Review: It is, simply, a thing of beauty, its hook quotient the highest of The Decemberists' discography.

Title: Dissolution
Review: Dissolution is entirely convincing in its maturity and intelligence. [25 Aug 2018, p.55]

Title: Goodbye, Killer
Review: The eclecticism is jarring--especially on an album that's only 32 minutes long--but the songs are frequently superb

Title: Elastic Days
Review: Like Zuma, Elastic Days takes a little time to warm up to, but once it’s sunk in, it’s as comfortable as an old pair of jeans.

Title: Foley Room
Review: Despite all the ingenuity on Foley Room, it’s hard for me not to miss the days when Tobin belonged as much to jazz as he did to any electronic genre.

Title: Essence
Review: By leaving her images blurry and her singing uncomplicated, Williams has found a way to capture the sound she hears in her head and obsesses over the recording process to find.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die II
Review: In the case of Twelve Reasons to Die II, the glass is slightly more than half full.

Title: Rainbow
Review: Rainbow is simply the record she needed to make. And at a time where most pop music is either designed by committee or drowning in beigeness, it’s also the kind of individual and achingly honest record we needed to hear.

Title: Complete Surrender
Review: Complete Surrender shows that Taylor and Watson are willing to stretch out and continue their evolution as they deliver a strong third outing.

Title: Golden Ticket
Review: The album's ear-catching finish endorses Golden Ticket as a rewardingly receptive, slightly slippery customer to the death.

Title: Dark Arc
Review: Some listeners will find this to be powerful rainy-day music, the kind of stuff to get lost in while staring out the window at the rain. Most of us, though, will run out of patience long before the end.

Title: Wine Dark Sea
Review: Wine Dark Sea is a brilliantly track-listed album, stronger as a whole than broken into parts.

Title: Honeycomb
Review: The playing is bright, relaxed and spontaneous. [28 Jul 2005, p.82]

Title: Shiny and Oh So Bright, Vol. 1 / LP: No Past. No Future. No Sun.
Review: Save the few fire-breathing dragon moments of Lollapalooza-era churn, it’s the Smashing Pumpkins in name only, and that ice cream truck has long left the gas station.

Title: The Broken String
Review: The Broken String easily takes its place alongside those classics [Wilco’s Being There and Ben Folds Five’s self-titled debut].

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: Last Day of Summer is surely weirder than their actual album material, but it's compelling to watch a band rooted in garage rock go so far out of its comfort zone, try some uncharted styles (jazz, prog, tropicalia, and psych-folk), and still come up with some winners.

Title: Lucky Shiner
Review: Each song has expert structure, shimmering melodies, and enough drums and bass to put these songs in the club.

Title: Welcome the Worms
Review: The fire dies down as the album progresses, but the infectious melodies remain. [May 2016, p.104]

Title: You Know I'm Not Going Anywhere
Review: What makes You Know I’m Not Going Anywhere frustrating is the knowledge that Grote has all the right ingredients (including Fridmann in this case), but somehow isn’t consistently stringing things together.

Title: Love You to Death
Review: An album packed with shimmering highlights.

Title: Delta Machine
Review: It’s hard to imagine anyone other than extreme DM reactionaries finding anything here essential besides the abovementioned tracks [“Soft Touch / Raw Nerve” and “Soothe My Soul”], the stirring “Secret To the End,” and the mid-tempo “Broken.

Title: Teenage Emotions
Review: He is at his most interesting on the few occasions where he slips into a sort of uncanny valley of pop music--a bizarro fantasia that he arrives at honestly, like a less satirical PC Music.

Title: Ladyhawke
Review: Brown has an unlikely knack for putting quality into cliched, classic disco and rock. [Holiday 2008, p.106]

Title: The Scene of the Crime
Review: LaVette is a proud interpreter, and even back in her earlier days she was covering David Bowie and Neil Young, but on Scene of the Crime her choices are a little less NPR-friendly than they were on the all-female critics darling roster of "Hell to Raise."

Title: The Magnificent Tree
Review: Classic embryonic vocalic beauty from Geike Arnaert still carries the translucence of the band's signature ethereality, and shines as hard as she did on the band's previous releases. However, musical composition on songs such as "Pink Fluffy Dinosaurs" and "Frosted Flake Wood" are more intricate and sonically defined.

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: The source of Swing Lo Magellan's charm, for it truly is a charming collection, is that it's a record that doesn't try be anything other than exactly what it is.

Title: Lust for Life
Review: Lust for Life is her most expansive album; it has 16 songs, stretching nearly 72 minutes. It also, in rare moments, hints at a wink behind Ms. Del Rey’s somber lullabies.

Title: X&Y
Review: Confident, bold, ambitious, bunged with singles and impossible to contain, ‘X&Y’ doesn’t reinvent the wheel but it does reinforce Coldplay as the band of their time.

Title: All About Tonight
Review: The EP concept behind All About Tonight may seem small, but like its predecessor, it delivers big.

Title: Apocalipstick
Review: It's a trade-off that many bands make as they progress, cashing in on the uniqueness of their original sound for something more palatable to the imagined masses. It almost never works out well for the band involved and despite a few bright moments where they almost get it right, it doesn't work for Cherry Glazerr here.

Title: From Out Of Nowhere
Review: From Out of Nowhere could be an ELO album from 40 years ago, albeit with a bit of added digital polish.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: Throughout the album, Yorke’s everyday enlightenment is backed by music of expanse and abandon. The guitars sound like pianos, the pianos sound like guitars, and the mixes breathe with pastoral calm.

Title: Knowle West Boy
Review: Butler might consider himself lucky he got out when he did, as Tricky’s ideas are scattered all over the place and Knowle West Boy is mostly a mess.

Title: Me and Armini
Review: This feels more polished product and will no doubt have a broader appeal as a result, but it is a treasure of a thing and the more people that hear it the better.

Title: Kicking The National Habit
Review: Almost everything about 'Kicking The National Habit' is righteously unfashionable.

Title: Dodge and Burn
Review: Dodge and Burn is nothing if not heavy-handed in its attempt at conjuring up the same gothic witchcraft The Dead Weather once mastered.

Title: Black Light
Review: It's certainly nothing unfriendly, and none of it would sound out of place on the duo's traditional weekend slot at Lovebox.

Title: Remembrance
Review: If your perfect musical Venn diagram contains Oneohtrix Point Never, Machinedrum and Terry Riley, Suicideyear will satisfy your equation. [Oct 2014, p.93]

Title: And Now That I'm in Your Shadow
Review: And Now That I'm In Your Shadow finds him at another peak. [#74, p.98]

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: Too much of Not Your Kind Of People is pedestrian, anodyne and utterly unremarkable.

Title: In the Belly of the Brazen Bull
Review: Bull drags on with minimal memorable hooks and far too much guitar feedback. [Jun 2012, p.76]

Title: Tight Knit
Review: With their boundaries and ambitions by now well established, on Tight Knit Cabic and company largely succeed in luring the listener hazily back in time and into Vetiver's comfort zone.

Title: Foreverland
Review: There's no mistaking Foreverland for anything other than the work of an artist who has chosen to give up his fight with the not-so-cruel-after-all mistress that is contentment.

Title: Double Dutchess
Review: Fergie struggles to balance the new with the old throughout the album. Where Stefani’s raw confessionals helped distinguish This Is What the Truth Feels Like, though, Double Dutchess is stuck in the past.

Title: Pilot Talk III
Review: Curren$y may not do "new," but he is very good at what he does: riffing on cars, money, women, weed, and obscure moments from television shows.

Title: Grand Archives
Review: The effort is palpable, but the songs never quite get off the ground. [Winter 20008, p.82]

Title: Skins
Review: Skins barely leaves a mark. The ideas aren’t original. The record is short--clocking it in at just 20 minutes--but feels extremely threadbare. ... The songs on Skins are shards, sketches. Even calling them demos feels generous.

Title: Green Naugahyde
Review: The writing is more a series of creepy pranks than a set of tunes, but Claypool, guitarist Larry LaLonde and drummer Jay Lane are a tight knottyrhythm team, and their propulsion under the comic vocals in "Tragedy's a'Comin' " and in the manic marching jam "Last Salmon Man" is no monkey business.

Title: A Time to Love
Review: These toothless, '80s-embalmed tracks... are the aural equivalent of Sleepytime tea. [28 Oct 2005, p.87]

Title: m b v
Review: The noise that's here is lovely, heartbreaking, expansive and raw. [No. 97, p.58]

Title: Light Up Gold
Review: Parquet Courts are especially versed in the clipped, repetitive buzz of Wire's '77 classic Pink Flag, but, like Pavement, they soften post-punk's cranky edge with the glazed, lonely wonderment of fresh, wide-eyed New York transplants.

Atkins makes the material sound genuine, largely because it is perfect for her. Where previously her slight, observational songs seemed barely able to carry her powerful voice, the emotional and musical heft of these styles enables her to really spread her vocal wings.

Title: HYMNS
Review: The problem with Hymns is that it chugs along with a series of stilted niceties that lack any kind of rhythm or emotion.

Title: Cool Uncle
Review: Were they to pare the album down, losing some of the studio excesses, Cool Uncle would easily stand non-ironically with some of the best AOR has to offer. As it stands, the album holds a number of fascinating ideas and carries an inherent reverence for both Caldwell and his era that keep things from falling into parody.

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: Given Mascis's croaking rasp this shouldn't work, but it does, because he's turned in his best collection of songs for a long time. [Apr 2011, p.104]

Title: Saint Cecilia EP
Review: Sure, Saint Cecilia fills itself with all inclusive lyrics that Grohl has become known for. Yes, there are some midtempo shifts that you wish you could skip over. But out of five songs, four are solid.

Title: Ugly
Review: For the most part, it works.

Title: Palana
Review: Plenty of musicians this diverse and dreamy can lose themselves beneath production textures or simply the weight of their own brain, but Hilton doesn’t shy away from indulging in pop, which is as experimental and transitional a form as any other.

Title: Into
Review: For now though, things are still at the experimental stage.

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You
Review: He still dabbles in more-chin-stroking fare, but he's able to ground his adventures in enough melody to preserve the album's flow--and your bearings.

Title: La ForÃªt
Review: It's business as usual, but there is not a damn thing wrong with that when it comes to this group.

Title: Tomorrow's Harvest
Review: Where Music Has the Right seemed grounded in the real world (albeit a twisted recollection of such) and Geogaddi straddled the line between Star Wars and The Sandlot, Tomorrow’s Harvest finds the duo launching their sound into Lovecraftian orbit. And it sounds terrific.

Title: Velociraptor!
Review: For Kasabian fans this will be a fine, perhaps even happy result--another album in a similar vein to satiate your lust for new music, but the nagging thought catches as it wonders how new, interesting or innovative any of this really is; the short answer is no, it's not.

Title: Cardinology
Review: If that makes it sound like Adams and company aren’t pushing musical boundaries this time, it’s true, but they’ve settled into a groove that works just fine for now.

Title: Catch My Shoe
Review: Catch My Shoe shares some 21st century dissent with new albums from Wire and Gang of Four, but the Ex's continual flow of ideas and collaborations has kept its members in forward motion, where their UK counterparts are coming back to the fire after smelling the smoke.

Title: Darker Handcraft
Review: It sounds ferocious and is going to have you feeling filthy and dealing with tinnitus afterwards, but nothing's going to stop you from rocking.

Title: World Music
Review: [World Music is] a wonder through the traditional folk and more amplified sounds of the planet's history, yet infused with enough of Goat's own character to all glue together.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Room on Fire is the sound of a tighter, more focused band.

Title: In the Marrow
Review: This is an interesting album, one that will reward repeated listening, but one can't help but think that it's a transitional album, and that Dead Confederate are building to something even bigger and more balanced down the road.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: Like many of the best indie-pop bands, this one is musically conservative. Rather than chase new forms and sounds, the members are content to perfect the mannered pop song, nodding to forebears and fellow travelers, from Prefab Sprout to the Postal Service. [30 Dec 2004]

Title: Play
Review: Unfortunately, the last third of the CD isn’t nearly as good as the first two-thirds.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: For the first time, Oberst sounds as if he's trying to conform his lyrics to his tunes, not the other way around. [4 Feb 2005, p.130]

Title: On Leaving
Review: The lyrics lack the indirectness of so much of The Blackened Air and Road to Ruin, just as the piano-embroidered instrumentation skims the surface of what the singer’s band once plumbed with all of its clawing and scraping.

Title: MantaRay
Review: An album filled with singles that should be instant hits.

Title: Native Speaker
Review: These songs are great expanses, sprawling and glorious.

Title: Angels and Devils
Review: Short of their obvious opposition, there is little here in the way of meaningful tension between the Angels & Devils.

Title: Crazy Love
Review: The album's polished, middle-of-the-road approach isn't exactly for everyone, but its agreeable heart doesn't hit any sour notes, either.

Title: Repentance
Review: This should be among Perry's higher-profile efforts in some time, with production by Andrew WK, and guest appearances by everyone from Moby to Brian Chippendale of Lightning Bolt. [Oct 2008, p.150]

Title: Utopia
Review: At 72 minutes, this is the longest studio album of her career. Björk doesn’t find love with three chords and the truth, she finds love through an endless interrogation of every note there is.

Title: False Alarm
Review: On False Alarm, though, they offer something that proves they’re still worth paying attention to.

Title: Hawk
Review: The Gothic undertones of the previous two albums have been slightly toned down, but not that much, and this time they also manage to rock out with some more bluesy and electric tracks.

Title: Quiet Signs
Review: Whereas Pratt once settled on a colder and more reserved state, Quiet Signs manages to present a more empathetic side of her that was once concealed. It's still quaint by comparison, though, a delicately-crafted acoustic set that offers insight into her deepest fears and truths without letting us encroach into her private space.

Title: Director's Cut
Review: But if Director's Cut is a tad superfluous, it's also gorgeous.

Title: Dodge and Burn
Review: White and Mosshart's collaboration feels like a tale of the proverbial nearly men--close, but no cigar.

Title: Is Survived By
Review: Whether or not you’re a fan of their earlier, grittier material or their newer, more polished recordings, Is Survived By is a massively engaging and surprisingly triumphant record, and you cant expect anything but for them to continue to add to their ranks of love-moshing fans with an album that is just so damn solid.

Title: The Head and The Heart
Review: For all the humming and picking, the songs feel too similar to each other to hold interest throughout.

Title: Get Back
Review: Shakedown and Sell Your Soul feel triumphant in a way indie-rock has rarely managed of late, while an intoxicating weirdness drives even their most anthemic moments. [Jun 2014, p.93]

Title: The Harsh Light of Day
Review: Fastball are, in general, a little wobbly on this CD, but their aim is true often enough to suggest that once they get the guest star syndrome out of their system, the hits could keep on coming.

Title: Exquisite Corpse
Review: Exquisite Corpse's saving grace is that there is enough variety to its ensemble of guest performers to keep the listener somewhat interested.

Title: Field of Reeds
Review: Field of Reeds may initially come across as inhumanely taut, straining, and indistinct to begin with, but this is the sound of precociousness finally arriving at a purpose.

Title: Road to Utopia
Review: A Brock-sung acoustic setting of We Took The Wrong Step Years Ago is a highlight, but the less said about how the massed saxes treat Down Through The Night the better. [Sep 2018, p.91]

Title: No Color
Review: It's cliched to remark on a duo's ability to sound like a full band, but the Dodos' virtuosic acoustic guitar playing and busy arrangements undeniably defy their numbers.

Title: Major
Review: The many-splendored guitar blitz of Major rings in the return of good old-fashioned butt rock, but played to the squarely measured rhythms of '90s emo and Northwest indie stuff like Built To Spill.

Title: Desolation Sounds
Review: The Southern gothic touches strewn throughout the album help make this their best set of angry anthems to date.

Title: Dept. of Disappearance
Review: It's difficult not to get swept away by, and even admire, the unrelenting sweetness of the songs [for much of the album's first half]. Eventually, though, it becomes equally hard not to gag on the twee preciousness.

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: The high points are so fantastic that their missteps are easily forgiven.

Title: To Willie
Review: Timeless and universal, everyone can identify with Willie Nelson's songs, as sung by Houck, as Phosphorescent's tales of heartbreak, wasted youth, and harsh introspection.

Title: Mysterious Phonk: The Chronicles of SpaceGhostPurrp
Review: It's scattered, without a singular vision, and successful nonetheless.

Title: Great Escape
Review: On their careening second album, the Rifles prove that they're a band to watch, especially on the title track.

Title: Bend Beyond
Review: You'll find records this year of greater agency, but you'd be hard-pressed to find one that renders pleasure with such poignant lightness, control, and willful attention to difference.

Title: Zeros
Review: Musical diversity has been embraced to better reflect his character, whilst a positive tone remains, even when he’s examining negatives. No longer is McKenna a teenager emerging at Glastonbury, he is someone for the generation he speaks for to listen to.

Title: Cheer
Review: Combining the passionate onslaught of hardcore with a reasonable portion of grunge and radio-ready power pop, the New York group's cynical punk tone often feels effortless. If you're just hearing of Drug Church or weren't sold on their two prior works, now's the time to stay for a sermon.

Title: Can't Touch Us Now
Review: Despite the departure of original member Cathal “Chas Smash” Smyth, the elements that made Madness one of the most beloved bands of the early 1980s are intact on Can’t Touch Us Now, their first album for four years.

Title: Living with a Tiger
Review: Paradoxically, despite--or perhaps even due to--its directness, Living With A Tiger is a challenging record, only revealing its full depth on repeated visits.

Title: Brand New by Tomorrow
Review: There is little to these songs besides Mark's Lennon-like voice and an unobtrusive piano and guitar. [Apr 2007, p.113]

Title: Individ
Review: Ten years deep into their career, the Dodos have never actually steered too far from their roots, but the loose, unselfconscious feel of Individ proves that there is something to be said for recognizing and playing to your strengths, trusting your chops, and simply feeling things as intensely as you possibly can.

Title: Rivers and Streams
Review: In all, Rivers and Streams confirms that Melnyk is quite right to make the big claims of himself which he does.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: [Their collaboration] makes for a consistently delicious contrast between the unruliness of sound... and the cool affectlessness of both their voices as every song bursts with the interplay of these two eccentrics' ideas.

Title: Waiting For Something to Happen
Review: Alienation, restlessness and lovelorn angst abound here, and Veronica Falls have lost none of their knack for blithely morbid romance. [Feb 2013, p.113]

Title: Intriguer
Review: Much of Intriguer leaves one yearning for the unbound pop of "Now We're Getting Somewhere" or the straightforwardly confident balladry of "Better Be Home Soon." [Jul 2010, p.104]

Title: Magpie and the Dandelion
Review: Perhaps the Avetts are best when they run a little bit loose and ragged, letting the tempos push a little bit hard, allowing their harmonies to clash and happy to have their loose ends remain untied. Often, this means that the ballads are just a shade too tidy.

Title: I Remember
Review: It occasionally loses focus, but overall the decision to open up has worked wonders.

Title: Down Where the Spirit Meets the Bone
Review: Williams has assembled many guest musicians this time around, but despite all the disparate talent, the album is a tight, coherent work that never devolves into self-indulgent jamming, even at an epic 103 minutes.

Title: Impeach My Bush
Review: Peaches goes easy on the syrup and heavy on the flavor and hands listeners a delectable, if slight, cherry bomb of an album.

Title: Dear Heather
Review: His sleaziness is hilarious. [30 Oct 2004, p.65]

Title: Lemonade
Review: In a year when the world’s biggest artists have put their necks on the line--Rihanna’s leave-me-alone, independent streak of ‘Anti’, Kanye West’s scatterbrained ever-changing doodle ‘The Life of Pablo’--Beyoncé can count herself as a risk-taker breaking new ground, up there with the bravest.

Title: You Are Free
Review: This mixture of revealing honesty and defiant self-confidence pervades the majority of You Are Free, an affecting and unforced 14-track album that stands as arguably her most diverse and rewarding effort to date.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: A few flashes of brilliance, but no sustained heat.

Title: There Is No Other
Review: Hushed, understated psychedelia and Laurel Canyon-influenced LP. [Mar 2020, p.95]

Title: Walls
Review: First emailed across the seas, then finalized in Vancouver, their music is to pop as hardcore is to punk, with the Joey Ramone fillip of Cooper's bizarre pronunciation.

Title: The Infamous Mobb Deep
Review: The Mobb aren't exactly reinventing the wheel here, but on album highlight "Timeless," the effect is beguilingly hypnotic.

Title: A Swedish Love Story
Review: Owen Pallet's new EP marks another few accomplished steps forward from his recent album, Heartland. [Fall 200, p.71]

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: They are so good, so natural on Lullabies to Paralyze that it's easy to forget that they just lost Oliveri, but that just makes Homme's triumph here all the more remarkable.

Title: Weapons
Review: The problem is that when they do attempt something different [as on some parts of this album] things go horribly wrong. [May 2012, p.100]

Title: Lisbon
Review: It's true the band has made a radical decision to turn down the volume on the wall of sound they've been building up since their debut, but in doing so they've turned up something else they've been fond of for so long: measured nuance.

Title: Damita Jo
Review: All this heavy construction is undertaken in the service of one of pop's thinnest, wispiest voices, and although Jackson's lack of vocal presence leaves a void at the heart of "Damita Jo," she's enough of a personality to create a few serviceable personas.

Title: Crimes
Review: Savage punk rock that shifts and shakes like the bleachers during a homecoming orgy. [Jan 2005, p.98]

Title: The Night Land
Review: On “Loser’s Hymn” and the closing “Dins El Llit,” they keep the pace brisk but downplay the drums, and the results, a kind of dance music with its head in the clouds, are both invigorating and meditative--like the album itself.

Title: Millport
Review: Millport is a welcome postcard from a busman's holiday taken by a fine songwriter. [11 Mar 2017, p.52]

Title: Ella Mai
Review: Mai’s album will likely bring her a couple of radio hits--“Sauce” is an undeniable heater. But a lack of focus means that, on her debut, the instant, infectious rush of Mai’s warm personality proves a little more elusive to find.

Title: Hell-On
Review: Hell-On is one of Case's moodiest solo records to date.

Title: Redemption
Review: In his raps, Jay Rock can come off as a reclusive hard-liner with a remarkable storyteller’s acumen and an internal logic that always feels sound. Few gangsta rappers are better at illustrating just how limited their options were and how undaunted they had to be to overcome them.

Title: Psychedelic Country Soul
Review: What arrives is an accomplished roots-music album that serves as a reminder of the band’s legacy.

Title: Glad Rag Doll
Review: Krall's smoky contralto lacks the pungency of Wilson's, but compensates with greater mobility.

Title: Halo
Review: Halo digs deep into the unknown and bring back unexpected brilliance. [Jun 2017, p.93]

Title: Orbit
Review: An album of miasmic, trippy electro-pop, heavy krautrock rhythms and sinuous digital funk. [Sep 2017, p.93]

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: It's even more disjointed and unpredictable than its predecessor. [19 May 2005]

Title: Man Mountain
Review: Man Mountain is an explosion of cinematic orchestration and lush 1960s guitars, cerebrally chill and simply extraordinary.... One of the best albums of 2002.

Title: The Bravest Man in the Universe
Review: It's eminently clear these producers know exactly when to assert themselves and when to stay out of the soul legend's way to achieve the most captivating results possible.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: Weller seems enthusiastic, upbeat and genuinely inventive across the whole LP, with only a couple of minor missteps throughout.

Title: Strange Friend
Review: Songs such as (Invisible) Friends veer towards the anthemic but don't quite ignite.

Title: Anak Ko
Review: On Anak Ko, she’s keeps doing it. The musical range is unsurprisingly wide, shifting from the swirling dreampop to dire guitar grind to smooth Seventies softness to Yo La Tengo-ish, country-tinged guitar pastorals to Nineties alt-rock. It’s all leveraged towards an unguarded sense of personal revelation.

Title: Dizzy Heights
Review: As the album hits its stride it heads squarely into AOR territory, and one or two tracks could have been a good minute shorter, but even tracks such as the pop-rock single Flying in the Face of Love are lifted by superior production.

Title: Ghost Stories
Review: As much as you care and as much as you want to feel sad, you can’t be blamed if after a listen or two, all you feel is manipulated.

Title: The Ship
Review: The emotional focus sharpens as The Ship progresses.

Title: Wildcard
Review: While the latter half of Wildcard constitutes a bit of a shuffled deck of genres, there’s enough of a kick to the album as a whole to warrant its title, and Lambert certainly has the chops to sell it.

Title: First Taste
Review: Magnificently, songs like Taste or The Fall are only energised by these diverse sonic signatures. The double-drummers are key, too: Segall’s in the left-hand channel, while frequent collaborator and multi-instrumentalist Charles Moothart is in the right.

Title: Introducing Joss Stone
Review: Her makeover seems too urban for her Starbucks-mom base and too retro for urban radio. [19 Mar 2007]

Title: Romancing
Review: There's a mighty gulf between those acts [Devin's musical influences] and scores of garage rockers long since forgotten, and it's one that can only be bridged with the very best songs. And those are what Devin doesn't have.

Title: One Track Mind
Review: "FBI" sounds like a comatose disco track being sung  in a toilet, but the default position is a weirdly bluesy take on Krautrock. [May 2013, p.75]

Title: One Day I'm Going to Soar
Review: It all suggests a promising future for the reinvigorated band.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: Rather than be pulled into the darkness, Harris boldly searches for meaning in this gorgeously reproduced world.

Title: Kiss Land
Review: He isolates himself inside long, slow-tempo songs that edge from seductive into oppressive--and, with their reverberating guitar chords and crisp, dominating drum sounds, will feel oddly familiar to anyone who's enjoyed a 1980s ballad by Genesis.

Title: The Soft Bounce
Review: Highlights include Mystery Jets’s Blaine Harrison wigging out Sabbath-style on the crunching Iron Age; Euros Childs sounding sweetly spaced-out on the gently circling Door to Tomorrow; and the Magnetic North’s Hannah Peel cooing airily over the Stereolab/Broadcast-style, dark psych-pop of Delicious Light--but the Soft Bounce is a trip best taken as a whole.

Title: Horehound
Review: All-star collective make unholy hot-and-sweaty psycho-blues racket.

Title: Fade
Review: Fade is a sign of perseverance for the group, as the album perfectly details just what is so essential and appealing about the group, and why there will always be a place for these guys in the world of indie rock.

Title: Put Your Back N 2 It
Review: Although the trials and tribulations Hadreas writes about don't always make for an easy listen, his music has an idealistic dimension to it, envisioning the best of all worlds where he can try to touch everyone without having to be anyone but himself.

Title: Human Ceremony
Review: Human Ceremony is an impressive debut from a band who seem positioned to make many more excellent albums if they can continue to do such a good job of mining the past for gold and revamping it in their own fashion like they do so well here.

Title: Screamer
Review: By opening up their sonic palette, Third Eye Blind has highlighted their sheer strength as a songwriting unit and demonstrated that any path they take, they'll throw themselves into fully and unreservedly. Sounding both fresh and classic, Screamer is a great place for new fans to jump on, or for previously jaded listeners to give one of rock's most underrated groups a fresh shot.

Title: Shrines
Review: The refrain in "Fineshrine" ("Get a little closer, let it fold/Cut open my sternum and pull/My little ribs around you") sums up Purity Ring with creepy efficacy, consuming and surrounding the listener. And as sweetly chirped by Megan James, it never seems like a bad thing.

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: On first pass the album might feel like a lateral or even backward step. After repeated spins, however, its subtler arrangements take up digs in your head like pesky squatters who one day, inexplicably, start doing chores or even paying rent.

Title: Native Speaker
Review: A minor criticism could arise in a homogeny of the individual parts, but that just might be splitting hairs.

Title: Towards
Review: Ultimately, on Towards, We Were Evergreen have moved slightly left of the indie pop center and achieved something quite interesting and enjoyable.

Title: Out in the Storm
Review: Each song is as grueling as it is thrilling.

Title: Modern Times
Review: If Time Out of Mind is the weathered, death-obsessed uncle who drinks too much and broods over things unchangeable and distant, and Love and Theft is the rakish cad gleefully dancing on the edge of the apocalypse, then Times is Theft’s clean-shaven, less-interesting brother, with a bit of schooling under his belt and a professional spit-and-polish finish.

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: Holiday Destination needs to be uncomfortable and it is, a beautifully realised disturbance of any remaining peace. [Sep 2017, p.92]

Title: Delta Machine
Review: The new album finds vocalist Dave Gahan and songwriter/multi-instrumentalist Martin Gore refining some familiar sounds and trying out some new wrinkles.

Title: Away
Review: Despite some conceptual shakiness and a few instances of turgid sentimentality, Sheff is doing fine on his own, continuing to detail unsteady emotional ground with a characteristic mixture of self-assurance and existential dread.

Title: Bottle It In
Review: Overall, you’re left the impression of an artist genuinely expressing themselves. It may not be his Born In The USA--despite what Vile claims--but Bottle It In ultimately succeeds in its intentions and further escalates Vile’s reputation as part of a rare breed of authentic songwriters. And that’s alright for now.

Title: ZABA
Review: Though tracks such as Flip and Pools are undeniably cool, you can sense the quartet straining to tick the right boxes rather than pursuing a sound that's theirs alone.

Title: Vanishing Point
Review: While Vanishing Point keeps the slack alive, it cries for an extra shot of venom and volume.

Title: Plastic Anniversary
Review: Plastic Anniversary is just extraordinarily clever, something to be marveled at more than moved by.

Title: Take Fountain
Review: All too often, this new material fails to leave much of an impression.

Title: Into the Light
Review: When there are fewer tracks, Anderson contrasts foreground sharpness with distant background. “House of the Setting Sun” and “Chimes” present fatigued leads pushed along by hazy, distant clouds of tone. What the new climate hasn’t changed is Anderson’s persistent restlessness, wandering off the road to find unusual details. Into the Light heads into the desert, knowing it’s hardly a deserted place.
Everything feels tactile rather than crowded. [Apr 2016, p.92]

Title: Word of Mouf
Review: "Word of Mouf" never quite meets the standard 'Cris set for himself with his debut.

Title: Ultra Mono
Review: Unfortunately, most of it sounds like Jason Williamson jogged into a pillar box. The guest musicians include David Yow and Jamie Cullum, a VIP list that draws attention to IDLES' own inadequacy. IDLES' by-numbers rock plod has none of the sensitive jazz swing of The Jesus Lizard nor can it match the unhinged ferocity of Cullum at his most feral. ... Three albums in and the hype has died down. The ideas are drying up. The lack of substance is wholly exposed.

Title: Junto
Review: Junto holds few surprises and its not the strongest album to sit in their catalogue, but it is reassuring to know that the boys are still making the music they love for a global dance audience.

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: It's their willingness to fall flat on their face while swinging for the fences that separates them from the focus-grouped inoffensiveness of their pop peers. The messiness of the whole thing seems to be the point, part of its audacity. In most artists' hands, that would be a recipe for creative bloat. Yet more than ever before the 1975 prove themselves masters of the form.

Title: Animal
Review: Each song will become the soundtrack for Mean Girls soccer moms and pre-teen pre-sluts everywhere.

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: Flying Club Cup would be a triumph even with those layers stripped away; that's not to say that the cultural patina obscures the "real" songs underneath, but its removal allows us to sidestep mind-numbing questions about authenticity and intention.

Title: Return of Mr. Zone 6
Review: Return is largely bereft of the chintzy, minimal Zaytoven beats dominating previous Gucci releases, and in their stead exists the dense ominousness Luger peddles so brilliantly.

Title: Red Carpet Massacre
Review: Duran Duran have updated their sound just enough to feel relevant, without embarrassing themselves in the process--no mean feat for a band in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Title: Ten New Songs
Review: Ten New Songs manages to sustain loss's fragile beauty like never before and might just be the Cohen's most exquisite ode yet to the midnight hour.

Title: Michel Poiccard
Review: Even when not stated explicitly, most of Michel Poiccard feels like a love letter to Velasco from remaining founder Johnny Siera; there's a sadness and longing tucked into even songs that aren't ostensibly about Velasco.

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: Unlike most things that labour under an impression of being overly, scarily brainy, it is anything but difficult to love Lese Majesty.

Title: More Adventurous
Review: All the broad-shouldered indie pop and big city folk we've come to expect, but so meticulously refined and consistently pleasing that its crossover ploys seem forgivable. [Sep 2004, p.124]

Title: Honeys
Review: While minor lulls can be found and their habit of zeroing in on daily life's mundane nuances risks self-parody, this s*** still rips. [Mar 2013, p.92]

Title: A Weird Exits
Review: It’s probably not the album in the band’s considerable catalogue that’s going to convert the unconvinced--it’s a bit too uneven to be considered for that position--but, for the first time in a while, Thee Oh Sees have their eyes fixed firmly on new ground.

Title: Conversations
Review: Over the course of a whole album, a little more ribaldry is required. [Aug 2014, p.81]

Title: The Balance
Review: It’s stuffed with generic accounts of relationships, life on the road, times with the band.

Title: Nocturnes
Review: It’s fun, but accomplished too, and shows how Hesketh has taken her knocks, used them and come back bolder, brighter and better.

Title: Shadows and Reflections
Review: Almond has certainly never sounded better as a singer than on this, largely a collection of covers of often obscure source material. [Nov 2017, p.102]

Title: The Liberty Of Norton Folgate
Review: An infectious love for their hometown and a sound that brings in soul, pop ballads, polka, Jamaica and Steely Dan makes this Wikipedia workout actually feel inclusive.

Title: Folie A Deux
Review: In Fall Out Boy's world, tongue-in-cheek always trumps heart-on-sleeve. That's certainly the case on Folie à Deux, their most exuberantly cheeky release yet.

Title: Juice B Crypts
Review: It would be hard to find an album to compete with theirs in regards of modernism or creativeness.

Title: Origins
Review: As far as simplistic and generic post-rock goes it’s fantastically inoffensive. Yet with the face of the genre ever changing, God is an Astronaut and their sixth are slowly becoming a relic of the past.

Title: Yours Truly, Angry Mob
Review: Call this album their application for recognition as one of the decade's major UK bands.

Title: Soul Punk
Review: He loses himself among all the references here, leaving an emptiness at Soul Punk's otherwise vibrant center. [28 Oct 2011, p.73]

Title: The Only Place
Review: Here they're going through the motions, missionary style, with mechanical jangly pop and the wince-inducing triteness of Cosentino's lyrics.

Title: Make Sure They See My Face
Review: The songs aren't terribly memorable, but several cuts offer imaginative mash-ups.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: Yet because the beats are so fierce and the flows so varied, there is no slogging through this 39-minute hurricane. It's been a minute, but RTJ have reminded us that, yes, rap music can be fun and opinionated simultaneously.

Title: Ekstasis
Review: The more time you spend with it, the more its structures make sense, the more the melodies begin to sparkle, the more the sense of some unsought truth fighting its way out becomes apparent.

Title: Pre Language
Review: Disappears have created a dark, at times dancey, record that very rarely lets up.

Title: We Used to Think the Freeway Sounded Like a River
Review: A sustained masterpiece is unlikely. Instead, this is a record with only flashes of brilliance, but what flashes they are.

Title: Mess
Review: Now seven albums deep into their career, Liars remain a lasting and distinguished presence, one that continues to question the confinement of genre and fashions their identity around a refusal to do so.

Title: The Ghosts of Highway 20
Review: Williams’ themes here aren’t new for her—love lost and found, mortality, the struggle to get right with God. But thanks to Frisell especially, the settings for Williams’ cracked, world-weary voice and vivid songwriting are indeed new. [No. 128, p.60]

Title: Leaders Of The Free World
Review: Elbow's lifeblood is equal parts rain and alcohol. [Mar 2006, p.111]

Title: The Best Day
Review: Whether its anger is aimed at an individual or an establishment, the energy on the Best Day sounds like the conspiracy before the rebellion, rather than the anarchy itself.

Title: Dirty Side Down
Review: Dirty Side Down is a tad long, but when the songs are this good, WP gets a pass. This is easily the band's finest studio offering in over a decade.

Title: Why Me? Why Not.
Review: Gallagher isn't as potent a personality as he was a quarter-century earlier, but his middle-aged control has its charms, too. He sounds relaxed on Why Me? Why Not., maybe for the first time ever.

Title: Con Todo El Mundo
Review: A set of limber, largely instrumental funk shot through with Asian, African and Middle Eastern melodies, each track sounds like it could have come off as jukebox single purchased from some dusty overseas record kiosk. [Feb 2018, p.29]

Title: Testing
Review: Though the finished project is as loose and incohesive as its title might suggest, there’s a lot to like about Testing.

Title: Modern Country
Review: An instrumental album that never fails to hold the listeners attention, with a plethora of quotable passages and delightful moments. A coming of age album.

Title: Splendor & Misery
Review: Splendor & Misery paradoxically stands as Clipping.’s most and least accessible albums.

Title: Rocket
Review: The raw and at times, ferocious navigation of the album soars in its earnest delivery and marks a career-defining release for (Sandy) Alex G.

Title: Napalm
Review: Napalm finds X fluctuating between trying to recapture the sound he perfected when he was cavorting with the Aftermath staff, and exploring elder statesmanship a la "Thank You" from 2006's Full Circle. When he goes too far in pursuit of either extreme, Napalm falters.

Title: Out from Out Where
Review: He's constantly finding new ways to micro-manage rhythm without losing the beat. [Listen 2 This supplement, 11/2002, p.15]

Title: Real Life Is No Cool
Review: the Norwegian superproducer has been intermittently working with Christabelle since 2001 and all the years of back-and-forth were clearly worth it, as Real Life is simply stellar.

Title: Melt Yourself Down
Review: Though repetitive, the record is consistently engaging, with plenty of distinct highlights.

Title: The Morning After
Review: Each EP has a handful of standout songs--the melodic thrust of "Make for This City" on Morning, the escalating drama of "Porcupine" on Night--but what lingers is James' controlled mastery of mood, how the band never pushes too hard yet never settles over the course of this quietly satisfying set.

Title: Ice Cream Spiritual
Review: Lovably noisy baltimore scallywags come good with their second effort.

Title: Unreal
Review: Fans of Yuck who are coming into Unreal hoping for and album as plentiful of hooks as that album might be slightly perturbed at first not to find anything as tight or punchy as something like “Get Away” or “The Wall,” but after spending time with the album you’ll find that each song possesses an airy, sing-songy hook that’s easy to latch onto.

Title: Mess
Review: Even if it's not quite as striking an achievement as WIXIW, it's a lot of fun and shows, once again, that Liars are unquestionably themselves no matter how much they push their boundaries.

Title: Sometimes I Wish We Were An Eagle
Review: Sometimes I Wish We Were An Eagle is a record of grand hopes and epic imagery, and powerful, uplifting music--the most accomplished of his 20-year career. [Apr 2009, p.102]

Title: Cerulean Salt
Review: Cerulean Salt isn’t boundary breaking, but it possesses qualities enough to leave one charmed, if not consistently captivated.

Title: The 1975
Review: The LP mostly forces unconvincing emo lyrics into a bloopy 1980s package.

Title: Nightcap At Wits' End
Review: The new album is singular in its conception and an impressive leap forward in terms of execution. [Nov 2020, p.20]

Title: Future Women
Review: At their best when strings and horns--even a sousaphone--let some air flood through a dense mix, they could even be an American Supergrass in waiting. [Sep 2006, p.89]

Title: The Home Inside My Head
Review: The Home Inside My Head cements Real Friends' place as new-school pop punk's lead dogs. [Jun 2016, p.102]

Title: Going Back Home
Review: A joyful, celebratory affair. [Apr 2014, p.92]

Title: Work
Review: Shout Out Louds have long been a case for the positives of going singles-only, and they probably keep that reputation  here. But by a minor degree, Work is Shout Out Louds' finest album-length statement.

Title: Music For Cougars
Review: These days, of course, the documentary vibe of the band's earlier stuff has transformed into an air of escapism -- not for nothing is one track titled "When We Were Young." But that hardly detracts from the crafty throwaway pleasures at which Sugar Ray still excels; in fact, it actually provides a touch of sweetness that helps temper McGrath's innate sleaze factor.

Title: The Spell
Review: The Spell cannot break free of the band’s successful formula without something a lot more challenging than this.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: Tio Bitar is Dungen's most realized album yet and should resonate with anyone who likes rock music at all.

Title: A flame my love, a frequency
Review: Colleen's most immediate and affecting LP to date.

Title: Tales of Us
Review: It's a haunting song cycle, one that might not necessarily appeal to their fanbase as a whole. But give it another listen; for all its subtlety, this is a role that Goldfrapp was born to play. [Aug-Sep 2013, p.90]

Title: Gold Past Life
Review: As good as the album sounds, though — and it sounds especially good on headphones. under the helm of producer Thom Monahan, who’s historically known how to put an atypical sonic spin on acoustic-leaners from Neko Case to Devendra Banhart — it’s as a lyricist where Johnson is really peaking here. There won’t be many albums in 2019 with as many quotable, cut-to-the-marrow lines as this one has.

Title: The Getaway
Review: The Getaway is generally a surprising success--the sound of a band having the intelligence to know when the time has come to move on and having the skill to actually achieve it.

Title: Out in the Light
Review: The frontman's voice is largely clear and earnest with grit where necessary and a dash of Neil Young's nasal falsetto, the kind of delivery just begging for a listener's impassioned sing-along.

Title: Loud City Song
Review: The result is an enriched soundworld, more ambitious than her much discussed debut, Tragedy. [Aug 2013, p.53]

Title: There is No Enemy
Review: Martsch's hitherto opaque lyrics are more revealing than normal, exposing sentiments of anger and loss. [Mar 2010, p.97]

Title: Someone to Drive You Home
Review: Ridiculously entertaining. [Jul 2007, p.98]

Title: Never Were The Way She Was
Review: Never Were the Way She Was finds these two highly skilled artists operating at the top of their respective games and is a welcome addition to the experimental minimalist end of the contemporary classical landscape.

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: This new release is a work of subtle majesty, sidestepping whatever you might think of as "folktronica" while still keeping everything from running into the red.

Title: Lemonade
Review: Pop culture's reigning diva appeared in raw form--a vulnerable mess and unapologetically enraged as she thematically confronted her husband and father's alleged infidelity publicly, through visceral imagery and emotionally loaded sonic offerings.

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: The Center Won’t Hold is a real-time examination of the fraying that takes its toll on peoples’ insides and outer shells during times both good and bad. Agitations about screen-borne life and unpleasant urges bounce off grander existential horrors; there’s no digging out of them, this record bellows, but thrashing around and attempting to find others to share the burdens will at least stave off malaise.

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: Baldi maintains many of his songwriting charms - the knack for melody foremost - but he's clearly made a sharp left turn in terms of the project's capabilities.  [#39, p.67]

Title: Algiers
Review: Generally this is fairly accessible stuff.

Title: Hot Cakes
Review: If the novelty had already worn off by the time of their second album in 2005, this comeback effort tests the patience beyond breaking point.

Title: TM: 103: Hustlerz Ambition
Review: He's better when he sticks to his native tongue--the street-cred-radiating plain-spokenness he calls "real talk."

Title: Boxer
Review: Boxer is a National album through and through but blessed with a restraint and self-assuredness of a band on top of its game, resulting in a startling masterpiece on par with Turn on the Bright Lights, Bows & Arrows, or any other austere tribute to urban alienation you care to name.

Title: Don't Panic
Review: While For Baltimore proves they can still write a grade A banger when they put their mind to it, too many songs are destined to have "must try harder" stamped on their report card. [13 Oct 2012, p.52]

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: Compared to the honed three-speed Cerulean Salt, the rhythmic scattershot of Ivy Tripp makes for a more exciting casual listen, but it does weaken the album’s aural cohesiveness. It’s a fair trade-off.

Title: Closer
Review: What's new? High pitch frequencies; cell phone samples; the vocoded & pitched-down techno-poetry; a clean aesthetic from DE9 era running roughshod over a dark palette; and the fact that it sounds utterly different to his previous material, despite the references.

Despite the lo-fi nature of the source tape, which was made in an ad hoc manner by a local friend, the sparse setting--just acoustic guitar and banjo--gives Dalton's distinctive voice plenty of room to do its thing.

Title: It Is What It Is
Review: On It Is What It Is, Bruner—unlike Pastorious—finds a way out, channeling his pain into great, uplifting art.

Title: The Show
Review: In the end, The Show is yet another pretty good throwback hip-hop album on which Masta Ace has been a central figure.

Title: Unapologetic
Review: The now-24-year-old's voice may be simple, but it's distinctive--and as defiant as her album titles.

Title: Act IV: Rebirth In Reprise
Review: The Dear Hunter might be better served by working in rein in its vast pretensions. [No. 124, p.53]

Title: Lanterns
Review: It is hard to parse all that's disparate here, and in searching for its most personal form, Son Lux unwittingly dipped into the uncanny valley of digital music trying to become human--something a little too perfect to believe.

Title: It Still Moves
Review: In all, My Morning Jacket may be a journey through the past, but it's also a solid step into something rock & roll has been missing for an awfully long time in the mainstream arena: melody, extremely catchy and well-written songs that aren't afraid of the mainstream, and a love of the great pop continuum that translates into something new.

Title: Let It All In
Review: Let It All In is a tighter, more relaxed LP, full of beautifully restrained, crafted songs.

Title: Coming Back To You
Review: While Ms. Doolittle does well with these hand-me-downs, the process feels oddly like a sequel to the “Idol” experience.

Title: LISm
Review: Those hungry for the more immediate release of her techno might find parts of the album tedious, but LISm‘s long-form arc rewards a patient listener.

Title: High Violet
Review: It's exceptionally crafted, it's gorgeously composed and it's remarkably rendered by a band that might just be the very best we have today.

Title: The Worm's Heart
Review: It’s neither better nor worse than Heartworms--which itself was very much a mixed bag--but the pleasures come in different places.

Title: Sha Sha
Review: Underscoring the songwriting skill he's been working at since age eight and over the course of 11 songs, he plays acoustic, folk-rock, alternative, power pop, and straight-ahead rock; his lyrics are consistently heart-sung but they aren't lite (he's got weight and bite too).

Title: Four Stars

Title: 8 Diagrams

Title: At Your Inconvenience
Review: His second album is a regression. A year on, the gaudy guitar loops and sleek hip-hop beats sound mundane.

Title: Grown Backwards
Review: Grown Backwards' restraint risks landing it in a coffeehouse ghetto that only asks for its music to be ignorable, but just because something can be ignored doesn't mean that it should, as the solid handful of excellent moments here proves.

Title: Isolation
Review: Isolation showcases just what made others scramble for her number: natural pop charisma and an ability to glide effortlessly between genres. [May 2018, p.113]

Title: My December
Review: Much of "My December" lacks the precisely engineered hooks that made Clarkson famous.

Title: Mirage Rock
Review: Yet it's too comfortable, old ideas diluted to homeopathic proportions, results half-hearted and strangely spiritless, songs feeling overly long.

Title: Vanishing Point
Review: [Vanishing Point is] raw and unrefined, it has as much energy and attitude as any of their previous albums.

Title: Kicking The National Habit
Review: It makes for a cool sound that might be too inoffensive at times but which grabs all the right places most of the time.

Title: Happiness

Title: Cobra Juicy
Review: We're treated to a blissful numbness, which is perfect for those who came here for the whacked out waveforms.

Title: w h o k i l l
Review: She deploys her superb music to address an issue so pressing few can stand to think about it: who kills who?

Title: Fight Softly

Title: Day & Age

Title: Closer
Review: It's only when the vocals kick in that this trip seems to be getting a little too long.

Title: Enter the Slasher House

Title: We're Not Talking

Title: Regard the End
Review: As always, it's historically rooted music fired by present-tense passion. [20 Feb 2004, p.67]

Title: Kala

Title: Metals
Review: On Metals Feist combines the sublime magic of her voice with songs that feature equally strong compositions to render an album that is easily one of the best of the year.

Review: The band crafts incredibly tight arrangements of complex, space-age country rock songs that require patience, vision, and time to create. Often, this approach is impressive. And, frankly, it is not always successful.

Title: Astronaut Meets Appleman
Review: There is an effortless vibe to Astronaut Meets Appleman can only be gained from a career doing your own thing and not caring about chat places and record advances. Anderson appears to be happy in his skin and has crafted nine songs that reference his past, but also hint to his future.

Title: 1000 Palms
Review: Most of the album is kinda ho-hum and overly mild in tone, as is Pitts's voice.

Title: Fake Surfers
Review: Gone is all the nervous tension that crisscrossed most of Finberg’s twitchy, dystopian vignettes, replaced instead with carefully plotted fuzz and a general hazy ambience that suggests calculated late-1960s ennui more than anything else. Overall, that’s a really good thing, especially when accompanied with the band’s seemingly newfound ability to ply their songs with unexpected twists and subtle new details.

Title: WALLS
Review: Although this album does replicate almost everything they’ve created it has that sense of maturity about it, showing that over the sixteen years they’ve moved on from their rebellious teen stage.

Title: Holiday
Review: The album is unique in that it gives a very personal look into an individual's experience with catharsis, and it's one more of murmurs and heavy sighs than screaming matches and broken dishes.

Title: YSIV
Review: Logic’s lyrical prowess continues to get in his way on songs like “The Return,” which sounds like a motivational song made for a late night Nike ad.

Title: Amanda Leigh
Review: Power-pop guru Mike Viola, of the Candy Butchers, is the album's producer and main co-writer, and the collection (recorded at Ducky Carlisle's Ice Station Zebra in Medford) is filled with his sweet, skewed melodies and smart, infectious choruses.

Title: Heartbeat Radio

Title: Loyalty
Review: Loyalty is an exceptionally affecting masterpiece, at once timeless and very much of its time, highly personal in its specificity and universal in its emotional accessibility and resonance.

Title: Distant Satellites
Review: Thankfully, the album’s final act is as convincing as its opening movements.

Title: Musique de France
Review: Musique de France is, if nothing else, a fascinating experiment in transcultural harmony.

Title: Jonny
Review: Speculation aside, the music that Childs and Blake have produced here is gentle, unassuming and good humoured. It won't change the world, but it will warm the hearts of those fortunate enough to hear it.

Title: Cee Lo's Magic Moment

Title: Victorious
Review: It’s all too nice, too safe, and ultimately, too predictable.

Title: If Anything
Review: They manage to skillfully maintain the the same semblance of being perennially on the verge of collapsing in a heap of broken guitar strings, trashed drum kit and feedback, while retaining the visceral gut-punch of the tightest,  heaviest metal badasses.  [Jul 2014, p.95]

Title: Panic of Girls
Review: If only the other half of this album didn't spiral off into wretched reggae stylings, this would be alright.

Title: Results May Vary

Title: Paradise Valley
Review: These new songs are so amiable that you wonder where they’re meant to take you. Often the breezy journey--while pleasant enough--leads to dead ends.

Title: Head Carrier

Title: Regeneration
Review: By shedding the smirking artifice that served Casanova so well, and hiring producer Nigel Godrich, the Divine Comedy may be treading dangerously close to the sounds of countrymen Radiohead, but the Divine Comedy are smart enough to give listeners just enough lyrical bit to throw them off the scent.

Title: Release Therapy
Review: Release Therapy is probably Luda's best album since Back for the First Time, but it's not like that's saying much.

Title: The Bravery
Review: There are countless other bands using electro blips to make us boogie and bang harder. [8 Apr 2005, p.65]

Title: Lost Channels
Review: While it might be criticised for not having some of the mystery characterising previous albums, Lost Channels is a blissful yet haunting record.

Title: Yes

Title: Idiology
Review: Does it work? It depends on your idea of "flow": If you don't mind sandwiching the Trent Reznorish "Introduce" and the Squarepusher-on-crank mess of "First : Break" between the opulent epics that comprise the middle and the end of the album, Idiology comes off as an inspired collection of irreverent hackery and emotional depth. [Jul 2001, p.79]

Title: Krystal
Review: Matt Maltese's second album persists with velveteen schmaltzy AOR; like yacht rock on a budget. His graceful croon, though, is more jaded this time, combining with the hollowed-out production for a deluxe dose of remorse. [Jan 2020, p.84]

Title: Lucky Old Sun
Review: Kenny Chesney does heroes George Strait and Jimmy Buffett proud on his latest set, which has a free-and-easy feel befitting its island inspiration.

Title: Venus On Earth
Review: Venus on Earth feels impulsive and rich, rippling with surf psychedelia and exultant brass swing.

Title: Deer Creek Canyon
Review: Deer Creek Canyon is dappled with sad-slow shuffles and lovely ruminations on escape, the roll of the seasons and her roots in Colorado. [Jan 2013, p.73]

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: The Collective's aspirations come off as bland and blurry, as if aspiration alone was the sole goal for this jam, spread out over three quarters of an hour.

Title: Our Endless Numbered Days
Review: Beam's voice is streamlined and a little too perfect for fans of his prior music who felt, with good reason, like Beam was serenading them from their living rooms.

Title: Fool's Gold
Review: The first half connects the mind and the body equally, which is why they are such successful songs. The second half of is just body music and that’s where it falls a little flat. That’s not to say it doesn't work at all.

Title: Drones
Review: The result is a claustrophobic classic that sharpens the focus of what is possible in the name of high-minded rock. [6 Jun 2015, p.50]

Title: Own the Night
Review: While the average age of Lady Antebellum's members is a relatively youthful 28, Own The Night is purposely old-fashioned, even geriatric.

Title: Business Casual
Review: Business Casual is the sound of Chromeo having wholly realized its vision. The only question is where does the duo go from here without becoming a tired party trick? Chromeo just might want to get out while the getting's still good.

Title: Secret Wars
Review: Secret Wars clamors like past Oneida albums dating back to 1997, but it also shows a band mellowing out without losing its charge.

Title: Tuskegee
Review: Acoustic guitars replace glistening synths, bittersweet steel guitars slide in to provide the patina of rural rootsiness, yet Richie still never really steps away from the polished sheen that characterized his musical heyday.

Title: Hot Cakes
Review: Frenetic take on Radiohead's Street Spirit aside, the tightly arranged songs here are pleasingly Queen, AC/DC, Lizzy and Leppard-aware. [Sep 2012, p.86]

Title: Working in Tennessee
Review: The album--recorded at Haggard's California ranch--benefits from a relaxed, among-friends vibe, and Haggard's more upbeat singing about his past.

Title: Attack & Release
Review: The title Attack & Release implies the best aspects of the Black Keys’ music, all sweat and hurt and sweat and ecstasy, but the album neither gives nor takes, neither emotional nor sweaty but still clammy-handed.

Title: Modern Worship
Review: There are many occasions on Modern Worship when the surging synths sweep you along with the force of a dopamine rush, but there are a few others when you're left with a nagging sense that Hyetal could take things that little bit further.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: There’s a sense of urgency on Somewhere Else, a need to keep searching and exploring. And she’s onto something.

Title: Phantom Radio
Review: This is an impressive record that occasionally tries to cram too many ideas into one place but more than makes up for it in sheer song-writing quality.

Title: Synthesis
Review: It frequently feels like one of those remix albums where tinkering guests have tried too hard to put their own stamp on proceedings, resulting in curios that are momentarily interesting, but will never replace the established versions in your affections on your playlists. [11 Nov 2017, p.50]

Title: Crash My Party
Review: Ultimately, Crash My Party is melodiously rewarding despite its sporadic lyrical missteps.

Title: World Wide Funk
Review: From the title track onwards, he slaps down 25 minutes of spring-heeled and rump-shakin' bumpin' Bootsy funk, which will pick up again after ballad Heaven Yes, gentler Ladies Nite, and the poppy Candy Coated Lover and Snow Bunny. [Dec 2017, p.93]

Title: Paper Trail
Review: Despite his often earnest lyrics, the radio-friendly party anthems, flirty come-ons, collaborations with A-list pals (Rihanna, Jay-Z, Kanye West, Lil Wayne, Justin Timberlake), and outstanding production prove this beleaguered bad boy still knows how to have a good time.

Title: The Breakthrough
Review: Someone get this woman some drama, pronto.

Title: Letters Home
Review: Bits of experimentation still poke through, especially on the dissonant, heart-rendering "Rabbit Foot," which neatly stitches up Defeater's past while pointing toward fresh dynamics and future chapter to come. [Aug 2013, p.86]

Title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
Review: Merriweather Post Pavilion is a perfectly organized record, not a note out of place, not a second wasted.

Title: Pure Comedy
Review: It works because it’s so astonishingly, genuinely clever.

Title: Bring Ya to the Brink
Review: If still a bit too far from the mainstream to make for a full-fledged commercial comeback (which "The Body Acoustic" might have provided if not for Sony's "rootkit" debacle), Bring Ya to the Brink recaptures Lauper's artistic relevance and stands as a hipper alternative to Madonna's "Hard Candy."

Title: Soul is Heavy
Review: At 15 tracks, Soul's tautness sometimes suffers, but Nneka makes her heavy-lifting sound first-rate virtually all the time.

Title: Human Performance
Review: Although there’s nothing as lyrically sharp as Content Nausea, as raucous as Sunbathing Animal or as brash as Light Up Gold, Human Performance hits all the right notes for a band with a lot of ground to cover.

Title: Interpretations: The British Rock Songbook
Review: It's hard not to appreciate the karma of some of the most well-worn rock standards of LaVette's hard-fought early years rendered new again through a voice time almost forgot.

Title: Alice
Review: Waits does nothing predictable here, and the structure of even the most forlorn tear-jerker is ambitious and avant-something-or-other. [Co-Album Of The Month, June 2002, p.106]

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: The album doesn't quite match their punishing live show, but neither does it betray their purpose or message: to fiercely silence the white noise of psychosocial oppression. It is one missive they convey without ambiguity.

Title: True Meanings
Review: Anyone ever touched by the likes of English Rose or Fly will find much to cherish here. [Oct 2018, p.113]

Title: Charli
Review: Charli is no doubt an album of too many features and too many parts, but it somehow all fits together in a way that allows her penchant for unconventional songwriting and her ear for an exciting melody to work in concert, creating a project better than most anything she’s done in the past.

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: I Learned the Hard Way is her fourth album with the Dap-Kings, and to say that it does nothing differently from its predecessors is essentially, among Daptone believers, high praise.

Title: Old Ideas
Review: Old Ideas remain a quietly surprising album, full of grace, full of sadness, but also, most importantly, full of life. [Mar 2012, p.90]

Title: II
Review: Somebody needs to boot Nielson off his why-fi connection: beneath the murk is the work of a riveting craftsman.

Title: Together Through Life
Review: Dylan shirks responsibility; he puts the onus on us. Fortunately, the impetus the album provides is all we need in order to define its brilliance.

Title: Welcome to Mali
Review: If the album is frustratingly uneven--if, despite moments of exuberance, it can also feel like a mundane grind--well, I suspect that also mirrors life in Mali. And almost everywhere else, too.

Title: Some Twist
Review: Throughout, it's the sheer quality of Nau's songwriting that truly impresses. [Jul 2017, p.89]

Title: Xen
Review: Not interested in following in anyone's footsteps, Arca borrows back the skeletal remains he made to West and creates new albeit strange life. Gorgeous and ghastly, Xen is no clone, but it may too resonate through generations.

Title: Out My Window
Review: Most of the album is swathed in hazy reverb; initially, this is pleasingly disorientating, but ultimately proves anaesthetising.

Title: Art Official Intelligence: Mosaic Thump
Review: It's clear that despite laudable ambitions, comeback albums should be focused and lean, not as flabby as this one.

Title: Escapements
Review: This is a strong record that's all the more powerful for being so wonderfully, majestically disjointed.

Title: Crown Royal
Review: On Crown Royal, Run DMC are looking back so much that their necks must be permanently turned in that direction. Not only does nearly every track attest to how legendary Run DMC are, nearly every track also quotes directly from at least one song off their first four albums. It gets downright pathetic, every song bringing out a strong feeling of déjà vu.

Title: Sound Kapital
Review: This album doesn't stray far from the formula of their previous work, but it isn't disappointing. It goes down smoothly and will keep your toes tapping until the very last beat.

Title: Radio Music Society
Review: Most of the record finds organic urban grooves, frosts them with sweet pop-soul hooks and serves them up hot and fluffy.

Title: Joy
Review: If you can't enjoy Joy, you will probably never enjoy Phish. Yet, to paraphrase a vintage Phish song, what's most impressive here is how much they seem to be enjoying themselves--truly, deeply, gratefully. It's nice to have them back.

Title: Party
Review: For the most part though, this is a party for one, best enjoyed curled up with few distractions in the twilight hours. Sit, contemplate, and be absorbed into Aldous Harding’s spellbinding realm.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: Nothing Was the Same doesn’t capitalize on Drake’s bipolar desires quite as well as Take Care did despite the condensation of everything into more digestible parts.

Title: Glow & Behold
Review: Glow & Behold feels like a safe play. [No. 104, p.60]

Title: Samsara
Review: While none of Samsara is necessarily bad, there are moments where tracks start to blend together and lose focus. This doesn't necessarily take away from the amazing moments of the album, but as a whole it could use a bit more variance. That being said, the record makes it clear that Venom Prison are destined to join the top of the new-school death metal pack

Title: News From Nowhere
Review: It’s as carefully and intricately produced as anything the group has managed to date, but with a blinding vibrancy added to its tonal pallet and outlook.

Title: First Flower
Review: First Flower feels like a reclusive album emotionally, lyrically, and musically--but it’s one that actively strives to break through. It feels like being trapped inside your own thoughts, battling with the kinds of choices that incrementally alter your life on a daily basis.

Title: Rose Golden Doorways
Review: Rose Golden Doorways will undoubtedly repel and attract, but its sheer force is spellbinding. [Apr 2020, p.94]

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: With more concern for melody and rhythm than partisan politics, they use modern technology and an open mind to nimbly skip between the opposing camps of black 70s Disco and white 70s AM Radio, but in their songwriting methods The Sisters embrace the now mythic open arms party spirit of the early dance movement.

Title: Jaime
Review: It’s a total departure, her kaleidoscopic mix of decades’ worth of R&B, hip-hop, blues, and gospel, steeped in trippy laptop sonics and deeply personal political urgency. ... “I just want Georgia to notice me,” she sings, confronting oppression with faint hope. It’s a strikingly bold moment on a record that’s full of them.

Title: Good Thing
Review: Bridges doesn’t entirely leave behind his old-school roots, but, while Good Thing is hardly the next Blonde or, indeed, 24K Magic, it leaves you with a greater sense of who he is: loved-up, and striving for a level of ambition that feels within reach.

Title: Raven in the Grave
Review: One hopes Raven In The Grave doesn't signify the last post for The Raveonettes as they are a joy to behold in this mood, and more than capable of producing a belter of an album when least expected.

Title: Fuckin A
Review: Uncomplicated, exuberant melodic thrash. [19 Jun 2004, p.57]

Title: Eternally Even
Review: This time around, the woozy, comforting psychedelia of old remains, the songs trickling into one another, sleepy synths sighing, purring and pulsating. But Eternally Even comes with the biggest serving of soul he’s cooked up yet, sexy basslines sizzling even as he looks death in the face for We Ain’t Getting Any Younger Parts 1 and 2.

Title: Ratatat
Review: The band's sound is both fresh and nostalgic, and so pretty that it seems overly harsh to criticize them too much at this point. It's just that Ratatat is good enough to suggest that, with a little more diversity, the group could do even better things.

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: As Hardcore closes, it beats its chest too, the subtleties of the album's earlier songs unfurled into those wonderful dramas of old. [12 Feb 2011, p.52]

Title: I Used To Be Pretty
Review: I Used To Be Pretty is an unexpected triumph from a band far too compelling to be a one-off.

Title: Ufabulum
Review: It's something that can be quite brilliant: to paraphrase Special Agent Dale Cooper--Squarepusher's path is a strange and difficult one.

Title: Urth
Review: Whether dabbling in light or dark, the Nottingham trio are never anything short of exhilarating.

Title: Clay Class
Review: Even with bursts of ill-tuned twang, Prinz and Horn's harshness is centered and tame.

Title: Everything Ecstatic
Review: Hebden is a voracious consumer and producer of ideas, although there is sometimes the feeling, amid all this glut and gusto, that they're ideas for idea's sake. [#256, p.54]

Title: Zonoscope
Review: Take Me Over makes a misplaced attempt at funk, which grates slightly, but it's hard to dislike the well tuned synths and dreamy choruses of tracks such as Hanging Onto Every Heartbeat. [Apr 2011, p.101]

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: In truth, a couple tracks could have been cut to turn this into an epic single-disc release of huge proportions, but it's still the best work that Nick Cave And The Bad Seeds have done since Murder Ballads.

Title: In Conflict
Review: His finest achievement yet.

Title: X
Review: There just isn't enough memorable music here.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: This is no mere regression into a tried and tested formula for the Duluth trio. Each of these tracks is more than their trademark guitar, bass, drum soundscapes with delicate vocals hovering above the mix.

Title: Early Risers
Review: Joining the fun are pals such as Ethan Miller, Stephen Malkmus and Cass McCombs, who add to the sense of chaos, but do not diminish the cohesion that make these diverse jams so stupidly, thrillingly rewarding. [Dec 2015, p.79]

Title: Nausea
Review: This is another lo-fi gem, and most encouraging is the fact that there’s apparently plenty more he can wring out of this particular sonic platform; he might not need slick studio production to genuinely capitalise on his potential.

Artist: Someone Still Loves You Boris Yeltsin
Title: Let It Sway
Review: Sway is a noticeable sonic upgrade from SSLYBY's previous two albums, which can be somewhat off-putting at first, Still, the progression suits the quartet rather fine. [Sep 2010, p.113]

Title: Black Gives Way to Blue
Review: ew singer William DuVall spends half his time replicating Staley’s nasal misanthropy and the other half buried by Cantrell’s vocals.

Title: EDNA
Review: The resulting project is Headie's most complete and compelling set to date. Pulling out all the stops for an expansive statement of self, in EDNA the Tottenham great provides an impeccable portfolio of his varied sonics, concretizing his place among London's finest.

Title: Stronger with Each Tear
Review: Blige's frequent problems with pitch control [on "I Can See in Color"] mar what should have been the album's finest moment. Instead, the song is just indicative of the larger problem with Stronger: None of the elements that actually work ever manage to do so at the same time.

Title: Beautysleep
Review: Beautysleep's weakness is that so many songs are pretty instead of awe-inspiring-- that she gives us only a little greatness.

Title: Along The Shadow
Review: Perfectly written, recorded and performed, Along The Shadow is less an emo revival than a full-on reconstitution.

Title: Love Keeps Kicking
Review: Whether you read the title as a refusal to die or a foolish attempt to cling on, it doesn’t matter; both are just as relevant, and Martha have gone some way to capturing as much of it as possible.

Title: Lonerism
Review: One of the most impressive albums of the home-recording era while still feeling superbly refined.

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
Review: "Emma" was gorgeous in its austerity, but its follow-up is staggering for its vision. Bon Iver's self-titled sophomore release will go down as one of this year's most arresting albums, drunk on its own impressionistic charms and oblivious to anyone's expectations but Vernon's.

Title: Beacons of Ancestorship
Review: Beacons Of Ancestorship is pretty much what the avid Tortoise fan would consider par for the course, in that its a veering cascade of inherent surprises that never fails to astound, amaze or disappoint.

Title: Hamburg Demonstrations
Review: Hamburg Demonstrations, for all its charm and cheeky wordplay and get-the-bar-to-its-feet swagger, doesn’t quite live up to the expectations that its forbear set for it. Nevertheless, this is millennial Brit-rock through and through.

Title: Cosmic Wink
Review: Williamson outlines her personal mythology; as a lover, a daughter and, by the closing Piano Love, a future mother, via songs sung in a resonant, often Patti Smith-like voice, over a heat haze backing of Rhodes piano and guitar. [Jul 2018, p.90]

Title: You Won't Get What You Want
Review: By far their most dynamic offering, Daughters have pulled off one of the great comeback albums and further cemented themselves as a band with such singular creativity that they're nearly peerless. It may not sound like the album you thought you wanted, but the open-minded listener might find it's precisely what was needed.

Title: Lodestar
Review: Lodestar is true to Collins' roots.

Title: Mature Themes
Review: After years of weird-ass bedroom recordings, Ariel Pink has upgraded his operation, and what he loses in stoner burble, he gains in high-def Sixties flashback triggers.

Title: Lost Themes II
Review: Subtlety is in short supply on Lost Themes II, with soaring guitar solos, industrial synthesisers and violent percussion throughout.

Title: Tarpaper Sky
Review: Crowell continues to stake his claim as one of the genre’s most learned and accomplished performers, and if there is a gripe it’s that, at 11 tracks, the party’s over way too soon.

Title: Going Back
Review: Most of Going Back is devoted to the tried and true, though, the hits that remain staples on oldies stations across the globe, and whenever Collins is singing "Heatwave," "Uptight," "Papa Was a Rolling Stone," "Jimmy Mack" or "Going to a Go-Go," the album inches away from being a labor of love and into pure nostalgia trip, but even then the album is pleasant enough that it's hard to complain.

Title: Twelve Stops and Home
Review: [They] are so busy trying to be Supertramp they've forgotten to add anything of themselves. [3 Jun 2006, p.35]
