Title: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love
Review: Deafheaven is a ambitious heavy rock band, a gathering of innovative musical minds, and one of the very best guitar bands on Earth. Ordinary Corrupt Human Love is strong evidence of all three.

Title: Supreme Balloon
Review: Supreme Balloon adds up to the duo's most consistently enjoyable albums yet. [June 2008, p.98]

Title: Justified
Review: The Neptunes' brilliant, impertinent, full-body funk is, for the most part, what stays with you from Justified; their songs, spacious and shot through with ecstatic aaahs, outshine their neighbors on the album.

Title: So Beautiful or So What
Review: Simon's openness and spirit of inquiry ensure that So Beautiful Or So What is never the work of a man slouched in complacency.

Title: Arca
Review: The discoveries Ghersi makes on Arca allow him to write his most relaxed and intimate songs. His work is still mysterious, but not as opaque--it doesn’t keep you at an arm’s length, instead he offers up his pleasures more readily.

Title: How To Become Clairvoyant
Review: The set is an enveloping mix of melody, mood and texture that speaks to Robertson's triple-threat virtues as a performer, composer and producer.

Title: Wild Crush
Review: As it stands, Wild Crush is their most complete, well-rounded and accessible record to date.

Title: Nouns
Review: This one's solider, more concrete -- even beautiful sometimes.

Title: Never Will
Review: The quality of the material on this album shows she's got a lot on her mind -- maybe more than she realizes.

Title: By Your Side
Review: A unique record that puts a contemporary spin on an era that modern music forgot.

Title: Ancestral Star
Review: Barn Owl are adept at handling their equipment though, and have crafted a sound world in which the effects are essentially instruments themselves. It's an impressively broad palette too--whilst this music is undoubtedly slow to unfold and demands considerable patience from the listener, it does not feel one-dimensional or short on ideas.

Title: Desolation
Review: Fans of Wolfmother and Pallbearer might see this as the second coming of Sabbath, if they liked more At the Gates. But those who are looking for a bit more fuzz won't find it. Melodies, not distortion, drive this album.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: A work like this is only self-indulgent if its accoutrements aren't justifiable. Wilco makes every note count on this album: however miraculously, it all manages to cohere. And the songs are undeniably stunning.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: Vocalist Inara George and programmer Greg Kurstin have an affinity for all things pretty and vaguely retro, as her exceedingly pleasant vocals and his lush production attest. It's a formula, yes, but one that works over and over.
The result is something of a left-field classic. [Nov 2008, p.114]

Title: No Said Date
Review: His aggressive but nimble flow is all over each of these songs.

Title: Walls
Review: For every captivating thing here, like the chiming, excited "Dressed Sharply", there are far too many songs that are frozen at mid-tempo, leaving the album feeling too uniform to leave much of an impression, either in individual moments or as a whole.

Title: Sleep and Release
Review: The band's dynamics are beyond reproach, and the album sounds fabulous. Problem: The quiet songs don't provide a proper outlet for the band's palpable tension, and Aereogramme stays quiet far too often.

Title: Monster
Review: KISS' new album, Monster, is a fantastic dog: Protective, loyal, fun to be around but ferocious when it needs to be.

Title: Baby
Review: The songs are big on riffs, hooks, choruses, sex and swagger, although there's enough going on lyrically to suggest more depth than just sharp songwriting.

Title: Some Devil
Review: The end results are a bit unwieldy, perhaps, and not always successful, but it is interesting and certainly different than a Dave Matthews Band record.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: Despite its faults, Channel ORANGE still marks Frank Ocean out as an intriguing and exciting artist. It's a contradiction in many ways: a far-from-perfect album that suggests a long and prosperous career; an artist without an exceptional voice who looks like he will instead become an exceptional voice.

Title: Tomorrow Is My Turn
Review: The exceptionally well-curated material is all drawn from women singers--if not always women writers--and does a fine job of placing Giddens at the nexus of a multiplicity of traditions. [Mar 2015, p.79]

Title: 100 Acres of Sycamore
Review: 100 Acres... drips with sonic gloss.

Title: El Rey
Review: One for the fans, but it would be churlish to deny that the Wedding Present still have plenty to offer.

Title: Keep It Hid
Review: Spun-out psychedelia, world-weary Appalachian bluegrass and soulful blues make up his first solo album, proving that in the right hands, nostalgia can become a delicate, authentic rediscovery rather than the clunky retread that so many settle for.

Title: Take Me Apart
Review: What makes Take Me Apart so stunning is its meticulous attention to detail, with new layers revealing themselves on the third or 37th listen. Its sonorous breadth is mesmerizing.

Title: Good Apollo, I'm Burning Star IV, Volume Two: No World for Tomorrow
Review: The aggression is still there, now tempered with lighter numbers like Feathers, but the whole thing still reeks of comic nerd sci-fi awesomeness.

Title: Birdie
Review: Beyond the necessity, Birdie is a record that teeters an indie/emo line with ease and a sense of hybridity. Press “play” for a sense of melancholic calm.

Title: X
Review: Taylor Swift bestie and duet partner, writer of songs for One Direction, management client of Sir Elton John, British singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran comes into his own on his sophomore album x--pronounced “mulitply.”

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: If the album isn't quite up to the lofty standards of their earlier work, it isn't off by much, meaning that Wincing The Night Away gives 2007 its first great pop record.

Title: Coexist
Review: 'Coexist' is a refinement and crystallisation of their debut.

Title: 1000 Palms
Review: Ultimately, 1000 Palms sounds like emotional throat-clearing, the transitional sound of a band finding their bearings, resetting their dials, and getting back on their feet in the wake of a lot of personal and professional turmoil.

Title: The Mountain
Review: The result, which is gentler and more eclectic than the Bastards' earlier releases, is also Wennerstrom's most glorious, a collection of salty, rousing rock'n'roll that'll leave you aching for a roadhouse, a sticky bar stool, and a chipped glass of bourbon.

Title: Unbreakable
Review: Unbreakable is much closer in sound and spirit to her peak self, and her most solid release in years.

Title: Morning Tide
Review: Creating a musical theme that stretches across the album isn’t a bad idea, but The Little Ones fail to pull it off, and the songs suffer from a frothy sameness.

Title: Rosebudd's Revenge
Review: In an increasingly-predictable rap universe top-heavy with trolling mumble-rappers and formulaic pop-trap beats, Rosebudd’s Revenge’s quiet-storm menace makes for a surreptitiously potent punch of heavyweight Hip Hop.

Title: Simply Grand
Review: Her voice is rich, finely textured, and more expressive now than when it hit r&b charts in the 1960s. But her recordings can sound monotonous. That's not true here.

Title: Islah
Review: Islah is one of the more exciting major label rap debuts in recent years, and one positive to being a Gates fan is that you’ll most certainly never get tired with him.

Title: 4REAL 4REAL
Review: Released just nine months after Stay Dangerous, 4REAL 4REAL flies well below the lofty standard YG set with his first two albums and smells of his eagerness to get out of his label contract.

Title: Scenery
Review: Unlikely to be turning on any new fans, this will no doubt please those who have followed King since her earliest appearance on Nas' Street's Disciple, yet there's really not enough here to grab onto to really move the soul and demand repeated listens.

Title: Have Some Faith In Magic
Review: Firing on all cylinders and exhibiting the canny combination of eminently danceable rhythms with big hooks and gorgeous synth melodies.

Title: A Deeper Understanding
Review: The album is more a distillation of the formula they toyed with on previous albums. It's not as new anymore, but it sure sounds great. [Jul - Aug 2017, p.61]

Title: I Know You're Married But I've Got Feelings Too
Review: If her tough-minded 2005 debut presented her as a scion to her family’s legacy, then I Know You’re Married But I’ve Got Feelings Too portrays Wainwright as a distinctive artist with a caustic sense of humor and a complicated family situation.

Title: Season High
Review: [The first track, "Celebrate" is] a stunning start--and thankfully, the songs that follow are just as strong.

Title: Enslaved
Review: Enslaved will be even better than Soulfly fans will expect, a delight for any listener that enjoys Max Cavalera's composition style.

Title: There's Always Glimmer
Review: Its gorgeousness isn't always matched by a real statement of intent. [Summer 2019, p.112]

Title: Pussycat
Review: Hatfield is protesting Trump because he offends her personally, and the specificity of her outrage makes Pussycat an unusually powerful protest album.

Title: Wasted Years
Review: Righteous indignation has long fuelled OFF!, but Wasted Years is the band at their darkest and most venomous.

Title: ESTOILE NAIANT
Review: The net result of the half-thoughts that make up the patten mythos throw the music into a certain light, depending on how it's received.

Title: The Wink
Review: True, this is not an easy album to warm up to, but despite initial hesitations, repeated listening may reveal more nuances.

Title: Gods of the Earth
Review: The album's primary footholds--those downstrokes; that kick drum; those poker-faced paeans to wizards and wenches--are as true, and as sinisterly black-and-blue, as doom metal gets. [May 2008, p.136]

Title: Short Movie
Review: No doubts about this: Short Movie is a masterpiece.

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: One of the most powerful hip-hop albums of 2007.

Title: Bicep
Review: Bicep have never been afraid to go for broke, and their debut album is all the better for it.

Title: Asleep in the Bread Aisle
Review: Roth's tight, witty debut lives up to the Internet hype that has swirled around him for months.

Title: Damn Right, Rebel Proud
Review: Damn Right Rebel Proud, typically, raises less convincing hell than plenty of current mainstream Nashville product.

Title: Pretty in Black
Review: The perfect antique Cadillac album.

Title: Try To Be Hopeful
Review: The positivity is never over the top, nor does the pure sincerity exhibited throughout ever feel excessively earnest. It’s this which sets this band apart from their indie-pop contemporaries, and makes Try To Be Hopeful a record which should be revered as a truly important piece of work.

Title: The Catastrophist
Review: The Catastrophist is another shining example of the band’s ability to forge multitudes of different sounds into something new--something singular, that can really only be described as, well, sounding like Tortoise.

Title: Exile
Review: A chilling example of naked ambition prioritising production style over songwriting substance.

Title: Lil Boat 2
Review: He aspires to be more than the face of so-called "mumble rap." Yet Lil Boat 2's best moments are when he reverts to the familiar.

Title: The Other I
Review: As accessible and dour as it is on the surface, it’s the subtleties that continually beckon you in for more and leave their mark upon your subconscious.

Title: Slo Light
Review: Slo Light's sky-high production values come at the expense of soul. [Apr 2014, p.96]

Title: The Deconstruction
Review: Great moments in great songs ('I love you, there, I said it') still seem to be deep enough waters for EELS to swim.

Title: The Diary of Alicia Keys
Review: Those expecting another album where Keys sounds wise beyond her years will bound to be disappointed by The Diary of Alicia Keys, since her writing reveals her age in a way it never did on the debut.

Title: Postcards
Review: In Postcards Pieta Brown has created a trip through her most personal and revealing moments with an honesty and confidence most wouldn’t even attempt.

Title: Sonic Citadel
Review: There is restraint here, an alien concept for a band of Lightning Bolt’s usual undiluted abandon, but there is also the gleeful harshness which makes them such a force of the underground music scene.

Title: Misery Is a Butterfly
Review: The expansion of their sound to include breathtaking strings and keyboards has proven to lift Blonde Redhead out of the post-rock mire and recreated them as a band finally worthy of their past praise.

Title: Wilder Mind
Review: They are 12 variations on vaguely Don Henley-inspired arena schlock, and in this transition, they've found a new bottom.

Title: Tape Deck Heart
Review: An intensely personal record, the process of listening to the dozen tracks here is as intimate--and sometimes as uncomfortable--as reading pages ripped straight from Frank's diary.

Title: Director's Cut
Review: Director's Cut succeeds, however, by axing the star cameos and thrusting some of her most powerful songs back into the spotlight. [Jun 2011, p.115]

Title: Tentacles
Review: Raw, beguiling psychedelia from Californian newcomers.

Title: Transparent Things
Review: The only complaint I have is that this disc clocked in just under 39 minutes, while it definitely wouldn't be bogged down by another 41 minutes of tracks like these. [Jan/Feb 2006, p.78]

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: Thanks to a couple of moments where they give in to the anthemic impulses, the rest of Slave... can afford to drift along at its own singular pace, with rewarding results.

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: His knack for alchemising an engrossing trip hasn’t deserted him yet.

Title: Two-Way Mirror
Review: The sound's good and getting better - a wig-out of surf rock, Stooges-style punk and hardcore thrash, with the occasional Bambi noise of 1960's folk peeping round a tree. [Aug. 2011, p. 106]

Title: Pinned
Review: Joy Division, Suicide and JAMC collide for a post-punk racket: ear-splitting and sublimely desolate. [May 2018, p.98]

Title: Onism
Review: The record’s best songs are imbued with real emotional weight.

Title: Lotta Sea Lice
Review: It’s a lovefest in the best way, and a worthy addition to both of their catalogs.

Title: Tomboy
Review: The woozy, reverb-rich result makes for great headphone swimming (also: infant appeasement!), but Lennox is at his best with a groove to submerge.

Title: Icky Thump
Review: With its fuller sound and relaxed flights of fancy, Icky Thump is a mature, but far from stodgy, album -- and, as is usually the case, it's just great fun to hear the band play.

Title: Real Life Is No Cool
Review: Just about all of the new tracks would make fine A-sides, though they all fall into place as part of a flowing album.

Title: We Are Little Barrie
Review: Barrie Cadogan is a guitar phenomenon. [Mar 2005, p.102]

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: The biting nostalgia of middle age runs throughout the lyrics and the band’s desire to produce something akin to ‘Automatic For The People’ is largely fulfilled.

Title: Slow Summits
Review: Slow Summits is an unhurried, understated masterpiece that should make fans of the band, and of music in general, glad that the Pastels have not only stuck with it for so long, but grown into the kind of group that could release something this warm and beautiful.

Title: Didn't He Ramble
Review: A confident advance on 2012's Rhythm And Repose. [Oct 2015, p.77]

Title: Death of a Decade
Review: It's had to imagine how long Ha Ha Tonka can continue to grow on each album, considering how good they've become, but if you're looking for music that's smart, ambitious, literate, and fun at the same time, Death of a Decade could well be your introduction to your new favorite band.

Title: Somnium
Review: Throughout, a twinkly otherworldliness is counterbalanced by rhythmic excursions evoking the passage between one liminal world and another. [Feb 2019, p.92]

Title: Unicorn
Review: Sadly there’s only one track here where singer Tigs’ urgent purr and the subtle combination of electronica and bouncy indie pop matches either of those two tracks: the mesmeric ‘Slick’. The rest is solid, but with New Young Pony Club back on the scene, tracks like ‘Two Hands’ feel unremarkable.

Title: ShadowParty
Review: The album is certainly steeped in the synthpop and post-punk genres so associated with their feeder groups, so much of this album feels very much in its comfort zone: a solid and pleasing sound with few surprises.

Title: Mindset
Review: Elements create a thick, clotted atmosphere which is enveloping but sometimes almost claustrophobic.

Title: The Stimulus Package
Review: The Stimulus Package finds him working the angles as sharply as ever. On this album, he swings like a trapeze artist between the extremes of solemn commentary and hardboiled boasting.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: Angel Olsen's volatile voice lends an undercurrent of real, immediate danger to the early garage-rock throwbacks of Burn Your Fire For No Witness.

Title: Red Bedroom
Review: A propulsive party mix of garage rhythms, keyboard blurps and lecherous guitars drooling all over the ladies' shoes. [28 Oct 2004, p.103]

Title: A New Found Relaxation
Review: A New Found Relaxation promises much but never fully delivers. [Aug 2020, p.33]

Title: EAR PWR
Review: Their music now comes wrapped in gauzy textures more reminiscent of local hero Toro Y Moi. [Jul 2011, p.111]

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: The overall effect is a more diluted sound, in keeping with the watering down of Skinner's diatribes.

Title: Forcefield
Review: Forcefield stands proudly on its own, a meat-and-potatoes rock record that swings for the FM fences and gets by on Monks’ considerable personality and the band’s seemingly limitless energy.

Title: Clark
Review: This really does come very close to the top of the pile. An essential opus from a truly essential artist.

Title: Court Yard Hounds
Review: Robison and Maguire prove capable of crafting galloping, catchy choruses for such songs as "The Coast," "Ain't No Son," "It Didn't Make a Sound" and "I Miss You."

Title: T R O U B L E
Review: When the album quietly disrupts its meditations is when it is at its most effective. Other parts of the album draw you in quietly, but the softness of these songs can lose its effect after a while.

Title: Yellow House
Review: Out of step with the modern world. [Sep 2006, p.108]

Title: Savages
Review: This is a welcome blast from an uncompromising band. [Nov 2013, p.93]

Title: Asymmetry
Review: Some of it wants to carry on the torch of its predecessor, other parts of it want to redefine Karnivool, and other parts don’t even seem to have any discernible purpose, like those god-awful interludes.

Title: Kingdom of Rust
Review: Even if the album loses its way with its final two tracks, you are left so exhausted by this stage that it almost comes with a sense of relief. By reinventing what they do best, Doves have fearlessly strutted back onto everyone's radar.

Title: Samurai
Review: Samurai is an often frustrating listen, but at a minimum, it is always interesting.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: Ultimately, this album ends up being a more naturalistic take on Calexico's sound; just because it's less stylized doesn't mean it's less interesting -- it just takes a little more time for Garden Ruin's power to reveal itself.

Title: Blurred
Review: Huxley's pop forays might not be for everyone, but there's plenty on Blurred to appeal to both his underground acolytes and, perhaps, a new crop of fans as well.

Title: Cherry Bomb
Review: An album whose sustained brilliance reveals both an artist liberated from the need to try too hard, and finally armed with more to express than sarcastic teenage angst. [Jun 2015, p.55]

Title: La Petite Mort
Review: “Bitter Virtue” pursues a familiar James theme--condemnation of repressive moralities--but elsewhere, things are more ineffectual.

Title: Freedom
Review: Despite his hip-hop roots and the presence of guest rappers such as Lil Wayne, it's Akon's buoyant pop sensibility that prevails.

Title: Hope for the Hopeless
Review: Hope for the Hopeless is the next move down a path that seems to be the right one for Dennen. More attention should only yield more acceptance and acclaim for this young rising star.

Title: Works For Tomorrow
Review: Works For Tomorrow just gets better and better with every successive--and necessarily louder--airing, to the point where it does indeed feel like another genuinely great Eleventh Dream Day long-player.

Title: Desire
Review: Desire is most memorable as a collection of amazing verses. Not only is there not likely to be better rapping this year, Desire is the kind of album that reminds one of why emcees matter and just how much they can do.

Title: The Constant
Review: Sensibly, Sumner steers clear of Caucasian reggae on her surprisingly strong debut, opting instead for polished, sullen synth-pop with husky, La Roux-style vocals. [Nov 2010, p.93]

Title: Writer's Block
Review: The instrumentation is superb, the record feels unforced, and the music is heartfelt.

Title: Love Me
Review: The record with a chirping synthesiser in the background that sounds like the dawn's birdsong. Tomas Barfod may not have produced a perfect album, but then when has love ever been about perfection?

Title: Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors
Review: Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors is much more compilation than album album, more than any of Big Boi's solo efforts to date.

Title: Restarter
Review: It's a deceptively simple formula, but one that Torche continue to twist into intriguing and utterly addictive shapes. [31 Jan 2015, p.54]

Title: Splendor & Misery
Review: Utterly uncomfortable, but with such an imaginative foundation that you can't help but feel invited back to try to learn a little more about the strange and beautiful world of clipping.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: The gypsy queen is in royal form on In Your Dreams - it's not just her first album in 10 years, it's her finest collection of songs since the Eighties.

Title: Outside
Review: While the rest of Outside may not deliver in such a manner [as “A Forest at Night”], it still showcases one of North America’s more unique and talented producers on his own terms.

Title: Love at the Bottom of the Sea
Review: The disc largely lacks the memorable song- writing Merritt is known for, and that deficit is only compounded by the misguided production.

Title: Waiting For You
Review: Limitations can be freeing, but King Midas seems to tip-toe around a great deal of Martin’s artistic inspiration. The album successfully shows off an under-heralded side of his work, but it’s a shame that the sonic violence was deliberately repressed, rather than skillfully incorporated.

Title: The Weight of Your Love
Review: Too many songs spend too much time doing precisely nothing.

Title: The Double Cross
Review: For Sloan, it amounts to another fine effort. [May 2011, p.88]

Title: Self Entitled
Review: There's nothing outstanding here but fans of the band will have no complaints, and for newcomers it's as good a starting point as any, with arguably the same ratio of clever understated brilliance to uninspired mediocrity as any other phase of their discography.

Title: The Devil's Walk
Review: It's okay to mourn Apparat's past and question his trajectory. Just don't ignore what rests at the center: a record that, if nothing more, soaks in the present moment.

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: Toledo’s first full band record, his first record with a producer, with a sound that is ragged but clean, emotionally raw but cleverly structured. It’s a record that engages heart and mind and viscera all at once, and if some of the songs go on longer than pop usually does, it’s because they have more to say.

Title: Under Color of Official Right
Review: More varied stylistically, it offers a powerful reflection of the band's consistently bleak worldview. [May 2014, p.116]

Title: Sorry for Party Rocking
Review: Sorry For Party Rocking is a dumb party record that knows it's a dumb party record.

Title: Hubcap Music
Review: Some fans may miss the hobo simplicity of yore. [Summer 2013, p.92]

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: The difference between mediocre and magnificent Morrissey records tends to be the music, and by that measure, Years of Refusal is the strongest of his three '00s comeback efforts.

Title: Sycamore Meadows
Review: I must say, raw musical elements aside, as a songwriter his storytelling ability alone wins the day. [Holiday 2008, p.106]

Title: how i'm feeling now
Review: A stirring and immediate listen, as Charli takes us with her on her lockdown emotional rollercoaster in real time.

Title: The Winter of Mixed Drinks
Review: Like its predeccessor, though, this set is a compelling document of brilliant truths and lies and dramatic threats and regrets. [Winter 2010, p.100]

Title: A Bad Wind Blows In My Heart
Review: This follow-up takes on a conventional band set-up, but it's as impressive, offering a crisply original take on the classic singer-songwriter approach. [May 2013, p.109]

Title: Blood From a Stone
Review: Her ability to sound so eccentric yet create music so inherently comfortable is no small feat; by now, we know that wherever she goes to write her albums, and whatever bric-a-brac she ends up playing, the end result is always going to be sublime, and Blood From a Stone is no exception.

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: Savages’ smart reorganization and shuffling of punk, post-punk, krautrock, and noise music into something brutal, jarringly confrontational, and completely singular is a breath of fresh air and an unignorable statement of power and resistance.

Title: No Pier Pressure
Review: On the gorgeous Jardine/Wilson weeper “Tell Me Why”, the doleful nostalgia is surprisingly clear-eyed.... Sadly, “that thing” goes missing on Kacey Musgraves’ kite-weight offering and electro throwaway “Runaway Dancer”, fronted by Capital Cities’ Sebu Simonian, with synths via McCartney’s “Wonderful Christmastime”.

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: Whether or not you've made your peace with the datedness of Indie Cindy, as well as the sheer pile of things you did not want to see the band do, are you going to put it on repeat? More than you think, but less than they hope.

Title: It's All In Your Head
Review: Head shows Eve 6 tweaking and perfecting their sound to become even more consistent and solid. [Aug 2003, p.104]

Title: Are You Passionate?
Review: A quietly retro mix of guitars and organ-fueled songs, the music simmers rather than boils over.

Title: Not To Disappear
Review: Not to Disappear is made as carefully and beautifully as you would expect--balancing the acts of remaining true and pushing forward. It does this with an air of self-assured calm and the clarity that a few extra years of being alive bring.

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: On her third LP, Shah displays the patience to let an idea stew. And she’s not moving on until she’s sufficiently chewed it over, swished it around her mouth, and dragged her tongue across her front teeth.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: They've crafted a cohesive sophomore effort in a world that doesn't require cohesion, setting them apart from their many, many peers. That's admirable.

Title: Lovebox
Review: Groove Armada continue to have mislaid that sparkledust. [Dec 2002, p.105]

Title: Mess
Review: Being a Liars album, it is magnificent.

Title: Trust
Review: Trust is easily the most beautifully sparse record you'll hear this year. [Nov-Dec 2013, p.95]

Title: How Big How Blue How Beautiful
Review: How Big How Blue How Beautiful is a record about maneuvering around and through matters of the heart--sometimes triumphant, sometimes sad, and always deeply felt thanks to Welch acting as tour guide.

Title: Conatus
Review: Otherworldly, weird and downright gorgeous. Siouxsie oughta be proud.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: Review 1: All the elements of timelessness are there, but the songs just don’t seem to live beyond the last note.  [score=73] Review 2: The Shins’ music has grown by leaps and bounds.  [score=90]

Title: On My Way to Absence
Review: On My Way to Absence offers many new areas of musical exploration, suggesting a more mature arranger.

Title: Where You Go I Go Too
Review: Lindstrom knows all the right moves to give his own brand of spacey disco an air of transcendence, but the result feels so effortless that his facsimile and the "real thing" become indistinguishable--a fake so real it's beyond fake.

Title: Strapped
Review: Strapped is an album that seems to both highlight the Soft Pack's strengths and glaringly reveal their limitations to this point.

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: A staggering, synth-smeared beauty of a record.

Title: Hello Exile
Review: The Menzingers established themselves as a group interested in moving forward—even if they wrote about those high school days. Hello Exile fails to follow through on that promise.

Title: Convenanza
Review: The album traverses a rich genre spectrum and incorporates contrasting moods and atmospheres that make for an exciting listen.

Title: Funeral
Review: He still has clear vision and awareness of his place in the hip-hop game. However, Wayne is not a great editor, and thus listening to Funeral can become exhausting about halfway through. While listeners may be fatigued, however, Wayne is far from it.

Title: The Dreamer
Review: James's voice is slightly diminished but not so as to sound like anything other than itself. She's the real deal.

Title: Night of Hunters
Review: Amos herself performs with an insistently flat calmness: when her 11-year-old daughter Natashya pops up on a few tracks, in character as a shape-shifting fox, she actually proves an odder, witchier, more compelling voice than her mother, who could be mistaken for her piano teacher.

Title: My Main Shitstain
Review: Give this album a very wide berth. [Feb 2011, p.120]

Title: Confessions
Review: Addictive R&B hooks and all-dancin', all-lovin' subject matter boosted with hot production tweaks. [Jun 2004, p.107]

Title: Undertow
Review: Three short instrumentals fail to muster the same energy. Interesting sounds abound, but they don't always connect, sometimes feeling less like music than collections of sound effects. At their best, though, Wolf Eyes evoke soundtracks to a lost drama whose characters are always in peril, be it from physical violence or internal torment.

Title: Illumination Ritual
Review: Not to say they've been turning out clunkers every two or three years, but there's a renewed energy and focus on Illumination Ritual that lifts it towards the upper echelon of their best works.

Title: Capo
Review: Capo is scattered and scrappy, which for Jones  is a comfortable landscape where oddball, sprawling, day-in-the-life numbers can sit next to stay-on-the-grind tracks, and Black Eyed Peas-parodies with no apologies required.

Title: Asa Breed
Review: As spirited as this effort is, there's not much here to worry James Murphy. [Jul 2007, p.99]

Title: Ex:Re
Review: She stands sonically naked, palettes limited and claustrophobic in their unrelenting mono-focus, in this fascinating but demanding debut. [Feb 2019, p.91]

Title: Process
Review: Sampha's lyrics are clever and his voice so inherently likeable that it works. [Apr 2017, p.116]

Title: WARM
Review: Warm is an easeful record: it offers its appeal without supplication, or insistence. It’s really rather lovely.

Title: Stockholm
Review: "In a Miracle" sounds like Aimee Mann after a warm bath. But Hynde can still flash her blade.

Title: Retribution
Review: Zubot’s production creates a sense of vastness, placing Tagaq’s voice low in the mix with strings and drums or conversely counterpointing it to instruments to create icy thick layers of noise. However, his maximalist approach fails the more poppy tracks. [Feb 2017, p.45]

Title: He Gets Me High
Review: He Gets Me High is definitely worth a listen, if not a purchase.

Title: Sun Giant
Review: At times, it sounds as though the band was still working through exactly how they wanted all of the various elements to work together, such that there are some immediate, hook-filled songs ("White Winter Hymnal," "Your Protector," "He Doesn't Know Why") and other songs whose more complex structures require more from the listener.

Title: Madame X
Review: Bold, bizarre, brazen and beguiling, Madame X is Madonna living her Latin American Life. Brilliant.

Title: Americana
Review: The album comes over as a political parable as much as an investigation into the spirit of place. [Jun 2012, p.56]

Title: Desperate Ground
Review: The Thermals are still a band in awkward transition resulting in a record that is reliably good by their own decent standards, but which fails to fulfil its very apparent potential to be great.

Title: Citrus
Review: While Asobi Seksu recordings have yet to fully capture their live excellence, Citrus is still an accomplished noise-pop album, one that suggests there is plenty of new life yet to be found in exhuming shoegaze.

Title: Sounds of a Playground Fading
Review: This certainly proves that they are still a formidable force in contemporary metal. [11 Jun 2011, p.50]

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: More vibrant and engaged with the world than they've sounded at any time since Whatever You Love, You Are.

Title: Bleed Like Me
Review: Much of it signifies nothing. [May 2005, p.96]

Title: Hello, Voyager
Review: This is a fascinating record that enjoys toying with musical boundaries and unnerving the listener.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: An incredible record.

Title: California X
Review: It’s its own thing, and a pretty good one.

Title: Double Bubble
Review: Occasionally they break from formula, but the tired beats and repetitive rhymes ensure Double Bubble would have even a Full Moon Party shaking their heads. [Sep 2008, p.104]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: Coming two years after his debut ‘Blunderbuss’, a vitriol-filled purge that dropped in the wake of White’s divorce, Lazaretto does sound like a transitional step.

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: Tightly structured, lavishly orchestrated, brilliantly realised. [May 2019, p.18]

Title: The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book
Review: A mammoth indulgence, an 80-minute justification of his own ill-defined status.

Title: Free Love
Review: Sylvan Esso have always made albums that demand to be listened to at the expense of everything else in your record collection. Free Love is no exception. It’s the pair’s most cohesive body of work yet, and despite its more left-field moments, possibly their most accessible.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: New York's experimental sonic collective continues to make challenging and rewarding music on Eye Contact.

Title: Uncanney Valley
Review: Uncanney Valley seems too bent on interrupting serious moments with corny jokes and bewildering asides to say much of anything about anyone else.

Title: The North Borders
Review: The North Borders is as ambitious a record as its predecessor, and it’s just as successful.

Title: Mary Star of the Sea
Review: Equal parts prog-rock pretension, spiritual rejuvenation and glam rock harangue.

Title: Ghost Stations
Review: “Riser” features Jaki Liebezeit-style tom-toms behind cosmic contrails of synth trapped in a cavernous ambience; while string synth and wordless vocal keening drape like fog around “Abandoned/In Silence”, whose clarinet line establishes accidental but apt echoes of the theme to Exodus.

Title: The Drift
Review: Despite its complexity, every twist and turn of The Drift is absolutely compelling.
If you're a fan of the old Blur material, this disc may not be your thing.

Title: Everyone Is Here
Review: Like many a Crowded House release, this new Finn Brothers album gains resonance with repeated listens, revealing subtle charms and musical accents over time.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: It strikes the prefect balance: accessible, yet with enough idiosyncrasy to make it more than just a formulaic retread of past glories.

Title: Queen
Review: When Minaj leans into her untouchable strengths as a rapper, things get really exciting and an album of tracks as strong as "LLC" or "Barbie Dreams" would be one for the books. As it stands, however, Queen is another chapter of Minaj's good but largely meandering and inconsistent full-length album output.

Title: From the Double Gone Chapel
Review: The duo have crafted a disc that grafts underground rawness (garage rock, no wave, electro, classic '80s goth) to their taut dance grooves. [Sep 2004, p.140]

Title: Flow
Review: It's a solid return to form.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: A solid debut.

Title: Emerald City
Review: Emerald City finds Vanderslice further along his yellow brick road to occupying a truely unique place in indie rock. [Summer 2007, p.77]

Title: Accelerate
Review: "Accelerate" pushes along with urgency but a lack of bite - like background music to a bar scene in an indie thriller. "Horse To Water", however, has the machine-gun fast delivery of "It's The End Of The World…" and a cart-wheeling chorus redolent of old times.

Title: Full Moon
Review: A very slick example of production-line soul. [Apr 2002, p.110]

Title: Ceremonials
Review: It's bigger, brighter and braver than what went before, and should elevate Florence even higher, with her Machine shoulder to shoulder.

Title: Neon Cross
Review: Jennings appears on the album’s penultimate track, the fine Hurts So Bad, where his harmonies pop out of an average song. It’s one of the few moments on Wyatt’s album where her usually honest writing feels more cliche than distinct. Jennings’ harmonies are fine, but it feels like the tune easily could've been cut. Still, this album’s got plenty of superb moments.

Title: Heart Blanche
Review: The standard dips slightly in the later stages, but the grooves throughout are sleek and snappy, and CeeLo himself has rarely sounded better.

Title: Puff O'Gigio
Review: A record where frequencies oscillate with a sense of embryonic discovery; by embracing the fantastical, XXL find a new frequency of their own.

Title: Thought Rock Fish Scale
Review: Even in its quietest moments, Thought Rock Fish Scale is an album brimming with passion and protest. It finds confidence in humility, power in relaxation.

Title: Turn The Lights Out
Review: It's a pounding alt-rock dynamo with its head sunk in Sonic Youth and Dinosaur Jr rarities.

Title: Tourist in This Town
Review: Allison Crutchfield isn't forgetting anything that went wrong on Tourist in This Town, but even if the wounds seem fresh, the theme is learning from what went wrong, and this album is the work of a woman who knows plenty and has the talent and desire to make something worthwhile out of the drama.

Title: With Light and With Love
Review: Long-time listeners will revel in the subtle sonic shifts but the rest of us are still waiting for the band to make that major artistic breakthrough we know they're capable of.

Title: Tower of Love
Review: Let's just say Tower of Love isn't out to offend or challenge or discomfit anyone. But the album's less simplistic than it comes on, obviously, its snugly melodies decorated with snaking structures and surprising instrumentation.

Title: Faulty Superheroes
Review: Save for the slightly teary 90-second trudge of "The Real Wilderness," it's a rollicking pummel throughout. [No. 121, p.58]

Title: We, the Vehicles
Review: Pretty damn good.

Title: Jordin Sparks
Review: It reeks of generic blandness. [Feb 2008, p.86]

Title: Transparent Things
Review: If you like the Hot Chip album, you'll love this.

Title: Audio Day Dream
Review: His singing on "Audio Day Dream" is fine; it gets the job done. Yet what arrests your ear are Lewis' ideas.

Title: Fixed Ideals
Review: Muncie Girls have foiled the sophomore slump with Fixed Ideals, and if they sound a bit less D.I.Y. this time out, they still sound like a smart and forceful rock band that can deliver great music while offering plenty of food for thought.

Title: Burn Burn
Review: The record doesn't particularly sound like anything Our Lady Peace has done in the past, but maybe that is what's so exciting about the quartet's seventh release.

Title: Tooth & Nail
Review: Weary then, but, as ever, authentic.

Title: EVENIFUDONTBELIEVE
Review: We are back in Glass Swords territory here, but the overall mix feels less calculated and more impulsive, the surprise release of the album a hint at the more simplified and raw strain of the Glass Swords pleasure principle on display here.

Title: Notes on a Conditional Form
Review: There are at least two too many instrumentals, and songs that stand apart on their own start to bleed together near then end. But the ambition and execution can't be denied. This is the 1975 operating at the peak of their powers.

Title: Under a Billion Suns
Review: What makes these weak attempts at earnestness all the more disappointing is that the music is great.

Title: O Soundtrack My Heart
Review: Like all the best instrumental music, it's evocative stuff: the trio's multi-layered blend of vintage synths, skittering beats and crashing post-rock instrumentation keeps your mind's eye busy with images of futuristic cityscapes, gallant space troopers and, on the riotous title track, Jean Michel Jarre and Vangelis teaming up to battle Rage Against the Machine for sonic supremacy.

Title: Fold Your Hands Child, You Walk Like a Peasant
Review: Belle & Sebastian's formula is beginning to see some wear.

Title: Charmer
Review: Another sweet viper's bite of post-Freudian dyspepsia from the singersongwriter who loves to mistrust.

Title: Electronic Earth
Review: While Labrinth makes the right kind of noise, and provides a window into himself as an artist, at a fleeting 10 tracks Electronic Earth doesn't exactly give away the farm.

Title: Not Even Happiness
Review: Each time you listen to it, you feel like you’re gaining a little piece of rare knowledge from the singer’s weathered and experienced life. It’s hard to fault an album that makes you feel such a connection, and Byrne’s latest does just that.

Title: Unmap
Review: It desperately needs some kind of visual accompaniment to, at least, add a cinematic legitimacy to the sound's sporadic mood swings. Worthwhile? Probably. But the world waits for the proper return of Bon Iver.

Title: The Incredible Machine
Review: the bigger question with any record regardless of genre should always be is it good? And The Incredible Machine is very good indeed.

Title: Primitive and Deadly
Review: It's another solid outing from this immortal rock unit. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.81]

Title: 12 Desperate Straight Lines
Review: The second Telekinesis album suggests that Michael Lerner's gift for hooky, college-radio friendly indie-pop shows no signs of abating.

Title: Thousand Mile Night
Review: As a whole, Tolchin's rootsy acoustic mix works for him, though he shines brightest on the folkier, more heartfelt tracks.

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: For every circuit-overloading workout like “Copy of A” and “Disappointed”, there are a number of tracks where Reznor reverts to the teeth-gnashing angst of old without the pig-marching blitzkriegs to back it up, applying undue pressure on the the songs’ brittle structures.

Title: Personal Appeal
Review: It’s bonkers, but it’s hard not to be wooed by Moore’s outsider charm.

Title: Seven's Travels
Review: The subject matter here is repetitive, pseudo-intellectual pandering runs rampant, pointless skits and mid-song dialogue sessions interrupt the flow, and most importantly, wasted beats fall at the hands of Slug's newfound penchant for verse-long tracks and poorly realized singsong bridges.

Title: And Then Like Lions
Review: This is a lovely record, prettily arranged and carried off with assurance, but it’s ultimately very difficult to escape the feeling that the real aim here was to deliver something of slow-cooked profundity.

Title: Harmonies for the Haunted
Review: The addition of elegiac, slower songs ensure that this post-punk quarter is only moving forward. [Oct 2005, p.85]

Title: Le Noise
Review: Le Noise is the sound of a restless and prolific artist striving to deal with the burden of his great legacy.

Title: Hold On Now, Youngster...
Review: Los Campesinos! are hyper-literate college kids out to make big statements from microcosmic situations, but the metaphors in the overly abstract lyrics often get away from Gareth and co-vocalist Aleks.

Title: Broken Dreams Club
Review: Broken Dreams Club may only be an EP, but if it's any indication of the future of the band, then Girls will sophomore soar, rather than slump.

Title: World, You Need a Change of Mind
Review: It's classy and airy, although so stylishly produced (with French house guru Cassius) that it can feel like a soundtrack to an imaginary Ideal Home exhibition of laboratory-like perfection.

Title: Give More Love
Review: What stands out most about Give More Love is that Ringo's vocals have matured stylistically from his trademark amiably blokeish tones, and are stronger and more expressive now. [Oct 2017, p.90]

Title: Rooty
Review: Yes, it's as good as the last one, maybe better.

Title: The Airing of Grievances
Review: There's emo in the tortured lyrics and E Street Band in the arrangements, both appropriate for a Jersey crew. And the sizzling, storage-locker production makes it all sound like a cage match.

Title: Trick
Review: As ever, so much depends on your tolerance for Treays’ desire to make “big statements”--the noise assault of Drone Strike feels a little too on-point--but this at least feels like Jamie T is being himself again.

Title: Turn Out the Lights
Review: It won’t be to everyone’s tastes, but if you like your music to sound as if it could soundtrack a coming of age montage in a particularly gloomy John Hughes film, you found your gal.

Title: Endless Falls
Review: Endless Falls' mix of old and new maintains Morgan's reputation as one of the most consistent, and consistently interesting, producers out there.

Title: Awake Is the New Sleep
Review: Awake is a distinctly flawed album; much of what's here is precious or forced-sounding.

Title: Pigeonheart
Review: Only occasionally does the survey of this interpersonal battlefield afford an optimistic light.

Title: Scream
Review: In truth, all of Ozzy's solo albums are patchy, but Scream lacks the killer that drowns out the filler. When lead-off single Let Me Hear You Scream is the most dynamic song on offer, you know you're in for an uneventful ride.

Title: Eat Me, Drink Me
Review: Eat Me, Drink Me is a bona fide creative rebirth.

Title: Stay Together
Review: As a self-styled pop record then, Stay Together is something of a failure, distinctly lacking in hooks, entertainment value and any sort of real ingenuity.

Title: Perfect Hair
Review: Perfect Hair is no doubt a great album, but its tendency to fidget between ideas leaves it the idea of cohesion in a shallow grave.

Title: Dodge and Burn
Review: Hang on for a wild, careening drive as the Dead Weather take you on a searing ride through gutsy, fiery rock and roll that’s powerful and relentless, not to mention well played and tautly produced.

Title: LUMP
Review: The sense here is of two artists drawing creative sustenance from new light. [Jul 2018, p.112]

Title: God's Problem Child
Review: There isn't a hint of fussiness and the songs and the performances are so understated, they only seem richer with repeated spins.

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: Years of Refusal isn't just the loudest thing Morrissey has done in the '00s, it's also the best.

Title: The Liberty Of Norton Folgate
Review: The Liberty Of Norton Folgate--a title which makes sense in context but is otherwise unlikely to be jamming up the ringtone sites--is Madness in both their pomp and their prime.

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: An unfashionable record, then, and that may be its best asset. With such low stakes and barely any emotional intensity, Father of the Bride won’t cement Vampire Weekend’s legacy. But after a highly strung decade on the indie-rock A-list, it gives them room to breathe.

Title: Destruction in Yr Soul
Review: Songs bleed into one another to enhance the experience, and you'll find yourself hitting the repeat button when it's all over. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.97]

Title: Sol Invictus
Review: It's a dynamically compelling set that taps Black Sabbath, Chic, Killing Joke, Elmer Bernstein and Paolo Conte, Mike Patton's extraordinary (six octaves) voice its focus. [Jun 2015, p.76]

Title: You Had Me at Goodbye
Review: You Had Me At Goodbye finds her experimenting with musical form, be it on chamber-folk eulogy "When The Roses Bloom Again," "Windmill Crusader's" skittish electro-pop or the droll "Antiseptic Greeting." There are moments of minimal charm here, too. [Apr 2017, p.26]

Title: That's The Spirit
Review: By entering the mainstream one limb (album) at a time, Bring Me the Horizon are merely reaping what they've sown, and longtime fans should already feel acclimated to the water.

Title: Your Majesty
Review: A diverse, accomplished album that manages to be unabashedly emotional, playful, and ambitious all at the same time.

Title: Visions
Review: Visions is a flawed but intimate glimpse into the fantasies of its creator, and while it might not act as a springboard to greater fame for Grimes, it's just as satisfying to hear her take her bedroom music into a darkened basement, away from the prying world.

Title: Rolling Papers
Review: Rolling Papers may be Wiz Khalifa's studio debut and his breakthrough record, but as far as mainstream rap goes, it's far from it.

Title: OH (Ohio)
Review: OH (ohio) gets the sophistication and tone right, but something's slightly off.

Title: Director's Cut
Review: At its best Director's Cut is a dazzling affirmation of Bush's genius as songwriter, performer and producer. Maybe one day we'll take her for granted again. But not today.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: It's pretty, yet rarely challenging.

Title: Future Standards
Review: Future Standards isn't quite "Howe Gelb, the Moonlight, and You," but it's closer than anyone might expect, and he plays lounge lizard here entirely on his own terms, and it's a thoroughly enjoyable detour for a multi-faceted artist.

Title: Face Control
Review: Face Control does have at least a few things in common with a good poem: it’s a carefully crafted, modest, personal work that’s as much about purging the demons and anxieties that have been kicking around in the author’s dome as it is about creating something beautiful.

Title: From the Valley to the Stars
Review: The rolling melodies, stately pace and closed-miked, out of phase vocals result in an off-kilter whole, tempered by contributions from the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra. [July 2008, p.111]

Title: Hypnophobia
Review: It’s pleasurable, but it’s hard not think that a little varying of the approach might pay dividends.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: It's that sense of humbling, childlike wonder that defines what they do with their weathered hands. And they do it as brilliantly here as they always have done, which is high praise enough.

Title: Nextdoorland
Review: While the band revisits and expands upon musical ideas from its past, Nextdoorland never seems like warmed-over Soft Boys history; the arrangements are exponentially deeper, the playing is energetic and economical, and the songwriting has clearly benefited from Robyn Hitchcock's twenty-year career.

Title: Anne
Review: It's equally beautiful and heartbreaking, a kind of gentle sadness pulsing through it. Anne doesn't dwell in sadness though, instead, it presents a touching and honest glimpse of some of the more unfair struggles we often face that leaves us searching for hope and, more importantly, answers, but it does so in a tasteful and dignified way.

Title: It's Frightening
Review: Building a forthright sound on upfront drums, piano and Stephen Patterson's angsty vocals, tracks including Burundi-drumming lead single Percussion gun and the suspenseful groover Right Where They Left are a winning balance of art-indie mope and pop energy. [Feb 2010, p. 113]

Title: Disgraceland
Review: It’s an album that displays great faith in the late 70s/early 80s nexus of bar rock, punk, and 50s nostalgia, meaning that its melodies, riffs, and aesthetic choices often charm (to a point), even as its narratives mystify.

Title: The Search Engine
Review: The patchwork of Orb-like sonic tapestries and guest vocals by some uncharacteristically gnarly rock veterans is not hugely original, but still manages to engage. [Feb 2012, p.84]

Title: Telekinesis!
Review: The album brims with quick 'from the gut' compositions that have been uncomplicatedly produced using simple instrumentation.

Title: English Oceans
Review: The group may be battling their more indulgent tendencies at times, but Drive-By Truckers always find a path back towards redemption somewhere along the line.

Title: The Things We Do To Find People Who Feel Like Us
Review: Teeming with hooks and lyrical calls to arms, The Things We Do is a unique record, one that rages with youthful vigour, but which couldn't have been made by anyone under the age of 35.

Title: Ten New Messages
Review: We’re treated to less-interesting takes on the work of Bloc Party and The Libertines, low on hooks and utterly devoid of interesting production quirks.

Title: Horses and High Heels
Review: In the end, Horses is another addition to a catalogue short on standouts.

Title: 99Â¢
Review: The fickle genres of 99¢ not only see Santigold challenging the rules of pop, but bettering herself. In writing for others, Santigold grows a backbone that defines her unapologetically bold sound, even if she doesn’t push her lyrics as far as she does the music.

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: As formulaic and boring a rock album as you’re likely to hear in 2005.

Title: Internationally Unknown
Review: Rat Boy works best on this record not giving the fans what they want--but something new.

Title: Delta Machine
Review: While it could have been clipped of a couple of tracks, overall the devil is in the glitchy, Fever-ish new details--and Dave has rarely sounded better.

Title: It Is What It Is
Review: The weight of loss, the pain of failed love, the bleakness of it all, combined with Thundercats effervescent playing, unique playfulness and a giddy sense of humor combine on It Is What It Is, resulting in the best album of Brunner’s career and one of the strongest of 2020.

Title: Venice
Review: The fact that Venice takes a few missteps before getting into full strut inevitably takes its toll on the overall body of work.

Title: On Your Own Love Again
Review: Pratt's succinct lines can spill out so naturally and conversationally it's hard to believe someone wrote them, except that she messes with the syntax a little, too.

Title: Lemonade
Review: Her boldest, most ambitious, best album to date.

Title: Language
Review: It’s a beautifully crafted, upbeat pop album, and MNEK’s voice is compelling and gorgeous; the only small quibble is it’s a tad long.Colour , a triumphal duet with Hailee Steinfeld, feels a little tacked on in an effort to emulate the success of his Zara Larsson collab Never Forget You, and the conversational between-song interludes likewise feel a little extraneous, if all part and parcel of MNEK’s unique, mellifluous Language.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: As America crumbles, Protomartyr have proved that they can be that cereus, blooming in the dark times we inhabit--and continue blossoming into a formidable and vital band.

Title: Romantica
Review: Romantica charges out of the gate with a new vigor, brightness, and sensitivity that, in retrospect, hasn't really come together within one package for them since maybe Bewitched.

Title: The Mysterious Production of Eggs
Review: The Mysterious Production of Eggs might wrestle with unsavory topics, but it does so with a shrug of the shoulders, a wry smile, and a heart full of awe-inspiring song.

Title: drukQs
Review: Drukqs is the most sincere album [James] has released since 1995's I Care Because You Do. [Nov/Dec 2001, p.131]

Title: HNDRXX
Review: HNDRXX is a reminder that no matter how hard he tries to shun his reputation as a hitmaker, Future remains one of the most reliable acts in mainstream music, his reluctance aside.

Title: Angles
Review: Most of Angles finds The Strokes trying as hard as possible not to sound like The Strokes. This is done, in part, by recycling the least palatable parts of their last LP, and interpolating them with weird, near-atonal choruses.

Title: Lie Down in the Light
Review: No shocking directions or paroxysmal about-faces, but Lie Down In The Light is still some glorious stuff, expectations met and mettle once again tested.

Title: The Long Road
Review: It offers a heaping helping of meat-and-potatoes rawk that never veers far from the sing-along template established by their hit ''How You Remind Me.''

Title: Free TC
Review: The recorded calls between Ty and his brother that crop up repeatedly develop their characters while the story, for T.C. at least, remains stagnant. Free T.C. places an emphasis on the intimate, human relationship between these two men.

Title: Lesser Known
Review: While the overall record is much more song-centered and even features honest-to-goodness vocals on many of the tracks, he's still basically stockpiling scraps from his childhood.

Title: Dissolvi
Review: With Dissolvi, Steve Hauschildt rediscovers his adventurous self while taking delight in the human element.

Title: Expect Delays
Review: Expect Delays chugs along at a pleasant pace – ‘Bad Year’ is particularly cheerful, considering its title. If there’s a delay to be had, it’s probably the fact that it takes a few listens to warm to the album as a whole.

Title: Death Peak
Review: Despite its otherwise grim title, it plumbs emotional depths even further and creates a more vivid and exciting picture of what Clark is capable of this late in his career, and why all of the hype surrounding him from the beginning was more than credible.

Title: Maths + English
Review: His post-genre American-mythos statement.

Title: AFI (The Blood Album)
Review: AFI has little in the way of stumbles and no real clunkers to speak of, but a sense of familiarity and repetition creep in before the finish. It’s not enough to tarnish the gems but a greater commitment to ruthlessness would have been welcome.

Title: This Is Forever
Review: Of course, nothing on This is Forever is really new territory; the 80’s influenced synthesizers, the electronic drums, the monotone vocalist, it’s all been heard before. It’s all been done so much better.

Title: England Keep My Bones
Review: England, Keep My Bones is Turner's most emphatic success and the best singer/songwriter album that will be released in 2011.

Title: Tramp
Review: Though it rarely rises above a whisper, Van Etten's captivating vocals and Dessner's subtle production ensure that Tramp is never remotely sleepy.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: A considerably more gothic affair than Funeral, a set that sometimes screams “overcompensation!”

Title: Central Market
Review: Which isn’t to say that the rest of the album isn’t impressive at certain points, though the law of diminishing returns weighs heavily here.

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: Gratuitously avant saxophone squawking mars some of the disc's best moments, but Xiu Xiu's knack for grafting lush hooks onto noisy post-rock remains seductive.

Title: (a)spera
Review: This kind of sophisticated indie pop and singer/songwriter territory is all her own, and (A)spera holds almost as much wisdom as it does hope.

Title: Contraband
Review: In a time when The Darkness is successfully parodying cock-rock, members of Velvet Revolver are still earnestly carrying the torch. Whether you think that’s noble or laughable will probably determine your opinion of this album.

Title: Mikal Cronin
Review: Cronin learned how to pack garage/punk fuzzbombs with big hooks as the Moonhearts' frontman, and he hasn't lost the ragged-and-reckless urgency here.[#81, p. 55]

Title: Luminous
Review: having traded in all their early attitude for non-stop blissed-out jamming, the Horrors' default mode--equable lassitude--is beginning to pall a touch.

Title: The Next Four Years
Review: The Next Four Years isn't the best record of the year, but it is the most honest--and sometimes that means so much more.

Title: Up
Review: After a couple of plays, you're struck by Up's sonic cleverness. Three or four listens and the lyrical complexity begins to bite. Finally, and insidiously, after perhaps six or seven plays, the melodies bury themselves in your head. [Oct 2002, p.112]

Title: Kiwanuka
Review: Kiwanuka could very well be one of the best albums of 2019. But Kiwanuka is also a beautiful, deep place that feels like it will be worth visiting, not just in the last month of this year, but throughout a listener's lifetime.

Title: The Hazards of Love
Review: Where past Decemberists albums rewarded delving deeply into the milieu The Decemberists had created, Hazards of Love fails to provide much worth that probing.

Title: Get What You Give
Review: The Ghost Inside are one of hardcore's brightest lights, and Get What You Give is a perfect example of heavy music with a high IQ.

Title: Suit
Review: Nice and musically diverse.

Title: Santana IV
Review: Santana IV is arguably the group's best lineup admitting they threw it all away, way too soon.

Title: Hair
Review: Hair works because even when the pieces aren't well integrated, they are often enjoyable listening.

Title: Shrines
Review: The Canadian boy-girl duo's debut is a whirl of delicate dream pop.

Title: Doctor's Advocate
Review: It doesn't live up to the nihilistic brilliance of The Documentary... But [The Game] doesn't fall flat on his face, either.

Title: A Small Death
Review: Listening closely to A Small Death all the way through is like watching a melodramatic foreign movie; spellbinding and deliberately paced with an ambiance that leaves you reflective but anticipating better times are (hopefully) ahead.

Title: Blood Speaks
Review: Sometimes you wish they'd let themselves go a little more, but there's much here to adore.

Title: Omnion
Review: His fourth album shows a continuing talent for both dynamite house beats and reframing idiosyncratic vocalists. [Oct 2017, p.105]

Title: Harmonium
Review: Amid the dippy Dear Diary lyrics and gratuitous string sections, however, are a few treasures. [12 Nov 2004, p.122]

Title: Dear Heather
Review: Leonard Cohen has had No Voice since he began recording at 33. But he has more No Voice today, at 70, than he did on Ten New Songs, at 67.

Title: SBTRKT
Review: This album is paced like a perfect DJ set--it reads the listener with incredible insight, combining the immediate and familiar with intense passages of warm-up, breaking to allow for moments of blank space and reflection.

Title: The Waterfall
Review: At its finest, The Waterfall balances between mad and magnificent.

Title: In the Zone
Review: She may be older now, but she still sounds like a little girl, which undercuts both the glistening, sensual midtempo grooves that dominate the album and the big, booming uptempo cuts that offer a change of pace.

Title: Revelation Road
Review: Her voice [is] a soft, soulful instrument that draws the listener in with seemingly minimum effort, then delivers whatever message she wishes to impart to willing ears. [Dec. 2011 pg. 94]

Title: Myth Takes
Review: Too bad about the self-important, chanted lyrics, which rattle on even when the band's trying to stretch out and groove. [Apr 2007, p.110]
2 picks up where the debut left off, with trace elements of Southern swampiness mingling with sun-kissed West Coast mellowness.

Title: Grinderman
Review: While the sound of pure snarl and glee is what melts the speaker cabinets the most, the overdriven menace of most these songs doesn't undermine their worth as songs.

Title: Clark
Review: Clark is anomalous but deeply rewarding. It's the type of release you could easily live inside for weeks and still find interesting nooks every single day.

Title: Blame the Vain
Review: This is inspired stuff from a rebel who still has plenty to offer.

Title: Metalmania
Review: All in all, Metalmania is a lovely little album.

Title: Elvis Perkins in Dearland
Review: Decent as these tracks are, the rest of the album never quite lives up to 'Shampoo's' potential.

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: Say what you will about influences on sleeves, this is pop music at its best: nostalgic and angst-ridden, but ultimately life-affirming. Shout Out Louds have found a winning formula.

Title: The Remote Part
Review: It's every ounce of Idlewild's potential fulfilled at once.

Title: Third World Pyramid
Review: If their classic records sounded like Newcombe on uppers, then this is the reverse: the whole record sounds protracted and dripping in molasses. Slow isn’t always bad, however. Psychedelia has a tendency to seem unhurried while keeping a tempo it can’t quite enjoy, and he hones in on a progression that works.

Title: Demon Days
Review: The results are reason enough for Damon Albarn's other outfit to finally pack it in.

Title: Fleeting
Review: Jones covers a lot of musical ground on this album, and it's all of high quality, confirming his place as one of the top-tier American Primitive guitarists.

Title: Strands
Review: The album is highly focused and engrossing, and continues Hauschildt's run of nearly flawless albums.

Title: King Animal
Review: King Animal undeniably draws its strength from the band's accessible Superunknown era, but also takes Soundgarden somewhere fresh.

Title: Dismania
Review: Though the sax draws you in, you'll stay for the trashy energy. [No.87 p.56]

Title: Epoch
Review: Irrespective of how you choose to approach it, the final installment of the trilogy that Hansen began back in 2011 fully underlines his strength, deftness and creative dexterity as a producer.

Title: Beautiful Future
Review: Well, there is a lack of faults, sure, but there’s not a lot that grabs hard.

Title: Wolf
Review: It may not have the global appeal of his OF stable mate’s Channel Orange, but it is certainly his most accessible and enjoyable.

Title: The Brink
Review: This is wishy-washy music for moody goth-lite teens. [Apr 2014, p.112]

Title: Warpaint
Review: A well-rounded and mature second album.

Title: Dumb Luck
Review: There are no great songs to speak of on Dumb Luck, and in fact there are just a few that I would hesitatingly call “good,” or more important, “memorable.”

Title: Negativity
Review: While the album title may aptly describe the plight, this is easily Deer Tick’s most complete album to date, proving that sometimes a bit of good comes from even the most dire of circumstances.

Title: Heard It In A Past Life
Review: Her singing provides the album's highlights. The instrumentation and production only serve to accent her voice and sadly often detract from the experience.

Title: Our Earthly Pleasures
Review: Our Earthly Pleasures, in contrast to the water-tight radio punk of its predecessor, overflows with ideas, even if it’s to the detriment of the material.

Title: Blood, Looms and Blooms
Review: Musically, this record definitely shoots what it was aiming for, but I wouldn't listen to it unless you are, or want to be, severely depressed or disturbed.

Title: Get Hurt
Review: Get Hurt is neither weird, nor, unfortunately, all that wonderful. [Sep 2014, p.116]

Title: Our Two Skins
Review: Payten’s writing is strong enough that she pulls off worthwhile takes on familiar themes. ... Her lyrics only falter when Payten sounds aware of her audience, becoming self-consciously clever.

Title: Field Report
Review: What could so easily be just another folky Americana album is lifted high above the norm by the sheer strength of Porterfield's quite brilliant songwriting. [Aug 2013, p.96]

Title: Black Cascade
Review: Black Cascade is impressive enough to vault Wolves into the top ranks of the highly idiosyncratic U.S. black-metal scene, allowing them rub shoulders with such standard-bearer bands as Nachtmystium and Absu.

Title: Carrion Crawler/The Dream
Review: Diehards and newbies alike will revel in its weird, wild well-roundedness.

Title: FM!
Review: It’s hard to work out whether this is an album, an EP or a playlist, and at 22 minutes long it’s difficult to feel fully satisfied and does leave you wanting more.

Title: Happiness
Review: Happiness promises the rough edges and absurdity of one era's pop, but for the most part gives the mum-friendliness of the next. Hurts would surely be better if they committed to one or the other.

Title: bounty
Review: Amid all the wanton airy-fairyness, this is just brilliant pop music. [Jul 2013, p.106]

Title: Chromatica
Review: On Chromatica, she seems too afraid or to removed from the Koons-loving side of herself to get too bizarre or to let the production dominate, two of Artpop’s best qualities. ... Chromatica functions as both stopgap escapism and yet another portrait of someone among us who’s trying to patch together her identity again.

Title: Turn The Lights Out
Review: [It] takes an echoed-up tack that's more Sonic Youth than Voidoids.

Title: Admiral Fell Promises
Review: Sitting down and listening to a full length album all the way through without outside interference is nearly impossible, let alone desirable. However, the solitary atmosphere and minimal elements of Admiral Fell Promises make it designed for just such a commitment.

Title: Sainthood
Review: This is a set of power pop with hooky choruses and chiming harmonies to go along with splashes of synths mixed in for throwback '80s flavor (especially 'Red Belt'). It makes for a 40-minute blast of smart songcraft.

Title: Disarm the Descent
Review: Disarm the Descent sees the Massachusetts quintet reinvigorated, leaving 2009's Killswitch Engage in their wake. [May 2013, p.86]

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: It's even prettier and easier on the synapses than D--also released this year--without sacrificing any of the complexities for which the Texans are renowned.

Title: Electric
Review: Electric isn't quite electrifying in the way that Very and Introspective and "What Have I Done To Deserve This?" are, but nearly every track has a moment or two that ignites seemingly long-gone enthusiasm.

Title: Spoon and Rafter
Review: Spoon and Rafter has no trouble making Ryan Adams seem like more of a farce than he already is, and it's deserving of at least half of the attention given to anything released by Wilco.

Title: Strength in Numbers
Review: Calla's sound continues to evolve as they explore divergent musical avenues within the context of potent, atmospheric alt-rock.

Title: Further Out
Review: Further Out does successfully sound genreless despite being referential of a half dozen genres at once and is presented as a continuous listening experience.

Title: Ghostory
Review: Ghostory is well on par with the strident ephemera to which followers of this project have become accustomed.

Title: Happy People
Review: This is a very real example of "that difficult second album." [Mar 2014, p.93]

Title: Junto
Review: Junto stands out not because it is breaking new ground, but because it illustrates how Basement Jaxx's patented busy-sounding tracks continue to be the superior version of what everyone else who is copying them is doing.

Title: Tomboy
Review: With Tomboy, Lennox valiantly accepts the responsibilities he once invoked on Prayer, now seeming to possess answers to some of the questions as well.

Title: DSVII
Review: What made M83 so great was its inclination to look forward as well as backward. Unfortunately, DSVII —like Junk— looks backward without bringing anything new to the table.

Title: You in Reverse
Review: A gorgeous set of spectral, ambitious and carefully crafted songs. [Jun 2006, p.188]

Title: Vanishing Point
Review: Think Ash covering Nirvana and you'll have an idea of just how bad an idea this album is. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.94]

Title: All Eternals Deck
Review: The album pays in cleft between Darnielle's left and right brains and strikes the perfect balance between wild imagery and plaintive sentiment. [May 2011, p.112]

Title: Penny Sparkle
Review: Certainly fans of the Blonde Redhead of old may damn Penny Sparkle with faint praise. Yet if Penny Sparkle veers a bit too close to Blonde Redhead meets Sade, it is mostly pleasant, and not for all of us is that word an epithet.

Title: Innundir Skinni
Review: Innundir Skinni is still a worthy achievement, it's emotional but not melodramatic; understated yet grand. But it is a mixture rather than a whole and lacks the cohesion of Arnalds' inspiring first album.

Title: Native To
Review: Native To is packed with well-executed, hummable stuff, but it wears thin quickly.

Title: Run the Jewels
Review: A rough and rabid ride.

Title: Medulla
Review: Without a doubt the most challenging collection of music she has ever released.

Title: I Forget Where We Were
Review: It’s a sensitive and technically more profound outing.

Title: Coming Out of the Fog
Review: There are times on Coming Out Of The Fog when Arbouretum seem to be a little too self indulgent and one paced, but each of these songs has a hook that digs deep and refuses to let go.

Title: Don't You
Review: Most of Don’t You aims for Babyface but lands somewhere around Surfacing-era Sarah McLachlan, except nowhere near as good.

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: In many ways, this is as radical, experimental and mind-expanding of a pop album as you’re likely to hear anytime soon, let alone by a festival headlining artist.

Title: The GOAT
Review: The songs here demonstrate his versatility by tackling new subject matters (relationships, love), expanding his reach with more big-name producers and features. He is no longer boxed in as a drill specialist but an artist with range, who can take that foundation and shape melodies that are on trend with 2020’s standards.

Title: We Are Science
Review: A churning, droning, sickly sweet nouveau-electro trip. [Nov 2002, p.94]

Title: Pylon
Review: Unlikely to win any new converts then, Pylon still remains a triumph of wilful perversity. [Jan 2016, p.113]

Title: Green Lanes
Review: Cooper and Hoare not only borrow, but fully adopt characteristics of traditionalist rock, like inoffensive lyrics, bland instrumentation, and unfettered nostalgia, all of which makes Green Lanes barely discernible from hundreds of other albums.

Title: Ray Ray
Review: Ranging from funk, R&B and soul to gospel and hip-hop overtones, Ray Ray delivers the goods.

Title: Cheatahs

Review: Waits' voice has always been an acquired taste, but those on the bus will appreciate the way he throws himself into every track as if haunting the characters like some sort of lunatic guardian narrator.

Title: Blood Mountain
Review: Intense, invigorating and beguiling.

Title: East of Eden
Review: It is at once too ambitious (in the recording process and change of milieu) and not ambitious enough (in its failure to push Bergsman’s music to unexpected and truly experimental places).

Title: Nightmare Logic
Review: Harder, heavier and more cohesive than their Manifest Decimation debut, Nightmare Logic is precise and snappy enough to win over hardcore fans too.

Title: Portico Quartet
Review: A mazy, fluid, ethereal suite of chamber jazz to get properly lost in.

Title: Oui Oui Si Si Ja Ja Da Da
Review: Why are you half-arseing your way through such a thick slurry of clod-hopping ska-by-numbers? Or wallowing in pits of cliché?

Title: Compton: A Soundtrack by Dr. Dre
Review: The Chronic and 2001 were simply collections of great songs and the order didn't matter much; Compton, conversely, is one giant song presented as a specifically sequenced album. While it succeeds as such--a lush, expensive-sounding art rap song-cycle--it fits the Doctor about as well as a baggy t-shirt. Dre makes great songs, not great albums.

Title: Quicksand / Cradlesnakes
Review: A monster of an achievement.

Title: Pop Etc
Review: [The songs'] punchiness and repetitiveness can quickly get on one's nerves, depending on your disposition.

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: Crack the Skye is Mastodon's most involved album to date, relying on hyper-intricate guitar arrangements and production nuance in service of its freaky inter-dimensional mythology.

Title: Punisher
Review: The maturation of Bridgers' craft, and influence of her peers, is apparent on Punisher. The songs alternate between tightly wound pop-rock ("Kyoto") and a soft concoction of folk-rock ("Savior Complex") and both sides feel focused and sturdy. Bridgers keeps getting better and Punisher affirms this.

Title: A Flourish and a Spoil
Review: The Districts end up finding an in-between, where emotional songwriting becomes the selling point, without being overdone.

Title: Blue Mountain
Review: A moving group of tunes worthy of any campfire.

Title: Rebirth
Review: It would be easy to think this might be the final great outing from such an important reggae music figure, but part of Rebirth's lore is that it sounds so fresh.

Title: Keys to the World
Review: For the most part, Keys To The World is a definite step forward and demonstrates that Ashcroft is finally hitting his stride as a solo artist.

Title: III
Review: Strangely, III doesn't sound like the work of a band at all.

Title: Damaged
Review: A profound melancholy suffuses the elegant and often sublime Damaged.

Title: Face the Truth
Review: Gone are the spotty moments that marred his previous solo work. Most important, Malkmus seems to be having fun again.

Title: Pete Yorn
Review: The performances outshine the material. [Dec 2010, p.119]

Title: Von
Review: Young, earnest, eerie, and overzealous, Von is a unique, almost belligerently unaffiliated piece of music that unsubtly blazons its idiosyncrasies.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: When everything here lines up the right way--and it more often than not, it does--Modern Vampires is the perfect album for the coming Atlantic summer. Think of it like saltwater taffy: bright and sweet, with plenty to chew on.

Title: We'll Live and Die in These Towns
Review: So here's what's brilliant about this band: the 11 songs here offer no solution, no way out and very little hope, making We'll Live and Die in These Towns as bleak in its own way as the Manic Street Preachers' The Holy Bible. The songs are brilliant, too.

Title: Peanut Butter and Jelly Live at the Ginger Minge
Review: No less of a passion-scratched, damp-sheet-scrumple of an affair than its predecessors.

Title: Picaresque
Review: “I am a writer, writer of fictions,” Meloy claims on “Engine Driver,” and that’s exactly what he does, but it’s what everyone else does too, the only real difference being Meloy hits the thesaurus and maritime literature a bit harder than most.

Title: You're the One
Review: The stripped-down arrangements and meditative flavor of the songs bring to mind such uncluttered efforts as 1983's Hearts and Bones or even Simon's 1972 solo debut.

Title: Blonde
