Review: Blonde is the sound of an artist urging his listener to be patient, and in this age of instant gratification, it is a refreshing, rewarding triumph.

Title: Erika Spring EP
Review: In the end, Erika Spring's solo debut falls into the category of pleasant experience.

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: They cram in so many styles it could easily come across too clever, like a band that claims to be equally inspired by Wu Tang, Cheap Trick and Cher. It doesn't happen. The tracks have a life apart from the name-that-tune layering that drives their sound.

Title: Sewn Together
Review: At their best, the Meat Puppets tackle swampy rock, erratic punk, boisterous country, ruminative folk, and seedy psych with equal authority, all while instilling a surreal scent of the desert.

Title: As High As the Highest Heavens and From the Center to the Circumference of the Earth
Review: It's an album that's easy to overlook, but careful listeners will be rewarded with a world of sound. [Apr 2011, p.122]

Title: So You Wannabe An Outlaw
Review: Earle sounds invigorated and relaxed, and these are some of his best songs in years. [No. 144, p.58]

Title: New Facts Emerge
Review: “Brillo De Facto” prove vaguely purposeful efforts on the surface here, a second, third and fourth listen reveals a band seemingly bereft of inspiration, regurgitating tame Fallisms with--and it really pains your writer to say it--riffs conjuring every middling young rural pub rock band of the early Noughties.

Title: Sorry For The Late Reply
Review: Arriving just at the right time for its message to feel truly resonant, Sorry For The Late Reply is a bold, brave, brilliant work.

Title: Songs
Review: Songs finds John Fullbright more concerned with the act of writing than with illuminating a subject.

Title: Iowa
Review: Iowa boldly follows up, notching maximum body blows in its unyielding production, while maintaining an odd grandeur in its professed pain and anguish, its struggle for individualism.

Title: Neon Golden
Review: With Neon Golden, the Notwist have created a daring album full of different sounds and textures. While this might sound like a textbook post-rock album, it is without a doubt a record firmly anchored by its pop sensibilities.

Title: Sleep Forever
Review: Yes, the distortion might be heavy, but when juxtaposed with soaring synths and Brandon Welchez's echoing vocals, Sleep Forever creates a kaleidoscopic landscape much more intricate than the duo's previous effort.

Title: The Moonlight Butterfly
Review: The Moonlight Butterfly won't allow The Sea And Cake to set the world on fire but with its reviving studio craftsmanship and exploratory attitude, it should happily smoulder in the ears of those who needed the band to deliver something just a little to the left of a self-defined centre.

Title: Air Lows
Review: Her fifth full-length Air Lows feels like a goth psychedelic ritual intended to plumb the depths of the listener’s unconscious; while the record doesn’t always hit its mark, the moments that do sustain momentum radiate a delectably gnostic hum.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: In all, this is a muscular yet not flashy outing from Gang Gang Dance, and its smooth confidence is a welcome respite from its self-indulgent neighbors.

Title: Broken Dreams Club
Review: As the second album looms, it's exciting to hear them sound so bold and articulate.

Title: The Duel
Review: Though Moorer's haunting characters delay the inevitable by juggling booze and pills, their stuggle ends with redemption. [16 Apr 2004, p.76]

Title: The Prodigal Son
Review: The Prodigal Son lives up to its title, a return to his earliest archival sounds.

Title: Terra
Review: This is music that needs to be ruminated on during late nights. [May 2011, p.79]

Title: Directions to See a Ghost
Review: With many songs over four minutes and often consisting of blantantly stoned self-indulgent "jams," some trimming is needed.

Title: Salton Sea
Review: The vision of Southern California terrain Barfod molds in Salton Sea seems strangely undead and haunting even at its most jubilant moments, creating a chilling sense of something epic and part-human.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: It is unusual for sure, but this is the beauty of Preliminaries. [Summer 2009, p.68]

Title: Youth and Young Manhood
Review: While rough and a little patchy, it's a cracking debut nonetheless. [Aug 2003, p.108]

Title: United We Stand
Review: Unfortunately, little of what makes this record so rewarding from the get-go surfaces on the back half.

Title: Stereo
Review: With a voice that aches like a hangover, Westerberg has long sounded like he's had an album of post-punk saloon ballads in him. Stereo is that album, and it's his best collection of songs since the Eighties.

Title: Italian Ice
Review: Clear-eyed, warm and stylish. [Jul 2020, p.20]

Title: Lust for Life
Review: As usual, it’s best listened to when you’re in your feelings, and since good news is in short supply, that might be often enough for her gauzy vision of love to feel like a balm, the more wide-eyed the songs the better.

Title: Brokeback and the Black Rock
Review: Black Rock is still filled with McCombs' spacious, isolating tracks ("Tonight at Ten," "Gold!"), which are best for lonely winter evenings.

Title: Believe You Me
Review: It works to the strengths of each, allowing Negro and Barwick their own spaces to shine while sculpting an overall, engrossing ambience around the pair.

Title: You Can Have What You Want
Review: The album’s less immediate than Can’t Go Back, and this is actually one of the things that makes it, in the end, probably more lastingly entertaining.

Title: No Fool Like an Old Fool
Review: Modest means and humble ends shape the character of No Fool Like An Old Fool.

Title: Odditorium or Warlords of Mars
Review: There are no formulas here, and that's a good thing, but one can't help but feel the lack of focus and discrimination it took to put together Odditorium or Warlords of Mars.

Title: Varshons
Review: Whether tackling Broadway showtunes or John Prine, or Simon and Garfunkel, the laconic alt-rocker nimbly transforms songs until they sound like they could be his own. That pixie dust extends to Varshons.

Title: Tales from Turnpike House
Review: Overall the LP falters too often.

Title: Forth
Review: Forth is a good, but not great Verve album, then, its glimmers of brillance all too brief. [Sep 2008, p.98]

Title: Travelogue
Review: The arrangements treat Mitchell's tunes as precious artifacts, making little attempt to seduce the listener.

Title: Darkness and Light
Review: With a producer and co-writer from outside the usual precincts of pop and hip-hop--the guitarist Blake Mills, who has worked with Alabama Shakes and Fiona Apple--Mr. Legend’s music turns less glossy: earthier and often spookier.

Title: Lie Down in the Light
Review: Lie Down In The Light is his most coherent LP since the bleak masterpiece "I See A Darkness." [Aug 2008, p.85]

Title: Hey Venus!
Review: Hey Venus!, then, is not the type of progressing heavyweight that has marked the output of later day Super Furries. As a shorter, lighter effort, though, it is every bit as tantalising, thickly coated in SFA-brand special sauce and still worth its weight in goal.

Title: 22, A Million
Review: Oblique lyrics provide few hand-holds; while his distress is palpable, it remains frustratingly nondescript.

Title: Just Us
Review: The tracks here, presented with the intention that other will use them as a creative starting pint, nevertheless feel fully realised, evoking a succession of fleeting states and ambiguous atmospheres. [Dec 2014, p.57]

Title: As I Call You Down
Review: The mellow vibes are appealing in their own lackadaisical way, but as the short LP approaches its conclusion it's hard not to wish there was just a little more discipline, perhaps enough to sculpt these pleasant sounds into full songs.

Title: Content
Review: Post-punk quartet's first all-new record since 1995. [Feb. 2011, p. 117]

Title: Suddenly
Review: It’s a treat to listen to the way such a masterful musician mines his own record collection for inspiration. What makes the album so spectacular, though, is Snaith’s voice. ... Throughout, his mesmerizing vocals elevate songs that might otherwise scan as banal.

Title: The Eminem Show
Review: It's a third album that avoids all the pitfalls of third albums: introspective without being self-pitying, expansive in scope without being pompous, exploring new directions without disappearing up its own arse.

Title: Water on Mars
Review: The result is like a more chaotic Nirvana or Dinosaur Jr, with gentle diversions into geeky indie, drone-rock and fuzz-pop that only enhance the racket-making around it. [Apr 2013, p.109]

Title: New Bermuda
Review: New Bermuda, if anything, is more overwhelming than Sunbather.

Title: Prisyn
Review: Even more audacious than No Trail and Other Unholy Paths, Prisyn proves Jaye Jayle's music can thrive as Patterson lets tradition go by the wayside.

Title: LUX
Review: The record accomplishes what Eno has proposed is ambient music's main purpose: to heighten one's sense of their surroundings while allowing their own narrative to fill the music with meaning and context.

Title: Pollinator
Review: Miraculously, the whole thing is given a neat completness by John Congleton's slick, electro-rock production. [Jun 2017, p.92]

Title: The Scene Between
Review: It’s a cohesive listen that doesn't quite translate into a cohesive statement of purpose.

Title: Warm On a Cold Night
Review: Luckily, the new songs here aren't just filler between pre-existing singles; in fact, there are so many standouts that any of these songs could work as a single.

Title: Battle Born
Review: Flush with stirring, singalong melodies, they construct exciting, catchy songs that draw on the dynamics of stadium rock established by classic bands.

Title: Sheath
Review: Ballistic but aimless.

Title: Going Down In History
Review: A soaring, Ian McLagan-dedicated Small Faces cover, "All Or Nothing," is the spiritual centrepiece of the set, but every song arrives with crisp melodies, burning guitars and impassioned vocals. [Apr 2016, p.81]

Title: Mondo
Review: It's unclear if the sentiments are intended as poignant or as punch lines. But on a set wired with this much sonic wit, the sincerity question may be moot.

Title: Mission Control
Review: Here the lyrics continue presentable insofar as they're audible. But what they, the riffs or the Whigs mean, no one knows.

Title: The Light in You
Review: Occasionally they over-indulge, and it’s certainly not their best LP, but it's easy to forgive them given the obvious love that’s contained within the tracks here.

Title: Divers
Review: It's a truly incredible album, a special album and a rare album.

Title: The Scene Between
Review: It all works rather well. [Apr 2015, p.102]

Title: Black Cadillac
Review: At times, Cash nails the knife-edge of hurt and love so adeptly, you feel like you're intruding on too-personal confessions.

Title: In Love
Review: The Birmingham quartet's debut album bears out the promise of their early singles and Delicious EP.

Title: How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb
Review: Atomic Bomb is a reduction of U2's most definable characteristics into a very basic formula: impassioned vocals lent extra gravity by Bono's wavering voice; guitars that chime like bells; thick, meaty rhythm section workouts; slowly seductive hooks that build to triumphant, emotional, endorphin-releasing choruses. And on that level, it succeeds admirably.

Title: Night on My Side
Review: It's almost disturbingly accomplished. [Jul 2002, p.103]

Title: Long Way Home
Review: For now, she’s created an unimpeachably well-crafted debut--something to gaze at, even if it is just a sequence of gazes itself.

Title: BE
Review: [The] familiarity brings you to the cereal, the soap and the market, and some people will be drawn to Be, okay with seeing the imitation. The rest are better holding off for Oasis’ inevitable reformation.

Title: Close Ties
Review: Close Ties shows that it's possible to be an experienced professional and still make music that's emotionally urgent and immediate; it's also a reminder that Rodney Crowell was and remains a talent to be reckoned with, and this album shows he's a long, long way from used up.

Title: Pala
Review: Friendly Fires' follow-up to their Mercury-nominated debut is a huge disappointment.

Title: Let's Go Sunshine
Review: There's enough variety to excite and warrant repeat listens; however, pacing suffers when the momentum is cut by otherwise pleasant tracks like "Fractured and Dazed" and "Picture Frame." These issues aside, Let's Go Sunshine is a mature progression for the Kooks, one that points in the right direction for the band's evolution.

Title: Street Safari
Review: Street Safari defies the sophomore slump with another collection of sharply crafted tunes that play like singles. It's a slightly more refined and thoughtful set on average, one that plays like an undergrad to Never Enough's skipping out on summer school, but it still struts and shrugs and keeps cigarettes in its shirt sleeve.

Title: Play With Fire
Review: Raging with a steady purr, Play With Fire might be an obvious follow-up to their 2017 debut—but that doesn’t mean it’s any less powerful or interesting. The LP sees L.A. Witch solidifying their status as the cursed love children of Black Sabbath and The Shangri-Las.

Title: Interplanetary Class Classics
Review: Iif you’re not in on the joke, the album might fall flat sporadically. Still, taken with the right level of salt, ICC is a brave, bold and multi-faceted experience that can knock one’s socks clean off.

Title: Gentle Grip
Review: Its best moments also its most agitated. For those of us keen on more of the same from York and co, let's just hope she keeps her beady eye on the anxieties of the everyday and not on paying a visit to outerspace.

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: Keyboard effects aside, it's the same-old same-old, and whether you love Snow Patrol or hate 'em, Fallen Empires will do little to change your mind.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: A double album slough of easy listening instrumentals. [combined review of both discs; #9, p.108]

Title: Adventures in Counter-Culture
Review: It's not to say that Adventures in Counter Culture is nothing but filler, far from it. The album ebbs and flows through its 15 tracks, each one playing part in a larger role of capturing Blueprint's purpose, which is to create a hip-hop album that goes against the grain of today's formula for success.

Title: True Love Cast Out All Evil
Review: Not unlike Bob Dylan's Time Out Of Mind, this is an album by a grizzled veteran of rock's rougher roads who proves in his late career that he still has great work in him. Perhaps even better, Erickson sounds remarkably confident and optimistic; for all the tumult of his life, he's happy to be living it.

Title: Aytche
Review: Aytche is, for the most part, an easygoing album, but an unsettling undercurrent runs through it as well. The muted thumps and ominous dissonance of “Chopping Wood” play like an ambient riposte to Bitches Brew.

Title: Fog
Review: The tracks are often tuneful, but they're too downtempo for anything but the chill room. [May 2002, p.74]

Title: Science Agrees
Review: Once, or if, expectations related to personnel are set aside, there are some meaty post-punk tunes among an uneven selection on Science Agrees.

Title: Afraid of Ghosts
Review: Produced by buddy Ryan Adams, and featuring guest shots from Bob Mould and Johnny Depp, Ghosts is a gorgeous, contemplative effort rooted in loss.

Title: Shaky Dream
Review: By maintaining forward momentum while having so much going on in every song, the band makes Shaky Dream an album that provides plenty of depth without sacrificing accessibility, striking a fine balance between catchy melodies and murky atmospherics.

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: On "Irresponsible Tune," leader Dave Longstreth harnesses the magic of bygone vocal groups like the Orioles and the Comedian Harmonists, singing about  "a world crooked, f***ed up and wrong" and, briefly, makes it right.

Title: After the Disco
Review: It's lovely stuff. [Feb 2014, p.90]

Title: More Light
Review: With the core ‘XTRMNTR’ team--the Scream, Shields, producer David Holmes--More Light, the Scream’s 10th album and first in five years, lives up to its bilious billing.

Title: Joyland
Review: It’s lucky for us that Joyland so often yields gems amongst the heavy strata of computerized monoliths.

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: [Thought there are] a few sweet moments on Sugaring Season--especially melancholic, piano-driven "Last Leaves of Autumn--it all feels a bit saccharine.

Title: Return of the Tender Lover
Review: With a seemingly renewed energy, Babyface is back in business with two records in the last two years, and Return of the Tender Lover sets the table for an even bigger return to the public eye forthcoming.

Title: Silver Eye
Review: Goldfrapp hark back to the bombast of a time when electronica was all about man (or woman) versus machine. On Silver Eye, the machines are ascendant.

Title: Paul's Tomb: A Triumph
Review: As a guitar record Paul’s Tomb may be, somewhat surprisingly, the best guitar record since, gosh, Pink (2005)?

Title: Saturn
Review: Saturn is quite the trip, more than worthy of its stellar name.

Title: Vespertine
Review: With Vespertine, Bjork has constructed a whispering wall of wonders, and instead of forcing everyone out, has invited the world to look through the cracks.

Title: Fragrant World
Review: There's a duality to Fragrant World that, sized up alongside its two predecessors, reveals an inherent character trait and a more troublesome trend. Bad songs turn into good songs, and good songs turn into better ones. [No.90 p.51]

Title: The Stage Names
Review: Sheff has proven himself again and again to be a gifted wordsmith, and Stage Names features some of his finest parlor room romanticisms and slacker-poet observations to date.

Title: Seasons of Your Day
Review: It is refreshing to hear Sandoval’s stunning vocals once again coupled with Roback’s guitars. The world is a better place for it.

Title: Transatlanticism
Review: It's Death Cab's slowest and most mature recording, and over time, hidden bits of magic reveal themselves brilliantly. [Nov 2003, p.98]

Title: Landing Gear
Review: There are no state-of-the-art flourishes (like Kanye West’s sped-up soul samples); he furnishes most of his own hooks, without the assistance of Auto-Tune, the now ubiquitous vocal effect favored by rappers who can’t really sing (Devin sings, and quite nicely too); and the only big-name rapper he invites is Snoop Dogg, with whom he shares some genuine stoner chemistry. Track after track (there are only twelve, and mercifully no skits), the beats land just so. And nowhere is he more confident than in his rhymes.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: My Name Is My Name is an album that listeners will either love or hate, with seemingly no room in between. It’s a bit much to take in upon the first listen, especially with so much hype behind its release, but with repeated spins and closer examination of the product, so to speak, the dope is as nice as advertised here.

Title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy
Review: The album demands a lot from our short-attention-span culture, but it's not time you'll feel like you've wasted. [Sep 2015, p.98]

Title: Dedicated Side B
Review: The dozen songs that comprise Dedicated Side B, all leftovers from the original recording sessions, are less musically adventurous than those particular tracks, but they double down on pillow talk, lending the album a uniformity that its predecessor lacked.

Title: Fool
Review: There are some songs that sound like they were last minute add-ons (“Alchemy” is so plodding you can almost watch time stand still), but taken as a whole, Fool still finds Jackson playing some of the best pop music out there, immune to fads and current trends.

Title: Pink City
Review: A finely crafted record, whose artfulness is mediated by informality. [Oct 2014, p.69]

Title: Musik, Die Schwer Zu Twerk
Review: Without any true sonic signifiers to really separate this record from Drozd and Coyne’s primary outfit, it simply feels like another of the Flaming Lips’ disposable ideas that are fun for a few weeks.

Title: Four (Acts of Love)
Review: Although Four may strike some despondent notes at times, it's a high point for Harvey's career. [Jun 2013, p.88]

Title: Modern Nature
Review: It's far, far better than anyone ever had a right to expect. [No. 117, p.53]

Title: Keep The Village Alive
Review: Kelly Jones seems particularly bereft of inspiration on Keep the Village Alive, with insipid lyric clichés harnessed to settings that resemble a swift rummage through an arena-rock record collection.

Title: All Day
Review: All Day offers a departure of sorts from Night Ripper and Feed the Animals, his previous releases. The composition of those two essentially follow the same furious blueprint, whereas All Day allows the musical ideas a bit more time to breathe and evolve.

Title: The Eraser
Review: The Eraser is a triumph.

Title: Last Summer
Review: The highlights are outweighed by tracks such as Glitter Gold Year, a half-formed sketch of jabbing bass and meandering riffs. [Jan. 2012 p. 120]

Title: The Electric Lady
Review: While the vibe's heady, the music can drift into syrupy cabaret or oversoft funk. But she maintains her chill over skillet-hot tracks like the disco-rocking "We Were Rock n' Roll" and the jumping "Dance Apocalyptic."

Title: Teen Dream
Review: Teen Dream is a lovely album, but there's more to admire here than to actually love. Oddly, that may not be a problem. [Feb. 2010, p. 94]

Title: Live it Out
Review: Despite questionable lyrics, it's a much more cohesive album. [8 Jul 2006, p.41]

Title: Host
Review: Producer Shane Stoneback resumes his role as the unofficial third member of the group, ensuring that Host, in spite of its dabbling in live instrumentation, springs from the same atmospheric vein as previous Cults albums.

Title: Them Crooked Vultures
Review: The biggest pleasure of Them Crooked Vultures is hearing three supremely gifted players fall together quickly and easily on songs built on simple riffs that sound like they were made up on a lark five minutes earlier.

Title: Everybody's Dying To Meet You
Review: The sugared melodies of Bitter Pill also go down smoothly, as does the lucently beautiful Intrusive Thoughts, and though a distracting feeling of déjà vu eventually takes root, the well-pruned runtime helps keep Flowers more or less in full bloom.

Title: Lip Lock
Review: Unfortunately, the concept-less and energy-deficient album leaves no room for anyone to make any lasting impression on the listener. [Jul 2013, p.89]

Title: Straight Songs Of Sorrow
Review: A masterful companion piece to Lanegan's unflinching memoir. [Jun 2020, p.88]

Title: Talk About Body
Review: Though it's a bit longwinded, activism and dance music collide on Talk About Body, which is a fiery and totally irresistible combination. [Feb. 2011, p. 71]

Title: Semicircle
Review: It’s a rousing party record, but when the music stops and the lights come on, it all blurs together into a fun but forgettable time.

Title: Weather
Review: Weather sees Hansen and co teasing out some new strands to their winning formula of blissful electronics. At just eight low-stress tracks, this isn't so much a headlong dash for horizons new as it is a gentle evolution, but you could do far worse than kick back and enjoy the weather.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: The oddball trio's new set is edgy and experimental, containing lurid imagery and bold use of dissonance.

Title: Benjamin Booker
Review: On close examination, his songcraft often stalls at the pupal (but promising) stage, but there is enough chutzpah here to steamroller such reservations.

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: This mysterious Swedish dream-pop band's music remains hazy--mucho echo, blurry harmonies, soft acoustic instrumentation buoyed by generous synth strings, and a bright white ambience suggesting both sunny Balearic beaches and blinding Scandinavian snowstorms. Yet its emotions are conversely vivid.

Title: Â¡Uno!
Review: Some of the dullest music released all year.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: All in all, there is freshness and intrigue for those that need it--and for those that don't, a reliable consistency with their 90s incarnation.

Title: Have Some Faith In Magic
Review: Have Some Faith in Magic is very pretty and very meaningless.

Title: Blinking Lights and Other Revelations
Review: It's an absolute must-buy release.

Title: Marlon Williams
Review: Given his richness of experience before he entered the studio, it makes sense that the nine tracks here are as so assured.

Title: Memory of a Cut Off Head
Review: It's a mesmerizing and haunting labyrinth filled with morbid storytelling, hurdling tempos and rhythms that would  perfectly soundtrack a meaningful coastal or cross-country road trip. [No. 149, p.61]

Title: The Trip
Review: Sadier's intonation can be awkward, but her compassionate yet detached voice remains as affecting as ever. [Nov 2010, p.97]

Title: Golden Eagle
Review: It's Macve's self-assurance and rounded expression that impress- that and her voice, a Lustrous and powerful instrument with a yodelling swoop that she wisely never overworks. [Apr 2017, p.32]

Title: Black Swan
Review: It's an expertly crafted pop record, sure, but Black Swan ultimately reduces to its primary points of reference without any broader context or sense of purpose.

Title: Reptilians
Review: A glut of midtempo dithering mostly takes up the second half, and while some of the songs situated there are decent on their own, together they congeal into an asymmetrical mess, exposing Reptilians' front-loaded wiring.

Title: Dear Science
Review: 'Dancing Choose's' title is pointed enough that the song almost doesn't need to prove that dancing on your troubles is powerfully therapeutic as thoroughly as it does, but that's just another example of this album's rare balance between craft and passion.

Title: Blackstar
Review: Even more than The Next Day, these seven tracks suggest the sounds inside his head are in sync with his long-time soul brother Scott Walker, though thankfully he remains on warmer terms with old-fashioned melody and emotion.

Title: Plumb
Review: The result is something that feels like an exotic journey and a familiar stroll all at once, and the comfort-to-exploration ratio is perfect.

Title: Only Run
Review: Their most eccentric, diverse sounding record to date.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: The Sea & Cake has dabbled in electronic grooves and Brazilian lilt throughout its seven sleek albums, but the band has never quite let it rip like it does on Car Alarm.

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: Strangers is a fundamentally passable album.

Title: Worlds
Review: He clearly has difference aspirations to many of his contemporaries, but on this evidence hasn't completely freed himself o f their influence. [Sep 2014, p.112]

Title: Release The Stars
Review: Release The Stars, if not a step forward, is at worst a side-step en route on to a knockout album.

Title: God Save the Clientele
Review: This is the sound of a band energized and fearless, starting to savor the precision, to move around a bit within their own tight parameters. [#17, p.83]

Title: folklore
Review: This is an album of Swift at her most knowing, pushing away the tabloid fodder that has often surrounded her artistry and magnifying the talent she's been honing her entire life. The melodies are full of warmth and round-edges, moving and twinkling on her whim as she indulges in one of the most most human and timeless past-times we have.

Title: Strands
Review: The tracks don’t so much develop as flow--and don’t so much flow as slide slowly, tidally, from one pole to another. Those poles are, to put it crudely, a smooth Badalamenti-like gloom and a more polyphonic, Vangelis-style choral sound. [Dec 2016, p.69]

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: Chicago's veteran alt-rockers haven't sounded this much fun in ages, their seventh album balancing their easy-going and experimental sides.

Title: Mr Beast
Review: The result is that we have a transitory album, but also a typically beautiful and subtle one.

Title: Rad Times Xpress IV
Review: Herrema and her group are obviously having a blast, and the fact that they have managed to blend so many disparate ingredients into a surprisingly potent brew is far more important than the supposition that they might not be taking themselves too seriously.

Title: Talk a Good Game
Review: The album quickly stabilizes with satisfying, if mostly unexciting, material. Other than the lack of European dance-pop, the main difference between this set and Here I Am is the presence of Rowland's most revealing and powerful song, "Dirty Laundry."

Title: Throw Down Your Arms
Review: You can't fault the songs, the playing or the voice, but these versions contribute little to the originals. [Oct 2005, p.117]

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: The result is a surprisingly jubilant follow-up, with the Richmond, Virginia-based singer-songwriter largely disposing of her delicate sound in favour of groove, R&B and '80s pop. [Jul 2018, p.116]

Title: One Day It Will Please Us to Remember Even This
Review: [They] have honed the legendary mania of the early records into a tightened combustion that is part "Personality Crisis" but also packs the matured anxiety and tattered-Sixties classicism of Johansen's 1978 solo debut. [24 Aug 2006, p.90]

Title: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes
Review: Social Distortion still hit as hard as they ever did - barring the obvious newfound musical influences. Anyone not yet convinced by Social Distortion probably won't find new evidence for greatness here, but for longtime fans, the six-year wait is more than worth it.

Title: Kiwanuka
Review: An album that's thoughtful, emotional, expertly crafted and often sublime. [Nov 2019, p.84]

Title: Alasdair Roberts
Review: Alasdair Roberts is not quite the equal of Spoils in terms of songwriting and is hardly as colourful as A Wonder Working Stone, but it is perhaps his most relaxed and effortless album to date.

Title: Be The Void
Review: There's not an obvious departure from their last few releases, but there doesn't need to be as the band has settled comfortably into their sound.

Title: Silver Tears
Review: Silver Tears is steeped in musical knowledge but delivered with a lighthearted touch and plenty of personality.

Title: Crack-Up
Review: At its most straightforward, Crack-Up features a digressive, segmented, prog-rock-style take on the sound of the band’s first two albums, with mixed results.

Title: No Man's Land
Review: There's a lightness of touch from Turner and his band (and producer Catherine Marks) that makes No Man's Land a welcome diversion. [Sep 2019, p.116]

Title: A List of the Burning Mountains
Review: A band that started with Can's hypnotic propulsion has ended up floating in Tangerine Dream's weightless free formity, but it's gorgeous stuff.

Title: Good Time
Review: The collection's 17-song canvas is sufficiently broad to hold the spirited, honky tonk-laced jaunt of the title track and the softly pulsating, organ-laced gospel of 'If Jesus Walked the World Today.'

Title: Away
Review: Away is a looser and more poignant than the band's previous releases ever hinted. [Oct 2016, p.95]

Title: The Shadow of Heaven
Review: All their songs unfurl slowly, gracefully... and some might say a little laboriously. Luckily, singer Jamie Lee has a voice that can just about carry his lofty lyrical themes. [Sep 2013, p.92]

Title: Phoenix
Review: It shows an artist no longer caught in his own artistic web, but someone watching his past selves struggle from a higher vantage point.

Title: Puzzles Like You
Review: There’s a wealth of experimenting going on in the studio with Puzzles Like You, and it creates a timeless A.M. radio sound. [#14]

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die II
Review: What it lacks is an interesting emotional--and thus truly cinematic--dimension.

Title: The Altogether
Review: The duo's most commercial and downright joyous album to date.

Title: A Deeper Understanding
Review: For the most part, it’s hard to deny that Granduciel has succeeded in pimping his wheels for bigger journeys.

Title: Spaces
Review: The variety of Frahm's career is captured with selective care, but Spaces' true achievement is transcending the summary nature of live records.

Title: Nightlife
Review: The problem with Nightlife is that, with the exception of “Hotel Suicide,” nothing really stands out.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: To those of you out there who crave immediate, wistful pop music that will make you smile about the future and make you cry about the past, you won’t find a better album this decade.

Title: To Syria, With Love
Review: Impossibly energetic, joyously extreme and a little bit exhausting. [Jan 2018, p.114]

Title: Bubblegum
Review: It's far from bad, but if you're still waiting for a Clinic record as great as the utterly seminal Internal Wrangler, keep waiting, and probably don't hold your breath.

Title: Time Off
Review: Time Off takes its time getting where it’s going, but deftly reaches its destination.

Title: Champ
Review: Back with less pressure, Champ packs that sweet sucker-punch we craved the first time around.

Title: Psychic
Review: For a record that wears its retro influences so openly, Psychic is surprisingly forward-thinking.

Title: Plague Park
Review: The small moments are the most memorable. [Summer 2007, p.80]

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: Even at its clunkiest, the album sparks.

Title: Who Needs Who
Review: If Dark Dark Dark are one of many acts who seem to define the realm of vaguely quirky and slightly winsome indie rock of the 21st century, the lean of the performances tends toward the quietly contemplative above all else, however much in a band context.

Title: They Were Wrong, So We Drowned
Review: The concept is difficult to follow and the music occasionally unpleasant. But the band’s willingness to stretch in new directions is refreshing.

Title: To Dreamers
Review: Kelley Stoltz is one of the millennium's great unsung auteurs. To Dreamers is frustrating though. [Nov 2010, p.102]

Title: Revelations
Review: The sound of an artist creatively re-energised, this is a revelation in all senses of the word.

Title: Transference
Review: Their seventh album, might be one of their best, with the band and leader Britt Daniel sounding as energised and playful as a puppy

Title: High Violet
Review: All the band's elements coalesce in a remarkably cohesive way to elicit the desired moods.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: This throws most of one's attention on the vocals, always the most engagingly evanescent aspect of their sound.

Title: Beautiful Trauma
Review: Pink reunites with trusted collaborators like Max Martin, Shellback, Greg Kurstin and Billy Mann on Beautiful Trauma. They help make the record sound both fresh and familiar, with occasional curves like the gospelized rave-up “I Am Here.”

Title: Hurley
Review: Hurley, named after the tragicomic Lost character (who also adorns the cover), continues this recent trend with no less than nine co-writers (for 10 songs), and an even longer list of featured musicians, including Michael Cera, who is enlisted to lay down some mandolin and harmonies for no discernible reason beyond his being Michael Cera.

Title: Cautionary Tale
Review: He doesn’t sustain the magic, however, with the result that Cautionary Tale is very much a front-loaded affair, the likes of Lightning and Thunder failing to spark.

Title: Beautiful Future
Review: This is just lazily done and disappointing considering it’s been marketed very well to appear mysterious.

Title: Projections
Review: As history lessons goes, it's a lively one. [Mar 2015, p.81]

Title: King of Jeans
Review: It's overrun by the dissonance of half-step progressions and minor-chord crunch, and it's constantly excruciating.

Title: Better Day
Review: Dolly steps up as America's cheerleader, to help fight the recession blues. [Oct 2011, p.100]

Title: Nights Out
Review: At its best, as on 'Heartbreaker,' the singing has the deadpan charm of Talking Heads or Kraftwerk, adding to the likeability of men who know its better to be a robot than a hippy. [Oct 2008, p.108]

Title: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy
Review: He samples atmospheric noodling from Aphex Twin and bombastic nuggets from Black Sabbath and King Crimson, and he gets help from some of the biggest names in pop, rap, and indie rock. West crafts these influences into a fever dream with a crescendo around every corner - the Beautiful Fantasy of the album's title.

Title: Get Awkward
Review: Even with song subjects nicked from movies, the only false thing here is the title: Get Awkward my ass. It's extremely difficult to imagine these hyperdrive darlings as anything but fully adept.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: Stunningly good.

Title: folklore
Review: A fully rounded collection of songs that sounds like it was years in the interactive making, not the product of a quarter-year’s worth of file-sharing from splendid isolation.

Title: Ugly
Review: Indie rock albums with this uniquely developed a voice don't come around often, especially not when it's this much fun.

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: Beneath the familiarity, Tame’s fourth is operating in a subtly different world. Where ‘Currents’ doffed its cap heavily to R&B within its pop smarts, creating his most commercial work yet, ‘The Slow Rush’’s ingredients feel slightly more disparate.

Title: Friends For Now
Review: There are some cacthy hooks buried deep in the goop. [Feb 2011, p.72]

Title: Volcano
Review: Every track on Volcano flows beautifully, almost overloaded with hooks and harmonies, and charged with rhythmic intent. But the soundscapes are infinitely brighter and weirder and more thrillingly modern.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Review 1: This is what they do- they don’t ape other bands. They ape pop music. And they do it better than any other band right now. [score=80]; Review 2: 33 minutes and 34 seconds of the SAME album! [score=65]

Title: Keep on Your Mean Side
Review: [A] bruising disc of post-modern blues.

Title: Strays
Review: This is a band consolidating their talents rather than simply showcasing them. [Aug 2003, p.108]

Title: Souljacker
Review: Taken as a whole, Souljacker comes off so bleak it overwhelms the album's strengths, like its memorably catchy melodies and sonically brilliant tracks.

Title: The Repulsion Box
Review: A wildly energetic record. [Jul 2005, p.120]

Title: Home
Review: Overall, the hybrids hold together: as their No. 1 single ‘Feel The Love’ has shown, this may well be an experiment with the mainstream that pays off big time.

Title: Home Counties
Review: Home Counties is Saint Etienne at their very best, blending breezy observations and harmonies with a deep seated emotion, centred around the need for a place to call home. In these uncertain times, a blast of hot sunshine and a listen to this record certainly make the world a better place to be.

Title: Purple Mountains
Review: Cries for help have rarely been so clear, self-aware, and funny.

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: While there are occasional flashes of brilliance on this 10th studio album, the missteps far outnumber the bright points.

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: Spotty, strange, all short songs and shitty sound, it's got the collagist careen of Bee Thousand and Propeller and the tumbling tunecraft of Alien Lanes and Under the Bushes Under the Stars.

Title: Begone Dull Care
Review: This time around they sound slightly more connected to genuine dance music, while at the same time stripping away some of the atmospherics to allow more of their subtle pop sensibilities to surface.

Title: Immersion
Review: Front to back, Immersion is pretty sturdy. But it also belies its title by not really plunging any real depths.

Title: LP4
Review: A good deal of the album (particularly the first half) uses the new-fangled instrumentation sporadically, as an afterthought to a slightly darker version of the duo's time-honored techniques. This is where LP4, though flawlessly produced, is messy.

Title: Time Team
Review: Time Team, while displaying shades of true brilliance, is simply an album that doesn't know what it wants to be, and makes the adjustment to compensate for its lack of identity far too late; which is odd, given how well it was doing up until that point.

Title: Are You Serious
Review: Iit’s an album that’s just as much indebted to love as a symptom as it is interested in it as a phenomenon.

Title: Electric Version
Review: Though not perfect, the New Pornographers are getting closer. [#5, p.87]

Title: Echoes
Review: With so many hip people in the studio, it's no wonder Echoes sounds like such a party. [Nov 2003, p.119]

Title: Powder Burns
Review: Musically, the album is as hard as the group has ever gotten.

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: So to sum up, insightful lyrics, great voice, and super production values add up to one of the albums to beat in early 2009. [Winter 2009]

Title: Gone Away Backward
Review: At a time when modern country feels like bloated spandex-and-Aquanetted pop-metal, Fulks defiantly embraces an unflinching traditionalism.

Title: Last of the Country Gentlemen
Review: To have four songs over 10 minutes on your debut is brave; when the record recalls Neil Young's sadder moments and explores the anguish of a break-up, it is foolhardy.

Title: Fist of God
Review: All in all, passably decent party music, but lacking in the divine touch its title might imply.

Title: She Has No Strings Apollo
Review: A raw, passionate record. [#14, p.135]

Title: The Black Album
Review: While it probably won't be remembered as his best album, The Black Album is his most personal to date and features some of his most compelling writing.

Title: Drip or Drown 2
Review: Gunna has a penchant for rapping over beats that include guitar, like on “Richard Millie Plain,” but he doesn’t use them for rock scabrousness. Instead, they’re caressing, soft-edged beds, elegant accompaniment for a rapper who makes his points with textures more than words. That said, there is a tenderness that peeks through here, not just in the gentleness of the sing-rapping, but also in some of the lyrics.

Title: Born Sinner
Review: Born Sinner is an honest account of Cole's growth and development, revealing his humble beginnings, challenging successes and bright future.

Title: Junk of the Heart
Review: They've perfected a kind of free-wheeling, self-conscious pop classicism with immediate surface appeal but little emotional depth, a disappointingly familiar amalgam of Coldplay, Cast, Arctic Monkeys and The verve. [Oct 2011, p.91]

Title: Coming Out of the Fog
Review: Their music, while distinctive, is a rather rudimentary and static thing, with a limited melodic spectrum. [Mar 2013, p.96]

Title: Mandatory Fun
Review: Mandatory Fun is not his best album (even if it, by far, has his most well-conceived meticulous promotional launch), but it is still very fun, virtually every parody being completely on point and capable of holding up to at least a few replays.

Title: Jason Isbell & The 400 Unit
Review: It’s just that, based on Isbell’s track record, it’s hard not to have an empty, unsatisfied feeling when listening to the rote Americana-lite he’s now turning out.

Title: Jessica Rabbit
Review: It's both far-out and potentially pack-leading. [Jan 2017, p.99]

Title: Peace Trail
Review: While it may not be the most musically involved album of his 50-year career, it’s persuasive evidence that Young still has a lot to offer.

Title: No Mythologies to Follow
Review: No Mythologies To Follow is a solid record, one that features a slightly older and more thoughtful MØ. It should make any fan of pop music look forward to what’s to come next from this gifted artist.

Title: Pines
Review: The main problem is that the wooly songs struggle to match the grandstanding conceit. [Feb 2013, p.101]

Title: To Find Me Gone
Review: Really, though, Cabic needs more “Red Lantern Girls,” a gauzy folk workout that hides and seeks until a brutish electric guitar prods the rhythm and heads for higher ground. It is everything the rest of the album is not: aggressive, terse, and surprising.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: These are glistening sonic fancies picked out in neon and Day-Glo. [May 2011, p.79]

Title: Disconnect From Desire
Review: The Edge has cited this New York loops-and-dance trio as a recent inspiration.

Title: Laulu Laakson Kukista
Review: group functions as a collective led by two born-again Christians, but the sounds they make suggest Christians of an extraordinarily mystical sort.

Title: Tales of a Grass Widow
Review: CocoRosie certainly revel in their unorthodoxy but this doesn’t always make for enjoyable listening; perhaps if their Tales Of A Grasswidow knew how to breathe, their macabre hymns might pack a little more pluck.

Title: amERICa
Review: AmERICa finds Wreckless Eric reborn in the USA, his home since 2011. Curmudgeonly, maybe, but a sly joy pervades. [Dec 2015, p.81]

Title: Don't Tell the Driver
Review: Turner’s unpredictable guitar work here is of a piece with the other elements in these compositions, but the ruffled imperfection of it all is quite beautiful in its difficulty.

Title: Red
Review: Good fun. [July 2009, p.84]

Title: Split the Difference
Review: If only all stupid rock music could be this intelligent.

Title: Petals for Armor
Review: Petals For Armor is a display of the multifaceted truth that is ‘femininity’; Williams’ rage is complex yet simple, primal yet now more discrete.

Title: The Wedding
Review: Oneida have never sounded more ambitious, yet they’ve kept their proggy impulses on a short leash; the flourishes serve the music, not vice versa.

Title: Pythagorean Dream
Review: While Pythagorean Dream serves the practical end of giving Chatham something that he can tour from town to town without having to school a new set of musicians for each performance, it’s not a compromise or even a reduction. It’s just one more chance to let him show what’s inside a sound.

Title: Supermodel
Review: With Supermodel, his goal is not to make you like him, but rather to give you a sense of what it's like to be him. He pulls it off, and he throws in plenty of hooks along the way.

Title: Citizen of Glass
Review: Her most ambitious work to date, both conceptually and instrumentally.

Title: Fields
Review: Gonzalez's classical guitar and weightless tenor float over soul jazz, Afrobeat, Ethiopian funk and krautrock, and the lyrics touch on spirituality and self-realization.

Title: Entertainment
Review: Professionalism is the order of the day, and most of Entertainment, recorded over two years and produced by Killers boardman Jeff Satzman, aims for the same middle ground.

Title: Time
Review: Time just feels far too fabricated, far too forced and well far too late.

Title: Blood Money
Review: Their new boss's hooks are often slicke rand less arresting than the minor-key grit they thrive on. [Jun 2006, p.142]

Title: Sexwitch
Review: Repetition is key to this music, but after several cycles, tracks begin to plod, broken up only by Khan's vocal work. The Sexwitch interpretations lose vital elements from the originals like horns, organs, and bells.

Title: Marry Me
Review: As with most any debut, Marry Me is imperfect and not without clear misfires, but with Clark’s unwavering confidence, the whole record seems clearly aware of this, and these failures still serve a purpose.

Title: Endlessly
Review: From the beginning of her career, Duffy's voice alone was clearly not her most potent weapon. Here, she oddly attempts to build an album out of it, not succeeding with anything close to the power and elegance of Rockferry.

Title: The Future's Void
Review: The Future's Void's often dazzling vignettes aren't quite as striking as Anderson's debut, but they show she's an artist unconfined by any one sound or perspective, and more than capable of engaging minds as well as hearts.

Title: Blinking Lights and Other Revelations
Review: Everett's double-album masterpiece, a definitive catharsis.

Title: Indistinct Conversations
Review: Built mainly from Powell’s knotty acoustic guitar explorations and lyrical musings that feel like fragments from an exceptionally perceptive diary, it’s the most satisfying Land of Talk album yet.

Title: M:FANS
Review: Music for a New Society was characterised by its sparseness and the space between its sounds. M:FANS fills them completely and yet retains the sense of dark weirdness; it is a completely different album that conveys the same disturbing, disturbed atmosphere. At 73 years of age, Cale is still making some of the most ambitious, exciting music out there

Title: Anxiety
Review: Throughout Anxiety, tracks fail to resolve--“Counting,” “Promises,” “Gonna Die”--and initially I thought it was a songwriting flaw, coming on so fantastically strong there was nowhere left to go. But .... On multiple listens none of this plays accidental--songs run aground as a means of setting the next episode in motion.

Title: Red of Tooth and Claw
Review: The changes Murder by Death have brought with Red Of Tooth and Claw are a sufficiently demanding and acceptable result.

Title: The Last Temptation
Review: Reveals little beyond the surface, and generally rehashes past formulas. [#13, p.96]

Title: Unbreakable
Review: Nearly everything here is top 40 or AC radio-ready.

Title: Cookies
Review: A little of 1990s' debut album Cookies goes a long way, but bouncy, witty anthems like 'You Made Me Like It' kick hard, whether they're meant to be ironic or not.

Title: No Devolucion
Review: Again working with Flaming Lips producer Dave Fridmann, they graft 4AD atmospherics ("A Darker Forest"), frosty power-pop hooks ("Magnets Caught in a Metal Heart"), and Mogwai pedal-effects crescendos ("Stay True") onto their post-hardcore template, which now churns even more fiercely with an expanded palette.

Title: Seaside Rock
Review: Wait till you hear 'Norrlands Riviera', the best thing Belle and Sebastian never did. Blissful.

Title: High Hopes
Review: A bygone feel permeates a few of the songs; the joyful saloon rock of Frankie Fell In Love takes listeners back to The River, and Down In The Hole recalls the more reflective Bruce of Born In The USA and Tunnel Of Love.

Title: On Your Own Love Again
Review: Perhaps working quietly away from bustle has helped the 27-year old craft folksy songs that--tape hiss and all--are magically out of time. They sit neatly alongside Sandy Denny, Nick Drake, Nico’s Chelsea Girl and Angel Olsen: ethereally beautiful with a dark undercurrent.

Title: Broken Side of Time
Review: Noel Gallagher-approved Alberta Cross's first offering fulfils the promise of 2007's "The Thief & The Heartbreaker" EP. [Oct 2009, p.105]

Title: Madness
Review: Sometimes the lyrics don’t match the energy of the music here, especially Jack Fowler’s guitar. They tend toward the blandly inspirational, with a handful of notable exceptions.

Title: Shake the Shudder
Review: There’s no reason not to throw on Shake The Shudder and dance it out, but like many fun-yet-hazy late nights, it doesn’t leave much of an impression afterward.

Title: Wig Out at Jagbags
Review: Even if Wig Out at Jagbags is quieter than, say, 2008's churning Real Emotional Trash, it feels looser than most of the Jicks records; the compositions are tight but the attitude is ragged, which winds up being more infectious and fun than albums where the songs drift but the instruments are tight.

Title: The Boy with No Name
Review: The boys deliver the same sort of agreeable Britpop they've made their name on, wisely realizing that ambition's really not for everyone.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: In terms of recording, speeding up, and trimming down he has produced one of his most intimate and exhilarating albums to date. [Summer 2008]

Title: The Letting Go
Review: The songs on The Letting Go that flirt with familiar forms... feel completely devoid of his pretentious tendencies. [Oct 2006, p.94]

Title: Chris
Review: The best songs on Chris are the outliers, the ones that are either fully intellectually-engaging or completely poppy. The songs in the middle, that plainly try to balance between the two, only underwhelm because of how common they feel.

Title: The Beekeeper
Review: Mainly there's either promising melodies (the "Crucify"-aping "Parasol") ruined by cringe-y lyrics, or decent lyrical ideas executed like a Yoplait commercial. ("This is sooo good." "Pirates good!" Cue bongos.)

Title: Helium
Review: Helium is known for two things, and one is its lightweight sound. Homeshake makes music the way he wants, and that's admirable, but hopefully, it doesn't get any lighter than this.

Title: Vapours
Review: Each maintains a newfound cool, which must be the result of Islands’ principal dudes realizing that they could live without one another, but that they’re far deadlier songwriters together.

Title: Big Black Coat
Review: It all adds up to their most rounded, consistently engaging record yet.

Title: White Wilderness
Review: With the orchestra, Vanderslice is able to maintain the best-friend-telling-secrets feel of his previous work, while expanding the sound to make it feel more like an orchestral soundscape of all your best friends telling you the same secret. Or maybe the secret is just much, much grander.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: What the songs might lose in pluck and idiosyncrasy, they gain in depth and craft, still letting Bird show off his rakish voice and trademark violin ripping. [#17, p.90]

Title: My Guilty Pleasure
Review: My Guilty Romance is not quite as good a record as its predecessor. It just doesn’t have the density of great tunes that made "Disco Romance" such an addiction.

Title: Songs From Black Mountain
Review: It's downright bad.

Title: Re-Mit
Review: It’s an unsettling, incomparable racket of The Fall at their wonderful, frightening best.

Title: Paperwork
Review: Nothing seems off-limits here.

Title: Oversteps
Review: Oversteps is reasonably accessible without compromising any aspect of what it means to listen to an Autechre album, which is the closest I can come to a formula for success when it comes to this band. It’s probably ten minutes too long in the middle, but the distinctive intro is a winner and the last three tracks are worth the trek.

Title: Oh My God, Charlie Darwin
Review: The album closes with a reprise of 'To Ohio'--possibly superfluous given the perfection of the earlier version, but the only marginal misjudgement on an otherwise largely faultless album.

Title: Incubation
Review: Taken as a whole, Incubation is an album that lures you into dark places in your brain rather than moving your body on the dance floor.

Title: Mission Bell
Review: The tone of the album is consistently mellow but not necessarily boring.

Title: Useless Coordinates
Review: Like their most obvious stylistic ancestors, Sonic Youth, everything feels primal and instinctive, chaotic but controlled.

Title: The Chronicles of Life and Death
Review: Welcome to tonight's Very Special Episode of pop-punk. [Nov 2004, p.130]

Title: Glow
Review: Listening in one session is like wolfing a hurried seven-course meal with post-dinner coffee and is roughly as messy. [Sep 2013, p.65]

Title: UN
Review: This is music made equally for headphones, clubs, and car stereos. This is as creative and re-playable as debut pop albums get

Title: The Silver Lining
Review: Most of it just falls flat, neither recapturing the glory days nor squarely moving the band into a new era. [#21, p.102]

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: With Father of the Bride, Vampire Weekend expand and re-contextualise their own creative universe, offer more questions than answers, take new risks, and open up new possibilities for their artistic future. In the process of doing so, they add at least a handful of brilliant tracks to their discography.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: Four years on and they have made a witty, hooky dance record in thrall to the rock operatics of Led Zeppelin and Queen.

Title: Untilted
Review: Unlike their many imitators, Autechre's music refuses to relax, ensuring them a longer radioactive half-life. [May 2005, p.106]

Title: Culcha Vulcha
Review: It teases and satisfies at once, which is why, unless you’re allergic to Snarky Puppy’s special charm, you’ll want to play this album over and over.

Title: Event II
Review: It's hard to complain much about Event II given Del's razor sharp wit and deft tongue skills.

Title: G is for Deep
Review: G is for Deep remains an album driven by lustrous compositions and like any good artist, Doseone's voice dutifully abides.

Title: Lulu
Review: It takes some commitment, and maybe a little homework, to get the most out of the album.

Title: Witch
Review: What does all this mean to the casual music fan? Invest in a reissue of Jeff Beck's Truth.

Title: Savane
Review: Probably the most gutsy, timeless recording of his career. [5 Aug 2006, p.29]

Title: The Red Thread
Review: But though the music is as good as anything they've ever done, rarely resorting to that downbeat, drunk-in-pub-tells-his-life-story tendency they've too often made their trademark, the lyrics are way below [Aidan] Moffat's usual standard.

Title: I See You
Review: The xx have taken in all the experiences and lessons they have learned since their breakthrough and come up with their most adventurous and quietly uplifting release to date. It’s so good, it may even banish those January blues.

Title: Alpinisms
Review: The effect is warm goth--New Order with more eros.

Title: Last Exit
Review: They do it better [than the Postal Service]--catchier songs, chillier production and more sophisticated beats. [Nov 2004, p.118]

Title: Mermaid Avenue Vol. II
Review: As on the first, the Bragg-written and sung music is the most convincing, since he captures the cadences and spirit of Guthrie's music. They sound like classic, weathered folk songs whereas Wilco's numbers are modern inventions, splicing music that is clearly theirs with Guthrie's words.

Title: The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place
Review: The quartet fills out the album by executing almost eactly the same formula [as the first track] four more times... and the dramatic shock wears off quickly. [Jan 2004, p.103]

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix
Review: Thomas Mars sings with a casual amiability so hard to resist that it helps carry Phoenix through some of the less immediate material on the album's back half.

Title: The Place We Ran From
Review: The whole enterprise should strike those who find Snow Patrol just a bit too mainstream nowadays as a step in the right direction--it's unfussy and smaller in scale, but nearly always compelling.

Title: Electric Balloon
Review: At best, it's eccentricity gone wild--there's no shortage of weird noises creeping in throughout--and at worst, just confusing.

Title: Technicolor Health
Review: "This will be a better year," sing the Shakes on 'Strictly Game.' If based purely on the imagination shown in this innovative album, it will be.

Title: Seeker
Review: Seeker borders on country outlaw ("Feel It All"), makes a good impression, and features A+ drumming, especially on the mellow hooks and slight shout of "Fire."

Title: GEMINI
Review: While some fans might prefer Macklemore with Lewis, Gemini is a reminder that before the multi-platinum singles, hit albums, and thrift shop threads, he could handle himself just fine.

Title: Peeping Tom
Review: Peeping Tom's almost exclusively synth-oriented songs (save the occasional bass and guitar) are ostensibly intended to highlight Patton's voice. This only accentuates his overwrought yet indifferent performances, however.

Title: Pink Friday
Review: Pink Friday lives or dies on Minaj's ability to fully embody all of the various personas she toys with, the singer, the rapper, the lover, the fighter, the tomboy, the girly girl, the big sister, the bitch. But she isn't always engaging, and she doesn't always sound at home with this material.

Title: Bigger Than Life
Review: Black Marble has seen a massive development with Bigger Than Life. Whether the record has proven itself to acutally be "bigger than life" is up for debate. But for Stewart's third LP, it's a solid effort and pleasant change of pace.

Title: Sensuous
Review: You really won't find a more interesting, intelligent or wonderful dream of an album as 'Sensuous' all year.

Title: Return the Gift
Review: It shows a band building a new outpost atop the summit of their achievements. [Nov 2005, p.124]

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Not since Talking Heads bowed out with their masterful 1988 swan song Naked has NYC been so dutifully represented by such a melodically robust collection as the 11 that comprise this eponymous redux of Vampire Weekend’s acclaimed “Blue CD-R” demo.

Title: How to Destroy Angels
Review: It's not Reznor's best or boldest work, but it's a promising first step down a new path.

Title: Waiting for the Sirens' Call
Review: Their best since Technique.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: Those fiercely loyal fans will be very pleased with In Your Dreams, a pit stop in her canon of rock folklore.

Title: Insides
Review: There might be doses of dancefloor energy through the Balearic string twangs of 'All I Want' and the pulsating, springy pads of Insides, but it’s definitely the dreamy, mind-expanding cuts that take precedent.

Title: The Magic Position
Review: Even at his laziest, Wolf sounds vastly more intelligent, committed and interesting than his supposed rivals, and "The Magic Position" is full of heart, warmth and beauty.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: A gloriously nuanced embellishment of the band's timeless virtue. [Apr 2015, p.91]

Title: The Sellout
Review: After listening to Gray's latest, The Sellout and going back to the music that had shifted through our slush pile unnoticed over the last decade or so, we're pretty stoked to find an artist making solid, soulful music beyond the confines of contemporary culture.

Title: Little Dark Age
Review: MGMT’s return to pop is a much more welcome surprise.

Title: Reconstruction Site
Review: There's a thin line between quirky powerpop and being They Might Be Giants. [Feb 2004, p.106]

Title: folklore
Review: Swift explodes the expectations of anyone preparing to call her music "diaristic," writing songs from different perspectives while putting her already-detailed work under a microscope. ... A content smile of an album on which one of the world's biggest pop stars, charts be damned, forges her own path and dares listeners to come along for the ride.

Title: Rather You Than Me
Review: Overall, Rather You Than Me is another example of Ross’ gift at making albums, even though he litters the radio with corny one liners.

Title: Danger In The Club
Review: Unfortunately, however, the band too often drops the tuneful troubadour for the drunken singalong.

Title: Siberia
Review: The return of wonderfully abstruse Nineties guitar-benders Polvo might not be the splashiest indie-rock comeback (that distinction goes to their Chapel Hill, North Carolina, homeys Superchunk). But it's one of the finest.

Title: Brighter Wounds
Review: Though hit and miss, Brighter Wounds is a solid addition to the group’s catalogue.

Title: Wounded Rhymes
Review: While the minimal production and closely miked vocals on her debut emphasized the pop hooks and her fragile voice, Li and producer Bjorn Yttling (Peter, Bjorn & John) give listeners a more all-encompassing, if familiar, sound on Wounded Rhymes, nestling her vocals amidst girl-group harmonies, psych organ and shambolic percussion.

Title: Kinky
Review: Kinky has the potential to transcend both the dance and Latin music genres, simply because of their ability to do just a little bit more than what’s expected.

Title: Dignity
Review: Her jump dancewards is curious commercially, but thoroughly worthwhile artistically.

Title: Language
Review: Language is short on originality, but Zulu Winter's polished musicianship and warm confidence may be enough to win over listeners who enjoy the bands they reference here, and when they do succeed in shaking things up it's enough to leave listeners wanting more.

Title: The Return
Review: This album signifies a moment for UK jazz but more importantly this a moment for Kamaal Williams.

Title: Play
Review: He gives indulges that portion of his muse on the instrumental-centric Play while also managing to deliver a collection that is consistently lively and fun.

Title: Throws
Review: As it stands, Throws is built upon a pile of production choices that are either indie-tastic or ill-advised, depending on one’s opinion.

Title: Along the Way
Review: McGuire's experiments with more conventional structures and arrangements don't always come off--the chuntering drum machines can makes things feel a little brisk and muzaky--but when he hits the spot, track titles like "In Search Of The Miraculous" don't seem too far-fetched. [Mar 2014, p.78]

Title: The Ship
Review: It's delightfully ponderous. [May 2016, p.48]

Title: Glow
Review: Many of Glow's songs are just-there, but a few manage to be engaging.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: This album will please Supergrass-adoring simpletons merely looking for a new album by their favorite band, but to everyone else it should be considered a major disappointment.

Title: Black Origami
Review: Dark Energy was already a significant left turn for footwork and Black Origami is a leap into the future from that, with probably only ‘1%’ (featuring Holly Herndon) from Black Origami sounding like anything on her first album.

Title: In Our Nature
Review: There's no denying the power of Gonzalez, and the draw of his voice and guitar. But it's better heard in small doses, as over the course of an album his chosen sound feels limiting. [Summer 2007, p.73]

Title: Melbourne, Florida
Review: No band will ever be able to replace the Go-Betweens or fill the void their demise left, but if Dick Diver keep making albums as deeply satisfying as Melbourne, Florida, the pain will be a little less severe.

Title: Wild Nights
Review: A certain blank-faced cool remains a part of their appeal, but it’s combined with some terrific songwriting.

Title: Li(f)e
Review: The end result is a new soundtrack for the same old song and dance: Sage still ekes out a chuckle-inducing rhyme here and there, but it’s nothing he hasn’t done before.

Title: Continuum
Review: With no edge to the songwriting and with such spit-polished, tasteful production, Continuum just doesn't convince as a heady, soulful rock album or as Mayer's creative quantum leap forward.

Title: Everybody Got Their Something
Review: Everybody Got Their Something has something for almost everybody... [Jul 2001, p.86]

Title: Overgrown
Review: Overgrown's biggest fault is lack of quality control; it's an uneven listen, with peaks like "Retrograde" segueing into the quotidian piano recital of "DLM," with an undistinguished back half that doesn't linger in the mind afterward.

Title: Currents
Review: Currents is a record you should be excited for, paying attention to and ready to consider the best of the year.

Title: Ecstatics International
Review: An album that as a whole sounds like a collage depicting a comprehensive list of everyone who's anyone from the past 40 years of popular music.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Orton has a flair for penning languid, spacious songs whose forlorn characters seem as adrift as the music's fleeting acoustic guitar chords and absentminded piano tinkles.

Title: Saturation III
Review: This is Brockhampton at their funkiest and most playful, but it’s also Brockhampton at their finest.

Title: The New Romance
Review: They present a united, often more supple front. [Nov 2003, p.131]

Title: Passion
Review: Passion may be an ambitious record from beginning to end, but listening to it is a breeze.

Title: Get Lonely
Review: Every line is razor sharp and yet brilliantly descriptive.

Title: Breakfast
Review: Overall Breakfast effectively blends alternative and hip-hop elements into an eclectic montage of fresh lyricism and bursting musical backdrops.

Title: The Earn
Review: The album is soulful, accessible, and devoid of the ignorance and shallowness that are trademarks of mainstream hip-hop.

Title: Upper Air
Review: Overall, you get the kind of lush musings that’ll soundtrack all the pivotal moments of your wayward summer romance. Blissful.

Title: Fox Confessor Brings the Flood
Review: Unsurprisingly, everything on Fox Confessor Brings the Flood is sublimated beneath Case’s vocals: music, momentum, the need for tunes.

Title: Conditions
Review: The Temper Trap relocated to london in May of this year in a bid to woo the uk: this is not a bad calling card at all.

Title: Polly Scattergood
Review: Beyond threatening suicide and playing coy with whispered vocals, Scattergood fidgets with the bad girl/innocent child dynamic, the juxtaposition of which is just tired enough to bear obvious, but still creepy, dividends.

Title: Negro Swan
Review: At times, Negro Swan crosses over from album and into a radio station from a world just outside ours; Dev Hynes has created a fabulous collection of cascading sounds.

Title: White Women
Review: Featuring the ever-glorious Solange on vocals, it’s a moment of gracefulness that showcases Chromeo’s evident knowledge of when and how to take things down a notch. As a result, it largely accounts for the mostly-pleasant ride that the duo take us on with White Women.

Title: Downtown Church
Review: Enchanting arrangements, glistening instrumentation, and Griffin's hypnotic vocals carry the day. [Mar 2010, p.86]

Title: Tape Deck Heart
Review: The production reveals his reckless yearning for more and contradictory desire for the safety of domesticity through its very slickness and reinforces the theme of Turner’s lyrics in this way. It’s a need trick, and Turner, his band, and Costey pull it off very well.

Title: Tape Two
Review: Everything suggests that, on the strength of this set, The Land of the Brave won’t need a referendum to prove its independence.

Title: Don't You
Review: ‘Small And Silver’ is a welcome break around the halfway mark, when their stock in trade is replaced with unsettling bass and an off-beat production. However, it’s only a hint of a promise to explore new territories and doesn’t go far enough to vary the album.

Title: Bad Vibes
Review: Gently strumming crispy chords or plucking glassy notes from his guitar, Shlohmo (like England's Mount Kimbie) finds fleeting moments of intimacy amid the bustle of urban life.

Title: Human Performance
Review: It’s easy to simply pore over Savage’s frantic wordplay--which peaks when evaluating kebab-wrapping techniques on ‘Berlin Got Blurry’--but the music is equally brilliant.

Title: Nellyville
Review: Nellyville will be the year's only record with a bigger-than-life number with Justin Timberlake, a capable ballad with Destiny's Child's Kelly Rowland, an acute dis of preachy rap veteran KRS-One, and an ode to the hip-hop footwear of choice. [#8, p.120]

Title: Run Fast
Review: Run Fast has many moments of darkness, but ultimately it’s a celebration: of growing up, of surviving, of wading through shit and coming out the other side.

Title: 12 Songs
Review: It’s not that Diamond has recorded a masterpiece, since quite a good portion of this is decidedly B material. It’s that the good stuff represents Neil at his best, exploiting his considerable knack for melody and structure to the fullest.

Title: La Di Da Di
Review: Unlike Mirrored or 2011’s underrated Gloss Drop, La Di Da Di is where Battles demonstrate their competence rather than their virtuosity; there’s never that moment of dominos falling to their death or the mutated instruments and real-time looping opening portals to parallel dimensions.

Title: Holy Vacants
Review: Somewhere between the clear narrative of Boy's Night Out's Trainwreck and the Dear Hunter's ongoing musical saga, it's one of the most compelling realized moments Trophy Scars' madness has produced. [May 2014, p.94]

Title: What a Time to Be Alive
Review: Not least of the record's triumphs is its vindication of a band at its peak even after all these years. [Mar 2018, p.94]

Title: Luminiferous
Review: This track [“The Lethal Chamber”], as well as Luminiferous as a whole, aggressively illustrates that High On Fire still deserves its place at the top of underground metal’s food chain.

Title: The Ride
Review: Amid all its big, primal energy there are enough ideas to suggest the fans' early faith is justified. [Jul 2016, p.94]

Title: The Ridge
Review: Though compositionally The Ridge feels less exploratory that Neufield’s previous work, it is still a moving document of her engaging, virtuosic playing.

Title: Contra
Review: Contra may not propose much of a rebuttal to those who thumbed their nose up at the band's past work, but it's not difficult to see how it could strengthen their core audience while netting them some new fans at the same time.

Title: Dancer Equired!
Review: Dancer Equired! should be required listening for any band looking to grow its brand in new ways without losing its core audience--and also for those who like their pop dirty, sweet, and fairly audible.

Title: Love, Hate, and Then There's You
Review: Love, Hate And Then There’s You isn’t entirely devoid of entertainment value--Stollsteimer’s misguided attempts to replicate the successful sound of the Kaiser Chiefs, Franz Ferdinand, the Strokes and other alt-rock radio staples at the time these songs were conceived turns out to be quite funny, however unintentional the humour.

Title: Weem
Review: Blessed with wisdom and a rare sense of poetry, Weem finds De Rosa revelling in glorious dis-connection from their roots.

Title: Ty Segall
Review: As much as Ty Segall is an album of potential singles material, it’s one of the most cohesive sets of music that Segall has released to date.

Title: Mauve
Review: In 2012, the album is still an impressive achievement and cements the trio's place as the absolute best band of shoegaze revivalists operating.

Title: Colt
Review: Recorded on an eight-track in her flat, Colt steadily emerges as a feature-length celebration of what solitude can yield when approached with creative ablution in mind and the right amount of inspiration at one’s disposal. Woods sounds at home in her seclusion and strikes a chimeric midpoint between electronic and acoustic worlds.

Title: Just Like The Fambly Cat
Review: What could have been a boring, belligerent, and bellicose introspective slide into the music industry dustbin has in fact turned out to be one of Grandaddy’s most listenable and likeable releases.

Title: End of Love
Review: [Barzelay's] sharp eye and endearingly nerdy voice enlivens his band's meticulous acoustic pitter-patter.

Title: If I Kill This Thing We're All Going To Eat For A Week
Review: When Mendel cranks things up, he's on shakier ground. [May 2015, p.107]

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: Ultimately, it's unfair and even glib to say this album doesn't hold water because it has no "Home" or "40 Day Dream," but all the same, one laments the loss of the magical, poppy Midas touch Edward Sharpe & The Magnetic Zeros once wielded with such ease.

Title: Food & Liquor 2: The Great American Rap Album Pt. 1
Review: What it proves to be is an exhilarating, uneven, thought-provoking, over-egged, over-long, lucid, barnstorming, soul-infused hip-hop album of a type that, as I may have mentioned once or twice or five times, you just don't get any more. Except, of course, you do, and here it is.

Title: Cupid Deluxe
Review: It’s an atmosphere soaked in deceptively mellow and melancholy neo-soul, another take on the worlds created by Sade’s whispered regrets and the Weeknd’s decadent obsessions.

Title: Tha Blue Carpet Treatment
Review: A strong statement from a veteran still pushing his artistic boundaries. [Dec 2006, p.170]

Title: I Speak Because I Can
Review: She found it in herself to make yet another gorgeous, melancholy, old-souled record.

Title: Ugly
Review: Ugly is ultimately an album that finally finds the Screaming Females completely confident in their own identity, no longer trying to straddle the line between their headier rock aspirations and the DIY punk scene that gave birth to them.

Title: When The World Comes Down
Review: The Rejects are best at small ideas with a long shelf life. "World" forgets that at points.

Title: Welcome to Goon Island
Review: Their power lies in drummer Pinstripe's jerky rhythms, which propel the band's adventures without lingering anywhere very long, which is sometimes a good thing.

Title: Gone
Review: If you like the idea of blog occupants such as Washed Out and Neon Indian but want to take the hazy filter off their Instagram souls, then 'Gone' could be for you.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: If Plant does nothing more on this album than draw attention to that Duluth, Minn., trio's music, he deserves praise.

Title: Bloodlines
Review: Although Bloodlines is a solid effort, it never seems to really take flight; alternately quiet and bold, it can’t seem to decide whether it wants to be a testament to Mathè’s artistic transformation or a kind of tentative experiment, to be abandoned if it doesn’t pan out.

Title: Do Whatever You Want All the Time
Review: Paradoxical as it may seem, the more structured version of the band that Do Whatever You Want All the Time presents just may be more exciting, and offer more potential, than what Ponytail were doing before.

Title: You Are All I See
Review: 2011 is a year for strong albums in general, and You Are All I See deserves to be ranked among the best.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: A peculiar but pitch perfect partnership.

Title: Harvest Festival
Review: When you get him on his own he's up for a big night out. Just don't expect him home til dawn.

Title: Us
Review: What gives Brother Ali's slice-of-life ruminations their impressive heft is the rapper's eye for everyday detail and the handmade appeal of his vintage-funk arrangements.

Title: Moonshine Freeze
Review: This is their finest work to date.

Title: Tales of Us
Review: The delicate guitar and piano figures and the sombre languor of strings behind Alison Goldfrapp’s breathy vocals create something akin to a cross between the dreamlike mythopoeism of old folk tales and the lush cinematic arrangements of Michel Legrand.

Title: Client
Review: Sorry ladies, a foreign accent, cheap synth sounds and zero hooks ain't cutting it anymore. [#5, p.111]

Title: Little Fictions
Review: For now, Elbow have created another record that comfortably matches up to anything they’ve released to date.

Title: Iv
Review: IV is simply packed to its dank rafters with monstrous riffs, muggy low-mixed vocals and more discordant amp noise than you could shake a deaf stick at.

Title: Brill Bruisers
Review: What subsequent listens reveal is the startling evolution of Newman’s songwriting.

Title: Stranger Than Fiction
Review: Looking back at Kanye West’s 808s & Heartbreak, there is much strength to be gained in weakness--Gates current momentum is fueled with that power.

Title: The Stepkids
