Review: It's immaculately produced and performed, full of gorgeous vocal harmonies, extravagantly wafting flutes and often arresting melodies. But for some listeners it might be wither lacking in rawness or uncomfortably in thrall to the past. [Oct 2011, p.100]

Title: Iron Flag
Review: More interesting than essential, Iron Flag may not win over those who gave up on Wu-Tang Clan around the time of Wu-Tang Forever, but the group's dedication to its own idiosyncratic path remains impressive.

Title: Luxury Problems
Review: It manages to evoke both void and overload simultaneously, and feels by turns oppressively dense and light as a feather. [Dec 2012, p.74]

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: The production values mean that, even though Powers' reverent anthems aren't a huge departure from what he's done in the past, the results have added gravitas.

Title: Mona
Review: Heartfelt, impassioned and sincere, Mona are reaching for the skies--and taking you with them!

Title: In Rolling Waves
Review: When it all comes together, In Rolling Waves is a thrilling, melodramatic ride through the regions where pop, electro and alternative rock crossover, and finally meet.

Title: SuperHeavy
Review: The quintet's debut is pretty good fun, fusing Stones-y raunch with brash Caribbean rhythms.

Title: Aerotropolis
Review: Sleeker but no less cartoony than her debut, it mixes freestyle house into her signature sound and comes off richer than anything she’s done before.

Title: Derdang Derdang
Review: As much fun as a desperado can have without going on a tri-state crime spree. [Oct 2006, p.214]

Title: Makes a King
Review: Makes a King, in comparison [to the Very Best’s early albums], feels a bit one-note, though they can still hit that one note hard.

Title: Ring
Review: Upon first listen, Ring is entirely  enjoyabe, but there's something about the second run through the loop that is transcendent. [Fall 2010, p.60]

Title: Gorilla Manor
Review: Gorilla Manor is listenable and inoffensive, but it doesn't express a single aforementioned component of its genre with any gusto.

Title: The Hardest Way to Make an Easy Living
Review: Most listeners won't care to follow this particular rabbit down the hole because of the bracing cynicism, paranoia, misanthropy, and betrayal they'll hear at every turn on this record.

Title: 137 Avenue Kaniama
Review: Bursting with invention, energy and occasionally cheesy synths.[May 2018, p.95]

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: It is his most enjoyable and well-rounded one in, like, an eternity.

Title: In Dream
Review: For now, Editors sound like a band in need of precisely what their name advertises.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: To say one of these albums is better than the other is basically beside the point-- anyone who buys one will certainly want the other, and both are fairly comparable as far as quality is concerned, anyway.

Title: Mountain Moves
Review: Vibrant and outward-looking, the record has a buoyant, dancified energy that flows. [Oct 2017, p.103]

Title: The Soul Sessions
Review: Thing is, Joss Stone does have an extraordinary voice, and the only misguided ploy on The Soul Sessions is a Roots-produced slo-mo cover of a White Stripes tune.

Title: Abbar el Hamada
Review: Third album Abbar El Hamada continues that [broad musical] path, though it eschews the largely acoustic nature of Soutak for a more electrified outing.

Title: amo
Review: Amo won’t satisfy all of BMTH’s fans, but it’s certainly accomplished, catchy and eclectic enough to bring in some new ones.

Title: Dose Your Dreams
Review: Lyrically and conceptually they are scattered, but instrumentally and vocally, there is an open-mindedness that rends you. Ironically, in an album that talks about dying, there is a never say die attitude that latches on and never lets go.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: Boards of Canada seems to be able to release albums pre-aged, so that all the things that might have bugged you a couple years ago now sounds like another part of why it's a classic.

Title: WHO
Review: A vigorous, if patchy comeback. [Jan 2020, p.114]

Title: The Capsule
Review: Capsule Sickness boasts a warmer tone, if one that lacks direction, unlike the fuller sound of Crux with its sharply distorted, decidedly un-humanlike “vocals”. Other tracks stalk the no-man’s land between noise music and techno, constantly threatening to stomp on any unexploded landmines just to see how impressive a sound that might make.

Title: Antifogmatic
Review: It is, truly, postmodern bluegrass-keenly self-conscious of its own brilliance.

Title: And Nothing Hurt
Review: This being a Spiritualized record, you should know exactly what to expect. ... The only minor gripe that you could have with the project is that it’s nowhere near as vital as Pierce’s recent collaborative record with Föllakzoid.

Title: Young & Old
Review: Likeable, featherweight pop. [Mar 2012, p. 86]

Title: Automaton
Review: Some may carp at the lyrics, but at 47, Kay retains pole position as pop's most revved-up playboy. [May 2017, p.107]

Title: Gold Medal
Review: Their craft has gotten way deeper than hey-ho blitzkrieg bop.

Title: Thrice Woven
Review: While the rest of the album doesn’t quite live up to the expectation set by its opening salvo, the longest journeys start with a single step. And as the first step in the next chapter of Wolves In The Throne Room’s story, Thrice Woven moves decidedly in the right direction.

Title: Neighborhood Watch
Review: The album is plagued by too many predictable bass lines and uninspired samples. [May 2004, p.163]

Title: Rocket
Review: It's unpolished and emotionally brave, in touch and free as the wind. It's really something. Quite a bedroom window, this one.

Title: Always Got Tonight
Review: There's as much rock here as there are dark, dreamy laments.

Title: The R.E.D. Album
Review: There's no doubt about it, there's greatness lurking in Game, and in R.E.D. Album. Let's just hope that from here on out he'll find the consistency he needs to truly claim that greatness.

Title: Cosmogramma
Review: Flying Lotus has made the strongest album to date with his amazing collection of sounds, beats and instruments; as good as you felt after hearing the sheer brilliance of "Los Angeles."

Title: Encore
Review: For the most part, Encore's strained, vaguely sad, regressive wackiness makes a lucid and compelling argument that Eminem should retire Slim Shady and let the real, serious Marshall Mathers stand up and be heard.

Title: The Entrance Band
Review: Their insides have been swapped: the dirty, heavy, colossal, dark-nastiness has been replaced with arena-rock aspirations and fresh-white, paper-thin production.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: It's both epilogue and prologue, yet these songs retain their own specific flavor, as R.E.M. map the borders between small clubs and large venues, between underground and mainstream, between rhythm and melody, between outrage and hope. That in-between quality still sounds invigorating so many years later.

Title: Oh My Sexy Lord
Review: Whether listening to them or foolhardily attempting to describe them, there’s little about Marijuana Deathsquads that’s easy, but that doesn’t make their third LP any less rewarding.

Title: The Magic Place
Review: The one-woman choir may seem eccentric, but by the last of these nine vignettes, Barwick has accomplished what few purveyors of such pristine beauty can. Through its oddities, The Magic Place shines.

Title: Sweet Kind Of Blue
Review: Recorded with Grammy winning producer Matt Ross-Spang and a host of Mississippi sessionerati, Sweet Kind Of Blue is perfectly soulful and understated.

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: Wondrous Bughouse doesn’t expand Youth Lagoon’s sound so much as pour neon-colored Kool-Aid onto it until it’s diluted to a point where it’s almost difficult to hold onto much of anything in these songs.

Title: To Lose My Life
Review: While that darkness gives the album its semblance of originality, it may prove incompatible with the group's mass-market ambitions.

Title: Of The Sun
Review: It distills what has made Trupa Trupa a must-see in past years at music conferences such as South by Southwest in Austin, Texas.

Title: The Same But By Different Means
Review: The Same but by Different Means is surprisingly seamless for a 22-track record. Like a Ouija board session, each track here feels part of a collective effort to access a realm outside our own. Sometimes, it leads to sustained moments of connection, like the radiant tropicalia sunshower of “Curtain of Rain.” At others, it yields sudden, surprising moments of rapture, like the beautiful melancholic chorus of “Hard to Say Bye.”

Title: Mean Love
Review: While Mean Love is his most experimental album to date, it’s also his most precise.

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: It doesn't help that Wilco is such a complacent album, so easily redolent of sounds and textures the band has called up in the past.

Title: Cedars
Review: If Cedars has an artistic failing, it's that the songs tend to blend together after "Almost the Same".

Title: Foundations of Burden
Review: Foundations of Burden is the sound of an already excellent band reaching their potential, and in the process setting a new standard for the genre.

Title: Secret, Profane and Sugarcane
Review: Despite T-Bone Burnett’s warm production, some excellent playing by the best bluegrass players around, and a few keeper cuts, Secret, Profane & Sugarcane falls all too easily into the middle ranks of Elvis Costello’s vast discography.

Title: The End Is Near
Review: Whatever excitement this album lends is, for the most part, borrowed by its pre-existing audience, and it's clear the Kadanes aren't going to challenge us.

Title: Love From London
Review: Love From London could use more of those surprising or insightfully startling juxtapositions that define his best labors. [No. 96, p.58]

Title: Big Balloon
Review: They are shaping their own pop form, and what an incredible listen it is.

Title: The Best Damn Thing
Review: It's a consciously lightweight pop-punk romp that appears to have been inspired by "Since U Been Gone," Kelly Clarkson's massive hit.
The softer focus fits them exceptionally well.

Title: Eats Darkness
Review: As a whole, Eats Darkness feels haphazard in a way that shades into self-indulgence.

Title: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier
Review: The record's emotional centre hits toward the end, so stick around for Your Moon, a cathartic downer backed by processed strings and 808 claps.

Title: Wilderness Heart
Review: Taken individually, the songs are beefy enough to satisfy stoner-rock munchies, but as an album, Heart is hardly cohesive.

Title: Performance
Review: In all, Performance is an immensely controlled assortment of what White Denim does best--which might please some and (eventually) bore others.

Title: Alfredo
Review: It’s an incredibly tight record packed with stellar performances, production and presence throughout. The blood, sweat and tears of hip-hop run through the album, but Gibbs has once again redefined what that means.

Title: The Trigger Complex
Review: A vibrant batch of new songs that still rail against conformity with slashing instrumental and lyrical fury, but also find room for the occasional “la-la-la” sing-along pop hook.

Title: Losing Sleep
Review: The sheer exuberance and joy with which these songs are delivered hint that another record would be a more than welcome artistic statement for a man who's made more than a lifetime's worth. [May 2011, p.83]

Title: Mowing
Review: His songs draw on his folk-rock roots, only to detour down mysterious and memerising byways. [Jan 2017, p.111]

Title: Fool Metal Jack
Review: The results on their 10th studio album are pleasingly baffling.

Title: Songs About Girls
Review: Songs About Girls isn't a hip-hop record, but a pop&B album of mellow head-nodders that veer between chilled-out soul and lite-electro funk.

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: The most surprising thing about Pixies’ first album in 23 years is that it holds so few surprises.

Title: No More Normal
Review: There is so much right about this album that it’s hard to criticise: Swindle’s vision to blend different worlds of underground music, together with his choice of features--as well as intriguing changes in pace--are what makes this album great.

Title: Love and Theft
Review: It may not be a better album than ''Time Out of Mind,'' but it glides from genre to genre with a sprightly glee, as if Dylan were traversing the American musical landscape in search of thrills, revenge, and reparation.

Title: Graveyard of Good Times
Review: Never overstaying its welcome despite its 16-track length, there are little pockets of unadulterated joy peppered throughout, specifically the buzz guitar-laced opener Headspace, and She Loves Anime’s electro-tinged tale of a boy who draws himself the perfect girlfriend.

Title: American Doll Posse
Review: Imagine an amalgam of The White Album, The Kick Inside and Professor Longhair, all conceived as an off-Broadway extravaganza directed by Julie Taymor.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: If this album is a mixed bag for West the producer, then it's a nadir for West the lyricist. [Jan 2009, p.114]

Title: Outbursts
Review: While the experiment with a more edgy, rock-oriented sound worked well for the British duo, singer/songwriters Olly Knights and Gale Paridjanian are obviously most at home with their comfortable brand of melodic folk-inflected pop, and that is the sound that makes up most of the tracks on Outbursts.

Title: The Morning Star
Review: The Morning Star is at once brave and solitary, gentle and bracing, provocative and spiritually resonant. It extends Bachman's reach, allowing him to paint the innermost dimensions of the world he perceives and cleave it open for light to flood in and illuminate it for us.

Title: Last Place
Review: Ultimately, though, for all its emotional tug, Last Place is solid rather than spectacular, with nothing quite matching the peaks of their first two albums.

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: If there's one thing that defines Midnight Boom, it's the new sense of fun that The Kills seem to have discovered.

Title: Heaven Is for Quitters
Review: Heaven Is for Quitters follows no pattern except that of disconnect, so while many of the tracks work as they are, it's far from a cohesive album.

Title: Upside Down Mountain
Review: A sumptuous immersion in Seventies California folk pop, it is the most immediately charming album he has ever made.

Title: Ancient Romans
Review: This double album (complete with lush art booklet) is styled like a toga party, but some tracks ("Fit for Caesar," "Lucretius") are closer to the 'shroom-chewing highlights of Pink Floyd: Live at Pompeii.

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: They're like a five-member Polyphonic Spree wearing Urban Outfitters, jacked up on Jolt cola, and rocking out in their garage with a bunch of instruments bought from a pawn shop. [#7]

Title: White Bread Black Beer
Review: Occasionally there's a little too much going on... Overall, though, Gartside remains intriguing. [Jul 2006, p.116]

Title: Harmony Avenue
Review: The music is punchy, with electronic and analog elements, but, in contrast with Fucked Up, there is absolutely nothing abrasive about the vocals, which are sometimes dominated by beautiful harmonies, as the album's title suggests.

Title: Palookaville
Review: His party jams... feel half-cocked, like Cook can't quite commit to the moment. [8 Oct 2004, p.114]

Title: Spacehopper
Review: Spacehopper proves Tripwires more effective than most at stepping out from under that umbrella without abandoning it. It is likely one of the best rock debuts you will hear in 2013.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: As it is, it's a very fine record from a band who are seemingly growing in stature, confidence, and ability by the day.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: The album's sound is frugal and full of space, but doesn't feel airy so much as eerie. There's a queasy, drugged feeling about the music on Wake Up Ghost that fits both the fragmentary lyrics and at least one of their themes.

Title: Winchester Cathedral
Review: In and of itself, Winchester Cathedral is a fine introduction to Clinic and an entertaining 35 minutes of evocative rock. But it's hard to believe that at this late date, having been together for seven years, the band can't find new modes of musical expression.

Title: Reassemblage
Review: The album is intriguing and accessible, yet just strange enough to stand out among all the other experimental electronic artists mining the early new age era for inspiration.

Title: The Shade of Poison Trees
Review: Sometimes one suspects he’s saving his best tunes for the next full-band Dashboard Confessional album. But then comes 'Fever Dreams,' 150 addictive seconds of falsetto and drum machine. It’s reason enough to be hopeful about whatever’s coming next.

Title: Psychodrama
Review: One of the most thoughtful, moving and necessary albums of 2019 so far. ... Tracks are at once astute and deeply personal in how they capture vignettes of everyday life and spin them into important lessons.

Title: Afterglow
Review: It’s gorgeous, moving and magnificent.

Title: Citizen Zombie
Review: Citizen Zombie is a lot of fun, which is both a blessing and a curse.

Title: NehruvianDOOM
Review: Interesting but inessential.

Title: Wildheart
Review: His third--and best--album moves farther away from beat-oriented R&B toward music that's heavy guitars, sex and hazy Cali vibes.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: For many listeners, Foxygen's influences will sound tired. But as they plunder the past, they're enjoying themselves, and the enthusiasm on this messy collection of songs is infectious.

Title: Blue Gardens
Review: It’s a potentially fulsome harvest E.M.M.A. has planted.

Title: Ignorance is Bliss
Review: An artist at the top of his game, with the newfound artistic freedom that Konnichiwa granted him but the energy of still having something to prove. It also confirms the 2010s grime revival as being more than a passing trend, and on this basis it’s stronger than ever.

Title: El Camino
Review: El Camino might be the weakest Black Keys album since 2006's Magic Potion, but the band certainly earned this celebratory joy ride.

Title: Marigolden
Review: Marigolden is yet another triumph, not only for Partisan but for the frozen tundra of America's Midwest.

Title: Now Here Is Nowhere
Review: It's sometimes hard to separate intentional mood-setting atmosphere from indistinct songwriting, but the album establishes enough momentum that the general cacophony becomes as epic as it's meant to be.

Title: What's Between
Review: A bravura production job, assisted by The Haxan Cloak, gives What's Between arcane depths. [Jul 2014, p.83]

Title: In The Future
Review: What really impresses on the quintet's sophomore stunner is the way Black Mountain effortlessly shift from devastating to devastatingly beautiful. [Feb 2008, p.117]

Title: Secret Machines
Review: The old fervour remains intact. In truth, their third LP holds few surprises. [Feb 2009, p.116]

Title: Silent Hour / Golden Mile
Review: Rossen's sprawling pop coupled with his subtly personal lyrics gives the album a bittersweet flavor that makes for some very impressive moments.

Title: Man-Made
Review: Review #1: If you love 4/4 time pop, this is for you. If you don't, you'll be converted. [score=80]; Review #2: If it has a fault, it would be an overall lack of immediacy... But this is still a damn fine pop album. [score=80]

Title: Born Sinner
Review: If Born Sinner proves anything, it’s that he’s not ready to take the fall, but he as a long way to go if he wants to rope off an area all his own in hip hop’s evolution.

Title: Blue Songs
Review: Blue Songs is a sophisticated and club-ready sophomore effort, even if--at times--it nearly crumbles under the weight of its own decadence and self-indulgences.

Title: Work It Out
Review: In places she sounds surprisingly like Andrea Corr, but she;s a winningly melodic songwriter. [Aug 2015, p.78]

Title: The Pursuit
Review: Too many songs on The Pursuit paint their singer as an un-self-conscious lout, too sure of his hand (“We Run Things”) or his taste (“Mixtape”) or his centrality in the world (“Wheels”).

Title: Age Hasn't Spoiled You
Review: Like fine wine, Bill Hader or Gillian Anderson, Greys are only getting better with age.

Title: Kill the Wolf
Review: What we have here is prog-folk of the highest order.

Title: Ring
Review: Ring is electic, beat-heavy, and easy to like. A sneakily confident debut that should please listeners at almost every turn.

Title: Oracular Spectacular
Review: Opener 'Time to Pretend' exemplifies this best, as the synths provide quirky cartoonish bounces to tales of fancy car whipping and coke snorting pipe-dreams. However, the record grows sluggish at certain points, particularly when they try to get super sentimental on that ass.

Title: Power
Review: The result is a fearless and powerful debut.

Title: Home
Review: As excitingly promising a solo debut as any.

Title: Polaris
Review: They've managed to serve up complexity in a deceptively digestible manner. [10 Oct 2015, p.52]

Title: Simulcast
Review: With ‘Weather’ it’s Saint Sinner’s vocals that give the project direction; when these are stripped away on ‘Simulcast’, it’s up to the listener to find a way though, to draw the conclusions. And it’s these personal conclusions that make ‘Simulcast’ arguably a far more engaging and interesting experience than ‘Weather’.

Title: VI
Review: VI is undoubtedly You Me At Six's poppiest effort yet complete with funky, melodic beats and synths along with relatable themes of relationships, feelings and late night adventures that perfectly straddles the line between pop and rock.

Title: Torches
Review: Regardless, even the harshest of words are unlikely to stop this album from being a success. And that, well, is kind of depressing.

Title: The Curse of Love
Review: The Curse Of Love is a neat record, filled with the mystic folk and lithe psychedelia that made them so refreshing back in the day.

Title: Pura Vida Conspiracy
Review: Pura Vida is more subdued (relatively speaking) than the group’s usual celebratory style, but the album’s best songs are still the most anthemic, the ones that sound the best alongside a hoisted, spilled beer.

Title: Synthetica
Review: For a large chunk of the album, the band seems to assume that Haines's ice-queen snarl somehow lends Synthetica's bland, hookless milieu a cool irreverence, but more often than not, what's supposed to be punk-ish detachment often plays like the group is bored by their own material.

Title: Sound & Color
Review: Sound & Color is not an electronic record. But it is strange and mystical and unexpected.

Title: Here I Am
Review: This album shows Rowland to be worthy of consideration in her own right.

Title: Arcology
Review: Where McRyhew's first full-length approached footwork with playful individualism, this record favours freeform acid and techno structures.

Title: The Official Body
Review: Overall, another great album from one of the UK’s best underground talents who may not remain so underground for long.

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: It’s a tap on the shoulder, a reminder, or a nostalgic look back that this collective works best at providing kitschy, alternative dance anthems for millennials hellbent on shaking it to something more organic.

Title: Mice Parade
Review: Mice Parade have never before been quite this accessible.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: You have to marvel that a 53-year-old man can still make music so brimming with adventure.

Title: Magnifique
Review: There is some charm in the Brooklyn duo’s method but, after five albums, it’s running thin.

Title: Violet Street
Review: But for all of the globe-trotting that went into Violet Street, Local Natives remain quintessentially SoCal: genial, approachable, and optimistic, even if their surroundings are liable to be on fire or crumbling into the sea.

Title: Lantern
Review: The 14-track effort staggers in its breadth, especially since the album never loses its central through line: his knack for spinning pretty, heavy, and pretty heavy tracks.

Title: Thanks for the Dance
Review: “Thanks for the Dance” isn’t really so much a last will and testament, then, as a hell of a heaven-bound balance sheet.

Title: What One Becomes
Review: The musicians' playing retains the band's typically muscular vigour, but has taken on extra nuance.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: Within the 11 tracks that make up her third full-length, Olsen’s strong and matchless voice pierces through fuzzed out guitars and massive organ riffs, allowing us to burrow into her mind.

Title: Bestial Burden
Review: Bestial Burden is not much fun to listen to, even for those of us who take great pleasure in noisy, abstract, unhappy music. So if you really need to hit bottom and feel about as misanthropic and nauseous as possible in order to bounce back, Bestial Burden might be just the thing.

Title: Alight of Night
Review: These songs are dull because they are about dullness, as sad movies are sad because they are about sadness.

Title: Tragedy & Geometry
Review: Hauschildt's new opus is certainly just as captivating and varied as some of his band's [Emeralds] best work.

Title: Amazones Power
Review: Amazones Power is a fresh, modern new chapter for Les Amazones d'Afrique, and one we can only hope will set a precedent for music and social justice in the new decade.

Title: Amber
Review: Clearlake have headed into deeper, darker waters. [Feb 2006, p.101]

Title: Ex Eye
Review: Ex Eye fuse together in a whirring blare of intricately constructed math metal, where each player can be distinctly heard weaving their individual musical craft within the group’s membrane. [Jul 2017, p.60]

Title: 4 Your Eyez Only
Review: 4 Your Eyez Only is a solid, short listen that relies on J. Cole’s strength and comfort zone, perhaps a little too much at times, but the underlying concepts continue to add a layer of depth to his artistry.

Title: Tanglewood Numbers
Review: One of his strongest and most focused albums to date.

Title: Langhorne Slim
Review: 'The Tipping Point' is typical of the album as a whole, a rush of hoe-down guitars and echo-laden drums topped off with a half-yelp of a vocal that recalls a slightly more unhinged Jack White. [July 2008, p109]

Title: Biophilia
Review: Even when she blinds her audience wit science, though, Bjork's vision remains remarkable. [Oct 2011, p.97]

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: Friendly Fire's real problem is that Lennon keeps coming up with airy melodies that recall his father's work, only they don't really sound like John anymore, they sound like Elliott Smith.

Title: From a Basement on the Hill
Review: This is an album about the seductions of oblivion, and a few of the more densely arranged songs mimic the characters in the lyrics, stumbling around without quite connecting.

Title: Wildest Dreams
Review: Most of what’s here isn’t memorable, but there is a steady flow of moments so ersatz that it is oddly listenable.

Title: Melophobia
Review: It can be a little sombre, a little raucous, and sometimes rough around the edges, but is consistent throughout. [Nov-Dec 2013, p.94]

Title: Kindly Bent to Free Us
Review: While Cynic's songwriting here is far from simple, their ability to create cohesion between the many elements at work in their music is a boon to the listener, providing the opportunity to enjoy the depth and complexity of the music without needing to spend an excessive amount of time trying to make heads or tails of it.

Title: The Courage of Others
Review: Furthermore, the way that 'Rulers Of Ruling Things', 'The Horn' and 'The Courage Of Others' arch effortlessly into trippier psych-rock inflected territory suggest a more expansive, weirder Midlake to come.

Title: Nextdoorland
Review: The psychedelic underpinnings of old are cleaned up a bit and the anger and bile that lay beneath the surface of the earlier material has been calmed, but there is still much to be enjoyed.

Title: Content
Review: The band that brought the funk to punk isn't in much of a dancing mood here.

Title: King Night
Review: Rave horns echo like WW2 sirens being played on a fucked-up ghetto blaster while the cast of House Of 1000 Corpses do their best Gucci Mane impressions--an interesting, if perhaps slightly contrived, oddity.

Title: Play It Strange
Review: Taken as pieces, these songs are prime 2000s indie rock; added together they make Play It Strange a satisfying step forward for the band.

Title: The Defenestration of St Martin
Review: Things perk up on the lovely Where There Are Pixels and the choired-up I Must be Jesus but it's one for the fierce-hearted and, as such, highly recommended. [Dec 2012, p.111]

Title: Write About Love
Review: Write About Love is a cracking pop album and a fine addition to a great band's already impressive catalogue.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Days of Abandon
Review: For now, it just comes off like an unnecessary retreat.

Title: All Time Present
Review: Despite the occasional nod to rock formalism, All Time Present achieves a scope only hinted at on Forsyth’s previous full-lengths.

Title: Plumb
Review: Plumb is a rich, complex album, with the songs spilling over into each other.

Title: Incorruptible Heart
Review: There's a soaring, unfettered confidence that Stark puts to amazingly good use on this record. [Oct/Nov 2012, p.129]

Title: Moveys
Review: The lyrics, though straightforward at times, come from a place of genuineness and vulnerability.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: Is White's nonchalant spectrum dabbling [found throughout the album] as interesting as the myriad variables of his own quirky sound? Eh, not quite. [No.88 p.60]

Title: Know Your Enemy
Review: Know Your Enemy is a fine -- if slightly long and somewhat fractured -- primer to the moods of one of Britain's most (self) important bands

Title: Goodbye, Killer
Review: Pernice's sixth studio album under the Brothers moniker is a palate cleanser that's more satisfying than most bands' main courses.
It is simply miserable, heavy, repetitive and cathartic. [18 Nov 2006]

Title: The Ugly Organ
Review: The best punk record you'll hear all year, articulate and amped all the same. [#58, p.86]

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: Crack the Skye follows Mastodon’s uncanny tradition of crafting a brand of heavy metal that is unabashed, mazelike, and above all, fresh.

Title: 18 Months
Review: The poorest served is hapless Ellie Goulding, struggling against the hurtling momentum of "I Need Your Love"; more successful is Florence Welch on "Sweet Nothing".

Title: One Word Extinguisher
Review: One Word Extinguisher doesn't shock the way Vocal Studies... did but, if his debut drew the vivid hip-hop/electronic blueprint, Herren convincingly takes his plans and constructs something big with the follow-up.

Title: Anastasis
Review: Anastasis demands intense, patient listening, though it rarely rewards it.

Title: London Undersound
Review: If it sounds suspiciously of coffee table, it is. But the coffee is freshly grounded, and thr table an elegant modernist sculpture. [Nov 2008, p.119]

Title: Peace Trail
Review: Unpolished and unhurried, Peace Trail is another charming stop on Young's long and winding road. [Feb 2017, p.108]

Title: 5 Years Behind
Review: Punk trio THICK emerge into the daylight clutching a dazzling debut album full of frenetic energy, laced with anger, humor, killer guitar riffs, and soaring punk melodies.

Title: Augustana
Review: Whether they're able to find their niche and create a sound that best exemplifies those talents in the future remains to be seen.  In the meantime, we'll have to cope with another unfulfilling outing from Augustana.

Title: Boxes
Review: Long-running bands that maintain success--a rarity in itself--do so by varying their sound and by exploring new ideas, by maturing with their audience. Boxes is a sloppy attempt to follow that charted path.

Title: Bigger Than Life
Review: With swaying synths, popping drums, synth melodies and wistful lyrics, it's Depeche Mode for the juicing era. [Dec 2019, p.96]

Title: I Am Very Far
Review: Fans who approach I Am Very Far carrying expectations informed by the group's earlier releases will no doubt find this to be Okkervil River's most challenging work to date, but it's also the group's most grandiose, thrilling, and brilliant.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: Eye Contact works because its bolshie drum patterns and metallic synth stabs, influenced by Jamaican dancehall and UK bass music, anchor it firmly in the near future, while Lizzie Bougastsos' strong and inventive melodies help make light work of what could come across like a pretentious muddle. [Jun 2011, p.85]

Title: Boxer
Review: Sometimes, the hype is right. [Jul 2007, p.170]

Title: Art Angels
Review: Art Angels wipes the fog from her lens and lays out her vision, clear and uncompromising.

Title: Multiply
Review: A silky, bright, singing-in-the-shower masterstroke of joy and elation.

Title: American Interior
Review: Because the songs are often about the tour or the people, the lyrics are often unrelatable, with one obvious exception: “100 Unread Messages.”

Title: Purple Noon
Review: The chillwave movement has always channeled nostalgia—warm echoes of a distant past, faded and warped into a new aesthetic. Purple Noon, though, mostly just elicits nostalgia for the glory days of chillwave itself.

Title: Humanz
Review: Amid a series of electronic soundscapes that incorporate club, dance hall, R&B and hip-hop rhythms and textures, Albarn packs the album with songs that speak to the instability of uncertain times.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: Morning beautifully captures what makes this album so rich: that delicate divide between grandiose and intimate.

Title: Amarantine
Review: This album is calm and relaxing almost to a fault. [26 Nov 2005]

Title: King
Review: Though long at 18 tracks, King's still got plenty of heavyweight hits. [31 Mar 2006, p.64]

Title: Unseen
Review: These songs slowly reveal loss, surprise and violence, but they take their time getting there, whether across a line or through an entire track.

Title: Shape The Future
Review: It's an album that doesn't chase any current trends nor try to emulate what they've have done before. N.O.W has successfully found a way to grow and invent but also stay true to their core ideals. It looks like they'll be around for a good while yet.

Title: 7 Days of Funk
Review: Even if this is Snoop's first album with a single producer since the monolithic, Dr. Dre-helmed Doggystyle, don't call it a comeback, call it lark, and a funky, welcome one at that.

Title: Semicircle
Review: The nostalgia lacks anything close to the authenticity that Thunder, Lightning, Strike achieved, and the sound of the 2018 version of The Go! Team struggles to get anywhere far from persistent annoyance.

Title: Venom
Review: The band's detractors will probably complain that the template remains firmly in place, and the band is aimlessly trekking through well-trodden terrain, but by returning to their roots, Bullet for My Valentine seem to have reignited the spark that made their early work so vital.

Title: The Silver Gymnasium
Review: Preferring to be a bit more refined, The Silver Gymnasium mixes maturity and depth with rare awkward moments which are more typical of a band that is musically in their late adolescence.

Title: Leaving Songs
Review: Stately, thoughtful balladry. [Jun 2006, p.115]

Title: Purple Noon
Review: He has this impeccable talent when it comes to picking the right sounds to liquidize his voice, even if that tends to muddy what he’s actually singing. It’s a shame that this time around Greene wants to distance himself from his two best records and early EPs, but Purple Noon is nonetheless an improvement over Mister Mellow because it brings most of what we enjoyed about his early work back – even if it’s not as heavily emphasized.

Title: Threace
Review: The payoff comes about a third of the way in, when the spirit of Foghat makes an unexpected appearance and everything goes boogie. [Oct 2013, p.55]

Title: Blank Project
Review: After 17 odd years of making solo albums, Neneh Cherry surfaces with the force of a jab rather than an uppercut. We appreciate the contact regardless.

Title: We All Belong
Review: Hold it by its edges and the experience of this album suffers––the rocky center is where we find personal truths writ well.

Title: Blues of Desperation
Review: Blues of Desperation rarely deviates from the burnished hard-rock-meets-raw-blues template last explored on 2014's Different Shades Of Blue. But everything comes spiced with clever melodic tics. [May 2016, p.106]

Title: Lex Hives
Review: Album number five is the sound of the law of diminishing returns finally kicking in. [Jul 2012, p.73]

Title: Double Up
Review: Those lyrics may seem slightly ridiculous, but between them and his thinly veiled metaphors for his need to perform cunnilingus (Sweet Tooth), Kelly's originality and talent for making instant club hits is un-fucking-deniable.

Title: Clash the Truth
Review: The beauty of Beach Fossils has always been in the tension between Payseur's disaffected deadpan and the band's super-visceral live shows (before Beach Fossils, he spent years playing in hardcore bands) and on Clash much of that post-punk energy translates seamlessly.

Title: Complete Strangers
Review: The lyrics ring true enough, but not forcefully enough to really resonate with any depth.

Title: ARTPOP
Review: The melodies here are fine, they do a job, but nothing backs up Gag's Warholian rhetoric or scales the barmy heights of Bad Romance.  [Jan 2014, p.116]

Title: One Bedroom
Review: One Bedroom... signals a return to the half-on/half-off inconsistency that marred all Sea and Cake albums except Nassau and Oui, as a handful of misfires trip up the flow.

Title: Sister Faith
Review: Sister Faith may not be entirely consistent, yet in the long run it proves way more heartfelt and genuinely bruised than a typical hardcore punk offering.

Title: Spooky Action
Review: Spooky Action is rollicking exercise in high-impact lo-fi rock that should more than satisfy anyone who has dug any of Loewenstein's projects in the past.

Title: Skilled Mechanics
Review: Skilled Mechanics is an intelligent, pertinent piece of work that shows just how fresh the ideas of Thaws remain.

Title: Understated
Review: Throughout, we get a wounded and fragile man setting his hope-filled heart to music.

Title: Nobody Knows
Review: The real irony of Nobody Knows is that it makes him sound like a more fully realized artist, but a more conservative one, too.

Title: Since We've Become Translucent
Review: The problem with Since We’ve Become Translucent is that it doesn’t measure up to the standards Mudhoney set with the undeniable gripping music they produced in their heyday.

Title: Sound of Water
Review: This is a quietly adventurous coming of age, as languorous and fuzzy around the edges as a summer afternoon.

Title: What One Becomes
Review: Sumac are an original voice in metal, and we certainly need more of that. However, as they currently stand, they're merely good. Really, the only thing stopping them from greatness is a lack of self-editing.

Title: The Sun
Review: The album also crammed full of innovative bleeps and squeaks - if you're familiar with Four Tet you'll know the sort of thing--which add more of a unique selling point which in the end isn't all that necessary, because this is a somewhat dazzling album from some great talents, and it has an abundance of riches.

Title: Unfurl
Review: Unfurl seems infinitely more meditative, vulnerable, and dare I say, spiritual than Dawn.

Title: Working on a Dream
Review: The end of the working day, the mark of Cain, to win, darling, we must pay--these phrases, variations on ones he's used previously, arise on his fifth studio album in seven years, until it seems his uncharacteristic prolific streak comes partly from lazy songwriting, maybe done with a set of Bruce Springsteen Lyric Magnets.

Title: We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves
Review: It's hugely enjoyable, even without any theoretical justification.

Title: Visiter
Review: With Visiter, the Dodos have made one of the year's best albums, one that mixes folk traditions with impressive sonics and texture. It only hints at what they may be capable of.

Title: Range of Light
Review: Range of Light is its own entity, and a promising if a bit one-note follow-up album by the talented S. Carey.

Title: I Get Wet
Review: Here, on one compact disc, is what's wrong with the music industry. [#54, p.110]

Title: No One Can Ever Know
Review: A tense and absorbing record that creates its own world for you to live in.

Title: 2014 Forest Hills Drive
Review: All these flights of fancy fly freely since the album lacks an anchor. 2014 Forest Hills Drive comes off as a great, experimental, and advancing mixtape, but it's insider to a fault, as slight as that fault might be.

Title: Shallow Life
Review: Those incessant choruses this band is so good at continue to dominate, and yet again, it’s what ultimately compels us to think of the album as decent instead of merely middling.

Title: Spirit Counsel
Review: Come for songs and you'll be left wanting, but as a holy distillation of Moore's influences, Spirit Counsel impresses. [Oct 2019, p.30]

Title: Feminist Sweepstakes
Review: That unholy alliance of punk guitar and drum machine now shows off the organic contours of "real" band interaction -- check out how smoothly they funkify with one another on "Fake French."

Title: Concrete and Gold
Review: The Foo sextet has made its hardest, yet most curvaceous and warm-blooded record to date. [No. 148, p.54]

Title: The Warning
Review: In terms of wide-ranging savvy, fizzing enthusiasm and the sheer brilliance of its dance-pop tunes, "The Warning" is shaping-up to be the "Demon Days" of 2006.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: For all its musical diversity, Turn Blue never sounds incoherent.

Title: Amoral
Review: The New Yorkers' debut is retro but refreshing. [Dec. 2010, p. 106]

Title: Keys to the World
