Review: An album of satisfying melodic warmth, Down Like Gold is a winter morning headphone treat. [Mar 2014, p.110]

Title: The Instigator
Review: Fans of the Old 97's most recent work will surely snap The Instigator up with glee; in fact, anyone who likes their guitar pop sprinkled with a little angst will be pleased with what Rhett Miller has come up with on his own.

Title: The Evening of My Best Day
Review: While political manifestos are never something attractively wedded to song, Jones keeps humanity on the record, mostly with supportive grooves and her tantalizing way with twisting a note.

Title: Evil Urges
Review: There are few fiery guitar freakouts, folk-influenced melodies, soaring space-rock bridges, or psychedelic flourishes here; instead, the empty space is mostly filled with serviceable falsetto funk and glassy-eyed yacht-pop.

Title: Neighborhood Watch
Review: Despite a few quality tracks, the album feels wholly uninventive and listless.

Title: PUNK
Review: With PUNK, CHAI have defied all expectations, decreeing that everybody to them is cute--and they don’t need to be.

Title: Rebirth
Review: Oddly, the production in most songs allows lots of open sonic space that reinforces the wispiness of her voice, which rarely ventures out of a mid-range comfort zone. Beyoncé she ain't, much less Alicia. [27 Feb 2005]

Title: Life is Full of Possibilities
Review: An album full of interesting possibilities, but only a few memorable songs. [Mar 2002, p.120]

Title: Losing
Review: Growing up is hard but Bully make it sound exhilarating.

Title: Big Inner
Review: Many have tried to recreate the vibrancy and laidback groove of vintage soul-pop, but to absolutely nail it you need to be someone truly cosmic. Amy Winehouse just about managed it, and Matthew E White is one other such person.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: Neon Bible may be a bold departure from the beloved Funeral, but the divergence is as inspired as the music itself.

Title: Come to Life
Review: This may be her strongest set of songs yet and, even if not every one of its experiments quite comes off, at least these are indicative of an artist who's not content to cruise on auto-pilot.

Title: Employment
Review: A mini-compendium of Britpop from the '60s to now.

Title: Patty Griffin
Review: This is one of Griffin’s most introspective albums, as she continues to move in this direction. Her fans will enjoy the lyrics and her, unique passionate vocals.

Title: No Cities Left
Review: There's a strange, almost perfectly equatorial divide between five largely stunning songs, and six that might shine brighter in lesser company. As arranged, it's jarringly half-brilliant and half-blah.

Title: Departed Glories
Review: As with nearly every Biosphere album, this one contains far more depth than it seems at first, so one shouldn't shrug it off if it doesn't cohere on the initial listen. It's music to get lost inside.

Title: It All Starts With One
Review: It's the perfect end to a blissfully gorgeous album--one that showcases Ane Brun as being at the forefront of the new wave of Scandinavian pop music.

Title: Kleerup
Review: 'With Every Heartbeat' is evidence enough that this man has talent. He just needs to use that Rolodex a bit more.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: An album of eerie, elusive beauty.

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: [It] tries putting everything from the buffet on your plate, even the Jell-O you're not going to eat. C'mon, sounding like a stripped-down version of the Stooges wasn't such a bad thing, was it?

Title: Same Trailer Different Park
Review: The finest lyricist to rise up out of conscious country since Miranda Lambert, if not Bobby Pinson himself.

Title: Closer To Grey
Review: Closer to Grey feels more like a loose assemblage of good-to-great tunes than it does a cohesive album, especially with the level of production perfectionism Johnny Jewel and company are known for. It's a curious piece of the never-ending Chromatics puzzle, and an excellent offering to tide fans over as the they wait for the next piece to fall into place.

Title: Tempest
Review: The coherence of Tempest is the hypnotic key to its charm.

Title: Our Pleasure
Review: Overall, Our Pleasure feels musically intricate on a new level--thicker basslines, much more pronounced drums and priding itself with a lot of guitar-driven character. It's them at their most distinct and honestly, most assertively powerful stance.

Title: No Geography
Review: Three decades after forming, hitting the reset button has unleashed this iconic duo afresh, demonstrating an insatiable ability to forge the perfect dance track, whatever the era. Go get your rave on.

Title: King Push - Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude
Review: Every note fits. Every key has a keyhole. And King Push proper would be hard-pressed to beat this small wonder of great cameos (the always-undervalued Jill Scott, sampled Biggie), productions (in a first, Timbaland manning the boards on the eerie “Untouchable”), and block quotes (“I’m the L. Ron Hubbard of the cupboard”) here.

Title: Voyageur
Review: Voyageur is gorgeously weathered ­heartbreak, straight from the gravelliest Ontario roads.

Title: Lost Time
Review: There's no question that many of Lost Time's lyrics are funny, but the attitude that fueled NVM feels crushed. In both the vocal delivery and the driving guitars, the vibe is damper, the color somewhat drained.

Title: Life is Full of Possibilities
Review: A matchless combination of scratchy indie rock and post-Oval electronics.

Title: Us
Review: As good as Loss was (and make no mistake, it was very, very good), Us improves on it in virtually every way.

Title: Goon
Review: Goon isn’t great, at least in terms of its ambitions, but it is a fine example of what might evolve from pure pop purpose.

Title: Hydrograd
Review: The frontman sounds great as ever, as on the powerful ‘Fabuless’ and ‘The Witness Trees’, but his usual conviction isn’t as present and the album feels largely colourless.

Title: Further
Review: Rowlands and Simons have a tighter grip on the material-an odd thing to say about an album with eight tracks built to sprawl, maybe, but Further really does flow from beginning to end, just the way its makers intended it to.

Title: The Chief
Review: The rapper, producer and crooner pulls all the stops on The Chief, resulting in a first impression that is a memorable one.

Title: A Trip to the Coast
Review: A Trip to the Coast his first album for five years, is full of the kind of sweet, slightly off-kilter songcraft and guitar pop that could result if, say, Lloyd Cole and Robyn Hitchcock were forced to breed.

Title: Not Without a Fight
Review: With Blink-182/+44 bassist Mark Hoppus producing, Fight does pack a wallop, enveloping frontman Jordan Pundik's angsty relationship paeans on a dozen compact, dynamic and hooky tracks in a mere 35 minutes.

Title: Something Like a War
Review: Something Like a War feels ambitious and searching, navigating the complex experiences of Bainbridge and their collaborators.

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: Rihanna's appearance aside, Mylo Xyloto is everything you'd expect from a Coldplay album.

Title: Living Thing
Review: Living Thing is a quirky, cranky little beast, determined to defy expectations.

Title: Tropical Storm
Review: Superfine pop moments never stifle the underlying Jamaican flavor... even if Beenie sometimes sounds a bit like a guest on his own album. [#10, p.114]

Title: Tones of Town
Review: It's not overestimating matters to call 'Tones of Town' a timeless masterpiece.

Title: The Concretes
Review: While the songs have a tendency to run together with an overall sameness, the album as a whole is greater than its individual parts.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Shapiro’s enchanting whisper of a voice guides you along, only occasionally bringing you back to earth with lyrics that speak of lost love and struggle.

Title: Autumn of the Seraphs
Review: Yet good songs alone do not a spectacular album make.  Autumn of the Seraphs shows no major songwriting leaps at all, but it’s still a fine indie-rock LP.

Title: Outside Closer
Review: If their last album seemed like a drastic change to their longtime fans, then Outside Closer will seem like more of a logical succession of sound.

Title: Suite 420
Review: Devin’s redundancy is the reason fans keep coming back. They won’t be disappointed by Suite #420, which features the usual set of chilled-out weed anthems, sex jokes, and old-school R&B beats, along with those great oddball numbers the Dude uses to break each album up.

Title: Shake The Sheets
Review: Using only guitars and drums, the Pharmacists whip up a powerful mix of wild abandon and subtlety that is a perfect backing for Leo's vocal dexterity and clanging guitar heroics.

Title: Fossils
Review: Gentle pedal-steel weepies and shimmering, folk-rock beauty are testament to her new-found freedom. [Sep 2013, p.92]

Title: Hard Islands
Review: Ultimately, it lacks the variety or the startling sonic leaps that would make it essential. Interesting, but no cigar.

Title: Heard It In A Past Life
Review: Rogers never once loses sight of that story [perpetual self-change] on Heard It In a Past Life, and the result is a laser-focused statement with nary a wasted lyric or synth line.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: Hive Mind, follows in the vein of "Ital's Theme" by focusing on warm, softly throbbing textural slides over insistent 4/4 rhythms to forge a kind of day-drifted vagabond music akin to the work of acts like Blondes or The Miracles Club.

Title: Hot Dreams
Review: These brooding, darkly shaded arrangements run the risk of being kitsch. But when Timber Timbre drop the horror pretense and focus on the neurotic ticks and inadequacies that come with romantic obsession, the band are at their best.

Title: The North Borders
Review: You have to wonder whether this is Bonobo appealing to the mass market he's engaged, building atmospheric pop that works better than his rumbles and snorts in a live setting.

Title: Flamagra
Review: It’s not a reversal of normal Flying Lotus material. We’re still dealing with confusion exemplified as a messy but ultimately rewarding tracklist, fear exemplified as music that is just off enough that it could feel terrifying, depression exemplified as little quirks and late starts scattered like jacks and marbles. The difference is that, for once, he’s not trying to fight it all off.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: The scattered approach showcased on this set needs polish and original thought to develop.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: At times, it's a touch muted, a little grey-out, but if this is Lennox staring down mortality, he comes out swinging. [Feb 2015, p.113]

Title: Funhouse
Review: Funhouse would be more fun if Pink went easier on the bad-love songs.

Title: Two-Way Mirror
Review: Considering all the trials and tribulations, Crystal Antlers can definitely look themselves in the, um, mirror with Two-Way Mirror and feel good about where they are and where they're still headed.

Title: Bangerz
Review: With its fresh, smart takes on youth, heartbreak, and modern culture, Bangerz is a record that could very well legitimize Miley Cyrus.

Title: My Guilty Pleasure
Review: My Guilty Pleasure is more cohesive, its production more varied, its songwriting more effective.

Title: Violence
Review: There's nothing here inviting enough to really convince floating voters, but Editors continue to thrive in their own dark universe. [Apr 2018, p.90]

Title: Phrazes for the Young
Review: Phrazes for the Young blusters its way through eight songs full of killer hooks and choruses, and then? Well, it’s gone, as fun and fleeting as a carnival ride that’s just a memory a few hours later.

Title: Requiem
Review: Though Requiem doesn't quite match the free-flowing intensity of some of Goat's earlier work, it's continually enriched by a fervent sense of joy and abandon, and an infectious eagerness to get lost in music. [Nov 2016, p.28]

Title: Feel That Fire
Review: On Feel That Fire he's found the midpoint between mirth and mope, as characteristic country barn-burners like the screw-it-'n'-drink sing-along of 'Sideways' mingle with themes of faith and fidelity to generate his most complete album yet.

Title: Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga
Review: Each and every hand clap and piano chord on their foot-stomping, flawless new album, now streaming on their label's Website, is obsessively placed.

Title: Ascent
Review: Ascent is stuffed with psychedelic guitar virtuosity, moments where Chasny leaves this plane and enters one of those transcendental, mind-freaked, head-tipped-back, eyelid-fluttering states that few are capable of.

Title: Waking Up
Review: Waking Up boasts enough intertwining pop melodies backed with anthemic vocals to show fans of the 2007 Timbaland-remixed track "Apologize" that OneRepublic can deliver more addictive hooks while still maintaining its own graceful and introspective sound.

Title: Earth Division
Review: They simply begin, evolve, repeat, and end, very much as though they were designed to play out while we directed our attention elsewhere.

Title: You've Always Been Here
Review: It’s the quarantine passion project created after too many days of 4pm drinking. It’s the existential crisis on Week 12 of drifting, structure-less furlough. It’s the desperate clutch at nostalgia that finds you trawling through your old school friends on Facebook at 2am, sobbing for A Simpler Time.

Title: Beach Music
Review: Complicated arrangements and gorgeous melodies reveal themselves to you as rewards for your patience. Over time, even the alien voices begin to sound natural, even inviting.

Title: Half Moon Light
Review: There are touches of roots rock and a distinct – maybe all-too-obvious – influence derived from Paul Simon and the slick R&B moves he incorporated in his mid-'80s solo work. At its best, though, and for the most part, the music is simple and beautiful and understated.

Title: Strange Friend
Review: The overall effect is more organic and rock. [Jul 2014, p.94]

Title: Trick
Review: He's had a reputation for being guarded in the past, but on Trick, we see him wear his heart on his sleeve.

Title: Candidate Waltz
Review: This is indie rock where the big hooks and bold arrangements never get in the way of the complex emotions at the heart of these nine songs, and that's why five years isn't too long to wait for music this special.

Title: Rituals
Review: It's a pleasant enough experience on the whole, but could've been so much more--and that is what's so frustrating with Rituals.

Title: Black Labyrinth
Review: Emotionally effective but quite different from anything he's done prior, it's an endearing, rewarding peek into Davis' interests outside of his day job.

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: There's more melody here than on previous Mastodon albums; opener 'Oblivion' even has a sweetly grungy Alice in Chains breakdown. And Brendan O'Brien's production does increase the fist-pumping factor in 'Divinations' and 'Crack the Skye'--the latter of which bites some of Metallica's Black Album rumble. But this is still a forbiddingly dense piece of post-prog rock.

Title: ZABA
Review: Moody textures outnumber memorable songs, but this is still a stylish and inviting debut. [Jul 2014, p.73]

Title: No Pressure
Review: No Pressure finds Logic all grown up and ready to give himself over to a new chapter. It's one of his best and most enjoyable albums, wrapping up an electrified run with his most clearheaded and honest material yet.

Title: Rize of the Fenix
Review: [The song] "Rize of the Fenix" is so powerful, so perfect, so representative of what these guys do well, what follows is almost sure to pale in comparison. Luckily, the highlights keep on coming.

Title: Moonlust
Review: It sheds their debut’s pastoral psych for a spacey romanticism, and in the process, its airy synthesizers and reverb’d guitars evoke a yearning that’s too vague and indeterminate to be a yearning for anything in particular.

Title: SASAMI
Review: Each song is like a little journal entry, lent emotional heft by Ashworth's use of repetition. [Apr 2019, p.114]

Title: Red
Review: Guillemots cram themselves into awkward fits, and Dangerfield has to squeeze the hardest--whether he's tying himself to a straightforward ballad instead of clamoring for the rooftops, or standing up for a fight when he's so much more comfortable slipping into a dream.

Title: Infinite Light
Review: If sophomore disc Infinite Light instead leaves only a pleasing afterimage, it's still dusky pause.

Title: Redeemer of Souls
Review: Overall the glory years seem a long way off and metal fatigue sets in long before the end of its 63 minutes. [Aug 2014, p.108]

Title: Heart's Ease
Review: The relaxed warmth carried over from Lodestar to Heart’s Ease affirms that she’s glad to be here.

Title: Hot Fuss
Review: Most of Hot Fuss slides by without creating much of a stir, but it's got too many memorable moments to be written off.

Title: The Golden Age of Grotesque
Review: What's surprising is that there's still so much life in what Manson is rehashing.

Title: Lush
Review: The crushing sameness of the existence described in Snail Mail’s music means that not every song on Lush is essential, but when Jordan hits, she hits a bullseye.

Title: Ratworld
Review: Ratworld wears its influences brazenly on its sleeves, but its execution is impressive, presenting an odd bird view of a world that is ostensibly its own.

Title: The Bride Screamed Murder
Review: Withstanding some strange experimentation - including a steamy a cappella version of the Canadian folksong "Peggy Gordon" and a sludged-out, seven-and-a-half-minute cover of the Who's "My Generation" - The Bride Screamed Murder is surprisingly accessible.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: The result is the Internet’s most musically diverse and synergetic album to date.

Title: 1000 gecs
Review: The guests skillfully mold the originals into creations of their own, while still preserving some of the songs’ initial ideas.

Title: Shapeshifting
Review: he overall result is in line with Studio's work or that of some of their Swedish contemporaries. [Feb 2011, p.69]

Title: Weather Diaries
Review: Weather Diaries is no Tarantula-sized affront to Ride’s legacy, but neither is it a Going Blank Again-style triumph of reinvention and focus. Weather-wise, it is an overcast day with a hint of sun: promising but never quite satisfying.

Title: Go Easy
Review: there is an impressive and ambitious sense of craftsmanship across the record that captures Blank Realm on the cusp of something truly special.

Title: King
Review: Sure, King's occasional lack of originality and sometimes sluggish wordplay could be cited. But that, of course, would only amount to throwing rocks at the throne. [May 2006, p.136]

Title: Perils from the Sea
Review: In a life of perpetual motion, Perils From The Sea provides a vital forward thrust. [Jul 2013, p.86]

Title: Law and Order
Review: Law is the perfect Indian-summer morning garage sale soundtrack album. It follows the mood flow to a T.

Title: Future Standards
Review: Future Standards feels a little too respectful, well-done but static and without much animating fire.

Title: My Best Friend Is You
Review: Disappointingly, she doesn't go all the way with this new, abrasive approach. Instead, she lets ex-Suede guitarist and Duffy mastermind Bernard Butler smother the album with corny string and brass sections that try but fail to impose a 60s girl-group aesthetic.

Title: Weather
Review: During its most striking moments, Weather is yet another example of Scott Hansen’s musical craftsmanship and excitingly it clearly illustrates the validity of his collaborative efforts with other musical artists. However the weighting on Weather is at times off-kilter and inconsistent, if Hansen can rectify and master this in future projects, he will likely be making the best music of his career.

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: In less talented hands, the dozen songs on this record easily could have sounded like a failed, high-concept art thesis, and to be perfectly objective, not every track really kills.

Title: Where the Messengers Meet
Review: Where The Messengers Meet might be the best MSHVB can do with their current MO, it's a remarkably compact album of emotionally-swollen, disillusioned folk rock -but you get the feeling that the band might be on the precipice of something much more titanic.

Title: Shut Up I Am Dreaming
Review: The poetry is too good, the gloom too cached in symbolism and fine melodies to feel trite or melodramatic.

Title: Â¡Uno!
Review: Free from grandly theatrical flourishes that were threatening to become things of creative captivity, ¡Uno!'s graceful manoeuvres confirm Green Day's status as one of the world's finest rock'n'roll bands.

Title: You're Welcome
Review: While the songs are undoubtedly strong on their lonesome, You’re Welcome is a record that begs to be listened to in sequence.

Title: Resonant Body
Review: Resonant Body is an inspiring release that demonstrates the healing qualities of dance music.

Title: Cry
Review: As with their debut, this album feels as though you’re being allowed a brief but intense insight into his self-contained world. Yet the vein of humour that ran through those earlier songs has been replaced by a deeper sincerity.

Title: Six Demon Bag
Review: This time out, Man Man's less sloppy but just as ramshackle, as if the snaps and crackles are the band's diversion from actually writing the record.

Title: Preteen Weaponry
Review: Oneida have always been a thick stew of different influences, but usually with a dash of originality to bind it together; Preteen Weaponry never rises above pastiche. Nevertheless, the band’s hypnotic drone sweeps through the album like a swift current — it’s enough to generate anticipation for their future travels.

Title: Eleventh Hour
Review: Vocally, Del may have lost some of his lyrical miracles and "spectacular vernacular" from albums past, but his unquestionably familar cadence hasn't budged a bit. [Jan/Feb 2008, p.104]

Title: Tender New Signs
Review: Whether it be the quaint elegance and flowing, reverb heavy guitars of kaleidoscopic opener 'I'm Gone' or claustrophobic haze of album standout 'Heavenly Bodies', there's little here that disappoints.

Title: Exai
Review: Exai shows they still occupy a special position in the current generation of forward-thinkers, producing music that couldn’t have been made at any other time other than now, unostentatiously trailblazing a path for others to follow in.

Title: TRUE
Review: True works as a whole and creates an unbroken mood and feel that is both nocturnal and strangely uplifting.

Title: Fast Man Raider Man
Review: While there are some moments of greatness (the menacing, psychedelic 'Dog Sleep', the mournful, pretty 'Don't Cry That Way'), the majority of this double album is dull, turgid and instantly forgettable.

Title: Tongues
Review: Tongues is a record of surpassing depth and ingenuity.

Title: How to Dance
Review: While McEntire’s aimlessness feels honest and satisfying in its questing, it also makes for an album with plenty of movement but less, perhaps, in the way of progress.

Title: Hymn and Her
Review: Make no mistake, though--the music of Hymn and Her is good, and the songs are almost always uniformly excellent examples of finely-honed pop songcraft. But when each excellent song sounds just like the slow, rainy Sunday pulse of a track that just preceded it, well, a few less hymns and a few more songs for rocking are in order.

Title: Crimes of Passion
Review: Crimes of Passion is a stellar fourth effort and may prove to be the defining record in what surely will be a long career ahead for the Crocodiles.

Title: The Unraveling
Review: The Unraveling is a dire yet vivid depiction of the American zeitgeist at a crucial time in the nation's history, and a decisive collection of songs these musicians clearly wish they didn't have to write.

Title: Fair Ain't Fair
Review: Refreshingly, he doesn’t resort to the type of left-wing broadsides that Bragg perfected, and instead dismantles his political and cultural targets through quirky stories and a mix of self-deprecation and sarcasm.

Title: Another Fine Day
Review: Like everything this band's made, it's long, sloppy, and uneven, but at this point that's the idea: here are a bunch of people who kind of know each other sitting down with some guitars.

Title: Decoration Day
Review: Few bands today are as good at telling a simple, straightforward, from-the-gut story like the Drive-By Truckers are.

Title: Alegranza
Review: It's the sort of release that will drive some listeners completely nuts simply because of the construction techniques, but it also powers forward with such a giddy energy that it's hard not to get wrapped up in it.

Title: Time on Earth
Review: While the slower, gentler moments are not without charm, large sections of the album land on the wrong side of the drowsy-dreamy divide.

Title: Hairball
Review: The version of the band audible on their second album is one that's on a sugar high and fuelled by a desire to create loud and fast music that doesn't skimp on the hooks.

Title: Entertainment
Review: Entertainment resurrects the group. Their music disconnects, only to connect again.

Title: Vermont
Review: This is an antidote to both Plessow and Worgull’s respective day jobs and the way they craft their soundscapes is admirable.

Title: Double Up
Review: Kelly's true genius is the metaphor-laden sex jam, and Double Up has some great ones. [Jul 2007, p.115]

Title: Brill Bruisers
Review: It's as accomplished and engaging as anything they've done.

Title: The Chemistry of Common Life
Review: Here, they combine hardcore punk’s combat-boot side with its tortured-noise side, layering what sounds like scores of tsunami-distortion guitars over an atomic-speed drum blitz to attain rarely witnessed levels of obliteration (think Black Flag reincarnated as psychotic yetis).

Title: Dead Son Rising
Review: While Dead Son Rising isn't likely to propel him back into the mainstream, it's an impressively bold affair that ensures his cult status will remain intact.

Title: Turn Out the Lights
Review: Her guitar and piano now come with string arrangements and a big, satin-finish production, which takes baby steps towards a mainstream audience, although perhaps some of her magical fragility is being lost.

Title: Goners
Review: Gibson's follow-up to 2016's Empire Builder finds her tinkering with the complexion of her sound, bringing piano and strings to the surface, mostly at the expense of guitar. It turns out to be a clever fit for the songs. [Nov 2018, p.29]

Title: Return to Cookie Mountain
Review: Almost wholly brilliant.

Title: Shine On
Review: It's when Jet explore the territory between their lodestars [AC/DC and the Beatles] that they go from being decent mimics to inconsequential imitators. [Nov 2006, p.96]

Title: Lonely Planet
Review: His most fully realized work yet, and also his most original. Bookended by a pair of gentle, ambient-leaning cuts, the record mostly ignores the dancefloor in favor of resting pulses and humid atmospheres.

Title: From the Ages
Review: Earthless are incredibly indulgent, sometimes to a fault, but they’re much too excitable to be called selfish or masturbatory. The dudes are once again just riffing here. It’s a trip worth taking, at least a few times.

Title: The Redeemer
Review: It's as intoxicating a listen as anything we've heard from the duo to date, drawing its power from the combination of Blunt's ideas, fluid and often semi-literate musicality, and world-weary persona.

Title: Rook
Review: The songs here tend to go nowhere for a quiet couple of minutes before bursting randomly into tightly composed melodrama, which could be mistaken for actually going somewhere.

Title: Animal Races
Review: A third LP of warm, retro pop jangle. [Oct 2016, p.100]

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: Adrian Thaws is another decent entry in the latterday Trickypedia, rolling along on circular bluesfunk grooves and furtive whisper-croak boy-girl vocals. [Oct 2014, p.79]

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: In Your Dreams winds up capturing the essence of Stevie Nicks, which -- as her previous three decades of solo albums prove -- is no easy feat.

Title: Who Me?
Review: It’s the bookends of Who Me? that shine some light on Wauters’ troubadour potential.

Title: Olympia
Review: Not all of Olympia’s added complexity works to its benefit, but the album succeeds as a necessary stepping-stone on Stelmanis’ path of artistic discovery.

Title: Isles
Review: While the album is described as a myriad of styles, there’s nothing to really demonstrate this: only the reggae and reggae-related genres are consistently and tiresomely reflected.

Title: 100th Window
Review: 100th Window meanders along, emotion-less and soul-less—albeit with haunting Middle Eastern flourishes.

Title: Feel Good Together
Review: The echoey vocals recall Nineties shoegazers like Ride, and the instrumental breaks suggest quality time has been spent with Pavement's Slanted and Enchanted.

Title: Powerballin'
Review: The constant talk of expensive cars, gyrating women and endless parties quickly becomes redundant--and boring.

Title: Earth
Review: Much of Earth is laidback and peaceful, centered around the cerebral “Brasil” and “Olympik,” which clock in over eight minutes, tickling the brain with swirling synths and dreamy lines about love and perfection.

Title: Hot Motion
Review: Their hooks seem to call to you from misty, far-off shores, promising mystical rave-ups. Drift in. [Oct 2019, p.91]

Title: Oxymoron
Review: What it lacks in punch it makes up for in being a more focused effort than its occasionally mixtape-esque brother, and thus, Oxymoron isn’t so much a backpedal for Q and TDE as it is a solid side-step.

Title: Shine
Review: Joni Mitchell's first album of new material in nearly 10 years is a return to the form that made her a star.

Title: You Were Right
Review: It's all fetching, if tough to fully love--which may have been Benson's intent all along.

Title: Good News
Review: His tunes are full of warm, woozy singsong charm.

Artist: S U R V I V E
Title: RR7349
Review: RR7349 mingles the tangible with the abstract to spur a novel meld of both imaginative atmosphere and gripping substance.

Title: The Curse of Blondie
Review: That isn't to say that The Curse of Blondie is a classic Blondie disc, but it's the first good one since at least Autoamerican, and features one of their best-ever singles in "Good Boys."

Title: Apollo Sunshine
Review: The band parlays its tuneful edification into an experimental collage, bouncing between art school rock, guitar-heavy psychedelia and keyboard hippiedom, yet interconnected by lyrics that are both shrewd and satisfying.

Title: Gold In A Brass Age
Review: Some songs just feel like they didn't develop as naturally as others. Some, such as "It's Late", feel in need of a few more sonic components to round out what the song is attempting to do. But there's an upside to moments like these as they show that nearly 30 years into his career, with a double-digit studio album count, David Gray is still exploring.

Title: Hush
Review: The band still have the knack with a melody, and there's always room for a winning formula melding atmospherics with a good tune, but somehow the addictive charm of the highlights of "Citrus" such as 'Thursday' and 'New Years' just aren't present on Hush, and you're left feeling underwhelmed.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: The pair's [singer James Mercer and producer Greg Kurstin] pop instincts ultimately prevail over more esoteric ambitions. [Apr 2012, p.86]

Review: Although some of the songs follow that same pop structure seen on the first half, by contrasting them with more experimental sounds (that are not hoping to top the charts), they have much more impact.

Title: The Argument
Review: All very highbrow and ambitious for sure, yet despite portentous advance warnings of material involving fallen angels, the Garden Of Eden and Dante-ish visions of Hell, songs such as the plaintive Morningstar and the Buddy Holly-aping rattle of Letting Me Out quickly prove Hart’s still more than capable of channelling his lofty ideals through good ol’ verse-chorus-verse.

Title: Journey To The West
Review: It probably made for a more interesting theatrical experience than it does standalone album, but if the form--expressive, exaggerated musical drama--is a bit unfamiliar, then Albarn's insidious tunes are not. [Oct 2008, p.101]

Title: Summertime '06
Review: It’s a major triumph disguised as a minor one--60 minutes of lean, inventive, important rap music that never pats itself on the back for being any of those things.

Title: Some Cities
Review: Like most of the cities Doves sing about, these songs are grey, drizzly, often unpleasant, and more often than not... very, very dull.

Title: In The Grace of Your Love
Review: Next to his material, In the Grace of Your Love sounds as forgettable as the dozens of nameless bands who came in Echoes's wake. The Rapture could still regroup on their next record, but it's difficult to see where they'd go from here.

Title: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always
Review: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always isn't Luke Winslow-King's happiest album by a long shot, but it feels like his best so far, and finds him expanding his musical horizons without losing any ground along the way. This is a top-shelf exercise in soulful blues with plenty to say to the lovelorn and the satisfied alike.

Title: No Mercy
Review: While T.I.'s measured, discursive rap style is heard at its best on scourging confessional duets with Eminem and, of all people, Christina Aguilera on the genuinely touching Castle Walls, Further promising collaborations with Kanye West, Pharrell and Drake end up having a rather more formulaic ring to them. [Apr 2011, p.97]

Title: Stellastarr
Review: There hasn't been a set of pretenders this convincing since Interpol. [#61, p.107]

Title: War & Leisure
Review: The L.A. soul explorer's fourth album creates a space where psych-funk splendor coexists with deep anxiety.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: What is clear is that the Arctic Monkeys of 2011 have produced, probably by a significant margin, the best British Rock 'n' Roll album you will hear this year, and on top of that there's the comforting sense that Suck It And See will only age well.
So maybe there's nothing here more interesting or deep or significant than what it is on the surface: a very beautiful record that means nothing more than what it is...

Title: Liberation
Review: A political record as grand, explicit, and opaque as Radiohead's Hail to the Thief.

Title: The Soul of All Natural Things
Review: Occasionally the album misfires. [Mar 2014, p.59]

Title: The Revolution Starts Now
Review: A couple of songs (including the goofy "Condi, Condi") seem out of place, but the heart of "The Revolution" carries the stamp of an artist and a patriot. [22 Aug 2004]

Title: Woman
Review: There are some infectious grooves here and there but they don’t crackle and snap the way they once did.

Title: Heron King Blues
Review: Evokes the same stark, road weary melancholy as Ry Cooder's score for Paris, Texas, but with a far more extensive sonic toolbox. [#240, p.57]

Title: Without Your Love
Review: Without Your Love ends up becoming a loose survey of Dexter's work instead the Nihjgt Feelings statement he intended it to be.

Title: Cold Roses
Review: For every two full blooms ("Cherry Lane," "Rosebud") there's a stem ("Mockingbird"), and a couple decent toss-offs ("Beautiful Sorta," "Dance All Night"), but such is Adams' double-album hubris.

Title: Reformation Post TLC
Review: The Fall are the best new band in Britain.

Title: Dead Zone Boys
Review: The record provides songs as unpredictable as the one proceeding it, incorporating multi-layered doses of percussion, fat synths, and ritualistic chanting that sounds as if it was yelped by Animal Collective’s evil step-sister.

Title: Lithium Burn
Review: While Lithium Burn is an easy album to empathize with, you wish it'd do more to make you root for the band.

Title: In Search of Harperfield
Review: Harperfield shines brightest when Pollock allows big emotion to weigh her tempo down.

Title: The Declaration
Review: Sleek but insubstantial fourth outing from R&B songstress.

Title: 200 Million Thousand
Review: 200 Million Thousand showcases some of their most satisfying [tunes] yet.

Title: Walking Cloud and Deep Red Sky, Flag Fluttered and the Sun Shined
Review: Mono singlehandedly redefines the concept of dynamics. They are very quiet, and then very loud. It will hurt your head.

Title: Out My Window
Review: Koushik has crafted an album that glows like a California sunset, even though he's actually a Canadian now living in Vermont. [Nov 2008, p.118]

Title: Music To Be Murdered By
Review: If they look hard enough, any artist could find criticism of their work online. That’s sort of the curse of the Information Age. But not everyone overreacts quite as much as Eminem does. But if his fears grow tiring, his lyrical ability can still give you something to admire, even if the album is somewhat uneven.
180 is structured like a gig, with the attention-grabbing hit followed by fun but less memorable tracks that build gradually in excitement.

Title: In Between Dreams
Review: Johnson appears to think that his smooth acoustic surfer music might need a retooling to reflect this scary new world.

Title: Fever Ray
Review: Who knows what Knife-man Olof Dreijer will bring back from his (literal) exploration of the Amazon, intended for an electronic opera about "The Origin of Species" (due September 2009); for now, this may be his sister’s most artistically satisfying album.

Title: No Shape
Review: Imperfect yet fascinating and occasionally gorgeous, No Shape once again expands and defies any preconceived boundaries of the Perfume Genius project.

Title: Wanderer
Review: This is a record with gentleness and vulnerability in abundance, but it's carefully crafted--it knows itself, and it knows when it's finished.

Title: Wildflower
Review: At 20 tracks long, however, it takes some serious listening to get through the whole thing, and a sense of sag in the latter third threatens to overpower on the first few spins. Essentially, this flower could've used a little more judicious pruning.

Title: A Coliseum Complex Museum
Review: Perhaps in the end it’s best to just say that The Besnard Lakes sound like themselves; they’ve certainly found a way to refine their own sound, and the jarring beauty that can be heard in A Coliseum Complex Museum is a prime example of it.

Title: Before The World Was Big
Review: Cleo Tucker and Harmony Tividad have already proven themselves as songwriters with a great deal of potential, and their debut record properly only confirms that they’re only just getting started.

Title: Let's Bottle Bohemia
Review: This album should really have been called Let's Battle Insomnia, in honour of its sedative properties.

Title: Luminous Night
Review: It's this combination of the simple and the intricate, the elegant and the forceful, that makes Luminous Night work so well.

Title: Worship
Review: While Worship occasionally soars on its own beautiful anonymity, it misses the bar set by a line of charismatic frontmen who exposed themselves through compelling narratives.

Title: Ready to Die
Review: Ready to Die is a weirdly exhilarating gem, thanks to Iggy's fiery eloquence and the Stooges' still-raw power. Apparently rock'n'roll can be an old man's game after all.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: It could have worked, but the dated production style bogs it down.

Title: The Eraser
Review: It sounds as you would expect: a desolate dreamscape punctuated by nervous drum machines. In other words, it's a bit Kid A. [Aug 2006, p.110]

Title: Joy as an Act of Resistance
Review: Everything about Joy As An Act Of Resistance is just so perfectly realised.

Title: Wildewoman
Review: The hummable, sing-in-the-shower refrains are there, but ultimately, its Wildewoman's lack of identity that limits its appeal.

Title: For Years
Review: For Years feels like the natural conclusion to the quest he quietly started back in 2010.

Title: 5 Seconds of Summer
Review: In truth, 5 Seconds of Summer are unlikely to replace their elders any time soon. But they do provide a nice alternative--one with fetching songs and just enough sass to stand out.

Title: Drums Between the Bells
Review: Drums Between the Bells at its simplest is often Drums Between the Bells at its best.

Title: Adam Green & Binki Shapiro
Review: As a homage to all the good things about ’60s easy listening this ticks all the boxes even if it feels too much like a re-hash of times gone by.

Title: Bionic
Review: Whatever the case, for Christina Aguilera, the x-factor has gone. The daring single minded focus has apparently been lost.

Title: Out of Touch in the Wild
Review: The music's one-dimensional emotional range is the Achilles heels of an otherwise gracefully dextrous affair. [Feb 2013, p.90]

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: Though I can't say this album has as many of these killer tracks as Xiu Xiu's previous albums, Women as Lovers is a satisfying installment for fans of Xiu Xiu's singular style.

Title: The Warning
Review: The quintet's refined funk tweaks the genre-busting dance rock of classic Prince and New Order with a modern, synth-happy sheen. [16 Jun 2006, p.77]

Title: Meds
Review: Molko still manages to carry songs with his affected, nasal delivery as the band provides a steady backbone.

Title: Gloss Drop
Review: Gloss Drop may be a less solid and coherent album than Mirrored, but it is still a remarkably promising follow-up. As always, the music is cerebral, engaging, technically stupefying, and utterly original.

Title: Ghosteen
Review: Yes, it can be painful, but there’s a beautiful catharsis contained within Ghosteen that makes it one of the most essential records of recent times – a lifejacket for anyone surfing that dreadful wave of grief.

Artist: S U R V I V E
Title: RR7349
Review: It's easily the most accomplished work yet from the mighty S U R V I V E, who tower over the majority of other synth-wave revivalists.

Title: Myopia
Review: There are many joys to be found within its brittle, opaque sounds but it’s undoubtedly an album that must be lived with for an appropriate length of time for these to fully surface. Yet, this isn’t a bad thing.

Title: Pop Voodoo
Review: You might cringe at some of the words, and you certainly wouldn’t play them to your young kids or their elderly nanna, but everyone in-between might just turn enough of a blind eye and enjoy Pop Voodoo for what it fundamentally is: an enjoyable trip of danceable funk.

Title: Around The Sun
Review: Where the two remaining musicians in the band appear to have gone astray, Michael Stipe sounds positively lost, never to be found again.

Title: White Lies For Dark Times
Review: White Lies For Dark Times succeeds when cool and carefree; when the album ups the energy, however, it’s channeled through the formulaic licks found at on any average summer-festival circuit, suggesting Lifeline’s high standards were an anomaly.

Title: Undertow
Review: A journey of self-discovery, confidence abounding like limits simply don’t exist.

Title: Electra Heart
Review: Marina Diamandis rivals Katy Perry for catchy hooks, commands with the swagger of Gwen Stefani, and even comes close to the ethereal vocal exhilaration of Florence Welch.

Title: Heartbeat Radio
Review: Imagine a less florid Rufus Wainwright , or Paddy McAloon without the lyrical smarts and you'd be getting close: he even claims Prefab Sprout - along with A-ha - as a key influence. [Dec 2009, p. 116]

Title: Love Letter
Review: On Love Letter, he does away with the freakiness and lays down a full record of slow-simmered, grown-man emoting. And it feels like a wayward husband who's finally come home for good.

Title: Hammer of the Witches
Review: Hammer of the Witches is the post-Midian release fans have been asking for while retaining the riff-oriented sound the band have been attempting for the past 15 years--only this time they’ve actually pulled it all off.

Title: Haughty Melodic
Review: Doughty is better off when laid bare or with a group of musicians that push him in new directions, rather than ones who simply back him.

Title: The Golden Echo
Review: It starts off brilliantly, but by the end of twelve tracks, it tapers off into an incessant and increasingly underwhelming performance.

Title: Riot!
Review: Riot! is immediately appealing because it focuses on sounds that have been neglected by the genre’s frontrunners. This is an uncomplicated album comprising of strikingly uncomplicated music, entirely lacking in 15 word song titles, Jay-Z guest appearances, and theatrical meta-concepts about performing in a rock band.

Title: No Pier Pressure
Review: Tellingly, Al Jardine and David Marks return here, their harmonies shining in the gorgeously dreamy Whatever Happened. [May 2015, p.93]

Title: Side Pony
Review: The retro vibe rules, captured with gleaming accuracy by producer Dave Cobb, Nashville’s roots-music it-guy (Chris Stapleton, Jason Isbell). If it sometimes feels a bit calculated, it's still pretty irresistible.

Title: Anarchic Breezes
Review: Occasionally plodding, and too ruminative by half, Anarchic Breezes is a journey in need of a destination, stuck between staring at the sun and gazing thoughtfully at its own navel.

Title: Ganging Up on the Sun
Review: The album is often as strong as Fountains Of Wayne's Welcome Interstate Managers.

Title: Ashes and Roses
Review: The uncluttered folk-rock arrangements and a voice that has acquired a richer Patina since her '90s country hits contribute to the loveliest and most profound album of her career. [Sep 2012, p.74]

Title: First Taste
Review: There are moments when some editing may have tightened things up and Segall’s lyrics are opaque even at the best of times, but for an album built out of experimentation, it is surprising how well First Taste links together; and most of the credit for that success can be given to those killer drums. ... Segall continues to blaze his own sonic path.

Title: In Between Dreams
Review: He's so laid-back, it's hard to tell when he's worked up. In more encouraging news, his tunes are meatier. [4 Mar 2005, p.72]

Title: Distortion
Review: Distortion isn't an easy listen, with its strict, difficult palette. But it's an endlessly fascinating and provocative one.

Title: Only In Dreams
Review: Only in Dreams, the second Dum Dum Girls album, seethes with a beautiful, raging confidence, louder and fuller than anything they've done before, and better than the onetime peers they're leaving behind.

Title: Hard Working Americans
Review: Hard Working Americans picked 11 cover tunes which deal with the hard truths of life among the working class, some recent compositions, and other, older songs that have remained relevant with the passage of time.

Title: Beautiful Rewind
Review: Even though Beautiful Rewind is a call to dance music's past, it's the contemporary, more experimental sounds that establish the album as a standout in both the Four Tet oeuvre and a growing collection of dance albums that pay homage to the past.

Title: City Music
Review: While City Music certainly doesn’t surpass Singing Saw, it’s a hell of a lot of fun to hear Morby take a walk on the wild side.

Title: Luxury Problems
Review: Luxury Problems is distinguished by the piercing vocals of Stott's former piano teacher, Alison Skidmore; looped, layered and heavily reverbed, they coil elegantly around Stott's brutalist constructions. [Jan 2013, p.83]

Title: Frankie Rose and the Outs
Review: Throw in a gorgeous Arthur Russell cover and you have a competent throwback release rooted in contemporary memes. [Fall 2010, p.67]

Title: Because of the Times
Review: Because of the Times validates the theory that the Kings of Leon are merely the Eagles in wolf’s clothing (or the Strokes in overalls), being that the album’s collection of tales, focusing solely on hard-living and harder women, are but hokey pulp fictions disguised with mellowed sincerity, played out on mythical dirt roads and overgrown farmhouses.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: There’s real talent here. However, these unflinchingly honest punks still have yet to figure out what to do with all the noise they channel.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: Despite all the lonely missives and political outrage, Oberst comes off more like a troubadour of hope. [Mar 2005, p.132]

Title: Lily-O
Review: Somehow at once entertaining, comforting, and challenging, Lily-O sees Amidon again pushing his distinctive perspectives through songs that belong to everybody.

Title: Destroyer
Review: Destroyer may shake and shudder but it never falls apart. [Jul 2019, p.81]

Title: The Rhumb Line
Review: While the first five songs on The Rhumb Line are uniformly strong, the album starts to lose its momentum just after cresting the halfway point.

Title: Cradlesong
Review: Cradlesong, his second persistently polite, numbingly polished solo album.

Title: The Soul Sessions
Review: The dichotomy of power and sultriness is the [final] track's greatest asset. It's that same duality that should provide Joss Stone with a career that knows no limits.

Title: Shadow of the Sun
Review: By the time the spacey, seven-minute "Ice" rolls around, Moon Duo have molded the album into a frothing, lively psych odyssey.

Title: Ringleader of the Tormentors
Review: As with everything Morrissey does, ROTT's resonance will elude those not hitherto fascinated by its master's voice. A shame, for in terms of pure musicality, ROTT is possibly his most ecumenical solo album, his most welcoming and loveable. [Apr 2006, p.89]

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: This is a band working at the very top of their game, and this album is a beautiful, brilliant beast.

Title: There's No 666 in Outer Space
Review: An album that is as fiercely imaginative as any the Sacramento-based group has released before.

Title: Tunnel Blanket
Review: If that's not your bag, then this won't convert you, but if intrigue you have; then check it out.

Title: Domesticated
Review: Domesticated is a blissful trip, managing the enviable feat of being inventive and comforting at the same time, and is highly recommended for all electronic music fans.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: He's purely elegant throughout.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: Majestic, glorious and not like much else you've ever heard before.... A strong contender for Album of the Year. [Mar 2004, p.107]

Title: Raise Vibration
Review: Raise Vibration's more serious shortcoming is its lyrics, which stumble whenever they reach for grand proclamations on the state of the world.

Title: Million Dollars to Kill Me
Review: Barry Johnson’s vocals remain huge, and riffs are still catchy, but in trying to expand their palate, their identity might just be starting to slip.

Title: Another One
Review: It’s a genial set.

Title: Sleep Well Beast
Review: This new material finds them in [a] more experimental mode. [Oct 2017, p.90]

Title: Blues Funeral
Review: Though a mixed bag, Blues Funeral does have its moments.

Title: Lovers Rock
Review: Very rarely, this album finds a moment of excitement. And when they do, you have to savor them, because you aren’t going to get another one for a while.

Title: Putting the Days to Bed
Review: A substantive collection of back-to-basics indie rock.

Title: Rooty
Review: The album misses the addictive funk of 'Red Alert', the off beat quirks of 'Yo Yo' and the engulfing production depth of 'Same Old Show'. But it's a powerful package and a proof that the Basement Jaxx have the confidence and vision to pursue their own path.

Title: Mariachi El Bronx (II)
Review: It [the first Mariachi El Bronx album] was a beautifully anarchistic move that's now spawned its second (more polished) album under the Mariachi El Bronx alias.

Title: The Hanged Man
Review: While there's plenty to like here, and more to admire, he's never made a record quite so challenging to love. [No. 146, p.54]

Title: Another Day on Earth
Review: A record that encourages global consciousness shouldn't sound so isolated and chilly. [Aug 2005, p.110]

Title: Rather Ripped
Review: It is indeed a really good record--but not a patch on their 1988 masterpiece 'Daydream Nation'. [17 Jun 2006, p.37]

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: Although the songs carry recurring tropes of eagles, devils and the sea, as well as her signature intricate guitar picking, the most haunting aspect is--considering this accomplishment--realizing the potential that is yet to come.

Title: Pearl Mystic
Review: Pearl Mystic is the best British psychedelic album since the 1990s; maybe more than that.

Title: Fever
Review: Although his group has made its mark on the metalcore underground, Tuck spends most of the Welsh quartet's new album spewing venomous tirades at a variety of villains who have done him wrong. But he does it in a polished fashion that makes "Fever" the band's most commercial outing yet.

Title: The Cool
Review: Lupe Fiasco and his producers--mostly Soundtrakk--have clarified the lyrics and brought out the hooks. The result is a three-act allegory that’s also one of the year’s best hip-hop albums.

Title: Lucky Day
Review: Another crop of dance tracks for the masses. [8 Nov 2002, p.106]

Title: Fading Trails
Review: The full-band songs rarely manage the sort of charismatic country-rock crunchiness that made What Comes After the Blues so endearing on repeated listen. On the other hand, the solo tracks can’t really match up to the almost uniformly excellent offerings on Let Me Go.

Title: Machine Dreams
Review: There's no way around the fact that most of Machine Dreams is icy electro-pop, but it is not as if the truly singular Yukimi Nagano, an enamoring vocalist, has switched to drone mode, forsaking her grounding in R&B.

Title: MAP OF THE SOUL : 7
Review: With each album, they continue on the path of self-discovery and maturity, pulling off yet another effortless display of pop prowess without forgetting the fans that have helped them along the way.

Title: Manic
Review: Her lyrical confidence is matched by the characterful production, which straddles R&B, country, trashy pop-rock, Kacey Musgraves-ish cosmic Americana and more. ... A major label pop album with real drama and humanity.

Title: Eight Gates
Review: Regardless of his or his label’s intentions, it’s possible to hear Eight Gates as a fitting tribute. In its blank spaces, it reflects the spectral quality of his greatest music, albeit sometimes for different reasons.

Title: Love and Distance
Review: With more room to breathe, the textured synthesizers come to the fore, and it is their melodic decoration that ultimately provides the saving grace. But without the electronic textures, Love and Distance is just Bryan Adams with a hip producer and a great drummer.

Title: Mo Beauty
Review: Mo Beauty becomes difficult to wade through as Ounsworth ventures further from his indie-rock roots. [Nov 2009, p.114]

Title: Working in Tennessee
Review: Now 74 and short half a lung, he's not making the best music of his life, just the best albums.

Title: The Altogether
Review: Unlike previous albums, The Altogether doesn't really take the listener on some mind-altering trip. It simply throws together some half-baked novelties, some wasted and underwhelming guest appearances and a bunch of rhythmic ideas that would have sounded infinitely better a decade ago.

Title: Conference of Trees
Review: A record that thrives on its biocentric themes, it’s one you won’t want to leave behind.

Title: Vanishing Point
Review: In other words, they haven’t lost a step as a band.

Title: This Is Another Life
Review: The execution of This Is Another Life may be its best feature, but “Villain” shows Lortz is at his best when he assesses the damage, rather than splitting it sideways.

Title: Silver Ladders
Review: It’s a wonderfully rich sound palette, and one that plays to the strengths of both musicians.

Title: Break It Yourself
Review: It's this sort of wide-eyed optimism [heard on "Near Death Experience Experience"] that lends Break It Yourself immediate appeal.

Title: Glitterbug
Review: They're onto something here. [May 2015, p.115]

Title: Scorpio Rising
Review: Not so much a step in the wrong direction as a step in far too many different directions at once.

Title: Swimming
Review: Most tracks float by in a pleasant if unremarkable funk-lite haze, but there’s an overall sense of Miller being older, wiser and more at peace than before.

Title: Welcome to the Drama Club
Review: Seemingly every track... contains nothing but raw bile toward those who have wronged Alexakis. [21 Sep 2006, p.88]

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Her ultra-high, almost kewpie-doll-like voice — which sounds autotuned even when it’s not — and previous tendency toward cheerleaderesque hooks wore thin quickly and threatened to become creative dead ends. Here, she’s found ways to reshape and reinvent them — and in the process, open up a whole new realm for herself as an artist.

Title: On the Line
Review: If you like quality songwriting delivered with panache, On The Line is on the money.

Title: California X
Review: Outstanding comparisons aside, California X are certainly capable of standing on their own.

Title: Underachievers Please Try Harder
Review: Nothing exciting ever happens, no new spins on the old-fashioned pop idiom or particularly colorful lyrical images, and the record's overarching lack of adventuresome spirit detracts from the grace of its individual songs.

Title: Ideal Woman
Review: Driven by a passion to tell real, meaningful stories- without shying away from gritty topics-using their music, Skinny Diet Girl deliver with Ideal Woman a creation that has strong messages encapsulated in a brilliant soundscape.

Title: The Classic
Review: No matter how much fun it appears to be for Wasser to try on all these different hats, developing a stronger focus on soul--or doo-wop, or girl groups, or R&B--would improve the impact considerably.

Title: Groove Denied
Review: The entire affair has a bewitching ease, an effortlessness absent from Malkmus’s artistry since the days when he wanted to name his solo debut Swedish Reggae. [Apr 2019, p.58]

Title: Culture II
Review: Culture II was never going to be a modest affair, in which three self-effacing twentysomethings quietly enumerated their blessings. Apart from some anxiety (“Tryna be like the Carters/Gotta be like the Carters” – Too Playa) and exhaustion (Work Hard), Culture II is wall-to-wall diamonds, watches, cars, chains, brands, fashion houses and exotic fauna.

Title: The Sellout
Review: The real problem with The Sellout is that it, in fact, wants to be a sellout but isn' a very good one. These blatant attempts to cash on famous names are weakest tracks here.

Title: Those the Brokes
Review: Redundant, needlessly long, Those The Brokes rarely matches the 60s California-dreamin' good-vibes pop of its successful self-titled predecessor.

Title: Game Theory
Review: It is an excellent album that has taken them seven long years to finally get to, but those are seven years that have been evidently well spent: After years of mediocrity and being, to some degree, marginalized -- just when the world needed them -- The Roots are back like never before.

Title: How to Get To Heaven From Scotland
Review: Moffat's drawn from a more experimental palette, illustrated nicely on his fine outing with ad hoc backing band The Best-Ofs. [Spring 2009, p.72]

Title: Time Being
Review: Thankfully, a Sexsmith misfire is a rare phenomenon, and the majority of this album is additional testament to his brilliance.

Title: Communion
Review: While he’s tugging at strings that have been otherwise picked up by the stable of Berlin’s PAN (M.E.S.H., Helm, and Visionist) or his Tri Angle labelmates past and present (Arca and Lotic), his extreme repetition of these familiar sounds pushes them euphoric.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: Ultimately, Mount Kimbie strip away any musical excess on Love What Survives, and leave raw vivid emotion.

Title: Before I Self Destruct
Review: If Destruct qualifies as a pleasant surprise, it’s only because 50 Cent’s last few releases set the bar so low. Still, for the first time since The Massacre, it’s once again intermittently fun to root for the bad guy

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Twista's overshadowed by West, but with jacked-up soul tunes such as Overnight Celebrity the result, who cares?

Title: General Dome
Review: The best tracks strike a raw nerve shared by Wye Oak and Battle's premiere efforts. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.86]

Title: Ashes Grammar
Review: Easily the blissful equal of jj or Memory Tapes, A Sunny Day In Glasgow are diffuse enough to avoid easy classification, and Ashes Grammar is easier to enjoy than it is to write about.

Title: Mission Bell
Review: Mission Bell, his fourth album on Blue Note, sharpens the payoff.

Title: You Should Be So Lucky
Review: Sung tentatively, a la Randy Newman. [Jun 2014, p.98]

Title: Matador
Review: Matador is a precise work of outstanding talent. While it may recycle the emotive wild card a little too often for some, any keen ear will be able to tell you this isn't some half baked solo project.

Title: Dreamcar
Review: Ultimately, while DREAMCAR's debut surely exists as a byproduct of No Doubt and Havok's various successes, the album stands on its own, magnified by each bandmember's most charismatic elements.

Title: Here If You Listen
Review: Here If You Listen is never less than gorgeously meditative, and in its cloudy, impressionistic swell bobs flotsam of unusual beauty. [Dec 2018, p.88]

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: The handsome melodic hooks and sturdy roots-music grooves, some of which are downright Tom Petty-ish, provide a hard-won equilibrium in songs about searching for relief from unspecified ailments.

Title: Drift
Review: There are sonic Easter Eggs for a thousand listens here, and it would take six pairs of headphones and an equal number of high-grade strains of weed to track them all down. Happy hunting.

Title: Workaround
Review: This is her most ambitious record yet.

Title: Neck of the Woods
Review: Structural over-tinkering is endemic on Neck of the Woods, an album that Silversun Pickups claim was inspired by horror movies; if so, they're the kind of horror movies where you wait a long time for twists you can see coming a mile away, with the visceral impact all but diluted by a glossy CGI sheen.

Title: Interplanetary Class Classics
Review: A wild work of twisted genius and more fun than rabies, that's for sure.

Title: Past Life
Review: It’s doubtful anyone will stroll about humming these tunes, but so too, it wouldn’t be at all surprising to find there’s something about them that’s all but impossible to shake.

Title: Dean Wareham
Review: It’s an album that humorously but honestly explores the tensions that arise in any long-term relationship, however in this case, the pressures--financial, political, or otherwise--seem to be coming more from without than within.

Title: Is This It
Review: Not since Oasis in their gloriously unstoppable and unapologetic heyday have we been given the opportunity to embrace such straight-ahead, ebullient, desire-fuelled guitar music.

Title: Wilderness Heart
Review: For a band that has made jammy excess and hippie-fied eccentricity vital parts of its musical DNA, the relative straightness of Wilderness Heart sometimes comes at the expense of distinctiveness.

Title: Amber

First up is “Funeral,” a swirl of blackened sludge that moves at the pace of, well, a funeral procession.

Title: C'mon, C'mon
Review: One of the best commercial rock albums of the year so far, and the sort of quality work that should dispel any skepticism about Crow's current hyper exposure.

Review: Confusing, in a fun way.
