Review: It's fantastic.

Title: Don't Look Down
Review: Even a goofy Eminem cameo (the "Allen Iverson of safe sex") can't save "C'mon Let Me Ride" from sounding like an over-the-top hookup plea, and "Final Warning," a domestic-violence drama, feels vaguely like tabloid fodder.

Title: Black Radio 2
Review: What began as a series of bold experimentations dressed in a warm fuzzy melding of genres feels half-baked second time around.

Title: What We All Come to Need
Review: Over all the album is pretty decent and enjoyable in its context. When it feels mediocre, it’s because the ideas, which once made this band and many post-metal bands so ahead of their time, have been caught up to.

Title: Push and Shove
Review: Push and Shove is a celebration of No Doubt's love for all things 80s pop and the Southern California ska scene.

Title: American Wrestlers
Review: Although there’s a vogue for the vintage production techniques and comfortable imperfect noisiness that pervades the record, it doesn’t always do American Wrestlers justice.

Title: Anthem
Review: Often lives up to its title, but they ought to find a kind way to break it off with the horn section. [Jul 2003, p.110]

Title: Awfully Deep
Review: It’s Manuva’s startling honesty which first impresses.

Title: Picture You Staring
Review: The best offerings here are “Blind Faze” and “2 Shy”, Fleetwood-fashioned tracks that sway playfully, celebratory in their own modest way. The rest doesn’t hit hard enough, and doesn’t even really seem like it wants to.

Title: Eyes Open
Review: Eyes Open is far from a horrible album. It’s easy to listen to, it’s melodic, and it’s well-read. But you’re a strong (or naïve) listener if you can get past the calculation, the number-crunching, the crassness with which Lightbody has taken aim at the MySpace demographic.

Title: Don't Stop
Review: Indeed, Annie’s given us a few winning singles but also a lot of glitz that can probably be ignored after one listen or two.

Title: Dear God, I Hate Myself
Review: New listeners will be immediately confronted with a couple of very catchy, horror-laced new wave anthems about fatal beatings and bulimia, and make that perennial first-Xiu-Xiu-experience decision: Do I buy this?

Title: Foam Island
Review: Sounds at times as much like an audio documentary of Cameron's Britain as a collection of electronic songs. [Oct 2015, p.62]

Title: Waiting For You
Review: Over half of the album's songs are filled with Robinson's bittersweet longing, brilliantly paired with some of Martin's most detailed, creative, and accessible production work.

Title: Human Animal
Review: The most impressive part of this album is that, throughout its entire tuneless, dissonant thirty-three-minute duration, Human Animal is rarely boring; it's filled with cool sounds.

Title: Somewhere Under Wonderland
Review: Somewhere Under Wonderland teems with lyrics full of rambling travelogue and mystical gobbledygook. Mr. Duritz sings them confidently, in a voice that’s not as laden with meaning as he seems to think, and preserving his shambolic nature.

Title: Morning World
Review: The album skates from tumbling tracks like “Pink” and “Morning World”—which are reminiscent of the slightly math indie-rock sound of the solid Polyvinyl band Aloha—to a jam like “It Starts At The Water,” which features static washes floating in and out of the atmosphere while an underground buzz burrows beneath a simple, chugging beat.

Title: Listen
Review: Listen throws a helluva lot at the wall, and not much sticks. [Oct 2014, p.89]

Title: Twins
Review: The music on Twins is more of the fantastically great quality we've come to expect.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Wide-eyed self-searching is this record's predominant mode, which Fleet Foxes do both lyrically and sonically, reveling in the process of discovery.

Title: Enemy Mine
Review: The record will prove inaccessible for those seeking a retread of the members’ more famous projects but works when approached on its own terms.

Title: Life is Good
Review: Life Is Good, finds him humbled and reflective after his high-profile divorce from Kelis. This doesn't diminish his impact, as these songs mix anger, nostalgia, and insight.

Title: Anvil Is Anvil
Review: Thoroughly enjoyable from beginning to end, the band have stuck to their formula and produced another decent if less-than-outstanding record.

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Starting with irresistible lead single 'Pork and Beans', a chunk of Weezer’s sixth album delivers the band’s trademark combo of crushing power chords, pop-culture references and a healthy dose of ironic self-ridicule.

Title: Blackstar
Review: At 41 minutes, Blackstar is a more concise statement than The Next Day and a a far, far more intriguing one, enticing you to follow Bowie further down this freshly-rediscovered, individualistic path where sonic surprises lurk around every corner--a journey that, at times, is not for the faint of heart. [Jan 2016, p.104]

Title: Conatus
Review: Slashed by shards and shadows, Conatus is Zola Jesus' best album to date.

Title: A Chorus of Storytellers
Review: Admirable attempts are made to emulate tourmates Lymbyc Systym on Blank Pages, but they fall short of that band’s visceral energy and edge.

Title: The Terror
Review: It's a dark, repetitive, uncompromising record, full of challenges and threats. [No. 97, p.51]

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: Bird has developed a finesse for off-kilter pop that takes mortality, confusion, and unexpected realizations as its subject, shaping them all into songs that are catchier, by their own terms, than most of Top 40 radio.

Title: LUMP
Review: Both artists sound far more liberated here than on each of their separate solo projects; it’s a collaboration many will want to continue.

Title: World, You Need a Change of Mind
Review: It's certainly a brave move to furnish it with such exotic pieces, but one that pays off beautifully. [Apr 2012, p.81]

Title: A Love Surreal
Review: Pleasingly, A Love Surreal eschews the idea of calling in favors, instead laying bare Bilal's own songwriting and production prowess.

Title: Thanks for the Dance
Review: While there's nothing radically off-blueprint in the finished article, it's obvious that every note has been pored over with love and respect. [Jan 2019, p.88]

Title: Shadow Temple
Review: The coolest thing about this mess of orgiastic sound is that it's totally possible to envision it being played live; it feels present, inside your skin, under your muscles, and inside your veins. Shadow Temple is physical music that evokes the spirit world; it rocks, but it soars too; creating a soundtrack for some kind of apocalypse.

Title: TRST
Review: Trust have a problem in Robert Alfon's unengaging, reedy mid-range quiver of a voice. [Dec 2012, p.114]

Title: Athena
Review: Athena announces a major talent in Sudan Archives. It’s original, exhilarating and unafraid to defy genre.

Title: Automata I
Review: Automata I is excellent on its own; its writing, production, and performances are all top flight. Additionally, it whets the appetite of anticipation for part two.

Title: Nothing Is Wrong
Review: Taylor's current side project, Middle Brother, shows his wilder, less studied side; this tuneful but sometimes bland set could use more of that.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Murder of the Universe
Review: Apologists will see it as a paranoic update of the doom-rock blueprint laid down by King Crimson and Amon Düül. Anyone else will be reaching for the paracetamol.

Title: Loyalty to Loyalty
Review: Loyalty is more low-key than its predecessor and less focused.

Title: Spooked
Review: A collision of Dylanesque surrealism and Bert Janschian finger-picking. [Nov 2004, p.114]

Title: SweetSexySavage
Review: A distinctly contemporary album that is in conversation with trendy, critically acclaimed R&B.

Title: Language
Review: Language is quite an impressive debut. Zulu Winter masterfully juxtapose adventurous and sexualized production with [mostly] touching, sorrowful songs. In other words, it's something you can dance to in public and reflect on in private. That's not an easy balance to maintain, but Zulu Winter does it well here.

Title: Praxis Makes Perfect
Review: Each of these 10 songs is a piece in the Feltrinelli puzzle, resulting in an album whose ambition suitably matches its subject’s big ideas.

Title: Crack-Up
Review: It confirms that rarest of achievements: a group somehow hanging on to the essence who they are, while pushing their art into thrillingly unforeseen places. [Aug 2017, p.99]

Title: Further
Review: Eclecticism has always been the strength of the Chemical Brothers and with their seventh studio album Further they continue to develop musically.

Title: PiÃ±ata
Review: Piñata comes with just enough to reduce the daunting 17-track length to a non-factor, although it drags a bit with overt nostalgia toward the fourth quarter.

Title: Pain Is Love
Review: Ja Rule's only real gift is for crafting undeniable pop hooks. That talent is underrated, but it still does little to cover up the rapper's derivative lyrics and crassly recycled 2Pacisms.

Title: Felt
Review: Abrasive textures win out over melody, and the odd flashes of In rainbows-era Radiohead only serve to underline the inaccessibility of the rest of the material. [Apr 2018, p.115]

Title: SMiLE
Review: The new Smile not only justifies its bearing, but also serves as a major triumph.

Title: Another One
Review: The whole mini album glows with a kind of stoned satisfaction; a peace of mind that can be found in even the most tumultuous of relationship struggles.

Title: Do Things
Review: Full of campy affectation presented with a shiny flourish, 'Do Things' is not fundamentally a bad album, but the constant happy-go-lucky nonsense, along with the un-imaginative songwriting, just seems a little contrived.

Title: Prog
Review: It's not likely this music will age spectacularly well, but so what?

Title: Way Down Low
Review: Way Down Low rivets with a fluid emotion lingering on Edmonson's subtlest articulation.

Title: Memories Are Now
Review: Memories Are Now is an inventive nine-song affair. [Apr 2017, p.112]

Title: Feed The Fire
Review: Certainly there are moments where you wish it’d venture down different paths--it’s Lindahl’s “Killer” record although Promise’s true killer is perhaps yet to come--but mostly it just feels good to watch this ruby red, Monster world burn.

Title: Love vs Money
Review: The-Dream has definitely bypassed the sophomore slump with "Love Vs. Money." The songwriter-cum-singer pushes the envelope production-wise (incorporating more of his Prince influences, among others) as well as lyrically.

Title: Here's to Taking It Easy
Review: There's no particular deficiency, but the new approach pushes the Brooklyn-based Athens, Georgia, band closer to the middle of the road than ever before.

Title: Highway Companion
Review: For about half of “Highway Companion” Mr. Petty’s reticence opens the songs to a sense of mystery. For the rest, he just sounds reserved and cagey, singing about restlessness but sounding all too settled. [24 Jul 2006]

Title: Fly or Die
Review: Fly Or Die has more in common with 10cc and XTC than it does Common.... Prog-pop album of the year. [Jun 2004, p.91]

Title: Patty Griffin
Review: Patty Griffin is a remarkable portrait of the artist and the experiences that informed these songs, and even by the high standards of her body of work, it's something special and is a potent reminder of her status as one of America's signature singer/songwriters.

Title: Modern Pressure
Review: As busy as things get on Modern Pressure, the less kinetic moments are afforded ample time to shine, with some of the LP's strongest bit arriving via breezy, sunset-ready, two-lane highway-worthy jams like "Roya" and "Impossible Green."

Title: Do You Want the Truth or Something Beautiful?
Review: This time the Mickie Most-omatic (phasers set to Winehouse) has dredged up someone so inauthentic she makes Duffy look like Johnny Cash.

Title: Ruins
Review: There is pain here. The results, though, are delicious. [Feb 2018, p.97]

Title: I'm New Here
Review: Not all of it works...But, as a radical overhaul of a career, it's a brave, brilliant and highly personal statement. [Mar 2010, p.83]

Title: Omni
Review: Producer Joe Chiccarelli curbs their proggy tendencies in favor of chromed-out, geometrically precise arrangements embedded with bull's eye melodic and instrumental hooks. [Jul 2010, p.115]

Title: Undertow
Review: This isn’t so much a progression as a rebirth.

Title: Napa Asylum
Review: So, this may be Sic Alps' best album to date.

Title: Imperial Wax Solvent
Review: A superb new Fall album.

Title: On Top
Review: One of the year's best knock-down-drag-out rock 'n' roll records.

Title: A Moment Apart
Review: While A Moment Apart has the foundations of a great album, ODESZA fall slightly short of the mark.

Title: Outside
Review: It's a record that captures their visceral live energy, always the band's strongest point, which was largely lost on the studio lapidary of their LPs. [Year End 2010, p.71]

Title: In a Warzone
Review: There’s a good deal of filler on In A Warzone, to be sure, but fortunately there are still some rewards awaiting those who stick it out.

Title: Ghostory
Review: It's an uninspired ending to what is generally a sharp, full-bodied collection of tracks from what is now an equally sharp, full-bodied duo.

Title: Glassheart
Review: Granted, much of the record is still given over to quaking ballads like Fingerprint--an area where Adele now has the advantage--but several tracks demand attention.

Title: Totale Nite
Review: It's fascinating territory and Merchandise sound like a band still exploring thier huge potential. [Aug 2013, p.73]

Title: My Old Familiar Friend
Review: A sturdy power-pop effort in the Paul McCartney vein, it projects an air of self-effacement.

Title: Britney
Review: It's enough of a reinvention to suggest that Britney will know what to do when the teen-pop phenomenon of 1999-2001 passes for good.

Title: Peasant
Review: Yet for all the tales of sonic Celtic carnage, Dawson’s sixth solo full-length, and second for Domino offshoot Weird World, is his most accessible to date.

Title: Carry Me Back
Review: Carry Me Home, the band's latest, doesn't suffer from a shortage of whimsy, but its surplus of cringe-inducing aw-shucks hokeyness is problematic.

Title: California Son
Review: The arrangements are suitably bombastic: there’s a theremin camping up the pub piano on his cover of Laura Nyro’s ”Wedding Bell Blues”. His version of Bruce Wayne Campbell’s (aka Jobriath) 1973 glam stomp “Morning Starship” really sells the wry/cosmic lyrics about a girl picking a rocket’s lock with her hairpin. ... Morrissey’s take on Joni Mitchell’s “Don’t Interrupt the Sorrow” is leaden jazz karaoke, stripping the original of all its haze and drift. The electro-stomp/harp, fading to reflective piano fade-out of his reworking of Melanie Safka’s ”Some Say I Got Devil”, makes a joke of his lifelong self-pity.

Title: Sam's Town
Review: Whatever Sam’s Town’s scant merits, the album reminds artists to be more careful about their role models—and to avoid Bono’s phone calls.

Title: Pageant Material
Review: Musgraves' willingness to address a life built on knotty contradictions give her songs resonance far beyond Golden's borders. [Jul 2015, p.82]

Title: The Spirit of Apollo
Review: N.A.S.A.'s dope beats and wet-dream collaborations make Apollo an absolute must-have. [Jun 2009, p.111]

Title: Big Fish Theory
Review: It makes for a challenging, dystopian listen, the blade runner to everyone else’s replicant.
A sprawling, ambitious 18-track effort that's hardly the cash-in it could've been. [May 2002, p.115]

Title: Clear Shot
Review: While they haven't suddenly become a different proposition, they are exploring structure and metre. [Dec 2016, p.88]

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: It takes a few spins to fully appreciate the complexity and ambitious scope at hand here, but this is the type of album that unfolds the longer one marinates in its charms.

Title: The Bronx (III)
Review: The band's third self-titled album deviates not an inch from the brutal style that's served them well since 2002. [Holiday 2008, p.92]
The crafty alt-country singer reimagines Swift’s blockbuster pop album as a polished roots-rock disc.

Title: The Spell
Review: Bewitching from front to back. [Jul 2006, p.192]

Title: Year Zero
Review: Year Zero doesn't just fall short of the promo campaign; it doesn't even rank among NIN's most adventurous efforts.

Title: Cydonia
Review: Cydonia is a welcome return to the sensual, dubby, progressive trance that marked its best early work... [#50, p.102]

Title: The Temper Trap
Review: The Temper Trap are touched by the brilliance of Dougy Mandagi, a vocalist with a set of pipes so extraordinary he could emote a Twitter feed. [Jun 2012, p.112]

Title: The House
Review: The House is an album of rare balance and beauty, managing to evoke hefty emotions and ideas while still feeling slight and ephemeral, never forgetting that this could all slip through your fingers at any moment.

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: For an artist whose past two albums were as impeccably curated as they were produced, the non-cohesiveness of Miss Anthropocene is bit of a disappointment, in spite of the record’s highlights.

Title: A Woman A Man Walked By
Review: Together, Harvey and Parish sound confidently experimental, like two soldiers daring each other to ever more stupendous feats of history.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: Parker's vocals have taken a noticeably more prominent role, often duetting with herself rather than her husband.... Songs like 'Four Score' and 'Holy Ghost'--where Parker takes the lead--are buoyed by unashamedly gospel-inflected chorales. And it works, wonderfully.

Title: Eden
Review: Eden certainly doesn’t shy away from her unique, occasionally weird filth ... Though her naughty, audacious, sideways, silly lines keep her cutting a unique figure in the dour, depressive world of modern rap

Title: Fake It Flowers
Review: Fake It Flowers is a true evolution, a record that’s stronger and fuller than beabadoobee’s earlier EPs and exemplifies the ongoing growth of her artistry.

Title: Becoming a Jackal
Review: There's depth, sincerity and beauty in abundance here.

Title: The Mountain Will Fall
Review: There’s a dispiriting aridity about The Mountain Will Fall, which lacks the joyous eclecticism of DJ Shadow’s earlier albums.

Title: Grinderman
Review: This is not a bunch of old blokes looking to recapture their youth; rather, Grinderman sounds like a freshly hewn and rudely vigorous chunk of leftfield rock.

Title: The Dusk In Us
Review: On The Dusk In Us, we have a handful of tracks that see Converge pushing at the boundaries of their sound, even escaping it entirely. This leads to some of the most accessible, catchy, and (uncoincidentally) most emotionally resonant work of their careers.

Title: Love King
Review: As bawdy, referential, and effortless-sounding as ever, Terius The-Dream Nash takes his long-playing love affair to the next level on this third solo effort, fading snappy summer-jam contenders into seething urban-rock suites.

Title: Leona Naess
Review: Her confidence blossomed this time around and vocally, she's never sounded so good.

Title: No Color
Review: The Dodos switchback moods and rhythms never settle and that's the prime joy of No Color. [Jun 2011, p.105]

Title: Andy Warhol's Dream
Review: It's heady stuff, but it helps that the songs are catchy as hell, and once acclimated to Sensor's nasally snarl, which falls somewhere between Wreckless Eric, Bob Dylan, Kyle Craft, and Ezra Furman, it becomes easy to see why he's generating such buzz from the very same machine that he rages against.

Title: Travelogue
Review: The arrangements... are ambitious and richly textured, producing work that rewards repeated listening. [Jan 2003, p.117]

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: Albums like Kiss Each Other Clean and The Age of Adz are so giddy with compacting layers and counter layers into the already mapped-out confines of their pre-existing aesthetics that they come across like snowflakes: each one is beautiful and unique, except that the detail is too small to see and anyways there's about a billion of them shits and you have to shovel the walkway and hope public transit isn't delayed. It's distracting, basically, because nothing gets a chance to breath.

Title: Tha Last Meal
Review: Tha Last Meal, mixed and largely produced by Dre (Master P is the executive producer), manages to sidestep the déjà-vu-all-over-again pitfalls by injecting the formula with sly wit, a healthy helping of cosmic slop, and, last but not least, some mind-bending production.

Title: Random Access Memories
Review: Random Access Memories confuses, disappoints and grates.

Title: Many Colored Kite
Review: There's nothing to diminish his status as a nearly great, albeit mostly unheralded, American songwriter. [Feb 2011, p.120]

Title: Rehearsing My Choir
Review: Thrilling prospect though it may be, the result is a disaster.

Title: Love Me
Review: Love Me is a gorgeous album, through and through.

Title: Murdering Oscar (and other love songs)
Review: Although most of the songs on Patterson Hood's second solo album predate the existence of Drive-By Truckers, they'd easily fit on any of his band's records--same low-life characters, busted dreams, and black humor, rendered in solidly gothic Southern rock.

Title: Shadows Collide With People
Review: Mercifully, Frusciante has toned down the screechy howl that made his earlier work almost unbearable, and while his songs aren't quite diamond-sharp, they have evolved into soft-focus pop tunes that display a keen melodic intuition and gift for beautiful torment.

Title: Working Men's Club
Review: From the rebellious energy that dances across the album to the twelve-minute shape-shifting epic of ‘Angel’ that closes out the record with giddy excitement, Working Men’s Club don’t know how to be boring.

Title: Heathen
Review: While the soul-searching is utterly sincere, the music is only intermittently successful.

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: It's not the music that sinks Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros, it's those lyrics: well-intentioned, certainly, but as deep as the bowl on a one-hitter.

Title: With Siinai: Heartbreaking Bravery
Review: A striking stop-gap for Krug and Siinai. [May 2012, p.87]

Title: American Gangster
Review: It is, really and truly, an experience.

Title: The Wink
Review: The Wink is a high-wire act that may find more fans among, say, free jazz listeners than conventional rock lovers. But even if the scratchy destination lacks home comforts, the journey is its own thrill.

Title: Le Noise
Review: It's not a completely successful experiment, but Le Noise is certainly an important moment in Neil Young's ongoing story.

Title: A Little Bit Longer
Review: The key to its success is that it is pitched perfectly between frivolous, disposable pop and meticulous mature craft, so as the Jonas Brothers continue to grow they might wind up losing that sense of fun that is integral to their music, but with this record they hit all the notes just right.

Title: Strange Little Girls
Review: Girls isn't as pop-friendly as 1998's From The Choirgirl Hotel, but Amos's take on Depeche Mode's starkly beautiful "Enjoy The Silence" is irresistible. [Aug/Sep 2001, p.120]

Title: Seven Dials
Review: Frame's always been an old soul, and the heartfelt Seven Dials is a welcoming return. [No. 113, p.55]

Title: Fist of God
Review: 'Heartbreaker' is a great song--musical, dance-y, poppy, and interesting--that puts the other artists-in-residence to shame. All the rest is jogging music.

Title: Hot Dreams
Review: This Canadian trio dispense a slow, seductive blend of blues and country that skulks in the shadows, whispering sweet nothings before baring its fangs.

Title: Vessel of Love
Review: All in all, the songwriting and production of Vessel of Love far surpasses any expectations that might spring to mind from the Buffett-esque label "tropical pop".

Title: Two Way Monologue
Review: An unexpected delight. [Apr 2004, p.132]

Title: Almost Free
Review: It's classic Fidlar. However, while the musical style's sure to leave fans scratching their heads, peer a bit deeper and you'll see their signature's very much there--it's just, well, diluted and funkier than ever.

Title: Another One
Review: While the instrumentation gives the impression of self-bricolage, made up of materials from Mac’s own private collection under a particular washed-out filter, the lyrics derive from common property, things like fragments of old clichés and easy rhymes.

Title: Indicud
Review: Cudi’s pitchy-dawg voice remains his own worst enemy.

Title: Understated
Review: A big, gorgeous old hug of an album.

Title: Amends
Review: “She Shines” displays fleeting snippets of raw emotion over chunky guitars, while “In Time”’s surging, punchy, melodious hooks bring some recognition of greatness to the forefront, but overall, the majority of the album seems pretty content with functioning on passive, prosaic ideas with little staying power.

Title: Within and Without
Review: Greene's efforts of merging the decidedly low-key sounds of bedroom music and the urban thump of hip-hop represent a good first step in the continued evolution of the genre, but in the end, the resulting efforts feel warped by the confines of Greene's bedroom pop dedication.

Title: Lift Your Spirit
Review: As great as the tune ["Wake Me Up"] may be, it’s Blacc’s voice that hooks you. It’s substantive, searching, and full of the depth modern soul men too often lack.

Title: Manual
Review: Manual elevates more often than it wallows, and most importantly, it never fails to surprise or entertain.

Title: Family
Review: The (mostly) astoundingly energetic Family is further justification of this band's fast rise and an album The Cast of Cheers can be proud of.

Title: Family
Review: It sets Vast Of Cheers up as just another cookie cutter indie band. [Jul 2012, p.96]

Title: Trees Outside The Academy
Review: Trying too hard to mimic his band’s tried-and-true telepathy with only karaoke-level results, it's easy to see he thinks he’s run out of ways to experiment.

Title: God Bless Your Black Heart
Review: Voyeurs of the disintegration of the human condition will be able to gorge on vicarious thrills to their black heart's content. [#246, p.62]

Title: Sing the Sorrow
Review: Sing The Sorrow soars with the kind of melodies hit singles are made of, yet it somehow persists with AFI's esoteric darkness. [Apr 2003, p.69]

Title: My Shame Is True
Review: When Skiba’s on fire, he’s one of pop-punk’s best tunesmiths; but when he’s coasting, as he is throughout My Shame Is True, his songs feel less black than beige.

Title: Colors
Review: Colors is Beck at his most exuberant, concocting weird, wonderful dancefloor fillers like a mad disco scientist. Good things come to those who wait.

Title: case/lang/veirs
Review: case/lang/veirs is an understated triumph, and a stunning addition to all three songwriters' discographies.

Title: Jordin Sparks
Review: Sparks and a cast of au courant pop producers combine that sense of sparkle, striving, and her powerful pipes for an age-appropriate, uniformly pleasant release that shouldn't disappoint those voters.

Title: Moonshine Freeze
Review: The cryptic nature of Moonshine Freeze impresses when at its uncompromising best, but it can occasionally underwhelm when she favors slimmer bare-bones arrangements. Still, these marked contradictions only reveal an artist who’s allowing herself to walk on a less purposeful path.

Title: Breakers
Review: So many layers unfold to their sound that even upon repeated listens their whispered secrets still have fresh moments to uncover.

Title: Malibu Ken
Review: With its 34-minute runtime, its cartoon cover art, and the pervading levity of Tobacco’s beats, Malibu Ken may seem at first like a minor work. But there’s nothing diminutive about a record this sharply written. It’s a side project every bit as substantial as Aesop Rock’s proper albums. That it also happens to be more fun than most of them is a bonus.

Title: Supermigration
Review: Supermigration may lack some of the euphoric moments of their debut album but these have been supplanted by a more rewarding, substantial set of attributes.

Title: Egypt Station
Review: The finest songs here land immediately and hum with urgency.

Title: Lost Property
Review: It may not have the instant listenability of We Were Here, and there are parts where it gets slightly bogged down but, in the end, it is another worthy addition to their catalogue.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: Fleeting moments of genius flanked by sketchy songs... [and] curious, dense production burying Eitzel's amazing voice under layers of maudlin instrumentation.

Title: Thanks for the Dance
Review: Although the fear was that Adam would be spreading his father’s legacy too thin, each track has the weight of a completed thought, not a sketch bulked out.

Title: Chinese Democracy
Review: The first Guns n' Roses album of new, original songs since the first Bush administration is a great, audacious, unhinged and uncompromising hard-rock record.

Title: Keel Her
Review: Across eighteen tracks, no matter how long they might be, quality control is bound to be something of an issue so alongside the cracking motorik electro instrumental of 'Overtime' we do get the morose 'Women Lost In Thought' or the noise-mess of 'Missing Time' but these are small detours from what's a pretty engaging record.

Title: G I R L
Review: G I R L sounds like the work of a much less interesting artist. But if Pharrell’s goal was to bring happiness to his listeners and vibrant tunes to the charts, then by all means he’s fulfilled his goal.

Title: ONoffON
Review: Unlike the clean, jagged, self-contained post-punk being revived in New York, Mission Of Burma's art-damaged music rattles and collapses, leaving amazing debris.

Title: Occasion for Song
Review: There's nothing but clouds on Occasion for Song, but rather than uninviting it's eminently listenable; an unflinching, graceful, truthful exploration of how to go on living when you've lost a friend, of how to recognize a world that suddenly seems that much darker and less hopeful.

Title: Colores
Review: An energetic and vibrant project, that is exactly what the music scene needed in such an uncertain time. One of J Balvin’s strongest projects to date.

Title: You Stand Uncertain
Review: In short, it is rare to find a producer who can craft many types of tracks so consistently well, but with You Stand Uncertain, FaltyDL has cemented himself as such.

Title: Salutations
Review: Salutations expands Oberst’s raw scratch solo Ruminations’ 10 songs into a messier, more glorious celebration of squalor and self-indulgence with a self-loathing chaser.

Title: Anthem
Review: On funkified tracks like "Get The Girl Back," the brothers expand their reach, inviting horns, handclaps, and shout-along choruses to the party. [21 Jun 2013, p.68]

Review: As ever with this band, it’s sure to be an idiosyncratic but beguiling direction, although there’s no hurry with so much to pick over on this thoughtful latest outing.

Title: Honeycomb
Review: If there's a quibble, 'Honeycomb' does lack variation of pace. Though it doesn't matter when the tunes are as consistently as good as 'Sing for Joy'.

Title: Learn to Live
Review: While Looking for Lucky incorporated some traditional elements into Hootie's brand of bland frat-boy rock, Learn to Live is strictly a mainstream country effort, and that doesn't always work to Rucker's advantage.

Title: Further
Review: The whole album works something like an expansion on the last three fuzzed-out tracks from Dig Your Own Hole. The Chems aren't in the same do-no-wrong zone they were when they recorded that stuff, but Further  brings them closer than anyone could've reasonably expected.

Title: Policy
Review: Policy is a dazzling execution of one man's crazed vision. [May 2015, p.91]

Title: Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends
Review: The sonic deviations may challenge fans who prefer that all of the band’s releases be a shade of “Yellow.” But more daring listeners will be relieved that Martin & Co. are exploring new territory.

Title: Junip
Review: More often than not, Junip can essentially be heard as an instrumental pop album with the music feeding and building off itself. After seeing parts of three separate decades together, Junip have finally worked up to what they can be at their best.

Title: M A N I A
Review: This is brave, baffling, bonkers and most importantly, absolutely brilliant. Strap yourselves in, it’s a hell of a ride.

Title: The Only Thing I Ever Wanted
Review: Vocally and melodically, Durant aims for nursery-rhyme simplicity, sometimes to her detriment. [Jun 2006, p.100]

Artist: Thee Silver Mt. Zion Memorial Orchestra
Title: Fuck Off Get Free We Pour Light on Everything
Review: Fuck Off Get Free We Pour Light On Everything is the most personal outcry of righteous indignation they've mustered. The result is something for a broader audience of like-minded people constantly muttering 'What the fuck?' at the world at large to connect with.

Title: Synesthesia
Review: At times, Synesthesia falls short of the brainy synth rock bliss Hands aim for, and while their songs are almost unfailingly bright and fizzy, they're not always especially distinctive. Still, even the least memorable tracks will make lots of listeners bob their heads whether they want to or not.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: [Filled with] fine, subtle moments. [No. 85, p.54]

Title: I'm Bad Now
Review: I'm Bad Now feels as much a modest masterpiece as Spring Hill Fair or Tigermilk. [Apr 2018, p.32]

Title: Microcastle
Review: The bolder sound signals that Deerhunter is now less concerned with the scarring effects of loss, conflict, and the passage of time, and more concerned with the ways to escape those things--even if that escape is fleeting.

Title: Lanterns
Review: Plan The Escape and No Crimes are largely uplifting, though the descending bass line and drum combo on Crimes sounds like Queens Of The Stone Age doing Go With The Flow Light; and pseudo-ripped Depeche Mode lyrics like, “All you ever wanted, all you ever need” make for the album’s most clichéd moment.

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: The consistently laudable performances and production of Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon make for something that appears effortless and remains engaging throughout its 70-plus-minute runtime.

Title: Coles Corner
Review: Work every bit as lush as that which recently propelled Rufus Wainwright to stardom. [Sep 2005, p.119]

Title: An Object
Review: An Object, as a conceptual aesthetic project, borders on brilliant. Yet the music itself is not immediately captivating.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: Mixed Emotions seems served just too late, and comes off as regrettably stale.

Title: Nobody's Smiling
Review: He set out to depict the pains of contemporary Chicago, but he ended up just making another Common album.

Title: Ruminations
Review: It features the Bright Eyes/Desaparecidos frontman alone with piano, harmonica and guitar, putting down songs never quite intended as an album. This sparseness means that the focus on Oberst is tight--maybe too tight. [Nov 2016, p.90]

Title: A+E
Review: What one quickly realises is that this is an accomplished record.

Title: Secret Wars
Review: Secret Wars is more than a good album. It's an incredible experience, taking you out of your daily life into a mysterious and mind-changing space.

Title: Hobo Rocket
Review: The claustrophobia of recording on a farm in western Australia may have contributed to Beard, Wives Denim‘s concision, whereas Hobo Rocket is a more freewheeling response to modern psychedelia.

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: His wordy narratives get hazy at times, but Sunday succeeds as a whirlwind tour through an overstuffed brain.

Title: Travellers in Space and Time
Review: 1960s-obsessed power-poppers discover the '70s. Time travel indeed. [July 2010, p. 102]

Title: Pleasure
Review: They are less successful when they step beyond these templates--the trippy "Surface" doesn't quite come off-- but this is a strong set. [Oct 2011, p.95]

Title: Tender Madness
Review: The appropriately titled Tender Madness, more or less backs that notion [go big or go home] up with 12 emotionally charged slabs of Foster the People- and Killers-infused highway anthems, of both the fist-pumping and soul-searching varieties, that flirt with mainstream architecture yet retain enough of a ramshackle, post-slacker luster to appeal to fans of Weiss' previous outfit.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: Like all of R.E.M.'s most recent albums, Collapse Into Now is flawed; a reflection, I'm speculating, on the fact that that band's working process is now flawed.

Title: Divine Providence
Review: As it is, Divine Providence is very good rather than truly great.

Title: Fatherfucker
Review: Some say electroclash. Wrong. This is rock and roll. [#5, p.103]

Title: Oxnard
Review: It’s less cohesive than the high watermark he set with Malibu, but hitching a ride back to Oxnard is a freewheeling and occasionally exhilarating quest into Paak’s sonic curiosity.

Title: Shangri-La
Review: Musically however, Shangri-La keeps things fairly light and upbeat, with plenty of memorable, chanted vocal hooks and a satisfying mixture of live and sequenced instrumentation.

Title: I Could Be Happy
Review: I Could Be Happy's covers vary so widely in quality that, in order to thrive, Nouvelle Vague may need to put their original concept aside for good.

Title: Athena
Review: This album explores that idea of opposites attracting and co-existing within one entity. It’s also a powerful, confident pop record tooled up to compete with the heaviest hitters (Paul White’s production is key, as it has been for Danny Brown and Charli XCX) while occupying its own uniquely ambivalent and querulous space. [Nov 2019, p.60]

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: What makes Ryan Adams so stunning is both its substance and restraint. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.73]

Title: In Love With Oblivion
Review: In Love With Oblivion is generic in the best sense of the term, a record that blasts a bright light through its otherwise dead sources.

Title: Golden Age
Review: Golden Age mines that elusive ground between the way things were and the way they're remembered, set to hypnotic acoustic and electronic instrumentation. [No.99, p.55]

Title: The General Strike
Review: The [same] sort of Clash-meets-Green Day agit-protest skate-punk Anti-Flag have been making since 1996. [May 2012, p.90]

Title: Snow
Review: There’s a moment in virtually every song where a single loose strand seems to break free and float skyward and it’s there, in the languid sway, where Snow truly takes hold.

Title: Moonfire
Review: There's plenty to enjoy.

Title: SVIIB
Review: SVIIB is a memorial, yes, but it's a glorious one. [Mar 2016, p.107]

Title: Kings Ballad
Review: Muldrow’s wonderfully flighty reverberations allow the listener to grow, to mature with her, to continually learn and blossom and thrive through the music.

Title: The Airing of Grievances
Review: This sense of being aware of our own impending death leading to a heightened sense of life sums up perfectly The Airing of Grievances, an album that bemoans the past, shrugs it's shoulders and raises a glass to the future.

Title: Weighing of the Heart
Review: Weighing of the Heart is, to me, an unripe album. The recording is slick and the mix is by the guy who mixed the last Gorillaz album, but I just don’t feel any outstanding music-making talent or skill. I see a marketable product.

Title: Dear God, I Hate Myself
Review: Xiu Xiu’s Dear God has at least three memorable post-punk anthems, including album opener “Gray Death.” For the most part, though, the album is a series of challenges.

Title: Blues Funeral
Review: Points in a direction that he'd almost certainly be wise to follow on future projects.

Title: 18 Months
Review: Harris's production has become increasingly homogenised and, despite the array of vocalists, everything here risks sounding the same.

Title: Sun Coming Down
Review: Sun Coming Down is succinct without being rushed.

Title: This Is My Dinner
Review: Yes, these are songs, supposed expressions of a character, but they are as artless, discursive, and slapdash as a to-do list or a diary entry; the central character seems to be only a deep sense of self-pity in need of external validation.

Title: Eat the Elephant
Review: Eat the Elephant is engaging, atmospheric rock done right with intelligent lyrics and ambitious themes.

Title: Sleepless
Review: It's an album that takes pleasure in its capacity to quietly, seductively surprise. [Aug 2018, p.28]

Title: Magic Time
Review: Missteps aside,  Magic Time delivers that familiar blanket on a chill winter’s day vibe, and Morrison fans will thankfully bury themselves under it.

Title: The Mysterious Production of Eggs
Review: Although The Mysterious Production of Eggs lacks the gleeful variety of Swimming Hour, it is obvious that Bird has created his most cohesive statement to date.

Title: What a Terrible World, What a Beautiful World
Review: While retaining the warmth and intelligence that has served them so well thus far, What a Terrible World… finds the five-piece at their most wide-ranging.... A fine return.

Title: Veckatimest
Review: Awesome in scope and execution, it's an album that's ultimately easier to admire than it is to love. [Jun 2009, p.108]

Title: Host
Review: Notably, the record is without the pair’s usual darkness, but ‘Host’ feels organic and true, like the first day of spring after a winter full of rain.

Title: Orcorara 2010
Review: It's ultimately a deep, unsettlingly immersive experience, yet it sanctions an almost unbearable intensity to be buoyed by a hard-won acceptance.

Title: Ex Lives
Review: Though the stouter vocals have given the band more confidence for moments of melodic bombast, occasionally they sound out of place.

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: When Smith gets a little feistier (his last resort), the songs feel more ambitious; but it’s the more minimal, quiet ones that hit home emotionally.

Title: Smile
Review: Near the album’s close, the psychedelic insanity of Ka Re Ha Te Ta Sa Ki is a whirlwind of pounding drums, circular chanting, spasmodic guitar noise and violent soloing that perfectly exemplifies Smile’s fusion of panicky, heavy abrasiveness and lush, melodic and dreamy sprawls.

Title: The Fiery Margin
Review: Startlingly original and yet somehow a nostalgic comfort in these worrying times, Roberts is one of the best we've got.

Title: Hopes and Fears
Review: The continual sense of aesthetic, structural and emotional conservatism constantly makes the listener feel short-changed, Singing Tom persistently pleading his own honesty and kindness and suitability and weakness.

Title: Emoh
Review: Emoh is full of quiet lyricism and Nick Drake beauty.

Title: Civilians
Review: While his unapologetically Dylan-esque vocals grate on weaker tunes, gems like the softly rollicking 'Time is a Lion' allow Henry to step out with a quiet roar. [Oct 2007, p.104]

Title: The Calcination Of Scout Niblett
Review: Calcination is a harrowing, emotionally draining 51 minutes; it can’t be judged on anything but its essences lyrically and musically, making it an abundantly successful endeavor.

Title: Demolished Thoughts
Review: With Demolished Thoughts, Thurston Moore solo albums have become more than fields of noise throwaways spiked with the occasional gem, more than Sonic Youth stopgaps.

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: No doubt they know to bury weaker material; the last few songs are less memorable.

Title: Alaska
Review: Daniel Tashian appears to be one of those songwriters from whom melodies simply pour, and there's barely a misplaced chord in this perfect miniature.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately is both vast and packed with detail. The songs expand and contract, one minute blasting open with the melodrama of a Roy Orbison ballad, the next zooming in with surgical detail as Hadreas describes ribs that fold like fabric, a tear-streaked face, an instance of post-coital petty theft.

Title: Fucked Up Friends
Review: Though the ideas can start to redundantly plod by the album’s finale, Tobacco’s quality control remains high throughout.

Title: Feast of Wire
Review: This is Calexico at their finest. [March 2003, p.86]

Title: Surf
Review: A warm, evocative pop-soul-jazz album that comes straight from the heart.
An effort largely filled with breathy, elevator-ready ballads, and jazzy uptempo ditties that never quite reach their potential. [12 Apr 2013, p.72]

Title: We All Belong
Review: They're totally authentic about being inauthentic. Like Guitar Bob, that makes them easy to love.

Title: Holiday
Review: More variety would help his cause, but Holiday is a graceful, emotionally affluent debut.

Title: American Interior
Review: It isn't quite as lovely as 2012's Hotel Shampoo and it isn't as otherworldly as his 2005 solo debut, Yr Atal Genhedlaeth, but it does manage to push his freewheeling spirit to the fore throughout and there truly is a sense that journeys long and important are being taken within and alongside the music

Title: Birthmarks
Review: Savor Luke Lalonde's chirpy blurts on "Needle" and "Ocean's Deep;" they're soon replaced by increasingly ironed-out dance pop that goes through unfortunate puberty over 12 tracks, from good to bad to worse. [No. 97, p.53]

Title: God Level
Review: These are tragic celebrations, Dionysian seances for the most schizophrenic of times. [Sep 2018, p.66]

Title: Ghosts I-IV
Review: A stunning collection of 36 instrumental tracks that is one of the most varied and ambitious releases of Reznor's career. [May 2008, p.104]

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: Now with his fifth album, Beam may not have abandoned his roots, but he's certainly stretched far beyond them.

Title: Gallipoli
Review: Gallipoli is the most acoustically rich Beirut album to date, with studio buzz and random dissonance deployed as musical texture more than ever before. [Mar 2019, p.35]
Jaar's samples might not seem obvious, but 2012-2017 can feel generic. Most tracks are just looped soul samples fastened to heavy kicks. They might be uplifting if they didn't feel so utilitarian.

Title: Up on the Ridge
Review: Dierks Bentley epitomizes the New Nashville ideal, but on Up on the Ridge he goes old-school with a set of acoustic bluegrass jams.

Title: Kasabian
Review: Sure this album may well sound awesome if you’ve just snorted a metre of charlie or recently breakfasted from a menu of ‘shrooms and LSD, but for sober ears it’s enough to drive anyone to drugs.

Title: Without Your Love
Review: Witchhouse appears unable to develop far beyond its basic origins, but Dexter instead hones, and in the process has produced something of a genre zenith--making slow-moving, essentially eventless music persistently compelling. No mean feat.

Title: Hitchhiker
Review: It’s this ability to take the familiar and present it in dramatically different forms, with the potential for rediscovery that this allows, which makes Hitchhiker--faults and all--a must-hear for Neil Young fans.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: Suck It blends the deliberateness of that record with the fleet-footedness of their still-stunning 2006 debut Whatever You Say I Am, That's What I'm Not and follow-up My Favourite Worst Nightmare.

Title: In a Space Outta Sound
Review: It's a perfect chill-out record, readymade for a sunny day or starry night, and it straddles the line between evolving style and signature sound brilliantly.

Title: Rain in England
Review: Rain in England, a therapy-session testimony that sounds like Soulja Boy having a Damascus moment in the champagne room over a beatless synth tide--is his least accessible.

Title: Good Arrows
Review: Such is Tunng's appeal, the ability to do the unexpected but also to make you smile with their lyrical vignettes and musical slights of hand.

Title: Hell Bent
Review: Elements of Jawbreaker, Pavement and even some riot grrrl gender politics rear their heads on their debut proper. The sound is beefier, but no less raw.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: Sir Lucious is all but hiccup-free, exceptionally consistent in its mad musical mission. Each track on the record is an explosive standalone statement within a greater unifying framework; it's an album, but these songs are pipe bombs.

Title: Libertad
Review: Velvet Revolver are a formidable collection of important figures from 80’s and 90’s hard rock, and this strong mixture of personalities lends their music a certain charisma, even when it isn’t particularly accomplished.

Title: Come Away with Me
Review: A showcase for Jones' remarkable voice, the disc captures a singer whose rare instinct for interpretation always serves the song, rather than working against it.

Title: The New Year
Review: For just under two decades, brothers Bubba and Matt Kadane have spent the majority of their time together crafting as near perfect slices of sonic Americana as they could.

Title: Plowing Into the Field of Love
Review: There isn’t a weak track on show. It makes Plowing Into The Field Of Love a truly impressive piece of work.

Title: The Dissolve
Review: Those who have managed to adjust to the attention deficit techniques of FlyLo or Prefuse 73 should have little problem in embracing Lynn's new approach, particularly as it appears to have resulted in one of the best albums of the year so far.

Title: MCIII
Review: MCIII is, in the end, the perfect sunny day album.

Title: Everything's Fine
Review: For an album so complex--one that’s simultaneously funny and fearless--it has an uncanny way of simplifying things

Title: Letters Home
Review: While Empty Days and Sleepless Nights offered songs that were entertaining enough without lyric booklet in hand, Letters Home is much more dependent on its story for emotional impact.

Title: Born in the Echoes
Review: The veteran duo and its guests are challenging and provocative throughout Born in the Echoes, even as they creatively blow up dance floors.

Title: Empire
Review: There’s no wild pretension and little real originality here, and it’s not going to change your life or make any critics’ Greatest Album lists, but it’s a lot of fun, and sometimes that’s all you want.

Title: Oceans Apart
Review: As far as the songs go, there’s not a bad apple in the bunch. And some, like Lavender and its wonderful one-note melody, or No Reason to Cry and its breezy vocals, are really terrific. But oooooh, the cheese in that sound.

Title: Threace
Review: Though their ongoing debt to the Krautrock canon remains evident, their stoner brew is now heavily spiced with influences drawn from Afrobeat, funk and space-rock. [Jan 2014, p.72]

Title: Here Comes the Cowboy
Review: Offenders and highlights aside, Here Comes the Cowboy might have been trimmed down to a solid EP or mini-album, but as a whole it just doesn't live up to the standards DeMarco set on his first three albums.

Title: The Outsiders
Review: On his fourth studio album, the terrifyingly creative The Outsiders, Eric Church pulls off what so many before him have tried: successfully merging the bedrock sounds of country music (plinking banjo, crying Dobro and a Hank Williams twang) with those of seemingly disparate genres like rock, heavy metal and especially R&B to create an utterly unique product.

Title: Blood of Man
Review: On his best album yet, Jennings goes much darker, with chilling tales of addiction, madness and loss, all wrapped up in fuzzy electric guitars, feedback and raw, distorted vocals.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: Despite the strength of this first offering, you can’t help but feel Foxygen haven’t quite reached their full potential.

Title: how i'm feeling now
Review: More than just an autobiographical document or a manifestation of Charli’s impressive work ethic, How I’m Feeling Now is her answer to questions about the viability of music in a crisis. It works better than anyone could have anticipated.

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: Let's Go eat A factory is not a brilliant album and of itself, but it does cast guided By Voices in a slightly different light. [Feb 2012, p.95]

Title: Salutations
Review: Releasing two similar albums in such close proximity might seem like a cynical attempt to double-down on the success of the first, but rather than feel like a re-release thrown together by label execs, these were the tracks as they should be; rich, nuanced, and steeped in major key melodies.

Title: Ecce Homo
Review: A challenging listen full of shifting, ephemeral environs marked by harsh, disrupting events, it's a deeply unsettling record about our ongoing becoming, and perhaps the science fiction soundtrack our brave new world deserves.

Title: Every Bad
Review: It's not a perfect album — at times it seems only a taste of the power that Porridge Radio will eventually wield — but it's an important album, a statement of purpose from a group with everything before them.

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: If you are a Beach House fan and want a shimmering soundtrack to serve as a backdrop for daydreaming, then Depression Cherry should fit the bill. For everyone else, your mileage may vary wildly, even within the span of one listen.

Title: Keep Me Singing
Review: Morrison’s voice has lost some of its sheer power, but he has retained all of its deep expressiveness, still every bit the otherworldly musical instrument it’s been for the past half-century.

Title: The Wonder Years
Review: Overall, it's hard to find much fault with The Wonder Years, and it's remarkable how cohesive it feels given that it's a compilation album.

Title: Theology
Review: Word-heavy, tune-light songs don't help... Worse, O'Connor's delicate voice can be heard puffing, straining and - horrors - singing flat!

Title: Swear I'm Good At This
Review: They've mastered the basics, but still have miles to go. [May 2017, p.26]

Title: Anchor
Review: Every move on the album is intentional and nothing is unchartered territory for Zammuto.

Title: Attack Decay Sustain Release
Review: Despite some other choice cuts, there’s no cohesion to hold it together.

Title: Okovi
Review: While it’s a release that might disengage fans of her more sub-rosa earlier material of yore, Zola Jesus has evolved into an artist where pop--born from a need to mend from trauma or otherwise--is no longer a recurrent secondary descriptor, but a primary one. Danilova has loosened the shackles that have made this remarkable metamorphosis possible.

Title: With Love
Review: As a 33-track double album, With Love has space for a small village's worth of memory lanes. [No. 100, p.61]

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: Pieces of the People We Love is a great funky dance record with guitars, and not much more. Luckily, it doesn’t need to be.

Title: Radio Retaliation
Review: Despite the politics, there are still a few more of the ethereal masterpieces Thievery Corporation have made a hallmark in the past.

Title: Twisted Crystal
Review: On Twisted Crystal, Guerilla Toss journey to the edge of the universe and grapple with the mysteries of human existence. Such adventures can be panic inducing, but here they conquer anxiety through curiosity, finding excitement and even solace in abstruseness.

Title: Romanian Names
Review: As for the claim that Romanian Names represents the pinnacle of Vanderslice's recorded output to date, the argument certainly holds water. The dozen songs are all inviting, catchy even, in their own way, and aurally consistent with the history of "sloppy hi-fi" production at Vanderslice's Tiny Telephone studio.

Title: Dark Matter Moving at the Speed of Light
Review: This is more than a nostalgia trip. [Apr 2005, p.102]

Title: Intuit
Review: Knopf only succeeds in doing more of what Menomena does best (which is to say, “better than Ramona Falls"): carving out handsomely arranged albums overstuffed with ideas.

Title: Hairdresser Blues
Review: It's a quick, occasionally dirty and sweetly affecting collection of ballads about ill-fated romance, the Bay City Rollers and letting go of love.

Title: Hard Bargain
Review: At the age of 64, Emmylou Harris has made an album as fresh and distinctive as any in her catalog, and Hard Bargain is a reminder that her evolution into a songwriter is one of the most pleasant surprises in a career that's produced rewarding music for nearly 40 years.

Title: The Pariah, the Parrot, the Delusion
Review: Though it often oversteps its own ability a few too many times, The Pariah, The Parrot, The Delusion is clear in aggression and ambition, rarely annoying listeners with undue hubris.

Title: Axe To Fall
Review: A huge array of guests help out, representing acts like Disfear, 108, Genghis Tron, and Neurosis. They are too many to list, but the bottom line is, they work. Whether they're yelling, singing, or laying down leads, they fit their songs. And that in itself is fitting.

Title: Synthetica
Review: That Metric were able to follow up their best record with another just as good is quite an achievement, hopefully something they will do again and again.

Title: Tha Carter III
Review: The album is listenable, exciting and succeeds in reigniting interest in hip hop and rappers that dedicate their life to become great MC's, not just hustlers.

Title: MAP OF THE SOUL : 7
Review: Their cultural impact is undeniable, and their work continues to push forward conversations about genre, language, and much more. There’s no telling what BTS will do next, but that’s what’s so compelling.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: Sisterworld is a slight and perhaps necessary comedown for Liars after the polar extremes of previous releases.

Title: Raditude
Review: Raditude is an album of surface appeal--there’s no heart beating inside these plasticized tunes.

Title: Reunions
Review: Isbell kicks up dust by looking backwards, and Reunions is at its best when he’s doing just that.

Title: The Book of Traps and Lessons
Review: While it isn’t as immediate as ‘Everybody Down’ or as viscerally brutal as ‘Brand New Ancients’, there is a new maturity here. Tempest is baring her soul, and scars, for the world to see – she doesn’t need to rage to get her point across. There is a powerful understatement to this album that yields more secrets with every listen.

Title: Care for Me
Review: Each note and phrase on the album is colored to depict this struggle. The instrumentation is bracing, almost as if played live for a crowd, but it has the intimate tenor and tone of Saba recording the entire thing alone in his basement.

Title: Pull My Hair Back
Review: She's made a hugely satisfying album of slinky electronic soul. [Oct 2013, p.71]

Title: The Evangelist
Review: It’s good to know he’s still in fine form and is going to keep on keepin’ on, but for now I’m more left waiting for the next Robert Forster album than able to really love this one.

Title: Open Season
Review: Don't look to Open Season to get your heart pounding or your blood flowing; it trades in less cathartic experiences.

Title: Imps of Perversion
Review: Throughout Imps of Perversion, Pop. 1280 find new ways to create their confrontational racket and the band definitely succeeds in incorporating these resh elements.

Title: Simple Songs
Review: Much like Black Messiah, a slightly more heralded return of another long-absent polymath, it rewards repeated listens, even if they’ll barely bring you closer to actually understanding it.

Title: Autumn of the Seraphs
Review: The band has crafted yet another delicate indie-pop bauble. Finely spun as it is, there's a hint of sinew.

Title: Blurred Lines
Review: Mixed with poppy tracks like "Top of the World," "Pressure" and Michael Jackson meets Hall and Oates ditty "Ain't No Hat 4 That," it's evident that Thicke has created his most fun and mainstream-friendly project yet.

Title: Ghetto Bells
Review: Sweet, subtle and quietly insidious. [May 2005, p.111]

Title: Our Version of Events
Review: Disappointingly, Our Version of Events, with the exceptions of "Heaven" and "Daddy", is as flimsy and mushy as they come.

Title: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
Review: Song after song returns to the same nightclubs for the same set of cocky put-downs and faintly misogynist come-ons. Meanwhile, the band fumbles through a sound that seems to have been assembled from pieces of retro-minded rock acts like The Strokes and Franz Ferdinand, but without the sense of purpose or history.

Title: Since I Left You
Review: It obviously has its high points and moments that drift a little more, but The Avalanches are definitely onto something with the release.

Title: Radum Calls, Radum Calls
Review: No matter the name, it's impressive that O'Hagan continues to examine this one small corner of the musical universe, still finding new ways to combine sounds in ways that please the ear and stimulate the mind.

Title: Into Colour
Review: Elsewhere the mood is flat and the tunes forgettable, Rumer’s muted voice lacking the mystique of the 70s folk artists she reveres.

Title: Let There Be Morning
Review: Let There Be Morning isn't designed to bowl you over with its size and scope; rather, it's a quietly compelling, lushly orchestrated affair that slowly but surely melts its way into your heart.

Title: A Fever Dream
Review: A Fever Dream is by far the most focused, making good on frontman Jonathan Higgs’ recent claim to NME that the songs “need each other”.

Title: This Silence Kills
Review: Cooing fragmentary, dreamlike lyrics in a fuzzy-warm purr, this young singer's kittenish vocal affectations will grate on some... [but] Dillon redeems her whimsy with promising nods towards Bjork, Joanna Newsom and Lykke Li. [Jan 2012, p.84]

Title: Leaders Of The Free World
Review: Leaders Of The Free World is an ambitious and beautiful album that confirms Elbow as one of the bands of our generation.

Title: Songs in A&E
Review: Songs in A&E retains all of the weight of its self-imposed seriousness, its capital A artistic gravitas, but unfortunately leaves the uplift of invention to the memory of Spiritualized albums it so readily evokes.

Title: My Everything
Review: The innocence in Grande’s voice helps her bring off the cliches in the more earnest material, like the soapy ballad “Why Try” or “Just A Little Bit of Your Heart,” co-written by One Direction’s Harry Styles. She proves less sure on more flip songs.

Title: Cupid's Head
Review: With each track developing at an imperceptible pace, this is subtle but irresistibly compelling. [Nov 2013, p.69]

Title: Paradise
Review: There’s an urgency to Paradise, with punishing drums and agitated guitars, but the band never quite embrace the obvious.

Title: Saturns Pattern
