Title: Working on a Dream
Review: Ultimately, Working On A Dream feels like Bruce Springsteen taking stock.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: The characters and artifacts that surround these songs feel artificial, like stock props, but the music that Del Rey pulls them through splits them open, shakes them to life.

Title: Evil Heat
Review: Their catchiest, most compelling record yet.

Title: Shields
Review: It sounds as if Grizzly Bear have spent their time away digging out the emotions that sometimes get buried beneath the technical fireworks. Speak in Rounds builds to a climax that – to use a phrase not much associated with Grizzly Bear – rocks, and furthermore rocks in a viscerally thrilling manner.

Title: Truth Is a Beautiful Thing
Review: There are ballsy moments--they just happen to be coated in the trio’s signature icy cool.

Title: Weird Sister
Review: They plug in and play their hearts out on their debut album, with twin-guitar fuzz-pop gems.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: Bankrupt! isn't nearly as devoid of new ideas as its title suggests, but it doesn't feel like quite the leap forward Wolfgang was compared to what came before it. Not that it necessarily needs to be.

Title: This is Eggland
Review: Producer Dave Fridmann has managed to effect the same kind of equilibrial magic he wielded with The Flaming Lips, bringing power and clarity to the Eggs’ churning psych-punk turmoil of guitars and synths, and balancing it with the plaintive anger of Holly Ross’s vocals.

Title: The Ugly Organ
Review: A potent piece of rock art.

Title: Moveys
Review: Flowing effortlessly between melodious vocals and blistering guitars, between reflecting on past feelings and accepting new eventualities, the majority of the album feels weightless.

Title: Holy Fire
Review: Foals remain the antithesis of a foursquare indie rock band. And yet nothing here is quite holy enough, or quite fiery enough, to live up to the album's billing.

Title: Life Fantastic
Review: A tastefully produced, solid entry into the Man Man catalogue.

Artist: Pantha Du Prince & The Bell Laboratory
Title: Elements of Light
Review: The results are at times brazenly brilliant. [Mar 2013, p.65]

Title: Primary Colours
Review: As bold and listenable as it is, Primary Colours is occasionally scattered, giving the impression that the band is trying on different sounds for size--although the fact that most of it works so well is actually more surprising than how different it is than their earlier work.

Title: The Sovereign Self
Review: On The Sovereign Self, they combine to remarkable effect. This is not an easy record, but it needs to be heard. Again and again.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Tao of the Dead
Review: While they did gain immediacy and a hint of their earlier punk energy, this is still some of the most densely constructed art-rock you're likely to hear all year, which only makes the quick process even more impressive.

Title: Maths + English
Review: The price of diversity is cohesion and there are points where Maths + English veers wildly off track.

Title: Sway
Review: The haze is fairly one-dimensional, but it's an engrossing path of melancholia. [Oct 2014, p.102]

Title: Detour
Review: None of the songs on Detour are without at least some merit, though a few are without any discernible marketplace value, save niche kiosks along I-40 or the occasional road tripper’s Spotify.

Title: Freedom
Review: Akon's philosophy of liberty also includes the freedom to reuse nearly identical hooks for 13 songs straight. That approach may bring him plenty money, but it yields only a few legitimately fun tracks, buried beneath a pile of boring retreads.

Title: Skins
Review: Skins is the sound of a band reinvigorated. [Apr 2011, p.98]

Title: Chain Gang of Love
Review: The beauty is in the album's concision and seamlessness. [5 Sep 2003, p.74]

Title: The Besnard Lakes are the Roaring Night
Review: Right now no one is making music this grand, this big, this moving with so much assurance.

Title: Lust Lust Lust
Review: Their fourth record, the stunning Lust Lust Lust, retains the Danish duo’s fetish for early pop harmony and surf guitar, not to mention shoe-gaze buzz in their concise, fuzzy bursts of tragic romance.

Title: Wooden Leather
Review: Features a more worldly sound and outlook.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: The whole package is a head-snapping reminder that when R.E.M. was on fire, you couldn't put them out with all the water in the world.

Title: Probot
Review: As rewarding as it is unpredictable.

Title: Earth to the Dandy Warhols
Review: Their sixth album (and the first on their own label) is their most self-assured set yet, veering from sparkling glam to funky New Orleans boogie by way of early Nineties shoegazing.

Title: Seeing Sounds
Review: Thematically starved, Seeing Sounds is nonetheless a sonic feast.

Title: A Flourish and a Spoil
Review: A freshly squeezed record with the pulp left in it.

Title: Assume Form
Review: For such crackling peaks, there are also times where it seems Blake has found himself at the forefront of a heady new genre, trap-schmaltz. ... Despite those shortcomings, Assume Form stands as Blake’s most coherent statement to date. The Spartan singer-songwriter tropes of his debut, the half-baked collabs of Overgrown, and the overlong The Colour in Anything fall away to reveal a more dynamic Blake.

Title: American Dream
Review: Just as the record threatens to get Too Much, as ‘How Do You Sleep Tonight’ wrings out its last notes, the crowning glory that is ‘Tonite’ kicks in.

Title: Solo
Review: Iyer structures this programme cannily, beginning with an inviting interpretation of the pop ballad Human Nature, unfolding over a rocking left-hand vamp and briefly darkening into a hypnotic drone.

Title: Autumn, Again
Review: It works as an introduction of sorts to this young band, who have a surplus of great ideas (and, hey, it's a free download). But it's little more than a starting point, a segway, an ice-breaker, to the much meatier discussion that Ashes provokes.

Title: Hair
Review: [A] feisty, psych-tinged hook up with Tim "White Fence" Presley. [May 2012, p.80]

Title: Matilda
Review: A fine line between unpredictable flair and china shop bull.

Title: Tanglewood Numbers
Review: Musically, he’s ditched the clean, plainly instrumented indie-country schlep of his previous efforts for something brassy, something downright soulful.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: Its unusual lineup of collaborators--including the Dirty Projectors’ Angel Deradoorian, percussionist Joey Waronker and Pet Shop Boys’ Neil Tennant--looks intriguing on paper, but their contributions are often barely audible; Danielle Haim’s appearance is a natural meeting of minds, however.

Title: The Beast You Are
Review: No matter who is in the lineup or what other activity Willis and Warren are up to, Big Business deliver exactly what you ordered time and time again. And that consistency is precisely what makes The Beast You Are such a thrill to listen to and carries with it a small pocket of disappointment.

Title: To Lose My Life
Review: On their debut, this trio of fashionably dour West London lads crafts wildly overwrought goth-pop weepers with choruses that would make excellent Robert Smith High School yearbook inscriptions.

Title: Skyline
Review: The production of this album in so short a time is nothing short of miraculous, and listening to it is an experience to savour.

Title: Conceived in Sewage
Review: While spirited in their performance, this brutal quartet lack the dynamism and versatility of label-mates Dying Fetus.

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: A strong contender for album of the year. ... Titanic Rising is remarkable for its breadth, effortlessly shifting from the 90-second ambient wash of the title track to Picture Me Better’s homespun take on the cosmic cowboyisms of Kacey Musgraves. Then there are Merings’ lyrics, evincing a similar shift in scale and scope.

Title: For Evelyn
Review: With its rich sonic landscape and Georgas' confident lyrics, For Evelyn is a great record, but perhaps more importantly, it also shows that Georgas is getting better and better with each release.

Title: UR FUN
Review: UR FUN is as concise, focused, and sparkling as of Montreal have ever been.

Title: The Fire
Review: Like the album's namesake, The Fire starts with a small spark that quickly builds itself into an emotional blaze that burns steadily across all 11 tracks, taking the listener on an exceptional musical ride.

Title: Tell 'Em I'm Gone
Review: It can be a little underwhelming but it is music with its heart in the right place.

Title: Dungeness
Review: The bleak landscape around Dungeness can provoke contrasting responses, and both the sense of malevolence (it’s the site of a nuclear power station) and stark beauty are well reflected on this masterly recording.

Title: Begin
Review: Many of Lion Babe’s ditties fall short of achieving anything in particular, making it a pleasant enough album, but one that is quickly forgettable.

Title: Back to Land
Review: It's the trickling-down of dusty record bins everywhere, reduced to simple essence and repeated till it hurts.

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: Sean Lennon continues to impress. [Nov 2006, p.104]

Title: Van Lear Rose
Review: Given a chance to be herself, Lynn responds with a powerful return to form. [28 Apr 2004]

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: It's impeccably well done: riffs and basslines lock together as tightly as a highway-bound engine, but, like an American vehicle, the problem is excess.

Title: In the Shape of a Storm
Review: Jurado possesses a gift for elevated simplicity, and this quality graces In the Shape of a Storm and gives its ten songs a pleasingly rounded shape.

Title: Compass
Review: Even as his piecework band stretches the sound in unexpected directions, Lidell--like a peculiar cross of Prince and Otis Redding--remains confidently true to his soul vision, creating a tense musical discourse that wrings raw emotion from each eclectic track.

Title: In the Dark
Review: At times, Parker Gispert's voice is buffed clean of any individual characteristics; at other times, it's contorted into a hackneyed imitation of Southern rockers such as Jim James. The album's best moments, unsurprisingly, are those in which the band lays off the mixing knobs.

Title: Feast of Wire
Review: This album solidifies their standing as one of the most endearingly idiosyncratic bands on the American scene.

Title: The State of Things
Review: The State Of Things will no doubt be a big hit. But if anyone ever takes the time to give it a good proper listen they will find that it’s a wafer thin album of posturing and poor word play.

Title: Walk Through Fire
Review: She's channeling her own experiences so they speak to the universal, just like the classic soul she loves. The result is an extraordinary record, one designed to be part of a grand musical tradition, and it contains enough emotion and imagination to earn its place within that lineage.

Title: Gauntlet Hair
Review: A few listens into Gauntlet Hair and its charms start to coalesce.

Title: Paper Trail
Review: He's embodied literature's most popular archetype--the survivor--by transforming his woes into a reflective, enjoyable album.

Title: Spirit
Review: You have to go back to 1993’s Songs of Faith and Devotion to find a more consistently flawless record from the band. Lyrically the trio is in top form.

Title: Palookaville
Review: Palookaville's highlights promise the sweat and smiles that have become Fatboy Slim's stock in trade, but its surprisingly dull lulls offer nothing more promising than a blank expression.

Title: Joy as an Act of Resistance
Review: IDLES aren’t being macho or destructive in suggesting that we might have to tear it all down and start again if we’re going to truly come together. This is the jarring sound of sensitivity in a new age of chaos.

Title: III
Review: Third time's still a charm with Philadelphian prog-folk contingent.

Title: Information Retrieved
Review: Even though Information Retrieved is an excellent album, it won't do a whole lot to win over anyone who has already decided that Pinback isn't for them. For everyone else, the album delivers plenty of the gloomy/sunny/plaintive/happy pop that has made them one of the more instantly recognizable bands in the indie landscape.

Title: The Secret Migration
Review: Those who like Mercury Rev like them a lot; so while The Secret Migration doesn't happen to migrate into new territory, they are the type of band that could go on making the same album forever and we wouldn't care.

Title: Candylion
Review: Qualities like intelligence, eclecticism and imagination sometimes seem to be in short supply in the music industry - Candylion encapsulates all these qualities and more and deserves a far wider audience than the cult status it will undoubtedly settle into.

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: Lacks the clever subtlety of innuendos on songs like "Can I" (featuring Tory Lanez) and "F&MU." "Bad News," "Everybody Business" and "Open (Passionate)" are the album's standouts, showcasing elements of Kehlani's strongest contributions to music thus far, and highlighting her ability to make vulnerability a strength.

Title: Dumb Flesh
Review: The totalitarian self-regard of these bombastic modular synth symphonies owes more to Queen’s One Vision than it does to Kraftwerk’s Man Machine.

Title: Humanoid
Review: With the exception of 'Hey You' and 'World Behind My Wall,' the album is melodically anemic and strangely low-key. Subtle is not a mode that suits Kaulitz.

Title: Oceans Apart
Review: The album is wonderfully cohesive. [May 2005, p.119]

Title: Rainbow Mirror
Review: For all its imposing scale, though, it lacks some of the dramatic finesse of classic Prurient. Fernow’s poetic lyrics, spoken or shrieked, have been a key hallmark of the project, and without them, these abstracted noisescapes lack the narrative character of his best work.

Title: Vulnerable
Review: Tricky hasn't planted his flag on any new territory, but he has gotten a stronger grasp of what has made him such an intriguing and important artist in the last decade. [#6, p.90]

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: For a country-punk prodigy, Loveless is only getting better with age. [Feb/Mar 2014, p.73]

Title: Petals for Armor
Review: Petals for Armor doesn’t offer up an easy redemptive arc towards happiness; it is a Herculean effort to pull yourself out of depression. But in letting us in on that effort, Williams has created something special.

Title: Ego Trippin'
Review: It's that he trivializes his own content--not the gangsta, braggadocio no one takes seriously anymore, but the pimp slime.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: Where its predecessor found Plant operating in a finely-tuned genre, Band Of Joy gives him an opportunity to explore his influences, and to colour a few choice odds and ends from the rock 'n' roll canon with his indelible mark.

Title: The Chemistry of Common Life
Review: They are like nothing you've ever heard before and everything you one day hoped you would, too strong for the charts and too corrupting for MTV.

Title: Syro
Review: What is missing is that impish, dangerous side, the famous contorted grin and all that it suggests: humour and horror, surprise and confrontation. [Nov 2014, p.89]

Title: Loyalty to Loyalty
Review: For those who can accept Willett's voice for what it is--a jagged, yet neccessarily appropriate fixture that suits the music's rough edges--Cold War Kids have made a record that will please the existing fanbase, and quite possibly earn some new pledges of loyalty. [Fall 2008, p.74]

Title: Good Mourning
Review: There's enough mayhem and murder to satisfy any Scarface groupie.

Title: The Less You Know the Better
Review: Shadow's production is wantonly flashy, but it can't mask his lack of flair.

Title: Avenged Sevenfold
Review: While straying from metal's path, they uphold its legacy of conservative politics. [Nov 2007, p.148]

Title: Infinity Overhead
Review: Its [closing track Close Company] guitars are huge, its drums are pounding, and it sums up the record perfectly: dark, sexy and gargantuan.

Title: Comfort Woman
Review: A perfect commingling of the spirits of dub reggae and mid-'70s soul and groove jazz.... NdegeOcello's finest moment on record thus far.

Title: Leave No Trace
Review: Not once does this record manage to clamber out of its self-imposed constraints of mediocrity; and for a band genuinely capable of blissful set piece tracks, that makes it mostly a somewhat distressing token.

Title: Love Is Here
Review: Starsailor is one of those wonderfully rare bands that manages to be gentle and sensitive while also rocking admirably.

Title: Electric
Review: [Producer] Stuart Price coaxes the best out of the Boys here for some of their finest dancefloor work since 1993's limited edition "Relentless."

Title: STAY DANGEROUS
Review: He doesn’t need to hop on the emo rap bandwagon and a more stoic presence is always welcome, but this feels like the first YG album that’s coasting on reputation rather than inspiration.

Title: Utopia
Review: Achingly dull, and self-regardingly solipsistic.

Title: Kill for Love
Review: Its power and poise never ceases for 90 wonderful minutes.

Title: All Mirrors
Review: All Mirrors is her boldest reinvention yet. [Nov 2019, p.30]

Title: Among The Leaves
Review: This type of rough-spun music isn't for everyone, but Among the Leaves is a valuable effort regardless of its pockmarks and dogged minimalism. Enjoy at your own risk.

Title: Blood Red Roses
Review: Blood Red Roses is as stylistically varied as its predecessors. [Nov 2018, p.37]

Title: Solo Piano III
Review: While those showier pieces grab attention on first listen, the more meditative ones slowly sink their hooks in, too.

Title: Brain Pulse Music
Review: BPM works its vibrational magic with quietude and organic peace, and comes across more like a n ancient Zen ritual. [Apr 2012, p.71]

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: It can sound almost laborious in its structural directness mixed with its lyrical opacity.

Title: Mosquito
Review: A confusing, intriguing record, then. Not their strongest, but there's a transition underway.

Title: He Was King
Review: Masterfully bleak and hyper-stylized, He Was King is music for the robot age.

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: Hesitation Marks, the new album from Nine Inch Nails, is both business as usual and remarkably prescient.

Title: Near to the Wild Heart of Life
Review: Near to the Wild Heart of Life isn't the record fans waited five years for. But backed into a corner, Japandroids have penned a truly great record filled with all the guitar hooks, shout-along choruses about nights spent drinking, sweating and longing to be somewhere else that we've come to expect.

Title: Slowly Paradise
Review: This is the organic culmination of our protagonist’s most singular travels, and he’s reached a most puzzling bliss.

Title: Lotta Sea Lice
Review: The idea of a Kurt and a Courtney making a record has a darkly funny resonance but the Nineties fantasy-rock pairing they really evoke is Stephen Malkmus and Liz Phair, the languid guitar surgeon and the causally incisive lyrical realist.

Title: I Am Me
Review: "I Am Me" has an awful lot of brooding teen-rock songs, none of which flatter Ms. Simpson's rather breathy, mannered voice. [24 Oct 2005]

Title: Flavors of Entanglement
Review: It's a cluttered affair with bleeping, buzzing lows (harshly ambient tracks like "Straightjacket" and "Versions of Violence") and a handful of humble high points in a pair of lovely piano ballads.

Title: Where Shine New Lights
Review: The album is like a gentle, sometimes terrifying solitary journey, a walk through foggy terrain with no absolute destination in mind, but one that takes the listener to places of new questions and different possibilities every time.

Title: Empty Estate
Review: It’s hard to call this a misstep at all, but its best quality is keeping hope alive for what will come next.

Title: Putting the Days to Bed
Review: It's Roderick's lyrics that really grip. [Nov 2006, p.118]

Title: No Burden
Review: As far as the music goes, rhythm guitar is the foundation here, and it ranges from Strokes-ian down strokes to slow-core. The drums are mixed prominently, giving adequate room to Dacus’ towering voice. The lead guitar is mixed oddly low, though. Many times throughout the album, when a blast of lead guitar is expected, we get it, but dang is it quiet and a little deflating.

Title: Aaltopiiri
Review: Despite the obviously electronic origins of most of the sounds, there are clearly thinking, imagining humans behind the scenes; this is about as un-clinical as electronic music gets.

Title: Perfect Hair
Review: The album does have its share of absurd, tangled, almost impenetrable lines, nasally sung patches that could definitely be called an acquired taste, and mutated, oddball production that’ll raise more than a few eyebrows.

Title: Skullsplitter
Review: Each song is so comforting, peaceful and downright beautiful that it’s like being lost in a wonderful auditory dream.

Title: Be Your Own Pet
Review: Even at its most ominous, though, the album never loses its verve or vitality. It's just one quick hit after another, a succession of aural whippets that last long after the record's over.

Title: Cat's Eyes
Review: Zeffira's facility with reeds, keys and strings ensures constantly interesting textural shifts, while the combination of Badwan's imperious, Scott Walker-esque baritone and Zeffira's varied vocal stylings recalls not just Lee Hazlewood & Nancy Sinatra but even the effervescent charm of The B-52s.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: Graves' earnest lyrics are purposely mixed far beneath the caustic instrumentals here, but when a few words do surface, we're treated to thoughtful (if only partial) confessions.

Title: Prom
Review: The nostalgia-heavy lyrical bent of some songs can read either sweet or cringe-worthy, depending on your birth date and sensitivity to sentiment.

Title: Annie Up
Review: The songwriting paints in broader strokes than the hyper-specific character studies of the debut. What the Annies lose there they gain in fuller, more ambitious arrangements.

Title: Ski Mask
Review: Perhaps Ski Mask's greatest virtue is that it demonstrates Islands' competency as a conventional rock act while dropping the occasional winking reminder that the band hasn't lost their ability to get weird.

Title: Where The Action Is
Review: Where The Action Is may not be the absolute rave-up the album title implies, but it is a remarkably incisive effort that ought to remind one and all what a singularly important ensemble the Waterboys were… and still remain.

Title: Darkel
Review: Generally there's a lightness here he'd do well to retain. [Oct 2006, p.118]

Title: Doomsdayer's Holiday
Review: Its ultimately about serving the power of the jam, an aesthetic of which Grails have a solid grap. [Year end 2008, p.82]

Title: Diamond in the Ruff
Review: It's one of those rap albums that's disappointing as often as slightly engaging, and oftentimes is hard to pinpoint exactly what's letting you down.

Title: Sparkle Hard
Review: When this album is good it’s superb--probably the Jicks’ finest yet; and when it’s less so--less focused, more haphazard and wilfully out-there--it’s still pretty damn great as well.

Title: Fishscale
Review: I'd be surprised if anybody, in any field, drops something this potent in the next nine months.

Title: Testimonium Songs
Review: By the album’s end, there’s no definable takeaway aside from the fact that Testimonium Songs would have benefited from being a true Joan Of Arc record as opposed to a small piece of a larger puzzle.

Title: Just Be Free
Review: This is music to be experienced, not read about or analyzed for political and sociological meanings.

Title: Saltbreakers
Review: Veirs here is at the peak of her game, and as refreshing as a lungful of oxygen.

Title: Faith in Strangers
Review: Faith in Strangers is long-form listening at its finest.

Title: Take Care, Take Care, Take Care
Review: Explosions In The Sky continue to tap into this special vector of imagination, emotion, and possibility, making everything that much more vivid.

Title: Channel Pressure
Review: It's an album that gets better with every play, with every peeling back of its more obvious, glossy layers. It especially repays headphone use, where each stutter, bend, warp, and pitchshift can be discovered and new subtleties can become apparent.

Title: Summertime '06
Review: Staples has so much to say in Summertime '06 that it’d be impossible to fully dissect in one listen, and his ingenious phrasing makes for a constantly amusing variety of vignettes. A record is only as good as the music that accompanies, though, and collaborative producer No I.D. delivers in spades and then some.

Title: Bushcraft
Review: Simply put, Bushcraft is the best Converge worship since the Power and the Glory dropped Call Me Armageddon in 2004.

Title: Limits of Desire
Review: Small Black successfully avoids a sophomore slump by harnessing their various sonic inclinations.

Title: Lucky Shiner
Review: Wonky beats and shimmering twisted tech melodies. [Nov. 2010, p. 109]

Title: Stone Temple Pilots
Review: Not that long ago, STP would have struggled to hit the simple sparkle of "Cinnamon," with its falling jangle and "Yeah, c'mon, c'mon" chorus. The sunshine is overdue, but it suits them.

Title: Get Ready
Review: Get Ready is one of New Order's better works, and that's saying a lot.

Title: Tooth & Nail
Review: Through its songs he conveys truths about this country in a way that few other English songwriters, if any, are able to do.

Title: Where the Messengers Meet
Review: Sad-eyed generalists with a knack for cinematic spookiness, they aspire to Wolf Parade's adventurousness, but often descend into lumbering, Interpol-style self-seriousness.

Title: As Is Now
Review: The great thing about Weller at this point is that he'll shuffle the deck every other song and often (if not always) come up with a face card. [Feb/Mar 2006, p.103]

Title: Forced Witness
Review: Forced Witness is a lovely album of '80s-ish pop, using synth and sax to find the space between Springsteen and the Bunnymen. [Sep 2017, p.24]

Title: Ouch
Review: The result is 12 exquisitely dreamlike, personal songs that also work as Krgovich's coming out album. [Nov 2018, p.89]

Title: Pang
Review: Polachek further distills her approach with a collection of deeply emotive songs that showcase her delicate vocals and intricate pop sensibilities.

Title: Loose Fur
Review: In its own fragile way, a delight. [Mar 2003, p.111]

Title: Country Music
Review: Throughout the album, Burnett's players (including guitarist Buddy Miller and Jim Lauderdale on harmony vocals) cushion Nelson's singing with warm string-band arrangements that never overpower his understated delivery.

Title: The Beautiful Stories
Review: While INVSN probably won't shock anyone sonically or lyrically, there is still definitely a spark of creativity and honest expression here.

Title: Heavy Rotation
Review: Anastacia’s voice--once described by a critic as a ‘human air-raid siren’--is still hard to love: when she reaches for the trembling high notes your first instinct is to duck under the table and lock your head between your knees.

Title: Settle
Review: Throughout, Settle will blind you with so much sheen you’ll want to tile your bathroom in it. Sadly, the London Grammar-featuring ‘Help Me Lose My Mind’ is a bit of an unnecessary cool-down.

Title: Invincible
Review: Jackson has lived a bizarre train-wreck life of mystery and tragedy, but following such a lengthy absence, Invincible just reeks of desperation and aimlessness.

Title: Game Theory
Review: If anything, the grooves have gotten tougher and funkier on Game Theory.

Title: 8 Diagrams
Review: Yeah, that’s 8 Diagrams--a knockabout set rather than a knife to the jugular.

Title: Nights in the Dark
Review: California X have a way to go as songwriters, but Nights in the Dark shows they're maturing into a top-flight heavy indie band, and if you want to hear a group that know how to make their guitars signify, this may be just what you've been looking for.

Title: Music for Insomniacs
Review: In Music for Insomniacs Berry has created a synth fantasia of dreamy soundscapes for the wakeful, but with a greater dynamism and more grandiose scale and momentum than most ambient music.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: The Crane Wife is an impressively realized song cycle.

Title: Sun Gangs
Review: With Sun Gangs it’s as if they've finished the whole cake and the house burst, bricks and mortar exploding through the sky like fireworks.

Title: Sugar Ray
Review: It's essentially more of the same.

Title: Funeral Mariachi
Review: It doesn't have to be anything more than the two things it certainly is: a tribute to a longtime bandmate and friend, one in which he gets to take part in spite of departing the planet, and a collection of songs which at different points are clever, funny, fulsome and moving.

Title: Cabinet of Curiosities
Review: He's made an album that sounds so good and authentically psych-like, and one that wraps the listener up in a warm embrace of misty melodies and cobwebbed arrangements.

Title: Seasons of My Soul
Review: [It] has the pleasing sense of an album made to the artist's vision rather than the focus-grouped demands of the marketplace: almost uniquely in its chosen milleu, Seasons of My Soul sounds like a hit album without sounding like all the other hit albums.

Title: Apar
Review: A long look in the mirror, the band’s fourth record proves an examination of reflection, best where predictable and worst where you see something surprising that doesn’t belong.

Title: Music from Another Dimension!
Review: The usual forehead-slapping decisions are here: goopy Eighties production, tired synth horns, a Diane Warren ballad.... The best thing about Music From Another Dimension! is the chance to hear Joe Perry and Brad Whitford play guitar.

Title: Fast Times at Barrington High
Review: Fast Times at Barrington High doesn't go to the hoop with every song, but it scores more than enough points to make it a career highlight, not to mention one of the best emo albums (whatever that means) of 2008.

Title: Varshons 2
Review: There's a DIY feel and bouts of slacker tomfoolery to Varshons 2. [Mar 2019, p.88]

Title: Still Trippin'
Review: Still Trippin' is, in turn, a satisfying listen for classicists and interested experimenters alike.

Title: All My Friends Are Funeral Singers
Review: It is another well-made and executed Califone album, and it stays completely true to their concept. Consistency is underrated.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: Eric Emm and Jess Cohen have produced an album is both substantially intelligent and undeniably fun in equal measure.

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: But even at its toe-tapping best, this quintet from Newcastle can’t convey a sense of passion.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: That's Oddfellow's overriding vibe, as well as its greatest asset: tighter songs and sturdier structures, with more room left for atmosphere, exploration, and subversion within them.

Title: Songs of Innocence
Review: While Songs of Innocence is more succinct, glossy and nimble than recent U2 outings, there is very little of the rawness, directness or spontaneity of youth to it--and precious little innocence.

Title: Wiretap Scars
Review: They put together nearly perfectly produced and arranged songs, tight and precise yet still urgent and fast.

Title: The Fame Monster
Review: Dirty dance-diva bundles new EP with reissued album.

Title: Sleep Cycle

By the end, it’s difficult not to feel as though you’ve overstayed your welcome.

Title: I'm Bad Now
Review: I'm Bad Now finds Nap Eyes somewhere in between their two former releases.

Title: He Thinks He's People
Review: It's almost one high point after another.

Title: Sweet Talker
Review: This might finally break Jessie J stateside, but by trying to be all things to all people, the soul is drained out of it.

Title: MCIII
Review: Cronin’s dulcet hesitance has given way to slightly meeker delivery. The hooks are there--in the engaging vocal counterpoint to a descending horn line on the bridge of "Say", for instance--but they’re difficult to appreciate.

Title: Emancipated Hearts
Review: Wareham's fragile delivery imparts an eggshell vulnerability to songs that track contemporary anxieties, such as "The Deadliest Day Since the Invasion Began", but finds its natural home in the lilt of the Incredible String Band's "Air".

Title: The Civil Wars
Review: Ultimately, The Civil Wars plays out lyrically insipid and completely oblivious to the fact that their vocals strive for meaningful but define overbearing.

Title: Neon
Review: As someone whose success has come mostly as a singles artist, Jay Sean fails to deliver anything quite as charismatic as any of his greatest hits on Neon, leaving the album feeling largely flat.

Title: Long Live the Angels
Review: Her return is lucid and uncluttered, placing all the expressiveness of her voice at its center.

Title: Tranquilizers
Review: Tranquilizers is a fitting companion piece to Velvet Change, providing two ends of the spectrum that Jones has found himself in. His evident comfort with this material is encouraging, but it’s clear that there’s still room to progress for Dog Bite.

Title: Moonlight
Review: While the rhythm section is fairly basic throughout the album, there are a few bright moments when simplistic rhythms turn into entrancing bass lines or brisk drum fills. So while these moments of musical clarity might make Moonlight worth a listen, they likely won’t warrant a plethora of repeat spins.

Title: What a Boost
Review: Complex and vibrant, What a Boost is an invigorating and engaging ride.

Title: Drill a Hole in That Substrate and Tell Me What You See
Review: A retreat from overt tale-telling makes these songs less immediate and localized but potentially more personal, both for Jim and his listeners, as he strips away the surreality and specificity and renders his murky ruminations more universally resonant.

Title: Portico Quartet
Review: A powerful, graceful album.

Title: SweetSexySavage
Review: She sometimes coasts on a singsong, nearly spoken flow that squanders the expressivity of her understated but resonant pipes. Yet haunting highlights like “Piece of Mind” and “Everything Is Yours” prove that beneath SSS’s padding, there’s a succinct, sassy, and sincere album waiting to be slimmed down to Kehlani’s own soul-searching essence.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: “I Never Learn” is a gorgeous opener, its fulsome strum of acoustic guitars graced by strings and backing-vocal cooings in anthemic manner; but from there it’s emotional pain writ large, with wan piano lines supplanted by grand, melodramatic resolutions.

Title: Stuck on Nothing
Review: The reality is Free Energy sound like ’90s rock berks Terrorvision. It’s not all woe--‘Bad Stuff’ is like an FM rock Pavement--but it makes us worry that Murphy might be losing his edge.

Title: On The Water
Review: Future Islands clearly wanted to tug some heartstrings this time around, and in the respect, On the Water is an unqualified success.

Title: Feedback
Review: Their most immediately pleasurable album. [Sep 2006, p.104]

Title: Madame X
Review: The pace plods on some mid-tempo tracks, but overall this is a personal, politically-charged mix of dark thoughts and good vibes. [Aug 2019, p.88]

Title: The Pinkprint
Review: If The Pinkprint is a letdown compared to The Blueprint, then Minaj brought it on herself. However, as a breakup album that takes heartbreak (or, more specifically, the feeling of having an infinite amount of love to give to an appreciative person) in every direction possible, it provides a template worth imitating.

Title: Room Inside the World
Review: This balance of immediacy and distance makes Room Inside the World Ought's fullest work to date. The members of Ought like to be out there in the Montréal music community, playing for and with people they know. You can picture these new songs suffusing a live setting, where bodies let go.

Title: Annual
Review: Annual feels like a one-paced, indistinctive first step into a new world and one that is begging for just the odd about-turn to maintain interest.

Title: Witching Hour
Review: Ladytron have decisively transcended any particular froth of trend that may have sprouted up around them. [#17, p.98]

Title: Future Politics
Review: It's the anti-hygge of records: cold, hard, and anything but comfortable. [Feb 2017, p.111]

Title: The W
Review: The W is a sonic gestalt that exists somewhere between the Queensbridge projects and OutKast's Stankonia, down the block from Lee Perry's Black Ark studios, two floors below A Tribe Called Quest's Low End Theory.

Title: Loud Like Love
Review: It’s a disappointing yet completely listenable effort that suffers for being nothing more than a new Placebo record.

Title: There Is A Place
Review: Note Eaglehurst/The Palace, an ecstatic workout that mythologises a shared house of Brit jazz tyros as an inspiringly sacred space. [Dec 2018, p.92]

Title: The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here
Review: Nothing sounds new, and yet it has no parallel in the old Alice catalog, because they were just so much weirder than we remember.

Title: The Worse Things Get ...
Review: The melodies are forthright, the arrangements are hand played, and Ms. Case’s voice is open and robust, with the richness of prime Linda Ronstadt and Patsy Cline.

Title: Instrumental Tourist
Review: Despite scattered flashes of brilliance, too often it's an album that feels unambitious, as though it's content to dwell in the middle ground where the two producers' back catalogs intersect rather than forge something new.

Title: Unbreakable
Review: Unbreakable makes small nods to adult pop, peppering the processed music with tasteful piano and light guitar riffs and keeping bright, danceable grooves to a minimum. But the material stinks worse than ever.

Title: Saturation III
Review: Saturation III is the shortest, hookiest, and best, though, for no better reason than they are cooking by now, pithily commenting on police brutality, drug addiction, and receiving head.

Title: Pines
Review: Pines dances between Sudol's ballad-heavy debut, One Cell in the Sea ("Sad Sea Song"), and her more dance-ready sophomore effort, Bomb in a Birdcage ("Sailing Song"), and Sudol's subject matter has shifted further from pining for a man and closer to self reflection and possible happiness.

Title: A Thousand Thoughts
Review: A Thousand Thoughts is a compilation, and it has to be approached without expecting consistency or some sort of discipline.

Title: Ode to Sunshine
Review: Loose, raw, a bit funky, it illustrates the band's knack for creating new-but-classic-sounding songs and getting them down on disc with a sizzling live feel. [Aopr 2009, p.87]

Title: The Great Escape Artist
Review: There's nothing here to match the wildly brilliant ambition of their late-80s/early-90s peak, but "Underground" packs a hefty punch, while frenetic closer "Words Right Out of My Mouth" sounds like an ornithophobic Stooges.

Title: Thrice Woven
Review: Not since acclaimed debut Diadem Of 12 Stars has Wolves In The Throne Room rocked this hard and steady; in its sustained racket, it approximates one of the band’s live shows, which tend to be all blistering blitzkrieg all the time, drone passages withheld.

Title: Cuttin' Heads
Review: Mellencamp's crackling, gorgeous Heartland pop resonates more now than ever--even if, at times, he sounds like he's ripping off his best guitar moves.

Title: Between My Head and the Sky
Review: At 76, her music remains truly vital: unsettling, touching, funny, undeniable.

Title: Eternity, In Your Arms
Review: It is by turns beautiful and brash, driven and divine. [18 Mar 2017, p.50]

Title: Nashville
Review: If you like intelligent song writing with killer sing-along choruses, then you desperately need this album.

Title: Colour Trip
Review: Their debut album, Colour Trip, is more of a nostalgia trip as they delve deeply into shoegaze, dream pop, noise pop, and generally seem to be auditioning for a spot on the Creation roster between My Bloody Valentine and Ride.

Title: Shine a Light
Review: Tells the story of musicians creating something brilliant and new with the well-worn pieces of their punk-indie-hardcore legacy. [Oct 2003, p.124]

Title: The Olympians
Review: From front to back, the quality is so balanced that there are no obvious peaks or lulls, though the tracks that incorporate harp and harpsichord stick out a little more for their uniqueness relative to standard soul-funk revivalism.

Title: This Unruly Mess I've Made
Review: TUMIM shows a regression to the mean, further establishing him as an above-average emcee whose runaway hype train simply ran off the tracks.

Title: Anthem of the Peaceful Army
Review: Millennials could use a band that can play instruments in real time, that exults in musical possibilities, that wants to make both a ruckus and a difference. On its debut album, Greta Van Fleet isn’t that band.

Title: In Love With Oblivion
Review: In Love With Oblivion stands as a solid second attempt for a group with a promising future.

Title: Repo
Review: On their sunnily deranged new album, Repo, Black Dice somehow manage to do away with context entirely, constructing music comprised solely of sound effects designed and recorded themselves.

Title: Glass Boys
Review: [The] unflinching self-reflection makes Glass Boys a more immediate album for Fucked Up, especially coming on the heels of such a performative piece as David was.

Title: Expo 86
Review: Yet perhaps in spite of themselves, the members of Wolf Parade--who also put in time with a handful of other bands, including Handsome Furs and Sunset Rubdown--are also improving as songwriters, crafting shapelier melodies and figuring out how to use rhythm to drive toward an emotional climax.

Title: News and Tributes
Review: A pretty disappointing work of rock ordinaire. [Jun 2006, p.112]

Title: Lover
Review: There is a brilliant album among the 18 songs, if only it had been pruned it a little.

Title: Ghosts of Then and Now
Review: With Ghosts of Then and Now, Illum Sphere strives to balance the ethereal with the earworm and, for the most part, succeeds.

Title: Believe You Me
Review: It's immensely listenable throughout, but at its best--with 'Vistate' and 'Cara Falsa'--it's truly spellbinding.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: Indie rock's maturing avatars of tense lethargy paint life as an epic fade. [21 Jan 2005, p.88]

Title: Vespertine
Review: Björk's latest is as delightfully eccentric as her choice in outfits, blending scratchy electronic programming with tinkling music boxes and squeezing her formidable voice into ancient-sounding harmonies or futuristic whispers.

Title: Alter
Review: Decadent, theatrical, and magnetic, Alter falters only when the band's ambitions get the better of them, but the album's slight unevenness doesn't prevent it from being tremendously exciting.

Title: Yawny Yawn
Review: The allusive, poetic intimacy of songs and singer are enriched, while an atmospheric haze keeps the concept loose. [Sep 2019, p.34]

Title: Golden Grrrls
Review: It's clear that the members of Golden Grrrls write enjoyable, harmless numbers with great ease. However, since these numbers are given little chance to grow, Golden Grrrls lacks staying power.

Title: Inventions
Review: Inventions sets aside such linear development; instead, in a track like “Flood Poems,” the background looms up and submerges the guitar and percussion. Still, the album does head somewhere; marches emerge as the beat strengthens in the album’s closing tracks.

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: It’s the instant gratification--the sheer consistency of fun--that makes Midnight Boom so irresistible to begin with. It is what it is, basically.

Title: In Rainbows
Review: Both artistically and in terms of a new business model, In Rainbows is a necesary masterstroke. [Dec 2007, p.96]

Title: Tasty
Review: After the patchy pleasures of 'Wanderland', 'Tasty' is a huge Roman orgy of an album.

Title: Death Of The Party
Review: [2018's debut's] Rousing tunes and harmony-rich arrangements marked them out as contenders. This second outing delivers on that promise. [Sep 2020, p.110]

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: It’s frequently a difficult listen, and not for the reasons Garbus intended.

Title: The Garden
Review: Gone is most of the musical adventurousness that redeemed the most seemingly cliché moments of the debut.

Title: Undercard
Review: Undercard peddles in a more mature, assured--though no less skeletal-kind of songcraft.

Title: Postcards
Review: The resulting appearances from the likes of Calexico, Mark Knopfler, Carrie Rodriguez and David Lindley are subtle and empathetic, blending easily into Brown's spare, atmospheric Americana. [Jun 2017, p.24]

Title: Level Live Wires
Review: He finally gives his dark, dense instrumentals room to breathe on his fifth album. [Sep 2007, p.136]

Title: Fake It Flowers
Review: Just as judging the past from the present can be a fraught undertaking, weighing up the throwback 90s indie du jour by the standards of the decade itself is probably unfair too, but you wish Beabadoobee could muster a little more period-perfect surliness.

Title: Family
Review: After a very strong first half, Family starts to get a little shaky in the home stretch.

Title: Body Faucet
Review: Reptar aren't afraid to grow up but they're gonna have fun getting there, and with Body Faucet they succeed in doing both.

Title: I See the Sign
Review: Amidon and his cabal of collaborators-- Nico Muhly, Ben Frost, Shahzad Ismaily-- have been merging chamber music with indie rock for awhile now (see also: Sufjan Stevens, Thomas Bartlett, Owen Pallett, Bryce and Aaron Dessner of the National), and their touch is nuanced and, on occasion, delightfully odd.

Title: Sixteen Oceans
Review: Four Tet marries the naivety of a childhood sensibility, the sublime immanence of nature, and the infinite possibilities of the imagination ingeniously and thoughtfully, and further imbuing them with a borrowed but genuine mysticism that is, as always with Four Tet, ultimately very satisfying.

Title: Hunter
Review: Her’s is a sound that’s daunting and distinctive, brash yet beguiling.

Title: The Time of the Assassins
Review: His flat baritone suggests he’s still new at this whole “getting angry” thing, but the dude’s got the damaged part down.

Title: Hard Believer
Review: The songs are best when they say the least, implying depths that are, perhaps, mostly in the listener’s head.

Title: Nouns
Review: There are songs on Nouns that seemingly defy you to listen, and not because they’re loud or crass or due-heavy on true-dat market-maneuvers and what I guess we can now safely call “aural assault”; and not because of the bad vocals, bunkered mix job, or the hundred and one other things that would make your parents, my professors or Celine Dion hate this album.

Title: Shape The Future
Review: With so much New Age nattering, here more than ever your enjoyment will depend on your own zeal for enlightenment and/or bong rips.

Title: Funeral
Review: Whether or not listeners make it through all 24 tracks on Funeral, it’s easy to see what Wayne is definitely in his own world. His rhyming remains unlike anyone else in the entire genre and despite this album not being his strongest, you don’t have to go far to find a Wayne quotable that inherently makes one admire his seasoned lyrical dexterity.

Title: EP-1
Review: Three out of the four songs are at least enjoyable.

Title: Good Sad Happy Bad
Review: Good Sad Happy Bad is ultimately an optimistic record; it tries to bring out the positive in some of the most negative sounds around.

Title: All That You Can't Leave Behind
Review: The band neither succeeds wildly nor fails. There are only a few reminders of the lackluster dance sounds in its recent work... Otherwise, what dominates are the straight-ahead rhythms that drove the early days.

Title: Black Cadillac
Review: Cash is an expert detailer who doesn’t pander to navel gazing, and was somehow able to produce a detached, yet emotional response to her grief.

Title: Filo Loves The Acid
Review: There is some extremely sophisticated signal processing going on here, resulting in complex subliminal sound patterns in the spaces between beat and the 303s’ scrolling and glooping. However each track is about relentless repetitions of one monolithic kick and one acid riff above all else. While the processing can occasionally resemble some of Tin Man and Cassegrain’s recent dismantlings of acid, which float in motionless seas of reverb, the primacy of the kick ’n’ riff lends the forward momentum of these tracks a glorious singlemindedness. [Sep 2018, p.52]

Title: Life of Pause
Review: Perhaps it isn't quite a fully realised picture, but Life of Pause still paints a very pretty sonic landscape.

Title: Songs of Experience
Review: A handful of tracks shoot for the anthemic uplift of vintage U2, but fall short. The only real left-field beauty here is Love Is All We Have Left, a token reminder of the Dublin quartet’s shimmering ambient avant-rock period.

Title: Free TC
Review: Free TC, dedicated to Dolla $ign's currently incarcerated brother, marries a diverse range of earworm-level hooks and genre-bridging rhythms to uncomfortably base themes.

Title: I'm New Here
Review: His first album in more than 15 years sees him back atr the musical vanguard--thanks in large part to XL boss and producer, Richard Russell, whose arrangements brilliantly frame the 60-year-old's rich burr and terse street poetry with brooding electronica and stark blues handclaps. [Mar 2010, p.106]

Title: FRIDAY FOREVER
Review: For a man who’s lived and breathed rave culture, his album about the experience is strangely lacking in highs.

Title: Hippies
Review: If Hippies has a flaw, it's only that it overstays its welcome by just a few minutes.

Title: Love Is a Four Letter Word
Review: Many of the hacky-sacking grooves on his fourth album settle for snoozy gentility.

Title: Sunbathing Animal
Review: Sunbathing Animal is not an immediate or cushy listen, but it is gripping; a considered and brutal reminder that Parquet Courts’ aren’t necessarily an accessible band.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: It doesn’t quite rank alongside their very strongest material, but there are still more rippling vocal harmonies and gutting one-liners than most bands could be proud of in a lifetime.

Title: Elephant Stone
Review: Elephant Stone is a thoughtful and concise album that showcases not only precise musicianship from all members of the band but a distinct growth in songwriting.

Title: Louder
Review: While the turbo vocal bursts on “You’re Mine” and “Burn With You” blend nicely with the poppier elements, several of the tracks, including the burbling “On My Way” and the title tune, feel a bit too calculated and anonymous in their production approach.

Title: Soft Control
Review: Whilst there are echoes of the bluster of Florence and the Machine and the minimalist soul of Jessie Ware here, Soft Control is a distinctive take on modern pop and an album with crossover appeal.

Title: Cuttin' Heads
Review: Mellencamp sounds like he's just hitting his stride. [19 Oct 2001, p.82]

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: To be fair, if it weren't for Lynch's lacklustre vocals and lyrics there might be a fairly solid collection of atmospheric retro rock 'n' roll here, but as it seems to be coming at the expense of his film career that's still not quite good enough.

Title: Shiny and Oh So Bright, Vol. 1 / LP: No Past. No Future. No Sun.
Review: There are moments of glorious burning distortion on Solara and Marchin' On, but its real riches are much more subtle. [Dec 2018, p.115]

Title: Running Out of Love
Review: Running Out of Love is absolutely true to the duo’s style and their assessment of today’s Sweden.

Title: Kunk
Review: Dope Body albums have been great in the past because they took familiar kinds of rock melody and put a sinister spin on them, reimagining American popular rock through a spit-smeared lens, reinvigorating it with the edge and causticity those songs could have conveyed in different hands. But they don’t do any of that here. On Kunk, they just screw around a bit.

Title: Dogrel
Review: This is the sound of vitality; of authenticity and ambition; of style, substance, and swagger all packed in to 35 minutes of vulnerable, honest pop music that is weighted with melancholy, yet buoyed by youthful vigor and touched, perhaps, by genius.

Title: Torches
Review: Time will tell, but this opening salvo will certainly leave you pumped up for further Foster kicks.

Title: Just Look At That Sky
Review: It avoids sounding too similar to their debut, but retains the likeable elements of that record with added gusto.

Title: Whiteout Conditions
Review: Newman, Case, and Calder are wonderful as always and with Newman providing the melodic earworms, Whiteout Conditions is another strong addition to the band’s already excellent discography.

Title: Strange Pleasures
Review: A welcome, and ultimately pleasurable return.

Title: Saint Dymphna
Review: Dymphna's genre distinctions are more sophisticated and nuanced. [Dec 2008, p.152]

Title: Delirium Tremens
Review: Harvey remains mostly reverential to his sacrilegious source, but Delirium Tremens is much more than just Gainsbourg fed through Google Translate. Rather, it amplifies the unsettling undercurrents that always stewed beneath Gainsbourg’s impeccable arrangements.

Title: Masquerade
Review: Clef sounds more invested in his music when he's appropriating other people's songs. [Jul 2002, p.109]

Title: Love 2
Review: Love 2 slithers beyond its sketchiness and proves ingratiating just the same.

Title: Brace The Wave
Review: It acts as a skilled and timely reminder of his own uniquely vulnerable vision as a songwriter. [Oct 2015, p.102]

Title: ACR Loco
Review: ACR Loco lives up to its title. [Nov 2020, p.83]

Title: This Unruly Mess I've Made
Review: Though This Unruly Mess I’ve Made is decent, its biggest failing lies in its quality control. For every good song, there are two mediocre and/or forgettable ones next to them.

Title: Collector
Review: Collector is clever, catchy and addictive, and gets better with repeat plays. You can only imagine he and Disq know exactly what they’re doing.

Title: 99 CENTS
Review: The Chicks on Speed brand of girl power won't scare a Geri Halliwell fan, but their chatty cynicism might make them question their ideals.

Title: Twelve Angry Months
Review: The concept is basic and brilliant: a song for every bitter month of a year of off-again/on-again romance, from splitting the record collection in January to “A token e-mail/ A drunken text/A sorry go-round of cell-phone sex” in October.

Title: Reggie
Review: Uptight types who want him to save hip-hop will hate on this one, but this ain't nuthin' but a party y'all, and a fun one at that.

Title: Honky Tonk
Review: The pacing is so languid, the dynamics so muted that I doubt this iteration of Son Volt would last very long in a real honkytonk.

Title: Arms Way
Review: Arm’s Way represents a step forward from "Return to the Sea" creatively if not as an artistic whole.

Title: Semper Femina
Review: Ms. Marling doesn’t cast herself as heroine or victim, angel or avenger. She does something trickier, and perhaps braver. Clear-eyed, calmly determined and invitingly tuneful, she captures each situation in all its ambiguity.

Title: Small Town Heroes
Review: You might call it a postmodern take on 20th-century American music, but it's so warm and welcoming that it never feels like an exercise in technique or a mere demonstration of knowledge.

Title: Feel the Sound
Review: Feel the Sound is such a consistent, and consistently smooth, pop album, that it might put you to sleep, or at least a musically-induced coma.

Title: IV Play
Review: IV Play succeeds in spades with its production and songwriting.

Title: Born Villain
Review: The truth is, though, there's just a lack of magic, a lack of something special going on. It's not bad. It's not good.

Title: Boronia
Review: There are a few standouts strewn throughout like "Jump the Gun," "So Tired," and "Laura," but mostly it's the kind of long-player that works best blaring in its entirety from the speakers of a sun-roasted beach cruiser dashboard on the way to someplace fun.

Title: Melody Road
Review: What makes a difference here is the general lightness of his new songs and Was and Lee's sympathetic production; the two play off each other perfectly, turning this into the first latter-day Diamond record to feel quintessentially Neil Diamond.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: Price’s work behind the boards, while often commanding, is hardly ambitious; running the tracks together to try and give Madge the "album" sound is noteworthy, but he’s picked the wrong pop-star to prod.

Title: Break It Yourself
Review: Bird conducts his experiments with the lightest of touches: his ingenuity matched by a gift for simple, lilting melodies.

Title: Warm On a Cold Night
Review: It remains evident that the pair stellar pop songs in their armoury, but their over-reliance on a standard formula finds this debut stuck in a bit of a creative rut.

Title: Revolutions Per Minute
Review: Revolutions Per Minute is an album that’s been a long time coming, and Kweli and Hi-Tek prove once again that there’s more to rap than club bangers, delivering another dose of socially and politically conscious music that’s more about opening people’s eyes to what’s happening in the world than telling them how to feel about it.

Title: Yes Lawd!
Review: Yes Lawd! cuts a deep groove and doesn’t let up for nearly an hour of R&B/hip-hop bliss.

Title: Haughty Melodic
Review: It's just a little sad to hear Mike giving in to conventionality, even if he does do it better than most.

Title: Angles
Review: Angles doesn't feel like an over-indulgent record, nor one that speaks of a dearth of ideas.

Title: Pray For The Wicked
Review: It's breathless and occasionally shallow, but never less than entertaining. [Summer 2018, p.114]

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Belong
Review: The 10-track set barely has a weak moment and actually ends too soon. It's like '90s alt-rock had a child who suddenly grew up beautiful.

Title: Furfour
Review: Furfour is packed with widescreen synthpop ballads like this [“Acid Ali Khan”], which is either a misstep or an admirable commitment to aesthetic consistency, depending on your taste.

Title: World Without Tears
Review: It's an album filled with appetites and their consequences.

Title: Eating Us
Review: Eating Us is a litle too tidy, their frazzled wildness cultivated into ordered orchards, but on tracks like the typically titled 'Bubblegum Animals,' BMSR still conjure a ravishing, stoned cyber-soul pinic. [Jun 2009, p.83]

Title: Blues Funeral
Review: Though the grappling guitars of 'Riot In My House' wouldn't seem out of place on an MC5 album, Blues Funeral doesn't always kick out the jams.

Title: The Air Between Words
Review: A collection of big, bouncy and immaculately produced club tunes, it brings together some fine productions. But it's also a tough record to love.

Title: Krieg und Frieden (Music for Theatre)
Review: Not ‘dance’ music by any stretch of the imagination, but beautiful all the same.

Title: Always
Review: At its best, it's both cathartic and transformative, harnessing the transformative power of empathy to politicize the personal and personalize the political.

Title: Kidnapped By Neptune
Review: Kidnapped By Neptune is one of those rare albums that's both sexy and dirty, and isn't guilty of trying to be either.

Title: As If
Review: On As If, !!! show that they've still got ideas, leaving listeners with one of the most enjoyable, if schizophrenic, dance albums of the year.

Title: Big Love
Review: At times, the overall veneer is a shade too clean, suggesting nothing so much as cocktail hour at a classy conference, but the fact that Hucknall and Simply Red choose to celebrate the softer, soulful sounds of the '70s by doubling down on the smoothness does separate them from the legions of neo-soul divas in the new millennium.

Title: Single Mothers
Review: Earle’s consistency is both his friend and his enemy on Single Mothers. In its quest for poignant empathy and delicate strokes of storytelling, it doesn’t vary much in tone.

Title: Ascent
Review: Mysterious and enfolding, Ascent seduces. [Oct 2012, p.90]

Title: I Grow Tired But Dare Not Fall Asleep
Review: Gone is much of the external noise – typewriter clatters, vinyl crackles and the whir of bicycle spokes – replaced by ambitiously ornate compositions. As on Dark Days, I Grow Tired feels spookily prescient.

Title: Goodbye, Killer
Review: This music sometimes feels spontaneous and casual, but the craft of Joe Pernice's songwriting remains as literate and melodically absorbing as anyone working in indie pop today, and Goodbye, Killer confirms he and his collaborators haven't lost their touch, and have even gained a bit or edgy nerve along the way.

Title: From Safer Place
Review: The songs ultimately blur into one extensive blast of rugged emotion and high energy, dazzling in their urgency and always threatening to crumble out of precise playing into unhinged noise.

Title: Hifalutin
Review: The only way that Lowly lives up to their name is their humility to push themselves to give more to their listeners--something they do exceptionally well on Hifalutin.

Title: Observator
Review: Despite standout moments within most of the songs, nothing on this album except perhaps the closing number, "Till the End", truly stands out as recognizably Raveonettes.

Title: In Your Honor
Review: Both these records chronicle the physical and mental graffiti of figuring out how to emerge from some very large shadows, including his own, with nerve and power. [Jul 2005, p.96]

Title: Deeper Woods
Review: Like a long walk in the woods, it's richly and deeply transporting. [Jun 2018, p.35]

Title: Human Question
Review: It’s worth noting that the band’s emphasis on songcraft, on making a point, pays off in a way that not every track here does.

Title: The Plain Where The Palace Stood
Review: It's hard to imagine droves of converts flocking to so abstruse a musical cocktail, but it's a welcome addition to the Grubbs canon, nonetheless. [Jul 2013, p.87]

Title: New Me, Same Us
Review: The general vibe is of music for well-upholstered hotel suites. [May 2020, p.104]

Title: Little Hell
Review: It doesn't shun country influences altogether, mind--when matched to the album's mood and Green's plain-speaking lyrics, they function to add a soulful feel to a set of characteristically lovely, melancholic songs.

Title: Everything Goes Wrong
Review: It's weirdly kind of a grower. There's nothing that immediately jumps out and announces itself as the 'Where Do You Run' of Everything Goes Wrong.

Title: grÃ¦

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: The Riptide glides by satisfyingly. [Sep 2011, p.83]

Review: While album three may require a reboot from The XX, that's for another day. Right now, when it comes to fusing indie rock and dance, no one pulls it off quite as elegantly.

Title: Youth

Review: In many ways, this is his 'Nylon Curtain.' [Sep 2001, p.160]

Title: The Remote Part

Title: Lex

Title: Chemical Flowers
Review: However, for as many tunes that feel dynamic in their constant morphing there are a good few that never quite find their way beyond a bunch of interesting noises.

Title: Cry

Title: Captain of None
Review: Captain Of None places Schott's voice front-and-centre and folds in her long-burning love for dub and reggae rhythms, making for her most approachable and otherworldly record yet.

Title: Nothing But the Beat

Title: The Deconstruction
Review: It feels like a career-straddling greatest hits collection in which all the ‘hits’ are brand new.

Title: Bloodsports
Review: Bloodsports is effortlessly superior to its predecessor A New Morning, and averages out roughly on a level with Head Music (though more consistent in quality).

Title: Fishscale
Review: The stories are as vivid, brutal, and thought-out as any noir.

Title: Blank Project
Review: Produced with finesse by Four Tet, whose ability to mix live drum grooves and electronic muscle is unrivaled, it's music that beats its own path, brilliantly.

Title: Canto
Review: Offers up one superb song after another.... Even if you don't consider yourself to be much a Latin music fan, do yourself a favor and check out Canto.

Title: Weather Systems
Review: Intricate and thoughtful, it recalls the work of Porcupine Tree's Steven Wilson. [Jul 2012, p.102]

Title: Ã·

Title: Suck My Shirt
Review: They're as committed as ever to rocking and having a good time, and that's something that thankfully seems to be getting even stronger the more they figure out what they're doing.

Title: The Grind Date

Title: Don't Give Up on Me

Title: R Plus Seven

Title: When I'm Free
Review: This album is one of empowerment and regained vitality.

Title: In The Future
Review: In The Future showcases a group who knows exactly what they're doing. [Feb 2008, p.101]

Title: Late Registration
Review: As ornate and bloated as West's ego. [Sep 2005, p.99]

Title: Inlet
Review: As dark and tonally blistering as anything they did in their early years, Inlet essentially finds Hum picking up where they left off in 1998.

Title: Sauna
Review: Sauna can be disorienting at times, too, but, more to the point, it has a peculiar way of making you feel like you’re listening to two overlapping albums that follow perpendicular impulses.

Title: Lollipop
Review: The fact that these titans of the US underground have collectively hoovered enough drugs and booze (and clocked enough jail time) to make Pete Doherty sit up and wonder makes their sheer longevity something to be marvelled at.

Title: Happy in the Hollow
Review: Above all, it’s the melodies that stand out, whether in the wonderfully whacked out melodies of ’You Make Me Forget Myself’ or pacy ripples of ‘Sequence One’, all delivered with an insouciance that’s rather satisfying in these times.

Title: Don't You
Review: This organic quality pops up every so often, as if to reinforce the human element of an album that relies so much on electronic flourishes to get its point across.

Title: Impersonator
Review: With such a wide-open sound, even the confusing and painful parts sound hauntingly beautiful.

Title: Captain of None
Review: The spacious long-form approach on these eight tracks really showcase Schott’s insistent, tactile, and conversation-with-yourself lonesome performance style. It’s great loner music, for those who own this about themselves but are ever casting a tentative eye toward the throng.

Title: Isolation Drills
Review: Ditching lo-fi aesthetics for a more radio-ready sound in the spirit of, say, the Raspberries or Badfinger, Pollard has wisely chosen not bury his songs in oblique lyrical references and muddy tape hiss.

Title: Songs
Review: Dismiss his second album, Songs, only at your peril.

Title: Lift a Sail
Review: On Lift a Sail, we see a Yellowcard that is no longer holding back.

Title: The Weighing of the Heart
Review: Schott's work here takes you to all sorts of places while all the while keeping your focus firmly hooked on the music, this beautiful music, at hand.

Title: Young & Old
Review: Young & Old proves it can still make shimmering beach pop even while anchored to the shore.

Title: Fire from the Sky
Review: Fire From the Sky is suitably heavy, grim but not ridiculous, and its best songs will remind listeners of Metallica.

Title: Monsters Exist
Review: This contrast, however, between bouncy or turbulent beats and contemplative or cosmic ambience, which recurs throughout Monsters Exist, is so dissonant that it effectively gets in the way of the album making a cohesive statement.

Title: Random Axe
Review: I just feel some little thing is missing, some insignificant morsel that should have no bearing on whether you explore Random Axe's Random Axe or not. By all means, dive in head first with comfort. Enjoy yourselves.

Title: East of Eden
Review: It's most beguiling when the eastern influences are to the fore.

Review: Bobby Ray has a little way to go to match his mentor's lyrical ingenuity, but as the first post-Lupe rap star he's already absorbed the most important lessons about form and function, inspiration and integrity. It's a great start.

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: There’s the feeling that, behind her mask of the anthropomorphic goddess of climate change, maybe, just maybe, this is Grimes’ most honest and reflective album yet.

Title: What Could Possibly Go Wrong
Review: A long time coming, the record is fully worth the wait, Dominic flexing his musical muscles in a genre-blending debut that sees him dip his toes into rap, hip hop, pop, rock, emo, and more. A sure-to-be-beloved album amongst Gen Z-ers.

Title: Busting Visions
Review: Ultimately, Busting Visions is a sprawling yet thoughtfully constructed album full of backwoods, sandals, and sunburn rock with enough slippery electric guitar work, backing vocals, chiming bells, plinky pianos, and various freaky percussion bits to qualify as a kind of modern-day hippie noodle-rock opus.

Title: Hypercaffium Spazzinate
Review: No matter how sobering Hypercaffium Spazzinate gets, Descendents keep things light by playing these wistful, grown-ass songs like teenagers.

Title: Pay the Devil
Review: Pay The Devil is for Van Morrison completists only.

Title: Uh Huh Her
Review: The single-mindedness with which she approaches these songs is ultimately responsible for much of the album's distinctive flavor. [#7]

Title: Tomorrow's Modern Boxes
Review: On the new album, Mr. Yorke is both instantly recognizable and less crowd-pleasing than ever. But for anyone who’s stayed with him this far, it’s worth following him further into the murk.

Title: Red
Review: Whether she's real-talking Jake Gyllenhaal ("We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together") or fantasizing about crashing "a yacht-club party" ... her self-discovery project is one of the best stories in pop. When she's really on, her songs are like tattoos.

Title: No World
Review: It's really unfortunate that Inc. hasn't been able to elevate beyond these very basic production mistakes; they give an impression that No World was either unmastered or mastered haphazardly.

Title: No Further Ahead Than Today
Review: Though the title track and "The Magic In You" recall his early triumphs, it's all a bit 'shoe-business' as usual. [Dec 2016, p.37]

Title: Time Capsules II
Review: At his best, Oberhofer packs emotional punches in the maniacal vocals of 'I Could Go', underscored by proggy synths, billowing flutes and a chorus that stomps around like a giant drunk toddler. Somehow, Oberhofer's melodrama makes getting dumped sound fun. If only he could keep it up over a whole album...

Title: Quakers
Review: Stuffed with bomb-ass beats and rhymes that will bang from Cali to Darlington.

Title: Indicud
Review: Overall, Kid Cudi is refreshing and lively thoughout Indicud, proving he can go off and experiment (like he did on WZRD), yet come back to the Day & Night Cudi we have all grown to know and love.

Title: Hurley
Review: Hurley is a reminder of why we fell in love with Weezer in the first place--the power-pop anthems, grungy rock songs, the gawd-awful yet quirky lyrics--it's all here.
So it isn’t better than Swift’s album, as that would be a pretty hard album to improve on. What Adams has done though is to look at it through another prism, and created a pure break-up album.

Title: Damage and Joy
Review: The album is as much a kind of career retrospective and odds-and-ends collection as it is a new creative document.

Title: The Deep Field
Review: As a whole, The Deep Field nails it. True, the songs are long, it is almost ceaselessly rich, and you're going to want to skip its first 30 seconds every time.

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: Just as Some Girls rejuvenated Mick and co., the Hold Steady’s latest finds the Brooklyn collective rediscovering the mix of morose jubilation and joyful myth-making they perfected a dozen years ago. Freed from the pressures of serving as Craig Finn’s primary creative outlet, the band has learned how to keep telling its hoodrat saga.

Title: Marry Me
Review: There are no apologies necessary for this wonderful debut album.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: With Channel Orange Frank Ocean has proven himself as one of the most significant artists in popular music today; his next effort will definitely have the potential to be a genre classic.

Title: Golden Xplosion
Review: He has been launched into the UK jazz marketplace fully formed, capable of extraordinary flights of dexterity and rhythmic trickery, yet also with a strong sense of fundamental musical language and compositional flair.

Title: Pyramid
Review: This is not music for the faint of heart, but it seems the Jaga Jazzist’s move to Brainfeeder has opened up for them yet more frontiers of space rock and jazz to conquer. Long may they reign.

Title: Lucifer
Review: Peaking Lights make music that turns limited means and an artsy angle into something profoundly universal.

Title: Mythomania
Review: Cryptacize's latest squanders the band's natural resource: singer Nedelle Torrisi.

Title: Bedroom
Review: Their execution is highly impressive, Bedroom may be retro in its thinking, but on this debut bdrmm have proved to be forward thinking in execution. An assured and brilliant debut.

Title: The Garden
Review: A quirky lo-fi wonder or the best album the '70s never had, "The Garden" feels like a lost gem, discovered in a box in the attic; a forgotten masterpiece full of tantalising sounds, odd voices and tingling ideas.

Title: The Flower Lane
Review: Crisp drum figures add punctuation, and a noodling sax help evoke a mood of traveling the city at night. [Mar 2013, p.91]

Title: News and Tributes
Review: This time around, the harmonies are less striking, but add a fullness to the group’s sound.

Title: White Trash with Money
Review: Keith occasionally appears to be stretching himself... but often seems to be coasting.

Title: Feel That Fire
Review: The album would be an enjoyable enough lightweight ride without those moments, but when they come, they are welcome. They also give the album an air of missed opportunity.

Review: The songwriting is certainly not poor and Glenn’s voice is far from shot, but what makes this album so average is the combination of the lazy arrangements and the poor production which makes the album sound as if the veteran vocalist is singing over a backing CD.

Title: Sheezus
Review: What Sheezus proves is that Lily Allen is still growing and evolving as a musician, and even with a few lesser tracks here and there, Sheezus is so far her best-yet mix of personal stories and overarching cultural commentary.

Title: Joy as an Act of Resistance
Review: IDLES believe that community spirit and togetherness will be what ultimately guides us closer to happiness as a whole, and in Joy As An Act Of Resistance they’ve created a monumental banner for the movement.

Title: Crazy for You
Review: What's the same is bigger and broader, bringing its faults into stark relief. This is, I stress, Best Coast's Proper Album, and so rather than Where The Boys Are's loosely defined "songs" we get Songs: feeble, noise-soaked throw-back translations of everything from doo-wop, girl-group, pop-punk, to pseudo-grunge.
The fact that the emotional extremes are few and far between makes the album difficult to wade through -- its impact would've been tripled with about half an hour lopped off, but where to begin?

Title: When the Pawn
Review: Fiona's brand of heartache is a welcome, dark respite from the avalanche of popcrap.

Title: Myths & Heroes
Review: It’s not entirely memorable, but it’s confident and varied.

Title: The Day Is My Enemy

Title: Living the Dream
Review: This is the sound of a working band locking in on their groove.

Title: Why Choose
Review: T this is an album about choice, and even when they occasionally flub in their decision making they still own it with pride and care.

Title: Shotter's Nation

Title: Love
Review: This is easily some of McMahon's prettiest and most accessible music, and it's also some of his finest. In its own simple, graceful way, Love adds more depth to the rest of Amen Dunes' work.

Title: Kinder Versions
Review: Kinder Versions is one of those precious pieces of art that is brand new but feels like it was always here, dragged from the beginnings of the world and rooted in elemental truth.

Title: The Last Broadcast
Review: Rich with melody and drama, even the band's experiments--like adapting King Crimson's "Moonchild" into the lush "M62 Song"--work.

Title: CCCLX
Review: There is nothing here that is going to cross over to the mainstream, and individually, the tracks aren’t even all that interesting, save perhaps for Le1f’s moment early on. The context provided by listening to the album all the way through is what saves it, what gives it a point of view.

Title: Strip Me

Title: Suck My Shirt
Review: Simply put, their sound has organically reached a more developed state. Each song brings something new to the table with few tunes just bleeding together.

Title: The Grind Date

Title: Lights Out

Title: The Coast Is Never Clear

Title: A Celebration of Endings

Title: 4everevolution

Review: The record’s high peak, “Upstate Blues,” displays more Kinsella influence (this time Owls) in its jazzy bursts. But the clever wordplay is all Weiss.

Title: Brainfeeder X

Title: World Wide Funk
Review: When the funk gets this good, with a relaxed, propulsive charm that belies the P-Funk density of the arrangements, why bother modernising?

Title: Civilian

Title: Saturnalia

Title: Loma

Title: Estudando o Pagode

Title: Civil Disobedience for Losers

Title: Aufheben

Title: Bangerz

Title: Front Row Seat to Earth

Title: A Perfect Contradiction

Title: Love at the Bottom of the Sea

Title: Made of Bricks

Title: Vicissitude
Review: Vicissitude is such a wispy, bloodless record that it’s hard to find anything to recommend about it.

Title: From Parts Unknown

Title: Bloom
Review: Beach House's fourth and most sumptuous album.

Title: Out Among the Stars
Review: Arrangements are unfussy--at least by today’s standards--and Cash’s rich, familiar baritone is in fine shape.

Title: My Main Shitstain
Review: It hardly feels coincidental that My Main Shitstain was released on a label called Big Dada, because that's almost exactly what it is: a statement that borders on nonsensical; cynically upbeat garage punk that's equal parts entertainment and introspection. Title: Under Branch & Thorn & Tree

Title: Mechanical Bull

Title: House of Spirits
Review: A must-have addition to already almost perfect catalog. [No. 110, p.55]

Title: Runner
Review: This striving for variety, and the fact the Sea and Cake run with every idea regardless of how soon it tires, is also one of their charms.

Title: Bish Bosch
