Title: Encore
Review: You’d believe this was a “Weird Al” Jankovic record had you tuned in halfway through.

Title: From the Valley to the Stars
Review: So, if you're with indie-pop’s backward-gazing contingent, or if you prefer it when ‘achingly beautiful’ actually aches, or if you want an example of style-versus-substance as a false dilemma--then get this record.

Title: Blonde
Review: As Blonde gets closer to the finish line, the same themes get explored again and again with a more collagelike musicality.

Title: Echoes
Review: Unfortunately, many of the underdeveloped rockers and plaintive ballads here are dance-floor-clearing duds. [Nov 2003, p.111]

Title: Hands
Review: Hesketh can write a damn good pop song, and whether that’s what caused the initial buzz, it's something hard to deny when presented with the cold, hard proof of Hands.

Title: More Parts per Million

Review: The album was not created lightly, and by no means deserves to be skimmed, but there’s a diversity and thirst within this album that stands to keep Early Riser remembered for some time, and will no doubt lead McFerrin to achieve the same.

Title: I Told You I Was Freaky
Review: Considering the circumstances, FOTC's second Sub-Pop outing, I Told You I Was Freaky, has some worthwhile moments.

Title: Singing Bones
Review: Their most sure-footedly solemn performances to date. [Nov 2003, p.114]

Title: Offend Maggie
Review: It shouldn’t offend, but it might be slow to engage.

Title: Evil Urges
Review: Heard back to back they almost make sense, but the sequencing here amplifies the disjointed feel of an album that facinates and frustrates in equal measure. [July 2008, p.108]

Title: Delta Machine
Review: The camp is layered on thick, just as it always was, yet this time it crosses the thin line these electro pioneers once walked with ease.

Title: Reality Testing
Review: Reality Testing, then, pushes into new territory so well that it erases the possibility of its existence as a one-time distraction, and its few major successes lead to expectations of a more unified version.

Title: Beyond the Door
Review: This, almost surreally, is only their seventh album and contains not a dull moment. [Sep 2019. p.83]

Title: Destroyed

Title: Let It Come Down

Title: Out Among the Stars

Title: Dream River
Review: Dream River is required reading, without a doubt.

Title: Coexist
Review: The world adored the xx's Mercury Prize-winning debut album xx. Coexist is, if anything, an even finer piece of work.

Title: Zoo
Review: [Zoo will piss you off if you think] their Fugaziish formative albums are sacrosanct and that any deviation voids them in the eyes of The Living Christ Our Lord Henry Rollins. Two, you hate loud noises.

Title: Owl John
Review: It's when Hutchison's sinister demeanor matches the darkness of the music that Owl John works best. [Oct 2014, p.116]

Title: Be Slowly

Title: Heaven and Earth
Review: A conceptual double album exploring earth (reality) and heaven (idealisation), is perhaps unlikely to sway the old guard, but it pushes forward with a purposeful vitality that was at times missing from his debut album, The Epic.

Title: Right Here Right Now
Review: It’s Shaggy’s support on an island-y ode to committed relationships that pops among a mix of passionate R&B jams and take-charge lady anthems.

Title: Sunshine Rock
Review: The lyrics paint a picture of discomfort and restlessness, which grows over the course of the album into a fully formed portrait of personal strength, creativity, and hard-eyed refusal in the face of the harassment of time.

Title: Home Again
Review: There will doubtless be more varied shades on future records, but for now, this pensive debut gives notice of a fine new talent. [Apr 2012, p.80]

Title: Take Care
Review: Take Care does a beautiful job of giving Drake the best group of features that complement his style while rarely outshining him.

Title: The Devil's Walk
Review: It's a midpoint between densely-orchestrated post-rock and ambient electro, and the results are pretty captivating.

Title: Two Suns
Review: The joy of "Fur and Gold" has vanished and taken some of Khan’s potential with it. This is request for their safe return, no questions asked.

Title: Seeing Sounds
Review: N.E.R.D's third album, an "Anti Matter" suggestion that devotees "tilt your head back and close your eyes" and try Seeing Sounds, bangs frantic enough to entice one serious auditory seizure.

Title: Authenticity
Review: What I realized listening to this studio masterpiece is that Phonte, Dwele, and Aloe Blacc are all former MC's with new grown and sexy albums out this year worth purchasing.

Title: Sam's Town
Review: With those sharp synth lines, and an interesting sense of melody, the Killers have made a good album.

Title: Sirens
Review: It is in this emergent, slightly surreal space between music and politics that Jaar’s syncretic talent shines through.

Title: No Sounds Are Out Of Bounds
Review: Overall it’s a baggy mixed bag of dub grooves and warmed-over house beats, dominated by an exhausting tower of babbling dialogue samples that, like No Sounds itself, rarely have much to say.

Title: No More Stories...
Review: It bears to be dissected because it is pretty much all over the place, even if what they wanted to achieve could be stored inside a magical pot of gold.

Title: Octahedron
Review: It shows that for the first time they really can do restraint, without compromising the overall impact of the instances where things are let rip.

Title: Atrocity Exhibition
Review: Atrocity Exhibition finds Brown back behind the lens, capturing raw emotion with grainy 16mm.

Title: Judy Sucks a Lemon For Breakfast
Review: Rather than delivering a post-modern mishmash, they effortlessly synthesise these elements, making themselves a candidate for the quintessential 21st century pop group. [Aug 2009, p.102]

Title: Dance Mother
Review: Take the repeats out of the equation and you're left with a decidedly mixed bag; just a few of Dance Mother's newbies manage to rival their older siblings' success.

Title: Animositisomina
Review: Songs such as "Unsung" showcase a reapplied talent for twisting archetypal metal riffs into new shapes.

Title: Here Come the Rattling Trees
Review: O'Hagan proves here once and for all that he's up to the job.

Title: Choral
Review: Choral sometimes feels staid and a little postcard-y: a pretty gesture that fails to eclipse the experience of actually going somewhere.

Title: The Time Is Now
Review: David may have worked hard to rejoin the pop firmament, but he seems slightly lost now that he’s arrived.

Title: Ukulele Songs
Review: Ukulele Songs is an album brimming with integrity and enthusiasm and, most importantly, it boasts great tunes.

Title: Scorpion
Review: The album is a hulking catalog of Drake in his comfort zone, a space in which his ability to create memorable music that sits perfectly in the cradle of the cultural zeitgeist is unmatched. Still, the excessive 25-song tracklist is a misstep.

Title: Colored Emotions
Review: This record represents a bold, imaginative first step for a young band that seems poised to take their sound anywhere.

Title: After the End
Review: While Merchandise hasn’t exactly figured out how to inflate their songwriting to match the scale of the giants who’ve preceded them, After the End still glows too vividly to be obscured by anyone else’s shadow.

Title: Punk & Poetry
Review: A convincing musical narrative for young life in the UK today. [May 2011, p.104]

Title: Songs In The Dark
Review: Some people may see Songs In The Dark as a curio, simply recorded for in order to keep the legacy of the McGarrigle canon alive and well. Yet it’s the black humour and obvious love for the material that lifts this into another sphere.

Title: Grand
Review: Grand isn't as majestic as its name suggests, with only a handful of songs moving past the anxious minimalism that permeated the last album. For returning fans, though, Grand provides a familiar brand of punk music for happy people, for lovebirds, for those who wish Mates of State had more swagger and less glockenspiel.

Title: Rest
Review: There are some songs, such as Deadly Valentine, that just seem to fall a bit flat, and considering that’s there’s only 10 tracks, it seems to be an oddly lengthy record. Yet, like most of Gainsbourg’s work, it oozes class and, at times, it becomes startlingly beautiful.

Title: Await Barbarians
Review: Intimate and involving doesn’t necessarily mean that the record is engaging, however, and some tracks wash over without an impression, ultimately making this feel like little more than an indulgent side-project.

Title: Love the Future
Review: Though there’s a lot to dislike, there’s also the bones of something interesting here. If only they’d stuck with making more numbers like the enticing Adam Green-ish gypsy pop of ‘Neal’, they might just have won us over.

Title: Side Pony
Review: They've honed their sound even further, zeroing in on a vintage-inspired, '60s soul aesthetic.

Title: Brave
Review: It's nothing more than modest music for mellow good times, but it's lively enough to be fleeting fun, with enough good tunes for a mild party, preferably one that's held at home.

Title: Grandfeathered
Review: Brash and bold, its juxtaposition of fragile synth lines and uncompromising slabs of aggression make for a compelling, if not occasionally familiar, listen.

Title: Oceania
Review: Oceania is best listened to in bits.

Title: Black Sun
Review: At times, the album draws more from drum and bass than from UK funky or any other bass music du jour.

Title: Reincarnated
Review: The Diplo-directed record is a somewhat sloppy mish-mash of reggae cuts that rarely attain an authentic air.

Title: My December
Review: There are no hooks, nothing to suck in the many adults that liked Clarkson's first two records.

Title: Art History
Review: California Wives' music is soft and pleasant and fully formed and vague. Their lyrics are ciphers.

Title: I Com
Review: She tries to be jokey, warm, even friendly on occasion--but she also sounds awkward. [Jul 2004, p.105]

Title: Total
Review: While his unique but resolutely unchanging styles of slap bass shards and cut-up vocal syllables works well in a balanced DJ set, it wears quickly over 22 tracks. [Jul 2011, p.94]

Title: As Long as You Are
Review: Despite no huge leaps forward sonically, there are some fantastic scenes set to song. [Nov 2020, p.83]

Title: Beautiful Things
Review: One of the most honest albums we've heard in quite some time.

Title: Heard It In A Past Life
Review: It sticks in the mind for a good while after and just keeps bringing you back in with fantastic production, brilliant pop songwriting and a central personality as easy to like and support as any on the current music scene.

Title: Because the Internet
Review: Because The Internet shows off his full array of talent (writer, musician, comedian) and makes him stand out from the rest.

Title: Weval
Review: With their debut full-length, WEVAL have proven that they're willing to approach their music with their ears wide open and their possibilities endless.

Title: PETRA
Review: An uncomfortable listen, especially the Big Star's Third-esque When I Think Of You, but also an album imbued with acceptance and dignity. [Nov 2019, p.93]

Title: Iron Balls of Steel
Review: Iron Balls Of Steel ultimately raises eyebrows more often than it does fists. [14 Jan 2012, p.51]

Title: Praxis Makes Perfect
Review: What Praxis Makes Perfect might lack in fresh musical directions--their percolating analogue-digital pop remains little altered--it makes up for in apposite italophile detail.

Title: The Heart Is a Monster
Review: The Heart Is A Monster is not only a stark reminder of why the band have been so influential, but it also underscores their status as modern trailblazers. [Jul 2015, p.97]

Title: The Paradigm Shift
Review: It's Korn's most significant album in a long time. [Nov 2013, p.94]

Title: The Far Field
Review: There’s only one misstep: the slower Candles turns into a dispiriting trudge. Otherwise, The Far Field is another accomplished, engaging set.

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: Garden Of Delete feels more like an audio showreel than a traditional album. [Nov 2015, p.51]

Title: Heroes to Zeros
Review: Heroes to Zeros, in spite of a few uneven tracks, makes the cut.

Title: Havilah
Review: A little too heavily indebted to fellow Aussies Nick Cave and The Triffids' late David McComb, even if that's not a bad place to be coming form. [Mar 2009, p.105]

Title: The Voyager
Review: Most of these songs are anchored on a foundation of smart, solid pop.

Title: In Our Gun
Review: In Our Gun has all the elements that made their debut so great, and then some.

Title: Everything Wrong Is Imaginary
Review: A swirling, guitar-driven headtrip. [Apr 2006, p.220]

Title: Shields
Review: Shields is an engrossing, beautiful work which could only come from Grizzly Bear, and only at this point in their career.

Title: When Machines Exceed Human Intelligence
Review: Not essential, but Warp completists will find much here to admire and enjoy.

Title: Panda Park
Review: 'Panda Park' is a strange record, though whether you think it's any good or not depends on your tolerance levels.

Title: Attack Decay Sustain Release
Review: Attack Decay Sustain Release defies such trite categorization and, ultimately, what it is or isn’t doesn't really matter. All you need to know is this is quality.

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: Flashes of contingent weirdness appear throughout the album, and the lyrics remain reliably sardonic, but the band surrenders too often to a prefab pop-rock idiom that isn't entirely their own.

Title: This Is Acting
Review: Whether we like her or not, Sia might be authoring the most iconic pop music of our generation. For this reason alone, This is Acting is worth at least one listen.

Title: Whatever It Takes
Review: While that's brief by 21st century standards, it's plenty and proper on a collection of songs framed in kinetic, inspired performances by one of the greatest soul bands to emerge in decades.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Having lost the shock of the new, this more tuneful follow-up privileges Krauss's pop instincts over Miller's mayhem.

Title: Electrified
Review: Electrified certainly isn't the most original album you'll hear this year, but crunchy pop like this doesn't have to work very hard to impress the indie set. [Jul 2005, p.176]

Title: Biophilia
Review: There's not a lot of replay value in Björk's new mode, but it still works humbly well and the computer visuals go a long way toward expanding on the fragile, chamber orchestra feel of the music.

Title: The Mosaic of Transformation
Review: The Mosaic of Transformation is a generous record, a gift from Smith to those who need to lock into their body, to move quietly and deliberately.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: Wincing the Night Away feels labored. Gracefully realized though it is, you can hear the three-plus years Mercer spent pondering how to satisfy the expectations his surprise classic had created -- and also how to remain fresh and true to himself.

Title: In Love With Oblivion
Review: It lacks many truly original hooks, but this is a nice updating of Count Five-style psych menace to file with fellow lo-fi '60s revivalists like King Khan and Dum Dum Girls. [May 2011, p.82]

Title: Hawk
Review: At times it feels like this music will rise above simple pleasure, to something more fearsome or fearless, something unquantifiable and haunted--for now, however, the dichotomy between male and female will have to do.

Title: The Serenity of Suffering
Review: Branching out, but not too far, Suffering is heavy enough to stand proudly in the Korn kanon, but not daring enough to be much else.

Title: Fair Youth
Review: Despite the energy and marching delivery, the band's musings often ring quite delicate. They're never fragile, however.

Title: Songs Cycled
Review: At best Songs Cycled deals in quick-pivot moments.

Title: Phoenix
Review: Phoenix is much more than what floats to its surface, and far greater than the sum of its parts. It's an album of stories.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Lyrically, Loveless can still hit a clinker ("Verlaine Shot Rimbaud") or two ("Head"), but the yearning in "Everything's Gone" and pain expressed with "Hurts So Bad" illustrate she's come a long way in expressing universal emotions.

Title: Damaged
Review: Kurt Wagner's conversational croak is, charitably put, an acquired taste. [Sep 2006, p.106]

Title: Alvvays
Review: Whether you’re looking to fall in love this summer or pine away unrequited, you won't find a better soundtrack than this.

Title: Every Country's Sun
Review: Vivid, compelling and unafraid of delving into new territory, Mogwai have found the ideal combination of progression and familiarity.

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: There's something weirdly compelling about hearing Fagen settle into this particular rut, especially on a set of songs about growing old in an age of terror.

Title: Field of Love
Review: The beats she’s produced on Field of Love, meanwhile, flirt with unabashed garishness and fully match the whimsy of her vocal theatrics like never before.

Title: Sex Swing
Review: This [‘I am William Corder’], the pinnacle of a truly masterful, sonic annihilation of a record, is a murder ballad not in the melodramatic gothic tradition, but something else, something transcendent, and like the rest of the record something terrifyingly transfixing.

Title: Nobody's Smiling
Review: For the most part, Common's been an almost staggeringly consistent presence in music for years, and then fittingly, his new album Nobody's Smiling, is as good as anything he's done.

Title: Sister
Review: A transitional record, then, one that seems to be leading to a masterstroke.

Title: Jukebox
Review: Marshall’s second album of covers, mostly continues the cleaned-up, virtually lobotomized aesthetic of 2006’s unfortunately heralded "The Greatest."

Title: When the Pawn
Review: Brion girds Apple's elastic melodies with off-kilter beats, giving her music a more rhythmic feel than it has previously had, while the singer herself runs the spectrum of grim emotions.

Title: Get Awkward
Review: Let it also be said that Jemima Pearl’s voice has improved in a myriad of ways; throughout Be Awkward, she wails, rally-cries, and (especially on 'Becky') croons with a range of emotions that were bereft in previous recordings. If there’s one thing Be Awkward has in common with BYOP’s first effort, it’s the fact that it runs a bit long.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: The tunes are basically chants and the drumming is more straight-ahead than "tribal" and when the vibraphone trips in after 40 seconds of 'The Ballad of Butter Bean,' you may not bust a gut laughing, but you'll probably grin. [June 2008, p.75]

Title: Clear Shot
Review: They're at their best when they keep it succinct, as on I'm Still Believing and Another Dimension. Their longer songs are less successful. [Dec 2016, p.115]

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: Despite its obviously short shelf-life, Welcome Interstate Managers is delicious power-pop, unpretentious, loose and perfect for teenagers driving down to Ocean City for the weekend.

Title: In and Out of Youth and Lightness
Review: Even if their whole style is essentially a throwback, there's plenty of room out there for throwback done right. But on too much of Youth and Lightness, they're not the machine they could be.

Title: Rennen
Review: As a soundtrack to a new era where we’re all through the looking glass, old certainties bonfired and every phone alert quickening the pulse, Rennen hits the right tone--its rhythms shivering and uneasy, its melodies veering from melancholy to euphoria in a single stride.

Title: MUDBOY
Review: Sheck masterfully transcends one-hit-wonder status throughout his debut.

Title: Before I Self Destruct
Review: Taken as a whole this album has a pleasingly morbid tone, in keeping with the best moments from 50 Cent’s first two albums. But context is this album’s undoing.

Title: Arcology
Review: Arcology, like its predecessor, is a genre study first and foremost, rearranging familiar elements according to McRyhew's own idiosyncratic vision.

Title: Constricting Rage of the Merciless
Review: This is not music meant to be enjoyed as individual songs, but rather as part of a larger, more visceral listening experience that, despite its often redundant quality (individual track differentiation is damn near impossible) and oppressive nature, proves highly enjoyable, if ultimately exhausting clocking in at just under 40 minutes.

Title: Paul's Tomb: A Triumph
Review: You’ve got death and exaltation, followed by a sly wink at rock history. Not a bad set of tools for making smart, defiant music.

Title: The Obliterati
Review: What really lifts this out of the ordinary is the undeniable craft that has gone into the song writing.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: This ain't perfect, nor is it exactly sui generis, but it still ought to bump up their summer-festival-lineup-poster font size by a solid five points or so.

Title: Just Like The Fambly Cat
Review: While there are hints of tiredness, Grandaddy are not leaving us with heads bowed. [Jun 2006, p.116]

Title: The Rainbow Children
Review: Unfortunately, the record is burdened by a pretentious, overarching narrative about "the Wise One" and his struggle with "the Banished Ones."

Title: Out of Season
Review: Gibbons' craft is making her desperate drama believable and compelling.... [But] the lack of memorable tunes is Gibbons' worst affliction. [#61, p.96]

Title: The Voyager
Review: The Voyager is not quite so easily summed up. It’s not anchored in one particular scene, but plays as broadly California, with sly nods to the Byrds in the guitars, the Go-Go’s in the vocals, and Randy Newman in the wry humor.

Title: Gorillaz
Review: Neither Brit-pop nor hip-hop, "Gorillaz" contains a motley, dub-influenced collection of songs that are, like Hewlett's drawings, an exercise in sophisticated immaturity

Title: If You Leave
Review: Both musically and lyrically, Daughter ain’t half as clever as they clearly think they are (people get serious and clever mixed up a lot, weirdly).

Title: Mst
Review: All in all, too little of Mst lets us hear Gretschmann shine within this chosen framework.

Title: We All Belong
Review: Even when a sense of agitation seeps in, as on 'Die, Die, Die,' We All Belong sounds truly inviting. Dig it.

Title: Sleep Well Beast
Review: Sleep Well Beast sees The National flourish with candid lyrics and diverse song craft, embodying the band’s continuing evolution and life’s constant change.

Title: Beautiful Future
Review: A fine mix of fantasy and reality, made by a band who never run out of ideas, sung by a singer too smart to fall apart and too excited by rock’n’roll to stop being stupid.

Title: Atlanta Millionaires Club
Review: Atlanta Millionaires Club is a masterpiece of claustrophobic intimacy that brings compelling immediacy to a time-tested story.

Title: Deep in the Iris
Review: Deep in the Iris is more concentrated than anything Braids have released to date. If its runtime is more approachable, the songs themselves are also more intense.

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: Powers is going all in on this one, inviting you into his Wondrous Bughouse and daring to pour light into an often dark place.

Title: Godfather II
Review: Though it boasts hard-hitting moments (see the supple uppercut of ‘Been A While’ and the dizzying double-jab of the JME-featuring ‘Call the Shots’), this sequel lacks the punch of its predecessor.

Title: Everything Goes Wrong
Review: While there's merit to the charges that songs suffer from sameness and that musicianship is a secondary facet of the band, the Girls' detractors don't consider tradition; walking in the footprints of Bikini Kill, Ramones, and other like predecessors who faced similar criticisms, their flaws serve to be their most interesting, differentiating features.

Title: Wovenwar
Review: It's a solid first salvo from a band who clearly have the chops to make a serious stir. [Sep 2014, p.105]

Title: Clor
Review: Even when it runs out of creative juice, Clor gets by on energy and production alone until the juices get flowing again.

Title: Elect the Dead
Review: His ambition is never entirely realized, and though his voice is versatile, his almost operatic style at times borders on annoying.

Title: Reaching for Indigo
Review: Her performance reinforces the thrust towards freedom that shows up in the other songs. She isn’t just playing with the women and men in the band; she’s rising above them, flying high and alone in the blue.

Title: Loud City Song
Review: Loud City Song is Holter's most polished work to date, and another example of how she upholds and redefines what it means to be an avant-garde singer/songwriter.

Title: Where All Is Fled
Review: Where All Is Fled builds on Hauschildt's Berlin-school/kosmische influences while exploring new dimensions, resulting in his most immersive, accomplished solo work yet.

Title: Big Dark Love
Review: Big Dark Love has big, dark secrets hidden away in its seams that call out for repeated listens until you can draw them into the light.

Title: We Don't Even Live Here
Review: We Don't Even Live Here is the weirdest, angriest, and best P.O.S album to date.

Title: Weather
Review: Tycho never loses sight of what he is known for: the skillful mastery of crafting brilliant ambient soundscapes from bare computer programs. And believe it or not, his sound here is that much more captivating.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: On Hive Mind, Ital delivers a refreshing approach to instrumental electronics, with equal disinterest for both the club and headphone scenes, pissing off Internet purists in the process.

Title: Nightbird
Review: Longtime fans will be comforted by Nightbird, even if it comes off like the fluff Giorgio Moroder might've rejected after a coke bender. [Mar 2005, p.138]

Title: No Coast
Review: Braid continue their story here, branching out in new directions and leaving room to wonder what comes next.

Title: Outside Love
Review: His arrangement choices are flawless. While guitar stays front and centre, piano, strings, group vocals and slide guitar make fleeting, effective appearances.

Title: Me First
Review: Sennett twists and turns his songwriting more when he's alone than he does with Rilo Kiley, and while playing spot-the-influences isn't hard... it's also pointless in light of the album's genuine warmth.

Title: Together Through Life
Review: The singer isn't up to tenderness and the accordion gets annoying. But the first two tracks are standards in the making, the last two tracks are prophetic and mean, and the blues in between are as pointed as the pop songs are long-winded.

Title: Taiga
Review: Taiga is more of an achievement than that; it’s the mark of someone who has truly taken their time over their work. Cooped up in a friend’s holiday home in Washington, Nika Roza Danilova crafted a small slice of perfection.

Title: Celestite
Review: Every bit as dense and nuanced as their more traditional work, Celestite might end up finding itself falling between two stools, but no-one could accuse Wolves in the Throne Room of going at this half-heartedly.

Title: She Has No Strings Apollo
Review: Few bands... make slowing down sound this risky.

Title: Immunity
Review: If you don’t drift off too early, though, it all resolves, making for a sonically rich and delicately nuanced album.

Title: Waltzed in from the Rumbling
Review: Their fourth full-length is eclectic and confident. [Jun 2016, p.78]

Title: Bad Vibes
Review: Shlohmo's "debut" LP arrives slightly bloated due to its own blind ambition, and might require a few taps of the skip button for a more rewarding listen.

Title: Armonico Hewa
Review: Linguistic detective work aside, engage with natural scenery through scattered sound, this album does.

Title: Combinations
Review: Most songs, including the single-worthy 'Come Clean,' are still built on soaring vocal interplay and a childlike sense of wonder.

Title: The Money Store
Review: Burnett's one-note anger may be fine for those who fetishise the punk-rock mode of expression, but the near-total lack of range in his vocal approach is a poor match for the careening thrill of the music, and wearyingly basic.

Title: Eureka
Review: Robert Schwartzman's best asset is his gift for breezy melodies, but Eureka's lyrics sag.

Title: Interiors
Review: It may not be quite as consistent as its predecessor, but Interiors showcases the continued development of a vital emerging voice in popular music and features frequent moments of shiver-inducing beauty.

Title: Pylon
Review: The musicality on Pylon remains suitably elastic.

Title: Manzanita
Review: There is nothing but earnestness and obsession in her songs, which risk both clichés and awkwardness as they reach for honesty. [31 Jan 2005]

Title: Blurryface
Review: The result is an album that doesn't quite reach the heights of Vessel, but nevertheless serves as evidence that one of pop's most daring duos isn't about to slow down--even if that means running into a few walls.

Title: American Dream
Review: Full of irresistible grooves, quotable lyrics, and moments of spine-tingling beauty, American Dream is a worthy addition to the LCD Soundsystem discography.

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: At their best--during the disc’s torch-lit forays inward, the piano-ballad title track and the forlorn 'We’re Looking for a Lot of Love'--Hot Chip get serious, delving into the up-late tangles and riddles of the 21st-century heart.

Title: All We Grow
Review: Like Arthur Russell, he marries such influences [of Steve Reich and Terry Riley] with an off-kilter pop sensibility. [Oct 2010, p.87]

Title: The Optimist
Review: It may not top what came right before it, but it still beats almost everything else that’s been released so far this year.

Title: Every Open Eye
Review: The Glasgow trio's second album builds on the stem-winding synth-surge of their arresting 2013 debut, The Bones of What You Believe.

Title: Electric Balloon
Review: Ava Luna are an exhilarating live band, and Electric Balloon is the first thing they've done that comes close to bottling that energy.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: As is the case whenever [Kurt] Wagner's velvet croon wraps itself around a night that ends so late it's already morning... there really isn't a critic in the world who can touch him. [combined review of both discs; Mar 2003, p.94]

Title: Solar Motel
Review: Solar Motel is Forsyth’s most traditional album in recent memory.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: It's fantastic, as is so much of Forgiveness Rock Record, a collation of so many talents that it's practically bursting at the seams.

Title: Death Magic
Review: The end result is 40 minutes of music that drain the listener’s energy and will.

Title: Coma Witch
Review: As good as the proper album is, nothing--absolutely nothing--will prepare you for the masterwork that is “Observer”. It is, in short, brilliance, pure magnificence.

Title: Stronger
Review: Certainly, part of the variety is down to the multitude of producers and writers on Stronger, but the album's success is entirely due to Kelly Clarkson, whose personality and professionalism turns it into her best album since her Breakaway breakthrough in 2004.

Title: Devout
Review: Mr Mitch’s productions are as fastpaced, tight and spirited as his DJ sets. He makes the most of these sparse landscapes, marking a path for a complex of emotions to bleed though. Part of the album’s charm is that Mitch doesn’t shy away from adopting a pop sensibility nor embracing love as his subject matter. [May 2017, p.51]

Title: Mellow Waves
Review: It's unfair he no longer sounds unique. As a transmitter for cute. stylistic oddness, though, he remains staunch. [Sep 2017, p.96]

Title: Mordechai
Review: Mordechai, for all its use of vocals, really shows off the chops and interplay of the drums, bass, and guitar at Khruangbin's core. Even the songs that didn't grab me at first are a pleasure to listen to for the way Speer, Lee, and Johnson play together.

Title: Closer To Grey
Review: Their music is timeless but pulls on nostalgic heartstrings—it can be goth, earnest, sad, happy, distant and close all at once. It scratches a very specific itch for atmospheric pop and rock music that most of their imitators still can't touch.

Title: All at Once
Review: More sprawling and expansive than their previous record, All At Once still struggles to contain the myriad charms of this archetype power trio. [Mar-May 2018, p.59]

Title: Ambivalence Avenue
Review: Ambivalence Avenue presents a livlier Bibio, tastefully absorbing hip hop and disco beats. [Aug 2009, p.104]

Title: Chickenfoot
Review: The resulting album is, as expected, old school chest-beating man-size heavy rock. [Jul 2009, p.104]

Title: Perpetuum Mobile
Review: It feels like one of the most uncompromising and oddly impactful offerings they've produced in many years.

Title: Satin Doll
Review: A free-floating space jazz run at Joni & Mingus's Goodbye Pork Pie Hat is typical of his approachable fusion. [May 2020, p.96]

Title: Overgrown
Review: Overgrown remains closer knit, and paradoxically less fragmented than its illustrious predecessor, ideas rotating core values guided by an affirmatively unseen hand. Which ultimately makes this an even better record.

Title: Hold On Now, Youngster...
Review: Spirited and frenetic, Hold On adds up to more than just the sum of the band's five-star libraries. [Apr 2008, p.100]

Title: Stunt Rhythms
Review: Stunt Rhythms is by far an auditory treat.

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: Though they fit snugly inside their vintage genes, the Kings manage to make room for a surprising amount of heart. [Mar 2005, p.85]

Title: Postcards From a Young Man
Review: The Manics' 10th offensive is a more playful beast than that--poignant, joyful and above all really, really loud.

Title: Lost Wisdom
Review: Elverum is reveling in his honest moment of awe. In doing so, he has sloshed away the Norwegian frost with a mittened hand, a frost that kept these songs so chilling.

Title: Ordinary Man
Review: 71 years old at the time Ordinary Man was released, Osbourne's voice in in great shape, sounding more or less like he always has. How he's making music this strong after riding the crazy train for more than half-a-century is anyone's guess, but the better songs here rank among his best.

Title: Feel It Break
Review: Stelmanis, bassist Dorian Wolf and drummer Maya Postepski have created something that plays as a carefully balanced, organic whole, like an inadvertent concept album. That's more a testament to the skill with which it's been put together than because it lacks standout moments; in fact, half the songs here could be released as singles, as Austra are as melodic as they are melodramatic.

Title: Skull Ring
Review: Overproduced, under-written, swaggering nonsense.

Title: Knowle West Boy
Review: Knowle West Boy is a survey of Tricky’s sonic versatility--straightforward rock and oppressive, moody atmospherics all have a home here--and it is frequently gorgeous.

Title: Sing To The Moon
Review: All in all, a bewitchingly beautiful debut.

Title: Distant Relatives
Review: Sadly, Nas brings self-importance to "Strong Will Continue," that's encumbered his latter career, but it's the exception on a broadly fruitful collaboration. [Jul 2010, p.115]

Title: Country Squire
Review: Childers walks the line of down-home idiosyncrasies and smooth popular jams with a star-making perfection.

Title: This Is How You Smile
Review: By the time you’re through to the end of the album, Negro’s precise refusal to have bullied you with his ideas means you’re happy to return to the beginning and let that sunlight in again. Central heating for kids. Lovely. [Mar 2019, p.57]

Title: Goodbye Lullaby
Review: Goodbye Lullaby seems as much about the singer-songwriter's self-examination - she co-wrote all the tracks and is the sole author on many - as about any outward relationships.

Title: The Worse Things Get ...
Review: The closing Ragtime offers a happy ending of sorts, but this is too honest a record about unhappiness and grief to deliver a neat, redemptive conclusion.

Title: Wolves
Review: Their strength is in their inclusivity--yes, they’re from a punk background, but this is melodic hardcore with killer choruses to stir the hardest of hearts, bursting with a positive energy that channels your adrenaline until passive listening becomes all but impossible.

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Monsanto Years
Review: “Living With War,” his 2006 album about President George W. Bush, was a dud, and so is this new one.

Title: Sing When You're Winning
Review: 'Winning'' is a winner, offering ample reason for connoisseurs of great pop to rejoice, whatever their age. Alternately wistful and witty, introspective and invigorating, it's arguably even better than ''The Ego Has Landed,'' Williams' 1999 Stateside calling card.

Title: Hendra
Review: A solidly satisfying set.

Title: Ceremonials
Review: By taking what worked about Lungs and amplifying those qualities to a natural, satisfying conclusion, Florence has made a near-great pop record that should afford her the creative freedom to do whatever the hell she wants next time around. She may be away with the faeries, but she knows exactly what she's doing.

Title: Be Strong
Review: Be Strong, in short, is superb: a joyous amalgam of disco textures and dancefloor stylings which never fail to bring a big grin to your face.

Title: KOD
Review: While there are moments where Cole comes off more as a condescending high school principal than earnest older brother, KOD is an overall strong effort that connects of emotional trauma, mental health stigma in the Black community and the real problem of drug glorification.

Title: Acolyte
Review: No question about it, though, Delphic are at their best when they're in the studio with Pearson. His production wizardry is a joy to behold on Acolyte.

Title: Innocents
Review: Closing track The Dogs (featuring Moby himself on vocals) does stretch things out somewhat, it doesn’t spoil the notion that Innocents, while maybe not the creative renaissaince hinted at, is Moby’s best album for some time.

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: Musically, his sixth Silver Jews album is a low-key treat, country-inflected folk rock goosed by melodies that conjure both the Velvet Underground ("Open Field") and Johnny Cash ("Candy Jail").

Title: Trouble
Review: Fourteen songs deep, each and every one is a terrific slice of electronic pop that definitely delivers astounding results.

Title: Muzikizum
Review: The London threesome behind X-Press 2 slaves to house's repetitious mechanics (check the ugly robot fart clouding "AC/DC") yet often transcends its self-imposed limitations through fastidious craft.

Title: In the Pit of the Stomach
Review: It's hard-edged, it's proficient and most certainly smarter than the average band.

Title: Quixotism
Review: The giant, immense void that swallows sound in Part 1 shows itself in Part 5 to be just another windmill, slain by Ambarchi’s guitar and studio magic.

Title: The Hunger for More
Review: An assured debut that scores as much for what it doesn't do as it does for its low-key, insidious rhymes and chrome-gleaming rhythmical clatter. [24 Jul 2004, p.49]

Title: Brill Bruisers
Review: If you have a grand desire to take on the world and want a suitable indie rock soundtrack, Brill Bruisers will certainly do the trick, and if this isn't the best effort to date from the New Pornographers, it most certainly doesn't disappoint.

Title: Born with Stripes
Review: With no clear-cut standout like "Nice Train" or "Dolphin Center," the record fights to find its footing on slacker-rock ground and never quite gets there.

Title: Heroes to Zeros
Review: The Beta Band have added muscle to their rickety rock chassis without losing their past work's wood-fairy charm. [Aug 2004, p.106]

Title: Plastic Anniversary
Review: Like other Matmos albums, it relies too heavily on the concept behind the album for merit. Plastic Anniversary is an impressive experiment with intriguing results; it's not, however, an album you'll likely find yourself revisiting time and time again.

Title: Whispers
Review: Ultimately, with Whispers, Rosenberg has crafted an album of sweet, hummable anthems for tender-hearted troubadours everywhere.

Title: The Dew Lasts An Hour
Review: Ballet School is an indelible entry into the synth-pop genre, and are at least taking the approach somewhat differently by using guitars.

Title: Electric Lines
Review: We are ricocheted between smoky soul, verdant groove, and tantalizing pop-electronica. [Apr-Jun 2017, p.80]

Title: Rispah
Review: Irrespective of genre or decade, 'Rispah' is an astonishing tsunami of emotion which above all, makes you feel alive.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped, Krug's first post-Wolf Parade LP, feels like ritual music infused with 1980s nostalgia.

Title: Tribal
Review: Imelda May's fourth album works best when she drops the bad-bad-girl stereotypes, but takes a few songs for her to hit her stride. [No. 112, p.59]

Title: Preservation
Review: Preservation hits the hardest when there are zero or few added ingredients to divert attention from the voice, the melodies and the words.

Title: Bish Bosch
Review: This very refusal to cohere, to make sense, to play the game of identity and otherness, of harmony and disharmony, makes Bish Bosch this year's only necessary work of art.

Title: Security Screenings
Review: If Surrounded by Silence was Prefuse 73 beside himself, or even ten steps behind himself, Security Screenings is a commendable return to the path blazed by One Word Extinguisher and its subsequent outtakes.

Title: All Love's Legal
Review: Almost nothing about it works.

Title: Music For Cougars
Review: Sugar Ray can sometimes try too hard to seem younger than their years, pushing the dance beats a little bit too hard, and Mark McGrath relies on some unseemly Auto-Tune, but even with this too-evident aural botox, the group remains a guilty pleasure that's a bit hard to resist.

Title: Gods of Violence
Review: The record surges without slowing down, expanding without adding burden. Moreover, it proves that, out of the old class, Kreator are among the strongest, crushed not by ego or commercial temptations.

Title: Catacombs
Review: Despite the sparser arrangements and increased focus on direct lyricism, it's every bit as aurally hypnotic as his previous work. It seems like he realized there was someone he really did want to sing to.

Title: Good Advice
Review: A wildly inventive yet mainstream sound that suits her lyrics. [Mar 2016, p.106]

Title: Milk Money
Review: This uneven album is mostly a vehicle for “Legos (for Terry)”, an accomplishment that’s not only worth hearing but good enough to leave you hoping for more like it, too.

Title: The Week That Was
Review: Of all the 32-minute concept albums inspired by Paul Auster to come out of Sunderland this year, it's comfortably the best.

Title: How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb
Review: A one-paced affair, enamoured with drawn-out ambient intros, crystalline guitars layered with reverb, four-note rumbles for basslines, choruses that go on forever and occasional, half-hearted stabs at “groove”. Meaning that it sounds EXACTLY as you would expect U2 to sound.

Title: Beyondless
Review: Iceage make unpleasant music, but their bland sentimentality is the most disagreeable thing on Beyondless.

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: The album's standouts, however, are the two collaborations with Tirzah, whose understated vocals fit perfectly with Tricky's unnerving instrumentation and help to reveal an artist who's still capable of surprising, disturbing and revelling in his own idiosyncracies.

Title: Charmer
Review: Charmer plies the familiar recipe on a bed of pealing guitars and burbling synths. [Oct 2012, p.84]

Title: In Between
Review: There are still instances where Young Prisms reaches back to their old method, but the undeniable presence of growth gives their old ideas a fresh spin.

Title: Darwin Deez
Review: Darwin Deez, a New York-based artist for whom the word "offbeat" seems to have been invented. Not that there are any in his music--all straight 4/4 and po-mo lyrics--but there are plenty of tunes, not a little charm and a fair old sense of humour.

Title: Let's Stay Friends
Review: Let's Stay Friends is LSF's comeback--and frontman Tim Harrington and crew have picked up precisely where they left off.

Title: Condors
Review: Experienced as a whole, Condors is a multi-course meal that features some familiar dishes and some foreign with ingredients that require a bit of acclimation-but they're all delicious.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: [Wrecking Ball is] unquestionably his most potent album so far this century.

Title: This is Eggland
Review: This Is Eggland takes no prisoners in its sonic bombast, and does not suffer fools gladly. Taking elements from krautrock in the oscillations of Silver Apples together with the slash and fury of riot grrlers Bikini Kill, the resulting dish is mashed up in a throwaway aesthetic.

Title: Epic
Review: From One Day's po-sweet surprise to DsharpG's shivery vocal/harmonium drones, each gear shift is proof of a compelling new voice. [Dec 2010, p.100]

Title: Local Honey
Review: Fallon speaks humbly of his work, but Local Honey, containing various other themes of home and love, is his highest achievement to-date.

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: By channeling her anxiety into wonderful, shaggy, relatable and supremely catchy songs, she’s made Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit one of the most compulsively listenable albums to come out so far this year.

Title: Velocity of Sound
Review: Velocity is one massive dose of extremely fuzzed-out pop.

Title: Chinese Democracy
Review: It's an exhilarating album. Seriously, after finally hearing these 14 tracks in their finished form I was so energized I wanted to climb a mountain.

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: The Queens have officially given us the first legitimate Album Of The Year candidate for 2005. [May 2005, p.130]

Title: Complete Me
Review: Complete Me is a clever, well crafted and painstakingly produced pop concoction that was well worth the numerous delays.

Title: Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded
Review: More than it's lack of rap, Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded suffers most from not fully being any one thing, as it's unable to balance multiple approaches into one package.

Title: King Push - Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude
Review: It isn’t overly ambitious, but after more than two years without an official release it is still a treat to hear Pusha T, even if he stays largely in his cocaine comfort zone.

Title: The Nacirema Dream
Review: Listeners might feel fatigued while sitting through the 75 minutes that this album has to offer. Regardless, The Nacirema Dream is an admirable achievement.

Title: Somersault
Review: Somersault raises the bar on 2013’s ‘Clash The Truth’.

Title: Ssss
Review: The New Wave equivalent of the Rocky/ Apollo rematch at the end of Rocky III.

Title: FFS
Review: When two such spiky forms collide you can’t expect everything to click, but FFS is still a wonder of gelling idiosyncrasies.

Title: Once Again
Review: Legend's lounge-track sentimentality often spills into schmaltzed-out Streisand-on-Broadway territory.

Title: Animal
Review: Here he frames her Valley Girl sneer with electro-glam arrangements that make brushing one's teeth ''with a bottle of Jack'' sound like an awesome way to kill the morning-after blues.

Title: Fragrant World
Review: Yeasayer's only triumph here is perfecting a niche they've already seemed to master.

Title: One Life Stand
Review: The real shift is in their attitude, which allows them to embrace earnestness and write some straightforward love songs. It’s a strategy that could have backfired, but instead it has inspired their strongest and most consistent album so far.

Title: Always Got Tonight
Review: A fine return to form, Tonight offers a relaxed set of moody songs about love, cheating, heartbreak, and other venerable topics, all delivered with passionate effortlessness.

Title: The Godfather 3
Review: Rather than cowering from a tumultuous year full of set-backs, he’s taken the opportunity to deliver a long-awaited, cohesive project built on depth, clarity and nostalgia.

Title: Nothing's Gonna Change The Way You Feel About Me Now
Review: Nothing's Gonna Change... is ultimately the kind of album you can curl up into, let the warm tones surround you and rest easy.

Title: Silver Age
Review: Mould's most mature album, and for that reason, it is definitely his best solo album, too. The Silver Age is not the best record of the year, but it is certainly one of the most unpretentious and easily liked records of the year.

Title: Cinder
Review: This album more than any other swiftly dispels the notion that the trio are condemned to register wary introspection through brooding atmospheres.

Title: Kisses on the Bottom
Review: The music ... floats over you like a light mist on a cool spring morning in an English garden as the sun glints through the haze.

Title: Cut and Paste
Review: Overall, Cut and Paste is a fine collection of Oscar’s old lemons made into lemonade--it’s refreshing pop music, but with a floppy fringe and a tote bag.

Title: AIM
Review: AIM may be not the magnum opus that Mathangi Arulpragasam is capable of, but the music world would be a good deal less colourful and quirky without her in it.

Title: Lush
Review: Lush marks the arrival of an immensely talented singer-songwriter who also still has much room to grow. It may not live up to those more exuberant expectations of an instant classic, but it’s still an admirable, skillful piece of music that leaves me excited for what comes next. In this case, Jordan hasn’t finished the race. She’s just arrived at the starting line.

Title: Modern Kosmology
Review: What makes Jane Weaver and Modern Kosmology such a joy is that it comes as sharp and welcome relief to so many of the serious and po-faced purveyors of cynically cosmic vibes. This is music that simultaneously celebrates and explores, that takes pop as its foundation and then builds a multi-layered space on it that welcomes one and all.

Title: Pure, Beyond Reproach
Review: From the zany club outings of his 2010 to 2011 releases with Night Slugs to the more restrained and conceptualised LPs of recent years, each record has been a milestone in the development of this most remarkable musician--his latest album being no exception.

Title: Restless Ones
Review: Restless Ones is a statement of collective confidence and ambitious vision. [No. 121, p.55]

Title: Hot Shots II
Review: Its most fully realized set to date.

Title: Sunken Condos
Review: Long a master of obfuscation, Fagen plays it straight on Sunken Condos, tightening his songwriting and letting his music swing, and the results are an absolute joy.

Title: Doris
Review: It's obvious there's still plenty of room for some maturing (especially with the group's approach to women), but it's nice to at least see a little progress to go along with the stunning music.

Title: I
Review: I is the result, four long, loosely-related tracks that bump and groove and thrum and throb, often hypnotically, sometimes with a lively intensity. As an idea of musical process reimagined, I is always interesting. But as music, it’s uneven.

Title: Nothing to Do
Review: It gets old quick, but this goofy dance punk record is fun for the first few spins. [Jun 2012, p.158]

Title: Era Extrana
Review: This is a far more serious record than its predecessor, but Palomo isn't always as assured in rendering the darker material.

Title: Passion, Pain & Demon Slayin'
Review: Passion, Pain & Demon Slayin’ seems concerned with little more than keeping up appearances. Hopefully, the high points of the album are a proper barometer, and Kid Cudi’s next destination is a sight better than this.

Title: Amnioverse
Review: It’s disorientating, harrowing, yet hopeful – the ending needed to complete the circle. The only thing to do now is go back to the start and enjoy it all over again.

Title: Lions
Review: While Lions roars with all of the classic rock bombast and Stones-y swagger we've come to expect from the Crowes, the album is sorely lacking in the magic that can only be achieved when the innately talented drive themselves to distraction in the pursuit of perfection. [May/June 2001, p.110]

Title: The Civil War
Review: This sounds like what writers for a comedy skit trying to make fun of avant-garde music would come up with. [#5, p.114]

Title: Hive Mind
Review: On Hive Mind, the positive impact of their time apart is quickly apparent. The opener, Come Together is mature and quietly devastating in spite of its perky rhythm, an emblem of solidarity in the face of senseless violence. There’s little else here in the way of political statements, though, to the album’s benefit.

Title: To the Sea
Review: If you dig Johnson, you will like this record. If you've heard a few songs and never been interested, little on this album is likely to change that.

Title: Probot
Review: From the opening rally cry of Venom's Cronos ("Centuries of Sin") to the eerie creep of King Diamond's closing "Sweet Dreams," Probot pulls itself up by its pewter bootstraps and shatters glass with undefeatable vocals.

Title: With Strings Live At Town Hall
Review: Beneath their limpid surfaces, Mark "E" Everett's songs are volatile dollops of emotional explosive. [Mar 2006, p.98]

Title: It's Frightening
Review: At 10 songs and 35 minutes, there’s no filler, not even on the obligatory final comedown 'Leave It At The Door,' which is all fluttery woodwinds and exhaustion.

Title: V
Review: Arguably The Horrors’ best album yet. V, it would seem, is for Victory.

Title: Young Enough
Review: Ultimately, Young Enough outshines a promising debut, delivering a steady mix of summery earworms and angst.

Title: Feels
Review: The recipe for their success is straightforward, but they do manage to indulge in some more experimental desires by pushing Geronimo’s voice to the margins of the mix on tracks like the psychedelic “Bird’s Eye.”

Title: Sort of Revolution
Review: Every track on Sort of Revolution would feel at home in a warm, European coffeehouse.

Title: Goblin
Review: Sometimes this anger is ugly and interesting. Sometimes it is shallow and shocking. But something tells me that, while I have no trouble dismissing loads of offensive hip-hop, I won't be able to write this one off so easily.

Title: The Drop
Review: There's little outright originality, but they're melodically strong and the male-female vocal interchange between Andreas Pallisgaard and drummer Jaleh Negari is captivating. [Sep 2013, p.107]

Title: Deeper Than Rap
Review: Ross' player's paradise can be a very nice place to visit--outfitted with a cushy synth groove and a strenuous T-Pain chorus, the Kanye West- and Lil Wayne-assisted 'Maybach Music 2' manages to be both triumphant and laid-back--but over the length of a full album it all feels a bit too familiar.

Title: Welcome to Sideways
Review: A contoured album that hits a sweet spot between kinetic and laidback.

Title: A Thousand Heys
Review: Once the initial shock of hearing this Mazes' brand of distorted but highly melodic rock wore off, it gave way to pure delight.

Title: Future Breeds
Review: The Vancouver-based geek-funk group are making a good fist of it on their fifth opus and, for the most part, Future Breeds crackles and fizzes with electro-punk-tinged invention.

Title: The R.E.D. Album
Review: If there had been some big singles, fewer guests and more of Jayceon being himself, this could well have been a real classic.

Title: Running Out of Love
Review: Rather than risk nestling ever-deeper into their cushy role as purveyors of twee-approved, candied indie-rock, The Radio Dept. have opted for a collection of songs that is as decidedly unapologetic as it is cemented in political sludge.

Title: Stereo
Review: [Stereo] is brimming with expressive, beautifully articulated songs that speak to both sides of his personality.

Title: Ben Kweller
Review: Effortless pop with an undenaible solo-era Stephen Malkmus quality that just makes you want to go on a long drive. [#22, p.100]

Title: Brand New Eyes
Review: Rough edges, like the curt bathos of the lyrics (which repeatedly mistake brusqueness for wit), may be improved in the future. Either way, the band's music is already as catchy that of Fallout Boy, without nearly as much of the put-on faux-cleverness.

Title: Wounded Rhymes
Review: At her core, this new snarling, burned Lykke Li is unfamiliar, perhaps even to herself, but it's to our benefit. We get to meet her all over again.

Title: Pure
Review: One has to give credit to an '80s new wave musician who can adapt and create contemporary-sounding music.... The album can comfortably sit alongside Marilyn Manson and Nine Inch Nails on store shelves. Pure doesn't drive like the industrialized adrenaline rush that is, say, Orgy, but the tracks' lingering and creepy pace leaves behind a different kind of impact -- it's more haunting than relentless

Title: Please Excuse Me for Being Antisocial
Review: At times, Please Excuse Me for Being AntiSocial feels like it's trying to offer something for everyone, and it becomes difficult to locate Ricch's personality among the different window dressings. Regardless, it's a strong collection and highlights how Ricch can mold himself into different styles and keep things exciting in almost any stylistic configuration.

Title: Jackleg Devotional To The Heart
Review: Notably looser is ‘Oblivion Overture’s classical, Fantasia-esque take on earlier track ‘Oblivion’, while ‘Morning Of My Life’ finds a softer side to Flemmons’s nasal vocals, accompanied by little more than soft plucks of guitar. When combined though, these opposing elements transform Jackal into a distinctly outright collection of songs.

Title: Delta Spirit
Review: Delta Spirit delivers a handful of superb cuts that have the band taking a modest step forward.

Title: Silent Cry
Review: The confidence of a band that took over a year to record the album is notable, and theirs is an assured voice.

Title: Queen of Golden Dogs
Review: What's most impressive, though, is Gainsborough's commitment to integrating classical music on Queen Of Golden Dogs. The results, far from being grandiose, are rough, eloquent and compassionate.

Title: The Sun's Tirade
Review: It's up to the label's high standard, a riveting composite of grief and filth like no other.

Title: The Moon & Antarctica
Review: But, due to poor track titling and a rather wishy-washy sound (first it's Rusted Root, and then the Pixies, then Frank Black and the Catholics), the album ultimately doesn't have much of a solid impact.

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: Its ambrosial melodies and austere instrumentation edify his canon of work, which has long been rewarding for its risky sensibilities and perseverance. Yet that’s what makes Wakin so curious; it’s Vile’s most derivative record to date.

Title: Original Pirate Material
Review: The Streets' novel pairing of dance music and wordplay hits the mark more often than not, and it's a step in a potentially interesting direction. [Nov 2002, p.93]

Title: Grassed Inn
Review: Grassed Inn is both beautifully stupid, and much, much smarter than you think. [Jan 2014, p.63]

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: By trying to please all demographics here, Clark gives little sense of who he is.

Title: Trouble in Paradise
Review: There’s a notable evolution here, and we see the lone Jackson strive for something you can sink your teeth into over the course of a few days, weeks, month, rather than something you can insufflate at a club in the space of a few minutes.

Title: Weird Revolution
Review: Anchored in the surreal goofball art rock, club beats and bubblegum punk that made anomaly hits like 1996's "Pepper" so cool, frontman Gibby Haines and gang sugarcoat their standardized tales of decay and hallucinogens but keep some delicious bitterness intact.

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: There is a ton of evidence of his genius at work here.... As an album, though, The Further Adventures of Lord Quas doesn't cut it.

Title: Nocturama
Review: The missing link between Murder Ballads and Boatman's Call.

Title: HYMNS
Review: What it lacks, though, is a sense of purpose, which is the precise thing this new version of Bloc Party needed it to have; they needed to make a convincing case as to why they still deserve your attention. Instead, they picked the worst possible time to lose their nerve, and turn in something so bereft of conviction and new ideas.

Title: Guidance
Review: Guidance has parts where Russian Circles deliver on the promise of their astounding career, and instances where one is reminded of their greatest hits. The latter may be less appealing to those acquainted with the Russian Circles discography, but the former is still a thing to behold.

Title: Ex Lives
Review: A spontaneous, short, sharp stab of a record but one that might have been great had it not sounded so rushed. [April 2012, p.101]

Title: Invasion of Privacy
Review: Cardi B has proved herself to be someone not to mess with in the rap game, and it's exciting to see her at the top of her game on Invasion of Privacy.

Title: Pour It On
Review: Overall, it misses Hot Chip’s outsider appeal completely, coming off as whingey and middle aged. Don’t bother.

Title: The Hawk Is Howling
Review: The Hawk Is Howling is a record that shows Mogwai's lips to be sealed, but speaks volumes about their depth and ingenuity.

Title: Heavy Ghost
Review: Apparently Stith shied away from any musical expression for years--in which case Heavy Ghost represents a quite spectacular plunge. [Apr 2009, p.87]

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: Introspective and tightly wound. [Sep 2020, p.26]

Title: Automaton
Review: They may not find new listeners after a seven-year hiatus, but Automaton by Jamiroquai is a strong return and experimental contribution to popular music from a band too often identified solely for one song and its striking video.

Title: To Survive
Review: Wasser’s a collaborator at heart (she was a charter member of the Dambuilders and worked with Lou Reed, Antony & the Johnsons and Rufus Wainwright, who guests on “To America”), and she sounds most natural when she’s backed by horns and keys and backing vox and slinky grooves.

Title: Strange Desire
Review: Antonoff may be popular but his songwriting leaves a lot to be desired.

Title: Lemonade
Review: The result is an album in which millions will find their own struggles reflected back to them, as therapeutic as it is utterly dazzling. If you've ever been handed lemons, you need Lemonade.

Title: No Mas
Review: No Más has three-fifths as many tracks in the same amount of time [as Jamz n Jemz], and for the most part, each track outstays its welcome.

Title: Made in China
Review: Made in China is a raw, angry album that is difficult to endure at points due to the emotionally naked lyrics, but the lo-fi, almost punky, music is a perfect fit.

Title: The Last Sucker
Review: Is The Last Sucker Ministry’s masterpiece closer to its career? Not totally, but it’s a powerful album that leaves you wanting more.

Title: Rising Down
Review: It might not be their best-ever album--Phrenology can still claim that title--but Rising Down finds The Roots reinvigorated, more passionate than ever.

Title: From the Ages
Review: It never really achieves the celestial heights of Cosmic Sky, every song after the opener feeling too much like an extended comedown, but From The Ages is an essential record for anyone who likes the sound of guitars sounding like guitars.

Title: All At Once
Review: Jollett's weighty musing are all but neutered by his determination to cover all musical bases but, as an alt-rock starter-kit, it's just about perfect. [May 2011, p.109]

Title: The Stage Names
Review: The band's arrangements are still wonderfully unpolished, so while these tunes should please anyone who buys CDs at Starbucks, they still pack some ragged glory of what makes the Austin collective so intoxicating on stage.

Title: Devil's Night
Review: Devils Night's high points are some of the most accomplished hip-hop we'll hear this year. But the balance between humor, shock, raw talent and psychosis that Eminem achieved on his last two albums is off.

Title: Emancipated Hearts
Review: Even at six tracks, it’s stunning how much life (and death) Wareham spreads over these tracks, and makes these tiny whispers of songs feel like the biggest secret anyone’s ever told you.

Title: Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)
Review: While Numan's work remains strictly sulky stuff destined to ruin any party, he proves he's not a robot at all on his most connectable, personal, and palpable album to date.

Title: Midnight Memories
Review: Midnight Memories takes the slight progression of Take Me Home and demolishes it.

Title: Phase Zero
Review: Morgan Delt's Phase Zero navigates that thin line between rêverie and acid trip, drawing an accepted state of temporary and discreet insanity.

Title: The Astonishing
Review: You might want to laugh at points, because a good deal of it is very silly, but somewhere within the second half, you’ll become just a little invested. By the grand finale, you might even feel inspired.

Title: Tomorrow's World
Review: It's early Erasure fans who seen likely to enjoy the '80s electro sheen of the all-action rhythmo-melodic hooks and subplots. [Nov 2011, p.100]

Title: Trouble No More
Review: If you really want to hear folk-blues played with rock'n'roll attitude then go back to Boomer's Story or Into The Purple Valley. [Oct 2003, p.111]

Title: Beyondless
Review: Lyrically, Beyondless is occupied with notions of excess, from the endless cycle of war, to switching one dependency for another, to indulgence and appetite. It works because the band fundamentally thrives in extremes.

Title: The Duckworth Lewis Method
Review: It's a record of beautifully constructed songs--pastiches, yes, but so perfectly rendered as to be melt-in-your-mouth lovely.

Title: Union and Return
Review: Union and Return is as much a continuation as it is a fresh start; as much as Wyatt's old approach might be missed, he doesn't need it to make compelling music.

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: A glorious, towering achievement. [#22, p.98]

Title: Robotique Majestique
Review: Robotique Majestique is compelling and eminently danceable, and it has as much visceral kick as cerebral appeal for the indie dance kids who demand both.

Title: Return to the Moon
Review: Return To The Moon is fully realised and offers plenty of intrigue, but .... rarely do they sound like a unit, and, surprisingly, Berninger is the one that ends up sounding a little lost. [Nov 2015, p.74]

Title: LCD Soundsystem
Review: After disappointing would-be breakthrough releases from so many of the discopunk frontlines, this is an album that’s more easily classifiable as “great” for what it isn’t, rather than what it is. It’s not inconsistent. It’s not a total deviation from what we know of the group. It’s never dull. And, most importantly--it is in no way a let down.

Title: Riot Boi
Review: Somewhere between the cuteness of Shamir and the scariness of Mykki Blanco you will find New York’s Le1f, a ballet dancer-turned-producer-turned rapper. Although his out-ness is a big part of the appeal of this warped and edgy party album, the nod to riot grrrl in its title hints at far wider-ranging agendas within.

Title: Hello, Voyager
Review: Its diversity, boldness and overall quality has compelled me to delve into Bozulich's past work with fresh, enthusiastic ears.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: The pair's [James Mercer and Greg Kurstin's] proclivity for spacious, languid moods helps Port of Morrow move smoothly from mod throwback shimmies (like the spindly guitar jam "Bait and Switch'') to the hypnotic, near trip-hop of the title track.

Title: C'mon Miracle
Review: It's classy, but also honest. Not a single emotion seems overplayed or exaggerated; you'll dance and sway to it because each song feels as organic as life, and the life it documents is nicely lit.

Title: Taking Back Sunday
Review: While this latest work may not meet the wild expectations of many long-time fans who yearn for a return to band's early glory days, it should be taken for what it is, as this current Taking Back Sunday is once again a new animal.

Title: Morning View
Review: Even at their most acerbic or delicately downplayed extremes, Incubus are compelling. [#184, p.137]

Title: Third Mouth
Review: Some wonderful and very carefully constructed material here.

Title: I Love The New Sky

Title: Dear Science
Review: If you're a fan, there's certainly stuff you'll enjoy here, but if you're looking for them to take another step forward, this might not suffice.

Title: Blanco
Review: The songs on Blanco first appeared on Bazan’s monthly 7” series, so it seems clear that using synthesizers was one way of differentiating them from their original versions. (He must like doing this, since his last album was a collaboration with the Passenger String Quartet.)   But he seems to be onto something interesting with this electronicized approach.

Title: Late Registration
Review: [An] even more ambitious, superbly crafted follow-up. [28 Aug 2005]

Title: Azari & III
Review: Really, though, its the earlier track "Lost in Time" that best sums up the record's appeal--on one level, it's about the dancefloor as an escape, while on another, it winks at the group's time travels.

Title: Ten
Review: After a few listens Ten emerges as an extremely clever audio novel.

Title: Here We Stand

Title: War Stories
Review: War Stories is another win for Lavelle.

Title: Gossip in the Grain

Title: Some Things Last Longer Than You
Review: This is an album significantly more than what it seems to be, at first, on the surface. To some, it will sound like just another melodic punk album with a predilection for pop--an angry retort at the grievances of being in your twenties--but it’s the kind of record that will stir and inspire you during moments of existential crisis.

Title: Colored Sands
Review: Luc remains an expert in experimental extremity, with Forgotten Arrows, reminding us that Gorguts were trawling prog-death waters long before Gojira. [17 Aug 2013, p.54]

Title: The Hex

Title: At the Dam

Title: Guilt Show

Title: Cost of Living
Review: The band's simmering anger are leavened by a sophisticated musical backdrop utilising brass and keyboards. [Sep 2017, p.109]

Title: AIM

As such, the album feels less like a farewell and more like a preview for her next reinvention, a midday snack before the full-course government takedown.

Title: Shields
Review: This is still a Grizzly Bear record, but thanks to a spin through the grinder of maturity, it's also now a Grizzly Bear that know when to hold back or let things flow in order to create an LP that connects emotionally. This was the one thing that its impressive but more technically minded predecessors often lacked.

Title: Something Shines
Review: Many of the songs on here just aren’t very memorable.

Title: Made Up Mind
Review: All in all, Made Up Mind is one of the more intriguing efforts from 2013.

Title: Temple Beautiful
Review: Temple Beautiful is the product you expect from this highly original and creative artist.

Title: The Cookbook

Title: High Noon
Review: High Noon is almost that special of an album, and, despite some minor inherent weaknesses, this is definitely one to purchase and check out.

Title: Wrath
Review: This confident follow-up is rawer, looser and altogether more agressive. [Apr 2009, p.97]

Title: Antidotes

Mostly that's fine, since sublimely hypnotic arrangements of horn bursts and techno glitch beats generally render meaning unnecessary. But all that yelping about "electric shocks" ("Big Big Love [Fig. 2]") might be better buried in a dub mix.

Title: Solo Piano III
Review: Chilly Gonzales has shown time and again that he’s a composer worthy of our attention and this is just one more instance that proves him right. Solo Piano III is Gonzales at his most traditional, but with hints of his more disarming inner ego.

Title: Marnie Stern
Review: It's undeniable that for her self-titled third album, Marnie Stern has made some canny decisions. This time round, several of the tracks are built around huge, stomping riffs, with the speedier guitar lines mixed further back to create more space, without sacrificing that-which-is-Marnie.

Title: Solarized
Review: There's a freshness uncommon to fortysomething men two decades into their career. [Oct 2004, p.110]

Title: Sheezus

Title: Fever Ray

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: Their conversational deliveries and every man personas, cultivated in the often self-effacing world of blog rap sometimes feel small atop sparse, up tempo production clearly inspired by the late '80s when larger than life mic controllers brought the color to often minimalist canvases.

Title: Innocence Reaches
Review: The amount of fatigue and cynicism baked into 14th album Innocence Reaches is not just a bummer; it's verging on ominous.

Title: Demon Days
Review: Spookier, blippier, and more on edge. It's also not as cohesive. [27 May 2005, p.136]

Title: True North
Review: True North shows flashes of their earlier work, and is a step up from their last album, 2010's The Dissent of Man, in terms of aggression.

Title: You Can Have What You Want
Review: You Can Have What You Want is like "Turn on the Bright Lights" (2002) without the drama, without a voice as deep or distinct as Paul Banks’, and without the hooks. Instead of all that, Papercuts opt for a vague, beige production and generally indecipherable lyrics that may or may not be about some kind of futuristic utopia/dystopia.

Title: Into The Murky Water
Review: It all adds up to a record for those who want thrills but don't want them dumb.

Title: Heavy Lifter

Title: Truelove's Gutter

Title: Destroyer
Review: Destroyer starts thumping with the first track and never stops; the tone might change, but the listener’s desire to stomp the accelerator on the open road won’t.

Title: The Life of Pablo
Review: There is much to be admired here, rather less to be enjoyed.

Title: Rain
Review: Rain balances sophistication and edgy smarts with a winning mixture of grace and confidence.

Title: Homesongs
Review: Nothing less than a whole new world will do, and Adem has created just that.

Title: Blueberry Boat
Review: The problem with Blueberry Boat is that, while it's a musical marvel, it's not an album that I'll keep listening to.

Title: Night Visions
Review: Dramatic and sweeping, the Las Vegas band works in the same vein as pop giants Coldplay, offering up track after track of hooky and emotional midtempo jams.

Title: Wonderland
Review: Altogether, it’s some irresistible glitter-on-the dancefloor delirium.

Title: Love King
Review: On Love King the slow-thumping '80s-R&B vibe suggests Prince is still a huge influence; even darling Nikki might blush at these racy tunes.

Title: American Idiot
Review: Against all odds, Green Day have found a way to hit their thirties without either betraying their original spirit or falling on their faces.

Title: Soldier of Love
Review: Lacking rhythmic hypnotism and relatable most to those who are experiencing solitude created by romantic desertion, this is not your mother's Sade album.

Title: Begin To Hope
Review: As if the synthesized strings and electronic dabbling weren't sad enough, [Spektor's] ascerbic voice has been all but lost in squishy couplets about making things better and needing to "know you."

Title: Room 29
Review: One can’t help thinking the ghosts and echoes of previous scandalous indulgences are rather betrayed by the project’s neat, sentimental manner.

Title: Here We Rest
Review: Jason Isbell and the 400 Unit's Here We Rest is not what you'd call easy listening.

Title: GINGER
Review: GINGER yields a sound that is more emotionally evolved than any album thus far. ... The result is BROCKHAMPTON have finally come of age.

Review: Musically, Madness still trade in pub singalongs powered by ska rhythms and music-hall jollity--but the jollity feels forced, and Suggs’ tired vocals suggest a man going through the motions.

Title: Thank You for Stickin' With Twig
Review: Business as unusual for Twig. [Oct 2015, p.83]

Title: 24K Magic
Review: Is anything here the equal of Uptown Funk? Not quite, but the opening three songs are excellent party starters. The mid-tempo cuts lack the lustre of the uptempo ones, and the album’s closing ballad--Too Good to Say Goodbye--isn’t as persuasive as When I Was Your Man off Unorthodox Jukebox.

Title: Sleeper
Review: With Sleeper Segall sounds almost, well, mature, and emotionally invested.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: With a hot guest list (Ciara, T.I.), this is bound to bump the clubs, but beyond that, it's clown time.

Title: Shelter From The Ash
Review: Shelter bleeds enough drone and bliss to make a pretty smear of reality.

Title: High Hopes
Review: There's a sombre edge to almost all these songs, even when the Hammond organ is wailing and the backbeat is a mile wide.... Morello's presence is crucial to the tone of the album.  [Feb 2014, p.65]

Title: ye
Review: Make no mistake, this is difficult to listen to. You will not be rewarded for multiple listens. It is what it is. It’s not enough, by a mile. West has clearly made this for himself first, and indulgence is deeply ingrained into the concept.

Title: A Deeper Understanding
Review: Produced differently, A Deeper Understanding could be really startling stuff; as it is, it feels like The War on Drugs have made an agreeable, fan-pleasing album to escape into and hide in, not to a record to take on the world--but perhaps that’s not such a bad thing in 2017.

Title: The Unraveling
Review: The Unraveling finds Hood and Cooley as fiery as they’ve ever been. If American Band proved that the Drive-By Truckers still had plenty left to say, The Unraveling shows that they can allow themselves a bit of fun in the studio while getting their message across.

Title: An Obelisk
Review: The songs here beg to fall apart but are kept in tight reign by Chris Wilson's drums and R.J. Gordon’s flurrying bass while Stickles and guitarist Liam Betson slay riffs and trade licks.

Title: Zeros
Review: This sophomore effort sheds off the fat and pins down his point: clout, capital, and dedication bubbling over into a synth-pop opus so deliciously evil and devastatingly singular it deserves its own cult.

Title: Hard Rain
Review: Hard Rain is not a bad album. It will very amiably sit, out of focus, in your field of vision as you do other things. It doesn’t, however, have whatever special something it needs to transcend the sense of a backwards referent.

Title: The Breakthrough
Review: Mary J draws on an eventful life to reach new levels of feeling. [7 Jan 2006, p.29]

Title: Saturns Pattern
Review: Weller’s renaissance has not come at the expense of his musical identity. The sunshine-pop haze of Phoenix is from the Tame Impala playbook, but you could imagine Style Council-era Weller singing it.

Title: Brute
