Title: In Our Nature

Title: El Pintor
Review: Throughout, the refreshed use of light and dark is notable and works. There is contrast and there is colour.

Title: Origin

Title: No Cities Left

Title: Teens of Denial

Title: Black Market Music

Review: Their third set hits a sweet spot between the futuristic soul of their debut and the synth pop of 2009's Machine Dreams.

Review: Heems and Kool A.D. might be deconstructing rap for the purposes of delivering ingenious and challenging verses, but Relax is one of the best capital R rap albums out this year.

Title: Meds
Review: If you are able to ignore the lyrics, you'll be rewarded: the choruses on Meds are catchy.

Title: Ski Mask

Review: Glass Animals sound like they are on the cusp of everything. There's a gap between their vocabulary and their sound, their choruses and their intros, their obvious intelligence and what they've produced.

Title: Jarvis
Review: A decade after he first set an impossibly hard act to follow, Jarvis Cocker has returned with an album that knocks not only his ageing contemporaries, but many of his descendents, for six.

Review: The focus on time and its ravages may seem to place this in 35-and-over territory, but Sexsmith's songs are timeless. [Mar 2007, p.136]

Title: Never Better
Review: P.O.S. has created something that sounds vibrant and alive, and stretches the narrow limits of the genre.

Title: Chuck
Review: An uneven but fitting swansong, then. [Aug 2017, p.100]

Title: Take Me Home and Make Me Like It
Review: Take Me Home in particular sounds like a bonus disc to a full album reissue. But they reveal new angles to the Big Star story. [Aug 2017, p.52]

Title: Up in Flames
Review: Though Manitoba's constructions are joyously slap-dash and defiantly experimental, he still manages to lure the listener in with woozy melodies and strangely beguiling textures.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: There's nothing overly complex or profound here, but try to resist the charm.

Title: A Weekend in the City
Review: Those hoping to be converted are likely still to doubt the 'voice of a generation' tag.

Title: New Chain
Review: In all honesty, New Chain isn't so very different from the rest of the Bushwick bulk. What is worth returning to, however, is the fact that the music offered is effortlessly lovely, memorable, well-transitioned, and oddly addicting.

Title: Ash Wednesday
Review: There's something about this album... that takes listeners by the hand, smacks them into reality and reminds them they're still alive. [#24, p.90]

Title: Open Here
Review: When they strip things back and leave space for each element to breathe--as on the purely orchestral title track--Open Here can be a joy, a deeply astute pop album that’s also often brimming with fun. While pushing their boundaries as far as they can go though, it sometimes makes for a record that can feel frustratingly cluttered.

Title: Superorganism
Review: The disorientating utopian ride you take when listening to this album in full will no doubt bring you glee, and maybe some weird dreams if you think about being a prawn too much.

Title: Standing in the Way of Control
Review: Think Au Pairs or Delta 5, but filtered through Bikini Kill and the Rapture.

Title: Raven in the Grave
Review: Here, they tinker with the formula slightly, shedding the surf drums, and adding washes of synth (usually a mistake, and so it proves). [Jun 2011, p.94]

Title: Winning Days
Review: A diverse and highly enjoyable ride.

Title: Intensive Care
Review: For all its rosy glow of nostalgia, it's essentially just another Robbie Williams album--occasionally spectacular, more frequently merely solid. [Nov 2005, p.116]

Title: Holy Fire
Review: On Holy Fire, the third album from the English band, the post-punk revival is given a newfound sense of depth, creating songs that are rhythmic enough to draw listeners, but hypnotic enough to leave listeners lost in their wide-open spaces.

Title: Solo
Review: Solo is Iyer's grand statement, and with it he has fulfilled his promise.

Title: I'm All Ears
Review: Depending on your taste for that kind of home-brewed, distinctively British weirdness, I’m All Ears is either a massive leap forwards or a sad lurch towards the middle-ground.

Title: The Cookbook
Review: While not every cut is a winner, Elliott does a fairly consistent job of gaining the listener's attention through her outrageous lyrics and performance style.

Title: The Modern Age
Review: She [Louise Wener] sounds more at ease in her delivery, and the knowhow is natural. On occasion with their less successful single releases you felt Sleeper were trying a bit too hard, but here it is refreshingly instinctive. The addition of more power to the lower end is very welcome too.

Title: Daemon
Review: Mayhem are restrained by an obsession with their past. [Jan 2020, p.85]

Title: Heligoland
Review: Then, six songs into a characterless album, one on which ambience takes precedence over tunes, 3D and Daddy G unveil three stunning numbers that compare with anything in their back catalogue.

Title: Baby
Review: Already it feels like they're playing to a rapidly disappearing crowd. [Mar 2012, p.89]

Title: Lifelike
Review: Elegant, unusual touches like these suggest Facs are still finding new complexities in their music on Lifelike, an album that demands and rewards close listening.

Title: On The Water
Review: On the Water is too uncompromising, too disinterested in being for anyone outside of its circle of two.

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: It's taken a while to get here, but Ultraviolet finally introduces a fresh talent who may not have too much to say just yet, but what's going on in the background goes some way to making up for such deficiencies.

Title: YSIV
Review: Logic rhymes in exciting ways, but the meanings can be a little strained.

Title: Beams
Review: It's not that Beams is a lighter listen than Black City, but it's certainly more honest.

Title: Damage and Joy
Review: Musically there is little to remember, lyrically some of this is challenging to forget. For a 19-year wait, this is a mild payoff indeed.

Title: Some Cities
Review: Anthemic, challenging pop.

Title: Gutterflower
Review: Gutterflower proves once again that they are masters at crafting instantly appealing pop songs.

Title: Shelter
Review: If you can’t conceptually get behind the concept of a metal kid giving up noise for beauty, you’re probably not going to like the record. Otherwise, check it out. It’s lovely.

Title: Tromatic Reflexxions
Review: The album is brilliant on its own terms: a party record with no fixed strategy, one that wiggles out of all responsibilities to the partier.

Title: The Pale Emperor
Review: It's about as close to aging gracefully as you could ever hope to get from a dude who used to call himself the Antichrist Superstar. [23 Jan 2015, p.69]

Title: Drifters / Love Is The Devil
Review: There are magic moments, but the overall effect might make you drift off rather than have you on the edge of your seat.

Title: Too Bright

Title: Electric Balloon
Review: The record keeps pulsating from one energy to another, suggesting art project and ritual.

Title: Spoon and Rafter
Review: A melancholy masterpiece.

Title: Outside
Review: Outside tastes like having returned to my favorite bar to find they've redone the menu. Only this time, all the improvements are positive ones.

Title: Magnificent Fiend
Review: It's a tighter, less primitive album than its predecessor, but as such, it has a lot more to offer as well.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: The Shins' second effort sparkles with a clarity that was not always evident on their debut and energizes with a spark and an enthusiasm that previously seemed forced.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: Infinite Arms is a surprisingly understated affair.

Title: Dark Light
Review: While the drop in adrenaline has left room for some good ideas, they’re not fleshed out well enough, and with the lack of a single flat-out rocker, there’s nothing to get excited or exhilarated over.

Title: Heligoland
Review: Instead of reintroducing the genre’s founding dub steps and club sensibilities, contributions from Massive Attack’s musical descendants (Blur/Gorillaz mastermind Damon Albarn, Portishead’s Adrian Utley) lend quieter atmospherics that amplify the emotion of the band’s mainstay whispers.

Title: Blood Red Shoes
Review: Their fourth album, self-produced and recorded in Berlin, finds the smart hooks and spiky lyrics all present and correct. [Apr 2014, p.69]

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: Boarding House Reach is easily one of the most layered and compelling releases of 2018, which furthers White’s legacy as one of the few remaining mavericks in music.

Title: Blacc Hollywood
Review: Melodies coast, but they don’t always stick; everything’s too mannered, too clean, and the album is marred by a clinicality further punctuated by its bonus tracks.

Title: My God Is Blue
Review: Sébastien invites you to follow him, like a sexy David Koresh, and with tunes like 'Sedulous', 'Pepito Bleu' and the aforementioned 'Cochon Ville' ('pig city' en Anglais), the call might just prove irresistible.

Title: Something Else
Review: Something Else--a sharper, more concise follow-up to 2006’s breakthrough but spotty, "The Evolution of Robin Thicke"--songwriter and producer Thicke is using the tones and rhythms of soul music for a bigger idea: dissatisfaction.

Title: Ladytron
Review: Their eponymous return is an immersive, invigorating and convincingly brooding stomp of disenfranchisement.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes extends and refines both the lyrical smarts and programmatically adventurous nature of Young Liars.

Title: Divine Providence
Review: Divine Providence apparently isn't a realm for the faint of heart, but those with the verve to vent their all may find it a welcome retreat.

Title: Fleeting
Review: Fleeting achieves something each Jones record has worked toward, to create a geography of sound, to make these notes from guitar and banjo feel like the creaks and groans of an old house, to make you picture the dust pluming off each plucked string, to see the motes drifting through sunlight pouring through a nearby window.

Title: Beautiful Thing
Review: While there's certainly no shortage of sonic experimentation woven into this relatively more adventurous album, the British singer-songwriter struggles to find an effective balance between the added electronic accoutrements and the minimalist core that informs his solo work.

Title: Blood Moon
Review: Blood Moon seems like Craft's real start, and one of the most exquisite soul-searching odysseys of this or any year. [Jul 2016, p.93]

Title: Magnificent Fiend
Review: When [Ethan Miller] bellows, "Lord, have mercy on my soul," the result is hokey, irresistible fun.

Title: Birthdays
Review: There’s no better way to shut out the din than by putting this record on.

Title: City Center
Review: While the descriptors may intimate a degree oof emotional detachment, this record ultimately is anything but, exuding ample warmth while engaging the listener at a deeply personal level, and auguring even greater things to come. [Summer 2009, p.64]

Title: Something to Die For
Review: The album's largely a series of almost good songs and will likely get a fair amount of play both on college radio and in clubs.

Title: NYC
Review: It’s great headphone music and would make a suitably dense soundtrack for a drunken stroll through the Lower East Side, where much of the inspiration for NYC was found.

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: Multidimensional. ... This rotating playlist of styles and sincerity will rankle with some--it's very earnest about addiction, love and our internet selves--but rather that than banal conformity. [Feb 2019, p.23]

Title: The Conversation
Review: Pleasant enough, but you may feel you've heard this conversation before. [Jun 2013, p.88]

Title: As If to Nothing
Review: Though some might say that Armstrong's music is powerfully evocative and serene, such people hate music and all its subtle possibilities and intricacies.

Review: It is something of a slow burner, and familiarity with their back catalogue will certainly add depth to the whole experience, but those who come to it cold will find the immediacy and vigour of the likes of Public Enemy No. 1 irresistible.

Review: The result is an affable album that soothes but rarely dazzles, and In the Cool of the Day winds up functioning better as a contemporary reading of older songs.

Title: WIT'S END
Review: Unafraid of bursting your bubble, Wit's End crawls and slithers slowly, touching upon the darkest of themes.

Title: Howlin
Review: Howlin' works impeccably as a whole. Equally uplifting and calming, it's the dancefloor via the beach.

Title: Amphetamine Ballads
Review: Amphetamine Ballads probably shouldn’t feel like quite so much of a breath of fresh air--there’s plenty of evidence to suggest that it wears its influences (or has them tattooed, probably) very much on its sleeve--but it carries a threatening urgency so often conspicuous by its absence nowadays.

Title: Witching Hour
Review: Witching Hour could stand to be about two tracks shorter, but its quality comes as an unexpected, and highly welcome, surprise.

Title: A Color Map of the Sun
Review: The result has to feel like a studio adventure! Whereas Daft Punk’s Random Access Memories was lavishly rich, Smith’s treatment of his session players manages to flatten all human serendipity and rhythmic nuance.

Title: CrownsDown
Review: The resultant album is free of the over compensating braggadocio and tired memes of ring-tone rap culture. [Fall 2009, p.75]

Title: Perfect Version
Review: Musically, Perfect Version isn’t flashy, but it sure is pretty. Chastity Belt records have a way of popping out at the listener with their shimmering melodies and catchy hooks, while this album is significantly more understated. But Shapiro’s hushed voice, delivered among reverberating guitars and atmospheric drones, invites the listener back for repeat listens.

Title: Words and Music by Saint Etienne
Review: Words and Music frequently sounds as dizzy with the joy of pop as Saint Etienne did 20 years ago.

Title: Fasciinatiion
Review: That Fasciinatiion isn't a revelatory departure is not to say that it is completely without merit. It is, however, undeniably lacking an air of excitement.

Title: Exciter
Review: 'Exciter' stakes a hell of a claim on bringing Depeche Mode into the 21st century.

Title: The North Borders
Review: The result is not, unlike many of his peers, a symphony of interlinking tracks, but a collection of individuals that, together, tell a unified story of emotion.

Title: Planet Earth
Review: A sound as sharp and renewable as anyone's in pop history.

Title: Hello Sadness
Review: The best moments remain the songs where the band moves as a unit, conjuring a sense of hope and elation, rather than falling back on tired, shouty punk cliches.

Title: A Better Version of Me
Review: Rainer Maria is the genuine collegiate article: impressionistic and overwrought.

Title: Fake It Flowers
Review: Too often, she jumps to John Hughes-isan climaxes without laying the foundation that would grant them the proper emotional heft. But Kristi shines as a guitarist and a composer; even the sternest skeptics might be forced to headbang once the power chords crash in on a particularly distorted chorus. Beabadoobee needs to punch up her script, but the set is perfectly lit.

Title: Fold Your Hands Child, You Walk Like a Peasant
Review: It makes good on Belle And Sebastian's urge for diversity while sticking to the transcendent pop that made its name.

Title: Invariable Heartache
Review: A low-key, highly engaging covers album. [Nov 2010, p.99]

Review: It underlines that Pottery have made a record meant for a party that never stops. Bobby’s Motel is surely a place with more to it than meets the eye.

Title: We Love Life
Review: Cocker's treasurable wit and the band's seventh album have taken a corporation bus ride out for strange, poetic interludes among the trees and the undergrowth.

Title: The Book of Traps and Lessons
Review: An always thought-provoking record.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: It's less flashy than previous efforts, but the thrill here is of witnessing a songwriter's talent maturing.

Review: Make no mistake, 'Don't Be Afraid Of Love' is so much more ambitious and downright joyful than we had any right to expect that it's a flooring jolt to the system long after the first listen.

Title: Boys
Review: The results are assuredly in Crocodiles' wheelhouse with the occasional surprise.

Title: Electric Dirt
Review: Helm blends the secular and gospel worlds with an almost seamless precision. Fans of the Band will love this.

Title: Beware
Review: Beware emulates and elaborates on the familiar, and Oldham's strengths as a songwriter and bandleader shape the album into something beautiful.

Title: ANThology
Review: Lyrically, they've got a ways to go.... That said, Alien Ant Farm shows some real potential.

Title: Dressed Up for the Letdown
Review: While "Dressed Up For The Letdown" is a classy, clever record, it is not one you can imagine yourself revisiting that often.

Title: Always Tomorrow
Review: Deeply satisfying on multiple levels, Always Tomorrow is great guitar pop and a bracing account of one person’s struggle to construct a new life. Free of sugar-coating or easy answers, it should speak to everyone who wants to take better care of themselves.

Title: Family
Review: It ends up being a more nuanced guide to the Thompsons' flawed but just-about functioning dynamic, divorces, remarriages and all. [Dec 2014, p.82]

Title: Under a Billion Suns
Review: The rock these four men so easily brandish is every bit the equal, if not the better, of that deployed by so-called peers half their age.

Title: All Your Happy Life
Review: It demands your attention, grabbing your head by the hair and forcing you to listen.

Review: Recorded with Thomas’s snarl up front and the band on screeching overload, they pile through new titles such as Welcome To The New Dark Ages and revisit Sonic Reducer and Final Solution, plus the Sonics’ garage classic Strychnine.

Title: Ssss
Review: Tremendous stuff.

Title: Belladonna
Review: At first blush, Lanois' music is flowery wallpaper, but on repeated listens the colorful textures sink in and evoke a hushed mysticism.

Title: Lease of Life
Review: It's intrinsically a strange album though, trapped somewhere between The Knife, Nineties acid house, Kraftwerk, New Order’s Technique album, and literally anything Eno did in the Eighties, but the warped pop sensibilities and gloriously plastic production make it a hidden gem.

Title: Lemonade
Review: Lemonade marks Beyoncé’s most accomplished work yet. It is the perfect combination of the sharp songwriting of 4 with the visual storytelling acumen of her self-titled record. Here, we see Beyoncé fully coming into her own: wise, accomplished, and in defense of herself.

Title: Paradise
Review: Slow Club is aware of their twee appeal--and uses it like a double-edged sword, throwing folk guitar solos, string sections, and ballads into the mix like a particularly well-timed punchline.

Title: Goodbye, Killer
Review: The guy knows how to make records you want to love. What's missing here, though, is that arrow through the heart moment where admiration and affection turns into adoration.

Title: I Like To Keep Myself In Pain
Review: Hogan's style is refreshingly simple, honest, and strikes its target on every track; whether she's tackling country, pop, supper-club blues, or uptempo R&B, she can sing it right and make you a believer, and I Like to Keep Myself in Pain is the triumphant showcase her talent has deserved for far too long.

Title: Now, More Than Ever
Review: Immersed in beautiful, stirring string arrangements, heartfelt melodies and an all-around warm and welcoming down-home folk feel, the new album is sincerely soothing.

Title: HoboSapiens
Review: He is clearly invigorated by the tensions between pretty and ugly, simplicity and chaos. [Nov 2004, p.130]

Title: Have Some Faith In Magic
Review: 'Have Some Faith In Magic' sees them unbuttoning those stiff top-collars and delivering some of their finest pop bangers to date.

Title: The Next Day
Review: A few tracks lack clear antecedents (see: the Jack White-aping “You Will Set the World on Fire”), and some simply lack cohesion, or at least enough melody to anchor them. But Day is also an excellent reminder that Ziggy Stardust, the Thin White Duke, and the lunatic who sang Christmas songs with Bing Crosby have all been coexisting in the same brain for decades.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: Lighter and more laid-back, with breezy melodies and fuzzy guitar-and-keyboard arrangements that sound built for a summer night's drive.

Title: Love Comes Close
Review: Cold Cave are neither here nor there. The pop hooks aren’t catchy enough, the ‘coldness’ too rote, the flirtation with eroticism simply an abbreviated spin on Depeche Mode’s “Master and Servant.”

Title: Home Counties
Review: It's a multilayered, detailed affair, which proves that 27 years after their debut, their edge is still keen. [Aug 2017, p.108]

Title: Girl on Fire
Review: Keys has rarely ever sounded so at ease, so downright sensual, as she does as her latest.

Title: All We Could Do Was Sing
Review: That’s not to say they don’t come across like an all-singing, all-banging Life Aquatic armed with pots, pans and whatever instrument comes to hand, but from the raw, stamping folk-punk to the string layered sea ditties, All We Could Do Was Sing is much more than it initially lets on.

Title: Coexist
Review: The xx has refined its sound, creating an even sparser atmosphere. But there is strength in this minimalism.

Title: Amygdala
Review: Amygdala is a thoroughly immersive album, possessing so many layers that it seems to change upon each listen.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: Only when Morrissey's wickedly funny side emerges does Quarry find moments worthy of sharing shelf space with his finest.

Title: Nothing Feels Natural
Review: The band only falters when they lean on stock symbols, as on the materialist-baiting "Pink White House."  If those lyrics sound lazy, it's only because Nothing Feels Natural is so taut and particular otherwise.

Title: Gimme Some
Review: Gimme Some delivers more than a few pop songs, a legitimate pop album written with the subtlety of a band that has come to appreciate, instead of run from, their hit-making ability.

Title: United Crushers
Review: It may not be as immediate as some of their earlier material, but it was a necessary endeavour for a band trying to make sense of the maelstrom of the modern world.

Title: Black Noise
Review: Where ["The Bliss"] bubbled and spat like hot fat, its meticulous construction overflowing with polyrhythms, Black Noise seems disjointed and overlong even though it runs for roughly the same duration.

Title: Dignity
Review: Duff set out to make an adult dance-pop record, with surprisingly successful results.

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: It is more fluid, more subtle; as such, it pulls you in gradually, irresistibly, its icy black under-current taking hold when you least expect it.

Title: Bromst
Review: The music becomes something like a natural process: one clean, simple sweep, but built from an insane complexity of detail. And there's enough to un-knot in there to make this a terrific step for Deacon--out from the sticky basements into a space where he can try to tackle the sublime.

Title: Pools of Light
Review: While groups like Thee Silver Mt Zion and Godspeed You! Black Emperor overegg everything, Moss works a far more thoughtful, nuanced seam. [Jul 2017, p.34]

Title: Quiet and Peace
Review: Ninth album Quiet And Peace is roughly one third quiet, peaceful and Chris Stapleton-like. ... elsewhere, All Be Gone and Lonely Fast And Deep recall the lumberjack Lemonheads of '93, but there's forward motion too. [May 2018, p.90]

Title: Do to the Beast
Review: The stylishly sleazy intensity is still there on their first record since 1998's excellent 1965, only with a wider palette.

Title: Bruiser
Review: The Duke Spirit still sound like The Duke Spirit.

Title: My Love is Cool
Review: It's a good album, full of high points, but it never excites in the way it threatens to.

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: An aesthetic watermark for Cave, a true high point in a long career that is ever looking forward.

Title: There's Always Another Girl
Review: In a time where it is possible for acts who made their careers in that early-90s cauldron of independent creativity to reform and remake themselves, it seems a cop-out to make such a risk-free album, especially since Hatfield had full creative control. Fan-funding could liberate, rather than stifle, even allowing experimentation; there's no boss to please, only fans to engage. But that doesn't happen at any point on There's Always Another Girl. Just more of the same.

Title: Immunity
Review: At 20, Clairo is already such a fully-formed artist that it’s nothing short of thrilling to envision where she’ll go from here. Immunity highlights her vulnerabilities while showcasing the full range of her formidable strength as a producer and songwriter.

Title: The Errant Charm
Review: The Errant Charm is, on the whole, immensely successful – a venture outside of a comfort zone,  a triumph for an artist who has consistently put out quality music only to be instantly likened and compared to a list of formidable influences, and an excellent soundtrack to hazy summer days and introspection.

Title: Blue Hearts
Review: Getting back in touch with his anger hasn't come at the cost of Mould's innate tunefulness. [Oct 2020, p.86]

Title: Nearer My God
Review: Plenty of artists put their every fiber of being into a record, but there’s rarely the overt drive to exceed one’s greatness that’s so insistent, it threatens to earn indie rock's most unintentionally revealing slight: try-hard. For most bands, it's an epithet. On Nearer My God, Foxing flaunt it like an Olympic gold medal.

Title: Victim of Love
Review: This is living, breathing music that avoids the trap of comfy nostalgia. [Jun 2013, p.94]
25 is very much Adele playing safe.

Title: In a Space Outta Sound
Review: Sadly the two best (read: different) tracks come at the end, a shame because you'll have probably put on something closer to actual music by then.

Title: Resistance Is Futile
Review: The album concludes with Nicky Wire’s grainy lead vocal on The Left Behind, a charmingly offbeat detour into 1980s indie-rock. More of these eccentric tonal variations would have been welcome on an album that emerges as a solid exercise in arena-sized anthemics, majestic in parts but not a career peak.

Title: Working on a Dream
Review: As an addition to a remarkable oeuvre, then, Working On A Dream has its worthwhile moments, but it's as a snapshot of a window of hope from an increasingly seasoned cultural commentator that it borders on the essential.

Title: Dormarion
Review: The album includes a perky Cure pastiche, a taste of synth-pop and some very Spoon-ish back-and-forth between fuzzed-out, noisy guitars, but the succinct, kinetic rockers are its high points, and leaves you wanting more of them. [No. 97, p.59]

Title: Varshons 2
Review: Listening to Varshons 2 is like catching up with a childhood friend--on surface level its pleasant, but as the conversation persists, the friendly emptiness becomes too painful to bear.

Title: Trouble Man: Heavy Is the Head
Review: Tip might be eager for another major hit. But fortunately, most of the album finds him delivering more modest pleasures, which, at least at the moment, work just fine, too.

Title: Suit
Review: Sadly, Suit, is exactly what it purports to be: the business-side of a duo of albums. And, in the world of pop, there’s nothing worse than sounding like business as usual.

Title: Ships
Review: None of Smith's previous records-- and in fact, very few indie releases this year-- have flat-out rocked like this one, with blaring trumpets signaling snares to exact their force beneath sweeping multitracked vocal choruses that simply won't stop crescendoing.

Title: Me First
Review: It’s ridiculously eclectic, yet uniformly affecting; a winter warmer that moves with a mysterious grace.

Title: These Days...
Review: Ab’s creative leaps are sometimes jarring at the onset, such as “Closure” featuring Jhené Aiko, a track that will be deeply unsettling to the National Association of Backpacker Excellence among others.

Title: XOXO
Review: Louris is nonetheless still on top form with Homecoming and his sublimely resigned Then You Walked Away is the pick of the three bonus tracks on the physical formats of the album.

Review: Earnestly sung lyrics in the vein of Jack Johnson or John Mayer, 80s-style instrumentation (percussion, guitar licks, synths), and constant rhythmic switch-ups are elegantly crafted.  This album isn't boring, it's just too polished for the raw sounds and styles it draws influence from.

Title: It's About Time
Review: This is not his finest hour nor his most groundbreaking, but just having him on the scene is enough--even if all he’s able to do is spread joy.

Title: Lavender
Review: A scary, fucked up kind of beauty. Consider Lavender a salve. Or, at least, an honest, genuine listen.

Title: Simple Math
Review: They've perfected the balance of gorgeous songwriting and rabid musicianship, so we can't wait to see what they do next.

Title: Handcream for a Generation
Review: Mood music, maybe. How to be conscious and happy at the same time.

Review: 17 endurance-defying tracks of gormless, soulless cookie-cutter corporate country, carting woefully trite homilies to smalltown values that leave the listener feeling uneasily like jackson's running from something. [May 2008, p.100]

Title: Comfort of Strangers
Review: Without altering her style drastically, Orton has broadened her approach on what is her most accomplished record to date. [Mar 2006, p.94]

Title: Something For All of Us

Title: The Spinning Top
Review: The Spinning Top, a really very enjoyable record, displays some of the finest aspects of the guitarist’s talents, but chief among them, those that pertain to Coxon the folkie, and acoustic guitar stylist.

Title: Beat the Champ
Review: Overall Beat the Champ will no doubt prove a hit with die-hard Mountain Goats fans, however as a standalone album it lacks a coherent sound.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: Wrecking Ball may be his angriest and most overtly political collection, yet the fury is contained in some of his most uplifting and celebratory music, so you can never be quite sure if he has come to raise the flag or to burn it.

Title: 20 Years In A Montana Missile Silo
Review: 20 Years in a Montana Missile Silo's glimpses at life's unknowability are disturbing, affecting, and always fascinating--and prove that Pere Ubu are as vital as ever in the 2010s.

Title: Seth Bogart
Review: His new self-titled record slips out of the leather jacket in favor of body-oiled synth-pop that balances between swagger-happy and tooth-rottingly sweet.

Title: Loose
Review: Unfortunately, the result is like a blind date where the chemistry doesn't quite click.

Title: Theater of the Mind
Review: Theater of the Mind, ultimately, is a difficult record to absorb. It’s not so much Ludacris’ persona that’s changed and yet this album tries to almost completely change his sound.

Title: The Time Is Now
Review: David takes the album title's sentiment to heart to such a degree, every song sounds like a cover version of whatever transient entries are currently topping the charts.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: Amidst a sonic atmosphere of clenched-fist roughness, one can find stark beauty and honest emotional value in the lyrics of lead singer Elias Bender Rønnenfelt

Title: Portamento
Review: Guitarist Adam Kessler's exit makes room for a more overtly expansive approach on the Drums' just as solid sophomore outing.

Title: More Than a Woman
Review: Braxton has gotten brave and ratcheted-up both the attitude and tempo.

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: The band is still good enough to put across (The Album)’s later songs, thanks to a buzzy ’70s sound that nods to George Harrison here, John Lennon there, and Tom Petty all over the place. But the “reaching for something indescribable” feeling of songs like 'Deeper Down' and 'One Wing' is sorely lacking amid the pat familiarity of 'I’ll Fight' and 'Everlasting Everything.'

Title: Antiphon
Review: The most effective songs on Antiphon are those that one-up the band’s former approach with confidence, skill and purpose.

Title: Ascent
Review: An unequivocally rocking set on which Chasny is backed by his former group Comets on Fire. [Aug 2012, p.56]

Title: White Stuff
Review: Hagerty’s guitar playing remains as unkempt as ever, but, touchingly, the duo’s vocals play tag throughout, augmenting one another’s frazzled joint vision as though no time had passed.

Title: Family Portrait
Review: With Family Portrait Ross From Friends (or Dr Geller as he prefers to be called) confirms enviable production skills that were already displayed on hype-building 12” releases, but is missing some songwriting nous that would have lifted the album up and made it a more consistently engaging listen.

Title: America
Review: Stein mostly carries an air of pleasant politeness, which rather fails to convey the darkness beneath tales of gambling addicts and bottles of bourbon in the fridge. [Aug 2017, p.38]

Title: In Another Life
Review: His well-aged craft shows on his fourth LP in 15 years.

Title: Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest
Review: Abstractions give way to specifics, and the result is a cascade of feelings, ideas, and images overlapping and enhancing each other in the listener's mind.

Title: Melodrama
Review: An album that captures the rise and fall of restless youth in a fluorescent, dazzling city.

Title: In The Dark
Review: In the Dark is an excessively fundamental album (guitars, drums, and bass, chorus-verse-chorus-that's all there), and viscerally, it's not too offensive.

Title: Melodrama
Review: There is a palpable depth of feeling and meaning in her songs, operating on both personal and universal levels, delivered with subtle dynamism and dizzying imagination. She is a breath of fresh air with the power of a hurricane.

Title: Majid Jordan
Review: On Majid Jordan, it's clear the Toronto pair have refined their sound, with subtle but meaningful touches that make for a stunning, cohesive work of art.

Title: Dying to Say This to You
Review: This stuff is often pretty infectious in spite of itself--you know, "so bad it's good." [Apr/May 2006, p.118]

Title: Cloud Nothings
Review: Cloud Nothings' self-titled debut displays Baldi's feral chops in natural light.

Title: Heathen
Review: A return to form. Definitely. [June 2002, p.108]

Title: Veckatimest
Review: Veckatimest works like a cash-back bonus, the more you give in to it, the grander the return.

Title: Radio Silence
Review: Pick up any one or two of these tracks (save maybe for those above "The One I Love") and they'll sound great--energetic, smart, everything you want Talib Kweli to be. The whole album at once is a bit numbing, but still worth listening to.

Title: The Black
Review: Worsnop may be gone, but the rage channeled into The Black has helped the group lift themselves back onto their feet, showing they are more than capable of carrying on without him.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: The hush on this mellow set may be due in part to Adams' recent hearing problems. Either way, it proves he doesn't need noise to blow you away.

Title: Clear Heart Full Eyes
Review: This is an album that feels as much like a series of compelling stories as it does a collection of fine songs. [21 Jan 2012, p.53]

Title: 31 Minutes to Takeoff
Review: He sounds as unflappable as the subject of his first hit.

Title: The Stoned Immaculate
Review: This LP helps demonstrate variance and unseen skills within those confines [infectious bangers and more romantic, nostalgic odes] to truly set Curren$y apart

Title: Heavy Ghost
Review: Yes, Heavy Ghost is weird, but Stith's melodies are simple and wonderful, making his experimentation easy to follow and, with his enchanting choral throughout, it's easy to get lost in every song--or even engulfed into a new fantastical land that you may never want to escape from.

Title: Offering
Review: With its sweet, dream-pop sound, Offering is an immediately likable record that is enjoyable on first listen. Repeated plays make it more lovable as the subtle, ultra-cool textures creep into your consciousness and make for dynamic and vibrant tunes with honeyed vocals. I think I've found my new guilty pleasure.

Title: Mondo Cane
Review: Even if this album is a genre exercise, it's still a very fine one. Mondo Cane pulls no punches, makes no apologies, and is impossible not to enjoy on some level.

Title: Brill Bruisers
Review: The electronic elements probably won’t quite be to everybody’s tastes, but even then, the energy with which they’re delivered should be enough to make up for it.

Title: I Am the Fun Blame Monster
Review: Suffice to say, Menomena are a hugely creative band, and with I Am the Fun Blame Monster, they've managed to make an album that's extremely accessible yet entirely unconventional.

Title: It'll Be Better
Review: It's short, boring, and occasionally aggravating, recalling the flatness of acts like Maroon 5 and John Mayer while never coming close to their likeability, and when you're being rocked off the stage by Adam Levine, it's not a good sign.

Title: My Maudlin Career
Review: As a unit, the group amassed some of the best music of their careers onto this singular, ‘effusively sentimental,’ career.

Title: Kiss of Death
Review: Kiss... doesn't astound, but Jada flexes impressive muscles as he grinds his heels into a well-trodden dance floor. [9 Jul 2004, p.89]

Title: See You In Magic
Review: It is a ‘safe’ record, one that plays to its makers’ long-established strengths without really stretching them--but fans of all the aforementioned predecessors are certain to find much to love across these 13 tracks.

Title: The Hazards of Love
Review: There are certainly enough good things about the album to let its more infuriating conceits pass.

Title: Watershed
Review: Watershed has friction, and friction brings heat. Those left cold by metal's po-faced tendencies might well warm up to it.

Title: After the Disco
Review: After The Disco is an unashamedly brilliant pop album that might just be the right kind of stuff to get you through the remains of winter.

Title: Older Than My Old Man Now
Review: Best of all is "The Day That We Die", Rufus Wainwright oozing mournfully with his dad about the way that familial potholes prove so difficult to repair.

Title: The Sunset Tree
Review: Cathartic and essential.

Title: Adam Ant Is the BlueBlack Hussar in Marrying the Gunner's Daughter
Review: Ant's famous sartorial attention to detail doesn't extend to the music here, as experimentalism meanders into the bizarre and unlistenable.

Title: Head Down
Review: Give this West Coast quartet credit for honing its sound on this, the group’s third album.

Title: Bitter Tea
Review: It’s true that they could probably benefit from a stricter censorship of their own endless creativity, but Bitter Tea is an uncontrolled outpouring of musical concepts in every way, and you sense that the Friedbergers wanted this.

Title: In Stormy Nights
Review: A work of absolute beauty, chaos, seductive darkness and cosmic light.

Title: Tender New Signs
Review: Tender New Signs is full of cracking tunes that help avoid the formlessness that effects-laden atmo-pop often slumps into. [Dec 2012, p.113]

Title: My Favorite Picture of You
Review: This terrific batch of songs needs no such handicap to be recommended as a perfect way for newcomers to start a musical relationship with Clark’s burnished Americana or for existing fans to continue theirs.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: It’s a reminder that no matter how badly you might think he behaves, Morrissey still does not mince words. And his music is vital because of it.

Title: My Finest Work Yet
Review: Recorded live without headphones or separate tracks, the sound is intimate and conspiratorial. The perfect polish of a meticulously assembled recording is set aside in favour of a sense of the room and the musicians in it, united in their organic performances.

Title: On the Outside
Review: A commanding return. [Nov 2005, p.131]

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: A lush and trippy affair with shades of Edward Lear-like surrealism and John Winston Lennon amid strawberry Fields. [Mar 2008, p.103]

Title: Maladroit
Review: Maladroit is a welcome - halfway - return to form.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: Darnielle finds equal grains of humanity and empathy in people crouched in the darkest corners and blinded by the brightest spotlights. It's not spirituality, escapism, or even optimism, exactly, that he's espousing--all you know is it's some kind of light.

Title: Dreamt for Light Years in the Belly of a Mountain
Review: Superb stuff. [23 Sep 2006, p.33]

Title: Revolverlution
Review: They might not be hip, they're not as innovative as they used to be, but they still make very good, even great music, and that's evident on Revolverlution. If only it were presented better.

Title: Dirty Jeans and Mudslide Hymns
Review: Dirty Jeans And Mudslide Hymns is full of typical John Hiatt tropes: old-timers and hard times, devotion and desperation, in roughly equal measure.

Title: Valhalla Dancehall
Review: Pugnacious indie squares up to all-comers. [Feb. 2011, p. 106]

Title: Things That Can't Be Undone
Review: It's thrilling and moving to hear Lund indulge his serious side on this gorgeously forlorn new LP.

Title: Join the Dots
Review: The difficulties seem to arise when melody and vocals are expected to step up and carry a track for them. They don’t, much more often than they do, which ends up leaving the listener (or this listener, at least) vaguely dissatisfied.

Title: Six
Review: Although titles like 'Suicide' and 'Drugs' may seem a touch overt, the songs are not overwrought cliches.

Title: I'm Gay (I'm Happy)
Review: Yeah, he hinted at this sort of consciousness on a couple of recordings in the past, but this is full-fledged social commentary.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: It's a grandiose (Rick Rubin produces), earnest affair that sheds the trio's earthy realness for a glossy veneer which is sometimes thrilling (the majestic 'And It Spread') but often, well, nothing more than an unconvincing stab at that most scary of concepts: mainstream country.

Title: Let It Beard
Review: Studded with occasional gems...it's also weighed down by a handful of jokey throwaways  and partially realised pop numbers among its 24 tracks. [Oct 2011, p.94]

Title: The Undisputed Truth
Review: Ali's unselfconscious candor engenders an intimacy between artist and fan that makes each new album feel like a letter from an old friend.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: The steady pace of mid-tempo tracks might deter some listeners; although there are tinges of mischief, a sudden shift in pace would certainty elevate the listen.

Title: Heartworms
Review: While Heartworms has its melodic pop moments and the band tries to remain indie-rock stalwarts, there seems to be a lack of cohesiveness between the songs. But one thing that remains strong is Mercer's ability to craft songs that are always interesting, otherworldly, and transport you to another universe.

Title: Shame, Shame
Review: With co-producer Rob Schnapf at the helm, Dr. Dog don't sound like mere imitators--they sound like an unusually hook-savvy indie band whose taut, touching songs about friendship ("Jackie Wants a Black Eye") and life on the road ("Station") begin as straight pop rock and take thrilling turns into psychedelia.

Title: Go! Pop! Bang!
Review: It may have taken three years for Go! Pop! Bang! to see the light, but fortunately, in Rye Rye's case, she has only gotten better with age.

Title: None Shall Pass
Review: The album is as solid as its maker's last name but so predictable you could set your Flavor Flav clock to it.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: Hip-Hop Is Dead... brings out the best in the emcee, who might have produced his strongest lyrical performance since Illmatic.

Title: Pocket Symphony
Review: An atmospheric downer.

Title: Rainier Fog
Review: They were always one of the most metal band of the alt.rock boom that emerged from their Seattle scene in the early 1990’s, but on Rainier Fog; there’s a beauty and an expanse--as well as a major chord or two--that sees the band evolving.

Title: Demolished Thoughts
Review: If your relationship with Sonic Youth  chiefly consists of boozily chucking yourself around to their sprinkling of indie-disco floorfillers, you may be surprised to know that Thurston Moore can 'do tender', let alone do it very well.

Title: Cloak and Cipher
Review: Cloak and Cipher won't wow you with hooks or musical prowess, but it does signal an exciting start for a band with tremendous potential, and it serves as an excellent first glimpse of a lead singer with loads of talent.

Title: Jumping the Shark
Review: At times, the simplicity of the melodies (the synths at times sound like readymade ones you'd find on a Yamaha keyboard) and decidedly uncomplicated drum machine beats may leave the listener wanting more, but they play into the notion of these characters being pathetic, exhausted and disappointed so well that there really isn't a need for much more.

Title: Kaputt
Review: Kaputt is eccentric and enjoyable, but it's no Infidels, which is to say it never quite breaks through its sonic limitations.

Title: No Hope, No Future
Review: The main problem with No Hope, No Future, though, is that very little here stands out above the accepted and expected norm. At times, there's a feeling Good Shoes have almost resigned themselves to a destined state of mediocrity.

Title: Brothers and Sisters of the Eternal Son
Review: Despite the heavy sonic resemblance, this road map back lands Jurado and Swift someplace new, slightly more thematic and worlds more dramatic. [No. 106, p.60]

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: It's not that it's post-rock-by-numbers, although at times it really is, but more so that it doesn't even sound like there are painters behind the palette.

Title: Endless Now
Review: A reliance on monotonous tempos and rhythms--and a disappointing lack of melodic variation--further make Endless Now fell curiously lethargic. [Sep 2011, p.112]

Title: Rise to Your Knees
Review: Rise is a welcome, if uneven, return.

Title: Road to Rouen
Review: An album of both phenomenal concentrated bits, as well as some disappointing gaps.

Title: The Clearing
Review: The Clearing may not be a slam-dunk for the neoclassical movement, but it serves out positive little tidbits of what the subgenre has to offer.

Title: Commune
Review: With some judicious skipping of tracks this is another eminently listenable set. [Oct 2014, p.109]

Title: Violet Cries
Review: Other groups have approached the issue of originality by genre-blending; but in the case of Esben and the Witch, it is their very faith  that ensures that the hollowness one feels while listening has a doubled quality, reflected not only in content but also in experience, leaving one with the ominous aftertaste of a doppelgänger encounter.

Title: Mechanical Bull
Review: Occasionally frustrating and sometimes even a little soapy, Mechanical Bull has its flaws, but it also brims with personality and passion. [Oct 2013, p.104]

Title: Kissin Time
Review: The production can be a little too clinical and antiseptic in spots.

Title: The English Riviera
Review: If Metronomy appeared glib in the past, here you'll find musical and emotional depth. [May 2011, p.91]

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: Easy-going and mellifluous, songs built on the simplest of patterns.

Title: Colliding By Design
Review: What could have been a nostalgia grab is instead the triumph of a band that chose to deliver on the initial promise of their seminal debut, not only to their faithful fans, but, more importantly, to themselves.

Title: Planet Pit
Review: It's similar to Pitbull's newest album, Planet Pit, which blends everything but the kitchen sink in a frenetic jumble that's facile yet unadulterated fun.

Title: Idle No More
Review: Its fusion of Brian Jones-era Rolling Stones paisley pop and Spectorian pomp pushes Khan and the Shrines beyond their usual JBs jones, but the album’s title speaks to a burgeoning social consciousness.

Title: Dungeonesse
Review: Ultimately the one thing truly lacking on Dungeonesse is the bright spark that makes pop stars so entertaining to obsess over.

Title: Black Rainbows
Review: Black Rainbows is a pretty good dress rehearsal. [Oct 2011, p.97]

Title: No Control
Review: With a good spread of melodies and hooks throughout, even if ideas do fly about like rice paper, it’s a strong development of a record.

Title: Liberty
Review: Liberty, her seventh album, feels like the record she’s been desperate to make for some time.

Title: Moodymann
Review: It seems an easy listen at first, but the scale is daunting. [Feb 2014, p.53]

Title: Empress
Review: There is nothing fly-by-night about Rita Ekwere, an artist in the classic mould – audibly from London, but gazing outwards. Empress feels hugely current.

Title: No Sounds Are Out Of Bounds
Review: While some will label these 12 pieces as evidence of Alex Paterson’s genius, the majority definitely won’t, and although it’s a well-produced work, it doesn’t bend or expand expectations. [Sep 2018, p.54]

Title: Without Warning
Review: The "Issa Album" was a full course meal while "Without Warning" ends up being more of a snack.

Title: i
Review: The only real problem with i is the sheer volume of excellence we've all come to expect from Merritt.

Title: Black Origami
Review: It's intricate and punishing, industrial and artful.

Title: Night Visions
Review: There are a lot of cosmetics present to cover up the band’s shortcomings, but not even the most epic posturing and glossy production can hide this record’s blemishes.

Title: Gave In Rest
Review: Unlike much ambient music, Gave in Rest isn’t made for background listening. In fact, only with volume can you fully appreciate the depth of Davachi’s creation.

Title: The Coast Is Never Clear
Review: The Coast is Never Clear's shortcomings fall in Beulah's tendency to recycle the same song and name it something new.... Nonetheless, Beulah is still making some of the most infectious and smart pop songs anywhere in independent rock.

Title: Phantastic Ferniture
Review: Phantastic Ferniture is pumped with enough care-free energy and catchy pop hooks to brighten up the darkest of days.

Title: Live a Little
Review: Live a Little... finds Pernice throwing off the shackles of overenunciation and fussy production.

Title: Ty Segall
Review: Ty Segall is his finest effort to date, a superb record and one that will help save rock ’n’ roll, which isn’t dead, it’s merely been regrouping.

Title: Here Comes the Cowboy
Review: Always exquisitely unbothered, the indie-rock poster boy now sounds like he can’t be bothered.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Once again the theme of emotional cleansing runs through much of the lyrics, though this particular well of inspiration has not yet run dry.

Title: Manhattan
Review: Skaters' knack for writing infectious melodies often offsets their enthusiasm, so although Manhattan is an uneven record, its bright spots still have capacity to shine like Times Square.

Title: Allergic to Water
Review: Her vocals throughout the album sound relaxed and carefree, with wordless bridges that convey a giddy exuberance beyond the power of any lyric to convey. [No. 115, p.55]

Title: Love This Giant
Review: Love This Giant is a sprawling behemoth, if not greater than the sum of its parts, then certainly twice as weird.

Title: Life Among the Savages
Review: While Life Among the Savages lacks the absolute highs of Quever’s previous work, it also lacks any lows, except for possibly the abrupt ending which leaves you longing for more.

Title: Desire
Review: Monch makes a lean 47 minutes seem epic in the best way.

Title: Saint Bartlett
Review: With its blend of classic Jurado themes and a new sonic palette, Saint Bartlett serves not just as an encapsulation of Jurado's career, but as a promising indicator of where he's headed.

Title: We Started Nothing
Review: We Started Nothing comes packed with a peppy parade of songs likewise steeped in electro beats and chant-along vocals.

Title: Gift of Sacrifice
Review: Three tracks, including the opener and closer, are short instrumentals that might have been elongated for further immersive and exploratory effect. Otherwise, the album is an off-kilter musical gift born of Osborne’s sacrifice of conventionality for weirder, wider possibilities.

Title: YSIV
Review: YSIV--the conclusion of his Young Sinatra series of mixtapes--is his most confident and accomplished release to date, shaking off some of the awkwardness that has long peppered his music.

Title: One Life Stand
Review: This is an imbalanced record, and one that leaves you frustrated rather than elated. But despite the blips, they have dished up at least two cerebral bangers here.

Title: The Wedding
Review: Wedding might not be Oneida's most way-out album, but it's as satisfyingly restless as anything in their catalog.

Title: Touch Down 2 Cause Hell
Review: The record isn't the home run Boosie probably needs. It could stand to be trimmed a bit.

Title: My Dinosaur Life
Review: Motion City Soundtrack have made the best album of their career and easily one of the best albums of 2010 or any other year. [Feb 2010, p.91]

Title: Gods and Monsters
Review: It’s all rather marvellous.

Title: Threace
Review: Threace possesses a wholly immersive sense of itself, and a free floating kinetic energy that is out of step with most contemporary riff-based music. Its command of sonic hypnosis is all the more impressive considering its brevity.

Title: For Those Who Stay
Review: This is a strong indie rock release that further establishes PS I Love You’s sound, improving upon it but not really do much to shift it. Maybe that’s a good thing though, because this album is a great listen.

Title: Automaton
Review: Automaton seems an audacious comeback, to say the least, but also strangely listenable.

Title: Guero
Review: Long live the king of hip. [May 2005, p.132]

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: A unique musical vision with a genuinely unique and beautifully skewed worldview to boot.

Title: Brilliant Sanity
Review: Brilliant Sanity is occasionally brilliant, but it could greatly benefit if it let go some of its sanity.

Title: Serena-Maneesh
Review: What truly makes this album stand out is the group’s sense of control.

Title: Prisyn
Review: One of Prisyn's finest qualities is that it sticks to a precise ten tracks, no filler, no needless privileging of quantity over requirement.

Title: Cancer 4 Cure
Review: The music is certainly some of El's most engaging yet, and should possess real lasting power.

Title: Black Butterfly
Review: Even in the heavier material on Black Butterfly these guys make more room for melody than they ever have before.

Title: Some Are Lakes
Review: Ultimately, LOT’s songs will dictate their trajectory, and principal songwriter Liz Powell sounds mostly up to the task.

Title: III
Review: While the experiment works, for the most part, in tandem with Devine and Hull's always thoughtful and occasionally profound words, the album becomes formulaic as songs reliably start as acoustic song, then gradually ascend into the atmosphere.

Title: Interzone
Review: This shift further into sounds of the dancefloor obviously comes with no hands in the air hedonism, they stick firmly to their monochrome formula but by adding flourishes of colour to their sound they've made their best album yet.

Title: Always
Review: Much like a pungent stilton, this is difficult prospect to recommend or advise against, especially if this is your first experience of Xiu Xiu. Dip your toe in the water, though, and there are bits to love.

Title: The Stand Ins
Review: Sheff straddles the line between precious and brilliant, warbling twisty, appositive-packed tales about life on the road and crumbled relationships over cranked-up, vaguely folkish rock riffs.

Title: Vitriola
Review: Vitriola is a fiercely political record, but one that seldom feels trite; married to the aggressive tone of a band back to make a point, it’s a razor-sharp lament of America in 2018.

Title: Elsewhere
Review: Elsewhere is a compelling debut, on which Moore has successfully revitalised the folksy feel of some of her earlier work. For a first album, it’s certainly a triumph.

Title: Out In The World
Review: It’s as though Jay is playfully toying around with genres without building a fully cohesive record. There are plenty of lovely moments on this LP, but without a clear structure it never truly acts as one.

Title: Space City Kicks
Review: Space City Kicks may remind us that Pollard spawned thousands of followers in the lo-fi and power-pop arenas, but it also assures that--even when he's not at his absolute peak--he is head and shoulders above his acolytes.

Title: Thunder Follows the Light
Review: Though the lyrical themes may lack potency, Thunder Follows the Light highlights Lee’s knack for composing beautiful melodies.

Title: Bye Bye 17
Review: It's clear that this is easily Har Mar's best album. Sure, the lyrics are still hamfisted, but they're not as bad as they were in the past.

Title: Africa Speaks
Review: As passionately exciting as anything in the classic Carlos canon, Africa Speaks is an album of highlight after highlight. [Jul 2019, p.87]

Title: True Meanings
Review: It’s a lengthy, beautiful work, and undoubtedly a late career high from one of the most important, courageous songwriters in the country.

Title: The Time of the Assassins
Review: Neither horrible nor great, Time of the Assassins is an unassuming album, a working holiday that was probably more enjoyable to make than for anyone besides die-hard Strokes fans to hear.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Decidedly more disco for Mitski, Be the Cowboy is a showdown of electrowave and her signature fretwork that brings a pop pep to heartbreak and humanity’s greatest gluttonies. With that formidable force of a voice, she forces us all to be the cowboy and lament for a while.

Title: Streetlights
Review: In 2010 he sounds derivative, uninspired, and starving for a paycheck.

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: Larceny and sharp, immediate hooks permeate everything they do, and so it is with Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action.

Title: As I Am
Review: Alicia Keys’ third studio album is an exercise in tightening the screws.

Title: The Odds
Review: On The Odds, MacKaye and Farina-on baritone guitar and a minimal trap kit, respectively---don't challenge their by-now established conventions, but wreak incredible havoc within them.

Title: No Cities Left
Review: At its best sounds like a suicidal combination of Blur and the Divine Comedy.

Title: Horehound
Review: The debut is by no means a hit-packed record, pop is firmly on the backburner here and thrillingly it's precisely this lack of obvious choruses and instead the bizarre little instrumental interludes, spooky stripped down ballads which build and build and attacking grooves that will have you coming back time and time again to it.

Title: Bitter Drink Bitter Moon
Review: The reality is that Bitter Drink, Bitter Moon is the musical equivalent of a grape soda--it tastes familiar, but it's just not quite a grape.

Title: Goddess
Review: It asks listeners to love it, and its creator, for both flaws and attributes. Fortunately, the latter far outweigh the former, announcing Banks as a well-rounded songwriter and singer that deserves a lot of the attention she has earned so early in her career.

Title: Silence Is Sexy
Review: Silence Is Sexy is yet another collection of pointed and intriguing meditations (in German and English) on love, life, poetry, and metaphysics, with part-time Bad Seed Blixa Bargeld's creaky grumble drifting in and out of Goth territory.

Title: Year of the Black Rainbow
Review: Unfortunately, "Year" lacks the grandiose thematic concepts of previous outings as well as an immediate single, like past songs "A Favor House Atlantic" or "The Suffering."

Title: Food
Review: Once you get over the initial shock of Kelis' raw-throated take on country-rock on "Friday Fish Fry," the culinary theme becomes another ingredient that never quite blends into a tasty dish. [May 2014, p.76]

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: Those who really love Frank Black and Black Francis' songs, as opposed to just their sound, will enjoy eavesdropping on him playing around with his work.

Title: Enclosure
Review: [The album is] somewhere between his recent acid house work as Speed Dealer Moms and his dramatic collaborations with Omar Rodriguez-Lopez and Wu-Tang acolytes Black Knights--and pretty much everything he's done to date. [No. 110, p.55]

Title: The Chemistry of Common Life
Review: Chemistry is a natural and seamless masterpiece that might never have happened but for the band's own need to thumb its nose at expectations.

Title: Mary's Voice
Review: The contemplative Mary's Voice may win over listeners who couldn't stomach the unrefined energy of The Music Tapes' older work, with artistic integrity intact.

Title: I'm Not Your Man
Review: Mainly, there aren't enough chances taken to keep you hooked in for the duration of 13 songs and this might be a case of selectivity leading to greater impact overall.

Title: Passive Me, Aggressive You
Review: It is a decent debut, with a lot of room for growth. [Feb 2011, p.66]

Title: Love & Hate
Review: It admittedly spends a lot of time in a downer mode--a more light-amidst-the-dark feel would feel nice--but this sophomore effort remains affecting and affirming in its own quiet way

Title: Liquid Cool
Review: Liquid Cool is at its best and most interesting, though, when Gonzalez’s sound plays with the way our brains and human interactions have been rewired in the modern age, raising the bar by creating impactful moments via osmosis.

Title: The Idler Wheel

Review: It’s a vivacious, impactful beginning which appeals both to the heart and the body. Yet, there’s also plenty of evidence of skilful management of sounds, elements being introduced and withdrawn at the opportune moment.

Title: Hypnophobia
Review: Impressively, Gardner's instrumnetals such as "Grey Lanes" and "All Over" show how he can effectively summon up an exquisite nostalgia for an invented '60s. [Jun 2015, p.76]

Title: Syro
Review: Imagine a mirror which distorts not just the reflection, but reality itself, and you have a fair idea of the stunning legacy to which Syro triumphantly belongs.

Title: Love Letters
Review: Love Letters is great. There’s potential here, and it feels like it had the ability to be a nigh-on perfect record, but for reasons obscured--probably the brick-subtle lo-fi-ness--it feels unfinished. It’s like a final draft.

Title: Dark Bird Is Home
Review: Everything here is well thought out and meticulously executed, it's just that Matsson makes it all seem so effortless.

Title: Storm Damage
Review: Storm Damage is generally a difficult scenario to weather, in more ways than one. Happily then, Ben Watt proves he’s got the desire and determination to see the situation through.

Title: Now Here Is Nowhere
Review: As challenging and glorious as rock can go when filtered to it's basic elements, but not without a whiff of indulgence.

Title: Hidden
Review: Hidden is not just the most original record to emerge from Britain this year, but the most unfathomable: an immaculate enigma.

Title: Born Under Saturn
Review: The album is executed slickly enough that this lack of cohesion isn't a huge problem. The goofy lyrics, though, owe too much to the hippy-dippy era.

Title: Light of X
Review: The sunny, country-ish melodies of opener 'Beathless' and 'Savorin' Your Smile' aren't quite matched by her limited voice, but when some darkness descends, as on 'Pictures Of You,' her perky nature adds a bittersweet twist to the added emotional weight. [mar 2009, p.104]

Title: Krystal
Review: At the end of the day, what Matt Maltese does best is conjure kitchen sink dramedies. And with ‘Krystal’, his ability to do that is as strong as ever. The melodies feel more like accompaniments to the stories; a canvas on which to paint. But the wry yet heartbreaking lyrics that accompany it shows an artist who has grown. As enviably funny as ever, but this time a little more self-aware.

Title: A Sailor's Guide to Earth
Review: Overall, the album is strikingly intimate.

Title: Sour Soul
Review: A vivid, pulsing rhyme banquet that's out-there, edgy and kaleidoscopic. [Mar 2014, p.96]

Title: Rudebox
Review: An absolute howler.

Title: Encyclopedia
Review: Look into this Encyclopedia and you'll find The Drums defining themselves for now and forever. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.75]

Title: Clapton
Review: Clapton and Bramhall also have pulled off a minor miracle in assembling an ad hoc group that manages to sound like a blues band whose members have been absorbing one another's abilities to the point of musical osmosis.

Title: Freedom's Goblin
Review: Freedom's Goblin cuts open Segall's brain and lets it all ooze out. Serve yourself up a spoonful of all that melodic goo, and enjoy.

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: It is missing the stable spine that gave the band’s earlier work such distinctive character, and their repetitious, two-dimensional songs bring the overall package down. Still, when the band is at its best, Fontaines D.C. delivers an irresistible cocktail of post-punk storytelling.

Title: BlackenedWhite
Review: Cuts like "64" and "Deaddeputy" prove that they too enjoy lyrically attacking everything in their way. [29 Jul 2011, p.72]

Title: Painted Shut
Review: It's easy to sound hyperbolic when describing the impact of Quinlan's voice, but she really does prove herself to be among the most captivating rock singers of her generation on Painted Shut. That her vocals are very nearly equaled by the music and the subject matter makes this album a notable one.

Title: The Boy Who Knew Too Much
Review: It's a Technicolor pop explosion designed for throwing your jazz hands into the air.

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: The simple truth is, you won't find a sadder yet more uplifting album all year.

Title: Little Joy
Review: Producer Noah Georgeson makes all the right decisions in keeping the sound warm, relaxed, and analog to cleverly use the past to give listeners an easy entry point into these pleasant, deceptively simple recordings. [Year End 2008]

Title: I Am... Sasha Fierce
Review: Sasha is an intriguing but diluted direction.

Title: Black Up
Review: Unsurprisingly, their music proves equally mysterious, the lava-like bass and shuddering beats suggesting a familiarity with dubstep's experimental margins. [Aug. 2011, p. 116]

Title: All Days Are Nights: Songs For Lulu
Review: In the world of the gilded musical scion, sixth album counts as stripped back. [May 2010, p. 93]

Title: Wild Animals
Review: Fans of the band will find enough familiar ground here, but Wild Animals shows a continued creative evolution at work.

Title: Rooty
Review: But sound for sound's sake isn't what makes the disc work; it's the recurring female singers, who add forlorn soul to the rhythms.

Title: Dead Language
Review: There are moments of growing pains, but they never overshadow the highlights here, of which there are many.

Title: Me Moan
Review: It’s exciting to listen to an artist just go for it, and that’s obviously what Me Moan is: an attempt to synthesize genres of music that don’t quite belong together.

Title: American Love Song
Review: American Love Song is classic Bingham.

Title: American VI: Ain't No Grave
Review: Fortified by his Christian faith, he lends a cracked gravity to souvenirs of cornball sentiment ranging in tone from Ed McCurdy's political "Last Night I Had the Strangest Dream" to Queen Lili'uokalani's escapist "Aloha Oe," which close an album that also includes the traditional title song, a Sheryl Crow number about redemption, "Cool Water," and the tenderest "For the Good Times" I've ever heard.

Title: Forth
Review: For the first four tracks, The Verve dig deep into their chaotic history to conjure the strange, intoxicating mix of stridency, shimmering beauty, pretension and vulnerability that made them so distinctive back in their pomp. And then the plot is suddenly lost, along with the tunes.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: No Cities To Love finds the trio facing inwards, rocking out in a tight space, writing short and punchy punk songs and just generally enjoying bouncing off each other once more.

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: While A Brief History of Love isn’t quite capable of recapturing the rush upon hearing “Bittersweet Symphony” or “This is Music” for the first time, the Big Pink’s reverence towards those songs and their era and everything they represented is extremely well executed. And greatly appreciated.

Title: Playing the Angel
Review: 'Playing the Angel' is hardly the most essential Depeche Mode album ever, but it is Depeche Mode doing what they do best.

Title: Devotion
Review: Despite the occasional tendency to soar above when her songs could benefit from some earthiness, in the main Ware's sheer, confident boldness carries the day.

Title: Ducktails III: Arcade Dynamics
Review: There are several memorable songs here, but the offhand, one-take atmosphere makes the project slighter than it might have been. [Feb 2011, p.50]

Title: Pala
Review: It seems Pala is Friendly Fires' successful attempt to translate their positivity-injected carnival live performances into a record. In the process, it just so happens they've delivered what deserves to be the soundtrack to the summer.

Title: Thumbtacks and Glue
Review: It might skirt the edges of twee but the follow-up to 2010's Die Stadt Muzikanten darkens and deepens as it unfolds. [Mar 2013, p.79]

Title: Manzanita
Review: Imagine Joni Mitchell if she'd made Miles after Mingus. [Feb 2005, p.92]

Title: The Crying Light
Review: The Crying Light shows Antony boldly, indefatigably following his own eccentric star.

Title: We Know About the Need
Review: Stuttering breakbeats, looped effects and suffusive psychedelia. [Feb 2007, p.72]

Title: El Pintor
Review: A return to form, it brims with fresh ideas, in everything from the looser production to the chordal detours that suggest the trio is ready to tweak its formula.

Title: Prism
Review: The single Roar is ruthlessly efficient in its bid to get the drunk and recently dumped member of the girls' night out party up on the table, using her WKD bottle as a microphone, and the rest of the album follows suit: if the ballads are standard issue, the faintly trap-inspired Dark Horse sounds like a hit single, as does Birthday and, for better or worse, the new jack swing parody This Is How We Do.

Title: Intriguer
Review: The House head honcho proved he's still a classy, clever tunesmith, and does so again here on Intriguer.

Title: Seth Bogart
Review: It's not quite Hunx and it's definitely not punk, but Seth Bogart is a blast.

Title: Smoke
Review: Smoke is his first off-center classic. [Fall 2007, p.77]

Title: Buck the World
Review: The problem with Buck the World is that it's largely inconsistent. There are 15 producers over 17 tracks. Sometimes it clicks, but other times it feels forced.

Title: Melt Yourself Down
Review: The music Melt Yourself Down make on this eight song, 36-minute debut album is insanely full of energy and ideas, a tumultuous barrage of snaky, infectious hooks and punishingly addictive grooves.

Title: Your Queen is a Reptile
Review: A provocative, anti-establishment critique of the blind idolatry received by the British monarchy and finds each of the nine tracks paying homage to Hutchings' list of notable women that he believes are worthy alternative monarchs. [Apr 2018, p.87]

Title: A Wasteland Companion
Review: Too much filler towards the end of the album detracts slightly, but this is another solid set.

Title: Here I Am
Review: The songs overflow with self-affirmation and confidence.

Title: Changing Horses
Review: While I certainly can't hold it against Kweller for trying something different and playing dress-up with a Nudie suit, Changing Horses nonetheless finds his half-assed over-countrification and half-assed under-countrification to be equally ineffectual.

Title: Loud Patterns
Review: While the comedown is expertly managed, one begins to pine for the glossier touches which Molleson clearly excels at. Nonetheless, it’s an album brimming with vigour and ideas from start to finish, and likely set to be one of the UK’s most engaging debuts this year.

Title: Late Registration
Review: A masterful sophomore disc on which every weak rhyme, guest and beat has been ironed out through months of hard work and several blown deadlines. [Oct/Nov 2005, p.120]

Title: From the Very Depths
Review: It may bear the mark of Venom, but it lacks the heart-stopping toxicity of its inception.

Title: Tweekend
Review: Tweekend isn't a giant leap forward for the Crystal Method, but it certainly doesn't keep them trapped in the past.

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: None of it means a damn thing beyond what it is. Which is just what they were trying so hard to achieve.

Title: Before the Age of Mirrors
Review: The busted up and agonizing forms that result accumulate into a hell of a record. Put on your black boots and stomp around in it awhile.

Title: The Sunset Tree
Review: The emotions on The Sunset Tree are raw. It's a testament to Darnielle's abilities that he reins in those emotions enough to create such a powerful and coherent exhibit of his internal life.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: Lightning Bolt begins with a spirited sprint before sputtering out and winding up in dullsville.

Title: Pure Heroine
Review: Nitpicking aside, Pure Heroine remains a lush, engaging experience.

Title: God Says No
Review: Here's music tailor-made for cruising down the road with the wind blowing through your mullet.

Title: We Knew It Was Not Going To Be Like This
Review: We Knew may be a less immersive listening experience than Kudos was, but it makes up for that by sounding better and having better songs.

Title: Tarot Sport
Review: The main problem with Tarot Sport is that it sometimes seems to be trying too hard, building drama into repetitive riffs by sheer force, urging greater and greater effort on listeners who are already a bit out of breath.

Title: Nothing Important
Review: Namechecks for Peter Beardsley and Peperami show eccentricity, but once you get used to his atonal delivery, Dawson emerges as a talented chronicler of the tiniest, realest details.

Title: Blood Money
Review: Too much of Blood Money represents something sad and fascinating-- two demons domesticated, two artists who have willfully transformed themselves into hucksters.

Title: Sky Swimming
Review: It's hard to imagine many people reaching for this album even for times of pensive reflection when there's such a preponderance of terrific mellow music out there.

Title: Autumn of the Seraphs
Review: Autumn Of The Seraphs is more of the same I have come to expect from Pinback--lovely harmonies and catchy hooks, all with an underlying emotional depth.

Title: Dig In Deep
Review: This is an LP brimming with rough-hewn fun that will leave fans grinning, tapping toes, and humming along, but it'll also leave them marveling at the unabashed panache and undeniable chops of this veteran songstress.

Title: Blackstar
Review: It’s trippy and majestic head-music spun from moonage daydreams and made for gliding in and out of life.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: By taking the piss out of himself and the cynicism out of his outlook, Bird’s songs are not only smart and sensible but joyous and full of hope.

Title: The Sophtware Slump
Review: The perfect soundtrack for workers clearing out their cubicles and trudging away after their short-lived high-tech careers abruptly ended. The 11 songs capture a bittersweet tone perfectly -- sadly witnessing cultural wreckage and detritus but finding glimmers of beauty.

Title: Kill Them With Kindness
Review: Kill Them With Kindness might be a rewarding listen, for example, for a Stars fan, but then again it might be better to stick with the more familiar originals.

Title: Battle For The Sun
Review: Producer David Bottrill (King Crimson, Tool, Muse) gives Battle for the Sun a lean, sharp sound, stripping away a lot of the synthetic weight that bulked up the group's last few albums.

Title: Long Island
Review: As Long Island is the most attractive and consistent Boog release to date, it is still a difficult proposition to say “hey, this band is for you.”

Title: Playtime Is Over
Review: Playtime Is Over is miles forward from the Wiley of 'Wot U Call It' and 'Who Ate All the Pies' but it sits uneasily behind Sway's One For the Journey and Kano's The Mixtape projects

Title: Fool
Review: He and his band sound focused and spry over eight beautifully arranged songs produced by Jackson and Pat Dillett. [Feb 2019, p.90]

Title: Get Color
Review: Get Color may not be as revelatory as its predeccessors, but its slight merits gradually ooze into the wounds it so fiendishly creates. [Fall 2009, p. 102]

Title: Hope Downs
Review: If there’s anything to criticise Hope Downs for, it’s its risk-averse approach, and tendency to become a one-dimensional listen, but as a debut record, it presents a band that know exactly what they’re doing, and proceed to do it very well indeed.

Title: Jackrabbit
Review: The foibles in surface-level character development thankfully get overshadowed for much of the album with the undeniable charm of the orchestral pop sound.

Title: All Is Dream
Review: Also worth noting is the vulnerability at work that's never surfaced before -- Donahue's voice takes on the pinched, high sound of Neil Young's on more than few songs, and it perfectly suits the sense of enchantment inherent in the album as a whole.

Title: Tourist
Review: Unfortunately, too much of Tourist seems like an amalgam of other things, whether it's the Coldplay-ness of their ballads or the distinct Super Furry Animals influence that's been with Athlete all along.

Title: In The Future
Review: Black Mountain won’t win any prizes for innovation, but their slightly bruised brand of retro is far more fertile than that of their contemporaries.

Title: Hit Reset
Review: There is far more variety on Hit Reset than you suspect the casual ear is going to give it credit for. The biggest talking point on Hit Reset, though, is that it finds Hanna on the lyrical form of her life--and that’s saying something.

Title: Grey Tickles, Black Pressure
Review: The album is a bold, idiosyncratic collection of songs crafted under intense time pressure after producer John Congleton insisted that Grant have all of the material ready to go before entering the studio. Such a challenge certainly seems to have focused the mind.

Title: Astronaut
