Review: Hart’s multiple layers of sound keep his unadventurous song structures from becoming trite; though Our Thickness is pure verse-chorus-verse-chorus fare with no flashy bridges or codas, it will still take months to dive into every piece of instrumentation.

Title: The Past We Leave Behind
Review: The Past We Leave Behind is lovingly crafted but too vague to live up to its title.

Title: Doom Days
Review: A record which thrives on evoking feeling and catharsis, while remaining committed to their personal influences, on Doom Days they’ve managed to deftly build a conceptual world not all too different to the one we’re facing right now, and that feels like a triumph in itself.

Title: Broken Dreams Club
Review: Girls are a band who release their intoxicating mist over time, making this mini-album a bit unsatisfying in quantity rather than quality.

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: It's the lyrics that make Smart Flesh truly shine.

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: Sober living has brought back Skinner’s musical fire, and it has given him a new perspective that is sometimes fascinating but too often cliched. [Winter 2008]

Title: Autotheism
Review: What drives the music is the tightly synched interplay between drums and guitars, and that, particularly as sharpened by Wes Hauch's surgically precise lead work.

Title: Know Your Enemy
Review: Cull the arrogance, the laziness, the ill-considered ignorance, the (that word yet again) sneering, and there wouldn't be a better album than Know Your Enemy, and not just of this year. Cull the brave lyrics, the moments of inspiration, the songs to treasure and the moments of honesty and, were it available in dogfood form, you wouldn't feed Know Your Enemy to your hounds.

Title: Tough Love
Review: A genuinely superior slice of small hours electro-pop.

Title: Trouble Man: Heavy Is the Head
Review: Trouble Man's not the album you'll be recommending to less devout followers of the T.I. saga the way you would have King or Trap Muzik, but it's easily the most satisfying to fans of those albums in a long time.

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: These are lifeless non-revelations married to engrossing tunes.

Title: Cool Choices
Review: On her own behind the piano or over drum programming, the songs sound sad in a somehow less convincing way, perhaps because so much of the rest of the record doesn’t try as hard to convince us of the hurt and does anyway.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: He's written some resonant songs. But he lost his nerve as a coproducer, going for stadium bombast instead of the unadorned grit these stories of hard times demand.

Title: The Air Between Words
Review: Martyn has an incredible musical heritage and series of works in his past, and it’s a shame that The Air Between Words simply is not as interesting nor as rewarding.

Title: Them Crooked Vultures
Review: Nasty riffs and sticky melodies are everywhere, buttered over by the androgynous harmonies that have made Homme a hard-rock anti-hero, but verse-chorus arrangements hold little interest. Instead, there are fascinating digressions, packed with surprises.

Title: Humor Risk
Review: Humor may not exactly be a love record, but its road-ready ballads and attitude toward life are a bit more encouraging than--and a perfect compliment to– Wit's dark ruminations.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: A whole that's less than the sum of its parts, a bittersweet pill that's best taken in small doses. [Feb 2005, p.88]

Title: At Home
Review: Several of the tracks are too short, as if in an eagerness for the songs to sit within a four minute pop structure, instead of discarding some of their ideas, they cram them all in and cut down the song length.

Title: Christmas Songs
Review: All songs are played relatively straight--nary a jingle bell in earshot--which is a good choice, as it offsets the devotional aspects of more traditional carols like ‘O Come All Ye Faithful’ and ‘Angels We Have Heard On High’.

Title: This Is Country Music
Review: His Stetson, clean-cut good looks and Music Row polish might grate with alt.country fans, but his classily understated writing turns mawkish sentimentality into affecting art.

Title: Electric Balloon
Review: The streamlining does much for the album, giving the songs enough space to let their varied and often contrasting influences meld nicely with the band's unique visions.

Title: Havoc and Bright Lights
Review: Havoc and Bright Lights is as soothing as a Sunday afternoon nap or a warm bath: it's music for when you know you're right where you want to be.

Title: Whatever It Takes
Review: Whatever It Takes will please existing fans more than create fresh adherents. There is nothing new here. Hunter and company dig a deep groove. The heavy musical rhythms both tie Hunter up and set him free.

Title: Age Against The Machine
Review: The album falters in spots because of the disparity of its urges. Age Against the Machine seems to want to ease Cee-Lo back into the Goodie Mob’s world while not-so-gently tugging them into his.

Title: Release The Stars
Review: As a whole, the album feels less definite, less driven, than the 'Want…' albums, which is both a strength and a weakness.

Title: Lost in Space
Review: Sonically rich, Lost in Space is home to some of Mann's most intimate storytelling.

Title: Hands
Review: Rather then shy away behind tricksy, overtly difficult melodies or instrumentation, Little Boots has created a pop record in the truest sense of the word; not only does it fizz by in no time at all, it also doesn't alienate or discriminate.

Title: West Ryder Pauper Lunatic Asylum
Review: Sounding more like Animal Collective than The La’s, in these times when one wrong move is seeing bands of Kasabian’s stature sink like stones, it seemed a brave comeback.

Title: One
Review: The limp rhythm section and layered guitars expose the rote melodies, ridiculously dull lyrics and cruise-control tempo. [27 Jan 2005, p.60]

Title: The Firewatcher's Daughter
Review: All she lacks is a really killer song. [Apr 2015, p.72]

Title: Time
Review: Time has its highs and its lows. It’s an album that doesn’t take itself too seriously. The lyrics may be tongue-in-cheek, but the craftsmanship of each song is nothing to smirk at.

Title: Kids in the Street
Review: Earle still hasn’t lost his way with downbeat ballads or the songwriting tradition as powerful renditions of both “Same Old Stagolee” and “If I Was the Devil” both attest, but in all, this album shines a bit brighter in mood and tone than his other more recent releases.

Title: Trouble in Dreams
Review: Luckily for him, his band Destroyer more than makes up for his occasionally strained croak, and "Trouble in Dreams," their follow-up to 2006's acclaimed "Destroyer's Rubies," is an unqualified triumph.

Title: Miami Memory
Review: The 70s soft rock inspirations hit the hardest on two of the most interesting cuts here, Far From Born Again and Bad for the Boys. The two tracks combine a jaunty, easy-listening sheen, with lyrics in the former that discuss sex work positively, and in the latter, that talk about the reckoning of abusive men.

Title: The Cold Still
Review: While certainly an accomplished progression from 09's "Union" in terms of tempo, it's still a bit too midlevel and the band might stand out from their contemporaries if they were a bit more rough around the edges.

Title: Brightly Painted One
Review: Brightly Painted One is an album of quiet, devastating beauty.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: Jay-Z’s latest does little to prove that he can come up with anything that isn’t entirely predictable.

Title: Belladonna
Review: A gorgeous, shimmering 40 minutes of music - a sonic road trip through parts unknown.

Title: Infinite House
Review: Some might consider it messy, and the old adage is, life is messy; well, the latter is true, which lends it its exhilarating beauty.

Title: Taiga
Review: Gone are the darker, more gothic underpinnings of her previous efforts, replaced by a shimmering, gossamer pop sheen that carries with it only shadow elements of her former sound.

Title: Highly Deadly Black Tarantula
Review: Their latest dismantles the genre boundaries often used to pen them in. [Dec 2015, p.79]

Title: Prisoner
Review: Though there’s some absolutely gorgeous production that recalls the lush sound and synthscapes of 80s rock, the songwriting is weighed down by clichés.

Title: EUSA
Review: Taken as a whole, though, EUSA is luminous, a grand gesture made up of the kind of small, gorgeous moments that will remind listeners of home--wherever that may be.

Title: Ahead of the Lions
Review: Each track follows the Rage Against The Machine model: Make music for the masses without diluting it for the bosses. [Nov 2005, p.101]

Title: For The Recently Found Innocent
Review: A risk of pastiche is never far away, but Presley staves it off with energy, songcraft, cunning and a renewed, relatively streamlined focus. [Aug 2014, p.81]

Title: Seeds
Review: Moving past melancholy into mild acceptance is a real accomplishment, but a difficult one to make compelling for an entire album. Seeds struggles in that regard, but has to be called a success.

Title: Lindsey Buckingham / Christine McVie
Review: Together, they’ve produced an album of cracking Mac-esque pop, most notably the clipped, catchy Feel About You and the tightly constructed first single In My World.

Title: The Beautiful Madness
Review: Joseph's craggy voice is perfect for such heavy-duty topics. [Sep 2020, p.28]

Title: Theater of the Mind
Review: Luda has suggested he wanted this album to have a cinematic through line, maybe in order to consolidate his diversified media representations, but Theater doesn't cohere in a manner that would satisfy anyone short of Paul Haggis, or anyone who has listened to an album by Prince Paul or Madvillain, for that matter.

Title: Gaslighter
Review: An album so full of emotion, it takes a while to absorb it all. It’s not perfect, and it’s not meant to be. But the juxtaposition of slickness and rawness somehow works, making the kind of statement the Chicks have been working toward since they first sang of mattress dancing and offing that unfaithful Earl.

Title: The Fragile Army
Review: The melodies are far more varied than on previous outings, and the sense of dynamics and balance of tension in these songs -- and the arrangements that accompany them -- are the most sophisticated this group has ever pulled off.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: There's something about this album that militates against devotion: a coolness that dampens the indie-pop energy and threatens to leave listeners entirely unmoved.

Title: North
Review: North exudes a consistent, subdued beauty that, at times, is almost too delicate to make a true impression.

Title: The Only Thing I Ever Wanted
Review: Sophomore album 'The Only Thing I Ever Wanted' is the work of a band with a keening melodic sense, akin to the development apparent in the prime works of, say, Idlewild or the Delgados, and, impressively, it does this without losing any of the idiosyncratic DIY charms that characterised its makers in the first place.

Title: The Shakes
Review: The Shakes is a record with raw energy.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Like a lot of albums produced by Phil Ek (by the Shins, for instance, and Fleet Foxes), you're impressed, but don't necessarily warm to it.

Title: Xen
Review: It’s a gracefully self-contained ecology--a sonic environment rich with empty and warm spaces, within which the listener is urged to breathe more easily and share in a queer feeling of belonging.

Title: Replica
Review: It's unlike anything else in Lopatin's discography, not just a bold step sideways, but something like an epistemological break from an artist whose work increasingly bears the weight of something like hegemony.

Title: Out My Window
Review: Out My Window, Koushik searches for--and at times strikes--the fine balance between structure and flexibility, rigidity and looseness, body and soul.

Title: pom pom
Review: If the 17-track Pom Pom does little to un-muddy the waters, within its exploded binliner of '80s FM rock licks, novelty squelch noises and other home-recorded debris, songs of splendour lurk. [Dec 2014, p.106]

Title: Nobody's Daughter
Review: A dismal and insipid collection of retrogressive mid-tempo ballads and textbook alt.rock moves.

Title: Aventine
Review: Aventine does not reveal its atmospheric charms instantly and the brief instrumental Tokka is a reminder she can veer too close to chamber music, but repeated listens unfurls all sorts of wonder. [Nov 2013, p.113]

Title: Warpaint
Review: Mostly, though, this lingered-over comeback offers sumptuous returns for those prepared to linger over it.

Title: Insides
Review: Much of the album treads familiar ground, not only to long-time listeners of Fort Romeau, but for any fan of the more minimalist side of House.

Artist: Pantha Du Prince & The Bell Laboratory
Title: Elements of Light
Review: The fluid blend of tracks makes it more of a single piece than a series of highlights and also-rans. [Feb 2013, p.108]

Title: Era Extrana
Review: The band's second disc improves on the "chillwave" (read: low-fi synth pop) of its 2009 debut, dunking dreamy early-MTV haircutband balladry in layers of psychedelic schmutz, almost hiding excellent songs in the murk.

Title: Acousmatic Sorcery
Review: Acousmatic Sorcery is an occasionally iridescent collection of songs, but at the end of the day it feels too tasteful, too self-consciously curated.

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: Producer Rick Rubin has made Metallica sound like Metallica again. [Nov 2008, p.116]

Title: Music For Men
Review: Ditto's one-of-a-kind voice still bestrides everything, sometimes gutsy and soulful, sometimes oddly sweet. [Jul 2009, p.130]

Title: There's No Home
Review: The emotional complexity--or rather, saddled contradictory feelings--aren't all that set her apart from her peers: She also draws on influences from outside folk which, largely due to her finger-style treatment and accompaniment choices, wind up adhering to a folk template.

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: The sounds here do at times recall territories previously mapped by Brian and RD James, with or without MDMA, but Song For Alpha still makes for an electronic listening album of particular quality. [May 2018, p.93]

Title: Dreaming of Revenge
Review: Ideas thin at the end ("Can Anyone Who Has Heard This Music Really Be a Bad Person?"), but when blithe builds to a six-string gallop on stilling closer "2 O'Clock," Revenge kills.

Title: Hubcap Music
Review: Hubcap Music finds Seasick Steve back on form, with an album steeped in gritty boogie and even grittier attitude.

Title: Pure Heroine
Review: 10 songs here, and not one loser in the bunch. [11 Oct 2013, p.72]

Title: The Historical Conquests of Josh Ritter
Review: The resulting album is as lean, rambunctious and snarling as its predecessor was stately.

Title: Heroes
Review: I decided that Lukas's stoned-hillbilly affect was just what his dad needed to distinguish this particular assortment of what-thes, why-hasn't-he-evers,​ and written-to-orders from rival entries in his unchartable catalogue.

Title: My Love is Cool
Review: Wolf Alice balances the difficult combination of seeming guilelessness and utter confidence.

Title: Dark Days / Light Years
Review: This rethink has by no means robbed the band of its tunefulness, as the snappy 'Inaugural Trams' readily proves. But the dozen minutes of 'Pric,' which meanders charmingly around the musical map, are more representative of an outfit which is at its best wild and weird.

Title: King Night
Review: It's been a hella long time coming and may, ultimately, be about as soul curdling as Sabrina the Teenage Witch, but Salem's first blood King Night is still an enjoyably daft crypt kicker.

Title: Crushing
Review: When Jacklin isn’t waxing philosophical on mind-body duality, she’s simply showing the special way she processes the world around her. The result is a profound statement that stands as an early candidate for this year’s strongest singer-songwriter breakthrough.

Title: Passion, Pain & Demon Slayin'
Review: PP&DS is self-indulgent, silly, messy and heartfelt. It's Cudi at top songwriting form, and the songs on it are arguably the best he's ever written.

Title: Futurology
Review: There’s plenty to be pleased about here.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: Ghost's new album may not uncover many of the verteran MC's still-hidden darts but, even 11 years after his solo debut, there's no denying that one of hip-hop's most vibrant voices in its comfort zone.

Title: Take Me Home
Review: The material is of variable quality.

Title: Yellow House
Review: Grizzly Bear are an Animal Collective that decided to go more intelligible and accessible instead of running naked through the woods on five hits of sunshine acid while screaming in tongues.

Title: Woke Myself Up
Review: Her voice shares the same dusky, stained-glass quality as Chan Marshall’s, strident but capable of fracturing at any moment.

Artist: Thao & the Get Down Stay Down
Title: We The Common
Review: Nguyen's rich, harmonic voice is up to the task, carrying with it the weight of more years than she's lived, and effortlessly mumbling and swinging around these compositions. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.89]

Title: The Believer
Review: Miller's compositions are typically well crafted and slightly artier than what you'd hear on, say, a Josh Groban disc, but this isn't too far off that sort of pouty boy bellowing.

Title: III
Review: While the album does tail off slightly towards the end, III is for the most part a solid comeback for Shiny Toy Guns.

Title: Wake Up the Nation
Review: That's just about a half-hour shorter than 22 Dreams, but the disc in turn is twice the fun.

Title: Excerpts
Review: Desperately, painfully arty but worthy of your recollection.

Title: Love, Shelby
Review: It's sad to see the rocker side that Lynne has unveiled in her live sets turned into histrionic failures like "Trust Me," "Star Broker," and "Jesus On A Greyhound." [Dec 2001, p.154]

Title: A Thousand Heys
Review: They've got all the right footnotes and they know their way around a hook, but A Thousand Heys doesn't carve out a distinctive enough place for itself amid this year's crop of guitar-wielding miscreants.

Title: Fire Songs
Review: Without shattering any paradigms, they’ve assembled a very listenable collection of songs that’d be a welcome addition to a Starbucks summer playlist.

Title: V
Review: V combines expansive arena-rock sonics with a heavy dose of lush electronics. Indeed, the stern synths and metal-bashing percussion of Hologram sound like vintage Tubeway Army, while the robo-riffing thunder of Machine falls between Suede and the Sisters Of Mercy.

Title: Our Shadows Will Remain
Review: Arthur is in a class of his own and Our Shadows Will Remain is a monstrous, memorable outing, his finest moment in a career that is thus far full of them.

Title: Heron Oblivion
Review: It's quite simply a thrilling, white-knuckle ride of a record. Its quieter moments are really just momentary respite from a soaring squall of sonic psychedelics.

Title: Remember Us to Life
Review: With Remember Us to Life, Spektor foregoes some of the whimsical narratives on previous albums and digs back into more personal thoughts, showcasing her inimitable vocals and piano talents.

Artist: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
Title: Planetarium
Review: The album has clearly been something of a labour of love for its creators, and feels remarkably homogenous for something produced by four highly individual minds via a mixture of live and studio performance over several years. If you like the sound of a big, camp, melodramatic slab of astrological sci-fi shot through with very earthly, twenty-first century hang-ups, Planetarium is a trip.

Title: The Magic
Review: Although Matsuzaki’s airy voice can be an acquired taste, overall, The Magic delivers fun pop melodies that require some patience. Rather than solely detailing a narrative, Matsuzaki also uses her words as rhythmic punctuation; that’s a key thrill of Deerhoof’s catalog, but can be a challenge to connect with.

Title: DÃ©jÃ  Vu
Review: The desire is there for more of that visionary spirit--though the suspicion lingers that with everything just simply too available, Moroder no longer has the focus and inspiration that fired his finest work.

Title: The Black Album
Review: A magnificent record. [Jan 2004, p.104]

Title: Pull Up Some Dust and Sit Down
Review: This doesn't rock, and it shouldn't. But it rollicks, skanks, and two-steps just fine.

Title: Neck of the Woods
Review: Something's horribly lacking here.  Namely, actual songs. [May 2012, p.53]

Title: A Sailor's Guide to Earth
Review: It's a telling indication of the degree of daring and sophistication at hand that artistic gestures which might have seemed contrived or ill-conceived in other contexts--like say, transforming Nirvana's "In Bloom" into a majestic country-souul ballad worthy of Charley Pride-yield some of the most startling results. [May 2016, p.63]

Title: Mountain Battles
Review: Kim and Kelly Deal have delivered their strangest record to date. [Winter 2008, p.91]

Title: Where It Hits You
Review: Classic heartbreak stuff. [Mar 2012, p.97]

Title: The Sovereign Self
Review: The breadth is a big part of the charm. [Jul 2015, p.83]

Title: Way Out Weather
Review: Way Out Weather's lines and contours are beautifully rendered. But there are times when Gunn's songs don't benefit from the extra exposure, when one misses Time Off's murkier, more forgiving production.

Title: Good Mourning
Review: The mean-spirited sounds of Good Mourning are easy to listen to, but hard to forget. [#17, p.132]

Title: Hot Shots II
Review: Celebrating nonsense and good sense, Beta Band make music from junk and found sounds, their quirky combo of serendipity and sample skills paying off in spades.

Title: 21st Century Breakdown
Review: Bloated, culturally inconsequential and decidedly average, the net result is a band getting far too high on an over-inflated sense of self-importance to the deafening chimes of cash registers the world over.

Title: The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place
Review: Explosions In The Sky are the only instrumental post-rock band that matters, and The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place is proof.

Title: The Girl in the Other Room
Review: Key to the success of the disc is Krall's stretch on the keys, making this her strongest jazz outing.

Title: Dagger Beach
Review: The plethora of unlikely choices adds a depth and tension to the songs, recalling a variety of unique reference points while creating the album's own remarkably strange, remarkably honest statement.

Title: Sheezus
Review: Sheezus has a few good points and some admirable intentions, but too often it misses the point.

Title: The Sun Dogs
Review: The Sun Dogs features solid, compelling songwriting and sounds wonderful; heavy, spacious guitars flare up amidst the smoke, and when these guys start to rip, there’s no stopping them.

Title: The Big Bang
Review: Busta seems to be treading water too often.

Title: Father Divine
Review: There isn't a weak track on "Father Divine," and though some of Ladd's lyrical styling can be uninspired... the album is packed with solid material.

Title: True Sadness
Review: Fortunately, they haven't forsaken their natural songwriting strengths. [Aug 2016, p.70]

Title: No Witch
Review: Unfortunately with No Witch, there just isn't enough excitement to hold the listener's attention for long. And while the group is to be commended for their artistic efforts, it could benefit from a more aggressive fusion of sounds on its next album.

Title: Totems Flare
Review: We’ve been shown angry Clark, blinded by passion and vigor, and we’ve seen drowsy, reverb-soaked Clark, but never before have the two parts struggled with one another in such a fascinating, rewarding way.

Title: Bubblegum
Review: Alt-rock blues darker and scarier than Jon Spencer or even Jack White ever imagined. [24 Dec 2004, p.66]

Title: The Golden Age of Apocalypse
Review: Equal parts futuristic space jazz fusion and hip-hop that does well to bridge the seemingly disparate corners of Thundercat's sprawling resume, Apocalypse is one of those rare modern jazz records that's remarkably unpretentious without having to cheapen the daunting complexity jazz is noted for.

Title: Skip a Sinking Stone
Review: It is an album-lover’s album, too as each track bleeds into the next, the transitions ooze, indistinct and lovely, making it hard to listen to one song without listening to every song. In a musical landscape powered by singles and populated by an insurmountable avalanche of new material, a record like this, which pulls like taffy and takes its time, really is a treat.

Title: II Trill
Review: The album is dark and menacing, and also better than the first "Trill," even if Bun doesn't threaten to slap anyone in the face with a pie a la mode.

Title: Help Wanted Nights
Review: Kasher wrote this as the soundtrack to his screenplay, but on this evidence it could debut on The Hallmark Channel.

Title: Black Sun
Review: Black Sun is spotty and rusted, and it is likely that it will be interesting to most for this or that track - a grimy slayer, a leftfield floorfiller - or for the fact that it has a fantastic musique concrète apocalyptic vignette featuring Flying Lotus for a coda.

Despite the attempts to recreate the dense power chords and pained whines that made Saves the Day emo poster boys, the formula fails when applied through Conley’s rose-colored vision of his own glory days.

Title: Chuck
Review: The Chuck Berry template rears its head, for better and worse, throughout Chuck.

Title: The Things We Do To Find People Who Feel Like Us
Review: There's something refreshing about a bastard of old who doesn't try to slow down his band's headlong thwack with stubble-stroking musing on midlife malaise or clunky lit-seminar over-trying. For these guys, noise will always be enough.

Title: The Way Things Fall
Review: Like horror films or ghost stories, the upside of ADULT.’s brand of dark paranoia is its visceral thrill; it’s as nasty as electro can get whilst maintaining a remnant of a reassuring pop edge.

Title: Isles
Review: Natalie Bergman and her brother Elliot are too inventive to get cast as style-rock band, experimenting with African thumb pianos, dub-reggae grooves, and sultry soul vocals with deep pass-the-dutchie raspiness.  [15 Mar 2013, p.62]

Title: Control
Review: While the form may feel familiar (think: a glitch-pop kissing cousin to Rufus Wainwright’s days as a balladeer, or a soft-shoe version of Patrick Wolf’s orchestral manoeuvres) a promising left-of-centre choice sets Fyfe apart from the pack of crooners.

Title: There's No Leaving Now
Review: There's No Leaving Now is another sweetly concise collection of ten songs by the eloquent Swede, whose nationality remains brilliantly masked by a Midwestern twang.

Title: Memories Don't Die
Review: Nearly everything he raps on Memories Don’t Die is something you’ve heard before, performed more ably elsewhere, and the few lines that aren’t are unbelievably simple-minded or straight-up witless.

Title: American Dream
Review: Murphy skillfully layers his sounds for tracks that somehow feel dense and airy at the same time.

Title: Amnesty (I)
Review: So as good as it often is, Amnesty feels like a missed opportunity, the first safe album from an act that once would have recoiled at such a thought.

Title: Holy
Review: Jayne’s music is at once disorienting and familiar.

Title: Open Season
Review: Sadly, Open Season's one-pace '80s guitar rock lags a bit behind the narrative. [May 2005, p.110]

Title: ISAM
Review: ISAM plays out like the soundtrack to some bizarre nature documentary: it continually pauses, goes off in another direction, halts again, then sits unmoving for a time, as though Tobin had been musically ghosting the movements of a tiny insect traveling along a leaf.

Title: The Beautiful Lie
Review: It might as well be Harcourt’s thesis: marrying the histrionic truths of the deeply aggrieved with the formal mastery of great pop. More often, Harcourt’s failed attempts at mimicking Jeff Buckley throw whatever genre he tries off balance.

Title: Que Aura
Review: The remarkable thing about Kelley Stoltz up to now has been how seamlessly he absorbs his influences, finds their essences and out of that irreducable core makes songs that are entirely fresh and new.

Title: Midnight Soul Serenade
Review: The duo does tweak their established formula, here and there, with varying results.

Title: Harmonicraft
Review: Rather than merely aiming at populism, though, Brooks has set a new personal best for what he's been doing for almost 20 years: turning pop anthems into earthmovers.

Title: Veronica Falls
Review: While the songs sound effortlessly crafted, there's a complexity to the melodies and structures that surprises on repeat listens.

Title: Dark Light
Review: Sisters Of Mercy fans will remain defiantly nonplussed. [Nov 2005, p.103]

Title: Graduation
Review: The bliss that does surface on Graduation is all in the grooves, which range further than West has ever gone before.

Title: Ventriloquism
Review: These are well-loved songs that Ndegeocello loves a little bit more, singing them with a rich, warm tone (she’s never sounded better) and backed by a band who know how to anticipate every bob and weave she might make. It’s one of her best.

Title: Protean Threat
Review: A record that otherwise skids wildly across art-rock history leaving steaming tyre tracks in its wake.

Title: Violet Psalms
Review: An album that challenges, even as it brings a 17-year band to its conclusion. As a coda for Frog Eyes, it's hard to imagine a more potent sendoff.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being
Review: Typically, the complaints against Wayne are that he's annoying, grating, and ubiquitous; but for the first time he's made himself seem uninteresting, which is far more career-threatening.

Title: Paperback Ghosts
Review: The album has that general feeling that we’re all fading away, grasping at moments of life, but there’s also a lit spark, a pulse running through it all.

Title: A Muse In Her Feelings
Review: From the harp-tinged starter of “No Good”, far across the twinkling lights, broken hearts and epiphany, to thunderous claps of “…Again” A Muse holds itself aloft, floating dreamily on a sea of feeling.

Title: O
Review:
Lucky for him, he has Lisa Hannigan on board on several tracks in this album--her breathtaking vocals almost manage to make this take of epic heartbreak to the backdrop of Irish lullabies worthwhile.
Almost.

Title: BareNaked
Review: Amounts to nothing more than a party of five million bland cliches. [11 Oct 2002, p.82]

Title: Atrocity Exhibition
Review: Whether he's rapping about stripping copper out of abandoned houses or addiction, Brown manages to wring humor and, somehow, relatability out of grim personal stories.

Title: The Lonely Position of Neutral
Review: It's a solid formula--trouble is, anything resembling emotional complexity gets blasted away by the heavy-metal howitzer of Don Gilmore's production. [Oct 2002, p.117]

Title: More Fish

The other album, where the Wave section of the album name is derived, which loosely comprises the first half of the album and revolves around a mythical group of vengeful drowned slaves, isn't just Lupe Fiasco's best but easily one of the greatest albums I've heard in recent memory.

Review: Squeaky genius.

Title: III
Review: III is a record for getting lost in your thoughts, rather than losing your mind on the floor.

Title: Down in the Weeds Where the World Once Was
Review: Down in the Weeds is still a Bright Eyes album, with its share of obsessiveness, narcissism, and angst. Many songs have their sights set on calamity, from climate disaster to Oberst’s failed marriage. And yet, there’s also a refreshing maturity, a perspective that seems a bit wiser, a bit less ready to revel in self-loathing. ... That culmination — from grief to love — is what truly makes these Bright Eyes songs feel new.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: Pop's understated delivery draws even the most skeptical of listeners in, bathing his hushed voice in beds of stark piano and tremolo-washed guitar.

Title: Voices
Review: Jordan wraps swelling, sing-along choruses and metal guitar outbursts with hushed confessions, distended melodies, and enough Gothy menace to make it sting. [17 Feb 2006, p.79]

Title: Rainier Fog
Review: Rainier Fog is more than just another Alice in Chains record; it's another step in the process of redefining their sound since their first comeback record, 2009's Black Gives Way to Blue.

Title: Undun
Review: [An] excellent record that anyone who wants to hear the graceful way by which hip-hop should age should add to their collections right away.

Title: Troubadour
Review: Whether he’s lamenting immigration hassles or imagining himself a depressed American kid fighting in Iraq, this Muslim fan of Biggie and Bruce Lee has a common touch. He’s a universal soldier, not an exotic novelty.

Title: Free the Universe
Review: A no-brainer, easy-to-enjoy production slate gets knocked around by its flaws just enough that even the minor, acquired-taste touches seem like just another bad decision.

Title: Flamingo
Review: What we have here is a Killers record made without the Killers that sounds like The Killers and is almost as good as The Killers, but not quite. [Oct 2010, p.101]

Title: We Got a Love
Review: Even though the record is irresistible at times, it's also a feedback loop of nostalgia that's creaking as it turns.

Title: Harps and Angels
Review: 40 years after his debut, the curly-haired songwriter continues to play to his strength: three-minute social commentaries that might sound bitter if they weren't so funny.

Title: Waiting for the Sunrise
Review: Perhaps in the winter this will all seem a lot less charming, but right now, it’s a nice soundtrack for a drive out to the coast or for porch sitting late in the evening.

Title: Semper Femina
Review: Semper Femina is a concise, dynamic statement from the English singer-songwriter, mixing breezy 70’s country-rock melodies with claustrophobic, fingerpicking folk, often on the same song.

Title: Grey Tickles, Black Pressure
Review: In its 58 minutes length, Grey Tickles, Black Pressure notches up fourteen masterful tracks with no down-swing, enchanting the listener until the very last words, "love never fails".

Title: Nothing Is True & Everything Is Possible
Review: It's the sound of grand ambition realised. [Jun 2020, p.98]

Title: Rebel Heart
Review: There are times you hope for a little more dumb fun--enter Diplo, who turns up on five tracks with his air horn and Caribbean beats and would be welcome on more--and there's at least one moody ballad too many. But then an aqueous bassline bubbles up and a surge of trance-y pulses sweeps you along to Madonnaland, where introspection and abandon engage in erotic acts of self-actualization.

Title: Ultimate Care II
Review: Ultimate Care II is reliably dream-like, the sort of album you never quite hear in the same way twice; passages jut out or fly under the radar.

Title: Soul is Heavy
Review: Even as Soul is Heavy struggles to balance the earthy and the abstract, Nneka's vocals prevent the album from curdling into run-of-the-mill radio r&b.

Title: Modern Guilt
Review: Modern Guilt feels like a vanity project: there is no attempt to reach out, none of the classic pop singles Beck has been revered for, just 10 inward-looking, unlovable tracks.

Title: Peace Trail
Review: All too often, though, Peace Trail sounds like another case of Young chucking half-formed ideas at the wall to see if anything might stick before moving on to yet another project. That said, there are genuinely powerful moments here that promise of better things to come.

Title: Lady in Gold
Review: An evolution in sound from its debut album, Blues Pills serve up a masterful mix of soul and blues-rock that ferments into a tasty, tasty witches’ brew.

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: I Can Feel You Creep Into My Private Life doesn’t quite hit the immense heights of her first two albums, but this is still Merrill Garbus doing her own thing--which is something that’s always worth paying attention to.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Having defined its gauzy sound on previous albums, Halcyon Digest Deerhunter finds the group expanding it with knockout results.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: At times a beautifully rendered album with surprisingly solid songwriting; it's an unashamedly nostalgic musical postcard from the American West Coast.

Title: Aerial
Review: 'Aerial' towers over the vast majority of even this year's embarrassment of riches.

Title: Grinderman
Review: This being Cave, classy lyrical dexterity is never far away. But here the fire and brimstone preacher is a little less po-faced than much of his back catalogue, allowing humour (still black as coal) to gain the upper hand.

Title: Sound Kapital
Review: Sound Kapital may be the best of the bunch-- a hard-hitting, spine-crushing work of post-industrial electro-punk that owes more to Suicide than Pavement. [Jul 2011, p.85]

Title: Chemical Miracle
Review: The Australian punks tone down the fury on album two, and manage to achieve so much without it.

Title: Here I Stand
Review: After a four-year break, Usher's fifth set is bursting with grown man, true-to-life tales like leaving his player ways behind ("Before I Met You"), falling in love ("Something Special," "Lifetime" and the title track), making love ("This Ain't Sex") and having a child.

Title: Persona
Review: Cinematic in scope and delicately constructed, the album grows from warm, organic techno (‘Persona’) through ambient electronica (‘Dreamer’s Wake’) to the insistent synths, drums and drones of ‘Hidden’. Lovely stuff.

Title: The Hex
Review: Despite its subject matter and context, The Hex is by no means a grim listen. It’s very much a continuation and, inevitably, a conclusion of the fine solo work Richard Swift did in the past, and a fitting and self-aware cap on a career that ended far too early.

Title: In Waves
Review: What's disheartening about In Waves is its lack of a clear identity; the band seem to be targeting too much at once.

Title: Eâ€¢MOâ€¢TION
Review: Carly Rae Jepsen and her production team try overly hard to be clever. In the end, what's left is a record that takes itself too seriously to be taken seriously by anyone else.

Title: Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts
Review: In Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts, M83 have created an ethereal electronic masterpiece, and one which, thankfully, doesn't sound like a relic from the Warp Records back catalogue.

Title: The Warning
Review: They are very good at making sleepy, hapless trip-pop sprayed with whimsy.

Title: Pigeons
Review: This psychedelic folk pop-athon of tickled riffs, snappy elastic basslines, shimmering synths and sweetly sung vocals is all dreamy eccentricity, with a bittersweet hint of rhythmic unrest, from start to finish, and should send Hidden Cameras fans into an amorous tizz after just one listen.

Title: Out of the Blues
Review: Occasional horns spice up the approach adding tasty seasoning to an album that shows Boz Scaggs at 74 is bookending a remarkable career by reviving a love of the refined soul/blues that began over 50 years ago.

Title: Complete Me
Review: A high-gloss, vocally gymnastic collection of '80s-referencing dance pop concerned with love and love gone wrong, can be a little full-on. [Aug 2009, p.107]

Title: Honeymoon On Mars
Review: The Pop Group’s name has always been a bit ironic, but strangely enough, a more focused, fine-tuned, pop sensibility is what they needed here to make this album a more accessible type of strange.

Title: The Law of Large Numbers
Review: While sentimental on occasion, and certainly possessed by a lovelorn spirit that should connect with all but the hardest of hearts, The Law of Large Numbers never comes across cloyingly, its content ably handled and expressed with the same cliché-free purity The Delgados mastered.

Title: The Light in You
Review: It’s not a reinvention, but Mercury Rev did their experimentation on their earlier records. Here they just get on with the job of sounding like nobody else, which suits them very nicely indeed.

Title: Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino
Review: The first listen may be surprising, but repeated listens illuminate that Arctic Monkeys remain progressive and energetic even when style and mood shift dramatically.

Title: Workout Holiday
Review: Songs begin fully-formed before spiralling into abstract drum loops punctuated by slicing guitars and vocal drones (‘Mess Your Hair’). At other times, the most perfect moments of Small Faces psychedelia or Velvet Underground basement pop will emerge from the most unlikely formless squalls (‘Sitting’; ‘Heart From Us All’).

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: For everything else there's Coldplay: reliable, built to move, and able to run on hot air alone.

Title: American Ride
Review: There's a little less bluster and bravado on Toby Keith's latest album, American Ride, and it's a welcome turn.

Title: Beach House
Review: Finding the best bits in these sleepy songs often feels like hard work.

Title: Athena
Review: Showcases her eclecticism in technique and execution on her magnificent terms.

Title: Quarter Turns Over a Living Line
Review: Quarter Turns Over a Living Line is neither an easy, nor comforting listening, and absorbing the entire album can occasionally leave the listener gasping for air. However, as a portrait of a dystopian 21st century musical landscape, there is little better than this brand of pure British blackness.

Title: Unravelling
Review: We Were Promised Jetpacks have pushed the bar for these bands even higher with the release of Unravelling.

Title: Lorraine
Review: Lorraine is evenly split between mercilessly detailed songs like these and frustratingly blank ones ("Sweet Disposition," "Rocket Science"), which feel like hollow templates designed to be inhabited by other, less imaginative singers. On those songs Ms. McKenna sounds complacent; discomfort suits her better.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: Large Hadron pop that'll frazzle yer neurons.

Title: Blood Money
Review: Most of this album is startlingly uninspired; no-frills rhymes were once this duo's main weapon; now they are its main liability. [1 May 2006]

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Rage sits alongside heartache and humor, the shifts in mood occurring with a dramatic flair and a disarming playfulness. The unpredictable nature feels complex and profoundly human, resulting in an album that's nourishing and joyfully cathartic.

Title: Golden Eagle
Review: Macve sings with real power as she glides from note to note in a dreamy glissando--although the Tammy Wynette-style catch in her voice is a quirk that is perhaps overemployed.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: But for all its momentary highlights, this is a record that doesn't tend to grow on you as much as sink and seep into your skin: and it does this slowly.

Title: Fool's Gold
Review: The spirited chants and intricate beats give Fool’s Gold unity, and the precision is inviting. They never break from their tight sound with a boldly original gesture, but there’s no need to risk spoiling this fun set of songs.

Title: Hamburg Demonstrations
Review: The album falls flat in just about every aspect. It’s not offensively bad, it’s inoffensively boring.

Title: The Declaration
Review: Ashanti’s still got a decent voice, but she’s badly in need of a better songwriting and production team.

Title: Peeping Tom
Review: There's hardly a stinker in the bunch. [Jul 2006, p.206]

Title: Death of a Bachelor
Review: Panic! At The Disco’s audience may perpetually renew itself with fresh teenagers, but Urie is maturing as an artist. He takes a lot of risks on Death Of A Bachelor, all of which pay off.

Title: Invariable Heartache
Review: Generally there's not too much straying away from the Nashville sound and Wagner's production keeps things sounding impressively full and remarkably fresh considering the age of the source material.

Title: Cost of Living
Review: While a few songs interject to maintain the rabid pace of earlier releases (“Because You,” “Somos Chulas (No Somos Pendejas),” “Tonta”), most come through with a mid-tempo energy that might fall flat were it not rejuvenated by dense song forms, disjointed and atonal harmony, and Ruiz’s characteristic snarl.

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: What We Saw..., then, is the usual Spektorish mixed bag of literate genius and "look at me" showboating.

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: She might be mouthy, trendy, shallow and opinionated without having all of the facts, but MIA creates terrific pop moments.

Title: The Bride Screamed Murder
Review: The Bride Screamed Murder, you see, all works when it really shouldn't, demonstrating once again just how the Melvins can somehow ensure their own very special brand of weird never quite becomes the norm.

Title: Shangri-La Dee Da
Review: Shangri-La Dee Da sounds like two completely different bands -- DeLeo's hard rock and Weiland's soft balladry. Happily (for Atlantic Records), the album has something for both slumming Papa Roach fans and growing Jessica Simpson fans. STP has enough talent to hold both together.

Title: Lady Antebellum
Review: At this point, Lady Antebellum is a group that seems to know the basics of contemporary country but isn't ready to move beyond them or redefine them for its own ends. Still, this is a good beginning.

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: Mr. West is often nowhere to be found, and more crucially, nowhere to be felt. Parts of this album - "Sin City," "The One," "Creepers" - feature what's easily the laziest music on any Kanye-related project, with no trace of his trademark meticulousness.

Title: Severant
Review: An intriguing sonic experience from start to finish, Severant is a bold left-field first offering from an artist who's quickly establishing himself as the intelligent dance scene's "one to watch."

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: Just like with White Stripes albums, the music rattles your brain like no other and gets better with age. [#20, p.97]

Title: Era Vulgaris
Review: This time around things are more industrial and complex but every bit as sleazy and intoxicating.

Title: Birdy
Review: The whole idea of Birdy sounds like a transparent attempt to court a more credible audience, but thanks to her haunting tones and a tasteful yet compelling production, it impressively avoids being the try-hard affair you'd expect.

Title: The Bridge (Concept of a Culture)
Review: While beats like 'Shine All Day's' electronic bounce feel odd at first, they gradually begin to make sense, while KRS-One's 'What If?' and the Supernatural-helmed 'Tribute To The Breakdancer' will keep the most ardent old-schoooler happy. [Apr 2009, p.108]

Title: Revival
Review: There are just too many pop stars here (Pink, Beyoncé, Kehlani) wailing anodyne hooks over glutinous beats. Perhaps the biggest problem with Revival – as with many latterday Eminem records – is the struggle of an intelligent fortysomething artist to evolve while somehow remaining true to the demands of his sniggery core audience of alienated males.

Title: Shine
Review: Don't be fooled into thinking it's the big American names that are carrying this record, because her lyrical wit, seductive soul vocals and Brit charm offensive prove she is strong enough to punch above her weight.

Title: Simple Math
Review: They seem satisfied enough with their place as one of the underappreciated underdogs of the American alt rock scene, and it's hard not to get a kick out of hearing such an independent spirit raging through this album, even if commercially, Simple Math doesn't quite add up.

Title: Field of Love
Review: Unfortunately, there are a few too many moments with a "more is more" approach, and they hold the record back.

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: It suits them well that as musicians that have worked their entire career just to get noticed; for their newest album, I Learned the Hard Way, to be a beautiful representation of what real, honest and true soul music really is.

Title: Homesongs
Review: Pulling every sound to its limit, Adem’s debut is glorious in its scope, maintaining a contemplative stride through bare instrumentation.

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: Garbage haven't released an album this immediate, melodically strong and thematically interesting since their self-titled 1995 debut. [Jul 2016, p.91]

Title: Phantom Brickworks
Review: It's exquisite ghostly piano and hypnotic loops transport you to a gauzy, fantastical netherworld. [Jan 2018, p.96]

Title: Gravity the Seducer
Review: For diehard fans Gravity The Seducer is replete with pleasing moments. For fans of novel musical statements, not so much. Listen, feel your mind wander, forget.

Title: It's The Big Joyous Celebration, Let's Stir The Honeypot
Review: For a lo-fi project, Celebration is a particularly imaginative, lengthy work full of vivid character portraits, using additional instrumentation and computer-generated distortion to expand far beyond the boundaries of more straightforward guitar-driven indie acts.

Title: Hunter
Review: Calvi remains in firm control on Hunter, but she lets loose more than enough moments of bliss to satisfy.

Title: Flourish // Perish
Review: Occasionally subtlety spills over into insipidness, but overall this is a masterclass in restrained beauty.

Title: Warrior
Review: Taken as a whole, this is another surprisingly enjoyable album from a pop singer who has managed to broaden her approach without losing her USP.

Title: Music Sounds Better With You
Review: It's hard to go into explicit detail on Music Sounds Better With You, simply because of how happily delightful it is.

Title: m b v
Review: It’s a good album, but not a great one, and though the long tail of history will eventually render such a long production time moot, it’s certainly not a record justifying the ludicrous wait.

Title: Yellow & Green
Review: They deliver 18 tracks of timeless, gimmick-free and inventive rock. [14 Jul 2012, p.52]

Title: El Camino
Review: Down and dirty, it grooves by on soulful power chords and Carney's relentless hammering of his kit.

Title: Real Life Is No Cool
Review: It's best when it's at its most trippy. Less effectove are the parping brass and chukka-chukka guitars on "Baby Can't Stop." Happily there's enough of the former to outweigh the latter. [Mar 2010, p.105]

Title: One Word Extinguisher
Review: Isn't so much a leftfield perversion of HipHop as it is a restoration of the genre to its avant garde roots. [#231, p.67]

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: Concerns over the band’s changing sound are summarily squashed under the furore of their zipping forward with the energy and heft of a dozen motorcycles.

Title: Build a Rocket Boys!
Review: The band didn't set out to create a hit-laden album that repeats the successes of their past. Instead, they've crafted an album full of beautifully lush melodies, intricate patterns, and soaring vocalizations.

Title: Bitchitronics
Review: The result is music that undulates and bobs, never really going anywhere, but accumulating density. [No. 101, p.52]

Title: Go Plastic
Review: In anybody else's hands, a blending of techy aesthetics and near-tender melodies would be a musical oxymoron, but in Squarepusher's, it is delicious.

Title: I Am Very Far
Review: The smooth shape of this album - there's no rising or falling action - and lack of a big concept won't replace 2005's Black Sheep Boy for diehard fans, just as the superior The Stand-Ins didn't in 2008. But Elvis Costello fans should holler.

Title: Songs of Experience
Review: Songs Of Experience will likely go down as a late-career classic. [Jan 2018, p.104]

Title: Ten Silver Drops
Review: These songs are painfully uneventful.

Title: Lo Moon
Review: Lo Moon isn’t afraid to step outside of its comfort zone, and it’s a big reason why the album feels like such a distinct triumph over the genre’s familiar tendencies and tropes.

Title: A Distant Fist Unclenching
Review: Instead of picking over internal ashes, Krill rotate and swivel, holding a lighter, as if looking more closely at the moment might make action possible.

Title: De Facto
Review: Most consistently enthralling album thus far. [Feb 2019, p.36]

Title: Out of the Shadow
Review: Out of the Shadow is a meandering musical path, but one well worth taking.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: The album bubbles over with insidious grooves, inventive samples, and lissome rhyming about things frivolous and fraught.

Title: Dark Sky Island
Review: The lyrics often mention homecomings; the music is a warm bath.

Title: A Million and One
Review: Most of the songs on A Million and One burrow between ecstasy and threat, Nova’s voice playing at the edges of those feelings.

Title: Sonic Soul Surfer
Review: Some of Wold's tracks here with a full band don't descend into pub-blues mediocrity. [Apr 2015, p.83]

Title: One Second of Love
Review: One Second of Love is artfully crafted.

Title: Skins
Review: All suggest that this band is in the process of remaking itself for a vital midlife. [Mar 2010, p.85]

Title: Optica
Review: Functional yet uninspiring, Optica is pop as Ikea catalog. [Jun 2013, p.104]

Title: Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager
Review: Kid Cudi's Man on the Moon II was released in a year where rap album sequels were common, but unlike most of the competition, this sequel has a very strong link to its predecessor.

Title: Shadow
Review: Bitter-pill catharsis. [Jun 2014, p.89]

Title: Office Politics
Review: Both confounding and compelling, Office Politics, like much of Hannon's work, feels a bit like a magnificently rendered lark, but as per usual, it's hard not to admire the craftsmanship.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: The album takes its cues from its stellar opener, "World Sick," which swells and booms and tries to embrace the global and the personal all at once, while never forgetting to swing.

Title: The False Alarms
Review: The False Alarms is marked by a frustrating lack of movement, direction, or variance.

Title: New Brigade
Review: A punk band with a Steely Dan fixation they most certainly are not, but in their best moments these kids do rouse something as opulently degenerate and self-destructively lax as the Dan's cleanest work.

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: While these [linking tracks] suggest Schneider's appreciation for the short-form work of electronic music pioneer Raymond Scott, they stop well short of giving Wonder the thematic consistency it seeks (and needs).

Title: Everything That Happens Will Happen Today
Review: An underwhelming collection that lacks focus and rarely lives up to the lofty aspirations of these two titans of modern music. [Fall 2008, p.79]

Title: Living With The Living
Review: Leo's melodic gifts don't keep up with his lyrics. [22 Mar 2007, p.80]

Title: Shadow Offering
Review: A sadder, wiser, and stronger album, Shadow Offering reflects big changes in Braids' world, but proves they're still at their finest when they dig into -- and sit with -- complex emotions.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: It's all so gentle that it's nearly sleepy, but in a nice way.

Title: Future Hearts
Review: It's a version of All Time Low that not only has zero interest in moving past its pop-punk roots, but is embracing them with more vigor and pride than ever, laying the groundwork for punk bands that imagine a world where "maturing" doesn't mean leaving behind what you grew up loving.

Title: Living With The Living
Review: Leo and company go over a lot of territory on this release, but it is not bothersome or a stretch; the band pulls off all of these styles very well.

Title: Major Arcana
Review: With its quaking rhythms, twisted riffage, and jet-black wit, Major Arcana is a redemptive ode to the broken bones that grew back together a little crooked--the ones that taught Dupuis how to walk in her own weird way.

Title: Hundred Acres
Review: Hundred Acres’ environment can occasionally border on the too-cozy and tender, and, as has been the case on previous records, certain songs simply wind down more than they come to any conclusion. Still, Carey ably shepherds the whole sentimental journey.

Title: The Information
Review: [A] darkly intelligent album.

Title: Resolution
Review: There are no concepts, no gimmicks, no frills: just straightforward metal, period.

Title: Be Small
Review: If kept short and sweet, Temple would have made a charmingly laconic record that blossomed in unconventionality, yet sadly here is muddled in his expansive means.

Title: Less Than Human
Review: If the DFA medium/message commands one groove rattling under a nation, Less Than Human is evidence enough that bot-genius Maclean is just the half-man needed to bang up the plumbing so that all faucets drip lightning bolts.

Title: Another Day on Earth
Review: If lightweight, it is often pleasant and amusing, if not utterly engaging.

Title: This Machine Kills Artists
Review: Across 17 tracks with titles like “Dark Brown Teeth,” “The Blithering Idiot,” and “Drunken Baby,” Osborne delivers concise down-tuned ditties full of booming vocal melodies and bizarro humor.

Title: The Birds of Satan
Review: Dave Grohl and Pat Smear both make cameos on the record, but high profile guests aren’t the album’s high point. That accolade goes to the gentle soft rock triumph of ‘Raspberries’, the shred-happy ‘Pieces of the Puzzle’ and the piledriving, ’70s-era Aerosmith ballad ‘Too Far Gone To See’.

Title: Scarecrow
Review: If this is indeed a swan song for Brooks, it's like calling it a career with a championship-winning shot at the buzzer.

Title: Hyperview
Review: There is nothing particularly revolutionary about the new record, rather it is a band finding confidence in a sound that’s new to them.

Title: II
Review: It's part Fairport Convention and part Led Zeppelin at the band's most druidic. [Jun/Jul 2006, p.121]

Title: Candy For The Clowns
Review: Although this by no means makes the album unpleasant to listen to, it's more likely to have you reaching for some of the classic albums of decades past than giving it a second spin.

Title: Lianne La Havas
Review: The set covers the trajectory of one relationship and was recorded in concentrated fashion, and it consequently plays out like a complete statement made by a self-contained crew. What's more, La Havas' lithe voice forms a tighter bond with the lyrics, and her gently ringing guitar rarely leaves her hands.

Title: A Thing Called Divine Fits
Review: Rather than a cohesive structured debut effort that was the product of a cooperative band, you have a Frankenstein-ian melding of cast off parts.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: By design, the new disc is less precisely crafted and more taken with posh, atmospheric grooves than hot power pop.

Title: Be Small
Review: Be Small connotes acceptance of the intimacy Temple can't seem to breach. [No. 126, p.57]

Title: The Rebirth of Venus
Review: Were the central conceit not so half-assed and Lee's lyrics not so shallow, Venus might qualify as actively misogynist in a way that could be interesting to engage and dissect. As is, the album is simple to an annoying, tiresome degree.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: The record is permeated with an air of bashed-out-before-tea desperation. [Jan 2001, p.106]

Title: Breaks in the Armor
Review: Previous Crooked Fingers albums have been more elaborately orchestrated, fortifying themselves; this one, even when cushioned by Liz Durrett's backup vocals, makes a wary peace with its own sense of isolation.

Title: Mala
Review: Mala may not stand as the zenith of the man’s catalogue, but it’s a highlight worth exploring and a dreamy journey for the taking.

Title: Blurred Lines
Review: What’s striking is how unambitious most of the rest of the album is, especially the half that’s produced by Mr. Thicke with his longtime production partner Pro-Jay.

Title: Animator
Review: The innocent timbre of her voice giving these songs a semblance of hypnotic, warped nursery rhymes. [Oct/Nov 2012, p.123]

Title: All I Intended To Be
Review: She draws in appropriate songs by Merle Haggard, Patty Griffin and Jack Wesley Routh, but excels them all with her own 'Not Enough.' [July 2008, p.104]

Title: The Libertines
Review: It's brilliant at points, exhibiting the casual, grimy grace that laced Up the Bracket through English countryside benders, sing-alongs, and pub anthems, but evidently, The Libertines are creatures of excess, and even a good thing can be overdone.

Title: Follow Me Down
Review: Rather than hone the traditional Appalachian discipline, the sensualist singer explores the possibilities of acoustic/roots music--conjuring songscapes, erotic tableau and enough tension to hold listeners transfixed throughout Follow Me Down.

Title: Heaven and Earth
Review: Despite the sheer weight of material on offer you’ll struggle to find an inch of fat. With its forward-thinking, deep-searching nature counterbalanced by a natural warmth and populist, groove-heavy approach, it’s another hugely accomplished work by a man whose prolific run of form shows no signs of abating.

Title: Tight Knit
Review: Tight Knit is a beautiful, lazy album of befogged West Coast dreams. [Apr 2009, p.107]

Title: No More Stories...
Review: Mew has succeeded in developing a good sound from some of the least hip ingredients imaginable, and No More Stories... feels like a consolidation of every stride they've made to date.

Title: Drone Logic
Review: Impressively, in a nod to Avery's crowd-pleasing and circuit-bending skills, this is a techno album that seldom sags. [Nov 2013, p.65]

Title: Shine a Light
Review: The group frequently wanders into still valleys before chugging back up, properly balancing bounce and punch--Constantines may be the best band since Archers Of Loaf to marry intelligence and brute force.

Title: Confessions of a Dangerous Mind
Review: The album’s overall production by his longtime main man 6ix sparkles like never before, and lends itself to the loosely thread, sharply needled conceptual-ism handsomely.

Title: Every Kingdom
Review: Throughout Every Kingdom Howard plays to his strengths, the greatest of which is his skill in crafting hooks.

Title: The Eraser
Review: Radiohead fans will obviously want to snag it up, but if you’re looking for melancholic electronic pop, there’s much better to be found.

Title: Paradise
Review: White Lung sound both heavier and more accessible on Paradise, once again proving that there's far more to this band than meets the eye.

Title: Savage (Songs from a Broken World)
Review: There’s much to admire about Savage, but it’s definitely one that you have to be in a particular mood to enjoy.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: What this record ultimately boils down to is whether or not you’re tired of the incessant vocoder effect. If you are, this really isn’t for you. But if it’s little more than a mainstream trend, T-Pain does it better than anyone.

Title: Alpine Static
Review: Dizzying psychedelic bong-fodder that requires neither psychedelics nor bongs. [Aug 2005, p.176]

Review: The songwriting, playing, and production here are inspired, kinetic, and far more accessible than ever before.

Title: Manipulator
Review: Manipulator affording him space to rise above his obvious points of reference and create the one thing no one envisioned for album number seven: Ty Segall as both uncompromised AND accessible artist. The complete package.

Title: Slow Air
Review: Swerving back and forth between the lanes of psychedelic road rock and dream pop, the album never reaches its intended destination. However, while directionless, the journey still uncovers beautiful moments.

Title: Starwalker
Review: Perhaps the most impressive thing about this album is how seamlessly it blends both creators' sensibilities.

Title: I Used to Spend So Much Time Alone
Review: On the band’s new album, her lonely psychoses are exposed and have taken center stage for an unapologetically dire, wistful listen.

Title: Visions of Bodies Being Burned
Review: Visions of Bodies Being Burned, like its predecessor, is macabre and monstrous in all of the ways that your leering curiousity would have it. It’s a taut exploration of hatred and hostility, one which stands shoulder-to-shoulder with its demonic older brother.

Title: Cause And Effect
Review: Not a game-changing comeback by any means, Cause and Effect is instead a satisfying return to form that manages to gracefully age Keane by invigorating a familiar formula with wisdom and honesty learned over a dramatic, life-changing decade.

Title: Von
Review: It's a long, occasionally ponderous listen... but it's an impressive and rewarding journey that moves between prog, space-rock and subdural transmissions in ancient alien tongues.

Title: Salad Days
Review: The music never seems to come from a place of desire to convey something true or honest from within DeMarco, but instead it paints variations of past emotions, interpret others’ honesty, gives a distorted remembrance of the past for a more entertaining present.

Title: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground
Review: Spewing more words per inch than an IRS vault, the effect is like primal scream therapy set to incidental music. [Oct 2002, p.101]

Title: Killer Sounds
Review: Killer Sounds is certainly flawed, but has an awkward yet indefatigable charm.

Title: Out of View
Review: Theirs is a likably punked-up take on the noise blizzard thing. [Feb 2013, p.74]

Title: New Moon
Review: The Men almost casually demonstrate a mastery of song-based rock & roll that usually comes from decades of work.

Title: Sea When Absent
Review: This is one of those genre puzzles that are rewarding to anyone with an adventurous appetite, even if your bright eyes’ve never gazed anywhere but ahead.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: No Cities To Love stares down its troubles, power and joy ultimately lying in the hands of the people who can write such songs. [Feb 2015, p.86]

Title: Rainwater Cassette Exchange
Review: The remarkable thing is that, even on an EP of accessible pop songs, Deerhunter effortlessly retain that shape.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: It’s enough for the compositions on The Man Who Died in His Boat to exist on their own terms, and it’s fascinating to see how exact a piece of music Dead Deer became in between takes.

Title: Fate
Review: Ultimately, this is a winner and though it may not offer the new, revelatory sounds and styles that some were hoping, in the end it wins out because of its heart.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: What once was futuristic now sounds nostalgic -- or to borrow a title from another member from the class of 1995, "Brand New You're Retro" -- and that's the appeal of Not Your Kind of People, for better or worse.

Title: Oxymoron
Review: Given TDE’s ever-increasing appeal, Oxymoron isn’t quite an elite offering, but it meets the difficult task of attracting casual fans without straying too far from the formula that attracted ScHoolboy Q’s core audience.

Title: Disturbance
Review: In this time when dank edgelords across techno and industrial music are still flogging the dead SS cavalry charger of suspect aesthetics and prissy growling, it's refreshing to listen to a record where you've never a doubt that the sturm-und-drang is in aid of righteous causes. May the Test Dept cogs keep on grinding.

Title: Sculptor
Review: There’s always the risk that proclaiming one’s difference from all the narrow-minded plebs will come over as whiny and entitled. It’s a trap Luluc escape through their music, not defiant or raging, but hushed and wistful. Steve Hassett’s guitar sounds like a dandelion clock blowing away on the wind.

Title: Broken Ear Record
Review: Although the group's previous outings routinely got bogged down in forced experimentalism, Broken Ear Record at least keeps the pace sufficiently frantic, which allows us to excuse some (if not all) of its more self-indulgent moments.

Title: Teenager
Review: Teenager is an important album for The Thrills. It represents a step forward for a band that was looking like it had lost its luster. [Fall 2007, p.83]

Title: Made Up Mind
Review: While they may stretch out for improvisational flights in concert, Made Up Mind is concise and compelling.

Title: As You Were
Review: The swaggering beasts of Wall Of Glass and Bold kick it off and Greedy Soul waves a musical truncheon in your face as producers Greg Kurstin and Dan Grech- Marguerat find the jugular on songs powered by riffs, choruses, hooks and lashings of attitude to keep up with their swaggering frontman.

Title: A Distant Call
Review: The once nitty-gritty production that better helped listeners live in Sheer Mag's retro world has been tidied up. Having polished up so much that the line between self-awareness and cliché is stretched thin, it's hard to tell whether a concept has been burrowed or held hostage all together. In many ways, the charm is gone. Thankfully, a song like "Hardly to Blame," finds ways to make the best of less-than-ideal situations.

Title: Lions
Review: 'Lions' is widdle-smothered great-grandadrock shite that Hendrix could whack off in ten minutes today, despite being dead. Pumped full of funk-rawk formaldehyde to stop the choruses dropping off, it boasts all the originality of a cloned baked bean and about as many tunes as a tractor makes trying to get out of a ditch.

Title: The Soft Bulletin
Review: A vertiginous rainbow swirl that crams so many ideas into so many tight spaces that each track is like a perfectly rendered Joseph Cornell box.

Title: Thumbtacks and Glue
Review: It's the orchestral pop of Red Rover, Red Rover and the others that sweep the album along. [Apr 2013, p.113]

Title: NEVAEH
Review: Hope and intimacy can be relayed through lo-fi production that flirts with the grittiness of field recordings. Though in rare moments on Nevaeh, that style approaches detachment rather than transportation, as on the meandering, minimalist ballad “bbygurl.”

Title: This Is Happening
Review: Not only has the band wrapped up the themes of the record with impeachable, spotless playing and production, but the man at the center of it all hasn’t lost his penchant for writing quality tunes either, as nearly anything you blind-spot off This Is Happening will prove.

Title: Automata I
Review: Automata I cherry-picks from some of the best elements of previous Between the Buried and Me records, while injecting their masterful sense of musicianship and structure.

Title: SIGN
Review: A few of the album's tracks are somewhat formless and not distinctive enough to make a lasting impression, but overall, SIGN is one of the more approachable Autechre releases in quite some time, and an easier starting (or reentry) point for listeners who aren't committed enough to plunge into their headier works.

Title: Alone In The Universe
Review: This is your echt ELO in all its familiar state of sub-Beatlesy woe.... Whether his form of “properly” meets with your approval will, of course, depend on your capacity to perceive virtue in the familiar and the sentimentally melancholic (and in brevity: Alone in the Universe clocks in at roughly 35 minutes’ duration).

Title: Emmaar
Review: Remaining true to your identity while also evolving and keeping an audience that’s always a moving target interested in you is a tough gig. On Emmaar, Tinariwen are up to the task.

Title: Singularity
Review: There is a distinct symmetry to the album with the effectiveness of the more urgent first half benefitting from the more ambient, immersive second, on an album that begs to be heard as a unified whole.

Title: II Trill
Review: Unsurprisingly, the atmosphere is often weigted with doom, though there's an intoxicating impetus to the tar-like bass and woozy funk. [Aug 2008, p.140]

Title: Still on My Mind
Review: Still on My Mind is another rich outing for Dido in every way. At its peak, it provides awe-inspiring combinations of singer/songwriter radiance and novel sonic manipulations and juxtapositions; at its weakest, it's still innovative and diverse enough to appeal to specific audiences and maintain Dido and company's willingness to expand their palettes and take their listeners to different places.

Title: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy
Review: With his music and persona both marked by a flawed honesty, Kanye's man-myth dichotomy is at once modern and truly classic.

Title: See You In Magic
Review: If the herky-jerky new-waver 'Total Bloodbath,' and the 'Ticket to Ride'-styled charmer 'Partner in Crime' find Reis comfortably adapting to the pop approach, the mix can also leave Reis hanging out to dry, particularly on the smooth '70s-Stones strut 'You've Got Nerve,' where the droning qualities of his rasp are overemphasized by a chorus that simply repeats the title ad infinitum.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: [These albums] are as much of a pendulum swing from Is A Woman as Is A Woman was from Nixon. [combined review of both discs; Feb 2004, p.90]

Title: EUPHORIC /// HEARTBREAK \\\
Review: The band sounds ready for battle, but too much time is spent slogging through the swamps of defeat, many of which are adorned with forgettable choruses and melodies that arrive at dead ends, only to bash themselves against the wall hoping for some kind of merciful respite.

Title: Hymn to the Immortal Wind
Review: If Hymn to the Immortal Wind does anything, it establishes Mono’s place among post rock’s top dogs, and for this reviewer, easily gives them the title. Everyone else is just generic or something.

Title: Art Official Intelligence: Mosaic Thump
Review: The freshness that figured into De La's previous four albums feels a touch staler here. (#78, p.116)

Title: Wheel
Review: It’s Laura Stevenson’s third album, and the third that leaves you feeling warmly disposed but unconvinced, gamely professing your interest to see what she does next time around.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Time to Die is far from a bad album, but unpredictability still suits the Dodos better than trying to fit into a more recognizable indie rock mold.

Title: MeYouWeYou
Review: A striking, satisfying album that balances the boldness of a debut with the experience Rocketnumbernine has gained since You Reflect Me.

Title: Under and Under
Review: It's a fair guess that he has a workshop full of chorus, flange, and delay pedals from that era at his disposal, considering that every instrument and vocal line is run through one effect or another, making most of the album unintelligible or indecipherable, but it's just that limitless, everything-including-the-kitchen-sink way of working that makes Blank Dogs so special and interesting.

Title: Images du Futur
Review: Images Du Futur feels like a great movie without an ending.

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: They responded with Death Magnetic, the best Metallica album since "Metallica."

Title: Sun on the Square
Review: A set that sounds hauled up from another time and place. [Aug 2018, p.111]

Title: III
Review: A well-done lo-fi pop album lost of the things we’re used to: contexts and whatnot that make both us and the analytical process feel much easier, helping us pretend that we really know what’s going on and how to get behind the ideas.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: Manson can still whip up an appealingly vengeful turn of phrase, but they retain a tendency to sound stiff. [Jun 2012, p.73]

Title: Mediation of Ecstatic Energy
Review: Thought has clearly been put into the sequencing of Mediation of Ecstatic Energy.

Title: The Lovers
Review: A compelling record then all told, and one which should hopefully ensure Marshall has the benefit of a label suitor for his next release if there's any justice.

Title: Sonder
Review: Not so much leaping between time-signatures as entire time-zones, the gristly riffs and ambient metal meanderings of ‘Sonder’ strive for a kind of stoic, sombre enormity, but they clash badly with Tompkins’ often slick pop vocals.

Title: Black City
Review: It's another misfire with a handful of great moments that point to something better.

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: THS’s move toward a purer aping of classic rock is mostly welcome and largely successful; the fallout is the loss of the band’s snaky, blunt riffing, their wit dissipating into a pool of honest rocking.

Title: The Distance Is So Big
Review: While the best moments on The Distance Is So Big have hooks to spare, “Scienceless” and “Public Opinion Bath” could’ve used at least one. It’s just hard to maintain that kind of optimism over the course of a whole record.

Title: Arms Way
Review: Arm’s Way may be technically impressive but ultimately a bit of a boring downer.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: The album is harsher, darker, and just plain louder than Low have ever been in their 10-year career.

Title: Junto
Review: Basement Jaxx has an inclusive spirit that defines their approach to both making music and disseminating it, and that vibe defines Junto more than any single style or song.

Title: We Are Sent Here By History
Review: Hutchings has suggested his Ancestors work is an update of the griot tradition - weaving social commentary into seemingly harmless party pieces. We Are Sent Here By History achieves more: transforming impending doom into an affirmation of life. [Apr 2020, p.92]

Title: Beast Moans
Review: This is easily the biggest disappointment of 2006.

Title: Microclimate
Review: This is bedroom pop that transports you to strange vistas made by a brilliant loner in a frigid room.

Title: White Lilies Island
Review: The actual tunes may not be particularly strong, but crucially, at the centre of it all Natalie croons and sighs with all the clear-eyed moonfaced sweetness of Juliette Binoche baking cakes. [Dec 2001, p.116]

Title: Distant Relatives
Review: Few best-of-both-worlds collaborations work as well as Distant Relatives, which pairs Nas' incendiary rhymes with the keening hooks and global rhythms that Bob Marley's youngest son favors.

Title: Help Wanted Nights
Review: There's the unmistakable whiff of eternal under-achievement that pervades cute but forgettable ditties like 'Share Of Men' and 'Heartbroke.' [Oct 2007, p.98]

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: It remains an awfully good first effort, and the boys clearly have some exciting ideas - not enough to fill the entire disc, but exciting nonetheless.

Title: Pure Luxury
Review: A-grade pop songwriting. [Aug 2020, p.94]

Title: The Seventh Seal
Review: This album still falls way short of what it could be, and I have to wonder how this even happened.

Title: Unfinished Business
Review: Jackson sounds as vital as ever in front of her live band, and has crafted a definitive album in a storied career. [#92, p.54]

Title: Happy Hollow
Review: Intelligent indie-rockers, look nor listen no further for your possible album of the year.

Title: Riceboy Sleeps
Review: Riceboy Sleeps can keep you company in your cubicle or gridlock traffic.

Title: The People or the Gun
