Review: The band isn’t in the same lyrical league as others of similar political persuasions. What they do have is energy, which makes about half the album enjoyable, in spite of lyrics that would sound more appropriate coming from a high-school freshman.

Title: Blank Face LP
Review: It’s not easy to homogenize the opposing forces at play, but everything here feels like a genuine rumble through a mind scarred and inebriated by the reality of gang life and chasing the American dream while the room spins.

Title: Valende
Review: Most of Valende's songs have that creepy nursery-rhyme thing that people who read too much Lewis Carroll would call "whimsy." [Mar 2005, p.132]

Title: Coin Coin Chapter One: Gens De Couleur Libre
Review: In spite of the album's wilfully hard-to-stomach intensity, [it] will appeal to fans of art music of many different backgrounds.

Title: Animated Violence Mild
Review: If previous Blanck Mass albums were each a step out from the shadow of Fuck Buttons, Animated Violence Mild shows that he’s outgrown the comparison altogether.

Title: Hello Sadness
Review: Hello Sadness is their fourth straight great album.

Title: What Kind of World
Review: Largely devoid of lyrical texture and detail, the universe conjured by World often feels bland to a fault.

Title: The Runners Four
Review: In the end, however, the band's stamina outlasts our own. [11 Nov 2005, p.72]

Title: Nobody Wants to Be Here and Nobody Wants to Leave
Review: Whilst not perfect, Nobody Wants To Be Here And Nobody Wants To Leave is, as the cliché goes, a return to form and the album of a band that has rediscovered what they’re good at.

Title: For My Parents
Review: To those who care about the small differences, it's another tremendously strong album from a career already littered with them.

Title: 12 Desperate Straight Lines
Review: 12 Lines is enjoyable enough to be worth its existence without seeming rehashed and a solid improvement over his debut.

Title: A Productive Cough
Review: What’s interesting about A Productive Cough is how accessible it is compared with the band’s past work.

Title: Czarface Meets Metal Face
Review: While the group’s mutual wit and sense of lyrical structure could elevate the flattest of records, the kineticism and gleeful weirdness of their individual work is bafflingly absent. Czarface Meets Metal Face is polished but never makes good on the thrills promised by their teasing enterprise ‘Ka-Bang’ off Czarface’s 2015 record Every Hero Needs A Villain.

Title: Wind in the Wires
Review: Wind In The Wires just feels a bit more hesitant than Lycanthropy, and while there are some great tracks, it doesn't quite have the same energy that his debut did.

Title: Lonely Avenue
Review: Intelligent, funny, heartbreaking atl-rock, Hornby lyrics music and vocals by Folds. [Oct. 2010, p. 92]

Title: Rejoicing In The Hands
Review: Rejoicing in the Hands is a remarkable album, and Banhart displays a range and gift for melody that belies his twenty-three years.

Title: Render Another Ugly Method
Review: All told, Render Another Ugly Method is a transitory step for Mothers, one that’s equally messy and compelling, showing that Leschper’s voice as a songwriter and singer remains her own, no matter how many effects she puts on top of it.

Title: Gargoyle
Review: His irrepressible, grizzled vocal is the master key to the soul that is often kept hidden behind the pewter façade, and it’s the desire for more glimpses into it is what makes Gargoyle as affecting as it is.

Title: The Astonishing
Review: An epic adventure that is, in every single way, truly astonishing indeed. [16 Jan 2016, p.51]

Title: Eyes on the Lines
Review: It’s not always the most memorable listen, though through its free-flowing divagations we finally begin to feel more empathy for an artist who’s too perceptive to hide behind his taut guitar accents.

Title: Old Fears
Review: Old Fears makes for a fascinating record, evolving gradually from start to finish and yet doing so in a way subtle enough so as to never jar nor stand out.

Title: Complete Strangers
Review: Cabic is most effective when he's closer to home. [Sep 2015, p.117]

Title: Unreal
Review: As Blumberg puts on his Neil Young hat and laments "I've got some things to do/Some private things to do" on closer "The Plan," one can't help but think that, although perhaps overly self-indulgent at times, Hebronix could well prove fruitful.

Title: Handcream for a Generation
Review: Cornershop have clearly been biding their time, not squandering it, returning with the kind of meaty, substantial, truly multi-dimensional project they've long been working towards.

There are enough hooks in this bouquet of confusing-if-passable genre-hopping tracks to keep him on the path to future hits, but nothing comes remotely close to the lightning in a bottle of "Old Town Road"'s accidental perfection.

Title: Shine On
Review: On "Surrender and Certainty" and "Song for My Father," which is surprisingly less saccharine than you might expect, it at least starts to feel like she's evolving as an artist. But those moments are few and far between on an album that feels longer than it is, which, I guess, is a desirable quality for what is basically glorified background music.

Title: Downtown Church
Review: Griffin could have skated on the success of her last effort, but Downtown Church is a gutsy move, one that's as haunting and original as anything in her past.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: Time, life, death, religion, New York City, and New York money are big topics to tackle in a 45 minute pop album, and Modern Vampires doesn’t even attempt answers to the questions it raises. Instead, it’s content to expound upon the Vampire Weekend aesthetic in inventive, imaginative, and undeniably successful ways.

Title: Different Gear, Still Speeding
Review: When it comes to carrying the torch for an earlier generation's idea of rock 'n' roll perfection, no one means as much business as Liam Gallagher.

Title: Barking
Review: The duo have remained one of the few constants in UK dance music. [Oct 2010, p.120]

Title: What a Terrible World, What a Beautiful World
Review: What A Terrible World continues to sharpen the band's sound. [Feb 2015, p.81]

Title: Veckatimest
Review: Even as they feature orchestras, women's choirs, and Beach House singer Victoria Legrand on Veckatimest, the album is still an intimate, ascetic affair.

Title: These Were The Earlies
Review: Imagin[e] the Beach Boys getting strung out in a field on cider midmorning in some alternative universe Texas, surrounded by retro-sounding DIY synths, a raggedy brass section, and a hippy cello player.

Title: Villains
Review: It's both organic and future-facing. A true metamorphosis, this album sees Queens Of The Stone Age shedding an old identity to discover new ways of playing the same song. [Sep 2017, p.84]

Title: Policy
Review: Although the sometimes scattergun approach to genre-hopping has its drawbacks, what’s great about Policy is the future possibilities it allows Will Butler.

Title: Crows
Review: If Crows was the first album from a new artist, it would certainly be hailed as the debut of a powerful new voice, and the fact that it comes from someone who has already been making fine music in notably different styles makes the accomplishment all the more impressive.

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: It's about as close a facsimile of the fractured and foreboding scattershot thoughts that haunt most of us at night as one can capture on record. [Feb 2008, p.115]

Title: Delta
Review: Though “experimental” may be a bit of an overstatement, the best parts of Delta prove that, in the hands of the right producer, Mumford & Sons remain capable of recording radio-ready earworms that challenge expectations (a little, at least) while still retaining the major qualities that made them superstars in the first place.

Title: boygenius EP
Review: For anyone still struggling to tell any woman with a guitar apart, the deft collaboration and complex collective songwriting on the boygenius EP is a great place to learn.

Title: Lala Belu
Review: Any fears his propulsive energy may have waned in exiles are quickly dispelled. [Mar 2018, p.111

Title: Saturdays = Youth
Review: Saturdays=Youth meaningfully diversifies M83's catalog while retaining Gonzalez's indelible fingerprint.

Title: In a Dream
Review: Things work best when the musical surroundings match their respective vocal style and they create something resembling the cinematic edge of Johnny Jewel's Chromatics. [Oct 2014, p.93]

Title: Pull Up Some Dust and Sit Down
Review: From the title's Depression-era jokes onwards, Cooder protests like it's 1939. [Oct 2011, p.96]

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: Twin Fantasy marks another leap in ambition. [Mar 2018, p.22]

Title: Modern Nature
Review: Modern Nature is a significant step forward for a band dogged by being seen merely as Britpop survivors that have never really moved on. This is evidence that they truly, distinctively have.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: Given that Morning Phase reveals similarly raw honesty and engrossing emotion [as Sea Change]--plus bears the mark of superior penmanship gained by a decade’s more patience and wisdom, the album is poised to be revered as one of Beck’s most potent collections.

Title: In a Poem Unlimited
Review: These tracks embody the heartache arising from Remy struggling with her place, and the place of her sisters, in the world of male power and dominance. [Mar 2018, p.57]

Title: Lonesome Dreams
Review: If the music grew much gauzier, it would cloy. But for most of the album, Lord Huron stays poised precisely at the edge of weightlessness.

Title: Jinx
Review: The record hits you in the spaces you didn’t realize were blank, like that moment that is the sliver between thought and expression.

Title: Strange Desire
Review: You’re unlikely to hear a more earnest album than Bleachers' Strange Desire this year, nor are you apt to find a release more faithful to the spirit and sound of Top 40 radio in the late, great ’80s.

Title: Destroyer's Rubies
Review: Destroyer’s Rubies is one of those rare albums whose literary value is so compelling as to make any imperfections simply blend in as an essential part of the storyline.

Title: HYMNS
Review: Hymns finds a fully-in-control Okereke, still tangled in the electronics of his solo albums (“Rock’n’roll has got so old, just give me neo-soul,” he admits on ‘Into The Earth’) fusing with Russell Lissack’s spectral shoegaze guitars to steer one of the century’s most pioneering underground bands into more mature and absorbing, if murkier, waters.

Title: Yoko
Review: Yoko isn't exactly what fans of the first three albums might be expecting, but it's still a Beulah album. [#5, p.99]

Title: Scurrilous
Review: While they're not without their spark and charm in places, PTH still frustrates as a band who struggle under the weight of their own ideas. [2 Apr 2011, p.52]

Title: Wayward Fire
Review: Pop music styles change faster than they wear out, and Mohager convincingly makes the case that there is more to say in the music of the '80s, even if fashion has banished it to its own radio formats and nostalgia tours.

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: Sometimes the pair slips into an uncomplicated groove, and the results transcend the duo's deep, signature whimsy to lift Gnarls Barkley into the realm of classic.

Title: Liars
Review: Each track bears the sound of a confident, secure band of artists who now know they are ready for prime-time, and can weather the onslaught of attention without compromise.

Title: The Illusion of Progress
Review: The title of Staind's sixth album is a bit of a misnomer, but there are a few new stylistic directions here.

Title: Brothers
Review: Yep, there's plenty of life here, but interest wavers when howling barroom guitar-note after howling barroom guitar-note wafts to the back of your brain.

Title: I Had A Dream That You Were Mine
Review: The one-man band that is Rostam Batmanglij enjoys co-billing status here as the pair deliver a follow-up that goes bigger and better in the way that a worthy sequel should.

Title: Becoming a Jackal
Review: Meticulous but only rarely precious, it's an album distantly haunted by Phil Spector's Wall of Sound, a luminous mesh of acoustic and electric guitars, bass, piano and organ, with airlessly thudding drums.

Title: Two
Review: It is an incredibly unique performance that builds upon the collective legacy of its members not by pushing them to their extremes, but by uniting them back to a rooted sonic aesthetic that all too often gets buried when they are apart.

Title: No Home Record
Review: It finds Gordon arriving as a solo artist, nearly 40 years after Sonic Youth released its first recordings, with one of the most challenging and intriguing albums of the year.

Title: Dreams Come True
Review: Dreams Come True was never going to reach the near untouchable height of his canon, but you'd be hard pressed to map out a better first attempt to break free from that diamond-encrusted leash.

Title: Wilder Mind
Review: The new instrumentation affords a more nuanced approach, from the thrumming bass, piano, tom-toms and subtly tingling guitar evoking the resolute support of “Broad-Shouldered Beasts”, and the keening, spacious synth textures of “Tompkins Square Park”, to the unison guitar thrash that opens “The Wolf.”

Title: Spend the Night
Review: It's full-on, one-dimensional and perfect. It ain't clever, but it could be very big.

Title: The Sermon on Exposition Boulevard
Review: You want back-to-basics? This is it.

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: It’s huge fun and sounds just as big.

Title: Easter Is Cancelled
Review: Easter Is Cancelled is a soaring and melodic evolution for The Darkness, a fresh step into maturation that retains their campy, fun-loving spirit without all the sleaze and filth.

Title: An Awesome Wave
Review: Alt-J's bizarre pop is ultimately rooted solidly in pathos, in a sort of blighted redemption. They favor cacophony for its ability to offset silence, enjoy spiraling out of control for its appreciation of the meticulous.

Title: Black Up
Review: Shabazz Palaces created an album that is deep, dense, cryptic, hypnotic, and beautiful in its own freaky way.

Title: The Understanding
Review: Certain artists’ albums sound like they’re effortless because they’re actually lacking in effort, but Röyksopp’s albums sound effortless because these guys are just that good at turning out great downtempo tunes.

Title: Parastrophics
Review: Mouse On Mars are returning in triumphant and rapturous fashion, both sealing their reputation as relentless innovators while basking in the glory as beacons of inspiration.

Title: Peace
Review: It's at its best on Drive, where throbbing bass and a giant chorus dominate, but then Peace slides--albeit stylishly--into a repetitive blur. [Oct 2013, p.102]

Title: Ambivalence Avenue
Review: Yes, Ambivalence Avenue is an album that defies expectations, and it is also Bibio’s most creative and penetrating release yet.

Title: The Lone Bellow
Review: This is a solid debut, made by a band that arrives fully formed and has a great future.

Title: Held In Splendor
Review: What would be even more effective is more focus on spanning dynamics and intensity, which can come naturally when shooting for something a bit more personal, but that doesn’t negate Splendor as a successful sophomore step.

Title: Babel
Review: Babel bowls along with the ebullient energy one expects of Mumford & Sons, like a cider-soused hoedown at an after-hours lock-in. But while this works to the advantage of their more rousing sentiments, it tends to iron out the subtler creases in some of the songs.

Title: Wanderlust
Review: The tremulous piano ballad “Young Blood” is far from the dance fodder singles of Ellis-Bextor’s past, while the sombre tone of tracks like “Until the Stars Collide” suggests that she’s re-positioning herself in the prim Nordic-diva territory of Agnes Obel and Ane Brun. A good move.

Title: Forever Sounds
Review: Forever Sounds (Shake It/Damnably) is a kaleidoscopic, sonic soundscape, engagingly recorded at John Curley’s (Afghan Whigs) facility, Ultrasuede Studios.

Title: High Society
Review: Though they may be more focused, Enon will never be straightforward, but that's one of the band's, and album's, strengths.

Title: Tempest
Review: Most of it is an inspired mix of blood and bawdiness.

Title: Uncanney Valley
Review: It’s fun, but not the comeback it could have been.

Title: Astronaut Meets Appleman
Review: The songs swing from cosmic and ethereal to mischievously earthy.

Title: Heaven To A Tortured Mind
Review: On Heaven To A Tortured Mind, Tumor harnesses his relentless curiosity to test the boundaries of rock and noise – and reinvents what we expect from both in the process.

Title: I Will Be
Review: It's a neat homage to '60s girl groups and C86 bands they inspired, spooked-out bubblegum delivered in singer Dee Dee's naive but infectious sing-song. [Jun 2010, p.98]

Title: Rock and Roll Night Club
Review: The cheeky nature of Rock and Roll Night Club inadvertently elevates its reputation--falling somewhere between classic pop and performance art, DeMarco's talent for writing hooks should spurn any attempt to call it novelty.

Title: Laws of Illusion
Review: Laws of Illusion is certainly not as arresting or as bold as some of the early highlights of her career.

Title: Physical
Review: Not everything here is riveting: Gurnsey’s narrative arc is a little underdeveloped.

Title: One Second of Love
Review: She's found a strong, vibrato-less voice that's confident but imperfect in funny ways.

Title: These Four Walls
Review: These Four Walls is like a 50-minute, 11-song tour through the Scottish scene’s past, present, and future, emphasizing how much of the country’s best pop music has been concerned with transporting listeners to specific places, so we can all linger there together.

Title: Meaning of Life
Review: Meaning of Life has few weak links, unfolding instead as an album-long emancipation for one of our best female vocalists, released from pesky contractual obligations and channeling her delight at that newfound freedom into songs that, while signaling a new stage in her career, appear to flow directly from both heart and soul.

Title: Always Strive and Prosper
Review: Always Strive and Prosper is arena rap in jet-set dance-pop drag, and while A$AP Ferg’s talent occasionally flickers when it’s directed in the wrong places, it shines brightest when he’s just being himself.

Title: We'll Be The Moon
Review: We'll Be the Moon doesn't always hit the mark, but it's an encouraging first offering proving that Fixers can walk the walk as well as they talk the talk.

Title: Swim
Review: Despite his chameleonic tendencies, Dan Snaith retains his singular identity as an artist--and Swim is a reminder that even at his most challenging, the man's compositional capabilities can dazzle.

Title: Sing in a World That's Falling Apart
Review: Despite the sense of chaos, there’s a level of sophistication and poise on show throughout. This record showcases Black Lips in a songwriting prime.

Title: 14 Shades of Grey
Review: Like a crisp Xerox of the band's multiplatinum Break the Cycle, with everything sounding bigger, brighter and tighter.

Title: Medulla
Review: Medulla may divide Björk's audience, but, combining intellectual rigour and sensual ravishment, it is brave and unique.

Title: The Balladeer
Review: The Balladeer will only help cement her reputation as one of America's finest musical artists.

Title: Bye Bye 17
Review: Tillman’s silken, Otis Redding–reminiscent vocals anchor funky, horn-driven R & B beats that match the swagger of Motown.

Artist: Conor Oberst and the Mystic Valley Band
Title: Outer South
Review: In short, arguably for the first time, Oberst gives us an album rife with liveliness--and it sounds like he had a damn good time making it.

Title: Never Will
Review: McBryde’s second major-label release, Never Will, is just as daring and deep, sometimes deceptively so [as Girl Going Nowhere].

Title: Relax
Review: On Relax, Das Racist, at worst, deliver an album that tries too hard to sound like every other rap album out there.

Title: Strange Weekend
Review: Sonically the songs are strong.

Title: Testify
Review: With nothing to react against and few new ideas to air, P.O.D. mostly operates in default mode, relying on hitmaker-for-hire Glen Ballard to inject the music with new life. Sadly, he doesn't.

Title: Amputechture
Review: You'd think these guys would've overheated by now, but they still love channeling chaos into one long river of song. [15 Sep 2006, p.77]

Title: Where You Stand
Review: Not everything is quite so Travis by-the-numbers--and with mixed results. [Sep 2013, p.88]

Title: Drastic Fantastic
Review: The Scottish singer builds on the promise of her first album with Drastic Fantastic.

Title: Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts
Review: The whole much greater than its parts, Dead Cities is creation imbued and then muted again.

Title: FR32
Review: The limp, autotuned love song “Happy” and drearily positivist “Good Morning” are lazy nods to the mainstream, but elsewhere Wretch is better served by the dark sparkle of arrangements featuring grimy sub-bass synths and itchy electro beats tinted with eerie vocal samples, thumb-piano and synthetic pan-pipes.

Title: The Blackest Beautiful
Review: Songs on Fake History sometimes sounded like they were simply vehicles for Butler’s frenetic performances instead of complete songs. That isn’t the case here, which means that most of these songs aren’t as immediate, but lack of immediacy is generally a good indicator of an album’s longevity, especially in post-hardcore.

Title: Songs of Love and Horror
Review: Offering more than mere updates of classics, Songs of Love and Horror also showcases the depth of Oldham’s catalog through obscure tracks like the slow, haunted “Most People” and the previously unreleased “Party With Marty (Abstract Blues).”

Title: Matangi
Review: Matangi again establishes M.I.A. as one of the most fascinating figures in modern music, but the personal voice underlying her material remains aggravatingly half-baked.

Title: The Eraser
Review: What makes The Eraser great is Yorke's singing. [Aug 2006, p.82]

Title: And Nothing Hurt
Review: More than any previous Spiritualized album, however, And Nothing Hurt feels like a mere set of songs, an accessible group of tunes that may be painstakingly constructed but are only casually connected.

Title: Drone Logic
Review: A nicely well-rounded debut album from an artist who's only been releasing music for a couple of years.

Title: Evolve Or Be Extinct
Review: [An album] that's up there with its maverick creator's best.[Feb. 2012 p. 105]

Title: Golden
Review: The mulch-platinum country trio's fourth LP is a refreshing return to form after the dull post-"Need You Now" phase of their career. [10 May 2013, p.67]

Title: Nothing
Review: Nothing finds beauty in exploring dreams of a human-free world. Kode9's strength has always been to show that serious scholarship and avant-garde instinct don't need to separate from dancefloor culture and here, he's made one of his clearest statements of that yet.

Title: The Drawing Board
Review: Not surprisingly, Art Department are at their lachrymose best not when trying to uncover house's absences, but when redrawing ever more finely what was always already there.

Title: Wolfroy Goes to Town
Review: Its biggest problem is that, from start of finish, it feels strangely reserved.

Title: Further Complications
Review: This is a record that's more intriguing than entertaining. Cocker's warmth and wit are in short supply, as is the sweeter side of his melodic gifts.

Title: The Fame Monster
Review: Only after being overwhelmed by the sheer visibility of her warp-speed relaunch did I realize how enjoyable and inescapable her hooks and snatches had turned out to be.

Title: Tromatic Reflexxions
Review: Tromatic Reflexxions sometimes seems to work like a Fall album, wearing you down with its relentless energy.

Title: The Miraculous
Review: As a composer, singer, and sound sculptor, Hausswolff is in full control on The Miraculous, balancing harshness and intimacy, heaviness and airy melancholy. It's an uncompromising view, but it's also welcoming.

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: Wonderful Glorious alternates between distorted rock and freewheeling country-pop interludes.

Title: Re-Mit
Review: Not wonderful, but certainly frightening. [Jul 2013, p.75]

Title: Red River Blue
Review: Red River Blue, alongside recent efforts by Blake's summer tour-mate Brad Paisley and wife Miranda Lambert, pretty much defines mainstream country these days – high-quality songs, great singing and musicianship, big production, and the same time-honored, predictable six or seven themes that we've all heard before.

Title: Afterparty Babies
Review: Over and over, we get the sense that Cadence makes records for that gaggle of kids on the album cover, for the look on their faces. If any of the rest of us likes it, all the better. It works: We’d like to know more about Mr. Weapon, and his buds.

Title: Pickin' Up The Pieces
Review: For Fitz and Co, few if any post-60s developments in black dance music are acknowledged. Still, when it's good and exciting, as on the standout Don't Gotta Work It Out, with its simply thrilling keyboard coda, considerations of originality become irrelevant.

Title: 9 Dead Alive
Review: Almost every track on this fifth LP is thematically inspired by a historical figure, which intrudes in the spoken passages of Sunday Neurosis, but otherwise inspires some of their most exciting music to date. [Jun 2014, p.119]

Title: Scramblers
Review: For Schofield, the word scrambler symbolises both a sort of opiate and a happy place from childhood, so the music highlights this dichotomy by fusing danger and warmth into an irresistible oxymoron. A sensation of the world ending while we carry on dancing. [Apr 2020, p.51]

Title: Harps and Angels
Review: It's his signature sound and Harps and Angels captures it sublimely, as the production--a co-credit to Newman's longtime associate Lenny Waronker and his latter-day producer Mitchell Froom--has no fancy accoutrements and he's written another set of quietly wonderful songs.

Title: Everybody Looking
Review: As it is, Everybody Looking feels like a slight step up from Gucci’s prison mixtapes, but not the major step that a Free Gucci statement album might warrant.

Title: Insula
Review: He tears apart square wave synths into sharp, staccato blocks and spreads them across Insula, twisting alien 8-bit into different melodies and frequencies. [Jul 2018, p.60]

Title: Olympic Girls
Review: A worthy, if more subdued, companion to Kacey Johansing's The Hiding last year. [Mar 2018, p.37]

Title: Oceania
Review: [Oceania] is a good stand-alone record, a bong-prog take on the alt-rock grandeur of Gish and Siamese Dream.

Title: Wilder Mind
Review: With new tools, they’ve taken liftoff from a proven formula when they really didn’t have to.

Title: Pushing the Senses
Review: I have to accept that the band I once loved is now nothing more than a distant memory. Songs such as 'Tangerine' and 'Crash' have long been replaced by the new sound which owes much more to Keane and Coldplay in their melancholic approach.

Title: Life, Death, Love and Freedom
Review: Blunt and stubbornly engaging, it may be Mellencamp’s most candid effort in years.

Title: Reservoir
Review: The air of melancholy on display throughout is as enticing as Beirut's. Impressive. [Nov 2009, p.94]

Title: Carry On The Grudge
Review: Shame he's keeping a twice-a-decade pace, but this album should stick to the bones for twice that long, likely longer.

Title: New Album
Review: New Album is the culmination of the band's ongoing experimentation that catapults its ferocious sound headlong into new territory.

Title: A Chorus of Storytellers
Review: The new ambition found on "A Chorus of Storytellers" has led the Album Leaf to its best execution yet.

Title: Animal Ambition: An Untamed Desire to Win
Review: The album is a welcomed return for 50, who sounds like his hiatus didn’t affect his ability to create his signature street records.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: His songs may reference antiquities like Ernest Hemingway, but the drum programmes, autotuned vocals and synth sequences are more modern than the usual country-rock favoured by septuagenarian troubadours.

Title: O Shudder
Review: Though the busy, Reichian loops help decorate the retro palette, it's the sort of intricacy that can encase art-pop in bulletproof glass, demanding admiration without meeting us halfway. At its best, though, O Shudder's timeworn skill is to combat looming adversity with verve and rhythm, emptying the mind through the body.

Title: The Sun Dogs
Review: This feeling of something ancient is instilled in The Sun Dogs, which possesses a strangely hard-to-pin-down sense of mysterious nostalgia, demonstrating that the creation of original music has not yet become a foolish ambition.

Title: Wyatt At The Coyote Palace
Review: This music reminds you how alone you are; it consoles you through its insolubility, comforts you by jabbing you in the chest and letting you know how complex the struggle is, how inaccessible we are to each other but just how universal our pain can be. [Dec 2016, p.63]

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: Pecknold and guitarist Skyler Skjelset have been writing teenage symphonies to God since they were actual teenagers, and that transcendent love of music shines through in their own songs.

Title: Jungle
Review: Combining the pop world’s two biggest current loves--forward-thinking dance music and throwback soul/funk--Jungle are ticking every box on the ‘perfect debut’ checklist, and they’re doing it with pizazz.

Title: Man of the Woods
Review: Conceptually muddled, qualitatively uneven fifth full-length.

Title: Down in Albion
Review: There is something dispiriting about trawling through so many songs which show glimpses of lucidity, even brilliance, but always seem to either nod off or descend into chaos by the end. [Jan 2006, p.120]

Title: Sound-Dust
Review: A major rebirth, relegating the chirpy melodies to expedients, relying less on Sadier's monotone singing, and reaching for new formats within the group's formidable compositional skills.

Title: Time of Dust
Review: A dusky delight.

Title: Caracal
Review: Ultimately, Caracal just doesn’t feel much fun, and even its highs are nowhere near Settle’s polished bliss.

Title: OLD
Review: With all these styles packed in tight, Old ends up being a maybe-inadvertent career retrospective for Mr. Brown, echoing his speedy and jagged evolution over the past few years.

Title: Ask the Dust
Review: This is ambitious electronic music rewarding persistence.

Title: Nothing Hurts
Review: The album coasts through 13 songs in just 29 minutes, making for a seemingly perfect setlist of distorted, high-energy punk.

Title: Stars Are The Light
Review: Stars Are the Light is a decent album that shows Moon Duo know how to put a new spin on an old formula. And while it may not make a big splash, the ripple effects can be pleasing.

Title: Getaway
Review: New Zealand supergroup the Clean once again makes a case that the world's most intriguing pop music comes from that small, faraway land.

Title: Requiem
Review: Needing to prove nothing, Goat have created one of the most definitive musical statements of 2016.

Title: Moment Bends
Review: My problem is that AIH don't really give much away. There isn't any real personality on show. It could be any musicians.

Title: If Anything
Review: One of the best albums of the year so far.

Title: The Third Hand
Review: Some sleepy stuff hurts his cause, but his best songs... combine vivid, polished tracks with solid tunes that pack a sneaky emotional weight.

Title: The Greatest
Review: You'll need to listen closely to understand and appreciate, but Marshall is worth it.

Title: No Elephants
Review: More a series of half-drawn soundscapes than actual songs per se, No Elephants comes across as an exercise in the abstract, in which the artist makes almost no attempt to color inside the outlines.

Title: You're Dreaming
Review: Don’t slot these guys into an Everly Brothers pigeonhole because not only is no one else releasing music like this, but the refined songwriting and flawless performances push these tunes into near classic territory.

Title: Flight of the Conchords
Review: Many songs play out like shared "private" jokes but succeed all the time. [Spring 2008, p.75]

Title: Maybe Today, Maybe Tomorrow
Review: The Essex four-piece rarely put a foot wrong. [1 Sep 2012, p.50]

Title: Blood Bitch
Review: Despite controversial lyrics, unconventional song structures, and a lofty concept, Blood Bitch somehow fits like a defiant glove against all the odds.

Title: Robotique Majestique
Review: The local duo has struggled to top its electroclash charades. Their solution? Lasers. On Ghostland's third self-produced LP, Robotique Majestique, mastered at the Exchange in London by Nilesh Patel (Daft Punk, Justice), that strategy largely translates into massive, Technicolor electronic interludes delving deep into Depeche Mode.

Title: We Disappear
Review: We Disappear is the brashest, most mainstream-sounding alt-rock record The Thermals have pulled off to date. It rarely pauses in its pursuit of hook-laced, punk-pop anthems such as The Walls and the bittersweet Thinking Of You, but it sounds especially jubilant on the best of its Grim Reaper-related numbers, Hey You.

Title: Tip of the Sphere
Review: In the face of so much uncertainty, it’s tempting to think that armageddon is the only answer. Whilst not standing toe-to-toe with the very best of McComb’s discography, Tip of the Sphere is as good a soundtrack to The End Times as anything he’s done.

Title: Severant
Review: More melancholic than mechanical, Severant is a testament to the strength of the human imagination.

Title: Brightly Painted One
Review: If the acoustic backdrop sometime slacks texture, there are no such qualms with the songwriting that demonstrates a novelist's eye for detail. [Jun 2014, p.83]

Title: Para Mi
Review: There are some lovely songs on Para Mi, though; you might just have to slog through some unfortunate synths and occasionally cringe-inducing lyrics to get there.

Title: Individ
Review: Altogether, the material is mature, technically proficient as ever, lively, and sounds rough and real; it’s hard to imagine Individ won’t be a hit with fans, intermittent or long-standing.

Title: Heartworms
Review: Heartworms is a slow-burning grower that rewards repeat listens but requires some commitment to love. [No. 142, p.58]

Title: Hairball
Review: He’s throwing his bleeding heart into the technicolor to make sense of it all. The kinetic energy between him and Currie makes this all palpable.

Title: Gimme Some
Review: They seem to have stopped trying to subvert their pop nous and accept what they do best, and for the most part it works a treat.

Title: The Stoned Immaculate
Review: "The Stoned Immaculate" is a perfect 2012 example of what I call hip-hop's Marijuana Mood Music era. Beautiful production through [sic] results in a gentle buzz, a mellow aural high that's relaxing and refreshing.

Title: The Reminder
Review: Though jangly uptempo ditties are nothing new for the Canadian singer-songwriter, it's these kinds of songs, seemingly constructed for radio play, that mar the otherwise radiant Reminder.

Title: Ego War
Review: Over 13 tracks, not one a filler, they mix everything from punk to electro, house and disco, and end up like a delirious collision of the Specials and Basement Jaxx.

Title: Escondida
Review: Starbucks should replace Norah Jones with Holland as its mood musician of choice; her compositional brew is smooth, with jolts of witty malice.

Title: Mind the Drift
Review: This (slightly) new direction is a fitting complement for the smart-assed menace that made the band such fun in the first place.

Title: Yeezus
Review: Each fluorescent strike of noise, incongruous tempo flip, and warped vocal is bolted into its right place across the record's fast 40 minutes.

Title: Reality Check
Review: Reality Check stands as a fun, frank and startlingly perceptive debut that surprises for all the right reasons.

Title: Sunbather
Review: It's not for the light-hearted, but Deafheaven have delivered a deranged, damaged, majestic treat here. [8 Jun 2013, p.54]

Title: No One Dances Quite Like My Brothers
Review: Vår manage to save a plodding midsection with tracks like the creepy, droney and dark Boy, proving they’re jacks of multiple trades.

Title: Fragments of Freedom
Review: The disc flirts with dozens of styles, with so much diversity from track to track that the album never quite builds up artistic momentum. But several moments are more than worthy of the band's legacy.

Title: In a Poem Unlimited
Review: Groovy and scintillating, but with depth and meaning to spare, In a Poem Unlimited is U.S. Girls--and pop music--at its very best.

Title: An End Has a Start
Review: It appears they have emulated themselves on their sophomore (and sophomoric sounding) effort.

Title: Good Bad Not Evil
Review: Other than the crowd noise, you’d have a tough time distinguishing the two albums. This is a good thing, as applying studio sheen to the Black Lips’ primitive mix of acid-damaged psychedelia and beer-fueled garage rock would be akin to putting lipstick on an orangutan.

Title: The Fine Art of Hanging On
Review: The Fine Art of Hanging On is another capably written set, but turns its back on the band’s pared-down folk roots in favour of baroque-pop arrangements that reach for the heights of Rufus Wainwright and Illinoise-era Sufjan Stevens, but don’t always hit the mark.

Title: Kingdom Come
Review: Kingdom Come is exactly the kind of rote product Jay-Z seemed to want to avoid when he "retired": It's a victory lap without a victory, a rare instance of a rap superstar blowing his own horn and yet sounding half-hearted about it.

Title: This Is... Icona Pop
Review: It has ten passable tracks and one certified super-smash that will either get listeners gleefully singing-along or reaching for the skip button. You decide.

Title: Harlan County
Review: It's a shame that he didn't become more well known, because the album is 10 songs of top-notch songwriting that never falters. [Jul 2011, p.90]

Title: Everybody's Got It Easy But Me
Review: Everybody's Got It Easy But Me answers Finberg's ever-withering worldview with playful, rambunctious performances, enhancing the I-just-wasn't-made-for-these-times pathos of his lyrics by essentially making him sound like an outcast within his own songs.

Title: Rapprocher
Review: It's a hit and miss affair.

Title: GO:OD AM
Review: Singles sales shouldn’t matter much to him now, because with GO:OD AM, he’s accomplished the dense, complex work that plays out with remarkable clarity.

Title: Till Midnight
Review: It's his best album in years. [No. 108, p.59]

Title: Young for Eternity
Review: Crackles with the cocky, hormonal exuberance of youth: it's a profoundly teenage album. [Aug 2005, p.126]

Title: Threes
Review: The newest incarnation of Sparta has that “trying too hard” sound to it, a sound that’s careful and measured, a sound that sounds just a little too bound to the studio for a rock band.

Title: Coles Corner
Review: Stylistically patchy but a sincere and winning catalog of his songwriting and vocal repertoire. [#10, p.106]

Title: The Ragpicker's Dream
Review: A decent album of roots-tinged songs that showcases his terse guitar style and detached vocals to solid if unspectacular effect. [Nov 2002, p.122]

Title: National Ransom
Review: Elvis Costello traffics in so many genres, it must be hard to focus on one. Here, he doesn't.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: The best thing about Garden Ruin is the way they look beyond country borders to engage with the wider world, both culturally and musically.

Title: Serfs Up!
Review: The truth is finally out. People are talking about the music. People are dancing. People know Fat White Family are better than maybe Fat White Family themselves think they are.

Title: Multi-Love
Review: By deconstructing traditional geometries of desire, they’ve made their most fully realized album yet.

Title: White Hot Moon
Review: Never mind that they still haven’t quite figured out the right formula; for all of their renewed gumption, improved production, and flair with the pen, Pity Sex remain limited by their narrow emotional range and over-reliance on their influences.

Title: Babelsberg
Review: The further you get into the album, the more you realise how integral the orchestral arrangements are.

Title: Baby Darling Doll Face Honey
Review: of the songs on Baby Darling Doll Face Honey have forgettable lyrics, bland, fuzz-wah guitar noodling, and an overwhelming sense of melodrama.

Title: End of Suffering
Review: Frank Carter used to be a stick of dynamite. Then a stick of dynamite with a longer fuse. Now his music is much more akin to a firework display. Long may he ignite the sky.

Title: The Mindsweep
Review: It's hard not to proclaim it as the best album of Enter Shikari's already impressive career. Yes, it's that good. [Feb 2015, p.89]

Title: All My Demons Greeting Me as a Friend
Review: While All My DemonS is a listen that’s at times varied, interesting and progressive, any connections made here are purely at surface level.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: Although the album is punctuated by spoken-word interludes--bits of poetry, self-help, comedy and tribute--it is designed to flow as a whole, gradually infusing a room like incense or the smells of home cooking. ... And Solange’s voice is sure-footed and playful, confident that the music will follow her every whim. ... Outside a few prominent guest raps, Solange and her musicians slip the collaborators into the background. This is her space, her sanctuary.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: Combines guitar-driven, slightly Weezer-esque songs with the odd moment of touching musical beauty. [#17, p.133]

Title: Worship
Review: A Place To Bury Strangers succeeds in one aspect: It produces music so hammering and explosively airy that it crumbles the very walls used to create such an echoed and amplified sound. It just fails to recognize that in doing so for almost 45-minutes straight, we begin to feel like we're getting buried alive under the rubble.

Title: The Trouble with Being Myself
Review: To call Macy Gray's new album, The Trouble With Being Myself, delightful is to minimize its sensual intelligence and considerable emotional depth.

Title: Hot Hot Heat
Review: At its best, Hot Hot Heat is a reminder of what’s made these guys consistently good and periodically great.

Title: Future Women
Review: All this ambitioin coagulates into an irresistible, tumbling, tune-filled whole. [Dec 2006, p.118]

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: It's not a bad album as much, but to anyone familiar with Lynch's other work, it's entirely predictable in sound and style.

Title: Era Vulgaris
Review: There has always been a slightly tricksy, proggy side to Queens of the Stone Age, but here the more episodic songs such as Run Pig Run lurch distractingly rather than flow. The result is more of a trudge than Queens of the Stone Age albums are supposed to be, not helped by the fact that Homme seems to have mislaid his lyrical wit.

Title: Here With Me
Review: There is not much on Here With Me that surprises or overwhelms, but that is not Jennifer O’Connor’s brief.

Title: Roll With the Punches
Review: This new CD proves how much he still loves performing. That said, the more emotional songs, such as Ruby Toombs’ weepy “Teardrops From My Eyes” Count Basie & Jimmy Rushing vindictive “Goin’ to Chicago”, sound better than the more fun ones. While Morrison shows that he still can stretch out a word or repeat it rat-a-tat style, the music’s more interesting when it doesn’t call attention to itself.

Title: To Be Still
Review: With this single self-produced masterstroke, Alela Diane has effectively shaken off all the ill-fitting labels of “new weird America” and “freak folk” and given notice that a warmly expressive and unique voice has arrived with stories to tell.

Title: BMX Bandits Forever
Review: Bowlcut romantics will swoon for twinkly samba "Saveoursmiles" and "Love Me 'Til My Heart Stops" on his 10th LP, but as wistfulness gives way to despondency on "Rust" and an anguished take on West Side Story's "Somewhere," Stewart's idiosyncratic path feels like an increasingly lonely one. [Jul 2017, p.25]

Title: Ensemble Pearl
Review: Ghost Parade and the sustained swell of Giant (which comes on like a less glacial take on Zeit-era Tangerine Dream) are frustratingly low-watt affairs, while Wray--featuring atonal viola from Mr Bungle/Bill Frisell collaborator Eyvind Kang--resembles the abstract strokes of Talk Talk’s Laughing Stock rather than doom-laden trailblazers such as Earth or The Melvins.

Title: Bitchin'
Review: The Donnas get the ball into the red zone from time to time on Bitchin', but they never really score.

Title: The Lady Killer
Review: If the de rigueur synthetic frills keep The Lady Killer from the visceral, tactile highs of the current soul revival, they do remind that artifice can often be its own reward.

Title: Madvillainy
Review: A glorious phantasmagoria of flow.

Title: Tidelands
Review: Moody, beautiful, nearly perfect.

Title: Lookaftering
Review: There's still something truly magical in the wistful clarity of her voice. [Nov 2005, p.131]

Title: The Official Body
Review: A dazzlingly creative effort, it might well be SHOPPING’s most complete, concise, and fascinating release yet.

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: In the end, Ultraviolet’s finest moments occur when Kylesa venture farthest from their proven strengths and step into the unknown.

Title: Room Inside the World
Review: Anxiety might still be rooted in Ought’s foundations, but by looking beyond it the four-piece have made their richest, greatest work yet.

Title: Dusk
Review: This time there is too little that snags the ear. [Nov 2016, p.114]

Title: Sugar at the Gate
Review: Largely insubstantial. [Aug 2017, p.97]

Title: What's Inside is More Than Just Ham
Review: Beneath the slightly grating kookiness, FEET's songwriting is genuinely exciting.

Title: Someday World
Review: Once one grows comfortable with the album’s prevailing electro-acoustic ambiance, the repetitive song structures do little to add energy to the beleaguered soundscapes.

Title: Basic Volume
Review: Over 15 tracks, however, progress stalls. For all Gaika’s articulacy--he also writes for Dazed & Confused--the downbeat haze in which he operates privileges numbness over passion and ire, qualities his arresting music merely hints at, rather than weaponises.

Title: The Eldritch Dark
Review: With such careful attention to detail, The Eldritch Dark isn't just an homage to the sounds of the past, it's also a gateway to another era in metal history that, with any luck, more bands will go into and explore.

Title: La Cucaracha
Review: Next to 2003's comparatively straight-shooting "Quebec," Ween's first studio album in four years is flush with quick right turns.

Title: Authentic
Review: Thirty years in, LL still spins taut couplets as often as he licks his lips and delivers them with nimble style.

Title: Silver Lake
Review: While Silver Lake sounds like a Vic Chesnutt album through and through, it's also a better than average introduction to the man's work.

Title: Hard Rain
Review: he 22a label founder flexes his expansive musical influences across ten new creations. One of the most exciting tracks here is “Buffalo Gurl”. Dividing its time between earlier R&B and sultry jazz chords, it’s the pick me up you didn’t know you needed. [Aug 2019, p.65]

Title: Zebra
Review: There is a very fine line between contentment and the utter absence of feeling, and while Zebra's production and mix is flawless throughout, it falls too often on the wrong side of that line.

Title: Trap Lord
Review: The rapper is an excellent tour guide through this warped landscape of thrills and chills, and even if Rocky remains the A$AP Mob's most obvious and outgoing choice, there's an argument to be made that the more interesting one is Ferg, a Trap Lord if there ever was one.

Title: Welcome Home
Review: These songs sparkle with a gentle joy, their warm softness as alluring as a swimming pool on a hot afternoon. [Jul 2019, p.109]

Title: Logos
Review: Logos feels familiar and assuring, another affecting dispatch from a corner of indie music that is increasingly starting to seem like one Cox pretty much owns.

Title: Man-Made
Review: This is a mature, reflective work (read: repeated spins are expected to reveal the deeper layers), the sound of a veteran group content with its cult status and simply playing to its strengths: Smartly crafted guitar-pop that will appeal to the faithful and perhaps add an adherent or two.

Title: The Altogether
Review: In ten years, you'll be mistaking their superficial work here for the Chemical Brothers, Crystal Method, or Fatboy Slim's big-beat bullshit.

Title: The Mountain
Review: The Mountain is a more diverse set than the old Heartless Bastards gave us, it's still rooted in the same emotionally direct songwriting and performing that is this band's trademark, and for all that's changed with the band, Wennerstrom has held on to her core virtues.

Title: A Perfect Contradiction
Review: It may be nothing new but her punchy, uplifting set of pastiche Sixties and Seventies soul, r’n’b and disco is perfectly pitched with just an appealing hint of exaggeration.

Listening to 7 is almost like spending time with a normally cheerful and sunny friend who’s angry at someone or something else: It’s a bit startling but not unpleasant or unwelcome, because it opens up another side to the person--and proves that they can still surprise you.

Title: Under a Billion Suns
Review: Their best record in years. [Apr 2006, p.218]

Title: Rattle That Lock
Review: A gentle watercolour portrait of the artist as a young man.

Title: SIGN
Review: There are times when Sign truly soars, though it never manages to eclipse what’s now a crowded sonic milieu.

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: The Odd Couple is the exhilarating sound of the band geeks and theater weirdoes taking over the school.

Title: Because of the Times
Review: Because Of The Times burns with all the invention and ambition that seemed to have been sucked out of its predecessor. [May 2007, p.108]

Title: Mastermind
Review: The album might not be nearly good enough to launch him into any "classic" conversation, but it also not nearly bad enough to be viewed as a sign of his impending demise.

Title: Dumb Luck
Review: At 40-plus minutes, Dumb Luck gets out just when the getting is good. [May 2007, p.93]

Title: Puff O'Gigio
Review: In these oneiric landscapes, lyrics won't guide you much. But that's fine, as there's plenty to stimulate the curious explorer.

Title: I Can Feel the Night Around Me
Review: Relaxing as it may be, the album works best as vague metaphor, affording the listener room to infer, interpret and apply personal meaning, independent of any direction by Hartley.

Title: Olden Yolk
Review: An album that cooks up a dreamy meld of contemporary indie-New York atmosphere and a trippy past seemingly frozen in time.

Title: Life of Pause
Review: It all amounts to the messiest, least consistent Wild Nothing release to date. It's also the most alive. [Jan/Feb 2016, p.60]

Title: My Best Friend Is You
Review: While it's clear that Nash's skills have advanced light years since Made of Bricks' bang-it-out musicality, one can't help but wish she'd finally figure out what the hell it is she's trying to say.

Title: Culture of Volume
Review: This album is perhaps even more ambitious than its predecessor and, unlike East India Youth's debut, finds the artist stepping out from the shadows to produce a stunning, transformative electronic record.

Title: Achilles Heel
Review: Nothing here is horrible, but nothing here is great.

Title: Monsters of Folk
Review: Spread over 15 tracks, the combination wears thin at several points, and several songs feel more like their creator's solo work than a composite product. Monsters of Folk has moments on undeniable beauty, though, and when the musicians pitch their voices atop one another--as they do to notable effect on the gorgeous "Slow Down Jo"-the benefits of teamwork are more than clear.

Title: Noble Beast
Review: It's less mopey than Bright Eyes, less pompous than Sufjan Stevens and better than almost everything else. [Feb 2009, p.103]

Title: Illumination
Review: The ex-Jam frontman careens from folky piffle to respectable bar-band stomp.

Title: Honeycomb
Review: It is a noble effort, modeled on Bob Dylan’s Blonde on Blonde, but the results are underwhelming.

Title: Hug of Thunder
Review: Hug Of Thunder is a welcome return by Broken Social Scene. Dignified, grand and full of life, let’s just hope we don’t have to wait another seven years for their next record.

Title: Thistled Spring
Review: Thistled Spring seems a really lovely idea; the lyrics are beautiful, the musical texture is auburn and wood-hued, smooth-sanded and multi-faceted. But there’s nothing that speaks to me.

Title: Hot Dreams
Review: More than any previous Timber Timbre record, Hot Dreams simmers sonically with the chaos lurking just below these surfaces. Rarely does such calm feel so utterly foreboding.

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: The problem with Maya is that the clamour around what she says seems to have begun influencing some of the music that she chooses to make.

Title: Torches
Review: Much of Torches doesn't aim much higher than being a fizzy soundtrack for windows-down elbow tans. Which is fine, but for all his ease at getting attention, hopefully Foster will want to command it more thoroughly.

Title: Sing To The Moon
Review: While unlikely, Mvula's fusions aren't aurally threatening: this remains a woman musing on the vicissitudes of love, while heavenly instrumentation shimmers around her.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: Despite having a lot in common with their first disc, there are some slight variations in sound that make Chutes Too Narrow even better than its predecessor.

Title: Strange Dreams
Review: The album might scare off some fans who were reeled in by his perky pop songs, but it might find a home with those who like their pop seriously murky and gray.

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: This is Suede right near their very best. They remain incurable, helpless romantics, barely able to control their wildest musical thoughts, and Brett Anderson sounds like he depends on them more than ever.

Title: XXX
Review: That's the magic of XXX: whether joy, sadness or disgust, Mr. Brown will make you feel something.

Title: Dedication
Review: It's an overheard confessional, or an electronic diary entry from a very sad masked man, and an artistically impressive and musically satisfying one at that.

Title: Future Hndrxx Presents: The WIZRD
Review: The lean guest list of trap all-stars Young Thug, Gunna and Travis Scott delivers solid if unspectacular support down the home stretch. Diehard Future fans, of which there are legion, will be satisfied. But at 20 tracks, The Wizrd runs overlong. Jewels like “F&N” (with its nifty beat switch), “Promise U That” and “Faceshot” run the risk of getting lost in all the streaming.

Title: Success
Review: If success means overpowering the senses with creepy, captivating dissonance, KEN Mode are clutching a real triumph.

Title: American Slang
Review: Make no mistake--that Jersey (GA's home state) vibe still lurks in the corners. It's just that his writing style is more distinctive here. It's also the sound of a band pushing itself while capitalizing on its strengths.

Title: Vision Valley
Review: One wishes they would spend a little more time plowing through the album while kicking amps and knocking over mic stands rather than changing things up.

Title: Bashed Out
Review: This album is about the layers that play out in a minimalist way. Each brush stroke, each note, is purposeful. This album doesn't scream "listen to me", it gently draws you in.

Title: Not Waving, But Drowning
Review: Short on visceral thrills, but long on soul and dexterity. [May 2019, p.108]

Title: Late Registration
Review: Mostly brilliant. [Aug 2005, p.88]

Title: Snares Like a Haircut
Review: They artfully balance soaring interference-cloaked anthems with dreamier My Bloody-style FX investigations. [Mar 2018, p.113]

Title: Devil's Playground
Review: Over-produced and under-inspired. [26 Mar 2005, p.51]

Title: III
Review: Astonishingly, rather than the sound of desperate barrel scraping (although surely the cupboard is now totally bare), these songs document a band that constantly sought to engage and push the boundaries of music.

Title: Jaime
Review: Howard's embrace of all the mess of life gives Jaime its sustenance. Her audacity is apparent upon the first listen, but subsequent spins are profound and nourishing.

Title: Tender Buttons
Review: Despite this record's twilight charms, the group may need to become more expansive if they want to head further out there. [Oct 2005, p.96]

Title: These Four Walls
Review: They don't have the lyrical complexity of the bands that they will be compared to (from a young U2 to the aforementioned Frightened Rabbit), but they do have the energy and that's a promising place to start.

Title: Good News For People Who Love Bad News
Review: While the album is not as cohesive a vision, many of its songs are more focused.

Title: In the Magic Hour
Review: In producer Tucker Martine’s hands (he’s worked with Neko Case, Punch Brothers, the Decemberists and Laura Veirs), O’Donovan’s music sounds light and atmospheric, her folk freed up by billowing electric guitars and sensitive percussion.

Title: Satanic Panic in the Attic
Review: It's hard to believe that a guy so apparently bombed out of his head... can concoct such well-crafted pop songs. [#11, p.98]

Title: Spring
Review: If this isn't Quite her own trip, she leaves intriguing tracks to follow. [Dec 2019, p.110]

Title: Closer To Grey
Review: Closer to Grey is the coldest, shiniest, most polished collection of songs released under the Chromatics banner. It’s chillier, darker and more sinister than anything else they’ve ever put out.

Title: Tirtha
Review: The music is at its best when it emulates an animated conversation, one voice leap-frogging the other with no one losing sight of the central theme.

Title: PHOX
Review: On this debut, not a single note is out of place.

Title: How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb
Review: Compared to All That You Can’t Leave Behind, it’s immensely sincere, well-thought out, and meaningful... [It] also happens to be loaded with hooks.

Title: ArrangingTime
Review: On this record, Yorn seems to master mood more than tune, but that winds up being to his benefit. This tonal elasticity gives ArrangingTime an enveloping warmth, one that is alluring even if it tends to shift concentration away from the songwriting that allegedly was his greatest strength.

Title: Static
Review: Cults' sophomore album sidesteps presumptions about a rising, major-label band and admirably finds contentment not in what they could be, but what they are right now.

Title: A Stranger Here
Review: The pre-WWII country blues that the 77-year-old honed under the tutelage of Woody Guthrie are in full bloom on 'The New Stranger Blues' and 'Soul of A Man'. [Spring 2009, p.77]

Title: Aytche
Review: Joseph Shabason plays saxophone with art rockers Destroyer and provides icy synths for the R&B outfit DIANA. His solo debut, however, is densely textured ambient jazz that is wonderful to immerse yourself in for 40 minutes.

Title: Restarter
Review: While it doesn't mine new territory, Restarter is the sound of Torche getting comfortable and digging in their heels.

Title: Can't Fly Without Gravity
Review: This busy collection is really just more free.

Title: The Midnight Organ Fight
Review: Their jangly melodies claw their way inside your brain just the same, making them latest in a long line of Glasgow bands to effortlessly combine celebratory sonics and miserablist lyrics into something singular.

Title: Black Moon Spell
Review: This album is louder, catchier and more memorable [than King Tuff]. It doesn’t break rules or upend conventions, but it fills its songs with more oomph and pressure than ever.

Title: Prisoner
Review: The album tails off after a strong start. Lyrically though, and as a view into Adams’ psychopathology, Prisoner is nothing short of fascinating.

Title: The Hiding
Review: [A] chilled collection both soothing and intoxicating. [Jul 2018, p.30]

Title: The Spine
Review: At least 40 per cent of 'The Spine' is really rather charming. [3 Jul 2004, p.65]

Title: Wolves
Review: Wolves is somehow even more polished, almost glossy to a fault with its compression and ladled-on sweetening of the distortion. At times, it veers dangerously close to latter-day Metallica.

Title: Alegrias
Review: Since Gelb started working mainly as a solo artist, these collaborations have arguably been his strongest, most convincing works. His collaborators have provided challenging but appropriate accompaniments for his florid musings.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: This is the best album of the year so far.

Title: About Farewell
Review: Alela Diane hasn’t upended the form, but that probably wasn’t her intent. What she needed was a port in a storm, and About Farewell is a very sturdy bulwark.

Title: Mental Illness
Review: These songs are crafted in the best sense of the word, with the lyrics delivering sublime twists that the music matches. As such, Mental Illness becomes something of a balm for troubled times; it's an album that finds reassurance within the darkest corners.

Title: Age of Unreason
Review: While these songs may lack the same kind of energetic rage that defined the band in their early years, they're still a formidable way of exposing truths and holding the powers that be to account. [4 May 2019, p.55]

Title: Caramel
Review: It’s hard to judge if the album has simply missed its mark or, as I suspect, he appears to have lost the enthusiasm and imagination with which he approached his first, vastly superior effort.

Title: Providence
Review: It's a daring album, and in its best moments, the listener gets a sense of how fulfilling and soul-cleansing its production must have been.

Title: LAX
Review: Though LAX has its debilitating faults, it certainly stands up with any rap full-length released this year, which for this point in Game’s career, might even make it a miracle.

Title: Everybody's Dying To Meet You
Review: Helmed by ex-Primal Scream and My Bloody Valentine producer Brian O’Shaughnessy, the band’s second release, Everybody’s Dying To Meet You is a shade more confident and fully-realised.

Title: Nabuma Rubberband
Review: Nabuma Rubberband is too uneasy, too unsettling, to guarantee a full-blown commercial breakthrough, but otherwise, they've cracked it all. [Jun 2014, p.107]

Title: Human Ceremony
Review: Sunflower Bean have enough homegrown ability between them to draw up a series of immersing and original compositions.

Title: Strange Peace
Review: It’s refreshing to know there are bands like METZ putting out such quality rage like the 11 songs on this most exceptionally enthralling hello for today’s youth to thrash along to with the same sense of reckless abandon their parents were able to extol as members of the Sub Pop Singles Club.

Title: Bromst
Review: His 2007's "Spiderman Of The Rings" was filled with good ideas but prone to novelty. Bromst goes a long way to reversing this trend. [Apr 2009, p.84]

Title: Never, Never, Land
Review: Lucky the men from UNKLE have such generous mates, without whom Never, Never, Land would tinkle and whoosh into oblivion.

Title: II
Review: A series of back-to-the-futurescapes that are both lush and subtly unnerving. [29 Jul 2006, p.29]
This sophomore release named after his hometown's zip code is raw and ready to fight, including taking down all the industry folk who helped hold up this second LP.

Title: Visions of Bodies Being Burned
Review: The dread that percolates throughout the album comes from the ominous production and burly subject matter, but Daveed Diggs' quick-witted and masterfully controlled flows amplify the anxiety. Like the masked killer in a scary movie, Diggs seems supernaturally several steps ahead at all times.

Title: Tahoe
Review: If $ucessor is the finality of the final, then Tahoe is the beginning that begins. Tahoe is a voice that emerges after the rupture, the voice that creates itself anew, settling into itself as into a home.

Title: DNA
Review: There’s a down-to-earth sense of crisp, hooky economy à la Mendes and Puth, gentlemanly horniness mixed with bittersweet innocence they wear well, even as grown men who know what it’s like to soldier their way to hard-earned redemption.

Title: Book of Ryan
Review: By providing a cinematic narrative throughout, Royce proves that he is more than a one-trick-pony witty lyricist. He's introspective and not afraid of laying down confessional lyrics.

Title: My Father Will Guide Me Up a Rope to the Sky
Review: Where it leads, and who dares to climb it, is irrelevant; the fact that it so dizzyingly hangs between spirituality and perversion, austerity and decadence, is enough.

Title: Chastity Belt
Review: These are stories about patterns of behaviour, like dreams that keep returning, or won't end. The way out, these songs counsel, lies in relinquishing. [Oct 2019, p.85]

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: While MacLean isn’t a self-conscious wit, he’s never seemed too invested in trying to not sound silly, and it doesn’t cost him. Sometimes, when the darkness gets heavy, his limitations add a much-appreciated levity. As Brody Stevens might say, “Enjoy it.”

Title: Animals in the Dark
Review: Adding to his old-time preacher's moan and expressive banjo, Whitmore utilizes a full band for the first time in this collection of songs lamenting corrupt authority in all its various forms. [Winter 2009, p.79]

Title: Rainbow Mirror
Review: The results isn't always compelling; at times the trio lean on cliched sounds--ominous synth tones, for example, or whirring stock effects--that have also crept into previous release. But more often, the pieces on Rainbow Mirror avoid banality through forced patience. The extended track lengths greatly benefit Fernow’s chosen range of sounds and moods. Given the room to stretch and develop, he and his colleagues maintain a level of subtlety throughout. [Dec 2017, p.56]

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: Slave Ambient continues themes of wanderlust and searching that were all over the other records, but as Granduciel sings of friends gone, of calling loved ones home, of trying to find his place in the world changing around him, the music behind him seems to be searching too.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: His strengths are all being restrained, but you can tell they're struggling to get free.

Title: The Hope Six Demolition Project
Review: This isn’t the best or the bravest music of her career, but Harvey continues to pave new ground. This time, she takes that responsibility very literally, exploring new places and inviting listeners into her strange universe.

Title: Beyond
Review: There is something almost eerie about how exactly the Dinosaur Jr of 2007 sound like the Dinosaur Jr of 1988.

Title: Careers
Review: Although most of Careers chugs along with a sandy roadside candor, some tracks, like the churning, heavy Planet Birthday or the clinically pulsing Hong Kong Hotel, play with disparate textures.

Title: PUP
Review: Pup have come out spitting, sounding like Dookie-era Green Day dipped in tar and broken glass. [12 Apr 2014, p.53]

Title: E = MCÂ²
Review: The production is glossed to within an inch of its life, the mood is cheerfully upbeat--or 'festive' as Carey might put it herself--and the entire confection rings out with bold, sassy, brutally executed intent.

Title: Ambitions
Review: Unlike the space disco of his past, Thomas's music now hangs together not with laser bursts but with silken thread.

Title: God's Son
Review: It's not all brilliant, but there's enough of brilliance here to convince.

Title: Futures
Review: A kind of Joshua Tree for the heavily pierced and mildly upset. [Dec 2004, p.140]

Title: Universalists
Review: On paper this should be a mess; on record it's a thrillingly chaotic sonic voyage. [Jun 2018, p.27]

Title: Origami Harvest
Review: It’s difficult to tell if the emcee is mocking a trend in rap—or simply perpetuating it. The air of poetic abstraction on the album doesn’t clear anything up. But elsewhere, the contrast in styles works more successfully.

Title: Full Closure and No Details
Review: Full Closure and No Details feels more like a journey to the closure Cohen seeks through her songwriting than an answer itself — and what an important and journey it is.

Title: Mystic Familiar
Review: He’s decided to take things a little slower, in the process creating his best, and perhaps most coherent, album to date.

Title: Mordechai
Review: The group sit deeper than ever in their grooves on their third outing, and the moments of tranquillity are even more zen. Mordechai offers a rich, meditative escape from the world, something more welcomed than ever in the current climate.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: The sound throughout--as ever recorded and mixed by drummer John McEntire--is gorgeous, and a nice reminder of how thoughtful simplicity can still carry a lot of weight.

Title: Coming Home
Review: It's all a pleasing time warp without turbulence, one with songs built more to evoke the past than to last in one's memory.

Title: The Nihilist
Review: The Nihilist feels like a collision of Gotham's manic energy and the otherworldliness that has permeated Kiwi music from Uncle Tim's Splitz Enz to Lorde. [Jul 2014, p.73]

Title: Exhausting Fire
Review: Exhausting Fire is the fourth--and best installment of what will hopefully one day be recognized as the finest thing going in the forward-thinking heavy underground. [No. 125, p.59]

Title: The Obliterati
Review: Packed with energy and furious with ideas. [#269, p.45]

Title: Last Exit
Review: Your tolerance level for the group will probably mostly have to do with how well you can stand the rather light vocal stylings and the sometimes lighter-electronics programming.

Title: Subiza
Review: For all the barbs that could arguably be lobbed at Delorean for wheeling out another variation of the near terminally exhausted formula, they sidestep any fatal criticisms by applying a hefty dose of summer exuberance to their White Isle pop that's near impossible to deny.

Title: Rather Ripped
Review: [Sonic Youth's] most openly “mature” disc, possibly their best since ’95’s Washing Machine, maybe even the almighty Daydream Nation.

Title: Stainless Style
Review: As a document of its time, then, Stainless Style is remarkably successful. Taken on the base level of being an enjoyable pop album, it also triumphs handsomely.

Title: No Kings
Review: No Kings, the second time Doomtree has stepped out for an all-crew release, is a triumph of musicianship.

Title: When the Pawn
Review: Part Jewel-with-tunes, part Tori-Amos-without-kookiness, it noodles, but only rarely.

Title: Boo Boo
Review: Boo Boo is fascinating as an exercise for Bear, and proves that Toro Y Moi has yet another viable direction to take their music in. At some point, Bear may need to chart a clear course for the project but for now it’s fun to hear him freely experimenting with new sonic palettes.

Title: Fucked Up Friends
Review: Black Moth Super Rainbow principal Tobacco's new solo full-length sticks to the formula established by his band, but adds a healthy dose of drum machine. [Fall 2008, p.87]

Title: What Will We Be
Review: It's easy to lay the rap on Banhart's drifting towards the middle of the road with the fuller, whole-band sound he's embraced, or the bigger labels or the greater notoriety, but the fault clearly lies with Banhart himself, who has become a lot easier to understand. [Fall 2009, p.56]

Title: Complete Me
Review: It's actually quite hard to decide whether Complete Me is a dreadful pile of over-processed, overloaded frippery, or if it's a work of genius. It could purely come down to whether you've got the stomach for it.

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: Notably talented musicians, expect that by their next album, Smith Westerns won't just emulate their influences, but fully embody what could become a unique sound. [Feb. 2011, p. 72]

Title: Sun Racket
Review: The band are less assured on the quieter numbers, however. The likes of Milk at McDonald’s and the dreamlike Sue’s are pleasant enough (and the former includes the arresting line “I don’t regret a single drop of alcohol”), but unlike their best work there is precious little in the way of nagging hooks to lodge in one’s head.

Title: Wet Will Always Dry
Review: An album that has Blawan back and showing us why he matters to us techno heads.

Title: Era Extrana
Review: Era Extraña does not flow as smoothly as Psychic Chasms but the influences are in all the right places and it seems that Alan Palomo is wearing them proudly on his sleeve.

Title: The Blueprint 2: The Gift & the Curse
Review: Jay-Z has upped the commercial rap ante once again.

Title: Rant
Review: It is clever and witty like the band is want to be, but when listening to Rant I stopped caring about the lack of instruments and simply enjoyed myself.

Title: TREAT MYSELF
Review: For the most part, the album is sickly sweet and filled with cliché lyrics. ‘Treat Myself’ is a frustrating listen, especially given Trainor’s track record for writing ear-worm pop songs.

Title: Some Echoes
Review: Never has Aloha sounded so tight, so completely in control of its sound, so assured of that sound.

Title: Disgraceland
Review: The Orwells ape highlights of the last 25 years of indie rock on their second album. [Aug 2014, p.78]

Title: Parodia Flare
Review: Tropics' debut album stands its ground as a promising start for an artist still figuring out exactly what he wants to say.

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: Perhaps Codes And Keys's seemingly illogical sequencing of songs makes sense if they wish to lure their audience into thinking it's as-you-were. But it's not: things are different and better. [July 2011, p. 110]

Title: New Eyes
Review: The classical elements are independently pleasing--as you’d expect when elements of Shostakovich, Mozart and so on are used--but by drenching it all in commercial dance production, the supposed ‘fusion’ becomes a bastardisation.

Title: Plague Park
Review: It's almost as if, released from the role of playing less weird anchor to Spencer Krug's art rock savant, Boeckner's figured out how to maximize and expand what he does best.

Title: Ultramarine
Review: Ultramarine moves Young Galaxy from being a great indie band to being a great band, full stop. The songs profoundly move the body and the psyche in equal measure.

Title: Meet Glen Campbell
Review: There are more examples of cover albums gone wrong than gone right. Thankfully Glen Campbell's new set, which finds him ably putting his own twist on tunes from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers, Foo Fighters, U2, Green Day and John Lennon, among others, fits into the latter category.

Title: The Red Thread
Review: Five years later, it's easy to be blasé about [Aidan] Moffat's disgruntled first-person narratives. [#154, p.68]

Title: Saint Cloud
Review: Katie is making a point of saying more with less, taking potent emotions and quietly tucking them into a plain white envelope for us to open and interpret. She’s as lucid as we’ve ever heard her, stripping down to her emotional core and daring us to make eye contact.

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: He could be a genius or he could be a lunatic; either way, one of modern filmdom's most debated and alluring figures has made an arresting album that successfully translates his visual surrealism to a new medium.

Title: Jungle
Review: The details of bandmember identities and backgrounds quickly become extraneous in light of the wealth of intriguing sounds presented on this incredibly well-constructed debut.

Title: Ride Your Heart
Review: Drawing on powerpop, new wave and girl group harmonies, this record is full of engaging tunes, doe-eyed dedications and wry witticisms.

Title: Comb The Feelings Through Your Hair
Review: Truly a bold step forward for the band, the album takes Grooms to their next plateau the same way Daydream Nation proved Sonic Youth's breakthrough almost 30 years earlier.

Title: Live Like You Were Dying
Review: McGraw uses references to death and suffering to camouflage rather ordinary songs, and rather ordinary singing.

Title: Incredibad
Review: This one fares better than most in audio form, but whether ‘Natalie’s Rap’ will be enjoyed by anyone who hasn’t already wet themselves at the video is debatable.

Title: The People or the Gun
Review: The album never challenges the conventions of a political punk rock record. Because so many political punk rock records have come and gone, Anti-Flag missed another opportunity to at least make The People or the Gun a little more compelling than its army of predecessors.

Title: This Old Road
Review: Recall's Johnny Cash's recordings with Rick Rubin. [Apr/May 2006, p.111]

Title: Lollipop
Review: Lollipop is their 13th Studio album, and one of their best. [Jun 2011, p.91]

Title: No Thrills
Review: It's boldly rendered, and somehow crafts a very human world from cartoon sonics.

Title: No More Shall We Part
Review: What makes 'No More...' Cave's best album since 'Henry's Dream' (which it most clearly resembles), is a return to melodrama (or rather the juxtaposition of melodrama with the album's ballads) where Cave crafts a deliciously potent mix of the visionary, the bizarre and the everyday...

Title: Oh My God
Review: While Morby's earlier concepts might have seemed somewhat looser and more liberated from the self-imposed constraints of such a project, Oh My God also feels like the apotheosis of his multivalent approach to the construction of music and myth. He is truly at the top of his game, and one can only stand in awe of this accomplishment.

Title: Asleep in the Bread Aisle
Review: Asleep in the Bread Isle is an everyday suburban rap album, if there is such a thing.

Title: Magnifique
Review: As with every Ratatat record, Magnifique leaves you wondering what they could do if they fleshed these out into actual songs with real singers.

Title: Frank
Review: Winehouse's record has the feeling of being allowed to grow on its own--without being meddled with and fussed over.

Title: Don't Forget Who You Are
Review: It’s a dispiriting affair--a mishmash of glam rock, lad rock and heavier indie rock that fails to ignite.

Title: Futurology

Every track -- whether reflective but swinging, like "Wild Honey," or poised, then pouncing, like "Beautiful Day" -- honors a tune so refined that each seems like some durable old number. Review: Dig deep and there's powerful drama and enigmatic subtlety in equal measure as the Cumbrian four-piece once again embrace understated electronica and invite favourable comparisons with Talk Talk.

Title: When You're Through Thinking, Say Yes
