Review: The band sounds fresh from their rest, aren't trying to be something they're not again, and most importantly, they sound young and sincere. Welcome back, Yellowcard.

Title: The Female Boss
Review: A lamentable debut all round.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: An intimate, introspective album that takes tentative steps to reveal the soul behind the star.

Title: HYMNS
Review: It's such a musically bare record. "Into The Earth" is the only song that feels like a rock song and it's also very soft and drab. So many songs riff off the same synth beats that HYMNS end up being a contemplative session that puts you to sleep as opposed to prodding at your mind.

Title: A Walk with Love and Death
Review: The tenacity and productivity of the Melvins is admirable, as is their ability to continue to push music into some of its darkest and most intriguing corners. What would be really interesting, though, is if the Melvins made fewer Melvins records and tried more projects like the one on the second half of A Walk With Love & Death. After 34 years, their output is at times just a little too breathless.

Title: Highly Evolved
Review: The Vines' place in the rock gene pool is shaped by elements of controlled guitar thrash, often complex harmony, bubblegum psychedelia and polished piano-driven ballads with an early Seventies whiff. [Aug 2002, p.116]

Title: Discipline & Desire
Review: Discipline plummets you into the band’s shadowy world but remains loveable--like a brighter, warmer Savages.

Title: No Thyself
Review: The surprise excellence of the songs and the music makes this the long-overdue fourth great Magazine album.

Title: All My Relations
Review: Warm and thoughtful as the intentions behind it, the music on Relations at times skirts close to the territory occupied by those Persuasive Percussion albums that clutter up used LP bins.

Title: Running Out of Love
Review: Running Out Of Love isn’t the sound of hectoring; it’s The Radio Dept. getting on with the business of making important records, being one of the most challenging, uncompromising and rewarding bands we have and proving that political music is as vital as ever.

Title: Cerulean Salt
Review: One of Cerulean Salt’s great triumphs is that we believe in these people, the album’s intimacy heightens its sense of realism, its characters feel living.

Title: Lady in Gold
Review: [A] polished second set by the Swedish '70s-inspired blues-psych outfit. [Sep 2016, p.99]

Title: II: Void Worship
Review: With music like this, the line between undercooked and overdone is a pretty fine one, but II: Void Worship shows that Pilgrim are a band more than capable of walking it with an album that's sure to find purchase with doom purists looking for something less fussy than the post-metal albums the genre influenced.

Title: The Powers That B
Review: By Death Grips’ standards, the first disc is significantly less dynamic than the second.... Jenny Death represents another step forward for Death Grips, a group that seems to have walked over the horizon and out of sight albums ago.

Title: Love & Hate
Review: Love & Hate is a massive leap in accomplishment for Kiwanuka.

Title: Humor Risk
Review: Though he used songs from the same recording sessions for both, Humor Risk is quite a different collection, accessible and verbose by McCombs's standards.

Title: Hardcourage
Review: He works in a middle ground, neither minimal or elaborate, making strong impressions by getting pushy. That’s what follows seduction.

Title: Sequence
Review: A record that awakens mysteries and meaning from sparse elements; a masterful ritual. [Jan 2019, p.67]

Title: Yawny Yawn
Review: The absence of instrumentation and arrangements beyond Ryder-Jones's lyrics and piano makes Yawny Yawn noticeably different from the original versions of the album's tracks. This is distinctive in offering a new listening experience focused on a direct and consistent style.

Title: Chinese Democracy
Review: The album fifteen years in the making that sounds like a slick but robotic imitation of what it might have been long ago.

Title: Consolers of the Lonely
Review: "Broken Boy Soldiers" lacked tunes like these, tunes with considerable weight, and these songs turn Consolers of the Lonely into a lop-sided, bottom-loaded album that's better and richer than their debut.

Title: Alligator
Review: [A] fine collection of city-weary poetry.

Title: Transit Transit
Review: Transit Transit is full of the sort of implausible leaps of imagination that normally only happen in your sleep.

Title: 99 CENTS
Review: It's funny and smart and a little annoying in large doses.

Title: Turn On The Bright Lights
Review: When it works, like on “NYC” or “Roland” it’s a dizzying and beautiful thing that leaves you starving for more. And even when it doesn’t work, it doesn’t fail – it’s just that at times the band seems unable to live up to their own standards and expectations.

Title: Scorpion
Review: The star’s hubris is no more apparent than in its sheer breadth and lack of quality control. At 25 tracks in total, Scorpion is way too long--even by Drake’s own standards--and simply doesn’t need to be.

Title: Young & Old
Review: The problem is, even at their best, Tennis's music seems inconsequential and frankly, neutered.

Title: Snowdonia
Review: Grief and hardship have changed Surfer Blood, there’s no denying that. But they deserve praise for making a record that still has its own joie de vivre and doesn’t completely overhaul the alphabet that has made the band a success in the first place.

Title: See My Friends
Review: The performers on this one likely count it among their career highlights, but those who have kept up with the quality of Davies' output in recent years may well be more interested in what he has yet to say rather than revisiting what he's already said so beautifully.

Title: Shoot for the Stars, Aim for the Moon
Review: With stakes this high and a legacy to consider, the end result may or may not bear much of a resemblance to what Pop Smoke had in mind. Nonetheless, he sounds alive here, a motivated and vibrant hip-hop talent actively pushing towards that next level.

Title: Permalight
Review: The Auto-Tuned vocals and cluttered background instrumentation on the title track represents a low point of the album. Luckily, the second half of "Permalight" moves away from electronics and finds Rogue Wave returning to its guitar-based, head-nodding roots.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: It is, of course, a very good album from start to finish--but you would expect that from an elder statesman of American alt-pop and one of the brightest talents of the current NPR-approved indie-rock scene.

Title: Stupid Things that Mean the World
Review: The more restrained, and slightly less expansive feel, of some of the tracks here perhaps makes the record as a whole feel slightly undercooked in comparison to its predecessor. Nevertheless it is another fine entry into the enviable discography of one of the most sadly underrated of British songwriters.

Title: Showboat Honey
Review: Although Showboat Honey isn't as instantly gratifying in terms of infectious hooks as his previous releases, solid songs that settle in with repeat listens make it a worthy addition to his increasingly reliable catalog.

Title: Native Invader
Review: It adds up to one of the most purposeful full-length statements in her quarter-century career.

Title: Apocalypse
Review: There’s a wealth of sonic variety on display but the concise run-time--clocking in at a fraction over 40 minutes--keeps matters focused and thoroughly engaging.

Title: The Unforgiving
Review: While her vocals alone are unlikely to gain Within Temptation too many new listeners, fans who have stuck with the band throughout their career will likely forgive The Unforgiving's occasional missteps.

Title: Such Hot Blood
Review: Such Hot Blood is best when it's at its most anthemic. [Nov 2013, p.101]

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: Making no palpable effort to crack the conventional with overflowing melodies and love songs, Bird instead latches up the intellect to create tiny packages of literature that make always leave you thinking--and snapping your fingers at the same time.

Title: Prisoner
Review: 'Prisoner' is unquestionably a captivating LP where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, since the cohesive nature of its songwriting is clearly intended to suit a beginning-to-end listening experience and enhance longevity.

Title: Good Arrows
Review: Here are very lovely songs, tempered by oblique though evocative lyrics; here are rustic landscapes juxtaposed with computer sounds and eccentric field samples; here is violence couched in the gentlest possible terms.

Title: WALLS
Review: Sadly, they seem content for the kind of mediocrity that designates you as the headliner Firefly and Bonnaroo call when someone else isn’t available.

Title: Elsie
Review: Bellowing hoarsely while ivories tinkle and muted guitars gently twang, he comes across like a scenery-chewing Method actor marooned in a stoic Ingmar Bergman flick.

Title: Lines, Vines and Trying Times
Review: Lines suggests that the Jonas Brothers simply don't have--or, more charitably, haven't yet developed--the chops to make it once the current teen-pop bubble bursts.

Title: Face Tat
Review: At times, the album may seem like it's made to confuse as much as thrill, but neither of those gets to the truth of Face Tat. Simply put, to paraphrase one of Hill's lyrics, it'll turn you into energy.

Title: The Golden Age of Glitter
Review: The Golden Age Of Glitter then, is a subversive record. Things may not be as they appear at various points throughout, but that’s no reason not to give it a go.

Title: Pause
Review: A far more sonically ambitious statement than its predecessors, perfectly fusing organic sounds with production techniques that are usually the preserve of underground dance producers or R&B mavericks.

Title: Foreign Light
Review: While Foreign Light trades some of his past eclecticism for a super-soulful hook-up with singer-songwriter Andrea martin, his acute ear for sasquatch basslines and simpatico collaborators remains undimmed. [Sep 2017, p.91]

Title: Hidden
Review: Barnett's blue-sky dreaming is actually a pretty accurate description of Hidden – heavily beat-driven, almost entirely absent of guitars, and laced with large amounts of elaborately arranged woodwind and brass. Does it work? Largely, yes.

Title: Sound Mirror
Review: Syd Arthur avoids any whiff of trendiness and just gets down to the business of writing and performing timeless music on its second record Sound Mirror.

Title: Pleasure
Review: Pleasure the album flows cohesively and poetically. [Apr - Jun 2017, p.80]

Title: The People or the Gun
Review: Even if People or the Gun does nothing to break new barriers musically, fans of their early work will be pleased to hear a return to form.

Title: Cuidado Madame
Review: As ever, it's wildly inventive. [Jul 2017, p.108]

Title: D
Review: Is there nothing they can't do?

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Her confidence trumps cute here.

Title: Dirt Farmer
Review: Whether reworking Steve Earle's 'The Mountain' or the traditional heart-tugger 'The Blind Child,' it represents a small yet very real personal triumph. [Dec 2007, p.121]

Title: Showtime
Review: These barren videogame shoot-out beats and textures don't do him justice. [17 Sep 2004, p.76]

Title: NY's Finest
Review: NY's Finest has everything you'd expect from this legendary producer. [Mar 2008, p.108]

Title: Unknown Rooms: A Collection of Acoustic Songs
Review: Unknown Rooms is admittedly an endeavor to listen to as a whole. But with the dense themes and music also comes reward: an acceptance for the unknown, and plucking the bizarre beauty from the inevitable.

Title: Join the Dots
Review: Songs pound onwards, elliptical guitar lines wrapping round and round, and there's an all encompassing feeling of travelling vast distances. Relentlessly, confidently and quite, quite spectacularly.

Title: Hall of Fame
Review: Needless to say, Big Sean may not have solidified his position in the rap hall of fame, but is certainly in the process of paving his way.

Title: Attention Deficit
Review: Overall, the ups far outweigh the downs.

Title: Lust Lust Lust
Review: Lust Lust Lust is an accomplished set. [Jan 2008, p.109]

Title: Modern English Decoration
Review: There is nothing new here, nothing especially innovative either. It’s just an album that consistently hits its target in a magnetic, mesmerizing way, and one that if you let it will swallow you whole.

Title: Crusher
Review: Like good goth, this is painful and exclusive, full of moody anthems and baritone melodies that won't cut through the static until the fifth listen or so.

Title: My Old Familiar Friend
Review: Not only does the music feel like filler and lacking in substance but the album itself feels like it’s only purpose is to merely keep music ticking over until something worthwhile comes along.

Title: Non-Secure Connection
Review: Non-Secure Connection needs – and deserves – several encounters before its treasures can be fully revealed. When they are, a record to stand beside his best achievements in recent years is the result. Hornsby is a fascinating and absorbing character, and the longer his creative surge continues the better.

Title: What Happens Next
Review: It’s hard to weigh out music so that it balances between intelligent and the danceable as the old Gang of Four did. Gill has made an excellent effort of it here but there’s some reapportioning that needs to be done.

Title: Room 25
Review: The pleasure of Room 25 is in hearing a master wordsmith turn words into feelings so that the feelings linger long after the words have stopped.

Title: Golden Greats
Review: Like its predecessor, Golden Greats meanders a bit too much and it places a little too much emphasis on surface, but when the surface sparkles like this, it's hard to complain too loudly.

Title: Celebration Castle
Review: What raises them above the hordes of young revivalists is their way with a cranky bon mot. [Jul 2005, p.121]

Title: Sprinter
Review: Each song works on its own terms, but many of the songs don’t seem to share terms.

Title: Cosmic Wink
Review: Cosmic Wink is largely free from inhibition though, documenting the big changes in life over beautiful, sweeping folk. While the album doesn’t hold all the answers, it’s still sure enough in its message to connect and remind you of the important things.

Title: Pink
Review: there's something in this that sounds just so much more intelligent than fannying around making devil horns.

Title: Post-Nothing
Review: Sure, there’s nothing at all novel about young dudes feeling immortal and wanting to get laid, but Japandroids infuse those well-worn tropes with enough energy and songcraft to make it feel refreshing.

Title: Sculptor
Review: Sculptor is a small gift coming at the right time, a 36-minute reverie that nonetheless remains rooted in waking life.
Blur have finally found a sound to match their name.

Title: Reptile
Review: As a slice of rootsy blues, it works nicely.

Title: Beyond
Review: It kicks ass.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: Dazzling moments don't come often enough to make up for flat ones.

Title: You Had Me at Goodbye
Review: Mostly You Had Me At Goodbye is an artist stretching out and eagerly grasping a whole new world, one that she should easily conquer. [May 2017, p.94]

Title: Shelter
Review: Though Alcest have left the majority of their metal signifiers behind, they've discovered another kind of heaviness via gorgeous, shimmering melodies.

Title: On Desire
Review: The epitome of indie clichés, Drowners have done nothing to break their mould, and On Desire does little to appease the want for something more.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: Not a bad album at all. In fact, at points it's really rather wonderful; it's just not quite the wall-to-wall fruity bangers one probably expected, but by no means as skip-heavy as the likes of Random Access Memories.

Title: High Hopes
Review: There’s a spirit of collaboration that is largely new, a genuine and warm-hearted celebration of past members’ contributions and a celebration of the rowdy, uplifting storm cooked up by the 18-strong modern incarnation of the group.

Title: Graduation
Review: At heart, he's still a producer not a rapper (which explains how badly he hits the mic at times, more on that later). He's got that hit-making part down pat... it's just that he can't make good hits anymore.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Flying Microtonal Banana
Review: Rich, imaginative, and more than a little strange.

Title: Emotions and Math
Review: Glaspy defies easy categorization and this solid, cleverly written debut is a testament to her sense of craft.

Title: Get Awkward
Review: By riding high on punchy impulses, Get Awkward ends up being a solid follow-up even if it doesn’t sound as instantly re-playable as the band’s charismatic first LP.

Title: Long Way Home
Review: Though she’s on the edge of slipping into Adele-esque poperatics, this is a bold and confident first LP from a producer--and singer--with great potential.

Title: Understand What Black Is
Review: Lamdin and Fatty have created sympathetic backdrops for the Poets to declaim over: lightly jazz-tinged reggae grooves, dubby production flourishes, spacious arrangements that allow for the Poets’ words to take centre-stage.

Title: The Assassination Of Julius Caesar
Review: They are masters of atmosphere and intrigue, and flirting with pop music has only further aided their chameleonic nature, with this being their most satisfying and diverse effort in many years.

Title: Steeple
Review: A resounding power chord marks the confident introduction to this fine debut album. [Nov 2010, p.113]

Title: Beams
Review: Beams, like Asa Breed, is front-loaded with the atmospheres and vocal manipulations that are bedrock to his best work. But Beams fails to evince the kind of songwriting growth that the vocal minority of his fans have been waiting for.
The debut album by indie's latest great white hopes, however, is notable mainly for its crushing ordinariness.

Title: Poison Season
Review: Bejar’s dismantled the old Destroyer sound, but he’s built something wonderfully disorientating in its stead.

Title: Black Cherry
Review: A dull compromise of artistic intent and marketability.

Title: Soul Music
Review: Yes, it’s possible to read Soul Music as some kind of commentary on, or deconstruction of, jungle. More people will probably interpret it as a collection of straightforward, canon-savvy bangers. That’s fine, of course, but it’s difficult to shake the sense that Special Request could have been something more.

Title: Utopia
Review: It’s an album you’ll want to return to again and again.

Title: Us
Review: Us is uplifting, thought-provoking, funny, heartbreaking, and bootyshaking.

Title: From Every Sphere
Review: From Every Sphere is the ultimate grower, which moves, in your mind, from quite nice to utterly compelling and addictive over a matter of days, or better, nights. [Album of the Month, March 2003, p.94]

Title: Regions of Light and Sound of God
Review: Regions of Light and Sound of God is all heated feelings and extravagant gestures. It is also what solo albums are for: the leader of a great band out on a limb, in rapt self-examination, getting weird and interesting.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: It's much less forthright and immediate than Inverted or Chutes, but it succeeds in spinning a web that draws you in; once caught you just want to lie back and absorb its gentle bounce.

Title: Cleopatra
Review: Ultimately, though, Cleopatra is simply Americana pastiche we've heard a hundred times before.

Title: Skull Worship
Review: It’s the sound of the Warlocks finally burning out on the most inward-looking album of the band’s career.

Title: Beauty Behind the Madness
Review: In the end, enjoying the Weeknd requires a certain suspension of disbelief, and that remains true on Beauty Behind the Madness. You really have to buy into his bad-guy persona.... For newcomers, there's a whole world to explore, and on Beauty Behind the Madness it's richer and smarter than ever.

Title: Memphis
Review: Magic Kids do pull off a winner with Summer, a sultry delight of abounding strings and tropical strums that, sadly, sounds out of place with the obvious eye winks scattered throughout. Memphis may borrow from such an imaginative time period, but their explorative range remains very limited.

Title: Ether Song
Review: When they're not straining to be anthemic, Turin Brakes still weave a seductive spell. [#14, p.143]

Title: Planet Earth
Review: Planet Earth is the sound of a working musician working, which makes it a bit of a passing pleasure, yet there's no denying that it is indeed a pleasure having him turn out solid records like this that build upon his legacy, no matter how modestly.

Title: James Blake
Review: The highs are notable. The problem is, Blake has put himself in a tight box, and when he strays out of it the material wavers [...]

Title: Strange House
Review: An undeniably good record. [May 2007, p.95]

Title: Always Ascending
Review: Always Ascending is a class act, polished, honed, several cuts above the mewling herd. New guitarist or not, Franz Ferdinand abide.

Title: Total Freedom
Review: Despite the underwhelming musicality of Total Freedom, many of these songs still pack some undeniable emotional force, especially the more joyful tracks like "Who Rescued Who" — a charming ode from Edwards to her dog. In her songcraft, Edwards remains dependable and enjoyable.

Title: On Oni Pond
Review: The album shrewdly brings order to the disorder, without streamlining away the band’s agreeably quirky identity.

Title: They Want My Soul
Review: They Want My Soul is more of a welcome return than a comeback, and too complex to be considered back-to-basics--especially when they reinvent the basics on each album.

Title: Under the Blacklight
Review: Under The Blacklight is by far and away the most accessible album that Rilo Kiley have ever made.

Title: Weather Diaries
Review: Weather Diaries is both recognizably Ride and a logical, tasteful update of its sound.

Title: Can't Wake Up
Review: Third proper full-length Can't Wake Up now completes his metamorphosis into an exceptional songwriter whose songs manifest into cinematic novellas. Characters living therein and their actions come to life in dreamy detail. Delivering them all, the singer's voice floats like a passing cloud along blooming stretches of reverberated chords.

Title: The Incredible Machine
Review: Sugarland are ruthless in their desire to leave no radio-ready trick untried, but in the end it's too much machine, not enough heart.

Title: Delirium Tremens
Review: Harvey's intimate understanding of Serge's rich catalogue allows him to smother markedly different compositions such as "Ce Mortel Enniu" (1958) and perverted mid-70s gear "SS Si Bon" and "L'Homme a Tete De Chou" with a menacing Bad Seeds swagger that unifies Delirium Tremens. [Aug 2016, p.76]

Title: The Magic
Review: Deerhoof show that pushing boundaries can yield fantastic results.

Title: Dormarion
Review: Dormarion should leave returning fans satisfied and new listeners hooked as Lerner continues to refine his skills and churn out strong albums.

Title: Highly Deadly Black Tarantula
Review: A filmic atmosphere is constant. [Jan 2016, p.96]

Title: El Tren Fantasma
Review: An evocative sonic portrait that juxtaposes the human-made sounds of the railway and the surrounding landscape.

Title: Mechanics of Dominion
Review: Mechanics of Dominion is too heady for its own good, but still holds ground as a wonderful combination of influences and post-genre style. It takes time for it to reveal itself, and it’s usually worth the investment.

Title: Kleerup
Review: Yep, it's the face of a guy who just recorded an accomplished, cohesive debut, one that should please fans of "blog house" and Swedish pop alike. Now if only he owned a razor.

Title: Sing When You're Winning
Review: It's a tribute to Williams' almost delusional self-confidence that he sounds equally at home no matter what the musical form; he invests each track with an energy many of them don't deserve.

Title: Apollo Sunshine
Review: But it's in the repeated listens that Apollo Sunshine begins to slip into place. Once the ear is ready for the stylistic differences, you can put aside your surprise and start listening for the individual pieces, and that's where the magic of the band continues to show itself.

Title: Freedom
Review: He's a master of weaving his overdubbed vocals into rapturous gospel heights, as on "Flesh," and his cry of "Should've known better" amid the heartbreak of "Leaves" resonates long after the track is finished.

Title: Chaos and Creation in the Backyard
Review: No one was expecting Godrich to turn this noble British pop institution into Radiohead, of course. But the glimpses of greatness are enough to leave you wishing that bottle had prevailed and more in the vein of "Too Much Rain" had resulted.

Title: Kiss Me Once
Review: A booming, fun pop record that is refreshing by not attempting to be anything other, though that same inessentialism keeps the record from reaching transcendence.

Title: Last of the Country Gentlemen
Review: Gorgeous as much as it is terrifyingly heartbreaking, it's Country Gentlemen's ominous open-ended silence that unnerves most of all.

Title: Only In Dreams
Review: It showcases a remarkably assured collection of songs (at times sounding like The Long Blondes do surf-pop--in no way a bad thing) as well as a real depth and maturity to songwriting that dwarfs the offerings of its home-recorded predecessor.

Title: Fear in Bliss
Review: In places it lacks the character to make Horse Thief truly stand out, but this first outing is a fine enough place to start. [May 2014, p.111]

Title: ONoffON
Review: OnOffOn has an incredibly dense, thick sound, and it sags a little in the middle, but Miller can still write terrifically belligerent pop songs. [Jun 2004, p.96]

Title: Plague Park
Review: I find myself disappointed with Plague Park despite its elusive initial luster. The good news is it’s an easy fix: Hire a band.

Title: The Way
Review: The result is an urgent collection whose creative spark burns brightly. [Dec 2014, p.104]

Title: Trying to Never Catch Up
Review: This is the Strokes’ first record without its adherence to formula and form, with better guitars and bigger chords. And, you know, more fun.

Title: Same Trailer Different Park
Review: Ms. Musgraves has a sweet character to her sound, which allows her to deliver a cynic’s wisdom in the voice of an inquisitive child.

Title: Some Nights
Review: Listeners who come for the trio's Glee-approved breakout ''We Are Young'' will be happy with Some Nights' superior first half.

Title: Ex:Re
Review: While there isn't always a tonne sonically to separate this from Tonra's day job, it must be applauded for its brutal honesty and moments of pure poetry.

Title: Skyline
Review: A decadent listen seemingly begging for visual accompaniment, even Tiersen's propensity for nihilism can't sink Skyline's intoxicating, mud-splattered grace. [Jun 2012, p.156]

Title: Kiss Land
Review: Kiss Land is proof for the unconvinced: the Weeknd is a star whether he wants to be or not.

Title: Uh Huh Her
Review: It is a short disc (41 minutes), and not an entirely satisfying one: instead of stories and characters, we get a series of gestures, a few false starts, pockets full of poses. This is an album of shards, then. But they're sharp. [7 June 2004]

Title: Americana
Review: Showing himself to have lost none of his wit, melodic acumen or genuine love of and for people, places and things, Americana is as fine a late-career album as one could hope for. For long-time fans and neophytes alike, Americana is a treasure to behold.

Title: Two Eleven
Review: Brandy scores when her raspy-sweet voice soars during ballads and slow jams, and that's what stands out on this intimate, often ethereal collection, Two Eleven.

Title: Amber
Review: One of the most striking Brit-rock step-ups since Radiohead got The Bends. [17 Feb 2006, p.79]

Title: Splazsh
Review: Beneath the stray bits and hiss, Splazsh's stoned dance grooves and stumbling, slo-mo electro--an odd mixture of Moodymann, Burial, and Boards of Canada--pull you into a world as immersive as the title promises.

Title: New Bermuda
Review: Taking their sound into a much darker (and riffier) realm comes as a bit of a surprise, but the band pulls it off with such excellence and grace that the shift isn't even jarring.

Title: Homeland
Review: The innovative, at times baffling result is part performance art, part avant-garde symphony, with the occasional Kierkegaard joke thrown in for good measure.

Title: Together Through Life
Review: It's a shame that the album fails to hit, and in some ways, it's also a shame that it's not terrible, either.

Title: The Believer
Review: These fluid, unfussy songs don't quite stick in your gut the way the 97's' best stuff does, but give Miller a chance and he can charm you something fierce.

Title: Goddess
Review: Goddess weaves a captivating spell that many are certain to fall under. [Oct 2014, p.87]

Title: Order of Noise
Review: At its best, Vessel's debut LP for Tri-Angle, Order of Noise makes you cock your head and wonder why you'd never heard that particular high-end squonk used in the place where a low-end splomp would usually go, the cards moving too fast to pick out the placement. At worst, Gainsborough's reliance on the value of shifting cards seems to trump what the cards actually are, and the fact that those three cards aren't ever leaving your sight.

Title: Real
Review: The aptly titled Real gives listeners a satisfying and enlightening further glimpse into her world, one that will surely be expanding with thoughts waiting to be put to song for years to come.

Title: After the Disco
Review: Taken solely as part of the Broken Bells discography it’s their best effort yet: a textured, kaleidoscopic pop record that crackles with imagination, and hints at the sign of something brilliant to come.

Title: In My Mind
Review: Sledge is a very straightforward lyricist; he doesn't stunt, he yearns. His lyrics favor plainspoken confessions over catchy turns of phrase, and when the album falters, it's because his words reduce a pair of lovers to their mouths and hands.

Title: American Utopia
Review: While not expressly political, American Utopia can't help playing as a reaction piece.

Title: Final Transmission
Review: As a tribute, it is wonderful, but even without the terrible context in which the album has come about, Final Transmission is superb. [8 Jun 2019, p.54]

Title: Salton Sea
Review: As a solo artist, Tomas Barfod's a few steps away from achieving sweet and total bliss, but Salton Sea is plenty evidence that every step taken in the future will be worth documenting.

Title: Loom
Review: Loom becomes tiresome as it reaches its second half, and the lack of lyrical clarity, though sincere in execution, balances poorly against the powerful instrumentation.

Title: Judy Sucks a Lemon For Breakfast
Review: This is Cornershop doing Cornershop very well.

Title: Yanqui U.X.O.
Review: The usual barrage of angry cello instrumentals. [Dec 2002, p.103]

Title: Floodlight Collective
Review: Despite the similarities, there’s actually a few brief moments in The Floodlight Collective where Pundt one-ups the band he derivates from, but there’s unfortunately as many that are boring enough to negate any previous triumph.

Title: The Complex
Review: Although its inspirations, musical and conceptual, trace as far back as Kraftwerk, The Complex serves as a reminder that modern devices and glistening production values can be applied to the most primal creative instincts, if utilized by the right --  blue -- hands.

Title: Gimmie Trouble
Review: The punk dominates more than it ever did on its electro-tilted predecessors.

Title: Fading Lines
Review: She proves adept at so many styles within her chosen niche on Fading Lines that her next album could go in any of four or five directions and sound very good.
1989 isn’t a “crossover” success. It’s the album every subsequent blockbuster must now reckon with.

Title: Zeppelin Over China
Review: Lyrics are lovably askew and songs rarely breach three-minutes. In conclusion: more is still more. [Mar 2019, p.99]

Title: In Time to Voices
Review: It may be a skip away from the processes they know best but, in 'In Time To Voices', Blood Red Shoes find fresh invention.

Title: Interpol
Review: Instead of ending tensely and dramatically they are the final whimper and sigh of an album named after a band that have lost their way and aren't sure which direction they should be heading.

Artist: Jenny Lewis with The Watson Twins
Title: Rabbit Fur Coat
Review: Though the singer-with-backup music relies on formula that won't set anyone's life straight, her melodic chops--sweet as a writer, supple as a singer--put the songs across.

Title: Intuition
Review: Intuition presents a sampler of contemporary R&B styles from producers including Timbaland, Just Blaze, Butter Beats and Calvo Da Gr8, giving the collection a disjointed air.

Title: Adventures in Your Own Backyard
Review: Adventures in Your Own Backyard is a frankly exquisite, elegantly crafted gem.

Title: Yours, Dreamily
Review: Needless to say, Yours, Dreamily can occasionally represent a more challenging listen than other Auerbach-contributed music. Occasionally though, these guys soar.

Title: Give Up
Review: Like any worthy match, the coming together gives each aspect assets that they'd be wont to find otherwise, the eletroclashy bursting with depth and the indie-croon thankfully adrenalized.

Title: Apollo Kids
Review: When it's all said and done, Ghostface Killah treats Apollo Kids like a seasoned veteran would treat a game on the hardwood; he picks his spots, lets his teammates have their moments, and takes over when necessary. In that respect, Apollo Kids is another project we can tally up in Ghost's win column.

Title: Sagara
Review: So Sagara sounds necessarily and unavoidably at odds with itself, a not wholly successful balancing act that lands its objects within sight and some distance from where its artist intended, but the effort is commendable and important.

Title: Electric
Review: This is another in a seemingly endless streak of quality albums from Richard Thompson, a journeyman artist in the homestretch of his long career, whose best years never seem to be behind him.

Title: Sunbathing Animal
Review: Another mix of sloppy slacker-pop, warped, indie jangles and insolent post-punk expressionism, Sunbathing Animal nevertheless feels more assured of itself than its acclaimed predecessor.

Title: Cursing the Sea
Review: Contrary to the slipshod musicianship of their older peers, September Girls are more than competent unit that model themselves accurately with a toughened exterior, and most of the flaws arise out of its production inconsistencies; the most glaring being the distracting interchange between vocal clarity and obfuscation between tracks, and the whirring fuzz is stretched out far too thin.

Title: Sweetener
Review: Grande can really sing, which is a treat in this Auto-Tuned era. Her four-octave range has been compared favourably to Mariah Carey’s, but her style is far more delicate and understated. She rarely unleashes full power blasts but her delight in singing is transparent and her producers take full advantage, layering her all over the tracks.

Title: Yankee Hotel Foxtrot
Review: After a while -- a familiarity period if you will -- it becomes clear that these songs are not only fully realized, they're damn near brilliant.

Title: Load Blown
Review: You leave Load Blown feeling that Black Dice, unlike many of their kin, are actually genuine experimentalists--even if it's with the caveat that sometimes it all rather blows up in their face. [Nov 2007, p.96]

Title: METAL GALAXY
Review: From the creative songwriting to the engaging performances, Metal Galaxy is certainly out of this world. With its awesome blend of musical styles, all infused with some form of metal aggression, this record is BABYMETAL at their most adventurous.

Title: The Knot
Review: The Knot turns the cliche about sophomore slumps on its head by being much stronger than If Children.

Title: Lost Highway
Review: Luckily, Bon Jovi's country-music move yields just... one irritant. [Jul 2007, p.113]

Title: The Madness of Many
Review: Abasi's unique thump technique gives needed life to passages other technical players would simply pick their way through, as Reyes and drummer Matt Garstka lock in to drive these sputtering rhythms home with power and proficiency.

Title: Some Echoes
Review: Like a computer geek with a romantic streak, Ohio's Aloha straddle the line between trad songcraft and proggy virtuosity.

Title: Theater of the Mind
Review: While his previous effort, 2006's "Release Therapy," was much more the thematically tight album and deserved a concept, this loose set of tunes is all-together more entertaining, thanks in no small part to a highly inspired Luda and all the punch lines he lands.

Title: Myth
Review: The multitude of sonics on Myth prove Geographer to be something of musical adventurers, even if the various paths they travel down don't always lead to success.

Title: Tracker
Review: There’s effortless and effortless, and this is an album that verges on the predictable.

Title: Close To The Glass
Review: Eight albums into its career (nine, if you count Sturm, a 2009 film score), the band has lost none of its ability to aim boldly for the gut.

Title: Braindrops
Review: [“Soft Power” is] an engrossing, haunted fable, a way to link society’s obsession with conspiracy to our basic needs for security and comfort. It’s proof that Tropical Fuck Storm are still clever when they want to be, able to channel obsessive rage into real insight. Braindrops could’ve used more like it.

Title: Flourish // Perish
Review: [In Kind undermines the mood of the entire album with a series of acrobatic vocal yelps.] It's a shame, because otherwise this is a record of near-perfect beauty. [Sep 2013, p.88]

Title: Discover a Lovelier You
Review: The album succeeds in creating a dreamy mood that is both soothing and slightly unsettling. And yet this mood is relentless, and, ultimately, all the songs begin to sound the same.

Title: The Pinkprint
Review: While it's too early to tell if The Pinkprint is a classic, it's safe to say it's her best album to date. Minaj was finally able to out-rap herself and purge issues she's struggled with in private in her most exposed fashion yet.

Title: Faith
Review: It hasn’t completely reinvented the wheel for Hurts, nor has it allowed them to rest on old habits. Instead, it presents them at their most open – and in age of isolation, there’s much to admire in that.

Title: High Risk Behaviour
Review: High Risk Behavior is so full of hooks, personality, and humour that you might find yourself, wanting to play that 28-minute record again. It's a rare thing to want to hear a record on repeat, but rarer still is a record that you feel like you know having just heard it just once, and this is particularly true of the singles, which sound closer to 'classic' Chats than a lot of the album.

Title: Dear Catastrophe Waitress
Review: It's a rich, bright, clever and engaging album that should trash those lame prejudices against Belle & Sebastian once and for all.

Title: Untouchables
Review: Nothing here explains the reported $4.5 million budget. [28 June 2002, p.142]

Title: Monkeytown
Review: Monkeytown is the sound of two men working in harmony, perfectly in control of their machines. And it may just be one of the albums of the year.

Title: Silent Shout
Review: This is one of the most rich and accomplished albums of recent times. Essential.

Title: Heaven Is Whenever
Review: Their loud, rough and tumble early efforts on Almost Killed Me and Separation Sunday have combined nicely here with a sense of southern rock and pop rock from the past few albums to produce another gem for an amazingly consistent band with plenty of room left to grow.

Title: Blood Mountain
Review: Yes, sometimes more is better. [21 Sep 2006, p.82]

Title: That Don't Make Me a Bad Guy
Review: The 47-year-old Oklahoma native alters that repertoire somewhat with That Don't Make me a Bad Guy, sticking to accessible, down-home rock even as his singing ranges from new directions to bland drains on his natural character.

Title: Upside Down Mountain
Review: It's a testament to Oberst's enduring versatility that Upside Down Mountain can accommodate the antic creepiness of "Governor's Ball" as well as the transcendent uplift of "Time Forgot," but the album's moments of sentimentality make Oberst sound like just another chart-climbing purveyor of feel-good folky schlock.

Title: White Men Are Black Men Too
Review: The album won't win many new fans, but for those already clued in it supplies a fresh batch of engaging, abstract production and, especially in the meat of "Old Rock n Roll", a few meals' worth of food for thought.

Title: IRM
Review: As a pairing between two artists, the album works, though not nearly as much as it could have if both were at the top of their game.

Title: Oak Island
Review: Nightlands have created something that's utterly self-contained.

Title: Honeyblood
Review: While the album has its forgettable moments, there are points where McVicar and Tweeddale really show what they’re made of--and that, if you piss them off, you’re going to know about it.

Title: Songbird
Review: It's apparent Nelson doesn't share Adams's enthusiasm for the Fleetwood Mac and Grateful Dead numbers, but he's at home with Gram Parsons's $1,000 Wedding and Leonard Cohen's well-covered Hallelujah.

Title: Ghost Notes
Review: No longer ghosts, with this strong, same-as-it-ever-was album, Veruca Salt are now full-on zombies, the riffing dead. They don’t wanna go.

Title: FLOTUS
Review: It's all really cohesive, and while no tracks jump out as jarringly different, each one is filled with deliberateness and prettiness.

Title: Hamburg Demonstrations
Review: There is nothing here that is dramatically different to what he offered on his debut solo album, but the end result is charming and beautifully comforting nonetheless.

Title: Rock N Roll Consciousness
Review: While there will undoubtedly be some who bemoan the same failing within Rock n Roll Consciousness, there’s no way Thurston Moore is going to stop for anyone.

Title: Mountain Battles
Review: Despite its evocative title of raw sinewy snarl, Mountain Battles is, sadly, a narcoleptic disappointment. [Spring 2008, p.74]

Title: Miike Snow
Review: Their packed schedule has finally allowed space for this lavish eponymous debut. [Sep 2009, p.95]

Title: Dummy Boy
Review: Dummy Boy is one of the most unlistenable rap records of this year. ... He’s delivered a bland project. Often, it’s as though he took what was in his drafts folder and released it as a “studio album.”

Title: World Painted Blood
Review: Tom Araya's shriek has grown ponderous, and not until rosary-ripping closer 'Not of This God' do the four mid-fortysomethings bypass their rigid polkacore hopscotch for a devastating groove.

Title: Free Will
Review: The handful of breaks from his patented gutter raps aren't enough to compensate for the monotony in his dozen interchangeable guns-and-butter records.

Title: My Best Friend Is You
Review: Now 22, she's full-on pissy and proud, pulling from some reliable forebears on this fascinating follow-up.

Title: Abandoned
Review: It's truly an incredible piece of work that excavates the very core of human existence. [Sep 2015, p.95]

Title: English Tapas
Review: Williamson has never been mournful in quite the same way that he is here, nor so disappointed in what he sees around him, whether it’s politicians, musicians or just ordinary people. This comes through not only in the lyrics but in their delivery.

Artist: Thao & the Get Down Stay Down
Title: Know Better Learn Faster
Review: Know Better Learn Faster mostly sounds like a young artist coming into her own--in music and life and love.

Title: Good Luck With Whatever
Review: Wonderful. ... If the new album is short on the breakup songs that once were Dawes’ rueful bread-and-butter, this album’s two quietest songs are among the best Goldsmith’s written.

Title: Hobo Rocket
Review: Like many psych-heavy records today, the album doesn’t say much lyrically. The lack of deep lyrical content is an easy detail to overlook due to Pond’s complex execution of instrumentation.

Title: The Album About Nothing
Review: The Album About Nothing is his most personal piece of work to date, and also his best. That hair-trigger sensitivity can be off-putting, but it's also what makes him good at what he does.

Title: Secular Hymns
Review: Secular Hymns is very close to the feel of a Peyroux live show, and one in which she’s clearly having a ball.

Title: United States of Horror
Review: United States Of Horror is wired on a different kind of anger--these tracks seethe with violence and disgust, raging at dark political orders, economic inequality, racial tension and fractured society.

Title: All Hope Is Gone
Review: Occasional, more straightforwardly anthemic moments approach the mawkishness of Nickelback, but Slipknot remain showmen at heart. [Oct 2008, p.108]

Title: Kid A
Review: Not content to embrace familiar dance-music genres like trance (the way Madonna does when she's feeling experimental), the band delves into the most outré electronic music imaginable, from the amniotic soundscapes of Brian Eno to the industrial gristle of Coil. The result is Radiohead's best album...

Title: Ringleader of the Tormentors
Review: Longtime devotees may miss Morrissey's Smiths-era vocal histrionics, but his supple croon has matured into a thing of beauty. [May 2006, p.103]

Title: Here
Review: Here never becomes too cosy, there are also plenty of sparkling textural buzzes and blips to ensure that Teenage Fanclub's traditional consistency remains impressive rather than soporific. [Sep 2016, p.91]

Title: Group Therapy
Review: The magic is still there. [#53, p.73]

Title: A World Out of Time
Review: A World Out Of Time was recorded as a whole, a distinction that has some subtle effects on the album's sequencing and pacing without diminishing the elements of collage.

Title: Downtown Church
Review: The final number is “All Creatures of Our God and King”, a traditional hymn sung with piano only, and it showcases Griffin’s voice at its most pure, a fitting and mesmerizing end to an album that, regardless of one’s belief, is an uplifting, moving, and exquisite listening experience.

Title: Paracosm
Review: Greene's meticulous creations are still slow-rolling and thickly layered, but this time he and returning Animal Collective producer Ben Allen slather on less futuristic sounds.

Title: The Bake Sale
Review: The release of the Cool Kids' debut EP still radiated sonic excitement, a blast at once sharp, funny and intimate. Here, after all, is a triumph of absolute aestheticism.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: There are moments when all this earnestness turns sickly and Burns gets too serious about his gifts... but the eclectic moments of bass, banjo and French vocals... manage to jerk things back into focus. [#71, p.88]

Title: Moonshine Freeze
Review: While the record may fall slightly short of Bashed Out's high benchmark and its plethora of exceptional melodies, Moonshine Freeze remains a fine addition to This Is the Kit's already excellent back catalog.
The Gloaming is different because it gets at the lovely essence of the Irish tradition without sentimentality or dumbing down--and also isn’t afraid to make it modern.

Title: When I Pretend to Fall
Review: Heaves with harmonic charm. [Oct 2003, p.111]

Title: Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!!
Review: Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!! sees Cave at his wittiest and most relaxed, though perhaps also most detatched. [Apr 2008, p.53]

Title: Brainwashed
Review: Brainwashed is rich in warm Harrison vocals, couple with his distinctive slide guitar style. Unfortunately, it's also rife with often too-glossy production.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: The sound is still layered and textured, and those gut-achingly gorgeous seamless harmonies between Sparhawk and wife Mimi Parker are still there.

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: As singles, the LP works. But as a whole product, listeners could start wondering if they hit “repeat” by accident.

Title: Losing Sleep
Review: Rather than making Collins sound as though he's trying to play catch-up to what the current generation of indie-rock kids are doing, the co-writes and duets on the album simply come across as a logical progression of the kind of retro-minded, catchy rock that Collins has been writing and performing over the course of his career.
It is a short, sharp album, produced entirely by Kanye West’s former mentor No ID.

Title: Versus
Review: It’s an overegged pudding at times, but to its credit Versus is anything but polite; with brass and bass to the fore, Craig chips away at our preconceptions--he’s here for more than the black tie and polite applause.  [Jun 2017, p.61]

Title: White Trash with Money
Review: This is an addictive record, enveloping in its sound and memorable in its songs.

Title: Girl Going Nowhere
Review: Girl Going Nowhere, her unprophetically titled debut, is rife with autobiographical detail, rowdiness and sensitivity.

Title: Penny Sparkle
Review: A nicely composed mix, no doubt, and one that's often gorgeous to boot, but Penny Sparkle mostly sounds like a band getting complacent with age.

Title: Our Bright Future
Review: All the tracks on her eighth studio album, Our Bright Future, are as clear as her voice, and the lyrics are simple and honest.

Title: Antics
Review: Antics is ridiculously good. [Oct 2004, p.112]

Title: The Amazons
Review: This album is a belter, a shout-it-to-the-rooftops, punch-the-sky, yell-along-at-the-top-of-your-voice storm. It is crammed top to bottom with monster riffs, anthemic choruses and the sheer exuberant thrill of being young, in love, and armed with a fuzzbox.

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: With drums, strings, pianos, amps and backup singers, this is the biggest sounding record ever for a band that used to consist of one guy on acoustic guitar. [Apr 2008, p.81]

Title: Body Music
Review: Moving from urgent dance-pop (“Bad Idea”), to minimalist pillow talk (“Friends to Lovers”), to bassy underground undertows (“Lost and Found”), Body Music is the sound of AlunaGeorge just getting started--and they could go anywhere from here.

Title: Die Knowing
Review: On their third album since Andrew Neufeld moved to vocals, Comeback Kid were poised to strike out, but pleasantly, they instead knock Die Knowing out of the park.

Title: Mazes
Review: Mazes is all about songwriting growth, lyric melody, more elaborate textures, and accessible riffs. They underscore Moon Duo's heavy stuff and offer something refreshingly different in the process.

Title: NYC, HELL 3:00 AM
Review: The lulling confusion of NYC uncannily enacts the unstable identity of the city itself. Ferraro paints it as aggressive, oppressive, and unknowable; then offers an audio tour of its darker depths, rats and all.

Title: Life On Earth
Review: While it won’t be for everyone, and won’t be an album for all occasions, Life on Earth is a stark, devastating achievement.

Title: Reggie
Review: Yet for all the patchy unevenness that comes out in places, the album is also a consistently likable effort.

Title: The First Lady
Review: Her tightest set yet.

Title: Replica Sun Machine
Review: It’s definitely not album of the year (nor would it have nabbed that distinction in 2007 when it was actually released on the other side of the Atlantic), but the Shortwave Set bring just enough innovation with them to make this 45 minute disc worth your while.

Title: The Little Willies
Review: Maybe this isn't a major record, but it's thoroughly likeable record that doesn't lose its charm on repeated plays.

Title: As Is Now
Review: [His] most satisfying collection of material since 1993's "Wild Wood".

Title: False Idols
Review: False Idols comes close to vanquishing the spectre of ‘Maxinquaye’, comprising a fleshy and nasally return to form.

Title: Careless World: Rise of the Last King
Review: Attempts to keep one foot in the streets and another in the mainstream, and largely succeeds. [May 2012, p.102]

Title: Mar Dulce
Review: Tango remains the constant for Bajofondo, but the 17 tracks offer quite a few variations on a theme.

Title: The Best Little Secrets Are Kept
Review: It's hard to shake the empty feeling at the end of each these songs; The Best Little Secrets Are Kept has an inescapable, intentional tawdriness.

Title: Brothers and Sisters of the Eternal Son
Review: Sure, stripped-down, acoustic versions of the songs could’ve worked, but with help from producer Richard Swift, they’re fleshed out into psychedelic dreams dappled with field recordings, Latin guitar and Jurado’s serene vocals, raising existential questions that don’t quite get answered.

Title: The Grotto
Review: The songs, while as elegant and naturally paced as they've ever been, tend to merely drift along.

Title: The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends
Review: A terrific package. [Jul 2012, p.71]

Title: A Shut-In's Prayer
Review: Without sacrificing any of his detailed, anecdotal lyricism or thoughtful keyboard arrangements, Advanced Base managed to construct a record you can play over and over again without feeling so sorry for yourself.

Title: Useless Coordinates
Review: Useless Coordinates is not a new approach but a refashioning of past ideas as a powerful, vibrant tool to question the world through art. Drahla has nailed this concept.

Title: The Richest Man In Babylon
Review: One of their more intriguing works to date, capably blending vocal theatrics, spritual exploration and subtle songcraft in one sitting.

Title: It Had to Be You: The Great American Songbook
Review: Here, he sings against syrupy, obvious orchestral arrangements, driven by a beat that sometimes seems on the verge of a nap -- all of which encourages Stewart's worst habits: He sounds lazy, glib and uninvolved, just the opposite of when he still mattered.

Title: The Lady Killer
Review: As an album The Lady Killer achieves everything it purports to be. Its music is familiar enough to attract broad attention.

Title: David Cook
Review: Indeed, it's hard to distinguish Cook's sound from that of his own idols, like Our Lady Peace and Better Than Ezra.

Title: Big Station
Review: This is Escovedo's most diverse collection of material since 2006 John Cale production The Boxing Mirror.

Title: The Boxer
Review: While the adventurous Boxer pares off Bloc Party's ponderous streak, it leaves room for Kele's hopeless romanticism, and the end result hits in all the right places--head, hips and heart alike.

Title: The Amalgamut
Review: The only misstep is in the pacing.

Title: Golden Sings That Have Been Sung
Review: Whilst there are still examples of the kind of dexterous acoustic guitar playing now closely associated with Walker’s music, there is also a greater sense of space and time here, enabling Walker to place greater emphasis on his lyrics.

Title: Always
Review: While experimentation and weirdness still abound--as on the abrasively sung-spoke "I Luv Abortion"--Always seems much more tempered than past efforts, extending the poppy sensibility of 2010's Dear God, I Hate Myself.

Title: The Black Crown
Review: Although there are storming successes amongst the album's 11 tracks (such as 'Slaves To Substance' and 'You Only Live Once') The Black Crown falls a fraction shy of the pack-shedding statement it needs to be.

Title: Utopia
Review: Traditionalists might still wonder where all the nice steady beats have gone, why so little music here is anchored. The dominant message, though, is of limitlessness, of hope and, on Future Forever, of “a matriarchal dome” with “musical scaffolding”.

Title: Ask the Night
Review: Occasionally too sweet for its own good, Fink's atmosphere of perpetual twilight never fails to soothe, even as it unsettles. [Fall 2009, p.58]

Title: Synthetica
Review: On Synthetica, Metric isn't necessarily making a transition; they're simply taking stock of where they've been before figuring out where they're going.

Title: Evil Heat
Review: For all its attempts at hipster currency, Evil Heat reveals the needle-shaped creative hole where the drugs used to be. [#57, p.102]

Title: Hourglass
Review: A more electronic, better built, and altogether better deal than "Monsters," thanks mostly to the singer and-don't-you-forget-to-mention songwriter's better sense of self.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel
Review: Tell Me How You Really Feel is Courtney Barnett at her angriest and most vulnerable, but being a drinker of details means she can also blow the beauty of life’s little things up to full-size.

Title: Ghostory
Review: The album is so cleanly produced that it sounds like they can't afford a flaw. And ironically, it's this seeming aversion to being perceived as imperfect that holds them back.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: In many ways Boys & Girls it is as note-perfect an album as you'll hear all year, yet it's also often perfectly inert.

Title: Yours Truly
Review: The Long Beach ska punks have a new singer, a more melodic mellow bounce--and a lot less edge. [22 Jul 2011, p.73]

Title: This Gift
Review: Look beneath the surface sheen, then, and you'll see gratefully receive This Gift as the best, most complete, Sons And Daughters long-player to date.

Title: The Graceless Age
Review: I don't expect to hear a better album this year.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: Phoenix are no '80s copycats, but they occupy a sweet spot where influences and their own flashy banks of synths and treated guitars sound meaty and perfect together.

Title: The Music
Review: How anyone can describe Leeds' The Music as a "best new band" is beyond me. Unless they're over fifty, sport a footballer's perm and weep at Almost Famous.

Title: Beast Moans
Review: A muddled mess of convoluted textures that is at times, frankly, unlistenable.

Title: Forever Abomination
Review: Basically, this is exciting, skilled, fist-pumping, true-to-life stuff made by good-seeming guys who, in the end, aren't afraid to laugh, goof around, or make fun of themselves.

Title: Ten
Review: Not what you'd call an enjoyable listen, but one to be respected anyway, and also one that worms its way into your head.

Title: Grey Tickles, Black Pressure
Review: If there’s nothing quite as heartstopping here as Pale Green Ghosts’ Glacier, which doled out honest and profound advice to teens teetering on the verge of coming out, there are plenty of songs whose warmth glows brightly amid the black humour.

Title: C'est La Vie
Review: There’s gorgeous, candid song-craft at work, ‘C’est La Vie 2’ urging that “they say that love is easy if you let it be”. That self-reflection runs like a golden thread, particularly on the woozy ‘These Rocks.’

Title: Reset
Review: Reset is an enjoyable 42 minutes of dystopian aphorism and boasts more dense textures and a keener ear for juxtaposition than its predecessor. It's a definite progression; just don't expect it to tear down the firewalls of GCHQ any time soon.

Title: Wasting Light
Review: Even after several listens there's little here to really strike a chord with the long-standing Foos fan. That's not to say it's poor - it's far from that.

Title: The Hungry Saw
Review: The band were making good music before they split, and the revamped lineup have picked up right where the previous incarnation left off.

Title: Making Time
Review: Jamie Woon has dropped a second LP every bit as captivating as his first, and it’s hard to find any faults with this piece of work. Sumptuously slick, and with the humidity of a tropical locale. Make sure you make time for Making Time.

Title: Tempest
Review: on Tempest, his latest album, Bob Dylan mostly sounds insane. That volatility can yield tremendous rewards-- on the ferocious "Pay in Blood", it clarifies his nihilism, his cruelty-- but it can also be distractingly unruly, inching toward self-mockery, all wild undulation and hairball-retch. Which would be okay-- embraced, even!-- if the rest of Tempest didn't feel so rote.

Title: Our Version of Events
Review: What's magical about this album is how Ms. Sande's stance remains unmistakable regardless of what the backdrop is. It's not a flawless album, but rather one with a number of flawless moments.

Title: The Beast In Its Tracks
Review: He sets his bruised but unbowed soul against a stark musical backing and rediscovers the power of keeping it simple. Beautiful.

Title: Great Big Flamingo Burning Moon
Review: Execution-wise, it's perhaps a little too disjointed in nature. [Apr - May 2015, p.88]

Title: Third Law
Review: Just as deep and cosmic in scope as its predecessor, this album eschews traditional beats in favour of a primordial throb, a rhythm that seems to originate deep within the planet's core.

Title: Live from the Underground
Review: It breaks very little new ground--which does have the upside of the songs sounding catchy because you feel like you've heard it all before.

Title: Lemonade
Review: With all matters of the heart explored in extremely intimate detail it sees Beyoncé back on top of the pop world ready to slay like only she can.

Title: Take Her Up To Monto
Review: Monto occasionally overwhelms as its leading light pivots. Patience is rather vital as the album expands and Murphy continues to contemplate. There’s no padding here, but like any good trip into an intriguing mind you may emerge from the swell a touch dizzy.

Title: Recess
Review: Even at its biggest, it sounds disappointingly thin.

Title: Sun Giant
Review: It all adds up to a landmark in American music, an instant classic.

Title: Full Circle Nightmare
Review: There's nothing remotely new here--and his hyper-ventilating yelp won't be for everyone--but it's a rollicking 40-minute ride. [Apr 2018, p.108]

Title: Dark Sky Paradise
Review: His third and best record isn't that moment yet, but he's one step closer.

Title: The Shade of Poison Trees
Review: Carrabba’s keening grandiloquence may have lost some of its most explicitly cathartic qualities, but The Shade of Poison Trees remains his best work in years.

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: This is tough, honest, uncompromising beauty and the next great voice in music. [Apr 2005, p.86]

Title: Modern Guilt
Review: Nothing makes as quick of an impact as 'Crazy,' but give the tunes time and you'll find they stick around.

Title: Narkopop
Review: Voigt certainly hasn’t lost touch with electronic music, though Narkopop reclaims the sound of it that is most unmistakably his, while also giving it more variance in tone.

Title: Songs of Innocence
Review: Bono may have self-deprecatingly described Songs of Innocence as “the blood, sweat and tears of some Irish guys...in your junk mail,” but it’s not even that interesting--it’s just a blank message.

Title: Sparrow
Review: Sparrow is sharply constructed as an album, setting a mood with its first song and then finding variations on this lush, enveloping sound. It's a record designed for late nights, whether those nights are lonely or romantic.

Title: Ghost Blonde
Review: There's an ineffable quality to No Joy's music that truly works. [Dec 2010, p.51]

Title: Meteorites
Review: All in all though, Meteorites is a decent, if hardly vital, album from one of this country’s true national treasures.

Title: ilp
Review: Rarely do you stumble into a world so richly realized and so warmly, curiously inviting. [No. 104, p.58]

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: Patti Smith, Eddie Vedder, Peaches and Lenny Kaye are along for the ride, helping Collapse Into Now stand tall in R.E.M.'s richly diverse canon.

Title: Before A Million Universes
Review: Though it may have lost some of the urgency of their debut, Before a Million Universes has allowed the band to develop a level of genuine introspection rarely seen in the hardcore of today.

Title: Blacklisted
Review: Blacklisted's accompaniment is roundly excellent and evocative, but Case's voice is what really sells the record.

Title: Changing Tune
Review: Streamlines their punk blasts as they aim for a wider audience. [Oct 2012, p.98]

Title: Come with Us
Review: Too often, all it offers is the rumble of starting engines. [Feb 2002, p.124]

Title: La Petite Mort
Review: Solid but somewhat samey. [Jul 2014, p.109]

Title: Purple Naked Ladies
Review: The Internet still feels like an important first step, not only for its willingness to test the limits of current hip hop/R&B, but as proof that Odd Future is more than just a one-man show. [Mar 2012, p.108]

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: The King of Limbs is Radiohead's Sky Blue Sky–a reliably enjoyable record that follows a heightened run of musical genius.

Title: Death Song
Review: The more spacious likes of "Comanche Moon" and "Life Song" suggest an ambition to nail a headline spot at the UFO Club, which may not boast much novelty a half-century after the fact, but can still elicit a contact high. [Jun 2017, p.23]

Title: 200 Million Thousand
Review: Here they make less of an effort to conceal the pop smarts percolating beneath the slop-rock surface; catchy little gems like 'Starting Over' and 'I'll Be with You' help make this the most satisfying Black Lips album yet.

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: Ultimately, Allison is a pleasure to listen to even in the space where she floats right through your head.

If you already have the original download from last year, there isn't a ton here that's really alluring, although the three bonus tracks are all pretty good in an of themselves. If you haven't yet heard this one, its by all means time to pick it up.

Title: Secret Wars
Review: Secret Wars feels like a keeper, like an album I’ll pull out and play and still love ten years from now.

Title: The Orchard
Review: Disappointing return from orchestral indie types. [July 2011, p. 117]
21 is just a logical, major label extension of her girl-ish, diary-dream optimism.

Title: E = MCÂ²
Review: At the end of the day, however, E=MC2 is nothing more than a shallow imitation of its predecessor, the unexciting kid cousin of an arena-sized R&B watermark.

Title: Sharpen Your Teeth
Review: An oddity for sure, but much too good to be restricted to specialist alt-rock record retailers. [July 2002, p.122]

Title: Triangle
Review: In some ways, this feels like the album Susanna's career has been building toward; her music has always united the heart and mind, and she does so with striking creativity on Triangle.

Title: Blurred Lines
Review: "Take It Easy on Me" (produced by Timbaland and J-Roc), "Give It 2 U" (Dr. Luke and Cirkut), "Feel Good" (will.i.am), and the deluxe edition bonus cut "Pressure" (the Cataracs) are nothing like the title track's undeniable disco-funk groove, and not one of them is among Thicke's best. They do, however, lack desperation and help convey the album's prevailing casual, lighthearted feel.

Title: New Chain
Review: Where's the NoDoz? Chillwave may have officially become too chill, bros.

Title: Snapshot
Review: It's all meaty, squalling guitar riffs, foghorn blasts of harmonica, and a confusion of solid speed with actual excitement.

Title: Pedals
Review: Although it's been a full decade since their last release, United by Fate, Rival Schools don't miss a beat on this reunion disc. [Mar/Apr 2011, p. 88]

Title: Landlord
Review: Landlord is fantastic, crafted, big-stage trap with the lissom, conversational feel of a mixtape.

Title: Livin' on a High Note
Review: The production is restrained, leaving plenty of space for Staples's rich vocals, although some songs feel a bit too clean and reserved. It's all very pleasant but lacks the fire and passion we want from her.

Title: Walk The River
Review: For a band that once stood out for its too-much-ness, Walk the River now gives us too much of the wrong things: too many midtempo songs, too many minor-key acoustic strums, too many codas that outstay their welcome without really connecting.

Title: Local Business
Review: The group raging behind him on Local Business are minimalist punchers, cruiserweights mixing a little Thin Lizzy and Big Star pop-ulism in with the basement bile.

Title: Brave
Review: J. Lo's music has been upgraded from quite bad to merely bad. [Dec 2007, p.148]

Title: Anything in Return
Review: Anything In Return us ultimately a chill listen, but not a necessarily memorable one. [No. 95, p.59]

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: He's the kind of singer whose voice you instinctively trust. It's a resource that brings continuity to a fifth album touching on greed, death and dogs. [Feb 2015, p.72]

Title: Nausea
Review: Craft Spells’ previous work wasn’t bad, but Nausea is such an unexpected metamorphosis that Vallesteros could just as well have changed the band name. Even in a crowded dreampop field, this is music to bask in, whatever you call it.

Title: Pocketful of Sunshine
Review: Bedingfield's second record is slight but filled with hooky, crisply produced songs that sound great on a sunny day.

Title: So Beautiful or So What
Review: It's his best album since 1990's The Rhythm of the Saints, and it also sums up much of what makes Simon great.

Title: From King To A GOD
Review: If his discography to this point was the regular season, From King To A GOD could be a sign that play-off Maquina is going to be a problem.

Title: Trickfinger
Review: Trickfinger often provokes an engaging anxiety, but when Frusciante's not pushing at the edges of the form it can lack the magic of his otherwise unapologetically experimental solo work.

Title: Lovers Rock
Review: Lovers' Rock ranks among the finest albums of the year, as Sade, nimbly utilizing that distinctively smoky, vulnerable instrument that is her voice, weaves gentle yet insinuating odes to love and loss.

Title: Nosebleed Weekend
Review: On the whole, Nosebleed Weekend is a triumph, The Coathangers’ strongest top-to-bottom album and one that proves the band can maintain its essence as it evolves.

Title: Candy Salad
Review: The richly produced, melodically generous Candy Salad is plenty to chew on, but one can't help wishing its songs could be as vibrant as its sounds.

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: Despite Jenkinson playing every instrument, including his customised six-string bass, it does sound like a group effort.

Title: African Giant
Review: African Giant is a cohesive piece of work. The tracks have a subtle dancehall theme which threads through them. 19 tracks may have been too ambitious in this case but Burna Boy is an example of why African music is gaining popularity and becoming more mainstream.
Whether or not Joan of Arc are intentionally pulling back from some of the density of He’s Got the Whole, a bit too much space leaves stretches of 1984 less than solid in the process.

Title: Roadsinger (To Warm You Through The Night)
Review: Roadsinger is an improvement on his patchy 2006 comeback "An Other Cup." [Jun 2009, p.135]

Title: Relaxer
Review: Fans may balk at the curveballs--Hit Me Like That Snare is a louche garage-rock foray--but they telegraph the self-assurance that doesn’t rely on overcomplication.

Title: Red
Review: It's sexy, daring, and complete.

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: The end result is an unfortunate fact that while Death Cab For Cutie seems as capable as ever at expressing themselves, they are running out of things to say. Or, at least, things worth hearing.

Title: Worship The Sun
Review: There’s a definite progression in the songwriting and the tunes are soaked in the kind of timeless California sunshine you just don’t get from Brits.

Title: Cannibal
Review: While she occasionally goes too far even by the exceedingly lax standards of a Ke$ha record-really, "C U Next Tuesday?"--Ke$ha is in full command of her artlessness on Cannibal, marrying airhead kiss-offs with chirpily upbeat, ringtone-ready dance-pop.

Title: Fire in the Hole
Review: A few tracks bump, but for the most part, Lord Jamar's production couldn't make punks jump up, much less get beat down. [Sep 2004, p.114]

Title: Join Us
Review: Overall, there's less headbanging potential here than on their finest moment – 2001's Grammy-winning song Boss of Me from Malcolm in the Middle – but it doesn't matter. This is still a brilliant summer listen.

Title: At War With The Mystics
Review: Much of the CD is both beautiful and heartfelt. [7 Apr 2006, p.59]

Title: Jason Isbell & The 400 Unit
Review: There's no shortage of variety, but there's a slight feeling of colourlessness about it, a sense that none of the 11 tracks quite have the bit of magic that lifts a good album to dizzy heights.

Title: Try Me
Review: The entire thing is a cathartic art project that feels like the moment of forced calm after an exhausting sob. [Feb 2014, p.92]

Title: New Brigade
Review: All these lurches and groans and crashes and bangs and stutters and roars come together to form one consistently rousing, emotionally immediate whole. From them to you.

Title: This Unruly Mess I've Made
Review: Many of This Unruly Mess I’ve Made’s flaws could’ve very well been forgotten, or at least temporarily swept under the rug, had the actual music been good.

Title: Plunge
Review: Plunge is riskier than anything she has made before. It is sometimes harsh, often dissonant, frequently audacious.

Title: The Curved Line
Review: The Curved Line is a pretty harmless, quirky listen, and enjoyable enough if you've got a bit of a sweet tooth.

Title: Hold My Home
Review: Hold My Home is arguably the strongest record--with the most consistent highlights--that the band has yet to deliver, and it bodes well for their future.

Title: thank u, next
Review: Thank U, Next flaunts Grande’s emotional healing; it’s suffused with the joy of discovering that what didn’t kill her really did make her stronger. ... As eager as she sounds on Thank U, Next to embrace new ideas and attitudes, the album shows that she can still do the old-fashioned stuff--the big vocals that connect her back to Mariah and Whitney and Celine--when she wants to.

Title: Aloha Moon
Review: Their sound yearns for those Pacific nights, with a hazy moon illuminating San Francisco Bay. It's going to take a bit more than sparkles and glitter, though, to propel their intelligently crafted dream-pop a bit further.

Title: The Fall
Review: Here, Jones ties up loose ends, unafraid to sound smooth or sultry, letting in just enough dissonance and discord to give this dimension, creating a subtle but rather extraordinary low-key record that functions as a piece of mood music but lingers longer, thanks to its finely crafted songs.

Title: Last Place
Review: It's a subtler and darker sibling to The Sophtware Slump or Just Like The Fambly Cat. [Apr 2017, p.30]

Title: Cumbia Siglo XXI
Review: While it's not always clear what's on offer amid the density, there's always a sweetener on top to keep you coming back. [Sep 2020, p.111]

Title: In The Silence
Review: The everything-but-the-kitchen-sink promotional campaign--an appearance on Made In Chelsea here, a cover of ‘Wrecking Ball’ on Dutch radio there--might smack of desperation. Fortunately, In the Silence is more than good enough to dispel any such impressions.

Title: Seven Dials
Review: A long overdue return, and well worth the wait.

Title: Cupid's Head
Review: More than ever, Willner’s own soul is put on display through his repurposing of sound, and what results is both synthetic and organic, both detailed and blurry, further cementing The Field’s reputation in the electronic ether.

Title: Hollandaze
Review: This is a carefree release that is meant for our "reptilian" brain.

Title: Descended Like Vultures
Review: One of the year's best. [29 Oct 2005]

Title: Other Life
Review: Where the songs are slow, the fruity Bontempi keyboards are gruelling and the singing comes on like Jimmy Somerville weeping over a dead pet in a marbled mausoleum. But get past the Bronski Beat animal trauma vibes and Savage's other life is rich and full.

Title: Disappeared
Review: If anything, Disappeared reestablishes Spring Heel Jack as drum-n-bass experts, gifted at layered percussion, and erudite at unsettling listeners with an uneasy ambience.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: Hummingbird plays like a sophisticated and logical forward progression. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.88]

Title: Absolution
Review: A massive concept album that is so gluttonously huge-sounding that it makes The Wall sound like a Sebadoh record. [#10, p.94]

Title: Rainwater Cassette Exchange
Review: Rainwater Cassette Exchange confirms--Deerhunter may never make a loud or abrasive album again, but they have other, deeper fires, burning away fierce as ever.

Title: Lazarus
Review: Half brilliant, half laughable solo debut from Gym Class Heroes front man.

Title: Champ
Review: Champ, their second album, shows a slight advancement from Elephant Gun, with more complicated song structures and more creative instrumentation. [Summer 2010, p.86]

Title: You, You're a History in Rust
Review: A showcase of a band who have learned lessons and improved upon them, quietly getting better and better until something really special emerges.

Title: Cage Tropical
Review: While one occasionally wishes that Frankie Rose could get a few paces further out from under her own shadow, the best of Cage Tropical does something similar, taking her own retro influences and using them to leapfrog her way out of a creative rut.

Title: Kid A
Review: It is a kind of virtual rock in which the roots have been cut away, and the formal language -- hook, riff, bridge -- has been warped, liquefied and, in some songs, thrown out altogether. If you're looking for instant joy and easy definition, you are swimming in the wrong soup.... Kid A is a work of deliberately inky, often irritating obsession.

Title: Echo Ono
Review: Incandescence, in the age of fluorescence. [#39, p.69]

Title: Phoenix
Review: Bazan's voice is more full and powerful than ever, and the return to familiar writing processes pays off. Every note from every instrument expertly weaves together with pristine, yet organic movement, as if Bazan was a Baroque composer for string quartet.

Title: It's Decided
Review: The results are intimate yet expansive--a pleasing balance between post-rock sonic experimentation and traditional songcraft.

Title: Feature Magnetic
Review: Kool Keith trades verses with an array of guest stars, packaged with bare hooks and brisk running times. In most cases, he pulls his collaborators into his own orbit.

Title: Testify
Review: The most notable aspect of Testify, in fact, is how little P.O.D., or their guitars, have to say.

Title: Latin
Review: It won't be to everyone's tastes and it's clear with a name like theirs they won't be appearing on Fearne Cotton's playlist anytime soon, but there's an energy and vitality to Latin that's impossible to deny.

Title: Where The Humans Eat
Review: [His] roughhewn compositions shuffle along with a shambolic charm, giving the collection an earthy appeal and conversational warmth. [#16, p.96]

Title: Flesh Tone
Review: It's clear that Kelis has carved out a new niche for herself, dancing in front of the turntables till the lights come on, if they dare.
