Title: Love vs Money
Review: Cliche love songs, too many similar beats and melodies, and a lack of energy all pull the album down, and when the album is composed in a way that should be fully appreciated in its entirety, the lack of variety affect the album’s success even more.

Title: Dancing Backward in High Heels
Review: The result might have been sharper if someone other than Louis XIV's Jason Hill produced it; his washed-out murk and puddles of reverb render the whole thing a mess. Luckily, there's just no stopping Johansen and Sylvain.

Title: Petra Goes To The Movies
Review: Truly cinematic and imbued with humour and pathos, popcorn not included. [Apr 2013, p.94]

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: Focus too deeply, and it feels less like a collection of songs and more like a showplace for his sonic finery. As mood music, though, it's a sweet trip. [Feb 2020, p.83]

Title: Harry Styles
Review: Despite Styles' self-conscious references, his debut avoids indulgence. [Aug 2017, p.110]

Review: Trouble is, after one listen it becomes evident that MB hardly benefit from further investigation – they’re just another hipster band who got lucky.

Title: Sinematic
Review: A muddled attempt to signal contemporary relevance. [Oct 2019, p.88]

Review: His new project is even more deranged, much of its sounding like Butthole Surfers driving at you on a space-age steamroller. [Jun 2013, p.93]

Title: Highest Point In Cliff Town
Review: Impressively it's under a year after they signed to Heavenly and they've already released this very honest, charming slice of garage-pop

Title: In Guards We Trust
Review: Enjoyable, but the signposting towards "the good bits" can be a tad too obvious. [Jun 2013, p.86]

Title: See You Around

Title: Libra Scale
Review: R&B concept album about binmen turned superheroes. Yup.

Title: Forth Wanderers

Title: Life Metal

Title: LA Spark

Title: Four Stars

Title: The Suburbs
Review: One of the 21st century's most intelligent and satisfying bands (musically, lyrically, emotionally) have once again set out their stall, and once again produced a work of inspired resonance, capturing truth after truth, in all its muddled, human realism.

Title: Drawing Down the Moon
Review: Drawing Down The Moon marks a welcome return for Azure Ray, and makes for an oftentimes exquisite listening experience. It's just a shame that, when it comes to the songs themselves, much of the beauty is only skin deeP.

Title: 100 Miles from Memphis
Review: It may have taken her over 20 years, but today Sheryl Crow is retrieving and expanding upon those parts of her artistic sensibility that had always been there.

Title: Ray Ray
Review: Ray Ray hits more than it misses in its celebration of a time when George was making the mothership connection and Marvin just wanted to get it on. [Nov 2004, p.160]

Title: Zebra
Review: In reaching out to others, Georgopoulos is discovering his own voice for the first time.

Title: Push the Button

Title: Manafon
Review: Sylvian is front-and-center on every song, which is good because he provides the only rhythmic and melodic stability, as the instrumentals dart and scratch and feedback around him.

Title: Real Life
Review: Lyrically fascinating, charmingly vulnerable and compulsively danceable--this is how to do a debut.

Title: American Utopia
Review: Byrne filters grace, wonder and apocalyptic portent through his fractured worldview. [Apr 2018, p.95]

Title: Dusk
Review: Once again, a thoroughly pleasant aural experience; an enjoyable slice of dreampop that subtly introduces and shifts between a variety of influences to keep the listener interested.

Title: Chuck
Review: Chuck’s a wonderful piece of American music, and ultimately as enigmatic and elusive as the man who filed it on his way out the door.

Title: Personal Computer
Review: With only ten tracks, half of which are under three minutes long, Personal Computer feels just a few bits short of a byte and you may well find yourself moving straight onto Unknown Mortal Orchestra's back catalogue just to get some closure.

Title: Dead Language

Title: Savages
Review: Too many songs utilise the same plodding, mid-paced grooves and simple, one-line refrains. [5 Oct 2013, p.54]

Title: Gargoyle
Review: The songs, hard and soft, fast and slow, seem better than ever. Lanegan may sound like he’s done everything there is to do, but he’s clearly not done pushing into new territories and getting better.

Title: Random Desire
Review: While the key of Random Desire is mostly subterranean, when the serpentine build of The Tide breaks, the impact is undeniably soulful and powerful. [Mar 2020, p.88]

Title: Three Fact Fader
Review: Three Fact Fader is an impressive sophomore effort. Engineers have created a winning combination of English pop/rock.

Title: The Hour of Bewilderbeast
Review: Although a couple tracks towards the end don't work quite as well, it doesn't detract from the album as a whole very much.

Title: Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors
Review: While Killer Mike, Jai Paul and Big KRIT all earn their places, Kelly Rowland, Kid Cudi and Bosco are unnecessary decoration, and contribute to the overall sensation that this is a good album in need of a brutal trim.

Title: When You're Ready

Title: drukQs
Review: While there are a couple of tracks that are completely amazing, the album as a whole could have used a little better sequencing to make it more tight.

Title: Norman Fucking Rockwell!
Review: While “Norman F—ing Rockwell” may not win over too many of the unconverted, also like a Tarantino film, it finds Del Rey placing new sounds, ideas and scenery into her fairly monochromatic framework, while still remaining completely on-message.

Title: The Fire Theft
Review: Hard rock that is neither hard nor rock.

Title: Bromst
Review: Bromst is an excellent followup to a slightly more-excellent debut, and proof that Deacon isn't going anywhere.

Title: Wired Together
Review: Somehow contrives to bring us the worst of both worlds [of glossy dance floor beats and Manc rock swagger.] [Oct. 2011 p. 131]

Title: Workaround
Review: Unorthodox methods prove highly persuasive. [Mar 2020, p.27]

Title: Coup De Grace
Review: Coup De Grace has plenty to offer, but it’s not a big step forward from Kane’s previous solo work. If you liked that you’ll probably like this; if you didn’t, this probably won’t change your mind.

Title: Elephant Jokes
Review: The thing is, this isn’t a bad album. But it is so full of mediocre songs--as are most of the albums since the end of GBV--that one has to ask why he just didn’t save up all the great ones and make one really excellent album.

Title: Hefty Fine
Review: Hefty Fine proves only marginally more welcome than a Jerky Boys reunion.

Title: Nosebleed Weekend
Review: The Coathangers bring some good punk sensibility to the table but the majority of these tracks lack the velocity that would bring them into moshable territory.

Title: Battle Lines

Title: Wabi-Sabi
Review: A strikingly confident record. [Feb 2016, p.74]

Title: I Don't Run
Review: On I Don’t Run, the Madrid quartet wade through these messy feelings with confidence and exuberance to spare, taking us on a pleasure cruise through choppy waters.

Title: American Head
Review: Coyne’s quivering voice still captures the frailty of the human spirit, and his band have made songs that will draw tears from frazzled audiences until the Earth slides into the sea. Yet too many of his death-obsessed drug lyrics are lamely predictable and uninvolving, and swaddling his vocals in effects until he sounds like Rob Brydon’s “man in a box” doesn’t help.

Title: Invitation
Review: Many songs ache with Eighties troubled-youth flashbacks, especially the Pixies-loving "Brother."

Title: We Are Not Your Kind
Review: We Are Not Your Kind marks a supremely confident reassertion of their capacity to pulverise. [Sep 2019, p.116]

Title: Reflektor
Review: It’s an interesting, intermittently excellent album from a skilled group that could still use a little help in getting out of their own way.

Title: I Can't Go On, I'll Go On
Review: Frontman Ross Flournoy and his mates kick up a ramshackle jangle-pop racket that gets its energy from always sounding as if it were on the verge of falling apart.

Title: Cansei de Ser Sexy
Review: A gleeful throwback to early-1980's art-school pop.

Title: Forever Turned Around
Review: Forever Turned Around tows the if-it-ain't broke line, a choice justified by nuggets such as My Life Alone and Before I Know It. [Oct 2019, p.89]

Title: Earthology
Review: On this reassuring piece of big-bottomed exotica, the "Sahara swing" they concocted with Karl Hector is the tipoff. They love the continuity bass-and-drums lay below; I love the content koto and flute and malletophone add on

Title: LP1
Review: Drive All Night, with its chilled-out jazz backbeat, is a standout among her sultry tales of love. [29 Jul 2011, p.72]

Title: Avi Buffalo
Review: Avi Buffalo manages to toe the "slacker pop" line without ever giving us the sense they're phoning it in. [Winter 2010, p.62]

Title: Naomi
Review: There isn't quite enough to genuinely stand out from the crowd. [May 2013, p.98]

Title: Carried to Dust
Review: Calexico's dusty vistas make a welcome comeback.

Title: The Runaway
Review: Not all the songs deserve such painstaking embellishment, and several stumble while mixing 60s pop and 80s melancholy, giving The Runaway the feel of an elaborate souffle that doesn't quite rise to the occasion.

Title: Syro
Review: Richard D. James is back, and he’s still absolutely untouchable.

Title: Across The Field
Review: A fascinating and deeply rewarding journey through the ages. [Aug 2019, p.38]

Title: Settle
Review: It’s not perfect--‘Grab Her’ and ‘Stimulation’ both outstay their welcome and the glitchy ‘Second Chance’ feels like it’s from a different album--but it’s a consistently thrilling debut.

Title: Never
Review: The spring in their step has a dangerously sharp point to increase Never's allure. [Aug 2012, p.87]

Title: Peanut Butter
Review: Peanut Butter manages to double down on Weird Sister's considerable volume of bitter pills and sugar-encrusted euphoria. [Apr-May 2015, p.83]

Title: The Grand Tour
Review: There’s something almost mathematical and architectural about Brooks’ guitar aggregations but these qualities are conveyed humbly and unobtrusively throughout.

Title: Human Hearts
Review: Too much of Human Hearts feels like a retread of what they've already done on previous LPs. [Apr 2011, p.115]

Title: Good Time
Review: Good Time is a thoughtfully crafted, warmly contemplative survey of contemporary country sounds by one of Nashville's most dependable singers.

Title: Hail To The Thief
Review: An incredible album from a band that continues to redefine its boundaries.

Title: Love Without Fear
Review: If you want an album that is easily digested, doesn’t require much thought or attention, but still ticks all the right boxes in terms of beautiful guitar playing and vocal work, then it’s the one for you.

Title: Sukierae
Review: He's created a burbling paint pot of a record, one teeming with ideas, styles and reference points as diverse as Double Nickels On The Dime, but wholly recognizable as Tweedy-esque. [No. 113, p.60]

Title: I Get Wet
Review: So then, what is the excuse for a typically elitist music nerd to bow to Andrew WK's blistering tard-rock? That's right, folks: there isn't one.

Title: Congratulations
Review: The album's peppier tracks are front-loaded early, and even if the duo are capable '70s sylvan prog revivalists, the back end of Congratulations feels directionless.

Title: Generation
Review: A low-rent version of the Streets without Mike Skinner's wit, they're just a couple of palookas mouthing off in the pub. [Nov 2005, p.131]

Title: The Ownerz
Review: Guru is... pushing the same grim consistency that makes folks describe Gang Starr albums as 'solid', not budging, not boring, but not better than Moment of Truth. [#234, p.73]

Title: Future Crayon
Review: While the proper order from some of the previous releases is interrupted to make this new album work, having one-off bonus tracks like "DDL" (from the first All Tomorrow’s Parties compilation) and rare 7" B-side "Test Area" from the Echo’s Answer single in one place is an esteemed reward. [Summer 2006]

Title: pom pom
Review: It’s funny, melancholy, randy, touching, disgusting and deeply, deeply strange. It will baffle many--but at 17 tracks and 70 minutes, it has the feel of a magnum opus.

Title: Modern Times
Review: The veteran singer-songwriter has opted to retreat into old-timey blues, rattling off clichés about blind horses and hog-eyed towns while laying down a halfhearted soundtrack of brushed drums, plucked guitars and woozy strings.

Title: Happy in Galoshes
Review: Galoshes is a fascinating mess.

Title: Kazuashita
Review: It is hard not to hear Bougatsos refracted through the lens of Grimes, an artist who radically expanded on GGD’s commercial potential. In comparison, Bougatsos now comes up a little ephemeral.

Title: Hokey Fright
Review: The blending of their styles creates an alchemy that is intensely personal and oddly alluring.

Title: Departing
Review: It's exciting in its pacing, invigorated in its writing, and illustrious in its instrumentation. It's not mad - nor, indeed, prairie-mad - to think that this is an early contender for album of the year lists.

Title: English Oceans
Review: Nothing here reinvents the wheel, but the band are masters of their art.

Title: Remember Me
Review: With the majority of the tracks being in-and-around the two minute mark, Sage The Gemini presses the gas pedal too quickly before capturing your attention lyrically or sonically.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Albarn aficionados will, of course, lap it up, but for the rest of us, think of it more along the lines of a faintly beguiling curio in an otherwise fascinating career. [No. 109, p.52]

Title: Under Rug Swept
Review: Chiefly consists of lumpen and joyless AOR rock, with a few rhythm loops to give an illusion of modernity. [Apr 2002, p.104]

Title: Black Sands
Review: Black Sands is an album so fully realized that comprehending the places he still so obviously has yet to reach is staggering.

Title: Loose
Review: It probably won't appeal to all, and some of Furtado's fans may be hugely turned off by the more danceable tracks. Yet Timbaland has revitalized Furtado - this is the sound of an artist having the time of her life.

Title: The Hawk Is Howling
Review: Using a combination of brilliant textures and powerful, atypical chord progressions, Mogwai paint a picture equivalent to an auto-stereogram, popularized in those Magic Eye books 15 years ago. You almost need to loose your focus to let the music really sink in.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: True to form, the band deliver yet again on Car Alarm. [Nov 2008, p.155]

Title: Eye Contact
Review: It's challenging yet fairly catchy beneath all the layering. It's abstract vocally yet painfully direct musically. It's not for most yet potentially has crossover appeal at its heart.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: It's still not exactly accessible, but it's their easiest listen to date, and a damn amazing and amusing one, if you're feeling creative.

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth
Review: Anthems For Doomed Youth has plenty of reminders of why people fell in love with The Libertines in the first place.... For better or worse, the habit of both spinning and dwelling upon their own mythology remains too. [Oct 2015, p.112]

Title: Hombre Lobo: 12 Songs of Desire
Review: The sound is deliberately barren. The guitars never quite fill the space, and the drumming (credited to Knuckles) often has the mechanized indifference of drum-machine tracks.

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: Animal Collective's abstract and catchy sides are each constantly aware of what the other is doing.

Title: Wizard Bloody Wizard
Review: While another updating of Bloodrock/Blue Cheer/proto-metal is exactly what the world doesn't need, it's a different story when Electric Wizard puts such source material in the crosshairs to show the saturated margins how it's done. [No. 149, p.55]

Title: House of Sugar
Review: The newest record from Alex Giannascoli at times improves on the inscrutable, circuitous experimentation of his Domino debut, Beach Music. At other times, it refines the accessible but still characteristically sauntering country-lite of Rocket, his masterful second album for the British indie label. In other words, House of Sugar sounds like a middle ground between the two albums that preceded it.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: It is, as always, complicated, but addictively, intriguingly so. [Apr 2017, p.111]

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: Too much of Strange Little Birds is filler.

Title: Wrangled
Review: Wrangled lacks ambition.

Title: Paid tha Cost to Be da Boss
Review: Snoop unleashed. [Feb 2003, p.100]

Title: A Hundred Miles Off
Review: The band has seized upon that sloshy saunter that we love and turned it into an elaborate dance. [#20, p.94]

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: IX
Review: The strongest moments on IX, like on any of the band's albums, are those that manage to create a vast rock sound by building elements up to impressive climaxes before bringing them crashing down.

Title: Jim Noir
Review: Jim Noir works brilliantly on an escapist level, even though it rewards more active listening.

Title: Culture
Review: On Culture, their world is richly rendered, full of hopes and paranoia and unbridled joy.

Title: Dead Ringers
Review: Dead Ringers embraces zero-gravity keyboards, clean vocals, and the spaced-out guitar sprawl of the best Popol Vuh records. It’s the farthest he’s gone from traditional metal signifiers, but it’s proof that inky bleakness is no heavier than blinding light.

Title: The Psalms
Review: This is a unique and poignant album that was clearly a labor of love for all involved.

Title: Insides
Review: Spacy yet grounded, cosmic yet physical, Insides is a satisfying journey and Fort Romeau's finest music yet.

Title: Hardcourage
Review: It sounds like like a lot of learning and a lot of loving went into this album, and the result is FaltyDL at his most open.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: Like all the best of heavy metal, effortless dumb good fun. [Nov 2011, p.89]

Title: Audience of One
Review: His solo work tends to be more delicate--with Audience Of One capturing him at his most porcelain.

Title: The Body Wins
Review: Emotion is the string connecting the album's 13 songs, which don't quite feel cohesive but never fail to surprise.

Title: Ephorize
Review: By balancing on the tightrope between meme and icon, between relatable and aspirational, Ephorize emerges sounding remarkably human.

Title: New Life
Review: Despite being beautifully sung and slickly produced, Monica's seventh record is numbingly predictable.

Title: The False Alarms
Review: The False Alarms finds Fol Chen stripping off its makeup and taking a good, hard look in the mirror.

Title: Barking
Review: Thirty years into their collaboration, Underworld's Rick Smith and Karl Hyde continue to sit at the forefront of dance music innovation. Barking is just further proof that Underworld isn't going anywhere.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Perhaps the idea was to make the Dodos’ introspection more overt, or to cushion the songs’ cryptic reflections on breakups, commercialism, mortality and global warming. The intricacies do come through. But these songs will sound better after they’ve been roughed up onstage.

Title: Charmer
Review: Once again, we have a very good recording from a very talented singer, songwriter, and performer.

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: Overall, Wolf's Law largely oversteps the sophomore slump.

Title: Nightcrawler
Review: Pretty though they are, Nightcrawler's hazy songs have a slack sound and little personality. [7 Sep 2006, p.106]

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: The rock quintet wastes no time reestablishing its high-energy bona fides on Teeth Dreams.

Title: Earthly Delights
Review: Their fifth album still features plenty of trademark thrills -  Brian Chippendale drumming junglist breakbeats at heart-attack velocity, bassist Brian Gibbon's' riffs sounding like a grindcore group playing gabba - while the bark-spitting tempo-shifts of opener Sound Guardians wouldn't alienate the Metallica set. [Jan 2010, p. 96]

Title: Always
Review: Stewart's preoccupation--narcissism, sexuality, body horror--translate into a sort of febrile synth-pop, dotted with orchestral excursions and abrupt electronics. [Mar 2012, p. 107]

Title: Thick As Thieves
Review: There are some fine moments, chief among them the searing Ordinary World and the delicate ballad Lost, but there's a feeling The Temper Trap will never again match the bombastic euphoria of their breakthrough track. [Aug 2016, p.117]

Title: Lost Themes
Review: Carpenter’s limited instrumentation starts as a strength--these Lost Themes could stand with any of his horror soundscapes, as you can imagine a potential victim running through a dark forest, being chased by an unknown enemy, or haunted by a ghost that’s slightly out of frame but definitely in earshot. The sheer predictability of the formula, similar to much of the horror output, doesn’t stop the jump-scares.

Title: Pines
Review: It's beautifully presented in an absorbing blend of acoustic guitar, piano, cello, and the occasional tint of vibes or ambient colouration.

Title: Rockferry
Review: Duffy is a major talent, and Rockferry is little short of outstanding.

Title: Sleeping with Ghosts
Review: The album is overflowing with modern day punk-pop anthems, dressed up with technological marvels and justifiably bleak outlooks. [#5, p.89]

Title: Bloom Forever
Review: It’s hard not to listen to Country Home and its lyrics “I will hold on to / The part of me that is in love with you” without feeling like you’ve read a diary entry you shouldn’t have. Elsewhere, however, the album is surprisingly sunny: these are songs for festival picnic blankets as well as for holding on to your loved ones.

Title: The Triad
Review: Weber's trademark fusion of cascading chimes and subdued yet propulsive rhythm has expanded radically in scope. [Jul 2016, p.113]

Title: Neighborhoods
Review: Ultimately, Neighborhoods is a slightly awkward entry in the band's catalog that shows as much potential as it does flaws.

Title: Living Room Songs
Review: Living Room Songs may not exceed 25 minutes in length but this is still an album to luxuriate in and one that fans of traditional classical composers such as Arvo Pärt and Henryk Górecki will find to their satisfaction.

Title: Transfiguration of Vincent
Review: Transfiguration is a quiet record and might lose some listeners in it's sleepy summer melancholy, but M. Ward is the real deal.

Title: V
Review: The temptation to change hasn’t been enough to find a marked difference between V and the rest of Wavves’ catalog. Instead, like so many of the artists who find and stick to a personal aesthetic, few new fans will be gained, but even fewer will be lost.

Title: Firepower
Review: It's as sharp as can be, as powerful as an atom bomb, and exactly the sort of thrilling metal adventure you want from them. [17 Mar 2018, p.53]

Title: Cassadaga
Review: He is clearly searching for a more mature style. But the musical and rhetorical convolutions of “Cassadaga” are no substitute, yet, for the way he used to blurt things out. [9 Apr 2007]

Title: The Animal Years
Review: An album that sounds simultaneously deeply personal and in tune with confusing times.

Title: Nav
Review: More about creating a low-wattage soundtrack for chemical and sexual mischief than foundations for songs.

Title: High as Hope
Review: High As Hope is musically safe likely due to the subdued art pop grandeur heard in previous Florence and the Machine's albums. However, musical flourishes throughout the album add depth and affectation.

Title: Dark Red
Review: At times there's too much going on to be comfortable, but that sonic complexity also keeps things interesting. Shlohmo deserves kudos for making an instrumental electronic album that expresses anxiety, despair and sadness so vividly.

Title: All American Made
Review: Like Nelson's best Seventies work, Price's latest is both reverent and revolutionary, a traditional-minded statement that nevertheless blazes an urgent path forward.

Title: Awake Is the New Sleep
Review: He's never sounded more confident. [Mar 2005, p.134]

Title: Cadillactica
Review: This isn't a great rap album, it's just a great album. Period.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: Master of My Make Believe has the feel of being made deliberately difficult to listen to; obstructionist for the sake of being obstructionist, confrontational without really having anything to argue against - except what might, ultimately, be self-imposed expectations.

Title: Wonderful Crazy Night
Review: Even Elton-sceptics can take solace in how producer T-Bone Burnett continues to improve the veteran piano man by filling the interstices of his work with detail, rendering songs such as the rather good Claw Hammer at least 43% more nuanced.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: As always, the contrast between Adam Franklin's smooth pipes and his and Jimmy Hartridge's strident six-strings provides the sonic setting, enabling Swervedriver to put the brawn back in beauty.

Title: Collector
Review: With songs as good as these, there’s no need to grow up and stop slacking off.

Title: Tainted Lunch
Review: A mutant strain of noisy funk, hip-hop, subversive art punk and dirty disco. [Dec 2019, p.35]

Title: Odd Blood
Review: The result is simultaneously stranger and poppier, more celebratory and more serious.

Title: Bubba
Review: While 99% provided the initial space for Kaytranada to make his mark, BUBBA is where it matures.

Title: Golem
Review: The whole thing is executed with a sense of starry-eyed bliss. [No. 119, p.61]

Title: Lenses
Review: Even if Lenses' individual tracks remain as foggy as dry ice on the dancefloor, as a whole the album brings Soft Metals' music into focus, revealing them as a tighter, more versatile group in the process.

Title: In Rainbows
Review: In Rainbows, the band's seventh studio album and first since 2003's "Hail to the Thief," is dense and thorny, complex and beautiful.

Title: Living Legend
Review: Legend, like Gunplay’s professed diet, is a potent mix of uppers, downers and hallucinogens; it makes for a weird, and weirdly satisfying, trip.

Title: Stars of CCTV
Review: The triumphant "Star's Of CCTV" will be to guitar bands what The Street's "Original Pirate Material" was to the UK urban music: essential listening.

Title: Not Real
Review: Touchstones are many and include Delia Derbyshire (last year they collaborated with the BBC Radiophonic Workshop on an original score to the 70s sci-fi film Le Planete Sauvage) Can, Grace Jones, Moondog, John Carpenter and Grayson Perry’s pop folk art. But, once again, their sound is their own.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: RTJ2 is a fierce release.

Title: Own Your Ghost
Review: They rise to each other's challenges surprisingly well, with sinuous lo-fi beats brushing against saxes, woodwinds and vintage synths. [Jun 2011, p.96]

Title: Raise Vibration
Review: Kravitz knows how to sculpt not just sounds but a cohesive LP, and that kind of pro assurance when combined with his earnest hippie beliefs, make Raise Vibration a sunny, affirming listen.

Title: Self Help Serenade
Review: Marjorie Fair's plinky strums, orchestral swells and hummable lyrics are hard to dislike and impossible to love. [Aug 2005, p.111]

Title: The Datsuns
Review: It's pure driving music, the type that's fun to listen to while blasting through a deserted stretch of prairie highway, but it's also something you wind up immediately forgetting the second you stop for a bathroom break.

Title: Anian
Review: This cool, classy set is accompanied by an ambitious if uneven spoken-word album, in which writers and musicians reinterpret the songs in English.

Title: Shine a Light
Review: Impressively raucous. [#240, p.68]

Title: HiggledyPiggledy
Review: Admirably obtuse, Slug put the odd into prog odyssey with style. [Jun 2018, p.93]

Title: Heavier Things
Review: A sophomore effort that doesn't have as many drawbacks as one might assume.

Title: Metals
Review: The album itself is worthy of praise from any angle you choose to view it.

Title: Trouble Anyway
Review: Even more striking is the way she folds all this talent into her songs, keeping all the bits distinct while shaping them into a complicated, intricate whole that breathes like a living creature. Nicely done.

Title: Whelm
Review: Whelm is a Herculean debut.

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: Instead of being an especially bold or dynamic record, however, it only recalls the best moments of Quality Control and EP, seldom reaching their highest peaks.

Title: It Still Moves
Review: He claims his Dave Matthews-sponsored major- label debut was his chance to make a true band record, and I guess his boys are trickier than Crazy Horse, just not in any way you haven't heard before.

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: He's turned the clock back to the Fun Trick Noisemaker era of playful psychedelic indulgence that was the Apples' stock in trade before the unsavoury aspirations of indie-rock stardom took hold.

Title: Sung Tongs
Review: Before, it sounded like Animal Collective sought only to please themselves. Sung Tongs sounds like a concession to the rest of us, and that's not a very exciting prospect from such a unique and potentially great band.

Title: The Heist
Review: Flexing the same contextual muscle that helped make Atmosphere's Slug an MC for the downtrodden, Macklemore utilizes second album The Heist as a vehicle for dissection, pulling back the layers of skin that cover addiction, the music industry, materialism, and homosexuality.

Title: Haven't Got The Blues (Yet)
Review: The resulting poignancy of his honest songwriting is an amazing accomplishment.

Title: Working Out
Review: Given an open mind and time to unfurl, Working Out is a wholly absorbing record. [Mar 2014, p.107]

Title: Battle Born
Review: As ever, his lyrics sound better the less you think about them, but you know The Killers are getting it right because most of the time, you don't need to.

Title: Age of Unreason
Review: Anyone who's spent any time with Bad Religion will know what they are getting into with Age of Unreason. It's a good album that largely succeeds because the band are old pros. And because Graffin and Gurewitz have plenty of genuine anger and articulate that anger in interesting ways.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being
Review: When Wayne is on, he's one of the best in the game, but on Human Being he's just killing time with sub-par versions of his far more popular songs – this is a completely superfluous release that lacks the relevance and immediacy of his mixtape works and the quality-control of his albums.

Title: Nuclear Daydream
Review: The album becomes more intoxicatingly hermetic with each successive song, taking you as deep as you dare to go. [Nov 2006, p.79]

Title: Visions of Us on the Land
Review: It’s the real deal, the meat of his canon and bearing rewards for fans old and new.

Title: Sundry Rock Song Stock
Review: His most effortless success yet. Sundry Rock Song Stock is a breezy trip through the life of a confident and naturalistic performer, someone whose best work still may be ahead of him.

Title: Dose Your Dreams
Review: Dose Your Dreams is fucking ace. [Oct 2018, p.85]

Title: The Bright Mississippi
Review: Toussaint gives each of the instruments room to explore, breaking free of the structure of the song and marking it with his own distinctive stamp. It's this loose, spirited mood that makes the album's interpretations so smooth and effective.

Title: Barchords
Review: Jordanian remains pleasantly understated as a frontman, letting his voice and knack for raw melodies take the focus.

Title: Blood
Review: Blood proves to be another mixed bag. [Aug 2015, p.92]

Title: Sundowner
Review: Even without explicit elegies, there's a sense Morby is permanently watching something sink into the horizon, suspending what's left in beautiful songwriting amber. [Nov 2020, p.80]

Title: Palindrome Hunches
Review: Recorded in a primary school, the Reading warbler's third solo record is whimsical, pleasant and calming, with shades of Damien Rice and Regina Spektor.

Title: Recover EP
Review: Stop what you’re doing and get this EP, and keep going.

Title: Colors
Review: While that might mean Colors doesn't offer the depth and intrigue of most Beck albums, it does mean it's a fun confection. It's a record that's designed to be nothing but a good time, and that indeed is all that it is.

Title: My Shame Is True
Review: Listening back on the first couple of releases, its obvious Alkaline Trio has learned to inject more melody into their songs over the years, though My Shame Is True is closer to their punk-ier sound than the last few efforts.

Title: Here's Willy Moon
Review: Here's Willy Moon: this is music that is out there, it is not cooked up by consultants and marketers, it's a truly, genuinely strange attempt at something new--it may miss its mark but that's why it's fascinating.

Title: Heart-Shaped Mountain
Review: Shimmery background countermelodies of organ and mandolin bring a slightly psychedelic, dreamy sense of indie rock to an album that alternately evokes both '80s Los Angeles and '90s Scotland.

Title: From the Cradle to the Rave
Review: Whether or not Shit Robot is making grooves and beats that are unique and progressive isn't the point. The whole point of his work is to embrace the glorious past and then push the necessary knobs and buttons that are commonplace today to take it to a wonderfully hip-shaking new level.

Title: Human Animal
Review: A near-perfect balance of industrial threat, hardcore power and black comedy. [Oct 2006, p.134]

Title: Compass
Review: At times, Lidell seems determined to overcrowd his genuinely soulful and lyrically strong music, whether it's with silly, pitched-down vocals ("Your Sweet Boom"), laptoppy clicks, squiggles, and washes ("She Needs Me"), or blasts of aggro rock ("You Are Walking").

Title: 1000 gecs
Review: Some of the most interesting tracks on 1000 Gecs and the Tree of Clues come from less predictable pairings.

Title: Libertine
Review: Like so much of Gene's fine back catalogue, this is an album about the ways in which love can buckle you under and life can break you down, options closing in like the walls of an Indiana Jones dungeon.

Title: Starboy
Review: There are more tracks to like than not, even stretching all the way to the end of the record. If you want Starboy to be a good album, it can be that. It may require some personal editing. It also may require that you ignore what even the most sterilized tracks seem to be about.

Title: Everything She Touched Turned Ampexian
Review: With Everything She Touched Turned Ampexian, not only has the frustratingly prolific Guillermo Scott Herren delivered a blinding banger of a record, he’s upped the game that appeared indomitable on 2003’s "One Word Extinguisher."

Title: A Fool to Care
Review: One great pleasure that comes from listening to this album are the choices that Scaggs made in songs to cover, songs from R&B, soul, and country, any of which might pick up rhythms from jazz or Cajun music.

Title: Don't Give Up On Love
Review: He delivers 10 killer tracks which, defined by horns, organ and a defying-the-years-vocal-hit from Bryant, span the spirited How Do I Get There? and commanding One Ain’t Enough to the compelling A Nickel And A Nail and swooning Something About You.

Title: Real Estate
Review: Real Estate’s sound is imbued with the same sentimentality as the rest of the indie class of 2009, but with zero ambition.

Title: Thank Your Lucky Stars
Review: Mood is the driving force, making it function best as background music, if occasionally forgettable.

Title: Celestite
Review: There are absolutely stunning passages on here to be sure, but as a whole the record fails to really take your breath away like one would hope.

Title: Hoodstar
Review: Hoodstar only makes it all the more apparent that the St. Louis MC's overnight popularity was like lightning in a bottle.

Title: Rest
Review: Fans of spacey Nineties lounge-pop like Air or Broadcast will drift along happily to pillowy confections such as "Ring-a-Ring O'Roses" and "Rest," a collaboration with Daft Punk's Guy-Manuel.

Title: Bloom
Review: It's not the band's most immediate music, but the album's challenging mix of heartbroken words and aloof sounds rewards patient and repeated listening.

Title: Acousmatic Sorcery
Review: Out of its many blues like qualities the one that I see potentially defining the album as a whole is its rawness.

Title: Summer Make Good
Review: The album is much more consistent, more cinematic than anything they have done before.

Title: Spectre
Review: There’s a sense of exhaustion in Spectre, but it’s not an exhaustion with irony and a refuge in po-faced sloganeering. Rather, Laibach dramatise the exhausted nature of a political movement that seems unable to do anything other than follow the lines laid out for it by the social order it claims to oppose, or take refuge in a vague utopianism.

Title: M
Review: M is painfully bland and too on the nose.

Title: Head Carrier
Review: Their past is a double-edged sword, but that doesn’t prevent Head Carrier from having its own unique strengths.

Title: No Line on the Horizon
Review: No Line on the Horizon is a considered and nuanced work with significant depth beneath the dense, sometimes thorny exterior. Getting there, though, requires some work.

Title: Charmbracelet
Review: A step ahead of the J-Los of the world; a step behind what may prove to be a career pinnacle.

Title: Layers
Review: While Layers is not filled with party bangers or catchy, memorable hooks, Royce uses his album as a platform to create a dialogue with his audience.

Title: Last of the Great Pretenders
Review: His latest album isn’t a pop masterpiece, but that doesn’t mean that there aren’t a few enjoyable tunes that even non-fans should be able to find themselves hitting the rewind button a time or two.

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: The Hold Steady are very much a band for their existing fans. There’s not anything here, whether the bar-room blues of ‘Blackout Sam’ or the jazz hands-aloft ’T-Shirt Tux’ that’s likely to win outsiders over.

Title: Sing To The Moon
Review: Sing to the Moon is a bold and beautiful debut: airy and dense, soul and jazz, dark and light. Head in the clouds, toes in the dirt.

Title: The Paradigm Shift
Review: Korn’s follow up to ’11’s dubstep-infused ‘The Path Of Totality’ is a completely different monster to its predecessor, and for all the right reasons.

Title: Painting With
Review: Full of punch, the album still never quite reaches its destination.

Title: Threadbare
Review: It seems they’ve found land for their sea legs, regaining footing with a more profound focus by the likes of Cambria Goodwin, whose vocals nod toward Régine Chassagne’s sadness and the haunting of Victoria Legrand.

Title: Distortion
Review: Distortion isn't an easy listen, with its strict, difficult palette. But it's an endlessly fascinating and provocative one.

Title: In My World
Review: In My World is a counterpoint to McQueen’s recent work: while the introduction of vocals reveals another side to Matthewdavid, the humour--too often overplayed--is its weakness element.

Title: Visions
Review: Though it's well produced and confident, and goes deep into its web of influence, it seems so rooted in this moment that it feels transitory.

Title: Sun
Review: If there is nothing here as instantly transfixing as some of her past work, Sun comes alive on closer listening, revealing myriad depths and unexpected vocal turns.

Title: Lysandre
Review: It's easy-listening music for deeply uneasy times.

Title: Visions
Review: You'll have to search long and hard for a more original and distinctive album this year. [April 2012, p.100]

Title: Purple
Review: It's clear that they've tapped into something special with this new lineup and that from the tragic events they suffered through they've been able to reemerge bigger and badder than ever. Purple is their finest hour yet

Title: One People One World
Review: Only final track, The Way Our Lives Go, a slowish ballad, counts as a surprising divergence from the template. [Mar 2018, p.95]

Title: Monuments to an Elegy
Review: There's lots of good guitar playing, but no flashy riffs and absolutely nothing you'd call a solo. It gives Monuments its greatest strength: a self contained identity.

Title: Cease to Begin
Review: Cease To Begin is a fine, fitting return to familiar ground. [Fall 2007, p.91]

Title: Love Your Dum and Mad
Review: The weight of the album and the somber nature of its subjects can nearly get too much at times. Yet it’s the lightness and dexterity in Nadine’s voice and songwriting that means she has created an album of stories that will warm you and keep you company.

Title: Touch
Review: The influence of Beyoncé's massive hit "Crazy In Love" is all over Amerie's sophomore effort.

Title: I Will Be
Review: On the whole, I Will Be invites you to be whisked along by the sheer energy burst: the pots’n’pans clatter of the drums, the crackle and fizz from the amps and the bitter take on romance from Dee Dee herself.

Title: A Little Deeper
Review: A surprisingly mature debut record. [#3, p.87]

Title: Everything Ecstatic
Review: "Everything Ecstatic" pulses with imagination and subtle talent, choosing to follow a sweet technicolour road rather than take a harder, and far well trodden path.

Title: The Air Force
Review: Here, Jamie Stewart and his crew of arty innovators use the penchant for sonic deconstruction they honed last time round to take their project of disemboweling pop songs to a new plane.

Title: Mines
Review: Maturity suits Menomena's Mines just fine. [Summer 2010, p.79]

Title: RUFF
Review: They’ve landed on a fertile middle ground between their spark-and-buzz beginnings and those first wearier-but-wiser bends in life’s learning curve.

Title: Little Joy
Review: It's a sunny album with low aspirations, which in this case is a compliment.

Title: Can't Be Tamed
Review: When you get right down to it, not only is Can't Be Tamed a confused statement of a record, but it's a pretty boring listen as well, as Cyrus hits on tired old pop trends (AutoTune? Really?) as a way to deliver her quasi-edgy new persona to a much more intelligent mainstream audience.

Title: God Save the Clientele
Review: It cements the Clientele as one of the best pop bands around today.

Title: Rise Again
Review: Laswell provides an accomplished, opulent dub setting. But it's at blandish odds with the lo-tech wildness of Perry's own original Black Ark recordings. [Jul 2011, p.93]

Title: Coolaid
Review: The Swizz Beatz-assisted "Let Me See Em Up," "Light it Up" and "Let the Beat Drop (Celebrate)" rarely do much to stand apart from filler. These occasional misses aren't enough to water down the entirety of Coolaid, though, with Snoop's return to G-funk proving refreshing enough to keep listeners' thirst quenched.

Title: My Turn
Review: He’s trying to tell a story here, but he’s just not much of a storyteller—his bars keep the narrative going, but he doesn’t offer enough arresting imagery to make his scenes come to life.

Title: Serena-Maneesh
Review: Serena-Maneesh sounds like the kind of record many bands spend their entire careers trying to create.

Title: Voxtrot
Review: Voxtrot remains a compelling enough statement to justify the inordinate amounts of excitement thrown around the band, yet nowhere near a fulfillment of the enormous potential they’ve shown.

Title: From All Purity
Review: Celeste put out a sludgy doom-inflected black metal record; this year, Indian turned the equation on its head and put out a blackened doom record, that's equally depraved, nihilistic, and crucial for any fan of truly heavy music.

Title: Logos
Review: Like Animal Collective's best work, Logos manages to combine simple melodies with enough experimentalism to allow you to keep returning to the record with fresh ears, but not too much to reduce it to avant-garde mush.

Title: Insula
Review: Every track on this album is densely constructed, colorful, and unpredictable, and while it may seem lighthearted at first, it manages to cover a wide range of emotions. One of the most inventive debut albums of 2018, for sure.

Title: Noctunes
Review: The whole album unfolds at a pace somewhere between stately and glacial. [Oct 2015, p.93]

Title: Good To Be Home

Review: At the end of the first album on which he's managed to keep all of his organs inside his body, it's like Cox is finally letting us see his heart.

Title: Stillmatic
Review: While no album may ever top his debut's brilliance, this one comes close enough to make even his most passionate haters happy to hear the raw essence of hip-hop revealed in all it's true glory.

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: Tricky may not be reinventing the wheel, but his focus is sharper than ever. [Oct 2014, p.93]

Title: Deep Down Happy
Review: These 12 tracks are a furious, funny flag in the ground from a band who make absolutely no bones about who they are.

Title: Luciferian Towers
Review: There's little on this album that would sound out of place on any of their other works, but GY!BE's apocalyptic vision remains as relevant and powerful as ever.

Title: Maximum Balloon
Review: It feels like Maximum Balloon is a project that could inflate infinitely. Let's hope it does.

Title: For My Crimes
Review: It may not be the liveliest 35 minutes of the year, yet it’s filled with memorable imagery and some heartbreaking songs. For anyone who’s never heard any of Marissa Nadler’s work before, For My Crimes makes for an excellent starting point.

Title: Devotion
Review: Much like Ocean’s Blonde, Devotion unfolds and unravels in different ways upon each listen, giving you everything but never too soon. With it, Tirzah and Levi have created something fiercely unique, relatable and of the moment; one of the most crucial pop records of the year.

Title: Tracker
Review: Tracker may not quite reach the same heights as its predecessor--it features one too many misses for that to be the case--but it is another solid solo entry into his already impressive back catalogue and a record that Knopfler’s faithful following will undoubtedly delight in it.

Title: aloha
Review: Nothing is forced and no sound is extraneous on this desert-dry, whisper-close 12-song set. [Apr 2020, p.30]

Title: Fold Your Hands Child, You Walk Like a Peasant
Review: The group's lack of growth has begun to make their well-established talents wear thin.

Title: I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass
Review: I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass is a delirious jumble, the rare album that holds together because of the sheer audacity of its diversity, rather than being torn asunder by it.

Title: Folk Songs
Review: The familiarity of the material is offset by the uniqueness of the approach. [Aug 2017, p.104]

Title: Memphis
Review: A squashy gust of falsetto, horns, and strings buttress the swaying keyboard popper "hideout," but like many of these tracks, it's a little too twee. [Summer 2010, p.79]

Title: Black Dialogue
Review: Lif and Akrobatik have a long history, so they sound natural as brainy verse-swapping partners, and they're sharp throughout, whether they have their sights set on the Bush Administration or are simply batting boasts back and forth.

Title: Caught in the Trees
Review: What Jurado does most isn't necessarily what he does best, which is what makes the first half of Caught In The Trees so refreshing.

Title: KOCH
Review: An unsettling soundtrack of misanthropic club dystopias. [Nov 2014, p.99]

Title: Meir
Review: It’s weird, it’s creepy, it’s unstable, but man, there’s art here, something that few bands can boast.

Title: Shrines
Review: It's a record that effortlessly juxtaposes chopped up electronics and ghostly effects with James' supersweet voice to create eleven strange but simple pleasures.

Title: Listen
Review: Not only is none of this fresh, its fast-food vacuity is presented as proud branding.

Title: Lamp Lit Prose
Review: It’s an overdose of things that would, individually, be fantastic, but are made lesser by their combination.

Title: Boy King
Review: More so than ever on the new Boy King, Wild Beasts seem especially comfortable and confident with their wayward electro. Which only shows in the added coats of glitz.

Title: Sounds Good Feels Good
Review: For better or worse, that same sense of déjà vu pervades much of Sounds Good Feels Good, with the band borrowing liberally from its influences.

Title: Bones
Review: Bones is a fiery yet melodious modern rock album made by a band who may come to regret their name should they survive to become old hands.

Title: Prairie Wind
Review: Melodically, Young creates a comfortable, atmospheric lilt his admirers will instantly recognize. Lyrically, however, Young's lost his way.

Title: Universal Themes
Review: Aching, poetically quotidian observations permeate Universal Themes. [Aug 2015, p.89]

Title: Body
Review: For a trio that has reveled in building its own little worlds for three decades, Body feels newly reflective of our space and time, a stark and jarring statement about the precipice of modern life.

Title: Songs From San Mateo County
Review: At only 15 minutes, this Bay Area hardcore vet packs a lot in, resulting in one of the most fun and re-listenable records so far in 2019.

Title: Edge of the Sun
Review: Album highlight Cumbia De Donde, featuring Spanish guitarist Amparo Sanchez, is a goofy Mariachi riot that manages to incorporate odd, cartoonish electronic elements to great effect. The flipside is their increased tendency towards clichéd, characterless attempts at straight-down-the-line MOR.

Title: Significant Changes
Review: Significant Changes may well plunge you below the surface but by the time you reach final track Conclusion, tying in perfectly with the album's overriding scientific theme, we're ever confident that even deeper sounds are still to come from Jayda G.

Title: Not Yet
Review: Despite their monotone and their monoxide fuming, it's hard not to warm to Monotonix, especially when they catch fire. [Apr 2011, p.86]

Title: Adam Green & Binki Shapiro
Review: These aren't songs meant to jump out at you, but spend some time with them and little illuminations flicker to life.

Title: Fasciinatiion
Review: Ultimately, Fasciination has enough passable triumphs mixed in with the misfires that the album is brought to a level of acceptable fluff.

Title: Treasure House
Review: On Treasure House they find an impressive balance: classical, symphonic music melds with garage and post-punk, giving credence to the cliché that opposites attract, outstanding in its complex sounds and arrangements.

Title: Major Key
Review: As might be expected from a record this big with a rolodex this wide-ranging, Major Key is an absolutely mixed bag. Khaled utilizes full-speed-ahead intensity, big room trap, and syrupy R&B, all without leaving room to breathe. But then again, Khaled’s presence unifies Major Key.

Title: Traps
Review: Traps, gets plenty of mileage from those elements [sun, hot dogs, and babes by the pool], but it shoots them through with just enough worry and weary resignation to land them a notch above the typical empty-calorie summer jams.

Title: The Altar
Review: The Altar is more textured and artful than ‘Goddess’, BANKS growing into her role as a writer, upholding the sensual melancholia that characterised her debut. Yet, it still feels as if BANKS is fine-tuning her sound.

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: Nominally folk gospel, they embrace an array of styles from rock to dance, via unashamedly esoteric. [Oct 2013, p.100]

Title: Original Pirate Material
Review: Throughout the disc, his attention to detail and melody stretch well beyond his 22 years.

Title: Dungeonesse
Review: At times, the offering is inviting on the surface, but becomes a bit antiseptic or flattened once you actually get inside. [No. 98, p.53]

Title: Why You So Crazy
Review: Why You So Crazy is indeed a reflection of their uniqueness and disregard for predefined musical categories. In doing so, they manage to be both entertaining and exhausting; likely, an intentional contradiction.

Title: Blank Face LP
Review: Q is as distinct and powerful a voice in hip-hop as Kendrick, and he manages to bring the likes of Kanye West, Swizz Beatz, Anderson .Paak, and Vince Staples to Figg St. on one of the year’s best rap albums thus far. The only real dissonance here comes on Miguel collaboration “Overtime.”

Title: When We Stay Alive
Review: It is a transformative synthpop journey exploring how our worst moments shape us as individuals for when we are at our best.

Title: Shobaleader One: d'Demonstrator
Review: It's an excellent way for Jenkinson to branch out and try something different--his playing and programming is definitely up to his high standard--but aside from the sweet retro vibes, it's hardly a classic.

Title: All You Need Is Now
Review: Leave A Light On, for example, sounds an awful lot like the Rio-era ballad Save A Prayer. Unfortunately, these doppelgangers are the album's best songs, which makes you wonder why the band bothered.

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: An enjoyable yet essentially average release that plays it very safe, sticking close to preconceptions and relative “rules” of electro/synth pop without straying too far from the groundwork set down by the figures from another era it quotes and, to some degree, replicates.

Title: Servant of Love
Review: If anything, this is more consistent and satisfying record, one that emphatically places her at the forefront of modern roots music. [Nov 2015, p.72]

Title: The Glowing Man
Review: While albums and concerts get to end, the knowledge that real lives carry on scarred by real-life tragedies like the one related make The Glowing Man a fraught record to hear.

Title: Father of Asahd
Review: Father of Asahd isn’t perfect, and the celebratory baller vibe can get a little tiresome at times. However, this time round, whenever Khaled shouts “Another one!”, his catchphrase, it actually feels merited. DJ Khaled’s true talent lies in bringing people together.

Title: Family Crimes
Review: Here, together again, they pick up more or less where they left off, slipping subdued hooks into strummy reveries and spiking easy breezy tunes with jarring, occasional violent lyrics.

Title: Mazy Fly
Review: Spelling continuously reinvents herself and her sound. What at first listen may turn many off bears repeated listening, through the often terrifying kaleidoscope of sound is a melodic pop centre.

Title: Donuts
Review: A schizophrenic palate of honeyed soul, downbeat electrix, timeless hip hop and bare-knuckle beats, these 31 tracks (spread over 44 minutes) are packed with triple the hooks – and suffer from attention deficit disorder (to the listener’s benefit).

Title: De-Loused in the Comatorium
Review: Its musical adventurousness proves intoxicating.

Title: The Journey Man
Review: The double album structure adds texture to the record’s length, avoiding monotony. Goldie clearly still owns his sound and endows it with a unique vision on The Journey Man.

Title: Ty Segall
Review: It's a welcome, and much needed, breakthrough. [Apr 2017, p.118]

Title: Wave
Review: There are some glitchy electronic beats and questionable structural turns during the album's back half that feel a little bit out of place, but the overall vibe remains one of deep and heavy existential pain. Wave is an acutely overcast album, but Watson's gift for melody, narrative lucidity, and retro-pop sensibilities help to keep things more melancholic than maudlin.

Title: Out of Nothing
Review: If only Embrace gave us more of the spacey, Mercury Rev-style psychedelia of "Near Life" (sans McNamara's poorly mumbled vocals), it'd be easier to forgive their lack of imagination.

Title: Dum Spiro Spero
Review: It's extreme in a way that corpse-painted clowns will never understand--but as an expression of raw, wounded humanity, it stands as Dir en Grey's most captivating, compelling and soulful release to date. [30 Jul 2011, p.50]

Title: Neon Bible
Review: Bombast occasionally gets the better of the songwriting, but that's a small complaint on an album that gets nearly everything just right. [10 Mar 2007]

Title: Robyn Hitchcock
Review: Hitchcock remains a master at being both melodically and lyrically intriguing.

Title: The Bravest Man in the Universe
Review: Barring any idiomatic prejudices against the contemporary production techniques, there are no glaring missteps here.

Title: Crybaby
Review: Intimate but grand, Crybaby is a triumph.

Title: Strange House
Review: Although packed full of nerdy Sixties tributes and Spider Webb's dizzying antique organ sound, it's not stuck too far in the past.

Title: Chase This Light
Review: The record is crisply produced, with jittery, epic songs that just happen to be about getting older and maybe a little more cynical. [Nov 2007, p.125]

Title: Another Day on Earth
Review: Despite some affecting songs and intriguing production quirks, it lacks that kind of magic [of his 1970s albums]. [Jul 2005, p.113]

Title: Disappointment Island
Review: Its sturdy set should also prove a worthwhile find for those interested in offshoots of math rock, or a kind of controlled virtuosity suited for rainy-day instrument workouts.

Title: It's Alright Between Us As It Is
Review: Overall, It's Alright Between Us As It Is is yet another solid entry into Lindstrøm's discography. It doesn't re-invent the wheel in terms of genre or what we expect of the Norwegian producer, but it just keeps things ticking along with exciting and unexpected flourishes at every turn.

Title: Better Oblivion Community Center
Review: Succeeds as a standalone work, regardless of its authors’ statuses in the indie-folk world.

Title: I Love You, Dude
Review: The key feeling could be summed up in the album title, in a way -- it's not necessarily that the album is all about love, but it's definitely about warmth and happy energy with a definite male slant, a blissed feeling over the heavy crunch and impact of the music.

Title: Living With War
Review: OK, more news event than musical milestone. But a really great news event.

Title: Flockaveli
Review: Waka barely bothers to write rhymes, but Flockaveli is hypnotic, focusing attention on the details beneath the bombast.

Title: Nausea
Review: The messy trip-hop of 'If I Could' and screeching synth line of 'First Snow' mean Nausea lacks consistency, but it's a clever and rewarding record.

Title: Pieces In A Modern Style
Review: Orbit makes these compositions so much his own that "Pieces" doesn't seem like much of a departure from Orbit's "Strange Cargo" series of solo ambient albums.... beyond the whiff of new-agey preciousness that hangs over the project, the record is beautiful and moving.

Title: Soldier of Love
Review: Soldier is sumptuously melancholy, exquisitely beautiful R&B, perfect for crying on a very expensive sofa.

Title: Spaces Everywhere
Review: The band does what it does best, which is couch surreal oddity in unstoppable catchiness.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: Collapse Into Now suffers somewhat. It's good. But it's no Reckoning. Or Document. Or Automatic For The People. Or...

Title: Ventriloquizzing
Review: Fujiya & Miyagi are an invigorating mix of the cerebral and the visceral. In a just world, they'd be the new lords of the dancefloor.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: While Pedestrian Verse feels like the most comprehensive Frightened Rabbit LP in the band’s nearly 10-year career, it also forgoes some of the band’s restless charm in the process.

Title: Colour the Small One
Review: 70 minutes to savor, to let the words run through you, to let the melodies wrap around you.

Title: You, Forever
Review: These songs come with fuzzy edges, a puff of smoke, a gentle wobble. It's Owen's solid songwriting skills that tether them to Earth, though. [Summer 2018, p.109]

Title: You
Review: Their labour of love, You, shows dedication, unencumbered enthusiasm and an eye for detail that perhaps under scrutiny of millions would not exist. Put simply: it's pretty bloody good.

Title: The Way
Review: The short, sweet The Way packs enough pop-tinged punk energy and emotion to satisfy Buzzcocks faithful, at least.

Title: Long Way Home
Review: Låpsley is nothing if not diverse, but she manages to retain a bespoke, trademark sound throughout Long Way Home.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: It's protest music, damn right about moral abstractions rather than those finely limned characters good little aesthetes get gooey about, and for me a cathartic up.

Title: Acousmatic Sorcery
Review: A bundle of raw, karaoke machine-recorded songs reminiscent of early Devendra Banhart and the more emotive work of Wesley Willis. [Mar 2012, p. 87]

Title: Love Kraft
Review: Love Kraft emphasizes contemplative beauty over the manic propulsion of the band's early work.

Title: Always Ascending
Review: So while Always Ascending is certainly a return to form in places, it certainly isn't perfect, particularly in its middle run. ... Overall, it's a pleasant feeling to have a good Franz Ferdinand record again, like a warm hug reminding one of a simpler time only slightly bastardised by ten years of regressive politics and is seemingly inspiring many of these bands to redress the balance.

Title: Jamie Lidell
Review: The constant zipping and zapping of its final five tracks almost cause the album to become bottom heavy, but thankfully the just-right 'So Cold' and the lovely 'Don't You Love Me' keep it from going completely overboard.

Title: Black Swan
Review: When alone, the sweeping choruses that swarm Athlete’s fourth record, Black Swan, shoot for the rafters without any substantial emotional anchor—the songs get lost in the clouds.

Title: Tempest
Review: When it all comes together, like the play it takes its name after, Tempest is turbulent, dark and wondrous.

Title: Be OK
Review: The most charming cuts are the perky title track and Michaelson's wistful, ukulele-equipped take on 'Over the Rainbow.'

Artist: Todd Rundgren, Emil Nikolaisen, Hans-Peter LindstrÃ¸m
Title: Runddans
Review: This is 39 minutes of three musical visionaries spreading their wings and breaking down barriers. [Apr-May 2015, p.86]

Title: JESUS IS KING
Review: With only three songs stretching beyond the three-minute mark, the album is mostly made up of short sketches. Some are perfectly fine little ditties, but without more full-bodied tracks to act as support, Jesus Is King is a suite that constantly feels like it will blow away in the breeze. Confronted with the task of creating songs about religion, West delivers a set that lyrically is as thin as Bible paper.

Title: Adult Nights
Review: At times old-fashioned, Wild Light doesn't feel stuck in the past. There's plenty of mid-tempo despair here--perhaps too much--but on songs such as 'Future Towns,' the band is finding nostalgia in better days that might never come

Title: Peanut Butter
Review: Joanna Gruesome have adapted, honed and stretched their sound on Peanut Butter, and though nothing here sticks in the brain quite like ‘Sugarcrush’ or ‘Secret Surprise’, their tip as one of Britain’s brightest new hopes is more than backed up on this showing.

Title: In My World
Review: In My World is an argument that the drugs are getting better, and maybe even too good, but it proves that freaky hallucinations are hard to string together, and that the impish can be irksome when clever is pushed to its limit.

Title: Heavier Things
Review: An equally available yet more sophisticated album.

Title: Doggumentary
Review: While a dozen singles will probably be lifted from Doggumentary, as an album experience it's an utter dogg's breakfast – as might be expected from a project that credits no fewer than 20 different producers and 35 engineers.

Title: 50 Year Trip: Live at Red Rocks
Review: After half a century, it’s clear that he still retains an eternal energy and enthusiasm. It’s little wonder then that this 50 Year Trip proves such an exhilarating journey at every stop along the way.

Title: Fed
Review: I believe that if you can get past the record’s obvious shortcomings, there is quite a bit of beauty to be found.

Title: Together We're Heavy
Review: This is a record of outrageous range and unprecedented panache.

Title: This Addiction
Review: While This Addiction might not be perfect, it's a more than respectable entry into the band's already sizable canon, proving that though they may be in that rarified group of punk-rock lifers, Alkaline Trio aren't done evolving yet. [Mar 2010, p.89]

Title: Folk Songs
Review: Folk Songs is a smart and emotionally effective exploration of the folk tradition that respects musical history without being chained to it, and it's an experiment the Kronos Quartet would do well to repeat in the future.

Title: Dream On
Review: Hooking up with producer Patrik Berger (Robyn, Charli XCX, Icona Pop) has given her music an explicit clarity. His prowess in the studio with some of some of the biggest leftfield pop artists of recent times gives an impressive breadth to the sound which manages to sound both large-scale and minutely detailed, the unfussy execution perfect for Boman’s introspective and unassuming vocal delivery.

Title: Exclusive
Review: Exclusive seems aimless, an album where Brown is doing what he's told versus being the anchor of his own ship.

Title: Emmaar
Review: For better and worse, surprises on Emmaar are scarce if there are any.

Title: Between My Head and the Sky
Review: Between My Head And The Sky is an intriuing record, crackling with an excitement that most new artists would struggle to generate. [Oct 2009, p.97]

Title: Nobody Knows
Review: It’s not a mulligan by any means, but more a second round of laying all his raw talent out on the table before the unraveling of his mystery begins.

Title: Broken Ear Record
Review: It's less glossy than either of its full-length predecessors... and in addition to a bit of grit there is a stronger rhythmic center to what is happening here as well.

Title: Exai
Review: This much material is exhausting to make your way through, the stretches between moments of genius way too long.

Title: Return to Love
Review: Return to Love is a sticky, sweat-drenched spiritual that commands attention with each wrenching power chord. Far from any aesthetic bait-and-switch, the album marks a slow maturation, a deep breath of chordal refinement that for once feels like an honest distillation of form.

Title: Nightlife
Review: Phantogram drives straight through, with a clear purpose, no rest stops.

Title: Grrr...
Review: Simplifying things is fine, of course, and Bishop Allen does quite a bit with a little on Grrr..., but there are small moments when it feels like the band is putting a glass ceiling on these songs.

Title: Let It Rain
Review: [The] material [is] often so simple in construction that a check of the enclosed lyric sheet is sometimes necessary to ensure the songs really exist. [Jan 2003, p.102]

Title: Smile
Review: Smile finds them advancing that set melodic agenda and playful rearrangement of classic rock DNA. [June 2008, p.109]

Title: Poseidon and the Bitter Bug
Review: A fascinating listen on its own, Poseidon flashes back in fine fashion on how the Indigo Girls sounded two decades ago.

Title: White Crosses
Review: Mostly known for delivering folk-punk anthems, Against Me! delivers a no-fuss rock collection with its latest release.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: Turn Blue may not rock as resoundingly as past works, but the added soul in Auerbach’s vocals, and the extra beauty of the tunes, give the album a slow-burn warmth.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: On the whole Infinite Arms is an album buried under the weight of its own sound. It's hard to know how this album could have sounded with less ham-handed production, but as it stands the mix here feels like some sleight of hand.

Title: Lights Out
Review: It’s simply not striking enough to elicit a stronger response than this, as well polished as it may be.

Title: The Thrill of It All
Review: Much of it feels comfortable; at 25, Smith can still sing the hell out of the kind of love songs he could sing the hell out of when he was 20. But he’s grown, too, and The Thrill of It All is best when he stretches out of his comfort zone.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: Hypnotic Eye is little more than a decent record with a few ideas above its station.

Title: Flashy
Review: Much of the record satirizes plastic surgery and oversexed macho men, but despite the ironic humor, there’s a compassion in the music that’s unexpected coming from a band best known for a Taco Bell–referencing novelty hit.

Title: Stumble into Grace
Review: She is still in the forefront of genre-transcending artistry.

Title: The Worse Things Get ...
Review: A listless cloud of heartbreak penetrates every crack and many moments teeter on the maudlin, but The Worse Things Get has fight, too.

Title: WZRD
Review: These bedroom demo-sounding efforts are primitive. {Jun 2012, p.85]

Title: Perfect
Review: Fair has always had a tendency to get too cute in his lyrics, but there’s a contagious positivity to Perfect, even if it’s often oversimplistic.

Title: Beyond the Pale
Review: Anyone pining for the arch twig-insect dandy of old, preening over driving beats and gyrating to wayward early electronics, will find much to love on this album.

Title: Ungrateful
Review: Sadly, it plonks them squarely in the polished but unremarkable heartland of inoffensive US shopping mall metal. [Jun 2013, p.99]

Title: Body of Song
Review: Body Of Song finds Mould creating familiar-sounding music without simply rehashing fan favorites.

Title: The Redeemer
Review: The Redeemer finds Blunt adding a series of potent new weapons to an already well-stocked musical armoury. [Jun 2013, p.88]

Title: Ignatius
Review: Rather than trying to please the club, the ladies, the hardcore 30+ crowd, the younger fans, and everyone in between, Jadakiss has released a cohesive, satisfying album that is easily one of his best efforts. More of this, please.

Title: La Isla Bonita
Review: Results are varied.... Luckily, Deerhoof's blahs are better than most people's best. [No. 116, p.57]

Title: Mozart's Mini Mart
Review: Mozart’s Mini Mart, his first LP since On The Hot Dog Streets (2012), is militant and magnificent--as oddsome as dress wearing-era Kevin Rowland, as socially astute as Sleaford Mods, as mythomaniacal as Kanye West.

Title: Sunny Border Blue
Review: This is more of simply Hersh and an acoustic guitar than her last effort (1999's Sky Motel), but that just gives the appearance of other instruments greater effect. The emotional weight of her often unorthodox sentiments comes from subtle mastery of dynamics.

Title: Lux Prima
Review: Everything across Lux Prima feels completely right; familiar yet new, revealing more of two beloved figures without losing what made them great all these years.

Title: Traffic and Weather
Review: Record geeks beyond repair, the songwriters still lace the more accessible material here with their trademark wit.

Title: Emperor of Sand
Review: Drawing as much from their past as well as their present, Mastodon refuse to go extinct just shy of two decades of music-making. Emperor of Sand is at once emotionally powerful and musically arresting.

Title: The Origin of Love
Review: The fact is, The Origin of Love is simply a good record by one of the UK's more undervalued pop songwriters.

Title: More Adventurous
Review: Lewis' crisp alto shines on every track... Unfortunately, the songs (and especially the lyrics) don't give Lewis the support she deserves.

Title: Run the Jewels
Review: The vibe is somewhere between the coherence of an album and the casual flow of a mixtape.

Title: The Great Depression
Review: The thrills come when he jumps off the cross and gets on the dance floor. [Nov 2001, p.129]

Title: For Paris
Review: For Paris has an avant-gardist taste, and the homemade artwork and written statements ring sincere.

Title: Fast Man Raider Man
Review: Fast Man Raider Man is simply too long, and, as such, a dilution.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: In throwing his emotional locker wide open, Frank Ocean has made a tender, engrossing classic.

Title: Strut
Review: A selection of his own trademark cliches. [Oct 2014, p.90]

Title: Range of Light
Review: Much like Bon Iver's output, Range of Light delivers a set of songs with a fixed sense of place and a nostalgic sense of time.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: [A] taut, intense collection of songs.

Title: You Know What It's Like
Review: You Know What's It's Like presents the emotional cente of dal Forno's work with a clarity previously absent from either band. [Nov 2016, p.55]

Title: Violet Cries
Review: Theirs is a music of doomed melancholy –- plaintive, dark, and uneasy.

Title: 151a
Review: When it starts, the overt prettiness and ornate, layered arrangements are very reminiscent of Owen Pallett, but very soon it veers of in some lovely tangents, although it inevitably comes back to string-laden, experimental pop.

Title: Out of the Woods
Review: Much of the album has a cheesy '80s vibe. [#17, p.93]

Title: The Complex
Review: Even emotive guests like Tracy Bonham and Dave Matthews can't heat up The Complex's frosty, dullingly drum-driven aesthetic. [2 May 2003, p.70]

Title: Earth to the Dandy Warhols
Review: Merging the sounds of space rock with an element of trance and a smattering of early Velvet Underground experimentation, the group ends up with an enticing album that holds a fresh mix of sounds.

Title: Sunny Border Blue
Review: Teetering between darkness and light, Hersh's somersaults have never been more compelling.

Title: Harverd Dropout
Review: The Florida rapper’s limited strengths and many weaknesses become highly detectable on Harverd Dropout. Under Pump’s control, the album piles up songs without structure, lines without meaning, and hooks without melody; it’s utterly tasteless.

Title: Bad Penny
Review: Spectrals' debut is mellow and accessible without being boring even though it has less fuzz than fans might be used to.

Title: Making Mirrors
Review: [Making Mirrors] showcases a risk-taking, self-possessed artist, with mixed results.

Title: Farm
Review: Farm isn't the kind of Dino record that has a keeper single like 'Start Choppin'' or 'Feel The Pain.' Instead, it boasts some of Mascis' biggest departures under the Dino name. [Aug 2009, p.110]

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: With Extraordinary Machine, she shatters already sky-high expectations.

Title: ANIMA
Review: Anima is slightly more songful than Yorke’s previous solo record, 2014’s “Tomorrow’s Modern Boxes.” “I Am a Very Rude Person” and “Impossible Knots” both ride funk grooves that recall Atoms for Peace.

Title: Stiff
Review: White Denim sound as strong as ever on Stiff, even when the itchy undertone of the songs begins to rise to the surface.

Title: Carry Fire
Review: The album's roots go back to Zeppelin's immersion in English folk and American blues, but here Plant displays everything he’s learned along the way; Carry Fire's sophistication and mystique place it among the most ambitious and evocative albums of his legendary career.

Title: Haha Sound
Review: Broadcast invokes the spacier reaches of Brian Wilson and Syd Barrett-era Pink Floyd, but Haha Sound is a retrofit well-tailored enough to wear a cloak of its own.

Title: Island
Review: Island isn’t an album that provides any easy hits – it’s more of a record to luxuriate in and discover its charms gradually. Lockdown conditions mean that it’s easier than ever to immerse yourself in this grandiose music, and those that do will find much to lose themselves in.

Title: Before Today
Review: His seventh album bristles with ambition, merging influences ranging from hair metal and Merseybeat. [Jul 2010, p.136]

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: Depression Cherry doesn’t always have the emotional heft, or melodic impact, of their 2010 breakthrough Teen Dream or its follow-up, 2012’s Bloom, but the duo’s knack for crafting thoughtful, enveloping songs makes their return more than welcome.

Title: Singularity
