Review: A deeply passionate, impossibly noisy twee record.

Title: Animal Races
Review: Animal Races is an homage to a bygone era, and a terrific one at that, so while it's far more influenced than it could ever be influential, it does have the potential to inspire sentimentality among those who lived through the era to which it devotes itself.

Title: Gossamer
Review: The onetime bedroom artist now makes first-rate pop anthems, gleaming rocketships of sound that wouldn't sound out of place on the radio next to Rihanna or Nicki Minaj. The tone might seem out of step with the lyrics, but it speaks to a certain resilience.

Title: Kveikur
Review: Kveikur is as melodic and, in places, as fragile as anything the band have released before.

Title: Gigaton
Review: Almost 30 years into a career you would once have put money on ending within five, Gigaton suggests Pearl Jam might still be around long after Trump is a distant memory.

Title: Pocketful of Sunshine
Review: It's good clean fun, entertaining and inoffensive.

Title: Play
Review: Play is a modest, charming little record built on a few simple ideas, and a winner on its own low-key terms: Moby has made the first electronic blues album.

Title: The Decline of British Sea Power
Review: While some of their songs deliver nothing more than noisy twaddle, British Sea Power are a formidable band when they choose to simply stop making sense.

Title: HIVE1
Review: Overall, While HIVE1 may not satisfy those hungry for melody and immediacy, it provides a rich and rewarding experience for those patient enough to listen attentively. [Apr-May 2015, p.80]

Title: Silent Movies
Review: Silent Movies is able to take all of the disparate descriptions above and press them into one unifying album. Marc Ribot really ought to have the opportunity to score films more often, because the results can be breathtaking.

Title: I Like It When You Sleep, for You Are So Beautiful Yet So Unaware of It
Review: When you sleep... has a much more distinct and iconoclastic character than their slick debut, drawing from the effervescent, percolating polish of early '80s Hot 100 pop that they flirted with on "Heart Out.".... That doesn't mean that When you sleep is consistent by any stretch. It's 75 minutes long, which could mostly be solved by trimming the four (!) lengthy ambient tracks on the record.

Title: It Won't Be Soon Before Long
Review: Listen to this record and you realise that by comparison, Robbie Williams does actually have some soul. And if that's not a damning indictment of one of the most execrable records you're likely to hear this decade, I don't know what is.

Title: Paper Gods
Review: Paper Gods feels like a Duran Duran-shaped helium balloon, impressive, shiny, but oddly empty inside. [Oct 2015, p.96]

Title: Public Warning
Review: It's all very funny and cheeky, but after a full album's worth it grows cloying, like a good Saturday Night Live skit that's two minutes too long.

Title: i,i
Review: There is lots of prettiness and some innovative production, like the tumbles of wordless vocal on iMi, gently insulated by downy static; Vernon’s gospel holler and falsetto curlicues will always make ears prick up. But frequently, including on iMi, his melodies are uninspired, feeling like the first thing he came up with while woodshedding around the backing track.

Title: MGMT
Review: Considering it’s only 44 minutes long, MGMT’s self-titled third album feels much lengthier. This is partly due to the dense layers and constantly shifting textures, but it’s also a result of the abrasive digital distortion shrouding the psych-pop jams, making it a tiring listen even at its most melodic.

Title: High Crimes
Review: This is shiny modern rock with a scuffed heart and a sense of constant restlessness of spirit. [Jun 2019, p.89]

Title: Megafaun
Review: Yet aside from that one cut, Megafaun's self-titled album seamlessly integrates an easy-going tuneful-ness with a nearly mystical devotion to tone and texture.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: It’s with his latest masterpiece, 808s & Heartbreak, that he has demonstrated, with impeccable skill, that he is supreme, yet again.

Title: How To Become Clairvoyant
Review: On his first album in 13 years, Robbie Robertson resumes his fascination with the great American mythos.

Title: Where It Hits You
Review: Tracks such as "Epilogue to a Marriage" here, serve as a reminder that there's always room for the real thing, and you'll know it when it hits you.

Title: Free the Universe
Review: Free the Universe is, after all, a party album, and by using an energetic mix of faces both famous and obscure, Diplo keeps his grungy dancehall rave running on all cylinders.

Title: Any Human Friend
Review: From the arresting cover (a comically unsalacious shot of a semi-naked Hackman holding a piglet to her breasts) to the startling contents, Any Human Friend signals Hackman’s coming of age as an artist with real purpose and  star power.

Title: The King is Dead
Review: A relatively understated delight from a band few might have suspected capable of understatement.

Title: Hush
Review: As far as listening experiences go, you can certainly do a lot worse than sitting back in your chair, being consistently affected by Asobi Seksu's sunlit wandering. Unfortunately, it would probably be better for Hush if the band stepped into the shadows every once in a while.

Title: See You On The Moon
Review: There's something awkward about the whole: the album wins attention but doesn't keep it. [Jun 2010, p.95]

Title: Youth Culture Forever
Review: 'War Cry," the album's longest track at more than 11 minutes, sums up the band's problem with its blend of barely audible vocals and meandering guitar solos that go from metallic shredding to simple repeated clusters of notes without building much tension or release. [No. 109, p.59]

Title: Hell Hath No Fury
Review: Listen to the beats and you'll find The Neptunes' best work in years. [27 Jan 2007, p.31]

Title: Resilience
Review: Resilience mostly lives up to the promise of its moniker, delivering another well-executed, purely fan-centric collection of testosterone-fueled, post-grunge/processed metal jams with a complete disregard for subtlety.

Title: Supermigration
Review: Supermigration pulls its punches here and there, but the closer, "Rainbow Collision," lives up to its hippie-friendly title with an epic swell.

Title: The Loves of Your Life
Review: Leithauser's voice is its usual delicious scuffed-up howl, the music covers a broad indie-rock sprawl, but the focus here is the stories. [Jun 2020, p.102]

Title: Black Sarabande
Review: His latest is an unhurried flow of ambient piano pieces that, despite the implications of the title, are only momentarily dark and far from risqué, perhaps at times more suited for those soft intimate moments made for two, or most certainly personal reflections made for one.

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: Sundown is still considerably boring when compared to the likes of the Kings' first three albums. It's also too long, the back end sacked with faceless mid-tempo songs devoid of hooks that can't compare to the mini-epics up front.

Title: Rented World
Review: Rented World might not be quite the landmark that it’s predecessor was-- it’s unlikely to be a fixture of too many album of the year lists outside of the punk scene--but regardless of the accolades it may or may not win, it is evidence of a band who know exactly what they want to do, and have little trouble in achieving it.

Title: Devout
Review: This is an album of breath and sigh, baby’s gibberish and parent’s confession. It’s also a complex and layered meditation on fatherhood and family, rich in emotion, textured and capacious; it’s a long exhale--stately, calm, joyful.

Title: Part of the Light
Review: Part Of The Light finds him in dream-like mode, and though he'll never rival Guy Garvey for loquacity, he's so comfortable in his own skin that To The Sea details a cheery trip to the seaside and his voice soars where it once growled. [Jul 2018, p.112]

Title: Ring
Review: Not only is Ring one of the few albums to feature the Nepalese stringed instrument the sarangi and a structure inspired by Homer's The Odyssey, it's also a fresh, creative debut that more than fulfills Glasser's potential.

Title: My Ride's Here
Review: It rocks harder (and louder) without stinting on the musicianly colors that have always redeemed his sessionman whomp.

Title: Internationally Unknown
Review: While a smidgen of originality wouldn't go amiss, there's plenty to compensate for it in the way of exuberance and humour. [Feb 2019, p.88]

Title: Good Girl Gone Bad
Review: Truly, this is music for the ringtone generation.

Title: Rodeo
Review: Scott goes for spacey sounds, stoner vibes and vocal filters, but despite the eclecticism, he's too elusive and bland for Rodeo to amount to a stylistic--let alone a subversive--statement.

Title: Contra
Review: As the watery floating of "I Think Ur A Contra" draws the album to a close, it becomes clear that not only did the members of Vampire Weekend succeed in creating an excellent sophomore album; they've managed to survive long enough to outlive their hype and its attendant backlash.

Title: Wondervisions
Review: Wondervisions, its lyric-less debut full length, does not fall short on its abilities to stir emotion.

Title: Pleasure Boy
Review: While, depending on perspective, the album's a bit shallow on dignity, it goes a long way on atmosphere and seductive, despairing style.

Title: The Resistance
Review: The Resistance, shows growth from the band's previous releases and proves that it's primed for a global musical takeover.

Title: Midnight Memories
Review: Here there are spirited, pitch-perfect replicas of the Who's power-chord bombast ("Best Song Ever"), Van Halen's louche boogie ("Little Black Dress") and Def Leppard's stadium-sized glam ("Midnight Memories").

Title: High on Jackson Hill
Review: High on Jackson Hill doesn't quite trump "Fables" the way that album outclassed its precursor, but it's hardly accurate to call this a disappointment.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: Frightened Rabbit's best material rivals brothers-in-brood the National and Arcade Fire, and even their B-level stuff is better than that of most acts working in this vein. But unlike those leading lights, these guys don't have the pop instincts to throw in the occasional punk scrappers, chamber-folk interludes, or disco rave-up to keep things from getting monotonous.

Title: The Mountain Will Fall
Review: It broadly makes for a winning reboot, from the old-skool hip-hop stylings of The Sideshow and the urgency of Nobody Speak, a collaboration with Run the Jewels, to the more menacing atmosphere of Depth Charge and the jazz inflections of Ashes to Oceans. It’s not without its longueurs, however.

Title: Seer
Review: [The] only complaint is that the rest of the LP doesn't quite sustain the power of these two tracks ["Petrichor" and "Sharp Stones"]. [No. 107, p.55]

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: Comedown Machine has done the best thing The Strokes could have done.

Title: Avonmore
Review: Avondale is Ferry teasing at the possibility of something more and never quite delivering.

Title: This Path Tonight
Review: Actually, resigned existentialism suits Nash well on his lean, reflective new set.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Review: Their sound is an accident born of naivety, but their unabashed love for '80s indie is unmistakeable. [Feb 2009, p.89]

Title: Soft Airplane
Review: With a lack of lyrical development, an emphasis on sound effects is insufficient to make Soft Airplane memorable.

Title: Smile
Review: There’s nothing on this record to equal the giddy delight of Perry’s greatest hits. No fireworks to light up the dance floor, but enough to raise a smile.

Title: Everything Is
Review: Nine Black Alps' raucous nod to the early '90s sounds more heartfelt than the work of so many of their countrymen who can't get past the '80s. [#19, p.96]

Title: Spooky Action at a Distance
Review: Although influences aren't hidden ... it's [Pundt's] own voice here. [May 2012, p.82]

Title: Startin' Fires
Review: Blake Shelton is nowhere near as compelling as his girlfriend, Miranda Lambert (who shows up to lend guest vocals to the cheeky 'Bare Skin Rug'), but this sensitive Nashville hunk definitely knows how to craft a sturdy country tune.

Title: Big Wheel and Others
Review: Big Wheel and Others represents McCombs’ most transient yet memorable volume of song-carved verse yet.

Title: Ghost People
Review: It demonstrates his considerable talent as a producer, for he has crafted a cutting edge album that is extremely engaging and enjoyable.

Title: Yuck
Review: Even with the growing pains, Yuck has learned well from the best and it probably won't be long before this group starts to teach some lessons of its own.

Title: Young Man in America
Review: A fierce, melodic affirmation of sadness and grief, love and lust, attachments formed both strong and precarious, Young Man in America is a marvel of a record from start to finish.

Title: A Written Testimony
Review: An album that dares to tackle life's big questions head on. [Jun 2020, p.101]

Title: We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves
Review: American producer conjures up dazzling electronics. [Aug. 2011, p. 123]

Title: Rise Ye Sunken Ships
Review: Songs typically travel from the spindly to the epic, and extol the virtues of living life to the full.

Title: Serpents Unleashed
Review: With Serpents Unleashed, the scratchy, scrappy Skeletonwitch of old is gone. Beneath that shed skin lurks something far vaster and scarier--but no less sinisterly inviting.
Their sound is now more stark and metronomic than ever before.

Title: Are We There
Review: While Are We There can be taxing at points, by its end, you’ll be overcome by the feeling that you’ve shared in something profound.

Title: Free
Review: As a detour from rock & roll, Free is a fine and compelling study of the mind and mood of Iggy Pop at the age of 72, and if it's clearly the work of an older artist, that works to its favor, a pointed contrast to the abandon of his youth but with no less gravitas.

Title: A Weird Exits
Review: A Weird Exit has an immediacy and coherence that was missing on previous outing, 2015's Mutilator Defeated At Last--a fine album, but not as hooky as this one. [Sep 2016, p.80]

Title: Scarlet's Walk
Review: The new album's themes show that Amos is energized with stories to tell once again - making Scarlet's Walk at once ambitious and also one of her most moving collections yet. [Nov 2002]

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth
Review: There’s enough fun here to justify Anthems’ existence, which really is a lot to say for an album that for so long seemed like it would never exist. If it acts as a one-off return for fans, it’s an amiable, if un-revelatory set.

Title: Ultra
Review: Zomby changes style a frustrating amount, and all of it crawls along at a painstaking speed. He's gone for something different here, which is commendable, but the end product, sadly, comes off more pretentious than deep.

Title: Light Falls
Review: Light Falls retains the epic nature of Wrekmeister Harmonies' earlier offerings, but the scope is much more intimate, direct, and accessible. As a result, it may resonate with some as even more powerful.

Title: To The Sunset
Review: We should've seen this one coming. And still it's a gut punch. [Sep 2018, p.89]

Title: Pause
Review: Hebden has a rare ability to make his delicate instrumentals engaging and unpretentious.

Title: Singularity
Review: There are spoken words buried in these machine-like architectures, only the tone, not the sense of them coming through the music. It is a rather lovely space that Hopkins creates, lyrical but inhabited, precise and well-lighted and buoyant.

Title: Have You in My Wilderness
Review: She doesn’t convey specific messages or exhaustively detail narratives, but to listen to each song on Have You in My Wilderness is to inhabit a feeling in all of its pain and all of its glory.

Title: Dusk and Summer
Review: Dusk and Summer can be as ponderous and precious as a Hallmark card, but it succeeds because Carrabba has found music as intense and bittersweet as his deep, deep feelings. [29 Jun 2006, p.68]

Title: To Pimp a Butterfly
Review: It's a challenging, ambitious combination of words and music that becomes increasingly absorbing over time. [Jun 2015, p.103]

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: If it's pop thrills a go-go you’re after, you’ve got it.

Title: Brighter
Review: Songs are built with obvious hooks and structure, and are lyrically intimate, keeping them in line with the slick electro flavor and emo sentiments of Miike Snow and VHS or Beta.

Title: Nick Waterhouse
Review: It’s an all killer-no filler set that’s the culmination of everything Nick Waterhouse has accomplished for the past nine years. He might have plenty bugging him, but with soul music this joyous and exuberant, you’ll be too busy riding the groove to care.

Title: Garden of Arms
Review: The confidence in their new record is clear, if only because their vocals sound more boisterous than ever, but for the most part, the experimentation is the problem.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: Really, the sad emptiness of these raps needs little explication from me.

Title: Ghosts of the Great Highway
Review: Ghosts of the Great Highway is propelled by excellent songwriting, rich, heartfelt vocals, and solid musicianship.

Title: In Colour
Review: Jamie XX has rearticulated dance music once again. This is an album that surfs from one emotional peak to the next. It’s an album I was actually sad to have end.

Title: El Camino
Review: They sound like a band who think they've made the year's best rock'n'roll album, probably because that's exactly what they've done.

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: This fourth outing puts to bed both Tonight's frantic lonerism as well as any notion of a second night out with Alex Kapranos' equal-opportunity, Jacqueline-and-Michael seducer. [No. 102, p.56]

Title: Now Only
Review: If you choose to look for the metaphors, there's beauty and even redemption to be found in Now Only; if you don't, there's a kind of quiet acceptance in the numbness.

Title: Maladroit
Review: Maladroit is the emo equivalent of '70s arena rock -- a bracingly cocky attitude that tag-teams with its partner, navel-gazing.

Title: Siesta
Review: Siesta may be a celebration, but it keeps it low key. You’ll find yourself refreshed, minus the clean up. It’s a salve for a tiring year.

Title: Whoop Dee Doo
Review: Equal parts The Runaways and Weezer, but still going, and still good.

Title: Hurricane
Review: Jones's fans with long memories will certainly want to hear the first four tracks, but the robustness, of sound, modernity of arrangement and cool, hard, clarity of distinctive delivery that once suggested her style would always sound fresh just fades away. [Nov 2008, p.110]

Title: Wonderland
Review: Similar to the likes of Animal Collective, it weeds out the ordinary pop listener to reward the fan devoted to deciphering its layers.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: This is far from conventional rock, but it's rock as viewed through Cale's dark shades and skewed outsider sensibility and as such, one of his more successful and consistent outings.

Title: A Thing Called Divine Fits
Review: A Thing Called Divine Fits might seem the Platonic ideal of indie rock collaboration, but the most memorable moments have Boeckner's signature.

Title: schlagenheim
Review: As a whole, Schlagenheim is an imperfect, intriguing debut: behind the overheated prose lurks a young, self-conscious band who clearly aren’t as fully formed as the hype suggests, who are still capable of misdirecting their undoubted talent and haven’t quite clicked that intelligence is best worn lightly in the balance between art and heart. But it’s still early days.

Title: Seaside Rock
Review: They've come up with a non-vocal album that surprises and delights. [Nov 2008,  p.112]

Title: Electric Lines
Review: On Electric Lines, Joe Goddard shoots for something eclectic and exciting, but settles for something sporadically enjoyable at best.

Title: Quazarz: Born on a Gangster Star
Review: The group’s most ambitious work yet. ... As if heard through alien ears, the arrangements have a weird, woozy character, with the abstract beats and trickly, liquid synth parts punctuated by unusual instruments like the bass clarinet on the opening “Since CAYA.”

Title: Let Go
Review: Virtually every song on Let Go hits its mark in one way or another, dispensing consistently remarkable moments that range from the sweet minor-key swoon of "Blizzard Of '77" and "Neither Heaven Nor Space" to the sleek, bouncy new wave of "Hi-Speed Soul."

Title: Saturn Return
Review: The effortlessness with which the Secret Sisters articulate their musical ambitions places Saturn Return among recent country-roots gems from songwriters like Jason Isbell and Pistol Annies. If working through their struggles has been a strange process, the wait was more than worth it.

Title: Kitchen Sink
Review: It's bolshy, uncompromising and demands to be played on repeat. [Aug 2020, p.36]

Title: Shedding Skin
Review: With its introversion and focus upon the everyday in both subject matter and imagery, the appeal of Shedding Skin depends partly on your appetite for people watching. [Mar 2015, p.48]

Title: Night Train
Review: Overall, Keane's efforts to move beyond pigeonholing succeed more than they fail. [Jun 2010, p.107]

Title: Hasta El Cielo
Review: In rethinking them together, this just might be the band’s most unified piece of work. The ability to harness such rich diversity in sound is what makes this band stand out.

Title: Begin Again
Review: It’s an entertaining assortment of Jones unrestrained.

Title: Pluto
Review: Pluto wears that influence loosely, without ever feeling formally indebted to it.

Title: Shelter From The Ash
Review: A fine album for autumn.

Title: Art in the Age of Automation
Review: Portico's rejuvenated quartet status brings with it more of the jazz-influenced stylings that first made their name, [Oct 2017, p.36]

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: Lovelorn, honest, poignant and emotional in the best way imaginable.

Title: Everything's Getting Older
Review: The net result, a tapestry through dark alleys and along river banks, makes for an entertaining listening journey.

Title: Old Wow
Review: As sad ballad follows sad ballads towards the close, Old Wow is not as well-paces. Nonetheless it's full of resonant music. [Feb 2020, p.94]

Title: Negative Capability
Review: These songs may be scorched with an unavoidable yearning quality, but they find her standing at a new creative peak: ‘The Gypsy Faerie Queen’, co-written with Nick Cave, might rank among the best songs either have written, while ‘Born To Live’, her piano-led paean to departed lifelong friend Anita Pallenberg, speaks of our corporeal impermanence with a calm but unswervingly frank honesty.

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: Wilco is a Great Band, if you like stuff that’s boring. And a lot of people seemingly do.

Title: Heal
Review: Same Emotions, meanwhile, sounds like a lovingly recreated homage to the soft rock of Journey, Toto, et al. Best of all is his deeply personal tribute to the late Jason Molina. [Aug 2014, p.113]

Title: Myths of the Near Future
Review: It’s an immersive, art-school-bred aesthetic that, three or four times on the band’s debut album, makes for some very good music, too.

Title: C'mon, C'mon
Review: Crow sounds as if she's trying too hard to show us that all she still wants to do is have some fun. [May 2002, p.91]

Title: Western Stars
Review: Between 1975-84, he made Born to Run, Darkness on the Edge of Town, The River, Nebraska and Born in the U.S.A.—five outright classics. Though Western Stars doesn’t rise quite to that level—it’s an impossibly high standard—Springsteen’s latest entry in such a storied catalog more than holds its own.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: You could never truly expect a truly cohesive album from Santigold, and she's met expectations.

Title: The Beginning
Review: The Beginning is a depressing listen, not because the music's that bad, but because it implies that even the most successful pop producer on the planet can't afford to indulge in anything that might be construed as intelligent or interesting, lest the masses run away screaming in terror.

Title: News and Tributes
Review: Too often, though, as on the lacklustre title track 'Favours For Favours' or 'Thursday', it has to be said that the new beast just isn't as feisty as the one-trick pony of old.

Title: O Shudder
Review: They've made an undeniably great record that hits the sweet spot between distinction and accessibility. [Mar 2015, p.93]

Title: What Chaos Is Imaginary
Review: Tracks like ‘Swamp and Bay’ bring us punchy indie rock, and ‘Hoax and the Shrine’ give us woeful nursery rhyme acoustics befitting to a reflective train ride in a coming-of-age film. A development for Girlpool, and one of sheer enigmatic bliss.

Title: An Omen
Review: Maandig remains the primary vocalist; yet she is MIA on many of the vast orchestrations that feel like Tattoo leftovers.

Title: A Situation
Review: Every single moment of ‘A Situation’ feels dreadfully real and groovy as heck, so prepare yourself mentally - you may start to believe the matrix is real.

Title: Achilles Heel
Review: One of the most easily forgettable albums in recent memory. [#7]

Title: Why There Are Mountains
Review: Although Joe has now reverted to the boring D’Agostino, the feral noise-pop his band creates is as vicious as ever.

Title: World Eater
Review: It might not hit Dumb Flesh’s dancefloor highs but with decent headphones and a windswept night there’s points on here that are damn near-transcendental, although the damage left might be permanent.

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: While he has talent and likability, it's a shame this album is not a little freakier, a little riskier--a little lonelier.

Title: Sometimes I Wish We Were An Eagle
Review: While the dewy-eyed mood of his last album, "Woke on a Whaleheart," suggested Callahan's romantic entanglement with Joanna Newsom had turned his brain to mush, this miraculous return to form finds the artist formerly known as Smog losing his girl, but rediscovering his mojo.

Title: Spring
Review: It is a hazy path through a dusty landscape of sadness and enlightenment that never arrives at answers or certainties, but shimmers with an eternal mystery. [Dec 2019, p.90]

Title: Positive Songs for Negative People
Review: What Turner lacks in lyrical bravura he makes up with arena sized melodic hooks. [Sep 2015, p.95]

Title: Happy Now
Review: Stripped of the band’s famed essence, the agitated pop of yore is foregone in favour of something that sounds formulaic and uninspired. ... The results are something akin to a terrifying amalgamation of Muse and Duran Duran.

Title: Blade of the Ronin
Review: Even those who decided years ago that this album was going to be great will be hard-pressed to find a great rap record here, only a sporadically enjoyable one.

Title: Theater of the Mind
Review: We've watched this movie more than a few times, but it's always fun to see this many talented pals cutting loose together.

Title: Unsound
Review: Mission of Burma continues to make some truly glorious noise on Unsound.

Title: The Bright Mississippi
Review: There is sleaze here and funeral swing, and sass to spare. [Jun 2009, p.105]

Title: Do Things
Review: Do Things has a few missteps, but May just keeps smiling and charging forward.

Title: White Hills
Review: Monstrous stoner-psych jams from, of all places, Williamsburg. [July 2010, p. 95]

Title: The Hollow
Review: If you're looking for a solid heavy record to give a spin, give The Hollow a chance.

Title: The Diary of Alicia Keys
Review: If she's going to make us read her diary entries, she's going to need something more compelling than this litany of cliche and hackneyed need-a-man Bridget Jones-wailing. [Feb 2004, p.72]

Title: The Final Frontier
Review: The Final Frontier, its scratchy, clattering intro resembling The Mars Volta and signifying that this national institution's quest for adventure remains unabated. [Sept. 2010, p.98]

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: Effectively embracing the entire history of the band's sound, the album sprawls over an hour, and has so many peaks and valleys it's practically topographical. [Apr 2005, p.98]

Title: The Fatal Feast
Review: Following a David Cronenberg-style instrumental intro that whets the appetite for straight-to-video gore, The Fatal Feast flails forward with the professional bounty hunter creed "Repossession."

Title: Lessons in Love
Review: Lyrically, Polite rarely strays far from a seducer's template, but the way in which he sells the cliche is compelling.

Title: Memento Mori
Review: Memento Mori, Flyleaf’s second album, is precise, muscular and alluring, full of crypto-Christian imagery and husky riffs.

Title: Faking the Books
Review: Their sound is an interesting polyglot, one as easily accessible to dance minimalists and brown corduroy-wearing emo boys, and with nary a compromise. [Apr 2004, p.86]

Title: Bones
Review: There’s so much bone-crunching texture that it claws your ears like a gnarled kitten. Past the theatrical dins of songs like Flight and This Time, though, there are simple pleasures in the cinematic darkness of I Am the Others and the folksier Undone, which strikes a balance between complex rhythms and alluring acoustic guitar licks.

Title: Waxing Romantic
Review: Waxing Romantic is an impressive blend of top-notch songwriting, inventive production, and strong performances, the kind that vaults Bretzer to the same lofty heights of his influences.

Title: Rembo
Review: The end result is a triumph; a late-night drive that starts somewhere in '90s Michigan but arrives home, in a gloriously disorientating future. [Aug 2017, p.90]

Title: Viet Cong
Review: Viet Cong aren't quite home yet, but they're getting there. [Mar 2015, p.100]

Title: Storyteller
Review: Story may not tell listeners much about Underwood’s inner life, but she’s never owed or offered that. She makes good songs sound great, and that’s enough.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being
Review: For most of I Am Not a Human Being, it seems like Wayne has forgotten how to write a verse. He's all about couplets now.

Title: Ma Fleur
Review: Neither jazz nor trip-hop nor any other label you might care to slap on it, Ma Fleur delineates an immensely moving, utterly distinct night-time world which is a pleasure to inhabit.

Title: Young Man in America
Review: A sorrowful, yet captivating collection of songs, ensuring that Ms. Mitchell continues to snap at the heels of PJ Harvey in the female singer songwriter stakes.

Title: Puff: In The Air Without A Shape
Review: Puff doesn’t grab your attention directly. Rather, it occupies your subconscious, leaving vestiges of melodies and lyrics behind that lie dormant for stretches of time, resurfacing intermittently and maddeningly.

Title: We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions
Review: We shall overkill, he means.

Title: The Journey Man
Review: This is his first proper solo LP project since ‘Saturnz Return’, and it’s brilliantly, bloody-mindedly Goldie: a slew of deep d’n’b grooves offset by beatless lounge-blues arias and glamour-soaked jazz club noodlings.

Title: TRUE
Review: Avicii's genre-hacking whimsy may seem decadent or oblivious. But it's undeniably optimistic--inspiring, even.

Title: The World Is Yours
Review: The less devout should keep a pinch of salt on stand-by. [Oct 2007, p.100]

Title: Right Here Right Now
Review: Sparks still sounds like she's finding a voice of her own.

Title: Hearts
Review: Pitched somewhere between synthed-up '80s mood-out and electronic-infused shoegaze, the Swedish duo I Break Horses may have a slightly off-kilter name, but Hearts  is a fine, if often derivative, debut album, a classic instance of a band knowing who and what they love, but not to the point of making it their own.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Things improve considerably when the pair abandons the preening street-cred game; Moffat and Middleton seem finally to realize that if they're going to make a love record they might as well not half-ass it.

Title: A Picture Of Good Health
Review: The follow-up to 2017's excellent debut Popular Music, A Picture of Good Health finds Hull, England four-piece LIFE at their most angrily buoyant.

Title: Leucocyte
Review: More than any other recording issued by this excellent band, Leucocyte captures the art of music making at the moment of conception.

Title: Out of Silence
Review: His sweetness and melancholy are as palpable in the composition as they are in the performance and, ultimately, that's why the live-in-the-studio recording of Out of Silence cannot be dismissed as a stunt: such a simple, yet kinetic, production is the only way to do justice to songs are rich as these.

Title: Faithful Man
Review: This new album feels like a lost gem recently unearthed.

Title: De-Loused in the Comatorium

Review: Electric Endicott confirms that the gifted outsider who allowed us to glance into his psyche on You Think You Really Know Me hasn't stopped pursuing his singular vision of twisted pop music, just as he still hasn't figured out how to deal with the opposite sex, and who knows: if he ever did, he might never be able to make music again.

Title: Songs In The Dark
Review: An album drenched in familiar swathes of charm, pathos, elegance and black humour. [Dec 2015, p.90]

Elsewhere, "Reach Out" and "Can I Go On" provide the kind of anthemic rallying calls we collectively get behind Sleater-Kinney for.

Title: i
Review: Tracks as smart as the dreamy, melancholy character sketch "Irma" and the lyrical album-closer "It's Only Time" suggest how Merritt can top 69 Love Songs: one song at a time.

Review: Moffat's half-sung, half-muttered confessionals still lurch between the pulsing beats and pensive instrumentation but the tone is now more funereal than carnal.

Title: Sick Scenes

Title: Berlin
Review: Confident, crunchy, and catchy as hell.

Title: Noble Beast

Title: The Decline of British Sea Power

Title: Reward

The influences have either been thoroughly shrugged off or thoroughly absorbed, and what we get here is a frankly remarkable set of ten songs that lead us from our comfort zone almost imperceptibly to a very very strange place, and then once more out of the woods and back to more recognizable territory.

Title: Ukulele Songs
Review: Ukulele Songs is lovely as it breezes by, but it doesn't promise a very long shelf-life.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: Thankfully, there are just enough flashes of brilliance to save it, even if much of the album comes across as a really expensive demo.

Title: Bright and Vivid

Title: Non-Fiction

Title: The Milk of Human Kindness

Title: Yellow House
Review: Yellow House is a keeper.

Title: Shapeshifter
Review: An impressive and diverse follow-up to an already-impressive debut.

Review: The album disappoints. [#32, p.58]

Review: Fun for all the family. [May 2020, p.28]

Title: Good Bad Not Evil
Review: At times, it feels far too self-consciously hip; at others, the roughness of their songs is fantastically ready.

Title: The Lamb

Carlson's guitars, clearly the focus, get to step back from the angular and the lugubrious. Instead, red-lipped riffs flutter over careful and precise percussion, evoking crimson dresses striding down gold corridors. And underneath it all--the star player--Adrienne Davis’s steady, world-eating thud has never sounded better.

Title: Swimming
Review: Whatever headspace produced Swimming, it captures this perfectly.

But it's here that they've finally come into their own, where Jack and Meg White finally seem not only comfortable with the path they've chosen, but practiced, precise and able to convey the deepest sentiment in a single bound.

Title: Animal Joy

Review: Even with Gonzalez windy guitar strums taking a definitive backseat, Gonzalez purists will not be able to resist the charms of his friends in Junip. [Summer 2010, p.79]

Title: Blade of the Ronin
Review: While Vast Aire and Vordul Mega rarely hit the heights of their former lyrical ingenuity, their stream-of-consciousness rapping style remains one of the most potent forces in hip-hop.

Title: Get Born
Review: The best tunes here have that boys'-club vibe of the best early-to-mid-'70s hard-rock bands, dead-on and nailed.

Title: Maths + English
Review: Where once he growled his rhymes through gritted teeth or abortively gulped them down altogether, now the beats let him breathe. [Jul 2007, p.113]

Title: The Glorious Dead
Review: The Glorious Dead is an achingly self-aware throwback record, focusing more on the strength of each song than the album's overall structure.

Title: Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino
Review: He shares the ennui, dissociation, irony and unfulfillment of his particular celebrity destiny, coupled with a biting and original take on a more widely shared quotidian anxiety that listeners will note with nods and laughs and hums of recognition. But a hit or two would have been nice.
The songs hold to simple instrumentation and simple structures that allow Adele's raspy, expressive voice to develop the story in the verses before she delivers the hook.

Title: Earthquake Glue
Review: The songs are getting samey. [Sep 2003, p.102]

Title: Singularity
Review: In self-reflection, Hopkins deconstructs Singularity; for all its avenues, detours, desperate reaches and anxious retreats, true inner peace rests on a foundation of simplicity. A modest concept, often taken for granted.

Title: Brainfeeder X
Review: The set's ordering is exemplary, especially given its size, but diving in at random reaps the richest rewards, throwing up unexpected complements and contrasts. ... It's a trip for devotees and newcomers alike. [Jan 2019, p.41]

Title: Dark Bird Is Home
Review: Though Matsson more often sings solo, both on this album and throughout his discography, the supporting vocals add a new layer to his work, elevating it to a level he hadn't previously hit. [Apr-May 2015, p.86]

Title: Last Exit
Review: What worries me about the obviously talented Junior Boys is their tendency to round their corners. The music is so safe, so pleasant; it's not hard to imagine it in the Starbucks CD rotation without raising an eyebrow.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Despite its delivery, Kamikaze is very resolutely an old-fashioned album: 45 minutes and 13 tracks long.

Title: Fever
Review: Like the soundtrack of a very bad Jazzercise class.

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: Tune-Yards latest is a record dominated by the society it both critiques and is a part of.

Title: Galapagos
Review: The group's ambition is admirable, but they come unstuck on the over-egged samba shuffle of "Lost Winter," while even Florence Welch might consider "Mellotron" to be a bit much. [Mar 2013, p.76]

Title: American V: A Hundred Highways
Review: This is not a 'commercial' release, at least not in the commonly construed meaning of the word. If you had to be picky, you could say that nothing has the impact of that cover of Nine Inch Nail's "Hurt" or Nick Lowe's  "The Beast In Me". But that's beside the point.

Title: Serpent Music
Review: While it doesn’t always work, it’s Yves Tumor’s use of field recordings that gives Serpent Music an ambulatory quality.

Title: A Short History of Decay
Review: A Short History Of Decay is raw, honest and painful: listening to its 10 songs feels like intruding on someone’s personal grief.

Title: Beautiful Thing
Review: Kinetic and heartfelt, Beautiful Thing lives up to its name and delivers some of Taylor's finest solo music yet.

Title: We, the Vehicles
Review: Sure, emo bands cry over their myriad problems all the time, many of which are delivered either as mopey confessionals or with Gerard Way-ian gothenticity, but rarely are they so post-apocalyptic.

Title: Alright, Still
Review: If the pop dreams get slightly tarnished by the graffiti put-downs of 'Not Big' (her ex has a 'size problem') and 'Alfie' (her brother smokes too much dope) then that's not too worrying. With a personality this size, this isn't the last time you'll be hearing from her.

Title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
Review: With Merriweather Post Pavillion, Animal Collective have refined their distinctive vision, once again proving they are ahead of the pack. [Feb 2009, p.1114]

Title: Amputechture
Review: Amputechture shows a band honing their eruptive sound and bringing it into tight focus for the first time, routinely pushing their music to the wall without ever risking a breach.

Title: Rize of the Fenix
Review: And so, just like that, Tenacious D are back.  They're funny, they're absurd and they're hotter than a phoenix.  Sorry, fenix.  Let's just hope we don't have to wait another six years for the next one. [May 2012, p.52]

Title: Amen & Goodbye
Review: Where this album sets itself apart is with Roche, her contributions otherworldly and out of time, strange Wicker Man chants both charming and sinister. Her siren song laces Amen & Goodbye's best moments.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: A schzoid excursion into the fake plastic glitz/sorid underground duality at the heart of Los Angeles. [Winter 2010, p.64]

Title: The Stimulus Package
Review: Another hip-hop comfort blanket, The Stimulus Package reminds us a dope loop and a capable MC justify their own existence.

Title: Push the Button
Review: An album full of beat-wise psychedelia. [27 Jan 2005, p.61]

Title: Asleep In The Back
Review: Seems that after all the pale imitators, Radiohead finally have a competitor worthy of healthy comparison.

Title: Eat Pray Thug
Review: His solo debut is packed with syntax-mangling wordplay. [Apr 2015, p.95]

Title: Ships
Review: It isn't fair to Smith to imply that Ships is Danielson's play for a Stevens-level breakout, but the record is definitely an assured, ambitious follow-up to 2004's ramshackle Brother Is To Son.

Title: A Funk Odyssey
Review: 'A Funk Odyessey' takes you on a journey of eye-closing triteness.

Title: Lesser Known
Review: Since Dan Deacon is a personal friend of Boeldt's, it's no surprise that club music would rub off, but even when the wheels start spinning and electro funk is cross-referenced, the all-too-cute, retro '80s aesthetic is ever present.

Title: Jessica Pratt
Review: Listeners who prefer their folk flashier or wrapped around memorable, poppy hooks might find Pratt's approach meandering or bland. But those with a more patient ear will find her a worthy and quietly distinct heir of Baier, Bunyan, and Dalton's homespun sound.

Title: Shut Up I Am Dreaming
Review: Shut Up I Am Dreaming is pure bedroom art-pop with a thin Britpop glaze that is as poignant and self-effacing as it is self conscious and pretentious.

Title: Wolves
Review: Stylistically speaking, the 11-track set doesn't deviate much from the formula the band established on its prior outings, but it will no doubt please longtime fans just looking for something new to pump their fists to.

Title: On A Distant Shore
Review: His facility with the form is evident on songs like “Easy To Love”, which aptly has the smooth, easy manner of a standard, and more dramatically with “On The Waterfront”, which renders solitude in epic fashion. ... Elsewhere, he reverts to form with the rolling blues arrangement of “Love This Way”, with his signature piano to the fore, and terse blues guitar punctuating his account of being “lost inside the darkness and the howling wind”.

Title: Paradise Valley
Review: Eleven songs that hit the mark where last year’s overwrought "Born and Raised" mostly missed, Paradise Valley is a more lyrically restrained and less generically reflective affair. And musically, it’s bigger, more accomplished and more approachable.

Title: Electric Light
Review: While producer Paul Epworth’s contribution is accomplished, adding a dynamism that maintains our attention throughout, the record seems to lack an underlying theme. Bay has been a bit too clever for his own good, and on Electric Light fails to latch onto a identity that makes him truly unique.

Title: Flux Outside
Review: The Royal Bangs don't just grab you by the throat and demand your attention, they threaten to rip apart your speakers, drench you in your own dancefloor sweat, and leave you begging for more.

Title: Plunge
Review: Plunge is a very unique album that can be as melodic and intimate as it can be chilling and alien. After repeated plays, all of these aspects end up being enjoyed since it is apparent that these songs were built with an honest, emotional grit.

Title: Wet from Birth
Review: Perspiration trumps inspiration, as madly sawing strings and short-circuiting robot bleeps compensate for the lack of hooks. [Oct 2004, p.120]

Title: West
Review: At times it can become something of an amorphous blob, with songs blending into one another, but the highlights of Home and Flight ensure that there's something tangible to hang on to.

Title: Passionoia
Review: For all its wit and occasional beauty, Passionoia lacks the killer anthem that would make the band genuine subversives rather than cult wags. [Mar 2003, p.102]

Title: Harps and Angels
Review: Sharp, incisive, funny and at times even heart-rending in the context of some beautifully-judged rag/country/Dixie-land songs.

Title: With Light and With Love
Review: There’s a rare moment of foreboding on the briefly gloomy ‘Feather Man’, but the likes of ‘Shining’ and the Avi Buffalo-style ‘Only The Lonely’ are representative of an optimistic and sprightly record.

Title: Redemption's Son
Review: Redemption's Son achieves a sophisticated marriage of traditional songwriting craft and avant-garde production.

Title: Splitting The Atom EP
Review: On Splitting The Atom, though, the duo simply sound like they’ve run out of ideas, unsurprising given the opening half’s attempts to re-visit an album over 18 years old.

Title: Crosseyed Heart
Review: By the end, you find yourself wishing he was just a little more prolific.

Title: You Are Free
Review: You Are Free demonstrates a subtle, hopeful change in sentiment--a relief from Cat Power's melancholy.

Title: American Gangster
Review: He's not a real gangster, but he is a real poet. And like the greatest of American poets, he admits that, very well then, he contradicts himself. American Gangster contains multitudes.

Title: Jet Black
Review: Too many of the songs settle into lackluster grooves, and pairing those grooves with Vermue's style-over-substance vocal affectations makes the album less than memorable.

Title: Tomb
Review: Tomb benefits from having a slightly cleaner sound and the results are remarkable. Tapping into the potential his past albums only hinted at, It's polished just enough that the songs boast a greater clarity but without losing any of the homespun intimacy of his previous recordings.

Title: Each Other
Review: Somber and yet stirring, Each Other is an album that encourages shoe gazing, day dreaming and simply settling into quiet contemplation.

Title: Dethalbum III
Review: The band's latest volume, Dethalbum III, features some of Small's best melodies and instrumentation to date.

Title: Something For All of Us
Review: Great sleepy Sunday-afternoon music, but it could have been more than that.

Title: Universal Mind Control
Review: Although Universal Mind Control represents a serious step backward from the successes of his recent projects with Kanye, it would be remiss to say the album is the death knell for Common's career or that he has fallen off in any significant way.

Title: Legion of Boom
Review: The Crystal brothers score low on originality, but they certainly know how to make cheaply pleasurable noise.

Title: Music Kills Me
Review: Gets lost somewhere between camp and institutionalism.

Title: Central Market
Review: The combination of synth, loop techniques and no-joke instrumentalists playing wild and unconventional rhythms is totally over-the-top, but that’s exactly what makes this album so dazzling.

Title: Youth Is Only Ever Fun In Retrospect
Review: For the most part the songs are full to bursting with youthful melodies that lift the weight off the more serious of topics.

Title: Hamburg Demonstrations
Review: There doesn’t appear to be much of a connection between any of the songs, and you’ll have to be fairly willing to wander through the wreckage to find much of any delight.

Title: I Sell the Circus
Review: I Sell the Circus, in other words, can’t quite shake some of Pollard’s tendencies to keep us guessing, tendencies often employed to the detriment of consistency. Ricked Wicky, though, never goes full oddball.

Title: One Bedroom
Review: A fizzling delight, jettisoning previous jazzy inclinations in favor of a gorgeous electronic pitter-patter that sets off Prekop's velvety, mourning vocals. [#14, p.143]

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: Muse used to sound like a Radiohead tribute band; now they sound like a Muse knockoff. [Aug 2006, p.81]

Title: Paracosm
Review: The range of Paracosm helps Greene present himself as more of a singer/songwriter than a producer, though the former part of that dynamic still lags.

Title: Always
Review: This is an album that need proffer no apologies for its dramatic, overwhelming and salutary take on darkness and light.

Title: Cenizas
Review: Cenizas creates the precious illusion of space and motion. [Jul 2020, p. 109]

Title: July Flame
Review: Here is a winsome, lady-driven response to the wood-chopping likes of Midlake, Fleet Foxes and My Morning Jacket that remains refreshingly sweet.

Title: Write In
Review: Happyness's second LP is deceptively well thought-out, deftly constructed around unusual chord changes, and laced with subtly eyebrow raising sonics. ... Making you wonder just how impactful this able trio might be if they properly pulled their finger out. [Jun 2017, p.106]

Title: III
Review: III is a cinematic album undertaking a complicated subject. III and the accompanying music video are culturally important points of contact with the realities of addiction. As such, the Lumineers deliver the album with compassion and clemency.

Title: Days
Review: These tracks are so instantly memorable, so curiously familiar--and so uninspiring, despite their loveliness.

Title: Need to Feel Your Love
Review: Just good old-fashioned hard rock that's guilt free and easy to love.

Title: Mythomania
Review: Mythomania is overdriven, with sparks flying from the bolts in its neck and fruit machine cherries lining up in its vacant eye sockets. But it sounds perfect somehow.

Title: Banga
Review: Banga feels like both a return to form and a renewal.

Title: Lex Hives
Review: As a whole, Lex Hives serves the same purpose as just about every Hives album thus far: dance, let yourself go, and have a good time.

Title: In the Pink of Condition
Review: In the Pink of Condition is the work of an artist fully in control of his sound and vision, and Hawkline delivers exactly the album anyone who's been following him wanted.

Title: Every Kingdom
Review: The shimmering finger-picking and angelic backing vocals of Old Pine build a cosy fireside vibe, but elsewhere the upbeat hoedowns are less impressive. [Nov 2011, p. 92]

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: Mike Cooley steps up with some much-needed light contrast to Patterson Hood’s darker lyrical impulses, which are well represented here, sometimes with touching poignancy and others with blunt force trauma.

Title: Call It Love
Review: Call It Love is an enticing work, but despite its many pleasing qualities, it doesn't quite stand out from the oversaturated electronic dream-pop scene.

Title: Coles Corner
Review: An album of gorgeous, lush songs.

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: The ultimate draw is Antony's voice, and within the first two seconds of the album, it should be very clear to even the most unaware newbies that Antony has an amazing Nina Simone/Brian Ferry/Jimmy Scott vibrato, a multi-octave siren that would sound painfully lovely no matter what he was saying. Lucky for us, he fills that promise with worthy syllables.

Title: Didn't He Ramble
Review: He might ramble sometimes, but his ramblings are like the songs of angels.

Title: Forever
Review: On Forever, Holograms take lofty themes and personal trials and make them a communal experience.

Title: HERE
Review: In a year of superb, politically charged albums by black American artists, Alicia Keys’s sixth record is a standout, on which her signature piano takes second place to her urgent voice.

Title: Mississauga Goddam
Review: A more straightforwardly uplifting listen.

Title: Take The Crown
Review: Take the Crown lapses into the same grandiose self-help talk and too-slick production that's marred his recent albums.

Title: Take Back the Universe and Give Me Yesterday
Review: Really, if your parents don't dig this, there's something wrong with them. This is music for the drive to pick up the kids from soccer practice, or to the doctor for dad's yearly prostate exam.

Title: Ordinary Man
Review: These 11 songs feel like a loose mixtape, flitting among a half-dozen moods and motifs in what feels like a methodical quest for streaming placement.

Title: Master of Disaster
Review: His richest and most consistently satisfying release since the late '80s.

Title: Levitate
Review: So short and concentrated, the album feels like a style exercise rather than a major work, but it nonetheless finds Cutler refining his skills and presenting the best version of his 1992-via-2020 approach yet.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: First Impressions may not be the best Strokes album, but damn if it doesn't feel like the last. [Jan 2006, p.88]

Title: Blondes
Review: Despite retaining a relaxed, lightly psychedelic feel, Blondes' songs are properly functionalist grooves.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: Their fifth album together since 2002 maintains an astonishing standard comparable even to that of original legends like Aretha Franklin and Otis Redding. [Jan 2014, p.122]

Title: Wondervisions
Review: Delicate Steve flaunts every loose end, every unfinished seam. It might be testing to find the threshold of musical coherence; it might just be having a well-plotted lark. But if Delicate Steve's music were any more polished, it wouldn't be half as intriguing or anywhere near as much fun.

Title: My Love Divine Degree
Review: Defiantly lo-fi production rather hampers the attempts at big-budget symphonic soul, but the clubby bangers such as "It's In The Love" and "She Ran Away" work magnificently. [Jul 2017, p.26]

Title: Dents and Shells
Review: Dents and Shells matches the intensity and concision of Impasse, while adding an organic, spontaneous feel to the proceedings.

Title: The Ghost in Daylight
Review: The Ghost in the Daylight (Warp) is a quieter, more overtly folky album than 2007's Western Lands. There is no obvious focal point - nothing like gorgeous, pick-clawed "Trust" from the previous album - only a series of acoustic songs that flare gently from rueful nostalgia to sudden melancholy.

Title: Leave No Trace
Review: With the debut, the main argument against Fool's Gold seemed to be that they were appropriating too much African influence, sounds they didn't have a right to, into what was primarily pop. With Leave No Trace, I'd say they've gone too far the other way, eliminating the eccentricities and exoticisms that made them interesting.

Title: Point
Review: More rounded and less determinedly schizo than Fantasma, Point is a great album of delicious odd-pop made by a whimsically modest genius.

Title: Paranormal
Review: The best thing about Paranormal is that it sounds exactly like an Alice Cooper album. [28 Jul 2017, p.50]

Title: Another Fine Day
Review: Although plucky, Another Fine Day never quite eclipses its members' better-known efforts.

Title: Sister
Review: That Godrich is a master at harnessing restless energy should be no surprise. Here is further proof. [May 2020, p.112]

Title: Boy King
Review: A fifth album u-turn that few could pull off, Boy King is the sound of a band reborn. The core elements are all still there--that falsetto-baritone play-off between vocalists Hayden Thorpe and Tom Fleming as prominent as ever--but they’re glitched-up and garbled.

Title: Americana
Review: Americana is consistently melodic and witty, even if its mellowness sometimes verges on the sedate so that you fancy a burst of garage-guitar power chords from “baby brother” Dave to fire things up a bit. It’s an impressive comeback.

Title: Marauder
Review: Raw but refined, familiar but resolutely strange, Marauder seizes that fine balance of retaining the old while introducing the new; the sound of a band at ease with themselves, it could well be Interpol’s finest album in a decade.

Title: Out in the Storm
Review: Out In The Storm bares out the wound-baring pitch. The injuries remain, but its crunchy riffs, sharp melodies and forthright vocals comprise Crutchfield’s deepest, most direct emotional diagnoses yet.

Title: The Shadow of Heaven
Review: An exquisite album by anyone's standards.

Title: Chasing Yesterday
Review: Chasing Yesterday really isn’t a bad album as such: it’s alright, it has its moments, it’ll do.

Title: Poses
Review: While there's certainly nothing on Poses so riveting as to signify a rock revolution, there's something to be said for the virtue of a simple crooner operating at the top of his game. [#51, p.122]

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: There's nothing minimal about the music, which is cleanly produced, smartly textured hippie shamble.

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: There's just incredible depth to The King Of Limbs, and if you're impatient, you'll miss it.

Title: False Idols
Review: The issue that plagues False Idols is that we only ever seem to hear the seed of each idea. Credit goes to Tricky for variety, but it would be a more rewarding experience if we were able to listen to the songs evolve and develop.

Title: Loney, Noir
Review: Rarely does an album ingratiate itself so immediately and so quickly wear out its welcome.

Title: Continental
Review: Really, there are few surprises here, but there is a crucial one, which is that Continental gradually reveals itself to be a solidly constructed and rather strong collection.

Title: Confident Music For Confident People
Review: Confident Music For Confident People is exactly what it says on the tin. It's also the most unashamedly addictive record you'll hear all year.

Title: The Con
Review: Somehow The Con is even more obsessive sounding than Tegan and Sara’s earlier work, and it’s probably even better; it could well be one of the year’s best albums.

Title: Use Me
Review: There isn't a wasted moment on the album, an expertly crafted triumph that succeeds by balancing addictive production and a concentrated thematic focus. Beyond the technical, Use Me is also an inspiration, a cathartic rebirth for Gunn where she can take full credit for doing all the work, embracing the pain and cleaning her wounds with strength and confidence.

Title: Logos
Review: Cox's great virtue is that he wears his experimentation lightly; though meticulously orchestrated and teeming with digital feints, these songs feel wonderfully spacious and derive an easy-going charm from his hazy vocals and their one-take recording. [Jan 2010, p. 117]

Title: The Besnard Lakes Are The Dark Horse
Review: Throughout, interest is held with dynamic and textural changes, more than an inherently riveting musical idea. But the album’s much more than just stoned jams.

Title: Pop Psychology
Review: While Glenn gamely belts out every song like it's a Broadway audition, his band's appeal remains some distance short of universal. [Aug 2014, p.111]

Title: Starboy
Review: His guests include Lana Del Rey, whose affectless manner makes her a perfect match for him; though the best grooves here come courtesy of Daft Punk, bookending the album with the scudding title-track and Michael Jackson homage “I Feel It Coming”.

Title: Ibeyi
Review: The brilliant "Oya" places the sisters' voices front and centre, swinging from Bjork-like vocal gymnastics into a Yoruban spiritual. Elsewhere, Russell winds the pair's cajon and Bata beats into wonky boom-clap rhythms that smartly complement the romantic "ghosts" or "Think Of You." [Apr 2015, p.77]

Title: Eat Pray Thug
Review: Eat Pray Thug is 11 songs in 40 minutes with the most emotional moment, "Flag Shopping," up soon at track five, paving the way for the intense trilogy that closes: "Al Q8a," "Suicide by Cop," and "Patriot Act."

Title: Devotion
Review: ny quibbles are minor here though, for Devotion is a truly impressive debut album from yet another talented British singer.

Title: The Good the Bad and the Funky
Review: [Tom Tom Club] come this close to surpassing the raw energy, vibrant power, and rhythm-fresh approach of their now-classic eponymous debut.

Title: The Altar
Review: The high points of The Altar are nearly perfect, but these are outnumbered by a massive middle section comprised of unremarkable, uninspired filler.

Title: Treasure House
Review: It’s not so much that these two work well together, but that they work well in spite of each other. There are obviously two very different musical personalities on show, but where they meet is a convenient hinterland that somehow manages to honour the music they love.

Title: Holy Ghost!
Review: Ultimately, the songwriting isn't quite weighty enough to sustain a full album. Worth a check if you're a previous fan.

Title: Son of Evil Reindeer
Review: Son of Evil Reindeer has a fun, collaborative atmosphere which produces some truly unique moments. [June 2002, p.123]

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: 50 Words for Snow is extraordinary business as usual for Bush, meaning it's packed with the kind of ideas you can't imagine anyone else in rock having.

Title: Trouble Will Find Me
Review: Trouble Will Find Me is impeccably sequenced, even at thirteen songs the rare National record that doesn’t contain “the one song they should have obviously left off.”

Title: Prisoner
Review: They're tight in the way that only the threat of bottling can foster.

Title: Alright, Still
Review: Enough of Alright, Still works -- as pure pop and on the meta level Allen aims for -- to make the album a fun, summery fling, and maybe more.

Title: A Bath Full of Ecstasy
Review: Tracks like "Hungry Child" and "No God" are huge, highly focussed anthems that would boss a festival stage. For all of the album's welcome contradictions, however, this focus does hold it back a little. ... But at the right time, in the right company or on the right dance floor, it's a powerful high that also has a message.

Title: Cool Uncle
Review: The mix of guests, which includes Deniece Williams, CeeLo Green, and Jessie Ware (who once covered Caldwell), add to the album's cross-generational character.

Title: Ultra
Review: Ultra is also Zomby’s most experimental record in ages.

Title: Everything Is Love
Review: Everything about Everything is Love feels superficial, from the artists’ constant pronouncement of their love for each other to their engagement with topics like fashion, art, watches (this gets its own category), social issues, how great their friends are, sports, and, indeed, their own lives. The most boring aspect of the album is its centerpiece: the couple’s obsession with their wealth.

Title: Babel
Review: Babel is the more subtle and accomplished album. [No. 92, p.56]

Title: The Wild
Review: The only misfires include Brother, an old-tyme shanty à la the Decemberists whose Back On The Chain Gang-style background chants are an uncharacteristically tacky production choice. Still, The Wild is full of serviceable songs and outstanding playing, with Banwatt once again proving he’s one of the best drummers in the biz.

Title: Black Mountain
Review: Black Mountain is as mundane, bleak, and hollow as the cover art would suggest.

Title: In Our Heads
Review: Three good tracks [songs, "Motion Sickness," "Ends of the Earth," and "Flutes,"] do not an album make - and, unfortunately, this is the sum of the worthwhile moments on In Our Heads. Elsewhere the album is pure drudgery, remarkable only in its dullness.

Title: Gilding the Lily
Review: The resultant sound is crisp and lovely, and on a clear mission to please its other (the listener, maybe?).

Title: Free Nationals
Review: The Free Nationals’ supreme musicianship is unquestionable, but they more often than not seem to require an outside presence leading from the front to really bring it all home.

Title: SASAMI
Review: A collection of songs that are superficially alluring but, bar standout "Morning Comes," rarely captivating. [Apr 2019, p.36]

Title: The Colour in Anything
Review: If there’s a downside to Anything, it’s the exhaustive length: 17 heart-trying wisps-of-songs that near the 80-minute mark, akin to needing a tissue and buying a Costco pallet of Kleenex.

Title: You, You're a History in Rust
Review: One of my favorite albums so far in this very young year.

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: The songs on WWSFTC all hint at loss, limitation and aging, with Spektor's poetic sensibility and passionate singing giving the LP a wrenching sense of vulnerability. [No.88 p.59]

Title: From When I Wake the Want Is
Review: The follow-up has richer, dreamier contours, but the mood is gaunter. [Sep 2018, p.94]

Title: Qualia
Review: The mood of the album is always upbeat, ending with the forward looking “Vorfreude 2”--the German word meaning an anticipation for future pleasures--and doesn’t venture into any of the weirder, harder, filthier, squelchier corners of electronic music.[Nov 2017, p.66]

Title: Don't Believe The Truth
Review: A big stinking pile of rubbish.

Title: Wounded Rhymes
Review: Sonically it's a super-charged take on the girl-group sound, with thundering drums, multilayered vocals, heart-wrenching lyrics and loads of echo-all of which contrasts with her honeyed voice.

Title: Star Wars
Review: The record’s impromptu release was surprising; that Star Wars delivered on all of the excitement surrounding it is anything but.

Title: Human Performance
Review: Human Performance is the first album you could describe as your typical Parquet Courts record--it gathers their best tricks in one place, along with new ones you wouldn't see coming.

Title: New Moon
Review: New Moon has extended the the group’s realization of their own freedom.

Title: The Ghost Of Hope
Review: This moving yet strangely exhilarating album is a distant relative of The Residents’ 1979 album Eskimo, their sonic studies of Arctic culture.

Title: Habitual Levitations (Instilling Words with Tones)
Review: On Habitual Leviathans, the group are more powerful than ever: but it’s a confident power that requires minimal chest thumping.

Title: The Magic Numbers
Review: The Magic Numbers is one of the best pop albums of the year.

Title: Boxer
Review: While Boxer lacks a knockout punch like last album’s 13th round uppercut “Mr. November,” all scorecards still have the National besting David Berman to remain indie rock’s “Great White Mope.”

Title: Dead
Review: As good as Hastings’ production is, however, it is Young Fathers’ vocals that make Dead great.

Title: Man on the Moon: The End of Day
Review: This first official release is a soul searcher and may require more patience than your everyday debut. Still, the chilly, complicated Man on the Moon perfects the futuristic bleak-beat hip-hop Kanye purposed a year earlier, and rewards the listener with every tripped-out return.

Title: III
Review: III is a triumph that takes pop and redefines it, and may come to be seen as a watershed moment for the group as they hit full stride.

Title: Infestissumam
Review: Whatever Ghost's intentions, they've definitely managed to carve out a niche within the increasingly fragmented world of heavy metal, and while purists may revile them for their insolence, it's their insubordination that ultimately earns them a place in the genre.

Title: Lovehatetragedy
Review: The group's secret weapon is the way it so vividly captures the storms of confusion, anger and self-recrimination that swirl around inside a boy.

Title: Everybody's A Good Dog
Review: There are not many people out there doing retro-sounding albums that aren't a mere repetition of something that's already been done several years before (and probably better), but Diane Coffee manages to be hopelessly nostalgic without sounding déjà vu.

Title: Death Lust
Review: Death Lust is an extreme album in which Williams bares his raw, overcome soul over ear-splitting guitar noise. As harrowing as it can be, it’s transcendent rock music that feels unparalleled so far this year. Durham Region should be proud.

Title: IV
Review: Though not their best record, IV is nevertheless an excellent addition to the group's staggeringly consistent discography.

Title: Bandana
Review: There was a lot riding on this album to be a worthy successor to Piñata, and Gibbs and Madlib ended up with something that unfortunately doesn’t come close to those heights, but something that’s still worth thoughtful evaluation and plenty of discussion.

Title: Peace Trail
Review: Peace Trail is a hard record to get a hold of at times. The songs are so bare-bones--and, at times, meandering--that it feels a bit tossed-off.

Title: Marnie Stern
Review: It all adds up to Stern's most fully realised, most rounded album yet, and a huge step in her evolution as an artist.

Title: DNCE
Review: Thankfully, the group ultimately finds its groove with retro, funk-heavy tracks like new single “Body Moves” and “Blown,” which is about exactly what you imagine it is. It’s better for the band—and everyone else--when they don’t overthink it.

Title: Unrest
Review: Oye's single-minded thematic focus and velveteen baritone hold everything together. [#14, p.142]

Title: Hotel Paper
Review: If not as catchy (or stroppy) as Avril Lavigne, she is never less than efficient. [Aug 2003, p.102]

Title: Angles
Review: If nothing else, Angles makes it impossible to predict where the Strokes will go next.

Title: Just a Little Lovin'
Review: Instead of paying tribute as concept, Lynne owns these songs, taking inspiration from the renowned blue-eyed soul singer to create her own sober renditions of indelible melodies from the '60s and '70s.

Title: Deleter
Review: The most interesting moments on ‘Deleter’ arrive when the band embrace ’90s dance in all its euphoric, Technicolor glory. There is still plenty here for fans of the band’s more melancholic, anxiety-ridden electronica, but there’s some much-needed escapism to be derived from getting lost in Holy Fuck’s tripper soundscapes.

Title: Late Registration
Review: Late Registration... definitely mines familiar terrain, but West’s zeal for clever wordplay juxtaposed with his unflinching confidence makes for a charismatic and often electrifying punch.

Title: Hyperion
Review: Advice for Gesaffelstein: ditch the singing guests, and experiment more with the danceable dimness.

Title: Dva
Review: Everything from the synth work to the drum tracks sound the same, and this, on top of the fact that Emika’s vocal delivery rarely changes, makes the album slightly (but only slightly) disappointing.

Title: A Small Death
Review: A set that honors and acknowledges more than wallows.

Title: Margerine Eclipse
Review: The band is crisp and tight, with daring songwriting and arrangements. [Mar 2004, p.111]

Title: The Afterman: Ascension
Review: While the album isn't full of the kind of revelations that drop jaws and illicit gasps, the emotion here is a much-needed place of solace and solidity in a mythos larger and more involved than Heaven's Fence itself.

Title: Beware and Be Grateful
Review: These aren't ferocious songs and they aren't always playing with everything on the forefront, and it's compelling to see that; the band has rounded up the edges of their songs and put them into the ground.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: While his tortured, guttural delivery comes off as the lunatic ramblings of an abusive boyfriend, the actual lyrical meat of The Last Romance rings with the uncomfortable, ugly truth of facing your hungover self in the mirror the morning after a one-night stand.

Title: The Incessant
Review: It’s a challenging and, at times frustrating listen, with great melodies getting lost amongst the feedback--but it begs your attention nonetheless.

Title: Girl on Fire
Review: In spite of that fresh blood [of collaborators], Girl on Fire basically delivers the same payload as Keys' other albums; it's a collection of handsomely crafted, gorgeously sung ballads interrupted by several overworked anthems about the value of perseverance.

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea reveals more poetic, as well as playful, layers with each listen--and above all, underscores what an inviting songwriter Berman is, whether he's taking a darker or lighter approach.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: On the whole, Our Love To Admire delivers exactly what's promised, which for fans will be exactly enough.

Title: Riot Act
Review: The most quietly adventurous, intriguing document the group has assembled in ages.

Title: Man It Feels Like Space Again
Review: Indulgent and trippy and sometimes off-kilter--but a whole heap of fun.

Title: Skull Ring
Review: While the results aren't classic, they're at least presented in a classic style.

Title: Kris Allen
Review: Despite scoring writing credits on an impressive nine of these 13 tracks, Allen gets himself stylistically lost somewhere between Fly White Guy Avenue ('Can't Stay Away') and Bleeding Heart Boulevard ('The Truth'), while rarely visiting original territory.

Title: The Blow
Review: No-one actually ever put out a request for an indie Pet Shop Girls, but thank goodness The Blow decided to do it anyway.

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: I Love You, It's Cool is admirable in large part because its ambitions are every bit as subtle and difficult to quantify as its pleasures-- you don't have to call it "adult indie," but it feels like conflicted indie rock for adults.

Title: Chant Darling
Review: Chant Darling doesn't hit strike that balance often enough, and very few of these songs allow such a glimpse of the musician behind them. Ultimately, Lawrence Arabia's carefully tailored influences have the same effect as that stage name, as if Milne was intent on absenting himself from his own album.

Title: Who Sent You?
Review: It's uplifting, even life-affirming.

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: It's good, but it's not essential.

Title: Make Way for Love
Review: It’s obvious where Marlon Williams’s influences lie but he expertly melds his roots with elements of chamber pop and ‘50s heartbreak amid a sea of textures. Make Way For Love is nuanced, subtle and evocative.

Title: Interstellar
Review: Frankie's doesn't bear the weight of an obviously solo effort and at once succeeds in creating music that rivals any full-band effort from any of her peers.

Title: Coolaid
Review: Casting such a wide net over the span of 20 songs ends up being a gift and a curse as the brighter moments risk getting dimmed out by extremely ambitious attempts that fall short. Running so long ensures filler and repetitive topic material, but overall Snoop makes a strong case against ageism as he fuses the adult contemporary and Gangsta Rap genres.

Title: Last Building Burning
Review: Seriously, these songs feel like Smashing Pumpkins demos--grainy, rough, atmospheric--like if they were made in a garage, and I think that's exactly what CN wanted to achieve. Rough, raw and rugged, but still jangly, catchy and head-poppy enough to leave you wanting more.

Title: Is the Is Are
Review: Repeat visits are sure to unearth more of the band’s thought process, but there's a lingering sense that less could've been so much more.

Title: Cosmic Wind
Review: Overall, Cosmic Wind is free of obvious flaws. But while it's a pleasant album, there's no song distinct enough to elevate it from passive listening.

Title: Bored Nothing
Review: Ultimately, it’s all just too lazy. Yes, I know that’s the point, but this really is slacking overkill.

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: Jurassic 5 is sophisticated and mature, yet it's energetic, fresh, and still knows how to have a good time.

Title: Isolation Drills
Review: Guided By Voices sound more assured than ever before, reflecting on the travails of life in a rock’n’roll band with uncommon honesty and power.

Title: Halo
Review: There are sturdy melodies on the quietly charming Cosoco or Cálculos Y Oráculos, but even an apparently conventional song is soon transformed by her edgy and intriguing off-kilter soundscapes.

Title: Quiet Nights
Review: The line between dreamy and sleepy is a fine one, and many jazz singers have fallen on the wrong side of it when attempting bossa nova. Diana Krall, however, negotiates it skillfully on Quiet Nights, her first album of all bossas.

Title: Modern Blues
Review: The results rate with his best work, by turns reflective and attacking, on which lyrics sparkle and music breathes and flows with a sure touch.

Title: Compassion
Review: Compassion is a major grower, but this is because its fusions don’t all immediately translate. Barnes profits from holding onto some of the answers.

Title: White Bread Black Beer
Review: Features some of his most beautiful, introverted and delicate tunes yet. [24 Aug 2006, p.94]

Title: Black Bubblegum
Review: Even though the surface is smoother and and the vocals less garbled than usual, it’d be a mistake to read Bubblegum as a true unmasking. Filters swaddle Copeland’s voice throughout, distorting and distending it but stopping short of intelligibility; lyrically, he’s striking a tricky balance between deadpan nihilism and pop troubadour nostalgia.

Title: In The Future
Review: Too quick and severe on the brakes, Black Mountain stunt their own grandiosity in the name of dynamics or patience.

Title: Kill The Moonlight
Review: Yet another brilliant pop record for the college radio crowd.

Title: Sundown Heaven Town
Review: On the disc, co-produced by McGraw and longtime collaborator Byron Gallimore, the singer stretches a little more than usual--and takes a few musical chances.

Title: Easy Tiger
Review: It is focused — read: not insanely self-indulgent — in a way that recalls albums of his like “Heartbreaker” and “Gold."

Title: Regional Surrealism
Review: Brian Eno famously stated that "ambient music must be as ignorable as it is interesting". The problem is that, whilst Regional Surrealism certainly succeeds in providing a pleasant musical backdrop, it is rather more the former than it is the latter.

Title: Green Language
Review: Isolating his experimental tendencies to specific tracks leads to some uneven pacing on the album's second half. Otherwise, Green Language fully delivers, serving as a fascinating turn for an artist who earned his reputation by essentially bashing fans into submission with bass.

Title: Same Trailer Different Park
Review: Musgrave just paints a picture of their shared solitude, and she lets us see our absurd selves in the lives of others.

Title: Quieter
