Review: Ratcheting up the glimpses of honesty found on The Redeemer, it is his most transparent collection to date.

Title: BlakRoc
Review: A hip hop album of raw and unusual playfulness. [Jan 2010, p. 118]

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: Even more meandering than its celebrated, if somewhat cold, predecessor. It's also more confident, more coherent, yielding an all-enveloping warmth that's entirely resistant to any iPod shuffle function. [Jul 2004, p.119]

Title: Fall Be Kind
Review: This is Animal Collective at their finest folks, inviting everyone in to see them at their peak and loving the freedom that comes with being on top of the world.

Title: Disappeared
Review: Spring Heel Jack exist in that increasingly exciting no-man's land where clubland and modern jazz call a truce and have a kickabout.

Title: Spiritual Songs for Lovers to Sing
Review: On Spiritual Songs for Lovers to Sing, Roberts and Hoorn deliver a beautiful album filled with bombastic, gothic and anthemic hymns that aim for deliverance.

Title: Model of You
Review: Model of You is neither sparse nor overstuffed, relying on a few, highly polished elements to make up each song and allowing each of them ample space to unfold.

Title: Into the Lime
Review: From the barroom country-rock of Shouting Match to the tear-stained seasonal misgivings of A Very Sorry Christmas, the whimsical warmth of If Only You Knew Her and the back porch baroque of Out Of The Lime, this is perfect and brilliantly realised melodic pop.

Artist: Willie Nelson & Asleep At The Wheel
Title: Willie and the Wheel
Review: It was worth the wait: Nelson's laid-back croon acts as a warm dishrag over the fiddle, pedal steel, cowboy harmonies and roadhouse jazz of Western-swing revivalists Asleep at the Wheel.

Title: Brain Thrust Mastery
Review: It’s a mixed bag then: sometimes they hit bull’s-eye, other times they miss the board altogether, but the erratic results reveal a band dragging themselves out of their comfort zone.

Title: Something to Tell You
Review: It’s hard not to feel that, had they let them run a little wilder, Something to Tell You might be a richer album. For now, they seem content in their comfort zone, striving for--and occasionally achieving-- glossily depthless pop perfection.

Title: The New Danger
Review: It’s largely half-baked in its execution.

Title: Rebirth
Review: The album's drawback lies not with the producers or the material, but with Lopez herself.

Title: The Waterfall
Review: His juxtaposition of dreamy, doors-of-perception tunes and frustrated romantic ones can feel odd, but the musical brilliance keeps the project in focus through to the angst-ridden, Harry Nilsson-like folk of “Get the Point.” Just don’t expect a light listening experience.

Title: Crown Royal
Review: The Queens trio still flow properly and cut a dash.

Title: The Wild Feathers
Review: While The Wild Feathers clearly have the chops, what remains to be seen is whether they can develop their own voice separate from their forebears, and separate from what fans have come to expect.

Title: Psychic
Review: The sound of Psychic is meticulous and luscious.

Title: The Crying Light
Review: As music, it's simply exquisite--more controlled and considered than anything Antony and the Johnsons have done and sure to linger in the minds of listeners for more than a season.

Title: Soused
Review: Haunting, jarring, and oddly beautiful, Soused defies the idea of “easy listening,” but its singular vision and harnessing of the avant-garde makes it one of the year’s most compelling artistic statements.

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: King of Cowards
Review: King of Cowards confirms it’s Pigs that deserve to have their cake and eat it. But it’s also an open invitation to join in the overindulgence with a complete lack of contrition. To gorge on the fruits of their labour is to feel utterly replete, that said, I’m not one to turn down thirds. More more more more more more more!

Title: My One and Only Thrill
Review: Gardot mixes jazz and R&B with elegant string arrangements and acoustic guitars to beguiling, small-hour effect. [Mar 2009, p.98]

Title: Blackout
Review: Spears’s fifth studio album is her most consistent, a seamlessly entertaining collection of bright, brash electropop.

Title: Song Up In Her Head
Review: If the disc drags in places, Jarosz makes up for it with a pair of smart covers: Tom Waits' 'Come On Up to the House' and a take on the murder ballad 'Shankill Butchers' that betters the Decemberists' original.

Title: Lanterns
Review: While the creative process might be something that's constantly changing for Lott and Son Lux, the one thing that's remained consistent is the level of quality, making Lanterns an album that easily lives up to, and even exceeds, any expectations fans would have for the project.

Title: Wolf
Review: If you’ve made your peace with his artistry, the rewards are considerable.

Title: Down To Believing
Review: The taut and engaging first half of Down to Believing juxtaposes formidable country-rock like "I Lost My Crystal Ball" and the garage-rock-at-heart "Tear Me Apart" against more poised and controlled expressions of emotional unrest.

Title: The Soft Cavalry
Review: There’s a pleasing weightlessness wending its way through The Soft Cavalry’s 12 tracks, alternately augmented and offset by Clarke’s lyrics, ranging from tender to grim to destructive. On paper, that reads as confusing; on the record, that stew of emotional expression coheres nicely, each ingredient blending with the others in Clarke’s dream pop base.

Title: The Hawk Is Howling
Review: Hawk makes marginal stylistic advances that it could stand to omit, and it lightly retreads stuff that needs no recapitulation.

Title: Between My Head and the Sky
Review: The good news: Ono, as usual, doesn’t need our approval--not just because she’s rich and famous and fuck you, but because her music stands on its own.

Title: Blood of Man
Review: Blood of Man sounds like that album's [2004's "Use Your Voice"] companion piece, merging the same traces of folk, roots rock, and small-town storytelling with a simple increase in volume.

Title: Tennessee Pusher
Review: Tennessee Pusher pushes their envelope further still. [Oct 2008, p.149]

Title: Uncle Dysfunktional
Review: At its best, in its stoned funk and stewed grooves, there’s enough to suggests they could even fulfill their early ambition to be the "Sly and the Family Stone of Salford." Double double good.

Title: Amoral
Review: Ultimately, it's the stuff of a common nightmare--creepily thrilling, but not worth reliving.

Title: In Ear Park
Review: Without a heavy-handed disposition, Department of Eagles manages to convey the sentiment of another time while reaching a modern audience.
The virtuoso musicianship largely eclipses Henry Tremain's insipid vocals. [Feb 2013, p.112]

Title: Sun
Review: Its songs are mostly amalgams of tired pop music tropes/techniques and trite realizations

Title: Faded Seaside Glamour
Review: After a great start, Faded Seaside Glamour loses its way and ultimately fails to inspire.

Title: Konkylie
Review: The sequencing of Konkylie could be slightly better, but the ability to write a great tune is definitely with these Saints. [Jul 2011, p.88]

Title: Overgrown Path
Review: Throughout its brisk playtime, Overgrown Path evinces an airy touch with transitions, a knack for phrasing (the pauses and extra beats always find their right place), and an invidiously deft hand for crafting verses equal to their choruses.

Title: Hit Reset
Review: Hit Reset, the Julie Ruin’s second album, is super-spunky.

Title: Changing Horses
Review: Unfortunately, not all of Changing Horses is nearly as inspired, particularly the mainstream country pop of 'On Her Own' and rudimentary 'Ballad of Wendy Baker,' but Kweller still lassos up a good time for good ol' boys.

Title: American Tunes
Review: A step left of center yet still striking familiar chords right on time, Allen Toussaint show us his understated brilliance one final time.

Title: James Blake
Review: Using lo-fi digital techniques to play up rough edges and raw emotion, Blake's rare talent is to make music so naked seem unshakable.

Title: Dirty Work
Review: On their fourth album, All Time Low get stranded between bratty snot-rock and witty power pop.

Title: Major Key
Review: The problem with the fantasy of a major Khaled Album though, is that, like a summer blockbuster, Major Key is too front-loaded.

Title: All Your Happy Life
Review: Gloomy, grey but definitely not dull, The Wytches have cast another stellar spell.

Title: United States of Horror
Review: Ultimately, United States of Horror is more than just a collection of songs. It’s exactly what Ho99o9 intended it to be: a blistering manifesto for a disenfranchised America.

Title: Paracosm
Review: Overall, Paracosm is an impressive return from an artist who is still learning his trade.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: While some songs drag, others are absolutely enchanting. [No. 95, p.55]

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: The album teeters on adult contemporary but never lets go of Maxwell's characteristic playful glint. Anyone remotely interested in his sound should pick this up.

Title: Family
Review: The resulting record never splashes too far out of the gene pool... but it creates a pleasing coherence along with a slightly sentimental glow. [Dec 2014, p.100]

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: It's a sweet musical reprieve from radio presenters with beaming suicide smiles gracing subway posters with snappy catchphrases.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: Although Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy has the dizzy invigoration and winning enthusiasm of an excellent first album, it also suffers from a kind of first-disc immaturity, an urge to pack everything in at once and as early as possible, rendering it top-heavy and inconsistent.

Title: Tinsel and Lights
Review: Those who appreciate what she does well can recognise that in her own understated way, Thorn belongs in the pantheon of the truly great British female singers, and this is another worthy addition to a back catalogue of consistently high quality.

Title: What Is Love?
Review: What Is Love? is a superior compilation, but it's held together by Clean Bandit's winning way with a catchy, wistful tune. [Feb 2019, p.111]

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: Twin Fantasy leaves no doubt that Toledo is a strikingly gifted and thoughtful songwriter who also has a firm grasp of how to make his material work in the studio, and isn't afraid to think on a grand scale.

Title: Black Sea
Review: Black Sea is a headphone album, packed with fragile, briefly presented sounds that seem in constant danger of escaping unheard.

Title: Songs for Our Mothers
Review: They claim to be writing about politics, death and sex on this record, but Songs For Our Mothers offers so little that’s actually new. There’s no light to shine, no tales to be told and no ground to be broken. Nothing to see here.

Title: Another Country
Review: Merritt's pure voice is mostly accompanied by gentle piano on a set of songs that ultimately lack the fire of her earlier work. [June 2008, p.100]

Title: Run the Jewels 3
Review: Every track is a killer. [Mar 2017, p.54]

Title: Trap Lord
Review: He still lacks the kind of technical rapping skill that made A$AP Rocky reach star status. Regardless, A$AP Ferg has constructed an album that surpasses the quality of Rocky's Long.Live.A$AP from earlier this year.

Title: Pang
Review: Pang is such a coherent musical statement that when something doesn’t fit, it stands out. Polachek restructured the album somewhat late, swapping out five songs; what’s left is a sweeping, delicately latticed album with a few odd pop songs. They’re not bad pop songs.

Title: Dealing With Demons I
Review: There’s little to distinguish its 10 tracks from each other, beyond Wishing’s stark, startling verses. It’s a shame, because Fafara clearly believes in what he’s doing, and this is far from a bad album. It’s just not enough to reach beyond the faithful.

Title: Float
Review: With Float they’ve delivered another strong album that is more assured than their other records, and offers a hopeful energy.

Title: I Aubade
Review: More a holding album than a great step up. [Aug 2015, p.111]

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: While so many bands at their status revert to bloated contentment or some vague idea of rockist salvation, Mylo Xyloto finds Coldplay successfully continuing to explore the tension of wanting to be one of the best bands in the world and having to settle for being one of the biggest.

Title: Honky Tonk Time Machine
Review: What’s interesting about Honky Tonk Time Machine, though, is that, as eager as Strait seems to reclaim his commercial clout, the album doesn’t downplay his perspective as an aging grandfather at a moment when country music is dominated by youngsters.

Title: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground
Review: No longer does he sound on the verge of breakdown with every aching syllable, no more pent-up jadedness---this is pure, cheerful post-orgasmic clarity.

Title: Yuck
Review: In fact, a lot of the album may be confused for being from another time period. But nostalgia works in the band's favor on this first release--even though it wears its influences right on its sleeve.

Title: Jekyll + Hyde
Review: On one hand, some of experiments fall well outside Brown's songwriting wheelhouse, like the hideous seven-minute butt rock "Junkyard," or the vaguely offensive Caribbean-lite "Castaway." On the other hand, the album is a showcase for what's clearly a versatile group of musicians, and its strongest five-song stretch turns on a dime from pseudo-gospel with bagpipes ("Remedy") to pop-country ("Homegrown") to big band ("Mango Tree") to heavy K-Rock fodder featuring Chris Cornell ("Heavy Is the Head") to lilting country-folk ("Bittersweet").

Title: June Gloom
Review: More subtle now, but Alice and Kacey are keeping us guessing.

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: As with all of The 1975’s escapades, it ought to be a disaster. Instead, the showpiece triumphs as an unlikely paragon of social media-era pop. In a glass bottle, tamed and ridiculed, the inferno is strangely beautiful.

Title: Scorpio Rising
Review: There's no reason to buy any other electronica CD this year.

Title: I Phantom
Review: Make no mistake about it, I Phantom is a fantastic record.

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Charming debut from flirtatious Scandinavian popette.

Title: Louden Up Now
Review: Sound[s] like the most genuine "no wave" tribute album yet. [Jun 2004, p.83]

Title: Every Open Eye
Review: With Mayberry's recent participation in the discussion of misogyny on social media and in music, it's easy to view these songs through the lens of feminism, but it's just one of the many compelling facets of Every Open Eye's overall scope.

Title: Six
Review: While, the Black Heart Procession does an excellent job of musically embodying October's primary mood, they'd do well to remember that it's a month made more bearable by the occasional flash of Indian summer.

Title: Etiquette
Review: This is nicely-conceived pop music that keeps things concise and interesting.

Title: The Same But By Different Means
Review: He has a fascinating rhythmic sense, phrasing almost like a man who is writing down his words as he sings them, which gives the record a strong sense of immediacy and almost improvised spontaneity. And yet the accompaniments are more elegantly constructed than that implies, a beguiling mixture of harmonic squidge and tight metrical control. [Apr 2019, p.57]

Title: Old Money
Review: Old Money is as trippy and fantastical as Rodriguez Lopez's work with Mars Volta without the beat-you-over-the-head prog fury and yelped vocals intensity that causes much of Volta's music to bend under its own pretentious weight. [Winter 2009, p.77]

Title: Immersion
Review: Showing an impressive savvy in inviting perhaps unlikely artists to collaborate with them also leads to some of the record's highlights.

Title: Harvest Festival
Review: Freed from the expectation of neatly crafted songs, Goddard gets in touch with his dance roots on a collection of largely instrumental grooves. [Jan 2010, p. 119]

Title: Everything Else Has Gone Wrong
Review: This is the sound of an ever-curious, shape-shifting band finally finding the confidence to tell us who they really are. But they are not telling us anything we didn’t already know.

Title: Phase
Review: The potential is there for this to be very good, but the fact that it’s so comprehensively safeguarded limits it hugely.

Title: A Small Turn of Human Kindness
Review: A Small Turn Of Human Kindness really does sound like some bad shit has gone down. To this end, you have to assume HM have succeeded in their intentions, although they tend to be sardonic and inscrutable by design.

Title: The Bloom and the Blight
Review: The increasingly frequent transitions between the finger picking subtlety of old to such newfound rockage are, however, simply too jarring for satisfactory listening. [Nov 2012, p.84]

Title: Near to the Wild Heart of Life
Review: The lyrics are maybe a bit more intricate this time around, but they still rely on open-hearted platitudes about life lived hard and love without restraint, the eternal human struggle between the righteous path and inclinations to darkness, and, of course, well-timed “whoa-oh” shouts than can sometimes say it all.

Title: Honey
Review: At nine lean but often seemingly formless tracks, Honey feels raw and incomplete, like a work in progress--and maybe that’s the point.

Title: Regeneration
Review: Regeneration, the Divine Comedy's sixth album, could find fans on either side of the Atlantic, as it's their first to pay as much attention to the sound as to the songs.

Title: Aufheben
Review: Ignore the arch titles and you'll find some lovely psych pastiches. [Jun 2012, p.69]

Title: Golden Eagle
Review: Golden Eagle is a wonderful collection of songs and tales that ultimately find a sense of redemption. Over its ten songs Macve displays an innate talent for exquisite songwriting and storytelling in a voice that is just jaw-dropping.

Title: Waterloo to Anywhere
Review: While the album is a fun first listen, it's in taking that second and third spin of Waterloo to Anywhere that the band's infectious quality becomes a full-fledged epidemic. [Sep 2006, p.142]

Title: Life Without Sound
Review: It's a solid pop-rock album, but until they learn some new tricks, Cloud Nothings will just have to continue their search for whatever they're looking for.

Title: Amyl and The Sniffers
Review: Amyl and the Sniffers is a thumping, screaming, wailing magnet for misfits, losers, and outcasts, a clarion call for rejects and mis-shapes that is also an obscenely, outrageously good time.

Title: Karmacode
Review: Though obviously unconcerned with finding a place in the mainstream, this release just as cool and catchy as anything by Evanescence.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: Their third album Infinite Arms glows with that familiar sound, a sound born with an American heart.

Title: Metals
Review: There is nothing quite as uplifting as those previously mentioned numbers, but Metals remains as wonderfully organic and distinct as its predecessors

Title: Artificial Fire
Review: Despite the album’s length, none of the songs feel unnecessary, and each critic seems to be picking a different favorite, illustrating the diverse sounds on Artificial Fire.

Title: The Stand-In
Review: There's no question that The Stand-In is a step-up from her previous effort; her delivery and songwriting show a confidence that previously lacking. However, The Stand-In is no stand out.

Title: Widdershins
Review: He's most successful when stripping down his lyrical ideas and melodic underpinnings to their simplest expressions, in a live-in-the-studio trio format. [No. 150, p.55]

Title: One Track Mind
Review: These songs stick in your head in a way that 15-minute guitar jams never do, while still maintaining a bit of hoary mystery at their core.

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: New guitarist Matthew Simms has refreshed Wire's sound. [Apr 2013, p.79]

Title: Mean Everything to Nothing
Review: The unabashed emotion in their all-out approach will surely appeal to fans of raw yet sentimental Southern rock, Weezer and Modest Mouse followers, and angst-ridden teens.

Title: Rejoicing In The Hands
Review: It’s as simple as songwriting can get; as striking as songwriting can get.

Title: Admiral Fell Promises
Review: His Bob Dylan-esque voice combined with the hauntingly beautiful arrangement of the classical guitar throughout Admiral Fell Promises is hypnotic, trapping listeners in a melancholy spell of wonder.

Title: Freedom
Review: Freedom never seems to settle on a single direction, but it’s hard to say whether that’s good or bad.... But it’s when Refused attempts to sound modern--through ultra-slick production tricks and modern sonic collage--that the album truly falters.

Title: Nouns
Review: No Age is certainly an adventurous band, but its sound here suffers from too much repetition.

Title: Two Dancers
Review: The eccentricities are still present, the quirks still correct, but everything has been shepherded into a more cohesive, frequently more melancholy, totality.

Title: Shade
Review: This 13 track set sees the band tapping back into that essential ingredients of their core sound.

Title: Blessed
Review: Combined, the result is a dynamic, human album, one that's easy to fall in love with. Highly recommended.

Title: Dear God, I Hate Myself
Review: Now seven full-lengths into their career, Xiu Xiu have hit a milestone with Dear God, I Hate Myself. Over 12 songs, they condense the best aspects of all their previous albums to craft what may prove to be their finest hour.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: Though the songs are broken up into two- and three-minute arrangements, they seamlessly blend with the interludes to create a continuous mood piece designed to be absorbed in one 38-minute listen. In contrast to the more traditional song structures and insinuating melodies on “A Seat at the Table,” the new album lacks a signature tune. Only the reggae-flavored playfulness of “Binz” cuts through the haze on the first few listens, though shimmering moments of beauty flutter to the surface throughout.

Title: Touch Down 2 Cause Hell
Review: His latest album loads several compelling rounds of rage and heartache, and no egregious duds (though "Spoil You" really is pushing it).

Title: Pura Vida Conspiracy
Review: This reeled-in style seems like an extension of their exhaustion and desire to create something laid-back that would give them a chance to breathe and really examine what they’re doing and why, rather than trying to hustle and do everything at breakneck speed all the time.

Title: Bottom of the World
Review: Allen is quite the philosopher on The Bottom of the World as he ponders the meaning of life, sex, and dreams to a sparse musical accompaniment.

Title: White Noise
Review: A hint of what Pet Shop Boys would sound like with guitars. [Apr 2003, p.72]

Title: The Raven
Review: Reed has once again stretched the boundaries of popular music and, in doing so, has honored Edgar Allan Poe's illustrious legacy, along with his own.

Artist: Pantha Du Prince & The Bell Laboratory
Title: Elements of Light
Review: Weber's creative theoretical and instrumental approach is unique, but the abrasive and connotative tonal qualities of the carillon often overshadow the colourful subtleties of the finer details of his delicate arrangements.

Title: Puberty 2
Review: As bawdy and unpredictable as anyone is in their first puberty, Puberty 2 shows Miyawaki indulging her whims with a devil-may-care attitude--the result is an incendiary self-portrait.

Title: Nocturne
Review: While a slight step forward, Nocturne, like all of Wild Nothing's output to date, still inhales all of its influences--the women, the hurt, the favourite records stuck on late night repeat--and exhales them in to a beautiful, swirling, ethereal cloud.

Title: Up
Review: Full of the obscure and deranged moods that made Security alternately delightful and demented, this album revels in craggy vocals, thumping beats, esoteric instrumental sounds and a general feeling of beautiful dread.

Title: The Embers of Time
Review: The best cuts have staying power. [May 2015, p.80]

Title: Clues
Review: The result is far from flawless, but Clues sparkles in the rough.

Title: Overpowered
Review: While the commercial potential of her new album may be up for debate, as a showcase for Rosin Murphy’s talent, Overpowered is an enormous success.

Title: We the Best Forever
Review: As usual, his imperial victory-march hip-hop songs are fun, and mildly exhausting.

Title: Tallies
Review: It doesn't just repeat the past, it mines it for gold while tossing out the dross, a process that works to refine this record until it gleams like a precious gem.

Title: Ad Infinitum
Review: While not entirely experimental, Ad Infinitum explores darker and more mysterious territory than Telekinesis has in the past, a fitting direction for this more mechanical journey.

Title: Mess
Review: Its coda features a lone, breathy synth that unfurls like a tattered flag planted high atop a snow-covered peak, and, like the band’s best work, the song is comparable to little else in the pop/indie landscape—a far cry from the tepid feel that permeates too much of this Mess.

Title: The Tipping Point
Review: Returns to hip-hop basics.

Title: Monkey Minds In The Devil's Time
Review: Steve Mason is realizing his musical vision confidently, typified by the jump between the rather moving sampling of Brazilian commentary from a glorious Ayrton Senna lap, complete with soaring engines ("The Last of the Heroes"), to the pained yet undoubtedly uplifting, piano-led gospel of "Lonely."

Title: TFCF
Review: On TFCF (short for Theme From Crying Fountain) Andrews comes into his own. The tracks might be loosely structured, ideas, samples, field recordings and styles scattered by the dozen across the album’s 33 minutes, but it’s a sense of a distinctive songwriter exploring fracturedness across a broad spectrum from the dancefloor to the introspective. [Oct 2017, p.64]

Title: Pe'ahi
Review: Despite their varied approach, though, these songs remain pop nuggets with hummable melodies, swathed in layers of distortion but maintaining their sweet appeal underneath.

Title: It's Me Again
Review: Shuffles between romantic ecstasy and agony with tempos crawling and Tweet stretching out lush melodies till they're barely recognizable.

Title: Taiga
Review: What's so brilliant about ['Taiga'] is how Yoshimi finds spiritual connections between unlikely genres. [Oct 2006, p.102]

Title: Out of View
Review: The album has its super-twee moments but is never insufferable.

Title: Quit the Curse
Review: The record makes no indelible mark on your day--I imagine this skirting the periphery of most year-end lists, the perennial shut-out waiting flustered at the gates (“I’m sorry, you’re not on the list”)--but it’s detailed enough to add dimensions to the scene Burch sets.

Title: Who Needs Actions When You Got Words
Review: You would call Drew the most exciting rapper Britain has produced since Dizzee Rascal, if that didn't sound like such faint praise.

Title: Heaven Is Whenever
Review: [The departure of keyboardist/multi-instrumentalist Franz Nicolay] Far from having a negative affect on these 10 songs, The Hold Steady have flourished in this slight change of tack, with frontman Craig Finn's inimitable, narrative lyrics as stirring as ever.

Title: Begin To Hope
Review: There's a fearless, uninhibited confidence to Spektor's voice, not to mention a delightful whimsy to her music, that sets her apart from artists like [Fiona] Apple.

Title: American Central Dust
Review: The song themselves are thoughtful, ambling between folk, country and mid-paced roots-rock. [Aug 2009, p.100]

Title: The Livelong Day
Review: It's frequently unsettling listen, but never a joyless one. [Dec 2019, p.110]

Title: Fool's Gold
Review: It doesn't require a lyric translator to hear the exquisite sense of regret that permeates a song like "Ha Dvash," but the sheer exuberance of the music keeps spirits soaring. [Feb 2010, p.88]

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: El-P's uniquely, beautifully harsh vision remains undiluted.

Title: The Solution
Review: The Solution is a deeply schizophrenic record, one that completely divorces Beanie's cocksure swagger from his introspective depth.

Title: Scenery
Review: These songs aren't in line with much contemporary R&B, but reach for something more retro, and on tracks such as Teach You, a kind of Broadway grandeur. The strange result is that they in fact sound refreshingly modern. [Apr 2019, p.113]

Title: Sushi
Review: Sushi sounds enthusiastic but slight, with generic synths and run-of-the-mill dubstep-inflected bass lines.

Title: Flower Boy
Review: Flower Boy is a fascinating, singular effort from Tyler, The Creator. He’s crafted a record that finally measures up to a promise that has always been there.

Title: Liberation
Review: An ambitious, if flawed new album that once again tries to include many different things on one release, but unfortunately stumbles in several places.

Title: This Is the Sonics
Review: This Is the Sonics is an outstanding return to duty for one of the great primal rock & roll bands of the '60s, and if they don't sound like kids, the flame that fueled their best discs is still burning bright, and they're louder, crazier, and wilder than most bands a third their age.

Title: Pushin' Against a Stone
Review: Pushin' Against a Stone showcases a stunning and unique new voice.

Title: Innocence Reaches
Review: By lacking any resonant peg and showing little advancement, the record feels like a question mark, a gray spot on the timeline.

Title: m b v
Review: m b v is an impressive work, one in which adventurous and nostalgic listeners alike will find something to appreciate.

Title: Lasers
Review: Instead of retaining his distinctiveness, as mainstream rap has become more like Lupe, so he's begun to sound more like everyone else on Lasers

Title: Slowdive
Review: It’s conservative enough to satiate longtime fans, yet lovingly crafted to such a degree that it confuses you into thinking that its reached its full potential when it could've been so much more.

Title: Painting of a Panic Attack
Review: A record made up of excellent songs, with a few great ones chucked in to raise the bar.

Title: Motto
Review: We knew Sky Larkin had potential. It’s been more than followed up on with Motto, surely one of the best albums of the year.

Title: Postcards

Title: Found In Far Away Places
Review: That the band never lose themselves in the process of these myriad digressions is impressive to say the least, but what's most notable about Found in Far Away Places is how fluid the ride is.

Review: Schmilco is a deeply personal work. It’s also an album that so sincerely accepts maturation beyond supposed stasis, or prurient middle-age crises, that it should make us drop the term “dad rock” as a pejorative and accept that it can also be used as a description of high art.

Title: Evil Spirits
Review: Visconti busies it up, eking out build-ups and layering the ambient sound of a crowd arguing on We’re So Nice, while closer I Don’t Care gets jazzy. Overall, though, this is a well-behaved, orderly Damned: stoic, steady-handed and spirited.

Title: Here With Me
Review: Produced by John Agnello, Here With Me features a small roster of musicians, including her regular backing trio, who do a fine job of complementing O'Connor's melodies without intruding on her personal space.

Title: Parallel Memories
Review: Mr. Mitch goes full experimental, recalling the work of similarly minded artists such as Evian Christ and Shabazz Palaces, albeit in a more muted way.

Title: MCIII
Review: Cronin’s previous album was something of a messy listen, and MCIII doesn’t offer the solution. But behind the debris, there are glimmers of shimmering greatness.

Title: Nothing's Gonna Change The Way You Feel About Me Now
Review: Restlessness and drive applauded, but oh for the sound of those demons.

Title: Combat Sports
Review: It’s short and easily missed, but catch it and you’ll be able to feel the excitement, freedom, and, perhaps, relief of a band rejuvenated.

Title: Back to Black
Review: A guileless, brutal breakup album that can sit with the best of them, set to the sounds of music's finest early rock moments. [17 Mar 2007]

Title: Knock Knock
Review: If Knock Knock is a more conventional album than the more psychedelic and twisted Amygdala, it’s also a more affecting one. The fact that some of the guests appear more than once (Murphy gets two turns, as does Sophia Kennedy, the vocalist who released her strong debut album on Pampa last year) lends cohesion, and the production is extra lush.

Title: Heart Blanche
Review: This new album is as quixotic and wilfully idiosyncratic as his previous oeuvre. [Jan 2016, p.88]

Title: One Beat
Review: S-K swagger like they never have before, eschewing the filler that made their last few records drag. [#9, p.157]

Title: Weather Diaries
Review: If any shoegazers are primed and ready to make the most of this second chance, it's Ride.

Title: The Fame
Review: Empty lyrics are all part of the game when it comes to creating pop music--and Lady GaGa looks to have hit the jackpot here with her blend of sassy attitude, metallic beats and sharp, incisive songwriting.

Title: Means
Review: Fews sound excited by the prospect of overreaching themselves on a debut that has flaws, but is alive with possibilities.

Title: Beast Moans
Review: It's ultimately pretty patchwork. [15 Dec 2006, p.85]

Title: Stadium Arcadium
Review: Neither disjointed embarrassment of riches à la  The Beatles nor conceptual magnum opus like  The Wall,  Stadium Arcadium is two hours of sometimes middling, sometimes masterful, mostly pleasurable mainstream rock.

Title: Let The Dominoes Fall
Review: Thier latest dusts off their usual blend of late-'70s Clash-styled punk, ska and dub reggae, but applies topspin via 'Civilian Ways,' a bluesy folk exercise inspired by the return of Armstrong's brother from Iraq. [Sep 2009, p.92]

Title: The Longest River
Review: Chaney is a major talent, whose record doesn’t just suggest that there’s greatness ahead. The record is great.

Title: Bliss Release
Review: There's an appealing open-heartedness about the debut from Australian psychedelic poppers Cloud Control, a sense of wide-eyed, slightly fried wonder.

Title: All Melody
Review: Across 12 songs and 74 minutes, All Melody functions as a single, cohesive piece of music, with recurring themes interwoven throughout. It’s easy to get lost in the album and then, hearing a familiar motif, come up short, as if turning a corner in a long hallway and wondering if you hadn’t passed the same spot just a moment ago. It’s a pleasantly disorienting sensation.

Title: Gone Away Backward
Review: Recorded in three days and stripped down to folky fundamentals, Gone Away Backward may be Fulks’ most cohesive, best-realized album yet.

Title: Pawn Shoppe Heart
Review: An unflinching major label debut, as well as a straight rock album that straddles confidently that tricky space between rawness and posturing. [#10, p.95]

Title: Godfather
Review: Godfather is no mere retread, not the sound of youth but an idealised memory of it. [Mar 2017, p.56]

Title: BlackenedWhite
Review: It's clearly a release intended for hardcore Odd Future fans.

Title: 100 Miles from Memphis
Review: While it's admirable to hear an artist with such a well-established aesthetic branch out, 100 Miles from Memphis doesn't stretch far enough to work as either a contemporary soul record or as a purely retro-minded tribute.

Title: Froot
Review: After closing the door on her Electra Heart era, Marina Diamandis knew she needed to reinvent her persona. Froot achieves just that, adeptly flirting with chart sugar on the title track and “Better Than That” but more often than not, digging her heels into raw, nail-biting reality.

Title: You Could Have It So Much Better
Review: Simply great.

Title: Security Screenings
Review: There's no arguing that it's pretty entertaining.... But there's the nagging sense that it's all sound and fury.

Title: Rise and Fall, Rage and Grace
Review: The album's latter half contains some welcome pop moments--'Nothingtown' and 'Let's Hear It for Rock Bottom' make going nowhere in life sound like hot fun--but the standout melodies often take a back seat to the diatribes, and Holland doesn't back up his disaffection with many good reasons to rally behind him.

Title: Baby I'm Bored
Review: As with his last two releases, Baby I'm Bored is gutted by under-worked, inconsequential two-minute ideas.

Title: Blues of Desperation
Review: The tunes here aren’t necessarily in a class with some of the material Bonamassa has recorded in past years, songs by blues giants like Willie Dixon or writers like John Hiatt and Tom Waits. But they suit the artist perfectly.

Title: Strange Keys to Untune Gods' Firmament
Review: The sheer sense of sprawl created by the two-disc release, accentuated by the sometimes sudden shifts between songs as one variety of feedback suddenly cuts in to replace another, creates its own involving logic.

Title: The Believer
Review: Sticks to the mold of its hook-y predecessor.

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: I’ll Sleep When I’m Dead is a triumph that will, like its predecessor, take years to unpeel.

Title: Miracle Mile
Review: It's possible that the cumulative deadening effect of Miracle Mile is intentional, or that the contrast between the vacuous music and the spiritual ennui of the lyrics is supposed to be ironic. But Miracle Mile doesn't seem smart enough, musically or lyrically, for that to be the case.

Title: Set the World on Fire
Review: Second album is polished, though its anthemic pop-metalcore suffers from thinking its better than it is. [Aug. 2011, p. 119]

Title: Modern Times
Review: Might be the most upbeat feel-bad album of 2006.

Title: KOD
Review: There might not be any outright smash hits ready for radio and curated streaming playlists, but it’s a well-paced album with strong replay value.  Cole doesn’t sacrifice any inch of rhythm or melody while detailing his cautionary tales.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: Producers Mike Elizondo and Rob Cavallo smooth away many of the rough edges, and it's the tracks that escape the industry sander that are great. [Mar 2013, p.87]

Title: Mandy Moore
Review: There's nothing on this album quite like the guilty pleasure of "Candy," her textbook pop number from "So Real."

Title: The Medicine Show
Review: The Medicine Show is her biggest-sounding album this century. [May 2019, p.84]

Title: Lithium Burn
Review: While angular, skittering tracks like Stutter and album opener Haircuts/Uniforms add post-punk energy and experimental variety to the album, they also kill the mood.

Title: Almanac
Review: Hamilton's languid, Hope Sandoval-style cooing occasionally struggles to keep pace.... But when they're aiming true, Widowspeak strike gold. [Mar 2013, p.111]

Title: Making A Door Less Open
Review: Making a Door Less Open isn’t as memorable as its predecessors on its own: Toledo’s vision as a whole never feels truly fleshed out, representing the first legitimate misfire in the career of one of this generation’s most talented indie-rock songwriters.

Title: Alela Diane & Wild Divine
Review: This is a vivid selection of songs underscored by a bittersweet poetry.

Title: Black Noise
Review: Mostly, though, these elegant ­orchestrations of techno beats and ­sinuous, looped ­melodies ­suggest an aural equivalent to time-lapse ­photography – and seem equally ­revealing of our world.

Title: Benji
Review: Not his most graceful, but certainly his most strikingly personal, Benji is another colourful stop on Kozelek's glorious journey into the light. [Apr 2014, p.119]

Title: Lousy With Sylvianbriar
Review: Overall, Lousy With Sylvianbriar is a satisfying link in bringing Barnes’ musical progression full-circle, but at times he seems to forget what made him so good at this stuff the first time around.

Title: The Lillywhite Sessions
Review: More of a curio than a proper follow-up to May’s Deafman Glance, and is likely to be of far greater interest to DMB completists than the casual listener, but it makes for an at times intriguing project.

Title: Langhorne Slim
Review: The overproduction of the record is a constant detriment: a large part of Langhorne’s charm is in the rawness of his sound and his unrestrained vocals, but these songs lack the wild-eyed, howling passion of his earlier recordings, even if lyrically they are much stronger than his previous songwriting efforts.

Title: Grey Oceans
Review: More often, however, CooRosie appear uninterested in the listener's experience--and that can make Grey Oceans a bit of a slog. The cost of their commitment is you.

Title: Something Else
Review: The visuals that come along with the music and skits create a Cirque du Soleil-meets-Hip-Hop atmosphere as Tech N9ne and his star-studded cast propel you through ups and downs throughout the album all while staying on track with fire, water, earth theme. [Sep 2013, p.99]

Title: Whole New Mess
Review: It’s a record of personal growth in its most authentic form. It’s nice to finally hear the whole story.

Title: Thanks for the Dance
Review: It’s a beautiful, fitting send off to one of music’s finest lyricists and an excellent postscript to an incredible career.

Title: The Man Upstairs
Review: Sure, the eccentricities of other solo efforts like Eye or I Often Dream of Trains are missing, but to complain about that would be asking for a lack of honesty that The Man Upstairs simply refuses to provide.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: No Cities to Love exceeds all expectations of what a reunion album should sound like by not sounding like a reunion album.

Title: With Teeth
Review: Reznor seems to have finally grasped that listening to a NIN album should not be as torturous as whatever artistic agony went into its creation. [29 Apr 2005, p.145]

Title: 100 Days, 100 Nights
Review: There's much more to this band and album than the throwback aesthetic. [Fall 2007, p.98]

Title: Insecure Men
Review: The vibe is smart, slightly soiled. [Apr 2018, p.28]

Title: Dedicated
Review: Jepsen’s knack for lyrics that hit on the mostly-fun but often-fraught world of romantic relationships is also still in full effect.

Title: Love is Dead
Review: So much goes right here, but in scrubbing their songs of imperfections, they've also magnified their flaws. Though not quite stuck in neutral, it will certainly please the band's ever-expanding fan base while not really moving the needle creatively enough to convince sceptics that their initial opinions were unfounded.

Title: Out of Sight
Review: This time Fussell has a full band to flesh out his vision, providing front porch grooves that carry the same kind of woody resonance as those of The band. [Jul 2019, p.91]

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Fetch the Bolt Cutters will not disappoint. Released with little warning nearly a decade after 2012’s The Idler Wheel…, the album sees the now-42-year-old songwriter proving that she’s still more than capable of telling off partners, detractors, and others who have done her wrong, all while picking apart the inner workings of her frantic mind. But what sets Bolt Cutters apart from its predecessors is that, for the first time, the scales tip more toward resilience than agony.

Title: Hang
Review: Hang is the product of a very experienced and talented band carefully crafting a set of songs. And they’re damn good.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: On Chutes, Mercer’s voice is singing right next to you, and the change works wonders.

Title: Babes Never Die
Review: Overall, and despite a brief lull, Babes Never Die is enjoyable from beginning to end. Peppered with catchy choruses and heroic riffs, and with sing-along moments galore, it's much fuller, better rounded and more complete than 2014's Honeyblood.

Title: Year of the Gentleman
Review: It's no surprise that Ne-Yo sings about women on his excellent third album, Year of the Gentleman.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: It's a concise, tidy sounding album, with little of the noise leakage of old. [May 2011, p.51]

Title: Relapse
Review: There was a time when he did these things for our id, for our deeply rooted disgust at our own celebrity culture and so at ourselves. But here he’s not standing in for anyone, working himself into a feverish sweat solely for his own satisfaction.

Title: Beware of the Dogs
Review: Beware of the Dogs is a melodic, memorable package overflowing with promise.

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: For now, Mogwai is happy and ready to stay more firmly planted in the present and the physical. It's a beautiful album, sure, but most important, it's a fun one too.

Title: Lady From Shanghai
Review: It's a rich and layered work that refuses to be easily summed up. [Jan 2013, p.69]

Title: We Live in Rented Rooms
Review: Yet as wretched as his characters often are, Cornog always affords them the dignity of their own volition.

Title: Far
Review: Here she leaves behind the flaky-as-adorable posturing long enough to salvage Far from its role as capricious sideshow, and so, too, long enough for listeners to get a glimpse of the songwriting talent that lurks beneath the peculiarity.

Title: Travellers in Space and Time
Review: Basically, the album plays out like hit song after hit song. Love or hate the new direction, the Apples have made a long, long career out of constantly changing and reliably creating songs and albums that overflow with hooks and happiness. This may be their hookiest, happiest album yet.

Title: One of the Boys
Review: The bulk of Boys is sufficiently well put together; the generally witty pop walks that tricky line between edginess and accessibility.

Title: Tied to a Star
Review: It’s a calm, beautiful oasis in Mascis’ coruscating career path, prettier even, because of the carnage before and after.

Title: Joy Comes Back
Review: Covers include The Four Tops' Loving You Is Sweeter Than Ever cooked into greasy Southern soul, and the title track, where, backed by Derek Trucks on slide guitar, she delivers the hymnal straight. [May 2017, p.96]

Title: Come to Where I'm From
Review: Arthur's shortcomings as a lyricist make his emotional palette seem as limited as his sonic palette is varied and, however layered the production, his songwriting nearly always follows suit.

Title: Supreme Blientele
Review: Ultimately, while this crowdedness [from guest appearances] prevents Supreme Blientele from feeling like a definitive statement from Gunn as a rapper, the album can still function as a fine entry point to the fast-growing catalog of an ascendant rap cult hero.

Title: The W
Review: It's about as good a hip hop album as you will hear this year. Correction: Make that great.... It's hip-hop that plays to the streets and the suburbs with equal intensity, intelligence, insanity and integrity.

Title: Anniemal
Review: Not since the days of The Tom Tom Club, Bananarama, and "Lucky Star"-era Madonna, has dance-pop been this fun, this bouncy, this unabashedly optimistic.

Title: MASSEDUCTION
Review: Five studio albums in, it feels more like another new beginning, and pretty close to a masterpiece.

Title: Tales from the Realm of the Queen of Pentacles
Review: A great overall effort.

Title: Tropix
Review: It is the most artfully rendered and sophisticated recording in her catalog, the work of a mature artist in full command of a sonic language. It's also a hell of a lot of fun to listen and dance to.

Title: Hunter
Review: It’s Calvi’s most complete record yet. It grasps the catchiness of her debut, and kneads in an increased sense of maturity in her delivery of topical subjects, brought together with seasoned production and her expectedly dexterous, mighty voice.

Title: King Push - Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude
Review: Most of its 10 songs last just two or three minutes. It's too good to be a mixtape and too short to be an album, raising the stakes even higher for the album proper.

Title: Quarantine
Review: Quarantine is the addictive soundtrack to some kind of science fiction nightmare.

Title: Partners
Review: It’s a testament to Broderick’s talent that even on an endlessly intriguing and clever record like this, he can still play straight to the heart.

Title: Multiply
Review: Multiply sacrifices cohesion in its quest for stylistic diversity, but it’s a bravura tour through the smooth sounds and hot jams of yesteryear.

Title: Jonny
Review: If gentle psych-pop is very, very much your thing, you may fare better with Jonny, but otherwise the overriding impression the album will leave you with is that it would have made a really strong EP with some judicious pruning.

Title: Hang
Review: At first the wackiness is too much to digest, a sort of “you don’t have to be mad to review this, but it helps!” Yet against the odds, Hang does reward patience.

Title: Bashed Out
Review: The assembled talent takes This Is The Kit’s traditional folk to the edge of the avant-garde.

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: They’ve tossed a simple, solid album in our lap, thrown up the deuce and strolled out the door, take it or leave it.

Title: The Next Day
Review: His innovative days may be long behind him, but Bowie's melodic gifts remain undiminished and his lyrics appropriately ambiguous.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: Big, bold and joyful, it's exactly what a great pop album should be. [Jun 2015, p.105]

Title: Underneath The Owl
Review: Underneath The Owl is unquestionably the best album of the Gamblers' career thus far. [Apr 2009, p.132]

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: Without the hip-hop beats that peppered her first album, the songs here lack a sprinkling of brashness--a little of the Kim and Kanye touch would have helped.

Title: Through the Windowpane
Review: Not all of Dangerfield's maverick ideas work - he should steer clear of under-accompanied singing for a start - but when they do take off, Guillemots really soar.

Title: Mourn
Review: While still struggling a bit to overcome their influences, still sound no less than incredible and compelling on their debut.

Title: No End
Review: It gets a bit noodly-doodly at times, but with some stand-out moments, notably the lovely, meditative grace of the bass and guitar alliance in "XII."

Title: Pageant Material
Review: Every pretty melody, every sweet-tart lyric, every vocal and instrumental flourish... they definitely earn her--to borrow a title-song reference--a 4.0.

Title: Rain
Review: Most tracks are sophisticated, jazzy pop songs and ballads about relationships, but the angry young man of yore occasionally peeps over the parapet. [Feb 2008, p.102]

Title: Darkel
Review: What Darkel does offer is more of a good thing: songs that sound like the follow-up to Moon Safari, if Air weren't so progressive.

Title: Slow Gum
Review: It is such a thorough conglomeration of influences that it mostly manages to avoid sounding derivative.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: As enjoyable as The Whole Love is-and it's an appreciable improvement over the wan Wilco-it still has some of its predecessor's slight, low-stakes feel.

Title: Yeezus
Review: Kanye West doesn’t give the listener a second to realize the album is more a masterly response to a masterpiece than a masterpiece itself. With one sweep of the hand, West brushes away expectations. And then he sticks you squarely across the face

Title: Josephine
Review: Plenty to like, but it's hard to love Jospehine. [Summer 2009, p.61]

Title: Sob Story
Review: It’s always good to know there’s someone out there still doing straight-up guitar pop without irony or pretense.

Title: A Lesson Unlearnt
Review: An assured first step. [Aug 2015, p.114]

Title: Oh My God, Charlie Darwin
Review: Just as Waits has the power to infuse you with familiarity with the return of a chord, so do the songs of Oh My God, Charlie Darwin, like an embroidered pillow on an old porch that says ‘home sweet home’.

Title: Destroyed
Review: Destroyed is an album created in the middle of the night for the middle of the night. Disappointment awaits those seeking anything more.

Title: Major Without a Deal
Review: He's a hollow rapper with no unique trait or style. He drifts through songs such as "Love You/How I'm On It" and "Young King" with no real concept of flow or knowing when to change tone.

Title: The Broken String
Review: Just as the record threatens to flatten into artifice, they bust out their best Clash and Cheap Trick moves on 'Middle Management,' gleefully shattering the porcelain into smithereens. [Jan 2008, p.82]

Title: Jaakko Eino Kalevi
Review: The lovely Jaakko Eino Kalevi, the most coherent album so far from the former Helsinki tram driver, is a gem.

Title: Rainy Day Music
Review: The group envelops the different elements of music available to them-- from folk, to rock, to Gram Parsons-influenced pop-- in such a way that is alternately enjoyable and excessively off-putting.

Title: Trick
Review: The full, colourful spectrum of Jamie is on show here, as broad as it’s ever been.

Title: Cinderland
Review: The album feels intimate and delicate without sounding rustic. The album always maintains an undercurrent of fear or despondency, but it never gets too overbearing, and stays intriguing throughout.

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Monsanto Years
Review: The new [album] sinks decent riffs and an earnest message in unlistenably didactic lyrics.

Title: Sunset Kids
Review: This is his best record yet. [Sep 2019, p.87]

Title: Major Arcana
Review: Rather than merely rehashing sounds of yesteryear, Speedy Ortiz add modern rock ’n’ roll strokes to their take on fuzzy noise pop.

Title: Dylanesque
Review: Dylanesque is the rare album of Dylan covers that envisions the songs in unfamiliar musical settings, and it does so without sacrificing the soul of the lyrics.

Title: Afterparty Babies
Review: As a knowing send-up of youth culture, Afterparty Babies can be both funny and obnoxious.

Title: New
Review: Even if it’s not McCartney’s most engaging record outright, New is a breath of fresh air for what could’ve been a frustrating sigh.

Title: Human After All
Review: Some of it is tough and unforgiving... and some is pure pop plastique. [Apr 2005, p.89]

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: A profoundly emotional, uncynical brand of songwriting that showcases Antony’s obsession with nature.

Title: Ice Cream Spiritual
Review: With J Robbins producing and the vastly improved sonics, you have a much clearer idea of what everyone is doing. Little things are important with this band, and here, you can actually make them out.

Title: Noble Beast
Review: Poetry has always been another tool in his box, but here more than ever, it seems that the lyrics serve as an instrument, not to be separated from the rest of the music, and helping to create a seamless but showy overall sound.

Title: Traffic and Weather
Review: Their songs are either shitty soft-rock or worse, wink-nudge pastiches like the new-wavey 'Someone To Love'.

Title: Of the Blue Colour of the Sky
Review: It just feels like all the wacky studio noise takes away from what could have been a really fun album.

Title: No Shouts, No Calls
Review: Warmer than previous efforts. [#25, p.102]

Title: WE ARE CHAOS
Review: At just ten tracks, it’s an easy listen. Of course, some of them have more repeat playability than others, but there are none that feel like filler.

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: The good news is that this album proves they are top-level purveyors of pop. The bad is that the eccentricity that once flowed freely feels forced.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: The album won't blindside you or beat you over the head with anything - but it'll sure leave a mark.

Title: The Other
Review: This “psychic reset” has reinvigorated Thomas, and even if the results are sometimes a bit messy, there’s no way you can call this record boring. Long live King Tuff II.

Title: Triage
Review: Methyl Ethel have reached great new heights with this stellar effort.

Title: Crimes of Passion
Review: The new record basks in Endless Flowers' sunny afterglow, but the songs here are brasher, nervier, and a lot more fun.

Title: Pala
Review: Naturally, each successive track is more feel-goody than the last; every chorus is a confessional, a burst floodgate, a pleasure in a few minutes.

Title: The Voyager
Review: All together, The Voyager’s balance of frothiness and fearless introspection make it something pretty special.

Title: Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends
Review: While they fight shy of radical "Kid A"-style reinvention, hats should be doffed to Coldplay for at least having artistic cojones to mess with a winning formula. [July 2008, p.101]

Title: Radlands
Review: For everyone else, the predictable melodic twists and some truly awful lyrics will likely prove too much to endure.

Title: The Red Light District
Review: Ludacris includes thoughtful rhymes on "Child of the Night" and "Hopeless," but his humor is still his biggest asset and the reason he commands respect. [15 Dec 2004]

Title: Welcome Joy
Review: They're more likely to be judged on face value, but that shouldn't do them any harm. [Sep 2009, p.95]

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Rather than being a disappointment, Be the Cowboy's point of view provides a brilliant twist, one that channels all the unease, unpredictability, and intuitiveness of Mitski's previous work--even for those who don't take in the lyrics.

Title: Break It Yourself
Review: Though it's a lengthy record, at just over an hour, it's a rewarding one.

Title: The Way I See It
Review: The album was Grammy-nominated, and deservedly so.

Title: Mas Amable
Review: It may be dreamy and easygoing on the surface, a chill album to set the vibe of a room. But it's filled with deep moods, careful details and weird, intense rhythms. The best way to hear it is to slow down and appreciate each little thing passing by.

Title: Drones
Review: Great in parts, but flat and clumsy in others, Bellamy’s bid to become more serious appears to have stunted what he does best, which is operatic excess fuelled by volcanic emotion.

Title: Life, Death, Love and Freedom
Review: His world-weariness feels legitimately earned rather than affected keeps Life from being just an exercise in pessimism.

Title: Invented
Review: The first six songs include plodding modern rock that sounds like the Offspring's "Gone Away," an attempt at dark disco with clumsy lyrics and cheeseball pop. But if you stick it out, you'll be rewarded: Invented's second half features gorgeous "Littlething," Adkins' top-notch duet with Rachel Haden and Linton's punchy "Action Needs An Ambulance." [Oct 2010, p.112]

Title: White Chalk
Review: It's a brave and brilliant refocusing of her energies, virtually a rebirth. [Oct 2007, p.91]

Title: Ten New Messages
Review: While not everything hits the mark... there's enough here at least to draw comparisons with the aforementioned Britpop mainstays and keep them among the forefront of 2007's elite.

Title: I Love The New Sky
Review: The connective sense of an on-the-hoof holiday from the day job, plus emotionally deep and humorous lyrics, make this a winner. [Summer 2020, p.98]

Title: Konnichiwa
Review: Konnichiwa is a landmark in British street music, a record good enough to take on the world without having to compromise one inch in the process.

Title: I Thought The Future Would Be Cooler
Review: Preventing such weighty topics from becoming too exhausting are the upbeat instrumentals with which they've been paired.

Title: Clearing The Path To Ascend
Review: The amount of technical and emotional ground that YOB are able to carry across these four tracks is phenomenal, and makes Clearing the Path to Ascend the album that marks the band's return to the height of their power.

Title: Era Vulgaris
Review: They continue to find some clever ways to do a pretty dumb thing. [Jul 2007, p.112]

Title: Sonic Highways
Review: Sonic Highways is an attempt to channel a different musical energy, but it's one that Grohl does a far better job capturing with his camera crew.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: Editors show they're ready to take over with the spacious, stately love-conquers-all tune "The Weight of the World" or the pop-philosophy of the twitchy, pulse-pounding title track.

Title: Proof of Youth
Review: Proof of Youth is exhausting; otherwise its sweetness is irresistible.

Title: Sisyphus
Review: Sisyphus is a tragic waste of a vivid storyteller.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: The first new Garbage album in seven years is like a film sequel where familiar characters haven't changed much – especially Manson,who still cherishes the wary alertness of adolescence.

Title: Man and Myth
Review: It's not easy or cheery, but it's loaded with old gold. [Oct 2013, p.85]

Title: To Realize
Review: It's always great to see a band showcase all of their strengths but when you can take everyone by surprise it's going to require just that much more skill.

Title: Day After Tomorrow
Review: She boils songs down to their bare essences, and colors them in simple, evocative ways.

Title: Country Sleep
Review: The emotive finesse of ‘Cherry Blossoms’ might further the calls for a shoulder to blub on, but chugging full-band showstopper ‘Ramona’ shows Yellen’s songwriting to be as rich as his voice.

Title: Showroom of Compassion
Review: Fans of the band's old stuff should find plenty to love, even though it all feels pretty familiar.

Title: Alela Diane & Wild Divine
Review: Backed by a solid country-rock band (including two guitarists who claim co-writing credits on more than half the songs), her new sound is perhaps more indebted to Nashville than the West Coast's folk scene, but it sounds its best in the neutral territory between both camps, neither subscribing to nor rebelling against any single genre.

Title: High on Jackson Hill
Review: It might seem like a weird time for an up-and-comer like Immaculate Machine to put out what’s essentially a “transition album” this early in their career, but as High on Jackson Hill proves, not only is this band capable of pulling off any style they want to try, but they do so with good taste and undeniable charm.

Title: Volume 1
Review: The band seem more intent on rocking out and having a good time rather than impressing. [Apr-Jun 2017, p.78]

Title: Pigeons
Review: It's harmless, head-spinning fun. [Jul 2010, p.92]

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: The studio remains the band's fourth member and their wind-tunnel intensity is a constant. The compositions are more focused this time round, however, while quiet-loud dynamic shifts are more arresting.

Title: Held
Review: Held is one of those albums where the moods and methods are a constantly moving target while the overall sound, somehow, comes out unified.... This is deep stuff.

Title: Hombre Lobo: 12 Songs of Desire
Review: Hombre works best when it fully embraces its titular beast: 'Fresh Blood' finds excitement in a brooding groove, and rattles when Everett literally howls. Unfortunately, those are exceptions: The rest of the album just isn’t cohesive enough to entice much repeated listening.

Title: Forever So
Review: A wonderful start.

Title: Veckatimest
Review: All bets aren’t necessarily off in terms of whether or not Grizzly Bear have hit their plateau--recall that we did this with "Yellow House" in 2006; oops--but it’s hard to imagine them giving us more to enjoy in one sweeping statement than they have here.

Title: Lovers
Review: It’s that sense of timelessness--and, yes, mood--that makes Lovers such an essential collection both for Nels Cline fans and anyone who believes in the beauty and power of jazz.

Title: Night Driver
Review: Unfortunately, Night Driver's opening and closing tracks either fade together all too quickly or wade too far into an unpleasant '80s pool. [Jan/Feb 2016, p.57]

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: The band isn't doing anything that hasn't been done before, but damn if that doesn't seem to matter a lick while listening to the record. It's just too youthful, effervescent, and charming.

Title: Falling Down a Mountain
Review: Color me pleasantly surprised. The Hungry Saw, it turns out, actually revitalized Tindersticks, spurring the band to an unprecedented level of productivity.

Title: The Allegory
Review: His beats are generally chunky sample flips and simple loops, but he also has an ear for a good sound. But if you’re listening to a Royce album it’s because you want to hear the guy rap. To his credit, Royce has the rare effect of a rapper’s extreme technical ability making him seem limber instead of rigid.

Title: The Libertines
Review: An extraordinary record... It's not, nor is it intended to be, easy listening. [Sep 2004, p.94]

Title: Humbug
Review: Not every song hits the mark, but the Monkeys should be applauded for spreading their wings and not dropping like stones. [Sep 2009, p.100]

Title: Girls and Weather
Review: Their Achilles heel is a lack of slow, gut-wrenching ballads, something they'll surely have to put right if they're to win Mr Rowland's blessing.

Title: Damaged
Review: Even more subdued than usual. [12 Aug 2006, p.32]

Title: Eric Bachmann
Review: We can certainly add this gorgeous new album to the list of things that we take warmly to our hearts during these trouble times to help us make some brief sense out of it all.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: This Detroit outfit have restrained their post-punk intentions somewhat, playing with more textured compositions rather than blunt assault of their earlier material. This proves to be the perfect swirling yet steady backdrop for frontman Joe Casey to spin his cheap beer-fueled freeform yarns of lost souls and tortured romantics. [Oct 2017, p.83]

Title: Take Off Mode
Review: Far removed from the developments of the Teklife collective and other figures of the scene, DJ Nate stands out just as much as he did at the beginning of the decade.

Title: Scarlet's Walk
Review: Scarlet's Walk not only evinces Amos' musical maturation, it's also the singer's most ambitious lyrical work.

Title: Let Us Never Speak of It Again
Review: Let Us Never Speak of It Again is the sticky, panting, sexually deviant album Louden Up Now should have been.

Title: In and Out of Youth and Lightness
Review: Free from the shadows of their past, it seems Young Widows have found an infinitely darker place to dwell.

Title: Easy Wonderful
Review: There's something happily uncomplicated--and at times proudly uncool--about his band's sixth album, Easy Wonderful, like a 1990s Baja hoodie that you can't bring yourself to throw out.

Title: Hannicap Circus
Review: Flaccid beats mean that his solo debut -- despite guest spots from Eminem and Big Boi -- too often falls flat.

Title: Dangerous Woman
Review: Held together by Grande’s skyscraping voice, Dangerous Woman throws a lot at the wall and, brilliantly, most of it sticks.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: Still likeable in their simplicity, and sweet in their execution, one has to wonder what might have been if there were just a touch more coffee in the studio. [Oct 2011, p.97]

Title: Changes
Review: Bradley effectively draws you in with his voice and leaves you deep in thought with Changes, all the while grooving back and forth.

Title: Music Speaks
Review: It helps that her smooth voice sits so comfortably on the songs, content to illuminate their fine tunes rather than over-embellish them with flash.

Title: Stop Mute Defeat
Review: As long-time residents, the pair are understandably incensed and concerned over recent developments in the US, along with their city’s ongoing corporate makeover, translating their rage into a seething Xtrmntr for modern times that is undoubtedly their best, most relevant work to date yet.

Title: Moonfire
Review: Moonfire is a perfectly nice album, one that would provide a suitable soundtrack to a warm, summer evening. However, if you're looking for something to captivate and engage you, then look elsewhere.

Title: The Abandoned Lullaby
Review: Overall, The Abandoned Lullaby is a texturally interesting marriage of genres, but hardly a unique one. As solid as the music sounds, it's just not special enough to crave, making this collaboration rather forgettable.

Title: Hobo Rocket
Review: Pond still appreciate the glue of a hummable pop hook and the intoxicating pyschedelia of headphone tricks, but the most satisfying way to hear Hobo Rocket is turning it up as loud as it’ll go.

Title: Hydrograd
Review: Reflection supplants rage on “The Witness Trees,” while “Song #3” is a heartfelt, hook-heavy paean to love’s salvation that’s among Stone Sour’s most pop-savvy moments. ... [frontman Corey Taylor] still spits out words heated enough to melt earbuds on ragers including the near-thrash kiss-off “Somebody Stole My Eyes” and the aptly, awesomely titled “Whiplash Pants.”

Title: More Arriving
Review: More Arriving is a giant step for Korwar, who pushes musical boundaries to the breaking point as his tunes articulate righteous anger, passion, pain, and pride with a militancy that emerges from the plight of human decency itself. Brilliant.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Flying Microtonal Banana
Review: Flying Microtonal Banana is essentially the same King Gizzard album from last year, updated for the sake of its own consequence. But it's also better than most other albums of its sort, specifically because King Gizzard appear able to coherently piece together a fun anthem with a sense of musical direction.

Title: The Path of Totality
Review: Despite all the electronics, there's no mistaking The Path of Totality as a Korn album...and one of their better ones to boot.

Title: Condors
Review: Condors, is a restless, richly-detailed amalgam of intricate, glitchy electronic ambience, guitar reverberations that range from gently acoustic to furiously rockin', and ethereal to keening female vocals that recall Kazu Makino of Blonde Redhead, Nicole Barille of mr. Gnome, and Bjork.

Title: Reincarnated
Review: There's a winning sincerity to his sunny jams extolling peace, love and gun control; even the weed anthems feel less phoned-in than usual.

Title: Release The Stars
Review: It feels more like a collection of tracks than a cohesive work.

Title: This Old Road
Review: Kristofferson is dead-on here, razor-sharp, economical in his language, and to the bone in his insight.

Title: DÃ©jÃ  Vu
Review: Déjà Vu could have been Moroder’s own Random Access Memories, which had guest vocalists all pulling together to create a masterpiece. Instead, it’s just a bit random.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Robin Pecknold's well-chronicled bout with writer's block and three years later, Helplessness Blues has arrived, and the good news is that it unquestionably sounds like a Fleet Foxes record-which is to say: warm and exquisitely pretty.

Title: Welcome Home Armageddon
Review: Ferocious and beautiful--Funeral For A Friend sound more like themselves than they have done in years.

Title: Wolfroy Goes to Town
Review: With Oldham's melancholy vocal occasionally cast against the sweetly anguished Angel Olsen, the songs ponder God and humanity with religiously quiet intensity

Title: Head Above The Water
Review: As on Power’s previous albums, there is a delicious tension between the ethereal succour offered by her voice and the turmoil these thrumming songs are processing. Often, wordless emoting is the only solution; Power’s tones flow like starlings above her mantric guitar and that of her partner and collaborator Peter Broderick.

Title: Overgrown
Review: It’s the ideal sophomore LP: Blake emphasizes and magnifies his finest assets (the croon, the dark romance) for the sake of a better song.

Title: The Godfather 3
Review: G3 is heavy on bangers, with all tracks whizzing by in two or three minutes, and the album constantly stays sharp and exciting.

Title: Just Us
Review: Much here feels underdeveloped. [Jan 2015, p.71]

Title: No Devolucion
Review: By combining these previously worked on sounds in new ways Thursday have created an album that is not only new and unique, but also unmistakably their own.

Title: Amanda Leigh
Review: Listeners are advised to ignore the authenticity issues and focus on Moore's catchy tunes and warm voice on Amanda Leigh.

Title: Sidewalks
Review: Matt and Kim has lost a bit of their musical soul in attempting to reconcile their rough, campy sound with mass-appeal polish, and as a result, Sidewalks lacks a considerable amount of the bite of its predecessor.

Title: DAZE
Review: Part of the success of Daze is how fully Brood Ma commits to his sonic palette without committing to a singular musical style.

Title: Lost & Found
Review: There’s a diversity of stylistic approach and yet a singularity of vision that few artists are able to combine so early on.

Title: We Are Catchers
Review: With the help of former Coral man Bill Ryder-Jones, Liverpool's We Are Catchers (aka Peter Jackson) has captured the melancholy essence of Beach Boy Dennis Wilson's solo album 'Pacific Ocean Blue' and distilled it in the murky Mersey to produce this confident debut.

Title: Hotel Shampoo
Review: Subjects resulting from such reveries include imperialism, the environment and the more familiar home turf of love and longing. Nobody does it better.

Title: Midnight
Review: On Midnight, everything’s come undone, often for the better. In a few places, it recalls “Tango in the Night,” Fleetwood Mac’s lustrous last (noteworthy) gasp from 1987. Ms. Potter doesn’t quite have the tragedy Stevie Nicks so effortlessly channels, but she nonetheless finds moody pockets for her voice while the band hones a chilly take on brisk rock.

Title: World of Joy
Review: World Of Joy, ultimately, is impounded by its own musical influences.

Title: Yes, It's True
Review: Even with the group’s slight retraction, it’s that madcap sense of wonder and lofty ambition that helps keep Yes, It’s True healthily afloat.

Title: Lazers Never Die
Review: Major Lazer have never been bashful about appropriating musical styles where ever they find them; every song they make seems to be trying to remix the entire global street culture all at once. On Lazers Never Die they manage to duct tape all their influences together into a fun, listenable package.

Title: Everything Ecstatic
Review: Everything Ecstatic doesn’t come together as solidly as prior Four Tet releases, but it unquestionably contains the blueprint for far greater explorations to come.

Title: Weapons of Mass Destruction
Review: Dragged down by too much unremarkably brawny fare. [27 Jan 2005, p.60]

Title: Hungry Bird
Review: The melodies and arrangements, spiked with trombone and banjo, are simultaneously edgy and refined.

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: As darkly elegant as that pairing might be, no 3 manages better when its somber front is married to blithe surrealism, a feat jj accomplishes with skill and regularity.

Title: Saint Cloud
Review: This utterly beautiful balm of a record feels less like a confessional, and more a vessel for warmth, serenity and worldly wisdom. [May 2020, p.114]

Title: Heal
Review: The title couldn't be more appropriate--it's an album about the healing power of music, a testament from someone who made it through, a shout to keep going.

Title: Back to Basics
Review: Sadly, CD2 is a disastrously misjudged, cartoon homage to juke-joint jazz. It is awful. [Oct 2006, p.122]

Title: Trench
Review: Take my recommendation and forget about the most deeply conceptual parts of this concept album--which just seems like a lot of work--and enjoy the many parts of Trench that don’t require a thirst for symbolic origin stories. There are plenty of these, like “Morph” and “My Blood,” which sport falsetto R&B hooks, somewhat in the tradition of the previous album’s best track, “Heavydirtysoul.”

Title: The Alternative to Love
Review: The Alternative To Love to be a quality rock album that covers several genres in influence and doesn't deserve to be punished for not being as good as its predecessor.

Title: Music Kills Me
Review: All the clichés from French pop and house music collected in one shiny package.

Title: Father of Asahd
Review: Although instant, maximum commercial impact is no doubt the primary objective, the album does come across as more considered than the average Khaled LP.

Title: Highway Queen
Review: The Nashville-based artist loads songs with sometimes five or six guitars, and while she roots all of them in country, there are outreaches to vintage rock ’n’ roll or western soul. The precise genre sometimes remains elusive, but Lane’s boldness never wavers.

Title: Unpatterns
Review: Unpatterns feels like less of a discrete instalment in a collection and more an accomplished blend of the two things James Ford and Jas Shaw do best--gigantic, open-armed, open-air pop, and femur-fracturing analogue techno.

Title: World On The Ground
Review: Ten spare, spacious folk-Americana songs, many of them lovely, and the instrumentation is subtle and beautiful. [Sep 2020, p.87]

Title: Bossalinis & Fooliyones
Review: Bossalinis & Fooliyones is a perfectly plain little rap album, one that's 70 minutes long for no real good reason and comes and goes with little remarkable occurring either good or bad.

Title: I Can't Go On, I'll Go On
Review: So many bands confuse being laid-back with being comatose that it's good to hear a band who give their richly layered tunes some heart and soul.

Title: Deftones
Review: A modern, commercially-viable, carefully crafted rock record that also sounds violent, deranged and desperately, incurably sad all at the same time.

Title: Tennessee Pusher
Review: The band’s mix of creativity and credibility, serious and strange is yet again a delight to experience.

Title: Plain Spoken
Review: If his bitterness is unavoidable in the lyrics or in his voice, his music softens his bite, turning these tunes into melancholy laments instead of invective, so there winds up being a bit of a needed cushion to Mellencamp's straight talk on Plain Spoken.

Title: Everyone Is Here
Review: Nothing has really changed at all.

Title: National Ransom
Review: Recorded in 11 days in Nashville and LA, National Ransom sees Costello continuing his obsession with bluegrass and Americana, under the watchful eye of producer T-Bone Burnett. [Dec. 2010, p. 104]

Title: Isles
Review: With songs largely based around Natalie's love of soul and melodic '60s pop, Wild Belle have a less frenetic, if still hypnotically languid take on NOMO's world fusion sound.

Title: 100 Proof
Review: American Idol haunts this artistic breakthrough.

Title: Fortress
Review: Basically, Fortress will surprise some and maybe even anger others. But with the right Feel Good mindset, it can be a wonderful journey through the mind of some a.) interesting people or b.) interestingly intoxicated people. Plus, there are boobs on the cover.

Title: Recovery
Review: So is Recovery a classic album? No. But is it an essential one in shaping Eminem's future? Absolutely.

Title: Nothing as the Ideal
Review: The result is an excellent sounding but slightly flat affair as the band settles into life as a trio.

Title: Epoch
