Review: Most of the time, however, Epoch sounds like the album Ulrich Schnauss has been promising for a decade. [Feb 2017, p.38]

Title: Warm Slime
Review: Thee Oh Sees conjure sweet, sticky fuzz, and there's very few spaces on Warm Slime to take a breath, or think about what you've heard. Then again, it's this very saturation that makes Warm Slime such a natural high.

Title: Up in Flames
Review: These laptop-pop fractals... deliver spectacular hip-hop drum breaks and the sort of mile-deep multi-tracking that makes digital technology so much fun. [Listen 2 This supplement, Apr 2003, p.12]

Title: Lover
Review: Lover does not sound like the work of someone desperate to command the pop zeitgeist and yet is all the more likely to do so. Instead of trying to be all things to all audiences, it plays to the strengths of a witty songwriter in love, eager to tell anyone who will listen exactly how she feels.

Title: Everything Must Go
Review: A familiar blend of clipped funk, jazz nuances and airy musings. [Jul 2003, p.113]

Title: Are You Serious
Review: A lifelong troubadour whose wandering ways have seemingly found some respite as a Los Angeles family man, the native Chicagoan cracks open the door and reveals himself in a way that manages to strike an elegant balance with his more cryptic tendencies.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: Supergrass has gone from energetic, young and roughshod to energetic, veteran and polished.

Title: Now
Review: It all sounds great, too, with contributions from a vast array of players and producers, including Matthew Koma, Jacquire King, guitarist Greg Leisz and fiddler Gabe Witcher. The problem is Twain’s singing. ... [Her voice is]  lower and less flexible than before, and that works out OK in the slower, moodier stuff here. That’s not the case, though, in the uptempo material, which feels flat and robotic.

Title: Secret, Profane and Sugarcane
Review: Pairing with producer T-Bone Burnett (who helmed 1986's rootsy antecedent "King of America") and a distinguished pickup band of country heavyweights, he gives his typically fussed-over tunes a tent-revival authority.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: Repeated listens draw out its infinite flaws, its awful smugness, and remind you that were this not A Radiohead Album it would have been consigned to the pile marked 'Not A Patch On Aphex Twin' last week.

Title: Illinois
Review: Take away the album's conceit, and Stevens' artful songwriting -- and voice -- still remain.

Title: Spell My Name
Review: Spell My Name shows Braxton hasn’t lost her broad vocal range or her ability to slot into multiple mood playlists. It has everything you want from a full-bodied R&B record: songs to cry to, vibe to, and make babies to.

Title: Moosebumps: An Exploration Into Modern Day Horripilation
Review: Automator's cinematic drama provides a stirring backdrop for the Doctor's prolix self-celebration, the ribald "Polka Dots," sinister "Power Of The World" and woozy "Flying Waterbed." [Jul 2018, p.27]

Title: The Beginning
Review: Consider it a musical Snuggie for tottering Valley party girls--it will feel marvelous in the cold, drunken and lonely hours of the night.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: Amnesiac plays like a streamlined version of Kid A, complete with blatant electronica moves and production that sacrifices songs for atmosphere.

Title: Stay Gold
Review: The sound on Stay Gold is what suits him best: heart-on-sleeve Americana that’s equal parts earnest and exuberant.

Title: Rockferry
Review: Duffy's the Clay Aiken of nuevo "soul."

Title: Capacity
Review: There's plenty more heavy material to uncover (including a song called "Coma"), though it's all wrapped in a captivating musicality that combines the power of folk storytelling, poetry, and rock angst. In the case of Capacity, it's a quiet power.

Title: Dreaming of Revenge
Review: Somehow the 28-year-old has created possibly her most sophisticated release yet. [14 Mar 2008, p.75]

Title: All Nerve
Review: On the fifth Breeders album, the songs are all cinematic movement--hiding, escaping, screaming in the meadow, running for the exit.

Title: Try This
Review: Armstrong... gives it a welcome sense of cohesion.

Title: Not Even Happiness
Review: With Not Even Happiness she’s spreading her wings musically. There’s more polish to the production, yet the joy that is her storytelling, heartfelt singing and inventive guitar playing are the songs heartbeat.

Title: Underneath The Pine
Review: The resulting record is a shiny, dreamy affair that retains all the hooks and feel of the first album but adds some energy and pop immediacy.

Title: The Runaway Found
Review: The Runaway Found is an incredibly focused first album, giving evidence of how serious the Veils are about composing a stylish, quality sound.

Title: Dirty Gold
Review: Haze's impetuosity may've harmed Dirty Gold's commercial prospects, but the purity of her intent speaks volumes. [Mar 2014, p.94]

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: Strange Little Birds is a record that’s human to its very core, revelling in flaws and failures, but never losing hope. And in that way, it’s the perfect mirror for its creators’ 22-year career.

Title: Beneath the Eyrie
Review: A little too straightforward. [Oct 2019, p.110]

Title: Trouble Will Find Me
Review: They might shake, they might tremble, but The National remain a safe pair of hands. [Jun 2013, p.86]

Title: Parallax
Review: Parallax, unrealised masterpiece or not, sounds like the man in his bedroom with a thousand songs to leave unexplained.

Title: Truelove's Gutter
Review: Truelove's Gutter is a beautiful album. [Oct 2009, p.113]

Title: "Awaken, My Love!"
Review: It’s at once a homage and a parody, equally aware of that era’s excesses and its glories, of the way that the most memorable 1970s R&B merged sensuality, activism, humor, toughness, outlandishness, futurism, soul roots, wild eccentricity and utopian community spirit. That’s an extremely high bar, but at its best, “Awaken, My Love!” recalls many of those virtues.

Title: Colour Trip
Review: Digs aside, Ringo Deathstarr could probably stand on its own if it wanted to. [May 2011, p.86]

Title: Cascade
Review: The formula remains potent. [Aug 2015, p.71]

Title: I Never Learn
Review: She sounds every bit the wounded princess, unwilling to let anyone help her pick up the pieces as she delivers these lovely, sad songs from behind a shroud of her own making.

Title: Blood Oaths of the New Blues
Review: Blood Oaths is perhaps the closest to plainclothes Wooden Wand has come.

Title: Scale
Review: A lean, focused record, Scale is Herbert's best record to date, and a must-buy for any dance-music fan.

Title: Cardinology
Review: Even at his slightest--and Cardinology is pretty slight--Adams always turns out likeable ear candy.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Higher Than The Stars
Review: This EP marks a vital point in POBPAH's artistic development, a chance to see that they aren't willing to just sit back and repeat themselves. It's a pretty good listen, too.

Title: SremmLife 2
Review: Hotter singles make their debut a better buy, but for a group pegged as a one-hit wonder early on, SremmLife 2 dispels that myth with style.

Title: Better Day
Review: The melodies aren't as strong as those on Backwoods Barbie but Dolly Parton's wit, sincerity and plucky pragmatism allow her to get away with simplistic advice like: "Lead the good life, just treat this planet right and try to all be friends" and icky lines about painting pretty rainbows in the sky.

Title: No Elephants
Review: [Her high-pitched vocals] restricts her melodies a bit too much for their own good, and some more dynamic performances near the album's end can't save it from fading in a poof of uneasy effervescence. [No. 95, p.55]

Title: The Moon & Antarctica
Review: A visit to desolate regions... a 60-minute, 15-song treatise on isolation, displacement and a seemingly bottomless spiritual void.

Title: Afrodisiac
Review: Afrodisiac is Brandy's fourth consecutive durable showing, fluffed out with a few innocuous — if still very listenable — filler moments, but it is stocked with a number of spectacular -- and emotionally resonant -- singles that wind up making for her most accomplished set yet.

Title: 3D
Review: Though not what Lopes or TLC will be remembered for, it's a solid effort. [Jan 2003, p.124]

Title: Pale Green Ghosts
Review: Pale Green Ghosts reaches a personal level that can feel fascinatingly intimate or witheringly so. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.93]

Title: The Cure
Review: Brighter than Bloodflowers, denser than Wish, The Cure presents Smith as a wild-haired sorcerer's apprentice, conducting another mad symphony of infatuation and angst.

Title: Encore
Review: The album has a familiar shortcoming: Once again, Eminem is guilty of not knowing when to stop in the studio. [8 Nov 2004]

Title: Concrete Love
Review: Although the The Courteeners are newly mature, they're oddly not yet their own men. [Oct 2014, p.69]

Title: Anxiety
Review: In its more luminous moments, it also contains enough to suggest that there is still a great album lurking somewhere underneath the Ladyhawke moniker.

Title: Bottle It In
Review: Bottle It In does enough to keep himself and his fans happy, but it leaves waiting those of us that wish a bit more from him.

Title: Always
Review: This showcases Stewart's proclivity for macabre imagery and borderline perversion waging war with his pop-songwriting expertise.

Title: Too Much Information
Review: As a literary exercise, it’s convincing; as a listening one, it’s mixed.

Title: Mysterious Phonk: The Chronicles of SpaceGhostPurrp
Review: The somnambulant nihilism of his one-trick flow and the risible machismo of choruses quickly wear out SpaceGhostPurrp's welcome. [Aug 2012, p.87]

Title: Femme Fatale
Review: While Spears' vocals are inevitably the least impressive element of any given song, she doesn't exactly disappear into the production on Femme Fatale; she settles into it, game for whatever and confident in the hands of trusted professionals who know how to best utilize her.

Title: The Conversation
Review: This isn’t the album to convert the cognoscenti to the Texas cause, but those willing to listen without prejudice will find in these warm, well-crafted songs a perfectly seductive soundtrack to their summer.

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: By giving a wide berth to the safety of the post-rock label they've long despised, Mogwai have recorded some of their finest songs since "Mr Beast."

Title: WILL THIS MAKE ME GOOD
Review: Hakim provides consolation that is flavorful and tripped-out. Moreover, it's a little reassuring that he's able to flash some of his pitch-black, bone-dry sense of humor. The first two lines of "Crumpy" in particular should not be missed.

Title: Blue Smoke
Review: Fans will find much to love in Blue Smoke, and while nothing here approaches "Jolene" or "Coat of Many Colors" or "Here You Come Again," songs like the title track or "Banks of the Ohio" wouldn't feel out of place on a playlist next to these classics.

Title: ARTPOP
Review: For better and for worse, Artpop meets the mandate (of cranking up the cray). It's a bizarre album of squelchy disco (plus a handful of forays into R&B) that aspires to link gallery culture and radio heaven, preferring concepts to choruses.

Title: 10 Songs
Review: In standing mostly still, Travis have found contemporary eddies swirling around them.

Title: Persona
Review: Just about all of it is enjoyable, but not much of it sticks.

Title: Lost in Space
Review: Devoid of obvious weak points, Lost In Space sounds sad without ever becoming schmaltzy.

Title: Black Laden Crown
Review: Black Laden Crown is at its best when the band keeps it slow and low, as they do with great success on workmanlike candelabra-burners like "Last Ride," "Skulls & Daisies," and "Pull the Sun" and it's in those solemn moments of churning, Jim Morrison-esque torment and woe that Glenn Danzig sounds the most sinister and at ease.

Title: Uproot
Review: DJ/Rupture knowledgeably traverses a world of ominous meditations, complete with anxiety about his entitlement as a curator.

Title: Many Moons
Review: In the end, Many Moons appears exactly as advertised: an album that showcases many different faces of the same essential thing. These songs won’t spark any revelations with their musings on time and the subconscious, but they might just transport you to a place that feels like a pleasant dream.

Title: Quazarz: Born on a Gangster Star
Review: Overall, the beats here are funkier and a little more jagged than they are on the preceding volume, highlighted by the whomping bassline on "Moon Whip Quäz," Thundercat's bob-and-prickle low end on "Since C.A.Y.A.," and what resembles a contorted hybrid of Prince's "Delirious" and Urban Tribe's "At Peace with Concrete" on "That's How City Life Goes."

Title: Dark End of the Street
Review: For the most part Marshall gets it spot on, but when she doesn't she only serves to highlight the quality of the originals.

Title: Nothing Valley
Review: Nothing Valley is an intense, hugely engaging listen.

Title: A Dramatic Turn of Events
Review: The bulk of A Dramatic Turn Events finds Dream Theater perhaps too settled into their ways.

Title: Trouble in Dreams
Review: TID might be Bejar's most pompous, profane, and pastoral record, but it's also his least "intelligent," rational, or linearly clever.

Title: Death of a Decade
Review: On Death of a Decade, Ha Ha Tonka takes the harmonies and anthemic melodies one step further.

Title: â€
Review: Justice essentially have two modes: funky techno built with filthy overdriven synth sounds and gleefully daft disco/'80s pastiche so shiny as to be almost reflective. Both are held together with a studio rigour that makes the record bounce out of the speakers so forcefully that the moments of synthesis, where the sound coheres into its trademark elastic groove, become utterly addictive.

Title: Routines
Review: The versatility of core members Auscherman, Kevin Krauter, and Keagan Beresford--each of whom writes, sings, and swaps instruments--affords them chances to try on different masks, a huge strength despite some inevitable flat results.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: After the wild beach party of 2007’s Volta and the shiny wonders of 2011’s Biophilia, Vulnicura is a windswept trek of a record. But one which gradually repays its difficulties with the raw exhilaration of survival.

Title: All About Tonight
Review: All About Tonight wasn't recorded to reach a new audience, so much as shore up Shelton's fan base while furthering his chosen marketing experiment.

Title: Serpent Music
Review: The middle of the album explores a stranger kind of sample collage, stitching together unlikely sounds and moods. At first the shift seems odd, but after a few listens it becomes clear that this is where things really get interesting.
Even if you appreciate Havoc's reliability, you'll miss Prodigy's unpredictable diction.

Title: Dealer
Review: The Albatross darted fitfully and stretched out in all directions, while Dealer pulls all of Foxing's influences inward. Inverting his typical role of making burly post-rock bands sound delicate, producer Matt Bayles (Isis, Caspian) boosts Foxing's fragility.

Title: Edgeland
Review: Hyde's stream-of-consciousness lyrics are more rambling than visionary.

Title: Orc
Review: The best part about it is the Oh Sees manages to make this shift while still sounding like themselves, holding true with some killer bursts of distorted guitar and psychedelic reverb throughout.

Title: You Are There
Review: While the group are certainly impressive in performance, they can't break free from an almost mechanical feel that lingers and really holds the album back.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: A marvellous little menagerie of smart, eccentric guitar pop full of arty tics and tricks. [13 Aug 2005, p.58]

Title: Asiatisch
Review: The most striking aspect of Asiatisch is the confidence of Al Qadiri's sound, demonstrating that the quality of her music has finally caught up with her artistic ambitions.

Title: Discodeine
Review: Discodeine settles too comfortably into a consistent four-on-the-floor groove that ends up sounding an awful lot like a rut.

Title: Ashes and Roses
Review: She's been treading water artistically for years now, recording and re-recording slight variations on the same polite, coffeehouse-folk album, and Ashes and Roses is just as lifeless as its predecessor.

Title: Emmaar
Review: While the Tinariwen formula may be familiar, Emmaar sees their sound refined without losing any of the group's rebel edge and defiant spirit.

Title: Son
Review: It nudges toward a slightly more experimental sound--lulling without being tedious, compelling without diddling into pretension, and always perfectly mesmerizing. [Jun/Jul 2006, p.114]

Title: Only By The Night
Review: Only by the Night is long on astral, arena-ready largeness, with blippy keyboards, droney guitars and whoa-oh-oh backing vocals.

Title: Retriever
Review: He's shot truer and more heartfelt arrows than these. [Jul 2004, p.122]

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: The whole thing works beautifully, more with each listen.

Title: Gore
Review: Running at you full-steam ahead, seeing red and gutting you. This album is testament to the trials and tribulations they've endured and more so, how they've risen up.

Title: From Kinshasa
Review: The music is consistently either thrilling, evocative or moving.

Title: Girl on Fire
Review: Her technical brilliance remains stunning; it's now matched by her maturity and modernity. [Jan 2013, p.74]

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: With shorter, tighter songs far more reminiscent of 80’s post-punk than Southern AOR, Aha Shake Heartbreak can only be considered a pleasant surprise.

Title: Life Processes
Review: Every part of Life Processes seems meticulously calculated with such antecedents in mind, laid out in every detail and implemented exactly to referential specification.

Title: Love Over Will
Review: It’s not necessarily perfect, with a number of its brief 13 tracks sounding like unfinished sketches, but somehow the sum total adds up to an engaging, if unsettling, minor masterpiece.

Title: Dudesblood
Review: [A] curiously eclectic record.

Title: Caveman
Review: Caveman have followed-up CoCo Beware with a solid effort that retains some of the looseness of their debut. However, with the added label pressure, that looseness sometimes feels forced.

Title: The Atlantic Ocean
Review: Swift hasn’t put out a bad record yet, but The Atlantic Ocean is his most solid effort yet, his best attempt at managing the dark-lit record store in his head.

Title: Blue Album
Review: This might be quality above innovation, but it’s also maturity above cliché, and above all, passion over cynicism.

Title: Better Luck Next Life
Review: There's an unsettling haze that inches along with Better Luck Next Life, due in part to vocal duties shared among the off-kilter pairing of Jeremy Cox and Jigmae Baer.

Title: We Are Undone
Review: Two Gallants’ rulebook may be dusty, weathered and well-worn, but there’s a familiarity to what they’re doing that can’t help but make We Are Undone a thoroughly enjoyable listen.

Title: The Follower
Review: It is, if anything, even denser, more dimly lit, more seamlessly contoured [than 2013's Cupid's Head].

Title: Orbits
Review: Not enough bold venture, too much going round in circles. [Jan 2013, p.110]

Title: Gargoyle
Review: Gargoyle takes the electronic bedrock of its 2014 predecessor Phantom Radio and kicks it up a notch. [Jun 2017, p.109]

Title: Positive Songs for Negative People
Review: Turner leaves behind considerable wreckage with Positive Songs--in ways both cathartic and clumsy. And as usual, he goes down swinging.

Title: After the Disco
Review: The songs, sonically and structurally, don’t sound contemporary at all. At best, they sound like disco by way of these two artists, both of whom have been making similar songs for five, maybe ten years.

Title: Zeros
Review: It's a clever set, no doubt, and ably built. But for the Soft moon's work to sound weightier, Vasquez may need to push his limits more aggressively. [No. 94, p.59]

Title: The Tree of Forgiveness
Review: There’s not much more than half-an-hour of original material here, but there’s a quality to the stories in these songs.

Title: White Women
Review: No fillers on White Women, good to go for the duration of the evening. [Jun/Jul 2014, p.84]

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: Meiburg’s voice is a wonder throughout, wonderfully fragile on ‘Hidden Lakes’, tearing it up on ‘Corridors’. A wonderful album.

Title: Pure Heroine
Review: With lyrics steeped in critical thought and slathered with confidently modulated vocals, Lorde is the antithesis of pop schlock, making Pure Heroine a project well deserving of the commercial attention it's been receiving.

Title: Palookaville
Review: Slim still loves blabbing repetition and dropping yapping vocal samples into the gobs of the dull, and this helps make Palookaville less a reformation than merely his latest and quite bland big beat manifesto.

Title: American IV: The Man Comes Around
Review: Ultimately, Cash is the type of musician that you'd like to hear take a shot at each of your favorite songs. So it's hard to fault him for the covers on this album that don't quite work.

Title: Unrest
Review: Despite sagging a bit in the middle, Unrest skillfully skirts the myriad ways this kind of variety project could go wrong.

Title: Short Movie
Review: This is Marling at her finest, but as she’s proved five times in a row, the best is always yet to come.

Title: A New Tide
Review: Their latest, A New Tide, is their most accessible set yet.

Title: Zipper Down
Review: Jesse Hughes and Queens Of The Stone Age main man Josh Homme's capacity for throwing out sexy grooves has only improved with age. [3 Oct 2015, p.52]

Title: Is Survived By
Review: On Is Survived By, they've outdone themselves.

Title: Strawberry
Review: There's more distortion, less naturalism.

Title: Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not
Review: To be frank, it’s pretty much business as usual for Dinosaur Jr on Give A Glimpse Of What Yer Not, but when the formula works this well, what’s the point in switching it up? Love live the fuzz.

Title: Neighborhood Watch
Review: Chunky, hook-laden songs like Tryin' to Breathe and This Way show a newfound sonic confidence, but Dilated Peoples remain astoundingly dull MCs, delivering earnest and predictable rhymes.

Title: Exai
Review: Some of its songs deserve to be cut into halves, while others should have been chopped wholesale. With those snips, Exai would be a really good Autechre album that summarizes the various successes of their career in an hour or so. As is, it's as much a frustrating obstacle course as it is a grueling marathon.

Title: With Siinai: Heartbreaking Bravery
Review: There's a purposeful simplicity to its narrative approach and a concreteness to its imagery--even when our narrator sounds less than engaged.

Title: Bamboo Diner in the Rain
Review: Bamboo Diner In The Rain won’t necessarily catapult The Wave Pictures much further forwards in terms of commercial appeal, but as a self-proclaimed attempt “to grow inwards” it’s a strangely satisfying go-to collection for those already convinced of the group’s lateral charms.

Title: Paul's Tomb: A Triumph
Review: It'd be nice if they'd push themselves a bit harder to break some new stylistic ground, as with a sound like this compelling, it's obvious that they aren't lacking in sheer imagination and songwriting talent to do so. [Spring 2010, p.63]

Title: Jaakko Eino Kalevi
Review: His vocal lines are often so casually intoned that they mingle imperceptibly with those of his back-up singer Suad Khalifa, over gently pulsing twilight liaisons that yearn to be a little more sophisticated than they actually are. [Jul 2015, p.77]

Title: Teen Dream
Review: Teen Dream is kind of MOR, it would go down a treat at a dinner party, there are boring bits and the doleful DIY magic of the debut seems to have more or less run out. But it’s shot through with more than a handful of heartstoppingly wonderful moments.

Title: Non-Believers
Review: The only thing that’s the least bit ambiguous is the supposed theme that inspired the songs, a fascination fraught with themes of discovery, isolation, alienation, and ambiguity. Heady stuff, for sure, but propelled by enthusiastic melodies, Non-Believers becomes the kind of album that can woo even the most reluctant listener.

Title: Pattern Is Movement
Review: An enticing record emerges, boasting intricate instrumental latticework with the smoldering focus of slow jams. [No. 108, p.57]

Title: Friend and Foe
Review: No filler, not one outtake, Friend and Foe succeeds in living up to the hype of Menomena's first LP by growing wiser with every loop of sax and blast.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Where its predecessor corralled modern versions of The Canterbury Tales that the band's foxhunting moniker continues to evoke, Pecknold's Helplessness relies on a suitelike flow in the absence of greatest hits.

Title: Wasting Light
Review: The Foo Fighters may have ballooned in size over the past few years and if it took them going back to their roots to make an album this good then so be it, but when all is said and done Wasting Light is as an example of how to be a globe-eatingly massive band and still sound young, hungry and, above all, important.

Title: Alegranza
Review: El Guincho has only himself to get along with, but you'd never know it just listening to his album. [Dec 08/Jan 09, p.78]

Title: Views
Review: Taken on its own, it’s another sumptuously produced, artfully crafted statement from one of the few rap stars with a truly individualistic aesthetic. It’s also too long and stubbornly low energy, nowhere near the knockout Drake’s been building it up to be since practically before he began recording it.

Title: Probot
Review: The year's first great metal album. [19 Feb 2004, p.67]

Title: Beach Music
Review: There's nothing not to like, but at 13 tracks in just 37 minutes, it's all rather slight. [Nov 2015, p.76]

Title: Alive to Every Smile
Review: Wratten's finest post-Field Mice LP. [Dec 2001, p.98]

Title: Mad Love
Review: It's all slick, sassy and infectious, but she's clearly capable of being much more besides. [Dec 2016, p.109]

Title: Confrontations
Review: It’s atmospheric, infectious and enjoyable.

Title: Lost & Found
Review: On Lost & Found, Smith is defining her own destiny. In the process, she confirms that she is special and rare, an asker of impossible but necessary questions.

Title: Celebration, Florida
Review: Plenty of bands try to re-create Bob Dylan's mid-'60s apex, but Celebration, Florida sounds like it's conjuring Dylan's mid-'70s Rolling Thunder Revue period.

Title: Beautiful Rewind
Review: Free from any external pressure to conform, Hebden has managed to make a wholly uncompromising record that remains compulsive from start to finish. [Dec 2013, p.115]

Title: Alone
Review: Much of the material is unmemorable, making this feel longer than the album's 46-minute running time.

Title: Ratchet
Review: Ratchet is instantly likeable and oh so infectious. A great pop album through and through, there's enough here to keep you dancing all through the summer.

Title: A Hundred Days Off
Review: After a while, the music becomes repetitive and, well, uninteresting.

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: As ever, The Hold Steady achieve their best work when their playing is loose. When the songs are filtered through the bottom of a shot glass. When they sound like the best bar band in the best bar you didn’t know about until the moment that you found yourself in it at 3am in the morning. On the basis of ‘Thrashing Thru The Passion’, that band are back.

Title: Hamilton: An American Musical (Original Broadway Cast Recording)
Review: It’s 46 songs of verbose, intricately delivered raps, spun from a story with enough character to have already made it a New York Times best-seller. There’s a lot of ground to cover regardless of medium.

Title: Exposed
Review: Though her voice has yet to fully develop and lacks the uniqueness running through her bloodline, it's clear she landed a major-label contract on the basis of her talent.

Title: Demolition
Review: Its songs are sketchy but affable, with a confidence that makes the half-hooks sound almost indelible.

Title: Thank You For Today
Review: A benchmark DCFC record and, barring a surprise drop from The National, the most immersive alt-rock album you’ll hear all year.

Title: Nothing More to Say
Review: Their debut album is shadowed by tragedy, lead singer Dan Klein having succumbed to neurological disease shortly after its completion. His keening falsetto is at the heart of the record, a set of elegant, tortured love songs that occasionally betray Klein’s anguish.

Title: Seasons on Earth
Review: Despite her love of folk traditions, and a classic voice, Baird keeps these songs from ever feeling dated.

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: Strawberry Jam, 2007’s strongest album so far.

Title: Reservoir
Review: Oftentimes the lyricism and themes, although relatable and poetic, are somewhat cryptic and ambiguous. However, what Gordi has accomplished here is absolutely a successful debut full of honest feeling, introspection, and self-therapy all through beautifully-composed folktronic landscapes that are sure to mesmerize.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: As for the songs themselves, putting aside tragic and Autotuned context, some work and some don’t.

Title: Escape From Evil
Review: Escape From Evil feels like a case of one step forward, two steps back.

Title: We Disappear
Review: You can hear the anxiety, claustrophobia and desperation pour from every fuzzy guitar, from every snarl. Yet it is also a remarkably upbeat sounding record, with infectious riffs, thumping drumbeats and an overall rich, joyous punk rock sound.

Title: Trapped Animal
Review: Animal is a study in patience and makes one pine for the visceral indulgence of the past. [Fall 2009, p.60]

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: Music this sparse, this abandoned and this beautiful... you can never have too much of it.

Title: Darlings
Review: While it lacks the raw, jubilant catharsis of a Broken Social Scene release, Darlings is both understated and refined, showcasing the many facets of Drew’s romantic songwriting.

Title: MHz Legacy
Review: Like a fine wine and all that jazz, they have grown into a formidable group, and MHz Legacy proves that.

Title: Crawling Up the Stairs
Review: While it's interesting to hear Grace pour his heart out on 'All Of The Future (All Of The Past)' in a pained fashion, it makes for a record that doesn't really demand repeated listens.

Title: Ten New Songs
Review: Ten New Songs is all introspection, closer in sound to a technologically updated Songs From a Room.

Title: Two Suns
Review: Two Suns doesn’t have to parade itself around as a concept album to prove that music has always been, and always should be, about telling a story, as Khan does here.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: Rarely has an album exemplified the 'body and soul' paid so much lip service in House music so willingly. [Apr 2008, p.58]

Title: Something for Everybody
Review: The twelve tracks of Something for Everybody are tonally monotonous (except for No Place Like Home, the requisite piano ballad near the end), and seem focused on placating long-time fans looking for a nostalgia trip.

Title: The Future's Void
Review: The album is an obvious step-up right from the start.

Title: Same As You
Review: It's 20-minute closer Unrelenting Unconditional, however, which steals the show with its spectacular reimagining of Miles Davis's epic early '70s experiments in transcendental jazz-funk. [Apr 2015, p.108]

Title: Invicta
Review: The production is big on bluster and stadium-sized punch, but, sadly all of the passion's also been squeezed out here. [19 Feb 2012, p.51]

Title: This Is How You Smile
Review: Helado Negro has managed to craft an emotionally powerful classic with This is How You Smile.

Title: The Gathering
Review: Appropriately for an album called The Gathering, the esthetic Arbouretum achieves feels somewhat monolithic--overarching and whole instead of neurotic and splintered--and in this manner should provide healing properties for a psyche battered around by all the little specifics of daily life.

Title: Dumb Luck
Review: The album almost has a mix-tape esque feel to it and the staggering amount of guests has much to do with this.

Title: I Don't Run
Review: Neither the songs nor their delivery are perfect, but that's perhaps the point. [May 2018, p.30]

Title: Everything Is New
Review: The makeover has done him proud. [Aug 2009, p.108]

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: It’s ecstatic music, surely; and intense, too, even as it’s joyful.

Title: It's Blitz!
Review: Between its violently happy songs and its softer ones, It's Blitz! ends up being some of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs' most balanced and cohesive music.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: Blunderbuss is good, damn good, and its' few missteps unthinking.

Title: Witness
Review: The title track draws on gospel traditions to confront police killings--“Not everybody that’s brown can get the fuck on the ground”--while in “Overtime” and “Believe”, Booker expresses the desire for faith and direction in a rootless world.

Title: Stranger in the Alps
Review: A kind of urban folksiness runs deep through the record, and the strummed softness of ‘Would You Rather’ even features Bright Eyes’ Conor Oberst. The downbeat vibe is cut through by unmitigated banger ‘Motion Sickness’ but Strangers In The Alps is definitely album for the sad times.

Title: See You Tonight
Review: The boy next door has definitely left the building.

Title: All About Chemistry
Review: But if "Chemistry" is a pure-pop sugar rush, much of what follows is equally sour, often falling into the thematic trap that snares so many post-hit albums: lots of songs about how success is really hard on rock stars and their girlfriends.

Title: Tranquilizers
Review: Despite a few obvious highlights and stuff worthy of mention, you’ve heard this all before and, unfortunately, done a whole lot better.

Title: WIXIW
Review: WIXIW puls[es] with strange, inimitable energy.

Title: Quarantine
Review: It ends up being a mixed bag of give and take, but as an assault on all senses it always manages to succeed.

Title: Chaosmosis
Review: The bracing, sometimes violent collision of rock ‘n’ roll and dance music that’s powered Primal Scream’s best work has been melted down here into mercurial droplets--shiny and radiant, to be sure, but ultimately non-descript.

Title: Demolished Thoughts
Review: Though Moore's lyrics are a bit more obtuse, this could just as easily soundtrack a breakup as Sea Change could.

Title: Monsters Exist
Review: With just nine tracks, Orbital once again prove that their chosen genre of music need not be so devoid of emotion or variety, and why they, despite the time off, continue to remain at the top of a heap heavily populated with copycats.

Title: Wavvves
Review: The result: an album exuding wall-punching energy, ugly noise, and raging nostalgia for stale bong water and sunburn.

Title: Mosquito
Review: Mosquito is not without highlights, but it requires some patience to unearth them, because when this record is bad, it's loudly, brazenly bad.

Title: Bang Bang Rock & Roll
Review: It's like the debut, but slightly different, definitely better.

Title: Demolished Thoughts
Review: Whereas that album [Several Shades of Why] revealed the Dinosaur Jr frontman's surprising musical and lyrical range, Demolished Thoughts only reveals Moore's particular limitations.

Title: Sucker
Review: A damn fine album from Charli XCX, one that doesn't waste any time getting to the sugary center of the London chanteuse's signature dance pop.

Title: Instrument
Review: After eight albums that synthesize post-rock, home-listening electronica, and dub, the trio otherwise aren't up for much of a shakeup in their approach. None of the remaining seven instrumentals is novel, but they're all enjoyable on some level, cunningly shaped as ever.

Title: Take Me to the Sea
Review: If you like your rock tight, shrill, and speedy, this one could be for you. Problem is, as rendered, Jaguar Love's spastics are at war with groove and less than supportive of their progressive ambitions. [Fall 2008, p.86]

Title: Spinnerette
Review: Spinnerette sees the former Distillers leader at the head of a band not dissimilar to that run by her husband, Josh Homme. [Jul 2009, p.101]

Title: Antidotes
Review: Antidotes is really a pleasurable record that found itself displaced by its worn-out, second-hand clothing

Title: Shallow Bed
Review: Dry The River have made a very good debut album.

Richard Dawson is an eccentric but clear-eyed observer of the human condition, and just as he brought something fresh to the U.K. folk tradition on 2017's Peasant, 2020 reveals how he sees the details of everyday life in a way that slips past most writers. And if it isn't always fun, the honesty and passion in this music deliver more than enough reward for your time.

Title: Crazy Love
Review: The neo–Rat Pack crooner makes a few too many soft-rock concessions on his new studio disc, Crazy Love.

Title: Fake Songs
Review: Liam Lynch is about as funny as the plague, and even that had its moments in Monty Python. This doesn't have any.

Title: Bleeds
Review: Working primarily as a storyteller, Bleeds finds Manuva exploring a cultural landscape dominated by violence, tragedy and “hard bastards” across ten paranoid masterpieces.

Title: Raw Honey
Review: The music is genuinely rich, and creates a strong nostalgia for a musical era gone by.

Title: New View
Review: New View is best appreciated with a deep and unhurried engagement, as the full album in full fidelity offers many distinctive pleasures.

Title: Asa Breed
Review: Much of Asa Breed sounds like TV On The Radio with more exacting production and a more pensive disposition.

Title: Both Sides of the Gun
Review: The rap on Ben Harper's music up to this point has been that it's been too derivative. This could be the album where he finally transcends that. [23 Mar 2006, p.61]

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: Bewitching.

Title: Songs and Other Things
Review: Songs and Other Things' mid-tempo pop feels tossed-off, like Verlaine couldn't have been bothered to do more between walking the dog and a few dart games.

Title: Are You Serious
Review: As ever, he showcases a poetic turn of phrase and hopscotches across a dizzying array of styles. [May 2016, p.69]

Title: The Hunter
Review: Hinds hasn't delivered a logical sequel to Crack The Skye, but The Hunter triumphs in a less profound, more immediate way: It's the first truly fun Mastodon album.

Title: Versus
Review: Comprising eight new songs plus There Goes My Baby, the new set alternately bumps and throbs as a reinvigorated Usher further paves his comeback path.

Taylor's original 1989 is made even more interesting and worthy of discussion by Ryan's overtly classic rock-ified version, while Ryan's version is intriguing as both a personal expression and a reaction to one of the biggest albums we're likely to see come along in our lifetimes.

Title: Render Another Ugly Method
Review: Render Another Ugly Method is an album which demands careful listening, almost as it pushes away the listener, inviting interpretation as it rejects it. Often thrilling, it is rarely less than compelling.

Title: All Hands on the Bad One
Review: All Hands on the Bad One finds the Northwest power-trio at their most melodious, playful, sarcastic, and punchy-- both musically and lyrically.

Title: Water Curses EP
Review: While the tracks appear softer edged, they share "Strawberry Jam's" tangy, bitterweet flavours. [May 2008, p.49]

Title: Live Like You Were Dying
Review: While McGraw may not be the greatest of warblers, nobody in country can touch him at conveying emotions too deep to express in words.

Title: Vapours
Review: Though there is an overall whiff of the 1980s about Vapours, it sidesteps the traps of either sounding trendily vintage or indistinguishable from the rest of today's Reagan-era impostors. It works best, however, to think of the album as a return to "Return to the Sea," only, as its title suggests, in a hazier, less opaque form.

Title: District Line
Review: District Line is a fine showcase for the differing sides of ex-Hüsker Dü/Sugar frontman Bob Mould's repertoire.

Title: Untilted
Review: There's not a lot here to grab onto unless you're willing to immerse yourself in a world of totally alien sensation. If you are willing to accept the challenge, there is a chance you will find yourself significantly changed by the experience.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: Embodying that impervious inner spirit that Kafka called the Indestructible, where the possibility of perfect happiness exists in spite of everything else, its calm resignation defines what A Moon Shaped Pool strives for. In honing that potential from start to finish, Radiohead have excavated their most accomplished album in at least 15 years.

Title: Hyperview
Review: The reverby haze that now surrounds Title Fight mostly works to their favor, but perhaps they could benefit from bringing some sharper elements out of the mix, or some new dishes to the shoegaze table.

Title: Ctrl
Review: On Ctrl, SZA proves that you can be confident yet insecure, sexual yet crave affection and genuine connection, and empowered and still prone to falling for bad boys and all the drama that entails. SZA is the real deal and yet another example of how some of the most interesting, complex, sophisticated art being made today is being made by R&B artists.

Title: Tape Recorder
Review: Tape Recorder is an apt name for its unvarnished sophomore LP, which resembles a demo.

Title: There's No Leaving Now
Review: It may prove hard for Matsson to get heard above the quiet din made by so many others who clutter his field, but he's one of the all-too-few worth listening to. [Sep 2012, p.94]

Title: Ghosts I-IV
Review: It's meant to be taken as surface, perhaps skimmed for samples, but generally to be used as mildly unsettling mood music--a specialty of Reznor's, to be sure, but he's better and scarier when his ideas are more finely honed than they are here.

Title: The Practice of Love
Review: It may be her subtlest, most approachable album yet; though its ideas are just as complex and provocative as those of Blood Bitch or Apocalypse, Girl, there's something welcoming about it that engages the hearts and minds of her listeners fully.

Title: Tuns
Review: The nine tracks on this record are nimble, charismatic, and ultimately make for an enjoyable if unspectacular listen.

Title: Join the Dots
Review: It's only when hazy melodies begin to pierce the fog that their psychedelic rock strikes the right balance between hooky immediacy and cosmic ambition.

Title: Golem
Review: Their new sound might scare off some of the psych lovers who dug their debut, but for anyone looking for some weird heavy rock noise, Golem fits the bill.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: Master of My Make-Believe lands with a bit of a thud in contrast; lots of filler propped up by a few far-out pop jams, possessing as many ups and downs as her 2008 debut record.

Title: Weird
Review: Far from reclusive, Weird is a gregarious, idiosyncratic pop album that invites the listener to meet it on its own terms, but Hatfield is absolutely fine if it's rejected. She's cool being on her own.

Title: Run the Jewels
Review: Of the two rappers here, Killer Mike gets the most quotable lines, turning simple statements into punchlines and investing each syllable with a sense of rhythmic possibility.... Despite abandoning some of the more layered and mannered production flourishes of his solo work, El-P still packs these songs with stray details--the roar of a tiger, those gorgeous organs, the squeal of a dolphin--that can be jarring on first listen but gradually reveal themselves to be essential.

Title: Get Born
Review: An efficient if fairly joyless hybrid of the Stones, AC/DC and Oasis. [Nov 2003, p.109]

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: Bad rap is no way to repair a bad rep. [21 Oct 2002]

Title: The Rising
Review: He sounds as genuinely hurt and confused as any of us, but if he's gained any insight into that hurt or confusion, he's not about to express it.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: Plastic Beach proves that he's most truly himself when he turns into a cartoon.

Title: Purple Naked Ladies
Review: An endearingly scattershot take on spaced-out R&B, complete with drug fetishism and a load of moves apparently copped from the Neptunes.

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Fetch The Bolt Cutters is full of visceral, jittery, wonderfully imperfect performances that make the album feel like a dreamlike concert at Largo.

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: If anything, Gloucester County proves that Smith is willing to let his unique style mature, which may at some point provide some insight into one of the underground's most elusive personalities.

Title: Payola
Review: By simply moving with the times, Desaparecidos have managed to skirt that issue entirely, making Payola a surprisingly vital return we never knew we needed.

Title: Azel
Review: It's complex music but with enough of a melodic charm to hook you in, easy to appreciate but hard to fully grasp. [May 2016, p.104]

Title: Communion
Review: Communion plays out like a kind of fever dream, a delirium of cold sweat and disturbing visions in which there are only brief moments of daylight before you're plunged back into the maelstrom once more.

Title: The Tourist
Review: A little moderated, perhaps, but more mature too. For the first time in years, we are able to imagine that Ounsworth’s best work might still be ahead of him, rather than behind him.

Title: Locked Down
Review: There are a few moments when Auerbach's production touches threaten to distract from the grooves, but the overall quality is so impressively high that the occasional misstep is quickly forgotten.

Title: Graffiti on the Train
Review: In conclusion, solid record, but it simply does not hit home hard enough.

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: This is why Dye It Blonde is truly a success: the band have moved from the garage noise-rock sound to a much more atmospheric one wherein the noise is harnessed into multiple layers of melodic instrumentation.

Title: Pawn Shoppe Heart
Review: Offers all the kicks of a souped-up kit car roaring down the open road.

Title: Love Yes
Review: Love Yes feels like a radical step forward for the Brooklyn-based group. It’s a coming of age struggle wrapped in the slick, veneer of Eighties glamour, and ultimately TEEN’s synth-pop dreams are hard to beat.

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: A joy from start to finish. [Dec 2003, p.124]

Title: Solo
Review: Iyer structures this programme cannily, beginning with an inviting interpretation of the pop ballad Human Nature, unfolding over a rocking left-hand vamp and briefly darkening into a hypnotic drone.

Title: Woptober
Review: Although he’s far from a punk, the caricature we’ve come to know as Gucci Mane has shed a chunk of his unrepentant hood mentality in favor of a wiser narrator of the trap. Once he fully discovers how to convincingly put that into the music, the world had better brace itself.

Title: Abandoned City
Review: The concept might sound dry, but Bertelmann's kinetic approach always sound alive. [Apr 2014, p.110]

Title: AMOK
Review: Yorke's second album away from Radiohead is surprisingly accessible for one so extensively jammed then spliced together by machines.

Title: Reformation Post TLC
Review: A dispirited, half-baked record. [Jun 2007, p.156]

Title: Emperor of Sand
Review: With Emperor of Sand, Mastodon remains one of the most distinctive bands of its ilk, but like a beach that’s been combed over many times before, there’s precious little left to discover this time around.

Title: Music For the Quiet Hour / The Drawbar Organ EPs
Review: Shackleton, if there was any doubt, can do big picture and tight focus equally well; he can lead us into the future musically while digging in his heels against the one that's actually in store.

Title: Is This It
Review: Simply put, Strokes have every quality rock'n'roll requires from its finest exponents and Is This It is where they come together.

Title: Further
Review: Richard Hawley hasn't strayed too far from a successful formula. What he does introduce is a deliberate sens e of brevity, keeping songs tight and focused. [Jul 2019, p.29]

Title: No Closer to Heaven
Review: Musically, the pop-punk sound has been largely abandoned (save for, perhaps, recent single 'I Don't Like Who I Was Then') in favour of something more forceful and nuanced.

Title: Anoyo
Review: Going back to make a new album from sessions that had already been used could have ended up sounding overworked. Instead, Anoyo is the counterbalance to what has been done. These albums shouldn't be compared, but taken in together.

Title: The Spinning Top
Review: It’s sickeningly impressive. Yes, Coxon’s stormed through the Davey Graham Advanced Finger-Picking Guide but he hasn’t forgotten to flip it over and write some of his best ever songs.

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: Night Thoughts is a record that deals poetically and bravely with the shadows that start to grow as we age and life's responsibilities weigh heavier on our shoulders. Brett Anderson seems as comfortable writing about the aging process as he did chemical smiles in the backs of Volvos and bored suburban housewives done in on sleeping pills etc, something that bodes well indeed for the future.

Title: Hung At Heart
Review: Hung At Heart is not a particularly forward-thinking album with all of its 15 songs dealing in homespun 60s grooves, but this is a largely irrelevant quibble when the songs are this good.

Title: American Utopia
Review: In other words, it’s a David Byrne album: cerebral, but with an irresistible beat; and exuberant, but in a way that is self-contained. And if America right now is something less than a utopia, Byrne is a force for positivity, exhorting us all to do better.

Title: Summer of '13
Review: Even if elsewhere the electronic elements occasionally err toward the passe, ultimately, this is as spirited as it is an unexpected cavort through altered sonic pastures. [Jun 2016, p.94]

Title: Pigeonheart
Review: Throughout the album DM Stith acts a man far off into the galaxy, oscillating between space and sound, and without much vocalizing, extends a gracious hand to the listener as well.

Title: Monolith of Phobos
Review: At its best, it sounds like a long-lost Pink Floyd album actually meant to be synced to The Wizard of Oz (the album's title track and "Mr. Wright"); at its worst, it evokes old Tame Impala (the first movement of "Cricket And The Genie" and "Boomerang Baby"). Basically, it's a win-win situation either way.

Title: another eternity
Review: As a whole, the album could do with slightly more counterbalance to the several anthemic tracks, but the delicate final song, Stillness in Woe, is a welcome, dreamy reprieve.

Title: Hall Music
Review: Hall Music, continues this reticent foray, concealing its quaint charms until six or seven concentrated plays have been sucked up and digested.

Title: Hope In Dirt City
Review: Another solid and easy to recommend effort in a discography that already has a couple.

Title: Apocalypse, girl
Review: This album deserves the attention of a penetrative PhD dissertation. [Apr-May 2015, p.83]

Title: Fantasies
Review: The story here though is the album's simmering, intimate moments--and despite the fanbase-building qualities of their new-wave past, the more the group embraces an inky, ambient future, the better it  could get.

Title: Friend Opportunity
Review: This doesn’t seem so much a pop internalization of Deerhoof’s unique talent as it is a kind of album-costume where they adorn the talents of other bands.
On 21, she sounds refreshed and poised to attack.

Title: Acousmatic Sorcery
Review: What is present is that instant-click connection between artist and audience that only comes with the most naked of performances--Monotony is one such riveting recital, sketchy yet complete--and Beal's commitment to documenting the minutiae alongside the meaningful in comparable detail ensures that even-handedness permeates the entire set.

Title: Weezer (White Album)
Review: The White Album not only matches the sounds and feelings of Buzz Bin-era Weezer, but also the craft.

Title: Vengeance Falls
Review: This is a proud and focused heavy metal album that eschews current trends in favour of great songs, massive grooves, blazing lead breaks and a disarming air of combative euphoria.

Title: Django Django
Review: While it doesn't quite live up to their early hype, it's still an encouraging first offering, suggesting that they might do with album number two.

Title: A River Ain't Too Much To Love
Review: Callahan is back on track. [Jun 2005, p.104]

Title: Pro Tools
Review: Pro Tools could be called a return to form, but since GZA never lost the form in the first place, it would be more apt to say that he's kept the peak form he already had and just honed his lyrical tongue to an even sharper and more polished edge.

Title: World Wide Funk
Review: Modern production simply won’t allow for the kind of warm frictive depth in the low end or biteable chunkiness of beats those albums revelled in--but as a dazzling showcase for Bootsy’s still-ill skills it’s great, always problematising what could be politesse with the sheer deranged drive behind Bootsy’s shades, always plumbing for excess as a watchword. [Nov 2017, p.54]

Title: Writer's Block
Review: When these Swedes get whacked by romance, they cushion the blow with a reed-kneed bedroom boogie that shimmies while evoking decades of great escapist groove music. [Mar 2007, p.141]

Title: Touch
Review: Touch has a better batch of songs than All I Have.

Title: Duality
Review: Duality is a full-blown orchestral dance-pop masterpiece that will make you throw your arms in the air with glee, even if you think you should know better.

Title: Everything Else Has Gone Wrong
Review: Everything Else Has Gone Wrong is about getting through troubling times with grand gestures, projecting those emotions in the most outward way possible. And, coming back from that absence, demonstrating their steady growth as musicians with a joyful disposition that is contagious.

Title: Pond Scum
Review: Oldham's rewriting of his own songs sometimes turns into a queasy compulsion.... There are some stunning revisions in this collection. [Mar 2016, p.62]

Title: Free All Angels
Review: It's a damn good pop album, with a little muscle behind its melodies to boot.

Title: Floreat
Review: While musically it can get a bit precious, Carlyle gleefully delivers lyrics that jar wonderfully with their polite musical frames.

Title: Things That Can't Be Undone
Review: The pairing of Lund and Cobb on Things That Can't Be Undone is a feather in both their caps; as an album, it forges a new path in country music, yet remains exceptionally close to the tradition's heart.

Title: Evil Friends
Review: Danger Mouse’s fingerprints are all over all of these songs, and it’s easy to see parallels with some of his other projects, but in many ways Evil Friends is the most quintessentially Portugal. The Man album the band has released. It’s also undoubtedly their best.

Title: Long Way Down
Review: There's also something a little too contained, cling-filmed and... Keane-ey about it's measured percussion and guitar swells. Which leaves you feeling that although this is a very good record by a very talented young artist, it's probably not a patch on catching him live.

Title: From Out Of Nowhere
Review: Like its predecessor, Alone in the Universe, this album is entirely good-natured, firmly in the lineage of classic ELO, without ever quite hitting the heights of the past. ... How far this autumnal romance will go remains to be seen but, for now, what a pleasure it is to have Lynne back.

Title: Circus
Review: "Blackout" seemed like it signaled a more club-orientated path for Spears, like Madonna or Kylie Minogue, but Circus is a hodgepodge of pop themes that never really finds a face.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: Plant has steadfastly resisted a return to the Zep fold; Band of Joy makes us glad for that.

Title: Us
Review: Where it differs from the debut is in lyrics that are heartfelt but deliberately less personal than Me.

Title: Kiss Land
Review: Sonically, his oeuvre has bridged the divide between barren and lush. Lyrically, he has perfected the motif of narcotized horror.... This is the real deal.

Title: Shrink Dust
Review: Shrink Dust is still very much a CVG record, just one that you can cozy up with a little easier.

Title: Love After War
Review: The second half is dominated by ballads made for seduction (with more than a little preening). They don't offer much in the way of development from Thicke's recent past but they should get the job done.

Title: No One Dances Quite Like My Brothers
Review: No One Dances Quite Like My Brothers switches  so jarringly between moods from track to track that it doesn't really know what it's supposed to be. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.91]

Artist: I Love You But I've Chosen Darkness
Title: Fear Is on Our Side
Review: The band's accomplishment on Fear Is on Our Side is that no matter what direction the song goes, the journey is always worth it, the ending is a satisfying resolution.

Title: Silver Wilkinson
Review: So while it’s still tough to classify his sound, Silver Wilkinson is Bibio’s most streamlined recording to date.

Title: Saint Cloud
Review: The further you get, the sharper the writing becomes and the more introspective and unique the album feels.

Title: Modern Guilt
Review: There isn’t anything outlandishly overdone on this album as Beck offers a more stripped down approach. These are obvious efforts to return to a more cohesive, solid form and with a steady dose of subtle harmonies, crafty melodies and hooks, interesting instrumentation and oh yeah, two songs that feature Cat Power, Beck doesn’t disappoint.

Title: Summertime '06
Review: While unrelentingly committed to his personal story, Vince rapturously integrates dense and conscious-filled narratives of his inner life, packaged vibrantly over layered and unpredictable production executively produced by No I.D with support from DJ Dahi, Clams Casino and Christian Rich. Among 20 tracks, there's no filler to be found.

Title: Kish Kash
Review: A naggingly problematic record, with a void at its heart that no amount of cool celebrity mates can quite conceal.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: Nothing Was The Same is straight to the point, and in just over an hour, Drake closes the book on Take Care, yet opens the chapter to a brighter future. [Nov 2013, p.89]

Title: Requiem
Review: There is a feeling of higher power, an all encompassing truth or consciousness that pervades the album, and provides the thread to link their myriad sounds. Rather than an end, this feels like a reincarnation.

Title: Breaking Kayfabe
Review: Breaking Kaytabe is without a doubt one of the most impressive releases you'll hear all year, regardless of genre.

Title: Minor Victories
Review: Overall the experiments that succeed om Minor Victories pull the weight of the ones that don't and the collective product is praiseworthy from the standpoint of its dispersed alchemy alone. [May - Jun 2016, p.95]

Title: The Third Gleam
Review: Stripped of any studio sheen, the songs hearken back to the siblings' early work when they were still sculpting their heartfelt hipster hobo aesthetic.

Title: Will
Review: On the self-produced Will, there's an extraordinary confidence behind Barwick's voice and arrangements.

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: With its prowling, piano-led menace and barely contained fury, Extraordinary Machine offers ample confirmation that Apple is far darker than your average singer-songwriter. [Jan 2006, p.126]

Title: It's Never Been Like That
Review: A puny, ill-conceived record in comparison to both Alphabetical and its predecessor United.

Title: Culture of Volume
Review: Thankfully, it’s always Doyle’s intention to break down boundaries, even if he’s ticking verse-into-chorus boxes. As a result, music is the real winner.

Title: X
Review: Chris Brown's sixth album is adventurous musically and a total mess lyrically.

Title: End of Love
Review: Since all the lines make sense, and almost all the stanzas almost make sense, you keep waiting for the songs to make sense. And waiting, and waiting, through calm, memorable arrangements that are never in a hurry.

Title: The Rising
Review: Anyone hoping that this reunion with his old band would mean Springsteen's found his focus and was ready to rededicate himself to the freewheelin' spunk of his "classic" period will surely be disappointed with The Rising.

Title: Life in Slow Motion
Review: [Gray has] stepped up his own game with richer production, bigger arrangements and a renewed sense of purpose that makes songs like "Alibi" and "Disappearing World" sound like his most epic work yet.

Title: Flower Boy
Review: Flower Boy shows thoughtfulness can be freeing. As Tyler, the Creator embarks on a journey of self-discovery, he becomes close to whole.

Title: Trouble Man: Heavy Is the Head
Review: By combining the deep-bass beats and fast-spitting rhymes of Trap Muzik with mature, more-to-the-story rhymes, Tip finds himself back in the limelight. [Feb-Mar 2013, p.89]

Title: Summerlong
Review: The album is one of the standout releases of the year, and also leaves you wanting to experience the Rose City Band live as soon as we are allowed to do that again.

Title: Morning World
Review: Recorded in just ten days, Morning World stands as Teen Daze's most effortless work to date, coming off thoughtful and patient without ever succumbing to the burden of "style."

Title: Black Soul Choir
Review: Lyrical references to Charles Bukowski and Elizabeth Carter score egghead points, but the real smarts are in the taut and tight delivery of the 10 tracks.

Title: The English Riviera
Review: The type of punch Metronomy now pack is differently varied, and instead of relying on catchy melodies, its excitement and originality is now more broadly sourced.

Title: Strange House
Review: The band bolster their indie credentials by touching on everything from Joe Meek (Thunderclaps) to the B-52s (She Is the New Thing) and the Fall (Excellent Choice).

Title: Inferno
Review: The long view is serene, but it boils with nattering subtext. Robert Forster makes lean, minimal, elliptical songs about the struggle against time and self. He makes it look easy, but buried contradictions suggest that it’s not.

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Their strength is that, musically as well as sartorially, they’re unafraid to plunder and repurpose styles previously considered naffer than Bluetooth headsets.

Title: The Cold Still
Review: Their strong suits are Nathan Nicholson's forlorn warble and the pop hooks that pepper quiet melodramatic, minor-chord rock songs like Locked In The Basement. [Mar 2011, p.98]

Title: Plain Spoken
Review: Mellencamp finds his own delicate melodies, including some of the prettiest of his career. Their finery offers a sweet contrast to the increasing grit in his voice and bile in his lyrics--the most incisive of which take dead aim at himself.
Henry Tremain does a fine job replacing the ever-inventive Stuart Smith on vocals. His lyrics aren't that much fun to sing, but they're nice to read.

Title: Miike Snow
Review: The debut album by these producers-turned-trio comes after blog-bait remixes galore, including a nice enough Postal Service-ish Vampire Weekend makeover, but there's little of those fine young Columbians' infectious exuberance here.

Title: Things We Lost in the Fire
Review: It's not too ambitious to suggest few other releases this year will match its grace, humanity and power.... A magnificent album.

Title: Love Is The Plan, The Plan Is Death
Review: Whilst this is a lovely, well-made album, nothing separates it from countless other acoustic folk recordings.

Title: Starboy
Review: He remains an exceptionally talented vocalist, yet none of the many studio wizards represented in the album's by-committee structure is capable of wrenching him out of his usual morose rhythms. To be fair, none of them really try, playing to his basic talents while also coddling his laziest inclinations, swaddling songs in scintillating soundscapes that coat these sour centers in layers of sweetness.

Title: Everybody Wants To Be On TV
Review: With Everybody Wants To Be On TV, they've given those masses what they want. But there's nothing for the discerning music fan.

Title: Tough Love
Review: Tough Love is a tour de force album, one that nails heartache with sophistication and class.

Title: El Pintor
Review: At a concise 10 tracks clocking in right at 40 minutes, there doesn’t seem to be much fat to trim on this record.

Title: The Mountain Will Fall
Review: The repetition of the word “mambo” over another messy beat fails to do much. There’s too much going on to really make much sense of what’s happening. Shadow quickly makes up for that with two of the most alluring tracks on the record. “Ashes To Oceans” features British jazz composer and trumpeter Matthew Halsall, providing a gorgeous contribution to the already haunting composition. On “Pitter Patter,” rain-fall piano notes permeate the track while producer Bleep Bloop and Nite School Klik associate/trap producer G Jones give it an ethereal feel.

Title: Third World Pyramid
Review: Nine-minute meanders and sub-standard I Am The Walrus clones aside, Third World Pyramid furthers and spreads out the BJM sound.

Title: David Cook
Review: The producers give David Cook's clutch of bombastic verse-chorus- verse rockers an impressive melodic sheen, one well suited to Cook's husky, expressive vocals.

Title: Release The Stars
Review: It's a glorious tangle of excess.

Title: Magic Mountain
Review: Clunkers aside, Magic Mountain comes closer than any previous offering in providing the kind of excitement Black Stone Cherry generate live, and showcases their most refined songwriting to date.

Title: Comfort
Review: Cole's beats may differ but she speaks the same language of shadows and longing. [Sep 2013, p.100]

Title: Strike A Match
Review: Strike A Match runs the risk of becoming a little too chaotic as Aggs and Rodgers throw everything in at once; their flair for reflective lyricism sadly becomes a little lost in the crowd.

Title: South
Review: Her lilting angelic voice and ethereal alternating waves of electronic and acoustic musical accompaniment make Nova's contemporary folk-pop tunes perfect for TV-styled teen angst and lessons in love.

Title: Firewater
Review: It may not be their best album, but where it doesn’t really add to their legacy, neither does it really tarnish.

Title: Bird Songs
Review: Sticking mostly to his usual tenor sax instead of adopting Parker's alto, Lovano isolates the strands of Parker's musical DNA and shows how they're part of the music's ongoing regeneration.

Title: Synthetica
Review: There's a lot of kinda clichéd and heavy-handed stuff.

Title: The Suburbs
Review: The Suburbs is a really good record, but it's clear that indie rock is not in Kansas anymore.

Title: Days Are Gone
Review: It’s not revolutionary, life-changing ‘high art’ but right here, right now Haim’s sassy, enthusiastic, ‘one for all’ joie de vivre feels freshly invigorating, infectious ...basically, a drop o’ the good stuff.

Title: Revelations
Review: Variety has never been Audioslave's strong suit. [Sep 2006, p.102]

Title: The Sister
Review: As heart-stopping as The Sister is, though, it feels more like an appendix to her body of work than a fresh, essential sequel.

Title: Single Mothers
Review: The Tom Waits-ish jazz of the title track, the slinky CCR-ish trundle of "My Baby Drives" and the gentle pedal-steel-led-weeper "White Gardenias" confirm that Earle's quieting of his demons has lost him little. [Nov 2014, p.73]

Title: Rockferry
Review: Husky-sweet and preternaturally seasoned, Duffy's delivery is as pungent as it is unaffected, and the songs, which the singer co-wrote, follow suit.

Title: This Is... Icona Pop
Review: Even when they're shouting, they do so in a particularly musical and distinctive way, and although their smash is one of five This Is… songs the duo had no hand in writing, they nevertheless suggest a consistent sense of authorship through the intensity of their shared ecstasies and frustrations.

Title: The Cost
Review: Alas, 'The Cost' is closer to the Noughties ipoddery of 'sensitive' folksters like Damien Rice or James Blunt than a Fleetwood Mac or a James Taylor.

Title: The Moon & Antarctica
Review: An absolutely awesome album.

Title: Want Two
Review: Showcas[es] Rufus as one of, if not the best songwriters of his generation. [19 Mar 2005, p.59]

Title: Indigo
Review: With just about enough sonic variation to keep things interesting, there’s a more pristine, altogether more polished feel to this collection of tracks no doubt the result of an artist who’s getting closer to refining their craft.

Title: Sexwitch
Review: It's this momentum that makes Sexwitch such a transcendent album, and some of the most exciting music any of these artists have made.

Title: Success
Review: Although Success is a very solid album, from a band that have already proved themselves consistently capable of churning out suitably bad-tempered and obtrusively loud material, it’s hard to feel it’s anything we haven’t heard before, which makes it far more underwhelming than its generally high quality content suggests it should be.

Title: Coma Ecliptic
Review: Coma Ecliptic is an exquisite masterpiece. As with most opaque works, it takes many listens to fully appreciate everything here.

Title: Help Us Stranger
Review: The beauty of The Raconteurs is in the timeless joy of hearing two world-class songwriters, cut from two very different sides of a similar cloth, come together to make something if not greater, then at least as good as the sum of their considerable parts. And in that sense, Help Us Stranger succeeds, and then some.

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: This album, like its predecessor, is stunning. [Fall 2007, p.91]

Title: Close To The Glass
Review: With guitars or electronics, the Notwist projects a sense of isolation and displacement.

Title: SremmLife
Review: The palpably effervescent joy of Rae Sremmurd feels untainted by the ills of reality and stands against a backdrop of contemporaries like Shmurda and Chief Keef who use their as a way of combating the grim reality of inner city rot.

Title: Dark Days + CanapÃ©s
Review: Dark Days And Canapes feels both bleaker and more robust than [earlier works]. [Sep 2017, p.28]

Title: Dream Wife
Review: Dream Wife’s self-titled debut is a satisfying and infectious trip of lo-fi indie pop that starts 2018 off with a much needed shot of adrenaline.

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: Producer Bjorn Yttling, who brings in his Peter Bjorn & John bandmate John Eriksson and, on many of these 12 tracks, a full string section to add a kind of lush power to the group's melodic drone.

Title: The Coast Is Never Clear
Review: Uplifting, exuberant gloom. Tremendous. [Oct 2001, p.108]

Title: Jp3
Review: With Jp3, Junglepussy has successfully pushed her artistry forward without sacrificing the personality that established her as a dynamic force. Although her crass content isn’t meant for everyone and she has yet to have a proper crossover moment, the sophistication of this project demonstrates her underrated status is just moments from being erased.

Title: Cadillactica
Review: Cadillactica is an album where an artist launches a superior second act while losing none of the essential elements that made the first so powerful.

Title: Drones
Review: Muse have always been ridiculous and overblown, but at least they used to be a ton of fun.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: This is more than an album, this is a moment in music history. Enjoy it.

Title: Loose
Review: The strangest thing about Loose isn't its irregularity, but the simple fact that this doesn't sound like Nelly Furtado at all.

Title: It's Me Again
Review: A much smoother ride and more cohesive entity.

Title: Let the Ocean Take Me
Review: Even though the band isn't doing anything that listeners haven't heard before, the album's lyrical depth will reward fans who take the time to sit down and really explore the record.

Title: From Here We Go Sublime
Review: If you like minimal electronic music at all, you must seek it out.

Title: White People
Review: More attention seems to have been paid to assembling the cast than finding something for them to record. [Dec 2004, p.98]

Title: Midwest Farmer's Daughter
Review: Daughter is best when it's specifically first-person, when Price bends country to fit her own story rather than bend herself to fit the form.

Title: Rammstein
Review: Injecting their trademark sound with fresh flair, RAMMSTEIN is one of the band's best efforts, a potent distillation of all the elements that have endeared them to fans for two-and-a-half decades.

Title: The Afterlove
Review: While the lyrics may be banal and inoffensive--bar a few moments of pause-and-rewind strangeness including references to “modern friends” and “beautiful” mothers (not his)--the music is actively risible, with Blunt having adopted a watered-down version of Justin Bieber’s asinine tropical house.

Title: Between the Times and the Tides
Review: Between the Times and the Tides cements Ranaldo's role as a dreamer and poet who can remain true to himself and reveal new things at the same time.

Title: Switzerland
Review: For a bunch of comedians, the Electric Six sure are talented musicians. [Dec 2006, p.189]

Title: Pink Friday
Review: Pink Friday, while certainly far from profound, is neatly rooted in predictability and vulgarity. But then again, would we have Minaj any other way?

Title: Fanfare
Review: The follow-up isn't quite so startling [as his debut] and the horrible guitar indulgence of Dear Friend is his first major misstep, but assisted by Jackson Browne, David Crosby, assorted Heartbreakers, Roy Harper and Wilco's Patrick Sansome he's evolved. [Dec 2013, p.117]

Title: Honeyblood
Review: Those artists who standout from the rest of the pack do exactly this with the additional knack of killer songwriting, and Honeyblood fortunately have that going for them in an abundance.
Through it all, and sometimes in spite of ambitious arrangements, Jones proves himself to have a way with poignancy and yearning melodies that stick.

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: King of Cowards
Review: With stoner rock's monotonous thrum as a template you're always going to have to work a little harder to break through with something genuinely interesting, and Pigsx7 don't always manage it here. [Oct 2018, p.84]

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: Just a Souvenir reveals itself to be a solid record, up there with the best of Squarepusher's work--as any good performer knows, you always leave the audience wanting more.

Title: "No Flashlight": Songs of the Fulfilled Night
Review: With No Flashlight, Elvrum is shifting the focus of his music onto himself. It’s unclear whether this is the smartest move to make, in light of his obvious production mastery.

Title: Eight Gates
Review: Short, spellbinding, almost painfully beautiful album. [Sep 2020, p.96]

Title: Love Will Find A Way
Review: "Love Will Find a Way" closely echoes the levitating version on Pharoah Sanders' like-titled album, all the while seeming to inch toward "Love's Holiday." It ends this invigorating album just as effectively as the blueprint began its parent release.

Title: Visions
Review: Grimes has come into a cleaner, more distinct version of her IDM self, albeit one still influenced by Aphex Twin, TLC and Enya.

Title: Chiaroscuro
Review: A record whose middling between arena aspirations and headphones listening feels less of a fusion and more of a compromise.

Title: Hard II Love
Review: He sounded breezy and at ease [on 2014's "Good Kisser"], finally confident enough to date women his age. So it’s a little disappointing that on Hard II Love, Usher’s eighth studio album, he hasn’t managed to hang onto that effortlessness. But there’s plenty to like, starting with his voice, which sounds better than ever.

Title: At War With The Mystics
Review: Mystics still has plenty of weird, shining moments to solidify the band's unique spot in rock, but the schizophrenia may leave you a bit jarred. [Apr 2006, p.84]

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: Although they indulge more textures this time, they don’t stray so far from Dogrel’s art-punk blueprint to the point of losing themselves. It’s just that the palette is wider and more pronounced. If anything, their chiming, noisy guitars and messy arrangements only fit their highfalutin aspirations even better.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: Heard consecutively, these songs sound disappointingly like one another, and while one good belter about the pain of unrequited love is a blessing, nine in a row turns out to be real drag.

Title: Age Against The Machine
Review: This warm, wonderful record is a joyous, head-spinning delight.

Title: E Volo Love
Review: The best moments ion this latest from Francois Marry come with added West African sparkle. [Feb 2012, p.86]

Title: I Am King
Review: These 11 tracks play on every ounce of rage you've ever known. Be afraid of them all. In the best way possible.

Title: Imps of Perversion
Review: Not everything works on Imps of Perversion, but it's still a strong second album that broadens Pop. 1280's horizons without sacrificing their pummeling impact.

Title: ESTOILE NAIANT
Review: Estoile Naiant is an invigorating, perplexing journey through the post-modern contextual climate of the information age that has synthesized an almost completely new narrative for the future generation of music, one that is both progressive and retrospective all at once.

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: On Daze, Vile’s amorphous, ambient drones continue to solidify into sharp shapes with defined edges.

Title: No, You C'Mon
Review: Some of the weakest, most un-affecting songs that Kurt Wagner has ever written. [combined review of both discs]

Title: Familiars
Review: Unwieldy on paper, it comes to life through odd, prickly phrases, but the music cuts deepest. [Aug 2014, p.93]

Title: Space City Kicks
Review: There's a whole gamut of compressed pop guitar stylings; some leap out, others don't. [Feb 2011, p.95]

Title: Frantic
Review: Frankly, this is total yuppie shit--competent and unobtrusive.

Title: The Red Light District
Review: Everyone's always complaining about how CD's have too much filler, but this one could use a little more: more big-name guests, more novelty songs and, most of all, more slow jams. It's that rare hip-hop album that might have been better if it had sounded more like a mixtape. [13 Dec 2004]

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: Lone soul genius Cody ChesnuTT's in dazzling form on Landing on a Hundred, which must be the most impressive crowd-funded album ever.

Title: The Monitor
