Title: No, You C'Mon
Review: The real fun is to be had on No You Cmon, as Lambchop gets much more adventurous and bold in their musical arrangements.

Title: Killing Time
Review: Killing Time is no breakthrough, but it does pack actual hard-rock crunch, not just sure-shot emo punch.

Title: Discovery
Review: Not enough of this album delivers on the promise of [lead single] "One More Time."

Title: Blueberry Boat
Review: In the end, that's the best gift the Furnaces have to offer, the simple power of their own joyful racket and clatter, the pure holy hell they always seem to raise.

Title: Speak Now
Review: Speak Now is no pop masterpiece, though it's sure to be hailed as such in some circles.

Title: Funhouse
Review: Funhouse is more haunting than amusing, but the solidarity that comes along with her recent divorce serves as the effort's muse and proves to be her best partner in life.

Title: Red Letter Days
Review: It's hard not to wish that the album had a bit more of the quirks and muscle that gave Breach its backbone. Without it, Red Letter Days isn't quite as forceful, but it is accomplished, melodic, and attractive.

Title: Noctourniquet
Review: For those who respect The Mars Volta for continuing to evolve after all these years, their latest offering will continue to inspire hope in the band's future.

Title: Bloom
Review: Well beyond the already stellar dismissal of heteronormative storylines in pop love stories, Sivan finds a wealth of ways to bring about fresh reflections on age-old themes with undeniable charisma.

Title: Black Panties
Review: Regardless of the reason, it’s safe to say that Kelly is fighting all sorts of social norms on Black Panties, from sex talk to issues of race and economics. The way he’s going about the issues might be a little bit clunky, to say the least, but it’s admirable that he’s even tackling them.

Title: This Island
Review: If This Island failed musically but still got Le Tigre's message out, it could be counted as a minor success. But at this critical juncture in their career, Le Tigre seem tame.

Title: Antenna
Review: A truly remarkable progression, and a great album to boot--Antenna is the work of a band that's constantly moving forward.

Title: Holy Hell
Review: It's as an articulation of grief that this record speaks most powerfully.  [Jan 2019, p.106]

Title: New Me, Same Us
Review: Now more than ever, the escapist quality of music cannot be underestimated. Little Dragon heartily delivers on that front throughout New Me, Same Us, opening the door to a candy-colored world where the beats are chill and every word is sung softly by Nagano.

Artist: Yoko Ono / Kim Gordon / Thurston Moore
Title: YOKOKIMTHURSTON
Review: With more focus and restraint, there's no reason to think Moore, Gordon, and Ono couldn't have really run with their collaboration and made something great. Instead, YOKOKIMTHURSTON feels like an overly conceptual exercise. Maybe that's by design, but a little melody would have gone miles here.

Title: Old Friends
Review: There is a solid amount of quirkiness to realize and I Was A King surely have a knack for turning out strong songs but maybe next time a 'less equals more' approach would be more fitting.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: The Whole Love is much more encompassing of everything vital in the Wilco catalog, the twangy, the noisy, and yes, a little of the leisurely.

Title: Death Is The Only Mortal
Review: In rippling the delving guitars and gripping drums with a tenacity that is tough to deny, The Acacia Strain find themselves again with just the right recipe--giving us a much more concentrated opportunity for catharsis in the key of anger.

Title: Unsound
Review: Mission of Burma have successfully walked that fine line between being consistent and running out of ideas.

Title: Good Girl Gone Bad
Review: Lyrics are once again an Achilles high heel for Rihanna.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: When it really hits, as it often does here, the music of Grouper creates a feeling that can only be defined as awe, an uncanny mixture of wonder and dread that nobody does better.

Title: Hunted
Review: Neither an audio-verité release or a fully-fledged, star-studded duets album. It's quite interesting, but that's all. Now, with this out of her system, she can move on.

Title: Paul's Tomb: A Triumph
Review: This release feels freer, though--not easier, necessarily, but delivered with a clarity of purpose not quite as muddled, consumption-wise, by sheer weirdness as was their previous LP, Tears Of The Valedictorian, for instance.

Title: Volta
Review: Where even her most divisive albums have managed to push her artistic boundaries, Volta feels limp and strangely empty-- almost unfinished.

Title: The Futureheads
Review: The Futureheads reclaim pop punk from the Warped Tour crowd -- and revive it in the process.

Title: Destroyed
Review: The guy's not a bad water-treader. Destroyed follows the understated elegance of 2009's Wait for Me even deeper into Ambient land; written on tour during sleepless nights in hotel rooms around the world.

Title: Ire Works
Review: I can't help but admire the wondrous technicality of the band members, but I wonder if they could have deployed it in a more tasteful way.

Title: Heartland
Review: Impressive in both scale and execution, Heartland succeeds not just due to Pallett's sizable talents, but his belief in his even larger ambition.

Title: Promise Everything
Review: With Promise Everything, Basement have returned stronger than ever, and have taken great care to capitalize on the most effective aspects of their previous sounds to make a dynamic and cohesive whole here.

Title: The Road From Memphis
Review: He's no fool: the result is an even more potent clutch of instrumentals, punctuated with the occasional vocal from Sharon Jones and some surprising male singers, including The National's Matt Berninger and Lou Reed.

Title: The Open Door
Review: Many of these theatrical, midtempo songs run together.

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: For all its highlights, however, Ta-Dah is haunted by the thought that the Scissors Sisters can't keep this up much longer.

Title: Point
Review: Point is less a stylistic mash-up and more a stylish exploration of mood and groove. [Feb 2002, p.98]

Title: Dungeonesse
Review: [A]  light, infectious, effortlessly cool debut.

Title: What About Now
Review: Bon Jovi's 12th studio album finds them on familiar ground, arena-pleasing blue-collar anthems of everyday struggle sitting alongside overblown power ballads.

Title: Kin
Review: The overall effect is of a band who have experienced life's slings and arrows but now exude both tenderness and wisdom. [Jul 2016, p.106]

Title: Constant Bop
Review: It’s a great album to listen to on headphones--the level of detail and the clarity of the aesthetic choices really become apparent.... It’s bliss.

Title: Getting Paid
Review: It's all played with an energy and focus that will impress even the most die-hard fan of '70s prog who claim "they just don't make 'em like that anymore".

Title: Faith in Strangers
Review: The most fully formed and wholly unique record in his discography.

Title: Jiaolong
Review: Jiaolong boasts nine timeless dance-floor bangers that resurrect a moment.

Title: How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb
Review: The record does sound good when it's playing, but [its] conservatism is what keeps HTDAAB earthbound and prevents it from standing alongside War, The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby as one of the group's finest efforts.

Title: Aquarius
Review: Aquarius heralds an essential new voice, one that coheres 100 current ideas about women, sex, sadness and musical restlessness in one excellent album.

Title: Gossamer
Review: It is both heart-wrenchingly introspective and jubilant.

Title: Glass
Review: These are superior soundtracks for sure, but just a little low on levity. [Dec 2016, p.93]

Title: Silver Landings
Review: Between its warm sonic patina and the personal nature of its material, Silver Landings stands as Moore's most mature work to date, making for a strong if understated comeback.

Title: Heartstrings
Review: Heartstrings lacks the killer song that would bring Howling Bells the success they undoubtedly crave. [Jul 2014, p.109]

Title: Feature Magnetic
Review: Here’s a Kool Keith album you don’t need to take in 20 minute doses. Lap it up. [Dec 2016, p.71]

Title: Albatross
Review: A record of imposing and frequent beauty, Albatross never crosses the line into grandiose bombast.

Title: Made in China
Review: Hatfield tears through 12 songs, posturing and pouting over caustic guitars and leaving her singalong hooks raw and unedited. [13 Aug 2005]

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: Still, despite its light-handed approach, Carrie & Lowell strikes with a sort of urgency unparalleled across the composer's 15-year career. Each song feels like a demon Sufjan simply had to face sooner than later.

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: Swing Lo works best at arm's length, admired like a diamond rather than held like a carbon-based life-form. [Aug 2012, p.91]

Title: Black Cherry
Review: While their artistic risk-taking is commendable, unfortunately the same can't always be said for the results: Black Cherry sounds unbalanced, swinging between delicate, deceptively icy ballads and heavier, dance-inspired numbers without finding much of a happy medium between them.

Title: Retribution
Review: A difficult but thrilling listen.

Title: The Midnight Sun
Review: Elegant and focused, the album was written, recorded and produced in the same bedroom as his first LP--with the same supersonic attention to detail. It's only his ambitions that have changed.

Title: Jigsaw
Review: Sov never quite recaptures the brash personality and cutting-edge sound of her first album. The beats here are more pedestrian, the lyrics more tentative, and for all her talk in the press notes about resuming her career (after a six-month break) with a sense of control over her music, Jigsaw sounds more like an album without a firm direction than the wide-ranging statement of purpose she meant it to be.

Title: In This Light & On This Evening
Review: It's a curiously dated backdrop that, although sitting well with Smith's occasionally pompous lyrics, does no favours to the singer's foghorn baritone; a problem that might have been saved by some radio-friendly tunes, which are notably thin on the ground this time. [Nov 2009, p.90]

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: Her voice has grown huskier with age, the songs are barely there, and hip-hop producer Mike Elizondo doesn't have the delicate hand that's required to bring them to life.

Title: Slow Air
Review: They've still got a solid ear for dreamy, yet captivating melodies, but with the confidence to push their sound in new directions and see where it takes them.

Title: Don't Let the Kids Win
Review: Due to her diverse strengths, Jacklin’s songs differ greatly--but where for some that may result in an inconsistent tone, Jacklin strengthens the album by honoring its emotional core at all costs. Tracks jump from genre to genre without losing their hypnotic quality.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: Blak and Blu pays off; it's not a perfect album, but it is bold and exciting.

Title: The Private World of Paradise
Review: The Private World Of Paradise does have a somewhat rustic, indie-rock feel, though augmented with a greater wealth of instrumentation. [No. 107, p.61]

Title: Changes
Review: An inescapable sense of conviction makes it transcend nostalgia. [May 2016, p.106]

Title: Happy Ending
Review: A stew of attractive singalong folk pop that looks to evocative kitchen sink drama for lyrical inspiration. [Feb 2014, p.83]

Title: Call The Comet
Review: Call the Comet is a tuneful, energetic collection of songs that evoke a youthful 54-year-old who still has plenty of good ideas up his sleeve.

Title: Memories Are Now
Review: Hoop’s experimental tack often requires repeated listens, but it’s creativity and not mere quirkiness that ultimately leaves  alingering afterglow.

Title: RTJ4
Review: RTJ4 supersizes their outsider aesthetic without squandering any hard-won authenticity. Icy disquisitions on the missing soul of modern America jostle with good-natured boasts from the golden age of hip-hop, yielding a remarkable hit rate.

Title: You Can Play These Songs with Chords
Review: As you might expect, the overall quality of the songs isn't quite up to the standard of the best Death Cab for Cutie albums, but it comes close enough to entertain fans who aren't die-hard completists.

Title: A Colores
Review: As good as it sounds, it simply fails to make a statement.

Title: Anak Ko
Review: The record and its seamless transitions from one heavily enticing, tender, and softly delivered track to the next paints a captivating and enthralling self-portrait.

Title: Food
Review: Food is a fabulous and immediate record, rich with muted brass and low-key electronics.

Title: Millport
Review: Throughout its just-over-30-minute runtime--very punk--Graffin and company take on everything from gospel, Americana, and bluegrass to Crazy Horse-esque pre-grunge and breezy Laurel Canyon country-pop, and that they do so with such gusto makes Millport feel like less of an outlier, and more like guys making the best of a power outage.
Mostly, though, 21 sounds as though it was built around Adele's presence.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: For the first time, Longstreth seems all too human, acknowledging failings and opening his inner landscape outwards.

Title: SAWAYAMA
Review: Raw artistry paired with rich heritage makes for a magnificent, spine-tingling first album for Rina Sawayama.

Title: EarthEE
Review: EarthEE finds that magic spot where the feet are grounded but the head's floating on a cloud. [Apr 2015, p.111]

Title: Trinity (Past, Present and Future)
Review: Trinity is a more diverse album than their last, but there are times when the songs feel too disjointed.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: Creating a suite of well-turned if unnecessarily understated antiwar songs, she's a gifted, strong-willed minor artist bent on shaking England in particular.

Title: Adult Nights
Review: Wild Light certainly will not be pegged as the most original, best dressed or smartest band in Indie Pop, but the group wears all of Indie Pop on its proverbial sleeve and seems fit to carry the Indie Pop flag--at least for a little while.

Title: Delusion Moon
Review: It’s not so much a Meat Wave as it as an all-consuming fleshy tsunami. Although this breed of cut-the-brakes punk is obtrusive and in-your-face in all the right places, it offers little else in terms of versatility or gear changes.

Title: The Drift
Review: This is out in the margins, removed from 'pop' and 'alternative' genres by the scale of its reach, its bloody and bold ambition. It is complex, multilayered, densely plotted, wordy. It's also scary, harsh and bruised.

Title: In The Seams
Review: It's a wholesome piece of work that just keeps on giving.

Title: Ducktails III: Arcade Dynamics
Review: Arcade Dynamics, then, falls somewhere in between the cleaned-up Real Estate sound and the noisier aesthetic of Landscapes.

Title: The Killer
Review: It's the producer's most immediate album and tightest display to date.

Title: The Blueprint
Review: Blueprint is his best since debuting with Reasonable Doubt in 1996.

Title: Wallpaper for the Soul
Review: In the end, Tahiti 80 have made a record worth listening to, even worth recommending to others, but one that fails at its primary, stated goal: to wallpaper your soul.

Title: Songs
Review: Songs is an accomplished second album, that sees Woodhouse building on the foundations of electronica-tinged outputs that you'll quite easily appreciate and enjoy.

Title: Conversations
Review: It's a gorgeous album, though, and a perfect one to settle in with as a night dwindles toward its end. [Jun-Jul 2014, p.88]

Title: Sound & Color
Review: [Brittany Howard's] performance only confirms that she's the kind of pop vocal talent that only comes along a few times in a generation, while Sound & Color as a whole is proof that Alabama Shakes have got the chops to be a lot more than Muscle Shoals revivalists.

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: Although there are some clumsy similes and metaphors, and a surplus of astrological references, its lyricism is undeniable, abundant in pithy rebukes and come-ons. And while the predominantly crawling tempos can have a tranquilizing effect, there's nuance to nearly every cut with high-level songwriting to match.

Title: Fits
Review: With so many disparate elements spliced together, Fits should be a terrible mess, but the Texan trio exercise glorious control throughout, ensuring that every blast of noise has its tender counterpoint.

Title: Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager
Review: Man on the Moon II, the sequel, is still a bumpy listen, but it tweaks his formula enough to at least hint at the massive promise Kanye sees in him.

Title: TH1RT3EN
Review: The Deth's 13th album (how'd you guess?) gravitates between classy thrashers and hokey anthemic rock with scorching guitar work and Mustaine's snarling voice expectedly leading the charge.

Title: Horses and High Heels
Review: Producer Hal Wilner again helms this follow-up but the chemistry proves more fitful. [Apr 2011, p.80]

Title: Challengers
Review: While no one can argue that it’s not an accomplished and distinguished collection of songs, the doubts still remain--albeit fainter than before--as to why one would choose this collective over at least half-a-dozen similar-sounding yet ultimately superior bands.

Title: The Shepherd's Dog
Review: Beam has managed to tweak and in?ate his signature sound without sacri?cing any of its considerable charm.

Title: Mutant
Review: The downside of the now-ness, the resistance against static definition, is lack of resolution. Mutant is hard to listen to, sometimes in a salutary way and sometimes not.

Title: Partners
Review: This record falls into all the icky, celebrity duet traps.

Title: Hot Motion
Review: They have achieved the almost unachievable in 2019, a rock album that is required listening from start to finish, rather than being a collection of singles and skippable filler. They ought to be applauded for this, and the record ought to be lapped up by a public longing for depth and heft in its music.

Title: Cassadaga
Review: A restless, questing work.

Title: Something to Tell You
Review: Handily, 70s soft rock is a well-worn vector for such feelings. And if there is a nit to pick with Something to Tell You, it is that Haim’s balance of R&B and soft rock has leaned too far in favour of blowsy wallowing, and away from R&B’s clever sonic feints and tough-girl postures.

Title: Real
Review: The music is more refined than previous Loveless albums. With the exception of the sonic roar in "Same to You," the pleasures on Real turn on instrumental subtleties.

Title: Punish, Honey
Review: It all makes for riveting listening for anyone willing to let Vessel punish--and reward--their ears.

Title: Benjamin Booker
Review: His debut lives and breathes the Deep South, from the Chuck Berry references (most effective on opener 'Violent Shiver') to the slower, more hushed tones of 'I Thought I Heard You Screaming', which sees Booker take his vocal cues straight from Bobbie Gentry's late-’60s peak.

Title: Puzzles Like You
Review: Puzzles Like You... is not at all Halstead's best work, and what has sounded simple and subtle before begins to feel simplistic and blunt; the songs here move with an energy that seems either forced or mocking, and on the whole embrace the kind of triteness they used to offset.

Title: The Big Dream
Review: This is an unrelentingly difficult record, with all semblances of pop music and even melody eschewed for a Hound of the Baskervilles trudge through a gothic swamp.

Title: You See Colours
Review: While debut album 'Faded Seaside Glamour' suffered from a mild dose of ADD, sprawling and meandering into atmospheric noodling between its smatter of acid-in-your-candyfloss pop hits, with 'You See Colours' Gilbert has sharpened his pop stiletto blade.

Title: Sistrionix
Review: It is a thoroughly unironic, seriously fun, rock record, in which seizing the day (well, the night), settling scores and the importance of making one's own money are explored in detail, with leering electric guitar and crashing kit.

Title: Ambivalence Avenue
Review: It helps that Wilkinson sings sweetly, too, distancing and layering his vocals for that dewy, lost-in-the-woods effect. [Aug 2009, p.87]

Title: Dance on the Blacktop
Review: Nothing's third album is something of a safe bet: fans of the band and/or genre will still enjoy this, while Agnello's name being attached may turn a few extra heads, but it is feasible that the whole 'nu-shoegaze' movement is running out of steam.

Title: Luciferian Towers
Review: It’s still a functionally and otherwise dazzling work, one that sits nicely among the band's compositions.

Title: A Productive Cough
Review: If you're fond of the notion of rock & roll as folk music, A Productive Cough is something you'll want to hear, an album that captures the roar of the masses in an unexpected way, and if you've loved the songs of Titus Andronicus as much as their music, you'll find this isn't quite so different as you might think.

Title: My Shame Is True
Review: A nice rebound from the fan service of its predecessor, showing that even this late in the game, Alkaline Trio can still write better songs than the vast majority of their contemporaries and take them to uncharted waters when it feels right.

Title: In Love and Death
Review: For the most part, it's standard shouty punk designed to appeal to white male American virgins... Yet, they surprise. [Dec 2004, p.147]

Title: Plumb
Review: Intellectually and musically, it's more like a rose bush in winter: thorny, twisty, and hinting at tantalizing beauty. The more time you spend with this album, the easier it is to get caught.

Title: Peeping Tom
Review: Once you get past the shock tactics, Peeping Tom is little more than a pile of dated Linkin Park-style sludge. [2 Jun 2006, p.83]

Title: Something Else
Review: A more structured back to basics approach really works for them. [Sep 2018, p.94]

Artist: Jenny Lewis with The Watson Twins
Title: Rabbit Fur Coat
Review: A dozen remarkable tracks. [Feb 2006, p.78]

Title: The Seer
Review: The Seer won't be for everybody, but deserves to win new converts.

Title: Preparations
Review: On the whole, it's not a big departure, or a grand statement. [Fall 2007, p.87]

Title: Allas Sak
Review: Things mostly stay low-key and subtle, with Ejstes's guitar growing righteously wild just once, on En Dag På Sjön, one of several instrumentals.

Title: X&Y
Review: When he moans his verses, Mr. Martin can sound so sorry for himself that there's hardly room to sympathize for him, and when he's not mixing metaphors, he fearlessly slings clichés.

Title: Shriek
Review: Wasner’s vocals seem more confident and assertive now, as if she’s come of age. Still, there are moments on Shriek just yearning for a clever guitar melody or screeching solo.

Title: Heathen Chemistry
Review: It's hard not to find this album kind of disappointing, a confirmation that no matter what they do, Oasis Mach II will never have the sheer abandon or thrill as Definitely Maybe through Morning Glory.

Title: Twisted Crystal
Review: They’ve left the cutting edge musically, which can have valuable results, but here it feels ambivalent and a little tidy.

Title: Fold Your Hands Child, You Walk Like a Peasant
Review: Ultimately, despite all its self-defeating limitations and annoying, fey affectations, this remains a superb record.

Title: The Last Word
Review: Opening cut "I Got You" promises faith and solidarity "even if they start to build that wall," and both the strident funk of "Above The Law" and the testifying "Pressure" lament the rise of inner-city crime. [May 2019, p.30]

Title: You Were Right
Review: A winner from top to bottom. [Jan 2014, p.100]

Title: The Year of Magical Drinking
Review: A powerfully uncomplicated rock album.

Title: Blink-182
Review: Blink-182 have found a new, angrier way to never leave junior high. [Dec 2003, p.135]

Title: A Lesson Unlearnt
Review: On A Lesson Unlearnt, the insights on love are articulated both from the position of the one being sought and the one seeking affection, offering an entry point for anyone who can identify with love's effects.

Title: Land of CanAan
Review: There's barely a wrong-placed note on the whole magnificent album. [Jun 2013, p.81]

Title: Grime MC
Review: It’s testament to JME’s influence that he’s able to pull in such heavy hitters, but also to his talents on the mic that he’s never overshadowed.

Title: Shangri-La
Review: A wry and considered thing. [Oct 2004, p.128]

Title: Heligoland
Review: [The album] sees the reunited Grand "Daddy G" Marshalll abnd Robert "3D" Del Naja proving they can still corner the market in atmospheric glooom, even if their era-defining days have passed. [Mar 2010, p.90]

Title: A Little Bit Longer
Review: It's unfortunate that much of their sophomore effort is submerged in an ocean of heavy-handed production, so deep that the boys' natural talents struggle to break the surface.

Title: The People's Key
Review: The People's Key just doesn't have the emotional pull that others do.

Title: Fortune
Review: Not all of Fortune is so unctuous, but none of it is inspired.

Title: Worship Music
Review: On the (relatively) bright side, there's the root-level pleasure of hearing hard-boiled riffs performed with a minimum of fuss.

Title: Rooty
Review: The nerve of it all is breathtaking. Turbo-beats poke up a gospel-jazz revivalist meeting, a mariachi band wanders into the hazy disco sashay of 'Broken Dreams', a Gary Numan sample gets bludgeoned to credibility in the Van Helden-esque pogo of 'Where's Your Head At?'.

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: A winner. [May 2007, p.106]

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: The overindulgence comes off as an indistinguishable wall of sound and, even worse, as a terrific bore.

Title: Metal Resistance
Review: This album seamlessly flits from one brilliantly bold idea to another with no dips in quality.

Title: Kicks
Review: The album is also horribly sequenced, pushing its best tracks down after a morass of prettier, more insipid melodies had fluffed you.

Title: The Trials of Van Occupanther
Review: A truly delectably odd album of archaic echoes and future-classic choruses.

Title: Sucker
Review: Sucker is just an exceptionally good pop album.

Title: Holy Vacants
Review: This then, is a solid album of phenomenally crafted songs.

Title: Shed
Review: The first long-play offering by these Pennsylvania teen punks might just be one of the best punk rock debuts of the year.

Title: Dutch Tvashar Plumes
Review: Dutch Tvashar Plumes is dominated by exquisitely expressive forms of abstract techno.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: The duo’s music was always full of the small details, but they now conspire toward something bigger.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: Feelings are always “heavy” or a “burden,” and love is consistently “dark” or “light”; it’s thematic territory that feels stale for the band, and the result is an album that aspires to talk about the complex nature of relationships, yet has nothing meaningful to say.

Title: April
Review: Throughout, Kozelek connects memory to emotion with masterful strokes.
All told, it may be the best set of songs Rouse has yet to offer.

Title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy
Review: Tragedy reflects the wild mood swings associated with those suffering from bipolar disorder; raging one moment, euphoric the next before settling into a seemingly bottomless depression. And like those suffering, it’s not always a pleasant listening experience, but when it’s on, it’s some of their best and most musically mature work yet.

Title: Don't You Think You've Had Enough?
Review: This is state-of-the-art pop music with an irresistible sense of rough and tough feminine glamour. Do not miss out.

Title: Antibalas
Review: In all that attention to detail, there's flair and fire enough to quash the qualms and revel in people doing something over and doing it right. [Sep 2012, p.97]

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Worlds Apart
Review: This is the best album Trail of Dead has ever made. [#13, p.94]

Title: Algiers
Review: There's not a lot of post-punk, no-wave or noise to be found here, but more so a very topical sound for the right now. [No. 122, p.53]

Title: Wild and Free
Review: For his latest release, Wild and Free, he rarely feels the need to stray outside this tried and tested outline: Each track bounces along with a carefree groove and exudes blissful vibes without really offering anything fresh or innovative, but is there really any new ground to break in a genre that reached its creative zenith over 30 years ago?

Title: Water for Your Soul
Review: She dives into world music on this album, with interesting results. [No. 123, p.61]

Title: The Blueprint 3
Review: Just as The Blueprint 3 seems to have pulled it off, it peters out in a mass of indistinct tracks.

Title: New Maps of Hell
Review: New Maps is a terrific sounding record; at least two-thirds of it begs many repeated listens.

Title: Muzik
Review: Sure, there are a ton of bands pursuing a very similar sound and feel as Dolorean are on Muzik, but their style, the strength of their songs, the sweep of their melodies, and the strong emotional core revealed by their lyrics and vocals push them ahead of the pack.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Only in closer Grown Ocean, with crashing cymbals and trilling woodwinds, do you get a sense that Fleet Foxes are actively trying to impress you. Even then, though, you're impressed all the same.

Title: Ten
Review: Fueled by the expert bustle of his trio (including bassist Tarus Mateen and drummer Nasheet Waits), he's given to expansive, sparkling showpieces; solo, he coaxes the still spaces between the notes into a cadence of their own.

Title: Principe Del Norte
Review: Much of Principe's second half finds him repackaging the first half with plodding disco beats that make the initially exciting melodies seem boring the second (and third, and fourth) time around.

Title: Drops of Jupiter
Review: The music fails to gain any momentum until track seven, and by then, Train's lucky the listener's still spinning the CD.

Title: The Music Scene
Review: The Music Scene is a good album, but one that is hard to get excited about.

Title: You Can Do Anything
Review: True to form, this third record pootles around before, ultimately, achieving lift-off.

Title: New Hymn to Freedom
Review: This is a superb album by three supremely talented musicians. More than that, it is an ideal reminder of the perfection that--even in today’s digital climate--can still be reached through letting three such talents simply play in a room together. Undoubtedly one of the true highlights of 2018.

Title: Fantasies
Review: This Canadian-American hipster quartet's first record in four years has an electrophile slickness, not to mention a set of catchy songs.

Title: Diamonds On the Inside
Review: Diamonds on the Inside's breathless Rolling Stone Encyclopedia of Rock whirlwind is tiring, at best.

Title: Imperial
Review: 'Imperial' is an evolving and ever-involving shard of artistry by a true original on his 'Victorialand'-era form nonetheless, and that's got to be cause for celebration.

Title: Ghosteen
Review: A rich, shifting tapestry of grief, beauty, tailspinning disorientation, and illuminating snatches of lucidity.

Title: Ten Silver Drops
Review: The Machines' laser-light-show-ready atmospherics don't entirely compensate for the lack of a single as catchy as their last album's "Nowhere Again."

Title: Turn On The Bright Lights
Review: Interpol's virtue lies in the way its music unfurls from pinched openings to wide-open codas.

Title: Some Cities
Review: Doves’ strength lies in their careful sculpting of the sonic and the emotional, and here they’ve restrained their palette and scope so much that the result is grey.

Title: Pain Is Beauty
Review: Every album tells a story and, thankfully, Wolfe’s story changes all the time, a morphing type of self-expression with completely pure intent.

Title: Keep It Hid
Review: It is an album in the original sense of the word, offering a coherent display of Auerbach’s influences.

Title: With the Tides
Review: Rockist textures and lush dreamscapes that could very well be the Cocteau Twins take on heavy metal.

Title: Jukebox
Review: She doesn’t outdo the originals. Instead, like a fan, she claims them by pondering them.

Title: State
Review: Those that deem this effort too weird or erratic are best advised to consider the deluxe edition with its live bonus disc recorded with the Metropole Orchestra at the Paradiso in Amsterdam.

Title: Tropics of Love
Review: Amid the cheap preset funk and curdled interludes, Bouaziz enchants with moving pieces such as "Heartbeats" and "Hero." [Aug 2014, p.74]

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Lykke Li manages to combine Feist’s beautiful crooning with Robyn’s playful spunk in her own impressively unique way.

Title: Fuzz
Review: From the opening cut of “Earthen Gate” the songs nudge, heave, shove and then finally bulldoze their way to your hearts.

Title: Sparrow
Review: What lingers longest on this remarkable record is an uplifting sense of resilience. [Jun 2018, p.26]

Title: Snowflake Midnight
Review: What ultimately saves Snowflake Midnight from following The Secret Migration up the band's collective keister is the song positioned to serve as its climax, 'Dream of a Young Girl as a Flower.'

Title: You Want It Darker
Review: It feels like the most human of his late works, with acoustic instrumentation carefully balanced alongside drum programming and vintage keyboards.

Title: Relax
Review: Often Patrick Wimberly's production renders their pop-cultural culling too literally.

Title: Your Future Our Clutter
Review: The Fall are the most predictable and unpredictable band in Britain.

Title: Wonderful Rainbow
Review: Stellar noise pollution. [May 2003, p.99]

Title: Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace
Review: Grohl and Company sound like Bob Seger fronting for your garden variety modern hard rock group.

Title: What Chaos Is Imaginary
Review: It's easy to lose your way here, as there aren't many big choruses to hook onto; and by the time we reach the generic shoegaze of "Roses," the duo seems to have misplaced their own compass. Still, they say not all who wander are lost, and Girlpool have at least tracked several potential paths to pursue on the next overcast journey.

Title: Time on Earth
Review: As reunion/comeback albums go, Time on Earth is outstanding.

Title: I Love The New Sky
Review: It’s all crowned by the confidence of I Got This, which reconciles Charlatans-esque country-soul Hammond to classy baroque-pop ba-ba-bas in a way that is unabashedly uplifting.

Title: TH1RT3EN
Review: Basically, it's a Megadeth album; no more, no less, no change. [Jan 2012, p.124]

Title: Vestiges & Claws
Review: A few shuffling moments suggest Sunday pub lunch surrounding by Bugaboos, but when Gonzalez hits his meditative stride--Every Age's there-is-a-season stateliness, the post-rock smudges of What Will---he owns the room. [Mar 2014, p.98]

Title: Putting the Days to Bed
Review: Roderick has a disarming command of how swelling choruses and careful harmonies can push a song from good to great.

Title: Xenoula
Review: There are traces of Bjork and in the childlike voice exploring its surroundings, Yoko Ono, but the fantastical world Xeno creates is entirely her own. [Feb 2018, p.116]

Title: 7 Days of Funk
Review: While Snoop's voice is an easy match for the sound--both are low-key but hard-hitting--most of the tracks don't quite cohere.

Title: DiCaprio 2
Review: DiCaprio 2 exemplifies what the ideal student of the game sounds like--someone who's conscious of how a hook presents itself, how to control their delivery and how to diversify their lyrical bonds.

Title: Jinx
Review: Jinx isn’t really a narrative anyway, more a fine assemblage in which a slightly eldritch weirdness is balanced with pop nous. It certainly feels like Crumb are on the cusp of something here.

Title: Lonely Planet
Review: Lonely Planet is a pleasing collection of well-crafted, often beautiful sketches, and while they may not always end up anywhere specific, you'll always enjoy the journey nonetheless.

Title: Critical Equation
Review: Not every song is a slow ride--True Love and Heart Killer are bluesy folk stompers--but on the likes of the luxurious Buzzing In The Light and Critical Equation they allow themselves to revel in dreaminess. [Jun 2018, p.110]

Title: For the World
Review: Ed Askew will continue to write, observe, reflect, and create visions and words. This result is timeless enough to remain there if one wants it.

Title: The Greatest Story Never Told
Review: Even though there were a few points at which this album dragged for me, (see back to back six-minute songs), there is no doubt that this is not only a strong debut for Saigon, but a strong album that indicates he'll be a force in hip-hop for years to come.

Title: With Love
Review: While With Love is an ambitious and entertainingly composed undertaking, offering glimpses into Zomby’s varied inspirations, it can still be frustratingly piecemeal and somewhat self-indulgent.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: The result is Björk’s most frighteningly intimate album to date.

Title: Camp
Review: Gambino can really rap. Scratch that; he can really, really rap, plus sing and emote and put on a show better than 90% of his hip-hop counterparts.

Title: Midwinter Graces
Review: Perhaps where Midwinter Graces suffers most is that it will be resigned to the world of the holiday album, making brief appearances from only late November to early January, garnering at most a passing mention the rest of the year. At the very least, though, it is a holiday record that will be remembered once a year.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: Nothing Was the Same doesn't show large amounts of growth, but the small changes to the sound and the slightly wider net his lyrics cast make it worthwhile.

Title: El Tren Fantasma
Review: Watson packaged up the month that he spent riding the train, using his original recordings, adding his own narration, throwing in some interviews, and creating something magical.

Title: Astro Coast
Review: To some extent, Astro Coast comes off like a muscular, radio-ready version of music that would've been found on a limited-edition 45 back in the mid-'90s. But the way Surfer Blood balances escapism and grit is a neat trick, and one that never really loses its sense of wonder.

Title: Watersports
Review: The result is a wild and unpredictable album, Watersports, which navigates styles and time-periods like a patient veering in and out of consciousness.

Title: Wooden Head
Review: Wooden Heads is a Byrds-worshipping, bummer-in-the-summer mystery. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.104]

Title: Dissociation
Review: Dissociation is an impressive album and a perfect endpoint to a very noisy and varied body of work.

Title: Love and Curses
Review: Love and Curses is a rock ‘n’ roll record with neither pretense nor manicure, a clean glimpse into rock’s exposed essence.

Title: Nashville
Review: These are great songs, regardless of categorisation. [Mar 2005, p.101]

Title: Gloss Drop
Review: Stripped down to a three-piece since Tyondai Braxton's surprise departure, Battles' sophomore effort may not have a nailed-on stand-out like their debut's Atlas but their dizzying electro-prog has a great deal more focus this time around.

Title: American Tunes
Review: A country-gospel stab at Ellington’s “Come Sunday” badly misses the mark, and Toussaint’s innate funkiness is only lightly felt, sometimes sacrificed for too much tastefulness. There are still many American treasures here.

Title: Heligoland
Review: Overall, though ‘Heligoland’ is a puzzling and frustrating listen. Some good tracks can’t hide the fact that this is the stuff of an identity crisis. It’s one thing to call on your famous friends to put flesh on your bones. It’s another if you leave the listener wondering if you’ve any spine at all.

Title: Nude With Boots
Review: This band is still nearly as big, as slow, as lumberingly loud as they were in the days Kurt Cobain was trying out for a spot on bass.

Title: Living Legend
Review: While his long journey has finally paid off, Living Legend lacks it factor to have listeners clamoring for a follow-up anytime soon.

Title: The Way I See It
Review: On his third solo outing (and first for Columbia), songwriter/producer Raphael Saadiq takes the listener on a smooth carpet ride that seamlessly weaves the feel-good essence of soul music's storied roots.

Title: Dizzy Heights
Review: Dizzy Heights is a bold, wonderful affair. [Mar 2014, p.113]

Title: Do Not Disturb
Review: Inevitably there’s nothing here to rival the dark majesty of Van der Graaf Generator’s classic 1970s work, and newcomers should start with Still Life, Godbluff or Pawn Hearts. But Do Not Disturb is a worthy addition to the group’s canon and--if this is indeed their last album--a fitting end to an illustrious career.

Title: Careful
Review: At their best, Boy Harsher capture the bittersweet feeling of being young, in love and on the road, oblivious to the inevitable spin-out.

Title: Big Station
Review: What raises Big Station above the ordinary is the ease with which Escovedo explores his place in the world, whether through love's hard fought redemption or life's barrel-scraping moments. [Aug 2012, p.97]

Title: Savage Hills Ballroom
Review: While Savage Hills Ballroom awkwardly stretches to make universal points from Powers' personal distaste, his personal heartache results in the most truly resonant moments.

Title: Nellyville
Review: Outside of "Pimp Juice," the album sounds weighed down by the commercial pressures of going multiplatinum the last time out. After five tracks, one cannot help but wonder what might have been had Nelly not gotten so pop so quickly.

Title: The Prodigal Son
Review: Ry Cooder’s long investigation of the permutations of the blues and possibilities of justice comes to rest here in the religious balm which remains inseparable from American music.

Title: Innocence
Review: Built around harmonies that only siblings seem to muster, there is a neat balance struck between angry noise from self-enforced isolation and a pastoral quality that strikes into the heart of America in a direct bloodline from CSNY and The Band.

Title: Art and Life
Review: More than justifies the hype.

Title: What Will We Be
Review: What once made Banhart such a strange bird--roaming from jazz to folk to indie pop, often within a single song, as on the impossibly catchy 'Chin Chin & Muck Muck'--now seems almost mainstream, as if the rest of the pop world has not only caught up with him, but left him in its dust.

Title: The Fine Art of Self Destruction
Review: These folk and country-tinged tunes are melodic, deft and emotive. [Dec 2002, p.108]

Title: Padded Room
Review: Padded Room is still a solid, well-crafted effort.

Title: Grey Tickles, Black Pressure
Review: Grant has a fascinating combination of wisdom, world-weary cynicism and righteous anger; it never grates.

Title: Alegranza
Review: The joyous problem: All the repitition, all the sunshine, all the sound can get tiring. But the same goes for anything that releases endorphins this ecstatically. [Oct 2008, p.122]

Title: Bloody Lovely
Review: Only the moody, foreboding ‘Over It’ hints at the pair testing their own boundaries; otherwise, this is another solid Deathrays outing.

Title: Banga
Review: Smith leads one of the best and sturdiest bands in rock... and their intricately scored psychedelia is a running high in Mosaic, the title stomp, with its yowling-wolf lick and Nine, an extended beguiling jam that suggests Smith fronting her own Doors. [Jul 2012, p.89]

Title: Beautysleep
Review: An album full of songs so lethargic, it sounds like it needs a nap halfway through. [Apr 2002, p.71]

Title: It's All Around You
Review: It's All Around You has both serious ambience and serious grooves, it rocks occasionally, and it doesn't dip into jazz nearly as much as some of their past releases.

Title: The Repulsion Box
Review: A raucous blend of rockabilly, country and '80s indie rock best listened to before a heavy night of Caledonian pint-drinkin'. [Sep 2005, p.112]

Title: Sugar
Review: Sugar, by comparison [to "Wrecking Ball"], feels laboured. [Sep 2010, p.91]

Title: Hey Everyone
Review: While there is plenty here that's impressive, the odd change of gear wouldn't go amiss next time around. [May 2009, p.110]

Title: The Money Store
Review: The Money Store might be the very definition of acquired taste, and will most likely alienate the vast majority who attempt to give it a spin, but it's undeniably an extraordinary record.

Title: Sorceress
Review: While Heritage is the strongest of this new trilogy, as well as laying the blueprint for this current era, Sorceress is able to push the adventurous qualities further to outstanding effect.

Title: Our Endless Numbered Days
Review: Our Endless Numbered Days is cleaner, more diverse, and generally sparser than its predecessor, and, given the apparent limits of Beam's former setup, it's also an astoundingly progressive record: Beam has successfully transgressed his cultural pigeonhole without sacrificing any of his dusty allure.

Title: Obsidian
Review: Obsidian is a brave and necessary record that builds on Baths’ glitchy poignance.

Title: LP3
Review: There's nothing intrinsically flawed about what's otherwise a solid instrumental record, but so much of it feels so close to many of the things happening on the radio and the pop charts right now that, 90 seconds into a song, the mind might start wandering and wondering what this kind of stuff would sound like with Wale or Rihanna on top of it.

Title: Don't Let the Kids Win
Review: As a whole the LP’s similar tempos and approach cause the whole thing to float by like a long-lost memory, nice when you’ve clasped on to it but soon it’ll be running through your fingers and out of sight.

Title: Challenge Me Foolish
Review: Breakbeats have become fashionable again, so a dusted-off track like “Undone” doesn’t sound quite as dated, with Paradinas playfully bouncing between tympani boom, percolator bip, and dramatic background strings. ... But “Bassbins” also shows that the more aggro and cartoonish take on it (which anticipated the rise of breakcore) remains out of fashion for good reason.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Reign is more nuanced and varied in sound than Treats was.

Title: The Tarnished Gold
Review: The key word for this album is pretty.

Title: American Capitalist
Review: This kind of constant drive away from the more watered-down sound of a lot of their post-grunge contemporaries and toward metal is something that allows Five Finger Death Punch to stand out in a genre that's easy to get lost in.
While O floated along pretty much at one consistently delicate pace, 9 finds Rice exploring a wider range of musical expression. [#16, p.97]

Title: The Bride
Review: It’s not a quick fix to the pain in her heart, but it is part of the essential journey, one that may be fabricated but feels all too real nonetheless thanks to Khan’s riveting and insightful storytelling.

Title: Everything Under The Sun
Review: If Everything Under the Sun often seems a bit candy coated, it's a high grade of confectionary that they serve, and most folks who get a taste of this album are likely to come back for more.

Title: I Speak Because I Can
Review: I Speak Because I Can is, without doubt, an album to really delve into, and one to lose yourself in for hours. Added to that, it asserts Marling as one of this country's most talented young songwriters; our Conor Oberst or our David Berman.

Title: Nervous
Review: Much of Nervous is a little heavy for what is, on the surface at least, a gentle, lilting folk inflected album. However, there are moments of utter joyfulness to be found.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: So if Thr33 Ringz fails to shock, consider also that it fails to disappoint.

Title: Tides
Review: Tides [is] a somewhat unbalanced listen, with both genuine highs and a few frustrating lows.

Title: Her Majesty the Decemberists
Review: A thrilling listen. [Dec 2003, p.140]

Title: Jeff Bridges
Review: Bridges' country-fried drawl gets wonky (see the shuffling "Blue Car"), but when the pieces come together -- as on laid-back, folksy charmers like "Everything but Love" and "Maybe I Missed the Point" -- the result is as comfortable and unpretentious as the Dude's bathrobe.

Title: After the Disco
Review: Another beguiling collection that merges New Wave and dance sensibilities with winsome pop melodies.

Title: Honky Tonk
Review: In the end, Honky Tonk is a slow burn, Farrar musing on life as scenery flashes past the van window, and the redemptive power of music.

Title: Let The Dominoes Fall
Review: This album, the band’s seventh, feels familiar in structure, packed with the usual two-minute bursts of aggression. But it’s improbably weighty and ponderous and unusually slow moving for a band that specializes in gnashing.

Title: Some Racing, Some Stopping
Review: The songs are much more confidently realised. [May 2008, p.100]

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: His songwriting style remains largely unaltered: eloquent, abstract, stream-of-consciousness rambles, tiny bits of which manage to lodge themselves in your brain. But his talent is most apparent as a composer.

Title: Celebration Rock
Review: This is not the sound of settling.

Title: King of the Beach
Review: Shards of digital distortion and self-indulgent instrumentals are pretty much gone. What remains is a novel reworking of the California surf punk formula.

Title: Definition of Real
Review: He comes across as a Southern-fried early DMX with his unabated aggression; raw, explosive verse; and hints of conscience.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: Lyrically, however, the album is just another soul-searching journey, and while he may be getting too old to call a “boy genius”, he's not lost any of his wistful intelligence.

Title: Work
Review: Work finds them owning their sound, and treating the nostalgic pangs they stir as a platform from which to express something sincere. The result is a record a little less giddy and more workmanlike than prior SOL albums.

Title: kin
Review: Fans of electronic music take note: iamamiwhoami is a powerhouse, and they have the songs (and videos) to prove it.

Title: Callus
Review: An album that’s disorienting at its catchiest, harrowing at its ugliest, and more than willing to run both of those modes at the same time.

Title: 4REAL 4REAL
Review: YG regains some of the energy that made his early output stand out, though all the new elements he brings into focus--from the spirited features to his tribute to Nipsey--feel tacked-on and half-hearted, well-intentioned but not well thought out.

Title: Some Say I So I Say Light
Review: While there are some good songs on Some Say it is often a frustrating listen, which is all the more disappointing given Ghostpoet's potential as an artist.

Title: The Future's Void
Review: This record feels even more pinpoint-focused than her first--perhaps thanks to its recurring themes--and the shaking, distorting sounds she's wrapped around her voice are as beautifully unsettling as her words.

Title: The W
Review: Although roughly half as long as Wu-Tang Forever, The W is every bit as erratic and overreaching. If Forever was a great single album hidden in a messy two-disc set, The W feels like a good six-song EP nestled inside an uneven album that seems to take its cues from the half-assed weirdness of ODB's N**** Please.

Title: The Light of the Sun
Review: There's nothing cerebral about her lyrics; she's a captivating, blunt performer, here emphasizing classic arrangements and raw emotion over poetic invention.

Title: Anxiety
Review: The majority of the tracks on her second full-length, Anxiety, teem with chilled vocals, crunchy guitar, and keyboard blurps that move hips to sway before showing their hollowness as soon as one steps off the dance floor.

Title: Where You Go I Go Too
Review: On his debut album, he shoots for the stratosphere and lavishly scores.

Title: The Universe and Me
Review: The Universe and Me offers more evidence that, as time goes by, Guided By Voices’ other songwriter may be aging more gracefully.

Title: Galore
Review: This sweet-and-sour debut that is more original than your average pop thing.

Title: The Atlas Underground
Review: Frustrated, hungry, and full of rage, The Atlas Underground is a rallying cry set against an inventive and propulsive backdrop that inspires a physical response as much as thoughtful action.

Title: Ivywild
Review: Those willing to put forth the effort will be rewarded with a beautiful, stimulating and eclectic album that stands alone in a genre of its own making.

Title: Georgia
Review: Perhaps there’s not that one killer single that will turn her into an instant sensation, and those are bound to emerge, but what she’s cultivating with Georgia holds more value: that of creating an essential body of work that is unaware of any imperfection, coming from a mind that’s overflowing with a glut of ideas.

Title: LUX
Review: Lux is a surprisingly rich experience that's difficult to fault. It's not the most startling record Eno's ever made, but it probably is his most successful ambient work.

Title: Leaves Turn Inside You
Review: This is Unwound's Kid A, in that they've turned their back on the rock in favor of something more atmospheric, but even more significantly, they've tossed out all the old recipes and made the future unpredictable. Problem is, they've fixed something that wasn't broken. [Jul 2001, p.85]

Title: Until In Excess, Imperceptible UFO
Review: It’s slower, dreamier, with songs that prize atmosphere above immediacy.

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: Not since 1992’s "Your Arsenal" has he combined barbed wit and fast-moving, backward-glancing guitar rock so piercingly.

Title: I'm Not Bossy, I'm The Boss
Review: This funny, convincing, unembarrassed collection proves she's no cartoon.

Title: Astronomy for Dogs
Review: Some of the tracks will endure, but as a whole the album’s timelessness is limited by its own camp posturing. Still, it’s quite a fun ride. [#17, p.82]

Title: Stephen Malkmus
Review: It will remind you that Stephen Malkmus is one hell of a songwriter, whether you like him or not.

Title: For Emma, Forever Ago
Review: Although For Emma, Forever Ago works best as a concise listen, as each song segues naturally into the next, tracks like 'Blindsided' and 'For Emma' quickly rise as shining standouts.

Title: Yellow & Green
Review: Their third album totaling 75 minutes and spread, slightly unnecessarily, over two CDs, it reaches unexpected new heights in the pantheon of 'metal bands who mellowed out'.

Title: Honey
Review: Honey's intentions are noble but the results are mixed. [Jun 2016, p.69]

Title: Offend Maggie
Review: Remarkably, there has not been a dip in quality: simply put, Deerhoof is as strangely consistent as they are consistently strange.

Title: Incarnate
Review: Despite still occasionally erring towards po-faced earnestness, his [Jesse Leach's] impassioned and fiery performance ensures that Incarnate is a brash reaffirmation of this band’s superiority over their peers.

Title: I'm Going Away
Review: I’m Going Away is striking for its group sound; the Furnaces play with more air around them, more flexibility and interaction.

Title: Jim Noir
Review: His continually entertaining and tuneful approach should pick up many more fans over the summer, and those that found their way in through tracks such as 'Eany Meany' won't be in a hurry to up sticks either.

Title: The Hungry Saw
Review: It’s not an incredibly remarkable record, but when a band is this consistent for this long, it’s hard to fault it.

Title: Work (Work, Work)
Review: Continuing a penchant for darkness established on 2009's 'Marry Me Tonight', Work (Work, Work) is probably as grim a sounding record as you're likely to hear.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II
Review: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II represents not only the most overt and successful attempt to capture the patience, subtlety and fluidity of Earth's talented cast, but also the most accurate document of their patient, stoical and determinedly psychedelic ethos.

Title: Lunglight
Review: Drowning pop compositions in jittery polyrhythms is indie rock's move du jour, but the Shaky Hands aren't trendy; they make fine-boned, classic rock'n'roll in the Strokes' vein.

Title: Together
Review: The guest list is impressive. But it'd take a very straight face to refute the frequent echoes of The New Seekers or Fleetwood Mac, while "Silver Jenny Dollar" sounds like something Mike Batt might have knocked up for The Wombles. [Jun 2010, p.97]

Title: Have One on Me
Review: To devotees, however, it sounds very much like a second masterpiece: a different kind of epic to "Ys," and one with enough hooks and charms to ensnare at least a few Newsom agnostics. [Apr 2010, p.82]

Title: How The West Was Won
Review: hile its takes on classic swing, psych country and postpunk pop are understandably fragile and lacking wallop--an inevitable consequence of age and getting your kids in your backing band--How The West Was Won is shot through with a wonderfully wry reinvigoration.

Title: Dagger Beach
Review: The lack of structure makes these songs feel experimental, but not sufficiently to commit to being out there in a remarkable way.

Title: Britney Jean
Review: Far too much of Britney Jean defaults to EDM-by-numbers and the numbing lyrical repetitiveness that appears to be Will.i.am’s calling card.

Title: Nothing Is Wrong
Review: Those looking to rock out won't find many headbanging opportunities here, but Nothing Is Wrong works well as driving music, particularly if the scenery outside your windshield matches the sepia-toned music.

Title: All That Emotion
Review: She ensures these songs keep it together. [Sep 2020, p.88]

Title: Give More Love
Review: Inevitably they’re not reinventing the wheel, yet it’s still good to hear Ringo’s non-voice (heavily treated), and his drumming skills are undiminished.

Title: Love King
Review: Third albums often represent the moment where an artist's sound either gels or falls apart. With Love King, The-Dream has narrowly skirted an artistic rut by staunchly holding his ground. But he can't keep making the exact same album for much longer.

Title: I Loved You at Your Darkest
Review: A well-earned victory lap for a band that pulled itself back from the brink of oblivion to sound stronger than ever. A source of pure joy, indeed.

Title: drukQs
Review: In-between the chaos and peace, 'Drukqs' induces a whole host of emotions using acid squiggles, plucked piano strings and 80s electro-breaks.

Title: Reflektor
Review: As it stands, Reflektor is Arcade Fire’s most diverse and sonically interesting work to date.

Title: Wrong Creatures
Review: On Wrong Creatures, it's refreshing to hear a band so wrought with spiritual and emotional demons find their rock & roll grace and let it rip.

Title: I Speak Because I Can
Review: I Speak Because I Can is an album of elegance and brilliance. Marling has developed from her debut, and her voice has grown both physically and lyrically.

Title: Ghosteen
Review: Ultimately, all are visions, alternately haunted and comforting. Subtle evolutions in mood and instrumentation come to peaks that are made all the more stunning by their scarcity.

Title: Contraband
Review: It is a rare, fine thing: the sound of the perfect A&R sales pitch turning into a real band.

Title: I Like To Keep Myself In Pain
Review: This is Hogan's first solo album in 11 years and her best. [Aug 2012, p.96]

Title: The Bronx (III)
Review: Certainly the LA punk mob have a free-spirited approach to life – as rebellious and American as the Stooges or Jack Kerouac – and every bit as compelling.

Title: Messes
Review: It’s easy to indulge a reverie when it’s a vivid one, and Messes invites you to lose track of time for awhile with it.

Title: KIN
Review: It’s smoothly produced by veteran producer Tony Hoffer, and each track has a radio-friendly sheen to it and a catchy chorus. Which is all very nice, but it’s disappointing news for those of us who prefer Tunstall at her more experimental.

Title: Black Yaya
Review: It's an eclectic mess that, when performed with such a light touch, just gels.

Title: Some People Have Real Problems
Review: Some People is stuffed to the rafters with love songs but they're never precious or cloying, even when the arrangements soar to rousing string/brass/choir-laden climaxes, or when the lyrics are comprised of little more than a string of clichés .

Title: Harps and Angels
Review: Harps and Angels belongs up there with "12 Songs" and "Sail Away" as one of Newman’s greatest works, regardless if he took 20 years to get it out into the public.

Title: Sculptor
Review: Randell and Hassett are a formidable musical team, certainly, with both skill and vision to spare. They proved that on Passerby. Sculptor, on the other hand, seems like it’s searching for the right path forward, with both glimmers of hope and rough patches.

Title: Motion
Review: Ultimately, Motion is somewhat of a scattered album with some shining moments.

Title: Who Needs Who
Review: Unusual musical flairs pop up all over Who Needs Who... [but] the style never becomes the substance. Likewise, the drama behind the album's making doesn't overwhelm the music.

Title: Angel of Retribution
Review: A preposterous, highly-entertaining return. [Apr 2005, p.104]

Title: Harmonium
Review: Admirable, if not necessarily lovable.

Title: I Remember Me
Review: The Oscar-winner is an understated powerhouse on her second album.

Title: In the Absence of Truth
Review: In the process of adding new facets to their sound,  Truth winds up reinforcing self-imposed limitations.

Title: V
Review: The duo's intoxicating sense of endless sonic possibility remains, but the many lovely moments rarely amount to memorable songs, and several shout-outs to its still-enchanting debut fells like cruel teases. [No. 112, p.57]

Title: Octahedron
Review: it’s an excellent change of pace for the band, and proves that they can indeed write spacey, esoteric mid-tempo songs instead of...well...spacey, esoteric breakneck songs.

Title: The People's Key

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty

Title: Cry

Title: Gemstones

Title: Cadenza
