Title: Ghost Town
Review: Owen leave behind the emotional outbursts of his collaborations with his brother Tim in Cap'n Jazz, Joan Of Arc and Owls, but keep a quieter, suburban rage alive on his sixth album. [Dec 2011, p.121]

Title: Cardiology
Review: Cardiology dials down the sparkle, which is kind of a bummer; plodding fake-U2 anthems such as "Right Where I Belong" are definitely not Good Charlotte's sweet spot.

Title: Almost Free
Review: Produced by Grammy-winning producer Ricky Reed (Twenty One Pilots), the troupe also trades in the lo-fi blades of Too for a polished maturity without sacrificing any edge.

Title: Life Love Flesh Blood
Review: It's a svelte, consummately accomplished change, although Burnett's reliably polished, sometimes even laidback, settings allow plenty of room for grit and sweat. [Apr 2017, p.32]

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: The freedom of expression and thematic irregularity that we hear while listening to Edward Sharpe and the Magnetic Zeros is a fabulous release from the traditionally despised contract that constrained Ebert’s first and former band, Ima Robot.

Title: Forever Neverland
Review: A masterpiece that puts MØ firmly on her own pedestal as an individual artist rather than a recurring feature.

Title: While I'm Livin'
Review: Without regret, Tucker takes the intuitive songwriting of these younger collaborators and proudly inhabits their biographical approximation of her nine lives with earnestness and ease.

Title: Folk Art
Review: Of the many excellent and diverse projects Joe Lovano has produced and won critical acclaim for, this ranks with his very best, as strong an album as he has ever produced, with musicianship at an extremely high level, and well-conceived compositions that continue to identify him a true original.

Title: Man Alive!
Review: Holding to Marshall’s wavelength requires a little more investment than the dingy music asks for, but that’s not to say his shadowland of the heart lacks nuance.

Title: You Are Not Alone
Review: You Are Not Alone is a solid outing that somehow amazingly manages to be both secular and sacred at once, and there is a stripped-down timelessness to it.

Title: Living in Extraordinary Times
Review: "Overdose" is somewhat overwrought but works as it moves along and further sounds join the vocal. "Trouble" is a shadow version of late-'80s/early-'90s James, more proof that a whole album, or at least an EP, of these three demos would be most welcome. As it stands though, Living In Extraordinary Times is a triumph for the band as their great songs continue to move to new territory.

Title: Dancing at the Blue Lagoon
Review: While Dancing at the Blue Lagoon brings Cayucas' shortcomings to the fore, more often than not it's more blandly pleasant than irritating, serving up a watered-down tropical drink of an album that just doesn't connect the way Bigfoot did.

Title: Defying Gravity
Review: Defying Gravity builds on the skill set that gave listeners "Love, Pain & the Whole Crazy Thing" and takes it further, seamlessly combining hook-laden crafty songwriting with a pop sensibility in the modern country vernacular that blazes a new trail and underscores Duke Ellington's dictum that there are only two kinds of music: good and bad. This is a shining case in point for the former.

Title: Not Even Happiness
Review: The result is a record that’s concerned about faith, death, and the metaphysical. It’s heady stuff but grounded with vignettes of everyday activities--a beautiful, comforting second work from the singer.

Title: Take Care, Take Care, Take Care
Review: With subtle sonic shifts (such as chanting on the almost-poppy "Trembling Hands"), the songs are reliably dynamic, turning hushed beats and lightly scratched guitar into overwhelming drama.

Title: Television Man
Review: Sure, the songs' formulaic stop-and-spurt attack can wear on the listener's ears after a while--but this is an album well worth risking tinnitus for.

Title: Congratulations
Review: Cowbells and organ chords set the frenetic pace for this crazed and eerie take on surf music that namechecks the godfather of ambient in its punkest track.

Title: Sugar
Review: The idea of "wounded optimism" applies to Sugar as a whole, at least from a listener's perspective. There's just enough good material here to believe that the problems with the record represent a temporary misstep, or a flawed approach, rather than a fundamental change in the band.

Title: Prisoner
Review: Ultimately Prisoner is tethered by sturdy, familiar images of tightropes and trains. [Mar 2017, p.94]

Title: Jerusalem
Review: The eclectic, pan-genre disc opens -- as did 2000's Transcendental Blues -- as an unabashed rocker, but this time around Earle uses the heavy artillery to underscore weightier worldly themes.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: There’s an eerie blandness to the mood that is initially off-putting but turns into a surprisingly compelling, subtly evocative combination of sadness and contentedness.

Title: Melt
Review: The harmonies never reach the heights of say, Toro Y Moi--though Night In The Ocean's fusion of hip-hop thud and buzzing shoegaze guitars shows a welcome willingness to try. [Mar 2012, p.113]

Title: Wallop
Review: Alas, genuinely surprising moments are scarcer on much of Wallop, with rudimentary workouts outnumbering the fresher like of "$50 Million" and its super-charged Chic groove. [Oct 2019, p.23]

Title: Volume 3
Review: All in all, it’s just good fun. And more than a little bit clever.

Title: A Hundred Million Suns
Review: It’s all so methodically planned that even standout radio-wave surfer ‘Take Back The City’ and producer Jacknife Lee struggle to stamp fresh life into this mega-selling formula.

Title: Zeitgeist
Review: Zeitgeist’s orgy of avalanche rhythms, cascading riffs and sky-licking guitar is as grandiose as ever (the solo on "Tarantula" sounds like a nuke hitting a Guitar Center), but the bombast is softened as Corgan reaches out for shame-sharing community.

Title: Masts of Manhatta
Review: For a record that, thematically, trades in adaptation to new environments, Masts of Manhatta boasts real structural depth, as Bonham finds an effective balance of contemporary folk and modern rock.

Title: Sha Sha
Review: Three or four songs short of a really strong album. [Oct 2002, p.107]

Title: Year of Meteors
Review: Deep meaning and well-crafted pop.

Title: Æ’IN
Review: A remarkably assured and instinctive piece of work, one that speaks of good times on the dancefloor while not being afraid to throw in more poignant and affecting emotions, all wrapped up in clothing that falls nicely on an ambient blend of disco and house.

Title: Psychedelic Country Soul
Review: While the more mellow moments may turn off some of the more alt fans of alt. country, most longtime fans will find this one just dandy. [Mar 2019, p.90]

Title: Food
Review: While it remains almost impossible to dissociate Kelis and early collaborators the Neptunes, it's more difficult imagining a better creative alliance--at this point in her career, at least--than the one that shines here.

Title: Such Pretty Forks in the Road
Review: Throughout the album, Morissette crafts a raw, often uncomfortable, narrative. In the portrayal of imperfection, Such Pretty Forks in the Road creates space to encounter profound disquietude.

Title: Christopher
Review: Despite the self-therapy and tonal lulls, Christopher is a highly listenable affair that produces two truly outstanding moments.

Title: Riceboy Sleeps
Review: It's true that Riceboy Sleeps is no departure from New Age, is in fact a strengthening of at least Birgisson's place at the centre of its indie iterations. But it also takes the formula of another band a lot of people like and bends it just enough to make that formula interesting again.

Title: Psychodrama
Review: It all culminates in Lesley, a staggering, 11-minute exploration of toxic masculinity and domestic abuse. “Tell a yout’, if you got a brain then use it,” he raps, early on; Dave’s doing that, but has much more in his armoury than just brains.

Title: SUGAREGG
Review: What prevents Sugaregg – Bully’s third album, and Bognanno’s first as a totally solo entity – from feeling like a period piece is that the retro approach isn’t exclusively put to the service of buoyant, indelible tunes. Instead, Bognanno uses this mercurial mode to record her experiences with bipolar disorder. The theme leads to another set of opposites surfacing in the lyrics, a series of starkly frank psychological insights that are at once coldly analytical and wildly evocative.

Title: Eat the Elephant
Review: Keenan balances the constructive dissemination of contemporary society in his own unique way and, in the process, rather surprisingly, may have just made one of the most prescient albums of the year.

Title: Arcadia
Review: As far as solo jaunts go, this is one she should be immensely proud of. It's Macomberesque as opposed to Borrellian.

Title: Everything That Happens Will Happen Today
Review: Everything That Happens is a brilliant addition to a creative partnership that has yielded so much and shouldn’t have taken 27 years to rekindle.

Title: Save Rock and Roll
Review: With the emphasis--ironically--more on “Pop” than “Rocky” it’s not as dynamic with contrast as the more accomplished Folie à Deux yet it’s a charming, convincing and much welcome comeback.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Even where Sounds Of The Universe resembles a self-help manual, it does so with commanding tunes and a ring of truth. [May 2009, p.102]

Title: Blonde
Review: This is an album of mostly beatless soul whose heart nevertheless pumps vividly and loudly throughout its 17 tracks. [No. 136, p.61]

Title: Is This It
Review: A heartily uplifting brew of scruffy street style, swear words and stammering pop tunes which sweat musical history. [Sep 2001, p.99]

Title: Light Asylum
Review: Light Asylum works best if approached as a work of fantastic campness; after all, this would explain the whip-cracking sound effects on IPC.

Title: Now We Can See
Review: It is in reality a bit boring, a bit generic, and a bit aggravating.

Title: Heart's Ease
Review: It's as touching, beautiful and dark as any of Collins' records, and even pushes her sound into new territories. 65 years into her recording career, that modern approach to folk music is still yielding treasures. [Sep 2020, p.24]

Title: Hard Love
Review: Hard Love delivers frontman Tim Showalter's hard stuff in exponents. Add this depth of relay onto Showalter's loaded visions, and it sounds as if the universe itself is groaning. We are out of our seats for this one.

Title: Between Places
Review: The band’s songwriting chops are evident on Between Places, and it’s refreshing for a debut to err on the side of being too ambitious, when so many new indie bands nowadays suffer from the opposite problem. But the content of these songs doesn’t quite earn their epic execution.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: Hummingbird proves that these guys are maturing into a sound that's both singular and wrenching with severity.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: A trio of high-profile tracks near the end of MNIMN offer the best of both worlds in terms of Pusha T catering to the Top 40 crowd and still supplying the uncut raw fans expect.... Sadly these moments are inconsistent and broken up by generally ill-fitting production.

Title: Into The Woods
Review: If anything on Into The Woods Brock and his merry men (including drummer Richard Chadwick and keyboardist Tim Blake) conjure, not the mellowness but the magic and mystery, even malevolence, of nature.

Title: City Beach
Review: Where Jackson occasionally seemed as if they were in a rush to jam as many styles into their sound as possible, Cunniff digs deeper into her idiosyncrasies, creating music that feels unhurried and flows easily.

Title: Half The Perfect World
Review: World is like stumbling into a jazz café at closing time. [22 Sep 2006, p.94]

Title: Gauntlet Hair
Review: Gauntlet Hair are surely a band to keep an eye on, and their first full-length is an exciting listen, but now that they've got that rhythm section thumping for us, let's get some clear choruses to shout along to.

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: The slightness of this album is hard to hold a grudge against, but ain't nothing oh-my-god necessary about it either.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: Ultraviolence, a collection of mid-century ballads spiked with blues-rock, is a stunning accomplishment. Its eleven songs whimper and howl, soothe and taunt, hypnotize and thrill.

Title: Kill The Moonlight
Review: This is simple music, driving music, perfect music for getting a good bath from the asinine perils of nu-metal and modern rock.

Title: Lenses Alien
Review: It is a more mature record.

Title: Heroes
Review: [Nelson] moves effortlessly from pop country balladry to well-heated Western Swing. [Jul 2012, p.94]

Title: Release Therapy
Review: Release Therapy is solid; disappointing only when weighed against Luda's prodigious talent. [Dec 2006, p.89]

Title: Permo
Review: Charmingly wobbly Edwyn Collins-produced debut. [Dec 2017, p.96]

Title: Strapped
Review: Strapped isn't groundbreaking, especially by the standards The Soft Pack have set for themselves.

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: 'Cuckoo Cuckoo' is another moment in which Animal Collective reach a new level of compositional mastery and broaden their territory.

Title: My Woman
Review: These are controlled, tempered, well-steered songs, capable of navigating genres. [Oct 2016, p.104]

Title: Warning
Review: Green Day have created a great punk-meets-rock album.

Title: Freedom
Review: Boldest album to date, Freedom highlights "Miki Dora" and "Skipping School" grapple with masculinity and its illusions. "Satudarah" offers stoned-eye hallucinogens.

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: It's a far cry from the lo-fi surge of Cerulean Salt, but Crutchfield has progressed beyond that breakthrough LP, and begun the next phase of a career that's only trending upward.

Title: Tentacles
Review: Crystal Antlers need to allow the sounds of their instruments to serve a compositional goal in this way more often, rather than simply using them to bash through their songs.

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: Boys in Girls in America is one gargantuan anthem short of, and two bits of filler long on, the band’s Born to Run.

Title: Sauna
Review: The about-faces make for an engaging, challenging listen, but by the end it all seems a bit vague.

Title: Low in High School
Review: His 11th solo studio album Low in High School is a mixed bag of brilliance and dross. There are some genuinely interesting new explorations while other tracks are deeply disappointing. Disconcertingly uneven, yes, but not safely predictable.

Title: Marigold
Review: What is clear is that the album adds to Pinegrove's growing status as one of the most talented recording and touring bands in the land. Marigold brims with the promise that any sustained run of the band's current line-up will yield a multiplicity of their best moments.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: No Cities to Love spends much of its running time reminding us not what Corin Tucker, Carrie Brownstein, and Janet Weiss can do but what other configurations of players can't.

Title: Mama, I'm Swollen
Review: Diehard fans will continue to bray for "The Ugly Organ 2," but Swollen features better songs, stronger playing, and Dylan-level lyrics, making it the band's most cohesive work to date.

Title: IRM
Review: Where her previous album was ethereal and ephemeral, IRM is exciting and eclectic.

Title: Reachy Prints
Review: The pleasures of Reachy Prints are deceptively complicated, and it's another masterclass in how lightness needn't be thin or naive. [May 2014, p.72]

Title: The Preacher's Son
Review: Mostly tepid adult-contemporary black pop. [22 Jan 2004, p.69]

Title: 200 Tons of Bad Luck
Review: Despite these head-scratching derailments, 200 Tons of Bad Luck brings the gloom in Biblical doses.

Title: Music To Be Murdered By
Review: Eminen’s 11th album offers over an hour of the world’s greatest rapper blasting away on all cylinders. It is the first great album of 2020, so lethally brilliant it should be a crime.

Title: Emoh
Review: The lack of distinctive arrangements eventually diminishes the songs' individual merits. [#9]

Title: Tomorrow Right Now
Review: His idiosyncratic rhyming style can grate without the leavening presence of other rappers. [Apr 2003, p.116]

Title: Lucky
Review: On record five, their lovely, surging melodies suggest a minor-league Coldplay, while singer-guitarist Matthew Caws recalls a lost golden age “when I could fix anything with sound.”

Title: (II)
Review: While not as immediately striking as either Crystal Castles (I or II), the streamlined sound allows more maneuverability and subtle variety in the actual songwriting.

Title: Wild Smile
Review: Sporting three singers/ multi-instrumentalists in Austin Fisher, Quinn Walker (Fisher's cousin), and Pan, along with drummer/ keyboardist Brian Aiken, there's a kaleidoscopic twist of fresh ideas throughout Wild Smile that offers something new with each trip through these tracks.

Artist: S U R V I V E
Title: RR7349
Review: The perils of nostalgic resentment notwithstanding, many listeners will find the foggy atmospheres and neon-lit cityscapes of RR7349 irresistible.

Title: Reflection
Review: Although essentially a radio-ready pop aperitif and nowhere near the cultural touchstone of Beyonce's album, Reflection nonetheless works as a Revlon ad-level post-feminist girls' night out with plenty of vintage '90s R&B swagger.

Title: From Here to Eternity
Review: This is long-form drone perfection. [Sep 2019, p.91]

Title: Darkness Brings The Wonders Home
Review: This is Smoke Fairies' strongest, most urgent album to date. [Apr 2020, p.93]

Title: Scratch My Back
Review: His voice, still a dynamic instrument that can leap from meek to menacing, is very much out front, prowling over spare, sometimes lugubrious reworkings. At the album’s best, the results are head-spinning....At its worst, a few songs feel plodding and insular.

Title: On the Line
Review: There are dark undertones--drug references mainly--but Lewis is no moper. [Apr 2019, p.32]

Title: Here and Now
Review: Their ambitions may get the best of them on Here and Now, an album that finds frontman Chad Kroeger volunteering to "kick a hole in the sky."

Title: Song Yet to Be Sung
Review: Farrell's silvery adenoidal baritone scissors through bass-heavy raggamuffin beats, dreamy swells of keyboard-fueled atmosphere and ticklish breakbeats -- and the slapdash aesthetic somehow coheres. [Aug 2001, p.79]

Title: Simulation Theory
Review: The group has scaled down a bit (how much bigger could they get?) writing, rhapsodizing and crooning about lighter topics than usual. Similarly, the group--along with co-producers Rich Costey (Interpol), Mike Elizondo (Eminem, Fiona Apple) and Timbaland (Jay-Z, Missy Elliott)--has also changed up its sound with a mix of electro-punkish riffs and sprightly beats filtered into its densely layered orchestration. ... Refocusing their ambitions in a way that won’t alienate fans but also keeps them anticipating whatever might come next.

Title: At the Dam
Review: The album sounds as billowing and ethereal as one would expect from a solo harpist, but Lattimore's sense of experimentation gives her a distinctive sound, and At the Dam is simply a magnificent album.

Title: The Magician's Private Library
Review: Such is Sitek’s influence on the record that it takes you a little while to get to know the real Miranda. While initial listens find her songs somewhat opaque, they gradually open up to reveal their emotional depths.

Title: Cobra Juicy
Review: Cobra Juicy employs a richly flourished amount of instruments and sounds that are catchy and full of life.

Title: Scholars
Review: The album is an ambitious and adventurous set of music that's every bit as engaged as anything they've ever released, and there's an undertow of discovery that makes their new music an adventure worth a spin or two.

Title: The Music Scene
Review: The Music Scene adds new knots to Blockhead's sly, ironic take on boom-bap, incorporating shifting structures that spiral into changing tempos, half-remembered snippets of soul horns and gnarly old guitars, and occasional drifts into hazy, shimmering psychedelia. Sadly, this fog thickly enshrouds the back half of the disc as the tempos stagnate, rendering it inert and crying out for a shot of adrenaline.

Title: Let the Record Show: Dexys Do Irish and Country Soul
Review: It all makes for an excellent follow-up to 2012’s comeback album, One Day I’m Going to Soar.

Title: Carnival of Souls
Review: Though its concept may remain opaque, Carnival Of Souls compels. [Oct 2014, p.116]

Title: Incarnate
Review: As a whole, Incarnate improves on the creativity and restlessness offered by Disarm the Descent. There is a lot more ambition, confidence and above all, passion here.

Title: World Music
Review: Beautifully realised, immaculately recorded, and one of the year's loveliest vinyl artefacts to boot.

Title: Interiors
Review: Neither a work of nostalgia nor a move away from the blueprint that made them so special in the first place, this album demonstrates that artistic quality cannot be confined to a specific place in time.

Title: Pressure Chief
Review: Although Pressure Chief isn't a bad album, several of its songs come off like b-side compliation fodder rather than a batch of fresh material.

Title: DSU
Review: At its best, DSU cycles through that duality with aplomb, which will serve as an excellent introduction to his gigantic discography for all new fans.

Title: Life and Times
Review: As immediate as Life and Times isn't nearly as diamond-hard as "Copper Blue," which is a great part of its appeal: it flows naturally, the music never pushes, it settles, comfortable in its own skin.

Title: Future Women
Review: They make a better Shins than a Stooges. For anyone looking for a relative of the former with an interestingly rough sound and loads of potential, the M's are good to go right now; but the rest of us are stuck mining gems from amidst muck, like normal.

Title: Arrow
Review: Often you wonder exactly what you're hearing; you just know you haven't heard it before. [Aug 2020, p.87]

Title: Field Songs
Review: Field Songs is Whitmore's masterpiece thus far: unflinching, stubborn, demonstrative, and inspiring.

Title: Jeff Bridges
Review: Jeff Bridges is all quiet and sepia-toned, dripping like molasses in dollops of hammy pedal steel, placid acoustic guitars, and Bridges' cracked vocal chords.

Title: The Meth Lab
Review: Too often, the album is weighed down by pedantic, average beats and too many run of the mill guest verses, indicating Meth's generosity is a bit of a weakness. Ultimately, it dilutes The Meth Lab's potency.

Title: Trouble in Paradise
Review: La Roux returns on its own terms, with at least five minutes and 40 seconds that capture tremendous artistic growth and expression.

Title: Enjoy the Company
Review: These songs show a band in its prime-and cast a much wider net of influences, finally shaking that garage band label, bringing in folk, country and some damn fine bar room rock.

Title: Winter Kills
Review: Winter Kills thrills with the same potency the band have wielded throughout their career. [24 Aug 2013, p.54]

Title: Electric Balloon
Review: Each song is so powerful and crafted you can’t help but buy into whatever it is Ava Luna are trying to sell you.

Title: Hardly Electronic
Review: Hardly Electronic is a mature and polished album from a band confident enough to let their influences guide their sound without overshadowing it. Longtime fans will obviously snap this up, but anyone with an interest in classically-minded pop arrangements and great songs will find much to like on this unexpected gem from the Essex Green.

Title: The Milk of Human Kindness
Review: It’s similar enough to past efforts that one can trace his artistic trajectory with a steady arc, but it’s the point in the arc where the slope takes a radical increase, making the name change seem like an appropriate signifier.

Title: One by One
Review: It's hard not to wish that the songs stuck in your head the way they used to, even if it's still enjoyable as a whole.

Title: Drifters / Love Is The Devil
Review: Love Is The Devil draws more obviously from film music, creating a moving, mostly instrumental platter loaded with evocative drones and coarse textures. [No.99, p.55]

Title: For Now I am Winter
Review: The results meld as mood music of the highest variety--dense yet delicate, edgy and yet elegiac.

Title: Castlemania
Review: All in all, Castlemania is a fairly loose and scattered record.

Title: Essence
Review: As halting, spare, and downbeat as its predecessor was giddy, verbose, and, okay, downbeat. [Jul 2001, p.125]

Title: Thank You For Today
Review: “Summer Years” is the band’s earnest indie-rock sound distilled to its purest essence, and “When We Drive” is an elegiac look at long-term relationships through the metaphor of a road trip--but there’s no “Doors Unlocked And Open” or “Ghosts Of Beverly Drive” to shake things up. It’s another solid Death Cab For Cutie album, but it lacks vitality.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Days of Abandon
Review: The leap taken to get to this record isn't as jarring as the one from the debut and Belong, and its standout songs—such as "Simple and Sure" and "Eurydice"—are grounded by the huge, uplifting choruses we expect (and adore) from Pains.

Title: Nights Out
Review: his new record is a fine one, Nights Out picking up where 2006 debut "Pip Paine (Pay the £5000 You Owe)" left off; styles reeled in and stripped for parts which are reassembled, re-wired, into something oddly-cohesive.

Title: Mother
Review: The union between the two musicians (one entrenched in Cretan folk and medieval music, the other in instrumental rock and post-punk) is the alchemy which makes this record both structurally cohesive yet subtly and, somewhat contrarily, diffuse.

Title: GN
Review: It has to be said that this is more of a nice vibe record than it is one full of great standalone songs, but when the vibe created is as utterly charming as this, that can only be a minor gripe. [1 Jul 2017, p.52]

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix
Review: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix is an absolute blast, rich in ringing guitar and euphoric synths but thankfully light on fromage and staid rehashes. [Jul 2009, p.130]

Title: Bless Your Heart
Review: Bless Your Heart simultaneously reinforces and extends the favorable first impression left with the premier album.

Title: Hinterland
Review: Hinterland feels less like the spirit of the dance floor and much more like the crush of a weaponed march. [May 2015, p.98]

Title: Year In The Kingdom
Review: Tillman's intimate, close-miced voice, does lend Year in the Kingdom a lonesome, somber tone, one Tillman-- a funny, amicable dude, if you've ever heard him clowning on himself at a Fleet Foxes gig-- would do well to shake on occasion. Next time, maybe; for now, the stout, supine Year in the Kingdom, Tillman's second fine record of the year, will certainly do.

Title: Music for the Age of Miracles
Review: By the time MacLean gets around to a spoken-word revisit to an old haunt, "The Museum Of Fog," you're happily along for the surreal ride. [No. 146, p.55]

Title: Tomorrow Morning
Review: Eels' latest, Tomorrow Morning, is far too insular to mean much of anything outside itself. It's an exercise in self-referentiality, which might be more impressive if the music didn't sound like the folk-with-beats path Beck was smart enough to avoid.

Title: The King of Nothing Hill
Review: 'The King Of Nothing Hill' manages to effortlessly stir a Trans Atlantic cauldron of retro flavours, sleazy soul, avant-garde darkness, soundtrack cool, breaks, head nodding jazz sophistication and electronica sus.

Title: Keep It Like a Secret
Review: Recalls last year's fine Halo Benders release, The Rebels Not In, the album Martsch recorded with Beat Happening's Calvin Johnson and former Spinanes and current Built to Spill drummer Scott Plouf. And that's not a bad thing at all.

Title: Bittersweet World
Review: Bittersweet World is the first time that she has made a record that lives up to her happily empty persona, something that's truly fun junk.

Title: Cause And Effect
Review: Unfortunately, it’s little more than a bland exercise in pop that the band needs in order to sell records and tour again.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Heavy-breathing sex chants with a heart of darkness.

Title: Static
Review: It’s an album about what happens next rather than looking back. They might be a band in thrall to the 1960s but this is a record that tells us to live in the now.

Title: Ungrateful
Review: At times, the quintet deliver the solid grooves and renowned, catchy singalong choruses that have engaged their adoring fan base, but for too much of the time Ungrateful sounds a bit flat and tired.

Title: Secret Machines
Review: On the new one, the drums still thunder and the space rock vibe is intact, but something is missing--and I’m not sure that something is Ben Curtis.

Title: Born Under Saturn
Review: For a band consisting of four members, Born Under Saturn is both remarkably adventurous and eclectic.

Title: Weezer (Black Album)
Review: Of course, The Black Album is not completely void of redeeming qualities, and there will likely be many listeners who are pleased with what they hear at times. Those listeners, however, may not be those who fell in love with the version of Weezer that existed in the middle of the ‘90s. Instead, the listeners within that sector may feel something comparable to watching a good friend make a bad decision.

Title: On the Impossible Past
Review: On the Impossible Past is an impeccably crafted melodic hardcore record by a group ready for it's close-up.

Title: O Shudder
Review: "Drips" hovers between Hot Chip and late-period XTC, while the meticulous detail of "Babymaking" and "Don't Sit Back (Frankie Said)" recall lost studio gems like Rosie Vela's Walter Beck-helmed Zazu. [Mar 2015, p.75]

Title: Born to Sing: No Plan B
Review: His 35th solo studio album is his jazziest: the warm brass and catchy, sweet melodies recall 1970's Moondance. But the music's velvet glove delivers some of his hardest-hitting lyrics.

Title: Ty Segall
Review: This stripped-back, honest approach exposes the inconsistencies and vulnerabilities of the man, while also bringing to the exterior the charisma and charm of a laissez-faire psych icon.

Title: American Gangster
Review: When the natural flow of Nas' rap elevates 'Success' to one of American Gangster's best songs, you kind of wish Nas could have just had the same idea and done the album himself. It shadows the finale of the album, even the tight, appropriately grand title-track that finds Jay-Z at his breeziest.

Title: Marissa Nadler
Review: For this fifth album, she changes tack again, gaining in clarity what she loses in originality. [Aug 2011, p.94]

Title: Universalists
Review: That’s the beauty of Universalists: there’s no use trying to pin it down. What’s more, doing so discredits its core thesis: music is music, plain and simple. Gat manages to capture the ecstasy of his live performance, while expanding his production and experimental practice to a global, and—dare I say—universal palette.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: It is powerful but blunt electronic pop; hooks always aimed to tear, melodrama at an uncomfortable volume. Still it often works.

Title: Drift
Review: Drift is a fabulous introduction to a burgeoning beat-making talent, one of the finest since edIT’s Crying Over Pros For No Reason, but Thing’s next record will likely be his One Word Extinguisher.

Title: Peaceful, the World Lays Me Down
Review: All in all, Peaceful, the World Lays Me Down, even with its mortality obsession, is mostly a statement of nothing, but at least it sounds good most of the time.

Title: Blossoms
Review: Blossom shows much promise for AI-augmented composition in the realm of electronic sound. It's unlikely that a software version of the Beatles will exist in our lifetime, but Purgas and Ginzburg have proven that the boundaries of technological possibility are completely mutable.

Title: No Pressure
Review: As well as weighty statements, there is a sense of closure here.

Title: The Anteroom
Review: The Anteroom sometimes creeps and lurches like an old car stuck in rush-hour traffic.

Title: Mosey
Review: This is ain't your average country record.

Title: Heavy Is the Head
Review: Stormzy came out swinging for his second album – it’s big, it’s broad and it is mostly brilliant.

Title: Things We Lost in the Fire
Review: Measuring out grief and resilience with a steady hand, these are the best songs of Low's quiet career. [Feb 2001, p.98]

Title: The Naked Truth
Review: Things go downhill as petty vindictiveness and insignificant beefs become the preferred themes. [Jan 2006, p.114]

Title: White Pepper
Review: White Pepper, their seventh studio album, could be Ween's most accessible release yet.

Title: Era Vulgaris
Review: It's not so much that the songs themselves are weak, just that many of the choices made in them are.

Title: Godfather
Review: He's a mover and shaker who has every right to look back in pride, in personal pride. Godfather is the reaffirmation of a status.

Title: Get Ready
Review: Even for fans not needing much convincing, Get Ready is a "grower," an album whose focus on sublime songcraft and introverted delivery reveals its secrets slowly and after many listens.

Title: Antisocialites
Review: Antisocialites doubles down on Alvvays’s strengths while also helping the band carve out a stronger identity within their well-established sound. By highlighting the band itself, Alvvays one-up their exciting debut.

Title: RTJ4
Review: This is the sound of RTJ staking their claim as one of the all-time great hip-hop duos. [Aug 2020, p.112]

Title: Amputechture
Review: Sequenced into one long, continuous piece of music, most of Amputechture's tracks arrive at impressive jazz-fusion pit stops that are all too brief.

Title: Cemetery Highrise Slum
Review: While Miller and co. occasionally go too big in their goth-y appropriation of ’90s grunge and alt tropes, the album features a fair share of subtle emotional moments to combat them.

Title: Prior to the Fire
Review: On its sophomore album, Priestess pulls no punches and delivers all blows in menacing fashion, borrowing heavily from the gods of metal's yesteryear.

Title: American Saturday Night
Review: From sterling ballads to punchy rockers, it's a classy set. But the initail post-Obama musings of Welcome To The Future already seem dated and, as ever, it's hard to know where the buyer will come from. [Aug 2010, p.124]

Title: First Ditch Effort
Review: Musically, the band is still in frenetic first gear, proudly sticking to its well-tested formula of power chords, metal-infused riffs, and biting humor. That sameness dulls some of First Ditch Effort’s luster, but it’s still a spirited late-career entry for the veteran punks.
Whether due to Gurnsey and Void’s developing rapport, or the honing of their collective sound, 25 25 packs the immense sort of punch that descriptions of their live shows recount.

Title: Loose Fur
Review: A pleasant if somewhat plain folk-rock record, less adventurous than either Wilco's or O'Rourke's own recent outings. [#227, p.68]

Title: Lovers
Review: There are a few moments that miss their mark--recent single “Someone” has a forced keychange that belies its soaring effortlessness--but for the most part, Lovers is a slick, listenable debut with a strong sense of direction and poise.

Title: Edge of Everything
Review: It's bleak and brutal, but it's never suffocating, and it encourages reaction and resistance. There's even some light shining through during "Post-Scarcity Anarchism," when a much brighter, more hopeful melody emerges through the frazzled synths and piercing noise flares. A few ambient interludes somewhat dull the album's impact, but relentless, abrasive pounders like "Futures Betrayed" and "Quantum Unfolding" provide the bulk of the program.

Title: The Runners Four
Review: Interesting, unique, weird and inviting.

Title: Two of Everything
Review: Two Of Everything is a sure-footed progression from 2009's self-titled debut, thanks to the warm co-production of Dan Auerbach (Black Keys) and the pair's willingness to push the sonic envelope into the outre zone, even embracing bagpipes. [Sept. 2011, p. 96]

Title: Good Mood Fool
Review: You can see how easy it would have been for Luke Temple to be complacent here; he had built up a solid reputation in the indie world and it would have been simple to release a toned-down Here Goes The Magic album. But instead we ended up with this album and I, for one, could not be any happier.

Title: Painted Ruins
Review: The superb Painted Ruins, an album that captures the fear, confusion, and wonderment of what it's like to be alive in 2017. [Jul - Aug 2017, p.56]

Title: Soft Money
Review: The results are mesmerizing. [#13, p.90]

Title: Errol
Review: Errol makes the listener work for its pleasures, but they're worth it. [Apr 2020, p.112]

Title: Whip It On
Review: Little more than comic book soundbites, wilting in the jagged, feverish shadow of their illustrious forefathers.

Title: The Dirty South
Review: Although this could get tired eventually, the Truckers haven't run out of stories yet, and their acute awareness of themselves and their forebears suggests they'll know when to say when.

Title: The Unseen In Between
Review: It's understated excellence at best, perhaps a little inoffensive at worse, and entirely a continuation of the aesthetic the Brooklyn-based guitarist has honed for the last two years. [Feb 2019, p.27]

Title: Within and Without
Review: The entirety of Within and Without is a mishmash of half-recalled thoughts sterilized in a cloud of sh*t production.

Title: Salutations
Review: Salutations is good, but it is apparent it could have been better. Rather than swing for the fences, Conor and crew settled for a base hit that didn’t move any runners on base.

Title: Dark Bird Is Home
Review: While these songs still have Matsson's trademark melancholy at heart, there is a new kind of gladness and hope to them too. [Jun 2015, p.112]

Title: Notes of Blue
Review: Farrar, with his ever-changing band, has been doing this decades, but it seems like by looking back further, he’s found a way to energize himself going forward.

Title: Silver
Review: Milking the most that they can out of their straight-up duo lineup, Yun and Cundiff show the limits of what they're working with, for better and worse. Since the format only allows for so much variety, many of the tracks on Silver tend to run together.

Title: so sad so sexy
Review: While this might not be the most pivotal ‘sad pop’ record from someone who arguably coined the genre, it can stand toe-to-toe with the best of them and few albums have ever been as appropriately named as so sad so sexy.

Title: Record
Review: For the most part Record strikes a nice balance. Thorn's voice has gotten deeper and huskier with age, but those developments work well to underscore what is newfound confidence, even brashness.

Title: Beaucoup Fish
Review: Furious techno stomps and mellow streamlined electronica clash head on with Karl Hyde's often nonsensical vocal style, pushing the group forward yet sticking close to their original blueprint.

Title: You Could Have It So Much Better
Review: Far more than a sequel. [3 Oct 2005]

Title: Re-Mit
Review: OK, it’s not pretty, but it’s pure Fall. And that’s what makes them a difficult band to feel disappointed with, even if the release is, like Re-Mit, something of a second-rate offering.

Title: Couples
Review: Couples is simply a successful attempt to sound both different and better.

Title: James Blake
Review: The highlights here are subtle, but many.

Title: Imperial Blaze
Review: The album sags toward the middle, but when he sticks to his strengths, Paul is arguably the ablest pop ambassador Jamaican music has ever had who isn't surnamed Marley.

Title: Mary's Voice
Review: While Koster's childlike enthusiasm, meandering, impressionistic lyrics, and Anglophile steampunk posturing may be the very definition of twee (or tweed, in this sense), like Willy Wonka, it's hard not to admire his Luddite tenacity, especially in an age that prefers instant gratification to pure imagination.

Title: Paramore
Review: [Guitarist Taylor] York is Ms. Williams’s collaborator throughout most of Paramore, and they have pushed the band beyond pop-punk without abandoning momentum or the big, catchy chorus.

Title: The Drawing Board
Review: When Art Department stick with their signature sound, even though it might not be exactly unique--it's easy enough to trace a lineage through seminal Chicago jack tracks, early-'90s disco house and the sleeker end of electro-clash to contemporary peers like Soul Clap and Benoit & Sergio--the results are nothing short of mesmerizing.

Title: Body Faucet
Review: The ideas are all there, they just don't fit together properly yet. [Sep 2012, p.110]

Title: The Sound of Music
Review: Essentially, the album is business as usual for Laibach, which means that if you're in on their grand scheme, it's another exquisitely orchestrated laugh riot.

Title: Till Midnight
Review: Ragan's insightful writing lends itself to both anthems and love songs, revealing the singer/songwriter's maturity and savvy. He just needs to trust his vision more.

Title: Cerulean Salt
Review: It's confessional solipsism, lacking the musical compulsion to make one care.

Title: Lifetime of Love
Review: Whilst certainly disjointed and disorientating in its execution, this first full Moon Diagrams showcase is an oddly gripping sonic ride that suggests that there is plenty of artistic life beyond the drum stool for Moses Archuleta.

Title: Amadjar
Review: Tinariwen's music has a beating heart to it and a genius for connecting the group's specific experiences to a broader audience. No one puts the soul of the Sahara into music so intimately and ingeniously as Tinariwen, and Amadjar is a particularly well-polished jewel.

Title: The Exodus Suite
Review: Typical of many timeless albums, the whole of The Exodus Suite is greater than its impressive parts. Carve 50 minutes out of your life and spend time reveling in its thought provoking, often mesmerizing and riveting pleasures.

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Now we get Cuomo name-dropping Eddie Rabbit, Joan Baez and "a Cat named Stevens," which makes Weezer sounds like a retread of "Built To Spill," who did the recycled-classic-rock-cliché thing back in 1999. Did it better, too.

Title: From Here To Now To You
Review: Johnson is back on sunnier acoustic ground here, exploring interesting open tunings on some of the crispest songs he's ever written.

Title: Love is Dead
Review: The handful of songs produced by the band themselves—“My Enemy,” the brooding new wave track “God's Plan,” and the gentle ballad “Really Gone”—stand out in their deviation from the glossy, monolithic tracks helmed by producer Greg Kurstin.

Title: thecontrollersphere
Review: "Holiday Call" and "Black Lion Massacre" aren't among Barnes' best songs, but they are bold and show that he's an artist who is eager to challenge himself rather than stick to what has become a very successful formula.

Title: Detroit House Guests
Review: Adam Lee Miller and Nicola Kuperus have used a familiar creative trope--the artist in residence... Fittingly, Nitzer Ebb's Douglas J. McCarthy, whose own dislocated, radical electronica feels like an overt influence. [Apr 2017, p.97]

Title: Follow Me Home
Review: Reflecting the Top Dawg Ent. rapper's lyrics and tone, the album is unapologetic and rugged, but sounds anything but rough.

Title: I Am Easy to Find
Review: At 68 minutes long and 16 tracks, its length becomes an issue during a third quarter which drifts. But as an exercise in breaking with consistency, I Am Easy To Find shows The National remain open to new possibilities after all.

Title: A Small Turn of Human Kindness
Review: This quartet have honed thier lumbering heaviness into something both glorious and at times funny. [Aug 2010, p.82]

Title: Hysterical
Review: After a fair-to-middling second album they took a self-imposed break before returning with this excellent effort. [Oct 2011, p.83]

Title: Push and Shove
Review: The very elements that made No Doubt popular in the first place have disappeared.

Title: Donuts
Review: Years from now these "Donuts" will still be just as fresh as the day they first hit the store.

Title: Resolution
Review: The record is their most musically ambitious to date, while still maintaining the unrelenting, thrash-influenced Southern heavy metal they do best.

Title: Oddments of the Gamble
Review: The only weakness of oddments is the occasional breaks in the overall flow, moments where tracks fade away too soon or stretch on too long, or where a massive peak is dropped off immediately into a spacy low. But these breaks are infrequent, only jarring because of the comforting haze the record consistently meets.

Title: The E.N.D.
Review: The E.N.D. (Energy Never Dies) is a mess of pop/dance/rap crossover.

Title: Something Like a War
Review: That’s the fundamental issue of Something Like A War: Kindness, in their efforts to cultivate and redistribute softness as a universal tenet, forgot the key rule of living honestly—your vulnerabilities must be specific enough to connect with.

Title: Cole World: The Sideline Story
Review: Cole World: The Sideline Story is a well-rounded effort, and deeper than most.

Title: The Silver Gymnasium
Review: It’s one of the most honest albums I’ve heard, but even better, it’s told with expertise.

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: None of the songs on "Yours to Keep" lack a naggingly memorable chorus; none is remotely inaccessible; and none is less than excellently crafted.

Title: Tassili
Review: Perhaps most impressive is that in what is arguably the band's most traditional record to date, Tinariwen manages to loop in highly recognizable people and sounds without any effort.

Title: Intriguer
Review: Their second collection since coming back together out of solace following that loss makes it clear that to group leader Neil Finn, there's still musical business to finish for this band.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: There is a sweet strand of diversity, subtle or otherwise, permeating the record and points towards the coming together of comfort and talent.

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: While this release is ruminative in nature, the temperament isn’t far removed from the classic record with which this release shares a striking visual resemblance.

Title: Jessica Pratt
Review: Sometimes Pratt’s nervousness about being looped into a scene extends to her album’s production. Some songs are cloaked in hissing tape, and her lyrics can be difficult to make out.

Title: Begin Again
Review: Every track seems to hint at a grander version than what was delivered, but the loose ends and modest scale are alluring, since they appear to offer an insight into how this fiercely imaginative, quietly fearless singer/songwriter challenges herself.

Title: Son of Evil Reindeer
Review: The focus remains upon Lightbody's gauche romantic vignettes; nirvana for those who believe the world could usefully sustain a second Lou Barlow, but over an album's duration akin to persistent immersion in lukewarm herbal tea. [Sep 2002, p.104]

Title: The Last Ship
Review: Unfortunately, the set doesn’t quite command as a fully realized piece.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: Darnielle [is] a songwriter still worth paying attention to.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: Ultraviolence prioritizes mood over innovation, classicism over experimentalism, and is better for it.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: Oberst always projects a spiritual generosity unknown to most footloose troubadours who can’t commit.

Title: Graveyard Whistling
Review: Graveyard might actually be the most country Old 97’s record in years, while maintaining the sticky sweet melodies the band has always nailed.

Title: Rush to Relax
Review: In the end, the unexpectedly loose, protean feel of Rush to Relax makes for a wholly satisfying step forward from one of Australia's finest bands of the first decade of the 2000s.

Title: Believe You Me
Review: The musicians' sensibilities combine to create a bliss pop which doesn't simply evoke the spirit of summer, but allow it to bleed into every chord. [Oct 2012, p.64]

Title: Keel Her
Review: It may not be entirely successful, but it could well be looked back on as the acorn from which a bigger tree grew.

Title: Odd Blood
Review: While it’s still the arrangements that will continue to impress, the words and overall sonic ability speaks paramount to what Yeasayer is capable of.

Title: Los Angeles Police Department
Review: Pollie's sulky tenor is perfectly suited to these tales of heartache and lost affection, with muted backing tracks that intensify the tear-soaked scenarios that bring him solace. [No. 142, p.57]

Title: Human Performance
Review: So while this fifth album is tighter and cleaner, it’s far from chart-ready. Instead it wears its pre-punk to post-punk influences proudly.

Title: Exai
Review: As always, it's a lot to take in; even after a dozen listens, the album's too oblique to really register in the memory. That slipperiness does nothing to diminish the moments when things really stick, though.

Title: Kinky
Review: This is international music, not intended merely for Kinky's native Mexico. Actually, it's more intended for trendy music cultures such as those of Europe and the U.S. -- a sort of Spanish update for the early 2000s of the late-'90s electronica/rock sound associated with groups like Prodigy and Primal Scream.

Title: The Cloud Making Machine
Review: It doesn’t always work, and the record has a scattered second half that undercuts the sonic unity of the first, but the best moments here are as starkly affecting as any of Garnier’s past work.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Room on Fire is a passionate, 32-minute burning effigy of the seemingly insurmountable expectations fans and critics had for the record.

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: Unless you have a natural predisposition towards the enjoyment of self-consciously nerdy vocals and jangling harmonic songs taking a 'sideways looks' at life, Sky Full Of Holes will leave you completely unmoved.

Title: Little Sparrow
Review: Little Sparrow contains some of the most beautiful and affecting music Parton has ever made...

Title: The Bloom and the Blight
Review: It's one of those albums you could listen to again and again.

Title: No Blues
Review: No Blues is their best album yet. [Dec 2013, p.109]

Title: Ruins
Review: First Aid Kit’s latest may be a slightly more conservative gesture than their last record, but it synthesizes their many musical strains more fully than ever before.

Title: Love Is Here
Review: Starsailor are the U.K. equivalent of the Goo Goo Dolls.... You may well like Love Is Here, but it could take a while before you admit it to yourself.

Title: Some People Have Real Problems
Review: It’s good-girl soul for the Starbucks set.

Title: Country Sleep
Review: The 23-year-old Nashville resident's keening voice can drag you in with either the acoustic intimacy of 22, which resembles the stark folk of Father John Misty, or the electrified rock of Ramona. [Mar 2013, p.95]

Title: Walk Between Worlds
Review: Sonically never less than knowingly enormous, but concise at eight tracks, Walk Between Worlds is sure and strong. [Mar 2018, p.91]

Title: The Beast In Its Tracks
Review: There is plenty to enjoy here, though many of his long-time fans will be hoping for a return to the bigger picture next time out.

Title: Mastermind
Review: When push comes to shove, there are only about three songs here that merit that kind of mindshare--and none of those come close to his best singles. By his standards, Mastermind is technically a good album, but neither timely nor memorable.

Title: The Capsule
Review: They're far from failed experiments, but they do reinforce the notion that Necro Deathmort are much better at making atonal soundscapes. [Jul 2016, p.112]

Title: Beyond the Sun
Review: He's delivered a sincerely meant yet curiously staid and pedestrian tribute.

Title: On Reflection
Review: Overall, this is an album with fleeting moments of joy, but these are not sustained.

Title: Nine
Review: A spiritual follow up to 2003’s ‘Untitled’, ‘Nine’ sees the trio as confident adventurers. Dealing with the ideas of despair, loneliness and longing, the record doesn’t shy away from the shadows but you’re never far from a dash of hope.

Title: Drone Logic
Review: It sits together as a cohesive body of work rather than a fragmented collection of club moments.

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: It's the amped-up riff in the middle of Offspring Are Blank that best sums up their playful approach. They often flex their muscles without feeling the need to land a killer blow. [Aug 2012, p.97]

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: There's a potent '80s smoke machine-ambiance wafting through the plush, slow-fizz synths and padded percussion that fill their debut full-length. [Oct 2013, p.100]

Title: Savages
Review: Savages is a feisty record that returns to the familiar blend of hardcore, thrash and groove metal.

Title: Real Animal
Review: Sweeping violins and take-no-prisoners guitars co-exist in producer Tony Visconti's gorgeous glam frame for Escovedo's visionary sound.

Title: From the Double Gone Chapel
Review: Shards of Joy Division guitar crisscross punk-funk basslines and mournful electro shivers.

Title: Soft Hair
Review: But more than anything else, Soft Hair is about intimacy, creativity and a zest for life--two singular musicians liberated by collaboration.

Title: To Believe
Review: Swinscoe has a knack for both producing lush orchestral movements and picking worthy collaborators. On To Believe, they are unfortunately not more than the sum of their parts.

Title: LP4
Review: It is instrumental rock music that is experimental, emotional, colorful, and engaging, while skillfully blurring many musical boundaries.

Title: Hollywood's Bleeding
Review: It will be a surprise to learn which tracks aren’t singles yet; there’s at least five more hits to be spawned from this thing, and we’ll never hear the end of it.

Title: Warm Heart of Africa
Review: It’s all a part of the open exchange in the Afropop community that gives The Very Best their lush and addictive sound.

Title: Go Forth
Review: At this point they have worked through their formative stage, and prove themselves capable of delivering a solid album with diverse songwriting and a consistent style. And even if that style sounds derivative and summons the inevitable Dischord comparisons, it's impressive nonetheless.

Title: The Heist
Review: Macklemore's a mix of all of the above with some distinctive qualities, and with Lewis putting that kaleidoscope style underneath, The Heist winds up a rich combination of fresh and familiar.

Title: Final Straw
Review: A remarkable return. [Oct 2003, p.130]

Title: Black Noise
Review: At 70 minutes, Black Noise is a big, dense listen but also the kind of album that rewards investment.

Title: Love Will Prevail
Review: As ever, Ragon's lyrics are highly evocative if not outright provocative.

Title: Visions
Review: It's a bummer that Visions ended up as a fever dream of a record: unnecessarily oblique, listlessly long (48 minutes!), and painfully shapeless.

Title: Iron Flag
Review: The Clan's lyricists remain as aggressively word-drunk as ever, balancing the music's pop conciseness with oblique rhymes that compel repeated listening. [Feb/Mar 2002, p.116]

Title: Relaxer
Review: At times their idea-heavy songs can feel weighed down by cleverness (the Primus-y "Deadcrush"). But Alt-J can create a dark beauty that's like moonlight on an English moor.

Title: Collapse EP
Review: While James is here less austere than on Cheetah EP and less eccentric than on landmark release Richard D. James Album, Collapse nevertheless proves to be a serviceable Aphex Twin release at this point in his career. His knack for finding interesting textures and layers hasn’t been compromised nor has his willingness to build off of previous styles in his oeuvre.

Title: Ferndorf
Review: It’s his intensity of focus coupled with an impressive range of motion that gives this album its real strength and maturity.

Title: The Centre Cannot Hold
Review: The Centre Cannot Hold displays a different facade of the artist than the ones presented in Aurora and By the Throat, yet at the same time, it glimmers with a similar energy and purpose. By projecting the state of reality into his music, Frost can transcend it and produce a work of art as a result.

Title: Vide Noir
Review: Even when the concept stumbles, parts of Vide Noir are pretty enjoyable listening anyway, like the flecks of psychedelic guitar across the title track and the filigree detail and sensual current of “Moonbeam.”

Title: Sport
Review: Throughout, Sport is crude, queasy, sometimes shockingly ugly, and often quite funny, in a madcap, slightly threatening way. It thrills and it mystifies in equal measure.
It's an enthralling listen, proving once and for all that they deserve the wide success of fellow travelers like Radiohead and Sonic Youth.

Title: Surprise
Review: This surprise is an entirely pleasant one. [27 May 2006, p.33]

Title: Ultimate Care II
Review: At once atmospheric, industrial and experimental, Ultimate Care II is kind of like Lou Reed’s Metal Machine Music had the old geezer from Freeport, N.Y. crafted it out of love instead of vitriol.

Title: All That You Can't Leave Behind
Review: Subtle breakbeat drumming and glistening guitar be damned, Bono will ruin a song. And so the story goes for the entire album-- one of the band's finest, if not for the tweeting and hooting of The Fly and his grating lyrics.

Title: The Night Creeper
Review: While the artwork borders on the iconic and the concept is very much in sitting with the band’s oeuvre, musically, The Night Creeper is a sub-standard addition to the canon of one of the most promising bands in modern rock.
Plenty of nightmare visions of Skid Row LA, but really no fun at all. [Jan 2013, p.93]

Title: How Animals Move
Review: It's obvious that most of the songs have been meticulously worked over, and as a listener you're thankful for it, but as an album it feels like the paint has hit the canvas at random.

Title: The King of Whys
Review: Songs rarely adhere to one form, instead taking bits and pieces of Kinsella’s career and making them all sound fresh. It’s the kind of record that will appease Owen fans, but it’s lush enough--and inspired enough--to suggest that Owen is perhaps the best it’s ever been.

Title: Synesthesia
Review: Hands play the instruments that induce you to dance and hear those sounds that make you want to feel it all.

Title: No Kings
Review: Overall, this is a pretty interesting effort that is very genre-bending in its approach.

Title: After Robots
Review: Blk Jks's own voicee is utterly compelling. [Oct 2009, p.107]

Title: forevher
Review: The only real issue that Shura faces on forevher is that the record can be too much of a good thing. The psychedelic grooves that back the project can almost be suffocating, not allowing melodies or choruses to flourish on tracks that feel like a huge hook could bring them to perfection.

Title: Sunny Border Blue
Review: Astormy soundtrack to one woman's inner life that swings from acoustic guitars to explosions of layered vocals, electric guitars and the occasional lonely horn or piano.

Title: Mug Museum
Review: Predictably, then, it's all too easy to 'find' (read: go searching for subconsciously or otherwise) shifts in the Welsh singer-songwriter's sound on this follow-up.

Title: Slash
Review: Slash goes through all the proper motions (distorted guitars, squint-eyed staring-into-the-distance guitar solos, loads of star power), but the end product doesn't satisfy me on a visceral level, and closer examination only magnifies the fact Slash can't establish instant chemistry with just any name he pulls out of his address book.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: Most of the tracks are about as blank and sterile as an airport terminal.

Title: Volume 3
Review: Prepare for more cute, wistful, sad-but-sunny retro-pop songs that'll hit a lot of people's sweet spots, and make other people want to punch a LOLcat in the face. [10 May 2013, p.67]

Title: Business Casual
Review: Their one great idea grows tiresome over an album's length. [Oct 2010, p.88]

Title: Drowners
Review: Drowners prove themselves competent in making a tight indie rock album full of enjoyable melodies, but their strict adherence to formula and professionalism is undermining and can be dull.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: "Black Balloons" is built on a riff exactly like Bon Iver's "Perth" sped up, and hearing the grating lyrical wail of "Columbia" and you're left wondering if so much time away was a result of writer's block. [Feb 2013, p.90]

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: Even without his electric axe (and accompanying pedal board and crater of Marshall stacks) Mascis is still a virtuso.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: Dave Longstreth conjures up something resembling a clear picture from all the record’s wildly disparate elements, and ‘Dirty Projectors’ serves to unify his most experimental moments with the door-opening impact of ‘Bitte Orca’.

Title: May You Be Held
Review: For those not moved by this more unhinged side of the band, MYBH may prove disappointing. ... Still, MYBH makes the case that the field recording that plays out album closer "Laughter and Silence" is now as integral a part of the Sumac sound as any other. If you're willing to consider a musical choice like that to be just as "heavy" as a lurching dirge or a colossal chug, then May You Be Held will prove a rewarding and expansive listen.

Title: Mechanics of Dominion
Review: Minimalistic on its outlook and yet with a rich instrumentation, traditional on both its inclusion of classical and folk influences, and still forward-thinking and experimental. It is an act that has been standing between these worlds, bridging them together better than ever in their most potent work yet.

Title: 100 Lovers
Review: Although DeVotchKa's fifth album finds the group less interested in wildly crossing borders, it's still the sound of a seasoned traveler-just one who's finally found a comfortable resting place.

Title: Blood Pressures
Review: It's an album that deserves the limelight, regardless of how it got there.

Title: Rock Steady
Review: About half of 'Rock Steady' is just great, a career salvage job to compare with Madonna 's 'Ray Of Light'.

Title: Something Else
Review: There are mixed results as some tracks on Something Else feel like the band are going through the motions, while others flow with more energy.

Title: Public Warning
Review: Her subject matter is goofier, her flow is dumbed down and her beats are staler.

Title: Blues Funeral
Review: Blues Funeral generally succeeds because Lanegan knows exactly what his audience wants and is willing to play to his strengths.

Title: Intimacy
Review: They are so solid and so confident that it seems inevitable that they will get many chances to slowly drift into more daring lands. But without more risk, they may be destined to make albums like Intimacy--accomplished and intriguing, but not life changing, not classic. [Year End 2008]

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: Wakin On A Pretty Daze comes into focus with context, though, as does any accomplished record.

Review: The result is somewhere between the Pet Shop Boys' meticulous dance pop and the driving keyboard rock of acts like Zero Zero.

Title: Overpowered
Review: Not once does Overpowered really drag its feet, but it never truly impacts with the might one could possibly expect from an artist with such a fine pedigree.

Title: forevher
Review: Each of its 11 songs luxuriating in an unhurried, pillow-soft airiness that draws you in, as opposed to giving up secrets too willingly. Free of expectation, Shura's found her own pace. [Oct 2019, p.108]

Title: Here Lies Love
Review: The roster's promising and the concept is offbeat enough to be brilliant. The execution? It could have been a lot more inspired. Unless you come to the record already a die-hard fan of each and every one of the guest vocalists, you're going to find yourself skipping around in search of highlights.

Title: Sempiternal
Review: Sempiternal sounds like a record that wants the world--that's all of it, not just the bits where longhairs dwell--which is refreshing for a metal record in 2013. [30 Mar 2013, p.52]

Title: Crazy Itch Radio
Review: Like a nervous listener station-surfing for the next big fix, Crazy Itch Radio is the end result, the space where successive sounds subconsciously collapse upon each other.

Title: Warning
Review: Green Day's melodies are as delicious as ever, and the band continues to integrate acoustic guitar into its sound without getting all granola on us. But as a songwriter, Armstrong's neither here nor there, unable to fully abandon his goofball roots but not stretching far enough to score the breakaway great album he's always seemed capable of writing.

Title: I Grow Tired But Dare Not Fall Asleep
Review: His latest offering is powered by some lovely, liquid bass playing that offers a silvery thread through the textured mélange of disjointed electronic noises, splintered guitars and ghostly traces of strings. It is certainly not for everyone. But Ejimiwe’s relentlessly downbeat delivery may have finally found its moment.

Title: Light
Review: The biggest problem with his reggae is simpler: He's unequivocally terrible at it. Not only do we get fake patois, but also raging electric guitars and cluttered hip-hop production.

Title: To Realize
Review: There is a certain rhythm that begins to form with constantly being pulled along and feeling as though this will be the moment everything crescendos. Prepare yourself To Realize presents a Sisyphus-esque journey that can be exhausting.

Title: California Nights
Review: Like its predecessor, it’s a little too long, but California Nights reaffirms the things that Crazy for You had me believing and The Only Place had me doubting; that Cosentino is a fine songwriter with a keen ear for melody, that Bruno’s guitar work is the perfect foil for her.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: There’s no pure pop moments like Losing You and she may never generate the same amount of press inches as her elder sister does on a regular basis, but this third album is an endlessly compelling one.

Title: The Incessant
Review: The Incessant has a wealth of great ideas baked into the sediment of a wholly unremarkable collection of songs but boasts enough personality to still be worth giving the benefit of your doubt.

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: Unfortunately, it seems the group is more interested in refining, rather than re-defining, their craft, whose torpid mechanics bear no mystery, no guts behind all that glamour.

Title: The Seduction of Kansas
Review: The follow-up amplifies the hooks, widens the scope, deepens the wordplay.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: Lost In The Dream is calmer and more confident than previous efforts, songs stretching out beyond the six-minute mark if the feeling is right. [Apr 2014, p.83]

Title: Hearts
Review: Hearts is not an album of change, but one that revels in the joy of what you know.

Title: Show Your Bones
Review: It's only when they change pace on "Cheated Hearts" and the equally poignant "Dudley"... that Bones makes its mark as a worthy successor to Fever. [Apr 2006, p.98]

Title: La Radiolina
Review: The jumble of languages and sounds gives La Radiolina the feel of a noisy, colorful street bazaar where there's chaotic beauty on the surface and a certain poetic logic that runs underneath.

Title: To Believe
Review: To Believe doesn't rush along the cutting edge, but after 12 years absent, it hits this particular spot in time and space: sombre, tense, watchful, looking for calm, but gathering storms. [Apr 2019, p.92]

Title: Drone Logic
Review: The times have changed enough in the music world that Drone Logic won't get the same recognition and acclaim that albums by Underworld or the Chemical Brothers (or even Plastikman or Orbital) received 20 years previously, but it's every bit as good and expansively musical as anything from that era.

Title: Reunion Tour
Review: Sampson's penmanship here is the most minute and observant among a recent batch of great songwriting

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: Their third album in as many years, JJ continue to gather a pace and 'No.3' will surely propel them further into hearts and minds.

Title: Quicken the Heart
Review: There’s an unshakeable feeling that they’re going through the motions a bit too frequently and that this represents a step backwards for a once fresh and exciting band. Unfortunately, it seems the curse of the third album may have struck again.

Title: Injury Reserve
Review: Injury Reserve is as cohesive a hip-hop album as one can hope. This is thanks, in large part, to Parker’s ever-so-versatile production, though also, I think, Groggs’ and, in particular, Ritchie’s growing scepticism with modern hip-hop culture, and a heightened awareness of its pretensions.

Title: Dealer
Review: There are so many moments of catharsis despite a few songs feeling repetitive or filler. It's bold, jammed with raw emotion and to top that, brutally honest.

Title: Guilt Mirrors
Review: Despite the album's daunting length, Harte rewards listeners with some of his most affecting and expressive music yet.

Title: Half of Where You Live
Review: It's unfortunate for Half Of Where You Live to be released so close to something so perfect [Trust EP], but the change in direction leaves a probably ill-deserved lingering sense of sadness. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.99]

Title: Eight And A Half
Review: The result, while a bit surprising, is entirely satisfying.

Artist: Working for a Nuclear Free City
Title: Jojo Burger Tempest
Review: In all, it's a magnificent, ear-catching jumble. [Fall 2010, p. 64]

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: For an outfit that's never denied its plastic-coated glamour, Garbage exits Not Your Kind Of People remarkably well-preserved.

Title: Slideling
Review: Slideling eschews all of McCulloch's recognizable quirks and endearing pretensions, replacing them with slick generic “mature” songs and arrangements that make Coldplay sound adventurous.

Title: 99Â¢
Review: It’s initially fun to play spot-the-references, but in the best moments the sounds are harder to pin down.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: On the surface, Beirut has nothing in common with classic rock, except that Condon also knows that a memorable tune can bring disparate cultures together as persuasively as any fancy arrangement.

Title: Living With The Living
Review: An impassioned, angry and devastating document.

Title: Saturdays = Youth
Review: Anthony Gonzalez nurtures nostalgia but isn't enslaved by it, and Saturdays=Youth teems with equal parts ache and pomp as a result.

Title: Untilted
Review: As mechanised as their rhythmic focus can be, there is flesh, bone, and brain beneath the near industrial barrage of beats.

Title: White Pepper
Review: Ween is so satisfying because they're making something that's at once smarter and grosser than the competition.
They might be old, they might be poorly and they might be running scared from their wives, but on 13 Black Sabbath roll back the years and sound young again--and blacker than ever. [Jul 2013, p.102]

Title: Autumn
Review: By all intents and purposes, Autumn is the definition of true, unadulterated bluegrass with only a few modern amenities tossed in for good measure.

Title: Wildflower
Review: The Avalanches bag production, they roller-coaster; got to be jokers, they just do what they please. [No. 134, p.51]

Title: Between the Times and the Tides
Review: If nothing else, this album is a guitar fetishist's dream, and sounds like it was a joy to make, too.

Title: Both Ways Open Jaws
Review: Both Ways Open Jaws is an album that is best when taken as a whole and wholly intriguing trip into that most treacherous and elusive of terrains: the happy marriage of eccentricity and pop song craft.

Title: Breakthrough
Review: It's about as weird and wonderful as you'd expect from a guy who looks like he's been living on a commune for the past ten years.

Title: Molina & Johnson
Review: Molina & Johnson's treasures are there, as long as you listen closely. [Jan 2010, p.95]

Title: FIBS
Review: She’s the type of restless innovator that doesn’t stick with the same style for too long, and FIBS is a joyful, energetic follow-up to her debut. [Nov 2019, p.56]

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: Without a steady beat to ground it, Orton's music tends to float into the ether. And unfortunately in the case of Sugaring Season, this means many of the album's best, moving moments fade into the background.

Title: Lighght
Review: While Lighght has its highlights, there is simply too much questionable fluff surrounding the good ideas.

Title: Bromst
Review: This muscular follow-up ratchets up the internal tension until his exuberant toy-town techno becomes a shot of pure musical adrenalin.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: Through thick and thin, Tribe embodies the fully fleshed out idea of the Hip Hop their impassioned audience clamors for: work that’s soulful, thought provoking, and gripping enough to transport minds away from strife to another world sonically.

Title: Savage Hills Ballroom
Review: The vocals make Savage Hills Ballroom an acquired taste, but those who enjoy a bitter pill will swallow it whole. [Oct 2015, p.117]

Title: Ultra
Review: With Ultra, Zomby might have finally removed any remaining warmth from his sound: the album is cold to the point of inaccessibility.

Title: For Ever
Review: This music still tends to slip into the background, affable but never striking.

Title: Rebirth
Review: Specifically though, Rebirth absolutely boasts some of the best tunes that Cliff's recorded since his string of successes surrounding the international releases of The Harder They Come.

Title: The Age of Anxiety
Review: Pixx has created a debut record that shows her to be a fascinating prospect, and though significant turmoil informed the record, the pay-off is equally as great.

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: The music is unlike anything Cloud Nothings has done before, and that's a good thing.

Title: Always Ascending
Review: The result is quiet success. [Mar 2018, p.25]

Title: Rot
Review: If maturity is on the Bad Boys’ lyrical agenda on the sardonically titled Rot, letting up the pace is not.

Title: FRKWYS Vol. 9: ICON GIVE THANK

Title: Human Hearts
Review: Maritime's musical development has become a compelling narrative of its own, each subsequent record in many ways both improving upon and elucidating the last.
