Title: Chromatica
Review: Infectious, exciting and even a little hedonistic during some of the most confusing of modern times, now’s never been a better time to get lost in this new destination.

Title: Lucky Old Sun
Review: Chesney's sincerity is never in question, but his songs are uniformly garden-variety and obvious no matter how they are dressed.

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: Blessed with great songs, wonderful arrangements and vocal performances that seriously raise the bar in our expectations of what she's capable of, it is a record that shows real artistic growth in every area and is destined to become a classic that rivals Trailer Park and Central Reservation.

Title: Ignore the Ignorant
Review: While Ignore the Ignorant isn't perfect--Gary and Ryan Jarman's guileless vocals don't always jell with their slick surroundings--it is unquestionably some of the Cribs' most accomplished and diverse music.

Title: May The Lord Watch
Review: Easily one of the best records released in 2019, superlatives only go so far.  ... “May the Lord Watch” only solidifies Little Brother’s place in the pantheon of great rap duos.

Title: Monkeytown
Review: The album may be scattershot, but perhaps that doesn't matter so much when it's delivered out the barrel of a 12-gauge.

Title: The Rite of Spring
Review: The Rite should elicit gasps, not cock eyebrows—the latter of which is the most extreme reaction the Bad Plus manage to provoke.

Title: Ropewalk
Review: The result is an album teeming with hooks and melodies butting up against countermelodies, and a crisp, vibrant pop production.

Title: Security Screenings
Review: The great moments aren't enough to carry a convincing musical thread throughout the record. [#12, p.92]

Title: Tarot Sport
Review: Tarot Sport goes far beyond it's sonically daunting reaches and succeeds at being a deeply emotional experience.

Title: Half The Perfect World
Review: Peyroux is a wonderful singer and this collection of songs is her best yet.

Title: I'm Gay (I'm Happy)
Review: I'm Gay (I'm Happy) isn't sly and intertextual, it's an alternate universe beholden only to its own laws.

Title: Popular Songs
Review: You still get an album's worth of pristine, beautifully constructed songs that enhance Yo La Tengo's literate reputation.

Title: Murray Street
Review: Murray Street achieves that rare thing for any band - real consistency.

Title: Corsicana Lemonade
Review: True, not every album needs to make a statement; sometimes it’s just nice to have music to listen to with your eyes closed and your brain off. But they can do better.

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: It is Mastodon's ability to blend such grandstanding flourishes with a powerful sense of songcraft that suggests Crack The Skye might be some "Master Of Puppets" breakthrough for the Atlanta quartet. [May 2009, p.98]

Title: Remedy
Review: One of the best Americana records of the year.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: This is a dull album, revealing how over the space of three records, Mr. Albarn and Mr. Hewlett have moved from wacky conceptualists to self-satisfied dilettantes.

Title: Widow City
Review: Widow City is endlessly enjoyable, yielding new detail every time you slip through its song mazes. [Oct 2007, p.59]

Title: Sun Giant
Review: Fleet Foxes' full-length debut showcases a gift for folk-adjacent mini-epics that evolve in unexpected directions yet never lose their organic center. [Summer 2008, p.102]

Title: Also Sprach Zarathustra
Review: Overall, for a band that will soon enter its fourth decade of activity, Laibach sound impressively fresh and relevant. I am sure Also Sprach Zarathustra will raise many eyebrows, but also receive critical acclaim for its effective minimalist approach.

Title: Fuzz
Review: On this album, the influences are acknowledged and respected while still managing to sound original.

Title: DSU
Review: The more you listen, the more obvious it is that Alex G is a bright new talent in his own right.

Title: Haunted
Review: Unfortunately, Haunted reverberates with tired samples, rehashed echo effects and beats so plodding they could stop a metronome.

Title: The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book
Review: The most pleasingly direct yet musically adventurous hip-hop long-player you're likely to hear all year.

Title: Freedom
Review: Even with the subtle narrative running through the record, McMahon’s songs gain resonance less from their lyrics than from the forward pulse of his music.

Title: Ulfilas' Alphabet
Review: Sundara Karma have grown both personally and musically with this album and they have delivered a follow-up that is confident and utterly fearless. With more direction than their previous entry, Oscar Pollock’s weird and wonderful mind becomes the main spectacle and something to truly admire.

Title: The Diary of Alicia Keys
Review: See, there're a good few cracking singles on here, but there are also occasions when her wistful classicism leads her down blind alleys.

Review: These are effective dancefloor tracks that contain secret burdens o f menace or anxiety. [Dec 2012, p.68]

Review: Sounds like a step backward.

Review: The Jackson-White reboot casts the song as a swampy, country vamp, and while it isn't a horrible idea in theory, it does feel contrived and a bit of an unnecessary pander. Even with that misstep in mind, though, it's pretty tough not to root for Wanda Jackson and The Party Ain't Over.
There’s a good amount of experimentation here, and very few misfires.

Title: Widow City
Review: The libretto/story/concept of the album is of absolutely no interest to me, and it won't be to you either.

Title: Melody Road
Review: There are no duds on his first all-new album since 2008--just 12 stripped down soft-rock tracks, not too heavy on the strings, hitting consistently hard whether Diamond plays the winsome crooner ("Something Blue") or the bummed-out belter ("Alone at the Ball").

Title: The Getaway
Review: The Getaway is about as good as you can hope for from a band who will, without reservation, hang out in a car with late-night-TV cornball James Corden with lavalier mics forcibly affixed to their naked torsos (a bit of movie magic I’d be okay never having properly explained, frankly).

Title: Small Mercies
Review: Small Mercies may not be quite as immediate as The Age of Anxiety, but it's fizzing with energy and ideas that prove that Pixx the right person to sing about what's wrong with the world.

Title: Survival
Review: Survival is a listenable album, but the songcraft leaves something to be desired. It seems like Hardy needs to find a way to play to her strengths more consistently, and it will make her songs more effective.

Title: Goblin
Review: Those songs are products of an ambition that hasn't quite been tamed, but on the majority of Goblin, Tyler genuinely uses his creative freedom to create the fantastic.

Title: In Colour
Review: What we're left with is an uneven album that's rarely as profound or as meaningful as it tries to be.

Title: Lights Out
Review: The new face of lo-fi bedroom pop. [#39, p. 67]

Title: Two Thousand
Review: For all the improved minutiae, French Kicks simply can't shed the "boring" tag.

Review: The result is a (surprisingly) coherent and effective soul-and-funk-inspired album that doesn't try to overstep itself. [Summer 2009, p.62]

Title: w h o k i l l
Review: On the follow-up to her 2009 breakthrough album, "Bird-Brains," Merrill Garbus (aka Tune-Yards) again creates a clamorous assemblage of warm, overdriven kitchen-sink instrumentation, field hollering, layered stacks of processed vocals and a sonic smorgasbord culled from the world cafe-only more so.

Title: Love
Review: As long as McMahon is singing, Amen Dunes will never sound quite like anyone else--and on Love, he sings better and more ambitiously than ever.

Title: DOVE
Review: A little indie olive branch, Dove is as welcoming as it is welcome. [Jul 2018, p.108]

Title: El Pintor
Review: It’s a characteristic success and a massive delight to the fans that their return as a three-piece yields something as excellent as El Pintor.

Title: Steam Days
Review: Steam Days is a worthwhile--if slightly unseasonal--listen.

Title: Welcome to the Fishbowl
Review: [Welcome to the Fishbowl] is aimed squarely at the mainstream. These songs are genetically engineered to be both supremely catchy and intensely wet.

Title: Freedom
Review: Freedom is nothing more than an exercise in competent stadium rock.

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: Several Shades of Why gives us that softer, gentler J Mascis. But it's not kids' stuff -- these are lullabies for adults, offered up with a compassion that doesn't come easy.

Title: The Search
Review: The Search is a potent reminder of why Farrar was and is one of the watershed artists of the alt-country movement.

Title: Green and Gray
Review: Pile hold on to all the anxiety and fury of youth here, but present their dissonant squalls with a mature, metered patience that just adds to the slow-boiling listening experience.

Title: Trouble in Paradise

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver

Title: Follow Them True
Review: Urgent, uncompromising, intelligent--Stick In The Wheel are the bristles on the clean broom the UK folk scene badly needs.

Title: Hopes and Fears
Review: Basically, this is a fantastic band releasing twelve brilliant songs, and it's not only the best guitar album you'll ever hear with no guitars on it, it's one of the best this year generally.

Title: Junip
Review: These considered songs are slow to blossom but, like Junip, they're worth the wait. [May 2013, p.104]

Title: Between Two Shores
Review: It's a beautifully recorded and unmistakably classy outing that resonates deeply. [Feb 2018, p.95]

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: If Codes and Keys started at track 7 and kept the momentum going, it could be a great record. Instead it's a good one with great moments from a band that's clearly getting better with age.

Title: BarragÃ¡n
Review: At it's best, Barragan sounds like typically inventive musicians sleepily phoning it in. [No. 113, p.54]

Title: Admission
Review: There’s little to fault here in all honesty; it plays everything right and does so with a near flawless execution. Though one could argue it’s a little one-dimensional in terms of almost exclusively working with one style, as I said earlier, it nails the way these songs are presented.

Title: Ultimate Success Today
Review: Ultimate Success Today is convulsed by End Times thoughts of collapse and an American dream eating itself. [Aug 2020, p.111]

Title: Real Estate
Review: Despite the summery song titles and the beach balling associations that might follow these guys around, this music transcends the notion of seasons.

Title: The Besnard Lakes Are The Dark Horse
Review: Intriguing, unpredictable and far from ordinary. [Mar 2007, p.110]

Title: Love Letters
Review: Love Letters isn't the next move many expected from Metronomy following the astute pop of English Riviera, but it's a logical move and likely the best one possible for a band as imaginative, unconventional and talented as this one.

Title: In Ear Park
Review: Rosen and Nicolaus stride forth as songsmiths of a much more assured vintage, harp, piano, brass and chocolatey harmonies coming together in vividly orchestrated numbers. [Nov 2008, p.94]

Review: It's upbeat, fashionable and sounds great in the background when you're only half paying attention. Rather than seizing his moment in the spotlight, Parker sounds like he's just enjoying the journey.

Title: Alopecia
Review: For me personally their sound isn't progressive any more--it's regressive.

Title: Just Like The Fambly Cat

Title: The Valley

Review: It's All True runs the risk of feeling samey, but the album never gets sleepy, which should settle any debate over its function in the boudoir.

Title: Blonde
Review: For every low point there’s the unquestionable standouts.

Title: Sun & Shade
Review: At their most stripped-back, Woods have always been arresting – but here they realize some of their most beautiful work yet.

Title: Pythons
Review: Despite this dark lyrical shift, the group is still aping sunny surf-rock and collegiate-pop tropes.

Title: Romanian Names
Review: This is not Vanderslice’s most sonically adventurous record overall, but it does not need to be. His most powerful songs seem often, at first, the most unassuming.

Title: DOVE

Title: Horses and High Heels
Review: Horses And High Heels is another impressive entry in her catalogue, as genuine as anything she's done since the 1979 classic Broken English.

Title: Gold Medal

Title: Silver Age
Review: Mould is at the top of his game on Silver Age.

Title: Legends Never Die
Review: For fans of RA The Rugged Man, this is essential. For fans of early Eminem, this is essential. For everybody else, if you can ignore the swearing and appreciate the intricacies of RA's rhyming, you'll undoubtedly enjoy this because at least 80% of this record is straight up dope hip hop.

Title: The Waterfall II
Review: [“Spinning My Wheels”], and the album as a whole, fit these odd times and the excellent song kicks off an album which slots in well with the band’s varied past offerings as Waterfalls II drifts into and out of psych, folk, late-night disco and jam band spiked arena rock.

Title: Human After All
Review: Portraying the state of pop as a series of predictable formulae long since exhausted by corporate superstructure, Human After All more than lives up to its name, rendering a metaphor for failure on the grandest yet simultaneously most personal of terms.

Title: We Are Not Your Kind
Review: More than anything else, We Are Not Your Kind feels locked-in on a personal level -- that aforementioned sense of melancholy resides uncomfortably close to the surface throughout -- and that human touch resonates, even as the band unleashes volley after volley of tribal rhythms, scorching riffage, and fathomless decibels.

Title: Aftering
Review: Continuing in the direction of Fred Thomas' previous two albums, the equally outstanding All Are Saved and Changer, Aftering is filled with vivid descriptions of particular moments from throughout the prolific songwriter's life, as well as more general encapsulations of the bleak, uncertain feelings clouding the landscape of late-2010s America.

Title: Any Day
Review: Eschewing electronic production flourishes in favour of some analogue authenticity, Any Day eventually settles into its groove. The melodies are intricate and layered, but the impressive musicality is outweighed by a lack of urgency.

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Fetch, which blossoms more and more with each listen, feels giddy too; high on romance and rhythm and the surreal gift of being alive.

Title: What Will We Be
Review: It’s not surprising that What Will We Be sounds, then, like a relaxed, slightly crisper take on the ideas that informed his previous release. This haze of lazy Tropicalia, occasionally interrupted by an indulged moment of proggy vamp, isn’t necessarily a compromise.

Title: Strong Feelings
Review: Here's one of the best records you'll hear in 2014.

Review: Revival is no rerun. It is Fogerty getting back to work--and finally acting on his own advice.

Title: Space Is Only Noise
Review: This teetering restraint masks the true weirdness of Space Is Only Noise. I could understand someone finding the intensely self-contained Space a bit claustrophobic, but the album is most rewarding when you just grab a seat at the table.

Title: The Physical World
Review: A lot has happened in 10 years, but DFA’s approach to making ferocious music certainly hasn’t.

Title: X
Review: X is one of his least ambitious releases.

Title: Policy
Review: Policy may just be too slight to be successful, forcing its shortcomings to be amplified even if there are, in fact, many things to enjoy about this record.

Title: Love Kraft
Review: Their greatest album. [#17, p.93]

Title: Now
Review: But for all its stylish exuberance, 'Now' is an album full of wonderful sounds that's lamentably thin on songs.

Title: Halcyon
Review: The main flaw of Halcyon is that it occasionally feels a bit too much.
It's the first time Adams has sounded completely worn out and spent, bereaved of either the craft or hucksterism at the core of his work.

Title: Ire Works
Review: Ire Works is a thrillingly hostile racket containing 13 wild bursts. [Dec 2007, p.110]

Title: Stitch of the World
Review: Throughout, the songs are delivered with a powerful undertow that recalls Emmylou Harris' Wrecking Ball. [Feb 2017, p.33]

Title: Young Prayer
Review: Think of Young Prayer as the demos deemed too spectral, too elusive, to be revisited for [Brian] Wilson's new take on Smile. [#249, p.61]

Title: Me First
Review: Addresses the stained beauty of all things LA via psychedelic washes of keys, honking sax and country stomp. [May 2004, p.100]

Title: Quality
Review: He manages a harder edge without completely sacrificing credibility.

Title: Giants Of All Sizes
Review: Elbow have proven to be one of the most reliable and entertaining rock bands around and Giants of All Sizes has plenty of spectacular music to make it a 2019 top 10 contender.

Title: Traversa
Review: The album is invigorating and repetitive in the way that walking is invigorating and repetitive.

Title: Vespertine
Review: The best album of Björk's career

Title: Put Your Back N 2 It
Review: A delicate collection of near-gospel songs for the brokenhearted.

Title: Rare
Review: While none of these 13 songs attempt the subtle weirdness of “Bad Liar” and the emotional thesis—self-love!—can be a bit one-note, Rare is the 27-year-old’s most cohesive record to date. ... But it’s difficult to come away from Rare with any real perspective on who Gomez is other than that she doesn’t want to be the person she was, whoever that similarly mysterious shadow was.

Title: Olympia
Review: Yet the cameo-packed Olympia shares far more with Ferry's recent solo stuff than it does with Roxy's early-'70s art rock; lusciously arranged lounge-funk workouts.

Title: Powerplant
Review: Music is cathartic for Girlpool, allowing them to share their honest expressions while simultaneously allowing the listener to impose their own perceptions. This is a delicate balancing act that takes most artists years to master, but Tucker and Tividad provide enough give and take to make the overall experience one of constant intrigue.

Title: Otero War
Review: Emotions and feelings are generated clearly, but more overt references to specific story elements (characters, settings, plot) would carry Otero War to another level. Otherwise, it’s hard to shake the notion that this sounds just like another breakup album.

Title: Superwolf
Review: Superwolf is Americana at its most grim. [Apr/May 2005, p.134]

Title: It's a Myth
Review: It’s A Myth an easily enjoyable release that doesn’t waste any of its brief and surprising burst.

Title: Fake It Flowers
Review: The leap from bedroom-dweller to teenage riot instigator has been a swift and fruitful one, and what could be considered derivative is genuine in every sense. Circumstance might dictate that bedroom songwriting is back on the cards for Bea as the slow crawl to the return of live shows continues, but there’s a rock-solid foundation for the years to come.

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: Though it rarely makes good on the promise of her earlier songs, Cheap Seats is polarizing, and by now most listeners will have already decided whether or not they can stomach Spektor's peculiar kind of verite, glass-half-full optimism.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: [Mt Washington is] an early contender for song of the year, with Local Natives themselves current frontrunners for unexpectedly brilliant comeback of 2013.

Title: The Knot
Review: The record isn't a failure by any stretch; there is enough going on to make it at least worth a listen or two if you love the sound of 1990s American indie rock as much as Wye Oak do.

Title: Rome
Review: Of course the question arises: is Rome the greatest thing 2011 will offer? Hardly. Nevertheless, I'll vouch to name it the most ambitious album of the year.

Title: Infinite Moment
Review: On Infinite Moment, the Field proves that he's such a master of his craft that he can generate the same excitement from briefly moving outside the box as he can revelling back inside it.

Title: Angles
Review: Though this band was routinely slapped with claims of 1970s plagiarism upon their arrival, it's unlikely that many people have ever mistaken a Strokes song for one by Lou Reed or Television. So it's ironic that their mimicry can be uncanny on Angles.

Title: The Monitor
Review: Stand too clsose to the bagpipes, harmonica, scream-along choruses and a constant artillery of thundering drums, and your ears are gonna get powder burns. [Apr 2010, p.130]

Title: The Virgins
Review: Slinky but less than earthshattering debut from buzzy manhattanites.

Title: Sewn Together
Review: Although the band remains on an independent label--oddly enough, Megaforce, which wouldn’t have touched anything this psychedelic and mellow back in its own heyday--they’ve chosen to continue on in a similar ‘90s-nostalgic vein.

Title: From Here We Go Sublime
Review: If Willner doesn't hit at least some of your pleasure centers, well, forget your ears-- your nerve endings might actually be dead. Even three months in, it's a safe bet that From Here We Go Sublime will wind up 2007's most luxuriant record.

Title: BarragÃ¡n
Review: Barragán, the follow-up to that 2010 misstep [Penny Sparkle], course-corrects well, incorporating the most interesting elements of that electronic side trek while returning a few steps closer to their strengths.

Title: Not Too Late
Review: Subtlety was a defining characteristic of her first two records, and it carries over onto "Not Too Late," where even the differences are understated and discreet.

Title: Dark Matter
Review: It's Newman's ability to paint such a scene [narrator's wife, on her deathbed, defending him against their concerned and/or churlish offspring] with humor, affection and honest humanity that makes his albums so thoroughly worth the wait. [No. 145, p.60]

Title: Rock Action
Review: After you've listened to Rock Action for the first time, you may be hard pressed to believe that Mogwai merely wrote these songs; you'll feel as if they created these symphonies out of thin air, pulling gorgeous sounds from within the deepest recesses of the human soul. Eventually you'll come back down to earth and realize that Rock Action is by no means divine...but it is very, very good.

Title: Take Off Your Pants and Jacket
Review: Yet when they stop arsing around for the sake of it, Blink-182 write some very good pop songs. [Aug 2001, p.124]

Title: The Scene Between
Review: It’s got moments of music that sound like life. And when the songwriting is interesting and the melodies evocative, what you need is something to keep up what they’ve built.

Title: Grassed Inn
Review: Realm's refusal to shut up after a radio-friendly 180 seconds, surely, make them all the more cherishable. [Feb 2014, p.96]

Title: Shaking the Habitual
Review: Sporadically brilliant, perhaps it is The Knife’s Inland Empire--a fearless piece of work with its own logic, one that shears away all safety nets.

Title: Midnite Vultures
Review: He's got the beat rate up and lots of faux funk happening.

Title: Pussy's Dead
Review: As a whole, the album plays out a bit unevenly, with some distinctive artistic peaks and a few mis-plays made in the name of experimentation. Still, with the long gaps (six years) between each of their releases, it's hard to fault Autolux for making a worthy stab at reinvention.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: Pop sensibilities are allowed to swell over, into and around each other; each song blends the seams of the core into a fragmented, disjointed, appropriately-meshing of sounds and in the end, Love this Giant is a magnificent triumph because of it all.

Title: Tha Carter III
Review: Though wrong and stupid kinda work (in a good way!), Tha Carter III is more a balanced, self-conscious synthesis of everything viably great about Lil Wayne, hyperbolic or not, than the penultimate statement of the MC’s “legendary” status.

Title: I'm Not Dead
Review: The music here is a weird mish-mash of FM rock, folky ballads, and funky, poppy dance tracks. It makes for a diverting, interesting listen - but not a totally successful one.

Title: The Light in You
Review: While it's lovely to have them back, this album is more of a pleasant addition to the Mercury Rev catalogue than a defining moment.

Title: Kinshasa One Two
Review: Kinshasa One Two is worthwhile both as a cause (all proceeds from sales go to Oxfam) and as an experiment, albeit one that requires some judicious editing to extract the tracks that really count.

Title: La Isla Bonita
Review: Closer Oh Bummer, sung by drummer Greg Saunier, is a straightforward moody rock song--at least for the first three minutes, after which a striking doomsday-meets-Thriller breakdown erupts, reminding diehard fans that the band members are still weirdos but also keeping fair-weather listeners at a distance.

Title: New Wild Everywhere
Review: The result is an album that is altogether pleasant, but just doesn't do enough to distinguish itself on the map from the rest in its genre.

Title: Cry Cry Cry
Review: The greatest and most wonderful surprise is that Cry Cry Cry burns with the passion of a debut.

Title: Songs For You
Review: On Songs for You, Tinashe shows off how adept she is at flitting between genres, hopping on moody, woozy R&B, sun-dappled G-funk, ’80s pop, acoustic devotionals, club-worthy drum ’n’ bass and skittering trap, sometimes in the span of a single song without so much as straining her airy, but substantial soprano. There are a few songs left over from a scrapped album with RCA, but here, they feel part and parcel of the vision Tinashe has for herself.

Title: Emerald Valley
Review: Filthy Friends are suave, soothing, and anthemic—especially on "One Flew East"—but Emerald Valley is caught in an awkward slowness.

Title: The Mountain Will Fall
Review: While there’s a certain amount of showmanship--he’s certainly still got skills--more often than not it sounds like he’s simply going through the motions.

Title: Transference
Review: Transference is the victim of an unfortunate irony--the more honed, the less it cuts.

Title: Slow Air
Review: While the atmosphere of Slow Air enthralls with captivating layers of sedated synth and breathtaking reverb, the stunning production quality can’t save Still Corners from sinking into the increasingly crowded waters of the dream pop scene.

Title: Synesthesia
Review: Too often, elements of the LP are unrecognizable from that of its competition.

Title: Ys
Review: There is still something unsettlingly Renaissance fair-meets-Wind in the Willows about her music, yet something lovely lives there as well. [24 Nov 2006, p.109]

Title: Doris
Review: It’s a work as notable for its technical achievements as its nuanced themes, and that’s almost as impressive considering that so many artists lack in one or both of those fields.

Title: Ill Manors
Review: Solid, purposeful, and crafted in a manner that betrays both Drew's age and the album's hurried road to release, Ill Manors makes heavy-hitter number three for the rapper, suggesting that Plan B doesn't issue albums, just milestones.

Title: Tell 'Em I'm Gone
Review: It’s Cat Stevens singing rhythm and blues, with a combination of originals and covers that showcase attractive playing (legendary guitarist Richard Thompson helps here) and production (cue Rick Rubin). Best of all, his voice remains intact, providing a familiar and favorable sound.

Title: Back to Land
Review: The overall pace, sequence, and vibe of Back to Land finds the Shjips teetering on the edge of classic rock mania with enough restraint to keep things minimal, mystical, and interesting throughout.

Title: Drowners
Review: It’s the record’s most easy-to-appreciate moment, but whether there’s enough to the rest of it to ensure its makers aren’t soon to be forgotten remains to be seen.

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: While it lacks the iconic significance of his debut, BLACKsummers'night is a record more than worthy of Maxwell's talents, because it trades the physical sensuality of his earlier work for a deep emotional resonance, the performance of an artist whose focus and attention to detail gives his expression a singular veracity.

Title: Neva Left
Review: Neva Left is unfortunately, yet predictably, another mixed bag. The good tracks are effectively updates to proven formulas, which when matched to more imposing beats, show Snoop hasn't lost his touch.

Title: Country Sleep
Review: A gorgeously warm, fuzzy album by a man wise--and sad--beyond his tender years.

Title: We'll Never Turn Back
Review: If her album is musically uneven at times, her artistry and strength continue to shine as undimmed beacons.

Title: SIR
Review: While the nine-year break has seen the duo barely switch up their instrumentation--Warren Fischer is still blasting drum machines and moody synth underneath Spooner’s vocals--the band’s friend and new producer, R.E.M.‘s Michael Stipe, seems to have generally smoothed the scruffier side of the duo’s compositions.

Title: Girl Going Nowhere
Review: The forceful sound of Girl Going Nowhere may camouflage the subtleties of her songwriting, but it's also an asset, as the production, along with her powerhouse voice, demand attention.

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: Further Adventures of Lord Quas is a record that can satisfy the cult fan just as it will sate anyone who has an open mind to music that creates its own barriers.

Title: Good Mood Fool
Review: Temple’s unassuming sound can often hide how experimental he is. Not so on the lysergic electronics of ‘Sue’, which swirl like watercolour dreams.

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: It's not perfect... Overall, though, this is a long overdue, welcome comeback.

Title: Computer Controlled Acoustic Instruments pt2
Review: While acoustically generated and devoid of any heavy electronic processing, the results are much darker and stranger than anything on Syro, with ominous detuned metallic percussion and mangled piano noises taking the place of bright, bubbling, acid synth lines.

Title: Lodestar
Review: Collins herself brings a demotic charm to whatever she sings.

Title: We Are Born
Review: While We Are Born occasionally lapses into the anodyne, overly tasteful pop-folk balladeering of Sia's past, overall it's a charmingly cheery, light-hearted romp looking nowhere but sweetly, sanguinely forward.

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: Bar rock for the smart set. [3 Jun 2005, p.82]

Title: The Bravest Man in the Universe
Review: At times the dribs of Gorillaz-style glitch don't quite fit, making some songs on The Bravest Man in the Universe feel more like clever remixes than organic moments. Still, Womack shines.

Title: La Roux
Review: This is adequate debut, but La Roux will need to move beyond brittle pastiche if they hope to reinvent such overfamiliar ingredients. [Jul 2009, p.91]

Title: Fandango
Review: Cloaked in fuzzy melancholy, Fandango is one for dreamers. [Jun 2013, p.94]

Title: Favourite Colours
Review: The Sadies' best album yet.

Title: Mirrored
Review: Battles unite process and expression, making playing that’s as quantized and mechanical as Kraftwerk sound as wild and urgent as Albert Ayler.

Title: Wolf
Review: With Wolf, Tyler, the Creator is exciting again: maybe not as the ringleader of the Odd Future empire, but as a producer who just turned 22.

Title: Tonight: Franz Ferdinand
Review: There's plenty of evidence on Tonight... of attempts at broadening their palette, but it's usually by substituting jerky guitar for jerky synthesizer as the lead instrument. [Feb 2009, p.110]

Title: Geogaddi
Review: Where Music flowed with a pastoral warmth, Geogaddi feels colder and more mortal, bound to the tension between its upper and lower registers. [May 2002, p.78]

Title: Pain Is Love
Review: The tracks on this album contain the right beats to make listeners' heads bounce. But more thoughtful music lovers will simply shake their heads at the profuse profanity and misogynistic philosophies Ja Rule perpetuates with Pain Is Love.

Title: Off Off On
Review: Off Off On captures something of how the world is right now. It has moments that encourage us to turn off and seek escape, but at the same time also provides energy to help us to re-engage with the world. In short, it’s a perfect soundtrack to help us through these pandemic-dominated times.

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: Less ambient and more grounded than the preceding tracks, it's the one song on the album you wouldn't want to hear at the party; rather, it's a subtle, evocative slow-burner best saved for the cool air and the long walk home.

Title: A Chorus of Storytellers
Review: A Chorus of Storytellers is an evocative, full-bodied record from a band nearing the peak of their powers. [Winter 2010, p.68]

Title: Milk Famous
Review: The collaborators are rubbing off in the best way, and the bulk of these tunes are not second-rate imitations, but fully realized--and seriously catchy--originals.

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: The pair has picked up a supporting cast and loads of confidence for Girls' second album, Father, Son, Holy Ghost.

Title: No One Else Can Wear Your Crown
Review: For every track that falls short, there is another where they hit a sweet spot.

Title: Come to Where I'm From
Review: Enlisting a heavy-hitting cast of helpers -- from the best unknown drummer in the world (Carla Azar) to one of the most creatively pure producers around (T Bone Burnett) -- Arthur has transformed a dozen of his best compositions from the skeletal coffeehouse-ready material they surely were at conception into richly-textured and deeply emotive mood pieces.

Title: Radium Death
Review: Whitmore might only occasionally let that rock ‘n’ roll animal out from time to time, but that scarcity--coupled with excellent pacing--is exactly what makes it so exciting.

Title: Please Be Honest
Review: Please Be Honest certainly has its charms. But for the first time in Pollard’s career, Guided by Voices isn’t the main event--which, for the band’s legions of fans, is surely a loss.

Title: Someone to Drive You Home
Review: Put simply, this is fantasy pop, performed to perfection.

Title: Be Brave
Review: Reviewed as a whole album though, it must concede that buying Be Brave would be like paying for two songs played at different speeds and in different keys fourteen times over, an unwise choice that would eventually leave many wondering just what the hell is so different between Friday in Paris and Da Da anyway? I've got to tell you, after these past couple days, I can barely even tell anymore.

Title: An Imaginary Country
Review: It’s verily comfortable existing the background, but instead of becoming wallpaper, the music fills the container of the room it’s played in and settles beautifully into the atmosphere.

Title: The Seer
Review: Just be thankful that the new Swans are as clever, as terrifying, and as proficient in their craft as presented on The Seer.

Title: The Mosaic of Transformation
Review: Though it finds Smith at her most reserved, The Mosaic Of Transformation feels like a breakthrough, melting the pop-savvy hooks of her past records into one gorgeous, rarefied sound, as invigorating and smooth as electricity flowing through circuits.

Title: Smile
Review: Smile is their exquisite-corpse sequel, a near-automatic exercise in drawing inspiration from anybody but themselves.

Title: Free Your Mind
Review: The major misstep on Free Your Mind is eschewing those decent lyrical impulses in favor of rather limp and unaccomplished (and repeated!) inanities such as “free your mind” and “shine on,” phrases that should be confined, respectively, to the lexicons of aging hippies and Roger Waters.
4:44 is just about the safest way Jay-Z could have re-asserted his dominance: smarter raps over soulful beats over a very concise runtime.

Title: Bionic
Review: If nothing else, it all proves that Aguilera is a woman of many parts, which may be the point of this occasionally brilliant and brave, occasionally teeth-gritting and stupid album.

Title: Invincible
Review: To really care about this album you have to be able to get into the pure hard sounds of the dance-track percussion and the way Michael tends to garnish them with his voice.

Title: She Wolf
Review: Yet while these tracks might bring Nelly Furtado's Timbaland-fueled makeover to mind, there is more to She Wolf than glossy dance-pop. [Dec 2009, p. 124]

Title: Ignorance is Bliss
Review: Maybe it's the tedium of a career spanning nearly two decades, or a shred of complacency settling in after winning the highly coveted Mercury Prize in 2016, but Skepta seems subdued on Ignorance. A decent album, but not his best.

Title: Flower Of Devotion
Review: Detailed production and collective growth as performers meet with a songwriting style that grows more distinctive with each new release, making Flower of Devotion a further step up. Some of the heartbreak and healing that defined the last album carries over, but more than anything Dehd grows deeper into their sad, summery twilight sound.

Title: Whoop Dee Doo
Review: All too often the album lacks the requisite light and shade to make for a consistently enjoyable listen.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: All ten of the songs here are grandiose and muscular in the great tradition of Spiritualized songs.

Title: Eat Me, Drink Me
Review: The results are too often less-than-inspiring, and our Marilyn’s music has not established the sort of consistency required to atone for this lack of drama.

Title: God's Problem Child
Review: The album's greatest treasures are sadder and subtler, finding their place within the Willie trifecta of love, loss and loneliness. [No. 142, p.59]

Title: Believers
Review: If Bondy's been searching for a suitable solo identity, Believers may be his charmed third time.[#81, p. 54]

Title: Handwritten
Review: The lyrics are a little more personal, the band a little more developed - it seems that this is the start of a new and exciting chapter for The Gaslight Anthem.

Title: The Endless River
Review: A suite of mostly instrumental moods and fragments, The Endless River rolls like a requiem through familiar echoes.

Title: Heartless
Review: An exciting follow up to 2014’s Foundations Of Burden that edges the band’s sound forward while keeping sight of what they do best, Heartless is a glorious open wound that bleeds melody. Right on.

Title: What Do You Think About The Car?
Review: Smart, engaging lyrics are a widespread and continual theme on McKenna’s initial offering.

Title: Eyes Open
Review: The band's naked ambition would be offputting if it didn't come wrapped in such resounding choruses.

Title: Human Ceremony
Review: Human Ceremony isn’t anywhere near fault-free, but its charm arrives when the trio get ahead of themselves.

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: Teens of Denial takes its power from its absence of blind spots, its lack of Freudian suppression. Toledo looks long at himself and us, a sort of nauseous survivor of modernity. Sometimes just the looking itself is enough.

Title: Fetch
Review: The results are a no-less-entertaining 33 minutes of madness, like a Ramones album spun at 78 rpm. [Jan 2014, p.123]

Title: Fundamental
Review: Fundamental is the group's most inspired album in nearly a decade.

Title: Black City
Review: Dear's tempos here are mostly slow, never rising above moderate, and the result is an anxious but exhilarating journey through the night.

Title: The Waiting Room
Review: Though Tindersticks is no longer angling for the pure dramatic sweep of its ambitious ’90s records, it remains a unique band, maintaining a sense of creativity (and making beautiful music) while working within limited themes.

Title: Reflections
Review: As a whole, the album rejects traditional song structures, though the final three tracks (“Shy”, “Fade Away” and “Make Believe”) are arguably the most melodic on the record. Such a duality implies the sheer range of Diamond’s artistry, so much so that it would be criminal to label her a “new kind of popstar”. Simply put, she is a new kind of star, an artistic voice that stands out in the tumult of the modern musical world.

Title: Damita Jo
Review: That it'll be her most scrutinised release is a problem, because its stilted, wearying, obsessive concentration on an uncomfortably forced notion of it's creator's sexuality means it's the only album she's made in the last dozen years that doesn't merit such focussed attention.

Title: Idealism
Review: Idealism shows off plenty of blaring synth riffs. [Jun 2007, p.92]

Title: We Come From The Same Place
Review: We Come From The Same Place, then, is a delightful record, catchy enough to keep the listener’s attention, and with enough substance for them to return to it time and time again.

Title: Push the Button
Review: While there aren't as many heart-stopping productions as on 2002's unjustly neglected Come With Us, Push the Button proves the Chemical Brothers have retained the innate curiosity necessary to keep them blazing trails for years to come.

Title: Distant Relatives
Review: Distant Relatives is this African contradiction explored further with hip-hop, dancehall, and by way of samples, jazz, and African music showing the way. It's a royal and a striking reminder of why these two artists have reached legendary status.

Title: Zammuto
Review: It's hard to recall an album so invitingly unfamiliar, so beguilingly hard to parse, so full of "wait, what was that?" moments... since the first Books album. [No.86, p.61]

Title: Fortune
Review: Fortune is never terrible. It just feels cripplingly pointless.

Title: Ghosteen
Review: Ghosteen is not a blissful or comfortable album, but it is a hopeful one. The gaping wound of ‘Skeleton Tree’ is scarring over as Cave pulls away from the past’s savage undertow, content in the knowledge that peace will come. It’s a paean to how all things bright and beautiful can be thrown into blinding relief once you’ve known real darkness, another open letter straight from artist to audience that cuts right to the core of what means to have loved, lost and loved again.

Title: I See You
Review: There is a sturdiness to the xx. The band’s innate talents for melody and texture, even when expressed in the wrong proportions, persist.

Title: Orc
Review: Despite all of the quixotic ups and downs in the tunes the album never loses its sense of purpose or momentum.

Title: Temper
Review: However disparate its geographic points of reference, Temper is an artistically consistent, tonally temperate, record--depending on your taste, maybe a little too balmy and dispassionate.

Title: Cupid Deluxe
Review: It’s an effortless but unpredictable experience. Hynes may not turn up until midway through a song, but he glides seamlessly into the album’s comfortable atmosphere.

Title: Odyssey
Review: A taut, economic album with emotional songs at its heart. Yep, we’re as surprised as you.

Title: Flamagra
Review: Ellison remains keen on confronting and articulating his inner quarrels in the name of taking weirdness to the masses, and in doing so writing a new chapter in the pantheon of great Afrofuturist music.

Title: Circuital
Review: My Morning Jacket no longer sound like a band of curious adventurers perpetually at odds with their former selves, and consequently deliver an album that plays like a sort of kid-in-a-candy-shop, take-a-little-of-everything thrill ride. Predictably, results vary.

Title: Copia
Review: It sounds exactly like Eluvium, only with an organ and not a guitar, and with more overt classical aspirations than before.

Title: Rap Album One
Review: Approach Rap Album One is an acquired taste that's worth acquiring because it isn't for everyone, but it's excellent.

Title: Almanac
Review: While the songs retain their verse-chorus-verse clarity, the newfound breadth of the music orchestrates and enriches lyrics that take the long view.

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: Ambitious and uneven.

Title: Along The Shadow
Review: This album sets the band on their surest footing for years and proves that Anthony Green and friends can still hang. After all this time away, that’s more than enough.

Title: Is the Is Are
Review: Is The Is Are nails all of nostalgia's sonic signifiers, without any of the retrograde guilt. [Mar 2016, p.100]

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Monsanto Years
Review: Young hits the equilibrium between songwriting and performance best when he brings his heart to the table through rebellion, and these nine tracks geared towards environmental ignorance at large do the trick.

Title: A Grand Don't Come For Free
Review: 11 frenetic, oddball, and extremely original tracks. [Jun 2004, p.154]

Title: New Brigade
Review: The rest of the album sees the group continue to rip from the history of punk to make something decidedly fresh.

Title: This Is What The Truth Feels Like
Review: The pop-rock of the album’s first half is relaxed, breezy, intimate, and dull; the twitching beatscapes of its back end are tense, fiery, theatrical, and void.

Title: Haunted
Review: As uncomfortable as it is beautiful, Haunted's intense personal nature is both disturbing and compelling. It is less an album than an experience.

Title: JESUS IS KING
Review: Jesus Is King is impersonal, repetitive, boring, and somehow too long at just 27 minutes. Some albums grow deeper with subsequent listens; Jesus Is King shrinks.

Title: The Waiting Room
Review: Picking up right where A Certain Distance left off, the Seattle-based producer's latest LP shows the same passion for methodical soundscapes, which are no less thoughtful for their glowing warmth.

Title: Writer's Block
Review: The album is laced with spacey, distorted guitar fuzz, delicate '60s pop melodies, groovy basslines and winsome lyrics that coalesce into a unified group of songs from start to finish. [17 Feb 2007]

Title: Zee Avi
Review: The breadth of Avi’s influences is apparent on her self-titled debut album, but she still creates a unique and extremely charming persona of her own.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: Car Alarm is essentially Everybody II; an album that subtly stretches the group’s formulaic parameters with rawer production and looser instrumentation but without cementing any concrete boundary-changes.

Title: Smoke + Mirrors
Review: Evocations of everyone from Coldplay to Peter Gabriel to Queen remain intact, with that first band’s specter looming largest over the moody, dirge-y, electro-tweaked proceedings. The album hits its most interesting and feverish spike with the furtive yelps and rhythms of “Friction.”

Title: One of Us Is the Killer
Review: On One of Us Is the Killer, everybody is firing on all cylinders and DEP sound just as urgent as ever. [Jun 2013, p.94]

Title: The Future's Void
Review: EMA has crafted a wide-eyed, open-eared, reasonably horrified, digi-noise drone-folk treatise about the soul-sucking, privacy-wrecking qualities of online life.

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: Over inventive arrangements that feature more live instrumentation than on any other Streets album, Skinner gives maturity a fresh coat of meaning.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
