Review: Its first half features some of the group's sweetest pop confections since those massive singles, while its second delves into the muggy Barrett-isms of their more recent work.

Title: The Diary of Alicia Keys
Review: An hour of heartful, artful singing enhanced by dense, yet fuss-free arrangements. [Jan 2004, p.106]

Title: Tired of Hanging Around
Review: 'Tired Of Hanging Around' is one seriously pissed-off, paranoid, twitchy record.

Title: The Marshall Mathers LP 2
Review: It is a testament to Eminem’s enduring talent that the album never feels laboured or even slightly dated. Instead, it is a perfect reflection of the world of Marshall Mathers in 2013.

Title: No More Shall We Part
Review: A highlty nuanced album which is at once razor sharp, and rich in new openings and possibilities. [#206, p.60]

Title: Working Men's Club
Review: A compelling, grimy darkness ripples throughout. [Nov 2020, p.82]

Title: Lay It Down
Review: From the gentle fire of the first, and title track, this is Green in the role of Love Man and in very fine form. [July 2008, p.100]

Title: Vamala
Review: Glam folk never sounded such a good idea. [Mar 2015, p.105]

Title: Stankonia
Review: As the tracks shift from smooth R&B to frantic, drum machine driven beats, Outkast prove able to pull from a big enough bag of tricks as rappers to remain unpredictable. The problem is that they come out of it all without having left any defining mark on the songs. It's almost as if Stankonia would be more memorable if the duo stuck to one sound, one rhythm, and one train of lyrical thought.

Title: Melbourne
Review: The songwriting is pretty much entirely solid, and there are brief flashes of idiosyncrasy, but this album boils down to being a product of the excitement of influence and just being young playing and writing music, without ever remotely threatening to stand up as something worthy of all the critical saliva that’s already dripped onto bedroom carpets worldwide.

Title: La Isla Bonita
Review: La Isla Bonita is harder, edgier and noisier than 2012's Breakup Song, but just as charming, off-kilter and curious.

Title: The Beginning
Review: Unforgivably bad.

Title: Hug of Thunder
Review: Hug of Thunder thrives in these quieter moments, which depart from band's established sound in order to play to specific vocalists' strengths. The album's more discordant and propulsive tracks are more of a mixed bag.

Title: 12 Desperate Straight Lines
Review: For 12 Desperate Straight Lines, the songs are still there, only this time some of the looseness of the self-produced sessions comes into play and the end result ends up being a marked improvement.

Title: American Interior
Review: A work of typically broad imagination, not everything on American Interior fully clicks into place. Yet when it does, there’s more than enough to suggest that Rhys need not cease his eternal voyaging.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: For a group of guys who are now 22 years on from their debut album and 15 years past their prime as one of the biggest and most important groups in rock ‘n’ roll, Lightning Bolt is a strikingly stellar set of songs that belies the band’s democratic nature.

Title: Britney Jean
Review: Britney Jean, her first album released in her thirties, is a subtle shift away from frantic bangers and into more forthright songwriting.

Title: On the Line
Review: On The Line may not be her strongest work, no matter how much it aims to be but it proves that Jenny Lewis doesn't need to try too hard to become one of the greats. She's already been one for a while.

Title: Moon 2
Review: A series of disconnected ideas rather than one concentrated work. [Oct 2018, p.24]

Title: Dirty Computer
Review: With funky guitars riffs and breezy melodies, Monáe's latest effort manages to resemble a throwback and tribute to the Purple One yet avoids feeling too nostalgic.

Title: Coconut
Review: Coconut seems to be a "transition album": A sometimes-exhilarating, sometimes-WTF layover between a possibly played-out formula and exciting new sounds on the horizon.

Title: The Documentary 2
Review: The Game is literally inseparable from his influences. He doesn’t digest them as other rappers might; instead, he wears them like brands. He too is joined by oodles of guests, a striking show of support for a midcareer rapper who’s pugnacious to boot. Both Kanye West and Drake appear here, and in strong form.

Title: Cat's Eyes
Review: Cat's Eyes is the rare side project effort that feels as (if not more) fully realized than the band from which it borrows members.

Title: METAL GALAXY
Review: Babymetal are still at their best when they hover around their initial idea—harnessing the energy of metal and J-Pop into high-flying hybrids. ... Otherwise, Metal Galaxy teems with embarrassing gimmickry.

Title: WIXIW
Review: While 40-plus minutes of these experiments may start to drag, Liars' ability to work in hooks and structure to oddball electronic music is both admirable and pleasantly surprising.

Title: Happy in Galoshes
Review: STP singer on the solo comeback trail.

Title: Mini Mansions
Review: It's different. It's well-written. It's emotive. Those three things are hard enough to find in music these days, let alone in one place.

Title: AMOK
Review: Far from capturing their kinetic live energy, AMOK feels as isolated, distraught, and feeble as the characters littered about in Donwood’s tragic portrait.

Title: The Brutalist Bricks
Review: Leo has now produced more Pharmacists records while we've been at war than not, and in a world that still needs Fugazi's oppositional fire, The Brutalist Bricks' Dischordant burn is welcome.

Title: Nature
Review: Valet's third LP is proof that hazy guitars and dream-pop vocals aren't just for smoke-filled basements. When done right, anyone can take the journey and float with the music rather than get buried inside.

Title: Tenacious D
Review: Not since Bob and Doug McKenzie have two jokers nailed the clod-metal aesthetic so accurately: Nearly every lyric here comes straight from your high school's bathroom wall.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: It’s a broad net Terje casts here, flitting through myriad styles but he always ensures they’re congealed in order to give the record a cohesiveness and rigidity.

Title: The Both
Review: They work hard to make it a true collaboration, and due to that effort and the high quality of the songs they each brought, it works amazingly well.

Title: Lollipop
Review: Recent Meat Puppet albums have had an ephemeral presence in record shops, particularly in the UK, appearing on a variety of labels and disappearing from the racks not long after release. With music so focused on the transitory nature of things, it seems strangely appropriate.

Title: Foundations of Burden
Review: An effort that is even more emotionally ambitious an undertaking, and all the more wounding for its beauty.

Title: Yellow & Green
Review: Yellow & Green documents the evolution of Baroness from great metal band to great band.

Title: ken
Review: Like one of Lynch’s filmic worlds, ken is elegant and perverse, a reflection on where we came from, and the unbelievable place we seem to have ended up.

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: It’s Not Me, It’s You cooks up nostalgia for Allen diehards, but the elements have been shuffled and re-imagined with pulsating dance tracks that are surprisingly fitting.

Title: Diver
Review: An intoxicating brand of synth-pop that's slicker than a Gordon Gekko coif.

Title: How I Long to Feel That Summer in My Heart
Review: There are no shocks or surprises, but instead, How I Long... thrills us softly, its tiny layers and details all intricately woven together into a cohesive and aesthetically delightful tapestry.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: Freed from the aesthetic demands of an odd-couple partnership, Big Boi (Antwan Patton) improves on the standard set with 2003's Speakerboxxx, an ostensibly solo work crystallized inside a double-album set, delivering a record that's rigidly focused and almost uniformly strong.

Title: Warm Heart of Africa
Review: Instead of approximating a hodgepodge of the 21st century's musical memes, this debut LP takes on a life of its own, authenticity snobs be damned. [Fall 2009, p.68]

Title: Monsters Exist
Review: Overall, there’s as much room for the head explodeGIF in Monsters Exist; as there is in a WhatsApp group-chat post philosophy lecture.

Title: neo
Review: So Pitted is constantly poking and prodding at its audience with a wicked glee and demented smile. [No. 128, p.61]

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: I Learned the Hard Way is yet another work of impeccable late-’60s nostalgia by the flagship act of Brooklyn label Daptone, where soul revivalism is a way of life, from crack horn section to period recording tools to throwback art and typography.

Title: Tenderheart
Review: The songwriting and performances on Tenderheart pop when he integrates up-tempo and driving qualities with soft and steady vocal deliveries, aspects presented by both the excellent title track and the out-and-out rocker single “Trouble”. But, Outlaw closes the album similarly to its opening: quiet, subdued, and largely opposite the feelings he creates in its middle.

Title: Pink City
Review: Pink City is a real winner, and listeners will be swayed by its gentle beauty, all obvious comparisons that may seem pertinent be damned.

Title: Strange Geometry
Review: A more satisfying disc than its predecessors.

Title: Fly International Luxurious Art
Review: More fine than fierce, Fly International Luxurious Art may not be on the man's top shelf, but it's a sturdy and entertaining effort well worth its place in the Chef's catalog.

Title: Liberation
Review: There is something unceasingly engaging about Trans Am. [Apr 2004, p.122]

Title: Three
Review: Bloom is a little over 21-minutes of relentless noise pool of percussion and clatter that’s somehow relaxed by the gently pressed piano keys that methodically pierce its surface, a contrast that rests the mind over the length of this track when it might otherwise induce anxiety.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: It's an album about what war does to the aggressor, as much as what it does to the vanquished victim.

Title: Biophilia
Review: When Bjork's supernatural voice soars in "Thunderbolt"--"Craving miracles"--soul easily trumps software.

Title: Rugby Thompson
Review: It is a skilfully wrought glimpse into that dream.

Title: Nanobots
Review: They still craft songs as if they’re assembling a robot, and they make sure to throw so many of these short tracks on the album (25 in 45 minutes) that you’re bound to find a few that will hit the pleasure buttons just like the old days.

Title: see you tomorrow
Review: Karen's spectral, childlike voice sounds like it's been beamed in from a haunted 19th-century log cabin. [Feb 2020, p.29]

Title: Visiter
Review: This is cerebral twisted folk that's as wistful as it is strident. [04 Apr 2008, p.63]

Title: Beings
Review: Listening to Beings though makes one thing abundantly clear: Lanterns on the Lake are one of Britain's most crucial bands of the present moment.

Title: MDNA
Review: Luckily for fans of music and controversy alike, Madonna's compulsions reap musical dividends as she continues to bang into a dance-tastic G-spot, and the results are part sour, part sweet.

Title: Kill The Moonlight
Review: It’s that rare record that’s equal parts innovation and familiarity, or what one might refer to as a perfectly designed and executed experiment in indie aesthetics.

Title: Heritage
Review: The Swedes' 10th album, Heritage, is a brave, melancholic and often beautiful heavy rock record that revels in the warm, analogue tones and shimmering mellotrons of the pre-punk 70s while still exuding a sense of wonder at new ideas.

Title: Flashmob
Review: His synapse-fusing take on acid-house, however, first showcased on 2005's OK Cowboy, reamins an underground phenomenon--this sequel won't alter that. [Nov 2009, p.114]

Title: Aufheben
Review: Much like the Socialist commune they share a part of their name with, BJM retains the mysterious cult image that attracts a few but repels many.

Title: Dig In Deep
Review: Raitt's signature slide guitar is back out front; it shines throughout the recording. Her earthy singing voice, with just a hint of time's grain, is more disciplined and holds more emotional authority than ever before. It soars through a song collection balanced between rough, rowdy rockers and searing ballads.

Title: Where You Stand
Review: Where You Stand picks up where you last left them--no matter where that was along the way.

Title: Bloom
Review: In 2006, it seemed like Beach House couldn't outlive Beach House. In 2012, Bloom is the bar to clear.

Title: Scars
Review: Scars is the strongest Basement Jaxx album since 2001's "Rooty".

Title: The Black and White Album
Review: Sonically they've tweaked their punk-pop vibe, even employing the hip-hop-flavored Pharrell Williams for one cut. Happily, that gambit--the danceable ''T.H.E.H.I.V.E.S.''--pays off.

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: Beautiful stuff. [Jun 2019, p.116]

Title: Fast-Moving Clouds
Review: The contrast between the style and the subject matter is so arresting that you kind of wonder what will happen on the next record when Nelson is, perhaps, not mad anymore.

Title: Me Moan
Review: Unfortunately, Me Moan doesn’t really deepen Gibson’s exploration of this novel niche. Instead, it feels mostly like a country record that still has one foot in the sample-based electronic aesthetic that previously defined Gibson’s work.

Title: The New Life
Review: Girls Names does not dwell on the dourness, but conquers and transforms it into a solace--a sound resulting from some hallucinatory fever like a Max Ernst painting, realizing the shadowy dimension parallel to this existence.

Title: Hallelujah Anyhow
Review: It’s all quite pleasant, nicely played and sung and recorded, but perhaps a little distant. These tunes flow by like sunny afternoons and when they’re done you can’t remember much.

Title: Heaven
Review: Twelve years after their formation, the East Coast five-piece have created their finest album to date.

Title: Eight Houses
Review: It feels distant and phoned in.

Title: Ancient Romans
Review: Throughout the album the sense is of rough experimentation, a kind of direct curiosity in the collision of sampled loops, echoed vocals, bursting bass, and random moments. Stallone's echoed vocals, however much a stylistic commonality in some corners, act as further random hooks, a slightly stupefied but never incoherent series of reactions.

Title: Jesus Piece
Review: It's more focused than he's been in awhile, and while you couldn't call an album featuring 2Chainz, Rick Ross, Meek Mill, Lil Wayne (twice), Future, Young Jeezy, Chris Brown, Common, Pusha T, Jamie Foxx, J. Cole, Kendrick Lamar and more "lean," Jesus Piece is less all-over-the-place than The R.E.D. Album.

Title: Secular Hymns
Review: The French singer renders smoky blues. [Oct 2016, p.100]

Title: Urth
Review: Kagoule have captured the energy, thrills, uncertainties and anxieties of being a teenager and bundled it all up in an exciting debut album that thrills from beginning to end. More importantly they've done it on their own terms.

Title: Paradise
Review: She's sometimes bogged down by her own weightiness, but Paradise won't stall her slow but steady climb. [May 2017, p.104]

Title: Six Cups of Rebel
Review: [A] rock-inspired electro-alien world that Lindstrøm has carefully crafted.

Title: Hypercaffium Spazzinate
Review: Muscular production from the Blasting Room's Jason Livermore brings Stephen Egerton's melodic guitar to the forefront, and Alvarez and Stevenson's lockstep percussion sounds downright youthful.

Title: The Way Out
Review: If there's a lesson to be learned from The Way Out, it's that we need little more than the sounds of each other's voices to find comfort--or in the Books' case, to crank out yet another masterwork.

Title: The Mix-Up
Review: Tossed-off, underdone, monotonous, unfinished, and redundant maybe, but not bad.

Title: Silence In The Snow
Review: The Florida foursome still manage to top themselves with each outing. [Nov 2015, p.96]

Title: Born Like This
Review: With too much hip hop content to recycle cliches of its own making, it's exhilarating to discover someone out there is still willing to test the limits. [Jun 2009, p.132]

Title: Smile
Review: Though excellent in brief parts, much of the album is still worrisome, at times specifically seeming to document a band running out of steam.

Title: The Magician's Private Library
Review: It’s ambitious for a debut, and for the most part Miranda is able to keep up.

Title: Lotta Sea Lice
Review: Courtney Barnett and Kurt Vile are on top of their respective games on Lotta Sea Lice, and hopefully the magic will not stop at one record.

Title: Black Noise
Review: The third full-length from Hendrick Weber maintains the high quality of previous efforts while pushing certain elements of his shoegaze-y, minimal-inspired techno sound further.

Title: Ruins
Review: Their voices complement each other so naturally and so gracefully that it’s easy to forget how much craft there is in these songs, and how much ingenuity they put into their vocals.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: Overall, a confident, clear-headed quantum leap beyond their previous work.

Title: Bambino
Review: The studio mix is excellent, and sample-heavy interludes provide a welcome break from what at times seems like a label compilation. One unifying thread, however, is the playground-fidelity sampling and the prominent, plucky bass, which gives the album a Parliament-ish, heavy funk overtone.

Title: Swanlights
Review: Hegarty's fourth album strictly follows the template laid down by his previous records: fragile, sombre and wistful, always dominated by that extraordinary tremulous voice, seemingly forever on the brink of bursting into tears.

Title: Cause And Effect
Review: Cause & Effect plays to their strengths. [Nov 2019, p.112]

Title: From Here to Eternity
Review: Dunn's ability to subsume the subject into his detailed sonic landscapes with minor shifts in the onslaught of drones speaks to this album's ability to impact a wide-ranging listenership. From Here to Eternity serves as a masterful articulation of the power of ambient music.

Title: What's Between
Review: What's Between provides some compelling glimpses at Kelly's cimmerian headspace, but knowing that he possesses the ability and the vision to flesh out his own ideas, it's hard not to be left wanting more.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: Meiburg and the group have swapped the muddy tranquillity that kept them muted and unheard for a daring dose of starry eyed wonderment that really should unleash the groups collective wings, enabling them to fly higher than ever before.

Title: Rennen
Review: Despite his obvious production chops, Sohn the popstar seems merely an uninspiring iteration of the current trend for singing an irritatingly affected brand of the blues.

Title: Avi Buffalo
Review: The band comes together neatly, covering a range that encompasses stripped-down recordings and wider-canvas anthems. Avi Buffalo make songs that, at their best, remain lodged in one's head for days.

Title: Forever Turned Around
Review: Ehrlich and Kakacek are perfectly in tune with each other, evoking ache and yearning on every note. If the record is not as immediately grabbing as Light Upon the Lake, it’s because it’s a slow burn, driven by a deep desire that blooms into a heart-wrenching splendor.

Title: A Dotted Line
Review: If there isn't much spark, there is a surplus of warmth; the trio is comfortable and relaxed, and it's hard not to succumb to such friendly, familiar vibes.

Title: Noonday Dream
Review: The result is not a focused or sharp record--but it doesn’t need to be. The allure of Noonday Dream comes in its willingness to swell and expand, before Howard sits up and starts kicking, slowly but precisely, to steer the track in a new direction.

Title: Other Life
Review: It takes a good deal of bravery to write and record songs that are so naked and unflinching, and it pays off: Savage's courage and palpable investment in the material makes it easy to connect and empathize with his subject matter.

Title: If You Leave
Review: There are a lot of topic sentences about If You Leave that won’t tell that story--the defiant moment, clearer and less guarded revelation--but it’s captivating to watch Tonra shake off the burden she’s locked herself up with.

Title: On Desire
Review: There's parts of On Desire that feel all too familiar, and there's parts that simply don't work. For every negative though there's a melody or lyric that makes it shine, and for that, the band are worth sticking with, at least for the time being.

Title: Revelation
Review: True, Newcombe's fondness for repetition allows him to take half an idea and stretch it out until it disappears into a chorus-less fug. But it's all pleasingly reassuring, like stepping into a well-curated vintage furniture shop.

Title: Out of Touch in the Wild
Review: The rock vibe of past records is all but gone but not completely as the final song, “Brio” smokes along.

Title: Nightmare Ending
Review: It's a long glorious exhalation of energies not actually dissipated, as it seemed for a while, but only multiplying in force under suppression.

Title: Intoxication
Review: The slick Shaggy sex formula is intact, plus he steps off the well-worn with booming first single 'Church Heathen,' already scorching JA parties with its keen indictment of religious hypocrisy, and 'All About Love,' featuring his raw, ragged, utterly compelling singing voice. 'Body a Shake' comes harder than before.

Title: Iteration
Review: Nostalgic, dramatic and not exactly short on synth, Iteration is the kind of album necessary to help us battle through the rest of 2017.

Title: Black Swan
Review: The band's experimental side (the side that made them good) has suffered, as if "Wires" was the new blueprint on how to write successful songs.

Title: One Track Mind
Review: The washy blend of acoustic dirges, blown-out guitar tones, and lonely psychedelic character sketches solidify into an increasingly accessible sound from this once ungrounded act, without losing any of the group's character or inspiration.

Title: DÃ©jÃ  Vu
Review: It hardly bears Moroder's personality at all.

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: There are a couple of moments where she still feels like the sum total of a very tasteful record collection, where she struggles to make herself heard over the echoes of Joni Mitchell and Dylan's thin wild mercury sound. More often, though, she cuts through her influences, and rings out loud and clear; when she does, it's a very diverting sound indeed.

Title: Sequel To The Prequel
Review: The bawled slur that passes for Doherty's vocals is less agreeable the older he gets, while the flaccid grunge plaints and raggedy punk thrashes have diminishing appeal.

Title: Caer
Review: For a 13-track album, the majority is forgettable and doesn't live up to the colourful elements of Lewis's previous releases. The lack of energy on Caer leaves a longing for more originality and creativity he has once given us.

Title: Idealism
Review: Despite the echoes of their past on this second long-play set, Digitalism's perfectly timed return is more about fondness than contempt.

Title: So Much Fun
Review: Thugger has performed vocally like this before on Jeffrey, lyrically like this on Slime Season and emotionally like this on Beautiful Thugger Girls but not consistently have they all converged together like this, forging the ultimate Young Thug Voltron. Plus, this top-notch performance has been spread across such perfectly paced beats. Quite literally, the production on this album is just a blast.

Title: Imarhan
Review: An assured, ear-opening debut.

Title: Interiors
Review: If another goal of art could be said to remove humanity, if only for a moment, from the physical world by using the tools of the very same physical world, Interiors has followed all the rules of architecture to make a building that floats.

Title: Everybody Looking
Review: It will please fans looking for Another Gucci Mane mixtape. Everyone else will likely find it a bit spotty. Certain songs fall into familiar--now six- or seven-year-old--formulas. His vocals, no doubt out of practice, sound a bit rusty. But most of all, it just feels unfinished, rushed.

Title: Vapor City
Review: It's the intricate musical subtleties Stewart weaves through them that blow your hair back.

Title: Magnificent City
Review: Magnificent City is lazy and inept, devoid of force and inspiration and chemistry.

Title: Observator
Review: While the album may improve on its predecessor, Observator still finds the Raveonettes engaging in far too many self-indulgent habits: They've left Hot Topic, but they don't seem to know where they're headed next.

Title: A Fever Dream
Review: Musically, there’s a playful restlessness throughout, with rock and electronica constantly being twisted into imaginative shapes.

Title: My True Story
Review: It's a tasteful genre exercise that employs old-fashioned conventions with strategic license.

Title: All That You Can't Leave Behind
Review: The chaotic electronic density of U2's last few efforts has been replaced by sticky, bite-size tunes -- sporting candy-sweet choruses that are often underlined by unabashed words of love.

Title: These People
Review: These People functions as a pleasing adult alternative record.

Title: Gold Record
Review: For the most part Gold Record is a deftly woven and cosily feathered little nest of songs. Settle in.

Title: Sigh No More
Review: Thanks to a volatile mix of the uplifting and gloomy--there's a bitter murder tale ("Dust Bowl Dance") and lingering visions of death ("Timshel")--Sigh No More transfixes.

Title: Cherry Bomb
Review: Musically, he is maturing before our very eyes.

Title: Satan's Circus
Review: The vibe is ultimately too sterile to be compelling, let alone truly malevolent. [5 Jun 2005]

Title: Any Day
Review: The electronics of their earlier work are pared back, leaving their comfort zone reupholstered with goose down. But it’s no great shakes, because the Sea and Cake are one of those bands who essentially put out the same album over and over again, which doesn’t matter all that much--no one else sounds remotely like them.

Title: The Head and The Heart
Review: If well-crafted folk-pop leaves you feeling lukewarm, by all means join the naysayers; otherwise, I'll be on the side of those dancing and singing along.

Title: I-Empire
Review: I-Empire is so in thrall to Edge's guitar sound circa 1984 it could almost be the work of a /u2 tribute band. [Dec 2007, p.112]

Title: Poses
Review: Although ever so slightly more modern in feel than his critically adored 1998 self-titled debut, Poses is still built upon Wainwright's mastery of highly composed, early-20th-century popular-song styles. [July 2001, p.86]

Title: No Boys Allowed
Review: Though Hilson sings like a sweet-voiced dream throughout, No Boys Allowed is muddled and devoid of the gutsiness the title leads us to expect.

Title: IV
Review: Indeed, they can rock. But, inevitably, their writing here lacks the epic imagery and themes that cemented the rock gods into the canon, and thus doesn’t bewitch in the same way. Black Mountain defend the temple ably, at least.

Title: Skeleton Tree
Review: The songs are pillowed by vaporous electronic backing that recalls the slow-moving, aquatic drift of Push The Sky Away and the sonic explorations of Cave and Ellis' Minimalist Soundtracks. [Dec 2016, p.26]

Title: Sonic Boom
Review: Will it provide decent accompaniment for a Gene Simmons blood-belching performance in a packed arena? This big, dumb, catchy record passes that test.

Title: Giants Of All Sizes
Review: Perhaps their greatest album since their Mercury Prize-winning breakthrough The Seldom Seen Kid, released over a decade ago.

Title: The Heart Speaks in Whispers
Review: Rae feels light here, no longer weighed down by her past and suddenly able to address pain with emotional wisdom. The Heart Speaks in Whispers is a summer record that reveals the warmth in silver linings.

Title: Quazarz: Born on a Gangster Star
Review: Both albums [Quazarz: Born On A Gangsta Star and Quazarz vs. The Jealous Machines] deliver uneasy commentary on modern times, and the music that supports it is as equally challenging.

Title: 'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!
Review: As it is, it's a new Godspeed album and it's a good one, but when you have set your standards as high as they have, it can only seem like a failure. [Nov 2012, p.59]

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: It's easily his most personal work yet, and even though the story of his mother's difficult life is hardly universal, the results are deeply moving and richly evocative.

Title: Horrorscope
Review: It's another conventional rock record, thrashing guitar hooks and throbbing bass lines are in place, but frontman Max Collins has lyrically improved.

Title: Our Love
Review: [An] irresistibly immersive fourth album. [Nov 2014, p.89]

Title: Saturdays = Youth
Review: Like it or not, the 1980s are part of who we are and Gonzales' homage to the decade is the closest thing to perfect he's achieved.

Title: Anything Goes
Review: Kelley and Hubbard are genial enough hosts but the preponderance of monochromatic, midtempo tracks--occasionally featuring awkward, rapid fire rap-sung interludes--blend into an indistinguishable blur that may be sufficient while the party lasts but aren’t as memorable after the buzz wears off.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: If this is indeed the next stage of Moore’s career rather than just another one-off project, it’s an assured, though sporadically underwhelming, soft launch.

Title: Of the Blue Colour of the Sky
Review: Bursting with promise, OK are more than their name suggests.

Title: Everything Now
Review: More comfortable in their dancing shoes, Arcade Fire have it both ways on Everything Now, zeroing in on our modern malaise while taking inspiration from more concise dance-pop styles.

Title: The Fool
Review: At times, as on Free, there’s a danger of things crossing into the formulaic big-pop sound the Mumfords have spread through the charts. But more often, these songs – written with Passion Pit’s Michael Angelakos among others--are imbued with enough subtle strangeness to remain beguiling.

Title: High as Hope
Review: It’s raw, human, stripped of all excess and laid bare--and it’s quite possibly the most beautiful thing the band has ever released. Near perfection.

Title: Declaration of Dependence
Review: Percussion is nowhere to be found on the group's latest release, Declaration of Dependence, and the pair's Simon & Garfunkel-esque harmonies are less dynamic than they once were. But there are still plenty of bright spots.

Title: Engineers
Review: An incredibly warm and organic sounding debut.

Title: Random Desire
Review: This new solo album is at its strongest when Greg finds new ways to express himself. Where there are traces of the Whigs’ soul power, as on Sempre and The Tide, it’s hard not to compare the songs unfavourably to his day job.

Title: Franz Ferdinand
Review: This is a terrifically exciting debut, imbued with a zest, energy and songwriting flair that warrants -- perhaps even commands -- some sort of attention.

Title: The Exodus Suite
Review: Genre-bending but with a common gothic ambience throughout, Gemma Ray is equal parts story teller and musician as she skillfully intertwines a diverse collection of 12 independent chapters in the form of songs that stand strong individually, but intensify when put together.

Title: Significant Changes
Review: It’s Jayda G’s own vocal work that ultimately unites Significant Changes, accenting hooks with fizzy ad-libs, steering tunes with sprawling falsettos and resounding in the deep.

Title: Sexwitch
Review: At worst, Sexwitch marks a fascinating detour in an already accomplished career.  At best, it’s a creatively adventurous standalone release. In actuality, it likely falls somewhere in the middle.

Title: Rotten Apple
Review: [It] works best when he's rapping alongside guests.

The likes of "Do Exist" and "The Loop" come close, but the lack of those few really memorable synth-pop gems stops this very good album from being an excellent one.

Review: All shallow, all pure as a result--pure escape, pure delight, and, as the cavalcade of gospel postures at the end makes clear, pure spiritual yearning.

Title: Party Rock

Review: True to form, the album commands nothing less than the gluttonous nature of its mainspring: a hearty, robust experience that demands an insatiable appetite.

Review: The Crying Light--a haunting collection of ballads that play like transmissions from a mournful, elegant alien--nearly equals its predecessor.

Review: A delight, from start to finish.

Title: Burning the Threshold

Title: The College Dropout
Review: A flawed, overlong, hypocritical, egotistical, and altogether terrific album.

Review: It’s exceptional stuff.

Review: The real measure of Knoxville's success is that it always feels it has ended too soon.

Title: Watching Dead Empires in Decay
Review: Truthfully, this is a record not for the faint of heart as listening to it may cause palpitations, but those brave enough to journey into Kirby’s mystifying landscape will be fascinated with the rotting corpse-like stuff that he brings to the table under this pseudonym.

Title: Carnation
Review: If it often gets over on mood rather than message, Gibson turns out to be an impressively good mood guy, and the production (by Gibson and Randall Dunn) gets the details right, making Carnation sound like a middle-of-the-night album for a man whose sense of style is matched only by his knack for poor choices.

Title: Psychic Lovers
Review: Though Psychic Lovers sometimes feels a little labored, it proves that the seemingly accidental brilliance of Dinner's earlier music was anything but.

Title: Underwater Cinematographer
Review: Although several of the tracks on Underwater Cinematographer lack a certain individuality, the remainder brim with creativity and the notion that there's something spectacular around the corner.

Title: We Built a Fire
Review: Repeated listens bring a number of sounds to the surface--a hint of heartland twang, plenty of pop melodies, and an endearing messiness (evident in the half-sung, half-shouted background vocals)--but We Built a Fire is mostly concerned with mood, which it casts during the first minute of running time.

Title: Putting the Days to Bed
Review: Even though Days To Bed is littered with the sort of tunes that indie pop fans obsessively search for, it suffers the same fate as the group’s previous releases. By the time you reach the final 25% of the album, you’re more than ready to go to bed — and not in a good way.

Title: Didn't He Ramble
Review: There's a real craftman at work here. [Nov 2015, p.111]

Title: Evil Urges
Review: They're not the first current band to find new value in the big sounds and large lapels of Fleetwood Mac and the Eagles, but appear to be doing so without irony and something approaching childlike zeal.

Title: American Gangster
Review: The "Gangster" portion of the record is, as you'd expect, effortlessly strong.

Title: In a Dim Light
Review: Complex, and replete with glitches, slow beats and breakdowns, In A Dim Light is as captivating as 'Condors', yet with an evident sense of renewed direction and focused calm and quietude.

Title: The Spirit of Apollo
Review: That overstuffed guest list doesn't necessarily work to the exclusive benefit of The Spirit of Apollo, as sometimes the clutter makes it hard to hear precisely what kind of music Zegon and Spiegel are trying to make here.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: There is no shortage of shimmery songcraft here.

Title: Change
Review: Showcases a band testing themselves by going down an untravelled road while still maintaining their identity.

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: Coldplay rage in their own lovably goofy way.

Title: Pure Comedy
Review: The music stays cozy, supportive and unobtrusively inventive, placing luminous details behind Mr. Tillman’s sympathetic, ever melodic voice.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: Ashes & Fire might mark the first time he could ever been described as simply dull.

Title: Club Nites
Review: Far from the fools of their name, Dumb are onto something pretty magnetic.

Title: High Violet
Review: High Violet sees no need to tinker with a successful formula, and because of that it's less a step forward than a refined restatement of well-known strengths.

Title: Swisher
Review: It’s something you can really sink your teeth into--and derive pleasure from its airy and light techno journey into the skull.

Title: Luxury Problems
Review: Though he's had plenty of strong releases in the past, this one has the inspired feeling of an artist truly finding his footing--a breakthrough, in other words.

Title: The Diary
Review: It’s an album that’s a handy reminder of how inseparable weirdo experimentalism is from the badass mainstream in hip hop.

Title: Humbug
Review: This is oval-shaped music, circling around the tracks; it’s accomplished, but not particularly infectious.

Title: Centipede Hz
Review: Simultaneously the most and the least pop record of the autumn.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: Fortunately, Darnielle's writing usually carries it, grounding his songs to keep them memorable and offer entryways back into something that continually seeks the transcendence its title suggests.

Title: Doo - Wops & Hooligans
Review: Doo-Wops & Hooligans kicks up no fuss, and shortchanges on its promise of both doo-wop and hooliganism.

Title: Never Better
Review: It's a tumbler, a series of good thoughts that get lost in development.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: A shake up in the lyric department would be nice to see next time around, but on this outing Lana Del Rey is able to sell it with striking vocal performances and breathtaking compositions.

Title: Consolers of the Lonely
Review: Consolers of the Lonely is heftier than its predecessor, both in its Led Zep-go-garage wig-outs and in its cosmic balladeering.

Title: E = MCÂ²
Review: E=MC2 is Carey's most-fun album, and her best.

Title: Dusk
Review: Ultimate Painting may not reach the commercial heights of either guy's main band, but it is fully the equal and in some ways more interesting. Certainly if you're a fan of Veronica Falls or Mazes, you'll want to check this out right away.

Title: Sic Alps
Review: Sic Alps towers above the rest of the ample retro garage acts today, in both scope and measure.

Title: Spiritual Songs for Lovers to Sing
Review: It’s a combination that is gratifyingly peculiar and, thanks to a knack for satisfying toplines, holds a significant amount of jubilant appeal.

Title: Heartbeat Radio
Review: Heartbeat Radio is Lerche's most eclectic outing yet, with no overarching concept beyond a consistent level of excellence.

Title: Resistance
Review: A memorable, albeit inconsistent, record by an unabashed futurist steeped in funk, jazz, electronica, and everything in-between.

Title: Hope In Dirt City
Review: Hope In Dirt City is the most soulful and hazy he's ever sounded.

Title: Hour of the Dawn
Review: Like the rest of her discography, Hour of the Dawn a short and sweet collection of music for and from the heart, only this time around it's played right from the guts.

Title: Reflektor
Review: Listen closely enough to Reflektor--and give it the patience that clearly went into its recording--and that old Arcade Fire burns. It’s just a different kind of flame.

Title: Salon Des Amateurs
Review: Whether or not these songs are ever played next to the latest dance music sensation at a club, Salon des Amateurs is a bold, accomplished work that ranks among Hauschka's most exciting albums.

Title: Cope
Review: It certainly sounds like black and white and red, but while it’s quite clearly in a better way than a sunburnt penguin, its attempts at something completely dramatic and bold aren’t quite as successful as Spielberg’s iconic scene.

Title: America's Velvet Glory
Review: The Molochs are on their own trip, one that spins old ideas with new energy.

Title: Wonky
Review: Wonky restores the Hartnolls' reputation among electronic music's greats. [May 2012, p.103]

Title: Owl John
Review: Hutchison may seem down on himself on this record, but the music is full of creative energy.

Title: The Only Place
Review: Elsewhere, the tunes sag rather than sing, and Bethany Constantino's lyrics about being bored and lazy become cloudily familiar.

Title: Earthly Delights
Review: The highlights demonstrate that these guys have yet to exhaust their uncanny vision, but by and large this is Lightning Bolt doing a Lightning Bolt album.

Title: Be Good
Review: With a gift for creating memorable melodies allied with a strong storytelling narrative, he comes across like a sophisticated jazz version of Bill Withers. [Apr 2012, p.94]

Title: Islands
Review: A lovely, emotionally poignant album that moves Durant’s music far ahead of her somewhat gauzy, even reticent debut and into far more accessible waters.

Title: Bittersweet World
Review: She has to, you know, sing. You can tell she's not into it.

Title: Volcano
Review: Volcano may rank as more of a technical progression than an artistic one, but it’s no less impressive for that.

Title: Citizen Zombie
Review: The Pop Group’s signature mode of deviant funk, with dub effects and tangled guitar distortion wielded with razoring disregard for polite taste, is still disconcerting and the focus of their anger is still sharp, albeit refracted through allegory and apocalyptism.

Title: Born This Way
Review: Please enjoy someone actually putting a bit of effort and imagination back into pop, and keep the sneering and lazy comparisons in check. Not that they can take anything away from what is, simply, a marvellous record.

Title: Constant Image
Review: For all the remarkably fluid dialogue in Constant Image, none of that would matter if the songs didn’t connect in the first place. And reader, boy do they! Songs like 'Punching Up' and 'Pressure' sound like lost gems that popped up on your local college radio station.

Title: Logic Will Break Your Heart
Review: It’s not a pretty record; while of course, being at times a very pretty record.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: World Peace is a frustrating experience, moving too quickly between temperaments and overstaying its welcome by a good 20 minutes.

Title: The Garden
Review: The Garden differs from their debut, Simple Things, and its followup, Where It Falls, in that it scales back the soundscapes in favor of a more upbeat, organic, and song-based sound. [#14]

Title: Phosphene Dream
Review: Sorta silly lyrics like "Rollin' fast down I-35/Supersonic overdrive" indicate the road that Phosphene Dream navigates: It's all blacktop stretching through reverberating vistas--ultracool if a little predictable.

Title: Song For Our Daughter
Review: Marling's seventh solo LP has the clarity, mastery and quiet strength of a folk-rock classic. [Jul 2020, p.110]

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: Throughout the two albums, Lambchop effortlessly and repeatedly cross country, rock, soul, jazz, and cinematic borders.  [combined review of both discs]

Title: Silent Hour / Golden Mile
Review: Rossen brings to this EP the meticulous craftsmanship we've come to expect from his work, but in Silent Hour he's created something rare: a rendering of isolation that feels sincere but never maudlin.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Clocking in with 14 wide-screen songs, "Forgiveness Rock Record" sounds trim and taut at nearly every turn. McEntire's nimble production keeps all the layers distinct, even when the band is whipping up a tender maelstrom of fey orchestration.

Title: Spiral Shadow
Review: Whether bellowed by Philip Cope or sung with witchy intensity by Laura Pleasants, just about every song has a chorus that immediately stamps itself on your brain. In that sense, Spiral Shadow is damn near a pop album.

Title: Rose Windows
Review: Judging by Rose Windows’ now final album, the shame is that differences, whatever they were, could not be overcome because a growing, developing collection of musicians was just beginning to dent the consciousness of a much larger audience. Instead of eagerly anticipating their next move, we are therefore left to cling to their last hurrah.

Title: Nocturama
Review: Cave has managed to move away from the stifling atmosphere and the false captive environment of No More Shall We Part and somehow create a Cave world where The Bad Seeds can indeed stretch, howl, riff, sniff, grind and bark with a freedom unheard on record since 1993's Live Seeds. [Album of the Month, Feb 2003, p.84]

Title: Reality Killed the Video Star
Review: Like the verbal tricks he loves to employ, the appeal of Robbie Williams might still be too tricky to be truly universal. But this album proves that he is a great brain teaser.

Title: Illinois
Review: Stevens is simply one of the most talented artists creating music right now, period.

Title: Paradise
Review: It's not sonically unique. Yet there's a charm here.

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You
Review: Somewhat hit or miss pastiche pop, Parallax Error Beheads You is harder to like that it should be.

Title: The Facts of Life
Review: If you like well-constructed pop/rock music with female vocals, it's definitely worth a look.

Title: Let The Dancers Inherit The Party
Review: With an occasional propensity for mindless wigouts slightly curbed, it's windswept anthems a-go-go on their best album for years. [May 2017, p.96]

Title: Dirty Baby
Review: DIRTY BABY is a singular accomplishment, presented in a fashion that demands more of the listener's attention but buy pays off handsomely.

Title: Sea Change
Review: A great record to play at 3 A.M. [#10, p.112]

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: Titanic Rising presents an immensely elegant journey to a different place and time; in equal parts beautifully delicate and powerful.

Title: The Betrayed
Review: Whether a fanbase reared on moshpit anthems is ready for such artful desolation remains to be seen, but as an exercise in skin-shedding and score-settling The Betrayed is brutally effective. [Feb 2010, p. 103]

Title: Gentle Stream
Review: With prog moodiness and pastoral folkiness both hanging heavily over The Amazing, it's the more psychedelic edges that twirl around the songs, dragging them into tangled and weird territory, that makes Gentle Stream occasionally exceptional.

Title: Idlewild
Review: Idlewild is a dazzling album. [Oct 2006, p.124]

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: Nine Types Of Light suggest they're settling in nicely. [May 2011, p.78]

Title: Save Your Season
Review: It's all too hammy, too rich to absorb.

Title: Banks
Review: It's a strong album and shows once and for all that Paul Banks doesn't need Interpol, Interpol needs him.

Title: Tha Carter IV
Review: The stream-of-consciousness id that Iggy Pop might once have envied is still on display, but here it feels corralled into a pen of predictable similes and metaphors.

Title: Chemical Chords
Review: On Chemical Chords, there’s nothing in the 14 pleasant-sounding tracks that we haven’t heard them sing about--in breathy, jazz-cat-inflected French--several dozen times before.

Title: The Stoned Immaculate
Review: It works just fine and follows the blueprint of most major label projects today. The thing is that, in doing so, Curren$y loses some of the magic that makes him a true original.

Title: Louden Up Now
Review: The music is still missing one crucial element—hooks. There really aren’t any of which to speak, and no amount of production skill and instrumental finesse is able to mask that.

Title: Grey Oceans
Review: http://www.tinymixtapes.com/music-review/cocorosie-grey-oceans

Title: Varcharz
Review: Two of the last tracks, “Bertney” and especially “Retphase,” end up succeeding where most of the album is lacking in finding the perfect balance between left-field beats and compulsive rhythms. Too bad the rest of the album doesn’t hit the same mark. [#15]

Title: Bloodsports
Review: Suede deserve some credit for being one of the few reunited bands to actually risk their reputation by recording a new album and whilst there is nothing on 'Bloodsports' as gloriously epic as 'Stay Together' or as bat-shit crazy as 'Introducing The Band', it should be viewed as a partial success.

Title: Quiet and Peace
Review: Buffalo Tom provides a warm blanket on a cold, dark night of the soul. [No. 150, p.51]

Title: Revelation
Review: Familiar BJM territory perhaps, but they still inhabit a different, more enticing cosmos to their peers. [Jul 2014, p.87]

Title: Pretty Ugly
Review: DVA is most successful when he edits out the excess and focuses his production on a handful of strong elements. As a producer, it's self-control, not talent, that he's lacking.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: This record isn't a revelation, perhaps, but it is rewarding nonetheless.

Title: Half Smiles of the Decomposed
Review: As a send-off... it's not quite the full parade. [Sep 2004, p.104]

Title: No Better Than This
Review: It might sound like a stunt, but results in a deeply felt and surprisingly enjoyable exploration of American Vernacular music. [Sep 2010, p.93]

Title: Fear Fun
Review: Tillman varies things up on Fear Fun, reveals an adventurous palette, and makes what may be his best album to date.

Title: CYRK
Review: Le Bon is doodling, but as she refines it, CYRK becomes a clear piece of work with a well-clarified core.

Title: We Have Amnesia Sometimes
Review: These ambient drones might sound unfinished, but in their unhurried, unpretentious vibrations they capture the timeless yawning void of our current daily existence, the perennially narcotized blur of our homebound, shutdown society. (It’s also, um, great music to write to.) If you’re sympathetic to Yo La Tengo’s less formal and radio-friendly moments, you might respond well to this one.

Title: God Loves Ugly
Review: In a hip-hop landscape littered with studio gangsters, pimps on wax, and thugs in need of hugs, Slug proves yet again on God Loves Ugly that the bravest move a rapper can make is simply to be himself.

Title: Prairie Wind
Review: Seems largely unable to go far beyond generic musical stylings and rather lifeless, matt[e]-finish reportage. [Nov 2005, p.97]

Title: Sister Cities
Review: This record really scrapes past [No Closer To Heaven] with so much more heart and soul. ... The most well-produced and expansive sound I've heard from TWY.

Title: Regifted Light
Review: Baby Dee may be writing about slugs and snails, cowboys and pie, but she is a serious artist worthy of sincere consideration.

Title: The Violet Hour
Review: As impressive as the early singles were, the material on The Violet Hour is often commensurate, sometimes superior.

Title: Seeds
Review: Although she is a great poet and lyricist, a little restraint would help in these situations. Seeds is still a great record nonetheless, and shows Muldrow hasn't yet lost focus since Umsindo.

Title: Oh No
Review: Oh No is a gorgeous and deadly pop music manifesto that proves yet again the sad girls are not vulnerable and silent subjects.

Title: Surfing the Void
Review: In defence of Surfing the Void, it's certainly not an album I'd describe as 'bad' per se--it's just a massive disappointment.

Title: I Hate Music
Review: They’re love songs about persistence, and that’s embedded in the sound of the record; you don’t need a lyric sheet to hear it.

Title: Kala
Review: Her most anticipated follow-up is again the most cross cultural jam you'll hear this year. [Sep/Oct 2007, p.129]

Title: The Both
Review: New Wave heartthrob and master songcrafter Aimee Mann gets welcome vocal and guitar snarl from Ted Leo, a post-punk heartthrob in his own right whose unfussy attack benefits from Mann's melodic and harmonic touch.

Title: Terroir Blues
Review: At 23 songs... his second solo full length is as bloated as a rummy's liver. Still, it's good.

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: Death Cab still sound like Death Cab, but Codes and Keys is undoubtedly the least pop record they've made since breaking through to the mainstream with their last indie-situated effort, 2003's Transatlanticism.

Title: Paper Trail
Review: Though you'd be justified in hanging this writer for conflating person and persona, you're asked to contemplate the uneasy positivity that chacterizes Paper Trail's three mot popular songs. [Dec 2008, p.74]

Title: Lo Moon
Review: These kinds of lyrics paint pictures that can be simultaneously morose and inspiring, avoiding the stock repetition of 2010's mainstream love songs by imbuing them with the bold creativity and vicissitude of songwriting in the '80s and early '90s. All in all, Lo Moon is an impressive debut.

Title: 24 Karat Gold: Songs From The Vault
Review: The result is the best sounding and most consistent collection of solo Nicks since her '80s peak. [Dec 2014, p.90]

Title: Waiting For The Moon
Review: Few bands can get away with being in a holding pattern like Tindersticks.

Title: NY's Finest
Review: With NY's Finest, Pete Rock, whose place in hip-hop is alread firmly cememted alongside masters like Premier, may not go beyond expectations, but he certainly meets them comfortably.

Title: Night on Fire
Review: Clogging their previously supple grooves with banal guitar bluster and noxious singing, VHS Or Beta don't set the Night On Fire; they just dampen your spirits. [Oct 2004, p.148]

Title: VII
Review: While the band’s penchant for steadying, shimmering guitars and unexpected use of instruments certainly appears on VII, it’s not enough to overshadow this album’s lack of originality.

Title: (Breach)
Review: Generic, maybe, but very nicely done. [Nov. 2000, p.117]

Title: One of the Boys
Review: Where it hits the mark, One Of The Boys is sparky and accomplished--though entirely disposable--pop.

Title: The Private Press
Review: The Private Press is a more diverse collection of styles and sounds, and still surpasses anything else out there.

Title: The Livelong Day
Review: They approach the tradition with an awe and wonder that especially percolates into the instrumentals. ... Their most extreme statement yet. [Dec 2019, p.89]

Title: There Is No Elsewhere
Review: Their latest warms the electronic pot with quirky pastoralism--brass, melodica, clattering-teacup percussion and tangible emotional warmth. [Oct 2018, p.94]

Title: Joy
Review: Joy is a journey not to be missed.

Title: After Laughter
Review: Where 2013's Paramore found the group tentatively transitioning from their pop-punk roots toward a multi-layered '80s synth-pop sound, After Laughter reveals them having beautifully completed the transformation.

Title: Go-Go Boots
Review: If the music on Go-Go Boots is less physical than what the Drive-By Truckers  typically deliver, it's emphatic and passionate, with an impressive sense of dynamics and as much soul as these folks have ever summoned in the studio -- they've rocked a lot harder, but they've never cut a more natural and telling groove.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Eminem was really rapping across an entire LP again (something I’d never say elsewhere: Rihanna is not missed), stans were going to like it too much, while his inflammatory remark is sure to prevent most any of the unconverted from being able to engage with the music itself.

Title: Are You Serious
Review: There is some devastating music on Are You Serious, and there is some beautiful music, too; often these passages are one and the same. It sounds like a natural progression for Andrew Bird, yet in places it’s like nothing you’d expect from the singer. It is, for these reasons and many more, a triumph.

Title: Love Songs For Robots
Review: Whilst it’s a brave attempt to explore new lands outside their comfort zone, it’s one that isn’t quite as rewarding and rich as Patrick Watson would have hoped.

Title: Love Is a Four Letter Word
Review: For a listener who's only been aware of Mraz by reputation, this is no instant-fix point of entry. It relies on past experiences, knowledge of what the artist is capable of rather than anything he delivers with consistency across these 12 songs.

Title: The Dew Lasts An Hour
Review: It's '80s pop, but not as you know it. [Sep 2014, p.69]

Title: Cold House
Review: It's definitely a great step for the group.

Title: Infinity on High
Review: FOB could've cut an album's worth of club hits and still found an audience. Its refusal to do so shows it still knows the difference between selling records and making fans.

Title: You Are Not Alone
Review: At 71, Staples still knows how to hang tough and shows no signs of slowing down.

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
Review: Despite its hype, its expectations, its blown up sound, and its many production flourishes, Bon Iver is nothing more than a solid placeholder album.

Title: Hotel
Review: Impeccably made, hedonistic, lovelorn, catchy, compelling. But spiritual, messianic, visionary? Not by a long shot.

Title: Hang Cool Teddy Bear
Review: As is generally the case with Loaf's oeuvre, the ridiculousness of the enterprise is redeemed somewhat by a recognition of its own absurdity. [Jul 2010, p.112]

Title: Americana
Review: The rest is solid if rarely spectacular, with the Crazy Horse rumble making a welcome return to Young's modern day repertoire.

Title: Furfour
Review: The duo's sad, passionate vocals readily recall peak-era Depeche Mode, but the instrumentation is much more organic, and the production is far more atmospheric and multi-layered, even verging on hallucinatory at times.

Title: Lupercalia
Review: While he succeeds fairly well at ensuring that Lupercalia spends its every minute displaying his emotions on its sleeve, it's fairly safe to say that this record won't exactly storm the charts.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: It's derivative and is a near hybrid of Mew, the Postal Service, M83 and Empire of the Sun, but it's perfectly likeable without ever inspiring outright love.

Title: Yuck
Review: It's the seamless simplicity in which the record flows that defines this masterful debut.

Title: Imperial Blaze
Review: Every single cliche held dear with the English language appears to have been right-click-Synonymed here.

Title: In Our Bedroom After the War
Review: The edge is smoothed down here, the bitterness outweighs the resignation, and strangely, the two sound stronger on their own. [Oct 2007, p.112]

Title: Open Your Heart
Review: Open Your Heart is smartly sequenced to metabolize genre and morph like a masterful DJ mix, subtly rationing out its true peaks even while seemingly going full-throttle throughout.

Title: Stuffed & Ready
Review: Stuffed & Ready is their finest accomplishment yet of such a daunting endeavor. And with its personal perspectives on the effects of the current cultural zeitgeist, it is not simply a great rock record, but an important document in the early days of 2019.

Title: Fever
Review: By far Kylie's best album to date.

Title: Nursing Home
Review: Let's Wrestle has developed a studied, wide-ranging brute that embraces their oddball wit to a greater degree.

Title: You Had It Coming
Review: What's missing is the modern edge that would give Beck's fiery playing a better context. Too often, the techno-funk rhythm driving the action here sounds stiffly electronic, like a Chemical Brothers castoff from the Nineties.

Title: Renacer
Review: Renacer paints a clear portrait of a band lacking the courage and will to abandon the tendencies they have clearly grown out of and no longer stand behind.

Title: When the Heart Emerges Glistening
Review: Akinmusire easily trumps Truffaz in the area of technical skill. His agile delivery and rounded, even-tempered tone recall facets of Kenny Dorham and Dennis Gonzalez in terms of burnished beauty and melodic alacrity.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: Mercer staggers from self-doubt to self-righteousness with each song, concealing razor blades inside his caramel-apple anthems. [Dec 2003, p.133]

Title: Busted Stuff
Review: Busted Stuff does strip away some of the Lillywhite mystique, dropping the exaggerated façade of "lost classic" status, but it further illustrates that Matthews' discards are often more compelling than his hits.

Title: Vespertine
Review: If there's one question to be raised with the album, it's that it's all simply so lush and nice that on some levels it fails to excite.

Title: Man of the Woods
Review: Unfortunately, Man Of The Woods’ thematic depth hasn’t quite caught up to the rest of his ambition. It’s not a fatal flaw, but it does make for a record that’s not quite as transcendent as it was built up to be.

Title: Real Gone
Review: Tough going and very samey, both in sonics and lyricism. Even if you enjoy the basic template, you may well run out of steam before the end.

Title: Never
Review: Levi's gift lays in kitschy nuance that is inherently pleasurable. And by diving into more conventional songs on Never, she loses a bit of this endearing personality.

Title: The Album About Nothing
Review: Throughout, Wale captures the weight of facing criticism and prejudice, of being an outsider looking in. Unfortunately, all that weight sinks his ambition as often as it lends his words impact.

Title: Live Forever
Review: As intriguing as Strange's music already is, Live Forever demonstrates that there's still tremendous potential left to unlock.

Title: Scintilli
Review: Scintilli slowly builds an all-absorbing world, [with] tension between fear and beauty. [Nov. 2011, p. 139]

Title: Public Domain: Songs from the Wild Land
Review: His music remains lively and contemporary even when he reworks traditional songs old enough to have their copyrights lapse into the public domain.

Title: Hexadic II
Review: At times the album becomes a little difficult to follow, with the momentum failing during the twists and turns of songs such as the slightly ponderous 'Vile Hell'. However Chasny often manages to claw back interest by adding slight colouring to the stark instrumental palette.

Title: The Way Out
Review: Partly cartoon, part Sesame Street, and with a healthy dose of consequence-free childish threats and violence, A Cold Freezin' Night is a welcome distraction to the meandering electro-drone that populates the rest of the album. But from here on in, it's a case of the law of diminishing returns.

Title: Earthtones
Review: Earthtones is a refreshing, playful set that hits a sweet spot between classic smooth soul and Jurvanen's pensive soft rock.

Title: Someday World
Review: The record is full of texture, and while it maybe isn't essential listening, it's a nice addition to both catalogs. [No. 109, p.55]

Title: In Limbo
Review: The airy-fairy aggression sometimes misses the mark. [Oct 2012, p.112]

Title: The Messenger
Review: So, no, Marr isn't exactly reinventing rock here--he already did that. The Messenger feels more like a tribute to his youth, to his home, and to all the musicians he's worked with over the past three decades.

Title: Destiny Fulfilled
Review: While it's no surprise that Destiny Fulfilled showcases advanced production values, the songwriting and vocal abilities are just as impressive. [Jan 2005, p.81]

Title: The Sunset Tree
Review: The Sunset Tree is one of the most volatile, affecting and coherent records he’s made yet.

Title: This Is Not The World
Review: Their sound is as big and manic as it’s always been, and the melodies as infectious, but the content slinks away from even the prickly personal politics that populated their first singles.

Title: No Mercy
Review: No Mercy takes T.I.'s recent experiences and frustrations, and effectively bottles them up into a potent and complete work.

Title: Ten
Review: Ten turns out a few good songs, but there are better solo records by each of its members.

Title: Smother
Review: Maybe it's because we've come to expect these guys to knock us out with each album, but Smother can't help but feel like a misstep.

Title: 1000 Days
Review: 1000 Days swings wildly from Black Sabbath-style paranoia to delicate Van Dyke Parks weirdness with an increasingly erudite command of garage rock while still managing to maintain much of the enigmatic charm of their previous releases.

Title: What Now
Review: Resonate with them, and you learn to speak about yourself in a way that carries meaning--and this is what What Now does best. Take a walk with this in your headphones and look at the people passing by; you’re allowed some isolation among others.

Title: Dear Life
Review: While there’s nothing that tugs at the heartstrings as much as Metarie did all those years ago, Dear Life is a reminder that Brendan Benson remains a terrific songwriter. He’s still too much of a quirky proposition to make it big, but Dear Life is a great big burst of sunshine in an all too dark world.

Title: Shrines

Title: The Ghost in Daylight
Review: An exquisite, unexpected gem. [Jun 2012, p.102]

Title: Sea of Cowards
Review: The Dead Weather have released another quickly recorded batch of entirely unmemorable, unpleasantly limp rock music showcasing Jack White’s increasingly irrelevant take on garage, blues, post-punk, and guitar refuse.

Title: Thank You Happy Birthday
Review: Though some of these songs would work well on their own, as a full length, they lack fluidity, consistency, and an overall theme that usually binds songs together.

Title: Providence

Title: Defying Gravity
Review: The album, co-produced by Urban and Dann Huff, has a smooth, lush sound that fits the material like a well-tailored suit.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: Her worldly-wise tone can still come over a little smug but give her time – she'll grow younger than this yet.

Title: Glacier
Review: Glacier is a journey.

Title: Out of the Game
Review: Wainwright shows that his pop legs, while shaky, haven't lost their footing. [No.87 p.60]

Title: Positive Force
Review: Happy music can sometimes seem superficial or lacking the emotional depth that music is "supposed to" capture. On the contrary, this album seems enlightened. It's happy and deep and complex and present, all at the same time.

Title: Young Prayer
Review: Rather than being a well-planned effort, the record is perhaps a means of casual, off-the-cuff catharsis for the artist. [#8, p.116]

Title: A Sleep & A Forgetting
Review: Simplicity is A Sleep's best value.

Title: Celestite
Review: For those who can keep up, some exultant and righteous highs await.

Title: Eagulls
Review: A single-minded, yet ultimately baffling experience. [Apr 2014, p.95]

Title: Erotic Reruns
Review: For the Yeasayer fans who enjoy their stranger stylings, this will fall out of rotation quicker than others; that doesn't make it bad, just not a favorite.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: Low has found what they do well and occasionally even exceed the standards they've set for themselves, but the stoicism and gradual build that comprises the band's best songs is at times defeated by their lyrical disinterest and repetition.

Title: Settle

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: A band clearly in awe of Jarvis Cocker's lyrics and the sound of spiky guitars. [Jul 2005, p.119]

Title: Naomi
Review: The Cave Singers find a way to remove the corniness from a jammy folk album, instead building Naomi with honest lyrics and a soothing ramble of guitars. [Apr 2013, p.86]

Title: Magic Potion

Title: Paradise
Review: There's a clearly dynamism between the couple, resulting in a unified performance and all that lets them down is a weakness in some of the songs, where a greater commercial edge might have initiated more interest. Sophisticated Steel City pop.

Title: Pacific Daydream
Review: Pacific Daydreams certainly doesn’t achieve the grandiose aims from the aforementioned inspiring proverb. That said, thankfully it is still a solid record which should satisfy fans.

Title: Dark End of the Street
Review: On the surface it’s all nicely put together but almost all these covers lack the passion.

Title: Wrong Creatures
Review: This album, like their previous works, except Howl, will do nothing to damage their legacy. Again, being non-threatening should not be viewed as a crime, especially here. Wrong Creatures scatter nearly great songs amongst forgettable ones.

Title: Hello Happiness

Title: Avonmore

Title: Favorite Waitress

Title: Miracle Temple

Title: Lion

Title: Kicking The National Habit
Review: This is reggae-inflected rock filtered through Gorillaz-style genre restlessness. [31 Mar 2006, p.65]

Title: DNA
Review: Well-manicured music that cannily plunders contemporary chart sounds and plonks a pitch-perfect harmony on them.

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: Their best album since BAGIA, possibly longer. [Apr 2014, p.92]

Title: Era Extrana
Review: For all of the fine craft on display, there's little obvious emotion. No matter, though, as there's room for everyone, and this makes for ideal driving music and it should sound sensational in a club.

Title: Roots & Crowns
Review: Things are more cinematic here, with every melody weaving through a mise-en-scene packed with dramatic incident. [Nov 2006, p.101]

Title: BLACKsummers'night

Title: Group Therapy

Title: Around The Sun

Title: Velociraptor!

Title: Be Your Own Pet

Title: Shine On

Title: Collisions

Title: Z

Title: Teenage Hate

Title: Little Dark Age
Review: A record that embodies a whole world of vulnerability, confusion and unsteadiness without losing shape. [Mar 2018, p.102]

Title: Some Cities
Review: Some Cities is not as strong as its two predecessors, but it does continue the band's run of consistently pleasing albums.

Title: A New Testament
Review: Overall, A New Testament is an improvement on Lysandre and demonstrates Owens’ ability to adapt to a multitude of different genres.

Review: Off-kilter energy, and their trademark honesty abound, LIFE - who received accolades such an ‘Album Of The Year’ listing from BBC Radio 1- prove with their second album that they are a quality band capable of making stand-out records more than once.

This is lacking neither imagination nor creativity, and is another transfixing exhibition of the beatmaker's command. The tracks are a little longer on average but still rarely exceed two minutes. What few tracks eclipse the mark never drag.

Title: A Loud Bash of Teenage Feelings
Review: Self-aware but undaunted, every moment sees the band pushing at the walls, daring to take it bigger, promising to make it more open.

There won’t be another album that comes out this year that sounds anything like this one.

Title: Remind Me Tomorrow
Review: Remind Me Tomorrow stands comfortably alongside Van Etten's finest work but also, excitingly, quite aside from it. Van Etten continues to amaze, move and impress with every move.

Review: Try as she may to distract with her strut and style as Skylar Grey, what resonates is the same kind of melodic turn of phrase that was apparent back when she was calling herself Holly Brook.

Title: Boxer
Review: A patchy, flawed effort.

Title: Crimes of Passion

Title: Caveman

It's also a notch or two down from her best, due to a handful of songs (mostly in the album's latter third) that aim for Gauthier's typically hard, simple honesty and instead land in the territory of gloomy repetition of aches and pains one would expect from this type of project.

Title: Under a Billion Suns
Review: Rollickingly great fun to listen to. [4 Mar 2006, p.31]

Review: That smile will have a difficult time leaving your face.

Review: Only takes a small step forward. [Dec 2005, p.108]

Title: Impressions

Review: In short: challenging stuff. [Dec 2016, p.113]

Title: Absolution

Title: Observator
Review: The record may not be their masterpiece, but it is an important piece of a surprisingly strong career.
