Review: It's not at Radiohead's level, simply because it's not as conceptually coherent; the lyrics may shock but they don't bite; the production (save for "On Sight" and a couple of others) is interesting but barely truly revolutionary within his own career arc, let alone when we count other contemporaries such as M.I.A. But while it might feel like an opportunity missed, at least Yeezus feels real.

Title: Slow Summits
Review: Nothing unduly groundbreaking here, yet at the same time always brutally refreshing.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: What makes Collapse Into Now so satisfying is that it isn't a return to form so much as a realization that the band R.E.M. are now isn't necessarily a bad thing to be.

Title: Black Velvet
Review: The result is naturally a bit of a mish-mash, but all of the material is terrific and the sequencing makes this seem like a finished product.

Title: Recording a Tape the Colour of the Light
Review: Less sparse than open, the songs resist the build-and-release structure that most other Montreal acts utilize, and they also refuse to ride a groove or play with distracting orchestration.

Title: Me and Armini
Review: Torrini captures a few joyful infatuations followed by a lot of lingering wounds; she’s vulnerable but never conquered.

Title: Sky City
Review: It's most persuasive setting is deluxe drive-time melancholia, purring with understated classicism. [Sep 2015, p.69]

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: Yet, something's missing. An emotional engagement, perhaps, because they sometimes seem positively embarrassed to play from the heart.

Title: Time Capsules II
Review: This is not his creative masterpiece, but there is no doubt that one is yet to come.

Title: The Chaos
Review: The emphasis is on big, radio-friendly choruses, four-part harmonies giving an euphoric dimension to their punk-influenced sound, with less of the earlier complex angularity. [Jun 2010, p.127]

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: Finn’s writing is sharper than ever, the various narratives driven less by the wordy exposition of yore than acute observation, devastating detail, by turns exclamatory, epigrammatic and grainily authentic.

Title: Scorpion
Review: Scorpion doesn't even come close to being one of his best; instead, it's a one-trick record stretched out into 25 endless tracks by an artist who's so deep into the self-obsessed, self-pitying rut he created for himself that he can't see daylight anymore.

Title: Revelations
Review: Its rote alternarock thrills are meagre vittles compared to the revolutionary metal the principle players have wrought in the past. [Oct 2006, p.110]

Title: American Utopia
Review: Left to his own devices, Byrne comes home to a screwball hymnal mode that, for all the lyrical left turns, can feel a little too predictable. [Apr 2018, p.29]

Title: Dear
Review: It’s psychedelic in a chthonic way and sounds as though it was recorded live in an underground cavern. It’s easily their most minimalist recording, a carefully monochrome study in sludgy drones.

Title: Starboy
Review: Despite an overlong hour-plus runtime and surplus of filler, Starboy does have highlights. ... But for longtime fans that believe the Weeknd is one of the major R&B artists of the decade, Starboy will ultimately seem like a disappointment.

Title: Afterglow
Review: Eventually the piano-based songs grow repetitive, while retaining their lush romanticism.

Title: D
Review: It doesn't matter whether White Denim are playing glowing, Lee Hazlewood-style country or chugging, meaty metal: the sound is always unmistakably their own.

Title: No Way Down
Review: Expanding and improving upon their already striking debut, No Way Down is a stunning accomplishment on so many levels: the amount of care and attention to detail that so clearly went into its creation; its stylistic uniqueness; and its sheer, subjective beauty.

Title: HYMNS
Review: Themes of loss, grief, and finding meaning in one’s life are buried deep within the subtext of the record. It’s just a shame that after listening to Hymns, we’re no closer to finding any kind of revelation or spiritual bliss.

Title: Shadows Collide With People
Review: Full of a lush, bubbling beauty that proves Frusciante's personal rehabilitation has taken his music further than ever.

Title: Luminous Night
Review: Chasny has completed the move started with "School of the Flower" into a more polished sound and Luminous Night seems to be the finest example from this new period of Six Organs of Admittance.

Title: Green Lanes
Review: Listening to the beautiful, restful and balanced sounds of Green Lanes, one hopes that they do indeed continue to work together for years and years.

Title: Pale Green Ghosts
Review: John Grant's songs can be characterised by extreme restlessness and the state of suffering mental and physical discomfort within one's being. The irony and often confronting honesty he brings to these problems ensure Pale Green Ghosts is extremely engaging and often engrossing. But Queen of Denmark it is not.

Title: Seeds
Review: The band is as sharp and bold as ever, finding new facets of a sound they spearheaded more than a decade ago.

Title: Sun
Review: Marshall still manages to wring pathos out of her work, if not to the same degree and not in the same way.

Title: Beerbongs & Bentleys
Review: Beerbongs & Bentleys contains banger after banger; it's an incredible drug-induced album.

Title: As High As the Highest Heavens and From the Center to the Circumference of the Earth
Review: Influences are obvious but the balance between light and dark is perfect here.

Title: Hypnotic Underworld
Review: The music is fantastic, but the sinking suspicion that there's something else going on that you can't possibly fathom becomes pervasive by album's end.

Title: Malody
Review: It’ll be a shock to the system for Futureheads fanatics anticipating herky-jerky guitar pop, but with the distraught Monster Again, nakedly vulnerable Thunder Song and the graceful, elegiac titular song standing out; it makes for an intensely cathartic and wholly absorbing experience for listeners prepared to dump their preconceptions at the door.

Title: Semicircle
Review: The instrumental smorgasbord can feel a little claustrophobic, as on the clattering All The Way Live, but overall The Go! Team's relentless party vibe emerges undiminished. [Feb 2018, p.96]

Title: Chaosmosis
Review: The rest of the record, for all its flash, leaves us in some bland middle ground- lacking the impact and craft of great pop music, but too fleeting in its appeal to work as anything else.

Title: Yesterday Was Forever
Review: Yesterday Was Forever was a record paid for by fans, and made for the fans.

Title: Rebound
Review: As on her previous albums, what makes Eleanor’s songwriting feel magical are the stories she tells and the tiny details she drops in.

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: This album rocks harder than 2003's The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place, and it's more sinister, too. [Mar 2007, p.67]

Title: The Sellout
Review: Nothing here will dramatically alter the arc of Gray's career, but The Sellout yields several jams worth hearing.

Title: Twenty-Five For The Rest of Our Lives
Review: Twenty-five for the Rest of Our Lives, their latest, is by far their best to date.

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: On the one hand, no 3 can sound frustrating unfinished. It seems as though something substantially more satisfying would have been attained had the band just stuck with it for a while longer. On the other, it's an enjoyable enough distraction not without its merits. Just don't think of it as the proper progression from no 2.

Title: By The Way
Review: Overall, the album leans more toward the melodic end of their oeuvre, but they have grown into this kinder, gentler mode organically, progressively working toward this groove little by little, album by album.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: It's far from an implosion, far from spectacular.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: Faced with the unexpected, Prass evolved, trading inward-facing confessionalism for outward-facing perseverance and releasing one of 2018’s minor masterpieces in the process. Plus, you can most certainly dance to it.

Title: Deep Trip
Review: e. This all-or-nothing approach makes Deep Trip an exhilarating listen that's just as capable of amping listeners up with its vital punk energy as it is freaking them out with its surging undercurrent of mind-altering sludge, making for yet another feather in the cap of Sacred Bones and their ever-growing lineup of head trip-inducing bands.

Title: Rispah
Review: The melodies drift rather aimlessly but the wonderfully groggy textures will stay with you like the best kind of sonic Valium. [Aug 2012, p.75]

Title: Party Store
Review: Michael Collins' garage rockers do Detroit techno. [March 2011, p. 97]

Title: Loud City Song
Review: This album is the sound of an excellent singer, songwriter, arranger, and, I’d argue, thinker translating those strengths into some of the most stirring music you’ll hear this year. Loud City Song may not be loud, but the echo it makes is unforgettable.

Title: California Nights
Review: Their third album is another impressive set.

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: The Future Will Come's title seems presciently loaded, its content primed for a mainstream meet'n'greet. [May 2009, p.108]

Title: The Age of Fracture
Review: The problem plaguing The Age of Fracture is inconsistency; the filler material is unmemorable and a little bland.

Title: Innundir Skinni
Review: Incidentally, this is what the title Innundir Skinni translates to loosely in English-- "under the skin"-- an apt description for Arnalds' gentle, peculiar and powerful music itself.

Title: Reality Check
Review: It's one big, horny wink--halfway between charming and totally sleazy. [Apr 2008, p.78]

Title: 100 Miles from Memphis
Review: Crow has returned to the kind of music she loved as a kid growing up in the shadow of one of America's hottest soul hotbeds. The result finds her sounding more at home and effortlessly exuberant than she has since Tuesday Night Music Club.

Title: Division Street
Review: Simon's songwriting can feel slight but in a dolorously cute way.

Title: Hendra
Review: Lyrics are reflective and well written--Watt is also a published author--but a middle-age malaise runs through these 10 tracks.

Title: Ancestral Star
Review: It's an atmosphere-setting collection, with little in the way of memorable riffs or melodies. But that's the point: Earth has needed to slow its roll for a minute now. Here's the inspiration.

Title: Babes Never Die
Review: As a whole, it’s derivative, but (mostly) enjoyable.

Title: American Idiot
Review: There's still plenty of spunk in to be found in this Sgt. Pepper-lite.

Title: The Magic Place
Review: The Magic Place, Barwick's first release on Asthmatic Kitty (after two self-released albums), trails a dreamlike reverie across its 45 minutes.

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: This time the hits outweigh the misses.

Title: Young Narrator in the Breakers
Review: Pavo Pavo have achieved a collection that eschews the obvious, being undoubtedly hip yet simultaneous geeky in its references, and the resulting work is a real gem.

Title: Personal Life
Review: During the course of 10 catchy, snappy, lo-fi pop-punk songs, an incredibly personal, heartfelt narrative unfolds, full of ups and downs. [Oct 2010, p.120]

Title: With Love
Review: You just don’t get a sense of the depth and variety of the history Zomby is trying to encapsulate. Also, much of With Love‘s second half is made up of loping, rather dull dub and dubstep.

Title: Panic of Girls
Review: They unapologetically rip into this album with a pulsating and mangled electro-pop opener called "D-Day", and rarely, if ever, lapse into giving people a poor photocopy of Parallel Lines.

Title: Tha Carter III
Review: Tha Carter III is a monumental album full of powerful, self-defeating statements that obliterate rap’s internal logic without offering too much more than indifferent bong logic in return. Judged, however, as a collection of singles and quotable verses--the criteria on which we’ve been grading hip-hop records since the end of disco--Tha Carter III is an agonizing piece of work.

Title: Far
Review: She's making a bid for the mainstream, even recruiting ex-ELO mainman Jeff Lyne to her corner on five tracks, including grandiose highlight 'Human Of The Year,' a three-minute distillation of the album's overriding facination with religion. [Aug 2009, p.104]

Title: Go Tell Fire to the Mountain
Review: Go Tell Fire to the Mountain, and WU LYF in general, are a band handicapped, seeming less like an actual group and more of an experiment. In what? In determining how much vocal pain listeners are willing to endure if the underlying music is actually pretty good.

Title: Beta Love
Review: When Mr. Miles gets too literal, as on "Binary Mind," you can begin to feel cornered. Far better is his bittersweet keen on "Angel, Please" and "For Once" and "Is It Too Much," songs of direct melodic and emotional thrust.

Title: The Disco's of Imhotep
Review: Bullish and forceful, The Disco’s of Imhotep is also a work of considerable intricacy and mystery. Jamal Moss aims high and rarely overreaches, making the album not only ambitious, but a welcome blast of modern house that would live up any club night.

Title: BiRd-BrAiNs
Review: If you relish a challenge, and like music to brace you as much as entertain you, then this should fit the bill. Like no-one else very much, but very much herself, it is one woman's raw, open and compelling testament.

Title: Spoils
Review: There is a clarity of musical and lyrical vision here that is rarely found in modern music.

Title: Ibifornia
Review: These squelchy tunes pack much summer sunshine, and even kitsch jungle noises on the title track. But the long-range outlook is a little more mixed.

Title: Swoon
Review: It would be thrilling to hear a Silversun Pickups record which finally shakes off all their influences and creates something entirely their own. Swoon isn't quite that record, but it takes them closer to that goal, and is a seductive, intricate thing of beauty in itself.

Title: Wayward Fire
Review: Mohager ultimately forgets there's a fine line between homage and aping, but if your dream gift is a time capsule from the Reagan Years get ready to discover your new favorite record. [Jul 2011, p.107]

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: Hesitation Marks follows the musical lineage that began with The Fragile, but it surpasses recent NIN albums thanks to a deeply personal thematic core and a willingness to push the songwriting into territory that is often dancier and poppier than listeners have come to expect from the band.

Title: The Documentary
Review: This no-talent is masscult rock at its most brazen.

Title: Relax
Review: Their unique perspectives on racial and class identities are perspectives that hip-hop needs to remain vital, to remain that genre that united so many other groups throughout the genre's dominating decades. And the best part is that they fulfill that role while still joking.

Title: The Weather Station
Review: Tense and uncertain, The Weather Station will keep you tuning in.

Title: Lazaretto
Review: You suspect that getting on the wrong side of White would be inadvisable. Thankfully, he has channelled his demons in Lazaretto to create one of the great break-up albums of recent years.

Title: Breakfast
Review: Ultimately, your Chiddy Bang tolerance rests on your ability to endure the self-consciously cute.

Title: Songs You Make at Night
Review: A record that lands with such hazy panache, transporting its listener into a nocturnal wilderness where dreams are limitless. The record is undoubtedly a strong return to form for the folktronica vanguards and potentially the signalling of a second coming for the band.

Title: Innocence Reaches
Review: Though Innocence Reaches is more than a bit disjointed, offering a mix of styles previously explored and newly absorbed, it's an up-tempo pleaser with songs that promise to be handpicked fan favorites--if with little consensus.

Title: You Know I'm Not Going Anywhere
Review: You Know I'm Not Going Anywhere is a sonic and lyrical breakthrough for the Districts, a record that's years beyond anything else in their catalog.

Title: The Reminder
Review: Whereas her last album's smoothed-out eclecticism could be both daunting and empty, The Reminder is equally diverse yet more full-blooded.

Title: Darling of the Afterglow
Review: Classically trained, the breadth of Ainsworth’s talent is laid bare on Darling Of The Afterglow.

Title: The Spiral Arm
Review: Though still meditative, they're now more dynamic. [Jan 2020, p.24]

Title: Breakin' Point
Review: The songs get you moving just enough. The melodies and lyrics gently grab you by the ears.

Title: Hunter
Review: A soaring, feverish conflagration of sense and sensuality. [Sep 2018, p.90]

Title: Forever Today
Review: While Forever Today doesn't break any new ground for I'm From Barcelona, it's a refinement that's resulted in the band's most consistent album yet.

Title: Inside the Rose
Review: The powerful fusion of the electronic and the classical crucially allows the brothers to lightly grasp the hands of their listener, and guide them through dreamscapes of cosmic beauty, searing light and haunting darkness.

Title: The Fall
Review: An electronic album that manages to sound intimate, late-summer warmth turning to autumnal melancholy, and a cartoon band that suddenly seems a little fragile.

Title: Night Melody
Review: t’s a record about how the night is more than just an expanse of time to sleep through or drink away. Indeed, through West’s eyes, it’s much more: a richly populated terrain where life can be discovered, avowed, and confronted, even in the darkest of corners.

Title: This Is Happening
Review: With This Is Happening, Murphy remains far ahead of pretenders trying to steal his thunder. [Jun 2010, p.107]

Title: Songs of Innocence
Review: [Songs Of Innocence] has only a handful of standouts.... This is a serious mis-step that might win a week's worth of good publicity, but could foreshadow a year's worth of bad.

Title: It's All In Your Head
Review: There's little here that Our Lady Peace, Foo Fighters, Everclear and a half-dozen other post-grunge bands don't already do better.

Title: Wolfroy Goes to Town
Review: Definitely for the faint-hearted.

Title: Widow City
Review: This record's delightful and wholly original; no one else could possibly have made it.

Title: Left
Review: They have developed into an almost evangelically uplifting and powerful rock unit.

Title: Ratchet
Review: [A] dazzling modern dance album. [Jun 2015, p.94]

Title: Yes, It's True
Review: The continuing resemblance of their lyrics to motivational speeches may still grate on non-fans. [Oct 2013, p.88]

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Murder of the Universe
Review: Prepare for all the fiery guitar solos, vocal howls and whoops, and the ever-present double-drummer attack and honking harmonica you could ever need. Overall, Murder of the Universe is an audacious, wild masterwork by a band who can never rest.

Title: Around The Sun
Review: Structure trumps texture throughout: "Make It All OK" is a formally tight breakup ballad, with spiritual overtones, that could fit neatly on a good singer-songwriter record, and others are arranged semi-acoustically, highlighting Stipe's cleanest melodies and most inviting vocal performances in years.

Title: WLIB AM: King of the Wigflip
Review: This mixtape-style collection is more ramshackle than his most celebrated work, but it's still packed wirh inspired funk. [Dec 2008, p.127]

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: No Cities To Love is a triumph. Not only does it meet every one of our over-the-top demands as fans, it serves as a great entry point for those new comers who have yet to be introduced to one of the most important bands of the last quarter century.

Title: Stories Don't End
Review: The result confirms there are few bands that can mix past and progress like these fellas.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: On what may be her best album, Polly Harvey offers a portrait of her homeland as a country built on bloodshed and battle, not so much a police state as a nation in thrall to military endeavour, however impotent and wasteful that has become.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: It may not be the best Wilco album ever, but with care and consideration it may well turn out to be your favourite.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: The Thrills' external, sometime vaccuous pinching is clearly self-conscious, a carefully premeditated breach of expectation that causes more of a wince than a flash of pleasant surprise.

Title: Boys and Diamonds
Review: Never mind the cultural appropriation bollocks, here's ethnotronic industrial pop.

Title: Sun Leads Me On
Review: Half Moon Run may still be exploring a road that travels between Django Django's left-field indie pop and the wintry harmonies of Fleet Foxes, but the scenery is damned fine. [Nov 2015, p.89]

Title: After Hours
Review: Even though the subjects may not be sung about with as much grit as they once were, they are certainly darker than the pop genre that's entrapped the artist in recent years.

Title: It's A Corporate World
Review: Dale Earnhardt Jr. Jr.'s dedication to branding has earned them plenty of attention, but on It's a Corporate World, their music too often feels like an afterthought.

Title: Living With The Living
Review: Leo manages to skip from tender, unadorned romantic pop crooning to full-throttle punk yowling to Celtic-flavored folk-rock without losing the listener, the beat, or the message.

Title: The Getaway
Review: Fans will probably find The Getaway an improvement on 2011’s I’m With You, citing tunes such as Detroit. Sceptics will continue to boggle at their enduring charmlessness, a problem not even Danger Mouse can fix.

Title: Christmas Songs
Review: Despite valiant efforts at punking up "O Come, O Come Emmanuel" and "White Christmas," this is starting to sound like a bad joke. [No. 105, p.52]

Title: Spend the Night
Review: But for all The Donnas' ongoing charms, Spend The Night tempers them with a faint whiff of predictability.

Title: The Flower Lane
Review: Its songwriting, production, and delivery harbor no risks, and therefore the album safely passes by its listeners without leaving anything but a want for something a little more lively.

Title: Long Gone Before Daylight
Review: The electronics of Gran Turismo has been supplanted by an organic sound with countryish overtones (see Live and Learn) that suits Persson's melancholy lyrics.

Title: Get To Heaven
Review: Get To Heaven feels both like a band at the peak of their powers and self-consciously dialing everything up to 11 before things go up in flames. [Jul 2015, p.90]

Title: Anywhere I Lay My Head
Review: You might wish there was more from Waits' 70s barfly period--what would Johansson have made of Christmas Card from a Hooker in Minneapolis?--but it's a measure of this album's surprising allure that you're left wanting more.

Title: First Taste
Review: An overwhelming sense of fun pervades First Taste, as further epitomized in a couple of wacky drum solos that are so maniacal they'll bring a smile to your face. All in all, Ty Segall's obviously having fun as a result of being chiefly interested in entertaining himself.

Title: Together Through Life
Review: While Dylan's grim-reaper ruminations are familiar territory, Together Through Life does offer some surprises.

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: The Hold Steady will probably never match the thrill of their first three releases, but Thrashing Thru the Passion is the most enjoyable record they’ve made in thirteen years.

Title: Doko Mien
Review: In the wrong hands this mish-mash could be a colossal disaster, but delivered through the inimitable vocals and presence of Eno Williams, it melds gracefully. [Apr 2019, p.31]

Title: The Animal Years
Review: There's something subtly majestic and quitely engaging about the music of Josh Ritter. [#13, p.88]

Title: Herd Runners
Review: Aldred is in top form here, and with Elliot's help he's unearthed a music box filled with undeniable loveliness, but the songs are as fleeting as they are lustrous; museum pieces without placards.

Title: Mr Beast
Review: They vacillate between flotational devices and skull-crushers. [Apr 2006, p.91]

Title: Heartthrob
Review: The across-the-board quality of Heartthrob earns it the merit as yet another high point in the Tegan and Sara discography. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.89]

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: Post-millennial indie boy-rock has taken a savage beating here. And it may prove the best it’s ever had.

Title: Silver Wilkinson
Review: Both J Dilla and the recently revived Oval come to mind at moments of Silver Wilkinson, but this is a sound as English as Virgina Astley. [May 2013, p.66]

Title: Who Is the Sender?
Review: Fay is now in his 70s, and his beautifully hymnal fourth studio album contains sublime, heartfelt ruminations on nature and the world from someone who knows his time is running out.

Title: Dude Incredible
Review: It doesn’t challenge expectation, but equally it does nothing, puts nary a single step wrong, to risk their reputation as a preeminent act of their kind, and of our times.

Title: Fading West
Review: The bulk of these songs feature clichéd lyrics and arm-waving call and response construction.... That said, there is talent and maturity in the song craft, production and playing.

Title: Everything Must Go
Review: Fagen and Becker perfected their airless craftsmanship years ago, and it works as well now as ever.

Title: Burden of Proof
Review: This is the biggest Benny album to date, but he doesn’t lose what made him great and such a beloved underground rapper. His boasts are as strong as ever, and his flows are cold like the air in the Buffalo streets.

Title: Heavy Metal Music
Review: It's a visceral, straightforward assault,, and what really shines through is a grasp of songwriting that was once sorely underused and a sense of commitment and passion that was never really in doubt. [27 Jul 2013, p.52]

Title: Some Cities
Review: Some of the radio-friendly oompa of ‘The Last Broadcast’ has been cut back, and the new record bears more resemblance to their debut ‘Lost Souls’ in its ashen-faced detachment and bloodied-yet-unbowed pride.

Title: Go To School
Review: Go To School is a misstep--the sound of talented young musicians over-reaching to the point of unlistenability. [Oct 2018, p.93]

Title: Let the Good Times Roll
Review: [A] flat-out sensational album. [May 2015, p.77]

Title: Jay Stay Paid
Review: A record that not only tops any solo offering that the late James Yancey released during his lifetime, but also rivals Slum Village’s “Fantastic Part 2” and his own “Donuts” as his finest full-length effort.

Title: VYP (Voice of the Young People)
Review: Though there’s slick, occasionally dynamite production from the likes of the Runners and Scott Storch, the lyrics rarely rise above defensive boasting (“One Hit Wonder”), frigid sex raps (“What It Is [Strike a Pose]”) and rote autobiography (“College”).

Title: Low in High School
Review: This album is partisan, powerful and controversial. [Dec 2017, p.87]

Title: Viet Cong
Review: An ambitious and rewarding debut.

Title: Return to the Ugly Side
Review: The duo is quite adept at keeping the dopey momentum going, but without a respite or a break in the haze, Return To The Ugly Side is often impenetrable. But that's kind of cool--a half-hour album that stretches out (or drags on) to feel like far longer.

Title: Forever
Review: Where his debut was concerned with building on his formative years, this incubated follow-up hatches a newly minted worldview from the embattled singer.

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: In taking back the rawness of [their] first e.p., the band have simultaneously acquired the courage to experiment with a surprising number of styles. [#9]

Title: The Chronicles of Life and Death
Review: Half the time, Good Charlotte sound like Blink-182 after the snip, the other half they sound like the Backstreet Boys without the songs. [16 Oct 2004, p.48]

Title: Universal High
Review: It's a refreshing step away from the anti-culpability of 'nice-boy' singers like Ed Sheeran and the ilk. Ultimately, the record is a lot of fun and will sit best with those who avoid taking life and love too seriously.

Title: Delirium Tremens
Review: His finest and most interesting yet. [Aug-Sep 2016, p.92]

Title: Desperation
Review: For an album that was certainly not recorded spontaneously, Desperation sure sounds spontaneous.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: The album seamlessly strolls from soaring numbers like "Lights Out" into a more stripped-down second half before ending with the gorgeous and inspired "Windows."

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: It’s an intriguing and refreshing listen.

Title: Dissociation
Review: In all its clean and high moments, in all its jagged dreams and nightmares, Dissociation is an album that will not only make music lovers think about the Dillinger Escape Plan, but will remind music lovers the gift that music is.

Title: Rehumanizer
Review: There is nothing wrong with working a beloved genre and working it hard; however, if faithful imitation is substituted for inspiration and energy, the results tend to be kind of underwhelming.

Title: Mature Themes
Review: Mature Themes is another satisfying step in Ariel Pink's evolution--an album as melodically, hypnotically addictive and surprisingly danceable as it is arcane.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: It’s the sound of Low passing up the opportunity for a twentieth-anniversary blow-out and opting instead for a quiet get-together with old friends.

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: Seventh Tree ultimately may have club-happy "Supernature" devotees shaking their heads, but for those of us who cherish all things weird and wonderful in the land of Goldfrapp, it is a welcome (and much-needed) return to form.

Title: Dum Spiro Spero
Review: It's far from easy listening but it's an approach that's won them legions of devoted fans in the process and comes close to reducing many of their peers to nothing more than musical footnotes in the larger scheme of things.

Title: Now Here Is Nowhere
Review: There are moments when the Secret Machines imitate their influences a little too closely, and at times the brothers' voices aren't as imposing as the arrangements. But for most of "Now Here Is Nowhere," the Secret Machines make music that matches the scale of their ambitions.

Title: My Main Shitstain
Review: In order to get that these three people from Bordeaux and a drummer from Berlin are the genuine maverick article, one just has to grab a listen. And be confused. And delighted. And frustrated. And appalled. And strangely aroused. And then listen to track two.

Title: Another Fine Day
Review: Beyond the elemental pleasures of imaginative, passionately delivered rock and folk, "Day" offers a set of songs with a consistent viewpoint and emotional reach. [25 Jul 2006]

Title: Greendale
Review: Greendale has a tattered, buzzing, demolike sound, rude as any Young has put out.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: Fresh off his triumphant "Fishscale" series, the thinking-thug’s MC once again shows why he’s the alpha Wu-Tanger: palpable street authenticity, classic taste in R&B (Stax, Motown) and the breakneck rhyme virtuosity of hip-hop’s golden age.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Though it’s a record perspiring uncertainty and the fear of becoming stagnant, Be The Cowboy is Mitski’s most personal and confrontational thus far. It’s violently poignant and the mark of an artist who’s barely tapped into her singularity.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: Perhaps the biggest thing to take from 808s and Heartbreaks is the well-knit structure of the album. Every track finds it’s spot and the fact Kanye West is always on topic lyrically makes 808s and Heartbreaks a desirable, interesting listen.

Title: Galaxy Garden
Review: For listeners that like their electronic music with a pulse (both literally and figuratively), this release will be a rewarding experience.

Title: Sounds From Nowheresville
Review: The mediocrity taints the entire record and makes one wonder how it all went so wrong.

Title: I Bet on Sky
Review: Though lacking the infernal dynamics of 2009's Farm, there remains sufficient compensation to delight Dino devotees. [Oct 2012, p.88]

Title: There Are Rules
Review: Suffice to say, the once-beloved Kansas City quintet are not Radiohead, and whilst they may have left their pioneering, emo-infused pop-punk behind over a decade ago, nothing quite prepares the listener for the insipid snooze-a-thon they've concocted here.

Title: Menos el Oso
Review: Prior to this record, Minus The Bear had a reputation for jokey song titles and bloodless precision, but here, the band reinvents itself as a purveyor of nightmares.

Title: I'm New Here
Review: The album sounds heavy and elusive, like a field recording, and it will surely be studied with the most powerful of cultural microscopes, but its author will just puff cigarettes and chuckle.

Title: Expectations
Review: Expectations is an insistent but uneven album that points toward greater musical ambitions than it achieves. The sound is pleasantly aquatic and soft-edged but fussy and overwrought, as though its architects were worried that too much downtime might spur listeners to click away.

Title: Do It!
Review: The result is some of the loosest, most facinating music of their career. [Apr 2008, p.92]

Title: Tempest
Review: It's on "Early Roman Kings" that the various strains come together most effectively, with Hidalgo's organ added to another Muddy Waters blues-stomp groove, and Dylan blurring history again in his depiction of the titular Romans "in their sharkskin suits, bowties and buttons, with their high-top shoes" – neatly underlining the gangsterism of imperial invaders of all eras.

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: While the record might have benefited from some more discrimination on the cutting room floor, it's still a focused, complete record and a pleasurable listen.

Title: Musik, Die Schwer Zu Twerk
Review: Though Electric Würms may not be breaking boundaries any time soon, they’re doing this on their watch and no one else’s.

Title: Dudu
Review: A worthy follow-up and tonal cousin to B Boys' strong debut, Dudu hits its mark.

Title: Museum of Love
Review: Museum of Love is a nonformulaic, hard to pin down, quirky and danceable album.

Title: Bonxie
Review: Mumford & Sons-style tunes are still part of the package, but Man on Wire possesses a depth absent from their old songs, while the highlight, Between the Saltmarsh and the Sea, is a sumptuous fusion of folk and electronica.

Title: Calling Out
Review: In short, Calling Out's not a bad shout if you're looking for something calm and unruffled to soundtrack the summer. [Aug 2015, p.104]

Title: Stay Gold
Review: You’ll just go with the flow and appreciate the sheer songcraft of a journeyman who could probably release an album as solid as this every year without breaking a sweat.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: Our Love to Admire is the perfect soundtrack for an eighth grade dance, but for actual adults who know better, it’s best to avoid this mess.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: As an art experience, Honeymoon is gorgeous, and needs to be heard in context with her atmospheric home-made videos. But as pop music, it can fall a bit flat.

Title: Watershed
Review: Watershed, the new Opeth album, broad enough to encompass death-metal pummeling as well as cello and English horn, is typically engrossing--symphonic, and in a way organic.

Title: Pink Friday
Review: Pink Friday is full of boring....the most confounding thing about Pink Friday is that it lacks style, lacks weirdness, whatever your opinions of how deeply that weirdness goes.

Title: Tourist in This Town
Review: Allison’s debut Tourist in This Town shows she certainly has the potential to go it alone too, provided it’s on her own terms.

Title: The Long Goodbye
Review: It's sleek and distinctly studio-based, with live instrumentation taking a backseat to plush soundscapes that could only come from some fancy knobwork. [#5, p.92]

Title: reputation
Review: At the heart of Reputation lies a sequence of songs that chart the rise, fall and fallout of a fleeting relationship and offer a masterclass in pop songwriting along the way.

Title: Strange Geometry
Review: Another understated near-masterpiece from a band that doesn’t need to make a bang to make a deep impression.

Title: Return to Cookie Mountain
Review: As music for airports, the album hums along like a tension-age sedative, but if it was meant to be a grand artistic statement by an acclaimed band with a distinctive vision, it's pretty much static.

Title: IGOR
Review: IGOR is a commendable, yet flawed album, one that further challenges what we can and should expect from a rap album in 2019.

Title: Reality Testing
Review: Lone tunes are nothing if not growers--but there’s no question that this is one of our best artists on the form of his life.

Title: Icky Thump
Review: The new album manages to hone the at-points-aimless progressive aspirations of Get Behind Me Satan into sharp, clear-cut musical growth.

Title: The Lonely Position of Neutral
Review: Its tight-as-a-drum musicianship and the sense of threadbare vulnerability resonating in singer-guitarist Kevin Palmer's songs elevate the band above the ever-expanding pack of like-minded acts.

Title: Live from the Underground
Review: [A] competent, if rarely distinguished, major-label debut.

Title: Quality Street Music
Review: His involvement in the actual song-making process may be limited, but his ear for the finished product shouldn't be understated.

Title: Super Extra Gravity
Review: Nina Persson sings like a warmer Aimee Mann, and the songs manage to deliver their payloads without clobbering you over the head, or schmaltzing out.

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: The biggest problem with When Fish Ride Bicycles is the overall dull presentation and atmosphere.

Title: Weirdo Shrine
Review: At 11 tracks that clock in just over half an hour, it’s done too quickly. But we spend just enough time in La Luz’s nocturnal surf world to push repeat and return again, an action the best albums always provoke.

Title: Ghosts of the Great Highway
Review: Ghosts of the Great Highway is one of those albums that you want to have around for when life gets you down.

Title: Mindset
Review: Two dark, roiling 22-minute tracks that conjure up a world of nature in turmoil. [Feb 2012, p.97]

Title: Blue Eyed in the Red Room
Review: A meditative mix of blips and strums. [4 Mar 2005, p.75]

Title: As You Were
Review: As convincing as Liam Gallagher is when he audaciously boasts that he's "got the Midas touch" early on in the album, As You Were doesn't ever quite turn to gold.

Title: Explains
Review: Sonically, Explains is breezy, effortless, and warm as a Pacific Ocean sunset, and its laid-back vibe helps tame some of Field's more manic, pop culture-laden diatribes like "Light Brang" and "Where."

Title: Be More Kind
Review: Beautifully arranged and commandingly composed, Be More Kind is a great work from an expert in his craft. [5 May 2018, p.55]

Title: Tempo
Review: There are thrills galore for fans of the Knife and Róisín Murphy (like Murphy’s Hairless Toys, Tempo is inspired by ball culture documentary Paris Is Burning), and nagging hooks too.

Title: Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not
Review: Overall, while they're not reinventing the wheel here, this is a very enjoyable album and their best work since 2007's Beyond.

Title: MartyrLoserKing
Review: It pulls from rock, punk, noise, industrial, hip-hop, and even African tribal music. Lyrically the album is among the first to take this kind of look at hacker culture as well as how the definition of the artist and art have changed in the digital age. Regardless of genre, this may well end up being one of the best and conceptually most important albums released this year.

Title: Just a Little Lovin'
Review: Lynne has crafted a disc that--while not exactly transcendent--still manages to go to emotional places that remain unattainable to your run-of-the-mill pop vocalists.

Title: Likewise
Review: While it doesn’t wield the heft of a Hop Along release, Likewise demonstrates Quinlan’s adept melodic sensibility and enviable vocal delivery. It’s a short, sweet collection, easily digestible and ripe for revisiting.

Title: Marauder
Review: ‘Stay In Touch’ is a hip-shaking highlight, and the one true surprise here, but largely Marauder simply sees Interpol proving their worth once again, and their prowess for creating bleak, blackened indie rock that’s full of feeling.

Title: Front Row Seat to Earth
Review: In this album for insane times, Mering has attained universal connectedness while allowing us into her own excruciatingly cathartic purview, no easy feat.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: While there may not be a song to soundtrack an Amazon advertisement in this bunch, it'll work nicely to soundtrack bleary summer nights–probably for years to come.

Title: Fetch
Review: Sane comparisons elude Melt-Banana, but your mouth will froth and your tail will wag every time you Fetch.

Title: A Black Mile to the Surface
Review: The result is Manchester Orchestra’s most confounding, thrilling, and unintentionally loopy album yet.

Title: Silver Wilkinson
Review: Even with some of its more unpredictable moments, Silver Wilkinson offers a scenic route through Bibio's music that showcases its depth as well as its breadth.

Title: FIDLAR
Review: FIDLAR will make you want to pound a case of the cheapest beer you can find with these guys, it’ll make you want to crank it up as loud as it will go in whichever of your friends’ cars.

Title: Evil Urges
Review: Evil Urges explodes the band's sound with the same kind of creative leap that Wilco took on "Yankee Hotel Foxtrot" and Radiohead took on "Kid A."

Title: Big Black Coat
Review: While it still falls short in holding attention from start to finish, Big Black Coat signals a welcome return. Junior Boys created their most uncomplicated album yet, which still holds their signature style, and with it comes a jagged body of music made soft to the touch thanks to Greenspan’s buttery vocals.

Title: Disc-Overy
Review: All but a handful of the tracks on Disc-Overy are quite ruined by this appalling Black Eyed Peas gloss.

Title: Eyes At Half Mast
Review: On Talkdemonic's third stab, Eyes at Half Mast, the novelty seems to be thining, and O'Connor and Molinaro finally sound limited by their tools.

Title: Undertow
Review: Their second outing makes no effort to remap their coordinates: they remain riffy, distorted, full of nocturnal energy, possessed of rollicking good tunes, but also open up a more expansive goth-rock strain on indie-radio cuts. [May 2015, p.94]

Title: Futurology
Review: Futurology isn't just the best album the Manic Street Preachers have made this century, it's arguably the best album of the year. [Aug 2014, p. 206]

Title: Bandana
Review: As the culture is currently enamored with more rhythmic patterns than the meat on the bone, Freddie Gibbs and Madlib have undoubtedly proved they can compete without compromising their composition standards.

Title: ÃgÃ¦tis Byrjun
Review: At its best, the album seems to accomplish everything lagging post-shoegazers like Spiritualized or Chapterhouse once promised. However, at its worst, the album sometimes slides into an almost overkill of sonic structures

Title: Aerial
Review: Even if Aerial doesn't set the world on fire, it's good to hear Kate Bush again, and to hear a record that sounds so organic and grounded.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: Yes, and it's just as frustrating, too, and fiddly and awkward and self-conscious and self-important and neurotic and panicky, and as often ugly as it is beautiful, and as often pompous or irrelevant as it is profound. Just as you've come to expect.

Title: Songs in A&E
Review: That this is Spiritualized's most vital and compelling set for a decade suggests that his muse has been galvinised by his near death experience. [May 2008, p.61]

Title: Two Fingers
Review: Modern cityscapes, dilapidated by neglect, spring to mind when listening to police-dissing banger, 'What You Know.' Its police-siren chorus is the one moment of levity on a somewhat harsh release. [Spring 2009, p.77]

Title: Good Thing
Review: Classic soul opener Bet Ain't Worth The Hand sounds like the Philly soul of The Delfonics, but it's not long before we're into more up-to-date sonic shapes witht he dislocated beats of Lions. [Jun 2018, p.109]

Title: Strange To Explain
Review: Strange to Explain sounds like the result of carefully considered choices in songwriting and production. Without losing the unfiltered emotion that makes them so compelling, Woods reach a new maturity with these songs. Fifteen years into a tirelessly curious evolution, the band sound more comfortable and surefooted here than ever before.

Title: Trees Outside The Academy
Review: Trees Outside The Academy is a relaxed, organic record that charms without really trying, and perhaps the closest Moore will ever come to the lost Moby Grape album. [Sep 2007, p.57]

Title: R Plus Seven
Review: R Plus Seven doesn’t have quite the disembodied weirdness of Replica, but it’s no less accomplished, another intriguing chapter from an artist whose work remains alive with possibility.

Title: The 1975
Review: It's almost as if the songs were constructed by way of algorithm.

Title: Deeper Than Sky
Review: While the shock has worn off for their follow-up, Deeper Than Sky makes up for the lack of surprise by being even better executed.

Title: ASTROWORLD
Review: The modulation and echo treatments on the vocals, combined with the frequently torpid tempos, nonetheless make Astroworld ideal for being pumped through an (18 and over) amusement park's sound system near closing time, when the challenge of hitting all the rides has started to turn into an overindulgent, overheated chore.

Title: Brute
Review: Despite the forcefulness of its concept, Brute thus often feels less like music of protest than music of exhaustion, confusion, and diffuse rage. This can make for an oppressive and tiring listen, but at best its effect is unsettling, and suggestive of traumatised detachment--a familiar enough reaction to the barrage of grim reports that make up the daily online news churn.

Title: Cosmogramma
Review: Because in constantly mutating just when you begin to pin it down, drawing everything around in before rearranging atoms before your very eyes, Cosmogramma proves itself time and time again as mind-meltingly boundless as a black hole.

Title: Post-War
Review: Introducing some very welcome rock rhythms to his blend of folk and fingerpicked Delta blues, Ward’s disarmingly sweet fourth album squeezes big themes into modest but bewitching tunes.

Title: Selling My Soul
Review: The productions are steeped in soul and R&B, offering a more upbeat and clean sound than the usual Wu murk and a Masta Killa companion to Ghostface's retro effort Ghostdini the Wizard of Poetry in Emerald City.

Title: A Different Kind of Fix
Review: This album is a great one, and proof that the band are able and willing to develop and grow their music.

Title: Transfixiation
Review: Transfixiation is at its best, however, when a little restraint casts its own spooky shadows.

Title: Strange Peace
Review: Truth be told, Strange Peace’s series of succinct bludgeonings are more a case of ain’t-broke-don’t-fix and the appointment of likeminded racket fetishist Steve Albini as producer comes less as a surprise than foregone conclusion.

Title: National Ransom
Review: It's a lot to take in, but his aim is true as always.

Title: Meir
Review: They're still wildly unpredictable--and still committed to not singing in English--but the dichotomy between the adrenaline rushes and chill-out moments seems a bit more purposeful.

Artist: Beth Jeans Houghton & The Hooves of Destiny
Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose is a success, in that it captures what Beth Jeans Houghton has been doing in her live shows for the past couple of years, without diluting or rushing it for the sake of a time-specific tag.

Title: Technology
Review: Clocking in at just under an hour across 14 songs, about 12 of which could easily be singles, Technology is engaging, fun and an early contender for album of the year, plus the album of this band’s career.

Title: Magnifique
Review: Magnifique is less than immersive.

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: Fourth outing for the hirsute folk/pop alchemist. [Feb. 2011, p. 107]

Title: The Marriage of True Minds
Review: When that results in music that sounds like music, it's great.
A sinister, slinky catwalk with sharper melodic angles and a propulsive, post-punk groove. [#75, p.99]

Title: Manipulator
Review: With 17 tracks stretching over 57 minutes, perhaps some judicious editing could have trimmed the excess, but this remains a major step forward for Segall and a logical extension of a direction he was already headed in.

Title: Murray Street
Review: Consider Murray Street to be Sonic Youth's calmer, more introspective journey into the science of sound, one filled with just as many gifts as their earlier, more hard-hitting works. It's filled with rewarding listens.

Title: Songs for Silverman
Review: Not only is Folds singing better than ever, and not only is his song-writing oozing confidence - but the musician in him is also at the peak of his powers; the piano playing is just mesmerising.

Title: Take Me to the Alley
Review: Throughout the album, which the singer produced with Kamau Kenyatta, Porter matches these cozy sentiments with modest, small-scale arrangements--mostly keys, bass and drums--that sound shaped more by the gigs he's played over the last three years than by any desire to experiment in the studio. But Porter’s resting state is a compelling one.

Title: The Terror
Review: There's always been a relentless optimism hidden behind the Flaming Lips' unique brand of pop experimentalism.... Which makes their understated 13th album, The Terror, an evocation of a bleak, post-apocalyptic future, such a striking contrast.

Title: Midnight Memories
Review: As a whole, Midnight Memories isn’t a genre game-changer. But in terms of the One Direction catalog, this record is exactly the right move: There’s enough personality, charm, and dramatic solos to satisfy fans, and enough incremental moves toward artistic credibility to at least give the band a chance at an enduring career.

Title: Mr Twin Sister
Review: Favorite records tend to draw us back in again and again because they offer a specific, familiar feeling, yet it remains difficult to rate, categorize or even define an album as restlessly mutable as ­Mr Twin Sister.

Title: The Heart Is a Monster
Review: Many of the album’s finer moments come in the slower, more abstract compositions.

Title: MetaL MetaL
Review: At times they pull in too many directions at once. [Jun 2015, p.116]

Title: Infinity Overhead
Review: Infinity Overhead's smorgasbord of sounds should please every level of Minus The Bear fan.

Title: Don't Let the Kids Win
Review: Don’t Let The Kids Win shines brightest for its clear, and charismatic narrative voice.

Title: Celebration, Florida
Review: The Felice Brothers are not what they used to be. The band has grown, and not all of the growing pains are pretty. Some of the tracks on the new album, such as the dirge "Dallas" and the plodding "River Jordan", could use some of Simone's energetic drumming.

Title: Tennessee Pusher
Review: OCMS's scrappy, fervent playing--live, the band is a mesmerizing mess of strings and sweat--reinvents old-time for a whole new generation.

Title: Wait For Me
Review: While it may be Moby's darkest record yet, Wait For Me should, at very least, serve as an optimistic sign that Moby's independent creative juices are still flowing.

Title: Seems Unfair
Review: Second LP Seems Unfair offers the kind of melodic prowess, lyrical wit, sensitivity and social awareness that harks back to the days of Felt, Hefner and The Smiths with the band capable of effervescent, wonky guitar attacks more in keeping with the early material of Stateside benchmarks Weezer, Pavement and more recently, Waxahatchee.

Title: Crystal Fairy
Review: Though there are near misses on Crystal Fairy (like the riffs that don’t quite reach heavy metal territory in “Secret Agent Rat” or the teeth-gritting introduction of “Under Trouble” that does more to incite annoyance than apprehension), the album succeeds far more than it falls short.

Title: Pageant
Review: The songs on Pageant are immediately catchy on first listen, but they have a melodic, lyrical, and instrumental power that will make them evergreen for years to come.

Title: The Understanding
Review: Röyksopp have little left to say aside from what others have said more clearly in the past.

Title: Playing the Angel
Review: The album skillfully and confidently showcases all of Martin Gore’s songwriting strengths.

Title: Sorry For The Late Reply
Review: Unfortunately, there are too many missteps for this to feel like any kind of progress on their debut, even if the sentiment behind the tracks remain essential. Sløtface clearly still have much to say; they just need to work out a way of rediscovering their voice.

Title: Devils & Dust
Review: Stands somewhere between Nebraska and Joad in terms of impact and quality.... But this album doesn’t merely find the middle ground between those two earlier releases: Its best songs break new ground for Springsteen.

Title: Jackinabox
Review: The arrangements are much tighter than ever and cover up whatever lyrical deficiencies the charismatic, freewheeling attitude of the band doesn't.

Title: Expectations
Review: Expectations surpasses any you might have had.

Title: Loyalty to Loyalty
Review: Throughout the album, haunted-saloon piano and reverb-choked guitar conjure a murky, wobbly misaligned version of old R&B.

Title: Superwolf
Review: Superwolf contains some of [Oldham's] most startling work yet.

Title: Avenged Sevenfold
Review: The end result is a safe, predictable record that could very well be Metallica-lite (like the new Metallica), in addition to being pretty close to silly.

Title: All Eternals Deck
Review: While the other songs, intelligent pieces of art that they are, may intrigue, it's disappointing that only one song here compels us to really feel anything.

Title: Sunken Condos
Review: For all Fagen's obsession with precision, this still feels like a remarkably relaxed, quietly confident album--sleek, urbane and sophisticated.

Title: All Hell Breaks Loose
Review: Yes, it ultimately makes for predictable stuff, but Black Star Riders play bullshit-free unpretentious rock. [15 Jun 2013, p.54]

Title: Paris
Review: Why settle for pseudosleaze like Peaches when Paris delivers the real thing? [21 Sep 2006, p.82]

Title: Elsewhere
Review: Her thickly textured voice anchors what might otherwise feel like a scattered collection of morose songs exploring insecurity, loss and a loosely nebulous sense of yearning.

Title: Rub
Review: These songs offer a smart inversion of the usual gender roles in mainstream music, all set to a propulsive, bass-heavy backdrop. [Oct 2015, p.81]

Title: Peanut Butter and Jelly Live at the Ginger Minge
Review: It's hard to believe at first listen, but they've got nuance.

Title: Latin
Review: The Toronto-based collective goes all out on its third album, Latin, which features lead members Brian Borcherdt and Graham Walsh's spacey keyboards and effects supplemented by the powerful live drums and bass of their touring personnel.

Title: Crossing The Rubicon
Review: This is a well-rounded album that is as artistically rich as it is sonically pleasing. The Sounds are going to be around for awhile.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix
Review: Whilst Wolfgang Amadeus... is clunker-free, with high points from start to finish, allow me to abandon my critical faculties and gush about 'Love Like a Sunset Part 1', as this instrumental is by far the most incredible moment of the album and also quite possibly the best thing they've ever done.

Title: You Tell Me
Review: It will be interesting to see if You Tell Me is the start of something long-running or just a one-off. However it turns out, the album works as another argument in favor of the on-going genius of Peter Brewis and as an impressive introduction to the lovely music of Sarah Hayes.

Title: California Son
Review: California Son may not entirely succeed in repositioning Morrissey as a righteous protest singer, boldly crooning truth to power, but in fleeting moments like this [like on "Some Say I Got Devil"], it confirms him as a peerless modern practitioner of deep song, the pop artist who can divine, even in the work of the singer of "Brand New Key," lorca's dark, abysmal spirit of duende. [Jun 2019, p.28]

Title: Amputechture
Review: Where 2005's harrowing Frances The Mute strikes the right balance between inspiration and indulgence, the Mars Volta loses its equilibrium with Amputechture. [#73, p.96]

Title: Valtari
Review: The eight tracks of Valtari, which, while pleasant, are somewhat underwhelming examples of the band's formula.

Title: Just Go
Review: Just Go, slightly more so than Coming Home, tends to be a happy (and comforting) medium between Richie's familiar approach and contemporary R&B.

Title: Crush Songs
Review: The lo-fi bedroom lullabies on Crush Songs do have a pretty simplicity, but it's ultimately a sleepy listen with a lot of half-formed song sketches. [12 Sep 2014, p.62]

Title: Trick
Review: Sweet, intimate and tender, Trick is a tempting treat.

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: Sadly, much of Welcome Interstate Managers is bogged down by forgettable midtempo slush. [Aug 2003, p.104]

Title: Devotion
Review: Devotion goes down a little easier is both its strength and a feature that proves a bit disappointing in the end.

Title: Title
Review: Trainor may be talented, with a large voice and a witty writing style, but over the course of the album she crosses the line from confident to smug.

Title: Wind in the Wires
Review: At 21, he has the raconteur’s wit of a younger Nick Cave still buoyed by the weightlessness of possibility.

Title: Dear Miss Lonelyhearts
Review: Certainly this record is relevant, and maybe even worth listening to with some regularity. But I can't help but feel that this album is just a watered down Arcade Fire rather than the aural adventure that others seem to hear.

Title: LEGACY! LEGACY!
Review: Woods embodies the cultural makeup of Chicago, tackles the multiplicity of identity, and balances her dominance with flawlessly selected features that build her up. ... This record could be the basis for a college course or used as an actually accurate history book.

Title: Laws of Illusion
Review: Her songs fall easily on the ear, her rhyming schemes are adroit and she writes intelligently on serious subjects.

Title: Cinder
Review: Cinder keeps things reserved, letting the sad-eyed melodies teeter around the room at a drunkard's pace.

Title: Confess
Review: The infectious beats and catchy hooks are still a driving force, but Lewis has abandoned the bedroom vibes to surge ahead with full-on amphetamine-induced vigor.

Title: No Boys Allowed
Review: Warm and confident throughout her second album, Hilson is becoming hard to ignore.

Title: One Beat
Review: All of One Beat is strung loosely together by a common plea: for awareness, for understanding, and, most of all, for holding onto hope.

Title: Space Gun
Review: Space Gun is one of Pollard’s best. ... Unlike almost all the rest, there is virtually no filler here.

Title: There's No Leaving Now
Review: His third album is likely to disappoint fans and critics listening for those big, emotional climaxes, but Matsson's career has been defined by his ability to find new ways to paint with a limited palette.

Title: Parastrophics
Review: A wicked density of engaging audio elements that practically demands full immersion. [Mar 2012, p.88]

Title: Personality
Review: Personality's not a start-to-finish winner like Glass Swords was, but it's refreshing and gratifying to hear Scuba step out from the shadow of the Berghain and dreary discussions of the "dubstep-techno crossover", and start to release some music that sounds like it was fun to make.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: Just about everything on Sky Blue Sky, even soft-shoe skiffles like the title track, will likely sound better live.

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: When Longstreth uses his newfound focus to shake up his methods... the results are often startling.

Title: Into The Woods
Review: Bassist Haz Wheaton and drummer Richard Chadwick provide the solid underpinning, while Brock's knack of fashioning and delivering strong melodic and verbal hooks is plentiful in evidence. [May 2017, p.46]

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: When Fish Ride Bicycles is an energetic and fun summer album with lots of warm-weather references and car talk.

Title: 3 Doors Down
Review: Taut musicianship, well-crafted songs and potent vocals make this a landmark album in an already multiplatinum career.

Title: The Budos Band III
Review: They've rapidly become the standard bearers for the funkiest of instrumental soul, and III suggests they could keep doing this thing for several albums before it even begins to approach boring. We should all be as similarly stoked.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: I'm In Your Mind Fuzz
Review: It rates amongst the best three or four post-millennial psychedelic rock records. [Jan 2015, p.95]

Title: Is This It
Review: Delivers the goods in spades. [Nov 2001, p.94]

Title: Psychic
Review: All dark atmospherics and empty space, Jaar’s spectral production for collaborative project Darkside creates the void where rhythm, and seemingly time, are allowed to infinitely float on.

Title: White Stuff
Review: If, after an absence of 19 years, you are happy to engage with a band who are reprising much of their musical and lyrical themes whilst also dipping their toes into unexplored (and poorly realised) terrain, then no doubt there is much within White Stuff which will tick all of the appropriate boxes. But, oh man, that Kool Keith track.

Title: Free Yourself Up
Review: Maximizing that powerful female energy is Tennessee-raised lead singer Rachael Price, whose dusky, highly resonant vocals, reminiscent of Dusty Springfield, ground the album with a warm virtuosity. It also doesn't hurt that Kearney, guitarist Mike Olson, drummer Mike Calabrese, and touring keyboardist Akie Bermiss frame her in earthy, organic arrangements with a tactile, live-in-the-studio feel.

Title: Let's Wrestle
Review: Even with these flirtations with violins and brass, Let’s Wrestle are still the band they’ve always been: self-deprecating, scruffy and charming.

Title: Broken Side of Time
Review: A brave but clumsy attempt at expanding and refining the EP's dressed-down folksy rock, Broken Side's sound never coalesces enough to truly electrify, and though the ever-reaching, sprawling coarseness that Alberta Cross mines so well is still present here, it's noticeably less profound.

Title: The North
Review: The North's ultimate undoing isn't that it exudes so much schmaltziness, but that it sounds awkwardly and almost unconsciously dated, similar to the most recent offerings from indie-pop rockers Minus the Bear and Cold War.

Title: The Now Now
Review: A record that’s more reflective and human than you’d ever expect from a band of literal cartoons.

Title: All I Intended To Be
Review: Restrained, graceful and poised, the lady remains country music's finest ambassador. [July 2008, p.103]

Title: Free at Last
Review: Having graduated from knuckleheaded threats to a more hardened ghetto perspective that sometimes blossoms into tender complexity, Freeway sounds at home, particularly over the sweetly weeping keyboard loop that grounds 'Reppin’ the Streets,' the album’s best track.

Title: Anime, Trauma and Divorce
Review: Remarkable. ... The 12-track project explores the collapse of a marriage, financial turmoil, anxiety, self-doubt and self-care. A lesser rapper might sink in the mire, but Open Mike has always been dope on the mic, and ‘Anime, Trauma and Divorce’ find him at his best.

Title: Sonic Nurse
Review: Sonic Nurse neither disappoints nor surpasses expectations.

Title: Luna
Review: When ever Gordon Anderson admits to being "lost inside the chasms of my mind," therre seems little hope for the rest of us. [Nov 2008, p.87]

Title: Appeal to Reason
Review: There's nothing here you haven't heard before from Rise Against--or, indeed, from Bad Religion before that. But producers Bill Stevenson (of the Descendents and All) and Jason Livermore keep the music moving at a breakneck pace that gives everything the gleam of urgency anyway.

Title: My Garden
Review: On Dahlia's debut, My Garden, she transcends the sum of her seemingly disparate influences, proving herself to be a relatively distinct artist, even if her risks don't always pay off.

Title: The Great Escape Artist
Review: They may talk it up as a brave new step forward, but their first album in over eight years can't really be viewed as other than a retrograde move for Jane's Addiction.

Title: Schmilco
Review: Schmilco is Wilco’s most musically simple and emotionally resonant record in a decade, gorgeously naked and efficient.

Title: Another Country
Review: Merritt isn't one of alt-country's most distinctive vocalists; her singing here is wide open and affectless, occasionally to the point of near-anonymity. But instead of making the tunes on Another Country seem forgettable, that quality actually ends up inviting you into the material

Title: Tip of the Sphere
Review: Tip of the Sphere is Cass McCombs’ most elegiac and profoundly literary album, a eulogy for the end of times and a mass articulation of the absurd world of modernity.

Title: Rehearsing My Choir
Review: The twosome's sincere kitchen-sink music and lyrical pathos mean the tales of Chicago life unravel like a good Paul Auster novel. [Dec 2005, p.150]

Title: I Thought The Future Would Be Cooler
Review: The sound of a band running on empty. [Jan 2016, p.115]

Title: Un Autre Blanc
Review: There are moments on Un Autre Blanc that do feel close to unpalatably slick, but for the most part, the high production values here allow for Keita's music to come through with feeling rather than glide through the uncanny valley.

Title: A Laughing Death in Meatspace
Review: A Laughing Death In Meatspace is by no means easy listening: the playing is off-kilter, strange bursts of noise erupt from instruments, songs dissolve into a maelstrom of noises; the production, mixing and mastering bear traces of the album’s speedy composition and release; and the lyrics invite us to contemplate, without histrionics or self-deception, precisely how fucked we all are. It’s hot with anger and full of ugly truths about the ways we live our lives; and the effect is compelling.

Title: New Maps of Hell
Review: On Maps, BR breathe new life into their formula--short, fast and melodic Cali skate-punk ditties led by the always politically and socially aware growlings of lead singer Greg Graffin.

Title: Now Here Is Nowhere
Review: They are also the rare psychedelic band who keep to the point -- there are no digressions into noodly space jams to obscure the way.

Title: Rad Times Xpress IV
Review: Black Bananas mostly keep things tight throughout the record. [#39, p.66]

Title: Be Small
Review: The sun may be setting, but an album as self-aware as Be Small is a blinding signal of light and hope.

Title: Frankie Rose and the Outs
Review: She excels when she stacks up layers of her ghostly choirgirl voice within a more lush framework. [Nov 2010, p.114]

Title: Everybody Wants To Be On TV
Review: Unfortunately, Scouting For Girls occasionally meander out of their depth. [May 2010, p.102]

Title: Evangelist
Review: While there’s a compelling dark energy to the stark, fuzz-riffed uptempo tracks (the bass-driven God Song oddly recalling U2 when they strip things down), the telepathic power of the ensemble is best realised on spectral slowies such as I’m In Love Tonight, featuring deeply resonant viola from Bad Seed Warren Ellis, and epic Never Feel This Young.

Title: In Colour
Review: The record is filled with solid, sunny pop melodies.

Title: Modus Vivendi
Review: While Shake occasionally excels at crafting musical gems out of dark paranoia, her themes are stretched somewhat thin over the course of the whole record and on some tracks she ends up sounding listless.

Title: Hood Billionaire
Review: There is very little to write home about here, and for the most part it feels very hastily made.

Title: Faith and Courage
Review: O'Connor's most coherent record since 1990's ''I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got"

Title: Saturdays = Youth
Review: On fourth album Saturdays=Youth, the warm synthesizers are still in play and Gonzalez’s propensity for beguiling bombast is undiminished, but by imposing structure and melodic discipline on these sprawling compositions, he’s made them even more elegant and effective.

Title: Lost Girls
Review: The record is elevated by surreal moments and powerful songwriting that could only have come from Khan, whether in the palpable carnality of The Hunger, or the Middle Eastern synth patterns of So Good. She may not have intentionally set out to make this album, but it’s a blessing that she did.

Title: Avi Buffalo
Review: Continue to muse, and this strange, wonderfully unexpected work of art becomes one of the most mature (and stirring) narratives on intimacy, fidelity, and hesitant honesty heard in a long while.

Title: Something for Everybody
Review: With most of the original brain trust intact – brothers Mark and Bob Mothersbaugh and Gerald and Bob Casale, plus ex-Nine Inch Nails/Guns n' Roses drummer Josh Freese – Something for Everybody sounds effortlessly fresh.

Title: Overdrive
Review: By Shonen Knife's standards, Overdrive does sound like some sort of hard rock album, and the attempts to make like Kiss, Thin Lizzy, or Deep Purple come off better than one might expect, though Yamano's guitar skills are less impressive than those of the average metal axe slinger.

Title: Dirty Dancing
Review: Uncomfortable deliery and thin lyrical content suggest that utilising vocals isn't their strong suit. [#223, p.69]

Title: The Redeemer
Review: Blunt’s past records steeped that sincerity in reverb or in incomprehensible in-jokes-the beauty was in the blur. This time around, he’s figured out that he doesn’t look too shabby in focus either.

Title: Age of Transparency
Review: Age of Transparency is his best album yet.

Title: Types of Wood
Review: So unashamedly beaming with the spirit of 1991 that it should be wearing a flannel shirt and a woozy expression. [22 Apr 2006, p.41]

Title: Miike Snow
Review: Here Christian Karlsson and Pontus Winnberg hook up with indie boy Andrew Wyatt, manhandling his plaintive love ballads until they explode into freewheeling electro fantasias.

Title: Shlon
Review: Shlon is in some senses a return to his roots, combining the lush Arabic romance poetry of collaborator Moussa al Mardoud with Hasan Alo's techno arrangements. [Jan 2020, p.28]

Title: Awakening
Review: Awakening isn't going to change anyone's life, but Sacred Reich sound like they're having fun, and on thrash records like this one, that can be worth its weight in gold.

Title: Under Color of Official Right
Review: No matter how dark and overcast the basic mood of the album is, Under Color of Official Right never feels claustrophobic or overbearing, the production opening up just enough to make things expansive, almost majestic in their own way.

Title: Semicircle
Review: The result is another eclectic, iconoclastic record that doesn't sound like anything else happening in the world. That the Go! Team can sound as fresh and inventive on Semicircle as they did when they started is an impressive, almost miraculous, feat that defies nature and defines triumphant joy.

Title: In Conflict
Review: A sustained chamber-synthpop reflection on the idea of romantic and sexual turmoil, the album is also a tangle of confessions and absolutions, artfully and bravely unresolved.

Title: Time To Die
Review: If they tend toward the opaque, a soothing vibraphone or twinkling guitar arpeggio is never too far away. [Oct 2009, p.108]

Title: Forgetting The Present
Review: Forgetting The Present is the latest and most perfect union of Remember Remember’s distinctive blend of styles. Expect that record to stand for as long as it takes for their next album to appear.

Title: Overgrown
Review: Always confident in his ability, here he conjures sublime moments with "Retrograde" and ""digital Lion" before violating each with curdled klaxons, his voice throughout pitched persuasively somewhere between Antony Hegarty and Jeff Buckley. [May 2013, p.67]

Title: Towards
Review: The majority of the record is just not memorable enough.

Title: X&Y
Review: X&Y is well crafted and enjoyable, but it’s bloodless and distant. It feels manufactured, a piece of product in the march to become the Biggest Band in the World.

Title: New Moon
Review: New Moon shows The Men, who have always been admired for their ability to pull such diverse influences but held back for their lack of originality, expanding their horizons and coming into their own.

Title: Wall of Arms
Review: It's too easy to mistake them for any number of other bands--Editors, Maximo Park, The Futureheads all spring to mind--but if it's not original, it's still done weell. [Jun 2009, p.125]

Title: The Evangelist
Review: The Evangelist isn’t a Go-Betweens album, but it’s more cohesive than any of Forster’s other solo albums, and more moving.

Title: Shapeshifter
Review: The sophomore record sounds like a concept album about change: changing relationships, changing surroundings, changing perspectives and changing within oneself, often without even realizing it.

Title: ACCA
Review: It does feel like she is yet to fully reach the potential of her unique style and we are perhaps still awaiting something truly impressive that "All the Things" hints at. However, it's certainly very interesting listening to her sonic journey on the way towards that goal.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: The Bones Of What You Believe is an exceptionally strong debut where every track is a potential single.

Title: The Renaissance
Review: The Renaissance is the logical extension of this exploratory work, coupled with Q-Tip’s need to, once and for all, step out from behind Tribe’s long, dominant shadow, and in many respects (if not all), it succeeds wildly in both dimensions.

Title: Sleep Well Beast
Review: Sleep Well Beast, like all The National’s albums, occupies troubled territory. These are songs about the fleeting impermanence of joy, compared to the lingering bruise of despair, and how hard it is to live in this unfairly weighted emotional space. It’s a struggle embodied in Matt Berninger’s enervated, murmurous baritone.

Title: Pageant Material
Review: Though her songwriting partners--Nashville A-listers Luke Laird and Shane McAnally--are on board again, the acuity is lessened.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: A Seat at the Table is intensely rich and gracious in its candor, so much so that it’s quieter, painstakingly personal moments are every bit as robust as direct aggression. Its soulful flow is luscious and languid, and simply dazzles in the graceful, airy beauty of Cranes In the Sky, where Solange’s voice floats to stratospheric altitudes.

Title: From a Basement on the Hill
Review: Freed from the more formal sound and circumstances of his previous work, Smith indulged without being indulgent, and the revelation here is the exuberant, instinctive, playful and daring sonic pilot who was hidden inside the meticulous craftsman of such albums as "XO" and "Figure 8." [10 Oct 2004]

Title: Noonday Dream
Review: On Noonday Dream, he expands the Cornish landscape that has impacted his previous work and brings in sounds and instruments that spark the imagination for places further afield, in the most exquisite way.

Title: I Am Not A Dog On A Chain
Review: It finds Morrissey wandering down some interesting musical avenues. [May 2020, p.109]

Title: Music from Another Dimension!
Review: With tracks like "LUV XXX," "Beautiful," and "Lover Alot," everyone's favorite dude-looks-like-a-grandma just can't let go of that screechy horndog rock.

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: Lese Majesty is a trip to be sure, but the destination remains unclear. [Sep 2014, p.114]

Title: A Shadow in Time
Review: Even without knowing anything about Basinski himself or the climate in which he’s created his work, the listener herself would still be able to create their own world around it, such is the power of his music.

Title: Fresh Blood
Review: A more straightforward affair, and--though still a delicious record--slightly less eye-opening.

Title: Maladroit
Review: Be forewarned: There's not much along the lines of "Island in the Sun" here.... Still, there are plenty of smart hooks and catchy vocals throughout.

Title: Hush
Review: Despite their gift for undeniably soothing melodies and luminescent keyboard and guitar textures, the duo’s album falls into the “grower” category, and it’s possible that less resilient listeners won’t stick around to be dazzled by its early morning shimmer.

Title: See Mystery Lights
Review: The pair's cryptic lyrics can get lost in the shuffle at times, but Bechtolt and Evans offer enough interesting musical ideas to keep the listener engaged.

Title: Fragments of Freedom
Review: Unfortunately, a couple of the early tunes are so slick as to lose all feeling, while some of the lyrics are dumber than a doormat, but as party albums go, this will keep you up for a while.

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: A work of faultless skill and assured sophistication, The Take Off and Landing of Everything positions Elbow as one of the most quietly ambitious and rewarding acts of our generation.

Title: Hopelessness
Review: When Anohni sings about mass graves and drone strikes, it doesn’t feel like a lecture. It can be strangely empowering. For all its bleakness, Hopelessness leaves you feeling anything but.

Title: Agora
Review: The unpolished feel of Agora is a bit striking for a Fennesz release, but it's clearly just as carefully considered as his other albums, and makes a welcome addition to his catalog.

Title: Sleepwalking Sailors
Review: Don’t expect an ordinary cruise through placid conditions; this is music for those who love weathering a storm.

Title: Return of Saturn
Review: There is no doubt that Gwen Stefani is currently the most hyped up singer in the world; nevertheless, that doesn't change the fact that she possesses one of the worst singing voices in pop-rock history.

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: A couple of tracks feature liberally processed vocals, but the singing acts less as a melodic agent than as one more source of instrumental texture.

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: Most of Minutes is honed, metallic pop with a hip-hop stride and a wake-up kick.
