Title: Fabulous Muscles
Review: Sonically, it's well-tempered between its beat-driven and its acoustic pieces; lyrically, a unique, personal pain drips out from Stewart's whispered vocals, providing the driving force of Muscles' challenging, diverse ensemble.

Title: The Feast of the Broken Heart

Review: [It] sounds more like a continuation of Pinback's 2004 high-water mark, "Summer in Abaddon." This is, of course, a good thing. [27 Jan 2007]

Title: More Faithful
Review: It's a record built less on borrowed nostalgia and genre fetishism and more on earnest, risk-taking creativity and mixing genres in weird sonic chemistry experiments.

Title: A Woman A Man Walked By
Review: Polly’s second joint album with Parish couldn’t be more eclectic in its breadth and scope.

Title: Home Again
Review: There's obviously more to come, but this eagerly awaited debut disc doesn't disappoint.

Title: To the Sea
Review: Johnson considers the world's woes with gentle reflection rather than recrimnation, along the way hoping to illuminate his son's path to finding his own truth. [July 2010]

Title: Paris
Review: She's convinced an army of writers and producers... to furnish her with above-average R&B to pant suggestively over. [Sep 2006, p.108]

Title: In Your Honor
Review: It is clean, polished rock with a vaguely punk edge that stays within a clear set of boundaries but in doing so manages to appeal to indie-kids and metal-lovers alike.

Title: Salome
Review: The result is a maelstrom of noise, both ominous and ecstatic, doomy minor chords and cloud-parting major riffs.

Title: Happy Now
Review: Andy Gill's guitar work is still distinctive and angular on tracks like "Toreador" and "Don't Ask Me," but the band seem intent on lending the old with the new. [May 2019, p.23]

Title: Commonwealth
Review: Canada’s answer to the Fab Four, Sloan, are still charming after 23 years together.

Title: SASAMI
Review: At times the album that little bit too airy. As skilful as Ashworth is in crafting delicately spun melody--the jangling harmonies of ‘Morning Comes’, or the gentle lull of ‘At Hollywood’--her full force and potential truly reveals itself when the shadows burst out and take over, dragging her shoegazey soundscapes to the edge of the void.

Title: Life is Full of Possibilities
Review: Pretty, brittle, subtle, full of surprises, and disarming in its ability to set moods, Life Is Full of Possibilities is a masterpiece that places Dntel near the top of the heap of electronic artists working in 2001.

Title: Fetty Wap
Review: The whole of the self-titled Fetty Wap album is remarkably inoffensive and uninspired.

Title: The Blue Depths
Review: The Blue Depths is an album first and foremost and is assembled as one. Therefore, it should be listened to that way; because the aura it creates around the listener--particularly through headphones--is nothing short of spectacular.

Title: Ad Infinitum
Review: While not as immediate a confection as past releases Ad Infinitum is Telekinesis' Golden Record. [No. 124, p.61]

Title: Travelling Like the Light
Review: Nothing quite matches that burst of bile ['Crying Blood'], but the title track--choir and all--is heavenly. [Jul 2009, p.118]

Title: Camp
Review: Although Glover plays the part of rapper exceptionally, he needs to do a little more to stop "n****s asking whether this dude's for real or not".

Title: The Traveler
Review: Rich with amped-up fiddles, mandolins, accordions and harmonies, it's vibrant, hook-laden and addictive. [Aug 2015, p.77]

Title: Forever
Review: Aside from a couple of ponderous, buzz-killing instrumentals, Forever is one long rave.

Title: Sweet Disarray
Review: A rare debut, as well crafted as it is likeable.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: After the novelty wears off, the keeper is his typically blunt 'Nice to Be Dead'--"It’s nice to be underground/Free of the ugly sounds of life"--which happens to be the album’s one electric-guitar rocker.

Title: Sweetener
Review: Ms. Grande backs up her statements with song-and-dance mastery. ... She’s her own choir, support group and posse. While a few guest vocalists (Mr. Williams, Nicki Minaj, Missy Elliott) provide a little grit for contrast, Ms. Grande sails above any fray, past or present. Her aplomb is her triumph.

Title: Ex Lives
Review: Much of ex-Lives is encumbered by well-trodden ground turned muddy and attempts at atmosphere. [Apr 2012, p.96]

Title: Trouble Will Find Me
Review: While catharsis never comes, there are glimpses of light coming through at the edges, and a sense of perfect order among the chaos.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: [Adebimpe's] singing is consistently riveting, and the oddball mix gives it room to flourish. [Apr 2004, p.138]

Title: (II)
Review: By focusing on the scars that aren't always visible on the surface, Crystal Castles have delivered their most consistent album yet.

Title: WARM
Review: When he sings, he doesn't seem to be singing from some ivory tower. And when stripped of the confines of a band dynamic, that relatability is even more naked and genuine. Warm is Tweedy unfiltered, a gift that begs to be shared.

Title: So Long, See You Tomorrow
Review: There are times when it feels sporadic and fragmented--with so many different elements crammed in to each track--but ultimately, it is the sound of a band pushing themselves further than they’ve ever gone before.

Title: Cherry Bomb
Review: For all their blown-out abrasion, though, Tyler’s harder tracks never dazzle the way West’s industrial experiments did. They merely cloy.

Title: Paris
Review: She sings like a woman who has heard of something called singing, can't be sure of exactly what it might entail, but is fairly certain you do something a bit like this. She sounds both distracted and bored stiff, as if making an album is keeping her from the more serious business of standing around a nightclub in a pair of really enormous sunglasses.

Title: West Ryder Pauper Lunatic Asylum
Review: Thing is, most of the songs on West Ryder Pauper Lunatic Asylum, while never outright abhorrent on their own, just aren’t tight enough to keep from being devoured by all the sonic excess.

Title: Apricity
Review: Syd Arthur never forget to write a tune for the sake of muso self-indulgence. There is a lightness to Liam Magill’s voice: it’s soulful without over-emoting, like Paul McCartney or Glenn Tilbrook.

Title: II
Review: The production is minimal, leaving II feeling pure and honest.

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: Rarely before have the pair achieved [moments of transcendence and preserving them in amber] with this much grace and finesse. [Sep 2015, p.68]

Title: Short Movie
Review: The best tracks showcase Marling’s ability to fuse her meandering musicality with her forceful passion.

Title: Little Red
Review: Little Red should rightly see Katy B cement her ascent to the stratosphere, joining the rest of dance music’s glitterati.

Title: 4x4=12
Review: With the illuminated big head and all, Canadian producer Joel Zimmerman's Deadmau5 alias is a blast to see live, but you can also bring quite a bit of that tech-house-meets-slammin'-electro excitement home with 4 x 4 = 12.

Title: You Are We
Review: The production values on You Are We are perfection--too many metalcore records overproduce until notes feel clinical. But ‘Feel’ builds and drops like an avalanche of brilliance, Taylor’s voice firing off a round of vocal ammo with ease.

Title: Sailing to Philadelphia
Review: Sailing To Philadelphia often sounds outright anachronistic, from the "Sultans Of Swing"-like "What It Is" to James Taylor's voice on the title track, yet it never comes across like another old English coot courting Baby Boomer record buyers. Knopfler's ability to keep his talents in check serves the music, which benefits from the simple structures and tiny (but significant) guitar flourishes.

Title: The Next Logical Progression
Review: Gift of Gab is a craftsman, and achieves goal to provide uplifting music.

Title: All My Relations
Review: The eight tracks here are more high definition than most of what he's done in his career, with all the various noisy elements easily distinguishable and with more depth than usual.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Days of Abandon
Review: POBPAH's third LP lunges confidently into all the right places, emitting sunshine, glee, rainbows, sugar and sparkles as it goes like a sweaty unicorn running a marathon.

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: His dazzling feel for 21st-century psychedelia pushes this well past nostalgia tripping--and while the verbal abstraction gets thick, there's serious pleasure in plumbing it.

Title: Summer Bones
Review: None of these tracks are throwaways. [Apr 2015, p.92]

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: Cruel Summer is a mistitled fireworks show from Kanye West and his G.O.O.D. Music label/roster/empire, one that comes off as mixtape-minded follow-up to his flossy Jay-Z team-up Watch the Throne.

Artist: I Love You But I've Chosen Darkness
Title: Fear Is on Our Side
Review: Casts [their] this-is-not-a-love-song songs in an ultraviolet, goth-shoegazer glow that stretches [their] glistening guitar ripples to Mogwai-like proportions. [#71, p.100]

Title: Emotional Mugger
Review: Sonically, Emotional Mugger lands somewhere between all of these records [Manipulator, II, and Ty-Rex], maintaining the cohesion and (relatively) streamlined arrangements of Manipulator but nodding to the scuzzy ’70s hard rock of the latter two and Segall’s trademark haywire, lo-fi garage.

Title: Acrobats
Review: A significant step onwards from their acoustic debut, Acrobats finds the trio developing a taste for the electric, which adds miles to their creative horizons.

Title: Dawnbreaker
Review: Sauser-Monnig's songs retain a sense of early-morning introspection that lingers. [Aug 2019, p.29]

Title: All The Way
Review: Refusing facsimile, Galás’s music attains its weight and power not from its oddity but from its humanity. [Apr 2017, p.53]

Title: Thunder Thighs
Review: These tunes feel huge, enhanced by a newfound confidence, choirs literal and adhoc, and the snap-bracelet rhyme schemes of pal Aesop Rock. [No. 82, p.54]

Title: Nothing
Review: The most complicated forms of techno and footwork are built simply, from the ground up, and on Nothing, we hear the simplicity of each component and how it all comes together to make the music that we love.

Title: The Smell of Our Own
Review: This is the stuff memorable summer days are made of.

Title: Electric Light
Review: This adds up to a solid album that presents as an immediate difference to what went before, even if it does not roam too far from the grounds of its creator’s past. That certainly doesn’t mean it can’t be enjoyed. Electric Light is a thoroughly immersive ride that shows James Bay has plenty of ideas brimming in that now hatless head.

Title: A Celebration of Endings
Review: Biffy Clyro have delivered an album of restless invention, substance and style that arrives like a spray of water on the arid expanse of this saddest of summers.

Title: With Love
Review: A truly stylish but somewhat overly long affair.

Title: CALM
Review: CALM is occasionally inspired, sometimes incredibly stupid, and most of all: surprisingly fine.

Title: Mic Tyson
Review: These verses could've fit on any of his past records or mixtapes. But the production on Mic Tyson ties them together nicely.

Title: Yours Truly, The Commuter
Review: Yours Truly is more cohesive than many of those past albums, a comforting hybrid of west coast beauty and stark, isolationist expanse that bodes well for his solo career.

Title: Wrong Creatures
Review: It’s their most accomplished clawing-back so far of the basic dark rock’n’roll street-smarts that were lost as they cast fruitlessly around for new directions with projects like the acoustic album Howl and the awful noise-scape effort The Effects Of 333 (their very own Metal Machine Music).

Title: The New Classic
Review: The New Classic will never be a classic, but it isn’t anywhere as bad as anyone will expect it to be.

Title: Wonderful Rainbow
Review: At its best, though, this album is like having a beautiful girl hit you repeatedly over the head with a baseball bat.

Title: Apple
Review: A staggering and potent amalgamation of numerous genre influences, but it also has moments of information overload, where its boundarylessness becomes too much.

Title: Franz Ferdinand
Review: The first great rock album of 2004. [May 2004, p.102]

Title: Fortress
Review: Protest the Hero is having fun with their creativity here, and Fortress is a better album for it.

Title: You Won't Get What You Want
Review: Daughters’ accessibility is directly proportional to their uncompromising compositional choices—hypnotic dissonance, martial drums cranked to incapacitating volumes, scathing vocal repetition, all rendered through impossibly vivid production. This is not music interesting in growing on you: it consumes and dominates.

Title: Velocifero
Review: Ladytron's strength is its sure grasp of Pet Shop Boys-style pop songcraft, which weaves memorable melodies into songs about anxiety-ridden love affairs and the ennui of a Sunday afternoon in a world where God is dead.

Title: Bye Bye 17
Review: Take the fake phone call and run, don't elephant walk, away. [No. 98, p.56]

Title: Unreal
Review: You get something that's very lovely and poetic and melancholy and vulnerable and unspeakably beautiful. [No. 100, p.54]

Title: Soft Hair
Review: Every so often, the album strikes that tricky balance between queasy and cute.

Title: Evolve Or Be Extinct
Review: Quality is spotty, though. [Feb 2012, p.106]

Title: Souljacker
Review: The whole back half of Souljacker drops into a range between plain bad and plain vanilla with only the occasional standard deviation above musically amusing.

Title: Nighttime Stories
Review: Through the years, the band has sculpted their sound into full-fledged metal, and as the burly, serpentine tracks Arteries of Blacktop and Full Moon, Black Water attest, they incorporate palm-muted riffs and Sabbathy doom with much aplomb—even if the latter closes the album with delicate, melancholic guitars, saying goodbye to their departed loved ones with gentle compassion.

Title: Too
Review: This new batch thrashes with abandon (“Punks”) and displays a remarkable leap in instrumental maturity with its airtight chord progressions and unhinged shrieks.

Title: Celebration Castle
Review: They’ve attempted to tighten up where their debut hung slack – shorter, less songs, less room to drag. Yet dragging is all that Celebration Castle does, falling deeper into the garage-meets-new wave dichotomy that looks good on paper but would require considerably more talent to execute.

Title: Where It Hits You
Review: The Athens-based multi-instrumentalist is joined by an assortment of similarly rootsy musicians who help flesh out some of these generally atmospheric yet always moving pieces, many of which only reveal their subtle allures after repeated playings.

Title: Stains on Silence
Review: Girls Names do a very good job of keeping the drama, intensity, and twisted emotion in place while taking the music into darker, odder realms. It's pretty far from the poppy place the band started at, but their journey remains one that is very much worth following.

Title: 99Â¢
Review: Remove the four or so songs that never seem to do more than bubble happily in an unambitious realm of chanted hooks and rehearsed quirkiness, and the result is an album fit for anyone with the slightest predisposition for fun.

Title: La Roux
Review: La Roux's dedication to their aesthetic makes this an album where the songs are variations on a theme, and on the rare occasion where the songwriting isn't razor-sharp, the style threatens to overtake the substance. However, that devotion also makes La Roux a standout, not just among the many other '80s revivalists, but the entire late-2000s pop landscape.

Title: Galore
Review: There’s pretty of sunlight on Galore, but no heat or friction, as everything from the production to Pepperell’s enunciation is so glassy that all of these somersaulting hooks might as well be gibberish.

Title: Felt
Review: Ocean’s no extrovert, but he’s an intersection for a wide array of listeners, and Felt exhibits a porousness that could also attract new and more varied fans of Suuns. Perhaps, in the end, we’ll all want it weird.

Title: David Comes to Life
Review: It's a true testament to the band that its windswept glory-rock stays exhilarating for nearly 80 minutes.

Title: Timez Are Weird These Days
Review: It may not be game-changing and it'll be slaughtered by those who have a hatred of hipsters/fun. But it's harmless entertainment, and London gets full marks for what he's best at--experimentation.

Title: The Wave
Review: The album arguably gets worse as he gets better, particularly in “Quicksand”, with its Coldplay-esque promise to “patch you up, we’ll work it out”.

Title: Ghost Notes
Review: Gordon and Post haven't missed a beat. In fact, they might be better than ever.

Title: Helter Seltzer
Review: Helter Seltzer offers a master class in grandiose indie-pop and how to maximize the potential of the simplest of sounds. [No. 133, p.58]

Title: Ripe
Review: Slower tracks such as 'Just Say Yes' and 'Blush' veer too close to blandness, though the power chords of 'Sex Without Love' and humorous idolatry of 'What Would Jay-Z Do?' revitalise. [Nov 2007, p.141]

Title: Finding Forever
Review: Finding Forever is something to be admired, even if it is uneven.

Title: American Head
Review: For a band that's spun fanciful yarns from the farthest reaches of time and space and the inner recesses of their own minds, this grounded perspective could be another interesting change of direction. But for now, it feels more like a retreat.

Title: Behind the Sun
Review: After more than 20 records, Motorpsycho remain inexhaustible in their creativity, fully, energetically, in command of a musical vision that is boundless.

Title: White Pepper
Review: Ween are at their best when they either dive headlong into ridiculousness or play it totally straight (admittedly, they don't do the latter very often). Here, however, they walk a rickety platform between those extremes and frequently fall into the ironizer's pit.

Title: Golden Grrrls
Review: The bursts of bright energy and amateurish enthusiasm on Golden Grrrls shine on wondrously for several minutes, but after a while the limitations of stunted musicianship and repetitive songwriting take over.

Title: Melophobia
Review: Cage the Elephant sound bigger and more polished here, but it’s Shultz’s lyrics that have grown up the most.

Title: Biophilia
Review: Only "Virus" connects in the way Bjork's best work can, uniting the fundamental optimism and wonder underlining this project with music that sounds otherworldly yet welcoming.

Title: Emmaar
Review: Tinariwen still speak to the world as outsiders, but now they are telling us more about ourselves than we knew before. [Mar 2014, p.92]

Title: Heligoland
Review: Haunting vocals by TV On The Radio's Tunde Adebimpe and Mazzy's Star's Hope Sandoval calm the jitters here, but the crew have gotten comfy just tripping out, but they sometimes forget the hooks. [12/19 Feb 2010, p.105]

Title: Golden Ocean
Review: Whoa, is it ever tough, but wow, is it ever great.

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: It sounds so damn joyous. [Nov 2005, p.134]

Title: Guero
Review: The production lacks the loose-fit liveliness and lightness of touch which was The Dust Brothers' trademark back in the mid-'90s. [Apr 2005, p.114]

Title: Graduation
Review: Thing is, though, that for every failure Graduation puts me through it has many a saving merit that only the nigh witless audacity of Kanye West could afford

Title: After the Disco
Review: After The Disco deserves to be heard and delivers a truly pleasant listening experience, rousing even, when the hooks hit the spot. But--and perhaps this is what the duo insightfully intended when they gave the album its title--don’t expect a party.

Title: Glad All Over
Review: The Wallflowers have always been a band that excelled at bringing new life to things we'd heard before, and that remains true on Glad All Over.

Title: A Thousand Heys
Review: Whether Mazes are a band that to stand the test of time remains to be seen, but this is an enjoyable, exciting and mostly excellent snapshot of their lives as they are right now; and you can't help but want to join them as the days grow longer and the nights lighter.

Title: Twentytwo in Blue
Review: Sunflower Bean have all the ingredients at hand to achieve something truly spectacular. And they’re right on the precipice.

Title: Beat 'Em Up
Review: 'Beat 'Em Up' is not shit but ain't exactly loveable either. However, it does confirm that Iggy Pop can still kick up a fuss with the best of them even if the end result isn't as legendary as the man who produced it.

Title: Source
Review: Deeply melodic, brilliantly played, and blessed with a spirit that feels generous and boundless. [Oct 2020, p.26]

Title: Another Day on Earth
Review: Another Day On Earth is more blank than frank, a journey through a hollow land, more discreet than it needs to be. Imagine a recording in which every human error has been scrubbed, like coffee grounds off a formica counter.

Title: Visions of Bodies Being Burned
Review: It tries too hard to pay homage to horrorcore tropes, like the chopped-up horror movie samples and heart-pounding bass, and sounds too polished as a result. It’s horrorcore for people who don’t want to listen to the real thing. Clipping. is an incredibly innovative and talented group, especially in creating entire worlds within their songs, but at their most inhibited, they come off as try-hard.

Title: City of Refuge
Review: Three weeks spent writing and recording alone has resulted in a cathartic outpouring that's both half-baked and hauntingly memorable.

Title: The Union
Review: The best tracks see the pair sparring over hymnal slow-burners that feature contributions from Neil Young, Brian Wilson, and Booker T. [Dec 2010, p.108]

Title: Offend Maggie
Review: Offend Maggie is head-spinning bliss from beginning to end, and proves that the quartet are the best prog-rock post-punk Afro-Oriental art-pop folk-jazz band in the world.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: The good--no, the astonishing--news is that this constantly engrossing record repays a decade and a half's faith and patience. D'Angelo has scuttled down the digital chimney with an early Christmas gift with long-lasting rewards: not just one of the best records of 2014, but one that will stay with you throughout next year, too.

Title: Cosmogramma
Review: Cosmogramma bursts with inventiveness; I've found myself careening around my apartment to sounds I don't recognize as of this Earth. That Lotus takes these vibrant ideas and sets them to pulses that move asses is incredible. Apparently everyone else is bouncing along in agreement.

Title: Dig Out Your Soul
Review: More than anything else, there’s a feeling that Dig Out Your Soul might actually be their best album in over a decade. In other words, not quite the fabled, oft-promised “Best one since fookin’ "Definitely Maybe!"" but certainly the best one since fookin’ "...Morning Glory."

Title: V
Review: Every song clocks right in that radio sweet spot between three and four minutes, and nearly all of them go down like candy, but collectively the final product is an album with all the surprise and individuality of a Now That’s What I Call Music compilation.

Title: Learn to Sing Like a Star
Review: Further proof of Hersh's glittering place in the rock firmament after two decades of making music. [Mar 2007, p.112]

Title: Comb The Feelings Through Your Hair
Review: They’ve found a way to wedge different sonic elements together, creating an assemblage of oft-quoted elements that feels fresh and vital even when its tone turns elegiac.

Title: Arthur Buck
Review: The duo's valiant attempt to circumvent the buzz-kill of pre-meditation can only take them so far, however, and Arthur Buck is not without the odd dud. [Jul 2018, p.89]

Title: Shotter's Nation
Review: Doherty is no mad genius--he's just mad, and it shows in Nation's slipshod execution and undernourished songcraft.

Title: Build a Nation
Review: The music? Thrilling as ever.

Title: Upper Air
Review: This record is like a pale version of their biggest fan in its shoe-shuffling awkwardness, and though each track sounds far too timid for single release, that is perhaps Upper Air's defining charm. [Aug 2009, p.103]

Title: KOCH
Review: At times, KOCH is so microscopic it feels like there’s barely any place left for this music to go. But Gamble keeps finding new ways to take it apart and reassemble it, to the point where something so closed off, so concerned with the smallest of gestures, feels thrillingly open.

Title: Ilo Veyou
Review: Exudes warmth. [Dec. 2011 p.94]

Title: The Making Of
Review: Despite a few too many sanitised, lounge-y moments, overall this is an enjoyable first effort. [Oct 2015, p.102]

Title: Slaughterhouse
Review: Whether you want to doubt it or not, there's just too much right about the self-titled Slaughterhouse for this album to be wrong.

Title: Tuxedo
Review: It's hard to imagine a record more slick and fun than Tuxedo arriving any time soon.

Title: Back to Love
Review: Where Hamilton's past albums have lured in listeners with their slow, sensual pull, Back To Love grabs them outright with the soul man's punchiest, most immediate batch of songs yet.

Title: Fatherfucker
Review: 'Fatherfucker' is one motherfucker of an album.

Title: Shriek
Review: It's certainly not Dungeonesse II, despite the superficial similarities. It's still got that rough-hewn, faltering-gear quality that bubbles up to make the group's most basic indie rock gems uniquely their own.

Title: Cuts Across the Land
Review: Even on repeated listens, the search for the showy dazzle of The Killers, the lyrical tomfoolery of the Kaiser Chiefs or the sheer stadium smartness of Franz Ferdinand proves fruitless, and it becomes apparent that, in an age where indie's proving to be the stronghold of overachievers, 'Cuts Across The Land' may have missed its moment.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: "Man on a Wire" is electric, and Not Your Kind of People's title track deftly threads blues licks through a '60s psychedelic needle. But too often the tomorrow-is-now thrills are missing here.

Title: Symphonicities
Review: Sting has shown he's a rocker who knows how to scale up.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: A subtle hallucinatory pastiche. [Jun 2007, p.92]

Title: Sea Island
Review: Music this haunting is more universal than local.

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: What's great about this album is they've managed to wield the same monolithic power riffs but make them count, with melodies and ideas way more consistent than before.

Title: Black Noise
Review: By melting away the distinctions between one sound and the next, Weber pronounces that he’s far more interested in affect than effect. Here he also notes that he shares perhaps more in common with the shoegazers than the beat architects. Yet, this mush of sound, sweet as it may sometimes be, may be the album’s only major impediment, as it can at times dull the impact of certain songs or passages.

Title: Utility
Review: Overall then: heavy, strong and not that long… but not really designed for dabblers.

Title: Days Are Gone
Review: HAIM bounces from strength to strength on a pop rock journey that hits on nearly 20 years of touch points.

Title: Quiet Signs
Review: Quiet Signs has a slightly jazzier, more soulful feel than her last, folkier outing, with a faint nod to Joni Mitchell on Poly Blue and perhaps even a hint of the Drifters’ On Broadway to the beguiling, sumptuous Here My Love.

Title: Give You The Ghost
Review: It's the interpretation of a human voice that elevates this record beyond a curious obscurist record and makes the simmering (but never boiling over) electronica truly shimmer.

Title: The Embers of Time
Review: The critics may long for drama and scandal, but The Embers of Time often demonstrates that a simple life could be for the best. Here, it certainly makes for enjoyable listening.

Title: The Winter of Mixed Drinks
Review: Any listener who has experienced the emotions associated with a romantic split should appreciate the album.

Title: In the Morse Code of Brake Lights
Review: The sheer, exhilarating high of early albums is gone, as is the laser focus pushing through to the end of songs. There are more sideways glances, more pauses. They can sprint when they need to, but not forever. This release proves that they don't have to anymore.

Title: Love Yourself è½‰ Tear
Review: Love Yourself: Tear shows off each individual member’s qualities fairly and acts as a well-structured introduction to a wider global audience that is all too eager to pick out negatives.

Title: Retribution
Review: She produces a cumulative effect that's both shattering and exhilarating. [Jan 2017, p.31]

Title: A Wasteland Companion
Review: It is perhaps three songs too long, but A Wasteland companion is, nonetheless, a welcome return to form. [May 2012, p.85]

Title: Brutalism
Review: Brutalism showcases Pierce's knack for portraying the thrilling and terrifying sides of romance and juxtaposing joyous moments with devastating ones.

Title: Evermotion
Review: What we’re left with is a somewhat novel approach that’s bolstered by improved songwriting, but ruined by a sheer lack of direction--or anything interesting to say.

Title: Total
Review: The timing may be off, but Total transcends trends to be one of the year's best dance records, and a likely cult classic in the making.

Title: Ringleader of the Tormentors
Review: Quite honestly, he's never sounded so alive and free - or, more importantly, human.

Title: Marnie Stern
Review: One of Stern's greatest strengths is that she never relies on any tried and true shorthand when it comes to self-expression.

Title: VOL. 4 :: SLAVES OF FEAR
Review: In essence, this album sounds like Death Magic if Trent Reznor had gotten a hold of it. They’ve subverted the congenial elements associated with their last record to make some of the band’s darkest incarnations yet.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: Pageant exists in a rarified echelon of R.E.M. records, alongside Murmur and Automatic for the People as one of their unimpeachable classics.

Title: Peace
Review: Tracks like Drive, Novocaine and Black cloud sound like the soundtrack to a 1980s brat-pack comedy, nut the sheer vim and vigour with which they're delivered still make it a rock 'n' roll rush. [Jan 2014, p.116]

Title: Young for Eternity
Review: Chock full of indie anthems that possess the straightforward bravado of early Oasis singles, the punch of Ash's finest moments and Kurt Cobain's ear for a pop hook amidst the noise and confusion. [#19, p.101]

Title: Crimes of Passion
Review: San Diego’s Crocodiles have absolutely nailed album number four.

Title: The Big To-Do
Review: The Big To-Do suffers from the opposite problem, with its workmanlike consistency belying its lack of truly astonishing highs.

Title: Mail on Sunday
Review: He joylessly repeats all the tired tropes of Southern party rap (brand-name fetishizing, drug-trade mythologizing, stripper-bitch glorifying), and the album's best track has already been let out of the bag.

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: Some couplings are brilliant.... Too often, though, the sheer familiarity of Girl Talk's building blocks detracts from his particular accomplishment.

Title: Underworld
Review: Underworld might not reach every peak it aims for, but it tugs on the heartstrings in all the right ways.

Title: Ibibio Sound Machine
Review: The highs and lows come from the instruments. The richness is in the brass section. But there are no emotional lows, only funk lows and disco lows, which, in emotional terms, are virtually highs, the landing places in a bouncing run.

Title: Scheherazade
Review: Haunting songs rooted in old-time country, Southern Gothic and humming electric ambience. [Mar 2016, p.72]

Title: Sempiternal
Review: Sempiternal is one of the most breathtaking and engaging albums of the year.

Title: Matador
Review: Not only is the music a step forward, the songs are too--and Coombes revels in their delivery.

Title: The Foundling
Review: There is no album in her catalog like The Foundling; it's a terrible beauty whose jewels gleam darkly, endlessly. Its songs hold truth for anyone who has either shared this experience or merely has the willingness to ask difficult questions with an open heart.

Title: Future Hndrxx Presents: The WIZRD
Review: On The WZRD, he spends most his time refining his formula or simply being lazy. Either way, it’s clear that Future is way too comfortable.

Title: Born This Way
Review: The more often she changes, and the broader she spreads her net musically, the less distinctive her art becomes.

Title: America's Child
Review: There's no faulting Shemekia Copeland's voice. [Sep 2018, p.91]

Title: III
Review: Though it's Moderat's strongest record, III isn't quite all killer. The very Field-like "Finder" bounces its vocal loop into the pocket, but it doesn't show off the songcraft found on songs like "Reminder," which might have sprung from a solo album by Thom Yorke.

Title: Worship Music
Review: Anthrax's tenth album, Worship Music, should rightfully be seen as a triumph.

Title: Forced Witness
Review: Forced Witness is perhaps too heavily grounded in the sounds of the decade [early '80s], to the point that a "heard it before" spectre hangs over the album.

Title: Miss Universe
Review: Even the mildly satirical skits, which don’t quite work, prove her desire to create a proper album, rewarding repeated listening.

Title: Overgrown
Review: At its best, Overgrown brings to mind Frank Sinatra's iconic In The Wee Small Hours, a record that acts as almost a thematic analogue in its lonely tone and ultimate embrace of love as a painful yet beautiful emotion.

Title: The World's Best American Band
Review: On The World's Best American Band, White Reaper knock it out of the park, drive over it in a noisy Mustang, and deliver nothing but a good time.

Title: Hurry Up, We're Dreaming
Review: With less of the anxiety that marked his earlier albums, that world is a joy to get lost in over and over.

Title: Take Back the Universe and Give Me Yesterday
Review: What's most striking is simply that they are able to take such a drastically different tack with this album and still end up sounding like the same band.

Title: Snow Bound
Review: It's an inconsistent album, with some songs slipping by in a swirl of sameness but there is enough here from a heartfelt and unique creative mind to keep interested in the band at a renewed and deserved high.

Title: Moody, Standard and Poor
Review: The songs are powerfully wiry and declamatory.

Title: Neptune
Review: The Spirit still play hard-to-get, which helps to avoid any ridiculous moments on this polished sophomore effort, but they're often too stand-offish to even challenge the listener, let alone push the envelope that their influences have so neatly prepared for them.

Title: I Bet on Sky
Review: It's everything to be expected: Dinosaur Jr. sounds relaxed, takes a laid-back approach and still manages to make an album that stands up next to everything else that the band has released since its resurrection.

Title: Apocalypse, girl
Review: Apocalypse, girl is a shift toward orchestral pop after the noisy rock of 2013's Innocence Is Kinky, but Hval loses none of her avant-garde inclinations in the process.

Title: Songs
Review: There may be arguments for Rusko's moves here; it's just that they're not very well executed.

Title: Mirrors the Sky
Review: There's so much to like about Mirrors The Sky that could've been loved instead.

Title: METAL GALAXY
Review: Everything fizzes and bursts and explodes with neon delight that sounds, genuinely, like nothing else on earth, but has a delight to it that's oh so familiar. [5 Oct 2019, p.53]

Title: Goon
Review: Some of the exhaustion on Goon is a lack of emotional range. The continued packaging and shrinking of love and misery for commercial consumption, something Jesso Jr. doesn't do cynically, but he does it so well and so often.

Title: Invisible Hour
Review: The melodies are strong, but they have a moody, hopeless character that perfectly fits these tales of missed connections and love gone terribly wrong. [No. 110, p.57]

Title: Forth
Review: Are the Verve back? Maybe. Definitely.

Title: Wild Nights
Review: While the guitars are grimier and the drums hit harder, Pins haven’t totally smothered their sound in engine oil.

Title: Invitation Songs
Review: If these songs constitute the Cave Singers' most pronounced attempts at transcending standard folk tropes, it's the gentle, percussion-free lullaby 'Helen' that ultimately proves most successful.

Title: Babes Never Die
Review: It’s easy to make comparisons with contemporaries--namely the likes of Best Coast--but Stina Tweeddale and Cat Myers transfer so much personality to their tracks that a deeper, more lasting impression is given.

Title: Chop Chop
Review: As the album title hints, the songs were recorded in quick, live takes and condensed rather than stretched unnecessarily. This all works to the greater good and marks Chop Chop as a triumph of substance over sophistication.

Title: You Forgot It In People
Review: Like no other pop album you've ever heard.

Title: Skeleton
Review: Most of Skeleton is an endless rush, sounding like up-tempo versions of the Pixies' surf-rock choruses. [#71, p.93]

Title: Sound Kapital
Review: A side project gets slicked up for a close-up.

Title: Black Dialogue
Review: On the whole, Black Dialogue emerges as a triumph, an impassioned 12-track hip-hop manifesto even a mother could love, assuming of course, she hasn't affixed a Bush/Cheney sticker on the bumper of the family station wagon.

Title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
Review: Merriweather Post Pavilion is so gorgeously confident that it fulfills expectations and more.

Title: Achilles Heel
Review: Ultimately, Bazan continues to sound more like a distillation of Wilco's Jeff Tweedy and The Counting Crows' Adam Duritz than the latest flavor of pop star.

Title: Cows on Hourglass Pond
Review: Hourglass Pond is an off-balance album. If you played the album to someone who didn’t know Tare had a new album, it would be very unclear where it belongs in his discography.

Title: Double Exposure
Review: Kelley Stoltz, Michigander with a heart full of British singsong, delivers pure pop nostalgia on Double Exposure.

Title: The OOZ
Review: All that aimlessness is certainly on brand for the hazy expanses Marshall so clearly wants to create, but like the seeping unctuousness for which the album is named, it threatens to engulf his more potent songs.

Title: Powerplant
Review: With only two songs passing the three-minute mark, this is blink-and-you’ll-miss-it angst, but deserving of your attention nonetheless.

Title: Star Kitty's Revenge
Review: A recording not to be missed.

Title: Emotions and Math
Review: These songs are raw and beautiful. Glaspy's voice is roughened, tremulous and hypnotic. Her guitar playing is characterful and advanced. Be sure to leave a space on those end-of-year lists.

Title: Plans
Review: Gibbard's angelic vocals sag with the weariness of a man who's gazed at his navel all his life only to realise there's nothing but fluff and darkness.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: Channel Orange is as dazzling as it is baffling, rarely staying still long enough to get a grip on.

Title: Arrows
Review: There are glints of light here and there, and some saving humour in the 26-year-old's lyrics.

Title: Maroon
Review: A borderline adult-contemporary sound that's catchy and exuberant enough to gloss over the intermittently dark verse.

Title: As Is Now
Review: One of his more satisfying solo albums.

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: Whether it inspires bosom-heaving, jersey-rending, or chopper-flagging, Explosions in the Sky will have true believers again faint with praise.

Title: Sigh No More
Review: Every hoedown on Sigh No More-- every rush of instruments in rhythmic and melodic lockstep-- conveys the same sense of hollow, self-aggrandizing drama.

Title: We Know About the Need
Review: This is a sprawling album of warmth, stuttering electronics and rural psychedelia. [#24, p.96]

Title: Blowback
Review: It's too lightweight and silly to appeal to those looking for musical innovation, and the songs aren't focused or fully developed enough to grab new fans. Mostly, it's just a really annoying album.

Title: Stay Alive
Review: Once the allure of hearing Grace so stripped down wears off, the record begins to sound like what it is: glorified demos for an Against Me! album we'll never get to hear. Even at its most vital, Stay Alive never escapes the sense that the pandemic has one again cheated us out of something better.

Title: Phantom Power
Review: Beneath the sweetest of the album's retro harmonies, though, lurk harsh synths and dark thoughts. [Oct 2003, p.128]

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: Hammond doesn't out-write his band -- several songs here get vague -- but Yours to Keep is more expansive than the Strokes, and sweeter.

Title: Tranquilizers
Review: Just as pretty but more purposeful than Jones' previous output, Tranquilizers makes good on the promise of Dog Bite's debut and then some.

Title: Psychedelic Pill
Review: He's still evolving, and though the double CD Psychedelic Pill is far from nostalgic, he's spending a helluva lot of time looking back. [No. 94, p.61]

Title: Always Got Tonight
Review: May be the best CD of his career. [Feb/Mar 2002, p.112]

Title: Badlands
Review: Under 30 minutes long, Badlands is a short burst of concentrated energy that gradually slides into less compelling instrumental murk.

Title: async
Review: async is the work of an authentically great artist that may well be entering a rich new phase of his 42-year career.

Title: The Horizon Just Laughed
Review: Profoundly authentic, nostalgic, and graceful throughout, The Horizon Just Laughed does nothing less than reaffirm that Jurado is one of the best songwriters in the business.

Title: The Avalanche
Review: Mike Kinsella has made not only one of his sincerest works to date, but also one of the most brutally honest albums of the year.

Title: All Hell
Review: Gibson avoids awkward genre mash-ups with memorable vocal melodies and a knack for seamlessly matching timbres of the traditional and contemporary.

Title: Mastermind
Review: Mastermind is a powerful album, an album with an identity, and one that has some solid songs and a handful of hits. Ross delivers just what he promised.

Title: A Different Forest
Review: That this focuses entirely on the unadorned piano may feel like a step down from those who embrace his more adventurous works. The instrumental chops heard here, though, stand on their own very well, and reveal another side to Hauschka’s music — and, perhaps, create some ambiguity as to where he might head from here.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: It is a record marked by a weary wonder at the departure of something huge from the world – Victorian invention and enterprise, the ages of steam and discovery, the impossible cruelty of empire, all fading into a half-remembered dream.

Title: Encore
Review: Encore is a perfectly good record. ... But one can't help but wonder how Dammers' wayward genius might have added a level of glorious unpredictability to proceedings. [Mar 2019, p.22]

Title: Ultramarine
Review: It’s no slight to say nothing on Ultramarine matches its opening triad--not much does. The remainder of it is solid, though it shows a band still using established pop framework in lieu of a personality.

Title: Our Blood
Review: With pedal steel by Buddy Cage (Dylan's Blood on the Tracks), ominous percussion by Sonic Youth drummer Steve Shelley, and Buckner's usual subtle craftsmanship, he creates wasted-night rhapsodies that demand you lean in close--however warily.

Title: Oceania
Review: Billy Corgan can't ever quite muster up the magic of the Pumpkins' early years because, to be honest, the songs just aren't good enough.

Title: Kodama
Review: Alcest strive for balance once more here, and for the most part, they achieve it.

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: Smart Flesh won't grab you with big hooks or infectious grooves, but listen long enough, and it'll sink its teeth right in to you.

Title: CVI
Review: Royal Thunder display a soulful sonic acumen that's as dynamic as it is compelling.

Title: Bat Out of Hell III: The Monster Is Loose
Review: This is a musical just waiting to be staged.

Title: We're New Here
Review: Throughout, Scott's old-soul narratives are reborn through Smith's atmospheric beats.

Title: Mended With Gold
Review: Mended With Gold shines and wilts in equal measure. For each injection of bombast draws the band further and further from their essential qualities. And yet, this departure, too, was inevitable.

Title: Lucky
Review: The group’s fifth disc is an infectious collection of bright rock songs (Whose Authority) and calm, soothing numbers (See These Bones).

Title: The Red Thread
Review: The music offers few surprises this go around, relying instead of the tried-and-true guitar arpeggios, atmospheric noises and orchestral, rainy-day crescendos.

Title: Through Water
Review: Through Water refines her sound: heavy piano chords; wistful, solipsistic duets with her own pitched-down voice; high, ethereal backing vocals; and low, mournful synth pads like artfully arranged clouds.

Title: Disc-Overy
Review: The best tracks are the more thoughtful reflections on youthful memories, such as "Illusion" and "Snap"; the worst is the turgid pomp-rock-rap crossover "Written in the Stars", ominously scheduled as his next single.

Title: All Delighted People
Review: In the love affair of listeners to this EP, an overly ambitious singer-songwriter who seems to be far more into growing artistically then creating genuine songs will force fans and detractors alike into the arms of another.

Title: Indigo Meadow
Review: Produced by John Congleton, the album bridges the quartet's trademark dark reverberations with the fun-house psych of 2010 breakthrough Phosphene Dream, only with more studio effects than all four sides of The Beatles and an emphasis on the Doors' Soft Parade-era organ.

Title: Caracal
Review: Caracal is consistently good but also feels manicured and safe.

Title: In The Future
Review: This is definitely a solid album from a band that is surely to get better.

Title: GENE
Review: Like the obtuse artists that LA Priest takes notes from, the best moments on Gene come when these perspectives are deeply inward looking and warmly welcoming at the same time.

Title: From the Valley to the Stars
Review: From the Valley to the Stars has hills that rise close to "El Perro del Mar's" peaks, and its cohesive vision is a pleasure to behold. At the same time, though, it harps on its themes with an overzealous single-mindedness, occasionally letting flimsy stuff support an overarching conceit that requires foundations of marble.

Title: (Breach)
Review: There's one big knock to be made against ''Breach'': It lacks the spark of the new, the original. Both lyrically and musically, Dylan works within traditional forms rather than pushing at boundaries... Dylan is more craftsman than innovator (in this way he resembles John Mellencamp), and some listeners will be put off by the feeling they've heard it all before.

Title: Anak Ko
Review: Despite these variations, discernable influences, and the involvement of collaborators, the comforting Anak Ko is more unified in tone than prior releases and benefits from its marriage of immersive sound design with consistently engaging songs.

Title: This Is Country Music
Review: When folks start calling you the greatest country artist of your generation, you'd better deliver. This Is Country Music does.

Title: Rakka
Review: Rakka contains some of Ripatti's most thrilling and unpredictable sound design, but taken in one sitting, it's hard to know what to do with it.

Title: Head Above Water
Review: Overall, Head Above Water is a collection of eclectic tracks and done well this could make for an element of surprise that keeps your ears perked in anticipation. Here, however, it makes for sonic inconsistencies that leaves you dissatisfied, wanting the bigger and better things that Avril is definitely capable of.

Title: Elaenia
Review: The album is not without its flaws, mostly coming from the disappointing length and one filler track. The record only lasts seven songs, and with the flood of ideas that Shepherd clearly brings to the table, it’s a damn shame we don’t have more time in his world.

Title: Black Noise
Review: This is a special album, make no doubt about it, casting its spell as it makes both a moving memorial and an example of raw talent. If techno with a soul is what you're after, then look no further than this.

Title: Underneath The Rainbow
Review: The overall effect is dizzying--a revolving door of treatments and narrators--but usually hits the spot.

Title: America Give Up
Review: America Give Up comes out swingin' from the first bell and barely lets up.

Title: LP3
Review: Though glimpses of possibility exist (“Falcon Jab” and “Shempi”), and the album is a more coherent and epic expression than previous works, it still fails to excite and mobilize.

Title: Among The Leaves
Review: With 17 tracks, Kozelek proves that he in fact can write a song under the five-minute mark, can be bright and bereaved in equal measure, and can even have a little fun doing this whole music thing.

He can sound awkward navigating Swift’s vernacular of haters and mad love, but when he plays up his strengths--the fingerpicking and strings on “Blank Space,” or changing the “Style” lyric “James Dean daydream” to “Daydream Nation,” a nod to Sonic Youth--the universality of great songwriting shines through.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: Talkie Walkie isn't on a par with Moon Safari, and proves far less daring than 10,000 Hz Legend. But it manages to hold up, in its own punch-drunk, electronically unstable way.

Title: Chain Gang of Love
Review: Their whisper-thin, doo-wop harmonies, fuzzy guitars and barely-there percussion make the Strokes seem like Led Zeppelin. But that's not a bad thing.

Title: Bare Bones
Review: Peyroux doesn't need to abandon her trademark loose-limbed style, but she needs to push at the edges of it more.

Title: Sudden Elevation
Review: Sudden Elevation sacrifices her native tongue and most of her earlier tweeness, while retaining her capacity to move and enchant. [Mar 2013, p.93]

Title: Nothing Bad Will Ever Happen
Review: Nothing Bad Will Ever Happen, as a whole, doesn't contribute anything terribly original to the genre, and as such doesn't make much of a lasting impression on the listener.

Title: Celebration Castle
Review: This record is solid and merits a listening, particularly for fans of similar straight-ahead rockers like the Constantines.

Title: Never
Review: From moment to moment, Never's oddball quality can be a blessing, but it becomes more of a curse when the moment passes and there's little besides disparate pieces to hold onto.

Title: Outside Love
Review: A bit more raucous and a hell of a lot more cohesive than 2006’s "Axis of Evol," Outside Love finds frontman Stephen McBean (who also leads Black Mountain) continuing to rewrite the 1960s, with much improved results.

Title: Throws
Review: The sound of two talented men messing around and letting off steam in a studio. Much livelier than Tunng. [Jul 2016, p.81]

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Kamikaze finds Marshall Mathers revelling in his Slim Shady rabid underdog role, fulminating at critics, boggling at Lil Yachty, and sneering at the Migos flow on Not Alike. How riveting all this finger-wagging is probably depends upon your birth date.

Title: No More Lamps in the Morning
Review: She delivers twisted, nostalgic jazz, flanked by her Spanish husband's eerie Portuguese guitar.... Lovely. [Mar 2016, p.98]

Title: Moon Tides
Review: Moon Tides is a daydream, not a rollercoaster ride, and if you’re not enchanted with the album from its earliest moments you’re unlikely to find anything that will catch your attention down the line.

Title: Come Back to Us
Review: The album bears Rogue's signature yet versatile voice and simplistic guitar-driven arrangements that recall his eponymous band's first album with the occasional grand gestures of Rogue Wave's later work.

Title: The Way
Review: With 10 songs running just over 40 minutes, the disc is compact and taut.  That helps makes this a moderately successful return for a veteran singer and occasional songwriter who always seems one hit away from the mainstream audience that threatens to constantly elude her.

Title: Public Warning
Review: A full-length debut strong on deft, cheeky wordplay and blessedly free of the usual hip-hop clichés burdening her American counterparts.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: Hercules And Love Affair are at their best when they cut loose and damn the consequences. [Apr 2008, p.110]

Title: Clay Class
Review: Clay Class is nearly an indie classic. All that's missing are tunes--not quite enough of those bits.

Title: Pop Trash
Review: Most of the album is, in fact, pop trash.

Title: Pleasure
Review: A record that is demanding and compelling, though often beautiful. [Jun 2017, p.90]

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: Incorporating harp, horn, clicks, clacks, reeds, bells and strings in other more "typical" Múm songs like 'Dancing Behind My Eyeballs,' they breathe a bit more breath and color into their swaying, hypnotic pop music.

Title: Say It
Review: By focusing inwards, Born Ruffians have done that whole 'maturing' thing that us reviewers like to talk about, and created a much improved piece of art.

Title: All Eternals Deck
Review: Perhaps the most striking moment here, though, is not one that offers anything new to Darnielle's still-expanding sonic palette, but rather one that reaches back to the past.

Title: Side Pony
Review: It may take a leap of faith, and it’s hard to imagine how convincingly Lake Street Dive can pull off this slick, immaculately produced studio album on stage, but once you let yourself go with the disc’s flow, it’s tough not be engaged by the sheer vivacity and likeability of a set that sounds like it was plucked out of a time capsule.

Title: Sorceress
Review: There are a couple of songs that feel a bit like half-sketched filler, means that Williamson’s fourth album may not come across many people’s radar. Yet for those who do chance upon it, there’s much to enjoy.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: These songs puncture the gloss, so they make the greatest first impression, but that glimmer remains the reason to get lost within Ryan Adams: his blend of song and studio craft turns this eponymous album into the equivalent of a substantive, new millennial version of the Eagles' Long Run.

Title: Widow City
Review: It’s a decided step forward, more confident and comfortable than they’ve ever sounded, and with (as always) a few unfortunate exceptions, an incredibly strong collection of songs. [Fall 2007, p.73]

Title: What One Becomes
Review: Alternating between unsettling dissonance and bludgeoning force, the North American act’s sophomore effort showcases a crossbreed of stoner metal, sludge and noise that both enthralls and frightens the listener.

Title: Human
Review: Like John Mellencamp and Bruce Springsteen, Stewart has done a reasonably good job of making his music millennium-friendly without alienating aging baby boomers for whom the occasional Tom Waits cover is adventure enough.

Title: The Block
Review: Like "Red Carpet Massacre," The Block is proof that it requires more than the best producers and songwriters to make good pop music

Title: Bloom
Review: Bloom is a fun record, dreamy and vulnerable and urgently horny. Sivan has a fresh perspective, and his force of personality enlivens tracks that otherwise might sound conventional. His best songs perform a kind of magic, with sentiments that feel universal to all of us and as personal as a fingerprint.

Title: 10th Avenue Freakout
Review: Freakout is a struggle between balance and shambles; the compositions constantly wobble beneath a gravity that threatens to bring them down for good and to render Broder’s brain inane for all time.

Title: Singularity
Review: There’s no prescribed narrative, but Singularity still tells a grand story--a synesthetic evocation of how it feels to be alive.

Title: I Am Gemini
Review: Overall, Cursive has put a tremendous amount of work into the idea and music for Kasher's somewhat twisted story, and it shows.

Title: Coexist
Review: Its low frequencies, irregular rhythms and slow-burning dance beats creep into the songs and draw us in deeper.

Title: Sondre Lerche
Review: All in all, the album feels like the slightest bit bloodless, the older, wiser Lerche a little less than the yearning teenager we once knew.

Title: Business Casual
Review: The record opens with a powerful three-part salvo crafted for maximum dance-floor penetration.

Title: 100 Miles from Memphis
Review: Crow's obvious joy is infectious, but even this former Michael  Jackson backing singer can't make a new I Want You Back seem anything other than redundant.

Title: Love Me
Review: Ultimately, with Love Me, Barfod has crafted an album of highly engaging, emotionally resonant pop music that's as creatively rewarding as it is accessible.

Title: 10 Futures
Review: 10 Futures categorically sounds like an album that was made for the sake of it, for the joy of it.

Title: Mary Star of the Sea
Review: As Zwan create a louder and less obviously pop eclat than the Pumpkins, they also turn more minimal. Their first record has one theme: the electric guitar. [#14, p.140]

Title: Yes, It's True
Review: It's only on a frazzled but euphoric Raise Your Head that DeLaughter achieves the sonic rapture the Spree promised from the outset. [Oct 2013, p.109]

Title: Tales Don't Tell Themselves
Review: While frontman Matt Davies' transition from apocalyptic yoof-preacher to hoodied motivational speaker will definitely leave listeners with an extended sense of self-belief, the winsome angst that once drove songs such as "Streetcar" has all but disappeared.

Title: Heavy Metal Music
Review: The album just offers up a heaping pile of midtempo heaviness that harkens back to Metallica's middle years.

Title: The Cost
Review: Singer Glen Hansard moves from quiet introspection to earnest Jeremy Enigk-like wailing and back again, all the while reminding you just how rewarding a listen The Cost is.

Title: Without Warning
Review: Like most projects that get recorded without the guise of a meticulous A&R, Without Warning’s billing never exceeds the expectations of any artist--rapper or producer--let alone offer a glimpse of what allows these individuals to rank amongst 2017 Hip Hop’s most popular figures.

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: As always, Stevens' precise details makes his songs ring through with truth. [Apr - May 2015, p.87]

Title: Because the Internet
Review: As a concept album on man's most abstract concept, Because the Internet is more than worth the download.

Title: Dirty Side Down
Review: On its eleventh studio recording, Widespread Panic sounds more like itself than it has in years. Dirty Side Down is the sound of a band returning to the comforts of home.

Title: The Invisible Man
Review: A typically bruised and beautiful collection of lovelorn ballads, Raymond Carveresque character studies and darkly romantic confessionals.

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: Comedown Machine [is] reliably solid, mostly enjoyable, slightly disappointing for reasons that are difficult to articulate.

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: Animals is a raucous and hugely entertaining effort that doubles as a virtual "Name That Tune" game. [Nov 2008, p.164]

Title: Plumb
Review: Plumb is a good bet for the end of year polls already.

Title: OnMyRadio
Review: A couple dramatic moments don't quite take full flight, and a handful of tracks are tepid and unmemorable, but OnMyRadio is mostly another set of sturdily constructed laid-back R&B.

Title: The Power Out
Review: Music that at once revels in and transcends rock traditions.

Title: Teflon Don
Review: Ross's greatest tool is still his presence, which vouches for the strength of his persona when his lyrics can't.

Title: Kill The Moonlight
Review: The arrangements, referencing indie-rock more than participating in it, pile on heft to the small-life tragedies: Matt Brown's sax toughens up Spoon's welterweight ranking, while [Eggo] Johanson's piano gives it roots, rag, and bonus rhythm.

Title: A Rush of Blood to the Head
Review: It's an album of outstanding natural beauty, an organic, wholesome work.

Title: Mountains of Sorrow, Rivers of Song
Review: Ballads like "Chill In The Air" and "Burden" have a stately gait, but Lee is more engaging when he turns playful huckster. [Jan 2014, p.75]

Title: Sailing to Philadelphia
Review: True, Knopfler's basic approach remains the same - as a guitarist, he is still enamored of the minor-key finger-picking style of J.J. Cale, and as a singer/songwriter, he remains enthralled with Bob Dylan. But in one song after another on this album, you get the feeling that he started out playing some familiar song in a specific genre and eventually extrapolated upon it enough to call it an original.

Title: Hey Ma
Review: If you liked James before, then they won't disappoint you now. [Fall 2008, p.81]

Title: Tell Me If You Like To
Review: Disposable lyrics and an overly polished sound doesn’t necessarily mean that this is a bad album, though--it’s not, although it is likely to get lost in the midst of this year’s more thought-provoking and risk-taking albums.

Title: Adore Life
Review: With fearless approach and razor sharp delivery, Adore Life is so bruisingly intimate that it feels like a surgical hand taking grasp of your gut. When Savages speak, you listen.

Title: Passion, Pain & Demon Slayin'
Review: Pharrell Williams and Andre 3000 add support on this hefty but intriguingly experimental 19-track marathon, while Willow Smith adds weirdness to Mescudi’s trademark humming on the dub hip-hop of Rose Golden.

Title: Please Daddy
Review: While the intimacy of the songs makes this a challenging listen, there is a humbling bravery here.

Title: Camp
Review: Vastly talented, he brings rare articulacy to the thorny subject of black self-image, particularly the problem of breaking down the barrier of ghetto authenticity.

Title: Saturnalia
Review: It's a gloom that suits them both. [Apr 2008, p.112]

Title: The Dutchess
Review: Where the likes of [Gwen] Stefani and co manage to tie eclectic albums together with the strength of their personality, Fergie never actually comes close to showing what she really sounds like, leaving "The Dutchess" as an exceptionally random R&B mixtape.

Title: Light of X
Review: It’s a stretch to call anything timeless, and singer-songwriters aren’t about to go out of style any time soon. At the very least, it’s another 12 songs just waiting to be plucked for the montage scenes of next season’s prime-time dramedies.

Title: Do to the Beast
Review: Dulli is a man still capable of the best in sweat-soaked R&B flavoured rock ‘n’ roll, but he now has a range of subtler, more graceful maneuvers too.

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: With Holiday Destination, Nadine puts a critical magnifying glass over why we should do just that [fight for something better than what we currently have].
