Review: If Sia spent more time at the piano, and/or hired Robyn to write her a couple of tracks, the results could be marvelous.

Title: Arcology
Review: Busy and engrossing, Arcology marks an exhilarating development in Thug Entrancer's sound.

Title: Cause I Sez So
Review: Against considerable odds--'Cause I Sez So is a bit of a hoot. [Jun 2009, p.95]

Title: Sermon on the Rocks
Review: Sermon On The Rocks is a wild ride, with producer Trina Shoemaker adding vivid colours to the singer's rolling rock gospel. [Dec 2015, p.78]

Title: Roses
Review: Roses may not immediately grab hold--and it's lacking one strong single to pull listeners in--but it's well-constructed adult pop that's unashamed of being either adult or pop.

Title: Lip Lock
Review: A couple more bitchy bits like this ["Wanna Be"] and the album could win over old fans with ease, but if Lip Lock isn't mean enough, well, neither is Eve. She's sweeter than before and musically more adventurous.

Title: No Holiday
Review: At 18 songs, “No Holiday” is basically a double album, one that sits somewhere along a continuum of epic works that includes the Clash’s “London Calling” and Liz Phair’s “Exile in Guyville.” The determination, the vision, the energy — it’s real.

Title: Aa
Review: So many genres collide on Aa it can feel like being trapped in a virtual karaoke machine. [Apr 2016, p.102]

Title: Knuckleball Express
Review: What makes Knuckleball Express slightly different from previous Hex albums is that the songs seem slightly straighter, though it’s a matter of moments before the apple cart is upset and a whole packet of noodles is scattered over the mix. [May 2020, p.52]

Title: The Flower Lane
Review: The record feels akin to 40 minutes of stoned stargazing in a college dorm room. And the kid down the hall has yet to add substance to the conversation.

Title: Leveler
Review: August Burns Red have set their own bar even higher on Leveler, and have done so for all of their scene in the process. The album is certainly among the most memorable releases so far this year.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: Drizzy’s candid lyrics about battered egos and insecure relationships were refreshing early on in his career, but the persona is wearing thin as he recalls how rich his melancholy has made.

Title: Tiger, My Friend
Review: Psapp's music is so beautifully complex that upon first listen it might seem a bit haphazard or amateurish -- with all its bells, whistles, whizzes and whirrs -- but after repeated listens, the oddities take on a precise purpose and fit perfectly within the melodic structure.

Title: In Evening Air
Review: Drawing from a few different traditions while making them their own, Future Islands prove here to be a well-versed group of wild, woolly storytellers.

Title: At Best Cuckold
Review: But because of its uneven idiosyncrasies and its cheeky self-flagellation, At Best Cuckhold sounds like Avi Buffalo’s coming of age story.

Title: The Age Of Immunology
Review: The Age of Immunology is, simply, a masterpiece.

Title: Girl on Fire
Review: ["When It's All Over"] itself is one of the worst here, mercifully outnumbered by the merely adequate and the few standout songs.

Title: I Had A Dream That You Were Mine
Review: Leithauser and Rostam have clearly tapped into the long, illustrious history of the great American pop standard for inspiration on these dynamic new songs, offering up their own inventive twists on the art form to keep the expressive dialogue going for a whole new generation.

Title: One Kiss Ends It All
Review: Overall, One Kiss Ends It All is a little uneven but still an enjoyable piece of cosmic pop, and once you get past the occasional stutter, there is a lot to take from this one. If only every day could be Saturday.

Title: Modern Mirror
Review: Adding in the duo’s pressing commentary about narcissism and digital romance, both of which bear heavy relevance today, Modern Mirror is goth aestheticism for the now and just maybe—the decade to come.

Title: Goodbye Country (Hello Nightclub)
Review: A triumph, possessing a universal appeal that extends beyond the dancefloor straight to the heart. [Sep 2001, p.100]

Title: Hermits On Holiday
Review: Most of Hermits on Holiday is pretty spontaneous and free-form, but it rarely lapses into the stuff of jam-band nightmares.

Title: Great Big Blue
Review: Though the easy-to-follow lyrics and even easier-to-follow melodies throughout Great Big Blue make it ripe for every summer playlist under the sun, the result is of genuine collaboration and friendship, giving it a charm beyond its obvious summery sheen.

Title: Endless Now
Review: there's a little too much here that's predictable or worse still, forgettable. [Sep 2011, p.91]

Title: Wake Up
Review: As with many records that share Wake Up’s exuberant qualities, the individual tracks are largely hit-or-miss.

Title: Power
Review: Morgan sings and raps on the LP, the first time they've used their voice on their records. That helps make Power their most accessible release. The singing is charmingly unpolished.

Title: Art Official Intelligence: Mosaic Thump
Review: Each track is a treat - a sensible, lo-cholesterol treat, maybe, but still packed with oddly addictive rhymes and beats.

Title: No Geography
Review: Their mega beats endure on No Geography, but this is also a stupendously successful splicing of past and present.

Title: Arrows
Review: Not a bad song on the album. [Oct 2013, p.96]

Title: Sun
Review: This is easily her fullest-sounding, most animated record to date, dense with layers upon layers of sound... and copious multi-tracking of Marshall's intimate, elusive, dispassionately soulful voice, which is richer and more versatile here than ever before. [No.91, p.51]

Title: From Here We Go Sublime
Review: It’s fair to say if you don’t find anything worthwhile somewhere in this record, you probably just don’t enjoy electronic music.

Title: Yankee Hotel Foxtrot
Review: It's a gripping darkness that doesn't often lift. It's hard going, but it's worth it, and that is undoubtedly their point.

Title: Another Fine Day
Review: For a bunch of jokesters, these guys deliver some seriously good music.

Title: Shut Down the Streets
Review: For the most part, though, Shut Down the Streets manages to avoid the ennui nipping at its heels, and in its best moments, reinforces Newman as both a skillful wordsmith and a masterful purveyor of Dylan-esque folk rock.

Title: The Remote Part
Review: While it doesn't have as many flat-out terrific songs as its predecessor, I'd venture to say that The Remote Part is the record that Idlewild has wanted to write all along.

Title: Dead Son Rising
Review: Dead Son Rising is neither terrible nor extraordinary.

Title: Here's to Taking It Easy
Review: Try it out, it's definitely worth it, just not anything you'll be rushing to your guitar to emulate. Or maybe it is, if you're in to taking it easy.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: I'm In Your Mind Fuzz
Review: Their longer songs at times dissolving into aimless jamming. The quieter ones, meanwhile, have a tendency to drift past prettily but inconsequentially.

Title: Cobblestone Runway
Review: Despite the odd bump Sexsmith could be in business at last. [Dec 2002, p.111]

Title: Ruins
Review: The new album’s particular saving grace is its self-loathing streak, the sense that scales have fallen from eyes and that Stay Gold’s nebulous disaffection has soured to regret.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: Nas pushes lyricism and technical virtuosity to the forefront here, stretching both his own boundaries and those around him.

Title: The Last Rider
Review: he Last Rider is yet another confident stride along that path, and anyone with a passion for smart and savvy grown-up pop is enthusiastically urged to follow him wherever it leads.

Title: The Creatures in the Garden of Lady Walton
Review: It won’t be everyone’s cup of tea. My Brightest Diamond’s Shara Worden sings on over half of the tracks, and her operatic voice is at times jarringly high. But it’s also soft and masterfully controlled, never distracting from the nuanced soundscapes bobbing in the background.

Title: The Art Of Love & War
Review: The album is filled with lush, suavely undulating ballads that have Ms. Stone cooing quietly and intimately.

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: This more open, organic process comes through on the songs, providing E and company with a refreshing amount of creative freedom after the relative confinement of doing a conceptual three-album trilogy.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Arab Strap's most affecting album yet. [#71, p.86]

Title: Miracle Mile
Review: Miracle Mile is the most varied Starfucker joint to date. It’s also one of the prettiest party records you’ll hear this year.

Title: The Colourful Life
Review: Cajun Dance Party aren't doing anything too unique or special here, but they do what they do with conviction and guts--and that's enough to make this a very good debut.

Title: Boys and Diamonds
Review: Boys And Diamonds is a madcap trek around the postmodern musical landscape of a world on the brink of catastrophe.

Title: Let's Go Extinct
Review: A thoroughly satisfying and intriguing record that pushes Fanfarlo toward new boundaries.

Title: Mise En Abyme
Review: The tensive sentiments that lurked the prior compositions are now in focus, beginning with an ever-mounting wave of vocal crescendos. Each layer adds weight, and each disharmony adds tension.

Title: Sirens of the Ditch
Review: This is a remarkably mature and impressive debut from an artist who seems like he's just getting started and his best stuff lies ahead of him.

Title: Hands All Over
Review: Really this is lead singer Adam Levine's show. Thus, the band's success lives and dies with his delivery. That delivery remains technically sound, though as a whole, the band underwhelms here.

Title: Pale Fire
Review: It's less direct than before, but still strangely, powerfully beautiful. [Jan 2013, p.103]

Title: English Oceans
Review: Basically, this is the sound of a band happy to be coasting, which can be a chore to listen to.

Title: 6twenty
Review: A crank-it-up-Friday-night blowout that's pure exuberance. [Apr 2003, p.74]

Title: Present Tense
Review: The album’s electronic feel sharpens the idea of sterility and a frictionless modern life, while providing, as British electronica has done since the days of John Foxx, a lexicon for existential nothingness.

Title: No Mercy
Review: Mostly, the album shows that T.I.'s lyrical side is not worthy of much attention.

Title: Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace
Review: This is another fine album from Grohl and company.

Title: Visionland
Review: Banditos light-heartedly plough a furrow of 60s garage-psych, soul, blues and country with a punkish good-time sense of savvy.

Title: Into the Blue Again
Review: In its many moments offering something warm and comfortable, Into the Blue Again might have been able to gain the status of one of those albums that could settle restless nerves, but this undercurrent of coldness counteracts this idea, leaving some tracks unsatisfying, passable rather than pleasing.

Title: Black
Review: Black feels like the embodiment of the masculine midlife crisis, with a similar lack of self-awareness on the part of the protagonist, even when he’s expressing realizations and moments of self-discovery.

Title: Indigo
Review: More complex ruminations are few and far between, with Tatum too often getting bogged down in generic binaries, from the fire and rain dichotomy on “Canyon on Fire” to a fickle romantic partner always “pulling me close” and “pushing me back” on “Oscillation.” Delivered with Tatum's vocals so prominent in the mix, these trite lyrical moments blemish Indigo's otherwise pristine musicality.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: It's an impressive work from a genuine legend and as a response to our current situation, leaves us with a pertinent message: in Bruce we trust.

Title: Moody, Standard and Poor
Review: It's all about perfect guitar tones, what frontman Rick Froberg doesn't say and the space Obits give their songs to breathe--even though it's evident it's not for lack of technical ability. [Apr 2011, p.115]

Title: Almanac
Review: Whereas Widowspeak suffered a touch from homogeny, Almanac casts its entrancing firelight in a variety of attractive bearings.

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: They sound joyous even when they're miserable. [Oct 2006, p.96]

Title: Fallen Angels
Review: He’s back with a second deeply felt, imaginatively reworked batch [of songs from the Great American Songbook] on Fallen Angels.

Title: Go
Review: It's ... very much worth your while. Many bands should wish that their most impressive work was as good as Motion City Soundtrack's least impressive.

Title: Wake Up Now
Review: Nick would do better to stick to his signature rippling guitar on the ethereal ‘Infinite Trees’, the quietly sensual ‘Lullaby’, or, best yet, the charming ‘Remembering’, which chugs along with a jolty percussive joy.

Title: Dumb Flesh
Review: A danceable memento mori, Dumb Flesh is mischievous, poignant, and quite likely Sacred Bones' most accessible release of 2015.

Title: In a Perfect World
Review: All told, there's a lot of bodice-ripping emotion to take in, and it's this, rather than the lack of original ideas, that makes In a Perfect World hard to take in large doses.

Title: Conditions of My Parole
Review: While the album can, at times, feel unfocused, that's also the point of a project like Puscifer, which allows us to take a look inside the mind of one of the most creative frontmen of the last 20 years.

Title: Mount Ninji and da Nice Time Kid
Review: It's appropriate imagery: Mount Ninji is a hedonistic party in a trash heap.

Title: Painting With
Review: You’re left with an album on which smug self-indulgence is matched with genuine inventiveness. Painting With won’t change anyone’s mind about Animal Collective, or even help the undecided make theirs up.

Title: Peace Is the Mission
Review: The more restrained moments, such as hit single Lean On, nicely accentuate the crazed moombahton intensity of tracks such as Blaze up the Fire.

Title: Hemingway's Whiskey
Review: Monochromatic can also be read as reliable, giving the people what they want and with Chesney, that's an easy, relaxed good time…it's just, now that he's in his 40s, he makes records designed for a quiet weekend afternoon at home instead of a Friday night kegger.

Title: Wu-Massacre
Review: Though the tight, cohesive, filler-free 12-track project sometimes feels more like a super-sized EP than a proper album, it’s worth remembering that Enter The Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) changed hip-hop with just 13 tracks.

Title: Stockholm
Review: She still knows how to hone a catchy melody. [Summer 2014, p.88]

Title: Knuckle Down
Review: Knuckle Down looms as both a pleasing musical achievement and a disappointing move.

Title: The Ecstatic
Review: It's always great to see one of our better artists achieving a return to form, but it's usually successful with leveled results. But on The Ecstatic, Mos Def is certainly back and he has released the best hip-hop album of the year, so far.

Title: It's a Bit Complicated
Review: Complicated shows a real grasp of musical history. [Jul 2007, p.99]

Title: Beyond the Pale
Review: Beyond the Pale contains plenty of sharp songwriting, but despite the intrigue of its premise, it may have benefitted from a more thorough commitment to making a proper album.

Title: Future
Review: Future improves upon his 2016 output. Although the 17-track, hour-long affair lasts way too long, Future sounds fully engaged.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: The vocals on You’re Nothing, however, are much more emotive and indicative of a newfound acknowledgement of the singer’s vulnerability as a frontman. The result is anything but sappy.

Title: Fandango
Review: Fandango tries to revel in its excess and overreaches far too often to be considered a success.

Title: Heathen Chemistry
Review: A step up from the previous two tossers. [12 July 2002, p.84]

Title: Olympic Girls
Review: Her most powerful album to date, both vivid and serene in its uncanny way of slowing the pace of time. [Mar 2019, p.61]

Title: D
Review: An audacious, adventurous, unclassifiable fourth album from the newly expanded Austin natives: this is a seriously self-assured sonic experience.

Title: Familiar Touch
Review: DIANA blend genres and provide a real sense of intimacy on Familiar Touch, a deeply personal and musically rich collection of songs.

Title: Freetown Sound
Review: One of the most sincere sonic statements of the year.

Title: Bobbie Gentry's The Delta Sweete Revisited
Review: Lucinda Williams' version of Gentry's iconic "Ode To Billie Joe" leaves much to be desired but. ... Overall, this one's worth it. [Mar 2019, p.30]

Title: Augustines
Review: Augustines has always been capable of creating rousing songs, but this is an album full of them, and it never once feels too much or overstated.

Title: These Were The Earlies
Review: Given that it’s a collection of EPs and singles, These Were the Earlies is predictably all over the map, a problem exacerbated by the Earlies’ wide-ranging stylistic ambitions and long-distance collaborative methods.

Title: Dizzy Heights
Review: The overall sense of experimentation arguably makes Dizzy Heights Finn’s most surprising and accomplished release since Crowded House’s Together Alone, the work of confident tunesmith daring to stretch himself.

Title: Yawn
Review: The ex-Coral songwriter is unafraid to experiment on Yawn, and--aside from a few songs that lose a little of their immediacy due to similar tempos and an abundance of shoegaze guitar--the likes of Mither ('Is that your key in the door / Nothing else would mean more') showcase Ryder-Jones as one of the most distinctive, comforting and essential voices we have.

Title: Volume One
Review: Deschanel's songs are simple and sad tales of heartbreak and missed connections, with hooky melodies and not a single artless moment to be found.

Title: Innerland
Review: The album’s production works against it, however. Beyond proficient, it's so clean and glossy your attention slides off the album. You long for a little grit and texture to really bring the music alive.

Title: Shiny and Oh So Bright, Vol. 1 / LP: No Past. No Future. No Sun.
Review: The main problem with Shiny is that half of its tracklisting is dedicated to mid-tempo rockers that are only fractionally better than 'Knights of Malta.’ ... With some more time and care, ‘Silvery Sometimes’ could have been an unimpeachable addition to the Pumpkins canon. As it stands, it suffers the fate of being packaged in what will likely go down as one of the worst albums in the band’s discography.

Title: Total Freedom
Review: These are unsparing accounts of tough subjects, but Edwards navigates each song with tenderness and humor, allowing her to tear apart old idioms (“Love is blind/Whoever bought that line must be a real sucker”) or invent new ones (“Love is simple math/I can be a total pain in the ass”).

Title: Matter
Review: While Grobler's music often bursts with light, frivolous energy, this album has an undertone of dissatisfaction that's new.

Title: Settle
Review: It’s one of the most gleeful and replayable debuts of 2013.

Title: Less Than Human
Review: It suffers less from a lack of competence than a general lack of inspiring tracks and the consistency of swiss cheese.

Title: Safe in the Hands of Love
Review: The music found on Safe in the Hands of Love thrives. It's just as boundary pushing but at the same time, it offers easier access points to the complex and often messy but brilliant world of Yves Tumor.

Title: God Bless Your Black Heart
Review: Twisted, mangled, and deeply submerged under the layers of bewitching muck are brilliant melodies with sonorous strings hidden between double-tracked guitars and gigantic, mesmerizing choruses.

Title: DOVE
Review: Although there mightn’t be a Feed The Tree or Super Connected to be found this time round, Dove is a coherent collection that retains Belly’s essence while acknowledging the passing of nigh-on a quarter of a century.

Title: World Without Tears
Review: She is simply magnificent.

Title: Czarface Meets Metal Face
Review: When the MCs are actually on the mic, backed by 7L’s super-rugged boom bap production, there is much to love.

Title: False Priest
Review: While some may regret Barnes's toning-done of quirkiness or ambition, False Priest plays to his best qualities while minimizing his weaker ones.

Title: Heartwork
Review: If one thing about The Used’s eighth LP stands out above all others, it’s how thrillingly modern it sounds.

Title: Lights Out
Review: It's a seductive indie-rock Pygmalion.

Title: Dreams Come True
Review: This full-length debut confirms Taylor's love for Arthur Russell's underwater electronic grooves, but these fussy, avant-prog slow jams rarely come up for air.

Title: Trouble
Review: The five numbered tracks of Trouble total a monolithic 82 minutes and trace heaving faultlines of their own making. [Sep 2016, p.73]

Title: Oceania
Review: For a Tarot-themed rock album made by an immortal megalomaniac, it's actually OK. Especially the loud bits.

Title: Chaos and Creation in the Backyard
Review: There's no question that in places, it's a tad too twee. But what we're hearing is an artist honestly following his muse--always a compelling event. [16 Sep 2005, p.84]

Title: The Understanding
Review: By turns frantic and tired, jittery and soothing.

Title: AMOK
Review: AMOK is a surprisingly unassuming album in that way; each song has worthwhile hooks and accessibility is favored over abstract experiments.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: The more intelligible lyrics and mid-fi production keep things entertaining and give it the feeling of a fully fleshed-out work.

Title: Three
Review: Tracks such as ‘Answer’ contain more light, pop-ridden sensibilities, yet it’s with the grittier, heavier-sounding choruses where Phantogram are at their best.

Title: Painted Shut
Review: While Hop Along’s frontwoman’s vocal still acts like a pummelling, emotive and unmistakable instrument, Hop Along’s sound has expanded accordingly on Painted Shut to fully accommodate her storytelling.

Title: The Deserters
Review: Now and then she mistakes bland tastefulness for classy restraint; otherwise, subtlety is The Deserters' chief charm.

Title: The Element of Freedom
Review: Keys never gets gritty, she remains reserved, never letting her singing or arrangements obscure the melodies or the classy veneer of the entire proceedings. All this determined detachment keeps The Element of Freedom from packing a primal, passionate punch, but there is charm in Alicia's enveloping, quiet cool.

Title: If Not Now, When?
Review: The sound Of Your Laughter and The Guessing Game are Get It On-style glitter boogies; by contrast Stay Now and All That Glitters reveal a more fragile side. [May 2015, p.92]

Title: Mondo
Review: Catchy, easily danceable, and consistently engaging, the album has arguably few stale moments. [Jun 2012, p.152]

Title: Half-Light
Review: Batmanglij has a boyish, intimate tenor, charming when not overdoing the breathy, verge-of-a-giggle delivery. Ultimately, though, it's the gorgeously inventive tracks that steal the show.

Title: Tricolore
Review: If their debut album doesn't quite match the boldness of their claims, it's a delicious little thing.

Title: Cry Pretty
Review: It is all gloss and shine, with sadness at industry-approved levels of maximum efficacy. Take 75% uplift, add 20% melancholy, top up with 5% not actually contentious controversy, and voilà: Cry Pretty.

Title: Flockaveli
Review: Flockaveli is poised to become to the Trap South what Group Home's Livin' Proof means to graduates of NYC's Golden Age: a producer classic littered with verses so whack they become endearing in their special way.

Title: Heart of My Own
Review: Heart of My Own sounds more produced than Oh, My Darling, but not for lack of quality. Despite the yearning lyrical plotlines, the warmth exuded from the woodsy harmony of Bulat’s voice mingling with the amalgamation of guest instruments cozies even the bitterest of winter days.

Title: The Concretes
Review: Definitely mysterious, but the songs on this record are obvious when it comes to the Concretes’ influences.

Title: Rips
Review: Her new band's no-frills approach incorporates doo-wop melodies and Joan Jett anthemics without ever being cutesy or overthought. Clearly, she's no novice at heartache.

Title: New Moon
Review: The Men have simply absorbed another musical language and are trying to speak through it and the other languages they’ve spoken through on previous albums, trading Spacemen 3 or The Buzzcocks for Dusty Springfield (“Freaky”). Some don’t work (“Saw Her Face,” parts of “Half Angel Half Light”), some do really well (“The Brass,” “Electric”).

Title: North
Review: North is an album intended to be accessible, and it embodies its time and place more honestly than most records released this year--which is a risky thing to say while also acknowledging that the title refers to a time as well as a place: the Northern England of Joy Division and The Human League.

Title: To Pimp a Butterfly
Review: Kendrick can’t be Pac or know everything it took to be him, but he isn’t going to let doubts stop him from making groundbreaking music. With To Pimp a Butterfly, it’s never been more apparent that he’s doing just that and prepared to stride past any and all obstacles.

Title: Do Not Engage
Review: Black and Miller aren’t as bluntly exposed as on their earliest records, but they still keep Diamond’s production bracingly in check for a sound that preserves a pervading visceral punch.

Title: Como Ama una Mujer
Review: The problem is that Lopez easily ages herself by a decade or two. In other words, Mama Lopez is probably going to love this album.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: While there are some lovely sounds on Somewhere Else... but it's hard not to yearn for something more.

Title: Jukebox
Review: This is Cat Power as strong and mature as we know her today.

Title: Wounded Rhymes
Review: Wounded Rhymes is an album that has not escaped unscathed from its wounds.

Title: Breakthrough
Review: Breakthrough splatters so many short ideas across its 47 minutes that a front-to-back listen is wearying, like hearing a dozen erratic interludes mixed in with a handful of lengthier sketches that are no more settled.

Title: None Shall Pass
Review: It's heady but funn stuff, eased along by bluesy, turgid grooves from frequent collaborators Blockhead and El-P, as well as Aesop himself. [31 Aug. 2007, p.65]

Title: Stay Positive
Review: Stay Positive isn't so much of an instant gratification, but a record that reveals more with each listen. [Aug 2008, p.131]

Title: In Case You Didn't Know
Review: This second album is characterised by cheesy, soul-flavoured pop.

Title: Bubblegum
Review: In the end, the album’s rather limited scope is justified by the masterful detail with which it is rendered, granting the listener limited entry to a place most of us wouldn’t want to stay long.

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix
Review: Though the album trips lightly from slinky roller-skate jams ('Fences') to near Brit-rocky rave-ups ('Lasso'), the underlying vibe is both retro and somehow outside of time--like a memory made sweeter than the real thing it recalls.

Title: Stone Rollin
Review: He doesn't just rediscover the past, he remakes it.

Title: soil
Review: Overall, soil is a courageous effort where serpentwithfeet's bravery pays off.

Title: The Color Before the Sun
Review: While many of the songs on The Color Before the Sun do fall into a certain post-hardcore formula that’s used over and over again throughout the album, the journey presented therein makes the difference.

Title: Paracosm
Review: Each track bleeds into the next with seamless precision, borrowing each other's fantastical effects from both mid-century analog plug-ins and modern digital tricks.

Title: EUSA
Review: Evocative and enriching, Tiersen’s Eusa is a faultless work.

Title: Post Pop Depression
Review: There’s not an ounce of fat on these eight, energised tracks. Everything is sharpened by the awareness of mortality and there is alchemy’s in Pop’s ability to infuse such resignation with real electricity.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: It’s Album Time is an impressively balanced and varied record.

Title: Stories Don't End
Review: Stories Don't End barely registers upon the first spin (it's easy pop for the millennial generation), but if given the time to percolate, it produces a damn fine cup of coffee.

Title: A Corpse Wired For Sound
Review: This album is not great as background music, because its dark emotion can be oppressive. However, it's a record full of detail.

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: After an average third LP and a four-year hiatus, the art-rockers are once again all kinds of excellent.

Title: Deep Politics
Review: Big ideas trade blows with mere doodles, but the resultant concoction is easily the band's most rewarding work yet.

Title: Let's Stay Friends
Review: Most notably is how these songs manage to seem loose, fun and deliberate all at once.

Title: Man Mountain
Review: More Michael Caine chill than Sean Connery cool, but equally suave. [Oct 2002, p.88]

Title: Endless Flowers
Review: On Endless Flowers they wisely embrace that amorous but no less powerful approach to indie pop originally deployed by charismatic acts such as the Modern Lovers and Different Class-era Pulp. Pleasingly, it's a guise that fits them as perfectly as their sunglasses.

Title: Antibalas
Review: They appear to have moved back into full-on Afrika 70 revivalism. [Sep 2012, p.73]

Title: Bat Out of Hell III: The Monster Is Loose
Review: The whole thing is, of course, ridiculous. But Meat's beat manifesto should be treasured as the last chapter of a remarkable rock trilogy.

Title: Heron King Blues
Review: Heron King Blues, for all its successes, is not an album for Califone rookies.

Title: Furr
Review: Furr is the work of an assured band that are in confident command of their craft.

Title: People and Things
Review: The more expansive arrangements suit McMahon's hyper-expressive singing, especially on a handful of cuts ("My Racing Thoughts," "Platform Fire") with keyboards by veteran session player Patrick Warren. But occasionally they make McMahon's songwriting feel less distinct than it has in the past.

Title: The Renaissance
Review: Some of this works wickedly--'Believe,' the D’Angelo track, is a keeper, as is 'Gettin’ Up,' a charismatic come-on--but there are just as many small missteps.

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: The King of Limbs demands some deep immersion for comprehension, just as a traveler from a foreign land must lose himself in the culture to understand where they are.

Title: Down in Albion
Review: Even the strongest songs... are hobbled by sickly vocals and Mick Jones's pallid, needle-thin production. [Mar 2006, p.109]

Title: Trouble Will Find Me
Review: For now though, as an album, as a piece of art, it’s beautifully painted but the colour palette needs to expand substantially.

Title: Ester
Review: TTTs are not the only young group on the block to be melding detached female vocals, distant percussive rattles and guitar effects, all swaddled in a sonic fog, but they're better at it than most.

Title: 20 Years In A Montana Missile Silo
Review: Thomas might have this new album down as the James Gang teaming up with Tangerine Dream, but PU exist in a world their own, one that bears only passing resemblance to reality.

Title: One True Vine
Review: The mood is sombre, the pace slow-to-mid and Staples means every word she sings.

Title: Lenses

Title: Days Are Gone

Title: Demonstration

Title: Oxnard
Review: Later lyrical transgression aside, the LP is a pleasurable thrill ride.

Title: Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends
Review: Coldplay's desire to unite fans around the world with an entertainment they can all relate to is the band's strength, and a worthy goal. But on Viva la Vida, a record that wants to make strong statements, it's also a weakness.

Title: Let the Record Show: Dexys Do Irish and Country Soul
Review: A smart running order helps, but it’s the performance from Rowland and his cultured set of musicians that pulls the project off.

Title: Masana Temples
Review: Masana Temples is a comparatively accessible release from Kikagaku Moyo, despite rooting itself in a reality outside of our own. The ease with which these tracks can be entered leaves one wondering whether this utopian vision--for all its gestures at peace--could be closer to us than we thought.

Title: Lynn Teeter Flower
Review: Taylor sounds too much like thousands of other winsome distaff troubadours.

Title: Mount Moriah
Review: Dominated by shuffling drums, slow southern rock guitar licks, and pedal steel, the music on Mount Moriah is unobtrusive and reserved--at times almost too much so--but there are some fine flourishes in these songs, which feature members of Megafaun, St. Vincent, and Bowerbirds

Title: California
Review: California isn’t a perfect record, nor does it need to be. It displays a band getting back on the right page with great energy yet struggling a bit to find equilibrium.

Title: Off the Record
Review: Clearly, Bartos carries the romance and self-aware humour of the “classic” Kraftwerk in his genetic code: the sweet, buoyant, dignified and melodious Nachtfahrt and Hausmusik, for example, breathe the same rarefied European air which rendered The Man Machine and Trans-Europe Express such heady and immaculate touchstones.

Title: Breach
Review: Breach does a lovely job of sounding both murky and ethereal; an important but difficult combination of affects for the genre in question.

Title: Life on Display
Review: Without the blue-eyed soul conviction of the original, it's enough to make even second-tier grunge has-beens like Seven Mary Three seem like innovators. [Dec 2003, p.145]

Title: Seeds We Sow
Review: Buckingham needs the tension of Fleetwood Mac to bring out his best work. He can get too quirkily self-indulgent on his own, but this new solo album, Seeds We Sow, has moments of considerable beauty.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: Aside from the added guitar riffs and post-punk tones, Stars stick with a lush string section and neatly placed horns throughout, and their romantic appeal stays largely intact.

Title: Hypercaffium Spazzinate
Review: There are times when their elementary to songwriting can make them look as if they’re stuck in their teenage angst, which is expected considering their genuinely fun play on nostalgia is quite detrimental to their brand. But the tunes do stack up, and when it’s delivered with this much conviction, that’s reason enough to rekindle that loyal, longstanding friendship with their most ardent fans.

Title: Shields
Review: Shields pushes and prods at musical boundaries in a similar way to Talk Talk's 1986 masterpiece, The Colour of Spring.

Title: Secret House Against the World
Review: Early Buck albums had all the professionalism of a late-night weed experiment, but Terfry is growin' up and it shows.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Time to Die by itself isn’t a bad album, necessarily, but it’s not even close to the same level as Visiter and what made Dodos different to begin with. I hope that on their fourth album, these guys return to their roots.

Title: Hello Happiness
Review: “Sugar” carved out a path to the dancefloor, but it also made Khan sound like a heavily filtered singer-for-hire as she belted out the hook. The song anchors “Hello Happiness,” and the remaining six tracks are essentially more of the same, with Khan’s voice rarely in the forefront. Her vocals become just another texture in stretches of the title track. ... “Too Hot” provides the sole exception. ... It’s terrific.

Title: The Art Of Love & War
Review: The strength of the album rests not on one aspect. From the dense lyrics spanning a wealth of topics to the perfect production, The Art of Love & War proves that Stone isn't going anywhere.

Title: b'lieve i'm goin down
Review: While B’lieve I’m Goin’ Down, at least as far as its words are concerned, is more interesting than it appears on the first few spins, that’s not quite enough to make it a memorable listen.

Title: hopeless fountain kingdom
Review: Where Badlands established Halsey as one of the more talented and dynamic artists of her generation, Hopeless Fountain Kingdom is both overambitious in theory and mundane in practice.

Title: Fourteen Autumns & Fifteen Winters
Review: Fourteen Autumns & Fifteen Winters is aptly named, its brumal sonics occupying the emotional chasm between melancholy and salvation. [#17, p.93]

Title: Microshift
Review: Microshift finds Hookworms drawing a line under their history and taking their first step on a new adventure. They’ve not put a foot wrong yet.

Title: Life Fantastic
Review: Though it may not be treated as an important album in the broader scope of music, it is an important album for Man Man, and one that is likely to age gracefully, just as Man Man appear to be doing.

Title: Yes Lawd!
Review: There’s also great ingenuity in the shorter interludes comprising little more than random chatter over a simple melody (Can’t Stop). An album with this much flair and originality is hard to fault.

Title: Diaper Island
Review: Creating such a tightly-knit record is a simple style a myriad of singer-songwriters have lived by, and in that sense Diaper Island feels just as uncompromising, if in a different way, as the equally miserable Blood on the Tracks.

Title: Ride Your Heart
Review: Bleached have discovered that they have a canny knack for inoffensive rhythms, melodies and harmonies which will immediately appeal. But where this record needed to provide an abrasive counterpoint in the lyrics, they’re more sickly sweet than the music.

Title: Only In Dreams
Review: This is a dark and heartfelt affair. [Dec 2011, p.82]

Title: Sidewalks
Review: With little more than plinking and repetitive, if deliriously catchy keyboard riffs, straightforward dance-punk beats, and jocular vocal whimsy, their third record keeps the party going hard - even if it's more the cake-and-ice-cream variety.

Title: Zonoscope
Review: Zonoscope is far from an outright failure, just more severe of a backslide than expected.

Title: Hats Off to the Buskers
Review: In a vacuum, Hats off to the Buskers exists as a charming, innocuous piece of work, perfectly fine for mass appeal; in the real world, Falconer and company are gonna have to grin and bear just a few more Arctic Monkeys references.

Title: Sonic Citadel
Review: While the proceedings might be more restrained than usual on the '80s hardcore-aping Husker Don't and Sabbath clatter of Halloween 3, if you think Lightning Bolt have softened you're very much mistaken. [Jan 2020, p.110]

Title: Crazy Itch Radio
Review: If you boarded the good ship 'Jaxx back in the Nineties, Crazy Itch Radio won’t see you throwing yourself overboard any time soon. If you were waving it away from the shore, though, this won’t see you splashing your way through the sea to catch up.

Title: Option Paralysis
Review: For years, Dillinger Escape Plan have been the metal standard-bearers of dizzying, time-signature torture, though they have occasionally eased up to construct NIN-damaged, alt-rock superhero fantasies. The band's fourth album gives these two personalities their most seamless marriage to date.

Title: Wilderness Heart
Review: Rather than adhering to type, Black Mountain now have a catalogue of songs that respect and rival their influences.

Title: Courting The Squall
Review: This is the best album Garvey has worked on since The Seldom Seen Kid.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: This album shimmers.

Title: To Survive
Review: Voice and piano are to the fore, but Wasser's orchestrations pulse and ebb like living things. [July 2008, p.102]

Title: Inner Journey Out
Review: Perhaps a wee bit too derivative for some--Tres Warren’s scuzzy washed-up vocals evoke Anton Newcombe. Still, there’s enough here to trigger intrigue should you make the effort.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: It'll inevitably be pigeonholed as post-house or something equally asinine, but for now, it exists without definition, and for that we can be grateful.

Title: Feels Like Home
Review: The most heartening thing about Feels Like Home is the utter absence of fussiness, or second-album overthink. It extends the Come Away With Me template while never echoing the earlier songs.

Title: Sunbather
Review: The mood stays ominous, even as sonic details thrill headphone-equipped headbangers.

Title: MartyrLoserKing
Review: Williams doesn’t rely on heavy-handed sloganeering, and is more than capable of a light touch, administering impressionistic yet prescient lyrics that are indicative of his beginnings as a spoken word poet.

Title: The Physical World
Review: On too much of The Physical World they sound like a pale imitation of themselves. [Oct 2014, p.108]

Title: Nozinja Lodge
Review: A beguiling, uplifting listen.

Title: You in Reverse
Review: The vulnerable sound that you known and love--all slide guitar and open chords. [May 2006, p.94]

Title: X&Y
Review: Unusually accomplished, fresh, and emotional.

Title: Paper Trail
Review: His apparent claims to have had "no choice" in his most recent legal entanglement--attempting to procure machine guns from an FBI cooperating witness--do him little credit, but the skilled, catchy choruses of On Top of the World, Whatever You Like and current UK hit Live Your Life suggest he is still a strong "buy".

Title: The Art of Pretending to Swim
Review: Villagers fans will no doubt love this record, which has the capacity to obtain a new fanbase with O’Brien’s newly found sound.

Title: Pinch & Shackleton
Review: It is difficult to pick any more jewels off this dance floor diadem, making the most as it does of the long player context.

Title: Victorious
Review: Missteps matter little on an album that proves a minimal tour de force, home to some of the most simply enjoyable music in Hood’s 20-plus-year production history.

Title: Moms
Review: Moms is an album that you will probably end up liking, and liking a lot, though it is also conversely an album that is hard to enjoy with its heart-on-its-sleeve sentiment and the realization that its creators might not be the most affable guys on the planet.

Title: Have One on Me
Review: Were brevity the chiefmost virtue of popular music, "Baby Birch" would be a turgid waste of time, rather than the deft and skillful creature it is. The same sentiment goes for the rest of the album; there is a depth to the material here that rewards--nay, demands--repeated scrutiny.

Title: Wicked Nature
Review: Even though it’s not overlong at only 55 minutes, it still feels bloated and unnecessary.

Title: Themes For An Imaginary Film
Review: Like the phantom motion you feel laying in bed after long hours in transit, Themes for an Imaginary Film is bound to stick with you, drawing you in deeper with each turn of the ignition.

Title: Never Better
Review: From front to back, the album's an acquired taste, and even if it's not the big paradox that an album mixing punk ethics with rap virtuosity might risk becoming, it doesn't have a universal appeal, especially for heads leery of anything that might approach the misnomer of "emo rap."

Title: A Corpse Wired For Sound
Review: It makes for an exhausting and engrossing listen, and ultimately can’t be anything but a life-affirming statement.

Title: A Thousand Shark's Teeth
Review: Frustratingly, what should be the album's best song isn't on the album.... A creative chameleon with endless wells of technical skill, Worden stuffs Shark's Teeth with studied know-how.

Title: Before We Forgot How to Dream
Review: The effects are over-stylised, however, rendering her impressive vocals precocious, ad the uniformly mid-paced tempos can become wearying. [Aug 2015, p.80]

Title: The Unsemble
Review: Sure, no one is going to mistake this for an Einsturzende Neubaten or Jesus Lizard album (and most definitely not a Silver Jews disc), but the links to those acts can still be felt in the music here, making this self-titled debut an impressive collaboration between a trio of rather impressive collaborators.

Title: Sonic Citadel
Review: Sonic Citadel is a showcase for titanic, incisive riffs, gnarly yet immediate, accessible. [Oct 2019, p.56]

Title: Start Something
Review: [Lostprophets] mine the acts of groups like Faith No More and Incubus to put a more palatable edge on the sluggish nu-metal genre.

Title: Storytelling
Review: An occasionally jumbled, yet undeniably pleasant, collection that unsurprisingly feels like a hybrid of a proper Belle & Sebastian album and a more traditional film score.

Title: Double Night Time
Review: No part of stately songs like the instrumental 'Nocebo' and especially the would-be pop hit 'Ruthless City' sounds desperate for attention, but they pay attention back with warm details that prove all the more wowing for their restraint.

Title: POWER
Review: While never the strongest lyricist, ‘Power’ sees vocalist/guitarist Sam McTrusty roll out an unending series of lines that are overt to the point of self-suffocation. ... ‘Messiah’ and closer ‘Praise Me’ are stronger cuts, though as with much of ‘Power’, they’re unfortunately lost amongst the plethora of untidy songwriting on show.

Title: Iteration
Review: The best thing you can do is let Iteration’s rain-soaked neon lights wash over and see what you feel.

Title: Lies for the Liars
Review: It seems as if they've done everything possible to distance themselves from their original, much more interesting sound, opting instead for songs with barely enough hooks and coherent structures.

Title: Shackles' Gift
Review: The music is too futuristic--and, more bizarrely, too rooted in Indian Ocean folk roots--ever to get weighed down in heaviosity. [Mar 2015, p.96]

Title: We Are The Night
Review: For every catchy electro-dance, there's a tune that leaves you scratching your head.

Title: Civilian
Review: Even as it limits the album's appeal as much as it does the band's chances of broader success, Wye Oak's stylistic purity is a virtue in itself.

Title: Heavy Lifter
Review: The result is a more coherent set of tunes that don't veer far from Hovvdy's established ruminative demeanor.

Title: Vespertine
Review: 1997's Homogenic, also a mixture of heavy beats and strings, was not as varied or complete as this album, and while Selmasongs, last year's soundtrack to "Dancer in the Dark" (in which Björk starred), was lovely in its own sweeping, cinematic way, Björk has surpassed herself with this new work.

Title: The Stars Are Indifferent to Astronomy
Review: The band sticks to their guns but in doing so produce a record that's so nonprovocative that the music doesn't truly assert itself.

Title: Lady in Gold
Review: Forget the sophomore jinx, this set delivers on the promise of that first album and then some.

Title: M:FANS
Review: If M:FANS represents a world that is colder and less forgiving than the time and place that spawned Music for a New Society, it also confirms that Cale is still a strong and vital artist, and one capable of offering two very different sets of perspectives on these songs that are both bold and compelling listening.

Title: Return the Gift
Review: I'm sure purists would prefer to snag the recently remastered originals as opposed to this Gift, even though those older fans would be able to appreciate this album most.

Title: Wake Up the Nation
Review: An astonishing landmark, and great record, wherein the Mod once again becomes The Modernist. [May 2010, p.94]

Title: Transference
Review: The decision not to focus on immediate pop hooks is really a blessing, though, as this album showcases Spoon at their loosest and most diverse.

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: Ridiculously innovative.

Title: My Krazy Life
Review: There’s no desire to transcend West Coast inner-city values, and YG does traverse the hyphy and nighttime sounds with aplomb. But the thrills do have a comedown at some point. For the album as a whole, it’s the potentially ephemeral replay value because of its on-the-nose focus on 20-somethings mayhem.

Title: Look A Little Closer
Review: Bibio's [Ambivalence Avenue] had two things Look a Little Closer is missing, namely context and a true sense of discovery.

Title: Anywhere I Lay My Head
Review: Anywhere I Lay My Head is a starling achievement not because Ms. Scarlett has simply managed to cleverly re-imagine some assemblage of Tom Wait songs, but rather, because she has seized upon precisely why they affected us so much the first time round. [Spring 2008, p.91]

Title: Urban Turban - The Singhles Club
Review: Full of life and sunshine. [No.87, p.53]

Title: Take Me Home
Review: The cheesiness, loads of filler, and overly glossy production are still present and hinder much of what the album had the potential to accomplish.

Title: Talk About Body
Review: A firebrand debut album, Talk About Body celebrates the struggle and freedom in defying easy classification.

Title: Diamond Rugs
Review: This ain't no Chickenfoot; this is the really really real deal.

Title: Don't Get Lost
Review: There’s plenty more to like. The imaginary soundtrack piece Fact 67 is full of neat Sturm und twang; Dropping Bombs On The Sun is a pretty, hazy piece with a spooked Parks vocal that lives up to the title. If you like Ornette Coleman and all that jazz, then Don’t Get Lost is your friend.

Title: Ohms
Review: In terms of epic grandeur, though, Ohms somehow surpasses even the band's most ambitious middle-period work. If past albums in the Deftones discography defined key points in the story of your life, you can expect to be thoroughly engrossed by the latest chapter in a remarkable musical journey that, against all the odds, just got more compelling.

Title: Vermont
Review: Vermont make their retro intentions more than clear on their self-titled debut.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: This real-life fairytale is made up of myriad difficult home truths but Marling's hejira, her flight to freedom, makes for absolutely compelling listening. Oh, and there's a happy, redemptive ending to boot.

Title: Everything Goes Wrong
Review: This is fun music that is all at once euphonic, brash, unsophisticated in its simplicity--but powerful for that same reason.

Title: Hey Hey My My Yo Yo
Review: Their heavenly mix of mix of giddy silliness, pop smarts and pop culture overload makes Hey Hey My My Yo Yo a fun-filled, joyride from beginning to end.

Title: Before the Poison
Review: Unless you dig Nick's poetry, grab the Polly songs and run.

Title: Endless
Review: For the most part, the musicality--much sparser than the maximalist sonic feasts of his earlier work--still holds the same synesthetic power of the past, even for those who don’t claim to have the ability to see sounds.

Title: The Age of Adz
Review: Sufjan's proficiency with larger-than-life arrangements has always been one of his strongest qualities as a musician, and across The Age of Adz he wields that proficiency, brazenly, like a kind of weapon.

Title: Heavy Mood
Review: There's a lack of progression from previous albums that makes Heavy Mood a bit of a disappointment.

Title: i
Review: The marked contrast between the deadpan vocals and the lightness of the music mostly works, although because of the limitations of Merritt's vocal range, he is not always able to project the same depth of feeling detailed in the songs' lyrics.

Title: Live Like You Were Dying
Review: More of the album comes down on the right side of chest-thumping versus heart-bearing. [3 Sep 2004, p.77]

Title: A Better Version of Me
Review: Rainer Maria still sit solidly in the emo-core genre, yet avoid producing music that is maudlin or obvious. In fact their graceful approach to music is exactly what disguises their insightful and detailed lyrics.

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: A 10-track masterclass in spectral, psychedelicised pop, it's awash with great tunes and soaring arrangements. [Nov 2006, p.117]

Title: Liz Phair
Review: Phair is a fine lyricist, and although she's lost some musical identity, she's gained potential Top Forty access.

Title: Are We There
Review: She gives everything, and it’s impossible to be unmoved.

Title: Feedback
Review: It's original member, turntablist Nu-Mark, who still provides the highlights. [Aug 2006, p.96]

Title: Secret House Against the World
Review: Pick out the antihero tracks and one or two missteps and you have every Beck album (no typo) crammed into one disc with more wit and charm and weird science and heartache than that dude’s cumulative catalogue.

Title: To The Sunset
Review: Musically, she does something different, bringing what she needs to each song, breaking away from genre into something that you could shelve on about any rack, and probably should.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: Beck produced Morning Phase himself, and while that makes for a cohesive listen, consulting with another trusted producer could have coaxed out some of the freewheeling unpredictability that once characterized his music.

Title: Cut With the Cake Knife
Review: The exquisite nature of this slices of dappled pop genius is a joy to behold.

Title: A Blessing and a Curse
Review: Musically, A Blessing and a Curse is the Truckers' least complicated album. [May 2006, p.93]

Title: Static
Review: Cults is a pop band--albeit a very distinctive one--and Static only works when the band delivers on the melodies that made its debut so compelling.

Title: The Life of the World to Come
Review: He's still writing finely observed vignettes that manage to intersect life as we live it with life as we wish we could live it, and as such, he has more in common with a short story writer than he does with the typical singer/songwriter.

Title: Honky Tonk Time Machine
Review: Eighties pop shine cut with pedal steel/fiddle poetry, Texas swing, cantina blues and achingly-crooned nostalgia that generally doesn’t feel hard sell, even when things gets treacly. Which of course, they do.

Title: Fireplace: TheNotTheOtherSide
Review: A confused but compulsive listen. [Feb 2017, p.60]

Title: Shock City Maverick
Review: He's more grounded... and his evasive, abstract beats underpin his vocals less randomly. [Dec 2004, p.124]

Title: The Ecstatic
Review: Though his vigor falters toward the end, The Ecstatic remains by far his strongest, most deeply felt work in ages.

Title: In The Grace of Your Love
Review: I will say In The Grace of Your Love makes the last five years without The Rapture seem a lot more empty, sometimes you don't know what you're missing until it returns.

Title: Adore Life
Review: Adore Life is a great set of songs. Savages have created an equal-but-different follow-up to Silence Yourself. While it can’t have the surprise of their debut, Adore Life demonstrates evolution and exploration that Savages will hopefully continue to embrace in the future.

Title: Men's Needs, Women's Needs, Whatever
Review: But all the marquee names in the world wouldn't mean a thing if the Cribs didn't step up in the songwriting department, and the trio answer Kapranos' ready-for-prime-time production with chart-gazing tunes.

Title: God Loves Ugly
Review: Though the lo-fi D.I.Y. production slows the momentum on a handful of tracks, when Slug's rhymes and producer Ant's beats click, the results are as good as underground hip-hop gets.

Title: High Hopes
Review: It's well within the Boss' right to try and freshen up old material, especially 18 albums in, but this one lacks a through-line beyond the distracting (and occasionally straight-up embarrassing) Morello.

Title: Bad as Me
Review: A work of pure, true genius.

Title: The Light in You
Review: The delicate songs quickly exposing the thin line between pretty and cloying. However, salvation arrives with the euphoric chorus of Are You Ready?, swiftly followed by Sunflower’s easygoing pop charms.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: "Sky Blue Sky" feels more collaborative than the past few Wilco records... The dozen tunes here reflect the more organic sound of a band playing in a room, with musicians turning ideas into grooves, which in turn become songs.

Title: Fever
Review: If you liked Embrace, You'll like Fever. If you're looking for something novel, you might have better luck at a bookstore. [Spring/Summer 2010, p.107]

Title: Reality Check
Review: The gimmick factor is high, but when one gets past all this, the songs on Reality Check are simply catch-as-hell pop tunes with a hormonal teen's penchant toward the lustful and reactionary. [Spring 2008, p.84]

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: Despite many excellent tunes, a continual emphasis on effects makes the album slightly grating in parts, feeling a bit like a Wire and Frampton Come Alive! recurring super group nightmare, in which the best and worst aspects of Seventies rock music are forced to combine to beat the Russians.

Title: Traveler
Review: It's not his most cohesive batch of songs.... But for a man who creates songs of which he says, "To me, they're for everybody to play," there's no reason not to include a little bit of this and a little bit of that.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: Heartfelt, spirited, lyrical, moody and mostly magnificent pop rock.

Title: A Sleep & A Forgetting
Review: The album is a bit of a departure for Islands in sound and even more so in content, but rather than a misstep, A Sleep & A Forgetting fits neatly within the band's catalog.

Title: Ctrl
Review: Featuring savage and often heartfelt, diary-like ruminations, CTRL pushes against the borders of convention lyrically and sonically, placing it on the upper echelons of potential ‘Best Of ’17’ lists.

Title: Dog Whistle
Review: The production is slicker, the songwriting more considered, and the statement more solidified. Peppered with spoken-word interludes, Cashwan-Pratt laying himself bare like never before, Dog Whistle is a manifesto for everything Show Me The Body’s early days promised.

Title: It's Up To Emma
Review: Throughout, Niblett’s lonesome, PJ Harvey-like voice and grunge-bitten guitar are central, while disorientating snare cracks serve to underline her forlorn tales of domestic crises.

Title: Less Than Human
Review: For some, the absence of human warmth may prove the album's ultimate flaw. Still, until there are humans out there making music like this robot, we'll settle for it.

Title: In Spades
Review: It's Dulli's band, and what he's delivered here honestly satisfies.

Title: Most Messed Up
Review: Most Messed Up is a full-blown, album-length expression of the Old 97s’ vintage, railroad-beat careen stripped of all embellishments.

Title: A Hundred Days Off
Review: Underworld's grooves pump with less impact now, but they make them work harder and with more diversity.

Title: Loud Hailer
Review: Beck has never made a record quite like this before, one that radiates knowledge and tempers cynicism with hope and hope with cynicism. Thank goodness we have it now and for all time.

Title: Mystery Hour
Review: Mystery Hour is quite an accomplishment professionally and personally, as Bagg and Hill are congruently creative and confessional in expressing their arc with eloquent honesty and striving, novel artistry. Each track freshly reveals a part of their puzzle with style-shifting panache while simultaneously ensuring that the LP flows cohesively.

Title: awE naturalE
Review: Often on 'Awe Naturale', the songs are suddenly cut off before they get into their stride and leave you wanting more of their soulful jams with a rap twist. Regardless, this is a largely enjoyable debut from this versatile duo.

Title: Different Gear, Still Speeding
Review: Different Gear, Still Speeding is not without its faults. But it manages excess and grandeur far more gracefully than Oasis' own overblown collection, Be Here Now.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: The album is much larger and brasher than it would first appear--the closer it hews to a mix of sad-sack indie pop and elegant, monied Patrick Bateman commercial 80s sounds, the better it works.

Title: Yeezus
Review: Yeezus isn’t his masterpiece, but it's an integral piece of an eclectic collection that will one day provide a window to an artist who will either become an insane Howard Hughesian eccentric or mellow into reality TV Kardashian fatherdom.

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: The first Seeds LP without co-founder Mick Harvey, Sky is full of tiny sounds--plinking guitars, pulsing bass, lazy subtle drums.

Title: Wovenwar
Review: Taken as the debut album from an entirely new band, which it should be, Wovenwar shows great promise, even if it all feels a bit familiar.

Title: Arrow
Review: As Arrow progresses, we get a clearer sense of how she's beginning to understand what she seeks. And though we're never exactly sure what it is, her music leads us to a full conclusion.

Title: Dear
Review: There are stray blasts of righteous melody, like the anthemic crescendos that erupt from the placid surface of “Beyond.” But most of Dear’s sonic earthquakes seem designed to rattle the bones, not catch the ears.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: While there's no immediate pop hit present a la "Feel Good Inc" or "Clint Eastwood" to get sucked into straight off, Albarn's ability to juggle his rotating ensemble cast and still spin a cohesive yarn for all of sixteen tracks remains something to behold.

Title: Kannon
Review: Kannon will leave other neophytes feeling awed by the complexity and physicality achieved here. [Jan 2016, p.70]

Title: Tomorrow Morning
Review: Creativity sometimes croaks when domestic bliss walks in, but not here. [Sep 2010, p.96]

Title: No Mythologies to Follow
Review: Despite its strengths, No Mythologies To Follow is still a touch green. [Apr 2014, p.115]

Title: Bluefinger
Review: Bluefinger is the best overall solo record Black has released in a long time, but it's still only good, not great.

Title: Santi
Review: Most of the album is forgettable, or worse.

Title: In Our Bedroom After the War
Review: Not Stars’ best, and far from their worst, but an album’s worth of the usual string-laden drama-pop seems a thin substitute for what today’s kids are seeking.

Title: They Were Wrong, So We Drowned
Review: Though it might not be the most easily digestible subject matter, it melds thought and execution as well as any concept album in recent memory.

Title: Bang Bang Rock & Roll
Review: Bang Bang Rock and Roll is still the most welcome, here's-mud-in-yer-eye debut since The Libertines' Up the Bracket.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Ending with a brief, queasy reprise tease of 'Wrong,' Sounds of the Universe concludes anticlimactically, an echo of its promising start.

Title: True Love Kills the Fairy Tale
Review: You can give True Love Kills the Fairy Tale several spins and still not remember which lilting melody goes with which crashing, reverby drum-fuzz-and-synth lick.

Title: Rips
Review: All that's left are tightly compacted songs that may not have a reflective gloss to them, but instead light their own way.

Title: The London Sessions
Review: Blige’s co-writers, including UK-to-US success stories Disclosure, Emeli Sandé and Sam Smith, find striking ways to frame Blige’s voice without distracting from its richness and emotional range.

Title: Chris
Review: For a flag-waving LGBTQ artist riding the transgender express, the secret of Letissier's crossover charm is that she never lets polemic get in the way of a slick hook. It may be pop with a purpose, but first and foremost it is pop with a damn catchy chorus.

Title: The Feast of the Broken Heart
Review: While Butler has for the most part an uncanny ability to match singer to material, his own personal lyrical touch is left slightly remote (he co-wrote many of the songs with his collaborators). Instead, he's a curator par excellence who's once again assembled an aggressive and varied collection of voices who together form an earnest plea to choose compassion over division.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: With their third album, the War on Drugs continue to recreate classic rock in their own image and in doing so they created a classic album of their own.

Title: Chaosmosis
Review: Chaosmosis has its moments, but it sure is patchy.

Title: Gigaton
Review: Outside of the soaring Retrograde, a prime example of how Pearl Jam has ultimately matured, most of Gigaton shows a band whose collaborative efforts and expertise can still resonate if they open their minds to the challenge.

Title: Passionoia
Review: Unfortunately a lot of the record falls a wee bit flat.

Title: We are Beautiful, We Are Doomed
Review: For Los Campesinos! to come up with such a strong follow-up not even a year after their last is an amazing feat.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: The compositions on Connector are firmer, more contained than they've been since 1997's Audoditacker.

Title: Four
Review: [Four has] the density that made Bloc's angular edge so full, rich and round in the first place. [No.90, p.54]

Title: Dismantle & Rebuild
Review: There seems to be a number of ideas thrown together into the mix and this does result in the collection sounding a little confused towards its conclusion but there are many highlights before this point that suggests The Ramona Flowers are likely to be around for a long time.

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: But vintage doesn’t mean nostalgic. 'Dirty Old Man' is the pissed, hilarious antithesis of his wide-eyed ’70s signature 'Old Man,' and it rivals Nick Cave’s 'No Pussy Blues' (see Grinderman) as the year’s best song about a deranged, horny graybeard.

Title: Effra Parade
Review: Some may fine the ambient, tree-hugging Willow (Interlude) hard to stomach, however, and the lyrical flair that can elevate a debut album is sometimes lacking. [Apr 2014, p.91]

Title: Ritual
Review: A few of the tracks have a moment, usually a chorus, that you might want to play back a few times. But like Editors, taken as an album there's nothing unique, rewarding, or even merely engaging enough to be worthy of another spin.

Title: What Chaos Is Imaginary
Review: Songs like All Blacked Out and Chemical Freeze are suffused with melancholic ambiance, where descending minor chords provide a fullness to their otherwise spare arrangements.

Title: Bark Your Head Off, Dog
Review: Bark Your Head Off, Dog continues the Hop Along tradition insofar as it is sharp, well-produced indie rock accompanying Quinlan's bold lyrical earnestness. This is the band's hallmark sound, so loyalists can rejoice. What is different this time around, however, are broader and more grandiose instrumentation.

Title: Lungs
Review: It's a bold, inventive record that bristles with energy and passion.

Title: The Monitor
Review: The band have taken  Bruce Springsteen's influence, twisted and distorted it and made a quite remarkable album that lives up both to its rebellious, riotous ambition and its rich musical heritage.

Title: Real
Review: The acoustic Clumps strips down for a particularly moving two minutes, but for the most part, Loveless commits to the stunning sonic evolution. Embrace it.

Title: Riot On An Empty Street
Review: Riot's tales of lost loves and existential confusion shimmer with precise harmonies, memorably melancholy melodies, and rich but restrained arrangements. [6 Aug 2004, p.80]

Title: Ma
Review: If you’re already a fan of Banhart’s recent work, this slots firmly into that leisurely, often lovely vibe. He has shifted away from the quirky “freak folk” of his early years into something just as odd, even subversive, around its edges, but far more relaxed and enjoyable.

Title: Bird Dog Dante
Review: While it's unlikely that Bird Dog Dante will win him many new fans, its curious, intimate, casual approach will certainly appeal to those who have embraced Parish's earlier--and no less idiosyncratic--recordings.

Title: The Slideshow Effect
Review: The Slideshow Effect is, likewise, a small gem worth treasuring.

Title: Dirt Farmer
Review: As wonderful as it is unexpected, Dirt Farmer is a strong candidate for comeback of the year.

Title: Not Music
Review: Not Music is all over the place in the best possible way, and fans who love Stereolab's gracefully intellectual side will especially appreciate it.

Title: Between My Head and the Sky
Review: This is a deeply focused, wonderfully colorful, and deeply expressive work that showcases a collaboration between mother and son and displays depth, strength, creativity in spades, and intense beauty.

Title: Sumie
Review: Her ability to micromanage is clearly great. It’s not the most unique take on folk, but it is rife with charm; her intimate, sympathetic sounds soothe the most restless minds.

Title: Kaputt
Review: Bejar's ninth disc detours into all manner of early-Eighties smoothness - glassy New Wave bass lines, blue-Monday synths, turquoise- sport-coat saxophones, backup singers straight off a Steely Dan record, all filtered through the obtuse, literary bent that turns Destroyer albums into such fun puzzles.

Title: The Letting Go
Review: It’s been years since he sounded this responsive and attentive.

Title: The Weirdness
Review: The problem lies in the fact that The Stooges have nothing left to say.

Title: Indestructible
Review: It often lacks the charge of inspired discovery that accompanied its '90s predecessors.

Title: The Original Faces
Review: These ninety-second-ish ditties are too gaunt and echo-ridden to stand alone as memorable singles, but within the tempestuous framework of the album, their vulnerability hits like a late-summer thunderstorm.

Title: Warrior
Review: Auto-Tune, deployed all over the record, turns Kesha's voice into a robo-squawk, and not in a good way.

Title: Murray Street

Title: Deeper Than Rap
Review: Even if this isn't much "Deeper" than the average Three 6 Mafia album, the glitz and guts of Deeper are a big step up, making Ross sound like a Miami-fied version of Young Jeezy.

Title: Grid of Points
Review: Grid of Points is the sound of what’s left after the winds have subsided. It’s astonishingly beautiful and astonishingly, painfully real.

Title: Free Spirit
Review: A very credible record with no real mistakes--but no real personality, either.

Title: Ceremonials

Title: Eden
Review: Everything on Eden more or less works, though it’s a definite step down from Ephorize.

Title: Policy
Review: Policy's highlights maintain a precarious balance between classicism and cataclysm, but the album often tips too far in either direction.

Title: Sonic Citadel
Review: Sonic Citadel is Lightning Bolt at their most poppy and accessible.

Title: The Way I'm Livin'
Review: This is a nicely balanced album that you could listen to repeatedly and still discover fresh, exciting touches with each new listen.

Title: The Five Ghosts

Title: Quiet Signs

Review: The Savage Heart is often just that,uncompromisingly breaking new, often bleakly fertile, ground for the band, showing they can still evolve emotionally.

Review: The Starlight Mints weren't excessively ambitious in the studio and the coolness of Built on Squares makes for a pleasant listen while capturing a band in the making.

Review: Song for song, it's better and more consistent than Head Music... thanks partially to Stephen Street's focused, flattering production, but also due to a sharp set of songs.

Review: The only reasonable offering on 'How Does It Feel' is the multi-layered and kaleidoscopic lead single, 'Painted'. Elsewhere, it's the kind of standard by-the-numbers electro-pop that's likely to soundtrack your next visit to the local department store.

Title: White Chalk
Review: Constantly brilliant. White Chalk is an amazing album, racked with beauty, stricken with fragility and haunted with something otherworldly.

Review: Cold and sweet all at once while perched atop a reef of moody Krautrock, Let the Blind Lead has a progression that melts more than it floats.

Title: Junip
Review: A fuller, more focused version of the sound they introduced on Fields, this set of songs is worthy of being Junip's namesake album.

Title: Impressions
Review: Impressions is thrumming with big ideas, bigger choruses and is imbued with the pearly wisdom learned from rolling with life's punches. [4 Mar 2017, p.53]

Title: Camila
Review: The raunchy come-hithers you assume have been dropped in late in the day can be as boring and samey as piano ballads. But here, Cabello acquits herself well as an R&B vixen.

Title: One Love

Title: No Shape
Review: Here, we have Hadreas’s desire to transcend his body and self--the no shape of the title--and glorious, inventive, shape-shifting music to match.

Title: Ode

Title: Drum's Not Dead
Review: This is music that relies entirely on feeling, and while not for everyone it is music at its most impulsively, spontaneously creative.

Title: Tight Knit

Title: Born This Way

Title: Plaza
Review: Even if Quilt don't always find the answers they're looking for on Plaza, they've found some of their most confident and cohesive music.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: No youngsters this side of Arcade Fire (who record for the Chunk's Merge Records) articulate ambivalence with such skill or heart. Few even try.

Title: PLECTRUMELECTRUM
Review: Neither Art Official Age nor PLECTRUMELECTRUM aims to be a legendary Prince record, but both hit their marks anyway.

Title: Moonlight

Title: Shrink Dust
Review: Chad VanGaalen's world is weird, but never just for weird's sake--his creations spring from deep inside the singular, twisted mind of their creator, and Shrink Dust is the closest we've come yet to getting inside his head.

Review: More than anything, Glazin's sneer'n'strut is just too much of a pretty good thing: One or two at a time, these songs work wonders, but over half an hour, the Boys' retrograde sneer and strut proves a bit too safe and samey.
