Title: Black Laden Crown
Review: Because of the time lapses involved in recording the material, the album sounds uneven and sometimes stale, sadly lacking the Misfits punk rock kick that he managed to reboot into early Danzig offerings with producer Rick Rubin. Of note, however, is the closing “Pull The Sun”, a majestic hovering ballad where Danzig drops the Jimbo stance to elevate his group and his more subdued vocal to a higher rock pinnacle. [Jul 2017, p.60]

Title: Mother
Review: This is a record of stormy intensity, hauling its emotions up to the mountainside to expose them to the elements. [Mar 2018, p.115]

Title: Heroes
Review: An appealingly misshapen collection of classics, contemporaries, and originals.

Title: Sparkle Hard
Review: Sparkle Hard remains an entirely worthwhile pursuit that resides within the upper echelon of Malkmus’ post-Pavement output. The way he experiments and progresses his sound is admirable, and it has resulted in some must-hear moments on this very record.

Title: You Are All I See
Review: You Are All I See suffers from the exact same problem that plagued another act with a helium-voiced frontman: Passion Pit on their 2009 album Manners. Instead of delivering full products that capitalize on their immediate strengths, both albums pad their triumphs with overdramatic bluster storms that fail to really go anywhere, and it's kind of a shame.

Title: Snow Bound
Review: There’s something off in the way that the euphoria attaches to the chillier depths of his songs. It’s unsettling enough to suggest that it maybe could be interesting if it worked, but it doesn’t quite.

Title: Urban Turban - The Singhles Club
Review: Mostly, it's funky pop, half-deconstructed and relentlessly optimistic. [Jun 2012, p.71

Title: Green Language
Review: For his second album, also released on Warp, Rustie indeed slows it down a bit and peels away some layers, but he does so without making any concessions to politeness.

Title: All Yours
Review: Their third and strongest album, pitching them closer to Captured Tracks labelmate Mac DeMarco. [Oct 2015, p.84]

Title: Angles
Review: Comeback albums, it seems, are not just for other bands to do.

Title: Poses
Review: With Broadway-worthy new standards, and a strong supporting cast, Wainwright delivers a flawless, flip-flopless performance. [8 June 2001, p.76]

Title: Yours Truly, Angry Mob
Review: Like its predecessor, the Kaisers' second album is patchy, but does have moments of brilliance.

Title: Songs About Girls
Review: The only thing wrong with this largely excellent album is knowing that will.i.am has better stuff up his sleeve.

Title: Carter Girl
Review: She's in fine eloquent fettle, sinking her heart into the ever-resilient material. [May 2014, p.71]

Title: We are Beautiful, We Are Doomed
Review: At just over a half hour long, it's more EP than album, but even these (ostensible) B-sides make for a giddy and infectious sprint.

Title: For The Recently Found Innocent
Review: The end result isn't as wholly immersive or adventurous as the White Album­-like lo-fi wonderland of 2012's Family Perfume, but paired with last year's succinct Cyclops Reap, Innocent makes the perfect gateway drug to Presley's lysergic canon.

Title: Folk Art
Review: With Us Five, Lovano has found a flexible and exciting working band, a group that can play down the center or off on the side, that can swing joyously or reach for the heights of abstraction.

Title: Savage Times
Review: As a whole, Savage Times is a chaotic, yet interesting album.

Title: James Blake
Review: London singer-songwriter attempts to annex the middle ground between Benga and Anthony Hegarty. [March 2011, p. 96]

Title: Before This World
Review: Before This World, though not a particularly remarkable album, reacquaints us with an old friend, one who we wish would visit more often.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Sounds like it was recorded in a tin can and constructed from leftovers off the group's debut.

Title: Introducing Joss Stone
Review: She has talent to burn, but rather than challenge herself, Stone has chosen to throw herself on a multi-million dollar bullet train to the centre of mediocrity.

Title: Finally Woken
Review: The audio equivalent of a warm bubble bath.

Title: Age of Transparency
Review: Age of Transparency is as emotionally compelling and musically creative a work as has been released this year.

Title: Hunter
Review: This is the album we've been waiting for, whether we knew it or not.

Title: Mangy Love
Review: This is shrewd, layered music that demands the songs be mulled over and scrutinized; even if that may not provide answers to questions McCombs poses.

Title: Need to Feel Your Love
Review: It’s just as intense in terms of either volume or passion as their self-released EPs, but the album’s somewhat surprising emotional and stylistic eclecticism prevent the band’s library of overcharged ’70s-style riffs or its maximalist energy, epitomized by singer Tina Halladay’s wailing typhoon of a voice, from becoming too fatiguing.

Title: Stumble into Grace
Review: Lovely, heartbreaking, and just diffident enough to get perspective on this bittersweet old world. [26 Sep 2003, p.94]

Title: Nikki Nack
Review: For tUnE-yArDs, definition remains elusive and extraordinary.

Title: Title
Review: While the 21-year-old singer rocks more sass and self-empowerment on her full-length major-label debut (which, confusingly, shares a name with the four-song EP she released in September), she's also charmingly old-fashioned.

Title: Ode to Sunshine
Review: Despite Delta Spirit’s anarchic (i.e., creatively opportunistic) sampling of everything from cold war folk to the Cold War Kids, when the band members hit their stride--as on the rumbling, locomotive grooves of piano-stung epic Americana on 'Trashcan'--Sunshine becomes nothing less than an ode to musical joy.

Title: Sunlight on the Moon
Review: Unexpected exits drop like hailstones throughout the Athenian psych/pop institution's 13-track 13th album. [No. 103, p.55]

Title: Tower of Love
Review: It's cute--like a super furry animal, perhaps. [Jan 2006, p.127]

Title: Spoils
Review: The way Roberts' often high-pitched brogue wraps itself around sentences is pretty as hell; his voice has never sounded better, nor has it been recorded this clearly before.

Title: Tassili
Review: The collaborations jump out at the listener, but they account for only half of the album's 12 songs; in some cases, the guests are barely noticeable. Much of the rest is recognizably Tinariwen, and there are plenty of solid tunes here.

Title: Homesongs
Review: [A] mesmerizing debut.

Title: Out of Season
Review: Disarmingly intimate. [Dec 2003, p.87]

Title: Old Yellow Moon
Review: It might be a record looking to the past, but it has Harris and Crowell doing some of the best work of their careers. [Apr 2013, p.103]

Title: False Idols
Review: A return to a winning formula, if not an emphatic return to form. [Jun 2013, p.79]

Title: The Age of the Understatement
Review: This isn't just a novel idea that is haphazardly hashed out but rather, the work of two impeccable musicians and it's a fine addition to either musician's catalog and a brilliant one at that.

Title: Feed Me Diamonds
Review: MNDR's debut full-length, Feed Me Diamonds, is filled with choruses of "ooh whoa oohs" and other shots at those easy hooks that you can't stop whistling. But the material doesn't connect with the proper force.

Title: Deleter
Review: Despite there being little opportunity for euphoric release, it's easy to lose yourself in Deleter's darker, more brutal moments. [Mar 2020, p.119]

Title: Abundance Welcoming Ghosts
Review: Picking out parts is really beside the point – the album works as a restless, searching, gorgeous whole. Morris and his band have never been better.

Title: Real High
Review: An artful mix of focus and atmosphere, Real High may be Nite Jewel's finest moment to date.

Title: There Are Rules
Review: There Are Rules doesn't contain a single tune that lingers afterward.

Title: Play On
Review: No amount of hackneyed songwriting can undermine Ms. Underwood’s voice, which is consistently impressive, capable of pneumatic thrusts. It enlivens plenty of moments here.

Artist: And So I Watch You From Afar
Title: Heirs
Review: Fretboard noodling far outweighs any emotional or intellectual potency, and Heirs continues to leave ASIWYFA stuck between a rock solid live show and a hard-to-place recorded direction.

Title: Brother Sister
Review: Brother Sister feels bigger than just the siblings, but it is essentially a gentle folk record with lovely instrumentation and gorgeous harmonies. With Sean primarily on guitar and Sara on fiddle, and both sharing vocals, the sound comes across at times like a full band but it’s usually just the two of them making stirring music.

Title: Invaders Must Die
Review: The Prodigy has been treading water for a few years, most likely looking for the inspiration, sentiment and spooky samples which they now unleash on Invader Must Die--a treat for anyone with a thirst for the twisted and ferocious. [Winter 2009, p.92]

Title: The Expanding Flower Planet
Review: An imaginary world is striking not because of its contents, but because of the way in which we view them--detached, overwhelmed, inspired--a feeling Deradoorian captures with exciting promise on her debut LP.

Title: Elaenia
Review: Shepherd is among London's most sought-after DJs, known for marathon sets that span everything from disco's deepest cuts to feel-good hip-hop. But here he steps away from those club sounds in favor of a fully immersive experience that's unbounded by genre.

Title: Motherland
Review: Natalie Merchant has made an album of elemental beauty... she's never sounded better. [Jan 2002, p.140]

Title: Chalice Hymnal
Review: On Chalice Hymnal, they’ve added another solid story to their growing skyscraper.

Title: Rebellious Soul
Review: Rebellious Soul doesn't have quite the impact of Michelle's 2010 mixtape, What's the 901?--curiously, there's little fighting talk here to match the superb Hit 'Em in the Mouth--but it has enough to confirm the emergence of a vital voice.

Title: Amadjar
Review: Never resorting to cliche, they continue to be just as inspired by the universal themes of love, politics and nature as they always have been. Their musical delivery is just as heartfelt and forceful for it.

Title: Days
Review: These towering moments stretch thin across a record lost in a comatose state of traditional, if beach-bumming, rock-pop tedium.

Title: Love, Shelby
Review: The edges have all been sawed off of Lynne's sound by producer and co-songwriter Glen Ballard, and she appears as a positively wimpy adult.

Title: Songs for the General Public
Review: The ideas in ‘Songs For The General Public’ are rich, creative and often funny, but its musical staying power is lacking.

Title: Yoko
Review: A switch in approach and sound definitely worked for them, and fans shouldn't be put off by Beulah's toughened confidence.

Title: Terrible Human Beings
Review: Rather than saturate Terrible Human Beings with these thrilling, if grotesque, excesses, the Orwells use them sparingly, which strengthens their impact and punches up the flavor of an otherwise measured album.

Title: Joan of Arc, Dick Cheney, Mark Twain
Review: The balance of unsettleing noise and artistic appreciation wavers perhaps a little too much and, as admirable a band as they are, wrapping your ears around their album unfortunately proves to be a little too much work.

Title: No One Deserves Happiness
Review: Despite the misery that inspires and thrives within their suffocating work, the band shows a remarkable sense of vitality, inspiring to longtime and new fans alike.

Title: The House
Review: As with most of The House, songs like the folk-inflected opener "I'd Love to Kill You," the Eastern-tinged "The Flood," and the yearning and pretty "Red Balloons," take time to build and grab you slowly with deft, biting lyrics and Melua's lilting, burnished vocals.

Title: Vacation in Hell
Review: Competent but not always compelling.

Title: The Ghost in Daylight
Review: Bristol songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Nick Talbot's fourth album for Warp is a gorgeously hallucinatory affair, marking a slight shift towards late-80s/early-90s psychedelia.

Title: Mid Air
Review: On Mid Air Buchanan has consoled us with signature world-weary comfort and has done so finely.

Title: Sheath
Review: Some of it hisses and gurgles like early Future Sound Of London. [Oct 2003, p.118]

Title: Go To School
Review: In the end, the love you take from Go to School will be equal to the tolerance you have for an even more undiluted version of The Lemon Twigs. Your call.

Title: Flamingo
Review: It's clear from Flamingo that Flowers accounts for the lion's share of talent in The Killers, and if they ever go on definite hiatus, their fans can look forward to more consistently good material in the form of Flowers' solo albums.

Title: Up All Night
Review: Razorlight's debut has more hooks than a fishing rod factory, and the advantage they have over Oasis (in addition to not sounding anything like them) is that they haven't had their arses kissed enough to disappear completely up them yet.

Title: Silver Tongues
Review: Through the overdriven riffage, juggernaut rhythms and starey-eyed James Cox's foghorn yowling, some proper and highly dynamic songcraft does emerge. [Apr 2019, p.93]

Title: Picaresque
Review: "Picaresque" is by far the Decemberists' best work to date.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: As ever though, Liars emerge with their own sonic identity intact - you can 'hear' LA in the chaos, disquiet and vast, starving spaces of these songs, but they remain a band that don't surrender easily to their surroundings.

Title: thank u, next
Review: So thank you, “Ari”, for a lovely listen. I have to confess, I’d like a bit more vocal grit. Maybe that’s up next.

Title: Creep On Creepin' On
Review: They could turn even the hardest kids at school into pissy wrecks with the elegant dread-heart blues of this, their fourth album.

Title: The Powers That B
Review: The Björk-based art piece works better when consumed as album number two.

Title: The Remote Part
Review: Merely good-but-not-great.

Title: Soul of a Woman
Review: When all is said and done, Soul of a Woman cements itself as a fitting send-off for a woman who flat-out owned the stage and spearheaded a scene, transcending the notions of “neo” and “revival” to make music that was impassioned and pure. Sharon Jones lives on every time you press play.

Title: Depart From Me
Review: Confident non-jumpers shouldn't be concerned that this disc weeps with you're-always-dying-inside woe-is-my-love-life misery.

Title: A Fever Dream
Review: It might just be Everything Everything's most human record to date. [Sep 2017, p.107]

Title: Italian Ice
Review: This flawlessly conceived follow-up draws from many of the same influences yet broadens her boundaries. It’s every bit as potent and expertly arranged, putting it in play as an early contender for one of 2020’s finest albums.

Title: Blues With Friends
Review: Suitably weathered by age and experience, [Dion's voice] hardly gathered rust and has retained its lustrous power and soulful richness. Co-producer/multi-instrumentalist Wayne Hood wisely pins that voice to the centre of this fabulous record, with A-listers very much in supporting roles. [Summer 2020, p.86]

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: By and large, though, the players justify their flightiness.

Title: LP1
Review: Few debuts possess such control and ambition all in one; LP1 is the rare album that manages to sound both lived in and completely futuristic.

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: With a little more time to perfect their style, the War on Drugs would be well-positioned to win converts for both camps, and also their own.

Title: Internal Wrangler
Review: It's one of those releases that reminds you that with all the experimenting and genre-blurring, there is still something simple and nice about an album that takes fairly base elements of rock and roll and creates a disc that's highly catchy.

Title: Short Movie
Review: Marling's fifth takes vast steps forward musically, as ever. It's more defiant and distinct than anything she's done before. [Apr 2015, p.74]

Title: They Want My Soul
Review: While their eighth album doesn’t take any major left turns, it brims with life, ideas and energy.

Title: The Future's Void
Review: There are some quite beautiful and pop-infused moments to be found sprinkled across the album despite the best efforts of EMA and her co-producer Leif Shackleford to keep away from the ears of the commercial fraternity.

Title: Salon Des Amateurs
Review: As with all of Hauschka's music, Salon Des Amateurs takes place at an awkward apex between being "beautiful" and being merely "pretty". This is actually quite an important distinction, because the album never decides whether its pop music or classical music.

Title: Stay Home
Review: It's when they forget themselves, when the mood deepens and melodies tighten, that the Beets show who they really are. You see it often enough on Stay Home, but you'd also think those talents could shine brighter if they got off the couch and stepped outside their safety zone.

Title: Big Echo
Review: Ultimately, the lushness is merely an entry point, and the influence-ripping distracts, but doesn’t derail: Big Echo is best enjoyed for its clutch of memorable moments pinned on a pretty backdrop.

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: Every song ends like a firework finale and fragile chords explain more about the human condition than words ever could. [Jan/Feb 2006, p.78]

Title: 99Â¢
Review: The whole album drips with Caribbean zest, the tropical bounce of 'Can't Get Enough Of Myself' and the pumping 'Rendezvous Girl' balanced by eccentric slowies such as the oddball power ballad 'Run The Races'. There's plenty more too, candied but with class and pop bite.

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: Tracks such as the arresting Human League-meets-Georgio-Moroder fusion 'One Day' and the gloriously uninhibited finale 'Happy House' remian an irresistible invitation onto the dancefloor. [May 2009, p.113]

Title: The Soft Cavalry
Review: Atmospheric, cinematic, dramatic, evocative. [Summer 2019, p.87]

Title: Mental Illness
Review: This is a solid addition to Mann's estimable discography, the kind of record that sets a mood and sustains it for 39 craftsmanlike minutes.

Title: 100 Acres of Sycamore
Review: Dramatic and ravishing, 100 Acres of Sycamore is some achievement.

Title: Dance Mother
Review: Even when they occasionally stumble ever so slightly under the weight of their own ambition, the reckless, adventuring spirit that comprises Dance Mother is one of the compelling things that makes it sound like one of the more exciting debut albums to emerge in long while.

Title: The Soft Bulletin
Review: The Soft Bulletin echoes the oft-mimiced Smiley Smile by The Beach Boys, with its psychedelic wobbliness, songs-within-songs and airy termperament.

Title: Dear Life
Review: Style and contentment. [Jul 2020, p.104]

Title: Let The Dancers Inherit The Party
Review: This album incorporates nearly all of the many facets that make British Sea Power memorable, and it's their strongest overall effort since Do You Like Rock Music? in 2008.

Title: PROTO
Review: While "Godmother" confounds with its sci-fi babble, the likes of "Alienation" and "External" suggest that a tune is a tune in any language. [Jun 2019, p.29]

Title: Under the Boards
Review: Chris Conley's juvenile lyrics and whiney vocal tone submerge the band's music.

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: Coxon rocks it in a class of '77 Brit-punk style that'll make record-collecting fetishists in search of Adverts and Chelsea demos soil themselves. [Dec 2006, p.198]

Title: Ready to Die
Review: They've bottled the lightning in an album of satirical wit, edgy intelligence and what fans crave most of all, raw power. [Jun 2013, p.105]

Title: Ten Thousand Fists
Review: [The songs'] unrelenting wallop, growling guitars and mock-operatic choruses tend to blur together even as they're kicking your ass. [Oct 2005, p.137]

Title: A Place To Bury Strangers
Review: A Place to Bury Strangers may not be easy for would-be record buyers to find--it's currently limited to 500 copies and put out by, um, Killer Pimp Records--but it's worth every effort.

Title: Summer Sun
Review: As irresistible at its peak - the luscious 'Little Eyes' and a lovely interpretation of Big Star's 'Take Care' - as it is baffling at its prog-jazz edges, 'Summer Sun' is the crowbar that pries open the door into a world of left-field beauty.

Title: Electric
Review: A vigorous 11-song collection that keeps the lyrics and melodies straightforward, allowing the complexity and uniqueness of his guitar-playing to burst through.

Title: Rispah
Review: Playful and emotional if a touch polite, it's marked by moments of genuine greatness.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Deerhunter have long proved themselves to be one of the most inventive bands around and the most deserving of the boatloads of hype and bandwidth that has been devoted to their work. Halcyon Digest solidifies that notion even as they sound like they are evaporating into the ether.

Title: Younger Now
Review: Younger Now blends pop-rock and pablum country fare that is so restrained, so thinly produced, it seems like her lovably goofy personality was hobbled throughout the recording process.

Title: The Lion's Roar
Review: As it is, The Lion's Roar is a quality release, but due to the stand out tracks being placed at the front and the end, the middle section feels weaker than it is, making the overall impression of the album suffer.

Title: Pure Comedy
Review: Pure Comedy is definitively a headphone album; where I Love You, Honeybear made you swoon with its overt eclecticism, the gems here need to be unearthed after a few excavations. The album’s pacing does not help matters, burdened with a middle section that dares you to fall asleep and counts on a deep love of Tillman’s voice.

Title: Wilderness Heart
Review: Wilderness Heart is probably the best new utilization of the Iommi/Page/Lynott grab bag you'll hear because, to put it simply, it's going to appeal to men AND women.

Title: Anywhere I Lay My Head
Review: This is a brilliant album that will no doubt top some ‘best of 2008’ lists, but it’s hard to work out if it’s a one-off or not.

Title: All Night Long
Review: Los Angeles rock revivalists Buckcherry waste no time getting down to business on their latest album.

Title: Nostalchic
Review: Whilst Nostalchic is Lapalux’s most full-bodied work to date, it’s also one of the finer examples of how the recent house-meets-r’n'b explosion can be executed with subtlety and finesse.

Title: Double Negative
Review: A dystopian masterpiece.

Title: Holy Fire
Review: Holy Fire is Foals’ masterpiece because it ties in the rhythmic nature of their debut, the soul of the second album, producing finally the rhythmic soul of its own.

Title: Learning
Review: So sublime are these ten spectral soundtracks to the minutiae of a modern lover's tribulations that their sorrow is translated into something more uplifting than unsettling.

Title: PHOX
Review: Although some tracks may blend together on initial listen, PHOX ultimately serves as a colorful debut from a promising young band.

Title: Bottomless Pit
Review: Bottomless Pit will clearly not be for all hip-hop or punk fans, but it is impossible to deny that this album, just like the rest of the duo’s catalog, is doing a much-needed service to both genres by experimenting with them in unimaginable ways.

Title: Instinct
Review: Beneath the distractingly high-pitched, multi-tracked vocals and tastefully tribal drama, there's nothing more threatening than a synthesized Florence + The Machine. [Jul 2012, p.107]

Title: Ghosteen
Review: The anguish a parent feels for losing their child is harrowing and Ghosteen masterfully captures Cave's grief and spiraling rumination on mortality.

Title: Charli
Review: Alongside indulgently unadorned ruminations on fear and love, the record is boundlessly liberating, decadently indulgent, and irresistibly danceable. Aitchison has delivered her greatest work yet.

Title: See My Friends
Review: The occasional highlight isn't enough to make up for the cloth-eared versions of timeless songs found elsewhere on the record, or to cover up for the fact that See My Friends is a mostly soulless, and an entirely pointless album.

Title: Safari Disco Club
Review: Julie Budet chirps exclusively in French, which helps her Auto-Tuned singsong remain vaguely mysterious, even if her childlike melodies are far simpler than the subtly finessed synths.

Title: Dents and Shells
Review: Picks up where 2002's Impasse left off, with Buckner at large in a dusty, wide-screen landscape of brushed guitars, weeping pedal steel and decorous strings. [Dec 2004, p.114]

Title: Valentina
Review: While this isn't going to make you toss your copy of George Best, it shows the guy still has some gas left in his tank and is far from embarrassing himself.

Title: Junip
Review: As with his solo output, Jose Gonzalez has a clear vision for his music's direction, and he sticks to it with admirably rigorous discipline here, making the majority of Junip more steady than indistinct. [No. 97, p.57]

Title: Crossing Muddy Waters
Review: The most natural and relaxed John Hiatt album in years...Hiatt's voice has never sounded better; its course edges sometimes straining for high notes works perfectly with this craggy, unpolished music.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: The songwriting is the driving force behind the album, and any reservations about whether or not Frightened Rabbit would transform into radio-friendly M.O.R. are swept away.

Title: Fall Heads Roll
Review: If there's a method to this madness, you definitely won't find it here. [Nov 2005, p.101]

Title: Ether Teeth
Review: For all the homemade, quirky charm on show here -- and the album has plenty of wide open, lyrical moments -- Ether Teeth leaves behind a lingering, moody, melancholy aftertaste. [#231, p.60]

Title: Weather Diaries
Review: All four members are back in the fold and each one sounds like they're playing with purpose and energy. [Jul 2017, p.82]

Title: Volume 3
Review: Instead of cleverness, the polished songs indulge here sentimental broken heart. Bandmate M. Ward is mostly content to stay out  of the way vocally, but he builds up a castle of retro-instrumental heartbreak for Deschanel. [Jun 2013, p.102]

Title: Hold Time
Review: These new songs have lofty melodic ambitions but aren’t dedicated to the kind of journeying Ward’s lyrics imply.

Title: From When I Wake the Want Is
Review: While the subject matter and style aren't vastly different to anything Kathryn Joseph’s done before, the progression here is more of a tasteful expansion of what came before it. In terms of finding new ways to express oneself with honesty while staying true to what makes you special, this album is a roaring success.

Title: Tyranny
Review: While these "in-between areas" are not always sonically pleasant, you can't accuse them of being dull; they make Tyranny the compelling album that it is.

Title: Pain Is Beauty
Review: While it's possible Pain Is Beauty would have benefited from some more time spent songwriting and fleshing out the overall direction of the album's sound, there's still more than enough impressive songs to make this a worthy addition to the Chelsea Wolfe catalog.

Title: Age Against The Machine
Review: So out gores the vintage, spiritual sound of 1995's nourishing debut Soul Food and in comes a job lot of dizzying electronica, schizoid stylistic shifts, screeching strings, sonorous sub-bass and beats verging on hi-NRG. [Oct 2013, p.90]

Title: Eight
Review: The end result is a very ambitious piece of psychedelia-tinged indie rock that rewards patience with some truly inspired tweaks on the typical slow-jam formula.

Title: Morningwood
Review: Morningwood does a great job at imitating, and they have spirit. But their spirit does not translate well to good listening, nor does it provoke the underwear-dancing and air guitar it hopes to achieve.

Title: The Archer
Review: Savior is a commanding narrator of heartache and revenge, singing of blood and tears over piano and reverb-drenched guitar, demonstrating a star quality that belies her 24 years. [Feb 2020, p.33]

Title: Warzone
Review: An inventive way of uniting her body of work, Warzone furthers her legacy as a promoter of peace and understanding.

Title: Silences
Review: It’s all a bit wonderful, actually.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: Almost every aural detail is simply pretty, every guitar texture inviting, and perhaps the most impressive part is that it’s here just one year after Times and Tides.

Title: Say Anything
Review: There's sax and doo-wop here, but Bemis is at his best yelling stuff like "I can't define myself through irony …and self-deprecation!" over taut punk pop.

Title: Children of Alice
Review: Keeping up with Children of Alice's quicksilver changes and hypnotic passages requires listeners' full attention, but it's well worth it--these ever-transforming soundworlds honor the magic that Broadcast tapped into with Keenan while suggesting an equally fascinating way forward.

Title: Ruins
Review: Wherever you listen, Ruins pairs tough truths and tender melodies with tremendous expressive punch, from the piercing self-investigations of the title-track to Hem Of Her Dress, where heartache and rage merge with raucous honesty. Meanwhile, Nothing Has To Be True hews beauty from transformative circumstance.

Title: Nothing's Gonna Change The Way You Feel About Me Now
Review: In many ways, it's his best work yet and does a great deal more to solidify his growing reputation as one of America's premier songwriters. [Mar 2012, p.89]

Title: Like a Rose
Review: This blend of contemporary attitudes and classic sounds is insinuating and addictive, particularly because at nine songs, it's too brief--once it's through, the album practically begs you to start all over again.

Title: Worldwide Underground
Review: Erykah Badu still hasn't found her way through the haze.

Title: Unleashed
Review: "Beer for My Horses," a rangy duet with Willie Nelson, and easy grooves like "Ain't It Just Like You" don't chase away the overbearing taste of "Red, White and Blue," the album's centerpiece first single. [#9, p.150]

Title: Warnings
Review: Warnings is a triumphant, timely, and life-affirming return.

Title: Dead to Me
Review: Ending with what sounds like a tape spinning off its reel, it's a welcome break from the amorousness of the remainder of the album, which is charming, but may have a harder time finding a place in your record collection during the year's colder months.

Title: Total Strife Forever
Review: While Doyle struggles to balance his various musical elements--the opening 10 minutes is sheer drudgery--he has a nice way with layered vocal harmonies, which deserve more regular exposure.

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: Ignore the lyric booklet and you have one of the more impressive albums of 2004.

Title: Summer Make Good
Review: Does Summer Make Good maintain the peak established by its predecessors? In a word: no. But that doesn’t mean it’s not good, because it is; it’s just not quite as magical as the others.

Title: We Are The Night
Review: While you may know what you're getting with a Chemical Brothers album, they remain damn good at what they do.... You get the impression that their next album may have to be a bit more adventurous if they're to survive.

Review: Their clichéd soundbites aside, there's much to enjoy on this typically ballsy and no-nonsense follow-up to 2011 breakthrough Pressure & Time.

Title: Escape 2 Mars
Review: This eco-themed, sci-fi clad concept album bristles with electro-pop sounds (Light Years, the OMD-ish title track) yet retains Gab's furrowed-brow lyricism and singular approach as he forges his own space within this changing landscape. [Feb 2010, p. 105]

Title: Worship
Review: There's not enough conviction or charisma on the surface of Worship's dulled sandpaper to break the skin, let alone get under it.

Title: 5 Seconds of Summer
Review: Although everything is rendered with a high-shine gloss and sanitised precision that makes it more saccharine than Sex Pistols, there's still an enjoyment to be had on a basic level. [5 Jul 2014, p.53]

Title: Cuts Across the Land
Review: A reminder of artists like the Breeders. [Mar 2006, p.122]

Title: All My Heroes Are Cornballs
Review: Through AMHAC, JPEGMAFIA has attempted to produce something so questionable, unique and conflicted in its elements, that on first glance, it’s uninviting and dissonant. This goes for the use of his close friends giving faux unfavourable comments about the record in the PR campaign too. Yet that friction he creates and the doubt at the front of your mind makes you concentrate more, breathe in every element and realise its undeniable quality.

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: Once I Was An Eagle represents a bold, adventurous step forward that’s resulted in her most fulfilling work yet.

Title: Piece by Piece
Review: Every song aims for the monumental, a strategy that’s competitive for radio play but wearying over the course of a whole album.

Title: Songs You Make at Night
Review: Songs feel shy of messing with the familiar. [Sep 2018, p.94]

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: It all makes for an album which is strangely boring; the baroque detailing becomes an inaudiable blur. [Dec 2008, p.65]

Title: Wake UP!
Review: The 10 tracks on her debut are all lovingly crafted, but the languid atmosphere means that they sometimes drift into each other.

Title: Acid Tongue
Review: Lively and loose, cut with collaborators including her talented Scottish boyfriend Johnathan Rice, spooky folkie M. Ward and actress-singer Zooey Deschanel, the 11 songs (many of which she has performed live for years) encompass Southern-gothic folk, Appalachian blues stomps and 'The Next Messiah,' an eight-minute, Who-style rock mini-opera.

Title: On Sunset
Review: Ever the magpie with a love for shiny trinkets, Weller slips in West Coast Santana-style guitar, Middle Eastern drone, hand claps and honking tenor. References are introduced and then discarded at will. ... Intriguing, to say the least.

Title: Under a Billion Suns
Review: Mudhoney these days, for all their pioneer status, mostly just sound like a regular, decent rock band. [Apr 2006, p.105]

Title: Seasons of Your Day
Review: Sandoval and her collaborators may never modify the melancholy torch that they bear, but they keep that fire masterfully for those of us who still have a yen for patient, no-frills sounds that happen to serve as a miracle balm.

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: There are plenty of throwaway tunes, and the sound quality is decidedly lo-fi, but what's most surprising about this three-CD collection is the number of good songs.

Title: Radlands
Review: There's more emphasis on guitars, and they appear to have ingested a whole load of pharmaceuticals, but at heart they're a great pop band, and their ability to write a heart-rending tune certainly hasn't been hampered.

Title: What Went Down
Review: What Went Down sounds like a collection of songs built for the stage, and that's not a bad thing, especially since Foals have become an absolutely formidable live beast. It's just hard not to miss the breathing room and layers that defined the band's past work. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.62]

Title: Hold Time
Review: Behind the flourishes, Ward sounds as moony as ever, singing beautifully sad songs about mortality and feeling lonesome.

Title: City Sun Eater in the River Of Light
Review: All of those tracks work because they’re never played as straight genre experiments; they all sound first and foremost like Woods songs, even when they draw from a different vocabulary than any that came before.

Title: Taiga
Review: Taiga is a more mainstream album than people may be used to from Zola Jesus. But that is not a bad thing.

Title: Audio Day Dream
Review: ADD is certainly one of the more interesting AmIdol-related records, but so much commotion without construction is ultimately as forgettable as Jordin's pageant-winner trifle, and perhaps a little more tiring to get through, too.

Title: At Best Cuckold
Review: Sometimes Avi Buffalo’s entrance into the gauntlet of the undisguised voice leads to a pretty song or two, maybe a moment of blissful pop; but more often than not, the songs whimper without much intelligible emotion.

Title: The Digging Remedy
Review: Tracks can occasionally patter past without triggering the same fight-or-flight response, but when their machinery really gears up, they remain masters of electronic mood. [Aug 2016, p.115]

Title: Oh No I Love You
Review: Oh No I Love You is a warm affair and a slightly more together reflection of Tim than I Believe was, and the accompanying remix album with cosmic re-works by the likes of Seahawks is a bonus too. This deserves to find itself in as many homes as possible.

Title: A Flash Flood of Colour
Review: The positives are overshadowed by petulant observations to politics which is hard to take seriously when dire lyrics like "Yabba dabba do one, Son."

Title: Red Velvet Car
Review: Red Velvet Car has something of a meditative mood -- the punchy Townshend  power chords are used as color, not fuel -- triggered somewhat by a preponderance of textured, acoustic-laden arrangements and miniature epics, all elements that hearken back to Heart's golden age yet wind up feeling right in line with their vibe in 2010.

Title: BeyoncÃ©
Review: The songs are alert to the current sound of clubs and radio, but not trapped by it; the refrains are terse and direct, but what happens between them isn’t formulaic. And while Beyoncé constructed the songs with a phalanx of collaborators, they all know better than to eclipse her creamy, soulful voice.

Title: Cells
Review: Cells remains more a collection o would-be club anthems than an album. [Dec 2012, p.104]

Title: Blank Project
Review: It’s a very puzzling record, but the last thing you should do is try and puzzle it out: just go with it and you’ll find its strange charms working much more quickly than you might have thought at first.

Title: Destroyer of the Void
Review: It would seem that Destroyer Of The Void is an album that manages to both impress initially and continue to reveal virtues well into repeat spins; a trick that ensures the satisfaction of all manner of listeners, and one that reflects Blitzen Trapper's growing reputation as something of a must-hear.

Title: Riceboy Sleeps
Review: Riceboy Sleeps is an elegiac set of powerfully evocative songs, functioning at its best as lovely background music while flipping through the pages of the art book it's bundled with. Listened to unaccompanied and in its entirety, the experience is frustrating and unpleasant, and its bloated feel renders a lot of it impotent.

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: Women As Lovers may be his best yet. [Mar 2008, p.107]

Title: OK Cowboy
Review: OK Cowboy is a full-fledged album, with a satisfying ebb and flow that shows that Arbez's sound has several sides to it.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: Their most mature set to date.
13 gets tiresomely monolithic and ponderous.

Title: Human Performance
Review: Fortunately, throughout the rest of the album, the band writes songs that allow them to excel as they stay well within their limitations. These are tight, economical pop songs actually worthy of Pavement comparisons in terms of not just sound, but melody.

Title: Upland Stories
Review: With his old-timey Upland Stories, Fulks matures into an important voice.

Title: Gulag Orkestar
Review: Ignore the clunky lyrics... and Gulag Orkestar is an infinitely more appealing album.

Title: Caligula
Review: Hayter is classically trained, and there is emotional as well as technical brilliance to the way she expands her vocal palette here.

Title: From Here on In
Review: At 16 tracks, the melancholy mood lingers a bit long, but hey, if you can handle some meandering in your Britpop, then Here's something for you.

Title: Grasque
Review: Grasque proves to be the group's most elusive outing to date, favoring icy, often formless melodies that come and go as they please, and existential lyrics that periodically dissolve into ghostly, wordless repetition.

Title: Attack & Release
Review: Danger Mouse hasn't commandeered his charges' muse and forced The Black Keys to change, simply encouraged them to co-operate and collaborate for the first time. Clearly, company becomes them.

Title: Stray
Review: Bateh’s sequencing is masterful, but take some of these songs out of the album’s broader context and many lose their steam. It’s not particularly kind to the casual listener either—this is an album for those fully committed to being a fly on the wall of this jet-black joyride.

Title: Ghostory
Review: What used to feel like surfing amid the cumulonimbus suddenly feels like snorkling in soup.

Title: Better Oblivion Community Center
Review: It’s full of charming melodies, carefully placed harmonies, and biting lyrics from two of the most influential songwriters around. Some days you just get lucky.

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: What remains is a band conflicted about how to stretch and how far to stray from a winning formula, between living up to expectations and confounding them.

Title: Most Messed Up
Review: Sure, the twitchy alienation of their earliest records is long gone, but the Old 97's are still fighting the good fight against respectability.

Title: Tassili
Review: The power of Tinariwen lies not only in their ability to communicate that idea musically, but most crucially in their ability to make such a simple idea sound fresh and profound.

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: Freighted deep with lugubrious rolls of oily bass, sandy inhalations of desert strings, holy intonations and salty lust, Push the Sky Away is the audio equivalent of bathing in the Dead Sea.

Title: Tough Love
Review: These radio-ready confections teem with smart hooks and fuller choruses.

Title: Heritage
Review: Fortunately Grellier includes enough moments of excitement to keep Heritage less of a soundtrack album and more a French disco LP stripped of vocals.

Title: Hall Music
Review: In the end, Hall Music is an enjoyable but paradoxical album, both an expansion and contraction of Svanängen's palette.

Title: Ersatz GB
Review: Ersatz G.B. offers no easy explanations, but instead twists and excites the listener's brain with unexpected phantom bewilderments. [Dec 2011, p.100]

Title: The End of That
Review: The End of That has more outstanding moments than La La Land, but whether those highlights are enough to neutralize Plants and Animals' weakness for occasionally derivative kitsch depends on how much their fans are willing to overlook.

Title: Fine Line
Review: Fine Line is very much a document of a 25-year-old deep in the process of figuring out not just what kind of musician he wants to be, but what kind of person. The path from cookie-cutter boy-band member to bona fide rock star is one fraught with a lot to prove both personally and publically, and yet it’s one Styles seems to be navigating with an eagerness to learn, to experience and to experiment.

Title: Green and Gray
Review: At 53 blurry, delirious minutes, it's a lot to take in. (Better suited for that might be the more melodious, less dense Dripping or this record's chronological and spiritual predecessor, A Hairshirt of Purpose.) But it's a strong step forward, and offers no more or less than exactly what Pile are all about.

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: It's arrogantly risky. That's their best feature. [Jun 2003, p.100]

Title: Ontario Gothic
Review: Gothic is another solid set, but you can also feel Hildebrand finding the borders on a sound that has the potential to sound limitless.

Title: Communion
Review: Communion clearly packs a unique set of quirks, diversions and comedowns. [Sep 2009, p.102]

Title: Asiatisch
Review: It's immersive and transgressive, if you care about this stuff.

Title: El Tren Fantasma
Review: Brilliantly textured, brilliantly sensitive, unrepeatable by its very nature-this is a great example of a sound recordist's art.

Title: Run Fast
Review: The album contains some of her best lyrics.

Title: See You On The Moon
Review: It's still a quietly engaguing offering blessed with a lyrical lightness and organic Tucker Martine production. [Jul 2010, p.135]

Title: Illegal Moves
Review: Illegal Moves is just as powerful a statement about the urgency of the times and the reactions we should all be having, because being entertained doesn’t have to mean being disengaged. That Sunwatchers make their calls to arms sound so fun doesn’t diminish that power--in fact, it just might be the most important part.

Title: Stand Up
Review: The official return of the DMB shows them in full force and stretching way Up.

Title: Melodrama
Review: Melodrama's swirls of strings and bursts of glimmering synths show a pop star in her prime.  Between rage, elation, and all of the mistakes in-between, Lorde is more self-aware than she's ever been.

Title: Antiphon
Review: Is it Pulido? The absence of Smith? The third act crawl? In truth, all play a damaging part. Despite these irks, Antiphon is everything that it needs to be; a new beginning, loaded with promise. That's enough for now.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Theirs remains a gallows wit. [Nov 2005, p.112]

Title: Overcome
Review: Overcome is but a grain in the sand on an oversaturated desert; a metal album you'll enjoy while you play it but won't ever be something you‘ll yearn to hear.

Title: Asleep In The Back
Review: More in the vein of Built To Spill's Perfect From Now On than the latest Doves or Travis albums, Asleep is structured as an epic, almost prog-rock album that, once spun, reveals itself as a comfortable listen, containing a number of classic pop songwriting turns within its vastness.

Title: Boxer
Review: If there is one thing that might be wrong with this album -- besides an uneventful last third -- is that the album might be too tailor-made for music critics worn out by music fatigue, hype fatigue, and irony fatigue.

Title: Souljacker
Review: Strange stuff, but oddly appealing. [Feb/Mar 2002, p.111]

Title: Weezer (Black Album)
Review: With The Black Album, Weezer once again sounds insufferably uncomfortable with the notion of aging by devising the musical equivalent of getting hair plugs. ... A compilation of tracks lacking in quality and spat out at the end of a conveyer belt.
The end result is a kind of low-flying elation that only these experienced noirists could deliver.

Title: Throw Down Your Arms
Review: An imposing act of pop interpretation. [3 Oct 2005]

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: You have to wade through a lot of plaid-shirted, porch-rocking psychedelia before you get there. The patient pilgrim, though, can look forward to unearthing the widescreen Laurel Canyon-birthed wonder of 'Your Protectors' after one or two plays.

Title: Sulphur English
Review: A captivating fourth album from the Richmond, Virginia outfit that casts a woeful eye over Trump’s America. [Jun 2019, p.56]

Title: Think Tank
Review: True, Think Tank is flawed. There are many, many things wrong with this album.... But the record’s peaks are extraordinary.

Title: Time's All Gone
Review: Waterhouse's own voice is slightly under-recorded, but the musical settings--the understated Telecaster twang, the honking horns, the rumbling tom-toms--always churn with the right degree of roadhouse charm.

Title: Cotillions
Review: Perhaps the album doesn't sound like country music, but Corgan has assembled the album with country ideals, keeping the music and emotions direct but also relaxed, and that rigorous stylistic aesthetic makes Cotillions one of his better solo albums.

Title: Upside Down Mountain
Review: It's still familiar emotional portraiture, but these scenes often appear through a high-powered telescope instead of a magnifying glass. [Jun 2014, p.106]

Title: Talahomi Way
Review: He seems perfectly content to let these small-wonder songs shuffle out unobtrusively into the world, and it's come to feel like a comforting spot to return to every couple of years or so.

Title: Appeal to Reason
Review: Because of the current pop landscape's shift away from melodic rock it's impossible to tell if Rise Against will ever break out, but it's nice to know that, either way, they're still making aggressive, well structured pop-minded hardcore.

Title: A History of Insolence
Review: Naomi Bedford’s intriguing background in folk and rock, and political activism come together on this varied set of songs about “freedom, dissent and strife”, which show off her compelling, no-nonsense vocals and ambitious range.

Title: You're The Man
Review: You're The Man is a bitty, madly varied collection. ... But as a series of discrete and individually brilliant EPs, it's a fascinating documents of the myriad directions that Gaye could have investigated at his creative peak. [May 2019, p.48]

Title: Byen
Review: We can't help but hope that after eight years, he may have tried something a little more off the beaten path. That being said, fans will surely enjoy more Torske in their lives, and Byen is Bjørn Torske at his most idyllic.

Title: Clash the Truth
Review: Clash The Truth is an accomplished album that should see Beach Fossils leave behind lo-fi slacker pop's balmy evenings.

Title: 7 Days of Funk
Review: It's a welcome sign of life from an MC who many assumed to be over the hill, and where it fails, it fails on its own terms--and that's a kind of success in itself.

Title: Quality Control
Review: It is truly exciting stuff from a group that represents a sagging genre's vitally bright future.

Title: Poseidon and the Bitter Bug
Review: Poseidon and the Bitter Bug is not only solid all the way through, it feels fresh, clean, new, and chock-full of beauty.

Title: The Spine
Review: Alas, for all its genuine charm and the way the two Johns genre-hop without leaving footprints, The Spine lacks the spark of true greatness. [Aug 2004, p.119]

Title: M
Review: M displays gift for balancing atmosphere and songcraft that will reward numerous listens.

Title: Collisions
Review: It is the closest you’ll get to The Bends in 2005.

Title: La Bella Mafia
Review: Like a prize fighter coming into her own, Lil' Kim finally realizes her true potential on her third Atlantic effort.

Title: The Slideshow Effect
Review: In all, this is an album that you might want to really like, but ultimately you'll probably feel a bit cold and aloof at the general lack of variance in the band's sound.

Title: New Gods
Review: New Gods is an unusually good album.

Title: Enter the Kingdom
Review: It's clear Matthew Milia has the talent to do any number of things, but thankfully he's happy to continue making music, and Enter the Kingdom is yet another reminder that Frontier Ruckus are one of the best things to come out of Michigan since Faygo Redpop.

Title: Leaving Atlanta
Review: The band's debut was kind of a crumpled, nicotine-smudged affair, but Atlanta feels brighter, less muddled, not polished but certainly tidier around the edges. Smith's voice remains a friendly, mid-range yawp-- emotionally precise if not always entirely on-key.

Title: Darwin Deez
Review: Darwin Deez is a guy who has clearly created a persona to deliver his material, but that doesn't disguise the fact he has a lot of talent and has a made an album that proves he's a 21st century indie pop prodigy with a promising future.

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: The Chicagoans' sophomore full-length is tightened and scrubbed clean of a few of the layers of reverb that doused their debut, bringing to the forefront an ambitious and dexterous level of songwriting that belies their ever-so-slightly-post-adolescent ages.

Title: Back to Basics
Review: Labored production isn’t the only problem.

Title: The Errant Charm
Review: The result is the band's balmiest, most relaxed outing to date, with enough down-tempo hooks to score a whole summer's worth of beach trips and barbecues.

Title: Dissociation
Review: Dissociation might be the final stop on this journey, but in 10 years, it's also the first thing we'll point to when people ask why these guys are still relevant.

Title: Down To Believing
Review: It’s a brave album, at times raw with anger.

Title: Some Rap Songs
Review: Some Rap Songs is the rare album by an immensely talented lyricist who deigns not to pull out any fireworks, opting to sink into the cushion’s of a therapist’s couch in the search for an honest work of art. It’s a delicate statement of restraint, and in this case the process shows more of the artist than ever before.

Title: Wondervisions
Review: Like the guileless ballers on the screen, Delicate Steve's got surprisingly smooth moves, and the album lets you see the wonder of each one. It goes for the layup every time, sinks it, and you'll have no problem cheering along.

Title: Voices
Review: VOICES employs music as a forum for activism, spreading sentiments of unity, tolerance, and compassion throughout a pensive, sweeping, and goosebump-inducing song cycle of drones, arpeggios, and keyboard figures. In the wake of a surge in anti-liberalism, oppression, bigotry, and bloody violence and unleashed in the middle of a global pandemic, it's a becalming rebuke and a heartening conduit for hope, reflection, and radiance.

Title: More Than Just a Dream
Review: Nearly everything that made Fitz And The Tantrums interesting has been thrown out the window for More Than A Dream. Fitzpatrick has run out of anything interesting to say, instead relying on awful cliches. [Jun 2013, p.96]

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Even the half-hearted retreads ("You Talk Way Too Much," "Between Love & Hate") cashing in on the notoriously unwashed NYC quintet's debut can't muster a wink.

Title: Holy
Review: Jayne and company do manage to pull off a few tracks that capture the old fire and brimstone of classic LAL, but the shiny textures and generic songwriting are too much to overcome, rendering Holy a disappointing addition to the band's previously strong catalog.

Title: By the Way, I Forgive You
Review: The most emotionally direct and revealing album she’s to released to date.

Title: Another Life
Review: Another Life captures the ecstacy and catharsis of bodies exchanging sweat and petrol, crushing each other in unison. [Oct 2018, p.48]

Title: Do Whatever You Want All the Time
Review: This is punk rock that's both intellectually challenging and young at heart.

Title: Build a Nation
Review: What torpedoes Build a Nation is the heavy cream of reverb and echo that drowns the vocals.

Title: Cold Roses
Review: An enjoyable, if surprisingly safe, collection of roots rock. [Jul 2005, p.102]

Title: Brilliant Sanity
Review: As a whole Brilliant Sanity is as fresh as it is reminiscent, as catchy as it is challenging and thoughtful--a welcome nod to what has been, with a firm eye on the horizon.

Title: amERICa
Review: Heartbreaking, heartwarming, Eric's still very much a contender. [Jan 2016, p.92]

Title: Gold Cobra
Review: So is it any good? Does it matter? Limp Bizkit are bigger than ever before so getcha groove on, stop taking things seriously.

Title: In Our Heads
Review: Fifth album In Our Heads features its share of cerebral hip-shakers but the group has enough other moves to keep things varied.

Title: A Church That Fits Our Needs
Review: Lost in the Trees rethink of the music of grief and catharsis, turning this album into a loving and lively wake without neglecting either the precariousness of life or the horrors of death.

Title: Policy
Review: Policy is enjoyable enough, but one hopes that for its follow-up, Butler takes time to find the most accomplished realisations of his material.

Title: Let Us Never Speak of It Again
Review: Out Hud’s new-found pop smarts leave you hoping that they’ll drop the instrumentals and devote a whole album to songs.

Title: Ghost Stories
Review: Coldplay is always going to be warm, nostalgic, melancholy, pleasant, innocent and good. They’re as much a warm word and an arm around the shoulder now as they were when they first showed up.

Title: No Better Than This
Review: No Better Than This is a step beyond his best work, revelatory and free, the sound of a man who's unshackled from commercial considerations or outside influences. And ironically, it's a record that could've been made in 1954, which means it comes out of the speakers sounding remarkably fresh and new.

Title: Delta Machine
Review: Delta celebrates brooding faith and slippery solace without scrimping on Depeche's trademark blackstrobe punishment.

Title: End Times
Review: In the long, twisted canon of break-up albums, Everett doesn't only miss the mark, but makes arguably the first serious misstep of his career.

Title: Whispers
Review: While Mr. Rosenberg can be affecting, the narrowness of his vision can be suffocating. Most of the time his lyrics are like teenager’s scribbled poems.

Title: Negative Capability
Review: The Gypsy Faerie Queen, co-written and performed with Cave, and the Lanegan-scored They Come At Night, addressing the attack on the Bataclan, are among the LP's finest moments, but it's Born To Live, a tribute to the late Anita Pallenberg, that proves its most stirring. [Dec 2018, p.107]

Title: Last Year Was Complicated
Review: The best songs here to showcase Jonas as an artist come toward the end, when Last Year Was Complicated trends away from its production excesses.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: The best-sounding Decemberists record to date. [Nov 2006, p.103]

Title: Ullages
Review: Monotony is a problem on Ullages--you long for Eagulls to move beyond the confines of their soundscape and extend their emotional range.

Title: Liverpool 8
Review: Liverpool 8, which stands happily beside Starr's recent hits compilation, holds its own as a companion piece to McCartney's similarly vital "Memory Almost Full," and makes a nice day off from having to like Radiohead.

Title: Untilted
Review: Since barreling into parts unknown, the further advances made by Sean Booth and Rob Brown have been subtle at best, and the most intriguing sounding bits of their eighth album, "Untilted," usually arrive in the midst of something more familiar.

Title: Red Barked Tree
Review: Red Barked Tree is the most successful product to date of this examination. [Feb 2011, p.86]

Title: Rat Farm
Review: This fourth record in six years is another gem, a touch rockier than 2011's saccharine Lollipop, but no less sublime. [May 2013, p.95]

Title: Forever
Review: There's no gentle way of saying this, so let's cut to the chase. This record is, quite simply, useless.

Title: There Is No Year
Review: The poem isn’t great, but the music is as electrifying, unpredictable and chaotic as ever.

Title: Trouble in Shangri-La
Review: Shangri-La is one of those archetypal "it takes a few listens" albums -- although even songs like the meandering title track do eventually make an impression.

Title: Remember the Night Parties
Review: There is a palpable sense of indifference throughout the first half of the record. [#15]

Title: Drunk
Review: Drunk’s a chill listen, but it’s also a restless one.

Title: The Blue Depths
Review: It’s simply constructed, confidently attempted and ultimately, radiantly accomplished. And much like that couple [on the album back cover], the album’s missteps are present but there is enough good to prove this is a solid effort.

Title: Destroyed
Review: The album would truly shine overall if it didn't contain too many songs that are less songs and more experiments in sound. That's not to say this is a major problem, but instrumental, orchestral arrangements seem strange when they come 12 songs through a 15-track LP.

Title: Wired
Review: It's a record with an electric crackle, a halogen glow. [25 Feb 2017, p.52]

Title: Blood Mountain
Review: The perfect entwining of brain and brawn. [9 Sep 2006, p.37]

Title: Eyehategod
Review: Lack of variation in the tracklist is the token criticism against Eyehategod records, and while this one has its monotonous moments (the stoned drone of the seven-minute “Flags and Cities Bound”), the memorable riffs and refrains come in swarms.

Title: A World Out of Time
Review: Committed psych, folk and early metal music crate-diggers could probably reference a vast and rich collection of LPs from the '60s and '70s that Eternal Tapestry's work fits nicely alongside.

Title: Angry Cyclist
Review: Quaintness is what their fans look for; you just sense that there might have been an even more searing political bent lurking beneath on Angry Cyclist that never quite pierced the surface.

Title: Attention Deficit
Review: The darker moments like 'Contemplate,' where he explores insecurity against an elegiac Rihanna sample, prove he's best as a doubter, not a hater.

Title: 4:13 Dream
Review: Amid the frenzied melancholy, there’s filler and a histrionic misstep or two, but for those willfully lost in the perpetual adolescence Smith has always documented, here’s the new soundtrack to Saturday night.

Title: Miss Machine
Review: Giant mutant rats are running about the place with gasmasks and guns. Their eyeballs are electric red, firing lightning bolts of acid, spit and shit and blowing up the place and the furniture.

Title: Born on Flag Day
Review: The likes of "Little White Lies" (lost love as spirit death), "Straight Into a Storm" (found love as rock and roll life), and "Song About a Man" (grandpa) translate perfectly into their long-diddled dialect.

Title: Hear the Lions Roar
Review: Somewhere on the feral fringes of indie civilisation, Half Japanese remain kings of their own tiny jungle. [Feb 2017, p.28]

Title: Head Over Heels
Review: Music this nakedly derivative requires sharp pop instincts to be successful, and tracks like these prove that Chromeo are still able to create magic within their well-worn source material, even if they are retreading old ground.

Title: Rooty
Review: Despite Rooty's many delights, it feels like Basement Jaxx didn't really know how to top Remedy. [Aug 2001, p.127]

Title: Ogilala
Review: Whether Ogilala will count as one of them remains to be seen. Like its author it too is both fascinating, brilliant and unlikeable by turns. An interesting curio in an always-compelling career.

Title: MAGDALENE
Review: The album is a knotty meditation on the process of separating self-perception from public perception, and of twigs’s reclamation of her body and work as hers and hers alone.

Title: Vows
Review: For the most part, Kimbra's invention is a marvel to behold, as her enchanting and swooping jazz-pop tones glide across a veritable feast of sounds

Title: Blood Pressures
Review: The songs' little jabs infect the listener again and again: they suck you back in even as they draw a little blood, but never quite a gushing wound.

Title: Faithful Man
Review: As strong as this set is, it still faces the originality conundrum. Rather than a group of songs individually composed and packaged under the banner of a soul album, Faithful Man can occasionally feel like one extended, vaguely monochromatic exercise in proving the vitality of a brilliant yet aging art form.

Title: A Quiet Darkness
Review: This grandiose set of songs cobbled together from decaying sound scraps has all the ominous mystery and majesty of a silent twilight, and all the implied struggle of the abandoned structures where and from which it was created.

Title: Sweat
