Review: The album is carpeted with generic riffage, shredding and mouldy memories of heavy rock's past. [Oct 2010, p.106]

Title: A Mad & Faithful Telling
Review: Urata's slurred warble leaps into soaring vibrato, and the group's eerie throb of violin, accordion, and sousaphone has never felt so cinematic.

Title: Black Up
Review: Black Up points toward hip-hop as a source of headphone albums as the Seattle collaborative offers intriguingly fractured surfaces under their vocals, alternating brain-tweaking minimalism with jarringly complex rhythms and vinyl-ripped ephemera.

Title: Go With Me
Review: Go With Me certainly isn't a bad record by any means, but it just doesn't have the originality and lasting value that will keep people coming back for repeat listens.

Title: Hard Lessons
Review: Strongly evokes a member of Foo Fighters attempting a modern Americana album, and as such is largely a punky take on the stomping arena country of Brad Paisley. [Aug 2019, p.36]

Title: The Sister
Review: This is a singer's album, one that luxuriates in the pure, lovely tones of Nadler's warmly intimate, darkly insistent voice. [No.87 p.57]

Title: Everything Is Beautiful
Review: The songs on Everything is Beautiful, by contrast [to Everything Sucks], are warm and sun-dappled; reminiscent of the uplifting, gospel-influenced hip hop of Chance the Rapper.

Title: Letters Home
Review: Letters Home gives something to write home about, bringing to mind Have Heart's swansong, Songs to Scream at the Sun, while simultaneously containing Defeater's best material to date.

Title: Fake It Flowers
Review: The songs on Fake It Flowers are far from superfluous. Rather, it’s evident that Kristi revives the sound—which was predominantly represented by straight white men—in order to infuse it with her own life and experience as a Catholic school dropout and daughter of immigrants.

Title: The Circus
Review: The Circus isn’t terrible. In fact it’s very listenable; genre-wise it falls somewhere between Beatlesy ballads and Billy Joel’s 'The Piano Man.'

Title: Public Warning
Review: For every moment that Sov's supreme wit and impeccable cadence is fitfully showcased on Public Warning!, there is a moment when her gifts are squandered amidst anxious beats that try to compete with her huge personality.

Title: Running Out of Love
Review: This is a record that has finally seen the light of day after a bitter dispute between the band and their label. That something so beautiful and politically charged can emerge from the embers of conflict can only be a positive thing.

Title: Birth of Violence
Review: With melodies that are stretched thin and simplistic lyrics that feel even more so next to the sophisticated arrangements, Birth Of Violence’s dark beauty is like standing outside watching the stars in winter: stark, beautiful, and a little numbing.

Title: Neighborhoods
Review: They've gone all mature, come to terms with their past and kicked on to the future too.

Title: Waxing Romantic
Review: While it may not be the most unique or innovative record, Waxing Romantic is certainly sincere.

Title: Universes
Review: Though his abilities with oddball party jams are unquestionable, Davis proves he can be equally compelling when he tones it down a notch.

Title: Out of Nothing
Review: Whereas before Embrace always harboured that tendency to fuss over minutiae, to pore over every detail with such attention that betrayed self-consciousness, their fourth studio album, Out Of Nothing, finally sees them free of their own fastidiousness.

Title: Outer Peace
Review: Overall, the first half of Outer Peace sparkles, but there is a disappointing limpness to the second part which suggests that the ideas ran out and two EPs of excellent material could have been produced instead of one album’s worth of work.

Title: HIVE1
Review: There's nothing wrong with making demands of the listener, but there's little to no reward to be found across these eight increasingly alienating compositions.

Title: Life Without Sound
Review: The two records are essentially similar in their mood and effect, and the snag with this album is that it follows the formula set by its predecessor uncomfortably closely.

Title: Goldenheart
Review: Complete and correct, Goldenheart is a triumph.

Title: Stay Gold
Review: For all the dusty byways covered on Stay Gold, First Aid Kit shows to be wise beyond their years.

Title: Cardinal
Review: There’s no flash here, just a finely crafted batch of searingly personal indie rock songs. Unless you never had to grow up, it will resonate.

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: Keys and Codes, which inverts the title of Death Cab's last record, feels slapped together, which is disappointing when you consider the array of talent present.

Title: The Slow Wonder
Review: Lets you better appreciate his knack for weaving glorious pop songs out of change-ups and mixed signals. [Jul 2004, p.109]

Title: This Path Tonight
Review: With producer Shane Fontayne adding dimension and tension to the music, Nash’s first album of originals in 14 years is marked by hope and possibility shadowed by loss.

Title: One Breath
Review: [Not only is] One Breath a consistently captivating listen, but Anna Calvi a compelling artist.

Title: Since We Last Spoke
Review: RJ and his sampler wander the record crates of shared memory, and come up with progressive rock and Northern soul songs that have little to do with anybody's idea of revival.

Artist: And So I Watch You From Afar
Title: The Endless Shimmering
Review: The Endless Shimmering displays ASIWYFA's unrelenting optimism, and demonstrates their mastery of their singular brand of math-grunge.

Title: The Devil's Walk
Review: If anything, the album isn't obnoxious or overproduced, and those who are more forgiving of beauty-mongering landscape pop likely have a year-end list candidate. Those who are into Apparat's more adventurous work and collaborations, though, should pass.

Title: Endless Now
Review: Male Bonding can't help but balance themselves on an axis of sweet melody.

Title: Bestial Burden
Review: Bestial Burden is immensely captivating and exquisitely structured, another unique offering from an unparalleled artist.

Title: Save Your Season
Review: Krautrock-tinged, distortion-clouded synthpop covered in soft blankets of breathy, post-Cocteau's vocals... Just breathe it in. [Dec. 2011 p. 98]

Title: World On Fire
Review: While World On Fire isn't the finest thing Slash has, or will ever, put his name to, it still shows an iconic talent doing what he does very well. [6 Sep 2014, p.52]

Title: Romanian Names
Review: Romanian Names holds the unfortunate and surprising distinction of being the very first John Vanderslice album to feel like just another John Vanderslice album.

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: It’s a relief then, to find that – despite Fontaines DC’s own misgivings – they still have plenty more of note to say.

Title: STAY DANGEROUS
Review: Stay Dangerous is an off-the-cuff chronicle of an artist who's gotten too big - at least in his mind--for his own good.

Title: Living Proof
Review: There is no nostalgia about Living Proof. [Dec 2010, p.96]

Title: Deep Trip
Review: Too many records are boring. This one is visceral and scary, which is an improvement.

Title: Song & Dance
Review: If some of these drifting, piano-rich tunes aren't reworked into dream-state Ibiza sunset bangers by next summer then, frankly, the world is dancing to the wrong beat. [Mar 2013, p.98]

Title: See Mystery Lights
Review: A generally rambunctious mid-fi indie electropop sitting at an odd remove from the band’s devotional cause.

Title: Shriek
Review: Shriek is perhaps not what we expected from a Wye Oak record, but it’s blinding nonetheless, and, while destroying any preconceived notions of the band, lodges itself near the top--if not at the top--of their canon.

Title: Hocus Pocus
Review: These tunes sound like they're built out of yard-sale detritus, salvaged and held together with masking tape, chewing gum, anger and sentimentality. [Nov 2003, p.112]

Title: With Love
Review: What could be mistaken for something approaching a masterpiece reveals itself as far more hollow.

Title: Marry Me
Review: In the studio, it’s a totally different beast--a little soggy with orchestral coloring and the 24-track fuckery often seems rote. Taking St. Vincent at face value, Marry Me can be an enervating listen because Clark is playing against her strengths.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: It's arguably Mercer's and the Shins' most satisfying achievement.

Title: Monomania
Review: Monomania is an easy album to become monomaniac about.

Title: La Sera
Review: La Sera is still a solid collection of lush dream pop that is a trip down memory lane worth taking.

Title: right on!
Review: It’s a record that’s full of interesting ideas that needs a few listens to appreciate its subtleties, which are ultimately very rewarding.

Title: The Fool
Review: The Fool, which took nearly six years to finalize, incorporates coastal psych and voluminous noise-pop with a dash of Spector-flecked harmonies.

Title: Seraph
Review: There are plenty of good ideas here, but plenty of bad ones, too. [Sep 2015, p.77]

Title: Here
Review: If you want progression, look elsewhere. Here is ‘just’ another routinely radiant TFC album.

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: Both familiar and surprising.

Title: Seeing Other People
Review: One of the only things missing from the album is flow between tracks. Songs hit a satisfying ending, but then fade out and move to a track that doesn't connect to what the listener just heard.

Title: Heavy Is the Head
Review: A solid album but also not a surprising one. To boot, the main thing that grounds this album with a sense of time and place is the political side of it.

Title: This New Day
Review: Live, there's little doubt, these tracks will find their own groove and grow, but here they're like show dogs, primped and primed and hard to love.

Title: Little Fictions
Review: Unlike its predecessor--where the weight of the past sometimes bogged down the tempos, too--Little Fictions moves.

Title: King of the Beach
Review: It's half-baked as well, never distinguishing itself from other rock & roll throwbacks.

Title: Red River Blue
Review: Shelton continues to shine as a singer, especially on the heartfelt "I'm Sorry'' and the title track, a tender duet with wife Miranda Lambert.

Title: Dizzy Heights
Review: Dizzy Heights is an apt title for an album airborne with vertiginous harmonies and references to astronauts and flight.

Title: Crimson
Review: Alkaline Trio's shtick isn't as cartoonish as that of goth-punk outfit AFI, but it can be a bit silly.

Title: 4 Your Eyez Only
Review: Cutting through the tedium reveals a moderately engaging narrative of low level criminality with solid insights ranging from the cloying to mildly provocative. [Feb 2017, p.59]

Title: Aphrodite
Review: Aphrodite is her most unified work in ages.

Title: Friendly Fires
Review: Quite what has held back the milieu of meandering morons that make up the music scenes mid range, mid class, middlemen is probably this intelligent and creative leap; crossing genres and keeping your opus open and fresh.

Title: Apollo Kids
Review: If you still have a stomach for violent, vulgar content, this is recommended.

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: Dreamy and digressive, Parker’s songs meander and drift as if going nowhere before suddenly switching track. It can be hard to get to grips with, but there is purpose to such apparent waywardness. Meditative lyrics grapple with the relentless passage of time, lending emotional grit to his woozily blissful jams.

Title: Born Sinner
Review: His riffs on racism, homophobia and misogyny have more lyrical cunning than insight. But when it comes to twisting himself into Kanye-size pretzels of career-oriented real talk, he's a champ.

Title: Simple Math
Review: Simple Math is a perfect interpretation of an imperfect man's life, and hopefully just another chapter in  the larger story Manchester orchestra have yet to reveal. [Jun 2011, p.105]

Title: Suddenly
Review: The three singles—“Home,” “Never Come Back” and “You and I” ... follow the trajectory of Caribou’s previous and most successful commercial album, Our Love, in the conjunction of dance, R&B and psychedelic electronics, and will likely capture the same level of attention for it. Yet there is also much to like in the quieter, more contemplative cuts where frail, gorgeous shreds of melody reside in intricate electronic settings.

Title: Space Zone
Review: In spite of its occasional missteps, it ably bridges futuristic synthscapes with the rhythmic dexterity of footwork's foremost practitioners.

Title: Life Is People
Review: Although Fay's fan base is likely to remain meager, those who Life is People touches are unlikely to hear a more inspiring album this year.

Title: Fever
Review: It's their confident leaning on heritage-metal in particular that sets Bullet For My Valentine apart from local contemporaries Funeral For A Friend and Lost Prophets, but it's also that strength that holds them back.

Title: The Return of East Atlanta Santa
Review: The Return of East Atlanta Santa leans on this lighter, more playful side of Gucci’s personality, proving along the way that back to business doesn’t have to mean an absence of fun.

Title: King Animal
Review: It's neither a trainwreck nor a masterpiece, but it stirs the senses in all the right ways.

Title: Queen of Golden Dogs
Review: It's also as if Gainsborough is processing his overwhelming emotions in real life, and though his erratic compositions are sometimes too slapdash to bear, his refusal to ever settle is commendable.

Title: Born To Die
Review: What Born to Die isn't is the thing Lana Del Rey seems to think it is, which is a coruscating journey into the dark heart of a troubled soul... What it is, is beautifully turned pop music, which is more than enough.

Title: Avatar
Review: Freedom rock at its most liberating. [Jul/Aug 2006, p.116]

Title: Turn Out the Lights
Review: Turn Out the Lights is a rich, moving work that creates a communion of sorts, an acknowledgement that the little victories are worth embracing even if salvation seems utterly out of reach.

Title: The Deserters
Review: It is a lush thing that, were we writing for a certain type of women’s mag, might have us reaching for words such as "candles" and "bubble bath."

Title: Blue Roses
Review: Those with a low tolerance for navel-gazing are advised to steer clear, but there's plenty to cherish here.

Title: Chain Gang of Love
Review: The Raveonettes have something the Mary Chain lost around the time of 'Automatic': an understanding of how to make a tight three minute pop song feel exhilarating.

Title: Endless Flowers
Review: The blindingly sunny Endless Flowers is an album appropriate for the beginning of the summer, all popsicles, poppy beats and poolside parties coalescing into warm nights

Title: A Weird Exits
Review: It’s comfortably strange territory, and while it might not open any new or mind-melting doors, Thee Oh Sees remain rampantly good fun.

Title: Cedars
Review: It's painful, joyful and glorious. [#5, p.98]

Title: Crown Royal
Review: The Ishtar of comeback albums -- overdone, underinspired, and marketed to within an inch of its life.

Title: At the Down-Turned Jagged Rim of the Sky
Review: This is life At the Down-turned Jagged Rim of the Sky, which isn't a devastatingly beautiful one, but it's still engaging in its own deep, personal way.

Title: Nellyville
Review: A winning combo of thick club cuts, hands-in-the-air call-outs, pop ingenuity and a perfect balance of entertainment and realism in his rhymes.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Fleet Foxes mostly seem content to plug away at the atmosphere established on their debut. The big question on "Helplessness Blues'' isn't where the songs will go, but how much distanced reverb will be featured on any given cut.

Title: Sun Structures
Review: At every turn there are moves unarguably adjacent to Revolver, The Zombies, early Byrds, and, in the title track strident harmonies, The Mamas & The Papas.... The tunes throughout, though, are original, and infectious. [Mar 2014, p.94]

Title: Off With Their Heads
Review: Both anxious and anthemic, the third most famous band from Leeds, England (behind Gang of Four and the Mekons) lobs social commentary as sharp as drummer Nick Hodgson’s ties, and tackles subjects as brainy as evolutionary biology ('Like It Too Much,'), the tenets of self-help ('Tomato In the Rain') and gender politics ('Remember You’re A Girl'), all at breakneck speed.

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: This could be Modest Mouse's finest hour were it not a little long - the nuances are occasionally rather swamped by the effort of listening to the hour-long record through.

Title: New Moon
Review: One can make out here and there traces of American roots music, but those are alas, buried within the breathtaking bluster, ’cos ultimately, you can’t separate The Men from the noise.

Title: Sewn Together
Review: The second album of their third coming aims for the spontaneity of the early recordings, pushing those buried melodies to the surface. [Jul 2009, p.93]

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: Perpetual Surrender's highlights might have had more impact if they were collected on an EP, but DIANA have a unique enough perspective--and enough potential--to make the album worth a listen for anyone who loves synth pop in any of its incarnations.

Title: Slicker Than Your Average
Review: This is one of the most subtle male R&B records in a good while.

Title: The Boy with No Name
Review: While the first half of the record is promising, however, the band loses steam toward the end.

Title: Romance Is Boring
Review: Los ­Campesinos! now sound a little less like a series of twitching climaxes, and they're the better for it.

Title: Everything to Everyone
Review: The record feels uneven, as the oscillation between frivolous and serious makes both less convincing. [Nov 2003, p.108]

Title: Slow Summits
Review: Slow Summits is full of carefully arranged autumnal tunes: thoughtful, intimate, unaffected and wistfully romantic. It's secret music worth sharing.[No.99, p.56]

Title: Mangy Love
Review: Mangy Love is a terrific, bizarre album made up of familiar parts rearranged into something new, unfamiliar, and offbeat.

Title: Sick Scenes
Review: Though Sick Scenes is unlikely to win the band legions of new fans, it’s a record that sits comfortably alongside the rest of their canon while acting as an affirmation as to why, in 2017, a decade after their debut, Los Campesinos! are just as important now as they were ten years ago.

Title: Imperium
Review: Purposefully lo-fi, it would be easy to dismiss as self-indulgent nostalgia, yet its quirky charms and understated directness more often than not outweigh its faults.

Title: Rubber Factory
Review: Shockingly well done... a remarkable album. [3 Sep 2004, p.73]

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: Julian Casablancas continues to sing as if roused from a deep sleep, the rhythm section keeps the tunes as puckery tight as the band's trousers and guitarists Nick Valensi and Albert Hammond Jr. balance melodic strumming with some impressive shredding.

Title: FROM DEEWEE
Review: Some tracks will work better live, but consider the experiment a success. [Jun 2017, p.112]

Title: Somethin 'Bout Kreay
Review: Kreay indulges the full breadth of her influences, turning Somethin into a series of wan genre studies.

Title: Sweet Sour
Review: All in all, then, the record showcases a dynamism present but not fully realized on their critically acclaimed (and still excellent) debut.

Title: Strange Weekend
Review: Strange Weekend's gauzy dream-pop is almost incapable of provoking anything but love.

Title: The Besnard Lakes are the Roaring Night
Review: But even weaker songs are still not a wasted trip, flickering with sharp moments and dazzling effects. In this way, the album asserts itself as a refreshingly pointed piece of chamber pop, a starkly serious work that plays as big but never portentous.

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: One of the consistently brilliant musicians working today hasn't let us down yet.

Title: Miami Memory
Review: These are tender anthems, even if some won't be readily singing lines like "eating your ass like an oyster" in a festival field. [Nov 2019, p.22]

Title: Ash
Review: In the end, Ash is many things: militant, vulnerable, and tender; it is urgent yet unhurried, its sharp edges unapologetically exposed. It is rooted in struggles and seeks victory, not deliverance. It is not only memorable, but indomitable and beautiful.

Title: MG
Review: A shockingly vital, crackling, unencumbered solo instrumental record. [No. 120, p.55]

Title: Monterey
Review: Pretty road ruminations. [Jul 2015, p.96]

Title: Fever Dream
Review: His songs are resonant with the weight of experience, and his musical settings, even in their relative sparsity, are powerful and at times nearly elegant.

Title: Realism
Review: The Magnetic Fields’ eighth album, provides yet another example of why Merritt belongs on the shortlist of America’s greatest songsmiths.

Title: When I Pretend to Fall
Review: It's just straight rock and roll, really, and I mean really straight rock and roll.

Title: The Afterlife
Review: Cut during the same sessions as Trust in the Lifeforce of the Deep Mystery, it's not a collection of outtakes or even a sequel, but a holistic mirror image that comes from the same sphere of aesthetic investigation and font of inspiration.

Title: White Chalk
Review: White Chalk, wholly self-contained and uncompromised, is a work of literary depth and complexity.

Title: In Between
Review: It's easy to get the sense that the intent is to let the jangling shoegaze wash over you, and if some of the lyrics stick, that's fine. But that's the thing-- they rarely do, and neither do several of the songs.

Title: Earth to the Dandy Warhols
Review: The set is somewhat of a shambolic affair, wherein kernels of good ideas get blown out, jumbled up or lost in execution.

Title: Mama, I'm Swollen
Review: The emo-punk angst is cut with little of the band's trademark wit or ingenuity: Most of the songs plod bloodlessly to an inevitable, pointless climax of noise, sour humor, and teen nihilism.

Title: Twin Cinema
Review: With more developed ideas than Mass Romantic and a more cohesive sound than Electric Version, it's their most consistent, confident, and best album to date.

Title: Emotional Traffic
Review: Mr. McGraw has never sounded this casual. It doesn't suit him.

Title: The Weight of Your Love
Review: Editors' fourth retains their customary grandeur and gloom, but with a new immediacy and surety, as Tom Smith matures into a truly commanding frontman. [Aug 2013, p.86]

Title: Shangri La
Review: The result isn't the clean-up job it might've been; Bugg, 19, still sings with a nasal edge that wouldn't last more than a round on "American Idol." Yet the songwriting here feels more evened-out, less appealingly pugnacious than it did last time.

Title: Never, Never, Land
Review: Compared to 'Psyence Fiction''s ruthlessly cut glass exterior, this is a rounded, more human record, considerably less calculated and therefore far more approachable.

Title: Great Vengeance and Furious Fire
Review: Great Vengeance and Furious Fire is too uneven to be great, but its handful of fantastic singles makes for an extremely promising debut.

Title: Everything's the Rush
Review: The dizzy, euphoric racket is occasionally brought earthward by lyrics that hint at darker troubles.

Title: Django Django
Review: Smart guys, smart record.

Title: Winning Days
Review: There seems to be a hollowness, a lack of soul, an empty Big Mac carton where this album's heart should be.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: Clocking in at a mere 32 minutes, the album is conceptually and sonically tight.

Title: Love's Crushing Diamond
Review: It is minimalist yet lush, hopeful yet rooted in a stark and sometimes grim reality.

Title: Sees the Light
Review: Overall, Sees the Light is as successful an album as La Sera was.

Title: Citizen Zombie
Review: The band may castigate the apathy endemic to the masses, but it doesn’t wallow. It instead throbs, bristles, and ultimately galvanizes, vividly documenting what’s been lost in our comfortably numb political complacency while brazenly providing a template for what can be done to re-gain it.

Title: New Maps of Hell
Review: It's business as usual for Bad Religion, the US punk rock stalwarts recently restored to full power with the return of guitarist Brett Gurewitz. [Sep 2007, p.100]

Title: BeyoncÃ©
Review: Beyoncé is better than good, slickly packaged, created with the best of intentions yet still comes off as a postmodern mash of hubris, sincerity and gloss. It will be a hit regardless.
Difficult to fault, [yet] it's equally difficult to get excited about.

Title: The Camel's Back
Review: While The Camel’s Back demonstrates a clear progression in Psapp’s worth as songwriters and musicians, it becomes easy to ignore what they accomplish creatively as the ears only pick up on its “cuteness” factor.

Title: Derdang Derdang
Review: ABO keep the music tight and enclosed to match the lyrical mood, making Derdang Derdang a succinct, purposeful statement.

Title: Twenty-Five For The Rest of Our Lives
Review: This melodic yet dynamic punk seems to have been created in the early '80s, a high compliment and one the band is likely to embrace far more than the realization that the disc's title is impossible to fulfill.

Title: Wild Strawberries
Review: Nice enough, and the climax of the title track is truly transportive, but no real departure from previous form. [Mar 2015, p.56]

Title: Eat at Whitey's
Review: Whenever Everlast lays back and spins stories and tall tales on his own, his blend of folk, rock, blues, rap, and pop culture clicks.

Title: Magic Chairs
Review: For now, the experience of listening to Magic Chairs is a frustrating one: the sound of a group with one foot remaining in art-pop territory and the other pointed toward an arena-sized sound. Efterklang might pull off either mode, but their occupation of the same space is a source of unwanted friction.

Title: Volta
Review: Her vision is worth the price of submission. [Jun 2007, p.90]

Title: Brightest Blue
Review: A confident return from an artist now comfortable in who she is.

Title: Circular Sounds
Review: Stoltz knows that sometimes the best way through anything, from hangovers to hopelessness, requires just good pop, a steady beat and the sound that everything’s okay. That’s what he does very well.

Title: Shoot for the Stars, Aim for the Moon
Review: It’s a shame there are not enough songs where Pop’s talent can shine on its own. Only six of 19 tracks feature Pop Smoke solo, not including the intro, outro and “Dior,” which is a bonus track that also appears on all of his previous tapes. ... However, there are still many highs.

Title: Alice and Friends
Review: Nothing is entirely serious. It’s all in fun--and it is fun, fortunately.

Title: Hell-On
Review: Case’s restless exploratory impulses are contained within relatively conventional song structures, with much more compelling results.

Title: Tender New Signs
Review: The only problem here is that the genre is taken to the extreme, and can blend together to the point where the album seems like one massive track.

Title: Settle
Review: There’s nothing very new about the sound, but there’s a freshness and intelligence in the Lawrence brothers’ discovery of it.

Title: Asa Breed
Review: Throughout much of Asa Breed, Dear achieves a serendipitous balance between the uplifting and the eerie, the hummable and the hypnotic, the tuneful and the texturally adventurous.

Title: Surf
Review: While written with absolute precision and poetic skill that rivals the best rappers currently working, Chance's words tumble from his mouth effortlessly, as if he's already done with the verse by the time he recites it, looking to what's next.
He fails to come up with an album that keeps up the standard set here by a couple of standout tracks such as "Strawberry Wine" and "Nightbirds."

Title: The Messenger
Review: The massively influential Smiths guitarist finally makes the solid solo debut he should've recorded a quarter-century ago.

Title: Veckatimest
Review: Veckatimest's only down side is a touch of preciousness, a need for refinement that, unchecked, might nudge Grizzly Bear towards the polite rather than imaginative. It's a small quibble. For now, this is almost perfect.

Title: Manual
Review: The overall effect is a carefully constructed, complex yet breezy, psych-pop collection. [Dec 2015, p.69]

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: Nothing on this album quite lives up to the previous "Give Me Every Little Thing," but in the end, Maclean does make the case that he should continue hanging around the mixer for many years to come. [Winter 2009, p.100]

Title: News and Tributes
Review: Inspirational stuff.

Title: The Meetings of the Waters
Review: While some of these experiments don't work--the riotous "Babushka-Yai Ya" is messy and, ultimately, skippable and "Euphoria" lacks any exultation--others cast Regan in a new light.

Title: All Things Under Heaven
Review: The band focus on capturing moments rather than arranging songs, interspersing tracks with tone poems including Millenial Prayer.

Title: The Day Is My Enemy
Review: The music is mid-paced pummel of snarling electronic bass and beats through which Liam Howlett's nutty synths occasionally sail like a haunted bumper car. [May 2015, p.78]

Title: Pressure
Review: On Pressure, the solid if routine follow-up to Trap or Die 3, Jeezy doesn't deviate from his standard set of themes. He's still rhyming about his rise from the bottom, the product he's shifting, and all the disposable wealth and women that have come with it, all the while castigating would-be detractors and snitches.

Title: Goths
Review: Songwriter Darnielle expertly renders the acute emotions of adopting a new tribe and the resignation that life often forces. [Jun 2017, p.89]

Title: Living Room Songs
Review: Apart from the aptly titled "Film Credits," which, worthily, plays much like a ode to Max Richter, the music on the remainder of the album is left to unsatisfying and grey piano suites that don't sound destined for a more open setting nor benefit from the intimate setting of Arnalds' own living room.

Title: Everything Must Go
Review: Everything Must Go is a profound disappointment.

Title: Strange Pleasures
Review: It's more of an adept fusing of very distinct styles into something interesting and almost factory fresh, if not quite to the level of the bands they are drawing inspiration from.

Title: Escape From Evil
Review: While Hunter seems more enamored of radio hits by the likes of Gary Numan and Flock of Seagulls here, Lower Dens never quite settle into an easy genre hook.

Title: Secrets Are Sinister
Review: While the quartet’s earlier efforts maintained a shoegazey vibe, that’s mostly been abandoned this time around in favor of more straightforward (and less interesting) songwriting. [Year End 2008]

Title: Once Upon a Time in the West
Review: The Brithish band takes its attention away from the variety and finds a moderate middle ground. This makes The West slightly generic and much more acceptable at the same time. [Fall 2007, p.79]

Title: 'Til Your River Runs Dry
Review: While Burdon himself remains indignant, and indomitable, his tenacious stance is coached in songs that rarely measure up to the classics credited to him early on.

Title: Waiting for the Sunrise
