Review: You could argue Wolfmother’s ballsy and carefree hi-octane music is all just innocent fun, ideally washed down with a six pack of tinnies. Yet it’s utterly devoid of soul and intelligence.

Title: Youth
Review: Here, his pool of talent is confirmed in the spare xylophone beat to “Youth” and the ingenious, slinky grooves to “Lightwork” and “They Don’t Know”, a frisky pass-the-mic showcase between Tinie, Kid Ink, Stefflon Don and AoD. But given the sharp drop-off in notable guest talent this time round, compared with Demonstration, he certainly needs to make changes.

Title: A Different Kind of Truth
Review: Van Halen have found their dazzle without a hassle.

Title: The Last Broadcast
Review: The darkest feel-good record of the year. [14 Jun 2002, p.100]

Title: Pilot Talk II
Review: A minor release for Curren$y still bests most major hip-hop releases, and this Pilot Talk sequel relishes in the rapper's expanding set of skills.

Title: Painted Ruins
Review: Painted Ruins stops short of fearlessly exploring new musical terrain, instead content to approach the familiar from new angles.

Title: Unfidelity
Review: Unfidelity exhibits sonic DNA from all corners of pioneering electronica. [May 2014, p.93]

Title: Total Strife Forever
Review: This is music that’s meticulous and expansive without ever falling into the trap of being boring or self-indulgent.

Title: Freetown Sound
Review: Dev Hynes' work--populist, experimental, healing, agitating, straightforward, multi-layered--demonstrates this unfailingly. Prince's radical pop spirit lives on in many artists. But none are channeling it more fully, or artfully.

Title: The Pinkprint
Review: Nicki is more personal, more timeless and more connected to her own artistry here, serving some of the most superlative work of her established career on The Pinkprint.

Title: Benjamin Booker
Review: It's a pleasure to report his studio debut catches the spark. [Dec 2014, p.103]

Title: Forever
Review: You can hear the isolated perspectives that it was made in creep into the finished products, which doesn't take away from the songs but adds a feeling of being stuck in some faraway dream to even the most immediate of the band's glowing pop tunes.

Title: The Beautiful Struggle
Review: While he's still the 21st century's answer to KRS-One, a rapper who is simultaneously intelligent and engaging, he needs to work with producers who are capable of sharing that vision with the masses in an equally engaging way. At times "The Beautiful Struggle" achieves this perfection combination, and at other times you're left loving the lyrics but lacking in headnodding dopeness.

Title: Computers and Blues
Review: His fifth and final Streets album turns into his best since "A Grand Don't Come For Free." [Feb 2011, p.123]

Title: American Nightmare
Review: The musical flourishes and pitch-black noir that run like a current underneath American Nightmare bring the album into a wider world.

Title: El Rey
Review: If you've been sticking by the group for long, you'll be rewarded by El Rey's brutal honesty, hard-won wisdom, and first-rate songcraft, and you'll relish the sound of a band trying to recapture a brilliant sound from their past and succeeding completely.

Title: Hail to the King
Review: By the album's second half, Avenged Sevenfold can't help but let loose their guitar shredding theatrics a bit, and their personality starts to shine through as the tempo quickens and tracks take flight to unabashed height

Title: WALLS
Review: Producer Markus Dravs (Coldplay, Mumford & Sons) does an admirable job of translating Followill's signature slurred delivery and the band's muscular jangle into thicker arrangements, though the result can feel generic.

Title: jj nÂ° 2
Review: This level of quality is ridiculously hard to challenge, which may be part of the reason jj n° 2 has remained on the hipster tip despite that it isn’t very hip.

Title: Stars Are Our Home
Review: It's a pretty indulgent affair (Halstead has acknowledged this) with most songs clocking in close to or exceeding the five minute mark; the last couple of tracks are disposable.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: If you wade through some horrid lyrics and mediocre songcraft, you will find You Are The Quarry stands solidly as a long overdue return to a formative sound. [#7]

Title: Crybaby
Review: Essentially, Crybaby is an album that achieves exactly what it set out to do.

Title: Light After Dark
Review: Sadly, though, Ain't Nobody's by miles the most interesting four minutes on Light After Dark, which suggests Maguire is another startling talent whose every point of interest has been sandblasted off between being signed and getting her album out.

Title: Full Circle
Review: There’s no grandstanding on this modest yet confident record. Rather there’s the humility, humour, wisdom and hard-won truths of country music at its best.

Title: Red
Review: It's frustrating, then, when Swift reverts back to type. Too many of the songs on this bloated 16-track album revisit the gently strummed verses and characterless choruses of her previous work.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: The more time you spend with Ambassadors, the more clearly that commitment and joy comes through.

Title: A Blessing and a Curse
Review: A Blessing... is perhaps a more personal and introspective record than usual. But truly there's still a lot to marvel at. [Apr 2006, p.112]

Title: A Blessing and a Curse
Review: A Blessing and a Curse easily qualifies as the Truckers’ most straightforward album.

Title: Sticky Wickets
Review: Once again, they have come up with a lovingly crafted tribute to the idiosyncrasies of England’s summer sport, and those who approach it as a bit of harmless fun will be humming these songs with a smile on their face at least until the final ball of the Ashes series is bowled.

Title: Animositisomina
Review: The sustained ferocity on display here is admirable. [7 Mar 2003, p.72]

Title: Art Angels
Review: Crackling with radio-primed hooks, whipsnap breakbeats and Boucher’s helium-pitched vocals, Grimes’ third album makes a convincing strike for playlist ubiquity, with a healthy dollop of the oddball chucked in.

Title: American Slang
Review: After their breakthrough, The '59 Sound, the Jerseyian punks appear to have taken a Green Day-like career shift: finding a concept that struck a chord and beating it to death like one of the down-and-out ciphers in the B-movie quality Springsteen worldview they've constructed.

Title: Hard Boiled Soft Boiled
Review: This album confirms Odonis Odonis as one of those rare bands who marry noise and melody and do it well.

Title: God of the Serengeti
Review: This album is a violent frenzy maxed out to the “nth” power, so it may not be for everyone; however, most who embrace hardcore hip-hop will undoubtedly love this album.

Title: Power in the Blood
Review: She has lost none of her power in the interim.

Title: Rausch
Review: Rausch is something to get lost in, a long stroll free of the noise of modernity where the little details can draw near and take your breath away with their simple beauty.

Title: War Room Stories
Review: Like a butterfly flapping its wings in the Amazon causes a hurricane on the other side of the world, Breton’s attention to detail has made the all-encompassing tone of War Room Stories differ vastly.

Title: Histoire de Melody Nelson
Review: Andy Votel’s encyclopedic liner notes and a Gainsbourg interview make this version the definitive reissue for the as-yet unsullied.

Title: Future Ruins
Review: For all the grim despondency, this is an album steeped in the acrid stench of beauty. [Mar 2019, p.88]

Title: Live Wild Die Free
Review: Scandinavian pop clearly plays an influence alongside contrasting splashes of psych-rock and raw, grungy punk, and the unique little fantasy worlds they create with it are a great form of escapism.

Title: Head Cage
Review: A more focused sonic direction would have been more potent and a more adventurous one would have been more exciting. Still, every track delivers a bruising and it’s hard to imagine anyone interested in the group being disappointed by the album.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: One of the most striking facts about this record is that it doesn't sound definitively like the work of one or the other, though occasionally you will catch a whiff of something one or the other has created in the past.

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: Yes, there are a lot of reasons to hate Scissor Sisters. But this brilliant debut is not one of them.

Artist: And So I Watch You From Afar
Title: Heirs
Review: Whilst there are fragmented glimpses of influence peppered throughout, the record remains very true to And So I Watch You From Afar’s sound; too much at the beginning, but brilliantly later on.
Fresh-faced wunderkind aces his debut. [Oct 2011, p.118]

Title: Instant Money Magic
Review: Much like funsize Snickers bars, there's a gooey joy to be found in the brevity, but especially for us this side of the Atlantic, there are bands who have improved on the formula of twee-punk/whatever you want to call it.

Title: The Midnight Organ Fight
Review: It's Hutchison's utterly believable desperation and frank lyrics that push the whole thing from good to great.

Title: Lonely Twin
Review: The album us one that easily endears itself wit its gentle, tuneful touch and just enough hazy heft to keep things interesting. [Jul 2011, p.86]

Title: Vapor Trails
Review: Rush sound like they're slowly but audibly running out of puff. [July 2002, p.118]

Title: The Soft Bulletin
Review: The Soft Bulletin is sparse and enchanted, like the band has awoken from a long dream spent spinning in outer space.

Title: Lost Themes
Review: The icy synths of "Vortex" and "Fallen" evoke vintage Carpenter dread. But the prog-pomp of "Domain" and "Mystery" are the aural equivalent of too much CGI.

Title: Skit I Allt
Review: It's to Ejstes credit that he's stayed his course, continuing to pull together nostalgic and post-millennial sounds instead of chasing a mass audience that he probably couldn't have kept anyway.

Title: Dead Media
Review: Hefner is new at this, so things get clumsy. But it's endearing, because [Darren] Hayman's melodies and the idiosyncratic worldview he espouses are still irresistible. [#53, p.79]

Title: Country Westerns
Review: This is raw, honest Americana featuring a punky edge that connects due to the power and passion it’s played with and inspired by.

Title: Motherhood
Review: For as many as will be impressed by it, there will be plenty for whom it’s just a headache. If you’re willing to stick with it though, you’ll be rewarded with many sonic gems – and some thought-provoking ideas thematically.

Title: Take Off Mode
Review: Take Off Mode doesn’t forge any new paths so much as it retreads old ones. ... That said, Take Off Mode’s most retro moment is also its best.

Title: Andorra
Review: Andorra belongs on a hip continuum but something about it still feels slightly cold--it's a druggy album that's too precise to be made with drugs, a lush album that’s too filigreed to be emotional.

Title: BareNaked
Review: The funniest thing since Ravyn-Symone's Here's to New Dreams.

Title: Clear Heart Full Eyes
Review: What's left are halfhearted Hold steady wannabes and dull stabs at poignancy.

Title: The Scene Between
Review: You will hear better records than The Scene Between this year; none will put a bigger smile on your face.

Title: Emoh
Review: He delivers 14 sweetly sombre neo-folk tunes that reveal just how subtly pervasive the man's influence really is. [Mar 2005, p.108]

Title: I Hate Music
Review: [Superchunk] crafted an album of effervescent ebullience, fusing joy and sadness with a skill that built on their two decades of existence.

Title: Mine Is Yours
Review: Cold War Kids seem to be aiming for something more akin to Kings of Leon, and the songs bear this out. [Year End 2010, p.69]

Artist: Dan Le Sac vs Scroobius Pip
Title: Repent Replenish Repeat
Review: Repent Replenish Repeat follows in much the same vein as 2010's prickly The Logic of Chance: glitchy industrial-electro grooves and jerky, uncomfortable rhythm programmes, over which rapper Scroobius Pip inhabits the grey area between maverick articulacy and feral antipathy.

Title: South
Review: Heather Nova has ventured out on South, delving into the pop side for her own inventions. Fans who aren't accepting of such a move might be critical; new listeners might find South her easiest album.

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: This is a stunning album, bristling with astute and funny words, glorious tunes and delivered in performances all the more impressive for sounding so utterly effortless. [Mar 2008, p.80]

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: Sincerity of intent is one thing. But they've got the music to back it up.... This is Scissor Sisters' first Greatest Hits collection. [Feb 2004, p.70]

Title: Love Letters
Review: Love Letters may not guarantee that Metronomy are the kings of their sound, but they still have a seat at the table.

Title: Atheist's Cornea
Review: Throughout, shimmering walls of guitar give way to echoing, spacey psychedelia; riffery and frantic drumming; tuneful asides and emotional rampage.

Title: Edge of the Sun
Review: Edge of the Sun is a strong album that continues the upward trajectory that became stronger as the lessons of albums like Garden Ruin took root.

Title: Red Carpet Massacre
Review: Less impressive are the band's own art-rock statements. [Dec 2007, p.116]

Title: Evil Friends
Review: Evil Friends kicks out the jams, heightens the hits, and rolls it all up in a trippy joint.

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: There certainly seems a lot to unpack in Father Of The Bride, and at times there almost seems too much crammed into the album.

Title: Rocket
Review: Throughout, G straddles clarity and complexity with deceptive ease.

Title: Berkeley to Bakersfield
Review: Whilst Berkeley has an obvious theme, there’s a feeling of movement and diversity on the album, and the ideas are put forward in such a way as to make this album relevant to modern life and not just California.... Bakersfield takes on an altogether different style again; we’re headed to the country, and it’s entirely understandable why these songs were grouped and recorded separately.

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: Striding through metal, dancehall, space pop and dubstep, our multicultural mascot has littered MAYA with politicized sonic motifs: from marching drums, gunshots and modems to heavy machinery and blaring sirens. It's loud, proud, and taking no prisoners.

Title: Go Tell Fire to the Mountain
Review: A shrewdly self-marketing, purposefully confusing gaggle of musicians and visual artists, WU LYF--which stands for World Unite/Lucifer Youth Foundation--plays music that's an exhilarating blur, swathed in echo and cymbal sizzle.

Title: American Tragic
Review: At a relatively brief nine tracks, the record is a perfectly paced blast of dark pop that deftly reflects Fortune’s growing prowess as a songwriter.

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: I Love You, It's Cool prove Bear in Heaven's 2009-10 success wasn't a fluke, and given two years, they can deliver another album of ebullient jams.

Title: Screamworks: Love in Theory and Practice
Review: Old-school romantic Ville Valo croons as often as he screams, so that even when aiming for the stylistic median, a bit of local weirdness oozes forth to make Screamworks more interesting than it's designed to be.

Title: No Shape
Review: His fourth LP feels like a statement of defiance, strength and unabashed beauty. [Jul 2017, p.112]

Title: Galaxy Garden
Review: Cutler's surgically meticulous programming skills and ear for mesmeric melodies.... elevate this follow up to 2010's Emerald Fantasy Tracks above simple ['90's techno] homage. [Jun 2012, p.106]

Title: Suck It and See
Review: Arctic Monkeys continue to carve out a consistently thrilling career on possibly their best record yet. [May 2011, p.75]

Title: Untitled
Review: Even if the music isn't extraordinary, Nas himself is legendary on "Untitled" - and as long as racism is relevant, so is this album.

Title: Hang
Review: Tension may not be the defining characteristic of Foxygen's sound this time around, but it's still there, bubbling up furiously beneath the sparkling surface.

Title: The Pale Emperor
Review: The Pale Emperor is downright ambitious when it wants to be and lazy when it can get away with it.

Title: Have One on Me
Review: It is a stunning and ambitious piece of work; one for the ages.

Title: Jacuzzi Boys
Review: There are many (too many?) bands in 2013 playing this kind of raucous garage rock, but thanks to the perfect production, the high-quality hookage in every song, and the nuanced yet powerful performance The Jacuzzi Boys deliver, there are precious few bands doing it better.

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: With Attack on Memory, Baldi's never felt more alive or more authentic.

Title: Thing of the Past
Review: Thing of the Past contains no original songs (although it's unlikely that anyone without a nasty crate-digging habit will recognize most of these tracks), but Vetiver are awfully well suited to the material, and Cabic's vocals--sweet, smooth, and golden--shine.

Title: Hard Bargain
Review: Some of the story-songs are drippy, but that voice remains dry.

Title: Hypnotized
Review: Dream Police feels here like its own project, like a stand-alone band just getting started. With that feeling comes excitement and discovery, but also a learning curve.

Title: A Moving Picture
Review: It's just a shame his parochial worldview is often at odds with his music's overreaching grandstanding. [Mar 2013, p.94]

Title: Cheer
Review: The versatility shown here adds yet another notch to Drug Church’s (and Kinlon’s) bedpost as one of the most exciting bands around in a genre that doesn’t often do much experimentation or progression.

Title: Regifted Light
Review: Regifted Light doesn't seem built to shock or cajole, but to connect with all sorts of people, and to last.

Title: Praxis Makes Perfect
Review: What stops the record being preposterous, what keeps it charming and fun throughout, what makes it okay for ‘Mid Century Modern Nightmare’ to rhyme “bourgeoisie” with “cups of tea” is the presence of Gruff.

Title: Surfing Strange
Review: It’s a familiar story to hear DIY bands frustratingly avoiding their past strengths once they secure some proper studio time; both records have a more “mature” sound than their lo-fi predecessors, but I find the songwriting largely forgettable.

Title: Playtime Is Over
Review: Beatwise, Playtime culls Wiley's best dubs from the last year, with tracks like 'Bow E3' and '50/50' flexing textbook mastery over grime's sludgy polyrhythm.

Title: The Argument
Review: Musically scattergun, with vintage rock ‘n’ roll rubbing shoulders with post-rock sounds, there’s much to admire about this bold artistic statement.

Title: Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace
Review: Grohl often shows off his sky-high vocal range, award-winning ear for bridges and choruses and penchant for ending opuses with dark, pitch-perfect shrieks.

Title: Barbara Barbara, we face a shining future
Review: An album on which Underworld reestablish themselves as supreme dance music architects.

Title: Technicolor Health
Review: Technicolor Health amply delivers on the promis of their 2007 EP, "Burning Birthdays." [Apr 2009, p.86]

Title: No Mercy
Review: The electricity that defined T.I.'s early career-dexterous lyricism molded effortlessly to trap rap essentials -- feels further away than ever before.

Title: reputation
Review: The sparkling, writerly synth-pop of 1989 has been jettisoned almost entirely, replaced by thudding trap beats, Vegas EDM, melancholy Drive-wave synthesizers, and splashes of Miami bass. More often than not, it works.

Title: Like a Rose
Review: Although there exist exceptions, like the gorgeous “Used” (in which Monroe drops this corker: “Used, like a house where a family lived until they died and there’s a soul in every room”), the record as a whole slithers into a sort of unsatisfying middle ground.

Title: Collection
Review: At 20 years old, Allison is only just getting started, and Collection is a tidy introduction to Soccer Mommy that points towards her vision of bringing her contemplative songwriting to a more potent and energizing level.

Title: Load Blown
Review: Load Blown, superficially, is more of the same; sample some 30 second clips online or in your local record store and it's believable that this is a continuation of what they've been doing the past few albums. The entirety, however, exhibits otherwise, and isn't nearly as fulfilling.

Title: Oczy Mlody
Review: These pendulum shifts--from frustrating to fascinating and back again--play out within the songs themselves.

Title: Miss Universe
Review: Miss Universe is an intimate record full of personal fears and emotions, but these are of wider, universal relevance. They should resonate with us all.

Title: The Unnatural World
Review: Ultimately, The Unnatural World is a frustrating album.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: "First Impressions of Earth" would be better at 40 minutes than it is at 50-plus, and the Strokes' vision still has a definite ceiling, but Julian Casablancas' songs and ever more congested-sounding voice fight mightily to claim a new creative range.

Title: Hate
Review: Loud, large and unrelenting, Hate is stunning, orchestral pop.

Title: Eucalyptus
Review: Avey Tare’s stream of vanishing sounds, creaking floorboards, and silently intonated lullabies is romantic in its faded resemblance to our radiant, ever-growing environment; but as with Portner’s newly adopted city of Los Angeles, the supposed nature exists purely as an extension of the human desire to create and actualize what we see in our minds.

Title: Choir of Echoes
Review: Peggy Sue may always be a little too quirky to reap the mainstream success of some of their contemporaries, but their versatility is a strength they can bank on in the long run.

Title: Bass Drum of Death
Review: A new punk classic.

Title: Rapor EP
Review: Grossi's ability to deftly assimilate these more pop-oriented artists into his oeuvre is a testament to his growth since You Are All I See, resulting in his most confident release to date.

Title: Damaged
Review: Even though the songwriting's tight, the uniformly delicate touch of adult contemporary arrangements will leave you struggling to stay awake till the album's end.

Title: I Like It When You Sleep, for You Are So Beautiful Yet So Unaware of It
Review: Despite opening big, bright and airtight, I Like It When You Sleep... gets boring-melty during dream-gaze reveries like "Please Be Naked" and "Lostmyhead." Even so, when they hit the right kind of moody sheen ("Somebody Else," "Loving Someone"), the 1975 are an enjoyable balance of desire and distraction.

Title: Nerve Endings
Review: Without over-embellishing it at all, you won’t find too many albums in the quintet’s chosen genre that betters the quality, consistency and diversity of Nerve Endings.

Title: Shall Noise Upon
Review: Shall Noise Upon succeeds in fits and spurts, but as a whole, it lacks the continuity that is an essential ingredient for a career-defining record.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: Relatives in Descent manages to sound more thoughtful and introspective than 2015's The Agent Intellect without sapping the strength of this great band; quite simply, as a bit of record-making, this is Protomartyr's most impressive accomplishment to date.

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: She’s becoming an increasingly agile performer, rapping, singing, and everything in between. It Was Good Until It Wasn’t channels all those skills into sterling R&B that feels like a homecoming of sorts.

Title: Nektyr
Review: The record is strikingly patient and meditative, even to the point of being hypnotic.

Title: Take The Crown
Review: Even with that less-consistent Side B in mind, there's still no denying that Take the Crown remains the most wildly entertaining album Robbie Williams has released in years, unabashedly broad in appeal but immaculately well-crafted, at times even rivaling Williams' best work.

Title: Sorry for Party Rocking
Review: It's topped off by truly terrible rapping, which often turns otherwise groan-inspiring instrumentals into jumbled, maddening filler.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: It's marked by the fresh excitement of mapping out new territory rather than the more craven pleasure of wallowing in nostalgia: an object lesson in the value of not giving people what they want.

Title: Slipway Fires
Review: On 'North London Trash,' 'Burberry Blue Eyes,' 'Hostage Of Love' and the histrionic 'Blood For Wild Blood,' Razorlight have matured beyond bubblegum rock and may yet answer Borrell's prayers for immortality. [Dec 2008, p.100]

Title: High Expectations
Review: Mabel’s gorgeous silky vocals soar, the glossy production is stellar, but the exuberance and effervescent attitude that make tunes like ‘Don’t Call Me Up’ so brilliant aren’t found throughout.

Title: Antarctica
Review: Antartica might fall short of the punk-pop immediacy of debut album cuts like “Motorbike” and “Goodbye Texas,” but it’s another fortifying garage punk record, hellbent on trying to shake you out of your shoes. After two punk stunners, this Los Angeles trio has every right to apply “caution hot” stickers to their guitars.

Title: Ancient Romans
Review: It's reliably hypnotic stuff, although the final two seemingly interminable tracks d o expose Stallones' rather rudimentary chops. [Sep 2011, p.96]

Title: Feminist Sweepstakes
Review: Feminist Sweepstakes wants to be a terrifically fun album, yet with no deviation from the ceaseless politics and endless drum machine beats, things go stale.

Title: Gallipoli
Review: Condon’s constant obsession with anachronism occasionally yields lovely, even compelling results. Other times, listening to his music feels like talking to friends from high school you’ve lost touch with. There’s good stuff here, but ultimately, it’s hard to be excited about something that feels so seriously entrenched in the past.

Title: Watch Me Fall
Review: The dozen brief, ridiculously infectious tunes on Watch me Fall come wrapped in arrangements that run from frenetic punk to bouncy Britpop to wistful balladry.

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: Gone are the peak-time weapons that peppered Drone Logic; instead Avery teases us with tension and texture, ebbing and flowing his way to something truly hypnotic.

Title: Ones and Sixes
Review: Low have been indie rock's most economical songwriters for 20 years and running, but their 11th LP takes a bold step toward pop.

Title: LP5
Review: It’s not a game-changer of an album, but the game is certainly changing and Apparat is playing for the right team.

Title: Wed 21
Review: Overall, from the Hail To The Thief-like guitar line and giddy chorus of Ferocisimo to the undeniable Eras, Wed 21 is an album that might not change any lives but is full of surprises nonetheless.

Title: My Love Is a Bulldozer
Review: Venetian Snares is a veritable virtuoso when it comes to drum programming, and as was to be expected, My Love is a Bulldozer is littered with downright slick percussion.

Title: Down Where the Spirit Meets the Bone
Review: This album stands with Williams’ strongest work and represents that rare thing in American popular music and its culture of celebrity.

Title: Down To Believing
Review: If the album has a fault, it's in sequencing, with some of stronger moments low in the pecking order. [May 2015, p.99]

Title: Glow
Review: Glow is all inspired aces and a can't-miss release for funkateers or nu-disco fans.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: It is hard to shake the feeling that these songs may actually be leftovers.

Title: Ibeyi
Review: A hypnotic collision of cultures and influences, of tradition and innovation.

Title: Chuck
Review: The spiky quartet furnish their usual shouty vocals with grinding riffola and twiddly guitar solos, just as the rest of the post-Linkin Park world are realising nu metal wasn't such a good idea.

Title: With Us Until You're Dead
Review: The array of styles that are spliced together--space rock, electronica, trip-hop, orchestral flourishes--fail to add up to a cohesive whole. [Sep 2012, p.97]

Title: Brothers
Review: The old stomp is still here, but Alabama has stoked The Black Keys' dark side. [June 2010, p. 93]

Title: Ratchet
Review: Ratchet is an exciting first look at an artist in development.

Title: Bespoke
Review: In spite of this second half lag, Daedelus continues to exhibit a tremendous capacity for distilling disparate ideas into something personable.

Title: Kintsugi
Review: Its 11, quietly assured alt-rock growers let Ben Gibbard's appealingly detached vocals and quality-controlled lyrics do the heavy lifting. [Apr 2015, p.94]

Title: Growing Pains
Review: Growing Pains is an edgier record than "The Breakthrough," but Blige has definitely lost or just outgrown the brassy urgency of her twenties.

Title: See You In Magic
Review: Add the Night Marchers to Speedo's roll of triumphs and feel free to rank See You in Magic as one of his finest moments. It's really that good.

Title: Vulnerable
Review: Vulnerable contains its share of lemons, but there is a spark, an energy, that hasn't been heard from McCracken's voice in a while.

Title: Women's Rights
Review: It's unlistenable dreck. [No. 126, p.55]

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: Thunder, Lightning, Strike is simply amazing. It is filled with boundless, glorious noise, sewing together flamboyance, quirkiness, sturdy sampling, and a well-traveled feel that can take you anywhere you want to go.

Title: Furfour
Review: Furfour is not an album that will change the world. Tracks come and go leaving only occasional ear worming melodies and are largely bereft of sing along moments. It is, however, quite possibly the most interesting listen you’re likely to get all year as each play will reveal something you didn’t catch before and for that reason alone, it’s one that needs to be heard over and over.

Title: Lift Your Skinny Fists Like Antennas to Heaven
Review: On earlier releases, the traces of anger, sorrow or despair rippling through the found voices seeded roaring rock improvisations that empathetically rooted and resisted the calamities visited upon them. But the improvising on [Skinny Fists] falls within beat parameters too tightly determined to generate any really useful dissonance. [#200, p.66]

Title: IRM
Review: IRM is a swirling mess of sounds and signifiers, tied together in how irresistible it all is.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: Armchair Apocrypha is ultimately another object of strange and unique beauty from this inventive songwriter and performer.

Title: VOIDS
Review: Despite the time off and lineup shake-ups, album No. 6 bears all the hallmarks of the band's 15-year career.

Artist: Avec le Soleil Sortant de sa Bouche
Title: Pas pire pop, I Love You So Much
Review: There are so many ideas, grooves and interesting deviations on Pas Pire Pop that it is impossible not to be drawn in by it. Rather than being overwhelming, it’s a record that stuns with its hypnotic and jubilant rhythms.

Title: Iv
Review: At times, they sound like Black Sabbath might, if Tony Iommi had ever misplaced his genius for memorable riffs. Far better is when they harness their power more constructively. and fragments of tunes emerge from the sludge. [Jun 2017, p.112]

Title: Sam Baker's Album
Review: Baker's style is physical, thick, dense: woozy bass, murky keys and drums that kick hard enough to stir up dust and gleam in the dim light coming in through the basement windows. [Jun 2011, p.60]

Title: A Bigger Bang
Review: Despite its lack of an anthem to replace "Start Me Up," it certainly beats Tattoo You or anything else going back to Exile except Some Girls.

Title: All We Love We Leave Behind
Review: Thrilling stuff. [Dec 2012, p.109]

Title: so sad so sexy
Review: Lykke Li’s songwriting is strong here, but the excess of electronic manipulation sometimes resembles a bedroom experiment.

Title: Parastrophics
Review: Rather than switch directions, or dig deeper into familiar turf, Mouse on Mars sound re-energized here, broadening and brightening their loopy forward vector.

Title: Join the Dots
Review: No matter what confection the band prepares, the melody is the cake and the trippiness the frosting, making Join the Dots one of the most non-head accessible psych rock records since Tame Impala’s breakthrough.

Title: Jarvis
Review: A collection of songs that proves nearly as personal, as socially aware, and as deft at intertwining the two, as was Pulp’s 1998 opus, ‘‘This Is Hardcore.’’

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: Viscerals
Review: A strange, unruly offering. The momentous, squalling dissonance of the curtain-raising Reducer seems to signpost where they’re going, but then they spin off into a twisted, eight-track labyrinth.

Title: Heavy Mood
Review: What feels missing from Heavy Mood is specificity: Where are the characters, and what became of those kids passed out on the lawn? The heart of Heavy Mood is lost its in own sloganeering.

Title: 1 Time Mirage
Review: Not a satisfying record, nor a fully rounded one, but one that suggests so much future exploration. [Oct 2018, p.56]

Title: Side Pony
Review: Side Pony is a solid starting point for anyone who has yet to discover the band.

Title: I Need a New War
Review: Finn is operating at a whole new level of finesse here, and gifts us something truly beautiful.

Title: One Day It Will Please Us to Remember Even This
Review: What's most remarkable is just how like the old Dolls this new record sounds. [Aug 2006, p.92]

Title: The Four Worlds
Review: A wonderfully poignant album that leaves you wanting more, The Four Worlds is proof that restraint can sing louder than excess.

Title: Fever
Review: Although the album is full of brilliance, album opener ‘Marina’ stands headstrong above the others in terms of scope and grandeur, a dirty distorted guitar solo coupled with an African style instrumental and tribal chorusing sees ‘Fever’ go from commendable to a masterpiece.

Title: Forever
Review: There seems to be an innate knack for melody on display here that produces several moments of pop joy.

Title: Song Yet to Be Sung
Review: The fusion is sweet yet corny... and occasionally it's just baffling. [Aug 2001, p.132]

Title: California X
Review: It’s one of the young year’s best all-out rock records, the kind of fantastic full-length that some kid in a garage will one day look back to themselves, maybe when plugging that guitar in for the first time.

Title: Asleep on the Floodplain
Review: Chasny has distilled all of his impulses and obsessions-- slow drones and brisk picking, solemn mumbles and cheery riffs, ponderous lyrics, and ruminative instrumentals-- into 43 muted, marvelous minutes.

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: It roars with confidence and vigour. [Sep 2019, p.106]

Title: Ã·
Review: These songs are more believable--touching, even, if you’re not put off by the milky expressiveness of his voice--than the multiple attempts at rapping.

Title: Phrenology
Review: All the experimenting produces inevitable indulgences (take Amiri Baraka--please!), but even throughout them, each backbeat from drummer ?uestlove hammers an exciting new sound into place.

Title: The Last Laugh
Review: It is to Costas and Burton's credit that they have fashioned such an enchanting album from such an unpromising premise.

Title: Guero
Review: Finds [Beck] consolidating his considerable talent by combining all his disparate influences into one coherent collection of songs. [#15, p.90]

Title: In Time to Voices
Review: Fizzing with ideas, their future looks bright. [May 2012, p.93]

Title: Arrivals
Review: At fifty minutes long, and without a single climax, Arrivals becomes exhausting in its maturity, composure and homogeneity. And while it is a great album to chill, think and lose yourself in, it doesn’t seem to shed much warmth, much emotion.

Title: Satanic Panic in the Attic
Review: It's hard to imagine a better psychedelic-pop record this year than Satanic Panic In The Attic. [#64, p.102]

Title: WIT'S END
Review: Wit's end is so sparse and downbeat that it occasionally verges on the drab. [May 2011, p.91]

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: This is an album restless in its search for the new, the sound of White's reinvention in progress, scorching the Earth in anticipation of what might follow. If it misfires on occasion, it's certainly never dull. And if it never quite reaches its destination, it's still quite a ride. [Apr 2018, p.84]

Title: Radical Connector
Review: A warmer, more leisurely update of 2001's Idiology, Radical Connector foregrounds vocals to more inviting, song-minded ends.

Title: Queen
Review: The fuddy-duddy stance--thou shalt rise from the streets and compose by hand with paper and pen--feels bitterly defensive, even when Minaj lives up to her boasts about her hard-won craft, which on Queen is almost all the time.

Title: I Am Me
Review: No matter how hard Simpson tries, no matter how foreboding the surface, beneath it all she's still light and frivolous. But that doesn't mean, by any stretch, that this is bubblegum music, since that term implies that this music is frothy, fun, and, most important, hooky, and I Am Me is none of those things.

Title: Fading Trails
Review: One of Molina's strongest, most interesting records yet. [#73, p.96]

Title: The Big Freeze
Review: A decade after making her solo debut, Stevenson has found her sweet spot as a singer-songwriter.

Title: Hall Music
Review: Loney, Dear hasn't changed much, and that's what makes this inimitable album such great company.

Title: We're New Here
Review: Scott-Heron's voice sounds just as prime as it did last year, except this time around Smith has adorned the versions with added beats, synths and keyboards for a fuller, richer sound.

Title: Exile In The Outer Ring
Review: Exile In The Outer Ring explores complex subjects without reducing them to empty soundbites and neat conclusions.

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: As with a lot of Morrissey's latter-day solo material, its target market appears to be people who heard the Smiths and thought: if only this stuff was less beautifully nuanced and original, a bit more ungainly and predictable, then we'd really be getting somewhere.

Title: Now Only
Review: While that sense of conviction and commitment remain true in this new release, the six songs presented here are evidence of extending a singular moment into an ongoing musical arc. By persisting with a subject matter that was fleeting, Elverum joins his music to other contexts and considerations that were not pertinent the first time.

Title: To The Sunset
Review: To the Sunset isn't splashy: it's handsome and layered, alluring upon the first impression but revelatory upon revisits.

Title: Kings & Queens
Review: A provocative and inventive second album. [Sep 2009, p.96]

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: Newman has pushed his voice to a human place, upon a mantle, as if finally proud of the boys. Good show. [No.97, p.61]

Title: Makers
Review: Unfortunately, bare-bones arrangements, train songs, and good intentions are no shortcut to supposed authenticity, and still less are they a guarantor of overall quality.

Title: Labyrinthes
Review: What Labyrinthes lacks in instant anthems, it makes up for in rich melodies, grand orchestration, and blooming arrangements, that stop short of bombast. [Jun 2009, p.92]

Title: Immersion
Review: There are still a little too many US FM radio pop-metal vocals, but happily there's also plenty of fierce, melody-laced drum & bass action that will please festivals and dancefloors the world over.

Title: Robyn
Review: Fantastic all of the time.

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: Overall this record feels like a pocket in time and the breeze of nostalgia is welcome in parts but is wholly unsatisfying.

Title: Coracle
Review: Whether as background music for one's day-to-day or as a receiver of one's full attention, it is truly an enjoyable record that is prepared to fill whatever space is asked of it.

Title: Highly Deadly Black Tarantula
Review: Unusually for the average album (which this is decidedly not), every track here is distinctive; a cinematic, mind-scramblingly complex yet cohesive mini-epic.

Title: Edge of the Sun
Review: Much of Edge Of The Sun is as comfortable as an old pair of slippers.

Title: Guero
Review: 'Guero' contains several familiar sounds merely repackaged and freshened up - remnants of the party album mentality of 'Midnite Vultures' sit next to the eclecticism of 'Odelay' and the folk sensibilities of 'Mutations'. What negates this is the conviction with which it's all delivered.

Title: Something About April II
Review: On Something About April II, Younge emerges as someone more interested in creating new classics than new samples.

Title: Mosaics Within Mosaics
Review: Mosaics Within Mosaics, much like life, will float past you in a complicated, blur, but there are so many important, beautiful moments to learn from when you let them, rather than trying to pin them down.

Title: Strangeland
Review: Frontman Tom Chaplin continues to imbue it all with freshness and wonder making Strangeland an inviting place.

Title: Broken Ear Record
Review: It's flighty, frustrating, and at times a little frigid, but intelligent and never lacking in momentum.

Title: Eureka
Review: Eureka finds the guys stuck between pining for the golden days and looking toward the future, resulting in a track list that's sometimes tuneful and often haphazard.

Title: Human Animal
Review: This is a densely structured journey through intense pummelling and dervishes of electronic noise.

Title: Short Movie
Review: Short Movie stretches its cohesive motifs through all thirteen tracks, without sticking to a plot or forced narrative structure. Instead, the themes of self-reflection and search for belonging and identity move you wantonly through the album.

Title: Nude With Boots
Review: The results are surprisingly tame, if not un-rocking.

Title: Beauty Behind the Madness
Review: Beauty Behind the Madness leaves one feeling just as estranged from Abel Tesfaye’s depraved character as previous releases boasting less adhesive tunes.

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: Over its brief 26 minutes the songs crest and fall within a fairly narrow band, and when one feels like it’s about to peak and explode, the group instead will pull back a bit. There are shifts and changes aplenty, and there’s certainly no risk of tedium, but this is a reserved set of songs nonetheless.

Title: Watershed
Review: If anything, the group's latest is another musical masterpiece from a band known for putting out musical masterpieces.

Title: I'm Not Well
Review: Their diverse tunes are rough and smooth in all the right places. [20 Aug 2016, p.68]

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: Say Yes to Love is a potently wrought 22 minutes of febrile noise-punk that contains enough in the way of hook and subtle invention amidst its familiar battery to stand up on its own feet.

Title: The Light of the Sun
Review: Here, she returns to R&B like she never left: With its earnest introspection and earthy   textures - not to mention guest spots by Eve and Anthony Hamilton - The Light of the Sun has a distinctly early-aughties vibe, recalling an era when tempos were slower and voices less Auto-Tuney.

Title: I Started Out With Nothin' and I Still Got Most of It Left
Review: It all proves that Seasick Steve is at his strongest when he’s playing solo.

Title: Riceboy Sleeps
Review: It all combines to make a delicate, sad, little record, but one that ripples with beauty.

Title: Home Again
Review: While Home Again rockets with infinite promise and closes on the moody brilliance of the Dan Auerbach-assisted "Lasan," the interim doesn't always clear that high bar.

Title: What Is Love?
Review: Melodies are frequently forced and characterless, and many songs possess an almost computer-generated quality: either riddled with counterintuitive combinations (Sean Paul singing about the sacrifices of single mothers on mega-hit Rockabye) or resembling other people’s work (the unbearably twee We Were Just Kids is steeped in Ed Sheeran-style nostalgia; the lyrics of Out at Night resemble a poor man’s Nice for What).

Title: Cripple Crow
Review: Banhart brings the peace and love, but not the understanding. [Sep 2005, p.104]

Title: Coaster
Review: Beneath their notorious humour, 11th studio album Coaster is less angry than previous political witch hunts, but Fat Mike and co still love to offend.

Title: Life After Defo
Review: Like some of his peers, Woolhouse can be a little too subtle for his own good, but on Life After Defo, he's crafted a promising debut with a distinctively cozy take on life's bittersweet moments.

Title: Demon Days
Review: Like the Gorillaz's self-titled debut, Demon Days goes the way of most auteur projects, its oversize idea load making for a trip equal parts peak and valley. But also like the debut, Demon Days is better than it has any right to be, featuring singles stronger than anything released under the Blur banner since, you know, that "Woo-hoo" song.

Title: Field Music (Measure)
Review: They have limited their ensemble to traditional rock strictures with the odd brass section and string quartet thrown in at opportune moments, and there’s very little else that you could do to describe it. As they say, it is what it is.

Title: Scorpion
Review: What it all adds up to is an effective commercial album, littered with potential singles, taking few risks and adding little to hip hop culture.

Title: New Again
Review: Such obvious imitation [of U2] isn’t good strategy; it diminishes well-made songs. Taking Back Sunday is better off merging its old blurted troubles with its new attention to detail.

Title: Uyai
Review: [A] melting-pot maelstrom. [May 2017, p.107]

Title: The Canyon
Review: For a band that has evolved from screamo to such thoughtful artistry, The Canyon is a stunning offering.

Title: Smoke
Review: While his contrived sonic and visual aesthetics do much to explain the thinness of Smoke, they do not justify it.

Title: Winter
Review: Clearly inspired by the recent critical upswing, but beholden to no one, this is the creation of a band with an utterly focused sense of identity. The result is gloriously uneasy listening for the masses.

Title: IRISIRI
Review: The impulse to cast off cultural standards dictating how music should sound dominates IRISIRI, which seems most interested in articulating femininity outside the constraints of patriarchal expectations.

Title: Fantasize Your Ghost
Review: Cunningham and Stewart also know how to write a killer pop melody. [Jul 2020, p.33]

Title: Robyn
Review: The hooks come off-kilter and all killer.

Title: Solaris
Review: Indebted to hard-edged Chicago acid-track producers like Adonis and Armando, Parkes constructed brittle, distorted drum-machine breaks (instead of the usual: endlessly tweaked skittery breakbeats) and matched them with claustrophobic analogue effects, most of which hark back at least a decade or so.... In all, Solaris is just as dense and intensive a production as most of Photek's previous work -- for better, but occasionally for worse -- but the range of styles points to a more ambitious future.

Title: The Departure
Review: More than once, in fact, the album surprises with moments of rock gusto. Wilson’s trademark balladry is still in full force, but musically this is a much rawer affair than anything previous album ‘There Are No Saints’ could have foretold.

Title: Tassili
Review: Tassili is a very different album from any Tinariwen have recorded before, and they're proving to be a band of considerable range as they build a catalog of varied and excellent albums.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: It’s surer and more satisfying than either of those previous albums [El Camino and Brothers], and seems less labored.

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: Across 14 varied tracks, Avery's compositions become engulfing, such is the pull of his palpable textures, dense soundscapes and tantalising beats. [May 2018, p.24]

Title: Divers
Review: She takes a bold, explorative leap into the centre of her own mind.

Title: color theory
Review: A darker and more complex record, it displays a newfound maturity in Allison's arrangements and a decidedly higher set of stakes.

Title: Deluxe
Review: Even if its ambitions aren’t that grand, then at least Deluxe is a far better way to spend 30 minutes than many other 2016 releases shackled with the blanket terms “indie” and “post-punk”.

Title: Payola
Review: Ultimately, the band ends up playing off each and every strength, backed by Oberst doing what he does best.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: Top-down pop that sparkles like a lifeguard's teeth. [Jul 2003, p.109]

Title: Herd Runners
Review: Hearing one of these songs by chance would be perfectly inoffensive, but listening to an entire album of them just feels like a chore.

Title: Geocidal
Review: Recorded in sessions at a French convent and a San Francisco studio and featuring analogue electronics alongside strings, brass and woodwind, Geocidal is monolithic.

Title: Strange Peace
Review: Metz, whose fusion of sludgy guitar tone, boiled-down hardcore attitude and smartly sardonic lyricism, if not quite outright throwback, certainly has the quality of a studious tribute. [Oct 2017, p.32]

Title: The Air Conditioned Nightmare
Review: The Air-Conditioned Nightmare is ultimately an experience as disorienting as the sensations and emotions that Woodhead describes, strangely beautiful one minute and aggressively ear-splitting the next.

Title: Rituals
Review: While The 1975 don’t own radio-rock just yet, Rituals feels a little too much like Deaf Havana have lost sight of their own signature, while hammering at the heels of Healy’s.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: Modern Vampires quite often touches brilliance, and does so without audibly straining for 'maturity' or pushing hard to be some po-faced Great American Album.

Title: Universes
Review: While the music he creates on Universes is not quite from another planet, there’s definitely a spirit of exploration that makes it a joyous listen throughout.

Title: Christmas Songs
Review: A stinging reprise of ’93’s ‘American Jesus’ serves as a timely reminder that these perennial bastions of articulate dissent haven’t gone soft on us quite yet.

Title: Sing When You're Winning
Review: This is undoubtedly his best record...

Title: Overgrown
Review: At it best moments, Overgrown proves that the two sides of James Blake—the dancefloor oddball and the crossover songwriter—can exist side by side, but it also demonstrates that, at least right now, the balance between the two is totally off.

Title: Ships
Review: The hooks are nearly endless, each catchier than the last, and each song features a Technicolor array of instruments that create a perfect sonic version of the mildly psychedelic album art that comes with every Danielson release.

Title: Jump Rope Gazers
Review: Jump Rope Gazers is crammed with fizzing indie-pop tunes, and not unlike Camera Obscura’s Tracyanne Campbell or Alvvays’ Molly Rankin, Stokes has an innate talent for crafting beautiful bittersweet effervescent indie guitar pop. The Beths take the chiming indie template and energize it, infusing it with their own personality and sly wit.

Title: Lift Your Skinny Fists Like Antennas to Heaven
Review: This ambient/noise/psychedelic amalgam is limited by tedious repetition and a lack of emotional focus.

Title: American VI: Ain't No Grave
Review: It doesn't tell us anything we didn't already know about Cash in his final months, nor does it sound like an attempt to re-brand an icon or re-shape a legacy.

Title: The Plot Against Common Sense
Review: You won't mistake it for anyone else's, and an artist as singular as Falkous always deserves our attention.

Title: The Raven
Review: Often falters distressingly.

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: For an album unabashed in its intimacy, the bigger moments are all that more rattling. Not everything turns a new corner.

Title: Know-It-All
Review: Know-It-All has sweet spots, but doesn’t match the promise.

Title: Personal Life
Review: Personal Life is hardly a failure; much of it is excellent. But it's also missing that anger-meets-energy urgency that made the Thermals' early albums so undeniable.

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: It's Not Me, It's You is a wonderful record, and, better than that, a pop album brave enough to have a go at defining the times.

Title: Control
Review: This album includes boasts a brilliant storyteller, amazing music, and, most important, beautifully delivered lyrics.

Title: Forever Turned Around
Review: The songs may not be as individually memorable this time around, but it’s perhaps the better full album. And boy, will it keep you warm throughout fall into winter.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: Jay-Z, being Jay-Z, spends most of the time banging on about how rich he is, how brilliant it is being married to Beyoncé, and how irritating it is that some people don't find him quite as wonderful as he does.

Title: Dopamine
Review: The songs are wrought elaborately enough.... Yet this album seems carefully calibrated not to disappoint the conservative fan.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: Suck It and See (English slang for "give it a try"), slows the pace but ultimately feels even more detached.

Title: Prism
Review: Prism shows a more mature side to the singer, an ability to really connect with her experiences whilst still producing absolute pop smashes. It’s a combination that suits her very, very well.

Title: The Great Escape Artist
Review: The Great Escape rarely moves past generic dance-floor thump and sway. [Oct 2011, p.100]

Title: Rabbits on the Run
Review: Carlton's wheels are finally spinning forward, but they don't gain much traction.

Title: III
Review: While there's nothing on here that feels quite as urgent as Nichijyou, last year's track recorded with Jehnny Beth from Savages, it's still a beguiling collection of songs. [Jul 2014, p.103]

Title: Days Are Gone
Review: Those allergic to smooth pop-rock may find Days Are Gone hard going. Paradoxically, given this is an album of clever mash-ups, Haim's one straight-up R&B tune might actually be their best.

Title: Until The Colours Run
Review: [A] frequently sublime follow-up. [Oct 2013, p.105]

Title: Haunted
Review: Lyrically, Haunted progresses from timid to defiant, and ultimately to triumphant. Musically, Poe drifts confidently from trippy beats and spacy sounds to straight ahead rock and mellow, melancholic numbers, though not always in such a way as to strictly parallel the dramatic flow of the album's lyrics. All that means, though, is that this is a dynamic collection of songs and not merely the kind of high-minded rock opera that quickly goes from interesting novelty to pretentious joke. Ignore everything but what comes out of the speakers, and you've got a pop treasure that is as innovative and insightful as it is immediate and unforced.

Title: The Greatest Story Never Told
Review: Whether you've been patiently waiting for five years or just recently got into Saigon's music, The Greatest Story Never Told delivers a stimulating message that is as cautionary as it is entertaining.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Be the Cowboy may not hit the highs Mitski is capable of hitting, but it's still a solid effort from one of today's best artists.

Title: Can't Touch Us Now
Review: This isn’t the work of a group that has nothing left to say but is, instead, evidence of a group unsure of what it should say.

Title: Outside Love
Review: Outside Love, two years later, is another solid effort with a handful of quite good songs--and only a few embarrassing ones.

Title: Flashmob
Review: In truth, the majority of this largely monotonous second outing becomes a one-size-fits-all affair, and you’re left digging around in this hallucinogenic haze for a new high.

Title: Love Is a Four Letter Word
Review: He's re-engaged the formula of sweet, James Taylor-ish vocals, lyrical inoffensiveness... and a laid-back Jack Johnson-like musicality where 5/6 embraces cruise ship reggae. [May 2012, p.101]

Title: Are You in Love?
Review: With hooks as deep as heartbeats, this has the sweep of the desert dunes in it. [Apr 2020, p.93]

Title: The Trials of Van Occupanther
Review: The warmth and the easy familiarity enable The Trials of Van Occupanther to stand on its own.

Title: The Airing of Grievances
Review: Each play of Grievances is like that triumphant, sweaty bar show, right there in your room.

Title: For Evelyn
Review: While her sonic template, modern and spare yet lush, works wonders for “Don’t Go,” it’s otherwise isolated moments — the discordant saxophone blats pulling her toward St. Vincent in the danceable and lopsided “Waste”; the chewy synth bassline of “Crazy [Expletive]”; and the line “When you left me, I was ready for you to leave” in “Walls”--that suggest an excitement the songs can’t quite sustain.

Title: Too Many Voices
Review: Stott again collaborates with opera singer Alison Skidmore on decaying digital laments, warped twilight anthems and claustrophobic club bangers; stuttering songs of mourning for 21st century club culture. [Jul 2016, p.93]

Title: Songs of Experience
Review: It may not even share the same ambition as ‘No Line On The Horizon’ however, it’s an undeniable improvement on their two misfiring predecessors, marking this collection as their most cohesive and heartfelt in almost 15 years.

Title: Puberty 2
Review: Mitski’s career has been one of anonymous toil followed by intense critical promise with Bury Me at Makeout Creek, at last delivered upon with blinding clarity in Puberty 2.

Title: Blackbirds
Review: This is a melancholic album, but a determined, thoughtful one. [Mar 2015, p.80]

Title: Tha Carter IV
Review: He's still getting more women than a taping of Ellen, but on Tha Carter IV – his most emo album to date – it sounds like what he really needs is a hug.

Title: Backwoods Barbie
Review: Surprisingly agreeable return from the High Priestess of country kitsch.

Title: The Spirit Indestructible
Review: It's not all bad, of course-if you prefer your sugar with a side of C-rate bounce, there are things here with which you most certainly could spend your Saturday nights.

Title: All Day
Review: The real enjoyment of any Girl Talk album stems from picking out the first hint of a song, mentally scanning your iTunes and figuring out what it is in time to fully enjoy it before it's gone. Or, you could also just stop thinking and enjoy all of it.

Title: Walking Cloud and Deep Red Sky, Flag Fluttered and the Sun Shined
Review: Lacks the clarity of some of Mono's earlier work.

Title: Brighter Wounds
Review: The arrival of his first child and Trumpism, shadowed by a friend's death, have filled Brighter Wounds with heightened bliss and anxiety. [Mar 2018, p.94]

Title: Valere Aude
Review: It's an interesting diversion for Romans, and might just be the most admirable part of Valere Aude.

Title: Beautiful Africa
Review: Being from her country means contending with the legacies of some of West Africa’s most internationally successful artists; at this point, I’d say Traoré fits comfortably alongside her forbears.

Title: Dying in Stereo
Review: It's like taking hip-hop of the early '80s and jettisoning it into the now: update the metaphors, the references, and the technology but not the beats, the flows, or the vocal stylings.

Title: We Are The Night
Review: We Are The Night is the most listless album they've made—and maybe not coincidentally, it's also one of the lightest.

Title: SVIIB
Review: There is not one weak track on here. [Jan/Feb 2016, p.58]

Title: Wham! Bang! Pow! Let's Rock Out!
Review: You get the feeling even the band think the joke's wearing a bit thin. [Jan 2019, p.106]

Title: My World, My Way
Review: But for all these guests and all of Silkk's versatility, My World, My Way still suffers from the same formulaic production -- all bleating synths and skittering drum programs -- that makes all No Limit productions seem indistinguishable.

Title: Rhine Gold
Review: Rhine Gold is an album that demands scrutiny, and it's definitely worth taking the time to engage in.

Title: Silent Movies
Review: Whatever ensemble he employs, and in whatever style he plays, unpredictability is a major component of his M.O. Silent Movies is no exception, and his formidable technique services music that continually thwarts expectation.

Title: Rockferry
Review: Duffy's not a belter, but she boasts a cool power that is immensely aided by the cleverness of Rockferry's instrumental settings, which employ mostly acoustic instruments for a warmer sound that, in combination with Duffy's vocal prowess, stays sweet, soulful and satisfying.

Title: Acid Tongue
Review: Only a talent as major as Lewis could half bring it off.

Title: Keep On Moving
Review: It’s a one-trick pony album sure, but what a trick.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: In the face of hysterical expectation, the Strokes have resisted the temptation to hit the brakes, grow up and screw around with a sound that doesn't need fixing -- yet.

Title: Excuse My French
Review: When these mantras connect, they’re indelible. When they don’t, it’s like being smacked in the face repeatedly with an iced-out chain.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: Laura Marling continues to impress on her third outing, though the transatlantic influences are becoming more apparent.

Title: Ocean Eyes
Review: It’s all very pretty sounding on paper, but in reality lazily produced and poorly written.

Title: Royalty
Review: Where “Sleep” excels as a quality addition to his catalog’s stellar collection of panty-dropping and baby-making songs (see: “Take You Down,” “No BS”), others fall and lean towards prosaic.

Title: Solaris
Review: For Solaris, Photek sticks to his signature style of clinical percussion etching a variety of danceable rhythms. Of the 11 tracks, only "Terminus," the disc?s opener, is truly jungle. The rest of the album features a technophile's gift bag of futuristic dance cuts... Most all of it's gorgeous stuff, and high praise is in order.

Title: Underneath The Pine
Review: There isn't the clarity that characterised his lovelorn debut. It's a minor criticism, though, and one that doesn't tarnish an album as equally rich in invention as his first offering.

Title: Minus Tide
Review: True to the album name, Minus Tide is one body of work that lacks the aggression that initially made Lemonade so exciting.

Title: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier
Review: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier is a feel good record, genuine in all the ways that a beautiful composition should be.

Title: Welcome to Bobby's Motel
Review: Even when they slow down, there's a lot of excitement in Pottery's music. Though they frequently threaten to steamroll over anyone within earshot of Welcome to Bobby's Motel, the band have so much fun that their listeners probably won't mind.
