Review: The industrial and atmospheric elements of the album all convey a sense of searching and often of rushing away from one thing and toward another. Even the blurred cover image of Hatchie suggests a feeling of constantly being in motion. It is through this searching and continual movement that Hatchie etches her own lines to define her persona through her music, constantly propelling herself and her ideas in new directions and trusting that we’ll keep up.

Title: Infinite Worlds
Review: The Cameroonian New York dweller threads a singular narrative obsessed with the singer's sense of place, or lack thereof.

Title: Weirdon
Review: Weirdon is a melodic and enjoyable rock album.

Title: Joanne
Review: Joanne is certainly not the all-conquering opus it was intended to be and will prove divisive, but it remains a daring and exciting record, delivered from one of modern pop’s most unique and singular voices.

Title: Chaos and the Calm
Review: Chaos and the Calm churns out pleasant but forgettable, festival-ready anthems.

Title: Poison Season
Review: There’s enough allure in Poison Season’s oddities to make it highly listenable.

Title: Losing Feeling
Review: No filler here. That's the glory of an EP, but also of No Age. [Fall 2009, p.73]

Title: Unpatterns
Review: Unpatterns is actually more engaging and accessible than Simian Mobile Disco's past work, perhaps because no gimmicks or distractions cloud the band's analog alchemy. [Jun 2012, p.84]

Title: Mirror Mirror
Review: Sons and Daughters add to their canon of murder ballads, then finish the album with the sound of a rain storm on a beach enveloping Bethel's ghostly vocal, a sound that seems to linger long after it fades from earshot.

Title: Cloud Nothings
Review: The result is another fantastic step forward, though not without some growing pains. In the transition from basement to studio, one component has yet to come into full focus: Baldi's voice.

Title: Moondagger
Review: Far from the naval-gazing, self-conscious banality one might expect from such a young artist, Moondagger is filled with moments of philosophical prowess and intelligence.

Title: Supernature
Review: So the form of vaguely electroclash pop delivered with frighteningly robotic efficiency has been mastered, but the content itself is the problem.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: Large parts of Blak and Blu are spent crooning falsetto soul numbers or cranking out chunky rockers in the vein of the Stones and Bob Seger.

Title: Don't Tread on Me
Review: There are no missteps on the album, and the group's faithful will have plenty to rock with. But Don't Tread on Me still feels like one to grow on instead of one to remember.

Title: Dirty Vegas
Review: As much as the vocals, however, the fault for Dirty Vegas lies with the unambitious production; Dirty Vegas make a crossover group like Underworld sound positively edgy in comparison.

Title: Lost Domain
Review: Despite the dark moments, Lost Domain keeps the flame. [Dec 2014, p.119]

Title: The Big To-Do
Review: Musically, the DBTs manage a decent range--from big, squalling rockers to teary, lap-steel balladry--albeit without throwing any great surprises. Same old story, to some extent, but one worth hearing again.

Title: Visions
Review: Visions is a remarkable outing for Boucher in that it manages to showcase her knack for spinning bits and pieces from all points on the musical spectrum into crafty, easily digestible pop.

Title: SweetSexySavage
Review: SweetSexySavage, because of its consistency, can be run through easily, especially in a car with the windows down and the bass up. Feminism, rebellion, and plain old badassery pour from Parrish’s lips, and her melodic sensibilities are sharp enough keep you engrossed.

Title: Psychic
Review: Psychic simply doesn’t leave a lasting memory when one considers the work as a whole.

Title: Fossils and Other Phantoms
Review: Their spooky, sexy, dark folk is kept bare and bolshy, like Laura Marling with sex and humour.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: Has Jay-Z made another classic? Only time will truly tell, but my gut says MCHG will ultimately fall just short of classic status. Where does it rank among his now 15 albums? I’ve got it somewhere in the top third.

Artist: Conor Oberst and the Mystic Valley Band
Title: Outer South
Review: It feels a little too soon for this overstuffed, 16-song collection where Oberst's cutting social commentary is dropped into a maelstrom of charging guitars and barroom backing vocals.

Title: Ensemble Pearl
Review: It’s as if the quartet decided to pay tribute to one of O’Malley’s chief inspirations: Earth. That sounds dull, but there’s something hypnotic about these songs.

Title: Falling Faster Than You Can Run
Review: Ggood voice is nothing without good songs, and Rateliff comes with plenty of ammunition on Falling Faster Than You Can Run.

Title: So Runs the World Away
Review: There are ten other very fine songs here, this album shows Ritter developing continually, and there's potential for greatness, in time.

Title: Get What You Give
Review: The Ghost Inside still smack like a wrecking ball. [16 Jun 2012, p.53]

Title: Division Street
Review: Division Street is Simon’s sweet step into the twilight sun.

Title: FIDLAR
Review: FIDLAR is a punk-spirited rock & roll record whose original source material is alive and a millimeter below its vinyl surface.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: Over length of 12 tracks, the soul/G-funk stuff becomes a little one-note, while the Disney-fied material lacks the charm that makes Prass such an engaging, idiosyncratic performer.

Title: Don't Weigh Down the Light
Review: Things can get twee--but this feels like a tiny church in that forest, sacred and touching. [Jul 2015, p.92]

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Miss Anthropocene thrills when it reveals a refined, linear evolution of Grimes’ long-standing interest in rave nostalgia and alluring pop music from around the world.

Title: Wuthering Drum
Review: Toher's music has become more powerful as he's made it more delicate, and Wuthering Drum is a compelling debut that casts a lingering spell.

Title: Disconnect From Desire
Review: It's airy, synth-heavy and loud, and it moves like a glacier.

Title: Mermaid Avenue Vol. II
Review: The emotion flows as true as the music.

Title: VII: Sturm Und Drang
Review: The public’s appreciation for Sturm und Drang is genuine because the music is intelligent and authentic. Lamb of God is everything a metal band should be in 2015 and so, so much more.

Title: I Am
Review: At the end of the day, I Am’s overall passable production and flashes of potency and strength keep it afloat for a time.

Title: Seeking Thrills
Review: Even when it’s clumsy, Seeking Thrills never feels manufactured. It’s a passion project, a result of trial and error, the singular product of someone learning to write for her own voice.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: All the evidence anyone needs that the 50-something Weller is in the midst of a supersonic prime. [Mar 2012, p. 98]

Title: Playing with Fire
Review: This disc is just as disposable and dumb as you'd expect.

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: Key to the success of 'Broken Boy Soldiers' is the relatively restrained musicianship.

Title: Alice
Review: The album's songs do not attack you with bombast but rather smother you in a slow burn, like gathering frost suffocating a mournful shut-in.

Title: Fall Be Kind
Review: The band’s trademark solemnity and repetitive downtempo styles prevail in the final three tracks, making you feel like you’re treading in a swimming pool of honey--in a good way.

Title: Feral
Review: When RVG get it right, the results are deeply affecting. ... The weaker moments — “Little Sharky & The White Pointer,” “Prima Donna” and “The Baby & The Bottle” — could easily have been excised for a sharper listen. It’s not that anything here is cringe-inducing, it’s just that because the band’s sound is so straightforward, the songs need a little spark to make them stand out.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: There are moments where the weirdly wonderful pagan pixie princess pokes through. [Jul 2011, p.90]

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Deerhunter has come into its own, and the halcyon result is not to be missed.

Title: Reflection
Review: On the debut from Fifth Harmony (which formed during the second season of The X Factor, in 2012), high self-esteem feels like a party.

Title: Violet Cries
Review: The group have been around for well over a year without arousing much of a stir, and the monumentally tedious poesie-rock of Violet Cries offers few hints that this should change.

Title: Sleep Mountain
Review: What they're actually releasing is passionate, urgent, full of music that swoops with the geometric elegance of flocking birds, but shows scant evidence of original thinking.

Title: Wiretap Scars
Review: They've managed to broaden the nervous-tic angst-rock of their previous band into something more readily adaptable without reducing it to mealy-mouthed pop regurge.

Title: Outside Closer
Review: Surging volume is still far outweighed by wispy melancholy, but the contrast is rewarding. [Mar 2005, p.104]

Title: Medicine County
Review: Thrilling third from the ex-Headcoatee's duo. [May 2010, p. 93]

Title: Jet Plane and Oxbow
Review: With Jet Plane and Oxbow, Shearwater achieve not only their grandest statement to date, but their most grounded as well.

Title: Time To Die
Review: It seems silly to declare Time To Die too well put together, but it's not always the shapest knife that gets the most use. [Oct 2009, p.110]

Title: Logic Will Break Your Heart
Review: A similar osmosis of Bunneymen and Chameleons' dramarama as Interpol. [Mar 2004, p.106]

Title: Twin Cinema
Review: By turns darker and more challenging than 2003's dazzling Electric Version. [Oct 2005, p.96]

Title: Safe in the Hands of Love
Review: Safe In The Hands Of Love is a fascinating synthesis of rock, plunderphonics, bass music and noise from an artist that remains stubbornly undefinable.

Title: One Life Stand
Review: One Life Stand is the classic pop album they've always threatened to make. [Mar 2010, p.96]

Title: BLUE
Review: While Blue’s electropop soundscapes are hardly a great move forwards from their first two projects, there are genuinely majestic emotional moments to savour here.

Title: Do Things
Review: Sticky and overblown, this could be an album that gets old after a few listens. Lucky for us, it just doesn't. [Jun 2012, p.146]

Title: Ganging Up on the Sun
Review: Both expansive and dreamy. [23 Jun 2006, p.69]

Title: Gettin' In Over My Head
Review: Too many lyrics are more serviceable than insightful or inventive. [20 Jun 2004]

Title: Critical Equation
Review: Dr. Dog is a band that can write a hell of a great song. But on Critical Equation, they're mostly treading water.

Title: A Season in Hull
Review: This lo-fi, devil-may-care air translates well to record, with A Season in Hull capturing and accentuating the band’s characteristic camaraderie and casual, Jonathan Richman-esque charm.... Admittedly, the stripped-down setup has drawbacks too, leaving the material with nowhere to hide and exposing an uncharacteristic patchiness.

Title: Karaoke Angel
Review: Karaoke Angel is a beautiful surprise from Sarlé, whose career as a solo artist has only just begun.

Title: Electra Heart
Review: Electra Heart is too professional to be truly terrible, but it's never clever enough to be more than merely toytown.

Title: Similes
Review: But it’s not float-away, background material; these songs poke and prod while clasping you close, the embrace warm but never completely comfortable.

Title: Time to Die
Review: It's not nice, but Electric Wizard prove here that sometimes to achieve perfection, all you need is hate. [20 Sep 2014, p.53]

Title: Lianne La Havas
Review: Lianne La Havas is boldly authentic and infused with passion.

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: Like a late-night screening of Blue Velvet, it may be hard to get through, but impossible to ignore. [Dec 2011, p.121]

Title: Jay Stay Paid
Review: While it is neither as monumental as "Donuts" nor as exemplary as the "Dillanthology" discs, Jay Stay Paid is close to a must for any casual Dilla admirer.

Title: American Dream
Review: Whereas LCD’s previous album, This Is Happening, felt coherent as the project displayed a love of disco, American Dream feels happy sampling from many of the band’s established recording styles.

Title: Let's Go Extinct
Review: The results are sparkling, upbeat and infectious. [Apr 2014, p.73]

Title: Voices in a Rented Room
Review: This is not an uplifting listen. [Apr 2014, p.91]

Title: Bird Songs of a Killjoy
Review: Although it runs a bit too long and some songs blend together, Bird Songs of a Killjoy is a heartwarming and enchanting listen. It’s as far from a killjoy as you can get.

Title: Hospitality
Review: In the end Hospitality is a solid pop album through and through.

Title: Allways
Review: Allways showcase a band reconfigured as a kind of hippy Meters. It's an unlikely transformation, but an appealing one. [Dec 2018, p.93]

Title: In Roses
Review: Everything is organic, unforced and so subtly constructed that much of the time you don't so much hear the songs as feel them. Beautiful. [Feb 2014, p.91]

Title: An End Has a Start
Review: Editors have acquired a sense of urgency and emotion they lacked on "The Back Room." [Aug 2007, p.98]

Title: Know-It-All
Review: Too often here Cara is let down by bland arrangements and underbaked melodies, from the Swift-by-numbers of opener Seventeen to the banal balladry of Stars.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: It's safe to say her new album is another fascinating, furiously beautiful work that maintains her position as England's reigning folk princess.

Title: Yours, Dreamily
Review: Yours, Dreamily is tight without purpose, bordered where it should be wild, and only occasionally feels alive at all.

Title: Dancing Backward in High Heels
Review: While the New York Dolls struggled to balance past and present on their previous reunion albums, Dancing Backward in High Heels is a product of the here and now as defined by two guys following their muse in their own way, which is just what they should be doing at this stage of the game.

Title: Point
Review: Given his prior eclecticism, it's stunning to hear the unified, boldly conceptual approach Cornelius takes on his new Point.

Title: Something for the Rest of Us
Review: Something for the Rest of Us is every bit as easy on the ear as each of their albums has been since 98's big-league breakthrough, Dizzy Up the Girl.

Title: Rattle That Lock
Review: Rattle That Lock is a small, intimate album that maintains Gilmour’s impeccably tasteful quality threshold throughout.

Title: Flies the Fields
Review: Dense soundscapes that seemingly start in progress and stretch invisibly, yet infinitely, in all directions. [Apr 2005, p.118]

Title: Heartthrob
Review: It's bright and shiny and perky.... But it also risks being faceless--it's Tegan and Sara's least personable, most superficial record. [No. 95, p.60]

Title: Who You Are
Review: It's well-meaning, well-crafted and confused. Sometimes versatility can be a vice.

Title: Here We Stand
Review: Back for round two, sophomore album Here We Stand doesn't quite bring anything new to the table, but does carry on in the same fun, brash rock tradition of the debut.

Title: The Black Magic Show
Review: The result is a sound of un-epic mopeyness, more surface than interior and arguably more truthful because of it. [Apr 2006, p.84]

Title: Dying to Say This to You
Review: Their newfound nods to pop music... overshadow the expected balls-out rockers. [Apr 2006, p.220]

Title: Dark Days + CanapÃ©s
Review: [A] sensitively-written and fearlessly-recorded album.

Title: Ribbons
Review: A seamless fusion that casts a low-key but binding spell.

Title: On Top
Review: Rye Coalition send up a prayer for that emo addict who's done with Rainer Maria but keeps AC/DC in the closet. [Apr 2002, p.122]

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: When it comes down to it, it ain't gonna change your world any.

Title: Dependent and Happy
Review: This CD version has some outstanding moments, and at times is a masterful lesson in dream-like production.

Title: Ontario Gothic
Review: Ontario Gothic is an amazingly precise, contextually aware work that’s very easy to listen to as just beautiful music, but it’s also an album that asks the listener to try for more.

Title: Range Anxiety
Review: A minimum of chords are played with minimum effort. Generic lyrics abound.

Title: rEVOLVEr
Review: It gives credit to his cheerily assured worldview that Pain's roboto soul sounds like inspiration.

Title: Title
Review: She just needs to read more self-help than she spouts, and show us that she has more depth than bass.

Title: Dancer Equired!
Review: There's a glint of genius in these songs that's best realized if you turn this album up as loud is it can go and think about relationships and stuff. Even if noise/lo-fi/shitgaze is showing its wrinkles, its heart still beats strong here.

Title: Pick Me Up Off The Floor
Review: This blend of warmth and invention is what's so appealing about Pick Me Up Off the Floor: the shape may seem familiar, but the construction of the songs and the inventiveness of the performance keeps it fresh and surprising even after the first listen.

Title: All Nerve
Review: Not everything on All Nerve works. But then, perfection was never the aim for Breeders; instead, they’ve provided something vital, visceral, completely modern. In never once looking back they’ve re-captured the incessant energy that drove ‘Last Splash’, and given us something to take its place.

Title: Grand
Review: Even though Grand is a bit toned down from Matt and Kim's first albums, it maintains the spunk, high energy and carefree attitude that caught people's attention in the first place.

Title: ii
Review: Liima still recognizably sounds like Efterklang, but it seems like there's less pressure for them to construct a monumental statement here, and the group seem to enjoy their freedom.

Title: Fantastic Planet
Review: Easily the most joyful and extroverted of Lipstate's albums at this point, it also feels the most vibrant and engaging, gracefully exposing a world of endless blissful layers for the audience to stargaze upon.

Title: Melodrama
Review: She is intensely self-aware and, accordingly, is able to take all the inelegancies of youth--the stumbles out of nightclub doors, the clothes strewn across the bedroom floor, how apocalyptic that first heartbreak feels--and turn them into something exquisite.

Title: Out of Season
Review: Out Of Season's usefulness as ambience almost trumps its self-importance and paucity of standout material. [Dec 2003, p.136]

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: The sweetness of Strawberry Jam is savvily balanced by the sour, or at least the edgy. [Oct 2007, p.98]

Title: Mise En Abyme
Review: Mise En Abyme is a lot to unravel, but that disentanglement is its own reward. Cousin has plundered his experiences to create a yearning LP that nevertheless feels welcoming (and, more importantly, honest) every step of the way.

Title: Roosevelt
Review: There are few surprises in Roosevelt's brand of dance music, but that seems decidedly the point; the synapses it triggers feel like the most welcomingly comfortable sort of sparks, firing on familiar-but-welcome cylinders.

Title: Love Is Dead
Review: Unfortunately, it translates into kohl-eyed pantomime, rather than cathartic music, with lyrics so hopelessly trite they sound like a feel-good tract for preschoolers.

Title: Cursing the Sea
Review: Caoimhe Derwin and Jessie Ward’s guitars have perfected that Jesus And Mary Chain kettle-whistle sound, lending a haunted air to otherwise energetic stomps like ‘Heartbeats’ and ‘Talking.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: Aside from the aforementioned pair of tracks [Control and the title track] that hit dark pop highs akin to Garbage's best, this is just another solid disc from solid musicians, no more, no less.

Title: Lovers
Review: [A] splendid debut for Blue Note. ... Backed by a brilliant ensemble of strings, wind and percussion, Cline's guitar creeps stealthily through arrangements elegant and enigmatic, lush and low. [Sep 2016, p.71]

Title: Gumption
Review: As an album, Gumption meanders quite a bit, occasionally to the point of feeling detached, but its glimmers of gold make for an ultimately compelling listen.

Title: Expo 86
Review: The band come up with hooks aplenty, delivering anti-pop gold on the guaranteed-to-disappoint-no-one Expo 86. [Aug 2010, p.156]

Title: Embrace
Review: Embrace plies its trade with a neat mix of musical proficiency and stylistic flexibility. [Jun 2009, p.93]

Title: Down to Earth
Review: Jem's Dido-like vocals are consistently a soothing treat, but on the whole there's a sultriness and spark missing from the material.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: It's a less alien, less disturbed and thoroughly lighter record. [Nov 2005, p.104]

Title: Hungry Bird
Review: What strikes me is that past Clem Snide albums had their stronger moments, but also their weaker ones, while Hungry Bird, for all its time in development, is more solid throughout, delivering its 10 pop songs with a consistency that shows the band continuing to develop its sound.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: We can only parse this album as that of a brilliant group still trying desperately to reconcile its awkward youth into an identity, but only managing to hide behind a few ten-year old audio masks.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: With Oberst, there is little filter; the gems and the rubbish all emerge from the same place. Oberst's talent and his unevenness are all of a kind.

Title: Flight of the Conchords
Review: Somehow, even after you know all the punchlines, the tunes are solid enough to still bear pressing ‘repeat’.

Title: The Black Market
Review: The band manages not to compromise their sound, but on The Black Market, the formula is growing stale.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Fishing for Fishies
Review: Closer ‘Cyboogie’, the cheesy, sci-fi-inspired lead single from the LP, is by far the most tepid of the set, as if marking the roll of the end-credits and a collective sigh of relief. With that being said, do not doubt that King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard still know how to kick ass.

Artist: Conor Oberst and the Mystic Valley Band
Title: Outer South
Review: In many ways, Outer South feels almost like a coming of age for Oberst. His voice is way stronger than it has been in the past.

Title: Neon Golden
Review: The Notwist are, for me, the band New Order never had a good enough singer, or a creative enough programmer, to be.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: With Mind Bokeh Bibio recognizes that our happiest, hands-in-the-air, hedonistic moments are shadowed with memory. A bit of hiss, crackle or distortion can evoke the sadness under the celebration.

Title: Working in Tennessee
Review: Working In Tennessee is often sleepy to the point of being narcoleptic. Still, even when he strains to hit notes, which he does often, Haggard sounds like he's enjoying himself.

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: Borrowing liberally and transparently from Bright Eyes, the Cure and mid-1960s chamber pop, the band sublimates familiar expressions of indie gloom with string flourishes and twink­ling piano lines, giving Olenius both a shoulder to cry on and, in soaring songs like 'Tonight I Have to Leave It,' a source of joy.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: When I Never Learn aims for pop, it's the hazy Shangri-Las variety; the melodies are Li's lushest to date, but the smoke never clears around them.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: The achievement here is that each song feels like its own distinct world.

Title: The Child of Lov
Review: He’s created an incredibly ambitious, soulful avant-garde debut.

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: Corny and bombastic, their latest is also ambitious, impeccably built, and apt to induce fits of uncontrolled fist pumping. [14 Jul 2006, p.81]

Title: Voyager
Review: While it might seem like there's a little too much going on here, the top-notch production, artistic collaboration, and devotion to the space-age vibe results in a satisfying and unexpected gem.

Title: Take The Crown
Review: It's safe, something of a retreat from past endeavours to a sound more suited to commercial returns in the present.

Title: Freedom Highway
Review: A timely, arresting album.

Title: All Mirrors
Review: Monumental and intimate in equal measure, All Mirrors' boldness is exceeded only by its profound emotional resonance. Angel Olsen's talents were always apparent. Here, they seem limitless.

Title: WARM
Review: This record comes on like the voice of a friend, confessional and familiar-- full of small, important reassurances.

Title: Tidelands
Review: They tend to stay in their most comfortable wheelhouse -- bluesy roots rock -- but, as before, their incredible vocal harmonies carry the day.

Title: Nothing's Lost
Review: Nothing's Lost is a well-meaning record that just got its priorities mixed up. These tech'd-up tearjerkers can out bench press anyone in terms of sonic fodder, but the album is whiny, transparent, and a colossal hodgepodge.

Title: Costa Blanca
Review: Exotic, hip and exuding an effortless charm, Costa Blanca is a sophisticated treat from start to finish. [Jan 2014, p.120]

Title: The Cosmic Game
Review: Hampered by lazy beats and an overabundance of world-music window dressing. [25 Feb 2005, p.102]

Title: Embryonic
Review: For all its flaws and failings, for all that you may never feel like listening to it again, it's hard not to be perversely glad Embryonic exists.

Title: Alight of Night
Review: Quite simply, Alight Of Night is one of the most breathtaking records these ears have been partial to in a long while, and even if Crystal Stilts never make another record, their legacy is assured.

Title: Warpaint
Review: On their self-titled follow-up, the all-female quartet's gift for ringing, skeletal guitar lines, slyly defiant lyrics and keening melodies remains intact.

Title: Secrets Are Sinister
Review: Secrets has its finger on the pulse of mainstream radio, judging from its oppressive sonics. But stuck between a tired, nebulously elucidated artistic direction and their own nebulously elucidated commercial aspirations, they just sound a whole lot like the major-label also-rans that they actually are.

Title: The L-Shaped Man
Review: Ceremony have a strong handle on this style [Ian Curtis'], and after nearly a decade together, these new clothes fit them quite well.

Title: Smoke + Mirrors
Review: Lyrics and delivery suggest Imagine Dragons adhere to old-fashioned rock band idealism, but nothing is allowed to get in the way of a sparkling hook.

Title: Crimson
Review: Overall, the band seem to be running long on ambition and short on ideas. [Jul 2005, p.172]

Title: The Amulet
Review: Longtime listeners will know the drill, but newbies looking for some frame of reference might want to imagine Sigur Rós, Mew, and Sunny Day Real Estate in an art school lunchroom brawl.

Title: Shout It Out
Review: Uptempo jams like ''Waiting for This'' shimmer with top-shelf songcraft; Motown vet Bob Babbitt even sits in on bass. But sometimes you wish these whiz kids would act their age.

Title: Traditional Synthesizer Music
Review: The timbres of the modular synth, in my opinion, are dull, but that doesn’t mean that Venetian Snares hasn’t created interesting music from his machines.

Title: Love at the Bottom of the Sea
Review: Their liberal word-cram of mixed meter and sea-shanty pentameter is on full display on instant jaunty novelties.

Title: V
Review: V is the record that has finally given The Horrors a set identity. Perfecting every element they did so well on their four previous records, V is a pure and unadulterated celebration of The Horrors.

Title: Mind Hive
Review: Simms certainly knows how to deliver Wire energy - compact, disciplined, no waste, no spray, as on Primed And Ready. There are also lovely moments of Wire pop here. [Mar 2020, p.87]

Title: Thank You For Today
Review: Thank You for Today marks the stirring opening of a new chapter in this band’s already storied history.

Title: 1634 Lexington Avenue
Review: 1634 Lexington Avenue is the album Smith through his wandering and woodshedding has been promising for decades now. It is retro to be sure, but free of artifice or false appropriation. He is personally invested in these songs and it shows. Essential.

Title: Teenage Dream
Review: Perry delivers the gurl-gone-wild stuff with requisite sass, but she actually sounds more engaged on "Not Like the Movies" and "One That Got Away"--quieter cuts that recall her singer-songwriter days at L.A.'s Hotel Cafe.

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: Dabke lives or dies by its ability to make people move, and although Souleyman is no-frills, and borderline gruff compared to other dabke performers, there’s something in his stentorian singing that’s irresistible.

Title: Some Nights
Review: Lyrically vapid, auto-tuned and stadium-aspiring choruses like these, with their hands-in-the-air, mugging-with-your-mates quality, are so lacking in imagination that they make "feel-good" feel really, really bad.

Title: Paracosm
Review: Paracosm is, at the very least, beautifully rendered wallpaper, and it’s hard to blame Greene for living in this fantasy for as long as he possibly can.

Title: Out in the Storm
Review: Out in the Storm is perennially bright, with its melodies maintaining a serrated edge that ensures the sound remains robust, immersive and hard-hitting.

Title: Heavy Love
Review: Heavy Love is a supremely self-confident record. [Mar 2015, p.85]

Title: Petrol
Review: Petrol, a looser, messier album, does a better job of communicating new ideas, and its emotional depth feels less gestural and more genuine.

Title: In the Pink of Condition
Review: Whether the songs zip like ‘Ringfinger’ or sprawl like ‘Rainy Summer’, they all feel very much of one piece, giving them a cumulative strength beyond their individual merits.

Title: Film School
Review: The guitar work is clean and atmospheric, the vocals light and poppy and the rhythms playful to reflective, but we've been here before.

Title: Phantom Brickworks
Review: There’s a widescreen vibe to these tracks; with their patient, sometimes nearly imperceptible cycles of accretion and subsidence, they feel as much like landscapes as they do music. But they’re vistas that have been internalized and made personal, and that process--along with the calm majesty of the songs--is the source of Phantom Brickworks emotional sweep.

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: Wilco (The Album) adds yet another chapter to the story, and if this band's relevance is to continue going forward, then let the resilent closer 'Everlasting Everything ' score our impending sunrise. [Summer 2009, p.90]

Title: In Ear Park
Review: Songs begin lethargically and the vocals and instruments grope at each other, struggling to agree on how to establish the rhythm. Once they coalesce, each blooms, but the tracks refuse to linger in the thrall of the climax.

Title: Stranger Today
Review: Stanger Today is the sound of a band doing what they want, knowing how to do it and, most importantly, having a blast doing it.

Title: Before We Forgot How to Dream
Review: A remarkable piece of work for someone so young. [Apr-May 2015, p.86]

Title: Want Two
Review: More, and even better, of the same--one of the dead-cert Albums Of The Year. [Album of the Month, Apr 2005, p.96]

Title: The King is Dead
Review: The King is Dead is a few layers of vocal harmony away from being a Fleet Foxes record, which is fine, but the Decemberists are at their best when they sound like themselves.

Title: Soviet Kitsch
Review: Traces of Joni Mitchell, PJ Harvey, Björk and Cat Power are all proudly on display in the unpredictable arrangements and off-kilter emotions.

Title: Bitter Tea
Review: Bitter Tea is nearly abstract to a fault, but that doesn't always take away from its finest moments, which are in abundance. [#13, p.85]

Title: Evil Heat
Review: Gillespie's lyrics will never win any Nobels, but the musical excitement generated here is impossible to deny.

Title: Ukulele Songs
Review: The songs, a handful of covers and about a dozen originals, aren't terrible, but the ukulele gets really old, really quick.

Title: Napa Asylum
Review: As their odd tics, off notes, and bevy of stops and starts build up, the logic of their approach becomes clearer and more addictive. In that sense Napa Asylum, with 22 songs stretched over 45 minutes, is probably the best Sic Alps full-length so far.

Title: Blessed
Review: Blessed, like Williams' best efforts, finds the blessings within the blues.

Title: 99Â¢
Review: The album is presented as a consumerist critique, intentionally blurring the line between artist and product, but the quality of the songs varies too widely to pull off an actual concept album.

Title: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground
Review: The Ritalin generation may have found its Bob Dylan. [#9, p.143]

Title: The Wave
Review: It will obviously appeal to most long-term Keane fans (even without Rice-Oxley’s trademark tinkly piano chords) but anyone who’s gone through a bit of a tough time in their lives will find this to be comforting succour.

Title: The Weight Of The Sun
Review: Shape of Light harbours hues of Nick Drake, but occasionally Modern Studies' mellow beauty drifts into Enya-land. [Jun 2020, p.90]

Title: Silent Alarm
Review: Many of the tracks (including "Positive Tension" and "This Modern Love") are so choppy and discontinuous as to give you the same nauseous feeling you get when you hear a Mars Volta record.

Title: Hang
Review: Utterly theatrical, it represents without presenting; evokes without mentioning; transports without moving. It's as fake as the time we're living in, and as fascinating as our own decadence.

Title: Star Treatment
Review: Whilst Star Treatment might funnel a lot of influences into its carefully woven songs, it is still a fiercely idiosyncratic work.

Title: Goon
Review: Jesso's winsome melodies and gorgeous chord changes never fail to hit the spot. [Apr 2015, p.103]

Title: Everything Touching
Review: Everything Touching is far more direct, less convoluted, often shamelessly anthemic.

Title: The Week That Was
Review: Bewis has brought the album to the brink in just eight tracks. [Fall 2008, p.85]

Title: I'm Not Dead
Review: It's when Pink steps outside of expectations that she turns exciting.

Title: Tenderheart
Review: It’s hard to follow any Ry Cooder assisted act, but Outlaw coalesces around his own, more intimate sound. We can always use an honest, unpretentious Sunday morning album to enhance the usually easygoing mood, and for those moments Sam Outlaw’s unassumingly enjoyable Tenderheart hits the mark.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Halcyon Digest isn't always a cohesive listen, but the record gels where it counts--it's all great.

Title: The Atlantic Ocean
Review: If you’re reading this, stick with it. It has some real rewards in the back end--my only hope is that the songs were recorded in chronological order, to suggest that this is the direction Swift will take future albums.

Title: Cold Spring Fault Less Youth
Review: Clocking in at a breezy 37 minutes, Mount Kimbie's second album feels a bit slight by the time it's finished, though not because it's short on great ideas or compelling tunes.

Title: Rising Down
Review: Playing against typecast, Rising Down is not an appropriate soundtrack for your next fraternity party or bong load. It's more of a call to arms. Radio Raheem might well be proud.

Title: Yonder Is The Clock
Review: A record so concerned with repeating the strengths of an album past that it forgets to chart its own path.

Title: Watching Dead Empires in Decay
Review: Even more than on past outings, Kirby seems drawn to a sense of disconnect, refusing to let the elements of each track interact with one another. Yet Dead Empires is also rich with experiments and surprises. [Nov 2013, p.60]

Title: Skeleton
Review: Skeleton romps along at a joyful gait peppered with breathless harmonies and squalls of noise and subverts some familiar tools along the way. [Nov 2008, p.87]

Title: Getting Away with Murder
Review: This is grade-A grade-B pop metal. [Oct 2004, p.120]

Title: Tomorrow's Hits
Review: Tomorrow's Hits is an easy album to admire--this is The Men stretching out and aiming for new targets--but a difficult one to fall in love with.

Title: From the Corner to the Block
Review: Corner is sort of like ["Ruckus'"] older cousin, as it finds Galactic enlisting a monster guest list of MCs to rock over its densest grooves to date. You'd think the results would vary more than they do.

Title: Revival
Review: Revival is so uninspired and lost that picking it apart is a hopeless affair.

Title: Evolve Or Be Extinct
Review: For all its innovativity and dogged determinism, the album's latter moments just can't compete with the top heavy appeal of its opening tracks.

Title: To Syria, With Love
Review: The rave presets of old will appease older fans while the more intricate synth work will satisfy more recent converts. Still, it’s the deeper tunes here that point to an intriguing future.

Title: Medulla
Review: All in all, though, Medúlla is far too busy. Even when you're experimenting, the less-is-more rule still applies.

Title: Esker
Review: A neat sampler of MacKay's unshowy virtuosity, at once brisk and mellow. [Jun 2017, p.33]

Title: Supernova
Review: Supernova’s experiments aren’t all triumphs by any means, but, given how painless it would have been to stay the course, LaMontagne is to be commended for taking on a challenge at all.

Title: Tha Carter II
Review: The album is listenable, exciting and succeeds in reigniting interest in hip hop and rappers that dedicate their life to become great MC's, not just hustlers.

Title: The Alternative to Love
Review: The Alternative to Love is tipped to be his big breakthrough album, and it's easy to see why. It's full of bright '70s power-pop choruses, infectious guitar riffs and the kind of laid-back breeziness that suggests most of these songs came to him in his sleep.

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: Propulsive, addictive, ego-driven bursts.

Title: False Priest
Review: Of Montreal will always appeal to anyone looking for a world to get lost in. Is it too much to ask for him to visit ours once in a while?

Title: Far Enough
Review: The record often leans on familiar garage-rock tropes, so much so that it often dips into homogeneity and predictability. But the band also leaves plenty of room for McKechnie’s booming vocals, by far the band’s most impactful instrument.

Title: Tour de France Soundtracks
Review: Has all the hallmarks of classic Kraftwerk.

Title: Havilah
Review: Havilah broadens the Drones' sonic palette and continues to carve out a sound that is uniquely theirs, and in that sense it's an accomplishment, but wrestling with the record's dark subject matter makes it a difficult listen.

Title: Dangerous Dreams
Review: A case of too little, too late, nothing on Moving Units' full-length debut Dangerous Dreams does anything to disprove the feeling that the dance-punk scene is at best overcrowded and at worst approaching rigor mortis any day now.

Title: The Spark
Review: Ultimately, The Spark presents a baffling listening experience. Almost every song on the album poses as an unremarkable backdrop onto which the band fiddles with elements of everything from grime to orchestral arrangements with virtually no successful results.

Title: Everything Is
Review: Unsatisfying.
Ultimately, this is the best album The Artist Formerly Known As Squiggle could possibly have hoped to make in 2006.

Title: Send
Review: A taut, brutal collection which is as strong as anything they've released in their previous incarnations. [June 2003, p.65]

Title: Western Stars
Review: A lushly orchestrated set of throwback, country-tinged folk pop that, despite some resemblance to previous works like Nebraska and The Ghost of Tom Joad, sounds like little else in his catalog. Frankly, its sheen is off-putting at first. But once you settle in, the set reveals some of Springsteen’s most beguiling work ever.

Title: Remedy
Review: The duo's self-proclaimed "remedy" is nowhere near as revolutionary as the hype would insinuate, but it does offer its distinct pleasures

Title: Little Honey
Review: And though those positive vibes yield some correspondingly fun tunes, the disc feels a bit underwritten at times.

Title: O Soundtrack My Heart
Review: Woodly prog rock for weird beards.

Title: Push the Button
Review: The album suffers from serious momentum problems. You get something that hammers in a good and interesting way and then a few minutes later it's like the tap of a blue tit's beak on a milk bottle top.

Title: When I Pretend to Fall
Review: Brainy, brooding, classically "indie" guitar music. [#16, p.121]

Title: Strange Desire
Review: Strange Desire is like a John Hughes film without the nuance and humor, all ‘80s schmaltz and all catharsis, or at least attempted catharsis.

Title: Safe in the Hands of Love
Review: On his Warp Records debut, Safe In The Hands Of Love, Yves Tumor joins the ranks of Arca and SOPHIE at the millennial generation's pop vanguard, a group whose fluid approach to music and imagery is eradicating the gap between underground and mainstream.

Title: Born Like This
Review: Fortunately DOOM is unable to completely shake off his own best and worst habits, and so Born Like This contains its fair share of the rapper's classic screwball set pieces.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: Wise Up Ghost is a fearless, invigorating gut-punch of a record, one that never settles and surprises from start to finish.

Title: Permission to Land
Review: It's that subtle streak of accomplished mischief that separates The Darkness from the multitude of marginal bar bands that still play this stuff for real.

Title: IV
Review: At their best, Black Mountain approach '70s rock with a 21st century mindset, and that's the sort of sound and feel that make IV so effective.

Title: Absolute Dissent
Review: The tracks are long, grinding and relentlessly angry about the state of the world.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: Anger has always been at the root of Low's modus operandi; the difference, ultimately, is that where once it lurked behind marble pillars, it now stomps and snorts like a pig on a griddle. [29 Jan 2005, p.59]

Title: Have One on Me
Review: Have One On Me is so enrapturing, so imaginative and so delicate, that it feels safe to say that in five or ten years time, you’ll go back to it and discover brand new things--whether they be the meaning of a song you’d never fathomed before or a simple amuse-bouche of a beautifully constructed oboe phrase.

Title: More Issues Than Vogue
Review: Even the weaker moments are elevated by a raw vocal that growls with bubbling emotion. Love’s trials and tribulations never sounded so exquisite.

Title: Vicissitude
Review: In its own subtle way the album delivers on the promise and intentions of Turning the Mind.

Title: The Illusion of Progress
Review: Ballads have always been his forte, a convenient vehicle for his quivering sensitivity and accidental melodicism, yet it's still startling how slow The Illusion of Progress unfolds, as Staind rarely muster the energy to move beyond midtempo even when they deign to crank up their amps for anthems of mild alienation or vague inspiration.

Title: Welcome oblivion
Review: Welcome Oblivion confirms that the music world needs a band like How To Destroy Angels, too. [2 Mar 2013, p.50]

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: Until Gibbard can harness this newfound happiness with the kind of lyrical flair his fans are used to, Death Cab remain in danger of being, well, just another indie band.

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: There's a familiar elemental tone to the Dirty Three's latest album – except this time the oceanic influence is replaced by snow and sky and rain.

Title: Stony Hill
Review: There are diversions into pop and hardcore dancehall but overall it's a strongly enticing release. [Dec 2017, p.91]

Title: Mala
Review: Almost everything here is pretty good when you sit down and concentrate on it, but there little that jumps up and demands your attention.

Title: The Family Jewels
Review: The closer she gets to herniating herself trying to convince you that you're listening to a crazy avant-garde ­artist making pop music by accident, the more convinced you become that she's a canny operator writing pop songs and then dressing them up in a multicoloured afro wig and glasses with eyeballs on springs.

Title: Boca Negra
Review: This isn’t just sonic research; it’s a real album, paced and considered. It feels good.

Title: Norman Fucking Rockwell!
Review: As a mood piece, Norman Fucking Rockwell does an admirable job preserving Del Rey’s mystique while moving her sound forward.

Title: Kaleidoscope Dream
Review: Miguel has impeccable songwriting chops and a deceptively supple voice, not to mention total command of both.

Title: Calico Review
Review: Calico Review may leave the listener feeling a little parched, too, as it doesn't paint as bright and stirring a picture as either of its predecessors.

Title: No Way Down
Review: New album No Way Down is one of the year's best so far; its title apt for vertiginous synths and strings that litter the mix like vapour trails on pure blue sky.

Title: Happy New Year
Review: Happy New Year is unpretentiously unique, challenging and eclectic.

Title: Seven Swans
Review: Stevens' most personal and focused album.

Title: Gravez
Review: It may be easy to enjoy at the time, but this third full-length leaves no lasting impression.

Title: Healing Is a Miracle
Review: Healing is a Miracle is easily Barwick's most intimate – and intentioned – foray in years.

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: Serving as the final part of a trilogy that includes the much feted records Rook and , the album is an epic feat of baroque pop craftsmanship, something akin to an update of Scott IV  or Dusty in Memphis for the new millennium.

Title: Kindly Bent to Free Us
Review: This isn't a slight dip in quality, it's an avalanche.

Title: Saturn
Review: Saturn isn't afraid to show her playful side. [Dec 2018, p.105]

Title: New Seasons
Review: The first studio release by the Sadies in three years represents a big sonic advance.

Title: The Magnificent
Review: It's just hard to find much of Jeff himself in these amiable, head-nod-friendly, immaculately crafted but ever so slightly sterile tracks.

Title: E = MCÂ²
Review: It's still very much a Mariah album--and a very slick and stylish one--with all the sweetness and swagger that entails.

Review: With one foot in the classic NYC underground scenes that paved the way, ‘Underneath’ is pure bass-led, disco ball-flecked Studio 54, while the dance-punk footprints of ESG are all over ‘Cities’’ irrepressible hook and ‘Compromised’ tips a hat to godmother Debbie Harry. ‘Gentle Grip’ sounds timeless.

Title: Pacific Daydream
Review: Pacific Daydream is both exuberant and plaintive; it’s full of songs about past joys and present loneliness, recalling friends and lovers who are no longer part of the singer’s life. ... But there’s a whole pop apparatus around him--a tambourine shaking, a firm beat, happy backup voices--to insist that Weezer’s kind of music is far from extinct.

Title: Going Out in Style
Review: Boston's finest prove that far from having nothing left to say, they're just getting started. [Apr 2011, p.114]

Title: Babel
Review: It's very much a 'if it ain't broke' album and, for now, that's okay.

Title: In The Maybe World
Review: The overall effect is too solipsistic and immature to take you close to the title's imaginative world. [Aug 2006, p.96]

Title: Sunshine Rock
Review: Bob Mould is not pulling up stylistic roots on Sunshine Rock, but it’s still breezier than his average, thanks in part to the use of an 18-piece string section on much of the album. [Mar 2019, p.62]

Title: The Big Roar
Review: The welsh trio have taken their time to reach this point, but with The Big Roar they have taken their opportunity with great style, producing what I think is a mature, clever and exceptionally listenable record from start to finish--and that's a mighty thing.

Title: Unstoppable
Review: Unfortunately the album is filled with blank and unspecific emotions that without Mr. LeVox’s pyrotechnics, are distractingly dull.

Title: Some Rap Songs
Review: Well, it can be [dour]. But it’s also ecstatic. Make no mistake: This is an album by one of the best rappers alive, elbowing slant rhymes and assonance into his disses (“Please do abort, I could feel when you’re forcin’ it / Still in a bore riddim”) and exhaling those singularly oblong sentences of his (“Galaxy’s the distance between us by Christmas,” he describes one foundering relationship).

Title: Beat The Devil's Tattoo
Review: Every single one of the lyrics is either a really, really lame Spacemen Zero drug innuendo (the – hey! – 10-minute epic ‘’Half-State’), about ‘twisted’ love (the – hey! – ‘stripped down’ ‘Sweet Feeling’s Gone’) or mentions “highways”.

Title: Konnichiwa
Review: Reclaiming his own identity, Skepta is now properly equipped to amplify the sound just above its dank, underground incubator.

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: Thankfully, Danielson's music is interesting enough to look past some of these lyrical drawbacks.

Title: Burned Mind
Review: For such a tortured swarm of piercing feedback-drenched feedback and electronically-manipulated electronic manipulations, this record feels surprisingly coherent, almost to the point that it’s comforting.

Title: Ruff Draft
Review: While still lush in its own grimy way, Ruff Draft represents the harsher, more experimental end of Dilla’s palette.

Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: It is a funereal album whose spark and anger is obscured like the smoldering foundations of a burnt out city.

Title: Myth Takes
Review: "Myth Takes" ... should see the festive art-rock collective bop its way out of cult status, as each of the 10 cuts on this album adventurously cascade through genres without ever losing a groove. [10 Mar 2007]

Title: All The Roadrunning
Review: The tension between their vocal personas--she's ever hopeful, he's relentlessly glum--is the highlight. [21 Apr 2006, p.73]

Title: Surrender
Review: Hutchcraft might be the real problem here: he’s good at what he does, but he only does one thing: big and sad and serious.

Title: Good Luck and Do Your Best
Review: Bound to give you that warm, fuzzy feeling.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: Simply another shimmering LP from a truly original band.

Title: Mirage Rock
Review: Even when Band of Horses go for broke, the South Carolina-bred Bridwell exudes the laidback gravity of a down-to earth Southerner.

Title: Pretty in Black
Review: Put it this way: the Raveonettes have got one serious retro fetish. [#15, p.95]

Title: Get Guilty
Review: Newman’s second solo outing, Get Guilty, is a baroque-pop gem, on which he displays remarkable tonal control via crafty arrangement.

Title: OIL OF EVERY PEARL'S UN-INSIDES
Review: In SOPHIE's most intimate work yet, she subverts pop motifs into the catchiest form of self-assertion, reminding us all of why pop music still matters.

Title: Cumbia Siglo XXI
Review: Cumbia Siglo XXI is easily Meridian Brothers' most satisfying outing to date. While no less insane than its predecessors, its musicality is as abundant as it is adventuresome. Further, it pays tribute to cumbia even as it exaggerates and satirizes it with almost familial warmth and affection.

Title: Quit the Curse
Review: Quit the Curse is consistently hooky and elegant, and though it slumps with a few lax, jangly rhythms, it’s nothing less than a pleasant stay to her sighing thoughts and apprehensions.

Title: Passionoia
Review: A greater combination of accessibility and subversion would be nearly impossible to imagine.

Title: Edgeland
Review: This is sweetly strange and often emotional music--an album of disquieting tone poems and outlandish lullabies.

Title: Welcome Home
Review: If the album's greatest sin was simply sonic banality, it would be a lot more palatable. Far worse is the cynical nature of the album's roosty overtures.

Title: Mirrors the Sky
Review: Throughout Mirrors the Sky, Lyla Foy's warm and comforting voice remains the focus.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Nonagon Infinity
Review: It makes for something of a experimental jam session where its members are trying to perfect a unified sound alongside different lyrical approaches, which strike a fine balance between campy sci-fi imagery and silly, doom-laden metal tropes. And yet, once it’s fused all together it comes across as one big slab of raucous, careening psychedelia. King Gizzard are still grounded to their garage roots.

Title: Winning Days
Review: About as personality-free as rock music gets. [Apr 2004, p.115]

Title: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier
Review: It's tuneful enough but, really, the case for the dismantling of 2010's nostalgic apparatus starts here. Less hypnagogic pop, more over-the-hillwave.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: His flows are lazy, uninspired, and flat out boring.

Title: 200 Years
Review: The most impressive aspect of 200 Years, especially considering it as the debut of a new collaboration, is its overall aura of cool confidence.

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: It's the tension between Homme's conflicting impulses that pressurizes Lullabies to Paralyze's highest points and accounts for its lows.

Title: Hippo Lite
Review: At one point, Presley claims, he and Le Bon used the sound of a frog’s ribbit for an instrument. It’s here where Hippo Lite verges towards sounding like music that was only ever made for its makers, rather than an outside audience. In a quest to discover simple living free of consequence, Le Bon and Presley can, at times, get lost in their own little bubble.

Title: David Comes to Life
Review: The eighteen tracks and eighty minutes presented here don't hold a candle to 2008′s The Chemistry of Common Life but I truly admire the tenacity of this outfit to push on toward such a lofty venture.

Title: Graduation
Review: Grating bouts of narcissism aside, Graduation contains killer pieces of production: 'Stronger' uses Daft Punk's 'Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger' to practically revive Eurodisco, while 'Champion' snarkily snatches its hook from Steely Dan's 'Kid Charlemagne.'

Title: Forcefield
Review: After repeated listens the songs reveal themselves to be some of the catchiest, most joyful few minutes of jagged guitar-driven pop mastery you've heard all year.

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: It Was Good Until It Wasn’t is the latest work demonstrating the 25-year-old’s profound emotional intelligence. Its 15 tracks waft in as though carried by a summer breeze; Kehlani’s crystalline vocals shine through arrangements of sedate beats, jazz piano motifs, and luxurious twangs of Spanish guitar.

Title: This Is Us
Review: Most of the songs are just complete misfires.

Title: Quakers
Review: Ladies and gentlemen, let me introduce to you, coming all the way from left field, the best album of 2012 so far.

Title: Anthem of the Peaceful Army
Review: Production-wise it's the compressed, tidy sound du jour that flattens out dynamics; it would be interesting to hear them recorded on some funky old analogue gear, to add a bit more grit. [Dec 2018, p.92]

Title: Bat Out of Hell III: The Monster Is Loose
Review: Meat's voice is there, the cover art rules, but something vital is missing. [Nov 2006, p.102]

Title: Temple Beautiful
Review: On one hand, it's raw and stripped down, but on the other it's expertly crafted.

Title: Fear Fun
Review: [Fear Fun is] packed with sardonic, self-effacing songs that recall the finest traditions of harmony-soaked West Coast folk-and-country influenced rock'n'roll. [Jun 2012, p. 68]

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: While this is drastically experimental by their standards, there is nothing here you haven't heard done infinitely better many times before.

Title: The Tree of Forgiveness
Review: The Tree of Forgiveness is autumnal John Prine, but it's also a potent reminder that his remarkable skills as a songwriter and his rough-hewn excellence as a singer haven't failed him yet.

Title: Yeezus
Review: It’s not quite godlike, but Yeezus certainly feels like it was created by a higher power.

Title: Real Gone
Review: Real Gone... is Waits’ grittiest work to date and is an excellent introduction, for those unacquainted, to his hard-boiled thirty-year run.

Title: Engravings
Review: With references to house, dub, and instrumental rock all stitched together into a looping, building tapestry that manages to be both visually and emotionally evocative, this is certainly an album that will keep your interest long into the next fad.

Title: Sunlight on the Moon
Review: Sunlight on the Moon is not the best Elf Power record, which would be a tough task for a band with so much great output, but it’s another sign of the band’s lasting sound and continued growth.

Title: Don't Look Away
Review: Don’t Look Away is a supremely confident album from a songwriter who has found his place and knows his music. It completes a trilogy which is essential listening for anyone who wants to hear why the psychedelic lineage of the past 50 years is fresh and alive.

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: For all its shortcomings, Watch the Throne is still damn good.

Title: NehruvianDOOM
Review: NehruvianDOOM isn’t the first attempt to recreate Golden Age Hip Hop in the 21st century, but it’s an exceptionally creative take on the now-classic sound that succeeds in offering an enjoyable--and at times quirky--listen.

Title: Unapologetic
Review: Even the club bangers ("Phresh Out the Runway" and "Numb," featuring Eminem) are heavy with bass that rumbles more in your chest instead of rattling your feet. Ballads work well for Rihanna, and this album has two of her finest.

Title: Rules
Review: Rules finds The Whitest Boy Alive turning noticeably paler, peddling a shade of Ralph Lauren yacht-rock that would make Hall & Oates blush. [May 2009, p.105]

Title: All Delighted People
Review: It's a staggering return from his alleged creative crisis, a terrific addition to his discography, and a wonderful addition to an already fantastic 2010.

Title: Glasvegas
Review: Glasvegas is determinedly provincial, insisting there is grandeur in everyday lives. But what sounds rousing in Britain can sound sodden and overwrought to American ears.

Title: EVOL
Review: Despite the bloodlettting and reckless spending, Future just sounds bored. And occasionally lazy. [Apr 2016, p.50]

Title: The Milk of Human Kindness
Review: The range of styles is impressive, which trumps the lack of logical or elegant transitioning. Snaith may be showing off, but at least he’s backing it up with strong and memorable arrangements.

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Ultimately an excellent record. Where the message is muddied, thankfully the music is often, simply put, beautiful.

Title: The Triad
Review: One hates to say it of a pleasant record, but much of it seems like background music for shiny-looking bars, where people pose around before the action starts.

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: [It has] abundant warmth, melodiousness and spontaneity--and fewer full-tilt stylistic shifts than earlier records. [Jan 2012, p.127]

Title: Summerlong
Review: In an increasingly fraught world, it’s an unashamedly sunny sound. It makes for a gorgeous record in which to lose yourself for 40 minutes.

Title: Medicine County
Review: Medicine County is a scattered disc, for sure, but its simple joys are ripe for the plucking.

Title: Physicalist
Review: On Physicalist, Forma, mind-bogglingly skilled with their synthesizers, push themselves further and further into new territory--almost literally--as they pare back, slow down, spread out, dig into the (American) soil beneath their feet.

Title: Putrifiers II
Review: The music here never has too clear of an antecedent, and the directions the album takes are generally unexpected-unsurprising for a band with such fondness for the unusual.

Title: (a)spera
Review: It’s a Giving Tree scenario, spun out with strings and a subdued power-ballad build, and it sets the stage for the worldly decay catalogued throughout (a)spera with the help of several gifted collaborators.

Title: The Physical World
Review: The Physical World confirms everything we'd hoped for: DFA still know how to produce unstoppable energy, they still know how to push a bass guitar to its full capacity and they still know how to inject tonnes of fun into not just their product, but the wider spectrum of music itself--and there's not much more you can ask for, especially after so long.

Title: New Energy
Review: Though far from perfect, New Energy is one of Hebden's most intimate and personal albums, with all the idiosyncrasies that come with that.

Title: Untitled
Review: Ho & bling free rap of the highest thought provoking order.
