Review: He smartly revisits songs from Bruce Springsteen ('The Hitter') and, for those who miss the raw, hungry Jones, he delivers a roaring rendition of Tommy James & the Shondell's 'I'm Alive.'

Title: Mungodelics
Review: Mungodelics remains an uneven effort in design alone, promptly adding another layer of mystery to this hard-to-pin-down duo.

Title: Hairball
Review: Hairball is their most open, breezy album to date.

Title: Luv Is Rage 2
Review: As for today's singing rappers, Vert fits in comfortably next to the likes of Fetty Wap and French Montana, and I have little qualms with calling him a better writer than the latter. The production is a little bit more of a mixed bag.

Title: Shape Shift With Me
Review: This is a winner, another great release from a band that, really, has no problem delivering great albums. Shape Shift with Me occupies a perfect middle ground between their last two discs, and that's a very special, and unique, place to be.

Title: Don't Stop
Review: Some of these songs do, of course, belong on the radio: They’re saturated with production effects catered to a generation that calls its designer drug “ecstasy,” all wrapped around indulgent hooks, sentimental lyrics, and a sweet voice airbrushed into flawlessness. But Annie flaunts too much.

Title: Six
Review: The 13 songs on Six are rich and exquisitely constructed, perfectly-pitched baroque riffs and orchestration are juxtaposed with searingly compelling lyrical imagery.

Title: Departure
Review: This album can't be written off purely as a repetitive mess--this is the sound they were going for, after all, and when they rely less heavily on repetition, drones, and electronics, they find some decent material.

Title: Us
Review: She is as captivating as ever, but the rougher edges have been removed slightly giving us a more polished, and immediate, album.

Title: The Republic
Review: Tthe 15 pieces within hum with oddly soothing tones and rhythms, like New Age music swimming through mystical Roger Dean-esque topographic oceans.

Title: No Blues
Review: The finest songs here are as solid as any other rock music you’ll find in 2013.

Title: The Bird and the Bee
Review: Space-age pop that cunningly combines bossa nova languidity with Beach Boys-style lushness.

Title: Sweet Sour
Review: Band of Skulls' clean tone and unabashed take on rock positively scorches at every point on the album.

Title: Love and War
Review: West Virginia singer, songwriter and guitarist Brad Paisley has proven himself a wizard at striking a canny balance among earnestness, whimsy, social awareness and party-hearty celebration. With Love and War he’s conjured another 16 tracks that skillfully traverse those lines.

Title: Soft Fall
Review: The album's first half explores the same musical territories as Nocturne--the chiming euphony of a hundred things happening at once, the guileless melodic patterns that wander up the scale and back--but it does so in lifted fog. [No. 92, p.59]

Title: Muchacho
Review: A raucous centrepiece it is not. A soundtrack for a nightcap alone though? Absolutely.

Title: London With The Lights On
Review: There is nothing not to love about it.

Title: Put Your Needle Down
Review: An updated Dylan song, Dirty Lie, and the gospel-bound River Jordan add variety to an enjoyable if uneven set that's a big step forward.

Title: Nephew in the Wild
Review: Musically, Nephew in the Wild feels like a logical progression from Ashworth's past work; lyrically, however, it isn't always as clear of a step forward.

Title: Miracle Temple
Review: For an album whose most apparent traits are simplicity and broadness, Miracle Temple's best moments are pretty idiosyncratic.

Title: Magic Potion
Review: Anyone possessing their previous output will find little in the way of reinvention. [Oct 2006, p.96]

Title: Under the Iron Sea
Review: If this is what happens when Keane attempt to delve into darkness, the mind reels at what these guys would sound like when they’re in a good mood. [#14]

Title: Renegades
Review: From a pounding rendition of "Pistol Grip Pump" by West Coast hip-hoppers Volume 10, to a snarling, grunged-up assault on Bob Dylan's "Maggie's Farm", singer Zack de la Rocha and company deliver atomic thrills with revolutionary fervor. Still, anyone hungry for new insights into this uniquely righteous band, or looking for evidence of risk-taking, may feel shortchanged.

Title: Need to Feel Your Love
Review: With Need To Feel Your Love, the band broadens its horizons without losing what made ‘em so promising in the first place. That’s always a tricky line to walk, and Sheer Mag does it with gritty grace.

Title: Recommended Record
Review: Recommended Record may flit between styles but it’s a cohesive and polished third effort from the band.

Title: Want Two
Review: Where Want One emphasized his ability to soar, Want Two drowns him in costumes; his range actually sounds restricted when you hear the same droopy-lidded croon against such varying backdrops.

Title: The Hungry Saw
Review: What will draw fans old and new to this record, however, is the melancholia of Tindersticks frontman Stuart Staples' vocals, which become especially poignant on the forlorn 'Other Side Of The World.'

Title: Evil Spirits
Review: Although the band haven't really made a notable album since the close of the '70s, this ten-track, 42-minute LP stands as some of their most focused and stylish work to date.

Title: Mature Themes
Review: Simply put, Themes is Pink at his most vivid.

Title: The Man Upstairs
Review: While there is nothing particular off about this quiet, solid collection--consisting of little more than Hitchcock’s voice over quite acoustic guitars and the occasional piano and cello--it’s still a pretty muted, low-energy affair that is not immediately memorable.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being
Review: I Am Not a Human Being is kind of a crummy album, rife with laziness and repetition.

Title: Year of Meteors
Review: Showcases her luminous vocals, rich lyrics and subtle arrangements. [Sep 2005, p.120]

Title: Devouring Radiant Light
Review: Tracks such as the blistering “Temple of the Sun” take no prisoners, taking little time before exploding into the kind of full-frontal assault we’ve come to expect from the heavier side of metal. Elsewhere “The Luminous Sky” takes a more frenetic approach though feels no less uncompromising, while “The Sacred Soil” closes out a record that not only shows exactly where Skeletonwitch are in 2018, but also where contemporary metal is at as well.

Title: Body Talk
Review: So, while Robyn shows that her body can certainly do the talking, when it comes to walking the walk she's prone to stumbling in directions she should avoid.

Title: The Scene Between
Review: It all sounds amazing on the first couple of listens, but the wheat (songs like the title track and “Did You Know?”) separates quickly from the chaff. Regardless, The Scene Between opens up a whole new lane for an artist that would have been easy to write off.

Title: Sycamore Meadows
Review: It’s an ideal time to simultaneously start over and glance back, which Walker does on Sycamore Meadows, trading the glammy style of his prior solo work for competent, traditional radio rock....Then again, you’ll need a high threshold for boorishness to enjoy his frequent autobiographical nostalgia for substance abuse, pubescent defloration and venereal disease.

Title: Future Nostalgia
Review: Future Nostalgia is an artist in total control. It’s built on such an addictive carefree spirit that it’s hard not to let loose and go with it. The greatest pop star of this generation? That’s for you to decide. But Future Nostalgia makes a very convincing argument that Dua Lipa just might be.

Title: The Seldom Seen Kid
Review: The bass-fuzz stomp and chain-gang holler of 'Grounds for Divorce' couldn't be more immediate, Guy Garvey refusing to let emotional intelligence blackball a decnt tune. [Apr 2008, p.106]

Title: Invention
Review: Invention has very few peers, in my opinion. Though Schlammpeitzinger's Collected Simple Songs of My Temporary Past and Andrew Coleman's Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt come close, I'm firmly resigned that I'll not hear a more effortlessly charming album this year.

Title: Consummation
Review: An enchanting record of twists and turns.

Title: Dust
Review: Halo's records have always posed tricky questions, and Dust features her most complex and engrossing yet.

Title: Old Money
Review: Once again it's a showcase for some dextrous prog-jazz metal guitar work that on occasion veers dangerously close to tuneless skronking. [Mar 2009, p.104]

Title: Smother
Review: As Wild Beasts records tend to go, Smother is par for the course in terms of its opulent eccentricities and its magnificently polished arrangements. This time around, though, the Beasts have been tamed. Frankly, that's a disappointment.

Title: Panic of Girls
Review: This album is a wellspring of the bandmates' combined creativity and an ode to free-spirited artistic expression. Bravo.

Title: Orchestrion
Review: It's very melodic (though not very melodically surprising), and technically mind-boggling. But harnessing all this awesome machine power to make just another Pat Metheny Group album without the group seems a bit of a missed ­opportunity.

Title: Horehound
Review: Her voice simply doesn't have the heft to project the necessary menace. Despite these occasional missteps, though, Horehound establishes the Dead Weather as a fully-realized band with a sufficiently distinctive point of view that deserves serious consideration as more than just a one-off side project.

Title: Wasting Light
Review: This is a largely unimpressive album. [9 Apr 2011, p.50]

Title: The Highway
Review: The Highway contains some of Williams' most potent songwriting.

Title: Highway Queen
Review: It is the second half of the album that actually shows why country persists against all odds: at its best, it is unafraid of telling stories that dig deep into ordinary lives.

Title: Reality Killed the Video Star
Review: Millennial ‘It’ Boy gets the horn on eighth album.

Title: Darkel
Review: The whiff of soft-rock schmaltz is occasionally close to overpowering. [16 Sep 2006, p.36]

Title: Introduction
Review: Some of the catchiest songs he's ever written.

Title: Friend Opportunity
Review: Longtime fans might lament the loss of a second guitar and the balls-out thrashing that sometimes came with it, but on certain levels it may be a blessing in disguise. A leaner Deerhoof allows other facets of the band to shine, most notably Greg Saunier's drum work.

Title: Hotel Valentine
Review: To say that the album sounds like Hatori and Honda picked up right where they left off downplays its specialness, but there's no denying it sounds like Cibo Matto had never stopped playing together.

Title: The Monitor
Review: With five songs clocking in at more than seven minutes, often thanks to detours down E Street, it's a big-idea album that feels small and personable, even as it's kicking you in the shin.

Title: Wild Nights
Review: The results are serviceable. [Jul 2015, p.111]

Title: This Time
Review: This Time isn't Sigel's strongest endorsement as an emcee--that would be The B. Coming--but it is a testament to his impeccable ability to select production.

Title: Memento Mori
Review: Momento Mori is a good album, with the awesome 'Set Apart This Dream' and 'Again' shining with their anthemic choruses and deft use of pop melody. The tragedy is that it could have been great. [Dec 2009, p.108]

Title: White Lilies Island
Review: A surprisingly agreeable, if lightweight, disc.

Title: Mirror Traffic
Review: Everything you could want from a wizard, a true non-star. [Sept. 2011, p. 100]

Title: Evil Genius
Review: There's a little less bravado for its own sake; instead, we are offered reflections on the differences in the man's life since his last release from jail. He's married, off of drugs and, as the album's cover shows, ripped now.

Title: Vestiges & Claws
Review: ‘Leaf Off/The Cave’ and ‘What Will’ are the strongest of the 10 new strands to this web, yet it is hard to assign priorities to what is a consistently good album.

Title: Civilians
Review: So many of his songs sound damnably similar, blanded-out by his pinched rasp and seeming disinterest in melody.

Title: A River Ain't Too Much To Love
Review: A River Ain't Too Much to Love is a subdued, plaintive collection of songs that accompany silence; they encourage reflection without guile and unveil themselves without a hint of studied artifice.

Title: Your Wilderness Revisited
Review: With Your Wilderness Revisited, William Doyle hopes to bring you along on a magic carpet ride through suburban England, where you will find new ways of experiencing pathways, front gardens and parked cars as though they were entirely new concepts.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: Turn Blue is pure searing sexiness, hotter than a Nashville afternoon. Their best yet.

Title: Michael
Review: Michael may very well contain the best material Bundick has released throughout his already stellar career.

Title: The Feast of the Broken Heart
Review: Although Feast comes packed with Europeans and expats (Butler currently calls Vienna home), the rhythms strike with Yankee assertiveness, the vocals now direct yet far more diverse.

Title: Berkeley to Bakersfield
Review: While the result can’t be dismissed as a gimmick, the best tracks of both would have made a great single album. Spread out over two shorter ones, the effect is diluted.

Title: Impeach My Bush
Review: Her rock-oriented approach here will please some, but such a genre-hopping exercise is only occasionally provocative.

Title: Aphrodite
Review: Although the album is an exercise in euphoric clubland dreaming, tracks Closer and Everything Is Beautiful remind us there is perhaps a more sincere side to Kylie that is often overlooked.

Title: Out of the Shadow
Review: The bicoastal milieu of Out of the Shadow is apparent: It reflects both a lush, sunny "California Dreamin'" temperament, and Gotham's grimy, melancholic disposition.

Title: And Nothing Hurt
Review: There is great humanity to And Nothing Hurt, a collection of wistful, wounded observations, the work of a person wearied by the world, but no less in love with it for that. There is hope and joy and naivety here, even as Pierce sounds like he’s been kicked in the groin before recording another cracked vocal.

Title: Wonderful Wonderful
Review: Wonderful Wonderful finds them more comfortable in their own skin: They've managed to condense their operatic impulses into an album of tight, relatively low-key pop songs.

Title: Lulu
Review: There's an insurmountable disjunction between the sound of Metallica doing their nut in the background and Reed's papery old voice rambling away upfront.

Title: Heart Head West
Review: Regardless of Heart Head West’s stretch of sweet-and-sour ballads, its lack of textural and rhythmic variety leaves you hungry for something heartier.

Title: Serena-Maneesh
Review: One of the most intriguing walls of sound since My Bloody Valentine circa Isn't Anything. [Jul 2006, p.97]

Title: On the Outside
Review: Unleashes a torrent of bloated, if occasionally lovely, romantic anthems that aspire to cosmic insight, yet settle for greeting-card corn. [Sep 2006, p.112]

Title: Okovi
Review: A decade-plus of refining this particular sound has led to the purposeful pop of Okovi, her sixth album. Danilova’s vocal performance momentarily recalls darker and more secretive Sia songs.

Title: Afrodisiac
Review: Recalls Janet Jackson at her best.

Title: Marlon Williams
Review: While he doesn’t know quite where his strengths lie yet, tracks such as Strange Things and Lonely Side of Her boast a ghostly, weathered quality that compensates for the odd hillbilly dud.

Title: Black Traffic
Review: There are some pretty nice tracks on there, but nothing as strong as the previous peaks.

Title: Universal Themes
Review: It’s hard to move past this when there’s so much going on but, whether we expect to like it or not--which mostly translates to whether we expect to be able to put up with him or not, we owe it to Universal Themes to try. Despite his behaviour, it's still a great album.

Title: Wyatt At The Coyote Palace
Review: Wyatt At The Coyote Palace shows us a performer whose energies are intact and whose music and lyrics retain their ability to provoke, charm and occasionally disturb us.

Title: Tweens
Review: Tweens pulls no punches, though; this is basic music and these are basic words expressing basic emotions.

Title: Brighter
Review: Even though Brighter falls short, in this context it does illustrates that the indie WhoMadeWho infuse their dance with has more funk and attitude than most.

Title: Talahomi Way
Review: An overall mood of sub-tropical Pacific torpor (albeit well conveyed and executed) does get a mite soporific over the course of an album, or a handful of them, or a career's worth.

Title: Shout It Out
Review: Aside from the trio's penchant for maudlin and borderline campy lyrics, there's little about Shout it Out that isn't infectious.

Title: It Is What It Is
Review: Bruner’s playing—and, increasingly, his writing as well—is so distinctive he’s able to own it even as he tones down his outsize personality. Many modern artists have mined these sounds, but few have honored them quite like Bruner does on It Is What It Is.

Title: Heartstrings
Review: Heartstrings is a succinct outing that charms. [Jul 2014, p.86]

Title: Magnetic Man
Review: Tracks such as "Boiling Water" wouldn't sound out of place in a naff holiday resort. There are notable exceptions, though, such as "Fire" feat Ms Dynamite.

Title: Rose Mountain
Review: This is the record where the Females escape the punk shadow that’s long threatened to typecast them.

Title: Storytone
Review: Storytone presents the same 10 songs twice: compellingly naked save for a guitar or ukulele, then dressed to kill in Hollywood strings and big band brass. [Dec 2014, p.119]

Title: Diver
Review: A lot of the songs are solid hits in the making.

Title: Psychic Chasms
Review: Never ominous and always bright, Psychic Chasms is fantastic brain candy in the vein of electronica or millennial psychedelia.

Title: The Universe Inside
Review: The group's first two post-reunion albums were fine and deeply satisfying, but The Universe Inside goes someplace most fans would never have expected. It's bold, challenging, and dreamlike stuff that stakes out new territory for the band and unexpectedly succeeds on the level of their best work.

Title: Horizon
Review: Incorporating a sense of scale and sounds that highlight the ingenuity and curiosity that sits are the heart of the trio, Horizon is a celebration of the trio’s vision and collective experiences. Wherever it takes them next, let’s hope it continues to be as enthralling as this.

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: Slave Ambient is a well-crafted and euphoric album, but somehow it doesn't have much that sticks out.

Title: Something About April II
Review: This is music for pleasure now. [Mar 2016, p.49]

Title: Leave No Trace
Review: Leave No Trace is an enjoyable time, but the party peaks early.

Title: The Waterfall II
Review: With the exception of “Wasted,” with its hard-rock guitar and raging solo, there’s a gentleness and a sweetness to The Waterfall II that is easy to get lost in.

Title: Aftershock
Review: While the band's elemental sound doesn't show much in the way of innovation, the spirit of true rock is so strong within it that it doesn't really matter.

Title: Stand Up
Review: DMB's five nimble instrumentalists... take Putumayo globalism to a Sigma Chi frat party. [Jun 2005, p.107]

Title: Trees Outside The Academy
Review: You’d be even more surprised to hear that it features 'songs'--proper, beautiful, well-crafted songs.

Title: Ages
Review: There is nothing bad about the album. At the same time, there is nothing impressive about it either, nothing that really grabs on and won’t let go.

Title: Esoteric Warfare
Review: Esoteric Warfare won’t be seen as Mayhem’s best album--there was never any chance of that. However, it’s as good as its predecessor, and every bit as vile and crushing as you’d expect.

Title: Take My Breath Away
Review: Take My Breath Away begins expansively, but rather than proving to be a promising start the opening track turns out, in fact, to be the highlight.

Title: De-Loused in the Comatorium
Review: Contrary to nearly every other band in music today, the Mars Volta suffer from an abundance of ideas and concepts, not a lack thereof.

Title: Broken Ear Record
Review: This is a record that brattily demands total attention, and as such, will either be lauded as a bold journey, or derided as pretentious indulgence.

Title: Tranquilizers
Review: The truth is Tranquillisers has no teeth; being neither truly reprehensible nor in the slightest bit memorable.

Title: Duper Sessions
Review: A bit uneven.

Title: Out of the Black
Review: There is still a huge amount of enjoyment to gain from Boys Noize and that overrides some of the consistency issues.

Title: Quiet Signs
Review: Quiet Signs is an utterly captivating record from its first second to its last. [Mar 2019, p.116]

Title: Future Politics
Review: On Future Politics we find Austra revolving on the spot, caught in a flattering beam of light but still hovering on the brink of taking those first, brave steps towards a radical utopia.

Title: POST-
Review: According to Rosenstock, it was recorded with friends in secret, and finished just before it was released. You can hear all of that in these songs, which crackle with urgency and fun. POST- feels less like an album and more like a document of tightly knit people working hard to make something that feels cathartic and good.

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Vampire Weekend's eponymous debut, with its wide range of references rationed across a collection of brief pop morsels, proves the early fascination was no fluke.

Title: The Chronicles of Life and Death
Review: Good Charlotte have obviously put a lot of effort and imagination into Chronicles, and if it comes off as slightly awkward in parts, well, isn't that part of growing up? [Nov 2004, p.135]

Title: Comfort of Strangers
Review: The record was recorded in two weeks, and many songs sound as if they are first takes, with cracks and stumbles preserved.

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: Iit never feels forced or like she's making some kind of push. It's unhurried and natural and real.

Title: Remember Terry
Review: Maybe it's missing a little bit of the thrill that came along with hearing TERRY for the first time, but there isn't much anyone can do about that. All the band can do is keep cranking out these kinds of smart and snappy pop songs an album at a time, hopefully for as long as possible.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: Aside from initial single "Stone Letter" and its vitriolic chorus, most won't come away humming many of the hooks or melodies, the way one might after listening to a Faith No More album.

Title: Good Girl Gone Bad
Review: Three consecutive Timbaland productions, including one suited for a black college marching band and another that effectively pulls the romantically co-dependent heartstrings, enhance the album rather than make it more scattered.

Title: Moaning
Review: At their best melodically, Artificial lopes on Pornography-era Cure beats to a rousing Interpol angst chorus. Further on through, the various '82-91 moves become too familiar and the mood of despond too oppressive. [Apr 2018, p.95]

Title: Red Barked Tree
Review: The reason it all works is because with repetition and familiarity comes discipline and rigour--and Wire still have a lively and open relationship with both of them. [Feb 2011, p.57]

Title: Strong Feelings
Review: It sounds timeless, and oddly familiar. But subsequent listens add intrigue. [Feb 2014, p.70]

Title: We Are Born
Review: Known for her past collaborations with English electronica band Zero 7 and more recently with Christina Aguilera, Australian artist Sia Furler shines bright on her own on her newest release.

Title: BlakRoc
Review: Instead of acknowledging that they perhaps have something unique to offer and trying to put their own twist on rap, the Keys attempt to strip down their sound to fit within hip-hop genre norms--the result being the taming of many gifted rappers whose time would have been otherwise better spent.

Title: Rave Tapes
Review: Rave Tapes sees Mogwai doing what they do best in the way they’ve always done it. For better or worse, this is archetypical Mogwai.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: It's still considered the band's last album as an underground presence, so it holds importance as something monumental in the band's development. As an album, Lifes Rich Pageant is enjoyable and clean.

Title: Platinum
Review: On Platinum, an old-school country wisecracker that's one of her all-time bests, she's funny as hell.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: This record is a wholly singular work; not only does it defy expectations of what a Flying Lotus album should sound like, it totally obliterates any preconceptions about what can be released by a remotely popular contemporary musician.

Title: Cydonia
Review: Cydonia is a stillborn relic, flawed throughout by chronically stunted ambitions.

Title: Teen Men
Review: The purely audio side collected on this debut album is artfully coiled Vampire Weekend world pop.

Title: In the End
Review: In the End is a moving album and a worthy epitaph for O’Riordan and the band’s legacy, but it leaves you wanting something more, something you’ll never get to hear: the comfort of knowing everything worked out OK. It’s a reminder that grief lingers.

Title: Blade of the Ronin
Review: It's not exactly pushing these MCs towards a new rap revolution, tapping the past and present but skipping predicting tomorrow, but it's consistently engaging without overpowering the stars of the show.

Title: Show Your Bones
Review: As before, the band's willingness to ground itself in human emotion sets it apart.

Title: The New Monday
Review: There are moments where things becomes a little sluggish, though perhaps a stumble here and there can be expected when an album tries to fit so much into a short space. For the most part though, The New Monday is a valiant attempt at distilling Detroit’s musical culture into a single, cohesive record.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: Cranking the urgency and confrontation of last year's self-titled debut to neck-breaking intensity, RTJ2 is an urgent, paranoid album for a violent, panicked time.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Taken as a piece, Somewhere Else can’t live up to those giddy heights, but its sweetness is still to be savored.

Title: Fox Confessor Brings the Flood
Review: Case's genius as a writer, evident from track to track, stems from her ability to write lyrics that conjure up amazingly clear images but that still leave the songs as a whole up to interpretation.

Title: Earthology
Review: Guest appearances from the venerated likes of Percee P and M.E.D. and Mr Lif & Edan prove these Brothers' breakbeats more than pass muster. But it's the more adventurous instrumentals that impress most. [Mar 2010, p.92]

Title: To Survive
Review: It's much darker, more contemplative territory; the songs are like intimate nocturnes located somewhere between classical and soul.

Title: Conversations
Review: Conversations is an impressive album, in many ways a unique one in this current landscape--though you sense that the best may be yet to come.

Title: Free Reign
Review: Whilst it's unlikely to win over many new fans, it will certainly keep those who have been with the band so far content.

Title: Banks
Review: This solo album is stuffed with aloof, adolescent apocalyptism and self-regard set to lumpy, mechanistic beats and cluttered arrangements.

Title: Antarctica
Review: Steve Albini recorded the sessions, and he's done a typically fine job of putting this music on tape with accuracy but no needless frills, and Antarctica suggests Flat Worms have a longer and more diverse future ahead of them than one might have first guessed.

Title: No Manchester
Review: Delightful and frustrating.... There’s one disappointment: there are only seven songs here (five of which are repeated as live versions), and they don’t include any classic Morrissey-Marr Smiths songs.

Title: Any Port in a Storm
Review: SACW get a little too ragged for their own good in places, but Any Port is still a fine ersatz blast from the past that manages to speak to modern-day insecurities.

Title: Kick Up the Fire, and Let the Flames Break Loose
Review: By combining elements of metal, pop, jazz, and electronica, the Cooper Temple Clause create a broad album that is subtle and meticulous as well as driving and bombastic.

Title: Hot Cakes
Review: Hot Cakes is definitely worthy of throwing more than a few devil horns the band's way.

Title: North
Review: It's unclear what the band has been doing during its lengthy hiatus (their last full-length was released in 2002), but keeping up with current music trends was evidently not on the to-do list.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: Although critics of Morrissey's solo career have justifiably argued that his post-Bona Drag ensembles haven't met the Smiths' lofty bar, World Peace Is None of Your Business is the first Morrissey album that's often stronger musically than it is lyrically.

Title: Undun
Review: The album is complete in itself. It's just 39 minutes, made brief to be listened to as a whole.

Title: Business Casual
Review: So, it's formulaic, it's 'retro' in a really kitschy way, and Business Casual sounds pretty much the same as their 2004 debut, Fancy Footwork; and still, Chromeo are fucking great.

Title: Dreams in the Rat House
Review: There's a certain defiant spirit and explosive danger that noises its way through the "retro," thumbing its nose and daring you to call it just kitsch. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.97]

Title: In the Dark
Review: The 11-song set draws from some of the Big Apple's more established rock outfits, but still keeps the DIY feel of the Whigs' previous albums.

Title: Almost Free
Review: There are moments where gusto, melody and thunderous guitar riffs meet to powerful effect but there are some tired moments to wade through to get there. [Feb 2019, p.27]

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: Granduciel’s songs envelop you. As soon as you understand the lyrics for one song, another song buries words in hushed reverb.

Title: Queen
Review: Whether Nicki Minaj is the rightful queen of rap is up for debate, but the album, despite having several songs that were more filler than functional ("Sir," "Majesty," "Chun Swae"), highlights her ability to adapt to an ever-changing sonic landscape.

Title: Aesthethica
Review: It may come to define or utterly transcend metal; but it doesn't matter because this album is in its own class. Anyone remotely interested in heavy music needs to encounter Aesthethica at least once.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: While it's far from perfect, Casiokids have done well to polish their sound, even if they've not yet quite decided what they want to be when they grow up

Title: Contra
Review: Ezra Koenig's songwriting is effortless and breezy, and the Afropop rhythms are as strong as ever.

Title: True Sadness
Review: Underneath their smart stylistic kinks, however, lies a fundamentally old-fashioned imagination. [Aug 2016, p.107]

Title: Blonde
Review: The sprawling haziness still lingers, but the songs are sharper and studded with guests. [Nov 2016, p.24]

It’s the social commentary that makes this experimental album feel vital and unifying. Okereke lyrically eviscerates the politicians who’ve caused divisions based on race, wealth, sexuality and gender, but also offers a vision of hope and a desire for England to rebuild.

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: Over the course of the 38-minute album, these nouvelle cuisine portions amost add up to a satiating whole. But it's good enough you'll be hungry for more. [Winter 2010, p.94]

Title: The Unraveling

Review: With Open Your Heart, The Men have taken that breath. And it's only made their hearts beat faster.

Title: Underneath The Pine
Review: That Toro Y Moi's new record Underneath the Pine is distinctly a product of his songwriting, without sounding exactly like his 2010 debut, suggests that chillwave may still have some legs to it after all.

Title: Heaven
Review: The Walkmen are inching closer to the mainstream, while remaining utterly distinctive. [Jul 2012, p.112]

Title: In Ghost Colours
Review: Although In Ghost Colours is certainly a step up in terms of how cohesive it sounds, it loses some of the spontaneity in the process.

Title: The Savage Heart
Review: The venom and rage of the Jim Jones live experience is captured  more effectively on this third album than its predecessors, but there;s also greater depth to the playing and writing. [Nov 2012, p.76]

Title: The Golden D
Review: Sounds more like a toss-off by a drunk band in the studio.

Title: Weezer (White Album)
Review: The White Album is, hands down, the best Weezer album since... well, since it became so hard to agree on what the last great Weezer album was.

Title: I'm Not Your Man
Review: Her pearlescent lightness is still there in her sweetly sung cut-glass vocals, but in place of acoustic twangs there are heavy lidded licks and an overall louche noir. Grunge and shoegaze set the tone this time: the diaphanous guitar chimes enveloping like a cape.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: Ambitious, risky and occasionally rambling, this is a song cycle best absorbed in a start-to-finish listen. [#73, p.93]

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: It opens with the raucously bluesy 'Nothing Too Much Just Out Of Sight,' a promising start. But before long, McCartney reverts to pop messiah mode and tries to turn each tune into some grand statement about love, life and/or world peace in the hope that positive vibrations might inspire people of all races to join hands and sing along as one. Really.

Title: Overlook
Review: Taylor's whispery, timid voice sounds restrained on nearly every track. Coupled with repetitive lyrics and monotonous rhythms, Overlook is a yawn-inducing piece.

Title: Narkopop
Review: Grand intermeshing spinneys of lush ambient sound, distant pounding beats, lonesome horns and glimpsed shadows of melody that hint at Beethoven, Mozart and older Teutonic ghosts. [Jun 2017, p.89]

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: Born Again is superior to its predecessor in nearly every respect.

Title: ken
Review: The words, as always, tap into the subconscious, making different kinds of sense depending on when you hear them, though that meaning may be more a matter of you than the words themselves.

Title: Marks To Prove It
Review: Marks To Prove It remains oddly unsatisfying.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: When all of it works in perfect synch, the record hits a sweet spot that is both nostalgic and completely contemporary, illuminating how forward-looking the cross-continental collaborators were at their peak.

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Though there isn't a dud in Apple's back-catalogue, she has never sounded quite so liberated and artistically sure-footed as this. [Jul 2020, p.86]

Title: Broken Side of Time
Review: There's excitement her in 'ATX' and the title track, but when the bluster's died down, disappointingly little is left. [Oct 2009, p.89]

Title: Supernova
Review: The resulting arrangements are masterful affairs that frame LaMontagne's material with great taste and flair. [Jul 2014, p.90]

Title: Transverse
Review: Like all great live albums (Live at the Apollo, Double Live, After Dark), it will make you eternally thankful that someone had the foresight to hit the record button.

Title: Head In The Dirt
Review: HEK’s second album makes him sound more confident, distinct and comfortable in his own skin but thankfully not more fancier than his 2011 debut.

Title: The Hour of Bewilderbeast
Review: With 18 songs that clock in at over 63 minutes, The Hour of Bewilderbeast meanders too much, and the quirky pacing (there are many random instrumental interludes) makes it difficult to enjoy as a whole. But taken in sections, it's a bit of a grower.

Title: The DEFinition
Review: There's nothing wrong with this record... Yet it's only on Feel The Beat, in which he lets his ego off the leash, that LL gets into gear. [Oct 2004, p.128]

Title: Future This
Review: The album sags in the middle, descending into slick electro-rock territory worryingly reminiscent to Garbage, but the good songs are terrific. [Feb 2012, p.81]

Title: Mug Museum
Review: It’s still clear, though, that she has too many ideas not to be able to take them somewhere interesting once settled into a new life. File under ‘transitional’.

Title: This Generation
Review: This is just one of those albums that works great either as a stoney throwback or a party-starter.

Title: King
Review: [He] still knows how to make palpitating street anthems. [May 2006, p.91]

Title: Eat Pray Thug
Review: The love songs on this record are nothing to shrug off, but Heems is at his best when he’s politically charged. His messages are so strong that it seems strange to dilute them with pop songs.

Title: Cease to Begin
Review: Each sound lingers, and each stretched-out moment is welcome. [Nov 2007, p.114]

Title: A Different Kind of Fix
Review: They now dart in yet another direction, devising a shuffling indie-dance style that recalls variously the infectious syncopations of Talking Heads, the baggy grooves of Happy Mondays and the campfire psychedelia of Animal Collective, but somehow manages to sound homogenously all of a piece.

Title: Magpie and the Dandelion
Review: Too many edges have been sanded off the brothers' music, and whether the blame lies with Rubin's influence or the accelerated writing pace, the result is an album devoid of the band's usual charming lyrics and adroit melodies.

Title: Hexadic II
Review: Not as violent as Hexadic but no less unsettling, this is a strange and fascinating album from an artist who continues to evolve. [Feb 2016, p.80]

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: It retains their signature blend of folk-rock songcraft and miasmic guitar-drone textures, but in a more purposive manner.

Title: Dear John
Review: This is a bold howl for attention from the backwoods of folktronica. [Apr 2009, p.89]

Title: Pocket Symphony
Review: A big, heaping spoonful of bland. [Mar 2007, p.96]

Title: Parades
Review: It harnesses large spaces, allowing songs like 'Caravan' to blossom into something more orchestral than you'd expect; fitting for a band whose name translates as 'reverberation.'

Title: Instrumental Tourist
Review: All in all, Instrumental Tourist offers more proof that these two are undisputed masters in their field, regardless of how necessary a collaborative effort like this really is anyway.

Title: Here
Review: It may eschew the rough edges of their earlier records, and adhere to the templates the Fannies have used since Songs, but when you’ve got the formula just right, and have the songwriting chops of three of the finest melodic songwriters these isles have to offer, then the result cannot be anything less than sheer joy in the here and now.

Title: Xen
Review: It’s not quite the full spectrum of colours, but there’s an ambitious scale within its palette that allows Arca to craft the textural masterpiece that Xen quite often hints at being.

Title: Morning World
Review: No major leaps have been made and no showstoppers have been added. An effort to buck convention make have actually just made the project slide a few steps backwards.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: Well, they already have the careers. With Wise Up Ghost, though, they now also have a great album.

Title: Anxiety
Review: On the whole, Anxiety lacks the addictive quality of its predecessor, and it's certainly less musically interesting.

Title: You Will Never Be One of Us
Review: Nails constructs towers of noise tall enough to blot out the sun.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: His antiquated fantasies still very much belong to him, but it's still a joy to peer inside them--even if the canvases they're displayed on have shrunk ever so slightly.

Title: LP4
Review: Four albums on, Mike Stroud and Evan Mast have barely altered their instrumental electro/indie/hip-hop hybrid, except to expand and refine its tasteful details.

Title: i,i
Review: The singles have zing, the pacing is superb, and the back half is just as fun as the front. With i,i, you feel the whole last decade: the exploration, the lessons learned. i,i is a mature masterpiece and a stunning marriage of ambition and technique.

Title: Monuments to an Elegy
Review: This sunny half hour lacks an overarching aesthetic or a big, ten-minute cathartic blowout.

Title: Victorious
Review: The riffs are certainly bigger and ballsier than those on the past few records, but Stockdale seems to have lost his personal line to the gods of the ’70s and is left settling for the lesser players.

Title: Goddess in the Doorway
Review: All the star power in the world can't save sub-par material.

Title: Heron Oblivion
Review: Yes, notes and chords are fun and all, but these songs are precisely-controlled messes, and beautifully so. Simply put, Heron Oblivion is a guitar-centric record for those who thought Marquee Moon was too linear.

Title: Swanlights
Review: Fans are unlikely to be disappointed, but if you're expecting a new direction, look somewhere else. [Nov 2010, p.52]

Title: Turn It Up
Review: Turn It Up is a wasted opportunity, weighed down by beige soul ballads and cheap-sounding R&B that could have been cranked out for any talent show contestant. [Oct 2009, p.113]

Title: Monkey Minds In The Devil's Time
Review: Like Boys Outside, Monkey Minds casts Steve Mason as a gifted songwriter, a world-worn bringer of anger, melancholy, hope and melody. [Apr 2013, p.96]

Title: The Shakes
Review: A mixed bag, then, but still uniquely one of Herbert's own. [Jul 2015, p.107]

Title: The Eternal
Review: It's well-built, yes, but almost too well built, many parts sounding like they've been lifted directly from SY's vast back catalogue and slotted into place, like a jigsaw that needed completing, rather than the sprawling documents of noise and confusion this band's name is built upon.

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: The Golden Archipelago presents a direly meditative culmination.

Title: Animal
Review: Overall Animal is a dumb album. Where it tries to be empowering and fun it comes off sounding like a spoilt brat singing the American Pie script through auto-tune.

Title: I Hate Music
Review: Only the most jaded misanthrope could truly hate I Hate Music.

Title: Key Markets
Review: It is not very hip, and it doesn't really hop, but Sleaford Mods have arguably come closer than anyone else to creating a uniquely British form of rap: rant music.

Title: Oxymoron
Review: The wonders never cease on this adventurous and street-tough effort, but they never sort themselves well, either, and with accessible highlights like "Blind Threats," "Break the Bank," and "Man of the Year" all bundled toward the end, this LP requires a surprising amount of patience.

Title: Libra Scale
Review: If a little dominated by this trio [Champagne Life, One in a Million, Beautiful Monster] the rest of the album also develops the cool soul player theme nicely, with offers of mind sex and a considered approach in slick fusion.

Title: Terms of Surrender
Review: The National’s busy polymath Aaron Dessner is producer, bringing this excellent album, full of fear and succour, into focus.

Title: Ice Level
Review: Founder Carlos Hernandez has a tendency to mask his arrangements in more noise than they need, dynamics buried in the resulting fracas.

Title: Earthquake Glue
Review: Hazy, almost-there stadium anthems that don't quite fill the stadium. [Sep 2003, p.115]

Title: Future This
Review: It largely succeeds.

Title: Surrender to the Fantasy
Review: Surrender To The Fantasy is a reminder that Magik Markers is sort of an absurdist band at heart, willing to moon their audience and then have an intellectual conversation about it.

Title: Last Man Standing
Review: Nelson's voice has lost none of its wry warmth, his fretboard fingers little of their astonishing agility. And the songs here are terrific. [Jun 2018, p.33]

Title: The Antidote
Review: Martey is a definite improvement. [Jun 2005, p.106]

Title: Fossils
Review: The polished sound, when combined with O'Donovan's occasionally wispy vocals and recessed guitar, fails to propel the album. It lacks both weight and momentum, or at least enough mood to set Fossils apart.

Title: A+E
Review: You're left wishing the album drew a little more blood.

Title: World of Joy
Review: There's a second-half tail-off, but enough in the first half to keep up the sugar rush.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: World Peace is unquestionably the most subtle and decorous Morrissey album for many years, possibly since the hallowed Vauxhall And I. [Aug 2014, p.84]

Title: Lulu
Review: The bulk of Lulu sounds like your dad's drunk friend reciting his self-penned erotica over a melting ReLoad cassette.

Title: Free To Eat
Review: Plague Vendor have captured the feeling of youthful defiance that spurred the genre's pioneers to action, and while their debut might not be long enough to be the soundtrack to your late-night antics, it's the perfect album to light the fuse on a night you probably won't remember in the morning.

Title: We're Your Friends, Man
Review: 90 minutes of sensitive, surreal lyrics and wailing wig-outs which make J Mascis sound like Julian Bream. ... You'll enjoy it. [Feb 2019, p.90]

Title: Roadsinger (To Warm You Through The Night)
Review: The artist formerly known as Cat Stevens hasn't lost his knack for melody. But with clunkers like ''When I hold your hand I could fly a zillion miles with you,'' he could use a lyrical refresher course.

Title: Brighter Wounds
Review: On average, it's not one of Son Lux's catchier albums, but it is spellbinding, strange, and moving, and still as far away from expectations for a piano, guitar, and drums trio as any in existence.

Title: Up, Guards and at 'Em!
Review: Those three seconds of stuttering electronica simply take their reputation for leftfield experimentalism too far. Thankfully, such wilful pretension buggers off, and the rest is a more quality-controlled set.

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: Other than on "Answers to Your Questions," it's not real pretty when O'Rourke steps to the microphone. Most of his songs stab at a Tom Waits-style balladry but end up sounding more like schmaltzy Steely Dan castoffs.

Title: Dead Reckoning
Review: Yes, the hellfires still burn, and the hearts are still black, and the end is ever nigh. But this time the songs are infused with a contemporary heartache that sounds far closer to 2011 than to the 1931 Depression-era vibe the band typically evokes.

Title: American Doll Posse
Review: Ambitious, high-concept albums are one thing, but Posse's just a boring mess.

Title: Come with Us
Review: 'Come With Us' sounds immediately familiar, but this is often problematic, redolent of prior work by both themselves and others.

Title: HiRUDiN
Review: No shortage of flamboyant tunes. [Jun 2020, p.27]

Title: On Oni Pond
Review: Man Man have crafted an album here that, without betraying their old fans, makes their music accessible to a wider audience.

Title: If I'm Honest
Review: If I’m Honest starts with a barnburner about lacking suds (“Straight Outta Cold Beer”) and ends with a call to Jesus (“Savior’s Shadow”). It’s a trajectory seemingly dictated by Country Albums For Dummies.

Title: MeÃ° suÃ° Ã­ eyrum viÃ° spilum endalaust
Review: So Med Sud I Eyrum Vid Spilum Endalaust is just another Sigur Ros album, but if I can be the first to say it, our "first vital band of the 21st century" is starting to feel old hat.

Title: Ravedeath, 1972
Review: Hecker's latest seems to ultimately be about making peace with our mortality, and as such is his most powerful album yet.

Title: Noah's Ark
Review: Your enjoyment of this album will depend on how open you are to cats meowing, telephone rings, and French spoken-word passages weaving in and out of the songs.

Title: Swisher
Review: Though the songs on Swisher are occasionally a little too long--even the shortest is more than five minutes, and ‘Andrew’ nearly 10--they’re mostly dynamic and varied enough that boredom never really has the chance to set in.

Title: Kitsune
Review: The truly standout moments come throughout in the form of Emma Ruth Tundle's brittle and breathy vocals.

Title: Retriever
Review: Sexsmith's best album yet.

Title: Dreamland
Review: The nostalgia would be overwhelming were it not for Bayley's ability to offset it with woozy, elastic beats. [Aug 2020, p.102]

Title: Pop Voodoo
Review: If Ryder continues to hone his happy medium, the Pop Voodoo might wind up being just the beginning of a late career renaissance.

Title: The Window
Review: In refusing to pander, either to easy nostalgia or to current trends, she touches on something timeless.

Title: No Time For Love Songs
Review: For his part, Jennings deftly plays to the duo's strengths and surrounds them with a complementary sonic environment that dips and swells in all the right places, helping to keep the Mastersons just slightly adjacent to Americana's more obvious paths and in their own unique little world.

Title: Tales of Us
Review: Tales of Us unveils yet again how talented Goldfrapp truly is as together Alison and Gregory continue to craft music that does not pigeonhole them into a set genre; they simply make exceptional music.

Title: Admiral Fell Promises
Review: Judged as an expansion on Kozelek's craft, Admiral Fell Promises is a slight effort; it offers intimate perspective, sure, but the object of observation remains the same.

Title: Walking Like We Do
Review: Certain songs work better than others: “Dog Eat Dog” tries to tackle social injustice but lacks real bite; “Don’t Think”, though, has all the swagger and defiance of vintage Blondie. Most impressive is how much more confident The Big Moon sound as a band.

Title: Curse Your Branches
Review: Still a little dry at times, Curse Your Branches is saved by its attempts at lightness and levity, a positive step which shakes the singer out of a funk of self-serious gloominess.

Title: Broken Politics
Review: On her latest album, Broken Politics, time has not dulled any of her strengths--the mother-of-three still writes couplets that hook you instantly, and has lost none of that firebrand lyricism. Her art, ever poetic, is even more entrenched in the political than previously.

Title: Teenage Emotions
Review: The back half is full of heartbreak, happiness, and all things teenage life over some really good instrumentals varying from trap to reggae to ballads. It has arc. It has feeling. But for some reason, Yachty thought that bragging about himself, calling out haters, and trying to prove that he can rap (he shouldn’t so much) was more important than creating something focused and sincere.

Title: Stankonia
Review: Scattered among the jewels are shiny bits of glass that aren't as valuable as they might be.

Title: Who Sold My Generation
Review: Seattle three-piece Night Beats swoop into Who Sold My Generation oozing confidence. [Mar 2016, p.77]

Title: Neon Icon
Review: The bottom line is that you walk away with a pretty solid collection and the realization that RiFF RaFF probably isn’t going to fade away.

Title: Volume Two
Review: As impressively specific as those sonic ideas are, though, Deschanel's songwriting here is less distinctive than it was on "Volume One." Too many of the tracks bleed together in a well-appointed mush of major-minor melodies and hand-me-down lyrics about the inevitability of heartbreak.

Title: Solo
Review: There's an intriguing version of Michael Jackson's "Human Nature" and tunes by Monk and Ellington alongside originals that lurch from freaky modernism to stately classical. [Oct 2010, p.108]
This brand of tell-all genreless rock may seem impenetrable at first, but a few listens is all it takes before you’ll be hooked by Richard Dawson’s paranoia, honesty and poetry.

Title: Eternal Recurrence
Review: Unlike her boisterous debut album, it is a calming listen that lends itself to journeys into inner space, even if the lyrics can sometimes be distracting.

Title: Petals For Armor I
Review: Petals for Armor doesn’t offer up an easy redemptive arc towards happiness; it is a Herculean effort to pull yourself out of depression. But in letting us in on that effort, Williams has created something special.

Title: R Plus Seven
Review: Disquieting divinity, duly delivered.

Title: You're Welcome
Review: There was an inherently intriguing incongruity between his Brian Wilson-inspired melodies and the unfathomable level of DIY grime with which he rendered them on the first couple of (self-recorded) Wavves albums. Absent that tension, Williams's melodies must be judged by their own ingenuity, and on that count, the ones on You're Welcome, especially those in its back half, too often fall short of the mark.

Title: Until the Quiet Comes
Review: Until the Quiet Comes is cluttered and schmaltzy. [Nov 2012, p.59]

Title: The House
Review: Austere without the compulsion of self-restraint and experimental without the drag of formlessness, The House confirms Porches’ primacy as indie-dance mavens.

Title: KIN
Review: The result is 11 dazzling, fabulously hooky pop-rockers. [Oct 2016, p.95]

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: Like every other album, there are the trademarks we've all come to grow and love from the band and by the end of this, all of the most loving adjectives one could shower on an album will be spread all over The King of Limbs.

Title: New Life
Review: A slickly produced collection of largely generic, meandering songs about self-affirmation in the wake of heartache and romantic disillusionment.

Title: Time Stays, We Go
Review: There’s everything here that those in the know have come to love and expect from The Veils, but there’s also a window in for the rest of you--especially those not-quite goth, dreamer-types lurking over there, I see you with your Low lyric tattoo and Yeah Yeah Yeahs t-shirt.

Title: Something for the Rest of Us
Review: There's enough here to satisfy the faithful, if nothing to enlist new recruits. [Oct. 2010, p. 108]

Title: Locked Down
Review: An album that could've easily come from other Mississippi River stops where horns and funk pump through the bloodstreams-Chicago, Memphis or St. Louis.

Title: Valtari
Review: Ekki Mukk is a gossamer-light, if strangely riveting voice in the wilderness, while Varoelder drifts agreeably off into softly chiming waves of yearning desolation. Less stirring are the ambience-flecked, tympani-tickled meanderings that fill out much of the rest of the hour. [Jul 2012, p.90]

Title: Animal Companionship
Review: It could all be too cute for its own good but some inspired darker moments elevate the whole to the level of a Raymond Carver short story collection set to music by Joan Of Arc-era OMD. [Nov 2018, p.90]

Title: Screen Memories
Review: Screen Memories feels like the cryptic overspill, gnomic fragments of ideas and visions embedded in gloriously baroque synth-pop. [Dec 2017, p.109]

Title: Anthems
Review: The album itself consists of 11 tracks of unimaginative pub rock that, at best, rips off The Darkness, and at worst comes across like a bunch of teenagers in their first band.

Title: Encore
Review: [His] voice bulldozes everything in its path, flattening melody and obliterating nearly every sentiment on this overzealous album. [Feb 2018, p.24]

Title: Stiff
Review: Variety comes in the form of a gently funky soul interlude midway through that highlights the versatility of James Petralli’s voice. But rather than complementing the rest of the album it betrays Stiff’s lack of cohesion.

Title: Gossamer
Review: Their second disc is roomier and more varied.

Title: Post-War
Review: Whereas his previous long-players were primarily personified by their hushed beauty, dusty experimentation, and nostalgic romanticism, Post-War pushes forward a more boisterous and band-orientated vision for Ward’s sturdy songwriting.

Title: Give Up The Ghost
Review: Carlile still prefers sobriety to levity but it never feels affected; it's music that gets under your skin and cuts to the bone.

Title: The Balcony
Review: The Balcony is a debut as polite as potpourri. [Oct 2014, p.106]

Title: Demi
Review: It’s too bad that her new album, Demi, sounds like such a decisive return to teen pop.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: An exuberant return to old-school form.

Title: The Next Day
Review: It demands that you listen to it in this moment, not that you give it an easy ride because this is the man who made ‘Heroes’; and its songs more than live up to the demand.

Title: Fuckin A
Review: Fuckin A is as stupidly (and gloriously) irreverent as its title, all adolescent three-chord slams and snotty, self-championing chants, a seamless extension of the urgency introduced on More Parts Per Million.

Title: Flamagra
Review: Flamagra is still more accessible than either Quiet or Dead! and this is most likely due to Ellison’s choice of vocal collaborators. [Jul 2019, p.49]

Title: Head Down
Review: Head Down sounds highly-charged and fresh. [Dec 2012, p.84]

Title: False Priest
Review: False Priest generally packs the kind of shock and awe that made 2007's Hissing Fauna such a delight.  Throw in some deft work at the boards by one of today's hottest producers and a couple of guest appearances by notable female vocalists, and you've got one of 2010's most colorful releases.  It's not for everyone, but that's half the fun of it.

Title: Everything Else Matters
Review: There are a lot of bands working this angle in the early 2010s; Pinkshinyultrablast is one of the best, and their debut album shows exactly why.

Title: A Youthful Dream
Review: Arguably the album's biggest weakness is that its muffled, messy production doesn't lend itself to the best songs. Still, these guys are just kids and their potential makes them likeable enough.

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: Quasimoto is Madlib at his most creative and compelling. [May 2005, p.83]

Title: Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not
Review: The band keeps its aesthetic, but it keeps twisting it into new shapes. This shape might be the most personal one yet, and it’s as impressive and lasting as anything the band has made.

Title: The Money Store
Review: The Money Store is Death Grips's next move, and they sound surprisingly ready to engage a wider audience.

Title: Azel
Review: [Azel] finds him maturing rapidly. [May 2016, p.93]

Title: Red Dirt Girl
Review: Red Dirt Girl is a model of tasteful genre blending: a little bit country and a little bit electro-ambient pop.

Title: The Fool
Review: Despite all evidence to the contrary over the past 30 years, post-punk doesn't have to be built out of cold, sharp angles. The Fool, the full-length debut by Los Angeles' Warpaint, coasts instead on a humid, hazy, oozing pulse that's less ice age and more malarial swamp.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: Sweet Heart's melancholy tunes are still grand, their orchestras soaring and their choruses rousing, even Phil Spector-orian in the epic kink, but they're more tightly wound than on previous efforts.

Title: Small Town Heroes
Review: Her folk-roots music feels both ancient and modern.

Title: Wrath
Review: Wrath opens and closes with spans of placid subtlety--a welcome touch that doesn't make up for all the raging roteness in between.

Title: The Way Things Fall
Review: The inevitability implied in The Way Things Fall's title is delivered in its songs: far from sounding like a concession to anyone or anything, its directness makes this one of Adult.'s most confident and satisfying albums.

Title: Stranger Things
Review: Though the London band don’t exactly attack in a fist-raised blaze of mega-riffs, they hit hard all the same with quick, sharp, and consistently executed blows of effortless songwriting.

Title: Faithful Fairy Harmony
Review: Foster's is an oddly moving, crepuscular and dream-like world to get happily lost in. [Jan 2018, p.91

Title: Southsiders
Review: The disc is at least 20 minutes too long, with Slug coming off like he's simply recycling the same lyrical ideas in the last third of the album. [Jun 2014, p.104]

Title: Cope
Review: On this fourth full-length, their existential musings are bolder than ever.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: Their sixth collection is broad, bouncy and almost entirely forgettable.

Title: Folie A Deux
Review: It's simply another sturdy album that plays up what Fall Out Boy does best: rocking the arena with barely a second to catch your breath.

Title: Â¡Dos!
Review: It's an excellent Green Day album--one of its best--a catchy, revealing work that surprises with its willingness to explore ideas that the band members may not have invented, but which, fed through Green Day's filter, become theirs.

Title: I Like Fun
Review: The set includes some tender spots, but dire wins the day. Thankfully, it's on occasion leavened. [Feb 2018, p.94]

Title: Big Love
Review: He's a little too old to be playing the lecherous pick-up merchant on tracks like "Tight Tones;" but the lovesick swing of "The Old Man And The Beer" rather suits him. [Jul 2015, p.83]

Title: Champ
Review: There's nothing supremely bad about this record, but there are no surprises either. It's just--well, there.

Title: All Around Us
Review: All Around Us stands as a puckish, blustery, peculiar creation recommended for a good pair of headphones.

Title: We Still Go to Rodeos
Review: Whitney Rose's We Still Go to Rodeos stands out as among the best of these contemporary albums. Rose wrote the dozen stellar tracks (there's not a bad one in the bunch) that range from traditional country ballads to rocking rave-ups.

Title: Look At Us Now Dad
Review: A celebration and a middle finger as Banoffee reclaims her strength across tracks driven by wonky pop sensibilities and a drop of infectious playfulness.

Title: Loney, Noir
Review: These songs are full to the brim with ideas and a charming naivety - but there's a major hurdle that ultimately compromises the enjoyment: the vocals.

Title: Our Version of Events
Review: In comparison to the drudge that is contemporary mainstream American pop and R&B, Emeli's folk-inflected soul/pop is Nina Simone and Bob Dylan all in one.

Title: Strange Land
Review: What Schaff's everyloner routine lacks in subtlety, it makes up in a certain fraught, occasionally uncomfortable relatability.

Title: New York in the '70s
Review: A pop culture enthusiast, Luke Haines once again shows his uncanny ability to beat vivid and idiosyncratic new narratives from leathery sacred cows. [Jun 2014, p.111]

Title: Unfurl
Review: Unfurl is much like RY X’s previous record Dawn, though tinged with moments of evolution. Lined with a rawness that could be sometimes overlooked; it seems to find solace in giving an emotional response to me from its creation.

Title: Groove Denied
Review: Groove Denied can’t help but feel like a minor effort. It’s essentially his answer to McCartney II—the sound of a veteran artist with two beloved bands under his belt reveling in the freedom to indulge a latent fascination with the latest gadgets.

Title: Complete Surrender
Review: For all the flash and flair, the freshest, most intimate moments here are the result of holding back.

Title: Everybody's Dying To Meet You
Review: These are tracks that have the ability to win over those who wrote off Rachel Kenedy’s vocals from the first album: it’s a step forward for weird-voiced frontwomen all over.

Title: The OOZ
Review: Even after many spins, the album still reveals unheard layers as you shift your focus around Marshall's isolating masterpiece; it'd be profoundly depressing if it wasn't so brilliant.

Title: Light
Review: He's aiming for a wider crossover audience with a blend of dancehall, rap and rock guitar solos. Several tracks have the kind of mobile-waving choruses you'd normally associate with a boy band.

Title: PARTYNEXTDOOR TWO
Review: The highs of PND 2 have replay value, and the lows--though there are certainly more of them--blend with the rest of the album as it plays in the background of a bedroom.

Title: Spacehopper
Review: The album begins to lag toward the end as the slower tracks drag their heels, but it’s still an impressive debut.

Title: Introduction
Review: Introduction serves both as a reminder of Thompson's often overlooked sense of humour and an exploration of certain cliches endemic to the pop song, but most importantly, it just rocks. [#266, p.63]

Title: The Late Great Whatever
Review: There’s not a whole lot here that really distinguishes itself from similar material. However, the Lovely Bad Things do their shtick fairly well, and there are some outstanding moments as outlined above.

Title: Fur and Gold
Review: Fur and Gold is not the greatest album of the 2007, but it’s certainly the most breathtaking.

Title: Closer
Review: Unlike previous efforts, Hawtin shows a hint of humanity here.

Title: Sweet Talker
Review: As these 12 tracks go by, the quirks that made Jessie J’s previous albums notable have been replaced by the hugeness of failsafe producers; and she has taken a step back from the songwriting.

Title: Spot the Difference
Review: Although this is never less than excellent fun, the originals are still the best. [Dec 2010,. p.96]

Title: The Shakes
Review: There is a sense, though, that the nuances and detail of The Shakes need careful unpicking. It might be a return to dance music, but it’s far from disposable.

Title: Big Bad World
Review: Plain White T's are ultimately as bland and banal as the clothing they take their name from. [Dec 2008, p.133]

Title: Big TV
Review: As a whole, though, the album’s overall feel is still deadeningly generic.

Title: Two Way Monologue
Review: Think swoonsome pop at its most non-cynical but with a left-field twist. [Aug 2004, p.98]

Title: Radioactive
Review: Much has been made of Yelawolf's Southern rock fandom, but Radioactive is more an ode to the Southern hip-hop movement that started to seep across the world a decade ago.

Title: Lysandre
Review: Even with the thematic ties running throughout Lysandre, it isn't overly ambitious: The 11 songs clock in at less than half an hour, and the main musical theme that shows up in nearly every one of them becomes a wearisome prop by the end of the album.

Title: BE
Review: It's the album's deft balance between Sitek's freewheeling and darkly ambient aesthetic and the familiar sub-Beatles melodies that make BE a bold leap forward in the mould of Paul Weller's recent psych-inspired reinventions. [Jul 2013, p.71]

Title: Braindrops
Review: This is emphatically a headphones listen, especially for picking up the quieter moments of cacophony. It’s in the noisier moments that you’ll really appreciate having a good sound system for the album.

Title: The Way It Is
Review: Cole's street-savvy Oakland, Calif., upbringing gives her vocals depth and her songs a genuine, lived-in feel. [8 Jul 2005, p.69]

Title: American IV: The Man Comes Around
Review: Cash might surprise with his choice of covers, but in nearly all of his selections, he locates some personal meaning, or introduces new emotional elements.

Title: Silver Age
Review: In truth, [Silver Age] is simply just a pretty not bad retread.

Title: On Your Own Love Again
Review: On Your Own Love Again is something else again, at least a personal landmark and maybe a classic. Simple, straightforward, but more than it seems, this is one of the best albums of 2015 so far and marks the emergence of a very distinctive songwriting talent.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: So it comes as no surprise that the harmonic progression does not cadence as the listener might expect; the ear wants one more chord, but Pecknold and his backup singers simply end. There's nothing more to say.

Title: Blame It On Gravity
Review: The songs move between love and regret and between restlessness and loneliness.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: As is the risk with such serious-minded albums, a few songs err on the side of heavy-handedness... but Arcade Fire's raw passion and heartfelt ambition remain intact. [#75, p.90]

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: The lyrics brim with grouchy wit. [24 Mar 2007]

Title: Songs for Singles
Review: Now, recorded as a trio in the aftermath of guitarist Juan Montoya's exit, the eight-track Songs for Singles makes a case for the power of three.

Title: King's Disease
Review: King's Disease is a record that's occasionally swollen with too many ideas, backed up by lazy rhymes and unsavoury politics. Thankfully, with impeccable production overseen by executive producer Hit-Boy and bolstered by a slew of excellent guest features, Nas overcomes these pain points to pull together his most satisfying project in close to a decade.

Title: Play
Review: Although it may appear frantic, Play is an eclectic and coherent work where Moby accesses an array of sounds from his milieu of influences.

Title: At Weddings
Review: While simple and often musically somnolent, its heart-wrenching effect is ultimately hard to shake.

Title: Drums Between the Bells
Review: Drums Between The Bells is challenging and complex, but evocative, rewarding, and not altogether fragmentary, not even (or especially) when you bust up the long-playing order.

Title: The Dream My Bones Dream
Review: The songs are gorgeous, lyrical, chimerical, the arrangements weighty, complex and cool. [Jan 2019, p.89]

Title: Songs in the Key of Animals
Review: The old cliché about double albums is that most could be greatly improved if edited down to one disc, but that doesn’t hold true here. Animals is an anomaly: a two-disc set without enough solid material for even a single LP.

Title: Goodbye Lullaby
Review: Whether Goodbye Lullaby was all a tad over thought, or whether she's just holding back, the finished product falls significantly short of Avril Lavigne's own capabilities.

Title: The Week That Was
Review: It’s one of the oddest beauties of the year so far.

Title: Restarter
Review: Restarter is remarkably composed and perfectly balanced, demonstrating Torche's ability to continually refine their doom-pop/melodic hard rock approach.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: It's certainly the group's most cohesive album in ages.

Title: The Agent Intellect
Review: If these guys don't have the loftiest ambitions ever, it needn't matter when The Agent Intellect makes post-punk feel like purest rock'n'roll.

Title: 1000 Palms
Review: There’s no deviating from this formula as 1000 Palms is a disappointingly reclusive step for a band whose once-bright star might have finally stopped flickering.

Title: Soft Metals
Review: A good start to your evening--but certainly not capable of carrying the whole night.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: It's got some of his best pure songwriting yet, but no earth-cracking riffs. Still, as a treatise on loss and its schizophrenic aftermath, Blunderbuss is a purposeful success.

Title: Dust
Review: For an artist never exactly afraid of taking risks, Dust still finds new forms of experimentation, moving beyond dance toward something softer and more reflective. Halo juggles new elements with gorgeous sparseness that gives weight to each sonic addition.

Title: It Is Time for a Love Revolution
Review: Ultimately, he sounds confused--he wants to bare his soul and boogie on, but the boogie isn't nearly enough. [Mar 2008, p.97]

Title: 4 Your Eyez Only
Review: On Immortal, he tackles paranoia and police brutality in ways that are both heartbreaking and bluntly nihilistic, while Foldin Clothes is a blissful and unapologetic diversion into domesticity ("I never thought I'd see the day I'm drinking almond milk"). Elsewhere, his earnestness comes off as unwieldy in moments that precariously sit on the cusp of sleepy sentimentality.

Title: Un Dia
Review: Listened to absentmindedly, its deep, rumbling groove and overlapping rhythmic lines may initially seem nothing more than an artfully assembled soporific swirl. Live with it a while, though--give it time and space in order that it may weave its beguiling spell--and delights aplenty unfurl.

Title: No Answer: Lower Floors
Review: It’s the clearest, most detailed record in their vast catalogue.

Title: Battle Born
Review: In many ways, Battle Born will live up to everything you wish of it, just not every Lanois-Lillywhite-and-O'Brien-helmed second.

Title: Lulu
Review: LuLu is a work that invites derision, an album that wallows in a tarpit of ugliness.

Title: With Us Until You're Dead
Review: It plays to all their debut's moody, elegant, widescreen strengths while illustrating the changes since. [Sep 2012, p.86]

Title: Grassed Inn
Review: By making concessions to clarity, Blank Realm have only amplified their inherent weirdness. As such, this thing is a fucking kick in the pants.

Title: Matangi
Review: M.I.A.’s most consistent work since her debut. ... Yes, her myriad ideas are still tumultuous, but there’s precious few other musicians out there attempting such an ambitious and impassioned collage of words, rhythms and concepts.

Title: So Long, See You Tomorrow
Review: It’s a mighty lunge forwards for the four-piece.

Title: The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here
Review: A brooding, groovy, muscular album, The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here is a more mature and thoughtful application of Alice In Chains' undeniably powerful aesthetic.

Title: Otherness
Review: Bainbridge reveals himself here not as an exhaustingly pseudy hipster but rather a songwriter of singular depth and emotion. [Nov 2014, p.114]

Title: Some Things Last Longer Than You
Review: Their debut has hooks sharper than new scissors. [10 Sep 2016, p.52]

Title: Zipper Down
Review: Sexy, fierce and occasionally very, very silly, this is an album made to be played on jukeboxes in backwater biker bars the world over, loudly.

Title: Red Carpet Massacre
Review: Red Carpet Massacre is largely just a ham-fisted example of what happens when fame, ego and squandered major label cash equate to a sad, missed opportunity.

Title: No Control
Review: Overall No Control comes across as a cohesive and original piece of work.

Title: The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends
Review: The triumph of Heady Fwends lies the way it sands off the rough edges off 2011's excess and whittles an honest, enjoyable set out of the mire while coaxing a wealth of unexpected voices into the fray without losing its way.

Title: Metals
Review: Slinky, spooky, superb.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: Sisterworld is an impressive record which lurches menacingly between euphoria and tranquility. [Mar 2010, p.89]

Title: The Agent Intellect
Review: Protomartyr save their best for the final half of the album beginning with the buzz saw, fuzz chug of “The Hermit”, moving into the splashy moroseness of “Clandestine Time” and recent single “Why Does It Shake?”. But it is on “Ellen” when The Agent Intellect truly peaks.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: From "Jeopardy" on, Run the Jewels 2 is uppercut after uppercut.

Title: Hands
Review: Hands is both exciting and inconsistent, an uncertain step in very much the right direction.

Title: Alice
Review: The wig-out-in-wonderland title track has a poppy, Donovan approach before its unsettling phased climax. [Apr 2017, p.99]

Title: Own Your Ghost
Review: The album lags a bit on a few songs where it sounds like one half of the group had the majority of the say during the writing process. These instances are few and far between though, leaving the rest of the album as an intriguing concoction of two bands coming from polar opposite sides of the musical spectrum and meeting in the middle to make something new.

Title: The People's Key
Review: Every line is laid with the rich sense of rhythm and texture that he's mastered over the years, but it still adds up to very little: a wildly spiritual record without any spirit.

Title: The Satanist
Review: At the end of the day, there is little doubt that listeners will enjoy The Satanist, because it provides in copious quantities what has made Behemoth a staple in the extreme metal community for over twenty years, while keeping their shortcomings to a minimum.

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: It's human where Radiohead are impenetrable, but complex where Coldplay are banal.... Elbow remain unquantifiably great.  [Sep 2003, p.100]

Title: Funeral
Review: Reveals added nuance with every listen. [Jan/Feb 2005, p.102]

Title: Apocalypse, girl
Review: Apocalypse, Girl is at once plaintive, savagely ironic and disconcertingly funny.

Title: Ripples
Review: It's Brown's voice that holds it all together. [Mar 2019, p.24]

Title: We're Not Talking
Review: Their second LP contains songs of remarkable quality. [Nov 2018, p.106]

Title: Subiza
Review: Subiza is the culmination of a years-long growing process in which Delorean was able to synthesize its influences into a sound all its own. It isn't flawless, but it could be this year's most perfect summertime album.

Title: Glow
Review: For all of the advantageous production choices, Glow comes with a certain stylistic parity that keeps it at bay after the second listen.

Title: Us
Review: Songs that are as euphoric as they are charming.

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: After an auspicious introduction Oblivion With Bells has disappointingly descended into an irreconcilable docile abyss.

Title: Everyday Demons
Review: Their default position is to panel it: hard-driving Zep-worship so unvarying in its pace that Everyday Demons comes on like one long undead riff plus a lot of yawled guff about about being an ‘Evil Man’ with ‘Demon Eyes.'

Title: I'm With You
Review: It's the heart of the matter, and the song that sets the bar. [Oct 2011, p.122]

Title: Let's Bottle Bohemia
Review: The Thrills continue to crank out buoyant melodies that keep singer Conor Deasy from downing in his bittersweet lyrics and brokenhearted vocals.

Title: A Hundred Million Suns
Review: A Hundred Million Suns is rife with the sense of a band striving to be taken more seriously, whether through rocking more manfully, displaying a more sophisticated subtlety, or simply stringing together three ponderous, already-overlong songs and calling the impenetrable result a 16-minute stand-alone epic.

Title: When I Have Fears
Review: Lyrically, The Murder Capital are less direct than Idles and Fontaines, but musically they're more expansive, bringing a brooding brain-twisting gothic feel. [Sep 2019, p.30]

Title: Spreading Rumours
Review: Their second LP retains the goofy amiability of their debut and cranks the Nineties influences.

Title: Kingdom Come
Review: Kingdom Come is a solid record, and entirely worth the cost just to hear Jay-Z spit a new song, but in the end it just can’t live up the expectations it tattoos all over itself.

Title: Indigo
Review: A well put-together record, just lacking in heart. [Oct 2018, p.119]

Title: Old Growth
Review: Nearly everything else on Old Growth consists of middling blues-rock with impressive soloing but negligible heft.

Title: I Want That You Are Always Happy
Review: A collection of songs which rings with the same deeply felt, universal truths of Bon Iver's For Emma, Forever Ago and Ryan Adam's Heartbreaker. Chillingly authentic. [Aug. 2011, p. 100]

Title: Pawn Shoppe Heart
