Review: Sounds too clean and constrained.

Title: pom pom
Review: Pom pom is probably the most accessible, easy-on-the-ear and enjoyable music of his career, without any asterisks.

Title: Nothing as the Ideal
Review: Recorded at Abbey Road in London, the eight-track set makes good use of the legendary studio's analog infrastructure, peppering the proceedings with fragmented loops and rewinding reels, all the while maintaining a radiant classic rock core. It's also the group's heaviest outing to date.

Title: Untitled
Review: "Illmatic" was stylistically brilliant and incalculably influential, but Untitled is a more mature, emotionally-driven, and philosophically-complex piece of work. It’s also a masterpiece.

Title: Born Sinner
Review: Born Sinner is a real grower, one that in many ways completely exceeds expectations and demands your attention.

Title: Unravelling
Review: Unraveling is cut from a richer, darker cloth than their earlier works, making it a bold departure and a tense new direction well worth exploring.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: There may be nothing explicitly political in the songs on Be the Cowboy. But there’s plenty implicit, from the DIY American mythology of the title, to the way the songs validate voices that are shaky, hurting, irrational, and damaged, while also being smart, wry, powerful, and deserving of love.

Title: Mise En Abyme
Review: Mise En Abyme hunts that sensation of flux and liminality, unearthing warmth in a landscape of paranoia.

Title: We're New Here
Review: It's a dub reimagining that takes the material further out, into a soundscape whose fractured dubstep tones, sped-up samples and drum'n'bass beats only occasionally work in its favour.

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: A charming album. [May 2006, p.128]

Title: Pebble To A Pearl
Review: The material on what's intended to be her big breakthrough is however unispired. [Mar 2009, p.80]

Title: Surfing
Review: What's more surprising is just how good it all is, the tunes great, the mood fun, the album infectious. [Mar 2009, p.92]

Title: Beware
Review: Beware is one of the more playful entries in the Bonnie "Prince" Billy canon. It's also one of his fullest sounding records.

Title: Los Angeles Police Department
Review: Overall, Pollie presents a wistful and warm little microcosm that subtly builds on the foundation of his debut.

Title: Steal Your Face
Review: The band continues to mine their particular brand of post-hardcore, danceable, free-punk madness--with satisfying results.

Title: Born in the Echoes
Review: The latest from the U.K. duo hits harder and lower than their last album, 2010's Further, with guest-vocal turns from artists as varied as Q-Tip and St. Vincent over tracks that could've torched an outdoor rave in 1995.

Title: Skying
Review: While Skying is not as large a leap forward as Strange House to Primary Colours was, it's still the work of a band firing on all cylinders, and an exceptional offering from a group that, out of nowhere, is quickly becoming one of the most exciting young acts around.

Title: Some Loud Thunder
Review: This time around, no celebratory hand gestures are required.

Title: A Hundred Things Keep Me Up at Night
Review: It sounds like almost exactly the same record, just not as slap-in-the-face fresh. Still, if it’s more of the same, at least the same is pretty good.

Title: Expansion Team
Review: DJ Babu looks to the old school for his mix of melody and beats, giving the whole project a fluid and classy feel with more than a nod to their heroes, Run DMC. [#184, p.130]

Title: Adult Nights
Review: Adult Nights is sweet and upbeat--so relentlessly so that at times it comes off as a little facile.

Title: One Kind Favor
Review: The ache, the anger, the elegance and the edge of Mr. King’s blues are undiminished and authentic.

Title: The Diary
Review: The album is recognisable in name only. Only a few songs register in their entirety as actual conceivable moments that the artist would have presumably been comfortable releasing.

Title: Sour Soul
Review: On the impressive Sour Soul, the Canadian trio that built its profile through Odd Future and Gucci Mane covers bangs out rich blaxploitation-invoking live instrumentals, providing a perfect canvas for the Wu-Tang Clan vet's vivid rhymes about dodging police, jewelry and, oddly enough, yoga.

Title: Legion of Boom
Review: Too many tracks get bogged down with a straight-ahead progressive trance formula, where zoning out feels more suitable than attempting to move your feet. Still, because the good stuff is so darn good (and it is), it is easy to brush aside any missteps.

Title: Free Your Mind
Review: Nearly every track is a highlight; these are accentuated by brief detours into psychedelic space.

Title: With Us Until You're Dead
Review: The album's only real flaw is a penchant for sketchy, banal lyrics that can jar with the imaginative and highly polished musical backdrop. [Oct 2012, p.71]

Title: Underachievers Please Try Harder
Review: Captures a portion of the wispy bedsit magic that used to mark some of The Field Mice's best work and boosts it with the lush, "Hazey Jane II"-like chamber-pop of Belle & Sebastian's first flourishes of glory.

Title: Encore
Review: Overall, Encore is a worthwhile listen. It obviously suffers from many of the problems that dance music albums generally suffer from but it does well to show off Snake's ear for hooks just as well as his ear for drops.

Title: Of Course You Are
Review: Pollard’s sheer output is intimidating. However, as this album proves, his quality control may be as good as anyone’s in the business.
Each of the songs is a short film: with an atmosphere and a story and a sense of drama. That makes her an artist to whom attention must be paid.

Title: Upside Down Mountain
Review: Although Upside Down Mountain could do with a little more lyrical variety and structural experimentation, it is strong.

Title: At Your Inconvenience
Review: A depressingly compromised second LP from an artist yet to meet  his early promise.

Title: The Mystery Lights
Review: It's steeped in the snotty multi-coloured psych of the Elevators, the Seeds, Os Mutantes and, via the parping Farfusa of "Follow Me Home," early Doors. [Aug 2016, p.80]

Title: Born to Sing: No Plan B
Review: Like Dylan, Born To Sing will probably be an acquired taste for some (the jazzy backing may put some off, as may Morrison's tendency to incessantly repeat lines and start scatting every so often), but it's yet another example of his sometimes erratic genius.

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: She hits rock bottom on the repetitive, bland Daydreaming. It really does feel like a daydream, this whole idea of crowning a new female rap queen.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: Barely enough for five years of waiting and hardly up to the old standard.

Title: No Color
Review: It may have taken Long and Kroeber some time to crack the tough nut of a thoroughly radiant album but unlike their namesakes, The Dodos have only ripened with age.

Title: The New Danger
Review: Not all of it works... but the 'What's Going On'-sampling 'Modern Marvel', mumbling folk-soul of 'Boogie Man Song' and widescreen shuffle of 'Champion Requiem' prove that not all hip-hop albums come with an expiry date. [23 Oct 2004, p.51]

Title: Deceiver of the Gods
Review: On Deceiver of the Gods, they are satisfied with plugging 10 new anecdotes into 10 songs they’ve made before and, unfortunately, will most likely make again.

Title: Jade Bird
Review: Jade Bird is an album of loose change, a pocketful of shiny, well-written nuggets that might give off a lot of flash individually but when put together don’t equal the sum of their parts. Thankfully, Bird’s singular musical style--a chalky blend of roots-rock, country and pop--and her mighty, mighty roar cancel out any thematic fumbles entirely.

Title: All of Something
Review: All of Something is a unique fusion of sounds that cements Sports' songwriting as a compelling mix of impressive and inventive.

Title: Warmer Corners
Review: It’s smart, depressing, inoffensive pop perfect for a rainy day.

Title: Isolation Drills
Review: From GBV's earliest days, Pollard has displayed, in almost equal measure, a talent for catchy melodies and for daring eccentricity, with his best songs balancing the two instincts. That dynamic pervades Isolation Drills, with the tension producing some of the most instantly enjoyable songs of Pollard's career while maintaining a strong sense of experimentation.

Title: Anoyo
Review: But where Konoyo was a more visceral invocation of the electronic sublime, Anoyo stretches out and creates space for the reeds to be heard amid the splices, obstructions and reversals of the Los Angeles based producer’s typically stratified sonic design. [May 2019, p.67]

Title: A Black Mile to the Surface
Review: Full of textured, wide-screen soundscapes, the record dips its feet in electronic waters, yet retains the emotional vulnerability that has always defined the Atlanta band. There’s an extra dose of sinister unease, too, especially on ‘Lead, SD’ and ‘The Moth’.

Title: Utopia Defeated
Review: The influence of earthy sub-Saharan blues is readily apparent on the choppy fretwork of ‘Walrus’, and the raw loops he creates by on-the-fly sampling have universal appeal. Similarly his voice, with its soaring inflections and echoes of Sting and Jeff Buckley, is a hugely effective tool.

Title: Valley Tangents
Review: Valley Tangents takes long, deep breaths, fuzz guitar scrawling over meandering piano in a humidified room. [Jul 2012, p.69]

Title: Where Does This Door Go
Review: Despite dipping into hip-hop and reggae, there are footnotes to ’70s pop throughout. That doesn’t diminish the sheer pleasure of the tunes’ playful intentions, but Hawthorne’s DJ crate-digging tendencies seem to be bleeding into his songwriting.

Title: This Is Acting
Review: While Sia has declared her awareness of the cheese factor in her hired-gun material, with its broad themes of self-empowerment and survival, she has a real gift for making it palatable.

Title: Life Among the Savages
Review: All told, with Life Among The Savages Jason Quever’s Papercuts has crafted a near-perfect collection of contemporary baroque pop ruminations on the modern condition, one of isolation, sadness and an affectation that requires us to present an outward façade not generally indicative of the emotional turmoil raging within.

Title: Chambers
Review: Though enjoyable, it may land in a limbo, too simplistic for fans of great chamber music or its challenging modern variants; too classical--lacking bells, whistles, samples and beats--to make it more than pleasant dinner party music for people coming from the indie side.

Title: America Give Up
Review: America Give Up is a fantastically-promising debut album full of charm and potential. So, until the Strokes release their next masterpiece or pack it in altogether, enjoy this bunch of upbeat, tousle-haired tunes.

Title: An Omen
Review: With Atticus Ross, Reznor pieces together wintry electronic headphone epics and deftly threads Maandig's ghostly sensuality into enigmatic tapestries. [30 Nov 2012, p.73]

Title: American IV: The Man Comes Around
Review: He's at the height of his powers here, as vital and relevant as ever.

Title: Every Country's Sun
Review: The once-lairy Scots' high-volume potency remains beyond question. [Oct 2017, p.92]

Title: Clapton
Review: The music throughout is sequenced brilliantly, with a cohesion that almost defies logic.

Title: Santana IV
Review: Santana IV rolls back the years to the time when the band melded spicy percussive Latin grooves with searing blues-rock. Seraphic-voiced Ron Isley fronts a couple of tunes but it’s the spacey, psychedelic instrumental, Fillmore East, and addictive salsa-rock of Anywhere You Want To Go, that impress the most.

Title: The Altar
Review: Banks packs enough energy and zeal at the starting line to duly lay waste to whoever was foolish enough to break her heart.

Title: Expo 86
Review: While this is definitely a darker album, the fuzzy synthesizers help to give the songs warmth, preventing the album from becoming suffocating.

Title: The Serenity of Suffering
Review: The Serenity of Suffering is easily Korn’s most diverse release; featuring melody, aggression, new sounds and old staples in just about equal measures wrapped into some of the band’s strongest songs in years.

Title: Be Strong
Review: The 2 Bears possess charm aplenty in their music making, and with its sheer love of light comic touches, Be Strong is certainly not short on that.

Title: Histoire de Melody Nelson
Review: Lush and languorous, velvet-robe decadent and soft-focus steamy, Histoire is a make-out record and a gross-out record.

Title: Heligoland
Review: Sure, it's a logical progression from 100th Window, but because their progressions are neither commonsense nor predictable, it's difficult to predict how it will hold up in terms of posterity.

Title: Teen Dream
Review: Teen Dream’s best material comes up front (“Zebra,” “Silver Soul,” “Norway” “Walk in the Park”) , and there’s a bit of a sag in the middle (“Lover of Mine,” “Better Times”), with songs that are pretty enough, but without any big payoffs.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: Admire feels oddly reined in, a transitional record by a band not yet willing to completely let go of the past.

Title: Rhine Gold
Review: Choir of Young Believers have created a singular sonic world all their own.

Title: Clark
Review: Even when Clark is firing sounds at bewildering speeds, it's never a chore--in other words, it's a lot more fun than Clark's reputation might suggest.

Title: The Illusion of Progress
Review: Most of all, the music packs as much punch as ever--and more variety, as Staind sometimes departs from its rock-metal power ballads for tunes that suggest Pink Floyd and even Brit band Oasis in the chiming-guitar pop of 'All I Want.'

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: Nine Types Of Light is an album that manages to blend experimentation with a welcoming accessibility that proves pop music can still be bold this far down the line.

Title: All The Time
Review: Further focus is rewarded with a deeper experience, sadder and more upset than you might hear the first time.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: A powerful return to form.

Title: The Love EP
Review: Bailey Rae's The Love EP is a short, but great listen with some of the finest love songs ever written.

Title: Let's Dance Raw
Review: Raw is a perfectly executed version of what Westerners might call global kitsch: a series of evocative tourist postcards showing sunny scenes from Rio and Honolulu.

Title: Tranklements
Review: Considering the Black Dog's immense volume of output over the previous few years, it's remarkable that the group's attention to detail and uniquely stern sound remains. And yet, for all the output that preceded it, Tranklements isn't merely another Black Dog album.

Title: Noble Beast
Review: Bird probably could have stood to cull a few of the weaker numbers, and with the additional room, might have reworked a few of the selections from Useless Creatures into experimental pop songs, thereby tempering his lack of risk taking on Noble Beast.

Title: 10,000 Days
Review: As daunting as its title suggests. [Jul 2006, p.114]

Title: Heartworms
Review: After a decade-plus in which they've evolved from cult heroes to respected major-label denizens, the Shins still prove capable of delivering a few surprises.

Title: The Rebirth of Venus
Review: He overreaches on occasion, but more often pulls off the sort of trick he manages with 'Families Cheating at Board Games,' merging faith and offbeat, cerebral underpinnings to forge quirky slivers of fresh perspective.

Title: Loso's Way
Review: Despite smirk-worthy lines, Loso's chest-thumping slickness feels less than fresh.

Title: In The Seams
Review: There’s a bit of guilt in sneaking a peek, a bit of unnecessary personal fluff and a few deeply held secrets that are gifts to receive. Ultimately, what’s most impressive about In the Seams is that Jones chooses to portray Saint Saviour in this way and stick with it throughout the entire record.

Title: The Information
Review: Despite the album’s plethora of stylistic shifts and breakdowns, there’s a solid coherency to The Information that allows it to flow from beginning to end without the listener losing interest.

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: At least Pixies didn't try to fake their way into recreating every aspect of their former glory. But the music here is so unfortunately forgettable.

Title: Into The Woods
Review: An altogether more positive attempt to commune with nature. [Jun 2017, p.88]

Title: From the Ground Up
Review: Throughout the album, whether he's coming off like a rootsy road dog or a post-Tin Pan Alley piano balladeer, Fullbright consistently displays a level of lyrical finesse that would be impressive in an artist with twice as many years behind him, which only bodes well for his future work.
By turns languidly bluesy and as stark as an oak branch against a February sky, her music is a treasure, and this record fills in a story-line with far too many gaps.

Title: Madame X
Review: Madame X is certainly a fluid album, but one tempered by Madonna’s solid confidence in her own aesthetic decisions.

Title: MDNA
Review: It [the song "I'm a Sinner"] makes you crave her next album, not this one.

Title: Animal
Review: It's effective, not good. More tellingly, it's catchy in spite of Ke$ha, not because of her.

Title: Gift Of Screws
Review: With the trusty Mick Fleetwood-John McVie rhythm section giving lots of sonic wallop, this is more than just a Mac album without the female vocalists: Buckingham seems to be rediscovering some sort of idealism.

Title: The Night Is Young
Review: For the most part, The Night Is Young manages to be simultaneously familiar and strange, commercial but emotionally weighty, grown-up without being boring: a musical grey area that grows curiouser all the time.

Title: I Am Shelby Lynne
Review: So why doesn't "I Am" quite hit the mark? Blame it on producer Bill Bottrell, best-known for his work with Sheryl Crow. Simply put, he lays it on a little too thick.

Title: Give More Love
Review: Starr remains fond of late-period Beatles, goosed with a bit of arena rock volume, and since he's working with a group of well-seasoned pros, this guitar pop is all well crafted and amiable.

Title: LoveLaws
Review: The more you listen, the harder is gets to place this record in a rundown of the overall Warpaint output.

Title: Spring
Review: Opener “Lily” falls into this liminal ground, as does “Blue Spring,” and while these tracks don’t seem pointed towards anything particularly urgent, their instrumentation (like the rest of Spring) remains rich and resonant, each component part augmenting the others.

Title: Crooked Shadows
Review: Perhaps Carrabba still writes lyrics in broad terms, but this willingness to sculpt his sounds on the softer side indicates that he's discovered a way to sustain this allegedly adolescent music well into his adulthood.

Chapman is an artist who has never had a problem with upending creative expectations, and if 50 isn't the sort of music many of his longtime fans would expect from him, it's also passionate, literate, and the work of an artist who wants to make the most of his late-era career. Not many artists sound this determined and engaged, especially at the age of 75.

Title: Avi Buffalo
Review: The record could be accused of wearing its influences a bit obviously, but as Wilco, Flaming Lips and Mercury Rev borrowed from Neil Young, progression essentially comes through a degree of regression and, although Avi retreads familiar ground, he still adds his very own unique footprint to his band's debut.

Title: Ghosts of the Great Highway
Review: A gorgeous record brimming with unhurried songs. [#61, p.108]

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: Every song is a piano recital, a punk rock concert, a tone poem, an art project, a dizzying expanse of white noise, a beautiful mess. But over Gallowbird's Bark, you begin to wonder the appeal of it all.

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: Last Day Of Summer is as good as anything White Denim have ever done. [Jan 2011, p.80]

Title: All The Time
Review: All the Time is filled with tracks that get the delicate balance right between experimentation and a love of an uncomplicated pop tune; between nostalgia for the past and a dedication to sounding like the future.

Title: Every Kind of Light
Review: The time apart has made the Posies come back fiercer, louder and heavier.

Title: Stay Together
Review: Overall it feels like a kind of gentrified pop: synthetic and nondescript, but predictably appealing all the same.

Title: ENERGY
Review: With Energy, Disclosure continue the refined, radio-friendly takes on house, U.K. garage, and more that made them stars, but find plenty of room to expand into new territory.

Title: Negative Feedback Resistor
Review: Off record, the band’s ideas about getting free are much more urgent, inventive, and contemporary than those psych clichés. Sadly, the band's stylistic conservatism has such a blurring effect on their records that any three tracks contain its total rewards.
Like many of his records, it's more of a collection of songs than a 'play from beginning to end' affair.

Title: The Lillywhite Sessions
Review: At times the distortion's kicked on ("Diggin' a Ditch"), or things venture into broken free-jazz ("JTR") or psychedelic madness ("Monkey Man"), but outside of the stylistic shifts the album plays it earnest.

Title: Happy New Year
Review: There's no unifying principal here-- just songs that are kinda psychedelic, kinda groove-oriented, and kinda long. While not exactly a disappointment, Happy New Year is a whole lot of "kinda," a record built around hesitancy that clutches the payoff tight in its arms.

Title: Little Red
Review: The ballads will be the tracks from Little Red to own the charts for the foreseeable future, but it’s on the 5am dancefloor that Katy B’s second album will score its biggest impact.

Title: Get Awkward
Review: Get Awkward is mostly more of the same but with more hooks, more wit, and a hell of a lot more emotion.

Title: Steeple
Review: There are certainly things to enjoy here, but too often Steeple is searching for its soul. It's a soul that will probably forever be caught in a bygone time.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: It's not a record to dissect or fall in love with, but rather a diverting, casual listen that brightens up the best part of an hour.

Title: Tomorrow's Modern Boxes
Review: A diverting, stoner-friendly 39 minutes. [Dec 2014, p.89]

Title: Everything Now
Review: The music glistens and gleams. ... An intoxicating ride. [Sep 2017, p.34]

Title: The Haunted Man
Review: While the album's comparatively restrained arrangements occasionally wilt in the face of Khan's fierce melodrama, The Haunted Man is still a worthy, often gorgeous entry in the Bat for Lashes canon.

Title: Forward Motion Godyssey
Review: Despite the lesser tracks on the record, Forward Motion Godyssey is a strong sophomore attempt from Post Animal. The band still have yet to truly define their unique identity, but as they are now, they are one of the stronger genre-bending psychedelic rock groups around.

Title: Ventriloquism
Review: The greatest strength of the album is that you don’t think of the original artists while Ndegeocello is singing. Some will feel she’s been reckless with beloved jams, others will fall in love with them all over again, and many will discover a new side of them even if they’ve heard the original a million times.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Some of the songs here are forgettable in the extreme.

Title: White Wilderness
Review: Though lyrically intimate, White Wilderness is a grand affair. [Feb 2011, p.72]

Title: Performance
Review: Performance doesn’t necessarily take White Denim in a drastically different direction, but it captures so many of the different sides of the band’s multi-faceted sound that it feels expansive and wholesome.

Title: Some People Have Real Problems
Review: Her fourth album brims with sunny hooks on its best tracks, and the alluring opener, 'Little Black Sandals,' affords her a rich, layered backdrop.

Title: New Roman Times
Review: A sweetly embittered geopolitical epic. [Dec 2004, p.124]

Title: Repo
Review: The only negative here is a lack of structure between songs, which makes Repo feel like something dropped in a pile at your feet.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: It's human connection despite the odds that has been at the heart of Bush's music from the beginning. With 50 Words for Snow, she casts the theme in a bolder and bleaker light than ever before.

Title: The Voyager
Review: It’s an incredibly well-observed, poignant look at what it means to be Jenny Lewis right now, yet lacks the indefinable quality to make it a classic.

Title: Crazy Itch Radio
Review: Their best album since... Remedy. [Sep 2006, p.131]

Title: Thank Your Lucky Stars
Review: In its own way, Thank Your Lucky Stars is just as rewarding as Depression Cherry, and arguably more immediate. Instead of releasing another mammoth effort like Bloom, they've delivered two smaller-scale triumphs that can be appreciated separately or together.

Title: Savages
Review: Savages is meant to be taken as both a warning and a rebel yell, and Cavalera and company connect on both levels, offering up an audio invoice for our past transgressions and a shot of adrenaline for the war ahead.

Title: Canta Lechuza
Review: At times doubts can surface as to whether it can fully work but against not inconsiderable odds he ultimately manages to pull it off, delivering on the whole an impressively irregular album of Latin-inflected laptop folk.

Title: Gold Cobra
Review: Time hasn't been kind to the once-popular amalgam of metal and hip-hop known as nü-metal, and it's been absolutely brutal to former scene king Limp Bizkit

Title: Culture
Review: Migos never try to recreate anything they’ve already done, but simply deliver more music that reflects their contagious, unadulterated flow. Culture is an album where they seize a moment of much-deserved success.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: X: The Godless Void and Other Stories
Review: Another rewarding helping of tuneful art-rock that moves their initial Sonic Youth fixations into far more expansive fields. [Feb 2020, p.108]

Title: SBTRKT
Review: There might not be anything on SBTRKT to bowl people over like Woon or Blake, but there's plenty to stick with after the next big thing comes along.

Title: Gandadiko
Review: It’s hypnotic in and of itself, and all impressions are purely in the ears/mind of the listener.

Title: Bionic
Review: Daring as some of the tracks are, they overwhelmingly loop her vocal around a generic house lick that has the effect of giving her very little to do vocally.

Title: Pink
Review: Color me unimpressed.

Title: Wooden Aquarium
Review: Both songs [Vapor and RIPP] provide interesting interludes in an otherwise pretty average album.

Title: Hold My Home
Review: Unfortunately, Hold My Home is not another baby step in the right direction, but rather a collection of slack-jawed tunes surrounding one or two borderline gems.

Title: The Tyranny of Will
Review: As is the case with most overstuffed hardcore albums, The Tyranny of Will lends itself well to a cherry-picking approach; keep some riffs and ideas, and toss the ones that don’t stick.

Title: Rebirth
Review: Although the cleaner melodies and pop polish seem to mute the rapper's stream-of-consciousness salvos, he still shines on "Drop the World," featuring Eminem.

Title: The Ascension
Review: There’s a stunning candour to the lyrics, though it gets a little stodgy in the mid-section and, at 80+ minutes, is a little more verbiage than the typical album. Yet we’re dealing with an untypical songwriter, and the last two tracks are among the best he’s ever written.

Title: Stranger
Review: Lean, at some point, gets lost in the wall of sound. And still it feels like the most essential music of his career: no longer an outsider looking in, but an artist fully embodying himself.

Title: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
Review: The disc reveals a few hard edges but offers optimism even as it explores the thornier corners of human behavior.

Title: Bedroom Tapes
Review: Without knowing it was made by a young Paul Woolfword, it might come off simply as passionate and touching hardware sketches with classic techno components. Nevertheless, these tapes show signs of promise in Woolford's ability to work within his limitations to create something powerful and personal.

Title: Poses
Review: Overall, Poses is more daring (and, at times, more mellow) than its predecessor, mostly because Wainwright has densely packed images and sounds in a way that is less immediately catchy and more complex.

Title: Rewild
Review: Needless to say, for a band only formed in January 2008, not only is this release very ambitious, but also well meticulously well crafted.

Title: So Far Gone
Review: The songs that were already previously available on "So Far Gone" are a winner and the new songs don't bring Drake down off the high cloud he's already on.

Title: Hippopotamus
Review: The result is an album which will satisfy fans of all the band’s distinct phases without necessarily ingratiating itself to anyone. [Oct 2017, p.61]

Title: Bring on the Comets
Review: These are high-flying songs in search of a place to land, and the warmth and seeming innocence of Pfunder's voice combined with all the familiar electro-disco trappings make this a record worth hearing for anyone not ready to let the past go without a fight.

Title: Grand Champ
Review: Too little stands out to make Grand Champ more than an uneven contender.

Title: Love In Flying Colors
Review: In 2013, it takes a certain level of bravery to make R&B this open-hearted, joyous, and musical. U.K. acts like 4hero, New Sector Movements, and Bugz in the Attic were doing it in the early 2000s, but none of them put it together quite like this, in one concentrated shot, with the songwriting on the same high level as the productions and arrangements. This crew is elite.

Title: On the Line
Review: The final result on display in On the Line--from the somber waltz of “Do Si Do” to the swell of strings at the climax of “Taffy”--is a new high watermark for a musician who’s never been willing to let a little rain get the best of her.

Title: Nepenthe
Review: Depending on your tastes, Nepenthe either marks Barwick's progression to a higher, more emotionally powerful and resonant place, or she's managed the musical equivalent of Instagramming her album.

Title: In the Court of the Wrestling Let's
Review: The tension between those two poles--refusing to grow up and yearning to move on-- is the emotional engine that drives the band and its impressively confident record.

Title: Mind Chaos
Review: The problem is not so much with the contents as with the packaging. ‘Mind Chaos’ is a pop record, and, as a pop record, it kind of works – it’s full of chart-friendly singles and sung by a bunch that are bound to find themselves doted on by 13-year-olds.

Title: Album of the Year
Review: May be his most mature, fully realized offering to date, though not necessarily his most thrilling.

Title: Beach Music
Review: Despite its experimental elements and trippy sensibility, Beach Music is relentlessly intimate, moving, and hard to shake--a notable trait for a young if experienced recording artist.

Title: Is and Always Was
Review: Personally, I wouldn’t be that interested in going back to Is And Always Was (what’s in a title?) again. For devout followers, not new converts.

Title: The Consuming Flame: Open Exercises in Group Form
Review: Given the album’s length and density, it resists close reading; if there is an organizing logic here, it is not readily apparent, although brushed drums and choppy vocal effects provide thematic through lines, and the occasional recurring motif lends a sense of narrative cohesion. But the music often unspools with natural ease.

Title: Black and White
Review: Across these varied tracks we hear Wretch 32 in all of his lyrical glory, making good on the promise he's shown since day one.

Title: There's Always Glimmer
Review: On her debut album, There’s Always Glimmer, Margaret’s violent view of songwriting translates to 34 minutes of serene and perceptive storytelling.

Title: Dolls of Highland
Review: Taken together, Craft delivers a fun and loose breakup album replete with colorful characters, memorable tunes, and an even more memorable vocal delivery--a noteworthy debut.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: Ultimately Hadreas has, with this album, proven his own hypothesis: you don’t necessarily have to blow things up to move forward.

Title: The Graceless Age
Review: It’s a well-crafted debut from a worthy new artist, but it’s competent rather than compelling.

Title: Out of the Black
Review: Most of the tracks sound pretty familiar, though, with just enough new tricks to avoid feeling like a complete rerun.

Title: Melbourne, Florida
Review: Melbourne, Florida is an exciting progression to old fans, and a solid entry point for new audiences.

Title: I, Gemini
Review: The more you listen to this record, the more it impresses you, even if their name is downright awful.

Title: Electric Circus
Review: Although he can be self-righteous, scattered, and grim, a team of truly youthful-minded producers is there to color the gray.

Title: Venus On Earth
Review: Venus on Earth proves that world-pop fusion needn’t be a pastiche of watered-down musical tropes, but rather something vital and soul affirming--a fever to embrace.

Title: Different Shades Of Blue
Review: The problem here, though, is that with the exception of the above songs ["Love Ain't a Love Song," "Oh Beautiful!," "Never Give All Your Heart," and "Trouble Town"], and maybe one or two others, the songs on Different Shades of Blue shade toward the generic side of things, and no matter how wonderful and gorgeous the guitar tones may be, it's hard to make a generic song sing memorably.

Title: Panic of Girls
Review: They reportedly had some difficulties securing a label for this release. And Unfortunately, it's easy to see why; Girls hits the panic button pretty early on. [Jul 2011, p.78]

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: Despite all the influences blowing through the ether, the resulting songs lack the dynamic range of their most obvious inspirations, each charting a familiar trajectory through a slow build and release of cacophonous guitars and caterwauling vocals that gets old around the five-minute mark.

Title: Move Like This
Review: Long after we thought we'd heard the last from them, the Cars have made their darkest, most romantic album. It pulls you along.

Title: The Duel
Review: The raggedy, pared-back approach puts the spotlight right back where it should be: on Moorer herself. [May 2004, p.106]

Title: Aftershock
Review: Aftershock is another worthy entry into Motörhead’s long discography, with 14 rollicking tracks of brawn, broads, and blazing riffs.

Title: I Bet on Sky
Review: I Bet on Sky fits nicely within the band's catalog, former and present. [Aug/Sep 2012, p.109]

Title: Havilah
Review: Sidewinding bass lines and slashing guitar help pull together ballads of marital woe ('The Drifting Housewife'), epic rock­outs ('I Am the Supercargo'), and rousing takes on regret ('Your Acting's Like the End of the World').

Title: Jacuzzi Boys
Review: Comparisons to the Smith Westerns (“Be My Prism”) and Yuck (“Dust”) may be inevitable, but the Jacuzzi Boys retain enough of their previous humor and urgency (“Rubble”, “Hotline”) to stand on their own.

Title: Hold On 'til the Night
Review: Word to Greyson: Hold on to 13 as long as you can.

Title: Anna Calvi
Review: Calvi's outstanding vocal tone and arrangements carry the emotional punches, while her lyrics can occasionally take a backseat role.

Title: Xen
Review: His time alongside Gesaffelstein added to his understanding of the space between beats, and the emotive power of these hesitations.

Title: Earthly Delights
Review: It’d be rather too easy to sketch this as a record suitable only for chewing off your own tongue to: in fact, just like the Hieronymus Bosch triptych it appears to name-check, Earthly Delights is actually a work far richer in tone, shade and technique than its lurid sheen might suggest.

Title: One Bedroom
Review: A warm sonic cocoon with synthesizer veins, it possesses the rare quality of making the listener feel like an active ingredient of the music.

Title: American VI: Ain't No Grave
Review: If there were any justice, Ain't No Grave would be the last album released under Cash's name. It is not only a compelling contribution to his legacy, but an offering that closes the historic American Recordings series with the same stamp of quality that began it.

Title: Destroyer's Rubies
Review: Bejar is so wound up in his own idiosyncratic mythologies, so hopelessly himself that some fans have already said it sounds like a greatest hits record; appropriate that a meta-rocker’s final frontier is his own reflection in the mirror.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: Even more devastation stems fro Iain Cook and Martin Doherty's sophisticated and catchy layers of synthesizers and vocal loops. [Oct 2013, p.82]

Title: Silver Wilkinson
Review: If Silver Wilkinson is supposed to be a journey, it sounds like Mr. Wilkinson got a little lost along the way.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: On Collapse Into Now, they sound like they'd rather be a band than a legend, which must be why they keep pushing on.

Title: Confess
Review: There is a subtle grandeur to George Lewis Jr.'s voice and musical nature.

Title: Alberta Cross
Review: Alberta Cross' familiar '70s rock soundscape is lush and relaxed--ideal for the self-reflection that's fostered by long drives, Sunday afternoons and quiet dinner conversations with friends.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: You’re Dead! is experimental and often ambient, but has so much attention to detail and raw talent (Herbie Hancock, Angel Deradoorian, Kendrick Lamar) that it could never be background music.

Title: Divide and Exit
Review: The Streets' Original Pirate Material crossbred with The Fall's Grotesque, it's nasty and brutish, but mercifully short. [Jun 2014, p.83]

Title: The DeAndre Way
Review: DeAndre's repetitive chants and thudding beats are likely to yield more commercial successes for his resume. And while they may not win over the Recording Academy, they can be fun in moderation.

Title: Anastasis
Review: While Anastasis is typified by lengthy songs and sometimes rather ponderous beats, Gerald is in her element on Kiko. [Sep 2012, p.95]

Title: On My One
Review: Bugg has always had one foot in the past and that’s fine, but On My One might as well be an official challenge to The Strypes in the ‘parents record collection’ department--though a mercifully more bearable one.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Ultimately, Kamikaze’s length and curtailed guest list make it less grueling than Revival, but Eminem’s indignant grandstanding has no discernible relation to the rap world he complains about.

Title: EGOLI
Review: Across a baggy 18 tracks, Egoli maintains a sense of purpose, but only comes into sharp focus when a particular artist grabs the reins.

Title: Let's Stay Friends
Review: Everything clicks on Let's Stay Friends, from blasts of Rocket from the Crypt bombastic rock on The Equestrian to Fugazi-sharp guitars backing Tim Harrington's feverish, controlled vocals on Patty Lee.

Title: News and Tributes
Review: While less exuberant and love-me-or-else desperate than the debut, News and Tributes is energizing in its own right, full of asymmetrical hooks and surprise detours.

Title: Excerpts
Review: overall Excerpts is an evocative, sophisticated and charming record, awash with imaginative atmospheres, that looks back to the past for inspiration without ever wallowing in sentiment.

Title: Absolute Truth
Review: Absolute Truth rights the ship with enough whistling milkman melodies to sink the Titanic. [Sep 2016, p.95]

Title: Cosmic Ocean Ship
Review: Todd's new album, Cosmic Ocean Ship, is full of songs that contrast the chilliness of urban settings with the call of the exotic, and come down strongly in favor of the latter.

Title: Waterloo to Anywhere
Review: It doesn't sound like a masterpiece; then again, it does nothing to damage its maker's reputation, which is more than you can say for Doherty's post-Libertines efforts.

Title: Slugger
Review: Slugger isn't a perfectly polished, radio-ready set of glossy chart-topping pop tunes, but an infectiously fun foray into shimmering, socially conscious synth-pop.

Title: I'm Your Empress Of
Review: A bold and entrancing set of songs, it’s hard not to see what a big leap forward she took on this album.

Title: Everybody Got Their Something
Review: It's a sassy section of sultry soul and urban vibratos, yet a snarling demeanor asking for a little respect also peeks through the dozen-song set list.

Title: Knowle West Boy
Review: There is a static-y scratchy cackle running through Knowles West Boy that gives ut the energy of a classic reggae record and a post modern work at the same time. But then at the same time, there is a just-recently-became-dated tone to Knowles West Boy that feels like Tricky is trying to scramble onto trendy bandwagons. [Fall 2008, p.84]

Title: Hopelessness
Review: The subject matter, then, is unrelenting. But Anohni’s impassioned delivery succeeds in making ecstatic music out of it, carried along by propulsive soundbeds; music that is equal to the apocalypse.

Title: This Unruly Mess I've Made
Review: The album isn’t necessarily a classic, or better than The Heist, but it does prove Macklemore is here to stay.

Title: Delirium Tremens
Review: Whether you enjoyed the first two excursions or you’re a Gainsbourg neophyte, Delirium Tremens is every bit as strong and enjoyable as its predecessors.

Title: The Chief
Review: The exclusion of US hit Classic Man (which soundtracks a key scene in the Oscar-nominated Moonlight) leaves the album lacking a truly memorable moment, but the Afrobeat-inspired A Little Bit More and the carefree, soca-style Some Kind of Way showcase a versatile, genre-bending talent.

Title: Charli
Review: Charli is a more-than-worthy follow-up to arguably the decade’s best pop release.

Title: May The Lord Watch
Review: Phonte and Big Pooh sound rejuvenated, and while 9th Wonder isn’t on this record (or part of the group), the beats compiled by Khrysis, Nottz, Zo!, Black Milk, and Devin Morrison have a sophisticated bounce, making this feel like an old Little Brother album without dwelling too much in the past.

Title: El Pintor
Review: The sum total is unmistakably, and welcomingly, Interpol. [Oct 2014, p.89]

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: [It] takes some persistance. [18 Mar 2006, p.35]

Title: Every Kind of Light
Review: The band is now more of a collaborative project than a Jon Auer-and-Ken Stringfellow-with-hired-guns proposition, and it shows in the eloquence of the songs here.

Title: Researching the Blues
Review: After 34 years of recording, the brothers think it's their best collection yet. Again breaking the artistic rule, they may be right.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: When the opening track of this third album features CSN-style harmonising about hotel lobbies, you wonder if they're trying a little too hard to sound like a burnt-out folk rock supergroup from 1971. [June 2010, p. 92]

Title: Six
Review: Despite their tendency to wade dangrously close to parody, the Black Heart Procession's continuing themes of despair, gloom and doom are still what make them so appealing as they continue to defy their sunny upbringing.

Title: Wishful Thinking
Review: There are little surprises on Wishful Thinking, but with that comes little letdown.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: Unsurprisingly Heartbreak is a grower. At first it does sound minimalist and sparse but the album is layered with delicacy and marked with a maturity.

Title: Communion
Review: Communion is a very good album; it’s just a shame it’s been spread out over the space of two albums.

Title: Quarter Turns Over a Living Line
Review: This is an astonishing album, but not an easy listen.

Title: Mura Masa
Review: Mura Masa’s nuance, confidence and obvious versatility betray his relative inexperience, and it’s increasingly clear that he is already a musical force to be reckoned with.

Title: Alone In The Universe
Review: The predictability of Alone In The Universe is its strongest suit, these are all cast-iron songs that will sit on an ELO retrospective beamed down from that spaceship in 10538 and nobody would imagine they were released 40 years after their golden age.

Title: The Ways We Separate
Review: Regardless of the inconsistencies, The Ways We Separate still leaves its mark.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: 'Port Of Morrow' is a glorious and confident return, even if it lacks a little darkness at times.

Title: Melbourne
Review: Unfortunately, Scott is more often than not lyrically uninteresting.

Title: Watersports
Review: If Watersports paced itself, if it weren’t afraid to be shorter, if it understood the power of precision, it could have been more awe-inspiring.

Title: Virtue
Review: This is a record where inspired ideas are constantly battling for oxygen with dubious ones.

Title: Tied to a Star
Review: This album’s most striking moments often come when Mascis commits unreservedly to the ballads.

Title: Sick Scenes
Review: Any nuance is stomped by hectic drums and background chants, but it's hard not to warm to people acting on the very human compulsion to make their presence known in case they spin out of reach forever. [May 2017, p.107]

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: While Maya certainly shows no diminution of sheer sonic ingenuity, it suffers from a shrinking of the spirit. [Aug 2010, p.112]

Title: Save Rock and Roll
Review: I can only assume the title Save Rock and Roll is intentionally ironic on their part because even they should know it's quite a stretch to call this rock and roll.

Title: Attack & Release
Review: The bottom line is that most of the songs here do fit well within the framework of their blues-rock aesthetic, and that's what makes Attack work as a Black Keys album.

Title: The Bird and the Bee
Review: This album maintains youth and vigor through dirty language and clean production, but eventually settles for something very middle-of-the-road.

Title: Embrace
Review: There are occasional lapses (‘I Run’ is textbook Embrace, and thus completely forgettable), and probably too few ideas to really sustain a record, plus of course Editors have made pretty much this exact album at least twice in the last ten years, but still--it’s a hell of a rug-pull from a band long written-off, and a reminder to some of us that everything should be approached with an open mind.

Title: Moon 2
Review: With its excellent fourth album, Moon 2, the band evokes a cosmic utopia of its own making and yet remains tethered to a relentless, earthbound groove.

Title: Red Dirt Girl
Review: Alternately sparse and lush, Red Dirt Girl can be seen as a companion piece to 1995's Wrecking Ball... The diverse production only adds to Harris' earthy songwriting, adding interest to what could otherwise be lulls during the more subdued songs, and really showcases the understated lyrics that the singer has slowly become recognized for.

Title: Love Is Here
Review: The band, while heavy on charm, is light in its ability to demonstrate any diversity in its songs.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: Oddly, the unconventional sequencing and measured pace of the album make the fragmented mess hold together quite well.

Title: Green Lanes
Review: While Green Lanes doesn’t exactly break new ground, it does refine their warm’n’cosy formula enough to interest.

Title: truANT
Review: A high-voltage treat. [22/29 Aug 2003, p.133]

Title: Just Be Free
Review: Just Be Free is a wonderfully functional album, displaying Queen Freedia at her very best.

Title: A Love Extreme
Review: A Love Extreme giddily steals from and collides with a kaleidoscope of genres, all without a trace of modern guilt.

Title: Time (The Revelator)
Review: A winsome, beautiful collection of songs... Welch has never seemed more assured, building a creatively expansive work out of modest ingredients.

Title: Paper Tigers
Review: The Caesars adopt a bombastic, arena-friendly brand of Sixties revivalism recalling that of... The Soundtrack Of Our Lives. Fortunately, the Caesars are good at it. [5 May 2005, p.74]

Title: Russian Roulette
Review: Perhaps his greatest achievement here lies in the construction, an LP that balances the rappers with the beats into a seamless record.

Title: July Flame
Review: July Flame is carefully composed, ever-deepening, glinting and glowing in new ways each time it’s played; there’s an inkling of something greater coming just around the bend, but for now it’s Veirs’ finest work.

Title: Us
Review: Empress Of takes listeners into a rich sonic environment on Us, while placing careful emphasis on the emotional territory she ventures into. The universality Rodriguez has sought to embody the record with is present, yet the vulnerability she is known for remains.

Title: Paralytic Stalks
Review: Paralytic Stalks is downright exhausting.

Title: Dear
Review: Packed with songs of delicious but unsettling despair. [Apr 2012, p.98]

Title: Confident
Review: Nothing else on Confident is quite as much fun [as Cool For The Summer], but Lovato's intensity never wavers as the album alternates between trap-influenced midtempo tracks like the Iggy Azalea-assisted 'Kingdom Come' and bombastic power ballads that show off her mighty vocals.

Title: Gone by the Dawn
Review: Gone By The Dawn is, at many turns, a lovely record. But it also seems to be a transitional record, as the group tries to find a more distinctive place for itself beyond '50s and '60s nostalgia.

Title: Electric Lines
Review: Though solidly enjoyable, Electric Lines could have benefitted from some more concretely original ideas to propel it forward. But when Goddard taps into his love for house, disco, and techno, his enthusiasm radiates through the speakers.

Title: Natural History
Review: While there's still no reason to call these guys accessible, there are moments here.

Title: Rat's Spit
Review: Lynch can be heard loud and (sometimes) clear here, floating among ideas that he finally allows to breathe. Despite the traces of anxiety written into the lines he sings, it’s a welcome respite when so much else has turned to smog.

Title: Fearless
Review: Swift's gentle touch is as enduring as her songcraft, and this musical maturity may not quite jibe with her age but it does help make Fearless one of the best mainstream pop albums of 2008.

Title: American Head
Review: The album has a slow chain drive narrative to it that feels as close to a recounting as anything the group has done. And there is a certain comfort in settling in for the album’s nearly hour-long journey to the before and the beyond.

Title: Indestructible
Review: Indestructible is the document of a band retaining their energy and refining their vision to be honest to themselves and their fans, while spitting venom in the eyes of their detractors. [Oct 2003, p.115]

Title: CAVES
Review: Caves may not have been the follow-up fans expected of her, but as Tristen's artistry continues to evolve, future left turns such as this will be welcome.

Title: Broken Bells
Review: He may have found the perfect partner in the Shins' James Mercer, whose moody pop sensibilities complement Mouse's muted time-capsule colors.

Title: The Black Magic Show
Review: Epic and memorable. [Jun 2006, p.188]

Title: Tremors
Review: Sohn casts his falsetto in blues-worthy scenarios--a one-man band balancing songcraft and heady post-dubstep production better than James Blake or Rhye, two inevitable comparisons.

Title: Chutes Too Narrow
Review: Seems to be the culmination and synthesis of a solid musical progression from good, yet uncertain and unchallenging, pop music to better, more confident, but still unchallenging, pop music.

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: With Nicolay (and those horns) back in the fold, the Hold Steady can provide strong melodies even when Finn isn't singing. It makes for a fun listen, and it's one of the most entertaining albums I've heard in 2019.

Title: The Spirit Indestructible
Review: Furtado isn't entirely successful; at times, the album is more impressive for what she intends to achieve than what she accomplishes. And yet for all its contradictions and clumsiness, it's hard not to admire The Spirit Indestructible, for it is that rare thing: a major-label album that bears the unmistakably messy, human stamp of an artist.

Title: Every Country's Sun
Review: A considered evolution from first minute to last, with no real enforced show in between, it may not be immediately obvious but by the end one truth remains clearer than ever, across a whole album--Mogwai can really do scale.

Title: The Mainframe
Review: The LP is repeatedly let down by its own exhibitionism.

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun
Review: All brilliant stuff, but a bit more self-indulgence and derring-do wouldn't go amiss next time.

Title: Good Evening
Review: Good Evening is unbelievably catchy and vintage but at times is weighted down by its own obscurity, sometimes becoming far too much background noise and not enough of an active listen to provide enough distinction between tracks.

Title: Heaven Is Humming
Review: An album s indebted to garage as it is to pop. [Sep 2019, p.27]

Title: MPLSound
Review: MPLSound might be the most pristine for what it ultimately lacks: the sense of real, lusty sin.

Title: Britney Jean
Review: As the album opener, [Alien is] hard to ignore but it inadvertently sets the tone for the rest of Britney Jean: she's not one of us and doesn't feel comfortable where she's at, and that uneasiness underpins the rest of this vaguely dispiriting album.

Title: SremmLife
Review: Coming in at only 11 songs, SremmLife is a lively surge of hedonism and recklessness.

Title: Intimacy
Review: Brave, individual and heartfelt, Intimacy offers treasure for fans old and new.

Title: Inside The Ships
Review: I can't say I'll be giving Inside the Ships more spins this year, but it's offbeat charm never felt like a waste of my time when I did, and that's more than I can say for most albums this year.

Title: Make the Best of It
Review: The fact that it's essentially more of the same might make it uninteresting to some, but to fans of the band or any of its widely known predecessors like Jimmy Eat World or Taking Back Sunday, that sameness will bring a welcome sense of comfort.

Title: Seabed
Review: Seabed is the worst of all worlds, all fluff without substance and repetition without meaning.

Title: Persona
Review: Each listen helps to start piece together the overall shape of the album, something which remains a little shrouded throughout. But its length, and depth, is also Persona's strength. An album to get lost in and to discover bits of wonder along the way.

Title: Burnt Offering
Review: Recorded live: there's a twisting, doomy intensity to these 10 instrumentals. [Dec 2014, p.73]

Title: Rokstarr
Review: Up-tempo club jams like "Break Your Heart," "Dynamite," and "I Can Be" sport melodies sturdy enough to support all the digital detailing, and power ballads such as "I'll Never Love Again" and "Falling in Love" do the gathering-steam thing as efficiently as more traditionally presented songs by Diane Warren or Kara DioGuardi.

Title: Passenger
Review: For all its deft arrangements and catchy chorus hook lines, Passenger feels unforced, spontaneous and timeless; indeed, such is its unaffected delivery that it might have been recorded 30 years ago or last month

Title: Heroes
Review: Inconsistency and lack of focus mars Heroes, which relies too heavily on misguided collaborations that don't add anything of value to the album.

Title: The Night Chancers
Review: The Night Chancers is Dury’s most accomplished work, its self awareness and innate understanding of genre and language shows the songwriter to be in the prime of his creativity.

Title: Meet the Humans
Review: These songs are strong enough to be recorded with minimal accompaniment and that instantly recognisible, hushed voice--but the best moments are when his love of electronica shines through.

Title: Real Gone
Review: His first, full-tilt protest record... he comes out swinging, in every respect. [Oct 2004, p.110]

Title: Anagrams
Review: The Liquid "I'm Turning Inside Out" and lyrically unsettling, Bon Iver-ish "Shine A Light On Him" are standouts in a quietly haunting set. [Aug 2016, p.83]

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: While the production values on the album are stronger, so is The Odd Couple's focus on Cee-Lo's voice.

Title: Strange Cousins From The West
Review: Freakonomics proves they still pack a punch, though. [Aug 2009, p.101]

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: Whatever he’s doing, the results are uniformly fantastic: rich, fascinating and moving, packed with gorgeous melodies and arrangements that feel alive, constantly writhing into unexpected new shapes.

Title: Hiss Spun
Review: Though it may be her second consecutive album to lean heavily on metal, Hiss Spun deftly incorporates a diverse range of sounds.

Title: Undone At 31
Review: Rather than a mundane breakup album rife with familiar tropes, Frawley channels his distress into a unique and engaging album that is easy to spend some time with.

Title: Circuital
Review: My Morning Jacket's new album, Circuital, does dial back the weirdness of 2008's Evil Urges.

Title: Hairdresser Blues
Review: Hairdresser Blues offers a more intimate window in to a more down-to-earth personal world, allowing room for that enormous persona to be folded back into the greater sum of Bogart's infectious songwriting personality.

Title: Madvillainy
Review: The wily creativity on display here is astonishing. [Jun 2004, p.114]

Title: Mapping the Rendezvous
Review: There's a certain modish charm to the opener, "Lucifer's Dreams," while "Finest Hour" show an aptitude for gentle balladry. Elsewhere, though, sub-Smiths smartarsery abounds. [Dec 2016, p.26]

Title: Once Upon a Time in the West
Review: To paraphrase Jarvis, you’ve got to wonder what exactly Hard-Fi are going to do for an encore--cos this is hardcore.

Title: Some of My Best Friends Are DJs
Review: Moments of playful mixing magic are at times followed by baffling inanity.

Title: No Mas
Review: Javelin don't yet possess the same kind of wit and invention of their most obvious forbearers, but there's enormous potential here, and the biggest compliment that can be paid to No Más is that it will sound best when reduced down to an audio tape and shoved into one of the boomboxes that Langford and van Buskirk so slavishly worship.

Title: Future Brown
Review: There is still enough variety in styles that make it a successful conjuring. And, once there, the free-form melting pot of production and vocals continues to satisfy.

Title: Eternal Turn of the Wheel
Review: What makes Eternal Turn of the Wheel so captivating is not so much the band's furious blend of rural sampling combined with their consistent prowess as black metal musicians, but the enchanting manor in which they craft the tracks.

Title: Sweating The Plague
Review: Some good songs emerge--"Ego Central High" is a glammy gem that makes its repetitiveness a virtue--but otherwise this is heavy listening that too often edges towards stodge. [Dec 2019, p.29]

Title: Native Invader

Title: Emperor's Nightingale
Review: Ultimately, Emperor's Nightingale is, despite its inconsistencies, a vital Stereo MCs album, a phrase you wouldn't expect to utter in 2011.

Title: The Official Body
Review: What's most unfortunate is that Shopping can do better--evidenced not only by their previous work but by a few stand-out tracks on this album.

Title: First Rose of Spring
Review: First Rose of Spring is the work of an artist who will never grow old.

Title: Dungeonesse
Review: The group's music is far more pointed and focused when she's standing at its center, proving that it's not just the parts (polished and hummable though they may be), but Wasner's transformative presence that ultimately sets Dungeonesse apart from the rest of the '90s-mining pack.

Title: Waxing Gibbous
Review: The combination of bile and hook, of wiry, mistrustful intelligence meshed in danceable synth pop works throughout the album, the contradictions bristling without overwhelming the tunes.

Title: Hologram Jams
Review: JL have dropped a weird pop record so humorously danceable that Ke$ha’s probably planning a collaboration as we type.

Title: Pause
Review: Without resorting to sappy new age or yuppie lounge cliches, Hebden has created a blissed-out ambient album for the post-rave generation.

Title: Ratchet
Review: It’s an incredible album strewn with highlights obvious and sneaky, the rare debut that holds up the weight of its backstory, with the added brassiness of assuring us that’s just him on the regular. Now we know.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: This could have been Costello's urban album, or his funk album, or his black album--but instead, it's simply his new album. [No. 102, p.54]

Title: Outside Closer
Review: "The Lost You" is a breathless, if unfortunate, peak. What follows are four miserable, mostly tuneless dirges that bring a slow death to [the] album. [#67, p.97]

Title: Tremors
Review: It’s by no means a flawless debut but it provides a perfect platform from which SOHN can only rise.

Title: Wolf
Review: We already knew he was a talented composer and producer, but Wolf suggests he now may just be the finished article.

Title: I Used to Spend So Much Time Alone
Review: I Used to Spend So Much Time Alone skilfully expresses complex and murky emotions with clear and concise lyrics.

Title: The Divine Feminine
Review: The listenability is at an all-time high, but the writing itself is still lackluster.

Title: Love and Other Planets

Title: Cut Your Teeth
Review: Kyla La Grange still has a voice you want to listen to, but two albums in, it seems like she’s still searching for the best music to set it to.

Title: Flamingo
Review: Many people who have heard Flamingo have said it sounds a lot like a Killers album. Wrong. It is more that The Killers' albums sounded like Brandon Flowers solo albums, with a bit of indie guitar on top to snare those Reading & Leeds headline slots.

Title: As Long as You Are
Review: It’s a listening experience that’s as satisfying and rewarding as those aforementioned records. With a band as assured and stylistically unique as Future Islands, a choice to stay in their lane can only mean more good things.

Title: From Every Sphere
Review: Harcourt would do himself well by spending a bit more time on his lyrics; a lot of the time it sounds as though he's just filling in the space between choruses.

Title: Fantasy

Title: Siesta

Title: Dear John

Title: Meltdown
Review: The band's melodies continue to be undeniable, but when guitar solos are added to the mix, the combination is electric. [#9]

Title: II
Review: While II has its stellar (and interstellar) moments, the band could use a little focus--otherwise they could risk becoming just a fuzzy memory.

Title: Underneath The Rainbow
Review: Underneath the Rainbow shoots for crossover appeal without compromising their tried-and-true aesthetic.

Title: Disc-Overy
Review: It's a super-confident debut breadth-wise, but a misfire in terms of depth--it stretches too far and ends up light on substance and personality.

Title: The Sunlandic Twins
Review: Occasionally masterful, frequently evocative, and consistently lovely.

Title: Indigo
Review: Glossy and glamorous, maybe, but it feels like a beautiful-designed dead end. [Oct 2018, p.37]

Title: Smile
Review: Smile is their exquisite-corpse sequel, a near-automatic exercise in drawing inspiration from anybody but themselves.

Title: placeholder
Review: With a singular perspective though, Hand Habits are in a lane of their own. [May 2019, p.111]

Title: The Search Engine
Review: The over-riding impression is that this is a tired, conservative and weirdly insular album.

Title: LCD Soundsystem
Review: Like just about everybody else these days, Murphy's more skilled at creating isolated tracks than making full-lengths, even though this particular full-length has few weak spots and unfolds smoothly as you listen to it from beginning to end. The bonus disc, containing all the stray single tracks, adds a great deal of value.

Title: The Evens
Review: The Evens’ self-titled debut does sound curiously like hardcoreless moments of The Argument polished and lengthened into full-fledged songs.

Title: Repave
Review: The limits of Vernon’s imagination and drive have yet to be truly tested, and based on the size of the sounds that he’s summoning here, the ceiling isn’t even in his sights yet.

Title: Process
Review: Over Process‘ 10 songs, Sampha executes a sonically adventurous vision that’s entirely his own and builds on his enormous potential.

Title: The Air Conditioned Nightmare
Review: After a promising start, the LP soon defaults to a brand of quirky, over-stimulated electropop that doesn't really do justice to Woodhead's smart, conceptual lyrics. [May 2015, p.72]

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: This LP could have injected some creativity back into 4/4, instead it settles for quaintness.

Title: Whiteout Conditions

Title: On Triple Beams

Review: The music is cinematic in scope, offering Armageddon and salvation in turn. [May 2020, p.25]

Title: Blonde

Title: Make My Head Sing
Review: Those heavier cuts are the album’s best--dark, dreamy and abrasive.

Title: Father Creeper
Review: It is a wearying listen, overcrowded and too loud and too harsh, and to engage actively with it is to feel your knuckles whiten with effort.

Title: Days Run Away
Review: Alas, they undermine themselves with a weedy production which too often gives proceedings a demo-ish air. [Mar 2005, p.99]

Title: Rome
Review: Few records will be made this year with such love and devotion, and you'll be able to tell it too. It's delicious.

Title: Kiss of Death
Review: No matter the number of bright moments, you can't help but feel that Jadakiss has his best days ahead of him.

Title: Eating Us
Review: Eating Us is still an unqualified success, the pop album that many followers in the footsteps of Kraftwerk have tried and failed to make.

Review: This is a vital debut that captures a dark, uncertain time, but counters displacement--in all its forms--with grace, nerve, and a spine-tingling call to arms, and perhaps just as importantly, a call to dance.

Review: For all this record’s hubris, the long-touted “generational voice” that is Alex Turner has never sounded more real, or more himself.

Title: Melted
Review: On the whole, this is the best album yet from Ty Segall, as joy-ride thrilling as the debut, as clearly delivered as Lemons, but with stronger, more varied writing.

Title: X

Title: Blackstar
Review: It feels as bold and weird as anything in Bowie’s back catalogue, sure to delight some and infuriate others.

Review: While the other material is good, these moments are great. [Sep 2014, p.104]

Review: [They] have taken their love of Fifties kitsch and Sixties pop off the Jesus & Mary Chain Gang of Love and down to the Velvet Underground.

Review: Despite having gotten a bit too caught up in imitation rather than innovation, the trio have succeeded in making an album that's accessible without compromising their artistry.

Title: Ivy Tripp

Review: A worthy and wonderful addition to [their] cannon. [Aug 2012, p.98]

Title: 99Â¢
Review: Although the bulk of the album oscillates between sarcasm and sincerity, the most fully realized songs transcend that spectrum entirely.

Title: Piteous Gate
Review: Whipple's previous PAN release, the Scythians EP, hinted at the greatness to come from this Janus club night co-founder, yet was a little too short to really demonstrate his true power. It took a full-length release to truly suss out the immensity of M.E.S.H.
