Review: Overall Open Here is joyful and reliably brilliant. [Mar 2018, p.108]

Title: Soft Friday
Review: This is cold-blooded revenge pop that strikes like a shard of shattered plate to the heart.

Title: You Will Know Nothing
Review: The African-influenced essence of the record carries it along with grace but ultimately this is about celebrating the potential of the riff as rhythm. [Aug 2018, p.28]

Title: Mauve
Review: With strong, fully realized statements such as Mauve, Ringo Deathstarr are making a strong case for being one of the most vital bands in shoegaze today.

Title: Yes, It's True
Review: Yes, It’s True starts out along a rather pedestrian path of nod-along rock-by-numbers.

Title: Home
Review: Home is a groovy, infectious and deeply listenable record, recommended for all fans of repetitive electronic beats.

Title: Hold It In
Review: Hold It In finds these crusty veterans meeting the threat of middle-age ennui with ingenuity and enthusiasm. [Oct 2014, p.57]

Title: Way Down Low
Review: From whimsical pop-like melodies to folk-tinged and saucy jazz songs and truly inspired covers, Kat Edmonson brings diversity to her second self-released album.

Title: Ghetto Bells
Review: More eclectic than most Chesnutt releases.

Title: Gliss Riffer
Review: Gliss Riffer is a magnifying glass held to that opening in one hand and an opium pill twirling between his index and ring fingers in the other, egging on the impending lucid dream that's been in the works for years. He's only now offering an audacious embrace.

Title: Olden Yolk
Review: Songs move at a satisfying clip, with modal harmonies and woody violin scrapes creating a misty, pensive atmosphere in which their analytical tales of fleeting urban encounters feel like ancient fables. [Mar 2018, p.31]

Title: Write Me Back
Review: Write Me Back won't totally please R Kelly fans who crave the silly pleasures of Trapped In The Closet, but it is without doubt an excellent record.

Title: Ascent
Review: Everything works and there's really nothing more a fan of either Organs or Comets could ask for.

Title: Sisyphus
Review: An ostentatiously operatic tour de force.

Artist: Beth Jeans Houghton & The Hooves of Destiny
Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: Has enough bright moments to ensure that Houghton will hone her experimentation in time.

Title: The Invisible Man
Review: While the San Francisco-based songwriter is still crafting unmistakably Eitzel-esque gloom tunes, his latest, The Invisible Man, is his most eclectic outing to date, veering from the low-key electronica of the opening track to the understated atmospherics of "Sleep."

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: It's admirable that they have made such a shameless ode to that which they deem most important to their musical output, or at least what they thought might sell, but the way in which it seems so forced and uncomfortable is the opposite of what anyone would have expected.

Title: Acrobats
Review: Acrobats drags a bit near the end, but there's no denying that it's a huge leap forward.

Title: Subiza
Review: Subiza is a dance album, make no mistake, but it's far from typical and it's blissful enough to be enjoyed at home in the midst of Beach House, Hot Chip, and LCD Soundsystem.

Title: This Path Tonight
Review: A gentle fleshing-out of tracks might’ve boosted it, but this is as close as the ever-youthful 74-year-old has yet come to doing an American Recordings. Autumnal, rather than valedictory.

Title: City of Refuge
Review: Although something of a melting pot, this is an original and accessible album, blending world influences with old time American music.

Title: Trophy
Review: Recalling contemporary debuts by names like Anna Burch and Madison Cunningham in terms of its polished sophistication, consistency, and fault-finding lyrics, Trophy introduces a songwriter fully formed.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: Their approach is eclectic, esoteric, and not easy on the ear, though it does have a restless energy which suggests it might work better live. [June 2008, p.97]

Title: Spoils
Review: With Spoils, Alasdair Roberts has delivered his finest work to date. [May 2009, p.95]

Title: BE
Review: Shades of light and dark ripple throughout and keep the listener guessing.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: Noah And The Whale would have done better to focus on the more organic sound they became quite good at than become just another forgettable crossover act.

Title: The Fall
Review: The result is avant-roots music that rocks, albeit gently.

Title: Light Up Gold
Review: Parquet Courts' over-the-top energy, speed, and succinctness makes the combination sound fresher than anything the original elements have managed in years.

Title: Expo 86
Review: Expo 86 feels divided down the middle, and both writers deliver some of their best work to date.

Title: b'lieve i'm goin down
Review: B’lieve I’m Goin’ Down is a quietly unexpected album. It feels very much like another Kurt Vile album, but close listening--or even not that close--will reveal some serious blues and some complicated dealing with it.

Title: You Know You Like It
Review: In a contemporary pop age of increasingly tired homogeneity, AlunaGeorge are a very welcome breath of fresh air.

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: For the most part, however, this is a gentle hybrid that, while not reaching the heights of either artists' best work, like Eno and Byrne's recent "Everything That Happens Will Happen Today", succeeds on its own terms, creating a new world without sounding too cloyingly contemporary, or too much like the work of ageing pioneers proving they can hang with modern times.

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: A few cuts ('Big N Bad,' '54321' or 'Step') don’t succeed in showcasing her talents as well as the rest of the album, but Ultraviolet succeeds in bringing together older Kid Sis favorites with new material, and--most importantly--is just a really fun party record.

Title: The Kid
Review: The music never changes, but with each new listen The Kid seems to deepen and expand as new details emerge, marking in reality a kind of growth on our part as listeners.

Title: Ritual Union
Review: Ultimately the effort is mighty, and Little Dragon is still clearly at the top of the electro R&B pile. But Ritual Union is a mixed bag, its feet uncomfortably divided between the dance floor and the couch.

Title: Biophilia
Review: Biophilia is a wonderful record in the most literal sense; it overflows with wonder. [Oct 2011, p.111]

Title: Grown Unknown
Review: These rather minimal tracks tempt because of Ices' fervor for ritualistic body percussion and headphone-ready mixing. [Feb 2011, p.73]

Title: Turn Out the Lights
Review: Baker is carefully balancing both sides without leaning too far in one direction, and though her songwriting is sharp, its fastidious uniformity makes the whole of it feel one-note.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: The most accessible album from Mike Hadreas (aka Perfume Genius) to date, without sacrificing any of his otherworldly strangeness and rich emotionalism. ... It is an album of vast depths that will reward a lot of listening.

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth
Review: It’s been well over a decade since Julian Casablancas & Co. have released an album as taut and wasted and sexy as Anthems for Doomed Youth.

Title: Ribbons
Review: A record that focuses on fleeting glimpses, on liminal evenings and burgeoning mornings, it’s imbued with sublime melodic flair and a lingering atmosphere that echoes after the final note has been plucked gracefully from Bibio’s well-served guitar.

Title: Ursa Major
Review: The formula is dependable and timeworn but ultimately successful, as Third Eye Blind follows the paint-by-numbers blueprint with stunning efficiency.

Title: Hannah
Review: Whether she is quite literally questioning her own happiness in "Hannah Happiness" or dealing with the act of sharing feelings with others in "Stranger Sat by Me," Read awakens the overwhelming feeling of second-guessing choices or misremembering a specific experience.

Title: Sunlit Youth
Review: Local Natives’ original components are still in fine working order, but evolution shouldn’t sound this unnatural. They tried, but their discomfort with the equipment stops the songs from fluorescing.

Title: The Tipping Point
Review: Ultimately, The Tipping Point is an ironic title, given the fact that the Roots sound like a group recharging its batteries rather than triggering a momentous shift in how it approaches its music and the world at large.

Title: Underneath The Rainbow
Review: It remains to be seen whether the lack of an instantly recognisable Lips sound of their own may thwart their wilder ambitions, but they're not lacking in tunes.

Title: Born Villain
Review: Subject matter such as the aforementioned romanticism is refreshing, and maybe that will be pushed to the foreground in future records, but it only appears in spurts on Born Villain.

Title: The Fine Art of Hanging On
Review: The Fine Art of Hanging On isn’t entirely free of faults. Hemming and co's way with the more downcast material is so compelling that, for all their strengths, some of the jauntier material seems lightweight in comparison.

Title: Tomorrow Will Be Beautiful
Review: It's an intense record that lingers in the memory long after it’s finished.

Title: All of Me
Review: It feels as if Estelle isn't sure what she's about.

Title: TM: 103: Hustlerz Ambition
Review: Despite the abundance of features (twelve), Snow's fourth studio album is indeed a win.

Title: Maniac Meat
Review: Not much has changed; it's just been both fortified and demented, buzzsaw harsh and woozily intergalactic.

Title: The Source
Review: Allen is inspirational throughout, creating a range of personalised drum patterns, and hey! You can dance to every darn thing. [Dec 2017, p.88]

Title: The Search
Review: Simple but effective sonic details — a chirpy horn arrangement, a reverse-looped guitar part — prevent “The Search” from feeling either preachy or repetitive. [5 Mar 2007]

Title: Whole New Mess
Review: If ‘All Mirrors’ took you to a lavish, creaky ballroom, then ‘Whole New Mess’ tucks you away in the cupboard under the stairs, the door slammed tightly shut.

Title: Aimlessness
Review: Essentially, Aimlessness is a jovial affair that promises more in its first half than it can deliver in its second.

Title: All or Nothing
Review: Even at times it's over-polished, at the very least, it's super-sized. [July 2008, p.113]

Title: Words and Music by Saint Etienne
Review: Saint Etienne's best LP since 1994 masterpiece Tiger Bay.

Title: Jericho Sirens
Review: This is a winner from start to finish. [May 2018, p.111]

Title: And Their Refinement Of The Decline
Review: This double-album is just as hypnotic, just as overwhelming, and awesome enough to win over a new battalion sleepyheads for the next six years and beyond.

Title: On Your Own Love Again
Review: Her lyrics feel like they're whispered directly into the ear; her guitar playing (the only accompaniment aside from the occasional flute) is even more meticulous. But the true leap is in the set's many quietly arresting moments.

Title: Hell Hath No Fury
Review: Concise at 12 tracks, the stylistic coherence seldom fails to engage. [Feb 2007, p.73]
DeMarco writes about life--both the heavy moments and the mundane ones--with economy and newfound grace.

Title: Scream
Review: The resulting Scream may not win any awards for brain cell power as far as titles go, but the 11 tracks contained within find the Prince of Darkness in fine form.

Title: Lateralus
Review: The band continues to rock in the Rush/Metallica eight-minute flexathon tradition: it may impress you with individual lines, but in the end, it excels mainly at musical gymnastics.

Title: Robyn Hitchcock
Review: The album is still as random as a Frenchman’s hat at times, though, and songs like Mad Shelley’s Letterbox and the superb 1970 In Aspic (‘Your bacteria are in me,’ intones Hitchcock, wide-legged and eyeless) couldn’t be written by anyone else. A worthwhile ball to put in his canon.

Title: God Save the Clientele
Review: This is a pretty modest band, albeit one whose supple melodicism is abetted by layers of detail, and whose songs tend to stick around just long enough to make their mark before gracefully bowing out.

Title: The Nashville Sound
Review: The pressures of everyday living crop up again on the confessional Anxiety and Something To Love, while White Man’s World serves up a thick slice of barbed social commentary. He’s at his most heartbreaking, however, on Chaos And Clothes, chronicling the aftermath of a doomed romance.

Title: Suspended Animation
Review: Although this LP is sequenced into tiny fragments of varying speeds of mood, the LP feels like one super-caffeine express fairground ride.

Title: Black Noise
Review: The use of reverberant instruments such as marima, bells and steel drums--as well as, on "Stick To My Side," the ethreal vocals of Noah 'Panda Beear" Lennox--give a real depth to his ambitious productions, and yet despite the elemental yearning, they retain a clubby toughness. Breth-taking stuff. [Mar 2010, p.90]

Title: Untouchables
Review: The riffs are cleaner and catchier than on previous records. [Aug 2002, p.126]

Title: When I Was Cruel
Review: It's no classic, but there are reassuringly unhealthy signs of life.

Title: Total Folklore
Review: This joyful little geode of an album--a 38-minute pocket of melodies that cluster, sparkle, and spike--has a powerfully anti-cynical energy to it,

Title: The Bride
Review: At times perhaps overly conceptual--Honeymooning Alone needlessly hammers the point home--The Bride also lacks more standout cuts to truly make it soar. There’s nevertheless plenty to appreciate here; just don’t expect much in the way of wedding playlist material.

Title: Realism
Review: The delicate melodies--sung by Merritt and various innocents, including longtime collaborator Claudia Gonson--make all the psychic mayhem go down smoothly, barely leaving a trace of blood on the floor.

Title: Until One
Review: Chained as they are to the demands of the dancefloor, there's a little room for subtlety in these frantic mash-ups of Coldplay and Empire Of The Sun, but then whoever did their thinking under strobe lights? [Dec 2010, p.115]

Title: Oak Island
Review: Oak Island, just out on Secretly Canadian, is a logical extension of that debut's theme and style, but is better crafted--or perhaps just better served--and stands as a good example of how subtlety can sneak up on a person and pack a desolate punch.

Title: Sunny Border Blue
Review: As usual, the results are exquisitely unsettling... [3/9/2001, p.82]

Title: Hall Music
Review: Hall Music offers some thrilling contrasts, both in style and mood, giving Loney, Dear's sound a more orchestral makeover.

Title: Fire
Review: Had they imploded in some bizarre gardening accident following the release of 'Danger! High Voltage' all would be forgiven. That single still sounds classic and retains the power to get Aunt Peggy off her seat at the wedding reception..... However, the rest appears to be have been cobbled together in a matter of hours.

Title: There Is A Place
Review: A lovely record. [Jan 2018, p.22]

Title: This Silence Kills
Review: Dillon's rustling electronics plink, twitch and occasionally spin out, set apart by a cutesy vocal style and eccentric lyrics that sound a bit like a baby-voiced Kate Bush.

Title: Broken Dreams Club
Review: It's an exhilarating taster of things to come.

Title: Dead
Review: The atmosphere isn't always strictly severe, knowing right when to let up with gorgeous melodies seeping through the chiselled cracks. These moments save the record from being vociferous without a cause, allowing the more vehement moments to speak louder than they would otherwise.

Title: Yesterdays
Review: Presented as a new studio album, it only manages to recapture the band's spirit, rather than its soul.

Title: For My Parents
Review: this is a Mono album through and through, so much in fact that this reviewer felt déja-vu during some of the more lulling parts. Depending on one's feelings towards the band, this will be a key factor in whether or not this is a worthwhile listen.

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: Condon's lyrics and his singing are nondescript at best, but Beirut retains a ragged majesty that can best be described as, well, French.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: It's a downer, sure, but if you've got the patience, this disc's subtle meditations have a way of working themselves into your heart.

Title: Visiter
Review: Visiter is an impressive sophomore album, a wonderful growth for the Dodos, and one of the year’s subtlest surprises, even if it took thirty listens to get there.

Title: Daisy
Review: Not so much a cohesive statement as an investigation of future stylistic destinations.

Title: Omnion
Review: Omnion, this New York outfit’s fourth album, finds Butler living clean again, producing slinky and varied club bangers alongside off-plan songs with greater undertow.

Title: Down in the Weeds Where the World Once Was
Review: Down in the Weeds is at odds with itself—where the band balances music that is ambitious in scope with some of Obert's most nakedly personal work. But just like his complicated and sometimes narcissistic persona, there's a good argument to make about how his over-the-top approach perfectly suits him. That aside, Oberst and his cohorts' generous offering does take them on new, unexplored territory while remaining true to his wry prose.

Title: By the Way, I Forgive You
Review: The album's best tracks are those where Carlile strides beyond the confines of orthodox pop-country. [Apr 2018, p.24]

Title: Ill Manors
Review: Ill Manors, depressing, blunt and provocative, fulfills one of rap music's most noble tasks--to touch the sore spots.

Title: The Capsule
Review: The whole album is a new frontier for Necro Deathmort, and it’s one worth exploring with them.

Title: Hit the Waves
Review: The songs so consistently mine the same material that it starts feeling like a portrait of our era as a deeply sad one, where lost souls abound.

Title: Strength in Numbers
Review: For the most part, Calla has become an uncompromising version of themselves: melancholy, desperate, but above all, unable to break free.

Title: Wheelhouse
Review: Don't let ["Accidental Racist"] dissuade you. Paisley still knows how to have a good time and standout singles "Southern Comfort Zone" and "Beat This Summer" continue to showcase this.

Title: Axes
Review: The band sometimes flails ineffectually, but more often it stays streamlined and urgent. [Jun 2005, p.109]

Title: Kala
Review: Here she is doing what she does best--weaving the sounds and statements of the people she's writing about into the song itself.

Title: Dark Black Makeup
Review: There’s a timeless quality to Dark Black Makeup that, again, probably has something to do with the band’s young age and built-in resistance to musical trends. It’s refreshing to hear a band that wears its influences on its sleeves without toeing the garage-punk party line, and it’s led to a surprisingly diverse collection of songs.

Title: Compass
Review: Lidell's bluesy wail goes head-to-head with a dense, churning groove in what can best be described as anti-R&B. [June 2010, p. 97]

Title: Memory Streams
Review: Memory Streams is both recognisable as a piece of work from the authors of their first four albums, but manages not to sound exactly like any of them. Instead it confirms them as increasingly assured musicians, carrying forward their first principles and playing like their lives depend on it.

Title: The Cold Still
Review: They have the relentless persistence needed to stick to the wall long enough (this is their third self-released album), but despite their striving for the grandiose (Kings producer Ethan Johns provides the country-ish bluster) and breaks (a spot in rom-com Going The Distance for last album "Union"), there's still that dark sparkle missing.

Title: Martha Wainwright
Review: Though accenting the vulnerability her vocals naturally possess, she manages world-weary honesty and summoned strength rather than contrived sentimentality.

Title: Creatures
Review: Creatures is an album as wonderful as it is unclassifiable, but it is aimed at those who like warmth with their edgy art.

Title: Pale Communion
Review: Relish the result of an intelligent, engaging act taking a new stand. [Sep 2014, p.90]

Title: Here We Go Again
Review: Along with some quiet surprises, there are also potential hits, including the first single/title track, where Lovato almost sounds like Kelly Clarkson's kid sister.

Title: Ten New Songs
Review: It's not inappropriate to think of Ten New Songs as an audio book of poetry with musical accompaniment.

Title: A Funk Odyssey
Review: Lurches from dewy-eyed sentimentality to vicious funk. [Oct/Nov 2001, p.105]

Title: Dancing
Review: Her lyrics see human experience both on an intimate and an epic scale: such expansiveness is well complemented by her music, even if the dancefloor only exists within her home. [May 2013, p.56]

Title: Food & Liquor 2: The Great American Rap Album Pt. 1
Review: He could use a little more production sugar to chase his socially conscious medicine on this restless, claustrophobic sequel. [5 Oct 2012, p.77]

Title: Invite the Light
Review: Invite The Light is music to soundtrack late-night drives on LA freeways and, when it works, it’s sublime stuff.

Title: Central Reservation
Review: "Central Reservation" is a decidedly grown-up pleasure and Orton is an artist who succeeds splendidly on her own modest terms.

Title: Authenticity
Review: It's a work of hushed intimacy and unabashed romanticism that uses synthesizers to create incongruously organic, natural-sounding grown-folks R&B.

Title: Airtight's Revenge
Review: Despite not being as mesmerizingly immense as some of his earlier output, the record is still a far-out journey of dramatics ("Restart" and "Levels"), hooky winners ("Robots" and "Think It Over") and real-world lament ("Flying" and "Think It Over"). In short, the wait paid off.

Title: Moosebumps: An Exploration Into Modern Day Horripilation
Review: Moosebumps tries so hard to replicate the debut that it ends up sounding a bit formulaic, even with an expanded budget and a wider sonic scope. It's still an impressive effort, and worth checking out if you're already a fan, but newcomers absolutely need to hear the original first.

Title: Heartthrob
Review: Their seventh album is a veritable bouncy castle of lush, up-to-the-minute indie synth-pop and blown-out radio choruses, less fussy and more whee than anything they've done.

Title: She Loves You
Review: The songs here often found their way into the group's tours for Blackberry Belle; this probably accounts for how much they resemble Twilight material, even as the original shape is maintained.

Title: False Priest
Review: False Priest is billed as a more collaborative effort, both on the production end with musical savant Jon Brion and in the spotlighted duets with divas Janelle Monáe and Solange Knowles.

Title: Lithium Burn
Review: Lithium Burn's relative straightforwardness makes it easy to enjoy these songs for what they are--and stands as a testament to the growth that comes out of compromise and sacrifice.

Title: This Is Country Music
Review: Even when the album isn't up to Paisley's typical standards, This Is Country Music is still an interesting, ambitious project from a man who need not apologize for the things he does awfully well.

Title: Beyond the Fleeting Gales
Review: It's a bit of a mess at times, but there's no denying that Crying's sense of fun is a major part of their appeal.

Title: Odd Blood
Review: Yeasayer’s greatest achievement is their balancing act, teetering between heartfelt and overly earnest, between invoking and pastiching past decades, between worldly experimentalism and token tourism.

Title: Illegals in Heaven
Review: With electronic pop maverick Lawrence English producing, they have, if not exactly tamed their sound, at least neatened it up.

Title: A World Out of Time
Review: The sound is not quite as clean as on Beyond the 4th Door, but there's an organic whole-ness and immediacy that makes up for murkier sonics.

Title: Fear Inoculum
Review: Fear Inoculum lives up to its daunting expectations with songs that showcase Tool in peak performance as musicians and compositional arrangers. For the diehard fan, there’s a lot to consume here. Likewise, the album offers little respite for the uninitiated; its accessibility comes in the form of its vastness and eerie psychedelia, not through hooks or common pop structures. This is deep prog-rock as only Tool can create it.

Title: Forever Endeavour
Review: Forever Endeavour is indeed a humble record, but as with its touchstones, the album's power lies in its simplicity.

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: Smith's vocals are spot-on throughout, save for the odd Mariah-esque trickle towards X Factor auditionee theatrics, and find themselves paired with as pitch-perfect a production as has been heard all year.

Title: II
Review: If there’s a quibble with II, it’s that like most doubles, it would be more effective as a single disc.

Title: Smother
Review: Wild Beasts continue to find finer ways of expressing themselves while still holding onto the primal passion they've always had, and Smother is some of their most accessible yet creative work.

Title: Freedom's Goblin
Review: Warbly vocalisms, impenetrably fuzz-encrusted guitar work, and boppin' elf grooves delightfully set the man apart from like-minded neo-hippies--alongside reverb avoidance and the occasional horns.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: By the time the second half of the album rolls around, the near-constant procession of sluggish tempos and downbeat refrains begins to wear.... These missteps aren't enough to erase the positive impression of Hypnotic Eye's best moments, but they may cause you to wish that Petty would just lighten up already.

Title: Ruins
Review: Ruins doesn't aim to re-write the indie-folk/country rule book, rather, the Söderberg sisters are just fine-tuning their craft and growing into a comfortable groove.

Title: Untitled
Review: The lyrics are all terrific; the beats, not so much.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: Casiokids received a one million Kroner grant from fellow Nordmenn A-ha for musical potential....A-ha can consider their money well spent.

Title: Ys
Review: The full orchestra doesn’t smack of overproduced grandiosity, which is a nice surprise. Less surprising, of course, is the album's incredible lyrical density. [#15]

Title: Yes Lawd!
Review: Yes Lawd! maneuvers through its 18 tracks with a gleeful sense of abandon. Like the work of the late producer J Dilla, Knxwledge’s rhythms take a few measures to lock into place, but when they do, weird patterns emerge.

Title: Dance on the Blacktop
Review: The narrative of Dance on the Blacktop is a hard-to-swallow reality check, but flourishes in the closing "(Hope) Is Just Another Word with a Hole In It." Nearing six minutes, the song is ambitious and rewarding. When Palermo's vocals and piano come to fruition in the mix, there is a sense of optimism, as though he might be smirking at his demons.

Title: Dolphine
Review: Dolphine’s songs are mystical, yes--but by no means are they not also tough, topical and profound.

Title: Upland Stories
Review: Musically it is more diverse [than Gone Away Backward] and his literary influences are to the fore. [Jun 2016, p.91]

Title: Face Tat
Review: It may sound cobbled together and unwieldy at times, but, then again, that's part of the magic of Zach Hill.

Title: Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino
Review: It takes a few listens for this space oddity to come into focus, but Tranquility Base gradually proves itself a rather daring reinvention. It’s poetic and expansive, subdued yet spellbinding--altogether, one giant leap for Monkey-kind.

Title: Born Again Revisited
Review: For an album so brazenly loud it leaves little impression; as a record supposedly about statements, it makes very few intelligibly. Most inexcusably, it lacks imagination.

Title: Hum
Review: Its calmness in the face of life’s trials is truly inspiring. That something so thoughtful and positive could come from such a turbulent time is someone’s life is astounding, and showcases just what a great songwriter Alain Johannes is.

Title: Showtime
Review: If Showtime isn't the equal artistic success of Boy in da Corner, it's slightly superior, stunning for the facts that it arrives so swiftly after the debut and is far from a retread.

Title: Sunken Condos
Review: This year's version features the usual relaxed jazz-pop grooves, sophisticated horn arrangements and tinder-dry ironic tone.

Title: Be Up a Hello
Review: Be Up a Hello is Jenkinson’s strongest album for a decade and is easily up there with his best work.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: While the band still has its head in the clouds, or beyond, it has made its finest, most listenable album to date. [Spring 2008, p.98]

Title: Unicorn
Review: Unicorn is that rarest of things: a record imbued with genuine talent and emotion which wipes the floor with the majority of its makers’ contemporaries, while calling to mind the classic vocals of Karen Carpenter and the pioneering spirit of Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Quite startling.

Title: No Keys
Review: “Stir The Sea” coasts on a choice yowly blues metal riff, but teased out slow jams like “Arcurlarius – Burke” are equally their forte. The vocal resemblance of Brian Markham and Meat Puppets’ Curt Kirkwood helps crystallise a bubbling under comparison with the latter, although Dommengang aren’t in The Puppets’ league when it comes to ingenuity or, frankly, personality. [Aug 2019, p.64]

Title: Servant of Love
Review: This project is far more adventurous in its presentation of a unique and provocative sonic palette.

Title: We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves
Review: Where the vocals are murky, the synthesizers have a queasy over-clarity, poised somewhere between the repellent and the sublime. [Aug 2011, p.58]

Title: The Good Life
Review: The stylized, old-time country of 'Hard Livin’,' 'Ain’t Glad I’m Leavin’,' 'What Do You Do When You’re Lonesome' or 'Lonesome and You'--yes there’s a theme there--frees him to find glimmers of humor amid the plaints.

Title: Phrenology
Review: With Phrenology, the cool Philly troupe remain head and shoulders above the rest by sticking to their well-defined course of smoky live beats, serious lyrics, stunning guests... and not one ounce of production from the Neptunes.

Title: How I Got Over
Review: From those opening, gorgeous, chords – their sultry delivery, their soulful demeanor, their jazzy glean, everything – signals that The Roots are back.

Title: Lovebox
Review: The album's wanton schizophonia results in such a switched-on pileup of styles that Groove Armada have earned their own rubric -- call it electrocrash, and consider it great.

Title: The Sovereign Self
Review: Well worth imbibing.

Title: DEATH RACE FOR LOVE
Review: The inventive melodies are consistently present and strengthened even more by his knack for hooks, like “Ring Ring,” a bona fide hit for the genre. But Juice begins to run out his welcome at this point, about two-thirds of the way into 21 full-length songs and one interlude. It can be hard to justify that long an album for most artists, and Juice, while bold in his efforts, doesn’t prove to be compelling enough to keep you engaged, especially with only three features (Brent Faiyaz, Young Thug and Clever appear).

Title: Grown Unknown
Review: By never taking her spare, mystical tunes down the typical singer/songwriter avenues, Ices sets herself apart from both the New Age and the folky acoustic guitar sets.

Title: New Epoch
Review: This is brink-of-apocalypse dubstep, wringing your guts with its internal tension rather than banging you over the head - without being didactic.

Title: Wrecking Ball

Review: If you’re looking for a roaring, well-executed good time, look no further: the Ponys are practically peerless.

Title: Lush
Review: Throughout the record, each line is given its own story. Every vocal feels deeply considered and felt, yet nothing is over-rehearsed. She knows precisely when to dial in and when to dial back, when to fully commit to her longing and when to step back and shake her head at it.

Title: Stade 2
Review: The album's a little too incoherent for even the most devout of electroheads.

Title: In and Out of Control
Review: Thanks to the production, the performances, and the songs, the Raveonettes have delivered on the renewed promise of "Lust Lust Lust" and made a very good, almost great, noise-pop album.

Title: Born in the Echoes
Review: Born In The Echoes is another example of Rowlands and Simons' magic way of making machines sing.

Title: Watch Me Fall
Review: Watch Me Fall isn’t evolution, but it is certainly maturation, the first physical testament of aging as a slog toward something better.

Title: A Little Deeper
Review: Like Craig David, Ms. Dynamite seems happy to pad ''A Little Deeper'' with a few examples of suave, heartsick R&B.

Title: The Waterfall II
Review: If this sounds musically dour, it’s not. My Morning Jacket is just too solid of a unit to get dragged under musically by James’ brooding musings. He never loses his strong melodic sense and is always ready to bring a retro-styled 70s soul vibe to the table.

Title: The Violet Hour
Review: Every so often a record pops up that seems to exist in some alien world, unscathed by hipster fads and driven forward only by its own gorgeous mindset. With 'The Violet Hour', The Clientele have made a beautifully haunting album of music to take drugs to make music to take drugs to.

Title: To Be Still
Review: To Be Still is beautiful and subtly splintered and cathartic in an honestly incomplete way. And it is, finally, that rare kind of album: one worth getting close to.

Title: World Of The Waking State
Review: A confidently created body of work that shows her strength in piecing together abstract compositions. [Oct 2017, p.65]

Title: Arms Around a Vision
Review: Ever changing and insightful, Arms Around A Vision never becomes staid or complacent.

Title: Killing Puritans
Review: Van Helden's compositional modus operandi doesn't vary much between the 11 tracks, but it's a combination that rarely fails to deliver a knockout punch. He introduces one element -- a vocal snippet or a jazzy drum break -- and milks it for a spell, before introducing a contrasting timbre. The two begin to climb in and around each other, as Van Helden tweaks and twists various effects, bringing the music and momentum to a dizzy, unsettling pitch.

Title: Heartworms
Review: The evolution and maturation of The Shins might continue at its steady pace with this record, but it’s all the better for the sense of nostalgia that pervades it, seeping from both its music and its lyrics.

Title: Kamaal the Abstract
Review: There are few high or low moments--which might put some listeners off--but texture and content, rather than pulse-raising histrionics, have always been Q-Tip specialties.

Title: Silver Dollar Moment
Review: If there’s a problem with the album it’s possibly in the even-ness of the tone throughout. The vocals are soft, tuneful and pretty, the tunes are melodic and often hooky but it’s not until the second last track--‘Snaps’--arrives with a bit more attitude and grit that you realise that this is what has been missing up until this point. That said, almost every track here would work as a single, or heard by itself on the radio – they’re all decidedly easy on the ear.

Title: Myth Takes
Review: Parts of Myth Takes [are] as close to commercial... as !!! can get without combusting. [Apr 2007, p.92]

Title: There Is No Love in Fluorescent Light
Review: Airy and danceable, There Is No Love in Fluorescent Light revives our faith in Stars.

Title: Rhett Miller
Review: Per usual for his solo work, he's made his strongest set yet.

Title: Dark Red
Review: Young, sexy, and chic, Dark Red is an album that undeniably is made for this moment, blurring the lines among past, present, and future in a way that could appeal to both EDM neophytes and history-obsessed nerds.

Title: Captain of None
Review: With its warm timbres and cushioning delays, sonically Captain Of None is Colleen's most approachable record yet. [Apr 2015, p.52]

Title: Fabulous Muscles
Review: Xiu Xiu nail their nebulous mix of new wave and post-punk gloom, but also lace their tunes with uncompromising experimentation and emotion. [Apr 2004, p.88]

Title: Shamir
Review: Exploring all that we give up about ourselves to make others feel comfortable, Shamir’s new take on pop songwriting is one that finally suits. Leaving enough scuffs around the edges to mark it out as his own, this is more than just album seven - it’s the start of a whole new era.

Title: HiRUDiN
Review: While it's not as brilliantly cohesive as Future Politics, Hirudin's exploration of losing someone and finding yourself sounds like the music Stelmanis had to make.

Title: Good Fruit
Review: TEEN’s sonic approach is chaotically diverse throughout and this very much feels like an album of two halves; when it captures the alienation and isolation it strives for, though, it soars.

Title: Last Patrol
Review: Last Patrol is easily Monster Magnet’s strongest LP in years.

Title: At My Age
Review: [A] finely honed collection. [29 Jun 2007, p.136]

Title: Pickpocket's Locket
Review: Pickpocket's Locket stands as some of Mercer's most urgent and terse work to date.

Title: Welcome to Mali
Review: Like all of Welcome To Mali, the underpinnings of 'I Think Of You' are fantastically layered, with a combination of precision timing and in-the-moment passion. [Winter 2009, p.68]

Title: Dreams Worth More Than Money
Review: He’s always been a reliably ferocious street rapper. DWMTM establishes him as that and something else: an artist with the ambition to go big and the finesse to stick his landing.

Title: Half-Light
Review: Half-Light is a good introduction to the solo sound of Rostam Batmanglij. It’s likely to remain more of a cult interest than establish Rostam as a star in his own right, but even when it becomes a bit unfocused it’s clear that Batmanglij remains a major talent.

Title: The Stand-In
Review: A logical next step then, which stays the right side of MOR. [Mar 2013, p.96]

Title: The Moral Crossing
Review: Leeds quintet serve up sonic catnip for post-punk nerks. [Dec 2017, p.96]

Review: There is self-deprecation and honesty to In an Open Field that combines with musical prowess to form a thoroughly enjoyable, thoughtful record. Few writers possess the melodic ability and communicative skill that Nicholas Krgovich does. He remains one of the finest pop songwriters along the coast.

Title: Journey To The West
Review: File under 'brilliantly out-there.' [Oct 2008, p.110]

Title: Tell Me I'm Pretty
Review: In their bid to capture the essence of their bluesy, garage rock, Cage the Elephant have effectively managed to lose the quirky personality they once had, and whilst Tell Me I'm Pretty is far from a homogeneous record, the tracks do have a tendency to bleed into one another, particularly on repeat listens.

Title: Dream Wife
Review: Dream Wife draw on the politicised ire of Le Tigre and Bikini Kill while putting their own fun, frivolous spin on things. [Feb 2018, p.111]

Title: Jules
Review: It typically takes young musicians quite a long time to find their unique sound, but we’re lucky to hear Julien Chang searching for his in real time.

Title: Near to the Wild Heart of Life
Review: Japandroids' ability to move the listener remains as powerful as ever. [4 Feb 2017, p.51]

Title: Shaken-Up Versions
Review: Shifting their past into their present, this intensifies retrospective beats with the primitive passion that’s always been at their core.

Title: Sic Alps
Review: This time out, there are strains of, say, Arthur-era Kinks, all crunchy clean guitars and sturdy vocal hooks. [Aug/Sep 2012, p.122]

Title: Sort of Revolution
Review: Simple, repetitive, often unsettling, Sort Of Revolution refuses to succumb to the obvious. [Jul 2009, p.93]

Title: We Don't Have Each Other
Review: Throughout, Campbell touches on one of his greatest lyrical strengths--his attention to detail--to bring scenes to life, while also being acutely aware of the underlying emotion and backstory just beyond the setting. It’s devastatingly effective.

Title: Adrian Younge Presents The Delfonics
Review: Anyone expecting a revival of the Delfonics sound we all know and love very well may walk away disappointed. Taken on its own terms, though, the record works.

Review: At first listen, you'll think this album is a disappointment and didn't live up to the hype. And maybe it didn't, but this isn't Bastard--it's an album with a much deeper theme and message, with just enough blood-thirsty lines and misogyny to hold the kids over.

Title: No More Shall We Part
Review: Occasionally he resembles a Pakistani Bryan Ferry. Is this a good thing? It is if you like Pakistani Bryan Ferrys. [#155, p.70]

Title: On
Review: Pop isn't an ambition for these smart people with other things to do, it's a discipline--the tunes strong, the beats solid, the vocals lightly yearning and pungently sweet.

Title: The Time of Our Lives
Review: Cyrus has always sounded older than her years, and as she leaves her teens, that's a good thing--especially since The Time of Our Lives shows her music is catching up to her pipes.

Title: Together
Review: In its crunchy guitars, rich harmonies and fist-pumping choruses, there's a warmth and positivity that, while occasionally too smooth, shows an admirable disregard for current trends. [Jun 2010, p.128]

Title: The Waterfall
Review: The music has stark contrasts that work well to portray the emotions of singer Jim James.

Title: Pushing the Senses

Title: Thousand Mile Night
Review: Tolchin's best work comes when he unburdens his soul. [Jan 2017, p.31]

Title: Quiet Nights

Title: From the Valley to the Stars
Review: From the Valley to the Stars is a fairly magical trip to the center of heartache.

Title: Flying Scroll Flight Control

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: In the cold light of day the album feels flat and utterly predictable.

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Just download the good stuff or buy the album and don’t expect much from Rivers because he never really gave you more than a few minutes of cheap thrills in the first place, which is plenty to thank him for.

Title: Teenage Dream
Review: By the end of Teenage Dream--hell, halfway through--it's apparent that neither Perry nor her collaborators had much to say that was meaningful, or even particularly interesting. It sure didn't stop them from saying it anyway.

Title: Mirrored
Review: Mirrored explodes with twisting grooves and obtuse angles. [Jun 2007, p.102]

Title: Back to Me
Review: Fantasia doesn't invest the songs with subtle emotion so much as she indulges in balls-out emotional overdrive, overloading these simple songs with histrionics that are compelling in the short term and even if they're exhausting over the long haul these full-throttle pyrotechnics make Back to Me her most interesting album.

Title: Goddess in the Doorway
Review: Goddess In The Doorway is the work of a man who is generally interested and occasionally inspired. [#184, p.135]

Title: How Animals Move

Title: Safe Travels
Review: This is a transitional album, it seems: there are a lot of attempts here to do something new, not all of them successful. Still, it will be exciting to see what they transition to.

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: At heart, Watch the Throne is a Kanye West production. It's more of a holding pattern than the seismic leap of My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy, but WTT  covers a ton of territory with aplomb; Kanye's hallmark versatility and tasteful maximalism as a producer are again in full view.

Title: The Small Hours
Review: He nails some sassy jazzy tunes mixed with poetic melancholia. There are still some lines that sound initially amusing in their absurdity.

Title: Factory Floor
Review: As a whole, it’s not so much sonically austere as utterly aesthetically totalitarian.

Title: Typical System
Review: What they're doing with their new wave affectations and post-punk sheen is absolutely creative and often subversive.

Title: Black Age Blues
Review: Black Age Blues is satisfyingly solid and reassuringly familiar a comeback as you'd expect. [Jul 2015, p.89]

Title: Manners
Review: Manners attempts to synthesize Michael Angelakos’ natural talent for dance music with more straightforward, heart-on-sleeve rock, but can’t quite commit to either.

Title: Band Red

Kaito are noisier, faster, girlier; Colk mispronounces her English not as a Marlene Marder homage but so people will think she's from Sweden. But the two share a rare, rambunctious sense that noise is fun and life is livable.

Title: Hell Hath No Fury

Title: Again and Again
Review: It's not like Again and Again is a terrible album; in fact, it's an almost uniformly enjoyable one.

Title: The Slow Rush

Title: Fortress
Review: Fans of kitchen-sink psychedelia will find few greater treats this summer.

Title: Livin' on a High Note
Review: Staples’ songs have never been short of heart and warmth, nor has she ever been the type to let much drag her down. But never has she been as deliberate about spreading her positive vibrations to the world as she is here.

Title: Tales of a Grass Widow

Title: Back to Love
Review: In spartan tracks that evoke but never imitate Al Green and Teddy Pendergrass, Hamilton whispers offers of courtly behavior he says would make Oprah jealous.

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: Unlikely to return them to chart orbit. [Mar 2012, p. 97]

Title: Once We Were Trees
Review: By scaling warm guitar lines, keen melodies, and a valuable sense of history, these Sparks continue to fly.

Title: Dark End of the Street
Review: The songs on the Dark End of the Street EP are well-sung and nicely arranged, but they are missing that vital thing that turns a song into a necessary document of feeling and experience.

Title: Return to Cookie Mountain
Review: The music beneath Cookie Mountain is an earthquake of nearly generation-defining proportions.

Title: Skeleton
Review: If you ever enjoyed the accessible moments of long-standing US indie-pop acts such as Modest Mouse or Built To Spill, but longed for them to stop with the eight-minute wig-outs, Skeleton is probably the album you’ve been waiting for; from Denmark via America.

Title: Critical Equation
Review: Dr. Dog’s music is usually far more engaging and inventive, so hopefully Critical Equation’s monotonous tedium is a mere blip.

Review: Its sound is hard but loose, rooted in sinewy beats by Patrick Carney, the Black Keys’ drummer, and spooky riffs by Dan Auerbach, its guitarist and singer.

Title: The Fire Theft
Review: A prog-rock field trip that will give Diary fans something (else) to cry about. [Dec 2003, p.128]

Title: Finally Famous
Review: With an album that highlights the lowlights and vice-versa of being an MC, Big Sean has crafted an effort that makes room for himself on the rap spectrum.

Review: A CD teeming with punchy choruses and crunchy guitars that are so five years ago.

Review: The Deserters produces a gently psychedelic kind of romantic chamber-pop. [Jan 2013, p.113]

Title: One Breath
Review: One Breath benefits from its variety and from a taste for experimentation which, striking subtle chords that invite the listener to stay and revisit.

Title: It's a Bit Complicated
Review: With Argos still writing gems and the band stepping up musically, Complicated should be as irresistible as its predecessor. For newcomers, it may be. For fans, it's still enjoyable, but familiar.

Title: Hurricane
Review: Even when she strays into overwrought moodiness during the disc's trip-hoppy second half, her menacing omnipotence has a way of willing you onward.

Title: Cage Tropical
Review: While this doesn't scale the heights of Interstellar, it's still a very good album from a fantastic artist. It's nice to have her back!

Title: Silent Shout
Review: While many electronic acts are trying their hand at folkier compositions and attempting to squeeze warmth from the digital realm, The Knife's Silent Shout opts for ice-cold distance. The record suffers nothing for it, instead coming out monolithic and beautiful.

Title: The Warning
Review: Here, [Hot Chip] beefs up the rhythms and tones down the indie-geek shtick. [Jul 2006, p.84]

Title: King's Mouth
Review: 12 meticulously crafted songs. ... Just as the preceding art installation invited viewers to enter its vast head of LED lights and wonder, this album does the same.

Title: Eating Us
Review: Perhaps unintentional by the authors of the music, BMSR triumph in crafting a nuanced and aesthetically superb effort. Their music is wholesome and sounds delicious enough to eat, what a treat!

Title: Gold Past Life

Title: The Fall
Review: If the hardcore fanbase feel a blanch coming on, this isn't all wilful eclecticism gone mad. King's work is The Fall's unifying factor that keeps it cohesive.

Title: Peeping Tom
Review: It's quite possibly Patton's most accessible album since his Faith No More days.

Title: In Between
Review: The familiarity of their sound and the ordinariness of their suburban laments do not breed contempt. Review: Save for the one glaring misstep, Punctuated Equilibrium doesn’t disappoint.

Title: Rook

Title: commontime
Review: As more challenging and artful pieces like The Morning is Waiting prove, the Brewises’ love for intricate harmonies will always go hand in hand with slick pop hooks.

Title: Hold Time
Review: The music here speaks for itself, whatever else Ward might be trying to say through it.

Review: The result is Gogol Bordello's best album in their 14-year career. [Aug 2013, p.94]

Review: Fortunately, when grooves meander and sometimes gets a bit ponderous, the band's creative instincts usually kick in to right the ship. [Summer 2010, p.83]

Title: Take The Crown

Title: Shake The Sheets

Title: Full Circle

Title: Moms

Title: Ribbons

Title: The Wild Hunt

[June 2008, p.59]

Title: Summer of the Shark

Title: They Were Wrong, So We Drowned
Review: A gigantic step backward.

Title: Under the Pale Moon

Review: These guys sound like they don't even understand why punks and classic rockers drink at separate bars. [Nov 2006, p.198]

Title: Fire Within

Title: The Letting Go
Review: A quite beautifully realised album.

Title: White Hills

Title: Volume X

Title: Suckfish
Review: It's hard to get out of Suckfish once it's on.

Title: The Worse Things Get ...

Title: Offend Maggie

Title: Barton Hollow

Title: Fleet Foxes

Title: From Kinshasa
Review: As with a lot of From Kinshasa, listening to it feels like arriving in a bustling, unfamiliar city, a very long way from home: a gripping mix of excitement, apprehension and sensory overload.

Title: Polymer

Title: Alpine Static
Review: Alpine Static unquestionably contains enough rock fireworks to warrant repeated listens.

Title: Ali & Toumani
Review: For residents of the 21st centurey, the sound is not nearly as exotic [as it was in 1980]....However, what is particularly striking about this album is the players' ease and familarity, both with each other and with their instruments. [Winter 2010, p100]

Title: PROTO
Review: The continuity stressed between body and tool, folk history and future, like the work of Meredith Monk or Björk, lures the listener away from the twin traps of techno-evangelist complacency and technophobic retreat with sweet inspiration.

Title: Interstellar
Review: Interstellar easily contains enough beauty to confirm that Frankie Rose is more than just the buzz-scene she once helped create and should provide lift-off into all manner of new sonic territories.

Title: We Still Go to Rodeos

Title: Blood Money
Review: A powerful and almost gleeful celebration of the horrors of the world. [May 2002, p.114]

Title: Before A Million Universes
Review: They don’t often get the time to build a song from nothingness to explosion quite as well as they mastered on their debut. It’s a powerplay that largely works, yet still takes enough rests to showcase a frantically beating heart and a definite intelligence underneath.

Title: Cover Two
Review: While the hypnotic cover of Talk Talk's "Life's What You Make It" may be the only moment here that doesn't distinguish itself enough from the original. Much more frequently, however, Cover Two brings out the best in Joan as Police Woman's music as she revisits some of her favorite songs.

Title: Everythings For Sale
Review: It’s something like Noname if she had a backstory closer to The Game. And just when it almost veers too close into Soulquarian-lite territory, Boogie drops “Self Destruction”, a vocally agile self-examination that reminds you why his contract was picked up by Eminem. [Mar 2019, p.65]

Title: No Luscious Life
Review: The likes of "Sauchiehall Withdrawal" and "Diop" add a few crumbs to the collective's heaving table, but there's plenty here to chew on. [Jan 2018, p.22]

Title: In My Own Words
Review: Although it's firmly in the commercial-R&B camp, it's got much more energy than those slickly produced records, and at times, the record's production verges on dirty.

Title: Book of Changes

Title: Escape From Evil

Title: Dark Red
Review: With Dark Red, he’s taken another turn, slipping out of the pop-shadowing path he was on in exchange for something darker and bolder, but compromised by its own disorder.

Title: The Catastrophist
Review: Tortoise may have become a little less cutting-edge in their old age, but within an area of the musical landscape which owes much to their enduring influence, they remain perennially relevant.

Title: Art History
Review: Take the record for what it is--a breezy, fun but ultimately unfulfilled attempt at an electro-pop statement album.

Title: The Imagined Savior is Far Easier to Paint
Review: The Imagined Savior Is Far Easier to Paint is provocative: its moodiness, myriad musical directions, and 79-minute length may be initially off-putting. What is revealed with repeated listening, however, is that this set's achievement is commensurate with its ambition.

Title: It Won't Be Soon Before Long
Review: If some of the ballads aren't as distinguished as the livelier tracks, they nevertheless are as sharply crafted as the rest, and the end result is that It Won't Be Soon Before Long is that rare self-stylized blockbuster album that sounds as big and satisfying as was intended.

Title: Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea
Review: If Nirvana and Robert Johnson are rock's essence for you, so's To Bring You My Love. But if you believe the Beatles and George Clinton had more to say in the end, this could be the first PJ album you adore as well as admire.

Title: Galore
Review: Too often, Thumpers fall flat.

Title: Chroma
Review: A lack of sonic variety and a mild sense of deja vu won't help to advance his cause. [Aug 2014, p.110]

Title: Everything Goes Wrong
Review: It’s also not a record where you’re instantly gripped round the neck, it’s more a gradual clamping before nails start to dig deep into the skin.

Title: My Krazy Life
Review: YG may just want to party, but the layered storytelling displayed here proves he could be the next transcendent, endlessly original West Coast superstar.

Title: Virtue
Review: The Voidz and Julian might not be the most predictable band to pin down, but there are at least some things that we’ve come to expect from them: whatever they do will be interesting, unusual and thought-provoking. On Virtue, they’ve hit the jackpot with a bonus ball--fun.

Title: Now Only
Review: The first time I listened to Now Only, it was raining and I cried for 10 minutes; after it ended, like a body after an exorcism, I felt lighter.

Title: Fishing for Fishies
Review: This thirteenth album finds them starting to sound like a band who deserve the billing [at Alexandra Palace]. [Jun 2019, p.85]

Title: The Night Is Young
Review: 2 Bears have hit a rich seam of easy-going melancholic euphoria. [Oct 2014, p.101]

Review: It's the best representation yet of the sheer force of the band live, a perfect half hour snapshot of the energy and aggression they've never properly captured on tape.

Title: Christmas In The Heart
Review: Christmas in the Heart is, in no particular order: delightful, silly, intimate in a somewhat phony way, gentle, cornball, crazy, dated, baffling and lovable.

Review: It is a bold, expansive body of work that should have all the praise heaped on it because, without warning, she dropped one of the strongest albums of the year on us.

Title: Sun & Shade
Review: While there's still a sense of DIY sound on Sun and Shade, the focus of the music has a much more communal feel.

Title: Daniel Powter
Review: Like [David Gray and Damien Rice], Powter writes faceless tunes landmined with unsubtle hooks that can devour your brain in less time than it takes for an expert barista to whip up a cappuccino. [Jun 2006, p.143]

Title: Plum
Review: It's a clunky end to a disappointing album; one that sounds less like a reinvention and more like a giant step down a path best left unexplored further. Maybe they can strip back down to a trio, get their pedals back, and return to being a first class psych band instead of second rate indie rock troubadours.

Title: Last Place
Review: Last Place is anachronistically introverted, and its tech references don’t quite make sense in the context of 2017. If it’s understood as a more human album then it works, but it is held back a little by the vestiges of the earlier, broken down and burnt out, Grandaddy.

Title: Dormarion
Review: Dormarion [is] his most mature album yet, and proves Lerner to be one of the more talented young indie pop acts out there today.

Title: Return to the Ugly Side
Review: Psych-pop and trip-hop revivalism collide with a pleasing consequence. [March 2011, p. 99]

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: The precedent is clear: Eighties post-punk, particularly the bony-riff geometry and dublike shadows of Killing Joke and early Siouxsie and the Banshees. So is the freshened, visceral impact.

Title: Gist Is
Review: Unfortunately, it seems the desire to be wild and innovative eclipsed the will to create songs that hold together.

Title: Kairos
Review: Kairos is an intimate account on how stripping things down to a minimum whilst keeping a clear focus on limitations can actually lay emphasis on more unique songwriting.

Title: Us
Review: Us struggles to consistently reach the vertiginous heights of “When I’m With Him” or Me, but at the album’s best, Rodriguez’s revealing narratives of fractured relationships and lonely adolescence strike somewhere deep, to the point that, if you listen close enough, her warm, whispery voice almost begins to sound like your own.

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: File under: very bad ideas.

Title: Garden of Arms
Review: Inter-Be was good, but this record proves the band can make a sound uniquely theirs. In doing so, they've also made something far more lasting.

Title: The Mountain Moves
Review: Unoriginal, yes, but while some elements can verge on sounding a bit tired in places, the notable musical lineage it follows gives The Mountain Moves the potential to be as timeless as it is conventional.

Review: He continues to fuse elements of hip-hop, R&B, funk, soul, and rock ‘n roll into his signature style. ... He’s won both of his Grammy for “Best Contemporary Blues Album” but his music is so different from most other entrants that he’s in a sense carving out his own genre.

Review: The pace is slow, the mood is solemn verging on the sepulchral.

Review: This potent return affirms Finn heeds his own advice. [Mar 2014, p.90]

Camper Van Beethoven, in their newfound maturity, addresses them all in a musical manner that reminds you that no one else sounds quite like them. Even still today.

Title: Destiny Fulfilled

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: I'd never wanted Calexico to change, but the new direction suits them well, proving that even in the face of radical metamorphosis, they remain as stunning and distinctive as ever.

Title: Not To Disappear
Review: Not to Disappear adds strong new strings to Daughter’s bow.

Title: Animal Races
Review: It’s a record that, for its infrequent misfires, delivers on the band’s desires to resurrect the spirit of rock ‘n’ roll.

Title: Roosevelt
Review: Given the album’s August release date, this is one of the nearly perfect LPs for the last few hazy weeks of a brilliant summer.

Title: Fever Dream
Review: The arrangements turn more delicate and acoustic as the songs grow more hopeful. [No. 131, p.61]

Title: Kill for Love
Review: If Kill For Love doesn't make you a Chromatics believer, nothing will.

Title: Compton: A Soundtrack by Dr. Dre
Review: Compton successfully crams the magnitude of his origin story into ambitious, densely packed sonics.

Title: America's Sweetheart

Title: The Way of All Flesh

Title: The Stage Names

Title: American Utopia

Title: Wyatt At The Coyote Palace
Review: Unsurprisingly, this is heavy listening.
