Review: For the Ghosts Within provides another oddly-shaped window into the labyrinthine mind of Robert Wyatt, nearly as vital in its own way as Shleep or Rock Bottom.

Title: 36 Seasons
Review: Without ever being outshone nor outright stealing the show, Ghostface does some of his best rapping in recent years and proves he's still got it.

Title: Everything All The Time
Review: A damned great indie rock record.

Title: The Invisible Man
Review: Nowadays, his voice has mellowed into a fearless croon that seems to suggest a down-home Boy George. [Jun/Jul 2001, p.108]

Title: Sepalcure
Review: As a whole the record is coherent, but contrast, juxtaposition and the element of surprise are the missing pieces of the puzzle.

Title: Insignificance
Review: The fly in the ointment is the lyric content, which plumbs depths of misanthropy that make labelmate Bill Callahan (Smog) sound like Bobby McFerrin.

Title: Dark Night of the Soul
Review: It's a shame if Dark Night of the Soul ends up relegated to a cult souvenir; it's truly exceptional as music.

Title: Gorilla Manor
Review: In an age of playlists, they've made a cohesive album. [Winter 2010, p.68]

Title: Sam's Town
Review: Taken as a body of work it is certainly more consistent than Hot Fuss.

Title: uknowhatimsayinÂ¿
Review: Relying less on atmosphere, tracks like Savage Nomad and Negro Spiritual reveal a rawness that balances his brisk delivery and minimal samples with renewed urgency. It comes with a caveat, though, as taking a more formalist direction puts the focus on technique rather than subject matter. And that's okay.

Title: Coming Home
Review: This debut sets a nice, if mostly safe, blueprint.

Title: Welcome Back To Milk
Review: Welcome Back To Milk is a powerful outpouring, but what lingers are the pauses for reflection. [Jun 2015, p.87]

Title: Think Tank
Review: The album shuffles and grooves like Fela Kuti sloshed on gin and tonics. [June 2003, p.100]

Title: Cut Your Teeth
Review: It’s an oftentimes stunning piece of neo-pop that’s enabled La Grange to catch up with the zeitgeist that so eluded her two years ago.

Title: All My Friends Are Funeral Singers
Review: It is brilliant, conjuring stark, cinematic imagery via Rutli's off-kilter antiquated lyrical motifs, and a vintage instrumental aesthetic that's paradoxically forward-looking. [Falll 2009, p.57]

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Robots is decidedly lowercase music, more a piece of his puzzle than a picture on its own.

Title: Aerial
Review: Considering the length of her hiatus, this is a remarkable surprise.

Title: MASSEDUCTION
Review: But for all its merits, much of the chaos on MASSEDUCTION tends to move rapidly in one ear and out the other, making it a pleasant but somewhat faceless affair.

Title: Blue
Review: Overall, Communions are a serviceable band. Blue is a fine record from an already fine group.

Title: Tyrannosaurus Hives
Review: "Tyrannosaurus Hives" is a good record, but one best dipped into rather than listened to in one go.

Title: Blood Rushing
Review: Blood Rushing is a beautifully lilting, melodious album.

Title: Release
Review: Admirers of melodic craft and pointed poetry -- even those stricken with synth-pop allergies -- should consider Release.

Title: Alpine Static
Review: Kinski have the potential, the skill, the other requisite intangibles to be awe-inspiring, but somehow they keep shooting left of the mark.

Title: July Flame
Review: It’s full of layered folk and indie-rock bucolia and plain-spoken but stretchy-thinking language, wherein everyday energies or objects transubstantiate into other, metaphorically richer ones.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: Of the two acts, Costello’s pinch of dry spice makes this set more his vehicle to champion, but both show a mutual, practical affinity.

Title: Abandoned Apartments
Review: Even if it takes a little more effort than expected to fall under the spell he's casting, Abandoned Apartments' finest moments make it one of Jay's best blends of dreamy surrealism and crisp-edged pop in some time.

Title: Orbits
Review: This is some outlandish stuff, to be sure, but in a sense-of-adventure kind of way that feels in keeping with the vague, in-title-only themes of futurism and space travel that Orbits centers around.

Title: Seeds
Review: Seeds is a credit to their bassist’s memory: staying true to the TOTR ethos of writing music that yo-yos between genres, its 12 expansive tracks make for a compelling and frankly splendid record that you should seriously consider adding to your collection.

Title: Radio Static High
Review: What drives each track home is the tight focus of the playing, riffs and ideas, each one the clockwork fuse on a ticking time bomb. [Oct 2015, p.60]

Title: Losing Sleep
Review: Despite being an album that appears to be made up of such personal and reflective lyrical themes, the tunes themselves mostly rattle by in a flash with less regard for steady contemplation.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately isn’t a perfect album. There are a couple of wormholes that Hadreas gets lost down and the sequencing causes a slightly jilted second half, but once these songs nestle in, they’re impossible to shift.

Title: Someone to Drive You Home
Review: Thankfully, it's even better than expected.

Title: Quality
Review: A little too close to the mainstream for comfort. [Jan 2003, p.91]

Title: Room on Fire
Review: There's something undeniably mechanical about Room On Fire. [#61, p.107]

Title: Nouns
Review: Though generally safe and un-"sexy," Nouns is the sort of album around which healthy musical communities could grow, and that seems to be the point.

Title: Descended Like Vultures
Review: A perfect mix of tender melodies and rock and roll. [#11, p.108]

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: This is an album that's far from complacent and what's most in evidence throughout is they're seeking to challenge themselves as much as their audience.

Title: Missiles
Review: The Dears left Arts & Crafts and cut their least entertaining album yet, Missiles, deciding to release it through the more populist confines of Dangerbird.

Title: Imidiwan: Companions
Review: Taken on its own merits, this is life-enriching stuff.

Title: Visuals
Review: While it's true that some of their pseudo-"prog" power is lost without Madsen's riffs, Mew's delivery is no less effective. Their ever-morphing vision has simply moved beyond terrestrial bonds and ascended into the expanse of the galaxy.

Title: The Magic Numbers
Review: It's classic pop, rejuvenated.

Title: Donkey
Review: Donkey is not the greatest thing since the peanut Kit-Kat, yet there's some indie-tastic fun with a hint of electro punk, a bit like The Gossip but swapping the Ditto scream for Lovefoxxx's sultry, breathily seductive whisper.

Title: In Conflict
Review: In Conflict might not be an autobiography the way you or I would write it, but make no mistake: the deeper you look into it, the deeper Pallett himself stares back at you.

Title: Seeing Other People
Review: There's a loose swagger throughout the nine songs. ... It seems that Foxygen rolled through Seeing Other People, making new music for the sake of making music.

Title: Bitte Orca
Review: Not only will you hum snatches, you'll parse lyrical bits, too: a basement-dwelling twentysomething high on Gatorade in an underpopulated housing development, a waitressing job for Solange Knowles.

Title: Elephant Shell
Review: As it stands, it's a really good album by a band that should've made--and still might make--a really, really great one.

Title: A Church That Fits Our Needs
Review: This may be one of the best records of the year so far.

Title: A Different Ship
Review: An unobtrusively profound statement, cradled in soft-focus melancholy, it's a willowy but towering expression of disassociation, and deeply moving.

Title: The Lovers
Review: The spaces in-between are almost as important as the notes themselves on a headphone album with which to brave the winter.

Title: The Reminder
Review: The Reminder sounds best on headphones, since its rich room tone and casual instrumental interplay is essential to the experience.

Title: If All I Was Was Black
Review: The lyrics sometimes reflect Tweedy's usual tropes as a writer, but Staples gives them a musical and emotional force that sets them apart. Her voice is in splendid shape for a septuagenarian, still supple and able to navigate the twists of the melodies while sailing confidently over the arrangements that fuse indie rock with the feel of '70s soul. ... Quite simply, this is an album America needs.

Title: ANThology
Review: Sounding like Alice In Chains covering early Heart, AAF have the grunge crunch thing in spades, but with the edges smoothed by dramatic melodies and soulful screaming.

Title: A Separation Of Being
Review: There's an appealingly alien quality to Joyfultalk's third album, a sound that drifts beyond familiar reference points. [Apr 2020, p.28]

Title: Slow Vessels
Review: When the music gets quieter there is an irritating increase in tape hiss. [Jun 2017, p.89]

Title: The Outsider
Review: While the hyphy tracks might scare some people off, they are the record's undoubted highlights.

Title: Awakening
Review: Delivers a punitive amalgam of classic West Coast thrash and bruising groove metal.

Title: Millport
Review: Millport might in large part be an homage or a genre project, but at least it’s a sharp and sophisticated one.

Title: Anything
Review: Here we get the full range of peaks and valleys from Martina's vocals, but the songs are a bit syrupy for those prepared for the menace of Maxinquaye-era Tricky.
The music roils and rumbles, allowing the group's folk roots to peek through, but it only sometimes rages or roars.

Title: The Bravest Man in the Universe
Review: The contemporary beats and intermitted uses of techno make this album youthful. For instance, Stupid has a stoic loop that runs through Womack's raspy cries and a sophisticated piano melody. It's a really beautiful blend of new and old.

Title: Girl Talk
Review: It’s a little preachy and confessional, but there’s truth in most of what Nash sings about on Girl Talk, at least for the ladies in the room who are still figuring out how to be capital-A adults.

Title: I Forget Where We Were
Review: [I Forget Where We Were] hangs together well, his David Gray/Damien Rice-like vocals resting on a bed of skittering drums, crafty guitar and fedback chords. Individual tracks take their time to get going (only one song here comes in under four minutes) and numbers such as opener Small Things break after two or three minutes to build back up from a pleasant plod to a sustained fug of sound.

Title: Meds
Review: Stellar. [May 2006, p.176]

Title: Stage Four
Review: The result is a beautifully sad collision of melody-drenched, aggressive art rock that retains plenty of the fast-paced intensity the band's perfected. [Oct 2016, p.90]

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
Review: It's at once majestic and gentle, a deep breath and a sigh that declares Vernon's transcendence of the turmoil and technique of his unique breakout record and establishes him as an artist who knows exactly what he's doing. Hallelujah.

Title: Personal Life
Review: The Thermals continue to give three chords and the (difficult) truth a good name.

Title: Falling Off The Lavender Bridge
Review: A million miles from thrash and punk, the twelve tracks here are an unusual mix of indie rock and country, with top class musicianship adding lots of depth and colour.

Title: Fly International Luxurious Art
Review: As befits its messy gestation, it’s a patchy affair.

Title: Hidden City
Review: There are moments of genius here and there, so do investigate if you find yourself humming Lil’ Devil from time to time.

Title: Ghost Culture
Review: 'The Fog' provides the LP's coda; part of me is surprised by the last-gasp dive into Gruff Rhys-esque psychedelic pop, but the rest of me is too bowled over by its beauty to care. It's the last in a dazzling array of surprises that show exactly why his label were so keen to snap him up in the first place. On this evidence, Ghost Culture is in for a very good year.

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: If anything, [Disc 2] is the real rip-off, as unsuspecting buyers will be shellshocked by these FX-laden, space-ambient settings. [Dec 2004, p.135]

Title: Love & Hate
Review: This is a landmark album for a previously forgotten musician, an incredibly neat and satisfying collection of songs.

Title: FIDLAR
Review: Once or twice they really hit the spot--No Waves could hardly be catchier, and Black Out Stout could have the Black Lips looking over their shoulder--but more often they don't.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: Even with all the name players involved, Albarn focuses the spotlight on the songs, which are terrific. [Jan 2007, p.92]

Title: Pray For The Wicked
Review: Granted, his sixth effort is as bonkers and creative as ever, but it could be that less really is more.

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: With its tight and at times almost arena-sized arrangements and clean--though not slick--production, the new version of the album, subtitled Face to Face, jettisons that entire aspect of the Twin Fantasy experience. For some who may have had trouble finding an entry point to the songs through the original album's lo-fi haze, this will be good news.

Title: Hell-On
Review: Hell-On is incredibly dense and eclectic; each moment sonically plays up Case's lyrics and her inimitable delivery--which can turn from tough to vulnerable, to casually wry and to siren-esque within a few lines. It's chock full of delicious attention to detail.

Title: My Bloody Underground
Review: As pastiche, this all makes for a fragmented and cumbersome back-to-back listening experience - utterly dominated by wild mood swings. But with so many independently functioning songs on offer, certain suites of two or three become hands down irresistible.

Title: Veckatimest
Review: The musical emphasis subtly shifts, from track to track and within tracks to create something that feels rather greater than the sum of its parts.

Title: Disappeared
Review: Spring Heel Jack's latest seems so willfully irritating, careening from one idea to the next, with little regard for such pop conventions as melody, rhythm, or harmony, that one can't help but wonder -- albeit fleetingly -- if it just might point toward a whole new style of music.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel
Review: Modest masterpiece of an album.

Title: Pull Up Some Dust and Sit Down
Review: The heartening sounds of an old master at work. [Oct 2011, p.117]

Title: Christ Illusion
Review: Sounds as hideously vital... as [Slayer] have at any time during their 23 year career. [26 Aug 2006, p.41]

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: The world's second-best co-ed lo-fi blues-rock duo are as sunny and merry as they've ever going to be, and that's not very sunny or merry. [Apr 2008, p.79]

Title: Oczy Mlody
Review: It amounts to one of the more dense, layered, anxious, and fun things they have released in a long time.

Title: Kveikur
Review: Even if it doesn’t have the same cultivated mystery or incapacitating demands of Agaetis Byrjun or ( ), Kveikur is every bit a return to form, tapping into its predecessors’ bottomless emotional wellspring for a Sigur Rós album that can be listened to casually or intensely.

Title: Miami Memory
Review: Cameron's third album, Miami Memory, is still some kind of monster, but it has drawn in its teeth and is laughing with the family.

Title: The Empire Strikes First
Review: Bad Religion sound more relevant than ever on their incendiary, political manifesto The Empire Strikes First.

Title: Pollinator
Review: Deborah Harry's voice has rarely sounded better, perhaps energised by material worthy to stand alongside the group's brightest back pages. [Jun 2017, p.24]

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: Xiu Xiu's music is all about discomfort, but Stewart and co. have become quite comfortable in this conceptual space, and are able to inhabit it like painters making wild, broad smears that intuitively cohere into a look that is distinctly theirs.

Title: Tourist
Review: Drama in music works perfectly fine in mediated, tactical doses, but for Tourist, the stakes are unrealistically high.

Title: Remember That I Love You
Review: For all the offbeat touches... Dawson's wide-eyed hope and wonder are the album's most affecting qualities. [Jun 2006, p.180]

Title: Louder
Review: Like a showtune from Wicked, Louder serves as an above average power-pop album that you can bust a lung trying to sing along to without any of that pesky “thinking” to get in the way.

Title: Babel
Review: "Babel" reveals a band happy to remain entirely Mumford - although a larger, smoother Mumford, offering fresh nuances and textures while emboldened by the promise of the initial mission.

Title: All Things Bright and Beautiful
Review: Like its predecessor, Ocean Eyes – an unexpectedly big US hit thanks to its flyweight lead single, Fireflies – this album suffers from a lack of substance.

Title: Fuckin A
Review: Even without a high-profile knob-twiddler [Walla] this would have sounded like their version of Husker Du's Metal Circus--a document of grace on the way to greatness. [Jul 2004, p.138]

Title: Diagrams
Review: Syrian Plains will get heads banging, while John is more likely to lead the dancing--and is the most joyful track on this generally bleak, occasionally repetitive album.

Title: so sad so sexy
Review: The album’s repeated motif of smoking and cigarettes as an addiction metaphor feels try-hard rather than smart. The best tracks are those that transpose the drama of Li’s best work to the album’s more explicitly pop context.

Title: Do You Know
Review: While it's nice to hear her pipes free of breathless pop production, it's a shame she ran with such bland, emotionally self-indulgent material for this crossover Do You Know.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Sounds Of The Universe also happens to throb with sonic originality and dark, complex humanity, and is a fine addition to one of the richest, most intriguing back catalogues in pop.

Title: Get Lucky
Review: Esteemed guests such as flautist Michael McGoldrick, accordionist Phil Cunningham and fiddler John McCusker ornament the arrangements exquistely, while  the Knopf's ever-tactile guitar continues to say more with three notes than most do with 20. [Oct 2009103]

Title: At What Cost
Review: It's authentic enough for natives to appreciate, but universal enough to maintain broader appeal.

Title: What Sound
Review: If there were any doubters about Lamb being the brightest, most talented singer/producer combo in electronica, What Sound is all the argument needed to the contrary.

Title: Transmission
Review: It seems a blinkered record, which can be admired for its defiantly non-commercial stance. It won’t win Fearless any new fans, and may distance Death In Vegas into more of a cult concern. All well and good if that’s the intent; otherwise, perhaps it’s time to draw the curtains, get some vitamin D and thumb through that ‘guest vocalist’ address book.

Title: V
Review: Though the 18-minute celestial sludge of "The Opulent Decline" conjures all the right imagery, you suspect Oneohtrix Point Never invariably got there first. [May 2013, p.67]

Title: Liz Phair
Review: Even the non-Matricized songs are full of useless keyboard riffs, tacked-on guitar solos and loads and loads of overdubbed Lizclone background singers. Never before has so much work been put into making somebody sound so ordinary.

Title: Timez Are Weird These Days
Review: The 23-year-old Trinidad- born Brooklyn MC's neo-retro hip-hop mashes up TV on the Radio's vocal cadences, old-school break-dance beats and the forlorn melodic tug of a Smiths fan (he dropped This Charming Mixtape in 2009).

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: The record is neither a failure, nor can I imagine is it a pisstake. No, this is Tom Jenkinson letting out his inner rock star, letting his guard down from the laptops a little bit more, and having sloppy fun.

Title: Heza
Review: To call Heza, the third LP from the New Orleans-based duo, more opaque would be an understatement.

Title: Tasmania
Review: Arguably Pond's slickest effort so far--a gorgeously nuanced set of damaged synth-funk and curdled power ballads that should finally see off any Grateful Dead comparisons. [Apr 2019, p.20]

Title: The Adventures of Ghosthorse and Stillborn
Review: Ghosthorse and Stillborn tends toward lazy, meandering nothings.

Title: Red Barked Tree
Review: Wire doesn't break ground on Red Barked Tree, but more than three decades into its career, the band's deceptively simple songs still exude subversive allure.

Title: Do Whatever You Want All the Time
Review: In Ponytail, that long-ago art project seems to have spawned the real thing – a band with an imprint and sound all of its own, with much of joy to share around.

Title: I Am Very Far
Review: The resulting I Am Very Far, which was produced by Sheff, feels both transitory and triumphant, successfully integrating the Austin, Texas-based collective's penchant for lovelorn, indie Americana with the wild abandon of 21st century pop music's increasingly blurry genre borders.

Title: Views
Review: The middle section boast a tougher, truculent edge reminiscent of last year's mixtape If You're Reading This It's Too Late. But it's during the final sequence that everything clicks. [#361, p.114]

Title: Have We Met
Review: It makes for immersive listening, even when tracks fail to sustain themselves. ... Despite its digressions, Have We Met is rich and varied enough to offer more than just throwback thrills.

Title: Manners
Review: On the whole, Manners mostly evens out into a consistently listenable experience, the joy of one absurdly successful track spread out in variations and reformulations across the entirety of an album with inevitable dilution in the process.

Title: The Concretes
Review: What's perhaps most interesting about the album is that it steers clear of most indie rock tropes.

Title: Twisted Crystal
Review: As wacky as their previous efforts but driven by a greater purpose, Twisted Crystal finds Guerilla Toss hitting a new high.

Title: Yours to Discover
Review: There are a few clunker lyrics--Grainger’s at his strongest when he’s singing about making love, not having sex--but overall it’s a worthy record from an artist who refuses to make the same one twice.

Title: Travellers in Space and Time
Review: There is absolutely nobody in the world but hardcore Apples in Stereo fans that need to hear Travellers in Space and Time, it's a record as slight as they come.

Title: Witness
Review: With Witness’ confounding combination of songwriting sloppiness and sleepiness, broad strokes are the really the best Perry can hope for these days.

Title: Music by Cavelight
Review: Blockhead injects enough emotional expression into the dusky downtempo tracks to separate himself from the knob-twiddling pack. [2 Apr 2004, p.66]

Title: Commonwealth
Review: Commonwealth offers a little something for everyone, no matter what you're looking for.

Title: The Grinding Wheel
Review: “Our Finest Hour” is a speedy thrasher about being able to accept yourself in new situations. Actually, Overkill did just that with “Shine On,” which features fresh areas of groove, dynamics and lyrical contemplation.

Title: Teens of Style
Review: By the end of the album, as the waltzing piano ballad "Oh! Starving" fades, it's impossible not to be knocked out by what has come before and be super stoked for what might come next.

Title: Honey Moon
Review: All of this exceptionally solid music is a remarkably beautiful thing to witness.

Title: Exposed
Review: Although DeBarge has nothing unique to say about falling in or out of love, what she does have--strong tunes, a nice voice and an ample supply of fresh-faced charm--is far more important.

Title: Scorpio Rising
Review: A curious but highly enjoyable mix of experimental beats and good old-fashioned guitar rock. [Jul 2003, p.92]

Title: Blood of Man
Review: Where the first half of Blood of Man comes easily and is more or less classic Mason Jennings, the second loses a step as it strays too far into a style and presentation that is both out of pace and place.

Title: Until One
Review: To account for the offensively retrospective nature of this trawl of commonplace dance-floor garbage (we're talking Coldplay, Candi Staton and Justice), I must assume, first, that they spent the last two years in a timewarp somewhere between 1993 and 2006. And secondly, that they spent this time in trashy commercial nightclubs, where glowsticks never die, dancefloors rotate and there's a price reduction for hen parties.

Title: Ufabulum
Review: While a number of tracks offer a solid melodic thread to grasp,m wade deep enough into Ufabulum and you'll find the sweetness a trap. [Jun 2012, p.160]

Title: A Different Arrangement
Review: The album is not without its bright spots, as much of the Brooklyn duo's soundscapes waver somewhere between engaging and downright daring.

Title: The Private Press
Review: An intentionally loose-strung concept of hip-hop and psychedelia, which at times loses focus.

Title: X 100PRE
Review: Bad Bunny feels less like part of the current pop landscape than an artist operating slightly adjacent to it. He is separated from the pack as much by a desire to take risks as by his roots.

Title: Wavvves
Review: Damned meets JAMC with a snifter of So-Cal pyscho-country-surf--on a series of hip, heady, lo-fi tunes, a large number of which seems to have the word "goth" in the title. [Aug 2009, p.95]

Title: Nighttime Stories
Review: The ebb and flow keep you constantly on your toes. [8 Jun 2019, p.55]

Title: Days Are Gone
Review: Days Are Gone, their long-in-the-baking debut album, is properly great, sounding effortless and breezy in a way that only something worked over like a jewel can.

Title: Eat Me, Drink Me
Review: It's not his best effort, but it's the perfect mood setter for your midnight absinthe and auto-erotic asphyxiation party.

Title: Cave Rave
Review: Overall, these songs are a fine reintroduction to a band that has worked hard to emphasize its strengths and come up with new ones.

Title: God Forgives, I Don't
Review: All the grandiose songs are clumped together in the album's first half, while "Hold Me Back", "911" (an ode to Porsche, not emergency workers) and lead single "So Sophisticated" represent the trap sound that propelled Rich Forever into redundancy.

Title: Late Registration
Review: It's a cleverly and thoughtfully composed album, bereft of filler and loaded with style and substance.

Title: The Betrayed
Review: Remarkably the chuck it all in and see what happens approach works, mainly because the superb sheen of production papers over any cracks. What we are left with is an inescapably solid album.

Title: Satan's Circus
Review: This slick homage to electronic hippie music sounds like two smart guys having genuine fun playing something they love.

Title: Impossible Truth
Review: This is all instrumental, and as in Billy Idol's haunting 'Eyes Without A Face' these are songs that say so much without ever saying a thing, piercing windows into the soul.

Title: Inside the Rose
Review: While you couldn’t say Inside The Rose goes beyond the furthest reaches of moments such as V (Island Song), from its predecessor, neither does it play things safe. Newcomers may feel that elements of Kate Bush circa Hounds Of Love or Hansa Studios-era Depeche Mode provide reference points, yet nevertheless, a track such as Beyond Black Suns is nothing but pure TNP: overlapping motifs, doom-laden beats, interweaving vocal lines and a song that resolves nothing, but does so with the utmost confidence.

Title: Good Souls Better Angels
Review: Better Souls Good Angels was written and recorded well before the pandemic. But the album, with its darkness tinged with glimmers of hope, its rage touched with tenderness, is very much one for our terrible time.

Title: Graduation
Review: West's writing and delivery has improved since "The College Dropout," though they're still marked by both a cleverness and a clumsiness.

Title: Visitations
Review: Unfortunately, for those who've been hanging around waiting for Clinic to eclipse its past achievements, Visitations feels like one step forward, too many steps back.

Title: Factory Floor
Review: A well-considered and promising debut album, one that knows just when to stop and breathe before breaking another sweat.

Title: The Woods
Review: The vicious licks laid down by Carrie Brownstein and Corin Tucker on "The Fox" are as punchy as anything I've heard them come up with, approaching something like Jack White if Jack White fell in love with The Experience instead of his Johnson. Amazingly, The Woods just picks up from there.

Title: Views
Review: Despite some intriguing musical excursions though Views is very much the Drake record in excelsis. It’s staggeringly long at 20 tracks and 80+ minutes, and is a grind for even the most ardent fan to get through.

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: Comfortably normal, the War on Drugs make for a nice tonic to the sometimes overly weird attitudes of modern indie-psych bands.

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: Though not blessed with the strength of his father's voice, he makes the most of Dad's knack for pretty melody. [Nov 2006, p.102]

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: This is an understated and promising first step from an unpredictable and distinctive talent.

Title: LP1
Review: Ultimately, a few things come from repeated listenings of “LP1″: First off, the writing and singing aren’t strong enough and come across as C-level Timberlake material. Two, without being surrounded by 1D, he shouldn’t sing high, flightily and airily, but rather stick to slow, low groovers. Three, Payno should find one or two styles that work best for him — and not put a host of other singers before him, male or female — and stick to them.

Title: The Next Day
Review: The rest of the album makes the distance between now and (Berlin) then of "Where Are We Now?" painfully evident, a pain heightened by Visconti's failure to convert this collection of session muso workouts into anything memorable. [May 2013, p.55]

Title: The Breaks
Review: Solidly crafted and splendidly written.

Title: The Lion's Roar
Review: The Lion's Roar is full of rich textures that unfurl around Klara and Johanna's bittersweet harmonies.

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: Wolf Parade do what they do better than anyone in recent memory.

Title: Junior
Review: She doesn't have a ton of vocal gravitas, and too much of the record is taken up by spirdery guitar explorations; its indicative that the soft, simple break-up lament "Sunnyside" is both the least musically showy thing here, and the most movin

Title: The Silicone Veil
Review: "Powerful" is perhaps the most fitting word, and though the strength of certain arrangements can feel all-engulfing, there are too many moments of near-inexpressible, extravagant brilliance on The Silicone Veil to deny Sundfør's overall accomplishment.

Title: Broke With Expensive Taste
Review: Her complete dominance over the sonic space of her debut reinforces Broke With Expensive Taste as a product singularly of her vision.

Title: Rise Ye Sunken Ships
Review: Rise Ye Sunken Ships is actually pretty great, but guys, just dial it down a bit yeah?

Title: Good Fruit
Review: Good Fruit is an album that wears its emotions on its sleeve, but never overplays them. Far from insistent, it’s perfectly pleased to offer just what you need, and nothing more. Take from it what you will.

Title: Magic Hour

Title: Chase This Light
Review: Not amazing, but steady and fun all the same.

Review: Goodman casts a spell on the listener with Sees the Light.

Title: All Hail Bright Futures
Review: This is almost dangerously infectious stuff from ASIWYFA. [23 Mar 2013, p.54]

Title: Jerusalem

Review: Touted as half 'Get Ready', half 'Technique', it lives up to every predictable stylistic retread that entails, to the point of self-parody.... Thank Christ, then, that the songs are so good. [26 Mar 2005, p.49]

Title: Moment Bends

Title: And Nothing Hurt

Title: No Shape
Review: Perhaps his most assured and confident album.

Title: ISAM

Title: Honest Life

Title: xx
Review: As overwrought as the lyrics are, the songs have an attractive, dreamy, atmospheric quality that helps the London band avoid embarrassing teen melancholy. It's also surprisingly hypnotic.

Title: Magic Hour
Review: Magic Hour won't blow your mind but it conjures enough spectacle to highlight why Scissor Sisters remain one of pop's smartest, most entertaining bands.

Title: Rennen

Title: The Electric Lady
Review: Monáe has gone ahead and created her own world, one with her own rules. Sure, it’s a world built on a foundation of Stevie Wonder, Michael Jackson, Duke Ellington, Ennio Morricone, and the countless other idea-seeds from which The Electric Lady grew, but it’s one Monáe has cultivated and shaped in her own distinct, unmistakable image.

Title: You Can Have What You Want
Review: By coloring within the lines of dream pop Quever has recorded a pleasant release but not necessarily one that goes beyond the normality of his band's moniker.

Title: Passenger

Title: Need Your Light

Title: Magus
Review: The album is their most sonically focused statement yet, primarily consisting of lengthy dirges with up-front growled lyrics that challenge concepts of ego and identity.

Title: Backwater
Review: Backwater, is a further refinement of their sound, fleshing it out and blanketing it with a gauzy patina that’s almost intrinsically appealing.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: This is a dramatic, ambitious album that dares you to rise to its challenge.

Title: Views
Review: Ultimately nothing here really out-pops last year’s dulcet hit, Hotline Bling, included as a bonus track. As ever, though, the detail--both lyrical and producerly--is pin-sharp.

Title: So This Is Goodbye
Review: In the end, Junior Boys' improved skills at constructing pop songs within their fantastic sonic template is more than enough to make So This Is Goodbye one of my favorite releases of 2006 so far.

Title: Disquiet
Review: Disquiet, the group’s fourteenth album, is their most direct and to the point release in some time.

Review: Zomby's early work stood out for the care with which it was created, but even given that, there's something startlingly mature about the production here.

Review: The result is vast and apocalyptic. [Dec 2015, p.81]

Title: Who You Are
Review: Divested of the slowies, this would have been a fine pop record.

Title: Hurricane
Review: Hurricane is classic Jones.

Review: Itâ??s the hyper-distinguishable leap from idiosyncratic-but-lovable to just-plain-lovable that makes Bromst--and Danny Boy himself--of increased import.

Title: X

Review: As a whole, the sophomore album is inconsistent, but when being eccentric is such a large part of a group's appeal, this is to be expected. Notwithstanding a few weak moments, many tracks are potentially their best.

Review: This is intelligent, knowingly silly music that should have no place in 2019. It’s anachronistic, beholden to its influences, and just a bit lightweight to be anything but a bit of a laugh. But, as this is 2019, and the real world is anything but a bit of a laugh, thank God for records like this. The world is in a dire condition, and International Teachers of Pop have given us a beautiful distraction.

Title: Alpinisms
Review: With a clearer eye to the cultures whose stereotypes they’re furthering, the Bells could have made a provocative connection between the European forms they’re comfortable with and any number of traditional Middle Eastern and Indian instruments and forms they’re interested in but not serious about.

Title: Shaking the Habitual
Review: They've never sounded more in tune with the materiality of sound or the sonorousness of the physical world.

Title: Centralia
Review: Centralia's seven lengthy essays proffer the duo's boldest, most immersive statements to date. [Mar 2013, p.88]

Title: Fork In The Road
Review: The outcome is more noteworthy for Young's stinging guitar work, passionate vocals and his powerhouse band's accompaniment than for finely crafted songs that add considerably to Young's estimable body of work.

Title: Feels Like

Title: Anak Ko

Title: No Boys Allowed

Review: While they might not whip up the same adoration, Another State Of Grace shows that there continues to be life beyond Lizzy. [Sep 2019, p.84]

Title: Kiwanuka
Review: This is an exceptionally compelling, absorbing, rich, and genuinely human piece of work.

Title: Gold Record
Review: ‘Gold Record’ finds him ploughing firmly against the grain. As the wider world collapses all around him, the prolific singer-songwriter has released the warmest, wittiest and most comforting work of his career.

Title: Hearts of Oak
Review: Insanely hooky and tortuous.

Title: Short Movie
Review: A commanding and sincerely fascinating listen that stands tall in a catalogue already awash with magic.

Title: Ringleader of the Tormentors

Review: Painting With is unmistakably an Animal Collective album, but in its eager familiarity, it ultimately neglects the one all-important quality of any Animal Collective record: novelty.

Title: Future Dust
Review: This is an album that shows a band who’ve grown stronger and unafraid to flex their muscle.

Title: Embers

Title: Whorl

Title: Crooked Man
Review: Despite the name, Crooked Man's greatest fault is ultimately how straight Barratt plays it.

Title: Christmas In The Heart
Review: It's a decent album with good intentions.

Title: Dust

Review: The big hooks are fewer and further between, but the meat in the middle is where the real magic lies.

Title: All The Right Noises
Review: Undulating melodies, exquisite sparkling detail and a sense of vast space all add up to a blissful listening experience.

Review: As they navigate these darker emotional waters, it's hard not to wonder what Hemming and his crew would sound like if they loosened their collars just a bit.

Title: Subiza
Review: They're called wankery chill-out names like 'Endless Sunset' and 'Infinite Desert' but are elevated above their base genre and boring titles by the general air of Animal Collective-gone-raving-down-Pacha.

Review: Perhaps inevitably for a first solo album, this is Mark Peters’ most personal work to date. It is the dissemination of music that has occupied his inner ear for decades, the soundtrack to countryside and habitats that have been a lasting part of his life. Because of that, Innerland has a deep set emotional significance and intimacy that carries beyond Peters and out to the listener.

Title: Lulu
Review: The whole thing comes off as either an expensive major label joke or nigh-impenetrable high art concept. Maybe both.

Title: Earthly Delights
Review: Music like this is a reward just waiting to happen and if you give it a fair shot, it will surely win you over.

Review: Here more than ever Bey indulges clashing impulses--between strength and escape, megapop and fresh sounds, big messages and resonant lyrics.

Title: Freedom
Review: This is not a terrible record, just a bland and misguided one.

Title: Cellar Door: Terminus Ut Exordium
Review: An underwhelming middle stretch aside, this cellar is worth exploring.

Title: Elytral
Review: Elytral may not be an easy record, but it is strangely affirmative and rewarding.

Review: A far cry from the piano-tinkling heard in formulaic modern pop, Krug’s ivories are often filmic (Barbarian), or musical-theatre enough to evoke Hugh Jackman or Julie Andrews singing amidst a mountainscape (November 2011).

Review: Cunningham is skilled in sustaining uncomfortable moments right up to a breaking point but he's also brilliant at making this self-contained, insular music sound sleek, modern and somehow appetising.

Review: Altogether elegant, moving, and often beautiful, Not to Disappear leaves Daughter, without question, on the heavier side of the emotional spectrum, but, like the Cure's "Dark Trilogy" 35 years prior, is sure to connect deeply with some listeners and stand out not only among pop contemporaries but among other emotive, textured indie pop.

Review: The shockingly honest debut is more comparable to the work of Sharon Van Etten than any of Williams' contemporaries in the pop-punk scene; not in the music itself, but the way both women use music as an outlet, in the aftermath of years-long relationships where they were demeaned and made to feel worthless.

Title: Timeless
Review: Timeless is a step up for will.i.am and a step down for Sergio Mendes, somewhere between decency and exceptionality.

Title: Future Crayon
Review: Future Crayon is a must for Broadcast obsessives and a good way for casual fans to explore some of the rougher edges of their music.

Title: More Parts per Million
Review: While the results aren’t exactly groundbreaking, they're undeniably loose, spirited and just plain fun.

Title: Someday World
Review: Someday World sounds quite like Happy Mondays at times, and rather like King Crimson at others.

Review: With Don't Do Anything, Sam Phillips has struck out on her own with a work that's among her most challenging to date, and it reveals that she's held on to the gifts that have made her one of the most rewarding singer/songwriters of her generation while adding fresh accents as she follows her muse with commendable courage and clarity.

Title: Finally Famous

Title: Golden

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: This is nowhere near a bad album. [#12, p.95]

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: Altogether, Father, Son, Holy Ghost is a complex record, one that doesn't quite fully realise Girls potential as great recording artists, yet equally suggests that bona fide masterpiece may not be too far around the corner.

Title: Rockferry
Review: The shadows come richly dark, and the brillance pierces. [May 2008, p.104]

Title: Sauna
Review: This hodgepodge of ideas, irregular pacing and abrupt transitions are oddly compelling; though it can be tough to make it to the end of the hour-long work, Elverum makes it worth it.

Title: Autobiography
Review: There isn't a song on her debut that doesn't paint in huge strokes. [Sep 2004, p.143]

Title: Lost in the Glare
Review: This newly winged Barn Owl glide on through celestial panoramas, a tempestuous sonic asteroid belt and heady, intergalactic drift. [Oct 2011]

Title: Yours Truly
Review: Minor missteps aside, Yours Truly is ultimately an impressive debut for Grande.

Title: Everybody Looking
Review: Gucci sounds more comfortable, confident and icier than ever before.

Title: Angel

Review: A hip-hop blues record is an interesting concept and in Koala's nimble hands, a unique listening experience.

Title: A River Ain't Too Much To Love
Review: Indispensable.

Review: The Canadian math whiz and artist formerly known as Manitoba proves he's just as calculated as he is cerebral, crafting music that feels equally clubby, fluid and submerged to back up the ideal album title.

Review: Kvelertak aren't creating any surprises on Splid, they are simply doing it better than they ever have before, showing they are greater than all the individual parts of their sound.

Review: The best part of Treats is that it makes you rethink the possibilities of this kind of music. It is possible for a former girl-group member and a former hardcore guitarist to get together to make an album that is more daring and more fun than anything you'll likely hear on Top 40 radio this year.

Title: Guero

The songs tend to flow into each other, although Antonoff and Del Rey’s partnership does result in some lovely musical moments.

That’s not to say these new songs are all gumdrops and sunshine, but it’s gratifying to hear an artist growing out of the framework that held up him at the start and drawing inspiration from new and different directions.

Title: Songs for Our Mothers
Review: As a musical representation of physical and mental decline, it is morbidly compelling. But in the wrong mood, it's a bit of a trudge. [Feb 2016, p.75]

Title: In Between
Review: The band doesn't need to say much, because that message is there in the music.

Title: Contra
Review: With the band now a known quantity, sophomore album Contra inevitably lacks the slaphappy dazzle of breakout singles like ''A Punk'' and ''Oxford Comma.'' Still, the album, recorded in Brooklyn and Mexico City, stays largely faithful to the sound they've built.

Title: Goblin
Review: It all sounds a little off, at times broken or aggressively annoying, an intentionally wobbly frame around an imagination that's churning at 1000 miles an hour. Call it avant-garde at your own risk, but at times this music has as much in common with electro-punk as it does hip-hop.

Title: Low in High School
Review: The 12-song album’s first five tracks are passable, if not actually quite enjoyable. Beyond this point, though, only the most hardened Moz fan should dare to venture. ‘The Girl From Tel Aviv Who Wouldn’t Kneel’ is an unbearable cha-cha-cha; ‘Who Will Protect Us From The Police?’ is lumpen electro; and least listenable track ‘Israel’ sees him deliver political polemic via the dubious medium of a piano ballad.

Title: The Private Press
Review: Accomplished and occasionally great as this album is, Endtroducing still casts the biggest shadow on it of all.

Title: Never Hungover Again
Review: Joyce Manor are more than comfortable with their own sound now--they’re effortlessly confident with it, and Never Hungover Again is a stark reminder of just how much fun you can actually have without alcohol pumping through your veins.

Title: Revenue Retrievin': Day Shift
Review: On the whole the batting average is much higher than even the best MLB players when it comes to hits on "Day Shift" so E-40 supporters should be kicking themselves if they didn't pick this up.

Review: Hypnotic channels occasionally, degrade into ruts, but more often this is a fabulous freakout. [Mar 2017, p.98]

Title: Quiet Nights
Review: Quiet Nights contains a few surprises, even if they are dressed up in slow finery.

Title: Threace
Review: For the most part Threace careens joyfully through a series of angular, happy-to-be-alive polyrhythms that are primal in their appeal.

Title: The Incident

Review: Throughout, there’s a disarming warmth and thoughtfulness, making for a pleasantly surprising late-career highlight.

Title: Exile
Review: If you’re able to look past the campy facade and accept that this is purely a record of glimmering pop, it’ll be something you’ll cherish.

Title: Brilliant! Tragic!

Review: A large portion of Black Metal resembles the kind of lo-fi, quantity-over-quality, solitary works of eccentrics who would have been at home in the mid- to late '80s on labels like Factory Benelux, Creation, or, well, Rough Trade.

Title: On a Mission

Title: Solar Motel
Review: [The] precisely arranged layers of keyboards and guitars have as many behind-the-door delights as an advent calendar. [Oct 2013, p.46]

Review: Keep giving it a whirl though and it becomes something rather exquisite.

Title: Idle No More

Review: Overlooking the nine subminute snippets‑-most annoying even at that length, with bows to the nine-second "Tick" and the 24-second closer‑-that leaves 16 songs that pretend to be songs, including one A plus, two clear A minuses, and six close enoughs.

Title: The Rose Has Teeth in the Mouth of a Beast
Review: More danceable (and vulgar) than previous releases.

Title: Hospitality

Title: Human Conditions
Review: At times he tries too hard, but there's much here to commend. [Nov 2002, p.114]

Title: Rolling Papers
Review: With a collection of songs largely indistinguishable from one another, this album exemplifies the struggle up-and-coming rappers currently face.

Title: Bitter Rivals

Review: Though it boasts a couple of heaters, A Thousand Heys butts up against the same problem faced by so many others working in this timeless but relatively basic template -- there are undoubtedly listeners who won't ever get enough of this stuff, but how can you distinguish yourself while still maintaining the spirit of your predecessors?

Title: Welcome
Review: The record could perhaps do with more of these vocal interjections, as it's packed with mostly instrumental grooves. However what there is comes extremely well layered and with a careful structure, well thought through but also retaining the potential for improvisation and a chance to cut loose.

Title: Soft Commands
Review: A batch of songs guaranteed to be huge hits as soon as we're all sucked into a giant time warp and plunked back down in 1974.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: It's another very good album from a band that's getting back into the habit of making them.

Title: Me First
Review: It's a thing of subversive beauty, a striking debut that's self-assured and captivating. [Mar 2004, p.104]

Title: New York in the '70s

Title: One Day I'm Going to Soar
Review: An accomplished piece of work, which, like life, has its blemishes and its triumphs.

Title: The Desaturating Seven

Review: Sometimes it sounds like he's trying too hard.

Title: The Terror

Title: Two Thousand

Title: Shine On
Review: Shine On is "new old rock" at its finest. [Nov 2006, p.136]

Title: Everything Under The Sun
Review: This US trio make a more than decent fist of their upbeat retro-music without ever quite shaking off the scent of pastiche. [Dec 2011, p.87]

Title: Our Nature
Review: Our Nature is too long and just not unique enough to really stand out among all the artists treading similar ground.

Title: At Least For Now

Title: Elephant
Review: It is stranger, thornier, and meaner than anything in the band’s past.

Title: Three
Review: Three is a Phantogram record in that it’s a well-crafted release, but it lacks the originality Phantogram prided themselves on.

Title: Curve of the Earth
Review: It’s the balance of maturity and melody that will keep you going back to this album. They’ve grown up, but then so have their fans. Let's just see where they go from here.

Title: New Amerykah Part One (4th World War)

Title: Thirst
Review: Akchote can still serve up a dancefloor banger when required. ... Although its on the album's closing track that he discovers the perect balance between artistry and energy, silken-voiced R&B singer Gallant turning Run For Me into a heady EDM ballad that elevates his signature beats to new heights. [Dec 2019, p.115]

Title: Honor Found in Decay
Review: While the execution has become more precise, more considered, the gigantic, swooping structures of the songs remain as thick and muscular as the Midgard Serpent, undulating around and encircling the world.

Title: Mala in Cuba

Title: The Hum

Title: Out of Touch in the Wild

Title: Wet from Birth
Review: Might not be enough to convince disbelievers, but to fans, it’s a gratifying addition to an already impressive repertoire.

Review: Somehow the music manages to be deeply exotic and familiar at the same time. [Jun 2014, p.50]

Title: III

Title: Fate
Review: Dr. Dog wear their influences on their sleeves. They also don’t seem particularly concerned about being the flavor of the week. These two things seem to rub a lot of reviewers the wrong way, and certainly, this album is more of the same. But it’s the most confident, complete outing since "Easy Beat." [Summer 2008]

Title: Daughter
Review: A beautiful and steady album about defying the roles others put you in and pondering what went wrong. It’s a heartbreaking project as well, peppered with upbeat but cutting songs. It may not be Loveless’s best album -- Real is impossible to beat -- but it ideally captures the indescribable greatness of her songwriting.

Title: Face Control

Title: Ocean Roar
Review: It is both gorgeous and fearsome, and one couldn't ask for anything more.

Title: Hospice
Review: A musical vigil primed to cut a path from bedside to festival stage. [Dec 2009, p. 111]

Title: Pattern Is Movement
Review: Pattern Is Movement is over before the listener is ready to be left alone. Not since Kid A has an album used its last song to create such an intense engagement with subsequent silence.

Title: The Soul of All Natural Things
Review: This is an album in possession of a rare innocence and charm.

Title: Release
Review: The sound of Pangaea doing his thang, then? Yep. Ahead of the game? On this evidence, most certainly.

Title: Man Alive!

Title: Rebel Heart

Title: Pro Tools

Review: While it feels great to have some undiluted Avey Tare material, he seems a little creatively restless here.

Title: Ash & Ice

Title: Push the Button
Review: It shows the Chemical Brothers, unlike their peers, are capable of adapting and surviving.

Review: The quality of the album isn't the issue, it's the qualities, the contradictions, the duplicity: it's what makes it as durable a listen as ever, but oddly empty when it comes to empathy.

Review: Man of the Woods is not an outright disaster but it is a significant disappointment--a record too preoccupied with image, volte face and forced “REAL” to fully engage as a coherent piece of craftsmanship.

Review: Rather than make a staid, serious statement album, the foursome keeps things loose and low-key, content to sound like postmillennial Traveling Wilburys but generally just being themselves.

Title: PHOX

Title: Dark Light
Review: A collection of irresistible pop-rock anthems. [Nov 2005, p.125]

Title: When the Pawn

This album is a reflection of that growth, and hopefully a promise for more of the same.

Title: Future Nostalgia
Review: Make no mistake, her risks are still very within the context of a 4/4 pop structure, but she still finds such color and joy in her surroundings it's hard not to get swept up in her energy. Such risk-staking, however, can still lead to a few moments that could've used a bit more polish.

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: The Strokes’ hallmarks--those lean melodies, that steely interplay among guitarists Nick Valensi and Albert Hammond Jr. and bassist Nikolai Fraiture, the urgency of Julian Casablancas’s vocals--are largely absent on Comedown Machine, their fifth studio album. In their place is a looseness that’s refreshing enough, until you realize these guys are perhaps running short on ideas.

Title: Wide Awake!
Review: In range, energy and freshness, this may be their best album yet.

Title: Here's to Taking It Easy
Review: Newfound confidence pours from the song and out onto the others.

Title: Soul is Heavy
Review: Throughout, Nneka's singing and rapping are inspired and deeply felt.

Title: Golden State
Review: Golden State is, inevitably, rather good.

Review: For anyone who legitimately enjoyed Blood Sugar, and think that they might actually want to purchase this thing, Stadium is unquestionably Red Hot Chili Peppers’ finest release since.

Review: Their music is generic, competently played, but breaking absolutely no new ground. Only someone utterly obsessed with hearing every pop-punk album ever, by anyone, should pick this up.

Title: AOI: Bionix

Title: Moonlight

Title: The Craft

Title: Flourish // Perish

Review: This is a joyful and respectful collection. [Feb 2013, p.107]

Title: The Seldom Seen Kid
Review: The Seldom Seen Kid is a stunning record, a career-best from a band whose consistency has seldom been matched by any British indie band this decade.

Title: Beautiful Thing
Review: Yo-yoing of tempos and moods aside, whether it is on the stripped-down “A Hit Song” or the jerky, David Byrne-esque “Oh Baby,” Taylor sounds pretty emotional, a sadness underscoring his signature vocals throughout.

Title: Blonde
Review: Frank’s rich sense of storytelling is still here, it’s just fragmented. But once Blonde’s ambiguity begins to piece together, it becomes something remarkable.

Title: Hiss Spun
Review: Listening to Hiss Spun is a punishing affair, but it's a rewarding one too. It's the sound of an artist not afraid to dig deep emotionally, and that challenges the listener to do so as well.

Title: Dance Mother
Review: Telepathe may not be superstars yet, but with Dance Mother--an album short in length but simmering over with ambition--they are certainly on the right track.

Title: Mutineers
Review: While Mutineers doesn't totally shatter preconceptions, there's a rare comfort in hearing an artist in pursuit of joy; and unlike the throng of relatively inoffensive twentysomething singer-songwriters littering the charts, Gray's songs have a timeworn quality that's far more charismatic.

Title: The Story So Far
Review: It may not appeal beyond their current fanbase, but it cements The Story So Far's position near the front of the pop-punk pack. [16 May 2015, p.53]

Title: Coral Fang
Review: The record sounds like a seamless amalgamation of the three Hole eras (punk, grunge and rock), with Dalle’s ska roots almost entirely supplanted in favour of a grungier muse.

Title: Mass Gothic
Review: Though it won't be every listener's groove, fans of baroque pop's lush overreach will find a lot to enjoy. [No. 128, p.59]

Title: Heat Lightning Rumbles in the Distance
Review: Fans of his [Drive-By] Truckers tunes will find much to love here.

Title: Rather Ripped
Review: Rather Ripped is a solid collection of songs smartly executed by a band secure in its legacy and refusing to go gently into that good rock night.

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: It's this ease of expression, both lyrically and musically, that makes Rewind The Film such a captivating listen. [Oct 2013, p.101]

Title: Is This It
Review: If you like one Strokes song, you'll like their whole album.

Title: Hairball
Review: Hairball doesn’t redefine its chosen genre, nor does it really refine it. It’s a straightforward album, one meant for windows-open listening on a sunny day.

Title: Abyss
Review: More than ever, Abyss proves that she knows when to unleash her full fury and when to rein it in, and the results are stunning.

Title: Hozier
Review: The more steeped Hozier gets in Southern influence the better: slow, hymnal Work Song disguises a love ballad as a spiritual to blissful effect, a perfect showcase for his rich, resonant alto.

Title: House of Baasa
Review: If at times the album works as dancefloor aerobic-pop, its true utility is in providing the soundtrack for two people to get lost in the vortex dance of each other's eternal-seeming embrace.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: There are a few head-scratchers,....but singer Caleb Followill has never been in better command of his beyond-his-years howl, and he's got monster hooks and melodies yet in his bottle of tricks.

Title: Jim Noir
Review: It brims with psychedelic electro-pop of the most inventively buoyant and sweetly retro-futuristic kind. [May 2008, p.106]

Title: Carnage Hall
Review: Kaputt excel at making complicated songs sound fun.

Title: American Standard
Review: The ghosts of more well-known recordings hover over “American Standard,” and they’re enough of a distraction to make one think that a better tribute to these compositions might have been a Taylor-curated playlist of the versions that originally captured his imagination all those years ago.

Title: Narrow Stairs
Review: Throughout Narrow Stairs, the band allows itself to open up, twisting and tinkering the same old style to their liking with mixed results. [Spring 2008, p.90]

Title: Helioscope
Review: Not radically reinventive, then, but Vessels deserve to keep their foothold on the post-rock face. [Apr 2011, p.100]

Title: The New Life
Review: The result is a stylish, intelligent record that does exactly what it set out to do: Girls Names have reinvented their sound and come up smelling of roses.

Title: Utopia
Review: Utopia feels like both a journey and a collection of statements that define and affirm who Björk is.

Title: The Endless River
Review: The Endless River belongs not in the pantheon of the great Pink Floyd, but in a hotel elevator.

Title: Singing Saw
Review: There's a strong sense of ambition on these recordings, a strong sense of purpose.

Title: Reflektor
Review: While Reflektor isn't so flawed as to strip them of their sash, it's a wobble on a podium, a needless error of judgement that could have been easily avoided had they heeded that other old truism. [Nov 2013, p.100]

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: The whole idea of Philly fruitcakes Man Man releasing an album that sounds like a dusted deconstruction of Tom Waits’s Swordfishtrombones--complete with grumbling old man affectations--on the same label that releases albums by Waits is too much of a nutty coincidence not to be a cockeyed po-mo parody.

Title: Watch Me Fall
Review: Watch Me Fall strives for but never achieves a more classic and accessible sound.

Title: Blue Cathedral
Review: Sometimes bludgeoning, always regal, Blue Cathedral is a calcified, hippified holy place.

Title: Endless Now
Review: Dinosaur Jr producer John Angelo coaxes dreamy harmonies from their skewed sound. [Sep 2011, p.114]

Title: Ology
Review: His first record reveals a felicity with language, a charismatic manner of singing, and a deep understanding of what makes a song work well beyond his years. Each track works on several layers. One can listen to it, make love to it, or just move to the beats.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: This is grown-up rock, with an adult swagger, from one of today's most gifted songwriting bands.

Title: The Monitor
Review: It lasts about two days, though, and even though the likes of 'Four Score And Seven' and 'To Old Friends And New' hum with energy and shoutalong choruses a little restraint would've worked wonders. An above-average Titus record is worth a dozen imitators, though.

Title: Dark Days / Light Years
Review: Playfullly irreverent and magpie-like as ever, and stuffed with inspired pop weirdness and great titles. [May 2009, p.119]

Title: Trench
Review: Trench is the sound of a band ratcheting up the ambition without ever being pulled down by an undertow of pretentiousness. It’s more low-key than ‘Blurryface’, but ultimately more rewarding.

Title: Come Feel Me Tremble
Review: Regret comes in many shades, but Westerberg never makes it boring or mopey. [Nov 2003, p.123]

Title: Glow & Behold
Review: They may be playing things that have already been heard before, but it’s a real pleasure to hear their take on the past.

Title: Beware and Be Grateful
Review: Overall, Beware And Be Grateful strikes a more satisfying balance of post-rock creativity and songcraft.

Title: Arular
Review: This is probably as close as anyone has yet come to achieving the visions of revolutionary global pop once advanced by the Clash and Afrika Bambaataa; it's equally enlightening to urban street kids and university eggheads.

Title: Kintsugi
Review: With Kintsugi, the cracks in the Death Cab veneer are undoubtedly visible, shiny or not. While many of the tracks fall flat, the vestiges of their prior form--confession and melody and, ultimately, charm--will likely still be evident enough to keep fans enamored.

Title: Broken Bells
Review: At its very best, when the collaboration clicks, Broken Bells boasts some truly marvelous songs, but these peaks are sandwiched between tracks that struggle to exceed colorless tedium.

Title: Torches
Review: The first half of Torches is its collective zenith, and although things pick up towards the end of the album by the strategically placed 'Pumped Up Kicks', you can't shake the feeling that Foster has simply stretched the party vibe over as many songs as he can before the momentum runs out.

Title: Flume
Review: Flume’s decision to try his hand at everything, whilst demonstrating his evident enthusiasm and frequent successes, comes at the price of the album’s coherency. Nonetheless, there’s a lot of potential here.

Title: Sentenced to Life
Review: Everything it has done, including the EP "Razor to Oblivion" and the album "Heavy Breathing," has been better than good. But Sentenced to Life (Southern Lord), its second album, reaches a new level of--how else to say it?--professionalism.

Title: Something
Review: The Brooklyn duo returns with material that stays true to its trademark song structure but turns the musicality up considerably.

Title: Alela Diane & Wild Divine
Review: There was mmuch to anticipate, but it falls short of the promise. [May 2011, p.114]

Title: To Syria, With Love
Review: To Syria with Love was assembled with an eye toward expanding Souleyman's audience. Given the production and the wide selection of textural palettes and tunes, it's a good bet he'll be successful. It will likely keep longtime listeners in the fold, too, although the raw, unhinged feel of his earlier recordings will be missed.

Title: Hit Reset
Review: While Mr So and So shows the gig perv no mercy, elsewhere Hanna’s bonehead-nailing, predudice-lancing manifesto reverberates, as ever, with humanity and truth.

Title: Guero
Review: 'Guero' represents a very clever man being clever enough to recognise what he's good at. [19 Mar 2005, p.58]

Title: Quiet Signs
Review: Though earlier albums saw her crafting a strange otherworld, the perpetual sunset hinted at before is painted here in new dimensions, making this set of songs her best and easiest to revisit.

Title: The Diving Board
Review: It may be too reserved for excitable fans hoping for I’m Still Standing sequels, but the purity and simplicity of this unadorned balladry (Can’t Stay Alone Tonight, The New Fever Waltz) may bring many who fell by the wayside back into the fold.

Title: Hidden
Review: It's genuinely surprising, beautifully wrought and announces TNP as one of the most powerful artistic forces in Britain today.

Title: Voxtrot
Review: It’s not like everybody’s playing a different song. Everybody’s playing the same song. It’s just that, for great boring swathes, that song sounds stubborn. It sounds like it doesn’t want to be played.

Title: Mixed Race
Review: Mild as it might be, Mixed Race is a solid effort from someone who insists on sticking around.

Title: Family
Review: The album’s 10 tracks are likely to frustrate as much as excite Thompson loyalists.

Title: Here Lies Love
Review: Here Lies Love is a sumptuous two-disc feast of harmony, melody, and Latin-accented grooves that the Studio 54-loving Marcos herself would likely appreciate.

Title: Caramel
Review: Caramel and Mockasin definitely takes you on one hell of an adventure. Even though it might leave you feeling a little softened and dehydrated, I can’t wait to re-lace up my skates and embark on the next one.

Title: Godfather Buried Alive
Review: While the J-Kwons and Juveniles enjoy the fruits of paradise and their Lexus helicopters, Shyne reminds us of the ones who didn't make it: the legions of his fellow Clinton inmates fighting to keep afloat under prison's psychic burden.

Title: From The Hills Below The City
Review: It’s certainly the best down-to-earth storytelling item to emerge in ages.

Title: Tour de France Soundtracks
Review: There are moments where the glory years are emulated.... Even so, after 17 long years, both band and audience deserve better than a wandful of magic and some rehashes. [Oct 2003, p.102]

Title: Everything's OK
Review: Green sounds in his element. [Apr 2005, p.100]

Title: ESTOILE NAIANT
Review: Much like its creator and artwork, it remains unidentifiable, borderline incomprehensible even, but never less than thoroughly enthralling.

Title: 'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!
Review: 'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend! sells itself.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: It’s essential listening not so much for its quality--uneven, if generally high--but for the strange place it occupies in Morrissey’s discography. Not since 1991’s “Kill Uncle” has he given us anything quite so puzzling.

Title: Too Weird to Live, Too Rare to Die!
Review: Panic! At The Disco have completely hung up their steampunk wardrobes to deliver one of the year’s finest modern-pop works.

Title: Believers
Review: We need to find a way to smoke this.

Title: You Make Me Feel
Review: Bryant spins vocal somersaults over a deliciously slow-burning, spartan accompaniment, while several Memphis veterans add some Allman-style rock wigouts. [Jun 2020, p.27]

Title: Singing Saw
Review: Beauty that can slice down to bone: double-edged and deep. [Jul 2016, p.108]

Title: The Dissent of Man
Review: are a few new wrinkles--the manic push-pull of "Meeting of the Minds" could almost pass for System of a Down--but it's generally overdrive-guitar heaven.

Title: In Waves
Review: New drummer Nick Augusto seems to be pushing Trivium toward a choppier and at times more primal sound, but for a band that was recently poised to evolve into something more sumptuous and ambitious, In Waves is a return to form Trivium doesn't need.

Title: Marry Me
Review: It's an orchestral record for those who prefer the simplistic, a darker one for those who prefer theirs twee, love songs for the scorned and sad songs for the content, an engaging and alluring combination that makes Marry Me nearly irresistible, and one of the better indie pop albums that's come around for a long time.

Title: Far
Review: Far snuggles between her previous efforts, linking the heady sweep of 2003's "Soviet Kitsch" to the roundabout pop treats of "Begin to Hope."

Title: Volume 1
Review: Singers aside, we have those subtle harmonies drenching every song, sparkles of synth, strings and flute, and those sunrise drums lifting everything. It’s utterly gorgeous and the best bits of Midlake still shine through.

Title: Relapse
Review: The further Relapse strays from narrative veracity, the more one suspects his fanbase feels he's tapping into his bottomless well for horror-show grandstanding.

Title: Paper Walls
Review: It's prototypical Warped tour rock - but, to be fair, at the top level of that particular realm, with thoughtful lyrics and tightly crafted guitar arrangements.

Title: MDNA
Review: An album that's competent, but equally perfunctory.

Title: Collisions
Review: The breakthrough record where Calla go from a whisper to a scream.

Title: Collisions
Review: In its best moments, Collisions has an edge that's grittier and more emphatic than its predecessor.

Title: Palindrome Hunches
Review: Though it may take some time to grow accustomed to, this is a record you'll want to wrap yourself up in.

Title: Playtime Is Over
Review: Playtime Is Over is exactly what we've come to expect from the garage sound of grime. It isn't trying to be anything it's not.

Title: ANTI
Review: It's an intriguing scrapbook of ideas and frequently enjoyable, but could use a banger or tow. [Apr 2016, p.112]

Title: Kiwanuka
Review: Ultimately, this is an album in which a troubled spirit seeks the relief of music to mesmerising and charged effect. And that is timeless.

Title: Ice on the Dune
Review: Ice on the Dune is a seamless suite of elegiac synthpop, with fairydust-flecked melodies, a perpetually peaking bass end, chord changes that reach into your heart, and fantasising falsetto vocals.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: Hypnotic Eye ends up a dynamic mini-album--but doesn’t quite sustain its momentum for an entire full-length.

Title: Delusion Moon
Review: For it's forty minute duration, Meat Wave's second record is one of the most engaging you're likely to find this year.

Title: Exai
Review: Booth and Brown are old hands these days, their territory firmly staked out. It’s gratifying to see, if only briefly, that they haven’t lost the element of surprise.

Title: Since We've Become Translucent
Review: Only one or two tracks capture that combination of venom, wit and old-time Northwest angst that made Mudhoney one of the grunge movement's standouts. [Oct 2002, p.88]

Title: Melophobia
Review: The resulting album is, at its best, ambitious and teeming with ideas and, at worst, one heck of a mish-mash of sounds.

Title: Temporary Pleasure
Review: It’s trashy yet too self-conscious for its own good, it’s lovingly crafted yet ultimately hollow, it’s dance music which veers from so catchy you can’t help yourself to chin-stroking music to nod at and appreciate.

Title: Nav
Review: NAV’s songcraft is sharp, but the lack of dynamics ultimately makes this debut feel one-note.

Title: True North
Review: While it's true that listeners looking for a more rounded rock record may come away feeling a little bludgeoned, the more important point is that for those along for the ride, time has done nothing to dull Graffin and Gurewitz's songwriting abilities.

Title: I'll Be Your Girl
Review: It falls into a very similar trap to the band’s last album, which started with a track that sounded promisingly fresh (“The Singer Addresses His Audience”) before immediately lapsing into Decemberists-by-numbers (“Cavalry Captain”).

Title: Hypnophobia
Review: Occasionally struggling to balance style with substance, Gardner nonetheless makes Hypnophobia much more than just an exercise in sonic adventurism. [No. 120, p.55]

Title: Widow City
Review: A gas, a blast. [12 Oct 2007, p.75]

Title: Powerballin'
Review: It's not that the album isn't good, it's that it pails in comparison to "Jackpot."

Title: Human After All
Review: Feels desultory and numb, verging on autistic. [Apr 2005, p.116]

Title: The Nothing They Need
Review: Wiry but not without weight, The Nothing They Need conveys an increasingly efficient model of Dead Meadow, saying its piece in eight unhurried, hash-hued visions.

Title: Song Yet to Be Sung
Review: Oddly enough, he not only makes it work, he makes it a whopping success.

Title: Other Life
Review: Other Life is a collection of poignant, emotionally powerful pop songs; but on a more conceptual plane, this album is a self-referential commentary on music itself, an intense examination--and, ultimately, an extremely heartfelt refutation--of the hollow, ironic appropriation that defines much of contemporary music.

Title: In Your Honor
Review: The most accomplished work of Grohl's post-Nirvana career. [Aug 2005, p.174]

Title: Nanobots
Review: Nanobots is, at the end of the day, a solid and immensely likable album.

Title: One Beat
Review: One Beat is ruthless with SuperGlue riffs that reach back a decade or more, from the Go-Gos pogo of "Oh!" to the stuttering Cure guitars of "The Remainder" to the Buzzcocks toolings of "Hollywood Ending."

Title: Songs of Mass Destruction
Review: Mass Destruction is Lennox's first album largely recorded in the U.S. (Los Angeles and Miami, as opposed to just London), giving the songs a slightly less chilly quality and a bigger, more expansive sound, but it's still a disappointment in the same way the Eurythmics' rock-leaning "Be Yourself Tonight" likely was to fans of "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)" and "Touch."

Title: Unpatterns
Review: Unpatterns is very now, yet by employing key electronic music touchstones it sounds classic as well.

Title: Challengers
Review: Challengers stacks up against the pillar of "Twin Cinema" just fine; it is the more restrained of the two, equally as satisfying, and more stylistically varied.

Title: Tarot Sport
Review: If "Street Horrsing" was a bit of a lark, then Tarot Sport plays an altogether more serious game. [Nov 2009, p.92]

Title: Watch Me Fall
Review: Watch Me Fall is even more melodic. Reatard classes up the joint a bit, smearing organ, hard-strummed acoustic guitar, and strings on the unrequited-love epic 'I’m Watching You.'

Title: Hell Bent
Review: Whether Potty Mouth are achieving anything new is besides the point--the important thing is that they feel fresh and relevant, whereas the punk of today has seemingly had its time, growing increasingly redundant and stale

Title: Frantic
Review: Frantic is packed with potential singles, as if he's decided it's not crime to enjoy himself, to embrace foolish things earthier than Avalon. This is classic Ferry, but full of surprises. [May 2002, p.92]

Title: i,i
Review: Vernon is an expert curator of his emotions, even if i,i needs to let a little more air in under the glass at times. [Oct 2019, p.110]

Title: Hold Time
Review: Yet for all the vintage analog atmosphere, the Portland, Ore., songwriter's sixth album continues to expand his Americana template with more of the classic AM pop sensibilities shown on 2006's "Post-War" and flooding last year's Zooey Deschanel collaboration, "She & Him."

Title: Keep It Like a Secret
Review: Built to Spill's combo of wry phrasing and explosive sound is more honed on this album than ever before.

Title: The Incredible True Story
Review: There's enough variation in energy and production to keep the listener engaged throughout, and several times there are sudden drops into another beat entirely in the middle of a song.

Title: Diaspora
Review: It’s GoldLink’s ability to seem at home in any space that makes Diaspora so coherent, and so specific to him, despite pulling music from all over. He is the anchor.

Title: All Thoughts Fly
Review: Unlike her song-based previous albums, All Thoughts Fly is instrumental, performed entirely on pipe organ. Its lush soundscapes find transcendence in the eerie and the sorrowful, much like Sacro Bosco itself.

Title: Balf Quarry
Review: Balf Quarry, their first album for Drag City, isn’t going to put a halt to those Sonic Youth comparisons. They’ve steadfastly stuck with the sound created on the Boss album for most of this venture.

Title: Lantern
Review: The problem is that Birchard spreads himself so thin in his rush to tick off all the stylistic boxes, some songs sputter into half-realized cliché.

Title: Molina & Johnson
Review: Written and recorded in 10 days, this debut collaboration is a testament to just how deeply these two songwriters sympathize with each other's work, revealing a shared penchant for evocatively detailed images that blossom into visceral narratives.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: This stream-of-consciousness head trip blends tricky, delicious melodies and slippery lyrics, yet never lapses into annoyingly smug artiness. [Mar 2007, p.88]

Title: Is This It
Review: For now, the Strokes have mastered their style; they have yet to come up with the substance to match it.... But the music leaves no doubts - more joyful and intense than anything else I've heard this year.

Title: Frozen Letter
Review: McGee may not know where he's going on his murky head trip, but he's a compelling enough guide that you want to follow him.

Title: All My Relations
Review: On record, it's certainly a jolt, and not just a pile of drum-driven aural overload, but something does get lost in the process.

Title: America Give Up
Review: A "more accessible, less-noisy Jesus and Mary Chain".

Title: Evolution
Review: The heavy songs on Evolution should please longtime fans, with a couple harkening back to the dynamism of Disturbed’s first couple of albums, but the glut of softer tracks may have been served better on a separate acoustic EP.

Title: Napa Asylum
Review: This sprawling mosaic of 22 songs has more room for melody and nuance than any of their previous albums, and they divine many moods and sounds within their fuzz.

Title: Electric
Review: He's written better collections of songs, but for fun, warmth, vigour and power, it' sup there with his best. [Mar 2013, p.86]

Title: The Waiting Room
Review: While McIlwain is operating within more rigid structures, another hangover from his ambient productions is that he can sometimes sound a bit directionless.

Title: Condition
