Review: Condition sits somewhere between the two [previous albums Dying and Dead], obscuring lovely melodies with disjointed electronica on deliberately self-destructive tracks like "Dissolve," the willowy "Colour Me Out" and "Coping Mechanism." [Apr 2017, p.39]

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: Our Ill Wills is generally an album of dispair and longing. [Summer 2007, p.77]

Title: Breakup Song
Review: Though their sound is undoubtedly unique, their music has become formulaic.

Title: Love is Dead
Review: Over two self-produced top 10 albums, Lauren Mayberry, Martin Doherty and Iain Cook, all graduates of alternative and post-rock bands, have refined a sound that keeps one foot in indie electronica, the other in modern radio pop and its heart in 80s synths.

Title: Andorra
Review: So slick is the production and so smooth is the transition from one moment to the next that Andorra suffers from an apparent reluctance to take us by the scruff of the neck and rattle us out of our mental Laconia.

Title: The Something Rain
Review: Forget diminishing returns, The Something Rain keeps Tindersticks' value high. [April 2012, p.105]

Title: Four Stars
Review: In any sensible home there's always room for some no-nonsense, Nuggets-era Garage rock, however, and for that alone the impossibly titled **** pushes plenty of the right buttons. [Jan 2011, p.142]

Title: You Are Not Alone
Review: The entire set speaks directly to the struggles and fears of an America desperately searching for some meaning and uplift. Staples and Tweedy have crafted a record with heart and grace, but also some toughness--all of them necessary if the goal is transcending troubled times.

Title: Reverie Lagoon: Music For Escapism Only
Review: The production allows the introspective oddness of Soto’s lyrics to show through better, lending them a really likeable, stand-out character.

Title: Babel
Review: There are images of walls and towers in nearly every song, but they don't serve as a unifying theme--a missed opportunity for an album named after a famous tower.

Title: Idlewild
Review: An awkward, uneven record that comes over like something they made in a week instead of something that was continually pushed back for more than a year.

Title: The Colour in Anything
Review: As with anyone complaining of love lost between pleas for it to return, it begins to become tiresome — no matter how smooth your voice may be. But Blake manages to make a whopping 17-song album transition seamlessly, holding your attention thanks to a careful execution of space between those very keys.

Title: Polymer
Review: Polymer is a summation of everything that puts Plaid rightfully on the same level of their innovative peers like Autechre, Boards of Canada and Two Lone Swordsmen. Creating worlds at once hermetic and immersive, Plaid’s music ticks along at a human level and envelops you in a protective, provocative cocoon.

Title: Glassheart
Review: As it is, it's simply the next Leona Lewis album.

Title: Pretty in Black
Review: The larger scope of the album bodes well for The Raveonettes... [but] it’s a shame that there are several clunkers mixed with such strong material.

Title: White Blood Cells
Review: This fine, fine album (quite possibly the finest of year) signals that the White Stripes have arrived. Hype or no hype, this is a band of significance...

Title: A Series of Shocks
Review: Like his last album, Leaning Over Backwards, A Series of Shocks is rich and spatially ambitious.

Title: Not Yet
Review: This new record is nothing surprising. It's everything that you'd expect. Right out of the gate, the message is clear: It is who it is, giving us a band, and an album, full of confidence and bruises. Yet by just being who it is, the music works, and, rightfully so, doesn't need to prove anything to anyone.

Title: Get Away From Me
Review: It's sometimes hard to tell who's running the show, the major label or the major talent.

Title: Ephyra
Review: When they do finally depart after a handful of shows later this month, Woman's Hour find themselves in the fairly unique position of having a small but well formed catalogue of work that's near flawless. As a result, Ephyra is a fitting epitaph.

Title: East of Eden
Review: East of Eden, in that sense, isn't so far from Studio's West Coast: a masterful, hypnotic album that draws on a world of influences but is ultimately limited by none.

Title: No No
Review: Much like switching on a 24-hour news channel, No No is engrossing for the first ten minutes or so. Then the parade of lurid images continues, and sure enough, they give you a headache.

Title: Woodstock
Review: Instead of putting their own offbeat stamp on danceable pop music, Portugal. The Man abandons their once-unique sound and retreats into imitation.

Title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
Review: Musically, Stewart's ambition to marry first-album Suicide with Einsturzende Neubauten and latter-day Scott Walker has been realised with aplomb. [Mar 2014, p.95]

Title: Any Human Friend
Review: Whether the subject is sex, love, equality or heartbreak, Any Human Friend offers up the perfect combination - lyrics to make you think and music to make you move.

Title: Wu-Massacre
Review: Enter Wu-Massacre a fun, but mostly forgettable affair that comes from three of the clan’s most prominent members; (Ghostface, Raekwon, Method Man) and for the most part ends up being little more than good-natured fan service.

Title: Helter Seltzer
Review: It’s not teeming with future classics, but it’s their most solid and replayable record since Brain Thrust Mastery.

Title: Headphones
Review: The mood of the disc is no less overcast than his usual material; it just makes more use of the celesta setting.

Title: Let Them Talk
Review: Let Them Talk is competent and heartfelt but far from necessary. [Jun 2011, p.87]

Title: Vultures
Review: It's not perfect by any means, but taking this for what it is, Vultures is a gnarly debut effort. [29 Sep 2012, p.52]

Title: The Wind
Review: It is a wonderful album that explores separation and endings and life’s journeys – and their inevitable end - in Zevon’s inimitable style.

Title: Nobody's Smiling
Review: He's nowhere near as agile as he once was, but that slack is picked up on a handful of collaborations with sharp young rappers like Lil Herb and Vince Staples. [Sep 2014, p.65]

Title: Avi Buffalo
Review: For those that can stand the fact that this lot really do possess some talent, this might be another slice of Sub Pop to add to the collection.

Title: Rooms of the House
Review: It’s a unique record, for sure, and one that deserves at least some of your time.

Title: Supermodel
Review: Forward isn’t always better. But for Foster the People, on Supermodel, it was the right direction.

Title: Stay Gold
Review: Stay Gold should surely find itself in contention as one of the best albums of the year as 2014 draws to an end.

Title: Virgins
Review: A daringly deconstructed soundtrack of the spheres.

Title: Malibu
Review: For its lyrical and musical scope, Malibu brings to mind a number of excellent albums, ranging from Stevie Wonder’s Innervisions to, yes, Kendrick Lamar’s To Pimp a Butterfly.

Title: Oh Inhuman Spectacle
Review: They may lack the immediacy of some of their more envelope-pushing contemporaries, but as sonic world-builders they excel, and certainly possess the acumen to expand those horizons on future outings.

Title: Let the Poison Out
Review: On balance, then, exactly 68.5% of this record is worth listening to.

Title: Metropole
Review: Songwriters Brendan Kelly and Chris McCaughan are in peak form and are far too self-aware to fall into that old trap; they know better than to chase capricious youth.

Title: Coco Beware
Review: The tunes wash over nicely, but ultimately fail to endear the listener. [Oct 2011, p97]

Title: Crack-Up
Review: Some may be unconvinced by the ambitious leap Fleet Foxes have made on album three, but there’s really no doubting the first-rate intelligence behind this uncompromising and ever-changing piece of work.

Title: Etch and Etch Deep
Review: An album-long search for new ways to express old thoughts, and far from any prescribed formula of tempos and buggery that would entail techno or drum n’ bass or other electronic information media.

Title: Honor Found in Decay
Review: Nothing here indicates they won't continue to rank among progressive music's leading explorers, well beyond those temporal musical fashions discussed earlier.

Title: Beat Pyramid
Review: Hypnotic repetition, mysterious soundscapes and recurring lyrical codes render this debut utterly engrossing and totally essential.

Title: Hurry Up, We're Dreaming
Review: Gonzalez wraps both hooks and hallucinations in bubbly melodies only occasionally bogged down by murky sprawl. [28 Oct 2011, p.73]

Title: Employment
Review: They develop, mutate, and swell in confidence until you’re faced with the last thing you expected - finally, a worthy successor to Blur.

Title: Both Sides of the Gun
Review: If in Both Sides of the Gun Harper is trying to show his audience what a wide variety of music he can cover, he certainly accomplishes that. But if he's trying to create an album that is really about him, he doesn't quite deliver. Ben Harper is in there, don't worry, but he can be a little hard to find.

Title: Release Therapy
Review: Release Therapy may not be the mature Ludacris record it purports itself to be, but that isn’t to say it doesn’t have some jaw-dropping confessional moments.

Title: Snares Like a Haircut
Review: Snares seems like a long EP--one that ends before it really gets going.

Title: Fuckbook
Review: Fuckbook is the best joke fake lo-fi cover album since Pussy Galore’s Exile, except with the added irony of the roasters becoming the roastees.

Title: Our Pathetic Age
Review: Our Pathetic Age reflects the way much of Shadow’s post-Endtroducing material has lacked structure, with the producer happy to throw ideas at the page, even if many of them don’t stick.

Title: Lupercalia
Review: The fabric of the songs seems imbued with joy, and it's testament to the quality of the songwriting that you don't feel alienated by what are incredibly personal lyrics. It's an all-inclusive love in, basically, and all the better for it.

Title: Vices
Review: While Peggy Sue never quite reached the dizzy heights of Mumford and Sons’ stadium-sized tours, their artfully woven narratives are more than double-tap worthy of it.

Title: VYP (Voice of the Young People)
Review: Not a bad debut, finally, but someone should tell her that speaking for the young people doesn't mean merely becoming Shanice with attitude.

Title: The Getaway
Review: As ever, California gets plenty of mentions, though there’s less filler than usual, the album reaching a yearning epiphany in the string-draped song for a son, “The Hunter”.

Title: Fire Within
Review: The album isn’t flawless, but it’s certainly better than many would expect from a girl her age. Fire Within is actually better than a lot of music that people far older and “wiser” are putting out.

Title: Out Calls Only
Review: There's enough bittersweet emotion to ensure his own personality seeps through. [Jul 2015, p.96]

Title: Hell on Heels
Review: None of this would work if the songs weren't actually good, but they're frequently brilliant.

Title: All Days Are Nights: Songs For Lulu
Review: So one third's great and two thirds grate, which is an improvement at least.

Title: The Besnard Lakes Are The Dark Horse
Review: Too big in their influences and scope to fit in even the biggest pigeonhole imaginable, The Besnard Lakes thankfully produce music chock-full of tunes and spine-tingly loveliness not seen since The Beach Boys or more recently the sheer joy and ridiculous grandeur of The Polyphonic Spree.

Title: Passive Me, Aggressive You
Review: A classic case of ugly and beautiful: TN&F's passive melodicism and aggressive innovation clash in a dazzling blaze of psych/sonic fireworks.

Title: Blackstar
Review: Blackstar is its own strange, perverse thing, the ­latest move in a boundlessly ­unpredictable career.

Title: Devil's Halo
Review: It would seem that on this album, Ndegeocello is less concerned with how emotion strikes a person (be it love, pain, or sex), but how people relate to that emotion. And in the process she creates the tightest, most emotionally potent work she’s produced since Bitter.

Title: The Richest Man In Babylon
Review: Hilton and Garza explore foreign cultures with wide-eyed curiosity and a taste for the unexpected.

Title: The Little Willies
Review: "The Little Willies" is several notches above a living-room jam. It is rehearsed, flowing, expertly produced. But it is still an album that has been hanging around the house all day in its sweatpants. [6 Mar 2006]

Title: Sauna
Review: No song on Sauna is going to make you sweat but every one will relax you and coax you into letting your worries seep on out of you. Like all his work, this record is a peaceful exorcism.

Title: Shame, Shame
Review: Balancing these cheery influences with the melancholy prose is the name of the game. The lively accordion and clanky piano on the song "Shadow People" recall Bob Dylan's 1974 country-folk single "Forever Young," but the cheerfulness seems to contradict Dr. Dog guitarist/vocalist Scott McMicken's strained lyric: "It's the right time for the wrong company."

Title: The Happiness Waltz
Review: What keeps it from the top is the lack of musical surprises. Still, these twelve songs will keep you warm as winter turns to spring.

Title: Pool
Review: The record is a bit too downtempo to be ideal party music, but it’ll make a killer soundtrack for your walk home from the party.

Title: V
Review: Five albums in and The Horrors have obviously found a new lease of life. This V is for victorious.

Title: Tempest
Review: As with the albums that have come in its wake, this one will be compared to 1997's Time Out Of Mind, the last truly great Dylan disc. Though not of that caliber, Tempest finds Bob Dylan still very much in the game.

Title: Someday World
Review: With its jarring synthetic brass--which is neither as charming or amusingly ironic as its creators seem to think it is--Someday World starts off on the wrong foot from the very first bars.

Title: Both Ways Open Jaws
Review: The second album from this mysterious French/Finnish indie-folk duo is every bit as eclectic and unexpected as the first.

Title: The ArchAndroid
Review: To say it's ambitious feels like damning with faint praise; its sheer musical scope--from the James Brown funk of Tightrope to the English pastoral folk of Oh, Maker--is spellbinding.

Title: Rain
Review: Ten very good to great songs, stamped with the signature of a musician who knows what he is about. That, kids, is what we used to call an “album”, and this is a very fine one indeed.

Title: Help Us Stranger
Review: A fun romp through the most succinct Jack White material in a decade, a collection of songs that will thrill crowds across the world until White moves on to whatever his next project is.

Title: Phantom Power
Review: There's a newfound depth to the Furries' music, a sense that no matter how hard the band tries to keep things positive, the darkness in the world has managed to encroach on its outlook and musical approach.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: As a whole, the album may not be impeccable, but it’s the best he’s released since 2010.

Title: The Glorious Dead
Review: They sometimes feel as second-hand as The Black Crowes, but The Heavy's capacity for rabble-rousing is a potent strength, which in music – if not always politics – isn't necessarily a bad thing.

Title: Magic Hour
Review: The production sometimes eclipses the songwriting.

Title: We Don't Even Live Here
Review: We Don't Even Live Here is a solid, confident step forward for the Minneapolis rapper, taking his confrontational punk-rap style and injecting it with a dark, danceable energy that sacrifices none of his signature hardcore edge.

Title: Slash
Review: This disc might not change your life, but it's an undeniably solid hard rock album that proves how much credit Slash deserves for the success of his former band.

Title: Enderness
Review: Even if there isn’t much meat here and the concepts are obtuse at best, the oddly titled Enderness (the beginning “T” is conspicuously, and intentionally, missing), taps into an enticing, low-key vibe that’s just as satisfying and far more personal.

Title: Invincible
Review: Though fatally flawed, Invincible does boast its fair share of sonic exhilaration. [#184, p.132]

Title: Alien In A Garbage Dump
Review: It’s arty, it’s farty, it’s at times strangely hypnotic and if you leave it on your record collection it will make you look really cool. If that’s your thing...

Title: Mudcrutch
Review: The songs are mythic Americana: With help from his bandmates, Petty creates a vivid cast of road dogs, strippers and junkies that conjures Gram Parsons' Bible-haunted Southerners and Robert Hunter's cosmic Westerners.

Title: Putrifiers II
Review: Beside Putrifiers II's guitar-fuelled thrills are a number of moments that find Thee Oh See's catching their winklepinkers on the pavement as they attempt to side step into more experimental, psychedelic territory.

Title: Emika
Review: This is the product of a dynamic and assured vision, one that retains an alluring sense of mystery.

Title: Feels
Review: It's on the sonic departures, though, that Feels strikes its most resonant chord.

Title: Security Screenings
Review: A disjointed affair on first listen, "Security Screening" eventually reveals itself as the mirror image of main man Scott Herren's multiple musical personalities. [11 Feb 2006]

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: In its 12 tracks, M.I.A. explores both what it means to serve as a sexual/romantic ideal in the Beyonce way, and what happens when a self-consciously political artist like herself confronts the sentimental streak deep within.

Title: Will the Guns Come Out
Review: The tracks jump in range between genres, but for the most part you can find a consistent punk sound woven throughout.

Title: Acousmatic Sorcery
Review: While Acousmatic Sorcery is interesting and occasionally even great on its own, it ultimately it feels very much like a hyper-creative and gifted artist trying to figure out what he's doing.

Title: Hollywood: A Story of a Dozen Roses
Review: Much of the production on Hollywood is swampy, but it’s a digital swamp. Mr. Foxx’s voice is slathered with so many effects that he veers toward anonymity.

Title: Scratch My Back
Review: This tribute to 12 of Peter Gabriel's favorite songwriters is a cool idea that turns into a stone bore.

Title: My Heart Has a Wish That You Would Not Go
Review: There are elements of everything from Radiohead to Sigur Rós and even the shimmering beauty of the Cocteau Twins, yet their sharp songwriting conjures up Snow Patrol with less obvious strokes.

Title: LP5
Review: As expected from Apparat, LP5 is an ambitious, inventive album which runs on its own intuition, fusing studio wizardry with honest expression to frequently thrilling results.

Title: The Black Parade
Review: This is a goofy record of bubblegum punk, with Queen lapping at its edges and enough good tracks to justify the smattering of empty screamfests.

Title: Another One
Review: Another One is a collection of a few of DeMarco’s best songs to date, all in a day’s work for this normal guy who just so happens to get a little wild on stage.

Title: Want Two
Review: Demanding and artful, he just may be this generation's Joni Mitchell. [5 Dec 2004]

Title: The Soft Pack
Review: There's little to make them noticeable today. [Winter 2010, p.69]

Title: Young the Giant
Review: California five-piece coming soon to a stadium near you. [Sept. 2011, p. 100]

Title: Children Running Through
Review: She has blossomed into one of contemporary folk's most enchanting voices.

Title: Corinne Bailey Rae
Review: If you don't mind the odd reflective moment, the odd luscious production value, then this has plenty to offer. [25 Mar 2006, p.37]

Title: Sewn Together
Review: They have shed their gormless, drifting amateurism and turned themselves into a classic American pop band. [Aug 2009, p.109]

Title: B-Room
Review: The lyrics and vocal delivery are just as clever as the sonic landscape, and it seems as if this album might be the high-water mark for a band many will mistakenly write off as just another indie act.

Title: I AKA I
Review: What’s left is something truly fresh, barely recognisable, a shuddering, bending feast of sound.

Title: Feels Like Home
Review: Feels Like Home is so inoffensive you have trouble remembering whether you put it on.

Title: Fifth Harmony
Review: It's the group's most cohesive album yet and a satisfying introduction to what Fifth Harmony can be capable of in their new era.

Title: Sermon on the Rocks
Review: Ritter draws liberally from the well of himself, others and the Bible, and it's a fun ride.

Title: Where The Gods Are In Peace
Review: With an album-long theme revolving around the ascent of an alien who joins forces with natives to save the world, Antibalas seem more than ready to push themselves to another musical level with Where the Gods Are in Peace.

Title: Up The Bracket
Review: The group's innate intelligence and almost shocking ability to forge something new and thrilling out of typical garage-rock influences always shines brightly through the thick Guinness fog.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: This is harsh, unyielding stuff, and most of this jolting album contains more the same. On her two previous albums, Lykke Li has been something of a floating presence, but everything about this album is intensely grounded.

Title: Good Thing
Review: Leon Bridges' sophomore record rings as an endorsement of his range. And that's a great thing for Good Thing, which tempers its pop-radio ambitions with unique bends on the age-old love song in this super-tight, 35-minute ride.

Title: Bitte Orca
Review: Bitte Orca signifies something exciting and all too infrequent in popular music: striving for a sound that doesn't have a definite audience.

Title: WE ARE CHAOS
Review: This batch of cadaverous Bowie-isms won't leave fang marks on your memory. [Sep 2020, p.68]

Title: Waking Lines
Review: Waking Lines is an ambitious premiere, but one that’s not had all it’s misshapen foibles ironed out. Patterns have, however, ensured that they’ll remain inside people’s heads for a considerable time to come.

Title: Tourist
Review: A very disappointing step backwards.

Title: The Bachelor
Review: When the dust settles around the closing notes of The Bachelor’s outro, 'The Messenger,' it’s clear that Wolf has achieved that rare artistic feat: total catharsis. And a beautiful batch of it, at that.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Forgiveness Rock Record might lack the romance of Funeral but it's far more alive than Neon Bible, with an urgency and energy that invigorates rather than drains.

Title: Sea Lion
Review: A strange, lovely trip.

Title: Re-Mit
Review: Some ace stuff aboard here.... But you do long for MES to turn up with a sheaf of structured writing, as per Hex Enduction, rather than a sozzled brainful of scattered grievances and in-jokes. [Jul 2013, p.86]

Title: Petra Goes To The Movies
Review: The arrangements are ingenious, emphasizing Ms. Haden's gift for mimesis: she can suggest the swoon of a string section as handily as the blare of a solitary bugle.

Title: Stay Alive
Review: Each is very different, but they’re connected by a sense of the time and space they were crafted in. It’s a collection of postcards from the edge that we’ve all been walking and one that’s utterly engaging.

Title: Charli
Review: Here she balances world-straddling confidence with unprecedented exposure of the anxieties and self-destruction that stymie her relationships, turning her from pop powerhouse to empathetic protagonist.

Title: Sunset Kids
Review: A few more rockers on the order of the Armstrong co-write “Strangers & Thieves” would have raised the overall temperature, but each of these 14 tracks is an exquisitely constructed gem.

Title: Savage Mode II
Review: In the end, you get 44 minutes of solid beats and bars and a handful of songs to put on your best-of playlists for Savage and/or Metro. That’s not the worst thing, but on Savage Mode II it feels like there’s both too much and not enough going on at once.

Title: Boys Don't Cry
Review: Boys Don't Cry isn't as satisfying a release as an original album would have been. But this is the labour of love whose genesis predates her debut. And it really does sound like another season in her soul.

Title: Mission Control
Review: It swaggers like prime Replacements, though with far better polish. [Jan 2008, p.103]

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: Kehalni’s lubricious vocals and tender slow jams are not for the faint-hearted, but there is a real core of emotional truth burning through these X-rated grooves.

Title: Alphabetical
Review: Perhaps they should stick to singles.

Title: The Fragile Army
Review: Sharpened writing invests these songs with plenty of hooks, yet manageable lengths insure they never overstay their welcome, always leaving you wanting more. [Summer 2007, p.84]

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: It's been a long time since Radiohead made records with an eye toward anything more than satisfying the band's own creative impulses, if it ever did. Those who are prepared to stick it out, though, may well find The King of Limbs worth the wait.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: Merrie Land
Review: He's mined this territory before, notably in Gorillaz's Demon Days, yet the very fact that the Good, The Bad & The Queen function as a band, drawing strength from their own interplay, gives Merrie Land a human resonance that echoes long after the final song ends.

Title: Magic Hour
Review: The overall affect is to transport us back to that pre-9/11 decade when “alternative music” really was an apt descriptor. Thankfully, it’s OK to give in to a bit of nostalgia on occasion.

Title: See You Around
Review: The songwriting is not quite as enigmatic as on that precursor project [case/lang/veirs]. ... The trio’s strengths lie mostly in the natural sweetness of their harmonies, a heartbreaking union of glowing melancholy underscoring the life lessons of songs such as “See You Around” and “Ain’t That Fine.”

Title: A Shut-In's Prayer
Review: The narratives are better developed and there are invariably a couple of lines in each song that hit home emotionally.

Title: The Weather Station
Review: The Weather Station is Lindeman's loosest, most confident album yet, but it may also prove to be her most deeply psychological; she doesn't hold back.

Title: Kish Kash
Review: Some of the most propulsive, ferocious music of the year as well as some of the most poignant.

Title: Change
Review: While the B-52's belatedly embraced electronics on 2008's Funplex, Change finds Wilson doing the same, but from a decidedly different vantage point, and it fits her beautifully; it's a successful musical reinvention that presents her talent in a whole new light.

Title: God Save the Clientele
Review: God Save the Clientele sounds like the work of the same band, but it shows them in a new, brighter light, broadened in both sound and outlook. In terms of sonics and tunes, these changes are welcome and logical, expanding upon the sound with which they made their name without sacrificing intimacy or risking coming across overcooked.

Title: Root for Ruin
Review: While Root for Ruin isn't the creative reawakening that Let's Stay Friends was, it might be the band's tightest and most polished album yet.

Title: Between The Stars
Review: The majority of the workmanlike Between the Stars, deftly juggles the muscular and the melodic without breaking a sweat in the process.

Title: That's Why God Made the Radio
Review: The album is an un- even but deeply touching work by a clearly flawed Great Band – one that, at its best, always aimed for the heavens, even if it didn't always reach them.

Title: Freedom
Review: Every track here is interchangeable, not only with each other, but with anything from his back catalogue. [Feb 2009, p.76]

Title: Far
Review: playing the freak also makes her blissfully unself-conscious, and that can be contagious. Nothing's more heartfelt than 'Wallet,' an ode to a stranger who lost his.

Title: Lost Property
Review: There's a warmth and careless spirit to 96, Rome and myriad others that hasn't always been there down the years, and they've seldom bettered Save You. It really is heart-warming to have them back on point. [Feb 2016, p.90]

Title: Pond Scum
Review: Though it has merit in the strength of its content, Pond Scum may be only one for the collectors.

Title: White Women
Review: Go ahead, laugh at tongue-in-cheek lines like, "You're a sexy socialite/ I wish you were a socialist/ Instead of worrying about your name on the list," but do so knowing that Chromeo is serious about getting you on the dance floor.

Title: Loud
Review: There's plenty of that spacey/dirty sound on Loud, even when the tracks don't fit the trance template. [Apr 2002, p.122]

Title: A Hundred Days Off
Review: The thundering beats, subdued vocals of indecipherable lyrics, and power packed riffs are all still there, but they've mellowed and everything is a bit softer around the edges.

Title: Load Blown
Review: Black Dice still belong in the DIY basement space but with Load Blown they’ve made their most accessible album yet.

Title: Wicked Nature
Review: Wicked Nature is a fateful folly that might just bear fruit. [Oct 2014, p.89]

Title: Monsters of Folk
Review: It's more jaunty nouveau Traveling Wilburys than folk rock summit as Bright Eyes' Conor Oberst, My Morning Jacket's Jim James and M Ward join forces.

Title: Us
Review: A joyous slice of orchestral prozac.

Title: B-Room
Review: Maybe it puts something of a low ceiling above its head by adhering too closely to the band’s recent efforts,  but while little here stands out above other Dr. Dog records, the songs are still plenty good.

Title: Empros
Review: Circles finds the band leaving a bit of the motorik behind for more melodic and dynamic territory. [#82, p.57]

Title: Outbursts
Review: ‘Sea Change’ is as epic as anything that came later, Knights’ vocal supplemented by a rich seam of orchestration, but much of the material here could have been lifted from those early recordings, where skeletal fret work frames angelic vocals. A return to the source.

Title: Drums Between the Bells
Review: The decision to vary the speaking participants helps distinguish each piece, and gives the album just the hint of variety it needs.

Title: You in Reverse
Review: You in Reverse... rejects the pithy pop of their 1999 breakthrough, Keep It Like a Secret, for spacey, stretchy tracks that emphasize their unique, virtuosic musicianship.

Title: Gentle Spirit
Review: It's engaging stuff. It just outstays its welcome a bit.

Title: Walk The River
Review: It comes armed with a pocketful of melodies and great musicianship. But yet somehow it doesn't convince. It's hamstrung in part by its length.

Title: All Aboard Future
Review: The result is a thrilling, hyperpercussive collection of laptop ditties mixed so cleverly that they'll sound great ticking through earbuds or booming out of dad's trusty Cerwin-Vegas.

Title: We Shall All Be Healed
Review: Lyrically, things are mainly annoying, although there are a few bits of amusing storytelling, and some interesting couplets.

Title: Alice
Review: You'd be hard-pressed to find sounds this spookily evocative anywhere outside the grooves of scratchy old 78s. [Applies to both 'Alice' and 'Blood Money,' 10 May 2002, p.80]

Title: Women as Lovers
Review: The songwriting of its back-half just doesn’t stand up to its front-half or the rest of the band’s catalog.

Title: Tomorrow's Harvest
Review: These 17 vignettes glow with Cold War paranoia, picking up where Threads, the most scarring piece of TV ever made, left off. It might also be the duo’s most accomplished album yet--and that’s coming from someone unable to remove the Hi Scores LP from his stereo.

Title: Harmony Avenue
Review: The net result is unexpectedly charming. [Aug 2020, p.30]

Title: Goodbye Terrible Youth
Review: Although the scattered nature of some of the songs keeps any single narrative from taking shape, the album is a significant improvement for a band that’s still coming into its own, still, in other words, in its youth.

Title: Heligoland
Review: With personnel changes and a series of guest artists the names of which ever-increasingly overshadow whatever actual sounds they're making, Massive Attack have fought a continual struggle to surpass 1994's 'Protection'.

Title: 10,000 Days
Review: Stupendously packaged, the music robustly mixed and often achieving new levels of bleak beauty, 10,000 Days is too strong a work to call a disappointment, but the constant need to fill out a CD to 75-80 minutes is threatening to become the band’s undoing.

Title: Fight Softly
Review: With sounds plucked from here, there and everywhere, it's an ambitious collection, but singer Ryan McPhun's gentle voice lends this second album by the Kiwis a beautiful tone.

Title: Geogaddi
Review: "Geogaddi" finds the Scottish duo ever adept at pushing the boundaries of electronic music without abandoning the hypnotically pacific nature of their sound.

Title: Sound & Color
Review: Notes may be reached, riffs rinsed, stop-start moments choreographed, but nothing’s being reached for, on appearance, at least--it’s all so brilliantly effortless.

Title: On A Distant Shore
Review: It’s a little regrettable then that his last officially studio album, coming out less than a year after he died, is so overproduced and kitschy.

Title: Napa Asylum
Review: Napa Asylum graces us with moments of understated beauty, and when it's not terrifying us with bad trips, leaves a feeling of contentment and fuzzy warmth with the world. However, 22 tracks is gratuitous and excessive, and the repetitiveness inherent in some of the tracks shows that quantity, and not always quality, swayed the making of the final cut.

Title: Unfamiliar Faces
Review: Matt Costa's sophomore effort, Unfamiliar Faces, finds the singer/songwriter delving into similar territory to his 2006 debut, "Songs We Sing," crafting hummable, somewhat intricate AM pop-influenced tracks.

Title: Brightly Painted One
Review: It’s tempting to think of Brightly Painted One as a “grower” of an album, and much of that depends on where you stand on the music/lyrics side of things. The problem is, for all of its evident beauty, it’s difficult to get inside – frustratingly so.

Title: FRIDAY FOREVER
Review: ‘Friday Forever’ is a solid record with an intriguing concept that unravels fantastically under Russell’s loosened leash.

Title: The Liberty Of Norton Folgate
Review: Nutty Boys regain former glories in full.

Title: Daughter of Everything
Review: John Schmersal's quirky falsetto lights up this debut. [May 2014, p.96]

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Belong
Review: Belong is a bigger, bolder, and brighter follow-up that adds new dimensions to the Pains' sound while nearly equaling the songwriting of their debut.

Title: Kala
Review: M.I.A.'s border-crossing dance pop is a revolutionary manifesto set to the victory-party vibe of the future. [Sep 2007, p.127]

Title: It Is What It Is
Review: What’s impressive is how Thundercat makes this music, with its complex structures and zigzagging rhythms, so human.

Title: Art of Doubt
Review: While Art Of Doubt doesn’t quite touch their previous high points, there’s still more than enough to keep many a Metric fan happy.

Title: Kubrick
Review: Named for characters from these films, the Soulsavers aimed to capture the emotion and atmosphere of each one. What results is, oddly enough, a lush work of gorgeous beauty for such dense and oftentimes disturbing movies.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: Her minimalist distillation of R&B, which takes into consideration not just the genre's rich musical history but also its penchant for social commentary, has resulted in a stunning statement that redefines the old chestnut about the personal being political.

Title: Astronaut
Review: Revitalizes Duran's early synth-pop magic. [28 Oct 2004, p.103]

Title: Tough Love
Review: For all its vulnerability, Tough Love is tenacious, too, brimming with R&B grooves and a whole lot of soul.

Title: Dedication
Review: Whether this is a one-off or a bridge to something more substantial, it's satisfying in the present and will likely increase in stature as years pass.

Title: Blackout
Review: Blackout may be more a tribute to the skills of the A-list producers who guided her through the disc than to any of her own talents.

Title: Love Yes
Review: The album is a significant step forward for TEEN; a dozen bright burning arguments that you can have your cake and eat it too with articulate, deeply felt but undeniably fun pop music.

Title: Maximum Overload
Review: Ultimately, there's little on offer to snare a neutral. For the zealot, however, new heights of melody and assurance await. [Sep 2014, p.93]

Title: Foundations of Burden
Review: Foundations showcases the development in the band’s songwriting skills.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: With Black Messiah, D’Angelo has silenced any doubters and re-confirmed his invitation as the heir apparent to the R&B throne, whether he continues to refuse the honor or not.

Title: Lucifer
Review: As the title of the soporific, sunbleached skank that is 'LO HI' suggests, 'Lucifer' is more a subdued warm bath of than a plunge into the psyche.

Title: Another One
Review: Though nothing on this record gives the impression of being overthought, there’s a familiar strangeness to his songwriting too.

Title: Dusty Trails
Review: Call this music "experimental easy-listening" -- neither strident enough to warrant serious commercial attention, nor sufficiently free-form to attract all the independent obsessives.

Title: X
Review: Actually, there’s nothing Sheeran does here that Mraz hasn’t done before, often more cleverly. Even so, Sheeran can write a hummable tune and, clearly, has something young girls love even more than looks: heart.

Title: It's All Around You
Review: While it may not match the exuberant authority of a band at the height of its powers, set by Millions Now Living eight years ago, it does manage to prove itself worthy, in its own way, of the distinct creative voice that high-water mark captured so well.

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Lyrics that once seemed cheeky and slyly referential back in the halcyon days of their 1994 debut (think ''Buddy Holly'') and 1996's Pinkerton (''El Scorcho'') have become tiresomely Seuss-ical on their sixth outing, Weezer.

Title: CMFT
Review: Taylor takes that responsibility as a solo artist and runs with it, throwing everything and anything into the mix; there are the standard sounds you’d expect from him, but there’s also country, blues-based hard rock, punk and some rap-rock thrown in for good measure. And therein lies the issue with CMFT: rather than those disparate influences somehow mixing to become a whole, they’re left to stand on their own. The more you listen to CMFT, the more it comes across as ‘Corey Taylor does (insert genre here)’ rather than something cohesive.

Title: The Soul Sessions
Review: Worthy of more than novelty status.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: No matter her self-presentation, her grip, the music is relentlessly Sad--and exhausting in its sadness.

Title: Trouble Man: Heavy Is the Head
Review: His eighth album exhausts with pointless proclamations of hardness, only occasionally turning inward to contemplate actual heavy issues. [21 Dec 2012, p.67]

Title: Castle Talk
Review: Screaming Females do not get me because I'm not surprised by them. I enjoy Castle Talk, but it's academic.

Title: My Bloody Underground
Review: His band's 13th album won't bring him the stardom he craves, consisting of amorphous drones in which the creative energy has been reserved for the titles. [May 2008, p.126]

Title: Combinations
Review: For a sophomore effort, Combinations makes for yet another strong debut.

Title: LEGACY! LEGACY!
Review: Just like these artists [poet Nikki Giovanni, singer Eartha Kitt, blues legend Muddy Waters, funk rebel Betty Davis, jazz greats Miles Davis and Sun Ra, literary icons James Baldwin, Zora Neale Hurston and Octavia Butler, poet Sonia Sanchez, iconoclastic painter Basquiat] resisted being boxed in, so does Woods’ music. These are songs that elude genre--a blend of trip-hop, rap/spoken word, R&B, gospel.

Title: Cocky & Confident
Review: Perhaps different production is all this LP would need for me to appreciate it, but I can only go off what I’ve got and this album is not up to par with Juvenile’s run from 1996 - 2003.

Title: White People
Review: Less charmingly loopy than [previous album So How's Your Girl], but the boys can still kick occasionally. [12 Nov 2004, p.120]

Title: Electrified
Review: Guitarist John Hill... generates enough raw power to mask the shortcomings of any old lead vocalist. Fortunately for this Denver foursome, it has one of the most exciting singers around today. [#68, p.91]

Title: Demon Days
Review: Innovative as it is satisfying.... It’s hard to imagine a more realized meld of hip-hop, electronica, and post-rock.

Title: In The Key Of Joy
Review: Nothing is lost in the process and tracks like "Bora Lá" with singer Rogê and Leporace, "Samba in Heaven" with Joans, and "This Is It (É Isso)" with Pascoal and Leporace, retain all the funky, soulful rhythms and hooky melodies that made Mendes' seminal albums so captivating.

Title: Giver Taker
Review: A debut album can often feel like an announcement or an artist statement: something that says, This is me, and this is my music. Anjimile unites that self-consciousness with an exploratory intention.

Title: Deportation Blues
Review: While Deportation Blues may have come from that place of great turmoil, it also further magnifies the dynamism and creativity that underpins BC Camplight’s work.

Title: Power
Review: Throughout the record there's a thoughtful restraint tot he compositions, swerving back and forth between quiet euphoria and shell-shocked dystopia. [Aug 2018, p.30]

Title: IGOR
Review: Though the mood of Igor is generally consistent, its songs are irregularly shaped, united by Tyler’s by-now signature keyboards, which are warm but a little sweet, and dance gingerly. As Tyler has gotten older--he’s 28 now--he’s become more willing to engage with emotions.

Title: He Gets Me High
Review: The saccharine harmonies are still present on the title track; they're just augmented with more expansive arrangements that bring out a welcome new dimension to the band's sound. [Apr 2011, p.114]

Title: Furr
Review: Blitzen Trapper's first release for Sub Pop doesn't just improve upon the promise of WMN, it expands its sonic horizons as well, narrowing the mixtape glee that fueled its predecessor with just enough maturity to lend it considerable weight.

Title: The Futureheads
Review: A sparkly, concise art-rock delight. [10 Jul 2004, p.47]

Title: Silver Tongue
Review: Doesn't quite hit home. ... Letting loose more might have benefited the flow. [Mar 2020, p.95]

Title: Ritual
Review: Taken individually, Ritual's songs can meander too much; as a whole, however, the album is a success. [Feb 2011, p.90]

Title: In and Out of Youth and Lightness
Review: It seems often as if the songs come to life more through sonic detail and aural shape (a variety of distortion tones, drum sounds, reverb ranges, and the like) than in compositional changes of direction, harmonic depth, or hooks. This doesn't, however, make the music dull. Instead, there's something compelling about the way Young Widows use these details--a shimmer, a hum, a scrape--for drama rather than relying on the often cheap dramatics heard in "heavy" music.

Title: I Am Easy to Find
Review: I Am Easy to Find feels like an old friend you’re pleased to keep around--even if, had you been introduced today, you wonder if you’d have been compelled to make the effort.

Title: Meaning of Life
Review: Yet for an album that promises revelation, Meaning of Life is full of generalities.

Title: 4REAL 4REAL
Review: It’s another solid album from an artist who like his late friend can crossover into a lot of areas (and arenas) given the chance.

Title: Ones and Sixes
Review: Sparhawk tentatively hits highs in Wayne Coyne territory, imbuing the canyon-filling swirls of background synths and simple, sad, jangly riff with echoes of The Soft Bulletin. “Spanish Translation,” on the other hand, is Low-core and lovely.

Title: Wig Out at Jagbags
Review: Few of his contemporaries possess a post-important-band solo discography as prolific and consistently great as that of Stephen Malkmus, but each new album firmly leaves his past in the dust.

Title: Battlefield
Review: As nice as it is to hear Sparks continuing to dabble in dance-pop, though, one wonders if it would have been a smarter move in terms of career longevity to try to build on the urban audience she started to cultivate with 'No Air.'

Title: AM
Review: "Do I Wanna Know?" and "R U Mine?" are a couple of satisfying stomps anchoring this collection of gold-tinted kiss-offs. [Oct 2013, p.82]

Title: Victim of Love
Review: Victim of Love may only be Charles Bradley’s second album but it marks another remarkable footstep in the life of its creator.

Title: The Big Roar
Review: It's equally ambitious, forceful and joyous as Courtney Love's high water mark. [Feb 2011, p.118]

Title: Rant
Review: It's far from self-indulgent; their song choices and clever arrangements make Rant a real, if unexpected, delight.

Title: Us
Review: An endearing, and wholesome end for an album so wonderfully content it it’s own bubble.

Title: Fading Lines
Review: One of the most infectious collections of pop songs written on an electric guitar this year.

Title: Sun Structures
Review: The songwriting is outstanding: striking and smart, concise and full, and James Bagshaw sings superbly throughout.

Title: Life After Youth
Review: Life After Youth is a welcome reminder of why Land Of Talk was missed, and a promising glimpse at a second chance.

Title: Scratch My Back
Review: Is this the groundbreaking work we'd perhaps hoped for during the album's initial release, an effort worthy of that preliminary giddiness?  Sadly, no.  Is it an interesting mix of tracks that confronts listeners with reimaging of songs so deeply tied to our heart strings we have no choice but to carefully imbibe and evaluate each note?  Sure.

Artist: Jenny Lewis with The Watson Twins
Title: Rabbit Fur Coat
Review: She benefits from solid production by Saddle Creek staple Mike Mogis, who tweaks her retro sound with synths and electronic blips, but it's the stark M. Ward-produced tracks that, while more traditional, showcase the Dolly Parton potential in Lewis's voice.

Title: Pilot Talk
Review: It's without a doubt the best hip-hop release of 2010, and might as well get ready to earn praise in the smart circles as one of the best overall releases of the year as well.

Title: Violent Hearts
Review: Violent Hearts occasionally plods, as on "No One," "Other Girls," and the opener "Believe," (at least before its delightfully messy climax). But more often it quietly impresses, revealing new melodic and harmonic strands with each subsequent listen.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: Exhilarating and violent.

Title: Shine
Review: Subdued but not entirely resigned, Mitchell sings in a strong, assured voice that’s still warm and welcoming, though lowered by decades of ecologically unhip tobacco smoke.

Title: Play
Review: Play sees Nashville superstar Paisley jam with an array of equally adroit pickers. [Dec 2008, p.111]

Title: Surrender Your Poppy Field
Review: While Surrender Your Poppy Field is less immediately approachable than the other albums from this period in the Guided by Voices saga, it's experimental, not meandering, and for fans with a taste for their more esoteric side, this will hit the spot and then some.

Title: Sounds Good Feels Good
Review: 5SOS finds a balance in their sound here that feels right for them, and ultimately the accurately titled Sounds Good Feels Good suggests there isn’t actually all that big of a gap between the boy band and pop-punk milieus, and probably never was.

Title: Open Here
Review: Open Here is another prog-pop masterclass from a band reflecting our times while remaining stubbornly out of step with them. [Feb 2018, p.23]

Title: Dents and Shells
Review: If Dents and Shells stands apart from Buckner's oeuvre in any way, it's in the prominence and evenhandedness of its instrumental arrangements.

Title: Eyes At Half Mast
Review: Eyes At Half Mast seems to be, on one level, an exploration of the horizons of the style of music that Talkdemonic themselves invented, but a lot of it retraces steps already taken, albeit with a noticeable upping of the proverbial ante as far as energy goes.

Title: Athena
Review: This project, as conceived by the artist, wraps itself in an Afro-futurist stance, an approach to neo-soul that feels right at home played next to the sounds of FKA twigs or Solange. But Sudan Archives still has room to grow while she defines her sound.

Title: Shine On
Review: You can practically hear the energy draining away as the album progresses and one song slides into another, indistinguishable by either melody or lyric.

Title: Perpetual Motion People
Review: His sax-heavy third solo album blows its own horn. [Aug 2015, p.75]

Title: Art Official Age
Review: [A] confusing, sprawling grab-bag. [Nov 2014, p.90]

Title: Beyondless
Review: Their ambition and drive is truly ‘Beyondless’, and that’s the galvanising effect and feeling you get as a listener when finishing Iceage’s latest statement album.

Title: We're Not Talking
Review: There's a seamless fluidity to how they're dependent on each others' input, and their contributions seem to suit their interests. It's an unerringly sincere look into a trio who are moving into adulthood, one stumble at a time.

Title: ERYS
Review: While ERYS occasionally drags over its seventeen17 tracks, it's an immersive experience that finds Jaden at his most vulnerable, processing his messy young adult feelings into a relatable and sonically exciting way.

Title: Bossalinis & Fooliyones
Review: Bossalinis & Fooliyones is, at worst, an amiable enough diversion, at best it's very entertaining.

Title: Tip of the Sphere
Review: Tip Of The Sphere represents McCombs' practised skill as a shaper of his own world, with pride in his craft, a deep respect for tradition and the drive to refresh it via his own, idiosyncratic iteration. [Mar 2019, p.18]

Title: Phrazes for the Young
Review: 'Ludow St' is lyrically smart, musically ambitious, more than any other track on Phrazes, it makes you wonder, if not regret, why the Strokes themselves never pushed the boat out this far. For that reason alone, it was worth Casablancas making this intriguing if imperfect record. [Nov 2009, p.98]

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: Nocturnal Koreans, the band’s 15th album, forgoes power for stillness, and manages the unprecedented: It’s the best thing they’ve done in 14 years.

Title: Secret Wars
Review: This time there's noticeably less fuzz and extraneous squall piled on top. [Feb 2004, p.92]

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: It's an album you can spend time with and understand as a whole work, and one that grows on you with each listen, revealing yet more detail and nuance.

Title: Waiting for the Sunrise
Review: David Vandervelde's latest full-length, Waiting For The Sunrise, is a a warm, comfortable, '70s AM radio throwback, layered with organs, reverb, and smoky heartbreak. [Fall 2008, p.84]

Title: Forth
Review: While Forth is certainly flawed and overreaching, there's enough to suggest that the Verve, assuming they're able to keep it together, can use the album as a foundation for something as compelling as their '90s output.

Title: Recovery
Review: Recovery is thwarted by similarly ill-fitting decisions.... The central salvation is Mather's enduring virtuosity. Throughout Recovery, he weaves dazzling internal patterns and clever word play.

Title: Storyteller
Review: She largely picks songs that serve as launch platforms for her ballistic-missile voice, but they don’t cohere into a whole identity.... If Ms. Underwood has developed a thematic specialty, it’s the woman-done-wrong anthem. The ones on this album are some of the better songs here.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel
Review: A much stronger set of songs. Her debut album's primary coloured backdrop having been swapped out for a richer, more nuanced palette. [Jul 2018, p.119]

Title: Crown and Treaty
Review: Crown and Treaty is at times wonderful, particularly on "Blue Sky Falls", "Joyful Reunion" and "Brugada".

Title: Equilibrium
Review: A perfect 41-minute album that balances wide-open melodic inventions with crisp, time-stopping grooves. [Listen 2 This supplement, Feb 2003, p.10]

Title: High Society
Review: High Society [proves] Schmersal capable of a good, straight-forward pop song. [July 2002, p.100]

Title: Broken Bells
Review: Broken Bells is an honest-to-goodness debut album--there are as many promising flashes as frustrating moments here. Mercer and Burton have obvious chemistry, but they need to blend more for true alchemy.

Title: Skeleton Tree
Review: Skeleton Tree is a testament to his art, his flaying honesty and his persistence in the wake of devastating loss.

Title: Astronaut Meets Appleman
Review: At first blush, this is not one of Anderson's most immediately engaging albums, but it has a meandering charm that works its magic over time.

Title: Cannibal
Review: Ke$ha didn't really set the bar for intellectual heft too high on her debut, Animal, so it seems like hair-splitting to mention that even with guilty pleasures like "Cannibal" and, uh, "C U Next Tuesday," Cannibal seems to be skimping on the cleverness.

Title: Carry On
Review: Maybe this is what living in France does to you. [Jun 2007, p.92]

Title: Future Nostalgia
Review: With this flawless effort, she manages to achieve both. Future Nostalgia could have just as well been titled "Future Classic."

Title: Citrus
Review: Citrus is the crossroads where My Bloody Valentine and Sonic Youth mingle. [Aug 2006, p.88]

Title: Haunted Cities
Review: Their 2002 debut was a surprising success, but Haunted Cities struggles to repeat the trick. [Sep 2005, p.100]

Title: Crazy for You
Review: Crazy for You is a soundtrack to bikini season as it's actually experienced, racked by impossible expectations and as high as the tide line.

Title: Morningwood
Review: It's hard to take the band too seriously, but the songs are debaucherous fun. [14 Jan 2006]

Title: Savage Hills Ballroom
Review: Savage Hills Ballroom is another strong, stirring release from Powers. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.68]

Title: Hey Ma
Review: Lyrics like those [in 'Whiteboy'] make up for the clunkers, but more importantly, the music itself sounds shockingly vibrant for a band only recently taken off ice.

Title: Foreverland
Review: If you're not a fan of strings, drama, and flamboyance, Foreverland is going to wear on you. But if you're a sucker for them, get ready for your fill.

Title: Eat at Whitey's
Review: An eclectic, intermittently rewarding album of first rate re-creations. But re-creations are all they are, down to Everlast's voice, which is beginning to sound like Redd Foxx's.

Title: Goodbye
Review: With a few exceptions, the rest of Goodbye remains little more than background music destined for life in service to candle boutiques and Saturn commercials. [Summer 2007, p.106]

Title: Few More Days To Go
Review: With much current pop eager to please, it’s thrilling to hear music played with such malevolence.

Title: Another Country
Review: It feels true to who he is today: an entertainer who is happy to reveal part of his heart because he now knows there's an audience who cares.

Title: Dancing at the Blue Lagoon
Review: There may not be as many earworms on this release, but they’ve approached it with patience and a finesse that allowed the songs to flourish into deep sonic explorations that leave the listener eager for more.

Title: Ruminations
Review: Ruminations feels like a comedown as such. His first solo album since 2014 ‘Upside Down Mountain’ features only Oberst, a piano, an acoustic guitar and the occasional flash of harmonica. It’s possibly his most reflective, nostalgic work yet.

Title: Two of Everything
Review: Olive doesn't have the strongest voice, but songs like "Traveling" and the choolin' "Strange Attractor" have a pure pop heart that blends beautifully with Auerbach's retro-rock aesthetic. [Sep 2011, p.93]

Title: Spoils
Review: There are plenty of fine moments in all the songs, whether it's a sudden burst of harmonies, or unexpected instrumental flourishes, from behind the singer.

Title: Escape From Evil
Review: [A] danceable set.

Title: Tarantula
Review: A marked improvement over the lively but uneven Let's Get Ready, Tarantula suggests that the raspy-voiced rapper's run at the top of the charts won't abate any time soon.

Title: You've Always Been Here
Review: It’s a solid enough debut that really comes to life when the band don’t play it safe. However, lacking the star power that’s expected from musicians like these (you’d never know who was in this band without being told) it’s little more than the soundtrack to a great Friday night down the local boozer.

Title: Glow & Behold
Review: They’ve evolved in shocking ways, but still remain loyal to their m.o., and thickly smother everything in a shoegaze glaze; culminating in a record that’s smoother, smilier and more adventurous than their eponymous debut.

Title: Saltwater
Review: Saltwater is a pretty record and the songs are clearly heavy with personal significance, but it was almost better when they were a little rough around the edges.

Title: Mountain Battles
Review: Steve Albini (Nirvana, PJ Harvey), among other producers, keeps things raw; indeed, the record's primitive art punk sometimes echoes Nirvana.

Title: Emoh
Review: 14 songs focused intently on melody and chord progressions, not licks or repetitive riffs or tricky drumbeats.

Title: Over It
Review: The project includes a host of features from some of the biggest names in the genre, who provide welcome (but somewhat unnecessary) co-signs as she herself manoeuvres with a standout level of artistry that leaves you in no doubt that she is indeed here to stay.

Title: Handcream for a Generation
Review: Difficult and easy, dance-y and indie, this is a transitional album that works on just about every level I can think of.

Title: Walls
Review: Understandably, the 76-year-old's voice has lost some if its technical precision, but the backdrops have light touch and when she growls Don't Lie To Me's motif, "How do you sleep?" or evokes "thunderclouds of alibis" on the imperious The Rain Will Fall, she oozes despair and fury. [Jan 2019, p.84]

Title: Pro Tools
Review: Never thought I'd say this, but RZA isn't missed--the budget production enhances a master lyricist's specialty by subtraction.

Title: You're the One
Review: Though not exactly a bad album, when contrasted to the remarkable Graceland and Rhythm Of The Saints, it sounds as arbitrary as a collection of B-sides.

Title: Almanac
Review: Niche though it may be, it is far more organic and authentic for experimenting with the folk model than the plethora of records churned out by ersatz acts.

Title: Black Up
Review: The calm rhymes juggle thoughts of black identity, paranoia, lust and possibility. Yes, hip-hop still has an audacious progressive fringe.

Title: Primary Colours
Review: If there's a more surprising album this year, we'll be, er, um, surprised; Primary Colours is one of the best albums of 2009 so far.

Title: All Is Dream
Review: Though their approach hasn't changed from the radically orchestral turn of 1998's Deserter's Songs, these songs are far more personal than their last set.

Title: X&Y
Review: Like Coldplay's two previous albums, only more so, X&Y is bland but never offensive, listenable but not memorable.

Title: Long Trip Alone
Review: As before, he continues to flawlessly integrate straight-ahead, unforced vocals into a riproaring sound.

Title: Happiness in Magazines
Review: The best Graham Coxon imaginable. [Jun 2004, p.97]

Title: X&Y
Review: It's a definite step backward from the passionate and substantial Rush of Blood toward the less mature Parachutes, somehow lacking something bigger.

Title: Ugly Cherries
Review: It's fun, it's queer and your straight friends will like it too because, ultimately, it's about being less alone. Everyone can relate to that. And the world genuinely feels like a brighter place with PWR BTTM in it.

Title: Fields
Review: Fans of Gonzalez's intimate solo bedroom folk may be taken aback by the kaleidoscopic bells and whistles of Fields, but the rest of us should be thankful the sales of those two previous releases have given Gonzalez andd his mates the freedom to indulge every whim. [Oct 2010, p.109]

Title: Rising Down
Review: Rising Down is pretty much same old same old.

Title: Graffiti
Review: A curiously faceless album that largely thumbs its nose at close reading.

Title: NehruvianDOOM
Review: Weighing in at a terse 32 minutes in length, spanning eight tracks plus an introduction, the album is a cohesive and methodical offering yet because of the constrained spin time, neither Bishop Nehru nor MF Doom have the space to flex their creative impulses and push the envelope in their respective spheres.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: Burn Your Fire for No Witness boasts an even more robust presence [as her 2012 debut, "Half Way Home"], thanks to production by John Congleton.

Title: Earthquake Glue
Review: Guided By Voices albums have become predictable, a shocking end for a group defined by its surprise delights.

Title: Sometimes I Wish We Were An Eagle
Review: The overlong 'Faith/Void' aside, this is another absorbing collection. [Apr 2009, p.100]

Title: Lonerism
Review: [A] brilliant album.

Title: The Alesha Show
Review: Even though her debut album didn't go off so well with her label, Dixon's latest album gives her another chance in the music biz.

Title: Anarchy, My Dear
Review: Like a good long-distance run, Anarchy rewards with bursts of sonic endorphins. [16 Mar 2012, p.69]

Title: Demon Days
Review: Danger Mouse sets a consistent tone that wryly chafes against Albarn's paranoia. [Jun 2005, p.105]

Title: Why There Are Mountains
Review: He’s certainly not the first kid to see the death of innocence in a “maelstrom of mail-order Marlboro memorabilia,” but he might be the first to sing about it--here’s hoping that future Cymbals Eat Guitars songs wrap such observations in similarly singular packaging.

Title: Dead Zone Boys
Review: The first half of Boys has all of the action, and the second side can't help but drag a bit.

Title: The Magic Whip
Review: Britpop’s giants are back, and they sound surprisingly the way we had hoped they would: melodic, contemplative and content as a single unit.

Title: Tha Carter III
Review: That said, it's not an instant classic, but it is the best rap album since Kanye West dropped "Graduation" last year.

Title: Dip
Review: As lush and expansive as his former work was taut and aggro - only the quality remains.

Title: Wolf
Review: It's complex, conflicted, and bipolar. Paranoid, even. Most of all, it reveals the harmless and empathetic character behind Tyler, the Creator's complicated persona.

Title: The Monitor
Review: The Monitor is ridiculously strident and frequently overblown, but somehow never slips into self-parody, which may only be true because it's obvious these guys are having a total blast indulging this hard. It's easily the most enjoyable rock record I've heard so far this year.

Title: Detours
Review: The roots-rock of Detours is old-school-sounding Crow now with a heightened consciousness of the world around her.

Title: Concrete and Gold
Review: Concrete And Gold is a straightforward Foo Fighters album, albeit one that does occasionally fulfill its promise to deliver both aural lavishness and maximum heaviosity. [Oct 2017, p.102]

Title: reputation
Review: Reputation is, too often, an ugly sounding album. But Taylor Swift has a superhuman knack for a stunning melody. Many of these songs are downright sweet.

Title: Jukebox
Review: Full of simmering restraint, Jukebox sounds lived-in and genuine, less a genre experiment than full fledged statement.

Title: Femme Fatale
Review: At its best, it sounds like a party, with a cutting-edge pop soundtrack. The question of precisely what Britney Spears brings to said party remains as imponderable as ever.

Title: Easter Is Cancelled
Review: Though brief nautical ballad Deck Chair is a skit too far here, there's a great bubblegum-pop song fighting its way through the exploded theatrics of Heavy Metal Lover, while silly song of thanks for the six-string We Are The Guitar Men is a virtuosic hoot. [Nov 2019, p.89]

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Behind the penny loafers and songs about commas, there's a bold band that can balance dextrous originality with an innate pop sensibility.

Title: I Still Do
Review: I Still Do is yet another solid collection of top-notch blues from one of the modern masters of the genre.

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Both youthful and novel--Li was twenty-one upon its release, which may explain both her occasional goofy vocal affectations and the hesitant freshness of her sound--it's hard to pigeonhole but refreshingly easy to enjoy.

Title: Croz
Review: David Crosby simply continues down a path he established for himself a long time ago, and even if he has encountered a few bumps along the way, this is a record of a man who has done everything he wanted to do with his life, and Croz emerges as the final piece of the puzzle.

Title: Stubborn Persistent Illusions
Review: Stubborn Persistent Illusions finds Do Make Say Think returning as restless and reaching as they’ve ever been.

Title: Dark Bird Is Home
Review: Matsson makes solid use of a band this time too, to flesh out the bare-bones folk-pop for which he has previously been renowned.

Title: The Duke
Review: The Duke is too scattershot, and Jackson doesn't quite know what genre to focus on.

Title: The Getaway
Review: Oddly enough, The Getaway starts to flounder whenever RHCP revert back to their old habits.

Title: Common Sense
Review: This is very much a post-Stormzy, post-Skepta, post-Drake-going-roadman album, and an important stepping stone along the path to the UK establishing itself as a bona fide world-beater at beats and rhymes.

Title: Climax
Review: Climax is both poundingly heavy and pleasingly melodic, at times recalling the Sisters Of mercy in their crossover pomp. [Feb 2014, p.71]

Title: Sleeping on Roads
Review: Taking into account the sometimes spotty songwriting and its overtly dreamy similarities to Mojave 3 (like if they'd had a back massage and 1200mg's of Valium), there isn't much to save it from solo slump status.

Title: Palookaville
Review: His... worst album to date. [#7]

Title: Making Mirrors
Review: Familiar they may be, but some credit has to go to De Backer for managing to weave these eclectic retro sounds into a cohesive affair.

Title: The Green EP
Review: Bibio isn’t reinventing the wheel here (or rather, the acoustic guitar), but when you’ve already hit the sweet spot, you don’t have to.

Title: This Is Happening
Review: Despite occasional flashes of brilliance it’s a patchy, derivative work.

Title: Re-Arrange Us
Review: Unfortunately there aren't a lot of opportunities to get caught in that lovely crossfire on Re-Arrange Us, a record that, for all its lush bells and whistles, finds the pair sounding as bare-boned and sparse as you'd expect a two-person band to be.

Title: Return of Mr. Zone 6
Review: Gucci, who was rap's most exciting figure a year and a half ago, is on a profound losing streak, and it's easy to hear The Return of Mr. Zone 6, his new street album, as an attempt to reverse that slide.

Title: Nothing Is Real
Review: He doesn't really offer sharp, pointed lyricism, but he does give the album a haze of depression capped by a few moments of catharsis.

Title: Melt
Review: As it stands today, they're just another band doing a very familiar thing--at least they're doing it really well.

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: What it shows is that if you're going to do the hits, the thing to do is pin them down, fuck them up and HURT THEM. [average of scores of 90 for Disc 1 and 70 for Disc 2; 16 Oct 2004, p.48]

Title: i
Review: Underpinning this wry melancholy are the winsome languor of Stephin Merritt's voice and the generous stash of tunes.

Title: Multiply
Review: Lidell has created an album of flawless, imaginative, and radical funk grooves.

Title: Denali
Review: Amidst an arresting collision of angular melodies, fractured rhythms and Davis' overpowering voice, Denali's self-titled debut is awash in the tortured melancholy of a woman whose relationship demons have driven her to the edge.

Title: Changes
Review: Changes redefines the Bradley Soul sound again. [May 2016, p.87]

Title: Dedicated
Review: With the release of her fourth full-length album Dedicated, the British Columbia native proves that although her destiny may be devoid of commercial super-stardom, she is a steady and unique songwriting talent, and the fire-hot E•MO•TION, although an exceptional triumph, was no fluke.

Title: The Silver Lining
Review: The nostalgia train is stalled by embarrassing platitudes and well-worn riffs. [14 Jul 2006, p.79]

Title: Cage Tropical
Review: Miserable but magnificent. [Oct 2017, p.39]

Title: After the Rain

Review: There's no denying that the darker mood suits them--although with Kevin Shields and co now out of retirement as well, it could be back to the drawing board again. [May 2009, p.119]

Title: The Things We Do To Find People Who Feel Like Us
Review: The Things We Do sounds like the product of an alternate reality in which Bruce Springsteen was a teenager in the 2000’s who spent all his time crafting the perfect instant messenger away notifications instead of ruminating on small town America. But Alex and his bandmates pull it off with sheer conviction and force of will.

Title: Planet Earth
Review: Planet Earth is a consistent, exhilarating winner from our reigning genius. [Sep 2007, p.121]

Title: The Dirt And The Stars
Review: Carpenter has been so consistent that calling Between the Dirt and the Stars her best album in however many years isn't particularly meaningful. Let's call it her best album since her last one.

Title: Go-Go Boots
Review: It's no reflection on him, but Go-Go Boots goes a long way to proving him wrong, suggesting a band that knows where all the bodies are buried.

Title: Deep Trip
Review: The mixture of mournfulness, savagery, lo-fi spirit and noise should appeal to psych fans and college rockers, metalheads and hardcore punks alike.

Title: Silver Age
Review: Silver Age's songs come across as a little homogeneous, but it's an exhilarating homogeneous mass, which is all that really counts.

Title: Too Many Voices
Review: Too Many Voices is everything but a claustrophobic piece of sonic art. On the contrary, this is Stott at his best, a composer whose futuristic music is well rooted in today’s world, one that is badly connected to material reality, without a locus, with an idea of time that is flexible, adaptable.

Title: Kicks
Review: Kicks certainly doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but it has a whole lotta fun copying it.

Title: The Difference Between Me and You Is That I'm Not on Fire
Review: Unfortunately, "She Will Only Bring You Happiness" isn't a single, and there a dozen other tracks to account for, none of which live up to that song's pop splendor, and few of which even come close.

Title: Sun Coming Down
Review: Sun Coming Down is Robin Hood-rich with pithy one-liners punctuated by Keen’s hi-hats, crashing through Darcy’s free-associating swarm of noise like that one person in every New York-based rom-com or sitcom wending his way through an avenue packed with people.

Title: Negro Swan
Review: An album, according to Dev, about “black depression, black existence and the ongoing anxieties of queer / people of colour”, Negro Swan is a record that radiates these tensions; subtle and amorphous, it’s not the most immediate listen, but it’s undoubtedly one with real weight.

Title: See the Light
Review: It's so steeped in New York's musical cliche of disco and glammed-up dance that it struggles to take flight under its own power.

Title: Bloom
Review: Bloom is a bare-faced record, thrillingly honest and defiantly queer, proving Sivan is one of pop’s most essential voices.

Title: Crazy for You
Review: The good news is, this album is going to garner a dozen swoons in her direction for each romantic woe she professes on it.

Title: Historian
Review: That gradual unfolding is one of Historian’s many delights. It’s not an easy album to wear out. It lasts, and it should, given that so many of its lyrics pick at time, and the way time condenses around deep emotional attachments to other people.

Title: Cassadaga
Review: "Cassadaga" is an insular, self-referential album that strives for depth and profundity and sounds instead like a high-school poetry reading, full of rhyming-dictionary couplets and banal pronouncements about life.

Title: Mohawk
Review: Mohawk is an album that feels great, imparts wisdom, drops sweet details and encourages both fandom and participation. If there’s fault to be found it’s in the record’s brevity.

Title: Our Endless Numbered Days
Review: A warm, gently beautiful album that rewards the patient listener.

Title: Carnation
Review: Carnation restores some of the eerie, discombobulated feel of his debut.

Title: Changes
Review: On “Changes,” he finally stakes his claim, honing a vocal approach that’s soothing, tender although maybe slightly tentative, a middle ground between comfort and reluctance. It is an effective album, and also a deliberately unflashy one — Bieber is consistent and confident, and also not drawing too much attention to himself.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: It's not quite hype enough to be pure party music and lacks the cohesive point of view that fosters a more personal connection with a record.

Title: Quarantine
Review: It's pervaded by numbness, claustrophobia, pain intensified to the point of dissociation. [Jun 2012, p.49]

Title: Hypnotize
Review: System Of A Down's music is highly layered and complex, but never succumbs to self-indulgence. Every track is tightly-coiled and urgent because, even while they're trying to broaden your horizons, SOAD are aware of the need to rock hard.

Title: The Way Out
Review: This electronic-folk duo, in the likeness of bohemian hedonists, turns meticulous attention-to-detail into bounding creativity--and something unequivocally bookish.

Title: Fading Trails
Review: What the cathartic Fading Trails might lack in foot-tapping motivation, it makes up for in passion and honesty and is highly recommended for those who like to dig a little deeper for albums that get better each time they are played.

Title: Within and Without
Review: It's an album you can hear without ever really noticing. Radox for the ears.

Title: ORO: Opus Primum
Review: Truly cosmic.

Title: Love, Hate, and Then There's You
Review: The new problem is a lack of texture: in aiming for big hooks and big bucks, they've thrown variety out the window. [Jun 2009, p.134]

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II
Review: An enjoyable, at times provocative companion piece, this one's a satisfying musical bath.

Title: FIBS
Review: With its huge, graceful scope, FIBS smirks slyly at any presumptions or hopes listeners may harbour. These fibs are alive – a thriving, amoebic album consuming the petri dish in which it was formed.

Title: Torino
Review: It's a bedlam of romance, a tender look back at first relationships and sexual romps, but with a bit of a smirk.

Title: Days Gone By
Review: Tune in, come down, and drift about because Bob Moses remain the masters of restrained bliss house.

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: Heavy, like delirious laughter looped ad infinitum, Lord Quas quivers with psychedelic rhythm.

Title: Situation
Review: Timelag-wise, the 1957 concept is as if some '60s songpoet had conceived an album about Armistice Day, influenza, the Palmer raids and Mary Pickford. Only that would have been a milestone and this isn't, which you can blame on heightened aesthetic expectations rather than the potency of this Canadian rapper's literary mojo.

Title: V
Review: It's hard to care about any shortcomings when the tunes are as masterfully crisp as they are on much of V.

Title: Graduation
Review: Musically, at least, it’s the most accomplished thing he’s ever done.

Title: Harlequin
Review: Harlequin is the product of five years of writing, refining, and arranging, and yet the record runs on a sleepy, easy vibe--at once one of its greatest strengths and potential stumbling blocks.

Title: The Secret of Letting Go
Review: The Secret of Letting Go retains that balance of experimentation and pure feeling, and sounds perfectly at home within Lamb's discography.

Title: Digging a Tunnel
Review: This is a musician who has simply absorbed a broad set of musical styles through a massively eclectic listening palette, and who sees no issue in crunching that together in one tidy little album. Embrace the chaos. You'll feel better for it.

Title: Company
Review: All irony aside, this bold debut is something to be admired--a creative and eclectic gem to be cherished and nurtured.

Title: Unreal
Review: Blumberg is a capable, if not particularly distinguished guitarist. He is also a songwriter with an unusual gift for sticky, familiar hooks and the issue here is that Unreal puts far more emphasis on the former.

Title: Star Treatment
Review: At its best, it’s quite thrilling.

Title: Gravez
Review: Gravez is scrappy, fun but unoriginal--free in spirit but limited in execution. [Jul 2013, p.105]

Title: Adult Film
Review: Musically, Adult Film is a smorgasbord of pop ephemera, with melodies crashing about like boozy butterflies, occasionally landing on an idea and then leaping back into the blue in search of less restrictive stimuli.

Title: Nightmare
Review: Nightmare is a completely different offering; even though it still has highly questionable moments, it's obvious that a genuine effort was put in, and that's enough reason to listen.

Title: The Pace of the Passing
Review: It's a pleasing collection of multi-layered poo songs in a manner that at times recall Sufjan Stevens. [Feb 2017, p.119]

Title: Bromst
Review: It's Deacon's most ambitious collection of recordings to date. [Winter 2009, p.71]

An album like 7 easily sets itself apart from any other record Beach House has recorded thus far; it's far more easier to write it off as a derivative indie album, but to do so would discredit the obvious effort it took to actually record something so different from every other album they've done yet.

Title: White Bread Black Beer
Review: The pristine, synth-heavy result certainly sounds worried over, sometimes to its detriment. [28 Jul 2006, p.67]

Title: Atonement
Review: A consistent, flawless catalogue that spans nearly three decades.

Title: Scale
