Review: [The songs'] politicism is woven so masterfully into the lush electronic pop medium that you’re never coerced into consideration of any one issue.

Title: Too Young to Be in Love
Review: There is real sorrow and feeling amongst all the fun and the record will hopefully see Hunx gain some of the attention that is way over due.

Title: Random Access Memories
Review: What Daft Punk have done on Random Access Memories could be seen as a methodically curated, musical museum of the future, rather than a conservatory for experimental collaboration.

Title: Solide Mirage
Review: One minute solid as a rock, the next seemingly in flux, Solide Mirage reveals itself anew with each listen: fleeting glimpses at a map into unknown territory.

Title: Love This Giant
Review: Byrne and Clark have managed to not only meet but exceed expectations, and created one of the year's smartest albums in doing so.

Title: Hannicap Circus
Review: Hannicap Circus is solid, filthy, fun, and everything else that you'd want from a less nimble Kool Keith.

Title: The Rising Tide
Review: The grandiose production, by Lou Giordano (Goo Goo Dolls, Live), matches the quasi-mystical visions mapped out in the songs....

Title: Love Is a Four Letter Word
Review: [Mraz] is taking the true-blue pop rock formula and expanding on it in ways other, less competent musicians fail to do in today's world of watered-down songwriting and formulaic radio.

Title: Costello Music
Review: Right now, their bouncing glamorama feels like the most important album you could own.

Title: Cenizas
Review: That such revelations can be borne out of isolation should be a comfort to us all right now, and Cenzias is a record expansive enough to open up even the smallest rooms.

Title: Pain Olympics
Review: Raw, and real, and often emotional, Pain Olympics is a turbulent journey through the world of this community, proving in itself to be a successful outlet for those creating it, while also offering solace and alliance for those that need it.

Title: Decoration Day
Review: Somber and smart, Decoration Day also manages to kick like a mule, and if isn't quite a masterpiece along the lines of Southern Rock Opera, it's strong enough to suggest the Drive By Truckers have another masterpiece in them.

Title: Skip a Sinking Stone
Review: Even when his quality control slips slightly, the music remains utterly beautiful, like glittering light on a river, or gossamer threads floating through the air on a summer’s day.

Title: On a Clear Day I Can See You Forever
Review: Sounding at times as though someone had isolated the synth track from a classic Hawkwind record, the music here is familiar and invites associations. ... Regardless, On A Clear Day is a pleasant affair.

Title: East of Eden
Review: Free of the patronising condescension that many Western musicians adopt when they embark on musical journeys like this, Victoria Bergsman has produced a marvellous, spell-binding album.

Title: Bitter Tea
Review: Alas, from [the first two tracks]... the pair slip first into mediocrity and then the standbys of those who have run out of inspiration: backwards recording and pointless noodling. [Jun 2006, p.115]

Title: Sunshine Rock
Review: Sunshine Rock does exactly what it says on the tin. A rock album that sparkles; a taut collection of Bob Mould cuts that fits timelessly into his ever-expanding legacy.

Title: Pageant Material
Review: Her music is as rooted in organic country and western traditions as ever, flush with cosmopolitan strings, instrumental banjo breaks, and generous portions of pedal steel, but the songwriting comes less organically, too often stretching itself thin over a genre that's historically benefited from a measure of simplicity.

Title: Glass Boys
Review: Everything from the swirly, '90s guitars to the harmony-laced background vocals just scream a band gazing far beyond their genre trappings. [Jul 2014, p.102]

Title: Cold Spring Fault Less Youth
Review: At a time when dance and electronic becomes increasingly homogenised by the mainstream, Mount Kimbie have released an album that still refuses to court the mundane.

Title: Koi No Yokan
Review: This fit and lean version of Deftones have turned negativity into vibrant positivity and channelled it into their cohesive and textured seventh full-length, Koi No Yokan--a record that will forever sit high upon Deftones' burgeoning list of impressive achievements.

Title: Stumble into Grace
Review: Those who want their Emmylou full of sweet, sad longing will play a quarter of this album to death.... Elsewhere, there's righteous anger and an assertiveness and sexuality to the love songs. [Nov 2003, p.128]

Title: What a Time to Be Alive
Review: There are plenty of power-punk melodies to ensure What A Time To Be Alive isn’t condemned to an early shelf life, even if to put it amongst their best work would be a stretch too far.

Title: Lisbon
Review: What draws me most to Lisbon is the exciting reinventions on the band's own formula.

Title: Irreal
Review: What they do rhythmically and spatially sounds great: the expanse, the air, the solid bass rhythms and percussive malleability.

Title: No, You C'Mon
Review: Whilst the songs on No You C’Mon don’t flow together as smoothly as those on Aw C’Mon, a number of them are of a similar ilk; lush, concise modern country that only Lambchop can do, the sound of a band from Nashville rather than a Nashville band.

Title: Junior
Review: It's an album that manages consistency without ever letting you get settled. Where each of her records has shown her brilliant musicianship, Junior is Kaki King's finest accomplishment as a songwriter.

Title: Raising Sand
Review: The pairing of the wily old tomcat and the classy country thrush turns out as magically in reality as it seemed unlikely on paper.

Title: Battle Studies
Review: Battle Studies, by comparison is relaxed and laid back, it’s feet in the air and stripped of extravagance with Mayer simply doing his thang with ease and pazazz.

Title: Spelled in Bones
Review: While Bones isn't as instantly accessible as its predecessor, it certainly provides more to mull over.

Title: Blank Project
Review: It’s rare that you get an album by an established artist that genuinely shocks and irrevocably repositions them. Blank Project is one of those albums. This is a hugely significant return.

Title: Cupid Deluxe
Review: A little more daylight would balance out the vibe. But that’s a minor complaint. In fact, on further listens it becomes the album’s appeal.

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: Perhaps Sky Full of Holes  will be that album to some impressionable youth whose idea of power pop revolves around Justin Bieber ballads, but for longtime fans it just sounds tired and dusty. Fountains of Wayne are still doing what they've always done, but I think I've finally grown up.

Title: Lisbon
Review: Reportedly inspired by two rainy trips to the Portugese capital, Lisbon nevertheless sounds like a continuation of the NYC outfit's 2008 turning point, You & Me, a dramatic din of last-call waltzes and dimly lit remembrances.

Title: Fear and Saturday Night
Review: The L.A.-based songwriter's fifth LP finds him focused solidly in the present. Fear still mines enough scarred grit to match Bingham's distinctive rasp.

Title: Beyond the Bloodhounds
Review: Beyond the Bloodhounds isn’t a blues record per se, but in the grand tradition of the blues, it creates space to look your demons in the eye and acknowledge their foul existence without necessarily doing much about them.

Title: Pilot Talk II
Review: There's immense lyrical potential, manifesting itself in lines like "Emotional luggage, nothin' of it, I don't check bags / I just carry on, leave that bullshit in the past," or "Master the flow, Alaska-cold / silent foot, assassin approach / high when I stroll / not even leavin' footprints in the snow," but it never quite carries over to the entire song. From that point of view this sequel is more of an afterthought to "Pilot Talk" than an afterburner.

Title: Shape Shift
Review: It's their first of several written live in the studio, giving it an immediacy that their two preceding records lacked.

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: Yet another firework-filled post-modern work of true art. [#24, p.89]

Title: Pile
Review: Pile arrives comparatively light on melodrama, brimming with live fast/die young missives instead, anthems of restless spirits who drink love and life from the same red plastic cup.

Title: Probot
Review: Unlike similar records... this has a unity of aesthetic purpose, a competitive wallop, even (kind of) a seriousness. [Mar 2004, p.127]

Title: TFCF
Review: Andrew spends TFCF discovering sounds that previous incarnations of Liars somehow never explored, whether it's the oddly majestic psychedelic flamenco of "Cliché Suite" or the brittle piano pop of "No Tree No Branch," one of a streak of surprisingly catchy songs on the album's second half. Amidst all the change, Andrew holds onto some quintessential Liars qualities.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: What's finally made it is an expansive, guest-packed 57 minutes that recall the Southern hip-hop bounce of 2003's 'Speakerboxxx', but with an added twist of maturity.

Title: Black Light
Review: If you are a serious Groove Armada fan you will love it or hate it, I doubt there will be an in between.  If you are just a music lover who is really digging the way electro and indie sounds have come into their own in the last few years than this is definitely for you.

Title: Do It Again
Review: Röyksopp and Robyn share so much sonic DNA that their team-up is almost self-defeating, blurring the distinction between the two to the point where their respective quirks are essentially scratched in favor of a cohesive but far too clinical production.

Title: Big Bad Luv
Review: Big Bad Luv can hold its own next to any of the great Americana-tinged rock ‘n’ roll records of the past, from Scarecrow to Full Moon Fever to Copperhead Road.

Title: Black Dog Barking
Review: Very occasionally, they come a school uniform away from actually impersonating their forefathers, but it's a formula they execute wit the same kick-ass conviction that earned them support slots with Iron Maiden. [18 May 2013, p.53]

Title: Beams
Review: Beams represents a cerebral and well-balanced opus that could well represent a peerless innovator at the absolute pinnacle of his legacy.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Unlike Treats, Reign Of Terror never feels new, fresh or exciting; it just feels like a chore.

Title: Relax
Review: They're deceptively laid-back satirists who deliver their smackdowns amid da-da streams of consciousness, sometimes with such subtlety that by the time the joke finally registers they're off on a fresh, equally strange and frequently hilarious tangent.

Title: Girls Can Tell
Review: Girls' melding of new wave and indie pop literally sounds timeless... [3/9/2001, p.82]

Title: Kin
Review: Though it feels disjointed at times, at its best Kin captures the emotional impact of changes and their aftermath.

Title: Kaputt
Review: Kaputt's allure fills up glasses with the finest Chablis in a Nagel print–filled room, and lets Bejar's newfound status as King of Hi-Fi unfold in all of its cryptic finery.

Title: Bless Off
Review: Bless Off is a single-minded beast of an album that seeks only to inspire the listener to hit the streets and take some risks, making a case for the idea that a life that isn't lived dangerously is a life that's barely lived at all.

Title: Robyn Hitchcock
Review: He remains a more psychedelic soul, as witness psych-rockers like “Mad Shelley’s Letterbox” and “Detective Mindhorn”. With a sort of repressed power anchoring its drive.

Title: Loose
Review: This is glorious, 21st-century Technicolor po.

Title: Dark Matter Moving at the Speed of Light
Review: This is an example of an innovator sounding only slightly better than his legions of lesser followers.

Title: FIDLAR
Review: Just occasionally the band drops hints that they might have a future beyond this loutish, two-dimensional debut.

Title: Untilted
Review: Untilted’s sound is warmer and rounder, but at the expense of sonic and rhythmic scope, initially a disappointment. It’s nice to report, though, that repeated auditions expose a new tightness in composition.

Title: One True Vine
Review: You Are Not Alone, her 2010 collaboration with Jeff Tweedy of Wilco, won Staples her first Grammy. The follow up is even better.

Title: Everything Is Recorded by Richard Russell
Review: At its least interesting, Everything Is Recorded is a compilation album, not a million miles from Albarn’s Gorillaz (fortysomething English guy makes hip-hop-derived album with stellar cast). But it is one whose centre remains tantalisingly unreachable.

Title: Excerpts
Review: By switching voices and languages, and throwing in string quartets alongside swooning electronica, he pushes different versions of reality, and while on the whole it slips into background noise, there are moments when Excerpts packs a punch. And there's plenty to capture a more vivid and patient imagination.

Title: Sports
Review: Weekend has crafted an aesthetically sound model of how a rock 'n roll band should work. It looks good, it knows how to talk to women, and some guys you know even think it's pretty cool.

Title: Perfect Shapes
Review: Perfect Shapes is a confident step forward. It all bodes well for whatever shapes come next.

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: While It's Not Me, It's You isn't quite the voice of wisdom, the Mockney chatter has been dialed right down. [Mar 2009, p.108]

Title: Because of You
Review: It's a little less immediate than the first album, but also takes Ne-Yo's case where it belongs: to the dance floor.

Title: xx
Review: It's hard to imagine their music getting much better. But it's not hard to imagine their lives getting much better. Which may be all their music needs.

Title: Hot Motion
Review: A stunning effort all-around, it is a pleasure to have Temples back, the prospect of where they can go from here is one of excitement and thrill.

Title: Put The Shine On
Review: The songs' relative lack of eccentricity makes CocoRosie seem oddly run-of-the-mill. [Apr 2020, p.25]

Title: Belief System
Review: Belief System is not only Special Request’s most definitive piece of work, but it will also, probably, prove to be Paul Woolford’s magnum opus.

Title: Days Go By
Review: So there are a couple of silly tracks - but then there were two silly Bennett sisters [in Austen's Pride and Prejudice]. Sadly, the remainder of the album is all Mary and no Elizabeth; devoid of life, wit, or energy.

Title: In the Belly of the Brazen Bull
Review: If you're over alt-rock, then Brazen Bull is going to do little to bring you around. But if you need a new guitar rock record, one that you can headbang to without irony, then the Cribs have delivered.

Title: Home on Native Land
Review: A sweet, joyously transgressive album.

Title: The Door
Review: On The Door, there is a sense that the sounds happening are not the products of the people creating them but rather those of some inscrutable (and vaguely dangerous) pulsing energy below our feet. It’s an amazing effect. And it’s created through the sheer power of quantity and repetition.

Title: Blueberry Boat
Review: Length is where the album fails.

Title: Play
Review: The ebb and flow of eighteen concise, contrasting cuts writes a story about Moby's beautifully conflicted interior world while giving the outside planet beats and tunes on which to groove.

Title: Just Say No to the Psycho Right-Wing Capitalist Fascist Industrial Death Machine
Review: Far more than a simple exercise in rock as violent fury, or as political vehicle for that matter, Gnod’s latest effort is yet another important musical statement from a group firmly at the forefront of everything good about British underground music. That it arrives in time to soundtrack such troubled times as these is, of course, a welcome bonus.

Title: Get Lonely
Review: Get Lonely is a record that requires multiple listens (itself a first) but which absolutely forbids them -- I've been unable to listen to it in one sitting after a month. Not out of its weakness or my boredom, but in its relentless despair and my weakness.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: The version of Low that helped define a subgenre remains recognizable throughout, but their sound has expanded.

Title: Return of the Tender Lover
Review: A satisfying mix of adult pop-soul love songs that evoke his early work. These amiable, adroitly produced and arranged songs confirm his inimitable knack for graceful melodies and effortless hooks.

Title: There's No 666 in Outer Space
Review: [It] has a charm that transcends your typical noise-splunk band. [Mar 2007, p.145]

Title: Exile In The Outer Ring
Review: The drone-folk sound of Gowns, the band the South Dakota singer/songwriter previously fronted, is still present, and while she retains a fondness for repetition, sometimes to her detriment, there's a faster, more insistent approach across tracks like "Breathalyzer" and "I Wanna Destroy." [Jul - Sep 2017, p.56]

Title: Run Fast
Review: Even through the heavier topics of illness and recovery, a melodic sense of dance carries the message, but what delivers the punch is Hanna's voice.

Title: Strange House
Review: Better then anyone could have hoped.

Title: Song For Our Daughter
Review: It's been a gradual recalibration and Songs For Our Daughter ruffles more of Marling's characteristic composure: she's feeling the breeze, focused, pressing keenly forward. [Jun 2020, p.24]

Title: Brass Knuckles
Review: Brass Knuckles sounds less like the product of a fighter who's ready to go back into the ring than one who's stalling for time.

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: Depending on your mood, there’ll be songs you’d happily lop off for a more streamlined listen, but by and large, all of these songs make the patchwork much more vibrant.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: Of all the newish dance acts digging on vintage disco and chicago House, NYC-based Hercules & Love Affair boast the smartest cuts and most range. [June 2008, p.66]

Title: Cold Beer Conversation
Review: In the end Cold Beer Conversation isn’t just another in a long line of superior releases, it’s a beacon of good writing, playing and singing. But it’s also all we could want or expect from a man who embodies the best that country music has to offer.

Title: Waltzed in from the Rumbling
Review: Plants and Animals have created something beautiful, even if it's not wholly original.

Title: Cypress Grove
Review: It's a modernization of his sound but not a bowdlerization; if anything, it's perhaps the finest realization of Holmes' blues. At the very least, it's certainly the liveliest and boldest album he's made.

Title: MG
Review: MG is an intriguing diversion that might appeal to Depeche Mode fans who were put off by the pure, minimalist techno of VCMG, and it could also come as a surprise to listeners who aren't DM fans, or haven't kept up with their later work.

Title: Swear I'm Good At This
Review: It's a kick in the teeth from start to finish.

Title: The Great Pretenders
Review: A great, and fun, album.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: This is the best and most complete set of songs Spiritualized have made since Ladies And Gentlemen.

Title: Dead Silence
Review: At times, the record is a grower. Off the bat, the singles sell the release but other numbers require additional listens to click. Having said that, once you hear that click this record is completely blinding.

Title: UGK 4 Life
Review: UGK 4 Life is a fitting capper to this Texas duo's storied career--nothing groundbreaking, just funky, rough-hewn, celebratory tracks.

Title: Release Me
Review: With its Motown feel, the title track finds singer Elizabeth "Z" Berg crooning about love gone wrong ("I wish you knew I'm not the one for you/You're not the one I need/And I can't stand you") over a harmonized chorus of "ooh's" from her female bandmates, but the vocals don't go down as smoothly as the Supremes. Meanwhile, it's on the standout cut "I Can See It in Your Eyes" where Berg settles into her most comfortable range and the group does its most believable impression of the Animals.

Title: Do Hollywood
Review: With one foot in the present and one foot in the past, The Lemon Twigs have produced one of the most striking, individual, and colorful debuts of the year.

Title: Highway Companion
Review: Highway Companion contains the most clear-eyed and hopeful songs that Petty has written in memory.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: Notice the way whole songs skulk past without you ever noticing; how half the material here is ornate but unmemorable muzak, with all the emotional force of a feather. [combined review of both discs]

Title: Heavy Rocks
Review: Heavy Rocks (2011) improves on the glam thrash of previous studio release Smile (2008) with two centerpiece epics.

Title: Coracle
Review: There's a sharp contrast between the twin peaks of Coracle and the rest of its material, especially when they try to pointlessly channel Spacemen 3 circa "Honey" and shackle that sound to some perfunctory beats on "Ecstatic Truth".

Title: Taste
Review: Despite a change in instrumentation and a palpable “lock” imposed on all of the sequenced bar-lines, he manages to maintain the sense of immediacy and ease.

Title: The People In Your Neighbourhood
Review: Keeping the intensity and power of their previous work, but much more agile and versatile in its approach, The People In Your Neighbourhood feels comfortably like Led Bib’s best work to date.

Title: As If
Review: As If  leans a little too heavily on the groove in the middle, with moments like "Funk (I Got This)" fading into the background, but it's reinvigorated towards the end by the riveting "Lucy Mongoosey", which uses another singalong chorus as an anchor, an introspective pause among all the dancing.

Title: Revival
Review: There’s enough growth here to accept the occasional stumble. Revival, like ‘Good For You’, is a damn fine, hook-laden surprise. Selena Gomez has found a voice worth paying serious attention to.

Title: Capacity
Review: The catchy songs are catchier; the melodies are tighter; the peaks and troughs dip higher and lower. ... If crossover hits were still a thing in the indie game, 'Watering' would be the low-key bridge to a more post-punk-savvy crowd. But other moments just fail to pop, like the title track that’s blown out and unfocused.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: Because past the pop songs, past the soaring (and let’s not make any bones about it, this album soars in places) this is a supremely clever album.

Title: The Bedlam in Goliath
Review: The Bedlam in Goliath is simply an immense album.
Prince is at his best when his music is unmistakably his. Half of the tracks on 3121 could not have been made by anyone else, but the slushy R&B ballads are not amongst them.

Title: Silver
Review: Those who are desperately clutching onto the past few months' sunny days and starry nights – or planning for Summer 2011 already – are likely to dig the unpretentious, casual atmosphere of Eternal Summers. For everyone else, there's bound to be something else out there better suited to pumpkins spice lattes and fall harvests.

Title: The Golden Age of Grotesque
Review: Seems to be his regular melange of jackboot glam and electro-metal spiced up with those endearingly juvenile stabs at pretension and subversion. [Jun 2003, p.94]

Title: Hoodstar
Review: If anything, Chingy has regressed since his debut, and his initially fresh style now sounds old.

Title: Playtime Is Over
Review: It's about the best a studio grime album can be.

Title: Good Morning Revival
Review: The problem is that for all the slick operations and glorious machinations of the marketing and production, this band has run out of steam; soulless without being undead.

Title: Twins
Review: It has the reckless spirit of a record that hasn't been over-analysed, but with an intense flurry of ideas from someone in the absolute prime of their creativity.

Title: Disgraceland
Review: There is a little too much grace and not enough diss.

Title: New Moon
Review: New Moon follows through on that promise but inevitably discovers that, when you do open your heart, blood gets spilled.

Title: Visuals
Review: Visuals spatters Mew's art-rock sensibilities on a pop canvas. [Jul 2017, p.111]

Title: Let There Be Morning
Review: The Perishers fail to elevate their brand of minimalism beyond the politely unobtrusive and fatally unmemorable. [Apr/May 2005, p.149]

Title: Out of Exile
Review: Deep cuts like "Man or Animal" are as hot as anything this side of Led Zeppelin II. [Jul 2005, p.95]

Title: Be Myself
Review: This is a rare album that is upbeat while also showing an emotional side that we all have felt from time to time.

Title: Swoon
Review: It's intimate, accessible, and--Pumpkins comparisons aside--fairly unique in today's scene. What more could one ask for?

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: For the most part, Ghost channels its shaggy sound into pop music. True, it's pop music that constantly threatens to erupt into noise or fade into silence, but it's still hard not to hum along.

Title: Soft Connections
Review: It's been a long time coming, to the point when it seemed it might never happen, but Soft Connections announces the reappearance of a major talent, one whom all fans of indie pop owe it to themselves to discover or rediscover.

Title: Colonia
Review: Beguiling, gorgeous stuff--and smartly funny, too.

Title: HIVE1
Review: It’s a private album, filled with in-jokes and notes that only make sense for Braxton himself.

Title: The Phoenix
Review: The Phoenix is, ultimately, a collection of immersive and impressively well-produced analogue techno tracks, bound up in a package with overt cultural references that tend to distract rather than add to the experience.

Title: Sleeping Operator
Review: A record that prefers to build up intensity before letting it ebb away, doling out flashes of propulsive rhythm in snatches and grasps rather than in the four-on-the-floor anthemic grooves favoured by so many bands these days, Sleeping Operator feels out of time, apart, distinct.

Title: The Seduction of Kansas
Review: The Seduction of Kansas is, all things considered, a solid second album. It builds on the promise of Nothing Feels Natural, and while it occasionally fumbles its own goals, it’s hard to fault Priests for aiming high. One can only hope that the radical ambition and sense of purpose on display here carries them far into the future.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: Not only does Bankrupt! propose a big, stadium-ready sound, it offers one that nearly suffocates its creators. [No. 98, p.59]

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: A giddy blend of nostalgia and invention that'll do just fine for starters. [Dec. 2011 p. 136]

Title: Unreal
Review: Unreal's feel is of the hangover following the hedonistic romp that was Yuck--reassembling a broken self into a positive whole, and taking an auspicious step in a new direction.

Title: Fall into the Sun
Review: For an album cast as a fresh start, Fall Into the Sun mostly feels like closure.

Title: Vessel of Love
Review: Album opener Angel Fire make it tempting to categorise Vessel of Love as an uplifting summer album. Yet Cook’s lyrics contain a haunting melancholia, touching on love and survival to create a bittersweet effect. There's a hidden depth to her breezy pop that will stay with listeners for days.

Title: Hotel California
Review: On the one hand, the album does very little of what Tyga’s best at and even when it does, Hotel California makes the strange move of bowing to Tyga’s biting prowess rather than original, ratchet works. On the other, everything here is done perfectly well and enjoyably; unless you’re focused on Tyga’s bars, taking him purely as a presence on some nice beats is not excruciating.

Title: RTJ4
Review: Because of the themes it addresses, “RTJ4” is indeed a hip-hop album chaotically reflective of the modern times and much needed for the same reason.

Title: The Private Press
Review: The Private Press is more solid an album than anyone dared expect from an older, wiser DJ Shadow, and though it won't be televising another revolution, I'd be lying if I said its celebratory pleasure centers didn't communicate directly with my own.

Title: Living Proof
Review: Whilst Living Proof is very much the blues, Buddy Guy's solos give this a rawness that swells with discord, and the result feels more akin to the avant-garde guitar days of Sonic Youth and Shellac.

Title: The Making of You
Review: You may have all the Pentangle you need, and all the Fairport Convention you could ever want to listen to. The Making of You won’t replace any of these favorites, but it can definitely carve a space out on the shelf next to them. Make some room. This stuff is good.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: The lush melodic sense that deserted Air on 10000Hz Legend has returned.

Title: Culture II
Review: Culture II ultimately feels less like a celebratory howl from the mountaintop than a transitional inventory dump. With its easily-trimmable 24 tracks, Culture II appears to be tailored to finesse chart rules, which count 1,500 individual song streams toward one full album sale.

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: Perhaps it’s deliberate that throughout The Take Off and Landing of Everything, hardly anything truly takes off. Instead the album dangles there, an effortlessly leaden exhibition of glum triumphalism--and an example of what makes Elbow, at its least potent, so subtly unsubtle.

Title: The Hum
Review: Throughout, The Hum is a thrilling testament to Hookworms' single-mindedness and conviction. [Dec 2014, p.112]

Title: The Boombox Ballads
Review: For the most part, this is a record about chasing a specific kind of pop aesthetic instead, which largely comes at the detriment of any kind of real connection.

Title: Surviving
Review: The album on the whole is a solid, self-aware addition to Jimmy Eat World’s catalog, and if the band’s modest strivers’ outlook has proved anything, it’s that there will be another. A band whose biggest song is against writing oneself off always has work to do.

Title: King Night
Review: This is not a one-hit wonder situation, or even an album with only one good song. With King Night, Salem exhausts all its resources in a singular moment, which leaves the rest of the record to suffer through its own paralysis and mediocrity.

Title: Antemasque
Review: Aside from the pleasantly Britpoppy "50,000 Kilowatts" and "Drown All The Witches," This is fast, fun, and full of piss and vinegar than one might expect from such seasoned campaigners. [Dec 2014, p.71]

Title: It Is Time for a Love Revolution
Review: It’s Time For A Love Revolution, his eighth LP, easily ranks among his highest achievements.

Title: Wind in the Wires
Review: It’s what Bright Eyes coulda done if he put the songs off I’m Wide Awake onto the canvas of Digital Ash.

Title: This Is My Hand
Review: This is My Hand is one big ball of skill, imagination and love of musical creation.

Title: False Idols
Review: Tricky seems to be doing some soul-searching--but the running time is long, and at least three quarters of the album is top-shelf.

Title: Hombre Lobo: 12 Songs of Desire
Review: Each track contains elements that sound similar in combinations of tone, texture and melody from previous records, so this album is not necessarily a knockout. However, the band’s artistic hybrid is delivered with a fervent honesty and steeped in an emotional intensity that may make it sound a lot like other Eels material.

Title: Gimme Some
Review: If the least they do is keep revealing new shades of the familiar, it's worth sticking around and seeing this band through.

Title: Hood Billionaire
Review: The sparse "Phone Tap" tells a tale of drug dealing paranoia, while the Big K.R.I.T.-assisted "Brimstone" is a remorseful hymnal. These moments are still few and far between, and the rest of Ross' tales of pushing fall short of revealing whether his ascent to boss status is factual or purely fictional.

Title: Initiation
Review: They say love is blind; on the basis of this intelligently balanced LP, though, it certainly isn't deaf.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: The choice, folks, is all yours. Would you like The Thrills? Or would you prefer some excitement instead?

Title: Long Way Down
Review: Long  Way Down is stuffed with bogus sensitivity, crystallisations of emotional disquiet couched in chant choruses, and polite piano arrangements reliant on a few chord-changes.

Title: Neuroplasticity
Review: Despite a greater focus on musicality, tunes remain hard to come by and Neuroplasticity (named for the brain's ability to form new pathways) remains a victory of mood over songcraft, which is to say, not all that much of a triumph.

Title: V
Review: The whole album is tinged just as much by melancholy as it is by hopeful optimism.

Title: Obey
Review: The album proves that Exploded View are at their best when they refuse to be constrained by reality, to listen to consensus or to obey, and instead, exist in the dazzling reverie of their collective dream.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: The Strokes don't have much of their own to say here. [Dec 2005, p.106]

Title: The Anthropocene Extinction
Review: These anthems drive their points home with unearthly force.

Title: Tales from Turnpike House
Review: Not much happens, which seems to be the point. [Jan/Feb 2006, p.96]

Title: Hell-On
Review: It shows that whatever life brings her, Case can turn it into something startling. [Jul 2018, p.108]

Title: Napalm
Review: What's delivered is another robust collection of business as usual, with the surprising diversions adding just enough dimension to the album to even it out.

Title: So Long, Astoria
Review: A fine trip down memory lane that celebrates the complexities of growing up.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: Most of the record is--sonically-speaking, rather than in terms of quality--classic Ghostface, but only a couple of these familiar tracks match the standard set on previous records.

Title: QTY
Review: QTY is as timeless, compelling and clever as you could hope for first time round.

Title: Art Angels
Review: Art Angels is a major victory for deep weird.

Title: False Alarm
Review: Some of the results feel either commonplace or, worse, flimsy and annoying – perhaps unwittingly.

Title: Feel Feelings
Review: An intelligent, stylish pop record.

Title: Crimes of Passion
Review: The album is diverting, pleasant, and completely undemanding; it’s the perfect soundtrack to a sunny afternoon or a road trip down the highway.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: It’s less catchy than Wolfgang but also more creative and more satisfying.

Title: English Electric
Review: English Electric--both melodically and artistically--stands as a rich, dignified entry in OMD’s catalogue.

Title: Snowflake Midnight
Review: Overall Snowflake Midnight isn’t quite the disaster that the disillusioned might have expected.

Title: Neon Golden
Review: Neon Golden often comes on like a radical update of New Order's Lowlife period, where mournful guitar songs are integrated into a mesh of clicks, pops, glitches and samples. [Mar 2003, p.96]

Title: Assume Form
Review: The limber Assume Form finds Blake with a new lease on life. We were lucky to have something as insightful and forward-thinking as James Blake; we’re luckier still to have this one.

Title: Raise Vibration
Review: It’s this line between cheesy and unbelievably cool that Kravitz hops back and forth over throughout the album, never convincingly staying on one side. ... Worth the price of admission is “Low,” a funk-tinged easy-groover about keeping a relationship grounded. It’s sexy, it’s smooth, and it’s dance floor ready.

Title: Amphetamine Ballads
Review: While Amphetamine Ballads is as exciting as any debut record in recent times, it’s also a reminder that the British ability to conjure depth from a sparsely coloured palette is as strong as ever.

Title: One Life Stand
Review: Marvellously, an uninspiring mid-section aside, this is still music to dance to. More than dance in fact; you can exult to this.

Title: At Least For Now
Review: For the most part these piano-led songs sound unique, the lonely despair of Cornerstone and the arresting lyricism of Condolence signalling an exciting new talent.

Title: Whatever It Takes
Review: From the heartfelt rhumba of I Don’t Wanna Be Without You and the title track – the perfect showstopper for the Harlem Square Club crowd--to Blisters, a captivating shuffle, and How Long, a going back to church blues, every song’s a winner.

Title: Under Branch & Thorn & Tree
Review: If there is a criticism to be made, it is that at times the whole thing can be a little too low-key.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: If anything, that’s the trick here: each time the listener pegs it with one of Albarn’s past sounds, the track subverts and confounds the expectation.

Title: Teenage Emotions
Review: It’s a graphic exemplar of the contemporary Atlanta sound: stark backing, nagging hook and staccato wordplay, as distinct from the lyricism that traditionalists hold dear.

Title: Shake Shook Shaken
Review: On the whole, they succeed by taking a careful layered approach. [Mar 2014, p.100]

Title: Pattern of Excel
Review: Pattern Of Excel succeeds during those little moments that capture Bannon's way with mood and melody.

Title: Glasvegas
Review: So believe it: this is the real thing, no-one’s crying wolf, not even Alan McGee.

Title: Hifalutin
Review: Lowly strikes their balances adroitly, but Hifalutin could easily have become another album--one that was more straightforward. [Jun 2019, p.94]

Title: Too Many Voices
Review: These processes are slow, sometimes painful and on multiple scales, but with each track and each album, the producer is changing our understanding of sound, data, memory and our own bodies in musical space. [Jun 2016, p.56]

Title: Antics
Review: Though Interpol couldn't be expected to surpass their previous heights, it's difficult to imagine a savvier or more satisfying second step.

Title: You Won't Get What You Want
Review: Whatever voodoo made their unapproachable sound so damn fun and cathartic is completely gone. In its place is a something altogether darker and uglier, but ultimately more brilliant and enrapturing than ever before. You Won't Get What You Want is Daughters finest moment and everything I’ve wanted.

Title: Handcream for a Generation
Review: A foot-stomping, bum-shaking good time from beginning to end. [May 2002, p.80]

Title: Evil Heat
Review: A letdown from the full-on intensity and imagination of their previous release.

Title: Civilian
Review: Baltimore multi-instrumental duo Jenn Wasner and Andy Stack have raised their game with this third LP. [Apr 2011, p.103]

Title: Forcefield
Review: Tokyo Police Club operates as a kind of derelict garage band, and their offbeat lyrical imagery and crunchy guitar-drum combinations work to enhance the album's messy, unpretentious charm.

Title: Futures
Review: It's just not ambitious enough, lacking the impact to draw new fans in while just about satisfying those already captivated by the band’s admirable class.

Title: Sunday Morning Record
Review: Almost worth getting a hangover for. [Jan 2014, p.119]

Title: The Isness
Review: It's the songs which seal The Isness's fate. [Sep 2002, p.100]

Title: A Healthy Distrust
Review: His style has finally caught up with his intellect, and while his beats are passable but unexceptional, his voice locks onto and scans over them so ferociously they're almost obliterated.

Title: Yolk in the Fur
Review: The first half of Yolk in the Fur [has] a cohesive and cinematic feel. ... The second half of Yolk isn’t as strong, but it still holds interesting developments.

Title: Finally Famous
Review: Finally Famous is a choice summertime rap rec­ord, complete with bright, breezy synth beats and cameos from Chris Brown and Mr. West himself. Prom King or not, Sean's clearly the life of the party.

Title: Laila's Wisdom
Review: While it's hard to pinpoint a track on Laila's Wisdom that is anthemic enough to be a dominant single, the project is a smooth, cohesive and powerfully insightful effort, which represents Rapsody's steadfast commitment to her craft.

Title: Wrath
Review: Wrath furthers Lamb of God's reputation for craft and innovation and argues to a broader audience that metal is a style rife with fresh ideas.

Title: Ambulance
Review: By using layers of shoegazey guitars and powerfully mic'd-up drums, they create soundscapes that combine Americana with English pastoralism. [Sep 2016, p.67]

Title: Keep on Your Mean Side
Review: There are a few moments of weakness on Keep on Your Mean Side - most notably where V.V. and Hotel get a little too repetitive or too simplistic for their own good – but it's easy to move past these minor instances without it detracting from the album too much.

Title: Rapping With Paul White
Review: It;s the mesmerising sonic weave which provides the intrigue. [Oct 2011, p.117]

Title: We'll Be The Moon
Review: Not terribly experimental then, nor especially genre-hopping, but let's not be sniffy; it's a very likeable cosmic pop record.

Title: Red
Review: Money and success can be just as good a fable as Romeo and Juliet, and Swift is deft enough to make a point of and poke fun at her fairytale stardom.

Title: Monomania
Review: It's an intense, sometimes violent, occasionally beautiful rock'n'roll record that once again proves the unpredictability and reliability of Deerhunter.

Title: Recurring Dream
Review: At 46 minutes, Recurring Dream isn’t an especially long album. But on the wrong day, at the wrong time and in the wrong frame of mind, it can feel like the longest 46 minutes in the history of all time.

Title: Take Off Your Pants and Jacket
Review: They don't mess around much outside their tessitura - they like to keep everything light, fast and punchy.

Title: Masterpiece
Review: Modern folk fans take note; it’s not every day we get the pleasure of hearing such an accomplished debut.

Title: Seabed
Review: Seabed never really gets out of first gear. The general vibe given off is that of a teenager moping about in his bedroom, albeit one with the skills to emote through slick, well-produced pop music.

Title: Dig Out Your Soul
Review: For those who have happily stuck around this long already Dig Out certainly won’t be the straw that breaks the camel’s back--by all means, it lightens the load quite considerably. But it does so with the dawning realisation that, 17 years and seven albums in, this is a high point in a career deficient in high points.

Title: Fade
Review: Few among us can craft an album as seamlessly fine as Fade. [Feb 2013, p.51]

Title: Life Is Good
Review: Punk can be a relative term, especially when applied to California. In comparison to The Pogues, Flogging Molly sound more like The Nolans. In fact, the Saw Doctors are nearer the mark. But all their rousing expat energy, best heard on The Hand Of John L Sullivan, can’t disguise a controlled finesse.

Title: I Am Gemini
Review: Gemini's theater-rock is no pain to listen to, but true drama queens will want to get their fix elsewhere.

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: Still, swirling in there with Yorke's apocalyptic surrealisms and his band's tricky rhythms, there's a beating heart that feels almost animal. If The King of Limbs doesn't feel alive to you at first, give it some time to wake up.

Title: The Redeemer
Review: It wanders more like a Hype Williams album would, and leaves that opening promise to dangle unfulfilled.

Title: Better Oblivion Community Center
Review: Better Oblivion Community Center isn’t an obvious step forward for either artist but it’s a generous and grounded collection of songs, showcasing the complementary talents of two of America’s most talented songwriters. By the crackling close of final track Dominos, you’re more than glad they opened their doors.

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: This is business as usual: string-laced Americana that ranks alongside other literate types such as The Shins or Midlake.

Title: Days Go By
Review: Two (incredibly) horrible songs aren't enough to discount the entire album, no. Yet it's unfortunate that Days Go By doesn't provide any delirious highs to counter its abysmal lows.

Title: Impersonator
Review: By utilizing a synth-based soundtrack just as organic, emotional, and unadulterated as Welsh’s voice and lyrics, Impersonator successfully matches man with machine and gives each an equally powerful, equally human voice.

Title: Froot
Review: Froot is another big, unabashed pop album astutely balanced with sufficient melancholy and restraint to stop it from all getting too Katy Perry. [May 2015, p.77]

Title: Phantom Punch
Review: For all the progress the record represents, Punch is a schizophrenic release.

Title: Ersatz GB
Review: It's not up there with their very best, but it's actually not that far off.

Title: Mutt
Review: The best moments are soft and strange. "The Corner" is a fabulous piece of folk understatement and emotional ambiguity, while the brilliant "Freefall" showcases Branan's willingness to stretch his voice to odd, ugly places in the service of transcendence. [No.88 p.53]
There's little here that's moves on from the kind of trip-hop balladeers that abounded in the late '90s or indeed the singer-songwriters that Sheeran admires such as Damien Rice or James Morrison.

Title: Psychic
Review: As a whole, it’s winningly Lynchian, and ballsy enough to open with an 11-minute song.

Title: Chrissybaby Forever
Review: Chrissybaby is 16 songs long, which might be more of this particular pleasant, low-stakes mood than you need at one uninterrupted stretch.

Title: Tentacles
Review: It’s safe to say Crystal Antlers have struck the iron while it’s hot, and while there’s no one else out there who sounds even remotely like them.

Title: Lonely at the Top
Review: None of this stuff is particularly groundbreaking, but it does what it does quite well.

Title: Key Markets
Review: Anger is still their foremost energy, but there is a much richer seam of humour than they like to let on.

Title: The Atlantic Ocean
Review: If the squelching synths of 'The Original Thought' irritate, the jauntiness elsewhere suggests he's thriving on a lack of commercial pressure. [May 2009, p.119]

Title: True Love Cast Out All Evil
Review: A fierce backing band, Okkervil River lends them drama, tension and a cinematic pomp that underscores the miraculous nature of Erickson's recovery.

Title: Southern Blood
Review: It’s not often anyone has the (albeit heartbreaking) luxury of being able to map out their own memorial, and Allman leaves us with his head held high and a record of rare beauty.

Title: Going To Hell
Review: The Pretty Reckless don’t do a great deal to prove the cynics wrong here. More frustratingly, they are undoubtedly capable of much better.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: The result is an intimate, poignant album, laced with rich production that enhances, not clouds, the songwriting itself.

Title: Woman
Review: Intimate and slow-moving, Woman is good but underwhelming.

Title: Coco Beware
Review: Coco Beware is actually such an inviting album you can keep it on repeat and just bask in the cozy melodies and gently propulsive percussion.

Title: Things That Can't Be Undone
Review: It's great credit to both Lund and his versatile backing bad, The Hurtin' Albertans, that such see-sawing through genres can sound so much like a singular piece of work. [Dec 2015, p.93]

Title: To the 5 Boroughs
Review: Fun, but hardly fresh.

Title: Heartland
Review: The whole sprawl of tooting loops, sawing violins and Pallett's unlovely operatic warbling feels gruelling and indigestible - prog stodge in a dashing post millennial disguise. [Feb 2010, p. 93]

Title: Rules of Travel
Review: This is as commercial as country gets.

Title: 4:13 Dream
Review: Obviously nobody's expecting them to record anything revolutionary at this stage of their career, but it's fair to say that this album will probably only get Cure enthusiasts excited.

Title: Some Things Last Longer Than You
Review: A bold first full album from a trio whose ambitions are clearly only getting bigger.

Title: After Laughter
Review: A gorgeously produced, hook-studded record with cocked-eyebrow trepidation adding a jittery edge--a combination that's very of-the-moment in 2017, even if it veers outside of pop's rigid lines.

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: As with anything that's trying to do something bigger and better, lessons of that magnitude can take more time to sink in, definitely longer than the handful of hours we've had to absorb what The King of Limbs might be all about. In that sense, the jury is still out on The King of Limbs and that's because there's always something more to Radiohead.

Title: Assume Crash Position
Review: A jam band to the core, they don't craft their "songs" any more cunningly, but the effect is more song-like. Then, after 52 minutes, there's an unbuzzy finale: four minutes of acoustic likembe and aged voice which I call a coda and you may call a bore. To my medium-fi ears, this is where to begin.

Title: It's Up To Emma
Review: On It’s Up to Emma, her sixth album, songs like “My Man” and “What Can I Do” are a bit of a shock--lusher, denser, subtler, their gut-punching intensity smoothed with sustained sounds.

Title: Favorite Waitress
Review: With Favorite Waitress, The Felice Brothers have elevated their songwriting without losing their rambunctious charm.

Title: Rivers and Streams
Review: Melnyk could use a bit more genuine mystery and less self-importance. [Dec 2015, p.52]

Title: No Elephants
Review: Germano's gift for conjuring otherworldly melodies is as strong as ever. That said, she's still, and will always be, a niche artist.

Title: Eagulls
Review: From the twin guitar salvos of Mark Goldsworthy and Liam Matthews through to Tom Kelly and Henry Ruddell's flawless rhythm section crowned by Mitchell's voice of reason, they're an unshakable and on this, their long-awaited first LP, an unstoppable force.

Title: The Altogether
Review: The Altogether is, all stated evidence to the contrary, a remarkable work. Why? Because it is the product of two brothers who, understanding that they can kid neither the audience nor themselves, mapped a musical course based on their root love -- musical energy -- and never strayed. [Sep 2001, p.147]

Title: All Day
Review: All Day is a more complicated mix than Girl Talk's previous albums, with more to notice on repeat listens. And just like everything else he's done, it's an exhausting experience.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: It's striking to hear a nearly 40-year-old outfit present one of their best albums yet. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.104]

Title: Food & Liquor
Review: The album might not become a rap classic, but it is easily one of the best rap albums of 2006, and maybe one of the top records of any kind to appear this year.

Title: Fuzz
Review: FUZZ is commanding and infectious--this could be the project Segall was born for.

Title: The Haden Triplets
Review: Each note has a purpose, and every musician playing or singing is doing a magnificent job bringing it to life.

Title: Field of Reeds
Review: Listening to Field of Reeds sometimes feels like taking a test and forgetting everything you thought you studied for. At the same token, its gorgeous production, control, and vision make it hard to turn away from.

Title: Nothing is Quick in the Desert
Review: That's not to say there's no "Boom and Proud" anywhere to be found on Nothing but it's not "Shut 'Em Down" level like those old Bomb Squad albums from the 1980's and early 90's.

Title: Easy Tiger
Review: Easy Tiger keeps it simple: beguiling melodies, an ace band, and Adams' elastic tenor.

Title: The Things We Do To Find People Who Feel Like Us
Review: Music saves the misfit kids, but not every pain can be walloped into submission. Beach Slang sound less interested in ripping that pain open and exposing its insides than they are in shouting over it, and The Things We Do can start to sound like an exercise in emotional extremes.

Title: The W
Review: All the big Wu dogs are here -- Ghostface Killah, Method Man, Raekwon, Genius, etc. -- and it sounds like they've been sharpening their skills like knives. They toss rhymes back and forth with the precision of a machine -- they're so good it's almost scary.

Title: The Greatest Generation
Review: It is my firm belief that The Greatest Generation has no real precedent in this community.

Title: The Heart Is a Monster
Review: The Heart is a Monster doesn't quite leave the impression mid-'90s Failure did, but despite less experimental approach and cleaner digital production, it's still a compelling listen.

Title: Are We There
Review: She has never sounded more confident. Van Etten’s fourth album marks the true arrival of a singer who’s been on her way for a long time, and thinking of her as anything less than a career artist is certainly a vast underestimation.

Title: Not Real
Review: Not Real proves a fun set--but whilst you can't help but admire Stealing Sheep for evolving their sound, with a few track tweaks it could have been an evolution which went so much further.

Title: The Shakes
Review: Some of Herbert's most engaging work since 2001's Bodily Functions. [Jul 2015, p.91]

Title: DS2
Review: Smartly abandoning the sappy balladry that alienated many on his debut album, Pluto, and trimming all the excess fat that made Honest, an otherwise solid sophomore effort, feel largely uneven, Future goes for the gut and DS2 can pack a wallop.

Title: Chapter V
Review: The acoustic guitars have largely been set aside on Chapter V, leaving Staind to pummel away at its troubles and hoping that people still have time to listen to self-pitying grown men moan about their dysfunctional childhoods.

Title: Reincarnated
Review: As it stands, the album has some decent songs but doesn't hold together as an album.

Title: Doomsdayer's Holiday
Review: Doomsdayer's Holiday shows a band pushing the limits of psychedelic post-rock and testing the boundaries of post-metal. [Dec 2008, p.142]

Title: Hard Candy
Review: Every one of these 15 songs is a perfectly-crafted masterclass in great American songwriting. [Aug 2002, p.99]

Title: Out of Touch in the Wild
Review: Arguably one of Dutch Uncles’ greatest strengths is that their music never sits still and is devilishly difficult to categorise, thanks to the intricate tapestry of expertly woven threads painstakingly constructed on each song so adroitly that it all fits together perfectly, without any single element being allowed to monopolise the listener’s attention.

Title: The Four Worlds
Review: It's deliciously hauntingly odd. [May 2018, p.93]

Title: Everyday Nothing
Review: Sensitive to a whole host of influences old and new, ‘Everyday Nothing’ is a confident, cohesive and finely-honed debut.

Title: You Are Free
Review: It's not exactly a party, but Marshall's songwriting and cooing delivery remain fierce and otherly, redolent of romantic encounters in strange wood cabins. [Mar 2003, p.114]

Title: You Can't Go Back if There's Nothing To Go Back To
Review: Dire and descriptive, You Can’t Go Back If There’s Nothing To Go Back To numbing melancholia is uncommonly compelling.

Title: Performance
Review: For a four-piece rock band from Texas, they still remain pretty difficult to classify and almost impossible to ignore. Play loud and enjoy.

Title: CHAMPION
Review: Grandiose in its bite, depth and soul, Champion lives up to its name.

Title: In The Future
Review: They put their cloudy heads together and came up with the power-chord-slashing and hobbitty keyboard werping goods but wisely didn’t lose all the dirty distortion and strummy acoustic bits.

Title: Vices & Virtues
Review: Above all, Vices & Virtues is a complete package that secures Panic! At The Disco as one of the most forward thinking pop-rock acts around.

Title: Zeros
Review: Not quite accessible to the unsuspecting ears, Zeros appeals in that inexplicable, morose way, propelled by a certain pleasure entwined with the chaos of the uncertain.

Title: I Grow Tired But Dare Not Fall Asleep
Review: With this, Ghostpoet has created another fantastic, authentic body of work, meeting those high expectations.

Title: Bionic
Review: Now, on her new album, Bionic, how has she decided to present herself? Mostly as a sexbot: a one-dimensional hot chick chanting come-ons to club beats.

Title: Sounds From Nowheresville
Review: Seems shambled and unfinished. [No. 85, p.58]

Title: Troubadour
Review: The trio are adroit musicians with pleasant vocal abilities--loving the falsetto--and if you look past the over-indulgences, the album is solid, if not particularly memorable.

Title: Uptown Special
Review: For all the technical charm that Ronson is able to pull off on this album, a lyrically nimble one with the employment of Pulitzer Prize winning author Michael Chabon, it never reaches sexy.

Title: Tin Star
Review: Once you hear any of them, you’ll want more, especially since this compact 32 minute disc ends way too soon.

Title: Fantasy Empire
Review: Drummer/vocalist Brian Chippendale’s delirious sing-song brings notes of fancy to tracks like ‘Dream Genie’, but Lightning Bolt’s aim remains simple: to batter you into ecstatic submission.

Title: Together We're Heavy
Review: It's hard to avoid a feeling of deja vu.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: While the connective tissue between the record’s highlights simmers at the same temperature as much of Low’s back catalog, The Invisible Way flows as a satisfying whole.

Title: Tripper
Review: Less dynamic and more ruminative than The Ruminant Band, here are 10 songs and a poky instrumental for country hippies manque and other shaggy folk down on the little luck they ever had.

Title: Ali & Toumani
Review: You get the feel of two of the world's greatest musicians in a room together, having a conversation and creating a document that will carry their legacy into the future. It is not challenging music. Anyone can approach it easily, and it is the perfect initiation to Touré's talents for listeners who haven't yet heard him.

Title: Aloha Moon
Review: Many of the songs on Aloha Moon hint at '80s soft rock, with their delicate guitar and drumming, while still providing a contemporary dream-like quality.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: His boldest, most impressive statement to date. [No. 114, p.55]

Title: The Terror
Review: As with most "difficult" albums, the more one listens, the more forgiving they become. [May 2013, p.77]

Title: Vespertine
Review: Vespertine is her most intensely private and intimate-sounding work, a journey through an interior world that is quietly ecstatic, erotic and playful.

Title: Nux Vomica
Review: A refreshingly passionate record.

Title: Shields
Review: [A] beautiful if vague fourth studio album.

Title: Makes a King
Review: Makes A King takes it up a notch: the same ingredients and patterns are there, but The Very Best now sound much more like a fully operational band, rather than a fortuitous hodgepodge of singing and sampling.

Title: Ambition
Review: Ambition nods to Ross' cartoon grandiosity in "Miami Nights," where Wale details his collection of luxury goods over a jubilant horn riff. Characteristically, though, the album heads in plenty of other directions as well.

Title: I'm Going Away
Review: It’s been a while since Fiery Furnaces released an album with songs that stick in your head. I’m Going Away, the Brooklyn band’s eighth release, is full of them.

Title: WIXIW
Review: An album that immerses you into its world, a headphones record that is at once both their most accessible and their most challenging, revealing new layers after every listen. Unpredictable, in the very best way.

Title: Soul Food
Review: The mostly original songs capture the gospel spirit in ballads (“The Highest”), funk (“Speaking in Tongues”), New Orleans second line (“Soul Food ll”) and driving blues rock (“Play All Day”) that will satisfy existing fans of any of the participants and win over some new ones too.

Title: Mockingbird Time
Review: Mockingbird Time, the band's first album in eight years, places them right back in the hazy glow of Laurel Canyon sunset. [Oct 2011, p.123]

Title: More Light
Review: Primal Scream haven't sounded this vital in at least a decade. [Jun 2013, p.97]

Title: Citizen of Glass
Review: This is an opaque and quietly intense missive. [Nov 2016, p.86]

Title: Afraid of Heights
Review: Afraid Of Heights sounds bigger and more ambitious than anything Nathan Williams’ former backyard solo project has ever recorded.

Title: Lover
Review: Even the bright spots in the album’s composition—the off-beat piano cascades in “Death By A Thousand Cuts” and the pulsating synth of “Cruel Summer” (thank you, St. Vincent) are particular standouts—are overshadowed by the musical anticlimax on most tracks, especially on “The Archer.”

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Sometimes I Sit and Think is in conversation with the likes of Marvin the Album and “Supernova,” Brighten the Corners and “Malibu,” Mellow Gold and “About a Girl.” The dream of the 90s is alive in Courtney Barnett. And with Sometimes I Sit and Think, it’s just been fully realized.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Stimulating dance music with infectious grooves. [#7]

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: The music doesn't impress much, serving as more a backdrop for Morrissey's lovely chops.

Title: Man-Made
Review: Ultimately, the album is weighed down by its very gentleness. [30 Apr 2005, p.64]

Title: Not Too Late
Review: Its ragged, unfinished nature illustrates that she's more interested in pursuing her art than recycling Come Away with Me, and if this third album isn't as satisfying as that debut, it nevertheless is a welcome transitional effort that proves her artistic heart is in the right place.

Title: Cuz I Love You
Review: There's nothing wrong with Lizzo's so-called "genreless," agenda-forward sound (nor did Pitchfork claim that there was, and I'm not one to side with their opinions as a rule), but it does lack a certain cohesion and maturity.

Title: Dose Your Dreams
Review: Dose Your Dreams is a dizzying mix of styles, often within the same song.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: Rooms Filled With Light never dips beneath beguiling. Most of the time it's really quite grand.

Title: Glow
Review: Compared to Fourgeaud’s 2005 debut, Smash, there’s a new clarity within the arrangements. Clarity that allows the album’s inspirations to excessively bleed through a disorienting IDM facade.

Title: Songs for the Deaf
Review: [The opening] quartet of tunes blows the band's wad, leaving the rest of the album scattered with only moderately cool mid- tempo metal, all of it delivered with gusto but not enough serious hooks to make anything stand out.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: For a handful of decent Morrissey songs – and, it must be said, some of his best ever vocal performances – we should be grateful. Ultimately though, for all these tantalising reminders of greatness, "You Are The Quarry" still feels like a man unnecessarily trapped by the limitations of his band and the extent of his loathing.

Title: Jet Plane and Oxbow
Review: Coming in at just over 50 minutes, it's the band's most streamlined collection of music since 2008's career-defining Rook, and their most vital offering to date.

Title: Noctourniquet
Review: It's a mess--not without some tidy bits--but what's better: these songs could be the death throes, finally, of these guys' unfettered id.

Title: Interpretations: The British Rock Songbook
Review: As promised, the disc is a journey through vintage British rock, but her simmering, brooding John cover shows just how freely she’s chosen to adapt some of the most famous songs in the pop canon. That liberty is well taken.

Title: Noctourniquet
Review: There are so many ideas battling it out here it takes numerous listens to make sense of it, but persevere and this is perhaps their strongest set to date. [Apr 2012, p.101]

Title: Engravings
Review: If Dagger Paths was a revelation, Engravings is a refinement, long to arrive but worth the wait.

Title: Long Trip Alone
Review: There’s no edge. No innovation. No energy. And precious few genuine hooks.

Title: This Is My Hand
Review: This Is My Hand should see her join him, her other collaborators and St Vincent in the US experimental pop pantheon.

Title: The Less You Know the Better
Review: Overall it sounds like the work of a man struggling to recall his motivations for making music in the first place.

Title: Fantasies
Review: Fantasies has solid musicianship, simple yet poetic and meaningful lyrics, a myriad of melodies, and hooks that are memorable and exciting.

Title: Unknown Rooms: A Collection of Acoustic Songs
Review: Unknown Rooms is entirely built on pure rests and negative space, the nerve-racking space of silence. Everything on the album sounds and feels distant, as if the sounds are emanating from the other end of a dark eternal hallway.

Title: Unreal
Review: Their [Daniel Blumberg and Neil Hagerty's] collaboration resulted in an album  that requires close attention to find the golden details hidden in its crevices. [Aug 2013, p.88]

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: Some thrills and spills, then--like West Ham--and the first fifteen minutes are as good as you could hope for from a band coming back to life after an extended period on the sidelines.

Title: El Pintor
Review: If the songs blend together a bit, that's called a style, and Interpol have always had that on their side. [Oct 2014, p.100]

Title: The Weight's on the Wheels
Review: Most of these songs are not quite up to Hart's usual caliber. His inherent charms are hard to deny; they just feel slightly threadbare this time out.

Title: Who Needs Who
Review: Art-pop triumph "Tell Me" puts it all over the top as the zenith of Triple D's young career. That's something to be optimistic about.

Title: Free
Review: Free is easily Iggy's most ambitiously left-field album since Zombie Birdhouse in 1982. [Oct 2019, p.90]

Title: Thank Me Later
Review: With its laid-back atmosphere and relevant lyricism, Thank Me Later  is a hip-hop album that successfully balances commercialism with art.

Title: Heligoland
Review: “Heligoland” comes across as an anthology rather than an album. It’s a dour collection of concepts and strategies — some successful — as Massive Attack ponders what to do after trip-hop.

Title: My Head Is an Animal
Review: On cutesy likes of "King And Lionheart," they're closer in spirit to the plague of emoters loosed upon the world by the success of Mumford & Sons. [Sep 2012, p.81]

Title: Hello Everything
Review: The sheer size of Hello Everything's scope dictates it's a bit of a sprawling beast, more a collection of moments than a cohesive record. Nonetheless, it's a consistently enthralling listen.

Title: Playland
Review: Marr’s singing is nice enough (check ''The Trap''). His most compelling voice, inevitably, remains his guitar.

Title: Big Wheel and Others
Review: Aside from the nine-minute rambling of “Everything Has to Be Just-so,” (coming at the end of the first disc, making it easy to skip), McCombs pulls off the rare feat of a double-disc that never runs short on inspiration or steam.

Title: Mars
Review: Although he's using sounds and influences from many of the musical hubs on the Earth, from Africa to America and plenty in between, with them he has created aural scenery that is so serene and heavenly that it couldn't possibly exist on our busy and frantic planet.

Title: Punk & Poetry
Review: At its finest, this album is indecently exciting. [16 Apr 2011, p.50]

Title: Trans-Continental Hustle
Review: Trans-Continental Hustle is an honest effort, but one that pales a little when compared to the Technicolor explosions of Gogol Bordello's back catalog.

Title: Banga
Review: At 65 [Smith] presents herself unburdened by age. She identifies on this album with voyagers, adventurers and her fellow artists; she's still determined to explore.

Title: Pink City
Review: Throw in some elegant, economical strings arranged by Owen Pallett and touches of harmonica, vibraphone and sax and you’ve got the best 32 minutes of music you’ll hear anytime soon.

Title: Find The Sun
Review: The trajectory remains far-out, each track a space station on Deradoorian's exhilarating trip. [Jul 2020, p.106]

Title: All Melody
Review: All Melody is remarkably well-rounded. It's not a techno album, it's not a classical album and it's not an ambient album, but it at times resembles all three.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: It might share some sonic similarities [to Sea Change], but it's an altogether brighter beast, built by an older, wiser soul who seems to have been taking a few years to work out exactly where he wants to be as an artist.

Title: Viola Beach
Review: The Warrington quartet was clearly in the process of defining their own sound.

Title: Songs
Review: With its 12 hushed and intimate tracks stripped back to the bare essentials--often just Fullbright's voice and guitar--the emphasis is on the strength of the songwriting (and, on Write a Song, the process itself).

Title: Disco Volador
Review: These kids know exactly what they want to do and they have the skills and imagination to make it work like an improbable magic trick. Which is what a band needs to beat the sophomore slump as decisively as they do here.

Title: Lil Durk 2X
Review: As Durk grapples with leaving his old life behind to create a better life for his sons, he creates his most gratifying and moving work yet. Lil Dirk 2X seeks rehabilitation but finds evolution.

Title: Dark Horse
Review: The addition of superstar producer Robert John "Mutt" Lange to the mix ensures that everything here is as radio friendly and mainstream minded as heavy guitar rock gets.

Title: Eternal Forward Motion
Review: While Eternal Forward Motion is most definitely a record that sounds like it would spit in your face before punching you, this isn’t simply moping around. These lyrics have a very real meaning, written for the voiceless millions of disenfranchised youths, growing up into a shitshow of someone else’s making.  [11 May 2019, p.53]

Title: Entanglement
Review: [A] neoclassical treat. [May 2015, p.78]

Title: A Moving Picture
Review: Ensconced in the current UK hip-hop trend of being both depressing and cheesy, 23-year-old James Devlin raps about weapons, swine flu and diabetes.

Title: Event II
Review: Deltron veterans will get the most out of this return, as their cherished classic goes from secret to high-profile, all while keeping the legacy intact.

Title: Somebody's Knocking
Review: The feelings of isolation that Lanegan has channeled into his music and lyrics are beautifully served by the influences that he’s using, and the result is an album that feels both current and historical. Most importantly, it’s another absolute masterclass crammed with songs that drill their way into your head and stay there.

Title: Lights and Sounds
Review: A strong effort that trades sunny-sounding rockers and breakup songs for weightier concerns of war and family, "Lights" conveys that maturity without seeming strained. [28 Jan 2006]

Title: Time To Go Home
Review: There isn't quite as much gleeful taboo-baiting on this second set, as they dig further and harder into the absurdity of being a young woman in America, and still make it catchy and fun as well as angry and melancholy. [Jun 2015, p.93]

Title: Lost in Space
Review: Michael Lockwood's production occasionally affects a sound akin to a Vonda Sheppard reared on black dreams and Russian literature. [Oct 2002, p.98]

Title: Charlene
Review: Tweet’s songwriting on Charlene is profound enough for us to feel something but doesn’t go over the top with wild emotions.

Title: Marigolden
Review: Sometimes, More is more. [Nov 2014, p.73]

Title: Shadows
Review: On Man Made, Teenage Fanclub seemed to be suffering a sort of rock'n'roll midlife crisis. Five years later, Shadows finds them at ease once again.

Title: Crush Songs
Review: It's lo-fi simplicity makes for a welcome addition to any CoCoRosie fan's collection. [Oct 2014, p.101]

Title: Devotion
Review: The middle section may lean a little too heavily on balladry, but if you're looking for 2012's most sophisticated pop star, you may just have found her.

Title: The Brutalist Bricks
Review: Although it may not be a punk album through and through, songs like "The Stick" and "Where Was My Brain?" embody the genre's spirit with pounding drums, frenzied guitars and rushed deliveries (the former cut clocks in at less than two minutes), while "Mourning in America" mixes the genre's chaotic arrangements and political bite with Leo's usual power-pop flare.

Title: The Carpenter
Review: The Avetts are clearly happiest when they're miserable. Which is fine, if you're in that kind of mood.

Title: Shiver
Review: Given Jónsi’s past solo releases and Sigur Rós’s discography, Shiver should have been much better than it turned out. While not a complete trainwreck, it disappointingly features a minimum of the signature greatness listeners have come to expect.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: A pronounced feeling of descent pervades Turn Blue.

Title: All Or Nothing
Review: All or Nothing is undeniably impressive, but at the cost of some of the heart that's as vital to Shopping's music as their brilliant interplay.

Title: Shine a Light
Review: An album ragged with last-ditch lunges of fuzz-noise and burnished vocals. [Feb 2004, p.99]

Title: Ultravisitor
Review: Repeated listens propel it towards sounding like his best yet.

Title: Hurry Up, We're Dreaming
Review: Hurry Up, We're Dreaming may have its flaws, but minor niggles aside it is a testament to the fine songwriting skill of Gonzalez.

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: It is not deserving of a Hurley-level bashing, and it’s too aware to be Pinkerton. It’s an album they could have made 10 years ago, but it’s also one that feels moderately current.

Title: Wild Things
Review: Wild Things is as likeable as it is cutting edge. [Aug 2016, p.113]

Title: Parastrophics
Review: It suffers from the problem that comes from trying to sustain that moment of pure ecstasy: it's incredibly fun, but after awhile it becomes exhausting.

Title: The Nothing
Review: Korn have always excelled at pain, but with The Nothing, this is the most authentic it's ever been.

Title: Seefeel
Review: The crashing waves of "O-OnOne" immediately align the new-look Seefeel with the aggressive ambiance of Oneohtrix Point Never and Emeralds, while "Airless," Peacock's serene vocals are assailed by coarse filter sweeps and the squeals of busted circuitry. [Mar 2011, p.99]

Title: Jassbusters
Review: Jassbusters has enough chops to pull off the kind of slick 70's MOR soft rock that seems to be Mockasin's bailiwick, but as a whole, there's just not a lot to these songs to keep things consistently interesting, and the album comes off as more of an indulgent lark in Mockasin's growing canon.

Title: American V: A Hundred Highways
Review: The dignity and sharp poetic instincts on American V are all classic Cash. [Aug 2006, p.89]

Title: Gang of Losers
Review: The Dears sound like a band who have finessed their vision and are ready, finally, to take on the world.

Title: Cobra Juicy
Review: Cobra Juicy drips with the group's trademark heady synthesizers, as well as infectious hooks and punchy electronica to craft their most melodic and accessible record to date.

Title: Ecstasy
Review: Signature oh-so-mellow, mumblin' beat, only this time with just too much remove and far too little energy to make it work.

Title: Gung Ho
Review: On Gung Ho-- much like 1996's Gone Again and 1999's Peace and Noise-- Patti and the band aren't exactly bad, but they hardly rock like they did back in '77.... when you listen to Gung Ho and forget about myth, legacy, mystique and all that crap, you have to wonder-- does Patti Smith really matter anymore?

Title: DOVE
Review: One might reasonably expect that a more mature edition of Belly would seem less fiery than what they delivered back in the day, and the craft of this album is all one could hope for, but there's a bit too much drift and not enough clear focus for Dove to qualify as a true return to form.

Title: From Kinshasa
Review: It could so easily have turned into a mess, but Mbongwana Star have made probably the most consistently listenable album to emerge from Kinshasa's rapidly evolving new genre.

Title: Pollinator
Review: Two or three weaker numbers drag quality levels down, but Pollinator contains enough vintage Blondie spirit to get the old juices flowing again.

Title: KIN
Review: What gives KIN its weight is Tunstall's craft. Invisible Empire/Crescent Moon proved that she could turn inward and be gripping but by turning that aesthetic inside out—this is an album about embracing the outside world--she's every bit as compelling.

Title: Kairos
Review: Casey Dienel and partner Shawn Creeden have created something that has a sense of the familiar yet also a simultaneous feeling of fresh investigation, a record with frequent moments of measured and finely balanced beauty but also a restive application of shifting textures to create a nuanced patchwork of sounds that keep their piquant flavour with repetitive listening.

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: While Watch the Throne is ultimately a minor entry in their canons, it's still a terrific snapshot of the friendship that has ended up defining mainstream rap.

Title: Ultimate Care II
Review: Ambitious yet oddly affecting, wash day need never sound the same again. [Apr 2016, p.111]

Title: Good Intentions
Review: Good Intentions is redeemed slightly by its incrementally improved production choices and impressive list of guest artists. The strongest songs on the lengthy album are those when NAV's juvenile lyrics and generic performances are enlivened by more talented artists dropping in to collaborate.

Title: The Russian Wilds
Review: The Russian Wilds captures the magic of on-stage jamming.

Title: The Last Word
Review: With The Last Word, The O'Jays end their legendary career on a peak.

Title: Better Luck Next Life
Review: Despite its psych-rock influences, the duo doesn't rely on a variety of instruments to convey the mood. Instead, the band doubles down on reverb, feedback, haunting vocals and doom guitar.

Title: A Grand Don't Come For Free
Review: Isn't likely to convert, say, your average Jay-Z fan.... Yet it works, and even seems refreshingly exotic. [21 May 2004, p.77]

Title: All You Need Is Now
Review: All You Need Is Now isn't Son of Rio, but it's the best album Duran Duran has released since then, a collection that manages what their best material always has, blending art with grand gestures and popcraft.

Title: The Cost
Review: The album is sophisticated and layered with deft orchestration. And yet, the band's songwriting and delivery display an earnestness and lack of pretension that's pure rock.

Title: Lost Horizons
Review: Simultaneously laid back and bursting with intensity, 'Lost Horizons' is a film score inviting each of us to direct our own personal movie.

Title: California
