Review: California is too long, but has the humour, pace, emotion and huge choruses of a classic Blink record. Mission accomplished.

Title: Blade of the Ronin
Review: Blade of the Ronin is a modest, dignified return for one of underground hip-hop fans’ long lost favorites. It won’t be a memorable record, but for fans who have waited this long for something new, it provides.

Title: Cala
Review: A fine piece of work from a criminally-underrated talent.

Title: Confessions of a Romance Novelist
Review: Lovingly co-produced with Paul (Mansun) Draper, Davies is on startling form throughout, layering spellbinding vocal harmonies and turning her hand to a long list of instruments with names few will even recognise.

Title: We Disappear
Review: The production, courtesy of former Death Cab For Cutie member Chris Walla, makes these songs, basked in an ambient wash, still feel wholly accessible.

Title: awE naturalE
Review: awE naturalE gives us a beguiling glimpse of an unfettered talent that most certainly is promptly, and most satisfactorily, on track.

Title: Strong Feelings
Review: Comparatively standard tunes such as To And Fro prevent Strong Feelings from being an unconditional classic, but that's tantamount to dismissing Toronto's CN Tower as a bit pointy.  [Feb 2014, p.91]

Title: MCIII
Review: Though mostly a one-man affair, he covers a lot of ground across the album's 11 tracks. [Jun 2015, p.86]

Title: The Lion's Roar
Review: A gorgeous, gripping study of English and north American folk music that covers as many of the genre's quirks as it can, without crawling from cliché to catastrophe.

Title: Ascent
Review: Ascent is an album that manages to find the perfect harmony between the normal and the weird, the dirty and the clean, the psychedelic and the straight. Put it in your psych-rock emergency kit. [No.90, p.60]

Title: Groove Denied
Review: Groove Denied is the sound of Malkmus truly untethered, and once you get past the initial jolt of its radical stylistic change, you’ll recognize it for being the great album it is. Don’t let the ascetic nature of the arrangements fool you. Malkmus is trying to blow our minds, and he succeeds spectacularly.

Title: Wise Up Ghost
Review: There are some missteps--the ballad Tripwire feels out of place in the general uptempo pace, and in (She Might Be A) Grenade, Costello lazily compares a girl to an atomic bomb (didn’t Green Day already do this?)--but when the album works, the band and the singer/songwriter sound more invigorated than they have in years.

Title: Love & Devotion
Review: Even when downcast, Love & Devotion is a sensual, lively record and anyone mourning the death of Air France should find much to enjoy here.

Title: Doug Tuttle
Review: It’s an album custom-made for deep headphone listening, and Tuttle and his cohorts pack the stereo field with incident and instrument.

With 7, there’s too little conviction to tell if a full project is something Lil Nas X wants to do. At best, there’s a set of half-considered songs. At worse, you’re left wondering why anyone fussed over Blink-182’s Enema of the State in the first place. ... It's not the work of a star, but a timid upstart. [5 Jul 2019, p.42]

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: Pre-interlude, Bankrupt! is trekking along the right path; it's a futuristic journey into a foreign place for Phoenix, akin to a soundtrack for an updated Lost in Translation. But things quickly go off the rails once it spirals out of the dizzying interlude of flashing synths, losing its sense of melody and purpose.

Title: Restless Spheres
Review: Restless Spheres never settles on one kind of terrain for long, but it exudes the assurance of an artist who has explored a range of styles over time and found his consistency among all of them.

Title: Our Nature
Review: Our Nature ties the song's stories a little closer to earth while allowing the music to dreamily swirl its listener into reverie.

Title: Viet Cong
Review: It's not fair to hold Viet Cong's hype against them, but an album this ordinary points to a generation of indie-rock writers trying, and failing, to pretend the bubble hasn't burst.

Title: Aphrodite
Review: The new set casts a spell with Stuart Price's signature preternatural touches, Minogue's breathy chirp and the hooky melodies of a varied crew of dance pop-focused songwriters and producers.

Title: RTJ4
Review: ‘RTJ4’ is by far Killer Mike and El-P’s most accomplished chapter, wrought with rage but injected with a humour and wisdom that offers razor-sharp clarity and, with that, an unapologetically raw and sobering take on our times.

Title: Unleashed
Review: Sadly, Keith's least-clever disc yet was almost completely written by him for the first time.

Title: A Better Life
Review: A Better Life is an entirely different beast, expanding on their debut’s vigorous garage-pop sound to create something darker, meatier and much heavier on all fronts.

Title: Get Rich or Die Tryin'
Review: More sonically adventurous than its mainstream look suggests.

Title: Tomorrow Will Be Beautiful
Review: The harmonies on Woman of Secret Gold might call to mind Harriet Wheeler of the Sundays to some; the chimes and cello accompaniment on the closing title track leave you wanting more.

Title: In The Spirit World Now
Review: Fusing elementary post-punk with a radio friendly pop sheen, In the Spirit World Now represents Ceremony's most accessible collection of songs to date. Which, depending where you sit on the Richter scale of hardcore to post-punk will undoubtedly divide segments of the band's fanbase.

Title: Rose Golden Doorways
Review: The album sounds like the process of ripping away at one’s own humanity in search of some kind of core; the music is colossal, destructive and all-consuming. ... Extraordinary, turbulent album.

Title: I, Gemini
Review: That a record so dark and ripe with nuance can also harbour such blatant pop sensibility belies the duo’s young age while serving as a testament to their rampant eccentricities.

Title: Beyond The 4th Door
Review: The group demonstrates admirable judgement, gesturing at entropy while craftily dodging its embrace. [Mar 2011, p.58]

Title: Fool's Paradise
Review: where Neuroplasiticy brilliantly built on Cold Specks' debut and breathed life into every track, Fool’s Paradise excels at singular moments and seems to struggle for air and space overall.

Title: Across The Meridian

Title: The Suburbs

Title: Bionic
Review: Sure, her voice remains full, brash, and loud. But ultimately, so much of what passes for hedonism on Bionic feels synthetic and compulsory.

Title: Freedom

Title: (K)no(W)here

Title: Honest

Title: Weighing of the Heart
Review: An album that improves with each listen, with an accomplished, ornate warmth.

Title: Lonerism
Review: This one's a beauty.

Title: Factory Floor
Review: Given the gestation period and polish, the humanity that manages to shine through this tight, crafted record is a triumph; the sound of a band having a whole lot of fun in the hope that ultimately you will do too.

Title: Y Dydd Olaf
Review: At once spooky and playful, romantic and angry. [Sep 2015, p.89]

Review: Though still no barrel of laughs--far from it--there is evidence of green shoots of hope here. [Dec 2016, p.91]

Going in that direction at the same time as their songs go in a much more immediately ingratiating one is a bold move for HEALTH, and here it pays off.

Review: At times the style itself feels like a copy of Rae’s hits instead of an organic creation, but The Chef does a good job of balancing the radio-friendly Rap with material his diehard fans crave.

Review: The thing is, despite the strength of the band (which also includes bassist Todd Sickafoose and guest Ivan Neville), much of the 12-song album feels like filler.

Title: Not Too Late
Review: Norah's most personal collection of songs to date.

Title: Oh Inhuman Spectacle

Title: Algiers
Review: In a similar context many other bands might have run dry by now. Not Calexico though, and 'Algiers' serves as a fitting reminder why they haven't.

Review: Tally this time: two heady club anthems, two B-side-ish vocal numbers, and lotsa bonus beats.

Title: Container

Title: Death Peak
Review: It is as purely individual a statement as the English producer has released yet. Happily, it’s also his most approachable, with the producer sounding more euphoric than he has in a long time.

Title: Evolution
Review: While longtime JLS fans may be satisfied with Evolution, those looking for either a smart reappropriation of sounds from the past or a daring creative leap forward will find themselves at a disappointing dead end.

Title: Rings Around The World

Title: Relax

Title: Out of Season
Review: The icing on the cake is in the little details.

Title: Human Performance

Title: Dear Science
Review: Deep Science should enhance TVOTR's reputation as one of the finest, forward-thinking bands around, along with fellow Brooklyn acts Animal Collective and Liars.

Review: It’s to their huge credit that they have made such an assured and immersive album on their own terms.

Title: Reward
Review: Magnificent and starkly candid new album.

Title: Face Stabber

Title: C'est La Vie
Review: ["Around The Horn"] inflates over a final few minutes into something uniquely epic. ... Lyrically, it's pretty baffling where "These Rocks," one of the albums' standout tracks, is the most openly confessional song Houck has written, set to a churchy musical swell, congregational and healing, the sound of a lifetime burden lifted by love. [Nov 2018, p.28]

Title: A Hundred Days Off
Review: A Hundred Days Off is enjoyably uninspired; it defines both "pleasant" and "unremarkable".

Title: Generation
Review: Generation betrays Audio Bullys' aspirations to say Something Important, undeterred by the absence of either insight or eloquence.

Title: Pick a Bigger Weapon
Review: Some who fondly remember Kill My Landlord or Steal This Album might initially wince at the less-abrasive sonics, but just as Riley's rhymebook includes more of himself than ever, so have his rhythms become more intimate and seductive.

Title: OCD Go Go Go Girls
Review: The songs of OCD Go Go Go Girls stand-up to a certain mood--one, passed a certain age, that's usually buoyant and beer-fuelled.

Title: Civilized
Review: While they are unlikely to blow any heads off, track like 'Graffiti Eyes' show that they haven't lost the knack of writing diverting pop songs. [Sep 2009, p.96]

Title: Black Noise
Review: Black Noise is slightly busier than Pantha du Prince’s sublime “This Bliss” (Dial) from 2007, a pensive, slender and tough album that remains his high-water mark.

Title: Monomania

Title: The Dreaming Room
Review: It's remarkably poised, perfectly calibrated vocal swells evoking the synthetic English pastoral of XTC or Julia Holter's experimental layering. [#361, p.112]

Review: What it isn't--quite--is the magnum opus it could be. The second half loses impetus.

Title: Buffalo
Review: Each to their own. For me, there's nothing here not to like, but even less to love.

Review: 6 Feet Beneath The Moon is an album of mixed emotions, a complex work of focused, driven highs and meandering, confusing lows.

Rather than congesting the listener with frantic Eastern European folk shanties, a poignant nobility and romantic notion of contemporary France permeates its way into your conscience with unbridled zeal.

Title: Dark Night of the Soul
Review: Few contemporary pop albums have spoken to the human condition so eloquently, and given the listener so much pleasure in the process, than Dark Night of the Soul.

Title: Rise Above
Review: This is either one of 2007’s most refreshing or most grating albums, and there’s a hair’s breadth in between. Swerving but creative, Rise Above may wear on repeated listens but still it connects more than it should.

Title: WIXIW
Review: Liars continue to stay delightfully fresh and impressively relevant through every careful reinvention.

Title: Renegades
Review: De la Rocha's rabid diatribes occasionally go overboard, particularly on the tracks (Eric B & Rakim's "Microphone Fiend" and Minor Threat's "In My Eyes," for example) that feed into the band's sometimes one-dimensional rap-metal groove. But when the band steps out of character -- as it does during its rudimentary take on MC5's "Kick Out the Jams" or its pacific reading of "Beautiful World" -- the results can seem truly transcendent.

Title: War Room Stories
Review: War Room Stories encapsulates art rock, tropical pop and various forms of electronica on a varied yet focused set that sounds as though it's not fallen prey to the usual second-album jitters.

Title: Black Boulder
Review: There isn't a bad track on Black Boulder and it is certainly an accessible crossover release that's suited to the long-player format. But it's not very original either.

Title: Natural Rebel
Review: There's nothing rebellious about the music and not much natural, either--but its immaculate anodyne tones are soothing, and that's superficially pleasing, even if it doesn't remotely seem attached to the Richard Ashcroft of lore.

Title: TerraForm
Review: The gambit [space-age sheen and quantised grooves] works on the trippy title track and the confrontational "If You Want It," but elsewhere it robs the band's hyper-rhythmic attack of its viscerally human feel. [Jan 2017, p.28]

Title: Event II
Review: There are a few too many “Get off my lawn, kids” moments, and the interludes are entirely unnecessary (hi, the Lonely Island), but as far as comebacks go, this album is anything but a non-event.

Title: In Your Honor
Review: This is by far their most realized and balanced attack. [#10, p.111]

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: The album's visual, an indie rock show tune on shrooms, but it's just difficult to take seriously hairy men smeared in war paint incoherently singing.

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: Every successful band eventually put out a bloated album, and for Northern Ireland's Snow patrol, it's Fallen Empires. [Feb 2012, p.84]

Title: With You Tonight
Review: Its fuzzy, dream-like patterns and navel-gazing can be hard to interpret, but there is a certain honesty and integrity that underpins the album.

Title: My Heart Has a Wish That You Would Not Go
Review: My Heart Has a Wish That You Would Not Go is an album that could accurately be described as “lush”, “layered”, or “lovely”... an achievement for a band that made its name in noise and cacophony.

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: Danielson's past successes may have been the work of a hundred voices gathering 'round to sing the same joyous song, but the most successful parts of The Best of Gloucester County embrace a different kind of communion altogether. Not just the community of Gloucester County, or New Jersey, or the indie rock or Christian communities, but one of all things.

Title: Defend Yourself
Review: Perhaps that’s the promise of a new familiar way that Sebadoh makes good on with Defend Yourself both thematically and musically, finding something to build on at last, after all the years.

Title: data Panik etcetera
Review: Still splitting opinion. Still weaving rich pop tapestries from whatever fibres take their fancy. They deserved better.

Title: ONoffON
Review: These are the songs of men who haven't changed their political opinions or been influenced by a new album since they disbanded. That sentiment makes OnoffON feel like a lost relic in spots rather than a dynamic new album by an underground legend.

Title: Baby I'm Bored
Review: 'Baby I'm Bored' is the album Dando's fans hoped he would return with.

Title: Home
Review: Home doesn’t successfully balance variety and cohesiveness, and as a result, Home sounds more like a collection of songs than a listening experience that is meant to be heard front to back.

Title: Goodbye Bread
Review: The 23-year-old deals in the kind of one-take, reverb-drenched, sugary psych-pop that mostly sounds effortless and might occasionally be genius. [Aug 2011, p.98]

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: It's a much quieter album than its predecessor, more interested in fingering the tears and rips in its luxurious, ambient textures than Black Up's intergalactic boom-bap. It pulses and shimmers like light bouncing off gold, burnishing Palaceer's radiant visions. [Aug 2014, p.51]

Title: Georgia
Review: Her self-produced Domino debut is an alluring tale of heartbreak and romance, framed by murky electro ballads and scuffed synthwave. [Sep 2015, p.75]

Title: Tassili
Review: There's still plenty to enjoy on Tassilli, but desert blooms fade fast when overwatered. [Sep 2011, p.65]

Title: It's All Around You
Review: For all their sonic salad-tossing, Tortoise can't fade guitarist Jeff Parker, the band's secret weapon and the one dude whose instrument connects them explicitly to their college-radio roots. [May 2004, p.107]

Title: GEMINI
Review: This is the same old Macklemore, stuffing all of his songs with drop-out catchphrases and horn solos and minutes-long American Idol-style belting, all starry-eyed and corny in the same way that, say, the music in a Broadway musical is.

Title: Pull My Hair Back
Review: Ms. Lanza, who is Canadian, moves with purpose and authority in and around the rhythms on this album which, produced by her with Jeremy Greenspan of Junior Boys, in places nods explicitly to Timbaland’s skittish production.

Title: Mystic Familiar
Review: For fans that saw the culmination of his artistic prowess in Gliss Riffer, Mystic Familiar will fulfill many of the same needs, but with even greater balance in execution.

Title: Second Love
Review: She’s more confident, done explaining herself. Moss’ dense paragraphs have been stripped down to just a few words, and the results are more poetry than prose.

Title: Bad Contestant
Review: At times joyful and at others surprisingly moving, Bad Contestant sets Maltese on the start of a path that marks him out as a true prodigious talent.  This is the voice of a true original. The future, it seems, is schmaltz.

Title: I Com
Review: I Com proves that this talented singer/producer is as adept at making her own music as she is playing around with others'.

Title: No Home Record
Review: No Home record offers few tunes you could whistle, but at it's best Gordon's no-wave din and take-no-shit snarl offer unabashedly militant thrills. [Nov 2019, p.87]

Title: All This Sounds Gas
Review: It's so immediately pleasing that the new moves in Stairs' repertoire take a while to sink in. [#32, p.57]

Title: Unguarded
Review: Unguarded is a sophisticated debut, steeped in a chilly, if still insulated atmosphere that strongly evokes '80s-era Kate Bush.

Title: Beauty & Ruin
Review: Beauty & Ruin deftly negotiates Mould’s intended arc, but that doesn’t mean the record is without disappointments.

Title: Eucalyptus
Review: It's hard to imagine the album's latent pacing and fragmented lyrical content piquing the interest of many outside of AnCo's hardcore fanbase, but it stands as a compelling step forward. [No. 145, p.61]

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: This third effort sees the band step into darker territory, blending detuned guitars and Sonic Youth-esque dissonance with infectious pop-punk hooks. [Mar 2012, p. 100]

Title: Elixer
Review: It's about average for albums from Prince proteges.

Title: Songs in A&E
Review: In sick times, with extreme politics on the rise and a fright-wigged bad Tory joke in charge of London, this is an album you can retreat to for succour.

Title: Homesick
Review: Homesick is a rocky album with songs stretching too long for their same-sound focuses.

Title: It's Never Been Like That
Review: It's Never Been Like That has the necessary edge of real art, but it's approachable right down to the final song, "Second To None," with its deep echo and thin lines.

Title: Uptown Special
Review: There’s plenty to enjoy in Uptown Special, even if there are some tracks that end up sounding insubstantial and a bit unsatisfying. If you’re looking for a party album, there are songs on here that will sound fresh for the rest of the year and beyond.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Upon repeated listens, the sorrowful undertow of Everyday Robots becomes a comfort, a balm for moments of alienation; it's the kind of record that when you're lonely, you press play.

Title: Kiss of Death
Review: [A] balanced mix of streetwise, club-ready and bedroom-bumping cuts.

Title: Mark of the Blade
Review: Sequence and flow, moods and styles, all form a coherent whole--albeit one that might have used a tad more judicious editing. But it's hard to fault a band for trying new things, especially when what they deliver is an album with far more hits than misses.

Title: Lost Girls
Review: Yes, nostalgia is a fairly generic formula. But listened to as a whole, the album positively thrums with sonic invention, managing to feel both fresh and full of intrigue. Khan once again demonstrates a knack for uncanny storytelling.

Title: The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book
Review: [A] tighter, indigo-deeper, more vision cohesive joint than its predecessor.

Title: Death of a Bachelor
Review: Ultimately, Death of a Bachelor marks the final transformation of Panic! At the Disco from egalitarian emo band to collaborative pop band headed with singular charisma by Urie the uncontested chairman.

Title: One Day It Will Please Us to Remember Even This
Review: All the reckless abandon the New York Dolls name conjures, the spontaneous handclaps, sloppy guitar-slashing and youthful over-indulgence that made those early Dolls recordings such a kick are sadly nowhere to be found here.

Title: KOD
Review: KOD, his fifth album, has the feel of a casual placeholder between bigger ideas--it has neither the grim purpose or intense emotional acuity of his 2016 LP “4 Your Eyez Only,” nor the cohesion of the prior one, “2014 Forest Hills Drive,” the record that set the terms for his new direction.

Title: Conatus
Review: Rather than radically reinventing the sound from Danilova's second full length, 2010's Stridulum II, Conatus comes across as a more fully-realized Zola Jesus production.

Title: Tragedy & Geometry
Review: Tragedy & Geometry is an emotional, slow-burning, hour-long journey that tests the limits of how captivating an exploration via ambient repetition can be.

Title: Babelsberg
Review: Ten tracks of seemingly upbeat alt-pop, Babelsberg is a record that on the outside appears bright and breezy, bordering almost on the whimsical. Dig deeper however, and it quickly begins to reveal itself as a wryly written document of current social and political climates.

Title: Work
Review: The record is expertly mixed and produced: It brims with fully realized moments, like a synth bit on “Anxious” that conjures the exact feeling of seeing an ex like someone else’s post on Instagram; the portamentos on “Slow Burn” should come with a vertigo warning. But the album’s mood is just sour.

Title: The Messenger
Review: This is a solid, enjoyable solo debut that’s certainly worth investigation if you’re a long-term Marr watcher.

Title: The Gold Album: 18th Dynasty
Review: We have 12 microwave-nuked approximations of Drake songs circa 2013 and Kanye songs spanning from The College Dropout to Yeezus, with none of the wit, soul, or edge.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: The lyrics resonate hard, though, felt most strongly when Rønnenfelt sings with broad expressive shouts.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: Every subtlety comes steeped in retro classicism.

Title: In The Future
Review: If you're not a fan of their weighty retro riffs, Into The Future is not going to sway you; but those who loved their self-titled debut will thrill to the darker, more convincing sounds of former single 'Stormy High' with its Plantish wails and solid Sabbathy riffs.

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: Lacking both the musical and counter-cultural thrill of the Brion recordings, this album turns away from a certain artistic "rawness" in the original recordings, razing away counter-melodies and acoustic decay for a well-polished delivery that presents the photogenic songstress in a more "flattering" light.

Title: Picture Show
Review: Picture Show may not have as much mainstream appeal as a song like "Animals", but it definitely shows a band honed in on creating enjoyable, addicting tracks that seem fresh without losing the hint of the past this album seems thankfully unable to shake.

Title: Lynn Teeter Flower
Review: Throughout, a cutback on shimmery electronic effects results in a lived-in sound; there's a shabby chic-ness to these songs, and also a believability.

Title: Reincarnated
Review: Intentions may have been good, but the result smacks of carpetbagging.

Title: Dip
Review: There are building blocks for something fantastic in most of these pieces, but only in two of them have they been used to make more than the sum of their parts.

Title: Kala
Review: M.I.A., undoubtedly the truest "outsider" to emerge on the pop landscape in ages, has crafted an album that, in its best moments, positions her as an impassioned advocate for the disenfranchised.

Title: The Trouble with Being Myself
Review: Macy's decision to team with [producer Dallas] Austin this time around gives her anarchic brilliance just the right creative counterbalance.

Title: Carrier
Review: There’s still much celebration to be had in Carrier; they just channel it in a way that’s not expected of them.

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: This album lays it on too thick... and declines the thematic burden of "Separation Sunday." As stories, on the other hand, the songs could convince anyone that kids have a hard time.

Title: awE naturalE
Review: Much here mediates around one unnerving groove. [May 2012, p.83]

Title: Rocket Juice & the Moon
Review: Albarn's best work has cheek, wit and a smart-alecky desire to shake things up. All this reverence doesn't really suit him.

Title: Dream River
Review: Here, we hear hints of funk, jazz, Americana and folk--and before you know it, the album’s ingrained itself.

Title: Antics
Review: While this is ultimately a more sophisticated record, it's probably a less obvious one, too. [#7]

Title: Painting
Review: [Painting] loses momentum. [Mar 2013, p.98]

Title: Punisher
Review: It's artfully rumpled, but the ragged angry gasps that close the record confirm Bridgers' songwriting isn't the effortless dream it seems. [Jul 2020, p.78]

Title: In a Dream
Review: In A Dream is brand new, but has the feel of a timeless dance record, the kind of record that is pulled from the crate on the most special (and danceable) of occasions.

Title: Shadow People
Review: The Limiñanas sound like they're too cool and nonchalant to even have a phone, much less use one to make a less than great record.

Title: Rammstein
Review: Rammstein have resurrected to bring us their seventh studio album. And boy is it the record we’ve all been waiting for.

Title: Finally Famous
Review: Finally Famous, which contains a handful of other tracks produced by No I.D. as well as collaborations with the likes of the Neptunes and Wiz Khalifa, is a slick triumph filled with muscular drums and rolling synthesizers.

Title: La Di Da Di
Review: For every urgent tune like the cinematic Non-Violence (whose bass jabs are pretty muscular), there are inspired variations, like the dreamy calm of Cacio e Pepe or the bejewelled hamminess of Megatouch.

Title: Comfort
Review: While not overly original, this album more than compensates for compositional complacency with its energetic delivery.

Title: Certified
Review: Revels in its own vulgarity. [23 Sep 2005, p.87]

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: Cast of Thousands is a great record, beautiful and emotionally powerful as well as musically inventive... a refinement and extension of their vision that will emerge as one of the best records of the year.

Title: Bloodsports
Review: In a way, it’s the most honest collection of songs Anderson’s ever written.

Title: The Book of Souls
Review: An album that wouldn't be out of place if it had come out 30 years ago.

Title: Heavy Is the Head
Review: it consistently hits a sweet spot. It is packed with memorable hooks – singles Vossi Bop and Wiley Freestyle are by some distance the least obviously commercial things here – but never sounds obvious or craven in its desire for chart success.

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: Is Indie Cindy good enough for the Pixies to keep going? Pretty much. [Jun 2014, p.113]

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: Clever and droll but also hypnotic and mysterious.

Title: Soft Commands
Review: Soft pop isn't everyone's favorite genre, and there are those who will find Soft Commands too sweet for comfort Still, even at its most pop-friendly moments, there's enough muscle and intelligence here to keep the album from cloying.

Title: Silesia
Review: Silesia is still a relaxing listen: and all of its intense sound swells still leave you with a feeling of peace.

Title: Hollow Meadows
Review: Worth every second of the wait. [Oct 2015, p.108]

Title: Dirt Farmer
Review: Helm takes material from a variety of sources and makes it all his own.

Title: Still
Review: Put them all together and you've got a drink that goes down hard, with a potent bittersweetness distilled by a master. [No. 122, p.60]

Title: Hell-On
Review: “Sleep All Summer,” which features Archers of Loaf frontman Eric Bachmann brings his harsh vocals to the forefront of the track, which unfortunately make it challenging for Case to standout. But it’s a small flaw in a gorgeously curated record that reveals Case is never really done reinventing herself.

Title: Octahedron
Review: Octahedron is the sound of a band treading water.

Title: Wave
Review: He lets the currents take it where they will, from the churning tumult of The Wave to the cresting, Bon Iver-ish Broken. [Dec 2019, p.113]

Title: Rough and Rowdy Ways
Review: At its heart, this is a serious work, with an underlying somberness. ... Almost 60 years since we first heard from him, the old protest singer is still composing extraordinary anthems for our changing times.

Title: Forth
Review: Forth is classic Verve, epic in scope, with layer upon layer of sound.

Title: The Black Crown
Review: Suicide Silence's third full-length maintains the visceral brutality that has characterized their output, even as it builds upon their unsettling strengths. [Aug 2011, p.120]

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: In the end Just A Souvenir isn't quite as consistent as it could be, but it offers a nice new direction that will likely have a bit more staying power.

Title: Gravez
Review: Gravez is a unified listen whose influences serve Hooded Fang’s greatest strength: infectious hooks.

Title: Lindsey Buckingham / Christine McVie
Review: They’re best when they work together, with the charming simplicity of the island-flavoured “Feel About You” and beach-strolling “Red Sun” contrasting nicely with the tart, twitchy urgency of “Too Far Gone”.

Title: Beat, Surf, Fun
Review: An indie pop masterpiece that's easily one of the best records to come out this year.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: In the end the record comes across as too much of a repeat. [#17, p.84]

Title: Clarity
Review: The outstanding “Clarity” is her first full-length album, full of songs that are stitched so tightly and varnished so brightly that they cease to be mere pastiche and transcend into something utterly new.

Title: We Need Medicine
Review: The Fratellis are quirky, and you almost have to accept that not everything will work to get to the moments of genius.

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: Amid such hi-octane dancefloor tracks such as this, current single 'Ready For The Floor' is, in context, pedestrian--its uncomfortable resemblance to Russ Abbot's 'Atmosphere' becoming more apparent with every listen.

Title: Ssss
Review: Ssss is absorbing techno to listen to and proof that well written music outscores clever production tricks any day of the week.

Title: Optometry
Review: After the initial bustle of a few extremely strong tracks, Optometry wanders blindly for far too long.

Title: Burst Apart
Review: As an exercise in maintaining artistic form, it's an indisputable success.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: Exciting as it can be, Boys & Girls could use just a little more shakin' going on.

Title: Amputechture
Review: It seems to prove a cardinal rule about art and ambition; if you paint in too many colors, you end up with mud brown. The Mars Volta could fill up whole galleries with canvases this color, and with Amputechture, have constructed another monochromatic monument to wild, uninhibited excess.

Title: Ishi
Review: Gengras's sublime drones--layers and layers of modular synth--evoke the spectacle and tragic history of his native California's wilderness. [Jun 2014, p.62]

Title: So It Goes
Review: On the whole, So It Goes covers a wide range of ground musically, sometimes making it hard to comprehend as a cohesive piece in its entirety. By doing so however, Ratking has made a rap album that is truly fitting for the modern New York.

Title: Loop the Loop
Review: Jenkins conveys his obsession with sound beautifully. [Apr 2016, p.71]

Title: Over and Even
Review: Subtlety and simplicity also define this set of acoustic songs. But like the verse, the terms understate the power and beauty of the subject at hand.

Title: I Tell A Fly
Review: Clementine clearly has things to say about some important topics, and it’s hard not to think they might reach a wider audience if they were a little less obliquely presented. Equally, there’s something laudable about an artist using their initial success not as a foundation for steady commercial growth but as leverage to get something like I Tell a Fly released and promoted by a major label.

Title: All the Beauty in This Whole Life
Review: It’s both sharp-tongued and warm hearted, an LP-length memoir that dabbles in political manifesto. But it comes over like an album Ali made for himself, and he sounds better off because of it.

Title: Mariachi El Bronx (II)
Review: As soulful and finely crafted as their debut of sorts, II is a glorious record.

Title: Hit Reset
Review: Hit Reset is a deliciously rowdy work in which Hanna flames negligent friends, cyber-bullies and idiotic lovers. [Aug 2016, p.77]

Title: Myopia
Review: These songs are obscured like frosted glass, as meticulously pretty and faintly unnerving as a porcelain doll. Though the album ends almost as quietly as it began, Obel’s whispery ambient fog lingers far longer.

Title: O
Review: Their third LP reveal a sweary rock toughness that suits them (surprisingly) well. [Nov 2008, p.120]

Title: Is This It
Review: The Strokes are not deities. Nor are they "brilliant," "awe-inspiring," or "genius." They're a rock band, plain and simple. And if you go into this record expecting nothing more than that, you'll probably be pretty pleased.

Title: Honest
Review: By all accounts, Honest reveals that Future's music was never a "right place, right time" story, but one that's unique and has staying power.

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: Although there is much to like about the album, it can be difficult to differentiate one from another.

Title: Factory Floor
Review: Whether it's the muffled, unsettling synths that peer out from underneath the groove, the mannered and highly potent collision of seemingly incongruous drum patterns, or simply the masterful arrangement, it all adds up to make a record that's difficult to second-guess and lots of fun to unpack.

Title: You Could Have It So Much Better
Review: The trick is to cede the idea that Franz Ferdinand are meant to deliver the cohesive, moving, traditional Statement Albums their debut may have misled listeners to expect. Some people-- earnest people, like Bloc Party, Sufjan Stevens, and the Arcade Fire-- will go on trying to fill that niche. Franz Ferdinand, though, aren't going to do that, and good on them: We can only hope they'll go on offering us cheeky, energetic surprises.

Title: Dirt Farmer
Review: Helm’s voice is still poignant even if it’s nowhere near as strong as it once was.

Title: Megaplex
Review: It takes from every era of the duo and amalgamates it in such a way that you it never feels forced or out of place. While we may miss those cutting riffs, they do more than enough to satisfy our thirst.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Belong
Review: The transition is subtle - the reconstituted tracks of Belong remain vehicles for near-perfect pop melodies, gentle self-deprecation, and wistful sentiments

Title: Wallpaper for the Soul
Review: Easy listening has never been this painful. [#57, p.106]

Title: Feature Magnetic
Review: Unfortunately, Keith is treated to some friendly fire here, as most of his cohorts outshine him.

Title: Detroit House Guests
Review: Adult succeeds here in crafting an unsettling musical experience--across which the familiar is recast in an uncanny new light--that's hell bent on subverting our beliefs.

Title: Royal Blood
Review: Even with a debut album, their ascent has been so steep the opening salvo feels like a premature greatest hits.

Title: Meet Glen Campbell
Review: The initially spectacular '60s orchestration eventually begins to wear, but the Witchita Lineman does imbue already good tracks like Tom Petty's 'Walls' and Travis' 'sing' with a genuine sense of grandeur. [22/29 Aug 2008, p.122]

Title: Ultra Mono
Review: This record fuses the first album’s goofy sense of humour with ‘Joy…’’s brazen manifesto for a healthier society. Despite their imperfections and the often justified criticism, IDLES are ultimately a good thing. The band want to take you on a trip and for you to enjoy the ride, and for the destination to be serene. Hold on tight.

Title: Totale Nite
Review: On Totale Nite, they manage to use small-scale elements--jangling guitars, cheapo drum machines, toy keyboards--to project the urgency of bands with louder screams and bigger amps.

Title: What The Dead Men Say
Review: All are multi-layered, offering moments of both beautiful intimacy and blazing rage. For most bands, attempting this juxtaposition would be disastrous, but here it sounds sublime, seamless.

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: The Take Off is not all that remarkable the first few times around, but it nonetheless hints at rewarding repeat visits. [No. 108, p.55]

Title: Sprinter
Review: Although Sprinter is a singular vision, it won't help rid her of the PJ Harvey comparisons, proving Torres to be musician unafraid of comparison, but even less afraid of compromise.

Title: Beautiful Dreamers
Review: The least idiom-specific tracks like those, diverted from familiar song-shapes, are the most eloquent--but Frisell would find it hard to do anything unmusical if he tried.

Title: 12 Desperate Straight Lines
Review: There are throwaways, but 12 Desperate Straight Lines moves Telekinesis in the right direction.

Title: Fair Ain't Fair
Review: The pop textures are more evident, the melodies are more hook-laden, and the overall vibe is more laid-back than past releases, varying in moods from positively gleeful to terribly melancholy.

Title: Shapeshifting
Review: On Shapeshifting, their first album for Paper Bag Records, Young Galaxy have found a sound that lives up to McCandless's compelling voice (it seems Ramsay has been reduced to a secondary role, save for opener "The Angels Are Surely Weeping"), and it provides an overall sensation very unlike their first two attempts.

Title: Zebra
Review: It is truly cosmic music, one that defies categorisation.

Title: Stills
Review: Stills explores its feelings of hurt and misgiving more deftly with its music than with its lyrics; if you’re sick of Dick and Barry types, the darkly-focused new wave avant-pop of Stills can still offer its rewards.

Title: Be
Review: Be won’t win many points for daring, but in terms of user-friendly hip-hop charged by a refreshingly positive undercurrent, it more than hits its hard-to-miss mark.

Title: Good Apollo, I'm Burning Star IV, Volume Two: No World for Tomorrow
Review: There's even hit-single potential--'Feathers' is unabashed radio-rock--that could make this weird bunch into the biggest cult band in the world. [Dec 2007, p.109]

Title: Resolution
Review: The Richmond quintet's usual uniformity of sound, production, and performance strikes many like a concrete dam, and Resolution takes 10-15 minutes too long to resolve, but there's no arguing with a rabid dog called "Cheated."

Title: White Men Are Black Men Too
Review: It’s chaos, the most extreme kind of hybrid imaginable. With that freedom, they sound more excitable and progressive than ever, like they’re chasing a pot of gold that contains endless truths.

Title: Infiniheart
Review: Contains some of this year's most original and moving songwriting, and displays a breathtaking virtuosity and inventiveness on the part of its creator.

Title: Pale Green Ghosts
Review: The risk pays off.

Title: Olympic Girls
Review: There’s so much room for everything to breath and flourish. Olympic Girls takes it slow, and we’re given the perfect chance for reflection through the mid-tempo bliss.

Title: Are We There
Review: Van Etten tackles heartache with refreshing sharpness, distilling complex sentiments into something beautifully simple.

Title: Staind
Review: You don't really hear that stylistic growth, though, on this slab of down-tuned chug-and-glug, which finds the band returning to the grim recriminations of early tunes like "Mudshovel" and "Suffocate."

Title: Holy Spring
Review: On Holy Spring he expands the minimalist palette of his debut Distant Early Warning. [Jun 2019, p.34]

Title: Endlessly
Review: Cool and clever without being contrived, this is sharp, commercially astute pop music that ebbs and flows to the rhythm of a very human pulse. [Jan 2011, p.84]

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: A few tracks (the fuzzy 'Fistful of Tears') miss the mark, but this is the necessary R&B return from one of our great--and seemingly lost--soulmen.

Title: Trust
Review: Much of 'Trust' dallies down the dark end of the street, where graceful Velvet Undergroundisms lounge around sharing tabs with gentle folk implosions.

Title: Too Many Voices
Review: Like his peers and predecessors, he utilized vocals to elevate his shuddering half-time low-end above mere physical and intellectual impact--and into the listener’s emotional realm. One listen into Stott’s roomy fourth LP, Too Many Voices, and it’s clear that’s exactly what he’s going for.

Title: No No No
Review: While pleasant in places, there’s a lack of drive about Zach Condon’s latest outing as Beirut.

Title: Nighttime Stories
Review: Nighttime Stories is a solid record from a unique band. Heavy metal is a genre born on riffs, and Pelican has those in spades. Purely instrumental records may be difficult to pull off, but Pelican has more than enough brains and brawn to show how well it can be done.

Title: Maximum Balloon
