Title: Me
Review: Me is a brilliantly confident album that fulfills--and builds upon--Rodriguez’s early promise. Recommended.

Title: Common Era
Review: The presence of familiar things makes their music go down easier this time around, but it remains a challenge, even after many listens, to feel like you understand what you're supposed to feel.

Title: Endless Now
Review: Male Bonding have stayed on course, but their sound remains as virile as it was.

Title: Love Is Overtaking Me
Review: Once you make the adjustment and accept these songs for what they are, ther are moments of loveliness. But for the most part, one can onlyy wonder what attracted Russell to indulge in this sort of stuff given his more renowned output. [Nov 2008, p.68]

Title: Christs, Redeemers
Review: The experience of listening to the album is a harrowing one, but the bevy of unexpected shifts, sidesteps, and complete submission into patches of noise makes it one of the more adventurous metal records of its type, and speaks to the long-fought amounts of work and thought the Body have put into their ever brutal, ever forward-looking sound.

Title: Future Breeds
Review: Expertly crafted and passionately played, there are enough hooks on Future Breeds to keep you singing along an new layer of aural insanity to keep discovering with each repeated listen. [Jul 2010, p.122]

Title: Fabulous Muscles
Review: It's exhilarating and rare to hear such bruised raw performances as these. [#242, p.71]

Artist: Laura Jane Grace & The Devouring Mothers
Title: Bought to Rot
Review: Grace doesn’t graduate from punk on Bought To Rot--she expands and elevates it with explicit revelations, fervent melodies, head-banging chord progressions and unruffled tenacity.

Title: I Will Set You Free
Review: Tunes that are both brainy and catchy, full of life.

Title: Homegrown
Review: Hearing these (sometimes very familiar) songs in this particular sequence is a journey, one that winds along a twisted road yet provides an experience as complete as its mid-'70s companion LPs. It's not a footnote but an essential part of Neil Young's catalog.
This experimental concoction Redd delivered is a hit-or-miss.

Title: Compassion
Review: Forest Swords was already becoming quickly respected for his deftness of touch when dealing with both musical and emotional tone. Compassion demonstrates he is very capable of weaving them together until they are intrinsically entwined.

Title: Permo
Review: With Permo, they display a self-starting urgency that keeps them up to speed with the turbulent here and now. [Jan 2018, p.114]

Title: A Different Ship
Review: Here We Go Magic move between more full-on hyperactivity in that vein from songs like "Make Up Your Mind" and "I Believe in Action" to the easier-going grooves of "Alone But Moving," but too often they don't do much with that.

Title: The Lumineers
Review: The general expansiveness of sound on songs like "Ho Hey" make this young group's eponymous debut uniquely American in all the best ways: gritty, determined, soaked in sweat and love and drive. There's nothing precious or affected here, just three dedicated artists opening their hearts.

Title: Tenderness
Review: Country-fuelled it may be, rather than the expected full-pelt rock, but so open is this letter that it easily succeeds in transcending genres. [1 Jun 2019, p.53]

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: On Wonderful, Glorious, Mark Everett not only has the songs but also a band capable of delivering the sort of breadth and depth of response he needs to keep the Eels vehicle moving onwards and upwards.

Title: Tha Carter IV
Review: For the last four years there's been no greater force in hip-hop, but this isn't the way President Carter should be launching his campaign for a second term.

Title: Liberation
Review: It’s a well-calculated offering from a living legend whose abilities are still very much intact.

Title: Possible Dust Clouds
Review: If there’s fun in her music, it’s somewhere between the anaesthetising effect of especially her more electric noises and the ecstatic release in her vocal, both too honest to be anything else but awkward. Fundamentally sociopathic. [Nov 2018, p.55]

Title: Preliminaires
Review: Iggy sings ballads. In French. With clarinet solos. He also dabbles in Dixieland jazz, spoken word, and chilled electro-lounge music on his 15th solo album. If that sounds hideous, or hilarious, it's actually a little bit of both.

Title: Twist Again
Review: It's a wonderful return for the much-underappreciated band.

Title: Super Extra Gravity
Review: Not quite as beautifully forlorn as 2003's Long Gone Before Daylight. [Nov 2005, p.123]

Title: The Past We Leave Behind
Review: The intensity rises and falls with the rolling hills, but the vistas remain the same, and the horizon never gets any closer. Despite the uniformity, there are clear highlights.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: Plastic Beach is a full blown hip-hop/trip-hop album and a prime example of how to stray away from one genre to dominate another. If Albarn has done anything with this project, he has shown his knowledge of flawless production and the ability to create aesthetically pleasing tunes.

Title: Venus On Earth
Review: The band itself is top notch here.

Title: Edgeland
Review: Mellow, abstract, and alluring, this worthwhile journey also offers Underworld fans a clear picture of Hyde's artistic contribution to the group.

Title: Just to Feel Anything
Review: There's real drama in the band's sweeping crescendos and ringing guitar chords; there's something genuinely affecting in their newfound emo overtones.

Title: Jiaolong
Review: Jiaolong may be a perfectly competent incarnation of Snaith's undeniable talents, but it doesn't quite induce the stupor it should.

Title: Stitch of the World
Review: An album that--biography aside--reveals the strength of merging personal vision with cooperative expression.

Title: Solaris
Review: Solaris is like no Photek album you've ever heard before: It's an album that celebrates both dance and relaxation, touching on deep house, trip-hop, and ambient, with (gasp) only one drum-and-bass track (the typically spare "Infinity"). Sentimentality for his musical roots and the desire to create music with a warmer, more human feel drive Photek on these 11 disparate tracks, and the outcome is mixed.

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: Though the album grows stronger as it lurches on, the trio's pursuit of bombast leaves the killer melodies lost in outer space.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: IX
Review: It at least proves that Trail of Dead are by no means a spent creative force, but they’re going to have to try harder to recapture the genuinely visceral energy of their classic records if they’re ever going to reach beyond their own fanbase again.

Title: Together
Review: Together is a good album that is catchy and full of hooks and does a lot of what we've come to expect from the band. Having said that, it's also a step down.

Title: Wretched and Divine: The Story of the Wild Ones
Review: It's like BVB's other output in that it's not perfect, but the high points are still pretty damn high.

Title: Godfather Buried Alive
Review: Shyne's Tupac-esque reflections on honor and mortality are penetrating, and suggest there are greater meditations yet to be unleashed. [20/27 Aug 2004, p.126]

Title: Up All Night
Review: Moore spends much of his debut album, Up All Night, outlining the pleasures to be had from hot women and cold beverages.

Title: The Drums
Review: What The Drums lack in originality and authenticity they make up for with some of the purest moments of fun and summertime joy this side of the next Eighties revival.

Title: Free So Free
Review: It's hard to see how much satisfaction this laconic talent must gain from fiddling with a formula he perfected in 1987. [Nov 2002, p.114]

Title: I Told You I Was Freaky
Review: It’s antithetical to quibble over issues of originality and cohesion when dealing with song parody, anyway; even when resting on their laurels, the Conchords have a singular ability to pen a damn funny song.

Title: Late Night Feelings
Review: Overall, this is one of Ronson's best works--a complete pop album.

Title: Skin
Review: Skin is the sound of Flume reaching for great heights and almost grasping what he seeks there.

Title: I Am All Your Own
Review: His songs are still gauzy and intangible, the breathy vocals offering lyrical wisps that only hint at turbulent emotions. [Aug 2015, p.58]

Title: American Dream
Review: It’s a beautifully produced, masterfully realized album, but it’s also a bit of a downer and an unusually slow burn.

Title: Excerpts
Review: While it brandishes a certain kind of insular brilliance, it's music more ripe for conversation or think pieces than headphones or the living room hi-fi.

Title: Quazarz: Born on a Gangster Star
Review: As you work your way through the new material, it becomes apparent rather quickly that Shabazz Palaces have elevated their jazz-damaged phrasing into a unique musical language. Butler, of course, responds to the music with idiosyncratic lyrics to match. ... Gangster Star leans towards a funkier, more upbeat mood.

Title: Caveman
Review: Their new self-titled album is both more refined and more expansive.

Title: The Sea
Review: It's to Bailey Rae's credit that never for one second does the album feel exploitative or mawkish, just truthful and real. [Mar 2010, p.94]

Title: How The West Was Won
Review: A consummately composed lesson in narrative songcraft, which tugs on the heartstrings as it sails into the sunset with Take Me Home. [Aug 2017, p.86]

Title: Goodness
Review: You don’t have to be a fan of punk music or emo to be a fan of The Hotelier, you simply have to appreciate genuine, earnest emotion.

Title: Integrity Blues
Review: At its worst, it's tired and turgid, but neither is it hopeless or without hope. [Dec 2016, p.109]

Title: Moody, Standard and Poor
Review: Dave Grohl is a veteran -- the world does not need another record from him. The world needs Obits.

Title: Turkey
Review: Turkey is less throwaway than its scrappy, Bandcamp-released predecessors. [Oct 2015, p.78]

Title: Complicated Game
Review: It’s an album that shows again and again that very few songwriters on this planet illuminate the oft-unfair rules of this game or the inner workings of the players quite like he can.

Title: Repave
Review: Volcano Choir puts Mr. Vernon’s voice and words up front and builds something like songs around them, often with crescendos marching toward full-scale choruses--enough to make the often inscrutable lyrics sound passionate enough to be worth puzzling out.

Title: Darkel
Review: Sometimes Darkel seems in danger of floating away on its flights of fancy, suggesting that Godin gives some of Dunckel's more whimsical ideas some grounding when they work together as Air. Nevertheless, this is a lovely working holiday, full of songs as shimmery and delicate as bubbles, and their slightness doesn't make them any less enjoyable.

Title: Hello Young Lovers
Review: A sweetly brain-scrambling experience. [Apr 2006, p.114]

Title: Surf
Review: Surf integrates a mish-mash of sounds, genres and guests into a relatively coherent whole, textured and nuanced in ways that demand repeat listens.

Title: I Get Wet
Review: There's no denying the over-the-top whomp of his music, the loudest and funniest metal you've heard in ages.

Title: Those the Brokes
Review: Many songs here are too long and similar in tone to the band's ubiquitous debut. But given time, the moments of real magic peek through.

Title: I Am Easy to Find
Review: Where once they relied on builds with big payouts, the soundscapes conjured on I Am Easy to Find harness restraint so effectively, instead of reveling in the melodies that champion the vocal riches over the intricate layering of guitars, Bryan Devendorf’s iconic rhythms and the space between everything. Even at 64 minutes, it’s a record that never feels bloated.

Title: A Certain Feeling
Review: As all over the map as A Certain Feeling is, it’s much more concise than the band’s 13-track debut, "Ears Will Pop & Eyes Will Blink." There’s not much extraneous fluff here.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: Outside the beats, the other surprise of Kamikaze is Twista's more worldly and thoughtful subject matter. [Mar 2004, p.184]

Title: Compton: A Soundtrack by Dr. Dre
Review: He seems to have found a new and more sincere voice, less bullish than we have heard him before, whilst using a fantastic roster of contributors to push the mood and narrative.

Title: Our Pathetic Age
Review: Its instrumental first disc a foreboding seas of sputtering synths, dislocated drums and disorienting ideas. Yet rare moments of beauty peak through. ... A similar wilful primitivism pervades disc two. [Dec 2019, p.95]

Title: Semicircle
Review: Cumulatively, the brassy blare and breakbeats are like Dayglo plasticine, now merging into an paterfamilias brown ball. [Feb 2018, p.27]

Title: Common As Light and Love Are Red Valleys of Blood
Review: The themes explored throughout the record’s massive 130-minute runtime are remarkably current--for example the Orlando shootings and the Paris attacks--and it’s these moments where the album commands absolute attention. Not even Kozelek can command it entirely for 130 minutes, though.

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Even if a few experiments fall flat, on the rest of Youth Novels Li is as witty and self-possessed, even if most of her songs brutally document her emotional masochism.

Title: I Forget Where We Were
Review: Howard expects you to meet him on his own terms and provides just enough aural enticement to give him not just one listen but a second, which is when I Forget Where We Were really begins to sink in its hooks.

Title: Model of You
Review: For the most part, Model Of You pushes Cloud Boat out into broader, more turbulent waters.

Title: Abysmal Thoughts
Review: Going it alone might not have been the most obvious next step for Pierce, however he has managed to maintain a catchy and consistent sound that justifies that decision.

Title: Fortuna
Review: Even at its bleakest, Fortuna reveals more colors and emotions at the band's disposal than Antipodes did, and its unsettled songs become oddly comforting and endearing with repeated listening.

Title: Heathen Chemistry
Review: Any good news – Liam’s decent fist of songwriting, the less oppressive sound, the professional playing – is rendered largely irrelevant by the gaping chasm where more decent songs should be.

Title: The Undisputed Truth
Review: With "The Undisputed Truth," Brother Ali improves as a rapper, while sacrificing none of the unique, personal touch that made "Shadows on the Sun" so impressive.

Title: Stay Positive
Review: Considering most of the album is spent describing what life’s like for the rest of us, it’s surprising Stay Positive ends on a relatively self-focused note, courtesy of album highlight “Slapped Actress.”

Title: The Magician's Private Library
Review: The Magician’s Private Library is Miranda’s personal baby but Sitek is the godfather, scavenging through all of the reading material. It’s a sincerely open recording and a true testament to what the human spirit is capable of--even when the odds are against it.

Title: The Ascension
Review: Surpassing the hour mark with some space yet to go, the record provides an expansive canvas for Sufjan to critique the flaws of humanity, at the same time finding room for the inward focus that made his previous offering so compelling.

Title: In Stormy Nights
Review: Difficult. All very difficult. But cheap dates get old quick, don't they?

Title: Sincere
Review: It’s way too often here that everything new and interesting about two-step gets brushed aside for suspiciously lite jazz and limp mixes of dancefloor hits.

Title: Everybody
Review: Everybody might be less than lustrous in their own catalog but tops most group's bests.

Title: Subjective Concepts
Review: Their Northwest hardcore sound may be derivative, but it represents the tendencies of its origins with convincing force, as their unrefined grunge tones and twangs almost make Subjective Concepts feel like an overlooked album from back in the day.

Title: Has Been
Review: It is definitely deserving of the cult status that it will inevitably earn. [Dec 2004, p.138]

Title: Devotion
Review: The arrangements are simple but elevated by deft touches of texture and mood, siphoning into hypnotic minimalism the essence of muted soul, garage, grime, R&B and the shattered club tracks that made the defunct London club Plastic People tremble in the early 2010s.

Title: Harvey Milk
Review: Harvey Milk has been referred to as The Bob Weston Sessions for some time; the remaster given to its ten songs serves to emphasise, rather than undermine, Weston’s keen ear for the dramatically heavy.

Title: Space Zone
Review: This collection by 18-year-old Chicagoan David Davis makes footworking beats accessible. [Dec 2012, p.106]

Title: VII: Sturm Und Drang
Review: VII: Sturm und Drang is the album that almost wasn't, but it's worth celebrating for the album that it is: another solid addition to the Lamb of God catalogue.

Title: Romance Is Boring
Review: Their sloganeering, haughtiness and mocking dismissal of their dislikes will always remain contentious, but never suggest they don’t mean it. This matters more to them than it does anybody else; Romance is Boring is the openly flawed but often brilliant proof.

Title: Faith in Strangers
Review: Despite a radical switch from digital to analog gear, the album is as bleak and as bracing as Luxury Problems.

Title: You've Always Been Here
Review: They sound positively in-your-face rather than isolated on garagey, throbbing stomps. [Jan 2021, p.27]

Title: Wonderful Wonderful
Review: Wonderful Wonderful is an album that doesn’t let the listener look forward to the next track, because the album is restlessly glancing backwards over its shoulder, haunted by past successes of The Killers, and the great artists who came before them.

Title: Elect the Dead
Review: It's not that bad an album--it's executed with all the gumption you'd expect from the SOAD mainman--but if you've heard any of the band's previous output you just don't need this in your collection.

Title: My Main Shitstain
Review: Dark, deluded and dangerously danceable, Paris Suit Yourself are the inspiration for wild dance floor seizures, or, at the very least, lucid gonzo dreams.

Title: Beat The Devil's Tattoo
Review: At its finest, the album serves as the ideal soundtrack for a fleet of lonely, grizzled bikers lost on a desert highway: slow-rolling and hardened, simultaneously seething, brooding, and wistful, and armed with the pride of vagrancy.

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: Wolf Parade is a great band, and while one will automatically think of Brock when they first hear You Are a Runner I Am My Father’s Son, (or any song featuring the first of the band’s two vocalists, Jason Krug,) many of the album’s strongest moments actually come when they more closely resemble other bands.

Title: Same Trailer Different Park
Review: Each track evokes an emotion, a giggle, a tear or a memory, but always a hunger for what’s next.

Title: b'lieve i'm goin down
Review: This darker edge lends substance to some of Vile's best songs to date. [Oct 2015, p.94]

Title: Spills Out
Review: The imitations/references spill out... But Spills Out is considerably less interesting and more cerebral, when Pterodactyl sounds like other bands.[#82, p.59]

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: Its real strength lies in the fact that it implores you to return for repeated visits to a world riddled with other people's cast-offs. Ironically, it recycles nothing; everything here is box fresh.

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: Teens of Denial is an album that works until it doesn’t. That moment will come at a different time for every listener.

Title: M:FANS
Review: M:FANS is less reclusive, just by virtue of its premise--Cale is collaborating with himself, the ultimate glum foil--but also because it fills every swatch of white space with his later-career electro-industrial leanings.

Title: Handwritten
Review: Cute he may be, but he has charisma that lasts no longer than a GIF, as Handwritten makes painfully clear.

Title: Sucker's Lunch
Review: On Sucker’s Lunch, Kenney presents each song with a fervor only teased on previous outings and she has never sounded more compelling. It will be exciting to see how she continues to shape her sound and identity going forward, but for now, at least, she has served up a delightful feast of music to keep us satiated until that day arrives.

Title: Star Wars
Review: Turns out Wilco are still full of surprises.

Title: Back On Time
Review: For music that is over 15 years old, Back on Time sounds as fresh as a sitar-wielding half-stepping daisy.

Title: Clay Class
Review: It gets repetitive after a while.

Title: Take Care
Review: The best of it affirms that Drake is shaping a pop persona with staying power.

Title: Nightlife
Review: It still cuts, just not quite as deep.

Title: Long Lost Suitcase
Review: Ethan Johns' stripped country settings on Willie Nelson and The Milk Carton Kids tunes immediately find Sir tom's grit and gravitas. [Nov 2015, p.77]

Title: Skins
Review: Skins takes that unrealized potential and cobbles together these tracks--basically b-sides and outtakes--strictly for fans who needed just ten more reasons to hear his voice.

Title: Back to Basics
Review: This rather bloated record should be regarded as a disappointment - an interesting one, but a disappointment none the less.

Title: Seen It All: The Autobiography
Review: He tends to repeat himself and his punchlines lack punch--but Seen It All is an album you can listen to start to finish and not hate yourself for buying it.

Title: Voices From the Lake
Review: The Italian duo have put together a timeless and beautiful dance record that slides easily to the top of 2012′s best.

Title: Fear Yourself
Review: Wrapped in the sonic wonder of Mark Linkous, Fear Yourself is more than a great record, it is a brilliant one.

Title: Dreamland
Review: For the tunnel-visioned Zeppelin fan, there's enough vintage Plant here to hold interest. [#8, p.121]

Title: In Colour
Review: In Colour breaks no new ground to be sure, but as an accessible crossover record it does a perfectly serviceable job. It's light, breezy and pretty, as ephemeral as the exhilaration of clubbing without really evoking the thrill of it all.

Title: AQUÎ›RIA
Review: It’s an album full of musical precision and technical achievements that ultimately reveals Boots to be exactly who he is: Jordan Asher, a prodigy producer eager to find his own voice.

Title: Know Your Enemy
Review: When it works, this can be pretty invigorating, but when it doesn't, it's utterly maddening.

Title: Sound Mirrors
Review: [An] assured, wildly varied, endlessly enjoyable album that finds Coldcut in a position even more unlikely than the podium at the Brits: dance producers at the top of their game, 19 years into their career.

Title: Love Comes Close
Review: Packed with lo-fi-meets-nu-rave parsings of UK post-punk discontent, the album’s distorted melodies are immediately catchy yet convey brooding emotional depth.

Title: 8 Diagrams
Review: Considering all that [has happened], it’s easy to be grateful for a quirky, uneven album like 8 Diagrams.

Title: Song For Our Daughter
Review: On Song For Our Daughter Marling intimately portrays her subconscious, the one that’s paved the way for her to survive to this point years before these songs were recorded, in its brutal glory.

Title: The Eraser
Review: Slight, but carrying a fair amount of weight, The Eraser isn’t a masterpiece, but it’s much more than solo-project divergence.

Title: Nothin' But Blood
Review: Overall, the effect of the album is mostly jarring. Gusty, but jarring.

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: Head-smashing songs like "Supermassive Black Hole" and "Invincible" all point to an album that strives to be nothing less than epic. It succeeds.

Title: Ruminations
Review: It's the most vital-sounding record he's made in years. [Dec 2016, p.110]

Title: A Healthy Distrust
Review: Francis... [is] a complex, fantastically literate and genuine wordsmith and poet. [#14, p.99]

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: The Windows operating system segue of Mark E. Smith ("Glitter Freeze") into Lou Reed ("Some Kind of Nature") is as apropos as used syringes littering Plastic Beach, which defines the disc's wasteland second half after "On Melancholy Hill." "Rhinestone Cowboy," meet "Rhinestone Eyes."

Title: A Fever Dream
Review: Where Everything Everything’s previous releases were as bonkers-crammed full of a surfeit of different stylistic tics, flourishes, embellishments and more not only from song to song within each album but even in every individual track, here, a definite sound and style has been settled on.

Title: Rated O
Review: It’s not that Rated O isn’t a good album. At least half of it is one of the best albums of the year. It’s that Rated O is just good enough and in a straightforward enough way to make you miss the Oneida that was about joyous, staggering confusion.

Title: The Empyrean
Review: John Frusciante has carved out a parallel world as a solo artist over a series of intensely personal and brilliantly realised albums. His 10th, The Empyrean, is his most ambitious to date.

Title: Man of the Woods
Review: Expertly appointed but emotionally inert homage to the place that he says made him.

Title: Hardcore Will Never Die, But You Will
Review: If Mogwai are looking for new routes to explore then Hardcore is a strong first venture.

Title: The Laughing Apple
Review: Yusuf’s vocals are a bit more gruff than in days gone by, but his whimsical tone maintains the fanciful and philosophical lilt once so essential to that early, engaging style.

Title: Blue Songs
Review: it is pretty much the same thing we all loved from Hercules and Love Affair. Does that mean this album is bad? No, it's fabulous. There was just no risk, no movement.

Title: Deep Down Happy
Review: In 12 songs, they make it pretty clear which side they’re on, and it looks like the winner - smart, engaged, and willing to crack a joke with the faith that their musical dexterity will speak for itself. Love them or hate them, dismiss them at your peril.

Title: Heavy Ghost
Review: It's Buffalo, New York-born David Stith's turn now to fashion a brilliant, hermetically sealed world that makes unabashed emotional connection. [Apr 2009, p.109]

Title: Goblin
Review: There are many arguments for and against Tyler's mouth and mind, but once the language barrier is crossed and ears become numb, the real brilliance of Goblin can be heard.

Title: Red Barked Tree
Review: As late efforts go, Red Barked Tree sounds alive, vital, and appropriately restless; and as aging rockers go, Wire remains well worth whatever wait comes next.

Title: Spoils
Review: Spoils delivers a series of eight meandering folktales, which wouldn't be out of place in a pub, and more likely borne from your average drunkard than a drunkard literary giant. [Spring 2009, p.106]

Title: Going Down In History
Review: Hard truths are faced down and bad voodoo gets annihilated throughout in unflinching, life-affirming, hard-rocking glory.

Title: Worship
Review: What is surprising is just how chief songwriter Oliver Ackermann shapes their face-melting shoegaze into something altogether more sophisticated. [Aug 2012, p.94]

Title: When The Devil's Loose
Review: Most of the songs light up, shine for a while, and pull back so suddenly that you feel a little betrayed. It's a shame these dry lullabies didn't surface earlier in our dreary summer.

Title: Spiritual Instinct
Review: Alcest don't pursue darkness or dwell in it; they understand it as a part of the unbearable light that holds everything in its embrace. The end of the journey on Spiritual Instinct, while deeply satisfying, signals yet another beginning.

Title: All Hands
Review: With a sound that’s one-third punk, one-third underground and one-third Yeezus, Doomtree’s All Hands is a work of lyrical importance covered up by synth notes and drum crashes, its messages left to be decoded by their fans.

Title: The People's Key
Review: This overflowing sense of self has done more to define Oberst than anything else, and it continues on The People's Key, spilling into the contemporary malaise he invokes and the often brilliant poetic associations of which he's sometimes capable.

Title: Old Ideas
Review: There's a distinct valedictory tone to his customary musings upon life, love and the spirit, with one track titled "Amen" and another "The Darkness". But if it is to be his last communiqué, at least the old smoothie's going down swinging.

Title: Utopia
Review: The result, by definition, breathes, which leads your ear initially to hear Björk’s voice as just another wind instrument; her lyrics don’t jump out the way they did in early stuff like “Hyperballad” or “Possibly Maybe.” But the words on “Utopia,” once they permeate your consciousness, are actually among her most intimate and affecting.

Title: Within and Without
Review: It's music for dreaming, the keyboard equivalent to shoegaze, reinforced by its song titles and vocals mostly mixed beneath the waves to gorgeously woozy effect. [Sept. 2011, p. 97]

Title: The Whole Love
Review: With The Whole Love, Wilco make noise-pop exciting again, perhaps because the pop part doesn't come easy.

Title: Who Do You Love
Review: Who Do You Love is yet more proof of Årabrot’s status as amongst Europe’s leading alternative rock acts.

Title: Always Got Tonight
Review: His eighth album again plays out his lonesome blues as the sincere struggle of a lovesick man -- and, as only Isaak can, he gets away with it.

Title: SR3MM
Review: SR3MM ends up being their clearest personal statement yet, finding their voices almost coincidentally.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: They were scratching at the surface of their emotional capabilities on their debut. With Hummingbird, Local Natives show that they can dig deeper.

Title: And It's Still Alright
Review: It's a late night listening record set in the candlelit environment of the human psyche and a worthy followup to Nathaniel's Falling Faster Than You Can Run.

Title: This Mess Is a Place
Review: While the second half of This Mess Is a Place is slightly less strong than the first (but only slightly), it still rings true with songs in which narrators repeatedly seem to be approaching friends and saying, "Hey, times are weird, but I'm OK, I think. How about you?"

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Orton delivers some gooey pop complete with sticky tunes and honey-dipped ear candy - yet it's heavy, disturbing, recondite.

Title: The Next Day
Review: An album that's thought-provoking, strange and filled with great songs.

Title: UNFLESH
Review: Although inescapably discomfiting, the music’s complex textures keep the listener snared.

Title: Trying to Never Catch Up
Review: Through all the fascinating genre shell games, the constant on Trying To Never Catch Up is a smart pop sensibility that rarely expels an unoriginal thought.

Title: The Gathering
Review: The results are shufflingly majestic, loaded with blissful truths and, it must be said, startlingly close to perfect.

Title: Wild Onion
Review: This doesn’t feel like yet more easy-trash, pool party punk (though it is that, and good at it), but something that has a preternatural songwriting zing and energy not predicated on just the fumbling charm of a stained ’80s metal t-shirt and Ronettes knowledge, but actual, like charm.

Title: From All Purity
Review: It’s all the necessary B-adjectives–bludgeoning, brutal, burly--but it’s something else too; Bloodcurdling.

Title: Bruiser
Review: Despite having many strong songs and a more focused approach, the Duke Spirit's third album is also their most uneven.

Title: Walk Through Fire
Review: This solo debut makes all the right moves to sail past retro on its way to timeless.

Title: Attention Please
Review: Here, the band focuses on building atmosphere and creating interesting soundscapes rather than high-volume noise. This is rare: quiet Boris.

Title: Grinderman
Review: Once our boy Nick begins his bellicose bellowing, there's no mistaking Grinderman's amped-up scorch for anything but another of Cave's darkly humorous creations of magnificent malevolence. Long may he howl and snort.

Title: All My Friends Are Funeral Singers
Review: So yes, All My Friends Are Funeral Singers is just another Califone album, but it's also a reminder of just what a special thing that is.

Title: Warp Riders
Review: Basically, what it comes down to is whether you can get past the thematic and lyrical silliness. If so, Warp Riders is a hell of a trip. If not--and truth be told, it's difficult--wait until The Sword's next album.

Title: Funeral
Review: Like The Fiery Furnaces' Gallowsbird Park, or Interpol's Turn On The Bright Lights, Funeral is a debut record that simply refuses to be ignored.

Title: Supernatural Love
Review: Acoustic or not, the killer grooves remain (try Lover or the title track), though downbeat pieces like Hear the Rain Come may need warmer weather to appreciate.

Title: The Trip
Review: If you want to hear this sort of thing done properly, you'll find happiness in the more sedate moments of the peerless Saint Etienne, but there's little to recommend The Trip. It's not much more than a Christmas bauble: shiny and polished on the surface, but with little of substance on the inside.

Title: God First
Review: The discrepancy between Steadman’s skill set and the kind of music he’s trying to make here is hard to overlook.

Title: Britney
Review: Many of the tunes are good for a romp around the kitchen (or the dance floor, if you prefer) but the girl is right when she says she is yet to come into her own both as a woman and a recording artist.

Title: Yr Atal Genhedlaeth
Review: Rawer and less accessible than [Mwng], it still contains many moments that will put a smile on the faces of die-hard SFA fans. [#9]

Title: Coral Fang
Review: Coral Fang finds The Distillers aping the bloodless Hollywood impotence of Hole's Celebrity Skin, their 'punk rock' inoffensive and utterly forgettable. [Dec 2003, p.113]

Title: Clap Your Hands Say Yeah
Review: A whatever-sticks debut with meritorious replay value.

Title: Murs for President
Review: Murs' spitball rhymes and thick beats have always showcased a proclivity for stardom, and they bear fruit on the soulful piano galumph of 'Time Is Know.' [Fall 2008, p.102]

Title: Rest
Review: Rest took seven years to come out, its long gestation fuelled by grief, and the finished product is nothing short of cathartic.

Title: Firepower
Review: The level of consistency remains high throughout a 14-track running order encompassing the belligerence of Evil Never Dies, and the title track, mid-tempo maulers (Lone Wolf) and epic closer Sea Of Red.

Title: Just a Little Lovin'
Review: Phil Ramone’s austere production seems designed to let Lynne’s voice carry the album, and that’s a big mistake, since she has neither the emotional range nor the soulful finesse to convey the real hurt at the core of this material.

Title: Youth
Review: While certain songs definitely stand on their own, the ability to capture a feeling throughout is what makes the album memorable and worthy of repeat listening.

Title: Bad as Me
Review: By shedding much of his fantastical baggage but none of his charm, he has created a nimble, playful little album that ranks among his very best.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: The volleying guitars of "My Gap Feels Weird" and friendly ferocity of "Rope Light" signal a group with the same playful spirit that made its best work roar (see: 1994's "Foolish"), but with refreshed energy from a nine-year nap.

Title: Ultra Beatdown
Review: Those in the know can attest DF is merely coming into its own after years on the touring circuit.

Title: The Inevitable End
Review: The Inevitable End will never be looked upon as a terribly uplifting experience, but its lyrical content treats heartache, despair, self-hatred, remorse, depression, and the fear of the unknown with utter respect.

Title: Mama's Boy
Review: As bizarre as LANY’s pivot to country pop is, they still manage to infuse it with enough charm where it doesn’t fall flat.

Title: Mutant
Review: Mutant is an album of contrasts, and Ghersi has an uncanny ability to let extremes interact with each other to create something new.

Title: Half Smiles of the Decomposed
Review: Half Smiles of the Decomposed isn't quite the guns-blazing finale I always imagined the last GBV album would be, but it never becomes a limp-wristed approximation of the band in any of its previous guises.

Title: Cells
Review: Although there are some memorable moments here, none of them come close to tracks such as Mars or The Dozens.

Title: The Hunter
Review: If not quite as mind-blowing as its best work, The Hunter provides a solid summation of Mastodon's musical range.

Title: Tip of the Sphere
Review: There are moments in early listens of the album when the attention begins to meander, only to be drawn back in by a lyrical quirk, or a sudden musical volte face, so that by the sixth roll about the turntable this seems a wholly differently textured record to when you began. [Mar 2019, p.121]

Title: Relapse
Review: It’s less a relapse than a rehash, less a comeback album than the kind of album artists need to come back from.

Title: AZD
Review: AZD marks a triumphant return for Actress.

Title: The 2nd Law
Review: Does this all meld together into the cohesive whole of a perfect album? Well, no, not really. But does The 2nd Law represent a band whose only limitations seem to be the high ceiling of their collective imagination? The answer here is an emphatic yes. [6 Oct 2012, p.52]

Title: TLC
Review: 2017's TLC are clearly more comfortable reminiscing, making their good-natured fifth less futureshock, more time machine. [Aug 2017, p.89]

Title: Howling, For the Nightmare Shall Consume
Review: Here, retaking the signature spell that Hellion and crew first conjured in the ’90s Cleveland scene, the band’s haunted hardcore gets a fresh coat of paint for the next stage of darkness. If you’re ready to enter the nightmare, this will get you howling.

Title: Get Hurt
Review: Get Hurt sounds like The Gaslight Anthem trying to figure out what kind of band they want to be.

Title: A New Tide
Review: Recorded in Chicago and Charlottesville, Virginia, A New Tide cobbles together elements of those scenes, but it ultimately lacks identity; it strives for diversity at the cost of imagination and quality songwriting.

Title: Meltdown
Review: A below par effort by their high standards.

Title: Lift a Sail
Review: There are moments of despair, but on the whole, Lift a Sail rings as an uplifting testament to love and human resilience.

Title: Fearless Love
Review: As far as a full-on comeback album, Fearless Love‘s songs as a whole aren’t strong enough to make for a great rock album, due to a lack of indelible hooks, yes, but also because nothing here really boogies.

Title: Given to the Wild
Review: Even at its best, Given To The Wild sounds like British Sea power without the esoteric charm, which is hardly the heartiest of recommendations. [Feb 2012, p.91]

Title: Life On Earth
Review: These vipers may be tiny, but there’s a bite to Fortino’s harrowing vocal that’s sure to leave its mark.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: While their ambition for evolving remains admirable, their apparent failure to understand their own strengths is troubling and undermines the promise they showed on their previous efforts.

Title: Making a New World
Review: Unfortunately, as a musical portrayal of the long-lasting echoes of WWI, its ideas are far more interesting than their execution.
Constantly questing without ever becoming indulgent, 4 is intoxicating. [Nov 2008, p.94]

Title: Outside Love
Review: This, then, is A-grade rock'n'roll--profound, damaged, brimming with wondrous dreams. [Jun 2009, p.104]

Title: Not Too Late
Review: Sonically, at least, the album takes only a small step away from the latte-lover mainstream.

Title: Wild Light
Review: What the album lacks in genuine surprises--it features fewer floor-filling basslines than its makers’ previous LP ‘proper’, 2010’s dance-designed ‘We Were Exploding Anyway’--it more than makes up for in comprehensive consistency.

Title: ANTI
Review: There is nothing wrong with Rihanna’s default dead-eyed vixen delivery--it’s one of the seven wonders of the pop world. But ironically, she actually sings the hell out of this record. If only more of these songs could actually carry the weight of Rihanna’s bid for freedom--a bid that is, ultimately, half-baked.

Title: No Mythologies to Follow
Review: The energy of this debut is tangible.

Title: Kunk
Review: This sort of noise and sludge ain’t for everybody, but fans of the Jesus Lizard, Pissed Jeans, or other such degenerates will take great masochistic pleasure in Kunk’s beatdown.

Title: Mr Twin Sister
Review: Their democratic process and persistence has resulted in an elevation of their sound.

Title: WILL THIS MAKE ME GOOD
Review: Although his 2016 debut, “Green Twins,” was a stoner-soul classic, his latest, “Will This Make Me Good,” is actually even trippier.

Title: We Love Life
Review: The band strikes the proper balance between ambition and pop instinct.

Title: Clockwork Angels
Review: Clockwork Angels sounds as mighty as its concept, with the well-balanced interaction amongst Lee, Lifeson and Peart.

Title: The Nihilist
Review: The Nihilist is a mind-melting blend of traditional songwriting and endless, restless experimentation. [Jun 2014, p.110]

Title: Stellastarr
Review: Too bad John Hughes isn't making the kind of movies he used to, because stellastarr*'s self-titled debut is a prom soundtrack worthy of Ducky.

Title: The Plot Against Common Sense
Review: A relentlessly insistent, unexpectedly danceable record which manages to be as engaging as it is wilfully bizarre.

Title: To The Bone
Review: It's all wonderfully executed. [Sep 2017, p.116]

Title: As If Apart
Review: He’s certainly carving out a niche that is very much his own, making for a colorful tapestry of sounds that are as uncanny as they are refined.

Title: Love From London
Review: As Love From London reinforces, he’s not relying on cleverness or humor as a crutch; even when he’s using elaborate imagery to explore a very simple feeling or situation, his sincerity never wavers.

Title: Fu Chronicles
Review: This six song collection from Daptone Records is a vibrant display of what Antibalas does best; fusing the spirit and soul of Fela Kuti with modern funky sounds.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: Long, luscious songs and cinematic melancholy are their usual preserve; their eighth album see these traded in for short, sharp shocks, metallic percussion, bullet-brusque sound effects, and frequent references to war, hate and death.

Title: Ash & Ice
Review: Because Ash & Ice somewhat ironically doesn’t have much of the icy immediacy that typically marks The Kills’ work, the album is one you need to live with to get the full payoff.

Title: Exiled
Review: Exiled is urgent and breathless from a band who need to be heard.

Title: Be Your Own King
Review: At times, all this loose-limbed craziness can become tiresome but like an excitable friend dragging you onto the dancefloor by the sleeve, they make it very a=hard not to join their party. [Apr 2013, p.97]

Title: Islah
Review: A cohesive, satisfying, fat-free full-length.

Title: Decemberunderground
Review: Decemberunderground carries a distinct whiff of missed opportunities.

Title: My Maudlin Career
Review: The songs work best when the band sticks to the balsa-wood wall of sound formula; they get into a spot of trouble when trying something different.

Title: Sun Giant
Review: Tone is an alchemic process, and Fleet Foxes produce gold with regularity, a stunning feat for such a young band. [Summer 2008]

Title: Beard, Wives, Denim
Review: The communal, freewheeling looseness is one of the album's greatest assets, as you feel as if you were a party to the making of the record in Eagle Bay, too.

Title: Guider
Review: They sound more into straight lines than catchy arcs, more into the moment than what came before.

Title: Soon Away
Review: ‘Jaded’ undoubtedly brings with it a glimmer of hope in an album that ultimately comes up short in delivering the fusion of intensity and melody that has served GRMLN so well before.

Title: End Times Undone
Review: End Times Undone neither elbows past nor dwells too much on Kilgour’s considerable legacy. It’s a frozen moment in a continuum, and it shines with suitable magic.

Title: Humor Risk
Review: Its oddball pop flavors and production style bring Ariel Pink to mind. [Oct. 2011, p. 101]

Title: Black Sun
Review: The irony is Black Sun is better-suited for the club. The album's sounds and ideas are large enough to fill a dark, echoing room.

Title: An Object
Review: They don't half make liberation and self-dependency sound miserable.

Title: Favorite Waitress
Review: Like many arch songwriters, the band tends to drop images and melodies from its favorite tunes into its work, phrases that add little sparks of frission to the Brothers' already strong melodic structure. [No. 110, p.54]

Title: Human
Review: The former "Moesha" star has never made a bad album, and she's not starting now with the appropriately rich and varied Human.

Title: Eyes on the Lines
Review: The lines referenced in the album’s title are not the kind to restrict or limit. They’re the kind to follow. The lines of an open road, rich with possibilities and rife with unanswered questions. Though whether the road is in this reality or another, remains to be seen.

Title: GINGER
Review: GINGER is new ground for Brockhampton, and a gentle nudge to others, urging them to go on their own paths of rediscovery and explore their roots. Thing is, we might need a bit more than a gentle nudge.

Title: Put Your Needle Down
Review: Put Your Needle Down shows that hometown versatility, bouncing from rhythmic, slick seventies rock to flirtations with New Wave to songs that could single-handedly make someone reconsider the sweeping generalization that pop doesn’t belong in country whatsoever.

Title: If All I Was Was Black
Review: Where Mavis' voice once a rangey, optimistic mezzo-soprano, her register has dropped dramatically to an emotionally rich, brassy contralto. It adds a growling intensity to lyrics that are dignified rather than angry. [Dec 2017, p.24]

Title: Other Truths
Review: It’s not often you find music that lives and breathes with such conviction that you find itself swept away in the charm of it all. That Do Make Say Think have achieved this lofty standard yet again shouldn’t come as a shock, yet it’s testament to their enduring talent that, at every turn, Other Truths continues to surprise and enthrall in equal measure.

Title: right on!
Review: It’s all immaculately executed (with help from Warpaint bandmate Stella Mozgawa on drums), just too often desperately unmemorable.

Title: Sculptor
Review: Employing a handful of tasteful collaborators, including J Mascis, Dirty Three drummer Jim White, and the National's Aaron Dessner, who co-produced Passerby, Randall and Hassett have made a record that boldly turns a corner while still slotting neatly into their already sterling catalog.

Title: Wig Out at Jagbags
Review: Wig Out is full of so much life and melody that it stands as a refreshing alternative to the increasingly homogenous state of indie rock. [Feb 2014, p.91]

Title: Goths
Review: While edgy, honest and witty observations are made about youth culture, there is a tendency to sprinkle moments of easy listening jazz throughout the record, which is a bit of a downer in a non gothic sense. Still, the brutal honesty and candor are present and much appreciated, one of the few characteristics that truly identifies a Mountain Goats record.

Title: Charmbracelet
Review: Who needs anti-depressants when you have Jesus and schmaltz?

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: It's a triumph of non-judgmental storytelling, delivered within purgative rock'n'roll.

Title: Pale Bloom
Review: Pale Bloom might be alienating to ambient fans who aren't familiar with how classical music works and would prefer appreciation not stand in the way of simple pleasure. It's easy to enjoy, a little harder to lose yourself in.

Title: Beneath the Skin
Review: Many of the songs are sturdy, constructed to support these grand ambitions, but these individual pieces are not as consequential as the big, big picture

Title: Ferndorf
Review: From this you'll gather that Ferndorf charms and frustrates in equal measure.

Title: Down to My Last Bad Habit
Review: The appeal of Down to My Last Bad Habit feels more Memphis than Nashville: it's Vince Gill's soul album, which is a welcome thing indeed.

Title: Vivian Girls
Review: The sound of three people ripping through hooky tunes without regard for pleasantries and taste is one of the joys of rock & roll, and Vivian Girls do satisfy on that account.

Title: More Fish
Review: Though "More Fish" lacks any real coherency, amid the flotsam is a marvelously random set of songs.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: He offers this glimpse of the soul beneath the swagger, and we like him better for it.

Title: I'm With You
Review: I'm With You is the sound of a band that continues to coast off past achievements.

Title: Electric Lines
Review: Even if Goddard is occasionally too reverent on Electric Lines, his love of electronic music--and the way it brings people together--is undeniable and infectious.

Title: You Want It Darker
Review: Using his remaining time, he’s not only putting his house in order, he’s tidying up ours too. You Want It Darker prepares us for his departure and, in turn, shows us how it’s done, so we have a road map--pockmarked by land mines as it is--in place when we reach that stage.

Title: The Obliterati
Review: Making up for lost time never sounded so good. [Aug 2006, p.88]

Title: The Sellout
Review: "Being herself" has resulted in her blandest record yet: it drifts from nondescript disco-pop and cloying R&B to woefully ersatz glam stomp. [July 2010, p. 132]

Title: Sun on the Square
Review: Rather than chasing trends or aiming for reinvention, the Innocence Mission seem content at this point in their career to carry on doing what they do best and expand on their trademark sound with another fine release.

Title: Wovenwar
Review: This is an instantly lovable, consistent and convincing debut, brimming with razor-sharp melodies and subtly expressed technical prowess.

Title: Triage
Review: ‘Trip The Mains’, perhaps Webb’s finest composition yet, appears to share its electrifying opening riff with Donna Summer’s disco classic ‘Hot Stuff’, before diving headfirst into a seismic chorus that’d shatter Blondie’s ‘Heart Of Glass’. Elsewhere, the haunting ‘Scream Whole’ begins as a soothing lullaby, before unravelling itself into a doomy slice of noir-pop. This momentum is intermittent though, disappointingly.

Title: Results May Vary
Review: The songs without hip-hop accents or full-on rage merely seem dreary and gray or derivative of vintage alt bands. [10 Oct 2003, p.121]

Title: Introducing Joss Stone
Review: [Introducing] contains her best songs and most relaxed, assured performances. [May 2007, p.112]

Title: High Hopes
Review: Post 9/11 sessions for The Rising yield early continuity ("American Skin [41 Shots]"), but once Springsteen goes Stax with full-on gospel rock ("Heaven's Wall"), High Hopes reveals its soft brown underbelly.

Title: Showroom of Compassion
Review: The harder they aim for radio, the more rewarding the result. Beneath the irony and compact cool, Cake is still a great little pop band.

Title: Fake Songs
Review: By turns alluring, obnoxious, and laugh-out-loud-funny.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: Keeps the orchestral Americana on an ambient, after-hours simmer. [Mar 2004, p.123]

Title: Under the Blacklight
Review: Either they're utterly serious about their flirtation with the mainstream or they're taking the piss with a wink. In both cases, the songs suffer a smothering slow death by context.

Title: Vessel
Review: There's great charm to these yearning tunes. [May 2018, p.28]

Title: Do It!
Review: Clinic has returned to making music that feels limitless. [Spring 2008, p.7]

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: It’s the songs that matter most on Crack The Skye, and the songs have rarely sounded stronger.

Title: Pura Vida Conspiracy
Review: Gogol are best when Hütz lyrically nuances the roiling energy; on "My Gypsy Auto Pilot," he goes back to Ukraine to find that he's a stranger in his old hometown.

Title: Around The Sun
Review: Undercut by passion and urgency. [Jan 2005, p.113]

Title: Life Is People
Review: It's not without a few syrupy moments, and it would be a push to recommend it over the old records, but there are some fine songs here.

Title: New Material
Review: In a world of easy sound bites and shallow narratives New Material has withdrawn from the spectacle to pursue a whole new goal--to teach you something about yourself.

Title: Space Is Only Noise
Review: Jaar, the son of conceptual artist Alfredo Jaar, can weave a heady spell, presenting himself somewhere between David Byrne and Ricardo Villalobos. [Jun 2011, p.85]

Title: Witching Hour
Review: The Witching Hour is the most urgent and immediate of their career. The earlier records were sort of toylike and plastic; this not only has a pulse, it has chilled blood in its veins.

Title: Thrice Woven
Review: Not quite a milestone then, but a release that’s set to be remembered for a very long time to come.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: [The] process of sonic expansion is continued apace on this latest effort.

Title: Telicatessen
Review: Rob Sonic absorbs elements of earlier electronica, industrial and IDM to create delectably expansive, engrossing parfaits of sound- this is perhaps the greatest space boogie funk record since The Cold Vein dropped.

Title: Romance at Short Notice
Review: Dirty Pretty Things move their music forward with this album, but they've sacrificed their clarity to achieve that.

Title: Candy For The Clowns
Review: Things start to become a bit samey three quarters of the way through the album.

Title: Ego War
Review: Ego War doesn't disappoint, offering an instant hit of raucous energy via choppy rave-house dynamics, high-density Daft Punk-style production and a refreshingly anti-epic approach to songwriting. [#16, p.114]

Title: Mettavolution
Review: Mettavolution is the R&G record where all of their gifts are on display and in sync; it sends listeners on a holistic journey of musical discovery and emotional resonance.

Title: 6twenty
Review: It almost goes without saying that the D4 kick the Vines, Hives, and White Stripes right square in their trendy asses.

Title: The Adventures of Ghosthorse and Stillborn
Review: The production is cleaner this time around, a mixed blessing that steals some of the band's messy, homemade charm in favor of a richer, atmospheric effect.

Title: Take Control
Review: Chugging clatter and repetitive shouting is still offensively dull, even if they don’t really mean it.

Title: Sun
Review: On [Cat Power] Marshall has changed direction yet again, abandoning her soul charm for something much less appealing.... But her natural grace shines through on "3, 6, 9"... and "Ruin."

Title: GREY Area
Review: At once soft and hard, fiery and vulnerable, Grey Area finds Little Simz thriving in her multi-facetedness.

Title: Torino
Review: For the most part, this is more of the same, which disciples will have no qualms about.

Title: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always
Review: There are moments of suffering, self-pity and, eventually, redemption throughout the nine tracks, and although there are some missteps, Luke Winslow-King's I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always is admirable in its undertaking, and definitely worth the listen.

Title: Threadbare
Review: It's actually more satisfying as a piece, a folksy ambience lapping up against muted psychedelia and reverb'd pop. [Nov 2009, p.102]

Title: awE naturalE
Review: Though the overall groove ("Don't funk with it," they advise on QueenS) is freewheeling enough to avoid being preachy, awE naturalE is implicitly political.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: The Strokes come across as a world-sized band that's tethering itself.... Nonetheless, this record is good. [Nov 2003, p.124]

Title: A+E
Review: Despite the quality of the execution, it's difficult to shake the sense that A+E has been done before.

Title: The Chronicles of Marnia
Review: Marnia isn't the single touch that shatters, it's the long, steady stare that gives way to embrace.

Title: Adventure
Review: Their obvious love of the Ramones’ weirder cuts is still alive and thrashing, and, admittedly, a lot of Adventure walks extremely familiar soil.

Title: Weezer (Green Album)
Review: Weezer have faced their challenge with confident, easy-going nonchalance, offering one hell of a tight little record.

Title: Eugene McGuinness
Review: What was once pin drop quiet is now grand; one soon adjusts however as the key to all of the songs here is the inner shell, not the protective exterior.

Title: Man Against Machine
Review: His primary weapon--and the quality that most sets him apart from the country stars who’ve surfaced in his wake--is his earnestness. The singer’s aggressive sincerity remains intact.

Title: Why Hasn't Everything Already Disappeared?
Review: Like ghosts that don’t know they’re dead, the songs on Deerhunter’s Why Hasn’t Everything Already Disappeared? wander about in a well-produced limbo almost in mourning for the death they can’t die. But they don’t know it, so--and this is the saddest part about it--they become what they deplore, all loss glossed over.

Title: Boys Outside
Review: He's turned a hard patch into something transcendental. However brief, however ephemeral, there's a sense of spiritual overcoming that encompasses not just his own history, but the experiences that listeners bring to these sad songs, as well.

Title: My ______ Is Pink
Review: The gamble was worth it as they have improved as artists and presented an album where you never know what will come next.

Title: Captain of None
Review: Schott's new material retains some of the music-box delicacy of yore, and her breathy singing is as slender as a reed. [No. 119, p.53]

Title: Black Gives Way to Blue
Review: It is a legitimately excellent record that lives up to (and sometimes even exceeds) the song writing standards set by the band on "Dirt" or "Jar of Flies."

Title: Friend Opportunity
Review: Gone are most of the scratching, scrunching noises that previously signified a low budget, and now there are crisp multitracked vocals. But the band hasn’t gotten any less imaginative. [14 Jan 2007]
The refusal to stick to one gender only adds to 1989‘s ubiquitous strength, making it less an album applicable to specific male/female relationships and more about relationships in general.

Title: Has Been
Review: This CD is beyond good or bad. It is from a world where concepts such as "unique" and "indispensible" live happily alongside "hilariously, brain-tearingly wrong".

Title: Mental Illness
Review: These are fine story-songs for any age, era or metal disposition. [Jun 2017, p.107]

Title: Albala
Review: A real gem.

Title: Untitled
Review: Hurrying urgently down the rushing veins of every song, colliding surreally poetic lyrics with thumping racket in a tense, on-edge mess, Untitled could well’ve put WALL on the same trajectory as their equally absurdist contemporaries Parquet Courts.

Title: Rolling Papers
Review: On Rolling Papers, Khalifa, the 23-year-old Pittsburgh rhymer responsible for the jersey-waving hit "Black and Yellow," manages to give life to those kinds of cash-gorged perma-baked cliches by warmly luxuriating in the space between pop's fresh-faced exuberance and hip-hop's easy arrogance--between skater and playa, Bieber and Biggie.

Title: Todd Smith
Review: This is a serviceable, lighthearted album packed with R&B collaborations. [10 Apr 2006]

Title: Analog Man
Review: Seldom has retro sounded so pleasingly stubborn. [Jul 2012, p.85]

Title: Everything in Between
Review: Unlike previous releases, there is not a dire need to shuffle back a few tracks to listen repetitively, but more of a, 'when I'm in the mood' feeling. No Age are certainly living in the moment, and Everything In Between has a similar retention factor.

Title: Hypnotic Nights
Review: The production may be a little cleaner, but the same knack for great fuzzed-out ditties is still there... a pretty good album.

Title: The Lovers
Review: As impressively deep as the music's pile may be, however, it's Marshall's towering voice that most recalls Elbow. [Dec 2012, p.109]

Title: Blemish
Review: A work of beautiful, desolate fragility.

Title: And Their Refinement Of The Decline
Review: This two-hour double-CD/triple-LP, their first product since 2001, is grand, somber, amelodic, arhythmic and slow, leaving plenty of time to admire the notes' altered states.

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: Elbow sound revitalised here with Garvey proving himself once more to be one of the most eloquent British songwriters around.

Title: Middle Brother
Review: Typical for a "supergroup," Middle Brother sounds more like a collection of strong musical personalities crowded into the same space than an actual band on its charmingly ragged, self-titled debut.

Title: Everyday Nothing
Review: Her stories are made believable by the authenticity of Bentham’s real-life everyday nothings that season each song and open our minds and hearts to the most primal feelings we encounter and the most insignificant events that take place in our lives.

Title: Kinky
Review: The album is witty and fun and will appeal to a wide variety of people. [Apr 2002, p.82]

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: Coxon is turning in some of the finest, most insightful guitar rock from either side of the Atlantic.

Title: The Anteroom
Review: How to Dress Well has never sounded more dejected, but maybe he hasn't been this invigorated, either.

Title: Embers
Review: Throwing Snow’s latest does not do justice to those environmental paradoxes. Instead, he hones in rigidly on a narrow conception of darkness and foreboding that grows stale. This rigidity gives the album a closed-off feel that ultimately constricts the flow of emotion and makes for a cumbersome listen.

Title: nijimusi
Review: Experiencing the music of OOIOO is an incredibly satisfying series of sensations that seems to form an exclusive bond between creator and listener. It's a plunge into unbridled creativity that is the true essence of psychedelia.

Title: Unpatterns
Review: Solid, polished, dancefloor-friendly, and other damningly faint adjectives.

Title: My Love Is a Bulldozer
Review: His tongue may be in his cheek at least some of the time, but parts of this album feel like the worst excesses of rock opera as applied to dance music.

Title: Semper Femina
Review: With Semper Femina, Marling is back on more assured ground, largely acoustic, with subtle arrangements and an exquisite use of strings that seem a natural, wholly fitting addition to her ever-expanding palette.

Title: Privateering
Review: The pleasure isn't in the gimmick or the dress-up, but in the disciplined play of emotion behind them.

Title: Breakin' Point
Review: There are a couple of tracks that veer rather too close for comfort to boy band and eurovision territory, but for the most part, assuming you like the better end of synth-pop, you won’t be disappointed.

Title: Herein Wild
Review: For the most part, it's an effective addition.... The only real snag here is Rose's voice, which sometimes sounds so detached as to be barely present. [Nov 2013, p.78]

Title: Be
Review: After blasting off into outer space with Electric Circus, Common returns to more solid ground with Be, but thanks to West, Poyser, and Jay Dee, the sounds are often nothing short of heavenly.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: Largely tosses out the loopy musical excursions and surrealistic pillow fights of past albums for a tighter, sparer approach.

Title: Velvet Changes
Review: All Velvet Changes creates is a disquieting malaise that deflects any attempt to penetrate its billowy, monochromatic, meaningless contours.

Title: Niggas on the Moon
Review: The songs feel more like eight variations on the same concept than eight distinct tracks. That's neither surprising nor unforgivable given the experimental bent of the band, but you can't help but notice the sameness when you listen to the album.

Title: Femme Fatale
Review: Gaga's music, let's be frank, is not that much better than, or even different to, that on Femme Fatale, but she knows the lingering appeal of playing dress-up.

Title: The Waterfall
Review: This record should be coupled with its predecessor but it without doubt exceeds its ambitions.

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: This may well be the most exhilarating debut of the year. [Nov 2003, p.107]

Title: In Search of Elusive Little Comets
Review: Little Comets have some energetic hooks and straight-to-the-point post-punk choruses that would make many of the resident bands in their native North East proud. There just isn't quite enough to get carried away about.

Title: The Altar
Review: Banks' list of grievances can get wearying, but the music's dour detail is alluring too.

Title: I Sell the Circus
Review: There’s an unmistakable feeling of sameness that runs through I Sell the Circus, which isn’t to say that it sounds tired--anything but.

Title: The Grand Tour
Review: James Brooks conjures the motorik rhythm and magnificent vistas. [Oct 2014, p.96]

Title: Blonde
Review: It’s a beguiling, meandering sprawl that rewards total immersion.

Title: Too Much Information
Review: The problem is that there is too little to dig into, to revel in. In many senses, Too Much Information is ultimately not enough. [Feb/Mar 2014, p.73]

Title: Electric Trim
Review: [Electric Trim] features conventionally structured songs that underline his country-folk and Americana interests, while amping up the psych-pop and orchestral alt.rock. [Oct 2017, p.36]

Title: Run Fast
Review: Art, love, personal and political ideology--all of it is delved into with gloriously unpolished gusto. [Summer 2014, p.91]

Title: Elaenia
Review: Shepherd's flawless Eglo catalogue had the power to coax his followers off the dance floor with him, and Elaenia's sophisticated sense of musical accomplishment ought to keep them there.

Title: The Argument
Review: It's still the best mix of fury and fluency since phony Beatlemania bit the dust. [Jan 2002, p.107]

Title: Blood Red Shoes
Review: Too often, the same formula appears with uninspiring choruses being too frequent; whilst these short, sharp bursts of fuzzy punk sound great in small doses, this collection will probably find itself confined to the shelf before long, as its longevity may be questionable with little poppy catchiness present.

Title: Painted Ruins
Review: In the end, the chief irony of Painted Ruins is that this album tackling the heavy subject of all things crumbling and passing ends up being the band’s most alive, cohesive offering.

Title: Mic Tyson
Review: Sean Price has rarely if ever lost a step and Mic Tyson is not going to be the time that he did.

Title: Paradise
Review: They haven’t completely ditched the relentless aggression--much of Paradise races past in an alluring blur of distortion and melody--but this is a welcome broadening of their palette.

Title: Dumb Luck
Review: The vibe here is mellow, unremarkable, and a touch contrived. [May 2007, p.85]

Title: Lonerism
Review: Themes of isolation and solipsism unfold musically as much as lyrically. Produced with help from Flaming Lips go-to guy Dave Fridmann, Lonerism surprises with layers of detail.

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: Make no mistake – the beats are still rigid, dabbling in taut funk and squelching electro as much as snotty punk moves and glorious polyrhtyhms. These nine songs, however, ring with a clarity of purpose and a true intent that was previously altogether lacking, presenting a far more cohesive image of Murphy and his many strengths.

Title: Imarhan
Review: Imarhan is the sound the band have spent their whole lives perfecting and it comes across like a best of. Given that they've probably got a lot more in the back catalogue that didn't make the cut for this album, there's definitely more to come from the Imarhan arsenal, but this is a great start.

Title: Nothing
Review: Nothing is a stark record, and I imagine not one that will be ringing out of club PAs on a regular basis. Instead, it joins the impressively swelling ranks of dance/techno/electro/house albums that reflect the inner workings of the individuals creating them.

Title: III
Review: III has a highly melodic crossover feel that is somewhat different to many of the players’ other, grittier projects, although the beats remain a little itchy. Songs about crowd mentality and medieval jesters are novel in theme but overthought and bombastically dramatic in their lyrical phrasing.

Title: ORCA
Review: Dapperton’s potential shines when he pushes himself, when it sounds like he’s making music for self-expression and fun, expanding his vocal range and messing around with reverb. He loses it inside of self-imposed pop formulas and strained symbolism.

Title: Songbird
Review: Nothing here sounds like it's been fully thought out or planned, and Songbird sounds all the better for it.

Title: The Monitor
Review: The Monitor more than cements Titus Andronicus's place in the indie rock arena. At its best moments, it reminds you of just how durable--and dangerous--a beast like rock 'n' roll can still be.

Artist: The Knife in Collaboration with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock
Title: Tomorrow, in a Year
Review: After three albums of encroaching conceptuality and quality, they’re cutting back on their known strengths in order to give everything over to the concept and the creative challenges it brings, never quite abandoning the listener, but requiring an undue amount of effort.

Title: Electrified
Review: Smiley-smart vocals, gung ho guitar, beaming hooks. [24 Jun 2005, p.165]

Title: I Can't Imagine
Review: I Can't Imagine is confident, assured, and fiercely independent.

Title: Something Wicked this Way Comes
Review: Colossal and cinematic, the fourth record from the Herbaliser is a timely achievement in music, a genre-bending statement of creative poignancy.

Title: Wait For Me
Review: It’s a remarkable work, and while Moby may find himself once more providing the soundtrack to every trendy restaurant and automobile ad for the next 18 months, what’s best about this record is that it’s just that: an album, meant to be consumed the old-school way, front-to-back.

Title: I Forget Where We Were
Review: While there are a few too many round-the-campfire gloom-fests on I Forget Where Were, there are also displays of real musical background. [Dec 2014, p.77]

Title: Theyesandeye
Review: Her slightly Alanis Morrisetteish voice can sound too mannered in places, and the songwriting is occasionally uneven, but the best moments--such as her whispered cover of the xx’s Angels--are truly lovely.

Title: La Isla Bonita
Review: This reckless abandon practically screams out of La Isla Bonita, but the record falls short of total reinvention.

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: The album offers huge choruses that suggest the New York City quartet might be the indie rock equivalent to K.C. & Tthe Sunshine Band. [#15]

Title: Indestructible Machine
Review: Indestructible Machine is as good as anything I've heard this year and marks the true, and truly defiant, arrival of what could be a serious talent.

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: Part minimalist dance record, part undulating sound collage, his new album serves as a scrapbook of nearly every idea Hebden has examined and cast aside during his career.

Title: Rise Up
Review: Sure, 70 million bong hits have rendered B-Real and Sen Dog confused political theorists (complaining about taxes during a recession? What up, Glenn Beck?). But when they write what they know, they strike a nice balance between visions of bong-water Armageddon and Nineties light-'em-up boom-bap.

Title: Rubber Factory
Review: It's just a shame that quieter moments such as 'The Lengths' sound a little weedy in comparison. [4 Sep 2004, p.72]

Title: A Dotted Line
Review: While they might not be better than ever, they’re at least what they once were and what they’ve always been in the collective memory: instrumental virtuosos and sophisticated songsmiths, all the while finding a way to make it look easy.

Title: Petits Fours
Review: A record that blends his trademark guitar squalls and characteristically crunching bass with feathery synths. [Spring 2009, p.65]

Title: Black Metal
Review: What is surely one of the year’s most frustrating releases.

Title: Laws of Illusion
Review: Country diva channels marriage break-on first LP in nearly a decade.

Review: Burst Apart is clearly the work of the same songwriter, but it never sounds like a mere retread. The Antlers' belief in this material comes through loud and clear, and it will likely resonate with a new multitude of fans, as well.

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: jj No. 3 is an irresistibly light-headed trip through lush, electronic pop. [Jun 2010, p.91]

Title: Inventions
Review: It's no "High Enough," but it is a damn fine collection of selected ambient works.

Title: In Search of Stoney Jackson
Review: These songs are alive, but there are too many cooks, and they clutter things with all their different ideas and approaches. Madlib's instrumental interludes are weird and compelling, which is no surprise, but because of the multitude of voices, his influence is more subdued than usual.

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Courtney Barnett has managed to expand her lyrical preoccupations and musical interests outwards and upwards, while still retaining the magic of her past peak. [Apr 2015, p.68]

Title: Old Yellow Moon
Review: The result is an album of solid country virtue.

Title: Natalie Prass
Review: This dream of an album sounds like little else currently in the pop field, and the fact that it’s a debut from a relative newcomer makes it even more impressive.

Title: Vehicles & Animals
Review: Rife with an irresistible charm, sly English wit, and supremely catchy choruses. [#10, p.98]

Title: The Bright Mississippi
Review: The inspiring combination lifts the album far beyond tribute material into sonic territory all its own.

Title: Pluto
Review: Pluto should be appreciated for what it is, an album of impeccably crafted, energetic, original music that is striving above all else to be popular and universal, even if such goals look less likely of being achieved than ever before.

Title: Origin
Review: Rakei's gently wistful tone fits the general mood, though it's something of a relief when he shifts gears. [Summer 2019, p.115]

Title: God Forgives, I Don't
Review: Lyrically it is all shamelessly hollow, but Ross's album is seductively swish, its production sophisticated and strings and saxophone abound. [Oct 2012, p.75]

Title: EUPHORIC /// HEARTBREAK \\\
Review: Euphoric Heartbreak is a more accomplished, interesting piece of work; a brutal but exhilarating listen. Yet without the hype that surrounded its predecessor, and with a distinct change of tact, it might struggle to find its natural home.

Title: Barbara Barbara, we face a shining future
Review: Barbara... is less massive comeback than slight return.

Title: Out Among the Stars
Review: Out Among the Stars is very much classic Cash.

Title: Shall Noise Upon
Review: Apollo Sunshine has finally created the audio beast we've been waiting for--a feast of emotions, sounds and additional weirdness. [Fall 2008, p.98]

Title: Kick Up the Fire, and Let the Flames Break Loose
Review: The first great album of the new prog revolution.

Title: Low in High School
Review: We have Low in High School, which is sometimes brilliant, sometimes infuriating, and 100  percent Morrissey.

Title: Shoot for the Stars, Aim for the Moon
Review: ‘Shoot For The Stars, Aim For The Moon’ showcases a multi-faceted artist only just discovering his potential. What makes the album truly stand out is that it serves as a testament to the strength, power and knowledge Smoke held in his ambition to go to the very top.

Title: Zonoscope
Review: Thanks to its beauty, warmth, and top-rate songwriting, Cut Copy remain atop the pile of dance-rock groups in 2011, right next to LCD Soundsystem. Review: Sadly, this follow-up shows signs of premature ageing. [Mar 2006, p.109]

Review: Sundown adds to pop’s current obsession with tropical house, while I Would Like is a good song without a proper chorus. But Larsson imbues each song with enough passion to see it over the line.

Title: Somethin 'Bout Kreay
Review: It's a pop album of awful pop music.

Title: Pop Trash
Review: A mediocre Britpop album.

Title: Shotter's Nation
Review: Doherty's presence, which is monumental, overpowers the rest of Babyshambles: Drew McConnell, Mick Whitnall, and Adam Ficek. [Fall 2007, p.72]

Title: Preliminaires
Review: This may be his best album since 1977's "Lust for Life."

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: Push the Sky Away’s rewards are interspersed among plenty of frustrating moments, yet even at its worst, it’s a fascinating album.

Review: Some songs work. He makes great use of Ethiopian-sounding jazz samples and M.I.A.-style children’s chants on ABCs, and excels while rapping over some of the album’s otherworldly beats.
