Review: On the album's first half, everything sounds correct but lacks any intoxicating, addictive spark.... [Yet] when its mood alters, somewhere around the metal wasteland of 'Lagoon Leisure', and things start getting sinister, then Regional Surrealism becomes (finally) exciting. The record transforms into a deeply disconcerting experience, all eerie shadows and claustrophobic spaces.

Title: Luminiferous
Review: Luminiferous burns hard, but it’s searching for an attitude adjustment that could make the flames grow higher.

Title: The Ownerz
Review: While it's not as immediately user-friendly as the group's early jazz-rap infusions, this album still bubbles with head-nodding boombox pleasures.

Title: The Slideshow Effect
Review: There's no doubt the songwriting is there--but the LP's best tracks ("All Our Wonder" and Old Haunts") share the lo-fi production that was a boon to the atmospheric beauty of their EP.

Title: Stadium
Review: Despite its unusual approach, it's warm, deeply felt, not all that dissonant, and oddly calming. Stadium is a quantum leap forward for its genre--whatever that genre may be.

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: Despite clocking in at a whopping 70 minutes, Car Seat Headrest pack enough hooks in to avoid lagging, thanks to Toledo's practice with his lengthy yet phenomenal earlier albums Twin Fantasy and How to Leave Town.

Title: Gist Is
Review: It’s an unapologetically impressive and precise record that could do more to reach out and connect, rather than just dancing off, expecting the listener to follow.

Title: I Like To Keep Myself In Pain
Review: As deeply rooted in American tradition as that sound is, it is never straightjacketed by nostalgia.

Title: Mississauga Goddam

Title: Yellowcard
Review: They've made a graceful exit here. [Oct 2016, p.86]

Title: Volume 1
Review: This is the least inventive product you could have expected from a bunch of varyingly inventive songwriters. Which is to say, it’s not much good at all.

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: The album's adventurous musical scope serves to further expand the mythos behind Ebert's ego-fueled, drug-addled, socio-religious musical experiment.

Title: Modern Country
Review: Modern Country is a beatific and expansive ambient record daubed in acoustic and electric guitars, analogue oscillations, some really scary bells and no words; its meaning can be fluid.

Title: Violet Cries
Review: Their debut positions itself somewhere sonically between the avant-gardism of These New Puritans and Siouxsie And The Banshees at their most stridently gothic. [Feb. 2011, p. 114]

Title: Themes for Dying Earth
Review: Themes is a record meant to sooth in its sensing of a crisis. It subtly implements the element of time, fashioning aspects like life and death into an intertwining of beautiful textures.

Title: One Second of Love
Review: One Second of Love feels like Nite Jewel attempting something like a proof of arrival, but mostly it's simply a high definition look at all of the strengths and weaknesses we already knew she had.

Title: Proof of Youth
Review: Even at just over 30 minutes, there's a feeling they're running short on new ideas. [Oct 2007, p.98]

Title: A Raw Youth
Review: A Raw Youth aims to sabotage meathead rock and succeeds. Le Butcherettes preserve all the best parts--the rush, the muscle, the vocalist as GOD--but expose the celebrated macho ego as a terrorising other.

Title: The Devil's Walk
Review: Mood music with a soul. [Oct 2011, p.112]

Title: The Orbserver In The Star House
Review: Everyone involved on this slab of hertz has brought far too much to the table over the years to dismiss this and the record really works.

Title: Clues
Review: Striking stylistic tics like this pop up all over Clues, and the contextualizing effect is undeniable: for good or ill, it’s nigh impossible to hear this album anew, free from preconceptions.

Title: Night Falls Over Kortedala
Review: For all the moments of heart-stopping splendour, the backing tracks sometimes sound as creaky as a "Prisoner Cell Block H" film set.

Title: Just a Souvenir
Review: Like any jam band, Squarepusher begins to outstay his welcome after the noisy bass and drum kit duke- out of “Planet Gear.” Thankfully, the idyllic guitars of 'The Glass Road’s' and 'Yes Sequitir’s' idyllic guitars and the retro-futuristic computer voice of 'The Coathangars’s' retro-futuristic computer voice keep these heavenly interstellar jams from sounding too analogous. [Year End 2008]

Title: In This Light & On This Evening
Review: In This Light and on This Evening dials it down so far that it doesn’t contain one track that comes close to the power of songs they seemed to toss off so effortlessly before.

Title: The Sun Awakens
Review: Sure, there are flashes of undeniable brilliance, but most certainly not the full wattage of the awakening sun as advertised--far from the record Chasny's capable of making.

Title: Feel the Sound
Review: Feel the Sound is not a classic, it's not a masterpiece, and despite its pristine delivery, it's not perfect. But it is an honest and genuine sampling of a band who continues to subvert expectations.

Title: Lost
Review: It's an ironic title for an album that's so sure, and even if his early fans frown as their dancing shoes collect dust, complaining about what doesn't happen on Lost seems silly when compared to the wonderful and intoxicating things that actually do.

Title: Superorganism
Review: Superorganism easily meets and exceeds the hype surrounding this talented group.

Title: The Glorious Dead
Review: This is a fun record. Sometimes that really is enough.

Title: Given to the Wild
Review: Given to the Wild is resolutely The Maccabees best.

Title: /\/\/\Y/\
Review: It all slides down very easily--but there's isn't much of an aftertaste. [Aug 2010, p.66]

Title: Brokeback and the Black Rock
Review: McCombs and crew have painted a portrait of endless highways, ghost towns, and sunburnt moments of ecstatic possibility.

Title: Abnormally Attracted to Sin
Review: Her 12th studio release, Abnormally Attracted to Sin, finds her in full command of her expanded arsenal, creating an overall sound that's as psychedelic as it is classic.

Title: The Difference Between Me and You Is That I'm Not on Fire
Review: Cryptic and cutting. [Aug 2004, p.108]

Title: Object 47
Review: That misstep ['Patient Flees'] aside, no band mocks harder, and Object 47 is a smartly sardonic piece of work on par with Wire's late-'70s heyday.

Title: The Good Life
Review: The 25-year-old Earle may have the false front teeth to show for his hard livin’, but he hasn’t yet figured out how to translate it into unique, memorable songs.

Title: Luxury Problems
Review: It's a thoughtful and meditative affair with a meaningful and felt collaboration at its core.

Title: Hitchhiker
Review: While eight have appeared in different versions spooned out on releases ranging from 1976’s American Stars And Bars, Rust Never Sleeps from 1979 (three tracks), Decade (the Nixon diatribe “Campaigner”) and one even as late as 2010’s Le Noise, there is an intimacy and rawness to these performances that is riveting and subtly powerful.

Title: In My Defense
Review: After a half-decade of life lessons, Azalea could have gone in a certain cathartic and mature direction. However, on In My Defense, she opted for a less gracious and, ultimately, exhausted route.

Title: Invincible
Review: The mix is such that the saccharine ("You Are My Life" and "Heaven Can Wait") is outweighed by the brilliant ("Whatever Happens" and "The Lost Children"), creating a record that is quite relevant while at the same time being experimental and fresh.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: While all of this still may not equal any great departure from before, anyone who had appreciated the newly charted direction on Everybody is sure to find the new songs every bit as strong and engaging. [Fall 2008, p.78]

Title: Galore
Review: This faith in the lives lived in the days before the darkness closes in grants Thumpers their transformative power and their unlimited naïveté its unique charm.

Title: The Deserters
Review: The odd over ethereal moment notwithstanding, the remainder of the album proves equally alluring. [Jan 2013, p.90]

Title: Discovery
Review: Listeners might tire of its mechanical edge, but luckily Daft Punk folds in a few more layers. Whether the listener believes it or not, Discovery postulates that club music can possess depth of sound and be more than a never-ending beat that simply marshals your body along with it. Thus, the songs are shorter, more eclectic and rife with hills and valleys of beat that urge you to stop and listen.

Title: Sleep Through The Static
Review: You'd be hard pressed to find anything to summon the blood and stiffen the sinew among the 14 songs on offer here. [Mar 2007, p.90]

Title: Sundry Rock Song Stock
Review: An album so profusely inventive, so alive to the possibilities of sound itself.

Title: Kasabian
Review: An unstoppable, intense and astonishing assault on the senses that gives a respectable nod to the past while it blazes a trail to the future. [#9]

Title: Road to Rouen
Review: Rouen is all long jams and breezy acoustics, the telltale signs of a band that feels it's time to sober up. [#70, p.110]

Title: Bonfires on the Heath
Review: Though Bonfires' pacing is erratic, the band keeps winsome romance close.

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: Separation Sunday isn’t quite on par with Almost Killed Me, primarily because it won’t stun listeners with its freshness.

Title: Specter At The Feast
Review: With the exception of the more melodious tracks coming in pairs and slightly hindering the flow of an otherwise excellent album, Specter at the Feast is a very good effort from BRMC, and an example of the continued revitalization that started sometime around Leah Shapiro’s arrival to the band in 2008.

Title: Demonstration
Review: Sonically, he's plumped for stark electronics that recall his teen years as a grime MC--a period recreated, with fellow rapper-turned-popster Dizzee Rascal, on the chilly Mosh Pit--but essentially the music is there to serve his observant lyrics.

Title: Summer Make Good
Review: While Múm's music has always posed a mysterious, melodic invitation to the listener, their latest offering feels flat at times, with very few signposts marking the way and even fewer landmarks inviting one back again.

Title: Amputechture
Review: It's solid, but as with Radiohead's Kid A follow-up Amnesiac, it highlights its predecessor's brilliance rather than asserting its own.

Title: Future Women
Review: One hell of a catchy album that gets better and better with each successive listening.

Title: Cloud Nine
Review: His debut album, Cloud Nine, is naturally very same-y--deep house wasting away in Margaritaville--but unfailingly gorgeous.

Title: A Billion Heartbeats
Review: It’s a wildly successful take on the world at large as the band enter a new decade. Far from just indie survivors, it seems like these Jets have still got plenty of fuel left in the tank.

Title: Alvvays
Review: Leaving themselves with no room for filler, the band set out to deliver on the promise of their singles, and we're thrilled to report that they've succeeded. Stardom beckons.

Title: Six Lethargies
Review: A challenging but far from inaccessible work. [Jan 2020, p.91]

Title: Something Dirty

Title: Frances The Mute

Title: Bare

Title: Lost Domain
Review: Dripping with raw emotion, Tim Wheeler's solo debut is a moving memorial to his father George. [Jan 2015, p.79]

Title: Waxing Gibbous

Title: The Seer
Review: The Seer delivers on its promise. It's an exhausting and maddening document, but one can't help but emerge from it filled with a renewed radiance.

Title: Culture of Fear
Review: While all of that emotional corruption may still tear their home planet apart, this trip-hop intergalactic train has reached its slice of space jazz heaven.

Title: Bloodlines

Title: Laws of Illusion
Review: All of McLachlan’s sonic trademarks are present and accounted for — dreamy keyboard washes, lilting rhythms, that angelic voice. They’re combined with her raw emotion in a beguiling manner that ranges from ethereal to rollicking.

Title: We Fall
Review: The arrangements provide a plush, tuneful backdrop for lyrics that proffer sympathy but also twist the knife.

Title: Colour the Small One

Title: Body Language
Review: You can’t help but get lost in Minogue’s music.

Title: Fetch
Review: Melt-Banana prove with Fetch that they can twist their peculiar universe into something more cordial, but one that forfeits a certain part of their penchant for risk.

Title: Mug Museum

Title: Microcastle

Review: The new industrial influences and heavily distorted textures work amazingly well at times, but after a few songs you find yourself longing for something resembling a melody.

Title: Beard, Wives, Denim

Title: Self Entitled

Title: Paper Trail

Review: The nearest to a rock record Thompson has ever made. ... A very good album. [Oct 2018, p.83]

Title: Divers
Review: Divers, her unusually tight fourth album, is full of lofty concepts (‘Waltz Of The 101st Lightborne’ sees time-travelling soldiers wage a futile war on their own ghosts) but her crafty tales, signposted by ornate folk arrangements, rarely outpace your imagination.

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: For the most part, Made In The Dark pulses with an unusual intelligence and creative bravery. [Mar 2008, p.101]

Title: Rewild
Review: It’s all very lush and fabulous, but also restrained and calculated to the point of coldness. If that’s intentional, they’ve pulled it off, but not necessarily to the album’s benefit.

Title: Dizzy Heights
Review: Finn sounds best when Dizzy Heights is at its dizziest, when he has to completely rethink how his voice fits a song. On the other hand, he sounds slightly less engaged on the more straightforward tunes, which perhaps don’t offer the same heady challenges.

Title: In Prism
Review: Even if it's not their best ever, it's a valid comeback that should appease longing fans.

Title: Negotiations
Review: Summers and Weikel work incredibly well together on Negotiations. Summers' haunting voice and shimmering guitars roll and intertwine with Weikel's drum and synth work effortlessly. It's an album that may take an extended listen, but once you key in, you won't shake it off.

Title: theFREEhoudini
Review: Currently billed as a precursor to the “official” new Themselves album that is to appear before the year’s end, the rejuvenation of his pioneering outfit that is heard on theFREEhoudini already feels like a mission accomplished.

Title: Octahedron
Review: Is Octahedron the band's best album? No, but if you dig on MV's unrepentantly "big" and meandering suite-driven concept-album thing, you won't necessarily be disappointed.

Title: If You're Dreaming
Review: The songs on If You're Dreaming, the second album from Anna Burch, don't so much play as they do float by.

Title: Wonky
Review: Further confirmation of the enduring strength of old-school electronic music.

Title: Under the Blacklight
Review: Under the Blacklight is at once more ethereal that anything Rilo Kiley has ever managed previously.

Title: Option Paralysis
Review: Option Paralysis may be considered a side-step by some, but there are so many exuberant flourishes and cleverly thought out harmonies that it's probably better to consider it a mind-boggling step over. The Dillinger Escape Plan isn't out of tricks just yet.

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: Wenu Wenu is a jubilant seven-track song suite that showcases the genre’s rhythmic and lyrical versatility.

Title: Rubberband
Review: While it was unfinished and framed in '80s studio tropes, their attempt to complete it with modern charts and muddy, hip-hop-styled mix weighs down what remains of the original proceedings.

Title: Get There
Review: A predominantly lush, lovely rendered debut that is never less than pleasant. Unfortunately, it’s seldom more than that either as these amiable tunes drift on a dreamy haze that threatens to slide into a memorable chorus or melody, but seldom does.

Title: The Practice of Love
Review: The Practice of Love is a powerful and joyous offering from one of the last artists anyone could ever accuse of playing it safe. Her unorthodox observations ('She found stretch mark cream / In an Airbnb bathroom') are, more so than ever before, full of wit, bite and beauty.

Title: Cold Roses
Review: Cold Roses’ first set is by-the-numbers, brokenhearted MOR fare, sometimes maudlin (“When Will You Come Back Home?”), infrequently dramatic (the piano-driven “How Do You Keep Love Alive”) and mostly forgettable. The second disc redeems Cold Roses from an even-less-enthusiastic recommendation.

Title: Legion of Boom
Review: To Jordan and Kirkland's credit, they let their guest stars shine without sacrificing the Crystal Method sound. [18 Jan 2004]

Title: Nocturne
Review: Minor criticisms aside, this is still a highly enjoyable record that knocks spots off most of the competition still tripping over each other's shoelaces to be the most shambolic lo-fi band in town.

Title: Alternative Light Source
Review: Despite the extended sabbatical, Leftfield’s muscular, invigorating presence remains undimmed.

Title: For Screening Purposes Only
Review: Without question, for all its eclecticism, "For Screening Purposes Only" is a dumb, disposable record that no one will listen to in 12 months' time.

Title: The Haunted Man
Review: The Haunted Man is so effortlessly emotive that it seems to demand that we demand even more from it. Or at least, it would, if it weren't so easy to get lost in the many layers of these melodies and start thinking about the ghosts that Bat For Lashes is trying to chase away.

Title: Innundir Skinni
Review: Simple, slightly silly but splendidly affecting, it's a telling suggestion that Arnalds will retain her endearingly obtuse edge, whatever language she favours in future.

Title: Human
Review: The huskiness that defined Brandy's prior work has been replaced by wispier and higher tones. The result is pleasant but far less ambitious than her last CD, 2004's "Afrodisiac."

Title: Music Tapes for Clouds and Tornadoes
Review: Clouds and Tornadoes ricochets back and forth between these three levels: the familiar, the unfamiliar but recognizable, and the unfamiliar and unrecognizable, and like Maddin and Katchor, it’s this tripartite feeling that gives the music its uniqueness while still feeling like an unearthed artifact.

Title: Impressions
Review: It's an indulgence for the ABBA fan inside us all, and sometimes we just have to give in. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.77]

Title: The New Danger
Review: Unfortunately, irrational moments like “The Rape Over” make you question the entire 17-track outing.

Title: American Life
Review: It's a record about being Madonna. [Jun 2003, p.90]

Title: 6 Feet Beneath the Moon
Review: At its core, Krule is showing all sides of his U.K. environment, and the multiple genres laced into the sparse backdrop are held together by an overlying somber grey fog. Peel that back and you have one of the most vital debuts of the year.

Title: Out Among the Stars
Review: It proves that even at his most uninterested, Cash couldn't help but make a record with weight, moral complexity and grim humor.

Title: The Beautiful Lie
Review: Harcourt's fourth album certifies his musical genius with songs that are catchy enough to be plastered all over the summer airwaves, bathing us in sweeping melodies and infectious beats.

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Monsanto Years
Review: This is Young the aged bellwether, raging about the state of the world with the focus of someone with little left to lose.

Title: Up
Review: The veteran artiste holds his ground on a collection that is sure to earn him the respect of not only his old fans but a new generation of listeners raised on sonic provocateurs like Beck, Nine Inch Nails, and Moby.

Title: The World's Best American Band
Review: Consistently cheeky, head-throbbing rock ("Judy French," "Party Next Door") meets shimmering melodies ("Little Silver Cross," "Daisies") that alleviate without losing momentum.

Title: In Time
Review: The Mavericks understand the potency of a band that plays as a solid unit and embellishes that sound accordingly--not quite brazen, but flaring with machismo.

Title: The New Classic
Review: Student’s complete commitment to character and form compensate slightly for the unrelenting weirdness of this project.

Title: End It All
Review: Quick on the draw, Beans bosses a bite-sized blitz of syllable practice.

Title: Some Cities
Review: As has always been the case with Doves, aural environment-building sometimes seems to be all the band has going for it, like on "Someday Soon," which uses sudden dramatic hushes and angelic choirs to pump life into a ballad that's practically melody-free. But at least the practice helps Doves make its few great songs count.

Title: Quiet Nights
Review: While fans looking for a classic, none-too-jarring soundtrack for a romantic evening surely will follow this record happily into their good night, Krall has offered us more than that in the past.

Title: Free Spirit
Review: On the new album, Khalid embraces a fuller sound that often harks back to the 1980s and 1990s, with pillowy synthesizers, tickling guitars and multiple layers of his own vocal harmonies.

Title: Ledges
Review: Ledges seems effortless in its creation. [No. 106, p.55]

Title: The Greatest
Review: Marshall wanders into lulling Orton/Portishead turf so often that it's easy to imagine some of these songs oozing out of the PA system at your local Banana Republic. [27 Jan 2006, p.80]

Title: Good Mourning
Review: Their best by a mile. [Jun 2003, p.100]

Title: Put Your Back N 2 It
Review: But where Learning drifted into the ether, this captivating follow-up thrives off harnessing his fragile sensibility to fulsome melodies.

Title: Crimson
Review: Crimson may not be AK3s best album, but it’s a welcome, mature effort from one of Vagrant’s best bands.

Title: Port of Miami 2
Review: Most of his 10th album, Port of Miami 2, is Ross exactly as you know and love him: the obscene boasts, the window-cracking bass, the speedboat cool, the various spins on raps-to-riches success.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Only Deerhunter makes echoes without egos, grounding even Bradford Cox's most wayward divergences in an all-encompassing blend of simple rock stylings.

Title: The Carpenter
Review: Save for the opening "The Once and Future Carpenter", about a woodworker who abandons his trade to wander, this second album is pretty dismal fare.

Title: The Marshall Mathers LP
Review: Aside from the horrifyingly detailed stalker narrative of "Stan" and the homicidal fantasy of "Kim," nothing on Marshall Mathers rises above the level of locker-room insults -- nearly every song seems to feature Eminem's giving someone the finger.

Title: The Open Door
Review: The Open Door is an exercise in how not to make a sophomore album (or any album for that matter).

Title: Making a New World
Review: Fans of Field Music will be absolutely overjoyed with this set, and of course, fans of '80s art rock will be in their element. Those put off by the unwieldy concept ultimately have nothing to fear – the WWI themes are completely ignorable, and so disparately connected that the only reason you’d ever know they were there was if somebody told you in advance.

Title: Creep On Creepin' On
Review: Creep On Creepin' On is a richly textured, intriguing piece of work that bears up well to repeated listens.

Title: Emerald City
Review: Throughout Emerald City, Vanderslice uses his celebrated producing talent to control feedback and mold it into an instrument as vital as the guitar and piano that are so central to his music.
It's definitely in the family tradition. [Oct 2006, p.112]

Title: Big Inner
Review: He's made one of the great albums of modern Americana, and one suspects that a reluctant star is born.

Title: Stubborn Persistent Illusions
Review: As a genre post-rock is certainly stubborn and persistent in the face of rocky times for guitar music, but its value is no illusion if Do Make Say Think’s latest is anything to go by.

Title: Deleter
Review: Tipping closer to dance-pop than noise-rock, Deleter is one of Holy Fuck's most finely tuned albums, yet the band sound as spontaneous as ever.

Title: Lost Horizons
Review: Think early Air meets hip-hop, the West Coast harmonies and Ultramarine-style tech-fok eccentricities merging with euphoric yet becalmed moodscapes. [Nov 2002, p.113]

Title: @#%&*! Smilers
Review: This time, the strong songwriting and astute musical arrangements combine to make Mann's latest her best album so far.

Title: Your Need
Review: Both celebratory and melancholy, this is an exceptionally strong album which effortlessly compels repeated listens.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: It may seem disappointing to those looking for further progress in one of the best American bands of recent times, but in the end it all comes down to the songs, and most of the ones here are little gems, perfect for a summer morning.

Title: The Forgotten Arm
Review: While the music here isn't as good as that on Bachelor, the strict structure does help give The Forgotten Arm direction, helping shape it into one of her more consistent albums.

Title: Savage Times
Review: Savage Times inevitably captures the tenor of its times as the Left Coast watched America turn rightward. [Mar 2017, p.26]

Title: Record
Review: In the wrong hands, Record’s subject matter could have been heavy going, but these songs are graceful, masterful, airy, bubbly and even a lot of fun.

1989 is a deeply catchy, sleekly-produced pop record with the slightly juiceless quality of an authorized biography, a would-be tell-all bleached of the detailed insight she’s trained us to expect from her.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: It's a knock-out.

Title: Ester
Review: An incredibly interesting debut album that's nearly as clever as its creators intended.

Title: Culture II
Review: It may well be overwhelming in the moment, but Migos have provided us with a lot to unpack as we await whatever comes next. Chances are, you'll like this album far more after the glut of material becomes a tad less staggering over some months.

Title: New
Review: [Working with four young producers] isn't necessarily an ideal recipe for coherence, but [Giles] Martin--the producer of the music for Love, Circue du Soleil's Beatles show, and for the Rock Band video game--keeps it under control.... with each song treated as an individual entity and allocated its own musical resources. [Nov 2013, p.64]

Title: Dylanesque
Review: More hit than miss. [30 Jun 2007]

Title: Twins
Review: In exciting displays of versatility throughout the album, Segall grimes it up then unplugs, freaks out then holds back, wails then moans--all in utter confidence.

Title: How to Be a Human Being
Review: How To Be A Human Being shows a band who know how to Frankenstein a song together, but can't bring it to life. [Nov 2016, p.107]

Title: The Bears for Lunch
Review: No new tricks, but there's life in these old dogs yet.

Title: Grey Oceans
Review: No matter your feeling on CocoRosie, whether love them for their innovation or hate them for their grating pretension, when you hear Grey Oceans you might find yourself missing those more challenging (or more inventive) days.

Title: Issues
Review: Issues put enough of their own spin on things to feel like something new, which feels like a praiseworthy accomplishment in an increasingly homogenous genre.

Title: Good Luck and Do Your Best
Review: This one feels more grounded, less frantic and, despite that constant pulsing movement, more at home. [#361, p.109]

Title: Empress
Review: This is R&B that is considered and it is timeless, done exactly the way that Ekwere clearly wants it to be done. Empress is brilliant. Ray BLK has earned a spot at the top of the R&B heap. Hand her the crown.

Title: MGMT
Review: The swampy, claustrophobic MGMT is never as interesting or smart as the crowd-pleasing sing-alongs on Oracular Spectacular.

Title: Thickfreakness
Review: Thickfreakness is an unrelentingly dour record - perhaps this music was best left in the past.

Title: Cope
Review: Indentations is the pleasing exception. A slowed down, emotionally visceral tune, it demonstrates that Manchester Orchestra have a real breadth in their songwriting.

Title: Painting of a Panic Attack
Review: Less swelling, more sand pits, the moments of crescendo here are few and far between.

Title: Leona Naess
Review: Sure, it takes some time to sink in, but once it gets a hold of your heart, it won't let go.

Title: Coco Beware
Review: The songs feel like the first days of fall, where you're clinging to that last bit of summer warmth while eagerly anticipating the slower pace of a city being cooled.

Title: Turn to Clear View
Review: It blends jazz, funk, dub and electronic sounds into a seamless, at times psychedelic whole. [Nov 2019, p.66]

Title: Milk Money
Review: By the end, the dizzying and beautiful piece expresses the fury and unpredictability of life while maintaining a zen-like calm at its core, finding clarity just as easily as it rises to chaos.

Title: Switzerland
Review: Switzerland lacks any track with even a tenth of the standout potential of Danger! High Voltage. And it's a critical absence for Switzerland, because there's nothing on this record that makes you want to hear it a second time.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: There is only one real slip - Stephen Fry's mood shattering appearance on the title track. [Dec. 2001 p. 123]

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: Wenu Wenu cleans up Souleyman's music just enough to place it in an expanded musical and sonic context that creates a new frontier without sacrificing its power.

Title: The Eternal
Review: There is an excitable, almost naive quality to its visceral riffs and enthusiastic name-checks of artists, poets and countercultural figures.

Title: Absent Friends
Review: While Hannon's aesthetic/literary weltanschauung is rather haughty, it succeeds by sheer force of intellect and style. [#11, p.95]

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: It's mostly a thing of pleasing lonesome grooves--but there are moments where it sounds like the Mahavishnu Orchestra tuning up.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: Flares dazzlingly on initial contact, but dims a little. [Jun 2004, p.92]

Title: A New Illusion
Review: There is great life and verve in these songs, teeming, irrepressible. Listen closely and you can hear the record breathing.

Title: American Goldwing
Review: About half of American Goldwing owes more to Faulkner than Jack London.

Title: Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys
Review: Danger Days definitely isn't worth it. If nothing else, it makes me interested to see where they'll go from here, but I find it saddening that the most likely future for them seems to be a breakup after this uninspired mess of an album.

Title: Gold Record
Review: The new record is pretty sparse in terms of its recording tones, very dry, and, in that respect, it owes a lot to skeleton-sparse Smog records like Kicking a Couple Around. But while that EP, another gem, seems to expand in its quiet moments, suggesting all sorts of dark narratives, heartbreak conceits, and hidden dialogues, the distance between Callahan's voice and the material he surrounds it here will leave some broader declarations up for grabs.

Title: Sucker
Review: Finally, a top 40 album that attempts to capture the restless energy of recent times and spit it out in a way that doesn't just feel good, but honest, too.

Title: thank u, next
Review: It’s contradictory, assured yet tender. It’s delicate but strong. It’s sweet pop music wrapped in an unbreakable metal shell. It’s beautiful but vulgar. It is, frankly, much more than we could have ever hoped for from her.

Title: Geocidal
Review: Geocidal is a fascinating listen purely for the fact that it acknowledges no boundaries: musical, geographical or otherwise. You may not love it; you may not even like it; but you'll pay rapt attention regardless. What it lacks in immediacy, the duo's debut album makes up for in sheer spirit.

Title: Welcome Home Armageddon
Review: FFAF have produced another pop-punk special with Welcome Home Armageddon--and, thankfully, they don't look like stopping any time soon.

Title: Capo
Review: Dipset's gruff second-in-command serves up a new set of drugged-up hustler tunes. [15 Apr 2011, p. 87]

Title: You're Welcome
Review: Originally whittled down from 40 songs Williams had penned from a jumble of sample-led ideas, You’re Welcome nonetheless features Wavves proverbial fuzzy guitar distortions and surf vibes, but includes his explorative forays into ‘70s psychedelia from South America, Cambodian pop and his obsession of ‘50s doo-wop.

Title: Loyalty to Loyalty
Review: Cold War Kids have exploded rather than refined their style here, which too often turns what were formerly strengths into liabilities and turns what were formerly liabilities into, well, even greater liabilities.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: Pleasant, yes, but not much more.... Too many of these 'songs' snap off at around the three or four minute mark, just as they start to get interesting.... It sounds consistently half-there. [#208, p.52]

Title: Ventura
Review: It's easy to imagine a superior album being made from sequencing it with the best of its predecessor. But there's a simple, unassuming quality that would be lost if you did.

Title: Catching a Tiger
Review: Cohesion will come soon; she's got all the nuts and bolts.

Title: i,i
Review: For the first time here, his ideas haven’t quite formed into a cohesive whole. All the other records felt complete works, this feels more like a collection. For all that really works on i,i, there are moments that feel unnecessary or out of place.

Title: Say It
Review: Their tics are still here--just listen to how they build the payoff of “Nova Leigh” from a variety of angles--they just aren’t the exciting focal point anymore. That’s probably better in the long run for the band, who have all quit school to rep Born Ruffians full-time, but doesn’t lead Say It to the mountaintop it could have shared with Red, Yellow and Blue.

Title: Go Forth
Review: A maddeningly spacy, fairly inconsistent, but very rich set of songs that capitalize on the leftover space from guitarist Gibb Slife's departure.

Title: The Ownerz
Review: There's plenty here to celebrate for consistency's sake-- because for what they've lacked in evolution, Guru and Premier have more than repaid in reliability.

Title: The Stepkids
Review: It gives all sorts of instrumentation the confidence to surprise us. [Nov 2011, p.102]

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: Lovely strings, flute and backing vocals occasionally shed some light, but mostly this is Cave playing it slow, hushed and haunted.

Title: Guero
Review: It sounds like a shadow greatest-hits album, a collection of also-rans offering intriguing variations on past styles.

Title: Hotel
Review: The slower stuff vagues out, and the bonus disc of ambient instrumentals ought to come with a controlled substance, but elegant relationship songs such as the torchy "Forever" suggest this talented softy has found a sensible way to come down from a multiplatinum high.

Title: North
Review: It's art music first and pop second. [Oct 2003, p.115]

Title: Deeper
Review: It’s sharp, the beats are punchier, and by utilising similar methods to production as techno, he's made his best album yet.

Title: The Neon
Review: Erasure has yet to really match the duo's early imperial phase, but here Andy Bell and Vince Clarke dish out the cosmic showstoppers with all the elan of their 30-year-old selves. [Oct 2020, p.31]

Title: Dig Out Your Soul
Review: Dig Out Your Soul continues Oasis' relatively impressive late-period resurgence.

Title: Yung Rich Nation
Review: It all sounds like a victory lap rather than a step forward, but perhaps that’s just as well.

Title: Trouble Maker
Review: They care not a whit about market share, EDM remixers or having annoying YouTube stars and/or rappers guest on their sessions, choosing instead to light up psychic votive candles for Joe Strummer, Desmond Dekker and Lemmy in order to capture the very same spirit those artists conjured all those decades ago.

Title: Attack & Release
Review: To be sure, it's an accomplishment and one that showcases the Black Keys' deepening skills but at times it's hard not to miss how the duo used to grab a listener by the neck and not let go.

Title: Any Random Kindness
Review: The band's second album finds HÆLOS expanding on their core sound while reminding themselves and the listener of just why they are such an exciting and intriguing outfit.

Title: The Body, The Blood, The Machine
Review: A little too homogenous to warrant many a repeat listen.

Title: Helium
Review: Fresh Air and Midnight Snack. Sagar sounds lethargic and detached, which may be the mood that he's going for; but when he sticks to the same tired motifs, it's hard to feel any more excited than him.

Title: Tomorrow's Hits
Review: Tomorrow’s Hits doesn’t boom like The Men’s early material (namely, 2010’s Immaculada and 2011’s Leave Home), but it’s more rousing instrumentally than last year’s New Moon.

Title: Locked Down
Review: A mystical brew of funk, gospel and delta rock.

Title: Somebody's Knocking
Review: There is something for every Mark Lanegan fan. It is also a good starting point for those unaware of his music. The only mildly bothering element is the production, since it doesn’t fit every tune. On the upside, there’s a rawness to the guitars and especially the vocals (most of the time they sound as if he’s singing in your room in front of you). Even so, during the multi-layered parts, some details get lost in a muddy pool of reverb.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: Underpinning the shots White fires at the world has always been a deep-seated melancholy that she brings out effectively here.

Title: Meltdown
Review: Ultimately, Meltdown isn’t as dramatic a failure as its title seems to be begging me to pronounce it--in fact it isn’t really a failure at all. It’s just a crucial dip in momentum.

Title: Road to Rouen
Review: Road to Rouen isn't entirely the stuff of rocking chairs and Sunday drives, but it is the first Supergrass record to champion an overall vibe over immediacy.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: The mood is more melancholy than the lineup would suggest — much of the album sounds like ''Waterloo Sunset''-era Kinks set to languid dub grooves.

Title: Let the Poison Out
Review: The Beets' newfound focus on recording quality could have easily highlighted shortcomings, but instead, the band found a way to broaden its sound by recruiting a member who exponentially adds to its worth.

Title: Build a Nation
Review: While Bad Brains never quite match the intensity of their early days, this is easily the best record they've released since Quickness.

Title: thank u, next
Review: Thank U, Next stands as what promises to be one of the best pop releases this year.

Title: Veni Vidi Vicious
Review: They almost vindicate the near-deafening hoopla that preceded this major-label debut. [10 May 2002, p.80]

Title: Familiar Touch
Review: If Perpetual Surrender had elements of woozy, chillwave, Familiar Touch is full-scale yacht-rock sophistication, with honed chorus hooks and silken arrangements rippling with precision curves. [Jan 2017, p.94]

Title: I Sell the Circus
Review: I Sell the Circus is an uneven collection from an artist clearly torn between the future and his past.

Title: Reverse
Review: In the sure hands of Pinhas and his comrades, Reverse is big enough to contain emotional multitudes.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: A uniformly strong collection of sharp-eyed, sardonic allegories.

Title: An Other Cup
Review: These new tunes are lovely, thoughtful and gentle, though they don't quite match his best songs.

Title: Tough Love
Review: It is tempered and classic-sounding. But the sounds are as itchy and oppressive as they are tasteful.

Title: Face Control
Review: Happily, their latest album, Face Control--recorded after the duo stormed the clubs of Eastern Europe for inspiration--is a huge improvement.

Title: Darling of the Afterglow
Review: Here, it’s clear Ainsworth understands the importance of experimentation, building something familiar yet otherworldly.

Title: Last Exit
Review: Greenspan... manages to fold elements of nearly a quarter-century of forward-looking pop into a distinct sound without sounding either conceptual or trading on contradictions or the smoke-and-mirrors of attention-grabbing eclecticism.

Title: Sunken Condos
Review: Donald's back in his self-referencing sweet-spot, and all's right with the world. [Nov 2012, p.69]

Title: Fear of a Black Tangent
Review: Busdriver is either an emcee from the future or the future of the emcee.

Title: Rare
Review: Rare is shockingly, and beautifully, upbeat.

Title: Diver
Review: Diver's appeal is immediate, its effect short and sharp. [Sep 2012, p.104]

Title: Mermaid Avenue Vol. II
Review: Displays a broader sonic reach than its predecessor.

Title: Double Down
Review: The smart-arse-ometer goes off the scale from time to time and a thin production hardly helps matters, but when Deez gets snappy on Kill Your Attitude and Melange Mining Co, he's far from a lost cause. [Oct 2015, p.104]

Title: SIR
Review: Sir is as extroverted as Spooner’s recent experiences, but some occasional, additional restraint may have added extra punch to its more introverted moments.

Title: You Can Play These Songs with Chords
Review: Takes us on a tour of how things got started and where they could be going.

Title: A Constant Sea
Review: After the third track “Christine” floats past like a lost Julee Cruise track on soulful blues guitar and vintage 50s’ keys, the LP takes a surprising but effective turn into heavy, murky territory.

Title: Blue with Lou
Review: A less-cluttered and more intimate take on “Remember You” might well have increased its potency as the closing cut. Nevertheless, the ‘less is more’ premise remains in effect just often enough on Blue For Lou to certify the record, name associations aside, as a memorable entry in the lengthy discography of Nils Lofgren.

Title: Magnetic
Review: It'll be too sappy for anyone who likes their rock raw, but if simpler pleasures tickle your pickle, there are few bands in this sphere pulling it off as expertly as the veteran Buffalo trio. [8 Jun 2013, p.54]

Title: Drum's Not Dead
Review: A stunning achievement and the first exceptionally great album of 2006.

Title: North
Review: It's a downbeat record that reclaim's dubstep's original dark energy and experimental imperative.

Title: Thin Mind
Review: Thin Mind speaks to the concerns of an age fraught with ennui and commodification; much-needed social commentary scored with the understated, melodic, often allusive edge that is the outfit’s creative stamp.

Title: Urban Turban - The Singhles Club
Review: Inconsistency's a little too much the watchword, but there are none more Something For Everyone.

Title: All This Sounds Gas
Review: Includes everything from Brighten The Corners-sounding pop blasts to comforting acoustic gems to dark rockers. [Nov 2001, p.91]

Title: Keel Her
Review: Taken as a three quarters of an hour lump, the narrowness of her vision is brought into sharp relief, as Keeler-Schaffeler struggles to salvage a bona fide record from admirably restless blogging.

Title: GINGER
Review: There are plenty of hooks here, but nothing to make a festival tent bounce like ‘Boogie’ or ‘Gold’ can. It’s a small criticism, though, on an album that resets Brockhampton’s compass and sees them straying away from the danger of implosion that ‘Iridescence’ seemed to suggest.

Title: Life Journey
Review: A little too shiny and over produced in places, but Life Journey is a trip worth taking. [Jul 2014, p.92]

Title: Ascent
Review: Despite a sharp shift in direction, the spirit of Ascent floats--sometimes upwards, at times skittish and swooping underneath clouds--but nonetheless rising.

Title: The Budos Band III
Review: With martial trumpets, cheap-sounding Farfisa organs and raspy baritone saxes, there are certainly nods toward Ethiopiques legends like Mulatu Astatke or the Wallas Band, tracks like "Rite Of The Ancients" and "Golden Dunes" add a rugged garage rock, and riff-based funk of "Black Venom" has a breakbeat that's just begging to be sampled by a bright hip hop producer. [Nov 2010, p.83]

Title: Drones
Review: Muse’s seventh album is--happily--anything but diminished.

Title: Nellyville
Review: Good-natured and breezy enough to make the hostility directed Nelly's way seem churlish.

Title: Heartleap
Review: This is the distilled, finely crafted essence of Bunyan: a hushed, reflective meditation of an album that seems to have the welcome effect of cancelling out the world around the listener.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: Magic.... Its rhapsodies present a portait of an artist at an early height of his powers. [Feb 2005, p.102]

Title: Colour the Small One
Review: Repeat listens reveal the album to be what the one-time Zero 7 vocalist describes as a "slow burner," a druggy mesh of acoustic guitars, keyboards, and lush, cinematic string arrangements.

Title: Kellie Pickler
Review: There are individual moments of accomplishment, but the album is like a Whitman Sampler, with a sweet tidbit for listeners in pretty much any stage of a romantic relationship, leading to a fairly scattered emotional palette.

Title: Black Age Blues
Review: Not only is Black Age Blues Goatsnake's best album, it is an instant classic of the stoner-doom hybrid and an earthy, electrifying endgame for rock & roll itself.

Title: I Feel Alive
Review: For there’s a lot to enjoy on I Feel Alive, but the general feeling of lovelorn listlessness can take its toll on a full listen.

Title: An Album by Korallreven
Review: If you give the album the chance it deserves you will be rewarded by one of the strongest LPs you are likely to hear this year.

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: There isn’t a single moment on EWBAITE when I wasn’t second guessing my feelings, and that makes it interesting to me, if not necessarily as interesting as some of their other post-reunion records.

Title: 10,000 Hz Legend
Review: The resulting mélange doesn’t always work, but the songs on 10,000HZ Legend still succeed often enough to override the record’s occasional shortcomings.

Title: The Sound of Music
Review: There's a couple of additions to the soundtrack in the shape of Korean folk standards "Arirang" and "The Sound of Gayageum" along with an address from the North Korean minister for Cultural Relations tagged onto the end.

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: Feed the Animals is a wonderful achievement, but don’t take my pseudo-intellectual pontification as proof of anything, go listen to it yourself.

Title: The Way Out
Review: It's been a long stretch since their last full-length album, 2005's Lost and Safe, but The Way Out exhibits the care the pair takes in meticulously crafting these constructions.

Title: Willowbank
Review: Willowbank is utterly charming, shimmering and another step in Yumi Zouma’s quietly fascinating evolution.

Title: Imperial
Review: The tracks give the listener a greater appreciation for RObin's contribution to the Twins. [#5, p.106]

Title: Youth
Review: In 13 songs, Wild Cub creates infectious, intricate electro-pop that blends ‘80s beats with electronics and synths worthy of the aughts.

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: Comes on like an evil Duran Duran making future music for damaged teens.... It's both disturbingly compelling and very, very wrong. [Jun 2003, p.112]

Title: The Wolf
Review: Just because W.K. has found his soft center lyrically, it doesn't mean the music has lost any of its hard core. [12 Sep 2003, p.150]

Title: Walk It Off
Review: The album as a whole finds a strange homogeny, and Tapes 'N Tapes keep exploring hip, leaving everyone guessing as to whether they meant to make such a confusing outfit or the pieces were just on sale.

Title: Skull Worship
Review: Although not quite being the pièce de résistance Bobby Hecksher and co. were hoping for, Skull Worship is a welcome return and when all's said and done, the musical landscape would be a much duller place without them.

Title: Moh Lhean
Review: Moh Lhean sounds a little more mature, but only relatively speaking. The project remains a creative burst of sounds, grooves, and stylized observation that's uniquely refreshing to those open to its quirky complexity.

Title: Streetlights
Review: There are moments here, but ultimately Streetlights pales against BlaQKout, the Kurupt/DJ Quik collaboration that dropped last year.

Title: Donkey
Review: For the most part, Donkey flounders in a sterile morass. It may well bring CSS to a larger audience, one that doesn't consider subversiveness an impediment, but that doesn't make it any less disappointing.

Title: Ripe 4 Luv
Review: Throughout Ripe 4 Luv you can sense that it’s taking every ounce of discipline Cook has to play these pop songs as straight as he does, so he can be forgiven for indulging a little kitsch at the finish line.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: Sweet Heart Sweet Light is infused with an uplifting lust for life.

Title: Overpowered
Review: The result is a delight. [Nov 2007, p.115]

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: Last Day Of Summer confirms that White Denim have a broad understanding of music as a whole... Their ability to synthesise this knowledge makes them one of the most thrilling forces in rock music right now. [Jan 2012, p.96]

Title: Charmer
Review: Her livelier numbers, of which there are quite a few, aren't exactly frivolous, but they have a pulse and plenty of color which, combined with album's concise running time, give Charmer the feel of an immediate, engaging pop record.

Title: Fields
Review: They may not yet have a strong enough aesthetic to make a great album, but they've made a unique, highly promising one that might soon create something which can bring Gonzalez's academics into the realm of something softer. In the way his best songs and covers were, and still could be.

Title: We Got a Love
Review: Although he doesn’t offer the genre anything noticeably new, he’s more than capable to keep the momentum going over a long player.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: Dirty Projectors is not quite that good [Primal Scream’s Screamadelica]--few records are--but it certainly drives a stake into the ground as to what guitar bands could deliver in 2017 if they would only open their ears and minds up a little.

Title: Silence Is Easy
Review: Sounds like Coldplay covering Barry Manilow.

Title: The Wild Hunt
Review: Innovative? Absolutely not. But as 35 minutes of 50-quid-bloke folky guitar music goes, it's near impeccable.

Title: Cover Two
Review: Joan Wasser's second covers set finds romance in Prince's lust-blind Kiss and innocence in the Strokes' Under Control. [Jul 2020, p.88]

Title: An Awesome Wave
Review: An Awesome Wave washes over its beached listeners, pleasantly cooling them for a second, then making its retreat back into an ocean of sameness.

Title: Two Dancers
Review: Much scruffier and far less inhibited than Coldplay, and way more compelling than Editors, Two Dancers is widescreen stuff nonetheless and an album that will carry them across more thresholds than their first.

Title: Nine
Review: Blink-182’s second album with Matt Skiba is ultimately subpar, weighed down by stereotypical lyrics and cloying choruses. Producers John Feldmann and Tim Pagnotta’s heavy use of compression makes NINE as in-your-face as possible, not giving the songs the necessary breathing room to develop without overproduction.

Title: Aa
Review: Nothing bores and the album moves through its track list with a purposeful flow, and while electro-trap fiends and "Harlem Shake" lovers may be thrown by all the artful noise, Aa still rocks the house, as Baauer evolves from meme generator to master craftsman.

Title: Art in the Age of Automation
Review: By focussing in on softer deployments of electronics and more subtle processing, and staying resolutely in an ambient soundworld, Art In The Age Of Automation does feel comparatively safe; well turned-out and nicely polished, but generally risk-free in execution.

Title: Sweet Talker
Review: Unfortunately, after that impressive opening salvo ["Bang Bang"], the album largely relapses on tired MOR pop.

Title: The Kiss of Morning
Review: Finally finding a palatable singing voice, too, the musical acuity shown here still places him very much in front of guitar-hero peers like John Squire and Bernard Butler. [Dec 2002, p.129]

Title: Older Than My Old Man Now
Review: This marvelous album will resonate with sons, daughters, parents, spouses or those mindful of their mortality. In other words: everyone.

Title: Qualm
Review: Qualm, is a victory lap. It is, on paper, an uncomplicated beast: a live hardware workout of claustrophobic, rhythmic acid techno. But her ability to draw out harmonic elements from the cacophony of it all is deft--that cassette tape feel is still evident.

Title: Natural Rebel
Review: Natural Rebel, sadly, is paint-by-numbers singer-songwriting. For a 10-track album, it feels hideously overindulgent--only two songs fall under the four-minute mark, and those still feel drawn out by plodding, bog-standard riffs.

Title: Mastermind
Review: This is Ross at his least cohesive and most clueless since his 2006 debut, Port of Miami.

Title: What's My Name
Review: What’s My Name dares you to continue listening, to see if you can make it through its first song without spontaneously combusting from second-hand embarrassment, a spectral groan of “Grandaaad” escaping from your ashes as they sizzle and singe. ... But perhaps opening with such a heinous song is actually a genius move. In isolation, they might not fare so well but, after that, nothing else sounds as bad.

You can hear an early, instrumental version of 'Someone Great' here, and it's pretty melody, twinkling xylophones and pulsing synths are mesmerising enough to take your mind off the pain of physical exertion.

Title: II
Review: The production on II is cleaner than on Fuzz's first studio album without ironing out the nooks and crannies of the band's sound (the report of Moothart and Ubovich's amps is just as fierce and buzzy as ever), and listeners who resonate to Iommic frequencies will get a righteous shake from this music.

Title: Stone Temple Pilots
Review: There are a couple groovy licks scattered here and there which are half decent, but otherwise it's a tepid exercise in mediocrity difficult to even feign interest in.

Title: Boys Outside
Review: So Boys Outside has its experimental elements after all, but only by degrees. Mason starts with sturdily constructed songs, then loosens the screws one by one.

Title: In Times
Review: Enslaved have hit a sweet spot with In Times, experimenting just enough to keep everything interesting while also offering up pure aggressive pleasure so decadent it seems almost indulgent.

Title: To Record Only Water For Ten Days
Review: The formula here is for Frusciante to carve tunes out of loose, cyclical riffs, a few basic samples and drum programmes and his own parched voice. Sometimes, as on 'Remain', the effect is slightly uncomfortable... Tough that out, and get used to the demo quality throughout, and there are some decent songs on 'To Record Only Water,' endearing for their rawness and honesty.

Title: As Long as You Are
Review: herring's poetic analysis of a recent break-up makes it all a compelling listen. [Nov 2020, p.29]

Title: Songs of the Plains
Review: The set walks a fine line with its retro-fetishism, but it manages to dodge hokey-ness thanks to Wall’s great voice, a low-key delivery, and invitingly haunted backdrops by legends like Lloyd Green (pedal steel) and Mickey Raphael (harmonica). Time-travelling lyrics help, too.

Title: Music's Not for Everyone
Review: When the band's clattering, it's great fun ("Why Not"), but leave the tongue-in-cheek (or is it?) spoken-word title track at home and release the rock instead.

Title: Theosophy
Review: As ever there are reservations about Molinari's blase attitude to the second-hand song title, but it's still a solid, engaging set. [Jul 2014, p.111]

Title: Femme Fatale
Review: As long as Brit keeps the ballads to a minimum and plays to her strength as a willing pop renegade (which she does here more than on any of her previous albums), she will continue to make exciting, groundbreaking modern music.

Title: Two-Way Mirror
Review: West Coast eccentrics' second ambitious offering. [Sept. 2011, p. 104]

Title: Portamento
Review: In the place of anthems, though, are carefully constructed gems making up a sequencing run so solid it takes a few listens to pick out the exact drop-off point.

Title: Try Not To Freak Out
Review: While pulling no punches in discussing anxiety or uncertainty, their sparky indie punk still evokes sunny days and exhilarating nights. [16 Sep 2017, p.52]

Title: Comicopera
Review: It's a portrait of an English radical at 62, but it's personal and emotional and neither strident nor stodgy.

Title: m b v
Review: Regardless of whether it’s an echo of the past or a bridge to the future, MBV stands as something potentially timeless--and immediately breathtaking.

Title: An Obelisk
Review: A Productive Cough felt more like a genre exercise than a passion project, and that’s true of An Obelisk, too, except this time the genre is a far better fit.

Title: Songs for the Deaf
Review: Queens Of The Stone Age are the greatest heavy rock band on the face of the planet and soon everyone will know it.

Title: iridescence
Review: Hooks sparse and structure loose, Iridescence redefines future pop.

Title: Beat the Champ
Review: Despite the unlikely set-up, there’s a classic archetypical feel to the set as a whole.

Title: The Fine Art of Self Destruction
Review: Malin convincingly wraps his tortured warble around the dust-caked tunes. [#14, p.139]

Title: X
Review: A savvy, shiny, slyly sophisticated set of thoroughly modern dance floor exercises, it's the record we hoped Girls Aloud might make.

Title: Negative Capability
Review: There won't be a better record released this month, and very few this year. This is one for the ages. [Nov 2018, p.84]

Title: The Astonishing
Review: Not just vast in musical scope, The Astonishing offers an entire Dystopian world of its own, not to mention exhibiting the potential to be an overblown Broadway rock opera, eye-frazzling sci-fi movie and nerd-delighting video game into the bargain.

Title: Destroyer's Rubies
Review: An amalgam of Streethawk: A Seduction's glam rock posturing, This Night's guitar-heavy psychedelia, and Your Blues' apocalyptic wordplay.

Title: Immunity
Review: The singer, born Claire Cottrill, delivers on that early promise on Immunity, which widens her sound without sacrificing the intimacy or the charm of “Pretty Girl.”

Title: Amici
Review: Perhaps because there’s no bass (Primo! has added Amy Hill on bass since Amici), Primo!’s sound lacks a certain grind and tumult--it’s more Grass Widow than Good Throb--but it’s sharp and fresh and a lot of fun.

Title: Strange House
Review: What the Horrors do, they do well. [Jun 2007, p.148]

Title: To Be Still
Review: The result: something greater than the sum of its parts, and one of this year's lovelier albums.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: This album proves that Bird is up there with the kings of US alt.country pop like Lambchop and My Morning Jacket.

Title: Temporary Pleasure
Review: Efforts here lack urgency and a necessity to blow the doors off the club apparent on previous releases.

Title: Love Me
Review: Barfod has more faith in his electronics, and when he’s playing something he trusts, he permits the songs to venture out and reach greater emotional heights. But that comfort doesn’t extend to his human players, and his hesitation to let go and explore permeates the album.

Title: Madvillainy
Review: An outlandishly imaginative collaboration.

Title: All Your Favorite Bands
Review: All Your Favorite Bands is an inspired record full of space, swagger and warm, analog glow.

The real magic on 50 doesn’t come from the coterie of younger tyros, but the great buck himself. The frailty of the 75-year-old’s voice (he’ll be 76 when this album comes out) can render homespun parables as biblical portents, in much the same way that Rick Rubin reinvented Johnny Cash as a latter-day Nostradamus.

Title: Centipede Hz
Review: Centipede Hz feels celebratory.

Title: Humor Risk
Review: Everything is still flawed and everyone unredeemable on this album, but as a whole it doesn't grip completely like past gems.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: With everything from the classic symphonic sounds of brass and strings to the creative dimensions of electronic sampling, synths and the violinophone, Mum certainly are experimental. The ambitious nature of which could be too much for some people though.

Title: La Grande
Review: As you listen, you can easily picture a campfire in a forest, stars in the sky and Laura Gibson, guitar cradled in her arms, mumbling her way through an upbeat breezy folk song that implies some inner sadness while at the same time being entirely optimistic and happy.

Title: Object 47
Review: Object 47 is not a horrible record; it just isn’t all that good. It has none of the flare found on the band’s trilogy of classics and is never quite able to free itself from not-so-desirable labels like bland and unchallenging.

Title: Blood
Review: When it comes together--as on the bumping ode to Jamaica "Green & Gold," and the spare "Wonderful"--this album demands, and rewards, all the attention you can give it.

Title: Sumday
Review: It's a compelling psychological study set to lovely tunes. [Jul 2003, p.114]

Title: Loud
Review: Rihanna's latest collection Loud is another sure fire assault on the charts and airwaves. It highlights exactly the best and worst of today's pop aesthetic.

Title: Wind in the Wires
Review: Lies somewhere between Kate Bush and a deranged Divine Comedy. [Apr 2005, p.124]

Title: The Atlantic Ocean
Review: Swift's stock-in-trade remains droll, gently roistering piano songs, mostly indebted to Harry Nilsson. [May 2009, p.97]

Title: Surfing the Void
Review: Even Klaxons' most ominously rambunctious tracks grind out plenty of bug-eyed dream-pop chants.

Title: Colour the Small One
Review: If her murmurous slurring defies full comprehension, her gentle sadness, hesitant beats and melancholic piano settings match the odd clear phrase. [Mar 2004, p.102]

Title: The DEFinition
Review: LL does DEFinition with a superstar panache that never gets into that dangerously cheesy Will Smith territory and keeps it streetwise without putting on a front.

Title: The Jazz Age
Review: [Bryan Ferry] corkscrews the concept in an instrumental tribute nit only to the very first cocktail'n'cocaine era but also to his own serpentine melodic gifts. [Mar 2013, p.101]

Title: Annie Up
Review: A lark evolves into a business proposition as an album of 10 inspired three-minute songs eventuates in an album of 12 expert three-and-a-half-min​ute songs.

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: It's funny: just when Mascis seems like he might be getting into a rut or regurgitating the familiar, he comes from the left and surprises, making everything new again.

Title: Levitation
Review: It has a tendency to be superfluous--a stray tabla rhythm is never too far away--but ultimately it’s a fun record that’s clearly born of love and dedication. That’s something to be commended.

Title: Animal
Review: An occasionally fun, occasionally catchy pop record that will log a few hits, move a few units and ultimately be forgotten once this particular pop trend goes the way of Crunk, Snap Music, the Power Ballad and all the other castoffs in the ever-expanding pop graveyard.

Title: Arc
Review: Arc is a missive from the heart as well as the head. [Feb 2013, p.100]

Title: Incubation
Review: The record packs familiar Function trademarks--industrial themes, hissing white noise, acid loops and retro rhythms--but the ideas fall short of reinvigorating the legacy established after Sandwell Disctrict's full-length, Feed Forward, landed in 2010.

Title: On My Way
Review: Top-notch stuff. [#7]

Title: Finally Rich
Review: Production from the likes of Young Chop, Mike Will Made It, and Lex Luger propel Finally Rich since it's evident that Chief Keef cares just as much about precise lyricism as he does about keeping the peace on the Southside of Chicago. [Feb-Mar 2013, p.91]

Title: Hippo Lite
Review: At times, the record is just classically Surreal, a bucolic unheimlich provoking a fleeting confrontation with the unconscious. What remains most alluring about this experiment’s broken logic is the sense that you’re furtively occupying someone else’s dream.

Title: None Shall Pass
Review: The album isn’t without its faults--its probably too long, and though the production may differ from other albums, it blurs together somewhat over the course of the album. However, there’s one song on this album that renders all such complaints irrelevant--the title track. None Shall Pass is undoubtedly one of the best things Aesop has ever done

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: With Last Days on Earth, the persistently-versatile Noah continue to set to music those picturebooks of get-togethers, easy plateaus and break-ups that we've all got stored in our heads and add to year-on-year – and, in the process, they've managed to forge some great big tunes. More or less irresistible.

Title: Genesis
Review: It's not exactly a convincing change of gears, nor is it particularly groundbreaking--unless you consider jamming as many four-letter words as possible into three minutes (on "As I Come Back") novel.

Title: Buoys
Review: A fruitful addition to Lennox's one-of-a-kind audial metamorphism.

Title: Out Among the Stars
Review: Out Among the Stars is a boon for fans of country music history as well as those who just can’t get enough Cash. More importantly, it highlights a missing link between the often disparate eras of a long and complicated career.

Title: XTRMNTR
Review: The music sounds lean and direct, focused but exceedingly angry, like the band received a collective kick in the ass from some higher power.... The first masterpiece of the new millennium... [#26, p.46]

Title: Little Joy
Review: This debut could've, should've and would've been more appropriate as a moody summer release for trips with the car windows down, but instead we're forced to keep 'em up as winter nags at our sleeves. [Holiday 2008, p.100]

Title: The Ballad of Boogie Christ
Review: Bare acoustic tracks with fuller band on upbeat tunes all sung in pleasing, husky tones. [Oct 2013, p.98]

Title: The Bronx (IV)
Review: This LA-based hardcore band turns out their most consistently solid set of songs yet; a dozen tracks of distorted guitars, machine gun drumming and throat-reddening vocals.

Title: Oshin
Review: It's an album in the true sense, each song a building block on an overall journey.

Title: Babel
Review: This is ultimately comfortable listening, befitting folk sounds of a resolutely un-freak variety. [Oct 2012, p.96]

Title: Kid A
Review: With Kid A, Radiohead has made the ultimate 3 a.m. stoner-headphone album, one that marks an entirely logical progression from -- if not necessarily an improvement upon -- the techno-but-not-really O.K. Computer.... Occasionally, it feels less like a rock record and more like a museum piece, and as a work of art, it's laudable. As an actual, listener-friendly offering, it leaves something to be desired: It's precisely the sort of record a band makes when it has endless amounts of time and money, and has spent long periods of time being told what geniuses its members are.

Title: Projections
Review: Projections, Fairhurst's first album, designed more for home listening than for dancefloors, is relatively listless, sometimes torpid, and often sounds more like a project than a form of expression.

Title: Cydonia
Review: Recaptures the formula that once, a decade ago, made them great. [Apr 2001, p.111]

Title: Sad Happy
Review: With Sad Happy, Circa Waves capture the broken dreams of youth and turn them into songs meant to be played at full volume before leaving you wrecked on the floor.

Title: Wreckorder
Review: Wreckorder is a hand-picked gift reminding us that it's the thought that counts. And to look down your nose at it would make you a snob.

Title: Blood & Chemistry
Review: It's mix of precision and passion reminds of Muse's debut. [Jun 2013, p.91]

Title: For My Parents
Review: Huge swathes of uplifting, chest beating, and grandiose magnificence populate this album, and it is almost impossible not to get swept up in the sheer pomp of the performance.

Title: Lost Themes II
Review: With Lost Themes II, John Carpenter and band have delivered an album that not only stands up to its predecessor, but surpasses it. In addition to eerie atmospherics, the album is laden with addictive grooves, and feels sharper.

Title: Django Django
Review: Unabashedly geeky and seam-splittingly stuffed with retro-futuristic flourishes, it's an utterly delight. [Oct/Nov 2012, p.129]

Title: The Devil's Walk
Review: A record for late, empty, lonely nights.

Title: Brothers and Sisters of the Eternal Son
Review: Brothers And Sisters Of The Eternal Son bills itself as a concept album, a road movie with no end, but the songs are tight, the meaning incidental and any big ideas play second fiddle to bewitching tunes and delicate harmonies.

Title: I'm Having Fun Now
Review: Its casualness sometimes surfaces in its tossed-off jokes or sing-song melodies, but that only underscores that Jenny & Johnny are having a good time -- and it's a good time that's easy to share even if one of the hosts doesn't quite hold up his own end of the bargain.

Title: Everything in Between
Review: Everything in Between is a triumphant leap forward from an already solid foundation, and one that cements the duo as one of this era's incontestably exceptional indie-rock acts.

Title: Postcards From
Review: All the pieces are beautifully composed and played, as you would expect from someone whose orchestral arrangements are sought by artists ranging from Gorillaz to Katherine Jenkins, but what Postcards From really needs is an accompanying, immersive Virtual Reality video experience that would allow us to see, and understand, what Brice heard.

Title: Ys
Review: The people who hear this record will split into two crowds: The ones who think it's silly and precious, and the ones who, once they hear it, won't be able to live without it.

Title: Cedars
Review: Are you worn out by your Travis and Coldplay CD's? In the market for some new Brit-Pop? Clearlake creates songs with equally appealing melodies to the aforementioned bands, while eschewing the relentlessly anthemic quality that occasionally mires the genre.

Title: Equivalents
Review: Sometimes, a cloud isn't just a cloud, and Morgan's Equivalents offers a space to ponder the difference.

Title: Monomania
Review: While Cox is no stranger to gut-spilling, it feels as poignant as ever on this record.

Title: Seeing Things
Review: There are pleasant moments, but by any measure Seeing Things as a whole is rather bland and featureless.

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: The really amazing thing about the album is how anthemic and affirming it feels despite the near total absence of proper sing-along choruses.

Title: Angel
Review: While Pleasure and C.U.T.S. evoke the nature of the dream, Angel, obsessive and occasionally trite, tends to tell rather than show.

Title: Liars
Review: If Liars have reached the post-masterpiece phase of their career where they hone their craft to a needle’s point, Liars is an absolutely brilliant jump-off.

Title: Blue Cathedral
Review: The trick to their aural freak-out is not too different from those in the past; it hides in the arcane black box manned by Noel Harmonson. The echoplex, with its Möbius strip of tape loop, warps the guitars and yowls like parallel sheets of Mylar and sheets of acid, focusing the entire band into ray-gun pulses that match the pounding of Utrillo Belcher.

Title: Feathers
Review: Space-rock aficionados will dig the zero-G atmosphere, but it meanders through excessive pockets better left unexplored.

Title: Here We Are
Review: Witty and blessed with deftness Citizens! may well be, but we're still a bit bilious from our musical diet during the noughties to thoroughly appreciate it.

Title: Relaxer
Review: This all-over-the-map approach makes Relaxer a bit dizzying and tough to digest at first, and yet you'll be immediately captivated and intrigued by its distinctive mix. And once you give it a few more listens, many of its varied songs will worm their way into your ears as some of this summer's best indie rock offerings.

Title: Pink
Review: Pink is their fastest, most instantly gratifying album.

Title: Songs of Praise
Review: Noisy but thoughtful, and frenzied but melodic. [Feb 2018, p.32]

Title: You
Review: The vocals alone would be a lullaby, but in this broken orchestra, they’re insomnia. Yet spending time with this record allows the burs to break off. If you give in to its strange terms, You is soothing.

Title: Love at the Bottom of the Sea
Review: This is Merritt in designer mood, playing with layers and music. The joy is found in watching it take shape.

Title: Candid
Review: The project doesn’t really find the band moving outside their comfort zone – indeed, ‘Candid’ is defined almost by how resolutely ‘Whitney’ it feels.

Title: As You Were
Review: Though As You Were kicks off with stadium-sized rock songs, some of the record’s most memorable moments arrive on its ballads.

Title: Electric Circus
Review: One problem: Common is an MC, not a musician. Which makes it difficult for him to achieve his lofty goals. Mostly he fails.

Title: Agora
Review: There’s no real new ground being broken on Agora, but it does make a good entry point if you’ve not been acquainted with Gilberto’s music before.

Title: Maritime
Review: Somewhere between Matmos and Ariel Pink, this is wickedly out there. [Sep 2005, p.110]

Title: Numbers
Review: It's that line between accessible and alienating that MellowHype have so brilliantly walked, making Numbers an engaging album from some of Odd Future's best and brightest.

Title: Emoh
Review: ‘Emoh’ is revealing at all times, but utterly dignified throughout, and it’s a wonderful solo record.

Title: Colour of the Trap
Review: Colour of the Trap, impressive an achievement as it is, is begging for diminishing returns.

Title: Bermuda Waterfall
Review: Along with the pseudo-bossa nova rhythms of "Naturally" and rolling melodic synth pop of "Heartless," the album takes gradual steps forward and shakes out to be one of Savage's more consistent collections.

Title: Periphery III: Select Difficulty
Review: The heaviest and catchiest thing the Washingtonians have unleashed--and the most moving, too. [23 Jul 2016, p.52]

Title: So This Is Goodbye
Review: So This Is Goodbye isn't just an improbable notch above 2004's Last Exit-- it's also among the best records you'll hear all year.
An over proliferation of fluffy beats and soaring strings may have you hankering for something tougher. [Jul 2015, p.91]

Title: Strays
Review: Strays masterfully re-creates the surface of Jane's Addiction's sound, but in the process neglects to capture the band's vulnerability, its many idiosyncrasies, or even the all-important sense that Farrell has much left to say.

Title: All Nerve
Review: All Nerve shrugs off any burden of a ‘come-back’ and becomes a truly rare thing: a wild, visionary, timeless rock album.

Title: Illumination
Review: Easily the most satisfying album of his decade-plus solo career, Illumination marks the first time in ages that Weller has sounded at ease in his own skin: mellow, upbeat, yet aggressive and gritty in all the right places.

Title: Dude Incredible
Review: It’s going to be hard for Albini, Weston and Trainer to ever top what we find on Dude Incredible. Worthy of filing alongside and above At Action Park and 1000 Hurts, it’s the sound of one of the great bands at the height of their powers.

Title: Limits of Desire
Review: The textures are excellent, the songs are OK, but as a whole, it just doesn't pack the emotional punch of earlier outings.

Title: Two Wounded Birds
Review: Two Wounded Birds are an exotic rarity; a band that performs pastiche without sounding anything other than utterly authentic. [Jul 2012, p.112]

Title: Miracle Temple
Review: Mount Moriah has certainly found more confidence in their identity, and Miracle Temple will be what defines them moving forward.

Title: Maths + English
Review: His straightest record yet, delving into crunk, rock, drum'n'bass and pop with varying results.

Title: Shooter
Review: Jennings may be most comfortable in front of a synth or computer, but on Shooter, he proves he’s never too far from his rootsy outlaw heritage.

Title: On Time Out of Time
Review: Basinski's latest effort is ambitious yet remains rooted in what he does best: instilling a multitude of visceral, yet ambiguous, feelings within his listener.

Title: The Deaner Album
Review: Some tracks don’t develop as much as you might hope, and as a whole The Deaner Album is a bit of a mixed bag, albeit with some winning flavours.

Title: Noel Gallagher's High Flying Birds
Review: It's all very appealing and completely listenable, if sometimes overreliant on mid-tempo rhythms with occasional surges in passion and pacing. [#82, p.56]

Title: Tyranny
Review: On Tyranny, that guy has simply worked too hard, and that sense of needless toil bleeds through in every bum lick, brick-walled sound, and garbled burst of noise shoved onto the record.

Title: Snow Bound
Review: Always a unique voice, Phillipps is as refreshingly conciliatory as he is arrow straight. It may be nothing particularly new, but it's the way he tells 'em. [Oct 2018, p.90]

Title: Rose Windows
Review: There's a strangely disarming quality to Rose Windows' second album. [Jun 2015, p.80]

Title: Public Warning
Review: At times Sovereign exceeds at being entertaining and at other times her simplistic lyrics, heavy accent and electronic beats prove to be too much to grasp.

Title: All Things Will Unwind
Review: Worden can be preposterously experimental - but she's always intriguing. [Dec. 2011 p.96]

Title: How Animals Move
Review: It's mostly a success, though its dominant tone of understated, rainy melancholia is unlikely to earn Parish a dressing room with a star on the door. [Oct 2002, p.108]

Title: Walking Proof
Review: This is a leap forward for Hiatt who delivers her most fully realized album yet.

Title: Restless Ones
Review: The combination of Wennerstrom's singular vocal style and the Bastards' multilayered guitars remains both lyrically commanding and musically transcendent.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: It takes a while for Mind Bokeh to get going, and once it does it's rather compelling, but after the uniformly excellent Ambivalence Avenue, the album can't help but feel like an overcast sky with too few rays of sunshine shining through. [May 2011, p.89]

Title: Get Guilty
