Review: Yet all of this feels like quibbling when surveying an album that's still devastatingly charming, consistently intelligent, and engaging on first listen.

Title: Both Lights
Review: Both Lights may be plenty gorgeous, but in Wyland's never-idle hands, that beauty proves fleeting.

Title: Full Circle Nightmare
Review: There's a country edge to songs like "Slick Delta Queen," "Exile Rag" and the surprisingly sweet "Bridge City Rose," the latter making a nice break from the self-centred tone of "Fake Magic Angel" and the Lou Reed-bitterness of "Gold Calf Moan." [Mar 2018, p.24]

Title: Healing Is a Miracle
Review: Her fourth album is inspired by a return to instinct. If it feels less ambitious than its predecessor, 2016’s Will – which explored acoustic settings from a Moog factory to a motorway underpass – it’s also more ravishingly beatific.

Title: Candylion
Review: Don't expect the gumption of Super Furries, instead bask in the mellow psychedelic ramblings of Gruff unplugged.

Title: Ode
Review: Full of understated elegance, Ode reminds us that Mehldau's is an increasingly significant body of work. [May 2012, p.82]

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: This is possibly not an album for those wanting immediate hooks and satisfaction, but it's a remarkable achievement and more proof - if any were needed - that Albarn is one of the most innovative and talented songwriters of his generation.

Title: Dystopia
Review: The band is brawny yet nimble, wriggling and writhing in a groove one moment, pivoting into pummel mode the next.

Title: Pinned
Review: The risks A Place to Bury Strangers take pay off more often than the stranger, near-failed experiments found on "Execution" and "Attitude."

Title: Fantasize Your Ghost
Review: Fantasize Your Ghost encapsulates the thrilling and sometimes terrifying joy of moving forward and finding the confidence within yourself to be exactly who you are — an album with enough depth and passion to fill a room, something you can listen to on a loop and never get bored.

Title: Songs of Innocence
Review: Yes, it’s big and shiny and sometimes bombastic, but it also takes chances and pushes forward the band’s legacy.

Title: Stephen Malkmus
Review: As accessible and eccentric as any album from Pavement's catalog...

Title: Days Gone By
Review: While there are elements to Days Gone By that still don't sit right, the album is an honest exploration of moods, and Bob Moses' unique combination of dance movement and introspective songcraft engages.

Title: Treats
Review: The combination of the music's essentials-- jackhammer riffs clipped from punk and metal, mid-tempo beats from hip-hop and electro, and supremely catchy sing-song melodies-- is striking on its own, sounding remarkably fresh and unlike anything else right now. But an even greater source of the record's appeal is how it doesn't sound especially referential.

Title: Feels
Review: Feels doesn’t trump earlier, more intimate Animal Collective releases. It’s just louder and messier.

Title: Stars of CCTV
Review: A steely-eyed desperation to succeed is transparent all through Hard-Fi's debut. [Aug 2005, p.112]

Title: Lucky 7
Review: In stark contrast to less talented producers who enlist MCs for name recognition alone, Statik’s posse cuts are the product of thoughtful placement.

Title: Funstyle
Review: It's a jumble of snarky (and funny) music-business skits and raps, junky computerized samples, tuneful near-pop songs with awkwardly overstuffed production, thudding cliches and, in tantalizing fragments, glimmers of her unsettling insight into character flaws, including her own.

Title: Free Spirit
Review: The El Paso-raised vocalist and composer kicks--or shuffles--everything up a notch with a handful of fresh producers (including Digi, Charlie Handsome and Hit-Boy), richer, more lustrous sounds, and further explorations into AutoTune.

Title: Dean Wareham
Review: They recorded this in James’s studio in Louisville, Ky., and nearly each song has a compelling depth.

Title: Black Mountain
Review: Comets on Fire, 90 Day Men and No Doctors all released albums within the last year that proved classic rock to be relevant in today's music community. The difference between these bands and Black Mountain is that it doesn't sound like the members of Black Mountain had to crush their souls to write their songs.

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: It feels like a resurfacing, like a promise, and it's a grand closer for this classically GBV (collection) album.

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: Vile could have chopped most of these songs in half and they would have worked just fine, but the overall effect wouldn't have been so blissfully druggy.

Title: Cigarettes After Sex
Review: It's a beautiful thing--its 10 songs have a drowsy, mizzled feel, reminiscent of the Cocteau Twins. [Aug 2017, p.103]

Title: A Small Death
Review: Crain has always been good, but on A Small Death she's genuinely great. [Aug 2020, p.92]

Title: Postcards From a Young Man
Review: Still raging, not drowning, their flame burns unfashionably on. [Oct 2010, p.110]

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: The richest, most dynamic album to the legend's name in decades.

Title: Damage
Review: In their quest to update the breakup record for those a bit too old to mope and stew in their juices, Jimmy Eat World succeeds here for the most part.

Title: Light of X
Review: The album is full of airy beauty and precious melodies sung in an angelic voice. However, there is not enough here to counter its delicate nature. [Year End 2008, p.83]

Title: Junk of the Heart
Review: While their play-it-safe approach may mean they're less likely to suffer the rapid sales decline of their contemporaries, they are now in danger of becoming indie pop's answer to Westlife.

Title: White Hills
Review: Not only do they add urgency to familiar psychedelic rock templates, but they pay just as close attention to the quiet moments as the raging ones--each track on their self-titled Thrill Jockey debut displays a careful layering of sounds and atmospheres.

Title: Hold On Now, Youngster...
Review: It is, however, undoubtedly a collection of many good songs. From start to finish, it’s a relentlessly difficult listen, and one that suffers from little in the way of dynamics or variety of tone.

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: Titanic Rising harnesses convention and refashions it into something singular. At once a document of this “wild time to be alive” and an escape from it, it’s often remarkably good.

Title: boygenius EP
Review: It’s when they come together on closer ‘Ketchum, ID’, an ode to the state of Idaho and the detachment of constant touring, that boygenius really comes into its own and sees the project become more than the sum of its parts.

Title: We Are The Night
Review: If we're to accuse Chemical Brothers of anything, it's trying to set a lofty new bar in the style they themselves created, and that no one else seems to be working anymore. [Sep/Oct 2007, p.128]

Title: Colors
Review: Beck has been working on Colors since 2013, and by the sounds of a recent interview, spent a lot of time trying to get the balance of “not retro and not modern” just so. He more or less nailed that bit, but what’s lacking from his Big Happy Pop Record is some kind of strong emotion that could elevate these songs above the “well crafted but innocuous” camp--something more than an idea.

Title: We The Generation
Review: There are unexpected pleasures in the margins. [Oct 2015, p.105]

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: What follows is the sound of a band trying and failing to forge a new identity - boy-band balladry, U2-style stadium rock and Metallica-esque melodic crunch are all attempted with predictably patchy results.

Title: Sound & Fury
Review: Distortion-saturated guitars, synthesizers squealing like tea kettles and tribal drums give country tradition a swift kick in the back side. This carnage doesn’t belong to a genre, it’s more like a feeling: Side 2 of Neil Young and Crazy Horse’s “Rust Never Sleeps,” ZZ Top demos after three cases of Tequila in a Texas roadhouse, a hurricane.

Title: Geogaddi
Review: Geogaddi is even more stripped-down and beautiful than Music Has..., BOC using simple circular rhythms and eerie samples to create an airless, ethereal ultraworld.

Title: There Is No Love in Fluorescent Light
Review: There Is No Love in Fluorescent Light is the sound of a band that know themselves. Stars speak to the truths we grapple with, and the internal nature of our emotional experiences. It's a gift to hear this realized.

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: It's a niche listen. But [...] it can be a charming one, too.

Title: Life In Cartoon Motion
Review: As admirable as Life in Cartoon Motion's eclecticism is, it could use more focus.

Title: Give You The Ghost
Review: Despite Leaneagh's claims that Auto-Tune and other effects are an attempt to render her voice just another instrument in the mix, Give You the Ghost is decidedly an album predicated on her vocals, even if it's not a "singer's album" in the traditional sense.

Title: Making A Door Less Open
Review: The album’s best songs show the potential of a more focused implementation of these styles. But if you’re willing to go along for the ride, you’ll find a lot to love in Will Toledo’s latest reinvention.

Title: Scorpion
Review: Scorpion might not be Drake’s most innovative work, but it does help to cement 40’s status as one of the best, and most consistent, producers of our generation, and sees Drake breaking ground commercially if not creatively.

Title: Feedback
Review: The only downside to "Feedback" is that by the time you reach the swinging latino rhythms of the instrumental finale "Canto de Ossanha" 52 minutes of hip-hop soul just won't seem like enough.

Title: Cadenza
Review: The group's palette is widening promisingly.

Title: The Helio Sequence
Review: Filled with some genuinely memorable moments The Helio Sequence show that if a band is open to experimentation and letting the light of the new day shine in, fascinating things can truly happen.

Title: Below the Branches
Review: Below The Branches is, maybe, the first perfect summertime album, absolutely brimming with brightness and charm.

Title: Nothin' But Blood
Review: Nothin' But Blood finds the hard-living and hard-playing one-man band Biram sounding as intense as ever.

Title: Return to the Sea
Review: There are some redeeming qualities, but for every success there are one or two failures.

Title: Hold It In
Review: They normally strike a few bullseyes per record though, and so it is with Hold It In.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: Despite Price's best efforts to infuse these songs with motion and finesse, Confessions never quite reaches its earlier heights after "I Love New York". When Madonna actually starts confessing, the album loses its delicate balance between pop frivolity and spiritual gravity.

Title: Roses
Review: Where Roses shines the brightest is via the textures that gild the album's edges.

Title: To the Happy Few
Review: To The Happy Few is precise and calculated. It lacks the irrationality and selfishness that gives a record its soul.

Title: Kintsugi
Review: The tautly controlled power of the performances meshes with the barely harness emotion of Ban Gibbard's impeccably sculpted, tortured lyrics. [Apr 2015, p.73]

Title: Everythings For Sale
Review: Everything’s for Sale will find an audience. Its gilded despair only leaves a greater impression with each listen. If there’s an album for the sad Instagrammer, posing in a beam of perfect light, copyrighted smile, only to heave a sigh, this is it.

Title: Dying in Stereo
Review: Northern State's skills and we-can-do-this exuberance transcend what otherwise might be shtick. [Aug 2003, p.116]

Title: So This Is Goodbye
Review: Furnished with seductive melodies, dry beats, translucent tonality and a variety of bouncing electronic arpeggios, So This Is Goodbye is filled with pure synth-pop oxygen.

Title: Ellipsis
Review: A rewarding evolution by a band that could easily coast on their rugged laurels. [Aug 2016, p.72]

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: Everything just gets better and better with Marling.

Title: Georgia
Review: It's palpable that the tracks are more at home on the stage, where you can feel the frenetic energy of the record itself, Georgia's boisterous on-stage persona coming through in abundance. On record, sometimes that energy gets lost in a noisy ether, her identity chopped and screwed into fragments.

Title: Skeleton Tree
Review: This is music so alive, real, raw, and occasionally frightening, that it forces you into its grip for its almost 40 minute running time, refusing to let you go. It might not be something that you would play that often given the intensity, but when you do, its emotional impact hits like a ton of bricks.

Title: Tremors
Review: SOHN is partial to sampling his own voice to augment the wounded confessionals. They stutter rhythmically and mix with a patchwork of minimal yet intricate electronics and low end beats to spine-tingling effect. [May 2014, p.118]

Title: Funeral
Review: Strikingly beautiful pop songs. [Nov 2004, p.142]

Title: The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends
Review: Their [the guest artists'] fresh influx of ideas on The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends creates new flavor profiles for the band's loopy psychedelic slurry.

Title: Sung Tongs
Review: Sung Tongs resembles the freakiest of '60s psyche, the outward fringes of Elephant Six-dom, the craziest excesses of Tom Ze -- yet it is a warm, deeply human work that winds its way into your heart.

Title: Collapse EP
Review: Like most Aphex Twin releases Collapse contains moments of queasy brilliance. [Oct 2018, p.48]

Title: The Woods
Review: [They] have made an evolutionary leap in rock. [Jun 2005, p.108]

Title: ATGCLVLSSCAP
Review: The late-album arrangement of these two outliers feels unnecessary and out-of-place. Two steps forward, one step back: such is the dance of courting other genres, even if the risks have helped keep Ulver vital.

Title: Stronger with Each Tear
Review: Stronger with Each Tear is a very good Blige album, if not quite a classic.

Title: Old Ideas
Review: He filters these gifts of poetry and keen observation through his bruised, romantic outlook, into a fully-formed album that sounds as if it was always in there, waiting to see the light of day. Or the darkness.

Title: Ledges
Review: Ledges may not match the intensity of his stage performances, but the album does portray Gundersen as an exacting songwriter who never lets self-reckoning curdle into self-regard and as an imaginative producer with a careful hand.

Title: I Go Missing in My Sleep
Review: I Go Missing In My Sleep is a collection of beautiful songs made infinitely more beautiful by the way they've been meticulously put together. The lightest touch lets Wilson's exceptional vocal sit effortlessly close, without sacrificing complexity or interest.

Title: Up From Below
Review: To be fair, Sharpe, a dramatic alter-ego for leader/singer Alex Ebert, does corral a few tunes infectious enough to last the distance on Broadway. [Sep 2009, p.90]

Title: Overpowered
Review: The result is a thoroughly modern pop album that will best appeal to ageing clubbers.

Title: Let's Bottle Bohemia
Review: It sounds exactly the same as the first record... Another solid, unremarkable effort. [Oct 2004, p.116]

Title: The Old Days Feeling
Review: This collection of rarities is a window into the mind of a restless but inspired talent. She isn't for everyone, but she is a break from safe.

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: All throughout, Lynch succeeds in taking often innocuous subject matter and turning it into a dark, sometimes humorous, but always anxiety-ridden event. [#39, p.71]

Title: Stay Positive
Review: The Hold Steady are mellowing, and it doesn't really suit them.

Title: Cranekiss
Review: Even without the haunting, almost phantasmagoric washes of guitar that dominated the previous two albums and despite the newfound prominence of robust and well-rounded melodic work that was previously largely swept aside by it, Tamaryn’s new late-80s/early-90s sensitive pop still possesses something of the signature melancholia that inspired her earlier output with Shelverton.

Title: Sweet Heart Rodeo
Review: This follow-up feels less homemade, but just as delicately adventurous. [Oct 2009, p.108]

Title: Whitechapel
Review: Whitechapel have reinvigorated themselves without reinventing the sound they became known for and, in the process, produced an appropriate follow-up to their sophomore success.

Title: Mordechai
Review: A a culmination of those travels as well as a homage to Houston. Laura Lee’s (bassist) homecoming provided her with the clarity that was needed to create the well-executed diversity shown.

Title: Steeple
Review: Steeple is a big, old hairy beast capable of stirring the most primal of instincts. [Dec 2010, p.115]

Title: Hummingbird
Review: Hummingbird feels wiser, grander, and more knowing.

Title: Thalassa
Review: Because she never fully commits to one mood or genre, it is difficult to feel fully immersed. Gika’s songwriting is sometimes too vague to resonate emotionally, and her delivery, though gorgeous, never feels fully unencumbered.

Title: Strange To Explain
Review: Strange To Explain might be about dreaming and escape but it's also about their limitations, our need for hoke and the importance of other people. [Jun 2020, p.31]

Title: The Forgotten Arm
Review: An unfussy affair. [Jun 2005, p.108]

Title: The Killer
Review: It succeeds, unequivocally, as usual.

Title: Seven Swans
Review: Like Elliott Smith after ten years of Sunday school. [May 2004, p.108]

Title: Fair Ain't Fair
Review: The album is loaded with arresting musical touches.

Title: And It's Still Alright
Review: Solo he's more ruminative. [Apr 2020, p.91]

Title: The Garden
Review: Zero 7 have perfected the formula for folk jazz that transcends definition and defies classification, always taking you on joyous rides that often end at a truly unexpected place. [Jun 2006, p.108]

Title: Gold Medal
Review: On Gold Medal, even when they fail, it seems as if that failure is a result of The Donnas trying to carve their own identity rather than just being a cute cover band that ran out of ideas.

Title: Ultra Mono
Review: Ultra Mono is an enjoyable but ideologically confused record and one in which some of IDLES best material must compensate for some of their worst.

Title: Invisible Cinema
Review: Invisible Cinema is the opposite of a silent film. The soundtrack is provided; the listener brings the visuals.

Title: Ultra Mono
Review: Like all IDLES releases, Ultra Mono’s biggest drawback is its lack of variety. Though the guitarists experiment with different tones, each song still has the same feel sonically. Likewise, Talbot’s vocals are monotone with little variety and his lyrics are sometimes simplistic. But IDLES make up for those flaws with its greatest strengths, the band’s passion, unbridled fury, and raw intensity. IDLES wears its passion and anger on its sleeve, delivering infectious rhythms, filthy distorted guitars, and snarling vocals to drive its message home.

Title: With the Tides
Review: South won't win any prizes for originality, but their songwriting is endearing enough to mask the stink of opportunistic career change. [Nov 2003, p.121]

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Like Stephen Malkmus or Kurt Vonnegut, Barnett looks at the mundane with a skewed perspective, turning it over in her mind and transmogrifying it into something extraordinary.

Title: Mouseman Cloud
Review: The 17 loose, grungy guitar-led songs here ... sound full of renewed energy. [May 2012, p.103]

Title: Man of the Woods
Review: As a pop-R&B hitmaker, he could let his genius producers do the heavy lifting while getting by on showbiz-schooled charm, but the styles he dabbles in here aren’t as forgiving of average songwriting. When Timberlake does commit to his theme, the results are mixed.

Title: O
Review: Clever, joyous and never patronising, O is a half hour bite of summer that’s perfect for fending off the darkening nights.

Title: Zukunft Ohne Menschen
Review: Zunkuft may be even more sleep-inducing than the average ambient album, but it's worth admiring for its robust, and not humorless, conceptual solidity.

Title: Sleeping Operator
Review: Ultimately the Barrs sound like themselves. [Dec 2014, p.71]

Title: Hoodies All Summer
Review: Thoroughly inspired as well as creative, Hoodies All Summer is arguably the best work of Kano's career.

Title: On Blonde
Review: They've birthed a catchy and danceable summer record which shows plenty of promise but falls short of something great.

Title: Trigga
Review: Filled with lust, desire and sexual journeys, Trey Songz reaches an expected level of mainstream success with Trigga, and while safe is always encouraged during sexual acts, perhaps Trey could’ve taken a few more risks with this album.

Title: Kill for Love
Review: Lacking a clear story arc or point of catharsis, Kill for Love drifts off into its own gorgeous gloom.

Title: Vehicles & Animals
Review: There are a batch of mighty tunes here, and a sound that, while hardly de rigour, melds some of rock's freshest, brightest lights to their own street-wise, archetypal city swagger and 'Mockney' wit.

Title: Spooky Action at a Distance
Review: Guitar work comes across as the strongest feature of 'Spooky Action At A Distance' – tricky arpeggios and impeccably crafted feedback combine to create bleary, Kurt-Vile-esque smokescapes.

Title: Everyday Demons
Review: Apart from two minor issues, the Answer has the right sound and feel on Everyday Demons and that does make them the perfect opener for latter day AC/DC: they work as pleasant appetizer for the main course.

Title: Showtime
Review: At its core, Showtime is a classic sophomore album in the hip-hop sense: puffy with bluster, brimming with indignation. [Nov 2004, p.107]

Title: You Are Free
Review: Mostly, it's Chan's wonderfully bold and understated piano and guitar work that makes 'You Are Free' what it is, a collection of shapely and becoming lo-fi oddities.

Title: 50 Song Memoir
Review: 50 Song Memoir is a rare example of Stephin Merritt offering a look into his offstage life, but just as importantly it's a reminder of why he's a truly great songwriter, and this ranks with his finest work.
A progressive, grown-up second collection, it ought to ensure Adele is around for 23, 25, 27 and beyond.

Title: The Search
Review: "The Search" is Son Volt 2.0, a modern, mature album that might be the group's best yet. [10 Mar 2007]

Title: Kannon
Review: Even as they add unimaginable depths to a deceptively simple form, Kannon reasserts their commitment to merely existing, unapologetically out of genre and out of time.

Title: La Petite Mort
Review: This is a resolutely up record, for the most part. [Jul 2014, p.92]

Title: We Are on the Edge: A 50th Anniversary Celebration
Review: Both a graceful tribute and a testament to these musicians’ questing vision.

Title: Beat 'Em Up
Review: Even at his least inspired he's got these funk-rap-metal boys beat.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light I
Review: Most of all, I'd like to list Angels Of Darkness, Demons Of Light: 1 amongst the ever-expanding and illustrious list of rock n' roll's most important albums.

Title: Supervision
Review: As an exercise in reclaiming control, in setting out her stall, it is a definite success, a hand-made pop exercise in an era dominated by algorithmic marketing plans. As a listening experience, though, it’s somewhat limited and frustratingly repetitive, ultimately paling next to La Roux’s previous heights.

Title: Wildest Dreams
Review: It's strictly a mood piece, complete with daffy lyrics about mermaids, bicycles and "Gypsy Tears." [Aug 2014, p.81]

Title: Kamikaze
Review: There’s nothing novel or exciting here, but at least they seem to be having a ball.

Title: Amber
Review: Compared to their offerings to date 'Amber' has the hardest edges, but it wouldn't be Clearlake if it wasn't soft in the centre.

Title: Beyond The 4th Door
Review: Almost without trying, the track becomes a perfect psychedelic blister--headstrong and hot, five dudes marching headlong in one righteous moment. Long live major-label debuts, then: This is the sound of Eternal Tapestry finally turning its instincts into conquests.

Title: Silent Earthling
Review: It takes some talent to blend elements of metal, prog rock, classic electronica (Brian Eno has been an acknowledged influence, and Rogerson will be releasing a collaboration with him in the near future), techno and hip hop into an album, but Three Trapped Tigers have pulled it off so convincingly here that it makes some of their previous material look unfairly clunky in comparison.

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun
Review: Once More 'Round The Sun's many positives are consistently seen in the best possible light.

Title: Second Round's on Me
Review: Dreary production from hometown benefactor Eminem does little to liven things up. [Aug 2006, p.82]

Title: Alvvays
Review: First albums rarely arrive catchier or more self-assured than this Toronto indie-pop quintet's frothy inaugural go. [9 Aug 2014, p.67]

Title: The Practice of Love
Review: For anyone who enjoys a dash of shimmering disco hedonism with their feminist theory, or who simply harbours a lingering respect for the sun-drenched joy of '90s trance techno, this album offers a richly rewarding dialogue with mainstream pop. Crucially, Hval understands well the strange, seductive, subversive potency of "cheap" music. [Oct 2019, p.28]

Title: Holly
Review: The singer has crafted an album that unfolds like a film: it’s brisk, self-contained and a little mysterious, and catchy enough to revisit again and again.

Title: Homesongs
Review: An open, emotionally congruent record that never tries to be clever and yet rarely seems dull. [Apr 2004, p.99]

Title: Try This
Review: Pink's delivery says more than her often wince-inducing lyrics, but it means enough to make Try This an engagingly revealing album.

Title: Nation
Review: A series of hard-rockin', tight tunes...

Title: Ego Death
Review: Ego Death as a whole a refreshing take on contemporary R&B, blurring the lines between the traditional and the contemporary to create something very much of the moment and yet still imbued with a timeless quality. Ego Death is a subtly defiant step forward.

Title: Dear John
Review: There are definite up moments in Dear John, but the odd mix of Svanängen's meandering melodies and melancholic vocals mixed with the bizarre samples and synths makes for a concoction that will either be adored or thrown out of a window in disgust.

Title: Punisher
Review: ‘Punisher’ is an immense album tackling the ugly and absurd sides to life with beauty, humour and self-awareness. It’s a unique reporting style and a key statement.

Title: Freetown Sound
Review: It’s often passionate, illuminating and fascinating, it frequently bears the hallmarks of self-indulgence, and some of it, you get the feeling, might only make sense to its author.

Title: The End of All Things to Come
Review: The musicians still churn out standard-issue heavy metal thrash à la Metallica to support Chüd's nihilistic pronouncements, usually sung in an enraged howl.

Title: Two Dancers
Review: Instead of spoon-feeding you how you’re supposed to react, they challenge you to understand them.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: The softer tracks find the group negotiating their path to maturity with confidence.

Title: High Hopes
Review: Too many songs disappoint, though.

Title: Dear Catastrophe Waitress
Review: The swollen, baroque-pop arrangements... may ruffle the band's more delicate followers. But the songs are always smart, and it's the music-librarian's humor that helps keep things from slipping into the maudlin. [Nov 2003, p.109]

Title: The Soul Sessions
Review: Stone shines on this impressive covers set.

Title: How to Destroy Angels
Review: HTDA's debut EP doesn't consist of dressed-up leftovers from The Slip: some of Reznor's obsessions remain recognizable, but having collaborators opens up the music and Maandig softens it, giving this EP a different feel despite some familiar sounds.

Title: In and Out of Control

Review: In short, a breezy DJ set attuned for meditative easy listening. When this approach clicks, the results are nothing less than sumptuous, a rich panorama of material organized by an artist whose greatest talents seem to lie in curation.

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: Apologies to the Queen Mary is almost an hour long, and there are certainly portions of it that aren't essential... but it's difficult to see where any fat could have been cut, as each track has its own fractured beauty.

Title: Between The Walls
Review: Between the Walls is not without its moments. Cleanly recorded and mixed, it serves as a nice palate-cleanser between courses of alt. Americana, folk, and neo-new wave.

Title: All I Ever Wanted
Review: I had to make several return trips to the lyric sheet to clear up which songs were love letters and which were screw-yous. But this sort of tone-deaf emotional bludgeoning tends to work in her favor on monstrous power ballads.

Title: Stranger Than Fiction
Review: He treats this debut album like a retail mixtape, and the result is a project that picks off from where The Luca Brasi Story left off. Unfortunately, these high points aren’t enough for him here to progress further.

Title: The Silicone Veil
Review: In this case, less is more. [Nov 2012, p.106]

Title: Scale
Review: A pleasure, featuring some of his most winging music since [Roisin] Murphy's Ruby Blue. [Jul 2006, p.118]

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Paper MÃ¢chÃ© Dream Balloon
Review: Fans of King Gizzard's earlier material may have trouble stomaching the bubbly nature of Paper Mâché Dream Balloon, but just as fellow Aussie psych band Tame Impala did with Currents, sometimes you simply need to take a chance and put out something unexpected--that the flutes on nearly every track end up working is just icing on this sweet cake.

Title: Uncanney Valley
Review: An agitated yet hook-heavy affair, these 10 cuts feel like an act reacquainting itself, slipping into a creative comfort zone that still requires a little polish.

Title: Painting With
Review: For all their organic methods, these Animals often come across so robotic and constricted--witness natural Selection's echoes of woozy Chicago house classic Washing machine--stripping those painstaking vocal arrangements of their humanity. [Mar 2016, p.94]

Title: Crawl Space
Review: Penultimate track "Your World" is perhaps the most forward-thinking item here; with the unusual mash of R&B and dream pop, it offers something novel, where some other parts of the album do have a tendency to be a touch heavy on paying homage to styles past. But the sounds and homages on offer are diverse enough that this is a minor quibble with what should otherwise be held up as a model debut album.

Title: Axe To Fall
Review: Staying true to a 20-year career of uncompromising extremity, it will take commitment to breach this seventh album's walls of noise. [Dec 2009, p. 113]

Title: Mellow Waves
Review: Overall, Mellow Waves sits nicely in Cornelius’ discography. Not as scene as Fantasma or exploratory as Point. This record uses the studio magic in a more utilitarian way.

Title: Requiem
Review: The chants, pipes and Afrobeat guitars might be facades, just like the masks and robes, but it doesn’t matter because the music underneath has real heart and soul.

Title: The Evening of My Best Day
Review: An utterly compelling, even riveting, selection of tunes that go from bright to opaque, to dark and back again by album's end.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: From the bottom of a spring-reverb well, Harris strums mournful, incoherent songs like "Vital" and "being Her Shadow," but intersperses them with creepy textural mood pieces. [Feb 2013, p.50]

Title: Happy Birthday
Review: A handful of fun tracks here, but no overly impressive. [Winter 2010, p.72]

Title: An Other Cup
Review: Yusuf hasn't missed a beat, as this is still the same sound he made famous on 70s staple "Tea for the Tillerman" and later perfected on "Teaser and the Firecat", and while it's certainly not as impactful, I'm comfortable saying that "An Other Cup" comes pretty close.

Title: Cry
Review: It's often said that love is better the second time around; whilst this remains to be seen, Cry is a grower and we look forward to love’s next incarnation.

Title: Hurts 2B Human
Review: It all adds up to an album that cleverly feels stylish and fashionable without abandoning the emotional gravity P!nk has accumulated over the years.

Title: Z
Review: [A] triumphant resurrection. [Nov 2005, p.96]

Title: The Assassination Of Julius Caesar
Review: Yet another album of utter genius in a stylistic vein that nobody in their right minds would have predicted from Ulver.

Title: Midwest Farmer's Daughter
Review: Price lives up to the hype by marrying hardscrabble traditionalism with modern narratives on her debut album, Midwest Farmer’s Daughter.

Title: Hefty Fine
Review: Hefty Fine finds the Bloodhound Gang in a Catch-22 -- they've never wanted to be anything other than a dumb, silly hard rock band, but their shtick is getting tired, yet they're trapped by the confines of what they want to be.

Title: Beaucoup Fish
Review: It shouldn't surprise anyone in today's age of shattered expectations that Beaucoup Fish is not as great as we'd hoped.

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: Heartbreak is an instance when that hoary music-biz cliche -- "They're better onstage" -- rings true; ironically so, since the Kings and producer Ethan Johns recorded Aha Shake Heartbreak live in the studio, with no overdubs.

Title: Street's Disciple
Review: Here Nas is on autopilot, churning out uniformly solid but unexceptional material.  [Oct 2004, p.183]

Title: EarthEE
Review: You can hear Badu’s influence across EarthEE, which flows as freely as its predecessor, but is more sonically detailed and rich.

Title: The Cost
Review: The Cost is hardly a poor album - in fact it's a quite good album - but after the release of so many gems, I find it difficult for it to completely measure up to the stiff competition.

Title: Be Brave
Review: There’s an intriguing, never pandering, blend of genres on Be Brave–from soul to blues to modern day indie rock-packaged as Texas blues–making the record a more interesting listen each time around.

Title: Cause I Sez So
Review: It’s just solid, classic Dolls, with all the swagger, muscle, righteous kitsch, and ballsy defiance you expect, plus some new twists.

Title: Cease to Begin
Review: Cease falters when it dips into mediocre balladry ('Detlef Schrempf,' 'Marry Song'), and at a scant 35 minutes, the album at times hints at greatness but ultimately leaves you wanting more.

Title: Asa Breed
Review: Dear joyously defies categorization. [15 Jun 2007, p.77]

Title: Eucalyptus
Review: While Eucalyptus is undoubtedly intriguing, it’s only occasionally enjoyable as music.

Title: My Turn
Review: The stuffed effort could be Lil Baby's attempt to showcase his growth. But one mark of artistic maturity is exercising restraint — less is often more.

Title: MCIII
Review: In short, if you liked what you heard on MCI and MCII, MCIII is more of the same, only slathered in lush arrangements with a little less of the raw outbursts of his earlier garage-y grunge sound.

Title: Free Your Mind
Review: It's time for Cut Copy to free its own mind too. [Dec 2013, p.89]

Title: MCII
Review: MCII sounds much more concise and meticulously assembled than any of Segall's efforts.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: "Misstep" is certainly a word too harsh for The Big Doe Rehab, which is more "uneventful" than "wrong."

Title: Target Earth
Review: If there were any doubts among the faithful about legendary Quebec prog-metal dudes Voivod being able to recapture the magic of their classic era in the absence of deceased guitarist Denis "Piggy" D'Amour, they're shattered within moments of the title track.

Title: Theory of Colours
Review: This album, on Ninja Tune offshoot Technicolour, presents an idiosyncratic take on electronic music that’s imbued with deep emotional content, yet danceable. All the while his engineering capabilities shine through, giving the album a polished touch.

Title: Far Side Virtual
Review: Such dedication to an aesthetic means Far Side Virtual gets a little tedious: It's 16 songs that aren't all that catchy but aren't exactly ambient either.

Title: The Dusk In Us
Review: There are some nods to years past, and most longtime acolytes will be satisfied with what is mostly testament Converge; but the band's causal nexus doesn’t exist in a vacuum, or in the grips of GodCity Studio, but out there, rooted in the mundane and then amplified to hysteria. Much of The Dusk in Us seems to obsess over the everyday, or maybe more accurately, our demons lurking on the cusp of day and night.

Title: Elephant Shoe
Review: Arab Strap's music is still fractured, Smog-like, and woefully beautiful. The group's pitted, narky ambience fuses Irvine Welsh with Brian Eno's Another Green World-- Elephant Shoe is ambient for the Tamazipan massive.... Arab Strap's depression is as addictive as their expression of it is alluring.

Title: It's Immaterial
Review: The record captures and remains stuck in a moment, circulating a narrative where memory serves and is replaced over and over again, like an acid flashback with a locked groove.

Title: The Point Of It All
Review: His singing throughout is flawless and expressive.

Title: Root for Ruin
Review: Les Savy Fav received high marks before, but this album proves this oft-comical band are no joke. [Oct 2010, p.116]

Title: LUMP
Review: If the results could always mesmerise and captivate as much as LUMP’s too-brief debut, perhaps we’d listen and follow suit.

Title: First Ditch Effort
Review: This is NOFX at their leanest, and it absolutely rips. [8 Oct 2016, p.52]

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: Le Voyage is as thrilling and replete with the unexpected as one might imagine a trip outside the Earth's atmosphere would be.

Title: Olympia
Review: Those hoping Eno's appearance would revive the art-rock experimentation of Ferry's early days will be disappointed.

Title: The Stars Are Indifferent to Astronomy
Review: The Stars is a reliably crisp, tuneful addition [to their consistent indie-rock discography], all racing snare hits, taut power chords, and Caws' emotive tenor.

Title: A Blessing and a Curse
Review: It's the kind of album that finds its own cozy place somewhere between Lynyrd Skynyrd and Leonard Cohen.

Title: Banks
Review: It is personal without actually being personal.

Title: Stone Temple Pilots
Review: It's not groundbreaking stuff, but it surpasses all expectations for a group who've spent almost a decade apart.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: It’s bold stuff, but if you were taking any solace that the Trump catastrophe would at least inspire some great art, The Future And The Past serves as Exhibit A.

Title: Yeah Ghost
Review: The music on Yeah Ghost is still Zero 7-but after a few cans of musical Red Bull.

Title: Beast Moans
Review: Ultimately, that’s the problem: No one can really decide where to take these songs, so everyone takes them everywhere.

Title: A New Place 2 Drown
Review: As a follow-up to 6 Feet Beneath the Moon, ANPTD lacks the charm that made his 2013 record amiable. This new work finds Marshall revealing himself through the sound of his combined musical sensibilities and artistry.

Title: Neuroplasticity
Review: Her voice is as mesmeric and worldly as ever, and the instrumentation is rendered in beautiful detail. But it’s tantalising to wonder what would have happened if she would have given herself completely to chaos.

Title: Stankonia
Review: Throughout, the music (produced almost exclusively by the group and its DJ) shines with the glint of successful experimentation. However, it never outshines the words, which is where the group has as much to offer, if not more so.

Title: Nightmare
Review: With imagery haunted by death and lyrical allusions to alienation and angst, Avenged Sevenfold's fifth full-length is almost impossible to appreciate unless you fit the prime demographic: tormented teenage boys.

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: 30 Years Of War aside, this is an album that finds the Manics in fine form.

Title: Sex Dreams and Denim Jeans
Review: I want to say “you’ve gotta hear it to believe it,” but there’s too much good music out there to waste your time on the bad--let alone the bad that knows it’s bad.

Title: Science Fiction
Review: Science Fiction is one of their most real and most effective pieces of art. Mike Sapone's production was spot on again and the cover of those girls jumping from a balcony more or less sums up what you need to do with this. Close your eyes and jump right in.

Title: Move Like This
Review: Out of retirement -- and on to the hard shoulder. [June 2011, p. 93]

Title: The House
Review: On The House, Maine is vulnerable, honest and strong--he soars on this, his best album yet.

Title: Treats
Review: Sleigh Bells have latched onto an exciting undercurrent in contemporary pop music and put their own distinctive stamp on it. In the process, they've made a hard-hitting album that will positively kill on the dance floor.

Title: Broken By Whispers
Review: Fey, coy, yet rich and deep, track after track on Broken by Whispers emits an exacting, well-crafted melodrama. Subtle electro touches only add to the wondrous acoustic guitars, wondrous and breathy declarations of love, and wondrous early morning seaside atmosphere. Those who balk at dreamy-boy nakedness will want to skip the bathos, but such people are called Americans...

Title: Living Well
Review: An album that, much like Pinback’s 2004 full-length Summer in Abaddon, is more immediate in its appeal but suffers from repeated listens.

Title: I Can Wonder What You Did with Your Day
Review: Despite some engaging song-craft, however, the album overall feels lacking in real substance and its fixations leave me blase.

Title: Invisible Cities
Review: The band is becoming, depending on how you look at it, either more like a classic jazz group—solos twisting well beyond the compact call-and-answer of formulaic Afrobeat—or something like a more world music-friendly Tortoise.

Title: Ritual Union
Review: Swedish electro-pop hipsters take understatement to a new high. [Aug. 2011, p. 117]

Title: Rakka
Review: Absolutely astonishing work, and easily up there with Delay's early-2000s masterpieces Multila and Anima.

Title: Persona
Review: This music is experimental and diverse in its sonic scope, but each unique sound is in service of its greater whole, making for a record that is undeniably the vision of a singular artist, a true auteur.

Title: Rated O
Review: Rated O is relentless enough and mean enough and playful enough to rope us in for 3 albums worth of music.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Somewhere Else is largely a more chilled-out affair than its predecessors. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.89]

Title: The High Frontier
Review: Languid and drone-heavy, The High Frontier is for the star-gazers that don’t get tired of looking up and wondering what’s out there, as opposed to going out and seeing what’s there for themselves.

Title: Tonight: Franz Ferdinand
Review: Taken as a whole, it’s the rare album that flirts with enough styles that it renders notions of classification irrelevant, and ultimately more of a Franz Ferdinand album than a dance album. [Year End 2008]

Title: The Blade
Review: Monroe sings these songs, many of which she co-wrote, with exquisite, bruised sensitivity.

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: The best tracks are the most pointed, because they go beyond technical style and really delve into each rapper's head.

Title: Civilian
Review: Here's one of the few first-quarter releases of 2011 that people will still be listening to in 2012.

Title: The Stand Ins
Review: The Stand Ins is a solid achievement cut from the same charming cloth, even if it doesn’t crisp in quite the same way "The Stage Names" did.

Title: Sundur
Review: The fact that the duo have chosen to deploy a stripped back approach to the album, and the fragile beauty this evokes, leaves little doubt that the pair are more than capable of weaving some seriously ethereal magic, even when they're miles apart.

Title: If I Should Go Before You
Review: It is music that asks for patience n an impatient age. [10 Oct 2015, p.52]

Title: Teen Men
Review: On record, Teen Men come across as your average, edgy modern pop combo, all shimmery, engaging songs with few constraints and even fewer darker designs.

Title: Something for Everybody
Review: Something for Everyone isn't a return to the halcyon days, but neither is it a deluded grasp for relevance, their sonic instincts still intact, the wheezy synths and buzzing guitars sharp and modern.

Title: Seasons of My Soul
Review: Seasons Of My Soul... rarely moves above midtempo or out of 6/8 time, and in its warm duvet of production it makes for a soupy listen, even more so on the second or third spin. But that won't diminish the album's efficacy as music for dinner parties or - let's face it - tender baby-making.

Title: All My Friends Are Funeral Singers
Review: They are doing the same thing they always do, which entails gorgeous and gracefully surprising variations on a deeply resonant motif.

Title: American Goldwing
Review: Sure, Blitzen Trapper attempt to vary the formula a bit--there's the jangly campfire number, or that one about astronauts--but when it comes right down to it, everything's all the same.

Title: Hail To The Thief
Review: While it’s unrealistic to expect another Kid A-like transformation, by pulling all those familiar elements together, Hail to the Thief sounds, well, a little familiar.

Title: Stuffed & Ready
Review: The garage pep of the band’s previous album, Apocalipstick, vanishes in favour of gloomy alt-rock and rain-soaked grunge – all cavernous bass and sludgy guitar – that inevitably crashes into towering, ferocious choruses. The effect is appropriately claustrophobic to Creevy’s insular theme, but difficult to endure across 10 incredibly samey tracks.

Title: Pretty Girls Like Trap Music
Review: There’s no galactic change to his style here, just a further refinement of it.

Title: Two Hands
Review: Big Thief’s power is in how they understand duality, both in the macro (with their two albums), and in the micro details. This record is best heard alongside its twin, but it’s equally powerful alone.

Title: Suicide Songs
Review: Rather than build on that record’s [The Shadow Of Heaven's] elegance and lightness of touch, MONEY have traded it out for something less polished, that’s often brutal in its emotional delivery. Not an obvious next step, then, but certainly a compelling one.

Title: Best of Times
Review: The elements that make up Best Of times were all there before, but even the band concedes that they have finally found their true sound. [Apr 2014, p.90]

Title: The Distance Is So Big
Review: The Distance Is So Big isn't as immediately accessible as previous Lemuria records, but overall, it has far more depth. [Jul 2013, p.100]

Title: Stephen Malkmus
Review: Beyond the bookish lyrics, Malkmus has composed an album of brilliant songs, with creative intros, off-kilter arrangements, and well-placed effects.

Title: Matter
Review: St. Lucia's splendid synth-pop allure has instant pop catchiness, but Grobler's willingness to wear his lyrics' romantic motivations like a badge of honor gives Matter a thrilling extra jolt.

Title: A New Place 2 Drown
Review: It's early morning or late-night music, and more than capturing a specific place and aimless time, A New Place 2 Drown is a soundtrack for a slowed-down pace of life.

Title: ken
Review: This is the kind that makes you want to go back and listen to his older stuff, if only to remind you he’s capable of wonders.

Artist: A Winged Victory for the Sullen
Title: Atomos
Review: This is a slow-burning, deeply resonant collection with a stirring potency and the capacity to truly wow.

Title: Are You in Love?
Review: Whether or not this will be Bulat’s breakthrough record remains to be seen. The sound sustains the suspense, but rarely does it leap out at the listener. It hardly matters though. Are You In Love? answers its own question with every repeated encounter.

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: It doesn't matter whether that future looks good or bad. Either way, The Center Won't Hold is a surprising path for taking an honest look at things, holding it together, and moving on.

Title: Abysmal Thoughts
Review: "I'll Fight for Your Life" makes up for its unremarkable melodies with a percussive synth pulse, while the charming "Head of the Horse" is a curveball ballad from a project that has always been better known for upbeat pop tunes. Beyond that, however, this album is a 50-minute slog.

Title: We Are Only What We Feel
Review: Though We Are Only What We Feel plods through similar tempos and uniform textures, Wäppling sings with enough character to keep the record from fading into the background.

Title: Goodbye Bread
Review: Goodbye Bread is a fitting development on an impeccable path. The depth accomplished through five albums is obviously grand and it's definitely as if Segall is purely improving with every passing year.

Title: 5 Seconds of Summer
Review: There's nothing desperately original about the 12 songs on their debut album.... But they're delivered with such winning enthusiasm that they make an old formula seem fresh.

Title: White People
Review: While "White People" certainly shows no lack of adventure... one is ultimately left wishing that Dan and Paul toned the wackiness down a few knobs this time around.

Title: Challengers
Review: What's immediately striking about Challengers is the unabashed mellowness of it all.

Title: Transistor Radio
Review: It's a deeper, more rewarding listen, rivaling End of Amnesia for Ward's strongest release to date.

Title: Disc-Overy
Review: Turn a deaf ear to the Cowell-connected producer Labrinth's uninspired Brit-hop beats and instead concentrate on the surely intentional comedy of Tinie's "I've got so many clothes I keep some of them in my aunt's house" and "I've been to Southampton but I've never been to Scunthorpe" (both from number-one single "Pass Out").

Title: Backwoods Barbie
Review: Parton victoriously retrains the focus back on the part of her chest that is truly meaningful: her heart. She also succeeds in producing a record that, after years of fine niche efforts in bluegrass and gospel, could actually make a bid for mainstream country radio airplay.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: Panda Bear Meets The Grim Reaper doesn’t push boundaries so much as it delineates the contours of Lennox’s comfort zone.

Title: Make Do With What You Got
Review: This is late-night listening that pulses with pain.

Title: Growing Up In Public
Review: Professor Green’s whiny rap and the tired chart-house riff detract from the power of the narrative.

Title: The Hardest Way to Make an Easy Living
Review: Not only are there scattered moments of lyrical brilliance on The Hardest Way, but from a producerly standpoint, it's probably Skinner's most accomplished and interesting record yet.

Title: Pickin' Up The Pieces
Review: Everywhere you turn, there's another neo-soul band trying to re-create, in some form or fashion, the classic sounds of Motown, Stax, and Philadelphia International artists. Title: Wild Go
Review: The tone is wistful and serene more than sad and heavy, but principal singer Nona Marie Invie still sounds like a femme fatale, with a coiled, spectral charm that suits the band's name. [Jun 2011, p.104]

Title: Junior
Review: King's voice, whether riding roughshod over her band's new found vravura arrangements or playing the smoky chanteuse, is still a decisive instrument of its own. [June 2010, p. 99]

Title: Duck
Review: As expected, Duck wants to please everybody and this is the reason it fails to take off. ... They prefer the safety of the comfort zone, although they fare much better when they show some grit.

Title: Telekinesis!
Review: Though the record could use a few more high points, there are enough hooky songs and exciting performances to make it very promising.

Title: Burnt Offering
Review: Burnt Offering has its own kind of subtlety, and most of it is in the interplay between meter, genre, and mood.

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: That he’s produced such a full, lush sounding thing packed with personality and life is impressive--but not surprising.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: With Sonik Kicks, Weller's silk-and-smoke voice sounds as good as ever, and his status as a soulful, folky, yet forceful songsmith remains ironclad. Next time around, though, an extra round of editing might not hurt.

Title: I Can't Go On, I'll Go On
Review: Even if you tend to avoid the genre of power-pop like some sort of rare disease, I Can’t Go On... provides an undeniably honest display of some quality rock tunes.

Title: Weezer (White Album)
Review: Sadly, there's a few too many tunes like (Girl We Got A) Good Thing--the sort of throwaway preppy drivel critics of Weezer think they sound like all the time--for this to sit alongside the band's classic work. [May 2016, p.90]
The music is accessible and poppy without dumbing-down the analog arrangements or their coffeehouse terrorist aesthetic. [#84, p.114]

Title: Tones of Town
Review: Tones of Town may lack the swooning immediacy of its predecessor, but it still sounds like a labor of love.

Title: God's Favorite Customer
Review: God’s Favorite Customer is the next chapter to Honeybear: the story of the hedonistic shroom-addled Hollywood waster who fell in love and started to grow up, even if the occasional pelvic thrust, sardonically raised eyebrow or over-dramatic fall to the floor wouldn’t go amiss.

Title: Battle Born
Review: Aside from "Battle Born", none of the other high points succeed against the influences The Killers have long been aping, much less against those times when the band has hit that sentimental ache that exists in all of us.

Title: Zeppelin Over China
Review: There is nothing necessarily new offered here in the way of direction or sound, however Zeppelin Over China adds a suitable chapter to the story of Robert Pollard, who recently celebrated releasing a mind-blowing 100 albums over the course of his career in various projects.

Title: The Decline of British Sea Power
Review: British Sea Power's slightly camp, wholly menacing, startlingly audacious debut is unlike anything you'll hear this year.

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: It seems that the more comfortable the principals get with Gnarls Barkley, the more haunted Gnarls Barkley gets. And it gets stronger, too.

Title: Silver Bell
Review: Silver Bell is generally best when it’s quietest, when Griffin’s vocals don’t have to compete with a denser sound.

Title: The Journey Man

Title: Black Up
Review: Black Up is best digested as a whole rather than tune by tune.

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You

Title: Flowers

Title: Spinnerette

Title: Def Leppard

Title: Mind Bokeh

Title: Come Home To Mama
Review: At the end of Come Home To Mama, I find myself most appreciative of Wainwright's confessional style of writing, how she reveals her main characters' flaws without shame.

Title: Out My Window
Review: Koushik effortlessly summons the hazy feel of running around stoned at noon on a summer day in hot pursuit of a grape soda or some other ridiculous craving to be satiated.

Title: Exile
Review: Ultimately, there's something delicious and monumental about Hurts.[Apr 2013, p.106]

Title: Rock Steady
Review: It doesn't strictly feel like a No Doubt album at all.

Title: Warnings
Review: Hypnotic stuff. [Summer 2020, p.100]

Title: Minus Tide

Title: Timeless
Review: An intriguing change of pace. [18 Feb 2006]

Title: proVISIONS

Title: Ciara

Title: Powerplant

Title: Ghost on Ghost

Title: Logos
Review: The tracks feel quickly and easily produced but fucking delicious.

Title: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
Review: This is thrilling, incontrovertible evidence of a major new talent in our midst. [Mar 2006, p.102]

Title: Red Gone Wild: Thee Album
Review: As big and as diverse as the guest list is, the album hangs and flows effortlessly.

Title: Go

Review: Unoriginality at its best. [#8, p.109]

Review: [Beware And Be Grateful expertly fuses] the complex rock of the band's early EPs with elegant, polished pop.

Title: The Unforgiving
Review: A concept album that doesn't get weighed down by the story line is a rarity, but it is something that Within Temptation succeed at with The Unforgiving.

Title: What About Now
Review: What About Now has enough always-darkest-before-the-dawn positivity and bland arena-country warm fuzzies to chock a true believer. [15 Mar 2013,, p.62]

Title: Hitch
Review: At times it almost sounds as if they know they've taken their current sound as far as it can go and seem palpably frustrated they can't figure out their next move.

Title: Higher Than the Eiffel
Review: Higher Than the Eiffel is most reminiscent of the work that Freestylers and Lo-Fidelity Allstars were doing eight to ten years ago. Both of them aged into their classic full-length statement with surprising grace, and made intriguing music long after most punters had deserted them.

Title: We Are Undone
Review: Stevens and Vogel have been playing together for almost 22 years now, if you can believe that, and We Are Undone is a fine addition to their catalogue.

Title: Divided by Night
Review: Here's the Crystal Method with a not-so-fresh batch of rave-rock jock jams seemingly designed to advertise a car you can no longer afford.

Title: Penance Soiree
Review: Someone still plays the Devil's music. [Jun 2004, p.98]

Title: Summer Sun
Review: Summer Sun is so mellow and pretty that it feels uncharitable to call it one of their weakest albums in recent memory; many bands would kill to make music this accomplished.

Title: Within and Without
Review: For his full-length debut, Greene teams with producer Ben Allen (Animal Collective, Gnarls Barkley) to revisit his '80s reveries, crafting Balearic bliss ("Eyes Be Closed") and refreshing New Romantic flounce ("Amor Fati"). He even invigorates '90s trip-hop's head-nod ("Before," the title track), making for an even better coast soundtrack.

Title: Hannah
Review: The album oscillates between emotional registers, balancing profound quiet with strummy, emphatic pleas about how we might better comport ourselves in the world; there’s a sense that even at their most gentle, these songs are transmitting something deeply earnest and hard-won. This is as true of Read’s lyrics as of her arrangements, which are newly rich and rewarding.

Title: Burned Mind
Review: ‘Burned Mind’ isn’t music; it’s a vision of a decimated future.

Title: Golden Ocean
Review: The loudest record [Hersh] has ever made, and even if few individual compositions leap out of the general roar, it sounds fantastic. [Apr 2005, p.116]

Title: The Velvet Trail
Review: Almond is at his best on the compelling torch songs that have long been his stock in trade. Winter Sun reflects on dwindling romance; The Pain of Never is swooningly melancholic. More, please.

Title: Tripper
Review: The only problem is that Johnson's tales aren't all that hooky. At least, not enough to buoy Tripper's soft and moody music.

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: It's the perfect record to listen to while you sit and wait for the next comet to pass, as Mascis sounds long shy of extinction.

Title: Depth of Field
Review: Depth Of Field, Blasko's sixth studio album, substantially persists with the gloomy synthesiser motif of its superb predecessor, 2015's Eternal Return, but locates an even more poised balance between the chilly melancholy of glam-electronica backdrops and the capacious warmth of Blasko's vocals. [Apr 2018, p.24]

Title: Life Is People
Review: The result a stunning, profound, moving and soulful record.

Title: Mystic Familiar
Review: A four-part story in the record's centre is propelled by a whirligig of percussion that rapidly becomes total overwhelm[ing]. But in its final 20 minutes the album finds steadier ground, allowing space for Deacon's undaunted imagination to come into its own. [Mar 2020, p.117]

Title: Double Roses
Review: More often, Double Roses settles for a tastefully ornamented Nashville smoulder. [Jun 2017, p.106]

Title: Why Choose
Review: Shopping make listeners lean in and pay close attention, proving along the way that they don't have to choose between tradition and growth to make a strong second album.

Title: Electra Heart
Review: Electra Heart is a reasonably fun listen, and even if it falls short of its stratospheric ambition, still has more to say than many of Marina's contemporaries.

Title: OIL OF EVERY PEARL'S UN-INSIDES
Review: Despite software advances, so many electronic producers are content to lapse into nostalgia or a safe, compromised emotional range; Sophie has crafted a genuinely original sound and uses it to visit extremes of terror, sadness and pleasure.

Title: Playland
Review: He may not be a born singer, or particularly vocally charismatic, but he sounds like he means it, and that's more than enough. [Nov 2014, p.94]

Title: Music For Men
Review: The weak spot, as ever, are lyrics that clasp to cliches without transforming them. So we get a song about a certain four-letter-word, and lines about rain or taking chances. On the other hand, the punchline of 'Men in Love' is pretty great, and Beth’s belting usually subsumes the stock imagery.

Title: Every Country's Sun
Review: Although Every Country’s Sun isn’t a flawless album (there are a number of tracks in the middle section that need more time to kick in), it shows us Mogwai nowhere near losing their touch.

Title: Everything's OK
Review: This is classic Green.

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: This album stands out because of its stadium-worthy aspirations.

Title: Everything in Between
Review: Their third album is their most conventionally songful.

Title: schlagenheim
Review: All four members of Black Midi are extremely young, wildly competent, knowledgeable about all sorts of music (classical, jazz, free improv, etc.) and willing to go way out on a limb. Schlagenheim is a really exciting start, which could lead in any number of directions.

Title: Built On Glass
Review: This record is intelligent, succinct in its ambitions, and more than anything, it’s pretty bloody cool.

Title: Poison Season
Review: It’s a surprise to see him employ such an economy of language, but Bejar can still command your attention with his sharp, romantic one-liners. He’s setting the scene by making a visceral impression with characters that feel alive, engulfed in their indecisiveness, driven with a theatrical imagination that’s as restless as it’s ever been.

Title: The Information
Review: He's turned his gaze back on himself and created a record that brilliantly summarises and even critiques his own past.

Title: Wilderness of Mirrors
Review: Wilderness of Mirrors isn't groundbreaking in general, but it is new territory for the often-cerebral English, and he puts an engaging, commanding stamp on this style of ambient overdrive hymn.

Title: Hug of Thunder
Review: More so than Forgiveness Rock Record, Hug of Thunder presents Broken Social Scene as a rock band making rock songs, a coherent montage rather than a patched-together highlight reel.

Title: Six Demon Bag
Review: A great album but, compared to their live shows, this is like listening to a circus. [Aug 2006, p.100]

Title: A Little Deeper
Review: It's Dynamite's choice of subject matter that distinguishes her from other R&B divas-in-waiting. [May 2003, p.110]

Title: Floreat
Review: The result is an album that will make many a listener feel like the cat that got the cream.

Title: Beyond the Pale
Review: It pulses with synths and electronic soundscapes overlaid by harp and violin, as if the early, experimental Pulp re-emerged as an electro Velvet Underground.

Title: Dark Night of the Soul
Review: Indeed, it's both comforting and sad to hear the audible fun involved in making this record.

Title: Yellow House
Review: The melodies are entrancing, made even more intriguing by their submergence within the reverb, together resulting in an album whose scope and sound are impossible to ignore.

Title: Gliss Riffer
Review: His fourth album, Gliss Riffer, continues that singular journey [the edge of pop and experimentation] and coerces elements of pop and madcap electronica into a convincing mix.

Title: Consummation
Review: On ‘Nothing Lasts’, the final song on the album, Schleicher seems to find peace after what’s been a fascinating but intense journey.

Title: Jungle
Review: West London synth duo Jungle claim to “bring the heat” on their debut album, but it’s more the languid haze of a holiday beach than the intensity of a dancefloor.

Title: Cee Lo's Magic Moment
Review: The dark songster offers a bright disc full of pudding-rich arrangements and a number of worthy soul hits--just with a little more twinkly tambourine.

Title: Millport
Review: Their punk training doesn’t quite lend them that particular grace. As a result, this can feel like a bit of a rough ride in places, albeit an intriguing one.

Title: Loma
Review: The band keeps a beautiful juxtaposition between major flourishes and minor dirges while the noise and dissonance never removes itself from the crevices of the songs.

Title: Palana
Review: Weird--but in a generally good way. [Feb 2016, p.75]

Title: Nothing Important
Review: Nothing Important is a remarkable record--at times deeply, painfully intimate, but also witty, bawdy, surreal, disquieting, nostalgic, brash and fearlessly individual.

Title: Vessel
Review: With a staggering 18 songs, Vessel may appear daunting at first, but quickly proves itself to be a sharp and smooth listen.

Title: Mature Themes
Review: Ultimately it just makes for frustrating listening.

Title: Augustines
Review: As a self-conscious play for stadium-rock ascension, it may prove successful. As a successor to one of the most honest and affecting debuts of recent years, however, it feels a little empty.

Title: Shangri-La
Review: The result is an ill-conceived concept album, one that, though characteristically sharp musically, feels flat and overwrought.

Title: Fingers, Bank Pads, and Shoe Prints
Review: Challenging, sure--but when it comes together, as on Kenny Loggins-sampling "Your Choice," exhilarating also. [Sep 2015, p.80]

Title: Pieces of a Man
Review: Pieces Of A Man is coherent, marrying the raw energy of trap with jazz-funk inspired beats. Black Milk’s instrumentals “Stress Fracture” and “Gwendolynn’s Apprehension” are remarkably complex both melodically and rhythmically. [Jan 2019, p.80]

Title: 100 Days, 100 Nights
Review: The band's reverence for its source material--all horns, Stax/Volt soul and he-done-me-wrong lyrics--occasionally gets so close that it's more clone than homage. But there's no denying the 51-year-old Jones' brutal, Aretha-ish voice

Title: White People
Review: Although White People doesn’t break any of the barriers ‘So…How’s Your Girl?’ did, it is none the less a graduation.

Title: Shame
Review: What they sculpt is impressive if not entirely unfamiliar. [Oct 2020, p.65]

Title: Only By The Night
Review: Essentially a funhouse mirror of 2007's far superior "Because of the Times," Only by the Night stumbles under the weight of its ambitions by lacking the songs necessary to support them

Title: You're a Woman, I'm a Machine
Review: A truly rocking dance punk album that fulfills on the promise of a dubious genre; other artists in this so-called movement have only hinted at something this fun and dance-able.

Title: Tides of a Teardrop
Review: The harmony between the two is captivating and eminently listenable; it’s easy to detect the seamless teamwork and understand why they’ve been so successful. Theirs is an airy sound, crystalline clear like splinters of sunlight in a hushed forest.

Title: Red Flag
Review: There’s far more good to be found on Red Flag than there is bad--this feels like the genuine follow-up to Saints And Sinners that Studio 1 should have been.

Title: Away
Review: It feels like a Sheff solo album in all but name, yet the change in approach has breathed new life into his work and helped him deliver an album that is both impressively bold in scope and magically intimate.

Title: Watch Me Fall
Review: Watch Me Fall includes some of his best sing-along jams yet.

Title: Midnite Vultures
Review: Midnite Vultures is the album of a great entertainer, not a great artist.

Title: The Stage Names
Review: The Stage Names shares the frenzy of pre–"Black Sheep" songs like 'The War Criminal Rises and Speaks,' and if it isn't as monolithic as the album that spurred the band's rise to "Believer"-subscriber prominence, it does contain several fine examples of hyper-articulate hysteria.

Title: Mirage Rock
Review: Mirage Rock is so lightweight and inconsequential that it really does seem more like an illusion than a record; it's wispy and indiscernible, as if the people who made it had no vision for what it should be.

Title: Syro
Review: Graying snobs once called this "intelligent dance music." Even now, few do it better.

Title: Rebirth
Review: It's a return to form and just what fans of Cliff's early work could ask for, but it's vital too, putting it on the man's top shelf, somewhere in the vicinity of The Harder They Come soundtrack and Wonderful World, Beautiful People.

Title: Goodness
Review: It presents itself as an almost impossible follow-up, but Goodness more than holds its weight, and shows its beauty in time.

Title: Aforger
Review: There are many highlights, to the point where it's evident this is just an exceptionally consistent record.

Title: Supper
Review: "Supper" is superior to the particularly subdued sound of its immediately predecessor, "Rain on Lens," landing closer to the Velvet Underground-inspired stomp of 1999's "Knock Knock."

Title: Wavering Radiant
Review: Some bands use studio trickery like an instrument, but Isis' straightforward tools avoid baroqueness even when the band is throwing deep.

Title: 1000 gecs
Review: By spotlighting upcoming artists alongside established names, 100 Gecs give an IRL boost to their ever-expanding community of internet collaborators on ‘1000 Gecs & the Tree of Clues’ while providing an exhilarating snapshot of pop’s alternative future.

Title: The Tipping Point
Review: As a listening experience, The Tipping Point is a decent album, a rough transition at best and a stumble at worst.

Title: Science Fiction
Review: Seething with anxiety and frontman Jesse Lacey’s trademark sarcastic self‑flagellation, and with a gorgeous production that gives the music space to breathe, it’s an emotional, intelligent work of grace and beauty.

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: It is Finn's particular gift to be able to set the listener smack in the middle of his songs, seeing what he sees, caring about the lives he chronicles. It is the listener's reward to find these stories scored by big, fat monster hooks, and effortless piano-driven melodies.

Title: Django Django
Review: It feels effortless. Even after repeated listening it somehow grows on you.

Title: Urban Turban - The Singhles Club
Review: With Urban Turbanm, Tjinder Singh reinforces his position as one of the UK's more engaging musical minds.

Title: Someday World
Review: At times the dreaded accusation of self-indulgence feels appropriate, and some of the songs here feel like sketches that still need fleshing out.

Title: Further
Review: Steadfastly chirping crescendos, whinnying breakbeat stampedes, and the odd evocative vocal.

Title: The Chaos
Review: Unbridled youthful vigor may now be but a distant speck in The Futureheads' rearview, but the joy of pop music still rings through in their every note.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: By taking various elements from not only their collective past, but also the work they've done separately, Radiohead has created something wholly new and utterly entrancing.

Title: Strange Peace
Review: To be clear, Metz haven’t turned into a pop band. They’ve actually done the opposite, incorporating harmony without going soft. The fact that so few heavy bands have been able to pull that off attests to how difficult it is. With Strange Peace, Metz make it sound easy.

Title: Don't Feed the Pop Monster
Review: At its best, Pop Monster injects plenty of fresh ideas into the Broods' repertoire, offering a handful of confident and polished gems that could have made for a stunning album if they had just sharpened their focus. Otherwise, lackluster inclusions that echo Lorde's sophomore shift dull the effort, which distracts from the excitement that occasionally shines through.

Title: Empire
Review: Empire arrives with the same frazzled mien as Oasis' What's The Story (Morning Glory); alive with paranoia, delivered with an unshakeable self-belief. It's relentless stuff. [Sep 2006, p.80]

Title: Tasty
Review: She doubles the weird factor. [Feb 2004, p.104]

Title: In Rainbows
Review: In Rainbows really does present Radiohead at their most full-blooded and confident.

Title: Cry
Review: It's about as vibrant and sweat-streaked as mainstream pop gets. [Dec 2002, p.105]

Title: Cool To Who
Review: There isn't anything innovative about their music, but every note of this album feels honest and considered.

Title: How Does It Feel
Review: As the album progresses, Plapinger’s vocals too often fail to engage, particularly on the more downbeat tracks, and there is a paucity of good ideas towards the end.

Title: Nobody's Daughter
Review: With Courtney Love the only original member involved, Hole's return is nominal, but Love's resurrection is very real....It's only when Love throws a pity party on a series of slow jams that sincerity eludes her.
Cohesive in its fragility. [19 Dec 2005]

Title: Back to Basics
Review: Ultimately, Aguilera's the only one of her peers with the vocal prowess to pull it off.

Title: Beings
Review: If the songs themselves sometimes seem to float by without fully grabbing the attention, when the melodies rise above the textures, as in The Blue Nile-style ache of Send Me Home, Lanterns On The Lake give us a glimpse of what might make them truly special. [Dec 2015, p.109]

Title: Loose
Review: It has at least seven killer tracks. [Jul 2006, p.101]

Title: The Sea
Review: It's to Bailey Rae's credit that never for one second does the album feel exploitative or mawkish, just truthful and real. [Mar 2010, p.94]

Title: Don't Believe The Truth
Review: As musically competent and beautifully-produced as this record undeniably is, strip the vocals and you'd be hard-pushed to identify it as being an Oasis album or enjoy it accordingly.

Title: Plum
Review: Wand are a special band, and the new emotional range suits them.

Title: EARS
Review: Antitheses abound--organic and electronic, modern and ancient, pastoral and urban. Combined, they create something extraordinary. [May 2016, p.91]

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: Acoustic guitar, harmonica and saxophone provide pools of warmth in the dusky depths.

Title: Little Red
Review: Rarely does a single album capture so much of what's right in a country's current moment in pop music.

Title: Conditions
Review: What the Temper Trap do devastatingly well is drape post-office-party mistake-hookup tackiness in the lofty imagery of global struggle....Elsewhere, the Temper Trap's pairing of sweeping portentousness with mundane douchebaggery is trickier to overlook.

Title: The Difference Between Me and You Is That I'm Not on Fire
Review: This set bogs down when the band flaunts its slow-chug technique at the expense of hooks and jokes. [#27, p.139]

Title: Dreamless Sleep
Review: There are a few too many tracks here that don't quite achieve lift-off. [Oct 2012, p.74]

Title: Keys to the World
Review: A deeply personal, occasionally lifeless but equally insightful passage into the latest chapter of Richard Ashcroft's life story.

Title: The Golden Age
Review: There's enough wide-eyed magic and spellbinding pomp here to make the adventure worthwhile.

Title: The Universe Inside
Review: It’s hard to believe this is the same band who bowed out with Ghost Stories. There they sounded uptight and reticent; here they are restless and free. The creative rebirth continues. Where to next? [May 2020, p.55]

Title: Downtown Church
Review: Fortunately for Griffin, the album boasts perhaps her finest performances to date, making Church an essential addition to her rich catalogue and a rewarding step in her ongoing emergence as more than just a go-to writer.

Title: Metropole
Review: This is a great album, one that carries the burden of growing up on its shoulders, but uses it for good instead of endlessly fighting against it, which punk bands need to do as they grow up.

Title: Tasmania
Review: The presence of tamp Impala's Kevin Parker in the producer's chair ensures that the sonic differences with his own band's sun-dried sci-fidelia are Rizla thin. However, frontman Nick Allbrook's rapier-sharp lyrics ensure that they still have their own livewire personality. [Apr 2019, p.114]

Title: Cardinology
Review: After this blisteringly good start, Cardinology settles down into a languid country-rock groove - beautiful at times, intensely listenable and professional, but probably not breaking any new ground.

Title: Pyramid of the Sun
Review: As a statement of intent from that band, Pyramid is promising in a shaky kind of way: it's clear that there's still creative magic to go around, but also that the old chemistry is going to be a tough one to reorient.

Title: Wire
Review: They may not be quite the same scrappy art rock brats that made Pink Flag and Chairs Missing underground classics, but they’re no less thoughtful and inventive in their songwriting approach.

Title: Upright Behavior
Review: It all feels a bit cosmic and a bit domestic, and that’s not unrelated to the way they play the songs--both tightly focused and freewheeling.

Title: Dip
Review: An incredibly pretty album with depth and scope.

Title: Pray IV Reign
Review: Those looking for timeless music on Pray IV Reign may find their prayers unanswered. But if you’re one of Jones’ longtime disciples, Capo’s got you covered.

Title: Rhine Gold

Title: Villains

Title: Hubba Bubba
Review: The inconsistency brings down the album as a whole and makes it a difficult front-to-back listen.

Title: Unfinished Business
Review: She's not ready to call time just yet. [Jan 2013, p.105]

Title: Future Brown
Review: The veneer slides aside to reveal more palpable excitement with the arrival of MCs from the UK grime contingent. [Mar 2015, p.48]

Title: Electric
Review: It's classic Thompson, packed with bleak stories of male failings, usually with a woman involved.

Title: In Animal Tongue
Review: Though at times a difficult listen, the album is at its best when Bozulich's voice is paired with haunting cello. [Oct. 2011, p. 108]

Title: Home, Like Noplace is There
Review: From start to finish there’s almost nothing to fault here.
