Review: The fact that it’s not doing anything particularly new doesn’t really matter because it’s hitting all the right notes and pushing all the right buttons. Most of all, just like their debut, it’s a lot fun.

Title: Sun Giant
Review: As with many releases like this, I wish the ride were just a little bit more bumpy just to throw off expectations, but nonetheless Fleet Foxes have put out quite an enjoyable little debut here.

Title: Manzanita

Title: Salton Sea
Review: It's ambitious, diverse, unique, and tonally and aesthetically complex.

Title: Todd Smith
Review: When LL teams with younger rappers... the album's momentum suffers. [23 Apr 2006]

Title: Dead Magic
Review: It’s an album certain of what it wants to be, but lacking in the naturalness needed to truly convince, let alone amaze.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: With Rick Rubin at the helm, employing his trademark austerity but not overdoing the dryness, the group swings for the fences musically, lyrically, vocally, and emotionally. Its batting average is sterling.

Title: I'm Not Your Man
Review: [“Round We Go” is] a roiling, overpowering emotional mixture, and it fits right in with what I’m Not Your Man wants to accomplish: a forthright treatise on sexuality and relationships, told with an uncanny sense of comedic timing and a penchant for reaching for the throat with its hooks, arrangements, and, most resoundingly, its lyrics.

Title: Marry Me
Review: Though her versatility is promising, Clark will be able to compete only when she figures out how to be one very interesting person, instead of five caricatures at once.

Title: Plastics
Review: Plastics represents a significant first step upon which the group can move upwards from, and it’s exciting to see what they do next. But it’s a shame they couldn’t carry the excellence through to the end of a record.

Title: Wild Flag
Review: That sense of teetering on the ledge of chaos, of mayhem fighting melody for control, makes Wild Flag a debut for the ages.

Title: Directions to See a Ghost
Review: By no means an awful record, but certainly a disappointing one.

Title: Tell Me I'm Pretty
Review: These guys aren't just reliving classic sounds, they're giving them a frantic sense of dread that's perfect for our own dislocated, paranoid times.

Title: Buoys
Review: A modest effort of just over half an hour. [Mar 2019, p.62]

Title: Between Waves
Review: Between Waves is an album created by a man who knows what he’s doing; and that’s the problem. He could create satisfactory albums till the end of days, but he’ll need to rip up the rulebook if he’s to grab people’s attention in this fickle age.

Title: Perpetuum Mobile
Review: Rather than fetishing these sound sources, Neubaten vacuum-pack the lot inside a hermetic and constricting production that is immensely disturbing. [#241, p.57]

Review: The album is plagued by similarly banal lyrics about sex and drugs that make his playboy image feel all the more superficial.... More positively, the poppier musical strategy perfectly suits his boyish vocals, and he sounds more open and less pretentious than ever before.

Title: We Are Born
Review: Not as good as we were hoping, but still strong enough to make us excited about the next chapter.

Title: Everybody
Review: The product of a band that clearly loves its formula enough to tease it a little, Everybody is another fetching expression of The Sea And Cake's never-changing moods.

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: While enjoyable and familiar, this set of songs reflects a band who knows what music they don't want to be making but haven't--at least, not yet--determined what it is they want to be defined by instead.

Title: Big Wheel and Others
Review: Throughout, McCombs hits a brilliantly unpredictable songwriting stride. [No. 103, p.57]

Title: Dirty Vegas

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: It's their best album in nearly 20 years. [Aug 2016, p.112]

Title: Franz Ferdinand
Review: The most ebullient British debut since Elastica. [Mar 2004, p.102]

Title: Believe
Review: On Believe, Disturbed takes the sort of jump that their heroes in Soundgarden and Pantera made after their respective breakthrough records.

Title: Rodeo

Title: Wild Flag
Review: It's a moment that feels like an emotional explosion – and it sums up everything great about Wild Flag.

Title: DiCaprio 2
Review: DiCaprio 2 surpasses everything the rapper offered before it, with his strengths in full focus at a level that can't help but remind of the career peaks of greats that came before him.

Title: To Be Kind
Review: It’s an insane and challenging, ambitious and exceptional work of art.

Title: Concrete Rose
Review: A lack of originality and too much filler mark Ashanti more as a pedestrian than the princess she purports to be.

Title: Unorthodox Jukebox
Review: It's appealing, generally engaging and all shot through with the confidence of a man who must feel he's got the hit parade Midas touch

Title: Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys
Review: The band's held on to its drive and focus, and the hits outnumber the misses.

Title: Don't Weigh Down the Light
Review: Not a great deal seems to be happening--then you are suddenly brought up short by the guitar that sings out on Back to You or the polyphony of Leaving Song.

Title: Royal Blood
Review: A tight bind of rhythm and noise, of chugging menace and sudden spikes.

Review: His characters are round and puzzling, not just sour. He uses bitterness not just as a good look but as a method of getting inside his characters.

Review: Ever so slowly, sounds build upon sounds, but it never seems overbearing. It's swaddling, enveloping. Nomad is music to get lost within.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: The result on The Whole Love is a work by a group of exceptional musicians who, four years into their collaboration, have melded into one.

Title: More Rain

Review: TSOM's strange, taut, heroic beauty invariably transcends irony. [Dec 2018, p.89]

Title: FOMO
Review: He's really coming into his own, and he'll have his masterpiece yet, probably a few of them. FOMO isn't one, but it sure is a lovely listen, something that completists will likely point to one day as some of the old guy's "good-but-not-great, early stuff."

Title: No Sounds Are Out Of Bounds
Review: The Orb have long made a virtue out of following their own path, and there are still times in No Sounds Are Out Of Bounds where this pays dividends, but there are also sections where they merely retread old ground with diminishing returns, making this an only half-satisfying LP.

Title: Bloom
Review: Bloom is an exceptional pop album, but maybe more importantly it’s a beacon for queer people who struggle to reconcile our neuroses--societal and personal--with our potential for joy and love.

Title: Girl Talk
Review: there are occasions on Girl Talk when we get glimpses of what another, better Kate Nash indie rock album would have sounded like.... Unfortunately, moments such as these are the exception, not the rule, on Girl Talk.

Title: The Mouse and the Mask
Review: The addition of Adult Swim characters into damn near every track isn't always seamless or clever, and the album could do without "Bada Bing" or Meatwad's intentionally painful bonus-track cover of Doom's "Beef Rapp," but otherwise, this stellar collaboration threatens to give underground synergy a good name.

Title: Hexed
Review: As a whole, Hexed may be CoB's most diverse and expansive-sounding album to date, ranging between their roots sound and adventurous experimentation. The synthesis approach found here makes for a compelling, deeply satisfying outing.

Title: The Besnard Lakes are the Roaring Night
Review: You won't find a more compelling wall of sound in many other places this year.

Title: Kindred
Review: While Kindred remains meticulously and impressively crafted, it just doesn’t carry the same emotional weight.

Title: Bright and Vivid
Review: Sweetly ambitious math-rock, put across with folky tunefulness and a girlish effervescence.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Mouse on Mars have successfully adhered to an important distinction regarding electronic music: to utilize vocalists as additional detail and atmosphere without ever fully depending on them.

Title: Days of Gold
Review: There's no mistaking Days of Gold for anything earthy, but this sonic thawing winds up emphasizing Owen's inherent sweetness in an appealing fashion.

Title: Ciara
Review: However good the other tracks are here, it's her indomitable track with Nicki Minaj, I'm Out, that powers this album.

Title: Just Whitney
Review: Appears and sounds more like a work-in-progress than a finished disc.

Title: The Thrill of It All
Review: Turning heartache into Top 40 magic is Smith’s strength--he famously thanked an ex for his success during a Grammys speech--but only a few moments here truly resonate emotionally. One of those is the staggering standout “HIM.”

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: In finding their way back to what works, it too often sounds rehashed to make it a true return to form the band has been yearning to find.

Title: In a Perfect World
Review: With time, greater individuality will come. Right now, this is an accomplished and emotive statement of intent, cinematic in scope and able to raise goose bumps at will.

Title: Boomiverse
Review: On past projects he has been comfortable sticking to a script he’s outlined for himself but here, he operates without rules. He isn’t bound by tempo, theme, style or even genre for that matter. All that appears to matter to Big Boi on Boomiverse is making good music that players can still bump in their Cadillacs.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: No great leaps forward from ‘Everything All The Time’ and ‘Cease To Begin’, just lovely, warm-hearted, full-throated harmonies and gentle melancholy.

Title: Internal Sounds
Review: Internal Sounds is a sparkling conflation of '69-vintage Byrds, early Burritos and psychedelic country helped along by the odd splash of boiling surf. [Oct 2013, p.74]

Title: Rockferry
Review: There's nothing dislikable about Rockferry - but nothing that dazzles, either.

Title: What Were You Hoping For?
Review: Twice as raw and thrice as hungry as anything the neo-soul mastermind has previously released, Hoping-from the title on down-is a full-throated, full-throttle challenge.

Title: Lucid Dreaming
Review: Consistently melodic, it’s packed full of hooks and almost suspiciously on-trend.

Title: Directions to See a Ghost
Review: The band call their dark noise "hypno-drone'n'roll", but they could do with less drone, more roll.

Title: Favourite Worst Nightmare
Review: Favourite Worst Nightmare finds the band getting louder, more aggressive, and, as a consequence, losing some of their youthful charm.

Title: Boo Boo
Review: All of this means that, in spite of the anguished self-interrogation that went into its making, this still sounds exactly how a Toro y Moi album should sound. However, Boo Boo feels like what we might call a coming-of-age album.

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: They sound like they'll probably end up being one of the most enduring bands of our era.

Title: Bon Voyage
Review: Beautiful things take time to properly come to life, and this is no exception; although this reading obviously comes in the aftermath of her accident, Bon Voyage sounds like a rebirth of sorts for Prochet.

Title: Choice of Weapon
Review: While the pomp and sense of urgency may be gone from the band's '90s heyday, this is a solid effort and a worthy choice for rock fans who want something loud to drive fast to.

Title: Walls
Review: With a decided mature edge over the Canadian twins [Tegan And Sara], vocalist/guitarist Kate Cooper and drummer/vocalist Damon Cox have reached their first pinnacle on their second album. [June 2011, p.106]

Title: Folklore
Review: Folklore is essentially the sound of an artist taking a risk.

Title: From a Basement on the Hill
Review: Exquisite, angry, sad and personal, basement is a beautiful swan song of one of this generation's best.

Title: Nocturne
Review: This is a gorgeous album of soundscapes that are able to stand up alone.

Title: What Have We Become?
Review: Anyone who enjoys their pop with extra wry and some sobering awareness should love What Have We Become?, but it's the Beautiful South faithful who will rightfully gush over the release, as these antiheroes have lost none of their touch or fatalistic flair.

Title: Hardcourage
Review: Hardcourage steps on from the broken UK garage rhythms that typify much of FaltyDL’s earlier work and into the sort of soulful, pleasurable house grooves occupied by the likes of Four Tet and Jamie xx.

Title: Cocky
Review: Lyrically, he's got one thing to say: Kid Rock is back, Kid Rock has lots of money, Kid Rock has the dames licked down, Kid Rock is hard. Which is all good when done properly, with wit, but Kid Rock is not clever, and he's not funny.

Title: Floreat
Review: Funky, funny, stately, strange, soulful and sensual, Floreat is a unique and unequivocal triumph. [Oct 2011, p.83]

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: So Divided
Review: So Divided attempts to unify the Austin outfit's operatic songcraft with the urgency of their "Days of Being Wild" to unlock 2003's The Secret of Elena's Tomb EP and overcome the trappings of the previous year's brilliant Source Tags and Codes, from which those days sprung.

Title: The Great Destroyer
Review: Songs like “California” and “Walk Into the Sea,” by far the sunniest, poppiest material Low has ever produced, shatter the mopey mold the band has so carefully cultivated, and to thrilling results.

Title: The Blueprint 2: The Gift & the Curse
Review: Overreaching but surprisingly solid.

Title: Soused
Review: The result is the most accessible Scott Walker album since Tilt, perhaps even longer. [Nov 2014, p.74]

Title: African Giant
Review: A swaggering, electric, and passion-fueled statement that lives up to the towering persona being put forth at its outset. ... African Giant is easily Burna Boy’s most cohesive and strongest project, with even the diverse list of guest stars—from Damien Marley to Nigerian rapper Zlatan to Jeremih and Future—being used expertly without overkill. Burna Boy is the true star at the center.

Title: Origami Harvest
Review: The result is a voyage through America that is both dreamlike and dystopian, exhausting but oddly compelling.

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: It's true that guitar-pop is all this is, but it's still bloody good stuff.

Title: The Harrow & The Harvest
Review: Gillian Welch returns after an eight-year drought with fifth LP The Harrow & the Harvest, an album sown with dry desperation.

Title: Animated Violence Mild
Review: Not surprisingly, many of the highlights of his fourth solo album – a treatise on capitalism and loss – nod to Power’s better-known band.

Title: Heartbreak Weather
Review: There are hints of experimentation, such as Nice to Meet Ya’s swaggering hybrid of Arctic Monkeys and Kasabian, but it’s the excellent title track’s flirtation with glossy, synth-tinged MOR that suggests where Horan might be headed next. Proof that it’s often the quiet ones you need to keep an eye on.

Title: Boo Boo
Review: At its peak, Boo Boo is Toro Y Moi’s most luxurious, if not remarkably lush effort since 2011’s Underneath the Pine.

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: We have this perfectly pleasant and assuming piece of synth pop, neighing through a vocoder with the dying breath of the shamelessly beaten horse of retro-futurism.

Title: The Body, The Blood, The Machine
Review: Without sacrificing aural excitement, they have polished their approach with a refined understanding of dynamics and a broadening of style.

Title: Run
Review: Heroic. [May 2015, p.100]

Title: Shelter From The Ash
Review: Although there are moments of striking beauty here, the guitar sounds become repetitive, and Chasny's vocal is not particularly convincing.

Title: Funhouse
Review: Pink continues to make everything she touches her own. She uses brains and brawn to turn the mainstream into a complicated place.

Title: The Sun Awakens
Review: The Sun Awakens is the record he's been promising. Where School of the Flower was a leap, placing his singing and guitar playing in equal measure -- though there were numerous instrumental pieces -- The Sun Awakens is the place they burst forth, fully entwined, completely formed.

Title: Be Set Free
Review: Be Set Free is the musical equivalent of a green bean casserole.  It’s not going be anyone’s favorite dish at the table, but everyone, young and old, will want a second helping.

Title: The Broken String
Review: Longer listeners will be impressed with the band’s evolution but will inevitably be let down with the lack of charm in these new recordings as opposed to their looser demo cuts.

Title: Wildcard
Review: For an album named Wildcard, there doesn't seem to a standout track. There are some very songs with strong emotional appeal and literate, artful lyrics such as the reflective "Bluebird", the love story "Fire Escape", the teary "Dark Bars", and even the comic "Pretty Bitchin'".

Title: Duets II
Review: Bennett fares better in gorgeous duets with k.d. lang and Aretha Franklin, and his romp with Willie Nelson is precisely as charming as you'd expect. But for an old pro like Bennett, there's a name for that kind of stuff: child's play.

Title: In Prism
Review: It's a sprawling, psychedelic masterwork, rife with knotty tangles of discordance and serpentine riffs.

Title: Ghost Notes
Review: Sometimes the songwriting relies too heavily on swelling harmonies and crescendos, and occasional lyrical clichés grate.

Title: Holograms
Review: Their self-titled debut LP packs a mighty wallop, matching a brutish, derisive attitude with whip-smart songwriting and compelling hooks.

Title: Planet Earth
Review: What actually lies inside Prince’s twenty-somethingth album is more than disappointing; it’s thinly if grandly produced, tapped with a veneer so dumbly decades behind any sense of interesting or intriguing taste that one can’t help but sit back and swallow the benign whole, thinking all along, Who the fuck even makes music like this anymore?

Title: Desire
Review: Desire is a taut and focused work that energizes, packed densely with typically Monch-like quotables that might take a couple listens to catch.

Title: Southern Hummingbird
Review: It goes down better if you concentrate more on her charming voice and the tracks, rather what she is actually saying.

Title: Easy Machines
Review: Easy Machines is ultimately more engaging, its mangled classic pop recalling Guided By Voices. [Jun 2017, p.105]

Title: Open
Review: It doesn't quite blow the emotional lid off, but Open is rich in subtle variations. [Dec 2017, p.88]

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: I prefer to think of Lookout Mountain as an album of pretty-good songs from a guy who has written some unbelievably great ones, and will, more than likely, write some more of that quality down the road.

Title: ATGCLVLSSCAP
Review: The album is one long ambient jam and precisely as exciting as that sounds. [16 Jan 2016, p.53]

Title: Holy
Review: Singer-songwriter Sam Jayne has an affection for classic rock and a great sense of whimsy about it.

Title: Shrines
Review: The band's ability to put repulsive images and to a danceable beat makes Shrines a knockout.

Title: Keep It Hid
Review: A highly accomplished solo debut from Auerbach. [Winter 2009, p.69]

Title: II Trill
Review: II Trill is obviously not Bun B’s defining musical statement; UGK has way too many classics in the bank for that. What it is, though, is a consistently great rap album by a consistently great emcee.

Title: Experiments In Time
Review: When the album finished, I immediately wanted to hear it again. And then again.

Title: The Mysterious Production of Eggs
Review: Folk songs given a rarefied air by his elegant wordplay and multi-tracked chamber strings. [Mar 2005, p.108]

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: Apologies To The Queen Mary is often unfocused, but it's plenty lovable.

Title: Future Nostalgia
Review: It’s an impeccably crafted, gleefully executed half-hour-plus of pop perfection that does meet the moment, maybe, in just reminding you how good it feels to be human. And to be in love. And to be in Studio 54.

Title: Mon Pays
Review: The use of the light, nimble calabash instead of drums helps craft a subtle, hypnotic sound that eschews the rock dynamics recently incorporated by the likes of Tinariwen or Tamikrest. This approach creates music that is somehow simultaneously vibrant and contemplative.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: "Tio Bitar" is an excellent follow-up to "Ta Det Lugnt," offering another far-out trip courtesy of Ejstes and his musical magic.

Title: Born To Die
Review: Tune out the background media noise and immerse yourself. [Mar 2012, p.94]

Title: No Treasure But Hope
Review: No Treasure But Hope is further refinement of what they've been doing in the past. [Dec 2019, p.89]

Title: Event II
Review: Event II is a satisfactory sequel, if not quite a gem on its own merit.

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: If this were purely an experimental electronic album, we'd overlook the lack of hooks, but even as such it's not particularly impressive.

Title: X Marks Destination
Review: While opener 'Trash' sounds like the sort of thing Bloc Party should have done after "Silent Alarm," most tracks are hurt by a real lack of lyrical depth.

Title: Ledges
Review: There are many fine moments here. [Apr 2014, p.76]

Title: A Moment of Madness
Review: With 17 tracks this album could be expected to take off to somewhere fantastic but, although we stay very much on the same page throughout the duration of the record, the pristine production of A Moment Of Madness is faultless.

Title: True North
Review: These aren’t stoical songs; nor are they blandly defiant. They speak a deep truth about ageing, and one that spikes several more humdrum cliches: age isn’t just how you feel, but an ineluctable fact; it isn’t just a matter of numbers, but very much a felt experience, and Chapman has delivered a beautiful continuum of musical experience since he emerged in 1969 with Rainmaker and Fully Qualified Survivor. [Mar 2019, p.48]

Title: Welcome Home Armageddon
Review: This is a fast-tempo, punk and metal-tinged homage to days gone by and those yet to come and, as a result, may well be the band's best effort since their much-lauded debut.

Title: Pala
Review: It's all done with such passion that the more sugared tracks avoid the risk of boyband smoothness, and will surely blast out across barbecues and festivals this summer.

Title: Murdered Love
Review: Murdered Love is a perfectly enjoyable and easily digestible slice of rap-metal.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die II
Review: The knotty lyricism and psychedelic rumble of 12 Reasons to Die II should be more than enough to keep Ghostface fans satisfied.

Title: Yours Truly, The Commuter
Review: The haunting tone unfurls itself further with every successive listen, making this an album worth returning to again and again. [June 2009, p.102]

Title: Honeys
Review: This is the stuff of vicious hangovers, unkempt hair being head-banged back and forth furiously, and eyebrow-raising debacles on public transport.

Title: In a Space Outta Sound
Review: In A Space Outta Sound spits some pretty standard jazzy hip-hop sounds, but for a lazy Sunday afternoon it could serve as a funky, stony soundtrack. [#13, p.98]

Title: Continuum
Review: Continuum is a gorgeously produced, brilliantly stripped-to-basics album that incorporates blues, soft-funk, R&B, folk and pop in a sound that is totally owned by Mayer. It's no stretch when trying to describe the sound of Continuum to color it in the light of work by such legends as Sting, Eric Clapton, Sade, Stevie Ray Vaughan and Steve Winwood.

Title: Hyperspace
Review: Overall, it's a glittering, multi-sensory synth-pop record that compels you to let yourself be transported through cosmic dimensions and the rich, textured under-layers of Beck’s creative psyche.

Title: American Gangster
Review: Judging by this surprisingly strong return to form, Jay-Z might want to consider spending less time in the office and more time at the movies.

Title: The Bake Sale
Review: The Cool Kids remember when hip-hop was a party. [Summer 2008]

Title: Basic Behaviour
Review: FRIGS half-convincingly communicate their agitation over piercing shards of noise. The band are at their best when the rhythm section takes charge.

Title: Black Rat
Review: The pair still aren’t in that DFA1979 category of combatively brilliant, just yet.

Title: the gamble
Review: An electronically based album rich in its own distinctive character.

Title: Big Music
Review: This is the first new Simple Minds album in recent memory that you’ll want to keep returning to.

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: The results--notably 'Cheap And Cheerful,' which suggests that Britney Spears' 'Toxic' made quite an impact on them and the chaotic 'Alphabet Pony'--are a revelation.

Title: Emerald Valley
Review: There’s are threads of heritage strung through Emerald Valley, not just in the vintage ‘70s/’80s guitar pop pedigree of the riffs and rhythms (“One Flew East,” “Break Me” and “Last Chance County” all from the second half particularly stand out), but also in Tucker’s lyrics and delivery, which are earnest and earthy without curtailing her natural dynamic.

Title: Sacred Love
Review: Rife with hyper-marketable flamenco guitars and jazz pianos, it's world music for people whose idea of adventure is a trip to Banana Republic.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: A brilliant record that serves as a perfect blueprint on how to make something new out of something old.

Title: Hidden Fields
Review: Devastating until the very last note subsides, this is arguably The Telescopes' finest record for over a decade. Prepare to be pulverised.

Title: Unto the Locust
Review: Machine Head is still a force in modern heavy metal.

Title: Showroom of Compassion
Review: Retaking the reins and returning to their indie roots, Cake delivers after the lengthy hiatus. New, old, different or not, Cake fans will have plenty to appreciate.

Title: Break It Yourself
Review: Whether contemplatively highbrow (the symphonic meditation "Hole in the Ocean Floor") or forlornly down-to-earth (the alt-country of "Fatal Shore"), his angst studies feel cathartic without seeming mean-spirited.

Title: Feels
Review: Despite its many wondrous moments, 'Feels' is not a record for everyone.

Title: Postcards from Paradise
Review: A rather predictable record. [May 2015, p.107]

Title: Suddenly
Review: For more than 20 years, Snaith has displayed a rare versatility and ability to keep things fresh. Suddenly is no different.

Title: Satin Panthers
Review: This is the sound of pigeonhole-free ambition slowly being realised, and it's sounding great.

Title: SMiLE
Review: This is pop music like nothing before it, or since.

Title: Push the Button
Review: The lion’s share of these tracks throb with a purpose that was mostly absent from their last effort.

Title: Life Is People
Review: Life Is People is superb. [Sep 2012, p.84]

Title: More Faithful
Review: The intricate layering of warped guitars and echoing vocals is all well and good for the background to summer fun, but for No Joy to be more than this More Faithful relies on these more intimate moments. Although these are sparsely scattered throughout they’re just enough to make More Faithful more than just a half-listened to soundtrack to road trips and festivals but an album with heart, confidence and intimacy.

Title: The Invisible Band
Review: This album is so lightweight and airy, it often consigns itself to the background.

Title: Loved Me Back to Life
Review: The finished product is almost a reinvention.

Title: My Favorite Picture of You
Review: Though there are some slow-burners on this record; songs that might not stick on the first or second go round, they are worth the patience once they finally click with the listener.

Title: Jamie Lidell
Review: [A] successful collection. [Mar 2013, p.91]

Title: Heligoland
Review: The album's dusty beats, pointed electronics, and cinematic feel are pleasantly familiar, at best they recall the band's past glory rather than pushing forward their legacy.

Title: Kittenz and Thee Glitz
Review: The perfect guest at your next guilty-pleasure dance party.

Title: Summer Sun
Review: Summer Sun, while constantly very good, is never creative, inspiring or great. [Editor's Note: Score listed is an average of three separate reviews/scores by this publication: 56, 60, 68]

Title: In Between
Review: This is the sound of The Feelies aging more gracefully. Simply put, like Here Before, this takes its place in their flawless discography as yet another gem. [Jan - Mar 2017, p.65]

Title: Face Tat
Review: Face Tat is less free-form than Astrological Straits, 2008's exhilarating, exhausting debut, but it's still a full 15 rounds of aural boxing. [Feb 2011, p.100]

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: Fallen Empires is typically and unashamedly arena-friendly bombast ... leavened by leader Gary Lightbody's often appealing insecurity.[Dec. 2011 p. 134]

Title: Phantom Planet
Review: Ambitious, uneven. [Feb 2004, p.96]

Title: Whorl
Review: On this evidence, SMD aren't quite there and the result is, sadly, a bit boring.

Title: Dream River
Review: At its core, this is a record about accepting and even embracing the smallness of human life, and how difficult that can be, given our damnably innate sense of adventure, ambition, and restlessness.

Title: Tower of Love
Review: Possibly cloying in large doses. [Jan 2006, p.112]

Title: Born To Die
Review: For all of its coos about love and devotion, it's the album equivalent of a faked orgasm-- a collection of torch songs with no fire.

Title: Planta
Review: They’ve used the time to come to terms with the loss of Cintra and create a sonic identity beyond his input, and it turns out that they didn’t really need him, and, just maybe, he was stalling their progress.

Title: Sea Lion
Review: Layered, and a bit rough-around-the-edges, Sean Lion is also a heck of a lot of fun, and marks The Ruby Suns as a young group to keep an eye on.

Title: Doggumentary
Review: Snoop's 11th album unevenly celebrates his all-over-the-map persona.

Title: Sagara
Review: It's a concise album, just 35 minutes, but its ethereality makes the time drift slowly: the percussive plink of a piano (or something like it), about 24 minutes in, registers as a decisive event.

Throughout these towering production flourishes, Adele's vocals cast an even vaster shadow: swooping, swerving, blaring brassily and cooing tenderly, a full orchestra unto itself that's theatrical, unpredictable, and dynamic.

Title: The Age of Adz
Review: Stevens ventures widely on this 85-minute disc to find the best way to express what turn out to be basic home truths.

Title: Transfiguration Highway
Review: This follow-up to 2018’s Might As Well With My Soul, in some sense, serves to highlight the band’s underrated ability to deviate from well-worn norms.

Title: Nixon
Review: The most fully realised Lambchop record, the most perfect blend yet of their alt country roots and their obsession with soul.

Title: Getting Away with Murder
Review: This is a determined little bastard of a record by a band in a bug-eyed, rhythmic sweat, who know it’s time to come out with their guns blazing.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Fishing for Fishies
Review: Fishing for Fishies is the freest the band have sounded in a while, and the record is all the better for it.

Title: Through the Windowpane
Review: There isn't a duff track to be seen, and you get the feeling the whole thing's been meticulously planned and orchestrated, with a mindset of giving us a record to cherish, something to put on when the chips are down, and that rare thing, one that will almost certainly be loved in equal measure many years down the line.

Title: Power
Review: This is a clanging, disruptive splatter of a debut, which speaks to the frustration of otherness through sheer feeling, rather than easily digestible vocals.

Title: Nothing's Real
Review: Nothing’s Real offers a fresh vision for pop’s new reality.

Title: Volume One
Review: Where the album suffers, however--especially in comparision to the Jenny Lewis record--is the absence of any real lyrical verve or personality. [Aug 2008, p.94]

Title: Parallax
Review: Parallax being Cox's most coherent record to date, it's harder to spotlight individual tracks, but individual settings stand out.

Title: Pollinator
Review: Despite the divergent inputs, Pollinator still has the feel of a coherent album that’s enjoyable, if hardly essential.

Title: Yours Truly, Angry Mob
Review: Kaiser Chiefs scramble to reclaim ground already won, sticking with lazily hooky songs sporting overcranked arrangements. The result? Charmless fare like the bombastic UK hit single "Ruby," and loutish lad-rock like "Thank You Very Much" and "My Kind Of Guy," which sound simultaneously pushy and forgettable.

Title: Snowdonia
Review: Getting these skills to jell means moving further away from the Surfer Blood that fans may be accustomed to, but Snowdonia hints at a rewarding payoff.

Title: Noble Beast
Review: Beast is his most instantly inviting album by far and vividly underscores his skills as a producer.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Lost Songs
Review: Lost Songs splits the difference between some of the more overly emotive/dramatic Trail of Dead featured on recent albums, and the frenetic, exciting Trail of Dead of its the early years.

Title: Banga
Review: For the rest of her 11th studio album she makes good on her word, drawing connections across history between cultures, generations and genres of music.

Title: Daytona
Review: Daytona stands loud and proud among Pusha T's best work. [Aug 2018, p.91]

Title: Babel
Review: Two albums in and Mumford & Sons still sound like a talented outfit fused to the starting block, paralyzed by the thought of having to truly race for their lives.

Title: Get Born
Review: There's no denying the disc's unbridled energy, and those who pine for a return to the booze-fueled days of '70s rock must find immense pleasure in Get Born's finer moments.

Title: Cassadaga
Review: Cassadaga is fulsome, epic, and swirling, by far Oberst's most sophisticated, seamless effort. [May 2007, p.89]

Title: Miserable Miracles
Review: Eray’s opening haze burns out to reveal stark, staccato drums, an urgent, discordant Juno lead and almost Orbital-esque bassline, providing a fine touchpoint for Blue Hour and Earth and Elsewhere’s tech-purist soundscapes: think Aphex Twin’s Ambient Works II. They're a fine addition, though an indulgence amid an album of otherwise brilliance.

Title: Saturns Pattern
Review: While it might not feature too many songs the faithful will be hollering for at gigs, it's crammed full of ear candy. [Jun 2015, p.98]

Title: Celebration, Florida
Review: An engaging diversion down a road which might be worth investigating further.

Title: Donuts
Review: Donuts is hip-hop, then, like “Howl” is poetry or Guernica is painting: the best aspects of a particular style, developed to their fullest and executed masterfully.

Title: Honor Found in Decay
Review: Honor found in Decay confirms that they are a metal band, yes--but one reminiscent of Silver Mount Zion or Swans as any more traditionally heavy-rocking concern. [Nov 2012, p.73]

Title: E Volo Love
Review: Overall, even through the rough spots, this is a project deserving of full attention.

Some improved diversity and novel musical ideas make 13.0.0.0.0 a much more interesting listen, though, and it's nice to hear a math rock band bringing more than just math to their songwriting sensibilities.

Title: Oh Land
Review: It's lush, detailed, frequently over-rich, but Fabricius' bright, perky voice and some generically kooky lyrics can't really carry the weight of the whole production. [Aug 2011, p.94]

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: A sort of gothy folktronica dominates songs like "Yes Men" and "Out The Way," with shades of PJ Harvey on the acerbic title track about refugees, while the crawling jutter of "2016" captures the dislocating agony of experiencing personal anxiety while "there's a fascist in the White House." [Sep 2017, p.37]

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: King of Cowards
Review: A66 is made thrilling by the gear change midway through, ditching its Sabbath crawl for a brutal climax. Nothing else quite succeeds in cutting through the downtuned murk, although riffs are uniformly monolithic and frontman Matt Baty's throaty bark is never less than entertaining. [Nov 2018, p.112]

Title: Green Language
Review: Originality may not abound but Green Language still remains an undeniably fun record to sink your teeth into.

Title: Jesus Piece
Review: Jesus Piece certainly isn't his best album, but if it ends up being his worst, then Jayceon's doing pretty damn good for himself.

Title: The Dreamer / The Believer
Review: It's a shame the God-bothering pomp of John Legend collaboration "The Believer" spoils it all at the end.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel

The album’s lead single, with its descending guitar notes and a Margaret Atwood reference, finds Barnett employing old tools to tackle a newsworthy social ill. It’s breathless and gutting, a short and sweet examination of sex and violence. It draws blood, but so does the rest of the album.

Title: The Process of Belief
Review: A MY-T-FINE punk rock album, chock full of swirling harmonies that came into fashion sometime around the Descendents rise in the mid-1980s.

Title: The Runaway

Title: Nothing Is True & Everything Is Possible
Review: Enter Shikari have the tools and drive to create something potentially mind-blowing, it’s just that they fell well short of the mark on this occasion.

Title: Second Round's on Me
Review: Eminem complements [Trice's] sinister outlook with equally gloomy production. [Aug 2006, p.140]

Title: Something For All of Us
Review: Throughout, Canning aspires to the rousing anthems that have made Broken Social Scene one of the best acts of the last decade, but he falls short. He’s certainly not a lemon in the BSS product line; he’s just an underwhelming model. [Summer 2008]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: Lazaretto, named after a place of quarantine for sailors, hurtles between moods and tempos, often within the same song.

Title: V
Review: V is like a peppy new Nissan Altima: It won’t give you too many problems; it won’t attract stares; it probably won’t get stolen. Its parts are reliable, though none have the pulse of “Moves Like Jagger,” the 2011 hit that gave this group new life.

Title: Veni Vidi Vicious
Review: The Hives explode where a hundred other punk bands are proud to rock.

Title: Voyageur
Review: The album, as intended to be heard, deftly captures the whiplash mood swings of a volatile relationship, showing how giddy exuberance and bitter despair can intertwine.

Title: Frantic
Review: Recalls The Bride Stripped Bare, Ferry's 1978 art-R&B lament. [#8, p.116]

Title: Supreme Blientele
Review: The 18-song offering is a cohesive masterpiece.

Title: Kingdom of Rust
Review: It gradually reveals itself as a lithe and texturally consummate work.

Title: Waxing Romantic
Review: Taken as a whole though, Waxing Romantic is a warm, enjoyable listen; one that suggests Bretzer has a voice worth hearing and all of his own.

Title: Head First
Review: This may be the most lovingly detailed synth-pop album since the golden days of Yaz and Kim Carnes. Yet expert execution doesn't always signal a good idea.

Title: A Woman A Man Walked By
Review: A Woman A Man Walked By is a side project in the worst sense of the term; a slight diversion that's really for Harvey completists only. [Spring 2009, p.66]

Title: Love Life
Review: Tamia does not to attempt to hit those high notes that Williams and few others have been able to reach, but she gets the feeling across. It's a fine finish to her best album yet.

Title: Infinite Dissolution
Review: It is their most holistic, inventive recording to date and ups the ante for anyone trying to follow them.

Title: Issa Album
Review: Issa Album needn’t be The Infamous, but it could’ve benefitted from a clearer and tighter direction.

Title: Born into This
Review: With few real rockers, Born is more disappointing than it had to be.

Title: Country Sleep
Review: Winston Yellen’s debut Country Sleep builds an intangible place you’re immediately delivered to upon first listen.

Title: Shock'n Y'all
Review: The hilariously blasphemous Jesus number, '80s-AOR-chorded tough-girl ode, Margaritaville-calypsoed frat-band lookback, and outlaw drawler about Willie's deadly herb all movingly balance muscle with vulnerability.

Title: Volume Two
Review: Like its predecessor, Volume II stands outside current production trends, and it’s built to last on its own modest terms.

Review: Sings Olivia Newton-John is an album nobody asked for but that’s partly what makes it special. Hatfield’s garage-bound arrangements scuff up the squeaky clean originals to likeable effect and she throws herself into the project with gusto. [Jun 2018, p.65]

Title: Reign of Terror

Title: Little Broken Hearts
Review: By placing so much emphasis on the stylish ever-shifting surfaces of its production, Little Broken Hearts never quite sinks in emotionally. Norah Jones may be pouring her heart out but it's been given an elegantly detailed sculpture that camouflages her pain.

Title: Cupid's Head
Review: On Cupid's Head, the Field demonstrates his expert ability to move forward with his craft while still retaining his signature voice.

Title: Corsicana Lemonade
Review: Corsicana Lemonade flips through a crateful of classic rock tropes, yet sounds spankingly "now." This extraordinary foursome just go from strength to strength. [Dec 2013, p.98]

Title: The Information
Review: Although The Information contains some of his most aware, intriguing lyrical head-scratchers yet, the familiar musical settings are something of a letdown from an artist famous for complete reinvention.

Title: Riser
Review: It's a sturdy, often absorbing record from a singer who is determined to be in it for the long haul.

Title: In Search of Harperfield
Review: It probably won’t break her out of the cult status in which she’s often resided, but for those who seek it out, it will prove an immensely rewarding listen.

Title: Shaker Notes
Review: Not everything sticks. Some of the lazing tracks verge on rudderless meandering, but as a whole, Shaker Notes is a fascinating detour.

Title: New Chain
Review: Small Black are more convincing when they move into sharper focus. [Dec 2010, p.96]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: Ultimately, without the abundance of the fitful, electrified abandon that permeated White’s past records--plus the fact that this album is clearly just another tiny sliver of the lexicon that may someday reveal his true scheme--some fans may feel moored on a lazaretto of dissatisfaction. Title: Reformation Post TLC

Title: Yankee Hotel Foxtrot

Title: Babel

Title: Voices

Title: No Love Deep Web

Title: Overcome

Title: Hoodstar
Review: The most memorable songs on his third album are decidedly buzz killers. [Oct 2006, p.96]

Title: Half of Where You Live

Title: The Way I See It
Review: The Way I See It doesn't break any new ground, but it's a very well-executed homage that serves to remind that classic soul is timeless.

Title: In a Poem Unlimited

Title: Corinne Bailey Rae

Title: Broken

Title: Lux Prima
Review: Lux Prima is an accomplished record--proof that two wildly different minds can work seamlessly together.

Title: Never
Review: Never is a bold step forward, but one that sacrifices the sugar-rush tweaking to solid if uninspiring ends.

Title: Nashville
Review: Rouse's primary gift remains his easy-flowing melodies, which are coaxed along by his cherubic rasp.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: After a boisterous first half, the backside of the album is a spiraling descent toward a grim and decimated collective soul. It’s both frightening and strangely captivating.

Title: One True Vine
Review: [Producer Jeff Tweedy's] his raw production lending itself to the Staples powerful presence.

Review: The album seems like it had the fat trimmed off in the studio and leaves the listener with a leaner-than-usual, but still enjoyable production. You’ll leave feeling full, but not stuffed.

When the Baroque arpeggios that close “The Station” enter a lockstep reminiscent of his synth-drone score for the 2017 thriller Good Time, for instance--it’s a musical thrill that renders questions about historical fidelity irrelevant.

Title: Boys Forever
Review: Boys Forever goes some way to making things alright, under or above ground.

Title: Chaos and a Dancing Star

Title: Strangers
Review: Strangers‘ ambition is its greatest asset, and because of Nadler’s own ambition, there is reason to believe she could get better still.

Title: Music's Not for Everyone
Review: Chain & the Gang sounds something like a slightly saner Captain Beefheart, a less arty Bongwater, or a whiter James Brown. [Feb 201, p.73]

Title: Infest the Rats' Nest

Title: The Cool

Title: Broken Ear Record

Title: Coriky
Review: All in all, this is a great album. Musically, it will be at home in the record collections of anyone who likes the previous bands the members of Coriky have been in. The lyrics are poignant and they’re delivered by some of the strongest voices punk has ever seen.

Title: proVISIONS

Review: The weird and promising thing is that it works without ever feeling natural. The actual coexistence of the earnest and the smoove stops being so striking after a while, but the best songs on Rules don’t let you forget there is one.

Title: 99Â¢
Review: Though 99 Cents is Santigold's most accessible work yet, it feels like the mainstream meeting White on her terms rather than vice versa, and the results are often irresistible.

Title: Head Carrier
Review: Two albums into their 21st century reunion, and the unhinged genius of early albums Surfer Rosa and Doolittle is largely lacking, replaced by the not unpleasant sound of old friends having a blast. [8 Oct 2016, p.52]

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: Clearly, this record is boring. Whether or not that’s a good thing remains up to your discretion.

Title: Welcome Back
Review: The album is livelier for its contradictions. [Oct 2004, p.124]

Title: Sleep Through The Static
Review: Dark sentiments are balanced by warm melodies and gently rootsy arrangements.

Title: Lemonade

Review: From Here We Go Sublime is fantastic all around, and it’s all the more effective for its restraint.

It’s still enjoyable to watch her figure it out.

Title: Soma
Review: Soma sits still, paralyzed by the weight of a sound that’s too big for this promising band to manage, at least for now.

Title: Lovers
Review: Lovers isn't instant, but perseverance brings great rewards. [Oct 2017, p.100]

Review: It’s bracing, familiar and flat-out exhausting all at the same time.

Title: Works For Tomorrow
Review: Furthering their Sonic Youth/Television post-punk quests. [Sep 2015, p.95]

Title: Bad as Me
Review: Bad As me is alive with some of his greatest yet. [Nov 2011, p.90]

Title: Shake The Sheets
Review: Leo proves himself emotionally enervating throughout, so it’s really a shame that Shake the Sheets isn’t half so sonically invigorating.

Title: Happy Birthday
Review: This 11-song Lp is less freak folk than freak scene, as the trio balances lo-fi guitar crunch with Chris Weisman's adenoidal vocals. [Jul 20120, p.93]

Title: Kisses on the Bottom
Review: Suggests that McCartney lacks anyone to tell him when he's had a terrible idea.

Title: Music Complete
Review: Hook's departure frees them to create their most varied and substantial work in decades.

Title: Faded Gloryville
Review: It has some of the year’s best country songs, plus a groove-heavy take on the Bee Gees’ classic To Love Somebody.

Title: Loved
Review: This record is not a reimagining of the band or a fresh start. Loved is an exercise in moulding what KEN Mode has always been good at into a perfect soundtrack for these times of great political uncertainty.

Title: Music's Not for Everyone
Review: Relying heavily on posturing and tired song structures, lacking the incisive commentary and pointed humor that it strives for, Music's Not For Everyone is a record that fails on many fronts.

Title: Why Love Now
Review: This is modern life sliced up with the precision of a medical scalpel and then force-fed through a high-density filter of piss and vinegar.

Title: The Unseen In Between
Review: Just bask in The Unseen in Between enigmatic glory.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: A Seat At The Table--like the headlines of 2016--is the score of black pain, black rage, black strength and black joy. And for everyone else enjoying the enticing R&B, it's for the rest of us to quiet ourselves, listen, learn and respect.

Title: Into the Wide
Review: An introspective piano ballad about a lover's never-ending faith, keeps Into the Wide earthbound and proves Delta Spirit to be a band of significant depth.

Title: The Sun and the Moon
Review: Too sappy for the cool kids, sure, but still a fine pop record.

Title: Field Report
Review: It would all add up to another listen-to-it-once bit of over-serious Americana noir if the songs weren't so good. But they're good.

Title: ONoffON
Review: Make no mistake: it may be a good two decades late, but ONoffON is the follow-up that Vs. has always cried out for. And as a result, it’s one of the finest records I’ve heard all year.

Title: Game Theory
Review: There are plenty of unexpected surprises to be found.

Title: Lovebox
Review: With Lovebox, they do another about-face, dirtying up and slowing down their song-structured house tracks into a grimy soul/funk/house/hip-hop amalgam. [March 2003, p.94]

Title: Into Forever
Review: Ultimately, although Into Forever might not quite hit the same consistent heights as the meticulously-crafted Modular Living, it’s still a respectable and forward moving addition to the Eat Light Become Lights canon in own right.

Title: One Second of Love
Review: Gonzalez is more fun when she's trying to be challenging than when she's trying to be fun.

Title: We Are Undone
Review: A sprawling, diverse affair. [Mar 2015, p.94]

Title: Nostradamus
Review: It all makes for a bewildering package, sometimes exhilarating, sometimes middling, and sometimes astonishingly bad, and while a good 45 minutes’ worth of Nostradamus is fully deserving of high praise, on a 100-minute double album, that’s nowhere near enough.

Title: Floating Coffin
Review: It’s great to have a thematically consistent and well-executed Thee Oh Sees album.

Title: Blue Lights on the Runway
Review: In short, Blue Lights on the Runway has it all.

Title: Smoke
Review: There’s wit and meticulous posturing in the hills: we’ll be waiting right here for tomorrow. After all, there are enough immediately delectable grooves in his eleven tracks today.

Title: Treats
Review: Sleigh Bells offer a thrilling ride. [Sep 2010, p.104]

Title: Equilibrium
Review: Shipp, whose restless vision is never clouded by grandiosity or pretense, has become the most important pianist on the scene today. Equilibrium is soul music for the mind.

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: Collaborations abound, and most of them work.

Title: Candylion
Review: Candylion isn't a major musical statement, but its idiosyncratic, nostalgic appeal is hard to resist.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: It takes more getting used to than their previous work, but it rewards even more for it.

Title: Assume Form
Review: Assume Form keeps that same desire [as The Colour In Anything] to break new ground, while taking it to the red line and managing to not outstay its welcome.

Title: Eucalyptus
Review: The free rein afforded by this latest solo effort renders most of these 15 tracks unrecognisable as songs.

Title: Amygdala
Review: Its visionary ambition recalls the fertile sprawl of Villalobos’ 2003 debut Alcachofa; baroque techno blessed with the carefree spirit of lounge music and Quiet Storm, dressed up in tie-dye, the music on Amygdala glows with an easy confidence.

Title: Where It Hits You
Review: An excellent collection of soul-bearing Americana.

Title: That's How Rumors Get Started
Review: Relatability charms never harmed Dolly Parton, and that's who you think of as these gargantuan melodies shimmer and soar. [Jun 2020, p.88]

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: While clearly wanting to be a legendary piece of extravagant and influential work, it suffers the most from its inherent apathy, a type of intangible element that makes it come off as equal parts careless and desperate.

Title: The Sister
Review: What is meant to sound intimate and sparse only sounds unfinished, and-dare I say it-downright boring.

Title: Familiars
Review: Familiars finds the Antlers on a new, magnificent level of heavy songwriting.

Title: See Mystery Lights
Review: Most of the album comes across as a weedy, irritating student pastiche of the DFA sound rather than something that deserves a place in its esteemed catalogue. [Sep 2009, p.105]

Title: Heritage
Review: Heritage is an infinitely more audacious beast, full of jazzy noodling, serpentine guitar leads, folky introspection and general acid-drenched freakiness.

Title: Hendra
Review: Modestly presented but appropriately self-confident in its dedication to craft, Hendra is a low-key but sturdy delight.

Title: World Eater
Review: World Eater does not seem like a doomsday device by design, though. It might sound like one now, but Power leaves open the possibility of it being his darkest transmission before the dawn of a new bright tomorrow.

Title: Plastics
Review: An album which blurs the line between retro and futuristic techno, yet always with an analogue soul.

Title: 13 Rivers
Review: With razor-sharp wit, a seemingly endless reservoir of imaginative guitar-playing, and a restless sense of musical adventure, Richard Thompson is still blowing away the competition, even those more than half his age.

Title: Blood Money
Review: It's hard to imagine another album in 2006 doing a worse job of justifying its existence than Blood Money.

Title: Naomi
Review: The simple moments are offset by grander, more exciting ones.

Title: Mind Over Matter
Review: Mind Over Matter has a fuller, brassier sound than this group’s debut, and especially emphasizes the guitars of Jacob Tilley and Eric Cannata.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: Like most albums by reformed bands, it reminds you what you liked without opening up an essential new chapter. [Apr 2015, p.84]

Title: The Sun Will Come Up, The Seasons Will Change
Review: While it may not be the collection of hits we were hoping for, The Sun Will Come Up, The Seasons Will Change is a little like a compilation of musical diary entries sprinkled with newly learnt wisdom: it’s fun, it’s new, and it’s Nesbitt's coming-of-age moment.

Title: Among the Ghosts
Review: If Among the Ghosts would have benefitted from more of a balance between those poles, Lucero’s latest demonstrates that they do the quiet stuff nearly as well as the loud.

Title: Surfing the Void
Review: Klaxons' ambition to stand apart from the grey indie hordes, to race by in a blur of outlandish rhetoric and pupil-dilating intensity, is admirable, but there are too many road bumps on this particular trip.

Title: Non-Fiction
Review: While not setting the world on fire, it nestles its way warmly into your heart, soul and dancing feet.

Title: Cocoa Sugar
Review: Cocoa Sugar finds Young Fathers at a fascinating juncture: opening up, moving forward, but still existing in a sonic hall-of-mirrors world of their own. [Apr 2018, p.104]

Title: Soul Punk
Review: Like any good album for the information age, Soul Punk is overloaded well past the point of saturation and its merciless in its attack, so it can be a bit overbearing, yet there's a real, vivid imagination behind its crystalline clamor.

Title: Siberia
Review: Siberia seems to have satisfied a need in Ideskog to break from production conformity, and while there are weak spots lyrically, its shadowy memories and hazy snapshots of the Russian railway emit a steady warmth you can return to.

Title: Higher Than the Eiffel
Review: Having been dumped by their label, and in turn voluntarily dumped this scheduled third record's first draft, Simon Franks and Tom Disdale have taken their time, entice Madness's Suggs and Mike Barson into cameos and emergwed altogether stronger. [May 2010, p.112]

Title: Uncanney Valley
Review: [Travis Morrison's] earworm melodies and piquant lyrical outlook are Uncanney's only source of nutrients. The rest are empty calories. [Nov 2013, p.94]

Title: SBTRKT
Review: This is an album that's clearly designed with immediacy in mind, from the ever-grinding bass to the generous supply of playful pop flourishes, and its best songs will get bodies moving by night even if they don't quite stick in the head the next morning.

Title: Public Domain: Songs from the Wild Land
Review: It's not that these songs are all obvious or overdone--this nonfolkie had never heard a few of them. It's that they're so soft they squish even when Alvin tries to rev one past you, which usually he doesn't.

Title: Designer
Review: Designer is a striking return, pursuing solitary aesthetic goals in a fashion both unrelenting and admirable. It perhaps lacks a little of the indefinable magic that made 2017’s ‘Party’ such a gripping experience, but in its ability to conjure bold, riveting songwriting it underlines Aldous Harding’s position as a truly remarkable artist.

Title: In Our Gun
Review: If anemic blues guitar riffs and half-assed attempts at white-boy soul were the only problems with In Our Gun, it might almost be passable.

Title: Citrus
Review: Where Asobi Seksu's first album seemed rushed, a little too experimental, and at times too loud, Citrus brings the right amount of noise, swirling affects, and sound balance.

Title: Dedicated
Review: There's a lot to love in Dedicated, but Jepsen tries to cover too ground even if they follow similar song structures, to the point where it may bring some boredom--it's best to stream individual tracks instead of listening to the album's fifty minutes straight through.

Title: Life Processes
Review: Life Processes sounds like mice playing Hundred Reasons covers. [May 2008, p.95]

Title: A Different Kind of Truth
Review: A Different Kind Of Truth sounds familiar in the best way.

Title: Moodring
Review: Nothing else on the album [other than single "My Love Is Like . . . Wo"] is quite so perfect a vehicle for Mya's predatory sexuality.[

Title: Born Again Revisited
Review: It’s a great record, but it’s as if the band made a pledge to skronk--a collective aesthetic noise decision.

Title: Supernova
Review: Unexpectedly exhilarating. [Jun 2014, p.79]

Title: Versatile
Review: It's disappointing to hear one of the all-time great vocalists turn in such mundane performances.

Title: Wolfroy Goes to Town
Review: Wolfroy Goes to Town haunts you quietly, in a private way that is, somehow, all the more devastating.

Title: The Union
Review: The Union brings up two very good points again and again: No amount of celebrity shenanigans or animated transgressions can eclipse the fact that Elton John is an absolutely amazing musician and there's a never-ending list of reasons why Leon Russell is your favorite musician's favorite musician.

Title: Temet
Review: Dramatic rock-style flourishes punctuate the rolling shuffle “Alwa”, and there are echoes of country picking in the brisk, stinging guitar fills of “Ehad Wa Dagh”. Most potently, there’s a Santana-esque flavour to the Afro-Latin funk of “Tamudre” and “Tumast”, the latter’s fiery, skirling guitar runs accelerating to a dervish frenzy.

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: It's this tightrope between bruised self-doubt and fun blasts of noise that gives Wolf's Law its emotional heft.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: On their third album, the band’s instrumentals radiate wit and warmth, like mid-80s New Order sloshing around in a sun-kissed sea--but it’s as a foil to some of Britain’s most idiosyncratic artists that Mount Kimbie really prove their mettle.

Title: Penance Soiree
Review: By simply playing by the rock 'n' roll rulebook-- whose article 17, section 4 strictly dictates that ego, excess and publicity stunts are to take complete precedence over, you know, songs-- Penance Soiree is one of the better straight-up records you're bound to hear from the genre all year.

Title: Wooden Aquarium
Review: Mazes confirm themselves as one of the most exciting British bands currently around. This is the result of what happens when three unique and brilliant minds are given the right facilities they need to make their vision happen.

Title: Distant Satellites
Review: It's as vast and cosmic as the title suggests. [14 Jun 2014, p.54]

Title: The Futureheads
Review: A punchy and exciting debut.

Title: Return of the Tender Lover
Review: A little more stylistic deviation like that could have helped Return of the Tender Lover feel more vital. Even when he's just dreaming of the past, though, the elegance of Babyface's songwriting remains untouched.

Title: The Virgins
Review: The melodies are often limp, the rhythm section disappointingly friction-free, and Cumming’s main lyrical M.O. is to name-drop coke constantly, like the doofus at a party who mistakes a key bump for a badge of cool.

Title: So Long, See You Tomorrow
Review: Bombay Bicycle Club might have veered all over the track, switching between the folk lane and the electronic one, elbowing indie-pop out of the way, but they still aren't setting the pace. [Mar 2014, p.112]

Title: Sometimes The Blues Is Just A Passing Bird
Review: There is distinct pastoral element at work in the Tallest Man on Earth's songs. He invokes the elements and the myriad forces nature: rivers, islands, rocks, clouds, birds, meadows, rainstorms, hail, forests, weeds, lilies and wheat.

Title: The Long Goodbye
Review: Like Belle And Sebastian, one of the main weaknesses of the group is that they're just to darn precious at times for their own good.

Title: Close to Home
Review: The music is superb, but it’s Mead’s subtle, witty lyrics that really take center stage on this record (like all his previous solo offerings).

Title: Parallax
Review: It sounds like a recipe for a dozen buzz bands this year, but Atlas Sound transcends the fads. Melodies shine through like faint stars through the window.

Title: Battle For The Sun
Review: Battle clearly illustrates efforts at sounding new, and undecided listeners may wonder why those efforts bore sweet moments with little resonance, a sugar pill for Placebo’s new era.

Title: The Haden Triplets
Review: The album’s center of gravity, always, is the Hadens’ vocal blend, which isn’t seamless or airless but rather a series of alert, intuitive micro-negotiations in the realm of intonation and timbre. At times you notice how much is actually happening, moment to moment, in that blend.

Title: Permanent Signal
Review: It’s woozy, dreamlike bliss and Mauro Remmidi owns it well.

Title: Heavy Meta
Review: Heavy Meta is most likeable when he directs those high standards inwards. ... More often though, Gallo is on the offensive, and his technically commensurate and frequently enjoyable garage rock gets entangled in a scornfulness that becomes a little uncomfortable.

Title: The Day's War
Review: Unfortunately, much of The Day's War relies too heavily on overly familiar chord sequences and featherweight angst, and it swiftly becomes hard not to yearn for a dash of the Biffy boys' brutish angularity to toughen things up a bit.

Title: Water Curses EP
Review: Simply put, it’s fantastic.

Title: Remember Us to Life
Review: These songs [The Trapper and the Furrier, Tornadoland, and Obsolete] are, ironically, more cinematic than anything found on her last album ‘What We Saw From The Cheap Seats,’ and that sense of drama helps make Remember Us To Life a return to form.

Title: Warble Womb
Review: A breezy 75-minute exploration of the lighter side of their vision. [Nov 2013, p.105]

Title: Ringer
Review: On Ringer, a generously portioned EP, Hebden dials back his frenetic eclecticism, instead turning out ambitious yet danceable techno.

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: [The songs] are confessional and vulnerable, yet so strong. Of the quiet songs, only the grungy dirge slows things to a crawl.

Title: The Secret Migration
Review: Much of the CD's faux poetry... sounds like the work of a New Age band. [20 May 2005, p.75]

Title: La Di Da Di
Review: As Battles evolve, they remain true to their unique mix of brains and brawn, and La Di Da Di just might be their most engaging music yet.

Title: Narkopop
Review: It can sound like being plunged into a dark, Dante-esque forest, with only a muted aortic throb to guide you home. Immersive, to say the least.

Title: Jessica Rabbit
Review: Sleigh Bells has grown up plenty since their 2009 lightning-strike arrival, but perhaps that strike is starting to feel like more of a distant memory than it should.

Title: Heron King Blues
Review: It’s about mood here. These numbers would rather glow than soar.

Title: amo
Review: The various dark and mechanical intermission tracks on the album make for the most experimental peaks and exciting signposts to the future, but nothing compares to ‘Nihilist Blues’, a robotic and apocalyptic blast of Eurodance featuring guest vocals and mad noises from art-pop icon Grimes.

Title: Someone to Drive You Home
Review: Over a strident indie-rock soundtrack, singer Kate Jackson comes across like a female Morrissey. [Dec 2006, p.138]

Title: Mess
Review: Mess gets caught in an odd trap in that it’s neither patient nor nimble.

Title: Saltwater
Review: With Saltwater but as a difficult second album goes, this is a total breeze rather than a mainsail-battering ocean storm.

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: In the end, it's the restraint, control, and unlikely expansiveness that make The Best of Gloucester County a strong and surreal step forward for Smith and his band.

Title: Fading Parade
Review: Quever has extended his transition into dreamy territory really well.

Title: Earthology
Review: While some of the instrumental workouts (like "Safari Strut") are loose and inspired, it takes a handful of appearances from backpack-friendly rappers Percee P ("Reverse") and Mr. Lif ("The Gift") to keep Earthology from fading into lava-lamp background grooviness.

Title: TerraForm
Review: If Terraform does little to diminish the notion that Roberts is one of the best kept secrets of Canadian pop, it goes a long way in promoting the idea that it's never too late to make a new discovery.

Title: Own Side Now
Review: Comparisons or not, Rose exceeded the expectations that her EP drummed up and delivered a beautiful and tender, youthfully energetic album that crosses the line Rose herself has been toeing so carefully between indie and country.

Title: This Land
Review: It’s an effective blend superior to earlier attempts at versatility, as on the Bright Lights EP and, during the aforementioned “What About Us,” comparable to the absorption of musical elements present on previous full-length studio albums like Blak And Blu.

Title: No Hope, No Future
Review: No Hope, No Future doesn’t always play to the band’s proven strengths, but it shows that Good Shoes are a thoroughly independent, even contrary band that's unafraid of change, even when it’s difficult.

Title: The Orbserver In The Star House
Review: This alliance with The Orb is positive for both parties, Perry providing a tighter rein on their tendency to meander, while they furnish him with a different terrain to his usual dub skanks.

Title: 1000 Forms of Fear
Review: In sound, composition and performance, Sia captures the melodrama of teen life, with all the lunatic exaggeration it deserves.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: If Sky Blue Sky is the product of Wilco's newfound clarity and cohesiveness, the album's paralytic ambiguity suggests they're also still in desperate search of a purposeful vision.

Title: Feathers
Review: The disc essentially finds the now-quartet cleaning up and living right and letting the world see them as they are; their tracks are marked by much clean-fingered guitar playing (the added guitar meaning there's six-stringing back-and-forth) and only a recreational use and abuse of wah.

Title: Peace Is the Mission
Review: There is no doubt Peace Is the Mission will suffer some criticism from dancehall purists, those exhausted by EDM and people who hate Diplo (a hate that he has certainly worked overtime to earn), but their maturation is palpable across the album's nine tracks.

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: A bleak and occasionally beautiful debut. [Oct 2009,p.102]

Title: Speed of Darkness
Review: Diehard fans might miss Flogging Molly's manic moments, but Darkness' lyrical depth--and sonic diversity--are incredibly rewarding. [Jun 2011, p.111]

Title: For Hero: For Fool
Review: The chemistry has changed, the music is harder, the frustration's more palable, and you can hear that this is some kind of a make-or-break moment. And this time they made it-- just.

Title: Fallen Angels
Review: Those who choose to embrace and eulogise anything the great man releases will no doubt laud Fallen Angels as another triumph, but the harsh reality is this is Bob on auto-pilot.

Title: Abandoned City
Review: The detail is wonderful, ghostly and rich, but the whole would have benefited from a clearer, less meandering navigator.

Title: Ta Det Lugnt
Review: What they said.

Title: Universal Themes
Review: There are spoken segments, garage-rock and pretty acoustic passages, too, but his default setting is intimate and minimal.

Title: Moon Tides
Review: A record of rivers and trees rather than streets and skyscrapers, it's a blissful and quietly cosmic experience. [Sep 2013, p.98]

Title: The State of Things
Review: Ultimately, the record is a tribute to McClure's charisma and unswerving self-belief.

Title: Cheap Queen
Review: On the whole, this is a record for comfort listening on headphones. Her voice is often intimately close in the mix, brushing up against your ear, unglamorous and unadorned.

Title: Nightmare Ending
Review: It’s a much more jagged experience; a patchwork as opposed to an exercise in consistency. In spite of this, or perhaps because of it, Nightmare Ending manages to be Eluvium’s most evocative and interesting work to date.

Title: Americana
Review: Given Ben Keith's death last year, it's the perfect merge: Young's rough-hewn organics and the raucous Crazy Horse.

Title: Give You The Ghost
Review: While it's an album prime for some excellent live renditions, it's the tendency to brood too much or even approach tedium at some points leaves further room for the development of this sound.

Title: Revelations
Review: Shamir represents what it is to be an outsider, with each of Revelation’s nine tracks teaching us to face our insecurities and embrace our weirdness. Even in the darkest times, Shamir’s brilliance continues to shine through

Title: Time Bomb
Review: This album is nothing but a parade of their '70s and '80s hard rock influences worn proudly on their sleeves. And for that, rock 'n' roll fans should be grateful. Time Bomb is one romping anthem after another almost clear through to the end, a "hidden" piano ballad that serves only further cement the band's status as a throwback to the days of overwrought arena rock.

Title: Serpentine Prison
Review: This collection allows his masterful lyrics and song-craft to shone through unfiltered.

Title: Son
Review: A grand experiment in vocal manipulation, Son makes Bjork’s Medulla seem like child’s play.

Title: EPHEM:ERA
Review: EPHEM:ERA cheats our trained cognition and creates a space for itself, playing with our restless thirst for difference, working itself into the gaps in our memory.

Title: La Costa Perdida
Review: Sadly, today there's nothing to distinguish Lowery and co. from scores of other unfocused bands trying to combine too many disparate elements.

Title: Quality Street Music
Review: Despite offering a variety of hip-hop today, the album lacks an honest feel, coming across like a batch of mediocre singles. [#255, p.99]

Title: Tidelands
Review: Tidelands, by contrast, finds the Moondoggies (and particularly lead singer Kevin Murphy) admirably striving to find their own voice, yet it's frequently a more crabbed and deliberate album than its predecessor. In other words, a quintessential example of artistic growing pains.

Title: Brilliant Sanity
Review: Brilliant Sanity's musings on uncertainty are some of their most confident songs yet.

Title: Getting Somewhere
Review: Moorer's understated voice doesn't always rise to the arrangements. [16 Jun 2006, p.77]

Title: Figure 8
Review: Smith has shifted his focus away from crafting the perfect pop epic; though this description fits several of the new tracks ("Son of Sam," "Junk Bond Trader"), there are just as many melodic fragments or simply structured ballads ("Everything Reminds Me of Her," "Somebody That I Used to Know").

Title: Saturday Night Wrist
Review: Their most well-rounded, focused record yet, one that comes scarily close to besting White Pony while heading in a slightly different direction at the same time.

Title: The Sound the Speed the Light
Review: The Sound The Speed The Light is as good as "Obliterati."

Title: Double Up
Review: His tenuous grasp on reality and good taste slips and he plummets into a tawdry, gratuitous and self-congratulatory flurry of misogyny, expletives and reggae.

Title: Gloss Drop
Review: Gloss Drop is a definitely strong final outcome.

Title: No Words Left
Review: The sweetness of her voice often masks tough sentiments. [Apr 2019, p.34]

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Fetch The Bolt Cutters is mostly the soundtrack of liberation, not recrimination, with Apple's piano keys, battering on the walls and barking dogs as its percussive, beating heart. [Jul 2020, p.27]

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: Quite unlike any other record you'll hear this year. [Nov 2013, p.116]

Title: Third Law
Review: By focusing on his aesthetic and retaining an interest in the possibilities that exist within slow music while setting himself time limitations, Porter has created a record that is as bold and as breathtaking as we might have ever hoped for, regardless of the projection it is set to generate.

Title: The Stage
Review: Though Hail to the King failed to live up to the royal expectations of its titular disguise, The Stage's grandiosity smells of overcompensation; Avenged Sevenfold's crown lies somewhere in between.

Title: Earth Division
Review: It's a beautiful EP deserving of repeat listening.

Title: Out of Control
Review: Out Of Control is, generally, yet another excellent album from a group who may have risen from a lot of people's 'guilty pleasure' to becoming full-on national treasures.

Title: Ancient Melodies of the Future
Review: With their intensely layered harmonies, pounding rhythms and Martsch's own nasal drawl, songs like "Alarmed" and "You Are" are sublimely hummable pop gems.

Title: No Better Than This
Review: [A] backstory is meaningless unless there are songs to back it up, and, like Mellencamp's other recent releases, Better more than walks the walk.

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: Depression Cherry’s particular non-specifics feel as full of breath and life as anything they’ve ever done--an album-length sigh as eloquent as a manifesto.

Title: Waiting on a Song
Review: “Shine On Me” sounds like a George Harrison out-take, while the kitschy-corny “Livin’ In Sin” (“Your touch is electrical/I’m so susceptible”) recalls The Beach Boys circa 15 Big Ones. But there are threads of sly invention woven throughout, most notably the unusual alliance of dobro slide and Bacharach horns that lifts “Wildest Dreams”.

Title: Psychic Warfare
Review: It's nothing we've not heard before from Clutch, but it remains superbly head-crushing. [10 Oct 2015, p.52]

Title: Visitations
Review: Visitations sounds more alive than anything since 2000's near-classic debut, Internal Wrangler. [Feb 2007, p.82]

Title: Dead Start Program
Review: John Tejada's fourth full-length for Kompakt is a succinct, incredibly focused album of complex, melodic techno tracks.

Title: Stateless
Review: It was great listening in on Hungtai’s world, a filmic mixture of life and life-that-can-be.

Title: Mercy
Review: It can sometimes feel like a  band trying on a variety of hats, although the songs themselves generally ring true, anthemic and delivered with a fistful of grit. [Apr 2020, p.30]

Title: Strays
Review: The songs rock -- and ferociously -- but that's pretty much all they do.

Title: Empire
Review: While there’s no doubt the songs from Empire will translate into amazing live shows, the repetitiveness of several tracks wears thin after a while in a less dance-friendly environment. [#15]

Title: TSOL
Review: Anyone with an appreciation for smartass MCs and a little of Fender-tapping would do well to give TSOL a spin. [Nov 2010, p.116]

Title: Strange Mercy
Review: St. Vincent reaches, and while she doesn't quite find it throughout, listening to the reach is certainly more interesting than listening to an album that answers just one of the questions again and again and again.

Title: Endgame
Review: This lack of identity admittedly fuels the indecipherable, entrancing mystery of the album, yet unfortunately this strength also equates to the album’s primary weakness.

Title: No Fools, No Fun
Review: There's a shared past that's evident in every moment of this debut, and that natural, relaxed camaraderie is the reason why No Fools, No Fun is such an appealing listen.

Title: Own Side Now
Review: While it may occasionally get too precious for some ears, Own Side Now is a tantalizing debut.

Title: Mother
Review: She hasn't entirely left the Chicks behind, but Maines has grown into something newly dynamic, and entirely her own.

Title: Escondida
Review: It's difficult to think of a more compelling sophomore record by a young singer-songwriter, Norah included.

Title: Conquistador
Review: The album suggests a full story, but it still seems paradoxically fragmentary. After its slow burn fades, after our hero has returned home, what’s best about Conquistador might be the sense of possibility it poses.

Title: Eat Pray Thug
Review: Eat Pray Thug is a remarkably moving opus condemning ethnocentricity and wallowing in relational grief.

Title: Logic Will Break Your Heart
Review: Disco, punk and pop, all in one bag.

Title: I Phantom
Review: Lif has managed to transcend the gimmicks and wankery that generally mar this kind of grand opus, and emerge with his strongest offering yet.

Title: Silent Shout
Review: There hasn’t been such an overtly bleak and dangerous concept album like Silent Shout in quite a long time.

Title: Power Chords
Review: Power Chords is much more lyrically mature and musically adept than your average garage rock record, and its teenage sheen might urge you to fanatically scroll the lyrics on your notebook or bedroom wall of choice.

Title: The Imperfect Sea
Review: Three albums in, it’s yet to be determined just where the younger Jeffes aims to take the group, but there’s a rigidity to The Imperfect Sea that approaches ordered desolation.
