Title: Our Version of Events
Review: This is a hugely impressive introduction to a dynamic, arresting talent.

Title: Keep It Like a Secret
Review: Beautiful pop symphonies that hit like a Louisville Slugger.

Title: Stony Hill
Review: His first solo album in a decade is an inspiring 18-track collection, flexing authority on roots jams and dancehall bangers, political meditations, and come-ons.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: He's turned in an electronic album that’s full of character without resorting to robot costumes or Pharrell bloody Williams.

Title: Hold On Now, Youngster...
Review: A glockenspiel in a guitar band? Freshens up the sound, they think. And they're right.

Title: Ghosts of the Great Highway
Review: The bottom line here is that Kozelek's aesthetic with Sun Kil Moon may not be radically different than his RHP project, but it is moving, graceful, and consciously beautiful.

Title: Lukas Graham
Review: It’s sweet earnestness in a shrewd, ambitious package. The music, like much Scandinavian pop, ignores genre to draw on whatever works, current and vintage.

Title: The Sunshine Underground
Review: Besides ‘It Is Only You’ and ‘Here Comes The Storm’, the mountain-shouting bravado of old tracks like ‘Borders’ and ‘Put You In Your Place’ has been dampened, but TSU is an intriguing new sunrise.

Title: Fallen Angels
Review: Even when he strains to keep in key or pitch, he manages to make a virtue of his shortcomings, bringing a sense of long-distance exhaustion to “All The Way”, and applying a sort of Gallic shrug to “All Or Nothing At All”, in stark contrast to the jauntier tone of Frank Sinatra’s and Billie Holiday’s interpretations.

Title: Magnifique
Review: Magnifique drags a bit, as can often be the case with instrumental tracks centred on repetitive patterns, but it demonstrates the band’s commitment to their oddball signature style.

Title: Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager
Review: As Drake and Kanye West have demonstrated, there's room in hip-hop for melancholic MCs who upend the self-congratulation that dominates the genre.

Title: The Anteroom
Review: The Anteroom is full of skittery electronics with hints of ambient and house textures that work as both as a marker for how outside of the margins Krell operates and how narrowly he deviates from his own previous innovations in the underground.

Title: Mono
Review: Never quite forsaking what brought them, they’ve created a new world for post-country country--as musically satisfying as it is hormone-peaking.

Title: Lulu
Review: An utter wreck that curiously, miraculously, might have been great.

Title: A Thing Called Divine Fits
Review: There's a chemistry between this trio, and a satisfying intensity to their focused electro jams.

Title: Wake Up the Nation
Review: Lean, mean and as uncompromisingly focused as its maker, this is an album for everyone's collection, and whilst Weller is perhaps not the man he once was, the man he is now is most definitely still a force to be reckoned with.

Title: Meet the Humans
Review: On his third solo album, Steve Mason veers dangerously close to that overfarmed damaged-earnest-sensitive-bloke territory, but luckily he doesn't seem capable of schmaltz or emotional cheap-shots. [Mar 2016, p.95]

Title: Forth
Review: Admittedly, the band's past catalogue sets the bar high, but Forth is an achievement, especially when considered in the context of so many failed attempts by others to return after a period of inactivity.

Title: New Brigade
Review: While it has been out in their native land since January and only recently been made available in this country through tiny New York-based What's Your Rupture?, this 12-track typhoon is exactly the kick in the ass our sorry punk community needs in the wake of Jay Reatard's untimely death.

Title: Friend and Foe
Review: The line between cheese and accessibility can be thin, and whistling or handclaps or a hidden track or an overt songwriting method can all reek, but Friend and Foe has, just as ostensibly, no wasted space. The hinge is in the balance the band manages with every inkling of sound or production seeming both spontaneous and stultifying, both labored-over and cast off.

Title: Lovers Rock
Review: Lovers Rock is an airy album, demo-like in its simplicity. It has none of the agression of a "comeback." In fact, Sade has never put out anything quite so ephemeral. [Jan 2001, p.114]

Title: Androgynous Mary
Review: Androgynous Mary is as morbid of a record as you’d expect from a bunch of L.A. punks. They’re disturbed, but entertained; they’re young, but disillusioned. If Androgynous Mary were a place, it would probably be a strange corner in the dark web controlled by Zoomers with good intentions and confused brains.

Title: BREACH
Review: BREACH, Lily’s first album for Dead Oceans, is a scruffier, more far-ranging record about developing a self in your twenties.

Title: You Forgot It In People
Review: You really don't know what you're dealing with until you sit down and take in the freewheeling beauty of one of the year's best.

Title: Diaper Island
Review: Sure, there are imperfections along the way, but this is an immeasurably intriguing and constantly developing journey that's best experienced alone.

Title: Unknown Rooms: A Collection of Acoustic Songs
Review: Unknown Rooms is very, very accomplished, giving the sense that Wolfe has realised the extent of her own ability and acted on it.

Title: More Light
Review: Sure, few will love everything on here but the hubris, yet the sprawling mess that is More Light can’t help but impress.

Title: Abandoned City
Review: It’s a worldly record in many ways, and though the core tenet is of his personal feelings, it works just as well as you what you’d probably assume the record to be about--abandoned cities.

Title: A Color Map of the Sun
Review: Each ["sides" of the double LP] is so good, it’s a toss up between which incarnation you'll end up liking most.

Title: Another Life
Review: Overall Another Life sounds like an illegal broadcast from an underground collective looking to inspire a revolution within those of a similar mindset. It may sound austere and unwelcoming, but if you’re on Amnesia Scanner’s wavelength then you’ll naturally tune into their determinedly experimental sound, and within it find a freedom and a groove that speaks to a different way of being.

Title: Animalore
Review: The end result is this expertly-crafted, inoffensive, hook-laden pop. Though it gets a bit silly in places, the core of this disc is far too good to pass up.

Title: Alice
Review: Alice is unique within Waits' unique discography, and it may be his most fully realized work. [Jul 2002, p.96]

Title: Calling the World
Review: There aren't enough original ideas here to know if Rooney can shine as a relevant, modern rock band.

Title: No No No
Review: No No No's a pleasantly nostalgic experience, but ultimately it feels insubstantial.

Title: Red Night
Review: Intoxication gives way to a sobering comedown, and hints at possible danger generally prove unfounded.

Title: Level II
Review: A fine album, offering quality tunes, if not clever punches. [May 2003, p.100]

Title: Noctunes
Review: Noctunes, unlike his previous records, is a work suspended in time, amorphous and entrancing, but ultimately too shapeless to hold its own weight. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.60]

Title: Title TK
Review: There's a lot of empty space in these songs, the better to focus on Kim and Kelley's up-front vocal harmonies and classically off-kilter lyrical ideas.

Title: Animal Nature
Review: The band's touch with songcraft, as opposed to groove science, is less sure. But they do have a way with a cover.

Title: Platform
Review: It's always drifting, skilfully, from challenging noise to fragmented affection in the most beguiling way possible.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: A disc that sounds like it's... 1998.

Title: Welcome Home
Review: Cohen's voice maintains the album's consistently floaty quality through these sparser tracks, making for a relentlessly dreamy set that's lost in thought and desire.

Title: Street Safari
Review: The firm foundation of the songs can be, at times, a little monotonous, a listening experience that not even the more jazzy guitar work can save. That being said, the band still oozes of swanky confidence.

Title: Life of Pause
Review: Like Gemini was to Nocturne, Life of Pause looks to be the rough draft of a new idea to be. Tatum still shows promise that he can combine that adventurous spirit and more fully encapsulating execution.

Title: The Impossible Kid
Review: Lyrical prowess is never in doubt, and neither is the idea that the MC is an acquired taste, but this wordy, extroverted, and capricious effort is an alive whirlwind with more pride than usual. That last bit makes it one of the most persuasive Aesop efforts to date.

Title: Happy Hollow
Review: [Kasher's] storytelling is still right up there with the very highest of Saddle-sitters. [#21, p.97]

Title: Fucked Up Friends
Review: Tobacco keeps things instrumental, lathering on freakish analogue effects but rejecting dance music's stylistic tics in favour of a pleasingly warped relative of space rock. [Aug 2009, p.112]

Title: Exquisite Corpse
Review: The 90 degree turns between tracks are endearing, like a cool mix-tape -- not cause for head scratching and folded arms.

Title: Home Again
Review: It seems a faintly ridiculous thing to say about an album that's so clearly busting a gut to sound 40 years older than it actually is, but it feels natural rather than forced or calculating.

Title: The Magic Whip
Review: Shorn of expectation and match fit in the middle of a long tour, four friends found each other again.

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: For aficionados of his gnomic genius, and there are many, this new collection provides further reasons to invest time and money in his eclectic works.

Title: Whiteout Conditions
Review: While The New Pornographers’ appealing quirks abound, their melodic gifts rightfully steal the show.

Title: The College Dropout
Review: He has his own personality: not a gangsta or a player but a diligent pragmatist. [Apr 2004, p.124]

Title: Pala
Review: Pala feels like a great shindig-starter, complete with wiggly, disco basslines and subtext-free lyrics like "All I want is to feel true love."

Title: Given to the Wild
Review: If only all bands had the guts and honesty of The Maccabees, maybe they'd get round to making third records as good as this.

Title: A New Found Relaxation
Review: Krivchenia has absconded with sounds traditionally associated with beauty, applied his twisted genius, and the result is A New Found Relaxation.

Title: Contra
Review: The 10 tracks appeal more with every play: initially sounding a bit like Paul Simon's Graceland being covered by 90s geeks They Might Be Giants, they will probably be among this year's most played and most joyful tunes.

Title: Double Exposure
Review: Like much of the rest of this fine record, [final song, "It's Summertime Again"] sounds like a forgotten hit beamed in from some beatific version of the past. [Nov 2013, p.77]

Title: The People's Key
Review: Oberst's voice trembles with the emotion of his youth, only ripped with spite instead of vulnerability. That solipsism has shifted to an even more detached universalism, which leaves little for the listener to connect with.

Title: My Favorite Picture of You
Review: His first album in four years and one of the best of his storied career.

Title: Magic Potion
Review: If the Black Keys sped up a little, their stodginess might feel more songful. [Oct 2006, p.94]

Title: Ekstasis
Review: Often very pretty, just as often very strange, Holter has crafted an album that reflects her unique vision, though it fails to captivate the whole way through.

Title: Kings & Queens
Review: This album is a stylized, slightly-paranoid romp sure to pluck the heartstrings of anyone who has ever lived life with reckless abandon.

Title: The Contino Sessions
Review: With their repetitive guitar riffs echoing against electronics, DIV aren't as flashy as fellow crossover masters the Chemical Brothers, but their appeal doesn't fade as quickly, either.

Title: Imperius Rex
Review: This is an impressive showcase for his fans.

Title: Venice
Review: With every album, Fennesz's music has become prettier and more accessible yet still retains his distinctive style-- and Venice is no exception.

Title: No Love Deep Web
Review: It's relentless top to bottom, but if you can get beyond the occasional groaning psycho-sexual screams there's a whole alternate network Death Grips have created.

The key to 3 is that the group might be less noisy, but ultimately they're no less weird, and if the album sounds like they're still making sense of their new configuration, their eyes are still on the buzzy prize, and this is a great, challenging, off-center rock album.

Title: So Far Gone
Review: So Far Gone shows that Drake is for real, and works as a tantalizing teaser for his first full-length record.

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: Some of the experiments here may work better than others in the long term, but it is far better that Beam is an artist prepared to take risks. His best work may be yet to come, while his writing remains vivid and evocative.

Title: Nick Waterhouse
Review: Nick Waterhouse (Innovative Leisure) occasionally comes off as a little too clean and polite. But when he loosens his tie a bit, Waterhouse brings a spark to his songs that transcends era and genre.

Title: Eyes on the Lines
Review: Making experimental music is certainly a noble calling. Sneaking the adventurous spirit of improvisation into a relatively conventional song-based record such as Eyes On The Lines, however: that's truly radical.

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: The album is imbued with a post-9/11 dread, which deters Fagen from recycling the nostalgia and Lynchian fantasy of his previous albums.

Title: Songs From San Mateo County
Review: Unlike many similar compilations, the album fits seamlessly into Molina’s existing canon—his work already blurs the line between “impulse” and “finished track.” And where his official albums tend to focus on a specific aesthetic, Songs From San Mateo County touches on every style he’s explored, making it the ideal entry point.

Title: Up, Guards and at 'Em!
Review: Described as a rallying call to guitar bands by Bowman, Up, Guards and at 'Em isn't distinctive or original enough to inspire anyone to swap their synths for a six-string, and instead, sounds more like a final nail in the British indie coffin than the shot in the arm it needed.

Title: Snares Like a Haircut
Review: Their call-and-response breakdowns are still as impassioned as ever on tracks like Drippy and Cruise Control, where they place the hooks and melodies right on the surface. The use of ambiance over their riotous songs isn’t just an asset, it’s also the essence of No Age.

Title: The Stoned Immaculate
Review: The Stoned Immaculate may not see Curren$y catapulting to new levels of lyricism, but the N'awlins native's wordplay is still high-- grade on the mic. [#253, p.89]

Title: Kill the Lights
Review: Bryan's fifth studio album is well-turned Nashville radio bait, trite yet undeniable, sure to drive up bar tabs in 50 states and beyond.

Title: Untrue
Review: That emptiness tempts a listener in, and puts you in its place--you, in a sense, step into the record’s point of view. This invitation to intimacy is a powerful move that most club music is simply incapable of.

Title: Supper
Review: Neither Callahan's trademark poetic gloom nor his even-keel misanthropy have been ditched in time for 'Supper', but it does see him breathing deeper than before and moving with a surprising spring in his step away from the claustrophobic intensity of his previous work.

Title: Love Letter
Review: It's easily the least sexually charged album in his discography, ideal for those who admire him as a singer, arranger, and producer but tune out the fantastical come-ons.

Title: Rubber Factory
Review: Some called their first two albums derivative, but with this third disc the guys wrestle their greased-up garage boogie until they own it.

Title: Pickpocket's Locket
Review: Although warmer, almost folk-rock, Pickpocket’s Locket is as visceral an experience as any Mercer project, albeit in a new way.

Title: The Ghosts of Highway 20
Review: Adult work, Ghosts hits the gut, the soul and the grey matter.

Title: What Went Down
Review: What went Down is their most fully realised yet. [Oct 2015, p.75]

Title: Tomorrow Is My Turn
Review: Raw and skiffly as you'd expect. [Apr 2015, p.95]

Title: Cinder
Review: Contains more than its fair share of exquisite melancholy and careering abandon. [Nov 2005, p.123]

Title: Need You Now
Review: The band is playing on the safe side on its less vibrant and surprising sophomore release.

Title: Feels
Review: The album is a confident yet ever-shifting debut, one that enters the crowded field of west-coast garage-rock bands and quickly claims its own dingy, fascinating corner.

Title: Blood and Candle Smoke
Review: Here, on Blood and Candle Smoke, he's perfected this method of songwriting and learned to record in a completely new way, to boot.

Title: Playtime Is Over
Review: With Playtime Is Over Wiley is finally living up to his reputation by achieving consistency without becoming mediocre; delivering a steady, honed set that's sharp enough to split flesh from bone.

Title: Mosaic
Review: It’s an honest album, and while you may not skip back to all of it, its jagged pieces all have their place.

Title: Beach House
Review: The sum of these elements could achieve greatness if not for one simple-yet-major falw: Beach House manages a memorable sound but not memorable songs. [#74, p.91]

Title: The Voyager
Review: There isn’t a weak track on the album--just varying degrees of excellence.

Title: Trouble Anyway
Review: The Trouble, with its richly twangy slide, spooky reverb and oblique enchantments, is particularly powerful, but throughout, Middleman’s voice is dark and engaging, her songs possessed of a deceptively subtle charm.

Title: Hot Shots II
Review: The quartet has cooled its eclectic babbling, and "Hot Shots II" whirrs and purrs like a gleeming silver sports car.

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: The Furnaces play with a whimsical charm, so the band seems more like an arts-and-crafts project than an occupation. [Nov 2003, p.113]

Title: LEGACY! LEGACY!
Review: LEGACY! LEGACY! is just as much a celebration of Chicago musical talent. ... It also demonstrates Woods’s vast talent as singer and songwriter. [Apr 2019, p.69]

Title: King Night
Review: The songs on this debut album are lethargic, syrupy, and sinister, with the rough-edged peaks of a maxed-out mix.

Title: Everybody Wants To Be On TV
Review: They peddle clichés about ugly ducklings and shagging that are so offensive they make a donkey braying into a bin sound like the ripe observations of a Charlie Brooker column.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: This is a truly magnificent record, and I think it’s going to end up being the album for which we remember Vampire Weekend.

Title: Backspacer
Review: This is a record made by mature men with perspective: full of reflection and eclecticism, finding space for both U2 guitar motifs and Buzzcocks solos.

Title: Warpaint
Review: Given Warpaint's complex, operatic highs, its experiments in minimalism and tranquility make for some awfully low lows, but there are worse things than a band that seems to be evolving in two directions at once.

Title: The Louder I Call, The Faster It Runs
Review: The Louder I Call... is another step forward for Wye Oak, a duo who still carry plenty of vision to inject some life into a form of indie rock that you don't hear that often anymore.

Title: I Will Be
Review: The summery feel and gloriously messy pop sensibility are at times great fun, but with something that is so derivative, it is hard to get too carried away without getting an urge to switch this album off and dig out the originals.

Title: Emerald Classics
Review: From their dream-pop origins, through their psychedelic sophomore, they have arrived at a spiritual revolution with Emerald Classics. It's a development to be proud of, to feel good about.

Title: Write About Love
Review: Overall, Belle and Sebastian Write About Love plays like a greatest hits, though not necessarily of former songs.

Title: Punctuated Equilibrium
Review: Wino aims to combine vocal and guitar swagger with psychosis in equal measure on Punctuated Equilibrium--the mark of someone who knows that one of the best things to do with electric guitars is to figure out how to stun the listener and make them queasy at the same time. So if nothing on the album ultimately surprises, it's still a great demonstration of ability.

Title: Higher Truth
Review: While Higher Truth never seems as self-consciously confessional as Euphoria Mourning, this mellow simplicity is an attribute: a relaxed Cornell creates a comforting mood piece that's enveloping in its warmth.

Title: Makes a King
Review: The Swedish-Malawian duo of Johan Hugo and Esau Mwamwaya decamped to a rented house on the shores of Lake Malawi for album number three. That apposite choice of location has paid off with a warmer, more pointedly African sound as insects provide environmental chatter and local villagers add laughs, jokes and musical accompaniment.

Title: Past Life Martyred Saints
Review: Past Life Martyred Saints is a fiercely individual record, made by a musician with a fearless and courageous approach to her art. Crucially, the desire to let such raw emotion out in song never feels forced.

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Thier debut album is one of the most inventive in recent memory. [Apr 2008, p.153]

Title: After the End
Review: After the End sounds like pretty much every other 80s-influenced indie record you've been hearing since what now feels like the beginning of time itself. Still, at other points, Merchandise do manage to provide a fresh take on the 80s.

Title: The Music
Review: A hollow release, the veneer of a good album covering up an otherwise unremarkable and sometimes disappointing collection of songs.

Title: Scarecrow
Review: As a final statement from one of the most important artists of the last decade, it's not exactly earth-shattering. But this eclectic, personal and heartfelt Scarecrow is still outstanding in its field.

Title: Sound the Alarm
Review: Sound the Alarm is ultimately just another good Saves the Day record.

Title: Too Much Information
Review: The music struggles to match the lyrical focus, sounding piecemeal and haphazard.

Title: Transistor Radio
Review: This one is just a little tiny bit less perfectly imperfect than [Transfiguration of Vincent], but it's still got all the warmth and gentle disorganization of its predecessor-- with a few more oomphy tracks standing in for Tranfiguration's most introspective meditations.

Title: The Golden D
Review: This is decidedly not for those who require slick and flawless recordings. It's not particularly an album for those who demand sheer brilliance every step of the way, either. For all its sonic oddities, The Golden D doesn't always have songs that rise far beyond mere ambition.

Title: Wanderer
Review: The swagger of Marshall's lyrics indicate a musician luxuriating in her maturity. [Nov 2018, p.105]

Title: Zipper Down
Review: Highlights are the punchy pop-metal of Got The Power and the greasy glamorama of The Reverend, replete with satisfyingly fuzzy guitar, but Zipper Down misses as much as it hits.

Title: Open Season
Review: Less chaotic and parochial, more serene and accessible, but no less magical. [May 2005, p.96]

Title: One Breath
Review: While the dynamics may be a little different, her wonderfully expressive, kaleidoscopic guitar playing and that voice, capable of alternating within the space of a few notes from a barely audible whisper to a wailing banshee, both remain as compelling as ever.

Title: Puzzles Like You
Review: Mojave 3's Great Leap Forward. [17 Jun 2006, p.39]

Title: Congratulations
Review: Listening to the new MGMT album requires similar preparations to those for a prolonged psychedelic experience: you may want to leave some time in your daybook for unexpected detours, and it'd be wise to erase previous experiences from your mind for fear that heightened expectations may not be met and mass bummerage will ensue.

Title: Scacco Matto
Review: This is a strong record, and one made with a singular artistic focus. Senni clearly knows what he likes, and he does it incredibly well.

Title: Here We Rest
Review: It's taken Isbell three albums to find his comfortable post-Truckers solo-artist groove, and on Here We Rest, he settles in quite nicely.

Title: Heavy Rotation
Review: Ultimately, though, it's her own barnstroming commitment and sheer affability that steer things safely home. [Dec 2008, p.123]

Title: East of Eden
Review: For East of Eden to be such an assured sophomore release, Victoria Bergsman has a kind of steely reserve to take herself further out of the picture on records to come.

Title: II
Review: Though parts of the album veer a bit too close to the synthetic hippie pabulum you hear upon entering the Nature Store, there's enough dark charm on Espers II to make it essential listeing for those of us who prefer our CDs caked with actual resin. [Jul 2006, p.208]

Title: To the 5 Boroughs
Review: Picking highlights from a release so well executed and downright ass-shaking is difficult.... 'To The 5 Boroughs' is a triumph.

Title: Outside Closer
Review: It demands the right frame of mind, temperament and that ideal rainy-day traveling environment, in which nothing works out. When you're in the middle of such a moment, Hood's there to provide the soundtrack for your emotional nosedive.

Title: Solidarity
Review: It all hangs together well, and is ably supported by the band's superb musicianship. [Nov 2012, p.87]

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: Sometimes the marriage of sentiment and sound is more obvious but it doesn't undermine the thoughtfulness of their restraint.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: Port of Morrow captures Mercer in a different era, and although questionable at times, it's a fruitful adventure that requires a little swinging and paddling.

Title: Animator
Review: This sumptuous sonic depth exceeds that of a live band, but still feels like something The Luyas will pull off live without a hitch. Evocative and avoiding narrative, brooding but warm to the touch, you'll feel compelled to return to these songs without actually learning the mechanics of their nature.

Title: 4:13 Dream
Review: The territory is familiar, occasionally too familiar....But it’s not a comforting nostalgic reprise; it’s another plunge into the maelstrom.

Title: Wildcard
Review: Lambert balances her high-spirited romps with more contemplative numbers, cooling off long enough to reflect without flagging Wildcard’s momentum.

Title: Devils & Dust
Review: Devils & Dust is remarkably self-contained and perfectly linear: here is the aftermath of The Rising, when the plains go quiet, the windows shut and we pray, pause, and plot our next move.

Title: Here's to Being Here
Review: Each and every single song on here is sprinkled with a certain something to make it outstanding all on its own.

Title: Poor Moon
Review: Poor Moon still feels like its developing, like it's unsure of what it will be yet. This makes their first full-length an uneven, sometimes frustratingly safe record, but it also makes it an album of some promise.

Title: The Sun Dogs
Review: This trance-inducing seven-piece evoke arcane loci, spirits and serpents. [Oct 2013, p.98]

Title: Rockwell
Review: Behind the whimsy she defies her own frailty. She stays on the move, with uncertainty wherever she alights.

Title: Rad Times Xpress IV
Review: Rad Times Xpress IV illuminates how well that music lends itself to more experimental renderings while the songs seemingly engineered to hold onto RTX's denim'n'leather constituency yield surprises.

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: Regardless of whether you share the Manic's collective outlook on life, and if you're not forty plus you might not, you can only take Rewind The Film for exactly what it is: a band who know where they want to be and are comfortable with that. And, interestingly enough, this is maybe the closest we'll ever get to really knowing them.

Title: You Can Do Better
Review: Many of the songs on this fourth LP begin promisingly enough, but some lose their way when frontman Alexei Barrow and bassist Kelly Southern pitch in with mildly hysterical vocals, the clashing combination descending into a shouty mess. [May 2014, p.113]

Title: Hello Everything
Review: Squarepusher's wide range is bound to disappoint some listeners.

Title: Carnivore
Review: For the most part, Ice plays with middle-age, cranking up the grumpy-old-man persona he established on 2014’s Institutionalized with tongue-in-cheek glee and riding it through the exploitation movie excess of Thee Critical Beatdown.

Title: Atlas
Review: These songs are Polaroid snapshots of friends, families, lovers, cul-de-sacs and empty highways. Some are perfectly, sentimentally fuzzy, and some don’t quite make it into the scrapbook.

Title: I Know What Love Isn't
Review: Jens sticks to what he knows, combining his spry guitar playing and razor sharp pop sensibility.

Title: Past Life
Review: The album as a whole is still more interesting than any of its individual parts, but now we can truly appreciate each and every fragment.

Title: You & Me
Review: Intimate, intense and beautiful, You & Me demands repeat plays and the Walkmen deserve a new respect.

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: Ultimately, under the unifying sound of Casiokids' youthful pop, African, Asian and Norweigan influences combine in blissful harmony to create the ultimate musical expedition.

Title: Fabula Mendax
Review: It’s an album that stands up on its own and remains, musically at least, a positive, upbeat and highly enjoyable album.

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: Change Becomes Us is a veritable compendium of everything that Wire has been up to since the late ‘70s, combining the bristling energy of the good old days, the electronic textures of the ‘80s forays, and the heftier rock of its 2000s output.

Title: Rook
Review: While Jonathan Meiburg’s uneasy high quaver has always generated the kind of simmering intensity that made Jeff Buckley so gripping and unnerving, canny tonal shifts give his introspective songs a bristling, heightened urgency.

Title: The Atlas Underground
Review: This is Tom Morello: Unfiltered, the work of a rap-rock renegade who answers to no-one, exploring new terrain well into the third decade of his career, an artist unwilling to rest on his legacy.

Title: Egypt Station
Review: Egypt Station is not without flaws. Quite aside from the misstep of Fuh You, it could use a trim. ... At its best, however, Egypt Station is an affirmation of an enduring talent, the work of an artist who has no need to try and be anything other than what he is.

Title: Para Mi
Review: Cuco transmutes various pop methodologies to create his own blend of burnout soul.

Title: Tambourine
Review: Finds her pushing her already considerable talents to new heights.

Title: More Is Than Isn't
Review: More Is Than Isn’t balances vocals with lyricless tracks but at the heart of it all is RJD2’s strength in producing impressive music.

Title: Her Mystery Not of High Heels and Eye Shadow
Review: An American oddball, for sure, but one to treasure. [Jan 2002, p.146]

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: Like a garish version of his label boss Akon, he's a singer/songwriter/producer who doesn't evolve much over this avalanche of releases and guest shots, but Thr33 Ringz proves he's much more aware of his limitations.

Title: Thank You Happy Birthday
Review: Taking cues from the Pixies and '90s grunge--Sell Yourself or Japanese Buffalo could be Pixies mainman Black Francis in a rage--but rowdier and caustic, they are compelling. [19 Mar 2011, p.51]

Title: Rub
Review: Rub is the first album in her career where the music feels as foregrounded as Peaches' persona, which makes sense, as she co-produced it with Vice Cooler.

Title: Faith in the Future
Review: Faith In The Future continues this rich work [of short story narrative in song], but with a new feel of quiet sobriety. [Oct 2015, p.107]

Title: Rainbow Edition
Review: Most of the tracks come in at under two minutes long; short drafts and ideas stitched together with smoky loops and obscure vocal samples. An atmospheric and pensive sound shrouds the majority of Rainbow Edition - the only thing missing is the underlying grooves that were found on their past releases, leaving some of these beats slightly too industrial and cold.

Title: Overload
Review: An album that can initially feel scatty but is held together by its creator's passion and poise. [Dec 2018, p.28]

Title: Alice
Review: Tom Waits has never made an album quite like Alice before.

Title: Live Forever
Review: Live Forever argues that life is not some march toward a peak, but a closed loop—one that’s tighter if you’re Black. The brilliance of Bartees’ debut is in how it carves out an expansive space within that loop.

Title: New Amerykah Part One (4th World War)
Review: Each listen to New Amerykah brings fresh rewards: it demands to be explored.

Title: Faith and Courage
Review: There's a lot going on sonically with this album, but it feels cohesive -- all its disparate elements are beautifully brought together by O'Connor's overriding openness and passion.

Title: Two Way Monologue
Review: Lerche gets his Burt Bacharach on, flavoring coffee-shop ballads with minor-key chicory. [Apr 2004, p.94]

Title: Vulnicura
Review: A self-consciously serious, elaborate, capital R Romantic dramatic statement that pulls no punches, more Greek tragedy than break-up album. [Mar 2015, p.55]

Title: Two Vines
Review: Their music palette may be limited but their style knows no bound. [Dec 2016, p.92]

Title: Crazy Itch Radio
Review: Maybe if they had calmed down a bit, Crazy Itch Radio wouldn't be Basement Jaxx's fourth best album. [Oct 2006, p.126]

Title: Evil Urges
Review: Evil Urges is easily MMJ's most accomplished and ambitious record, masterfully sifting through genres.

Title: The Fool
Review: The Fool often sounds like it was assembled by a spectacularly talented committee, like the minutes of the recording sessions are probably filed away in a sterile LA duplex somewhere.

Title: Sucker
Review: This year’s first great pop record bowls in with a rapturous celebration of the genre's rebellious, trashy potential (and a bottle of champagne and a pocketful of pills to boot).

Title: Eyelid Movies
Review: It should be noted that Eyelid Movies owes a great deal to Portishead's entire catalogue in terms of song structure, phrasing, and instrumentation. This might rub some folks the wrong way, but this album still manages a unique, cohesive sound that definitely merits investigation.

Title: Gang Signs & Prayer
Review: The south London grime don delivers a knockout debut that’s brash and pensive in equal measure.

Title: LOSE
Review: While the album may not fully scale D'Agostino's high bar, in attempting to make that leap Cymbals Eat Guitars have made their best album to date as well as a touching goodbye to a friend.

Title: Underneath The Pine
Review: Exactly a year since the release of his dreamy debut Causers Of This, South Carolina's Chaz Bundick is back with a very different and impressively cultured second album. [Mar 2011, p.105]

Title: News From Nowhere
Review: The impressions made are that the sublime, the relinquishing of the self can only come with work and time. “-” seems to come from a similar place as The King of Limbs’ latter tracks, which speaks to the notion of human fallibility and fragility, helping make News From Nowhere a decidedly beautiful album.

Title: Simple Math
Review: There are plenty of seeds sewn throughout Simple Math that could likely blossom into Manchester Orchestra's first real breakthrough, but here, we're stuck in the growing pains phase.

Title: Funeral
Review: Wayne’s unheralded 13th studio album proves that the 37-year-old’s flow can still be fearsome, even if his edit function remains iffy.

Title: The Physical World
Review: As it stands, it’s still one of the year’s finest and worth the wait.

Title: The Magic Place
Review: My only qualm with The Magic Place is with its song structure. Each of the nine songs starts sparsely, weaves into an intricate texture, bulges with layered loops and then tails off.

Title: Centipede Hz
Review: Centipede Hz is dense and unforgivingly full-throttle--you'll find no "Loch Raven" or even "Chores" here – and home to some of the band's best and most involved lyrics to date.

Title: Young Blood
Review: Obey the Brave's no-nonsense approach, boundless energy and verve, and catharsis-cleansing rage make the songs on Young Blood crackle with the out-of-control power of both the hungriest up-and-comers and all the institutions of power metal that came before.

Title: If I've Only One Time Askin'
Review: Like many of Romano's meticulous creations, it possesses all the hallmarks of a classic: a compelling, twisting narrative that bends the music to its shape.

Title: Two
Review: Ultimately, Two succeeds for the same reasons Owls did: by never acknowledging there were any expectations to be met and instead allowing the band to create without compromise.

Title: Antics
Review: Antics is so much more fun than Turn On The Bright Lights. [Oct 2004, p.107]

Title: Hold Time
Review: Hold Time is a wonderful, wistful collection of songs from an artist who has really started to hit his stride.

Title: Rub
Review: Lewd, bulshy, and gaudier than a kitsch ornaments warehouse with a sprung glitter pipe, Rub is a return to form, and hideously brilliant, garish good fun.

Title: Fish Outta Water
Review: Fish Outta Water may lack the demographic-tripping vibe that even a Jurassic 5 in turmoil could whip up, but it's a mostly winning debut that makes up in vocal prowess for what it lacks in hooks.

Title: Where The Gods Are In Peace
Review: Its songs are energetic and uplifting, with frontman and main songwriter Amayo's half-sung/half-spoken lyrics balancing snide humor with insightful commentary into the roots of the political quandaries we confront on a daily basis. [No. 146, p.53]

Title: What Now
Review: This album deserves your attention and is a perfect example of a group accomplishing and exceeding their full potential.

Title: Saltwater
Review: There's a lovely, skittering energy to the second album from Brazos, a restlessness that reflects the band's fitful existence.

Title: Ski Mask
Review: Ski Mask is almost certainly not Islands’ most accessible or enjoyable work, but it ranks with the band’s most forceful and accomplished.

Title: Trouble Maker
Review: Trouble Maker is up there with their best.

Title: Personal Life
Review: There are rare glimmers here, but maturity sure is sobering.

Title: Along the Way
Review: McGuire creates a journey that will absorb and transport any listener willing to let its sincere warmth and good wishes into their hearts. [Feb 2014, p.54]

Title: Bloodsports
Review: The quality tails off quite dramatically, with a string of unremarkable ballads closing the album, but this is still a pleasing return to something approaching their best.

Title: When It Falls
Review: Superior to its predecessor in just about every respect.

Title: GUV I
Review: He’s managed to inject this compact collection of eight tunes with more than a whiff of 90s alt-radio nostalgia, but the songs are hummable enough to rebuff anyone inclined toward cynical eye-rolling.

Title: The False Alarms
Review: This is Fol Chen's sharpest full-length yet, gaining cohesion from the often mechanically warped vocal presence of new frontwoman Sinosa Loa. [No. 97, p.55]

Title: New Relics
Review: At once sprawling and implosive, New Relics is simply just a relic for fans and other curious parties who want to plunge headfirst into this cascading and widescreen sound with a clutch of some great songs; the rest of it being little more than filler.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: RTJ2 is replete with razor-sharp lyricism and clattering, abrasive production.

Title: Seen It All: The Autobiography
Review: Backed by mostly familiar trap music production, Jeezy is steady (“Been Getting Money” is especially fine), but hardly inspired.

Title: Winter Hymn Country Hymn Secret Hymn
Review: Diminished by their willingness to splash about in the post-Tortoise shallows. [Dec 2003, p.124]

Title: Terms of Surrender
Review: On an album where Taylor nakedly reveals his most pressing moments of despair, it’s only in the album's handful of brighter moments that you wish for maybe just another small taste of the darkness. Taylor manages to flip his career-long look for the silver lining by acknowledging the pull of the worldly can only be put in a tidy little box for so long.

Title: Holy Ghost
Review: They [the songs] all sit well next to each other, but that feeling of “next to each other” rather than “supporting each other” can be difficult to shake.

Title: Rise and Fall, Rage and Grace
Review: Sounding closer to their more earnest Smash days, the songs are snappy to-the-point SoCal punk, albeit with a more polished sheen.

Title: Psychodrama
Review: A different kind of hero’s journey through the musical mind, Psychodrama feels less like a platform for clout than a starting point for self-help and paradigmatic change.

Title: Pawn Shoppe Heart
Review: Swathed from head to toe in ecstatic fuzz.

Title: Year In The Kingdom
Review: Though the sound remains dreamy, it's expansive; the melodic songs have a feeling of joy. [Oct 2009, p.101]

Title: A Loud Bash of Teenage Feelings
Review: A Loud Bash of Teenage Feelings might not be an earth-shattering departure from last year's full-length debut The Things We Do to Find People Who Feel Like Us, but it's a loud and beautifully fun ode to young outsiders falling in love, getting fucked up and revelling in their weirdness--and that's advice as good as any.

Title: Night Falls Over Kortedala
Review: The Swedish indie-pop singer shows a remarkably keen eye for detail, finding surprising moments of sweetness, poignancy, and humor in a variety of situations.

Title: Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager
Review: Whenever Mr Rager sets off on his next adventure we're ready, musical machetes in hand, to follow him into the undergrowth…

Title: This Island
Review: Even more staunchly pop than their previous records.

Title: Radium Death
Review: Mostly these dry, derivative, rather dreary songs of endeavour are a hard slog. [Jun 2015, p.84]

Title: Owl John
Review: [The album] is not so much a radical departure as a dalliance with a marginally more brooding, textural musical aesthetic. [Sep 2014, p.75]

Title: Nothing is Quick in the Desert
Review: Nothing Is Quick In The Desert shows them in fantastic form, sidestepping those laboured moments of musical correctness that made 2015’s Man Plans, God Laughs so patchy, and focusing on the kind of ear-popping chaos that made so much of 1994’s Muse Sick-N-Hour Mess Age so uniquely addictive. [Sep 2017, p.55]

Title: Fine Line
Review: The actual sound of Fine Line is incredible, and most songs have at least one great moment to grab hold of. ... While the music wades into the mystic, his songwriting, pointedly, does not. ... Styles doesn’t have the imagination of Bowie or another pop-rock touchpoint here, Fleetwood Mac, who took their lives and transfigured them through cosmic fantasia or Victorian grandeur.

Title: Nowhere
Review: Nowhere is Batoh's most provocative yet accessible solo album; its otherworldly strangeness is uncompromising, but somehow welcoming because of its deep focus. Its many textured ripples, fissures and psychic pathways resonate long after its playing timer expires.

Title: Callus
Review: It’s an album that needs the thick-skin its title connotes to listen--you won’t emerge from it feeling joyous, but you will emerge seeing a truth that will deeply unsettle.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Infest the Rats' Nest
Review: Like most King Gizzard records, it runs out of steam in the second half, but when ‘Infest’ rips it rips as hard as some bands who have been making this music for decades. Like the modern thrash revivalists, King Gizzard combine youthful energy with enough of their own inimitable style to make this excursion into the cobwebbed world of thrash fresh and interesting.

Title: The Fool
Review: While not perfect, The Fool is a very promising début that grows in stature on every listen. If you're willing to put the time in, this could easily live up to the hype.

Title: Endangered Philosophies
Review: What is said is interesting, and delivered with a fiery ferocity worthy of the howling big cat on the cover, but too often the dissonant noise serves to exemplify the disconnect between the engaging ideas and the impotence of their presentation.

Title: Reassemblage
Review: While never able to fully grasp the Japanese sounds they adore, Visible Cloaks nevertheless have created an album along the axis of Fennesz’s Endless Summer and OPN’s Replica, an abstract electronic album that’s readily accessible and an immersive listen.

Title: Sab Se Purani Bab
Review: It is highly electrifying, however, and ranks among the enigmatic, boundlessly exuberant vocalist's most joyous work.

Title: Electric Trim
Review: Electric Trim is Lee Ranaldo’s 12th solo album but it sounds remarkably fresh. [Oct 2017, p.59]

Title: Rules
Review: So, his odd decision to make Jamiroquai-like pillow-pop adds yet another string to Oye’s heavily-laden bow, but this is one we’d happily take the wire-cutters to.

Title: American Idiot
Review: The observations don't always dig as deep as they're meant to, and buzzwords occasionally stand in for insights, but American Idiot finds Green Day both shaking up its formula and applying it in novel and unexpected ways.

Title: Below the Branches
Review: 2006's album of the year may have arrived early. [Mar 2006, p.104]

Title: Brooklyn's Don Diva
Review: The production is bargain bin, and lyrically, she sounds leaden.

Title: Friend and Foe
Review: It sounds like a campfire sing-along at the most evil band camp in the underworld.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die
Review: At a time when many of his rap peers are even more desperately changing their sound to stay relevant, Ghostface Killah is cementing his relevancy by diving even deeper into what always made him such a unique artist.

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: He has bravely laid his songwriting gifts bare in their purest form.

Title: Let It All In
Review: The band’s template has barely changed over those years but that isn’t to suggest a lack of artistic growth. “How Deep It Goes”, the opening track from their tenth album Let It All In, is a prime example of their peculiar progression as it exudes the reassuring warmth of California songsmiths of yesteryear yet still somehow manages to wedge a wash of icy interplay between Huemann’s guitar and Matthew Pierce’s synths smack dab in the middle of the track. [May 2020, p.48]

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: If you’re new to Pixies, try this one first, then let the magic of their previous records blow your mind. If you’re already in love with their best work, a dalliance with Indie Cindy can’t hurt.

Title: Stuck on Nothing
Review: Stuck on Nothing opens strong, closes strong, and the intermediate tracks are interesting enough to maintain interest. Free Energy haven’t created anything cataclysmically new, but they have created an entirely likable pop album.

Title: Axes
Review: Axes isn't the stylistic leap forward that many might have expected after The Power Out. But what the album may lack diversity, it makes up for with surprising intensity and precision.

Title: Lisbon
Review: The Walkmen have done it slightly different this time, but I guarantee that after hearing this album, the brilliance of Lisbon will stay with you for the entire day, no matter what color the sky sitting above.

Title: Sisyphus
Review: Sisyphus is ultimately as off the wall a release as you’ll likely encounter this year.

Title: Girls Can Tell
Review: Their music is as strong as ever and they certainly deserve your attention.

Title: No Way Down
Review: A musical sub-genre rebooted. [May 2009, p.104]

Title: Diamond Mine
Review: The two together make magic: the songs don't feel like they've been crafted, rather that they just floated, fully-formed, into existence. Like the people Diamond Mine talks about, the songs aren't any one thing: they just are.

Title: NYC
Review: Hebden is clearly striving for dancefloor impact--but Reid's drumming is so untethered and, frankly, messy, that it sucks the explosions out of whatever bombs Hebden's trying to drop. [Dec 2008, p.60]

Title: The Electric Lady
Review: The Electric Lady is also a dazzling artistic statement, a fiendishly clever endeavor that oozes enough feminine charm, wit and charisma to endow dozens of regular pop starlets with.

Title: Maui Tears
Review: Maui Tears is a distinct return to form and one that reaffirms Sleepy Sun as a genuine force to be reckoned with.

Title: Ring
Review: Ring is odd and hypnotic, elaborate and approachable, dense and endearing. In the hands of any other musician, such aural acrobatics would end in failure. With Glasser, Cameron Mesirow not only makes the whole pastiche come together, but she makes it sound compelling, as well.

Title: The Raven
Review: A rewarding and self-consciously motley fest. [#227, p.60]

Title: Hollywood's Bleeding
Review: Post Malone curates as much as he creates, and there’s not a misplaced feature among the 10 spread across seven of these tracks.

Title: Push the Button
Review: While the album is based around the repetitive choppy hook and big beat, some quiet building moments of the heavy songs lack a sense of creativity and movement towards a real climactic edge.

Title: Food
Review: As Kelis herself once said, “Tasty.”

Title: Dilate
Review: This is a solid attempt by a band in thrall to electronic music to redefine themselves, but it’s their love of this music rather than their ability to explore its limits that is communicated by Dilate.

Title: Romance Is Boring
Review: Romance Is Boring would be better-served with more of the diversity that's found on these tracks. But those without dates on Valentine's Day should find some cheer in this danceable collection

Title: Music
Review: Mostly, as on Ray of Light, sophisticated production masks Madonna's shortcomings as a songwriter.... Often Mirwais is the real star here... It's his music that makes Music matter. [Sep 25, 2000]

Title: Nobody Knows
Review: As a whole it’s a bold, beautiful and uncompromising record.

Title: True Sadness
Review: Ultimately, True Sadness is a confessional set of songs, revealing in many ways and vulnerable in many others. However, honesty has always been an inherent element in their sound, so in that sense this album’s no different.

Title: Raising Sand
Review: You don’t have to be a fan of the country, blues or folk genres to appreciate the heartbreaking brilliance of this inspired collaboration.

Title: When The Night Comes
Review: Boyle is still at his strongest when he opts to bring the noise. [Jul 2015, p.102]

Title: Thistled Spring
Review: Thistled Spring, more nuanced and poised than its much-lauded predecessor, signals the ongoing work of a band far from finished, far from plumbing the depths of which it is capable.

Title: When I Think of You In a Castle
Review: They may have no trouble getting creative musically, but their lyrical content isn’t quite as inventive.

Title: Born To Die
Review: A delicious hybrid of Portishead and Nancy Sinatra.

Title: Lex Hives
Review: Much like the band's catalog, this record apes everyone from AC/DC to The Stooges with exuberant aplomb.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: Eye Contact solidifies the group's heavyweight majesty. Gang Gang Dance injects pop music with new life, leading the quest for newer sounds from ageless sources and mixing it all together in a critically irresistible way.

Title: The Grind Date
Review: Notably fresh for a group that's been rhyming for 15 years. [8 Oct 2004, p.117]

Title: Dusk and Summer
Review: It's difficult to imagine Carraba's earnest tenor appealing to anyone over the age of 20. [Sep 2006, p.107]

Title: Ruinism
Review: Ultimately, this seems to be his goal on Ruinism; to take you into a world of house and electronic music, where each and every artefact that you thought were held dear can be just as easily crumbled and recontextualised to create a whole new atmosphere. This is where which he wants you to venture, and not look back.

Title: Dear Science
Review: Dear Science has its moments, but these moments means less and weigh more. Pretty cool? Well, it's pretty alright. [Fall 2008, p.91]

Title: Deth Red Sabaoth
Review: After having worked out some of his (hopefully) passing interests in industrial and classical music over the past few years, Danzig has finally come close to once more nailing what he's known for--sick, spooky rock 'n' roll that isn't afraid of a little croon.

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: Add the pipes of Nancy Whang on most tracks--giving Future a boy-girl dynamic--and there's a distinct suggestion that the Juan MacLean might just become the Human League after all.

Title: Honeys
Review: Torture, disgust and danger are all here, but so too are some sharp-barbed observations on screwed-up modern living. [Sep 2013, p.90]

Title: The Planet
Review: The two musicians match well in terms of overall ethos, but at some points it feels like they just stopped listening to each other, and what should be otherworldly comes clunking to the ground.

Title: Transference
Review: Spoon's seventh studio album, Transference, strikes a balance between its early angsty indie-rock and the soulful deconstructed pop of its 2007 release, "Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga."

Title: Range Anxiety
Review: Twerps succeed in making decades-old style sound brand new again. [No. 117, p.61]

Title: Showtime
Review: What Dizzee Rascal has done with this record is find his own - profoundly satisfying - balance between grime's digital vortex of ringtones and car alarms and an older more contemplative electronic tradition. [Oct 2004, p.104]

Title: MeÃ° suÃ° Ã­ eyrum viÃ° spilum endalaust
Review: In this transformation, Sigur Rós have yet again set themselves apart from the rest of the music world, bridging genre gaps and inspiring many others to do the same.

Title: Of All Things I Will Soon Grow Tired
Review: Here's a band skipping from one musical fragment to the next with the reckless abandon of youth, trying out ideas, finding their strengths.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Somewhere Else is only rewarding if you can stay awake. [Feb 2013, p.90]

Title: Fluorescence
Review: Fluorescence represents equilibrium between the noise and energy of the first two albums and the dreamier soundscapes of Hush, while simultaneously refining the sound to the point where it is something distinctly Asobi Seksu's. More than merely going strong after four studio albums and two live releases, Asobi Seksu is better than ever.

Title: MONOVISION
Review: The individual tunes hold their own, but Monovision is a record where the whole means more than the individual numbers, since LaMontagne strikes a very specific mood -- one that's reassuring, even soothing -- and then manages to sustain it until the end.

Title: Nellyville
Review: A great pop album that reconciles his sudden wealth, attachment to home, and desire to rule the world.

Title: More Light
Review: More Light is not Primal Scream at their very best, but merely at their very good.

Title: They Were Wrong, So We Drowned
Review: For such menacing music, the overall effect is oddly inviting.

Title: TFCF
Review: TFCF might well be an Angus Andrew solo album under the Liars banner, but what he’s achieved here fits within the his band’s remit for consistently morphing and confounding expectation. More importantly, it’s heartening to see an album as intriguing as this emerge from such a traumatic time.

Title: Luminous
Review: Luminous is a great record, but it's an awkward bugger at times, and I suspect that in the long run the album will prove all the more rewarding for just that reason.

Title: Time (The Revelator)
Review: More than simply an expression of her music, Time (The Revelator) is a glimpse into the artist's personality.

Title: Black Noise
Review: Black Noise can't help but feel ever so slightly like a letdown after the consistently mesmerizing rapture of its predecessor. But make no mistake: Weber is still making some of the most enchanting electronica out there, and if this album brings him the increased exposure for which he seems well-poised, there are few producers more deserving.

Title: WIXIW
Review: WIXIW is an unqualified success and, now that LCD are no longer with us, its makers are truly are in a field of their own.

Title: Tooth
Review: Tooth works brilliantly as a whole, each piece building up tension to breaking point and refusing to offer resolution. [Jun 2016, p.48]

Title: Complete Surrender
Review: Even stripping off the gloss doesn’t help, because there’s not much under it.

Title: When It Falls
Review: In the end, this is a perfectly passable release if you need something to play in the background at your next cocktail party or if you're a dentist looking for something to play in the background.

Title: Devil Music
Review: It's an exhilarating rush, and even for a band that had never made the same record twice, it comes as a bit of a shock after the Men had been inching toward sounding like Bruce Springsteen or Tom Petty.

Title: God Loves Ugly
Review: [Slug is] suddenly one of the best alt-rappers around. [#9, p.143]

Title: Before The World Was Big
Review: It's brevity, meanwhile, ensures this sweetly, powerful group don't wear out their welcome. [Aug 2015, p.93]

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: The Century of Self
Review: Trail of Dead's post-major label debut, The Century of Self, may be the Austin institution's most conceptually complete work to date, a post-prog cathedral of mythical mini-epics, though it's by no means the band's masterpiece.

Title: Back To Forever
Review: Back To Forever strives for mainstream acceptance, and in doing so dilutes Lissie’s strengths.

Title: It Was Good Until It Wasn't
Review: A record that doesn’t always astound but has a fair few enjoyable moments, and some very effective vocal performances.

Title: Visitations
Review: With its lushly forbidding soundscapes and enigmatic lyricism, Visitations bears repeated journeys. [2 Feb 2007, p.123]

Title: Just Us
Review: jUSt is by no means a catastrophe, it's just too empty an artefact to recommend to fans of a band who once infuriated, teased, scalded, intoxicated and destroyed their listeners with effortless aplomb.

Title: Recording a Tape the Colour of the Light
Review: While it drifts away from the listener somewhat during its middle section, Recording a Tape the Colour of the Light is, for the most part, a captivating listen.

Title: Begin To Hope
Review: Always ambitious, occasionally experimental, and sometimes even radio-friendly.

Title: Villains
Review: Villains is the kind of album that sits at the back of class openly smoking a cigarette but still manages to ace its exams at the end of the year.

Title: Untitled
Review: Compounding shades of this all-encompassing bleakness and newfound furore to an already formidable plateau of emo, indie and shoegaze could just about make it mewithoutYou's finest work to date. [20 Oct 2018, p.55]

Title: Blossoms
Review: There’s a decent amount of groove and swagger here too, not least in the low-slung funk of Smashed Pianos, and singer Tom Ogden’s vocals, are pitched engagingly between the rough-edged croon of Alex Turner and the florid yelp of Brett Anderson.

Title: Top Ten Hits of the End of the World
Review: Top Ten Hits often sees a band with a highly stylized identity sitting inside of another band with a highly stylized identity. More often than not, these halves clash, one entirely overpowering the other, negating what makes the concept interesting.

Title: What Now
Review: Mostly, What Now is intent on being bigger and brasher than its predecessor, perhaps to avoid politely slipping into the background quite so easily.

Title: Jericho Sirens
Review: Their lengthy hiatus has clearly not dulled Hot Snakes' razor-sharp edge, one bit, making Jericho Sirens a very welcome return. [17 Mar 2018, p.55]

Title: The New Classic
Review: The New Classic establishes the Australian artist as a competent rapper with a decent ear for hooks, but that's about it.

Title: Mothers
Review: Ultimately, Mothers feels like a stepping stone to bigger and better things for Swim Deep.

Title: What Now
Review: The rhythm sections and synths have been crafted with a newfound appreciation for sound, but with unexpected, childlike curiosity. The lyrics retain a relatable amount of simplicity, yet they also portray an intimate exploration of self-worth and image.

Title: Come of Age
Review: Unfortunately, just like The Vaccines debut, there is very little to really make you stand up and take notice.

Title: The Living Infinite
Review: While The Living Infinite is certainly a whole lot of record, it's filled with enough vigor and creativity that it doesn't feel as though it's dragging along.

Title: Typical System
Review: What becomes clear is that, even when it is uneven, Typical Systems succeeds on good songcraft and—most importantly--heavy and convincing emotional weight. It’s an album that takes a toll, and then invites you back to take it on again.

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: It’s inoffensive, painfully so, with the smell of something run through focus groups from the get go, written and produced by committee to sell the greatest number of copies.

Title: Journal For Plague Lovers
Review: This is something unique, often flawed and often flooring, and as fine and fitting a memorial for its lyricist as could be imagined.

Title: Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors
Review: It feels rushed, like it needed more time for its many ingredients to blend.

Title: Sweatbox Dynasty
Review: Overflowing with gnarled pop melodies and stuttering beats, Sweatbox Dynasty may be decidedly askew, but the manipulations and distortions simply add character to what is in fact a very listenable album.

Title: Scintilli
Review: It'll be comforting to know that Plaid certainly haven't 'lost it', that said they haven't strayed far enough outside their comfort zone in order to do so.

Title: Comedown Machine
