Review: A singular experience, You Will Not Die is a theatrical jewel, the sound of a rich, vital talent moving briskly into the limelight. At times reminiscent of Kate Bush in its sense of performance, ANOHNI in its integrity, or even Marvin Gaye in its soulful, sinewy groove, this is an album to be cherished.

Title: Relaxer
Review: In Cold Blood follows and is excellent, with code-like vocals and a brass-funk cascade drenching a menacing chorus. Hit Me Like That Snare is alt-J flexing their nerdiness, and Deadcrush is great. The final three tracks of the record are painfully boring and terminally so.

Title: Donna
Review: A record to give reigning empress of dancefloor diversity Roisin Murphy a run for her hard earned. [Jul 2016, p.95]

Title: Broken Bells
Review: "high Road" is melodic enough, for sure, and Mercer is a clear-voiced singer, but the album's interest palls when Mouse's answer to life, the universe and everything proves to be "pedestrian breakbeat." [Apr 2010, p.83]

Title: Risk to Exist
Review: A record that fits neatly in to the Maxïmo Park canon, while seeking to distance itself from it subtly.

Title: Yoncalla
Review: Yoncalla isn’t earth-shattering--everything sort of blends together, as is often the way with most dream pop records. But what does it matter when it’s the sort of album that makes you feel good.

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: It's charming in every way, but still rooted in the pop folk that brought Beth to us in the first place.

Title: Aforger
Review: Aforger has a mysterious, almost uncanny quality to it beyond the more obvious emotional exorcism.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: The group have harked back to the more memorable songs in their canon, but this can be interpreted as largely derivative in some quarters.

Title: Fields
Review: Fields is intriguing in a low-key way that grows with repeated listening and will make Gonzalez fans into Junip fans.

Title: Eagulls
Review: The band surely know their strengths and have developed their sound, but the individual songs suffer when stacked on top of each other.

Title: No Wow
Review: They've traded amped-up aggression for seething sexuality without losing any of their muscular bite.

Title: Ripples
Review: A deeply mixed return, then, and perhaps not advisable as your first entry point to his solo work. We all know that Ian Brown can make waves; today he has chosen to make Ripples.

Title: Miss Machine
Review: When a band like the Dillinger Escape Plan is able to duplicate the intensity of the previous album, yet at the same time create music that actually possesses (gasp!) commercial appeal, daring to cause an uproar among dyed-in-the-wool hardcore fans, you know they're on to something memorable.

Title: Pangs
Review: It makes for warm, complex but ultimately rewarding listening--the forboding swell of Songs Of The Marvels, the smartly rollicking The Angry Laughing God--and is the sound of muscles being gently but confidently flexed.

Title: When The World Comes Down
Review: The manicured hooks on their third album show off AAR's drive, but the songs also show how normal these Oklahoma boys are, as songwriters and humans.

Title: III
Review: Most songs here sound like capitulations to overworked clichés.

Title: Silver Bullets
Review: The Chills’ most compelling album yet.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: The songs may be dense and literary, but they're also immediately potent on a purely visceral level, striking a perfect balance that makes for what's perhaps the best album in a year already thick with great material.

Title: The End Is Near
Review: The End is Near employs much of fans found so pleasant about Bedhead, particularly the impressive build-up of two and three bar melodies.

Title: Wild Young Hearts
Review: The songs on Wild Young Hearts are well written, and the band is tight. They put me in the mind of Earl Greyhound, those three-piece sets that really work.

Title: Assume Form
Review: [James Blake's] most fully-realised album to date. ... Dizzyingly romantic.

Title: We are Beautiful, We Are Doomed
Review: The band is still firing on all cylinders, even when they downshift into the textured, minor key electronics-and-acoustic guitar lament of 'Heart Swells/Pacific Daylight Time' or the instrumental snippet 'Between an Erupting Earth and an Exploding Sky' (strangely reminiscent of Mogwai’s 'The Sun Smells Too Loud'), and no one can make bitterly self-aware misanthropy sound quite as exciting as this band does.

Title: Bad Contestant
Review: Everything Maltese conveys feels like a direct connection to the mind that bore it. It feels filterless, and with the music playing its part perfectly, we're all privy to the cool, calm and collected, swooning and crooning, world that Matt Maltese sees. And we're all the better for it.

Title: Battle For The Sun
Review: [The album’s final track is] a satisfying conclusion to the band’s best album since 2000’s Black Market Music.

Title: The Monitor
Review: The Monitor is a near perfect union of cacophony and immature angst.

Title: Moodring
Review: Infinitely bland. [Oct 2003, p.111]

Title: American Tunes
Review: Toussaint masterfully irons oout the kinks and the dissonances from the city's music. [Jul 2016, p.77]

Title: Positive Force
Review: When Marion makes more creative use of his varied, globe-spanning influences, however, Positive Force is every bit as compelling as its predecessor.... [yet]  far too many of the melodic hooks are merely adequate, and he doesn't pull any surprises.

Title: Shake the Shudder
Review: While not as refreshing as the previous album, it still feels on occasion as if multiple pop crossovers could theoretically beckon, especially the songs fronted by guest vocalists, including Molly Schnick of early 90s riot grrrls Raooul.

Title: Born to Sing: No Plan B
Review: The music is fabulous, a sublime pulse of Hammond organ, trombone and piano. [Nov 2012, p.100]

Title: The Old Magic
Review: This series of albums has strongly suggested that Lowe is able to make the music he wishes to make, without any pressure of expectation or commercial improvement. Sometimes the old ones are the best.

Title: Welcome Strangers
Review: One of the album's greatest strengths is how it incorporates these experimental choices into something very musical, although that does mean you do occasionally miss what's below the surface on first listen. Different things rise to the top the more time you invest in the record, so if it's not clicking with you immediately, trust that it eventually will.

Title: Todd Smith
Review: His 12th album is so girly it should be wearing pink tights and a tiara.

Title: Neck of the Woods
Review: Neck Of The Woods may not coax many new fans to the Pickups' newly appointed Camp Crystal Lake, but it gives those already there something dark and sinister to mull over.
There's no "Chasing Pavements"-style killer, but she has murdered the Cure's "Lovesong" using Heart FM-friendly jazz-lite as her weapon.

Title: Lost Channels
Review: Though some tracks lull more than thrill, that seems to be the goal. [May 2009, p.114]

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: Right Thoughts Right Words Right Action is a welcome return, fusing a crowd-pleasing sound with some of Franz Ferdinand's most interesting songwriting. Track for track, it may very well be the group's most satisfying album yet.

Title: Loyalty to Loyalty
Review: Almost in defiance of poor sales and cult following, CWK and their charming second album embody everything you hoped music might be.

Title: A Few Steps More
Review: Sounds a hell of a lot like Stereolab.

Title: amo
Review: This album captures an occasionally combustible but largely uncomfortable sound of a previously fearless and pioneering band caught in a crisis of confidence, overriding their own musical instincts to pursue an idealised version of themselves they picture in their own heads.

Title: Ekstasis
Review: A work of transcendent pop beauty that finally explains the idea of "ekstasis" by leaving the listener beside themselves, in a state of rapturous joy. [Apr 2012, p.91]

Title: Fear Inoculum
Review: It's an impressive feat of engineering, but one that anyone other than ardent fans will struggle to find a way into. [Oct 2019, p.114]

Title: This Is Gap Dream
Review: This Is Gap Dream ends up being too truthful, as there’s rarely any indication Fulvimar intended for this to reach an audience far beyond himself.

Title: Excellent Italian Greyhound
Review: Excellent Italian Greyhound is vintage Shellac: stark, razorous and blackly comic, lurching into whatever time signature happens to possess drummer Tod Trainer.

Title: Ferndorf
Review: The sounds that Volker Bertelmann creates with(in) a piano is astonishing. [Oct 2008, p.112]

Title: schlagenheim
Review: It does little to dispel any of the mystery that surrounds the band, even while proving them worthy of the praise they've received across the pond.

Title: Cool Planet
Review: Cool Planet sits perfectly in the balance of effortless craftsmanship and half-arsed laziness. Just where it should be.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: Somehow, despite his success, Flowers understands that good music isn’t about what you have, but what could have been, and although his wife must wonder who he’s singing about all the time, the rest of us can press our face against the windows of childhood car journeys, and dream.

Title: Just Enough Education to Perform
Review: The clean-cut Stereophonics are the Black Crowes you could take home to your mom, only with stronger songs and without the high school histrionics.

Title: Shelby Lynne
Review: Lynne's rawest, most intimately person album since I Am Shelby Lynne broke with her country roots 20 years ago. [Jun 2020, p.34]

Title: Apocalypse
Review: What comes up as a whole is this odd but endearing blend of plainspoken nonchalance and almost limitless musical eccentricity.

Title: Blame the Vain
Review: Not that much has changed sound-wise. [Jul 2005, p.114]

Title: The Decline of British Sea Power
Review: BSP's performance art antics and throwback posturing come with a distinct set of innovations and surprises, and The Decline of British Sea Power proves that BSP have the song-power to back up their bullshit.

Title: Orcorara 2010
Review: Exquisite acoustic compositions meet Crampton’s taste for dissonance and distortion. [Aug 2020, p.54]

Title: Real Animal
Review: Taken as a whole, Real Animal shows a man content with the life he has lived, even as the rest of us hope that his final statement is still some ways off.

Title: From the Very Depths
Review: The band's 14th studio album shows them clinging to relevancy with grim resolve, and occasionally hitting the mark.

Title: Khalifa
Review: It delves as far as it can without hitting government-name territory, and for that the true fans will embrace it. But how many times can you retell the same story?

Title: That Don't Make Me a Bad Guy
Review: While most of the songs are well written and Keith attacks each vocal performance with his immediately recognizable command and swagger, not all of his production choices work.

Title: I to Sky
Review: With the exception of the Joy Division influenced 'City', the final third of the album drops the ante somewhat. The idea, though, that this sophomore effort may be laying the foundations for something even mightier cannot be ignored.

Title: Side Pony
Review: While the arrangements are loaded with clever touches, the LP comes off like an exercise in technique, preventing Price from reaching the transcendent moments she's clearly capable of. [Mar 2016, p.76]

Title: Not To Disappear
Review: Experience may be a cruel messenger, but Daughter’s success comes not from pulling away, but from embracing that. In doing so, Not to Disappear comes out the other side, not beaten and lost but vibrant and alive.

Title: The Orbserver In The Star House
Review: Scratch dances merrily over the electronics, but the two parties rarely connect in a cohesive way.

Title: The Sister
Review: The Sister is Marissa Nadler looking down and realizing that she has recently written eight good songs.

Title: Someday, Buddy
Review: The slow-motion misery of I Want Love is a little too drenched in its own fragile despair, but the lazy, wilted quality of Bad Mistake is better; a tired, grunge-lite lollop, more Stephen Malkmus than all-out macabre.

Title: American Supreme
Review: This is audaciously modern in its textural absorption of outre sounds from the 21st-century dance underground. [Dec 2002, p.136]

Title: I Used To Be Pretty
Review: Rough-hewn thrills abound. [Jan 2019, p.21]

Title: Soft Airplane
Review: The result is an album that is often brilliant, sometimes breathtaking, and never dull.

Title: Hotel Shampoo
Review: Hotel Shampoo is terrific, neatly channeling all of Rhys's wonderful eccentricities into an intelligent pop record.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: Hip Hop Is Dead is a lot like Nas himself: impossible not to admire, but hard to love.

Title: In The Seams
Review: The problem lies with the unrelentingly downbeat music. [Dec 2014, p.96]

Title: Peer Amid
Review: Peer Amid is the ultimate soundtrack for fighting your way to enlightenment.

Title: Earthquake Glue
Review: Earthquake Glue meets any GBV album that isn't named Bee Thousand or Alien Lanes.

Title: Clay Class
Review: Understated, sloth-like and quick-witted all at once.

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: Though Moz's vocal range has narrowed with age, he still delivers brilliantly titled odes to depression and hanging out on his own.

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: It works, sometimes.

Title: Stone Temple Pilots
Review: Said new record is what one would expect: wholly similar to their first three records in that it’s got three possible hit singles, a useless Side B, and is proudly derivative of at least six other bands. They are amusingly impervious to trends. So long as you can get your head around the fact that it’s, y’know, Stone Temple Pilots, this, their self-titled sixth full-length, is far better than any pointless reunion album needs to be.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: Psychedelic, kaleidoscopic pop...  heady and brilliant.

Title: English Oceans
Review: They’ve created a complex and detailed world, and English Oceans adds more memorable characters to it.

Title: The Trials of Van Occupanther
Review: While The Trials of Van Occupanther may never be more than a cult favorite, those seeking to till peculiarly American musical soil will undoubtedly reap a rewarding and plentiful harvest.

Title: Slow Focus
Review: Unfortunately, it often veers dangerously close to a corny dystopian sci-fi movie soundtrack, which becomes a little less cute with each listen.

Title: My Wild West
Review: Producers Curt Schneider and Bill Reynolds from Band of Horses have allowed a space and subtlety that add integrity to Lissie’s lyrics.

Title: The New Year
Review: This is exquisitely made, moodily complicated stuff, and if it doesn’t fit into the current landscape, that’s more our problem than theirs.

Title: Common Existence
Review: Common Existence is largely an enjoyable record that gives as much attention to mood and melody as muscle and might.

Title: Fundamental
Review: Fundamental offers pleasure as rewarding as The Magic Mountain or Glenlivet 18--indulgences best enjoyed as you approach the half-century mark, when your imagination is keen to leisured elongations of familiar tropes or newly appreciative of exotic sumptuousness.

Title: Sidewalks
Review: For a record that veers between hit and miss, there is a certain amount of charm and vibrancy that keeps one coming back for more.

Title: Emotions and Math
Review: Margaret Glaspy’s first album is a fabulous miniature, clocking in at just 34 minutes, that gets better every time you listen to it.

Title: Bones
Review: Outside of “Flight” and “Breath Out” all of the good moments are quickly washed out by waves upon waves of utter slog.

Title: Transparent Things
Review: Stereolab had similar starting blocks--there's no reason why Fujiya & Miyagi shouldn't become as notable. [Jan 2007, p.110]

Title: Witching Hour
Review: Working with a major label has brought a new sheen to the Ladytronic wall of sound. [Oct 2005, p.94]

Title: Before I Self Destruct
Review: Before I Self Destruct is still a fantastic juggernaut of a 50 album if you exit early, and a very good one even if you don't.

Title: Rather Ripped
Review: This is their radio-rock record, and it's not a tribute, it's as close to the real thing as they've come since they actually had a chance at radio play back in the '90s.

Title: Love Kraft
Review: Even by SFA’s lofty standards, the production on Love Kraft is little short of incredible.

Title: Lateness of Dancers
Review: An album of warm colors and earthy textures, Lateness is an album for warm sweaters and hard ciders, backyard firepits and late-autumn barbecues.

Title: Desolation Sounds
Review: As Desolation Sounds progresses, so the mood becomes more considered and expansive. [May 2015, p.105]

Title: Up in Flames
Review: His tracks are vibrant and imaginative, calling on fuzzed-out guitar solos and summer-day vocals that recall a raft of solid shoegazers.

Title: Last Summer
Review: There's not much screaming on Last Summer. Like I'm Going Away, it's a basic, modest studio-rock record, the kind common in the '70s, with flavorful detours reminiscent of that era.

Title: Happiness
Review: While Happiness never gets up and rocks, it's solid from beginning to end.

Title: Chief
Review: Chief, like Church's other work, walks the line between hard Southern boogie and softie singer-songster sap, but with plenty of chug.

Title: Wanderer
Review: Understated, beautifully crafted and always emotionally involving, Wanderer shows an artist who has found strength in her convictions, and a new pace of life.

Title: Tape Two
Review: You'll soon feel how all those slight musical differentials hoist the group's collective spirit, and how courageously the music's depressive candor strengthens their will to be alive.

Title: District Line
Review: District Line is essentially the same furiously melodic pop Mould played way back when. [Feb 2008, p.98]

Title: Blood, Looms and Blooms
Review: She could drop the dodgy cover of ‘Norwegian Wood’ and probably should, but that misstep aside this record’s an engagingly oddball, enchantingly out-there piece of avant-pop that could, with just a little more exposure, be celebrated as one of 2008’s best leftfield albums.

Title: Prism
Review: Prism [is] a tighter, cleaner record than its predecessors--there are no extremes here, nothing that pushes the boundaries of either good taste or tackiness.

Title: Bestial Burden
Review: With her heavily processed voice floating through the feedback, it's the remarkably detailed cry of a soul on fire.

Title: Era Extrana
Review: Era Extrana radiates with enough passion to make life more than a little woozy. [Oct 2011, p.105]

Title: Repo
Review: Repo improves upon past work and manages to cram more songs with more interesting ideas into the same space as previous releases, while simultaneously becoming a little easier to aproach. [Spring 2009, p.64]

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: “How long will it take to break the plans that I never make?” It’s a question that was inevitably begged by those previous celebrations of low-rent outlaw glamour, and, in attempting to answer it, Suede may have made their best album.

Title: Innerland
Review: Layering blankets of synths and keyboards as well as underlays of programmed drums and effects around his evocative guitar lines, makes Innerland an immersive experience, rich with flowing gauzy grooves and elemental ambient balm.

Title: English Oceans
Review: The result is a mixed bag of muscular rockers ("Shit Shots Count") and cinematic, brooding ballads ("Pauline Hawkins"), proving that a little teamwork goes a long way.

Title: Kila Kila Kila
Review: This is music that is both lovely to hear and challenging to ascertain at the same time.

Title: Fire
Review: As good as "Danger! High Voltage" is, the rest of this album is simply not worth it.

Title: Hopelessness
Review: Good pop is often pliable, its message broad or ambiguous enough for listeners to flex it to their taste. Political pop can be like this without compromising its message, but most of Hopelessness has no interest in pliability. It regards its audience as either fervent believers in Anohni's cause or a pop mass in need of blunt polemic.

Title: The Terror
Review: The nine songs ooze out with floating bits of atmospherics and noise appearing and receding in the murk while hypnotizing listeners via insistent synth and drum loops. [May 2013, p.88]

Title: Gang Signs & Prayer
Review: If Skepta’s ‘Konnichiwa’ was grime’s breakthrough, Gang Signs & Prayer is its blockbuster--an all-encompassing ride through human experience that’ll stand tall for decades.

Title: Ruinism
Review: Though far less accessible than his previous material, Ruinism isn’t the clinical listen it could have turned into. Its performers are never spotlit and yet its textures never lack a human soul. It is the kind of album that tends to frustrate a fanbase while cementing its maker as an artist for that very willingness to alienate the faithful.
Taken all together, 29 is a staggering piece.

Title: Nude With Boots
Review: Sure, there's a little too much filler, but this is pleasingly radio-unfriendly fare. [Aug 2008, p.140]

Title: Requiem
Review: In short, though this is a completely new face to Goat, a deeper, richer exploration of their abilities, it’s not a complete departure.

Title: The Balcony
Review: Beneath their poppier melodies and anthemic choruses underlies the D.I.Y. garage-rock ethic that inspired their quick ascent, and it's this mixture that places them firmly between the pop charts and dingy rock club basements.

Title: Keepsake
Review: While Pilbeam's gorgeous, dreamy melodies remain her main strength, a longer running time give her space to play with different ideas. [Jul 2019, p.29]

Title: Public Domain: Songs from the Wild Land
Review: As always, Alvin's guitar work is wonderfully supple and emotive, and stands out as the centerpiece of his arrangements. But, even more gratifying, a decade after leaving the Blasters, in which his brother Phil handled the vocal duties, Alvin has finally found his voice as a singer.

Title: Wilderness of Mirrors
Review: English subjects his ghostly pastoral chorales and haunted organ tones to crashing interrogations of harmonic distortion, transforming old worlds of meditative calm into a new decaying landscape of soaring despair. [Sep 2014, p.91]

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: It's Prince, it's Eno, it's PiL, it's The Coasters and all at once. At times, that jars. At others... it's as exhilarating as a kiss. [Jul 2004, p.124]

Title: Herein Wild
Review: It might be subject to less scrutiny had it not followed Interstellar, but then again, it might not be subject to scrutiny at all, and simply filed away with any other competent and unexceptional dream-pop.

Title: The Sweet Escape
Review: Erratic. [Feb 2007, p.126]

Title: Run the Jewels 3
Review: So the blessing and the curse of Run the Jewels 3 is that it’s still a Run the Jewels album, a promise that every song is good, nothing is bad, and depending on your mood you’ll either bask in the lack of tempo changes, pulchritudinous song structures, and surprising hooks, or you’ll seek out a more colorful record.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: George’s luscious voice and Kurstin’s distinctive production and instrumentation (he also rocks it out on Lily Allen’s new record and has played with Sia, Beck, and The Flaming Lips) lift The Bird and the Bee toward the heavens. [Winter 2009]

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: The juvenile wordplays, ironic pop-culture references, and narratives about sad-sack folks undone by mundane, everyday minutia that are among the band's trademarks remain fully intact: The content of the songs on Sky Full of Holes is, by and large, as wry and idiosyncratic as their songs have ever been.

Title: Infra
Review: What Infra is, is perfectly pretty, atmospheric, rainy day music.

Title: Losing
Review: Even at that short running time, Losing’s 12 songs start to blur together toward the end, but the album’s many charms keep that from becoming a liability.

Title: Heaven
Review: Heaven is a record with the power to grab your heart, like an ex-lover you just can't shake off--no matter how many years you've been without them.

Title: Hello Hurricane
Review: More than a couple of the mid-tempo light rockers here lack teeth, some of them even lack gums. We’ve heard Switchfoot as weepy soundtrack peddlers before, but Switchfoot the rock band, it turns out, is pretty darn good.

Title: Rolling Papers 2
Review: A bloated and expensive version of the rap he’s always made but without that signature effortlessness.

Title: Shine
Review: Five albums in, Wale remains one of the more mercurial talents in rap, with SHINE serving as further evidence of his abilities as an MC and a reminder of his lyrical radiance.

Title: V
Review: As a whole, the albums works on a cohesion, transitioning from stronger, more powerful tracks (“Dynasti”, “Dean & Me”, and “All White Everything”) to the remaining eight cuts, which are breezy, quiet, and, sadly, quite boring, thanks to cheesier lyrics and lack of production effort.

Title: Universal Audio
Review: A surprisingly adept three-minute pop formula record. [#7]

Title: I Know You're Married But I've Got Feelings Too
Review: Wainwright's songs are tight, cohesive and show real emotion.

Title: Future Breeds
Review: The tension between the band's hooky ways and their need to break away from them is almost palpable on Future Breeds, but pop wins this tug-of-war on its standout tracks.

Title: Soviet Kitsch
Review: There's a wealth of great material here... all diminished, to various degrees, by genre affectations.

Title: Dedicated to Bobby Jameson
Review: Push past the weaponised irony and you’ll find Another Weekend and Feels Like Heaven are his most seductive melodies since breakthrough album Before Today.

Title: This Old Dog
Review: In all, This Old Dog is a logical continuation of DeMarco's musical explorations, but the maturation of his songwriting is what gives it gravitas.

Title: More
Review: One of the best things about Ms. C as an artist, especially considering her indie-ish background, is that she hasn't been afraid to embrace plastic pop as a vehicle for self-expression. More importantly, though, having found success within this genre , Vitamin C here takes chances instead of relying purely on formula.

Title: Beware
Review: This is pure non-homogenised, heart-on-sleeve, downright meaningful music, the sort of thing The Wombats cry themselves to sleep over on a nightly basis. For that alone it’s worth a tenner of anybody’s money.

Title: Moon Landing
Review: He does manage to out-Mumford and out-Sheeran his countrymen on the rustic single "Bonfire Heart" (ironically, co-written with super-pop penman Ryan Tedder). Whether you want to hear James Blunt plowing that field is a conversation between you and your god.

Title: The World Has Made Me The Man Of My Dreams
Review: Ultimately, The World Has Made Me the Man of My Dreams, with its irony, sincerity, seeming contradiction, and elliptical paradox, is the most expansive, complex record yet released by this always provocative artist.

Title: AQUÎ›RIA
Review: While AQUARIA is uniquely Asher’s and probably unlike anything else you’ll hear this year--a mix of heavy, grinding industrial beats and quick, nimble lyrics that whiz by like the view of the landscape from a train window--the truth buried at the bottom of the bass drop is that Asher himself isn’t yet magnetic enough to make his own material shine.

Title: Future Breeds
Review: The songs blend together in a rather blatant way, and that really doesn't do the album's coherency any favors; despite their best efforts, Hot Hot Heat still hasn't crafted an "album" yet, only a decent collection of songs. That said, the songs here are built for live-show sing-alongs and are entirely easy to digest.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Upon repeat listens, there's not one point of Halcyon Digest that feels like it was overly thought out.

Title: Fate
Review: The Philadelphia group's fifth full-length release has a musical richness and depth of songwriting that weren't fully present on Dr. Dog's somewhat less-focused earlier music, though there were hints on "Easy Beat" in 2005 and "We All Belong" in 2007.

Title: Strange Clouds
Review: Strange Clouds is ultimately too weighed down by joy-killing self-importance to match [his] debut's hit ratio.

Title: About The Light
Review: About the Light is Mason at his most confident.

Title: Maze of Woods
Review: Maze Of Woods occupies a different plain, a more embryonic one that finds its stand out moments in a subtler way.

Title: Slowness
Review: While there are bands who share common ground with Outfit--These New Puritans, Hot Chip, Junior Boys--the appealing niche they’re easing into bodes very well for album three.

Title: Hallelujah Anyhow
Review: Hallelujah Anyhow may have been recorded swiftly, but the abandonment is still exquisitely detailed, as every listen to "Domino" reveal further nuance beneath the swagger. [Oct 2017, p.22]

Title: Laugh Now, Cry Later
Review: Unlike his early classics, Laugh Now stumbles occasionally and fails to keep the momentum going through the whole fourth quarter.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: If that presentation doesn't always hit the mark, the sentiment behind it often does, and the album never completely derails.

Title: Brain Thrust Mastery
Review: Brain Thrust Mastery contains a lot more variety than its predecessor, which, although enjoyable, blended together at times.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: Another extraordinary Decemberists album.

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: These half-arsed stabs at nu-AOR end up pleasing no one, least of all the band itself.

Title: Godfather II
Review: Godfather II isn't bad, but coming after a career highlight, it's quite disappointing.

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: RTRWRA neatly combines those familiar chantable choruses, punchy guitars, pleasant harmonies and simple, clever lyricism--all in all, a great vehicle for that smooth, too cool croon of singer Alex Kapranos.

Title: Bitter Rivals
Review: While "24" might be the best song Sleigh Bells have penned to date.... The rest of the album doesn't fare so well, and like the proverbial Potemkin village, its bravado is illusory, its songs precarious, one-dimensional façades that sag under anything more than a passing listen.

Title: Barbara
Review: We Are Scientists know how to create instantly catchy tunes, unfortunately they've yet to master making them stick in the memory bank.

Title: â€
Review: With loads of melodrama and not a moment of subtlety, Justice define the new-jacques swing.

Title: You Are Not Alone
Review: Staples isn't just a survivor. She's a great singer who is best when she gets to press onward.

Title: Motion to Rejoin
Review: The farther they wander, the more magnetic they become.

Title: The Life of Pablo
Review: The Life of Pablo has a lot going for it, but sometimes, even with all the best intentions, you can mess up a good thing just by virtue of being yourself.

Title: Pokey LaFarge
Review: Pokey will invite you to step away from the modern, more complex times and immerse yourself in a period of music from the mid western USA which formed the heart and soul of the country. It is a trip well worth it.

Title: Alice
Review: Alice is a major step forward for Meatbodies and one of the better garage punk/heavy metal/psychedelic rock albums anyone is likely to hear in 2017.

Title: Boxer
Review: Matt Berninger's murmuring, stream-of-conscious narratives are delivered with convincing melodrama, with few clunkers. [26 May 2007]

Title: Warrior
Review: Warrior, a moderate improvement of her disappointing debut Animal. [Jan 2013, p.106]

Title: I Remember
Review: The uncluttered production always feels reasonably on-trend, but too often these songs just aren’t catchy or inventive enough to be truly memorable. The result is another pretty decent album that doesn’t quite ignite.

Title: Balf Quarry
Review: It hits just as furiously and sloppily as all the old Markers standards, no matter its label, run time, or production quality.

Title: One Second of Love
Review: In the end, One Second of Love is enjoyable but slight: its stronger moments render the weaker ones particularly forgettable.

Title: X (No Absolutes)
Review: Prong have outdone themselves here, proving that they are still a force to be reckoned with and, ultimately, respected.

Title: Heaven
Review: Heaven is a testament to The Walkmen's triumph.

Title: Loner
Review: Loner is the sound of her undoubted talent turned feral. It's a wonderful, rollicking beast. [Jun 2018, p.94]

Title: Beautiful Rewind
Review: On Beautiful Rewind, Hebden displays the possibilities and complexities within the music itself.

Title: The Real New Fall LP (Formerly Country on the Click)
Review: as brittle, volatile and consistently riveting as any band out there, and even though no one could possibly take Smith seriously anymore, it insinuates that there's still enough justification here to warrant following The Fall's devious discography into one more decade.

Title: Absent Friends
Review: Patchy at best.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: Most of The Crane Wife consists of rehashes of Decemberists staples and by-the-books, cookie-cutter indie pop that runs the gamut between pleasant enough ("O, Valencia!") and barely tolerable ("Summersong").

Title: Steal Your Face
Review: In the fury of these cool-crushing rushes Mi Ami are exhilarating, roaring forwards, chasing risk like Can tied to the back of a pick-up truck and dragged across the surface of the sun.

Title: Ruff Draft
Review: Ruff Draft still feels like a limited-edition collectors-only curiosity.

Title: Take Fountain
Review: The band's return to the name might initially smack of a desperate reunion, but it's more than just symbolic: With Take Fountain, The Wedding Present reclaims its place as a thoroughly convincing vessel for pop heartache and joy.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: It's certainly a promising debut, just one hampered by a songwriting scope that strips it of its own vitality rather than informing it.

Title: Zeitgeist
Review: Zeitgeist fails to capture not just the spirit of the cultural times, but of the true Smashing Pumpkins. [Summer 2007, p.84]

Title: Diaspora
Review: Welcoming in the wider world as Goldlink's laid-back delivery flows with deceptive ease over Joke Ting's sinuous, tropical R&B, the Afrobeats-like bounce of Zulu Screams and Yard's captivating Caribbean riddim. [Aug 2019, p.111]

Title: Volume 1
Review: [A] sumptuous, immensely pleasurable throwback album. [May 2017, p.25]

Title: I Hate Music
Review: Rather than let heartbreak render the band static and immobile, Superchunk has thankfully turned to their faithful creative outlet of music once again, and the memories and spirit of their lost friends will resolutely live on in the stirring songs they have written to honour them.

Title: Brainwashed
Review: Stacks up remarkably well against the rest of his oeuvre. [22 Nov 2002, p.76]

Title: Magic Hour
Review: On this tight, 10-song reunion (minus singer-keyboardist Vivian Trimble), vocals still waver charmingly off-key, grooves still conjure a Nineties Lower East Side rent party.

Title: The Practice of Love
Review: While the two records share an airy, ethereal DNA, The Practice of Love is a far more palatable, more replayable affair – it just doesn’t seem to hit as hard as its sister, but very few albums do.

Title: Mark Kozelek
Review: Mark Kozelek is by no means a masterwork, nor is it the overwrought disaster it threatened to be, but instead another collection of songs from someone who just cannot stop writing, cannot stop releasing and, more often than not, hits the emotional marks he aims at, in however scattershot a way.

Title: Fading Lines
Review: Enticing, if inconsistent, this seems to be an album that de Graaf had dreamed of making, building on the pretty, prosaic folk-pop of her self-titled EP in 2013.

Title: Third
Review: That it’s Portishead’s best album yet is little short of miraculous.

Title: There's a Riot Going On
Review: There’s a Riot Going On’s theory doesn’t quite match up to its execution, and its parts are greater than the whole. So, is it more beautiful, or is it more boring? The problem is that it’s often too difficult to tell the difference.

Title: Widowspeak
Review: Their excellent debut album is a neat mix of somnambulant balladry and ragged high drama. [Oct 2011, p.105]

Title: Changes
Review: With no trace of the irony or detachment that's prevalent in so much modern music, Bradley and his band come up with yet another album that sounds like it was dug up by some reissue label specializing in obscure '60s and '70s soul.

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: On Ivy Tripp, Crutchfield creeps further into adulthood, expanding both her outlook and sound without losing the intimacy that endeared her to us in the first place.

Title: Coup De Grace
Review: Coup De Grace is Kane’s best work to date: punchy, cohesive and lots of fun.

Title: Brett Anderson
Review: On his lonesome Anderson is oppressively unimaginative.

Title: The Hungry Saw
Review: Powered by rattling drums, simmering organ, and Stuart Staples' resonant baritone, the first half of Tindersticks' latest is a can't-miss proposition....Too bad the disc's second half descends into a morass of half-finished, melancholic curios that mostly go nowhere lowly.

Title: Yanqui U.X.O.
Review: Stripped of some of Godspeed's hallmarks, including its creepy spoken-word samples and propensity for building to an overbearingly climactic full-on pummel, the disc's power lies more in its subdued shading and slow, methodical builds.

Title: Everything Was Beautiful, and Nothing Hurt
Review: Oddly enough, the early '90s feel which permeates the record, sounds fresh as a daisy in 2018. It would have been easy for Moby to get all punk rock and bombastic about the subject matter, but instead we get lush, mid-tempo trip hop. Kudos, sir.

Title: The Coast Is Never Clear
Review: A playful retro-pop event full of shifting moods. [Nov 2001, p.77]

Title: Aviary
Review: Aviary ultimately has the effect of looking through a new friend’s bookshelf, accessing the wild particularities of their mind.

Title: Realism
Review: By far his most listenable and fully realized work since 1999’s mammoth 69 Love Songs, Realism feels slight because it is. It’s hard to hear someone so adept with a poison pen preen instead of brood, but it’s also rewarding.

Title: In Ghost Colours
Review: Ghost Colours sounds like Depeche Mode on Lorazepam--dramatic, well enunciated and full of arpeggiated synthy goodness.

Title: Genesis
Review: [Domo Genesis] still talks about weed and weirdness, and sometimes with a star-studded guest list, as the killer "Go (Gas)" features Wiz Khalifa, Juicy J, and Tyler, The Creator. Mac Miller figures into the great "Coming Back", but the bits about Domo's family, his autistic brother, and his own search for self make this a meatier album than expected.

Title: Heart On
Review: The third album of the formula, the lovely-titled Heart On, shows that the Eagles of Death Metal have reached their limits, but not without a noble effort to keep on rockin’.

Title: Advance Base Battery Life
Review: Some of the more irregular numbers scream “demo” between their whisperings--think very early Arab Strap, midi beats in place of the crass Scottish semen puns--but overall it’s a solid little barometer, one or two cues offering insight into Casiotone’s current organic direction.

Title: Afterparty Babies
Review: His latest outing, Afterparty Babies, doesn't derail that path, but it struggles to stay on course.

Title: Paralytic Stalks
Review: It's more likely that Paralytic Stalks won't win Kevin Barnes any new fans, and may actually drive away some of his longtime followers.

Title: The Life of the World to Come
Review: The Goats have noble intentions, but their Biblicval tunes call to mind 7-11 praise music. [Fall 2009, p.59]

Title: Between Waves
Review: This incarnation of The Album Leaf asserts the resilience that has always held up their sentimental exterior.

Title: Life In Cartoon Motion
Review: "Life in Cartoon Motion" is like Scissor Sisters-lite: Retro disco with heavy doses of rollicking piano and funk. [31 Mar 2007]

Title: An Awesome Wave
Review: Young, yet somehow void of naivety. Vibrant, yet artistically matured.

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: Because there's an awkward squirm at Girls' core, a deviant devolution of classic mores, and that makes Holy Ghost something of a maladroit masterpiece.

Title: Now
Review: When Maxwell sings songs cultivated to melt a girl's heart ("Silently"), it sounds more like grand, fervent gospel than a cheap, fevered move.

Title: Contra
Review: Vampire Weekend's penchant for throwing an occasional obscure reference into their work doesn't change the fact that Contra is an obvious early contender for one of 2010's best.

Title: International
Review: International is brilliantly pop in substance and spirit.

Title: Playgroup
Review: His most impressive sound collage yet.

Title: The New Romance
Review: Pretty Girls Make Graves fall slightly short of their ambitions and capabilities, producing songs that are good, even very good, but less than what they’ve proved themselves to be capable of.

Title: Don't Weigh Down the Light
Review: Don’t Weigh Down The Light certainly rewards repeated listening.

Title: Fear
Review: The songs on Fear will stick in your memory too, especially ass-kicking, evil rockabilly numbers like “Lay Down in Bedlam” and “Devil Eyes”.

Title: The Lion's Roar
Review: There's a nourishing warmth in their bittersweet laments.

Title: Playing with Fire
Review: His constipated, region-nonspecific flow overwhelms even the most flamboyant beats. [Jan 2007, p.119]

Title: Blood Money
Review: Instead of the poppy makeover many anticipated, the Mobb's seventh album is a curious blend of gunz-money anthems, G-Unit-ized sex romps, and visions of the great beyond.

Title: The Contino Sessions
Review: The Contino Sessions is definitely a step in the right direction for the group in terms of continuity and development of their sound, but their are still a few hiccups that they need to work out.

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: Jack White missed, but in the best possible way. As weak as this record is, its extremely entertaining.

Title: Napalm
Review: Napalm is remarkably focused, not forsaking the established Xzibit sound but neither rehashing it.

Title: The Hex
Review: Altogether, The Hex is a complicated record of a period fraught with loss and psychic struggle for Swift, and its beautiful, twisted lyricism and memorably stylized sound rise to the occasion.

Title: Dead Zone Boys
Review: I'm all for musicians not taking themselves too seriously, but with such audacious, irreverent, and yet captivating material populating the bulk of the album, it is a supreme letdown to finish on such strangely muddled notes. Still, Dead Zone Boys is worth some serious attention.

Title: Pale Green Ghosts
Review: The production has a pristine, streamlined quality, with Grant’s vocals high in the mix, so the album’s blend of orchestral and squelchy electronic arrangements mirrors the clarity and grace with which he delivers his crude, self-lacerating ballads.

Title: Changing Tune
Review: Its bluster and sheen ends up burying the barbed poetry of frontman Mike Duce.

Title: Seven Horses for Seven Kings
Review: A masterpiece of sound design, that's no backhanded compliment. This album is the sort of sound design record that more sound artists should aspire to make.

Title: Communion
Review: Iif you’re looking for some pop perfection, this album displays it in droves.... However, things take a huge tumble when Years & Years try not to stick to their confessional-electronic niche.

Title: The Plain Where The Palace Stood
Review: This is classic David Grubbs--which is to say a joy, but also that it's unbashedly disparate. [Apr 2013, p.50]

Title: Leave Home
Review: A wonderful grab-bag of anomalous sounds that pilfers magpie-like from genre after genre as it charts its 41-minute course.

Title: Half Free
Review: With Half Free, Remy has made a brilliant, accessible, edgy pop record without compromising her ideals one iota--and hopefully has surreptitiously brought her into a wider light.

Title: That's Why God Made the Radio
Review: That's Why God Made the Radio isn't a bad album. It's just not the album everyone wanted.

Title: Barking
Review: While each track sounds different to the one that preceded it, they all manage to fit together as a coherent whole. Barking is still a credible effort and a pleasant listen, but it is also unremarkable and, had it been released by artists whose fame didn't precede them, it probably would not have made any waves.

Title: Release Therapy
Review: The anger is a new look for him, as is the role of political pundit or chronicler of social ills. And ultimately, Ludacris still sounds best on tracks like the NC-17 "Woozy." [Oct 2006, p.99]

Title: Season Sun
Review: Gulp suffers from the side-project lack of focus, but they have the capabilities to push their music to the edge on which they obviously live.

Title: Themes for Television
Review: There are moments of abject terror and suspense that perfectly sum up the show, that are flawlessly executed and deliver such a rush that you are swept along with them, and only after do you question what just happened. Like all the best things in life, this album is not what it initially seems.

Title: Heaven
Review: No One Ever Sleeps, even with harmonies from Robin Pecknold, feels not magical, but hollow and sluggish. At the rockier end, Heartbreaker adds Arcade Fire urgency and may score alt-radio love. The rest, however, is lukewarm. [Jul 2012, p.83]

Title: Because the Internet
Review: Because The Internet stands on its own musically. The project undoubtedly stands much taller when put in context of all the additional material released in order to create something bigger. [Dec 2013/Jan 2014, p.89]

Title: Possible Dust Clouds
Review: Whilst ultimately Possible Dust Clouds may fall short of being another truly seminal Kristin Hersh long-player--which will always be hard given the stiff self-competition of her own bounteous back catalogue--the renewed sense of dynamism, diversity and drive within confirms that there is still plenty of propulsive creative fuel left in the tank.

Title: The Underside of Power
Review: There’s a confrontational energy to The Underside of Power that encourages conversation, and not just rapturous abandon. It’s an unorthodox approach that immediately distinguishes them.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: The Century of Self
Review: Their sixth album enlists Michael Bay levels of volume and grandeur in the service of alarmingly generic, hookless power ballads and plodding prog etudes.

Title: Coexist
Review: Coexist is far from a bad effort. Gentle sophisticates that the XX are, however, it's hardly surprising that the cutting edge got a little too sharp.

Title: More Parts per Million
Review: They've still managed to convert their technological shortcomings into some fuzzed-out, genuinely energised rocking. [Jul 2003, p.113]

Title: Love Kraft
Review: A utopian epic, a sweeping musical argument for love in the time of Fallujah.

Title: Sorcerer
Review: As a follow-up to the massive, hypnotizing Overseas, Sorcerer is a concise distillation of Tonstartssbandht’s refreshing vision, a crystal ball portraying their intimate friendship, their cosmic noodling echoing deep into the nethersphere.

Title: Seeds
Review: This very quick, very pretty album is a good new look for TV on the Radio, and longtime fans will also feel at home with Seeds.

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: Mostly White sounds like a scrappy, abstract-leaning '80s-style battle rhymer who probably didn't win a lot of battles. Elsewhere, experimental detours dead-end: "Everything You've Ever Learned" feels like aimless twaddle with newly-unboxed digital toys. But at its best, the spirit of freaky free-play is thrilling and refreshing, a worthy end unto itself.

Title: Coral Fang
Review: The Distillers subtract a little of Joan Jett's poppy tunefulness and add (even) more aggressive vocals. If that sounds good to you, you'll at least like this album.

Title: Melt
Review: A white hot album that will leave listeners soaking up every note.

Title: Stay Trippy
Review: While the sense of humor that separates him from someone like Gucci Mane emerges at times, the brief grins are not quite enough to distract from the relentless, repetitive tropes that have come to define Juicy’s (and the rest of the rap game’s) lyrics over the past few years.

Title: Surfing the Void
Review: While still somewhat leaning on their flair for creating spacey cosmic hooks, Klaxons are taking a robust step forward, allowing themselves the chance to careen a bit without running entirely off the rails.

Title: The Color Before the Sun
Review: A degree of delicacy colors album number eight. [No. 125, p.55]

Title: MGMT
Review: They're doubling down on that sound [mad-hatter psychedelic sprawl of 2010's winkingly titled Congratulations] for Album Three, pushing their love of acid-tinged bubblegum right out the back door of the booby hatch, in a good way.

Title: Mothertongue
Review: Mothertongue oscillates between the comfort/terror of singularities and excitement/terror of potentialities, but the possibilities this duality affords for Muhly’s future work are frankly exhilarating.

Title: Memphis
Review: All that really matters for the moment is that their debut album is an unqualified success, a concise and perfectly-presented collection of first-class pop music.

Title: Supermodel
Review: Working on an epic, operatic canvas, Foster and his bandmates hide the spinach of existential angst into sweetly binge-worthy dance pop.

Title: Give My Love To London
Review: This album underlines she's more than a mere rock'n'roll totem. [Oct 2014, p.91]

Title: Working Out
Review: Arthur Beatrice running their race slow and steady has resulted in an album full of sophisticated pop.

Title: If All I Was Was Black
Review: One of the great successes of If All I Was is that it has the same levity as the anthems of the civil rights era.

Title: Summer of the Shark
Review: An uneven mish-mash of musical ideas that is only occasionally thrilling.

Title: Sleeping with Ghosts
Review: Ultimately, the anthems are as generic as they are hooky. [May 2003, p.123]

Title: Postcards From a Young Man
Review: Strings, gospel choirs, outeros inspired by Queen--the Manics' 10th album cranks up the drama, but in their hands grandiose needn't be a dirty word. [Oct 2010, p.94]

Title: Down 2 Earth
Review: The sound necessarily lacks the precision and propulsion of, say, house or grime instrumentals, and since nothing forces the listener to pay attention or move, Down 2 Earth disappears as it reveals itself.

Title: Eton Alive
Review: It's a unique kind of unhappy listening, too toxic on the universal scale to be bled out. But it leaves you galvanised, purged and recharged for the unending war against mediocrity. [Mar 2019, p.90]

Title: Replicant Moods
Review: Pharaohs succeed principally because they don't feel the weight of all those influences bearing down upon them.

Title: Cansei de Ser Sexy
Review: They're not the kind of band that ages well... [but] one hot summer is all they need. [Aug 2006, p.107]

Title: Introducing Karl Blau
Review: The most impressive thing about Introducing Karl Blau is how easily it could find itself slotted in the second-hand racks between Charlie Rich or Glen Campbell.

Title: Ã·
Review: A batteries-fully-charged assault on the pop charts from a performer skilled in musical osmosis.

Title: Biophilia
Review: Educational and emotional in a uniquely approachable way, these songs are a lovely part of a bigger picture.

Title: I Thought The Future Would Be Cooler
Review: The tracks themselves work if you can get past the contrast. That might even be what makes you love it rather than hate it. The problem is that if you’re going to have a deep concept behind your pop tracks then it really needs to be stronger or more current than something that has gone before.

Title: Not Music
Review: Not Music presents more of their signature future-retro pop exotica. [Dec. 2010, p. 114]

Title: Living Fields
Review: Portico still holds appeal for ambient music fans and those who embrace the fringe, along with Portico Quartet regulars who might find this trio's temperament a bit different, but the musical textures will be familiar.

Title: Sound the Alarm
Review: Saves the Day have given their fans nothing exciting, innovative, or new.

Title: Late Night Feelings
Review: Ronson’s ability to tap into each artist’s strengths and dig out their particular prowess allows each voice to shine through and own each individual track. This is what elevates the record to a guaranteed award winner and a truly empowering listen.

Title: A Woman A Man Walked By
Review: Although it's as uncentred as 2004's "Uh Huh Her," this album broadcasts confidence rather than confusion.

Title: Next Thing
Review: On an album that, from a musical perspective, seems incongruously loaded with self-doubt ("I'm 20, washed up already," "I don't know what I'm cut out for") the material is consistently hooky, endearing, elegant, and uncommonly candid.

Title: For My Crimes
Review: Long time fans of Nadler’s work won’t be disappointed, but overall For My Crimes feels like a bit of a missed opportunity. She may sing about throwing keys, but the reality is this album won’t be taking anyone’s eye out anytime soon.

Title: Every Country's Sun
Review: Every Country’s Sun feels honed, and passages of ponderous string-picking now flow serenely into the bursts of noise (1,000 Foot Face, Old Poisons) that make them such an imposing force live.

Title: Life, Death, Love and Freedom
Review: Though he may be contemplating mortality, Mellencamp, with his weathered snarl, still sounds remarkably alive.

Title: Original Colors
Review: The duo continues to tighten up the rhythmic oddities that initially defined them, cleaning up those frayed handmade edges just a hint more. [Oct 2011, p.100]

Title: White Pony
Review: Massive in pretension, slightly too long and gothic, but when all the pieces fit, you can't deny its unstoppable power.

Title: Awake Is the New Sleep
Review: Like a washed-up athlete, Lee's stuck reliving his glory years.

Title: Earth Suck
Review: They’re up to the challenge of taking their colossal metal sound to the next level by making it even heavier. They’re up to the challenge of crafting even more memorable songs.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: A compact, nine-song, 32-minute album that suggests an artist just hitting her stride, Li's new album seems to have pinpointed the locus of power in her voice.

Title: Conduit
Review: [The album] is their best in years, hitting upon just the right combination of melody, thrash, and hooks.

Title: Gliss Riffer
Review: At his finest, most expansive moments, Deacon renders this dilemma beside the point, but on Gliss Riffer, it's hard to avoid it; the battle between song and arrangement is staged in too small of an arena.

Title: The New Abnormal
Review: Abnormal offers something even better, possibly, than reckless youth: rock stars finally old enough to truly miss those good old days — and wise enough now, too, to give us the soundtrack these strange new times deserve.

Title: By The Throat
Review: The result is easily one of the more intriguing and overlooked releases of 2009, and an infinitely disturbing meld of visceral semblance and quiet complexity.

Title: Mad Season
Review: There's nothing lasting or substantive about the 12 tracks (plus one hidden one) that make up Mad Season.

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: With the release of this new album, There Is Love In You, he's shown his versatility in dancefloor culture while remaining true to his own soundscapes. The result of this new venture may be the most satisfying Four Tet experience since 2003's release of "Rounds."

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: It suffers from a lack of identity.

Title: Abyss
Review: Abyss weighs unnecessarily heavy at times--the obvious premise and barely-there smack drum of “Simple Death” doesn’t hold up against the other songs’ more nuanced examinations of the macabre subjects--but Wolfe makes a convincing case to follow her into the underworld.

Title: Keeping Up Appearances
Review: Patrick is found confronting familiar ideas of inner contentment alongside upbeat surface shine on this bittersweet work - full of charm and integrity

Title: Old Money
Review: Old Money is so far-reaching, it will likely piss off some of his fans while making others nearly swoon with its unwieldy rockist excesses. As for winning new fans to his cause? You bet.

Title: Creatures
Review: It's the type of album that shifts with every listen, making you discover unknown corners of certain songs, with nary a lowlight or highlight in sight.

Title: Dodge and Burn
Review: What makes Dodge and Burn such a terrific and complete listen is how much ground it effectively covers and how furiously it does so.

Title: Labyrinthes
Review: Nothing here quite matches the effusive, quirky 'Montreal -40C' from 2006’s Trompe-l’oeil, but 'Luna' sounds like Animal Collective gone mainstream and 'Dragon de Glace' sambas with Air--both fine rues to traverse, oui?

Title: For Emma, Forever Ago
Review: Bon Iver defiantly makes a small-scale statement on For Emma, Forever Ago, so much that if you don’t concentrate, you’ll pass this over.

Title: Animal Companionship
Review: Animal Companionship is a more sombre affair than it initially sounds as Ashworth uses animal love as a lens through which to dissect heartbreak and loss, broken lives and creeping morality. [Nov 2018, p.23]

Title: How Big How Blue How Beautiful
Review: Overflowing with stately songwriting and lyrical craftsmanship, How Big, How Blue, How Beautiful makes for a restrained but joyful return, and a collection that will last long after Welch’s broken bones are mended.

Title: Simple Plan
Review: There are some decent pop moments: 'When I'm Gone' is a seize-the-day anthem with a cathartic refrain. But most songs, like the angry barnburner 'The End,' are barely distinguishable from a dozen or so other Warped Tour bands.

Title: Murmurations
Review: But, too often, tracks such as We Go and Defender merely taxi along the dancefloor runway rather than take off and soar. [Jul 2018, p.116]

Title: Nili Hadida
Review: At times, she sounds mawkish or uncertain, and when the introspection becomes gloomily self-absorbed, some tunes are too slight to save the day. At best, though, this is soft, quietly determined pop.

Title: A Fool to Care
Review: These 12 songs map out a concise history of American soul, with a heavy dose of New Orleans strut.

Title: Torres
Review: It’s wrought with haunting, high-stakes emotions, but the strength of Scott’s voice means it never feels melodramatic or plainly vulnerable.

Title: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
Review: Such is the depth and quality of Turner's songwriting, it plays like a best of.

Title: Getting Closer
Review: As nice and welcoming as Getting Closer is, it'll never challenge you.

Title: Play Music
Review: Thieves Like Us look and sound like three yuppies trying out the music lark after being laid off by an investment banking firm.

Title: The Birds of Satan
Review: Taylor Hawkins indulges his '70s hard rock fantasy. [Jun 2014, p.98]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: Lazaretto will likely have little impact on his legacy one way or the other, but it’s a solid addition to his catalogue.

Title: American Kid
Review: American Kid is a triumph of songwriting and expressive singing.

Title: Seven's Travels
Review: Though leavened with self-deprecation and lacerating wit, Slug's unsparing self-analysis can feel a little solipsistic and oppressive, particularly over the course of the album's 70-minute run time.

Title: Dear Miss Lonelyhearts
Review: As a whole, it feels slightly temporary and detached, largely thanks to its uneven pacing and experimental streak.

Title: Sisterworld
Review: Liars successfully created a stimulating, challenging, and disturbing record and while it may click immediately for some, don’t get frustrated if you find yourself lost in the woods.

Title: Keepsake
Review: The album’s snappy 10 track run-list positively invites further plays, perpetuating this desire to keep the cycle going.

Title: Post-War
Review: It's a rare thing to find an album that is a real, unexpected pleasure to listen to all the way through.

Title: Townes
Review: Earle believes this is one of his best albums; he's not wrong. [Jun 2009, p.132]

Title: Prisoner of Conscious
Review: For all of its powerful lyricism, Prisoner Of Conscious is not a particularly dynamic listen.

Title: False Alarm
Review: Two Door Cinema Club have learnt how to harness their mainstream power while taking creative risks. They pay off almost every time.

Title: OH (Ohio)
Review: Consider OH the "most Lambchop" of Lambchop releases, as it swings through almost every tone in the band's history of influence-collisions, arriving at a soul of its own.

Title: Just Like The Fambly Cat
Review: Everything now seems as worn out and used up as Lytle's subjects, along with the imagery that brings them to life. [Jun 2006, p.108]

Title: Atlas
