Title: Empire
Review: For the most part Empire is every bit as powerful as its title suggests. [Oct 2006, p.96]

Title: Josephine
Review: With the title character appearing in several songs amid frequent descriptions of desert landscape, Josephine sounds like a concept album, at times tedious or academic....The Co. redeem these songs by creating beautiful scenery for Molina’s long, hard drive.

Title: Wavvves
Review: There’s an energy coursing through this, and records like this, that is undeniable....But there’s also your standard fare. Several of the songs sound the same. There are a couple of atmospheric tunes that add no atmosphere.

Title: Get Awkward
Review: Now they’re back, back, back (repetition absolutely necessary) with a second dose of barely-pubesced raucousness and, a mere two spins down the line, DiS is seriously reconsidering the prospect of having children, like, ever.

Title: Broken Lines
Review: It’s nothing revolutionary, but it’s nevertheless a formidable collection of songs by a formidable gathering of musicians.

Title: The Disco's of Imhotep
Review: Sweaty and ecstatic, elevated and pure, The Disco’s of Imhotep weaves quite the spell. This might be the most accessible Hieroglyphic Being album to date, but Jamal Moss remains out there on his own.

Title: How I Learned to Write Backwards
Review: The Aislers don't always hit their mark, perhaps because the disparate interests at work also contribute to some unengaging instrumental, noise and nearly spoken word pieces. [Apr 2003, p.103]

Title: Keep Your Eyes Ahead
Review: On their latest release since 2004's "Love and Distance," they seem to have figured out that it might be more effective to highlight the subtlety and grace of writing and arranging. [Winter 2008, p.96]

Title: Earth to the Dandy Warhols
Review: Earth To The Dandy Warhols finds the band back in track in all the best ways. [Fall 2008, p.80]

Title: The Argument
Review: This is really a leap forward.

Title: Hell: The Sequel
Review: On a major label debut, there is very little room to mess around and get experimental, but that's precisely what he's done. It's not a great effort from either end of the duo, and it frankly leaves one wondering what could have been for such a promising pair.

Title: Crave
Review: A triumphant return for longtime fans and a winning introduction for newcomers, Crave shows Kiesza has only gotten better at reinventing the idealism and big emotions of a bygone era for another generation.

Title: Jewellery
Review: Jewellery is an extraordinary introduction to a unique talent. [Mar 2009, p.101]

Title: Blissfucker
Review: Too many shards of ideas are shoved into the long songs, and Fickeisen’s flash sometimes borders on showmanship, a glaring incongruity for a spartan outfit like Trap Them.

Title: Bitte Orca
Review: Their seventh album remembers to add tunes, and is thus less baffling than before.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die II
Review: In the future, Ghost should do more of that heavy lifting, taking a cue from producer Adrian Younge, who provides his signature analogue flavour to sumptuous effect throughout.

Title: Heavy Mood
Review: The hobnailed thud and electronic clatter of Youth and Love riot force the seriousness but when they hit their exuberant stride, they pull on legwarmers and dance the night and cold away. [Dec 2012, p.88]

Title: De-Loused in the Comatorium
Review: The songs explode with creativity, fusing jazz riffs, tribal rhythms, hardcore bursts of noise, and addictive rock hooks into one of the most compelling discs of the year. [18 July 2003, p.73]

Title: Return To Annihilation
Review: While it’s certain that catastrophe is written all over Locrian’s high-concept Return to Annihilation, the experience is a step removed from the anxiety of early post-rock: here the listener trudges through the burnt-out husk of a world, its structures transfigured, estranged from their original forms.

Title: Lala Belu
Review: Tizita, like Lala Belu as a whole, feels like both a victory lap and the beginning of something new. It will be exciting to see what, at 71 years young, Mergia does next.

Title: Bloodiest
Review: If there's a downside to the rumbly growl emerging from the twisted minds of Chicago's Bloodiest, it's the sextet's unwillingness to push tempos beyond a snarling, hammer-slams-nail, mid-paced plod. However, when a gold-standard knuckle-dusting that’s part Swans churn, part Neurosis’ tribal stomp with Unsane’s propulsive groove is employed, does a lack of temporal variety matter? Probably not. [Feb 2016, p.102]

Title: Chocolate Starfish and the Hot Dog Flavored Water
Review: You'd expect better from a band so on top of their game.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Belong
Review: Not so much Teenage Fanclub as 'Loveless'-era MBV meets classic Cure at their poppiest.

Title: Mad Season
Review: Each song isn't particularly interesting or life-changing, but, damn, if every one of them doesn't boast a hook that sticks in your head until you're humming "We Wish You A Merry Christmas" just to exorcise it. For better or worse, this is talented songwriting...

Title: Black City
Review: The lyrical immediacy and intimacy lift Black City leagues above much of the disassociated drivel that's labeled vocal house.

Title: LUMP
Review: Lindsay’s wonky music, meanwhile--he plays most of the instruments--benefits hugely from the strength of Marling’s voice and persona. The only bum note is that there isn’t more Lump to treasure.

Title: Tomorrow's Modern Boxes
Review: Yorke’s meditations on the modern make Boxes thoroughly listenable but uneven. The album’s first half is noticeably more coherent and accessible than the challenge and trouble of the second movement.

Title: Fortress
Review: Musically the album is AB's heaviest so far, but it's never heavy handed. [Oct 2013, p.90]

Title: Towards Language
Review: Whether with Supersilent or on his own, Arve Henriksen has demarcated his own world of sound, communicating in ways that are sometimes inscrutable but always deeply felt. [Jul 2017, p.53]

Title: That's Why God Made the Radio
Review: A cloudless orgy of nostalgia.

Title: Edward Sharpe & the Magnetic Zeros
Review: On record, though--and particularly this one, which presents churchy performances in mixes both realistic and surreal--these same Up With People tropes don't work as well, particularly with prolonged exposure, as inferior follow-ups to promising debuts by the Polyphonic Spree and I'm From Barcelona have proven.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: He's less pimp than craftsman, packing more style--and more substance--into his four-minute-long songs than other rappers deliver in an entire album.

Title: Todd Smith
Review: Make no mistake about it, this is a formulaic album.

Title: SUGAREGG
Review: The album sounds even more emphatically Bully, with many of its hooky and grungy, visceral tracks examining the end and aftermath of a relationship.

Title: Lifeblood
Review: Infinitely better than their last album, and proof that The Manics are now capable of writing pop music that’s neither dull nor pandering.

Title: Mississauga Goddam
Review: Despite the strength of "Music Is My Boyfriend" and lush single "The Fear Is On", I continually find myself humming songs from the debut instead.

Title: Born To Die
Review: Much of her music aims to capture elusive emotions, yet she ends up spelling them out with literal refrains, banal narratives and sexed-up histrionics that leave little to the imagination.

Title: Once Upon a Time in the West
Review: The aforementioned 'The King' is a string-laden lament on changing times and love in their small pocket of the world, and it's better than most of the songs that precede it. But it’s not enough to pull Once Upon A Time In The West out of it’s own lumpen mediocrity.

Title: Hail To The Thief
Review: For all its muddied textures and sideways lurches, it is a magnificently engaging and expansive work. [Jul 2003, p.112]

Title: Jason Isbell & The 400 Unit
Review: On this new self-titled record, Jason Isbell and his band the 400 Unit sound like they’re still finding their legs.

Title: Play
Review: The guitar whiz cashes in his superstar chits for this largely instrumental album, an indulgence he's earned but doesn't quite pull off.

Title: Build a Rocket Boys!
Review: In their own, low key, understated way, Elbow continue to beguile and impress.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: Mostly it's the tunes that do the slamming. And though their lyrics may be too sincere for sophisticates, they're not sincere enough to suit the Avetts, a disconnect they'll tell you about.

Title: Victory Shorts
Review: If only Michaelson's lyrics could match theirs for social insight, devastating romanticism or sharp wit. Nonetheless, this second album gleams with promise.

Title: MTMTMK
Review: A slam-bang dance pop album of the first order, MTMTMK is technically an Africa-meets-Western-pop hybrid.

Title: I Tell A Fly
Review: It’s not an immediate album, but give a little time for the scattershot approach to sink in and moments of genius gradually reveal themselves.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: On their second album as Run the Jewels, noise-loving Brooklyn rapper-producer El-P and Atlanta's Killer Mike make the most explosive hip-hop you'll hear all year.

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: Teeth Dreams is nowhere near the best Hold Steady album, but it shows the band aging in a direction that fills us with… hope? Perhaps that’s all we can ask for.

Title: Contrepoint
Review: Out of something very, very old has come something deliciously new.

Title: Modus Vivendi
Review: Modus is essentially the antithesis of the half-baked works that arose from Kanye’s Wyoming sessions in 2018. It is the result of a handful of talented collaborators who provide enough eclecticism to balance out the bombastic sound of G.O.O.D. in-house producer Mike Dean.

Title: Quarantine
Review: An extraordinary, multi-layered, attention-grabbing record. [Aug 2012, p.87]

Title: Wilderness Heart
Review: Previous albums saw the band go for a murkier, more spaced-out vibe, but this time it's more about concision and songs.

Title: This is PiL
Review: Lydon's ever-inspiring love of de-dub postulates continually throughout the album – it's such a perfect return.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Dave Gahan's songwriting has improved since 2007's solo "Hourglass," but this Sounds like a mundane midlife crisis.

Title: All the Lost Souls
Review: Lost improves on the first disc at least five times over, partly because its starker focus might really take you back to...well, certainly not a club, but maybe an AM radio-equipped kid's bedroom circa 1973. [21 Sep 20007, p.80]

Title: Dua Lipa
Review: Those vocals are the magic ingredient, saving potentially limp tracks from extinction. But it’s equally impressive to hear how confidently the debut holds itself together, flitting between styles but always shining a spotlight on a legitimate pop sensation. She’s the real deal.

Title: I Will Set You Free
Review: There's much substance with the employment of piano, organ, synthesiser, guitar and horn solos, but the actual song structures and vocal performances don't share this same level of achievement.

Title: Oak Island
Review: The album is rich in texture but light on memorable melodies.

Title: Youth Code
Review: Regrettably the record and the band follow a formula at the expense of song composition.

Title: The Datsuns
Review: With so much apparent calculation involved, it makes sense that the group's self-titled debut is neither as good nor as bad as it might have been.

Title: Continuum
Review: With no edge to the songwriting and with such spit-polished, tasteful production, Continuum just doesn't convince as a heady, soulful rock album or as Mayer's creative quantum leap forward.

Title: Something
Review: Now an out-and out pop band, Chairlift veers towards the catchy on all 11 tracks of Something. [#39, p.67]

Title: Madame X
Review: Madame X not only amply rewards such close listening, but its daring embrace of the world outside the U.S. underscores how Madonna has been an advocate and ally for left-of-mainstream sounds and ideas throughout her career.

Title: He Gets Me High
Review: There's plenty to love here in the melody department, and Dee Dee's too great of a songwriter to make a complete dud of a record. [Oct. 2011, p. 80]

Title: Veckatimest
Review: This one is probably the closest rival to Merriweather Post Pavilion we’ve heard this year.

Title: Out of Ashes
Review: Mr. Bennington strives to sound sympathetic, but after a song or two it’s clear that his only sympathy is for himself; there’s no humility, much less humor or proportion. As real as his prolonged adolescent angst is supposed to be, it quickly curdles into narcissism.

Title: LP1
Review: LP1 is more than just a confident debut album. It's primordial in a way that Björk herself has often attempted but frequently short-circuited letting her cognizance get in the way.

Title: Underneath The Pine
Review: So what subgenre tag is appropriate now? Is this discogaze? Funkwave? Only time will tell.

Title: Alligator
Review: Painstakingly crafted, casually baroque music for people who get off a little bit on feeling blue.

Title: The Babies
Review: The Babies is a worthwhile enough diversion to make me genuinely excited for the next Vivian Girls record, and think that maybe Morby should stay in the spotlight and ask Woods to find a new bassist.

Title: L'ami Du Peuple
Review: As always, Kinsella comes across as well-read, thoughtful, and concerned, reflecting the veteran musician’s early Cap’n Jazz days as much as his new fatherhood.

Title: This Way
Review: This shiny collection of pop, folk, blues, country and rock is mostly about as emotionally engaging as watching Mr Spock watch paint dry... in the dark.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: In between the soul-searching, Fleet Foxes cranks out some pretty great singalong songs. And that's what it's all about, isn't it?

Title: Feathers
Review: Feathers may not have the heft of Dead Meadow's other albums, but it's easily its most listenable and satisfying from end to end.

Title: Drowners
Review: Drowners can’t inspire too much ill will or really any kind of strong reaction and that’s fair enough: it doesn’t deal in hot, dirty sex or catastrophic breakups, mostly drunken hookups and easy letdowns.

Title: Lady Wood
Review: Lady Wood is admirably lean and tightly focused, and though it doesn’t boast confessionals on the order of Like a Prayer‘s, it offers a peek inside the psyche of a smart, burgeoning young star.

Title: All Visible Objects
Review: These songs tend towards fuzzy sentiments—the words “love,” “life,” “light,” and “feel” are staples. Many of the musical ideas—tinkling pianos, plasticky strings and emotion-squeezing chord progression—have been part of Moby’s toolkit since the word “Go.”

Title: Ready to Die
Review: Throughout, he's supported by Stooges guitar riffing of brutal directness and simplicity, occasionally fattened by the horns that lend an apt touch of soul sleaze to the latter track.

Title: Two Suns
Review: Anyways, ignore the write-ups (uh, except this one), which won’t be able to help quoting all the spiritual mumbo jumbo about dualism, and enjoy what seems, to me, unstated genre practice at play on a very large stage.

Title: Sorry Is Gone
Review: A best possible blend of odd and good. [Dec 2017, p.96]

Title: Big Fish Theory
Review: Big Fish Theory doubles the ambition of Summertime ’06’s corroded soundscape but condenses that breadth within a tight 36 minutes.

Title: Pinewood Smile
Review: It’s just sad to hear the spark of reinvention that ignited their last powder keg of an album confined to a handful of tracks on a largely mediocre album. They can do better. They have done better. They will do better again.

Title: Born Again Revisited
Review: Times New Viking neither regress nor abandon their origins, offering instead a compromise where the harsh timbres commingle with increasingly more adept proclivities for memorable pop songs.

Title: My God Is Blue
Review: For all the talk of madness, it would seem more than ever that Sebastien Tellier knows exactly what he's doing.

Title: Praxis Makes Perfect
Review: The record alone makes for the latest solid effort from these two outsize talents, but the stage show ought to be the ideal way to enjoy it

Title: Bush
Review: Even though Bush looks backward, it proves he is once again ahead of his time.

Title: I Hate Music
Review: What amazes most, and there's much to marvel at here, is the childlike wonder and sprightly sense of play that still remains after all these years.

Title: Widowmaker
Review: This creative group of misanthropes have emerged a devastating proposition.

Title: Resistance Is Futile
Review: Beneath the surface sheen, Resistance Is Futile is a complex, multi-layer work. [May 2018, p.88]

Title: 'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!
Review: They use a quiet/loud formula to epic create drone-filled symphonies, which rumble, crackle and erupt perfectly.

Title: Lasers
Review: Obviously, Atlantic did not rape Lupe into releasing a soulless, automated, corporate record. The real irony is that Lupe's fans demanded this garbage be released.

Title: Beyul
Review: Yakuza continue to forge a specialized and strange alloy [of metal and experimental music] on Beyul. Don't expect to love all of their recombinations. Do, however, expect to be surprised by them.

Title: Face Control
Review: Together they've embraced more experience and experimentation for captivating results. [Winter 2009, p.100]

Title: Crossing The Rubicon
Review: The serious tone is a natural progression for the Sounds but Rubicon's downfall is that it's songs don't linger much after the music stops. [Jul 2009, p.128]

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: Pearl Jam's 10th album might offer little in the way of surprises.

Title: Divide and Exit
Review: With Williamson delivering street-ranter streams of consciousness over Andrew Fearn's frigid post-punk/jip-hop productions, it's possibly not for the casual listener out for a few laughs but there's much to invigorate in its unaffected, defiant slagging of hated jobs, metropolitan hipsters, Twitter and more. [Jun 2014, p.120]

Title: Lil Boat 3
Review: Even if Lil Boat 3 came out in a time without so much surface tension (is such a thing still possible?), it’d still feel sloppy and forgettable. The presence of personalities like Lil Yachty’s should be welcomed, but the execution still needs to be there.

Title: Elsewhere
Review: She may not over-emote, but Elsewhere still has burn marks around its emotional edges. [May 2015, p.97]

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: In its best moments, "Helplessness Blues" sparkles like some sort of divine plan, but a plan that knows the value of mistakes, surprises and even regret.

Title: Sonic Soul Surfer
Review: This sounds like Steve Wold, not Seasick Steve, and the result is an untidy, tedious affair.

Title: Negativity
Review: A perfectly acceptable retrenchment. [Nov 2013, p.105]

Title: In Defense of the Genre
Review: Defense of the Genre is the best major label release of the year, and the most surprising album to boot.

Title: Art Official Intelligence: Mosaic Thump
Review: This, like the last joint 'Stakes Is High', sees the crew making even more stylistic space between themselves and their very own creation of the late eighties, 'the daisy age'.

Title: Memory
Review: In many ways, Memory poignantly conveys how time has caught up with the Vivian Girls. It may look into the past, but the trio are not the same anymore both creatively and personally—and the time they took apart to explore other avenues works to their benefit. Armed with a deeper understanding of those trying times, and each other, the trio moves forward—and live in harmony with it.

Title: Chinese Democracy
Review: While few have ever actually accused the singer of using good judgment, Chinese Democracy shows him to be a man who, however divorced from reality, hasn't lost the instincts that once made him great.

Title: Homegrown
Review: It’s not all perfect: the previously-released title track clocks in as a fairly innocuous hoe-down, while the slightly uncomfortable spoken word midpoint of ‘Florida’ makes for a jarring addition. Still, when ‘Homegrown’ soars, it acts as further proof that few in history can reach the emotional peaks that Neil Young can.

Title: Warm Heart of Africa
Review: Malawi’s Esau Mwamwaya, however, is proof that even the West’s slickest and sickliest can be used well by inventive minds.

Title: Let's Get Out Of This Country
Review: The collection of ten songs on this album are mostly solid, with some real pearlers and a few that pass you by--but the band is so easy to listen to that you don’t need to be an established fan.

Title: Clark
Review: As the album advances, you get the sense that Clark is finally accomplishing what he claims to have been doing all along: making a techno record.

Title: Walks For Motorists
Review: Despite the different focus on Walks for Motorists, it’s less a reinvention for White Hills than an evolution from a prolific band with a restless streak.

Artist: Laura Jane Grace & The Devouring Mothers
Title: Bought to Rot
Review: In addition to the foray into pop-punk, the album elicits elements from several genres without settling on a single soundscape.

Title: "Awaken, My Love!"
Review: Only the limitations of his voice occasionally let him down--he doesn’t quite have the range to nail Awaken’s more ostentatious vocal lines. Still, it’s a minor gripe when there’s so much here to enjoy.

Title: Have One on Me
Review: As an album, it is huge, sometimes overwhelming-- but such is the strength and individuality of Newsom’s vision, it seems almost inconceivable she could produce anything unremarkable.

Title: Chasing Yesterday
Review: Chasing Yesterday has its flaws, but they’re far outnumbered by moments where it succeeds in catching up with its titular quarry.

Title: Texas Piano Man
Review: As unabashedly pop albums go, Ellis’ self-descriptive Texas Piano Man is a bracing alternative to the guitar-focused music that dominates the singer-songwriter field.

Title: Original Colors
Review: So while High Places have neatly avoided getting stuck in a rut on Original Colors, daring to reinvent themselves into a more motion-friendly group, fans of their first couple of albums should still find the overall mood sufficiently low-key to provide easy access.

Title: Leisure Seizure
Review: It's well-produced with some nice drums, but it simply has no reason to exist.

Title: Dark Energy
Review: Complex puzzles for nimble feet to crack, custom-built for dancing. [Apr 2015, p.52]

Title: Complete Surrender
Review: It’s direct, unflinching and explicitly pop: rarely have Slow Club sounded this full, this bold.

Title: Parallels
Review: One of Chung’s strengths is not overstuffing his music, but there are moments where Parallels’ nonchalance makes it feel like less of a full album and more of a holdover between more momentous projects.

Title: Death Song
Review: Death Song, their fifth full-length, is both unlike anything they’ve done before and also the most purely Black Angels album they have released.

Title: Frankie Rose and the Outs
Review: On this album she proves herself as something more (way more, in fact) than an eternal scenester and competent drummer.

Title: Luv Is Rage 2
Review: Nearly every song on Luv Is Rage 2 comes with a distinct enough hook to break up the limited set of things it does and subjects it ponders.

Title: Hypnotize
Review: Hypnotize has a little bit of everything: protest, pretension, comedy, brute force, delicacy, compassion, crassness, fury. [Dec 2005, p.143]

Title: Epoch
Review: On Epoch, Hansen, Brown and O'Connor are in the prime of their careers.

Title: Warmth
Review: On Warmth, Blondes haven't drastically improved on their sound, but they feel at home delivering ten more high-quality textural cuts.

Title: Born in the Echoes
Review: The Chemical Brothers continue to buck any notions of a creative burn-out with their strongest release in a decade.

Title: Years of Refusal
Review: The Manchester Mope now pushes in the opposite direction, ratcheting up the distortion, muscling up on his vocals, and emphasizing live-in-the-studio energy over overdubbed perfection. In the process, he has rarely sounded so urgent.

Title: Nootropics
Review: The disc turns more experimental as it progresses.

Title: Strange Desire
Review: Even the infectious energy of “Rollercoaster” can’t quite overcome a demo-like lack of polish that keeps the songs earthbound even as they reach higher.

Title: Where You Go I Go Too
Review: For some, this and the album's unabashed opulence may prove too much to stomach. For others though, Lindstrom has created a sophisticated and lovingly crafted album that despite its dance driven pulse will resonate with music lovers of all persuasions.

Title: A Time to Love
Review: As always, his heart's in the right place, but his pop brilliance has dimmed to the level of mere mortals. [16 Oct 2005]

Title: Plain Rap
Review: Plain Rap lacks the talents of Fatlip and Slimkid and it shows. The smart, polished Pharcyde backings - rich in jazz and rare groove - are still in evidence, but it's easy to miss the gawky verbals of all four rappers.

Title: Algiers
Review: The record’s constant hums and oohs at times whitewash even Algiers’ loftiest intentions, but the moments of clarity amongst all the murk mark the trio out as something staunchly individual.

Title: Minotaur
Review: At 25 minutes, Minotaur is slight but still a fine distillation of the band's deceptive charms and retains the sense of something very unsettling lurking at its core. [Oct 2010, p.105]

Title: Alight of Night
Review: Eventually Brad Hargett's depressive baritone voice will get you down, but not before it has demanded your attention. [Apr 2009, p.87]

Title: Priorities
Review: Whilst the album as a whole doesn't necessarily tread new ground, and admittedly is a little rough around the edges, it's a promising debut, and you can expect to hear more from Don Broco in the future.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: As ever Wagner’s voice is rich and warm, the instrument of a faltering singer that just gets better with age, cracked and croaked and delivering lyrics with a strange phrasing that makes the most indecipherable and idiosyncratic observation take on a wealth of meanings for the listener depending how they first, or last, hear it. [combined review of both discs]

Title: All Hope Is Gone
Review: While their peers pander to the mainstream, the masked musicians continue to honour their scene by staying true to their roots while broadening their sound.

Title: At War With The Mystics
Review: A record of jarring juxtapositions, a bunch of cool tunes that could[n't] care less about how they fit together. [Apr 2006, p.86]

Title: And Now That I'm in Your Shadow
Review: Jurado does downtrodden and mournful better than most, but concentrated strings of songs about being "restless 'til my death," "sadness in her eyes," and a hotel hospital add up to a tearstained emotional assault delivered with virtually no relief.

Title: All Hell Breaks Loose
Review: It may not eclipse past achievements but does point to a genuine way forward in a dignified and spiritual manner. [Jul 2013, p.84]

Title: Sorceress
Review: Much as Williamson charts her psychic growth, Sorceress also musically waxes.

Title: If the Ocean Gets Rough
Review: It's plenty catchy and big, but it's also wildly uncreative and predictable.

Title: Build a Rocket Boys!
Review: It's simply another excellent Elbow record. [March 2011, p. 98]

Title: Clues
Review: Yet get past the grating AF-isms and there’s some good tunes.

Title: Lamp Lit Prose
Review: The hodgepodge of ideas can make for challenging listening towards the end, but Lamp Lit Prose feels like Longstreth’s back having fun, playing with ideas, every listen offering up something new to discover.

Title: Songs Cycled
Review: The impossibly orchestrated compositions on Songs Cycled are constantly unraveling and being wound back in, making them a little bit hard to keep up with at times, but something amazing to behold nonetheless.

Title: Ta Det Lugnt
Review: It sounds unfiltered, raw, and rough, and the quartet's mixture of guitar, organ, fiddle, percussion, and flute (Jethro Tull in the house) makes it all the more authentic.

Title: Only Things We Love
Review: This is an album that might be best digested in smaller doses, in order to avoid the feeling that all these songs sort of just wash each other out--but there’s no denying that Blaqk Audio have stumbled onto something really entertaining here.

Title: Good Morning Revival
Review: Gimmicky moments are plentiful, but it's the box-fresh pop songs like "Misery" and "The River" that benefit most from their renewed sense of purpose. [Apr 2007, p.100]

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: The Scottish outfit have delivered again with jangly pop full of skittering guitars, self-flagellating lyricism, and whimsy under a pall of darkness that no amount of the big spotlight can dispel.

Title: Landing Gear
Review: Devin's target audience, on the other hand, embraces sleaze, porno, weed, and hip-hop with plenty of memorable stingers, and seeing as how Landing Gear delivers on all counts, fans of Texas' most blunted rapper will once again be pleased.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: The biggest glitch is the production - the myriad elements sound cramped for space.... Too bad, cuz Butler's lyrics, which replace coming-of-age angst with poetic explorations of global anxiety, politics and an excoriation of celebrity culture, put Funeral to shame.

Title: Two Hands
Review: Capping one of the strongest years a rock band has had in a while, this stands as a crowning achievement, the perfect record to close out a tumultuous decade and lead into one where the damage may be irreversible. Two Hands asks what responsibility each of us have going into the next era, offering no clear answers.

Title: You Can't Fight What You Can't See
Review: It seems now that the band is terrified of change, leaving them to rehash what their first five albums accomplished in lieu of actual progression.

Title: More Than a Woman
Review: It's so predictable and so painfully trendy that More Than a Woman might as well have a former Mouseketeer's face on the cover.

Title: Gentle Spirit
Review: There are times when Wilson's meandering style emphasis on ambiance turns on a twilight sound.

Title: Now We Can See
Review: An album that goes so far in proving that simplicity not only has its place, it’s also often the path to unmitigated greatness.

Title: Black Pumas
Review: Burton sings about interior voyages and the tracks were usually constructed by no more than two musicians; it’s music made at home, for home listening. That’s all well and good, since the duo has considerable skill, but this existential lonerism underscores a chasm between the pair and their influences. Unlike the icons of the era they find so inspiring, Black Pumas rarely look outside of themselves.

Title: American Head
Review: By track four, a whimsical-by-numbers reverie called “Dinosaurs on the Mountain,” American Head starts to fall off an American cliff. The tempos are slow enough to deflate even Coyne’s considerable charm, and the record’s rootsy, pastoral spin on the Lips’ sound is undermined by the band’s maximalist production ethos. Nearly every song is overstuffed with queasy synth textures and sleek, digitized strings, and Coyne can’t resist warping his vocals in a grab-bag of ugly processors.

Title: D
Review: While White Denim have a tendency to enthusiastically overcook things, ultimately it's their sheer audacity--allied to some strong tunes--that makes D hard to resist.

Title: Wilco (The Album)
Review: Like a slightly under-serving best of, though, we get glimpses of what they've done before, but nothing substantial enough to set a new high-water mark.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: Their sixth disc nails the familiar pleasure centers, but truly excites only when the singer casts manners aside. [24 Jan 2014, p.67]

Title: We Wanna Be Hyp-No-Tized
Review: The album is, however, still ramshackle and oddball where it counts. [Jun 2019, p.86]

Title: Tales of Us
Review: Tales of Us has a stately pace and woozy beauty, with cinematic orchestration of swaying strings over acoustic guitar or mossy cello.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: Without co-star Alison Krauss or marquee Texan producer T Bone Burnett, Robert Plant's latest solo outing suffers the expected sequel slump.

Title: Invaders Must Die
Review: A majority of IMD is destined to end up splattered across car adverts and in film soundtracks where the scene is of a pulsing, throbbing, energetic nature. Sadly, that won't lend it any more substance.

Title: Sorry You Couldn't Make It
Review: Swamp certainly has a knack for the genre's heartbreak. [Apr 2020, p.89]

Title: Cat's Eyes

Fall to Pieces is an audacious cri de coeur that ultimately finds strength in adversity where others might fall apart.

Title: Wired Together
Review: This is a piece of work in which good-quality ingredients have been handled without a great deal of tact.

Title: Give Till It's Gone
Review: Harper is in top form, crafting songs that succeed lyrically and musically, capturing much of the blues-driven energy of White Lies while mixing in a delicate simplicity that adds a layer of depth to the bluesman's latest effort.

Title: Curious Volume
Review: It riffs, it’s entertaining, but above all, it contains an existential joy that transcends recorded sound.

Title: City Center
Review: Every song in the first half of the album tries so hard to get somewhere, but just ends up breaking down when it becomes obvious there’s no end in sight.

Title: Fantasies
Review: Danceable though they may be, these songs are also fighting some pretty serious gloom.

Artist: The Ghost of a Saber Tooth Tiger
Title: Midnight Sun
Review: It’s an accomplished, enjoyable record from start to finish, regardless of references or lineage.

Title: The Libertines
Review: A thrilling, frustrating souvenir of a band whirling out of control. [Sep 2004, p.130]

Title: Gigaton
Review: This is just simple, honest-to-goodness, feel-good rock ‘n’ roll, and the world is better for it being out there. More like this, please.

Title: Darlings
Review: You get a good sense of just what kind of man Drew is on Darlings, reconciling monogamy with promiscuity, Broken Social Scene’s cheap-seats bombast with love-seat confidentiality.

Title: This Week
Review: Jean Grae continues to improve in every respect, but the negative aspect is that too many of the beats bleed into one another.

Title: Option Paralysis
Review: It's a war of emotion rendered in the most extreme tones and is more and more rewarding on every listen. One day, all bands will be like Dillinger.

Title: How Many Times Have You Driven By
Review: While a bit mercurial in nature, by its overall impression, How Many Times Have You Driven By is a grooving, otherworldly standout that establishes Vu as one to watch.

Title: Passage
Review: With Passage, Exitmusic has turned in one of the more ambition, evocative, and engaging efforts of 2012.

Title: Prophet
Review: Sonically, Knopf has never sounded more confident. [Jun 2012, p.82]

Title: White Lilies Island
Review: 'White Lilies Island' sees Imbruglia free herself from the Alanis Morissette-clone image that you sense was very much forced last time around and actually manage to carve out an identity, both in her vocals and as a personality.

Title: Here
Review: Here is a ruminative, inward-looking album of folk-inflected beauty.

Title: Don't Give Up On Love
Review: The septuagenarian reintroduces himself as a lively and supremely compelling singer. [Jun 2017, p.24]

Title: Y Dydd Olaf
Review: Y Dydd Olaf is a crucial minority language record, but Saunders' beguiling melodies and execution also make it one of the best British debuts of 2015.

Title: Worship
Review: Long term fans might find Worship not as visceral as previous outings, whilst those intrigued by occasional flashes of melody might find themselves beaten into submission by the album's oppressive nature.

Title: Terms of Surrender
Review: The record sounds warm, full and flirty; the snares hit you, the bass bounces and harmonicas and organs are as bright as California stars.

Title: The Electric Lady
Review: What a wild and wonderful listening experience this is: bristling with ideas, constantly shooting off at different angles but always replete with earworm melodies, plush with glittering sounds, charged with intelligent and emotional lyrics and underpinned by a syncopated rhythm section that shifts gears effortlessly from tightly coiled to blazingly expansive.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: No matter how contrived the sound, however, there's no writing this troupe off as lazy pastiche.... Give the People What They Want breathes passionate new life into the past.

Title: Victory For The Comic Muse
Review: [A] triumphant comeback.

Title: Why Love Now
Review: As a whole, this is a typically unpredictable and manic album. Musically, it couldn’t be accused of being subtle, but it does show a band pushing themselves to see where they can take their sound.

Title: Soft Hair
Review: Prepare to be taken on a journey around the pair’s sonic universe that touches on everything from US R&B, Nilsson-esque singer-songwriter numbers and back again, all under a heady sheen of studio shimmer that can feel woozy, psychedelic or just 110 per cent odd at any one point.

Title: Funplex
Review: The first album by the B-52's in 16 years sees the Georgia trash-pop veterans keep dull maturity at bay with 11 paeans to partying, space, deviant sex and sly protest politics .

Title: Libraries
Review: It remains delightfully messy and is all the more viscerally resonant.

Title: American Head
Review: Musically, it’s the ‘Lips at their most fully-realised. It may not get your feet moving but it’ll tug at the heartstrings. Each track builds up slowly like a rising tide that eventually envelops you. Compelling stuff.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: Thrilling and joyous, fierce and focused, the women sound like they’re having the time of their lives sinking their teeth back into the music together.

Title: Gravitas
Review: he uneven, occasionally locked-in Gravitas finds Talib Kweli energetically exercising his artistry free of any agenda but his own, and hopefully positioning him for a true return to form next time around.

Title: i,i
Review: If 22, A Million could come off as sometimes cold and always anxious, then i,i is the warm flipside, with songs that float and flutter, that call for resilience rather than resignation. ... This record finds power in its collaborations.

Title: Loud
Review: It is Rihanna's vocal--at once commanding, soulful and vulnerable--that anchors the song, and Loud itself, elevating it from a hit-and-miss collection into something oddly arresting.

Title: Central Market
Review: Central Market is a big album for an age that has acquainted itself with thinking small about the album both as a vessel for sound and as a standard-bearer for new aesthetic vision.

Title: Courting The Squall
Review: Lyrically, as ever, Garvey's skill lies in combining romantic poeticism with sandpaper wit. [Dec 2015, p.80]

Title: Bigfoot
Review: If emotional depth is what you’re after, these eight tracks are never likely to be your bag. But, if you can take Bigfoot for the sun-blushed, sweet-natured collection of songs that it is, then this could be the soundtrack to your summer.

Title: Oh My God
Review: Oh My God is Kevin Morby’s attempt at crafting his own post-modern American Songbook. The sound of a succinct vision--executed precisely as intended.

Title: It's Alive
Review: It's Alive is a debut that should appeal to both lovers of old-school surf pop and anyone who's into the modern "surf" noise-pop style, but always wanted more waves and less whine.

Title: No Said Date
Review: Masta Killa has delivered one the most urgent, straightforward Wu releases since the group's debut over a decade ago.

Title: Motion to Rejoin
Review: Brightblack Morning Light's intentions and actions are indeed admirable--they're committed advocates of much more than just drug legalization--but Motion to Rejoin struggles mightily to articulate a focus aside from tranquility.

Title: Open Here
Review: The result is an intriguing, if disorientating, sprawl of sound.

Title: The Warning
Review: 'The Warning' is a splendid combination of braindance and footdance.

Title: Peace, Love, Death Metal
Review: Often shambolic and in-jokey, it's also sensationally good fun. [May 2004, p.93]

Title: Love and Curses
Review: Musically invigorating, lyrically exciting, and thematically prescient from start to finish, Love and Curses gets my vote as the best album of 2009.

Title: White Women
Review: White Women is the closest Chromeo have come yet to fully realizing their sound, but it's also far from perfect.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: The wealth of talent on A Seat at the Table is well-showcased--it’s among the most exquisite productions of the year, each track silken-smooth and replete with quietly virtuosic instrumental flourishes—and in service of a story of pain and healing.

Title: The Ride
Review: Although mercifully less in line with the Kooks/Courteeners hegemony than their first album, The Ride is stodgily dedicated to the Real Rock cause, even while it's shooting for Alex Turner's autobiographical cool. [Jul 2016, p.71]

Title: Violet Cries
Review: While there are a few moments where Violet Cries' potent atmosphere turns meandering and atonal, this is still a promising and often captivating debut from a band with a bold sound.

Title: Pony
Review: His unique pop prosody and production skills, more sophisticated than ever in Pony, foretell that his sound will continue progressing to new creative heights, with the heft of catchy pop music and the inventiveness of its growing indie subgenre.

Title: Here Comes the Cowboy
Review: Here Comes the Cowboy may retain some of the disarming simplicity and emotional universality that has become DeMarco’s trademark, but it is ultimately an album that fails to welcome the listener warmly into its world.

Title: Lianne La Havas
Review: A jazzy, soulful, understated account of breakup and recovery, that shimmers like a gorgeous summer groove and lets La Havas’s tender singing and cryptic lyrics carry the bittersweet emotion.

Title: The Meanest of Times
Review: The Meanest Of Times moves beyond connecting the dots between working-class punk and ancient Celtic ditties, with surprisingly thoughful songs that explore lives shaped by drunken violence and Catholicism. [Oct 2007, p.100]

Title: We Love Life
Review: “Weeds,” an excellent tune which compares the English working class to this type of plants, is only one of the various epic, melodramatic tunes in the key of Scott Walker (who produced the record) present here that use elements of nature to symbolise aspects of modern society and the human condition itself.

Title: Amen & Goodbye
Review: Their fourth album largely abandons any subtlety in favour of a scattergun art racket. [May 2016, p.91]

Title: Warzone
Review: The sound of Ono gravely warbling "Imagine" at the close of Warzone may invite more ridicule from longtime haters. But believers in her musical vision will deem it very much of a piece with the boldness that marks these new renditions of many of her most furious songs. [Nov 2018, p.34]

Title: Ten New Songs
Review: [Robinson's] kind of soft rock-- closer to "I Want to Know What Love Is" by Foreigner than I'm comfortable with-- probably isn't going to score many points with the indie crowd, but it's not going to throw off your concentration for very long.

Title: Parting The Sea Between Brightness And Me
Review: While still drenched in anguish, regret and torrential riffs, Parting The sea gives Bolm's prose-dense vignettes and feral confessions the full punch and epic scope they deserve. [Jul 2011, p.112]

Title: Endless Scroll
Review: It is not the most groundbreaking sound musically but certainly innovative in approach and original in delivery and presentation.

Title: Afterglow
Review: If these songs have a certain melancholic charm, it has been obscured beneath an impenetrably bland sheen.

Title: Versatile
Review: For the most part, it’s a masterclass in jazz phrasing.

Title: A Walk with Love and Death
Review: Melvins have made exactly the album they wanted to. The result? This is one for dedicated followers only.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: At its best, Somewhere Else produces a few tracks worthy of putting on and dancing to in the middle of the night. At its worst, it's repetitive material that should've stayed on the cutting room floor.

Title: All About Tonight
Review: As pleasantly disposable commercial country, these tracks bat a solid five-for-six.

Title: Honor Found in Decay
Review: Despite flashes of greatness, the uneven, unfocused Honor Found In Decay feels more like a placeholder.

Title: The Competition
Review: Lower Dens have the right ideas for their music, but they’re not always the right ideas at the right time. This album, flawed as it may be, is still worthwhile for when the latter happens, like with the heated guitar work and wailing vocals of ‘Two-Faced Love’.

Title: Us
Review: Happiness hasn’t blunted his keen social insight, though, as he empathizes with latchkey teens (“Tight Rope”), reflects on friends trapped in the street life (“Slippin’ Away”), and rues slavery’s consequences (“The Travelers”).

Title: Joanne
Review: The less is more production suits her, and for a first time we get a real and lasting glimpse of Stefani herself.

Title: Distortion
Review: Whether Merritt's return to lo-fi will fly at Lincoln Center remains to be seen, but his melodic mastery is never in question. [Winter 2008, p.108]

Title: Doctor's Advocate
Review: Barring some last-minute surprise, he has made the best hip-hop album of the year. [9 Nov 2006]

Title: If You Wait
Review: Although at times they come close to overshadowing the subtle instrumentation provided by Major and Dan Rothman, it’s actually the intrinsic balance between the contributions of all three that defines their sound.

Title: Lights
Review: Outside of its immediate context, Lights is a sometimes great, always promising debut. It's an album about leaving home, and it works best when the contrast between the folk singer and the pop production chimes with the tensions between the pull of home and the allure of the city.

Title: Spine Hits
Review: Spine Hits feels too spacious, lacking the depth that both [newly-departed singer] Fannan's swelling vocals and improvised jams filled the band's two previous releases [with]. Regardless, Spine Hits is an enjoyable listen.

Title: Libraries
Review: Libraries nods more to Burt Bacharach, and the record can sag occasionally under the drowsy weight of his influence.

Title: Twist Again
Review: There's all sorts of other excursions as well; the benefits of having a home studio to get lost in.

Title: Here Comes Science
Review: TMBG's nagging pop tunes are useful mnemonics, albeit irritating ones. But there is no reason why anybody over the age of eight should listen to this. [Jun 2010, p.100]

Title: Harmonicraft
Review: Harmonicraft is a short, sweet collection of pop-metal confectionery, irresistible if not unforgettable.

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: At 19 songs and more than 75 minutes, Brighter Than Creation's Dark just barely slouches to excess, mainly because it finds the Athens, Ga., quartet at its most tuneful.

Title: Harlem River
Review: Harlem River sees Morby’s melancholic discomforts through a refreshingly soft lens.

Title: Radio Silence
Review: Kweli’s flow can feel rushed and sticky, as though he can’t articulate his thoughts as neatly as he can conjure them up. But his fans are loyal. Radio Silence will comfortably shore up the base.

Title: Secret House Against the World
Review: His hoarse-throated vignettes of smalltown weirdos are beginning to suggest a sketch-show parody of Tom Waits; enough already with the disillusioned, motel-hopping loners.

Title: Lungs
Review: It may be breathtaking in places, but Flossie's Lungs are just a bit too full of bluster.

Title: May
Review: Broken Twin may eventually necessitate more gusto and variation in tempo and dynamics should Romme want to further forge her plow forward. However, she intended for May to be a return to basics; with it, she has produced a compelling and painstakingly beautiful triumph of understatement.

Title: The Sunset Tree
Review: There’s so much here to enjoy, we can tolerate the occasional lyrical overreach.

Title: Performance
Review: Eight albums in, and some of that edgy math-rock experimentalism has been lost, along with two original members of Leon Bridges’ band. But what they now lack in raw, ferocious edginess, they make up for glorious driving riff on Performance.

Title: Future This
Review: Future This is a coherent, uniform proposition, a proper album, rather than a melange of posturing and botched experimentation, as was the case with A Brief History Of Love.

Title: Moveys
Review: While much of Moveys sticks to swaying, midrange tempos, they pick up the pace halfway through, on "At It Again," though the song hangs on to the, by then, well-established hazy, ruminative demeanor. Later, the ambling "Montana" incorporates slide guitar and harmonica without leaving this sighing, world-weary state.

Title: The Boy with No Name
Review: [Their] first [album] to sound authentically beaten up. [Jun 2007, p.101]

Title: You Are There
Review: After an hour of getting your heartstrings tugged with such intense proficiency, You Are There starts to feel no less egregiously manipulative than hearing Celine belt out "My Heart Will Go On" for the thousandth time in a Vegas ballroom.

Title: Jaakko Eino Kalevi
Review: A bit of a grower, Jaakko Eino Kalevi is a subtly enticing album that establishes his niche within experimental pop.

Title: Krieg und Frieden (Music for Theatre)
Review: Ring makes it work by resisting the urge to do anything that resembles grandiose. [Apr 2013, p.94]

Title: Seek Magic
Review: This is yet another one of those records about escapism, yearning for a bolt of light in the dark, an end to normality. And it finds it, to almighty effect; producing the kind of rapturous charge that no bedroom-dance record has ever assembled before.

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: By rights, Elbow should be pretty annoying, the same kind of lardy, overblown and overrated band as their compatriots Doves.... Yet there's something rather haunting and affecting about 'Cast Of Thousands', just as there was about 2001's 'Asleep At The Back', which raises Elbow far above most of their peers.

Title: Light Upon The Lake
Review: It’s all very pretty and pleasant, but whereas Smith Westerns burned with the emotions of their songs, Whitney seem rather more detached from theirs. Which, as easy-going as these 10 songs are, renders them more as temporary, unconvincing background music. It’s nice for a while, but their effects soon give way to the winds of truth and reality.

Title: Olympic Girls
Review: With a handful of impressive releases already under their belt, Tiny Ruins have outdone themselves here, with a full set of compellingly crafted songs that are enriched rather than overwhelmed by the fuller sound.

Title: Boo Boo
Review: It might take you a couple of spins to fully appreciate Boo Boo. At times, it’s very slow-moving, and some of Bear’s experiments don’t land. ... Don’t let the more experimental qualities keep you from listening to the record, though.

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: It's nowhere McCartney hasn't been before, yet it's still richer and more varied than he's been in years. [Jan 2009, p.116]

Title: My True Story
Review: Neville almost levitates through doo-wop, soul and R&B standards.

Title: Never
Review: Never is frank, fearless, and restless--a 14-song rattle bag of damaged samples, uneasy hooks, intuitive melody, and dry humor.

Title: Barbara Barbara, we face a shining future
Review: Barbara Barbara, We Face a Shining Future is never weighed down by its makers’ history.

Title: Just Enough Education to Perform
Review: Some of his most writerly songs to date.

Title: Unbreakable
Review: It's the ballads--a side of her repertoire that had taken a back seat to forgettable chart-chasers--that show Jackson's at her vocal and songwriting best.

Title: Sparkle Hard
Review: Sparkle Hard is at once his most sonically adventurous and structurally tight set of music in over a decade and easily stands among his most rewarding work with the Jicks.

Title: A Laughing Death in Meatspace
Review: Every track hits its target. [Jan 2019, p.27]

Title: Sun
Review: Sun is a rewarding return to a new Cat Power, one who seems more at ease with her music and herself than ever before.

Title: Blue Eyed in the Red Room
Review: It’ll be interesting to see where he goes from here. But until then, Blue Eyed in the Red Room is one to skip.

Title: Elephant Stone
Review: Cosmic concoctions of this sort are all too rare these days, so it’s rather refreshing to hear this sound revisited, particularly with the added investment in melody that Elephant Stone tends to allow.

Title: Whiteout Conditions
Review: There’s a drive and urgency about Whiteout Conditions that whisks one along regardless, their usual indie-pop mode here strengthened by layers of fast, bubbly synths and pulsing Eurocentric beats.

Title: Diamond Eyes
Review: Diamond Eyes is wild and serene, and I can honestly say its Deftones' best album to date.

Title: Every Feeling On A Loop
Review: The musical world is much better off for Johnson’s journey back from the brink and the delivery of Every Feeling On a Loop. He shows us that grasping on to the imperceptible curve of one’s little plot of land is not just cold comfort, but a cause for daily celebration.

Title: (II)
Review: The core elements are so big, like blasts of pure plasmic energy, that it sounds planet-sized.

Title: Beta Love
Review: Beta Love ultimately feels unfinished. [Apr 2013, p.109]

Title: Forget the Night Ahead
Review: Compellingly bleak is a tough mood to sustain, however, and tracks sucj as 'Interrupted' edge them toward generic stadium territory. [Nov 2009, p.112]

Title: H-p1
Review: It's easy to see how the impact of this sort of music might be lost on record, but White Hills put their studio to great use here, proving they can sound both impressively cohesive and totally baked.

Title: Innocents
Review: The results are expectedly familiar, fantastic and welcome.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: The balance of gold to dross still makes this album a keeper.

Title: First Ditch Effort
Review: This album shows that newfound purpose, and more importantly, it shows that NOFX is still NOFX no matter if they embrace the ‘76 or ’16 punk mentality and that they are that much better because of it.

Title: Room 25
Review: A blast to listen to.

Title: The Forgotten Arm
Review: Once the contrivance of The Forgotten Arm’s vaguely sketched plot device crumbles, there are still solid tracks to be found.

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: What we have here is easily Mr. Young's finest work in years, one that erases the memory of his well-intentioned but anemic 2006 protest album, "Living with War."

Title: Venice
Review: The most pressing problem is that Venice is rarely a challenging release.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: Condon's songs have always been flooded with emotion that sound both deliriously pretty and endlessly sad or foreboding, and The Rip Tide is no exception.

Title: Not Real
Review: Here technology is merely a vessel for a sound that remains pastoral and beguiling. Truly, a class act. [May 2015, p.95]

Title: Neon Icon
Review: This album gets a C+ because I really enjoyed the time I spent hating it.

Title: Sweetener
Review: Confident and empowered, Sweetener illustrates once again that Grande is an unparalleled pop chameleon.

Title: The Baby
Review: The Baby's combination of breezy melodies and vulnerability makes for an engaging listen well worthy of the promising designation.

Title: Yeah Ghost
Review: Besides a couple of limp late-album tag-ons, it appears that, for once, the kings of chill-out have gotten downright animated. [Fall 2009, p.96]

Title: Real Gone
Review: 'Real Gone' is not by any means easy listening. It is, though, possibly a new type of music. [2 Oct 2004, p.64]

Title: Silver Wilkinson
Review: Among the more production-heavy tracks, nothing comes close in terms of technical or intuitive savvy. Still, Wilkinson delivers solidly on the album's more organic offerings.

Title: Music from Another Dimension!
Review: Dimension delivers because of Joe Perry.

Title: Forever
Review: An album of bland and relatively anonymous adult pop that rarely gets racier than offering to "keep you up all night" and "make you holler."

Title: Threes
Review: As emo-tastic as Threes is, it merely sizzles in ways their debut singed. [Oct 2006, p.128]

Title: FR32
Review: Able to walk the line effortlessly between animalistic lyricism and tracks that are more melody-focused, Wretch has managed to paint a picture where the brushstrokes are appreciated by all.

Title: Giants
Review: They've kept their distinctive sound. [April 2012, p.106]

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: A record that anyone who’s ever demanded anything interesting from rock music should hear.

Title: Wildheart
Review: Focusing on Wildheart's overt eroticism is one way of listening, but it's impossible to overlook just how seriously he's taking craft.

Title: The Dirty South
Review: These rough, bitter, ruminative songs are slower, longer and wordier than those on Decoration Day. [Sep 2004, p.139]

Title: Sort of Revolution
Review: It's confessional late-night fare but the warmth of Fink's soulful voice is captivating. [Jun 2009, p.121]

Title: One by One
Review: The Foo Fighters' One by One, the band's first album since 1999, is densely packed with glum song titles, grinding beats, and moaned vocals. The result? Unexpected exhilaration.

Title: Mutant
Review: Almost every track has a fearsome radiance to its high end and even in those parts without drums or squared off structures, the surges of sound recall collective dancefloor ecstasies. [Dec 2015, p.44]

Title: Total Loss
Review: An intriguing new artist has found his voice. [Nov 2012, p.76]

Title: The Rising
Review: Springsteen's words may be weighted with the aftershocks of death, but the music, ironically, is animated; unlike ''Joad,'' ''The Rising'' is a pleasure to hear.

Title: Glasvegas
Review: There's much here to justify Alan McGee's awe. [Oct 2008, p.148]

Title: The Drug in Me Is You
Review: For most, the record will be too much--it's messy, it's overdone, it's arrogant, and ultimately it's disappointing – making Radke's return not really worth the wait.

Title: Peanut Butter
Review: The songs occasionally thrill but tonally it all becomes just a trifle exhausting about halfway through. [Jun 2015, p.107]

Title: Morning View
Review: Their movement toward non-nooky maturity continues here with tunes like the melodic and soaring "Wish You Were Here" and the dramatic "Warning"--each showing a more reflective and poetic side than before.

Title: Walk The Moon
Review: Individually, the songs are strong enough to hold their own, but after 11 tracks in a row, things get pretty samey.

Title: Welcome
Review: He’s much better at showing off his record collection on the well-chilled "Ice Castles," which purports to be a James Pants mix disc.

Title: Full Upon Her Burning Lips
Review: Drummer and percussionist Adrienne Davies again lays down a solid foundation for Carlson's slow motion riffage on instrumentals that eschew the more ornate sensibility of recent efforts in favour of a leaner, meaner kind of swagger. [Jun 2019, p.27]

Title: Chuck
Review: Chuck is Berry’s last inimitable flare, delivered in the nick of time.

Title: Eggs
Review: Here are miasmic, dizzyingly gorgeous songs built on the grandest and most romantic, but steadied by the hand of hook-loving classicists. Bravo! [Mar 2010, p.90]

Title: Powerplant
Review: Ultimately, Powerplant is a hooky, candid and sharp-witted portrait of young adulthood that engages with adept effortlessness.

Title: Trying to Never Catch Up
Review: Genuine hooks are oddly scarce.

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: Silence Yourself may not invent a genre. Silence Yourself may not give you something you didn’t have already. But it is so stark, so bold and delivered with such utter belief that you wonder why anyone would possibly care.

Title: Multi-Love
Review: Multi-Love demonstrates that the band isn’t beholden to a singular, lo-fi aesthetic. And for now, that’s more than enough.

Title: Sleeper
Review: His voice wafting in as it from across some great, wide divide, he drapes heavy-lidded seductions and portending cautionary tales over several decades of occultish folk, ritualistic rhythm and acoustic blues, from Bron-Y-Aur stomps to paralyzed lullabies. [No. 101, p.51]

Title: Here's Willy Moon
Review: Yes, he's a magpie--like, is My Girl really not a Ramones cover?--but Willy Moon is classy, forward-looking and 100 per cent on the money. [May 2013, p.100]

Title: The Age Of Immunology
Review: Magician's Success and the Can-does-The-Normal bleep of Backstroke could be missing soundtracks to some experimental Cold War animation. [Aug 2019, p.116]

Title: All Or Nothing
Review: Dance is the operative word across this tight 30-minute release, synths entering the spartan mix in an even more prominent way. This isn't the post-punk revival going disco, but it might be post-punk on a night out at the disco.

Title: Where You Live
Review: She's still on fine, if depressing form.

Title: Parallax
Review: It's a brilliant feat: to make a record about distance, Cox has written the most effortlessly approachable music of his career.

Title: Hug of Thunder
Review: Mostly, Hug Of Thunder feels like a sign of maturity to complement a more weathered and warm approach to songwriting that includes a lot of electronic pulses and skybound singalongs.

Title: Weezer (Black Album)
Review: Weezer's latest is an utterly skippable collection that'd be entirely unremarkable if not for the fact it was released by Weezer.

Title: Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots
Review: Where The Soft Bulletin was an intricate assessment of rock's potential, Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots is merely a rough sketch of a new musical direction.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: It could be said that a work as strong as Majesty Shredding cements Superchunk as an important band or a permanent indie fixture, but that's a bit of a misnomer. If anything this record is simply proof that Superchunk are going to make the music they want to make regardless of whether it fits into a modern context or not.

Title: Into the Wide
Review: This underrated band progressively unleash waves of measured ferocity over he turbine drumming of Brandon Young toward payoffs that are staggering in their intensity. [Oct 2014, p.71]

Title: Days Run Away
Review: Alright, so there's no 'Destroy The Heart', the lyrics are uniformly unremarkable, and the odd track is even, dare we say, a touch ropey... 'Days Run Away' is still better than it's got any right to be, and a marginally heroic homecoming with it.

Title: Love Keeps Kicking
Review: Every song here is expertly assembled, with the threat that they may crack and falter at any moment, but the band's unity holds everything together in a very pleasing manner. If there's any justice in the world, Love Keeps Kicking will be the record that sends Martha into the big leagues that they are surely destined to enter.

Title: Disturbance
Review: Basic themes remain unchanged. [Apr 2019, p.89]

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: The production doesn't always give Nicks's gothic imagery enough waft, but fans will love puzzling over which of her paramours she's recalling on Secret Love.

Title: Pattern of Excel
Review: Pattern of Excel is similarly idiosyncratic--it feels, in many ways, like a fistful of sketches torn from the notebook and tossed to the wind. Making sense of the ways they fall is part of the pleasure of this quiet, cryptic record.

Title: Second Love
Review: Second Love pays off most of all on those repeated listens--it’s not her most immediate collection of songs, but over time they reveal themselves to be her most rewarding.

Title: Taiga
Review: Most squarely accessible record to date, and easily the most pop album to come from an alumnus of Sacred Bones. [No. 114, p.61]

Title: Anak Ko
Review: Call it chill wave, call it dream pop, call her a bedroom producer - this album’s full of enough variety and adventure to make such generalisations moot. A real triumph.

Title: Paper Walls
Review: Unsurprisingly, the lyrics are direct and honest, while they've broadened their sonic palette to allow a tad more dissonance in with their urgent and propulsive pop-punk.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: Set in the more commercial contexts of Kelly Rowland features and the-Dream's fluorescent R&B, he can sound like a fish out of some pretty expensive water.

Title: II
Review: As with anything this ambitious, it occasionally over-reaches itself--but the highlights are magical, and should see Moderat reach ever bigger audiences.

Title: Let It All In
Review: As homeopathic remedies for heartache and life's unkindness, these reflective songs are persuasive and when the group decide to fly with the moment-seizing, easy-psych These Days Are Mine, it's doubly invigorating. [Feb 2013, p.105]

Title: Introduction, Presence
Review: Although their synth work and melodies are memorable beyond belief, this album’s poignance, delivered with a good-natured determination, is what takes the wheel and makes it a synth-pop milestone.

Title: Fanfare
Review: While his distinctive voice and keening melodies are as enchanting as ever, Wilson has added a cinematic heft that neatly avoids being saccharine.

Title: Gung Ho
Review: The album lacks nothing in substance, but in edge it could use a jolt.

Title: Forever
Review: The set oozes with timely funk beats and the kind of well-crafted songs that No. 1 hits are made of.

Title: Rainwater Cassette Exchange
Review: Ranging from translucent psych-pop to pummeling garage-rock, they're alternately assured and vulnerable, direct and subtle, light and dark.

Title: On My Way
Review: There's not a bad song on his new release and the more you listen, the more you'll like it.

Title: Tenacious D
Review: Take away the insane lyrics, and you’ve still got music worth listening to. Granted, it sounds like Journey being raped by Ronnie James Dio, but you have to admit that’s intriguing.

Title: Now What
Review: The big '80s-style production highlights her breathy-sexy vulnerability, but Presley's better when she rocks. [May 2005, p.123]

Title: Saturnalia
Review: It's the best thing either has done in a decade. [Apr 2008, p.116]

Title: Choreography
Review: Thomas doesn't completely capture the fleet shimmer of the best pop, but his songs are too much fun not to be taken seriously. [Aug 2016, p.108]

Title: Fallen Angels
Review: The final product, then, feels adrift: just off the coast of delivering a discrete emotional impact, offering a sporadic, self-reflexive charm for fans who smile at Dylan’s every left turn, whether in spite of themselves or on principle.

Title: Wanderer
Review: There's no danger of Wanderer outstaying its welcome, but while it's a brilliant return, it wouldn't be quite right too claim it as a triumph. Not because of the quality of these songs but because Wanderer is a record that know the cost of living and the price of losing all too well. [Oct 2018, p.82]

Title: Shields
Review: Shields is part spiralling indie rock, part wistful '60s pop. [Oct 2012, p.102]

Title: Humanz
Review: With a bit more focus, Humanz could have been an essential part of Gorillaz’s narrative. Instead, it’s a scatterbrained frenzy of emotion--which is what’s to be expected of anything immersing itself in the chaotic, logic-free nonsense of the world post-election.

Title: An End Has a Start
Review: The band's sophomore disc, which teems with drama and dark dollops of piano that swarm beautifully around singer-guitarist Tom Smith's clarion-call voice, continues to make good on the hype while again drawing on the past.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: It’s not all perfect. You could rightly question whether the Q-Tip/André 3000 duet Kids… has any place on a ATCQ album. Or whether a glut of guest spots including Elton John, Jack White and Kendrick Lamar are strictly necessary. Yet ultimately it’s the original, immersive Tribe vibes that conquer all.

Title: Ever-Roving Eye
Review: Ever-Roving Eye plays like a logical and slightly more daring sequel to his debut, moving forward into loose psychedelic shapes with pastoral chamber arrangements -- courtesy of woodwind player Paul von Mertens -- dotting the otherwise sparse landscape.

Title: This Is Gap Dream
Review: Like many slackers with a heart of gold, Fulvimar is full of interesting ideas on this record, but can't seem to put in the work to flesh them all out.

Title: Funeral
Review: If I were to have just heard the first half of the disc, I probably would have proclaimed it the best of the year as well.

Title: The Ghost Inside
Review: For the most part though, this is The Ghost Inside getting back to the largely straightforward, undeniably powerful mix of metal and hardcore they have always done so well.

Title: Underneath The Rainbow
Review: Underneath The Rainbow is more of an assault on the ears than anything else, although that’s mostly in a good way, as the band never lose sight of the style that first brought them success.

Title: ANTI
Review: This is an album that forces us to question the boxes we've placed Rihanna in all along.

Title: Gang of Losers
Review: Here's the thing about originality... You don't really need it when you play this proficiently. [Dec 2006, p.188]

Title: Bad Contestant
Review: Bad Contestant is a stunning debut with two very opposing personalities.

Title: The End of Silence
Review: It’s fair to say that, from a purely musical point of view, this is far from Herbert’s best work, but that’s hardly the point; The End Of Silence aims to unseat us and provoke a more profound engagement with the events around us, and to that end it’s a success.

Title: Third Album
Review: The album is perfectly suited for restless observation. It's like watching a sped-up time lapse of the tides, or nature evolving rapidly before our very eyes.

Title: Free Spirit
Review: It's frustrating, then, that Free Spirit's sanded-down sprawl more often than not threatens to suffocate any presence of a personality imbued in the music itself.

Title: 1-800 Dinosaur Presents: Trim
Review: The real power of this album is not only the showcasing 1-800’s collective musical prowess and their ability to mix and merge genres and style effortlessly to create music that sounds like nothing that has been released commercially in recent month, but of Trim’s vocals. Throughout the album he is the glue that holds everything together.

Title: The Trip
Review: It all makes for an engaging and frequently charming solo debut. [Nov 2010, p.114]

Title: Surrender Your Poppy Field
Review: Surrender Your Poppy Field proves he’s deepening rather than merely proliferating his music, continuing to grow up instead of growing old.

Title: Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga
Review: I think Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga is the album of this year and maybe of the next.

Title: I-Empire
Review: For all its cathartic lyrics, I-Empire is actually packed with dazzling, fast-moving songs, like 'Everything's Magic' and 'Sirens,' that bring together U2's widescreen guitar flights with tuneful, straightforward punk melodies.

Title: Wig Out at Jagbags
Review: Overall Wig Out at Jagbags isn't exactly a disappointing release, especially since it's far better than the breed of record many other artists multiple decades into their respective careers make. It is a frustrating one though.

Title: Shake Shook Shaken
Review: Unfortunately, there's nothing else that come close to matching its opening statement. [Feb 2015, p.106]

Title: A Bath Full of Ecstasy
Review: Amidst all the experimentation and extremes of this impressive album is a message about life: bathing in the moments of ecstasy will ultimately enable us to cherish and value life more.

Title: Cistern
Review: An orchestral score for a remembered expanse, it casts vivid shadows but avoids rigid form.

Title: Street Dreams
Review: He sticks defiantly to formula, hustling a string of synth-heavy, syncopated club jams. [#14, p.134]

Title: Introducing Karl Blau
Review: Blau places himself completely in his producer's hands. He digs into these lyrics and charts for all he's worth, delivering a gem that is as timeless as its songs.

Title: Wild and Reckless
Review: Wild & Reckless takes a couple steps in the right direction. This band’s optimum path, however, is still several steps away.

Title: Think Tank
Review: If it is the end, Blur has gone out kicking as always.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: Big Boi has exquisite taste in music, guests, lyrics and choruses--not to mention the knowledge and expertise of how to put a classic album together. And whoever bet against him just lost. Big time.

Title: Only In Dreams
Review: For the most part Only in Dreams is a sound that is firmly theirs.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Forgiveness Rock Record's thematic bent is mature, and that sense of gravity is embedded into the music, too.

Title: Gave In Rest
Review: We know intellectually it'd be impossible to make this music without modern recording technology, but it's still hard to believe this music came from the mind of someone with a car and a cell phone and a Twitter account. It feels like it's been floating around for eons in one form or another, waiting for someone to bottle it up.

Title: Smother
Review: In songs suffused with need and vulnerability, the music leaves itself open, waiting to be approached.

Title: Idlewild
Review: Deft, flawed, entertaining, thrilling, and disappointing, often at the same time.

Title: The Terror
Review: The Terror is a frightening trip, a fantastically cohesive album, and one that could have benefited greatly from a bit more editing and perhaps a little better track sequencing.

Title: Born This Way
Review: The record is blitzing, happily ludicrous, and plenty of fun for a while, but at the core there's Gaga, singing beautifully but clouded by all the readymade pop around her.

Title: All Days Are Nights: Songs For Lulu
Review: The music starts to grip most powerfully when it's more allusive and introspective.

Title: 100 Lovers
Review: Some of the album's instrumental tracks nod to the likelihood that Hollywood will come calling again soon, but 100 Lovers makes a case for DevotchKa's place being stage front rather than behind the curtain. [Feb 2011, p. 63]

Title: Beware
Review: The new Bonnie Billy record, Beware, is fuller in every sense of the word, from the choir of background singers answering Oldham on the opening track ('Beware Your Only Friend') to the way Oldham stops that song cold for a muted interlude.

Title: The Blue Hour
Review: While there’s a comforting familiarity that comes with all things Suede, it’s wonderfully shrouded on The Blue Hour by a very new, romantic and alluring strangeness. These are not hits to shake your bits to. Nor will these beats shake your meat. Rest assured, Suede remain the beautiful ones, but are just looking for beauty in ever more curious places.

Title: Light at the End of the World
Review: Erasure remain A-level, mid-tempo melody makers, crafters of classic romantic pop songs with electronica serving as the template.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Those who stick with Arab Strap will discover endearing wit and vulnerability in the duo's songs, as well as tender melodies and graceful acoustic playing. [Apr 2006, p.204]

Title: Gallows
Review: This is a raw, vicious and churning blast of a record. [25 Aug 2012, p.52]

Title: More Fish
Review: While More Fish is far from worthless, it's still a diluted product.

Title: At The Cut
Review: The musicians on the album--eight in total including Vic--seesaw between country, folk and indulgent Seventies rock, never reinventing wheels but generally giving the lyrical matter its appropriate platform.

Title: Folie A Deux
Review: Whether intentional or not, there's a certain glee to FOB's pop absurdity because their cheerfully careless genre-bending has no reverence: fitting all these sounds and jokes into a pop song is all a game and it's one listeners can share, whether they're playing spot-the-allusion or just succumbing to the sugary hooks clustered within one track.

Title: Summer Sun
Review: Summer Sun is a stunner, a subtle but substantial collection of non-sequiturs that displays the scope of Yo La Tengo’s tweaked-out serenity.

Title: Sukierae
Review: Listening to mid-period Wilco was, admittedly, never instantaneous, but you feel a more savage edit would do wonders with Sukierae.

Title: Cupid Deluxe
Review: Across the album, Hynes sings, writes, produces, and plays guitar, bass, keyboards, drums, synths. But this is hardly a solo act. In fact, one of the record's greatest strengths lies in its pitch-perfect deployment of guests.

Title: I Used to Spend So Much Time Alone
Review: The foggy nights of soul chronicled here lend Chastity Belt's bruised indie pop a weight that suits it. [Jun 2017, p.89]

Title: Preternaturals
Review: Whilst the exposure of O’Sullivan and Tucker’s pop heart has been more than welcome, one senses that there are many more sides to this complex, stubbornly esoteric collaboration that are yet to be revealed, and that’s an exciting thought indeed.

Title: Furfour
Review: There's something disarmingly joyous about it with only hints of the darker music that they also create. [Oct 2016, p.99]

Title: Indestructible
Review: Problem is, much of Indestructible, banks on the same old angst-mongering that has fueled a zillion rock-radio hits in the past 10 years.

Title: Elephant Shell
Review: The songs on Elephant Shell are a sensible progression from the Strokes-like hooks of earlier material, showing an increasing sophistication. As with before, the brilliance is in the brevity.

Title: Y Not
Review: The big guns are firing again on his newest release, Y Not, and to good effect.

Title: Raven in the Grave
Review: Hazy, dark, The Cure-ish dreampop with a Lynchian vibe.

Title: Bad Contestant
Review: This record contains meticulous instrumental arrangements and clever storytelling. It is protest music without the cliché heavy rock sound and direct lyrics. Instead Maltese uses satire to place pity upon the world but mostly himself, all delivered with a wry grin and a sparkle in his eye.

Title: MeYouWeYou
Review: MeYouWeYou is an ambitious and confident record from a band with enough smarts to keep one foot in the electronic realm while letting the other roam free.

Title: folklore
