Review: Even if Have You In My Wilderness is Holter's most accessible record to date, it's riddled with enough puzzles, lyrical twists and delicate refinement to remain intriguing listen after listen.

Title: Summer Sun
Review: Few bands are this awake to the possibility that music can be both droning and catchy.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: Less outre than much of Patton's work. [Feb 2013, p.80]

Title: Lost and Safe
Review: This decidedly literate songcraft has a range of ancestors, including Talking Heads, Sparks and David Grubbs, but three albums along, The Books are nailing down a distinctive soundworld of their own. [#254, p.54]

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: The sense of wonder in Fleet Foxes' songs is matched only by the discipline and talent that created this adventurous, evocative record. One which is already shaping up as an album of the year. [July 2008, p.98]

Title: Songs of Innocence
Review: A majority of Songs of Innocence shows the band fumbling around with current chart trends, settling for melodies and lyrics that are simply “good enough,” and generally making moves that reek of desperation instead of confidence, a stance that is very ill-fitting of U2.

Title: Here Come the Tears
Review: Here Come the Tears fits nicely in Anderson and Butler's catalogs and certainly beats anything they've done in the last five years, but it makes matters clear that all they'll ever do is release clones of what they once were.

Title: Wire
Review: Frontman Colin Newman's pointed lyrics can be gloriously dry and the measured melodies of the songs are fine. [May 2015, p.102]

Title: Falling Down a Mountain
Review: The album has a swagger that Tindersticks hasn’t shown since 2001’s "Can Our Love...," finding common ground between the rockier Velvet Underground and the mellower Rolling Stones.

Title: Write Me Back
Review: Sometimes the best results, though, come when Kelly drops the exercise completely.

Title: Bird Dog Dante
Review: For something put together with a supposed casualness, Bird Dog Dante is actually a remarkably industrious--albeit satisfyingly low-key--affair that stands-up as Parish’s most consistent and accessible solo album to date.

Title: Widow City
Review: Widow City goes on for a while--maybe too long. But it's quite a trip [Oct 2007, p.106]

Title: Black Mountain
Review: The disc is truly beautiful on the ears, filled with gorgeous dynamics, crisp, discordant playing and impressive production to boot.

Title: Wiretap Scars
Review: The anthemic cries for getting your crap in order are flavored with dashes of sonic experimentation and the knowledge of when to slow things down.

Title: Herein Wild
Review: It's her relentless musical alchemy that anchors the album, which finally finds Rose being herself, rather than attempting to sound like someone else.

Title: Insignificance
Review: Insignificance is the release that finds him hitting his stride completely, seemingly mixing little bits of all the different styles that he's poked around with and boiling it all down into a cohesive little release.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Days of Abandon
Review: It’s a little too smoothed out and indistinct now--most of the songs are well crafted but a little TOO well crafted.

Title: Ambition
Review: Ambition is just his latest pop grab, and in many respects, it's more realized than his last one.

Title: Tales of Us
Review: The mood is all of a piece, the songs are stronger, and nobody suggests lightening the atmosphere with a high-energy single. [Sep 2013, p.84]

Title: As Light Return
Review: They sound much heavier and quite unburdened by commercial notions. [No. 145, p.61]

Title: Tracing Back the Radiance
Review: Though it's unlike anything he has attempted before, the ambitious sounds of Tracing Back the Radiance still bear the distinctive stamp of his artistry, one that feels restless, nostalgic, and quietly hopeful regardless of the form it takes.

Title: PHOX
Review: Phox and its producer, Brian Joseph (a recording engineer for Bon Iver who worked with the band at Bon Iver’s April Base Studios), make the most of studio flexibility in songs that develop and transform themselves radically as they go.

Title: UNLOCKED
Review: UNLOCKED's best features are its brevity and simplicity. Songs drop in, do what they need to and cycle to an end without melodrama.

Title: Every Open Eye
Review: Every Open Eye goes down smooth, but it’s hard not to miss the moments of exhilaration that used to power the band.

Title: Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys
Review: My Chem's indulgent side still sometimes gets the best of them--the rave synths on "The Only Hope for Me Is You" belong on a different album. But they made a wise choice in closing with "Vampire Money," a No Wave spitball whose opening lyric is an (unprintable) fistful of garlic in the eye of "Twilight's" sexless family-values-noir.

Title: Notes on a Conditional Form
Review: A delightfully overstuffed collection that features some of their best and most immediately pleasing work to date.

Title: The Shade of Poison Trees
Review: Even at their most tragic and at their angriest, most of the tracks on the album are calls to empathy in unexpected scenarios, feeling pain as a means of catharsis and in turn acknowledging the pain in others after turning inward. The results are amazingly beautiful.

Title: The Isness
Review: Once you're name-checking Supertramp and ELO as major influences, it's pretty much over. [Aug 2002, p.114]

Title: The Virgins
Review: At their best, The Virgins come off as a pale imitation of The Cars. At their worst, it’s The Strokes meets Franz Ferdinand without any bite. [Summer 2008]

Title: Revelation
Review: Newcombe, encouragingly, has turned his career around from the dead-end fans feared, and while this may sound more like home studio two years of tracks solo project it is than a band effort, it will satisfy those who have stuck with BJM over the past 20 years, and it seems, will for as long as Newcombe keeps making records, more modest than before, but thoughtfully crafted.

Title: Mirrors the Sky
Review: If you’re hankering for a bit of masochistic pop, Mirrors The Sky will soothe the craving. And then destroy you.

Title: We Started Nothing
Review: Every song on this record pulsates with so many heart-thumping beats per minute, you'd think this was some newfangled cardiovascular exercise for ravers. [Spring 2008, p.99]

Title: Cervantine
Review: Several tunes put the talents of Bradford-based Hladowski siblings Chris and Stephanie to stunning effect on vocals and amplified bouzouki respectively. [Apr 2011, p.75]

Title: Own the Night
Review: Own the Night is mainly notable for the way it papers over emotional cracks (As You Turn Away: "No, we can't be friends/ I don't think I can take seeing you and knowing where we've been") with beige wallpaper.

Title: Exodus of Venus
Review: A welcome if particularly edgy comeback that positions the album as Cook’s finest, most riveting and intensely personal work.

Title: Made in the Manor
Review: While there's nothing here to equal his career-changing hit "P's And Q's," opener "Hail" comes close with its down-and-dirty signature riff. [Apr 2016, p.75]

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: Cat Power for the next generation.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Like Trailer Park, her first full-length, the new Daybreaker is less about melody and being lovely than about instrumentation and experimentation with the elements--electronic, acoustic, and lyrical.

Title: Rare
Review: The record she has delivered to kickstart a new decade is a career defining release, and from a pop star who is firmly back on top of her game.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: Listening to the ramalama of "Slow Drip" and "Hot Tubes" you can't help but cheer them on. [Nov 2010, p.102]

Title: Future Breeds
Review: Even though it's broken up by the occasional plodding piano number, Future Breeds can be a gauntlet of abrasive blasts of energy. Good thing, then, that it's so satisfying to make it out the other side.

Title: Living the Dream
Review: It never quite feels as reckless as you want it to. The car’s being driven more carefully, which might be good for the driver, but it’s less exciting for we passengers.

Title: On Time Out of Time
Review: It's a surprisingly approachable piece with an appeal far outside the experimental music community, which speaks to Basinski's ear for melody and grasp of emotion. Not many artists could turn a source as abstract as black hole recordings into music this beautiful.

Title: Clipper Ship
Review: Though only seven songs long, at least two--“Mallow T’Ward the River” and “One Can Only Love”--offer multiple movements that provide opportunity to explore more exotic environs.

Title: Fear of a Black Tangent
Review: The rapper's inborn goofiness just gives his words more bite. [Mar 2005, p.85]

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Visitor
Review: The best record of the three record of the three recorded with his new and far younger band Promise Of The real, it veers between raw fury an tender melodies. [Feb 2018, p.110]

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: Allen could’ve easily just rehashed the party-girl anthems of "Alright, Still," but while It’s Not Me, It’s You is as full of toe-tappers as Allen’s debut, the new album also has a big chip on its shoulder. Allen clearly has no intention of being mistaken for anybody else.

Title: Simple Songs
Review: It sounds fantastic as a study in symphonic-rock ambition and studio mixing techniques.

Title: Paper Tigers
Review: It isn't until the latter half of the album... that they find their own voice, and one that delivers deliciously sugary powerpop. [Aug 2005, p.102]

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Higher Than The Stars
Review: It helps to show Pains not as period fetishists, but instead a group of indie-pop aesthetes who seem to be able to operate comfortably within several different subdivisions of the genre.

Title: Pain Olympics
Review: With their documentarian dispatches from the meanest streets, Crack Cloud could never be accused of faking it. But the strange beauty of Pain Olympics is that it fills your heart even as it’s kicking you in the kidneys.

Title: Girl on Fire
Review: Girl on Fire is less a portrait of Keys's womanhood at a crossroads as it is another extension of a career spent predominantly navigating straight down the middle of the road.

Title: Thank You Happy Birthday
Review: As the hungover economy slowly gets out of bed and scratches itself, that's just what we need: one big melting pot of a party.

Title: 100 Days, 100 Nights
Review: The crowning achievement, though, comes with a fantastic slice of raw Southern soul, 'Humble Me,' that sounds like it came straight out of Muscle Shoals circa 1969.

Title: Icarus Falls
Review: It’s an inward, headphones-on plug into a young man wrestling with varying levels of success, from codependency and addictive behaviour to self-acceptance. It’s the sound of Zayn grappling with toxic masculinity.

Title: ye
Review: Over seven songs spanning 24 minutes, “Ye” is immediately disturbing (“I Thought About Killing You”), slightly exhilarating (“Yikes”), bafflingly underwhelming (“All Mine,” “Wouldn’t Leave,” and “No Mistakes”), and fleetingly brilliant (“Ghost Town”). The one thing it’s not is coherent.

Title: Echoes
Review: People are claiming The Rapture are geniuses, saviours and innovators but the simple truth is that they aren’t. [Review 1, score=70] One hates to frown on a band’s ambition, but you may find yourself hoping that next time out the band plays to their strengths the whole way through. [Review 2, score=75]

Title: Happy Songs for Happy People
Review: Happy Songs is epic and subtle, technically savvy and emotionally charged and visceral all at once -- in short, it's a summary of everything that is great about Mogwai's music.

Title: Violet Cries
Review: Named after a grim Danish fairy tale, Esben and the Witch pursues a narrow course on their first album, Violet Cries, a morose, pitch-black update of the '80s dark-wave template.

Title: What Now
Review: As a collection, What’s Now is peppy, confident and a little scathing but, like its title, it feels slightly too open-ended to make a real splash.

Title: The Earn
Review: With entertaining lyrics and even better themes, yU draws the listeners to his adventure that is The Earn.

Title: In Each and Every One
Review: [This fifth album] still sounds refreshingly unconventional. [Apr 2014, p.116]

Title: Keep You
Review: Keep You certainly succeeds in lyrical and atmospheric effect; there are just a couple compositional pitfalls that will likely work themselves out at live shows.

Title: Grassed Inn
Review: Grassed Inn anchors itself with sturdy, rhythmic melodies, which is the biggest testament to Blank Realm’s mission of increasing focus and tightening up their ship.

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: Twin Fantasy leaves no doubt that Toledo is a strikingly gifted and thoughtful songwriter who also has a firm grasp of how to make his material work in the studio, and isn't afraid to think on a grand scale.

Title: Sunbather
Review: The result is a perfectly flowing album that is, at times, as calming as it is chaotic.

Title: Raven in the Grave
Review: The untangled pop of In and Out of Control has been reconfigured and dipped in black eyeliner as the Raveonettes veer toward 1980s goth.

Title: Where All Is Fled
Review: At almost 70 minutes, Where All Is Fled may take a few unnecessary detours across its 14 tracks, but it's ultimately Hauschildt's most cohesive work. Here, he's matched his well-established talents as a composer of cosmic ambient with a new depth of artistic direction.

Title: Hunting My Dress
Review: It's far more fun, however, to sit back and appreciate the album as the dawning of a new, unique voice which, through its influences (both obvious and not-so), is blending styles and carving a niche in to the increasingly crowded canon of independent and original female artists.

Title: To the 5 Boroughs
Review: The beats bounce along happily enough... but the stripped-down sound focuses attention on the anti-Bush lyrics, and that proves to be the album's undoing.

Title: The Now Now
Review: Unfortunately, outside of those songs [Humility, Hollywood, Tranz, Sorcererz, and Lake Zurich] (which would have made for an excellent EP) The Now Now falls short, the grit and grandiosity of other Gorillaz records is absent.

Title: Tres Cabrones
Review: The initial feeling that this album is destined to be one of their many jokey, disposable ventures dissipates slightly as Osborne’s near-peerless ability with a brain-alteringly great riff takes hold.

Title: Crows
Review: Moorer's handsome voice is remarkably twangless here. Also remarkable is that the most indelible of her goth-chick musings is the happiest-sounding.

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun
Review: An album packed start to finish with some of Mastodon's best material to date.

Title: Gossip in the Grain
Review: It might alienate those who prefer him to wallow, but there's magic and bravery here. [Dec 2008, p.130]

Title: Cydonia
Review: Cydonia, like much of Orb's output, shows a dual inclination toward ambient backgrounds and melodic, Massive Attack-style foregrounds--a tendency no doubt encouraged by its additional collaborators, who range from a host of engineers to old friend Robert Fripp. However, considering how few electronic acts have translated the indulgences of studio tomfoolery into consistently great records, it's reassuring that Orb has weathered its unplanned hiatus and released another winner.

Title: Love Songs For Robots
Review: As a relaxing musical experience Watson has done a brilliant job.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: This luminously lovely collection is well-judged and intensely personal. [Feb 2013, p.74]

Title: Lost
Review: Simply refusing to be pigeonholed, the Danish producer has managed to stray even further from the lively electronic style that was his making.

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: It's not where you want to spend all of your listening time, but it's comforting at worst and occasionally fantastic.

Title: War Room Stories
Review: What War Room Stories makes clear is that the way forward is further exploration and boundary pushing. Unsurprisingly, given both their sound and their ethos, Breton are not at their best when static, but rather forging ahead--cramming the bare bones of their sound into new and unsuspecting genres and influences.

Title: Pagans in Vegas
Review: It’s too harsh to suggest that the band are coasting, since there are once more fragments of ideas, concepts and melodies which arouse.

Title: Regard the End
Review: In ditching the band ethic, they've tapped into the finest folk gothic traditions of death, suffering, misery and hardship and fashioned a paradoxically uplifting, transformative record of extraordinary power. [Album of the Month, Jul 2003, p.110]

Title: Shlon
Review: Part of Souleyman’s thing is upsetting delicate ears with his so-called vulgarity – it’s music for taxi drivers and party crashers. Likewise these swooning synth stabs may sound kitsch to discerning ravers, but the fun is heroically nonstop. [Jan 2020, p.69]

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: Change Becomes Us is an album throbbing with knowingly restrained anger, but with enough breathing space for it to be thoroughly enjoyed. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.97]

Title: Subjective Concepts
Review: Crushing riffs and ancestral memories of hardcore. [Aug 2015, p.98]

Title: Colorado
Review: The end result is another Neil Young album to add to the pile of the not-bad and the OK he’s amassed over the last decade, while a steady stream of archive releases highlight how great Neil Young can be at his best: as good as any artist in rock history, and certainly better than this.

Title: Safe Trip Home
Review: Lucky, then she's so musically warm and, like its predecessors, Safe Trip Home takes comfort in a sound that almost masks her unrest. Almost. [Dec 2008, p.127]

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: Ingenious in its conception as a soundtrack, weak and tedious as a standalone musical venture, an interminable experience despite its brevity.

Title: Porcelain
Review: Porcelain neither builds on the promise of Wiretap Scars nor cashes in on the band's gifted heritage.

Title: Pray For The Wicked
Review: The poignant album-ending ballad “Dying In LA” makes you wish there had been more tracks showcasing Urie’s pop-transcending emotive vocals.

Title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
Review: With Angel Guts Stewart once again manages to dig his nails into the grubby under layer, not returning with any transgressed beauty but instead stark honesty and brutal truth. You may want to turn away, but you might not be able to.

Title: Soma
Review: It's a smothering, enveloping textural experience, alternately threatening to cocoon or drown the listener.

Title: Parc Avenue
Review: In the end, Parc Avenue finds a band creating some amazing music, but still putting out some feelers along the way.

Title: Everything Now
Review: It leaves you yearning for an album that would have expanded the mature melodicism of those three tracks [“Electric Blue,” “Put Your Money on Me” and “We Don’t Deserve Love”]. Instead, their presence magnifies the smarmy, sophomoric awfulness of everything else here.

Title: Rated O
Review: Of course, it’s much too much, but the fact that it works at all is a testament to their commitment to well-honed rock hypnosis. Good luck finding the front door when it’s done.

Title: The Angels of Light Sing 'Other People'
Review: The mix of the album makes it very clear that any musical backing, inventive and immersive as it may be, is still simply backdrop for Gira's tales.

Title: Havoc and Bright Lights
Review: Morissette's poetic discourse of intimately describing her feelings still abounds, but is elegantly emoted here with cool restraint.

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: This is Devendra Banhart...eclectic and whimsical and poking genres with a stick to see if they'll bite. It's a little mad, a lot overstuffed, and probably a degree or two calculated.

Title: Figure
Review: Moments like Living Up to Let You Down are unforgettable; it’s just a disappointment the rest of the album isn’t even close.

Title: Debris
Review: Occasional flourishes reveal brilliance (‘Lost’, ‘Start Again’), but mostly it’s a homogeneous trudge through palpable emotional intensity. It culminates in some stunning imagery, which makes it worth the journey especially when you consider the relative brevity of the whole thing.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: The album’s 12 bloated, mostly mid-tempo tracks drone on and on, and even when they aren’t technically long they sometimes feel like they might never end because most of them fail to find a hook.
Seven albums in, and with a formula that’s kept its core elements largely the same, it’s largely Beach House by-numbers, but the pair have a gravitational pull that looks like it will never run dry.

Title: The Warning
Review: The slower songs on The Warning have a kind of raggedy, pioneering charm.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: Port of Morrow is transition time for The Shins.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: Despite their retro stylings, this Orange County, California band has served up a sixth album that is better (by leaps and bounds) than the punk-by-numbers that dominated their first two albums, 1989's Offspring and '93's Ignition. Further, Conspiracy has more well-written, hook-laden songs than anything found on their fluke indie hit, '94's fittingly titled Smash, or their too-boring-to-be-a-sell-out 1997 major label debut, Ixnay on the Hombre.

Title: Summer Bones
Review: Their best record yet. [21 Mar 2015, p.54]

Title: Crime Pays
Review: Crime Pays is Cam'ron's triumphant return to form....You also have an overabundance of skits on the album that generally are just there and not entertaining.

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: The songs on this album are echoing, but not distant; they connect on a personal level, and then pull the listener along in a mighty heave.

Title: High Society
Review: For all the divergent styles and blatant hero-worshipping to be found on High Society, the group never sounds derivative or misguided -- a rare feat, proving that despite numerous comparisons, Enon have indeed carved out their own fractured and unique musical identity.

Title: Brute
Review: It’s reminiscent of that doyenne of experimental electronica, Laurie Anderson--and that’s a heck of a compliment.

Title: Smother
Review: The ultimate beauty of Smother, though, comes from its subtlety as Wild Beasts continue to transcend conventional pop music with yet another great addition to their catalog.

Title: Music of the Spheres
Review: The production is perfect - not too cluttered, lush, beats melting beautifully into the now-understated guitar - and his vocals are warm and unpresuming.

Title: Van Lear Rose
Review: Nothing short of remarkable. [Jun 2004, p.102]

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Halcyon Digest is as comforting in its familiar feel as it is startling for its sonic variety.

Title: Man Mountain
Review: Nothing short of astonishing.

Title: In a Dream
Review: MacLean and his collaborators have mastered some but not all of the familiar DFA bag of tricks.

Title: The Massacre
Review: This time around he's tryin' too hard to be everything to everybody. [Apr 2005, p.97]

Title: Signs
Review: They lose their way when they amble in pub-rock fashion on the gormless Hard Case, but for the most part they’re as focused as they’re inspired.

Title: Universal Truths and Cycles
Review: GBV have made a record that should please any fan still listening.

Title: Get Away From Me
Review: So ignore the Doris-Day-meets-Eminem descriptions you’re seeing; this is more like Kate Bush meets Phil Ochs.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: Ragged glories from punk's oddball.

Title: New Bermuda
Review: New Bermuda doesn’t break down the walls of metal, instead it expands its confines, allowing Deafheaven to include subgenres that rarely mix while injecting more outside references. Ultimately, New Bermuda proves just how progressive of a genre metal can be, purists be damned.

Title: Secret Machines
Review: Adding electronic gurgles to heavy, prog-rock power chords, The Secret Machines recalls Rush and Black Sabbath at one end of the sonic spectrum ('The Fire Is Waiting') and David Bowie’s spazzier, punk-era edge at the other ('Atomic Heels'). In between those far-flung atmospheric poles, the band proves they’re more than just the sum of their seamless influences.

Title: Without Your Love
Review: In Without Your Love he shows that he’s evolved from sinister experimentalist to a creator of powerful and highly original songs.

Title: Isla
Review: Isla is nothing revolutionary. That's not to say that its originality is completely lost, but perhaps a touch more adventure and earnest into the mix would change the Portico Quartet's breeze into something much more powerful.

Title: Allas Sak
Review: While the execution has at times wavered over the years, Allas Sak finds the band fully re-engaged in the sound that it has staked out over the past decade--performing music that’s still as beautiful, optimistic, strange, and singular as ever.

Title: Stray
Review: M uch of ‘Stray’ could do with heeding its own advice; instead Bambara stay firmly on a strong but fairly predictable path.

Title: Close To The Glass
Review: Clatter arises from songs and songs from clatter, and it's maddening how so many of them seem to randomly end before committing to actual endings.

Title: Music For the Quiet Hour / The Drawbar Organ EPs
Review: There's so much blood and soul poured into Music for the Quiet Hour that it almost feels effortless. Along with the fascinatingly fragmented Drawbar Organ EPs, the box set presents what's either a closing chapter or a new beginning in the career of one of electronic music's most luminous illuminati.

Title: Cocoon Crush
Review: Cocoon Crush is, partly, the album that you’d imagine Future Sound Of London’s Lifeforms might have become if they’d had a million times the processing power at their disposal. Poised and composed. [Dec 2018, p.45]

Title: Laughter's Fifth
Review: Comes across as kinda dull.

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: Fleet Foxes is certainly a very good record, but it is kept from greatness by its failure to capture the communal feeling of its excellent, buzz-building live shows.

Title: Other People's Problems
Review: The results are atmospheric, rough around the edges but captivating, unique and extraordinary.

Title: Faith and Courage
Review: Faith and Courage speaks with the jaw-clenched directness for which O'Connor is both famous and infamous.... an album of approachable pop that's both defiant and diverse and that flaunts rock's swagger, electronica's experimentalism, folk's introspection and hip-hop's social critique.

Title: Who I Am
Review: N Jo’s fan base doesn’t care about calculation. They’re just the right age to buy into the workmanlike quasi-genuine rock of Who I Am. And there’s still enough of that original Jonas flavour to keep them interested.

Title: Bitter Tea
Review: Despite the oddball showpieces, the Furnaces have refocused the lens on their homemade-pop kaleidoscope, and the result is a unversally resonant album that's not just more joyful than it's companion; it's also more essential. [Jul 2006, p.192]

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: This sequel ups their ante further; there's inventiveness here that rivals Girls Aloud producers Xenomania. [Apr 2009, p.103]

Title: This Is Happening
Review: The ghosts of some of the greats are there for sure, but in the end, This Is Happening sounds like no one except LCD Soundsystem.

Title: Hyperion
Review: If it seems unfair to judge Hyperion’s weaknesses against the work of Lévy’s supposed peers, it’s equally frustrating that he hasn’t yet given us a real idea of who he is as an artist.

Title: forevher
Review: Steeped in vivid details of a queer romance, Forevher partners jubilant pop with its ideal mate: physically charged songs of electric devotion.

Title: Temper
Review: Temper is rewarding in a conventional way compared to the surprise of Precis, less something iridescent found in the sand and more the product of resourceful and masterly design.

Title: The Glass Passenger
Review: Jack's Mannequin frontman Andrew McMahon sticks to his formula of friendly piano and new-wave-influenced beats on his second album.

Title: Microshift
Review: The adherence to krautrockin’ repetition remains, but the proto-punk engine has been replaced by electronic loops and glacial synths. Suddenly, a band that once sounded most at home in strobe-lit basement dives now sounds primed for a late-afternoon slot at your roving summer festival of choice.

Title: Further Out
Review: Best of 2015? Maybe not, as Cloakroom could do well to add just a bit more variety to their sound. Nonetheless, they’re off to a rather auspicious start, as Further Out refines positive aspects of their debut EP and ups the production value immensely.

Title: Mountain Battles
Review: Mountain Battles is marginally more polished than "Title TK" but it still sounds as if it was recorded in one take in Steve Albini’s toilet. A good thing, as it turns out. The intimacy of is what makes it precious.

Title: Tired of Hanging Around
Review: Experimental it ain't, but this summer in a shiny flat box it is.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: You don't have to agree with the prognosis (even Nas has a change of heart by the end) to relish the furious eloquence with which it's delivered.

Title: Something to Die For
Review: The record as a substantial body of work comes complete with up-tempo numbers that are danceable but without an enticing hook, a few straightforward pop/rock tunes with tremendous choruses, and an album ending ballad that renders the album slightly indifferent, inconsistent and lacking an underlying direction and purpose.

Title: Mala
Review: So with equal amounts killer and filler doled out, Mala is a cake that comes across as half-baked.

Title: Dead Reckoning
Review: The contrasts of light/dark, father/son and sinners/saints never sounded so danceable. [Mar 2011, p.92]

Title: Permalight
Review: A jarring, but refreshing, makeover.

Title: There Is Love in You
Review: Hebden has yet again created a wonderful space where he can rightfully be called sui generis.

Title: American Saturday Night
Review: Here's an album where the marriage ballads are so meaty and convincing that the two exceptionally well-turned breakup songs seem like formal exercises, where a comedy number about fishing and beer would sound just dandy if there weren't so many subtler laughs on the agenda.

Title: Hiss Spun
Review: Though Hiss Spun probably won't end up as the best of her career, it may well be Wolfe's best so far.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: Taken as a whole, Animal Joy maintains the quality of Shearwater's earlier outings without quite taking things to the next level they're eminently capable of achieving.

Title: Black Bubblegum
Review: As with all of Copeland's records, surprising angles and intriguing touches are strewn throughout. But this is also an incredibly fun record, which is enough reason to play it over and over.

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: It's a conservative, preservative move by men who needed to reclaim their ground. But playing by those rules, Metallica wins.

Title: Songs of Praise
Review: Whether they're sophisticated or visceral, Shame's energy and confidence makes Songs of Praise an exciting debut from one of the most vital-sounding British rock bands of the late 2010s.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: It’s an absolute tour de force, a record full of drama and emotion and pleasure and pain.

Title: Orcas
Review: Orcas provides much to engage fans of both Irisarri and Pioulard, as well as lovers of languid, abstracted pop song craft.

Title: Living with Yourself
Review: To say that Living With Yourself is more closely related to the better solo efforts of Michael Rother or the breezy atmospherics of the Durutti Column would be accurate (and somewhat faint) praise, but it would fall short of recognizing just how versatile McGuire makes his instrument sound.

Title: Peer Amid
Review: The sound is physically propulsive, enveloping and mildly psychoactive. The beat pounds hard on the most lizardly parts of the brain, bringing a catharsis, a sheer rush of physicality.

Title: Human Conditions
Review: Ashcroft's mastery of balladry makes "Buy It in Bottles" his best since the Verve's "Lucky Man."

Title: Soused
Review: Although occasional representational sounds intrude on some tracks, it is Sunn O)))’s glacial, thundering voice that carries Walker’s conceptual project forward.

Title: Destiny Fulfilled
Review: There are simply too many stodgy slowies. [13 Nov 2004, p.57]

Title: Sirens
Review: He doesn't reveal many new tricks, but his knowledge of his own palette is masterful in every moment. More poetic and thoughtful than ever before, Jaar maintains an ability to fit seemingly disparate sounds together as if they were always meant to find each other.

Title: Hands
Review: For an album with crowded electro-pop instrumentation, the music isn't overbearing, and Little Boots' cheeky lyrics never lose any of their dry attitude.

Title: A Better Tomorrow
Review: RZA does his fair share of huffing and puffing on A Better Tomorrow (see hooks to 'Hold The Heater' and 'Crushed Egos'), but the widescreen production lacks the intensity to motivate a jaded clan.

Title: Emotional Mugger
Review: To call Emotional Mugger a celebration of excess, as sweet as it is, would miss the mark. (Although it’s no veiled warning, either--it enjoys itself too much.) No, this is a bender with an undercurrent of anxiety.

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: The collection instead represents more of an expansion on their current sound and scope, and finds a band still willing to take risks 40 years into an exalted career--still not caring what we think of it, but daring us to follow them where they lead before the Wire factory goes quiet once again.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: Overall, the writing feels sharper and stronger. Every chorus clicks, the melodies are uniformly beautiful, and they soar and swoop, the better to demonstrate Del Rey's increased confidence in her voice.

Title: Wilder Mind
Review: Marcus Mumford leaves his Irish-folk years behind and adopts a transatlantic burr for “The Wolf”, whose chugging riff and sappy lyrics (“You are all I’ve ever longed for”) pinpoint the album’s core failings: absences of both lateral intrigue and the elemental oomph its track-titles (“Broad-Shouldered Beasts”, indeed) hint at.

Title: Free at Last
Review: On Free at Last, he demonstrates that being forced to cool his heels since 2003 hasn't dulled the rough edges of his appealingly hectic flow.

Title: Now We Can See
Review: The album isn't a total disaster, though, there are a few songs that manage to overcome the record's flaws and deliver some excitement.

Title: Title TK
Review: Skeletal, fragmented, stumblebum, Kim and Kelley retain their knack for righting themselves with a tuneburst just when you thought they'd never do the limbo again.

Title: Burning the Threshold
Review: The music on Burning the Threshold is simply good--easy and reassuring, maybe, but masterful and in many places downright gorgeous, too.

Title: Brunei
Review: Williams manages to retain the transportative element of his previous work while slightly neatening the edges.

Title: Smoke
Review: Williams' songs are extremely repetitive, relying on MAX/MSP texture for their variance but proceeding at such a pace that it's easy to zone out, a tendency exacerbated by Williams' apparent three-note vocal range. [Fall 2007, p.77]

Title: The Happiness Waltz
Review: The music appears deceptively simple and unabashedly blithe at times, but regardless, the emotional undercurrent clearly comes through.

Title: Songs in the Key of Animals
Review: A Tuesday afternoon pool party of a record, Songs in the Key of Animals sounds like a great time was had by all, but that you kind of had to be there to appreciate it.

Title: Wonder Where We Land
Review: He’s proven mastery over his craft and shown that he can work with just about anyone and still put out some of the best product on the market.

Title: Zeroes QC
Review: Suuns' debut LP is pieced together from a few decent ideas and a lot of bad ones.

Title: Bleed Like Me
Review: Humongous hooks. [15 Apr 2005, p.77]

Title: 200 Million Thousand
Review: Yes, there are jokes and doo-woppy moments of light-heartedness, but this is a soupy, stoned, distressed-sounding album at odds with the Lips’ image as the world’s premier party band.

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: It's kind of cool, kind of confusing, and kind of boring.

Title: Endless Scroll
Review: Endless Scroll sets out to shake the listener from their complacency, because in this age there’s just no time for ambivalence. It’s a fantastic debut from one of the most exciting new bands around.

Title: Soul Journey
Review: It's the songs not the approach which set her apart. [Aug 2003, p.116]

Title: Bad as Me
Review: Though Waits holds a reserved seat in the small club of artists who don't put out bad albums, the whiff of wild youth hangs around Bad as Me as if it was recorded in back alleys, behind churches, and in bars after hours.

Title: Weirdon
Review: Purling Hiss’s rough but accessible rock, made with craftsmanship and taste, does a difficult thing. It pleases old indie-heads just as easily as it can draw in the new kids.

Title: Honky Tonk
Review: This recording feels more like a pleasant diversion rather than a necessity.

Title: Invasion of Privacy
Review: It’s not perfect, but the album is remarkably cohesive, the right length, and filled to the brim with songs that already feel like inevitable summer smashes.

Title: Take Care
Review: The result is both silkily seductive and moodily narcissistic.

Title: Revolutions Per Minute
Review: There's something magical about pairing Talib with Hi-Tek on production that transcends his already almost unlimited lyrical potential and creates an extraordinary experience.

Title: Leaves Turn Inside You
Review: A unique, epic effort from one of the most inventive and dynamic rock bands in recent memory.

Title: X&Y
Review: X & Y is uninspired adult pop that drops jaws only in its capacity to elicit yawns.

Title: Scream
Review: What we get when we put the pieces together: an album where every single song is approximately the same length; an album where you could take apart any one track, combine those segments with other stray bits of the album, and still have the same basic entity you started with; an album whose choruses consist of phrases like “No, that bitch ain’t a part of me” repeated eight times; an album that, above all else, does not want you to think about it too hard.

Title: Be Myself
Review: It may not be her finest set, but it captures the light/dark spirit that informed Crow’s best music and is a worthy addition to an already impressive catalog.

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: This is Coldplay getting in, delivering the tune, getting out, influenced by the discipline of cutting-edge R&B but still capable of testing arena acoustics with some supermassive bluster, glitterball lustre and classic Buckland glide'n'twiddle. [Dec 2011, p.46]

Title: Falcon
Review: There's an engaging sense of uncertainty running through these songs. [Mar 2010, p.96]

Title: Hot Shit!
Review: Coomes' slide work is effective and expressive. [#7, p.93]

Title: Earth to the Dandy Warhols
Review: [They've delivered] a spawling 70-minute opus devoid of drive or inspiration. [Oct 2008, p.83]

Title: Critical Equation
Review: The deep, pulled-back grooves of Critical Equation reveal the harnessed intensity of the songs and performances so deliberately that their myriad pleasures and embedded hooks will sneak up on you. [Jun 2018, p.27]

Title: I Need a New War
Review: The rambling nature of Finn’s delivery adds to the immersive storytelling, where listeners are focused on Finn’s lyrics--and what’s going to happen next to the characters in these stories--rather than worrying about hooks, riffs, or even the music at all. That isn’t to say that the album offers nothing in that area, but when Finn decides to figuratively dot his i’s, it feels like you’ve arrived at a momentous occasion.

Title: Black Soul Choir
Review: Sadly, the Norwegians promptly undo much of their good work by interspersing the bombastic rocking with acoustic cobblers like ‘Lovescared’ and the sort of excessive, pompous emoting that even Pearl Jam tend to avoid these days.

Title: Seeing Through Sound (Pentimento Volume Two)
Review: Seeing Through Sound doesn’t quite enrapture like Hassell’s 1977 debut Vernal Equinox or Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics, his renowned collaboration with Brian Eno, but it’s a satisfying, fully invested work.

Title: PUNK
Review: New cute or not, CHAI make a pretty strong blend of all the best bits.

Artist: I Love You But I've Chosen Darkness
Title: Fear Is on Our Side
Review: From note one, the listener is hermetically sealed into Chosen Darkness' unique musical universe where overdriven bass leads, pinpoint guitar lines and ominous synths hit with maximum impact.

Title: Jessica Rabbit
Review: The "uh oh"s that punctuate "Hyper Dark"'s shattered balladry hint at Jessica Rabbit's state of emergency, while "Torn Clean" is one of the band's prettiest songs yet. Contrasts like these have been Sleigh Bells' modus operandi since the beginning, but Jessica Rabbit's mix of brashness and finesse proves they can still thrill.

Title: All The Roadrunning
Review: It's got some fine, graceful tunes. [May 2006, p.128]

Title: Felt 3: A Tribute to Rosie Perez
Review: Aesop Rock proves he's also a viable beatsmaker--his spacey, highly textured production is easily the best in the Felt series so far. Slug's rhymes are better than anything on the last few Atmosphere joints and MURS is on point, as always. [Dec 2009, p.113]

Title: When I Have Fears
Review: With more than enough flagrant energy to satiate the average punk, The Murder Capital—still—is most affecting through its delicate and understatedly sad musings on life and death. In fact, the rest of the record sees the band tap into poetic introversion that is both broad enough to latch onto, yet intimate enough to impress your own experiences and fears.

Title: Calico Review
Review: They appear to have tired of Love and have been listening to far more Velvet Underground. [Oct 2016, p.105]

Title: Shine On
Review: If you get a kick out of glorious, ragged old rock'n'roll, then you'll consider it essential.

Title: Liz Phair
Review: Worst of all, the album closes with three decent songs, reminders of Phair's talent that are muted by what's come before.

Title: Come Back to Us
Review: This 13-track disc can be heard as a welcome return to basics. [Aug 2011, p.118]

Title: Trees Outside The Academy
Review: The album allows acoustic guitar to be the rule more than the exception. And the sublime melodies on 'Never Day' and 'Honest James' shine. Naturally, you can't take the boy out of art-school.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: A great album full of songs both uplifting and danceable, emotional and cerebral.

Title: Articulation
Review: At a time when mainstream house music is becoming more connected with both its past and the underground scene, ‘alternative’ interpretations like this are quickly becoming stale, and Articulation too often sounds as if it’s merely going through the motions.

Title: Beta Love
Review: This album may have been a growing pain in their attempt to evolve past their initial signature baroque pop, but it sounds like they missed a few steps that needed to be taken.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel
Review: Tell Me How You Really Feel is a wonderfully curated record, which manages to be both cynical and whimsical at the same time. The depth of musical ambition and of poetic expression deserve a suitably large audience’s attention.

Title: Own Side Now
Review: Rose still has plenty of time and room to grow, and across Own Side Now she sounds at times in search of a singular voice yet also utterly confident in her band, her arrangements, and her songs.

Title: A Hand Through the Cellar Door
Review: It may be a bit platitudinous, but Temple's delicate voice and songwriting make it an enjoyable listening experience.

Title: MTMTMK
Review: Their second still bears that warmth and immediacy ... but the decision to supercharge so many tracks with clubbier beats – in other words, to make them sound a lot more like the rest of the charts – is disappointing.

Title: Man About Town
Review: Containing 10 songs and with a running time of 30 minutes, it’s tantalisingly brief but never short of quality.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: Krug is a songwriter whose craft is best when met with the editing of other musicians--left to himself, however, we are left with a very forgettable retreat into his very OMD-obsessed psyche.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: Vulnicura is humanity at its most volatilely sublime.

Title: Black Origami
Review: What emerges is a baroque topography of movement and energy, culled from the explosion of an ultra-specific cultural context outwards, and then back into the dusk.

Title: Fool
Review: It's not easy to grasp at first, but it reveals van Dinther as a restless creative spirit, and seems to only hint at the directions his artistic career could take in the future.

Title: 9 Dead Alive
Review: 9 Dead Alive has strength, beauty and often a spirit of engagement with the tenebrous. At times, dialogues areunresolved, yet despite (because of?) this, there is vital music-making from two uncompromising artists.

Title: Evil Friends
Review: The songs themselves don’t shine through the production.

Title: Nothing's Real
Review: As with the best pop albums, it sounds like a greatest hits record. The songs flow into each other seamlessly as well as standing on their two own feet, which is an astonishing achievement.

Title: The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me
Review: Brand New took a huge step forward in 2003 with Deja Entendu, tossing away everything predictable about emo. But the leap on their third studio album is even bigger, and gutsier too: using rock’s earthly forces to amplify the heart’s greatest loves and fears, and in the process summoning the kind of grandeur that blows minds in bedrooms and raises fists in stadiums.

Title: The Last Rocket
Review: It may not bother the charts in quite the same way as ‘Slide’ did, but it’s more than enough to remind us that we should dismiss Takeoff, the solo artist, at our peril.

Title: Celestite
Review: The five tracks amble and pulsate and plod along in a way that feels consistent with the band and the genre.

Title: Rounds
Review: One of the essential electronic platters of the year. [#5, p.106]

Title: Wild Ones
Review: If you play this album really loud – and leave your brain marinating in formaldehyde on a shelf for a half-hour – it's crudely effective. Play it a second time, and you may want to kill yourself.

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: It's frustrating, because if you took Our Ill Wills' best moments and condensed them into an EP we'd easily be talking an eight or nine, but as it is, the second Shout Out Louds LP is a Jekyll and Hyde record that ultimately flatters to deceive.

Title: Good Grief
Review: Voices this vast require production just as epic and Shawn Everett (Weezer, Alabama Shakes, Julian Casablancas) brings the wattage of a Celine Dion Las Vegas spectacle without it feeling shallow or cheesy.

Title: For Now
Review: Some may scoff at the limited musical palette on tracks such as the La's-like Lazy Love, but beneath the bluff exterior beats the heart of a great pop band. [Jun 2018, p.109]

Title: Signed And Sealed In Blood
Review: This one may be their most devil-may-care, mixing hardcore blitz, Pogues instrumentation and Thin Lizzy swing.

Title: Deceiver
Review: Deceiver isn’t your Oshin or Is the Is Are, not by a longshot. Yet, while certain touchstones are present that give away that this is in fact DIIV, in a much larger sense we’re observing a band operating unlike they have before, and in the midst of that shift, they execute it stunningly.

Title: Endlessly
Review: It's when Duffy and co stop trying so hard that the album fairs best. [Jan. 2011, p. 100]

Title: Emotional Technology
Review: He's too reserved as a solo performer to keep things interesting. [5 Sep 2003, p.77]

Title: The Gus
Review: An album of odd stories, loose ends, beautiful turns of lyrical and musical phrase. We should be grateful for Mark Mulcahy, and for the persistent weirdness of The Gus.

Title: Love & Devotion
Review: The past is somehow devoured, processed and regurgitated to form a completely refreshing and new substance; this is heavenly stuff that marks a departure from the modern sound.

Title: Shrines
Review: Purity Ring have pulled off the feat of producing one of the year's most arresting debuts – a Grimm Tales for the 2010s, shrouded in the illusory threads of contemporary club music – while sounding like no-one else but themselves.

Title: All This Sounds Gas
Review: Like early Pavement tracks, PSOI's songs find pop hooks almost in spite of themselves.

Title: No Time for Dreaming
Review: Bradley, a 62-year-old ex-plumber and James Brown impersonator, has a raspy, infinitely pained voice but there doesn't appear to be any real interaction between him and the band.

Title: Hormone Lemonade
Review: A winning melange of tinny disco beats, retro-futuristic textures and layers of synth, it’s by far their most cohesive work to date; in its less inspired moments it feels literally (and presumably intentionally) monotonous, but at its best it’s an immersive, absorbing listen.

Title: The Trials of Van Occupanther
Review: The Trials of Van Occupanther is a beautiful piece of moody ambience, and an enchanting album that ultimately continues to reveal itself even after numerous listens. [#14]

Title: Everything Must Go
Review: Their signature tension between black blues gestures adn white boy harmonies has never been more vividly exploited than here. It'll keep you busy for months. [Jun 2003, p.95]

Title: Unity Band
Review: One of Metheny's best releases in recent times.

Title: Vices & Virtues
Review: If you were expecting some kind of creative transformation from the shakeup, this new album may be something of a disappointment, as Urie and drummer Spencer Smith return to the skittish, bombastic pop-rock of their debut.

Title: Soft Fall
Review: While this is a remarkably process-oriented album, Soft Fall is also some of Barthmus' most engaging work, especially on the tracks where tight song structures give form and contrast to his grandiose tendencies.

Title: Stadium Arcadium
Review: There's hardly any doodling or misfiring to undermine the sheer vastness of Stadium Arcadium.

Title: Together
Review: Together is the flawless execution of can't-shake-loose melodies, genius arrangements (oh, those group harmonies!) and production that leaves you energized.

Title: How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb
Review: Even at their most glibly bombastic, there's a melancholy undertow that they can't shake. [Album of the Month, Dec 2004, p.136]

Title: Desperate Ground
Review: By daring to show a bit of personality, the Thermals continue to prove themselves in today's musical landscape.

Title: Lost Time
Review: Their debut LP for Thrill Jockey feels more tightly composed.

Title: Felt
Review: Felt is a transportative album, a balm for troubled minds.

Title: Future Teenage Cave Artists
Review: If Future Teenage Cave Artists is the only cultural artifact left behind in an apocalypse, future generations will at least have an interesting scripture to use to rebuild.

Title: jj nÂ° 3
Review: It's the explicit handcrafted quality, indie rocks's loose regulations on sharp and flat, and a charming naivete that jj continue to pull off, despite their winking appropriations. [Winter 2010, p.63]

Title: VOL. 4 :: SLAVES OF FEAR
Review: It invents one of its own. Which at times makes for an unnerving and uneasy listen. Although stripped to a three-piece these days, the deafening crashes of percussion coupled with blistering pockets of pedal-induced noise aren't any less apparent.

Title: Darkness Rains
Review: There is just enough fun stuff with the band's basic sound and their occasional add-on instruments to make Darkness Rains an easy listen. But there isn't enough good stuff to make it a particularly memorable album. So it ends up being a record with a cool basic sound that doesn't stick with the listener for any length of time.

Title: New View
Review: Warm guitar and melted Wurlitzer electric piano help Friedberger's songs breathe and stretch into occasional instrumental bridges and codas. It's a more subdued record in general.

Title: Guider
Review: Much of what lends the album distinction is the tension created between the band's bold, confident projections and the more delicate core at their center. At times, that tension can be disorienting.

Title: Let It Come Down
Review: Let It Come Down is another masterfully made Spiritualized album, but its very ambitions sometimes overwhelm it.

Title: Year of the Gentleman
Review: 'Why Does She Stay,' forms the front end of a two-track patch of glorious gloom--the album's center, both literally and figuratively--complemented by 'Fade into the Background,' where he watches the one who got away get married.

Title: HITNRUN Phase Two
Review: While Prince is raging against the dying of the light, there exists no graceful innovation on HITNRUN Phase Two. Instead, Prince presents only an aped version of his one-time vitality.

Title: Atlas Vending
Review: The expansiveness of the sonic palette on Atlas Vending just gives the band more room to paint outside the lines. [Aug - Oct 2020, p.87]

Title: Now You Are One of Us
Review: Sure, 2004's God Bless Your Black Heart may be the Paper Chase's best album in terms of accessibility, but the band has taken its usual dark angle and bent it another hundred or so degrees toward further obtuseness.

Title: The Blade
Review: Her third LP imagines a 2015 mainstream by reflecting what it once was--Loretta and Dolly in the Sixties, sure, but also Emmylou in the Eighties and Reba in the Nineties.

Title: Tyrannosaurus Hives
Review: Tyrannosaurus Hives lacks its predecessor's cohesive vision, but it finds the band in excellent form, exploring universes beyond their own. One of the year's best.

Title: Stone Rollin
Review: Stone Rollin's rhythm-and-blues revival can't obscure Saadiq's songwriting talents.

Title: You Are There
Review: Another instrumental masterpiece. [Jun 2006, p.192]

Title: The Libertines
Review: The Libertines is a record of such raw autobiographical honesty that it carries a weight few others in 2004 can match. [Album of the Month, Sep 2004, p.94]

Title: Evil Heat
Review: Where Kraftwerk, MC5, and Miles Davis used to tempt them to excess, here the production unites their diverse influences, every track attacking the speakers like an angry lunatic thrashing against the walls of a poorly soundproofed room.

Title: Paper Gods
Review: While no reinvention, Paper Gods is both entertaining ad typically Duran-esque. [Oct 2015, p.75]

Title: The Tipping Point
Review: What the album lacks in ambition and social commentary it makes up for with deep soul.

Title: Universal Truths and Cycles
Review: The best songs have concise melodies and a likeable punch. The worst just sound like sketches, riffs a more traditionally ambitious group would have discarded. [#8, p.116]

Title: Traps
Review: While pleasant enough on a superficial level, the band's third full-length, Traps, falls short of the kind of coherent, compelling vision that would lift them up from intermittently-engaging mediocrity.

Title: City Sun Eater in the River Of Light
Review: A comfortable but nonetheless adventurous next step for this secretly brilliant band. [No. 131, p.61]

Title: Forget
Review: Although Forget might not usher in a new musical era, it's a near-flawless album and certainly one of the most impressive debuts we've ever seen. It might not change your life, but it will bury itself deep into your brain and make you feel good and warm for a couple of days.

Title: Yellow & Green
Review: A thrilling hard-rock epic.

Title: Means
Review: Means is shadowed and dizzying, sour and fleeting. The album captures the essence of an indie sound that's almost universally considered to be jaded, and proves that the genre may be weatherworn, but its framework is ripe for a renovation.

Title: Lenses Alien
Review: While they mainly hit a balance between shifting symphonics, subtle keys and pyroclastic guitar, sometimes--such as on "Plainclothes," a ballad/disco/punk-funk/noise jigsaw--there's just too much going on.

Title: Moonshine Freeze
Review: Stables’ impressive singing and highly mulled-over songwriting ensure that her creativity remains front-and-center, no matter who’s in the room with her. That said, her work is so intricate that some listeners might not find Moonshine Freeze under their skin all that quickly.

Title: Evolution
Review: Slum Village has little to say lyrically.

Title: Loose
Review: She’s found the perfect collaborator to match her voracious appetite for all things pop.

Title: Kykeon
Review: We might have heard these tropes a thousand times before, but on Kykeon, Rhyton use them to make something richer and more nimble than the flabby freak-out-by-numbers psych that's currently clogging up rock's bandwidth.

Title: Pursuit of Momentary Happiness
Review: Pursuit of Momentary Happiness isn’t as consistent as its predecessor, but its moments of punk gusto find Yak at their mightiest peak.

Title: John Wizards
Review: This is music that's instantly, wordlessly evocative while also invitingly open-ended. [No. 102, p.57]

Title: Silk Rhodes
Review: [A] wonderfully scrappy debut. [Feb 2015, p.95]

Title: The Universe Inside
Review: The Universe Inside might not be insanely memorable as a whole, but will still make for recurrent vivid flashbacks in the days after you’ve listened to it.

Title: Candy Salad
Review: This album will make for a perfectly amicable spring soundtrack, but in terms of a long-term shelf life it's be hard to imagine Candy Salad making it through the sweat and debauchery of the summer festival circuit in one relevant piece.

Title: Historian
Review: Even the less bristling episodes feel luminous and ecstatic, but mostly the magnificent Historian thrives on tension. [Apr 2018, p.94]

Title: Winchester Cathedral
Review: The complete, sublime magic that the band unequivocally showed in their earlier work is a little diluted here. [#7]

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: His latest fizzes with energy and smarts, and sees him letting his imagination off the leash to irresistible effect. [Jul 2016, p.70]

Title: Stay Positive
Review: Reliability is the Hold Steady's calling card, and on Stay Positive they don't stray far from the tried-and-tested combination of orthodox guitar rock and gritty, observational lyrics.

Title: Heron Oblivion
Review: It’s the pastoral style of Pentangle overlaid with crazed early-70s wah-wah duelling--think a pistols-at-dawn affaire d’honneur between Larry Wallis and Mick Bolton--and it’s very good indeed.

Title: Aphrodite
Review: Aphrodite is the work of someone who knows exactly what her skills are and who to hire to help showcase them to perfection.

Title: Peasant
Review: His overgrown rustic dream, though, is oddly modern and littered with fly-tipped rubbish, with free-ranging neo-folk mini-dramas drawing parallels between imagined past and haunted present. [Aug 2017, p.103]

Title: Lemonade
Review: Lemonade is Beyoncé at her most benevolent, and her most unadulterated. Treating her blackness not as an affliction but a celebratory beacon, Lemonade is a long overdue, cathartic retribution.

Title: Universal Truths and Cycles
Review: Universal Truths is not as raw overall as GBV's earliest efforts, but it seems much closer to their wonderfully chaotic live sound than the last couple of records have. [July 2002, p.104]

Title: Coolaid
Review: The Long Beach rapper hasn’t evolved much from his early years, but that lack of development is negligible when he does the West Coast sound so much justice.

Title: The Lillywhite Sessions
Review: He overthinks the rambling "JTR" and overstuffs the messy collage "Monkey Man."[Dec 2018, p.33]

Title: Load Blown
Review: Because the sound is based on repetition, yet it bounces off every wall it touches, the album can be like a bad trip inside the mind of a schizophrenic and new listeners may not be ready, but for the others who’ve supported the band in the past, it can be a welcome respite from the sound they’re used to.

Title: Chris
Review: Like Chris’ persona, the album is lean, unashamedly self-aggrandising and thrillingly audacious. Here, pop is a transformative power. Subverting male privilege to her own advantage, Chris has built an album of tunes that could not only top charts, but also change worlds.

Title: Beware
Review: This clash of the sincere and the facetious that makes Beware such a disconcerting album.

Title: The Suburbs
Review: With beats this straight and stolid, you'd better keep the anthems coming, and they do, almost.

Title: Varshons
Review: This is the real key to understanding Varshon: it can’t be a truly cynical attempt to recapture former glory because it’s too half-assed.

Title: Never Trust a Happy Song
Review: The more you listen, the worse it gets.

Title: Arctic Thunder
Review: Arctic Thunder is an honest, heavy and crushing effort.

Title: Causers of This
Review: Unlike, say, Memory Tapes though, Bundick doesn’t burn straight for a memorable hook, the pop elements of Causers of This trickling slowly from a frame that’s shaped primarily upon forms usually spied and assimilated by artists operating in more dance-savvy circles.

Title: I Don't Run
Review: This is the album where Hinds become a great band. They've got the songs, they've got the attitude, and they've got the sound; all their potential has been realized and it's a joy to experience.

Title: Bloom
Review: Where once this cut deep, extended, it discloses itself merely as pleasant and pleasantly familiar.

Title: True North
Review: With its high-minded lyrical concerns, its family-sized choruses and its authors' buoyant pursuit of what, in lesser hands, could be a restrictive musical form, True North is a superior addition to Bad Religion's already towering body of work.

Title: Le Noise
Review: Le Noise demands more effort than some listeners might be willing to put in, but at its best, it repays that effort pretty handsomely. In that sense at least, it pretty much sums up Neil Young's entire career.

Title: Sock It to Me
Review: With the increased polish and sheen, one can't help thinking that some of the charm is lost. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.103]

Title: Give Up Your Dreams
Review: In choosing to move down a more percussive path, the Phoenix Foundation set themselves a challenge quite different than those they had previously faced. 80-minute double albums are usually tough to follow, but they've chosen to reconnect with the spirit of the band rather than try to top 'Fandango' in a self-conscious manner, and in doing so have redefined themselves.

Title: The Black Dirt Sessions
Review: It's not the album that will define Deer Tick as a force in their own right, or McCauley as a songwriter on a par with his heroes, but The Black Dirt Sessions is the best set yet from this still-rising quintet.

Title: Centralia
Review: Much like the best of Eno's ambient work, Centralia is captivating without demanding attention, instead letting the listener wander into its web on their own.

Title: Migration
Review: A mind-expanding trip for sonic explorers. [Mar 2017, p.107]

Title: American Head
Review: Though the current incarnation of the Flaming Lips has been together since 2014, and thus responsible for these various digressions, the band has undertaken a sonic overhaul here that matches the emotional, sentimental tenor of Coyne and Steven Drozd’s new compositions.

Title: Black Mountain
Review: Black Mountain are about as referential as they come. But despite the obvious touchstones-- which, incidentally, fucking rule-- the band are affable and idiosyncratic enough to win over those who passed on recent retrofits like Comets on Fire's Blue Cathedral or My Morning Jacket's It Still Moves, and make those records' admirers practically cream themselves.

Title: The Unseen In Between
Review: Straightforward but elliptical; direct but enduringly rich; the unseen, in between. [Feb 2019, p.86]

Title: Food
Review: Food is good-time party fare packed with feeling; many of these songs would blend right in on a Soul Jazz compilation of rhythm and blues rarities.

Title: I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass
Review: Good luck finding a better straight-up indie-pop/indie-rock record this year (save TV On The Radio) that's as uninhibited, unique, and flawlessly all-over-the-place as I Am Not Afraid Of You And I Will Beat Your Ass.

Title: A Little Bit Longer
Review: Luckily, the New Jersey trio also continues to bolster its puppy-love perspective with an increasingly substantial brand of power pop that grows more palatable to the general population with each release.

Title: Take Me Home and Make Me Like It
Review: The Munster release makes for occasionally uncomfortable listening. [Sep 2017, p.66]

Title: Loney, Noir
Review: This is comfort music, and comfort never goes out of style. And while the aura of dreamy romantic abstraction is the same, Svanängen distinguishes himself from his peers on the structural level.

Title: El Camino
Review: The brilliance of El Camino lies in the fact that it is still perfectly modern, a step in the direction of legitimizing the use of vocal effects, multi-tracking and ultimately catchy choruses.

Title: Black Velvet
Review: Black Velvet is a collection of odds and ends and not a proper album, and sometimes it sounds that way as it moves from track to track. But it is full of the heart, soul, and spirit that Charles Bradley summoned every time he stood before a microphone, and this is a moving reminder of how much he gave us, and how much we have lost.

Title: Free Reign
Review: Free Reign is an album finds Clinic pushing themselves in directions that wouldn't have been considered years ago and it's to their credit that they possess both the will and imagination to do so.

Title: El Camino
Review: For 37 rollicking minutes, they give it the full gun, meeting the challenge of being the biggest garage rock band in the world head-on.

Title: Ultimate Success Today
Review: Rather than the rip-roaring, breakneck speed of the band’s earlier work, here songs are allowed to breathe and build more, taking surprising twists and turns is a highly satisfying way.

Title: The Back Room
Review: [They] possess a knack for tempering melodrama with minor keys and predictable beats. [Apr/May 2006, p.102]

Title: The Breakthrough
Review: Blige self-indulgently lets many songs on "The Breakthrough" run too long but keeps her sound fresh... adeptly weaving beats and live instruments, vocals and rapping, melody and rhythm in configurations alternately stark and lush. [11 Dec 2005]

Title: Bangerz
Review: Bangerz is a precise album that flits between bombastic and turgid; it is not very fun.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: While this new album lacks the immediate warmth of its predecessor there's much pleasure to be had wallowing in its rich patterns.

Title: Title
Review: The success of Lips Are Movin’ confirms that she’s no Eamon-style one-hit wonder; but Trainor might do well to study Duffy’s fate.

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: It doesn’t help that the production is full of weird echoes and indistinctness.... And yet, there are some genuinely good songs here.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II
Review: Instead of it being just another Earth 2.0 album though, the completed Angels Of Darkness, Demons Of Light is a successful experiment in sounding absolutely huge while doing so little, and the confirming masterstroke of Carlson's new direction.

Title: Transatlanticism
Review: Though there are quite a few slinking, introspective tracks on Transatlanticism, there are also a fistful of songs that have the left-field appeal -- not quite punk, not quite rock, not quite pop -- that brought a song like Jimmy Eat World's "The Middle" to the top of the charts in recent years.

Title: Seven's Travels
Review: Though it's not the emotionally draining follow-up many were expecting, Seven's Travels succeeds. Its saving grace is the fact that Slug and Ant remain ignorant of, or choose to completely ignore, the hip-hop conventions that have handcuffed similar artists for almost a decade.

Title: Uh Huh Her
Review: PJ Harvey can still pack a resonant, emotional wallop, even when the recording is devoid of frills.

Title: Can't Be Tamed
Review: A lot of its songs are ballads that ooze sap like an abandoned sponge.

Title: Believe
Review: At last, new metal has its answer to Depeche Mode's Black Celebration.

Title: Communicating
Review: Communicating also features some of her most direct lyrics and singing to date, and much of the album will undoubtedly resonate with listeners struggling to make connections or find meaning in their lives, despite their best efforts.

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: Sadly, Feed The Animals blends commercial US rap with rock classics with so little charm or skll, that even Jive Bunny is slightly annoyed you've used his name in vain. [Nov 2008, p.96]

Title: The ArchAndroid
Review: Monae's inexhaustible swagger and singular style sell both the high-concept theatrics and the schizophrenic sonics.

Title: Parallels
Review: While this sonic nonchalance means it can lack singularity and impact, Parallels feels like an organic and necessary evolution for Chung, his affinity for dense, hazy, dreamlike production still as mind-altering as ever.

Title: Beat 'Em Up
Review: Finding Iggy as confused as ever, Beat 'Em up ranks alongside New Values and Blah, Blah, Blah as yet another missed opportunity. (#209, p.60)

Title: Four
Review: The vicious "We're Not Good People" stuns with a pulsing, near-metal urgency that will lead you to act on your darkest urges - prior to playing the album again. And if you're not stupid, you will. [Sept 2012, p.88]

Title: Hendra
Review: Every element is in the right place but Watt is smart enough to leave some elements undone, giving the album a human heart that's evident no matter how deliberate the entire affair may be.

Title: Juice B Crypts
Review: Though the guests form a great deal of the fabric of the album, they do so on Battles’ terms, firmly entering their universe. No guest – not even Shabazz Palaces’ flowing verses on ‘Izm’ – steals the show. ... An album – that indulges the weird and wonderful side of Battles while also, simply, giving the people what they want.

Title: Build a Boat to the Sun
Review: Established fans will likely welcome the new developments; it's not a shift in style so much as in attitude, and her relatable introspection is in full force, just at a different stage--still searching but looking toward the light.

Title: Servant of Love
Review: Servant of Love is an album that needs a few spins to be fully appreciated, but it's as sincere, heartfelt, and artful as anything Griffin has released to date, and if the form may seem elusive to some listeners, the content is powerful and satisfying, a reminder of why Patty Griffin is one of our best singer/songwriters.

Title: Currents
Review: This is a record that demands your reflection and immersion, rather than just mindlessly wigging out.

Title: Wire
Review: If this album doesn’t bowl you over, it doesn’t disappoint either and rest assured that their next record will be something different that you didn’t expect either.

Title: Bon Voyage
Review: The whole experience is charmingly woah-dude in a way that never feels caricatured or insincere. Great pleasure is taken in employing the familiar apparatus and codes of psychedelia and, well, making them psychedelic again.

Title: Idiology
Review: Idiology refuses to cohere so completely that it plays out as part of Mouse On Mars's very approach; the duo hop from style to style, treating them like so many stepping stones to no destination in particular. [#206, p.72]

Title: Music Complete
Review: This is the first New Order album for a long time that sounds like it could only have been made by them.

Title: No Future
Review: Weirder tracks such as ‘System 100’ break the routine a bit, but it’d be nice to hear Moiré’s huge production skill with more variation of tone.

Title: Otherness
Review: Bainbridge reaches past the boundaries he set on Change of Mind, making Otherness a rich, varied examination of love and loneliness. But sometimes that sparseness he likes means there’s just too little to grip.

Title: Midnight Boom
Review: Florida-bred singer Alison Mosshart and British guitarist Jamie Hince built new tracks around the same sing-song rhythms. Their dark, sexy electro-rock sounds sharper and more memorable as a result.

Title: Sorry I Make You Lush
Review: Retains the tweak and squidge of his experimental, post-techno wanderings, but it's meant for feet rather than head. [Sep 2004, p.98]

Title: Apar
Review: This is music that desires to be clutched to youthful hearts and fill sun-bleached fields or golden coastlines; a hunger to delight that is so insatiable it’s rather tough to question.

Title: Ben Kweller
Review: A beautiful, touching collection of songs, and one which marks an important rite of passage in one man’s career, even if it doesn’t always feel like his best work.

Title: El Tren Fantasma
Review: Watson captures (or enhances) sounds in three dimensions, and the way he arranges them invites both immersion and reflection.

Title: Jersey Devil
Review: Jersey Devil comes with a real sense of sharp focus; cleverly worked melodies and handsomely crafted choruses come to the fore, pushing the woozy soundscapes to the back.

Title: Dancehall
Review: It's clear the Blaze are still passionate about the music they make, so listeners looking for an album full of songs like their earlier material are sure to be satisfied. Those looking for adventurousness and growth may not find all that they're looking for.

Title: The North
Review: The North continues to show off their skill and while nothing earth-shattering will be found here, it's something to fully bask in.

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: When the approach works, the results are bracingly exploratory; when it doesn't they're frustratingly half-formed. [Jul 2005, p.94]

Title: One Lost Day
Review: One Lost Day's songs may offer commentary about life's rough adventures but they also express openness, willingness, and tenderness as a result of them.

Title: Seer
Review: The album reaches its apex on the soaringly beautiful "Flight Song," evoking at once the best elements and most reflective shades of Eno, Aphex Twin, and free jazz saxophonist Marion Brown.

Title: Lover
Review: It’s an album with a lot of froth to it, but weighted froth — her most mature collection as well as her most fun one.

Title: I Grow Tired But Dare Not Fall Asleep
Review: Two nuanced, outstanding duets with French avant-popper SaraSara help lighten the all-consuming existential despair. [Jun 2020, p.91]

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: Father Of The Bride isn’t the shocking rebirth that might have been expected, given all of the information that trickled out about it over the past six years. Instead, it’s just far enough from expectations to surprise, but close enough to remain true. It’s a little messy and a little weird (and, again, a little long), but exactly the right record for Vampire Weekend right now.

Title: Warpaint
Review: There’s a jump in recording quality, but this isn’t always a boon to this sort music and can be a distraction here.... When they put their harmonies in unexpected setting, it works.

Title: Chromatics
Review: It doesn't stray very far from this template, but does just enough to suggest Genders has a few more strings to his bow.

Title: Come To Life
Review: An inspiring “is this even rap anymore?” record.

Title: Megafaun
Review: It might not be entirely mega, but there's enough to fawn over with this robust collection of breezy and inventive Americana.

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: It is some of Fagen's finest work to date.

Title: For Emma, Forever Ago
Review: Isolation doesn't get more splendid than this. [June 2008, p.100]

Title: II
Review: Seductive, maybe--but it rather lacks character of its own. [Sep 2013, p.92]

Title: Magpie and the Dandelion
Review: Not quite as organic as they seem, their perfection lacks taste despite its polish. [Jan 2014, p.117]

Title: Spirit
Review: The subtle flutter of her finest melismatics could give an open-minded person goose bumps. Her coarser melismatics, however, are the usual showoff BS and probably also a commercial prerequisite, like not having a harelip.

Title: Sun Bronzed Greek Gods
Review: It remains to be seen if the loose, congenial vibe of Sun Bronzed Greek Gods can be sustained for more than this EP's 19 minutes, but betting against Dom might be foolhardy.

Title: The New Year
Review: It's worth a purchase for the slow-building 'Folios' alone. [Fall 2008, p.87]

Title: Jake Bugg
Review: All in all, though Bugg's debut may not share the wordy precociousness of Conor Oberst's formative steps or the political astuteness of Willy Mason on Where the Humans Eat, it's his sheer earnestness and rare gift for writing simple, hook-filled tunes that ultimately charms the listener.

Title: It's All True
Review: It's All Real continues along the same lines: lush production, low-key bleeps and bloops, a hushed, lovelorn 2am ambience.

Title: Drum's Not Dead
Review: The trio's chanting, loops and metal-bashing framework is now fleshed out by some beautiful ambient-noise balladry. [Mar 2006, p.106]

Title: KOD
Review: J. Cole’s raps, but KOD sounds like someone who is either unfamiliar with drug abuse, or is completely unsympathetic to the dynamics of drug abuse in America.

Title: Quicksand / Cradlesnakes
Review: Califone's most confident and realized album.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: Every track emerges as ugly and joyless as the one before. [Oct 2004, p.127]

Title: The Glowing Man
Review: For a record seeking personal elevation via uncontainable energy, The Glowing Man doesn’t always glow often or energetically enough to help its listeners realize that it’s trying to attain such elevation.

Title: Humor Risk
Review: The results are sometimes funny, sometimes scary, sometimes touching, but rarely boring.

Title: Detours
Review: Detours clearly wants to be Bob Dylan but ends up being Bob Roberts instead.

Title: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes
Review: There aren't many punk stalwarts who can weave a tale of being down and out quite like Mike Ness, and for the most part he's in top form on this seventh studio release from Social D.

Title: Candidate Waltz
