Review: By any math, though, Candidate Waltz is a solid entry point, showcasing the band's mid-tempo stomps (reliably 4/4, despite the title) and Johnson's Zevon-cribbing rasp and wit.

Title: Blank Project
Review: Listening to it can be exhaustive, particularly during its clumsier second half, in which the narratives are duller (particularly Dossier), the musical progressions more stagnant (422). It’s undeniable, though, that this is a very original, fruitful record

Title: A Weekend in the City
Review: Okereke now sings instead of barking, and, well, oops on him.

Title: The End of Silence
Review: While the (simulated) exploration of the innards of this destruction may not make for the most hospitable or easygoing electronic album of the year, it undoubtedly goes some way to achieving its stated aim, even if its ethics could conceivably be indicted from the above-mentioned angle.

Title: Human the Death Dance
Review: As a primer, a first Sage Francis purchase, it’s fine; in light of his previous achievements, less so.

Title: Solid States
Review: Lyrically, this is among the sharpest and wittiest collections of songs this band has ever released. Add in the similarly fine music, and Solid States demonstrates the Posies have plenty of fresh ideas and great records left in them after three decades.

Title: Wavvves
Review: There's thrilling evidence of compelling, thoughtful craftsmanship.

Title: Band Red
Review: Though it's not quite as immediate as their excellent debut album, You've Seen Us...You Must've Seen Us, KaitO U.K.'s band red delivers more tightly coiled post-punk-pop with shouty vocals and elastic guitars, and also delves deeper into the group's experimental side.

Title: Some Racing, Some Stopping
Review: This disc isn’t something you’ll want to play loud. Instead, you’ll want to play it endlessly because the songs are first-rate, the songs are wonderful.

Title: You Will Not Die
Review: It’s an album that’s at times danceable and at others meditative, but always filled with emotional honesty.

Title: Total Loss
Review: When Krell is on, he's on. [Aug/Sep 2012, p.111]
What 25 25 is missing are those necessary bits of relief that were worked into their previous album.

Title: Wonderland
Review: The world of CEO remains an intriguing, if frustrating, place.

Title: I See You
Review: On “xx” and “Coexist,” the xx was using sadness as a kind of shield; its stylish monotony kept you from regarding the players as real people open to real connection. Here, in contrast, the music’s dynamics make you feel closely involved in what they’re singing about--the highs as well as the lows. I See You presents a band willing to be seen.

Title: Mechanics of Dominion
Review: The title track stomps and spins with strands of the Turkish music influence the ensemble collected with their 2013 album, Dalmak. The almost-finale “Northeast Kingdom” pleads for peace and respite, but Mechanics of Dominion is aware of how uncertain any meaningful resolution appears.

Title: Miss Machine
Review: Gleefully impurist and highly addictive. [Sep 2004, p.122]

Title: Croz
Review: A hauntingly quiet triumph, Croz gets under your skin and stays there. [Apr 2014, p.114]

Title: Folk Songs
Review: If there's one general criticism to be made here it could be that the album lingers a bit too much in a dark and dramatic mood (especially in the first four songs), but that's less an outright flaw and more a desire for more of the playfulness that appears in the second half of the record.

Title: Late Registration
Review: Practically every track on Late Registration is a glorious pop song. [Aug 2005, p.120]

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: The impressive thing about Strange Little Birds is how it feels simultaneously familiar and fresh, a record that echoes the past without being trapped by it.

Title: We Are the Pipettes
Review: The Pipettes are only fresh in the sense that they've appropriated Spector-influenced girl-pop for a new era.

Title: Wonderful Crazy Night
Review: As good as the tracks are, there isn’t that one real standout. Still, his voice sounds great, the songs are catchy and engaging but still well-crafted, and Elton and his band seem to be having a genuinely good time.

Title: Nursing Home
Review: Let's Wrestle are at their best on Nursing Home when the tension is visible: Whether this is the push and pull between their original sound and Albini's influence, or the clash of Gonzalez's casual vocals and Lightning's roaring bass, or the juxtaposition of adolescent male recklessness with anxieties of coming adulthood.

Title: American V: A Hundred Highways
Review: Thank you very much, Mr Rubin--The Man In Black is still with us. [1 Jul 2006, p.36]

Title: This is PiL
Review: An unexpectedly enjoyable late addition to a formidable body of work.

Title: Apar
Review: Musically it’s not a huge departure from Subiza, but if it ain’t broke there’s no point fixing it.

Title: Twelve Stops and Home
Review: There's something appealing about their brand of music with its light, sunny harmonies and direct choruses.

Title: Goes West
Review: The author's humanistic, heart-first approach, coupled with his songs' compellingly opaque expression and egoless playing makes reliability more rewarding. [Feb 2019, p.22]

Title: Grey Tickles, Black Pressure
Review: If John Grant never feels the need to write his memoirs, it’ll be because they’ve been played out for us over the course of these three brutally frank, flawed but ultimately human albums. Never less than enjoyable, the next chapter is bound to be worth the wait.

Title: Spelled in Bones
Review: Spelled in Bones digs further into Johnson's fondness for '70s songsmiths and production. Gone are Mouthfuls producer Brian Deck's glassy casements and miles of space, replaced here by a sound more rooted and wood-grained.

Title: Exile In The Outer Ring
Review: While this album isn’t what most people would consider rock, it definitely challenges the listener and succeeds at creating a world for the characters that occupy these songs and making the listener feel like they’re there for the experience themselves.

Title: EARS
Review: A modern new-age gem. [May 2016, p.79]

Title: Innerworld
Review: Electric Youth's debut is a well-constructed, carefully thought-out debut that belies its long gestation process and will make people who fell in love with them thanks to the Drive soundtrack very happy in a melancholy kind of way.

Title: Rainy Day Music
Review: There isn't much music on your radio dial that sounds so quintessentially bittersweet; the Jayhawks' old-fashioned gift is that they can make being lost sound sort of nice.

Title: As If
Review: It just isn't a consistent !!! album. But if it's any consolation, As If is still brimming with the ecstasy and feeling of freedom that you'd expect to be promoted by the band at this stage in their near 20-year lifespan.

Title: If Anything
Review: Greys are able to take these influences forward on tracks like "Cold Soak" and "Guy Picciotto," which seethe, howl and rock, combining the energy of hardcore with some of the more abstract sounds found in contemporary noise rock. [Jul 2014, p.74]

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: A bold, far-reaching and determined work that continues Brock's journey creating music both accessible and eccentric.

Title: Challenge Me Foolish
Review: An album that's alluring in passing, but might not have you doubling back for a closer inspection.

Title: Animator
Review: Time and time again The Luyas set themselves up in a soft kraut-like groove and fail to progress the song into something different, allowing it to fizzle out after four or five minutes.

Title: All You Need Is Now
Review: Déjà vu almost overwhelms The Man Who Stole a Leopard and Leave a Light On's echoes of The Chauffeur and Save a Prayer respectively, but this is Duran sounding as good as people remember.

Title: Brilliant! Tragic!
Review: The results vary: "Lost Weekend" is some kind of romantic peak, while the Lennon-esque "I Am the Psychic" is not.

Title: Talk About That
Review: Mayall proves that playing the blues is seemingly impervious to age. [Apr 2017, p.35]

Title: You Can't Take It with You
Review: The album has its moments, like a nice surprise bridge toward the end of the title track and the slowly building, percussive arc of “Circles.” But You Can’t Take it With You just fails to make a strong case for itself.

Title: True North
Review: Here Chapman obviously revels in his continued ability to mine the emotional, psychological, and spiritual terrain he did in his younger years as a songwriter, while adding experiential depth to his approach through a lifetime of profound musical development. In an enormous catalog, True North stands straight-up alongside his finest recordings.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: While there is much here to admire, at its overblown worst Neon Bible is one of those records that takes itself too seriously to be taken seriously. [Apr 2007, p.90]

Title: Dummy Boy
Review: DUMMY BOY is an insufferable 13-track farrago of anything from rock riffs to calypso drums, all pinned by 6ix9ine’s obsessive use of the “n” word, along with every other negative trope found in the gangsta rap of the early Noughties. ... Avoid.

Title: Innocence
Review: Singer Ciaran McAuley's words get lost in the dry ice a little, but a sense of quasi-religious wonder prevails. [Feb 2014, p.80]

Title: drukQs
Review: If refining one's vision rather than foraging for new sounds is the mark of emerging artistic maturity, then it appears that techno's jester genius has finally decided to grown up.

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: When Bear in Heaven's desire for duality-the confluence of ambience and pop-succeeds, it does so brilliantly. Ironically, it only manages these heights half the time.

Title: LoveLaws
Review: Confidently expressing vulnerability over woozy nocturnal soundscapes to create comfort and intimacy in a lonely, quiet place, LoveLaws will be your fireside companion.

Artist: I Love You But I've Chosen Darkness
Title: Fear Is on Our Side
Review: If the bulk of the album is for the car, the bar, the social occasion, then moments like ["Today"] are for headphones, bedrooms, intimate and solitary states. The presence of both increases the breadth of this assured LP, and establishes ILYBICD as being no longer a band to watch, but a band to listen to.

Title: Glasshouse
Review: The third LP from Jessie Ware sees her bring her diva mode to the forefront of her sound, but the lack of the scarcity and minimalism that saw her emerge at the turn of the decade results in the finished product lacking the effectiveness of her earlier work.

Title: Half-Light
Review: Longing and heartbreak are universal themes, but what Rostam does is make them accessible, thought-provoking in an artful manner that will serve him well in as he navigates his solo career.

Title: Anastasis
Review: Anastasis is certainly an accomplished record and one that fits well within Dead Can Dance's output, but it is a hard listen.

Title: My Woman
Review: A fascinating, affecting statement from a musician firmly in control of her artistry.

Title: Vapor Trails
Review: A welcome return.

Title: Powerballin'
Review: More consistent and satisfying than its predecessor. [14 Nov 2004]

Title: Scratch My Back
Review: Scratch comes off like a ponderous exercise in re-branding--an uncomfortable place to be for one of pop’s great innovators.

Title: Audio Secrecy
Review: Stone Sour has tapped into its full potential on Audio Secrecy, and it really shows when the album is heard in order, from beginning to end. The flow of the album is gorgeous, made all the better by the aforementioned balance between soft and heavy.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: Only By The Night is best viewed as a transitional record from a band who have quite literally done their growing up in public. [Oct 2008, p.98]

Title: Transference
Review: The album twisted and turned its already discombobulated songs around and around, never letting anyone get comfortable. It showed a more cerebral Spoon than ever before.

Title: Lucky
Review: Lucky’s music kicks high, the restlessness palpable. [Winter 2008, p.83]

Title: Ghost Stories
Review: Though a couple of songs feel undercooked—specifically “Another’s Arms” and album closer “O”--Ghost Stories mostly works.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: This is the best childhood summer holiday you ever had, condensed into 45 minutes of delicately arranged, beautifully performed, big, bright, cheery music. [Jul 2003, p.118]

Title: Ivy Tripp
Review: Crutchfield keeps her songs concise, and weaves in subtle forget-me-nots.

Title: Shriek
Review: Far too few of the songs are strong enough to really engage--so Shriek wafts by in a beautifully crafted haze.

Title: Domesticated
Review: Domesticated is a low-key album by Tellier's standards, but it captures the feeling that settling down is something to be savored, and it's got to be the most glamorous-sounding album about home sweet home.

Title: Wooden Arms
Review: It's Watson's voice we're missing most from the overwhelming instrumentation, and after hearing the Buckley-esque transcendence that his vocals are capable of, it's more than disappointing to hear them take second chair. [Spring 2009, p.106]

Title: Words and Music by Saint Etienne
Review: Words And Music expertly explores the intoxicated love of music and the sheer joy of being a music fan: feelings so universal that they will never be confined to particular eras.

Title: Jaime
Review: There’s a pop progressiveness coupled with an old-fashioned loneliness. It sounds nothing at all like Presley, but he lived in and understood those two worlds and might have appreciated the chance to bridge them in the way that Howard has here. ... Her distinctive vocal timbre is the twine that keeps Jamie wrapped-up tight. Not many artists can make loops and electronic sounds feel authentic, but Howard is more than able to keep them feeling warm and natural.

Title: Wild Crush
Review: The London trio has hit its stride, churning meatier, heavier grooves without sinking into sonic muck.

Title: Are You Serious
Review: Are You Serious contains more modes than songs, a diverse collection held together by Bird's voice and violin, and the sheer energy of the music.

Title: Lost Girls
Review: As a whole, there’s a loose sort of freedom to Lost Girls, as if Khan was able to summon the atmosphere and mystery that so often suffuse her music without sweating over it as much as usual. Her past work has sounded more rooted in the British Isles than Southern California, but she does the L.A. transplant thing with enough confidence that the presence of bloodthirsty vampire bikers doesn’t even sound like that much of a drawback.

Title: High as Hope
Review: Musically, High As Hope isn’t too far off from the operatic orchestration of her earlier work, which is the most frustrating thing about it. It does give the music a little more space to breathe, however, and adds a percussive through-line of handclaps, foot stomps, and prominent double bass that builds on the melodramatic vibe fans love.

Title: I Bet on Sky
Review: Even if the highs aren't as high, like the rest of the reunited lineup's work, there really aren't any noticeable lows.

Title: Hot Pink
Review: Hot Pink is an album that knows exactly what it is, and it’s the work of a well-crafted hip pop star with something to prove.

Title: Jungle
Review: By deliberately creating a sense of mystery around themselves, Jungle may have raised expectations that their music cannot yet deliver on.

Title: The Eraser
Review: One could imagine the dynamics, colors, and crescendos his bandmates might've added, and without them Yorke sounds hemmed in.

Title: G I R L
Review: This is pop music, and it's all in good fun.... I just wish the recipe would have included a touch more poetry.

Title: Light Upon The Lake
Review: The record’s finest moments relate to everyone’s lives, in one way or another. Whether it’s golden youth or present day regrets, there’s something to cling onto.

Title: Do It!
Review: On their fifth album, they crack the window, slow the motor (except on 'Shopping Bag,' a jazz-punk binge and purge) and take side trips into primeval glades where runic rites are conducted on acoustic guitars.

Title: BOBBY
Review: The record's general aesthetic stays the same, docile sounds, pitter-patter polyrhythms, and shimmering vocals, but the ear-tickling mutations along the way is the appeal.

Title: Everything Else Has Gone Wrong
Review: This fifth album immediately feels well adjusted and familiar. [Feb 2020, p.25]

Title: Try This
Review: The only thing missing is a killer pop hit to follow "Get the Pary Started." [Nov 2003, p.120]

Title: Bigfoot
Review: Though their name may seem like a mouthful, the quintet’s efforts equal an album that should be added to your playlist of summer hits immediately.

Title: Monuments to an Elegy
Review: If the songs don’t all match the Pumpkins’ early glories, Corgan is still carrying what he once called “the infinite sadness”, investing uplifting sounds with an undercurrent of melancholy.

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: Cruel Summer is half a classic and half a concession to mediocre talents.

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: It makes for a solid if unremarkable follow-up, the kind of release that buys a little more time for the Cool Kids to live up to their original promise.

Title: Riot On An Empty Street
Review: One of the prettiest albums of the year.

Title: Evolution
Review: They might have over-egged the acoustic balladry here, leading to their airiness unbalancing the syncopated beefiness elsewhere, but it's delivered so slickly and confidently that few fans will care. [20 Oct 2018, p.55]

Title: Freedom of Speech
Review: A pleasantly surprising, if patchy, return.

Title: Saint Bartlett
Review: Downtempo triumph from Seattle indie journeyman. [July 2010, p. 135]

Title: Green Language
Review: Whyte has made an LP that rises and falls gracefully, proving that even his brand of everything-all-the-time dance music has room for nuance and subtlety.

Title: Partners
Review: ["Sometimes" is] a knockout punch to an already gripping body of music and a fitting last word that cements this album not just as a heartfelt expression of love for John Cage, but for love itself.

Title: Some Nights
Review: The energy and personality which flood out of every melody give this album its own stamp of authority.

Title: Motherhood
Review: The result is a blisteringly progressive record - one that genuinely feels years ahead of its time.

Title: Pray For Rain
Review: Pure Bathing Culture’s sound is so consistent--melodic, but slightly gauzy and blurred around the edges--that one gets caught in the sonics, and the singing becomes just another texture in the recording. And it’s their strength with melodies that will keep listeners coming back.

Title: Rubber Factory
Review: Rubber Factory finds inspiration in decay, and signals a hopeful future for the Black Keys.

Title: Trying to Never Catch Up
Review: Positively exuberant. [Sep 2006, p.114]

Title: Content Nausea
Review: Savage and Brown are continuing their exploration of modern dread; anxiety as fuel for life's inherent mundanity

Title: The Gathering
Review: On The Gathering, though, the sonic vista is flattened out, resulting in a dreary, grayscale trudge of an album.

Title: Dead Blue
Review: They’ve consolidated on the progression made between their first two albums and in turn produced their finest effort to date.

Title: Kissin Time
Review: These songs sound more like her collaborators' than hers. [Mar 2002, p.120]

Title: Getting Away with Murder
Review: It seems Shaddix still writes most of his songs in purple ink in diaries with little locks on. [28 Aug 2004, p.56]

Title: Gathered
Review: Even though Gathered is very much a creative patchwork, it coheres thematically as well as musically, and sounds both sly and sincere. Howe Gelb's evolution from the most distinctive roots rocker in the desert to Arizona's most unlikely lounge singer is coming along nicely, and Gathered is a welcome addition to his catalog.

Title: Do Things
Review: As a whole, the album treads the fine line of genre fetishism and reinvention.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: This record isn’t gonna kick you in the head the way that BoC’s last two outings have on occasion done. The break beats aren’t gonna blow you away and there’s nothing here that’ll really get your blood rushing. If you give it the time, though, Campfire reveals itself as an truly beautiful piece of work, better produced and with a tighter sense of melody than the Sandisons have shown in past.

Title: Top Ten Hits of the End of the World
Review: Unfortunately, on Top 10 Hits of the End of the World, PR were so involved with their campy concept, they neglected to write and record music capable of carrying its weight.

Title: Kids in the Street
Review: The album plays its best cards early. [Aug 2017, p.112]

Title: It Is Time for a Love Revolution
Review: There's substance to 'Long Sad Goodbye's accusing lament for his late father and Vietnam's denunciation of the Iraq war, but Kravitz generally limits himself to muscular yet uninspired multi-instrumental expertise and sloppy-thinking hippitude. [Mar 2008, p.114]

Title: Cloud Nothings
Review: Cloud Nothings, the eponymous debut from the project of Dylan Baldi, is the work of another young mind who seems gifted beyond his years.

Title: The Spirit of Apollo
Review: On Apollo, L.A. scenemakers Squeak E. Clean and DJ Zegon pull in a wild roster of stars for what feels like a playful unity jam.

Title: In The Maybe World
Review: The balancing of ironic humour that raised a smile on earlier albums is absent here, which leaves us with almost nowhere to hide.

Title: Cass County
Review: Henley's discourses on ageing and feeling adrift in the modern world are poignant, and, on A Younger Man, painfully well observed. [Dec 2015, p.93]

Title: Joan of Arc, Dick Cheney, Mark Twain
Review: Kinsella and his crew finally seem to have found a way of expressing themselves that doesn't feel introverted and exclusive.

Title: Jackie
Review: Not for the first time, Ciara is suffering from a case of mixed-bag syndrome, a situation that seems even direr on the 16-track deluxe version, which has two unnecessary alternate versions of I Bet.

Title: Write About Love
Review: Write About Love also feels monumentally comfortable in its own skin. For a band that made its bones meticulously documenting awkwardness, that's a particularly impressive change.

Title: Pluto
Review: Pluto nicely refreshes current rap trends and offers some genuinely forward-thinking hooks.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: Where † crafted sly treasures out of gaudy detritus, single-minded as it may have been, Audio, Video, Disco simply settles for canonizing the forgettable.

Title: Oh Inhuman Spectacle
Review: They do a serviceable job in a handful of styles, and that’s nothing to sneeze at. Methyl Ethel could be your next favorite band, but they just have to pick what band that will be.

Title: As If Apart
Review: It’s warm, rewarding and a very, very comfortable listen. And therefore definitely not pysch.

Title: Isolation Drills
Review: Isolation Drills sounds like the real rock album GBV have always wanted to make...

Title: The Weirdness
Review: Cringe-worthy lines are unfortunately rampant through The Weirdness’s (long) forty minutes.

Title: Death of a Bachelor
Review: Like the soundtrack to a wedding reception, DOAB is Panic! At The Disco turnt up, both musically and lyrically. [9 Jan 2016, p.50]

Title: the gamble
Review: The Gamble takes some extraordinary risks, but the rewards are glorious.

Title: Hot Dreams
Review: Kirk's irresistible vocals lend the album all the quality it needs, and their lighter touches and some inspired choices really add depth to the monochromatic and claustrophobic formula.

Title: Ivory Tower
Review: This Boys Noize-produced return is nothing if not perverse. [Oct 2010, p.108]

Title: Who You Are
Review: This is dead-eyed pop with aspirations of being your comfort food but turns out to be a starchy soulless slop.

Title: Shape Shift With Me
Review: Shape Shift With Me has catchy anthems, heavy rock songs and speed rants; it's yet another excellent, and complicated, Against Me! album. [No. 135, p.52]

Title: Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers
Review: It's hard to shake the feeling that the National is highly influenced by and studied in the bands it emulates, but the album is still worth a listen for fans of moody country-tinged lounge music.

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: With brevity missing from Toledo’s musical toolkit (see the blame-deflecting “The Ballad of the Costa Concordia” and its 11:32 run time), the pain is exacerbated by songs that are simply too long to be memorable; what few hooks exist on Teens of Denial are quickly forgotten.

Title: Flamagra
Review: Even more than a Lynchian album, Flamagra is nothing if not a FlyLo album. As usual he lends himself to superlatives and clichés, the sign of a singular artist (there’s another) about whom there just aren’t that many descriptors.

Title: Women
Review: Women may not be easy listening, but it is rewarding listening.

Title: Causers of This
Review: Causers Of This’ infects your mind with pure psychedelia, splicing such conflicting sounds as soul, freak folk, hip-hop and electronica, and the result hits you like Animal Collective on a comedown, or Ariel Pink with Seasonal Affective Disorder.

Title: Juliana Hatfield Sings Olivia Newton-John
Review: About two or three songs into the album, you'll forget that it's a "concept" album and just enjoy it for what it is--a really strong collection of songs that just happen to come from an unlikely source.

Title: The Monitor
Review: Clocking in at just over an hour, The Monitor is a self-indulgent statement, to be sure--but some of the best ambitious works are often the most personal.

Title: The Agent Intellect
Review: Rather than back down from the precipice of decline and confusion, Protomartyr has reported the situation as they see it in The Agent Intellect, an uncomfortable, honest and ultimately excellent record.

Title: Atrocity Exhibition
Review: Atrocity Exhibition is a party rap album, a drug rap album, an emo rap album, and a post-punk album all rolled into one.

Title: Still Brazy
Review: Still Brazy is an artisanal, proletarian Los Angeles gangster rap record, less tribute to the sound’s golden age than a full-throated and wholly absorbed recitation.

Title: Blueberry Boat
Review: At times, Blueberry Boat sounds like it was made entirely out of the noodly bits that most other bands would junk for being too weird and difficult, but the Fiery Furnaces forge them into an album that's both more pop and more radical than Gallowsbird's Bark.

Title: Woke on a Whaleheart
Review: The sound of an artist refreshed and renewed. [May 2007, p.150]

Title: Weezer (Black Album)
Review: On tracks like Can't Knock The Hustle, Piece Of Cake and High As A Kite, the smartness and deceptive simplicity is lost under a wash of electronic beats and un-catchy melodies. ... They sound boring. [23 Feb 2019, p.54]

Title: The Morning Star
Review: The Bachman you know is in here but submerged deep in the unfamiliar; it is not really until the two gorgeous “Song for the Setting Sun” cuts that you get an unobstructed view of the man and his guitar.

Title: Fabulous Muscles
Review: The musical parsimony, cultural insularity, moral certitude, and histrionic affectations of these lo-fi artier-than-thous promise indie ideologues whole lifetimes of egoistic irrelevance.

Title: Last Man Standing
Review: Through it all, Nelson sounds as strong as ever.

Title: No No
Review: While the intellectual territory is familiar, it's explored with similar playfulness and ear for inventive juxtaposition as Papaich's fellow city dwellers Matmos. [Oct 2015, p.50]

Title: Something for the Rest of Us
Review: Something for the Rest of Us is an album to play on the drive home.

Title: Tumble Bee
Review: Following the birth of her first child, the underappreciated Laura Veirs recorded an album of mostly traditional folk songs for children, which has charm far beyond the nursery.

Title: Sam's Town
Review: Sam’s Town is so riddled with hackneyed clichés, pandering melodrama, and lazy songwriting, that we keep wondering just what gimmick Flowers will thrust upon us next in a desperate effort to hold our attention.

Title: Rooty
Review: Basement Jaxx do this so much better than anyone else, including Daft Punk, that you root for their mad programed sounds and unknown cast of determined singers. It's totally daft disco, sexy and sweaty, stupid and stupendous. This is pop.

Title: FM!
Review: Despite FM!'s brevity, Staples jams so much into every bar that it fully satiates, all while still managing to end so abruptly that it comes as a surprise. The electrifying thrill of FM! is a triumph for the rapper who remains at the top of his game.

Title: The Fool
Review: Shimmering psychedelic post-punk to get lost into.

Title: Haven't Got The Blues (Yet)
Review: With almost every line a zinger, Wainwright's cocktail of satire and over-sharing remains potent. [Sep 2014, p.117]

Title: In This Light & On This Evening
Review: While Smith & Co. may overuse a keyboard riff or two on In This Light, we shouldn't really let that sully this dark, majestic detour.

Title: Big Dark Love
Review: Best experienced in depressed darkness while contemplating your existence. [No. 117., p.59]

Title: El Dorado
Review: his songwriting and vocal performances give a picture of the coming of an important voice in the genre. Certainly one to watch.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: [He expands his reach] with the aid of producer-label boss Kanye West, guest ranging from The-Dream to Kendrick Lamar, and a steely gusto unmatched in hip-hop. [11 Oct 2013, p.72]

Title: The Rising
Review: There are more retro-sounding pop-R&B numbers with "sha la la" backing vocals than the subject matter might indicate, a stadium rocker, some soulful ballads recalling early Van Morrison, and stirring gospel. [Sep 2002, p.94]

Title: Undercard
Review: As Darnielle's first release on his new label, Merge, opening a new chapter in his career, Undercard may not be a total knockout, but it's an eminently worthy diversion from (or preface to) the main event.

Title: Thunderheist
Review: Thunderheist prove more winning than most, due to Isis' knack for calm, rhythmic flow, all one- or two-syllable rhymes and the schoolyard-inspired spelling out of words.

Title: Useless Coordinates
Review: The album is so cacophonous that it borders on the unpleasant. Yet there are redemptive moments. [Summer 2019, p.111]

Title: All Rise: A Joyful Elegy for Fats Waller
Review: Mostly, this project is a revelation and a thrill. It succeeds in making something old/new into something newer/new.

Title: Drowners
Review: Songs like "Unzip Your Harrington" and "Luv, Hold Me Down" aren't deep, but the charging-guitar shimmer and fun, facile choruses are pretty undeniable.

Title: Brave
Review: Expensive beats and uplifting material are offset by listless vocals.

Title: (I Can't Get No) Stevie Jackson
Review: The album works its minimal beats and retrograde high to near perfection, perhaps only because of it had the ultimate incubation period. [Aug/Sep 2012, p.118]

Title: X
Review: They've just made the best rock album since Andrew WK's 'I Get Wet'.

Title: Twilight of the Thunder God
Review: Twilight of the Thunder God merely refines these elements, but the tune-up is noticeable. In a discography filled with catchy songs, these are some of Amon Amarth's catchiest.

Title: Food
Review: Though occasionally subdued, Kelis brings a moody character to “Runnin’”, while Sitek offers subtle variations on the funk-soul style, edging into salsoul and swamp-rock on “Cobbler” and “Rumble”.

Title: AZD
Review: Musically, it takes listeners through a dystopian dance-floor dream universe, with the shiny but comforting hand from its cover as our guide.

Title: Let's Get Out Of This Country
Review: With [Belle & Sebastian] now seemingly lost to soft-pop pastichery, CO have come out of their shadow and flourished. [Jul 2006, p.84]

Title: Leave No Bridge Unburned
Review: Whitehorse's sophomore effort signals that this is one musical marriage that's only getting better with time.

Title: How We Operate
Review: Anyone who enjoyed Gomez for their more adventurous traits will be left in the cold by How We Operate.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: As dazzling, inventive and soulful as anything he's done. [23 Feb 2017, p.51]

Title: Young Prayer
Review: A restrained lamentation, a controlled elegiac mediation on the death of a loved one.

Title: Barracuda
Review: Whether it’s Mark’s influence, or Kinky’s own growth over the years (or maybe both), this album has universal appeal and its party-ready, rich sound is one that would be a shame to pass up.

Title: The Age of Miracles
Review: Mary Chapin Carpenter doesn't sound especially concerned with how much product she'll move on The Age of Miracles; instead, she's made an album that speaks with honesty and clarity about the mysteries of love and fate, and she communicates well enough that it's hard to imagine anyone who has ever thought about the ways life can turn on a dime not being moved by the beauty of this music.

Title: Bushcraft
Review: It’s an album of perpetual fruition, payoff meeting payoff with gratifying speed and the rush of riff-borne frenzy.

Title: Be Strong
Review: Although the first half relies on straight-up classic house beats and lyric imperatives to be stronger, work harder and get higher, they upend the formula with an oddball-pop sensibility, beautifully crafted melodies and general silliness.

Title: The State of Gold
Review: The result is mystifyingly boring and scrubbed completely of any evidence of human touch.

Title: You Can't Teach an Old Dog New Tricks
Review: A prophetically titled record that does exactly what it promises. [Jul 2011, p.94]

Title: Wondervisions
Review: Whether this is post rock, space rock or ad hoc it's hard to say, but who needs taxonomy when music feels this good? [Jan 2012, p.97]

Title: Songs
Review: As an overall piece of work, Songs flows seamlessly, with the consistency in mood and tone and meticulously crafted arrangements meaning not a note sounds out of place.

Title: Hell-On
Review: Images both earthy and heavenly make repeated showings, but case's vexing concern is troubled humans. [Jul 2018, p.88]

Title: Breakout
Review: Breakout is unlikely fodder for the razzle-dazzle road shows and 3-D concert films to come. As a portrait of the artist as a young malcontent, though, it's rarely less than fascinating.

Title: August
Review: It's a seductive, refreshing but gratifyingly purposeless ride. [Sep 2019, p.1110]

Title: Pieces In A Modern Style
Review: The most memorable tracks on Pieces in a Modern Style feel like high-brow Puff Daddy songs...

Title: Face the Truth
Review: If it's not a leap in the right direction, it's at least a big step.

Title: Gods of the Earth
Review: How scary/ridiculous the lyrics are is a matter of personal taste (or lack thereof), but it'd help if the production were more Scandinavian and less like, well, the Rocket from the Crypt rip-off band that singer/guitarist J.D. Cronise was in before he devoted his life to "Paranoid."

Title: Sun Structures
Review: Sun Structures is a simply wonderful record.

Title: Voxtrot
Review: Despite a few lyrical missteps ("Future Pt. 1"), "Voxtrot" is generally insightful and emerges as a promising debut. [26 May 2007]

Title: Paralytic Stalks
Review: You get the feeling Barnes is trying to bash you into the same twisted mindspace he himself inhabits, mixing up spiralling flute lines, cosmic rock and deranged show tunes.

Title: Change Becomes Us
Review: The real act of provocation here comes in the streamlining of what had been cacophonous material into a solid bag of actual tunes.

Title: Same As You
Review: The overall vibe here us one of relaxation rather than tension. [Apr 2015, p.93]

Title: EVOL
Review: His raps here still stick fairly closely to the trap-music conventions that have dominated the hip-hop scene in Future’s hometown Atlanta for the past decade or so.

Title: Forever Neverland
Review: Forever Neverland is an illustration of how modern pop should be--full of character, colourful and 14 tracks full of pop hit after hit.

Title: 808s & Heartbreak
Review: It is by far the strangest record he's ever made: a willfully sullen and uncompromising electro-pop album from one of hip-hop's biggest stars.

Title: Stand Your Ground
Review: A rather predictable and mundane package.

Title: iii
Review: The banality throughout iii detracts from any basic pleasure possible from the beats. [Jan/Feb 2016, p.57]

Title: Peer Amid
Review: He's a poetic if not somewhat mad genius on his own, but Peer Amid makes it clear Higgs is at his best pacing the prow of mighty musical vessel. [Mar 2011, p.99]

Title: Da REAList
Review: With some minor problems, some minor advancement, and some major moments, Da Realist is an overall winner from a rapper who keeps beating the odds.

Title: Lisbon
Review: Lisbon might leave plenty of listeners unsure what more the band has to offer us in the coming decade, but on its own there's little to be disappointed with.

Title: Young Hunger
Review: With Young Hunger, Manuel has carved out an album that hardly gives you a chance to wipe the smile off your face--or pull yourself from the dance floor.

Title: Alligator
Review: Berninger sounds smart and witty; but above all else, he sounds like he really went for it this time. [#15, p.105]

Title: White Chalk
Review: Even by her own unsettling standards, however, her seventh album is disturbing, a collection of smudged and spectral laments that appear to have been written before the invention of penicillin.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: Despite playing with pop forms, Set My Heart On Fire Immediately holds Hadreas's experimental shape, his artistic line. ... A slow burner, in every way. [Jun 2020, p.94]

Title: Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino
Review: Turner nails the concept, wallowing in warped dreams and painting widescreen soundscapes, but the foundation is wobbly; at a glance, it's impressive, but the slipshod details reveal themselves upon close inspection.

Title: The Temper Trap
Review: When it comes to developing and honing the craft of songwriting to present a signature sound with a variety of ideas, The Temper Trap fall short.

Title: Battle Born
Review: They too often edge into Meat Loaf/Jim Steinman territory, where every detail becomes a cause for operatic exaggeration and any clunky line or cliche sounds ridiculous.  [No. 93, p.56]

Title: Teens of Denial
Review: Most tracks last over five minutes and the longest comes in at 12. It gives the impression that Toledo is doing what he wants and making the music he wants to hear. You can’t help but love him for it.

Title: Chasing Yesterday
Review: There is always room in the world for another well written, classy pop-rock gem, and with Chasing Yesterdays Noel Gallagher proudly delivers 10 of them.

Title: Make My Head Sing
Review: While the lovelorn energy of Mayfield’s country ballads are often obfuscated by guitar fuzz, the new crunch fits her nicely.

Title: Under Rug Swept
Review: Is Under Rug Swept as good as Jagged Little Pill? Ultimately, no. [Feb/Mar 2002, p.108]

Title: XOXO
Review: XOXO, while broadening the band’s sound, becomes not a major shift, not even a detour really, but a refocus and sharpening of their hallmark jangly sound – brimming with country, folk, rock, and British Invasion power pop. It’s reinvigoration.

Title: Zebra
Review: A sweet, herbal fug hanging over proceedings, Zebra joins the dots between blissed-out Balearica, trippy kosmische, Eastern and Afro vibes and spacey jazz. [Sep 2018, p.91]

Title: Corinne Bailey Rae
Review: Rae's amiable competence marks her as a talent worth keeping tabs on, but the strength of Corinne Bailey Rae is fleeting, a triumph of mood over tangible substance.

Title: Popular Songs
Review: Playing like a welcome sequel to 2006's style-hopping "I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass," Yo La Tengo's 16th studio album finds the New Jersey trio bringing out Farfisa solos and celebrating ongoing couplehood.

Title: Forever Sounds
Review: Forever Sounds’ strength is in its emphasis on the sound of the band, echoing its increasingly confi dent, assured live show. [No. 129, p.57]

Title: Bleeds
Review: Although the second half of the album doesn't quite match up to the front, there's no sense it's dragging, either. [Dec 2015, p.88]

Title: The Music
Review: Sounds overproduced and underdeveloped.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: It’s Flowers’ unique presence--equal parts Wild West underdog and glitzy glam messiah--that really transforms Effect’s Reagan-era throwbacks into forward-thinking Instagram-age rock.

Title: Convenanza
Review: Through it all, in the music and in Weatherall’s characterful vocals, Public Image Limited is a clear influence. The album is at its best, though, at its most cosmic.

Title: Modern Dancing
Review: The joy TRAAMS have in pulling their songs taut and then letting them fly--an approach that shines particularly brightly on "Bite Mark"--is more palpable than ever on Modern Dancing, and the fun is infectious.

Title: Move In Spectrums
Review: Move In Spectrums is good—with more ambition it could have been great.

Title: We Are The Night
Review: On We Are the Night, the Chemical Brothers have switched from integrators to imitators.

Title: The L-Shaped Man
Review: On the whole, L-Shaped Man feels like a boring exercise: a band performing post-punk idolatry (Root Of The World could pass for poppier Public Image Ltd.) instead of bothering to try anything new.

Title: Blonde
Review: It’s just about impossible to live up to the hype that an album like this has been subjected to, but Ocean comes pretty close. Blonde is often a bit of a sprawling mess, but with some patience it becomes one of the most rewarding albums you’ll hear all year.

Title: Our Pathetic Age
Review: As is frequently the case with double albums padded with filler, Out Pathetic Age’s biggest problem is that too much of it feels disposable, anodyne, or tossed off. But Shadow still manages to get some strong work out of both himself and his guests, and he deserves credit for not trying to merely recreate the same trick over and over.
Patchier than Jacksonville. [Mar 2006, p.92]

Title: Yesterday's Gone
Review: Letting endless threads unravel, in vivid detail, this album might creep up on you at first, but make no mistake, its creativity and poetry will floor you.

Title: Range Anxiety
Review: If you're eager for a record that eats its influences raw in order to fuel a whole new world you'd better look elsewhere. [Apr 2015, p.112]

Title: Magnetic Man
Review: It's not spectacular but it is a reliable and solid effort. Whether this is a pivotal moment for the genre remains to be seen.

Title: Twerp Verse
Review: Their latest effort is a much-welcomed return to form.

Title: Lines, Vines and Trying Times
Review: If the Jonases come up woefully short in the sensitivity department, they (nearly) make up for it with songwriting that's far more flavorful than that on Fearless or on the JoBros' previous disc, last year's "A Little Bit Longer."

Title: Supermigration
Review: Most of the album feels too much like a work-in-progress.

Title: Through Low Light and Trees
Review: An extended pilgrimage to New Orleans allowed the longtime friends to hone the 11 songs that make up Through Low Light and Trees into something truly magical, and while the album is clearly the product of the green fields and misty mountains of their homeland, it's obvious that the time spent in the Big Easy had a profound effect on them.

Title: Yoko
Review: Everything is intricately wrought and calculated, perhaps in an overly accommodating response to fears of linearity. This fashionable awareness lends an almost palpable weight to the sound. It succeeds in adding depth and texture to the album, but sometimes overshoots the mark.

Title: Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers
Review: This is a very minor-chord affair. [Feb 2004, p.104]

Title: Sleep Mountain
Review: In merging the intimate with the majestic, The Kissaway Trail have achieved a rare, and subtle, balance. [Apr 2010, p.92]

Title: Godfather
Review: Ultimately, Godfather is a thoroughly enjoyable record, one that manages to leverage grime’s elemental sounds in a way that feels vital and forward-looking.

Title: FIBS
Review: FIBS takes listeners for a ride, so to speak, along the meticulously plotted rhythms of its very physical, narrative-free presentation, one that, in Meredith's hands, is both stimulating and engaging.

Title: Saint Cloud
Review: The songs here are at once deeply intimate and broadly accessible, like selections from an alternative universe where modern mainstream country radio isn’t all pandering, homogenized slop.

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: While Sound of Silver still delivers terrific buzzy dance-space jams ... it also contains wispy hints of New Order and Bowie... and Murphy's best song-making efforts to date.

Title: Sometimes I Wish We Were An Eagle
Review: 2007's stellar Woke on a Whaleheart found him miles from Smog's lo-fi folk prophesies, the music revived, almost jubilant. Eagle's halfway there but sounds preoccupied, his stoic baritone never giving too much away.

Title: Die Knowing
Review: Die Knowing is not the record that tries to re-capture the past, but rather combine the best of everything Comeback Kid has previously done. Boy did they deliver.

Title: Rest in Chaos
Review: Mixing humor with pointed social satire, Rest in Chaos finds Snider and his group tackling both darker moods and high-spirited rock.

Title: Harlem River
Review: Morby largely succeeds at taking us on his journey.

Title: Wolfmother
Review: An intriguing garage-rock thread runs through Wolfmother's songs, broadening their sound. [4 May 2006, p.56]

Title: Certified
Review: Part sex fiend, part revolutionary and part party-starter, David Banner certifies himself a rap powerhouse with "Certified."  [20 Sep 2005]

Title: Joyful Rebellion
Review: While k-os's antimaterialist ranting can wear thin at times, Joyful Rebellion builds and improves on the rich, organic, live sound that made his debut, Exit, such a left-field hit. [Nov 2004, p.162]

Title: The Devil's Rain
Review: The Devil's Rain is very silly indeed. [Dec. 2011 p. 136]

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: It’s this ability that makes The Big Pink so special for, beneath the dissonance, the artful posturing and the pop hooks is something far more enduring: these guys have got a soul and they’re not afraid to bare it.

Title: Understated
Review: Understated is a great album, but that's what we've come to expect from Edwyn Collins. [Apr 2013, p.97]

Title: Right Thoughts, Right Words, Right Action
Review: Kapranos and co have delivered what is simultaneously ‘just another Franz Ferdinand’ album and one of the indie records of the summer.

Title: History of Modern
Review: This 11th album refines their sound and gives it a modern productive tweak. [Oct 2010, p.112]

Title: X 100PRE
Review: As a debut album, X 100PRE succeeds at establishing Bunny’s ambition. With its bangers and sonic diversity, this release suggests that the Latin trap artist possesses the potential to shape mainstream music for years to come.

Title: Penny Sparkle
Review: Penny Sparkle is a welcome addition to the group's carefully curated discography. Longtime fans should be challenged to hear the band's growth, while new listeners are implored to seek out past works for comparison.

Title: All About Tonight
Review: On All About Tonight he's soused, flirty and convincing.

Title: Forever Sounds
Review: Calling Forever Sounds a masterpiece would probably be wildly premature, but this is a deeply satisfying work that reveals new pleasures with repeated listens, and reminds listeners this band is still expanding on what they do best.

Title: The Catastrophist
Review: The Catastrophist is not the over-confident reinvention or the rote revision of outmoded past albums that one might expect after a band’s seven year recording hiatus; it’s simply the next Tortoise record, and a rather good one at that.

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: Holiday Destination is Shah’s third LP, and is her most accomplished effort to date--superbly executed with an ability to make an austere backdrop insatiably compelling.

Title: Lazaretto
Review: The music is smart, diverse and tuned to perfectionist standards, but frequently the lyrics leave the listener wondering, “Where is White’s gut on this?”

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: At eighteen tracks, it never really drags at any point, and a lot can be said for Butler's captivating songwriting.

Title: The Unborn Capitalist From Limbo
Review: Its virtues lie in the quality of the songwriting, and the judicious arrangements: strings are used perfectly, to colour and shade rather than overwhelm. All in all, something of a gem.

Title: Volume 3
Review: There's not much in the way of surprises--this is swinging country-pop with a girl-group backbone, as has always been their way. The problem is that this sickly concoction is often overcooked.

Title: Politics Of The Business
Review: Targets all things "bling" with the same mix of bitter storytelling and star guests, only it's not as funny. [Jul 2003, p.111]

Title: SremmLife 2
Review: Rae Sremmurd is particularly well-suited to the carnival sounds of its debut, but in many places here feels as if it’s getting squelched.

Title: Pigeons
Review: Marked by inconsistent, not fully formed songwriting, Here We Go Magic's new tracks also make for an indecisive, if not bipolar, collection.

Title: Babes Never Die
Review: The real talking point is the poise with which Honeyblood have carried off a record on which they seem to have so completely trusted their instincts.

Title: Ruminations
Review: They’re not as overwrought as the earliest Bright Eyes records--recorded when he was in his teens and early 20s--but they’re just as pure and open-hearted, albeit with the (jaded) wisdom that comes with age, making it arguably his best solo effort yet.

Title: The Jazz Age
Review: It may not be an extreme reworking of song forms or a sudden return to action, perhaps simply another chapter in the various indulgences he enjoys, but in numerous ways, The Jazz Age is Ferry's most radical work yet.

Title: Cookies
Review: The whole midsection of the album is giddily enjoyable.

Title: The Allegory
Review: The Allegory plays out as Royce’s most consolidated offering yet. A definite career high-point for a rapper whose résumé spans over 20 years.

Title: Fantasies
Review: Fantasies finds her taking tentative steps toward optimism--the best possible outcome of getting back to basics.

Title: All the Lost Souls
Review: There's plenty to scorn on All the Lost Souls; Blunt loves a well-worn phrase, and his attempts at humor can be surprisingly crude. But he's onto something. He's not making background music.

Title: All Your Favorite Bands
Review: All Your Favorite Bands is plenty polished, but scratch the surface and there’s close to zero going on beneath it; it’s the kind of record that you’re in danger of forgetting before it’s even finished playing.

Title: The Feast of the Broken Heart
Review: Butler's troupe have always been unique--a dance floor-friendly manifestation of the dissenting, politicised queer underground--but now they're making transcendent music again, too.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: He may be coming to grips with the fact that there are limits to what you can do at the top, as his clash with Billboard regarding his Samsung deal showed, but that doesn’t stop him--lyrically, promotionally, or otherwise--from trying to push the boundaries out a little further.

Title: Open Your Heart
Review: The Men have decided to gift us with yet another 10 glorious songs.

Title: Sideways To New Italy
Review: Nothing quite comes close to ‘Cars In Space’ for desk-slapping earwormery, but with three singer-guitarists at play, the music chops and weaves with an impressive intricacy, always stopping itself short of self-indulgence. If you’re looking for a modern, uplifting celebration of all things riff, these boys have got your back.

Title: Nausea
Review: Where Craft Spells' previous release felt a bit lackadaisical, the more self-aware Nausea, with its themes of growth echoed in its synth crescendos, sports ambition.

Title: Keepin' the Horse Between Me and the Ground
Review: Over the 20 tracks spread over two discs, Steve lives every subtle nuance he wrings out of his voice or guitar. Now one of our most articulate links to a vanishing past, he deserves to be treasured.

Title: Traps
Review: This album is so soaked in self-pity that a track called "Madness" seems like a given. "Stone Froze Mascot" is a bad metaphor in and of itself - more self-pity, more of the same. Sound-wise, the album could use work, too.

Title: The Curved Line
Review: As fun as it is, a great deal of The Curved Line feels too laid-back to be spectacular. Only occasionally does it seem like it might be ready to explode.

Title: Day & Age
Review: Yes, parts of this album are just plain bizarre. Day & Age isn’t as genius as "Hot Fuss," but it has enough merits to keep its makers hit-makers, albeit odd ones.

Title: Room 25
Review: Room 25 is quarter-life crisis turned breakthrough, a balm through which Noname offers a taste of the simple sort of heaven that she's still searching for herself.

Title: Want One
Review: It's a staggeringly ambitious album with an emotional complexity the like of which is rarely seen in pop music of any era, never mind this one.

Title: Herein Wild
Review: It's the work of an artist at the absolute top of her game, and as a result, Herein Wild ranks as one of the best, most inspired and inspiring, albums of 2013.

Title: Microshift
Review: Immersive and lyrically heavy, but not without radiancy and light, Hookworms' ability to turn desperation into euphoria is a quality that makes this album a liberating, often healing, experience.

Title: Avatar
Review: Instead of knocking out another wall-shaking psych rock blast... Avatar comes off like a series of sedate recital pieces performed from sheet music while seated in the round.

Title: Under Cold Blue Stars
Review: Under Cold Blue Stars is a towering achievement. [Apr 2002, p.108]

Title: A Rush of Blood to the Head
Review: Dressed up in subtle strings and pianos, and given time to slowly breathe and develop beyond simple pop, A Rush Of Blood's 11 graceful tracks sparkle and swirl, occasionally escalating into a booming crescendo before dissolving back into delicacy.

Title: Comfort of Strangers
Review: Both her most musically spare and artistically complex [album] to date.

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: Fiona Apple’s fifth record is unbound, a wildstyle symphony of the everyday, an unyielding masterpiece. No music has ever sounded quite like it.

Title: The Terror
Review: While The Terror feels at first glance like an exercise in noise and disintegration, repeated listens reveal it to be a dark, challenging, and ultimately rewarding work of genius. It may be their best yet.

Title: Dear
Review: There's beauty amid the sonic desolation. [Sep 2017, p.116]

Title: Pools of Light
Review: The music is often troubling--as well it should be, given the context--but ultimately it is a trenchantly human record that is sweepingly cinematic in scope.

Title: Centralia
Review: Centralia, for the most part, goes back to the duo's tried-and-true dynamics for a seemingly exhaustive summary of the band.

Title: Pay the Devil
Review: Competent but unremarkable.

Title: Home Wrecking Years
Review: As a whole, Home Wrecking Years is worth a number of complete spins to let it decant and work its magic.

Title: Black Up
Review: That's Black Up's predicament: It wants to be experienced viscerally, but it's being stripped of life by over-intellectualization.

Title: Happy to You
Review: A coy, slow burner, it doesn't kick off properly until its latter stages.

Title: I Know What Love Isn't
Review: Snatches of flute, sax, and female vocal harmony vocals add sympathetic colour to these sad yet inquisitive songs. [Oct 2012, p.83]

Title: Range Anxiety
Review: No, not every song is a winner, and what doesn’t work has a tendency to suck the momentum out of the album, but when the elements lock into step, it’s stunning.

Title: Tweekend
Review: No one who bought Vegas will be disappointed by Tweekend, unless they're looking for some statement of artist growth. That's the only area where this album falters. It is otherwise a solid collection of thundering Big Beat grooves.

Title: Process
Review: Every listen throws up some new, previously unnoticed innovation.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: Much more realized than last year's Young Liars EP, it's also a bit more conventional.

Title: Nocturne
Review: Tatum has nevertheless produced an album that, despite its obvious glances back at the past, is smart, sophisticated and of its own pop moment.

Title: United States of Horror
Review: You’ll need a breather or two, for sure, but that’s the nature of great horror, regardless of what supernatural forces you choose to worship.

Title: Above the Prairie
Review: Eventually, the songs do sink in, but the reason to return to the album is its ability to conjure a specific feeling, whether it's the second the sun sets or the moment that paved highway gives way to backwoods dirt roads.

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: Taken as a whole, Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea stills far short of the Silver Jews’ seminal statements--namely 1998’s "American Water" and 1994’s "Starlite Walker"--but its mix of mischief and melancholy provides more than enough to keep David Berman in the game he continues to reassuringly and unpredictably play on his own terms.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Puberty 2’s only four-minute plus song was far and away its weakest, but here the songs are short, richly melodic, with layers of detail packed in--like super-compressed sad-pop bombs--and topped by Miyawaki’s vocals, at once commanding and plaintive.

Title: True Romance
Review: Minor quibbles aside (Set Me Free is a little over-wrought and clichéd), True Romance is a simply stunning record.

Title: Amanda Leigh
Review: Moore's sincerity and her pleasant vocals bring a great deal of charm to the project as well, and that goes a long way toward overcoming production that is perhaps a bit too slick to recall the homespun appeal of her favorite records.

Title: Pretty Little Head
Review: Adding some range to the offbeat persona she presented in 2004's "Get Away From Me," McKay comes on as a Harlem Holly Golightly, a twentysomething social activist with a disarming mastery of pop vernacular -- pop in the broadest sense, embracing cabaret, show tunes, old standards and a bit of '70s rock in the vein of Elton John and Cyndi Lauper.

Title: Super Collider
Review: Super Collider is so mired in midtempo drudgery and familiar hard rock (not thrash) tropes that it never really connects.

Title: Unbalance
Review: It's one of those odd albums where nearly every track sounds good, but it's all so singleminded and monolithic in its approach that taking it in as a whole almost feels smothering.

Title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy
Review: There are a few weak spots (Stickles' voice is much less suited for the closing ballads than the freight-train punk tracks, though the ballads better suit the surprisingly hopeful lyrics), but The Most Lamentable Tragedy is never less than interesting and rarely less than thrilling.

Title: Infestissumam
Review: Though not nearly as stunning as its predecessor, Infestissumam still has excellent moments, many courtesy of the rhythm section.

Title: Wolf
Review: He just keeps getting better at writhing around in this narrow space of homage and usually lands somewhere just between endearing and brilliant. [May 2013, p.67]

Title: Rebel Heart
Review: Rebel Heart, like its creator, pushes through the pain and, more often than not, lands solidly and with great grace on its feet.

Title: In Case You Didn't Know
Review: In Case You Didn't Know doesn't surprise, but it certainly fulfils.

Title: Four Year Strong
Review: Four Year Strong is catchy, polished and displays lyrical depths. [Jul 2015, p.96]

Title: Bleed Like Me
Review: They come across as a self-contained, insular studio band, with tunes aching to break free of the driving wall of guitars. [May 2005, p.96]

Title: Challengers
Review: Where melodies once surged with hand-clapping giddiness, they're now august and restrained, balladic, not bubbly--fitting songs strung between hope, resignation and regret.

Title: The Unraveling
Review: This is a good album, but it’s one of those albums that either has too much or too little of something.

Title: Paid tha Cost to Be da Boss
Review: Though Snoop Dogg never slipped from the charts, Paid Tha Cost to Be Da Bo$$ smacks of a comeback, and it's a great one.

Title: Strange Weekend
Review: Opener Drifting In And Out, a shimmering piece of dream pop, is beautifully realised, but the other nine songs fail to live up to its promise. [Feb. 2012, p. 110]

Title: The Classic
Review: Much as Get Direct and New Year's day cry to be fleshed out, the reggaefied Ask Me suggests another way forwards, while the fiercely intelligent songs Shame and Stay sum up all that's right about this most singular artist. [Apr 2014, p.112]

Title: EUSA
Review: Over time, however, a fondness for arpeggios becomes as predictable as island life. [Nov 2016, p.39]

Title: The Libertines
Review: No band in recent history has better captured the vertiginous experience of falling apart and loving it. [16 Sep 2004, p.79]

Title: Stay Gold
Review: At times the sisters risk being bogged down by a certain two-dimensionality, but they prove there’s more to them than a sparkling glumness with ‘My Silver Lining.’

Title: What Happens Next
Review: It's to Gill's credit that the band have retained their venom, spitting out terse rhythms and thick squirts of electronica. [Apr 2015, p.95]

Title: Mirror Traffic
Review: A sloppy and inebriated brand of psych-rock still serves as an ideal backdrop to S.M.'s hilariously irreverent storytelling-half silly, half serious and often poignant. This musical recipe really never gets old.

Title: A Crow Looked at Me
Review: As cathartic as the creation of A Crow Looked at Me might have been for this artist, we're obviously meeting him early in the soul-testing climb of this story's arc.

Title: Dystopia
Review: Interestingly, the tracks that fail to scale the same heights as those mentioned above don't take away from the general value of Dystopia, as there is enough underlying merit to be found.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: You're Nothing turns everything up--it's smarter, faster, catchier and noisier than their debut, more a Funhouse than a Rock for Light.

Title: The Ghosts of Highway 20
Review: The Ghosts of Highway 20 is otherwise characterized by its consistency, but what really sets it apart from Williams's previous album is its sense of emotional balance.

Title: Humanz
Review: The album seems pleasingly scattershot as it bounces from guest to guest.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: It's a balanced album by a spirit who seems anything but.

Title: English Tapas
Review: It returns to the sly humor, the hypnotic barking aggression, the occasional whiffs of wistful tune-ish-ness slipped in between robotic beats of Divide and Exit and maybe does it one better.

Title: WIXIW
Review: The latter half of WIXIW has enough to offset their plodding attempts to be experimental.

Title: The Fall of Hearts
Review: Inspiring and forward-looking, this album proves that at 25, Katatonia are still restless and refuse to rest on their laurels.

Title: The Day After
Review: The finest mainstream hip-hop album of the year.

Title: All Eternals Deck
Review: As usual, the North Carolina trio's latest is musically contemplative (mostly acoustic guitar or piano, bass, drums, maybe strings) and lyrically bountiful (camera-ready metaphors, idiosyncratic settings, characters with warts).

Title: In Waves
Review: Chops-wise, all is unimpeachable--but one ends up craving novelty. [Sep 2011, p.98]

Title: Prophets of Rage
Review: None of the tracks approaches the frenetic monstrosity of the Public Enemy song they're named after. But "Strength In Numbers" and "Who Owns Who" are some of the most ripping music anyone involved had made in years, and they're not all repeating themselves. [No. 146, p.59]

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Though it tails off toward the end, the second Weezer-Rubin collaboration (and the band's third self-titled album, out June 3) is a rush, starting with a sustained, four-song soliloquy on pop music's allure.

Title: Dark Night of the Soul
Review: Dark Night is a vocal showcase: Lynch, James Mercer of The Shins and Broken Bells, The Flaming Lips' Wayne Coyne, Iggy Pop, and several more stamp the tracks with appropriately brooding vocals. Only a few really stick, and not always in a good way.

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: Lots of singers set their dating woes to hard guitars and hummable melodies - Coxon just does it better than most.

Title: Jerusalem
Review: While on occasion disappointingly heavy handed, the more wistful moments shine through the murk. [Nov 2002, p.105]

Title: LP3
Review: Minor flaws aside, this new chapter appeases the demand for more epic tunes from a band that has so much to offer.

Title: Temporary Pleasure
Review: A couple tracks may become short-lived flings, but for the most part, the pleasure to be had from Temporary Pleasure will not be short-lived.

Title: Wounded Rhymes
Review: While her 2008 breakout, Youth Novels, was quirky and coy, Wounded Rhymes is hungry, dark, dirty.

Title: Run the Jewels 3
Review: The duo’s knack for high five-worthy boasts and massive one-liners remains undiluted. However, RTJ3 truly excels in some of its darkest moments.

Title: Gaslighter
Review: Dig deep, stick to your guns, “be a lot less guarded”, runs the message of this nourishing dose of laser-sharp country-pop boosterism.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Here, Canada's indie rock A-Team hasn't just reunited--it has border-hopped, aligning with kindred Great Lakes huddle-for-warmth art-rock communards in Chicago, where Tortoise leader John McEntire produced an antsier version of a great BSS record.

Title: VOIDS
Review: VOIDS is largely composed of lightly angsty guitar rock anthems and pseudo-emo ballads, with little instrumental sophistication to satisfy long-term fans.

Title: Diver
Review: It's amicable, it's friendly for the shoes, but it's like watching a mud-covered wild horse frantically kick at the locked barn doors.

Title: Conditions of My Parole
Review: Conditions of My Parole, featuring a supporting cast that includes Keenan's son Devo and ex-Mars Volta drummer Jon Theodore, reveals a more reassuring side of a singer better known for willful alienation.

Title: Walking With Thee
Review: For all of Walking with Thee's obvious musical accomplishments, its most impressive facet is the ability to transcend all the hype, hoopla and haranguing surrounding its release.

Title: Many Moons
Review: All told, Many Moons is not only worthwhile for fans of Real Estate and related projects, but for lovers of the honeyed melodies and genial jangle of the pleasantest of power pop.

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: Carrie & Lowell is the most harrowingly personal work Stevens has offered us to date; it also ranks with his most skillfully crafted albums despite its spartan approach, and it's a sometimes difficult but profoundly moving work.

Title: Soft Will
Review: It's a lovely place that Soft Will fashions here, but it sounds hesitant about pulling you in, perhaps because its creators are secretly concerned that you'll realize you aren't really going anywhere.

Title: The Grinding Wheel
Review: While the album does lose focus at times, loosening its initial invigorating grip, the jovial bounce of Let's All Go To Hades is a surefire live hit when you've had a few pints. [11 Feb 2017, p.52]

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: With any luck, Wakin On A Pretty Daze will go down as a document to the workman he really is.

Title: Radium Death
Review: Radium Death finds Whitmore at his songwriting and singing best. That said, his successful indulgence in rock & roll's various forms makes one wish he had just put the entire album on stun.

Title: Uh Huh Her
Review: Once you get acclimatized to the torturous messages and the dynamic, diverse musical accompaniment shifts from song to song, it becomes obvious that Uh Huh Her is one of Harvey's most rewarding albums.

Title: One Plus One Is One
Review: A record which is closer in spirit to the rustic eccentricity of his '...Bewilderbeast' debut, while still moving things forward. [19 Jun 2004, p.57]

Title: In Our Gun
Review: Buy this album and hold it dear, because you won't hear a better one any time soon.

Title: Virtue
Review: Virtue is the sound of honest confusion--messy, complicated and intriguing.

Title: Silence Is Sexy
Review: the "new" Neubauten is a stronger unit than it has been in the entire latter half of its existence.... Silence Is Sexy is brilliant, and Einsturzende Neubauten remains without peer. [#46, p.75]

Title: Swimming
Review: Swimming is ample evidence that Miller can pick up the pieces and continue evolving, his grasp on thoughtful, introspective hip-hop getting stronger by the album.

Title: Plastic Anniversary
Review: The project ultimately feels a little vague and indulgent. Though the sounds of plastic on offer are eclectic and the compositions joyous, Matmos seem to acknowledge climate change as a throwaway aside in favour of an avant garde remaking of physical theatre. [Mar 2019, p.55]

Title: Relapse
Review: While Jourgensen seems re-engaged with his music, he's also more disinterested than ever in the wider pop culture.

Title: The Sun Came Out
Review: The songs across this double album aren’t always particularly memorable, but they feel suffused with the warm glow that obviously accompanied the recording process.

Title: Dark Is the Way, Light Is a Place
Review: Dark Is The Way, Light Is A Place is largely proof that what Anberlin might now lack in immediate catchiness, they more than make up for in composure. [Oct 2010, p.111]

Title: Far From Home
Review: A glorious summer album.

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: The debut from London quartet Savages burns with a feverish sense of purpose: the sheer intensity with which She Will or City's Full are delivered is breathtaking.

Title: The Unsemble
Review: The Unsemble is an album that sounds like it was phoned in from a bunch of guys who clearly think they just have to turn up to the studio and the magic will flow instantly from the fingers of these master craftsmen.

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: Though they certainly do their fair share of sampling, they tend to use fragments as a means of fleshing out the battling, overdriven guitars, triumphant trumpet lines, and drum assaults that seem to break through walls with the barreling force of a thousand Kool-Aid men.

Title: Further Complications
Review: Neither Cocker's chewy structures nor his voice's subtle shadings are particularly well suited to Albini's you-are-there engineering. Fortunately, this collection of surging and reeling tunes is the former Pulp frontman's strongest since "Different Class."

Title: The Best of Luck Club
Review: Lahey stands out for her versatility. With buoyant wit, she rolls with the changes and delivers a lucid, omnivorous perspective that’s all her own.

Title: Person Pitch
Review: Somehow, these constant flourishes enhance, rather than obscure, the disc's plentiful catchy bits, giving Person Pitch a resonant, off-kilter charm. [Apr 2007, p.93]

Title: Island
Review: This is Pallett’s most ambitious album to date, filled with complex string sections, captivating melodies and the kind of lyrics that show a love for life seldom heard.

Title: To the Happy Few
Review: Medicine is at its best on To the Happy Few when it pushes its sound to the point of indulgence, then finds a way to pull everything together.

Title: Hate
Review: Hate is a beautifully gilded record, thoroughly nice and thoroughly listenable, and a mark higher than a lot of pop music with lofty intentions, but it doesn't move you to extremes.

Title: Norman Fucking Rockwell!
Review: Del Rey has certainly carved out her own niche in the world of singer-songwriters, much as the quasi-namesake of Norman Fucking Rockwell! did in the art world. This shows her refining that approach, adding a few new brush strokes here and there, but still providing a unique and fascinating tableau as a whole.
On (), the band steer their ghost ship into darker waters, erecting a vast, austere cathedral of sound, then sticking around to score a funeral mass inside. [Dec 2002, p.140]

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: A cache of hissy, vivid, occasionally creepy but mostly sweetly touching brain pop that stands proudly alongside GBV's ragged former glories. [Feb 2012, p.97]

Title: A Small Turn of Human Kindness
Review: The songs here all flow together, with intertwined parts and themes-a sludge symphony of sorts.

Title: Get Tragic
Review: Get Tragic, quite candidly, is a virtually perfect record. There’s nothing about it that’s out of place. It draws on the best parts of the band’s past history, catchy choruses, glam-rock guitars, electronic riffs that don’t leave your mind for days, mind-blowing lyrics--all combined with a glamour that lurks at the edge of the hometown you escaped, as the sun slowly sets.

Title: Innocence
Review: “Pontiak” and “ballad” were probably never supposed to be in the same sentence together, but the band’s insistence on its soft side for even a few songs is an exciting prospect that makes Innocence a diamond in the rough.

Title: Short Movie
Review: Short Movie lacks the seamless thematic and tonal cohesion of Once I Was An Eagle, but it offers more immediate pleasures.

Title: Original Machines
Review: For all Keely's best intents though, Original Machines falls short of genuine enlightenment; simultaneously too much and not enough. [Mar 2016, p.75]

Title: Radio Retaliation
Review: They were the first on the block with this particular subgenre and are still in front of a massive paxk following in their wake. [Dec 2008, p.72]

Title: Edgeland
Review: Far from a mid-life indulgence or quirky side project, this is a brave and beautiful album. [May 2013, p.102]

Title: My Woman
Review: The relentless heat of My Woman can be exhausting over the course of 10 searing tracks--the addition of a throwaway would give a weary listener time to regroup. But Angel Olsen’s fearless and eloquent embrace of raw emotions in all their messy splendor ultimately feels oddly uplifting, the way it always does when you witness a gifted artist at her best.

Title: Konnichiwa
Review: Konnichiwa isn’t just the sound of young Britain, but a bar-raising example of just how creative UK music can be.

Title: Yuck
Review: Strip away the noise and you'll realize that the charm of Yuck is rooted in fundamentals of great songwriting. [March 2011, p. 108]

Title: The Pinkprint
Review: If the late-add dance track confuses things, it's hard to fault Minaj. Throughout The Pinkprint, she's intent on channeling her talent to explore and document her many moods. The combination is often, if not always, intoxicating.

Title: Shape Shift With Me
Review: Shape Shift With Me doesn’t offer a lot in the way of answers, but watching her fumble her way through the questions is a pleasure, regardless.

Title: What a Terrible World, What a Beautiful World
Review: For now, it’s a record that gets better with each listen, a present-day anomaly. It’s the sound of a band unafraid of taking chances, and succeeding more often than not.

Title: Song For Our Daughter
Review: Song for Our Daughter brims with peaceful reflections that, even though Marling herself is just grazing her 30s, could seem like the work of an artist in their twilight years.

Title: Mudcrutch
Review: Mostly, Mudcrutch works for everyone: fans, the members who were left behind fame-wise, and Petty himself, who gets to look like a good guy for giving them a taste of what they missed.

Title: Tales from the Realm of the Queen of Pentacles
Review: At her brightest and her best.

Title: Broken Ear Record
Review: This glorious racket... has a beating, hideous heart to it. [Oct 2005, p.76]

Title: Flamagra
Review: Highlights are everywhere if you give them time to reveal themselves.

Title: What a Time to Be Alive
Review: As it is, the sense that absolutely nothing here has been left to chance--and that What a Time to Be Alive might have been a more interesting album if it had--is a tough one to avoid.

Title: You Could Have It So Much Better
Review: Sounds exactly like what you'd expect. [Oct 2005, p.132]

Title: Corsicana Lemonade
Review: It adds up to a challenging, taut, and inspirational 39 minutes of music you won’t be humming after the first spin. But, because of its confidence, integrity and diversity, you’ll be back for repeated visits.

Title: Lost Horizons
Review: Such perfectionism can easily be construed as soullessness, but I think what Deakin and Franglin are actually striving for here is to strike a balance between the warmth and humanity of their music's sounds and the machine-like grace of its flawless production.

Title: Soul 2
Review: His voice and interpretive skills are such, though, that most tracks fit him like a glove.

Title: Rocket
Review: An album that ultimately sounds curiously disengaged.

Title: Amnesiac
Review: Too tentative and slight to be genuinely moving.

Title: Sequitur
Review: This seeming juxtaposition of entirely retro leaning, concise pop sensibilities and massive, atmospheric tendencies shouldn't meld seamlessly, let alone adjoin each other, yet Hauschildt repeatedly finds a way to fit the pieces together.

Title: Mountaintops
Review: Mountaintops has plenty of upbeat romps, but the most compelling moments are the epic, minor-key laments.

Title: Horehound
Review: The Dead Weather is another slightly unsatisfying fling alongside The Raconteurs. [Jul 2009, p.84]

Title: The Haze
Review: If you’re a fan, rest easy knowing that PABH have done good. The Haze is their best yet. For the rest of you, make a bonfire of your Foo Fighters, Biffy Clyro and Bring Me the Horizon records. You’ve got no need for them anymore. PABH are it.

Title: Misery Is a Butterfly
Review: Despite sounding derivative at times, Misery... further refines [their] volatile mix with a touch of fidgety elegance. [19 Mar 2004, p.65]

Title: Kiss Me Once
Review: Full of sparkling hooks, the results do a good job of melding Minogue’s effervescent pop grooves with the dense, heavily treated vocals and deep sub bass of modern electro dance trends.... Subject matter and delivery are strained by coquettish pandering.

Title: Researching the Blues
