Review: Researching the Blues is a goddamn gem, crackling with energy, that totally celebrates the pure bliss and joy that rock 'n' roll can, and should be.  In short, it's everything that you were hoping it would be.

Title: Disaster Piece
Review: If it was all such axe-grinding, Disaster Piece might flag--but it has vision too.

Title: Stand Up and Speak
Review: Their electronic music brims with heartfelt emotions that anyone could understand.

Title: The Sermon on Exposition Boulevard
Review: Ambitious and sprawling, a mud-caked journey to transcendence.

Title: Nothing But the Beat
Review: Guetta might be one of the only people given partial credit for creating a sea change in pop music who's also unquestionably the least compelling example of that style.

Title: Command Your Weather
Review: Big Business may be broadcasting from metal's outer limits, but these knotty post-rock anthems dressed up in stoner metal might are as engaging as they are sonically demanding.

Title: Make My Head Sing
Review: Mayfield has insisted for years that love is treacherous and obliterating, and on Make My Head Sing... her guitar enacts that romantic violence. It provides an intriguing counterpart to her vocals, turning her inner monologues into something like an argument.

Title: AM
Review: Their music is suddenly sexier, no doubt a credit to Turner’s vision for AM, and continues to mature.

Title: Tremors
Review: While Taylor definite seems to prefer to approach his themes and ideas with a sombre touch, he’s not afraid to whack up the pace a notch or two, and it appears he actively enjoys getting stuck into dissembling standard percussive forces.

Title: Tomb
Review: Despite the album’s dark, damp, sepulchral title, light manifests numerous times on Tomb. In the dizzying chime of his careful fingerpicking and high-pitched howls, De Augustine captures love’s bright blaze.

Title: Ghosts of the Great Highway
Review: It's like everything that has always been great about the Red House Painters made a notch or two more exciting in the studio.

Title: Where Does This Door Go
Review: Hawthorne's songwriting, crisply appointed arrangements and effortlessly gratifying croon feel more casually confident than ever, making This Door a third straight slam dunk. [No. 101, p.55]

Title: Three
Review: It is slow, winding, and meditative, composed almost entirely of piano, bass, and drums, and builds outwards from minimal meanderings to overgrown thickets of instrumentation.

Title: Nothing Is Wrong
Review: You may not love it, but you'll probably like it, and that's enough.

Title: Shulamith
Review: Low-slung, dub-ish beats are appealing, though lead some tracks to Snooze Town.

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: Stewart remains a firebrand intent on creating skull-splintering sounds and society-skewering words.

Title: No Line on the Horizon
Review: It has the pomp and arrogance of their best work, enough new sounds and interesting new avenues to satisfy the musos and, at its core, is a very good collection of very good songs played very well. A little more silliness would go a long way, though.

Title: Only In Dreams
Review: Dum Dum Girls always know exactly who they are, play on their own strengths, and leave the audience fully satisfied and happy to come back for more. Simplicity rarely sounds this good.

Title: Cosmic Egg
Review: On this album, Wolfmother becomes a band worth paying attention to.

Title: Eyes Open
Review: Eyes Open dives headfirst into mainstream waters, hoping the strength of its intentions will be visible through the glossy bombast. It is, but it takes some surface-scratching to reach it.

Title: High Dive
Review: There's a lack of clutter to songs such as To The Open Spaces and the title cut, with its barely-there brass arrangements, which makes them simple pleasures, and among the best songs of her career. [Jun 2003, p.102]

Title: MeYouWeYou
Review: Tracks like "Steel Drummer" shade between euphoric rave and freakout energy, while "Black And Blue" has a distinct rock edge with its dark riffs and darker mood. [Sep 2013, p.63]

Title: Serpentine Prison
Review: The result is a set of forlorn ballads that start spare and gather beauty as they grow.

Title: Kintsugi
Review: So maybe Kintsugi isn’t a perfect effort. But like the ceramic art itself, Death Cab’s attempt at repatching was thoughtful, deliberate and, at times, really beautiful.

Title: Crazy for You
Review: It's weirdly powerful stuff this, couch-rock, heartbreak coated in cereal. And with this limelight-stealing album Best Coast are providing an amazing advert for dropping out, having mad crushes and doing very little other than getting high.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: Contains some of their best work, as well as some of their most indulgent.

Title: Show Your Bones
Review: Show Your Bones picks up where "Maps" left off, with the trio finding a middle ground between self-conscious primitivism and refined pop. [31 Mar 2006, p.60]

Title: Lala Belu
Review: These six new tracks flow neatly on from those recorded for Tche Belew 40 years before. [Mar 2018, p.95]

Title: Skying
Review: Skying does for early '80s psychedelic Brit-rock what Primary Colours did for post-punk, and both are as satisfying with such goals as one can imagine. Can their '90s Seattle grunge tribute be far behind?

Title: Let It Reign
Review: Let It Reign’s abrasiveness does little to deflect from its disappointing lack of ambition.

Title: My Maudlin Career
Review: My Maudlin Career offers soul and sophistication in abundance.

Title: Lust for Youth
Review: Overall there's little evolution from previous albums here. [Jul 2019, p.30]

Title: Nomad
Review: It remains to be seen whether Nomad reveals Bombino to be an artist of limited means or one who is making the occasional misstep on the way to something great.

Title: Bardo Pond
Review: Bardo Pond's self-titled is a massive, monumental piece of work, proving once again that this long-running outfit can still crank the heavy, mind-numbing psych that it's always been known for.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: Here's the solid, understated third album that digs in without trying to break new ground.

Title: The Crossing
Review: Its expansive ambition abetted by fellow travellers including Wayne Kramer and Peter Perrett. [Oct 2018, p.27]

Title: Woman
Review: Even if this [air of refined sophistication] can occasionally make Women feel a little bloodless, you have to marvel at the exquisite execution. [May 2013, p.76]

Title: Dude Incredible
Review: Shellac delivers a very spare and assaultive listen, 33 minutes that fly by and demand repeated listens.

Title: Love in Beats
Review: Undoubtedly one of his strongest. [Feb 2017, p.97]

Title: Oceans Will Rise
Review: Nothing spectacular, but something long-lasting and reliable. [Fall 2008, p.84]

Title: ASTROWORLD
Review: This is the sound of a musician who has worked to forge an entire world, an empire, around himself--we can peer in, but from afar, guessing at his motives and life behind the velvet rope.

Title: uknowhatimsayinÂ¿
Review: uknowhatimsayin¿ isn't Danny Brown's most anything, but it's the least a lot of things: least intense, least avant-garde, least worried about the world around it. And when we're talking about an MC for whom more is better, it's easy to feel like we've lost something essential.

Title: Welcome Back
Review: Songs like "Do You Remember" and "Wasting My Time" are tolerable but don't require repeated listening.

Title: Last 2 Walk
Review: Three 6 Mafia’s aspiration to evolve seems to have manifested itself on Last 2 Walk, from production to sound to lyrics. Having taken their novel sound to its lofty limits, it is time for the group to change and progress towards another musical frontier. However, their aspirations of progressing by melding Hollywood and the hood have largely failed.

Title: Woodstock
Review: While all that tinkering and aiming for the center have reached their payoff with the most commercially viable record of the group’s career, something of what made Portugal. The Man unique feels like it’s been lost.

Title: Tourist in This Town
Review: Tourist in This Town is sharply written, revealing a mordant, humorous understanding of Crutchfield herself and the people around her. There’s a vulnerability in these tunes that lives alongside the cleverness, so that we feel her angst, even as we appreciate her cleverness.

Title: LAX
Review: At 19 tracks, LAX is bloated and uneven, more often than not marked by weak beats and uninspired appearances. The Game’s skill and wit alone save this from being a complete disaster.

Title: Hunter
Review: Twice nominated for Britain’s Mercury Prize, Calvi has consistently delivered brilliant albums. This new era of openness only serves to push her to more relevant and engaging levels.

Title: Acid Tongue
Review: Jenny is a definitely a chosen one in the talent department, but she doesn't really let on.

Title: O
Review: The big, inescapable problem with O is that, aside from being derivative, Rice's songwriting is also unbearably repetitive-- he stubbornly relies upon time-tested singer/songwriter formulas (quiet acoustic strumming and sober, wavering vocals), and repeats them almost exactly the same way, every time.

Title: Masana Temples
Review: Kikagaku Moyo sound more assured than ever on this fourth album. [Nov 2018, p.32]

Title: Me
Review: Me is both a fabulous anthology of boisterous pop songs, and a timely, revelatory album for a lot of people to live vicariously through.

Title: Things Go Better with RJ and AL
Review: Seeming short at 40 minutes, it's a slight album, and it's marred by Blueprint's slavish devotion to his own goofy song-concepts.

Title: Surrender to the Fantasy
Review: On Magik Markers’ latest, Surrender to the Fantasy, the rough edges are further sanded down, the songs revealing interest in a diverse set of genre signposts.

Title: Replica
Review: Chugging, grinding, crackling, swelling, bubbling, babbling, these tracks don't sound like part of the natural world, but they do sound cognizant of the natural world.

Title: Pure, Beyond Reproach
Review: Pure, Beyond Reproach feels lost and directionless at times.

Title: The Tipping Point
Review: The Tipping Point has more soul, vision and musicianship than most bands muster in a lifetime. [31 Jul 2004, p.41]

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: Nine Types of Lights finds them boldly going forward with their most cheerful, party-centric effort to date. [May 2011, p.123]

Title: At War With The Mystics

Title: Fragrant World
Review: Its sound is bright, slick, and micromanaged.

Title: Caracal

Title: There's Me And There's You
Review: The result is a confusing confection that plays out like "Anti-Capitalism: The Musical." [Jan 2009, p.96]

Title: JESUS IS KING
Review: There are flashes of genius throughout, moments that insinuate where Kanye could go next with his music. In a sense, the album’s modest pleasures play to its (intended) message, which is supposed to be one of human fallibility and the prospect of improving oneself. But Kanye is eventually going to have to confront the serious limitations that his faith is putting on the range of his art’s expression.

Title: Convenanza
Review: Convenanza regularly dips into a bag of tried and tested moves that are little more than default settings: dubby basslines, plenty of space, echoes, jazzy trumpets that sound like deflating balloons and so on.

Title: In Love With Oblivion
Review: For all its clever-clever effects and pose-throwing, In Love With Oblivion is a big fun record meant to be blasted through the loudest speakers possible.

Title: No Closer to Heaven
Review: With No Closer to Heaven, Campbell and the Wonder Years have made an album that's more mature and thoughtful than before, but no less passionate and direct, and it ranks with their finest work to date as well as suggesting this band has an interesting and exciting future ahead.

Title: 1000 Days
Review: The unpredictability factor will cause some to turn to something easier on the ear, but if you were to persevere with 1000 Days, it’s very likely that you would appreciate it.

Title: The No-Hit Wonder
Review: Cory Branan may not have any hits--yet--but No-Hit Wonder shows that's sure not for lack of talent or a voice that makes his songs go down easy.

Title: Last
Review: Somehow the group manages, with masterfully restrained piano and strings, to wring joy from bygone heartache.

Title: Run Around the Sun
Review: These ebullient songs are clearly a joy for both the listener and the band.

Title: This Is What The Truth Feels Like
Review: There’s nothing even remotely inventive here.

Title: Dirty Projectors
Review: Dirty Projectors’ ornate arrangements can’t hide the fact that these songs are as direct and unguarded as Longstreth allows himself to get.

Title: Human Performance
Review: While Parquet Courts show here that they can tackle lost love brilliantly, some of the more interesting lyrics come from those where they portray the less tangible mental issues that are rife in modern society.

Title: And It's Still Alright

Title: B'Day

Review: The West Coast threesome's pillowy, nostalgic abstractions veer from the sweeping histrionics of M83 or breezy gestures of various Scandinavians toward a woozy, romantic restlessness

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun

Title: Strange Peace
Review: Strange Peace is more--more intense, more melodic, more brutal, more confident.

Title: Dumb Luck
Review: Dumb Luck can't help but sound like a compilation, with peaks and valleys directly correlating to a taste for the vocals.

Title: Ukulele Songs

Instead, Out of Range dishes out good feelings and Zen calm—more East than West. These days, we all need that sort of thing, regardless of your stance on sound baths.

Title: Minutes to Midnight

Title: Sonic Boom
Review: Classic and maybe even a little awesome, Sonic Boom makes that "hottest band in the world" tag much easier to swallow.

Title: The Jazz Age
Review: What we have on The Jazz Age is music that’s haunting itself.

Title: No Time

Title: Odd Blood

Title: Zoo
Review: It's punk rock by the numbers.

Title: uknowhatimsayinÂ¿

Title: She Has No Strings Apollo
Review: Though all the elements that make their music great are still present, never do they crystallize and come together quite like they have in the past.

Title: I Had A Dream That You Were Mine
Review: A finely observed, immaculately produced work, full of diversions, hooks, and charm.

Review: Robison's focus, on introspective ruminations and the vagaries of relationships, is relentlessly earnest. And as well-played as the music can be, lyrically it’s a very bumpy ride.

Title: Drift Code
Review: It is a very human experience, and if you can work past the occasional awkwardness of the vocal by spending more time with it then listening treasures await.

Title: The Bronx (III)
Review: Nevertheless, the casual listener will have little to soak up from here, only surface bruising. The masochists amongst us already know we’re gonna get our kicks from this.

Title: Ancient Romans
Review: You can't help but move along to some of the entrancing, pulsing drones found on Ancient Romans; altogether, another epic, grandiose, striking LP from one of the best and most underrated musicians of the moment.

Title: Speech Therapy
Review: Musically, the live instrumentation and golden-era feel to the production make this record an enjoyable listen.

Title: Absolutely Free
Review: The album swells, twists and turns, but rather than feeling helplessly meandering--a pitfall of the genre--it has an organic pacing that naturally starts and ends with each song.

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: A must for anyone still heavily rotating Moon Safari.

Title: Mura Masa
Review: Pure quality, from start to finish. [Aug 2017, p.109]

Title: The Id

Title: For Years

Title: Have One on Me
Review: Her latest firmly establishes her as a singer-songwriter to be reckoned with.

Title: Inside the Rose

Title: Malpractice

Title: Voyageur

Title: Before the Poison

Title: More Than Just a Dream
Review: It’s an album that’s hard to love, yet easy to like.

Title: Phase Zero
Review: The longing in Morgan’s voice separates this from whatever other indie pop record you tried and failed to enjoy this year. He isn’t concerned with hiding what records influenced him, only in making you remember why you loved them in the first place.

Title: Somebody's Knocking
Review: More than a few of Lanegan's longtime fans will be puzzled by his transformation into the party animal of the dark side, but his vocals are typically strong, and he sounds fully engaged with the material, happy to be visiting the VIP section of the Place Where Nothing Living Goes, and he's excited and challenged in a way he's hasn't sounded in a while.

Title: Congratulations
Review: There are nine tracks of somewhat forgettable spacey-psych 70's songs that are packed with confusion from start to finish. It sounds as if the band skipped a few pages, assuming that their immediate debut success would carry over with the risks they took for this one.

Title: Great Vengeance and Furious Fire
Review: The Heavy shines best on stage, where the band is an overwhelming force, but Great Vengeance is an entrancing peek at crush-worthy musical raw power.

Title: Field Music
Review: Effortlessly blends candy-pop conventions with the concise edge of punk. [Jun/Jul 2006, p.128]

Title: The Winter of Mixed Drinks
Review: Frightened Rabbit is mostly content to continue exploring the vein it tapped a couple of years ago. Fans will need to be slightly more patient, but they’ll ultimately be well rewarded.

Title: Love 2

Title: Graveyard Whistling

Title: Apex Predator - Easy Meat
Review: Honestly, 34 years deep, this is one of the band's best albums. [Feb 2015, p.92]

Title: Saint Cecilia EP

Title: Le Kov
Review: Gwenno is doing important work here, and for those willing to open their minds and step into the mythical land of Le Kov will find that they may not want to leave.

Title: Blood Bitch

Title: Compass

Title: Ricky Music

Title: Write Me Back

Title: Failed States
Review: This is easily one of their best albums, which is no small feat six albums into such an illustrious career.

Title: The Path of Totality

Title: New Skin
Review: Exhilarating or jarring, depending on taste. [Dec 2016, p.26]

Review: In the end, a necessary acquisition for fans or an easy way for newcomers to judge whether they are wacky enough to join the Major's cyberpunky reggae party.

Title: Mezmerize

Title: Ogilala

Title: Exo
Review: [A] thrilling and possibly definitive album, it's impenetrable, multifaceted, and irrepressibly imaginative.

Title: Wet Will Always Dry

Title: Asunder, Sweet and Other Distress

Title: Star Climbing
Review: The craft Zoot Woman bring to Star Climbing'a best moments continues to set them apart from the ever-growing number of similarly minded acts.

Title: Rough and Rowdy Ways
Review: Rough And Rowdy Ways is undoubtedly the work of an artist with one eye on his legacy, yet it’s so full of wit, mischief and life that it positively sings. [Sep 2020, p.52]

Title: Go Fly a Kite
Review: He hones his best Cars, Harry Nilsson and Wilco moves into a personally revealing breakup record.

Title: Modern Times
Review: Love And Theft was quite unlike any other pop album--apart, that is, from Modern Times, its direct and audacious sequel. [Sep 2006, p.72]

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: By my count, you've still got 50 keepers out of 69, give or take a few songs. And about a third of those sound like classics.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: If this album is less immediately impressive than its predecessor it’s because apart from tightening their arrangements the sound is still exactly what you expect.

Title: Minor Victories
Review: Minor Victories is the work of intimacy and candor. It goes beyond a one-off project and instead becomes a contained piece of longing and hurting. The cohesion behind it all should be the envy of any band whose members have the luxury of being in direct vicinity of one another.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: Under the cover of midnight, Del Rey has been exploring big ideas about eroticism, drugs, myth, the empty promise of YOLO, what it means to be a woman, and the American soul.

Title: Oceans Will Rise
Review: Production seals it all as taut and as giving as speaker mesh.
If you dug them back then, you'll likely dig them now. [Jun 2019, p.93]

Title: Grown Backwards
Review: [A] marvelously sophisticated, extremely political album.

Title: Be Brave
Review: With songs like “All You Can Hide Inside” revealing a flair for rough-around-the-edges ballads, Be Brave shows that the Strange Boys are growing--not in a self-consciously “mature” way, but enough to make them more than just purveyors of raffish garage rock.

Title: Trilla
Review: The huge guest list is also a plus since Ross would have a hard time carrying this album on his own, but when surrounded by talent he pushes a little harder and comes up with a handful of rhymes that aren't tired or clichéd.

Title: Clearing The Path To Ascend
Review: This seventh record still offers plenty for those who want an aural assault. [30 Aug 2014, p.51]

Title: ERAAS
Review: In all, ERAAS, though fully invested in the possibilities of their vacuum and their vocal prowess, are at their best when the instruments can breathe.

Title: The Talkies
Review: Overall this is a band that, by playing fast and loose with verse-chorus-verse, generate an addictive kind of noise.

Title: Medicine County
Review: Medicine County is more boisterous than 2008's Dirt Don't Hurt, but there's still something pleasantly lackadaisical about Golightly's delivery, and her songs never feel like they've been blindly co-opted.

Title: American Gong
Review: A glorious mess, just like our fucked-up world. [Winter 2010, p.100]

Title: The Bachelor
Review: The Bachelor is a thoughtful record whose greatest flaw is only that it’s overthought (though to the fans obsessive enough to fund it, that’s probably a bonus).

Title: Championships
Review: While the Audemars-Piguet and Rolls-Royce Wraith have not disappeared from the equation and Meek Mill’s affinity for the finer things is still intact, his conscience is the crown jewel of Championships.

Title: Slow Air
Review: Some of Still Corners' most intimate-sounding music, Slow Air's finest moments feel less like they're adopting the customs of a new land and more like they're adapting them to what they do best--capturing moods beautifully.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light I
Review: From behind her kit, Adrienne Davies keeps slow-mo time as new member Karl Blau thickly kneads deep ribbons of rumbling bass that counter Dylan Carlson's stately, dark holler melodies. The new moon suits them well.

Title: Radio Music Society
Review: [Radio Music Society] positions Spalding as an artist looking forward and back, a powerful stance.

Title: Delta
Review: There are standout moments--the aforementioned ‘Beloved’, the full-hearted chorus of lead single ‘Guiding Light’, the delicate tinkle of piano underpinned by a dog barking in the distance on ‘October Skies’--but you must sift through these sprawling 14 tracks to find them.

Title: Grand Romantic
Review: Fun. co-producers Jeff Bhasker and Emile Haynie help Ruess create richly orchestrated bombast with the right amount of sonic wanderlust.

Title: Never Never Love
Review: Listeners are left wondering if they’ve just gorged on an Anglo response to J-pop, a post (white-)boy-band attempt to alley-oop new jack swing, or the work of a Scissor Sister gone solo.

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: The great thing about this album is the same as was great about the last full length LCD Soundsystem album, and that is its effortless blend and execution of mix.

Title: Ode to Joy
Review: Such moments of challenging, bold experimentation (which Wilco hasn't really bothered with off-stage on this scale for a while), coupled with a set of by turns desolate and uplifting, strange and sweet tunes, makes Ode to Joy mandatory listening for anyone interested in the enduring creative potential of rock - sorry, folk – music.

Title: Some of My Best Friends Are DJs
Review: Anyone searching for a wholly absorbing listening experience should look (and listen) elsewhere.

Title: Planet Earth
Review: Planet Earth is one of those albums he makes when he's trying a little harder than usual, if not hard enough to alienate his core audience, which loves him for indulging himself.

Title: The Circle
Review: But even while Mr. Bon Jovi is sympathizing with the common man, the scrape in his voice is never wrenching. And while the arrangements are mildly darker than on the group’s previous albums, this group is still drawn magnetically to swelling choruses, its ambition of scale still grander than its ambition of import.

Title: Lucid Dreaming
Review: Though it may come across as an innocuous affair to some, Lucid Dreaming simultaneously triumphs as both a cohesive, introspective body of work and a bona fide pop record.

Title: Black Origami
Review: Sometimes the constant shifts can leave you reeling and wondering what Jlin is trying to get at, but it’s never long before they pick you up again and pull you back into it. This is the sound of a huge talent blossoming.

Title: Valley Tangents
Review: Blues Control are no longer noisy or childishly rudimentary, at least by most avant-yardsticks. Cho, on piano and keyboards, improvises with a new deftness; Waterhouse claws back a degree of rockism with thudding boogie drums and a guitar choked with the dust of its own basement.

Title: Not To Disappear
Review: It’s not so much sidestepped the perils of the second album as trampled them, taking the sound that won the band all those packed festival tents and driving it forward, matted and bloodied like Miles Teller at the end of Whiplash, no longer weeping and withdrawn but pulsing and alive. And it’s genuinely exciting to hear.

Title: Migration
Review: With Migration, Green blends the unexpected with the familiar and emerges with some of his most affecting work yet.

Title: Epiphany
Review: While the material is strong, this is all about Michele's stylish but subtle vocalizing and its jazzy inflections and nuances.

Title: Stay Home
Review: All in all, Stay Home is a step up from the Beets' debut, though it's hard not to imagine they're going to have to face the choice of either learning to play or hitting the creative wall some time in the future.

Title: No Color
Review: No Color isn't a bad album by any means - it's great at times, never less than good, and certainly better than could reasonably have been expected - but there's no sign here of return or retreat to their old strengths.

Title: Frances The Mute
Review: Frances bursts at the jewel-case hinges with Comatorium’s trademarks: musical inventiveness and wildly emotive vocals.

Title: Notes on a Conditional Form
Review: For an album as expansive and big-swinging as “Notes,” its hit rate is surprisingly high. The 1975 is still walking that tightrope of self-indulgence, but more often than not it has learned how to retain its balance.

Title: Stage Four
Review: Stage Four reverberates because it’s a concept album, the tracks linear and part of the greater whole.

Title: The Optimist
Review: On The Optimist, Anathema really do cement their title as one of the UK’s most revered rock bands, prog or otherwise: it’s a big jumble of ambitious ideas, executed near-perfectly--a mess, but a big, sprawling, dense, euphoric, beautiful one.

Title: The Book of Souls
Review: In fairness, we have heard the duelling solos, galloping Guitar riffs and Dickinson’s operatic Rock vocals all before, in that sense there’s nothing particularly new in form of style (but that’s no bad omen). Upon The Book of Souls the band do, however, sound tighter than ever, offering a raw atmosphere that makes the album sound as though it was almost written in order to be played live.

Title: Whispers
Review: There’s true beauty in this disc as Dico soulfully and honestly negotiates her way through the vagaries of love.

Title: Brilliant! Tragic!
Review: On Art Brut's fourth – and sturdiest – album to date, he delivers his wry recaps between sudden thrusts of guitar and rigid, right-angle percussion.

Title: Babel
Review: Consciously or not, U2-style evangelism is all over the Mumfords' bland but biblically titled second album, Babel.

Title: Star Kitty's Revenge
Review: She reinvents herself as a salacious digital temptress, crooning through soulful slow rollers. [Mar 2002, p.129]

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: As a cohesive album and a personal statement, Sound of Silver is superior in most every way.

Title: Serpents Unleashed
Review: Serpents Unleashed doesn't expand Skeletonwitch's armoury, but this band never disappoint. [26 Oct 2013, p.53]

Title: I Disagree
Review: As both a symbolic avatar for her life changes and a strong empowerment statement, I Disagree celebrates Poppy's rebirth as a pop-metal alchemist and unabashed rule-breaker.

Title: Four
Review: The album suffers some of the worst adjectives any musician can hear: boring, forgettable, and embarrassing.

Title: First Kiss
Review: The first few tracks are like The Black Crowes without the cosmic sophistication. [Apr 2015, p.104]

Title: Soul Music
Review: A thrilling creative renaissance on so many levels.

Title: South Broadway Athletic Club
Review: His [Brian Henneman's] Tom Petty-tinged voice and bursts of Rickenbacker guitar reinforce the familiar sound. Unfortunately he doesn’t always move with the times.

Title: Rub
Review: Her ideas and unabashed sexual allusions, certainly, are a good deal more interesting than her inflexible retro-electro rumble. [Oct 2015, p.92]

Title: Tallies
Review: [Tallies] inject sufficient Sunday/Cocteaus-ish vocal and melodic bounce to soften even the most calcified indie heart. [Feb 2019, p.93]

Title: Hypnotic Nights
Review: Hypnotic Nights continues with the Weezer worship introduced on 2011's We Are the Champions, but answers the fuzz-pop frivolity with equal doses of motorik groove and psychedelic drone.

Title: The Crane Wife
Review: Sometimes you wish Meloy would just put away his studied thesp-schlock and say, "Man, I'm sick of singing about Victorian peasants. I got dumped once. I want to write about that..." [27 Jan 2007, p.31]

Title: Little Broken Hearts
Review: This is a bold and engaging revolution. [May 2012, p.75]

Title: In League with Dragons
Review: The most impressive thing about In League With Dragons is that it’s the 17th Mountain Goats album, and Darnielle shows no signs of running on empty. This is an album that should excite existing fans of the band. ... It also works well as a gateway for new fans as the songs are catchy, the music is well balanced and when the band hit that sweet groove its glorious.

Title: Tommy
Review: Tommy is a kind of maximalist musical confetti, a mostly instrumental amalgamation of jazz, hip-hop, folk, and laid-back electronica. Disparate ideas flit in and out of these songs, often before the listener really has a chance to get acquainted with them.

Title: Sound & Fury
Review: It’s pure rock and roll: sleazy, slick and lots of fun. Sound & Fury marks another milestone for a remarkable artist.

Title: Origins
Review: Dragons’ producers Alex da Kid and Mattman & Robin have tamped down the epic flourishes and thudding bottom end that marked this album’s predecessor, “Evolve,” resulting in a more direct sound and message.

Title: Matangi
Review: The problem is that the record sat on the shelf for so long... that anything that may have once seemed fresh on the record now seems more than a little tired.

Title: Escape From Evil
Review: Look past the pastel surface-level familiarity of Escape From Evil and you’ll find that no matter what tool-kit a band is equipped with, superb songwriting and refined attention to detail and aesthetics always prevail.

Title: Phantom Brickworks
Review: Living up to its title, Phantom Brickworks proves a spectral set, a fragile sounding record that confidently conveys the intent of its creator. It may not win him any new fans, and old fans may even be puzzled at the lack of sunny beats seen on last year’s ‘A Mineral Love’, but it still stands as a great escape for those who like to get lost in sound rather than riffs.

Title: Manic Expressive
Review: Air and Zero 7 are perhaps the nearest reference points. [Dec 2001, p.106]

Title: Nobody Wants to Be Here and Nobody Wants to Leave
Review: Nobody Wants To Be Here And Nobody Wants To Leave will do more than satisfy existing fans of the band; new fans too would do well to start here.

Title: Melodrama
Review: Lorde’s overreaches and missteps are just as charming as the incisive parts, so she must be an icon. The board-manning Jack Antonoff’s over-reliance on synths and clicks limits what she can do with this new maximalism, and her insistence on, well, melodrama will occasionally mar her best writing, which remains in the shadows. She’s not a liability. But she can be a forest fire.

Title: Reflection
Review: It’s an album of fun, feminist pop that is simultaneously wise beyond its years (four of its five members are still in their teens) and refreshingly age-appropriate—and it effortlessly embodies the ideals grasped at by the girl power think piece wave, with a sharp, nuanced perspective that can only come from lived experience.

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: Darnielle's increasing love of full band arrangements--which aren't memorable--pushes him perilously close to earning the "soft rock' label. [Winter 2008, p.83]

Title: The Sea
Review: Even allowing for occasional swoops into blandish neo-soul, Rae has made an album she'll have trouble bettering.

Title: Gallipoli
Review: Throwaways make the ten-song album feel low on substantial ideas: there's enough material here for a solid EP, but it's rather thin for a full-length. Still, as a modestly enjoyable throwback to 2006, it gets the job done.

Title: Skeleton Tree
Review: Skeleton Tree offers little solace, but as the Bad Seeds’ 16th album, it gives the listener an experience that is unshakable.

Title: Hot Cakes
Review: A fun comeback album filled with screeching and penis jokes.

Title: Brigid Mae Power
Review: Despite its clear seriousness, Brigid Mae Power runs on that sense of newfound freedom. Power and Broderick find glimmers of light even in the darkest moments, and she learns to trust the kind of love that enables independence, after some period of coercion.

Title: Life Fantastic
Review: The experimentation found on Life Fantastic, for the most part, works rather well within the gypsy circus that is Man Man but even at its best it makes one wonder what it could have sounded like without the meds.

Title: Heads Up
Review: This time, the fiery furnace powering their new record comes from slashing open every membrane; letting ideas wildly collide like supercharged, excitable atoms. Brushstrokes and processes are all over this record.

Title: Hairless Toys
Review: It does reconfirm her knack for making grown-up dance albums unlike anyone else. [Jun 2015, p.106]

Title: Within and Without
Review: Much as its title suggests, Within and Without is a juxtaposition, matching an assortment of warm, decades-old retrograde styles with the despondent, isolated, and decidedly modern mood of Greene's alienated narratives.

Title: Nocturne
Review: On Nocturne, he's matured considerably as a songwriter, demonstrating a knack for the subtle nuances that make memorable songs tick.

Title: Life is Good
Review: Too many tracks here recount his salad days in the era "before Air Jordans."

Title: Get To Heaven
Review: Everything Everything have sculpted a masterpiece.

Title: Sounds From Nowheresville
Review: The unfortunate irony is that Sounds From Nowheresville doesn't sound much like a grand rejection of pop music at all. It just sounds a little bereft of ideas, and way too short.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: She’s created a world of her own, and on this latest record she sinks deep into its clutches.

Title: Rock n Roll Jesus
Review: Rumours of emotional maturity are exaggerated...but the reflective moments are best. [Dec 2007, p.98]

Title: We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions
Review: While this record remains absolutely likeable, it still sounds too much like the soundtrack for a concert that hasn't happened yet.

Title: A Better Version of Me
Review: If the whole record could be as good as the first ten seconds of "Artificial Light", it would be great. But it isn't.

Title: Lost Time
Review: They are definitely a marketable band (it’s no wonder Katy Perry ripped them off) and Lost Time is Tacocat’s biggest accomplishment to date--27 minutes of bubblegum pop that doesn’t lose its taste.

Title: Handwritten
Review: At 16, Mendes isn’t the artist he’ll be at 25, but he’s made a persuasive start--the adult-pop big league could yet be his.

Title: The Boy with No Name
Review: The band may have paved the way for the likes of Coldplay and Snow Patrol, but they still haven't found their "Clocks" or "Chasing Cars."

Title: Ride Your Heart
Review: Though there's an electric current coursing through Ride Your Heart, it's too often wasted on mundane material--which is especially disappointing given how zany and lyrically imaginative their previous band was

Title: Truelove's Gutter
Review: Truelove’s Gutter is a winner for his fans.

Title: Islands
Review: Some of the tracks are so light and delicate, you worry they might blow away in the breeze. But the pace occasionally picks up, as on ‘Highway Blue’ which whistles along on a jaunty groove, while a punchy horn section on ‘Good Ol Night’ adds further colour.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: "I Love You But I Don't Know What to Say" is a perfect finale to a near perfect album by a performer who seems, at least for the time being, to have learned to focus his wide-open talents on one narrow vein of material, and in the process has struck pure gold.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: Outgunned is a mess of unfocused energy and uncomfortably irrelevant sonics, an odd mix of cartoonish immediacy and tired youth-cult ideas that would be the perfect soundtrack to Itchy & Scratchy & Poochie: The Movie.

Title: Grid of Points
Review: Harris revisits the design of Ruins and guides it into a new form, one that's less immediately fulfilling, yet more stimulating, in a strange way. It's an album that's truly broken and poignant, and, most importantly, one that teaches us to see the beauty in our limited view.

Title: This Is Acting
Review: There are only so many times you can key into someone’s heart before they change the code, and after about 20 listens, the veneer crumbles a bit, and it’s a little too easy to see the gears turning underneath. But that’s not the most frustrating thing about the record; the most frustrating thing is that Sia has so much access to us and just doesn’t do much with it.

Title: Fuckbook
Review: An album full of cover versions is not really essential listening, although there are a few songs here reminiscent of the better covers from past Yo La Tengo albums.

Title: Alright, Still
Review: The music deliberately sits somewhere between glossy and unobtrusive. It shimmers enough to mask Allen's tepid singing voice but remains far enough away to allow her largest asset -- her snappy personality -- to take charge.

Title: The New Classic
Review: She dresses [her songs] up in the kind of shamelessly poppy hooks that make Top 40 programmers giggle in delight and "real hip-hop" heads shake theirs sadly. If this is the future, it's one strange place.

Title: Because the Internet
Review: The production is as rich as the raps, spanning pop, underground R&B, club music, and psychedelic experimentation. The project is further heightened by Glover’s knowing irony, his gift for hooks, and his visionary theme.

Title: Heaven
Review: On any other Walkmen album, just the hooky brilliance of the title track could be enough to declare this set a success, but there's never been one quite like this before.

Title: Major Arcana
Review: Speedy Ortiz take the most captivating musical elements of their forbears and push them to glorious new heights. [Aug-Sep 2013, p.100]

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: On Sugaring Season she captures both the melancholy and the confidence that comes with growing older really rather well.

Title: Undun
Review: The result is a remarkable display of creative unity and a stellar masterpiece sitting alongside the group's best work.

Title: DSVII
Review: What remains are a few fleeting moments of quiet beauty, and they do not appear often enough, nor are they substantial for an album of this length.

Title: Losing Sleep
Review: The production is solid and his voice retains that smooth edge that still carries with it the slightest sense of vulnerability.

Title: xx
Review: Spare, swirling keyboards and gently urgent guitar pluckings anchor this minimalist masterpiece, allowing Romy Madley Croft's plaintive, laudanumlike vocals to tentatively soar above the albumwide ache that is her and Oliver Sim's (e)vocation.

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: While debut albums are rarely perfect, you can't help but feel this one could benefit from some stringent quality control.

Title: Carry Fire
Review: For Carry Fire, Plant has written Lion In Winter love songs. [Nov 2017, p.96]

Title: Harlem River
Review: With Harlem River, Morby shuffles forthright, his sanguine tone assuredly focused on the cathartic inertia of travel.

Title: Wonderland
Review: Wonderland shies away from the textural depths the duo made their name on. But what the album lacks in psychedelic richness it makes up for with wild, off-the-cuff energy, and it sounds like Demdike Stare had a lot of fun making it.

Title: Picaresque
Review: Resembles the Arcade Fire if they were from the Renaissance era and rubbish. [23 Jul 2005, p.50]

Title: In a Dim Light
Review: This new full-length suggests that while Nedry haven't quite found their way there yet, the journey should be fascinating.

Title: The Waiting Room
Review: The combination of rich layered instrumentation, carefully orchestrated strings and Stuart Staples' evocative vocals give feelings of loss and loneliness a cinematic grandeur, yet their consistently strong recordings never lapse into sentimental excess. That is a balancing act few can manage, and the group pull it off yet again here.

Title: Give Up
Review: Some people who liked the more experimental side of Tamborello's DNTEL project will simply find it a little too boppy for their liking, but it's one of those little discs that practically drills down into your subconscious.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: The Future and the Past is a triumph, a coming-of-age that over-delivers on all Prass promised, and suggests limitless skies in answer to where she might go next. [Jul 2018, p.86]

Title: The Eraser
Review: Where The Eraser sags is in the middle, with tracks 3-5 falling particularly flat. Like too many of Radiohead's new songs, they contain a single weak idea dragged on interminably.

Title: Nothing Is Wrong
Review: It's as close to a perfect Americana album as there's been this year--fans of the California sound from CS&N to the Jayhawks will find much to love.

Title: Asa Breed
Review: Asa Breed feels too lightweight to recommend without caution.

Title: Nothing's Gonna Change The Way You Feel About Me Now
Review: This brevity [30-minute run time] doesn't make the record bad by any stretch, but it does make it feel cut off. The warm, gauzy sounds here invite deeper exploration, and instead Earle gets in and gets out all too quickly.

Title: Drum's Not Dead
Review: Much of Drum's Not Dead suggests a Ligeti score for The Blair Witch Project as played by The Residents. [Mar 2006, p.88]

Title: A Bigger Bang
Review: A Bigger Bang is just a straight-up, damn fine Rolling Stones album, with no qualifiers or apologies necessary for the first time in a few decades.

Title: Meet Glen Campbell
Review: Campbell doesn’t reinvent any of them, but he was never really an inventor. What he does is make a fine, if not spectacular, album that mostly plays to his strengths.

Title: Fields
Review: Gonzalez rarely writes full, indelible songs, but he's great at building enticing fragments into lasting moments.

Title: Underwater Cinematographer
Review: Now, we’re certainly all pro-happiness and exuberance, but the same doggedly optimistic message reiterated during several songs begins to sound more than a little shallow, even if such statements have a way of lending themselves more grandeur than they deserve.

Title: Ben Kweller
Review: He finally seems to be getting the hang of things. [Oct 2006, p.122]

Title: Bedouine
Review: Disarmingly intimate songs. [Aug 2017, p.102]

Title: Two Parts Viper
Review: Do not be deterred by Scogin's past endeavours; this is not a metal album--not even close. This is lyrical, groovy, poignant, unimpeded and, above all else, creative

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: If hippie leanings and a penchant for image-dense, nature-inspired poesy make Oberst a kindred spirit to Devendra Banhart and Joanna Newsom, he can also be hard-nosed.

Title: The Silver Globe
Review: Weaver’s voice is the key to the album: she can’t help but add melody, even when what lies beneath is the drone.

Title: Have We Met
Review: Have We Met, though perhaps less ambitious than Destroyer’s best work, is nevertheless their freshest and most enjoyable record in years.

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: An appropriate sonic companion so ethereal, any selenographer worth his weight in space could essentially disappear inside of it.

Title: Eton Alive
Review: Eton Alive captures the self-proclaimed “Best Band in the World” as wide-awake as ever, dolloping fun all over their music like it’s Daddies Brown Sauce.

Title: Everybody's Got It Easy But Me
Review: While the Intelligence may not sound quite as inspired here as they did on that album [2007's Deuteronomy], Everybody's Got It Easy But Me is still plenty of fun.

Title: God Says No
Review: A 12-song mess that veers unsteadily between the fuzztone freak-outs of his original concept and panicked-sounding rewrites of older Monster Magnet material.

Title: Pieces In A Modern Style
Review: From any conceivable angle, it is an indulgence...

Title: Ain't Ain't Ain't
Review: Not only does Fite sing more than speak-rap, he doesn't push oddity so hard. [Apr 2012, p.92]

Title: Have Fun With God
Review: As it is, Have Fun With God is never less than listenable but seldom more than vaguely pleasant. [Feb 2014, p.44]

Title: Music from Another Dimension!
Review: Aerosmith returning to the sound and fury of its '70s halcyon days is a welcome time warp.

Title: Pleased to Meet You
Review: It’s their tightest, freshest, most contemporary batch of songs, weatherproofed to stand the test of time.

Title: Juice B Crypts
Review: Judging by the results of Juice B Crypts, this revitalisation of purpose feels very much like something radiating directly from the artists themselves. Hardly a complete renewal or about-face, but rather a refining of methodology and intent, a distillation of what made them so exciting to begin with.

Title: Last Night
Review: Last Night feels like a cold academic exercise, as though Moby were compiling a collection of beats for future examination by an alien race curious about our after-hours ways.

Title: 137 Avenue Kaniama
Review: Baloji often presents a grand, cinematic vision here that can be thrilling in short bursts. Taken as a whole though, the sheer scale of 137 Avenue Kaniama can be a bit exhausting.

Title: Alone Together
Review: For the most part, the analog warmth of live instrumentation is employed thoughtfully, reminiscent, in some places, of some of the best tracks on Oddisee's fantastic Rock Creek Park.

Title: Ladytron
Review: Every Ladytron album has a few extremely low points, and on Ladytron those are “Run” (a part two to “The Animals,” not a particularly necessary one) and “Paper Highways” (the first part is great, as if wrought from iron wreckage, but it veers into a saccharine, completely misplaced chorus, like they handed it to Disney for a second). Much better as a ray of solace is the quietly experimental “Tomorrow Is Another Day.”

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: It would be more of a worry if Dye It Blonde's high points weren't so revelatory or well-executed because while it's not a conceptually brilliant record, there are enough triumphs to score a summer romance and get cut up on mix CDs.

Title: The Light in You
Review: While the sugary highs could give Van Dyke Parks an ice cream headache, it's hard to resist a work so clearly besotted with the power of music. [Oct 2015, p.78]

Title: Devastator
Review: Devastator is a fine and fully-formed piece of work, bringing the band rushing headlong into the present, but maintaining all the best elements of their past work.

Title: Illumination Ritual
Review: Overall, Illumination Ritual succeeds as a mood piece, even though it might not be quite as “illuminating” as one would like.

Title: Ultraviolence
Review: Del Rey sounds regally removed from the box-ticking modernity of her peers, a one-woman advertisement for the appeal of the unreal. [Aug 2014, p.113]

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: Ray Guns Are Not Just the Future builds on its predecessor with even tighter concepts and hooks born of a naturally strengthening partnership.

Title: Afraid of Heights
Review: The album is split up between the predictable pop-punk energizers that made 2010’s King of the Beach a pleasure, and a new avenue of slower, resolute tracks that lean on their lyrics. Williams, though, is not exactly a belletrist, nor does he try to be, and the words do function, proving to be revealing, dark and honest.

Title: commontime
Review: The addition of simple pop elements to Commontime and the fact that the Brewis brothers manage to keep cranking out music this intelligent and flat-out fun to listen to without ever having the slightest dip in quality, makes it one of their more interesting and rewarding efforts to date.

Title: Dancing Backward in High Heels
Review: This third comeback album unearths some of the band's less visible roots, in Broadway musicals, soul balladry, Stones-y orchestral pop and Fifties R&B.

Title: Paradise
Review: Paradise still sounds like the work sf an artist turning her face back, if somewhat slowly, toward the sunlight. [No. 142, p.55]

Title: Spirit
Review: The main drawback is that hip producer James Ford isn’t allowed to conjure up as much newfangled ju-ju as Spirit could stand. Songs like So Much Love could come from any era.

Title: Hyperion
Review: Despite some positives, Gesaffelstein isn’t able to recreate past glories, nor advance on them--or even successfully reinvent himself. By the end of it, you’re mostly left feeling confused and underwhelmed.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: I’m Wide Awake is an uneven product, full of everything there is to loathe and love about Oberst.

Title: Born and Raised
Review: The Laurel Canyon music scene of the '60s and '70s is a major touchstone here... and that ramble-tamble style suits him.

Title: Doom Days
Review: Doom Days is a vivid snapshot of humanity and an imaginative, adventurous levelling up from one of Britain’s most influential bands.

Title: Big Mess
Review: Until the band fully embraces their ping-pong guitars and surly one-liners ("I wish I saw myself the way you see me now"), Grouplove will likely remain a singles band rather than the new-R.E.M. their ambition hints at.

Title: GO:OD AM
Review: An interesting and infectious LP that's also his strongest to date.

Title: The Visitor
Review: For him, music is all about expression and collaboration. On The Visitor, he has crystallised those principles into a richly beguiling and inventive work that crosses musical boundaries effortlessly.

Title: So Runs the World Away
Review: Stirring stuff, and food for thought, too.

Title: Viet Cong
Review: Viet Cong's volatile brew often coalesces into something disarmingly catchy.

Title: Libertad
Review: This album blows the doors off its predecessor. Save a pair of disinfected ballads ("The Last Fight," "Gravedancer"), Libertad is all about hand-grenade chords, drag-racing riffs, and circus-tent choruses.

Title: Lady From Shanghai
Review: Although this is a far cry from the standard of their late Seventies heyday, the band have continued down their obscure path with little deviation, creating a sound which, although challenging and on occasion elitist, is there own.

Title: Upper Air
Review: I'm going to let the band off the hook for the holding pattern; in the meantime, we'll simply revel in the general loveliness of these 10 compositions, which utilize the debut's blueprints in the creation of sublime melodies, absorbing lyricism and delicate harmonic interplay.

Title: Ours Is Chrome
Review: Angry riffs and gigantic hooks build the base of the album and it's one heavily steeped in frustration and angst. Sadly though, as emotional and honest as the record gets, too many songs are forgettable and lack the punch possessed a couple years ago.

Title: Toy
Review: Musically, Toy is their most experimental and varied album.

Title: Smoke Ring for My Halo
Review: This record moves from cautious shine to swirling dark, showing all sides of the dubious kind of redemption hinted at in the album's title, but nothing is ever lost in these layers.

Title: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
Review: The record is starting to sound worn. [May 2011, p.105]

Title: Here Come the Tears
Review: There's nothing as great as "New Generation", "She's Not Dead", or "The 2 of Us" but there doesn't have to be, either, because the Tears have enough natural dynamism of their own to stand alone.

Title: It's A Corporate World
Review: The results occasionally jar, when Epstein's consistently elaborate productions overshadow the more pedestrian of Zott's compositions, but generally the sum of their parts is an equation to be savoured, and frequently produces magic.

Title: (I Can't Get No) Stevie Jackson
Review: No one's asking Jackson to bare his soul. Still, there's a surface-y, writing-exercise quality to many of these songs. (I Can't Get No) Stevie Jackson doesn't really give us much Stevie Jackson, just some clever jottings and puns and tunes he's scratched out in a notebook.

Title: Are We There
Review: It’s a truly fascinating listen.

Title: Glitter in the Gutter
Review: He retreats too often into dull AOR choogling. [Mar 2007, p.114]

Title: Fundamental
Review: A politically charged album that's free of musical sparks.

Title: 12 Songs
Review: The new album sounds great, but it has its share of filler, and Rubin's narrow vision means he lets some songs lie motionless when they might be improved by old-fashioned sweetening.

Title: Let It Beard
Review: What Let It Beard lacks in blockbuster hooks it makes up for in its rambling excess of melody, giving the appearance of effortlessness to what, evidenced by Pollard's lack of competition, is obviously anything but.

Title: Living Things
Review: It's largely the usual semi-hilarious histrionica to which we've become accustomed

Title: Hot Slick
Review: Hot Slick is the sound of a band enjoying themselves, having complete creative freedom, and doing things their way.

Title: Cigarettes After Sex
Review: Overall, chronically anti-romantic moments are eclipsed by sweet, somnambulant melodies that may not quicken the pulse but often hypnotize nevertheless.

Title: Rise Above
Review: Dirty Projectors leader Dave Longstreth clearly had more than a remake on his mind--a mind whose wandering ways will be worth following for years to come.

Title: Walking On A Dream
Review: I applaud the duo's unpredictability but wish they would calm down a bit.

Title: Breathe
Review: Breathe is Tiny Moving Parts' best work to date, and if math rock is your thing, it would be a crime to not check it out.

Title: Fear Fun
Review: Though he dumbs up his songwriting half the time by fearing fun literally as regards forward motion, don't give up.

Title: Under the Iron Sea
Review: Beautiful but strangely unhinged. [Jul 2006, p.100]

Title: Diploid Love
Review: Diploid probably has some ace songs, but you'll need an industrial belt sander to uncover them. [No. 109, p.55]

Title: 100 Days, 100 Nights
Review: They sound like they've matured in isolation, developing flavors that didn't exist in 1967.

Title: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
Review: Burn Your Fire, through increased complexity of instrumentation, creates a new dynamic--the vocal is more understated and reserved, less elusive and divergent --it's autonomy partially tethered by the whole ensembles balanced interrelation.

Title: Crimes of Passion
Review: A tastefully echo-bathed, psychocandy-flavored production job by the Raveonetts' Sune Rose Wagner, and you've got a soaring and psychedelic dream-pop stunner that will leave you wondering how being bummed can feel so inanely good. [Sep 2013, p.88]

Title: Kenny Dennis LP
Review: Fun and fully immersive, rewinds are rewarded with a plethora of intricate detail. [Jul 2013, p.85]

Title: Friends
Review: Friends so incessantly refers to its generic seasons-change premise that its emotional impact is wholly blunted by the album’s end.

Title: The Fray
Review: The group doesn't stray far from the template, turning in another batch of hooky mid-tempo songs that are pretty without necessarily sounding distinctive.

Title: And Their Refinement Of The Decline
Review: The listener who comes away from the two-hour experience of …And Their Refinement of Decline without becoming a bit misty at least once is too hardened for my friendship.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: Ryan Adams is a persuasively dark album, one defined by themes of struggle, instability, isolation, and regret.

Title: Earth Rocker
Review: It's certainly Clutch's most enjoyable album in a good number of years, and any fan of the group's post-Pure Rock Fury era would do well to give Earth Rocker a spin.

Title: i,i
Review: Bon Iver have imperceptibly moved from requesting close listening to requiring it, and i,i spins a mesmerising web of superficially insubstantial yet intensely majestic music. Listen closely and you can hear the language of pop being redrafted in real time.

Title: Dig In Deep
Review: Never mind dig in deep: this is an emotional excavation.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: Majesty Shredding lives up to its name and doesn't waste much time catching its breath, and along the way Superchunk delivers something that used to be expected of the band: an album on which every song sounds as inspired as the next one.

Title: Skeletal Lamping
Review: This feast isn’t without a good deal of filler.

Title: All That Ever Could Have Been
Review: It's all too easy to use adjectives such as glimmering and glacial when describing these kind of sounds but the music here is so expressive you can visualise the sights experienced by its makers.

Title: A+E
Review: Sophisticated it's not but, by and large, it's thrilling, the guitarist's zest for life evident throughout.

Title: Treats
Review: Abrasive and addictive, the duo have together discovered a chemistry that not only excites themselves, but almost anyone else who experiences it. [Aug 2010, p.122]

Title: Morning Phase
Review: So, largely unimaginative arrangements, flat delivery, a surfeit of vague ecological metaphors that wash like spray on the rocks (you can have that one for free, Mr. Hansen), and a lack of any sense of connection, of need, of reality.

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: Our Love to Admire will be looked back on as that tricky third record, the one it's cool to like best.

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: Like most of these top-shelf indie-pop tunes, ["101"] is cause for hoping Julian Casablancas loosens his songwriting grip on the next Strokes album. [Mar 2007, p.94]

Title: Night Driver
Review: This is the kind of record you could pack off to the beach for an entire summer then promptly forget about. Too bad. Lobsinger deserves more.

Title: Veckatimest
Review: This is a superb record, a spirted illustration of sepia-tinged Americana that feels linked inextricably with Animal Collective's "Merriweather Post Pavillion" as one of the not only most hyped, but also finest records of 2009. [Spring 2009, p.66]

Title: Timez Are Weird These Days
Review: Unlike the legends of BK past, London doesn't riff on drugs and housing projects, which in and of itself earns him a fair shot. He may be redefining what it means to be a rapper in the 21st century, but it wouldn't hurt if he practiced more rules of the game before changing it.

Title: Arms Way
Review: These songs may be less immediately catchy, but all of them have a moment in which they break away from their straightforward guitar-rock underpinning and allow strange, spacious moments to burble up from within.

Title: Prisoner of Conscious
Review: Despite everything he did right on this album, there are a few blemishes. [Jul 2013, p.88]

Title: Feral Roots
Review: "Look Away," with its inventive and Eastern-tinged, Led Zeppelin III-inspired acoustic guitar work, the soulful and contemplative title cut, and the breezy, psych-folk-rocker "All Directions," are administered with equal amounts of nuance and backbone, showcasing the band's versatility in both songcraft and execution, a feat made all the more impressive by their predilection for recording live in the studio. That craftsmanship, no doubt bolstered by the group's adherence to a rigorous tour schedule, is the glue that keeps Feral Roots from bursting apart at the seams.

Title: This Old Road
Review: An album that is not only one of the very best in his career but likely one of the best you'll hear from any singer-songwriter this year. [#13, p.86]

Title: Saturday Night
Review: It's a testament of the savvy of darcy and his producers Ross Gillard and Amy Fort that the new album's experimental passages are very much cut from the same cloth as more obvious crowd-pleasers like "You Felt Comfort," which shares the drive and jangle of "Tall Glass Of Water," and "Saint Germain," a dreamy haze of a song that demonstrates Darcy's gift for melody, absurd turns of phase and more pointed expressions of inner turmoil. [Mar 2017, p.38]

Title: Begone Dull Care
Review: The atmospheric Begone Dull Care feels more appropriate for a slick urban lounge than the dance floor, meaning it sounds fine without feeling like it has to be listened to.

Title: Walk It Off
Review: It's rare to pull off an album this succint and not invite boredom; it's even rarer if it fucking rocks. [May 2008, p.135]

Title: Curse Your Branches
Review: Regardless of the circumstances surrounding its creation, Curse Your Branches is Bazan's best album to date.

Title: Palace
Review: The way a latent power blends with an occasionally slightly gauche drama suggests early Radiohead. And, as with Radiohead, it feels like  the second album could be the key event, deciding whether these collegiate English sounds can enrapture the wider world. [Mar 2011, p.98]

Title: Sister Faith
Review: Metallic hardcore still gallops in short, sharp, steely blasts on a pair of two-minute openers, but Nineties grunge-dripping Seaweed now coats Ryan Patterson's punk heroes.

Title: New Wild Everywhere
Review: There's an easy likeability to Great Lake Swimmer's latest release. [Yet] many songs don't hold up on repeated listens. [#86, p.54]

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: Vampire Weekend banks on showering its tribal pop with lyrics poised for literary analysis, skimping pretentious by appearing completely natural.

Title: Christopher
Review: He mostly sounds like a fish out of water. [No. 95, p.57]

Title: TRST
Review: They're crafty enough to pack TRST with enough of their own quirks and curveballs to make for a surprisingly fresh debut, one that'll likely prove difficult to follow.

Title: Innocence Is Kinky
Review: Ultimately, the album’s heady diversity originates in Hval’s malleable voice, which alters style, approach, timber, and tone from one measure to the next.

Title: Floodlight Collective
Review: It's the kind of cohesive "album" album that's hard to find these days. [Spring 2009, p.72]

Title: Songs for the Saints
Review: He quietly champions racial harmony on “Get Along”, and embraces stylistic experimentation on the mandolin-driven “Pirate Song” as well as the reggae-tinged “Love for Love City”, which features steel drums and a guest turn from Ziggy Marley. It won’t be enough to alienate long-standing followers or to attract too many new ones, but Songs for the Saints is nothing if not heartfelt.

Title: Multiply
Review: The idea is to build a monorail between Aphex Twin and Stax Records; the songwriting eventually slacks off, but Lidell's performances don't. [Aug 2005, p.111]

Title: The Difference Between Me and You Is That I'm Not on Fire
Review: Granted, there are still "classic" two-minute exercises in self-immolation (the bleak "Icarus Smicarus" and pulverizing "Lucky Jim" stand out), but nothing that exceeds -- or approaches -- Dallas' chaotic brew.

Title: Joanne
Review: While its modernity is expressed by mixing and matching genres or adding digital zing to familiar tropes, for all its bravura exuberance and pop slickness it is old fashioned to its core.

Title: Sound Wheel
Review: A true counterpart to Car Ma, Sound Wheel is all the richer when coupled with the book's vision. On its own terms, it offers another intriguing side to Mosshart's persona.

Title: Flower Boy
Review: Flower Boy is the first time he’s been equally as forthcoming in his actual music. His flow has tightened up, and for a man whose voice basically destined him for rap stardom, he’s become even better at stretching his booming baritone into novel shapes, employing a plethora of flows.

Title: The Glow
Review: They're still mockingbirds, but what once felt derivative is now inching closer to vital.

Title: Ungrateful
Review: Ungrateful comes off as cluttered and confused. [Jun 2013, p.92]

Title: To Be Kind
Review: Despite clearly being intricately crafted down to the tiniest gestures--musical feats at this level of intensity and control don't emerge from half-arsed noodling--To Be Kind's songs also feel more fluid and open-ended than before, expressive and rich in possibility.

Title: Hold It In
Review: One of the Melvins’ most diverse and melodic, flirting with New Wave, glam metal, and psychobilly between epic guitar jams and gleefully twisted epics such as the closing “House of Gasoline.”

Title: Long Wave
Review: Long Wave seems like great fun for Jeff Lynne, less so for the rest of us. [Dec 2012, p.111]

Title: Noctunes
Review: A mysterious, sprawling listen that will baffle the masses, but reward patient listeners longing for an LP that is immersive, quirky and gently haunting.

Title: Divers
Review: Not only a deftly realised, enchanting meditation on time and its vagaries, the record is effectively a celebration of what we, as time’s denizens, are able to accomplish within it.... Divers is a colossal achievement.

Title: Rather Ripped
Review: Several tracks are up with their best. [Jul 2006, p.88]

Title: Mosquito
Review: Mosquito is a much-needed return to the days of ‘Fever To Tell’ and ‘Machine’--it embraces the band’s early, reverb-heavy sound but also tips its hat to the dance feel they’ve been honing in recent years.

Title: Panic Prevention
Review: For all the one-paced nature of its songwriting, wilfully lo-fi production values, inevitable Lily Allen comparisons and grating larynx, Panic Prevention is still an enthralling debut, and one that says infinitely more about the life of young Londoners than any amount of Bloc Party seriousness.

Title: Further
Review: They may have another breakthrough and forward leap again, but even if they don't, the comfort zone they've found still sounds pretty damn good. [Summer 2010, p.89]

Title: Cupid Deluxe
Review: Cupid Deluxe paints him as a producer and songwriter with massive potential that's only just begun to be realized. [No. 105, p.52]

Title: Flesh Tone
Review: This is one record on which his ultimate masterplan to weld R&B sass to thumping club beats comes good. [Aug 2010, p.84]

Title: Talk That Talk
Review: It's easy to criticise Talk That Talk but it's actually a fun and enjoyable record.

Title: Lala Belu
Review: With only six tracks, Lala Belu shows that being hypnotized is what we secretly want.

Title: Emancipated Hearts
Review: It may have taken more than a quarter of a century to come to fruition, but this lack of hurry is exactly what makes Dean Wareham's first solo outing so stirring.

Title: Graveyard Whistling
Review: The Old 97's still sound engaged, energetic, and as committed as ever 23 years after they released their debut, and Graveyard Whistling is evidence they're not short on fresh ideas either.

Title: Significant Changes
Review: Juxtaposing the escape provided by club culture's immediacy with the harsh realities confronted in the lab, Significant Changes sets a reality check to something danceable, but its success is wholly reliant on Jayda G's balanced presentation and steadfast commitment to both missions, tonal shifts like "Orca's Reprise" providing chill-out wind-downs for the party while the club anthems provide some sorely needed release.

Title: Wildflower
Review: The whole album flows like a rainbow-hued river animated by the spirit of generosity and wonder. [Aug 2016, p.116]

Title: Good Sad Happy Bad
Review: As a document of reunion between friends, Good Sad Happy Bad feels honest enough. On its own, it hits a note too lethargic and too muted to stick the way Levi’s past work has done.

Title: District Line
Review: It's as convincing and heartfelt as anything else here--and suggests that by incorporating disco into the rest of his music, even better things may lie ahead. [Mar 2008, p.96]

Title: Release The Stars
Review: Most of Stars ends up feeling like a sleight of hand; pay no attention to the lack of accessibility, but instead be distracted by the unecessarily grandiose 'I'm Not Ready to Love.' [Summer 2007, p.86]

Title: Trampin'
Review: Trampin'... is not a flashy album, and sometimes what's meant to be stately is sluggish instead. But though the revolutionary jolt of her early work is in abeyance, her fire still burns.

Title: Working Men's Club
Review: It’s the underlying sense of unease and something to prove that really adds the edge here.

Title: Racy
Review: Intrepid it ain’t, but sometimes the straightforward approach has its rewards.

Title: In Limbo
Review: TEEN is another in a long line of mildly interesting but ponderous offshoots from already established bands.

Title: Six
Review: A brief but compelling work from an important artist.

Title: Apocalypse
Review: On this collection of futurised soul and funk, Bruner shows skills as a songwriter too.

Title: Lover
Review: At 18 tracks long, ‘Lover’ is more sprawling and further from flawless than her 2014 pop crossover ‘1989’. But it succeeds in spite of its clunkier moments because Swift’s melodies are frequently dazzling and her loved-up lyrics are ultimately quite touching.

Title: August Greene
Review: Just as the album looks like it’s about to settle and prosper in this zone, in comes “Piano Interlude,” and the tone of August Greene shifts messily.

Title: Deserted
Review: Rarely do the Mekons get quite as loose as they do on Deserted, alternating between arid, nocturnal atmosphere that seems to emanate from Susie Honeyman’s fiddle and moments of near hysteria, as though their sun-baked brains have gone haywire. These songs take their time to wander about, even getting lost in the vast expanse--sometimes a little too lost.

Title: There is No Enemy
Review: There Is No Enemy is not a return to form. It’s a re-imagining of a band’s distinct and timeless sound.

Title: The Something Rain
Review: A well crafted and executed evocation of verdant indie pop that sticks with you long after it has sounded its final note.

Title: Sam's Town
Review: The highs aren't as high on "Sam's Town," but it's a better album overall.

Title: Red Letter Days
Review: A straightforward barnburner of an album.

Title: Hummingbird
Review: While there's nothing as immediately engaging on Hummingbird as Gorilla Manor's "Wide Eyes," the album compensates with beauty and seriousness.

Title: I Know What Love Isn't
Review: The album in a nutshell: a broken heart carried with poise, good humor and endless charm.

Title: Sweet Sour
Review: The trio continues mixing and mismatching, with both elements of Skulls' sound [Black Keys' rock and Radiohead's honey-eyed longing] feeling even more pronounced. [No. 85, p. 52]

Title: Scheherazade
Review: Longtime fans who have patiently waited for this resurgence will be thrilled with results that gently tug at the boundaries of their established sound. But even listeners new to the Freakwater experience can start here and work backwards through a rich catalog dedicated to the darker roots of Americana.

Title: The Crying Light
Review: It's an ideal January release, time enough for Antony's spacious, textured odyssey to sink in before those Album Of The Year polls come round again. [Feb 2009, p.104]

Title: Rock N Roll Consciousness
Review: The results are frequently riveting. ... A challenging listen, then, but that's its appeal. [Jun 2017, p.110]

Title: The Renaissance
Review: After myriad delays and label woes, it's clear the interminable wait for new material was worth it.

Title: Revolve
Review: Its wider emotional range and stylistic switch-ups, none of which is outside Newman's grasp, give it a slight edge.

Title: In Rainbows
Review: Elsewhere, it's business as usual--mostly amazing business, to be sure, but never entirely unexpected.

Title: Gauntlet Hair
Review: There's nothing on Gauntlet Hair that rivals the pop-minded immediacy or the floor-stomping clamor of "I Was Thinking...," but it still manages to wade deeper into an abyss that few bands manage to come out of successfully.

Title: Beacon
Review: Musically, they've come on. Kevin Baird's bass work – always a highlight – is finally showcased to full effect on the 'Rip It Up'-style swagger of 'Wake Up' and the jagged riffing of 'Sun', while 'Pyramid' features some seriously impressive guitar noodles.

Title: Drunk
Review: Drunk, as out-there as it can be, is an album totally high on its own unique ideas.

Title: Music for the Age of Miracles
Review: Throughout, The Clientele’s mellifluous breeziness accommodates fresh sounds without signs of strain.

Title: ARTPOP
Review: There are moments where she reminds us that she can still do wonderful things, but for the most part, Artpop shows us an artist who is trying to do too much all at once.

Title: Vertical Land
Review: Those expecting an ultra-stripped-back affair will be in for a surprise too, for although the album sustains and refines Sheppard’s core penchant for pointillist minimalism, Vertical Land is also arguably his most ambitious and elaborate statement to date.

Title: We Were Here
Review: The trademark use of acoustic as a lead guitar still sounds refreshing, and Knights' sweet and salty vocal style is still full of vulnerable charisma. [Nov 2013, p.88]

Title: Saint Bartlett
Review: The sound is quintessentially opiate--almost sleep-inducing--and upon writing that, it should be clarified as a compliment, kind of like falling asleep to NPR: It gives good information, but the undertones and lush notes can lull you to dreams.

Title: Just Us
Review: Faust has very little idea where they’re taking anyone.

Title: LP1
Review: Devon soul woman meets Dave Stewart, in Nashville. [Sept. 2011, p. 118]

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: Features some of Madlib’s most difficult and most accomplished production work to date.

Title: Blue World
Review: The musical quality is high, and it’s unusual among the saxophonist’s post-1959 studio recordings in reprising earlier compositions – he mostly featured new material. Coltrane’s rather unvarying dynamic level makes him a less effective film composer than his former employer Miles Davis, with his dramatic mastery – but Trane can’t be blamed for not fitting his music to the action, given that he had little idea what that would be. [Nov 2019, p.69]

Title: D-D-Don't Don't Stop the Beat
Review: If you think songs get into trouble past the three-minute mark and words are nothing more than things that fall out of your mouth, D-D-Don't Don't Stop The Beat is the record for you. [8 Aug 2003, p.71]

Title: Chasing Yesterday
Review: Chasing Yesterday is airless and compressed, more like an idea of a great rock album than an actual one.

Title: Tomorrow Is My Turn
Review: This is Americana in its purest form, where gospel, folk, blues, soul, and Celtic melodies all make sense on the same album when interpreted by a dexterous vocalist and multi-instrumentalist of Giddens’s caliber.

Title: The Great War
Review: Stories unfurl with an infectious nerdiness that undulates between giddy Boys’ Own exuberance and a museum curator’s painstaking attention to detail. [20 Jul 2019, p.57]

Title: Queen of the Wave
Review: An epic, widescreen journey which is busy and bonkers but constantly entertaining.

Title: Anxiety Always
Review: Adult. proves that there need be nothing fey or even particularly cheeky about synthesizer music. [#231, p.75]

Title: The Outsiders
Review: Church is a crafty, ambitious songwriter with a sensitive, rueful side.

Title: Milk Famous
Review: Milk Famous is consistent in the one way White Rabbits needs to be: At all times, it's adventurous.

Title: Double Exposure
Review: Double Exposure is exceedingly well-crafted. [No. 104, p.60]

Title: Glorious
Review: Dark and light, sweet yet savvy, layered but not overproduced--Foxes has created a work that embodies all these dichotomies and walks the line between them perfectly.

Title: Everybody's Coming Down
Review: While Kasher’s platitudes are presented as hard truths forged from experience, most of the time, it just sounds secondhand, scripts written by someone whose worldview has been shaped mostly by Cursive records.

Title: Release
Review: Equal parts wit, heartbreak, cool... and potential commercial suicide. [Jun/Jul 2002, p.112]

Title: Restless
Review: What's so impressive about Xzibit is his rhyme flow, which is one of the smoothest in rap and provides a wonderful contrast to his profanity-led ghetto dwelling lyrics. With Dr Dre providing beats for three of the tracks and overseeing the whole project, Xzibit now has the perfect musical canvas to accompany his underrated skills.

Title: Bromst
Review: Lo-fi freakster doffs cap to minimalism & screaming chipmunks.

Title: Saltbreakers
Review: This is not as good as its predecessor.

Title: No Time for Dreaming
Review: No Time for Dreaming wails in a world of "Heartaches and Pain" (see the memorable closing track), but Bradley's despair is never less than stirring.

Title: Heavy Lifter
Review: Hovvdy's balanced expressions between residual nostalgia and murmuring secrecy are worn in beautifully on Heavy Lifter.

Title: An Imaginary Country
Review: Tim Hecker’s beautiful meditations are inviting but still retain the edge of a seeker that isn’t quite finished with the trip.

Title: The Inner Mansions
