Review: Watered down and indistinct, The Inner Mansions falls into the same trap as Toro y Moi's Underneath the Pine and many other chillwave releases: Namely, that it's essentially a too-familiar collage of Holga-kissed sentimentality, running through its nostalgic musical cues like a mindless carousel slide projector.

Title: Panorama
Review: Hearing Jordan laying bare these experiences that sound more his own than ever over La Dispute’s most impacting collection of songs yet is something that will invigorate the die-hards once more and maybe (just maybe) finally impress the naysayers.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being II
Review: The beats are so simple that they’re a nonfactor, and there aren’t very many funny lines--which was Wayne’s most redeeming quality in the past.

Title: Tell 'Em I'm Gone
Review: These new songs should mesh gracefully with the classic music that rightfully made Cat Stevens a household name in the ’70s.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: At its best, Calexico does expand, opening the range of sounds to provide for new colors of expression; when it doesn't work, that open sound means a turn toward the basic, allowing prettiness to get in the way of sonic content.

Title: Salon Des Amateurs
Review: Salon des Amateurs is much more than striking the iron while it's hot, not just because of its singular attributes and styles but, frankly, it's yet another fantastic album in the span of a few months.

Title: Flies the Fields
Review: An enjoyable switchback ride through instrumental post-rock riff-making and full-on angst-ridden rocking out. [May 2005, p.87]

Title: Combat Sports
Review: The result is a fourth album both back-to-basics in a Ramone-next-door sort of way, but with renewed purpose and attitude, and eyeing new paths of punk-rock progress.

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: Just think of it as Diet Strokes. [#24, p.100]

Title: Lord Steppington
Review: No doubt, Lord Steppington is a niche album, but whenever a combination of 3rd Bass and Adult Swim is required, this one shows its pimp-hand with some dry, elevated humor.

Title: Break It Yourself
Review: For as much as this collection of songs feels like a band getting together to jam for fun, Break It also feels like one of the more cohesive albums in Bird's oeuvre.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: Conor Oberst doesn't sound much different from any of Bright Eyes' acoustic material, except that it is lacking in the bare honesty of his earlier albums.

Title: A Weird Exits
Review: Thee oh Sees have never done ‘Thee oh Sees’ quite as well as they do here, a riot of lucid cacophony, androgyny, glowing vignettes of loveliness, and two drummers caught in the most sublime lockstep.

Title: Obrigado Saudade
Review: A welcome addition to the avant-garde canon, an album that demonstrates the continuing development and growth of Mice Parade and Pierce.

Title: You Are Not Alone
Review: The production is bright and clear, and the arrangements showcase the star.

Title: This Modern Glitch
Review: The band's power chorus-penning know-how is evident each of these slick and sometimes over-polished ten tracks. [Jun 2011, p.125]

Title: Yesterday's Gone
Review: Yesterday’s Gone is one of the finest debuts you’ll hear for quite some time.

Title: Loved
Review: KEN mode are masters of their craft, and this is easily the equal of anything from the heyday of the genre on labels like AmRep and Hydra Head. While the more casual listener will find this heavy going, fans of the band, and of noise rock in general, are going to be stoked.

Title: Caramel
Review: In its own way, it's some of his strangest music, and might appeal more to fans who appreciate his willingness to try anything once than those expecting a repeat of his previous album.

Title: Monster
Review: KISS may have set out to sound like their old selves on Monster, but they strayed from the pop sensibility that made them great.

Title: Ego Trippin'
Review: Snoop Dogg's ninth album is perhaps his most progressive one to date.

Title: Forever Abomination
Review: It's Bummer Time, and in 2011 there is no better soundtrack for banging your head to oblivion.

Title: The Bells
Review: The resultant pieces feel so alive that you can almost sense the pressure of Frahm’s fingers alighting on each key as these solemn improvisations begin to weave their magic.

Title: The Spirit of Apollo
Review: The album is occasionally brought to earth by mediocre hip-hop, suggesting the project would have been better with a smaller, more focused cast.

Title: More
Review: C has described More as more adult than her debut, and while no one is likely to mistake her for Serge Gainsbourg, it does draw on far more respectable sources than those of her TRL peers, leavening her trademark sound with disco, new wave, and electronica. At her best, C sounds like an American, more mercenary version of Saint Etienne's lead singer, Sarah Cracknell, as she lowers her already-thin voice into a breathy, evocative whisper.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: These are the songs that don’t initially blow you away, but you find yourself coming back to months later.

Title: Remember My Name
Review: Remember My Name as an album isn’t going to change lives.

Title: Free TC
Review: His confidence is why he flies when he swings for the fences on his new album, Free TC.

Title: Miike Snow
Review: There's no lack of artists making similar sounding music--MGMT, Pop Levi, White Williams, and even Animal Collective come to mind--but Miike Snow is ambitious and fun enough that they're worth checking out.

Title: Before the Poison
Review: Before the Poison is poetic and unnerving; it stands alone in her catalog in the same way that Broken English did -- but this time, on the other side of the mirror.

Title: The Party
Review: Played entirely by Shauf save for the lush string arrangements, it’s a baroque-pop exercise with echoes of Seventies smarties like Harry Nilsson, Randy Newman and Steely Dan, though rather more empathetic than them. And less cynical.

Title: Drops of Jupiter
Review: Not only do many of the tunes have a similar feel, but Monahan, whose dusty vocals put the band on the map with the hit single "Meet Virginia" in 1999, is regularly drowned out by the soaring guitars and effects.

Title: Sirens
Review: An ambitious and eclectic album that packs tons of ideas into its runtime and manages to pull them all off with a great deal of style.

Title: Mr Beast
Review: With its plodding tempo, slow-woven guitars, melancholy piano chords and moments of crushing loudness, "Friend of the Night" is representative of much of the album, but Mr. Beast's best bits are those that dare to be different.

Title: Killing Puritans
Review: With Killing Puritans, Van Helden means to scramble and then reassemble house music like the Beasties' Paul's Boutique scrambled hip-hop in 1989. Like Paul's Boutique, Puritans initially seems chaotic and arcane, but with repeated dosage it starts to reveal itself as a pugnacious party album.

Title: Cloak and Cipher
Review: Lovely and bewitching, Cipher unfolds like an elegantly written novel. [Sep 2010, p.112]

Title: Speed of Darkness
Review: It's another diverse and engaging album from a band proudly aging like a fine malt whiskey. [28 May 2011, p.51]

Title: Goat Girl
Review: Funny, raging, unpredictable and electric, this is a record that feels alive.

Title: It Still Moves
Review: Answers an interesting question: What if, after The Bends, Radiohead had discovered pedal steel instead of Pro Tools? [Oct 2003, p.138]

Title: Heathen Chemistry
Review: Crackles with anger, energy, and defiance. [Aug 2002, p.156]

Title: I Disagree
Review: I Disagree is decidedly “post-genre,” tossing Poppy’s pop aesthetic into the shredder with heavy metal and industrial rock, previously only hinted at on the tail end of 2018’s Am I a Girl? “Concrete” shifts abruptly between tempos and genres, between commercial jingles and Beatles-esque chamber-pop, all shot through with roaring electric guitar riffs. That might sound incoherent, but it serves as a bold, deftly executed mission statement.

Title: Things Change
Review: Altogether, Things Change by American Aquarium is a quick-paced album from BJ Barham and a new line-up, with enjoyable and thoughtful lyrics and excellent music.

Title: Visions of Bodies Being Burned
Review: It’s a sharpening of the ideas introduced on Addiction to Blood, performed with clipping.’s classic graveness which only supports how scary this album can be.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: There’s no denying that the band has released a fully coherent statement.

Title: Supernature
Review: Her lyrics bring a hint of sadness to the space-dusted disco tunes. [10 Mar 2006, p.68]

Title: Revival
Review: Reassessing the past and reengaging with the present, Revival lives up to its name.

Title: Sweating The Plague
Review: Sweating the Plague shows Robert Pollard achieving the near-impossible; stringing together a steady decade of such strong material this late into his band's career.

Title: Pain Is Love
Review: Ja Rule seems to be more interested in movin' on up (to the pop side) than keeping grounded on the gangsta grid.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: A record that sounds like absolutely no one else on the planet. [May 2007, p.102]

Title: Teen Dream
Review: This Baltimore dream-pop duo, whose dense-fog organs, reverb-y slide guitars, and nodding harmonies feel as lush as a midnight walk in a wet garden. On their third album, those feelings now sound like actual songs, with swelling choruses and an all-encompassing ache.

Title: Oversteps
Review: By shifting the focus from the percussion to the melodic elements, the complexity has simply been made more palatable.

Title: Sebenza
Review: LV's South African explorations sound fresh in the current vogue for Footwork and trap rap references. [Sep 2012, p.73]

Title: Someone to Watch Over Me
Review: Boyle's versions are professionally executed but phenomenally dreary.

Title: Shine
Review: Shine isn’t dark. But it feels like an exercise in avoidance as if Wale took the advice to ease up too far.

Title: Powerplant
Review: The beefing up of Girlpool’s sound on Powerplant works marvellously in parts, but at points serves to dilute the individuality the pair presented on their debut.

Title: Gemstones
Review: His indie-circuit friends will be amused, but no one else will. [4 Mar 2005, p.73]

Title: Two Fingers
Review: A few rhythmically awkward moments detract from the album’s overall flow, particularly on 'High Life,' but chalk that up to two competing staccato production styles.

Title: Asking For Flowers
Review: On this mesmerizing third album, she’s mostly outgrown the obvious Lucinda Williams and Neil Young comparisons (the Crazy Horse-channeling “Oh Canada” aside), using her lustrous folk-rock melodies to dull the sting of her unsentimental tales.

Title: Juggernaut: Alpha
Review: Alpha is the brighter and longer disc of the two, varied in its execution by walking a line between challenging, progressive moments and more accessible fare.

Title: The Double Cross
Review: Sloan are craftsman who weld their good taste into charming miniatures, and if The Double Cross retains a hint of familiarity--not due to the source material but rather the workmanship--the group's level of skill assures that this is as comfortably satisfying as its predecessors.

Title: The Way The Wind Blows
Review: This is his best yet. [#15]

Title: Black America Again
Review: Whilst certainly not flawless, Black America Again sees Common deliver some of his most vital work and reaffirms his place in the discussion of greatest conscious rappers of all time.

Title: Angles
Review: Angles ends in a horribly frustrating manner, with none of the assurance of "Take it or Leave It" or "Red Light." No, Angles, even in ending with its strongest song, dies the way it lived: in sheer ambiguity.

Title: Yours, Mine & Ours
Review: Ultimately, the saccharine vocals are forgivable, but those who like their power pop with a little bite may find the sound a bit off-putting. [#5, p.115]

Title: Zipper Down
Review: Like Hughes and his signature ’70s-indebted mustache, Zipper Down makes familiarity refreshing.

Title: Swim
Review: Throughout Swim, Snaith employs similar tactics, getting something interesting started, seducing the listener, only to challenge them to stay on board as the song develops. [Spring 2010, p.69]

Title: Heavy Metal Music
Review: An incendiary cocktail of muscular grooves, designed to delight and thrill the metallic faithful. [Aug 2013, p.88]

Title: Bonfires on the Heath
Review: They all contribute to the consistency of atmosphere that makes the album in itself such a distinctively satisfying listen, and one in which anybody who makes the initial effort can immerse themselves entirely.

Title: One Day It Will Please Us to Remember Even This
Review: If you're heavily invested in the Dolls mythos... you'll be disappointed.... Still, One Day pleases us, especially since Johansen, Syl, and the new Dollettes don't try to replicate the old sound but opt for the rowdy professionalism of Johansen's '70s/'80s solo efforts.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: All comparisons aside, Collapse Into Now is one heck of an album.

Title: And Never Ending Nights
Review: Wilner hits a few gorgeous highs. [Mar 2012, p.90]

Title: An Other Cup
Review: Sounds astoundingly like an album from his '70s heyday.

Title: Wonderful Wonderful
Review: Wonderful Wonderful is the sound of a band rediscovering why they’re even making music in the first place, embracing their eccentricities instead of merely playing into what’s expected of them. It will never be anyone’s favorite Killers album, but it’s the most fun we’ve had with them in years, and a hopeful sign of truly wonderful things yet to come.

Title: Bankrupt!
Review: Phoenix gets the motions nearly right on Bankrupt, but that crucial snap simply isn’t there.

Title: Hard Bargain
Review: The 13-track set, produced by Jay Joyce, assures us that she's more than OK, with a still-luminous voice that can make the phone book sound like Puccini.

Title: My Way
Review: Focused and fighting fit, My way is proof that at 46 Ian brown is nevertheless prepared to go all 15 rounds. [Nov 2009, p.108]

Title: Tromatic Reflexxions
Review: Tromatic Reflexxions is a roaring success for both parties, blowing the fresh air of invention through an increasingly tribalist scene.

Title: Take Back the Universe and Give Me Yesterday
Review: But with gems like “Keep From Moving” and the country-tinged "Under the Tracks,” and even the vaguely disturbing, second-hand Bowie of “Lover’s Leap," the Creepers rein in their messier instincts, paring the proceedings down to smart, singalong and ultimately giddy jangle-pop.

Title: Digital Ash in a Digital Urn
Review: Digital Ash has the claustrophobic feel of a singer locked up with a computer, and it's distractingly chipper, like Rilo Kiley in their own Dntel homages; not every Bright Eyes record has to be an emotional epic, but Digital Ash feels like a practice run.

Title: The Naked Truth
Review: The Naked Truth could benefit from judicious cutting, but for its superior first half at least, it boasts the intimacy of a diary entry and the urgency of a kite sent straight out the penitentiary.

Title: The Hum
Review: Where the group from Leeds’ impressiveness lies is in their lighter, less mangled moments.

Title: Destroyer of the Void
Review: Things get more interesting when the band loosens up a bit on the multi-part title track; layered harmonies, elegant harpsichord and celestial synthesizers give way to a flamboyant mid-section with some unusually strident, glam-rock guitar.

Title: Exploding Head
Review: The back half picks up where the debut left off, full of inspired pieces of paranoia-inducing industrial guitar noise and moribund pop textures--it too often seems like a misguided attempt to connect dots for the listener.

Title: Tourist History
Review: Overall, this is a fine debut album that does exactly what it says on the tin. While they won't win any points for innovation, Two Door Cinema Club are going to find their way into a lot of people's hearts during 2010.

Title: Lookout Low
Review: It’s a slow burner - a passable Twin Peaks album that could, with time, become a great Twin Peaks album, but as of now, we haven’t quite gotten there yet.

Title: Beg for Mercy
Review: A pale retread of Get Rich... fashioned by lesser talents. [Feb 2004, p.69]

Title: Americana
Review: Even on the 66-year-old's 34th album, Young still has fire in his belly and fun in his fingers.

Title: Subiza
Review: The presence of mixers and various instruments is what recalls you the second and third times; mostly because you're too enveloped to look back now. But at the core of Subiza and at the heart of the sound is a tight-knit quartet that has already mastered the chemistry surrounding them.

Title: Arrow
Review: This is a grating, difficult, unsatisfying album.

Title: Paula
Review: The record is a failure, a virtual what-not-to-do guide for both songwriters and spurned lovers.

Title: The Sea
Review: The Sea is a richer effort than her debut.  Given its inspiration, it forges a darker and more sophisticated sonic palette.

Title: Whelm
Review: It's a careful and moody album, but fortunately, Dare has the grace to pull off his sonic and lyrical meanderings without devolving too deeply into self-conscious philosophizing or experimentation for its own sake, showing that he has both content and mystique to spare.

Title: I Love The New Sky
Review: On one level I Love The New Sky is simply a collection of engaging songs but on another it’s a call for togetherness, an appeal to stay strong and embrace life. Whichever view you take it’s very much a record for these times.

Title: Glynnaestra
Review: The album flows by with the scrapbooked flair of an intricately constructed sound collage, but one whose loose ends and experimental moments are firmly rooted in Krautpop rhythms.

Artist: Beth Jeans Houghton & The Hooves of Destiny
Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose is as restrained in its own way as it is vibrant; just over 30 minutes long, it shows that Houghton knows how to leave listeners wanting more.

Title: Walking With Thee
Review: The disc as a whole has sort of an austere quality that lets some of the fun out of the sails.

Title: Honeycomb
Review: Honeycomb is steeped in tradition, yet manages to buck it at the same time; while not all Pixies and Frank Black fans will appreciate its mellow maturity, it's an intimate treat for those who follow its lead.

Title: Riceboy Sleeps
Review: This is beautifully fragile music, not disposable but built to last.

Title: Tommy
Review: Dosh has indeed graduated from the sketchbook-like arrangements that marked his earlier work-- but Tommy's occasional tedium is a reminder that there's nothing wrong with doodling in the margins, either.

Title: Mount the Air
Review: An album of studied precision and endless textures. [Mar 2014, p.95]

Title: I Like Fun
Review: Sonically, it boasts richer textures than recent albums, thanks largely to the pair’s expanded touring line-up playing a greater role in the studio; a more fleshed-out sound than the occasionally irritating minimalism of yore. Arguably, the decision to beef up the instrumentation is designed to bring heft to the lyrics’ serious topics, even though the band are, as ever, likely to be preaching to the choir.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: In other world they might be drenched in sorrow, but here they're nice and introspective, like strategic resting points to make the glide that much more beatific.
Thier first albun of entirely self-penned instrumentals should finally see an end of [the world music tag], the fluid yet percussive tunes also impossibly nimble. [Oct 2009, p.116]

Title: Springtime Carnivore
Review: The Los Angeles-based artist's debut is one of the most promising starts of this year.

Title: Gettin' In Over My Head
