Title: Crawling Up the Stairs
Review: These instruments layer in complex, hypnotic patterns that drone in and over themselves, forged together to create less an emotional outcry than the hazy anguish of recalled emotion.

Title: Sirens
Review: Sirens proffers another string to his bow, its nine skittering essays overlaying richly textured, genre-melding electronic sound worlds with liminal song "structures." [Nov 2016, p.81]

Title: Plum
Review: In only two years, Wand has mirrored the maturation of the genre itself, moving from the youthful verve of “Tutti Frutti” toward rich, emotional terrain.

Title: American Dreamer
Review: Tastefully rendered and thoughtfully executed, American Dreamer invites you into its loose embrace while still maintaining a certain emotional distance. [No. 135, p.59]

Title: Pylon
Review: Pylon sees Killing Joke maintain the late-career renaissance precipitated by the original lineup reuniting for 2010's Absolute Dissent. [Nov 2015, p.77]

Title: Kinky
Review: All in all, a really great debut for this quintet.

Title: Mind Control
Review: It's an accomplished, evilly wrought set piece, but the acid-etched disco blues of "Poison Apple" is a standout. [May 2013, p.79]

Title: Grasque
Review: Grasque sometimes manages to make average pizza from excellent ingredients. When COYB are tenacious enough to boil a track down to a workable size, the result is a triumph. Often it can resemble unleavened music, stripped of the necessary rise and fall.

Title: Still Run
Review: The tracks are well-produced, but lack the soul to make a deep enough impact.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: This is probably the hardest Low album I’ve heard to appreciate, but it’s certainly worth it.

Title: Ugly Cherries
Review: Perhaps the true novelty of an album like Ugly Cherries isn't its glam presentation or its commitment to celebrating all things under a rainbow of pride. It's the heart-bursting sincerity that comes through in Bruce and Hopkins' eagerness to slather lipstick all over their chins and serenade their fellow weirdos in basements.

Title: Soviet Kitsch
Review: While Spektor possesses an intriguing voice, she uses it in such a cloying, affected manner as to be almost entirely off-putting.

Title: Augustines
Review: This is bigger, bolder, and better in every respect. [Mar 2014, p.97]

Title: California Chrome
Review: His music is remarkably creative and avoids sounding like a cheap novelty, or the audio equivalent of an ill-conceived Halloween costume.

Title: Strange Creatures
Review: If Strange Creatures show a grander musical approach, then lyrically they're still fascinated by the bleak detail of everyday life, even if lads-night-out-gone-wrong vignette Bonfire Of the City Boys and sax-peppered deadpan horror story Prom Night flip the mundane into something more twisted. [Apr 2019, p.110]

Title: Church With No Magic
Review: There's an exciting and engaging mini-album here but, across the album as a whole, PVT seem to be straining for a gravitas that their music does not entirely justify.

Title: Lost Themes II
Review: The band element is Carpenter's saving grace and is hopefully a sign of what's to come, as the potential for this project remains enticing.

Title: Elaenia
Review: Eleania demands focus, too, but pay attention to it and you'll be rewarded.

Title: V
Review: V is a solid, dream-inducing, quietly dramatic step forward for JJ.

Title: Semper Femina
Review: Semper Femina continues her decade-long hot streak with another collection of finely wrought vignettes on love, loss, and the empowerment that can be found in both.

Title: AM
Review: They’ve evolved certain factors of their sound and ventured into new territory, but AM is not so much a change of direction as it is an affirmation of all the musical elements that made the band exhilarating to begin with--inspired lyrics, screeching riffs and great melodies.

Title: I Had A Dream That You Were Mine
Review: A 1000 Times is an opening track as startling as it is oddly timeless, and if, when it debuted in July, it promised great things of this pairing, the resulting album certainly delivers.

Title: Rainford
Review: Rainford is a classic set of Scratch vocals: science fiction nursery rhymes, apocalyptic lullabies, their melodies light as air yet rocksteady. Scratch’s delivery at the age of 83 is like Dylan’s present-day rasp, no longer about hitting notes or even tone necessarily, but heavy with the weight of his personal and musical history. [May 2019, p.61]

Title: Songs of Mass Destruction
Review: The result is an album that captures the range of her styles, from the rhythmically charged pop of her Eurythmics days to the haunted, longing ballads of her solo career. If the two approaches don't always cohere, each is satisfying in its own right.

Title: Palace
Review: Chapel Club are another retro-indie band apparently eager to re-run the 1980s, albeit in slightly more musically adventurous manner than the likes of White Lies and Interpol.

Title: WLIB AM: King of the Wigflip
Review: For every track that delivers the expected, another does something quite extraordinary. [Oct 2008, p.72]

Title: Tour de France Soundtracks
Review: In essence, the group has adopted the smartest possible approach on Tour de France Soundtracks by simply making quintessential Kraftwerk music of a kind stylistically consistent with the music of its past but with subtle enhancements that suggest a connection to the present.

Title: Space Gun
Review: Overall, Space Gun gives hope for the continuing future of a band that’s already died twice. While there’s a few bumps here and there, this is the sound of a group drunk off its own energy and excited to be alive.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: Singer Joe Casey tacks flattened vocals to songs that move with a bristling crawl and occasionally explode into repressed fury. [Nov 2016, p.35]

Title: Animal
Review: It’s hard to remember the last time an album so flat and vacuous generated such a buzz.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: Pusha T is at the top of his game with sharply defined autobiographical tales and defiant, self-aware verses. He often dazzles with his smooth, cold-blooded flow and connects on virtually every song.

Title: Songs for Singles
Review: Instead of Meanderthal's rich sonics and expansive melodies, Torche about-faces into bracing, aggressive cuts like "Cast into Unknown" and "U.F.O." and even though "Out Again" delves into sludgy pop, it's done in such a lackadaisical fashion that's it;s clear that Brooks' heart is more in the faster, louder numbers. [Sep/Oct 2010, p.90]

Title: How To Become Clairvoyant
Review: Much of the rest, alas, suggests a gift not for clairvoyance but invisibility. [May 2011, p.94]

Title: The Con
Review: The Con is a startlingly dark, yet characteristically vibrant offering, featuring a band that’s learned to harness the energy-highs, while tempering pretty (even pastoral) pop-folk with a new, deeply-affecting brand of melancholy.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: The double in the room on Let England Shake is the whole modern world. PJ Harvey has given us a righteous scare.

Title: All Day
Review: For the uninitiated though, this is essential listening for any member of the iTunes set; crafting your next playlist will likely turn into a transcendental experience after you hear how uncannily Drake goes along with Flock of Seagulls.

Title: Boarding House Reach
Review: Boarding House Reach is a long, bewildering slog studded with these moments, which seem to be directly antagonizing you.

Title: The Blade
Review: The Blade further serves to position her as one of the premiere and rare female neo-traditionalists in the format.

Title: Need Your Light
Review: On Need Your Light, they finally hit the sweet spot.

Title: Colored Emotions
Review: The sound of this record is one that may have gotten them a record deal, but will not get them much of an audience.

Title: Space City Kicks
Review: It's just we know there's more to this guy than this sluggish, lifeless material.

Title: Phoenix
Review: Phoenix has been four years in the making, waiting in the wings to see the light. And now that it’s finally here, Phoenix is definitely worth checking out.

Title: Night Time, My Time
Review: Assured and assertive, Night Time, My Time plays like the darker, dirtier counterpart to fellow category-co-founders Haim. [No. 105, p.54]

Title: More Fish
Review: B-list Wu cronies contribute a few too many forgettable guest verses, but Ghost's technique has never been deadlier.

Title: Vows
Review: The rest of Vows is equally fresh and surprising, its genre leaps held together by Kimbra's pliant coo.

Title: AZD
Review: If you put in the effort this is one of the most rewarding albums of the year so far, but like pronouncing its title, don’t be surprised if you don’t get it first time.

Title: American Gangster
Review: This is the best music Jay-Z can make as a human--at least by my (his) definitions of what he (we) can do.

Title: Slick Dogs and Ponies
Review: Louis XIV has a considerable amount of work to do for listeners to regard them as more than aimless glam-rock fetishists.

Title: The Year of Hibernation
Review: Powers definitely has the compositional wherewithal to make something special--he just has to put more of himself into it.

Title: The Red Book
Review: The essence of what made Penguin Cafe Orchestra is here: the music is dreamlike and does indeed touch the heart of the listener.

Title: Evolve Or Be Extinct
Review: At his best on "Evolve or Be Extinct", though, he reaches a pleasing mixture of understated beats and slice-of-life rhymes that are occasionally profound. At his worst, songs like "Scar" have neither beats nor rhymes I ever want to hear again.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: Though this new political bent shows a heightened sense of maturity and substance, two of Morning's best tracks are poignant, unabashed love songs.

Title: Los Angeles Police Department
Review: None of these songs reach that lofty level [of Paul McCartney, Brian Wilson and Randy Newman], but fans of inward-looking popsmiths like Elliott Smith and Daniel Johnston (whose artwork gets a subtle nod through the graphics) will find some gentle little gems in this police department lost-and-found.

Title: The Glorious Dead
Review: They stick to their winning formula. [Sep 2012, p.88]

Title: Lisbon
Review: It offers a peppy antidote to You and Me, their especially downbeat 2008 offering, walking you through all the requisite Walkmen emotions: chipper resentment ("Blue As Your Blood," "Woe Is Me"), resignation ("All My Great Designs"), hung-over longing ("Torch Song"). But it's "Juveniles," the opener, that consolidates in one track all we expect the Walkmen to deliver.

Title: Songs of Experience
Review: Despite the blatant bid to sound modish and rejuvenated, U2 cannot help in certain respects but sound the same.

Title: D-D-Don't Don't Stop the Beat
Review: All the songs sound almost exactly the same. I don’t care! It doesn’t matter! Just dance!

Title: Resolution
Review: Frontman Randy Blythe still growls his guts out while his bandmates hammer away at economy-sized grooves that suggest an extreme-sports version of Southern rock.

Title: Happenstance
Review: Carried off with an impressive theatricality. [Jul 2005, p.104]

Title: neo
Review: Ultimately, what So Pitted have--besides a name derived from a YouTube video of a surfer waxing poetic about a perfect wave--is the discovery of a rad tunnel of sound where noise and melody can high five each other with impunity.

Title: The Golden Age
Review: True, he sometimes overdoes the theatrical flourishes, but high drama is what this record is all about, so he can be forgiven for that. [Jun 2013, p.108]

Title: Memory Almost Full
Review: Not quite double thumbs aloft then, but way fabber than it has any right to be.

Title: The Eraser
Review: The Eraser’s sound lies somewhere between the roiling beat soup of Amnesiac and a poppier sensibility.

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: An eyes-closed, head-bobbing masterpiece. [Oct 2002, p.86]

Artist: Someone Still Loves You Boris Yeltsin
Title: Let It Sway
Review: You could call it inconsistency, but you can tell they never signed up for the mission of steering the chasm of modern rock music. Instead, they're four guys doing what they want, culling their influences and breathing life into whatever construct emerges. But regardless of where it falls on the spectrum, it's always fun.

Title: We Slept At Last
Review: [A] coolly unnerving full-length debut. [Apr 2015, p.102]

Title: True Sadness
Review: There’s True Sadness, whose songs touch lyrically upon all things sad but with various shades of unsubtle sound to guide them. [No. 133, p.54]

Title: You Gotta Go There to Come Back
Review: What some see as derivative, unoriginal bollocks others view as honesty, craft and a lack of pretension.

Title: It's Alright Between Us As It Is
Review: Lindstrøm’s output can include 10-minute workouts of an avant-garde Boredoms track or the sort of polite female vocals people expect to hear on unthreatening dance tunes--Grace Hall’s pleasantries on Shinin’ fit that bill on his fourth solo album while the infinitely more interesting Jenny Hval crops up on a superior Bungl (Like a Ghost).

Title: Work
Review: The sonic references keep on coming throughout Work, but great songs do too.

Title: American Supreme
Review: Perhaps the strangest twist about this record is how much of it sounds more crude and antiquated than the duo's first two albums, which were released over 20 years prior to this one.

Title: We're All Gonna Die
Review: Too frequently, though, the new material doesn't have the constitution to withstand the heavy hand of producer and former Dawes guitarist Blake Mills. [No. 137, p.55]

Title: Wallop
Review: The ’90s were a decade very much in its feelings, and the best parts of Wallop are its most emotional.

Title: Where We Were Together
Review: The best pure indie-pop record of 2018 (so far) is not from Brooklyn or Glasgow or Melbourne or Olympia but Busan, South Korea. The album, Where We Were Together from the band Say Sue Me, is a perfectly paced fusion of jangling guitars, bouncing bass and sighed melancholy.

Title: Shaking the Habitual
Review: While some of the abstract material here is frustratingly opaque, how many other ‘pop’ acts can you name that would have the brass cojones to drop a near 20-minute track right in the middle of their record? Astonishing.

Title: Golden Ocean
Review: Only the album-ending title track tones down the noise, and even then, it's about as restrained as early Husker Du. [May 2005, p.132]

Title: Æ’IN
Review: Talabot has a knack for capturing the very specific kind of bliss associated with dancing on Mediterranean beaches at the height of summer.

Title: If You Wait
Review: The inner life of the walking wounded and the angst of embracing adulthood haven’t been this well documented on record in quite a long time and I can say without hesitance that If You Wait is a classic in the making.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: Though harder, happier and a little more direct, Animal Joy is above all a Shearwater record: swooping, eloquent, concerned with nature.

Title: All
Review: For an album that is so geographically and linguistically focused, ALL is strangely beautiful when robbed of all its context.

Title: Semicircle
Review: Semicircle won’t seem like a giant leap for the band but is yet another upbeat, buoyant addition to their canon, injected with an even greater sense of community spirit.

Title: Have You in My Wilderness
Review: Deciphering the message in her words relies on just how much time the listener is willing to devote to the album, but with music this brilliant, the task seems all the more alluring.

Title: Recess
Review: This already busy album becomes even busier with so many cooks in the kitchen, and shoots off nonstop fireworks as if this was Skrillex's audio variety special, sponsored by the wing of the stereo industry that sells, re-cones, or fixes subwoofers.

Title: She Remembers Everything
Review: Though Cash refrains from direct political speech on this record, she offers solace amid the political unrest, choosing to focus on personal connection rather than polarization as we near the end of a chaotic, divisive year.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: Band of Joy, by both reaching back and by yearning for a decorous new future, is an album that matters.

Title: Chill, Dummy
Review: A few dips and peaks throughout, but the elements seem to fall into place for a consistent and cohesive experience.

Title: This Unruly Mess I've Made
Review: Macklemore remains unsure of himself throughout, lacking the rapping skills and natural charisma needed to get things onto a surer footing. In the end, it’s a sadly fitting album title.

Title: Charango
Review: The entire album is a beauty.... The most adventurous album of their career. [Aug 2002, p.110]

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: Get Behind Me Satan may confuse and even push away some White Stripes fans, but the more the band pushes itself, the better.

Title: If All I Was Was Black
Review: If All I Was Was Black contains performances as powerful as any she has given.

Title: Good Grief
Review: It's a mostly dazzling performance, though on the histrionic Gone Insane, they get carried away by their own virtuosity. [Apr 2016, p.109]

Title: Sepalcure
Review: Deep tech sonics fizzle under analog warmth for this engaging LP, where Sepalcure demonstrate an outgrowth and combination of dub sounds, techno, and house so rife with flashy ideas that it's a miracle it actually works as well as it does.

Title: It's All Around You
Review: Although there are no new dimensions here,... this still feels like musical fresh mint. [#242, p.67]

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: The Shabazz sound is sprawling and promiscuous, but also deep, which might make for uneasy listening. [Aug 2014, p.79]

Title: The Diving Board
Review: John is still going strong and better than ever. A few listens to The Diving Board proves exactly that.

Title: Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers
Review: To the extent that it falls prey to unnecessary pseudo-sophistication, Sad Songs For Dirty Lovers comes off weak; to the extent that it maintains its own musical niche within the shattered-lover trope, Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers makes the shopworn surprisingly compelling.

Title: Nuclear Daydream
Review: It's the little touches that make Daydream so appealing. [Nov 2006, p.190]

Title: Skins
Review: Nineteen years later the band are in robust health, and Skins makes for an impressive, graceful addition to their catalogue.

Title: The Adventures of Ghosthorse and Stillborn
Review: CocoRosie has this fantastic ability to infuse humanity into their drum machines, and the warming result carries The Adventures to marvelous heights. [Apr 2007, p.102]

Title: Blank Face LP
Review: Blank Face turns away from the ambitious fusion of To Pimp a Butterfly, instead doubling down on a smoked-out atmosphere that points the listener’s focus toward rapping. That puts the onus on Q to hold attention for the duration of the record’s hour-plus running time, and he does so.

Title: Time Is Over One Day Old
Review: This may be the bleak and heavy masterpiece that BIH has been hovering around for the past decade. [No. 112, p.53]

Title: The People's Key
Review: The arrangements are pleasurable enough, less rootsy than before, with some skilled use of orchestration; but it's a shame to find such a gifted songwriter sounding so gullible.

Title: Doggumentary
Review: There are moments here that hint at brilliance of the West Coast veteran's early G-funk staples, which only underlines the fact that a more faithful sequel to his magnum opus would best serve his fans and his legacy. Doggumentary is far from that, its major player distracted by his desire to replicate modish hood-bangers and experiment in areas too far from his comfort zone.

Title: Sea Lion
Review: Move over, Devendra Banhart: there's a new bunch of bohemian music kooks in town. [Apr 2008, p.115]

Title: Control System
Review: Ab-Soul performs well in this complementary role and shows how versatile he really is, almost a west-coast amalgam of Brown and Kanye West, yet still a slightly weaker and more inconsistent sum than the parts.

Title: The Best Little Secrets Are Kept
Review: Pairs the thrilling hedonism of early-Seventies T. Rex and David Bowie with cartoonishly sexed-up vocals that make winking fun of glitter rock's excesses.

Title: Ultimate Success Today
Review: Apocalyptic music for apocalyptic times.

Title: Welcome Back
Review: A surprisingly tepid collection that might have benefited from a bit more preaching, or at least a bit more passion. [30 Aug 2004]

Title: Salad Days
Review: You can enjoy Salad Days for its unadorned flow and easygoing weirdness, or you can stop, reflect and be moved by its fresh honesty. It’s worthwhile either way.

Title: Fire Like This
Review: Blood Red Shoes still rocks out on most tracks, all riled up and restless, keeping the rhythms chunky and choppy on standouts like the defiantly-played and shouted "Light It Up," the revved-up guitar and drums of "Don't Ask," and the guitar jags and slamming drums on "Keeping It Close."

Title: The Datsuns
Review: The Datsuns' biggest problem isn't the style of music they're playing, though. It's the sub-standard quality of their songwriting, the uninspired performances on here and the fundamental lack of willingness to stretch beyond the safe confines of their older brothers' record collections.

Title: Woke Myself Up
Review: Reuniting her ex-bandmates adds a rock impetus to Doiron's more fragile solo work. [Feb 2007, p.74]

Title: Who Are You
Review: Having coloured in right up to the edges in previous projects, it's a pleasure to hear Ruscha exercising restraint on "Lights Passing By" and "Gravity Waves." [Apr 2018, p.35]

Title: Culture II
Review: While the bulk of the songs can’t disguise their rush-job origins, tinges of Trap Boy Magic do spring up from time to time.

Title: Carry On
Review: A surprising (if a little sad) return to form.

Title: It's Blitz!
Review: It’s Blitz! is the sound of a band reborn with new momentum, and on an album that requires dancing, the message is clear: It doesn’t matter where you came from. Just keep moving.

Title: The Menace
Review: Sounds like lovelorn, half-baked philosophy for the Mariah Carey set.... Lucky for Justine Frischmann and her reconstituted Elastica, rock 'n' roll doesn't require lyrical profundity, just great beats, riffs, and attitude. All are here in spades... [#47, p.90]

Title: Liberman
Review: Fueled by exploration and musical experimentation, Carlton’s reinvention finds her a long way from “A Thousand Miles”--and in a better place, artistically.

Title: Martha Wainwright
Review: Her songs are tough and earthy, hating mere prettiness when fieriness or forcefulness are required.

Title: A+E
Review: The combination of precisely crafted pop and fiercely imaginative arrangements results in a thrilling listen.

Title: Jason Derulo
Review: Derulo's desperation to cover all commercial bases is only matched by an inability to stamp his own personality on them.

Title: Hollywood's Bleeding
Review: More well-executed than his previous releases and undeniably catchy, Hollywood's Bleeding is a huge step forward for the guarded superstar, one that doesn't sacrifice the essential elements that made him such a surprise hitmaker, and pushes him even further into the pop-savvy landscape where he belongs.

Title: Medulla
Review: Bits of Medulla sound similar to Vespertine, but there’s a marked distinction in the means of delivery and enough change to keep things interesting.

Title: Roll On
Review: The Oklahoma singer/songwriter and multi-instrumentalist raises eyebrows from the get-go on his 16th solo outing, dipping into jazz for the gently swinging 'Who Knew' and the self-effacing 'Former Me.'

Title: Have One on Me
Review:
It’s unlikely that you’ll often listen to it in one bout, but whether beguiled one day by its exotic petals and blooms or the next by the less showy trees in the background, Have One On Me is 
an Elysian record that you’ll return to again and again.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Specifically, Mitski focuses on the loneliness of a "lone ranger" lifestyle and expresses it profoundly through the musical choices accentuating her lo-fi indie rock aesthetic.

Title: Curve of Earth
Review: Curve of Earth is not an easy listen, but the musicality keeps it from being a straight downer of a record. The songs here are uniformly well written and interesting even as the exorcism of addiction demons is at times oppressive.

Title: Invariable Heartache
Review: While Wagner's voice is not always up to it, Tidwell's authentic country pipes are the real revelation here.

Title: Layers
Review: Layers is a great step forward, a glowing promise on his next album, his ambitions will be fully realized.

Title: Ghost Blonde
Review: Ghost Blonde brings a glimmer of hope to those who feel that noise has remained stagnant, past overdue its last hurrah. As these set of songs pinpoints, there's still plenty to discover in a genre that has always shown itself as deviously minimal.

Title: The Iceberg
Review: Oddisee's all-round strengths as producer, mixer, and lyricist make for a more cohesive record, allowing for his personality and message to shine that much brighter.

Title: Like The River Loves The Sea
Review: Joan Shelley’s greatest gift is her approach to making music—to create a welcoming refuge from the world’s noise. A balm for our troubled times. A haven for those who need it, if only for an album’s length every couple of years. You’ll want to stay longer.

Title: Beacon
Review: The album hits a few highs; "The World Is Watching" enchants with swirling synth lines and intoxicating guest vocals from Valentina. The lows leave one wondering what could have been if Two Door Cinema Club had challenged themselves a bit more.

Title: Alasdair Roberts
Review: These self-penned songs feel so timelessly authentic they might have been dredged from the deep well of traditional British Isles song from which Roberts regularly sips. [Feb 2015, p.95]

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: Merrie Land
Review: While the Good, the Bad & the Queen are skilled at providing a wide breadth of styles here--from the woozy, carnivalesque organ of “The Last Man to Leave” to “The Truce of Twilight”’s militaristic chants--they especially succeed at conveying a crumbling and isolated Britain.

Title: Until The Lights Fade
Review: The record conjures an atmosphere of twilit sadness, but the songs themselves--languid and forgettable--fail to mark Stein out from dolorous troubadours past. [Oct 2018, p.116]

Title: That's How We Burn
Review: Much of the record is stuck in a good but not great sound from 10 years back.

Title: I Feel Cream
Review: I Feel Cream is Peaches' most pop-leaning album to date, though it doesn't comprise. [Spring 2009, p.67]

Title: Hurricane
Review: 'Corporate Cannibal' is the exception, and Jones, a miracle of nature at Meltdown, proves more fallible on Hurricane. [Nov 2008, p.64]

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: Anyone who has surmounted that hurdle will be delighted to discover that the album represents business as usual: 13 absorbing songs, sparingly orchestrated to concentrate attention on the lyrics.

Title: Fated
Review: Fated draws you in, and encapsulates a range of euphoric sounds, leaving you much lighter on the other side.

Title: Lonerism
Review: There's aren't a whole lot of songs here that really stand out on their own.... But the members of Tam Impala possess such boundless energy and obvious, puppy-like enthusiasm that it would be downright churlish to dismiss them. [No. 92, p.81]

Title: Then Came The Morning
Review: Part of the fun of The Lone Bellow is playing spot the influence: James Gang here, Staples Sisters there, Warren Zevon, Faces, lots of Crosby Stills Nash & Young. But to its credit, the band channels these icons with a commensurate amount of tact and respect.

Title: Blinking Lights and Other Revelations
Review: E is one of the best songwriters America has to offer, and he has made as personal, poignant, and ultimately redeeming an album that you are ever going to hear.

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: It all adds up to The Mountain Goats’ most musically sophisticated endeavor to date. In fact, the music is finally beginning to hold its own with the lyrics.

Title: Ruminations
Review: Though these songs were recorded hastily by some standards, their welding of forlorn lyricism and comforting listenability makes the songwriter admirable not just for his craftsmanship, but for his ability to pull through an arduous time with what could be a benchmark album in his already prolific career.

Title: Awake
Review: There are worse barbs to chuck at an album than that it would make a beautiful accompaniment to some breathtaking scenery.

Title: Congregation of the Damned
Review: It would be a disservice to how good of an album Congregation of the Damned is to say it’s not as heavy as older material in Atreyu’s catalog.

Title: Beat 'Em Up
Review: It's all third-rate bar band stuff.

Title: Front Porch
Review: It's hard to deny that Front Porch is Williams at her best. It took some time for her to come to terms with it, but this is an album that embraces Williams' legacy from the Civil Wars and incorporates it into her own musical personality.

Title: The Facts of Life
Review: Sparse, noir-tinged melancholia... If David Lynch should ever film a TV series in England, here are the soundtrack composers.

Title: Haha Sound
Review: In a world supersaturated with electronica, Broadcast are nonetheless bold, rare and crucial. [Sep 2003, p.97]

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: The core of any Low album, though, is the unearthly beauty of Sparhawk and his wife Mimi Parker's vocal harmonies, which, after 20 years, have lost none of their emotion-stirring power. [Apr 2013, p.90]

Title: Mirror Mirror
Review: Damned if they do and damned if they don't, it seems, but never sounding damned enough.

Title: Here Lies Love
Review: As each song features a different vocalist and each is a snapshot, it's difficult to tell which character is singing, to get emotionally involved or to keep up with the story without much refernce to the book. [Apr 2010, p.103]

Title: Girl at the End of the World
Review: If you do have another [James record], the chances are it’s stored away somewhere you don’t think about very often. The chances are, too, that The Girl at the End of the World, likeably well-intentioned as it may be, will end up in the same place.

Title: Interpol
Review: It is still familiar as an Interpol album, but it's certainly their most refined, elegant and frightening release. [Oct 2010, p.97]

Title: Get Color
Review: HEALTH will still be written off as noise, but for fans, it sounds like the quartet tapped into its groove.

Title: Feels
Review: If it isn't as formally shocking as "Sung Tongs," it's still a strong record. [17 Oct 2005]

Title: ONoffON
Review: The album doesn't break any new ground for the band, but finds Burma at the top of its game, mixing artful music, intelligent lyrics and controlled sonic mayhem.

Title: The Source
Review: A set of vigorous yet highly intricate arrangements of new material. [Oct 2017, p.60]

Title: United States of Being
Review: There's a true songwriter's ear buried beneath all the fist-pumping, and it relies on a well-honed melodic sensibility that borrows on classic power-pop tropes but introduces impressive key and tempo shifts.

Title: The Mouse and the Mask
Review: While this buoyant link-up is no disgrace, its main ingredients - copshow brass, cartoon flutes, professor voices - are fairly familiar rap tropes.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: An uneasy gamut of emotion imbues another exceptional Mountain Goats effort. [No. 92, p.51]

Title: B.o.B Presents: The Adventures of Bobby Ray
Review: There are many quirks with this album, but realise that it doesn't feel like a debut from a fully-formed artist, rather someone that intermittently flickers with potential and then dials it down to play it safe for the radio.

Title: Coming Home
Review: All the emo-rooted, posthardcore stylistic hallmarks are present and correct, embellished with a load of electronic arsing about on top, but the almost constant use of the same soaring ‘wo-ah’ pop hooks will soon have you wanting to hack your ears off with a pair of blunt scissors.

Title: Handwritten
Review: Handwritten houses some of Fallon's strongest compositions to date, and while it ain't punk, neither is The Gaslight Anthem.

Title: The Nihilist
Review: A few of Liam Finn's fans may be a bit puzzled by the more outré experiments on The Nihilist, but he's still writing great tunes and bringing them to life in an exciting way, and that--as much as the musical shape-shifting on these sessions--is what makes this album worthwhile.

Title: Hollowed
Review: No other album made by the countless electronic composers delves this deeply into places people fear to face.

Title: Afterparty Babies
Review: The boring beats and throwback rhyme flow (circa 92)--which is weak even by Edmontonian standards--put Afterparty Babies somewhere beneath Don Cash’s home demos and the outtakes from Organized Rhyme’s Huh? Stiffenin’ Against The Wall.

Title: Timeless
Review: A predictable, oversimplified, boring mess.

Title: When Life Gives You Lemons, You Paint That Shit Gold
Review: Add some beatboxing courtesy of Tom Waits (!), and you have an occasionally forced, yet boldly magnetic change of pace. [May 2008, p.94]

Title: Secret Wars
Review: All in all, expertly wobbling prog metal, constructed out of as few chords as possible.

Title: The Cost
Review: The Cost is an emotional trip worth taking, one that seems to move further inward in its focus and insight with each track.

Title: No Boys Allowed
Review: Her follow-up isn't merely eager to stand out but rather desperate, as if the studios in which it was recorded contained a clock counting down to the point of failure, the moment when Hilson would no longer stand a chance of being a ubiquitous, multi-platinum superstar.

Title: The Terror
Review: The Flaming Lips return with one of their most challenging, yet cohesive records to date.

Title: Humanz
Review: What Humanz lacks in memorable hooks, it makes up for in fist-clenching spirit--and We Got The Power sums that up best. [Jun 2017, p.113]

Title: Magic
Review: Chalk up at least some of this disconnect to Brendan O’Brien’s production, which is often so slicked down and smooshed together that it doesn’t just airbrush the band’s jagged edges, it sandblasts them.

Title: Ishi
Review: The headspace it produces is calming but frequently, dreamily surreal, and it often seems like a better place to live than the world outside it.

Title: 200 Million Thousand
Review: 200 Million Thousand provides a fair share of these moments and because of that you can say the album succeeds. It just could use a little more teenage head and a little less brains.

Title: I Love You, Dude
Review: Digitalism is at their best when immersing themselves in the trappings and embellishments of full-blown electronica, and they tend to suffer when trying to escape them.

Title: Go With Me
Review: Seapony is one of the best pop bands of 2011.

Title: Dose Your Dreams
Review: Vocal contributions from a slew of guests keep things unpredictable on a set which often feels like a multi-genre playlist. ... Time spent getting your head around this craziness is time well spent. [6 Oct 2018, p.55]

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: The only way you can't approach Best of Gloucester County is neutrally. And it takes suspendin' some serious disbelief to buy into the Danielson vision, but I think it's worth it.

Title: First Taste
Review: First Taste is a record exploding with ideas and interesting twists. [Sep 2019, p.109]

Title: Thank Me Later
Review: Thank Me Later may not have been the game-changing release everyone was hoping for, but we now have every reason to believe that the hype will ring true on his next album.

Title: Instant Money Magic
Review: Japanther sound more in touch than ever with the spirit of youth, excitement, and discovery that started the band 13 years before the release of this album.

Title: Psychic 9-5 Club
Review: At last, HTRK are inhabiting their own spotlight instead of disappearing into negative space, and by shearing off the mystique, they’ve become much more riveting.

Title: Everything Ecstatic
Review: Even if it is hard at certain points to cut through the thick fog of psych drum riffs, Everything Ecstatic leaves ears ringing like a loud summer afternoon in the city – sun-drenched cacophony that doesn’t quite know where it’s going just yet.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: Mind Bokeh signifies a union between sonic exploration-typically condemned to musical isolation by being defined as experimental -- and the consonances of modern pop music that are readily accepted by mass listeners.

Title: Rest
Review: With Rest, she grows more fearless as an artist while facing her losses, and the future, with courage and love.

Title: Bare Bones
Review: Predictably, the results are mixed compared to previous efforts--the quality of her performance remains extraordinarily high, but the material is spottier than usual, particularly when Peyroux stretches beyond her comfort zone and into newfound emotional real estate.

Title: All You Need Is Now
Review: The once bold, sometimes shameless Simon Le Bon sounds a bit tentative in this post-Killers world, and when compared to the tight, original, nine-track version of the album previously made available via digital download, this final, fatter version borders on "too much of a good thing." Fortunately, the emphasis will be on "good thing" for longtime Duran fans or anyone with a taste for melodic, synth-driven pop/rock.

Title: Signed And Sealed In Blood
Review: It's the Bostonians' simplicity that's most endearing though, and this is a terrific, hangover-inducing return to form.

Title: Singles
Review: Sometimes the lyrics are as uncanny as the voice.

Title: Dream River
Review: The arrangements on Dream River are almost as eloquent as his lyrics.

Title: Blume
Review: This is a broad, swaggering definition of jazz that touches on Nigerian afrobeat, Ghanaian high-life, grungy post-rock and vocal-led astral soul. Non-jazz fans might be drawn to Nerija's astonishing guitarist Shirley Tetteh. [Sep 2019, p.30]

Title: Street Sweeper Social Club
Review: Even as a record of adequate, vaguely politicized mook-rock, it mostly falls flat, whether by lazy lyrics or some uninspired drumming from Galactic's Stanton Moore, who adds plenty of percussive touches like the judicious cowbell of 'Clap For the Killers' but sinks more straightforward tracks such as 'The Oath' like a stone.

Title: Into Colour
Review: The question seems churlish: these are memorable songs, recorded with exquisite taste.

Title: Little Fictions
Review: All of it adds up to an album that feels quietly hopeful, making it a tonic for troubled times.

Title: The Private Press
Review: Few approach this style of record making with as much playfulness and gravity.

Title: Out in the Light
Review: His heart is worn clearly on his sleeve without becoming too overbearing and the final product is nothing short of profound.

Title: Throws
Review: Though it may take a few listens to reveal itself, Throws is a playful and inventive album that reveals little rewarding moments with each spin.

Title: Ersatz GB
Review: The [line-up] present on Ersatz G.B. were also present for 2008's Imperial Wax Solvent and 2010's Your Future, Our Clutter, records that showed enough touches of class, craft and ingenuity to reassure The Fall's notoriously hardcore following that the future was surprisingly rosy.

Title: The Cloud Making Machine
Review: While Garnier's trickling melodies and spare snares hint at mystery, mostly they leave you longing for a beat.

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: Give Indie Cindy an honest listen. If you have to, just pretend it's the new project of Frank Black, Joey Santiago and David Loverling.

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: Antony's musical presence haunts and hypnotizes long after he's left the stage.

Title: The Bravery
Review: If The Killers hadn't got there first with Hot Fuss, The Bravery's debut would have been revolutionary. Instead it is merely a brilliant pop record. [Apr 2005, p.115]

Title: The Suburbs
Review: It's common for heavily hyped albums to fall flat, but Arcade Fire's long-anticipated third LP hits with the satisfied thud of met potential.

Title: The Story of Sonny Boy Slim
Review: While he’s well served by the rugged immediacy of the mix--make no mistake, it’s an improvement--his songwriting lags noticeably behind his musical prowess. And he sings much of the album on falsetto, a thin part of his vocal range.

Title: Tongues
Review: It doesn't always work, but there are more than enough explosive moments to pick up the slack.

Title: If I've Only One Time Askin'
Review: He brings real feeling to his own compositions such as Let Me Sleep (At the end of a Dream).

Title: Blood in My Eye
Review: Desperately slim pickings... betray this release's roots as a mere EP. [Jan 2004, p.116]

Title: The Magic Gang
Review: The best thing about their self-titled debut might be their four-part harmonies.

Title: Jay II
Review: Jay Arner may be something of a misanthrope, but he cares enough to make great pop records for the world at large, and Jay II's juxtaposition of form and content only makes its pleasures more intriguing.

Title: Traveling Alone
Review: Traveling Alone feels more spontaneous and immediate than most of Tift Merritt's previous work, but it's no less beautiful or affecting for it.

Title: Flock
Review: The US debut of Damien Rice's former band turns sentimental mush into something palatable. [Mar 2008, p.97]

Title: Planta
Review: Some of the songs on Planta begin as dark as the worst in Interpol's catalog. It's really no fun, and the tone makes it a lot harder to choke down the lyrics. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.86]

Title: Crayons
Review: If we forget her Lenny Henry-esque Jamaican accent on the title track's Ziggy Marley duet, she's on sterling form. [Aug 2008, p.143]

Title: The Fame
Review: Icy love songs, shameless pop music that comments on its own shamelessness as it goes along: it's hard not to feel that you've heard a lot of this before.

Title: You Can Do Anything
Review: However much he hollers, Dave McCabe can’t escape sounding bored, and his often-schoolboy lyrics have begun to actively jar.

Title: Oh No I Love You
Review: Burgess always wanted to be a country soul man, on this album he has done it. [Oct 2012, p.87]

Title: Astronaut
Review: Duran Duran has a new lease on life, sounding more vibrant and exciting than it has in eons.

Title: Tassili
Review: Not "desert blues." Sadder than blues‑-too sad to be merely calming.

Title: Tical 0: The Prequel
Review: Kanye West's debut aside, it's the essential hip hop album of the year so far. [Jun 2004, p.102]

Title: Tender Madness
Review: Tender Madness is raw, yet alluring; it is unapologetically punk, with a better work ethic.

Title: Pure Comedy
Review: On Pure Comedy, Father John Misty is just about clever enough to glide entirely on his intellectualism, but by emotionally removing himself from his own narratives, he’s ended up making a record that’s smarter than it is affecting.

Title: More Parts per Million
Review: As with the best bedroom punk records, the bloody-knuckled passion and immediacy of these 13 rapid songs transcends any cavils about sound quality. [Oct 2003, p.130]

Title: Part II: The New December
Review: Fol Chen's commitment to writing music from a depersonalized angle is commendable as an artistic experiment-and more often than not, it surprises with unexpectedly beguiling hooks-but it's beginning to feel like its self-imposed mystery is a cover for its identity crisis.

Title: Pollinator
Review: Nothing here sounds forced. [Jun 2017, p.102]

Title: Thrashing Thru the Passion
Review: Even if the band’s guitar work isn’t what it used to be, Finn’s storytelling prowess certainly is, and along with his usual barrage of smartest-guy-at-the-dive-bar one-liners, an appropriate shift in his perspective as a lyricist is evident.

Title: Employment
Review: Kaiser Chiefs manage find their footing early on and this success forgives them their meanderings later on the disc.

Title: Death Is This Communion
Review: DITC will still melt your speakers. Jack Endino's clean yet full-tilt production fills out the sound, but it's drummer Des Kensel's ability to push forward and hold back--not simply pound monochromatically from start to finish--that truly creates the thriving, volatile atmosphere here.

Title: Lady From Shanghai
Review: Pere Ubu's first studio recording in three years is a suitably abstruse, challenging and dense record, and yet another example of how Pere Ubu remain at the very peak of experimental avant rock.

Title: Best of
Review: A classic compilation of a well-kept-secret of a band.

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: A great album, tweaked.
Some of the most evocative music of this century. [Dec 2002, p.97]

Title: The Law of Large Numbers
Review: Pollack's velvety, diction-rich voice shines on the syncopated, a cappella intro of "The Loop," and her idiosyncratic, mostly cryptic lyrics can be striking. [Apr 2010, p.104]

Title: Death By Sexy
Review: Hughes and his crew blow through the kind of drums 'n' acoustic booty jams that would make R.L. Burnside do ankle-grabs in his grave. [Jun 2006, p.188]

Title: Bright Ideas
Review: While McCaughan retains a lot of his vitality, he can't completely shake off the specter of comfortable maturity. [#11, p.116]

Title: Nick Jonas
Review: For Jonas, the new sound works well: He's sweetly confident while singing about all the adult lust that he has been suppressing in his music for years.

Title: Electric Lines
Review: The album (somewhat) finds itself towards its end, where Goddard’s sonic explorations and falsetto, paired with simple drum work, are better suited.

Title: More Light
Review: Frontman Bobby Gillespie’s lyrics still don’t sound as effortlessly cool as his breathy delivery (see Culturecide), but it feels like the band is back on the pulse of something.

Title: No Gravity
Review: Shontelle's diva vocal is pitch-perfect, but given Rihanna's bust-up with Chris Brown the domestic abuse subtext seems ill-judged at best. [Dec 2010, p.113]

Title: Wayward Fire
Review: While Wayward Fire generates most of its energy from the more aggressive electro-pop numbers, its subdued and romantic synth moments are well-crafted and catchy. [Jul 2011, p.84]

Title: Escondida
Review: Her jazz-tinged voice soars; the music manages to be both wonderfully austere and subtly strange. [Jun 2004, p.98]

Title: Standing in the Way of Control
Review: Unfortunately, the disc highlights a new hole: storytelling. [Feb 2006, p.92]

Title: We Loved Her Dearly
Review: If We Loved Her Dearly is any indication, Lowell has simply run out of material, if not ideas, musical or otherwise.

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: Twin Fantasy is not a perfect record—the latter half is bogged down by soundscape-y passages and spoken word, for one thing--but that only validates it as a powerful document of teenaged pain and longing.

Title: You're Better Than This
Review: Tthe record is a continuation of Pile as voice for a bizarre following that it simultaneously evokes and has, apparently, tangibly brought together.

Title: thank u, next
Review: At times the writing struggles to keep pace: The concepts behind songs like “needy” and “fake smile” are as relatable as they are predictable, and begin to stretch thin after a couple of minutes. Still, there is an awful lot to like.

Title: Boat
Review: Uplifting, powerful and sincere, Pip Blom deliver a rich, ocean-inspired debut that is instantly captivating. This is the opening chapter to something very exciting.

Title: The Black Swan
Review: Here and there this record finds its comfortable center. [16 Oct 2006]

Title: Sinking into a Miracle
Review: Sinking Into A Miracle is absolutely beautiful--otherworldly, often, and quietly ecstatic, in its own, strangely pop way. [Jan 2019, p.17]

Title: Time Was
Review: Time Was is a relaxed record, one that thrives on its melancholic mood. The pace is slow and methodical, but never boring.

Title: Off Off On
Review: Compositionally, Off Off On finds Stables at the top of her game to date. Pushed by Kaufman in new directions and with an ear towards experimentation in spots, the underlying tension of Stables’ music is spurred on by her lyrics.

Title: Ephyra
Review: Ephyra is an intelligent release, one that grows on its listeners far more than initial investigations would should suggest. Such things can be a double-edged sword however, and Ephyra is also a fractured record, the potential of which feels somewhat stymied by its own belligerence.

Title: Somewhere Else
Review: Somewhere Else may have the finesse of a professional with many years on the books, but it also has the languor that accompanies an amateur treading on uneven ground.

Title: Are You Serious
Review: Though the album has its moments of treaded water, the majority welcomes back the musician whose depth, curiosity, and high-brow intellect won us over in the ‘90s.

Title: Want Two
Review: It's more focused than Want One and as such packs more of wallop both musically and emotionally.

Title: Hyperspace
Review: A pristine collection that’s at once the past’s idea of the future as it is the here and now.

Title: Old Rockhounds Never Die
Review: Slightly mannered vocals; odd but good. [Sep 2018, p.96]

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: It is in the spaces between words and drums, and in the general structures of the songs... that El-P most clearly exhibits growth. And it is these points on the album that make I’ll Sleep an intriguing release.

Title: Devotion
Review: Devotion is a delicate, often gorgeous listen that flows remarkably well, though I can’t help but attribute its coherence to the utter lack of variation among its eleven songs.

Title: Let Love In
Review: This is music precision-built for vast stadiums. [Aug 2006, p.112]

Title: Devotion
Review: The songs lack the emotional pull of the duo's debut. Seeds of greatness are still evident, but this direction just seems like a dead end.

Title: Junip
Review: When the trio pulls back, they almost consistently find their sweet spot. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.93]

Title: Route One or Die
Review: Route One or Die is many things--immense, joyful, weird and above all aptly titled, as you'd be hard-pressed to find another debut album released this year --British or otherwise--that sounds so completely vibrant and alive.

Title: Utopia
Review: The Icelandic icon moves ever closer to the Platonic ideal of what it means to be Bjork. [Dec 2017, p.50]

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: Singer John Philpot's boyish sighs and teen-romance lyrics feel a little lightweight and non-committal, but the promised groove element plays dividends during the album's second half. [May 2012, p.67]

Title: Cody
Review: They’ve become better musicians, better songwriters and better at expressing life’s frustrations without jeopardizing too much of what made them so cherished in the beginning.

The music is a bright, shiny, and bland pastiche of electronic pop and faint nods to new wave and R&B. And the songwriting feels generic, a departure from the personable details that have made her a unique voice.

Title: Return of Mr. Zone 6
Review: Return of Mr. Zone 6 is Gucci's best album yet, whether you can still find better verses and hooks on the mixtapes or not.

Title: Rudebox
Review: After 16 songs ranging from electro-country to the parody-heavy We're The Pet Shop Boys and various quasi-conversational raps à la the Streets' Mike Skinner about losing his virginity, I felt the man should rope things in.

Title: Whoop Dee Doo
Review: We are treated to a collection of refreshingly care-free and up-tempo punk; well-crafted and not at all pretentious.

Title: Runaway's Diary
Review: It’s another classy notch in LaVere’s slowly growing catalog belt and shows her boundary pushing, restless artistry results in music that’s heartfelt, reflective, challenging and consistently compelling.

Title: American Interior
Review: It’s another excellent Gruff Rhys album then, tied around an unusual concept but not bogged down by it.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: Ryan Adams (the album) carries all the classic hallmarks of Ryan Adams (the musician), tightly condensed into an essential collection of polished Americana. [No. 113, p.52]

Title: Heaven To A Tortured Mind
Review: It is just one of the many avenues Bowie could have gone down, but the effect of what he has done is fascinating and wholly satisfying.

Title: Doggumentary
Review: Far from a behind-the-scenes veil-lifting, though, 'Doggumentary' largely ensures that the worst preconceptions of self-indulgent hip-hop remain in place.

Title: Run the Jewels 3
Review: This new album is the most successful of the lot--calmer but not remotely calm, more emotional but not at all tender.

Title: Cruise Your Illusion
Review: From the lean, scrappy production value to the grandiose guitar solos and Alex Coxen’s wobbling, vocal delivery a la Grant Hart, the record has the messy fingerprints of indie rock’s cherished first wave smeared all over it.

Title: Abyss
Review: However, as depressing as this might read on paper, Abyss has been constructed by Wolfe and co-writer Chisholm with meticulous care and awareness, making it not only her tightest LP to date but also much more enjoyable than its submissive melancholy has any right to be.

Title: Moment Bends
Review: The record plays like an old mixtape: a few songs you dig, a few you forget, and two or three you can't stop playing, that you can't keep from becoming part of a night the pictures can't do justice, of a packed dance-floor, of a girl you didn't kiss, of a midnight drive.

Title: Codename: Rondo
Review: If Ghostland Observatory's serious about more than modern raves, the locals need to bring in an outside producer (Austin's Wolfgang Gartner?) to help construct something fresh. Otherwise, the party's just about over.

Title: The Good Life
Review: The simple arrangements and hands-off production add to the gentle but decisive impact of The Good Life, and the result is a fine calling card for a young singer/songwriter who may not have worked out every last detail of his sound but clearly knows where he's going, and it happens to be a place worth visiting.

Title: Day & Age
Review: This is the Killers' spitball album, the one where they try everything and see what works while Flowers grasps for a relatable tone.

Title: Violence in a Quiet Mind
Review: Violence in a Quiet Mind is undeniably sad yet also affirming when considered in its entirety.

Title: Transnormal Skiperoo
Review: Finishing one of his records always leaves you feeling as if an enigmatic wanderer’s just left town. Transnormal Skiperoo, another quality addition to a too-short list of White releases, is no different.

Title: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love
Review: The fact that the album kinda sounds like so many things, very few of them usually adjacent to the genre, sits at the crux of the album's aspiration. Ordinary Corrupt Human Love is a critical reminder to card-carrying loyalists and new inductees alike of their own agency; that it's potentially revelatory, not sacrilegious, for the spectrum of black metal to include things outside of its purview.

Title: Turn On The Bright Lights
Review: Predictably claustrophobic listening.... When they come up for air, Interpol have the tunes to match all the mannered gloom. [Sep 2002, p.107]

Title: Love
Review: This is easily some of McMahon's prettiest and most accessible music, and it's also some of his finest. In its own simple, graceful way, Love adds more depth to the rest of Amen Dunes' work.

Title: Production
Review: Something of a mixed bag, "Production" teeters between grating aimlessness and uniquely dark, claustrophobically compressed runs through the Vocoder-happy lands of French house music.

Title: Life on a Rock
Review: Aside form one misguided reggae experiment, Chesney sounds right at home here.  [10 May 2013, p.67]

Title: The Muscle Shoals Recordings
Review: Their fourth album, The Muscle Shoals Recordings, is an outstanding 11-song offering that lives up to the lofty expectations of its namesake.

Title: Surrounded By Silence
Review: Prefuse 73 has defiantly asserted himself as one of the most important artists of his generation, ignoring boundaries and creating a landscape that recognizes hip-hop's original "anything goes" ethos. [Apr 2005, p.99]

Title: Welcome to the Dollhouse
Review: While DK's quest for pop domination falls short, the club-friendly Dollhouse cements their posh appeal. [May 2008, p.70]

Title: Mykki
Review: Its 13 tracks are more versatile in lyrical depth and vocal flow than before and, when added to his trademark intensity, are proof that Mykki's moved to the next level.

Title: Take Fountain
Review: As eloquent an emotional discourse as [Gedge] has mustered. [Mar 2005, p.101]

Title: Light Grenades
Review: The tearjerkers flow free on their sixth studio album. [Jan/Feb 2007, p.88]

Title: Last Night On The Planet
Review: At times Letherette overreach and their ambition to contort every trend of the last decade into a singular structure feels forced. The album flourishes where the beats are fortified by accompanying charisma.

Title: Resistance
Review: Resistance is evidence not only of the Souljazz Orchestra's abilities, but also of their audacity.

Title: Act IV: Rebirth In Reprise
Review: With some new explorations entwined, Act IV exhibits all facets of the band's alluring brand (extensive instrumentation, orchestral theatrics and experimental whimsy) in impressive form.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: It ultimately lacks cohesiveness and direction to evolve into something truly outstanding, but still remains intriguing enough to possibly earn points with the more adventurous listeners.

Title: Fragile Future
Review: Guitarist J.T. Woodruff has assumed all vocals duties, and his nasally whine is virtually indistinguishable from the hordes of similar sounding emo frontmen; that and disappointingly bland hooks make Fragile Future feel formulaic.

Title: The Carpenter
Review: They've become Auto-Tune-less pop stars, and The Carpenter will only brighten their shine.

Title: In the City
Review: The rest of Rudolf's self-produced debut is a middling rock record dressed up in sleek digital clothes.

Title: Fear Fun
Review: A striking, adept piece made accessible by Tillman's clear-as-a-bell voice, Fear Fun is the ideal companion for a weird headspace.

Title: Visions
Review: Over the course of an album even dogs will find the whistle register wearing, but taken individually these are sublime cocktails of post-geographical orientalism. [Apr 2012, p.79]

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: This isn’t just Almost Killed Me 2, it’s an exploration of what lies beyond that initial surface – and the truth ain’t pretty.

Title: Boomiverse
Review: From start to finish, Big Boi is so at ease with assured nonchalance that he blithely makes references to a mass murderer and an alleged serial rapist, and occasionally slips into some other juvenile business. Otherwise, he's in elite statesman form. He and his collaborators likewise don't seem all that concerned about the album's place in contemporary rap, and it's all the better for it.

But there's more to 3121 than the prickle of nostalgia: amid the title track's murky, unsettling groove and the grinding techno noise of Love, Prince sounds thrillingly alive, a veteran throwing down a cocky, confident challenge to any young pretenders.

Title: White Stuff
Review: Few would mistake White Stuff for golden age Royal Trux--the vocals are more subdued, the songwriting is more straightforward, and anyone looking for something as confrontational as "The Banana Question" won't find it here. But hearing Hagerty and Herrema stay true to their ethos after 30-plus years offers its own satisfactions. Consider the comeback complete.

Title: Fallen Empires
Review: The quartet are once again  playing it safe with their crowd-pleasing formula of surging riffs, queasily memorable choruses and lyrics which, like Mystic Meg horoscopes burn with portent while saying nothing. [Dec 2011, p.96]

Title: Hum
Review: Much of Hum has a brooding, measured Nick Drake-ish intensity, driven by fast, intricate folky picking. [Sep 2020, p.92]

Title: Twisted Angel
Review: Musically speaking, "Damn" is the only real memorable tune in the bunch. Which is exactly the expletive many of her old fans may express when hearing this often over-bombastic effort.

Title: I'm Bad Now
Review: Nap Eyes are mostly concise in their wanderings, but occasionally meander too far from the path.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: There's still nothing particularly radio-friendly here and plenty of weirdness to go around, but more than ever the free jazz influences and pulsating drones seem designed to serve the song and not just enhance the listener's physical sensations.

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: This follow-up work of pent-up aggression; of complete contrast to snappy pop-punk; has every chance of becoming the band's seminal work.

Title: Alone with Everybody
Review: Music that is designed to smother, to sedate, to lull the listener into a soporific state of boredom.

Title: Third
Review: Even though not every twisted move they make on Third pays dividends, considering the stakes, consciously fucking with their formula is a bold gamble for which they should be saluted.

Title: Dude, the Obscure
Review: Dude, The Obscure gets stronger as it goes, its second half filled with laments both specific (the complaint about a big-city wannabe in “NY”) and vague (the overarching malaise of “Lit By Midnight”).

Title: One of the Boys
Review: 'Mannequin' features some cleverly written lyrics, but Perry doesn't possess the grit or vocal prowess to follow through, and the title track is like No Doubt's 'Just a Girl' sans personality and conviction.

Title: Personal Record
Review: Broucek's analog approach gives each recording a warmth, and all of the separate instruments are given proper attention. Because of this and more, Personal Record is another fine entry in Eleanor Friedberger's career.

Title: Franz Ferdinand
Review: Frantic and rhythmic Scotpop with many echoes of so-'90s Blur in the sardonic jabs at middle-class bromides.

Title: Ski Mask
Review: Here, harmonies, bouncy synths and cheeky metaphors abound, and, besides a few clunky miscalculations, the record is an undeniably fun listen.

Title: Odditorium or Warlords of Mars
Review: This is their best yet.

Title: W
Review: Luckily Planningtorock, alias Janine Rostron, has delivered 'W', a masterpiece of art-pop experimentalism that gleefully expands on her debut.

Title: Le Kov
Review: Le Kov is not as cold as Y Dydd Olaf (which was based on a decades-old Welsh sci fi novel)--it’s less machinic and more organic, less 80s and more 70s. As such, it wavers a little, particularly in its second half, where the feel is a little too warmly indistinct, too hazy.

Title: Sister
Review: Sister completely one-ups the band’s debut from eight years ago.

Title: Goat Girl
Review: Earworm guitar licks and choir-like harmonies sprout unexpectedly from Goat Girl’s skeletal, unpredictable songs like wildflowers in landfill.

Title: Cruelty Without Beauty
Review: With songs full of piss and vinegar, Soft Cell's return is triumphant and toxic.

Title: Made Up Mind
Review: An all-round triumph. [Sep 2013, p.90]

Title: Compassion
Review: It is poignant and ragged with suffering, but it doesn't dwell there. It is also bright, optimistic and euphoric.

Title: We Fucked a Flame Into Being
Review: Languid piano, sleazy Rickenbacker, intellectual Lothario. Lethal. [Oct 2016, p.96]

Title: Virginia Creeper
Review: [His] gravel-like vocals envelop the album, while his well-travelled eyes ensure the lyrics are filled with knowing experience. [Mar 2004, p.109]

Title: A Written Testimony
Review: Filled with ghosts; confessions; jokes; an abundance of Jay-Z features and a prodigal son offering explanations for his disappearance and return. [May 2020, p.65]

Title: Gossamer
Review: A big moment is the ethereal R&B pastiche Constant Conversations, with Swedish a cappella trio Erato, but there are virtually no duds here.

Title: Ocean Roar
Review: Elverum has created an album that demands your time and attention, not to mention any memories you may be willing to part with.

Title: We the Best Forever
Review: It just goes to show that on a DJ Khaled album, you can't be Eddie Van Halen. You've got to be David Lee Roth.

Title: Thank You For Today
Review: It’s not that it sounds like 80s adult rock, but there’s something of artists like Bruce Hornsby and the Range here--something welcoming and accepting that feels awfully appealing.

Title: Side Effects
Review: Side Effects is largely devoid of these big bombastic moments, save the seven-minute incision "NY Money" that centres the album. Nevertheless, White Denim hurtle through the record's nine songs (as brief as many of them are) at a pace that can't help but keep the listener engaged and excited for what comes next.

Title: Rain
Review: The winsome 'Too Tough' is the best song here. Like with the rest of the album, it's a joy to deconstruct the song's craft (woah! Nice interlude!), but more of one just to listen.

Title: Mnestic Pressure
Review: Mnestic Pressure is a challenging but thoroughly stunning album that finds Gamble significantly pulling his vision more into focus than before.

Title: Welcome to JFK
Review: The specter of mortality haunts the proceedings. Despite all of this, it's a testament to Chinx's still-growing pop smarts that Welcome to JFK is sometimes a lot of fun.

Title: Drastic Fantastic
Review: Tunstall crushes the sophomore jinx under the stilleto heels of the white boots she wears on the album cover, delivering a confident and assured set that's fuller and a touch more electric than its predecessor.

Title: Maserati VII
Review: VII pursues no radical new directions for Maserati, but even though you sort of already know these songs, they still have enough engaging motion and kinetic force that if you ever loved them in the first place, you'll love them all over again here.

Title: Hell-On
Review: On Hell-On, Case once again spins the roulette with a treasury of surprises, stimulating lessons that are complex, thoughtful and articulate.

Title: Kasabian
Review: Kasabian's paranoid mindset is so in tune with the zeitgeist you almost imagine singer Tom Meighan has a sell-by date stamped on the arse of his corduroy strides. [4 Sep 2004, p.71]

Title: The Best of Gloucester County
Review: While he's always seemed comfortable in his own skin, Smith comes off as particularly self-assured here. [Feb 2011, p.63]

Title: European Heartbreak
Review: While it does contain a few songs that could be split off and saved, it mainly goes to show that she makes for a better melancholy dream pop artist than a singer/songwriter with her toes dipped in Americana and soft soul.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: Sounding like nothing else out there, distinct even from Tribe's previous work, We Got It From Here is political without being preachy, fun without being unintelligent and next level out while being street corner down. A superb swansong. [Jan 2017, p.71]

Title: Planet Earth
Review: Somehow these songs don't beg for a repeat listen.

Title: Young as the Morning Old as the Sea
Review: Ultimately, with Young as the Morning Old as the Sea, Passenger has crafted an album that, not unlike the oceans, fields, roads, and relationships that inspired it, remains with you, calling you to return.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: None of it adds much to Moore's legacy as a guitar innovator and post-punk aesthete, but you leave the record feeling as sweaty and beat as you would hauling a couch up to a sixth-floor walk-up.

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: These tracks are rescued by gorgeous chords and melodies, which give otherwise grey arrangements rich shades of melancholy and optimism. Avery had a knack for a hook back in the days of Drone Logic, too. His attitude to the dance floor might have changed, but the important stuff hasn't.

Title: Where The Action Is
Review: A little unwieldy in places, but still pleasingly timeless. [Jul 2019, p.85]

Title: Elysium
Review: Elysium is woefully short on what Tennant and Lowe do best, which is disarmingly sharp pop songs that stick in your head but also leave you thinking afterward. There are some good ideas at play here, for sure, but neither the music nor the lyrics do them justice.

Title: Who Needs Who
Review: A relationship breakdown between the band's two founders, singer Nona Marie Invie and producer Marshall LaCount, is laid bare, but with dramatic and beautiful consequences.

Title: Old Ramon
Review: Across Old Ramon's sprawling 70-minute set, Kozelek is still a master of his sly charade, disguising sprawling webs of complex guitar chords and considered narratives as humble, simple acoustic ditties.

Title: Scenery
Review: An album’s gotta end sometime, but these songs, two of the record’s most propulsive, seem to grab us by the arm to yank us into the shimmering neon starlight--and then it’s all over. If it’s good enough, the audience will linger through the credits. King could let it linger a little more.

Title: Runner
Review: It is great to hear them testing out other feels without losing an ounce of the consistency that has made them to toast of Chicago for all these years.

Title: One Bedroom
Review: Predictable. [#57, p.105]

Title: Raditude
Review: Driving yet jaunty guitars abound and backing chants fill the required spaces, yet it all comes across too much like a sub-par parody of their former selves.

Title: Ignorance is Bliss
Review: The chief pleasure of this album is how much it allows Skepta to be Skepta: an MC who always looks, waits, then darts between the traffic of his beats. This sensual pleasure goes beyond lyrics and into pure music, and should sustain his career long past his recent triumphant homecoming.

Title: If Only There Was a River
Review: It is a tease, an intriguing suggestion of possible next steps in the motion of one of this year’s most promising new singer-songwriters.

Title: July Flame
Review: It turns out Veirs hasn't actually abandoned instrumentations, she's just trying out a new kind. And what she ends up with is her best, most sophisticated record to date. [Holiday 2009, p.93]

Title: Crack-Up
Review: Crack-Up is perhaps Fleet Foxes' most epic and inventive record yet.

Title: Gandadiko
Review: Dark, minatory rhythms underpin stark lyrics telling of hard times in the north of Mali. [May 2015, p.95]

Title: Those the Brokes
Review: This sophomore set likewise has moments of indelible pop bliss, but too often veers off track with unnecessarily long songs and dull arrangements.

Title: Deep in the Iris
Review: The pill is somewhat sweetened by Braids' glossy new sound, a feelgood revamp that pairs swooning electronics with upfront drum'n'bass and will do some damage at large outdoor events. [Jun 2015, p.72]

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: His effort to overcome the body-brain gulf is more apparent than ever throughout No Shape follow-up Set My Heart on Fire Immediately, on which Hadreas loses control of not just his body, but his heart. As ever, his voice and music contort and warp in tandem with his anatomy.

Title: I Am... Sasha Fierce
Review: Beyonce still proves that she's an all-around good performer even though her attempt to branch out into an alter ego fails a little.

Title: Mansion Songs
Review: Overall the feel is sparse and desolate. [Jun 2015, p.89]

Title: Keep Me Singing
Review: Morrison delivers each of these songs with attentiveness; the material is consistently presented with finesse. Nothing further is required.

Title: Chatma
Review: This is the desert-blues album for fans of Can and Pink Floyd to sink their teeth into.  [Nov 2013, p.91]

Title: Gift Of Screws
Review: Gift proves that Lindsey Buckingham’s knack for writing catchy pop-rock chord changes is alive and well.

Title: Pure Comedy
Review: An absorbing, intermittently amusing album.

Title: Standards
Review: There’s a confidence and flexibility to his disparate themes.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Belong
Review: Its sound is now massive enough to match its big-hearted emotion.

Title: It's Never Been Like That
Review: All that's standing in the way of a major breakthrough is a certain facelessness, exacerbated by Mars's reticent style.

Title: The Stage Names
Review: The nearly impossible thematic scope attempted and deftly handled here is a tribute to Will Sheff's dexterity and range as a songwriter (if not a vocalist), and the band's chops for being able to keep pace.

Title: Finally Rich
Review: It's distressing, elementary and samey yet utterly unignorable.

Title: Epic
Review: Boasting a mere seven songs, Brooklyn-based singer/songwriter Sharon Van Etten's sophomore effort hardly lives up to the lofty promise of its name, but where Epic fails to deliver in size, it more than makes up for in sound.

Title: Rise
Review: Rise shows where the band’s three stars’ personalities unite in a Venn diagram and work together well. It’s just that these Vampires sound best when they’re sharing the same blood source.

Title: Ready
Review: What’s maddening and frustrating is that Trey has put out enough great material this year to make a truly brilliant album.

Title: Isles
Review: Without their smart lyrics and complex instrumentation, listeners would feel like they're listening to the same song again and again.

Title: Ancient Melodies of the Future
Review: Ancient Melodies of the Future sounds more like "vaguely familiar melodies of the past," but so do some of the best albums in rock.

Title: Siberia
Review: Sadly, Siberia is lacking any genuine spark.

Title: Mothertongue
Review: These three suites get under your skin in a good way, none more so than the final track, a haunting gothic tale of sororicide sung by fellow Vermonter Sam Amidon.

Title: Peace Is the Mission
Review: The best cuts here happen to be those hewing closer to Major Lazer's wake-and-bake dancehall origins. [No. 121, p.57]

Title: (II)
Review: It took me a few listens to accept the trance synth riffs that dominate, not to mention Alice Glass's increasingly melodic screeching, but the apocalyptic undertones are surprisingly effective with some sugar on top.

Title: Do You Know
Review: The pleasant surprise here is that she's co-written several songs that do indeed probe beneath the cover-girl, tabloid-ready surface of her life.

Title: Milk Famous
Review: Their third album deepens the rockist intentions with a track called "Heavy Metal" and a sound that's like Spoon or Fountains of Wayne dipped in distracted keyboard/noise-guitar ooze.

Title: The Search
Review: With everything it has going for it, it should be a lot better than it is.

Title: Fortune
Review: There's an open-minded exploratory edge to everything here, as if Black Prairie were delighted to discover that genres are really just in the mind of the beholder.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: They've still got a way with grand, sweeping crescendos and haven't forgotten that the build is as important as the payoff.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: A Ghost Is Born is a textbook example of an album created to fulfill expectations the band doesn't necessarily share.

Title: Endless Wire
Review: The album is inconsistent -- sometimes impenetrable, sometimes enlightening -- but always engaged.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: With Lost In The Dream and his band The War On Drugs, Adam Granduciel has made an incredibly strong case that his heroes should now be considered his peers.

Title: Interiors
Review: At it's best Interiors is alien and magical.... thought, it can also slip into a rather inaccessible coolness too. [Nov 2013, p.107]

Title: Dreamless
Review: While this doesn’t mark a new beginning for the band, it nevertheless represents a step down a different path that they’ll hopefully continue to follow.

Title: We are Beautiful, We Are Doomed
Review: Los Campesinos! continue to compose intelligent, well thought out songs, endearingly so, and eschew any trends other than the one they're setting for themselves.

Title: ArtScience
Review: Glasper has signaled an impatience with jazz on earlier Experiment ventures, but very definitely not on this one.

Title: Fossils
Review: Fossils is not only an auspicious debut, but one that lives up to, and at times even exceeds, the promise of its potential.

Title: Guesswork
Review: There’s a literary elegance to Cole’s compositions rare in the pop field—the late great Warren Zevon was one of the few contemporary songwriters who shared that quality—and these arrangements mirror that nuanced formality.

Title: The Futureheads
Review: This band is so exciting it’s almost unbearable.

Title: Master and Everyone
Review: A good album that finds Oldham retreating from the layered solemnity of his most recent releases in favor of a mood that is as intimate and delicate as it is bittersweet and biting.

Title: Let It Reign
Review: et It Reign's appealing mix of nostalgia and vitality proves that Barât can not just survive, but thrive outside of the confines of his other, storied band.
