Review: If Famous Monsters was a step back for the Misfits legacy, this is a bigger step in the wrong direction.

Title: The Black Album
Review: This is Jay-Z's suicide note and his glowing eulogy rolled into one. [Jan 2004, p.106]

Title: Smile
Review: A cover of 'Flower Sun Rain' by '70s Japanese supergroup Pyg sounds like the Super Furries, while a 16-mkinute doom jam with SunO)))'s Stephen O'Malley is as titanic as you'd hope. [May 2008, p.91]

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light I
Review: While Carlson and company continue to explore new influences (much has been made over the band's recent declaration of affection for Pentangle and Fairport Convention), Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light 1 sounds to me like a different manifestation of the same sound they've been exploring for some time now.

Title: Ether Teeth
Review: In keeping it complex, shy and out of the ordinary, Broder has accomplished a composition of delicate and post-modern-day-genius proportions.

Artist: And So I Watch You From Afar
Title: All Hail Bright Futures
Review: All in all, it's interesting but frustrating in equal measures, however it is sure to please fans who know what they're in for.

Title: Purple
Review: Baroness have delivered their masterpiece: an album grounding their cosmic heaviosity with earthbound, compelling drama. [Jan 2016, p.88]

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: The Echo of Pleasure
Review: Whether it's their brutal attempt at gloomy chamber pop on 'My Only', their embarrassingly direct ripoff of a My Bloody Valentine track on 'Anymore', or their goofy, oddly timed guitar licks on 'The Garret', The Echo of Pleasure results in being an incredibly vague arena rock statement, one that's hopelessly gasping for life (and critical acclaim). As Berman's vocals have clearly aged, so have his songwriting abilities.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: With his new album, Shifty Adventures In Nookie Wood, Cale is once again juggling gut-punches and brain-freezes.

Title: Harmonicraft
Review: The sense of brightness that was present (but kept at a reasonable distance) in the pretty good debut and the pretty excellent Meanderthal is amplified here, and many (most?) songs on Harmonicraft could fit comfortably into a more conventional arena setting than the ones from their murkier beginnings.

Title: The Divine Feminine
Review: Mac Miller isn’t a good rapper, and he definitely can’t carry a note, though he tries to do that a lot on this one. However, he has a vision of what he wanted this album to sound like and then carried it through with all the right producers and features, which is a talent in and of itself.

Title: California Son
Review: Versions of Jon i Mitchell's Don't Interrupt The Sorrow and Bob Dylan's Only A Pawn In Their Game are surprisingly persuasive. Elsewhere, it's like being imprisoned in the teenage Moz bedroom/brain. [Jun 2019, p.89]

Title: Blank Project
Review: Most songs are unfettered, with demo-quality mixes, a bare minimum of instrumentation, and over-exposed live drumming. Split between improvisatory and electronically assisted, the album's 10 songs navigate a raw zone.

Title: What We Lose in the Fire We Gain in the Flood
Review: Soulful debut from Omaha's answer to Duffy. [July 2010, p. 136]

Title: Out Her Space
Review: Out Her Space is Introducing’s twisted older sibling. Though some may be perturbed by the departure from Introducing’s Nashville direction, those open to Blau’s versatility as a composer and songwriter will find much aural stimulation in the united multiplicity of his works.

Title: The Noise Made By People
Review: Harkens back to the European pop of the '50s and '60s.

Title: Imperium
Review: Reaching even farther back to the jangling, surf-tinged guitar work of the ’50s and ’60s as inspiration, the three-piece has created yet another charmingly melodic record.

Title: Transangelic Exodus
Review: Transangelic Exodus is a scrappy yet poignant rock & roll narrative of inner conflict and acceptance; its songs are a confessional and confrontational commentary on a historic period when so much is possible, even as fear, hate, and paranoia still hold the reins of power. Its energy, vulnerability, rage, and crafty poetics are awe-inspiring.

Title: Tangier Sessions
Review: At a time when guitars serve more often as props than as centerpieces, this album is a wondrous reminder that the simplest palette can be used to paint the most profound results.

Title: Novelist Guy
Review: What’s exceptional about Novelist Guy is the ease with which he remakes grime in his own image, gifting it a breadth and charm and appeal others have struggled for over a decade to synthesize. [Jun 2018, p.62]

Title: Twerp Verse
Review: It’s their strongest album to date, and while Speedy Ortiz are probably never going to make that giant leap into the mainstream--they’ll always be a bit too abrasive and lo-fi for mass acceptance--Twerp Verse is the sound of a band standing on the verge of great things.

Title: drukQs
Review: The best work of his inventively mad career.

Title: Keep Calm and Carry On
Review: Keep Calm...is a perfectly good album, but it strives for nothing more.  [Dec 2009, p. 90]

Title: Emily Alone
Review: The resulting Emily Alone is a devastating, unapologetically vulnerable set of 12 ruminative guitar and keyboard songs, one of which is entirely spoken ("Still").

Title: GINGER
Review: Each of their albums experiment with genre, but GINGER is all over the place, never really sure what it wants to be. But moving forward, it seems pretty clear the group from that “BOOGIE” performance is a thing of the past, for better or for worse, and they’re attempting to evolve into something else. It’s just unclear if becoming the boy band of their dreams is the best use of their talents.

Title: Head Down
Review: A powerhouse of big riffed rock 'n' roll drenched in '70s sunshine. [Sep 2012, p.110]

Title: Terms of My Surrender
Review: The result is a warm, generally introspective but far from musty set that revels in predominantly acoustic material sung with Hiatt’s increasingly gruff, whiskeyed voice.

Title: Translated from Love
Review: The result is an unusual and likeable mix of country rock, rockabilly and excellent ballads. [Nov 2007, p.102]

Title: Pushin' Against a Stone
Review: “Organic moonshine music” she calls it, and no one could argue with that.

Title: What Now
Review: Sylvan Esso fans will fall deeper in love with the duo on this second album, while its casual onlookers won't be able to unlock their gaze. [Apr-Jun 2017, p.86]

Title: So This Is Goodbye
Review: While This is Goodbye does suffer, like Last Exit, from being a little too consistent (there’s very little variation in tempo or arrangement, or theme for that matter), it's as cohesive a listening experience as almost any album I’ve heard this year.

Title: Don't Be a Stranger
Review: Thankfully, more often than not Eitzel is on great form. [Nov 2012, p.82]

Title: Master and Everyone
Review: It is perhaps Oldham’s best work yet, and somewhat ironically, his most accessible as well.

Title: Back to Basics
Review: A truly soulful pop album, at least for one disc, Back to Basics is one of 2006’s best when Linda Perry’s fingerprints aren’t present.

Title: Tomorrow Forever
Review: All of these sounds may not surprise, but they're comforting in their familiarity, particularly because Sweet's execution as a writer and producer remains precise.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Amid all the beaming newness of Radical Connector is something familiar and unsettling. [Sep 2004, p.116]

Title: Babel
Review: The London quartet's hallmarks--plucky banjo, hard-driving acoustic guitar--are in place, but the songs are bigger and bolder, right down to Marcus Mumford's exuberant wails that now grind with more grit.

Title: Revelations
Review: The countertenor sings with an emotional, otherworldly raw power, whether he is conducting an imaginary conversation with an industry exec who dumped him (Games) or beautifully musing on coping with stress and pressure (Cloudy).

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: It's good to hear these hip-shaking hipsters cutting loose with such abandon. [22 Sep 2006, p.95]

Title: Phantom Radio
Review: It's more a big tent revival for existentialists than anything else. [Dec 2014, p.66]

Title: Build a Nation
Review: It's surprisingly decent. [Jul 2007, p.174]

Title: Digital Ash in a Digital Urn
Review: A painfully honest, emotionally draining album. [22 Jan 2005, p.49]

Title: Hitch
Review: While Hitch may kick off poorly, it more than makes up for it by back-ending the tracklist with some of the band's best work.

Title: Local Honey
Review: Another powerful record from one of the most profound talents of this generation of us born in the '80s and '90s.

Title: Wolfroy Goes to Town
Review: The entire thing is an absolute, unerring joy.

Title: Dirt Farmer
Review: The Band's Levon Helm turns in a modestly charming album of 13 cover songs. [30 Nov 2007, p.131]

Title: Golden Suits
Review: This'll be one to cozy up with come autumn. [Aug-Sep 2013, p.102]

Title: La Costa Perdida
Review: Fortunately, the band that helped establish the early indie ethos remains as odd and unrepentant as ever.

Title: Astronomy for Dogs
Review: Astronomy sometimes sounds like a British invasion LP given the remaster and remix treatment: dance-ready, fit for a plush couch and extra-plush headspace, and oddly misfiled in time.

Title: Business Casual
Review: The Montreal duo of P-Thugg and Dave 1 write hypnotic, theatrical disco beats reminiscent of Miami's late-'70s/early-'80s blow scene.

Title: Life Journey
Review: Some of the songs here are better than others (even with more than four decades of hanging out with everyone from Willie Nelson to Keith Richards, there is only so much cred you can breathe into a Paul Anka song), but there is hardly any track here that hasn’t earned the right to stay.

Title: Moms
Review: While Moms never reaches the earwormy heights that it leads off with, there's still a bunch of choice moments [throughout the album]. [No.91 p. 56]

Title: Harmonicraft
Review: All of this comes together to form a cohesive collection that flows effortlessly; without a doubt, it's one of the strongest guitar-rock records 2012 will yield. [May 2012, p.83]

Title: Elvis Perkins in Dearland
Review: Much like his 2007 debut, "Ash Wednesday," Perkins speaks through characters and, more importantly, though his musical arrangements to present a nuanced approach to musing on mortality and loss and loneliness.

Title: Heart of My Own
Review: Expertly and diversely arranged, the songs of Heart of My Own build and hover, often in surprising ways.

Title: Love at the Bottom of the Sea
Review: These 15 song-puzzles in 34:20 are sophisticated amusements all, although often the amusement is attenuated and one I get bored with before half its 2:38 is over.

Title: The Kingdom
Review: Ultimately, Bush devotees who lived through the alt.rock ‘90s will find much to love about The Kingdom. But it is also an album delivered with Rossdale’s customary style and panache, not to mention tunes that sit elegantly alongside the likes of Everything Zen and Swallowed.

Title: Country Music
Review: Willie didn't need yet another covers album to remind us of his transformative powers, but it's reassuring he still calls Country home.

Title: The Eminem Show
Review: He often riffs for too long, so by the time he's singing to his daughter on "Hailie's Song," you feel the album's nearly 80-minute length.

Title: Dirty Dancing
Review: While it's tempting to write it off as but one more retro paste-up, Swayzak's uncanny sense of texture, timbre, and space justifies an approach that otherwise seems like a drift toward Alzheimer's.

Title: Making Mirrors
Review: The lustrous "In Your Light" alone should see his name on billboards. [Mar 2012, p.87]

Title: The Deserters
Review: Unfortunately, the “To Here Knows When” cover is one of only three peaks in an otherwise unremarkable selection of songs.

Title: Everything Ecstatic
Review: Hebden has recalibrated his sound to something darker and more rhythmic, without losing a note of melody. [21 May 2005, p.66]

Title: All the Things That I Did and All the Things That I Didn't Do
Review: All The Things That I Did… takes a little time to truly unfurl, but over time it opens out into a wonderful, if occasionally heartbreaking gem.

Title: Lady From Shanghai
Review: They are super-tight and competent, but with an undercurrent of madness and chaos, a well-oiled machine that is infinitely more interesting because it might blow up at any time.

Title: The Hunter
Review: The Hunter, their finest album yet, is proof enough.

Title: Interpol
Review: Intentional or not, some of that transition seeps into the music, giving songs room to ramble but nothing resembling a core.

Title: Be OK
Review: A nice teaser to satiate fans between proper full-lengths.

Title: Picaresque
Review: It’s amazing to see how the Decemberists have grown. The songs from their first EP, 5 Songs, seem like a man and an acoustic guitar, where Picaresque feels like a full blown orchestra.

Title: By Default
Review: Aided by Pixies producer Gil Norton, they've audibly thrown everything at By Default.  [#361, p.107]

Title: The Miraculous
Review: Ceremony may have easily conquered the sophomore slump, but The Miraculous is the moment where von Hausswolff truly arrives as an artist.

Title: Gimmie Trouble
Review: Samey and inaccessible in parts. [5 Nov 2005, p.43]

Title: Parastrophics
Review: There are stretches, most notable the middle third, where the impulse to experiment obscures the user-friendliness, but nitpicking like this detracts from what we really should be acknowledging.

Title: Blood Rushing
Review: Under the deft guidance of Alabama Shakes producer Andrija Tokic, even her tendency to outbreaks of over-shrill soprano trilling sounds strangely compelling. [Oct 2012, p.79]

Title: Roll With the Punches
Review: His third album in as many years, while not among his most consequential, proves that, at 71, Morrison can still perform with gusto. [Nov 2017, p.98]

Title: Divers
Review: Divers steps outside of itself. Its lyrics are obscure, and its melodies are more variable and complicated than those of the “overstuffed gorge” some saw in 2010’s Have One On Me. At particular moments, though, it is plainspoken and personal.

Title: Candylion
Review: Ultimately, Candylion is more annoying than entertaining.

Title: Live Music
Review: A warm twangy sound, evocative of Southern, sun-paralysed afternoons. [Dec 2011, p. 100]

Title: Centipede Hz
Review: There's a higher percent of anxiety and queasiness mixed in amid the moments of pop bliss, and though fans of the glassy perfection of MPP may be initially disappointed, Centipede Hz sounds like another logical step in the band's evolution.

Title: Black Radio
Review: It's when the rappers stand down that it hits its stride. [Jun 2012, p.108]

Title: FFS
Review: For all of FFS’ deriding of being among others, the album as a whole makes a solid case for the beauty of the perfect combination.

Title: Shamir
Review: Shamir’s music makes the listener want to wake up. Listening to it is like being shaken awake, blinds thrown open. And it’s not like learning that anything sad or dull or particular was a dream all along.

Title: Wicked Nature
Review: Whether the record would have benefited from the band focusing more on fewer tracks is debatable, but Wicked Nature is in many ways a miniature triumph for an outfit written off by many as has-beens.

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: 69 elegant observations by a pop master.

Title: The Way and Color
Review: There’s good reason to think that some of the more middling fare on The Way and Color is no more than growing pains.

Title: Change
Review: Wilson, now 60, reveals a flair for conjuring up moods on songs that suggest the languorous drift from winding down to sleeping in. [Jan 2018, p.29]

Title: Band of Joy
Review: Co-produced by Plant and critically revered singer-songwriter-guitarist Buddy Miller, Joy is a mostly covers grab bag stitched together by Plant's sweetly urgent croon and finely crafted layers of sepia-toned instrumentation and vocals.

Title: Make Way for Love
Review: Make Way for Love is the soundtrack to a longing gaze across a mostly empty, darkly lit bar in which two lonely strangers find someone to spend the night with. It's a meditation on love--and perhaps, at times, simply on companionship.

Title: Tracer
Review: One of the most consistent EDM albums of the year, Tracer refuses to simply alternate between disco and electronica; it blends the two, and should prompt enough repeat listens to confirm Weiss and Takahashi's place alongside the pioneers they've collaborated with.

Title: Get Guilty
Review: Get Guilty is a stirring set of memorable power-pop, given a personal spin via Newman's habit of delivering hard-to-parse pronouncements, like some kind of mad-eyed, curiously convincing soothsayer.

Title: Let's Bottle Bohemia
Review: There's some startling songwriting on Let's Bottle Bohemia. [Oct 2004, p.104]

Title: Director's Cut
Review: An unusual and unexpected triumph. [Jun 2011, p.44]

Title: New Energy
Review: With Four Tet’s ninth album, New Energy, Hebden does something unexpected: He revisits previous sounds. There’s the low-key warmth of 2003’s Rounds, the free jazz at the heart of 2005’s Everything Ecstatic, the friendly thump of 2012’s Pink, the sprawl of 2015’s Morning/Evening. Downtempo nodders, beatless passages that flow into big bangers—he synthesizes all this into his most accessible listen since There is Love in You.

Title: Transference
Review: What we have here is a great album, un- or under-appreciated....What Transference does is it opens a space for this band to experiment within again.

Title: C'mon
Review: C'mon doesn't break much new ground for Low in the way that their last two records did, and that's clearly not the goal here.

Title: The Hunger for More
Review: Banks... raps each verse as if his entire career depends on it. [5 Aug 2004, p.113]

Title: Too
Review: Too is their leap into self-awareness and cheeky embrace. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.62]

Title: The Diet
Review: It's pretty weird. Not necessarily any weirder than your average Lambchop record, although it is, for the most part, considerably less gorgeous. [No. 124, p.57]

Title: There's No 666 in Outer Space
Review: Great musicianship does not a great album make, particularly when the singer is so out of his league.

Title: Gossamer
Review: This wet blanket is a sheer bore. [No.89, p.57]

Title: Be
Review: "Be" is certainly a triumph, but if it isn't quite the all-time classic Common was hoping for, that's because it sounds a bit too straightforward. [25 May 2005]

Title: Hell Hath No Fury
Review: Fury is a twelve step sequence of poisonous, caustic, and lithe rap.

Title: The Afterlife
Review: A work very much bigger than the sum of its parts. [Feb 2020, p.108]

Title: Comicopera
Review: Comicopera, his 12th solo record since 1970, has indulgences and longueurs, as all his records do. But it also has some burstingly beautiful songwriting.

Title: Ease My Mind
Review: The album drifts by comfortably and could benefit from a few surprises, both tonally and musically. However, there are definite standout moments, such as “Oh Oh” and the bouncy “Angel”.

Title: B7
Review: B7 is meticulous in its references to pop and R&B history, of which Brandy's own career is such an important facet.

Title: Burials
Review: "17 Crimes" and "Greater Than 84" survive with the band's flair for camp still intact. Others drown in pools of eyeliner.

Title: LEGACY! LEGACY!
Review: Like The Social Experiment project, as well as her last record, Legacy! Legacy! is about community, about legacies as heritage but also as that which is forged on the ground in the moment. Woods is a teacher and organizer, so it’s not surprising she encourages her guests to shine.

Title: Cheatahs
Review: An uber-melodious debut.[Mar 2014, p.96]

Title: Oh Fortune
Review: For this particular moment, though, Oh Fortune reveals that Mangan is still a lightweight.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: The only thing that keeps Oddfellows from being a thoroughly stellar album are the seemingly requisite filler tracks that simply do not last in your memory no matter how many times you listen to them.

Title: Theory of Colours
Review: An album that is stacked full of mind-transporting moments, rendered by carefully selected, produced and deployed analogue elements. It’s a lot to pack into 40 minutes, but it ensures that Theory Of Colours is not only a noteworthy debut album, but a statement of beautiful, fascinating intent from Dauwd.

Title: Edge of the Sun
Review: The ideas are fleshed out so well sometimes, and it's upsetting that I have to wait until 'City' to once again get to a place where the records conciseness is shared with its depth.

Title: Watching Movies with the Sound Off
Review: These sounds are heavier and Miller flows naturally in this element.

Title: Pearl Jam
Review: Pearl Jam is fully, comprehensively re-energized.

Title: Meadow
Review: Buckner's singular pipes and surrealistic lyrics tug the songs toward the esoteric, but the band pulls them back. [Oct 2006, p.95]

Title: Elixer
Review: Her ten tracks are disposable, and redeemed only by Prince’s extraordinary production ear.

Title: Nothing is Precious Enough for Us
Review: Nothing Is Precious Enough For Us sustains the antebellum lilt and spare arrangements of the first album. [Summer 2008, p.105]

Title: Knock Knock
Review: When the album comes to a close--with pulsing bass and swirling vocal layers slowly fading out--it feels like the end of some strange Odyssean journey, one that you may want to embark on again before long.

Title: The Prettiest Curse
Review: There may be some subtle shifts here and there, but overall, The Prettiest Curse revels in the simple pleasures of big hooks, chunky chord changes, and sing-a-long melodies.

Title: Petals Have Fallen
Review: Production-wise it tips a brim to the jazzy psych of the Brainfeeder crew, with some very gnarly riffs chopping through the boom-bap. [Feb 2015, p.77]

Title: Here and Nowhere Else
Review: Call it sustainable punk--the kind that doesn't need to burn out or fade away.

Title: Write About Love
Review: Playful yet touching at (almost) every turn, Write About Love may not shake any musical foundations but it certainly proves that Belle and Sebastian still can't be pigeon-holed.

Title: 8 Diagrams
Review: If as much heart and group energy went into the rest of the tracks, Diagrams might have been the electrifying re-entrance of the Wu-Tang Clan that fans were hoping for instead of just the minor miracle it is.

Title: Now What
Review: Despite hitmaker Linda Perry co-writing half of the album's original tracks, something is missing.

Title: Eton Alive
Review: As ever, Sleaford Mods are a voice that must be heard.

Title: No Line on the Horizon
Review: The album's ballyhooed experimentation is either terribly misguided or hidden underneath a wash of shameless U2-isms.

Title: Remedy
Review: Remedy is a mostly pleasant, forgettable dose of Americana.

Title: AM
Review: AM feels a considerably more self-assured album: heavy in a dramatic and confident way, conceptually strong and not without groove. [Oct 2013, p.73]

Title: Has Been
Review: 'Has Been' is just about as far as you could possibly get from your regular solo offering and as such arrives as one of the year's most strangely captivating albums.

Title: Yoyogi Park
Review: There are certainly moments of huge elegance and even dancefloor nirvana here, but the rigidity seems to stifle some of the magic in comparison to the album’s predecessor.

Title: Try Me
Review: Although most tracks on Try Me are taut and concise, they’re built around churning, sprawling riffs that feel far larger than the songs that contain them.

Title: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground
Review: [Oberst] infuses his figurative laments with a melancholy earnestness, communicating a more gut-wrenching breed of angst than the Limp Bizkits and Eminems of the world could ever hope to.

Title: I Am Very Far
Review: While the rich palette and varied arrangements are welcome, they also put load-bearing pressure on Mr. Sheff's songs, which feel intended more for evasive maneuvers.

Title: An Object
Review: It's moodier and murkier than No Age albums past, but no less galvanizing.

Title: Beauty & Ruin
Review: Beauty & Ruin--a lean, 12 songs in 37 minutes--finds Mould still monkeying with the formula. [Jul 2014, p.90]

Title: Matador
Review: It’s a solid, sturdy listen, with flourishes of electronics that bring sparkle, but much less of the pop sheen that was evident on Here Come The Bombs.

Title: The Suburbs
Review: It's profoundly self-serious, expertly workmanlike, occasionally transcendent, but lacking that childlike volatility, that glorious willingness to look and sound ridiculous. It's rare that so much nonetheless leaves you wanting more.

Title: another eternity
Review: The album is good, which is a component never worth underscoring. But it could be much more than that.

Title: Lux Prima
Review: Lux Prima certainly isn't Karen O's most urgent or explosive work, but it all sounds exceptionally lovely.

Title: Peaceful, the World Lays Me Down
Review: Their foppish indieboy spin on classic folk-rock is, more often than not, perfectly listenable. But you can't help but wonder, between all the gleeful strums and wizened howls, whether they possess the inner torment to carry off such worldly material.

Title: American Head
Review: If we force ourselves inside American Head, we find it full of intimate details that eschew social distancing. Breathe it in. [Sep 2020, p.86]

Title: For True
Review: Despite this motley bunch, the album's sound hasn't become a random genre gumbo.

Title: Trouble in Dreams
Review: He backs up all the contrived drama with the kind of gorgeously lush music critics dream about. [Winter 20008, p.81]

Title: Violence
Review: While the shift to a kinder and gentler sound doesn't live up to the spectacular music of past efforts, you can't fault the band for trying something new to broaden their appeal. And even with a few shortcomings, Violence still has enough alluring music to make it a worthwhile endeavor.

Title: Closer to the Bone
Review: Kristofferson has dedicated some of his finest work to family and friends and it's those songs that stand out on Closer To The Bone. [Fall 2009, p.75]

Title: Two Fingers
Review: Sway, however, doesn't command proceedings quite like Chuck D and the prosaic narratives of tracks like 'That Girl' are no substitute for verbal fireworks. Nearly though. [May 2009, p.101]

Title: Songs
Review: A confident, more expansive--emotionally and musically--annexe to his impressive, soul-baring debut. [Dec 2014, p.75]

Title: Outside Closer
Review: A modish conflation of acoustic guitars, violins, subtle electronics and artfully detached vocals, located somewhere near Amnesiac-era Radiohead. [Feb 2005, p.104]

Title: Goodbye Terrible Youth
Review: There’s a great and clear leap forward this time around, but this still has all the cornerstones of what drove so much attention: the ability to lull listeners through power pop or be taken in dreamlike trances, lyrics that take you on new journeys with every listen.

Title: Art Angels
Review: The first half of the album follows one knockout punch with another, with guitar-centric melodies underpinned by glitchy electronics that have more in common with 1980s post-punk and early industrial music than they do the pop mainstream.

Title: Signs
Review: An LP as disciplined as it is versatile.

Title: Oddfellows
Review: This may be a flashback to the sound of a decade prior, but after getting so far away from their metal roots, most fans will agree that this balance of creepy ambience and pummeling riffs is a welcome return to form.

Title: Smother
Review: It's hard to argue with the result anyway: Its slow build and aching vocals stand out as a purposeful moment of perfection on a record chock full of them.

Title: Bad as Me
Review: Co-written and produced by his missus Kathleen Brennan, Waits' songs--Bad as Me included--find their center immediately and stick like a record's skip.

Title: Overpowered
Review: She's melded the two sides of her history much more seamlessly; four-to-the-floor pop belters mix with touches of electronic and lyrical darkness to make one of the pop albums of the year.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: It’s a gorgeous, unreal place that Mount Kimbie evokes on Love What Survives, but dissonance leaks in through the crevices.

Title: Radioactive
Review: The self-proclaimed "White trash heartthrob" kicks off his show with a display of lyricism and content that aligns very closely with Yelawolf has always been about - sincerity, family, community and of course Chevrolet Caprice Classics.

Title: The Slideshow Effect
Review: The shift in styles more readily exposes the band's strengths and weaknesses.

Title: Trampin'
Review: This is a brooding, thoughtful work, a band stripped bare, naked music and raw emotion, beautifully sung and played with the command of a band that knows less is more is the key to great rock'n'roll.

Title: No Witch
Review: Though the sound may be different, The Cave Singers stay within themselves to make their best record to date.

Title: Big Red Machine
Review: More a headphones-type album than a radio-friendly one, what emerges are still songs before compositions or productions, though they may appeal to the more explorative indie rockers.

Title: Hip Mobility

Title: This Old Road
Review: For a studio album it sounds remarkably like a live one. [Mar 2006, p.90]

Title: Fuckbook
Review: Fuckbook is a fantastic, energy-fuelled riot of an album and--if you wish to view it as such--yet another brilliant addition to the embarrassment of riches that is the collected works of Yo La Tengo.

Title: After Hours
Review: After Hours certainly has its share of pity-partying. But there’s also a vulnerability that goes beyond the usual too-beautiful-for-the-world sulking. ... After Hours is one of the smoothest cocoons he’s spun.

Title: Stubborn Persistent Illusions
Review: This is an utterly triumphant, uplifting album.

Title: The Great Destroyer

Review: Ultimate Care II is still an engaging listen. Curiosity alone should be able to carry you through the first half of the track. It’s only towards the end when some honest-to-goodness notes are conjured out of the mix, announcing the Whirlpool as yet another avenue for ambient music.

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: Fish feels a little warmed-over.

Title: Employment

Still, it's hard to complain about too much of a good thing.

Title: Sexwitch

Title: La Futura

Title: Beautiful Lies

[Apr 2017, p.91]

Nothing sticks out; nothing disturbs the ear or the mind or the heart; nothing is objectionable. The flow might actually be TOO impressive, and the circular structure admits of no human fallibility.

Title: Amaryllis
Review: If it ain't broke, why fix it? And the results speak for themselves. [Apr 2012, p.108]

Title: Prisoner of Conscious

Title: Volta
Review: As with much of her past work, it’s almost embarrassingly human, sometimes sounding too close to you to believe it’s not your own.

Review: In small doses this perpetual explosion is often magnificent. [Sep 2013, p.66]

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: This formulaically old-school approach is both J5's greatest asset and worst liability.

Title: Everybody
Review: Despite flashes of unexpected vigour, Everybody is ultimately more variation-on-a-theme than it is wheel reinvention.

Title: Endless
Review: 46 minutes of music that plays like a mixtape, sliding from song to song, demo to demo, like scrolling through Frank’s hard drive of unreleased material. It’s an intriguing peek into his process, and it contains some of the rawest vocal takes he’s ever put out.

Title: The Blow
Review: There are some beautiful moments here.... Also some difficult ones. [Nov 2013, p.67]

Title: Twisted Tenderness
Review: Electronic, if not exactly rejuvenated, are rewired, recharged and, really quite good again.

Title: Nightbird
Review: They just sound bored. [Feb 2005, p.98]

Title: Scar Sighted
Review: The entire album pushes and pulls in such a manner, which is completely exhausting but ultimately cathartic.

Title: Lake Tear of the Clouds
Review: There are lots of lightly retro arrangements and nods to 1960s bubblegum pop. [Jan 2019, p.22]

Title: The Constant
Review: Predictably pristine, ultimately inessential.

Title: Xtreme Now
Review: X-Treme Now is an intriguing, often entertaining bit of art from a duo that seem locked into a long-running lark that sometimes, perhaps accidentally or even incidentally, delivers the genuine article, sometimes makes do with platitudes and sidelong, distancing glances, but more often than not is a summery slab of fun.

Title: Beat Pyramid
Review: Beat Pyramid crosses genres, sticks pins in everything it sees and manages to reference hip-hop, punk, new-wave, dubstep and everything in between. For that alone, These New Puritans should be applauded.

Title: Mosaics Within Mosaics
Review: It's a record just as baffling as it is beguiling.

Title: The Massacre
Review: All the ugly gangsta lies are here, especially as regards the brutalization of women and the business of death. But they're incidental to the mood of the piece, which is friendly, relaxed, good-humored, and in the groove.

Title: Beware the Fetish
Review: This is an album that resists being the Other, but also resists even entering into a discourse that would consider that the only position. It is music innately of itself, and a privilege to hear, even at a considerable distance.

Title: Lacuna
Review: Lacuna is a euphoric, ecstatic and effortlessly cool record which warrants your undivided and immediate attention.

Title: Mouthfuls
Review: Beautiful stuff: sunny with a sad undertow, like The Beach Boys, Beck and The Beatles put in a blender. [Nov 2003, p.110]

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: With keyboard and drum machine-led swirls, higher-pitched and echoed vocals, and an embrace for what could be called art-pop-not-rock, Moonface's Organ Music is very much in the right place for 2011.

Title: All You Need Is Now
Review: As a group of former heartthrobs with something to prove, Duran Duran are both a product of its time and a band with its eye on the future -- and they've finally managed to capture the titular sense of Now.

Title: Fasciinatiion
Review: It has great ideas brewing, but there are tons of bells and whistles in the production that upstage the songwriting, which admittedly is weaker than usual for The Faint.

Title: So This Is Goodbye
Review: This is dance music with unquestionable soul.

Title: Octahedron
Review: This is, however, their most mellow, reflective and tempered release yet. [Sep 2009, p.95]

Title: Culture
Review: Backed by production from Murda Beatz, Purps, Cardo, Zaytoven and Nard & B, co-pilots Quavo, Offset, and Takeoff sustain the hubris, excess, and immediate gratification adored by fans of gutter rap machismo while somehow bottling the very particular charm necessary for them to capture the hearts of pop-loving teens across the globe and carry rapping children’s lit live on the radio.

Title: Big Echo
Review: Big Echo is an immediate, inviting listen. It’s not breaking any boundaries of inspired expression, but for what it is it’s a fine set indeed.

Title: Invisible Hour
Review: The album’s arrangements and standout musicianship--including pedal-steel and slide guitarist Greg Leisz and Henry’s son Levon on clarinet--is a reminder that Henry’s extraordinary production work is second to none.

Title: Versus
Review: With its compact running time "Versus'' is in some ways better than the album that spawned it.

Title: In League with Dragons
Review: Dragons has taken some getting used to. With each listen, new details emerge.

Title: Regions of Light and Sound of God
Review: Regions of Light and Sound of God is a laid-back affair, hardly the max-effort of some Jacket jams, and one can feel James really enjoying himself. [Jan-Feb 2013, p.87]

Title: X 100PRE
Review: Bad Bunny conquered the singles game with ease. On X100PRE, he cements his place among the elite in Latin pop--and in pop music writ large.

Title: All Things Will Unwind
Review: It's a heady and abstract album that feels more like it should be studied than enjoyed.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: Depending on one's view, it could be heard as trance music for indie folks or prog music for electro pop fans.

Title: Red Letter Days
Review: They strive to be a classic band, crafting timeless songs that will still be fresh and relevant long after the competition sounds dated and quaint.

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: Contains his catchiest, most immediate compositions in decades.

Title: JUICE
Review: Despite being on the shorter side for an album release, Juice is carefully composed; it might not necessarily be a groundbreaking new release on the part of Born Ruffians, but speaks volumes in its playfulness nonetheless.

Title: That's Harakiri
Review: At 32 minutes, it’s a short album--but one whose brashness and pace you won’t soon forget.

Title: Beauty and the Beat
Review: With an awe-inspiring imagination in tow, Edan drops his own distinct magical mystery tour. [Apr 2005, p.101]

Title: No Love Deep Web
Review: Even at a meaty 46 minutes, the album still suffers from a feeling of writer's block.

Title: Beach Music
Review: Alex G’s narrators have often been traumatized, druggie, lovesick or inscrutable, and moving up the indie-rock circuit hasn’t made his new songs any more outgoing. Just the opposite: They are more cryptic and withdrawn.

Title: Mangy Love
Review: Indeed, this is one of those rare albums that reveals a little more with every play.

Title: All Melody
Review: An ambitious and unclassifiable album. [Feb 2018, p.88]

Title: V For Vaselines
Review: V For Vaselines has been released a few months too late, for V For Vaselines is a summer album.

Title: Work
Review: Epton On Broadway Part 1, delivers elastic electro-funk with a knowing Italo-inspired wink. It's a winning formula they never stray far from. [Aug 2019, p.112]

Title: Fold Your Hands Child, You Walk Like a Peasant
Review: Make no mistake, the vibe here is strange and quirky -- the band's affinity for the naïve sometimes makes for an odd listening experience. But once you've settled into it, Peasant reveals itself to be a thing of beauty -- its nakedness comes to seem like the most natural thing in the world.

Title: Glass
Review: Strings also form the structure of ‘Fuel The Fire’, one of the album’s standouts. And then there’s the ominous ‘Paradise’, which places light and darkness side by side in a tremendous exercise of juxtaposition. That same balance is present through the album and, combined with Illum’s knack for making everything sound so exquisite, makes it a superb little record.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: Though the overall sound of Ryan Adams may be a mask, hiding lyrics that are every bit as heartbroken, confused, lost, and struggling as ever.

Title: Kaputt
Review: Bejar's reckless approach to romance is almost certainly one of those things you'd live to regret, but that's the appeal of great artistic endeavours: when the writer can pull in his audience so completely that we experience all the adventure while risking none of the consequences.

Title: Holding Hands with Jamie
Review: Girl Band play ugly noise with a charisma and energy to drag them from the no wave ghetto, to somewhere bigger. [Nov 2015, p.89]

Title: Back to Me
Review: It's not that Back to Me is an unsatisfying listen; quite to the contrary, there are some smashingly rewarding moments on this release. It's just that if you have heard Failer, you're basically heard Back to Me already.

Title: The Big To-Do
Review: Per usual there's no flash whatsoever--just seasoned professionals delivering doggedly tuneful, meticulously detailed vignettes that are part Lynyrd Skynyrd and part Raymond Carver.

Title: Twerp Verse
Review: The result is a sharpening of Speedy Ortiz’s axe to grind. Succinct, wry, and in tune with its context, there’s plenty to unpick, here.

Artist: Beth Jeans Houghton & The Hooves of Destiny
Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: [Houghton's] first album of idiosyncratic banjo pop has been worth the wait.

Title: Broken Social Scene
Review: Absolutely stunning. [4 Feb 2006, p.29]

Title: Mala in Cuba
Review: The stabilisers are off for global fusion; the first ride could have been a lot worse.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: The party holds strong into the second half, where the comedown always muddles the songwriting a little. Surprise: Antony's dramatic ululations return to rescue the trawling sonics.

Title: Moaning
Review: Though it is steeped in a subgenre that often can seem tapped out, Moaning is a strikingly accomplished debut.

Title: Bounce
Review: Bounce is the sound of a group who know what they're good at and why. [Nov 2002, p.97]

Title: Lungs
Review: Florence's music is particularly sensitive to studio gloss; her singing is a fine balance between elegance and frenzy.

Title: System
Review: System is a one-paced, staid affair, where almost everything suggests a tired version of Seal's first hit, 'Killer.'

Title: Abyss
Review: Despite the overarching quality of the album, its continual, dirge-like range of instrumentation can become a little stifling and songs risk blending into one another.

Title: Hot Motion
Review: The sonic invention---fast-cuts between moods and styles, washy layers of aural colours--never gets in the way of the songs and the result is a triumph. [Nov 2019, p.116]

Title: Walking With Thee
Review: Clinic remember that Britpop is supposed to be fun. [Mar 2002, p.127]

Title: Rain On Lens
Review: Without a doubt one of Callahan’s most inspired collection of songs to date.
If you’ve ever been enticed by Spanish guitar, here’s your rock’n’roll introduction.

Title: Black Rainbows
Review: The record boasts maybe his finest solo single to date in 'Brittle Heart', plus a clutch of mid-tempo rockers that scrub up nicely--even if the seedy Soho glam of yore is replaced by a leadenly earnest tone.

Title: Say It
Review: Much of the material sounds rushed and half-finished, like a high schooler trying to write a research page paper during his lunch period.

Title: A Walk with Love and Death
Review: It finds the band indulging their darkest urges, often using nothing more than noise and soundscapes. Like everything the Melvins do, however, it remains compelling, clever, and absolutely unique. [24 Jun 2017, p.53]

Title: Flicker
Review: At its best, his songwriting is appealingly simple and straightforward: the title track offers an evocative portrait of a relationship that’s breaking down. But at times, Horan’s lyrics let him down a little.

Title: Turn The Lights Out
Review: Much of "Turn the Lights Off" is inspired by '80s artists who wanted to sound like they were from the '60s.

Title: Monuments to an Elegy
Review: Although his lyrics are as benign as ever, much of the music here doesn't just rehash what was good about the band's salad days, but bravely presents Corgan as an artist trying to stage one of the most unexpected comebacks in recent history.

Title: The Hurting Kind
Review: The Hurting Kind stands head and shoulders above Beulah for its mature vision, powerful focus, and poetic songwriting and production. This is White's finest moment thus far.

Title: Alvvays
Review: The lo-fi/hi-fi production values keep slickness at bay, resulting in something as warm, intimate and super-casual as an East Coast kitchen party.

Title: White Crosses
Review: White Crosses is all shiny and fresh and proudly expedient, without proving a thing except that Against Me! are fully capable of doing it again.

Title: Girls Can Tell
Review: At 36 minutes, Girls Can Tell packs more hooks than most bands fit into their entire discography... This is truly one of the most intense pop records since This Year's Model.

Title: Music Complete
Review: There is a spirit of adventure and experimentation in the album that is commendable.

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: Chrome Dreams II is effective despite the sonic clash because, on both the new material and the leftovers, the loud ('Spirit Road') and the soft (the soul ballad 'Ever After'), it’s unified by its call to give props to spirit and humanity, a sentiment that, whatever it’s wrapped in, never gets old.

Title: Sings Christmas Carols
Review: It comes off like Leonard Cohen if he kept his Biblical allusions strictly seasonal, and goes down as smoothly as rum-heavy eggnog. Quite captivating. Simple, and earnest, really.

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: And while at first it feels like an unholy, unhummable mess, the same solid gold charm which powered lead single "I Don't Feel Like Dancin'" to Number One, lurks at the heart of every track, and by listen five it's refocused "Ta-Dah" into a strangely enticing nether world, where it's forever 1974 and a cheap thrill or soaring pop high lurks round every corner.

Title: Tell Me How You Really Feel
Review: Clever turns of phrase and quirky observations still permeate Barnett's writing, and there are still jangly, toe-tapping jams like "Need a Little Time" and "City Looks Pretty," but there are also darker forces at work.

Title: MHz Legacy
Review: For now, MHz Legacy fits the group's journey quite well with strong highlights and a few struggles along the way.

Title: Joy Comes Back
Review: So Joy Comes Back might be on your shopping list, especially if you're already a Ruthie Foster fan, but take this advice: It's only half a great album, so keep it on the B side.

Title: Confess
Review: Confess is largely an impeccable sequel to an immaculate debut. [Aug 2012, p.82]

Title: Indicud
Review: Indicud won't work for everyone, but if you're a Cudi fan, this album finds him sounding better than he has in some time.

Title: Birthday
Review: Students of jazz, but with a love of avant-garde art punk and West African music, Pom Poko bring something chaotic to the table. ... But this is their bread and butter; the kaleidoscopic realm in which they thrive.

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: Neither MacLean nor vocal foil Nancy Whang has a strong enough voice for pop. Instead it's the surging 10-minute disco epics 'Tonight' and 'Happy House; that impress. [May 2009, p.89]

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: Though Timbaland’s productions always hold some sly surprises, “Magna Carta ... Holy Grail” comes across largely as a transitional album, as if Jay-Z has tired of pop but hasn’t found a reliable alternative.

Title: Feast of Wire
Review: Sure, with so much to hear and such a range of styles, the album can take a couple of listens before it starts to bloom. That said, after these requisite spins, one can't help but admire how smoothly Feast of Wire glides from track to track, style to style.

Title: Duck
Review: All in all, Duck is the sound of a band trying way too hard. [Sep 2019, p94]

Title: V
Review: Kowalczyk may have filtered some of the bluster from his lyrics, but he has wisely left the jagged edges in his music.

Title: Golden Era
Review: Del takes a trip down memory lane on Golden Era, but it's never as special or profound the second time around.

Title: Historicity
Review: Vijay acquits himself nicely on "Mystic Brew," effectively reinterpreting organist Ronnie Foster's impressive soulful mush for stately piano. [Fall 2009, p.74]

Title: WIT'S END
Review: Wit's End is even more hushed and sluggish than 2009's Catacombs, leaving lighter Dylanesque fare for depressive Leonard Cohen depths.

Title: Night of Hunters
Review: It contains the power and dynamics and splendor of her very best material, but because it is a work of classical crossover, any expectation of pop hooks or singalong choruses will be met with disappointment; consequently, its sophistication, elegance, and poetry will reward anyone who takes the proper time to absorb it.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: The duo's follow-up is a more relaxed affair. Though it, too, has cleverness to spare, the album is less cutesy and self-conscious than its predecessor. The beats are stronger, at times hitting with hip-hop force, and the music is fuller and more imaginative.

Title: Allways
Review: Allways is as mercurial as it is highly listenable. [Nov 2018, p.26]

Title: O
Review: With O, Markus Pop has reinvented Oval using new techniques to produce a challenging sound world that's simultaneously exhausting and fascinating.

Title: Them Crooked Vultures
Review: Believe it or not, though, this appealingly lightweight set of funky robo-rock jams actually makes good on Homme's promise.

Title: Basic Behaviour
Review: Even as they strain between varying poles, Frigs still manage to find moments of great, if sombre, beauty. That’s not basic at all.

Title: Algiers
Review: They can be packed to the brim with the thoughts and feelings of a whole collection of people. For Algiers, it is this ability to connect with hearts and minds that ultimately makes their record among 2015's strongest thus far.

Title: The Harsh Light of Day
Review: Well-constructed but largely uninspiring... Its lyrics offer little that's dynamic or artful, so what are listeners really left with? Decent melodies, to be sure, and nicely produced tracks... But deep down, the music and lyrics rarely match up, and few songs establish a mood for long enough to hang your heart on.

Title: Reptile
Review: A smooth and engaging affair, with consistently strong singing and playing from Clapton.

Title: Security Screenings
Review: At its best, the music's so hypnotic you won't miss [the vocals]. [24 Feb 2006, p.65]

Title: Destroyer of the Void
Review: On an album that quite simply comes up lacking in spots, they provide a healthy dose of the same brilliant elegance found on "Furr."

Title: how i'm feeling now
Review: Though it lacks the alien opalescence of Charli's best record, how i'm feeling now contains a different sort of thrilling delirium. It's fun and sometimes silly, made on the fly and under a tight deadline. But it's desperate too — a frenzied call for release, an ode to the love that keeps us going, and further proof that no other pop artist today can make the digital sound so disarmingly human.

Title: Furnaces
Review: Fifteen years after his debut, it was about time Ed Harcourt made a career-defining record. Here it is. [Sep 2016, p.106]

Title: Neptune
Review: For most of Neptune, the Duke Spirit graft sweet coatings onto a dark, swirling center.

Title: Fever
Review: Despite the lyrics failing to improve upon previous efforts, elsewhere Fever represents a significant step forward, and practically guarantees that BFMV will fulfil the expectations preceding its release.

Title: Touch Down 2 Cause Hell
Review: A pleasant surprise.

Title: Slaughterhouse
Review: All the controversy and hype aside, what’s most important is that these four rappers were able to put out a very listenable and enjoyable record. And to the surprise of many, there is nary a weak beat on Slaughterhouse.

Title: Gulag Orkestar
Review: A record of rare and strange beauty. [4 Nov 2006, p.33]

Title: Two Thousand
Review: Two Thousand is the rare follow-up miles-away better than its breakthrough predecessor. [Summer 2006]

Title: Any Day
Review: With Sam Prekop on vocals, though, a Sea and Cake album is genetically incapable of sounding like anything other than a Sea and Cake album.

Title: Southeastern
Review: It’s a poignant, reflective, and very often frank portrayal of humanity’s dual impulses authored by someone who has lived several chapters, yet knows the story is constantly being rewritten.

Title: Even In Exile
Review: Even if it’s a bit much at times, Even in Exile could well be the best record Bradfield has lent his voice to since 2009’s Journal for Plague Lovers; it’s not a classic, but a very strong, autumnal call to arms.

Title: Emotional Traffic
Review: Overall, though the lyric content is among the best on a Tim McGraw album to date.

Title: Saturday Night Wrist
Review: For most of "Saturday Night Wrist," Deftones contentedly let their instruments wander, inventing a meandering soundscape that broods in near darkness. [4 Nov 2006]

Title: Double Roses
Review: A whisper, sigh, prayer and somehow catharsis, Roses balms life’s harshness.

Title: Kelis Was Here
Review: A typical case of slack self-editing... Kelis was here too long, frankly. [Nov 2006, p.101]

Title: And Their Refinement Of The Decline
Review: Call it music for lucid dreaming, call it music for daydreams, or call it music for simply strolling in the dusk, this is another album that will stretch time and take you to another place.

Title: Dead To The World
Review: It may not quite give you the sheer electric shock jolt of their classic Meantime and Betty albums, but Helmet are still capable of bloodying your nose from 100 paces.

Title: Pedals
Review: Rival Schools have finally returned from an inexplicably long hiatus to demonstrate why they're such luminaries for today's post-hardcore hordes.

Title: The Suburbs
Review: Swelling at 16 songs and an hour-plus runtime, it's Arcade Fire's most ambitious and concept-driven effort to date.

Title: New View
Review: Like avowed influences Van Morrison and Neil Young, Friedberger on New View travels in fluid, seamless melodies, and uses them in service of lyrics that revel in poeticism.

Title: The Drums
Review: The album is overall fun, though it is at times repetitive and is best enjoyed in small doses.

Title: Glass Swords
Review: Th art here is ensuring that too much is in fact just enough, and Rustie is a master of it. [Oct 2011, p.51]

Title: These People
Review: There are outliers such as the horrible Britpop-by-way-of-Pet-Shop-Boys punchy greyness of Hold On, and the grating synth stabs on opener Out of My Body, but generally Ashcroft manages to relive his heyday nicely.

Title: Sound-Dust
Review: Tim Gane and Laetitia Sadier's prettiest songs since '95's Music For The Amorphous Body Study Center. [Oct 2001, p.116]

Title: Dead To The World
Review: Ultimately, though, after making such an indelible and unique contribution to the language of modern heavy rock, Hamilton continues to show that he's hemmed-in by the style he invented.

Title: Stephen Malkmus
Review: A swell record: personal but easy-going, distinctive, with a lot of picaresque personal narratives occasionally conveyed through exaggerated fantasy elements.

Title: Melody of Certain Damaged Lemons
Review: Certainly Blonde Redhead's most accessible yet.

Title: House of Spirits
Review: Those who continue to stick with the band will find themselves rewarded with another fine addition to an impressive catalog and an example of grown-up psych pop that's both calming and soul-searching, while never being anything less than completely enjoyable.

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: Throughout the record, Steve Mackey's production shimmers both warmly and vibrantly, sounding at once like a throwback from the 1980s and futuristic.

Title: Big Balloon
Review: It’s an unfettered display of eighties-evoking posing that suits them perfectly well, but it also sounds like a step back after they’d already figured out how to match their compositional smarts with a clear message.

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: Despite their reputation as torch-bearers of the new post-rock prog, it lacks the outrageousness of the ‘70s version of the genre and there’s an earnest sameness to these pieces that render much of it tedious beyond belief.

Title: Tropical Storm
Review: It's blatant commercial product, something for everyone.

Title: The Endless River
Review: As part of the greater whole of Floyd records, it’s an oddity, more relevant for its context in the band’s history than the music.

Title: Rainier Fog
Review: The main issue with Rainier Fog, though, is that the band never climbs from the very bottom to the very top of that mountain and gives us all of their range. They stick relatively close to base camp, a well-stocked, but comfortable mid-point that largely eschews dynamics.

Title: No Home Record
Review: No Home Record roils with just the kind of catharsis we need in Bad Timeline America. Play it loud, play it often, play it again.

Title: Fire Within
Review: A doldorous racket. [Dec 2013, p.86]

Title: Breakfast
Review: Grown up, spotlessly polished and now with full-fledged circuitry, these pirates are machines now, making Teleman’s debut nothing short of electric.

Title: Solar Motel
Review: Drawing from the rock pantheon as well as personal experience and fascination, Chris Forsyth presents a guitarist’s record that is decidedly group music, and Solar Motel should whet appetites and blow minds of shredders and weirdos alike.

Title: The Sermon on Exposition Boulevard
Review: The overall hush of "Sermon" occasionally leads down some sleepy roads. But with a real sense of creative spark at its heart, "Sermon" is a worthy entry into the Book of Rickie Lee.

Title: Dreams Come True
Review: The disparate parts align into a moody, liminal funk, orchestrating songs that obsess over a relationship irrevocably slipping away.

Title: Hitchhiker
Review: Beautiful, strange, and stoned, Hitchhiker lets us in on one of those nights.

Title: Glad All Over
Review: The Wallflowers don't abandon their identity as rock & roll classicists, they just now feel the freedom to mess around, and they've come up with one of their loosest, liveliest records that not-so-coincidentally is one of their best.

Title: Now We Can See
Review: Overall, Now We Can See is a bit uneven. Still, it's an interesting step in The Thermals, um, evolution. [Spring 2009, p.74]

Title: Soul Food
Review: It’s a catalog of strengths, a romp through sacred steel music, blues and Southern soul that often sounds as if it could have been recorded in heated performance.

Title: Baby Blue Abyss
Review: Baird’s weary, almost impassive croon and deadpan humour across both records can’t hide his serious resistance to our self-deceiving, digitally distanced lives.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: A record rooted in anxiety and mourning, We Got It From Here remains musically as dark and electrically relaxed as 1996's Beats, Rhymes and Life and 1998's The Love Movement.

Title: Singularity
Review: A comparable transition on Singularity, between "Everything Connected" and "Feel First Life," is made to feel seamless, less like a change in circumstance than an ascent onto some higher plane. Some will feel completely immersed in that; others might simply admire it from a distance.

Title: The Cookbook
Review: This is one helluva party LP.

Title: The Benoit Pioulard Listening Matter
Review: A bruised, heartsore set. [Jan 2017, p.104]

Title: Canyons of My Mind
Review: While you may wish this newlywed was a little happier, this is a superb, emotionally poignant album that displays and expands Andrew Combs’ impressive songwriting, musical and vocal talents.

Title: Scintilli
Review: Scintilli's pieces are as varied as ever, but carefully drawn, like working on separate days with blowtorch-on-metal or in purple and blue oils. [Oct. 2011, p. 113]

Title: Pearls To Swine
Review: Torres has traded away some pieces of the humanity that colored his earlier work in favor of a conversation about something elemental that's still waiting to be discovered. That doesn’t make for an immediate record. It makes for one full of enigmas, of beautiful and undefinable things that promise further revelations to come.

Title: Renegade Breakdown
Review: Davidson has easily transitioned between dim clubs and big festivals and learned to balance her acerbic ‘existential pop’ with hard-nosed techno. Drawing on the former, ‘Renegade Breakdown’’s appeal is in some ways broader, but she also risks putting off some of the initiated. On the whole, it functions as a reminder of the virtues of going against the grain and not playing it safe.
Roots folk doesn't get more organic than this.

Title: The Bride Screamed Murder
Review: King Buzzo, et al.'s 19th studio album is downright sugary, a sludge-pop romp that mostly plays like a distortion-charred version of the Bay City Rollers or Sweet.

Title: Pe'ahi
Review: It might be easy to take The Raveonettes for granted, or to cast them aside in favor of the latest flavor of the month. Like the rest of their 2010s output, the strength and near-brilliance of Pe'ahi show clearly what a mistake it would be to do either of those things.

Title: BREACH
Review: Fenne Lily’s latest record is as thoughtful and emotive as her first, confirming her as a rising star in the realm of singer/songwriters. [Aug - Oct 2020, p.86]

Title: Night of Hunters
Review: Not only is she an artist maturing and growing with her music, but in great Amos fashion, she is making sense of her past in a wholly original, intelligent way. And at this stage of her career, she's earned the right to a few spirit guides.

Title: Book of Travelers
Review: While Book of Travelers may be a less-immediate collection than some of his previous work, its contemplative nature is worth investing a significant amount of time in.

Title: Honeyblood
Review: While there's a small but significant gap between Honeyblood's outstanding songs and the rest of the album, it's still a debut full of moments of depth and moments of instant gratification--as well as lots of potential.

Title: Something for the Rest of Us
Review: Maybe the label was hoping to get back some of the Goo Goos' 90s magic, but that doesn't happen.

Title: A New Day at Midnight
Review: Comes off likea rave-era update of Van Morrison's blue-eyed soul. [Feb 2003, p.138]

Title: If I've Only One Time Askin'
Review: You won't hear a more open hearted, impassioned and lyrically rich roots album this year.

Title: 22 Dreams
Review: Apart from being the most eclectic and resourcefully imaginative solo album of Weller’s career, 22 Dreams also turns out to be one of his most consistent efforts.

Title: Instant Money Magic
Review: Amid the minor missteps and business-as-usual pleasantries, though, there is one winner of a track. Album opener “Wiggmann” finds Japanther supplementing their pop craftsmanship with an equal measure of ingenuity.

Title: The Night Land
Review: Each track takes you to some very unexpected places. In the process, each delivers feelings much more potent than a lot of the supposedly “emotional” dancefloor music currently flooding the market at the moment.

Title: Everything Under The Sun
Review: If a piano-pop song has ever put a smile on your face, Everything Under The Sun belongs in your collection. If that's never happened to you, well, why not?

Title: The OOZ
Review: No matter that feeling, illustrated with one distressed scene after another, filtered through a multitude of inspirations and a few bodily fluids, The Ooz is a completely engrossing work from a one-off.

Title: Endlessly
Review: Duffy is clearly striving for growth with Endlessly, but outside her comfort zone, she comes up short.

Title: Theosophy
Review: His fourth album is leaner and meaner than 2010's A Train Bound For Glory. [Jul 2014, p.77]

Title: Doo - Wops & Hooligans
Review: Mars has quite remarkably extracted themes from every one of those shows [The X-Factor], incorporating each into his debut, from glossy, over-sentimental ballads (Talking To The Moon) to an all-out, shameless dispatching of joy (Marry Song).

Title: Free For All
Review: Baha's production skills are clear across Free For All. Fans of instrumental grime artists like Slackk will find much to admire in the austere yet precisely constructed "Aliens," whose sense of space is uncommonly sophisticated.

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Miss Anthropocene is a deep, dark trip – shame the climate crisis bit isn’t also part of Grimes’s wild imagination.

Title: A Better Tomorrow
Review: Something is definitely missing on A Better Tomorrow: not necessarily the cryptic slang and mythology, but that RZA and the other members haven't found something to replace what stood them apart from the crowd.

Title: The Sovereign Self
Review: The quintet are a crack unit, powered by hard rock riffs, jazz and Krautrock-informed drums and flights of flute-based fancy.

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: Dark isn't a huge departure from the previous record, and it doesn't mark some major step in Hot Chip's evolution either. But there's something to be said for holding your liquor, keeping momentum, and showing the world that this whole ride is as wicked-fun as you thought it would be. [Winter 2008, p.92]

Title: M:FANS
Review: The original record’s improvisational nature is still here but hidden, its minimalist touches are scant.

Title: We Love You So Bad
Review: It's a short set, with just eight songs running a little over 20 minutes, but the poppy hooks come in gauzy droves.

Title: Client
Review: A pretty good album that, while not exactly groundbreaking, is a fine addition to synthpop's latest wave. [#23, p.83]

Title: Stuffed & Ready
Review: Creevy’s vocals are a controlled force, and it’s hard to image a woman who writes so incisively about her feelings ever recorded a song about grilled cheese. The potential was there from the beginning. It’s nice to see that they’ve realised it.

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: It's all a show with Kings Of Leon, and there's nothing they yearn for more than the chance to exercise their sexual prowess.

Title: Soul is Heavy
Review: For listeners ready to let go of expectations and embark on a musical ride, the journey will be well worth it.

Title: The Sovereign Self
Review: Whilst sounding altogether more psychologically and sonically cluttered, the challenges this album presents are as invigorating as its rewards--poetic beauty can still be found amidst the lysergic confusion.

Title: Tomorrow Is My Turn
Review: The bull horn power of Odetta and Bessie Smith’s sly blues are other touchstones on an agile, emotional record.

Title: Knowle West Boy
Review: Perhaps it’s not a full home run--it’s good, but more a retrenchment than a bold step forward. That’s OK, however.

Title: Sing the Sorrow
Review: As big and slick a rock record as you're likely to hear all year. [Apr 2003, p.101]

Title: Le Voyage Dans La Lune
Review: Le Voyage is, given its origins, a small wonder all on its own.

Title: III
Review: The album clearly fails to find the equilibrium or comfortable midway point between Espers’s debut and II that it seems to be seeking, nor does it make a strong case that such equilibrium is even desirable. At best, it’s a strong set of tracks that ultimately lack the cumulative force of those of the band’s previous two full-lengths.

Title: Salt on Sea Glass
Review: It may be true that That Dog and Cibo Matto only had limited commercial success and critical acclaim, but the sounds of Salt on Sea Glass indicate that they've both matured and outgrown the sound of their previous incarnations.

Title: Klang
Review: Their third album is another bony bundle of modern neuroses. [Apr 2009, p.108]

Title: World Be Gone
Review: Full credit should be given for bringing an extra dimension to the Erasure legacy, but World Be Gone makes for far from easy listening.

Title: Prog
Review: The Bad Plus has yet to release a truly flawless LP, but each new record shows that time and touring has only made the trio tighter and better.

Title: Ascension
Review: Not quite as candy-coated as Conqueror or as harrowing as Jesu, it's mostly notable for both Broadrick's high level of quality control (unless you just outright dislike his kind of music, his songs are always at least pleasingly consistent in tone and impact) and his increasing, perhaps unwitting, move away from song form.

Title: Computers and Blues
Review: From its cover in, there's a knowing, bustling swagger to The Streets' finale, if only in its relishing of a quick dart for the exit.

Title: Transit Transit
Review: With its deft blend of nostalgia and futurism, Transit Transit is not only a fantastic delivery on a forgotten promise, it's the best reason so far to be optimistic about 2016.

Title: Lust for Life
Review: Lust For Life may be a scattered, confusing record, but it's a beautiful ride--one worth repeated listens, even if Lana's intentions--like her enunciation--aren't always clear.

Title: Under Rug Swept
Review: Her personal revelations too often ring false and crass, and nothing undermines a confession like calculation.

Title: Naomi
Review: Ultimately, Naomi doesn’t stray too far from The Cave Singers’ previous output, but she, like any good muse, will captivate, invigorate and satiate.

Title: Art Angels
Review: Visions put Grimes on the map as pop's pure misfit but Art Angels secured her tangible place as the genre's most unconventional star. For those that doubted, she's done that thing she does, but better. More defined.

Title: Beams
Review: Minor complaints aside, Beams is a solid record, and a pretty good Dear album is nothing to be upset about.

Title: Teenager
Review: Musically, their songs are too brightly bland, so obviously designed for mass consumption and uplift that the tinny guitars and twinkling piano melodies end up sounding cheap.

Title: Views
Review: It’s a disappointment for an artist who’s managed to get better and better with every subsequent release up until this point.

Title: Another Language
Review: For the most part, This Will Destroy You finds its footing on the slow burn, crawling along at a snail’s pace, rarely straying from an established formula (quiet, brooding intro, slow build/hard dynamic shift half to three quarters of the way through, louder still) that, over the course of a whole album, can be somewhat draining.

Title: Party Store
Review: Releasing a covers album can be career suicide for some, due to the pressures of stripping apart a classic and making it your own, but Party Store is refreshingly not the case.

Title: Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys
Review: Danger Days doesn't sound like the future, but it does sound like the sate of My Chemical Romance's art. [Dec 2010, p.102]

Title: EP 1
Review: EP1 was a mixed bag.

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: It's a pleasure to listen to, and perhaps its sheer existence (thanks in part to crowdsourcing on Kickstarter) is a fact to be celebrated in itself

Title: Faking the Books
Review: Accessible enough for people who learn about new music from [NPR] and sonically interesting enough to appeal to hardcore electroheads. [May 2004, p.110]

Title: Blue Sky Noise
Review: Troubled frontman Anthony Green and his mates have embraced glossier production while reconnecting with At the Drive-In's teeming passion.

Title: LP1
Review: Sadly, the final product is so familiar and so shorn of genuine emotion that LP1 quickly loses any sense of identity and becomes standard fare, indistinguishable from any number of other recordings.

Title: Distortion
Review: He may be treading water a little until he really gets into his groove as the 21st century Sondheim, but Distortion at its best is beguiling and quietly devastating.

Title: Happy Hollow
Review: There’s an attention to detail and storytelling nous built up by those previous concept albums that makes further listening and exploration of Happy Hollow that much more rewarding.

Title: Everything Is New
Review: This time he's crafted a more parent-friendly brand of earnest pop that isn't quite as irritating, but is sadly no more engaging. [Aug 2009, p.101]

Title: Louden Up Now
Review: If you take away the 9 minutes of their already-released big single, you could probably squeeze a tight EP out of Louden Up Now, but as a full-length [it] starts with a bang and ends with sort of a whimper. Fun to filler in 53 minutes.

Title: Fever Dream
Review: Designated chillout areas and other blue rooms will find Fever Dream a worthwhile soundtrack, while longtime fans get that wistful vagabond indie-hop style once again, only this time it's transmitted from deep, blissful space.

Title: Myth of a Man
Review: Myth Of A Man doesn't feel like the whole story yet, but it's getting there. [Feb 2019, p.92]

Title: Off With Their Heads
Review: Erratic songwriting is evident from start to finish on the record.

Title: Miracle Temple
Review: Mount Moriah remains committed to a sparse, skeletal vein of Americana that values precision over ambition. That’s not to imply the album isn’t a rich and varied listening experience, but its ambiguities and complexities are shaded in charcoal, not paint.

Title: Scorpion
Review: Like most blockbusters, the script is predictable - topics include no-good men, being hard and how great Eve is - but this is designed for booming out of car stereos rather than close listening.

Title: Wide Awake!
Review: While Wide Awake! is perhaps less adventurous than the band's last two "proper" records, it is more sharply focused, with twists and turns that knock you off your dancing feet. [Mar - May 2018, p.58]

Title: Baby
Review: Baby feels more like a leftover relic from the '90s than the game-changer the genre needs.

Title: Violent Hearts
Review: As a full-length listening experience, Violent Hearts is a little much-- it runs just under a lean half-hour, but the relative lack of stylistic breadth covered makes a front-to-back spin feel longer.

Title: Cold of Ages
Review: If their self-titled LP represented a slight dip in the usual quality of this band, Cold of Ages represents a trip both back and forward--back to their earlier days in terms of material and the quality of the compositions, but forward in terms of recording quality, evolutionary potential, and available elements at their disposal.

Title: Finding Forever
Review: The rest of it though, is soulful and intelligent where 'intelligent' is not exclusive to 'good beats and rhymes.' Which is what it's all about.

Title: Some Loud Thunder
Review: The band... haven't leapt off in a new direction but have capitalised on the tension between Oundsworth's spiralling, just-about-to-fall-over vocals and the driving, zealous music that stops him from metaphorically sailing away into the ether.

Title: Skilled Mechanics
Review: While it isn’t without its moments, that is not enough to forgive the sub-standard R’&’B and lumpy rock crossovers.

Title: Hotel Last Resort
Review: Hotel Last Resort is a collection of music that is poised and deliberate, provoked and provoking. Not a record to be taken at face value, it begs for a conscious listen, start to finish. It affirms Violent Femmes’ place as one of the greatest contributors to both the punk and the American musical canon.

Title: True Romance
Review: They take their blue-eyed romanticism deadly serious, asking, "Wouldn't it be sweet if you could die from a broken heart?" like genuine kamikazes of love.

Title: Straight No Chaser
Review: Matching catchy pop songs and good production to hip-hop's most wanted, it all comes full circle in Straight No Chaser.

Title: White Chalk
Review: Polly has always done well to play outside her comfort zone, and in doing so on this album, she crafts a reminder more effective than her return-to-form attempt on "Uh Huh Her."

Title: Bleed Like Me
Review: They’ve returned to the clamorous, powerchord-packed rock of their debut, with the inevitable result that it sounds fixed firmly by the formaldehyde of fashion in mid-90s post-grunge.

Title: Father Creeper
Review: If this is his starting point, his future seems limitless.

Title: Crossing The Rubicon
Review: Front-loaded with buzzy riffs and cutting vocals, the third studio album from this Swedish band is bracingly ambitious, clearly designed to be heard in arenas and stadiums.

Title: Callus
Review: Unfortunately, Gonjasufi's attempt to turn his solidarity with the angry and the dispossessed into a musical concept is too blandly realized to be convincing.

Title: Yellow & Green
Review: This is an album of atmosphere, huge highs, crushing lows, melodies, crescendos and something entirely new that still sounds natural. Stunning.

Title: MG
Review: It gets on with the job in hand, never short changing the listener, and in the process providing a valuable insight into one of pop music’s great creative minds in the process.

Title: Mosquito
Review: Ultimately, Mosquito sees the band reenergised, trying new things and, generally, succeeding.

Title: Haw
Review: The arrangements are bigger, the language more dense, the symbolism darker. [May 2013, p.72]

Title: Album of The Year
Review: There's a stunning balance between fluid variations and deviations that in total feel like improvisation and the strictly confined, loping-in-circles gait of traditional hip-hop-a process which then lends itself to being described as simultaneously dynamic and hypnotic, loose and hard, jam and the jam.

Title: Not Music
Review: Not Music can feel a little like trying to solve a series of Sudoko puzzles, the brain fully engaged but the heart untaxed. [Dec 2010, p.97]

Title: Thee Physical
Review: Dubstep's increasingly Americanized impact can be sensed in the bass wobbles of "Black Nails," while trance's long shadow in turn crops up in "Real Is a Feeling." Not to mention the title and feeling of "Trancegender"--but why not go all out, after all?

Title: Elephant Shell
Review: Very minor, rather lovely and it rocks.

Title: Saturday Night
Review: Saturday Night is a confident debut from a creator who's best when he seems uncomfortable. So long as he keeps evading his comfort zone, Darcy's songwriting should remain potent for years to come.

Title: Steingarten
Review: Pole’s technique still relies heavily on the minimal, but Steingarten is garnished with a sonic density lacking on his first three full-lengths.

Title: My Heart Has a Wish That You Would Not Go
Review: Here, Aereogramme have created something more than deserving of all the praise lavished upon it.

Title: Walking Cloud and Deep Red Sky, Flag Fluttered and the Sun Shined
Review: The quiet/loud, quiet/loud thing has been going on for a long time now, and while Mono has things in common with everyone from Mogwai to the aforementioned groups, they're definitely one of the better bands I've heard doing this in a while.

Title: Narrow Stairs
Review: On its own, it has some great moments, and it is a very good pop/rock record.

Title: Isla
Review: Blending an almost futuristically elegant sense of atmosphere with flashes of raw, flesh-and-blood expression, Portico Quartet isn't the first to carve out such a pan-global sonic world, but it's created one that's welcoming to visit.

Title: Life on a String
Review: She lets [the songs] drift off into the kind of embalmed chamber music respectability often synonymous with the Nonesuch label.

Title: Life In Cartoon Motion
Review: It's irreverent, in-your-face, sexually nebulous, and infuriatingly catchy.

Title: Black Soul Choir
Review: The new outing from the Nordic rockers may not be as essential as Sister Faith in the long run, but it certainly makes for a highly pleasurable listen.

Title: North
Review: These are worn vintage sounds, but the songs here lack the choruses and hooks to invest them with fresh life, and Buttery's voice is forgettable. [Dec 2010, p.46]

Title: The Long Goodbye
Review: As a transitory album The Long Goodbye is uneven.

Title: Ghost Culture
