Review: RRD's tempo is beatific, fingerpicked guitar and violin cresting sweetly, though some fervent moments provide real highlights. [Mar 2018, p.90]

Title: Big Black Coat
Review: Casual and understated as ever, Greenspan and Didemus seemed to be making a point: Big Black Coat isn't the triumphant return of Junior Boys, it's just the next chapter in an ongoing story.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: Perfect Pussy is almost definitely a band to be experienced live rather than on record, but as statements of intent go, Say Yes to Love is an incredibly powerful one.

Title: Changing Horses
Review: Regardless of one's opinion on music that drawls, Changing Horses is worth your attention. [Mar 2009, p.106]

Title: The Sellout
Review: The problem with Macy Gray's comeback album is that, on it, she talks too much about her comeback album.

Title: Front Porch
Review: This may be the best, most natural and inevitable music she’s made.

Title: Obituary
Review: Latest recruits Kenny Andrews (lead guitar) and Terry Butler (bass) have brought renewed focus to both songwriting and sound.

Title: Smash Mouth
Review: As always, Smash Mouth is all but impossible to hate, offsetting its bald-faced mercenary intentions with a refreshing lack of pretension.

Title: Beyondless
Review: Beyondless largely speaks for itself. It does what Iceage have always done best: it challenges everything you thought you knew about them. It could be viewed as their most accessible album yet (it features guest vocals from Sky Ferreira, after all), but it’s not as simple as that.

Title: BiRd-BrAiNs
Review: Garbus’s peculiarities are often quite charming--often, not always, because there’s only so much so-called cute we can be expected to tolerate, and though Bird-Brains remains on the side of acceptability, it flies dangerously close to the line (er, wire).
The album plays to his strengths. It is more playful than his last LP, and also more finessed.

Title: Factory Floor
Review: This is music that demands to be played loud, and often.

Title: Control System
Review: Ab-Soul music fuses street-level concerns with the sort of erudite, rhyme scheme-fixated wordplay more commonly associated with rapper who value beats and rhymes over life. [Jul 2012, p.71]

Title: The Age of Fracture
Review: So, ear candy it is for Cymbals and The Age of Fracture. Whitney trumps fine art, and that’s okay.

Title: Spiritual Emergency
Review: Amidst the palpitated urgings of bass and the rapid skimmings of guitar, Fox’s drumkit emerges as the key figure here, the volatility of his technique underscoring the fact that, as soon as you efface the certainties and the contrived precision of the external world, the once incontrovertible dimensions of the self go with it.

Title: Brooklynati
Review: Whereas their 2006 disc, "Moonlighting," was across-the-board impressive but a tad monotonous, their latest hinges on memorable and unpredictable style jumps.

Title: Pain Killer
Review: A collection that plays into the group’s rock sensibilities without any loss of identity.

Title: So Beautiful or So What
Review: This cagey old pro makes room for stray nonsense phrases like "bop-bop-a-whoa" as well; spirited spirituality is his goal these days.

Title: Pageant
Review: Where Ugly Cherries felt spontaneous and carefree, Pageant feels more mature and considered.

Title: Friend and Foe
Review: Now that Menomena's technique feels less jarring and daring, though, the group has done a decent job of pouring its euphoric weirdness into bruised, beautiful songcraft.

Title: The Diary of Alicia Keys
Review: An enthusiastic album full of masterful strokes and electrifying intensity. [#23, p.98]

Title: Lantern
Review: They capture and transform generic ideas about space and environment in ways beyond the grasp of most bands. Sadly, this approach limits their accessibility; even so, theirs is a world well worth, at least, a visit.

Title: Low in High School
Review: Morrissey, at 58, once again proves himself a pop provocateur of enduring efficacy. [Dec 2017, p.100]

Title: Liberation Transmission
Review: Essential listening for mall rats everywhere. [Aug 2006, p.113]

Title: Before Today
Review: Before Today, while easily his best album to date, still feels like it's just the tip of the iceberg for this staggeringly talented songwriter.

Title: Resistance
Review: This is actually a joyful, bouncing album. [Oct 2018, p.68]

Title: One Breath
Review: One Breath is truly cathartic, but it will leave you a quivering wreck.

Title: Emotional Traffic
Review: Emotional Traffic isn't dramatically better, worse or all that different from what he's been doing since the beginning.

Title: Futures
Review: Ultimately, Futures is Bleed American Part Two. [Nov 2004, p.118]

Title: Humanz
Review: A boundlessly inventive and occasionally quite bonkers record that draws heavily on the input of its myriad guests. [Jun 2017, p.88]

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die II
Review: Adrian Younge's film score-like production on this latest team-up doesn't feel as atmospheric or inspired as their first go-round.

Title: Insignificance
Review: A pleasurable collection of comfortably played, understated, slightly skewed songs with smart lyrics. [#214, p.52]

Title: Hefty Fine
Review: There are already too many Bloodhound Gang albums in the world. This one should be recalled and recycled. Into something that's not a Bloodhound Gang album, obviously.

Title: Big Inner
Review: Matthew E. White's Hometapes' debut, Big Inner, is as frustrating as it is cosmically transcendent.

Title: Everything All The Time
Review: Whether cranked up high or turned down low, this music has a scrappy majesty. [Jun 2006, p.136]

Title: Grinderman 2
Review: The devil be praised that, rather than visiting the shrink or brothel to deal with his sexual dysfunction, the Grinderman went to the studio instead.

Title: The Chronicles of Marnia
Review: Marnia, a fantasy as daunting as it is revelatory.

Title: Midnite Vultures
Review: Beck's best when he's tweaking music he has a genuine interest in, giving new humor and affection to his nasty grooves.

Title: Used Future
Review: Used Future comes embedded in a murderous groove and with enough trippy melodies to give off a genuinely psychedelic edge. [17 Mar 2018, p.55]

Title: Shulamith
Review: For Polica, chilling out means going way below zero, resulting in an icy glitter that is seductive but ultimately freezes you out. [Dec 2013, p.112]

Title: Eagulls
Review: The Eagulls’ album does a fantastic job of funneling the band’s energy. That’s the good part. But as for the subtleties--the way that players interact, the fit between chug and melody, the depth that emerges with occasional negative space--you won’t find any of that here.

Title: De Vermis Mysteriis
Review: It is simple, it is pure, it is predictable, it is Another High on Fire Album.

Title: One Plus One Is One
Review: There are times when One Plus One Is One is simply too much, and the fresh spin that Gough brought to the British singer/songwriter tradition in his earlier work is missed, but he's still a fine addition to it.

Title: Traffic and Weather
Review: The left-bent, middle-class everymen in these songs are consistently disarming.

Title: A Rush of Blood to the Head
Review: A guitar record equally suitable for a lost weekend or a good cry. [Sep 2002, p.125]

Title: Blood Oaths of the New Blues
Review: It brings out the best in Toth both as a musician and a songwriter.

Title: Shape Shifter
Review: [Shape Shifter] has moments of s**t-hot playing (see the smeared runs on "Metatron"). But the arrangements, oversweetened with too many synthesizers, lean toward lite jazz.

Title: Panic of Girls
Review: The weakness is the music. [Aug 2011, p.79]

Title: Love in the Future
Review: Love in the Future is among Legend's best work, made for couples who are into one another for the long term while feeling a little daring and crazy.

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: As with many releases like this, I wish the ride were just a little bit more bumpy just to throw off expectations, but nonetheless Fleet Foxes have put out quite an enjoyable little debut here.

Title: Nootropics
Review: As a breathtaking study in grayscale minimalism, Nootropics is exquisite. But it dissipates the instant it touches air.

Title: Hyperspace
Review: Sometimes he hits pure signal, and sometimes it’s just background noise as he gets to wherever he’s going next.

Title: It's Me Again
Review: [Tweet] offers more mature and demure R&B this time out.

Title: The People's Key
Review: For all their diversity and maturity, these songs couldn't have been written by anyone else, and this welcome return shows that the three years since the last Bright Eyes album have been well spent.

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You
Review: It's packed with ideas, some of which work beautifully and some of which are just a joy to hear play out, but most of all, it's still a whole other world of pop music--an absolutely unique, enchanting, and irreplaceable vision of how the stuff can work.

Title: Everything Is Love
Review: It's also a sonic master class in marital counseling and commitment, wherein Beyoncé emerges with the upper hand and a contrite Jay is lucky she's so gracious. Vocally, it's a similar story: Beyoncé shines here, balancing light rap verses ("Apeshit" and "Nice") with some of the prettiest vocals she's recorded in years ("Friends"), while Jay offers his standard braggadocious bars that nonetheless make an impact for their occasional honesty and humility.

Title: Ecstasy
Review: Ecstasy is definitely a Lou Reed record for Lou Reed fans. If you're a happy regular shopper at Lou's Boutique, this one'll fit nicely on the shelf alongside all the others.

Title: Parachutes
Review: Following a path forged by fellow U.K. exports Badly Drawn Boy and Travis, still-wet-behind-the-ears quartet Coldplay prefers a folksy, familiar approach to guitar pop.

Title: Jeff Bridges
Review: Like many actors who try their hand at music, Bridges may have made this record because he could, and the acclaim for "Crazy Heart'' offered him a prime opportunity. It's so winning, however, because Bridges had something to say.

Title: The Beekeeper
Review: As a cohesive work, The Beekeeper holds together better than nearly any of Tori's more ambitious albums, but there's a certain artsy distance that keeps this from being as emotionally immediate or as memorable as her first two records.

Title: Exit
Review: Ambitious as some of that may seem, Exit never feels like a show-off record--just a thoughtfully put-together one.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: Tanlines's debut comes across as well-meaning but overly earnest, overly-invested and trying hard to do many things at once.

Title: World Gone Mad
Review: It's a solid enough LP, but it's hard to see this appealing very far beyond their fanbase. [Feb 2017, p.119]

Title: Designer
Review: Each of the tracks released from Designer so far has been engrossing – The Barrel, with its opaque lyricism (“show the ferret to the egg”), the equally gnomic Fixture Pixture, with its Air bassline.

Title: Rated R
Review: Despite the abundance of male influence on the record, from ex-boyfriend to songwriters to producers to mentors, Rihanna makes the sound her own, and fights back.
A decent follow-up from a band who has already proven themselves capable of much, much more.

Title: The Greatest
Review: It doesn't take a genius to see that this is a wicked concept on paper: Marshall's got the voice and the vibe to make it work, but there's a nagging sense that it wasn't properly planned out.

Title: Uptown Special
Review: As is, Uptown Special plays a little like a Spotify playlist on random--fun, and unexpectedly thrilling at times, but jarring and never totally satisfying.

Title: Free Reign
Review: Free Reign, co-produced by Oneohtrix Point Never's Daniel Lopatin, is subtler, jazzier and ever-so-slightly sexier than previous Clinic outings.

Title: Somewhere
Review: There are so many acts both past and present who sound exactly like this; there are moments scattered throughout Somewhere that feel a little derivative of some 90s alternative acts. So, while Somewhere is a good start, there’s a lot more to accomplish for Gum Country before they can really set themselves apart from The Courtneys – or other bands.

Title: Reggie
Review: I have no interest in warning anyone about this album's positive qualities, because they are so type-neutral. So are the negatives. Reggie is one of those veteran albums that could just as well not exist and no one would bat an eye.

Title: A Moment of Madness
Review: At 17 tracks, A Moment of Madness could be more taut and, frankly, have a bit more madness in the mix. Bizu is such a gifted vocalist that it would’ve been a treat to get a few less polished cuts.

Title: Weezer (Red Album)
Review: Aside from a few missteps like 'Everybody Get Dangerous,' there really isn’t anything to get all pissy about here because it’s an older Weezer willing to take a few chances and still doing what they want to do.

Title: Head Carrier
Review: There’s no denying that Head Carrier generally veers between sounding like an exhausted tribute to their former configuration to feeling something akin to a disposable Frank Black solo effort via a few conciliatory tracks.

Title: Pilot Talk II
Review: On the sequel, Curren$y and Ski go even further with that central idea, pushing into sleepy, smooth funk territory that fits Curren$y's rap style perfectly.

Title: No Cities Left
Review: It is true, this album does have songs and nearly all of them suffer the same fate: a few great ideas ruined by the need for everything to be so overblown and melodramatic.

Title: Contraband
Review: Mostly, it sounds like no more and a little less than one might expect (or hope for) from such a union: Scott Weiland singing over some relatively crunchy Slash guitar templates.

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: A fine record.

Title: West
Review: The greasy, hopped-up grooves of "Lazy Bones" and "Looking Out" aren't dramatic departures from West's overall drone-heavy aesthetic. But they do a lot to separate Wooden Shjips from similar bands, like the Black Angels and Dead Meadow.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: I have enough faith in this band to presume they’ll eventually see Only By the Night for what it is, as a fourth album hiccup that fails to play to their strengths.

Title: Viola Beach
Review: Despite the haunting narrative tied to the album, Viola Beach remains the sound of youth, hope, and possibility.

Title: Viola Beach
Review: [A] charming if slight collection, still worthy of your time, and not just to hear the aching, unfulfilled potential.

Title: The Messenger
Review: The Messenger duly wipes the slate clean and bursts with the same efflorescent skills that made Johnny Marr a guitar hero for the generation which had supposedly repudiated such a concept. [Mar 2013, p.90]

Title: Dead Cross
Review: Patton’s signature style is overpowering, transforming an opportunity to create something unique into another of his side-projects.

Title: Weapon
Review: Weapon stands as Skinny Puppy's strongest work since 1992's Last Rights; it's a testament to one of the few reformed bands still striving to push, not just themselves, but an entire bygone genre forward.

Title: Out from Out Where
Review: But for all its diligent progressivism, Out From Out Where collapses under its own weight, sounding every bit as stubborn and hermetic as Autechre's infamous Confield.

Title: Volta
Review: She's rarely sounded more alive. [Jun 2007, p.92]

Title: West
Review: Willner's soulful production, elegant and layered, recalls Daniel Lanois' work with Emmylou Harris. [17 Feb 2007]

Title: Consummation
Review: Consummation is a bold step forward and confirmation that Katie von Schleicher has a great deal to offer and should be creating satisfying music for a long time to come.

Title: Bad Witch
Review: Across the sixteen tracks that make up this entire project they’ve by and large avoided the awkward moments that have made listeners cringe on previous releases, they’ve finally nailed how to produce and mix Reznor’s voice so that his still somewhat heavy-handed lyricism doesn’t distract attention from the considerable craft that’s gone into the music, and they’ve found a way to organically explore new sonic avenues which mean that, while Reznor might feel like he’s trapped in a loop, doomed to continually find himself back where he’s already been, Nine Inch Nails are no longer simply repeating themselves.

Title: This Kind of Love
Review: This record’s way blander than the sassy hits she played.

Title: Gods of the Earth
Review: For the most part, it's all the same old bong-thrash, save for the record's one non-heavy trick: English-jig folk.

Title: Donker Mag
Review: Die Antwoord’s bombastic concerts and larger than life stage personas are not to be missed. However, this wild energy and devil may care attitude yield weaker dividends after being bottled and pasteurized in a studio that appears staffed by a cadre of rejected Saturday Night Live sketch writers.

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: This is exactly the type of ambition you want to hear from a young band. After making such a peppy, instant classic debut, they weren’t intimidated by the thought of a Sunday stroll album, and they reached newfound emotional and sonic heights in making one.

Title: The Night Is Young
Review: Rundell and Goddard are still crafting warm, well-balanced tracks, but the parts that reveal their personalities—namely the lyrics--are often awkward and strangely didactic.

Title: Celebration Castle
Review: Although less immediately catchy, Celebration Castle... soon warms up. [Jul 2005, p.94]

Title: Bloom
Review: It is a lot like Teen dream, but novelty is hardly the point: if Beach House are your type, then Bloom is unlikely to see the attraction wither. [Jun 2012, p.93]

Title: Hood Billionaire
Review: It's the beats, the cameos and the sheer momentum of Maybach Music that propels Hood Billionaire forward.

Title: Tomboy
Review: Sure, Lennox makes a lot of pretty noise on this album, but sometimes you just want to pluck him from his own sound waves and have him try to navigate them from the inside of a more firmly constructed ship.

Title: Citizen Zombie
Review: Citizen Zombie is more disciplined and linear than its epochal predecessors, yet it also reveals that its creators remain a force to be reckoned with.

Title: This Land
Review: This Land is the first place where Gary Clark Jr. doesn’t appear hemmed in by the past. The album may be informed by old sounds and forms, yet these familiar tropes feel fresh thanks to Clark’s idiosyncratic splicing.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: Three brisk, blood-pumping rockers pick up where the band's previous album, "Backspacer," left off.... Things falter when the band's love of '70s classic rock turns musty.... Inspiration returns on the title track, which rides Matt Cameron's roller-coaster drumming and richly layered guitars and keyboards.

Title: Excellent Italian Greyhound
Review: Greyhound has a loose, almost improvisational minimalism that straddles the line between engrossing and off-putting.

Title: Songs You Make at Night
Review: It’s a fine showcase for Tunng’s strongest set of songs in many years--happily, this seems to be one reunion that’s working out just fine.

Title: Life Metal
Review: More mellifluous than menacing despite its formidable display of power, Life Metal may be the richest work in the band's 21-year-mission to reconfigure Tony Iommi-worthy riffage into a soundtrack for mindful meditation. [May 2019, p.34]

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: In the end, though, Everything Is Borrowed's musical high points aren't enough to save it from its lyric sheet, and that, going forward, constitutes a real problem for Skinner.

Title: Wildflower
Review: A pastoral, wistful brand of psychedelia holds sway throughout this absorbing record.

Title: Highly Evolved
Review: OK, so it tails off towards the end, and there's something rather dishonest about a band so young releasing a track like '1969', but even then it's quite endearing to see them trying to build such an immediate mythology around themselves.

Title: 4eva Is a Mighty Long Time
Review: Big K.R.I.T. does a good job of separating the two personas at the end of the day. If the album was about 5 or 6 minutes shorter, it could have fit on a single disc but perhaps at the expense of the narrative. The double disc format really helps to drive home the point when the listener wants to switch from Big K.R.I.T.'s "Get Away" to Justin Scott's "Keep the Devil Off."

Title: Piano
Review: These are tracks that could easily be ballads slipped into a Hot Chip record, but where there they’d be bolstered with synths and programmed beats, here they are stark and knowingly bold in their simplicity.

Title: Out of Season
Review: Out Of Season makes Portishead's remarkable innovations sound like so much extra baggage to Gibbons' voice.

Title: Mantasy
Review: Whilst it isn't flawless, it's as accomplished as it is experimental and it seems to improve with each spin.

Title: Trust Me
Review: Trust Me opens with a triptych of horn-section-and-samples R&B numbers that bounce along pleasantly, even if they can't quite shake off the cut-price dancefloor feeling that permeates so much British pop; but they are still preferable to the succession of puppy-eyed ballads, almost wholly devoid of interest or edge, which follow.

Title: Swim
Review: Caribou's newest set, "Swim," which contains more electronic elements than its pop-traced predecessor, is a major step forward for Snaith.

Title: Labyrinth
Review: Kanda’s aptitude for melody is mixed and sometimes abandons him altogether, making the likes of Enigma and Garnet rudderless, but when he locks into one, his work becomes really compelling.

Title: Good Luck and Do Your Best
Review: Choppy beats and rhythms along with shuffling percussion helps create a feeling of urban movement and flux. There is a swagger to the songs that is hard to ignore--Panda has created the album that he has always hinted at.

Title: Meteora
Review: Harder, denser, uglier. [#15, p.128]

Title: More Light
Review: As it develops, it shows off a new side to them once again, one which wants to make records which draw on their experience rather than trying to do something completely new, and that in itself puts More Light up their with their best.

Title: Ssss
Review: The most potent and inventive electronica album I've heard in ages, a masterclass in punchy bleepscaping right from the low-register throb that opens "Lowly".

Title: Madvillainy
Review: All invention and no indulgence. [Jun 2004, p.110]

Title: Indie Cindy
Review: Indie Cindy delivers a relatively gratifying 12 track-journey that, at the least, yields some classic-sounding Pixies tunes.

Title: Favourite Worst Nightmare
Review: Favourite moves forward not one inch from Whatever, which is safe and reliable, but also repetitive. [#17, p.82]

Title: Lex Hives
Review: Lex Hives may not re-write The Hives' rulebook, it does offer proof that this band sounds heftier and, somehow, even more colorful than before. [2 Jun 2012, p.54]

Title: Welcome 2 My Nightmare
Review: This new nightmare falls short of the original, with several songs misfiring. [Nov 2011, p.93]

These heartfelt, confessional apologies are delivered via Jay’s most concise, straightforward album in years. 10 tracks and 36 minutes long, this is a filler-free return to form after 2013’s patchy and bloated ‘Magna Carta Holy Grail’.

Title: Anything in Return
Review: Return is neither a step up or down from 2010's wave-warping Causers of This or 2011's time-warping Underneath the Pine, yet it's not more of the same.

Title: No Time for Dreaming
Review: No Time For Dreaming not only prevails as a defining culmination of Bradley's lifelong musicianship to date, but also furthers the argument that Daptone Records can do no wrong.

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: It is more songful than anything Lopatin has done.

Title: HoboSapiens
Review: His most direct, energised and modernist work in years.

Title: No Wow
Review: It's a brutal record that changes you the same way prison changes a man.

Title: The Eclipse Sessions
Review: From dive-bar romps to plaintive reflection, this is his strongest collection for some time. [Nov 2018, p.30]

Title: In Light
Review: The formula of cramming 30 different songs into one is fun for a while, and it's invigorating, but ultimately it's hard to shake a sense of over-indulgence.

Title: Heavy Meta
Review: This is tough, smart, impassioned rock & roll with a sense of purpose and lots of swagger, performed with the confidence of a veteran and the scrap of a newcomer. It's heady stuff well worth your attention.

Title: Razorlight
Review: The solipsism and trite accounts of benders from the first album are still there, but the music has gone exceedingly soft.

Title: Sequel To The Prequel
Review: All in all, Sequel To The Prequel is a consistent and accomplished return from Babyshambles.

Title: 3001: A Laced Odyssey
Review: An excellent debut that flows perfectly and offers something new with every return.

Title: Real
Review: Loveless' songwriting on Real is sharp, economical and wickedly funny. [Sep 2016, p.77]

Title: Catacombs
Review: McCombs still has an ear for language and roll-off-the-tongue singing. His voice coats the lyrics like thick warm caramel on this one. Though often obtuse and twisted, McCombs includes some straightforward lyrics, as well, with some political commentary to boot.

Title: Peasant
Review: Peasant pulls every strand of Dawson’s work together to create something that might actually resemble accessible songwriting were it not so contorted by its own filthy humanity. It is utterly unique music, reminiscent perhaps of the complex, gnarled story-songs purveyed by Mayo Thompson and Joanna Newsom, but taken to much darker, more physical extremes.

Title: Born to Sing: No Plan B
Review: Fans of the old stuff who long ago wrote Morrison off will find their gripes sadly confirmed on Born to Sing: No Plan B, a recession album that's four years too late.

Title: I Hate Music
Review: This record is so good we don't need to focus on those details. With I Hate Music, Superchunk will once again land near the top of my year-end list.

Title: Benjamin Booker
Review: It’s tough and grimy but you have to wonder how many others are out there bashing out similarly trashy rock who haven’t gotten Booker’s breaks

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: Some of the arrangements wouldn't be that bad if they hadn't been sampled and sequenced to death. But if over-producing the life out of something is one thing, any use of the dreaded Auto-Tune facility is another. It runs through A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships like the plague to the point where numerous listens later I still have no idea what Matty Healy's actual singing voice sounds like.

Title: Jiaolong
Review: For those who seek out dancefloors in order to witness the unravelling of an electronic journey, this is one of only a handful albums this year to have delivered exactly that. Fewer still have done so with such distinctness.

Title: Rough and Rowdy Ways
Review: Rough and Rowdy Ways is the work of a man in love with language and philosophy, and, at 79, he continues to take the pulse of the zeitgeist with unerring precision. He ain't no false prophet, he's an artist, he don't look back.

Title: I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass
Review: What's most remarkable about this stylistic portmanteau is that every song is an original even though you assume several are among their shoulda-been-a-hit-but-wtf-is-it? covers.

Title: Possession
Review: Possession is buffed-up, scruffy and forthright gutter metal par excellence.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: A stunning effort. Solange creates such fully realized art that even when she may be expressing uncertainty and doubt, she’s charging herself--and her audience--with finding possibility.

Title: The Moon Rang Like A Bell
Review: Hundred Waters lay out all their cards on this album and use every single tiny part for all its worth.

Title: The Terror
Review: By matching their ever-evolving, exploratory musical ethos with less eager-to-please, more confrontational modes of performance, the album marks the moment when the Flaming Lips become whole again.

Title: Eton Alive
Review: Sleaford Mods' eleventh album is a remarkable leap on from 2017's English Tapas, a record of consolidation that addressed the strange situation that the duo found themselves in--going from a niche concern more accustomed to playing alongside noise artists suddenly given column inches and selling out massive venues. This progress has come hand in hand with a keener knack for more fully developed tunes to bolster Williamson's hectoring. It is also, frequently, a hilarious record.

Title: So You Wannabe An Outlaw
Review: More than a reclamation, Outlaw suggests the miles traveled imbue a more fluid application of his roots attack and tattered romanticism.

Title: American Interior
Review: It's another tour de force for Wales' musical explorer-in-chief, packed with the fine tunecraft, psychedelic references and experimental instrumentation we've come to expect from him.

Title: Fall Be Kind
Review: Thus, when not overextending the disappointing, unfinished musical projects on Fall Be Kind's, the Collective are busy beating their promising ideas into monotony.

Title: As If Apart
Review: While not discernably stronger or weaker than the record that preceded it, As If Apart burrows deeper into its maker's sonic pet obsessions. This is a work of accessible insularity, outsider pop from a tinkering songsmith who understands all the inner workings of the genre.

Title: My Way
Review: All shuffling beats and pub wisdom, it's same again for Brown's latest.

Title: Going Back Home
Review: If the production is too clean, it does at least reveal Johnson in glorious high definition with his Telecaster, simultaneously stabbing the chords while letting the licks bleed out with liquid heat.

Title: You're Dreaming
Review: At the heart of the mood is something that only comes naturally: the plaintive croon of hand-in-glove brotherly harmonies.

Title: A Weird Exits
Review: Time has been kind to Thee Oh Sees, who remain proper royalty in the garage rock universe and manage to shape-shift without losing their boisterous and impactful delivery.

Title: Overgrown Path
Review: For a record that initially seems nothing more than a charming little reverie, it's difficult to shake off. [Dec 2012, p.102]

Title: Your Future Our Clutter
Review: Oddball, but articulate, brimming over with a delight in language, "Bury" is a wonderful example of Mark Smith's transformative science fiction, and pretty much what one would hope to find on The Fall's first album for Domino records.

Title: Straight No Chaser
Review: Pretty much every song on Straight No Chaser is a future pop anthem of powerhouse proportions.

Title: Last Man Standing
Review: Willie Nelson, 85, keeps going from strength-to-strength, and Last Man Standing is the strongest yet.

Title: Æ’IN
Review: Modestly anthemic and quietly anthemic, ƒIN is worth the time of any music fan that considers themselves in the slightest bit interested in electronic music.

Title: Wreckorder
Review: Wreckorder;s main virtues--decent songs, solidly played--are also its downfall, and you end up wondering why Healy bothered taking a vacation only to stay at home. [Nov 2010, p.90]

Title: Winter Wheat
Review: The mood is pained, the production suitably spare, pushing the singer's understated lyricism to the fore. [Jan 2017, p.28]

Title: Revelations
Review: Bracing stuff. [Oct 2006, p.127]

Title: Junk
Review: The touch is lighter, with more interest in groove and atmosphere than climax. [No. 131, p.59]

Title: 4 Your Eyez Only
Review: With 4 Your Eyez Only, J. Cole deserves consideration for tugging at the heartstrings of listeners with raw human emotion but still leaves open the door to reach a musical zenith.

Title: Putrifiers II
Review: If it sounds like Thee Oh Sees have matured, you'd be right.

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: Night Thoughts grabs hold immediately and only tightens its grip with each listen.

Title: Dreams Come True
Review: Taylor doesn't get caught up in making his sounds too big, too large, or too much. He could, but he doesn't. He maintains control, doesn't get lost, and the result are nothing short of terrific.

Title: I Slept On The Floor
Review: Vincent's voice is so unusual and beguiling, it almost detracts from the lyrics, but they eventually punch through. ... Vincent and Another Sky enthrall. [Sep 2020, p.88]

Title: Blood Pressures
Review: Blood Pressures is a compelling forty minutes, and by the time we reach the closer, Pots and Pans, with a slider and twelve bar riffs to accompany its sultry, resonant admissions, you can barely imagine them any other way.

Title: Milk Cow Blues
Review: Misconceived is the polite word.

Title: American Head
Review: Far from a rehash of the band's previous glories, American Head feels transformational; at once magical and down-to-earth, it's the album the Flaming Lips needed to make and fans needed to hear at this point in their career.

Title: Hoodstar
Review: The majority of tracks scream "poor old bored celeb." [Nov 2006, p.139]

Title: Glitter in the Gutter
Review: Malin has seemingly adopted the persona and sound of his New Jersey counterpart Bruce Springsteen.

Title: The Platform
Review: DJ Babu's sample wizardry and scratching are impeccable, as are Rakaa and Evidence's agile rhymes, but their rigorous insistence on old-skool B-boy values leaves little room for risk-taking. [July 2000, p.106]

Title: Cosmic Wink
Review: Sultry, compelling and ever so slightly spooked, Cosmic Wink flickers and flashes like a series of time-lapse landscape photographs, but the place it documents is the heart. [Jun 2018, p.36]

Title: Lantern
Review: A relatively disjointed assembly of tracks seemingly drawn from working folders labeled like "athletic anthems," "theatrical intros and interludes," "almost pop," "space ballads," and "misc."

Title: Strange Trails
Review: "Fool for Love" wouldn't have survived the twisting soundscapes of the frontman's initial EP, but it offers the same sweeping vistas.

Title: August By Cake
Review: August By Cake is Robert Pollard's 100th album, and a double album to boot. Not only that but a great double album.

Title: Delta Machine
Review: It blows hot and cold.

Title: pom pom
Review: The first half or so of pom pom proves Ariel Pink is still a pretty formidable songwriter.... From there, the structure seemingly breaks away, as Pink indulges in further left-field whims that are often more novel than gratifying.

Title: Hendra
Review: There’s an aching pain that throbs throughout Hendra. But as the personal suffering that shapes the album is lamented, there is a clear cathartic quality to these songs.

Title: Transit Transit
Review: Transit Transit justly follows the digitalized distortion their debut paved, keeping a decidedly drab mood that permeates throughout the entire production.

Title: Future Brown
Review: It lives and dies on its guest vocalists: female MC Tink shines on "Wanna Party," as does grime veteran Riko Dan on "Speng." Elsewhere, a reliance on drab Auto-Tune crooning can drag. [Mar 2015, p.76]

Title: The Adventures of Ghosthorse and Stillborn
Review: It's not everyone's glass of absinthe, but Adventures will find a happy reception among listeners who want an occasional hallucination to go with their usual woozy drunkenness. [#75, p.94]

Title: No World
Review: The overall effect is pleasantly daydreamy, though the album quickly settles into one gear.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: Thr33 Ringz emerges as such a polished and self-fulfilling collection of hip-pop singles that it almost makes one wonder why T-Pain insists on drawing attention to the most derivative aspect of his musical career at the expense of some of his other, modest but real talents.

Title: Furr
Review: There’s no room for filler here; momentum carries on and roams wide but never eases.

Title: CrasH Talk
Review: At 40 minutes, this is easily Q's leanest LP. It would be meaner with the removal of the inane Travis Scott collaboration "CHopstix," the uncharacteristic single.

Title: None Shall Pass
Review: Essentially, it’s the effects of Aesop’s modesty that keeps him afloat above some of his equally skilled contemporaries. (This, in addition to the dope factor, more than makes up for the moment when the album overwhelms and shapes into a part-primal/part-industrial drone.)

Title: Metallic Spheres
Review: The only hint of intrigue comes 40-odd minutes into the record, when Youth takes up his mighty bass for "Chicago Dub," which briefly changes the pace for the better.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: It's a record that doesn't undermine their body of work, but nor does it stand out as a career-defining highlight.

Title: Again Into Eyes
Review: Again Into Eyes only truly perks up near the end when they call up their inner Psychedelic Furs on more straightforwardly swooning ballads like "Faith Unfolds."

Title: Derdang Derdang
Review: It's a journey through the West Country trio's brand of infectious bluesy garage rock and evocative of a head on collision between The Kills and the Arcade Fire.

Title: Hollandaze
Review: Hollandaze is an impressive debut.

Title: Franz Ferdinand
Review: Fearsomely post-post-punk, appealingly brazen, and ambitiously tight, they have indeed made The Album That Saved Indie.

Title: Meadow
Review: Meadow features Buckner's most focused work in years.

Title: Antidotes
Review: Fantastic. This is the best new band Sub Pop has worked with in years. [June 2008, p.131]

Title: Send Away the Tigers
Review: This is a band playing to its strengths.

Title: The Other Side
Review: While fans of Tonight Alive's debut will quickly fall in love with their sophomore effort, anyone looking for some powerful new emo-pop will definitely want to check this one out.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II
Review: For now, this is a hypnotic, well executed, if not altogether thrilling collection.

Title: The Rest Is Scenery
Review: If it doesn't reach the sustained invention of John Coltrane's odyssey in E, Africa/Brass, Youngs' talent for wringing emotion from base materials remain undimmed. [Jan 2017, p.102]

Title: Nothing Is Wrong
Review: Tay Strathairn's work on the keys shines on just about every song; Wylie Gelber maybe one of the most tasteful bassists ever, and Griffin Goldsmith's percussion is rock steady and incredibly impressive, especially considering his young age. But it is the sum of all these parts that makes Nothing is Wrong something truly special.

Title: Sparks
Review: It sometimes walks the line between close listening and a wash of sound, but it's intriguing from whatever angle it is approached.

Title: The Boombox Ballads
Review: Some structural confusion aside, it's easy to embrace his Johnny-Flynn-does-indie songs. [Oct 2015, p.98]

Title: SUGAREGG
Review: Bully’s third album is nonetheless breezy, it’s unapologetic in its raggedness, and even if they aren’t exactly reinventing the wheel they still align perfectly with each other and support Bognanno wonderfully. Bully are still pushing the painful narrative begun on Feels Like, and SUGAREGG is a continuation of those themes in a way that works powerfully for them.

Title: Family of Love
Review: None of it is forgetful and all of it is more than enjoyable.

Title: Peaceful, the World Lays Me Down
Review: Perhaps it's just that the rest of the songs aren't up to scratch, but this album is a simple case of diminishing returns--what appeared carefree and sparkly-eyed to begin with feels more and more calculated as you go on, what first seemed endearing ends up feeling a little irritating.

Title: Confessions of a Dangerous Mind
Review: Fun and compelling as such high points can be, nothing on this album reaches the strata of the title track.

Title: Around The Sun
Review: As arena folk goes, R.E.M. remain cooler than, say, the Wallflowers. Just barely. [8 Oct 2004, p.114]

Title: Homesongs
Review: Homesongs is his minor key playground, filled with masterpieces in the making. All you have to do to enjoy them is slow... down...

Title: Cut Your Teeth
Review: Pop’s going through a renaissance of sorts lately, or more accurately, the chart-dominating pop is, and alongside the aforementioned, La Grange is leading the charge of the nu-pop brigade. Avoid at your peril; the record’s not for missing.

Title: Get Born
Review: There's a raw urgency to the album that belies its dated influences. [Oct 2003, p.108]

Title: Destroyed
Review: Darkly neurotic, it captures the on-the-road loneliness and sense of dislocation perfectly. [Jun 2011, p.97]

Title: American Interior
Review: It's Rhys's empathy with Evans and the humour and pathos with which he conveys his young protagonist's emotions that makes this such a vivid and exhilarating journey.

Title: Shadows
Review: Lacking the hooks and spirit of subversion that framed most of their previous efforts, the songs of Shadows require patience and understanding to reveal oft-hidden strength of voice within.

Title: City of Refuge
Review: While the album is perhaps not as wholly satisfying as 2007's "In The Vines" and could benefit from a tighter structure, City Of Refuge, aided by contributions from Jana Hunter, Scott Tuma, and Sufjan Stevens, among others, sees Castanets craft passages of evocative, dusty beauty. [Fall 2008, p.74]

Title: Light Up Gold
Review: A finely crafted collection of indie rock.

Title: Louden Up Now
Review: Eighties punk-funk meets '60s idealism and reefer-toking? Make way for the hipster hippies. [#27, p.134]

Title: Stillmatic
Review: Sadly, the cuts that reveal Nas' depth and drive get lost in a jumble of sloppy filler.

Title: Pure
Review: Numan is now crafting music that sounds identical to his disciples. [Nov 2000, p.118]

Title: Airdrawndagger
Review: The album will wear thin on short-attention-spanned listeners who need their dance albums dosed with a bit more variety. [Aug 2002, p.79]

Title: Good Fruit
Review: While TEEN have covered all of this ground before, this is some of their most cohesive and satisfying music. As its title implies, Good Fruit is the result of thriving after hardship, and its sense of accomplishment is especially sweet.

Title: Hold on Pain Ends
Review: One of the most hard-hitting records of the year. [30 Aug 2014, p.52]

Title: Tetsuo & Youth
Review: It's a tricky muse, but every Lupe project has found a way to harness at least 15 or 20 minutes of his fluid, fleeting mind. Tetsuo & Youth is the most generous gulp he's managed in years.

Title: One of Us Is the Killer
Review: Overall, since their formation in 1997, The Dillinger Escape Plan have seamlessly fused math metal with aspects of pop and jazz, a trend that wholeheartedly continues on One Of Us Is The Killer.

Title: Music for Falling From Trees
Review: Music for Falling from Trees is somewhat reminiscent of Arcade Fire offshoot the Bell Orchestre’s debut album, yet it succeeds in being more of a set work, and has fewer indie signifiers, even with background noise and fuzzily mic-ed strings.

Title: Above the City
Review: This stop on the journey is pretty magical.

Title: Arcadia
Review: The delightfully obtuse and sometimes anxious sketches on Arcadia are what make it both enjoyable, and frustrating.

Title: Blank Project
Review: It’s a stark but warm-blooded product of avant-garde pop, just the sort of album you might have once hoped for from Ms. Cherry, whose singing is still limber and unlabored, earthy but cool.

Title: The New Abnormal
Review: The New Abnormal cements their continued relevance when many had been written them off, and as ever they don’t seem to care either way.

Title: Sentenced to Life
Review: Sentenced to Life mostly retreads 2010 Southern Lord debut Heavy Breathing, but with boosted boom and production clarity.

Title: Amnesty (I)
Review: This is an unpredictable album, thrillingly and engagingly so.

Title: Satanic Panic in the Attic
Review: Of Montreal have safely entrenched themselves as an institution in the indie rock world, and Satanic Panic shows them as dependable as ever for some of the best pop songs around.

Title: II Trill
Review: II Trill but never too trill, the second solo swagger from UGKer Bun B spins triumphant, Houston hip-hop ripped both in celebration of properly executed gangster prophecies and passed partner-in-slang Pimp C.

Title: Desire Lines
Review: Camera Obscura's done it again.

Title: Power of Anonymity
Review: Power of Anonymity is a masterclass in the sleight-of-hand that we call techno; there is virtuosity in the music's very attempts to sneak past under the cover of darkness. It may pass unidentified, but it will not go unnoticed.

Title: Love From London
Review: Love From London is by no means an Earth-shaking or life-changing record, but its virtues are plentiful, and so well balanced that its title is by equal measures sarcastic and sincere.

Title: The Slow Wonder
Review: Newman pens melodies that seem to have sprung from the collective unconscious and then encases them in bright, lush power-pop arrangements.

Title: Assume Form
Review: Assume Form casts Blake’s prior albums in a new light, as does the once-secretive young maestro’s new openness about his life and his struggles. What sounded like someone trying to dive down into the inkiest depths of his soul turns out to have been someone trying to swim up out of them.

Title: Night of Hunters
Review: Night of Hunters is a beautiful, smart record, but it's also, by design, an obtuse and insular album by an artist who already skews pretty far in those directions.

Title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy
Review: Where things ought to be reduced and given more purpose, they instead stampede into goodness-knows-where. Ambition doesn’t always equal perfection. Rock operas have their place, but this isn’t the pick of the bunch.

Title: Perpetuum Mobile
Review: Evern more so than on Silence Is Sexy... a few telling elements are deployed to dramatic effect here. [Feb 2004, p.98]

Title: Player Piano
Review: It's out with the neon-fugged, reverb-soaked beats of 2009's Seek Magic and in with straight-up, catchy tunes. [Aug. 2011, p. 100]

Title: Tales from the Realm of the Queen of Pentacles
Review: It shows that a talented, visionary singer-songwriter can comfortably do what she does so well, yet not be trapped by conventionality.

Title: All We Grow
Review: Down to the near-microscopic details, down to the faintest rough edge on his smoothest vocal landscapes, down to the last moments on the final track: it's a self-sustaining, well-rounded album that stands well without Bon Iver-especially without a drum solo.

Title: Mechanism
Review: Retro-kosmische pastiche is now firmly established as a lazy good-taste signifier, but it does not excuse mundane plodders such as "Turncoat" or "Motorbath." Thankfully, Soft Error move beyond retro-hipster orthodoxy on their best tracks. [Feb 2017, p.38]

Title: The Beautiful Lie
Review: Wading through almost an hour of smoky-voiced lonely-heart ballads like You Only Call Me When You're Drunk, Late Night Partner and Until Tomorrow Then is a yawn-inducing exercise that makes you question whether Harcourt's really this sad or if he's just putting on a lugubrious front.

Title: Good Bad Not Evil
Review: 'O Katrina!' which kicks off like any lovesick Nuggets stomp, then drops the line "I can't believe what's on the TV screen." We're not hearing about a jilted girl anymore, but a jilted city. And before that can sink in, another wonderfully scuzzy guitar solo is on its way.

Title: Britney
Review: Britney is by far her most personable album, the most consistently playful and the least wince-inducing.

Title: The Golden Age of Apocalypse
Review: Bruner has some pretty sweet, vibey chops that he deploys sporadically here. If cultivated, he could deliver that skewed-fusion, weed hazed love letter he's attempted here. In the meantime, best to let him noodle it out on his own.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: "I Wanna Talk 2 U", [is] just one highlight of an album which manages to be sonically inventive, dense and complex and melodically accessible.

Title: Neighborhoods
Review: The weighty aesthetic makes the punky bombast all that more effective and fascinating but also tends to swallow it up in an ocean of melodrama.

Title: Free at Last
Review: Behind-the-boards stalwarts like Bink and Dame Grease provide plenty of soulful hip-hop, but the chemistry isn't quite the same.

Title: On an Island
Review: In the end, Island makes Dave sound like he's just not enthusiastic about making music anymore.

Title: Until In Excess, Imperceptible UFO
Review: The Besnard Lakes' fourth album doesn't really add anything new to the heady concoction of symphonic shoegaze, doo-wop and spy stories they perfected on 2007's Are The Dark Horse, but it's always a pleasure to hear them work up a storm. [May 2013, p.67]

Title: The Future's Void
Review: What's most disappointing of all about The Future's Void is that, for all its heady ideas and pretty moments, in almost all ways it's a regression from Anderson's earlier work, a mishmash of half-completed thoughts that fails to ever fully connect.

Title: Tell 'Em I'm Gone
Review: The production and playing are beautiful throughout the album, and Yusuf’s voice remains remarkably preserved, still able to instantly spring from gentle introspection to emphatic eruptions. The record as a whole does suffer, though, from certain cover choices.

Title: Age Against The Machine
Review: The result is a set of gripping, euphoric grooves carrying raps that indicate a new-found maturity.

Title: Alpine Static
Review: Alpine Static, while inherently visceral, is also emotionally gripping.

Title: Modern Kosmology
Review: At all points Modern Kosmology feels like a single inspired continuum of pop songs. The confidence Weaver exhibits in holding them together in balance is well-earned and it is a satisfying spectacle that a rather underappreciated artist should find her moment nearly 25 years into her career.

Title: Sun Giant
Review: Although there is much to like about the album, it can be difficult to differentiate one from another.

Title: Korn III: Remember Who You Are
Review: Korn III (a reference to this lineup as the third incarnation of the band) moves forward more than it retrenches, referencing some stylistic trademarks while introducing some fresh dynamic sensibilities.

Title: Good News For People Who Love Bad News
Review: For all its transcendent moments, Good News ultimately fails to hold together all that well as an album.

Title: Brass
Review: Brass is certainly an easier record to wrap your mind around than Flux Outside. But, with one too many good-not-great melodies and that nagging sense that these guys are holding something back, it's also a whole lot less likely to get itself lodged in your skull.

Title: Asleep on the Floodplain
Review: With Asleep On the Floodplain, Chasny returns not just to his personal roots, but also to the roots of popular music itself.

Title: Bobby Fuller Died for Your Sins
Review: The overall mood is bright, hovering somewhere between the lyrical directness of Jonathan Richman and the West Coast energy of Tom Petty. [Mar 2017, p.37]

Title: One People One World
Review: Kuti and Positive Force don't let up at all during One People One World. Impeccably sequenced, it runs from strength to strength, dazzling with expansive sonic textures, killer arrangements, and a musical genre palette that exists seemingly without boundaries. As a recording artist, Kuti has been reliably consistent, but this date is his masterpiece.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: You’re Dead! is his most confidently structured work yet.

Title: New Epoch
Review: Just because Goth Trad now plays within comfortable parameters doesn't mean that New Epoch is a bad album,however it's more disappointing than it might have been had it not come from an artist who has a high pedigree for experimentation and purports to be mapping out a new identity for his homeland.

Title: Challengers
Review: Challengers certainly gets tastier after you’ve chewed on it for a bit.

Title: The Medicine Show
Review: In essence a tonic, The Medicine Show is a little bit more of what the world need now. [May 2019, p.93]

Title: Breakout
Review: On closer inspection, it's clear Cyrus is hell-bent on stepping out of that pop princess territory--but only just.

Title: 100th Window
Review: The downside is a lack of innovation that has always accompanied Massive Attack's recordings. [#3, p.86]

Title: To Be Still
Review: The poetry on To Be Still is sometimes a bit too delicate for my taste, but the songs show off much more than words alone. They display a quirky vocal talent and songwriting skill.

Title: Sirens
Review: Sirens runs swimmingly from track to track, and it’s ideal to consume it without a tracklist; listening as its samples, beats, and voices travel without a map or a compass. It’s clear Jaar wanted to do something similar to what the average listener considers to be an “album”, but making a strong case for his intentions takes patience. Contrary to pop music and accessibility at large, it works well in his favor.

Title: Field of Reeds
Review: Ambition often manifests itself into self-indulgence, and from the off you're convinced Field Of Reed could slip into said territory. But it's an exceptional case, where its makers hit the jackpot, where imagination runs riot and gets away with every daring feat, each one more foolish than the previous.

Title: Crush Songs
Review: More a record to crush on than fall in love with, but free it from expectations and it'll take a small part of your heart.

Title: The Church of Rock and Roll
Review: The Church of Rock and Roll is a transitional album from a band looking where to go next.

Title: Heroes to Zeros
Review: Dropping the experimentation down a notch seems to have allowed a great batch of songs to shine through. [#7]

Title: Loose
Review: Furtado's style-hopping nature makes her a never less-than-interesting artist, but it doesn't work to her advantage when it occurs within the same record, and that's what ultimately keeps Loose from cohering as a singularly great pop album the way her prior efforts did.

Title: Happy Hollow
Review: In the end it’s the guitars, which alternate from restrained, melodic jangles to serrated feedback screams, and the general sense that Happy Hollow chronicles life during wartime that hold these 14 tune together, hymns or otherwise.

Title: TFCF
Review: Acoustic guitar features, alongside synths, samples and field recordings, but for all their adventurism, these songs have structure. Still, diversity rules. [Sep 2017, p.32]

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: Even tighter and more flamboyant than 2009's Far, [What We Saw From the Cheap Seats] may be her best.

Title: Let Us Never Speak of It Again
Review: They're better at evoking turbulence than talking about it--efforts to cop '80s-pop vocals are overshadowed by the cascade and rumble of the instrumental long-players. [Apr 2005, p.102]

Title: Obsidian
Review: Obsidian makes for a totally immersive plunge and, depending on where you are with your own head when you listen, either a welcome gulp of fresh air in recognition or a chance to hold your breath and dive deeply into life’s darker materials until you have to come back up again.

Title: Ravedeath, 1972
Review: It might lack the narrative arc of 09's An Imaginary Country, but it's hard to imagine that 2011 will see many finer releases, of any genre.

Title: Ten New Songs
Review: Beneath the plasticky politeness is the same old wry fatalism that the likes of Smog continue to strive for.

Title: A Kiss Before You Go
Review: A Kiss Before You Go has its fingers in so many pies that it's unlikely to be appreciated entirely by many, but listened to in small portions, it's difficult not to be enamored by its inventiveness and inherent avant-garde charm.

Title: Life Without Sound
Review: It’s a chugging, nimble-footed affair, showing a matured and restrained group; no more eight-minute-plus pounding, slashing jams, replaced instead with a sense of clarity and focus, a driving, raw sonic thesis statement.

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: Both [discs] are full of surprises. [Oct 2004, p.115]

Title: Love Letters
Review: Metronomy must have many more experimental ideas to sift through before settling down with any one particular sound, just failing to come up with a compelling, powerful way to tell this story.

Title: California Nights
Review: Granted, they may not be reinventing the wheel, but the duo feel reinvigorated.

Title: To Believe
Review: To Believe is heartbreakingly brilliant: a collection of exquisitely assembled songs that appear delicate from a distance before revealing a close-quarters core strength. ... A triumph.

Title: Welcome to the Monkey House
Review: There are fewer acerbic-tinged, catchy pop tracks that made thier last two efforts so essential. [Oct 2003, p.86]

Title: Working Class Woman
Review: Davidson’s Working Class Woman is smart, intriguing and deserves to be heralded as one of the year’s most inventive releases--Lord knows she’s worked hard enough for it.

Title: Young Hunger
Review: For the most part this album, while as slickly produced as the classic pop it references, only faintly smoulders without igniting.

Title: Workaround
Review: Her debut LP eschews 4/4 rhythms to create a loose-limbed, free-ranging treat. [Feb 2020, p.91]

Title: Idiology
Review: This record isn't as masterful as the last, partially because they're trying out new things, many of which -- horns, vocals, ska(!) -- are old things. [Jul 2001, p.134]

Title: All Rise: A Joyful Elegy for Fats Waller
Review: This set manages to be reverent to Waller's original recordings, but since facsimile was never the goal, it also manages to create a completely new veneer for them, and the end result is a marvelous tribute that still retains its own shape and coherency.

Title: Tha Carter V
Review: The most surprising takeaway from Tha Carter V, it turns out, isn’t that Wayne still has music this vital in him. It’s that after all these years, there’s still more to learn about him.

Title: Excavation
Review: As the Richard Harris exhibition showed, by enabling us to momentarily confront our own mortality, morbid artistic meditations on death can be oddly and overwhelmingly uplifting.

Title: Slowly Paradise
Review: Chenaux has made a gorgeously hypnotic record that feels like a genuine break from life's often aggressive pace.

Title: Lotta Sea Lice
Review: By eschewing ambition in favor of intimacy, the album is both comfortable and comforting. While Barnett and Vile don’t travel far from their established sounds in their collaboration, the sum of their contributions yields fresh results.

Title: Missiles
Review: On the Dears’ fourth album, the Montreal melancholics take simple melodies and spin them into seamless epics.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: Its 10th full-length album in two decades as a band, the band pulls back from that intensity but adds layers of depth and surprise.

Title: God Level
Review: It is the best distillation yet of his tortured hustler mystique.

Title: In and Out of Youth and Lightness
Review: Future Heart is the album's standout moment because it represents a rare moment of cathartic release, the band finally letting their brooding rhythm swell into something nearly anthemic. Young Widows do it well, but a little less restraint would do them one better.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: But she's not attempting a simple 80's revival; for all the vaguely familiar hooks, there are also sustained, wistful overlays of strings and acoustic guitar that enfold the music like a haze of indistinct memory. [14 Nov 2005]

Title: AM
Review: Arctic Monkeys arrive at the end of AM a lot wiser than they may have appeared from the slow opening stomp of the LP.

Title: Kid Face
Review: Vanderslice's arrangements glide between loping acoustic strums, delicate picking, and stately piano chords, though for such a quiet affair, Kid Face has a surprisingly sturdy bottom end.

Title: Feels Like Home
Review: There simply isn't another singer working in pop music now that holds a candle to Jones.

Title: No Geography
Review: It certainly has a strong first half, opening with "Eve of Destruction" and "Bango," a pair of high-energy tracks that play to the Chems' strengths. ... Similarly, just-okay tracks like "We've Got to Try," while boasting some exciting elements, seem b-tier in light of past triumphs. That said, even b-tier work from the Chemical Brothers is worthy of interest--an opportunity to respect one's elders.

Title: The Historical Conquests of Josh Ritter
Review: What makes The Historical Conquests Of... a great album and not just Ritter’s foray into stylistic versatility is the integrity of his musicianship. The album is thorough; it is complete.

Title: Sexwitch
Review: A record unlike anything else you will hear this year.

Title: Do You Know Squarepusher
Review: His most diverse collection of songs to date.

Title: Give Up
Review: A pleasurable but uneven set that makes for occasionally compelling, but not addictive, listening.

Title: The Winter of Mixed Drinks
Review: The emotional immediacy of a jilted lover has been replaced with a series of tired metaphors, and as a result The Winter Of Mixed Drinks falls significantly short of its predecessor. [Winter 2010, p.82]

Title: Audioslave
Review: They just want to rock you into peaceful submission, and they are successful about 70 percent of the time. [Dec 2002, p.135]

Title: Slave to the Game
Review: It's the band--and Sturgis--who make Slave To The Game the most impressive album to date from the most underrated band in deathcore. [May 2012, p.72]

Title: Made in the Dark
Review: They're still a quirky band, no doubt, but now they're using those quirks to make their most accomplished album to date.

Title: Haunted Cities
Review: The whole package ends up having this strangely alluring glimmer. It's like discovering California Babylon after being lost in suburbia.

Title: Smother
Review: Overall, Smother seems to be missing purpose. I hear those careful ruminations on relationships, and I hear the pain that evidently went into this, but it leaves me cold.

Title: The Argument
Review: This is an encouraging partial return to form from an underrated talent.

Title: High Hopes
Review: The cumulative effect of this mass of old, borrowed, blue and renewed – covers, recent outtakes and redefining takes on two classics--is retrospect with a cutting edge, running like one of the singer's epic look-ma-no-set-list gigs: full of surprises, all with a reason for being there.

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: Political metaphors abound on this eclectically ramshackle collection. [Mar 2012, p.98]

Title: Blood Money
Review: Blood Money should be heard as a complete piece of music -- like watching a play -- and some tracks that might appear thin on their own will be revealed as far meatier in context.

Title: Everybody Come to Church
Review: A surprisingly coherent batch of soured psychedelia. [3 Oct 2015, p.52]

Title: Burn and Shiver
Review: Their second album only partially makes good on their promise, delivering a lovely package that lacks the emotional punch of last year's terrific self-titled debut. [#55, p.70]

Title: Glow
Review: Glow is an epic achievement, an album that bolsters its disco-flecked gems with 80s funk, Euro synth-pop and chunky 90s house tropes.

Title: KiCk i
Review: The main problem it faces is trying to successfully combine her new, slower palate with the tense, rapid-fire elements she's known for. To anyone who has been listening to her discography for long, this is clearly something that will be difficult for anyone to pull off. And to her credit, she tries.

Title: Semicircle
Review: Semicircle’s many pleasures--of melody, of tone color, of ideals never losing the beat--deserve an essay’s worth of exposition (no, really).

Title: A Love Extreme
Review: A Love Extreme is, as its title suggests, an album of sonic extremes, but those willing to sit through both discs will find a number of eccentric, engaging songs, particularly on side two.

Title: In Rolling Waves
Review: Their pop-rock noir is at its best on end-of-the-night anthems such as Hearts Like Ours and the suitably crashing Rolling Waves, or when it puts its sheeny spin on the xx's minimal house (as on Waltz).

Title: So-Called Chaos
Review: Once more, her songs become little more than cloying ruminations or sarcastic harangues aimed at those who want to squash her individuality. [28 May 2004, p.121]

Title: The Messenger
Review: The Messenger isn't an album that will blow any non-believer away. It is old fashioned, in many ways. [Mar 2013, p.65]

Title: Fading Trails
Review: With its restructured band lineup and multiple producers/locations, Fading Trails is unavoidably a somewhat dispirited and disjointed affair.

Title: Planet Pit
Review: Gotta get that boom boom pow? Look no further.

Title: The Western Lands
Review: The Western Lands offers more bang for your buck. [Fall 2007, p.96]

Title: Loose Fur
Review: Challenging, arresting and moving in equal measures.

Title: Thank You
Review: One or two of these songs might scan as tongue-in-cheek; nearly half an album's worth is a form of caricature, paying lip service to a millennial generation raised on hollow self-affirmations.

Title: Before Love Came To Kill Us
Review: The fearless formula, the genre-blending, the artistic craft on display marks Reyez's latest as one of the better albums in an already interesting 2020. Before Love Came to Kills shines a light on homegrown talent done great.

Title: Volume X
Review: Volume X certainly appears to have more than enough subtle moments and hidden delights to ensure its longevity.

Title: Coral Fang
Review: [Dalle] may be the New Courtney Love, at times even the Punk PJ Harvey, but she also has a depth of emotion that was last displayed by Kurt Cobain.

Title: Love & Hate
Review: It’s intimate and sprawling, personal and universal, affectionate and daring.

Title: A Funk Odyssey
Review: Not quite as effortlessly enormous as 1999's blistering 'Synkronised', 'A Funk Odyssey' nevertheless won't disappoint anyone taken with the band's direction on that record.

Title: Beacon
Review: It's taut, slick and more transatlantic than its predecessor but they lose some of the quirks that gave their debut much of its charm. [Oct 2012, p.112]

Title: Love Streams
Review: Luckily, Hecker has impeccable taste. Very few composers can achieve this kind of beauty or this kind of experimentation, and yet Hecker does both, time and time again.

Title: For My Crimes
Review: Nadler's cathartic inner journey isn't always as easy to empathise with as it is artfully expressed. [Oct 2018, p.88]

Title: Get Rich or Die Tryin'
Review: It's all good. Favourites switch with listens, and we can assure you that this record will remain on your deck all year.

Title: Slick Dogs and Ponies
Review: The moments of rocked-out swagger are fleeting and ultimately drowned out by a musical and lyrical heaviness that turns the album into a real downer.

Title: Father of the Bride
Review: This album has a more mature twang to it, musically and lyrically. And interestingly enough, it's pretty minimalist and their simplest-sounding stuff to date.

Title: Ecstasy
Review: While Ecstasy is essentially a concept album about the fantasies and realities of love and family, it includes as much sex, drugs, and rock n' roll culture as any of Reed's earlier work.

Title: Star Wars
Review: It's impossible to assess an album this thick with twists and turns in a few hours. But at this early stage, it feels rich enough to reward more listens.

Title: The List
Review: Overall, these imaginative interpretations would make Papa proud.

Title: The Underside of Power
Review: The Underside Of Power is righteous, vicious and vital. If the world is a stage, then at the moment it’s hard to think of a better house band than Algiers.

Title: Daytona
Review: The record’s simple presentation and briefness make for an engaging change from the epic crossover attempts of his prior LP Darkest Before Dawn.

Title: From Here on In
Review: All too often the guitar-led tracks expose their limitations.

Title: Fever Dream
Review: Luckily the album is the group's strongest and most enjoyable album to date. ... There are moments however when things quite work as well as on their previous albums, but these are the moments that are the most interesting and exciting.

Title: All This Sounds Gas
Review: Not only do Kannberg’s vocals sound more robust than previously, but the whole record has considerably more colour in its cheeks than Malkmus’s own recent solo effort.

Title: Crash My Party
Review: Bryan just can't match, say, Kenny Chesney's knack for lonely contemplation. Given the drinking songs he's best at, he'd be better off pretending spring break lasts all year long.

Title: Rhubarb Rhubarb
Review: Rhubarb Rhubarb is scuzzy but smart, surging between primitive playfulness and something more malevolent. [Dec 2014, p.83]
There’s depth here too--listen 10 times and you will still be discovering new things to enjoy: clever wordplay, a subtle melody. It’s a joy from start to finish.

Title: Surf
Review: There are too many impressive performances on Surf to focus on just one man’s achievements, and Chance has to be proud of that.

Title: In a Space Outta Sound
Review: Outta Sound shows a passionate and maturing George Evelyn that still had much to offer.

Title: Time of Dust
Review: Balanced by bitter barbs at modern snivellers and shysters in Time of Dust itself, the result is a compact but concentrated dose of poison.

Title: Strange Clouds
Review: B.o.B. has been adamant about his latest album being created organically, yet that doesn't justify the lack of cohesion or quality found on Strange Clouds.

Title: Black Peak
Review: They further develop their inventive and often thrilling fusion style by concentrating on songs rather than instrumentals. But the emphasis is on improvisation rather than predictable structures.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: Vulnicura is a harsh and demanding album, one to sink into with a good set of headphones. But it’s also Björk’s most--if not first-- personal record.

Title: Soft Will
Review: Everything on Soft Will is ringing, open, alive; there are croon-along choruses buoying every song. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.90]

Title: M A N I A
Review: M A N I A takes similar chances [as 2009's Folie a Deux] to more mixed results, as Stump belts out absurdly verbose lyrics over glossy, overstuffed tracks. But the album’s more experimental moments aren’t necessarily its strong suit. ... M A N I A hits its stride in the second half, with a pair of tracks that toy with religious imagery and waltz tempos, “Church” and “Heaven’s Gate.”

Title: Don't Be Afraid of Love
Review: Slick samples and buoyant melodies are in, dissonant atmospherics pretty much out. [Feb 2002, p.111]

Title: Ski Mask
Review: There's much to admire here, but when you’ve stared into the sun for too long, it’s hard to see the dimmer lights.

Title: Hands
Review: It’s the type of near-perfect, swooning synth-pop rush that Oakey was riding with the Human League in the ’80s.

Title: Three Futures
Review: Her latest is even more raw, offering conflicted images of emotional and physical release over bracing industrial-rock textures co-produced by Rob Ellis.

Title: Y Dydd Olaf
Review: It's glittering and electronic, its lyrics and title inspired by Owain Owain's dystopian science fiction novel, and its melodies underpinned with discordant notes and bric-à-brac sonic oddities--but it shares a similarly subversive edge to that record.

Title: Parodia Flare
Review: Ward's real saving grace on Parodia Flare is the guitar, which he utilizes in unexpectedly welcome ways to propel his compositions, keeping them from dissolving into murky keyboard washes.

Title: The Real New Fall LP (Formerly Country on the Click)
Review: Great by Smith's standards. Practically genius by everybody else's. [Feb 2004, p.74]

Title: Red
Review: There's a minor detail to enjoy in almost every song on here, but the whole is average to the point of being physically sickening for anybody who fell in love with their magical debut.

Title: The Golden Record
Review: While The Golden Record is far from perfect, and occasionally falters and fails to make the impression it should, there is much to recommend here.

Title: Nearer My God
Review: Nearer My God establishes itself as emo's first definitive document on digital-age despair.

Title: Nude With Boots
Review: It’s slightly less menacing, yet without a discernible drop in power, which should go down well in the burbs without alienating their hipster metal following.

Title: Little Dark Age
Review: Here, on their fourth LP, the duo--teaming up again with Dave Fridmann--appear to have entered some weird, parallel 1983. [Apr 2018, p.30]

Title: Vicious Lies and Dangerous Rumors
Review: Big Boi is the best thing about the album--and double props for staying true to his entire career's quest of never making the same album twice. But Vicious Lies And Dangerous Rumors as a whole? It's all over the place.

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: As well executed as the latter half is, it can feel a mite unsatisfying compared to the stripped-down stuff that sits at the top of the album. [Jun 2013, p.85]

Title: The Mirror Explodes
Review: It’s a noise-rock album you can play without annoying your friends, but it won’t aggravate the Tortoise worshipers in your group, either.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Worlds Apart
Review: It's killer stuff for any frame of mind.

Title: Days Run Away
Review: Although the record shows scant evidence that over a decade of rock music has passed, the band doesn't sound anachronistic or out of touch alongside its younger competition.

Title: Tongues
Review: More structured than its predecessors. [Apr 2007, p.102]

Title: Ringleader of the Tormentors
Review: A romantic, self-referential collection of songs that, even though we've heard this inimitable voice singing the same old tune for years, manages to avoid staleness. [May 2006, p.174]

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: On its sixth studio effort, Guy Garvey and company soar to new heights, even if the vocalist experienced a bit of personal turmoil in the form of a difficult breakup during the recording process.

Title: Pieces of a Man
Review: Though a versatile vocalist, Jenkins isn’t actually a Tier 1 rapper. His rasp can struggle when forced to take on too much, especially amid the prominent percussion and tough orchestration of something like “Ghost.” But this is a minor gripe within a major scheme. ... A gripping portrait of one human among Chicago’s 2.7 million.

Title: Alone with Everybody
Review: Admittedly, he seems to be missing a sparring partner like McCabe and thus, "Alone" often suffers a lack of tension. Still, Ashcroft's unabashed joy is rather contagious.

Title: Ouroboros
Review: Ouroboros is a perfect throwback to the lost art of the album-length format.

Title: Comfort Woman
Review: She shows the breadth of her talent and the depth of her sentiment. [Nov 2003, p.118]

Title: The Hanged Man
Review: The Hanged Man, despite some of its thinness and unevenness, is still a great record.

Title: Last Night On The Planet
Review: Letherette manage the notoriously tricky second album by delivering a reworked and revitalised version of the style with which they have made their name.

Title: That's Why God Made the Radio
Review: As a whole, That's Why God Made the Radio is not a top-tier Beach Boys album. But it's neither a reach nor hyperbole to say this final suite is among the strongest, most affecting music Wilson has ever recorded.

Title: Souljacker
Review: Souljacker is as strong as any of Eels previous albums, but even crawling through the muck there is a lot more joy and life here than heard before.

Title: Blackout
Review: It wants to be danceable, sexy, and a defiant response to the media shitstorm. It's not even that danceable.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: ‘You Are The Quarry’ sees Morrissey back in the ring, lean, limber and fighting fit.

Title: Lover
Review: Though uneven, Lover is a bright, fun album with great emotional honesty.

Title: Oxymoron
Review: It’s something special, just like it was always planned to be.

Title: Give My Love To London
Review: She’s Faithfull: volatile and unpredictable, intellectual and insightful, savage and soothing, and delivering in Give My Love to London as accomplished and compelling an album as she’s ever made.

Title: Night on Fire
Review: Immediately transforms VHS or Beta from disco revivalists into one of rock's best new bands. [Oct 2004, p.130]

Title: Cosmonaut
Review: The balance between these quiet, thoughtful songs, the needle-bouncing rockers, and the jumping Monkees-ish pop of tracks like "Stick Your Hand Up if You're Louche" makes for a thrill ride of an album, and a better example of modern guitar pop than Cosmonaut is pretty hard to find no matter where one might look.

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: The whole of the album is stunning and unique, and if the thematic gender-bending core of the album makes a few people ideologically shy away, then it’s truly a shame.

Title: Back to Basics
Review: Certainly a tougher and more traditional album than its two predecessors.

Title: Moms
Review: As memorable as the lyrics are on Moms, its biggest strength is the way Harris and Seim's already quite similar vocals and contrasting worldviews effectively intertwine.

Title: i,i
Review: The album seems to suggest that Bon Iver is transitioning from a band in the traditional sense of the word into a looser collective. Despite the album’s intense pessimism and anxiety, Bon Iver’s organization speaks to the power of forging a community to battle back against darkness.

Title: 1000 Days
Review: A few mis-steps aside, this is yet another strong showing from a band in the midst of a creative whirlwind, one that fortunately shows little signs of blowing itself out.

Title: Lucky Old Sun
Review: The album proves how vapid contemporary country can be: Very. Uh-huh.

Title: The Imperfect Sea
Review: It’s a growth record, and it shows Penguin Café coming into their own. It’s a beginning, but it’s imperfect.

Title: Cassadaga
Review: It isn't that Cassadaga is necessarily bad, but where I'm Wide Awake was compact and graceful, the new record lumbers, belaboring Conor Oberst's anguish about the state of the world.

Title: You Can Do Anything
Review: As this flits from widescreen country soul to palpitating Meat Loaf theatrics, the overriding impression is of a band that's having a blast. [July 2008, p.99]

Title: Kaputt
Review: Kind of like the whole idea of a disco album, a collaboration with a visual artist about African-Americans' tragic history is something you would never expect from Destroyer, and yet once you listen, it seems perfectly authentic, inspired, and essential.

Title: Weighing of the Heart
