Review: It’s all done with a precision and neatness that betrays Iqbal’s dance music roots, with each moment providing an aesthetic delight, from the medley of drumbeats that opens Eternal Passion to the liquid gold guitars that frequently surface.

Title: Tales of a Grass Widow
Review: They make albums that make you squint and stare at the floor and convince yourself you like it, maybe. And somehow, you’ll find yourself listening until you’re sure you do.

Title: Dead Drunk
Review: For the most part... the seemingly endless boundaries and subtly propulsive rhythms draw the listener into an engaging world of manipulated samples and shimmering loops.

Title: How To Get Your Record Played in Shops
Review: Donovan seems content to continue cranking out his own brand of lo-fi foggy fuzz. Boogie and chillin’, indeed!

Title: Red Yellow & Blue
Review: Born Ruffians are as eloquent in their summation of today’s indie rock style as any other likeminded band; in that sense Red, Yellow & Blue is as literate and aware as its title’s reference to primary colors implies. But knowingly limiting one’s scope to temporary fun predictably keeps the band from turning out something with lasting power.

Title: Images du Futur
Review: Images maintains an aura of continually mounting tension that keeps you anxiously captivated throughout its ten nervously haunting tracks.

Title: Inner Journey Out
Review: Let’s be honest: the [Brian Jonestown Massacre] hasn’t hewed to its classic sound in some years, so why not let Psychic Ills take on the drug pop mantle instead? As this album proves, they [wear] it well.

Title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
Review: Angel Guts: Red Classroom is his third album in under a year, and superficially it resembles many of Xiu Xiu’s others by draping wracked and fragile vocals over obtuse electronics and analogue atonality.

Title: Reflection
Review: Reflection takes a shallow look inward and a deeper look outward than you'd expect from a nonstop party.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: To say Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper is a textural album is probably stating the obvious, but it very much is, in a way where the individual tracks feel simultaneously adventurous and tamed.

Title: Father Creeper
Review: Spoek makes the "hard truths" sound like "real talk" while putting some of the world's most innovative rebel music underneath.

Title: Painted Ruins
Review: Painted Ruins is best enjoyed when you let each song carry you through its many twists and turns. And are there ever twists and turns.

Title: The Messenger
Review: The [emotional] connection is missing because of The Messenger's overarching weaknesses: the voice and the lyrics.

Title: Hexadic
Review: Albums such as this one will often be defined as ‘difficult,’ and the love of its content will derive more from muso appreciation than genuine affection. Six Organs of Admittance have sidestepped this by crafting a piece of work that diefies categorisation: it feels mathematically precise, painstakingly composed, entirely freeform and joyfully performed.

Title: Bullets in the Gun
Review: Only one of these tracks qualifies as obnoxious. The rest are solidly enjoyable commercial country, and there's something to be said for that.

Title: Violent Hearts
Review: The vocals are obscured, but nothing else really meshes.

Title: Last Building Burning
Review: A ferocious album that finds them diving headfirst into experimentation, it is filled to the brim with a driving energy that rarely lets up. Striking the precarious balance of melding their pop inclinations with uproarious noise, Cloud Nothings push the dial back in the right direction.

Title: Living Room Songs
Review: It certainly meets every expectation, albeit without stretching far beyond anticipated designs.

Title: The Fall
Review: There are a lot of innovative ideas, some strong moments, but also a good amount of filler. If you give it a spin, though, you'll probably find some hidden treasures in these songs as well.

Title: Backspacer
Review: Though it doesn’t hit with the same force as the early singles to which every future Pearl Jam anthem will be compared, it’s an oxygen rush nonetheless--one worth hoping for and high-fiving to when they unleash it live.

Title: Earth Rocker
Review: Clutch’s aim here was to try something different, and in stripping Earth Rocker of its fat, the band has revealed even more imaginative and powerful artistic muscle.

Title: Just to Feel Anything
Review: While some longtime fans may find Just To Feel Anything's retreat from the cosmos a disappointment, the album's relative conceptual restraint actually allows it to be even more emotionally accessible, inviting the listener into the trio's interstellar clubhouse instead of only letting us peak in from the outside.

Title: Thankful
Review: This debut has her trilling like Mariah Carey on fluffy R&B tunes. [Oct 2003, p.103]

Title: Half Smiles of the Decomposed
Review: It's hardly a career-defining collection. [Sep 2004, p.98]

Title: Beware
Review: The enigmatic nature of his music aside, Oldham invariably sounds like he's having fun making it, which makes Beware a warning only to those who place too high a value on simplistic clarity.

Title: By the Hedge
Review: In summary then, better than most if you like that sort of thing.

Title: Howl
Review: By the time the country twang of “Ain’t No Easy Way” hits with a massive drum-and-harmonica stomp, thoughts of Howl being a “Hey, let’s try this” album vanish, and the music becomes the entrancing jaunt of a band not necessarily finding itself, per se, but at least writing the best songs of its career.

Title: Total Life Forever
Review: There is stillness and hush here, and a depth of emotion they have never accessed before.

Title: Happy Rabbit
Review: The retro musical mood on Happy Rabbit fits the lyrical tone. [Jan 2017, p.24]

Title: Me
Review: At a time when Carly Rae Jepsen is turning to members of Vampire Weekend for new ideas, Empress Of’s self-produced music feels like a small victory for the future of pop.

Title: Nocturama
Review: Most people this pretentious or literary don't rock so hard or write tunes so good.

Title: Croz
Review: All in all though, a fair return.

Title: Asleep on the Floodplain
Review: Ben Chasny's annual solo folk extravaganza. [March 2011, p. 95]

Title: Good Mourning
Review: Alkaline Trio subvert their perky, zinging three chord mall-punk with misanthropy, melancholy and alcohol-sodden, world-weary wisdom. [Jun 2003, p.92]

Title: Master and Everyone
Review: Every knot has been planed away. It's hushed, wistful, 'cool,' acoustic, sweetly dolorous and subtly well crafted... and dull as corrective footnotes in a treatise on ditchwater. [#228, p.54]

Title: III
Review: This band may take their time between releases now, but they get exponentially more sophisticated and adventurous, not only in their composed material, but in their approach to making records. This is just stellar top to bottom.

Title: Banks
Review: It lacks cohesion, with eerie instrumentals featuring with gentle acoustic tracks, it is a noble attempt to progress a rather formulaic, albeit excellent, musical career.

Title: Fatherfucker
Review: More consistent and enjoyable than its predecessor.

Title: TLC
Review: As moving as it is to hear her and Chilli together for another album, the material is not up to par with TLC's past. Flashbacks are more likely than repeat play.

Title: Art and Life
Review: This record is just a party from beginning to end.

Title: Pool
Review: Experimental pop that feels for the warm electronic pulse of '80s futurism. [Mar 2016, p.100]

Title: Riot Act
Review: Eddie's heartfelt lyrics rarely cohere... [but their] grooves still sound taut, emotive, and world-class.

Title: Starboy
Review: Tesfaye can't decide if he's having the best time f his life or the worst. [Feb 2017, p.119]

Title: Night Work
Review: Jake Shears and Ana Matronic trot out those Bee Gees harmonies again over Moroder-style synth runs and glam guitars, delivering a stirring anthem about how for some disaffected folks, nightclubbing time is business time.

Title: Feels
Review: Feels is layered as no other Collective album before it. [#70, p.87]

Title: Shaking the Habitual
Review: The resulting album, unsurprisingly enough, contains their most texturally diverse work to date.

Title: Saturday Night
Review: Saturday Night is a record that is almost misanthropic in its progression, and an intriguing insight into Tim Darcy the artist.

Title: A Distant Call
Review: The more varied aspects of Need To Feel Your Love which made it such a fantastic debut, have mostly disappeared, resulting in a less rewarding listen. [Sep-Nov 2019, p.133]

Title: Eternal Turn of the Wheel
Review: Eternal Turn of the Wheel is as captivating as most any stretch of black metal you'll hear this year, even if it possesses a lifetime of questions that deserve to be asked.

Title: Woman
Review: If a woman were singing the songs on Woman, it would make for a great neo-soul album. The fact that a man is performing them elevates the album, making it one of the most confident debuts in recent memory.

Title: The Understanding
Review: What they do best is produce exceptional electronica for people that don't have the patience for extended instrumental passages and require things like vocals on regular intervals. With that precursor, The Understanding is probably one of the better electronica records to come out this year that thankfully doesn't involve MCs from Def Jux or was composed on a laptop.

Title: Typical System
Review: The five-piece isn’t interested in comfort, but rather an intensity created directly by that push-pull exchange, their strangely humorous song titles, and primitive, warlike lyrics.

Title: Way to Normal
Review: There is nary a weak link to be found. More than anything, Way to Normal is simply Folds’s way of showing us that, at 42, he’s still doing this piano-power-pop thing better than anyone else around.

Title: Admission
Review: Torche can get dirty as well, as evidenced by the gnarly, Alice in Chains-meets-Mastodon attack of "Extremes of Consciousness" and the scorching, aptly named "Inferno," but for the most part Admission administers seismic confections that vary in sweetness but always satisfy.

Title: Cherry Bomb
Review: At the end of the day, I enjoy Cherry Bomb, both for it's misanthropic noise and for its funkier and jazzier sides.

Title: Cold House
Review: Tender melodies, modern scrapes and traditional beauty merge into a gently unfolded whole that touches the soul with its silky aesthetics.

Title: Vespertine
Review: A beautiful, magical, mystical soundtrack; similar to Homogenic, but in a sense, more light-hearted and full of love.

Title: White Stuff
Review: Trux life feels more brilliantly warped than ever. [Apr 2019, p.114]

Title: Knockin' Boots
Review: Colourful and unconventional throughout, Knockin’ Boots keeps Julio Bashmore’s reputation for bangers firmly intact.

Title: Hurricane Bar
Review: Hookily retro, Kinks-style Britpop. [11 Mar 2005, p.105]

Title: Re-Engineering
Review: What makes Re-Engineering worthwhile is that the odd blooms Warwick coaxes from that soil are so pleasing to behold on their own terms. It's critical theory as easy listening that you can actually cut a rug to, if you're so inclined.

Title: All About Chemistry
Review: Semisonic's newest release, All About Chemistry, hits all the right pop spots, but will likely appeal to a very niche group -- the same group that embraced the easy, witty pop of bands such as Crowded House or Ben Folds Five.

Title: Matador
Review: The jaunty, energetic hints of Britpop cast aside, this is Gaz Coombes the adult man, writing adult songs, and they’re really rather great.

Title: For Their Love
Review: Shooting for the sweet spot of artists like Radiohead and The National, Other Lives embraces their tense, dramatic, theatrical, orchestral sound, and scope on For [Their] Love.

Title: Stay Positive
Review: If you know what's good for you, however, you'll drink the whole album in, because intelligently constructed and musically thrilling records like this are a rare, rare find.

Title: Out in the Storm
Review: Throughout, Crutchfield maintains a seething, triumphant line in catharsis that she channels into gruff college rock ad dreamy introspection. [Aug 2017, p.112]

Title: Cocoa Sugar
Review: Cocoa Sugar mystifies before it gratifies, but it reflects a modern global chaos as much as it does a personal one.

Title: All Nerve
Review: All Nerve is still a solid enough and welcome addition to The Breeders’ still slender yet always evolving canon.

Title: Paradise Gallows
Review: The apocalyptic tone that hangs over much of the record is suffocating, in the best possible way. [9 Jul 2016, p.52]

Title: Preoccupations
Review: Preoccupations is a more coherent, more accessible set of songs that proves this band doesn't need an edgy name to attract the attention they deserve.

Title: Unknown Rooms: A Collection of Acoustic Songs
Review: The tone and pace of Wolfe's voice don't really vary that much, and there isn't enough happening with the instrumentation to give the album any real sense of dynamism.

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You
Review: His maniacal energy is infectious. [Nov 2008, p.77]

Title: American Utopia
Review: Combined with the faux-naive, fairytale tone of the narratives, it makes for an irritatingly condescending experience. The lofty aimlessness is matched by musical settings.

Title: No Mercy
Review: On No Mercy, he sounds absolutely sapped of energy. And that's rough; nobody plays the ferocious livewire better.

Title: Old Ideas
Review: Old Ideas is not the man's latter-day masterpiece but its title is as bluntly honest as any you'll see this year, in more ways than one.

Title: ANIMA
Review: The textural depth of ANIMA grips, unlike past solo outings, and is ultimately even more rewarding when played on headphones.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: It’s a “grower” if there ever was one. And when it finally blooms in your ears, you’ll find yourself thinking “ah, so this is why I’ve been following this guy for all these years.”

Title: Parodia Flare
Review: An understated treat. [Nov 2011, p.103]

Title: Next to The Sun
Review: Her striking lyrics take aim at present-day bigots who clamor for closed borders—“Look how these brown hands cook all your meals/But mama says you want us all to disappear”—but she’s more concerned with the persistence of this foundational hatred, and with the people she loves, who have thrived “through so many moons” and continue to thrive in spite of racist brutality.

Title: Camp
Review: While Glover's exaggerated, cartoonish flow and overblown pop-rap production would be enough to make Camp one of the most uniquely unlikable rap records of this year (and most others), what's worse is how he uses heavy topics like race, masculinity, relationships, street cred, and "real hip-hop" as props to construct a false outsider persona.

Title: What Now
Review: it's not without charm, but you might find yourself wanting to like What Now more than you actually do. [Jun 2017, p.112]

Title: Leave No Trace
Review: There's a lot more discipline present on the band's second album, Leave No Trace, but it's not clear if that's an encouraging development.

Title: Futures
Review: While it may still fall short of the high-water mark established with Clarity, Jimmy Eat World’s latest is still a strong contender for the best album of 2004.

Title: Among The Leaves
Review: So its songs aren't exactly of the hum-along variety. No matter. There's no denying Sun Kil Moon's luminous glow.

Title: Stars Are Our Home
Review: Overall, Stars Are Our Home is a delightfully mixed bag that does rare justice to the term 'supergroup'.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: As romance, ethics, community and the economy collapse, Mr. Petty and the Heartbreakers offer two old-fashioned bulwarks: the solidarity of the band and the sinewy construction of the songs.

Title: Ripcord
Review: On Ripcord, time’s always slipping away, and that’s exciting. That excitement is kin to the grooves and rhythmic tricks propelling the album.

Title: Not Too Late
Review: While Not Too Late is a shade darker than her mega-selling, Grammy-winning template, it's highly unlikely to win all that many new converts, and fans may find this album a little bit of a slog in places.

Title: Lies for the Liars
Review: There's no denying the galvanic power of singer Bert McCracken's blowtorch vocals. [25 May 2007, p.84]

Title: The Soft Bulletin
Review: The Soft Bulletin provides an exquisite soundtrack to have blasting in the car at night.

Title: Bass Drum of Death
Review: While GB City felt fast and dirty like a fleeting glance with a stranger, Bass Drum of Death is a fully realized one night stand.

Title: Surprise
Review: What is startling about Simon's latest solo effort is how fresh and alive it sounds.

Title: Croz
Review: He's aware he's building upon a past he sometimes pines for, yet he's restless enough to forage ahead into new territory, but only when he's surrounded by cozy, familiar settings.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: Low give us a definitive chapter for where they are presently, and present it with more clarity and joy than we've heard from them in some time.

Title: Love Hates What You Become
Review: Altogether, Love Hates What You Become by Lost Under Heaven is artistic and dynamic, with enough exploration and experimentation to see the album and its tracks offered in a live active atmosphere as much as in solitude and wearing headphones.

Title: Sumday
Review: One of the major differences between this and other Grandaddy releases is that Lytle finally seems comfortable in his role as production auteur.

Title: Grinderman
Review: Grinderman isn’t angry and it isn’t raw, just a careful concoction of licentiousness and braying disdain ultimately monotonous and unexciting after the first four cuts.

Title: Rough and Rowdy Ways
Review: Rough and Rowdy Ways has little, if any, rock 'n' roll, but the sneer remains. Leonard Cohen and Tom Waits might vaguely peek in a little. Dylan has long lost interest in conforming to expectations, so it's no surprise that on a new record, he either satisfies all of them or none of them. He sounds like Dylan, whatever that is.

Title: Alice
Review: The sheer melodic gorgeousness of the finest songs here make Alice the pick of Waits's new matched set.

Title: Endless Wire
Review: It's the mini-opera that moves spryly compared to the proper rock album half.

Title: Cerebral Ballzy
Review: The songs are trite punk workouts without any real imagination and, whilst there's a reasonable amount of endeavour and vigour, they're unlikely to raise anything other than idle curiosity amongst the curious idle.

Title: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier
Review: A sense of awestruck wonder permeates tracks such as "Swallowed by the Night", though when Barthmus tries to deal in more human terms, with the inverse "Ebony & Ivory" schtick of "Shared Piano", the results are less successful.

Title: Blanck Mass
Review: While I don't understand a lot of the decisions made on this record, it is still undeniably an exhibition of some of the best sonic control and sound shaping around.

Title: Trouble in Dreams
Review: If you can't get enough of Bejar, you'll obviously want to check this out, but most others will feel like they've been down this road before.

Title: The Budos Band III
Review: The bass can get lost in the mix as well beneath all the moving parts. With the kinds of rhythms The Budos Band lay down, you need the bass up front and center. These qualms are minor compared with the overall delight the album conveys.

Title: Last Young Renegade
Review: Its delicate, sparse build-and-explode approach is largely typical of what Last Young Renegade has to offer--anthemic yet atmospheric songs that are subtly affecting.

Title: Loud City Song
Review: Although it takes more than a couple of listens for Loud City Song to feel like a cohesive album, the reward once you do is well worth the outlay.

Title: Oracular Spectacular
Review: Oracular Spectacular is a triumph of conceptual ambition, a series of fantastic voyages that avoids any of the navel-gazing such notions normally provoke. [May 2008, p.138]

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: Electric Arguments makes a gravity defying leap from his supine position atop past laurels with an album showcasing incredibly raw rock, complimented by totally-not-cheesy electronic production. [Holiday 2008, p.98]

Title: Madame X
Review: Her pop exists to exploit and sand off edges, packaging esotericism for the masses. It’s just that on Madame X, she is not merely dining out on other cultures; she’s whipping around drive-thrus.

Title: A Weekend in the City
Review: A Weekend in the City showcases what all the band's initial buzz was about, but twists and filters what might have been expected, leaving them open to praise for different reasons.

Title: I Still Do
Review: {I Still Do] offers a typical Clapton mix of covers and original material. The former are rather more impressive than the latter. [Jun 2016, p.72]

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: Neither engaging enough to be exhilarating, nor boisterous enough to be obnoxious, Perpetual Surrender simply gazes at its shoes without making much of an impression at all.

Title: Snowdonia
Review: Although those moments may be too fleeting to call Snowdonia a complete departure for the band, fans can will appreciate the added ambition here, on top of the elements they've come to know and love.

Title: Yesterday Was Lived & Lost
Review: New Build's arrangements are impressive and uncomplicated throughout.

Title: Stay Gold
Review: On Stay Gold, Walker falls into the latter camp, but if these songs lack a certain spontaneity, the craft is strong and Walker seems so eager to sound like a rock star that you just might mistake him for the real thing.

Title: Taking Back Sunday
Review: The whole thing is done and dusted in just under 40 minutes, yet zips by so fluidly that it feels half as long. [2 Jul 2011, p.50]

Title: Amadjar
Review: An almost biblical journey to freedom, Tinariwen have inspired compatriots from Tamikrest to Bombino, artists that encapsulate the struggle of a people, taking it to the world through music that truly brings people together.

Title: Leisure Seizure
Review: Like We Have Sound, Leisure Seizure feels inimitable not because of any great innovation or genius, but for the way it seemingly exists in its own perfectly contained universe.

Title: Two Hands
Review: The more Big Thief zoom in, the more magical they sound.

Title: In the Key of Disney
Review: Mostly, the album suffers from just too much of the patronizing, saccharine Disney vibe and not enough echt Wilson.

Title: The Route to the Harmonium
Review: The Route To The Harmonium feels like a return to the warmth of some of his earlier outings--not that he’s exactly satisfied--with a more mature Yorkston having crafted perhaps the album of his career.

Title: Black Up
Review: Following a pair of brilliant EPs, Shabazz attacks with Black Up.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: Ultimately, though, Dead Confederate's alt-country/grunge hybrid doesn't just feel like a compelling debut, it feels like a compelling new genre.

Title: Endlessly
Review: This time on Endlessly, she smartly taps a producer who wrote hits during that era: Albert Hammond accentuates her smoky, blues-tinged voice and classic Stax style while also bringing out her inner pop star.

Title: Mechanical Bull
Review: The band is just about out of transgressive fury, but they manage to muster enough rigor and discipline to keep Mechanical Bull kicking.

Title: In a Dim Light
Review: On In a Dim Light, Nedry never get as self-consciously slick as many of the bands that made trip-hop so dully tasteful in its later years, but they're still at their best when they're fully in touch with their volatile side.

Title: Stranger to Stranger
Review: Stranger To Stranger is poof positive that Simon isn’t simply still here, but he’s kicking with gusto. In a year where good news has been fleeting for classic rock fans, Simon’s latest is worth grabbing onto with both hands.

Title: Don't Tread on Me
Review: Fans of albums such as 2001’s  From Chaos and 2003’s promising Evolver will likely find Tread familiar and perhaps even comforting, but it’s unlikely to invite a new horde of fans as the album often sounds like an imitation of the bands 311 helped inspire in its decade-plus career.

Title: II
Review: Strip away the fug of patchouli oil and incense and you're left with little more than a shoegazing album played by Kula Shaker.

Title: Shaking the Habitual
Review: It’s an adventure.

Title: The Glowing Man
Review: Gira feeds on the drawn-out, high-tension passages of accelerating cymbal crashes and swelling guitar dissonance, many of which exist on the 25-minute “Cloud Of Unknowing.” But while the axis on which that track rotates features deconstructed, incohesive drum rolls and a kind of radiant summoning from Gira--one that bleeds and pools into negative space you didn’t know existed--the plodding, sinister rhythm that precedes it proves more hypnotic.

Artist: Someone Still Loves You Boris Yeltsin
Title: Let It Sway
Review: It's more than a return to form for SSLYBY--it's potentially their finest hour.

Title: Underachievers Please Try Harder
Review: What separates them from their peers is a refreshing feminine perspective that draws from '60s girl groups and the conflicted teenage angst of Leslie Gore.

Title: Modern Guilt
Review: Modern Guilt takes that album's insecurity in the face of technology running away with us, to a tightly-written 10 songs that in part seem to focus on what, precisely, we have done to the world; and how on earth are we meant to get back in touch with it?

Title: Jump Rope Gazers
Review: Fans of Future Me Hates Me will be more than pleased with Jump Rope Gazers, their latest album. Every one of their back catalog's strengths is not only present but amplified.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: Krug won't make any new fans with Organ Music, but that's not what he's trying to do here, anyway. He's just having himself some fun-or, as he put it, "lurching toward" his musical ideas "impulsively."

Title: Departing
Review: The relatively sparse and chilly tone of Departing ultimately feels less like a slump than a conscious decision to present itself as the wintertime counterpart to Hometowns' prairie summer.

Title: Twentytwo in Blue
Review: Though they sometimes still miss, Twentytwo In Blue stakes out the loss of innocence that comes with growing up, and it does it beautifully.

Title: Last Night Becomes This Morning
Review: Doughman sings of disenchantment and depression over a variety of lo-fi arrangements. [#12, p.97]

Title: A New Found Relaxation
Review: A New Found Relaxation suggests a New Mexico healing experience that’s both IRL and online. The samples move quickly, spiking the ambience with appropriate doses of anxiety.

Title: What Comes After The Blues
Review: The lyrics here lack the self-indicting punch that made MEC so unflinchingly great.

Title: Daytona
Review: Aside from the crisply brilliant drug poetry, the production, entirely by Kanye West, is another big draw. This is the roughshod style of cut-and-shut soul samples that characterised Bound 2 and much of Life of Pablo.

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: Death Magnetic is just about the best album Metallica could have made at this point.

Title: Shadow
Review: Shadow finds a band who can do more than just roar. [Jun 2014, p.114]

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: This is a strong, sometimes truly beautiful, maturation of Avery’s work as a producer.

Title: The Village
Review: Southern Africa is the music's muse, kept very cool by the jazz-brass, which lingers around her while she makes reckless instinctive-sounding moves from one note into another.

Title: Wet from Birth
Review: Not just a dance-rock band anymore, The Faint unveil a strong song sense with tunes as richly imagined, well-written and arresting as their titles. [14 Oct 2004, p.96]

Title: Don't Look Down
Review: For Ms. Grey, angst, melody and a hip-hop backbone are a promising combination.

Title: Starfire
Review: This is less organic, more brittle, and electronic than before and begs to be opened out in a live setting. [Jul 2015, p.93]

Title: Everybody Works
Review: Everybody Works has swept up the floors and straightened up the shelves. All the good stuff stays, but the lines are cleaner.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: Awkward moments of not, this group moves as one. [Apr 2013, p.76]

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: You’ve heard these sounds before, and you’ve felt these feelings before. The added value here, if you want it, is the organization and rigor of the blankness.

Title: Lord Steppington
Review: Lord Steppington is arguably his finest since Domo Genesis' No Fools mixtape, certainly an album on which his production is more freewheeling than it has been in a while, noisier, angrier, determined.

Title: lilac6
Review: Like the band's best '80s output, Lilac6 is the work of a bona fide songsmith. [Nov 2001, p.108]

Title: Wrote a Song For Everyone
Review: With help from a diverse coterie of peers, fans, and friends, Wrote a Song for Everyone offers fun and fresh takes on well-worn tunes.

Title: Book of Bad Decisions
Review: They balance killer musicianship and verbal panache with a bar-band mindset. Album of the year? Possibly, but that's just business as usual for Maryland's finest.

Title: Eggs
Review: Even when it slides and swivels to defy all definition, Eggs can be remarkably engaging if given the chance of repeat listens.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: Despite its lengthy gestation period, there is more than a hint of deja vu about The Campfire Headphase.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: Justice never lose sight of the big picture, aiming to blow your minds and sub-woofers with equal determination.

Title: Working on a Dream
Review: There is no pandering here, with Springsteen and the trusty E Street Band rocking and rolling with free abandon and sounding like they thoroughly enjoyed every single moment recording the album.

Title: If I Am Only My Thoughts
Review: The result is never less than amiable, but it also tends to slide past, like a pleasant daydream or an afternoon shadow.

Title: All Hands on the Bad One
Review: All Hands on the Bad One returns to concise song structure, making it more accessible and ultimately more satisfying.

Title: Two Parts Viper
Review: There's a quivering blues element to the sludgy stomp of Whether Terrified Or Unafraid, while elsewhere they twist the lo-fi fuzz into jarring alt.rock shapes, as Josh continues to serve up the deliciously unexpected. [10 Jun 2017, p.52]

Title: Great Escape
Review: The Rifles perservered, and if originality is not a strong point, their skill for crafting simple but immediate pop choruses makes uo foir it. [Nov 2008, p.109]

Title: An Other Cup
Review: Though the songs are all praises to the Creator (or His prophet), there is little sense of joy.

Title: Ready For The Weekend
Review: Ultimately, this is one party you might want to sit out. [Fall 2009, p.74]

Title: The Mountain
Review: The new rhythm section swerves and stomps harder than ever, making a racket worthy of Wennerstrom's voice--a veritable mountain of sound.

Title: Barchords
Review: Ultimately, the album's roomy sound and well-observed sentiments come across as byproducts of lived experience rather than of an extensive vinyl collection.

Title: Body Music
Review: AlunaGeorge have built a happy marriage out of the slick and the smart, and with Body Music, they just might manage the trick of making everyone else--from old fans to new ones; from critics to their record labels--happy too.

Title: All Nerve
Review: Mimicking the band's whole existence, it flickers between light and shade, its clouds fast-moving, sunshine blotted out before it breaks through. [Apr 2018, p.88]

Title: The Wolf
Review: The Wolf works best as a concept album about never surrendering the night when you got your first real six-string at the five-and-dime and were tryin' to break free. [Oct 2003, p.108]

Title: Ma
Review: Beautifully sweeping, unhurried strings are coupled with his whispered tones and gossamer Bunyan-Banhart harmonies making this a standout in an album with no shortage of heartfelt, melodious, Latin-flecked folk.

Title: Employment
Review: Try not to worry too much about where it comes from, or who else it may or may not sound like. Instead, enjoy a record that is quintessentially British, without pretension and most importantly, a whole lot of fun.

Title: Always
Review: Nothing's taboo in the surreal, often Fellini-esque reality [Stewart] concocts on the endlessly fascinating Always. [Mar 2012, p.81]

Title: The Disco's of Imhotep
Review: This particular release has all the textures, tinkles and poise the listener craves from Moss, while often arming them with some pretty hefty, distorted kicks and bass.

Title: Glad All Over
Review: It is probably Dylan's most distinctive statement. [Oct 2012, p.94]

Title: The Boombox Ballads
Review: The album is far from a lost cause. Sometimes, Two Lucky Magpies, Over And Out and the Bibio-esque titular instrumental are all lovely. But The Boombox Ballads annoys almost as much as it entertains.

Title: Unrest
Review: Much like KOC's albums, which tend to fade into the background as sonic wallpaper, the IKEA-sterile mood of "Unrest" does grow less distinctive by disc's end.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: I don't fault them for trying some new things, but the results are mixed at best.

Title: Designer
Review: The best moments on this record arrive when Harding’s playful approach to words syncs up with her playful approach to sound. The logic driving the end result may remain hidden, but its allure is undeniable.

Title: June Gloom
Review: June Gloom marks another confident step forward in the band’s quest to live up to their name in the indie-rock landscape.

Title: Los Angeles
Review: It's an inventive reimagining of hip hop with huge basslines underpinning the otherwise cinematic atmosphere.

Title: The Shade of Poison Trees
Review: The sugary 'Fever Dreams' and 'Little Bombs' sound threadbare, while glib homilies would shame the writers of Hallmark cards. [Dec 2007, p.115]

Title: Ignorance is Bliss
Review: Skepta is more than happy to satisfy his core fanbase. It’s something Dizzee Rascal struggled to find a formula for, so “Ignorance is Bliss” succeeds in that regard. Minus the terrible “Animal Instinct”, it’s easy to recommend.

Title: El Camino Real
Review: It doesn't take long to notice that the men of Camper Van Beethoven were having a lot more fun up north, while El Camino Real finds them playing with a technical skill that puts their early classics to shame but sounding curiously short on the joy and spontaneity that were once this band's trademark.

Title: Return to the Sea
Review: Those who felt like maybe they were starting to get Who Will Cut Our Hair When We’re Gone? only to be left out by Unicorns’ sudden dissolution should be reassured that Return to the Sea is a more rooted and confident effort.

Title: Shelter
Review: This is not to provide a blasting showcase for Chaney, as there is little ego on this record, and her talents at delivery and depth ripple through softly but persuasively.

Title: Feel Good Together
Review: Together, which was recorded during a period of lengthy down time for all parties earlier this year, is the sound of five guys bro-ing down, drinking beers and recording an album. It’s not the deepest thing ever recorded, but it is a fun little record that bears no pretense of seriousness.

Title: Goblin
Review: The repugnant misogynistic bullshit on Goblin sort of cancels any goodwill I have toward the guy. Particularly because it feels more like search engine optimization; Tyler makes no bones about his desire to hit the pop charts, and on too much of Goblin, he's doing it in the tawdriest way possible.

Title: Rock and Roll Night Club
Review: Rock and Roll Night Club is a confusing record, but not a mess. On the contrary, it's so deeply calculated that the intentions and possible motivations of its songs are likely to be lost on most.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Stunning. [Mar 2012, p. 96]

Title: Avonmore
Review: His own compositions show his romantic disconnection and crepuscular charm is undimmed.

Title: The Ascension
Review: With an 80-minute runtime, The Ascension feels overwhelming in its second act. ... But worried as it is, The Ascension isn’t without joy.

Title: Blood Money
Review: In terms of their long career of certified bangers it comes as a slight disappointment.

Title: The North Borders
Review: This is the sound of someone learning, brilliantly on the job. [May 2013, p.96]

Title: Life's Not Out To Get You
Review: The band have played it relatively safe, changing little from the upbeat pop-punk formula established on 2014's Wishful Thinking, but have still managed to cram some undeniably catchy moments into this new set.

Title: Scarecrow
Review: Country's biggest commodity takes the easy way out with a meticulously picked and produced batch of tunes (see: safe) that would be impossible to screw up.

Title: Power
Review: Power has a surprisingly cohesive feel, even as it shifts from the Beach Boys-infused harmonies of On Your Own to Prettiest Ones Fly Highest's hazy, Frank Ocean-like R&B, with only the slinky house beats of Cool Like Me sounding a false note. [Jan 2015, p.125]

Title: Perpetual Motion People
Review: Driven, hooky, moving. Better than Prozac or a sunny day. [Aug 2015, p.88]

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: One of the most flat-out enjoyable rock records in a long time.

Title: Masters of the Burial
Review: The music lover in Millan finds that stability in other people’s songs.

Title: All Day
Review: Gillis's vision becomes less orgiastic and more humanistic.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Lurching drum-machine beats, gentle piano chords, and somber string arrangements form the musical groundwork upon which Albarn sighs about the encroaching dominance of technology. If you’re the kind of person who shares this worldview, you may find Everyday Robots an often lovely demonstration of post-millennium tension. If not, the album’s monotony can fast become punishing.

Title: Hey Everyone
Review: Dananananaykroyd are, on this album's evidence, a fine band.

Title: Magnifique
Review: Songs are summery and bright, a more apt soundtrack to a road trip across Prince Edward County than to a night at an underground club.

Title: The Curse of Blondie
Review: Dub, metal, Okinawan folk, hip-hop and various strains of out jazz all inflect Blondie’s hooky popcraft, and they never pretend they’re something they’re not, such as young.

Title: James Blake
Review: Blake's songs are built around a single typically melancholic lyric and melody that he works over, kind of like an R&B singer, while gradually switching stylistic gears.

Title: The Bird and the Bee
Review: This is a record that gives up its secrets slowly, while being charming and delightful at every turn.

Title: Lover
Review: An album where the filler and the nuggets struggle for supremacy. ... Yet even those indifferent to Swift’s charms since she emerged as a teen-pop hitmaker in 2006 would probably acknowledge that she’s got a knack for writing hooks, and there are plenty of them on “Lover.”

Title: Call The Comet
Review: Call the Comet is more accomplished than compelling, but there is pleasure in hearing how all the parts fit together so tidily.

Title: Earth Division
Review: This is a case wherein open minds--and some patience--are likely to be rewarded.

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: Night Thoughts is another victory for the misfits.

Title: Shrines
Review: The record largely blurs together into a gloriously inscrutable haze, but certain songs resonate as sundry, singular experiences.

Title: Doom Abuse
Review: It's good--but not great.

Title: Love Keeps Kicking
Review: Martha's confessional and lovelorn themes fit perfectly in their revved-up pop framework. Love Keeps Kicking is a crystal-clear presentation of their powers, making equal space for the group's enduring stories of heartsickness, well-crafted pop structures, and blazing guitar work.

Title: The Amazons
Review: Presenting a portfolio of some of the best ‘rawk’ songs 2017 has to offer, The Amazons have remained consistent and have begun to embed themselves into the rich tapestry of rock ‘n’ roll with a bolshy stadium sound. If it ain’t broke...

Title: Poison Season
Review: Whether Poison Season is approached as an exhibition of those many individual pieces, or as an ensemble affair weaved subconsciously together, that conflicted point of view leads the listener to treat the whole LP as an exploration.

Title: Oceans Will Rise
Review: The Stills still aren't sure of their true identity, but at least those Interpol comparisons are way behind them. [Jan 2008, p.101

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: The elements are still there, but they aren’t fused in a way consistent with the hopes of those who foresaw The Strokes being the best rock band of our tim

Title: The Story of Light
Review: What The Story of Light shows in the end is that for every daring composition he gets right, there will be a few that are either too safe or not as well thought out.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: You're Dead loses momentum after "Never Catch Me." Much of the later two-thirds of the album is more atmospheric, reminiscent of 2012's more contemplative "When the Quiet Comes."

Title: Stop Mute Defeat
Review: Not all of the songs here find their mark, but it’s a fun ride nonetheless.

Title: Exister
Review: While it may not have that instant classic feel of Caution, it more than lives up to its older brothers in every way possible.

Title: The Difference Between Hell and Home
Review: 11 tracks with all the anguish that melodic hardcore thrives on, but with enough testosterone to keep it on the right side of whiney.

Title: DSVII
Review: DSVII is an undeniably florid soundscape of ‘80s pop culture touchstones. But hearing Gonzalez flesh these castoffs out into full songs through the lens of video game music feels like little more than an amusing experiment.

Title: Body Music
Review: Reid’s soundtrack is vibrant, but it can’t save the album from its own tedium.

Title: Stillmatic
Review: It's infuriatingly inconsistent.... But this album's bittersweet beauty lies in the fact that Nas cares. [Feb 2002, p.120]

Title: Many Moons
Review: Whilst not engrossing for the entirety of its running, Many Moons is still a pleasurable listening experience. It takes a few listens to get to the lyrical gems, which can often be remarkably revelatory.

Title: Sun Gangs
Review: Although less vitriolic than 2006's "Nux Vomica," his third album still throbs with delicious melodrama and anguished assertions.

Title: Lust Lust Lust
Review: Lust gives them the most emotionally substantive material they’ve ever had to work with, and yet there’s still that sense of detached restraint.

Title: Young Prayer
Review: It's the kind of record that will have a profound impact on a small number of people, be ridiculed by many more, and never be heard at all by almost everybody.

Title: SuperHeavy
Review: At its least enjoyable, however, you're struck--not for the first time in Jagger's extracurricular oeuvre--by a sense of star-studded pointlessness.

Title: The Invisible Way
Review: The Invisible Way is very good--and not just “good for a band that’s 20 years old.”

Title: Get What You Give
Review: While it may not be the Ghost Inside's best work--that title still belongs to Returners--Get What You Give is an impressive addition to their discography and will certainly boost their profile.

Title: Collection
Review: It largely manages to avoid vapid repetition and provides plenty of charm and promise for the future. [Sep 2017, p.37]

Title: After the Disco
Review: After The Disco is an exceptionally successful record filled with the type of uplifting melody we've come to expect from the pair, as well as more direct, clearer lyrics and an overall sharper edge.

Title: Ways to Forget
Review: The album captures little of the Opera's live spirit.

Title: In the Lonely Hour
Review: Just when you've started to grow weary of Smith's pity party, it's over. And there are enough moments of genuine musical, lyrical, and vocal virtuosity and soul to crack even the most hardened listener's icy heart.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: Iceage’s sophomore disc may not match the jagged punch and pulse of its debut, but it points the way toward an escape from its frigid, self-imposed cell.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: The amount of change from Ta Det Lugnt to Tio Bitar may be minimal, but this superb new album is no less rewarding.

Title: Face the Promise
Review: Because Seger has honed his craft to such a silver-bullet point, the album never feels like a retread; as on John Fogerty’s underrated Deja Vu All Over Again from 2004, roots-rock tradition seems renewed in Seger’s hands.

Title: Red Yellow & Blue
Review: Throughout Red, Yellow and Blue the timbre is really spare, but Born Ruffians show that you don’t need much else to create a compelling record.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: Great, better even than the last.

Title: Memory
Review: Guitarist Cassie Ramone and bassist Katy Goodman haven’t tweaked much of their fast-paced and fuzz-caked formula this time around, but they’ve certainly refined the hell out of it. Never has the band sounded so imposing in a studio setting, reining their once-uncontainable feedback into a beefy wall of sound.

Title: Wildflower
Review: Wildflower is assiduously intimate: lushly orchestrated, strictly mid-tempo and abundant with musings about balancing freedom and love. [Oct 2005, p.136]

Title: Constant Bop

Review: He's a modern master.

Title: High Risk Behaviour
Review: It’s hard to critique punk music. You’re judging exactly how much someone doesn’t give a fuck and how well they are at expressing that. High Risk Behaviour is an album you can blast on the highway while going 90 or one that you can watch live and get drunk and crowd-surf to.

Title: Eclipse
Review: Eclipse falls flat too often--eclipsing, some might say, the stadium-worthy songs we know he can achieve.

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: Their debut is yearning blog-pop, which might be a bit ‘2009 called...’ if songs like ‘New House’ weren’t just as sharp as their 80s, sax-ballad ancestors.

Title: R Plus Seven
Review: On R Plus Seven, it just sounds like triumph.

Title: As Light Return
Review: Throughout, Lawrie's voice is buried so deep in the mix as to be virtually inaudible, like a Mary Chain 7" slowed down to 33rpm. [Aug 2017, p.38]

Title: Somebody's Miracle
Review: Pleasant but dull.

Title: A Different Ship
Review: Sonically, it's jaw-dropping, particularly on headphones: every cymbal splash and synth squiggle purr up-close and personal. But most of these 10 tracks are so subtle, they might drift past unnoticed if you're not listening hard enough.

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: A trash-conscious blend of craft and humour gives them the sass, style and balls to sound like no one else around. [Mar 2004, p.111]

Title: Optica
Review: Thanks to the production, the overall strength of the songs, and the quietly intense energy the bandmembers put into their performances, Optica is a welcome return to form and solidifies Shout Out Louds' position as one of the best indie pop bands of their era.

Title: Every Valley
Review: Every Valley is lush and symphonic, more interested in expressing the human spirit of the mining communities than aestheticising the conditions in which they toiled.

Title: proVISIONS
Review: Now, at 52, Gelb’s music seems to have found a renewed vigour, a sharper focus. ProVISIONS not only has some lean 'n' lovely boy-girl ballads, wild mood swings and a frequent groove, but also a sense of intent.

Title: Only Run
Review: The most optimistic light to view Only Run in is also the most condemning; it’s not so much a fully realized album as it is a promising blueprint for songs that haven’t yet been written.

Title: Undermind
Review: The ballads are clunky and ponderous. The groove stuff, though... exists in that blissy stratosphere the Dead visited so often. [Aug 2004, p.138]

Title: Attack & Release
Review: The result is a flawless (post)modernisation of heartland rock that wears its lovelorn pessimism proudly on its ruffled sleeve.

Title: Nobody's Daughter
Review: Overall, Nobody's Daughter isn't a complete backfire, but it is proof that Love should hang up the Hole moniker and stick to her own solo career instead, since this release is basically a Courtney Love solo record that just happens to have a Hole logo on the cover instead.

Title: La Liberacion
Review: They fail to relocate it [their exuberance] on the follow-up, which if anything, is even drearier. [Sep 2011, p.104]

Title: Hubcap Music
Review: Recycled though some of these tales may be--his notable past tends to weave its way into much of his work--sung with his Southern drawl and playful hollers, Seasick Steve just about has the charm and vigour to carry them through.

Title: The Bachelor
Review: The Bachelor is quite a journey with a clear direction and theme. Wolf is going through an inner struggle and seeks to find a resolution.

Title: Mutable Set
Review: There are fleeting, faraway echoes of John Martyn at his wooziest, but Mills has crafted something very personal and individual.

Title: Ã·
Review: At best, we have a middling collection of songs that are going to sound great in a packed arena. At worst, it’s a pretty significant step back from X, and once the initial novelty of its release wears off, it’s unlikely to enjoy the popular acclaim or the longevity of its predecessor.

Title: Shrines
Review: The inventiveness in James's vocals draws attention to the lack of that quality in Roddick's production, which grows clichéd after a while.

Title: Sam Baker's Album
Review: All in all, most every cut on Sam Baker's Album is solid in its own right, but maybe 40 minutes is just too much, considering that the lines which box in the instrumental hip-hop genre become only more clear as the album pushes on.

Artist: Thao & the Get Down Stay Down
Title: Know Better Learn Faster
Review: On her sophomore KRS LP with the Get Down Stay Down, she sorts out emotional laundry via foot stomps and soul-searching.

Title: This Is Our Science
Review: It's a challenging, complex and sometimes brilliant album from an extremely talented artist who doesn't place limits on himself, though at times you may wish he had thrown a few small ones in there.

Title: Bitter Rivals
Review: Ultimately, Bitter Rivals offers the comfort of familiarity while being different enough to avoid breeding contempt.

Title: Fields
Review: Earthy, enigmatic and possessed of a refreshing lightness of touch.

Title: There's No Leaving Now
Review: With a voice that creaks like well-loved furniture and lyrics telling tales of the lives and losses of others, this album represents a career highpoint.

Title: Liverpool 8
Review: If you can deal with the nostalgia factor, it’s a pleasant but unremarkable disc.

Title: Cheatahs
Review: If you were someone who felt stood-up by Yuck’s follow-up to their self-titled debut, Cheatahs will follow through on the promise that great rainy Saturday afternoon shoegaze isn’t all gazing into a rearview mirror.

Title: Mudcrutch
Review: Mudcrutch is a grand old slice of classic country rock that not only serves as Petty’s finest work in almost a decade but is a mighty fine incentive for any long-defunct group with a hankering to dust off the drama and head back into the studio to quit their harboring and just go for it.

Title: Electrified
Review: DB's spry, Breeders-style way of recasting '60s and '70s rawk is enough to rescue it--and us--from tedium. [23 Jul 2005, p.50]

Title: Once Again
Review: His most impressive skill is echoing the laid-back charm of Bill Withers and the melodic instincts of Stevie Wonder. [Dec 2006, p.104]

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: She offsets an assault of cheekiness with confessions so intimate, they could have been drafted during an A.A. meeting.

Title: Floating Coffin
Review: Welcome back heavy bass and the practically patented echoing falsettos because John Dwyer’s mellow Putrifiers II mood is gone.

Title: Fork In The Road
Review: The sloppily played garage rock riffs complement the slapdash nature of the lyrics, and--as you might expect--it’s that loose, under-rehearsed and under-written methodology that is both the album’s strength and its downfall.

Title: In the Pit of the Stomach
Review: For a record that doesn't at all attempt to reinvent the two-guitars-bass-drums toolkit of punk-inflected modern indie rock, it's fundamental whole ends up being greater than its parts.

Title: We Are The Night
Review: We Are the Night is no departure, although it does reveal Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons showing some build-to-suit character instead of angling for the straitjacket-tight and over-serious dance music of their past ten years.

Title: Mastermind
Review: This album may be a step up from his previous outing, 2012's God Forgives, I Don't, but Mastermind hints that the Rick Ross story may have nowhere else to go.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die
Review: The most arresting of Twelve Reasons to Die's many pleasures is how out of time the album feels: Its pointed narrative distance from straight-faced gangster rap is very 2013, but the simple virtuosity of the small moments smacks of eras in both rap and soul that passed long before Ghost ever stepped to a mic.

Title: Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)
Review: The most compelling moments (“I Am Dust” and the title track) are like mechanized, sci-fi mini-operas, awesomely grandiose and yet disturbingly proximate enough to breathe all that fear right down your neck through your spine.

Title: Music for Listening to Music To
Review: Music for Listening to Music to borrows a little of Morrissey’s lyrical melodrama and a lot of Johnny Marr’s mellifluous guitars, which provide some of the album’s most arresting moments.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: Few other bands could provide properly sympathetic backing for a singer who delivers his roiling emotions in such sad, sleepy tones. [Oct 2004, p.112]

Title: Jackie Lynn
Review: The album does demand great attention. I can’t imagine any of these songs playing on the radio, or on one or two listens attracting new fans. Stalwarts of Circuit des Yeux and Haley Fohr will likely delight, however, in this new installment of her performance art.

Title: Go To School
Review: Featuring contributions from Jody Stephens (Big Star) and Brian and Michael's father Ronnie D’Addario, Go To School is a true beauty and a classic in its own right.

Title: Accelerate
Review: Accelerate is patchy at best, with only the blaring finale, ‘I’m Gonna DJ’, really catching the attention.

Title: Vertigo
Review: As ever, the single 44-minute track sis immersive; those coming to The Necks for a transcendent mindfulness session, however, may find it distinctly unnerving in places. [Dec 2015, p.75]

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: If nothing else, The Good, the Bad & the Queen is a clear demonstration of Albarn's maturation.

Title: Apex Predator - Easy Meat
Review: Musically, the band mixes its customary blast beat-driven grindcore maelstroms--the punishing one-two assault of “Smash a Single Digit” and “Metaphorically Screw You,” the layered, complex “Cesspits”--with industrial dolor (“Dear Slum Landlord”) and junk-bin clangor (the title track): caustic nods to influential circa-early ’80s noise-mongers like Public Image Ltd. and Swans.

Title: Revel In The Drama
Review: Against all odds, this is a brilliant second act. [Jun 2020, p.97]

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: Be it the ramped-up action of Dirty Three's wildest workouts or the cool-off come-downs that give their music a sense of closure and completeness, everything has a purpose and place on Toward the Low Sun.

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Visitor
Review: Listeners who've already given up on Young's current output are unlikely to be lured back by anything here, but for those of us still following his uniquely meandering path—in and out of the proverbial ditch--it's a ride well worth taking.

Title: The Good Fight
Review: Oddisee challenges uninitiated music lovers to engage with his ideas and his formidable body of work.

Title: The Silver Lining
Review: Sound[s] like a band that's discovered how to enjoy itself again. [Aug 2006, p.85]

Title: Dear
Review: While intended as a love letter to their longtime fans, this 23rd LP from the Japanese rockers feels more like an optimal entry point for newcomers.

Title: Champ
Review: Slowed down and keyboarded up, these tunes make what cares they do bear seem lyrical--carefree.

Title: A Kind Revolution
Review: So while the production isn’t as in-your-face as before, the flourishes that characterised those releases are here deployed to subtle effect on an album that’s only too happy to explore a variety of stylistic routes including blues, jazz, deep house and dub elements to make a surprisingly coherent and cohesive statement.

Title: Reads The Books EP
Review: The fusion of The Books' folk stylings and traditional instrumentation (cellos, banjos, clavinets) with Prefuse's hip-hop stutter-funk produces fresh moments, just not as many as desired.

Title: August By Cake
Review: A daunting 32 tracks and some typically uneven quality control. However, there's a renewed freshness here. [Jun 2017, p.106]

Title: What's It All About
Review: Metheny transforms balladic pop tunes into abnormally sophisticated easy listening.

Title: Traps
Review: Most of Traps keeps the toes a-tapping with happily-sung, sad-bastard references to bygone lovers, running out of weed and coming of quarter-age. [No.88 p.57]

Title: Winchester Cathedral
Review: A brand new bag of impossible shapes, rumbaing in esoteric formation. [#13, p.121]

Title: Virginia Creeper
Review: A fabulous, strangely soothing listen. [Feb 2004, p.100]

Title: Fast Forward
Review: Whether he is grappling with his confusion with the modern world in the searching title track, mulling the delightful aggravations of relationships on “If It Wasn’t For You” and the joys of making up on “A Little Smile,” or working up a froth on his rage, rattle, and roll version of Television’s “See No Evil,” Jackson is in peak form.

Title: Language
Review: For a band that spent a year in solitude writing and recording Language, Zulu Winter sound an awful lot like everyone else out there.

Title: Weather
Review: Weather is so deftly under-produced that you turn it up; so hazy and intimate you're drawn in close. [Jan 2012, p.98]

Title: SR3MM
Review: At this stage, both brothers realize they work better together, though SR3MM's unique format allows for a distinct look at the two very different parts of what make Rae Sremmurd tick.

Title: Kidal
Review: Kidal is first and foremost a kick-ass, spirited rock 'n' roll album that demands to be heard far beyond any 'World Music' specialist interest circles.

Title: Keep The Village Alive
Review: Occupational hazards aside however, this is certainly the band’s strongest in recent memory, and what it might lack in edge or novelty is well countered by craft and assurance.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: Yes, fourteen years is a long time to wait between records. But, when the end product is this good, it might just be worth the wait.

Title: Four Stones
Review: Simultaneously soaring and depthless, soothing and unnerving, solemn and joyful, McPhee's excursions feel weird, unknowable, as if the path we're on is both bright and labyrinthine, a certain route to the unknown. [Feb 2018, p.94]

Title: Nevermen
Review: With each layer adding something to the stew when time on their own endeavors allowed, Nevermen is a successful and forward-thinking act of sonic maximalism. [No. 128, p.52]

Title: Magnificent Fiend
Review: So there is a lot to love within this album. Its knowing winks to rock’s early ‘70s excesses and sage-like nods to the soulful marriage of rock and rhythm and blues exemplified by Sly and Curtis mean that we’re comforted rather than challenged.

Title: Performance
Review: Even with all the jazz, jams, and wonky improvisations, the nine tracks of musicians' music remain fun, unpretentious.

Title: Open Up Your Head
Review: With every listen, each song takes on a new richness, becoming something that will simultaneously become the sound of summer, yet a particular personal soundtrack that you’ll keep on coming back to.

Title: Be Slowly
Review: Those looking for 24/7  simple, saccharine sun and smiles may be jarred in a few odd points; but the rest of us can enjoy the added punch and intensity that Be Slowly brings to the table.

Title: We're Not Talking
Review: Packed with a convincing fusion of craftmanship, camaraderie and charm, We’re Not Talking certainly never comes close to a sophomore slump.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: Free of filler and definitely worth repeating, Hive Mind is the Internet we know and love, but tighter and more refined.

Title: Forth Wanderers
Review: Altogether, it's a rock-solid set, notable for good songs as well as a distinctive if simultaneously throwback sound.

Title: Home Sweet Home
Review: Kano's album is ridiculously good.

Title: There Were Wolves
Review: The lack of a reliance on the electronic merging with folk is the most interesting aspect to There Were Wolves; whereas it is essential to the appeal of Genders’ Tunng gang, The Accidental plays it straight, using those ever-present vocal sounds on top of primarily unadorned acoustic numbers.

Title: Shadow of a Doubt
Review: Check the great "Extradite" ("Man, I stay on point like icicles") for instant gratification or "Basketball Wives" for an abstract take on the Miguel-flavored bedroom number, then appreciate how this album goes 17 tracks deep and never runs out of inspiration or ideas.

Title: Ready to Die
Review: The result wears the weight of its history lightly, with the exception of "The Departed", a solemn tribute to lost Stooges.

Title: Immunity
Review: This is an intelligent and deeply human album and it would be no exaggeration to say that it’s already a modern classic.

Title: Home Everywhere
Review: Sometimes the album's constant zigzagging can create a bit of a discombobulated effect, but Medicine have never been the sort to adhere to any rules but their own.

Title: A Crow Looked at Me
Review: Pain is the crux of Elverum’s career, and without resorting to any of his brutally stark instrumentation, he offers his most sobering full-length to date, and likely of all time.

Title: The Only Place
Review: The Only Place delivers riveting drama in a rousing pop package, with Brion rescuing Best Coast from the fuzzed-out, lo-fi indie template, cleaning up their sound and enhancing the potential for mainstream appeal exponentially without diminishing their artistic credibility.

Title: Barchords
Review: There's a striking purity to this record. [Mar 2012, p.79]

Title: Elemental Themes
Review: Once again, probably not a highly sought-after sound, but then again, when an album is this well put together, who really cares?

Title: In Search of Stoney Jackson
Review: For an in-demand producer like Madlib, it might not be good business to give some of his most stunning beats to a relatively unknown group, but Jackson is brilliant enough to elevate Strong Arm Steady to the level of cult heroes.

Title: Shattered
Review: Some Reigning Sound fans might miss the harder-rocking side of the band, but if you're looking for ten new Greg Cartwright songs sung with real heart and soul, Shattered is just what you've been waiting for.

Title: Unleash The Love
Review: Lackluster as music and downright puzzling as a cultural artifact, Unleash the Love confirms that whatever you think of Mike Love's 21st century edition of the Beach Boys, he's better off doing that than trying to make music by himself.

Title: Leisure Seizure
Review: How long before the next Vek release remains to be seen, but Leisure Seizure will be stuck in your head long after you quit listening.

Title: Street Horrrsing
Review: It’s just the fucking jam, like some pulsing late-night bliss-out in front of a detuned television set whereupon everyone just sits on the couch exhausted but loving it.

Title: Spot the Difference
Review: Though this material has been rereleased ad nauseam, Squeeze obsessives will eat it up. For everyone else, it's a reminder that songs like ''Take Me I'm Yours'' have aged surprisingly well.

Title: Stay Trippy
Review: Stay Trippy may not be the album you play for doubters to prove the artistic merits of hip-hop, and its subject matter wears thin after a while, but damn if it doesn't sound good loud.

Title: Money and Celebrity
Review: Deep it is not, and its aspirations to be something greater keep it from being truly trashy fun, but there are enough energy and hooks to keep Money and Celebrity entertaining.

Title: Destroyed
Review: As with the majority of his work, the most notable tracks are all instrumental. [May 2011, p.89]

Title: Before the Poison
Review: A classic work...together [her collaborators] have created a near perfect, and wonderfully paced, stage for the singer. [Oct 2004, p.112]

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: In the hands of someone less witty and schizoid, a near three-hour epic would be unforgivable, but Merritt at play is frequently magical.

Title: 1,000 Years
Review: Corin Tucker's voice--always so uniquely emotive in the punkier contexts of S-K--looms uncomfortably over songs that sound scrapbooked from other '90s-centric acts (Liz Phair, Pavement) but never take on a form of their own.

Title: TO LOVE IS TO LIVE
Review: Although it seems Jehnny Beth has decided to go solo to express more of her vulnerabilities, by the end of To Love is To Live it’s hard to say whether we actually feel any closer to her. However, it also shows her chameleonic abilities as a vocalist, as she’s working with different styles and productions yet still sounding urgent.

Title: All Days Are Nights: Songs For Lulu
Review: The only things you hear on the album are Wainwright's voice and his piano, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. The problem is that he wants you to luxuriate in both when it's far more likely you'll feel like you're drowning, given how rarely Wainwright buoys the listener with an actual melody or memorable lyric.

Title: Under Pressure
Review: Just like Kendrick's stunning Good Kid, M.A.A.D City, Under Pressure is an autobiographical and odds-beating debut that arrives more fully formed than expected. Maybe all those mixtapes were all called Young Sinatra because the best was yet to come.

Title: I Will Set You Free
Review: All over the place, he takes you along for an engaging ride. [Feb 2012, p.97]

Title: Further Complications
Review: Steve Albini’s production retains some of the lushness Cocker favored on Pulp’s later albums and his solo debut, while investing it with a new punchiness. The approach ups the drama on Cocker’s tales of mid-life desire and failure.

Title: Traffic and Weather
Review: The everyday-ness of the songs makes them easily relatable, but, like a commute where traffic and weather happen on the 10s, the album starts to feel routine by the end.

Title: Pearl Jam
Review: Though few of these 13 numbers have the drama of tracks by the Who or Led Zeppelin, from whom the band draw much of their style, Pearl Jam play like men on a mission.

Title: Nothing Hurts
Review: It's lo-fi at its finest and a contender for one of the more impressive debuts of the year so far. Fans of the genre will lap it up and with very good reason: it's short, sharp and straight to the point.

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: While more than half the album flounders and meanders uselessly to arrive at roughly four truly worthwhile numbers, parts of Minutes to Midnight set the foundations for a whole new array of sounds that the band can and hopefully will pursue in the future.

Title: North Star Deserter
Review: The [guest] musicians have the good sense to know when to let Chesnutt's dry-leaf vocals and muted acoustic guitar carry the songs, and when to swell up and bring heightened Gothic intensity to the feelings of melancholy and dread. [Oct 2007, p.55]

Title: Hands All Over
Review: The rude guitar sleaze of Hands All Over, or the cocky glam-stomp in Stutter's verses show a band who are really at their best when they play pop music like the sleazy rockers they clearly are. In Adam Levine's mind, at least.

Title: Crash Love
Review: In no uncertain terms, Crash Love is an accomplishment that raises the bar for them as musicians and writers.

Title: Embryonic
Review: Embryonic is a true 21st century freak-out and it's only appropriate to end this decade with such an ambitious, intrepid undertaking.

Title: The Boxer
Review: In place of huge choruses and bombast, Kele offers an album heavy on tone, mood, and texture. Unfortunately, his efforts fail to make you forget the absence of things like hooks.

Title: Nobody Wants to Be Here and Nobody Wants to Leave
Review: Nobody Wants to Be Here and Nobody Wants to Leave offers a more nuanced musical narrative arc than any of the Twilight Sad’s previous albums. Where quiet moments have more often felt like necessary breathers to reload for further bombardment, here the dynamic shifts between the songs push things forward as much as those within them.

Title: Their Prime
Review: A brilliant and unexpected ride from start to finish.

Title: Return to the Sea
Review: The Frank Zappa/Neutral Milk Hotel/Muppet Show vibe doesn't always jibe, but that's half the fun. [7 Apr 2006, p.63]

Title: Spoils
Review: Its successor emanates a similarly yeasty authenticity, stretching songs into epic ballads, its acoustic guitars, bass and drums ornamented by a lattice of deftly plucked and strummed things. [May 2009, p.105]

Title: Eight
Review: The more adventurous shifts in style aren't without merit, but feel more curious than exciting.

Title: Water Curses EP
Review: Water Curses sits just shy of being worth the price of admission, even if the individual tracks are.

Title: Wavering Radiant
Review: It’s a proper album, in the sense that a divide is made at four of seven, the title track a segue between halves – its makers clearly bear download culture little respect, constructing their latest so that it’s best experienced as a whole, bridging arrangements as vital as the blustering bombast and constitutional inflections of grandly designed standout pieces.

Title: The Centre Cannot Hold
Review: To run with the cinematic analogies, I'd suggest that Frost is the musical equivalent of Nicolas Winding Refn, all neon lit brutality and state of the art emptiness. [Oct 2017, p.52]

Title: LAX
Review: The album, weighed down by a few awkward romance tracks and a well-meaning but ill-fitting MLK tribute, drags in the second half, and there’s no one moment to parallel the odd ache of 'Doctor’s Avocate.' But it’s once again more than the sum of its parts.

Title: Sundowning
Review: The whole album is marked by a pure, intense, feel, and Lukic's vocals don't need to be understood to hit you in your gut.

Title: Seeds
Review: Seeds is destined to grow and grow. Exhilarating stuff.

Title: Slow Air
Review: So safe they remain for Slow Air--with the same airbrushed slick of 2016’s Dead Blue, Greg Hughes and Tessa Murray pare back the fog machines and phone in a mostly forgettable series of pleasant enough new wave, as distant and vague as the storybook rainforest on the cover.

Title: Silver Dollar Moment
Review: Silver Dollar Moment’s vibrancy is at odds with the current mood of the world, but it’s also a vital indication of where we’re at now in terms of indie music’s trajectory. It shakes off any negative connotations of modern indie, particularly in the ‘landfill’ sense of the word, and reclaims it.

Title: The Cold Still
Review: Moments of band interplay showcase their collective ear for the nervously romantic-sounding post-punk that's helped inspire the group's sound.

Title: Smoke + Mirrors
Review: The combination of self-pity, grandiosity and leaden spirituality can get trying. And all those attempts at musical worldliness can feel like stylistic tourism.

Title: Thee Physical
Review: Nothing sticks on the LP, and the disc feels recycled, pedestrian and a bit exhausting--at best.

Title: White Bear
Review: This second album is laden with big, chunky riffs and swaggering anthems tailormade for waving scarves and throwing beer.

Title: Crooked Man
Review: As a producer, Barratt is the equal of anyone working today, but what’s most amazing is that even after 30-plus years, he still seems to be as connected with the magic of dancefloor moments as he ever was.

Title: Cavalier Youth
Review: The album is consistently tuneful, yet also pile-driving and monolithic.

Title: The Search
Review: The Search is protest music for the cryptology set.

Title: Carry On The Grudge
Review: Carry On the Grudge manoeuvres around post-adolescence with expertise. The void might exist, but at least now Jamie T is back there's someone to share the pain with.

Title: As Long As I Have You
Review: Muscular adaptations of Stephen Stills' How Far and Parliament's Get On Out Of The Rain stray into '70s Who territory, with stirring arrangements and hot Townshend licks, while his courageous tilt at Nick Cave piano ballad Into My Arms roils with heartache that can;t be faked. [Jun 2018, p.89]

Title: King Tuff
Review: More quality control wouldn't have gone amiss. [Jul 2012, p.104]

Title: Cocoon Crush
Review: Cocoon Crush is a portrait of an artist in transition. It’s rough around the edges, occasionally stunning, and always surprising.

Title: Angels of Death
Review: The arrangements of the album contrast between moments of minimal instrumentation, layered with her vulnerable vocal melodies that seem complementary of the overall theme. It could be felt at points that the musicality seems to move without increased colour, but it is only when you venture further into the album and the lyricism that it becomes clearer that this is likely to be understood as a reflection of the concept.

Title: Here We Rest
Review: The album is his most consistent and complete, finding room for singer-songwriter-type country, alt. country, harder rock and soul within a single record, while retaining a sense of direction and cohesiveness, as well as heart, soul and a satisfying emotional connection between artist and audience .

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Miss Anthropocene is a Kanye West of a listening experience. Strengthened by listening less hard and chilling out. Weakened by due diligence and the artist’s cerebral disconnect between what she's great at making and who she believes she is.

Title: Seeing Other People
Review: Mostly their ebullient sixth LP is clever and kooky enough to be cherished on its own terms. [Jul 2019, p.110]

Title: Punisher
Review: Tucked in among the record’s memorable melodies, clever arrangements and impressive guests are a steady stream of details that lend plainspoken perspective to Bridgers’ emotional highs and (mostly) lows. These kinds of details ground her work in the same way shading makes a still life painting pop. They make them feel not just sad, but real.

Title: Æ’IN
Review: His slow-burning music ... has serious cross-over potential. [Apr 2012, p.91]

Title: Dancing at the Blue Lagoon
Review: Rather than braving the road less traveled, Yudin doubles down on his replication of trite indie rock tropes.

Title: Psychic Chasms
Review: Whatever its origins, Psychic Chasms extols no actual reasons for being those ways, instead touching on now-expected tropes and empty gestures to fund a handful of ready-made critical anecdotes and popular opinions.

Title: Travellers in Space and Time
Review: An insufferable post-twee jaunt which represents the messy sound of a band fooling around with a studio full of toys.

Title: Detroit 2
Review: There are moments on Detroit 2 that feel special, but Big Sean himself rarely has anything to do with them.

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: Yet for all the sharp hooks and rhythmic twists, the album sags in the middle. [Apr 2008, p.127]

Title: Antifogmatic
Review: For all their peerless technical skill, it's the gutsiness they display throughout Antifogmatic that makes the album one of the year's finest, most ambitious records.

Title: The Lucky Ones
Review: Pitched somewhere between the Blues Explosion and Grinderman, it's an awesome racket, but the lack of time spent means the potential of 'Next Time' and the fevered 'New Meaning' have been lost in the rush to record. [July 2008, p.108]

Title: Songs for Singles
Review: Songs For Singles has a throwaway feel, albeit one with a lot of juddering, earth-shaking weight behind it. [25 Sep 2010, p.52]

Title: Gemstones
Review: Over the course of Gemstone's 15 tracks, Green's heavily enunciated, lumbering delivery become more irritating than a busload of thespians on their way to an audition. Thankfully, Green's elementary-school melodies, which call to mind Jonathan Richman at his silliest, ultimately save this album from the topical hell to which it aspires.

Title: R Plus Seven
Review: R Plus Seven feels isolated and eerily post-human. Musically it may be Oneohtrix Point Never’s most accessible work yet, but the emotional pull it exerts is minimal.

Title: Ali & Toumani
Review: This 11-track album--the second collection of collaborations by Touré and the Malian kora player Toumani Diabeté--doesn't sound like death. Rather, it's an early contender for the warmest, most life-affirming listen of 2010.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: To the relief of anyone who carries a torch for the reclusive genius, it's a beauty.

Title: Life Without Sound
Review: It seems as though Dylan Baldi has effectively evolved from a musical loner trying to go it alone to a mature frontman fully integrated in a strong and cohesive band. It seems as though Dylan Baldi has finally become a punk.

Title: Mr Beast
Review: The revelation of Mr. Beast is that it's the closest Mogwai have come to capturing the raw intensity of their live power. [#13, p.93]

Title: Desperate Man
Review: For better or worse, his new LP sidesteps largely hot-button debates. One exception is its opener, “The Snake,” a slithering, unplugged, dub-tinged parable suggesting strivers of all political shades consider their real enemies.

Title: Girl Talk
Review: Thankfully, while Nash has moved to a more extroverted, aggressive sound, she hasn't sacrificed any of the personal, intimate lyrics that marked the best of her early songs.

Title: I Speak Because I Can
Review: On I Speak Because I Can, her great leap forward after 2008's captivating Mercury-nominated debut, Marling deploys an archaic folk patois with convincing gravitas. [Apr 2010, p.118]

Title: News From Nowhere
Review: Its balance of electronic, acoustic and vocal elements, while initially impressive, is soon revealed to be a product of the lack of any forceful musical or textual elements at all. [Feb 2013, p.60]

Title: Always Strive and Prosper
