Review: Despite the occasional uncertainty, Always Strive and Prosper answers more questions than it poses. Ferg has clearly stepped up his game by delivering his most well-rounded project thus far.

Title: Conatus
Review: Mostly, though, Conatus gives you a more polished version of exactly what you'd want from a Zola Jesus album.

Title: In Ghost Colours
Review: Regardless of what kind of audience it ultimately finds, though, In Ghost Colours earns its smiles with a combination of ingenuity and easiness that you don't often come by, and for that, even in April, it already feels like a triumph.

Title: Relapse
Review: By letting Dr. Dre take over the low-end-funk production, and rhyming about things he actually cares about, he comes up with a more painful, honest and vital record than anyone could have expected at this late date, up there with "The Eminem Show" or maybe even better.

Title: OutRun
Review: It induces a heady sense of perpetual forward motion, whether graceful or full pelt. Stunning.

Title: Sea Change
Review: Sea Change not only signals a pinnacle in his career but may just be remembered, in an environment fueled by accelerating cycles of disposable culture, as one of this young decade's best records.

Title: Christ Illusion
Review: If you're the sort of person who only buys one metal album a year, then you'd probably be better off buying the new Mastodon album 'Blood Mountain' and going to see Slayer live but otherwise, what the hell are you waiting for...

Title: New Seasons
Review: As time passes, it sounds samey, though rich nevertheless.

Title: Welcome Back To Milk
Review: Produced by Bad Seed Jim Sclavunos, this latest project sees her moving away from the playful whimsy of her debut in favour of looser, gritter textures. [Jun 2015, p.75]

Title: OutRun
Review: Once you’ve finished Kavinsky’s OutRun, you’ll want to buckle up and ride again.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: As twelve equally matched moments of varied tone but consistent brilliance, it's nothing short of exactly what was expected--the start of something even bigger.

Title: Slicker Than Your Average
Review: This gentle, suave, insistent smoothie parlayed his direct lyrics and tricky beats into a strong straight r&b album in a year when contenders Raphael Saadig and Me'shell NdegéOcello got tangled up in form.

Title: Deliverance
Review: The album has a coherency that was absent first time around, and there is also a rattling freshness to the sound that Timbaland has rustled up.

Title: Human Conditions
Review: Further indulges his penchant for meticulously-crafted songs, exquisite production, and (sometimes painstaking) personal and spiritual introspection.

Title: Eat Pray Thug
Review: Eat Pray Thug is nothing if not awkwardly paced (the forgettable braggadocio of “Hubba Hubba Hima” clumsily follows “Home”), but it does manage a rare feat in being at once Heems’ most personal and political work.

Title: La Costa Perdida
Review: If you get past the fact that CBV aren’t trying to be radical or cutting edge, or even particularly contemporary, you’ll find a pleasantly undemanding, chilled-out record that’s the perfect soundtrack for all those warm summer evenings we’re crossing our fingers for at the moment.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: One shudders to think how wack the rejects are. [Nov 2004, p.156]

Title: Perils from the Sea
Review: Perils from the Sea skillfully bridges the gap between Kozelek's most recent offerings, which favored classical guitar and vocal over full-band arrangements, with the fuller sound of his Red House Painters and early Sun Kil Moon years, resulting in a listening experience that trades in the distant, narrative-driven opaqueness of Admiral Fell Promises and Among the Leaves for a newfound inclusivity that suits both parties.

Title: Gutter Tactics
Review: Disenchantment with the state of rap, and society as a whole, is a major underlying theme, but the statements never feel too preachy or in your face. Instead, the vocal freestyles hover just slightly above the music, delivered in an amorphous mumble that matches the sonic abyss of the background perfectly.

Title: Electric Light
Review: This follow-up displays an admirable desire for transformation. [Jun 2018, p.111]

Title: Blaqkout
Review: Neither artist disappoints on the LP and Quik continues to progress and go beyond the boundaries of traditional west coast hip-hop. Although I'm not sure if fans will ride down Crenshaw bumping a few of the songs on the album, I salute Quik and Kurupt for trying something new.

Title: Tears, Lies and Alibis
Review: Tears, Lies, and Alibis is an album worth buying mainly for two reasons. Firstly the opening track, Rains Came. It sits in what sounds like a familiar bed, but doesn't quite go where you expect it to, and is, this time, lyrically opaque. Secondly, you can drown in her voice. It is fabulous; not an in-your-face "listen to how many octaves I can leap" sort of way, but it effortlessly convinces you she's lived this stuff, and means every word.

Title: 1000 Days
Review: It's heady.... Wand delivers dynamic, lysergic rock 'n' roll. [No. 125, p.61]

Title: The Sun Awakens
Review: The Sun Awakens" is best described as a doom-folk record, encompassing the thick sludge of hyperdistorted electric guitar as well as the rattle and vibration of double-stopped riffs from his acoustic guitar.

Title: Under the Iron Sea
Review: An album to return to again and again, whose depth grows with every spin.

Title: Love Will Prevail
Review: If Nada! was the sound of punk rock overcoming itself, passing into its opposite, Love Will Prevail is the sound of it re-emerging once more, irrevocably altered by the journey.

Title: Man Against Machine
Review: With ripping guitar solos, Aerosmith-style strings and gospel-tinged background vocals, this is a record that could take Eric to Church.

Title: Gem
Review: GEM isn't just a fresh take on an old sound; it's an audit of the constraint placed on female artists in the past and a table-turning journey into what might have been possible if musical freedom meant more than obedience to parents, husbands and record producers.

Title: Reality Tunnels
Review: Ellis taps the pulse of his surroundings in manner akin to Massive Attack's Mezzanine. [Aug 2020, p.111]

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: Limited variety and specks of staleness can't ground the high points.

Title: It's a Myth
Review: It's a Myth is a stripped-down indie rock/hip-hop hybrid that says plenty and makes its own cool, low-key fun at the same time.

Title: Command Your Weather
Review: The tunes are pretty great too, but you'll be under no illusion that they're anything other than a rock band, and an explosive one at that.

Title: Under and Under
Review: The songs on this album all sound the same, and there are a lot of them.

Title: No Love Deep Web
Review: No Love Deep Web includes some of the group's most accessible material; "Lil Boy" and "Deep Web" are the type of glitch freak-outs over which Lil Ugly Mane acolytes and Crystal Castles fans can come together.

Title: The Historical Conquests of Josh Ritter
Review: The Historical Conquests of..., a sprawling diorama of down-home rhythms and thoughtful lyrics, isn't immediately striking. But there's a joy in unfurling the half-submerged melodies and wry, tender sentiments.

Title: schlagenheim
Review: Another six-minute effort closes the album, Ducter, and like all the album’s best tracks it manages to navigate all the band’s best checkpoints of note, showcasing those spellbinding vocals and extraordinary percussion as they tread a truly staggering path. Schlagenheim will open up a whole new bottle of weird, if you let it in. It’s Troutmask Replica for a new generation, or perhaps it’s Can attempting to recreate the madness that Captain Beefheart’s enigmatic classic contained.

Title: The Stimulus Package
Review: Freeway shares top billing here with producer Jake One, a journeyman recently rescued from G-Unit's dungeon and the collaboration provides Jake with a production showcase and Freeway with some much-needed cohesion. [Winter 2010, p.99]

Title: Congratulations
Review: MGMT seem determined to break the mold they made for themselves, and while they deserve credit for trying, the outcome just isn't as much fun as the MGMT whose tunes could punch up movie trailers.

Title: Within and Without
Review: Within and Without feels tentative and restrained; Greene has toiled in the chillwave hinterlands to finally release a beautiful debut, and he's good enough to let it ride.

Title: Wonders of the Younger
Review: Wonder of the Younger shows they're still expanding their songwriting palette with out sacrificing the hooks or pop smarts. [Dec 2010, p.114]

Title: Fingers, Bank Pads, and Shoe Prints
Review: Typical of a producer who makes music for battling, there’s more swagger than a pair of John Wayne’s chaps.

Title: The Greatest
Review: Like all Cat Power records, The Greatest is a mostly sad, heartbroken, hopeless, rainy-day affair; it just isn't damaged. For that reason, it's also going to gain her a lot of new fans.

Title: Beautysleep
Review: A few tracks sound blunt and under-realised, but mostly this is the sound of a champion artist getting good again. [Mar 2002, p.116]

Title: The Lights from the Chemical Plant
Review: Producer Jacquire King (Tom Waits, Kings of Leon, Norah Jones) gives each song a poppy slant even when the lyrical content wrestles with the jetsam of life.

Title: Zonoscope
Review: The refreshing thing about bands like Cut Copy is that they're consistent. Far too often do artists change direction throughout their careers and sometimes lose touch with that thing that made us all fall in love with them in the first place, but this isn't the case with Zonoscope.

Title: Kindred
Review: His third record perfectly distills Passion Pit’s mission statement to a mixture of musical nostalgia and energy that coalesces quite well with larger messages of accepting the past in order to embrace the future.

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: Family life and a well-earned break have given this one-time Gothfather new tricks that pure despair could never provide.

Title: The Menace
Review: The Menace is a far more varied and ambitious LP than the first and, one suspects, than the Elastica album we'd have got four or three years ago. A very pleasant surprise.

Title: The Search
Review: Aside from some standout songs, reactions to The Search are largely due to how you feel about the grungy, alt sound.

Title: Stadium Arcadium
Review: Stadium Arcadium ensures that graying Lollapalooza-era fans, indie teens, and rowdy lunkheads will all be satisfied.

Title: Strange Land
Review: Ultimately, Strange Land is a bold and successful leap into new and previously unexplored territory for Yellow Ostrich.

Title: Get Gone
Review: Haynes’ mellifluous voice hits home throughout, particularly effective on slower burners such as Tide and Keep Me, invoking a deeper hoodoo on Kingdom Come and Don’t Need It.

Title: Camp
Review: Producer Ludwig Goransson imbues the beats with a comparable degree of pomp, although we could have done without diversions into cheesy Swede-pop. [Jan 2012 p.88]

Title: Where It Hits You
Review: White's albums have tendrils that imperceptibly wrap themselves around one's attention; and such is the case here.

Title: The Sides and in Between
Review: While it’s not a perfect album, it certainly does its job of capturing the feel of getting behind the wheel and peeling out for parts unknown as the summer sun shines on.

Title: Still
Review: The musicianship is so uniformly good that you forget about it and allow yourself to be swept onward by the songs.

Title: Something in the Water
Review: Pokey LaFarge delivers something old and new on Something in the Water, and no matter how much he reaches to the past for inspiration and influence, he's able to make his music sound fresh and alive, and this is his strongest studio set to date.

Title: Fluorescence
Review: The most powerful moments here reimagine their sound at its best without ever retreading. The rest of it, however, glitters far too much for its own good.

Title: My Old Familiar Friend
Review: There have been worse ideas, it's true. All round, though, it feels like a man with a gun in his back, being forced to be upbeat. [Sep 2009, p.79]

Title: Compass
Review: In truth he doesn’t always seem to know his bearings, but he manages to make his confusion compelling.

Title: The Worse Things Get ...
Review: Neko Case’s sixth album is typically sumptuous and lusciously heart-rending.

Title: Zeros
Review: The 21-year-old might be trying to shake off any unwieldy labels from critics this time around, but he’s doing so in electric, entertaining and thought-provoking form. Climb aboard McKenna’s space shuttle, and let him transport you to a place where dancing and getting deep are equally encouraged.

Title: Feel Infinite
Review: Greene here pulls together abstract R&B, twisted 2-step and crunching house, skillfully adopting vocal techniques employed by his heroes, Masters At Work. [May 2017, p.91]

Title: Intimacy
Review: Intimacy might not actually be all that intimate, but it is a thing of rough, recycled beauty.  And if that isn’t worth getting beat up for, I don’t know what is.

Title: Shobaleader One: d'Demonstrator
Review: I wasn't fond of the Shobaleader One EP. It wasn't good. Shobaleader One: d'Demonstrator is no better.

Title: Tunnel Blanket
Review: Texas-based group This Will Destroy You is somewhere past the breakers, floating on a body of layered soundscapes and ambient atmosphere.

Title: Love, Shelby
Review: May not be as postcard-perfect as I Am Shelby Lynne, but it comes pretty close.

Title: Set Yourself on Fire
Review: It’s fairly impressive that Stars could make a record that comes this close to replicating its predecessor while still offering discrete pleasures of its own.

Title: The Shadow of an Empire
Review: He remains a formidable wordsmith, and a fast mover by the looks of things. However his career develops, it will be crucial for him to keep a tight hold of the bewitching elements that help make not just his debut, but also his latest, a refreshing listen.

Title: Ten Stories
Review: mewithoutYou managed to synthesize its various explorations into a richer sound, using the sort of palette necessary to adequately pummel the album's deep meditations while properly expressing the emotional potency they contain.

Title: Exo
Review: Gatekeeper's Aaron David Ross and Matthew Arkel crunch elements of '80s post-industrial dance, horror/sci-fi soundtracks and computer game music into an enjoyably garish whole.

Title: Top 5 Dead or Alive
Review: A top-notch Lil Wayne appearance plus an unofficial Lox reunion with Styles P and Sheek Louch guesting on the LP help put this one through the uprights, giving veteran Jada one of his best and most ambitious showcases to date.
The distinction between their sensibilities remain strikingly apparent. [May 2018, p.33]

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: A cohesive and satisfying listen crammed with generous melodies.

Title: Satis Factory
Review: A lusty, witty, charismatic racket. [Jul 2019, p.30]

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: Nas has made a passionate album to reawaken your love of the art and if your heart isn't thumping in your chest by the end then it's not hip-hop that's dead, it's you.

Title: Armchair Apocrypha
Review: The songs on Armchair Apocrypha are broader, more sweeping in content and delivery than their immediate predecessors.

Title: Head Above The Water
Review: There is a uniformity to the album. It has a pace and atmosphere that all tracks pretty much conform to, which in less skilled hands can be a problem. But here what we have is one of those records where your favourite track changes with each listen. One whose coherence and solidity allow you a little escape form everything, to a different place. A not altogether happy one, but a beautiful one nonetheless.

Title: True Love Cast Out All Evil
Review: While Erickson provided the 'text', Sheff had to present it with the right level of reverence, being careful to highlight, and not undermine, this record of struggle and redemption.

Title: Leaders Of The Free World
Review: Leaders Of The Free World contains songs as heavy and epic as the neo-prog of Elbow's first two albums, but it's strongest at its quietest.

Title: Heavy Is the Head
Review: Not only is it a drastic step up from an impressive debut, but it shows an artist keen to test himself emotionally, as well as artistically.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: The album finds the Orange County band playing to its strengths: furious, compressed bursts of wit and good-humored spleen.

Title: Graffiti on the Train
Review: The band's sound has changed, too--it's less triumphal and more cinematic, although the Krautrock groove of Catacomb sounds genuinely angry.

Title: Between The Stars
Review: The only problem is that the album is too long. [Feb 2015, p.96]

Title: Insides
Review: The album succeeds in meting out these many moods in a way that’s consistently listenable, for both those who use might use Coldplay as an entry point and the cynical veterans of a consistently dynamic electronic music scene. Insides is among 2009’s very best.

Title: Sagarmatha
Review: The mood, talent, and energy are present, but the lack of lyrics is off-putting and relegates the band's seventh proper LP to B-team status. [Feb 2009, p.103]

Title: My True Story
Review: What sets this collection of doo-wop and early rock era tunes apart from the jaded pack is Neville's peerless voice and crystal clear passion for the material.

Title: ONoffON
Review: By staying so true to Burma's superior style 20 years after it was emulated, it lacks the aura of innovation. [#10, p.90]

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: Watch the Throne is more notable for its general lack of impact. Neither as compulsively neurotic as Eminem, as languidly characterful as Snoop Dogg, nor as furiously articulate as Nas, the raps here represent a pretty mediocre, cardboard kind of throne, truth be told.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: The Offspring's most musically mature collection to date. The arrangements are tight and don't bore, which is sometimes the case with albums that feature similar-sounding songs.

Title: The Gold Album: 18th Dynasty
Review: Tyga has served up a solid effort with The Gold Album: 18th Dynasty, exploring new territory and pushing himself in a different direction than he’d gone during his ratchet past work. It’s just not necessarily a better one.

Title: Field Songs
Review: For what keeps Field Songs on the right side of unyielding darkness, what keeps it ringing with an affirming note of beauty, is the certain knowledge that however black it gets, "the sun's about to rise."

Title: The Life of Pablo
Review: A madcap sense of humor animates all his best work, and The Life of Pablo has a freewheeling energy that is infectious and unique to his discography. Somehow, it comes off as both his most labored-over and unfinished album, full of asterisks and corrections and footnotes.

Title: The Magnificent
Review: Recalls the early '90s work of A Tribe Called Quest. [Sep 2002, p.244]

Title: On
Review: Either annoyingly sweet or refereshingly well-adjusted, depending on your mood. [Oct 2002, p.107]

Title: Wrath
Review: Wrath demonstrates Lamb of God's superior musicianship and creative songwriting, but above all else, the band's desire to innovate without abandoning the formula that serves them well.

Title: Stainless Style
Review: Stainless Style's problem isn't the music so much as it is the ambivalent authenticity; it's impossible to determine if it's supposed to pay tribute to, make fun of, or be fully situated in the time and place of John DeLorean's rise and fall.

Title: Mikal Cronin
Review: We're treated with music that demonstrates a perfect niche between pop-accessibility and zany experimentation.

Title: Adore Life
Review: Adore Life, in particular, isn’t so much a maturation but a continuation for Savages.

Title: Epic
Review: As an album, Epic is disjointed in places, but as a collection of songs it's strong enough.

Title: The Plot Against Common Sense
Review: It's big and clever; also bloody brilliant. [Aug 2012, p.98]

Title: My Guilty Pleasure
Review: Agebjorn seems utterly uninterested in taking Shapiro to a new place--not even a different dance floor--and though you can't blame him for drawing out a good time, it feels as if we'd been here forever.

Title: Heart On
Review: Heart-On, despite its snarling, strutting riffs, feels disappointingly lightweight. [Year End 2008]

Title: Luminous
Review: After a while the tripped-out builds can feel formulaic, but the mind-altering textures and melodic flourishes are so gorgeously realized that Luminous’s feel-good charms become hard to resist.

Title: The Soul Is Quick
Review: This is some of Willner’s most enriching and captivating work yet.

Title: I, Gemini
Review: This meld of savoury-sweet singing, moreish melody, glistening texture, strange space and surprises galore makes I, Gemini the best pop-not-pop album since Micachu & The Shapes' Jewellery. [Jun 2016, p.47]

Title: Man of the World
Review: Often, it’s an insightful and engaging look into what it feels like to be of everywhere and nowhere simultaneously, without alienating anyone simply looking for a catchy pop song. It’s simply a shame that Baio didn’t alienate some of his own desires to wander through genres.

Title: Resurrection
Review: Their crafty wordplay of yesterday has been filed into more pointed jabs, bolstered by deliciously 2000s gang vocals.

Title: Changed
Review: The title track may be about rebirth, but on Changed, Rascal Flatts remains the same as ever.

Title: Arabia Mountain
Review: The nine tracks Ronson produced on Arabia Mountain (Deerhunter's Lockett Pundt helmed two; Black Lips produced five) show he's equally adept at plundering the garage, psych and punk treasure troves.

Title: Rat Farm
Review: If the fanboys and motorheads are equally turned off by it in places, you get the sense the Puppets themselves--who sound happier and more comfortable here than they have in years--would be perversely pleased. [No. 98, p.58]

Title: From the Double Gone Chapel
Review: A near-masterpiece. [Sep 2004, p.117]

Title: Not Waving, But Drowning
Review: He’s managed to successfully replicate the feeling of genuine emotion and human connection that drew listeners to him and his music on his first album, with his second likely to be just as prosperous.

Title: The Life of the World to Come
Review: Regardless of his collaborators or how he chooses to approach his songs, The Life of the World to Come is further proof of Darnielle's ability, evident since long before he traded a boombox for a studio, to imbue his imagery, his sentiments, and his many characters with astounding weight and power.

Title: Saint Cecilia EP
Review: The songs, some of which date back decades ("The Neverending Sigh" is 20 years old!), sound surprisingly consistent considering the recording session would be a rush job for any other big-time rocker.

Title: The Midnight Sun
Review: If anything, this album is better than his first, as he settles confidently on his recognisable but versatile sound.

Title: Alright, Still
Review: Alright's sparkly high-life beats... all gleam with upmarket panache. But strong medicine always requires a little sugar. [Feb 2007, p.82]

Title: Diorama
Review: [Daniel] Johns' much-improved vocals and flair for the theatrical complement his new, more inventive guitar style.

Title: I'm Not Bossy, I'm The Boss
Review: The album title promises much in the way of forthright antagonism and the Jessie J hair she sports suggests some kind of ironic statement on the chart mainstream, but the content fails to deliver, save for two isolated moments.

Title: Simulation Theory
Review: Most of Simulation Theory could be about our surveillance state and/or a relationship. The blurring results in clunkiness.

Title: Body Talk
Review: Robyn takes a range of styles from dancehall and rap to house and disco and melds them with her big pop sound featuring four-to-the-floor beats and thoughtful, unsentimental lyrics about love and loneliness.

Title: Hello Waveforms
Review: Essentially it's Ray Of Light without Madonna. [Mar 2006, p.108]

Title: In a Poem Unlimited
Review: The feminine focus of Remy’s music overlaps with the political in exact and contemporary ways.

Title: Kveikur
Review: Though Kveikur is more anxious and busy than a lot of their past output, it still possesses the heavenly quality all their other records so admirably held on to as well.

Title: The Lillywhite Sessions
Review: Walker plays it exceedingly straight, even when he's delivering good-time numbers like "Kit Kat Jam." This po-faced sincerity winds up underscoring Walker's debt to Dave Matthews Band--they now seem like a clear influence on his adventurous folk-jazz--while also highlighting the imagination behind the original set of songs.

Title: The Man Upstairs
Review: Intriguing and introspective, The Man Upstairs warrants considerable praise.

Title: Move In Spectrums
Review: More Than and We Both Know's saturnine piano chords offer a novel contrast to crisp synth-pop such as Somebody Who, where their talent for alluring yet artless arrangements really comes into its own. [Nov 2013, p.102]

Title: Acid Tongue
Review: Too much of Acid Tongue ignores what makes Lewis a compelling artist in favor of empty, not entirely successful style hopping.

Title: Head In The Dirt
Review: Head in the Dirt definitely bears all the hallmarks of an Auerbach production--fuzz, funk and stadium-ready choruses--and often it's difficult to tell whether El Khatib is merely serving as Auerbach's stand-in. But the catchiness of his songwriting ultimately wins the day.

Title: So Beautiful or So What
Review: It may be less exuberant and therefore harder to love at first, but it delivers the goods just as surely. And with Paul Simon now old enough to face the ultimate questions and to do so with a stunning musical sophistication, it may just be a complete classic.

Title: Cloak and Cipher
Review: She's good at finding obscurity, but sometimes not to her benefit. Ms. Powell wrote a lot of the lyrics on Cloak and Cipher with scrambled input from books and various other texts, and she doesn't do much to smooth out the results, savoring the disjunctive and the cryptic.

Title: Melbourne, Florida
Review: Just as charming as Calendar Days, and with a bit more pep. [Apr - May 2015, p.89]

Title: A Productive Cough
Review: Despite occasional attempts at restraint and the fact it’s only seven songs long, A Productive Cough provides Titus Andronicus with another bold manifesto. They might have varied the volume, but they’re still railing with their customary resolve.

Title: Knock Knock
Review: The magic of DJ Koze lies in the unique complex musical terroir he's built. [May 2018, p.93]

Title: To Pimp a Butterfly
Review: With all its superfly flourish and talk of Willie Lynch, Butterfly is heady and ambitious, if not unprecedented as subject matter.

Title: Good News For People Who Love Bad News
Review: Gone is pretty much everything they’ve learned in the last eight years or so, ditching all the progress they’ve made in favor of just making another Modest Mouse record. The results, needless to say, are disappointing.

Title: Velocity of Sound
Review: What's left is a tightly wound core of guitar, bass, drums, and vocal harmonies that naïvely captures the spirit and spunk of early rock icons the Kinks and the Beach Boys.

Title: Kiss Land
Review: It's in these moments--when he's paying attention to melody and songwriting--that Kiss Land demonstrates plenty of promise and tentative steps in the right direction.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: If Nothing Was The Same doesn’t resonate quite as consistently as Take Care, it’s because Drake and his in-house collaborator Noah “40” Shebib sometimes seem content to revisit that album’s sonic landscapes instead of carving out new ones.

Title: In the Now
Review: The production is generally safe but solid, and his ease with pop songwriting results in occasional cliches, but for the most part these are achingly sincere songs dealing with the aftermath of loss.

Title: The Only She Chapters
Review: Alas, a good third of the album meanders and there's a drab formlessness to his sonic fog. Fascinating but flawed.

Title: The Duke
Review: For the most part his tribute to Duke Ellington works in the way that should keep purist onside. [Aug 2012, p.96]

Title: Awakened
Review: That consistent album we're waiting for still hasn't come just yet.

Title: It's Never Been Like That
Review: Phoenix still hasn’t overcome the faults of their previous efforts. [#14]

Title: Patience
Review: Even when Mannequin Pussy venture to truly dark places, Patience is such a pure joy to listen to. In its biggest moments, Dabice’s raw edge is matched by equally colossal riffs, explosive energy, and surging momentum. Patience, is without a doubt, one of the year’s strongest punk rock records.

Title: Peace, Love, Death Metal
Review: Like all great garage rock, it all sounds the same, but that doesn’t matter.

Title: Dangerously in Love
Review: It's not so much that the most singularly talented and important soul singer of now has let us down, more she's tried too hard to please. [Sep 2003, p.105]

Title: The Competition
Review: He embraces a lush, widescreen sound with such vigor that even he can't keep up with, causing the album to lose some momentum as it settles into repetition. But Hunter's biting social critique is the focal point from start to finish, revealing his more vulnerable self in the process—a bold reinvention that should follow whichever direction he chooses to take from here on out.

Title: Warp Riders
Review: The riffs remain as ample and hard-hitting as ever, and with Matt Bayles (Isis, Mastodon) handling the production, The Sword have never sounded better.

Title: Ad Infinitum
Review: Ad Infinitum isn’t a palette cleanser or a holdover to the next conventional Telekinesis album--it’s a deeply affecting piece of work at a visceral level, suggesting that Lerner is an artist with crashing ambitions who’s willing to risk alienating his audience.

Title: Clap Your Hands Say Yeah
Review: Clap Your Hands Say Yeah is worthy of the attention, as it reveals a band of great ability and confidence brimming with ideas.

Title: Moon Landing
Review: More mopey ballads and ad-ready pop songs. [Dec 2013, p.92]

Title: La Sera
Review: This music is more about ambiance, with the luscious haze recalling a mood rather than shaping something distinctive. Has anything ever been so perfectly gorgeous and perfectly inconsequential all at once?

Title: Easter Is Cancelled
Review: It’s not a bad album, but it is hindered with a lack of understanding on what made the band so great to begin with. So, prepare to experience as many rough moments as there is smooth ones.

Title: A Head Full of Dreams
Review: The absence of those usual big arena hooks proves critical through the rest of the album, when the songs don’t quite hit home.

Title: Beneath the Skin
Review: Beneath The Skin is further proof that the Icelandic music movement is a near-unstoppable force. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.79]

Title: Reunion Tour
Review: Reunion Tour further cements the Weakerthans' status as legitmate rock 'n' roll tastemakers. [Nov 2007, p.172]

Title: Wakelines
Review: Butler performs the same job that Trevor Horn did with Belle & Sebastian--adding a widescreen pop ambition to McIntyre's flinty personal tales. [Nov 2018, p.34]

Title: Saturdays = Youth
Review: Though nothing quite reaches the heights of past work, there's ambience to spare on "We Own the Night" and the lush "Highway of Endless Dreams."

Title: The Empyrean
Review: While this album may mirror some type of personal imaginative journey for the listener, the truth is it is just too dreary and self-indulgent to endure in its entirety.

Title: Something About April II
Review: Something About April II is the rare record that allows you be spirited away without feeling dirty or voyeuristic. As though you sought to change some flaw in the past that shouldn’t have been changed at all.

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Sounds Of The Universe is Depeche's most tune-packed and sonically adventurous album for over a decade. [May 2009, p.82]

Title: Conditions of My Parole
Review: Conditions verges on dour, monochromatic humorlessness.

Title: Mountaintops
Review: Mountaintops is the first of their records to grapple with the everyday tribulations and banality of spending your entire adult life in a band-- with your Mate, nonetheless.

Title: When We Stay Alive
Review: ‘Feel Life’ and ‘Steady’ resolve this darkness, both euphoric and knowing - and beautiful sonically - while ‘Blood Moon’ addresses feeling disappointed in yourself, and what you need to do to push through and make things right. ‘When We Stay Alive’ is emotionally raw, elegantly presented and at many parts a real tear-jerker. Wonderful stuff.

Title: Sunbather
Review: A record everyone with half an experimental ear should experience, even if they run from it, screaming.

Title: The Cloud Making Machine
Review: Admittedly, not all of Cloud's most ambitious tracks work ou.... But in the end, it's Garnier's ambition, combined with his talent and professionalism, that make this an album worth seeking out.

Title: Everything in Between
Review: No Age's brief moment of near-mainstream notoriety may have passed by the time Everything in Between was released, but their growth as recording artists was progressing nicely and the album stands alongside Nouns as two of the finest noise rock/pop albums of the new millennium.

Title: In Ghost Colours
Review: In Ghost Colours achieves its success by striking the right balance between its competing genres--rock and electronic--without sacrificing either.

Title: proVISIONS
Review: While some lack musical polish, the brilliant 'Spiral'--with its images of Americans hiding away with guns and in churches and heading towards heart attacks and extinction--furthers his metamorphosis into one of the country's great musical elder statesmen.

Title: Heal
Review: That an album that sounds this vibrant and thrilling came out of such dark circumstance is a testament to the songwriting skills of Showalter. Pain never sounded so good.

Title: Carved Into Stone
Review: Songs as instantly gratifying as these don't come along every day. [May 2012, p.105]

Title: You Will Know Nothing
Review: Deeper cuts like "Voices at the Window," "Floating on Water," and the ethereal closer "You Ought to Know" deal in more abstract vistas, delivering different hues culled from the same retro spectrum, resulting in something that has more in common with the spacy, neo-psych-rock emissions of the Flaming Lips than it does crusty ethno-doom metal.

Title: There's Me And There's You
Review: There are some great moments, to be sure, but there are too many spots where the lyrics induce cringing and the electronic interventions sound more like gimmicks than real song elements.

Title: Motion to Rejoin
Review: Brightblack Morning Light has always been a druggie band; this time, however, the drug of choice is Dramamine.

Title: Upland Stories
Review: He may not be looking to “kill Saturday night” anymore but, with Upland Stories, Fulks has composed songs that are richer and more rewarding.

Title: Be Small
Review: Intricate and precise, Be Small doesn't demand attention--but slowly and very smartly, it secures it just the same. [Dec 2015, p.108]

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: It's the sound of Dirty Projectors just being themselves and fully justifying the royalty status Longstreth and Co. now enjoy.

Title: If You're Dreaming
Review: An intimate, close and enjoyably ambiguous record. [Jun 2020, p.94]

Title: For The Recently Found Innocent
Review: Passable psych-rock that rarely disappoints, but equally never really soars. [Sep 2014, p.117]

Title: In Between
Review: Despite intimations of mortality, there’s plenty of rocking and rolling left in this house.

Title: Lust Lust Lust
Review: Wagner and Foo have gone back to the rougher basics--distortion, echo and monastery-choir vocals--of their debut EP, 2002's Whip It On. But the simplicity is deceptive.

Title: The Mess We Made
Review: This record expects -- nay, demands -- multiple exposures. Its hidden delights and traps are equally patient.

Title: A Walk with Love and Death
Review: Many of these tracks barely scrape two and a half minutes. Crazed voices talk about “hair” and a “super-weird looking guy” while the deranged piano of a haunted ballroom plays for no one (“The Hidden Joice”). But it’s a fun, fairground of a record too, with a hare-brained 1960s Wurlitzer pop song (“Give It To Me”), dopey scat (“Scooba”) and silly names and phrases like “Chicken Butt” and “Eat Yourself Out”.

Title: Genuine Negro Jig
Review: Erasing the gap between the 1930s and today, this striking North Carolina trio brings a modern sizzle to the legacy of classic African American string bands like the Mississippi Sheiks, with fiddles, banjos, and even kazoos sparking an electrifying ruckus.

Title: I Love You, Honeybear
Review: Written around the time Tillman got hitched to this girlfriend, it's a hugely ambitious, caustically funny album about the redemptive possibilities of love, and being heartily sick of your own bullshit.

Title: Scorpio Rising
Review: Perhaps the duo is just second-tier to begin with, or perhaps they just let the needle swing too far towards the rock side of the dial, but the peak moments on Scorpio Rising offer little more than enjoyable nostalgia for overhead-projector light shows.

Title: Uptown Special
Review: An album of fresh pleasures is the pay-off, but don’t come looking to it for substance.

Title: Boss
Review: What separates Boss from any cynical cashing-in critiques is that the Markers went above and beyond to actually create an album that nearly contradicts their constructed identity.

Title: Monoliths and Dimensions
Review: With the explorations of additional instrumentation as well being more comfortable with silences and with echo, SunnO))) approach the freedom and abandon of the spirit-travelers alluded to in the titles and approaches on this, the band's best record yet.

Title: Working Men's Club
Review: By the time the record reaches it’s 12-minute close “Angel”, it feels like a great release. You’ve been put through the ringer with the abrasive “Cook A Coffee” (with plenty of shots at a certain, now former, Politics Live pundit) and “Be My Guest” and made it out the other side. Sweatier and ready to take on the world.

Title: Because of the Times
Review: The best thing, really, that can be said of Because of the Times is that it works the hardest trick: seeming deeply personal and inclusive, but still having an embrace elastic enough to be universally appealing.

Title: Goodnight Tender
Review: An unassuming venture, but capable and well executed one regardless.

Title: Love + War
Review: The more complex likes of Look Over Your Shoulder’s thrillerish build-and-hush tension, My Own’s dark and shifty Timbalandish textures and the moody, dubstep blues ballad of Forgiven, with its sunburst of a chorus, keep this lusciously atmospheric album well on the right side of smooth.

Title: White Chalk
Review: It's so alluring you have no choice but to follow. [Oct 2007, p.98]

Title: Outer Peace
Review: His chillwave sensibilities remain, but they’re bolstered by more direct elements from the popular hip-hop and disco funk sounds of today.

Title: 4:13 Dream
Review: Even with a dozen records behind him, Smith, when he puts his mind to it, remains a master at crafting concise masterpieces of bouncy pop majesty.

Title: Nightmare Ending
Review: Nightmare Ending may not be Cooper's most cohesive record, but it's a perfect representation of the indie-rock generation's most diverse ambient musician.

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Gentle, subtle, poignant, Barnett is almost crooning as she talks disappointment and expectation, and she has a photographer’s eye for detail when it comes to the otherwise mundane.

Title: Colors
Review: As both a quintessential entry into his catalog and a striking entry into mainstream popular culture, Colors once again cements Beck as a clever, ever-dynamic and enduring artist.

Title: The Civil Wars
Review: This is a limping, bloodless version of The Civil Wars, and if the band is to have a future they need to fix their issues, or else learn to channel the damage better.

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: It's free of gimmicks (Hey, an R&B record without Auto-Tuned vocals!) or trendy producers (No Kanye, no Timbaland; instead, guitarist Hod David does most of the work). No wonder BLACKsummers'night walks its own confident path down the artier fringe of R&B.

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: Earthbound offering from hyped to the heavens duo.

Title: Wraith
Review: While there has was never any doubting their psychedelic influences and their way with a groove, Wraith offers something more. Full of variety and unpredictability, like the best science fiction it maps out a dreamworld of our times, a tonic against the deathly thoughts of the small hours.

Title: The Weirdness
Review: Pop's lyrics about his penis and ATMs are beyond self-parody.

Title: TLC
Review: Album closer ‘Joy Ride’ does exactly what it says on the tin; it’s a joyous, perfectly assembled pop track. That’s not to say that the Kickstarter-funded LP is hit after hit--the bright and brash ‘It’s Sunny’ with its oddly theatrical tropes is a cheesy misstep.

Title: We Are Little Barrie
Review: Play[s] out like a fresh discovery that's strangely familiar--a '60s soul in a 21st-century outfit.

Title: At the Party With My Brown Friends
Review: Black Belt Eagle Scout has crafted an album to play any naysayer: At the Party with My Brown Friends will make a fan out of anyone.

Title: Hunter
Review: Hunter is a tempestuous album full of haunting, unsettling vocals; it resonates with evocative power.

Title: Stranger Me
Review: LaVere could rest on her lyrics alone, which are witty and feisty enough to stand on their own, but by giving her band boundless license to indulge any whim or eccentricity, she has crafted a well-rounded album that is already among the year's best.

Title: When You Walk A Long Distance You Are Tired
Review: Leschper meditates on creativity, identity and self-doubt in a voice that's equal parts Angel Olsen and Waxahatchee, while the music--played by a full band--runs the expressive gamut. [Apr 2016, p.76]

Title: I Am Gemini
Review: For all its tempo shifts and attempts at fun, Gemini sounds like the work of an ascetic band scared of pleasure.

Title: No Pier Pressure
Review: No Pier Pressure shows just what too many cooks can do to a Beach Boy's broth.

Title: Full Closure and No Details
Review: Her striking debut--recorded in 10 days and originally self-released on her own label--brims with as much honest emotion as it does uncalculated cool. [Jan 2017, p.23]

Title: Turn Out the Lights
Review: An album that turns its predecessor’s intimacy into something far more ambitious.

Title: Of All Things I Will Soon Grow Tired
Review: The results are extraordinary. [May 2012, p.79]

Title: The Waterfall II
Review: The Waterfall II offers no clues as to where My Morning Jacket might be headed, but as a document of what they were capable of in the studio, it's consistent, well-structured, and satisfying in a way the original was not.

Title: Don't Stop
Review: Fragrant ballads "When The Night" and "Marie Cheri" add a softer dimension to a bold collection on which Annie rarely puts a foot wrong. [Nov 2009, p. 81]

Title: Lucky Shiner
Review: The album feels like a nil-nil tie in soccer: lots of interesting parts, but ultimately lacking payoff.

Title: Sweet Warrior
Review: If you’re a lapsed Dickhead, Sweet Warrior would make for a great reintroduction to Richard Thompson. Likewise, should you require only one RT album per decade, this disc may well stand as his best of the 2000s.

Title: Hymn and Her
Review: Although little on Hymn and Her finds Earlimart venturing into new territory, there's a familiarity felt throughout that remains comforting, and sometimes that's just enough.

Title: Living With War
Review: In context, no song on Living With War is as simple as it may seem on its own--not a bumper sticker, not a pamphlet, not the slightest wrinkle in a Sunday morning pundit’s furrowed brow.  It’s a direct shot into the national discourse from a rock world that has been largely silent until recently.

Title: We'll Never Turn Back
Review: The angry funk of 'Down in Mississippi' proves too good to last, but only 'We Shall Not Be Moved' is (predictably) dull.

Title: Untitled
Review: This is a sprawling, furious, deeply ambivalent theme album about institutional racism, the failures of black leadership and the pathologies and promise of early-21st-century African-American life.

Title: Directions to See a Ghost
Review: Its muscular confidence and stylistic purity make it a must-listen for the psychedelically inclined, as well as an easy candidate for one of the best records of the year.

Title: Blurred Lines
Review: Nothing to see here.

Title: Marry Me
Review: It's an excellent debut, and hints at a potentially significant force in indie rock in the coming years.

Title: Thirteen Tales From Urban Bohemia
Review: A stoner's paradise from start to finish. Most pleasurable.

Title: Rockwell
Review: Rossi has worked well with producer Steve Albini to clean up the tracks, and pick up the pace, making them sparse and wonderful, like intricate machines.

Title: ERAAS
Review: This record can sound slightly off-putting at times, but that's what makes it so compelling.

Title: Grown Backwards
Review: A genuinely moving and wickedly fun record.

Title: Fasciinatiion
Review: For much of Fasciination, it’s the music that keeps the record afloat, because, even at his very best, singer Tim Fink doesn’t have much to say. [Summer 2008]

Title: Listen
Review: This is a very good album. The Kooks sound like a band rejuvenated. [Oct 2014, p.105]

Title: Myths of the Near Future
Review: The songs descend the same chords repeatedly and ponderously, as if the band were falling down the same flight of stairs over and over again.

Title: Diaper Island
Review: Sharper production focuses the singer's woozier tendencies, revealing a succession of hooks to adorn his take on Neil Young's grooving folk-rock and Blur's twisted indie.

Title: Home
Review: This is recycling as artistic endeavour. [Sep 2020, p.91]

Title: Wallpaper for the Soul
Review: More summery than a sombrero and probably just as unfashionable. [Sep 2003, p.112]

Title: 22, A Million
Review: Everything about the album is fragmented, and dizzying in the vein of Samuel Beckett’s Not I or T.S. Elliot’s The Waste Land. Even the lyric sheet is a glorious mess.

Title: The Village
Review: The Village largely whispers rather than shouts, and it's all the more powerful for it.

Title: Party Music
Review: They've also inflected the mix with OutKast's quick complexity; and, like 'Kast, the Coup have progressed from story rapping to more mercurial rhymes. [Oct 2001, p.125]

Title: Lost in Light
Review: On her second LP, Gothenburg's Sumie Nagano recites her depressive, wintry haikus in a soft, pure voice over some rather samey accompaniment. [Dec 2017, p.33]

Title: Wolves of Want
Review: The album, one that focuses on and attempts to make peace with various anxieties, is at its best when the distorted and confused clash with sunburst pop structures.

Title: Dirty Vegas
Review: For the most part, Dirty Vegas play up the notoriety by not straying too far from the template set by "Days Gone By." [Jul 2002, p.98]

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: By immersing himself even deeper into the world of dub music and its equally minimalist and maximalist tones and tropes, Grim Reaper sounds stronger than anything he's accomplished so far.

Title: Several Shades of Why
Review: Now we're meeting a new side of the veteran guitar god – a gentle, delicate and altogether more acoustic Mascis.

Title: Wild Mountain Nation
Review: A surprising record and a mess of contradictions--an okay band making a great record, classic rock songcraft made contemporary through sheer force of will, a quiet and loud album simultaneously, dancing along the lo-fi/hi-fi binary, a fucking record about Appalachia made by dudes from Portland!--that thrillingly, thinly, radiantly congeals.

Title: Fantastic Planet
Review: "Sisters" and "Growing" display a tendency to let her fascination with the moving gears trump the narrative movement that marks her best material. But fortunately, such moments are few and far between.

Title: In Cauda Venenum
Review: Opeth’s chemistry feels as tight as it is playful, heartfelt as it is engaging, as they explore a plethora of intriguing and majestic sounds. The instrumentation and vocals, in both versions, serve to present emotion and instrumental wonder. In Cauda Venenum is among Opeth’s strongest albums when it comes to the band’s progressive sensibilities.

Title: Morningwood
Review: Sounds like a band mashing all the current trends and ending up with nothing.

Title: Born This Way
Review: You have to admire the way Gaga fearlessly throws herself into, say, a disco mariachi arrangement on Americano, but she should be careful: her frequently righteous tone and overindulgence in clunky Catholic metaphors threaten to mire her memorable melodies in schlocky self-help proselytizing.

Title: What's Next to the Moon
Review: Without the thundering drums and over-amped testosterone of the originals, the songs are revealed as the beautiful blues-based writings they in fact are.

Title: Liquid Cool
Review: Its library-lite funk may be full of syrupy drift, but the progressions are crafty enough to keep the listener from glazing over.

Title: Matricidal Sons of Bitches
Review: A backstory so real you'll swear you've seen the flick. [Dec 2012, p.96]

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: The second album from Franco-techno duo Xavier de Rosnay and Gaspard Augé is decidedly less pop-tabulous than their career highlights to date.

Title: As I Am
Review: As I Am sees the piano songstress breaking free of her saccharine chains and delivering a streetwise, smoky set of real soul.

Title: Songs of Love and Horror
Review: This stripped-down set from the Palace/Bonnie songbook is a reminder of what a great singer Oldham has become. [Jan 2019, p.23]

Title: Cannibal
Review: Ke$ha doesn't branch out in any significant way here, so it's unlikely to do for her what the similarly packaged The Fame Monster did for Lady Gaga.

Title: Snowflake Midnight
Review: This Rev record is another triumph in which all is dream and this sometimes symbolism, the overall effect trippy, though less dark than of yore. [Oct 2008, p.102]

Title: Any Port in a Storm
Review: A stolid lack of poetry combined with Dermody's flat intonation could make Any Port in a Storm hard-going, were it not for his evident, dogged attempt to be Jonathan Richman fronting the Stooges, and a stoic faith in the goodness of life and the value of human endeavour that brims with hope.

Title: Paracosm
Review: For nine tracks in just 40 minutes, these are lighter than air and spry enough for your feet. [No. 101, p.60]

Artist: Jenny Lewis with The Watson Twins
Title: Rabbit Fur Coat
Review: Consider Lewis the Emmylou Harris of the Silverlake set. [3 Feb 2006, p.70]

Title: Vestiges & Claws
Review: Assessed independently, Vestiges & Claws’ progressions may be modest, but its adjustments cohere into a record of uncommonly evocative capacity.

Title: Swimmer
Review: Swimmer is mostly sweet and personable. Any listener who’s followed Moore and Riley for five albums running is probably somewhat invested in their relationship, and once again, they’ve rewarded that interest.

Title: Chills On Glass
Review: Chills On Glass has been sequenced, so that there are gaps between the songs big enough to drive a huge tour bus through, but each nugget is such an alien blast that you need a break to re-evaluate what just lubed past your lobes

Title: 9 Dead Alive
Review: There’s nothing as immediate as Ixtapa or Tamacun here, but there’s plenty of well rounded paeans nonetheless, and you’re sure to find something to adore if you’re a fan of guitar music, Latin music or heavy metal.

Title: Unsound
Review: [Unsound] is as rough, ragged and wracked as they've ever been, the likes of 'Dust Devil' and '7's' pushing needles thoroughly into the red.

Title: In Love
Review: Even though In Love is fun, Peace doesn't break any new ground. [Aug-Sep 2013, p.98]

Title: Libertad
Review: Libertad is much more like Audioslave’s second record, "Out of Exile": it shows the unbelievably low flair a supergroup can have, and how bland they can play, but finds them playing together anyway.

Title: West
Review: Perhaps an unrefined but fiery bar band would have been better suited to accompany such nakedly raw material.

Title: Little Honey
Review: For such a distinctive voice, disappointingly run of the mill. [Nov 2008, p.123]

Title: Living Theatre
Review: Living Theatre is the perfect intersection of nature and artifice, the very definition of what organic music can and should sound like, and it is a beautiful thing to behold.

Title: Kylie Christmas
Review: Throughout the album, Kylie sounds very game, merry even, and there's enough holiday spirit on offer to help even the grinchiest customer make it through the season with the bare minimum of humbug.

Title: Mid Air
Review: Many Blue Nile classics whispered their way to five minutes without outstaying their welcome, and there's plenty here that could have done the same. It's a minor quibble, however, when an album sounds as lovingly crafted, honest and subtly passionate as this.

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: Let's Go Eat the Factory unfolds with each successive listen.
It’s mostly a collection of decent tunes, polished to a blinding sheen.

Title: Interpretations: The British Rock Songbook
Review: Yet if the title is straightforward, the music often isn’t, with LaVette teasing out new emotional details from songs that seemed to have given up all their secrets decades ago.

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: The only mis-step on the album is "Boeing 737", a pounding, splashy stomp whose brash incoherence perhaps disguises a commentary on the twin towers attacks. It seems brutish and crude set alongside the rest of the album, which otherwise has the kind of stylistic and atmospheric unity that reminds one of what albums can offer that no other format can match.

Title: Fixed Ideals
Review: Whilst sonically Fixed Ideals can vary in its impact, Lande Hekt’s lyrics tell a relatable story in a crafty way, carrying the record all the way through.

Title: A Dream Outside
Review: It’s Gengahr's commitment to weirdness on A Dream Outside that puts them many streets ahead.

Title: Riot Boi
Review: Combined with schizophrenic production (Evian Christ, Boody, Balam Acab, Lunice) that leaps from horny trap to frantic electroclash, Riot Boi overwhelms with twists, turns, and surprises, all of which are exhilarating.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: Following an uncharacteristic hiatus, singer-songwriter Ryan Adams returns with this lovely, low-key effort.

Title: How The West Was Won
Review: This is guitar music at its most acerbic and romantic. [Aug 2017, p.110]

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: The Flying Club Cup is a good album. If you’re a fan of "Gulag Orkestar," it’s probably a great album. But aside from 'Cliquot,' it’s more of the same.

Title: Siberia
Review: With so many of its songs employing fade-outs, Siberia also has this palpably unplanned feeling, which doesn't always pay off.

Title: One Plus One Is One
Review: On the one hand, it's a little hokey: if One Plus One Equals One tried any harder to charm you, it would turn up on your doorstep with a bottle of Fleurie and offer you a footrub. On the other, the songs are Gough's strongest in years.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: Notwithstanding the occasional foray into jazz and blues, Black Messiah is much the same blend of miasmic boudoir soul, bare-bones funk and liberation songs that characterised his 2000 milestone, Voodoo.

Title: Enter the Slasher House
Review: At times, Enter the Slasher House feels like a carbon copy of Animal Collective, replete with effects-soaked hazy vocals mashed against high-tempo art-pop.

Title: At War With The Mystics
Review: Those farty sounds and the guy with the deeeeeeeeeep voice on "It Overtakes Me" are called "bells and whistles." That's what bands do when they don't have anything to say.

Title: Earthly Delights
Review: It is also a sound that on this, their fifth album, seems as resistant to change as the forces of nature and while seemingly limited in palette, is as expansive as it is inventive.

Title: When Machines Exceed Human Intelligence
Review: This is room-shaking, gut-quaking stuff. [Apr 2009, p.106]

Title: Painting With
Review: With every sound shoved forward in the mix, oodles of white space floats inbetween the sound-splats. Every moment is for the taking. Painting With marks an immediate, and physical new direction, and anything seems possible.

Title: Shine
Review: Though she transforms her preferred vocal delivery from a rough street-slang dialect to full-on harmonizing on her new album, Estelle fortunately avoids this condition on most of Shine, though her all-star production staff occasionally allows her split personality layering and superstar guests to crisscross, clutter, and exhaust the mix, particularly on “In the Rain.”

Title: Ambition
Review: Ambition leaves listeners to answer the simple question of whether they want an exceptionally unchallenging album to listen to for an hour or not.

Title: Devils & Dust
Review: Ultimately, Devils & Dust does not break new ground. In many ways, it is rather conventional -- a mostly acoustic collection that hearkens back to Bruce's origins as a singer-songwriter -- but it is this conventionality, in its acceptance of older American forms of music, where the disc hits its mark.

Title: Ribbons
Review: Instead of distracting, Ribbons' tangents add to its masterful feel--at this point in Wilkinson's career, his music is so rich that he can bring any aspect of it to the fore in ways that feel equally natural and surprising.

Title: Personal Life
Review: Personal Life may not be the band's most immediate album, but it's their best, a deep intimate record that's ultimately uplifting, quietly offering assurance and comfort on its trip into the mysterious zone of love and mortality. [Summer 2010, p.80]

Title: Afraid of Heights
Review: More often than not, Afraid of Heights points to a set of punk-rock signifiers rather than thoughtfully engaging with them.

Title: Rubberband
Review: Rubberband has been executed with genuine respect for the artist. There's enough greatness here to justify the effort. Even if we hope this doesn't launch a new kind of re-bop craze, it's still great to press play on another Miles Davis album.

Title: Horehound
Review: Horehound doesn’t sound like the first album from a tossed-off side project; it crackles with the intensity of a band that has been together longer than a few months.

Title: The Art of Pretending to Swim
Review: It's an impressive reminder of what made him so special in the first place. [Oct 2018, p.119]

Title: An Awesome Wave
Review: Alt-J crafts an ethereal ocean of sound that's remarkably cohesive-at once strange and familiar.

Title: Junip
Review: Junip's second album is enchanting enough to sell cluster bombs. [May 2013, p.88]

Title: Blue Eyed in the Red Room
Review: He can't muster much more than a compose-by-numbers Boards Of Canada kit that's destined for little more than wildlife documentary syndication. [Mar 2005, p.102]

Title: Women
Review: Produced by VanGaalen, this record explores a whole host of interesting sonic ideas, which keeps things nicely unpredictable.

Title: Suck My Shirt
Review: Suck My Shirt isn’t a huge departure for a band that likes their place in the garage, but it’s enough to keep fans busy without dulling the edges.

Title: Take Fountain
Review: Inevitably, it sounds dated. [Feb 2005, p.102]

Title: God Hates Us All
Review: Don't worry--eight albums into their reign, Slayer still sound like Slayer. [Sep 2001, p.158]

Title: Out of the Shadow
Review: Despite the band's penchant for uneven electronic dirges, Out Of The Shadow is a very accessible work -- perhaps too accessible for indie enthusiasts who thrive on innovation and sonic exploration.

Title: Maybe Today, Maybe Tomorrow
Review: As has been noted before, bands such as We Are the Ocean currently exist in a crowded market. Maybe Today, Maybe Tomorrow should give them a firm foothold in it.

Title: Since I Left You
Review: Quite possibly the best sample record ever made.

Title: II
Review: It’s an expert turn by seasoned professions thoroughly in their own comfort zone.

Title: Back to Black
Review: Back To Black is by far the best popular soul album I’ve heard this year.

Title: The Loves of Your Life
Review: By the time The Loves of Your Life closes with the joyous "The Old King," Leithauser stretches his music into a wide embrace of the past and present that's all the more impressive because it feels so lived-in and genuine.

Title: This Gift
Review: The pace is relentlessly uptempo, but the sheer feisty spirit and conviction with which it is delivered ultimately brooks no argument. [Feb 2008, p.102]

Title: Tiger Suit
Review: With commercial radio all about that urban groove thing these days, it's little wonder that the Scottish singer KT Tunstall decorates her Lilith Fair-style songwriting chops with electro-pop beats on her third studio album, Tiger Suit.

Title: Loud Hailer
Review: Lyrically this has all been done better before, but it does show that Beck is fully engaged with the world. Moreover, Loud Hailer’s often stunning tapestry of vampy rock, funk, Southern blues and wah-wah wizardry proves that all of his considerable faculties are as sharp as they ever were.

Title: Invincible
Review: Tired, frightened-sounding and hopelessly misjudged.... Hugely disappointing. [Dec 2001, p.116]

Title: The Sweet Escape
Review: Pharrell Williams' production and Stefani's fizzy personality make for an unexpected Christmas treat.

Title: Beast Epic
Review: It might not look like it's going to leap out and grab you, but Beam here launches a soft emotional ambush. [Sep 2017, p.87]

Title: Ghost on Ghost
Review: His fifth LP ties it all together with ethereal jazz-soul in summer colors, bolstered by the nimble swing provided by members of Bob Dylan's band and New Orleans horns orchestrated again by Tin Hat Trio's Rob Burger.

Title: Headphones
Review: Forget the easy Gibbard/Tamborello comparisons and look here if you seek more mope with your Moog.

Title: Goodnight Rhonda Lee
Review: Sets a high bar. But she clears it, with soulful, oddball, Jersey-girl-in-Nashville aplomb. [Sep 2017, p.96]

Title: (II)
Review: Witch House is an obvious influence, and you could question whether the former chip-tune terrorists are still as ahead of the curve as they once were. It hardly matters when they can come up with stuff like Child I Will Hurt You, a dream-state lullaby that is both beautiful and unbearably sorrowful.

Title: Ways to Forget
Review: Clock Opera's brand of mutilated pop music shimmers as a genuinely profound musical experience. Excuse the awful pun, but their time is most definitely now.

Title: The New Game
Review: Mudvayne write some decent guitar hooks (check the title track), but their imagination is parched, with most songs hewing to one formula: riff, whimper, shriek, repeat.

Title: Old Ramon
Review: 'Old Ramon' is a slight affair cut from similar cloth to '...Blue Guitar', fuzzy with distortion, hampered by less than inspirational songwriting.

Title: Awoo
Review: Genuinely affecting, and fun, pop music.

Title: The Dandy Warhols Are Sound
Review: Unfortunately, despite its improvements, the album still suffers from lackadaisical and unfocused songwriting. Sure, this record is quite a bit better than the one originally released, and kudos to the band for taking the time to prove their point.

Title: Four the Record
Review: The real strength here is the feline sharpness of Lambert's voice.

Title: Condors
Review: Particularly impressive is that the music never feels incoherent or thrown together. The band always, somehow, emerge with a compelling and coherent voice, albeit a strange and often dark one.

Title: Universal Audio
Review: Behind the surface sweetness of Emma Pollock's voice, the chiming guitars, the mellifluous folky lilt of the melodies and direct but deft production, these songs are as complex, adult and frequently as bleak as any the Delgados have ever written.

Title: A Walk with Love and Death
Review: "Black Health," "Sober-delic," "Edgar the Elephant" and "Cardboa Negro" are the most compelling tracks, showcasing a midtempo churn where McDonald's rock'n'roll pedigree really shines. ... Despite the presence of these successes, Death still sounds like a band treading water.

Title: To Survive
Review: To Survive, however, ignites enough fireworks of its own. [July 2008, p.1112]

Title: Pre Strike Sweep
Review: Blasting through 11 songs in less than half-an-hour, Pre Strike Sweep never settles into one mode or frame of reference for long. Instead, the album drags and scrapes itself into being for its entire duration, angry and bleeding and looking for new angles with every new riff, crash, and tortured scream.

Title: Don't Feed the Pop Monster
Review: The shift between styles can jar, but it's a move that give Broods' inoffensive formula a welcome burst of energy. [Mar 2019, p.112]

Title: Shrines
Review: Although the band's sonic stew isn't particularly remarkable or consistent (instrumentation oscillates between warm and comforting, and distant and anemic), their lyrics have a peculiar charm that keeps them alluring.

Title: Body of Song
Review: [Mould's trademark] coupling of aggression and tuneful economy is one of the chief attributes sometimes compromised on Body of Song.

Title: Bare Bones
Review: Peyroux still sounds like Peyroux, only more so. Which isn't a bad thing either.

Title: Carried to Dust
Review: Carried to Dust is a fine entry Calexico’s discography that both evokes a much-loved sound from the past and yet looks at the sun fading into the west, turns its horse towards the dying light, and carries on into the future.

Title: Wild Seeds
Review: The soft-rock paradigm with its classic Fleetwood Mac/Carole King references is self-limiting, but the songs are lucid and heartfelt in their graceful ruminations on the passage of time. [Sep 2019, p.34]

Title: Abyss
Review: Abyss may not be a go-to for either late-night or summer listening, but it ably solidifies Wolfe’s presence as a devastatingly unique voice in our current musical climate.

Title: Alphabetical
Review: Like Bread produced by The Neptunes. [Jul 2004, p.110]

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: It's his freest record, musically speaking, and in its bloodstained lyrics, which run the gamut from cautionary to vindictive to self-loathing, it opens up a side of White that previously has been impenetrable, wrapped up in his own self-mythologizing persona as he was.

Title: Hotel Last Resort
Review: Strange, inexplicable and uncomfortable are descriptions the Femmes’ are likely proud of. Their ageing indie audience expects nothing less and should be more than happy to check into this hotel of last resort.

Title: Magnetic Man
Review: This is less a statement about where UK dance music is headed than the sound of three men having the time of their lives, with scant regard for genre purists.

Title: Silver Landings
Review: Overall, Silver Landings finds Moore regaining her footing.

Title: MantaRay
Review: After a strong start, though, the album gets a bit flat, with some songs like 'One Mile Below' sounding dramatic enough but also too reminiscent of past Banshees/Creatures highlights to truly stand out.

Title: Exile In The Outer Ring
Review: Her ability to turn raw emotion into compelling and riveting music carries Exile in the Outer Ring, and the result is some of the best material we've heard from her yet.

Title: Bottomless Pit
Review: Death Grips pride themselves on constantly shifting and progressing from one release to the next. That unfortunately sometimes outweighs cohesion, but Bottomless Pit is tighter, more daring, and catchier than that.

Title: Dissolve
Review: Pulsing, hazy, addictive. [Nov 2017, p.100]

Title: Ambulance
Review: The whole work hits like a long-forgotten memory. Fans of Picture You, or of wistful atmosphere in general, will want to dig deep into Ambulance, and, to its credit, will find the room to do so.

Title: Young Love
Review: All in all, a noteworthy release that reveals more layers the longer you listen.

Title: Nevermen
Review: Delightfully chewy collaboration. [Feb 2016, p.90]

Title: MAGDALENE
Review: Sometimes elegance and grace are enough to spark a transformative introspective journey. It is a rare occurrence, but that's what FKA twigs has delivered with Magdalene.

Title: The Crossing
Review: All in all, it's the sound of a bunch of musicians from the top of the game performing at the top of their game. Ruthlessly tight, deeply soulful with tunes to keep you riveted to your stereo until deep into the night.

Title: Isles
Review: It’s about as exotic as a cocktail umbrella.

Title: The Errant Charm
Review: Your cider-drinking soundtrack for this summer is here. [Jul 2011, p.100]

Title: Spiral Shadow
Review: The 78-minute Spiral Shadow supersizes everything, from song lengths to layers of deep-focus space-rock effects, but the sprawling songs are still built around riffs as sweaty as a south Georgia summer.

Title: Man About Town
Review: Highlights album come when the songs stretch beyond Hawthorne’s solo comfort zone.

Title: The New Life
Review: If Cathal Cully's aim was to leave the past behind then he's succeeded resoundingly, and created one of this year's most ungainly beautiful records in the process.

Title: Human the Death Dance
Review: He rhymes like a champ. [Jun 2007, p.160]

Title: Humanz
Review: Humanz is another strong entry in Albarn’s lengthy and brilliant catalog. At its best, it doubles down on what Albarn has done right all along while also pointing in new directions he can go.

Title: Nomad
Review: It's a pleasant, if limited set, and though there are echoes of the mesmeric style of Tinariwen, he sounds more like the attacking Vieux Farka Touré with less ambitious guitar work.

Title: Diviner
Review: On his frequently divine debut album, Hayden Thorpe may well be a new man, untethered from his band, adrift in space and time, yet safe in the hermetic seal of an intricately designed vessel, but the desire for human connection will seemingly always bring him out of his shell and back down to solid ground.

Title: There Were Wolves
Review: If you liked the harmonies of that romantic duo on the Once soundtrack, you'll fall for these hard-headed, bighearted folkies.

Title: Aufheben
Review: Maybe at some points the eastern influences are more prominent, on tracks like 'Panic In Babylon', but on the whole it's classic BJM.

Title: I
Review: Overall, I is an interesting record, mainly due to Follakzoid’s uncompromising efforts to cross boundaries between electronic music and psychedelia. Nevertheless, it might be too much to take in in one setting, unless you really are in the mood or on drugs to drift away while listening.

Title: I'm a Stranger Here
Review: Their blend of bluegrass, blues and ragtime isn't unique within the current old-timey undercurrent of Americana, but frontman Pete Bernhard's songwriting contains enough contemporary flair to provide a solid backbone for the album's ten tracks

Title: All Is Illusory
Review: The album works more as a selection of striking individual pieces than a coherent whole; there are moments of brilliance here, but they're inconsistent, and the album has more than its share of false endings that muddle the pacing.

Title: Alarms In The Heart
Review: Dry The River have here proven that they hold their own distinct niche in our record collections, and are settling in to it nicely.

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
Review: This album just goes to show that when Vernon does manage to find that perfect balance of production and deep-in-the-gut songwriting, it is going to be shattering. Even the harshest critics among us may, for a moment, forget about our thumbs.

Title: A Celebration of Endings
Review: Decidedly bolder than 2016's Ellipsis, it is an album that revels in subverting expectations. [Jun 2020, p.88]

Title: Run the Jewels 3
Review: In short, RTJ3 is near perfect in its execution. They're so good at this that it seems almost unfair in its effortlessness.

Title: Gypsy
Review: The bluesiest tracks are best (Beat The Drum; Witness). [Oct 2019, p.92]

Title: Death By Sexy
Review: Sounds more fun on paper than it is in reality. [Aug 2006, p.111]

Title: Keep It Like a Secret
Review: Keep It Like a Secret is tightly wound clang, effectively understated in spots.

Title: Truly She Is None Other
Review: A sexy record, of a kind that no one else seems to be making anymore.

Title: Antisocialites
Review: Molly Rankin’s vocals throughout the record compliment the soundscapes perfectly, fanning disappointment with hope whilst exercising a great deal of control--and an admirable lack of bias--over her ponderings.

Title: Youth Authority
Review: The slower stuff often turns sticky--but the group wears their heart on the sleeve and, somehow, that tendency is more endearing as the Maddens turn into middle age warriors.

Title: Long Lost Solace Find
Review: Long Lost Solace Find has traces of Dinosaur Jr.'s most hushed moments, Anne Briggs' heartbreaking clarity, and the resigned grandeur of legendary artists like Karen Dalton or Nick Drake. It's a stunning turn of heel, and one that instills a sense of anticipatory excitement for where Polizze will take his music next.

Title: Galactic Melt
Review: Ultimately, Galactic Melt is like a good bartender: approachable without being overbearing, reminding you of past buddies while keeping a slight but not uncomfortable distance… and fading into context, so that when you wake up the next day there's nothing more than a pleasant gap in your memory.

Title: Losing Sleep
Review: With or without well-known collaborators, his old hard-nosed concision comes through.

Title: Gold Record
Review: Gold Record marks another stage in one of the most intriguing about-turns in recent American music. The curmudgeon of Callahan’s early records might now meet humanity with a wry chuckle and an observational benevolence bordering on empathy.

Title: The GOAT
Review: It is not the singularly engrossing experience that Die a Legend is, but it argues for him as an adaptable and unmissable talent, an unlikely star in a new major-label system.

Title: About The Light
Review: As a portrait of happiness, About the Light strikes its deepest chords when Mason acknowledges the long road he took to find it.

Title: Six
Review: More so than on predecessor The Spell, the Procession's ominous, gothic-baroque sound now suggest angular German Expressionist cinema and the raven wing atmospheres of Edgar Allan Poe as readily as The Bad Seeds. [Dec 2009, p. 94]

Title: The Trouble with Being Myself
Review: As ever, when the beats go uptempo, things go awry... but there's life in the giant-haired lady yet. [Jun 2003, p.98]

Title: The Golden Record
Review: Overall, I can honestly say that I enjoyed Little Scream and I'm interested to see what she'll do next.

Title: Natural History
Review: Natural History is an invigorating listen, which may say as much about today as it does about the band.

Title: Different Gear, Still Speeding
Review: This album, produced by Steve Lillywhite whose credits include U2, Dave Matthews Band and The Smiths, shows this band is ready to ready to compete for world-class status. Rock on.

Title: Hardcourage
Review: Hardcourage is an exceedingly worthwhile release from a producer that’s constantly pushing himself toward new things.

Title: Animal Nature
Review: Inevitably, some of the studio tracks suffer by comparison; you can imagine Barbarians as an irresistible call to arms in a Brooklyn basement, but it falls a little flat here. But there’s nifty production work elsewhere.

Title: Restless Ones
Review: The LP feels more casual than previous ones, but that's by no means a negative. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.79]

Title: Better Day
Review: Dolly's high lonesome Tennessee drawl carries nearly five decades' worth of hitmaking history, and lord knows how many centuries worth of Smoky Mountains folk wisdom.

Title: Untitled
Review: This album sounds like his band's final aria--the death scene.

Title: Expo 86
Review: The album is a perfect mixture of the band's first two records, blended with an equal part of their rock swagger and part their post-electro swing.

Title: Pearl Mystic
Review: Pearl Mystic is a promising debut from Hookworms, but whether it’s universally appealing is impugnable--there’s a suspicion that accessibility is not exactly on the top of Hookworms’ priorities; instead making interesting, immersive music to get lost in clearly is.

Title: Looping State of Mind
Review: The inanely literalistic Looping State of Mind magnifies that trend [toward expansionism], offering seven mutations of his trademark sound, in a newly expansive array of tempos. [#82, p. 55]

Title: SremmLife
Review: This is Snapchat-raised turn-up music, trendy and self-actualizing through its references to memes that come quick as they go.

As on Musicology, the beats get pretty wicked here... But while 3121 is no funkier than Musicology, it does emphasize speedier tempos and, two nods to Zapp aside, more conventional sonics. [6 Apr 2006, p.60]

Title: Everybody Got Their Something
Review: In a just universe, Nikka Costa, with her near-perfect American debut, Everybody Got Their Something, would become the ‘00s answer to Janis Joplin, Teena Marie and Like a Virginal Madonna.

Title: I Love You, Dude
Review: German electro poppers making a play for the festival crowds. [July 2011, p. 102]

Title: Tell Me
Review: Bumped up to the majors for Tell Me, like its predecessor produced by Auerbach, Mayfield evinces maturity in both her sonic approach and her writing. [Feb. 2011, p. 72]

Title: Body Music
Review: It is a wonderful debut effort, and all of the buzz and the attention they have garnered up to this point is likely only the beginning for AlunaGeorge.

Title: Collapse EP
Review: Collapse isn’t accessible per se, but it is a release which perfectly reflects the finest elements of Richard James’ oeuvre. It is a record liberated from convention, unafraid of failure and confident in its depth.

Title: Un Dia
Review: This is an adventurous and beguiling record that eschews the abrasiveness of Björk's more esoteric albums in favour of inviting the listener to explore its deeper reaches alongside the artist.

Title: Reform Club
Review: A little older and a little more experienced, the sound of Claro here is slower in BPM but more graceful as a result.
