Title: Leisure Seizure
Review: Nobody else writes songs like him. Alas, the twentysomething has a voice only a mother could truly love.

Title: Another Country
Review: Here her wonderful voice, smooth and warm with throaty twang and unforced power, has free rein to do what it does best on 11 fine new songs. [May 2008, p.111]

Title: Straight Songs Of Sorrow
Review: We should all count ourselves lucky that that role fell to a man willing to be this open and viscerally honest, and to translate it into music that salves the soul.

Title: Silk Rhodes
Review: This stuff can't touch Adrian Younge's Venice Dawn project, which released the dynamite Something About April in 2011, but it has its own charm.

Title: That Lucky Old Sun
Review: Sweetly and unmistakably, That Lucky Old Sun limns the sunset of Wilson's career, while still showing how California is at its most beautiful through his eyes.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: In the end, what really matters is that the superior Nothing Was The Same brings back the excitement of So Far Gone.

Title: Untitled
Review: Not consolidating or scaling back their ambition in the slightest, mewithoutYou continue to be one of indie-rock’s most consistently fascinating voices, and on ‘[Untitled]’ they’re as weird and wonderful as ever.

Title: National Ransom
Review: You'd be hard pressed to find an album as varied as Elvis Costello's National Ransom (his 26th, give or take).

Title: Gentle Stream
Review: [Gentle Stream] is gorgeous sun-dappled psych, crossing the lighter side of paisley underground with Nick Drake's dreaminess. [Dec 2011, p.93]

Title: Interplanetary Class Classics
Review: There will be more considered and crafted albums released this year, but few that are so much fun.

Title: I'm Your Empress Of
Review: It is not surprising that Empress Of has produced yet another gorgeous and memorable collection of songs, yet her consistency does not diminish the unique achievements of this album. This is a perfect album for finding comfort and beauty in the things and people closest to you.

Title: Clash the Truth
Review: With cuts like the melodically nifty “Taking Off” and the high-impact jangle-and-scree “Careless,” Beach Fossils find the right balance often enough.

Title: Solarized
Review: The entire disc is marked by diversity and ingenuity. [#13, p.96]

Title: Cotillions
Review: The concept of ‘Cottilions’ definitely deserves some applause. It’s a big, brave project for anyone to take on, and rather than disappoint or fail, it impresses, and in some places, it shines.

Title: Melodrama
Review: She didn't just write an excellent, expansive album that pushed her boundaries in all directions. She underwent a journey of catharsis.  With a dazzling set of songs, she's also given other broken hearts a path to the green light at the end of the tunnel.

Title: Somethin 'Bout Kreay
Review: It's not a very good listen, but it's kind of fun to watch someone be so free.

Title: Sleeper
Review: On Sleeper, the tracks with more of Villain are wholly better than those with less.

Title: Judy Sucks a Lemon For Breakfast
Review: This is the friendliest batch of neo-glam to come down the pike in quite some time, never catching fire but never really striking a match, either, and it's the least adventurous dose of eclecticism, too, with nary a sitar, Mellotron, or sample out of place.

Title: It's Never Been Like That
Review: The overwhelming sense is of a group needlessly hobbling themselves. [Jun 2006, p.110]

Title: Hard II Love
Review: While Hard II Love doesn’t include a song as cathartic as Usher’s “Climax,” from 2012, it’s full of smaller satisfactions.

Title: Visions of a Life
Review: In lesser hands, this kind of sonic disparity could be chaotic and confusing--but with Rowsell’s voice as the guiding light, Visions is a captivating, enjoyable ride.

Title: Tara Jane O'Neil
Review: While remaining as obtuse as ever, O’Neil’s newfound appreciation for singer-songwriter-dom presents some of her most personal work yet.

Title: If You Leave
Review: There's stark simplicity to Tonra's lyrics that's evocative enough to consistently land emotional haymakers. `[Apr 2013, p.99]

Title: We're Not Talking
Review: They still manage to hit that sweet spot where they seem uncertain about everything, except the music they’re making--smart, charmingly relatable, and definitely evolving.

Title: Because of You
Review: A likable little album.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: Nookie Wood finds him in rude creative health; a gruff, Pan-like affirmation of continuing musical restlessness.

Title: Comedown Machine
Review: Just like the band itself, it presents something of an ongoing identity crisis for the band, one that hasn’t figured out how to advance their sound except to put more meat on the bones.

Title: The Evens
Review: Pros: Farina is an excellent drummer and singer, and MacKaye hasn’t lost any of his righteous anger. Cons: with only two people you just can’t be viciously loud.

Title: HoboSapiens
Review: HoboSapiens is still dense and difficult for much of its running time, but the challenge comes from following the author through his many compositional twists rather than sitting through passages that drone on far too long.

Title: Engineers
Review: What sets Engineers apart on this full-length debut is their ability to build up a strong sound without anything being lost within it. [#9]

Title: The Golden Hour
Review: It defies, nay challenges, you not to tap your feet or, heaven forbid, dance.

Title: Canyons of My Mind
Review: A more sophisticated Harry Nilsson-like groove, but still keeping those Music City roots. [Jun 2017, p.95]

Title: Draw The Line
Review: Draw the Line is essentially another cog in the folksy wheel he's been spinning since "New Day at Midnight."

Title: Living in Extraordinary Times
Review: Living in Extraordinary Times marks a band still working at their full capacity, bringing new ideas and sounds while retaining what inherently makes James James--big choruses, danceable tracks, and timely lyrics.

Title: That Lucky Old Sun
Review: Wilson continues to rehash southern California culture with increasingly less perspective, further eschewing the untamed adolescent aesthetic by including stuffy musical theater elements and a top-down point-of-view that’s more clumsy analysis than sincere memoir.

Title: The Wild
Review: A welcome return to form.

Title: Acrobats
Review: A huge step forward for them and, hopefully, for their public perception too.

Title: Ancient Melodies of the Future
Review: Songwriter Doug Martsch again succeeds in striking an impressive balance between guitar-saturated bombast and impeccable melodic taste.

Title: In Time to Voices
Review: In Time to Voices is aggressive, it is irreverent, yet also very ambitious.

Title: Fundamental
Review: "Fundamental" is the sound of the Pet Shop Boys reborn, and mindful of the important role they fill in the pop family.

Title: Half Moon Light
Review: This album is a bold step into fresh creative ground for the Lone Bellow, but they seem to still be settling into their new musical home.

Title: Vespertine
Review: In the end, Vespertine commits its magic by daring to go places more obvious and more human than one would have ever expected. [#210, p.52]

Title: SuperHeavy
Review: The sad fact about supergroups is that they are rarely the result of any musical imperative. This is painfully confirmed on the debut offering from the alliance of Mick Jagger, Dave Stewart, Joss Stone, Damian Marley and A R Rahman, on which the assembled talents cast around for a style of their own without ever unearthing the natural chemistry on which great bands rely.

Title: Weather Systems
Review: Weather Systems stands with Anathema's finest work.

Title: She's In Control
Review: The album is just disappointing: full of slick beats of undisguised artifice and lacking the one thing all good slow jams need – namely, great vocals.

Title: Lifted
Review: Nash wants to prove he’s capable of soaring skyward. Whether his listeners are willing to follow him as he scales that cosmic plane remains to be seen, but for now, Nash offers all the inducement needed for them to at least consider making the climb.

Title: Art Official Intelligence: Mosaic Thump
Review: But despite collaborators as diverse as Chaka Khan, Busta Rhymes, and Mike D of the Beastie Boys, the album sounds more like the result of a raucous block party than of a careful marketing plan.

Title: Clear Heart Full Eyes
Review: The arrangements are simple, often pretty ... but mostly they serve to support the delivery of some of Finn's most evocative and well observed lyrics.

Title: Bonny Light Horseman
Review: It’s all very nice and a bit surprisingly, like your grandma’s favorite stew with some unexpected new spices in it. For an impromptu gathering of talents, Bonny Light Horseman feels very lived in. Here’s hoping it’s not a one-off.

Title: Gist Is
Review: By the time you reach the gentle conclusion of ‘Bonedigger’, it’s clear Adult Jazz will be inspiring their own army of rip-offs before long.

Title: Soft Commands
Review: Stringfellow has concocted a frustratingly obtuse record that's as beautiful and bold as it is shapeless and erratic.

Title: Heads Up
Review: At 52 minutes, it is no longer than your standard album, and yet it has seemingly bottomless depths and wide-open horizons that reward the listener with the possibilities of unending exploration. The fact that it can never be fully known makes it all the more revelatory.

Title: Wiped Out!
Review: The LA quintet still sound like 16-year-old boys.... Musically, though, their slick soulful pop-R&B is far more refined. [Dec 2015, p.94]

Title: The Age of Adz
Review: As important questions about music's worth in the age of free continue to swirl around him, Sufjan's still combating instant-gratification culture the best way he knows how.

Title: Lucky Shiner
Review: Lucky Shiner is a good argument for the album as a conceptual whole, and for a musical environment a bit slower than the singles-based landscape that birthed Gold Panda as an entity to be reckoned with.

Title: G I R L
Review: It’s catchy and shows faint glimmers of his true talent, but it comes off like a tossed off, half baked batch of outtakes from sessions where his more impressive music was produced.

Title: Sky Blue Sky
Review: This may be the best Eagles album the Eagles never made.

Title: When The Devil's Loose
Review: When the Devil's Loose might share some reference points with another singer/songwriter with a similar offhand affection for roots music, but A.A. Bondy seems to be developing a voice of his own despite all the surface similarities, and the result is a quietly powerful album of songs that cut deeper into the heart and soul than you might expect at first glance.

Title: Port Entropy
Review: Port Entropy, Shugo's fifth LP (depending on how you reckon Fragment, his 2003 CD-R self-release), decisively occupies the realm of the waking: the nimble, the abstract, and the exciting.

Title: Light at the End of the World
Review: When it all comes together, as it does on the amazing singles "I Could Fall in Love with You" and "Sunday Girl," the effect is intoxicating. Music like this makes you happy to be alive. When it doesn't come together, as on "How My Eyes Adore You", the result isn't unpleasant so much as tedious.

Title: Jaime
Review: There’s no track on Jaime that is likely to make waves – not in the same way as some of the better-known Alabama Shakes tracks, such as “Hold On” or “This Feeling” (the latter of which was recently used to remarkable effect in the final scene of Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag). But what lovely ripples it makes.

Title: IV
Review: Their fourth album reveals the breadth of the genre.

Title: Wolfmother
Review: Where fellow Aussie pasticheurs the Vines get more depressing the more they manage to sound like Nirvana, listening to Wolfmother's hilarious attempt to board the long-departed cock-rock bandwagon - singing 'She's a woman, you know what I mean!' as if they have never seen a woman, let alone touched one - is actually quite fun.

Title: Trouble Man: Heavy Is the Head
Review: This is a strong return to form for the self-proclaimed King of the South.

Title: Death of a Bachelor
Review: For all of its precocious, borderline bratty moments, Death Of A Bachelor is a remarkably nuanced affair. [Feb 2016, p.95]

Title: Love Hates What You Become
Review: They manage to pack such a powerful emotional punch across these 10 tracks. [Feb 2019, p.117]

Title: Galore
Review: On their charming debut, the four-piece fulfil their promise of being the edgy, sexually voracious Ace of Bass.

Title: Everything All The Time
Review: It takes a few listens to sink in, but Everything is transcendent, shimmering, layered, and smartass emo-pop fully ready for stadium saturation.

Title: Effra Parade
Review: A beautifully fashioned, classy and meticulously crafted background music, perfect for Sunday brunch among the NPR crowd.

Title: Changing Horses
Review: Changing Horses marks a defining moment in the songwriter's career, offering up a batch of pastiche-free country music that, like Ryan Adams' "Jacksonville City Nights," may be a promising sign of what's to come.

Title: Eucalyptus
Review: With a playing time of over an hour, and a reflective, more often than not formless complexion, even acknowledging its subtle whimsy and California roots, Eucalyptus goes by like a long drive through the plains, rewarding the patient and attentive.

Title: I See You
Review: The result is the most eclectic, multidimensional, and ambitious album of The xx’s young career.

Title: Phantom Radio
Review: This far into his career Mark Lanegan was unlikely to start making albums that are any less than engaging, but it’s still testament to his creativity and love of his art that ‘Phantom Radio’ is such a successful departure from bluesy rock and roll.

Title: Lights
Review: Aspiring to find a middle ground between her folk background and the burgeoning success of electro-pop is an enterprising objective, but it is one which Goulding predominantly succeeds in through her genuine sincerity.

Title: Carrier
Review: The sophistication suits the songs, which have a tragic seriousness without becoming a gloomy slog.

Title: Terrible Human Beings
Review: Terrible Human Beings can still be cherry-picked for catchy singles bound for algorithmic playlists, but  it’s impossible to overlook how much of the Orwells’ appeal is bundled into their persona as enfants terribles.

Title: Below the Branches
Review: There's nothing really new or earth-shattering about this album, but that's not a prerequisite for great rock & roll.

Title: Positive Force
Review: Positive Force will uplift you.

Title: Take Me to the Sea
Review: Write off Jaguar Love at your peril; this is one of the best albums of the year so far.

Title: Nav
Review: It's a lack of originality that turns the sound stale rather quickly.

Title: Honest
Review: Even if not everything on this album pulses with full intensity--the back half of it lags--Future is generally magnetic.

Title: Wooden Leather
Review: A significant step forward. [Oct 2003, p.179]

Title: Forever
Review: The Swedes have stepped it up in the songwriting department.

Title: Vieux Loup
Review: The Acorn remain elusive. [Jul 2015, p.69]

Title: Versatile
Review: He's added half a dozen of his own compositions in a similar style to this generous 16-track selection, which pays tribute to his jazz roots rather more successfully than his uneven homage to his R&B origins in September's Roll With The Punches. [Feb 2018, p.30]

Title: Asymmetry
Review: Asymmetry is their best yet. [Oct 2013, p.102]

Title: Security Screenings
Review: Herren never lets his music become too easy-going or the listener too settled. [Mar 2006, p.108]

Title: Crush Songs
Review: Not only are these songs about crushes, they feel just like one: emotionally intense, completely beautiful, and above all, fleeting.

Title: Love Yes
Review: Love Yes is a remarkable step forward for TEEN, blending the stylistic influences of their first two records to present a seamless and singular voice.

Title: Want Two
Review: A quieter, more intimate, and more demanding set than its predecessor, Want Two offers few of Want One's sweeping pleasures, but it cultivates a creeping beauty that's as satisfying in its own right.

Title: You Can't Imagine How Much Fun We're Having
Review: Slug hasn't grown a whole lot.... Still, his lyricism and delivery are generally smart and entertaining, and Ant's production goes even further toward making You Can't Imagine... a thoroughly enjoyable record.

Title: Nocturama
Review: This is one of Cave's best album in years, if not an immediate candidate for a career highlight.

Title: The Tourist
Review: It's not an easy album to love. [Apr 2017, p.98]

Title: Gang of Losers
Review: It's the band's fussiest, most elaborately conceived work to date. [Nov 2006, p.83]

Title: Bangerz
Review: It’s not the worst album in the world, but it certainly doesn’t live up to the acres of hype that have led up to it. It’s just rather average.

Title: Hard Islands
Review: His tunes have taken a tougher, more urban tone, with stand-outs 'The Turtle' and 'Basic Mountain' building to hard edged concrete peaks, drenched in acid Rephlex bleeps. [Jun 2009, p.85]

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: For people friendly to western pop traditions, there is little or nothing in the music to dislike, and lots to sing along with.

Title: Chapter V
Review: The real problem is sounding like Alice In Chains; afloat without a genre, the gang too often turn their emotional intelligence to making kinda dark, vaguely artistic middle metal. [Sep 2005, p.138]

Title: This Is... Icona Pop
Review: Basically, you can listen to all 11 tracks of This Is... Icona Pop and have a reasonable time, or you can put I Love It on repeat, forever, and have the time of your life.

Title: Blood Bank EP
Review: His new EP, “Blood Bank,” is due out on Tuesday on the same label, and three of its four songs abide by similar prescriptions [as “For Emma, Forever Ago."]

Title: Fork In The Road
Review: The resulting album is a ragbag of environmentalist/credit-crunch rants and rusty old chuggers.

Title: Throws
Review: The 10 songs of this debut album are all about character, change and companionship, from various angles.

Title: The Difference Between Hell and Home
Review: There’s a lot to appreciate, whether you like screamo, face-punching hardcore, pop-punk, or some combination of all those sounds and more.

Title: Collections
Review: Having been dogged with comparisons to Friendly Fires since their formation, it is ironic that this record perhaps sounds like the kind of misstep that the St. Albans band made themselves with their second album 'Pala'.

Title: Year of the Gentleman
Review: Ne-Yo is a stronger, more confident man than the one many remember licking his wounds on 'So Sick' from his debut album "In My Own Words" and 'Do You' from 2007’s "Because of You."

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: It seems - for the first time, perhaps - he's made one out of love for the artform alone rather than with the added motive of letting off a little barely-suppressed rage or feeling he has scores to settle, either with the industry or himself.

Title: Unstoppable
Review: Crisply produced, the album's biggest problem is the one that has always dogged Rascal Flatts: All the songs bleed into one another with rarely a shift in structure or mood.

Title: We Have You Surrounded
Review: This is the sound of an extremely skilled group of musicians working on every cylinder and impulse.

Title: Too Weird to Live, Too Rare to Die!
Review: Teeming with melodic hooks and reflective lyrics, Too Weird to Live, Too Rare to Die! is both hypnotic (the lingering closer “The End of All Things”) and beguiling (Far Too Young to Die” and second single “This Is Gospel”).

Title: The Smell of Our Own
Review: Gibb's mixture of gay and Christian imagery is potent, and his vision of music as a grand communal experience is backed up by some memorable tunes. [Apr 2003, p.112]

Title: Wild Young Hearts
Review: Leaving behind the soul-infused, gutter-punk leanings of their debut, this desperately craves the attentions of the MOR indie mainstream in a way so steeped in bathos that the over-produced sheen of the car-ad soundtracking title track shines less like superstar diamonds and more like sun off a bald man’s head.

Title: Move Like This
Review: Move Like This isn't a failure by any means. It's not the resounding triumph you might have hoped for, either.

Title: Heart of My Own
Review: It’s an album unlikely to reign in anyone who’s on the fence about adding a folk album to their catalogue, but sure to delight those who like their melancholy sentiments sung by a voice that is as dexterous as it is vulnerable

Title: Soft Sounds From Another Planet
Review: Soft Sounds is full of pretty interludes of ambient noise, mixed with shoegaze and electropop touches.

Title: Apocalipstick
Review: While Haxel Princess was full of goofy and relatable teenage dispatches, Apocalipstick shoots daggers. Now 19, Creevy sounds wizened and ready for battle.

Title: North
Review: Matchbox 20 has never made a record as cheerful or appealing or satisfying as this.

Title: CrownsDown
Review: I prefer the more minimal style of Them, which was sharply critical--and deeply personal--without being hectoring or bombastic. But listeners who enjoy picking apart seam-bursting sonic worlds will find plenty to explore here.

Title: Invisible Ones
Review: Fink stays close to the sonic templates of both Now It's Overhead and Azure Ray, but has less impact than either.

Title: Faded Seaside Glamour
Review: Despite some strong ideas and a few memorable songs, Faded Seaside Glamour remains notable mostly for the vocals: the album's ups and downs follow Gilbert's voice almost exactly, best when he's hitting high notes, mundane when he's not.

Title: Authenticity
Review: More moody, modern R&B that sounds like nothing else and reveals remarkable depth (there's even a little well-placed twang and some violin), Authenticity is neither an everyday nor an every-day album, unless playing it is necessary for the sake of convalescence.

Title: Don't Believe The Truth
Review: It's confident, muscular, uncluttered, tight, and tuneful in a way Oasis haven't been since Morning Glory.

Title: Wrecking Ball
Review: The musicianship and songwriting is easily on par with Magic and exceeds the output on Working On A Dream, and as a whole, Wrecking Ball stacks up considerably with The Rising, which to this day I consider a top-5 Springsteen album.

Title: Bang Bang Rock & Roll
Review: Every generation needs an Art Brut. [Jun 2005, p.100]

Title: The Deslondes
Review: The Deslondes provide a thrilling, original blend of American music that can’t be found anywhere else.

Title: Wildflower
Review: Even if it could never feel like a childhood's worth of lovingly curated music, and even if the shock of the new's way out of its reach, it's still another out-of-its-time, forensically assembled wonder.

Title: Sweet Sour
Review: Sledgehammer riff-filled rock doesn't need to be clever, but it sure as heck needs to sound like it's driven by full-pelt, carnage-causing energy. And that's where Band Of Skulls' second effort falls short.

Title: Perils from the Sea
Review: Perils from the Sea may not be a seamless collaboration, but neither artist has sounded so purposeful in his reverie in years.

Title: The Creatures in the Garden of Lady Walton
Review: They’ll soon become enraptured by what accompanies these highest-of-profile pieces: music that embraces the listener with a silken touch and seduces them with a beguiling beauty that, still, sits prettily beyond the clamour of convenient categorisation.

Title: At Swim
Review: Since her emergence as a solo artist, Hannigan has been drawn to all things nautical. On her third full length, she continues that fascination, treading new water and exploring new routes on many of the tracks, but still ultimately in search of new shores.

Title: Deeper
Review: Despite the change in scenery, the results are the same intense, fraught, pretty/ugly postpunk mishmash as ever.

Title: Spaces
Review: If, by chance, Spaces happens to be the very first record which you pick up by Nils Frahm, I must proclaim to be extremely jealous--you have a beautiful and highly rewarding journey ahead of you, my friend.

Title: Anxiety Always
Review: Anxiety Always is, to put it bluntly, one pissed-off album, a snide, sarcastic, bitchy commentary on trend-followers, relationships, and the brainwashed masses out there, and it's so up front in its condescension that you're taken aback at first, so punk-like is Adult.'s sound.

Title: Dead Throne
Review: There is a sense of urgency and maturity here that few in the genre will be able to replicate. So forget the throne, The Devil Wears Prada doesn't need it to prove that they've released the best metalcore album of the year.

Title: Bazooka Tooth
Review: Perhaps the producers have toned themselves down a bit just so Aesop can rock harder. Maybe they don’t want to steal his thunder. Whatever their motivation, the beats feel somewhat restrained, lethargic and lazy. But they are perfectly suited to Aesop’s limpid down-tempo rhymes.

Title: Compass
Review: Thankfully, none of Lidell's guests do much to blunt his funky trajectory. [Spring/Summer 2010, p.108]

Title: Finally Rich
Review: When Finally Rich works (and it often does), it's thanks to everyone other than Chief Keef.

Title: The Way and Color
Review: The Way And Color is an admirable, solid effort, surely paving the way for better material on the not so distant, sunset dripping, horizon.

Title: Directors of Photography
Review: It harkens back to the clever minimalism of The Platform, while incorporating all they’ve learned since their early days as a group. And though it is an uneven affair, it’s a welcome breath of fresh air in the hip-hop world of 2014.

Title: Anak Ko
Review: Like previous Jay Som records, Anak Ko might seem slight at first listen, particularly Duterte’s winsome coo, but the payoff for lingering in her evolving dreamspace is hefty.

Title: Kris Allen
Review: Sure, there are a handful of half-decent cuts included here, but even they have limited lasting value. Meanwhile, the filler (arguably half the LP) is mind-numbingly boring.

Title: I'll Be Your Girl
Review: There’s a sense of importance and profundity that emanates from practically every groove. Stirring, striking and flush with tunefulness and tenacity, I’ll Be Your Girl is more than a promising proposition.

Title: Delta
Review: On their fourth album, all pretense at rootsy authenticity is gone--this is machine-tooled stadium pop, with producer Paul Epworth in the Brian Eno role. [Jan 2019, p.22]

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: This celebratory nihilism defines an album that's sometimes dark and moody, sometimes manic and fun. There are familiar moments of quirky guitar pop ("Delete Forever," "You'll Miss Me When I'm Not Around"). More exciting is when Grimes goes big on reverb and club-sized beats.

Title: Four
Review: Four may be 2012's most exciting guitar album.

Title: Cause And Effect
Review: Cause and Effect isn’t Keane breaking any new ground, but in the quieter moments it’s surprisingly good.

Title: Making a New World
Review: An ambitious concept album about the aftermath of World War I. Even if you don’t feel the need to follow along with their historical lyrics, these 19 short songs are an entertaining, unpredictable listen.

Title: FIBS
Review: It’s a frankly overwhelming listen first time around, with everything tearing along at a hundred miles an hour, but it’s all fizzing and crackling so exhilaratingly that you’re happy to let her sweep you along.

Title: Island Intervals
Review: Recorded in Reykjavík with Sigur Rós collaborator Alex Somers and Múm’s Samuli Kosminen, the frosty twinkles and skittery beats complement Rhode Island-based Thibadeau’s alt-folk leanings.

Title: A Head Full of Dreams
Review: Clearly, the members of Coldplay haven’t completely shaken off their ghosts. But just as clearly, they’ve found joy again in “Dreams.”

Title: Here I Am
Review: The inherent blandness of Rowland's persona makes for too much roundly mediocre material.

Title: White Lilies Island
Review: Despite Imbruglia's big, pouty voice, it's all perfectly pleasant and quickly forgotten.

Title: Jim
Review: It's tempting to knock Lidell for being too derivative of Wonder and Donny Hathaway or for simply being the latest in a never-ending line of Brits mimicking the sound of Soulsville, but why bust up a party that's this much fun?

Title: An Album by Korallreven
Review: An Album assembles all the loose threads from previous bursts of inspiration to sequence a scenic panorama to get lost into.

Title: El Pintor
Review: Sadly, "Everything Is Wrong" announces another second-half fade, the back side congealing into the same zombie histrionics that sank Interpol. [No. 113, p.57]

Title: Last of a Dyin' Breed
Review: [The album] is full of reductive, radio-friendly hard rock. [Nov 2012, p.86]

Title: Excuse My French
Review: Excuse My French is a good album, possibly the best one the Coke Boy could make.

Title: Drum's Not Dead
Review: With their third album, Liars have succeeded in creating the near-impossible; a conceptual work that speaks to the emotions and the intellect simultaneously.

Title: Resin Pockets
Review: Resin Pockets plays like a found notebook of rapturous Proustian melancholy, everyday moments of dreamlike revelation assembled into weakly-strummed, frailly-sung almost-pop songs that embrace the beauty of transience and imperfection. [Jul 2017, p.87]

Title: Horehound
Review: Horehound's strengths are also its weaknesses--the rush with which it came together, the sense that it amounts to Jack White playing to type. But like Jack White, too, when it's good, it's very, very good. [Aug 2009, p.102]

Title: Sha Sha
Review: What 20-year-old Kweller lacks in crafting his own sound, he makes up for in crafting virulently infectious hooks, the kind that find you singing along despite the fact that you only have a tenuous grasp on the lyrics.

Title: Lulu
Review: While nothing else here is quiet as astonishing, ["Junior Dad" is] a perfect ending to the most extraordinary, passionate and just plain brilliant record either participant has made for a long while. [Dec 2011, p.80]

Title: How To Live
Review: How To Live uncovers an internal landscape just as wide open, much easier to get to, and even harder to escape from.

Title: Holograms
Review: It's nothing new, sure, but it's proof that mining from the past is a surefire way to keep things sounding familiar yet fresh.

Title: In Rolling Waves
Review: The band doesn’t seem to feel beholden to making a breakthrough--and In Rolling Waves may provide it regardless.

Title: Be Your Own Pet
Review: Much of the reason for bothering with BYOP lies in the absolute glory of hearing Pearl succeed in making every lyrical couplet she spews forth sound as if she's been drinking cider since birth and is ready to hurl... anytime... now!

Title: Tracker
Review: This skillful interweaving of Knopfler's personal past helps give Tracker a nicely gentle resonance.

Title: ken
Review: A set of songs seething with dark knowledge, as Bejar peeks behind the curtain of appearances in search of underlying motivations.

Title: The Soft Cavalry
Review: The Soft Cavalry has the full-vision flow of an album like Deserter’s Songs, wherein each track has a unique character and story to tell. If the writing process behind these songs was hesitant and searching, the production that has brought them to fruition, helmed by Clarke’s fellow musician brother Michael, is striking and confident.

Title: Dose Your Dreams
Review: Dose attempts to go everywhere and do everything. Opener “None of Your Business Man” is classic Abraham ascendancy (and the perfect anthem to quit your job to). “Torch to Light” introduces the double LP’s first moment of psychedelia, a new-ish venture for the band that’s sprinkled throughout. Mascis’s contribution on “Came Down Wrong” is, unsurprisingly, fuzzy, lackadaisical indie rock. “Dose Your Dreams” is disco. “Two I’s Closed” is a Beatles ballad. “The One I Want Will Come for Me” recalls shoegaze-y Cure.

Title: I Hear You
Review: There's plenty of promise to find within Arbor Labor Union's sanguine psych, but there's still a little further to go before the pinecones become trees with any real weight about them.

Title: Native Invader
Review: As ever with Amos’ more recent albums, it’s a bit overlong and some songs, especially in the album’s mid-section, float by without ever making much of an impression. ... Yet when Tori is on form, she still sounds as vital and exciting as she did 25 years ago.

Title: The Temper Trap
Review: Unfortunately, the only thing that The Temper Trap's self-titled album proves is that they may have been a one-hit wonder all along.

Title: right on!
Review: Jam is all well and good, but this record is at times lacking in the bread and butter of music--songs.

Title: Trouble
Review: Sweet at its core, but pleasantly dark around the edges. [Feb 2014, p.76]

Title: Lighthouse
Review: Lighthouse sees Crosby at his most stripped-back; rather than attempting to update his sound to suit the times it feels as if he has distilled it, leaving something akin to Essence Of Crosby, despite being crafted in cahoots with Michael League of Snarky Puppy.

Title: True North
Review: Bad Religion see no reason to mess with the formula. [Feb 2013, p.98]

Title: Wake Up the Nation
Review: "Wake Up the Nation," if anything, is at times too manically experimental.

Title: I'm Not Your Man
Review: Without being especially political, the album is resolutely female in the strongest, most self-asserting way.

Title: Life in Slow Motion
Review: Those who thought White Ladder would stand as Gray's crowning achievement may now have to think again. [Oct 2005, p.104]

Title: Sillion
Review: ‘Raising The Dead’ is a hopeful and tender ode to finding attributes of his late father in his newborn daughter. ‘Wandering Aengus’, meanwhile, is a Yeats-inspired piece of trumpet-covered beauty that sums up the record perfectly--peaceful, lush and well worth the wait.

Title: Sea of Brass
Review: Granted, Brass doesn’t exactly qualify as real rock, indie or otherwise. Still, there’s passion that’s gleaned from British Sea Power’s attempt at something bolder, a sweeping sound that literally echoes from the rafters.

Title: Go Tell Fire to the Mountain
Review: Go Tell Fire to the Mountain and WU LYF by extension soar on how excitingly singular they are; I want nothing more than to love this, just this, forever.

Title: Scintilli
Review: Scintilli is a disappointingly static record from a duo of born tinkerers.

Title: Impersonator
Review: By paring pop music to its core human elements, Majical Cloudz has written a record that’s bare enough to breathe inside.

Title: Let's Get Out Of This Country
Review: Yet for all its surface appeal, the record has a curiously soulless quality, a lack of vulnerability and humanity that undercuts most of its songs.

Title: Olympia
Review: Luckily, the songs are more often grand than boring.

Title: WARM
Review: Tweedy might be missing his band members, but the restless, resonant spirit that drives Wilco’s best records seeps winningly into WARM just the same.

Title: Dead Magic
Review: Dead Magic is a brilliant artistic statement, Anna von Hausswolff’s best self-definition to date.

Title: The Wedding
Review: "The Wedding" has some misfires, but vulnerability makes a promising new territory for Oneida. [23 May 2005]

Title: Inflorescent
Review: It can sometimes seem as though Friendly Fires are playing catch up for a post-EDM scene that largely sprung up in their absence. The cooing vocals and build-up/drop patterns grow a little tiring across the album despite their careful production, because they’re working in well-trodden territory in a post-Flume landscape. But there is a winning warmth to their music.

Title: The North
Review: Punchier production and more energetic songwriting point The North in the right direction. [Oct 2012, p.92]

Title: The Empyrean
Review: The notable tracks certainly makes this far away from a failure and the record as a whole is yet another solid presentation of Frusciante's unique take on his own solo career.

Title: Mykki
Review: Mykki is a well-crafted, incisive debut record that proves to be well worth the wait.

Title: Charity Starts at Home
Review: A well-balanced marriage of all of Phonte's musical inclinations.

Title: Animator
Review: As Animator fades out, however, all that's left is a lingering feeling equal parts hushed and disquieting. The Luyas' ability to cultivate a mood so thick with this album is a huge accomplishment, and the strangely beautiful world they've created in these songs is one worth revisiting over and over.

Title: Palace
Review: While flawed, this is still a very worthy record; a majestic realization of the promise shown by Chapel Club over the past two years and one equally suggestive of the what may be to come.

Title: In Between
Review: On In Between they ditch any SY trappings and go full shoegaze, removing much of the energy and dialing the tempos down to mid. It works really well, allowing the band to create a mood of wistful, well-produced melancholy that builds and builds until the album ends in a swirl of barely expressed emotion and guitar clatter.

Title: BLUE
Review: It's a rare moment of intrigue on an album that's generous in its beauty while leaving little to wonder about, a sky that never rains.

Title: The Mouse and the Mask
Review: Both guys are so irrepressibly playful that they get serious at their peril--they're better off as a nonstop musical goof.

Title: Iron Flag
Review: Although RZA tries crisply updating his trademark murk for the new rap age, the results rarely cohere. [Jan 2002, p.108]

Title: Amputechture
Review: Amputechture, with its obsessive exploration of religious fanaticism and the physical expression of devotional desire, is not an album wanting to be loved so much as feared and listened to with a sense of awe and taxed exasperation.

Title: Revolt
Review: It might not be wholly successful but that could be due simply to our unfamiliarity as listeners with music that manages to be different in an instinctive way.

Title: Requiem
Review: Tracks like “It’s Not Me” and “All-Seeing Eye” feel like works in progress and weigh down an already overlong album. Yet the album has its superlative bursts, like the fingerpicked coda of “Goodbye” and the gnarly biker metal guitars on “Alarms” and “Goatfuzz”. [Oct 2016, p.61]

Title: Bosnian Rainbows
Review: As art-rock abnegation, it's impressive. But when he teases flamboyance on the death disco "Morning Sickness," you long for a little more excess.

Title: Synesthetica
Review: While the album does make impressive strides, it doesn’t come without its shortcomings. Even at 39 minutes, the Synesthetica feels repetitive at times, small modifications made here and there to a tested formula.

Title: Seabed
Review: Occasionally distant, the restrained urgency of Dracula and soulful vocals of Closer ripple with an enticing warmth. [May 2013, p.113]

Title: Mirrored
Review: If the Flaming Lips mated with Marilyn Manson and ate Underworld for breakfast, the end result might sound something like Battles' debut album, Mirrored.

Title: Principe Del Norte
Review: Flashbacks to The Orb's Adventures Beyond The Ultraworld and the KFL's Chill Out are inevitable, but there are woozy hints of early Black Dog on "C," too. [Mar 2015, p.77]

Title: Velocifero
Review: On this produced-in-Paris gem, they beef up chilly synth-pop tunes with elegantly distorted guitar, German-industrial drum loops and plenty of goth gloom.

Title: Foolish Loving Spaces
Review: While this set is not as immediate as their first two albums, Foolish Loving Spaces winds up being the one that is most rewarding after repeat listens, an enjoyable, nostalgic ode to pure affection. Coolness be damned.

Title: 10,000 Hz Legend
Review: Apart from the slow-burning, spine-tingling opener Electronic Performers, though, the duo seem reluctant to exploit their remarkable gift for melody, and tunes are too often mangled or left to fizzle out.

Title: Primitive and Deadly
Review: The pervasive, blinding darkness that saturates this bleak, sublime music is driven by the band's collective desire to seek ecstasy in the very heart of the void.

Title: Bunny
Review: There are times on Bunny when Dear doesn't stray far from the hypnotic, hedonistic mood that underpins his dancefloor moniker, Audion. ... But Bunny really shows its teeth on Can You Rush Them. A smouldering, malevolent breakbeat stomp, its exhortation to "take back the streets" hints at America's political turmoil. [Nov 2018, p.86]

Title: Saint Dymphna
Review: Yet as compared to their previous efforts, the album is surprisingly accessible and at times almost poppy-a valiant attempt at distilling, or translating, the Gang Gang Dance experience into the album format.

Title: Southern Blood
Review: Southern Blood is a timeless regional soul album. [Nov 2017, p.31]

Title: La Vita Nuova
Review: Her lyrics as well as her performance may strike some listeners as overly literary, but there is method in these mannerisms. That unwieldiness becomes one of the album’s most appealing traits.

Title: Prisoner
Review: It’s full of layers and little emotions, rather than just being a slave to the bigger issues and emotions, and that’s what makes it authentic.

Title: Songs in A Minor
Review: Fusing R&B, pop, jazz, blues, throwback soul--hell, you name it--Keys delivers grandstand ballads (like the single "Fallin' "), midtempo music, diary-worthy lyrics and feminist funk as if they were all as uncomplicated as scales.

Title: Visitations
Review: A sobering reminder of how frustrating it can be when a talented group become tethered to their established aesthetic. [Feb 2007, p.118]

Title: II
Review: Craft and primitivism are often presented as opposites, but here they complement each other so completely that you couldn’t have one without the other. [Mar 2018, p.55]

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: Their latest successfully revisits elements of their thrash-metal prime, eschewing bloated self-indulgence for straight-up head-banging aggression, with decent riffs to match, thanks in no small part to producer Rick Rubin.

Title: Koi No Yokan
Review: They still deliver their challenging music with effortless ease. [[10 Nov 2012, p.54]

Title: Blood Pressures
Review: Given Alison Mosshart's recent adventures with the Dead Weather (and Jamie Hince's escapades with fiancée Kate Moss), it's no shock that the new Kills record presents a more expansive sound from the London-based blues-punk duo.

Title: Eat the Elephant
Review: Fourteen years on from their last outing, A Perfect Circle’s return to active duty as a living, breathing band is broadly speaking a good thing for the hard rock scene. Just don’t expect a record which silver plates their stellar reputation.

Title: Since I Left You
Review: 'Since I Left You' is proof that while being a vinyl junkie might not make you a teen idol, crafting a joyous, kaleidoscopic masterpiece of sun-kissed disco-pop definitely will.... Cool? Sure, whatever. Brilliant? Undoubtedly.

Title: Heartthrob
Review: As crushing as some of these songs are, Heartthrob never lets you feel the weight, but prefers to revel in emotions good or bad, most often while sweating everything out under a crystalline disco ball.

Title: Universal High
Review: Universal High is the reinvention we never knew we needed.

Title: AM
Review: AM's a heavy seduction, restless and all the better for it.

Title: Outside
Review: All in all, Outside is a solid third album and a return to form of sorts from a band clearly in the midst of a big transition.

Title: This Land
Review: The Texan singer and guitarist's fifth album feels like a one-man exploration of African-American music. .. The blues is in safe hands. [Apr 2019, p.110]

Title: So Long, Astoria
Review: The Ataris transcend the four-square melodic thud of their contemporaries with a gentle melancholy and poetic ambition. [May 2003, p.98]

Title: Elect the Dead
Review: while System of a Down would have given these songs more sheer brawn, Mr. Tankian’s versions are the next best thing.

Title: End of Love
Review: This smart and sophisticated country-rock however, is punctuated by uninspired songs that sound like outtakes from Recovering the Satellites.

Title: Does You Inspire You
Review: Swathed as it is in the kind of ’80s arrangements of flutes and chiming guitars that have rarely been allowed beyond Carol Decker’s lushest, most velveteen fantasies, this album is an open goal to accusations of trend-following revivalism. But, like Ladyhawke’s debut, the sheer quality of songwriting justifies any retrospective leanings they may have.

Title: Backspacer
Review: For the first time in years, Pearl Jam are seizing the moment rather than wallowing in it.

Title: Tired of Tomorrow
Review: A melancholy blend of shoegaze, hardcore and alt rock overlaid with Palermo’s dark and dreamy vocals.

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: White's commercial success has nothing to do with de Stijl or da blooze--just a strong, emotive voice delivering simple yet distinctive songs, which are fairly numerous here.

Title: Live Wild Die Free
Review: By all accounts, it’s in the crucible of live performance where this duo excels. But put on record, it all feels a bit lost in translation.

Title: Mazes
Review: Mazes proves that San Franciscan guitarist Ripley Johnson has not musically strayed too far from home. [May 2001, p.93]

Title: Zeppelin Over China
Review: There's an element of "always the same but always... the same" here--but when Pollard hits his cryptically emotive cruising altitude on Carapace or The Rally Boys the guitars accelerate around their pilot, his chose songwriting vehicle always flies. [Apr 2019, p.113]

Title: Wild Ones
Review: On his fourth album, Wild Ones, there's a distinct Flo Rida-shaped hole where his personality once was--and it's been filled with other people's songs.

Title: The Creek Drank The Cradle
Review: Spartan and unadorned, the naked sincerity of the record is heartbreaking.

Title: forevher
Review: forevher is a supremely catchy, slightly experimental (the horn sections in ‘princess leia’ couldn’t go unmentioned), but chiefly fun pop record that implements plenty of ideas that are completely new to Shura’s arsenal. ... With a sound this infectious and spellbinding, Shura has undoubtedly found her calling.

Title: Love Jail
Review: Love Jail is no masterpiece, but Wilson and his bandmates' instincts are most often good. There are far worse roadtrip companions.

Title: Beautiful Dreamers
Review: Ultimately, Beautiful Dreamers is a wonderfully balanced trio exercise.

Title: reputation
Review: Reputation showcases a grown-up Swift, that's for certain. But she can't yet shake the fabled girl-next-door persona she has always written into her songs, no matter how hard she tries to play the Bad Girl.

Title: Young Modern
Review: The entire album is seamless and offers new facets with each listen.

Title: In Our Gun
Review: The middling adult contemporary slop, although awful, isn’t what ultimately drowns In Our Gun. That blame can fall squarely in the lap of misguided attempts at moody electronica, something the band has more successfully dabbled in previously.

Title: Portamento
Review: The group's sophomore effort, Portamento, finds the band maturing but not yet mature, as it pumps out two-note New Order guitar riffs and whiny screeds against parents, religion, and its members' empty wallets.

Title: Black Holes and Revelations
Review: This is the band's most autopiloted effort yet, a hacked-up last-gen rehash of said space jams, only now with greater emphasis on glitz and glam. Somehow Muse, always loveably lame, have managed to take a turn for the lamer.

Title: Nothing But the Beat
Review: Guetta's trademark union of stadium trance and American R&B is represented in a glittering array of bling-encrusted collaborations (Snoop Dogg, Akon, Chris Brown) but they struggle to impose any distinctive personality on the overall mood of relentless rictus-grin-inducing euphoria.

Title: ZUU
Review: Curry has come a long way since he blew up and has fully solidified his place in the game. If ZUU isn't in your rotation, you're sleeping.

Title: All Night Long
Review: You can't too wrong when an albums starts with cowbell and kick-drum--and truth be told, you can't go too wrong with a Buckcherry album, period. [Jul/Aug 2010, p.88]

Title: 100 Lovers
Review: US gypsy folkies ramble aroudn the musical map. [Apr. 2011, p. 94]

Title: Rise Ye Sunken Ships
Review: Throughout the record, the songs' emotional undercurrent hinges on the subject and content.

Title: Seeing Through Sound (Pentimento Volume Two)
Review: The ambience is softer, the lights are dim, the rhythms echoing in the distance. While his first release, 1977's Vernal Equinox, just re-issued this year, might make the perfect place to start on a long journey with Hassell's work, this record will do just as well.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: What Audio, Video, Disco does best is show off what a pair of good producers can really do-namely, simplifying technical musicianship into head-throbbing dance music.

Title: The Clearing
Review: The Clearing feels lovingly erected, fashioned bit by bit.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: He's written better songs and told better stories, but Blunderbuss lends rare perspective on a man who generally lets image speak for him.

Title: Persona
Review: He's created an album that stands as one of his most evocative and ambitious so far.

Title: Out of the Woods
Review: There isn't a duff or thoughtless moment.

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: Even if the album is stagnant from an artistic point of view, Jones and the DAP-Kings really do their damnedest to make it seem fresh.

Title: Night Thoughts
Review: There’s less of the superficial swagger, more mature contemplation and reflection.

Title: Warp and Woof
Review: While Warp and Woof may not boast a banger to match "The Rally Boys" from their last double album from earlier this year, Zeppelin Over China, or the majestically dumb "See My Field" (from 2018's Space Gun), there are golden nuggets of melody and movement that are simply transcendent.

Title: Far Enough
Review: Authoritative, direct and exhilarating. [May 2020, p.100]

Title: Calico Review
Review: The trouble with studiousness is its tendency to inhibit invention, and such is the case here on their third long-player. [Oct 2016, p.23]

Title: Levon Vincent
Review: Thanks to its pared-down gear list and capricious flow, Levon Vincent feels like the work of someone left alone in the studio, sketching in real time with what's at hand and moving on. And that spontaneity gives it an even greater sense of intimacy.

Title: Seefeel
Review: Seefeel are definitely onto something new here, and it's worthy of the brand. [Feb. 2011, p. 73]

Title: Greendale
Review: Unlistenable, grade-A manure.

Title: Sun Gong
Review: Sun Gong is a two-part aural resonance-bath suitable for ultimate relaxation. [Dec 2017, p.106]

Title: Sunken Condos
Review: Simultaneously taut and lush jazz-funk-pop.

Title: In Between
Review: Between its moderate tempos and spartan production, In Between seems designed to turn as few heads as possible and at first even comes across a tad glum. ... With a little patience though, its sunnier side shines through. All the hallmarks of The Feelies' sound are present, but in a pleasantly subdued state.

Title: So Long, See You Tomorrow
Review: Ultimately, So Long, See You Tomorrow is highly engaging, thoughtful, kaleidoscopic pop music for citizens of the world.

Title: Fossils and Other Phantoms
Review: More often than not, Peggy Sue derive passion from poignancy, taking their listeners on a journey that makes having a broken heart interesting again.

Title: The Letting Go
Review: The pull of European cool against Oldham's usual rustic, heartfelt love poetry creates moments of sweet tension.

Title: Save Rock and Roll
Review: Admittedly, it takes a few listens for Save Rock And Roll to click, and some songs (“Alone Together,” “Miss Missing You”) are notably weaker than others. But overall, Save Rock And Roll is a blast of an album.

Title: Superwolf
Review: Full of sombre, skeletal and obliquely confessional songs, it's a crafted collection with ruminations on sex and loss. [5 Feb 2005, p.50]

Title: Tour de France Soundtracks
Review: There's more to Tour De France Soundtracks than a simple remake of the past.

Title: Pink Friday
Review: In the end, Pink Friday is an ambitious, glossy stunner if fashion week is your favorite time of year, but Minaj didn't earn her diva status this way.

Title: Hate
Review: The dramatic, melancholy undercurrents of string-driven pop nuggets "The Drowning Years" and "Never Look at the Sun" showcase the Delgados as the smart, cutting-edge descendents of the Carpenters: everything Belle & Sebastian want to be, but are too damn precocious to pull off.

Title: There Will Be No Intermission
Review: There Will Be No Intermission is a work of art. It’s as political a record as it is personal.

Title: Rio
Review: Not only are each of the songs on Río unique; they're all impressive, adding up to a complete full-length album experience filled with highlights.

Title: Decoration Day
Review: The best new-school Southern rock you can buy.

Title: "Let's Rock"
Review: "Let's Rock" is stripped-down, straightforward and ultimately, a blast. Not a single track meanders past the four-minute mark, bringing the band's best to the forefront: Fun jams chock full of Big Riff Energy.

Title: Flight of the Conchords
Review: But as a musical concern, the Conchords can’t hold a candle to [Tenacious] D, a shortcoming that’s much more apparent on this homonymous CD than it is on TV.

Title: Til the Casket Drops
Review: Malice and Pusha T are at the top of their game on most of the rest; even when they swagger on “Popular Demand (Popeyes),” the wordplay is so thick and weirdly inventive that it’s difficult to deny them.

Title: Atlas
Review: Something new has been born here; its parents are every form of dance and many forms of rock, and it rolls.

Title: Young Enough
Review: Building off a simple guitar note, the record’s slow-burning title track is perhaps the band’s greatest accomplishment yet.

Title: Elephant
Review: All the elements of previous White Stripes records surface again, but in weirder, more intense strains that don't break with Jack and Meg White's past, yet don't slavishly adhere to it, either.

Title: Room on Fire
Review: There's nothing about the quintet's second album that audibly acknowledges the impact of its debut.

Title: Burials
Review: Burials is an album that finds darkness everywhere. [19 Oct 2013, p.54]

Title: The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends
Review: Heady Fwends has racked up about one song's worth of decent material-only none of it is in the same song.

Title: Summer Sun
Review: Summer Sun sometimes sounds like a band treading water at low tide, but obsessively exploring the contours of a moment is what Yo La have been about from day one. [Jul 2003, p.109]

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: An album full of characters struggling against dead-end jobs, drug addiction and depression doesn't exactly sound inviting, but in the hands of John Darnielle, it's magic.

Title: Ready to Die
Review: Despite being crass and ill-judged, RTD is actually fun in parts, retaining vestiges of the band's visceral youth, but leavened with the perspective more behoving of men of a certain life-stage.

Title: High Off Life
Review: Rap has been around for four decades now, and you might have hoped it would have evolved beyond this kind of backwards, deeply misogynist, abusively macho, greed- and status-obsessed posturing.

Title: The Empire Strikes First
Review: The songs have the urgency and vitriol we've come to expect from the band, but there's one major problem: the spit shine production. [Jul 2004, p.128]

Title: LP1
Review: Spread over 17 songs that tick off genres with all the flair of an automated Spotify playlist, Payne’s anonymity remains the album’s default through line. Occasionally painful yet weirdly Payne-less.

Title: Intersections
Review: Intersections is colorful but not full of drivel or loquacious exposition. It isn't pretentious. It's just raw and fucking heartwarming. Grab it.

Title: Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz
Review: For the most it is a spaced-out, blissed-out trip that makes it hard to comprehend that it came from the mind behind Bangerz.

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: It's a thoroughly likable effort.

Title: Lotus
Review: Aguilera has always been an unstoppable force when she pours her heart and soul into her music-and not as adept at dumbing down her voice or lyrics for the sake of lightweight tunes or prevailing trends. Unfortunately, by focusing on the latter route, Lotus becomes disappointingly faceless.

Title: The Atlas Underground
Review: Pick and mix your own highlights, but as a one-sitting listen expect a bumpy ride. [Nov 2018, p.82]

Title: Sea of Cowards
Review: There is some real chemistry here, but for the third album, it may be advisable to pay more attention to quality control in order to make the truly epic album that is doubtlessly lying somewhere within The Dead Weather.

Title: To the 5 Boroughs
Review: The lyrics on To The 5 Boroughs are, with a few exceptions, a dismal failure.

Title: The Fame
Review: The Fame is a very unusual beast: a sparkling pop album crammed with infectious melodies that you somehow never, ever want to hear again.

Title: Pale Green Ghosts
Review: He’s made a motherf***ing exciting record, that’s for sure.

Title: Reflektor
Review: There are enough interesting motifs and musical adventuring on Reflektor that the negatives seem inconsequential on the whole.

Title: No Coast
Review: While No Coast is more resurrection than reinvention, hearing new Braid now after 15 years without drums up the realization that nothing has sounded quite like it since.

Title: Truly She Is None Other
Review: Golightly brings out rock'n'roll's original transgressive spirit. [#60, p.98]

Title: And Nothing Hurt
Review: It stands tall as a late candidate for the year’s best rock record. Spiritualized has added yet another chapter to its wild, dreamlike musical legacy, proving that rock isn’t dead and that maybe everyone else just isn’t trying enough.

Title: Folker
Review: There's a disarming simplicity and artlessness... with an increased emphasis on persistent pop melody over crafty wordplay.

Title: Short Movie
Review: There is more to Short Movie’s context than odd details, avant garde references and the philosophy of hippy shamans. Marling has long been able to trace a musical lineage back to heavyweights like Neil Young and Joni Mitchell, and this is cemented here.

Title: Hello Love
Review: While their talent keeps Hello Love engaging... the album is nonetheless The Be Good Tanyas at their most laid-back.

Title: Scars
Review: By closing the song with unadorned strings, Basement Jaxx seems to be finding feeling in its new efficiency.

Title: Breaking Kayfabe
Review: Pemberton’s crafted a uniquely engaging sonic statement that stands on its own legs.

Title: Demain Est Une Autre Nuit
Review: In their dramatic interplay they find their lust for perversion and compulsion, as if exploring the infinite degrees of their relationship with the same piquant allure of Gainsbourg and Birkin (albeit less warm and more interpersonally brittle).

Title: On the Line
Review: There’s loneliness, heartache and regret mixed with more than a pinch of decadence in these songs. The boozy, druggy indulgences match the haziness of the best songs, the self-medication of a generation of Los Angeles kids raised on broken families and bittersweet relationships.

Title: The Unraveling
Review: The Unraveling is another in a never-ending line of quality releases from Drive-By Truckers, but it's not a lot of fun.

Title: Like The River Loves The Sea
Review: The results are exquisite. [Sep 2019, p.34]

Title: Strapped
Review: For a band who made their name on straightforward, meat-and-potatoes indie pop, Strapped is all over the place.

Title: Stranger Things
Review: For better or for worse, Yuck no longer sounds like a band trying too hard to eclipse its own past.

Title: Choir of The Mind
Review: Choir Of The Mind is more often introspective and engrossing. [No. 146, p.57]

Title: All Things Bright and Beautiful
Review: Listening to an Owl City song is like speed-eating a box of Girl Scout cookies: You go from tasty to pukey in minutes.

Title: Seabed
Review: Everything is meticulous, not a note out of place--but this studied delivery is successfully supplemented with resounding soul, proving infectious indeed.

Title: Something
Review: In producing a focussed follow-up that completely transcends its litigious backstory, Chairlift have summoned a watertight case for the defence with Something.

Title: All
Review: The results--as evidenced by such songs as “Gwennilied,” “Aom” and “Koad”--are lush, lovely and inspirational, all exquisite examples of sublime repose simulated through delicate, dreamlike designs.

Title: Fallen Angels
Review: The arrangements on Fallen Angels are wonderful and sumptuous. Recorded with his longtime touring band, it’s easy to hear how working with this music has breathed new life into them as a performing unit. Their playing is loose, easy and natural, and they sound like they’re having a lot of fun.

Title: Third
Review: Released today, it instead feels like a staggering transformation and a return to form that was never lost, an ideal adaptation by a group that many people didn't know they needed to hear again.

Title: Uptown Special
Review: Despite the production and star power, no one element outstrips the others, except perhaps for Mystikal, who continues his reinvention as James Brown's heir apparent on the raunchy Feel Right.

Title: Enemy Mine
Review: Essentially, Enemy Mine is a showcase for the talent of the three artists involved. But it lacks the conviction of Frog Eyes. It lacks the focus of Sunset Rubdown.

Title: Virgins
Review: A record tremblingly alert to the darkness, it flickers like a candle in the gloom, a victory for the forces of good against all odds. [Dec 2013, p.107]

Title: Child Ballads
Review: These ballads in the raw are rough, tragic things--Geordie is hung for his crimes, there's a drowning in Clyde Waters--that lose their impact when pretty harmonies smother them.

Title: Felt
Review: While Suuns' albums tend to reluctantly hold your hand while guiding you through their universe, Felt reaches out and pulls you in. It may even make you dance.

Title: Humbug
Review: Gradually revealing its strengths, Arctic Monkeys have pulled off a rare musical trick of their own; they’ve finally made an album that grows upon consideration, a record that feels accomplished and complete.

Title: Cuts Across the Land
Review: You sense they need a couple of pure pop gems that the Mary Chain had submerged within the noise to perfect the classic sound they aspire to. [Jun 2005, p.95]

Title: Virtue
Review: There’s enough about Virtue to keep it interesting. There’s not enough to make it genuinely good.

Title: Bird Songs of a Killjoy
Review: Korkejian moves buoyantly alongside bouncy instrumentation, determined to get somewhere, but willing to enjoy the journey along the way. And what a beautiful sounding journey it is.

Title: Keepsake
Review: She doesn’t experiment much throughout her debut, but Pilbeam knows what she does best and sticks to it throughout. Her dream pop niche in the indie rock world is sure to win her loads of new fans going forward, and with her debut, she establishes herself as not only one of its rising stars, but also one of its best songwriters.

Title: Tales From Terra Firma
Review: It’s still occasionally a bit too ‘nice’ for its own good, but in a cynical world, sometimes a little hope and buoyancy doesn’t go amiss.

Title: Crime Pays
Review: The Harlem MC remains one of hip-hop's most compelling eccentrics, enlivening clichéd gangsta subject matter and pro forma beats with his deceptively virtuosic flow, and with taunts that work by wiggy word association.

Title: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy
Review: As a whole, the record is a brilliant display of Kanye's range and influences, an opus of dirty hip-hop laid over haunting classically-inspired melodies.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: Supergrass come crashing back to life with Diamond Hoo Ha, an album every bit as cheerfully gaudy and vulgar as its title.

Title: Mass Gothic
Review: The sound of a man finding freedom, it's an impressive reincarnation. [Mar 2016, p.112]

Title: Crush Songs
Review: This album is never afraid to speak its mind and voice its elastic relationship with love, pulled close only to be pinged apart.

Title: Dreaming of Revenge
Review: While not all of King’s attempts to focus her talent into ‘proper songs’ come off, when she nails it, we can’t help but agree with Dave Grohl that she’s one of the greatest guitarists in the world.

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: They'll change your life.

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: If you have a favorite Foghat album or can name a single member of Deep Purple, you will love Broken Boy Soldiers; fortunately, it doesn't end there. [18 May 2006, p.226]

Title: Silent Earthling
Review: Silent Earthling is far from an reinvention: it’s simply Three Trapped Tigers adapting and tinkering with everything that made ‘Route One Or Die’ such an exciting debut, to end up here with a leaner, more focused, brilliant second album.

Title: The Last Spire
Review: The Last Spire, their tenth and last release, combines all that the legends do well: snail-paced doom, upbeat Sabbath stoner rock and craggly sludge.

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: This pragmatic retracing of their heyday is a more than welcome return, an elixir for anyone who's missed the straightforwardly joyful noise of this indisputably seminal act.

Title: Sun
Review: Consider Sun the start of Cat Power's new musical life.

Title: On My Way
Review: It’s Kweller’s lyrics and voice that do it though; joy and melancholy combined to deliver pop as uplifting as Weezer and rock that’s as unsubtle as Kings of Leon, with anti-folk and Merseybeat along for what is a thrill-filled ride.

Title: The Ascension
Review: While Stevens often reaches great heights on The Ascension, he almost as often seems to get lost in his big ideas.

Title: Oshin
Review: In all, a dreamy plunge.

Title: Wheel
Review: Stevenson and her band have been improving in every aspect since their inception, and they've nailed it here on Wheel.

Title: Homosapien
Review: While the tension between live and synthetic elements is interesting to listen to, Homosapien lacks the kind of grand creative spark that's often born from this.

Title: The Boy Who Knew Too Much
Review: Mika's faith in the campy excess of Freddie Mercury/Elton John-style pomp pop is bracing. But over the course of an album, the shtick's charm erodes.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: With their latest album SJDK give the people what they want, even if they didn’t know how much they wanted it.

Title: In the Pit of the Stomach
Review: Suffice to say, the issues addressed here are as big as the music. [Nov. 2011, p. 142]

Title: A Dream Deferred
Review: The production is on point and the rhyme patterns are above average, but there's a distinct lack of cohesion.

Title: Blacklisted
Review: Case continues to refine her mix of alternative-country music and film-noir sensibility on Blacklisted.

Title: Invincible
Review: Invincible is an assembly-line bore.

Title: Wait To Pleasure
Review: This power trio makes no attempt whatsoever to hide their stylistic sonic cathedral. [Jan 2014, p.76]

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: Though it might not be their biggest or best album, The White Stripes might never make a bolder one. [#10, p.114]

Title: Bonxie
Review: Bonxie doesn’t contain too many surprises, and it doesn’t really have many answers to the bigger questions, but it does have a number of brilliantly written songs.

Title: Glow
Review: Content wise, Glow is everything you could want from a dance artist’s debut album. It’s produced well, it’s cheeky in parts, dark and suggestive in others and varied enough in regards to genre.

Title: Flicker
Review: It is hard to get overheated about something so determinedly tepid. And yet, dropped amid the frenzy of pop radio, Horan’s songs are immediately distinctive.

Title: A Wasteland Companion
Review: A Wasteland Companion belies its foreboding title, largely eschewing the hushed introspection that's cast a pall over previous efforts in favor of, well, a sound that's at least marginally more hopeful.

Title: There's a Riot Going On
Review: An album to savor, then, or forget.

Title: In Search of Elusive Little Comets
Review: Don't bet against them lighting up the indie firmament in 2011. [Mar 2011, p.106]

Title: Fortuna
Review: For the most part, Fortuna projects a confidence and self-belief that wasn’t all that perceptible on the rough-hewn Antipodes.

Title: No Shape
Review: With strident chords, spiralling melodies, and a shiver inducing delivery, No Shape might spend a lot of its time searching, but in being open about that the record presents Perfume Genius at his most realised.

Title: Devin Dazzle & the Neon Fever
Review: However, if 'Devin Dazzle And The Neon Fever' proves anything, it proves that Felix knows three years have passed since [Kittenz]. Now he's partying like it's 1984. It's a development of almost comical chutzpah, and it's one that he wears terrifically well.

Title: Microphones in 2020
Review: Intimate, absorbing. [Sep 2020, p.94]

Title: Cansei de Ser Sexy
Review: Cansei de Ser Sexy works not because of its ability to break new musical ground but because of its ability to borrow from other influences and use them in new ways to avoid sounding totally contrived.

Title: Autobiography
Review: [Courtney Love's] American Sweetheart is tragic and blasted and pissed-off and pathetic and desperate and sad; Autobiography is all those things, plus it has Fruit Stripe bubblegrunge guitars and insanely chewy melodies and an ear-tickling production job.

Title: Woman
Review: Halfway in the album starts to stutter like a mirror ball whose motor is on the blink. [Jan 2017, p.106]

Title: It's a Bit Complicated
Review: More so than the debut's, these songs fare like standup comedy on repeated listens: Once the punch lines are spoiled, who wants to listen to a joke again?

Title: Handfuls of Night
Review: Spending a little too long in the shallows of pastel-shaded easy-listening minimalism. That said, there are sublimely beautiful and lightly experimental touches here too. [Dec 2019, p.30]

Title: Less Than Human
Review: Less Than Human is the sound of James Murphy transforming the songs of a guy who has spent a nauseating amount of time fiddling about with Kraftwerk-y synths into an album as enjoyable at home as it is on the dancefloor.

Title: Widow City
Review: Factor in the music’s kitchen-sink vibe--anchored by a Chamberlin keyboard that triggers tape loops of various instruments--and the album is a lot to take in. But the task can be rewarding.

Title: Fishscale
Review: Will certainly stand as one of the best rap albums of the year. [26 Mar 2006]

Title: For All We Know
Review: Nao’s real flair, though, lies in embracing the old school and making it seem fresh. ‘Get To Know Ya’ and ‘DYWM’ both re-rub late ’80s soul and push it firmly into 2016 with crisp production and an effortless dancefloor feeling. More proof, if it were needed, that Nao--and her odd but addictive vocal--belongs up front.

Title: Lateness of Dancers
Review: Full of guest musicians helping to bring his songs to life, this latest record might be a little different to previous Hiss Golden Messenger outings, but it also might be his best.

Title: Stay Home
Review: Every song comes from the same mold that they've been working with from the beginning. And as the critical mass of messy hits continues to pile up, there are new revelations that rise to the surface, as well.

Title: Bubblegum
Review: Clinic have performed a remarkable metamorphosis for the melodic, dreamlike Bubblegum. [Nov. 2010, p. 106]

Title: Back on the Planet
Review: The LP is merely a collection of somewhat compelling, hip-hop-leaning beats that largely go nowhere; it's more like a dressed-up beat tape, and not a particularly exciting one at that.

Title: Showtime
Review: Do NOT approach this as a rap album, or you will be perplexed to no end. This is cerebral, intricate and inventive electronically-based music that is certainly hip-hop in ethic and inspiration, but channelled through a uniquely British conduit, interpreted by one of the more intriguing urban poets of recent times.

Title: Waxing Moon
Review: Bathed in hope and spiritual substance. [Mar 2020, p.93]

Title: DOVE
Review: It sounds, to its considerable credit, very much like the record that might have followed. [Jun 2018, p.24]

Title: Silver Eye
Review: There’s nothing new here, but you know what? That’s more than fine.

Title: 3D
Review: Perhaps 3D doesn't blaze trails like their other albums, but it never plays it safe and it always satisfies, and it's one of the best modern soul albums of 2002.

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: His voice must be heard to be believed. [Apr 2005, p.105]

Title: Change
Review: Change may be audibly bigger-sounding -- in a slick, professional way -- than previous efforts, but the new angle just drives the point home: The Dismemberment Plan deserve to be huge. [Jan 2002, p.82]

Title: NASIR
Review: The writing is so meandering and mechanical that little here feels intentional, even the gaps. And strangely, that’s the bittersweet takeaway: Nas the meticulous observer has been supplanted by Nas the nervous rambler. It doesn’t feel like an accident.

Title: Conor Oberst
Review: Largely, this is the introspective folk rock of Bright Eyes, though there's some welcome shift away from autobiography.

Title: American Idiot
Review: There are several duff tracks, certainly. And, sure, as a whole 'American Idiot' can easily be criticised for its simplistic, occasionally naïve sixth form lyrics, all round pomposity and general adherence to the group's tried and tested formula of punchy three-chord pogo-pop. But it's still a wonderfully entertaining, polemical punk rock record.

Title: Supernova
Review: The resulting arrangements are masterful affairs that frame LaMontagne's material with great taste and flair. [Jul 2014, p.90]

Title: Expect the Best
Review: Overall, Widowspeak sticks to its formula on Expect the Best, doubling down on conviction to a fuller effect. The familiar faded tonality now has punchier, richer hues.

Title: The Resistance
Review: It’s bonkers--hilarious, maddening, ridiculous and slightly shit--yet never dull.

Title: Set You Free
Review: His high-register hiccups convince you he's having more fun than a spring-breaker half his age.

Title: Kid Rock
Review: Song for song, this is better-written and harder-rocking than Cocky.

Title: Invaders Must Die
Review: From the first track through its final seconds, Invaders joylessly stomps through overly familiar territory. It's another lunkheaded, loud mash-up of rock and dance, a sound now so beefed-up and campy that it's perhaps only suitable for shotgunning cheap beer and practicing UFC chokeholds with your pals.

Title: Magnetic Man
Review: Worst of all, it turns out that commercially-minded dubstep is--perhaps inevitably--a much weaker prospect than its club counterpart.

Title: Visions
Review: Visions is marked by a number of characteristics that make up a broad swathe of forgettable, barely-there music-it sounds distant, cheaply produced, with songs that seem to flutter in and out of earshot rather than command attention-but it's executed with such personality, earnestness, and feeling that it feels so much louder and present than it really is.

Title: White Men Are Black Men Too
