Review: Flying Microtonal Banana is occasionally pleasant but mostly pedestrian. If anything, it’s a step back from the experimentation of last year’s fierce Nonagon Infinity.

Title: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood
Review: Shifty Adventures in Nookie Wood sounds like Echo & the Bunnymen or Simple Minds turned loose with an army of 808s and AutoTuners, and when left unwarped by gauzy effects, Cale's vocal delivery is alternately as morose as Joy Division's and as sneering as Nick Cave's.

Title: Family
Review: There's little spark, despite her admirable willingness to take chances. [Nov 3007, p.147]

Title: Pythagorean Dream
Review: There's something more naturally personal about Pythagorean Dream, in the way its multitude of vibrations emanate from Chatham alone.

Title: The Evangelist
Review: As on most Go-Betweens records, the melodies take time to sink in, though not the Grant McLennan legacy retrofitted with a Robert lyric about Grant's affinity for melody.

Title: Simply Grand
Review: Simply Grand is an album whose charms are too subtle to catch on the first spin or third, but enough listens will make it clear that the album's title is nothing more than a statement of fact.

Title: Let It Go
Review: Little here finds McGraw in a feel-good mode.

Title: Desperation
Review: Desperation is as refreshing as it is welcome. [Aug 2013, p.73]

Title: Ma Fleur
Review: It’s not just the recurrent meditations on mortality that makes Ma Fleur even more heart-rendingly beautiful than 2002’s Everyday, it’s also how The Cinematic Orchestra’s new album actually feels.

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: And with so much music, some cuts solidly fail, and some stand up to the best in the Bad Seeds canon.

Title: Leave Me Alone
Review: Leave Me Alone is flawed, but its flaws are what makes it so beguiling.

Title: The Colossus
Review: The multi-genre approach of The Colossus is refreshing.

Title: Lonely Avenue
Review: Both artists are gifted social commentators with a love for snarky, collegiate cynicism that hides a huge sentimental streak.

Title: Superwolf
Review: Frayed, fuzzy and undeniably excellent.

Title: Le Kov
Review: It's clear that she feels strongly about the words she is singing, and she inhabits every song fully. The music, words, and voice come together on Le Kov like fragments of the past put back together and made into a satisfying new whole that works as a lovely tribute to Cornish culture, while also solidifying Gwenno's place as an important artist.

Title: Locus
Review: The tone of Locus is unerringly dark with the repetition and harsh timbres occasionally tilting proceedings into the overly bleak, but there is enough overall nuance to keep the listener engaged for the duration.

Title: V
Review: It's all oddly refreshing, aurally exciting and a whole lotta fun. [Jun 2019, p.94]

925 is a cohesive, enjoyable, drug-infused debut about two longtime friends trying to make sense of being young in a dreary world. Despite a few hiccups, the record is a moody and exciting treat by an act to keep your eyes and ears on.

Title: Songs for the General Public
Review: Each song recalls the essence of a specific segment of '70s pop excellence, with just enough bizarre twists thrown in to keep things interesting.

Title: We Be Xuxa
Review: Here, as elsewhere, there may be subtext and hidden allusions but the important stuff is bouncing around on the surface.

Title: More Fish
Review: It feels somehow safe and experimental, foundational and radical. [Jan 2007, p.110]

Title: All in One
Review: Here the daughter of bossa nova creator Joao Gilberto has made an album that either drowns in its own sensuousness and sentimentality.

Title: What Will We Be
Review: For every throughly relised composition, there is a meandering fragment, great only as far as it goes. [Nov 2009, p.90]

Title: Jackinabox
Review: Sweet, vibrant and sunny songs with just as much invention and passion as 2000's buzz-building early EPs.

Title: Trouble in Paradise
Review: This polished set is pure aural candy from front-to-back and firmly re-establishes Jackson as one of Britain’s premier pop talents.

Title: III
Review: III's hazy, after-hours vibe is infectious, and these songs reveal fresh nuance with repeat listens.

Title: Poor David's Almanack
Review: That old-time, good-time vibe can occasionally dip into hokeyness, as the album title signals, but slow numbers like "Lindsey Button" and "Put 'Em Up Solid" are where the group excels. [Sep 2017, p.28]

Title: You Can't Imagine How Much Fun We're Having
Review: You Can't Imagine How Much Fun We're Having is proof that even in the world of indie hip-hop, you don't need to make a statement album to make a solid album.

Title: ENERGY
Review: Disclosure have always had an attention to detail in their production that gives the songs that much more depth, be it the irresistible breakdown one minute from the end of Douha (Mali Mali) or the fluttering arpeggios that populate closing track Reverie. And in this respect, as well as songwriting, structure and guest selection, they’re back like they never left.

Title: Shadows and Reflections
Review: Tunes like Burt Bacharach's "blue On Blue" and The Young Rascals' "How Can I Be Sure" are perfect for Almond's pirouetting croon. [Oct 2017, p.23]

Title: The Plain Where The Palace Stood
Review: The results, though often feeling abrupt and sometimes overly academic, are mostly warm and curious, stretching out in eternal open-endedness that isn't really looking for answers or understandable conclusions.

Title: System
Review: A brave, if samey, affair, System is undoubtedly sincere.

Title: 10 Futures
Review: 10 Futures may sound like a collection of individual tracks on the surface, but the more you listen the more it all begins to make sense.

Title: Lavender
Review: Musically, it’s a soothing sound--think Imogen Heap, Regina Spektor, Laura Marling and Tori Amos--that without attentive listening could be mistaken for a pleasant enough electronic-pop record. However, in Half Waif’s quest for some kind of calmness they’ve actually made an album that, inwardly, burns furiously.

Title: Clap Your Hands Say Yeah
Review: Sadly, [Ounsworth's] lyrics are a letdown.... When the tunes are this good, it certainly feels like a wasted opportunity.

Artist: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
Title: Planetarium
Review: Although overly padded and repetitious at times, Planetarium is a poignant, adventurous, and highly promising debut; if the quartet can trim the fat in the future, they’ll truly reach their potential.

Title: Scream
Review: Despite the occasional misstep, Scream shows that the bandmembers are ready and able to embrace their growing abilities.

Title: Oh My My
Review: Overall, Oh My My is another solid record from a group led by one of the best songwriters of a generation.

Title: Planet Pit
Review: He still enjoys bouncing his gruff voice off tropical beats, a vocal conguero, but all those 4x4 stomps from the Continent give him fewer opportunities to do so.

Title: Carried to Dust
Review: The band bring the tang of that elsewhere pop back to Carried to Dust, however, planting big-hook sensibility and the willingness to evolve within its Southwestern mood pieces.

Title: The Smell of Our Own
Review: The album almost sounds like an original cast recording of a musical -- the next best thing to being there, but not the same by a long shot.

Title: That's Your Lot
Review: Their debut LP serves as an impressive case for why--a mingling of youthful bombast and strikingly mature ambition, the songs here are anthemic, introspective, delightful. [Jun 2017, p.102]

Title: Holly
Review: With Holly, Waterhouse really comes into his own, branding himself as a retro crossover crooner whose immediate intent appears intended to instigate a ‘60s soul revival.

Title: Taking Back Sunday
Review: Anyone worried that the last decade had dulled TBS' edge, a listen to the post-hardcore rager "El Paso" confirms that it's never been sharper.

Title: For Use and Delight
Review: For Use And Delight is by turns plaintive and rocking, a wistful rhythmic journey into a band's true beating heart. [Nov 2015, p.90]

Title: Wallop
Review: An ass-shaking blend of disco, house, '80s pop with apparent self-awareness. [Oct 2019, p.92]

Title: Here in the Deep
Review: A mightily approachable and sometimes even fun album. [Nov 2015, p.88]

Title: Let England Shake
Review: Harvey doesn't preach, she merely describes, the lilting voice and the light melodies creating a surreal backdrop for mayhem.

Title: Drip or Drown 2
Review: Ultimately, Gunna sticks to his guns and delivers a solid effort that lives up to all the hype. He may not be the most innovative MC, but he continues to craft great bodies of work, which is what will cement his career, at the end of the day.

Title: Apocalyptic Love
Review: This one is cohesive and feels like a band affair, feels like an album, feels like it has the chemistry Velvet Revolver frustratingly didn't quite have but a certain other band had once upon a time when Slash was in that crew.

Title: ACCA
Review: The album is diverse: lovers rock meets gospel hymnals and Parisian waltz-dirges. [Feb 2020, p.94]

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Forgiveness Rock Record doesn't provide anything interesting to talk about in and of itself. Its actual thematic talking points, as far as I can tell, tend toward political pedantry.
This is an album that rings with the honed precision and craftsmanship of a job thoroughly done.

Title: The Lookout
Review: The Lookout certainly offers nothing that can't be immediately pegged as a Laura Veirs track. That doesn't have to be a bad thing. The joy of returning to an artist like Veirs comes in the subtle variation.

Title: The Epic
Review: This is wonderful stuff.

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: Tie on the celebrity blindfold, and Broken Boy Soldiers no longer seems like that much of an achievement-- just another case of men recreating their favorite vinyl deep cuts, if a bit more skillfully than most FM scrapbookers.

Title: Carrier
Review: It is among The Dodos’ best work--Carrier is a fitting eulogy.

Title: Barbara
Review: Barbara shows that We Are Scientists know what works for them, and even if it never quite breaks the barrier between pleasant and great, it's almost always enjoyable.

Title: The Golden Mile
Review: Ultimately, on the strength of The Golden Mile, the longevity of The Peth seems, at best, questionable.

Title: OLD
Review: Old is Brown’s best work. Complex beyond its two-sided structure, it is filled with narratives that collide, sentiments that conflict and resolutions that come to nothing.

Title: Lisbon
Review: Lisbon, like the rest of their music, is meant to be savored, the fullness of its songs allowed to develop over many listens.

Title: Delirium
Review: Ultimately, it's the unexpectedly appealing combination of Goulding's distinctive voice and the melismatic R&B bent of the songs on Delirium that makes for such an ecstatic listen.

Title: Last Place
Review: It’s beautiful and utterly captivating in its own way and, after all the band and Lytle have been through, that’s triumphant enough.

Title: Midnite Vultures
Review: Midnite Vultues kind of sounds like an album Prince would have made if he were more interested in being a geek than carressing his own ego.

Title: PLECTRUMELECTRUM
Review: The sound of him working with a lean combo is so refreshing, and a welcome first in his mammoth catalogue. [Nov 2014, p.107]

Title: i,i
Review: He's always taking a big swing. That alone is worth celebrating, but when he hits the mix right on i,i, all of these high-minded thoughts go out the window, and Bon Iver rises to something truly inspiring.

Title: Locked Down
Review: John has always had that deep gruff rasp, but backed by raw swamp boogie with lots of baritone sax, creepy female backing vocals and treated keyboards, he's sounding as dangerous and spooky as when laying down the gris-gris on "I Walk on Gilded Splinters" back in 1968.

Title: Contact
Review: The eight pieces here function as a drummer’s showcase, certainly, but Contact’s wilful limitations conceal an eclectic approach. ... Time spent immersed in Contact will reap reward. [May 2020, p.52]

Title: Heaven
Review: Their most consistent and accomplished album to date.

Title: Master of My Make-Believe
Review: There's a subdued, mid-paced feel to it, too, and this sense of somehow sad restraint holds it back from greatness.

Title: Weird
Review: Veering through infectious reflexions on self-imposed domestic isolation (“Staying In”), being contentedly single (“It’s So Weird”), confectionary-addiction (“Sugar”), rampant life commodification (“Everything’s For Sale”), the fake news-mired polity (“Paid To Lie”), personal body and space dishevelment (“Broken Doll”), these are some of the most consistently likeable Hatfield cuts of recent times.

Title: A Dream Outside
Review: This is savvy, intelligent music.

Title: All the Lost Souls
Review: Too much of All the Lost Souls is just pleasant ether, with Blunt showing a gift for drabness on forgettable ballads that make Coldplay seem like the Arctic Monkeys.

Title: Don't Wait Up
Review: This is a farewell album, but the band are going out at full strength. [Jun 2014, p.104]

Title: Satan's Circus
Review: Their most challenging record to date. [Nov 2004, p.102]

Title: Be Good
Review: The singing is immaculate all the way through, and there's plenty of blowing space from some dynamic improvisers, notably saxophonists Yosuke Sato and Tivon Pennicott.

Title: Eighteen Hours of Static
Review: A collection of astounding anthems for a new tomorrow, made by the disaffected youth of today.

Title: T R O U B L E
Review: The songs are stronger than ever, and the production remains recognisably the work of Hamilton’s hand.

Title: Shiver
Review: The parts of Shiver that strain to be fun and fresh can’t seem to break orbit from the grandiose mass of Sigur Rós, and the album leaves a sense of oppressive profundity in its bulky wake.

Title: LAHS
Review: Still relaxed, LAHS clouds over with less reverb, punchier drums, and – at long last – vocals at the front of the mix.

Title: Hey Everyone
Review: Everyone will find something appealing about Dananananaykroyd, no matter how small, but it’s difficult to imagine anyone truly loving this record, regardless of whether they judge it by its cover.

Title: Charlatans at the Garden Gate
Review: Her addictive debut is full of such moments: catchy refrains with multiple meanings, ear-tugging melodies with hidden hooks.

Title: Red Letter Days
Review: It's a strong effort, probably the kid's best thus far, and Dad should be proud.

Title: Remedy
Review: Like Old Crown's best stuff, it evokes a time our of mind. [Sep 2014, p.112]

Title: Recess
Review: There are almost no redeeming qualities to be found here, and the whole thing is shamelessly derivative, thoroughly lacking in any sort of creativity, and (worst of all) a logical point in Skrillex’s career arc, one which has been pointing downhill ever since 2010. Listen at your own risk.

Title: These Are the Vistas
Review: Amidst all the fun is a dynamic record that holds your attention.

Title: Fever to Tell
Review: Tefloning the lo-fi clang of their 2001, self-titled indie EP breakthrough with Interscope's sugar Daddy Warbucks, Fever to Tell sounds like a tenement rolling, garbage cans bashing some helpless gutter rat.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: A dystopian, focused pessimism that sounds (unfortunately) exactly like the world outside, but doesn’t sound quite like another band on the planet. A perfect soundtrack to nagging doubts and creeping realisations.

Title: Playing the Angel
Review: Like the best Depeche Mode, almost everything on the album will make an initial wowing impact while remaining layered enough in subtle details to surprise and thrill with repeated listens.

Title: Get What You Give
Review: The Ghost Inside do little to variate on the established metalcore sonic, even though they play that sonic well.

Title: Bestial Burden
Review: Bestial Burden works because of its methodical execution--a calculated piece of catharsis that towers over all other bedroom power electronics tape-peddlers. [No. 114, p.59]

Title: Empire
Review: Empire constantly changes its focus. [Oct 2006, p.99]

Title: Aventine
Review: A little string-plucking, some groaning cello and the odd beat adorn Obel's tightly focused set of songs, which approximate the sound of snow falling on a disused chapel while a solitary candle burns inside.

Title: Replica
Review: The voices on Oneohtrix Point Never's new album, Replica , were sampled from 1980s television commercials, an amusing sidelight for an album that is anything but crass and insistent (despite a track called "Power of Persuasion").

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: A guilty pleasure.

Title: Changed
Review: Changed marches to a deliberate beat, the tempos shifting only slightly when things get either insistent or gentle, the group layering its harmonies heavily on both the soft and loud numbers, giving every cut a candied gloss.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: This is the kind of bedroom folk pop E's done prettier--and weirder--before. [Jul 2003, p.111]

Title: Heavier Things
Review: Like [Norah] Jones, Mayer never lets his personality talk over his elegant melodies, but unlike her, he has range. [Oct 2003, p.112]

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: With Father, Son, Holy Ghost's exquisite, beyond-indie melodies, arrangements, and musicianship (the playful "Magic," the elegant "Just a Song," the fiery "Die"), he [Christopher Owens] and bassist-producer JR White flirt with perfection.

Title: The Fool
Review: Instead of utilizing the talented crew’s many particular strengths to create a unique and unified sound, The Fool comes out feeling like nobody in particular and everyone at once.

Title: Hairdresser Blues
Review: Whereas Too Young to Be in Love was the excited doodles of a crush's name in a notebook, Hairdresser Blues is the discarding of the love letters that came after.

Title: This Is Alphabeat
Review: While the first half of the album is more eclectic, the second half is just as groovy although less varied. Unlike bands like The Maccabees, The Kooks and The Wombats, the album holds up all the way through, never repeating the same formula song after song.

Title: Storm Damage
Review: It finds him in a reflective mood. It's a smart musical move, because Storm Damage showcases what a good lyricist he is. [Mar 2020, p.86]

Title: The Witch
Review: Here is an album that embraces every fibre of your being; generous in its awe-inspiring and beautiful moments. It’ll keep you guessing every minute of its hour long run. It’s uniquely Pumarosa and there’s nothing else quite like it.

Title: A Mineral Love
Review: His most intricate album to date, A Mineral Love is delicately constructed like tiny cells of a flower.

Title: 100 Lovers
Review: Devotchka has at least found a way to continue making tuneful, relatively entertaining music, as their contemporaries either verge on self-parody or have given up altogether. But nothing about 100 Lovers suggests anything more than another attempt to break even.

Title: Boy in da Corner
Review: When Dizzee thinks very deeply--worrying about growing up, about those around him who won't grow up, about dying before he grows up--he sounds like, what else can we call it, the real thing.

Title: Communion
Review: Too often their light touch turns lightweight, even wan.

Title: Hour of the Dawn
Review: Establishing her forceful new identity from the start, Goodman makes music with an infectious enthusiasm.

Title: Vanitas
Review: There is a catchiness to the song structures that occasionally brushes against an industrial influence.

Title: Devil's Night
Review: It's very difficult to see the tough-talking Devils Night as anything other than a slightly tweaked re-run of The Marshall Mathers LP. [#180, p.100]

Title: Music from Another Dimension!
Review: This then is an album that doesn't quite work, being as it is constantly in a state of conflict.

Title: Grave of a Dog
Review: Hayter brilliantly conjures atmosphere, but could perhaps hone some more arresting melodic progressions like her lament on Kingscorpse. It is Walker’s voice, blasted beyond melody into pure ranting expression, that seals the record’s strongest moments.

Title: The State of Things
Review: Things may go awry on He Said He Loved Me, where comedy Essex girls cheep-cheep the grating refrain, but as an updated take on the Specials' equal disgust and infatuation with urban life, it's impressive.

Title: Kinshasa One Two
Review: The music here definitely works best when this spirit of interaction is at the forefront, with potentially disparate musical ideas serving to complement and enhance each other.

Title: Title
Review: Aside from an understandable naivete, Trainor's weaknesses are her stylistic cherry-picking and her compulsion to appear adorably relatable and socially correct all at once.

Title: Swim
Review: Swim is quite dark; this is definitely pop of the bedroom sort, and despite Snaith's vocals usually being indecipherable, buried underneath hissing drum machines and meretricious synths, there's a pervading sense of intimacy to the whole thing.

Title: Tahoe
Review: Tahoe is a record for after the fall, after the collapse, a compulsive soundtrack for an age that is both post-natural and post-virtual. [Mar 218, p.46]

Title: I Get Wet
Review: Instead of rehashing rap and rock, he smashes up pop melodies, metal riffs and industrial beats with a hammer, creating something that teeters on parody yet heralds an enthusiastic return to the days when hair metal knew how to get the crowds loaded. [Apr 2002, p.65]

Title: Recording a Tape the Colour of the Light
Review: Recording's musical vignettes display equal parts languor and incitement. [#11, p.105]

Title: Ride Me Back Home
Review: The whole album encompasses issues dear to his heart.

Title: Jeff Bridges
Review: If you're a fan of Burnett's sound or just plain curious you'll find this a welcome project that does exactly what it sets out to do.

Title: Blondes
Review: The results, all shimmering synths and echo effects noodle along on 4/4, often for the best part of seven minutes, and we can't help but feel that some of this has been done before.

Title: Myth Takes
Review: Myth Takes is a record that's tough not to enjoy, even while you're wondering if you shouldn't.

Title: Non-Believers
Review: Whether you’re into it or not, it’s hard to discredit the remarkable solidness of the album, which, against most preconceptions, exists far outside the world of Superchunk. It’s everything a side project should be.

Title: Scale
Review: If Dani appeared on a few less tracks here, Scale may have been one of the year's finest.

Title: This Way
Review: It's her first genuine step forward... probably the best record she has cut to date.

Title: The Money Store
Review: A soup of electronic interference, exhausting percussion and smothering bass-cloud. It's stultifying like a bad case of screen fatigue; tangled and sparking - the sound of frazzled, short-fusing nerve ends.

Title: Valley Tangents
Review: The reality is that Valley Tangents just sort of floats by as background music even whilst actively listening.

Title: Rave Tapes
Review: Rave Tapes may not see them moving too far from their widescreen template but it’s an assured record that sees them draw from right across their rich palette of textures.

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: While the album has its awkward moments, there are enough slinkily wonderful tunes, gleeful beats and miments of genuine tenderness to make Skinner's transformation not just convincing but also really rather lovely. [Oct 2008, p.100]

Title: Lonely Avenue
Review: It has to be said that, considering how Nick Hornby is credited with writing all of the lyrics here, the usual Ben Folds key words are present and there's only so much 'bastard', 'shit' and 'fucking' I can take. Despite this concern, as well as being Folds' most musically accomplished outing since going solo, it does feature the magnificent phrase, "some guy on the net thinks I suck and he should know; he's got his own blog."

Title: America's Sweetheart
Review: ‘America’s Sweetheart’ throbs, chugs, thunders, blasts, romps, rants and rocks.

Title: In the Cool of the Day
Review: In the Cool of the Day is far from perfect, though. Moore's smooth vocal delivery suits the more minimal productions well, but it can become cloying when the backing track is too upbeat, such as on the irritating Up Above My Head.

Title: Electric Lines
Review: Home and Lose Your Love are pleasant, if earthbound, disco-house tracks bolstered by cut-and-shut samples of Brainstorm’s We’re on Our Way Home and the Emotions’ I Don’t Wanna Lose Your Love. But Truth Is Light is UK garage on non-alcoholic cava, and the dance tracks, with their interminable cosmic arpeggiation, have less poke than a 1980s hand-dryer.

Title: Confection
Review: It feels like a very French-pop-star gesture, extravagant and essentially useless, and perversely enjoyable for exactly those reasons.

Title: Trans-Love Energies
Review: It's clear that Trans Love Energies has been a long time in the making, but Fearless has managed to make it sound like a fresh piece of work.

Title: Iradelphic
Review: An album of solemn splendor, as exquisite as it is emotionally direct, grounded in jazz rhythms and an acoustic guitar.

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: This disc is pure Stewart - urgent, visceral electro-protest for the 21st century. [No. 85, p.59]

Title: Songs for Silverman
Review: The trouble with most songs on the album, even after several listens, is you'll be hard pressed to recall the melodies. [#10, p.110]

Title: Raskit
Review: It certainly won't spawn four number one U.K. pop hits the way his platinum-selling fourth album, Tongue N' Cheek, did, but it's a necessary re-evaluation and re-focus of his talents, and proves that he's far from finished.

Title: Always Outnumbered, Never Outgunned
Review: For all its sonic sizzle, Prodigy's fourth album feels frustrated. [Oct 2004, p.113]

Title: King Animal
Review: The group's first album since 1996 just sounds like the one they would've churned out in 1998.

Title: Ma
Review: While many of the songs on Ma offer serious meditations about what life is all about, Banhart understands the importance of both joy and pain.

Title: Shedding Skin
Review: Shedding Skin is a bold move for an artist so associated with a different sonic cadence, and kudos to Ejimiwe for trying to artistically reposition himself. Ultimately though, I would have liked to have heard more of an evolution rather than a complete metamorphosis from him.

Title: Settle
Review: A pop album brimming with imagination, vibrant melodies and, yes, a fair bit of formula.

Title: The Real New Fall LP (Formerly Country on the Click)
Review: Positively stomps and bristles, with Smith and his band summoning up the type of chutzpah not normally found in middle age.

Title: The Meadowlands
Review: The Meadowlands represents an impressive triumph of persistence over talent. [Oct 2005, p.121]

Title: American Gong
Review: The combination of this 'throwback to '96' sound with confident restraint, and that Quasi have already proven themselves to the die-hards, I'm going to call this timeless underdoggery.

Title: Tied to a Star
Review: J's mature-era peak continues. [Sep 2014, p.90]

Title: Fight Softly
Review: It may lack enough heavy hitters to equal the sucess of "Merriweather Post Pavilion," yet the aptly named McPhun has created a Technicolor, synapse-tickling delight. [Apr 2010, p.119]

Title: Providence
Review: It's not an altogether bad record and it ends on a bright note with two of its best cuts -- "Bad Advice" and "Deliver It" -- but for all of its amiable intentions, it comes across as short on personality.

Title: Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends
Review: Viva La Vida still manages to seem downsized compared to the band's gradiose early work. [July 2008, p.69]

Title: Clearing The Path To Ascend
Review: It’s a stealth band, working on the rack of riff and repetition, moving slowly toward loud, intense, orange-sky beauty.

Title: Chris Dave and the Drumhedz
Review: Keyboardist Cleo Sample and singer/songwriter Kendra Foster are among the variable cast that joins that trio, so the set unsurprisingly has the densely layered, spaced-out, and fiery qualities of D'Angelo's Black Messiah.

Title: Fishscale
Review: Ghost's Fishscale is the most creative album to come out of New York hiphop since his own 2000  Supreme Clientele.

Title: Wild Flag
Review: Considering the personnel involved, it's no surprise Wild Flag works as well as it does, or that it picks up in a familiar place. It's just nice when a super-group actually lives up to the title.
This is merely designed to please the diehards... if anybody else happens to like it or if it stumbles into a hit, that's merely a bonus.

Title: Latin
Review: The result is an absolute monster of a closing track that caps a seductively repeatable album, which speaks miles to the effort on Holy Fuck's strongest album to date.

Title: Good News For People Who Love Bad News
Review: A lot of major label-imposed ideas, like rhythm guitar and a heartbreakingly conventional new bass sound, combine to utterly ruin the record's first half. If you can make it through to News' innards, however, an EP's worth of something like better-recorded, more thought-out Lonesome Crowded West material awaits.

Title: Emperor of Sand
Review: Mastodon have written the most personal album of their career, and in doing so perhaps their most pertinent too.

Title: Nepenthe
Review: While it may be a tremendously personal album for Barwick, you can get lost in Nepenthe for not only its sheer beauty, but for its ability to evoke visual cues and tell stories with its music.

Title: We Get By
Review: Staples's fire is undiminished. [Jul 2019, p.114]

Title: Discovery of a World Inside the Moone
Review: For, as derivative and daft as The Apples are, it's impossible, like a scowling adolescent laughing at the antics of his irritating kid brother, to hate them.

Title: Revolutions
Review: Too many forgettable concoctions make this just another so-so DJ mix. [10 Jun 2004, p.91]

Title: The Errant Charm
Review: Unlike previous Vetiver albums, for The Errant Charm, songwriter Andy Cabic entered the studio with vague ideas rather than finished songs, and it shows.

Title: Shadows
Review: Shadows is a touch too twee at times, but more often, it impresses with its understated elegance and classically constructed melodies.

Title: Lamp Lit Prose
Review: A step forward into what lies ahead for Dirty Projectors rather than the complete self-immolation of its previous attempt. It seems, however, that while Longstreth has indeed found a 'Break-Thru' he still has some way to go if he's to return to his former glories which, perhaps, are now unobtainable.

Title: West Coast Highway Cosmic
Review: Mariani's ear for melody lifts it above the ordinary. ... Terrific. [Jun 2020, p.86]

Title: HYMNS
Review: In the end, Hymns is quite a listless journey.

Review: It’s conservative enough to satiate longtime fans, yet lovingly crafted to such a degree that it confuses you into thinking that its reached its full potential when it could've been so much more.

Title: Mind Bokeh
Review: Although Mind Bokeh can be expected to be a wilfully eclectic pick'n'mix affair, what he's actually going to pull out the bag can still surprise.

Title: The Ghost Who Walks
Review: Each composition is fleshed out as well as it can be, the end result still a kind of Appalachian wallpaper music that after further inspection and subsequent listens, leaves the record sounding much more flimsy than urgent. What impression it leaves doesn't last.

Title: I Phantom
Review: An album of flashing wit and giddy ambition. [Oct 2002, p.110]

Title: Thunder, Lightning, Strike
Review: I defy anyone not to seep happiness through the pores of their skin once in possession of this record.

Title: Persona
Review: This is an album that could have been recorded by any dance artist. There is very little of the personality that made Queen Latifah a star.

Title: Ravedeath, 1972
Review: It has many of the same sounds and instruments he relies upon-mauled pianos, organs, and guitars, mostly-but the way they're structured within the songs and as part of the whole are new. The record seems to have no center, no shining single moment, no climax or vortex. Instead it hovers lightly but ominously, like the notes in the songs themselves, hanging in midair without ever dropping to the floor.

Title: Celestial Lineage
Review: Celestial Lineage feels like the contemporary American scene's defining statement after San Francisco group Weakling's seminal 2000 offering Dead As Dreams.

Title: Sab Se Purani Bab
Review: Yoshimi’s mesh of voices is sometimes overpowering, although, as with Björk, that feeling of overpowerment is part of the deal, constructed to bring the listener to a place that feels like the edge of something--the singer’s endurance; the listener’s understanding--only to push them over into somewhere else entirely. [Nov 2017, p.61]

Title: In The Dark
Review: On In the Dark the band has paired its roadworthiness with greater ingenuity, and it finally feels like a fuse has been lit.

Title: Sinners Never Sleep
Review: For a record that could've gone in one of two directions, it manages the neat trick of going in both.

Title: Volume Two
Review: She plays the dewy-eyed ingénue a bit too faithfully at times, but there is no denying her legitimacy as a tunesmith, divvying her set between bouncy piano-pop, folk-flavored sing-alongs and orchestral anthems.

Title: Mulberry Violence
Review: Mulberry Violence isn’t ugly music by any stretch--all of the bleeding, shrieking noises are undergirded by rich chords, and Powers drops little moments of untouched beauty for us to get our breath.

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: Despite the occasional flashes of brilliance, Codes and Keys often feels like a half assed attempt at innovation.

Title: 1372 Overton Park
Review: With 1372 Overton Park, the walls of guitars are still there, but there’s also a Memphis horn section, female backing vocals, plentiful lead guitar, piano, a few sensitive ballads, and plenty of southern hip swagger. And oh what a difference those things make, without losing the sense that this is still a Lucero record in the best sense of the word.

Title: The Big Roar
Review: The Big Roar is the kind of epic-yet-intimate debut that does exactly what its title makes out in the most tactful of styles; an LP that ultimately delivers on every count on the four years of promise leading up to it.

Title: Hall of Fame
Review: Floating in a world over-saturated with hip-hop cliches, it’s not that the Detroit rapper doesn’t set himself apart from the rest of the genre’s newest, youngest and best MCs with these 15 tracks (18 for you deluxe edition fans), it’s just that he doesn’t set himself apart enough.

Title: A Lesson Unlearnt
Review: The variety of genres synthesised to generate this finished record show that they have absorbed life's lessons and reconstituted them to suit a unique outlook. The effect is a strangely familiar, yet singularly arranged thread of consciousness.

Title: Visions
Review: There's no doubt that Visions is an excellent album.

Title: The Fine Art of Self Destruction
Review: Rich in heart-rending beauty, tough-but-lovable gutter poetry, and plenty of genuine emotion.

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: For an album that, like every other Modest Mouse album, rattles on at an extended length, Strangers to Ourselves can desperately afford to trim the fat.

Title: Love Letter
Review: Kelly's default mode throughout Love Letter is needy like a Salvation Army bell-ringer.

Title: With Love
Review: Aside from its sheer heft, though, it's hard to imagine it converting anyone who doesn't already care.

Title: Before Today
Review: Pink has an amazing ability to surprise and does so again and again on Before Today.

Title: I Speak Because I Can
Review: I Speak Because I Can feels more professional than its predecessor, yet the album as a whole fails to capture the emotional power of Alas, I Cannot Swim.

Title: The Night Chancers
Review: Six albums in, Baxter Dury has realised a sound and lyrical approach that is unmistakably his alone. [May 2020, p.101]

Title: Do Hollywood
Review: At their best, they are capable of creating songs that take off like jet planes at dusk ("Hi+Lo"), strut wobbly like Paul Williams on a bender ("I Wanna Prove to You"), and hit the perfect spot between heartbreakingly sweet and just plain odd.

Title: Hearts
Review: Swedes channel shoegaze on strangely beautiful debut. [Sept. 2011, p. 113]

Title: Rainbow
Review: By slyly alternating between these two extremes throughout Rainbow, Kesha winds up with a comeback that's fully realized emotionally and musically.

Title: 24 Karat Gold: Songs From The Vault
Review: Unfortunately, 24 Karat is stuffed with too many stately piano-and-guitar ballads that return to the same theme of bygone romance.

Title: The Obliterati
Review: As the price of success, The Obliterati faces significantly higher expectations. Once again, though, Burma succeeds and surprises by playing to its strengths while moving forward.

Title: Process
Review: Process is a moving, musical autobiography of futuristic, soulful electronica and brittle r’n’b.

Title: Snowdonia
Review: Employing many of the same recording techniques that he used on Astro Coast, Pitts and company have come up with by far their best record since then. Sure, nothing here is as instantly memorable as "Swim" or "Take it Easy," but much of the material here could've passed as Astro Coast outtakes, albeit with a more mature spin.

Title: You Make Me Feel
Review: Don Bryant's third full-length LP You Make Me Feel is one that does just that. Feel the opening salvo of horns and salvation on "Your Love Is to Blame", soul-fired straight-right to the frontal lobe, the first of a one-two opening combination. The Octogenarian is laying down some of the hottest soul and blues on the planet.

Title: Un Dia
Review: Un Día's repetitions reward repeated listening; Molina's cascading, joyous vocals and clattering rhythms - on numbers such as 'Vive Solo,' 'Los Hongos De Marosa' and 'Dar (Qué Difícil)'--define a quirky and decidedly non-European sound.

Title: Dead Media
Review: It begins to wilt with tedium as it continues, as the drum machines and synthesizers give way to unimaginative organic instrumentation and bland, stale melodies.

Title: Silver Dollar Moment
Review: Silver Dollar Moment is a stunning debut, and if it doesn't quite reinvent the wheel the way that The Stone Roses did, it does have a uniquely sweet spirit and lighthearted beauty all its own.

Title: ORO: Opus Primum
Review: Italian doom merchants "Mammoth UFO"... can't duplicate the tight encapsulation of 2010 origin story Eve in 51 minutes, although 14-minute lunar landing "Empireum" could power Alien craft Nostromo.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: We’ve only got eight tracks here, about twenty or so minutes of music, but not a second of it is wasted, and just about every moment is brilliant.

Title: English Graffiti
Review: Whenever thoughts here turn to love, the results are not pretty.... But when antipathy rules, things go with a fizzy enthusiasm that’s quite infectious.

Title: Spiritual Mental Physical
Review: As a stand-alone collection though, it's vexingly stunted, and padded out with a few unnecessary additions to fill out its barely 30-minute run time.

Title: Oshin
Review: Its performances over the past year have generated much anticipation for DIIV's debut full-length, but Oshin doesn't connect the same way. [No.89, p.53]

Title: Annabel Dream Reader
Review: Annabel Dream Reader feels like the soundtrack to a Tarantino film.

Title: Good Luck, Seeker
Review: He continues to show why he’s been one of the best songwriters in the past four decades and again, despite what at times feels like a curious mix, he delivers the kind of gems that only he can.

Title: A Pill For Loneliness
Review: A Pill for Loneliness is another strong effort from City and Colour. It finds Green continuing to play to his strengths and continuing to move City and Colour's sound into new territory at an assured, steady pace.

Title: Future Me Hates Me
Review: Future Me Hates Me is more than proof that she and her bandmates made the right choice on refocusing their musical concerns--and it’s an absolute thrill to think about where this young band will take their talent next.

Title: How Do You Do
Review: His major-label follow-up wisely keeps the retro aesthetic.

Title: Going Down In History
Review: Going Down in History may not mark a sea change for Langford and company, but between the humor, the honky-tonk, and the affable, full-bodied sound, it’s an awesome chance to catch up.

Title: Moment Bends
Review: Overall Moment Bends is a return to form, if not quite as inspired as Architecture in Helsinki's best moments.

Title: Traveling Alone
Review: Traveling Alone is an eleven track collection that speaks to Merritt's vision and outlook.

Title: Soft Spot
Review: There's a melancholy at this music's core that Barzelay successfully resists by generally attempting to understand someone else's feelings rather than expressing his own.

Title: Beta Love
Review: The band's decision to eschew their trademark orchestration in favour of a more synth-driven sound was, sadly, a mistake.

Title: New Moon
Review: For now, though, New Moon stands as it is: a homey, gut-warming batch of tunes that erratically juggle nostalgia, craft, and ass-kicking abandon.

Title: Black and White
Review: It's performance, too, and about the dance of the music as much as words. When these align, his is a voice that sounds vital. But while Black and White is undoubtedly a relevant album to 2011, it's not always a good one.

Title: Underclass Hero
Review: Underclass Hero is a perfectly workable North American punk rock album. It’s got melodic suss and a snotty attitude to its credit, but not much else.

Title: For Use and Delight
Review: Lead guitarist Sean Thompson displays precocious virtuosity through For Use And Delight, spinning out bent-note filigrees that recall the work of his legendary namesake. [Nov 2015, p.81]

Title: Vapor City
Review: On paper Vapor City looked like Stewart’s descent into a sump of his own pompousness; in reality it’s anything but.

Title: Annabel Dream Reader
Review: The best tracks, like Burn Out The Bruise and Wire Frame Mattress, possess the lyrical degradation and sludgy rhythms of the early grunge ethos, if being tossed around with the surfing-a-graveyard sounds of L.A. antecedents from right before grunge, notably the Flesheaters and the Gun Club.

Title: Ego Trippin'
Review: "Why Did You Leave Me' and 'Can't Say Goodbye' are some grown-up songs, and Snoop probably has a whole album of them somewhere in him. But as long as the pothead-pimp shtick keeps selling, we'll probably never hear it.

Title: The Terror
Review: By facing down the exhausting nature of depression and loneliness (seriously, Coyne sounds so depleted that he can barely muster the dejection to sing, and yes, that's a compliment), the Lips have retroactively strengthened their entire artistic credo.

Title: Nursing Home
Review: If debut In The Court Of The Wrestling Let's was the giddy spin of a colour wheel, then Nursing Home feels ever so slightly more unified in tone and shade, and, if not exactly refined, than certainly a little tighter and more focused in its abandon.

Title: Ripe
Review: The twelve songs here drip with coatings of sentiment and sparkly instrumentation that are saccharine and plastic.

Title: The Stand-In
Review: Though some of the good-girl-gone-bad shtick has been sacrificed on the altar of go-for-it jangly pop, she's still as good as it gets when she finally opens her pipes on "Dallas".

Title: Couples
Review: The moody disco on Couples is both sleeker and spookier than the sexed-up indie rock of th Blondes' promising 2006 debut, "Someone to Drive You Home."

Title: Songs and Other Things
Review: Most of the 14 songs work as moments or hooks rather than as complete creations, suggesting the Verlaine coffee commercial may yet be upon us.

Title: Encore
Review: Like most DJ albums, unfortunately, Encore does little with its A-list guests.

Title: Cheap Queen
Review: At times, things feel in danger of being middle of the road, but that's made up for by heavenly moments and voice-of-a-generation lyrcs already drawing comparisons with Lorde. [Dec 2019, p.110]

Title: Dead Reckoning
Review: Dead Reckoning deserves to be heard by anyone with an interest in the ongoing evolution of rock music, or the darker side of the folk songbook, or just great songs played with power and conviction.

Title: Surgery
Review: Even when easing off the throttle, The Warlocks find ways to blow your mind. [10 Sep 2005, p.66]

Title: Sleeping on Roads
Review: It certainly doesn't sound that much different from a Mojave 3 record, if not quite as excellent due to the less than prime quality of some of the songs.

Title: Decoration Day
Review: The album boasts a handful of crowd-pleasing, party-starting cuts.... Yet more common are moments of startling beauty... and heavy doses of recrimination and regret.

Title: In Times
Review: We’ve got some Black Metal Muzak here, competent musically but too timid to go into the depths, emotional, musical or otherwise, that black metal should strive for.

Title: Ten
Review: As rap, this hardly registers. As political commentary, it’s too obtuse to make much impact. But as eclectic, genre-bending music with an ear for interesting sounds and a knack for making ambiguous lyrics memorable, cLOUDDEAD’s second effort is uniquely promising and satisfying.

Title: Real Life Is No Cool
Review: Once the shock of the new dissipates, what’s left is an impeccably assembled record worth indulging with the vigor that any of Lindstrom’s Christabelle-less work deserves.

Title: Everything Was Beautiful, and Nothing Hurt
Review: [A] sympathetic examination of the world's wounds.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: It probably won’t satisfy those who still yearn for a return to their ‘90s alt-rock beginnings but it’s a good starting point for newcomers. For the rest of us though, what this all amounts to, in the end, is another fantastic Radiohead album.

Title: @#%&*! Smilers
Review: @#%&*! Smilers walks its own path as a uniquely beautiful addition to Mann’s already impressive catalogue.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: It's like Scissor Sisters on tranquilisers. With a bit of ELO. And a dash of Ramones. And, with this eclecticism, a worrying lack of focus. [5 Jun 2004, p.57]

Title: Tallies
Review: This group of songs are vivid in colour, creating a warmth, unlike their contemporaries who cling to the depressing melodrama of these decades. By keeping it light, listeners will might find a second listen through all the more appealing.

Title: This is PiL
Review: It's an album that alternates between being rewarding and punishing.

Title: Last Building Burning
Review: By setting its course in the equal and opposite direction of Life Without Sound, it becomes its evil twin, a still-incomplete picture of Cloud Nothings. ... Yet Last Building Burning feels like a triumphant return because there isn’t as much pressure on it to do or say anything beyond its purely utilitarian aims. It slaps, shreds, and whips ass in whatever way you see fit.

Title: With Siinai: Heartbreaking Bravery
Review: It all adds up to Krug's most engrossing work yet as Moonface and his best album since Sunset Rubdown's 2009 LP Dragonslayer. [Jun 2012, p.154]

Title: Joy Comes Back
Review: Foster makes them all her own through her through her strong vocals and distinctive phrasing. She has a commanding presence and a nuanced sensibility that she learned in church as a young girl. You could say the music here is truly the rock of ages.

Title: Concrete and Gold
Review: In conception and execution, Concrete And Gold stands as Foo Fighters' most beguiling record to date. [Oct 2017, p.88]

Title: The Buffet
Review: The Buffet is better than just another R. Kelly album, but not enough to be worth saying so outside of a review, much less on a year-end list; call it a good one-night stand.

Title: Skelliconnection
Review: Despite any bugaboos, he's a plain great songwriter, and Skelliconnection is firmly above average.

Title: Everything She Touched Turned Ampexian
Review: The abstract hip-hop guru’s fifth full-length offering, in the tradition of wayward cut-and-paste instrumentalism, is one almighty mess.

Title: Mixing Colours
Review: This kaleidoscope of colors, minimalistic sounds, and levitating textures result in a kind of imaginative synaesthesia constituting a deep feeling of oneness. The oceanic quality in this otherworldly music is always present. In this regard, Brian and Roger Eno's Deutsche Grammophon debut represents a refreshing antithesis of today's harsh and accelerated times.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: This isn't Watch the Throne, full of rich and weighty contributions from a man who is still enormously talented. It's rap music as a transaction, with a host of stars and hip names wrangled together to convince you it's not.

Title: Forgiveness Rock Record
Review: Forgiveness Rock Record is not the sound of Broken Social Scene dumbing themselves down; it's the band taking their sound to its logical conclusion. Few people would've guessed that in doing so, they've stumbled upon their second straight-up masterpiece.

Title: We Don't Even Live Here
Review: Maybe there's a touch more swagger than solutions on the set, but Minneapolis' secret weapon really should have saved the title of his previous set, Never Better, for this one.

Title: Sequence
Review: The spacious nature of Sequence makes it a challenging listen even for those versed in experimental approaches. At times the band's long-winded emptiness is as easy to lose focus on as it is to be mesmerized by. Patient listening, however, reveals a tightly focused and deliberately crafted work by a band pushing their art forward at an aggressive pace.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Nonagon Infinity
Review: It's seamless, silly, but seriously good stuff. [Jun 2016, p.113]

Title: Green Language
Review: Unfortunately, Rustie’s seemingly inherent need to zig when expected to zag has resulted in an awkwardly stitched together ragdoll of otherwise intriguing and successful pieces.

Title: Transnormal Skiperoo
Review: Jim White’s latest collection of songs has a humanity about it that is too multifaceted to categorize in broad terminology or flowery descriptors and is quite possibly beyond adequate summation; overthink or undersell as much as you please.

Title: Eight Houses
Review: From start to finish, the record stirs with hazy horns and an obsession with elusiveness.

Title: Ivory Tower
Review: Gonzales isn't an innovative dance producer, and there's not much pop music in play here either, making Ivory Tower a rather run-of-the-mill soundtrack--one of the many that can't be separated from their films.

Title: Close It Quietly
Review: Frankie Cosmos continues to succeed at condensing the task of processing feelings down into short minute-ish long songs. The pace of the album is set at a brisk run, but it never gets sweaty, so you'd never notice how quick it is — or how hard it's working. Close It Quietly is composed and meticulous in flow, flawlessly delivering reserved passion.

Title: A Different Arrangement
Review: A Capable full-length debut from the Brooklyn darkwave duo. [Oct/Nov 2012, p.127]

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: Aided by producers Organized Noize and Mr. DJ, Sir Lucious Left Foot is a monster of an album.

Title: Adult Fear
Review: There's plenty to bliss out on here and Holy Wave prove strongest when they focus on the emotional core of their songs as much as on the waves of sonic exploration.

Title: Maraqopa
Review: His tenth studio record retains the open-air dreaminess of Saint Bartlett, but it also keeps his sacred sense of songwriting, his careful guitar fixtures, and his understated demeanor. [Mar 2012, p.84]

Title: Hard Candy
Review: Even when she wrestles with Pharrell's abrupt stylistic changes or lets herself get absorbed in a Timberlake melody, Madonna still finds her way back on top.

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: Each of its 24 tracks snaps and crackles with Schneider's sugary, peerless pop. [16 Feb 2007, p.76]

Title: High Violet
Review: American indie cult heroes get a little noisier, a little more obscure [June 2010, p. 104]

Title: Light of X
Review: Unfortunately, Richards doesn't play to her strengths often enough. Too much of Light of X slips out of straightforward and into simple.

Title: The Other
Review: In one sense, The Other is a logical extension of its predecessor’s more lustrous moments, like the jangly acoustic outlier “Eyes of the Muse” and the stargazing ballad “Staircase of Diamonds.” But the execution here is more sophisticated—and the overall tone far more serious.

Title: Hungry Ghosts
Review: As the album progresses, it becomes hard to listen to without wishing each song had its own kinetic, creative video. [Dec 2014, p.88]

Title: Nouns
Review: No Age turn noise into gold on Nouns.

Title: Death Is This Communion
Review: The primitive beauty of Matt Pike's dense riffs and Des Kensel's tribal rhythms should ensure that the Foo Fighters' frontman usn't the only one falling in love with the Oakland trio.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Radical Connector softens up the abrasive glitch techno and broken beats of 2001's Idiology to produce a more dance-friendly album, with their signature warped vocals taking on a house sheen and invading every track.

Title: Twentytwo in Blue
Review: It’s a perfect union if anyone finds the former too glossy and the other too gritty, but in occupying this middle ground, nothing here would qualify as potentially divisive protest music. In fact, there’s nothing divisive about Twentytwo in Blue at all.

Title: The Seldom Seen Kid
Review: The ebb and flow of the disc feels like it's advancing some unknowable plot, always the sign of a well sequenced disc but also the bridge between songs like the lovely 'Mirrorball' and the bluesy (in the get-the-Led-out sense) 'Grounds for Divorce.'

Title: It's All Around You
Review: Tortoise have created another batch of distinct, inimitable songs that strike a perfect balance between the academic and the playful, the immediate and the eternal.

Title: Dedicated
Review: While Jepsen has once again delivered a stunning hook-filled record that frankly gets catchier every time you hear it, Dedicated may not quite satisfy our lust for connection.

Title: Little Wild One
Review: Little Wild One continues to fill out the picture of Joan Osborne as artist, adding new shades of color to the portrait of a confident and exciting songwriter who is comfortable in her skin yet willing to continue striving for excellence.

Title: End Times
Review: With its stark arrangements, glimpses of social disintegration, and thirtysomething neuroses (see I Need A Mother), it really is close to a masterpiece. [Feb 2010, p. 94]

Title: Playing the Angel
Review: Shows a good deal more focus than their last two studio efforts. [Nov 2005, p.104]

Title: Kairos
Review: Casey and collaborator Shawn Creeden deliver a bold album that eschews their previous organic approach in favour of a more electronic direction. The effect is intoxicating. [Apr 2010, p.92]

Title: VOL. 4 :: SLAVES OF FEAR
Review: Health's dark musical aesthetic feels as fresh as ever. ... Now, that's not to say there aren't a couple misses like "Rat Wars", but all in all, the androgynous energy of Jake Duzsik on the mic is more than enough to shape another pulsating yet nihilistic soundscape that reminds us how Health ages well like fine wine.

Title: Little Honey
Review: While it shows that the 55-year-old barbed-wire country singer is wary of rock's trappings, Little Honey proves she's still crushed out on the music.

Title: The Holy Pictures
Review: It's the personal element that underpins this record's appeal. [Oct 2008, p.92]

Title: All Things Will Unwind
Review: All Things Unwind is a cohesive trek that leaves the listener enraptured by Worden's talent and undeniable magnetism.

Title: Something Like a War
Review: Sorrowful dance and defiant house beats wind throughout, bringing unity to the scattered sounds. [Oct 2019, p.109]

Title: New Me, Same Us
Review: Showcases [singer Yukimi Nagano's] full emotional range. ... Six albums in, now, as ever, Little Dragon deserve far more attention. [May 2020, p.94]

Title: The Great Depression
Review: Surely one of the rap game's most insightful voices.... The beats offer plenty of fresh surprises and the lyrics reflect DMX's increasing focus on introspection.

Title: Conditions
Review: Impeccably produced, Conditions is a legitimate contender for debut album of 2009.

Title: Feedback
Review: A record designed to ensnare the as-yet-uncommitted listener without abandoning their extant fan base. [Aug 2006, p.103]

Title: Made of Bricks
Review: Nash's bluntness and detail make for a good spectacle. [Feb 2008, p.96]

Title: Sound Mirrors
Review: Truly a master-class in beat-science from start to finish. [28 Jan 2006, p.34]

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: The music here remains identifiably and intrinsically Wire. [Jun 2016, p.82]

Title: Thrills
Review: She's onto some good shit here, but there's too much learning on the job.

Title: Haerts
Review: Everything is likable, and that’s the formula for successful pop. But ultimately, this is the kind of polarizing release that will see the indie purists drawing a line in the sand as to what they’re willing to call their own moving forward.

Title: LISm
Review: The words only hint at the true meaning of the piece; it is an experience that needs to play out in a linear fashion, felt and absorbed through multiple senses.

Title: King's Mouth
Review: The musical accompaniment to the installation works perfectly as a concept album, where heady instrumentals and psychedelic pop nuggets are intertwined with swelling strings and a nursery rhyme story narrated by The Clash’s Mick Jones.

Title: Welcome the Worms
Review: Welcome the Worms lacks an awareness as to how lethargic it can be. Its lack of energy can demonstrate how tiring life is, but it can bring discomfort to an audience that might want to rock to a devil-may-care attitude.

Title: The Antidote
Review: Try as you might, searching for vestiges of the ol' Morcheeba is futile.

Title: Peace, Love, Death Metal
Review: Splendidly queasy listening. [May 2004, p.100]

Title: Testify
Review: A sleek collision of burbling basslines, adversarial vocals and downtuned brutality. [Mar 2006, p.109]

Title: The Fire Theft
Review: Old fans may dislike their classic-rock ambition and orchestral gloss, but the Fire Theft could be the rare spin-off that equals its progenitor. [10 Oct 2003, p.124]

Title: Partie Traumatic
Review: The truth is that Youngblood writes terrific, instantly memorable pop songs, their fashionable new-wave cool rubbing against an urgent, almost disco undertow. [Aug 2008, p.141]

Title: New Album
Review: The occasional flaws are still fascinating twists of Boris' art-metal genome-and the rest of New Album tackles that mutation with beauty and brilliance.

Title: Permalight
Review: Overproduction ultimately damns this record as much as anything, with everything cranked to 11 and Rogue’s voice constantly reverbed. Permalight sounds like a band who’s incredibly eager to impress, which wasn’t how Rogue emerged on the scene, a singer of simple pop songs.

Title: Miss Anthropocene
Review: Miss_Anthrop0cene is the perfect Grimes record for 2020, delving into topical themes such as climate change with an eclectic mix of genres. It’s certainly her darkest, most ambitious project yet, and it works on nearly all levels.

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: If Lonesome and Moon are 10s, Good News is a 9 and Long Drive and We Were Dead are 8’s, then this gets 7/10. Definitely worth picking up for Modest Mouse fans, but those new to the band should start elsewhere.

Title: Elixer
Review: The third disc, Bria Valente's Elixer, is a tepid afterthought.

Title: Public Warning
Review: The contrived newer stuff suggests she should stop trying to impress US hip hop royalty. [Mar 2007, p.91]

Title: Weezer (Teal Album)
Review: It’s like live band karaoke, and everyone is invited, which is all this really boils down to at the end of the day. They’re not reinventing the wheel; they’re using it.

Title: Play
Review: In short, it's fun and functional, yet disposable.

Title: Dorothy
Review: Deceptively simple-sounding, beautifully constructed folk songs. [Jun 2017, p.95]

Title: Red Letter Year
Review: In this diary, the groove can be as meaningful as the words.

Title: African Giant
Review: The sometimes quite retro Afro-pop production can get generic though, when repeated across 19 tracks – the bright, throbbing electronic backing for Destiny makes you long for a bit more breadth – and the English language lyrics can lapse into rap cliche.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: They're five years ahead of their time. [#6, p.86]

Title: Let England Shake
Review: On Let England Shake, Harvey is not often upfront or forceful; her lyrics, though, are as disturbing as ever.

Title: Almanac
Review: Without a singular narrative to tie it all together besides Hamilton's lovely but noncommital exhalations, it's a little too easy to lose interest.

Title: I Bet on Sky
Review: This isn't a reinvention of Dinosaur Jr. so much as a sideways glance; a new angle to help us appreciate their wonder in a new light.

Title: Antipodes
Review: Starting at a bass-heavy point where crunch is more important than structure, guitarist-singer Joel Flyger nevertheless knows how to write a pop hook. [Mar 2013, p.108]

Title: Charleston, SC 1966
Review: In the end, Charleston, SC 1966 doesn't break any rules or new ground, and probably wasn't meant to.

Title: Everything Else Matters
Review: On Everything Else Matters, the band funnels the Kansas post-rock group Appleseed Cast’s delay-pedal wizardry and open-ended song forms into bright pop that’s more in line with Astrobrite alum Andrew Prinz’s Mahogany.

Title: If I've Only One Time Askin'
Review: Like all great Country records, Romano’s is cathartic--your heart aches for him and with him--and it is this emotive sway that makes the record a success.

Title: West
Review: Take out the organ, slow down the drums and you might confuse a few songs with Bay Area band Sleep's legendary Dopesmoker album. But it's the things that prevent easy comparison that make Wooden Shjips the kickass band they are.

Title: Flaws
Review: These boys have genuine pedigree--guitarist Jamie's grandpa was Ewan MacColl--and the confident acoustic textures and fingerpicking styles on display here show a real affection for folk traditions. [Aug 2010, p.77]

Title: All The Way

Title: Gorillaz
Review: It's at its best when it puts Albarn in situations that you wouldn't normally hear him in, but also stumbles occassionally with a couple tracks that feel rather tossed-off and others that feel like they could have come off a Blur b-side.

Title: Mug Museum
Review: While it may lack some of the focus of its predecessor, it retains every bit of its oddball charm.

Title: Blue Hearts
Review: Blue Hearts is Mould at his fiercest and most deliberate. [Aug - Oct 2020, p.87

Title: Ziggy Marley
Review: It’s rooted so firmly within his comfort zone that when he sings about revolution on Start It Up, it’s more eyebrow-raising than consciousness-raising.

Title: Invasion of Love
Review: Aldred's voice has also upped a register, his yearning falsetto perfect for pocket space opera "Progress" or the lubricious Al Greenisms of "Fingers Through The Glass." [Sep 2013, p.94]

Title: The Rose Has Teeth in the Mouth of a Beast
Review: This is a remarkably rich and complex achievement. [#267, p.52]

Review: On The Living Infinite, Soilwork have simultaneously stepped back to their past while maintaining their current sound, but they have also diversified their formula more than ever before--and they did so without a single filler track.

Title: Our Endless Numbered Days
Review: Beam has a lovely lilting voice, a light instrumental touch, and a casual flair for drama. [24 Mar 2004]

Title: Aquarius
Review: Tinashe's voice is pure and malleable, her lyrics suggestive and assertive. [Dec 2014, p.116]

Title: A Hundred Million Suns
Review: A Hundred Million Suns? Ugh. More like a hundred million yawns.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: First Impressions introduces some subtle new colors to the band's musical palette... but the pervasive sense of inert boredom, which has been noted as a strength in the past, is difficult to shake.

Title: The Evening Descends
Review: Few bands have managed to blend so many divergent sounds and styles together to make such an interesting, great-sounding, and cohesive [key word] record as Evangelicals have with The Evening Descends.

Title: Strange Mercy
Review: Clark's complex femininity, both self-possessed and keenly evolving, is what makes her music so powerful and fascinating.

Title: Finally Woken
Review: The joyful whole has a depth and swagger that is as life-enhancing as popular music should be. [Mar 2005, p.100]

Title: Rock n Roll Jesus
Review: Jesus spits in the face of good taste with such unbridled enthusiasm that it's almost possible overlook its more cringe-inducing tendencies. Almost.

Title: Down To Believing
Review: There is a neat cover of Creedence’s Have You Ever Seen the Rain but the best songs are her own heartfelt and brooding country ones.

Title: Come with Us
Review: A worthy successor to Surrender.... This is dance music that still outstrips anything else in its class. [Feb/Mar 2002, p.113]

Title: Drop
Review: Sometimes the album sounds backward when it isn't. Rarely does it sound like one person squeaking out notes in succession--more like a bunch of dudes filling a tape with improvisations, rewinding to the cool parts and haranguing some hapless studio engineer to razorblade it all together.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: For all its slavering over archaic ‘80s production cheese, The Desired Effect is a consistently impressive collection--probably the strongest Brandon’s produced since 2006’s ‘Sam’s Town.’

Title: Born Here Live Here Die Here
Review: Examines small-town origins, fatherhood, and matter of the heart with extra earnestness but few surprises. [Aug 2020, p.73]

Title: Pre Language
Review: Throughout, a spewing, pandering vitriol taints a band whose vivacity seems to be wearing thin.

Title: Tha Carter V
Review: The misogyny of Tha Carter V cheapens its moving moments.

Title: Love, War and the Ghost of Whitey Ford
Review: While accepting that his odd but beguiling hybrid of rap, country, folk, and Butthole Surfers/Tom Waits-weirdness will never eclipse 1998's platinum "Whitey Ford Sings The Blues" he's injected impetus into what threatened to become a stale formula. [Oct 2008, p.142]

Title: The Seduction of Kansas
Review: The Seduction Of Kansas is a fun, dancey funk-punk record that benefits from Congleton’s lightness of touch, proof that you can step outside your comfort zone and maintain your sense of self.

Title: Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers
Review: Each of the dozen laments on Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers balance catchy choruses, exquisite instrumental interludes, and the complex words of a man's grieving.

Title: I Used to Spend So Much Time Alone
Review: Beneath the edgy smarts there's always been an undercurrent of anxiety, and now they're plunging into choppy emotional waters, minus irony's lifebelt. [Jul 2017, p.26]

Title: Cannibal
Review: I can feel my IQ slipping a few notches with the passage of each track on this disc, and gloriously so: it takes brains and balls to make pop this smart sound so dumb.

Title: Historian
Review: Historian stumbles occasionally, with some songs taking a while to get up the hill, but it’s rewarding because it carries such weight and commands such attention.

Title: Trigga
Review: Until Trey adds another layer to his songs, whether it be humor, empathy or any emotion other than a caveman-like approach to sex; Trigga remains a hollow, if tempting prospect for men that may well woo your woman, but is unlikely to keep your attention after.

Title: Nation
Review: 'Nation' is not bad - it's taut and tense and if you buy it quick you'll get to hear their logic-defying cover of Bauhaus' 'Bela Lugosi's Dead'. But it's hard to reconcile 'Nation''s obsession with the scourge of globalisation with Sepultura's conversion from third world pioneers to just another angry hardcore band.

Title: Isolation
Review: Isolation works because Uchis displays impeccable command over her voice and her style. She bends genres to her will rather than allowing them to absorb her identity, making for an impressive effort that will only improve as it ages.

Title: The Hour of Bewilderbeast
Review: A slippery and surprising little record -- an oblique song cycle tracing a relationship from balmy beginning to corrosive end.

Title: Fever
Review: Not one weak track, not one misplaced syrupy ballad to ruin the groove. The winning streak continues.

Title: LP1
Review: LP1 takes the humid isolation of Twigs’ EP1 and EP2 and twists it into ten tracks of relationship Hail Marys. But there’s a subdued sense of strength running under Barnett’s pleas that translates into a dark confidence, and in that tension is where LP1 finds its best moments.

Title: Born To Die
Review: The worst thing about Born To Die is that even its great songs contain problems.

Title: Love Streams
Review: It feels ecclesiastical, like hymns for the digital age.

Title: Flume
Review: Streton definitely has the production chops to make a solid record. However, if he wants a great record, he needs to edit down that tracklist and sequence it for cohesion.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: When I Get Home, on the one hand, is a portrait of Solange, following the success of A Seat at the Table, leaning to the point of falling into all the most pretentious aspects of that record. On the other, When I Get Home is a complex and fascinating exercise in reconfiguring a whole history of black music for the post-modern age. ... Yes, When I Get Home is overbearing in the way it wants to announce itself as art, but the album also makes that easy to forgive.

Title: Going Back Home
Review: Even though this is done and dusted in just over 30 minutes, the raw rocking and joyous attitude will stick with you long afterwards.

Title: Candidate Waltz
Review: At its best, it's a net that holds you comfortably, but at times it's easy to get lost in the imprecision. The lyrics could use some claws (which, to be fair, few nets have).

Title: Dimensional People
Review: The problem is that this music, heard purely as a piece of product rather than as part of a wider performance with site-specific logic, leaves the listener with too much time in which to speculate what wider agenda the group may be spinning. [May 2018, p.54]

Title: Benji
Review: The sparse musical arrangements and haunting production only serve to heighten the album’s intimacy and ultimately render it a masterpiece of reflection and introspection, destined to be played on repeat in scores of late-night, tired, and lonely rooms.

Title: Beauty and the Beat
Review: The first three-quarters of Beauty and the Beat stands as something to be admired.

Title: Prairie Wind
Review: The songs are weirder and darker than their gentle melodies indicate. [Nov 2005, p.141]

Title: SAWAYAMA
Review: Perspicacious and personal, cool and colossally enjoyable, Sawayama is both a triumph over trauma and a paean to the power of effervescent pop in practically all its forms. [Jun 2020, p.98]

Title: As Long As I Have You
Review: His voice isn't built for such poignancy. This is a 74-year-old's dance record, not an elegy. [Jul 2018, p.27]

Title: Brill Bruisers
Review: Brill Bruisers is an enthusiastic correction in course, as well as a reminder that age doesn’t always equal solemnity or, for that matter, slouching toward self-importance of any kind.

Title: Music Kills Me
Review: Rinocerose's specialty is dropping an army of scratchy, shrieking guitars into the dumbed-down world of modern disco.

Title: Carboniferous
Review: Compared to prior outings, their Zorn-like freewheeling spirit has been toned back and songs feel more like actual "songs" with defined structure and greater emphasis on the individuality of the performers and the negative space surrounding them.

Title: Lonerism
Review: The way your patience is so handsomely rewarded is what truly makes Lonerism such an engrossing spectacle.

Title: Proof of Youth
Review: The Go! Team's folluow-up is densely packed enough to make Phil Spector's Wall feel like a screen door. [Oct 2007, p.160]

Title: Shogun
Review: So while fourth album Shogun is impressive, Trivium continues ro make "...And Justice For All" when they could do with a "Black Album" instead. [Nov2008, p.107]

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: A highly evolved exercise in absorption and restraint. [Dec 2018, p.28]

Title: Love Sign
Review: Love Sign dips a little too far into the Fountains of Wayne kiddie pool.

Title: Fires Within Fires
Review: Fires Within Fires is the summation of 30 years of experimentation in tonality and texture. Yes, Neurosis are firmly positioned within the extreme metal underground, yet their music, with its ability to generate images of beauty akin to those many of us have experienced in our own lives--not to mention the loss that accompanies them--challenges this categorisation. [Oct 2016, p.49]

Title: Some Nights
Review: [The band's] boundless enthusiasm could be teeth-grating even without Stars' overuse of Auto-Tune, but it's hard to dislike such catchy tunes and lyrics that are funny, sincere and oddly moving.

Title: SUGAREGG
Review: ‘SUGAREGG’ is eminently aware of its own fragility under its candy-coated shell, and with it a candid recognition of the fleeting nature of happiness and the work required to hold onto it.

Title: Frozen Letter
Review: Brief as it may be, Frozen Letter covers a lot of ground for Spider Bags--it has them gleefully offering us tasty kibbles of what they’ve always excelled at while also boldly paving themselves a new path forward.

Title: Pop Psychology
Review: If [a band] goes back to the well once too often, it can be derided for stagnating. If it takes a left turn, fans may bemoan the change of pace. Neon Trees, the Utah band behind the unavoidable “Animal” and “Everybody Talks,” seem to have split the difference on their third effort.

Title: You're Nothing
Review: A record that’s as jittery and unhinged as it is perversely spot-on.

Title: Ghosts of Then and Now
Review: Ghosts Of Then And Now is a rich and dynamic listen, threaded with a strong sense of purpose that's wonderfully engaging.

Title: The Manticore and Other Horrors
Review: There's nothing here that Cradle of Filth haven't done much better elsewhere. [10 Nov 2012, p.55]

Title: Crown and Treaty
Review: Songwriter Tim Elsenburg makes great strides forward with an ambitious cycle of songs about identity and history.

Title: Head Over Heels
Review: Chromeo specializes in upbeat, retro-embracing synth-funk—but, unlike others in a similar vein, the Canadian duo exists in an area somewhere between a come-hither wink and a seduction parody. On Head Over Heels, the group strikes a perfect balance between these extremes. Credit for this goes to the roster of impressive special guests.

Title: case/lang/veirs
Review: It’s not at all certain that this lovely, gentle record will ever get a follow-up--fortunately, it already sounds damn-near timeless.

Title: Diamond Hoo Ha
Review: Now Diamond Hoo Ha, find Supergrass mired in a sort of stasis. We always knew the lads were limited to just three chords; with efforts that feel measured, contrived, and dawdling, they finally sound like it.

Title: Mono
Review: There is a vibrant exuberance to these performances that, like its old-school audio, feels alive and fresh making the Mavericks one of the few bands better in their second act than in their first.

Title: I Like It When You Sleep, for You Are So Beautiful Yet So Unaware of It
Review: In the hands of other bands, this slippery focus might feel like genre whiplash or a bait-and-switch. Yet the album coheres shockingly well, thanks to smart sequencing and the vocal progression of frontman Matt Healy.

Title: In Technicolor
Review: Too much of the album feels restrained, unable to truly revel in the bliss of melody.

Title: Life In Cartoon Motion
Review: Mika makes music that sounds like vegetables with all the flavour boiled out of them. Blandness born out of a fear of doing anything new, interesting, or provocative. Blandness born from a fear of alienating a single person with a single piece of conviction in your music.

Title: Up and Coming
Review: The work on Up and Coming (ironic, I imagine purposefully, for a musician who is now 72 and long established as a master) is not busting boundaries. But it is excellent.

Title: Swoon
Review: It lacks some of Carnavas’ instant pleasures, but Swoon finds Silversun Pickups on the right path.

Title: Lost Wisdom
Review: This album sinks in, each listen dry rubbing the quiescent hums and lulls into the brain like a dream half remembered.

Title: Love's Crushing Diamond
Review: [A] collection of seven gorgeous, baroque-folk songs.

Title: Hidden City

Title: All Nerve
Review: The Breeders have released the rock album of the year so far.

Title: Cheers
Review: What redeems Trice is his workmanlike emphasis of craft over style. It's not flamboyant, but it's impressive.

Title: Viet Cong
Review: Viet Cong has only seven tracks and more than half don’t pass the five minute mark. Yet all are heavy, ingenious contraptions.

Title: Palace
Review: So they might be inserting themselves into a canon known for its critical consensus, but Palace is still a vital addition to the oeuvre, and richly deserving of the inevitable praise.

Title: Since We Last Spoke

Title: Earthology

Title: Mercy

Title: Rhubarb Rhubarb
Review: It’s still clear that The Voyeurs aren’t reinventing the wheel. But they’ve greased it with enough fun that it scarcely matters.

Title: Island Intervals
Review: Island Intervals starts with songs that pit the intimate and the epic against each other, that shift tempo, texture, and scope in fascinating ways. But that set of complications can’t sustain itself.
