Review: The issue with Lost in Alphaville, besides simply retooling earlier Rentals songs, is its feeling of playing it safe.

Title: Jonny
Review: Childs and Blake have created a record of outstanding songcraft, which salutes rock's past with a carefree spirit and its head in the clouds. Go Jonny, go, go go.

Title: Seabed
Review: This is a fun record, one whose effusiveness only reveals itself slowly, with repeat listens opening up more and more emotional layers hovering beneath its sleepy atmosphere.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light I
Review: He's produced an album that takes his current style just about as far as it can go. At the very least, those who have followed him this far should be satisfied.

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: I Can Feel You Creep Into My Private Life is a natural addition to the Tune-Yards catalog, a group of albums with songs so singular that practically every track seems like an evolution in the Tune-Yards sound.

Title: Conference of Trees
Review: Conference Of Trees provides plenty of evidence for Weber's continually developing ear for melodies and musically detailed arrangements, but there are other aspects of his past work that could have been left to one side. The Triad, his last full-length, at times felt twee and fussy, a problem that returns here in one section of the album in particular.

Title: Quality Street Music
Review: Quality Street Music serves as a vehicle for Drama to shine a light on some artists you may not have payed much attention to before while embarrassing and making caricatures of others, resulting in an unbalanced effort that reeks of songs constructed through emails and mix-and-matching rather than any real chemistry.

Title: Dissociation
Review: Every member is in top form here. Ben Weinman has crafted an eventful aural masterpiece.

Title: Continuum
Review: In the end Continuum feels like little-more than the self-indulgent effort of a possibly-peaked pop star.

Title: Otherness
Review: The results, often transcendent and inventive, incorporate gospel elements and "found sounds," while retaining the spirit of shaky DIY experimentation. [Nov 2014, p.95]

Title: Small Mercies
Review: The end result is a rewardingly eclectic mix, if not slightly discombobulating.

Title: When It Was Now
Review: It ain't exactly Bill Shakespeare (or Trojans), but it gets the job done.

Title: Escape From Evil
Review: The title may be a little hyperbolic, but what it lacks in realism it makes up for in groovy new-wave guitar licks, other-worldly instrumentation and production par excellence.

Title: Blood Like Lemonade
Review: You'd be a curmudgeon on to hate such a soothing, well-produced brew, but an undemanding soul to hear it as more than aural wallpaper. [Jul 2010, p.115]

Title: Continental
Review: Depending on how much Robin Guthrie you want in your life, Continental is either redundant or another reason to love him.

Title: Heard It In A Past Life
Review: While it sometimes feels like Rogers could be even bolder than she is on Heard It in a Past Life, it's a strong debut that shows how well she's growing into her fame as well as all the dimensions of her music.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: Marling has transcended the nu-folk movement and carved her own magnificent identity.

Title: Encore
Review: Encore never resonates the way his first three endlessly fascinating albums do.

Title: Fading Lines
Review: What you’re left with is the impression of an artist with her receptors fully open, resulting in a debut reaching far more emotional touch points than you’d expect.

Title: Rejoicing In The Hands
Review: Anyone who can sit down in such a short period of time and write this many unique songs has to have something abnormally genius working inside.

Title: Breakthrough
Review: It's a creation that's slicker and sleeker than the debut, but fortunately, it's not quite at the expense of Caillat's simple charms.

Title: Galore
Review: Listening to Galore kind of feels like growing up, as it perfectly balances a combo of bittersweet nostalgia, hopeful optimism and an impending sense of something bigger and better to come.

Title: Expansion Team
Review: The 16-track set showcases Dilated's combination of intelligent lyrics and mind-blowing production.

Title: Furr
Review: Enjoying Furr, then, depends entirely on your ability (or willingness) to ignore the heavy footprints of familiar musicians.

Title: The Lioness
Review: The mood here is much bleaker than the previous album, and there's more of a feeling a desperation in Jason Molina's vocals.

Title: Animal Ambition: An Untamed Desire to Win
Review: Despite being billed as his fifth album, it's nowhere near the level of his strong, yet largely overrated debut "Get Rich or Die Tryin'".

Title: Ephorize
Review: Her lyrical tricks are unexpected and endlessly quotable .

Title: Ex Lives
Review: Every Time I Die are moving in some promising new directions.

Title: Elysium
Review: New record Elysium finds them sounding once again like proverbial fish out of water, only with far less aplomb. [Aug/Sep 2012, p.113]

Title: Music for the Age of Miracles
Review: A work of lovely, floaty wonder. [Oct 2017, p.103]

Title: Life Metal
Review: It does thrillingly refine the group's electric explorations of numinous spaces both minuscule and gigantic. [Jul 2019, p.114]

Title: Living Things
Review: By refusing to play it safe, they'll further diminish their original fanbase, but such boldness is to be applauded.

Title: Fate
Review: Simply put, Fate is a refreshment of the sound that has been missing for so long.

Title: Cyclops Reap
Review: As it is, Cyclop Reaps has the aura of automatic writing, a stream of unfiltered imagery that is, intermittently, quite arresting, but as a whole shapeless and hard to navigate.

Title: In the Blue Light
Review: Simon’s song choices weave together to form a narrative on intolerance, the dangers of divisive thinking, impending mortality, the ebb and flow of love, ecological troubles and faith. Where less nimble-minded songwriters might flounder, his literary eye for the minutiae of life stands him in good stead.

Title: Dig Out Your Soul
Review: Dig Out Your Soul might not be the sound of envelopes being pushed, but its mix of kitchen-sink production and too many vague songs mark a deviation from business as usual that ultimately fails to deliver. [Nov 2008, p.105]

Title: Easy Tiger
Review: Easy Tiger plays like a tightly focused best-of compilation from Adams' past six or seven efforts. [Jul 2007, p.96]

Title: Pax Americana
Review: Pax Americana is something of a mixed bag of a return for Bratten. Its short runtime and nature as a mix of already released and new material making it feel more like an elongated EP than a cohesive album. It’s a record that takes its time shaking off a clawing desire to replicate its influences, but ultimately finds the form that led to Bratten’s best work again.

Title: Good Souls Better Angels
Review: As a songwriter and a storyteller, she’s simply never recorded anything quite like it. After so long in the game, it’s miraculous to hear her take such a fresh approach to her sound.

Title: Transference
Review: The somber, subtle hand instills Transference with a fair amount of grace, an impressive feat for a band known more for its indie irreverence than its elegance.

Title: Apocalipstick
Review: Deconstructing socio-cultural norms rarely sounds like so much fun. [Feb 2017, p.24]

Title: Big Black Coat
Review: All the songs on Big Black Coat sound like love songs, all eleven of them.

Title: Hozier
Review: In spite of its extra padding and occasional foibles, it's a strong debut and Hozier is far more commanding and convincing than so many other blues-inspired young turks lurking conspicuously in the alleyways of indiedom.

Title: The Believer
Review: The Believer may be a formula recording, but it still satisfies, for the most part, on the level of what it is: a finely crafted pop/rock album.

Title: Golden Grrrls
Review: The result is an accomplished debut that's a welcome--though not essential--addition to a growing number of lo-fi pop bands.

Title: The Heat
Review: The Heat compares favorably to PJ Harvey’s Stories From the City, Stories From the Sea, offering the same NYCentric references (“9-11 baby boom”), gruff, understated guitar work and narrative aptitude. These are Malin’s stories from the city and they don’t disappoint.

Title: Ring
Review: An ultimately frustrating listen, not because of the quality of Ring per se, but because of the undoubted class of record it could have been if only it were a little more thought through. Still, there's certainly enough potential to justify Glasser's rising reputation as a worthy heir to a certain Icelandic lady's throne.

Title: Noah's Ark
Review: It is the sisters' old-timey voices that capture and carry the beautiful eeriness of these minimalist songs. [#17, p.103]

Title: Almost
Review: The Ophelias' lyrics are at times impassioned, but the vocals are banal. Yet the maturity that arises from their individual and musical self-actualization carries Almost.

Title: Second Of Spring
Review: Revel in the poppy darkness of Beaches--sunset drenched “ba-ba-ba” vocals, upfront drums and twangy guitars--but also marvel as the Australian psych rockers draw out their swirling sounds into extended hypnotic workouts on this double album. [Oct 2017, p.64]

Title: Primary Colours
Review: The quintet's transformation from schlocky garage urchins to ambassadors of thrilling new-wave can largely be attributed to Portishead's Geoff Barrow, who, alongside Chris Cunningham, produced "Primary Colours," uncovering a formidable band beneath the haircuts. [Jun 2009, p.86]

Title: Come of Age
Review: They've honed their ability to be urgent and primitive, to write songs that make boys and girls want to snog each other, and added nuance and depth. Everything feels bold, fast and confident.

Title: Total Time
Review: Total Time’s earthly escapism has stars in its eyes and dirt under its fingernails.

Title: Hurricane
Review: Jones co-wrote all the material, and it shrewdly plays to her age and experience (she's 63), like a latter-day Marianne Faithfull with a Jamaican tinge and more of a bellow than a croak.

Title: Eclipse
Review: It’s rarely subtle sonically--synths come in bursts, bass lines thump like they’re reaching for the strobe lights--but Lewis’ seductive voice provides an irresistible tether.

Title: Living With The Living
Review: You almost get the sense Leo must be embarrassed by how good his last record sounds, opting instead to appease some imaginary punk ethic to the detriment of his songs.

Title: Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!!
Review: Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!! is ultimately a rock record more than it is an ideas record, but on both counts the Seeds bring it like a band half their age.

Title: Skip a Sinking Stone
Review: It’s an album to truly cherish.

Title: Eno Axis
Review: The songs boast a quality of spaciousness and delicacy that was rarer on 2018's otherwise very fine Lionheart. [Sep 2020, p.32]

Title: 1000 Days
Review: 1000 Days sounds like a Cory Hanson solo album and a stagnant development for Wand, who, instead of progressing toward a heavy psych sound patently their own, settle for a gentler, safer pop record.

Title: Tha Carter III
Review: Ultimately, Tha Carter III will have you believing in Wayne's greatness but wondering why, as often as not, he just isn't very good.

Full of expertly constructed, slightly neutered songs about heartbreak, 1989, which is to be released on Monday, doesn’t announce itself as oppositional. But there is an implicit enemy on this breezily effective album: the rest of mainstream pop, which 1989 has almost nothing in common with.

Title: Spiral Shadow
Review: Spiral Shadow might just be the album of the year so far. All hail the kings (and queen) of nouveau-prog.

Title: Fluorescence
Review: They've wrangled a tougher, just weird-enough synthesis, with "Trails" borrowing Yeah Yeah Yeahs' brio and "Perfectly Crystal" likely to impress fans of both Pet Shop Boys and Flaming Lips. [Mar 2011, p.83]

Title: Realisationship
Review: Realisationship might not always come together neatly, but Andrew Hung’s desire to push his own boundaries, whether that’s moving into that lo-fi zone or utilising his vocals, leaves you wondering just where he’ll turn n

Title: Welcome Joy
Review: Although the album is undoubtedly a more polished production than is "Invitation Songs," the percussion is obfuscated by a watery and murky mix.

Title: Pussycat
Review: As a collection of rock songs, it is deadly on the mark, a bulls-eye, a shot of sunshine and bourbon to your gut. It takes its place as the year’s most glowing record of despair, and joy? And as Juliana Hatfield’s best album.

Title: Unorthodox Jukebox
Review: The result is a record that makes the competition sound sad and idea-starved by comparison.

Title: It's Me Again
Review: Tweet is a contender again.

Title: Vivian Girls
Review: Though derivative of countless bands, Vivian Girls succeed in paring hazy nostalgia with big noise. It's simple and sounds good.

Title: Battle For The Sun
Review: The album may revive the band's career in North America, but for many of their loyal fans it will come as a major disappointment.

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: More about songs than weird jams, alternating between twisted retro rock and eccentric folk rock. [24 Mar 2006, p.71]

Title: Brooklyn's Don Diva
Review: A couple tracks and a few stray lines aside, these verses could have been dashed off by the MC at just about any earlier point in her career.

Title: Peace Trail
Review: As it is, Peace Trail is just another album to add to the teetering pile of evidence that Neil Young’s output is currently more erratic and confounding than it has been at any time since the mid-80s.

Title: Integrity Blues
Review: It's a soft, frail album Jimmy Eat World have here, but one that hits right in the feels. Hard. [29 Oct 2016, p.51]

Title: When Fish Ride Bicycles
Review: When Fish Ride Bicycles may pay homage to Chicago summers, but this duo rarely break a sweat, rhyming in dulcet tones about designer sneaks and tricked-out GMCs.

Title: The Life Pursuit
Review: There's still plenty about the group to satisfy long-time fans, and there's a wealth of quality and innovation to win them some new ones.

Title: Spring
Review: A sleepier song like "Blue Spring," which features pedal steel and sparse, strummed guitar, only provides contrast within a very narrow range of expression here, like when eyes adjust to dim nocturnal lighting, then notice the shadow of a stray moth.

Title: The Money Store
Review: The Money Store fits into modern hip-hop like a square peg on fire, a 40-minute straitjacket tantrum of vein-popping, slow-flow barks closer to Helmet's Page Hamilton than Harlem's Charles Hamilton.

Title: What Doesn't Kill You, Eventually Kills You
Review: Gay for Johnny Depp's Sex Vid Singles Club lacks a certain clarity in vision and sound. Or maybe that's the point.

Title: Nocturne of Exploded Crystal Chandelier
Review: This is a richly textured debut that creates a very agreeable collision between the organic and the electronic. [Feb 2011, p.100]

Title: The Blueprint 3
Review: Without its filler, this album could have been at least good, if not great. But, for better or for worse, this is what Jay wanted us to hear right now. It’s just a shame that it’s not entirely worth hearing.

Title: This Is My Hand
Review: The pressure of opposites can be a strong enough force to create bright and shiny diamonds. That’s kind of what happens on this album.

Title: Is This Thing Cursed?
Review: While Is This Thing Cursed? won't win over any more acolytes, or incite anything close to a Billboard pop-punk resurgence, Alkaline Trio diehards will find themselves, by turns, nostalgic for what came before and thrilled by what they hear now.

Title: Deep in the Iris
Review: By trying to be the band everyone wants them to be, Braids have sacrificed the qualities that made them so captivating. And that is one hell of a shame.

Title: Fade
Review: With Fade, they’ve come across ten songs that all sound tight and of course, refreshing, against the backdrop of what might be their most consistent album to date.

Title: I'm Not Well
Review: A near-constant crisis of confidence isn’t always the best character trait for a rock’n’roll singer, but this Devon power(ish) trio make it work on their solid debut album.

Title: Future This
Review: The fumbling effort to harmonize their irreverence and earnestness leaves the Big Pink ultimately stranded, and the result is a hook-deficient album that wears on the ears after only a few listens.

Title: Con Todo El Mundo
Review: The overall lack of lyrics--the most repeated line on the 10-track record is a simple, wistful “oooh”--is only a positive, letting the listener get fully, deeply lost in the band’s fertile psychedelic world.

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: GOD isn’t about sensory pleasure. It’s about sensory gluttony, auditory overload, and revelling in the difficulty of its pacing.

Title: Mass Romantic
Review: A record that's certain to be name-checked by pop savants 20 years from now.

Title: Snowdonia
Review: John Paul Pitts’ melodic prowess is what keeps me listening, even on a more chill album like Snowdonia. Something about his melodies and vocal timbre just hooks me and won’t let go. I just wish they would pump the volume back up!

Title: Oversteps
Review: This is their most assured, confident release to date and though it may not take the place of fan-favourite, it certainly deserves to be considered as the best introduction to Autechre’s oeuvre.

Title: The 1975
Review: It's a Gary Barlow idea of what indie music sounds like.

Title: Cosmos
Review: Give it a bloody good stereo and your full attention.

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: Its ambitions far exceed its ideas, and the record is sunk by the kind of sonic bloat normally reserved for self-regarding sophomore releases.

Title: Nootropics
Review: Nootropics is a slow burn that lingers long. [May 2012, p.78]

Title: Not Music
Review: In the end, it's not such a bad thing that Not Music shows Stereolab fans that they didn't always fully appreciate what they had until it was gone, even though a lesson like this can only come when it's too late

Title: City of Refuge
Review: City of Refuge seems more like a collection of ideas for three or four different albums than one complete work.

Title: Traps
Review: This two-faced record can be jarring, but the melodies stick, as does the venom in many of the lyrics.

Title: In Limbo
Review: It's easy to get caught up in TEEN's dreams without completely falling asleep, a tough act to follow with so many similar acts just simply getting lost. [#90, p.61]

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: [A] beautiful little album.

Title: Mississauga Goddam
Review: Even though Mississauga Goddamn isn't completely without flaw -- some of Gibb's lyrical and compositional choices are pretty obvious, for one thing -- it allows you, for a little while, at least, to escape from the everyday world.

Title: Beast
Review: There might be something deeper rolling around here than "There's nothing that will change me/There's nothing sure as shit" ("Bring the Fight"). Probably not, but if you want to bang your head, this will do the trick.

Title: As Good As Gone
Review: The music on the album is rarely as urgent as the image that adorns it, and never as explosive as the heavy artillery that is found on its back, but the disc has a more subtle appeal than both.

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: The band clearly dug much deeper and as a result they created bigger sounds than before. It can be seen as the positive impact of a collaboration that has lasted more than twenty-five years – even though drummer Janet Weiss recently decided to leave the band. Maybe the centre really cannot hold.

Title: Mellow Waves
Review: It’s the overall cool/warm Tropicalismo tone that’s most engaging about Mellow Waves, established through the light accretion of sparse piano, percussion, synth and guitar parts supporting his soft vocal on opener “If You’re Here”.

Title: Someday World
Review: Ultimately Someday World is undeniably disappointing. For something that promised so much and to deliver so woefully little is an injustice to each respective side of the partnership.

Title: Six
Review: This EP essays six bitter flavours of magic and loss, with sentiments which might be unbearable were it not for their unalloyed beauty. [Mar 2014, p.63]

Title: Summertime '06
Review: In a year of impressive solo rap albums, Staples has managed to create one that’s arguably the most idiosyncratic of the lot.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: To put it more simply, the record rocks and offers insightful commentary on the world we inhabit.

Title: Deep Down Happy
Review: So the debut album is done, and it’s a good one.

Title: Only For Dolphins
Review: Bronson's imagination, vivid as ever, makes up for the decreasing variation in his microphone approach.

Title: Destiny Fulfilled
Review: It's disappointing to find a glut of songs seemingly calibrated to appease the demographics. [Jan 2005, p.126]

Title: Climate Change
Review: Jubilant but spotty.

Title: The Way Out
Review: It's an undefinable musical culmination of our collective conscious-reminding us that the more we've changed, the more we've stayed the same.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: On Thr33 Ringz, more than ever, that robotic voice is just part of an effort to reconcile cold technology and warm soul.

Title: Radio Wars
Review: Too often on Radio Wars, velvet-voiced singer Juanita Stein seems content to hover around a handful of notes, and that makes it hard to distinguish this stuff from similarly styled fare by the Duke Spirit or Doves.

Title: Invincible
Review: We're placed squarely in Michael Jacksonland, a bizarre place where every sparkling street is computer-generated, every edifice is larger than life and every song is full of grandiose desperation.

Title: Two Wounded Birds
Review: Their eagerness to look into music's past only serves to make them sound timeless.

Title: Inner Song
Review: A welcome development is Owens' voice: this time, when deployed, it's positioned centrally. [Sep 2020, p.35]

Title: Silence Yourself
Review: On the London quartet's debut Silence Yourself, the group whips up a storm of aggressive rhythms, strident vocalizing, and six-string sheen as if the succeeding pop trends never happened and Gang of Four and Siouxsie & the Banshees rule the charts.

Title: Lovebox
Review: Lovebox takes them much too far down the path of production gloss, right on into the field of bland MOR electronica.

Title: Allas Sak
Review: The instrumental and compositional mastery on show is staggering. Whether it will make a dent in the consciousness of those who don't spend their time watching at the edges of the prog-rock firmament is another question entirely.

Title: Dirty Side Down
Review: Science or not, Widespread Panic's eleventh offering shows that after all this time, they've got something figured out.

Title: What If
Review: Although What If's nine instrumental tracks are heavily rhythmic, this is a refreshingly gridless and affecting music, with serrated clicks and muted arpeggios wandering organically in and out of time. [Apr 2017, p.30]

Title: Kaleidoscope
Review: Kaleidoscope isn’t going to kickstart Coldplay’s critical reappraisal, nor does it deserve to. But it rewards those of us who’ve stuck around with a few songs that capture the band at its best.

Title: Restarter
Review: Restarter has an unwavering groove. What it lacks in immediacy it makes up for in lasting appeal.

Title: Harkin
Review: While the straight guitar-janglers sometimes border on generic, the eerie psych-rock incantation "Red Virginia Creeper" and the clanging, reverb-drenched barbs of "Charm And Tedium" prove more rewarding. [Jun 2020, p.29]

Title: Seeds We Sow
Review: A much better way to think of Seeds We Sow would be as the album where Buckingham's creative restlessness finally, completely made peace with his history with one of the biggest bands in the world.

Title: No Color
Review: Now shorn of vibraphonist Keaton Snyder, San Francisco's The Dodos remain a three-piece with the addition of alt.country chanteuse Neko Case.

Title: Departing
Review: The songwriting is another matter. Where debut album Hometowns was saturated with specific references to Alberta, with little cinematic details that helped to flesh out the songs, Departing relies too frequently on stock winter imagery and generic love laments.

Title: The Magic Whip
Review: Blur have returned with inspiration to spare.

Title: Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea
Review: Chiming, richly textured and potently rhythmic, this is starkly, explicitly rock n' roll, and the back-to-basics approach beautifully frames Polly's tales of fear, love, sex, sadness, ugliness, and beauty.

Title: Born to Play Guitar
Review: It's best appreciated not as a legend's lap of honour, but for itself. [Sep 2015, p.75]

Title: Living Things
Review: Living Things" is simply a minor effort in an impressive discography, and one that should translate well to Linkin Park's live show.

Title: Weaves
Review: Weaves have written a good debut record that is unafraid to take chances, and to an extent, it signifies a band that will only get hungrier with time. There’s still in search mode, though, exceedingly pushing themselves to write clever pop songs that sometimes expose their calculated overconfidence.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: There’s something to be said for two masters of their craft talking jazz for the joy of it, but to me, the question remains whether or not this kind of jazz is played out.

Title: The Deconstruction
Review: Predictably overwhelming. [May 2018, p.27]

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: What this results in is an album that is just as frequently successful as it is frustrating.

Title: Hard Believer
Review: Whilst Hard Believer has its moments, this sense of playing it safe permeates throughout the record.

Title: Ascent
Review: Get lost in the haze.

Title: United Crushers
Review: United Crushers can come across as a draining listen, perhaps even an uncomfortable one to those accustomed to their earlier work. It takes a few listens to discern the resolve in Leaneagh’s lyrics, but it’s there.

Title: Law and Order
Review: Law and Order attempts to restore some sort of musical faith, but comes across as sounding like a narscisstic debut that only Jonathan Rado really understands.

Title: Ringer
Review: At four songs, Ringer is economical, but the diversity within its half-hour run time makes it surprisingly robust as well.

Title: The Only She Chapters
Review: The Only She Chapters is strictly for those who are already die-hard fans of Prefuse 73 and not really anybody else.

Title: Stay Gold
Review: Stay Gold features lush arrangements created by Nate Walcott and performed by members of the Omaha Symphony Orchestra. These layered sounds, so intricately woven to complement the sisters’ voices, create a completeness that realizes First Aid Kit’s musical maturity.

Title: The Town and the City
Review: Its stories of survivors and struggling lovers have a wistfulness that spills from the lyrics into the tone of David Hidalgo’s vocal performances and the warm guitar lines, which draw on blues, classic rock, and traditional Mexican musical flourishes.
At times, Adele's precocious talent feels prematurely aged by her material, and moments of levity are hard to find. But at its best, 21 is that rarest pop commodity: timeless.

Title: Strange Trails
Review: The band ensure they make music, which matches their aesthetic: airy, welcoming story-telling indie folk, which just happens to be painstakingly well considered and recorded. Ultimately though, where all this world building and curatorship comes to fall short is where it matters most: the songs.

Title: 32 Levels
Review: More a showcase of his production wares than an album, this collection still suggests Clams might produce a pearl yet.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: There's still only one Stevie Nicks – witchy, mystical and romantic.

Title: We Are Not Your Kind
Review: With all of the band’s nu-metal hallmarks at the forefront this time, We Are Not Your Kind sounds the more like the head-turning, self-titled debut they put out 20 years ago than any of their releases since. But what’s different here is a new sense of (gasp!) sophistication.

Title: Western Stars
Review: Western Stars is erratic in the first half, as Springsteen’s need for exposition sometimes grinds uneasily against the sweep of the music. But the second half is a profound pleasure. ... It makes you wish that Springsteen could dash off an album full of such country songs. Until then, Western Stars will have to do, and it does just fine.

Title: A New Testament
Review: Even when Owens isn’t operating at his peak, his work remains oddly intriguing--there’s a passion and honesty here, an uncompromising desire to follow his own vision.

Title: Two-Way Mirror
Review: After a decade of excellence from like-minded groups such as Liars and TV On The Radio, Crystal Antlers can't help but sound like a mildly intriguing afterthought, even if Two-Way Mirror holds the line in hopes of greatness to come.

Title: The World is Yours 2
Review: Although the surplus of features is at times overwhelming, The World Is Yours 2, is an extremely strong sophomore album.

Title: Blinking Lights and Other Revelations
Review: There's a good album underneath all the filler-- probably the Eels' best since Electro-Shock Blues-- but it'll take some editing to excavate it.

Title: Scream Above the Sounds
Review: While the U2-style arena-rock impressions that dogged Keep The Village Alive persist in places here, elsewhere Scream Above The Sounds finds Kelly Jones in more reflective mood, resulting in a more appealing balance of head and heart overall.

Title: Eternal Recurrence
Review: Eternal Recurrence is a fine, thoughtful piece of ambient drone-folk that is as challenging as it is assuring.

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: Humble and resigned to a fault.

Title: Parting The Sea Between Brightness And Me
Review: Where its cool and dynamic at first, by the time the albums over you get the sense that there was too much, too quickly, and something was certainly lost. While it may break away from the hardcore realm, giving these songs more room to grow and expand would have greatly increased the replayability of Parting the Sea beyond the first listen or two.

Title: Let It Come Down
Review: You could get lost for days in the depths of these arrangements, and still find something moving and transcendental at every gilded turn. It's a towering achievement...

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: Producer Dave Stewart has helped create an album that sounds exactly like the Nicks of myth: spooky, otherworldly, emotional and sassy, yet stalked by some undefinable melancholy.

Title: The Bachelor
Review: The Bachelor is the work of a hugely fertile imagination, skipping from the aforementioned Celtic folk to electro to glam, but one wonders how much more affecting Wolf might be if the grand passions were calmed down a little, the musical magpie impulses restrained a tad. For now, he's a little too much of a good thing.

Title: Life After Youth
Review: Although Powell's new land Of Talk is considerably more contemplative and understated, Life After Youth is an evocative and powerful step forward. [No. 142, p.57]

Title: Wildfire
Review: Wildfire is the work of a determined singer/songwriter who prizes craft over poetry or introspection. Platten specializes in skyscraping melodies and big, bombastic surfaces and these are the elements that not only fuel Wildfire, they distinguish it from the singer/songwriter's clear antecedents.

Title: Sundowner
Review: This is never going to replace your favourite Kevin Morby album, and it’s unlikely that it will make him new fans, but it feels like the kind of private delight that great artists bestow on their fans for their loyalty from time to time. Sundowner is Morby’s Harvest Moon, his Nebraska, his Hejira – a statement of intent made in the quietest way possible.

Title: BLAME IT ON BABY
Review: It's a sound we've come to know DaBaby handle on his own, but he invites industry peers like Quavo ("Pick Up"), Future ("Lightskin Shit"), YoungBoy Never Broke Again ("Jump") for the ride.

Title: World, You Need a Change of Mind
Review: It doesn't seem content with just being an enjoyable album, which makes it impossible for this listener to be content with its failure to live up to its own hype.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: The album has its moments, but you really couldn't call it the main event. [Jun 2009, p.99]

Title: You Tell Me
Review: You Tell Me is probably at its peak when it leans further towards these pacey, pop-infused moments. However, the handful of tracks that stray into ballad territory are still often striking--not simply due to the musical intricacies that lie within them but because Hayes' vocals evoke strength and tenderness in equal measure, giving them some real emotional weight.

Title: Mine Is Yours
Review: Mine Is Yours? You can keep it, thanks.

Title: Give Up The Ghost
Review: Give Up the Ghost is evidence that not only is she one of the best singers in modern folk-rock music, but that she can write a potent set of songs every time out.

Title: High on Jackson Hill
Review: If you really feel you need another Canadian choral indie troupe in your life, this is worth a punt.

Title: Wild Strawberries
Review: “Wild Strawberries” and “Enchanter’s Nightshade,” which occupy over 30 minutes of the album. They are mid-tempo, trad-to-the-max, predictable clean-tone psych-music.... Yes, there’s strong guitar playing, and the bass and drums plod capably, but it stays in the background and never enters the head. The record suddenly feels awkwardly escapist, and the listener is reminded that the whole disc actually feels rather laid-back.

Title: Cold Roses
Review: Cold Roses comes as a bit of relief, bereft of the posturing that so often attends Adams’ work.... That said, there’s also a sense of retreat that permeates the record, a willingness to offer the comforts of familiar tones instead of ambitiously taking chances.

Title: The King is Dead
Review: On The King is Dead, The Decemberists decided to fully immerse themselves in a style they've flirted with for years.

Title: Ghost Culture
Review: It's clear that he's arranged them with an ear for future extended mixes in which the pop songs fall away, leaving only the shuddering metallic chassis underneath. Maybe, in retrospect, it's his judicious sense of balance that holds him back: a few more extremes, and his next work might really sing.

Artist: Avec le Soleil Sortant de sa Bouche
Title: Pas pire pop, I Love You So Much
Review: In short, they make experimental rock sound so easy when the reality is anything but.

Title: An End Has a Start
Review: The songs get puffed and fluffed up but lose the wiry edge of "Munich," burying Chris Urbanowicz's guitar until it all sounds like Coldplay. Nice tunes, but louder, please.

Title: Kiss Me Once
Review: There’s more than enough in this album to keep her in that position--so, come for the gay brostep, stay for the songcraft and character.

Title: Mauve
Review: It's 2012, and the lush expanse of Mauve, both feet planted in 1991, still has the ability to spread over you slowly and entirely, like a veil of noise.

Title: Dark Young Hearts
Review: Dark Young Hearts shines with talent, pop tunes with those secret corners you think were put there just for you to spot. Lyrical flaws aside, it's an indelible mark of grandeur on our decaying decade.

Title: The Way
Review: Macy Gray is back, easily delivering on expectations.

Title: Gods of the Earth
Review: When it comes to the vocals, though, Cronise never delivers on the same level as the rest of the band’s work, and the longer Gods of the Earth goes on, the more distracting this weakness becomes.

Title: To Dreamers
Review: Who cares if Stoltz listens to the Kinks and Beatles too much when he sings like an angel?

Title: Asleep in the Bread Aisle
Review: The quality of Roth's rhymes varies wildly, from sophomoric to inspired, but when the two collide, as on the funky rant 'Bad Day,' he hits the sweet spot and the funny bone.

Title: Ribbons
Review: For all its apparent homogeneity, there’s considerable diversity in approach, with the resonant, vibes-like tones and cyclical guitar waves of “Strand” a continent apart from the shadowy, almost Krautrock manner of “Fog March”.

Title: Away
Review: Okkervil River is now firmly understood as what it always was: a collective of talented musicians sharing, for however long or briefly, in the vision of Will Sheff.

Title: White Pony
Review: At their worst, Deftones can sound almost like a parody of themselves. But at their best, the band fashions a heavy, claustrophobic atmosphere in which Moreno spins his dark, personal tales of misery and heartbreak against a backdrop of music that careens from the ugly to the beautiful. Most of the time, White Pony finds Deftones at their best.

Title: Invisible Hour
Review: Invisible Hour is poetic singer/songwriter fare at its best, and this is Joe Henry’s masterpiece.

Title: Heads Up
Review: It’s a journey through their journey, and of influences and styles we’ve all known and loved. But it has all the joy of something completely new, pulled together at the seams lovingly and beautifully into a patchwork that, at first, may feel like clash or confusion but in time feels full of strength.

Title: School of the Flower
Review: It is a beautiful result that, through the austere and effortlessly enchanting tunes, leaves you feeling the emotion infinitely more than any self-professed ‘emo’ might.

Title: Jackrabbit
Review: His predilection for marrying sublime pop melodies to bombastic arrangements laced with classical avant-garde flourishes has reached a new level of focus, and, resultantly, potency, on Jackrabbit.

Title: Mazes
Review: If the proceedings get a bit "same-y" at times, it's with good reason. Johnson understands the concept of expansion through repetition and uses it to great effect. As the album tumbles to a close with the eight-minute "Goners," the band's operational scheme seems stunning in its clarity.

Title: Sailing to Philadelphia
Review: Sailing to Philadelphia represents yet another high watermark in his impressive recording career.... If there's anything to quibble about here, it's that the CD's energy sags because it contains so many ballads and mood pieces.

Title: The Blue Hour
Review: It finds Suede wrapping up a triptych of records since their 2013 reunion and in doing so they feel positioned with one foot in the familiar camp of old while striding forward with the other into fresh, unknown territory. [Oct 2018, p.34]

Title: thecontrollersphere
Review: Thecontrollersphere is another thrilling addition to the Of Montreal catalog, but it's hardly a welcoming entry point for those unaccustomed to the depraved yet tantalizing world of Kevin Barnes.  For longtime fans though, this EP represents another exhilarating turn from one of America's most singular musicians.

Title: Scurrilous
Review: Classic/stadium rock and brainy trash collide in "Tandem" and "Moonlight;" "Termites" rocks like Minus The Bear, Overkill and Yes; and it's obvious someone's discovered Mahavishnu Orchestra abnd Primus. [Apr 2011, p.118]

Title: Dream On
Review: This lack of clear signposts can make navigating the nightmare-laden second half of Dream On a bit more difficult as the sound effects pile up and the tracks get denser.

Title: Sold Out
Review: Ultimately, Sold Out is not doing what its title cheekily alludes to. Although it traverses a variety of genres outside of footwork’s typical territory, DJ Paypal never relents on the actual practice of the juke: the core sound of the beat, getting danced on.

Title: Gunslinger
Review: Too often here he squanders his effort trying to pump life into flat material.

Title: Transatlanticism
Review: A lush, impeccably produced, musically adventurous, emotionally resonant examination of the way relationships are both strengthened and damaged by distance, the album surpasses Gibbard's other career highpoints, which is really saying something.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Flying Microtonal Banana
Review: For such an experimental concept, Flying Microtonal Banana still finds a box of safety and doesn’t try to get out of it too much.

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: The Rip Tide is moderate in ambition, and hardly a masterwork, if such things empirically exist.

Title: Pyramid
Review: While still offering glimmers of Jaga Jazzist’s undefinable, futuristic aspirations, the maximalist ethos of Pyramid ultimately comes across as oddly old-fashioned at a time when acts like 75 Dollar Bill are redefining the hypnotic potential of instrumental soundscapes.

Title: Sound Mirrors
Review: This is probably the best album we've seen in the new millennium from a mid-'90s techno producer.

Title: The Odd Couple
Review: The duo’s modern take on a classic sound runs throughout the new record, a worthy 13-song sophomore effort.

Title: Resolve
Review: Poppy Ackroyd chooses to move at a efficiently percussive pace throughout (best highlighted by the fertile and aptly-named "Time"), giving the album a post-modern atmosphere rarely explored on many classical-inspired albums, making Resolve an album hard to pin down and hard to categorize, but easy to adore.

Title: On the Ones and Threes
Review: Even in the heavier moments, the album plays with a cool, unruffled composure that seems more easygoing than prior outings, making for a comfortable, welcome return.

Title: Karma For Cheap
Review: A valuable new addition to the fringes of Americana.

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: What pushes I Learned the Hard Way towards being something truly brilliant as opposed to just very, very good is how well it works as a cohesive, well-rounded whole.

Title: Childish Prodigy
Review: Kurt Vile: 50% Velvet Underground; 50% The Jesus And Mary Chain. Childish Prodigy: 50% Velvet Underground & Nico; 50% Darklands.

Title: T R O U B L E
Review: The fruits of his change of mind are bittersweet and eloquent alt.pop songs that recall Bon Iver. [May 2016, p.82]

Title: Leave Me Alone
Review: It really only hopes to make you smile with smart twin harmonies and silly lyrics. On those terms, Leave Me Alone is a unqualified success.

Title: Beware and Be Grateful
Review: Beware and Be Grateful's main flaw: an occasional quirk overload.

Title: Long Way Down
Review: The most impressive thing about Long Way Down is how, despite being an album based on a simple, almost naïve set of concepts--being in love, falling out of love, the raw emotion of being young and not understanding the world yet--it sounds accomplished well beyond Odell’s years.

Title: Whitechapel
Review: Its peaks make Whitechapel the band's best album yet by a wide margin. [Jul 2012, p.98]

Title: The Inheritors
Review: The Inheritors is a fiercely original feast of experimental sound. [Jul 2013, p.76]

Title: Costa Blanca
Review: For while Costa Blanca superficially suggests a trip to some Euro-trash mall outlet, listen closer and you hear a dark, subversive critique.

Title: John Wizards
Review: John Wizards is, to paraphrase the anthropologist Claude Levi-Strauss' opinion on animals, "good to think with." But that won't make people want to listen to it. What will is its hip diversity, sunny disposition, and the fact that Withers never asks more of his audience than he's willing to give: A man of contract, he puts his clients first.

Title: Steal This Album!
Review: A relevant addition to System's catalog.

Title: Winchester Cathedral
Review: Minor aesthetic gripes aside though, ‘Winchester Cathedral’ is how you and I want Clinic to be.

Title: How I Learned to Write Backwards
Review: Another fine batch of eloquent, classic sounding pop songs, with a little bit of mustard added to it as well.

Title: Rise Up
Review: At 15-songs long the album can stand tall after the required trimming, making Rise Up a giant leap in the right direction after the lukewarm "Till Death Do Us Part."

Title: Walking On A Dream
Review: Walking on a Dream initially sounds as familiar as montage music in an HBO midday movie, but it will haunt your dreams.

Title: Unleashed
Review: For the most part, Unleashed puts the grits and gravy back into mainstream country.

Artist: Someone Still Loves You Boris Yeltsin
Title: Fly by Wire
Review: While Fly By Wire is pleasing, it feels like a daydream: lovely while it lasts, fading quickly, and hard to remember once it’s gone.

Title: Shortly After Takeoff
Review: Written from the heart and dredged from pop music's boneyard, Shortly After Takeoff feels like the album Christinzio has been working toward his whole career.

Title: Ultimate Painting
Review: Even though everything that Ultimate Painting have to offer has been heard before, the richness of their chosen source material- so utterly packed with hooks- puts them onto a winner.

Title: Meds
Review: Meds is as bare and honest as Placebo has ever been.

Title: Non-Believers
Review: It sounds like a Mac McCaughan record, which is a well-established concept even if this is technically the first Mac McCaughan record.

Title: Production
Review: What could have been a huge breakthrough instead sounds staid, as if he were so used to rocking the house that he didn't want to risk rocking the boat.

Title: Human Energy
Review: Human Energy is an exhilarating showcase for Stewart's continually mutating vision of abstract pop.

Title: Pink
Review: If Pink’s more evolution than revolution, it still stomps all over most of its close genre surroundings, leaving maybe Tiger Bear Wolf and The Woods as far as 2005 goes.

Title: Transnormal Skiperoo
Review: There is much here that is wonderful, but less of the tone set by the self-parodically chirpy 'Turqouise House' would have improved matters. [Nov 2007, p.132]

Title: Beware and Be Grateful
Review: The songs are engaging and incredibly catchy, but lack emotion ― that intangible quality that will take this feel-good record and give it staying power.

Title: Clear Heart Full Eyes
Review: With his first solo release, Finn hasn't gone too far away from his core aesthetic, but the move is enough to justify his own album.

Title: Year Zero
Review: Make no mistake this is NIN as usual, but [it is] an effortless, inspired, and unaffected Trent Reznor the likes of which we may not have had the pleasure of knowing for almost a decade and a half.

Title: Film School
Review: Right now, they're one unforgettable song from greatness.

Title: Faith in Strangers
Review: The album is another leap forward for the producer, refining his sense of songcraft and expanding his instrumental palette without sanding down his rough edges in the slightest. Faith doubles down on the industrial brutality of Problems, while also balancing that with a sense of hope and comfort rarely heard from Stott previously.

Title: The Liberty Of Norton Folgate
Review: The songs are wordy and disappointingly light on the knock 'em dead catchiness that was once their forte, but what The Liberty of Norton Folgate lacks in hit singles it makes up for in glorious ska/reggae arrangements and Suggs's perpetual chirpiness.

Title: Fully Qualified Survivor
Review: While all three ["Naked Ladies and Electric Ragtime," "Fishbeard Sunset," and "Andru's Easy Rider."] contain some magnificent guitar work, they are departures from what is otherwise an incredibly cohesive and great album.

Title: The Glowing Man
Review: Consolidation more than innovation, The Glowing Man still presents the current incarnation of Swans in its best light, as if this is the record the band has been working toward these past seven years.

Title: Pokey LaFarge
Review: Midwesterner Pokey LaFarge infuses would-be moribund styles with rare vigour, though lyrical concerns are anything but nostalgia. [Jul 2013, p.77]

Title: FROM DEEWEE
Review: They arrive at the settled creative space they’ve hinted at but never quite reached in the past.

Title: Green Language
Review: It’s most thrilling moments are the ones you’ve already heard before.

Title: Scholars
Review: By making a boldly experimental leap in a career already full of them, Dyer and Sanchez have created a surprisingly accessible record that shows off some of their best work to date. Whatever they call themselves, their powerful alchemy shouldn’t be ignored.

Title: Detroit Deli (A Taste of Detroit)
Review: If only rappers T3 and Elzhi had the personality to match the enticing soundscapes. [16 Jul 2004, p.76]

Title: Sleeping Operator
Review: Accomplished, shiny, but hard to get excited about. [Nov 2014, p.102]

Title: Judy Sucks a Lemon For Breakfast
Review: Cornershop's 2009 incarnation may not have the kinetic energy of the 2002 model, or the accidental pop brilliance of "Asha", but it isn't short on inventiveness.

Title: Paul Walker
Review: Paul Walker is painfully realistic, openly grim and socially unconscious, expressing a worldview that really, only Kindlon seems comfortable expressing in our scene.

Title: Sweet Disarray
Review: It's pleasantly pristine stuff from the still relative newcomer.

Title: Boxer
Review: Boxer works best as a mood piece; it's also the first National release to work as a whole, and it's the best album I've heard so far this year.

Title: California Nights
Review: The duo of Bethany Cosentino and Bobb Bruno move further toward mastering the [beach music] vibe on their third studio album, California Nights. They do so not by celebrating carefree romps along Pacific Coast Highway, though, but by inverting the Beach Boys' fun-fun-fun narrative.

Title: X
Review: X may be their niftiest since Adrenalize.

Title: What We Lose in the Fire We Gain in the Flood
Review: Thnakfully, as the album continues, the songs grow more developed as orchestrally augmented tracks "Right Place" and "LA Rain" showcase Burhenn's distinct vocal abilities. [May 2010, p.108]

Title: Anywhere I Lay My Head
Review: The whole set is heavily dosed with reverb and electro-swirls, perhaps to cloak Johansson's vocal limitations as much as to add psychedelia.

Title: Magna Carta Holy Grail
Review: Magna Carta Holy Grail is a solid example of a decent modern rap album and nothing more.

Title: One People One World
Review: It’s always been hard to translate the irresistible propulsion of Femi Kuti’s live shows into a comparably effective studio realisation, but with One People One World he makes a decent stab.

Title: Curtis
Review: It's a solidly above-average rap record, featuring a generous handful of very likeable songs and only two unqualified duds.

Title: Untitled
Review: Untitled should make no sense to any sentient being older than 18, but that isn't ageism, it's practical marketing

Title: The Photo Album
Review: As intelligent, bittersweet, angular stuff, whether it’s alt.rock, guitar-pop, or even emo is immaterial. Labels be damned - just call it great music.

Title: Rhythm and Repose
Review: The album is slow and steady without ever finding its pinnacle.

Title: Omnion
Review: Here, on My Curse and Cure and Wild Child, the lyrical remorse chafes intriguingly against the musical euphoria, while the title track sets Sharon Van Etten’s affecting vocals against swooning electronics.

Title: Defend Yourself
Review: The best that can be said of Defend Yourself is that it isn't embarrassing; they didn't lose the plot like the Pixies, and it's better than The Sebadoh simply because they got out of that L.A. studio and back to their roots. But it also doesn't add anything to the story or feel like it needs to exist.

Title: Another One
Review: At their best, these songs have a charm that's aching and amiable.

Title: Run to Ruin
Review: What keeps Nastasia from succumbing to grotesque melodrama is the razor-like incisiveness she brings to her lyrics.

Title: A Universe that Roasts Blossoms for a Horse
Review: The LP's title might suggest the randomised poetry of google translate, but Low Probability Of A Hug speaks a language everyone can understand. [Oct 2019, p.85]

Title: Departing
Review: There's no denying that Departing is miles ahead of where the band was a year ago and while die-hards will love Hometowns for a long time to come, Departing is absolutely the band's strongest work to date.

Title: Ode to Joy
Review: There’s nothing about Ode to Joy that is meant to set the airwaves afire. It’s raw elegance; a surplus of creativity delivered with equal portions of restraint.

Title: Volume Two
Review: The new album proves again that she’s not a dabbler, just as it proves again that she and Mr. Ward, her producer, share similar ideals.

Title: Twin Fantasy
Review: The results of Toledo’s re-imagination add up to enough to make this feel like more than just a perfectionist’s pursuit.

Title: Heartland
Review: Whatever you care to call him, the man’s come up with the goods.

Title: Ritual Union
Review: This band's gradual edging over the precipice of mainstream acceptance has been richly deserved; now, everyone should hear this dragon roar.

Title: Day & Age
Review: It's an odd record that finds room for an alien abduction, marimbas, family illness (the eerie 'Goodnight, Travel Well'), Spandau Ballet sax solos and Jona Lewie's 1980 hit 'Stop the Cavalry.'

Title: Black and White
Review: Stuffed full of prospective hits, Wretch's desire to rank beside Kanye and Jay-Z may not be that far fetched. [Sep 2011]

Title: White Trash with Money
Review: "White Trash With Money" is one of his best albums, partly because it finds a lighthearted way to smuggle recent years' redneck pride into this year's love-song boom. [6 Apr 2006]

Title: Let Go
Review: Most of it is pretty middle-of-the-road female singer-songwriter tripe.

Title: Spring
Review: It is a hazy path through a dusty landscape of sadness and enlightenment that never arrives at answers or certainties, but shimmers with an eternal mystery. [Dec 2019, p.90]

Title: No, You C'Mon
Review: Many of the songs... are short, some feeling cut off in their prime, others a little undeveloped. [combined review of both discs; Feb 2004, p.90]

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: Nocturnal Koreans is a testament to their continued relevance.

Title: Tourist
Review: Their horizons have broadened. [Feb 2005, p.102]

Title: Total Strife Forever
Review: A Major new British talent is born in William Doyle's solo debut, which sounds like the great lost album that Brian Wilson, Eno and Bjork should have made together. [Feb 2014, p.75]

Title: Heart Pressed Between Stones
Review: Full of eerie trembles and trills, Camila De Laborde's voice is similarly ethereal, if sometimes numbed, and she and Daniel Hermann combine to create glistening, immersive soundscapes. [Jan 2019, p.19]

Title: Late for Nothing
Review: Late for Nothing is a solid entry in this small but surprisingly fun subgenre of hyperactive metal.

Title: This Old Dog
Review: Hazier, more hypnotic, and like most sequels--yeah--not as effective, it’s hamstrung by an uncharacteristically grating synth refrain. While not bad, it’s hard to shake the feeling of déjà vu.

Title: Museum of Love
Review: Even if Museum of Love sometimes comes across as a sampler of DFA sounds past and present, it's an album that those who enjoy the label's output will almost certainly like, and a promising debut in its own right.

Title: Magic Hour
Review: Nostalgia-driven fan-funding is a useful way to see which short-lived phenoms have anything left in the tank, but Magic Hour suggests Luscious Jackson is a little too far removed from what drove the group to make music in the first place.

Title: This Time
Review: Ten tight tracks, and that includes the epic "Intro," puts this on the man's top-shelf, where it sits next to The Reason as the album's flashy little brother.

Title: Arular
Review: M.I.A.'s vivid debut already sounds like a booty-shaking milestone to rank alongside The Streets and Dizzee Rascal. [May 2005, p.98]

Title: Worship
Review: Worship doesn't break new ground, and it's arguably not even the greatest record done in this vein (or even the greatest record by APTBS, for that matter). But there's a diligent craftsmanship here and just enough attitude to carry the album all the way to the finish line.

Title: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
Review: Small quibbles aside, I'll Never Get Out Of this World Alive is a solid addition to Steve Earle's impressive body of work that should satisfy both faithful and new listeners alike.

Title: Pinewood Smile
Review: The Darkness have regained much of the joy, silliness and virtuostic songcraft that made their 2003 debut Permission To Land such fun. [Nov 2017, p.96]

Title: Emily's D+Evolution
Review: While Spalding never sounds anything less than original on the album, part of the beauty here is in recognizing her inspirations and reveling in how she has made them her own.

Title: Mareridt
Review: Amalie Bruun (aka Myrkur) returns in feral form with a fresh set of frozen warnings and blackened ballads. ... On “Funeral” she teams up with Chelsea Wolfe for a duet that never quite gels and feels frustratingly half formed, while “Kætteren” confusingly slips a sliver of traditional Scandinavian folk music into the mix. Even worse is end track “Børnehjem” where demonic child whispering over Myrkur’s medieval monkish chant evokes Blair Witch memories and ultimately drags the whole album down. [Dec 2017, p.60]

Title: Loud Patterns
Review: Loud Patterns is an overtly ambitious first album, which fittingly captures Molleson's "difficult to define" approach.

Title: Melodia
Review: Back from the brink of a long-promised implosion, the Vines sound like a band renewed on their first album since being booted from Capitol following dismal sales of 2006's muddled "Vision Valley."

Title: Evil Spirits
Review: A batch of songs that snap and snarl in all the right places. [May 2018, p.27]

Title: Silver Eye
Review: Silver Eye shows mo loss of conviction, a dense, meditative collection that explores cosmic mysteries and natural wonders without any wispiness. [May 2017, p.92]

Title: Porcelain
Review: There's just no getting around how much stronger Sparta are than so many of their peers.

Title: Laws of Illusion
Review: McLachlan simply sounds like McLachlan here, seemingly unaged by the seven years that have elapsed since her last record and unconcerned with new trends.

Title: Wildflower
Review: There are far too many children’s voices, snatches of birdsong, glissandi of saccharine strings, and always the half-heard, half-sensed thwack of Frisbee upon social media manager.

Title: Seven Steps Behind
Review: Seven Steps Behind requires being listened to in a relaxed manner without anticipation, treating the whole as potent, highly dynamic background music.

Title: Meet Glen Campbell
Review: The listenable authority of Campbell’s voice, especially on Foo Fighters' 'Days Like These,' confers the poise you suspect Richard Ashcroft was looking for while solo, but never found.

Title: Thumbtacks and Glue
Review: Hamilton writes very nice folk rock songs, the way a 1,000 song writers do, but he, unlike most of his completion, he also wires them with dynamite and blows them sky high.

Title: Speedin' Bullet 2 Heaven
Review: On a sonic level, much of this album is strong but the identity and continuity are lackluster.

Title: Parker Millsap
Review: One of the album’s more striking elements is its limited instrumental palette.

Title: Funeral Mariachi
Review: This is as riveting and beautiful a valedictory address as you could hope for from these underground heroes. [Jan 2011, p.95]

Title: Working in Tennessee
Review: At 74, one of American music's patriarchs sounds as sprite as ever, kicking off with a great honky-tonk anthem, the joyous title song.

Title: Sinking into a Miracle
Review: They take more risks this time around, but not in a way that alienates the listener. The result is a sublime collection of freely expressive grooves which uplift and inspire.

Title: The Feast of the Broken Heart
Review: [The album] is most notable for two typically saturnine contributions from unlikely electro diva John Grant. [Jun 2014, p.98]

Title: Good News For People Who Love Bad News
Review: A daring yet accessible disc.

Title: Back Into the Woods
Review: It's a gem for Harcourt fans and the sweetest of introductions for new listeners.

Title: A Wasteland Companion
Review: His seventh is his most vivid and varied yet.

Title: Parc Avenue
Review: Parc Avenue often strays too far into excess and departure for departure’s sake to enjoy the brand of a songwriter’s tour-de-force.... But as a fully realized and lovingly sculpted aesthetic, there may be few stronger full-length debuts waiting in this year’s wings.

Title: All At Once
Review: All At Once and Numb are instant, stadium-size anthems, and when the band sound as if they're trying to cover too many bases at once, Jollett's enthusiasm for a killer chorus and a good, dramatic yarn sees him home.

Title: My Name Is My Name
Review: This is certainly a fine album, pretty much throughout.

Title: Serpentine Prison
Review: If Berninger intended to establish an imprint beyond his day job, he certainly succeeded here. Once Serpentine Prison opens its doors, visitors will likely find it hard to leave.

Title: My Father Will Guide Me Up a Rope to the Sky
Review: My Father Will Guide Me Up A Rope To The Sky sounds more like the essence of Michael Gira than the Angels Of Light ever did, and ought to also serve as another broadside to the idea of reformations being inherently grubby and uncreative ventures.

Title: Every Valley
Review: Public Service Broadcasting's intentions are to be praised, even if the result is weak and unfocused. If the SDP leadership had formed a band, it would sound like this.

Title: Jiaolong
Review: While other possible sonic antecedents abound, the full album feels more roots than retro, old tools reclaimed to new ends.

Title: Desire Lines
Review: Desire Lines lacks the hooks of their best work, with no obvious hits.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: It’s a perfect album in every sense of the word, this album is timeless.

Title: Eight Gates
Review: These songs, Molina’s living animals, continue to make their way through the world, ensuring that their creator’s legacy lives on.

Title: Hail To The Thief
Review: The new songs have attitude, but they sound like outtakes from 2000's classic Kid A and 2001's lesser Amnesiac.

Title: Imploding the Mirage
Review: The 80s-loving Vegas crew delivers its strongest set of songs in years. [Sep 2020, p.68]

Title: Ire Works
Review: The band is clearly comfortable with the medium that it occupies between aggressive and technical post-hardcore yet is beginning to tread new territory.

Title: Fight Softly
Review: Fight Softly is, while not a game-changer, certainly a level-raiser. It glistens with pop immediacy, rollicks with breathtaking percussive interpositions, and clatters to a beat entirely of its own construct.

Title: Black Metal
Review: Its second half is abrasive to the extreme, but by this point the hypnotic album’s already worked its charm. If Blunt is ever to settle into a routine, this should be his blueprint.

Title: Sequel To The Prequel
Review: Nothing to rival ‘Time For Heroes’, then, but this as accessible, and as listenable, as anyone may have hoped for.

Title: Voyageur

Review: Wigflip is another document of Madlib weaving his near-impermeable armor of credibility despite some chinks. [Year End, p. 88]

Title: What Comes After The Blues

Title: The Raven That Refused to Sing (And Other Stories)

Title: The Understanding
Review: Even in its migration from the groovy '70s to the technocratic '80s, though, Röyksopp has become a lot cooler than it has to be.

Title: In Time

Title: All Hands on the Bad One
Review: Their brightest, most accessible album to date... the band is absolutely brimming with confidence and vitality.

Title: What's Next to the Moon
Review: Kozelek's sparse, haunting delivery can render even the basest material achingly affecting...

Title: Ring

Title: Self Help Serenade
Review: The hazy pop backing and too-similar melodies lend a rather homogenized sound. [#10, p.112]

Title: Them Crooked Vultures

Title: Funeral

Title: Melbourne

Title: The Preacher's Son
Review: It fizzles out with embarrassing speed.

Title: Pony

Title: Until the Quiet Comes

Title: Mar Dulce

Title: Arca
Review: It’s beautiful. The second half of the album, as mentioned earlier, is less interesting.

Title: Gutterflower
Review: Headed for a prom near you... it's the Goo Goo Dolls.

Review: After a pair of impressively strong solo releases, Craig Finn has made it a hat trick with I Need a New War, and the passion and superb craft of these songs make this a must for anyone who cares about American songwriting.

Review: Amiably lightweight. [Jun 2007, p.115]

Title: Soul of a Woman

Title: Charmer
Review: Thirty years in, Mann continues to charm, a hidden glint in her eye.

Title: That Lucky Old Sun
Review: Every single note feels forced, in hock to a sound and a set of attitudes that date from a time before many of us were born.

Title: Colfax
Review: It's a new band, a new sound, but the same old, marvellous songwriting. It's a killer combination.

Giannascoli's creativity is endless and as he continues his never-ending output of mysteriously disorienting and strangely familiar songs, he's becoming stronger and weirder with every album.

Title: Last Day of Summer
Review: What makes Last Day of Summer engaging has as much to do with White Denim's potential future as it does its roots.

Title: Catacombs
Review: This is an album of long, mysterious love songs to get lost in for days--seek it out.

Review: All these tracks, whilst lovely in themselves, are made ten times better when tethered together.

Gordon can be startling at times, and she does it all with a cool (a non-commercial, unreproducible cool, that is) that, as much as anything, makes No Home Record so particular to Gordon.

Review: An ambitious project, King Gizzard succeed into enticing you into fully absorbing yourself into their wild, bizarre universe.

Review: Corralling such a large cast into anything like a coherent vision is no easy task, but it's one that the Concretes manage with some aplomb on a consistently spectacular album. [Amazon UK]

Review: Recalling names like Tomberlin and especially Julien Baker, Ellis' melodies are much less memorable than her plaintive sentiments, likely limiting Born Again's appeal to the heavyhearted.

Review: Mysterious Phonk feels extremely private in ways that are powerful but not entirely sorted out yet. Purrp finds numerous occasions to talk about smiling in the face of a cold world, but even a facetious smirk never really cracks, and the world is cold in only the most brightly-lit, fantastical, and dystopic ways.

Title: To Dust

Title: Providence
Review: A superbly restorative tonic for troubled times. [Sep 2020, p.108]

Title: Ungodly Hour
Review: Ungodly Hour’s draw lies in the detail; not only the blink-and-you’ll-miss-it strangeness – Busy Boy briefly opens with tremulous blues that could have been recorded in the 1930s, while the highly entertaining Tipsy mixes casually threatening lyrics with curious percussion sounds – but in the slow-burn appeal of the pair’s vocal melodies, which are habitually inventive, ornate and hauntingly beautiful.

Title: The Heart Speaks in Whispers
Review: The Heart Speaks In Whispers is the sound of her getting it right again. [Jul 2016, p.105]

Title: Songs From Black Mountain

Title: All American Made
Review: By adding a decent dose of 2017 into her classic sound, Price creates something truly great.

Title: For My Crimes
Review: Far from showing signs of slowing down, Nadler sounds more focussed here than ever, continuing to challenge herself and evolve, with her eyes fixed firmly on the horizon.

Review: While it's hard to top some of the early solo work, it's easily his best album in more than a decade, and for the first time in years, he's made a record to stand beside those early classics. [Winter 2009, p.73]

Review: It is an acceptable listen--on par with the Kills’ previous record, 2011’s Blood Pressures--but your best hope for enjoying it is to manage your expectations.

Review: Those invested in the band’s slow-motion refinement of simmering melancholy will find that they’ve discovered yet more fresh nuance to that sound, as they seem to every time.

Title: Neon
Review: Neon feels confident and complete. [9 Aug 2013, p.75]

Title: Electric Lines
Review: There’s no doubt that Electric Lines will be the basis for some excellent live sets. But as an album, most of these songs offer too little innovation, too little variation, and too little life.

Title: Holy Wood (In the Shadow of the Valley of Death)
Review: Manson still has the most bloodcurdling scream in rock. But the flat-footed musical backing on "Holy Wood" leaves his delivery sounding strained, like an overburdened star left naked on an empty stage.

Title: Together We're Heavy
Review: Grandiloquent, glorious gobbledygook.

Title: Songbird

Title: Weezer (Black Album)
Review: Whilst it is undeniably their most experimental work, the record listens like an audio representation of Theresa May’s awkward robot-like dancing--confused, cringingly uncomfortable and desperately out of touch.

Title: Person Pitch
Review: A marvelous, hazy trip full of Beach Boys-inspired psychedelia.

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: It's not certain whether the acre to the desert forest has been crossed, but the feeling that abides is one of compassionate admiration for Stevens, not only for making this beautiful album of unfaltering rawness (and one which may even provide a crutch, a brutal one, for others), but for all of his work that has preceded it, music which frequently transcended the hurt of a life so wounded at its root.

Title: Honey

Title: The Mix-Up

Title: What For?

Title: Down Like Gold

Title: Jarvis
Review: It's lyrically depressing, but if you're down in the dumps about the ills of the world and frustrated by a lack of personal achievement, there's surely not a better companion piece to have to hand as you wallow.

Title: Holy Fire
