Review: John Talabot and Axel Boman share a rep for expressive, expansive rhythms aimed at forward-thinking dancefloors--music that can stand in its own right, away from the club. Thrust together, it's an approach that the Catalan/Swedish twosome maintain. [May 2017, p.91]

Title: Crack The Skye
Review: There will be naysayers among the band's extreme, tatted legions. But Crack the Skye is an awesome display.

Title: Future Women
Review: It's a dense, ambitious record that finally has the confidence needed to pull of the swagger they've been approximating.

Title: Caveman
Review: Caveman sounds like the next logical step from CoCo Beware. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.91]

Title: Gore
Review: It's a beautifully dark album. [May 2016, p.107]

Title: Knee Deep
Review: WhoMadeWho have been accomplished, even inspired, in the past, but here they emerge on a whole new level, displaying a subtle command of tension and release and an assured, seamless blending of rock and electronics, suffused with unfeigned emotionalism, which calls to mind the confidence and mastery of marquee acts like LCD Soundsystem and Radiohead.

Title: The State of Gold
Review: The State of Gold is a perfectly competent album, but after Pond’s 17 years in the music biz, competent isn’t enough. The primary problem with The State of Gold is that it exhibits a failure of imagination.

Title: Ecstatic Arrow
Review: Ecstatic Arrow is full of declarations delivered with such lucid certainty that they make a brighter future seem persuasively simple.

Title: Antidotes
Review: Antidotes might be a touch weird, enough to earn the badge of “musician’s music”, and its cryptic lyricism isn’t typical of a romp. But when Foals’ rhythms bristle and their guitars go colorfully spastic, the art house and dance house become one and the same.

Title: Chromatica
Review: Chromatica is not Lady Gaga returning to form, that would imply she’s ever had a dull moment - even Joanne held its own in a world of expectation - what is however, is an embellishment of who she is, both inward and outward, in a moment where the world needs beating, pulsating music to get lost in.

Title: This Path Tonight
Review: This is a no-frills type of record that prizes style over substance.

Title: Jay Stay Paid
Review: J$P‘s strengths might outweigh its weaknesses, but it’s just not enough. Also, this album feels far too long at a mere 60 minutes’ runtime.

Title: Information Retrieved
Review: [Listening to the album is like] a reunion with an old friend, but not necessarily a close one. For half an hour, you think "why don't we do this more often?" until it ends and you remember how frustrating they can be.

Title: Stranger on the Sofa
Review: Much more songwriter-based than [his] early discs. [Sep 2006, p.230]

Title: House of Sugar
Review: His songs are rarely constructed from a place of deeply considered meaning. Instead, they’re largely streams of his conscience: creations that invite listeners to cosy up in his world. On ‘House of Sugar’, it’s his most exciting invitation yet.

Title: Movement
Review: Movement is one of those lovely surprises that makes you think, "Of course that's how music should sound right now".

Title: My Ride's Here
Review: An eclectic, catchy opus that equals and occasionally surpasses his last really great release, Sentimental Hygiene.

Title: Hot Shit!
Review: Coomes and Weiss' compact set up maintans an awkward dynamic balancing natural elegance with barbed experiment to sustain the music's flux of design and accident. [#235, p.64]

Title: Return to the Moon
Review: The voice and their lyrics sit differently, somehow, against Knopf's arrangements, which can be by turns delicate, mischievous and furious. [Nov 2015, p.105]

Title: Positive Force
Review: If there's anything wrong with Positive Force, it's that it's better suited as background music than bearing up to intense listening; while the guitar lines on most of the songs here are deliciously difficult to whistle, they're all essentially fairly similar.

Title: Original Colors
Review: Original Colors isn't extraordinary music.

Title: Life in Slow Motion
Review: With "Life In Slow Motion" he's delivered an album so rich and deft that it pushes beyond the realm of the humble singer-songwriter, to earn him a place alongside the likes of Springsteen and Van Morrison as one of music's revered elite. Without question, this is a classic album.

Title: America's National Parks
Review: On this excerpt of the suite’s overture, “New Orleans: The National Culture Park USA 1718,” you hear the deep focus in their [Anthony Davis and Smith's] rapport; it’s an accurate reflection of the mood sustained throughout the work.

Title: Alpine Static
Review: Experimental longueurs and lack of vocals mean this trip's not for everyone, but out-rock fans should get on board. [Aug 2005, p.109]

Title: One
Review: One offers ten tracks of zipless triple-A folktronica -- bland, edgeless songs like "A Million Ways" that wouldn't even heat up the Ballroom D dancefloor on the final night of a Midwestern Regional Sales Conference.

Title: Watch the Throne
Review: They turn out to be pretty good influences on one another. Jay sounds generally reinvigorated: good-humored, full of nimble, intricate wit and atypically emotionally revealing, and if Kanye's rhymes occasionally remain as clumsy and crass as his personal life choices, he drops far fewer boners than usual. [#81, p. 56]

Title: In The Rainbow Rain
Review: The result is an album that's deeply affecting, but which—even if it is—doesn't feel quite as personal or authentic as much of the band's previous output. It's also their most anachronistic record to date.

Title: King of the Beach
Review: It's major-key and resplendently colored, owing as much to Orange County skate-punk as it does to the Beach Boys.

Title: Playland
Review: What’s clear is how badly Marr needs a foil, a counterpart, a collaborator, because on his own his ideas only seem to stretch so far, and so, sadly, does our good will.

Title: Discovery
Review: Occasionally, as on the gurgling electro-pop of "Short Circuit," the album actually manages to disappoint. But more often it provides the kind of intelligently produced yet universally likeable floor-fillers that keep even devoted hipsters from killing themselves when their relatives drag them to suburban dance clubs.

Title: Tanglewood Numbers
Review: A surreal, tender, revealing record. [Nov 2005, p.104]

Title: Will To Be Well
Review: While many of the album’s stronger tracks are also its most spacey and elusive, the sequencing emphasizes just how important the clicking, EDM drums are to the project’s core.

Title: Strays
Review: This is carefully architected to pack arenas.

Title: Infiniheart
Review: That's ultimately the sticking point with Infiniheart: VanGaalen's songs tend toward folly, yet it's impossible to discount his commitment to the material.

Title: Children Running Through
Review: Overall, this dynamic collection has something unexpected at every turn. [10 Feb 2007]

Title: The Deconstruction
Review: E's gifts as a songwriter and vocalist are still sharp, and if you've ever been partial to Mark Everett's slightly skewed but engagingly literate outlook on the world, then The Deconstruction should meet with your approval.

Title: Ceremonials
Review: As one of the last big album releases to close out 2011, it's highly fitting that Ceremonials should be considered perhaps the most beautiful and absorbing of them all.

Title: EAR PWR
Review: EAR PWR have concocted a gorgeous chillwave gem. [Jul 2011, p.115]

Title: The Air Between Words
Review: On The Air Between Words, Martyn comes off tranquil, playful and completely in control of his own kaleidoscopic world.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: In Your Dreams is an album about exorcising the demons of the past and moving forward toward the beauty lingering in our imaginations.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: The momentum and joie de vivre is intoxicating, and unlike many a transitional record, it's a genuine hoot, an unexpected blast of sunshine between the darkness of Fables… and the fires of Document.

Title: Older Than My Old Man Now
Review: The autobiographical Older Than My Old Man Now is a gleefully morbid summing up of his life in which he ponders childhood, family history, aging and death with an attitude of incredulity that he should be 65 and turning out songs like "My Meds" and "I Remember Sex."

Title: Feeling Mortal
Review: Mr. Kristofferson's voice wavers, indicating general pitch areas rather than specific notes, and he doesn't use it artfully to stress images or ideas as he rolls through the words. Some of those lyrics, though, can be dense and strong, working inside and outside the styles and structures of his best years.

Title: Invisible Ones
Review: If you're striving to restore faith in a world of "prophets, pimps, angels" and "whores," you gotta do better than Sarah McLachlan melodies and a rented Haitian choir.

Title: Charli
Review: With Charli, she attempts to capture the spontaneity of those releases [Number 1 Angel and Pop 2] in a more polished format; more often than not, she succeeds.

Title: A Moving Picture
Review: His breathless, this-really-matters delivery is ill-served by lines such as "Ain't a fan of vegetables/ It ain't about the peas".

Title: No Tourists
Review: ‘Timebomb Zone’s ugly rave onslaught strikes first – you feel the stretch of a wince appear. ‘Champions of London’ and ‘Boom Boom Tap’ follow up with a one-two punch; you never saw it coming. Maybe ‘Give Me A Signal’ would be a late highlight, and it is, unless you’ve heard ‘Higher State Of Consciousness’ more than once, or ‘Poison’, for that matter. You never stood a chance. The only reasons to recommend this record over its predecessor is that it’s shorter and doesn’t have Sleaford Mods on it.

Title: Minor Love
Review: Green can turn on the charm--countrified finale Blacken My Stay and Castles And Tassles are winners, and "castles and tassles and fatulent assholes" is a hysterical refrain - but overall, Minor Love is a curiously enervating affair. [Feb 2010, p. 95]

Title: Concrete Vision
Review: There's an overwhelming lightness to Concrete Vision, even when the lyrics veer into darker territory on tracks like the rippled ballad "True Love" or the title track. The comforting timbre of Kramer's voice keeps the vibe mellow and even-keeled, a lifeline throughout the record's changing synth textures.

Title: People and Things
Review: All in all, People and Things hits home as an almost surprisingly diverse record from Jack's Mannequin.

Title: Blood Mountain
Review: When the members of Mastodon decided to make an audiophile's wet dream of a metal album, they abandoned the vein-bulging spontaneity of their former selves.

Title: Government Plates
Review: Its idiosyncratic animus is something to behold, and even if you don’t like it, both the digital age and Burnett himself can reassure you with the verse, “Don’t worry; in a few, you’ll all be somewhere else.”

Title: Painted Ruins
Review: While perhaps coming up slightly short on the nuanced splendor of Shields and the instantaneous élan of its Veckatimest, Painted Ruins is a special kind of conquest. Be it via the unseen sparks that spring forth from heartbreak or the dizzying urges that stem from one too many late-night wrangling with one’s place in the world, this is music stemming from a place that few artists can access.

Title: You Are All I See
Review: With the influx of worshippers only getting stronger these days, Active Child is a welcome addition to the pulpit.

Title: Marks To Prove It
Review: Overall, Marks to Prove It feels a bit anxious, but that's not necessarily to its detriment, and four LPs in, the Maccabees are still making smart and sophisticated Brit guitar rock.

Title: Nothing is Quick in the Desert
Review: Nothing is Quick in the Desert--its 14th studio recording--flexes the group's stadium-rap muscle. This was an album specifically designed to be played live, and some of the subtlety and nuance that informs Chuck D's most incisive raps is missing.

Title: Infra
Review: By adding just the right amount of static to the sugar of his sweeping arrangements, Richter's created an album that's precisely balanced between accessibility and depth, desolation and joy, melody and noise.

Title: That Lucky Old Sun
Review: After taking care of some unfinished business in recent years, Brian Wilson shows he still has the stuff of conceptual brilliance on his eighth solo album.

Title: The Blue Room
Review: The effect shifts from sophisticated to just short of snooze inducing as the disc wears on and what starts out as tasty ends up as more of the same when the vibe stays locked in its classy, stylish, chill out groove.

Title: One More Light
Review: One More Light sees the band embracing its melodic core, and offering no apologies as they expound upon it.

Title: The Documentary
Review: A mostly rich and involving experience. [Apr 2005, p.98]

Title: Halcyon Digest
Review: Deerhunter aren't just revivalists, though: in the main this is timeless music, seemingly made with the conviction that loveliness will always be lovely.

Title: Modern Times
Review: It’s an intriguing and thoughtful and occasionally lively record, but it’s not the rollicking, randy good time some folks would lead you to believe.

Title: Happy to You
Review: The songs here are supremely catchy and delivered with the kind of sleek sheen you'd expect from a Katy Perry or Kesha record, but it's the inventive instrumentation and surprising twists they take that give Happy To You its edge. [May 2012, p.104]

Title: Let's Get Out Of This Country
Review: You might not find heartache as enchanting as this anywhere else.

Title: The Only Thing I Ever Wanted
Review: Their sophisticated studio treatments make every sound sparkle. [Aug 2006, p.84]

Title: Madman
Review: The styles vary while the tonality is so consistent, so dialed in that all feels seamless and the transition from gorgeous to gutbucket feels as natural as sunset.

Title: Waiting on a Song
Review: Ornate and sunny, the album is a love letter to '60s R&B and '70s soft rock, with lushly arranged strings peppering the songs, none of which are longer than four minutes-and, truthfully, none of which would sound out of place in an Urban Outfitters following a Leon Bridges power hour.

Title: Let The Dominoes Fall
Review: Sometimes observing that a band keeps making the same record is an insult. Not so with Rancid--and not when the records are this good.

Title: Life Is People
Review: Scrub away reputations and this album is so much stronger than the latter-day works of many of Fay's contemporaries.

Title: Quality Control
Review: Despite the fluid interplay of the four MCs and J5's evolving musicality, 'Quality Control' lacks the singalong pop immediacy of 'Jurassic 5'.... Quality then. But it's not the old-skool classic we'd hoped for.

Title: The Animal Years
Review: Through previous albums, his love songs and narratives have grown ever more phantasmagorical, and now he's writing oracular meditations. Love and war, faith and music, restlessness and a longing for home pervade his new songs, which might turn pretentious if they weren't so grounded in folky melody. [10 Apr 2006]

Title: Huncho Jack, Jack Huncho
Review: A competent collobarative tape that nevertheless proves that Quavo should stick to Migos and Travis to curating his own albums.

Title: Sleep Mountain
Review: Sleep Mountain lacks both the urgency and unhinged fervour of Arcade Fire and the inventive mischief of the Flaming Lips.

Title: Wed 21
Review: The warm human purr of her ethereal vocals is juxtaposed towith fluid electronic elements and the occasional welcome interjection of bluesy guitar and jagged off-beat percussion.

Title: From Far Enough Away Everything Sounds Like The Ocean
Review: Perhaps not sounding as exactly like the ocean as the title suggests, the Swedish trio have, however, definitely delivered the same magnificence any sea ever could, and chances are as soon as it’s ended you’ll want to dive straight back in.

Title: Silver Ladders
Review: A mesmerising slowdive into the sonic depths. [Nov 2020, p.31]

Title: The Unfairground
Review: His best in more than 30 years, he teams up with members of Ladybug Transistor, Teenage Fanclub, and others for songs heavy on rememberance but energized with chin-up horns and strings that'll sound fresh to fans of the Decemberists and Arcade Fire. [Apr 2008, p.92]

Title: Friend and Foe
Review: While they are not afraid to bang the drums and rock out, Menomena keep the majority of this album behind a beautiful mask of complimentary melodies.

Title: Funstyle
Review: Although the four infamous tracks might be regarded as novelties in the Liz Phair repertoire, the entire album plays as a fascinating experimental work of an artist trying to dodge your negative abuses by coming at it from unexpected angles.

Title: Opium
Review: Curious, gorgeous and a little bit off its rocker. [Aug 2015, p.109]

Title: The Mix-Up
Review: The Mix-Up may not be the cure for 2004's disappointing "To the 5 Boroughs," but it grooves nicely in the meantime. [Summer 2007, p.79]

Title: Into The Woods
Review: Sounding as hale and hearty as they did on last year's The Machine Stops, the rejuvenated band attain the same state of cosmic ragged glory several more times on Into The Woods. [Jun 2017, p.30]

Title: Alaska
Review: Pretty but lightweight. [Sep 2013, p.96]

Title: Another Country
Review: Elements of rock, folk, and blues pervade, and producer George Drakoulias (Black Crowes, the Jayhawks) stays out of the way, allowing Merritt’s voice to embody the songs, all 11 of which flow from start to finish, uninterrupted and primed for full-on stardom.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: The result is an album that is as notable on its own as it is in the historical chillwave narrative.

Title: Showtime
Review: Whereas Boy In Da Corner was the sound of a young man expressing the fear and frustration of growing up in a dangerous and bleak environment, Showtime reflects the confidence and ebullience of a maturing artist optimistically embracing a bright and hopeful future.

Title: The Bad Testament
Review: Each song on The Bad Testament sounds old, yet somehow unfamiliar, a portrait of the outlaw country bad boy as an old man.

Title: Donkey
Review: What’s important is confirming that you haven’t completely lost it, that you’ve still got the inspiration that made us listen in the first place--Donkey, however, is in danger of making us forget.

Title: Party Store
Review: The conceit of The Dirtbombs covering dance music is genius.

Title: The Miraculous
Review: The standout pieces are the lengthier ones. Perhaps, if you are already aware of her work on Ceremony, then The Miraculous will not be a surprise to you. But if you have not, then it may well be a complete revelation.

Title: Yesterday Was Forever
Review: Her winning formula back in 2010 was blunt honesty delivered in the form of spoken-word style poetry. Back then, she doled out witty, tongue-in-cheek observations and wry take-downs with ease. Attempts to recapture this style are marred by lazy rhymes and a delivery that’s often more just her speaking over the track.

Title: In Exile Deo
Review: Hatfield's finest work in a decade.

Title: Heavy Mood
Review: It's a tighter take on pop than their early records, but as the storming energy that kicks off Heavy Mood begins to ebb away the group begins to feel oddly charmless.

Title: Ensemble Pearl
Review: This debut itself is compelling but because, at last, it represents a clear synthesis of so many of O’Malley’s activities.

Title: The Wonder Years
Review: This is a Hip Hop album, complete with the wondrous elements consistent with a broader musical appreciation. And it just might be 9th Wonder's best yet.

Title: No Holiday
Review: Shattuck’s voice feels raspier and more raw on some of the album’s 18 tracks, a little less energetic, but the musical chemistry between her, McDonald, and bassist Ronnie Barnett remains untouched by time.

Title: The Village
Review: The songs are all traditional but are given a cool Scandinavian edge. [Mar 2013, p.75]

Title: Mourn
Review: Recorded in just two days, the excitement coursing through Mourn's entire 24 minutes (including the bonus track "Boys Are Cunts") makes its funny, scary, pissed-off punk that much more irresistible.

Title: Europe
Review: Their 2010 self-titled debut [was] all hummable melodies, clap-along rhythms, and poignantly turned phrases. Europe maintains these qualities and improves upon its predecessor in almost every way.

Title: Color
Review: Color is an album of two halves, with gloomier hues on side two. [Nov 2016, p.53]

Title: Our Two Skins
Review: Our Two Skins is an album full of emotions – sadness, happiness, hope, love, loss – and all of it deeply felt and straight from the heart.
It's a testament to their talent that by their seventh album they're still continuing to develop and reinvent themselves.

Title: Arc
Review: Inevitably, Arc lacks coherence; it's the sound of a band working out who they want to be.

Title: Immersion
Review: It's robotically humourless; imagine C3PO discovering ecstasy and synths and you're there.

Title: Family Crimes
Review: The vocals feel particularly watered down, a pastel blur that lacks the highs and lows that the Leopards had delivered in the past, the songs blending too anonymously into each other.

Title: Haiku From Zero
Review: Pervasive throughout is the sense that yearning for the unobtainable is its own reward, and the band successfully imbues Haiku from Zero with the notion that both pleasure and pain remind us that we’re alive.

Title: Deep Fantasy
Review: White Lung demand attention, engaging heart-to-heart conversations while simultaneously rioting.

Title: Dust
Review: It’s her most complete-feeling album to date, and never seems like Halo is trying to please anyone but herself. Yet, she also manages to create emotional bridges through the sincerity of her compositions.

Title: Yesterday Was Lived & Lost
Review: It's an encyclopedia of rhythmic assimilation, perfectly executed, nary a lovingly adopted concept out of place. Catchy as hell, too.

Title: The Bones of What You Believe
Review: They write very strong songs, but aural satiation sinks in over Bones‘ 48 minute runtime.

Title: The Redeemer
Review: An unmissable craftman. [Jun 2013, p.69]

Title: Phantom Punch
Review: It hits hard without sacrificing any of Lerche's classic pop appeal.

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: This is music that hits the head, heart and hips all at once.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: Repeated listens unmask 'Ryan Adams' as a great record, and a sleek departure from 2011's 'Ashes & Fire.'

Title: Recover EP
Review: The trio’s past experiences may explain how it manages to exercise a seasoned talent for both variety and control.... The two “Recover” remixes, by Austria’s Cid Rim and U.K.-based Curxes, are filler. They’re pleasant on their own, but neither can hold up to the original.

Title: Rokstarr
Review: Although Cruz’s downfall comes when he acts the player (‘Break Your Heart’, ‘Dirty Picture’), it’s obvious his real talent comes when he exchanges vocal manipulation for balladeering as on ‘Falling In Love’, and disregards romantic cynicism for a rather hopeful ‘The 11th Hour’.

Title: Sparrow
Review: Intimate songs like these needed such intimate music behind it. You’ve been invited in to the confessional and your job is to listen, learn and support.

Title: Magic
Review: Six years on he sounds like a man not getting nearly enough cuddles.

Title: Earthquake Glue
Review: Earthquake Glue sees a return to the satisfyingly stylistic cohesion of 2001's Isolation Drills, ... while retaining the impressionistic aural fug that's so key to the band's appeal. [Sep 2003, p.98]

Title: Tamer Animals
Review: Bar a few tracks that outstay their welcome, there is a lot to love about this album.

Title: Lollipop
Review: Ultimately, the refrain to "slow down" on "Orange" captures where the modern Meat Puppets seem to rest best: casual and contemplative.

Title: Everything Goes Wrong
Review: With 13 songs to sit through, it all sounds like the same riffs, verses, choruses, and rhythms in slightly different contexts. It also sounds like a big disappointment from a band that roared out of the gate with several nice 7-inch cuts and a strong debut album.

Title: Corsicana Lemonade
Review: The lyrics dwell on age, family and endurance, but the backporch party vibe imparts a warm glow to proceedings.

Title: Life on a Rock
Review: Life on a Rock ultimately seems less like a beach party album than Chesney stretching out with his ghosts.

Title: Armonico Hewa
Review: Armonico Hewa proves that OOIOO are far from running out of ideas.

Title: Bad Blood
Review: Lyrics are corny and sometimes funny.

Title: Ersatz GB
Review: Everyone already knows what to expect and, largely, they'd be right.

Title: Abyss
Review: Abyss neatly encompasses the totality of her career, synthesizing the artist’s prolific catalog into her strongest and most ambitious album yet, a cavernous chasm filled with beauty, brutality, and endless possibility.

Title: Radlands
Review: Their boldest and most fantastically frisky record to date.

Title: Off With Their Heads
Review: Off With Their Heads deftest creations may fall just short of the Kasier Chief debut's ruddy-faced string of exhuberant big hitters, 'Never Beat A Beat,' 'Addicted To Drugs' and the huge 'Like You Too Much' are still sizeable cut above some of "Yours Truely's" tepid misfires. [Nov 2008, p.104]

Title: Buoys
Review: The aquatic theme of the album is appropriate and in line with the atmosphere Lennox’s quirky, gentle guitar-plucking consistently evokes. But this, nor the occasional flashes of beauty throughout the album, are enough to recommend Buoys’ unremarkable lonely beach music.

Title: Shake The Sheets
Review: If Shake the Sheets lacks the subtle, nuanced excursions of its predecessor, it's redeemed by an urgent, unrelenting focus.

Title: You Have Already Gone To The Other World
Review: You Have Already Gone to the Other World, produced by Deerhoof's John Dieterich, is their best yet. [May 2013, p.65]

Title: Super Taranta!
Review: This is more like their "Give ‘em Enough Rope," a perfectly fine extension of that first energy burst, one that deserved to be milked a bit.

Title: Kissin Time
Review: There’s nothing wrong with collaborators -- and Faithfull has picked some good ones -- but the quality seems to be directly linked to who is behind each song.

Title: Underneath
Review: If the Grammy-nominated Forever was their blistering hellscape, Underneath is a glitchy, industrial wasteland.

Title: Rad Times Xpress IV
Review: Wallop[s] you upside the head with an acid-induced mash-up of rollicking glam, gunky metal and ghetto-fabulous art rock.

Title: Whorl
Review: [A] solid offering in a drizzle of bleeps. [Oct 2014, p.79]

Title: Coexist
Review: It's exciting to hear the minimalist U.K. trio approach their new-crush odes with such austerity in Coexist.

Title: Thirteen Tales From Urban Bohemia
Review: They may not always transcend their influences, but even when they don't, they make wallowing in them a helluva lot of fun.

Title: James Pants
Review: A slightly sinister brand of enigma is a key component of his shtick, but it's hard not to wonder what this leftfield pop talent might come up with if he were asked to produce something a bit more crisp and definite.

Title: Kodama
Review: Kodama is one of 2016's most arresting releases. [15 Oct 2016, p.53]

Title: neo
Review: At times (Pay Attention To Me, Rot In Hell), their chief inspiration point seems to be Nirvana’s seething grind through Devo’s Turnaround, but their gleeful dedication to deafening scree also calls to mind both No Age and TAD’s 8-Way Santa.

Title: Magnifique
Review: On album five, they still manage to experiment and sound as fresh as they were when they spat out 'Seventeen Years'.

Title: Friendly Bacteria
Review: For much of the album's remainder, Carthy sticks with the melting pot approach that he and Greater Mancunian peers like Rae & Christian helped codify over a decade ago. [Jun 2014, p.93]

Title: Alice and Friends
Review: Alice and Friends doesn't produce often in that department [solid hooks], relying instead on the kind of raw energy that fuels a good house party.

Title: Blood Like Lemonade
Review: While Blood Like Lemonade offers nothing new, its depiction of a seasoned group reveling in their own nostalgia makes for good listening.

Title: Sleeping Through the War
Review: Sleeping Through The War is the embodiment of a gentle giant: huge in presence but unwaveringly accessible.

Artist: Thao & the Get Down Stay Down
Title: We The Common
Review: It’s a rollicking, exciting and inspiring tussle in a corner of Thao’s cheerful quilt of a discography.

Title: Obsidian
Review: Despite the density of the music, Obsidian is a wholly immersive experience, setting Baths back on course.

Title: New View
Review: New View is a lush and beautiful record that stands comfortably in such heady company.

Title: Stranger to Stranger
Review: A distinguished and captivating extension of, rather than a dramatic departure from, his rich body of work.

Title: Searching For Zero
Review: For the majority of tracks, they succeed in their goals. It’s only when looking back at the whole picture, somehow the pieces don’t quite appear to fit.

Title: Revival
Review: The title Revival is no hype: Fogerty is again in full command of his talent for blending heartfelt writing with irony-free meat-and-potatoes rock.

Title: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love
Review: Deafheaven’s brilliance has long been hung upon the pursuit of a truth, like documentarians before they hit the edit suite. These songs are filthy, dank, often devoid of light, but like a weed emerging from a pavement’s crack, there’s something resembling hope there. A suggestion that maybe there’s something more.

Title: NYC, HELL 3:00 AM
Review: Listen to NYC, HELL 3:00 AM close enough and you’ll hear them drumming at the windows of your mind’s storefront.

Title: ShadowParty
Review: For fans of this particular era, ShadowParty's debut offers welcome satisfaction, breathing new life into the familiar with fresh ideas and a freedom unhindered by the burden of the beloved acts from which they originated.

Title: bounty
Review: Higher-proof versions of both music and visuals exist, but these songs stand up all by themselves. [Jul 2013, p.85]

Title: America Give Up
Review: This is mainly just sunny, disintegrated, low-stakes rock music. [Mar 2012, p.84]

Title: Feel the Sound
Review: A playful effort that comes from an ease with pop hooks and power-pop chords, a knowledge of how to employ a steady beat.

Title: Pinch & Shackleton
Review: It's a beguilingly well-delivered statement in a dialect that was sidelined in favor of the cult of bass or the florescent synths. [Dec 2011, p.53]

Title: Wild Winter
Review: Feels like a sideways step. [Jan 2016, p.113]

Title: No Blues
Review: After a few tracks, you may find yourself seeking relief with your favorite method of self-obliteration. [No. 105, p.56]

Title: In Light
Review: This is not music that hangs around in the brain, for reasons that aren't particularly clear.

Title: Blink-182
Review: Someone should put Blink 182 out of their misery.

Title: Double Figure
Review: Double Figure forms a mysterious narrative filled with enough breaks and builds to keep the most jaded beathead more than satisfied. [Aug 2001, p.96]

Title: Beacons of Ancestorship

Title: The Alesha Show
Review: Certainly enough to impress the judges. [Jan 2008, p.93]

Title: Endless Now
Review: In essence, Male Bonding provides much of the same on its most recent addition, Endless Now. But with their unique knack for incorporating melody while still maintaining the urgency, energy and punk nature of their music, more of the same is just fine.

Title: Made Up Mind
Review: Considering the improvisational skill, malleability and performing traditions of the sprawling group, this is just another solid recording on a long, strange evolutionary trip. [No. 101, p.60]

Title: Broken Bells
Review: Unlike its creators' best prior accomplishments, Broken Bells doesn't seem prepared, or even attempting, to cross over. Nor does it feel like a new direction or outlet for either artist-- it's more of a nice detour.

Title: Third Time to Harm
Review: Third Time to Harm is a visceral pleasure, celebrating brawn over brains and shout-along choruses (“What pretty parasites!”) over songwriting complexity.

Title: Master
Review: A muted trumpet melody and wordless chorale drift through Siren Spectre's gorgeous intergalactic ambiance before space-disco juggernaut Responder tunes into the transcendental infinite--a glitter ball in one eye, the other on the cosmos. [Dec 2013, p.86]

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: Their inimitable fury and drive is intact. [Sep 2019, p.18]

Title: Because I Was in Love
Review: These are gallingly sad, often crudely simple folk songs, interlaced with menace, though her assertions of agency are just as bracing as the dark parts. [Jan 2018, p.105]

Title: No No No
Review: With the drums intimately booming and the occasional zap of an analog synth snaking across the formalist woodenness, the blessed simplicity of the arrangements on No No No makes one cry out for a more adventurous artist to place in these settings.

Title: Spine Hits
Review: While the overall sound is brighter, it's also largely rather weedy, and trading in the once colossal stoner riffs for languid neo-folk doesn't really suit this five-piece all that well.

Title: Annie Up
Review: They’re too big to fail though, so lightning half-strikes plenty here.

Title: Bloodiest
Review: This is the first real “must own” art rock record of the year. Besides Blackstar, of course.

Title: Dream a Garden
Review: Latham's plaintive voice sounds like it's emanating from some romantically ruinous daydream. The effect suits the mood but makes his lyrics difficult to decipher, which is frustrating given his pointed message.

Title: The Imperfect Sea
Review: Richly layered and astutely arranged. [Jul 2017, p.96]

Title: New York City
Review: Thanks to their increasingly varied sound, the Girls remain aloof and unknowable. They have us right where they want us: behind the velvet ropes.

Title: Quazarz: Born on a Gangster Star
Review: Gangster Star is a light, trippy confection, reinventing R&B with rippling electronics and slippery, Prince-like funk. [Aug 2017, p.31]

Title: Grown Unknown
Review: That kind of less-is-more approach, where all the clutter is shaved down to a paper-thin framework, is where Ices produces her most affecting material, potentially sketching out a new strain of inspiration for her to follow next time out.

Title: Don't Get Lost
Review: In the end, Don’t Get Lost is very enjoyable, yet the main downside is its length.

Title: Broken Lines
Review: This is a clever hybrid of prog, hard rock and dance; there’s even a full-blown power ballad (that’s part The Tubes, part Kate Bush atmospherics) in the shape of All We Have Is Now.

Title: Be the Cowboy
Review: Be the Cowboy largely dispenses with the distortion of Mitski’s guitar-oriented recent work, getting all the fuzz out with intro track “Geyser.” What’s left are short and thwarted pop songs. (Only two are longer than three minutes.)

Title: Good Thing
Review: Certain sections of Bridges’s audience are likely to define themselves against modern forms, so there is a risk here. But Bridges handles the transition deftly.

Title: Strange Geometry
Review: The slight nods to accessibility and the decreased stylization might disappoint some of the faithful at first, but Strange Geometry grows more appealing with repeated listening.

Title: I Am All Your Own
Review: Although not strikingly different from earlier work, I Am All Your Own appears more terrestrial and less transcendental. This being a refreshing new granting-of-access to his style.

Title: ORO: Opus Alter
Review: Discount the general masses not attuned to UFOmammut's unique but long-established formula, and their dedicated followers shan't have to expend too many of their remaining neurons grasping the full enormity of the band's accomplishment, even though this second sibling falls just short of its elder twin overall.

Title: Reality Killed the Video Star
Review: The more you delve into it the less you find, because it’s all affectation.

Title: WARM
Review: As the lovelorn ‘From Far Away’ floats by, desolate and broken, haunted by the ghosts of art-rock guitars and phantom electronics, it’s clear that Jeff Tweedy still isn’t comfortable on well-trodden roads and that Warm has moments that upend Americana as beautifully as ‘Yankee Hotel Foxtrot’ did with US indie rock. One to let simmer.

Title: (III)
Review: You'd have to say that III is a good Crystal Castles album. But given that II was a great Crystal Castles album, the trend isn't going the way that you'd hope.

Title: Born Like This
Review: While the album is more a series of word puzzles than a memoir, it does occasionally illuminate the man behind the mask.

Title: Fashionably Late
Review: The songs themselves are a disaster. Everything is trashy and over the top, but generally rubbish too.... Basically, this is probably the worst album ever created by a serious group of musicians.

Title: Walk The River
Review: While there is nothing here as magically refined as 'Made-Up Love Song #43', and Dangerfield's lyrics sometimes veer into fromage-land, Walk The River represents a must-have for those with pop tastes.

Title: Before the Poison
Review: The combination often proves too bleak.

Title: Duskland
Review: These songs are bittersweet, haunting yet hopeful, and endlessly listenable.  Duskland is Cale’s golden hour.

Title: Evil Friends
Review: Where Broken Bells is pensive and slow, Evil Friends is hyper-caffeinated and energetic, and better for it.

Title: Generation
Review: What's that sound? That's the sound of a barrel scraping and a career being flushed down a toilet.

Title: Mouthfuls
Review: A stunning bit of psychedelic folk-rock.

Title: Alpocalypse
Review: Alpocalypse is a fine reflection on our world as it stands in this modern age, and well worth a listen, if only for a laugh to brighten up your day.

Title: Banga
Review: If only her music might just occasionally match the freeform, flighty, extravagant nature of her words.

Title: Civil Disobedience for Losers
Review: Civil Disobedience for Losers is easily one of the best pieces of Melvins-worship to come out in a while.

Title: Steal Your Face
Review: Per usual, the music is skewed and exhausting (in the best way imaginable) and the rhythmic interplay between bassist Jacob Long and drummer Damon Palermo is fantastic.

Title: A Constant Sea
Review: Heliotropes show a surprisingly mature and focused control of their formula on A Constant Sea, luring you in only to eat you alive.

Title: La La Land
Review: La La Land blows that template sky high, expanding and expounding upon the band's sound in a way that is utterly thrilling while still retaining all the muted joy and gentle perfection of "Park Avenue." [Winter 2010, p.65]

Title: The Miraculous
Review: There’s nothing wrong with a good glacial pace, but Von Hausswolff’s slowly unfurling arrangements, as well as her reliance on the organ as the primary rhythmic vehicle, occasionally make the record tough sledding.

Title: Science Fiction
Review: Brand New has put in the work, making a record that erases any doubts about whether the final product would live up to eight years of mystery and hype. And it’s effectively erased its past by making good on every far-flung expectation placed upon it.

Title: The Big Dream
Review: At the very least, the album should convince diehard Lynch fans that the director’s self-imposed, semi-retirement from filmmaking is bearing some very interesting artistic fruit indeed.

Title: Echo
Review: Vocal heroism is Ms. Lewis’s game, and she plays it ruthlessly, with an unselfconscious gusto evocative of classic Whitney Houston or Celine Dion.

Title: Welcome the Worms
Review: For the most part, Bleached’s style of rock and roll is best suited to short, vicious tracks that get in, chug a beer, high-five the host, then get out. Welcome The Worms loses some its punch strictly because of its runtime. It’s not long for an album, but it’s long for this kind of album.

Title: True Love Cast Out All Evil
Review: Okkervil River--with frontman Will Sheff as producer--defers to the chief, allowing Erickson's gruff voice to reign over woozy background vocals ("John Lawman"), punchy brass sections ("Think of as One") and Ebow lullabies ("Birds'd Crash").

Title: Vulnicura
Review: A strange, intoxicating and utterly brave record. [Apr 2015, p.86]

Title: Daylight
Review: Daylight works best when Potter is steering the ship. Even with the considerable and seasoned talents of Valentine, Nocturnals alum Benny Yurco, and keyboardists Larry Goldings and Benmont Tench behind her, Potter commands the room.

Title: SBTRKT
Review: Representing UK production at its best, SBTRKT's self-titled album is playful yet gritty.

Title: My Bloody Underground
Review: Everything on My Bloody Underground suffers from Newcombe’s chronic lack of focus, leaving the entire mess sounding like half-assed sonic sketches farted out in a friend’s basement over a woozy weekend.

Title: My Favourite Faded Fantasy
Review: The album flows as if it were a mixtape of Rice songs to a former lover.

Title: Wenu Wenu
Review: A couple of slower-paced moments, ‘Khattaba’ and ‘Mawal Jamar’, drag a little, but 'Warni Warni' is undoubtedly the best Syrian-folk techno banger you’ll hear this--or any other--year.

Title: Supernature
Review: The super-synthetic ethos of the album starts to rub against your skin; the band's retro dance-music collage feels less like innovative referencing and more like flat pastiche, and the simplistic little-girl lyrics add nothing.

Title: The Loneliest Man I Ever Met
Review: The notion of Kinky Friedman as a reflective song stylist might take some getting used to for some fans, but The Loneliest Man I Ever Met shows he can pull it off better than most would expect, and if his singing is a long way from perfect, the heart and soul are present at all times.

Title: Ex Eye
Review: Ex Eye’s self-titled debut is an intriguing amalgam of black metal, progressive rock, minimalism, and free jazz while not sounding of a piece with any representative artist from those genres.

Title: Silence Is Easy
Review: If all goes well, people will forego the bad songs and concentrate on the really good ones, and Starsailor will get the message to go subtle and tight. [#8, p.102]

Title: Underachievers Please Try Harder
Review: They are unprepossessing in style, dainty and sweet in quality.

Title: To Be Kind
Review: It might be the most accessible Swans album yet. The long stretches of abstract noise are draped over some surprisingly catchy hooks. A few moments might even qualify as singalong road trip anthems.

Title: These Days...
Review: That Ab-Soul tries to do both makes for a pretty entertaining ride, even when he technically falters. Ambition changes the definition of success, making this Ab-Soul record a better experience that can be picked apart.

Title: Sistahs
Review: Tender and defiant, it pays respect to its history while resolutely facing the future.

Title: Tape Two
Review: Tape Two sees them moving further away from a classic De La Soul template into something deeper and darker.

Title: Into Forever
Review: They've constructed their most diverse and arguably finest collection to date in fourth long player Into Forever.

Title: Forever
Review: A frothy soufflé of an album, heavy on the groovy dance beats and go-girl goodwill, light on profundity.

Title: So-Called Chaos
Review: She's lost track of almost everything that made her music marvellous. [Jun 2004, p.101]

Title: The Cookbook
Review: Proves incontrovertibly that she doesn't need Timbaland's beat mastery to create a compelling album.

Title: This Addiction
Review: This Addiction promises exactly what the title describes, as most older fans will eat this up.

Title: Standing in the Way of Control
Review: This is a transitional album: many of the songs seem underwritten without all that noise on top; sometimes it sounds as if the band is still trying to figure out what to do with its tense, restrained new sound. [23 Jan 2006]

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: There are more twists and turns, more textures, than on any other McCartney album in the last 20 years, and if it's a little messy, so be it: it's better to have Paul letting it all hang out instead of hanging back.

Title: The Loon
Review: The Loon is a rare thing: an indie-rock record that's as lovable as it is bewildering.

Title: Rapping With Paul White
Review: Some will call it noise, others a beautifully complicated symphony. In the end, you're not quite sure where you've landed, but you're glad you took the trip.

Title: Love Your Dum and Mad
Review: For all of Dum and Mad's unebbing intensity--it never gets overbearing, it retains a dynamism through Shah's magnetic voice--she makes you want to stay in the darkness with her.

Title: Cancer 4 Cure
Review: Cancer 4 Cure is as hard and vital as anything El-P has ever released, and that's no light praise.

Title: The Grind Date
Review: Their jabs cut and the beats burn. [Nov 2004, p.118]

Title: America
Review: America is a profound statement; splicing Fuck Buttons with Sigur Rós in a state-of-the-union address balanced between hope, despair and an accomplished collision of strings, brass, soaring choirs and beats.

Title: Standards
Review: So even as Tortoise integrate guitar surrealism and edgier motifs into their palette, they also progress their unique relationship to electronic music and hip-hop. [#82, p.139]

Title: Perpetual Surrender
Review: In many ways Perpetual Surrender is the average British weather forecast; patchy, dull and cloudy with occasional sunny spells. Room for improvement.

Title: The Bride
Review: This is a beautiful, beguiling, disturbing and rewarding album of love, loss, grief and recovery from one of the most intriguing singer-songwriters currently active in British music, of either gender.

Title: Geneva
Review: While it may seem as if Geneva is all over the musical map, the opposite is acually true--the map's just been redrawn. [Nov 2009, p.114]

Title: D-D-Don't Don't Stop the Beat
Review: Ultimately, though, the resolutely rubbish recordings--distorted, trebly drum breaks, scratchy guitars, monotonous voices--and near-total absence of melody, might test your stamina for mindless entertainment. [May 2003, p.104]

Title: Hospitality
Review: [Hospitality is] accomplished and bright, with more room to grow.

Title: You
Review: The whole record is very carefully balanced.

Title: Yuck
Review: The secret is their infallible way with a tune: tracks such as "Get Away" and the single "Georgia" possess a beguiling melodic charm that illuminates the lo-fi boy/girl vocal delivery of Blumberg and his sister Ilana, bringing uplift where once all might have been gloom.
He's a bona fide hitmaker with a colossal YouTube following, working in the argot and style of his own generation

Title: Celebration, Florida
Review: The new sounds end up grating against the vocals, which will always sound whiskey-soaked, and playing against the band's strengths. [May 2011, p.88]

Title: Beneath California
Review: For music fans that like their art on the more confrontational side, 22 minutes of Beneath California on your headphones will be time very well spent.

Title: Going Places
Review: Going Places is a monolith, the cacophonous capstone to a career that never settled for less. It’s two guys arriving at their musical endpoint, culminating nearly a decade of work with one final refinement.

Title: Together We're Heavy
Review: Thankfully, the music overpowers DeLaughter’s weak voice.

Title: Transfixiation
Review: If the album has a flaw, it's a lack of structure and differentiation; as the music progresses, songs become less distinct and less compelling. [Mar 2015, p.90]

Title: Trouble Will Find Me
Review: Trouble Will Find Me is the Brooklyn, N.Y., indie-rock band’s sixth and most deft album yet, a haunted and lugubrious meditation on loss and despair.

Title: YHLQMDLG
Review: Yo Hago Lo Que Me Da La Gana (or I Do Whatever I Want) convenes a family reunion of his favorite rappers and reggaetoneros to produce a genre-promiscuous work of reggaeton a la marquesina: a more street-savvy form of reggaeton once deemed so risqué that it was criminalized and relegated to garage parties across Puerto Rico throughout the Nineties.

Title: Communion
Review: Most tracks feel as if they'd fit neatly onto classics from The Who, The Kinks and even The Band, but none of the Swedes' songs stand out too far from behind their influences. [Winter 2009, p.106]

Title: A Hundred Miles Off
Review: The songs are still full of lush guitars and dense, clattering percussion, but offer the added bonus of being more grandiose and emotional.

Title: Admiral Fell Promises
Review: Kozelek plays beautifully, but without orchestration, his songs (which tend to run upwards of six minutes) start to seem directionless.

Title: Jamie Lidell
Review: Fans of Lidell (or Prince, for that matter) won’t be challenged, but Jamie Lidell is proof that sometimes execution really is king.

Title: II
Review: It's a handsome downer of a record. [15 May 2006]

Title: Haunted Painting
Review: Sadie Dupuis wears many hats, and the product of her impulse to try everything pays off: a well-crafted record that balances weighty lyrics with eminently catchy songwriting.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: Nonetheless, this is impressive, mainstream stuff. One hope their bluecollar heart will win out over their white collar power pop head. [May 2010, p.83]

Title: By the Horns
Review: Darker, wiser, and more personally reflective than her work with Angus, By the Horns strikes a nice balance between standard, confessional singer/songwriter fare and radio-ready alt-pop.

Title: The Courage of Others
Review: This unrelenting but beautiful melancholy forms the glut of Courage. Beauty is key here, especially with a song like “Bring Down,” where an otherwise depressing dirge is given liftoff by Smith’s sweet harmony and a twittering flute.

Title: Tasty
Review: With Tasty, Kelis has left the roller-rink, returned from outer space, and she's back on her own two feet on terra firma-- unfortunately.

Title: My Wild West
Review: If Lissie's still searching for her best expression, My Wild West comes closer than before.

Title: Matangi
Review: The middle of Matangi, including the masochistic grind of “Bad Girls” and the hard dancehall influence of “Double Bubble Trouble,” contains uncommonly straightforward songs that would’ve fit easily on Rihanna’s last two albums. M.I.A. doesn’t stint on the bangers, though.

Title: Wasting Light
Review: Recorded in the garage of frontman Dave Grohl's home in Encino, Calif., the 11-song set is an explosive, high-octane burst of rock energy from a 16-year-old band that is tightly honed and righteously raw.

Title: Come Home To Mama
Review: Come Home to Mama deserves praise; despite having a bland title, it's the album where Wainwright finally comes out with some ideas. The problem is that when they do work, they don't really go anywhere.

Title: Turn Blue
Review: This is another step along that path of evolution destined to appear on end of year best album lists, and (ducks from those crazed blues-starved fans of old) it’s quite possibly The Black Keys’ own best ever long player.

Title: Relapse
Review: His flow is so good, his wordplay so sharp, it seems churlish to wish that he addressed something than his long-standing obsessions and demons.

Title: Such Fun
Review: The band retains an experimental edge, but it’s all-too-often now embodied in clinical genre-hopping, meaning that for all its ostensible claims, Such Fun just isn’t as fun as it should be.

Title: The Scene of the Crime
Review: Despite her co-conspirators, LaVette proves again that she's the star of the show.

Title: Octahedron
Review: Octahedron lacks sparkle enough to raise it above previous creative highs--it’s a recommended affair, at times truly scintillating, but it doesn’t quite deliver to the extent where all caution can be tossed to the breeze.

Title: Mezmerize
Review: Mezmerize's strongest moments are when the band drops the eccentricities and just rocks out.

Title: Infinite Worlds
Review: Infinite Worlds is accomplished and stirring, but it’s also sprinkled with surprise intimacies, distinguishing it as one of the most remarkable and challenging releases so far this year.

Title: Local Honey
Review: Local Honey is an inside record that's better-suited for humid mornings and overcast afternoons than the open highway. In looking stridently inward, Fallon has crafted his most homespun and relatable outing to date.

Title: Some of My Best Friends Are DJs
Review: If Some Of My Best Friends Are DJs doesn’t do anything that wasn’t done on his enthralling 2000 LP Carpal Tunnel Syndrome -- and if, at a scant 35 minutes, it’s almost over before you notice it’s on -- it’s still worth hearing.

Title: In the End
Review: In the End exemplifies the defiance that The Cranberries, and O’Riordan herself have shown throughout their career. Defiance of the status quo, defiance of violence, and ultimately defiance of death. It’s unmissable, unquestionable and unforgettable.

Title: Havilah
Review: Havilah will remain as yet another great record from one of the most talented acts currently playing rock music.

Title: Can't Be Tamed
Review: Throughout Can't Be Tamed Cyrus seems checked out of her vocal performances, singing with neither the tween-queen enthusiasm of her Hannah Montana material nor the confrontational energy of 2008's Breakout.

Title: Bonfires on the Heath
Review: For those who cherished the late, great Go-Betweens, Galaxie 500 and The Zombies, take heart--here is your new favorite album, filled to bursting with shivering tremolo guitars, surrealist poetry and the sort of melodies that made the kids’ knees buckle whenever “Time of the Season” graced the airwaves.

Title: Astronomy for Dogs
Review: If nothing else, Astronomy For Dogs should be heralded as a step in the right direction after six long years of wandering.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: It’s a playful, fantastical response to some serious life changes.

Title: 12 Bit Blues
Review: A very unusual blues record that's also a very unusual Kid Koala record, putting aside his typical playfulness and reminding us that he can truly move us with his turntablism, as well as amuse.

Title: Out of Touch in the Wild
Review: Out Of Touch In The Wild feels like an album album, with the tracks naturally feeling their way to one another, but with enough stand out moments to show how far Dutch Uncles have progressed since they recorded that debut in Germany.

Title: Romantic Comedy
Review: Appealing and in tune with admirable influences but ultimately lacking the sort of unpredictability or drama that can make these the songs that saved your life rather than reminiscent of ones that can.

Title: Steal This Album!
Review: The singer's curious persona is mirrored by the musical pyrotechnics, Queen meets Rage Against The Machine in a metal production of Godspell!, an inventiveness and fury that makes their MTV contemporaries look as dynamic as lard models of Linkin Park.

Title: Nocturnes
Review: All but gone is the glitzy, retro-leaning synthpop maximalism that dominated her first record, replaced here by a remarkably expansive sonic palette and a newfound poise that hardly falters from start to finish. [No. 98, p.57]

Title: Truelove's Gutter
Review: Hawley has made an exceptionally perfect album with Truelove’s Gutter: it’s endearing, uplifting and absolutely beautiful, what else could you ask for?

Title: Myths of the Near Future
Review: This debut can't quite capture the wide-eyed euphoria of a Klaxons live show, but readymade anthems like "Golden Skans," "Totem on the Timeline" and "Magick" will energize dance fans and rockers alike.

Title: New Magnetic Wonder
Review: [It] approaches the peak the Apples hit with 1999's Her Wallpaper Reverie.

Title: Hit to Hit
Review: It all adds up to a fun meander to help you waste away a summer afternoon.

Title: Martha Wainwright
Review: Wainwright's barbed lyrics about love and relationships sound like she scrawled them on a whiskey-soaked night. [22 Apr 2005, p.62]

Title: Man of the Woods
Review: With his fifth studio album, Timberlake isn’t re-inventing the wheel, but he solidly continues to experiment with R&B, funk, pop and soul, with Americana creating an interesting layer.

Title: Ministry of Love
Review: Ministry of Love does come off like something of a fashion victim, sounding expensive but uncomfortable, looking good but doing little to stand out.

Title: Sold Out
Review: It wasn’t too long ago that Paypal himself was working his happy hardcore fanaticism into the footwork bass lines. While those hardcore elements are non-existent on this effort, the whimsical spirit remains.

Title: Arrowhead
Review: This is artfully bracing listening. [Sep 2008, p.55]

Title: Origin: Orphan
Review: S, no watersports this time, but a wee triumph nonetheless. [Dec 2009, p. 100]

Title: Look To The Sky
Review: [A] beautiful and calming record.

Title: The Spirit Indestructible
Review: Main producer Rodney Jerkins keeps the beats tight and hooks polished, but Furtado's flaming identity crisis makes this cringe listening.

Title: Wait To Pleasure
Review: Contrary to the band’s name, there are a lot of joys to be found in Wait To Pleasure.

Title: Beautiful Rewind
Review: There’s certainly nothing on Beautiful Rewind with a hook as memorable as ‘Locked’, from last year’s Pink. When Four Tet hits that sweet spot between fragile beauty and gritty pirate radio music (as on the aforementioned ‘Aerial’ and ‘Buchla’, for instance) however, you really feel as if he’s onto something.

Title: Level Live Wires
Review: Despite all the different guest appearances, Level Live Wires never feels hodge-podge or unsteady.

Title: Inside The Ships
Review: This time around, tuba, chanter, cymbalom and (apparently) paprika add to the nuance by which, at their best, Tarwater seem to stretch sound and time.

Title: Hug of Thunder
Review: Unfortunately, aside from a couple of other stronger tracks (‘Gonna Get Better’ and ‘Towers and Masons’ – one of Brendan Canning’s contributions), the rest of the album isn’t something I have a desire to return to.

Title: Rituals
Review: Team Ghost and Fromageau have a number of good ideas, but the band's biggest downfall stems from the fact that they sometimes condense too many of these ideas into too small a space.

Title: If the Ocean Gets Rough
Review: On his debut album... Mason's dour tendencies were neatly offset by his ramshackle musicianship, but here the rambunctious clatter gives way to a sound more smooth, adult and portentous

Title: Diamond Eyes
Review: Above all, it’s a mature album: Deftones skirted the obvious response to their tragedy, realizing that the left turn is a more rewarding journey.

Title: You in Reverse
Review: An album that does his low-key legacy well, mixing classic rock-influenced guitar solos and quaint folk sounds with psychedelic effects and high-pitched melodies that put Rush's Geddy Lee to shame.

Title: You Are All I See
Review: The biggest caveat of this album is that the retro aesthetic mars Grossi's attempts at emotional connection--it tries to resonate, but by tapping into our memories of heartstrings and not our actual heartstrings, it falls short. But as production goes, it's a success.

Title: The Stage
Review: They have blown the creative doors off, cramming an insane amount of ideas into 74 minutes of prog-metal bombast. Their knack for a chorus is as apparent on the shorter, sharper likes of Paradigm and God Damn, but it’s the outrageous opulence of towering ballads Higher and Roman Sky, and the overblown, starry-eyed Muse-ings of 16-minute closer Exist, that make this such a satisfying forward leap.

Title: Dark Red
Review: The album is a full hour long, and though most of the songs are captivating, a few tend to drag.

Title: Spiritual Songs for Lovers to Sing
Review: The music matches the rhetoric, and it's an undeniable triumph. [Jun 2016, p.109]

Title: Preliminaires
Review: Where "Avenue B" was a pretentious mess, Preliminaires is flawed but significantly more successful.

Title: On Your Own Love Again
Review: On Your Own Love Again is a timeless record by a remarkable talent only just starting to show what she can do.

Title: So Jealous
Review: The brittle harmonies make So Jealous a little tough to warm up to, but combined with the thick-handled melodies and punchy arrangements, Tegan And Sara's look-at-us swagger generates drama.

Title: Hopes and Fears
Review: Hopes and Fears contains more hooks than most pop groups manage in their careers.

Title: Missiles
Review: Its triumph is in its intimacy and honesty. [Dec 2008, p.134]

Title: Psychedelic Pill
Review: The foursome may be interrupted by time and circumstance, but whenever they find themselves in a room together with their instruments they pick up the conversation exactly where they left off.

Title: Switzerland
Review: A whip-smart, 13-song satire on FM-radio machismo and lyrical cliches. [Nov 2006, p.140]

Title: Life After Youth
Review: A solid, consistent return that sounds like the band never left.

Title: Blossoms
Review: Logically, Blossoms doesn't have the sort of strangely human touch of Emptyset's 2017 releases, but it's still a compelling, somewhat frightening hybrid of organic and synthetic processes.

Title: Volta
Review: Every song on Volta sounds like it was birthed in no fewer than 10 months, if not five years. "Fun" hardly has an opportunity to enter the picture when Björk's now seemingly permanent fastidiousness remains her métier.

Title: Way to Normal
Review: Although he seems to have rediscovered his panache, the music supporting his narratives is still lacking the originality of his best work.

Title: Who Needs Who
Review: An epic ambition that bolster Nona Marie Levine's lightly burnished vocals. [Nov 2012, p.96]

Title: Shrines
Review: Pulling the entire effort back from the precipice of cliché is the immediate charisma of vocalist Megan James, particularly engaging when hurdling over cleverly constructed lines of wordplay.

Title: Echtzeit
Review: Even at its strangest, Echtzeit still feels thoroughly calm and relaxed, as the trio is more than comfortable with venturing into uncharted territory.

Title: Blame It On Gravity
Review: What sounds like leftovers from Miller's last solo effort and bizarre surf-rock-inspired numbers rear their ugly heads, leaving these Lone Star Staters in jeopardy of repeating the grade. [July 2008, p.158]

Title: Breakthrough
Review: Breakthrough never quite lives up to its title. But the songs that do diverge from the formula even slightly-like the Greg Wells-produced "Fearless"-offer delightful relief, and perhaps a taste of what could be if the singer were to dig deeper.

Title: There is No Enemy

Title: Something For All of Us
