Review: Non-Fiction is just blandly lazy about developing its representation of women, like it is about everything else. That lack of specificity renders the album ironically hindered by its own overt conception: a story album unable to sustain interest as fiction, non- or otherwise.

Title: Good Advice
Review: Bulat's pipes and songwriting prowess flourish, more than in her prior folksy, singer-songwriter LPs.

Title: Palookaville
Review: As usual, his willingness to please gives the disc its fast-food kick. [Oct 2004, p.113]

Title: Aabenbaringen over aaskammen
Review: They sound truly beguiling. [Feb. 2012 p. 101]

Title: Personality
Review: It's an important album for Scuba, as a means of transition, of mastering his new craft. It's just not a terribly important album for the rest of us.

Title: 100 Miles from Memphis
Review: Nearly every song overstays its welcome; what may have felt like a bunch of great jams in the studio grows tedious over the course of 12 tracks.

Title: Acolyte
Review: There are flashes of brilliance here, but you do long for a wink or a flicker of wit. [Feb 2010, p.88]

Title: Brand New Abyss
Review: Even the more listenable songs on Brand New Abyss, such as “So There” and “The Woman You Want,” sound more like a successful regurgitation of past sounds and ideas than anything new. And while that’s not a bad thing, it’s not enough of a reason to spend time listening to the new album.

Title: They Were Wrong, So We Drowned
Review: Unlistenable. [Mar 2004, p.96]

Title: May The Lord Watch
Review: Phonte and Pooh have released the best Little Brother album since 2005’s The Minstrel Show. In doing so, they’ve reaffirmed why LB means something special to so many people and proven the improbable is still possible.

Title: From the Ages
Review: San Diego triangle Isaiah Mitchell, Mike Eginton, and Rocket From the Crypt propulsionist Mario Rubalcaba hurtle third studio LP and first since 2007 into the void atop a gloriously earthen pachyderm crunch on four tracks.

Title: The Waterfall II
Review: In case the meditative ruminations were missed elsewhere on The Waterfall II, the closer reaffirms the band's emotional shift in spite of the struggle.

Title: UGK 4 Life
Review: UGK 4 Life leaves listeners wondering where they might go next, and even if sated with one last release still lamenting that those further steps—gargantuan or tiny, toward greatness or overreach, whichever—will necessarily be solo, uncontrasted by that inimitable, nimble, lascivious whine we’ve lost.

Title: The Thrill of It All
Review: To date, the only real distinction of Smith’s music is his voice--and though he’s a talented singer, even that’s dulled by songs this predictably vanilla.

Title: Random Spirit Lover
Review: The shrewdly crafted Random Spirit Lover is the most satisfying batch of songs Krug has ever released.

Title: Peace Is the Mission
Review: There are some glimmers of pop gold.... But those moments are overshadowed by dated cheeseball synth presets, uninspired choruses, goofy samples and clunky rhythm programming.

Title: Bare Bones
Review: Bare Bones is a beautifully slow-cooked album that encourages us to look on the bright side. Not a bad message these days.

Title: Terms of My Surrender
Review: Hiatt sounds throughout as if gargling a box of frogs in some eternal late-night New Orleans backroom. And it's glorious. [Aug 2014, p.90]

Title: Master of Disaster
Review: A too-well-buried treasure. [Aug 2005, p.129]

Title: How I Long to Feel That Summer in My Heart
Review: This is one striking album from start to finish.

Title: Quaristice
Review: Quaristice demands to be heard, but stubbornly refuses to be the soundtrack of your life. That's art, and perhaps it's only pegged as "difficult" because it won't sing along with you; neither will the Chrysler Building, but that doesn't make it any less beautiful.

Title: Futures
Review: An inviting, maturing album that still shows enough vitality to still be classed as a good rock album.

Title: The Runners Four
Review: The Runners Four displays intuitive melody and a childlike disregard for convention that's captivating enough to overcome any saccharine tendencies. [Dec 2005, p.116]

Title: Feels Like
Review: When she lights up a guitar rant like "Trying" or "I Remember," she sounds like the world is caving in on her, but that doesn't stop her from standing her ground.

Title: In the Belly of the Brazen Bull
Review: The group's fourth album confirms that their default setting is a bit four-square nuts-and-bolts punk pop. [Jun 2012, p.92]

Title: Transit Transit
Review: Autolux's evolution isn't quite complete, but Transit Transit is an album made by a band ready to keep heading down the road. [Summer 2010, p.76]

Title: Allas Sak
Review: Allas Sak is a nice enough record. It sounds exactly like Dungen. No surprises.

Title: Stains on Silence
Review: The frustration comes from Stains on Silence's propensity for a feeling little bit too rough around the edges, unfinished almost, despite it’s reworking.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: Weariness gives way to willingness as Solange unpacks and ultimately celebrates Blackness, from the politics of Black hair in Don’t Touch My Hair (featuring Sampha) to a reclamation of Black masculinity in Scales (featuring Kelela).

Title: Kingdom Come
Review: He's grown up, alright. With the energy Jay brings to most of these tracks, you'd think 30 was the new 60.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: Del Rey has struggled to back up her provocations with substance. Ultraviolence was an exception, a singular breakthrough. Honeymoon is, sadly, a slip and fall after a promising stride forward.

Title: Made of Bricks
Review: While not yet distinct enough to escape [Lily] Allen's shadow, as an empathetic soundtrack to similar growing pains Nash's debut hits its mark. [Sep 2007, p.86]

Title: At My Age
Review: At a mere 33 minutes, "At My Age" leaves listeners wanting more, but then, that seems to be part of Lowe's seduction technique.

Title: Born Again in the USA
Review: It’s not often that a side-project produces an album that deserves anything more than a footnote mention. Loose Fur deserves its own cult.

Title: Figure 8
Review: A strong collection of lush, densely arranged power-pop and inimitably intimate ballads?

Title: Be Brave
Review: They could have retread the same musical territory, but instead they deliver a record that’s remarkable in its maturity and--most of all--its ability to be replayed again and again.

Title: Dream On
Review: Swedish pop producer Patrik Berger brings a new clarity to Boman's work without disturbing the delicacy of her performance. [Feb 2020, p.25]

Title: Dragonslayer
Review: Dragonslayer is a lither, more athletic Sunset record--easier to like, easier to understand.

Title: Belladonna
Review: Whereas Eno's purest ambient music has such an organic abstractness the listener stops thinking about what is actually producing the sounds, Lanois favours guitars, which links his music more to established styles. [Jul 2005, p.110]

Title: English Tapas
Review: There are glimmers of musical progression on Sleaford Mods’ ninth album: Jason Williamson sings the odd line, and there are even occasional choruses. But, pleasingly, for the most part it’s business as usual.

Title: The Bronx (III)
Review: You can't help but feel that had they cut loose more often--as they do on the album's highlight, 'Ship High in Transit'--and put a bit more punk in their rock, they would have made the record they'd like us to believe they did.

Title: Songs for Our Mothers
Review: From referencing Harold Shipman in a song title to taking a moral high ground to the view of secluding yourself with drugs, Songs for Our Mothers presents an insignificant manifesto.

Title: Perfect Version
Review: Perfect Version rivals no Chastity Belt album and its nebulous delivery causes its songs to often slip through the listener’s hands. However, none of that is really the point of the album. ...  A clearinghouse and a reset button, Julia Shapiro needed Perfect Version and we need the album precisely for that reason as well.

Title: Crooked Doors
Review: Tori Amos fans will be thrilled, but those hoping to continue on a hard-rock bender will be left puzzled. [May 2015, p.100]

Title: Skull Ring
Review: That's the problem with Skull Ring: It's the work of an artist who should be looking within himself to create a modern-may masterpiece, rather than trying to catch a spark from either his chart-topping successors or the band he once fronted so triumphantly. Both acts, in their way, give a whiff of desperation.

Title: Death Magnetic
Review: Death Magnetic at least proves that 40-something millionaires can make a valiant fist of recapturing the fury of youth. Sadly, though, it seems that Metallica will never be 20-years-old again.

Title: Back Home
Review: Heartfelt? Yes. But who would have ever thought Eric Clapton's music could become so disposable?

Title: Love Is Not Pop
Review: The sonic touches Hagg adds to her songs only makes them better. The combination of their gifts has resulted in something pretty special, possibly the best work either of them has done to date, and hopefully something that will continue.

Title: Soul Music
Review: Spurred by excellent, challenging production, the record maintains an adequate sonic distance from its inspirations, and the bonus disc's excellent selection of remixes fosters a dialogue between jungle, house, and techno's past and present.

Title: The Heart Speaks in Whispers
Review: Rich with on-point retro-futurist sounds, such as the gem-like, sultry neo-soul of Green Aphrodisiac. ... But there’s some unwelcome pandering to all markets in ghastly guitar ballad Stop Where You Are, a misstep looking for a Coldplay album, and a couple of tracks where smoothness wins out over personality.

Title: The Lucky Ones
Review: The eleven tracks here are tight, raw, and marked by insistent thumping rhythms and taught chunky riffs, laying the groundwork for one of the band’s most straight-ahead rock albums in years.

Title: With Teeth
Review: Trent Reznor has run out of ideas.

Title: Oracular Spectacular
Review: It's almost like neither [Dave Fridmann] nor the band could decide whether they were making an electronic or rock record and in dithering between the two settled on the awkward, frustrating middle ground.

Title: The Sun
Review: You can occasionally hear [Adem's and Hebden's] trademark sounds punctuate these proggy, Tortoise-like instrumentals. [Jul 2007, p.102]

Title: The Budos Band III
Review: Engineer Bosco Mann's work here exemplifies the principal that it's better to capture the sound right than to try to fix it in the mix. Then you can spend the mix getting the balance right, making some sounds stand out and others blend just right. Such is the case here; this record simply sounds right.

Title: The Sun Came Out
Review: The Sun Came Out, whether intentionally or not, is an album for singers, but often it's the music that elevates the songs and prevents even the slickest moments from falling into the AOR mire.

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: The band put their flag in the ground as the most intriguing musical voice we have, creating a bombastic, immaculately put together portrait of modern life.

Title: Exploding Head Syndrome
Review: Musically not that dissimilar to Pete Kember's work as E.A.R. or Randall Nieman's Fuxa, it's a far cry from The Telescopes' noisier excursions and for all its sinister overtones, actually proves quite a soothing listen in the right context.

Title: Thumbtacks and Glue
Review: [Hamilton’s voice] carries the wispy, breathy feel of an Iron & Wine, but where Sam Beam’s rustic vocals float like a leaf down a sunny river, Hamilton’s putters out like a deflated balloon, and he comes off as hesitant and unassuming.

Title: Live a Little
Review: If there were any criticism to be leveled at this album, it's that it is a little bland around the edges.

Title: Realism
Review: Realism is yet another solid gold deposit in one o the truly briliant pop music discographies of the past 20 years. [Winter 2010, p.69]

Title: Ske-Dat-De-Dat: The Spirit of Satch
Review: There's no doubt that Skee-Dat-De-Dat...Spirit of Satch is a project of love, but by the closing stages there's no getting away from it; the album is a bit of a... drag.

Title: I Never Learn
Review: You are either in the mood for this depth of wallowing or you are not.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: But as opposed to Blink, which powers straight ahead with scatological juvenility, the Offspring bridges punk with change-ups of metal and traditional rock and brings a more sarcastic wit to its observations of male teen angst.

Title: Endless Now
Review: Fans looking for a haphazard exercise in DIY should revisit the band's earlier effort, but will nonetheless be greatly rewarded by this deftly crafted slacker opus.

Title: Riot Act
Review: Those waiting for another record as challenging as 'Vitalogy' will be left disappointed. But 'Riot Act' is the sound of a band entering a powerful middle-age. They still deserve your attention.

Title: Condition
Review: Condition often has a slight avant-garde feel to it, but it's ultimately an album full of songs that sound like they've been raised with the sole intent of wanting to jump out of the speakers.

Title: Orc
Review: Dwyer's crew are oft-cited as the world's most exciting live rock band; they're also making some of its most exciting rock records. [Sep 2017, p.93]

Title: Here's to Taking It Easy
Review: Here's to Taking It Easy rests in the lines between love and heartache, celebration and mourning-and all of it is draped in a muted, silo-high production that cuts the hard edges off the record's darker moments.

Title: OX 2010: A Street Odyssey
Review: Although it's an imperfect effort in some regards, the somewhat conceptual OX 2010: A Street Odyssey testifies to Vast's highly developed steez, and does so with complements from MCs who effortlessly jibe with his arcane rhyme selections.

Title: The Inheritors
Review: Listeners won't walk away with a clear narrative about The Inheritors, which is designed for nonlinear exploration. It doesn't pay off all its risks—at times it gets too blurry to follow--but this album sounds like little else.

Title: Jericho Sirens
Review: Packed with a surfeit of nimble guitar lines, they draw their forces together into an expertly crafted portrayal of raw anguish that surpasses any nostalgic commemoration. These mature punks sweat out their energy with vigorous and eloquent playing, and in doing so, also show their younger peers how it's done.
The band has ripped elements from early L.A. hardcore, '90s powerviolence and screamo, and it wields this arsenal of influences to deliver big, sharp hooks. [No. 93, p.59]

Title: Distractions
Review: As a soundtrack for a wide variety of scenes, Distractions enhances Chen's reputation as one of UK club music's most adaptable artists.

Title: The Fall
Review: Easy listening princess goes indie-goth.

Title: The Jazz Age
Review: Ferry devotees will love it, and so might plenty of others.

Title: Venus On Earth
Review: Nimol's vocals are as beguiling as ever, Ethan Holtzman's Farfisa organ still swirls, Zac Holtzman's guitars still chime and chunk, and Paul Dreux Smith's drums clang happily along.

Title: Hell on Heels
Review: The songs have the feeling of rejuvenative writing, small experiments in genre and style for artists versed in country's classic modes but who rarely get to fiddle around with them.

Title: The Something Rain
Review: The album's highpoints, particularly "Show Me Everything" and "This Fire Of Autumn" showcase a band who seem to have rediscovered new ways of putting together their already impressive constituent parts. [Mar 2012, p.101]

Title: She's In Control
Review: The best ’80s-revival funk made by white Canadian hip-hop kids since, like, ever.

Title: Hold On Now, Youngster...
Review: More variety is needed and it's all been done before, but rarely with such a sense of fun. [Apr 2008, p.108]

Title: A flame my love, a frequency
Review: Colleen continues to craft uniquely personal experimental music with a clear artistic voice, and her latest release might be her greatest achievement yet.

Title: Waves Are Universal
Review: Without the production pizzazz that made Slowdive so compelling, Goswell is left somewhat adrift. [#7]

Title: Blood in My Eye
Review: From the amateurish cover art to a succession of clumsy diss tracks aimed at Fiddy, Blood in My Eye merely makes the Tupac disciple look desperate and directionless.

Title: Kazuashita
Review: All in all, this is a good album. While it has some magnificent moments, it doesn't quite come together enough to make a for a completely stellar ride.

Title: Let the Record Show: Dexys Do Irish and Country Soul
Review: An unqualified triumph. [Jul 2016, p.73]

Title: Lights From Paradise
Review: To sum it all up succinctly, there is no shortage of psychedelic jams to be found throughout Quest for Fire's Lights from Paradise.

Title: Nextdoorland
Review: Nextdoorland is one of the rarest of things: a reunion album that captures the spirit of what made the band special in the first place.

Title: Afraid of Heights
Review: Waaves offer some addictively catchy tunes that, while somewhat empty and lacking in substance, are still good, hazy fun.

Title: Wavvves
Review: The second album has the more obvious and combustible singles. But there’s nothing on the second album that comes close to the 1-2-3 punch of 'California Goth,' 'Wavves,' and 'Lover.'

Title: Fantasy Empire
Review: Fantasy Empire, with its discernible riffs, moments of relative calm--and even, dare it be said, choruses--is the best entry point for anyone curious about a powerhouse which has, up to this point at least, operated on the blustery, splattered neon fringes of noise rock.

Title: Family Crimes
Review: Family Crimes sees Skygreen Leopards light years away from the experimental, communal folk sounds that they were drawn to in their earliest days, but still retains the same distant dreaminess, though it's more dedicated to melody than any other chapter of the band's epic, shifting discography.

Title: Time to Die
Review: Not to be outdone by US stoner-rock peers Sleep and Earth, who have records out this year, the Dorset satanists have spat out this eighth album.

Title: Floating Features
Review: Despite its many nostalgic elements, Floating Features represents a new start in a new city, and though it often looks inward, it’s grounded in the present and glances towards the future.

Title: All Around Us
Review: The songs grow overly long at the end (the title track is a bit of a bore), though the album is consistently beautiful, if not always ear-catching.

Title: Good Girl Gone Bad
Review: Beyonce's superstar status is not in danger, but she should hand her A&R man a copy of this album.

Title: The Alternative to Love
Review: The heightened production values... sacrifice a bit of Benson's scrappy charm, but they also yield several sparkling should-be hits. [25 Mar 2005, p.71]

Title: Holy Fire
Review: Holy Fire is the sound of a band utterly on form and completely on top of their game.

Title: Keep on Your Mean Side
Review: Once upon a time rock'n'roll was all about the sex you really shouldn't have. The Kills haven't forgotten. [Apr 2003, p.108]

Title: Waiting For The Moon
Review: A heart-meltingly wonderful return to form.

Title: The Bela Session
Review: Your more serious fans and completists will probably find something like this a welcome addition to their collection. Despite it not offering many revelations or surprises, The Bela Session still serves a fun little snapshot of what was soon to be one of the more creative and influential 80s post-punk bands in their infancy.

Title: Abaporu
Review: The new sound stands up straight as the original iteration, but is backed by the depth of his previous work.

Title: Cardinal
Review: While the lyrics are what everyone will talk about, it’s Hall’s voice that makes them work. That insistent yelp, straining to create melody without being beholden to it.

Title: The Only Thing I Ever Wanted
Review: Like Stereolab backed by the Muppet Babies. [Jun 2006, p.114]

Title: Holiday Destination
Review: This is a well thought-out record and is clearly something that has taken several years to coalesce and construct. Though the political edge can sometimes distract from the beauty of the instrumentation, articulation and overall composition, it never gets boring, with little twists and turns that get better upon every listen.

Title: Observator
Review: Even when the band allows its minor-key impulses back in, the album feels pleasant, in a late-summer-sunset kind of way.

Title: Reunion Tour
Review: The band's latest, Reunion Tour, appeals directly to your brain.

Title: Love + Fear
Review: There are suggestions of better directions not taken. [Jul 2019, p.113]

Title: Florence
Review: As delicate as these songs are in terms of construction (simple guitar parts, barely-there percussion and Hayman’s vocals--it’s the first album he’s done as a truly solo artist) they really pack a punch.

Title: Someone to Watch Over Me
Review: Someone To Watch Over Me has the makings of a perfectly solid mopey-piano-girl album, largely eschewing chest-beating for a coarser-grained approach that serves the singer rather well.

Title: Happy to You
Review: As it turns out, beneath all the shattering percussion, well-timed sound crashes, and plethora of borrowed ideas, Happy to You is rather skeletal.

Title: The Heat
Review: Whereas the fucked-up, punk attitude [Ryan] Adams feigned on Rock'n'Roll was based on little more than pique, The Heat is all genuine passion, brimming with energy, anger and great tunes sandwiched between the dense guitars. [Jul 2004, p.114]

Title: Love King
Review: Nash is admirably committed to the natural, elegant flow of a capital-A Album, and throughout King, we segue seamlessly from his ennui to his libido to his sexual/financial prowess and back again.

Title: Walk Between Worlds
Review: At times, it teeters between nostalgia and self-parody. .... But you can forgive the odd-slip-up, because the whole thing sounds so joyous. [Mar 2018, p.115]

Title: Kasabian
Review: Kasabian is brash, loutish, and seems liable at times to cut you; the consistent kick drum beat throughout it is like a great party's heartbeat. But like the roustabout in the corner, drinking all the lager and scratching up your old records, it can be more loudmouthed than substantial.

Title: The Stage Names
Review: While this album isn’t as riveting as earlier Okkervil River CDs, there’s plenty to enjoy, and plenty of reason for hope.

Title: Ventriloquism
Review: The quartet, occasionally joined by players such as Doyle Bramhall II, Jeff Parker, and Levon Henry, roams fluidly through funk, roots music, and unclassifiable stylistic amalgamations, like they're doing so on an intuitive level.

Title: The Guest
Review: Sing-along melodies and breezy hooks are strewn throughout.

Title: Little Hells
Review: Most of Little Hells is musically quite simple, giving the sense that whatever Nadler has to say rests entirely in her sound, not in the songs themselves

Title: BOBBY
Review: It's lively in its drowsiness, which may be the album's most compelling and distinguishing contrast.

Title: Le Noise
Review: Young's sandblasting electric guitar sits handsomely alone before eerie rumbling atmospheres.

Title: A Healthy Distrust
Review: The rapper's ferocity makes him a good fit for punk label Epitaph. [11 Feb 2005, p.63]

Title: Freetown Sound
Review: Freetown Sound finds Hynes at the peak of his powers, mixing his best songwriting and production yet to powerful, purposeful effect.

Title: Nearer My God
Review: It's Foxing in a new shape, a first-hand witness of the evolution of a band that were really good just the way they were. While these changes may not be welcome with open arms, the thoughtfulness and artistry deserves a round of applause.

Title: Warm Heart of Africa
Review: Cameos by Vampire Wekend's Ezra Keonig and Tamil rapper M.I.A. add to a joyous but knowing smorgasbord that will play equally well in a Lilongwe disco or Shoreditch/Brooklyn trend hole. [Oct 2009, p.107]

Title: Invisible Storm
Review: Turin Brakes have made an album which is "OK". No dizzying heights or subterranean lows. You may raise an eyebrow every now and again, but nothing about this music grabs your attention and holds it.

Title: Born Like This
Review: Born Like This is still a damn fine record, but it’s too inconsistent to do more than simply satisfy your DOOM craving.

Title: Universal Themes
Review: Universal Themes is still overwhelmingly heart-on-sleeve, human; if it's not universal in the specifics, then it is in the way it rawly depicts experience.

Title: In Our Nature
Review: This is a sparse, minimal and unassuming record that's unlikely to hit anyone over the head with its innovation, but Gonzalez accomplishes much while sounding like he's doing very little.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Mostly, though, The Dodos’ little quirks--the lack of bass, the blustery drumming, the lyrics that threaten to say something profound but never do--irritate rather than intrigue.

Title: Give the People What They Want
Review: It’s a triumphant comeback.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: I can't stress enough how brilliant this record is, how pertinent and valuable its songs are to our lives.

Title: Last Patrol
Review: Dark, desperate and full of great tunes, this is rock'n'roll at its black-hearted best. [Nov 2013, p.90]

Title: Close Ties
Review: There's no arguing with craftsmanship like this. [Jul 2017, p.88]

Title: The Warning
Review: The Warning shows us a Hot Chip both familiar and unexpectedly progressive.

Title: Seeds
Review: Ms. Muldrow has been making records for six years, and Seeds (SomeOthaShip Connect), the newest, produced by Madlib, is the strongest yet.

Title: Dummy Boy
Review: The production on Dummy Boy is amazing. Tay Keith, Scott Storch, Murda Beatz and Ronny J among others lace 6 with some beats that match his "wavy" sound and style perfectly. The tracks are heavy on the bottom and have lots of room for 6 to flex his sing-song melodic flow.

Title: News and Tributes
Review: Like mid-'80s Scritti Politti, News And Tributes is pop music made by young men loath to sell their intelligence down the river. [Jun 2006, p.114]

Title: We're All Gonna Die
Review: [Producer Blake Mills] deftly applied his gift for song-serving ornamentation and transformed sluggish Dawes into an aggressively inventive band. [Nov 2016, p.26]

Title: The Wack Album
Review: The Wack Album feels awfully short on fresh ideas.

Title: 10,000 Hz Legend
Review: On their second proper longplayer, Air project that melancholy forward, depicting romantic recollections from a future world in which "technology" has attained sci-fi levels.

Title: Xen
Review: Xen remains as singular--and often as brilliant--as the rest of the Arca catalogue.

Title: Jake Shears
Review: There are nods to Scissor Sisters with some honky-tonk disco and references to the demi-monde. But there are also extraordinary tracks of looped beats and grainy heartbreak. [Oct 2018, p.84]

Title: Red Beans and Weiss
Review: Bohemian legend and walking R&B encyclopaedia Chuck Weiss is on great form on this latest album.

Title: Furious Angels
Review: The greatest album ZTT never released. [Oct 2003, p.134]

Title: Semper Femina
Review: Having entered the limelight early, the 27-year-old singer/songwriter has now settled into a comfortable groove to on this finely honed career highlight.

Title: Blunderbuss
Review: Despite all the critics desperately wanting White to continue being our modern-day rock savior, the record can't have it both ways [being both a pointed statement about the pains of a break up and a collection of daring, wacky and eccentric songs] -although it's still a blast to hear it try.

Title: A Hundred Million Suns
Review: Ultimately, Snow Patrol offers more bark than bite here. [Winter 2008]

Title: Onism
Review: Taken together, for its somewhat lofty inspirations and complex construction, Onism is above all a fun listen, full of discovery, whimsy, and musicality. And it's got a good beat.

Title: You're The Man
Review: A fascinating jumble of ideas, some of them fantastic. Too confused to be a great lost album, or indeed a coherent collection, as a snapshot of both its creator and soul music in turmoil, it’s perfect.

Title: Okovi
Review: It’s a philosophically messy record, and it goes without saying that it cannot offer us any answers to life’s big questions, but what it can and does do is reorient the questions we ask on the subject, and that can be infinitely more valuable for our understanding of death in the end.

Title: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love
Review: Too often the crossover strategy mires these songs in the most banal cliches of dream pop and arena grunge. [Sep 2018, p.29]

Title: Jake Bugg
Review: The teen delivers poetic social realism. [Nov 2012, p.90]

Title: Security
Review: Seven years on from their first album, Antibalas have developed into an unexpectedly varied, sophisticated band.

Title: Silver Tears
Review: He's at his best, however, when he takes it all very seriously indeed. [Feb 2017, p.96]

Title: Black Record
Review: Only two original members remain--David Thomas, also of Pere Ubu, and bass guitarist Craig Bell--and their approach feels oddly inconsistent. [Dec 2015, p.90]

Title: Battle Born
Review: With their simultaneous emphasis on the pedal-to-the-metal triumphalism of rock's yesteryear and their ultimate submission to tomorrow's grinding machinery, the Killers' new album may as well be called Battle Born This Way.

Title: The Flip Is Another Honey
Review: The Flip isn't a flawless effort; "Boy + Angel" and a few others lack punch. But updates to tracks like Cheap Trick's "Southern Girls" and Thin Lizzy's "Running Back" shine.

Title: Kannon
Review: Kannon is Sunn O)))'s most sparse offering in years, but the experiment in meditative metal minimalism is more than capable of shooting listeners towards a higher plane of consciousness.

Title: Sound of Silver
Review: Murphy's willfully pretentious métier, his intentionally inadequate lyrics, and his monotonous sequencing expose a genuine fear of dance.

Title: MAP OF THE SOUL : PERSONA
Review: Although it's only the first piece of the puzzle, on its own, Map of the Soul: Persona is a fitting celebration for a group at the top of their game.

Title: Dark Comedy
Review: Whether it's through casual observation or the to-the-bone identity struggles, Open Mike Eagle's overlap between amusing insights and uncomfortable truths makes for one of the most compelling indie-rap listens of the year so far.

Title: Cursing the Sea
Review: To be fair, there are a few songs that skew close to paint-by-numbers lo-fi indie rock but this is a record that refuses to hew too neatly to expectations.

Title: Playland
Review: Playland is better than its predecessor in pretty much every respect. The songs are better, the palette broader and there's a genuine sense of Marr hitting his stride as a solo artist. [Nov 2014, p.103]

Title: Changes
Review: The production is unpolished, warm and organic. It had to be. When you hear the pained fury in his rendition of Black Sabbath's Changes, it's clear it would be an affront to modernize Bradley's unvarnished howls.

Title: Man on the Rocks
Review: Imperfections aside, this is a strange, oddly compelling addition to his catalog.

Title: The Living Infinite
Review: If you like Soilwork, this is the album you've been waiting over a decade for.

Title: Nextdoorland
Review: For the people who love this band, their sound, and Hitchcock's songwriting, this album will definitely not disappoint.

Title: Meaning of Life
Review: There’s lots of filler, too, such as Go High--based around a Michelle Obama speech--and the body-positive pop of Whole Lotta Woman, which sticks a little too closely to the Meghan Trainor mould. Despite this, the strong, 90s diva-ish mood suits Clarkson’s belting vocal style, as she ushers in a more soulful phase with class.

Title: Seasons of Your Day
Review: It’s the aural equivalent of sweet syrup—slow, molasses-y and utterly satisfying.

Title: In the Dark
Review: You could call it "rock on autopilot". It would be a good description. If you asked some space creatures to create an album of banal Earthling arena rock, they might very well create In the Dark using a tentacleful of the simplest mathematical algorithms.

Title: Tuskegee
Review: He's a pop artist of substance, and as such brings a touch of class and sufficient flavour of another genre to the mainstream to make music that's interesting and lasting.

Title: Twice As Tall
Review: The result is songs that are intricate but still tricky, in the way African rhythms can be, but there’s a comforting palm wine-y warmth – regardless of his almost perpetual fury or often tedious boasting, Twice as Tall is usually more urbane than urban. And crucially, the singer is totally in tune with what his fellow millennials expect from their music and their cultural experiences.

Title: Aesthethica
Review: There's no let-up, no pretty acoustic interludes, just full-on musical onslaught.

Title: Everything All The Time
Review: Packed with plenty of oddly memorable moments. [Apr/May 2006, p.101]

Title: Whitechapel
Review: This record takes everything the band has done in the past and gives it to us in a rather different, yet just as captivating way.

Title: Vows
Review: Kimbra's American fame may have come on the heels of someone else's single, but there's a vision here that's entirely her own.

Title: Storytone
Review: The orchestrations also let us focus on Young as a pure singer, rather than as a holistic musician. And he’s a remarkably effective one. In his aged, spindly whine lies a world of emotion.

Title: Bush
Review: The drawbacks to Bush are few and far between though, and even these complaints are more like minor annoyances.

Title: Immortalized
Review: Immortalized isn't without its duffers. [22 Aug 2015, p.51]

Title: Black Hours
Review: While we should never compare a solo artist with their band’s work, when the template they’ve already set over the years is so very strong, and when they don’t at any juncture try to reset it, the feeling of missed opportunity is perhaps potent and hard to escape.

Title: DÃ©jÃ  Vu
Review: An album that plays too safe in its thirst for hits. [Jul 2015, p.110]

Title: Bird Songs of a Killjoy
Review: The more upbeat swing to the songs doesn't dull the crispness of her songwriting. [Jul 2019, p.90]

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth
Review: Anthems for Doomed Youth proves conclusively that they are somehow still standing. Drunkenly swaying and swaggering, but still standing proud and tall.

Title: A Sufi and a Killer
Review: It’s a stunning, genre-transcending record that should appeal as much to fans of the esoteric, fuzzbox-psychedelia unearthed by Andy Votel and the Finders Keepers label as it will those fond of dubstep, the spliff-frazzled paranoia of trip hop, J Dilla’s vision of cerebral, emotionally rich hip hop, the head-in-the-clouds acid folk of Marc Bolan’s Tyrannosaurus Rex and dust-blown, voodoo-tweaked blues.

Title: Electronic Earth
Review: This debut from Tinie Tempah producer Labrinth sits comfortably in the Kanye West school of autotuned mid-youth crisis, yet this album isn't without merit.

Title: Forever
Review: It’s simply the worst of generic pop music--the kind that’s existed for decades, just with a fresh new coat of EDM slapped on.

Title: Glacier
Review: The entire album, an inspiring instrumental accomplishment that moves at a glacial pace, puts Jamison in the leagues of some of the better ambient musicians going today, and on only his first real foray into the genre.

Title: Half-Light
Review: It’s honest, personal and wholly relatable. Rostam may have defined Vampire Weekend’s sound, but with Half-Light he begins to define himself.

Title: High Expectations
Review: As a debut album it goes over well, with a convincing display of versatility and quality songwriting that firmly establishes Mabel as a force to be reckoned with in UK pop.

Title: Common Existence
Review: It may not receive the attention its predecessors did, from me at least, but it's an impressive return to form; that in and of itself is worthwhile.

Title: Fly International Luxurious Art
Review: For all its unintended sonic drawbacks, Fly International Luxurious Art goes a long way to remind everyone of why Raekwon is one of the greatest to ever wield a microphone.

Title: Big Echo
Review: Big Echo won't change the direction of modern music but it's such an easy, pleasurable listen that it can't fail to enrich whatever environment it's played in. Unreservedly recommended.

Title: Girls and Weather
Review: Girls And Weather is so cloyingly cheerful and eager to please that it might as well be "Big Brother" audition tape.

Title: Pretty Little Head
Review: Candy-coated and a teensy bit tart, Pretty Little Head grows in delight with every bite.

Title: Blisters In the Pit of My Heart
Review: Relatability abounds on Blisters In The Pit Of My Heart, perhaps not least on retail romance tale ‘Precarious (The Supermarket Song)’ where “I’m like an unexpected item in your bagging area” emerges as a contender for lyric of the year.

Title: Cross Record
Review: Her eerie, seductive first solo outing takes your brain to a new plane. [Sep 2019, p.93]

Title: Wrecked
Review: While the sound splashed across Wrecked is quite gripping (exceptionally gritty electronic that heavily works the industrial angle), the lack of distinction within, and contrast between, tracks makes it tough to get behind.

Title: Guilty Pleasure
Review: Power ballad 'What If' reveals that Tisdale can deliver the radio-ready goods, and 'Tell Me Lies' is convincingly spunky. But the rest of the material, as racy as it sometimes is, doesn't give the singer room to comfortably let loose.

Title: Rome
Review: Burton and Luppi don't entirely lose their identities in the desert vistas of Rome--the record has all the crisp conciseness of a Danger Mouse production--but they might have created a better story than a record.

Title: WIXIW
Review: There's lots to love about WIXIW, but it is all so much the band's own creation that anything less than experience falls severely short of capturing it.

Title: 12 Stories
Review: 12 Stories, a record full of humor and pain, remorse and reckoning, is one of the very best country debuts of 2013.

Title: Physicalist
Review: With Physicalist, Forma have issued a gorgeous statement that extends beyond being a culmination of their previous work. This LP is an example of a collective approaching its zenith.

Title: Nostalchic
Review: Lapalux has found his home at Brainfeeder, with Nostalchic and its masterful genre crossings a fitting first release.

Title: Side Effects
Review: There's plenty of different music at your disposal, and you never know what comes next. The album is wildly and refreshingly unpredictable.

Title: Wooden Aquarium
Review: A really strong album that shows Mazes growing in just the right way, adding some maturity and substance without sacrificing the things (great songs, youthful energy) that made them worth hearing in the first place.

Title: Pageant
Review: What makes Pageant a great record, and a convincing document of queer life, is the balance between earnestness and droll humour, a push and pull that can be traced back through the work of Rufus Wainwright, Pet Shop Boys and The Smiths, right back to Susan Sontag's definition of camp as an expression of this duality in 1964.

Title: She
Review: She does sultry and cool well.

Title: Alaska
Review: Their hometown makes itself known--lots of songs are accented with steel guitar--but the instrumentation stays delicate throughout.

Title: Familiars
Review: What a pleasure that Familiars is familiar primarily for its quality rather than its qualities.

Title: Death Becomes Her
Review: Death Becomes Her is an album from an artist who in now beginning to realise her possibilities, not just as a producer but as a performer, and as such she wants to get everything out there, squeezing every last idea into the album. And sometimes her take on pop music might be a little too abrasive to reach the playlists of many a commercial pop station… for now.

Title: Nothing is Precious Enough for Us
Review: Though Nothing's eerie lullabies are sweet in their own sing-songy way, the album's more energetic moments only serve as a frustrating indicator of Thibodeau's potential—if only he would think outside of his usual (voice) box.

Title: Spark Seeker
Review: It's a record well worth listening to, and such a myriad of sounds.

Title: Lush
Review: At its core, Lush is partly a remarkable debut, for the solid shape it's delivered in, mostly cohesive, conceptually speaking, but it's true that the cohesiveness of Lush lacks any true dichotomy to "spice" up the album.

Title: Interpol
Review: As meticulously as these sounds and instruments are recorded, as beautiful and haunting as they sometimes sound, they don't add up to more than one or two truly memorable songs.

Title: Hot Dreams
Review: Hot Dreams isn't perfect, then, but it is different--and genuine experimentation always demands attention.

Title: The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place
Review: Explosions in the Sky doesn't shift as suddenly or jarringly on Earth Is Not a Cold Dead Place; the quartet has applied more structural predictability this time out, but is still quick about setting the sad butterflies in your stomach to fluttering.

Title: The Ground Our Sky
Review: A frontier bliss-out. [Dec 2019, p.96]

Title: Glass Swords
Review: This album is loud, obnoxious, personal, and a hell of a lot of fun.

Title: Aphrodite
Review: Sometimes dance pop with this much gloss and unabashed glee is relegated to the realms of guilty pleasure, but Aphrodite is that rare representation of perfect production that is just pleasure, pure and simple.

Title: Stitch of the World
Review: Tift Merritt and her wonderful band deliver big time with this record ...  Despite it being very early in 2017, it's safe to say this album will be on many year-end lists come December.

Title: In Space
Review: Mostly fantastic. [#11, p.109]

Title: H-p1
Review: Some listeners might run screaming but the band's tenacity is admirable, which keeps it exciting.

Title: Wizard Bloody Wizard
Review: If you compare this to past triumphs like Come My Fanatics and Dopethrone--albums that pushed doom metal into heavier and more joyously drug-addled territory than ever before--Wizard Bloody Wizard falls a spliff or two short of the mark.

Title: Evolution
Review: They might have over-egged the acoustic balladry here, leading to their airiness unbalancing the syncopated beefiness elsewhere, but it's delivered so slickly and confidently that few fans will care. [20 Oct 2018, p.55]

Title: Menos el Oso
Review: A sublime success. [Jul/Aug 2005, p.103]

Title: Slow Focus
Review: At times bleak and nigh on disturbing yet always thick with complexity, it's a record which takes many, many listens to get to grips with and rewards repeat listens with almost unbelievable depth.

Title: Atlas
Review: Atlas is a perfect return to form for Parkway Drive.

Title: Different Gear, Still Speeding
Review: Full of derision that the less talented one out of Oasis is going to be found out on his own? You won't be dissuaded.

Title: Radio Wars
Review: The way that Howling Bells constructed Radio Wars relies on strong melodies, hooks, songs, songs that aren’t really there, ideas not quite developed.

Title: Crush on Me
Review: It’s remarkable how Crush on Me comes off as two albums in one. One album, containing “Heels” and “Haunted House,” is a less abrasive version of SOPHIE’s work with Mozart’s Sister, which ends up as a hyperventilating version of the alt-pop singles that litter playlists everywhere. They’re all executed well; they’re certainly done with the most gusto possible. But the familiarity gets a bit much. ... The other, better album in Crush on Me is an alt-rock throwback.

Title: Grinderman
Review: It sounds terrific, in a turbulent fashion. [9 Apr 2007]

Title: Mythologies
Review: A psychedelic, textured sound that's a leap forward from their already-impressive debut album.

Title: Where Does This Door Go
Review: Upon a first listen, Where Does This Door Go may be a lot to take in, as it covers a wide range of sounds and styles in its 52-minute runtime, but it also packs an immediate punch, and Hawthorne’s growth as a composer is evident by the end of the first song, making this easily his best album to date.

Title: When The Devil's Loose
Review: A tightly constructed record, its hushed instrumentation and Southern Gothic lyrics give it a melancholic mood, one that Bondy handles beautifully. [Dec 2009, p. 117]

Title: Let Love
Review: There's more than enough for a killer accompaniment to his book, but as a standalone album, Let love needs a tougher edit. [Oct 2019, p.106]

Title: All 6's and 7's
Review: Gimmicks abound on this dark carnival of an album, and if you can't hang with some murder talk and misogyny, it's best to stay away, but this fat, epic effort is still a swift thrill ride and doesn't bore despite its size.

Title: Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts
Review: Dead Cities reinforces the French pair's penchant for distorted vocals and cheesy synthesizers, but the tracks here ultimately add up to far less than the sum of their assorted parts.

Title: Rapprocher
Review: Class Actress still sound a little too weird to truly break through (and if they toned that weirdness down, this record just wouldn't be as interesting).

Title: The Church of Rock and Roll
Review: Like with Foxy's previous efforts, The Church of Rock & Roll shines in its ballsy rejection of modern pop stereotypes, however, the new album slips in its contradictions.

Title: With Love
Review: For an artist so intent on self-mythologizing--with his grand pronouncements, rare interviews and mask-wearing anonymity--With Love feels like a surprisingly comprehensive piece of work. But it's still a rambling outpouring of quick-fire songs.

Title: Four Year Strong
Review: Four Year Strong sees the Massachusetts four-piece at their most refined, eleven tracks that not only succinctly sum up their fourteen year history but confidently remind the world at large that they’ve still got something to offer.

Title: Goon
Review: A succession of producers--including Ariel Rechtshaid, Patrick Carney of the Black Keys and Jesso’s chief collaborator, former Girls bassist Chet “JR” White--have smoothed the fragility and murk of Jesso’s demos into a 70s-inspired production that accentuates the similarities between his songs and those of various vintage songwriters.

Title: (II)
Review: There's nothing surprising or too far outside their comfort zone.

Title: Double Cup
Review: Emerging as an outgrowth of Chicago house music, the principle formula is one that combines bubbling 808s and low end with angular snare patterns and looped snatches of vocal samples. It can often prove a jarring prospect in the first instance, but DJ Rashad’s Double Cup is a coherent and appealing starting point for the curious.

Title: Your Queen is a Reptile
Review: This is jazz that’s best heard at maximum volume. [Apr 2018, p.62]

Title: Can't Wake Up
Review: Between the obvious stylistic growth of Shakey Graves and Rose-Garcia’s ramped up creative appetite, Can’t Wake Up presents itself as the definitive album of the project’s discography. It masters its own atmosphere, swelling with confidence at each and every turn while inviting all who listen to join in. It only gets stronger as it goes on.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: Run The Jewels has again pushed rap away from regular rhythms and rhymes and into territories that they’re still calculating the dimensions of. May they never reach the sum of such remarkable parts and continue to exclusively Run Them Jewels fast.

Title: Need to Feel Your Love
Review: Need to Feel Your Love continues to dance along the line separating proto-metal and power pop, but leans more often toward the latter. Bassist Hart Seely’s slightly crisper production lets you better savor the jangly acoustic strums underpinning the power chords, while liberating Halladay’s singing from the payphone fidelity of those earlier recordings.

Title: The Warning
Review: A highly entertaining album, and perfect for blasting during hot summer days.

Title: Comma
Review: There's a more pronounced sense of drive and velocity. [Aug 2020, p.36]

Title: Slow Sundown
Review: If Holy Motors are limited in range, they show genuine skill at bringing their one mood to vivid life.

Title: Better Oblivion Community Center
Review: The songs on Better Oblivion Community Center are contemplative rather than declarative, granting the artists a chance to approach sorrow in a cheekier manner and find reserves of hope amid the wreckage.

Title: Re-Engineering
Review: Re-Engineering is very much an album designed to be played as a seamless whole. It's warm, fun, curious and deeply entertaining.

Title: You're Dreaming
Review: There's a '60s simplicity that's instantly engaging. [Feb 2016, p.93]

Title: Render Another Ugly Method
Review: It might sound a bit much on paper, but Leschper's thought processes result in fantastic music--think Warpaint gone deconstructivism-crazy. [Oct 2018, p.115]

Title: Dreamt for Light Years in the Belly of a Mountain
Review: The sound remains crisp, ensuring that its rough-hewn beauty shines through. [Oct 2006, p.104]

Title: Back to Black
Review: It's precisely Winehouse's lyrics... that raise this expertly crafted set into the realm of true, of-the-minute originality. [16 Mar 2007, p.67]

Title: Give You The Ghost
Review: It starts losing its nuance halfway through, creating a distraction from the effort as a whole.

Title: Mostly No
Review: If Mostly No lacks genuine innovation, the album more than compensates with a radiating glow of veneration.

Title: Time to Die
Review: Electric Wizard are arguably the most revered band of the doom metal genre since Black Sabbath themselves, and on Time To Die, they remind us why.

Title: Spirit
Review: Exactly zero songs on Spirit come close to matching 'Bleeding Love.' On the album, she fares best when not allowed to overindulge in her sterling voice as on the haunting electro kiss-off 'Take a Bow' and the svelte power ballad 'I Will Be,' co-written by Avril Lavigne.

Title: Circus
Review: The clubby, adventurous pop on her sixth album--her first since getting committed and losing custody of her kids--would have made a fine follow-up to 2003's In the Zone.

Title: X
Review: Charmless kiss-offs (“Don’t”) and sappy sentiments (“People Fall in Love in Mysterious Ways”) dominate otherwise, landing with the thud of the authentically uninspiring.

Title: Demolished Thoughts
Review: There's no reaching out to new audiences here nor attempts to break ground, just an accessible expression by an artist with the freedom to do just that.

Title: Devin Dazzle & the Neon Fever
Review: [Its] Atari-quality grooves and soulless Berlin homages reek of '80s hipster trash. [4 June 2004, p.80]

Title: Both Ways Open Jaws
Review: Both Ways Open Jaws will strike you as both new sounding and classic, as both fresh and rooted in tradition. Most importantly, it will strike you as a treasure, and probably, as the best album you have heard in a long time.

Title: Rain On Lens
Review: While it isn't his best work, Rain on Lens shows that Callahan is proving to be frustratingly hard to pin down, but capable of unleasing brilliance at any given time. [Nov 2001, p.94]

Title: Without Your Love
Review: After two impressive EPs for Tri Angle, his debut Without Your Love continues to thrive on subterranean nighttime pleasures.

Title: Arular
Review: Arular is what The Coup’s second record set out to be but wasn’t: Party Music, both for the warehouse hedonists and the basement dissidents.

Title: Beyond the Pale
Review: A resounding comeback. ... The best thing Cocker has done since Pulp, and that is very good indeed.

Title: Carrion Crawler/The Dream
Review: This is a colorful mix of styles, filled with feedback, mangled solos and manic vocals, and rocking like The Cramps on a good night. [Dec 2011, p.100]

Title: High as Hope
Review: The most rewarding Florence and the Machine full-length yet.

Title: Nothing Hurts
Review: But while you’d think the group’s hard-punching sound might be sloppy considering how it comes on so fast and furiously, it’s surprising how little wasted energy there is on Nothing Hurts, with most of any excess burned off of the album’s lean and mean half-hour running time.

Title: Jumping the Shark
Review: His delivery is low, wounded, yearning; despite the rockist structures, the keyboards and drum machines rattle in a pale imitation of the grandeur he’s seeking, like the last scene of Aguirre.

Title: Signs of Light
Review: Things work better when they balance the impulse to hulk things up with their natural traditionalist intimacy.

Title: Another Country
Review: His new album is also self-penned, with mixed results.

Title: Hit Reset
Review: While the music of The Julie Ruin may not have as much of the anger and purpose that colored her earlier work, it feels like some of her most personal music yet, a reclamation of herself as a musician.

Title: In Light
Review: The debut album from Lafayette, Louisiana's Givers plays with a loose, ebullient spark that sounds borne of considerate friendly jamming. [Jul 2011, p.85]

Title: Modus Vivendi
Review: Although ‘Modus Vivendi’ has oodles of instant appeal, the minute the rule book is thrown out the window, Shake is at the top her game.

Title: Overjoyed
Review: In all, Overyjoyed sees Half Japanese play it considerably safer than they used to, and there’s bundles of pop-rock glory to enjoy, but it’s still more than enough for loyal fans to breathe a sigh of relief.

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: Come Around Sundown is, and it ends up being no different from a lot of the phony populism in the air these days.

Title: Love Behind The Melody
Review: Finally the loverman is back. [Mar 2008, p.100]

Title: Headphones
Review: Headphones is a welcome experiment for a songwriter who was getting dangerously close to repeating himself. [#9]

Title: Fear of a Black Tangent
Review: His delivery is exhilarating, but it made me nervous, jittery. It’s kind of like Miles Davis scatting, but instead of a trumpet he’s playing the entire writing staff of The Simpsons.

Title: King
Review: An absence of memorable narratives, punch lines and wordplay makes the songs pass without distinction.

Title: Sharpen Your Teeth
Review: The collaborative nature of Sharpen Your Teeth, of course, yields a few missteps.... There are some damn fine moments here, though.

Title: Spacehopper
Review: When Tripwires push so far out of their confines that the boundaries can’t be seen, the uncertainty and frustration of the lyrics starts to make more of a connection. Unfortunately, too often on Spacehopper they stick too close to the traditional patterns of orbit.

Title: Beast Epic
Review: Beast Epic is a worthy addition to the Iron And Wine catalogue and an example of an album that improves the more and deeper you listen to it.

Title: Detours
Review: In Detours' subdued second half, though, Crow lays off the social commentary to address her own recent rough patches, with lyrics that grow more absorbing and intimate as Bottrell's eclecticism simmers down.

Title: Modern Nature
Review: Having set high standards for two-and-a-half decades, Modern Nature serves as another prized addition to The Charlatans' already wealthy canon.

Title: Bat Out of Hell III: The Monster Is Loose
Review: That he fails is not the fault of his individual performance; it's the fault of botched execution.

Title: Many Levels of Laughter
Review: At barely more than 30 minutes of lingering in spacey grooves, Many Levels of Laughter may not be as focused, but it certainly shows another intriguing, clever songwriter on the rise.

Title: Time To Die
Review: The band seems to have decided musical chops and precision production are more important than ideas, turning Time to Die into a startlingly streamlined affair that passes without leaving much of a mark.

Title: The Rose Has Teeth in the Mouth of a Beast
Review: Matmos have created a digital manifestation of their own personality, one that would be done more justice through psychoanalysis than musical description.

Title: Let Them Talk
Review: To his enormous credit, Laurie never sounds like a dilettante among this group; he holds his own, working his way into the marrow of the songs, playing credible piano throughout the record.

Title: Out of the Blues
Review: The Walroth material absolutely sparkles, with "Rock and Stick", the album opener, having the heat and smoothness of a sports car in the sun, and the kind of groove that will satisfy fans of Silk Degrees. Scagg's voice is affected by age but not to its detriment.

Title: Fits
Review: On its third LP, Fits, the Austin outfit White Denim thrives with wailing, wavering guitars, fuzzed-out basslines, and spiritied shouts. [Fall 2009, p.60]

Title: The Union
Review: Elton John has said that The Union, his collaboration with rock/pop/R&B legend Leon Russell, is an effort to bring Russell the attention John feels he deserves- including entry to the Rock And Roll Hall Of Fame.

Title: Odd Blood
Review: An overcooked vanity piece from a band inflated by praise, Odd Blood heads in every direction at once.

Title: Fetch the Bolt Cutters
Review: The result of Apple’s self-imposed social distancing is the stunning intimacy of the material here — a rich text to scour in quarantine. Her idiosyncratic song structures, full of sudden stops and lurching tempo changes, adhere to logic only she could explain, which forces you to listen as attentively as though a dear friend were bending your ear.

Title: America
Review: With its multiple parts, its recurring motifs and its thematic hutzpah "USA" isn't easy to parse or process, but it's not impenetrable; Deacon remains committed to pop forms and rock songwriting despite his concert-hall inclinations.

Title: Unleashed
Review: There is care and artistry throughout.

Title: Night Melody
Review: West, when left alone to his devices, is able to transform emotion into the esoteric, colluding synthesis into vibrant, organic swaths of sound. Rhythmically taking jabs like hesitation marks, throwing caution to the wind.

Title: Life Without Sound
Review: Life Without Sound is the next logical step in Cloud Nothings’ upward trajectory.

Title: Theology
Review: The second record falters with a clunky combo of Celtic rock and leaden hip-hop rhythms that squashes the fragile, hook-free tunes. [Jul 2007, p.100]

Title: Channel Orange
Review: For now, the best tribute you can pay Channel Orange is that, while it plays, you forget about the chatter and just luxuriate in a wildly original talent.

Title: I Was Born Swimming
Review: While I Was Born Swimming never goes into the unfamiliar, Williams' gushing charm is more than comforting enough to feel what it's like to exist somewhere in between destinations.

Title: Battle Born
Review: This is a production in search of an album, a massive empty shell, a big expensive nothing.

Title: Night Falls Over Kortedala
Review: Each song unfolds so effortlessly one imagines it springing forth, fully formed, with the same exaggerated inevitability of a cartoon bubble sprouting above his head. [Fall 2007, p.74]

Title: Fleet Foxes
Review: A number of contemporary indie bands attempts to strip-mine mountain ballads in the service of indie pop, but none has melded the impulses as effortlessly and captivatingly as Fleet Foxes manage on "Blue Ridge Mountains" and "Oliver James." Sublime.

Title: Gentle Stream
Review: The Amazing like to entice and then awe, always bringing songs back to the guitars, which sound like they're being played by a real human person, until they burst into shards of jagged, whirling rainbows.

Title: Ellipsis
Review: Clearly Biffy Clyro see themselves as strivers, a band that charges relentlessly forward. But at times, listeners might wonder if they’re headed in any interesting direction.

Title: Searching For Zero
Review: Cancer Bats' most experimental album might also be their catchiest.

Title: Don't Look Away
Review: If the album’s mind is fixed on a future world, it is an open-ended one. The tendency at this point might be to assume that all imagined futures are dystopian, but the spirit of Don’t Look Away and the sum of the pictures and story fragments Tucker has strung together in the record are reflected in its title: the good, the bad, the beauty, the fear...don’t look away from any of it.

Title: Aviary
Review: The mayhem, the confusion, the hysteria, Holter has learned to embrace all of it, and by reflecting it honestly in her music, she has shown the rest of us that whilst we live in alarming times, empathy and love continue to stand strong. Aviary will be a challenging listen for many, but its message needs to be heard.

Title: Before The World Was Big
Review: Before the World Was Big is a record that will help you appreciate the 'good old days' whilst you're still in them; it's a record that will make you feel okay about the unsettling aspects of the future and it's a record that will make you wanna hug your pals and never let them go.

Title: The Beautiful Madness
Review: Delivers assurance, class and a timely, powerful study in historically ingrained racist ideology. [Sep 2020, p.89]

Title: MONOVISION
Review: If you enjoy a record that can gently coax a cathartic tear or two, Monovision fits the bill. [Aug 2020, p.88]

Title: Gimme Some
Review: This might be a more natural and relaxed PB&J having the time of their lives, but it certainly doesn't find the band at their most creative.

Title: Acrobats
Review: Even with these small blips, Peggy Sue have made the transition to a darker and bolder sound with ease.

Title: Everything Touching
Review: The dizzying craftsmanship evident on this debut LP is never an obstacle.

Title: Widdershins
Review: Full of heart, courage, and passion, Widdershins finds Grant-Lee Phillips going from strength to strength after The Narrows, and it ranks with his best solo efforts.

Title: America
Review: For all of its denseness, America feels as panoramic and wonder-filled as the cross-country travels that inspired it. [Sep 2012, p.99]

Title: Greendale
Review: A soothing, gentle rock'n'roll opus.

Title: The Idler Wheel
Review: The Idler Wheel… is a really incredible album, where Apple has quite cleverly developed musically in just the right way, creating something utterly distinct and different to her earlier work whilst still retaining all the characteristics that won fans over to begin with.

Title: Song For Alpha
Review: Daniel Avery has a specific set of tools in his arsenal and these are sometimes spread a bit thin, but Song For Alpha is still a worthy follow-up to 2013’s Drone Logic and an enjoyable listen.

Title: Serfs Up!
Review: Serfs Up! feels like a giant leap forward.

Title: Not Music
Review: Inasmuch as Stereolab have accomplished pretty much everything they could, Not Music feels like a passive retread.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: The 19 songs form a 39-minute-long cohesive whole which looses its meaning once shuffled or reorganised. What could come across as a mash-up of jam sessions slowly reveals its internal coherence.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: You can smell the impotent melodic desperation a mile off.

Title: Fits
Review: Fits is sublime, sexy, unmisable. [Jul 2009, p.99]

Title: Reptilians
Review: I know the band can write damn good songs and they have proven that before and prove it here, but until they address the main problems (the still heavily reverberated vocals for one) or really venture out into something different (there is life beyond pasting snippets from philosophy lectures) I think history will keep repeating itself for these guys.

Title: Manafon
Review: However central Sylvian’s bleak commentary, the weight and suggestiveness of this record gives it a sense of unpredictability, possibility, almost an openness beyond itself. It’s absolutely superb.

Title: Soul
Review: Seal's David Foster-produced tribute to classic soul is a figure skater of a collection, all elegance and grace. But some of these songs require the more aggressive approach of a hockey player.

Title: Transference
Review: While the bandmates sound like the veterans they are on Transference, Spoon brings to this new level the same prickliness and elusiveness that has informed all of its previous albums, and that has attracted devoted fans intent on parsing every word and note.

Title: Indigo Meadow
Review: Indigo Meadow is an assured, exciting piece of work.

Title: Konk
Review: Pritchard hits new high notes and rises to the challenge of the vibrant melodies and finely tuned choruses. With guitarist Hugh Harris coming out of the shadows, the Kooks' ambitions look well within their reach.

Title: II
Review: A pall of unrest certainly permeates the record, but II feels of a single entity, one cloaked in fog but backlit by strobes.

Title: Size Matters
Review: A disappointing barrage of lethargic metal. [Dec 2004, p.137]

Title: Get Lost
Review: His latest is dedicated to "the spirit of the summer night sky," and that's an accurate, if slightly cornball, description of these six impressionistic guitar instrumentals.

Title: Warm On a Cold Night
Review: Warm On A Cold Night is essentially a pick-up line delivered in Andy’s charmingly unfinished croak, wrapped in sensual synths and slick basslines.

Title: II
Review: Sounding like it was recorded in a musty shoebox, II nonetheless overflows with tweaky charm.

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: While it's not as subtle or as elegantly constructed as Beast Rest Forth Mouth, this record has a kineticism and momentum that Beast lacked.

Title: Eye to the Telescope
Review: Tunstall has Norah Jones's throaty catch, Dido's warmth, plus a winning way with a soaring chorus. [Jan 2005, p.130]

Title: Warpaint
Review: It’s impressively wrought, but save for the more propulsive, swingy shuffle of “Feeling Alright”, there’s a Novocaine numbness about it that makes it hard to love.

Title: Lenses Alien
Review: What's most impressive about Lenses Alien is that Cymbals Eat Guitars, after a couple of years on the road, sound like a band now instead of a recording project. [Jul 2011, p.79]

Title: Torres
Review: It's easy to imagine her getting very famous, because Torres doesn't wash the songs out with its prettiness.

Title: Torino
Review: In Wedding Present terms, Torino is Cinerama's Seamonsters. [Aug 2002, p.99]

Title: Be Your Own Pet
Review: Sweaty, sloppy and desperately quick. [Jul 2006, p.102]

Title: Time Was
Review: Still entrenched in disciplined modal drones and repetition, the group existing as a duo adds new color and dimension to its meditative sounds, giving the listener a sense of real mystery and excitement in what once felt simply obscured.

Title: British Road Movies
Review: The album is at its best, though, when Butler is cranking up the big rock and Jackson belts out melodies as straight and clear as an empty motorway. British Road Movies has plenty of that, and if it's not quite enough to make anyone forget the Long Blondes, it's a definite reminder to keep in touch with Kate Jackson.

Title: Marble Skies
Review: So far so good--and if anything it gets better.

Title: By the Fire
Review: It’s with By The Fire that Thurston Moore goes properly into orbit. Make no mistake; this is an album that stands shoulder to shoulder with the very best of his alma mater.

Title: NASIR
Review: Nasir is among the weakest Nas albums, but there’s nothing spectacular about its failure. It is, simply, the one thing Nas has avoided being all these years, through revolutionary highs and car-crash lows: dull.

Title: Seeker Lover Keeper
Review: Most often, the result is greater than the sum of its parts. [#39, p.69]

Title: Kish Kash
Review: There's a recurring sense of enforced jollity.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: A Seat at the Table, her third full-length album, is the work of a woman who’s truly grown into herself, and discovered within a clear, exhilarating statement of self and community that’s as robust in its quieter moments as it is in its funkier ones.

Title: No Shape
Review: It has moments of populist ambition (the soaring chorus of the lead single, “Slip Away,” for example) and self-consciously arty experimentation (“Choir”), and it’s a credit to Hadreas and producer Blake Mills that its 13 tracks sound as seamless and cohesive as they do.

Title: Requiem
Review: The music itself is far from nondescript, and if judged from this angle, and on its terms, Requiem is a flawed, unique, and immersive experience.

Title: Stellastarr
Review: Stellastarr's bold, cinematic sprawl demands a certain kind of tolerance, and might require a few listens before you're able to fully adjust to its dramatics, but Christensen is, in the end, an oddly convincing leader, and, if nothing else, you'll at least be stuck to your headphones trying to guess his next move.

Title: Daytona
Review: Another rare instance of an artist coming up with a classic a decade after what seemed like the peak of his career (Clipse’s Hell Hath No Fury), and the only thing that could’ve made it better was if he pre-released “Infrared” so that Drake could’ve responded and we could’ve had an album with “The Story of Adidon” on it.

Title: Soul
Review: As it turns out, the 45-year-old English singer's exploration of Soul comes up short in interpretation as it retreads ground long since broken by others.

Title: A Different Ship
Review: Highly recommended.

Title: Soft Will
Review: Soft Will is certainly pleasant enough (which shouldn’t really be what you’re striving for with a rock album), and I’m sure is being hailed by indie taste makers everywhere who like their rock on the sterile side.

Title: The New Classic
Review: Although a few late quarter misfirings render the album’s title misleading, there is too much good here to say with a straight face that Iggy will amount to nothing more than a flash in the pan.

Title: Ryan Adams
Review: Adams occasionally steps into a puddle of shallow adult-contemporary tripe that even his incisive personality and increasingly tamed voice cannot save. Those basic imitations of past great Adams tunes are few and far between on Ryan Adams, particularly when weighed against some of his other recent albums.

Title: When Machines Exceed Human Intelligence
Review: No amount of boulder-sized low-end can disguise the fact that, even when these tracks work, they usually feel like they're missing something major. And that something is a vocalist.

Title: Silver Eye
Review: If nothing here quite reaches knockout-blow strength, fine--it doesn’t really need to. Goldfrapp have found their platonic ideal, and that’s ideal indeed.

Title: Hot Shots II
Review: The key problem lies in the album's occasional sense of underachieving drift. [Aug 2001, p.104]

Title: Chuck
Review: His final album--and first since 1979--not only demonstrates the durability of the musical format he pioneered but also proves his indefatigability as an entertainer. [Jul 2017, p.25]

Title: Too
Review: Fidlar goes balls to the wall.

Title: Dressed Up for the Letdown
Review: Hypnotic and strangely thrilling. [Feb 2007, p.86]

Title: Antidotes
Review: Antidotes feels like riding a tea-tray down an icy mountainside. [Apr 2008, p.106]

Title: Unfollow the Rules
Review: A straight-ahead album of gorgeous, elaborate, amusing and affecting songs.

Title: Allergic to Water
Review: “Harder Than It Needs to Be” finds DiFranco hitting her stride, as it optimizes her knack for blending different musical genres—in this case, jazz with country and blues—and for delivering wisdom through clear, no-bullshit vocal inflections. If Allergic to Water had drawn upon these strengths more consistently, the album might have yielded a more delicately handled, astutely observed meditation on social and cultural issues that demand just as much attention now as ever.

Title: Let Us Never Speak of It Again
Review: Let Us Never Speak of it Again is bor-ing.

Title: Yankee Hotel Foxtrot
Review: Wilco's most rewarding work yet. [#34, p.60]

Title: She's In Control
Review: These '80s-trash connoisseurs have everything electroclash lacks: full-bodied grooves, self-deprecating idiot grins, and--what's best--sax solos. [20 Feb 2004, p.66]

Title: Quality
Review: Quality is a very conflicted album. On one hand, many of the tracks are close to the level mind blowing, production and rhyme wise. On the other hand, some of the tracks are just plain boring and muddy.

Title: Out from Out Where
Review: The focus on a single mood occasionally threatens to lead only to a creative dead-end, but Out from Out Where arguably betters its successors by coming together as a single work.

Title: Coming on Strong
Review: Preposterous, touching and brilliant.

Title: Sounds Good Feels Good
Review: Their second LP shows off their musical knowledge and ambition without getting in the way of their own preternatural adorableness.

Title: You Had It Coming
Review: Guitar-heads will automatically buy this, but it also deserves to reach any audiences excited by imaginative music working outside commercial boundaries.

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: All of the pop-coated rock that was immediately catchy, aggressive, melodic, seductive, melancholic, and driven from those two albums [Garbage and Version 2.0] can be found here – from the ramped up, unrelenting beats to the bright electronics and propulsive guitar lines, to Shirley's changeable, ever-engaging vocals.

Title: Rap Album One
Review: It's only when he applies his production tricks to his own voice on tracks like "Reflection" when things tend to go awry. But its this experimental bent that makes Rap Album One stand out, and deploying these skills judicially in the future will undoubtedly pay off on the evidence of this solid, eclectic debut.

Title: Specter At The Feast
Review: The album certainly finds the fiery BRMC of old rekindled, with the band wisely applying the lessons they’ve learned over the years to fortify their bold but familiar sound that, while not approaching a reinvention by any means, at least represents a definite rebirth.

Title: Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest
Review: Before putting it on, make sure you have an hour to yourself to just let it wash over you. Callahan’s ambition and essence haven’t been diminished by him being in a good headspace. He’s a man born to tell stories, and he’s no less of a storyteller than he was in his early 30s.

Title: Salt
Review: The sad country warmth of "Play the Game" and the starkly fingerpicked front half of "Soon" are soothing in their implied heartache, inviting listeners to lean in and try to untangle McMahon's lyrics through her downcast mumbling. Sadly, those same mumbled vocals sometimes become a hindrance during the slower sections of the album, distracting from the otherwise well-written songs. Still, delivery affectations aside, Salt serves as a solid introduction to this sensitive and engaging artist.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: These guys do so many things well--now if they could only find their weird again. [No. 95, p.52]

Title: Travellers in Space and Time
Review: Robert Schneider has always been an expert tunesmith, which makes the potentially disastrous transition from garage rock to super hi-fi feel like a natural extension of The Apples' ambition. Not only has the evolution been seamless, but an expanded mastery of studio technique has only served to buttress a fine collection of songs on Travellers.

Title: David Comes to Life
Review: Between the overlong, overstuffed songs and arrangements, ridiculous album concept and lyrical conceit, there's no room left for the vicious, hurtling energy that first impressed me on Hidden World's best songs.

Title: Nighttime Stories
Review: True to its title, Nighttime Stories' best moments appear late.

Title: Triage
Review: Webb is capable of nimble vocals, but he often opts for a deliberately strained tone, as if trying to push his woes through his colon. His gift for hooks means that even this peculiarity will find fans.

Title: Junk
Review: Messy, complicated, capable of star turns, it’s clearly a record Gonzalez needed to get out of his system.

Title: Here's to Taking It Easy
Review: Yet his voice still ambles all around the beat, and the production is calculatedly bleary, with horns, guitars and piano all entangled, as if two or three bands are playing the same song. Phosphorescent's perpetually woozy aesthetic is intact.

Title: Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not
Review: The thrill it provides will send a shiver of recognition through anyone who grew up with The Specials, The Smiths or Parklife. [Album of the Month, March 2006, p.86]

Title: Friendly Fire
Review: An album of angry, guilty, sad -- and often stunningly pretty -- songs. [5 Oct 2006, p.68]

Title: Heaven Is Whenever
Review: Despite the veteran group putting in a valiant effort, Heaven Is Whenever will largely be known as "the transitional LP." Hey, at least Bobby Drake's drums still sound exceptional.

Title: Get Behind Me Satan
Review: Hardly an alienating, experimental listen... White hasn't written such an accessible set of songs since 2000's De Stijl. [Album of the Month, Jul 2005, p.88]

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: Celebrates the little people with full powerpop majesty. [Jul 2003, p.108]

Title: Maniac Meat
Review: Maniac Meat is only really disappointing when compared to what came before, because try as it might, it can neither supercede nor outdo its predeces at it's own game.

Title: Go-Go Boots
Review: Despite the band's place in the alternative country/Southern rock movement, this album is still full of some yarns that should have never been woven.

Title: Dean Wareham
Review: Even if Dean Wareham isn't quite the sound of an artist shaking loose, its consolidation of strengths is something to admire.

Title: Defend Yourself
Review: When Defend Yourself starts attacking, it's as if Clinton never left the White House.

Title: Shutting Down Here
Review: A committed listen to O'Rourke's latest iteration reveals the piece to be understatedly eloquent, its movements and progressions restrained yet effective.

Title: Shine
Review: Joni Mitchell's first album of (mostly) new material in nine years is reminiscent of a chapter from the singer-songwriter's past--not her famous, acoustic balladeering Blue period but her subsequent, jazzier albums.

Title: Geist
Review: A touch more volume on the instruments and a bit of extra distance between one man's mouth and his microphone, this might have been a blissful exercise in studied yet clamorous rock music.

Title: Age Against The Machine
Review: The result is both an ambitious concept album and a glorious booty-shaker. [Oct 2013, p.68]

Title: Cheatahs
Review: The overall effect is warmly intoxicating and that the album comes so close to matching up to the records it's in thrall to means you can forgive its obvious debt to others. [Mar 2014, p.110]

Title: Beauty & Ruin
