Review: All the components are there, Joey Santiago’s guitar work is still impressive, Lovering’s drumming is still vigorous, but the problem is Black Francis himself. The compelling songwriting that completed Pixies is no longer there.

Title: Stories for Monday
Review: For a band who ultimately decided to soldier on, the album can feel unbalanced, but still delivers all the belting feel-good choruses that made you fall in love with the Arizona crew back in 2009. [Mar 2016, p.100]

Title: Still Life
Review: Merging deft production with stark, diary-entry songwriting on opener 'Too Much Love' (for dancing in low light with strangers) the south London electronic trio find a balance between melancholic subtext and the thrill of a beat you can sway to.

Title: Victory For The Comic Muse
Review: 'Victory for the Comic Muse' is the Divine Comedy's finest album since their post-Britpop Chris Evans-approved heyday.

Title: My Way
Review: Unlike Summertime: Willie Nelson Sings Gershwin, Nelson's limitations aren't a hindrance, and the arrangements aren't excessively polite, which means My Way is an appealingly light record: it's performed with more affection than reverence.

Title: Good Souls Better Angels
Review: She writes about toxic masculinity and abusive relationships with racing candour, and she sings with a fresh, unnerving snarl that weaponises her signature twang. [May 2020, p.35]

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: Madlib has formed a tighter frame around his productions than ever before.

Title: Motivational Jumpsuit
Review: Even as Motivational Jumpsuit faithfully approximates the grainy fidelity and 60-second dosages of Bee Thousand and Alien Lanes, it can’t maintain the same dizzying standards of pop euphoria throughout.

Title: New Material
Review: With their third LP, New Material, they dive into it headlong, getting closer to Munro’s stated goal than ever before.

Title: Future Crayon
Review: The Future Crayon, like Tender Buttons, is a little predictable at first but grows more complex after several listenings.

Title: Jessica Rabbit
Review: Jessica Rabbit is the work of a band in stasis, but also one who sound desperate to pull themselves out of it.

Title: Where You Go I Go Too
Review: When you consider that the first song is only a minute shy of half an hour long, this collection of epic ambient disco revisionism definitely counts as a full-fledged artistic statement.

Title: Reign of Terror
Review: Everything is enormously compressed, then amplified: it's claustrophobic and oppressive, but without having any particular power.

Title: The Search
Review: NF also shares Eminem’s shrillness and distorted sense of volume, rapping like he’s putting on the world’s loudest Punch and Judy show. He spends much of The Search darting in and out of an overbearing rappity-rap snarl-yell that can cut right through you if you don’t relate to his roiling anger.

Title: Beyond
Review: The spiraling, distortion-drenched guitar solos, the cracked and ruined moan of Mascis, the passive-aggressive romanticism, the relentless beat, the pedals, the sheer turbulent volume...it's just like Where You Been? all over again, with all the positives and negatives that the comparison implies.

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: An almost austere album, the production deliciously dry, forcing lyrics and beats to share the foreground. [Nov 2002, p.106]

Title: Love + Fear
Review: Love is where the album falls short of delivering--containing most of the pre-release singles and the mainstream Clean Bandit collaboration ‘Baby’--there are few moments where it feels like the signature Marina. ... The Fear half of the album is riddled with concern and confusion about life itself and the darker emotions that come with it. Opener ‘Believe In Love’ sits near the top of Marina’s most captivating songs.

Title: Open Season
Review: Neatly cut and effortless in its melodic simplicity.

Title: STONECHILD
Review: The pages of Stonechild sometimes read like wives' tales and folklore, but the morals found within should resonate with any modern wanderer.

Title: For The Recently Found Innocent
Review: So basically, it's another weird, great White Fence album, only the bass is a little clearer, the drums a bit louder, and there's less tape hiss. Only die-hard four-track fanatics could complain about that.

Title: Art Angels
Review: When it all clicks, it's a perfect pop moment. The worst that can be said of Art Angels is that its maximalist ambitions sometimes overshoot the needs of pop.

Artist: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
Title: Planetarium
Review: There are some lovely moments. ... But ultimately, the impossible ambition of Planetarium looms over every single moment. [Aug 2017, p.89]

Title: The 1975
Review: It's all promising, even if their debut leans harder on style than substance.

Title: Odd One Out
Review: It’s a charming and defiant debut, and one that encapsulates the GIRLI mindset, heartbreaks and all.

Title: Leave Me Alone
Review: Part of what makes Leave Me Alone such a blast is the impression it gives of Hinds as a tight-knit girl gang, on and off record.

Title: Blade of the Ronin
Review: Their prevailing operatic bleakness has barely changed in the intervening 14 years. [Jun 2015, p.72]

Title: Brave Faces Everyone
Review: What we have here will likely go down in history as the band’s magnum opus. It’s just so fucking massive and Netflix-level binge-worthy. Without a slow song or acoustic number, Brave Faces Everyoneis ten tracks of loud, abrasive rock music that should connect with anyone who’s life isn’t perfect.

Title: Donkey
Review: Donkey is the mediocre second outing Brazilian electro rockers CSS – will it show that they have more substance beyond being a mere good-time party band?

Title: Giraffe
Review: His diluted indie-whine does become obnoxious over the long haul. [Mar 2003, p.104]

Title: A Deeper Understanding
Review: Opener Up All Night moves through the formulaic pop gears as smoothly as Don Henley cruising along the Pacific Coast Highway, while Holding On is a slickly realised mid-tempo foot tapper. However, shorn of the novelty factor, such middle-of-the-road material remains better suited to balmy summer nights and drivetime radio than to repeated home listening.

Title: The Life of Pablo
Review: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy remains the apex of West's maximalist visions, and while The Life of Pablo certainly aims high, it isn't as consistently pointed in delivering both music and message as its big-budget predecessor was. And yet, it remains a modern gospel that is undeniably West's own, with a handful of vexatious moments peppered throughout the undeniably visionary ones.

Title: Word of Mouth
Review: On Word Of Mouth he's finally built a viable path between those old and new worlds. [Mar 2014, p.115]

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: John Neff’s expert, dreamy pedal steel and Shonna Tucker’s soothing, pitch-perfect harmony -- somewhere between Lucinda Williams and Neko Case--make Brighter another solid entry in the band's catalog.

Title: The Other I
Review: It's dreamy stuff, but it's nothing on their 5K-rated, self-titled 2012 debut album. [15 Nov 2014, p.54]

Title: If All I Was Was Black
Review: Staples is in strong voice throughout, yet on All Over Again, the closing folk blues look back on a lfe lived without regrets, she sings even lower than usual, sounding her age--impossibly wise and dignified. A fitting end to a great record.

Title: Hollow Ground
Review: It's a wonderful debut, and even if Clarke and Cut Worms veer away from this sound in the future, at least he will have left the world this one slice of genius retro-pop.

Title: Fundamental
Review: There's little on PSB's album that matches the big twizzly dunce-hatted glory of their 'Very' peak. [20 May 2006, p.33]

Title: Lovers
Review: A record that is rich, varied and a little crackers as well, Lovers will certainly stand as one of the best debut albums of the year.

Title: LM5
Review: Ultimately, despite a few high points, LM5 is so scattershot, both thematically and musically, that it’s hard to find much to grab onto.

Title: Molina & Johnson
Review: It sounds nothing like their other bands, and only shares that feel with their solo work. This, these twelve fragile, creaking, beautiful songs, is the sound of Molina and Johnson.

Title: Inside The Ships
Review: Inside The Ships is one of their most entertaining yet confounding albums. [Oct 2011, p.101]

Title: Think Tank
Review: Sure, it might be easier to accept if it was called a Damon Albarn solo album, but that's splitting hairs. A lousy album is a lousy album, no matter who gets credit.

Title: Valley Tangents
Review: Blues Control are one of the most intriguingly unclassifiable outfits in contemporary music, putting forth music that is clear and refined while also being absolutely incomparable.

Title: La Costa Perdida
Review: As ever, it's an eclectic mix of styles.

Title: The Day After
Review: The real story here is Twista's rapping. [9 Oct 2005]

Title: Fastlife
Review: As a vocalist and a presence, Jonas is a flop.

Title: Air Lows
Review: Nothing feels forced or amplified for impact. It’s a humble and understated sound and one that endears me to her as a human. The tracks and the overall narrative are succinct, though I wished the trip was longer. When the album finished I was compelled to play it through again.

Title: Time Team
Review: This is an album worth living and breathing to at least attempt to become acquainted with its wealth of emotional nuances and playful eccentricities.

Title: HYMNS
Review: For those expecting the worst ahead of Bloc Party’s return, Hymns is likely to validate all their fears. Change may have been unavoidable after losing two influential members, but to change beyond recognition is almost an insult to the original band’s legacy.

Title: RUFF
Review: If it's not the group's finest work, it has a genuine emotional purity and reaffirms Born Ruffians' place on the Canadian indie rock scene.

Title: It's Me Again
Review: Unfortunately, the songs aren't always as good as the sounds, but the best ones are dazzling.

Title: Untitled
Review: The California band's doomy gothic arias sound unsettling and bold once more. [Sep 2007, p.91]

Title: Extralife
Review: Extralife is a record infused with apocalyptic dread, a collection of campfire sing-alongs for the end of days. As well, it's an oddly beautiful record, comfortable in its unsettling contemplations and rapturous.

Title: Tribal
Review: The feel is antique and wearily repetitive. Only the sexed up Wicked Way and the deft and tender Little Pixie, about her baby daughter, offer any light and shade. [Jul 2014, p.92]

Title: The Platform
Review: The most alluring aspect of The Platform is the array of finely-crafted beats assembled by Evidence and DJ Premier protégé The Alchemist, which are in turn juggled and sliced at will by the hands of DJ Babu, the oft-forgotten man in the hip-hop equation.

Title: Burnt Up on Re-Entry
Review: He has not made a classic here, but he may have made an album which allows him to do so again in the future.

Title: A Strange Arrangement
Review: At worst, A Strange Arrangement has a couple lulls; at best, it’s one of the most enjoyable records of the summer. Highly recommended.

Title: The Something Rain
Review: It may not be a Tindersticks classic, in the same vein as 1997's sublime Curtains, but The Something Rain is a record full of mystery and intrigue that will keep you listening--and discovering new things each time--for a good while.

Title: Get Guilty
Review: Get Guilty is best enjoyed in chunks, as nearly all the tracks are great pop songs. But a full listen through can be an ordeal.

Title: By The Throat
Review: It’s not only an addition to 2009’s unassailably fantastic class of ambient music, but in a way is unique to that class for the menace with which it’s threaded.

Title: Albatross
Review: You'd think there wasn't much left to do with the roots-oriented rock formula, but Albatross proves that there's plenty of life and passion and intelligence left in the genre.

Title: I'm Not Your Man
Review: Her new found confidence comes through in spades here and the end product is a record that shines with a captivating vibrancy.

Title: Assume Form
Review: Assume Form is aggressively pastel and suffocatingly serious. He has lost the playful sense of surprise that guided his falsetto’s agile twists and turns on his debut.

Title: Goon
Review: There's not much one can do to deny the emotional weight or the eerily '70s character of Goon; it's probably best to settle into the La-Z-Boy, flick feathered hair off of your polyester lapel, grab a box of tissues, and let it be.

Title: High on Jackson Hill
Review: Therein lies the personality crisis of Jackson Hill: The sole connecting thread for all these tunes is a band whose love for its craft just barely surpasses what a hodgepodge mess it often is.

Title: Delta Spirit
Review: A lovely, thoughtful album.

Title: A Grand Don't Come For Free
Review: Upping his narrative ante, Skinner goes all-in on Grand, a bold follow-up that sounds beguilingly slight and dry until details start sketching its story.

Title: Winning Days
Review: Winning Days is still more interesting than any album by obvious progenitors Oasis because the good parts come up at the most random moments--spontaneous solo here, appealing harmony there.

Title: Lindsey Buckingham / Christine McVie
Review: They’ve reunited in the studio for this succinct collection of gentle pop-rockers, familiar yet far more strange and beautiful than 2013’s brittle Fleetwood Mac EP.

Title: Quicken the Heart
Review: The painstaking introspection here seems to stem from a need to use their success and exposure to deliver some definitive, U2-sized message when really they're so much more relatable when they're awkwardly sorting out their psychological messes on the fly.

Title: The Long Goodbye
Review: This is heavy stuff, but Ahmed’s wry wit and laser-focused delivery ensures that it doesn’t feel overwrought.

Title: Raditude
Review: Raditude seems intent on establishing itself as a now album, sacrificing any sort of cohesive vibe for a pop-friendly disc designed for car stereos to be turned to 11.

Title: Black Laden Crown
Review: The fact is, on Black Laden Crown, Danzig seems to have reached the conceptual and sonic epiphany he’s been searching for since the end of Danzig 4. The production issues may dampen this epiphany to a degree, but a production problem in of itself is not enough to buckle the dark message behind the computerized choices.

Title: Visiter
Review: It's a winning formula The Dodos repeat throughout Visiter, and yet never run into the ground.

Title: Visiter
Review: A lyrical and musical knockout, spearheaded by the miraculous 'Fools,' Visiter could be one of the best albums of the year. [Spring 2008, p.82]

Title: Binaural
Review: A seething, furious album; a declamatory statement against cynicism and passivity and the simple injustices of everyday life.

Title: Man on the Moon: The End of Day
Review: Cudi too often assumes some sort of higher ground even though his self-pity is flaunted no differently than any other tacky rapper accessory.

Title: Dangerous Woman
Review: The album glides through styles, maintaining a slightly menacing yet sexed-up vibe throughout.

Title: 3 Pears
Review: It's as fresh as any music he's ever made, and one of his very best albums.

Title: Faded Seaside Glamour
Review: Though Faded Seaside Glamour proudly wears the jacket of its influences for all to see, the band stitch it up so well that you could never accuse it of being a knockoff.

Title: Volcano
Review: If Temples needed to prove that they were more than talented revivalists, then Volcano should silence the doubters. Sure, you’re unlikely to find a Stormzy sample buried within its midst, but Temples’ second statement shows that innovation and notable progress can still sound classic.

Title: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes
Review: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes is a solid reboot for Social D, with singer and songwriter Ness navigating the current lineup of the band through a churning confluence of Stones-y blues and country twang.

Title: The OOZ
Review: The OOZ drops at our feet like a piece of poisoned fruit, a masterpiece of jaundiced vision from one of the most compelling artists alive.

Title: Pacific Daydream
Review: Pacific Daydream can be read as a bitter reaction to the Trump era and geo-political chaos, or maybe it's just a set of (mostly) great tunes that provide light relief from it all. [Nov 2017, p.114]

Title: Rewild
Review: A frequently startling record of no little beauty--which threatens to launch a new, esoteric generation of Williamsburg wonders.

Title: Hyperion
Review: These tracks [with pop collaborations] amount to unremarkable radio fare and dilute the artistic voices of all involved. ... The instrumentals have more bite.

Title: She-Devils
Review: Despite all of its sonic busyness, the vast majority of which falls in the category of charming rather than challenging, the album ultimately comes off as a little goofy, fun, and full of promise.

Title: Wet from Birth
Review: It’s all over the place, yet perfectly fresh and maligned.

Title: Last Summer
Review: Perhaps the biggest hurdle for Friedberger's solo endeavor will rest in separating herself from the past nine LPs she's released with her brother, but Last Summer succeeds on its own, casting a softer light on the singer's chaotic image.

Title: Sycamore Meadows
Review: A new high point for the already accomplished Walker.

Title: The Midnight Organ Fight
Review: The Midnight Organ Fight's bloodied-but-unbowed lyrics stand up to repeated listening even on the fastest cutes. [Summer 2008, p.106]

Title: Alvvays
Review: They certainly have their sound down (reverb-laced guitars, big choruses, surf-tinged moments), but there's a lack of variety here.

Title: Walking On A Dream
Review: Empire of the Sun's debut offering of electro-pop experiments and dancefloor daydreams is well timed indeed, arriving just as the buzz surrounding MGMT's "Oracular Spectacular" has started to recede.

Title: Sidewalks
Review: These two have always been more about energy than depth, more about the bobbing head than the stationary keyboard. Let's hope it stays that way.

Title: Shulamith
Review: Shulamith is by all means not a bad album, providing just enough thrills and spills to warrant repeated plays. But by expanding and deepening their sound palette, Poliça lose out on some of the original charm that helped make them unique.

Title: Con Todo El Mundo
Review: Khruangbin’s takes this new mode of listening and injects its own singular and developing personality into the playlisting of modern music.

Title: SuperHeavy
Review: [Songs swerve] between undistinguished reggae, so-so pop and indistinct blues-rock. [Nov 2011, p.92]

Title: Howl of the Lonely Crowd
Review: Old indie hero Edwyn Collins of Orange Juice produced the band's sixth album, and the joy is palpable.

Title: Absent Fathers
Review: While the album’s primary appeal may come from the rich storytelling in Earle’s songs, the musicality on display is nothing to balk at either.

Title: Major Key
Review: Like all of his albums, Major Key is a mixed bag, fitting for a maestro who traffics in a blend of chest-thumping and humility that’s both as comical as it is prophetic.

Title: Around The Sun
Review: The first REM album to really disappoint. [2 Oct 2004, p.60]

Title: The Colour in Anything
Review: Blake's third album (all 76 minutes of it) reaches back to the abstract electronics and agile, brittle beats of his early EPs while pushing his songwriting towards new levels of sad urgent grandeur. Blake's bell-clear tenor has never sounded more wounded--or more ethereal.

Title: Quality
Review: He's proven that he can do some beautiful long players, but this just sounds like someone else's greatest hits. Which isn't to say it's not one of the top 20 albums of 2002, because it is. But it shoulda been Top Ten.

Title: End Times
Review: Through a dozen terse, exposed songs Mr. Everett proceeds from bittersweet memory to guilt to resentment to a kind of acceptance. Even the glimpses of self-pity stay matter of fact.

Title: Yuck
Review: None of these songs is an inferior version of other songs on the album; each dangles from its own distinct nostalgic thread.

Title: Other Rivers
Review: Too often, though, this feels like folk music on cruise control despite the attempts to introduce subtle electronic elements to the background of many of the songs, like a Fence Collective recording gone a bit wrong.

Title: Views
Review: Given all the resources he has, the album may have been too big to fail, but he’s still maintained enough of his unique talent that it’s unlikely anyone could have done it better.

Title: An Other Cup
Review: The old Cat Stevens, who pondered earthly loves and sorrows and spiritual yearning, has been replaced by a songwriter who finds all his answers in faith. [13 Nov 2006]

Title: Going Back Home
Review: The pair attack a chunky selection of bluesy Wilko originals with gusto.

Title: Nootropics
Review: It is a delicate alchemy of tight metronomic grooves and carefully parsed instrumental interplay, to the point where nothing steals the show.

Title: Yuck
Review: The lyrics sound like the work of very young people striving for depth--Suck rhymes crucifixion, benediction, addiction and affliction in a kind of religion-and-drugs bingo--but given that they are very young, that can be forgiven.

Title: All That Echoes
Review: The singing is warm and temperate, emotionally expressive without any sign of strain. But there’s an intriguing tension in some of the other material.

Title: Futures
Review: Futures goes back to the band's roots, sporting 11 sparkling gems that carefully balance balladry with bombast.

Title: Sexorcism
Review: Disappointingly one-note.

Title: New Path
Review: Essaie Pas have gone beyond cliche and fandom to make something that truly speaks to the dynamic thought and droll humour at the heart of Dick’s writing.

Title: Mended With Gold
Review: RAA don't have the element of surprise like they did on the originally self-released Hometowns, and it doesn't slowly ingratiate the way Departing did, but Mended With Gold proves Edenloff's songs of lost love can sneak up on you even when the music hits you square on the chin.

Title: Hold Time
Review: It takes a minute for the standouts here to stand out, but it's an enjoyable wait.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: They’ll never be one of the greats, but Band of Horses have proved that they’ve near mastered the art of making quality, old-fashioned rock ‘n roll.

Title: Nothing Feels Natural
Review: Like Bodies and Control and Money and Power, the LP thrives on an economy of force and purpose.

Title: Emerald City
Review: The album, like most of Vanderslice’s albums, meanders along like a pleasant afternoon: it is all fair weather and blithe breezes, fairly consistent in both tone and tempo.

Title: One Bedroom
Review: One Bedroom does tend to lag in parts, perhaps lost in the legacy of the band that created it, but in the end it comes off as an unified organic being, both necessary and pleasant.

Title: Sillion
Review: Johnny Flynn's fourth LP pivots on the English songwriter/actor's distinctive voice, which echoes older UK folk even while wrapping itself in modern indie roots.

Title: Hail To The Thief
Review: There's something for everyone here. [Jul 2003, p.120]

Title: Slowdive
Review: Slowdive is a surprisingly joyous return to the fray. [May 2017, p.90]

Title: Hopelessness
Review: Some tracks come across like impromptu recording sessions where ANOHNI worked through recently-penned material over production pieces messed around with just before she'd arrived at the studio. Still, there is enough in this unexpected assimilation of talents to hold intrigue.

Title: The Sleepy Strange
Review: The Sleepy Strange offers seven mid-tempo rock songs, most with the inevitable country leanings that a pedal steel creates. These pieces lack anything even remotely resembling a sense of direction or urgency; Japancakes' songs don't travel from Point A to Point B so much as wander up and down the street in front of Point A and dig odd little things out of the lawn. Some listeners will love it, while devotees of single-minded purpose will positively hate it.

Title: Hawk
Review: It's a rich, insinuating sound, and there's plenty more of it on Hawk. But there are also several twists that make this much more than just a rehash of a proven formula.

Title: A Thousand Thoughts
Review: This has the potential to serve as a good sampler for those interested in the ethnomusicological side of contemporary chamber music.

Title: Old Flowers
Review: With the voice of Linda Ronstadt and songwriting gifts of Joni Mitchell, there simply isn't anything to dislike about Old Flowers. [Jul 2020, p.84]

Title: I Can Wonder What You Did with Your Day
Review: I Can Wonder toys with genres with resilience and resolve, resulting in something for everyone.

Title: Hundred Acres
Review: Ultimately, the album sounds confidently beautiful. While some may not be as memorable, songs like "Meadow Song" make this album one of S. Carey's best.

Title: Sirens
Review: The Chilean producer has released collaborative records, scored films and released a series of incredible 12-inches, Nymphs I through IV. And yet, for all of the sonic breadth of that material, none of it quite prepares listeners for Sirens.

Title: Mudcrutch
Review: Mudcrutch might be about wrapping up unfinished business, but there's plenty of new life in this old, thankfully resuscitated band.

Title: Pinned
Review: Pinned isn’t a memorable record; it’s a cacophony of ideas that don’t pan out. While it has bursts of substance, they soon trail off, or are abandoned instantly.

Title: Lysandre
Review: Lysandre justifies its own existence by virtue of its own wide eyed wonder, its own vulnerability, and its giving sense of heart.

Title: Social Cues
Review: Social Cues feels like the sound of a great band in desperate need of some down time. [Jun 2019, p.88]

Title: Wet from Birth
Review: This is well-muscled, heavily mascara'd dance music. [Sep 2004, p.99]

Title: West of Eden
Review: What we’ve got now is a world full of millennials that have grown up to make art about these injustices. HMLTD have done just that, focusing their trials and tribulations through a magnifying glass to burn us mere ants. And oh, how I love a bit of self-immolation.

Title: Beware
Review: Some will long for Oldham’s minimalist era, but Beware is still an engaging record from one of the indie world’s best songwriters.

Title: Yesterday and Today
Review: These iridescent sound experiments tell a thrilling story poles apart. [Summer 2009, p.72]

Title: Emika
Review: With Emika, then, the hiding is over, her close-up appearing clearly on the cover of this varied and impressive 12 song record.

Title: The Wonder Years
Review: The Wonder years have not only delivered a genuinely great pop-punk record but a genuinely great record, period. [8 Oct 2011, p.50]

Title: Look into the Eyeball
Review: Without the strength of material to prompt the question of whether Byrne should be taken at face value or not, the songs on Look Into The Eyeball simply glide by unobtrusively, and Byrne's romantic sentiments start to sound like Paul McCartney at his blandest. [#208, p.53]

Title: Wolfgang Amadeus Phoenix
Review: Very few dance albums are, and in the end, that’s what Phoenix created--a dance album, possibly the most enjoyable one since "Oracular Spectacular."

Title: The Defamation of Strickland Banks
Review: And whaddayaknow, this ugly duckling – out of a hoodie and into a tux – turns out to have a fine white soul voice and has followed a record you couldn't bear to hear more than once with a record you'll want to play over and over.

Title: Someone Out There
Review: Every single song breaks new ground for Morris – even the simple title track, which admittedly could have been found down the back of Chris Martin’s sofa.

Title: New Moon
Review: New Moon is their most purposeful beast yet.

Title: Back to Me
Review: Impressively reconfirms why she's alt-country's brightest rising star. [May 2005, p.111]

Title: I Need a New War
Review: He’s gone as far as he can go, done all he can. He’s lost in a bursting world of endless storefronts, in an America he no longer recognizes. He hasn’t a clue what he needs, only that he needs it. Songs as easy to imbibe to as to heave a sigh to, these are fogged, fading portraits for the ages. We all need a new war.

Title: The Golden Age of Grotesque
Review: There's nothing that catchy here - Manson seems to have used all his best hooks already. But it's not terrible, and it sounds good LOUD.

Title: Time to Die
Review: It’s great that Electric Wizard are still around and are still pushing the limits of heavy music--not just for metal itself, but for British metal in particular.

Title: Avatar
Review: If there's anything to lament about Avatar, it's that its moves towards accessibility, narrative, and more diverse pastures probably won't help to broaden Comets' fanbase.

Title: Signs Under Test
Review: [Signs Under Test] satisfies the soul without losing its precision-tooled digital lustre. [Mar 2015, p.97]

Title: The Search
Review: In both vocal cadence and lyrical content, NF falls somewhere between Eminem and Twenty One Pilots' Tyler Joseph, while channeling the former's rage and the latter's emotive introspection. As such, The Search is a heavy and emotionally exhausting listen, brimming with troubling allusions to suicide and soul-baring pain.

Title: Mogoya
Review: The result is an impressive, attacking set, but then Sangaré has always been adventurous.

Title: Send
Review: Forget the new school of post-punk bands. None of them approach the intensity and rhythmic engagement of Wire, still flying the pink flag of twisted rock after all these years.

Title: VII: Sturm Und Drang
Review: The production is dense, thin, and minimal, the guitars and drums pushed tight to give all these lyrics extra oomph.

Title: Here's to Being Here
Review: Even though the album's production aims for and achieves a vintage AM radio sound, Collett's willingness to subvert the conventions of songwriters like Dylan or Kristofferson makes Here a definitively modern record and perhaps the first of Collett's solo albums to sound like a real classic.

Title: Delusions of Grand Fur
Review: In general, you can tell that a lot of thought has gone into Delusions of Grand Fur. This is true of the well-crafted songs themselves, but also of the fluid trajectory of the album and the powerful lyrical subject matter.

Title: Across Six Leap Years
Review: Other versions are so microscopically different from the originals that you wonder why they've bothered. [Dec 2013, p.71]

Title: Ether Song
Review: Builds considerable muscle to the skeletal frailty of intricate guitar work while commendably maintaining all which was good of their debut.

Title: Western Culture
Review: Although not for the casual music listener, the song ["Legacy of Neglect"] and the album work not only because of Leonard's good melodic and dramatic instincts, but because he is equally charismatic with both quiet acoustic song and outraged, off-balance rock. In this way, the album's riveting album rock-slash-exasperated art rock is reminiscent of figures like Bowie and Reed while remaining completely idiosyncratic.

Title: Player Piano
Review: Like the craft of the best tracks here, the album itself describes a smooth and clearly bookended parabola, an unexpectedly rainbow bridge, but one that, unlike the most well-known of these, is a pleasure, not a revelation.

Title: Our Inventions
Review: The whole occasion is more intimate this time around, with vocalist/keyboardist Valerie Trebeljahr's sleepytime vocals nearly lulling you into a head-swaying trance.

Title: Repave
Review: Repave is integral to retroactively understanding Vernon's canon and also establishes a path forward from the runaway success of his past.

Title: Unbreakable
Review: Unbreakable is the mature album, free of commercial ambition, her all-too-breakable brother never made.

Title: Back to the Web
Review: The band's ability to rock out at the drop of a hat proves a pleasant surprise among the dopey reverie. [Jun 2006, p.115]

Title: Zeroes QC
Review: These songs are rarely exciting in their movement and few listeners will hear the album as more than just a good debut, but like The Velvet Underground and The Smiths, some styles never go out of style.

Title: Crown Royal
Review: Really, this isn't really a Run DMC album, they're just guests on it.

Title: Crazy Ex-Girlfriend
Review: Crazy Ex-Girlfriend would have been impressive if it was just a showcase of her strengths as a singer or as a songwriter, but since it is both, it's simply stunning, a breakthrough for Lambert and one of the best albums of 2007, regardless of genre.

Title: Starboy
Review: Some of the most exciting songs on Starboy are the least expected. ... But brevity is almost too central here: Some songs (“Love to Lay,” “Nothing Without You”) have barely any verses at all, largely relying on pre-choruses and choruses.

Title: True North
Review: The band excel at giving fans perfectly plotted two-minute bursts of disgust and attrition, epitomised by the splendidly immature, "F*** You." [Feb 2013, p.69]

Title: Raising Sand
Review: The most remarkable collaboration since Norah Jones and the Foo Fighters is also one of the best albums of the year. [Nov 2007, p.92]

Title: Held In Splendor
Review: For now, Held In Splendor is a promising, if limited, stepping stone.

Title: Isolation
Review: Thundercat, Damon Albarn, Tame Impala's Kevin Parker, and a slew of Kendrick Lamar collaborators (Sounwave, Steve Lacy, Badbadnotgood) all make contributions, but the vibe is hers alone. ... Uchis is a woman on the verge, willing to share her vertiginous thrills and spills. Thank her later.

Title: Another Language
Review: All the standard atmospheric touchstones get brushed aside here in favour of a deeper, more meditative experience. [20 Sep 2014, p.53]

Title: Suite 420
Review: Nobody expects maturity from Devin, even though he jarringly mentions that he has a 17-year-old son, but he usually makes eternal adolescence sound a lot more fun than this.

Title: Czarface Meets Metal Face
Review: Yes true believers these villains are definitely up to no good, but they're just the anti-heroes you've been looking for. With beats and rhymes more punishing than Frank Castle, Czarface Meets Metal Face is the hip-hop for everyone who's had it up to here with mumble mouthed singing emcees.

Title: Alice
Review: The melodies on Alice are easily the most direct Waits has written since Blue Valentine, but are more elegant than even those found on Foreign Affairs or Black Rider.

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: Smokey Rolls down Thunder Canyon may be his best so far.

Title: Doris
Review: It’s not always focused, and it’s not always perfect, but that’s what real freedom feels like.

Title: Lady Wood
Review: While there aren't as many standout singles this time around, the Swedish singer impressively maintains a consistent tone throughout, and its two-part structure adds to its listenability as an album experience.

Title: Happy in the Hollow
Review: You will have gathered from this that Happy In The Hollow makes a positive impact, its occasional loss of focus an asset rather than a fault as the music runs free. TOY make music notable for its mood, groove and texture, if not always finding a killer melody.

Title: Why Love Now
Review: Why Love Now is reserved in its sonic experimentation. But for a band as sharp and capable as this one, that’s not really a problem. Beneath the acerbic jokes, Korvette is a humane and considerate writer and performer.

Title: The Getaway
Review: Co-opted as they may be, the best tracks tend to be the ones that aren’t attempting to mine old hooks for new hits.

Title: The Bake Sale
Review: The Bake Sale is way too good for posturing.

Title: Clay Class
Review: Their change between 2007 and now may be incremental, but it's enough to qualify as a definite improvement on their debut.

Title: Anak Ko
Review: The project is stunning and displays a wonderfully acute understanding of what it should do. Duterte knows exactly where this album should stand within her own discography and that of the wider world. Its song-writing is calculated without betraying itself to rigidity and its honesty is telling without falling into a trap of timidity. Anak Ko owes a lot to Duterte’s awareness of how simplicity can breed beauty. Its greatest trick is the delicate fittings of nuance amongst deceptively uncomplicated compositions.

Title: FIDLAR
Review: The spirit of drunk adolescence, cramped kitchens and broken valuable endures on their frightfully fun debut. [Mar 2013, p.101]

Title: Throw It to the Universe
Review: TSOOL may be growing more understated as they mature, but this dependable album demonstrates again that classic rock played by its attentive fans can remain dignified and confident.

Title: My Father Will Guide Me Up a Rope to the Sky
Review: It's an album that marries the buzzsaw abrasion of past Swans' albums with the country-cum-death-blues feel of his work with Angels of Light. That's an easy way to explain it, anyway.

Title: Life Is Sweet! Nice to Meet You
Review: A solid second record with tinges of brilliance, it’s another fine piece of work from the busiest man around.

Title: Riot Boi
Review: When given adequate space, Le1f once again succeeds just being the best and most honest version of himself.

Title: Saturns Pattern
Review: When he indulges in a wash of Vox organ and a rush of 12-string guitars, or when he updates Curtis Mayfield on "Phoenix," they play like transmissions from the past on an album that is focused on the now, and the willful, harmonious collisions of history and the future give Saturn's Pattern its kick, while the warm thrum of the grooves gives it its soul.

Title: Honor Found in Decay
Review: The record doesn't abandon the moody sprawl of the band's last few full-lengths, but it does help restore urgency to an aesthetic that seemed in danger of growing soporific.

Title: We Are Little Barrie
Review: We Are Little Barrie is a stunning debut for sure, and the kind of record both old-school classic rock dads and groove-loving young kids should be clambering over each other to buy.

Title: Teen Dream
Review: This is both the most diverse and most listenable of their three full-lengths, and yet it never seems like a compromise. It feels like the product of careful, thoughtful growth, bringing in new influences--bits of mid-1970s Fleetwood Mac, sparkling indie pop, even a few soul and gospel touches--while maintaining the group's core sound.

Title: Welcome to the North
Review: All that stands between this young English foursome and Perry Farrell-ian Valhalla is a lack of a truly rippin' axman. [Dec 2004, p.124]

Title: Master and Everyone
Review: There's nothing aggressive or urgent about the record, and oddly, that works in its favor.

Title: A Dotted Line
Review: A Dotted Line is a work of supreme songcraft; one might call it a “return to form”, but from the sound of it, the form was never gone in the first place.

Title: No Home Record
Review: No Home Record is impossible to listen to without making reference to her former band, yet it stands alone as the finest work of a magnificent, imposing talent.

Title: Adult Baby
Review: Like any other juvenile, Adult Baby boasts the areas in which it could grow further, such as sharper lyrical flows or maybe mixing up the instrumental homogeny. There's only so many times you can hear a snare and cymbal conclude a movement. Yet growing up means making a few mistakes, and to her credit, Mikano leans into every single one to learn something from it.

Title: Aw C'Mon
Review: Over the course of 24 tracks, we get taut grooves set on Al Green cruise control, lots of havin'-fun-in-the-studio byplay, and the occasional spritz of rude fuzz-box gutiar to give all the gold-leaf detailing some shape. [combined review of both discs; Mar 2004, p.97]

Title: It's a Bit Complicated
Review: The band's arrangements show a more robust sense of melody than they did on their debut.

Title: Real
Review: The sassy European and fraught, fatalistic Bilbao also have their moments, though there’s too great a reliance on mid-tempo numbers and the proto-punk aggression hinted at sadly fails to materialise.

Title: Working Class Woman
Review: Thankfully, Davidson doesn’t hide behind irony for the entirety of this record. She never over-relies on a single set of muscles, she flexes them all.

Title: Love Me Back
Review: She finds the plaintive center, the kind of soothing intimacy that almost seems like the way we'd sing to ourselves in times of trouble.

Title: Dark Bird Is Home
Review: Dark Bird Is Home sounds carefully constructed, and Matsson keeps things simple rather than making easy moves toward a grandeur that could bury his songcraft.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: One of the few pop singers whose albums are best appreciated in their entirety and not lopped off into "hit singles," Madonna... has succeeded at creating a dance-pop odyssey with an emotional, if not necessarily narrative, arc.

Title: Lookout Low
Review: Cadien Lake James' shifts upfront are the most sonorous for sure. ... Yet at times, as on Colin Croom's "Laid in Gold," which borrows a classic riff wholesale, their sepia-tinted Americana is hugely enjoyable but painfully derivative; at other, less engaging times, they end up sounding more like a poorly angled throwback, as on "Better Than Stoned," which strangely comes across as a little juvenile on record but, happily, is an absolute blast live.

Title: Master of Disaster
Review: The tunes would be a whole lot better with careful pruning.

Title: How I Got Over
Review: This disconnect actually amps up the album's tension and energy, as if that first half was the uphill struggle, and the rest is the triumphant sound coming down from the summit.

Title: Friendly Fires
Review: Friendly Fires is teeming with ideas, and although the record's consistent sound can be exhausting--there is no release, no relaxation in tempo--it's encouraging to locate a new band with too much passion, so much that it can hardly execute its ideas on one page.

Title: Wallpaper for the Soul
Review: You've heard all this before, but it still sounds glorious.

Title: Black Light
Review: Their best and most cohesive album since 1999's "Vertigo." [Mar 2010, p.111]

Title: Kompromat
Review: ‘KOMPROMAT’ is an album that cements I LIKE TRAINS once more not only as a force to be reckoned with but as a band who are able to deliver a delicate critique on society.

Title: Always Returning
Review: As consistently lovely as this music is, one yearns for sharper edges to break up the pervasive languid drift. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.74]

Title: Fields
Review: Gonzalez's classical guitar and weightless tenor float over soul jazz, Afrobeat, Ethiopian funk and krautrock, and the lyrics touch on spirituality and self-realization.

Title: BarragÃ¡n
Review: The tense chemistry has been, to some degree, recaptured. [Oct 2014, p.68]

Title: Swoon
Review: The fuzzed out riffage and ethereal interludes are in place, but Swoon lacks the diverse textures, clever lyrics, and emotional depth that the Pumpkins honed over a 10 year span. And this is as it should be.

Title: Something to Tell You
Review: Something to Tell You doesn’t attempt anything new and keeps it safe, though, and when your best track is yet another sanitized extract of Tango in the Night, well, that’s not saying much.

Title: The Con
Review: Canada's Quin twins fairly blaze through The Con's 14 compact, supercharged tracks. [Oct 2007, p.109]

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: Maybe the problem with The Politics of Envy is that these tracks just sounded too good playing back on shiny studio monitors to a roomful of old friends. If he's struggling to say something about the wider world, maybe Stewart should consider a retreat into his own eccentric interior.

Title: Love vs Money
Review: That alpha-jerk machismo is mitigated somewhat by the intoxicating future-soul sonics on songs like 'Right Side of My Brain.' But The-Dream's vision of romance mostly plays like a nightmare.

Title: Super
Review: With everything lathered in exquisite, 90s-sounding euphoria, the duo prove to be irresistible, once again.

Title: Everyday Nothing
Review: Bentham may have struggled writing this album, but the results exude confidence and ambition. Whilst it draws heavily on the slacker sounds of the 1990’s, Bentham brings the genre firmly into 2020 with her fresh take on what it’s like to create in a time where inspiration can be hard to find.

Title: Tongue N' Cheek
Review: It unquestionably adds up to a pop record sharp enough to be the bratty but irresistible younger brother of Lily Allen's "It's Not Me, It's You."

Title: MTMTMK
Review: The follow-up [to 2009's Warm Heart Of Africa] is similarly energetic and eclectic. [Aug 2012, p.83]

Title: Heartthrob
Review: The tunes and recriminations seem to cut deeper than ever on their seventh album.

Title: Oak Island
Review: Oak Island has a deftness that makes it hard to resist, but some songs disappear under the weight of everything that's transpiring.

Title: Animated Violence Mild
Review: In many ways, Animated Violence Mild feels like the inevitable sequel to World Eater. Where that album used the full force of Power's music to rail against the world's injustices, this one reflects the resignation, frustration, and emotional overload of its time in its startling and moving tracks.

Title: Young Hunger
Review: Like Within and Without, it's no overhaul, but Young Hunger has a much more immediate presence, more direct in both a melodic and emotional sense and generally with a lot more 'oomph'.

Title: The Red Light District
Review: If you like loud choruses, ceaseless energy and the bug-eyed extremities of crunk, look no further. [15 Jan 2005, p.43]

Title: Expect the Best
Review: Expect the Best stands out amongst other reverb-drenched indie rock for being exceptionally well composed.

Title: Infinite House
Review: The art-rock band’s third LP Infinite House combines tentative dips into R&B and soul with a firm foundation in jittery, spindly, angular NYC rock, resulting in pop songs with a deliberately nervous, ungainly, everything-but-the-kitchen-sink feel to them.

Title: Rivers and Streams
Review: This is music that has gloriously outgrown its unfamiliar origins and deserves to be embraced wholeheartedly.

Title: Has Been
Review: It's that sobering confessional quality that gives the album an unexpected dose of depth and grace.

Title: Good Souls Better Angels
Review: If there’s a downside to the electricity in Williams’ veins on Good Souls Better Angels, it’s that the gentler material doesn’t have quite the same impact.

Title: Consolers of the Lonely
Review: Sometimes The Raconteurs' competence and professionalism get in the way of their fieriness, particularly in moments that sound like a White Stripes album given a coat of '70s AOR polish.

Title: Welcome to Goon Island
Review: Peer behind the pose, owever, and you'll find a sparky outfit whose towering tunes, such as 'Sun comes Up,' match their lofty ideas. [Sep 2008, p.115]

Title: Dark Days / Light Years
Review: It is a pleasure to report that the latest SFA opus is a joy from start to finish.

Title: A Crow Looked at Me
Review: There is sad music, which is to say music that deploys lyrical or musical motifs meant to connote misery. And then there is this album, which mostly exists in a space beyond those concerns. It is an album because a musician made it and it is broken up into songs, but it is also a diary, a balled-up tissue, found art.

Title: See You On The Moon
Review: The result might not be her most accessible album, but it’s certainly her most rewarding.

Title: Afraid of Heights
Review: Their kings of the beach crown may have slipped a little nowadays, but Wavves still offer plenty of no-frills fun.

Title: The Family Jewels
Review: There is a savvy depth evident throughout ‘The Family Jewels’ which simply cannot be ignored; fun, serious, poppy and unorthodox, it is an album full of contradictions, but one which rarely fails to entertain.

Title: Shadow of the Sun
Review: After an album, 2012's Circles, where it seemed like the duo may have been running short on ideas, adding Jeffrey on drums and shaking up the working arrangements have helped to make Shadow a sterling return to form that gives their best album, 2001's Mazes, a run for its money.

Title: Rebel Soul
Review: His recorded albums, and even his mesmerizing live show, have gradually incorporated a country sound. That trend continues on his latest, the rewarding 14-song Rebel Soul.

Title: Musicology
Review: A casual exhibition of Princeliness, stocked with a handful of old tricks but no new ones.

Title: Home Before Dark
Review: It's sure to please its predecessor's fans, but the filler-to-killer ratio here is skewed a little too far in the wrong direction.

Title: The Trials of Van Occupanther
Review: Despite [some] fine moments, occasionally Van Occupanther can feel a little too slick and one-note.

Title: Dance Mother
Review: Busy and Melissa have made a record that shimmers with possibilities, mapping out an alien territory that’s eerily inviting. Now it’s time to build on it.

Title: Exorcism of Envy
Review: An interesting experiment.

Title: National Ransom
Review: Over the course of 16 tracks, Costello flexes his stylistic muscles and exercises that famously acerbic wit.

Title: Slow Focus
Review: As clever as Fuck Buttons are at cobbling together unlikely juxtapositions, they're master builders when it comes to tension and release.

Title: Invisible Ones
Review: [Doesn't] always make satisfactory listening. [Dec 2005, p.104]

Title: Shields
Review: Here, the band has returned from the cold with a tight, extraordinary album that is lush and satisfying--yet still in the corners just a little bit sad.

Title: My Heart Has a Wish That You Would Not Go
Review: Whereas their back catalog centered on decidedly un-rogue waves of distortion, My Heart Has A Wish That You Would Not Go is a collection of quiet, often surreal songs that border on balladry.

Title: Your Wilderness Revisited
Review: On Your Wilderness Revisited, Doyle sheds himself of the bad habits he developed as an emergent successful recording artist in East India Youth and takes on the role of the Proustian artist. He takes pleasure in and extrapolates beauty from the suburbs that raised him, and takes pains to share that beauty with us.

Title: Hope Downs
Review: It's entirely addictive--one fix and you're hooked. [Jul 2018, p.36]

Title: WHO
Review: If this LP isn’t so groundbreaking as Tommy, it’s definitely a logical extension of The Who By Numbers and certain preferable to the forced and pedestrian It’s Hard.

Title: Trapped Animal
Review: Die-hard Slits fans who aren't put off by the band's newfound professionalism or the greater reliance on keyboards at the expense of guitar will find their faith rewarded by Trapped Animal.

Title: The New Abnormal
Review: It’s not the early, edgy Strokes, but what they’ve grown up into. Maybe the Strokes won’t make new friends with this album, but old friends can get closer.

Title: Up on the Ridge
Review: His voice is too plain to deliver the pathos in songs like Buddy Miller's "Love Grows Wild." But the record succeeds on high spirits, sterling guest stars (Miranda Lambert, Jamey Johnson) and covers like U2's "Pride."

Title: Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded
Review: Cut the iffy pop off these 19 tracks and you're left with Roman's true four-star empire, but as it is, Roman Reloaded is a frustrating mix of significant and skippable.

Title: Codename: Rondo
Review: Dig those snippets and Codename: Rondo just might be this weekend's soundtrack.

Title: Milk Famous
Review: In lieu of memorable choruses, indie nerds will enjoy this disc of earthy space-pop as a complete experience without any aesthetic hiccups.

Title: Backwater
Review: Backwater is a mature, rich effort that's likely to see Kllo continue on their ascent.

Title: In Our Nature
Review: These songs are never less than lovely, but they're never really more than lovely either.

Title: Slugger
Review: Shinier and poppier than anything Speedy Ortiz have done, Slugger is Dupuis’ attempt at putting politics into pop. The results are a thrilling and fizzing triumph.

Title: Snowflake Midnight
Review: The results are uneven but rarely dull.

Title: The Black and White Album
Review: The Black and White Album is an extraordinarily (perhaps inordinately) confident album. [Winter 2007]

Title: Sallows
Review: Anamai may not be as pummelling as a HSY record, but their metaphysical weight makes up for it, producing an even more striking result than Mayberry’s other band.

Title: In Our Gun
Review: A little more emotional chaos, a dash of the dark stuff, might make such avuncular campfire grooves more worthy of our time and money.

Title: Passover
Review: [Passover] can be frustratingly sparse in places. [Apr 2018, p.106]

Title: Hannah
Review: Hannah is another solid piece of output from a dedicated and thoughtful lyricist.

Title: Ten
Review: Everything they do is infused with an undeniable, albeit sometimes unfathomable, psychedelic spirit. [Mar 2004, p.92]

Title: case/lang/veirs
Review: Far from the sort of thrown-together collaboration that is generally de rigueur, case/lang/veirs stands out because it remains an accurate representation of the sum of its parts, a catalog of what makes its three artists great.

Title: Hotel
Review: If Moby has accomplished anything with Hotel, it's that he may have become the rare musical artist equally despised by both of modern music criticism's warring camps.

Title: The Chronicles of Marnia
Review: There's something exhilarating in listening to her think out loud--the sureness of her songwriting battling the part of her brain that knows the song will never be enough.

Title: Sleeping on Roads
Review: The aching sensitivity of many of these lonely acoustic compositions is balanced against an inventive backdrop of instrumentation.

Title: Believe
Review: The beats here are deft as well as driving. Surprisingly, EDM stylings such as the juddering bassline of As Long As You Love Me work well with his plaintive and still unmistakeably teenage voice.

Title: Lifeblood
Review: An often mediocre record, with a few peaks and an awful lot of troughs.

Title: Pussy's Dead
Review: The high proportion of psychedelic plods make this record feel like a missed opportunity--elegantly wasted, but wasted all the same. [May 2016, p.104]

Title: X
Review: x's first third is not without its issues but there is charm, not to mention the feeling that Sheeran really is trying to raise his game. A pity, then, that the remaining 35 minutes is alternatively as generic and simpering as it gets.

Title: Inji
Review: Weirdly wonderful. [Jul 2015, p.78]

Title: The Mouse and the Mask
Review: It's a fun ride. [6 Oct 2005, p.154]

Title: Anarchy, My Dear
Review: Say Anything have always been a hard pill to swallow for some, and while Anarchy doesn't change that, it shows that they have far more than just the one spanner in the toolbox.

Title: Moderat
Review: The result is pragmatic but also quite creative and surprisingly catchy.

Title: Semicircle
Review: Overall, whilst Semicircle does contain obvious flaws, this chapter of The Go! Team is here to have a good time and hopes you are too. And who can knock them for that?

Title: The Expanding Flower Planet
Review: The Expanding Flower Planet feels like an album full of trap doors, where a single, unexpected sound can deposit you into new worlds.

Title: Everybody Split
Review: The album in hand makes a taut, succinct statement, bristling with angst and melting into melancholy. It is rather good in the mysterious way of rock records; hard to say what it does better than the other records, but it does it all the same.

Title: Infinity Machines
Review: Their fondness for 17-minute improvisations demand a certain stamina, but there's a strung-out beauty to Infinity Machines that eases you in gently. [May 2015, p.73]

Title: Sensuous
Review: No doubt Oyamada has a fine ear for sound design, but he handles his tunes with antiseptic gloves. [May 2007, p.88]

Title: Band Red
Review: In the tradition of all great girl-fronted punk bands, from Sleater-Kinney to Elastica, it's not what Kaito has to say, it's the way Colt sings it.

Title: Enemy Mine
Review: Listeners who have managed to remain immune to the trio's idiosyncratic brand of "thespian rock" will no doubt find much of Enemy Mine unlistenable. That said, fans of manic melodies, bohemian pageantry, and synapse melting lyricism have no greater modern champions than Bejar, Krug, and Mercer.

Title: Paralytic Stalks
Review: At the end of the day, Kevin Barnes is really trying to make good pop. Paralytic Stalks is just that, bombast and all.

Title: Balls
Review: A profound disappointment... few songs lift themselves above pedestrian tedium. [Nov 2000, p.117]

Title: Heaven Is Whenever
Review: Although former member Franz Nicolay's piano parts are missed, the Hold Steady have still managed to craft a great record for a barbecue on a hot summer day--and for the hangover the next morning. [Jun 2010, p.105]

Title: Electric Slave
Review: Meet the new boss, same as the old boss.

Title: American Gong
Review: Quasi's reappearance with their most consistent album in a decade feels appropriate.

Title: Run the Jewels
Review: In the end, it’s exactly what you would want and expect from the two skillful musicians. Run the Jewels is an album that was perfectly executed for the summer.

Title: Yr Atal Genhedlaeth
Review: Yr Atal Genhedlaeth sounds like a one-off; a palette cleanser for the Furries’ frontman. It doesn’t rise to the level of Rhys’ work with his day job, but then again, it isn’t meant to.

Title: One Bedroom
Review: In a time when consistency is rare, and integrity even rarer, the Sea and Cake have made an album that highlights where they've been.

Title: The Scene of the Crime
Review: It gets better with each listen, and stands so far outside the realm of anything her better-known peers are doing today that it's almost scary.

Title: Nobody Knows
Review: It’s possible to like this record in theory while imagining one that’s 50 percent more enjoyable.

Title: Vampire Weekend
Review: On their debut, Vampire Weekend mostly earn points the old-fashioned way: by writing likable songs you'll be glad to revisit next month.

Title: IRM
Review: The subject matter subverts her inherent sensuousness, but this is still Charlotte Gainsbourg singing-- at times, she can't help sounding like the cooing French goddess her father helped popularize. It's dead sexy, reborn.

Title: Life on Other Planets
Review: On the one hand, there's an abundance of energy and some great songwriting; on the other, there's less focus here than on either of their previous two releases.

Title: Summer of the Shark
Review: It's the beautifully austere, grown-up pop album we've been waiting years for Mac McCaughan to record. [Jun 2003, p.97]

Title: Pickin' Up The Pieces
Review: What they lack in consistency they make up for in intentions. It's soul for all the right reasons.

Title: VOL. 4 :: SLAVES OF FEAR
Review: It’s a heavy record for heavy times, but another intriguing example of what the trio can achieve, even when they’re burdened with the weight of the world on their shoulders.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: He might have the Midas touch when it comes to genre, but when it comes to his last word, Terje is wise enough to say it in his first language.

Title: TLC
Review: Overall, a solid album, just not quite up to the legacy.

Title: We Are the 21st Century Ambassadors of Peace & Magic
Review: For a band that just started writing pop songs, this sophomore LP is an impressive outing.

Title: Frankie Rose and the Outs
Review: It's hard to deny the simple, joyful throb of this half-hour treat, and Rose has an unusual weapon she's willing to use early and often – harmonies of massed voices, whose affectless trilling lends the buzzing and twanging guitars an oddly liturgical taste.

Title: The Ragpicker's Dream
Review: About as far removed from Dire Straits as it can be.

Title: Bish Bosch
Review: It's a bastard of a listen--a rare, tough piece of meat too savory to spit and toss aside.

Title: Into The Future
Review: Into The Future is a heroic act of denial, nonetheless. The remaining Brains still burn with magnesium-strip intensity. [Jan 2013, p.82]

Title: Future Women
Review: As sophisticated as these songs are, it's The M's' offhanded performance that really sells them, giving Future Women the feel of a particularly solid live show. [Apr/May 2006, p.111]

Title: Fifth Harmony
Review: Fifth Harmony isn’t offensively bad, in fact, it sits quite comfortably with many other acts dominating the charts at the moment. But it’s too safe, too by-the-numbers, too beige to stand up to even Fifth Harmony’s previous work, which carried more lyrical and musical heft.

Title: For Evelyn
Review: Deftly deploying percolating electronica, natural instruments and overlapping vocal lines all the more emotionally gripping for the studied semi-affectlessness of Georgas's intimate delivery, Walsh transforms good songs into a great record. [Aug 2016, p.112]

Title: Chroma
Review: It’s a more evolved release for sure, and with less it seems Eugene McGuinness can actually achieve more.

Title: The Less You Know the Better
Review: Its only commitment is to a subtle antagonism, and it ignores pretty much any worthwhile development in pop, rock, electronic, or hip-hop music since the turn of the century.

Title: That's How Rumors Get Started
Review: From her visceral chemistry with her collaborators to their razor-sharp take on Americana and — above all — Price's deeply personal lyricism, there are plenty of elements that make That's How Rumors Get Started one of the year's strongest country releases.

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: They didn’t quite manage to move past The Seldom Seen Kid on Build a Rocket Boys!, but with Take Off, they’ve both cemented their place as a British institution and hinted that their best might yet be to come.

Title: The Silver Gymnasium
Review: There's a strange disconnect here, one that might be ironed out by facing the past head-on rather than treating it as a concept.

Title: Life Fantastic
Review: While there are definite left-field aspects to Life Fantastic, fans of crossover-indie rock groups like Modest Mouse and Spoon should be able to get behind the angular pop of "Shameless" or the backwater bluegrass-rock of "Life Fantastic."

Title: Paramore
Review: This is their longest album and has the highest stakes, and succeeds.

Title: The Courage of Others
Review: But there’s a strong presence to the album, with its meticulous atmosphere and granite consistency of tone. The chiming guitars of a pair of Erics (Pulido and Nichelson), and the tasteful work of a the drummer McKenzie Smith bring gravity to the band’s gloss on psychedelic folk.
