Unfortunately, the exuberance that bursts out of the clutter of his best songs is a characteristic seen too rarely here.

Title: The Big Bang
Review: The fifteen-song album may have two or three cuts too many, but the core of The Big Bang... is some pretty damn good hip-hop

Title: Ten
Review: They've sadly cranked up the wackiness. [Apr 2004, p.108]

Title: Double Vision
Review: Slick guest artists Tyga and Kid Ink help the listener bridge the gap between the album's maverick moments and the sweet songs aimed at teens, and with smooth-voiced Royce showing equal grace with love and lust, Double Vision becomes the great and infectious model for a 2015 pan-global pop album.

Title: Catastrophe Keeps Us Together
Review: Often echo[es] early R.E.M. with better articulation. [7 Apr 2006, p.59]

Title: Clash the Truth
Review: Picking standout moments is as difficult as finding instances where the record’s charm wears off--there’s not a stage where the latter ever happens, but such is Beach Fossils’ way of doing things there are never really any huge lifts in quality either.

Title: System
Review: His dance-pop tunes are surprisingly fresh and emotionally meaty, without a hint of complacency.

Title: JUICE
Review: Another stellar collection of smart, sweet, and silly songs from some of Canada’s best blog-era indie rock survivors.

Title: Smother
Review: It'd be reductive to try and describe a timeless album like Smother as a step up from its two predecessors, or even as a surefire Mercury contender--although it is, on both counts.

Title: Red
Review: The biggest problem with Red is that as obvious as Datarock's aesthetic is, it's still boring, and it doesn't stick to the tracks at all.

Title: Sundown Heaven Town
Review: It's hit-or-miss.

Title: Dark Matter Moving at the Speed of Light
Review: Disparate dance genres mesh with impressive (and infectious) ease. [Oct 2004, p.113]

Title: Blue with Lou
Review: Lofgren's voice is crackly, but plays perfectly. [May 2019, p.30]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: The band that has most closely followed his lead--the Black Keys--sticks to conventional takes on American genres, but White treats them with something fresher: a sense of menace.

Title: Congotronics
Review: Truly remarkable... Fans of Fela and the Ethiopiques discs will dig this, as will fans of the Notwist, Prefuse 73 and Aphex Twin.

Title: Soused
Review: There’s simply not enough sonic variation going on here to make Soused nearly as compelling as its respective creators’ past efforts.

Title: I'm Glad Trouble Don't Last Always
Review: On I’m Glad Trouble Don’t Last Always Luke Winslow-King continues to demonstrate his growth as a songwriter and entertainer capable of bringing new energy to time-worn Country Music tropes.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: They're better when they're reflective, not reflexive, as on the galloping, careening 'Be Somebody' and the mournful 'Cold Desert,' but the album lacks the hooky rock the band once pulled off so effortlessly, even when thry weren't trying. [Fall 2008, p.91]

Title: Mountain Battles
Review: With material as good as this, we can bear to do without Pixies for a while yet.

Title: ilp
Review: It’s an extremely mature record that tackles the world’s biggest most important theme, love, with confidence and assurance.

Title: Be The Void
Review: Be The Void matches guitarist Scott McMicken's clever lyrics, precise riffs, and quivery vocals to the rare glottal gift and intricate bass work of Toby Leaman in this jumble of freaky throwbacks, reflective ruminations, and spontaneous psychedelic bursts.

Title: Together We're Heavy
Review: An enormous, symphonic, sprawling, highly ambitious, far-reaching work of wonder. [17 Jul 2004, p.48]

Title: Drag It Up
Review: While they may have traded in some of their youthful punk rock spastic enthusiasm, they've replaced it with a world-wise wit and a smart approach to how a rock & roll record should be made in 2004.

Title: Feelin Kinda Free
Review: Feelin Kinda Free sounds like the work of a less dour and far more subversive band. Despite the subject matter and often funereal pace, it’s anything but a drag.

Title: Clay Class
Review: An unfettered sonic experiment from a commercially unconcerned duo, Clay Class, whilst often pushing itself successfully into unexplored melodic territory, feels unfinished, difficult and hesitant.

Title: Stray Ashes
Review: JBM has concocted a glorious half-dream of a third album. [Aug 2013, p.93]

Title: Cherish the Light Years
Review: Swirling Euro-melodies reminiscent of Depeche Mode, thudding and shuddering synths, and his coolly quavering baritone mark "Burning Sage" and "Confetti" like a pox.

Title: Unpatterns
Review: This is SMD's deepest, moodiest record to date. [Jun 2012, p.85]

Title: Shelter
Review: A typical shoegaze/post-rock album that, while beautifully constructed and breathlessly blissful, doesn’t recreate the same level of escapism for the listener that rendered Alcest’s past works so overwhelming and otherworldly.

Title: Grime MC
Review: Betters his 2015 landmark, Integrity. [Mar 2020, p.119]

Title: Are We There
Review: There's alot of her here, and the connections are all her own. [Jun 2014, p.89]

Title: Herein Wild
Review: Except for the dissonant pep of Heaven, Rose’s careful vocals float among bittersweet synths for 37 minutes of dreamy Cure- and Bangles-evoking pop.

Title: Up On High
Review: Up on High will sound like nothing much the first time you listen, but stay with it, because the songs are soft and unassuming, but excellent, and they’ll catch you in the end.

Title: High Country
Review: A 70s classic rock party, then, but one with a few new guests.

Title: Watch the Fireworks
Review: A likeable, modest debut. [Oct 2007, p.101]

Title: Nocturnal Koreans
Review: This mini album sees Wire once again looking askance at modernity via cryptic cynicism, bassist Graham Lewis's obtuse lyrics reaching new levels of vexatious impenetrability.

Title: Yes
Review: On their excellent 10th album, the music leans toward the ornate, with snatches of Tchaikovsky and spaghetti-Western atmospherics enveloping the synths and house beats.

Title: IRM
Review: Though the album hits a few sleepy troughs along the way, it gets progressively stranger and more aggressive, with distorted bass (“Trick Pony”), tribal drumming (“Voyage”) and T-Rex-style boogie (“Dandelion”) giving Gainsbourg room to stretch.

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: A belligerent surge of dub-influenced electro-rock and angst-ridden sloganeering.

Title: Young Enough
Review: Circling around Eva’s sharp, twangy vocals, the band’s second album is a gargantuan step forward, and one packed full of iron-clad mantras.

Title: Kiss of Death
Review: Kiss Of Death is uneven: Like Kiss Tha Game Goodbye, it suffers from an apparent desire to satisfy every demographic at once.

Title: Lousy With Sylvianbriar
Review: The melodies, meanwhile, avoid obvious hooks, in favour of tension and knotty complexity. This rescues Lousy with Sylvianbriar from dreary rockism.

Title: Listening Tree
Review: Overall, Listening Tree is all about Tim, and his deep closeted skeletons and inner demons, which are far too abstract to be even remotely relatable or fun to sweat it out to their exorcisms.

Title: Twisted Angel
Review: Let's hope Nashville will take her back, and quick.

Title: Immolate Yourself
Review: It’s a confident outing from an outfit with all the right reasons to be confident, a unified and often arresting record with few qualms about what it’s supposed to be.

Title: Lady
Review: Wray and Walker’s transatlantic pairing is beautifully natural.

Title: I'm Not Bossy, I'm The Boss
Review: Unfortunately, much of the album shrouds the transparent emotions in slick production, most egregiously O'Connor's multitracked vocals. This is not a new problem for her, but it's particularly vexing in that it sugarcoats songs that should be anything but.

Title: A Certain Trigger
Review: As much as a lot of the tracks are just bluster + accent + guitars, there are some melodies hidden along the way and the bluster + accent + guitars here are better than those pimped by the likes of The Others and Kaiser Chiefs and so on and so forth.

Title: Varshons
Review: Its choice of selections successfully reinvent the familiar and/or introduce the less well-known. [Jul 2009, p.104]

Title: Why Me? Why Not.
Review: Why Me? Why Not. is not the swaggering, confident album you might expect. Rather, there is a vulnerability and a sense of humility to go with the polished songcraft. While the musical influences are pretty standard Liam Gallagher fare these are surprisingly accomplished, memorable songs. The lasting, overall impression is of Gallagher discovering a belief in himself as an artist rather than simply as a singer in a rock 'n' roll band.

Title: Teen Dream
Review: Leaps and bounds over the act's earlier material, "Teen Dream" allows Legrand and Scally to truly come into their own while leaving the listener aching for more.

Title: Pyramids
Review: Sure, they're a very raw talent, but a formidable talent nonetheless, and this record's peaks hint at even greater musical epiphanies to come.

Title: Satis Factory
Review: The rollicking, Rivieras-evoking organ-rock tune "Berlin Weekend" is just one of several other worthwhile stops on a 12-track album that ups the ante on an already attention-grabbing debut.

Title: Dreamcar
Review: Apart from running repetitive with no real memorable tracks in the back-end, it's the cheese factor that ends up hampering the show.

Title: Initiation
Review: The whole record is coated in a dense echo-fug, and is completely and utterly one-dimensional. But that, to be quite frank, is the strength of Initiation.

Title: Hypersonic Missiles
Review: What’s here doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but it’s very well done.

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: Nine Types of Light proves how hard this quintet can hit, experimental New Yorkers or love-sick idiots.

Title: The Futureheads
Review: As all sugar-highs go, this can leave you a bit lightheaded before it's over. [#8, p.109]

Title: VII
Review: One-third of VII has the quintet living up to the folk/country billing with upbeat, chaw-spittin', porch-sittin' classics-in-waiting and depressive ballads presented in Eric Earley's stark, storytelling style. The other two-thirds have skittering keyboards and soulful backing vocals. [No. 103, p.52]

Title: Recess
Review: It's spectacular, almost exhaustingly so.  [28 Mar 2014, p.63]

Title: The Versailles Sessions
Review: Serious deep headphone (or loud stereo) listening, this is certainly no toss-off.

Title: Manipulator
Review: Despite being Segall's longest, packing 17 tracks into just under an hour, it’s also his most focused.

Title: Farm
Review: The last half of Farm starts suffering from verse repetition, slower songs never matching the ballast of 'Ocean in the Way.' Farm does reach beyond 2007's "Beyond."

Title: Miami
Review: Miami frustrates and falls well short in terms of capturing hearts as readily as it will minds.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: Throughout, the lyrical clarity and emotional honesty of the band shine through, creating an album that is as much uplifting as it is in parts bleak.

Title: Lost Friends
Review: As far as debuts go, the Sydney trio have made a solid first step here. They’ve got half the job worked out in spades. Now, they just need to work on making it memorable.

Title: Songs for Our Mothers
Review: The unruly palette endures throughout, with dirges, ersatz country and cracked pop variously suggesting Clinic, Throbbing Gristle and Blackpool cults Ceramic Hobs. Lyrically, trigger warnings may be necessary. [Feb 2016, p.110]

Title: Antibalas
Review: Antibalas is musical democracy in action, and an inspiring example of a band practicing what they preach.

Title: The Disco's of Imhotep
Review: It's foundations are suitably raw, emotional and, more often than not rhythmically muscular. And yet, by skillfully offsetting this by weaving in strands of Afro-jazz, the pervading mood is one of calming, introspective reverie. [Sep 2016, p.93]

Title: On Time Out of Time
Review: Basinski is a true master in the way he can overlay true emotion onto his subject matter, and there’s a sense of sadness for these black holes in their destruction and rebirth and the fabric of spacetime they tear apart within that. To close out with that sense of wonder and discovery relieves the weight of his material.

Title: Junip
Review: Whilst there are a couple of noteworthy exceptions there is simply too much here that simply slips into background music fodder.

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: Ultraviolet is brimming with the artist's down-to-earth candidness.

Title: Irreal
Review: The Musicianship is on point, the recoding crystal clear. But as a listener, it feels difficult to penetrate the album's inky darkness, and you suspect they like it that way. [Feb 2015, p.77]

Title: I Can't Go On, I'll Go On
Review: The lyrics are particularly generic, even for a pop band, and they render The Broken West’s mission obsolete.

Title: Palms
Review: Accomplished but a little safe, perhaps, Palms is nevertheless an intriguing project worthy of a sequel. [22 Jun 2013, p.52]

Title: You & Me
Review: The songwriting has never been stronger or more eclectic.

Title: Images du Futur
Review: On an album that rarely shakes off its shroud of unease, Suuns paint a pretty bleak picture of all our tomorrows, but their own dazzling Futur looks assured.

Title: Detours
Review: Detours is so good that even the middling songs are chock full of taste treats.

Title: 1000 Forms of Fear
Review: Luckily, Sia also puts those pipes to good use on her own material, including her dynamite new album, 1000 Forms of Fear.

Title: All My Relations
Review: All My Relations boasts a syncopated charm that stems from the freedom of groove inherent in jam sessions. But the album’s spiritual elevation comes from Gastelum’s songwriting process.

Title: Brand New Eyes
Review: This is a realisation, and an affirmation, of Paramore's musical craftmanship and potential longevity.

Title: Pressure Chief
Review: The perkiness and quirkiness are paper-thin. [Dec 2004, p.112]

Title: This Old Dog
Review: Iit goes deeper and sees our protagonist at his most mellow and introspective.

Title: Invincible
Review: Ultimately, the record runs too long, losing steam halfway through.... Fortunately, Jackson was clever enough to front-load this record, loading the first seven songs with really good, edgy dance numbers.

Title: Little Dark Age
Review: For better or worse, Little Dark Age is an album for its time: moody, backward-looking, a little depressed. ... This is a soundtrack for the long hangover.

Title: Ganglion Reef
Review: It’s fun, sure, but it’s also thrillingly restless, at times almost desperate.

Title: War Stories
Review: Amid the many features and incredible dynamism that mark every UNKLE full-length, there are no songs to grab onto and little of real essence.

Title: I'm All Ears
Review: “Hot Pink” reads clearly like “BIPP”-era SOPHIE, with its urgent metallic breakdowns and deep, heavy bass lines, while the high synth registers and spatial ambient of “It’s Not Just Me” conjecture a Generation Z folk-pop-disco hybrid. As a more mainstream addition to the avant-pop trajectory of artists like SOPHIE and felicita, however, Let’s Eat Grandma are not nearly as disruptive and original. [Sep 2018, p.49]

Title: Hip Mobility
Review: Frustrates as much as it entices, even more so than the Mikael Jorgensen & Greg O’Keeffe album, its older spiritual twin. ... For the third album in a row, Jorgensen has proven himself to be masterful at carving arrangements so that all the parts work in tandem in a perfect balance between form and function, not a skill to be taken lightly or under-utilized.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Murder of the Universe
Review: Murder is hellishly dark, terminally weird and subsequently very funny.

In some small-minded circles, country has a junior-varsity rep, while pop is the Olympics. And Swift wants us to know she’s ready for her shot at an all-around gold medal. With 1989, she should earn at least a silver.

Title: Distance Inbetween
Review: Ultimately, The Coral aren't doing anything they haven't done before, but the greatness of these songs is undeniable and the production is slyly inventive enough to to keep us hooked. [Apr 2016, p.115]

Title: Tales of Us
Review: The album has a movie score feel, but this time every track is its own short film.

Title: Aforger
Review: Dare’s vocals have lost none of their emotive brutality; the juxtaposition between his delicate voice and the brutal messages he conveys still fascinates, just as his experiments with heavy synth and drone alongside a solitary piano sound impossible, yet somehow work.

Title: Heathen
Review: A soul-searching set that recalls such pre-"Let's Dance" collections as Heroes and Scary Monsters (And Super Creeps).

Title: Contact
Review: This record is better placed alongside, rather than in opposition to, Chardiet’s prior two releases. It’s another excellent entry in her catalogue of searingly distressing, and physically exhausting, noise.

Title: Mug Museum
Review: This Welsh singer-songwriter wears her love of the Velvet Underground proudly, particularly on Mug Museum, her third album, which jingles and jangles even when the subject matter turns dark.

Title: The Element of Freedom
Review: It's surely a compliment to suggest that someone as abundantly gifted as she is can do better than this enjoyable, occasionally brilliant but disappointingly generic record.

Title: Soul of a Woman
Review: Jones remains emotive yet controlled, her artistry enhancing the warmth of her delivery, taking a sound from the past and making it still new and still vibrant. This one is a time machine of sorts, but it looks back to push forward, fulfilling the persistent vision of Soul of a Woman and Sharon Jones.

Title: Blacklisted
Review: Blacklisted rings with lost voices and strange journeys, and does a better job of balancing hope, innocence, and darkness than just about anything I’ve heard in a while.

Title: Todd Smith
Review: The album doesn't really push the creative envelope and relies too heavily on guests at the expense of the principal artist. [15 Apr 2006]

Title: Sounds Of The Universe
Review: Its 12th full-length album fits neatly into its discography while sounding contemporary and building on the trio's lean electro-rock.

Title: Bitchin'
Review: Bitchin' offers little you haven't heard before--even if you haven't heard a Donnas record--but it should go well with a beer or six.

Title: Boy
Review: Her work on Boy should be sufficient to satisfy her longtime followers and perhaps draw some new onlookers into the fold.

Title: Shaken-Up Versions
Review: It’s a bunch of great dance tracks that should preserve their live sound in its natural habitat.

Title: hopeless fountain kingdom
Review: For now, we’re left with a deeply imperfect and too-often derivative album that is not without its charms, but won’t exactly help form the connection with the average listener that Halsey long ago established with her core fanbase.

Title: Protean Threat
Review: This album is a success, albeit one that does little to distance itself from the releases that came before it. Each track shares the percussive and wonky tone of Face Stabber but Dwyer knowingly infuses enough melody into the highlights to make for a few key standouts.

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: A nuanced masterpiece. [Feb 2004, p.88]

Title: Ghetto Bells
Review: Despite the talents of the musicians here, on several tracks the music simply lacks the physical strength to handle the lyrical weight of Chesnutt's material.

Title: Kamaal the Abstract
Review: Buried at Track 7, the developed rhyme, unkiltered time, unsettling keyboards, and Kenny Garrett sax coda of "Abstractionisms" deliver what the flowery "Caring" and the endless "Do You Dig U?" emphatically do not: the "brand new sound" the finale only brags about.

Title: Black Cherry
Review: Glazed soul music that's both lucid and ambiguous, that chimes simultaneously with Donna Summer, John Barry and Suicide, beautifully schizophrenic and poised on the edge of ruin. [May 2003, p.91]

Title: Holding All the Roses
Review: Holding All the Roses delivers on every promise Blackberry Smoke have made to themselves and their fans.

Title: Total Loss
Review: His improved state of mind, and the superior production on some of the tracks, does bring the music on occasion perilously close to the RnB blandness to which this is presumably supposed to provide an alternative.

Title: Binaural
Review: Pearl Jam returns to peak form with a 13-song collection of driving power rock reminiscent of the band's glory days of the early to mid-1990s.

Title: United Crushers
Review: Ultimately, like a hipper London Grammar, Poliça are too dreamy and refined for their own good.

Title: Body Music
Review: AlunaGeorge could well be challenging old touring partners Disclosure for pop crossover supremacy this summer.

Title: My Krazy Life
Review: My Krazy Life is a solid debut. [Apr/May 2014, p.81]

Title: KiCk i
Review: KiCk I offers up an even broader palette than previously, while keeping up a steady diet of trademark dissonance alongside those slightly more overground ambitions.

Title: BE
Review: BE starts with a bang but ends with a whimper.

Title: Maroon
Review: But there are more moments when all-too-human messes lurk beneath the veneer of producer Don Was' perfect pop tracks, moments when the relentless sunniness of the music is pierced by sober themes (the last song, "Tonight Is the Night I Fell Asleep at the Wheel," is a graphic account of car-wreck carnage) and dark, psychological-profile assessments. In turning the snarky level down a notch, Robertson and Page haven't sacrificed the band's good-time giddiness -- they've just opened things up a bit.

Title: Highway Hypnosis
Review: With Highway Hypnosis, the cool kid sets the trend yet again--now floating almost entirely away from the bass, Moolchan cranks down the tempo for a decisively more urban flair that draws from the streets of Lisbon, Atlanta, and London in equal measure. And somehow, even with all this new swag, our sneaky protagonist loses none of the prankster wit that turned heads in the first place.

Title: Synthesized
Review: It maintains the basic tenets of electronic music, but rarely pigeonholes itself, allowing for musical contrasts.

Title: Band of Brothers
Review: The melodies are familiar, but the stuttering guitar style and weathered, laid-back vocals are still unique, still oddly touching.

Title: Order of the Black
Review: With the dust having settled around Zakk Wylde's unexpected departure from Ozzy Osbourne's band, better attention can be paid to Order of the Black, the new album from Wylde's Black Label Society.

Title: Transcendental Blues
Review: The writing shines throughout... Steve Earle seems able to do anything he cares to.

Title: Dark Is the Way, Light Is a Place
Review: While they might miss some of the drive that the band brought to the table in their earlier work, the depth of slower and more spacious songs like "Take Me (As You Found Me)" should ultimately prove more rewarding in the long run.

Title: From King To A GOD
Review: What the rapper lacks in flow experimentation and dexterous rhyme-craft, he makes up for with his knack for sincere storytelling.

Title: The End of Silence
Review: A triptych of glitchy, dissonant beats, shards of white light and fractured, ambient interference. [Aug 2013, p.91]

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: Morph the Cat is too complacent, too enamored with its own lacquered contours.

Title: Wire
Review: A touch of monotony creeps in, although they keep it at bay through sheer volume on the closing, eight-minute "Harpooned." [Jun 2015, p.84]

Title: We Are Not Your Kind
Review: This is grounded, back to basics writing that becomes the breath of fresh air for the album. This is the record the band should have come back with post Paul Gray’s death; it has all the hallmarks of what made Slipknot great in the first place, but it contains a lot of the good elements that came from .5: The Gray Chapter as well.

Title: Merriweather Post Pavilion
Review: Has the album of 2009 been unleashed in January? I can’t see anything else coming near it.

Title: OLD
Review: Throughout, his rhymes hit the mark, whether he’s painting a bleak picture of the Detroit streets, battling his own demons (loneliness, molly, more molly) or rapping at length about drug-dealing without glorifying it Rick Ross-style.

Title: Feel Infinite
Review: Feel Infinite is warm and inviting, a taut mix of R&B love songs to finding your true self on the floor.

Title: All I Need
Review: All I Need had the potential to be so much more than mediocre and forgettable.

Title: Mirrors the Sky
Review: Occasionally you might seek more variety in the tones and washes, but Foy has worked hard to create something that feels of a piece, and there’s no denying the talent at play here.

Title: Fits
Review: Fits feels like the band's formal first LP--lots of what makes them unique, and then those somewhat awkward "growth" points. That initial itchiness, in other words, never really goes away.

Title: Utopia
Review: Utopia, for all its new tricks and ideas, still sounds very much like a Björk record, meaning it will neither disappoint her dedicated base nor catch the casually interested much off guard. Still, if you're hungry for it, there's plenty here on which to chew.

Title: Leveler
Review: This kind of contrast between light and dark makes Leveler a wonderfully dynamic album that is musically engaging with mercifully few bass bombs. Theological differences aside, metal fans would do well to give this one a chance.

Title: ENERGY
Review: 'ENERGY' sees the duo step out of their comfort zone, engaging with an array of previously unexplored artists, genres and themes. They have wholeheartedly refined their vision and approach as artists.

Title: Flower Boy
Review: This is a quiet, mellow album that works better as chill out music than work out music. ... Well worth checking out, especially if you thought Tyler was a one-trick pony.

Title: A Hundred Miles Off
Review: The Walkmen haven't changed much since B&A... but they've honed their nervy talent chiseling lines of post-punk history.

Title: In The Spirit World Now
Review: They fare better as a dancey new wave party band than they did emulating Joy Division on their album before this, but for all its energy and drive, Spirit World is light on truly striking songs.

Title: Bell House
Review: Bell House is a slight work--10 tracks in about 23 minutes--but its songs feel sturdy, as if they’re anchored by DIY ethos and a solid rhythm section.

Title: All at Once
Review: The intensity of the music and interplay between the trio remains firmly intact and stronger than ever.

Artist: The Knife in Collaboration with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock
Title: Tomorrow, in a Year
Review: All the different ways to think about Tomorrow, In a Year seem to have the opposite effect of the one that was intended. They constrict the listener’s imagination and don’t allow for any room to breathe.

Title: Belladonna of Sadness
Review: Turner’s retro snap, crackle and pop and Ford’s studio shimmer polish Savior too much out of the picture, leaving her sounding like an imitation, rather than the real thing.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Malcolm Middleton’s electric and bass guitars have never sounded so big, and they’re better that way.

Title: I Shall Die Here
Review: This is music that looks death square in the face and screams back at it, announcing its life. [May 2014, p.69]

Title: Girl
Review: It's actually an album that sounds like a band experimenting with their sound and gently steering it towards a new direction rather than a radical fully formed departure from their former output.

Title: Pickin' Up The Pieces
Review: Fitz & the Tantrums is the kind of band that communicates best in concert, but this album serves as a fine proxy and party-starter.

Title: For Ever
Review: Somewhat muted follow-up. [Oct 2018, p.111]

Title: The Airing of Grievances
Review: This is the kind of record you'll spend days rocking out to. You'll get lost walking around listening to it (I know I did), think about quitting your job to relive the days when a record like this was all that was allowed to matter.

Title: Colorado
Review: Colorado feels more focused than Pill, especially so the backing vocals. [Nov 2019, p.87]

Title: The Migration
Review: All told, The Migration is an exciting and surprisingly fun album filled will take listeners on a journey through its soaring heights, provided they're brave enough to handle the thrills.

Title: Pacific Daydream
Review: With at least half of these songs, there is almost nothing to say, nothing to be baffled by, nothing to argue about, and for that sad, whimpering reason, Pacific Daydream can probably be called Weezer’s worst album.

Title: Tongue
Review: The album unfolds and reveals itself like the rolling hills of Tuscany, the outer-reaching moments tempered by Simon’s delicate touch and deft ear. Tongue creates a world built from the snug comfort of rain and the quiet joy that comes from solitude.

Title: Starcrawler
Review: They’re not world beaters yet, but Starcrawler’s creepy appeal shouldn’t be underestimated.

Title: iSouljaBoyTellem
Review: This follow-up to his commercially successful debut is a mind-numbing bore that has a few well-produced club tracks by Mr. Collipark and Polow Da Don that slightly mix up the successful formula (chant, be inane, repeat).

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: Whether you will enjoy this ultimately depends on whether you're more of a rocker or a dancer - indeed, some people much preferred the mellower sound of their last record - but there's little denying that this album misses a lot of the urgency and sheer emotional energy of the band's first two LPs.

Title: Record
Review: It is the best and most meaningful music Tracey Thorn has made in a long time.

Title: Change
Review: With Change... The Dismemberment Plan feel little need to show off with self-conscious musical ostentation and excess, instead choosing to focus themselves on making a fantastic, understated and involving record.

Title: UNLOCKED
Review: Denzel’s flows are as hungry as ever, at times managing to channel the untamed spirit of DMX (see “Diet”) while Kenny’s production is the ideal mix of weighty drums and potent bass. It’s an energetic listen and one that can hopefully act as some sort of cure for Old Heads Syndrome – the belief that no one is making real hiphop anymore. [Apr 2020, p.68]

Title: On The Water
Review: Their dreamy, romantic and melancholy music is the perfect accompaniment to hope, the kind that can pull you through, and in a time of timidity, they are true believers.

Title: Death Magic
Review: HEALTH have never sounded as focused as they do here. These are sounds that will grab you by the hair and drag you where you need to go. It’s control of a potentially unpleasant, entirely intoxicating sort.

Title: The Blessed Unrest
Review: All in all, The Blessed Unrest is a well conceived effort, but not sans flaws.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: What saves the thing is, well, Moore’s style is so ingrained that to some extent this really will start to sound more natural with time.

Title: Life Is Sweet! Nice to Meet You
Review: But what comes through now is the strength of the songwriting, and his willingness to try out new things.

Title: The Looks

Title: Tribal

Title: Willie and the Wheel
Review: Decades in the making, this collection of swing classics as interpreted by Willie Nelson and Asleep at the Wheel doesn't disappoint.

Title: King Night

Title: Don't Stop
Review: Anyone who can bring real emotion to lines like “How does it feel to hear your songs on the radio? / And does it hurt to hear your songs on the radio?” deserves to be a real star.

Review: If Interpol-an album that plainly documents a band stretching itself as far as it can unimpressively go-is what a large number of indie fans are going to settle for in this day and age, I can't help but shake my head and sigh in response.

Title: amERICa
Review: If it all sounds a bit vintage, at age 61, he's earned the right. [No. 126, p.61]

Title: Hold Time

Perhaps it is the satisfaction of a band returning to their natural territory, or perhaps it is a marriage of the energy of the record with the spirit of its times, but Cloud Nothings have never been better.

Title: House of Woo
Review: House of Woo may be playful and irreverent, but that shouldn't disguise its status as a potent exploration of sound.

Title: Untitled
Review: [Untitled] is not a comfortable listen. It feels like something not meant for our ears--an incredibly spiritual and private moment that’s bound to compelling scripture and woeful, debilitating memories. It’s unfiltered passion that evades qualification; something to which we’d be performing a disservice by assigning a title.

Title: No Blues

Title: Delta Spirit

Title: Strangeland

Title: Night Music

Title: Terrorbird
Review: With 33 tracks in 42 minutes (each averages around one minute), the four-piece is anarchic and weird, yet -- best of all -- still strangely maintains a certain charm.

Title: Twerp Verse
Review: This is the most listener-friendly and accessible that Speedy Ortiz have ever been. But the band hasn’t left behind their heavy grunge sound, despite what many long-time fans will think when they listen to Twerp Verse. They’ve just given their sound a clever makeover, and taken the next step in their evolution as a band by doing so.

Title: Bright Like Neon Love
Review: The results are both familiar and fresh and should delight anyone disappointed by New Order's recent album.

Title: Vices & Virtues

Title: English Graffiti

Title: Devin Dazzle & the Neon Fever

Title: Proof of Youth
Review: It's hard to pick a favorite track from the album. It simply all works on Proof of Youth.

Title: A Hyperactive Workout for the Flying Squad

Title: Minotaur
Review: Minotaur is as essential as anything else the band has released and whether as part of Bonfires or on its own, the record stands as a welcome addition to their legacy as one of the great indie pop bands of their era.

Review: At times, that there’s as much “subversive” pop music as there is music that is supposedly being subverted, not all of it as deep as advertised. Poem, thankfully, is far more thoughtful about it than most.

Title: Open To Chance
Review: It's just a lovely collection of songs, in which the serenity of voice and understatement of band create a humane intimacy rather than anything more mystical. [Oct 2016, p.32]

Title: Balf Quarry
Review: Balf Quarry, however, sees Elisa Ambrogio and Pete Nolan emerging blinking into the sunlight as they continue to excavate the more focussed sounds of last album "Boss."

Title: Red Letter Days
Review: Mediocre to its very last note, it reminds you that mediocrity is indeed far worse than simply awful.

Title: Content

Title: Twentytwo in Blue

Title: Grown Unknown

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: She’s clever and sharp with her lyrical daggers, and she’s frighteningly aware of the impact of her own voice.

Title: Transatlanticism
Review: It's just comfortable and pleasant enough to convince yourself to stick around - never good enough to be satisfying, nor bad enough to be disappointing.

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun

Title: We Are The Night
Review: On We Are the Night, Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons pull out all their tricks, delivering an album of euphoric psychedelic electronica, quirky guest appearances, and danceable grooves.

Title: Color

Title: Waking Up
Review: Second album Waking Up is a set of polished arrangements so middle of the road they make Snow Patrol sound like Animal Collective.

Title: Crosseyed Heart
Review: Crosseyed Heart would have benefited from some trimming; it could’ve done without a few of the riff-rockers and the ballad “Suspicious”, a rehash of “This Room is Empty” from the Stones’ A Bigger Bang album and “Wicked as it Seems” from Main Offender. But the album’s virtues outweigh its longeurs.

Title: Blur the Line
Review: Somewhere along the line, this became an amazing band, and songwriting/arranging this masterful elevates Blur The Line to modern-classic status, fully justifying the 5-star rating applied at the top of this review.

Review: Beneath the lyrics live a less-than-cohesive batch of songs. But when the band allows each track a little more breathing room, they show some growth and have a good time doing it.

Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: If you take one thing away from this debut, take away the fact that it's thoroughly deserved.

Review: On their third album, a major-label debut with one of rock's great titles, the trio wears a newly polished sound proudly, while not coming close to straddling the sell-out ledge.

Title: Discodeine
Review: Amid its sluggishness, Discodeine sparkles intermittently--but too rarely.

Title: Lonerism
Review: Lonerism is a life raft for the abyss of song-induced self-reflection it inspires.

Title: History of Modern
Review: Upon first listen, the crew miss the mark with the unfortunate single, "If You Want It," a trainwreck attempt at a new audience. However, there is nary another song on the album so reprehensible. In fact, there are at least 5 cuts that will have many of you reaching for your disco biscuits and hoping for a Skytel page with the coordinates of an epic warehouse sweatfest.

Title: Uneasy Laughter
Review: The songs here mostly lack the sonic power and impact of those on its predecessor, but they do accomplish the not inconsiderable task of making Sean’s angular guitars sit alongside Pascal Stevenson’s synths congruously on tracks like ‘Ego’ and ‘Keep Out’. Post-punk bands of various eras have transitioned to new wave over the course of three or four albums, but Moaning have done that with just two.

Title: Former Lives
Review: Gibbard has better demonstrated his strength as one of the best songwriters of the last decade in the past, but ardent fans will appreciate the effort here.

Title: IGOR

Title: Feast of Wire
Review: Calexico has crafted an album that's rich in variety, yet still manages to maintain a cohesive sound throughout.

Title: You Could Have It So Much Better

Title: Jason Derulo
Review: As a performer, the smooth Derulo--made even smoother by Auto-Tune--delivers it all so effortlessly that none of that persuasive debut hunger comes through, making this stylish and short set one to admire rather than advocate.

Title: Thrice Woven
Review: The second half of the album lacks the spirit of its first two transcendent tracks. ... But, for those first 19 glorious minutes, Thrice Woven skirts the eye of the storm, flitting between untrammelled power and celestial beauty with a finesse that few can match.

Title: Violent Waves
Review: Circa Survive have managed to stay both relevant and utterly compelling – not just surviving but thriving.

Title: Chromatics
Review: It’s largely inoffensive and bland, with a few above average moments, and has a tendency to fade into the background.

Title: Malice n Wonderland
Review: But too often on this album Snoop is a fuddy-duddy, domesticated and palatable.

Title: Hear the Lions Roar

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth

Title: Senior
Review: It can't be said that Senior fails to meet its modest wallpaper-ish aims, yet it hardly represents the best Royksopp has to offer.

Review: An optimistic and heartfelt album. [Aug 2002, p.165]

Title: Kellie Pickler

Title: Let Me Come Home
Review: Let Me Come Home never really develops into the lump in the throat it wants to be, though it certainly isn't for lack of trying.

Title: Harlem River
Review: Harlem River is a journey worth taking and an excellent debut from an emerging singer/songwriter.

Title: Curse Your Branches
Review: Despite its undercurrent of outrage, Branches--which expands Pedro's folksy sound with creamy keyboards, processed drum beats and the occasional spritz of glam-rock guitar.

Title: The Richest Man In Babylon

Title: The Third Hand
Review: An instrument-juggling, one-man-band approach that recalls the romantic, psychedelic pop of the Zombies and the textured electronics of Radiohead.

Title: The Seer
Review: This is an album that vindicates maturity, long years of toil, cumulative effort, resilience, patience, wisdom.

Title: Live from the Underground

Title: Phantom Radio
Review: Left to his own devices without any interference from outside interests, and an astounding album of dark, sultry music like this is what you get in return.

Title: Hopes and Fears

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: Welcome to Condale is a refreshingly ambitious, variegated take on the 80s both conceptually and in its execution.

Title: The Power Out
Review: Equally inspired by The Raincoats and Jacques Brel, The Power Out veers from one inspired genre tribute to the next, if it never quite cements the band's identity.

Title: Secondhand Rapture
Review: It does not always work, but in short, orchestral bursts, MS MR demonstrate that they can transcend the confines of goth synth-pop, and produce one of the most memorable debuts of the year.

Title: Bitter Honey
Review: A bit too cleverly loaded with cultural critiques, winks and nods. [Apr 2006, p.207]

Title: Shrines
Review: Despite minor niggles, such as the slight lack of scope in sound, Shrines is a confident debut that justifies the hype.

Title: Lost Girls
Review: She gives you everything, expecting nothing in return, lavishing you with luxurious, gothic glamour and saturnine pleasure. A modern masterpiece.

Title: Halfway Between the Gutter and the Stars

Title: Lasers
Review: Lasers works best when the grabby hooks, electro beats, and conscious rap rants are all turned down a notch.

Title: Plastic Beach
Review: Ironically, these individual pieces don’t add up to an overall masterpiece, possibly because the narrative is convoluted and strained, getting in the way of the pure musical flow, but also because it’s hard not to shake the feeling that this is a transitional effort, pointing toward a day when Damon Albarn will feel no need to front a band, not even in a cartoon guise.

Title: Stranger in the Alps

Title: Clinging to a Scheme
Review: The Radio Dept. have cleverly managed to conjure up music with a thoroughly minimal feel, despite this hive of activity instrumentation-wise.

Title: Strapped
Review: Strapped's thirty-something minutes of southern California rock doesn't turn the page on anything new, but is still a worthy listen. The album holds true to the band's striped-down signature sound from their last two albums, with a sprinkling of a few stand out tracks.

Title: Eating Us
Review: Eating Us works as a pop record and tends to be only as good as its songs, as opposed to the monochromatic statement of purpose that was "Dandelion Gum." Luckily, these are some pretty good songs.

Title: An Awesome Wave
Review: There's undeniably something new and intriguing going on here. [Jul 2012, p.95]

Title: Songs About Girls

Title: Kittenz and Thee Glitz

Title: Chemical Chords

Title: The Return

Title: Gallowsbird's Bark
Review: It pulls from a grab bag of influences, from Bob Dylan to Broadway, The Who to honky-tonk, and tosses them around with apparent abandon. In spite of this (or maybe because of it), The FFs spin all of this into a sound that's consistent, yet almost magically unique.

Title: Poemss

Title: Love And Its Opposite
Review: Taken individually, each of Love and Its Opposite’s songs is impressive and affecting. Strung together as an album, though, their sulky nature becomes oppressive.

Title: Get Awkward

Review: Thumping Mark Hollis-style piano and ominous scuttling backbeats add another satisfying touch to a recommended collection.

Review: Trans-Love Energies is a fine return and a worthy addition to the catalogue of a band whose path has become more of a fantastic voyage than a standard career.

Title: Hearts of Oak
Review: Leo's racial politics are serious and confused in that familiar white-guy-in-D.C. way, but word-heavy, wound-up gems such as "Hearts of Oak," "The Anointed One" and "The Ballad of the Sin Eater" prove he knows how to turn political conviction into punk energy.

Title: Yes Lawd!
Review: What’s astonishing here is the way they manage to forge a sound nearly as rich and original as that of America’s most blunted.

Title: The Phoenix
Review: The Phoenix shouldn't shock those who know the producer's past.

Title: Totems Flare
Review: He may be pushing boundaries and himself less urgently than before, but in doing so he’s made his most palatable and varied record to date.

Title: Headphones
Review: Considering how strong a songwriter Bazan has proved himself to be on the last few Pedro discs, the results here are mildly disappointing. [Jun 2005, p.164]

Title: The Sound the Speed the Light
Review: It would've been easy to let The Sound cruise from there, filling it with solid also-rans. But the energy level and commitment continue unabated.

Title: The Voyager
Review: Ultimately, the pop sheen Adams applies on The Voyager is at odds with Lewis' songs. By always opting for directness, he's failed to let her do justice, musically, to the darkness of her inspiration.

Title: Engravings
Review: Engravings is the sound of a man walking out into the coastline with his headphones on, the epic, Saxon past showing through the fog and playing with the Anglo present’s love of electronic music.

Title: The Weather Station
Review: These songs--even the quiet ones--are bold, messy, unflinching, humming with life. [No. 147, p.61]

Title: FM!
Review: FM! is definitely more centrally focused than either of those EPs [2014's Hell Can Wait and 2016's Prima Donna]. And even if this is just an off-hand project Vince recorded quickly, it's a hell of a one-off album that's full of charm and lyrical depth paired with fantastic production. Tune in.

Title: Slowdive
Review: Along with the melodic, melancholic vocal mumblings and minimalist drum beats, the overall atmosphere is that of a hazy, underwater dream.

Title: Not Music
Review: The signature post-rock and cleverly monotonous Stereolab aesthetic is still present, and continues to be refreshingly innovative.

Title: Politics Of The Business
Review: While Politics of the Business follows in the conceptual footsteps of its forbears, its all-too-literal sense of moral responsibility does get a tad tiresome, occasionally sagging into diluted dogma.

Title: One by One
Review: It's rock that draws power from its determination to struggle onward.

Title: The Meetings of the Waters
Review: This is a very welcome return of a singular talent. [Jun 2017, p.112]

Title: Fingers, Bank Pads, and Shoe Prints
Review: This new LP is understated by comparison, with fewer jarring moments and more shifting grooves.

Title: Kiwanuka
Review: An album that could have been a grueling downer from start to finish. Instead, it’s a testament to perseverance, determination and a vivid creative imagination from an artist who seems to have finally found himself, and that’s profound enough.

Title: The Eraser
Review: It sounds exactly like you would expect a Thom Yorke solo album to sound: twitchy electronic beats, doomy washes of synthesizer, backing vocals that are invariably high, wordless and ghostly.

Title: Only Revolutions
Review: Only Revolutions has enough in the way of nous, intelligence and tunes to broaden their audience immeasurably. [Dec 2009, p.122]

Title: Many Moons
Review: Many Moons is the fussy, neat feeling we already know of him. The only real change is that we now have to look deeper and listen more closely to invoke a powerful connection between artist and listener. If the songs were more engaging, this would be easier to do. However, they all resolve to their same base parts, and thus become more forgettable than the feelings Real Estate's best songs have conjured.

Title: Titanic Rising
Review: Titanic Rising is a revelation. These opulent, sculptural songs have sacrificed none of Mering's idiosyncrasy, or ability to unnerve. [May 2019, p.87]

Title: Fluorescence
Review: Joyful and experimental in equal measure, Fluorescence is an album that challenges you without you even realising.

Title: Do Not Disturb
Review: Do Not Disturb, VDGG’s 13th album and their third since regrouping in 2005, bears little evidence of engagement with music’s outside world, but it’s creative and sprightly on its own terms. [Oct 2016, p.61]

Title: Rebirth
Review: Concocting the world's finest excrement-related rhymes, Rebirth is most definitely a flop, terribly unsexy, and contains surprisingly few shit jokes.

Title: Eyehategod
Review: There aren’t any real surprises at work on Eyehategod, and that’s just fine. Its relatively simple approach of no frills instrumentals meets raw, demented vocals feels surprisingly fresh in its earnestness.

Title: This Is Not a Safe Place
Review: This Is Not a Safe Place is not, in the end, the classic Ride Mark 2 release that its first three songs so casually tease. But it has enough joy, verve and invention to suggest that Ride could get there one day.

Title: You Are the Quarry
Review: But just when he seems more relevant than ever, Morrissey has somehow contrived to make an album that sounds incredibly dated.

Title: Content
Review: They're as challenging as they were in their heyday throughout Content. [Year End 2010, p.70]

Title: Bish Bosch
Review: It's still one giant leap into the unknown, with all the notions of genre once again gleefully sidestepped. [Dec 2012, p.82]

Title: i
Review: Many of the witty, lovelorn pop songs here can stand beside any in Merritt's formidable catalogue.

Title: Radio Wars
Review: Radio Wars demands its listeners heed that siren song, and it's truthfully hard to resist.

Title: This Week
Review: Like Talib Kweli... she mixes precise diction with writing that's high on observation and metaphysical promise. [Dec 2004, p.137]

Title: Basses Loaded
Review: Rather than making a sharp left turn on Basses Loaded, the band instead pays homage to their long, curious history by plugging in with some longtime cohorts, making an unholy ruckus, and once again not giving a damn about what we think of it.

Title: A Woman A Man Walked By
Review: PJ Harvey can be exhilarating, thrilling, or offer up a disturbingly hysterical variant on black humour, but she ain't fun. A Woman A Man Walked By is kinda, sorta fun.

Title: King of Jeans
Review: There’s a blunt but effective wit at work here, pressed into the service of misanthropy.

Title: The Invisible Band
Review: It feels self-consciously downbeat and rustic, with a Gomez-style, recorded-in-a-shed sheen which belies Nigel Godrich's pristine, state-of-the-art production.

Title: Staind
Review: Nu-Metal stars release a solid effort. [Sep 2011, p.52]

Title: Joanne
Review: Joanne still represents a striking course correction for Lady Gaga. By abandoning the dance club for the dive bar, she may have tossed aside her status as a pop star once and for all. But Gaga has emerged as something better and truer.

Title: Lamp Lit Prose
Review: Lamp Lit Prose is his shiniest, airiest, even catchiest set of songs. The new record exchanges the jarring, glitchy electronic intrusions and arid trap percussion he used on “Dirty Projectors” for the springy guitar lines of older Dirty Projectors albums, bringing out their warmest tones.

Title: Midnight
Review: Amid synth-y disco ­dalliances ("Alive Tonight") and soul-funk workouts ("Your Girl"), she leaves room for snarling riffs on "Look What We've Become" and acoustic boom on "Empty Heart," reminiscent of Sheryl Crow's "Leaving Las Vegas."

Title: The Oracle
Review: Though built mainly with recycled material, "The Oracle" has fresh moments, such as the scrappy delivery of "What If?" and the up-tempo snap of "War and Peace."

Title: Gimme Fiction
Review: It's exactly the record that everyone hoped Spoon would make. [#15, p.98]

Title: Is A Woman
Review: Another mature masterpiece from America's finest. [Album Of The Month, March 2002, p.94]

Title: Girls In Peacetime Want To Dance
Review: It’s an excellent album by a band who seem to be permanently brimming with life and ideas, a glimmer of warmth to lighten the dark depths of winter.

Title: You Will Not Die
Review: You Will Not Die is a strikingly intimate album that succeeds despite some occasionally lead-footed pacing and stilted theatrics.

Title: Even In Exile
Review: Jara's story gives a dramatic, yearning quality to the libretto that suits Bradfield's epic style, and allows a sense of unity to emerge through individual songs. [Sep 2020, p.27]

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: Daniel Lopatin's newest Oneohtrix Point Never album is one of the more unique, powerful recordings to come out this year. It's uncomfortable but distinctly compelling.

Title: Imperfect Harmonies
Review: It's an easier to admire than to love. [18 Sep 2010, p.58]

Title: Heard It In A Past Life
Review: The palette can feel restrictive, and the lyrical matter predictable. It’s a stepping stone, a moment of reconciliation and recollection from a talent who is just about to surge ahead.

Title: Desire Lines
Review: Desire Lines is undoubtedly a Camera Obscura album, but it might be their first that is more suited to quiet winter nights inside, rather than the sunny side of things that dominated their sound on their previous albums.

Title: Settle
Review: Sometimes uniformity is no bad thing at all--when you get the formula right, that is--and Guy and Howard Lawrence prove just that on their debut LP.

Title: Passive Me, Aggressive You
Review: It's a welcome escape, but it doesn't have the shape and form of something worth escaping to and remains at best a quality xerox of pop music today.

Title: All We Love We Leave Behind
Review: All We Love We Leave Behind will sit alongside the very best. [6 Oct 2012, p.53]

Title: La Grande
Review: One wouldn't expect Gibson's latest to bowl over any audiophile chasing the wow!-factor, but for the patient, contemplative listener, La Grande-- much like the campfire depicted on its cover-- is a record worth warming to.

Title: Syre
Review: A lot of the otherworldly iterations might make it difficult for some of his peers to grasp, especially if you don’t have the time to properly digest it. SYRE requires patience, a thorough listen and acute attention to detail otherwise it’s just going to sound like a strange pontification on existentialism that the casual listener simply doesn’t have the time to decipher.

Title: Clear Heart Full Eyes
Review: Clear Heart Full Eyes is a low-key triumph, containing some of the most emotionally satisfying work Finn has yet produced. [Feb 2012, p.82]

Title: Lovers Know
Review: A record that requires some time to get acquainted, and rewards repeated listening. [Aug-Sep 2015, p.66]

Title: Telling It Like It Is
Review: In stark contrast to last year's effort, Marching Church have learnt to restrain their pandemonium in the name of melody-and are well on their way to becoming experimental rock flag-bearers.

Title: Conceived in Sewage
Review: Sure some songs (“Heaving Acid”/“Parasitic Eruption”) are indistinguishable, but for the most part this record sweats malice in a straightforward, pulverizing kind of way.

Title: Radio Retaliation
Review: Booming basslines, clubby beats, high production values and a guest list that includes Brazil's Seu Jorge, sitar lady Anushka Shankar and Afrobear star Femi Kuti make it a safe backdrop for just about any bar anywhere in the world. [Nov 2008, p.121]

Title: Bitter Drink Bitter Moon
Review: After a handful of muddled, upbeat tracks that mar Bitter Drink's middle, the band settles into its skin again with "Ditch Lilly," a meandering sprawl that lets its ink-black atmosphere slowly seep through.

Title: Welcome Joy
Review: Emphatic yet rarely overbearing choruses, all delivered in a subtle manner, will always bring me back to the road. The Cave Singers have mastered the art of give and take.

Title: Ecstatics International
Review: Ecstatics proves to be only half the album it thought itself capable of being.

Title: Young for Eternity
Review: Swings from rapid-fire rockers to acoustic-inspired melodic pieces. [Feb/Mar 2006, p.97]

Title: Pennied Days
Review: It's one thing to make a great debut album, and quite another to make an equally effective follow-up. Night Moves have done just that on Pennied Days, an indie pop marvel well worth your attention.

Title: At Home
Review: There are two completely different EPs within this album stitched together with a tenuously thin thread. One is dark, one is light and unfortunately the thread does not bind them together as a cohesive musical statement.

Title: Matilda
Review: Cited as a missing link between Radiohead and Massive Attack following their self-titled 2007 debut, the Leeds outfit here start to live up to the hype. [Mar 2011, p.115]

Title: The Black Magic Show
Review: The guitar work is straight out of the Velvet Underground/Television songbook, and the production begs for comparisons to the Strokes or Interpol. That's not to say being compared to these folks is bad, it's just that those comparisons don't reveal how unimaginative The Black Magic Show really is.

Title: Ashes & Fire
Review: The recordings have the warmth and pop of a vinyl record, creating a perfect environment for Adams to honor his influences.

Title: Ad Infinitum
Review: He has freed himself up enough here to find a renewed sense of purpose, without losing sight of what has drawn listeners to his music in the first place.

Title: Talk That Talk
Review: It's sure to sell on brand recognition alone, but I doubt a series of mannered and soulless hooks are going to find much life outside of the European remix circuit.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: As You As You Were already feels like a festival anthem in waiting. Stunningly good music.

Title: A Blessing and a Curse
Review: Finds [Drive-By Truckers] turing from the social concerns of 2004's Dirty South to the more personal with career-best results. [21 Apr 2006, p.75]

Title: The Circus
Review: After the huge success of his second critically-acclaimed album like ‘Pieces Of A Man’, this small EP steps into the big boots it needs to fill before Mick Jenkins’ next outing. ... Delightfully dainty.

Title: Heaven
Review: Heaven comes across as a more or less triumphant culmination of the Walkmen's first decade, and the fact that happiness fits the band better than anyone could have expected is just a welcome bonus.

Title: Taiga
Review: Their inspired, eclectic mix of sounds and textures is always playful, but Taiga's powerful playing and sophisticated arrangements make it OOIOO's most mature album yet.

Title: Joy
Review: Unsurprisingly, their second joint venture has the white-knuckle ride aspect you’d expect from musicians who produce new music seemingly at will.

Title: VII
Review: VII is Blitzen Trapper’s strongest album to date, with years of musical experimentation having come together in the band’s own mad-scientist brand of cosmic Americana.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: Some of the album's most arresting moments come as the dust settles.

Title: It's Album Time
Review: It’s Album Time is a lock-tight demonstration of how crucial time is in the cultivation process. As a result, Todd Terje curated one of the most enjoyable albums that will cross our desk this year.

Title: Loud Like Love
Review: Against the odds Placebo are growing old gracefully. [Sep 2013, p.89]

Title: A New Testament
Review: A New Testament makes for a comforting, occasionally gorgeous listen if you can set aside your preconceptions.

Title: Folker
Review: It's hard not to walk away with the feeling he's capable of better than this.

Title: When I'm Free
Review: Jazz and trip-hop shade this darkness. [Oct 2015, p.96]

Title: All Your Favorite Bands
Review: The power of Goldsmith’s words elevates it all to the next level.

Title: Outsiders
Review: A notably mature-sounding record full of gnarly guitars, scrunchy Hammond organ and tuneful innocence lost. [Jun 2018, p.92]

Title: Mirror
Review: The list of reasons to be angry have grown exponentially in the brief intervening period, so it only makes sense that Mirror is the way it is. Staring into the abyss is rarely this stupefying and spectacular.

Title: Wire
Review: A collection that feels like a fresh bookend to their first three classic albums. [May 2015, p.115]

Title: Chuck
Review: [Their] penchant for pastiche has evolved... into full-blown plagiarism. [9 Oct 2004, p.57]

Title: Providence
Review: With highly catchy choruses on ‘Heart of Mine’ and ‘Deliver It’, it’s obvious that the band can deliver the pop sheen they are known for. But while reaching for style, it is only by exception that they achieve their usual substance.

Title: Ode
Review: It bears a lot of replaying.

Title: Visions of Us on the Land
Review: Though the collab with Swift has resulted in easily Jurado’s most fascinating records as a songwriter, the wide-open road might be a little too inviting at times--because occasionally you need to consult a map for fear of driving off the end of the Earth.

Title: I See You
Review: Their extroversion is by no means a dead-end and does show ample potential, but analogous to stepping out into the light after a period of darkness, one must become accustomed to the surrounding brilliance. At the moment, The xx’s vision is mildly blurred with sunspots.

Title: At Home
Review: Dream pop is rarely celebrated for its attention to melody, as it usually places texture and atmosphere higher up on the totem poll, but At Home would have benefitted from a few more melodies that were capable of sticking with the listener past the album's running time.

Title: Dear Science
Review: No two tracks are the same, none could be anyone else. This is one irresistible party: the joy Adebimpe was looking for is right here. A great, great record. [Oct 2008, p.154]

Title: Mosaics Within Mosaics
Review: A lot of W.C. Hart’s lyrics are preoccupied with the idea of locating yourself within the whole whorl of the earth-psychedelia-human experience, be it from underneath, above, sideways, chronologically, anyhow, anyway, somewhere between the “rock and stars and sand.”

Title: Physical
Review: Physical boasts one hell of a range of tracks, some suited for dancing but all suited to telling Gurnsey's favourite story. With it he's created a new and independent take on house proving that Gabe Gurnsey is not just a member of Factory Floor but a solo artist in his own right and style.

Title: Seeker
Review: The resultant raggedy, in-the-moment feel suits the Neil Young-ish "Show Me" and harmonica-hinged "Guardian Well," as well as "I've Got Reason," less so "Feel It All," which drags its feet over five minutes. "Lost A year" is a sax-assisted winner, though. [Nov 2019, p.24]

Title: The Age of the Understatement
Review: Turner's new side project, a collaboration with Miles Kane of Merseyside indie-poppers the Rascals, is a shameless nostalgia trip--and it's still compelling.

Title: Is This It
Review: Plenty of bands have hooks and good songs and retro-garage sounds, but none compares to The Strokes.

Title: The Scene Between
Review: The Scene Between is another breathless, time-collapsing rush of dayglo, retro, lo-fi indie spunk, cutting back on the hip-hop inflections, schoolyard chants and cut-and-paste sample collage to focus squarely on melody. [No. 119, p.55]

Title: Quickies
Review: As with other Magnetic Fields projects, some deeper cuts succeed more than others. Still, any lows aren’t particularly low.

Title: Mirror Traffic
Review: As ever, there's a jamming seam throughout the Malkmus landscape, with the likes of Brian Gallop descending (or ascending, more appropriately) into freeform guitar passages that, while inevitably slightly indulgent, are never less than engaging, tuneful and, above all, enjoyable.

Title: Blacklisted
Review: A rare record from an extraordinary artist, and one of the year's best.

Title: Everybody's A Good Dog
Review: Fleming may have lost some of the outsider charm that bubbled through the first Diane Coffee record by going big, but he went big in such a sure-handed and spectacular way, it's hard to complain too much. In fact, an album this crazy and good deserves nothing but praise and adulation.

Title: Layers
Review: Six albums deep on the solo tip, Royce’s introspective side clearly shines through on Layers.

Title: Love is the Law
Review: For all its pleasures, though, Love is the Law feels a bit overstuffed at 17 tracks.

Title: Pearl Jam
Review: The band socks away the adventurous experimentation that dogged some of its most recent records to investigate a post-September 11, war-ravaged world overflowing with urgency and significance.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: Lennox lost his father to brain cancer in 2002 and the experience has floated through his music ever since, but never has his songwriting been so tragically pointed. There's no ambiguity here, only the gaping emptiness that the absence of a parent leaves behind.

Title: Ben Kweller
Review: This is the 25-year-old singer-songwriter at his most personal. [Oct 2006, p.208]

Title: Music for the Maases
Review: Embraced by trance, breakbeat, and house DJs alike, Maas has been heard in almost every sort of dance setting, so he's earned the right to his own compilation. [2/2001, p.85]

Title: Lifetime of Love
Review: Lifetime of Love is a strange album, where songs with differing emotional foundations, sonic palettes, aural pace and textural aesthetics mesh into a cohesive whole. As Moon Diagrams, Archuleta has created a world where introspection, catharsis and redemption can envelop you and become something porous, to be inhaled and lived in.

Title: Hiss Spun
Review: [Producer Kurt] Ballou’s signature crushing heaviness may have become a cliché in some circles, but paired with Wolfe’s beautiful voice and brilliant writing, it's a match made in heaven.

Title: On My Way to Absence
Review: Ineffectual hippy grumblings that will make you want to sleep. [4 Jun 2005, p.58]

Title: TRUE
Review: Worst-case scenario: that initial dreamlike spell wears out its welcome long before the album's 38 minutes are up. Best case: you've had a stressful day and True really hits that sweet, relaxing spot.

Title: Escapology
Review: Musically and vocally, there's few surprises but at least lyrically he's moved on from clever-ish wordplay and inane love songs, to tell tales of being generally screwed-up at the hands of the multi-million dollar pop machine.

Title: Open
Review: I can’t think of a record I was less eager to go back to a second time, and I can’t think of a record I changed my mind about more on the second, third and fourth time, except maybe the Necks’ last one.

Title: The Bedlam in Goliath
Review: For the most part, this is the heaviest record that they’ve recorded and the most far-out as well.

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light II
Review: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light, Vol. 2 is a looser affair, showcasing Carlson's improvisational chemistry with long-term percussionist Adrienne Davies, bass player Karl Blau and cellist Lori Goldston. [Mar 2012, p.102]

Title: Viola Beach
Review: Still, while their lyrics could be fine-tuned, it’s hard not to warm to a quartet whose obvious pleasure at being in a group pervades every adrenaline-charged note.

Title: Instinct
Review: They're at their strongest when at their hardest.

Title: I Love You
Review: Her new album does nothing new--we've been here before.

Title: Violent Hearts
Review: They've really only got one trick. But it's a treat, all the same. [Oct 2011, p.98]

Title: Happy Songs for Happy People
Review: The Stephen Kings of menacing post-rock, it seems that in absence of Young Team's glorious cacophany their tremendous build-up often comes to nothing. And it sounds as though they've come to terms with that.

Title: Holy Ghost
Review: While the shift towards tempered indie rock often robs Holy Ghost of the instant gratification of early MoBo, there isn’t a single clunker lyric that was wedged in for the sake of cleverness.

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: It’s a sincere album that is as friendly and rewarding as any of their previous works.

Title: Weezer (Green Album)
Review: Feels a bit repetitive and perfunctory the first time through, but it's resolutely unpretentious and airtight throughout, without a wasted moment or false move.

Title: The Truth About Love
Review: Maybe not a wholly successful album then, but at its best, The Truth About Love proves that Pink can still credibly compete with the pop stars she helped to inspire.

Title: Relatives in Descent
Review: Very few other bands are working at the level of aggression, precision, intensity and intelligence that Protomartyr musters. Relatives in Descent is yet another record from this outfit that you can’t afford to miss.

Title: Paul's Tomb: A Triumph
Review: A volatile brew of uneasy drama and emotion from a band that, on this showing, should always record live.

Title: White Women
Review: There’s a fine line between irony and referential lightheartedness. We all need a vehicle to convey emotions, after all, and Chromeo’s is more stylish than most.

Title: Power Chords
Review: There’s a unique heart hidden deep with every album he creates, and Power Chords is no different. Open yourself up to the world of Krol.

Title: How The Thing Sings
Review: On How The Thing Sings, Orcutt reveals a more open vision. [Oct 2011, p.58]

Title: Wild Seeds
Review: There's a cosmic/romantic wisdom to highlight One Way Or Another and Two Dreamers' sunshine classicism. [Sep 2019, p.96]

Title: Lush
Review: There's still a mumblecore sulkiness to Jordan's delivery that drags some songs down, but on tracks like the fingerpicking marvel "Let's Find Out" and "Deep Sea," she finds a distinctive voice all her own. [Aug 2018, p.33]

Title: Turn Blue
Review: It's meticulously executed but slightly (and sleepily) monochromatic.

Title: Close To The Glass
Review: On Close to the Glass, the results are more fractured and schizophrenic than ever.

Title: Sepalcure
Review: From ambient juke to haunting, slo-mo house, their debut album kicks and caresses in equal measure.

Title: A Short History of Decay
Review: Musically simpler and less baroque than The Graceless Age, the album's autobiographical arc is conversely harder to glean, its lyrics more oblique. Murry's greatest ability, however, is to make the listener wince uncomfortably while peeking through their fingers at his captivating, compulsive honesty. [Aug 2017, p.88]

Title: Quebec
Review: There's something here for everyone, to be sure--but closer to Ween's antic hearts, something to annoy everyone as well.

Title: Disappeared
Review: While it doesn't flow with the breathless ingenuity of their earlier albums, it's still a cut above 90 percent of today's electronica. [#147, p.109]

Title: Spills Out
Review: The dichotomy between the agonies of face-melting and beatific singing has long been a Pterodactyl motif, but this time the guitar wizardry takes a nonetheless threatening backseat to the structure of the songs.

Title: Shake The Sheets
Review: Leo's singing (showing a few traces of a soul side) has never been more confident or convincing.

Title: Curtis
Review: 'My Gun' is one of the best tracks Fifty's lent his name to; Adam Deitch and Eric Krasno's skilful production keeps the tension bubbling just below the surface with a muted hard rock guitar riff; 50's rhyme and flow is more varied and expressive than his usual monotone drawl.... The remainder of the album is as inconsistent as Fifty’s career to date.

Title: If the Ocean Gets Rough
Review: Weathered and intelligent, these songs resonate like folk antiquities from another age. Even more remarkably, they never sound forced. [Apr 2007, p.116]

Title: Creaturesque
Review: The practice spent fiddling with slower and more methodical tracks on the excellent "Purpleface" EP shows its effectiveness plainly here. [Summer 2009, p.100]

Title: Foil Deer
Review: Foil Deer isn’t an easy listen but it is a compelling one.

Title: Loom
Review: This is the rare offering of post-Smiths jangle that doesn't rely on pomp or posturing.

Title: Let's Face the Music and Dance
Review: An exquisitely contemplative turn into 80.

Title: Sung Tongs
Review: But despite its flaws, or perhaps because of them, this remains organic folk-pop at its bewildering best.

Title: Goodbye Lullaby
Review: The problems arise on Goodbye Lullaby when Lavigne compartmentalizes her softer side, to the point where it eclipses her finger-jabbing cheekiness.

Title: Social Rust
Review: It's a scuzzy Swans-like behemoth. [Oct 2014, p.77]

Title: Carefree Theatre
Review: Some of album's more pedestrian elements slide by — bouncy, sing-song verses that Pitts can obviously write in his sleep and which come off as a bit insubstantial sometimes, the whole thing threatening to blow away with the faintest breeze. Carefree Theatre is certainly pleasant enough to get swept up in however, and a good capstone to a decade's work.

Title: A Place To Bury Strangers
Review: The self-titled album brings the listener into a glorious sound world of first rate noise-pop and never lets go.

Title: Hell Hath No Fury
Review: The stark beats are the best Hugo and Williams have built in years. But its themes--dealing, girls--require more lyrical innovation to compel. [Feb 2007, p.105]

Title: Look into the Eyeball
Review: Often thought of as ahead of his time perhaps Byrne is now in the perfect position to articulate the angst of socially unskilled western white men who find themselves taking over the world via new technology. The album's glut of different rhythms speaks of a man trying to find his groove.

Title: Brick Body Kids Still Daydream
Review: Mike Eagle manages to balance the sense that he is speaking for many with the certainty that no one else could do it quite the same way.

Title: Oh My God
Review: One of his strongest bodies of work to date. It’s a richly textured piece of work which sees him expertly display his ability to make listeners find intimacy in vast soundscapes.

Title: Sounds Good Feels Good
Review: When compared to their debut, the maturity of Sounds Good is evident. [Nov 2015, p.95]

Title: America
Review: A dash of extra variety, and an increasing ability to transform clever layers of sound into well-structured songs, make this his best contribution to date.

Title: Apocalypse
Review: Throughout this solo effort--his fourth, for what it's worth--Callahan mumbles ever onward like a charmless, tranquillised version of Giant Sand's Howe Gelb. [Apr 2011, p.55]

Title: War Room Stories
Review: so far, so arty. [Mar 2014, p.108]

Title: Welcome Joy
Review: It's just there was the expectation of more, and this has left me a bit cold.

Title: Once More 'Round the Sun
Review: Because the wealth of emotional depth is brought to the forefront and propelled by the inner workings of Mastodon’s almost-perfected prog-as-hard-rock paradigm, this album really is an interesting development for the band.

Title: A Piece Of What You Need
