Review: The introductory kiddie voice and opening guitar scrape establish this second album as White's show; mariachi-style brass fanfare, Appalachian-hoedown fiddling and plenty of Roman-candle solos soon follow. [June 2008, p.76]

Title: A Bad Wind Blows In My Heart
Review: What’s most disappointing about the album is how Ryder-Jones has almost completely abandoned taking any sonic risks. His vocal is dulled and rasping throughout, and the songs never blossom like those on If..., seemingly hamstrung by his limited range.

Title: If There's A Hell Below
Review: Even with Black Milk's limits as a rapper, If There's a Hell Below is a solid album. Black Milk nails the line between being retro and forward-thinking, between street and backpack, between nostalgia and honesty.

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: Expansive opener, 'Crocidile' finds them locked into the pulsing techno groove that made 'Born Slippy' so maddeningly addictive. [Nov 2007, p.148]

Title: In Colour
Review: It is exceedingly rare to find a producer who does so much, with so little, that he distilled from, again, so much.

Title: Stories Don't End
Review: After a while the regretful, melancholy tone wearies one's sympathies.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: They may not be particularly youthful anymore, but there's plenty of transcendence to be found on this record.

Title: I Am Very Far
Review: It's a scattershot collection of rougher material, lacking the concision and continuity that made 2003's Down the River of Golden Dreams and 2007's The Stage Names such defining works.

Title: Mary's Voice
Review: It may have taken him a few tries but through Mary's Voice, Koster has finally found his own.

Title: The Man Upstairs
Review: To a drumless folk palette of voice, guitar, piano and cello, he deftly blends his own compositions with covers of The Psychedelic Furs, Roxy Music and The Doors into a sweetly morose song suite that examines the heartsick mature male, post-love affair, wondering what it's all about. [Oct 2014, p.110]

Title: Body Language
Review: Long stretches prove mysteriously hookless, arid, or burdened by Minogue foregrounding a voice that withers in the glare of the spotlight.

Title: Congratulations
Review: Overall, MGMT's refusal to co-operate with the listener jars with the crisp and professional production – which, despite Sonic Boom's involvement, is more Van Dyke Parks than Spacemen 3 and leaves Congratulations sitting somewhere in the middle, not complex enough for the prats, but too obscure for the jerks.

Title: Back to Love
Review: He sounds marvelous.

Title: Moon Tides
Review: It politely demands your attention; it wants to transport you elsewhere, to a place in which to daydream and reflect. Hindman and Versprille were absolutely right to go it alone; they’ve made a beautiful album.

Title: It's All True
Review: By no means is It's All True a masterpiece; the duo don't stick their necks out enough to entertain that notion. But by creating a palpable tension between smart songwriting and their knack for texture, Junior Boys have pulled a legacy back from the brink of indifference.

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: Welcome to Condale is a study in tactless excess, the sheer volume of inebriating nostalgic moments intended to overwhelm the lukewarm medium by which they're delivered.

Title: A Christmas Cornucopia
Review: Annie Lennox is robustly reverent on A Christmas Cornucopia, putting the full and frequently rough power of her voice behind some of the sternest old carols, with devout verses that are often omitted.

Title: For My Parents
Review: For My Parents isn't likely to go down with your Slow Riot for New Zerø Kanadas or Spiderlands, but there are times when it seems to break new ground.

Title: Warble Womb
Review: While it's not necessarily Dead Meadow's masterwork, it shows a band growing into its sound and mellowing nicely without sacrificing any of its radiance by exploring less extreme territories.

Title: High
Review: Royal Headache's execution is so straightforwardly 1977 that it almost teeters on generic garage-rock pastiche. The saving grace is this album's undeniable heart and soul.

Title: Strawberry
Review: Wussy reaches for transcendence and finds it. You wish it would go on forever.

Title: Love in Shadow
Review: As impressive and imposing The Deal and What One Becomes are, Love in Shadow stands in a league of its own. The change of perspective, the stylistic deviations and the smooth transitions between different modes make Love in Shadow appear as a pivotal record for the band.

Title: What Now
Review: What Now is accessible in every sense of the word, but after several spins, it'll pull you much deeper than one might initially think.

Title: The Con
Review: The Con is undoubtedly as sweet as it is short.

Title: Major Key
Review: His bottomless stock of anthemic crowd-pleasers may not be game-changing, but few albums this year have come preloaded with this many obvious singles.

Title: The Wake
Review: The Wake signals a new chapter for Voivod; they stand (again) at the blade edge of creative imagination and visionary execution in the world of extreme music.

Title: Art and Life
Review: Diasporic dancehall reggae, spruced up and polished around the edges, but essentially retaining the artist's signature style.

Title: On and On
Review: With On and On, this Hawaiian surfer's croon evokes the mellow-yellow moan of Donovan but without the weirdness that made that psychedelic folkie compelling.

Title: Soused
Review: A powerful mix of dramatic, slow-moving sound and Walker melodies and narratives. [Nov 2014, p.99]

Title: Murmurations
Review: It feels like a fitting release for the duo who’ve been going for so long. The search for new ideas is always on, and with this one, they’ve found a winner that offers something a bit different, while not alienating.

Title: Mama's Gun
Review: Mama's Gun is the female companion to D'Angelo's ''Voodoo,'' with which it shares a reactionary pseudo- sophistication that too often substitutes good taste for good tunes. It's soul music for people who -- wrongly -- think rap is dumb and contemporary R&B is simplistic. Unlike D'Angelo, however, Badu has a nuanced voice that pokes through the bland surfaces; sometimes she manages moments worthy of her forebears, as on the slinky ''Bag Lady'' and the syncopated ''Booty.''

Title: Swanlights
Review: The fourth Antony and the Johnsons  album is more diverse and positive than 2008's The Crying Light, with familiar concerns of death and alienation broadening into family, human bonds, and the joys of love.

Title: Transparent Things
Review: The difference between a wholly derivative artist and Fujiya & Miyagi is that they take their influences and condense them into one. [#17, p.91]

Title: Take Her Up To Monto
Review: While the album features several standout tracks and stunning vocals, as a whole, over-shined production and mashed-up genres obscure Murphy’s strengths.

Title: Tired of Hanging Around
Review: You have to go back to Costello, The Beat or Smiths to find a catalogue simultaneously as hummable and as disturbing as McCabe's. [May 2006, p.102]

Title: Yours, Dreamily
Review: By and large, as per its title, Yours, Dreamily is a downtempo treat, tailor-made for sundazed summer evening drives with the window down. [Sep 2015, p.87]

Title: After the Disco
Review: With After The Disco--Broken Bells’ second full-length album--Mercer and Burton up the ante with a set that builds on the promise of their debut and fleshes out that aesthetic into an even stronger set of songs with loftier ambitions.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Worlds Apart
Review: Simply put, 'Worlds Apart' is a delicately violent piece of art.

Title: Game Theory
Review: They've resurfaced sounding dark, mysterious, and pissed off.

Title: Arrows
Review: Despite those candid confessions, Arrows never bows to Scattergood’s self-indulgence, given the swooning synths and other cosmic confections.

Title: Ultimate Victory
Review: A cohesive and complete album in the world of Southern rap.

Title: Tales from Turnpike House
Review: An endlessly enjoyable sophisticated pop album.

Title: Luciferian Towers
Review: The nine-piece evoke America's open spaces in a beautiful bluster of feedback and reverb. [Nov 2017, p.28]

Title: Overexposed
Review: 'Sad' is an Adele-apeing weepie, 'Payphone' has a guest rap from Wiz Khalifa, and both 'Lucky Strike' and 'Fortune Teller' feature cod-dubstep breakdowns.

Title: Joyland
Review: Joyland has a coherent feel of low slung rock'n'roll and Morricone twang. [Apr 2015, p.96]

Title: End of Suffering
Review: We have to wait for the final, title track for the end of suffering. That Carter’s young daughter Mercy is on the recording ramps up the emotion and hopeful vibe of this acoustic ballad. It’s a much-needed resolution to an album of full-throttle catharsis.

Title: Why Love Now
Review: With riffs weighted so they're heavy enough to bludgeon, and vocals that feel like they're being torn straight from the larynx, the album is a tour de force of high octane refrains and filth-driven focus.

Title: The Sound of Music
Review: Of course half the fun is in hearing how the band have transformed oh-so-familiar songs into something quite different, and transform them they truly have.

Title: Every Kind of Light
Review: It's nice to have the Posies back in the studio again, but Every Kind of Light isn't the triumphant return fans might have hoped for.

Title: Modern Nature
Review: Their most remarkable record in years. [Feb 2015, p.95]

Title: Yours Truly
Review: Ariana Grande's debut LP is a surprisingly varied affair for a 20-year-old Nickelodeon star with a devastatingly strong voice.

Title: Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)
Review: Sadly, the thrust and thunder of "Love Hurt Bleed" and "We're the Unforgiven" resemble brutally overcooked Nine Inch Nails off-cuts, but for the most part Splinter is a solid and intriguing effort from an artist comfortable with his position in life. [Aug-Sep 2013, p.92]

Title: Fade
Review: Fade finds YLT at their most wistfully contemplative; a thought only softened by the paradox that this might just be one of their best yet.

Title: Made Possible
Review: The band is tinkering here, and it says something that the album still feels traceable to no other source.

Title: A Moving Picture
Review: Devlin’s talents as both lyricist and rapper are never in doubt, but for all the album’s pomposity and scale, musically speaking, it feels like a big step backward.

Title: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped
Review: Organ Music Not Vibraphone Like I'd Hoped is about as ambitious as 35 minutes of music can get, and Krug gets an awful lot out of one instrument here.

Title: Gold
Review: Adams continues to grow as a songwriter.

Title: Bloodstreams
Review: It's chaotic, panic-inducing and downright delirious. [5 May 2012, p.53]

Title: Â¡Dos!
Review: Dos!, the aptly named second part of the trilogy, is relieved of the weight of expectation and, though it was recorded at the same time as the first, sounds less strained.

Title: Jackrabbit
Review: The performances are strident and lean, suggesting the players are every bit as invested in delivering the best reading of Ludwig-Leone's complex and often gorgeous songs as he was inspired in creating them.

Title: Lions
Review: The heart of Lions lies in the best ballads the band has ever waxed, such as the Led Zeppelin III-esque "Soul Singing" and the churning "Losing My Mind."

Title: Total Loss
Review: Total Loss is a beautiful album, all ambient longing and sadness and spectral pop, rising and falling without warning - no other artist gets more emotional effect out of leaving things not quite finished. But it still feels not quite finished.

Title: A Brief Inquiry Into Online Relationships
Review: Despite the often bleak themes at play on the album, there's also a refreshing hopefulness on many of the tracks that speaks to Healy's own recovery and willingness to say yes to even the most frothy pop trend. However, taken as a whole, the album is often as disparate and difficult to wade through as the social-media landscape it hopes to comment on.

Title: Fate
Review: Strict modernists may chafe at the band's unapologetically backward-glancing aesthetic, but the rest should happily succumb to the shaggy charm of Fate's easy-like-Sunday-morning ramblings.

Title: Hundred Waters
Review: By relying on their talent and confidence, the fivesome takes the listener to a futuristic setting, one where '60s British pastoral music fuses with electro in order to fill a hole in the musical landscape.

Title: Humanz
Review: A listener might be impressed by the scale of the experience, but ultimately there is something missing--intimacy?--missing. [Jun 2017, p.30]

Title: Here I Stand
Review: He sounds much more convincing on syrupy ballads like the Dre and Vidal-produced title track, which lyrically and musically sounds more passionate and more adult than Usher ever has.

Title: Drift
Review: Drift is a step up from Devil’s Music (2016), which attempted to recreate Leave Home’s career-making abrasion with little of its viscerality. On the other hand, with nearly every song on the album performed in a different style, Drift lacks the cohesion of The Men’s less acclaimed albums.

Title: Working Class Woman
Review: All filtered through Davidson's signature brand of deadpan humour, this is a hilarious, challenging dance floor record, and you're going to have to take it seriously.

Title: The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here
Review: With a running time of nearly 70 minutes for just 12 songs, The Devil Put Dinosaurs Here can be overwhelming; the arrangements of several songs are amorphous, and tunes such as “Phantom Limb” and “Hung On A Hook” could benefit from an editor. Despite these small quibbles, the album is solid.

Title: Trust
Review: Harsh but striking. [Dec 2013, p.92]

Title: Here and Nowhere Else
Review: It's brash, ballsy and, above all, fun.

Title: Music To Draw To: Satellite
Review: This record is not going to win over anyone who is already skeptical of ambient music, but for those of us who have always loved this kind of stuff, Music to Draw to: Satellite provides a beautiful respite from the noise of everyday life.

Title: Restriction
Review: Restriction certainly has its moments, but you have to wade through a lot of dross to find them. [Feb 2015, p.73]

Title: Big Bad Luv
Review: He beefs things and takes a full-band approach on Big Bad Luv, which contains almost as many hooks as it does Moreland’s hard-earned kernels of truth.

Title: Songs of Mass Destruction
Review: The music is dominated by the same pounding pop-disco beats and thick textures that have defined all her record. But now Lennox sounds like she's been rubbed raw by life. [Oct 2007, p.111]

Title: Dancing Backward in High Heels
Review: Under the lipstick and howling-Stones guitars, the Dolls always aspired to the rough-granite poise and battle lessons of great blues and soul.

Title: Dream River
Review: There’s plenty to chew on with his latest, Dream River. And that’s just the lyrics, whose weightiness is given more heft by his controlled baritone.

Title: Pocket Symphony
Review: Pocket Symphony winds up feeling strangely transient, accomplished and genuinely likeable but also forgettable.

Title: Perfect Darkness
Review: Perfect Darkness further reinforces his reputation as the closest there is to a latter-day John Martyn. [Jul 2011, p.102]

Title: The Wild Hunt
Review: While his latest may not be as triumphant as his debut LP, Shallow Grave, The Wild Hunt is a worthy effort indeed.

Title: Half Free
Review: Half Free is both a revelation and a breakthrough, one that finds Remy elevating her songwriting panache while carrying a certain mysticism that seems grounded in both plausibility and commonality.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: In striving for more self-less version of self, Pecknold and his excellent band have made an album that embraces modesty.

Title: Cruel Runnings
Review: Sure, Cruel Runnings is a bit of a one-trick pony--but, you have to admit, it's a pretty great trick.

Title: Skeletal Lamping
Review: Given that the record is so nominally personal and probing, it’s telling that there is not one moment of transcendence, or relief, or acceptance, or melody, or substance.

Title: Oui Oui Si Si Ja Ja Da Da
Review: All you need to notice about Oui Oui... is that, together, these musicians can still rustle up a synergy no other band can imitate. [Dec 2012, p.102]

Title: Charity Starts at Home
Review: This is sophisticated music for the adult soul.

Title: Finally Rich
Review: Rapping with his affectless slur and bricklayer's tempo over rolling, mid-speed beats, Keef (who was criticized for mocking a murder victim, his rival, on Twitter) seems unshakably confident but profoundly directionless.

Title: Becoming a Jackal
Review: [O'Brien's] portentous lyrics, falsetto-prone quaver, and Simon & Garfunkel tunefulness are essential to the album's appeal.

Title: The London Sessions
Review: While The London Sessions takes her in fresh new directions, Blige's own identity remains the dominant flavour. [Jan 2015, p.98]

Title: Metals
Review: The music, however, remains sophisticated and rhythmically feisty (pun thoroughly intended) even when so thoroughly keyed down.

Title: Anniemal
Review: Anniemal is pleasant enough to listen to; when I played it in my car while I was stuck in traffic, it helped take the edge off. It reminded me of music heard in malls, peppy and buoying, but not so compelling as to distract you from the clothes.

Title: Issues
Review: Issues' debut album is not only a more cohesive effort, but it's the immediate answer to naysayers who say claim the band will immediately fade away into irrelevancy.

Title: Together Through Life
Review: In a time where we could have fairly expected another state-of-the-world sermon, Dylan's thankfully stopped the overdone end-is-nigh bell-ringing that's characterised his late-period, allowing the ghosts of romances past and present to permeate Together Through Life.

Title: This Is Not The World
Review: The Futureheads have defeated the machine at its own game and made a record that’s every bit as vibrant and vital as their 2004 debut.

Title: Margerine Eclipse
Review: Margerine Eclipse is a decided improvement upon their last three albums, discarding the dense and difficult song structures that plagued those albums.

Title: Spiderwebbed
Review: Those looking to capture a mood, to dive in to something soothing for just over half an hour, would be well advised to kick back and let the music wash over them

Title: I Am a Bird Now
Review: These bluesy spirituals are so raw they bleed. [Mar 2005, p.136]

Title: The Sophtware Slump
Review: Grandaddy sound like a lo-fi ELO and, in frontman Jason Lytle, possess an admirably unusual songwriter. Sophtware Slump is more coherent than their 1997 debut Under The Western Freeway, Lytle having settled on a theme: knackered electronics.... Cheap, cheerful and utterly charming.

Title: Release Therapy
Review: It's understandable that Ludacris wanted to show off different parts of himself, but in doing so he didn't have to forget about what fans already knew.

Title: Christ Illusion
Review: The good news is that this is the band’s strongest music since Seasons in the Abyss. The bad news is that, compared to their vaulted ’80s output, the album lacks intensity.

Title: Shake the Spirit
Review: Its sonic audacity is so bracing, it's relatively easy to forgive the lyrical stumbles, which crystallize on the dirty puns of "It Girl," but that's nearly beside the point because, unlike Love Stuff, Shake the Spirit never seems indebted to Elle King's idols. Instead, it embodies her own bold, bawdy heart.

Title: I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning
Review: Where Ryan Adams replicates old records, this is something new. [Album of the Month, Feb 2005, p.72]

Title: America's Sweetheart
Review: Love has nothing new to say and no better way to say it.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: Animal Joy falters where it mistakes crude simplicity for reinvention.

Title: moon
Review: Moon's classic-sounding melodies and instrumentation have a timeless if deceptively simple beauty that's different in all the right ways from Raymonde's former band, and that's exactly what makes Snowbird such a worthy successor.

Title: African Giant
Review: He empowers all to be ‘African Giants’ on an all-over entertaining album, demonstrating that he’s one for his people.

Title: No Said Date
Review: An impressive album in the best tradition of the Clan... Had this album come out in 1998, people might have hailed it as another Wu classic.

Title: Truth Is a Beautiful Thing
Review: If there's any downside, it's that their sophomore album doesn't do anything to distinguish itself from its predecessor. But you know what? When you write songs that are just as strong as your past work, evolution is less of a necessity. If it's not broken, don't fix it.

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: The dramatic arc of these songs is built around the way instruments lurch into place and dance drunkenly around one another before staggering off once again.

Title: The Mountain Moves
Review: You don't need an encyclopaedic knowledge of LA-based folk-rock to enjoy the rough-hewn vocals and gnarled, grainy guitar play of these London-based chums-of-Mumford. [Jun 2013, p.107]

Title: Tongues
Review: Despite its misfires, Tongues does make for an intriguing listen, and the record is punctuated with the occasional highlight.

Title: Cocoa Sugar
Review: None of these influences are worn on Young Fathers' sleeves and Cocoa Sugar is further proof that when the band puts something out that you can prepare for a unique, engaging listen.

Title: Girls In Peacetime Want To Dance
Review: Atlanta-based producer Ben H Allen (who has worked with Animal Collective and CeeLo Green) has beefed up their sound, although a taste for clean sonic lines and cheesy keyboards retains a power to grate.

Title: Meir
Review: Nobody could question the fact that these guys mean it with every fibre of their being, and Meir is music to make Norway proud; a new majestic fanfare to welcome hog-riding warriors into Valhalla.

Title: IV Play
Review: IV Play finds Dream delving into more sounds and styles than ever before.

Title: Nothing
Review: Despite its conceptualist sonics and firmly placid surface, Nothing still winds up as Kode9’s most unsettling and miserablist release to date, as well as his most emotionally resonant and straightforward.

Title: Boy in da Corner
Review: If Boy In Da Corner marks the beginning of distinctly British hip-hop, the genre's standards are already impressively high.

Title: Dept. of Disappearance
Review: Lytle's melodic warmth provides a protective layer against the heartbreak and horror. [Nov 2012, p.101]

Title: Desert Dove
Review: Michaela Anne has been on a steady rise since her 2014 debut Ease My Mind. Desert Dove will certainly steepen this trajectory. She is deservedly a major emerging voice in country and Americana circles.

Title: Rapprocher
Review: Especially in today's digital context, the album feels torn between big-P pop a la La Roux or happy-mode Goldfrapp (or, at least, Annie circa 2004) and the darker, broodier likes of Ladytron.[#81, p. 55]

Title: Love Is Not Pop
Review: El Perro's brand of pop is certainly easy to love, and a cozy sort of organic warmth--characterized by thick, resonant drums and keys, and treated guitars that seem to lurch and lumber with the slightly irregular rhythms of real life--pervades the new record.

Title: It's Real
Review: On It's Real, Ex Hex have taken a more nuanced approach to their songwriting. Songs are given a little more space to breathe with hooks taking a little longer to bed in. On the whole, the added polish provides a little more rock 'n' roll oxygen, but at times the songs could do with a little more spit.

Title: Supermodel
Review: The band’s songs are as dense to listen to as they are to contemplate.

Title: The Bravery
Review: We're reaching critical mass for new wave nostalgia, but we might have made room for your debut if there was something we could dance to. [#10, p.109]

Title: Yours to Keep
Review: The best record the Strokes should have released after "Is This It."

Title: Write In
Review: They write songs that make you feel good, and sound good, whenever they come on, and they do it in such a way that you truly feel like you’re listening to them for the first time.

Title: Mungodelics
Review: [Their indulgences] can be tiresome--"People On Strong Stuff" plods without purpose--but equally provides passages of uncontained elation. [Nov 2012, p.79]

Title: Milkteeth
Review: Dare may share some vocal similarities with Jeff Buckley and James Blake, but the overall effect is utterly distinctive. [Apr 2020, p.106]

Title: Careless World: Rise of the Last King
Review: Even though he remains a cipher, his surroundings are lush.

Title: Big Boat
Review: On Big Boat, their rambling new album, veteran producer Bob Ezrin (Pink Floyd, Alice Cooper, Lou Reed) does his best to emphasize the band's considerable knack for genre-bending exercises.

Title: Every Kind of Light
Review: While the lack of further experimentation in the songwriting becomes tiresome after a while, overall the band seems comfortable and happy to be playing together again.

Title: Altid Sammen
Review: Whereas the band's grand ambitions have sometimes led to music that can feel unduly grandiose, "Uden Ansigt" and "Verden Forsvinder" mark a welcome return to the more intimately scaled music of their early years. [Nov 2019, p.25]

Title: Please Be Mine
Review: "Fool" embodies this power structure as she manages to forge together all ranges of her nostalgic vocalizations and eclipse them outright with a full-on frontwoman wail. Feats such as that can only be pulled off with pedigree and talent, both of which Molly Burch debuts in spades on Please Be Mine.

Title: Golden
Review: As a pop product, the album performs its function--and it’s commendable of Minogue to experiment with a different sound. It’s just a shame to hear a pop queen like Kylie seeming to buy into tacky generic artifice because it happens to be in vogue.

Title: Obey
Review: The missteps are few enough they do little to tarnish what the band set out to accomplish, and the stronger songs here prove Exploded View is becoming more thrilling, ambitious and confident with each release.

Title: Puberty 2
Review: The songs sway with gravitas and hit home whether you’re wrestling with innate and confounding dependence (‘Crack Baby’) or trying to pilot your own mental health (‘Happy’), Mitski feels dedicated to those who, for once, just want to set their own pace.

Title: The Gloaming
Review: Not for the casual listener, but enormously rewarding if you hanker for some NY loft space in your croft house. [Feb 2014, p.115]

Title: Fast Food
Review: This terrific second album from the ex-jazz singer Shah carries with it a clear air of assurance. [May 2015, p.81]

Title: A New Nature
Review: The end result is a little too loose, maybe, missing the urgency of their previous effort. [Sep/Oct 2014, p.74]

Title: Seen It All: The Autobiography
Review: It’s by no means a bad record, but won’t be the trap pioneer’s most memorable either.

Title: World Eater
Review: It’s an engaging listen and a jarring template that perfectly captures a disquietened and uneasy era.

Title: Look To The Sky
Review: While retaining the melodic approach of his debut, the singer-guitarist has shaped some additional, more diverse sounds. [Dec 2012, p.88]

Title: Temporal
Review: With Temporal, Julia Kent continues to craft cerebral yet accessible epics, encompassing a vast spectrum of emotions using a limited set of tools.

Title: SVIIB
Review: A moving synth-pop paean to the pair’s powerful relationship and a fitting finale to their School of Seven Bells project.

Title: Padded Room
Review: The Joe Budden on Padded Room, however, is focused and hungry, spinning dense, psychological yarns that build for dozens and dozens of bars. Budden scratched and clawed for his second chance, and he hasn’t squandered it.

Title: Another Country
Review: Stewart still has the voice and, on the gravelly rocker Please and the Steve Harley/Jim Cregan co-write A Friend For Life, the songs. But the rest is best avoided. [Dec 2015, p.86]

Title: Release
Review: This is a long soft sigh of an album, suggesting not a sudden relief of pressure but just a pleasant exclamation of contentment.

Title: Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots
Review: Even by their standards, Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots is astonishing.... Plainly, this is music abnormally alive with possibilities.  [Album of the Month, Aug 2002, p.96]

Title: Albala
Review: For anyone who has enjoyed the great guitar music coming out of Mali in recent years Albala is essential listening.

Title: Drums and Guns
Review: Dependable? Yes. Beautiful? Definitely, yes. [Apr 2007, p.107]

Title: English Electric
Review: English Electric acts as a rejoinder to those who think that synth-pop is best left to the young.

Title: When I Have Fears
Review: The Murder Capital offer authenticity, honesty and truth aplenty, it has already become difficult, if not impossible, to imagine a vibrant music scene without them and there is a sense that this album is only the beginning of their compulsive journey.

Title: The Information
Review: Overall, this collision of dirty loops and polished pop is Information you need. [Dec 2006, p.198]

Title: Everything to Everyone
Review: Their rhythms jump all over the place and their vocals are so determined to land that punchline that it all ends up sounding like one smarmy mess.

Title: In a World Like This
Review: They seem stuck returning to the same predictable song structures and turgid melodies that made them famous in the first place.

Title: Quality Street Music
Review: The man behind the Gangsta Grillz mixtapes and the man literally behind T.I. and his Grand Hustle crew continues to do the improbable on his 2012 release Quality Street Music.

Title: The Third Hand
Review: When it is instrumental, it’s “Get It,” which seems a timid remake of Since We Last Spoke’s title track, or it’s “Murs Beat,” which, tellingly, has no Murs. Some of the rest sounds like a softer, more overproduced, and generally shittier version of the Cars. The rest of the rest sounds like something duller than that.

Title: Ellipse
Review: Her voice, by turns flighty and forlorn, has an honest personality often missing in pop. [Summer 2009, p.98]

Title: Trouble in Shangri-La
Review: Offering her strongest material since her 1982 landmark, Bella Donna, Nicks is radiant as she vamps through guitar-charged rockers that deftly balance her signature poetry with sticky pop hooks.

Title: Bring It Back
Review: Plucky, precious and sometimes cloying.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: Source Tags & Codes
Review: Their finest record to date and the most blistering, blissful album to be released by anyone in years.

Title: Aromanticism
Review: Bereft of any shine or polish, Aromanticism is a piercing debut collection of songs of remarkable intensity.
A messier, more elf-indulgent affair than its predecessor. [24 Mar 2006, p.68]

Title: Close To The Glass
Review: Close To The Glass is full of charming, understated yearning. [Apr 2014, p.94]

Title: OCD Go Go Go Girls
Review: Their first proper LP reflects its jittery title; it's brimful with melody, scuffed guitars and singer Shaun Hencher's scuzzy vocals.

Title: Marci Beaucoup

Review: While it might lack a rave-up pop number like Everybody Works’s infectious “1 Billion Dogs,” Anak Ko offers plenty of reasons to follow Duterte down whatever road may lay ahead.

Title: Natalie Prass
Review: While the tracks rarely challenge the listener with bold experimentation or chord progressions that range much beyond major-and-minor resolves, Natalie Prass provides a concise amalgamation of R&B, funk, baroque pop, and soul with a consistent through-line.

Title: Warpaint
Review: Expansive and enveloping at the same time, this set of songs puts Warpaint's past and future in perfect balance--one of the best things a band can do on their second album.

Title: W
Review: Less pretension, more tickling the perimeter of pop perfection next time please, Planningtorock--you can skip the beer belly though.

Title: Anthem
Review: The usual blend of knockabout punk rock, nutty-boy ska and witty lyrics. [Jul 2003, p.108]

Title: G I R L
Review: G I R L may have benefited from a few more introspective trips back to the drawing board.

Title: Brick Body Kids Still Daydream
Review: His new one, easily his headiest, is a concept LP built around Chicago's Robert Taylor Homes, a famously mismanaged housing project destroyed 10 years ago.

Title: Such Pretty Forks in the Road
Review: By Morissette’s standards, Pretty Forks is a vulnerable, sedate, ballad-heavy album. Most of those ballads are unobtrusive, with songwriting-template piano and strings plush and regular as amphitheater seats.

Title: The Ecleftic: 2 Sides II a Book
Review: Loaded with pop culture commentary and often directly naming social names, The Ecleftic is sure to stir up some emotions from not only the famous, but from the general public as well.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: X: The Godless Void and Other Stories
Review: Their 10th album sounds as though they had been sitting on it since [1994]. [Jan 2020, p.84]

Title: The Bride
Review: She’s flipped the script on us, and in doing so has created her most cohesive work--and maybe even her happiest ending yet.

Title: The Morning Star
Review: The folk comes juxtaposed with industrial creaks and eastern drones, the virtuosity tempered with scrabbling wildness. [Sep 2018, p.96]

Title: Crosseyed Heart
Review: The relatively low ratio of octane riffage means many of these songs hinge on Richards's worn, oaky voice. His low, craggly growl suits the rock songs well, and he manages perhaps the tenderest vocal performance of his career on the reggae-infused “Love Overdue.”

Title: Closer To Grey
Review: This is world weary pop, but it’s completely uncynical. Reserved and melodramatic at the same time, it doesn’t worry about the incongruities, satisfied to be both wilted and very alive.

Title: Union
Review: Guitars jangle and fuzz to no clear purpose, the rest of the instrumentation plods behind, and singer Wayne Petti fails to convince. [Dec 2012, p.103]. [Dec 2012, p.103]

Title: Fast-Moving Clouds
Review: Fast Moving Clouds is superb smart pop for a lazy afternoon; it's also an impressive first salvo from Sarah Bethe Nelson, who as both a vocalist and a songwriter confirms she's an artist to watch.

Title: The Still Life
Review: Laurent-Marke's facility for pleasant minor-key ruminations remain her strong suit, but the "stillness" of which she speaks all too often sounds like a stifling lack of urgency. [May 2013, p.85]

Title: Back to Land
Review: Wooden Shjips' approach with Back To Land is akin to seduction rather than press-ganging. Smooth and lustrous throughout, this collection should see Wooden Shjips emerge from their subterranean lair to reach a deservedly wider audience.

Title: Taking One For The Team
Review: It’s hard to fault them for sticking to that template since it was what helped turn the band into superstars around the world. But as Simple Plan moves outside of their musical comfort zone, it would be great to hear them mess with the formula a little more.

Title: Never
Review: It's a lot to take in, sure, but each listen is as fresh as the first.

Title: Will the Guns Come Out
Review: Songs are taut and brief, the guitar/drum arrangements stripped to absolute basics and El Khatib squawks his lines as if his switchblade is giving him grief.

Title: Color
Review: The results can veer wildly from the alluring to the downright alarming. Yet Gately's ear for melody holds it all together. [Dec 2016, p.106]

Title: Vulnicura
Review: Bjork’s Vulnicura represents a return of sorts to standard song form after the experimental Biophilia, its nine long tracks evoking the emotional confusion following a break-up.... But throughout, Bjork’s own vocals are the stumbling-block.

Title: Waiting for the Sirens' Call
Review: A fine distillation of everything New Order have been. [May 2005, p.176]

Title: Roots & Crowns
Review: Instead of wandering into opaque experimentation, as they’ve been known to do in the past, they corral those unruly elements into a series of hummable, memorable tunes.

Title: Bahamas is Afie
Review: Bahamas Is Afie is a triumph in soulful, roots music, and instead of just trying to sound old-timey, the record is full of personality.

Title: Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager
Review: With Man on the Moon II: The Legend of Mr. Rager, it seems he's on the road to finding what works, with varying degrees of success.

Title: Gravity the Seducer
Review: Hard-driving Helen Marnie-sung tune Melting Ice, meanwhile, is surely Ladytron's steely attempt at self-aware irony.

Title: Rehearsing My Choir
Review: On Rehearsing My Choir, the Furnaces are just defiant because they can be, indulging every impulse but neglecting to make any of them even remotely compelling. [#70, p.96]

Title: Keep It Hid
Review: Black Keys singer-guitarist Dan Auerbach opens his first solo outing with an acoustic country blues that sounds utterly authentic but signifies mainly as a museum-quality reproduction. Fortunately, the rest of Keep It Hid hews more closely to the Keys’ scuzz-encrusted, blunt-instrument assault.

Title: Go Away White
Review: The proceedings sound loose, yet focused but never disappointing. [Apr 2008, p.160]

Title: For All My Sisters
Review: The major fault one might find with For All My Sisters lies in the fact that with so little let up, there’s little to distinguish one song from another.

Title: Kaleidoscope
Review: Titled after a soothing interlude from the band's 2015 LP, A Head Full of Dreams, this five-song EP continues that album's mood of tranquil satisfaction.

Title: Super Extra Gravity
Review: Super Extra Gravity is too deft to be too dark, though-- there's joy in its catharsis.

Title: Clear Shot
Review: Fortunately, for every formless track, there are two more like the brilliantly buoyant "Dream Orchestrator," a glimpse of 21st century psych-pop at its finest. Moments like this make Clear Shot TOY's most ambitious and rewarding album yet.

Title: Taiga
Review: The language barrier and discord makes the record incomprehensible, but nearly everything is still as intoxicating and entertaining as hell.

Title: Froot
Review: It's the explosion in Diamandis's songwriting that's most noticeable here. [May 2015, p.107]

Title: Short Movie
Review: The new developments in sound and style of Marling's fifth album--and the way her leading-lady status continues to evolve--leave it as her most captivating yet. Just watch the movie and don't worry too much about the run time.

Title: Numbers
Review: Numbers proves that MellowHype are capable of making a good album without employing the over-the-top antics or shock themes they initially used to capture attention.

Title: Easter Is Cancelled
Review: Easter Is Cancelled may not be high art, but it doesn't need to be. It is that rare delight: a return to form following a lengthy period of artistic stagnation.

Title: Careful
Review: While the palette of sounds Boy Harsher plays with on Careful can seem limited--brisk drum machine loops, oscillating synths, and Matthews’ haunting incantations--the group finds ways to make each song sound distinct.

Title: Spiritual Songs for Lovers to Sing
Review: Hoorn’s sultry vocals; swirling, gossamer textures; and grand orchestral arrangements tirelessly interact with the record’s musculature to develop and bring to life the exquisite and anthemic anatomy of Spiritual Songs For Lovers To Sing.

Title: Can't Be Tamed
Review: At times Can't Be Tamed feels perfunctory, getting the job of showing Cyrus is growing up without making her too mature for her still-young fan base and little else.

Title: Adore Life
Review: Harsh, aggressive, hungry, and urgent, Adore Life is everything a Savages album should be. Unexpectedly - and this proves its greatest success.

Title: In Reverie
Review: Chris Conley's metaphorical lyrics remain earnest enough, but because of studio trickery, his vocals sound annoyingly nasal. [Oct 2003, p.120]

Title: Electric Cables
Review: Love gets to indulge his sweet tooth over a whole record. That freedom turns out to be part blessing and part curse, his delicate-as-a-feather jangle and wispy vocals eventually wearing just a little thin.

Title: Plumb
Review: One minute it's like listening to early Genesis, the next Smile-era Beach Boys, the next XTC and the next, um, 1980s Genesis.

Title: Chastity Belt
Review: Chastity Belt is proof positive that bands don’t need to simply spin the wheels when they’re going through periods of transition, waiting for the solid ground to return beneath their feet before they get going again.

Title: Weird Drift
Review: This is a dreamier affair, lighter than air music that floats along like a wispy breeze; unfortunately, last year’s effort seems to have set a standard which has clearly proven difficult to recreate.

Title: Go To School
Review: Go to School is an artistic statement on a grand scale, and it cements their reputation as world-class songwriters. It’s a once-in-a-generation epic.

Title: Coverage
Review: Moore's voice has grown stronger, she updates the covers with some youthful enthusiasm, and, well, these songs are hard to screw up.

Title: Return the Gift
Review: Time has not dulled the group's scarily tight musicianship. [15 Oct 2005]

Title: Government Plates
Review: The focus is less on total mayhem and more on creating droning dystopian soundscapes that MC Ride might occasionally hop on to yell over.

Title: The Fact Facer
Review: The Fact Facer is a nuanced, multi-leveled listen that stands with the best things Amos--and anyone covering similarly adventurous terrain--has done.

Title: Citrus
Review: That shiver of foreignness adds interest to what is essentially a frothy pop sound, as does the occasionally mesmerizing distortion.

Title: God Help The Girl
Review: God Help the Girl should probably just be viewed as a flawed work or a semi-successful adventure by a solo artist who needs his band to be truly great.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: It's the sound of a man confronting his own inevitable end with humour and dignity. Let's hope he doesn't move on any time soon. As band OF Joy proves, this particular wellspring is far from dry. [Oct 2010, p.82]

Title: Body of Song
Review: Body of Song is patchwork and spotty, dappled with a handful of sparkling additions to Mould’s estimable catalog.

Title: The Brink
Review: The Jezabels are a talented collective, but I find their latest set half as compelling as it could have been. The Brink remains grounded when it should soar.

Title: Are We There
Review: Are We There cuts deep into the skin of its creator and finds Van Etten more exposed than ever.

Title: The Truth Is Here
Review: No one aspect of Ali's personality really dominates. The Truth Is Here is all the stronger for it, and that can only be considered a good sign.

Title: Lese Majesty
Review: While there are songs of undeniable artistic invention (“Dawn in Lexor,” “#CAKE”) there are also moments of ostentatious indulgence, intellectual handstands that feel like ends in themselves. But then, that’s always a hazard with a band this original and audacious.

Title: Our Endless Numbered Days
Review: Beautifully recorded, this is intimate seduction for voice, elegant finger-picked guitar and not much else. [May 2004, p.93]

Title: Depth of Field
Review: Clever and very subtle grown-up electronic pop that beats with a broken heart. [Mar 2018, p.93]

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: It’s an honest delivery, but they are essentially preaching to the choir.

Title: Body Music
Review: Body Music shows R&B continuing to expand its scope, stealing the cues of hip-hop and electronic music, which draw strength from their omnivorous appetites.

Title: My Everything
Review: For her second album, My Everything, Grande has picked a set of songs so lyrically bland, sonically inoffensive, and artistically empty that they produce a zero-impact experience--musical vanilla fro-yo poured directly into your ears. It's by no means painful; there are even moments of fun.

Title: Tulsa For One Second
Review: It’s elegantly expressive music where warm tones from cold machines cut to the quick of human emotion.

Title: Hard Love
Review: Written by a person whose conscience seems to keep him from having too much fun, Hard Love is a conflicted yet summarily good record that breathes new life into good ol' rock'n'roll.

Title: Lookout Low
Review: OHMME add depth to the harmonies on seven of the 10 songs and the overall sense is of five people as excited by playing together as they were at their first rehearsal nine years ago. [Oct 2019, p.114]

Title: Libertad
Review: With filth, loose morals, anger, frustration, big guitars and even bigger choruses at every turn, it's got all the DNA of a pure-bred rock classic.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: The Campfire Headphase is enough of a genre bender to finally introduce this music to a well-deserved new audience. [Dec 2005, p.94]

Title: Spiral Shadow
Review: Spiral Shadow assimilates both paradigms as if Jane's Addiction and Kyuss shared leathers.

Title: Face Control
Review: It is a step forward for an artist with a wealth of potential and a tremendously moving voice. Should he cease his overzealous grab for stylistic and thematic conventions--or perhaps if he simply learns to cover more ground--there’s a good chance Handsome Furs will reach a level of maturity and sophistication at which their current offering merely hints.

Title: Dark Red
Review: Where Bad Vibes had a dynamic range of feeling, Dark Red is melodramatic to the point of being alienating.

Title: Inner Journey Out
Review: It’s a psychedelic North American road trip, coloured in by touring member Brent Cordero’s Farfisa and Wurlitzer, adding a fleeting but panoramic sense of wide blue yonder here, and a taste of honey there, to these otherwise introverted and haunting tunes.

Title: Until Spring
Review: Limp and uninspiring, this is a disappointing effort considering the potential the band initially showed back in 2009.

Title: Impersonator
Review: It’s refreshing and still, a fine listen; Impersonator is in the end, its own refined identity.

Title: Heligoland
Review: It still warms the blood to hear those trip-hop synths roll on the slow-burning "Flat of the Blade" (with some acid loops thrown in for good measure), but Massive Attack's arsenal has expanded and the resulting onslaught is nothing short of brilliant.

Title: Reflektor
Review: There is so, so much content, so beautifully and flawlessly presented that it can be baffling at times. The Suburbs, to many, was decade-defining music. Reflektor, I feel, through both content and design, will be artist-defining.

Title: All Night Long
Review: A right dirty dose of LA rocking is in order courtesy of Buckcherry, and boy, is it great to have them back!

Title: Wild Flag
Review: They're not reinventing the wheel, hell they're barely even reinventing themselves, but that's a good thing on this occasion, as they've created an album that will appeal to fans both new and old.

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: Seventh Tree is bound to ruffle a few electro-feathered fans, but there’s no denying it’s a venture that sets the pair into new experimental territory.

Title: Are You Gonna Eat That?
Review: Just as the two's previous solo projects, the music will probably not sit well with most hip-hop heads, but it's the perfect LP for each of their respective fan base.

Title: Teens of Style
Review: It's one young man's proper opening salvo cast as an entire genre's dying breaths. But for a last gasp, it sure sounds vital.

Title: At Weddings
Review: At Weddings shows Tomberlin tapping into a tentative inner strength, creating a soothing record that ends up resisting its self-doubts and reaches out its hand.

Title: In This Light & On This Evening
Review: Not even superproducer Flood (U2, Depeche Mode) can save the postpunk singer from misery. Or from overacting.

Title: Tears on Tape
Review: Suffice it to say, Tears on Tape is a sentimentally sweet, sonically stunning, and beautifully packaged album.

Title: Party Music
Review: Imperfect, definitely. But only because perfection is on the table.

Title: What a Time to Be Alive
Review: Another great Superchunk record. What a Time to Be Alive bristles with anxious energy; even by Superchunk’s over-caffeinated standards, it keeps an unrelenting pace.

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: Wondrous Bughouse is a delicious collage: provocative, allusive and consistently engaging.

Title: Salutations
Review: Though Salutations is one of Oberst’s most demanding albums, it’s also one of his least ambitious, even before taking these new arrangements into account.

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: The songs are filled with jokes - but the punch lines often turn into epiphanies.

Title: Baptism
Review: Somewhere along the line in his career, he fully absorbed his pantheon of Sixties and Seventies influences and began to sound like no one but himself. The confidence that results from that growth -- along with the knowledge that comes from having made records for fifteen years -- is apparent throughout this album.

Title: Sale El Sol
Review: Sale el Sol never once sounds disparate or overworked -- it's sunny and easy, its natural buoyancy disguising Shakira's range and skill -- but listen closely and it becomes apparent that nobody makes better pop records in the new millennium than she does.

Title: Heroes to Zeros
Review: A raging success. [#7, p.72]

Title: Dark Sky Paradise
Review: Dark Sky Paradise is a big leap in the direction of the ideal Big Sean full-length.

Title: Down to My Last Bad Habit
Review: It’s a pleasure to report that country music’s ultimate good guy has once again crafted an excellent collection of new music with his 18th album.

Title: Run the Jewels 2
Review: Headphone rap of the highest order, tracks on this sequel hum and groove, laced with texture and hidden sonic accents.

Title: Cut With the Cake Knife
Review: While its ingredients are undeniably basic--all of the songs are built from a few period-appropriate keyboards and chugging drum machines, and that’s mostly it--what makes Cake Knife so consistently endearing is how effortless it all sounds.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: Gone are any remnants of yesteryear's "rock music" ideology, thrusting Radiohead into a mature state of potentially their best work still to come.

Title: Swoon
Review: Swoon improves on the Pickups' 2006 debut, Carnavas, with less slavish writing and more articulated dynamics.

Title: Kathryn Calder
Review: Her own albums--this is the third and most transparent--reveal grander structures and a singular perspective, as she sings with tuneful equanimity about deep, unresolved, enigmatic struggles.

Title: Burner
Review: Damn odd. [Jul 2005, p.186]

Title: Sing Along To Songs You Don't Know
Review: The songs are generally slow, samey, and sleep-inducing, and the lyrics, any language differences notwithstanding, are hard to take seriously, even for a guy who raved about I'm From Barcelona.

Title: Out of the Black
Review: Out of the Black works either on the dancefloor or at the workstation, offering beat nuts from the Front 242 generation to the Deadmau5 kids their deep, dark, and delicious fix.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: On Shootenanny!, they take a solid first step toward crafting their opus a la Yankee Hotel Foxtrot or Soft Bulletin. [#6, p.81]

Title: The Route to the Harmonium
Review: This is music to get lost in, for headphones, and for your head. Yorkston’s talents as a writer drive these songs (he has also released a memoir and a novel in recent years). Phrases leap out, some delicate, some devastating.

Title: Big Fish Theory
Review: This lean, tightly structured follow-up ramps up the intensity. Built around raw, electronic productions, it also showcases his ability to rhyme with devastating candour over wildly varying beats. [Aug 2017, p.111]

Title: Wild Winter
Review: If you want a Christmas album from Smoke Fairies, then you're the target market for Wild Winter, though the previous caveat still applies--you're sure to enjoy it, but the guests at your Christmas party might be puzzled.

Title: For Use and Delight
Review: If your promised land is full of warm harmonies, rich guitar, and well-crafted songs of cosmic country rock then you’ve died and gone to heaven.

Title: Bliss Release
Review: Bliss Release is perhaps a little too derivative to justify the classic status it's been afforded in the band's homeland, but it's still a delightfully charming debut, made even more impressive by their hastily assembled beginnings.

Title: Club Nites
Review: This effort lacks the element of surprise that enlivened their previous album and the songs aren't all quite at the same level, but for sheer smart-punk action, Dumb are clearly still something special. Club Nites suggests they have plenty more albums worth hearing left in them, and this album deserves a spin on your listening device of choice.

Title: Electric Arguments
Review: A few late-album glow-stick groovers abruptly shift the vibe to rave-era bliss, but until then, turn off your mind and float downstream.

Title: Ancient Future
Review: It's this constant dynamic of push-pull throughout that makes Ancient Future a compelling listen.

Title: Gamel
Review: On the whole, though, Yoshimio and OOIOO honor that infinite and elusive history on Gamel without ever losing their own present.

Title: Konk
Review: Konk is the perfect example of the modern indie record: bright, breezy, demanding no great investment from its listeners but enjoyable to jump around to. [May 2008, p.128]

Title: Island Intervals
Review: Islands Intervals basks in a stately, other-worldly beauty akin to Sigur Ros and Icelandic folk artist Asgeir. [Mar 2014, p.112]

Title: Lover
Review: Lover is a fabulous record, full of super-fun standout pop hits that make your heart burst. It oozes with Swift’s much more palatable upbeat sass. She’s in love and also thinking about different kinds of love.

Title: The Wild
Review: While more uptempo than his fans may have been comfortable with in the past, the project has a noticeable sense of growth and maturity about it. Coupled with incredible production, The Wild reaffirms why Raekwon's been so revered all these years.

Title: Rotations
Review: The chamber ensemble expanded the possibilities for them immensely, but it’s unnecessarily timid at times. Overall, though, Rotations is a successful venture from a duo who have carved a niche but refuse to just whittle mindlessly.

Title: How to Get To Heaven From Scotland
Review: It’s clear this ‘Falkirk miserablist’ has finally found contentment.

Title: Ghostory
Review: Most of the songs are littered with cosmic debris, but fortunately it's all relegated to the background so as not to interfere with the percolating pace.

Title: Creation
Review: Ultimately, with Creation, the Pierces have delivered a lovingly crafted album that showcases their creative growth.

Title: The Far Field
Review: This is pop music designed to give you all the feels, and even with a disruptive pseudo-reggae track thrown into the mix ("Candles"), Future Islands prove that they can do it better than anyone else right now.

Title: Morningwood
Review: Their gutsy spirit, while not "soul" exactly, does allow the band to dodge flippant dismissals of poseurhood. [Jan 2005, p.90]

Title: Jennifer Hudson
Review: She has a magnificent voice that deserves a lot better than this formulaic pop and soul.

Title: Life on Other Planets
Review: Most of these concise, super-catchy tunes are as unself-consciously traditional, and fun, as an undiscovered cache of British Invasion rock. [#14, p.143]

Title: Tomorrow Morning
Review: Overall, Tomorrow Morning is a good, but far from great, record.

Title: Expansion Team
Review: Dilated Peoples continue to hold down hip-hop's middle ground with inoffensive mic purism and sophisticated production a la mid-'90s DJ Premier. [Dec 2001, p.158]

Title: Dear
Review: Dear could have been the end of the trip. But a quarter of a century in, Boris remain alert at the controls as they pilot their craft into uncharted galaxies, boldly going where no group has gone before.

Title: Ripe 4 Luv
Review: There are few traces of the musician Cooke has presented himself as previously, but if this is how he wants to strike out on his own, the comparisons to his other bands should be incredibly short lived.

Title: Antisocialites
Review: Alvvays were the perfect band to listen to when a need arose to forget about life. Despite its title, Antisocialites doesn’t manage to accomplish the same thing.

Title: Broken
Review: Broken is more diverse than "It's Not How Far," however, is its refusal to be hemmed in. [Fall 2009, p.67]

Title: The Seer
Review: Anchored by three tracks stretching past 19 minutes with only momentary lapses of Western conventionality, The Seer stands as an immense and jarring homage to unpredictability.

Title: Reeling Skullways
Review: Bass Clef may have created a solid album, but, in the end, this lovely exercise leaves a sense that it was all a bit too easy for him.

Title: Tears in the Club
Review: Kingdom's debut album is all pop. Not in the formulaic sense, but in its sophisticated amalgam of everything that is skilled and aesthetic from both mainstream club production and underground dance subgenre. [Mar 2017, p.49]

Title: Live it Out
Review: Obviously nobody would pay attention to her smart lyrics if the music didn't compete, but, largely, it does.

Title: Hypermagic Mountain
Review: There are no breathers in Hypermagic Mountain. There are only a series of knuckle sandwiches in the form of throbbing, distorting, gesticulating low-end ear bleeders.

Title: The Bachelor
Review: While The Bachelor is not a bad listen, it takes a little more energy to understand than seems fair for what it delivers.

Title: Daughter
Review: Throughout, she pulls no punches, her razor-sharp lyrics demonstrating a singular wit and vulnerability. [Dec 2020, p.35]

Title: Crazy Ex-Girlfriend
Review: Backed by ragged, loud guitar work and production that is full but not slick, Ms. Lambert sounds like a brash rabble-rouser, an emotionally insightful spark plug. [29 Apr 2007]

Title: The W
Review: There's a quality of randomness on The W that prevents it from cohering as an album. But even if it's just a collection of songs, The W is undeniably impressive, packing the kind of gritty, aggressive anthems that have been notably missing from most of the recent Wu solo albums. [#82, p. 148]

Title: BlakRoc
Review: Mixing nasty guitar leads with cavernous beats, the Black Keys have crafted a dark, sprawling opus that's convincing in its commitment to a unique sound.

Title: Impeach My Bush
Review: There's more meat on this album's bone than on the laughable Fatherfucker. [#21, p.99]

Title: Hard Working Americans
Review: Though most effective as a droll raconteur, Snider here relies on covers of songs by the likes of Gillian Welch and Lucinda Williams; fortunately, guitar wizard Neal Casal is on top form.

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: Linkin Park's ambitions are nearly palpable, but songs likely conceived as homages end up sounding too close to their sources. [26 May 2007]

Title: Transit Transit
Review: Transit Transit maintains a puzzling lack of urgency for an album so long in the works.

Title: Come Down With Me
Review: They’re still doing it better than anyone else; ravier than Foals, more fun than Fuck Buttons, flexing more post-hardcore muscle than Metronomy. It’s just that we kind of hoped they might surprise us again. That said, if they’re not pushing any new envelopes, Come Down With Me is still satisfying on its own terms.

Title: The Church of Rock and Roll
Review: This could be the record that provides that breakthrough [to mainstream].

Title: Fine Line
Review: Fine Line is a compelling document of an artist coming to life.

Title: Knoxville
Review: Maybe it shouldn't be altogether surprising that Knoxville is brimming over with bravura displays of improvisational nous. Similarly, it would be hard to find a finer study of the suppression of the ego; each musician's signature sound serving to continually complement, but never saturate, the artistry of the others.

Title: Belomancie
Review: It's an album that holds plenty of rewards for those willing to take the time to explore its odd twists and turns with an open mind.

Title: Painting With
Review: Animal Collective still lay down a challenge. It's the sound of a band refreshed.

Title: Take the Kids Off Broadway
Review: It's got that first-take impulsiveness to it, full of tics and eccentricities, and that lack of pretention lets us see Foxygen as the characters they truly are.

Title: Ivory Tower
Review: He reins in the Liberace-meets-Lenny Bruce schtick on his sixth album, a curiously anodyne effort helmed by Berlin electro buccaneer Boyz Noize. [Oct 2010, p.89]

Title: Anthem
Review: Unfortunately, their sixth studio album, Anthem, has neither the undeniably sweet earworms of their first effort nor much of the catchy soul-rock they’ve produced since.

Title: Black Sheep Boy
Review: Sheff's novelistic lyrics and the dextrous blend of country, folk and nervy indie-rock suggest a band approaching the peak of their powers. [Aug 2005, p.87]

Title: Pinewood Smile
Review: Pinewood Smile has got more jokes than ever, and it’s the first time the Darkness don’t evoke 1974 or 1984 so much as 2003--and they’ve never sounded more dated.

Title: Indicud
Review: It's an entertaining, vibrant, and artistically filling album, so consider it a "presents" effort and enjoy the show.

Title: Storytone
Review: Sure, these mirrored LPs--10 songs given lavish orchestral arrangements and also offered as solo performances on a bonus disc--might be stronger as one cherry-picked set of unrepeated songs. But it wouldn't be half as interesting.

Title: Lover
Review: Like its predecessor [Reputation], Lover shines when the bombast is stripped away and the songs are humble and discreet, even muffled.

Title: Astro Coast
Review: Led by a yearning frontman getting his Morrissey on, it's a debut that's boyishly and buoyantly charming. [Aug 2010, p.126]

Title: My Wild West
Review: Sometimes, as on “Shroud,” the introspective songwriting isn’t strong enough to sustain the bold attack and the seriousness can feel confining.

Title: Spot the Difference
Review: The game at the core of Spot the Difference may be mostly meaningless, but it tricks us into a different kind of comprehension, granting a new face to songs that now no longer seem as stale.

Title: Chris
Review: She just writes fantastic songs: the melody of 5 Dollars is perfectly poised between sweetness and melancholy; What’s-Her-Face frames a lyric about self-loathing with an ominous cloud of electronics; Damn (What Must a Woman Do?) conjures a crowded dancefloor at 4am so effectively you can virtually feel the perspiration dripping from the ceiling. It is an album about pop music as much as any of the other topics it addresses.

Title: Sing To The Moon
