Review: It’s all lovely, although some songs drift into pretty but insubstantial washes of sound, so the album may not quite pack the punch needed to change her fortunes.

Title: Our Love
Review: Like most Caribou albums, Our Love is a grower.

Title: Let There Be Morning
Review: As simple and dopey as Bright Eyes' I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning, only sleepier.

Title: Silver Bell
Review: It may not have a story of a lost classic, but it has the music of a freshly discovered treasure.

Title: Eyes Wide, Tongue Tied
Review: Jon Fratelli proves a cleverly withering lyricist. Nearly all the songs treat lovers as thieves, imposters or liars.

Title: Static Tensions
Review: Along with fellow Georgia natives Mastodon, Kylesa have crafted one of the metal albums to beat this year.

Title: New
Review: New is the sound of an old dog having fun with some old tricks.

Title: Six Cups of Rebel
Review: There are good ideas scattered about on the record, but when you have to pass through several minutes of cacophonous effects and layers of sound, it can get a little exhausting.
DeMarco, sans Elvis pitch-shift, delivers some quality tunes on 2.

Title: Madame X
Review: It is an intriguing, often brilliant, though occasionally awful record.

Title: BeyoncÃ©
Review: While there isn’t a chart-smashing Single Ladies or Baby Boy in the mix, the resulting 14 tracks (plus 17 videos) make her most complete album to date.

Title: Take Me to the Sea
Review: Johnny Whitney's helium-pumped, Brian Molko-meets-Freddie Mercury squeal is very much an acquired taste--perhaps for some it will prove insufficuently offset by his bandmates' post-punk adventurism. [Sep 2008, p.92]

Title: Ten
Review: Gen-Y stoners who'd trade their favorite bong to inhale a hip-hop Pink Floyd, the exchange line starts here. [May 2004, p.108]

Title: Sisyphus
Review: Though the elements don’t always hang together, there’s no shortage of intriguing ideas.

Title: The Third Hand
Review: It sadly turns out to be an unsettling piece of evidence that he's lost without someone else's pre-existing sounds to extrapolate from and transform.

Title: Songs for the Deaf
Review: The year's best hard-rock album. [6 Sep 2002, p.86]

Title: Kill the One You Love
Review: Less visceral than Beach House and more rhythmic than Trespassers William, GEMS creates its own distinct shade of contemporary dream-pop. Usher’s angular guitar work and layers of synths provide a luxuriously designed sonic backdrop for Pitts’s doomed romanticism.

Title: Once I Was an Eagle
Review: It’s easily the most charming she’s ever been--she's no master hunter, but she doesn't need to be.

Title: Places Like This
Review: The band offers their richest, most eclectic accompaniment yet. [Sep 2007, p.122]

Title: Fuego
Review: With sharp production and some of the better compositions Phish have managed in ages, Fuego ranks among their best studio albums, capturing strands of the frenetic, cartoonish, darkly cautionary, and open-hearted expressions that make their concerts such moving experiences, but which often get lost when the tape starts rolling.

Title: Suck It and See
Review: While the reins of pomp have certainly been reined in somewhat, it's hard to shake the suspicion that Suck It and See is further evidence that Arctic Monkeys are still Britain's best guitar band--albeit one that'd be even better if they ever decide to truly lunge into the unknown.

Title: Semicircle
Review: Since they’ve never really been able to top 2004’s Thunder, Lightning, Strike, that means that everything on Semicircle is fun, but not much of it is super fun. It’s kind of like going a field trip; technically you’re not at school, but it’s still school.

Title: Lady in Gold
Review: It's hard to find anything here that will break them out of the retro-rock ghetto and into the 21st century. [Sep 2016, p.102]

Title: Shape The Future
Review: Overall, this is an impressively diverse set of tracks, Evelyn has demonstrated his capability of working in a myriad of genres with a number of collaborators, yet in its entirety, the record feels slightly lost.

Title: Contra
Review: The songs are meatier and dimensional, emboldened by whirling electronics, taut guitar solos, harder drums, disparate textures and moods, and a lyrical self-awareness that perhaps life isn't just one big basement dance party.

Title: Hot Fuss
Review: So, it's plain that The Killers have made a record more concerned with artifice than artistry. If the intent is to place their album's principal teases on the next Now That's What I Call Music compilation, then bravo.

Title: Generation Freakshow
Review: An album that could have built on the promise of the last, and instead dilutes it in an almost certainly vain pitch for chart success.

Title: Feel Feelings
Review: Feel Feelings is a richly satisfying album. Soko demands the same commitment from her listeners that she put into making these songs, but as she combines happiness and sadness into something beautiful, the honesty in her music is mesmerizing.

Title: Centipede Hz
Review: Centipede Hz is an album that both gazes up into the cosmos, and stares down into the dirt--and perhaps that's not so weird.

Title: It's Blitz!
Review: Fuller backdrops don’t inhibit Karen O at all. She still sounds unguarded and madcap, sometimes girlishly vulnerable, sometimes indomitable.

Title: Meir
Review: They expand upon the thrills of the last record with acerbic aplomb, catching us unaware with hooks and then relentlessly, lovingly, plugging away at the daily, death-y grind.

Title: Arabia Mountain
Review: Awash in trippy reverb and surf-rock riffs, Arabia Mountain is further proof that the Lips have matured.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: X: The Godless Void and Other Stories
Review: Summation of their best recorded moments, X echoes the pulverizing claustrophobia of Source Tags & Codes (2002) and sheer aggression of bone-crushing 1999 debut Madonna, erecting walls of drill-bit noise and floating ennui codas.

Title: Ages
Review: Ghost Wave get comfy in simplicity, tone, and tempo, and maintain that true course for the rest of the record. There’s a great, mid-60s Stones energy that runs underneath Ages that keeps the whole thing hearty and on its heels. But Paul’s faux-lysergic lyricism peppered throughout is never as focused as something like the Stones' “19th Nervous Breakdown”, even though he matches that jaunty cadence often.

Title: DNA
Review: The main duty of pop is to be catchy, and it's a duty which DNA mostly shirks miserably.

Title: Her Majesty the Decemberists
Review: The Decemberists are stuck in the past while innovating with an eye on the future.

Title: Seeking Thrills
Review: It’s difficult not to wish that the entire album was full of the same ingenuity as its first half, because there's so much potential and talent evident in those first tracks. It’s still early days, though, and the huge themes and inspirations Georgia plays with in Seeking Thrills showcase a true rising star of British pop.

Title: In Our Bedroom After the War
Review: Their fourth album toughens things up immeasurably. [Oct 2007, p.114]

Title: The Endless River
Review: Pink Floyd's final farewell doesn't deliver anything particularly unfamiliar to those acquainted with the Gilmour years. However, The Endless River serves its purpose as well as a collection of unreleased material can--it remembers an integral band member while reflecting on past glories in a reserved, respectable fashion.

Title: Imploding the Mirage
Review: What the Killers have yet to learn from the later Springsteen is subtlety. If bombast is not your thing, this is not your band. Imploding the Mirage says some nuanced things, but very loudly. The best things about Flowers’s writing are twofold: the upfront carpe diem spirit here, best captured in lines such as: “We’re all gonna die!” And then there are the more elegant turns of storytelling.

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: With Cruel Summer, Kanye's corralled an impressive roster of allies and contemporaries to make a sleek, state-of-the-art album that's not half as good as one of those more modest old offerings.

Title: Sisyphus
Review: Sisyphus is almost certainly the greatest hip-hop folk-tinged electronica with a deep techno pop groove record you'll ever hear.

Title: Memory
Review: Memory isn't just their best record, it makes good on all the promise they displayed early on and will hopefully shut their critics up once and for all.

Title: Microcastle
Review: It may end angrily, but when it’s all said and done, Microcastle is a blissful retreat from the known.

Title: Fever Ray
Review: It's captivating stuff, with the gnomic lyrics adding to the implied oppostion between the natural world and the machines used to make the record. [Apr 2009, p.108]

Title: Bright Sunny South
Review: Bright Sunny South doesn't stray too far from Amidon's previous work, but still suggests his development in its gorgeous production, increasingly deft arrangements, and a general sense of greater confidence and vision throughout the record.

Title: Content Nausea
Review: Altogether, it offers a glimpse of what Parquet Courts could turn into. The future looks promising.

Title: Dedicated
Review: They’re about the feeling--everything tween inside every grown adult, and thus they are still unmistakably Carly even as she tries on new sounds. When Dedication falters it’s in the latter half, where her producers seem to be trying to chase pop, or at least Spotify “airplay,” by making her sound like everyone else.

Title: October Road
Review: Carefully written, elegantly performed, and generously emotional, it's another work by an artist still at his creative peak.

Title: This Is Not The World
Review: What matters is The Futureheads have made significant artistic and personal inroads to make sure their fans' enthusiasm rises to match theirs. [July 2008, p.158]

Title: Let It All In
Review: The best of these blues and folk-indebted songs carry the faint warmth and reassuring whiff of an old pub as frontman John Bramwell reflects wittily on life's disappointments. But there's a pervading drabness that they struggle to shake.

Title: Halcyon
Review: Her second album, however, belatedly delivers on all Goulding's latent promise.

Title: Street Sweeper Social Club
Review: Though a floundering economy, bombed-out GOP and a season or two of corporate bailouts have provided them with a fat barrel of fish to shoot, this rap-rock hybrid simmers instead of seethes, never quite mustering the blood-boiling rage of its principals' previous material.

Title: London Zoo
Review: As an album, London Zoo is simply more engaging. Kevin’s production is intense but club-ready, and the lyrics are righteous and relevant.

Title: Heroes to Zeros
Review: The Beta Band have reached out into traditional rock dynamics with mixed results.

Title: Green Twins
Review: Green Twins is high on sonic invention. [Jul 2017, p.108]

Title: As I Am
Review: Lacking the chutzpah of Beyonce or a signature voice to rival Mary J Blige, it's another curiously polite mix of soul and pop hip hop. [Dec 2007, p.118]

Title: Nothing
Review: Even by Hyperdub’s standards--a 20-year lineage of beats birthed and incubated in London’s most soot-smeared corners (grime, dubstep) and Chicago’s windwept streets (footwork)--this is not a light record.

Title: Lenny
Review: While it's hard not to wish that Kravitz's music was just a few degrees better than it actually is, he has improved over the years.

Title: Teenage Dream
Review: Those two qualities [Perry's sex appeal and goofy, self-effacing charm] are out of balance for most of the album, resulting in awkward jams like E.T. (Futuristic Lover) and Peacock.

Title: Sam Sparro
Review: As good as he evidently is as an arranger for the modern pop market (props, too, for song-penning collaborators Paul Epworth and Anthony 'Eg' White)--lacks lyrical consistency: for every neat tongue twist guaranteed to have you mouthing the words back in the shower the next day, there's some truly atrocious couplet that's best forgotten before it's heard.

Title: Black Acetate
Review: Cale squanders whatever momentum he accrued on the estimable avant-pop of 2003's HoboSapiens by adorning these new songs with such unflattering, generic alternarock textures that they often render their author unrecognizable at best, and irrelevant at worst.

Title: Greetings from California
Review: Greetings From California is an album that shines a light on The Madden Brothers' mature side. [13 Sep 2014, p.53]

Title: Storyteller
Review: Carrie’s never been in better voice, but a little more control in the production would have served her well.

Title: I'll Sleep When You're Dead
Review: Already the best hip-hop release of 2007, and it ain't even close. [Mar 2007, p.68]

Title: New Blood
Review: New Blood isn't always as astonishing but that's fine.

Title: Darling Arithmetic
Review: Pared-down arrangements place O'Brien's exceptional songwriting at the forefront of each track. His voice and words, a paradoxical mix of worldly weariness and childlike delivery, are still present, and as enduring and endearing as ever.

Title: Infiniheart
Review: These are really, really beautiful songs. [#11, p.116]

Title: Everything Was Beautiful, and Nothing Hurt
Review: It is the best thing Moby has done in a long time.

Title: Hometowns
Review: Hometowns, the band’s just-reissued 2008 album, is a well-crafted bit of folk that needn’t stand on the shoulders of giants.

Title: These Were The Earlies
Review: It's not half-bad, providing you can get over the fact that the Earlies have yet to find a sound to call their own.

Title: Keep It Simple
Review: The album is front-loaded with these relatively energetic tracks. Much of the rest ('End of the Land,' 'Song of Home') is resigned, reflective and spiritually attuned, but not always keenly focused.

Title: October Road
Review: An album of rich, subtle melodies, championship-level guitar playing and lyrical depth. [Sep 2002, p.115]

Title: Days of Gold
Review: To paraphrase J-Kwon, everybody in this beach gettin' "Tipsy" (another song title here), so drink up.

Title: The Electric Lady
Review: The album’s first half is fantastic.... The album’s second ‘suite’ is mellower and less consistent.

Title: Straight Songs Of Sorrow
Review: Over the course of an hour, Straight Songs unloads a lifetime of pain. But there is a happy ending to this story. Whereas much of the album has him merely “hanging on”, by Eden Lost And Found – a track built from a mobile phone recording of his wife messing around with an old Casio keyboard – he has embraced survival and moves towards his new dawn with, if not quite piranha teeth, then a mischievous, Cheshire cat grin.

Title: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes
Review: Ness' songs tackle his experiences with hard, unforgiving honesty. [Feb 2011, p.99]

Title: Gutter Rainbows
Review: Despite limp production, Kweli is often a great presence here, and fans certainly won't be disappointed.

Title: The Runners Four
Review: The band use trad tools... and trad tricks... But there's nothing trad about their cock-your-head tunings and lose-your-balance rhythms. [Dec 2005, p.100]

Title: Our Two Skins
Review: On Our Two Skins, Payten reckons with big decisions and big changes, claiming them as part of her life to beautiful effect.

Title: Omoiyari
Review: This album is the first work by Kishi Bashi that feels like a mission, and it’s that same sense of purpose that drives Omoiyari to be the most beautiful and impactful piece of his catalogue.

Title: BDL Bipolar
Review: It all adds up to a baggy and frequently baffling record.

Title: Popular Songs
Review: That these experiments hit their mark is a testament to how shrewdly Yo La Tengo has crafted their aesthetic over the years: They know exactly how hard and in what direction to push.

Title: We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions
Review: We Shall Overcome lets us revel in the sound of a man who no longer confuses unplugged with uninspiring--and who isn't afraid to mix in some merriment with the message. [28 Apr 2006, p.134]

Title: Swim
Review: Much like Four Tet's recent switch in focus towards club-friendly sonics, Caribou's Swim leaps into fresh, uncharted territory for the producer, but nonetheless retains the artist's unmistakably inviting and lovable style.

Title: Here Come the Rattling Trees
Review: Revealing Rattling Trees as a soundtrack from the jump puts the Llamas at an advantage and a disadvantage. It helps to explain the structure of the album, which kicks off with an overture that touches on all the melodic themes to be heard later, followed by quick instrumental bits that precede actual songs. But without the full text of the play or a chance to see it before hearing the music, these pleasant-but-slight songs become more negligible.

Title: Fragile Future
Review: Emo fans will be satisfied; dabblers will have their assumptions about the genre confirmed.

Title: Electric
Review: Electric is a return to one of his best attributes, the snarling electric guitar. [Mar 2013, p. 95]

Title: Ready to Die
Review: [A] robust studio resurrection of his alliance with guitarist James Williamson.

Title: Petals for Armor
Review: On her solo debut, Williams goes beyond all expectations to create an experimental and multifaceted picture of pain as she opens up the door into a new decade of her life.

Title: Uncanney Valley
Review: Pay no attention to the lyrics (pretend you’re foreign or something), concentrate on the music, and you might just enjoy yourself after all.

Title: As I Am
Review: Her fourth album starts well with the flashing anger of 'Go Ahead,' but only the Stax-sampling 'Where Do We Go From Here' is half as interesting.

Title: Love Me Back
Review: There are times when the album relies too much on vintage soul staples, with songs like Stuttering coming across as pastiche, but then the strident beat of Love You Long Time and the Elliott-produced dancehall-influenced closer Luv Back remind you of how versatile that voice can be.

Title: Reflections
Review: For the most part, though, Diamond’s debut album sparkles. Harnessing heartbreak and combining it with wickedly odd production, ‘Reflections’ is a shimmering collection of unconventional pop songs. After all that speculation, Hannah Diamond is human after all.

Title: The Drop
Review: What makes the record a success is the way Pinkunoizu harness their varied ideas and refine them into something accessible and engaging.

Title: Help
Review: It's an exhilarating racket, to say the least. [Sep 2009, p.88]

Title: Awake
Review: You'll be comfy, you might spot some pretty things on the hard shoulder, but ultimately it doesn't get you anywhere.

Title: In Our Nature
Review: In Our Nature is every bit as lovely as "Veneer," obscuring its darker moods in music as delicately bewitching as a morning mist.

Title: III
Review: III is a record that fluctuates between the joyous and the melancholy over and over, making those many contrasts of dark and light all the more impactful.

Title: Devotion
Review: As comfortable as the Beach House sound is, it's the uncomfortable moments that are most seductive.

Title: Folie A Deux
Review: And while this all may sound suspiciously over-indulgent, the fact is these self-styled 'soft-core' rockers are fulfilling their own prophesy.

Title: Instinct
Review: Overall, this is a daring, dynamic and dramatic debut.

Title: Absolution
Review: Like Coldplay on A Rush of Blood to the Head, Muse sound like a band who are at the top of their game. Their confidence carries you through the album's excesses.

Title: Roses
Review: [Shows a] lack of development involved in either the music or the creators' worldview.

Title: Ruins
Review: For most of its running time, you won’t want to move anywhere, either. Maybe don’t stay that way forever, but frequent returns to Ruins in the coming years are guaranteed.

Title: Stone Temple Pilots
Review: Loaded with heady guitar trips and crunching grooves, all topped off with flamboyant frontman Scott Weiland’s soulful vocal (which sounds all the better for his newly cleaned-up lifestyle), this is classic STP.

Title: Unapologetic
Review: Unapologetic makes a compelling case for Rihanna knowing what she's doing. This most compelling of pop phenomena still has something new to offer.

Title: A Little Deeper
Review: Ms. Dynamite's debut album is heady stuff, punctuated by groundbreaking beats, seductive vocals and melodies that lodge themselves firmly into your cranium.

Title: Sister
Review: Dark and syrupy in tone, with just the right amount of haze, as if from sacred smoke, Sister is a fine addition to the witchy, ritualistic hard rock that's leaving an ever-darker mark on aggressive music.

Title: Dear Miss Lonelyhearts
Review: After the wet noodle that was 2011's Mine Is Yours, California indie purveyors Cold War Kids come back al dente on Dear Miss Lonelyhearts. [May 2013, p.84]

Title: Algiers
Review: Easily their most accessible album, Algiers is also Calexico at their most expansive and very, very best. [Oct 2012, p.94]

Title: WIT'S END
Review: It will be intriguing to see where Cass McCombs goes next. A little more light and shade wouldn't go amiss, yet even his dark side is eminently loveable.

Title: Former Lives
Review: It's simply a charming patchwork collection of songs from just shy of the last decade that never found a voice amongst the catalogue of Gibbard's other projects.

Title: The Dutchess
Review: A shameless solo debut full of Eighties-style electro bangers.

Title: Molly Drake
Review: This is Molly Drake’s record, her story, and she tells it with heartbreaking beauty.

Title: Lost Property
Review: If Turin Brakes' world-view has changed little over the years, their embrace of the craft of record-making has only improved, and Lost Property is an impressive document of their skills in the recording studio.

Title: Aerial
Review: You could lose yourself for days here. [Dec 2005, p.142]

Title: Love Remains
Review: Love Remains is a striking debut, one that speaks to how we listen to and remember music we love, and the impact it makes on everything else we hear.

Title: Murdering Oscar (and other love songs)
Review: Devoid of the brawn that makes the Truckers so powerful and without a complementary voice off which to bounce, Hood's songs fall into a folksy rut.

Title: Jungle Rules
Review: Jungle Rules is full of summer vibes, and makes a perfect addition to not only Frenchie's catalogue but any summer playlist--which is to say it was worth the wait.

Title: The Art Of Losing
Review: Some cuts have a quick sugar-high effect--once they fade, they're about as fresh as overchewed bubblegum. [7 Mar 2003, p.72]

Title: Last Evenings On Earth
Review: Only the occasional squalling, free-jazz meltdown gets in the way of letting the good times roll. [Jun 2016, p.114]

Title: Slaughterhouse
Review: There isn't a whole lot of blood in Slaughterhouse, but it is a thrill ride, and an exhausting one at that.

Title: Everything Now
Review: So view Everything Now as a glass half empty due to its inconsistency or as a glass half full of standout singles. You won’t be able to ignore it though, which, in today’s crowded musical landscape, is triumph in itself.

Title: Down to the Lowest Terms: The Soul Sessions
Review: The best songs give Arrington the room to sprawl out and flex those ever-charismatic vocals, nearly untarnished by the sands of time.

Title: We Are the Pipettes
Review: While We Are the Pipettes often swells and soars... it doesn't come near the symphonic grandeur of the best of 60s girl pop. At its best, however, these pocket-sized songs still burst with verve and vitality, mixing heart-pumping melodies with carefree, almost conversational vocals.

Title: For Crying Out Loud
Review: The result with For Crying Out Loud is that it has bright moments but ultimately adds to the collection of below-par efforts that will do little to extinguish the elitism scorn that they attract.

Title: You & Me
Review: It’s not a showy record, but one that when peeled apart reveals itself to be a darker and more engaging album than on first listen. But not only that, as it might also be the best thing they’ve ever done.

Title: Xe
Review: Xe is a complete ecstatic experience itself as well as a dynamic text that reflects (on) these structural limitations that we employ in making sense of experience.

Title: God's Problem Child
Review: At times, Nelson’s nonchalance makes some of the more topical concerns on God’s Problem Child feel a tad hackneyed. ... That leaves plenty of space for the other veteran songwriters to slip Nelson their own meditations on aging.

Title: The Lady Killer
Review: With The Lady Killer, Cee Lo Green is out for blood. Track after track, he triumphs.

Title: Zeroes QC
Review: When they strip down everything down for the closing pair Fear and the onomatopoeic Organ Blues, the nape hairs rise even higher. [Mar 2011, p.100]

Title: Coming on Strong
Review: Could pass for a set of lo-fi synth demos Sir Paul McCartney cooked up one long weekend for shits and giggles. [Feb 2006, p.130]

Title: Rockin' the Suburbs
Review: But for all of its snickers, ''Suburbs'' is serious business -- a pop fantasia that seals Folds' rep as the Cole Porter of underclass underdogs.

Title: In Love
Review: There is something intangibly magnetic about In Love, and it feels like a wonderful, igniting record--when so many other “indie” records fail to stir any emotion other than indifference.

Title: Volta
Review: "Volta," much like "Medulla," is an appealing series of collaborations and musical ideas that do not quite jell in their final, recorded versions.

Title: Endless Wire
Review: So they've got sprawl and focus issues. But this underproduced mess of an album also has an abundance of magnificent, quirkily anthemic songwriting.

Title: Expansion Team
Review: A more polished sonic effort than Dilated's 2000 debut, The Platform.

Title: Reincarnated
Review: At its best, this album is nothing more than a passable appropriation of pop reggae in 2013.

Title: Ungodly Hour
Review: It’s not a full-bore masterwork: the first half of the record packs a stronger punch than the latter. But it’s a more cohesive, complete listen as a result of tighter sequencing. The Ungodly Hour is a soothing salve for a world on fire.

Title: Simulation Theory
Review: As a neon-lit tonic to Drones, Simulation Theory is bang on the money. But as an exploration of a new frontier, it's a genuinely exciting musical adventure in its own right. [10 Nov 2018, p.53]

Title: Wasting Light
Review: Wasting Light isn't perfect, but its flaws are essential to its being.

Title: The Assassination Of Julius Caesar
Review: Through musical discipline, a poetic sense of self-expression, emotional honesty, and rigorous intellectual curiosity, Ulver reveal not only what remains possible in synth pop creatively, but the aesthetic abundance that was there all along.

Title: Alone with Everybody
Review: Alone With Everybody is a good album with great moments.

Title: OH (Ohio)
Review: Whatever: just?listen to the damn disc.

Title: My One and Only Thrill
Review: These are slight, subtle progressions but what impresses is how thoroughly My One and Only Thrill lives up to the promise of her debut, offering another album that is as enchanting in its sound as it is in its substance.

Title: Fabulous Muscles
Review: Angry, desperate, and bleak, but this time coupled with a sense of hope and compassion, Fabulous Muscles is a major step forward for Jamie Stewart and Xiu Xiu.

Title: The Private World of Paradise
Review: Everything here is painted in varying shades of gloom and lit by flickering candle flame, but every now and then, illuminates something quite gorgeous.

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: The overall portrait is that of a fruitful collision of four like-minded, talented artists bursting with ideas, and smart enough not to take their own genius seriously. [Fall 2007, p.78]

Title: The Brink
Review: Mary's revelatory, palpable desire and seemingly newfound strength permeate all of The Brink, leaving you with an impression of the Jezabels as a band that's (in spirit) one part singer/songwriter, one part stadium rock god, and, ultimately, all woman.

Title: AOI: Bionix
Review: Loose, relaxed, and enormously enjoyable.

Title: Actor
Review: A few songs could slim down, but the star gets in and out of her dream sequences seamlessly, already thinking of her next line.

Title: Mandy Moore
Review: Sweet as she may be, there's nothing in Mandy Moore's bubblegum world that makes her stand out from the wallpaper of Disneyland background music.

Title: Sea of Cowards
Review: But as with “Horehound,” “Sea of Cowards” is all about the volatile vibe rather than songs. When the vibe works, it’s a decent approximation of the band’s top-shelf live show. But beneath all the “Hustle and Cuss,” the tunes just aren’t there.

Title: Elytral
Review: Synths and drum machines dominate, courtesy of Epworth and producer Thom Monahan, lending Elytral a seemly patina of '80s dark-pop. [Oct 2017, p.26]

Title: A Written Testimony
Review: As an album and summation of why so many people have revered Jay Electronica for so long, A Written Testimony was absolutely worth the wait. Let’s just hope the next one arrives sometime this decade.

Title: Pyramid of the Sun
Review: Despite their brevity, the songs are repetitive, wanky and almost impossible to differentiate. They make you yearn for the days before genre cross-pollination.

Title: Sir Lucious Left Foot: The Son of Chico Dusty
Review: It's eclectic, electrifying, eccentric and more than a little bit ludicrous, but Sir Lucious's ambition is as infectious as its madness is dazzling.

Title: Days Go By
Review: 'Days Go By' doesn't catapult them back to their prime; there's a lot of issues that can be picked out, be it recognisable musicality or questionable song choices. Having said that, when The Offspring do get it right on this record, they are great.

Title: Atlas
Review: Through lulling endless days to fretting thoughts about the future, they remain the same bunch, capable of making the impossible sound almost too easy.

Title: Raditude
Review: Raditude is just the latest and fullest articulation of Cuomo's wincingly sad desire to become a mainstream success, [Holiday, 2009, p.79]

Title: The Runners Four
Review: By turns jubilant, confused, afraid, angry, sad, relieved, all pretty poignant, yes.

Title: Strawberry Jam
Review: The sixth album by this neocommunalist, neopsychedelic quartet improves on 2005's "Feels," flashing more shards of tune to lure the coeds with the Coleman PerfectFlow InstaStart Lanterns over to their adamantly unkempt campfire.

Title: Supermodified
Review: A superbly stealthy assault on the ears, stroking and unsettling in equal measure.

Title: Anthem
Review: 40 minutes of soul-searching and bittersweet recollection that nevertheless rocks with major-league efficiency.

Title: Generals
Review: Where Bright Eyes lyrics lumber, The Mynabirds are aflight.

Title: The Soul of the Hour
Review: The Soul Of The Hour rumbles onward with fearsome nocturnal dread, if paced with sufficient patience this time to allow the odd shaft of illumination to seep in. [May 2014, p.87]

Title: The Child of Lov
Review: Williams has figured out his sounds, but he’s still working towards his voice.

Title: International Teachers of Pop
Review: It’s a self-assured, hook-laden set, and it’s exciting to imagine what they’ll do next as they settle into their roles.

Title: In Colour
Review: The incessant hooklines cloy a little after repeated listens, but that’s hardly the most damning criticism of a pop band.

Title: Dungeon Golds
Review: The sound is very much mid-’60s Beach Boys/Byrds pop stuff.

Title: Curtis
Review: What the two boil down to is that a parvenu mastering pop music for money has turned into a made man running on vanity. I find that this renders his expert trivialization of murder and such rather less piquant, and I think he does too--that an audacious formal delight has become routine.

Title: Permalight
Review: Unpretentious, streamlined and--as Rogue himself proclaimed--overwhelmingly "up up up." [Winter 2010, p.65]

Title: Instrumentals 2015
Review: It feels like a resumption of a music that has been going on uninterrupted, in private, like it was music playing itself forever. [Jul 2015, p.48]

Title: American Kid
Review: It's a record that manages to sound deeply affectionate without being sentimental. [Jun 2013, p.70]

Title: Achilles Heel
Review: The band's attempts to diversify the tone are not always successful.

Title: Sudden Fictions
Review: Cerebral and discomforting. [Aug 2020, p.89]

Title: Go To School
Review: Lemon Twigs commit wholeheartedly to the bizarre narrative that Go to School is built on. Leaving no ridiculous tangent or exaggerated flourish unexplored, the result is a larger-than-life spectacle grown from strange but excellent songwriting.

Title: Field of Reeds
Review: Quiet, diligent, and touching--this could very well be These New Puritans’ masterwork.

Title: Donkey
Review: Mostly, Donkey is undone by a dearth of really memorable, infectious tunes.

Title: No One's First and You're Next
Review: Growing more comfortable with their talents, maybe they’re learning that you don’t always have to work so hard and worry so much. Sometimes, you can just float on.

Title: Acolyte
Review: From a palette of familiar reference points, they've created a fresh, vital sound that could prove to be the basis of an impressive career.

Title: Americana
Review: There's plenty to like about Neil Young and Crazy Horse's first work together for nine years, a collection of cover versions of essential American tunes.

Title: King Push - Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude
Review: King Push's Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude is a damn good record, but it is not flawless.

Title: Unity Band
Review: The themes are typical Metheny: sensuous Latin grooves, synth-guitar fusion, folksy ballads, a good deal of jazz swing – and the rhythm section is mindboggling, not to mention beautifully recorded.

Title: Brass
Review: Aside from a few inconsistencies, the change in sound is quite revitalizing and proves that there is more to Royal Bangs than a serious case of musical ADD.

Title: Diaper Island
Review: Hard to imagine any of his future albums beating this one, but it's entirely possible, and all signs seem to point toward this inventive young producer/songwriter being on the rise.

Title: The Quilt
Review: Gym Class Heroes' Quilt is very, very much of its time: it skates by on the surface, which is appealing for a while, but in large doses it can seem like too much empty style.

Title: MeYouWeYou
Review: This is actually a deeply groovy album, beautifully produced and full of sparkling detail. [Sep 2013, p.108]

Title: Inspiral Carpets
Review: Inspiral Carpets sounds like the band did back in 1989 on their Dung 4 demo. [Nov 2014, p.92]

Title: The Grand Tour
Review: ‘Flatlands And The Flemish Roads’ evokes feelings of motion, ‘Ode To Viennese Streets’ a sense of relaxation, but strip away their titles and the concept evaporates, leaving a warm but undemanding album.

Title: Room Noises
Review: Room Noises is the perfect escape for girls who've outgrown their My Little Ponies but aren't quite prepared for more adult outlets of expression, and that of course is its downfall.

Title: Burn
Review: The album goes on to balance thunder and reflectiveness surprisingly evenly.

Title: Dear Science
Review: They haven’t exactly lost their sense of intrigue, it’s just that on Dear Science it all sounds a lot less intriguing.

Title: Paranoid Cocoon
Review: It also probably means that we'll be getting something new from Nau the next time around. Switching between musical characters is obviously Nau's default setting, and for all of its pleasantness, Paranoid Cocoon, in the context of his career thus far, feels like transition music over a costume change.

Title: Secret House Against the World
Review: It's highly unlikely that Buck 65 is ever going to become the cash cow that his paymasters probably thought he was going to be, but let's hope that he is invited to keep on presenting us with his skewed worldview; a beautiful painting seen in a shattered and blood stained mirror.

Review: Here, as on 2005’s "Takk," Sigur Ros have chosen to distill their rapture epics into shorter, more accessible bursts of swelling beauty. Yet this album still offers all the signature touchstones that make the band so deliciously unlike their post-rock contemporaries.

Title: Stay Positive
Review: The sound is more varied and lighter on its feet with touches of harpsichord and banjo but anchored by the Hold Steady's signature: thick, humid arena rock, a high-pressure system of cresting guitars and pianos that injects these dramas with tension and embraces all their contradictions and ambiguities.

Title: Freeman
Review: The resulting 12 tracks find Freeman both revelling in and lost within this musical yin and yang.

Title: America
Review: It's unfathomably exciting stuff.

Title: The Chronicles of Marnia
Review: The way Marnie plays is fresh, but she does hold true to some central tenets of rock’n’roll in her fizzing songs: invincibility and defiance.

Title: Immolate Yourself
Review: Their smoky, atmospheric ballads are too languid by half, but Telefon Tel Aviv's bright melodic palette keeps Immolate Yourself from descending into a dull fog.

Title: Complete Strangers
Review: After six albums, Cabic has yet to build a discernible and discrete identity for this band. It remains the ongoing also-ran from a loose freak-folk confederation that’s splintered in a dozen surprising ways.

Title: Celestial Lineage
Review: Olympia, Washington's Wolves in the Throne Room have made their most accessible album to date.

Title: Brett Anderson
Review: Gone is the Suede-lite of The Tears. Instead we get acoustic guitars, lush string arrangements and the previously cagey Anderson pouring his heart out. [Apr 2007, p.92]

Title: Lasers
Review: Lupe seems to have accepted that Lasers is not the masterpiece he originally set out to make and is prepared to move on. Maybe we should follow his lead.

Title: I and Love and You
Review: More than anything, I and Love and You proves how miscast the Brothers were as folkies, because their ambitions are so much larger.

Title: AOI: Bionix
Review: De La Soul returns to classic form relishing their status as one of hip-hop's longest running acts and flaunting their roles as hip-hop's cerebral older brothers.

Title: Share the Joy
Review: It does eventually resolve into "I Heard You Say," a dash of wintry Mamas and Papas pop. Sadly, the trio regresses from there, simply shining up versions of the same old loose, punky love songs they've been hawking for years.
It's sometimes a difficult listen, there's a lack of lucidity and guile that at times leaves the less striking tracks to come across rather samey.

Title: Days
Review: Days is a step in the right direction, but we're hoping they can challenge themselves to do something greater on album three.

Title: Varcharz
Review: This is an impressive record in many respects, and its hooks and patterns only emerge after many plays, but it's also an oddly distant one.

Title: Body Language
Review: It's hottest moments are tepid at best. [Feb 2004, p.77]

Title: Nine Types of Light
Review: The sort-of-romantic themes and sort-of-funk grooves lend a greater unity than usual, but save for a few tracks, the general impression is of lots of bustling, itchy industry – the scratchy guitars, the scuttling beats, the dying-firework synths – to no particularly attractive end.

Title: Para Mi
Review: The tone of the album is almost suffocating. Just as Cuco’s vocals submerge under the cloying, bolero sensibilities of “Far Away From Home” – as do we, with this all-encompassing misery.

Title: Suck My Shirt
Review: The attitude's still present and correct, but there's also a nagging, Pixies-like surf melodies of Drive and the serrated riffs of Springfield Cannonball. [Jan 2015, p.122]

Title: Kisses on the Bottom
Review: As a vocalist, this may not be his natural forte, but he takes great care with the songs, and that palpable love is enough to make Kisses on the Bottom worth a spin or two.

Title: Graffiti
Review: Try-hard, but ultimately mediocre R’n’B comeback from disgraced singer.

Title: Mutual Friends
Review: Mutual Friends, a loose song-cycle, is entirely winning.

Title: Revelation
Review: Its freshness proves that ten years after their 2004 breakthrough, the band is as lively as ever and, in some sly subtle ways, better than ever too.

Title: Wolves of Want
Review: This is a feel good album about terrible times.

Title: Blanck Mass
Review: Blissed-out analogue synths, the swell and drone of ambient rock and epic, beatless, drawn-out melodies characterize the debut. [Aug. 2011, p. 104]

Title: Universal High
Review: It’s a natural-sounding progression that confounds the expected developments ‘a guitar band’ should make and instead adds a glorious musical technicolour to a set of songs to soundtrack the summer and beyond.

Title: Life After Youth
Review: Some of that punchy vitality has been lost, but never does it obscure Powell’s ability to add bold expressions to her fine-grained accounts.

Title: Nightmare
Review: Avenged Sevenfold continues to sound like five different bands on every album, none of them particularly good.

Title: The Bride
Review: The most memorable song from the back half of the album, “In Your Bed,” sounds like it could have come from a different set of songs, judging by its lyrics.) As a result, The Bride goes past dreamy and into lullaby territory after a while, and the listener’s engagement with the music may drift off as well.

Title: Zeitgeist
Review: While not enough to stand among the best the Pumpkins have to offer, Zeigeist nonetheless stands fairly well on it's own

Title: Winter Hymn Country Hymn Secret Hymn
Review: Easily the best work that the group has done.

Title: Feedback
Review: In the future, the guys in Jurassic 5 need to do a better job picking their friends and their song subjects.

Title: Whiteout Conditions
Review: Some of the songs feel too sterile and Pornos-by-numbers; others are derivative in a way the band rarely is. Overall, it would have been more successful as a five-song mini-LP than as a full-length.

Title: Voices in a Rented Room
Review: On the strength of the songs here and the pitch perfect atmosphere they’ve conjured it would be criminal if we didn’t hear more from them in the future.

Title: Tearless
Review: By the end of Tearless, Amnesia Scanner’s singular vision, for all its moments that both stun and disgust, has seeped its way in. There’s no looking back.

Title: Loud
Review: So, in a strange way, Loud is an extremely successful album for Maas: it rids him of the trance tag, has enough vocal dance-pop to win over even more admirers, and is so diverse that everyone will find at least one enjoyable track.

Title: SIGN
Review: Highlights a voracious creative appetite and their relationship's enduring strength. [Dec 2020, p.87]

Title: In Search of the Miraculous
Review: Indie-goth, shoegaze, post-punk, all of these descriptions fit but none of them can begin to tell the whole story and with the arrival of In Search of the Miraculous there is a sense that this soulful, anthemic, continually evolving band are just getting started.

Title: Salad Days
Review: While those individual songs are great, they generate the urge to listen to the whole record in its entirety which, in the end, may not be as healthy and carefree as the title and arrangements would have us believe.

Title: Everything She Touched Turned Ampexian
Review: His latest LP, Everything She Touched Turned Ampexian is another sinuous but seamless blend of the organic and synthetic, embodying the hand-in-everything spirit of hip hop.

Title: Broken By Whispers
Review: This is music to listen to when you're either very depressed, in order to feel the camraderie, or when you're very happy, in order to mellow out.

Title: Blinking Lights and Other Revelations
Review: Calling an Eels album personal and somber seems redundant, but compared with the guitar-rock discord of the two preceding albums, this return to meticulously crafted pop miniatures seems even more inward-directed. [24 Apr 2005]

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: This is the most important artistic statement from NIN leader Trent Reznor since the late '90s.

Title: In the Dark
Review: There's nothing staggeringly new happening here, but it's all deftly delivered and sure to find favour. [Mar 2011, p.106]

Title: King Night
Review: By creating a world so comic-book vivid, each track stands and walks in its own desolate, saturnine world. But it's a world where the dead want to be alive and the alive would rather be dead. The creation of warped minds, Salem just made a monster.

Title: Purple
Review: Through it all the rejuvenated Baroness is totally inspired, not only to be making new music but also to have the ability to make new music. And you can hear it.

Title: Wheeltappers and Shunters
Review: For all its thematic focus and political commentary, Wheeltappers and Shunters is quintessentially Clinic; at once pointed and oblique, its bad trips and cheap thrills are a subversive rebuke to a sanitized notion of the past, present, or future.

Title: Four
Review: [On album's first half] the melodies are sturdy and the lyrics catch. Later, the titles get sillier (''Stockholm Syndrome''), and the guitar-jam vibe turns as dull as every real-life guitar jam. But when Four ends, your ears are guilt-free.

Title: Still Trippin'
Review: Still Trippin’ doesn’t have the crossover punch of DJ Rashad’s Double Cup, which definitely influenced it, but the potential is there just the same.

Title: Piano
Review: On his third solo album, he's found a niche that suits him. [Jul 2016, p.81]

Title: Red
Review: Red is more a poor parody of the genre than a booty shaker.

Title: Random Axe
Review: The supergroup concept is an invitation to self-indulgence, but Random Axe burns through 15 tracks--some of them about 60 seconds long--in about 40 tight minutes, making the trio more than the sum of its considerable parts.

Title: Liminal
Review: [A] strange and compelling work.

Title: Lessons in Love
Review: Lloyd still serves up a satisfying sophomore suite.

Title: 100 Acres of Sycamore
Review: But while it's sometimes a little too understated for its own good, 100 Acres of Sycamore is a never less than a charming and emotive U-turn suggesting that Regan now realizes where his talents lie.

Title: By The Throat
Review: By the Throat demands those kinds of complex distinctions, though. Its radiance is a dark one, and its most sinister moments lead to deliberate calm.

Title: Bangerz
Review: For all the mash-ups, Bangerz feels stitched together in the dark, and the attention-seeking begins to grate.

Title: Goons Be Gone
Review: No Age's latest is not ground-breaking, but it doesn't need to be. It's an enjoyable rock record from a pair of sonic auteurs whose instincts for DIY noise-punk are as strong as ever.

Title: Rock Steady
Review: The disc is bubbling with techno effects, a loose interpretation of Jamaican production and a (welcome) severe case of ADD.

Title: The Navigator
Review: The record is proof positive that an artist is ever evolving, and change is never something to be feared. Her talent and prowess as a musician and artist remain proven, nay, reinforced, by the alternative direction she takes in The Navigator, and, while different from precedent, there is much to love in it for Hurray for the Riff Raff fans, both new and old.

Title: Closer Than Together
Review: The Avetts have been doing this for too long and are too accomplished as songwriters to make an album that's a total dud. The good stuff on Closer Than Together is really quite excellent. But when the balance is just a bit more good material than mediocre (or worse) material, you start to question the production choices involved.

Title: Coming on Strong
Review: Restlessly inventive, Hot Chip also manage what many bedroom eclectics don't: crafting a genuinely organic, proper album, and the relaxed enthusiasm that drives this debut is absurdly infectious. [Jun 2004, p.94]

Title: Stankonia
Review: It takes a few listens to pull everything together, but given the immense scope, it's striking how few weak tracks there are. It's no wonder Stankonia consolidated OutKast's status as critics' darlings, and began attracting broad new audiences: its across-the-board appeal and ambition overshadowed nearly every other pop album released in 2000.

Title: Let Me Come Home
Review: It is an elegant and, quite frankly, utterly beautiful record.

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: At 72 minutes, his fifth release is too long and needlessly precious at times. [28 Sep 2007, p.106]

Title: Rooty
Review: Rooty is the second straight triumph from a pair of producer/DJs who look set to carry the torch for dancefloor electronica in the years to come.

Title: Something Shines
Review: Sadier seems to have taken a new direction with Something Shines, finding a nice middle ground between her last two albums, yet somehow erring a little too far on the side of safety.

Title: All These Countless Nights
Review: A little bit of growing up wouldn’t go amiss.

Title: Yours Truly, The Commuter
Review: With this album, Lytle has established himself as a solo artist who does not so much distance himself from his previous band as successfully scratch an itch for sounds that have been missing from the music landscape for quite some time.

Title: Criminal
Review: There are no easy answers or happy endings here; as Vasquez grows more skilled at expressing his pain, he delivers his bleakest--and most cohesive--music yet.

Title: Conduit
Review: If you came in as I did in 2008 on what might have been their most eclectic and defining record, you might find this a little less appealing simply for its lack of emphasis on the melody and dialed up screamo.

Title: Song Feel
Review: This album's been seven years in the making and it shows. Many of the songs, including most of the instrumentals, might've sounded fresh sometime back, but I find myself forgetting them as soon as they're played through.

Title: The Monitor
Review: this passionate record sounds more true to the E Street Band's spirit than do the absurdly literal Bossisms of the Gaslight Anthem. The Monitor is maybe 20 minutes too long, and by the end you'll be as exhausted as exhilarated, but there's the promise of a rare and vivid talent here.

Title: Sky Trails
Review: It’s a pleasure to report that he’s come up with something much more tangible than a mere phoned-in hash of former glories.

Title: Twins
Review: To have a release that's altogether thrashing, infectious and emotional achieves a depth that the slew of garage rock revivalists today fail to encapsulate.

Title: Tambourine
Review: Tambourine is a remarkably mature, confident, and commanding release that defines then rides its groove with no low points.

Title: Blackstar
Review: Halfway through and it's breathtakingly apparent that David Bowie isn't so much back on the horse as riding bareback towards a cliff-edge. [Jan 2016, p.86]

Title: I Am Gemini
Review: I Am Gemini is Cursive's weakest record by a disheartening margin.

Title: Gary Go
Review: Epic pop has a new face, and it belongs to Joe 90. [Jun 2009, p.122]

Title: Away
Review: The paucity of any full-on rockers may drive some listeners back to the group's more propulsive, earlier works, but the sullen, sweet, and soulful Away rewards a patient ear.

Title: A Perfect Contradiction
Review: She sounds a tad daft masquerading as a feisty Harlem mama on the Pharrell-produced I Can't rely On You, but her uber-gutsy delivery still charms. [Apr 2014, p.90]

Title: Foil Deer
Review: The echoes among unhinged riffs on “Good Neck,” “Raising the Skate” and “My Dead Girl” speak to the unity of Speedy Ortiz’s vision, as well as its limitations; the spikiness that gives the music its appeal also turns it abrasive over the long haul.

Title: The High End of Low
Review: Assuming they haven’t all grown up by now, Manson fans will adore every dark, juvenile flourish. For the rest of us, The High End Of Low serves as a cautionary tale of artistic regression.

Title: About The Light
Review: Well-conceived, vibrant, and executed with attitude and aplomb, About the Light is a career standout for Mason.

Title: Currents
Review: Currents is all about the wide lens. It’s not the landscape worth falling in love with, but the way Parker gives us a tour. Let it happen, and it will carry you off somewhere much further away than you realized was worth visiting.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: Considering how the album's style draws from each era of R.E.M.'s evolution, Collapse Into Now plays as something of a greatest-hits package.

Title: New
Review: New is as apt an album title as you'll find: Not only does it announce McCartney's first batch of original songs in six years, it also celebrates the idea that pop music can still invigorate, inspire, and surprise--even if you had a hand in inventing it.

Title: Zoo
Review: For the majority of the record, Ceremony is quite comfortable being average. Neither laudable nor terrible, Ceremony's music sets an easy target, hits the mark, and then moves on to the next task.

Title: The Thread That Keeps Us
Review: A song cycle that straddles inescapable anxiety and persistent optimism. [Feb 2018, p.24]

Title: Fork In The Road
Review: The music saves this album from certain disaster--an idea that, at its root is perplexing at best, is executed in an even more clumsy and confusing way.

Title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
Review: It is shocking, it's exciting and it doesn't attempt to give any easy answers or clues as to its real intentions.

Title: Bon Voyage
Review: With Bon Voyage, it genuinely feels as if Prochet got lost in her sounds and let it lead her. In her own musical liberation, Prochet makes something bizarre and stunning.

Title: Little French Songs
Review: It's Bruni's intimacy that's the album's most alluring aspect.

Title: Younger Now
Review: At its worst, Younger Now is inoffensively bland, wasted Dolly Parton talent aside. Songs like "Love Someone" are dead on arrival with their lifeless energy and forgettable hooks.

Title: Prophets of Rage
Review: The combination of Chuck D and B-Real’s wholly different vocal deliveries is a revelation throughout: the former’s commanding baritone and preacher’s power contrasting beautifully with the latter’s nasal sneer and street-smart menace. Similarly, the chemistry between Morello, drummer Brad Wilk and bassist Tim Commerford has never been in doubt, and here, while generally less aggressive than they were in their youthful pomp, that effortless ensemble groove ensures that none of these tracks will fail to free minds and asses.

Title: The Whole Love
Review: If it's not quite the landmark that was Wilco (the album), it's not far behind, as absorbing as any you'll hear this year.

Title: We Global
Review: The overall stylistic consistency that made Listennn unusual now makes for an exhausting hour.

Title: No Control
Review: The band's hazy rock songs benefit from a nice polish and these are a couple of nice 'n' sleazy summer anthem jams here. [Apr-May 2015, p.89]

Title: My Favorite Picture of You
Review: This is his first studio album in four years, and it shows he’s not lost his touch.

Title: Rock Steady
Review: Not since Aqua has a group of cartoon-fixated, stylistically scatterbrained lunatics sounded so entertaining. [Feb 2002, p.121]

Title: Demolition
Review: When Adams sticks to the pop-rock mode, he can be dynamic as well as one of the cleverest pop thieves since Nick Lowe.

Title: Broke With Expensive Taste
Review: Broke has instances of stunningly original songwriting and there's rarely a dull moment, but it's more a kaleidoscopic 'story so far' than a complete manifesto.

Title: Ventura
Review: With sumptuous harmonies and a live band locked in on every track, .Paak finds a sweet spot between throwback soul and the 21st Century dancefloor. He sounds like the best version of himself. ... An exceptional return to form.

Title: Creatures of an Hour
Review: No particular melodies, images, or moods really stick out from the vast, dreamy atmosphere that washes over you while you're listening.

Title: Given to the Wild
Review: It's an album that bucks a trend rather than starts one: an elegant and unexpected leave-taking from the indie landfill.

Title: Chill, Dummy
Review: With Chill, dummy, P.O.S avoids retreating into the program of Never Better, while also one-upping his prior outing.

Title: Younger Now
Review: Who knows which Miley Cyrus will emerge after the rootsy and real Younger Now, but we recommend enjoying Country Miley for as long as she lasts.

Title: Collections
Review: Delphic's determination to bring together so many possible new directions proves the album's undoing, and it peters out towards the end.

Title: Unseen
Review: There’s nothing in the way of a bold step forward on Unseen, which is the wooziest collection of songs they’ve put out in quite a while; this is very much an album for the wee small hours.

Title: Oh My My
Review: Their most diverse-sounding album yet.

Title: Remember That I Love You
Review: With Dawson, the focus is on the lyrics, with her music tending to serve as a mere platform for sprawling, humorous stories whose serious subject matter contradicts the childlike catchiness underpinning them.

Title: Poison Season
Review: Nearly 20 years on, Destroyer is still as surprising and inspired as ever.

Title: Exile
Review: It's on close personal terms with magnificence.

Title: Outside
Review: It's a cleaner, catchier Tapes 'n Tapes that, despite often flaunting rather than infusing its influences, may actually leave you humming its tunes.

Title: Lord of the Birdcage
Review: While not on par with essential solo Pollard fare like Not in My Airforce, Waved Out or From a Compound Eye this cohesive, flowing work motors by and, as always, his stirring songs reveal themselves and their riches through repeated listens.

Title: El Che
Review: While Rhymefest is a rock-solid rapper--this is the guy who once beat Eminem in Scribble Jam, after all--he also blunts his own impact with corny jokes.

Title: Migration
Review: Migration is a sparkling, crisp display of Green’s ability to completely immerse a listener, and it’s strong as it’s ever been.

Title: Ghosts VI: Locusts
Review: The music turns much darker Ghosts VI, which, by proxy, makes it the more interesting of the two. ... Unlike the first Ghosts collection, these albums feel like distinct artistic statements.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Despite its flaws, Connector stands as one of their best.

Title: Christ Illusion
Review: For the most part Christ Illusion is flabby and arthritic. [Oct 2006, p.126]

Title: Hold On 'til the Night
Review: Chance may be too young to understand the complex emotions he writes and sings about, but he sure makes it seem as though he does.

Title: Anxiety
Review: Ashin, in giving so much of himself away, leaves little scope for the kind of mystery that might enable his musical settings to transcend their functional pop status. [Feb 2013, p.60]

Title: Stay Gold
Review: Stay Gold is First Aid Kit's most lush and shimmering work to date. [No. 111, p.55]

Title: Ta-Dah
Review: Similarities to their debut are much easier to find than differences, although the songs aren't quite as memorable (except the single "I Don't Feel Like Dancin'") and Ta-Dah is slightly samey in comparison.

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: A few tracks ease into each other too easily and are forgettable, but there’s still an overall sense of growth and fruition.

Title: Weird Kids
Review: There's a bit more maturity and personality to some of these tracks that speaks of a band coming into its own. Still, for fans of their first two releases, Weird Kids provides plenty of the snarky sendoffs and he-said/she-said breakup rockers that drew people to the band in the first place.

Title: Liars
Review: The stylistic buffet has enough strength to survive a handful of duds.

Title: You Can't Go Back if There's Nothing To Go Back To
Review: If this really is the end, You Can’t Go Back... is more than a worthy addition to the story of a band who leave behind one of the--if not the--richest catalogues in sunny-side-down American songwriting; only a few slightly stale rehashes of familiar templates towards the end keep this from achieving the lofty standards of, say, 2009's We Used To Think The Freeway Sounded Like The River.

Title: Fourteen Autumns & Fifteen Winters
Review: The songs on Fourteen Autumns are loud, and graced with long-line melodies that are easy to hum, but there's nothing quick or disposable about them.

Title: Former Lives
Review: In terms of overall quality though, it has to be said that things noticeably pick up in the album's second half, as any traditional indie rock sensibilities that Gibbard may have initially had start to recede and are replaced by a grittier, slightly more abstract edge.

Title: Here and Nowhere Else
Review: With Here And Nowhere Else, they’ve thrown the first punch, and it hits you square in the jaw.

Title: 22, A Million
Review: For all its undoubted oddness, what’s striking about the album is how straightforwardly enjoyable it is.

Title: Foam Island
Review: They've become powerful songwriters since they focused on the craft in 2010, and Foam Island shows it off more than anything else.

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: Sounding big may be a pretty good way to get a support slot with the biggest bands in the country and, in time, the world, but after a point you need more to say.

Title: Made of Rain
Review: Comfortably their finest outing since 1982's Forever Now. [Sep 2020, p.113]

Title: Continuum
Review: Where his earlier music was a parade of bright primary colors, these plaintive melodies come in delicious shades of gray. [Oct 2006, p.138]

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: The prime intention of Wolf's Law is to overwhelm with bluster, muscle and noise, to orchestrate us clean out of our boots.

Title: To Pimp a Butterfly
Review: This record is so expansive that it's tough to wrestle into shape, even as it overflows with wit, smarts and a masterful skill of the language and phrasing.

Title: Minutes to Midnight
Review: There's no great leap into maturity... They've kept their salient feature--scorching, adolescent tantrums--unchanged. [Jun 2007, p.109]

Title: Swoon
Review: The Silversun Pickups show here that they've got a competent grasp of the amp-frying guitar soundscape, but someone needs to teach them how to write a decent rock song.

Title: 3 Doors Down
Review: 3 Doors Down--the band and the album--won't be breaking any records with this release, but they have produced a solid, if not spectacular, collection of a dozen tunes for their fans, who have been waiting two years for something new.

Title: Faded Seaside Glamour
Review: Genteel, eminently tuneful. [24 Jun 2004, p.179]

Title: Losst and Founnd
Review: There may be none of the heart-tugging vibe of octave-spanning “Without You”, or the abundant melody of “Everybody’s Talkin’”, but Losst and Founnd resurrects a treasured voice in songs full of vim.

Title: Superabundance
Review: It's a decidedly bummer affair, and even though the aggressive tempos suggest they're willing to fight against the crushing weight of existence, there's no relief to be found anywhere in Dartnall's lyrics--not in material goods, not in your fellow man, and certainly not in romance.

Title: I'll Be Your Girl
Review: It shows a refreshed band, back on the chase to find new ways of songwriting, with strong melodies and intriguing lyrics remaining a constant. I’ll Be Your Girl is the start of this new chapter, and it’s a wonderful place for them to begin again.

Title: Recess
Review: This wobbling between attempts to impress the dance music cognoscenti and to make songs as purely delightful as "Coast Is Clear" defines Recess, and occasionally bogs it down.

Title: Goodbye Country (Hello Nightclub)
Review: In sharing its predecessor's desire to cover every musical base, Goodbye Country (Hello Nightclub) suggests a continued identity crisis.

Title: All Melody
Review: Kacirek and Müller are credited, but it's difficult to discern their contributions to the piece. The title All Melody seems to refer to the singularity of the sounds combining together. It also suggests that while empty space is often a major element to the album, what is present is entirely melodic, and purely based in emotions.

Title: Trick
Review: A return-to-roots record that works most successfully when it rebels against itself, Jamie T's vision of revelation isn't something to be easily shrugged off.

Title: Third
Review: Portishead seem to be playing against intuition at every corner.

Title: The Pale Emperor
Review: On The Pale Emperor, he sounds both inspired and rejuvenated; for the first time in a while, the most interesting thing about Manson is his music.

Title: In Defense of the Genre
Review: Bemis may be seeking to defend the emo genre, but his album instead illustrates the difference between run-of-the-mill emo--which, indeed, comprises most of the genre's output--and the imaginative, skillful tunes that flourish here. The only major downside is the album's length.

Title: More Than You Think You Are
Review: Matchbox Twenty now seem almost dignified, a fact that is as much a tribute to their advancing abilities as it is to how shamelessly their sellout successors suck.

Title: Gaslighter
Review: By blending early-21st-century pop savvy with the storytelling that made country music so crucial to the American canon, Gaslighter is all fire and nerve, performed by three women whose musical bona fides are rivaled only by their rock-solid backbones.

Title: Private Suit
Review: PJ Harvey's frequent collaborator John Parish produces, and he brings a dark, melodramatic, and very theatrical sensibility to the songs that is much more interesting--and a much more flattering setting for Carol Van Dyk's expressive but limited vocals--than the straightforward guitar churn that dominated the last couple of albums.

Title: Good Arrows
Review: Good Arrows is still a series of beautiful songs for that part of us all that just wants to stay in bed all day.

Title: Rotten Apple
Review: Trademark G-Unit, pakced with a few thunderous club jams and too little else. [Oct 2006, p.128]

Title: My Everything
Review: Despite its shortcomings, My Everything succeeds in its primary objective. This is a pop record, clear and simple.

Title: Grand Romantic
Review: It shows how Ruess might succeed on his own as a good-hearted Midwestern boy--not quite a star, but someone capable of appreciating their light.

Title: Curve of the Earth
Review: Curve of the Earth is an ode to the uncertainty of the quarter-life crisis that somehow manages to make that awkward entry into maturity sound bittersweet and beautiful at once.

Title: The Queen of Hearts
Review: Occasionally it feels a little too theatrical--as on Willie O' Winsbury--but its roots are in the right place. [Aug 2017, p.95]

Title: Maximum Entropy
Review: It’s impossible to ignore the actual music, it’s so damn loud! And so stuffed up by the production, which is all there is. The end result is songs that that are so bright you might imagine you’re about to be blinded.

Title: Throw Down Your Arms
Review: The concept works better than you might think. [3 Nov 2005, p.94]

Title: Two Vines
Review: Two Vines may not be the group's masterpiece, but it is their most consistent album yet. Their mastery of modern pop sounds, ability to craft melodies that have a timeless quality, and the real connection they provide to people who want their frivolous pop music to have some depth and meaning, is impressive.

Title: Stockholm
Review: All in all, very little on Stockholm stands out, despite the best attempts by all involved.

Title: Pro Tools
Review: Even if they're slow to arrive, GZA's full-lengths rarely disappoint. Pro Tools is no different, but with so many divergent projects and experiments from the Clan filling the five previous years, this throwback also proves the crew's original formula still works splendidly.

Title: The Forgotten Arm
Review: While nothing on The Forgotten Arm is brand new for her, it's a natural evolution from what her fans have gotten used to, the minor-key laments and regrets of Bachelor No. 2 and Lost in Space.

Title: Skying
Review: While in some sense these tracks are truer to the band's past than Skying's more formally ambitious cuts, that only convinces me that the Horror's biggest leaps forward are the ones in which they follow other musician's great ideas to new places.

Title: Last Summer
Review: Wonky, wordy, connective - a Tapestry for the Williamsburg set.[Dec. 2011, p.93]

Title: Don't Believe The Truth
Review: Sure, for 11 songs, these blokes can grind out toe-tapping Britpop, but there are no heart-pounding anthems here. [10 Jun 2005, p.107]

Title: Researching the Blues
Review: If you like rock tunes with sharp melodies and earworm choruses, Researching the Blues isn't likely to give you anything to complain about. It's an album that feels, at its best, effortless. Other moments, however, feel too effortless, and as a result there are some missed opportunities.

Title: The Chaos
Review: They have always had an unabashed sensibility for writing three-minute pop songs and this record is stuffed full of them. The Futureheads have made exhilarating order out of The Chaos.

Title: King Night
Review: For all the calculated horror show element, much of King Night is very pretty and nuanced, trading in shivering beauty rather than infernal fury, with an aching world weariness running Marlatt and Holland's more lucid vocal turns. It's just a shame Donoghue has to dopily blunder in there every now and again, the dimwit henchman to his evil scientist colleagues.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Paper MÃ¢chÃ© Dream Balloon
Review: There can't have been a better 1968 record in all of 2015. [Dec 2015, p.90]

Title: Dance Mother
Review: Dance Mother has a few bright spots: the para-diddling drums at the beginning of 'In Your Line' give it a real open-air sweep, the song itself is straightforward and affecting, and “Devil’s Trident” features buzzy synthesizers that open up a bracing, jittery mood. But most of the rest isn’t all that engrossing.

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: Maxwell's voice is so unusually rich and supple that at best, as on the mercurial 'Bad Habits,' you cannot help but disregard his fondness for cliche.

Title: JESUS IS KING
Review: Despite the occasional lyrical misstep, Jesus Is King is a wonder of production, housing some of West's most focused and inspired work since 2013's Yeezus.

Title: White Chalk
Review: White Chalk shifts between comforting melancholy and supremely discomforting performativity with preternatural ease.

Title: Half Free
Review: This is the unmistakeable sound of a star being born: this is an album with something to say, in a voice all of its own.

Title: Accelerate
Review: Accelerate isn't quite as irresistible as some people might have you believe, but you can't help feeling glad they stuck around to make it.

Title: Heaven To A Tortured Mind
Review: It’s so heart-rending you could keep yourself wrapped inside its comfort for hours and not come out. To all those troubled minds and torn hearts clinging to the past, this is utterly heavenly.

Title: V
Review: V's spiraling, cathartic anthems often collapse under their own weight. [21 Sep 2001, p.84]

Title: Past Life Martyred Saints
Review: As an album, a glorious rawness and disregard for verse-chorus-verse simplicity runs throughout, but it strains for cohesion.

Title: Degeneration Street
Review: As ever, the gravel-voiced Lightburn sounds as if singing for his life rather than his supper yet, without sacrificing that epic feel that always set this band apart, he's broadening his horizons. [Apr 2011, p.101]

Title: Wrote a Song For Everyone
Review: While quite meaty in itself, this is odd and not necessarily called for. [Jul 2013, p.88]

Title: Divers
Review: Divers is another meticulous masterpiece from one of the songwriters of her time, an album that’ll still be spellbinding generations from now.

Title: Shields
Review: It's a warm-blooded record, beholden to analogue gear and flawless mastering--one destined to fit snugly on a turntable rather than to live as ones and zeros on your iPod.

Title: My Woman
Review: My Woman is a new watermark for Olsen. It somehow elaborates on the disparate missions of both Half Way Home and Burn Your Fire For No Witness while reaching out into the unfamiliar spaces of dreamy synthpop and more hook-driven, pop-oriented songwriting.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Review: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart can easily be at the forefront of this scene because, simply put, they have the best hooks.

Title: Actor
Review: Her voice seems small and fragile, but it's her most effective instrument, and it affixes a tight lynchpin to the album's broadly creative themes, leaving it glistening with ghostly elegance.

Title: End Times
Review: End Times sounds like a record that could, maybe should, be performed from a psychologist's couch. But it's an intriguing dialogue nevertheless.

Title: High as Hope
Review: It's an album that makes you feel the real Florence Welch is only beginning. [Aug 2018, p.106]

Title: I Am Alive In Everything I Touch
Review: Songs like “Heaven, Hell and Purgatory” will beat you down only to lift you up again, it’s a sonic ride worth taking.

Title: Undun
Review: If one can express disappointment in undun, it's that it sets out to tell a story and tells it well, but delivers a short story or a novella where fans of The Roots would have undoubtedly preferred a full length novel.

Title: Load Blown
Review: Possibly the most confident and successful of this third phase of Black Dice, the pieces here make no claims to exist as anything but the welcoming and obtuse freaks of rhythms gone awry.

Title: Strangers to Ourselves
Review: Strangers isn’t bottled lightning like The Moon & Antarctica or The Lonesome Crowded West, nor does it contain a magnitude 9 single like Good News or Ship, but its unwieldy stature and combative stance compliments Modest Mouse’s storied discography.

Title: Coexist
Review: Deceptively uneasy listening at times, but worth the effort.

Title: Mission Control
Review: The album sounds like something complete, that survived the changes that were necessary to make it.

Title: What Will We Be
Review: Tellingly, 'Angelika' and 'Maria Leonza' only get comfortably loose and silly when halfway finished. With a Strokes-y guitar part and a driving backbeat, the innovative '16th & Valencia, Roxy Music' is hopefully what Banhart will be in the future. [Dec 2009, p.108]

Title: Source
Review: Where the jazz content is foregrounded however, the music is less convincing. ... Garcia’s tone bears more than a passing resemblance to Kamasi Washington’s, with a similar paucity of harmonic complexity and grandstanding solos conveying an earnest seriousness that mistakes widescreen emoting for genuine emotional content. [Sep 2020, p.52]

Title: All of a Sudden I Miss Everyone
Review: Explosions in the Sky... are like the Kronos Quartet with big amps and John Bonham in the back, exploring the composed details in their music before blowing 'em up.

Title: No Pressure
Review: Building upon labyrinthine beds of sound and plump rhythms with lyrics that are both funny and frank, Logic is in his best, kid-like Q-Tip mode.

Title: Because of the Times
Review: Not quite a soaring rock masterpiece, but certainly a bold move that achieves a variable degree of success. Because of the Times proves that Kings of Leon have the ability to change move into new territory, as so many of their garage peers from five years ago have failed to do.

Title: Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!!
Review: It’s not surprising, then, that a number of the tunes on Dig!!! Lazarus Dig!!! sound familiar. Besides the ones that sound like rewrites of Iggy Pop and Leonard Cohen rewrites, Cave and crew aren’t above recycling their own work--'More News From Nowhere' is just a riff on 'Deanna.'

Title: Await Barbarians
Review: Well aware now of what he likes to do with Hot Chip and what he likes to do eponymously, Taylor’s efforts here are enough to sate fans until the next solo project arrives.

Title: KoKoro
Review: The LP expands her sound, but it does little to wrench her out of the darker-shade-of-twee headspace where she’s resided for years.

Title: She
Review: It's not only a testament to her sheer persistence as an artist, but also a powerful soul record that showcases her remarkable vocal talent with a concise collection of expertly performed songs.

Title: Primal Heart
Review: Primal Heart is a collision of hard electronics with light sprinkles of au courant R&B making for Kimbra’s most mainstream statement yet.  ... However, her most ambitious efforts don’t quite reach their apex, causing her somewhat cocky assertions to land flat.

Title: World Peace Is None of Your Business
Review: The album has its fair share of filler.... But, at its best, World Peace feels like a perfect penultimate episode in the last season of a beloved TV series. [Aug 2014, p.66]

Title: Emmaar
Review: It’s a truly absorbing listen, almost effortless. For a band that have been through so much turmoil, they convey so much beauty.

Title: Raise Vibration
Review: It's heroically earnest and not a little preposterous, but the singer's charisma carries it over the line. [Oct 2018, p.112]

Title: Gravitas
Review: he uneven, occasionally locked-in Gravitas finds Talib Kweli energetically exercising his artistry free of any agenda but his own, and hopefully positioning him for a true return to form next time around.

Title: Threace
Review: On Threace, the group’s second full-length for Drag City, Cave’s heart still beats to the motorik pulse, but they’ve broadened out their repertoire to include some of the other groovy, stoney sounds of the 70s.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: The results are hit or miss going forward.

Title: The Slideshow Effect
Review: Memoryhouse push their indolent, Sunday morning music as far as possible into the depths of recollection.

Title: Feel It Break
Review: her band's seedy synth pop more often recalls Kate Bush's dramatic art songs and the Knife's ghostly techno-pop (and more specifically, the soured vowels of frontwoman Karin Andersson).

Title: The Return
Review: This is a talent to watch, The Return laying down an impressive statement of intent, a marker of Sampa The Great’s potential. This will surely grow with subsequent releases, and it is exciting to think of where she could go next.

Title: Bottle It In
Review: The album’s second half becomes noticeably more lo-fi as it draws to a close, with the band laying down instrumental nebulas into which Vile allows his voice to languidly recline. It’s a hazy ending to a bear of an album, but one that rewards those who stuck with it through the 80 or so minutes.

Title: Golden
