Review: Golden contains several songs that sound custom-made for rolling the window down and turning the volume up.... However, any Lady A disc has to contain at least a couple of heartbreaking ballads, and they don't disappoint here.

Title: The Fall
Review: The strange, yet awfully satisfying, collection of tracks certainly won't attract new listeners to the Gorillaz catalogue, but synth-infused pop tracks like "Revolving Door" or "Hillbilly Man" will appease most listeners.

Title: The Fragile Army
Review: Flute and horn fight for breath alongside swampy vocals, and a heavy-handed rock bombast doesn't hide a dearth of hooks or memorable pop melody. [Sep 2007, p.110]

Title: Cyclops Reap
Review: While it is a shame that some of these ideas don’t feel more fully fleshed out, there are still plenty of moments that set characterise White Fence as some of the most interesting ’60s-tinged music being released.

Title: Hotspot
Review: Through it all, Tennant and Lowe feel as confident and progressive as ever, honoring their signature sound while continuing to push it into the future.

Title: Because of You
Review: Because of You mostly reminds us of the Ne-Yo Problem. He wants to be bad, but chickens out at the last minute.

Title: Happy Birthday
Review: Thomas' craft is tremendous for a newcomer, especially in an indie-rock moment that needs it.

Title: Yanqui U.X.O.
Review: While most of Slow Riot and at least parts of Skinny Fists shine through from a distance, much of what makes this album great is its painstaking detail.

Title: Love Letter
Review: His decision to ditch the club and retreat to a more conventionally romantic setting allows him to let his voice take center stage, which is where it should have been all along.

Title: Intimacy
Review: Rushed it may have been, but here Bloc Party seem to accurately reflect post-relationship blues: confused, introspective and stung.

Title: The Third Hand
Review: The record loses momentum when its latter half settles into decompressed electronica, but RJD2's daring innovation and unconventional melodies are enough to cement his reputation as hip-hop's most adventurous musical astronaut. [Mar 2007, p.63]

Title: Seek Warmer Climes
Review: Seek Warmer Climes is itself predatory--but with a delicate, skeletal shudder, it turns that hunger into a lonely howl.

Title: Alegranza
Review: It’s hard to know what to make of such attention to individual moments in an album so devoted to the overall spectacle; it’s harder because those privileged moments are spread so sparsely throughout.

Title: Familiars
Review: The album's focus on horn arrangements and roomy, dreamlike production gives it a singular feel, one where listening through the entire album feels not unlike wading through a field of tall reeds as an inexplicably sad autumn day fades into twilight.

Title: OK Cowboy
Review: This is an album that leaves you in absolutely no doubt that, at the very least, Pascal Arbez-Nicolas is the best thing to come out of France since Daft Punk. [30 Apr 2005, p.63]

Title: Celebration, Florida
Review: Celebration, Florida doesn't simply reflect the hubbub of America as the Felice Brothers see it. The album becomes a part of the spectacle, which is surely not what the band intended.

Title: Blue Film
Review: On casual listen it’s a perfectly pleasant electro-classical record. But despite the considerable technical talents of its creator, it could be by just about anyone.

Title: Mangy Love
Review: Mangy Love would succeed even without lyrics. Produced leisurely with Rob Schnapf (Elliott Smith) and Dan Horne and featuring 21 extra musicians, this is McCombs’ richest ever recording. Sublime flourishes abound.

Title: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes
Review: Hard Times and Nursery Rhymes is throwback after throwback, the album where the roots-rock traditionalism that has always been the counterweight to Ness's punk modernism finally comes crushing down on the whole Social Distortion enterprise.

Title: Furr
Review: Singer-guitarist Eric Earley accesses the haunted Americana Wilco nailed on "Yankee Hotel Foxtrot," with big nods to mid-'60s Bob Dylan, early-'70s Neil Young and the country Grateful Dead. [Oct 2008, p.78]

Title: Idlewild
Review: OutKast’s brains and playfulness sparkle throughout "Idlewild."... But despite the new, jazzy trappings "Idlewild" is more superficial than OutKast’s older albums.

Title: What Is There
Review: The album has a Side A and Side B feel to it with the first half comprised of layered, dense tunes as is mixer Blake’s penchant. Side B (if you will) lightens the sonics a bit, giving the band more room to breathe and, for these ears, an easier listening experience.

Title: Gaslighter
Review: The management of tone throughout is also masterful and consistent. For all the shifting that occurs within individual songs, it’s always anchored to place by restrained instrumentation and artful, deliberate counterpoints between highs and lows.

Title: Brothers
Review: Entirely produced by the Black Keys (except for the Danger Mouse-helmed song "Tighten Up"), the pair's latest album, Brothers, lures with its spooky throwback sound, preternatural grooves and dark bluesy jams.

Title: The Evens
Review: Nothing ever explodes on The Evens, which eschews Fugazi-style noise in favor of subtle dynamics and unsettling clarity. [#68, p.92]

Title: Pala
Review: A headlong rush of an album, Pala is accomplished, bold, and very, very danceable; everything Friendly Fires' debut promised and more.

Title: Shadow People
Review: There are truly transcendent moments on Shadow People, they’re just nestled in among the ones that never quite lift off. Add it all up and The Limiñanas remain a very cool band, which is a perfectly fine thing to be.

Title: Era
Review: The very hooky, liltingly pretty "Nothing Lasts" shows that Echo Lake would be pretty great if they dropped all the aspirations of epicness and just made simple little pop songs instead. They do reach for the stars on Era, however, and they end up shining just like the brightest of them.

Title: Frozen Niagara Falls
Review: This is a great album, and it's incredible to see Fernow again broadening the scope of the noise genre.

Title: Torture
Review: It's clear that the gore-obsessed band shows no signs of slowing down.

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: Aside from these conceptual assertions that it evokes, Feed the Animals is a good record. Though it’s broken up into 14 tracks, it functions best (and as Girl Talk intends) as a single 53-minute mash-up.

Title: Tarpaper Sky
Review: The tunes are a panorama of Crowell's favoured styles.  [Jun 2014, p.91]

Title: Beings
Review: It’s an album that may not crack the Top 10, but to those who succumb to it’s beguiling atmosphere, this is a record that will live with you for some time to come.

Title: Sensuous
Review: While undoubtedly charming in it’s naivety, it also feels slight and transitional, filled with a sense of thin momentary distraction.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Everyday Robots is a graceful and beguiling album from an artist that continues to explore, mature and surprise us with each release. Not bad for a debut album.

Title: Twelve Reasons To Die
Review: Ghost's raps are more Staten Island than Sicily. [Jul 2013, p.76]

Title: Not Your Kind of People
Review: This comeback album suggests a hiatus spent in a cryogenic freezer. Which is to say that they sound the same ... only rather less vital.

Title: Double Up
Review: The reaction Double Up provokes makes you think of the scene from The Producers when the opening night performance of Springtime For Hitler ends and the camera pans on to the audience: open-mouthed, frozen, aghast.

Title: I Am Not Afraid of You and I Will Beat Your Ass
Review: Their best since '95's Electr-O-Pura. [Oct 2006, p.127]

Title: Love and Other Planets
Review: Unfortunately, Adem’s efforts to take his music to new places result in the abandonment of much of what made Homesongs so appealing.

Title: Out of the Woods
Review: Call it Everything About The Girl. [Mar 2007, p.99]

Title: White People
Review: As eclectic as these 13 songs are, they all sound of a piece: Experlty cut and finished with fine details. [Nov 2004, p.135]

Title: Mezmerize
Review: Mezmerize doesn't fail to be unique.

Title: The Bronx (IV)
Review: Matt Caughthran's vocals have never been stronger, more melodic or capable of holding centre stage. Yet coupled with the slicker sheen to the LP (self-made in their new home studio) it has pushed some of their material into territories traditionally inhabited by the totally underwhelming.

Title: You Will Never Be One of Us
Review: Loathing permeates the band's third album like xenophobia at a Trump rally. Emulating Black Flag gone grindcore, You Will Never Be One of Us beats brief thrashers "Parasite," "Made to Make You Fail," "Violence Is Forever" senseless with merciless precision.

Title: Dangerously in Love
Review: Beyoncé never met a ballad she didn't like. Out of Dangerously in Love's 14 tracks, a staggering eight are the kind of overwrought, no-tempo love songs even Toni Braxton has the sense to avoid.

Title: Walking On A Dream
Review: Although Empire tries mightily, they collapse underneath too many ideas before the record is even half over.

Title: Blue Gardens
Review: Blue Gardens is really well put-together with love and affection sown directly into its seams. Another future classic from the Keysound camp.

Title: Afraid of Ghosts
Review: Finally, a grown-up album from the oldest kid at the party. [Apr 2015, p.92]

Title: Dummy Boy
Review: His blend of garish Day-Glo net art and brawling homage to the glory years of DMX and Onyx may be a commercially effective millennial update of Rotten Apple thug rap. But aesthetically, his distinct lack of lyrical talent and annoyingly hyperactive presence often undermines the whole thing.

Title: Dead
Review: The balance between pop and experimentalism is very fine but Young Fathers strike it with exuberant ease.

Title: The Evolution of Man
Review: This is a rock album for those whose idea of rock heroism is Red Hot Chili Peppers, U2, or maybe Muse if they're feeling a bit crazy. If that's you, you'll bloody love it. Everyone else will have to hope Example's evolution is just the beginning.

Title: The Apple and the Tooth
Review: Starting right where Ambivalence Avenue left off, Wilkinson’s strides on his inspired high with The Apple and the Tooth are again, an exceptional thing to witness.

Title: Take Me to the Alley
Review: It’s more of a slow burn and a slight step backward from Liquid Spirit’s dynamic nature. The results are nice, but with too few standouts, Alley breezes by.

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: Chatten’s monotone downtrodden vocals with direct lyrics (not going much deeper than their titles) dominate the songs. This style will either pull in the listener or alienate as the woe is me gloom follows each song like a small rain cloud.

Title: Solo
Review: To make so many overt references to his musical heroes while never losing sight of himself speaks to Iyer's own command. His improvisations have such clarity and vision, and it's rare that he stretches things any longer than necessary.

Title: A Little Bit Longer
Review: Too many of these songs get bogged down in chord changes and lyrics likely to sound worn-out even to a 10-year-old.

Title: Le Noise
Review: There are a couple of Young's obligatory, wandering acoustic ditties to water down the already short track list, and Lanois' soft touch seems to render antiseptic even those few moments of feedback and reverb.

Title: Didn't He Ramble
Review: Didn't He Ramble shimmers, saunters and charms; Hansard has never sounded so good.

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: Instead of having to suffer the middling albums for years before some sort of payoff, you get a nice mixture here, and thankfully the ratio is reversed in favor of the solid material.

Title: The Mountain Will Fall
Review: The methods have changed but Shadow's unorthodox sense of rhythm remains reassuringly familiar.

Title: Hysterical
Review: They make a decent stab at it.  But with such an overfamiliar sound, it smacks too much of the World Cup exit montage. [Oct 2011, p.117]

Title: The Black Parade
Review: This is one to file alongside 'American Idiot', 'Doolittle' and 'Nevermind' on your greatest US rock albums shelf.

Title: Haha Sound
Review: It's certainly very cleverly composed and constructed but ultimately sounds aloof and impenetrable and, as a result, somewhat devoid of emotion.

Title: Undun
Review: undun clocks in at well under an hour, Questlove said he wants it to be "ADD proof", a running time that also magnifies the importance of the third of the album that's purely instrumental. It's on these vocal-free tracks that The Roots truly show what they're capable of.

Title: Make Way for Love
Review: Whereas his debut self-titled album was a perfectly serviceable slice of alt-country, it wasn’t really distinctive enough to stand ahead of the pack. That’s all changed with Make Way For Love which, at times, contains some of the heartbreakingly beautiful songs you’ll hear all year.

Title: The Beginning
Review: Peas leader will.i.am mixes up house and disco beats, Chic and Slick Rick samples, wonky Moog hooks, crunchy guitars, and '70s funk bass into one of the year's wildest sonic stews.

Title: Dead Drunk
Review: For fans who are obsessed with seeking out everything Animal Collective, Black Dice, and experimental noise related, it's a fine bet, but for others this is going to rub the wrong way, which I suppose is part of the point.

Title: High Violet
Review: With High Violet, The National has graduated from being a critic's band. Now it belongs to everyone.

Title: The Shepherd's Dog
Review: This record is vast, playful, and most importantly, an absolute joy to listen to.

Title: Some Are Lakes
Review: Produced by Bon Iver's Justin Vernon, cuts like 'Yuppy Flu' and 'It's Okay' are steeped in morbid imagery, but Powell's passionate delivery makes this set life-affirming.

Title: Red Gone Wild: Thee Album
Review: He's in fine form, spitting a string of mishievously witty quotables over grimy old-school samples. [30 Mar 2007, p.71]

Title: Donkey
Review: Polished instead of rough, thoughtful instead of brash, Donkey isn't an outright failure, but it certainly is an odd and sometimes disappointing move from a band that didn't necessarily need to change its direction.

Title: The Only Place
Review: The record is sophisticated. [Jun 2012, p.78]

Title: Down There
Review: This is strictly a headphone listen--or, more likely, non-listen. [Nov 2010, p.108]

Title: Heart on My Sleeve
Review: By emphasizing melody and feel over art and angst, Lambert's come up with a debut that goes down quite smoothly.

Title: Deeper
Review: Deeper represents an exquisite documentation of post-punk's darkest hour.

Title: Gathered
Review: Gathered is a lovely collection of songs that offers sonic variety, wit, wisdom and intimate moments seemingly issued straight from the heart.

Title: The Sides and in Between
Review: Ultimately, Sides and in Between is an exercise in nostalgia, but there is a good-natured, homespun vibe at play throughout that helps to smooth out some of the more overtly retro trappings.

Title: Lifetime
Review: Lifetime is marked by aesthetic and personal conflict, and while it doesn’t uncover easy resolution, its beauty (and it is a remarkably beautiful record) derives in large part from the acceptance, or even embrace, of those conflicts as what generates a lifetime’s meaning.

Title: Youth Novels
Review: As things stand, a lot of people are going to fall in love with this new young talent, and her ambitious and creative debut. But Lykke Li is likely to stay a cult curiosity for now.

Title: Let's Be Still
Review: It's a beautiful set of sweeping prairie ballads. [Jan 2014, p.122]

Title: White Women
Review: Derivative though White Women often is, and knows it is, Chromeo's level of engagement remains well above #TBT posturing.

Title: Spills Out
Review: Spills Out is a satisfying album that puts a unique spin on otherwise trite indie-pop touchstones and a marriage of dissonance and charm seamless enough that, at times, it's almost difficult to tell one from the other.

Title: Back to Me
Review: Fantasia's rough-hewn vocals shine best on "The Thrill Is Gone," which features a similarly raspy  Cee-Lo Green.

Title: Justified
Review: Justified is just sound and posturing, with no core.

Title: Employment
Review: Essentially, 'Employment' is a very British record; an entirely Britpop creation spawned ten years after the event.

Title: Decemberunderground
Review: Singer Davey Havok continues to impress with his range and ability to quickly turn from a throat-searing scream to a bare-boned croon, as does the entire band's consistently exciting approach to songwriting and their music aesthetic.

Title: This Is Not The World
Review: The Futureheads are the Futureheads on their third full-length, This Is Not the World--rhythmically anxious, melodically electrifying, and almost mechanically precise.

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: With Rehab, Ghostface proves his tried-and-true technique has plenty of juice left in it.

Title: Blowback
Review: Much of this fascinating, infuriating record is defined by his commingling of HipHop, Electro, dancehall, and, most problematically, stadium alt.rock... Some of it is just odd enough to work. [#209, p.62]

Title: Brightblack Morning Light
Review: Most of the material is as impressive in sound as it is atmosphere.

Title: This Dream Of You
Review: These days, a classic croons are cool again. Witness the 90-something year old Tony Bennett or the ongoing admiration for Sinatra, Bobby Darin and others that share that seemingly romantic repast. In that regard, This Dream of You offers comforts you can count on.

Title: Augustines
Review: This time, with their newest album, the band seem to want to give something back, and whilst obviously somewhat dark at moments, it comes loaded with joyous and celebratory sounds.

Title: Atrocity Exhibition
Review: Rich, deep, full of wit, rapid fire lyrics and fantastically unusual production, it’s Danny Brown proving yet again that he is one of the most exciting rappers working right now.

Title: End It All
Review: These are collaborations worth hearing, but in no way at all do they add up to an end product that is particularly memorable or consistently engaging.

Title: Soldier of Love
Review: They’ve plied a unique blend of jazz, world, pop and soul for more than a quarter-century, and now they add heavier beats, craftier production and a wider arsenal of sounds and styles.

Title: Piano & a Microphone 1983
Review: It’s Prince as few have heard him: inspired, unrestrained, playing for no one but himself and the engineer who pushed the record button. Clearly this isn’t for everyone. But those looking for a glimpse into the artist, mostly pre-global fame, working out new and old material, will find it an invaluable and unique addition to his already bulging catalog.

Title: Sunlight Makes Me Paranoid
Review: Elefant frontman Diego Garcia must have memorized nearly every song by the Cure while he was growing up, because his band's debut album, Sunlight Makes Me Paranoid, is a shameless, abstract pop mix, a solid indie pop record heavy in new wave aesthetics.

Title: LOSE
Review: LOSE is captivating because it uses all the right tricks.

Title: Welcome to the Dollhouse
Review: These gals are older, more cohesive, and more enchanting than before, plus Maxim-approved.

Title: The Morning After
Review: Comprising eight tracks and running to just over half-an-hour, it's a crucible of stark arrangements, contemplative moods and subtle hooks; never earth-shattering yet consistently, discreetly affecting.

Title: Cage the Elephant
Review: Cage the Elephant didn't exist until 2005, but as this self-titled album demonstrates, their ability to be influenced by alternative rock and classic rock simultaneously is a definite plus.

Title: Something for Everybody
Review: Obsolescence isn't the real problem with Something For Everybody, Devo's first album since 1990-instead, the disc suffers from simply sounding like a weak iteration of itself.

Title: Kill the Lights
Review: Kill the Lights isn’t consistently pleasing, but it does represent a progression and evolution from Luke’s previous material.

Title: 8 Diagrams
Review: Minus ODB, the collective's most charismatic member, and rife with in-group strife, 8 Diagrams is a long way from the hip hop revolution, "Enter The Wu-Tang (36 Chambers)." It still ain't nothin’ to fuck with.

Title: Phoenix
Review: There's still a lot of soul-searching at mournful tempos, but reconnecting to his roots has made for a fine set of songs. [Feb 2019, p.93]

Title: A Wonderful Beast
Review: A Wonderful Beast feels more like a partially successful experiment than a fully realized meeting of the minds, but Johnson, Carney, and Branch complement one another better than one might expect, and this shows Johnson is still game to try new things and push the boundaries of his musical comfort zone.

Title: Girl with Basket of Fruit
Review: After that early-onset dizziness subsides, Girl With Basket of Fruit loses its power and makes little impact, as if these songs were menacing storm clouds that simply drift into and out of town without leaving a trace. It is heavy but hollow, muscular but oddly meaningless, built with streams of images that, however vivid, are the lyrical equivalent of inert gas inside combustion chambers.

Title: True Romance
Review: Early exploits including a ridiculous rhyme about T-Rex amorousness ("Dinosaur Sex"), jabs at vapid art-school scenesters ("Art Bitch" and "!Franchesckaar!"), and some indecipherable indie-dance vocoding ("I Wanna Be Darth Vader"). True Romance is a strident departure from those frivolities so far as solid, true-to-aim songwriting is concerned, but the divergence and a touch of the silliness remains.

Title: That's How Rumors Get Started
Review: Make no mistake, Price is her own artist. Nicks' recordings may have inspired Price, but the material on this album shows just how much she has developed as a unique and talented artist.

Title: WYW
Review: A typically obdurate outing from an always captivating contributor. [15 Apr 2017, p.52]

Title: Sunshine Rock
Review: Sunshine Rock is bitter and hopeful, full of rage and promise. It’s an album that defines a moment in all its ugliness and the rare moments of beauty that we have to keep fighting for.

Title: DÃ©jÃ  Vu
Review: Several of the album's tracks might not hold up if not for Moroder's brilliant production work tying it all together.

Title: Invaders Must Die
Review: The Prodigy's fifth studio album sounds just like The Prodigy should. Only leaner, harder, and even faster than before. [Apr 2009, p.96]

Title: Nocturama
Review: Often funeral-march slow, but there are also flashes of passionate energy.

Title: Ladytron
Review: This is a record that feels handcrafted for the fans that waited so long for new material. Had you already previously invested in their icy yet sleek sound, then Ladytron is a welcome, if not wholly groundbreaking, return.

Title: Wolf's Law
Review: The Joy Formidable proves on Wolf's Law that it can create grandeur and awe by letting contrast and touch speak volumes more than overpowering brute force can.

Title: The Sunlandic Twins
Review: Barnes' bright-eyed, bushy-tailed vocals are at times trying, but there is substance and craft behind the unrelentingly catchy ditties.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: The whole thing sounds like they had a blast. [Jun 2013, p.88]

Title: Almanac
Review: Lashings of reverb and experimentation with acoustic instruments draw the music into something much more evocative.

Title: Young for Eternity
Review: [A] sterling debut. [Mar 2006, p.122]

Title: Just Like You
Review: Falling In Reverse have given fans the rare gift of an artist stepping back to the sound they originally fell in love with. [Apr 2015, p.89]

Title: Dreams Come True
Review: Having heard Taylor's fingerprints over a dozen fine records, it's great to finally hear one that he can call his own.

Title: Junip
Review: Gonzalez's intricate, mellifluous guitar playing is not front and center, but committed followers of this side of his artistry will certainly be satisfied.

Title: Preteen Weaponry
Review: The incredible ride finishes not with a bang but with a whimper. Preteen Weaponry isn't much more than a 39-minute sonic experiment for a band seeking a new direction, but it's such a mindfuck to listen to, who cares where it ends up?

Title: Paid tha Cost to Be da Boss
Review: Not since his debut has the Doggfather been any higher. [#12, p.155]

Title: Swing Lo Magellan
Review: Dirty Projectors has never done so much with so little, a rare feat reiterated by the disarming, insistent standout, "Gun Has No Trigger."

Title: AJ Tracey
Review: With his debut album he firmly establishes himself as one of the leading lights in UK rap (if there were any doubts), and in a year where some of the scene’s heavyweights are also dropping albums, it won’t be a surprise if AJ’s project is rated as among the best of them by the end of 2019.

Title: Candylion
Review: On paper, it looks so wide-ranging as to be in danger of coming out gloopy and overdone; as it turns out, Rhys glues everything together with a crisp sense of confidence. [Feb 2007, p.98]

Title: Libertine
Review: It runs longer than an hour, and no matter how much you liked the Smiths you probably don't hav ethe patience for that much Gene. [#56, p.89]

Title: One Life Stand
Review: Hot Chip's impressive musical facility remains, it's merely a little out of focus. [Apr 2010, p.102]

Title: Widdershins
Review: Phillips’ melodies are solid and simplistically accessible, never swamping the lyric’s articulate message; protest songs have rarely been so polite in their persuasiveness.

Title: Boy
Review: It’s another glorious achievement for an artist who has created so much amazing art since arriving into the world fully formed way back in 1982.

Title: Sepalcure
Review: It's too cavernous and intangible to dance to but too wired for relaxation.

Title: Adult Nights
Review: Adult Nights is an engaging debut from a band that wears its sunny California influences as well as if they were born and bred there.

Title: Music For Men
Review: As a musical statement of intent to the throngs of the newly interested, Music For Men shows a clear picture of who Gossip want to be--a New Millennial Madonna for whom Danceteria never closes. But for those who have been following Gossip's career, waiting with bated breath to see how the band will evolve, this new record may feel a little too much like they are still Standing in the Way of Control.

Title: Sonic Nurse
Review: The Youth sound rejuvenated. [Jul 2004, p.108]

Title: Blood Mountain
Review: "Blood Mountain" is a strong record by a powerful band nearing an ideal of cohesion.

Title: Life In Cartoon Motion
Review: The massive dip in quality towards the end, including the progressive worsening through closing, bonus and hidden tracks, is disappointing, considering how well the album begins.

Title: Smile
Review: At first it seems she’s bounced back undaunted: galvanising opener Never Really Over thrums with fizzing electro synths; Daisies pushes back against detractors with brio. Yet there’s a creeping lethargy, a sense that, at 35 and about to become a mother, Perry’s kitschy shtick of old doesn’t quite fit any more, but that she hasn’t found a way forward she can connect with.

Title: 7 Days of Funk
Review: The name of this project might be 7 Days of Funk, but there’s enough groove in this mofo to last a lifetime.

Title: Benji
Review: This guy has written 40-plus albums of material, so it's saying something that Benji is one of his more challenging listens.

Title: Emperor of Sand
Review: Working again with producer Brendan O’Brien, Mastodon maintains their polished technical expertise. The album is clean but not scrubbed of feeling.

Title: One Life Stand
Review: Fuller than usual of slow songs and piano ballads, One Life Stand is their mellowest, most thoughtful effort so far — which means it carries the risk of also being their most boring. (Contrast is one of their secret weapons, though it didn't seem like such a big deal until now.) But keep listening: slow to reveal, its charm is just as slow to fade.

Title: Victim of Love
Review: His quiet, reasoning delivery works beautifully, and reminds one of the singer's instinctive ability to transform a song. [May 2013, p.91]

Title: Crystal Castles
Review: Such blipping and beeping stay true to the pair's beginnings as an eight-bit band, but Crystal really pushes all the right buttons when factoring wistful melodies into its playful computer glitches. [21 Mar 2008, p.57]

Title: Both Ways Open Jaws
Review: This terrific sequel feels bigger and better. [Dec 2011, p.81]

Title: All at Once
Review: Although not every song is essential in its own right, as a whole, All At Once congeals beautifully; in the era of the single, this is a real album, touching on themes of autonomy and control both in a personal and a wider political context.

Title: boygenius EP
Review: All these songs stand out for their craftsmanship and collaboration, not only between three artists but also three friends.

Title: The First Days Of Spring
Review: This is a beautiful album. Moving rather than maudlin, uplifting rather than depressing.

Title: What a Time to Be Alive
Review: It’s a hurricane of pop-punk fury with as much ferocity as anything the band recorded 25+ years ago.

Title: Always Ascending
Review: Like their past work, subpar filler holds the album back. It’s worth joining them for the climb, just know that it’s going to be an uneven ascent.

Title: II Trill
Review: This time out, he's a single short and couple songs too long, but his back is strong enough to carry the weight, proving once again he's one of the Dirty South's most reliable voices.

Title: Manic
Review: The real problem is that the best ideas are outvoted by frustrating ones, leaving us with little touches like the short, yelping-like sound in the second verse of More or the distorted vocals that end killing boys. There are some good moments here, but even the best of them can’t help Halsey get out of her own way.

Title: The Invisible Man
Review: This time out, Eitzel has built his arrangements around spare keyboard lines, atmospheric electronic samples, and percussion loops that blend with his voice and acoustic guitar to create an effect that suggest a more spare, organic version of Portishead, or a Jon Brion production that's stuck in a blue funk. But the new surroundings suit the songs quite well...

Title: Impossible Spaces
Review: Suffice to say Impossible Spaces itself is a journey, and one of the more all-encompassing ones I've had the pleasure of taking this year.

Title: Rockwell
Review: Her songs together paint a picture of a forthright, plangent character who, like Frida Hyvonen, mines experience for universe-level significance.

Title: MAGDALENE
Review: By its close, FKA twigs is an unstoppable force of nature.

Title: We Can't Fly
Review: While it's important to have ambition, Deluca probably should have stuck to the sound he does so well. His desire to stretch makes We Can't Fly a misfire of an album. It would have made a nice EP though.

Title: All Days Are Nights: Songs For Lulu
Review: All Days Are Nights is the sound of the man doing what he does best: bruised, tender, emotional and, at times, quite brilliant music.

Title: Feel That Fire
Review: It would be nice if some of the titular burn could be felt on Dierks Bentley's fourth studio album, but Feel That Fire is an atypically cautious, calculated affair from one of Nashville's best singer/songwriters of the 2000s.

Title: DS2
Review: It has little of the far-reaching ambition of Honest, but what it lacks in bold strokes, it more than makes up for in consistency.

Title: Let It Come Down
Review: Pierce enhances his trademark electro-scapes with rich gospel choruses and grand orchestral flourishes for operatic effect.

Title: Information
Review: Information is a decent effort that unfortunately doesn't quite bite as hard as it should.

Title: Reality Testing
Review: There’s a lack of precision, with a flabby middle section finding ‘Begin To Begin’, for example, looping aimlessly. Yet when it hits home, Reality Testing more than justifies Lone’s tag as one of the most flexible, dextrous producers in the game.

Title: 12 Memories
Review: That title is an overstatement, but the album does offer a few more memorable tracks than its predecessor.

Title: ANTI
Review: This, for better or worse, is clearly the music Rihanna likes: leftfield, stoned and strange. It is Rihanna without hits. This strange album, released without warning over the internet for free, may well be a reflection of the fact that not even her own backers really expects this to be a commercial blockbuster. It is more an exercise in rebranding, transforming the hit girl into a serious artist.

Title: Nightcrawler
Review: Pete Yorn’s songs sound so damn good, it’s easy to assume they’re not smart.

Title: Big Bad World
Review: One can’t help but be at least slightly impressed at the precocious skill with which these polished musicians craft songs so completely shiny and empty.

Title: High Expectations
Review: Sometimes they feel almost too airbrushed, with Mabel playing it a little too safe to qualify being described as wholly original or progressive. There are moments of talent and flair, but it would’ve also been refreshing to hear more personality (and less autotune). Nevertheless, it’s an album that contains some real highlights.

Title: An Object
Review: An Object scales back the ambitious and ostensibly ambient sound of Everything in Between (2010), but it remains gloomily meditative.

Title: If Songs Could Be Held
Review: Thomas may have been perfect for a second- or third-tier Lilith Fair stage, a place where people expect slow, introspective, sweet songwriting. However, if she hopes to capture a larger audience, she may want to first capture herself a faster metronome.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: By not reinventing the wheel, Hercules and Love Affair have surprised us with a great debut album. [Summer 2008]

Title: Take Me Apart
Review: Her debut full-length fuses together jagged textures, vaporous synths and her versatile voice into forward-thinking R&B animated by its restless innovation.

Title: It's Frightening
Review: When Patterson says, "While you're out taking aim, and taking orders." It sounds like an indictment, and is one of the many small touches that litter this near-perfect second album. [Spring 2009, p.68]

Title: Washed Away
Review: If shiny, groovy, melodic, finger-snapping, guitar-led pop-rock is your tipple, you’ll want to guzzle down Washed Away in one.

Title: Caer
Review: There are some meandering points on Caer, but Lewis Jr.’s sobering narrative on piano finale ‘Runaway’ ends things on a poignant high-note.

Title: To Be Still
Review: At her best, on the eerie 'Every Path,' she's mesmeric enough to lure ships onto rocks, but come the inevitable 'Later...With Jools Holland' appearance, older viewers may be forgiven for thinking Dolores O'Riordan has changed dramatically. [Mar 2009, p.96]

Title: I Disagree
Review: Essentially, this is sugar-rush, hyperactive pop music for people with the attention span of a gnat.

Title: III
Review: While Finder is as relentless as they come and Intruder punches harder than chase & Status, The Fool details life in a court during the Middle Ages interestingly enough and there's subtle beauty in Eating Hooks. [Jun 2016, p.114]

Title: Elastic Days
Review: The balancing between folk and rock is still present; the songwriting is straightforward, yet endearing. Even though this is not a revolutionary work, it shows that this guy is a great, skilled songwriter and Elastic Days displays all the wisdom he has gathered through the years.

Title: The Bird and the Bee
Review: The record fits snugly into a certain nameless musical genre that can be found in martini bars and designer-label boutiques the world over, a mish-mash of recognizable sounds and influences that's enjoyable but ultimately hollow.

Title: All The Roadrunning
Review: For a better taste of Harris' harmonizing abilities, try her recent collaborations with young'uns like Bright Eyes and Ryan Adams.

Title: Octahedron
Review: Octahedron  will appeal to elderly prog fans immune to attention deficit disorder, who have the patience to let its charm gradually unfold. [Aug 2009, p.111]

Title: Olympia
Review: The growth in Austra from Feel It Break to Olympia is palpable throughout.

Title: Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts
Review: A Herculean instrumental epic of beautiful depth, staggering grandiosity and extraterrestrial soundscapes. [#7]

Title: Parallax Error Beheads You
Review: Jacobs works in a peerless vacuum located in a hazy plot point on the pop timeline, located somewhere in-between outright sugary pop and nerdy bedroom electronica.

Title: We got it from Here... Thank You 4 Your service
Review: This album succeeds in its goals despite the heartbreaking passing of Phife Dawg while it was being recorded, and even though I had accepted "The Love Movement" as their last chapter all those years ago, this is a much more fitting end.

Title: Make Sure They See My Face
Review: He remains a singular performer, one who can't be overwhelmed by the usual Neptunes production. Williams' typically sparse 'Loose Wires' sounds simultaneously like Kenna's surefire smash--how could that Michael Jackson-inspired hook miss?--and the proof, thanks to its android-crooning verses, that the world will only see Kenna's face on his own, refreshingly distinctive, terms.

Title: Worlds
Review: Although it doesn’t sound quite like EDM, Worlds manages to retain the thrilling rush of emotions that the best raves inspire.

Title: My December
Review: "My December" offers an appealing if uneven snapshot of a girl with a big voice and big emotions who's in transition.

Title: Apocalypse, girl
Review: Sumptuous, but still challenging. [Jul 2015, p.92]

Title: The Grind Date
Review: A great hip-hop album, an accomplishment that whipper-snappers in both hip-hop and the pop-music world at large would benefit from attempting to emulate.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: Go Go... is never less than delightful--at its best like Belle & Sebastian having a stab at Portishead. [Oct 2007, p.99]

Title: The Golden D
Review: A largely useless excuse for a bored millionaire to air out his late-night bedroom recordings at the expense of the kids.

Title: Shall Noise Upon
Review: It is in this purely innovative way that Apollo Sunshine’s melodies are intoxicating, their lyrics epic, and their harmonies luscious--the more this album is listened to, the more the listener is impressed with the knowledge that there is something very powerful at play in this music.

Title: Rugby Thompson
Review: Rugby Thompson is one of those hard albums to critique in that as hip-hop it is inoffensive, and yet when it comes to pushing the boundaries of what the art and music could be there's literally nothing you could point to as innovative or revolutionary.

Title: Expo 86
Review: Expo 86 emphasizes the fact that novel beginnings are meant to prosper whilst winking at the past from time to time.

Title: Oceans Apart
Review: [A] sonic sheen (and the punchy rhythm section) gives the songs an immediacy that the previous reunion records have lacked.

Title: Highly Evolved
Review: The record's big-rock sound works against it, as does its back-and-forth swing from melodic Britpop to room-filling volume.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: Vulnicura is smooth and whole, even as its singer lies shattered.

Title: Hard Love
Review: All this noise stays in service of the songs, which remain as self-reflective and personal as ever.

Title: Storytone
Review: The songs on Storytone glide between those highs and lows with very few false moves, making this one stylistic detour that takes Neil Young very close to his artistic home.

Title: Transfixiation
Review: For a band so obsessed with death, and its erotic possibilities, they sound utterly alive on Transfixiation.

Title: Voices in a Rented Room
Review: Maybe they were trying to evoke Leonard Cohen’s Songs From a Room but they came up with something sweeter (albeit noir-ish) in the process.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: The relationship between the music and Albarn’s voice deepens the album’s theme.

Title: I Love The New Sky
Review: While I Love the New Sky would have been a near-perfect nine-track LP, it's a rare treat that Tim Burgess can give fans something so inspired and inspiring this deep into his career.

Title: Transcendental Youth
Review: It's another perfectly observed collection of songs made real by Darnielle's deceptively plainspoken poetry.

Title: Set My Heart on Fire Immediately
Review: The slow, contemplative songs on Set My Heart on Fire Immediately are hit or miss. Most are moving mood pieces with intricate melodies, while some are bland and skippable. The best Perfume Genius moments are with the dynamic upbeat pop songs, jam-packed with hooks and danceable grooves. Throughout the album, Hadreas forms complex sonic textures out of the thoughts tormenting his psyche. The result is an album that thrills at times, invites quiet reflection at others, but is always interesting.

Title: Myth Takes
Review: Their best yet: it’s multi-faceted like no release before it (from the band’s catalogue), and each and every nuance is super funky.

Title: Little Sparrow
Review: Her taste in cover material is slightly idiosyncratic, but that does nothing but add luster to the program...

Title: Lost Wisdom
Review: These songs may be threadbare, full of holes and silence. But together Elverum and Doiron have made something achingly intimate, so that it feels more complete in its fractures.

Title: Grinderman 2
Review: Indeed, Grinderman 2 is actually a far more listen-able record, with far more replay value, and this is what I'll remember when I find myself nostalgic for the dumb simplicity of the first album.

Title: Pastoral
Review: Not only is Bernholz preaching to the converted, she’s also preaching to an audience who pride themselves on their tolerance for enduring hostility. It might make for a more engaging performance than straightforward listening experience, although Bernholz’s ingenuity does reveal itself.

Title: Adam Green & Binki Shapiro
Review: This 10-track ode to the joys of a sad, sweet, mellow but occasionally dark and atmospheric love song is arranged with tender loving care and produced with just enough reverb to remind you of girl-group classics

Title: Free Reign
Review: As Free Reign shows, when Clinic take their time, they can build up a bewitching groove.

Title: New Material
Review: New Material is certainly not more than the sum of its parts, which causes problems for a band that thrives on the whole, rather than moments of individual magic. It leaves much of New Material ambling by.

Title: Record
Review: Record is solid, without a bad song on it, though with that said, aside from "Queen," "Guitar," and "Go," not much really stands out.

Title: You Can't Take It with You
Review: You Can’t Take It With You sounds like a proper album par excellence, gelling together with a cohesiveness so many strive for but never really hit.

Title: Mini Mansions
Review: Fun, if inessential. [Aug 2011, p.93]

Title: Maladroit
Review: With Maladroit, Weezer has finally given the full punt to the nerd-rock label they sorta invented and always shunned, settling instead for being our generation's version of Cheap Trick.

Title: Wooden Mask
Review: It's the instrumental miniatures that impress the most. [Oct 2016, p.31]

Title: In Advance of the Broken Arm
Review: In Advance of the Broken Arm is at least two songs too long. Yet Stern's manner of weaving together fiercely subjective, lyrical daydreaming with Olympus-level fret-searing finally means that the album justifies the majority of its many decisions.

Title: Wrote a Song For Everyone
Review: These two tracks [“Mystic Highway” and “Train of Fools”] are so strong that one can’t help but wish Fogerty had foregone the duets altogether and recorded a solo album of original material.

Title: Within and Without
Review: Greene's best trick: Using those elements of the past while crafting an album that sounds like a beautiful, dreamy future.

Title: In Conflict
Review: In Conflict is his masterpiece--if not the best album of 2014, certainly the most profound. [No. 109, p.59]

Title: Never, Never, Land
Review: Never, Never, Land not only escapes the expectations and pitfalls that dogged Psyence Fiction, but succeeds on a new set of strengths.

Title: Memphis
Review: Too much of Memphis sounds like a pale copy of a much more impressive band, and Magic Kids really need to find their own, less cloying, voice if they're going to produce something worthwhile.

Title: Beauty Party
Review: While conscious rap often comes off as dour, this is a thoroughly enjoyable record, dignified and jiggy all at once. [Mar 2003, p.94]

Title: The Big Doe Rehab
Review: The ensemble crew can't maintain the promising start. Aside from a few lyrical bullets, 'Paisley Darts' doesn't quite live up to the potential of its title.

Title: All That Must Be
Review: Ultimately, All That Must Be is a glowing album that plots the psychological journey of its creator through the often un-navigable waters of change. Yet somewhere in the Bermuda Triangle of real life, Fitzgerald found his strongest compass.

Title: Islands
Review: Her eclectic song structures and subtle melodies with a tendency to stick help give these songs an indeterminate specificity, like confessionals where her audience can fill in the details with whatever needs unburdening from their own souls. Maybe the sense of place in her music, then, is whatever place it needs to be, for whoever needs it.

Title: Breaks in the Armor
Review: Bachmann may be taking a stark look at things, but rarely had bleakness sounded so appealing.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: Blak and Blu's production (by Rob Cavallo and Mike Elizondo in collaboration with Clark) is too polished and processed for its own good, but if this album isn't likely to change your life, it will make an hour of it a lot more interesting, and there's no arguing that Gary Clark, Jr. is a talent strong enough to match his record company's hype.

Title: The Incident
Review: Stellar 12-minute opus 'Time Flies' teems with Pink Floydesque arrangements and moving lyrics, while 'Octane Twisted' offers up massive guitar riffage that you can bang your head to.

Title: MDNA
Review: No, MDNA can't be hailed as Madge's best ever album, and it may not contain the most thought- provoking lyrics of her career (perhaps an intentional tongue-in-cheek poke at the current state of pop music?), but it is the reigning Queen of Pop's most inspired work since Music, as well as the highly addictive record Madonna celebrants have been craving.

Title: Gang of Losers
Review: Lightburn’s tendency toward over-the-top melodrama has evolved into straightforward and heartfelt lyrics of love and loss. [Summer 2006]

Title: Twelve Nudes
Review: Twelve Nudes is a protest album—indeed the brief and bustling "Blown" opens with the straight statement "Trans Power!"—it's also a fantastic, filthy, punk rock record that offers to cement Furman's growing reputation as one of the best and, coincidentally, most important artists working today.

Title: Kveikur
Review: While energized, Kveikur doesn’t break away from Sigur Rós’ safe spots.

Title: Going Back Home
Review: Brawling tunes steeped in vintage rock & roll, with Daltrey setting his maximum-R&B yowl on full bluster against Johnson's slashing attack.

Title: Sheath
Review: LFO's gift is an ability to strip Detroit's electronic music of its soul, punishing any soft southern edges with a brutal attack of noise, while still managing moments of subtlety and consistently adventurous beat programming.

Title: Be Set Free
Review: These are mediocre, and sometimes painfully inept, approximations of classic lovelorn folk tunes. At a short 38 minutes, the times aren’t changin’ fast enough.

Title: Reformation Post TLC
Review: Tender and loving it might not be, but one of the albums of the year? Definitely.

Title: Waiting For The Moon
Review: The perfect introduction to Tindersticks' queasy, cinematic elegance. [Aug 2003, p.133]

Title: Chemical Chords
Review: Endearing hints of '60s pop glow faintly beneath the frictionless surfaces of Gane's loops, chirps and austerely percolating rhythms. [Sep 2008, p.84]

Title: I'm Only Dreaming
Review: The Texas crew have created a piece of art that probes into what it means to love and be loved with real intent and passion. If you’ve slept on this band up until now, it’s time to change that.

Title: Everyday Nothing
Review: Bentham is very good at what she does. She’s a distinctive songwriter with a penchant for avoiding the obvious, and her songs have a way of lingering, with melodies that scroll through your head like a news ticker.

Title: White Noise
Review: Though the Manchester duo might not be completely on par with the bands they emulate, they more than earn an A for effort while crafting some wonderful melodies along the way.

Title: Laila's Wisdom
Review: Laila's Wisdom is Evans' lyrically broadest and musically richest work, yet it doesn't have the sprawling quality of the first album.

Title: Compassion
Review: Forest Swords' second record is simplistic on purpose, but that doesn’t make it feel less empty.

Title: Our Inventions
Review: The arrangements stick to an effective coast-and-surge model of development: The tracks skim low and then tilt upward with the addition of a drum or synth part. It's a stock trick that works well, and Lali Puna use it with unusual tact.

Title: Some Rap Songs
Review: Some Rap Songs may be a brief exercise, but its ambition and the--largely successful--execution of its ideas demonstrate that the enigmatic Earl is as fascinating as ever.

Title: Hope for the Hopeless
Review: For those still enthralled by the lyrical twists and midtempo folk-rocking of 1972, this record will be manna from heaven.

Title: Tyrannosaurus Hives
Review: Thirty minutes of chugging and howling, you go from one killer riff to another with barely a millisecond to recover. [17 Jul 2004, p.46]

Title: New Path
Review: Beyond simply making surface references to scramble suits and fields of blue flowers, Essaie Pas connect to something deeper--real human emotion.

Title: We Fucked a Flame Into Being
Review: An imperfect first outing that nonetheless shines with the promise of something better ahead.

Title: After Laughter
Review: An undeniably hooky record that strays from its grunge-rock roots and finds the band in a place where they’ve found the fun in their craft once again.

Title: The Future Will Come
Review: For much of The Future Will Come, however, Maclean frustratingly boxes himself into the synth-pop format of the Human League.

Title: C'mon
Review: If you can cope with the intensity, tracks such as Done and the almost unbearably sombre $20 draw a mesmerising beauty from their anguish. [May 2011, p.119]

Title: Man on the Moon: The End of Day
Review: There's a good, possibly even a great, album in here somewhere, but Kid Cudi doesn't get very close to finding it.

Artist: Brian Eno, Jon Hopkins & Leo Abrahams
Title: Small Craft on a Milk Sea
Review: There's no doubting that sounds are placed together, weaved and treated expertly and Small Craft On A Milk Sea can, save its more aggressive moments, flow over and around you therapeutically.

Title: Head First
Review: On Head First, the singer's bandmate-producer Will Gregory creates a pitch-perfect neon-lit '80s wonderland with Hi-NRG bass lines and plenty of that fat synth sound made famous by Van Halen's "Jump."

Title: Finally Woken
Review: Jem’s deadpan tones sound like a slightly huskier, sluttier Beth Orton, and while nothing quite matches the beguiling "They"... she strikes the odd thimbleful of gold.

Title: Cat's Eyes
Review: Whether telegraphing heartbreak, world-weariness, or menacing intent (the latter especially on the Psycho-meets-Bad-Seeds nightmare of "Sooner or Later"), Badwan and Zeffira excel at heightening their musical senses simultaneously to the graces of the Heavens and the billowy depths of Hades.

Title: Machineries of Joy
Review: Learning the lessons of its predecessor, then, album number 5 is an intelligent distillation of everything that people cherish about British Sea Power and what makes them a truly Great British rock band.

Title: Mouseman Cloud
Review: Mouseman is essentially another 17 tracks for completists hankering to mine the singer's ceaseless compendium of songs in search of new nuggets. [#85, p.58]

Title: Villains
Review: On the whole, Villains isn’t Homme’s strongest collection of songwriting. That said, it’s the first Queens Of The Stone Age album where the sounds behind it are consistently strong enough to carry the load.

Title: Yesterday and Today
Review: Yesterday and Today, the sophomore effort from The Field (nee Axel Willner), can be easily understood as part of the tradition of moody follow-ups a la In Utero: a pairing of a signature sound with willful experimentalism.

Title: I Love You, Dude
Review: I Love You Dude is offensive in its banality, and other than that it's so mundane that it's tough to even want to care.

Title: Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots
Review: As strange as it is wonderful.

Title: Shootenanny!
Review: Shootenanny! has all the soft harmonies and lush production of 2000's Daisies of the Galaxy, but while that masterpiece was an homage to symphonic pop, this one is rooted in Southern blues.

Title: Slow Focus
Review: This is the first Fuck Buttons album that feels like post-invasion music. Victory lingers, but it also stings.

Title: Otherness
Review: There's only one track with any forward motion, and it's the overly slick and one-dimensional "I'll Be Back." Otherwise, Otherness is mostly murky and overcooked ballads, without hooks or much emotional impact.

Title: Other Arrangements
Review: Millsap may not have Swift's reputation and his break from his country past is not much of a repudiation of it, but Other Arrangements reveals the depth and range of Millsap's singing talents in his search for a bigger audience.

Title: The Pains of Growing
Review: The album's remainder employs assorted hit-angling producers connected by pop success with young women. The Pains of Growing is consequently more fragmented and less consistent than Know-It-All, but Cara makes the best of it, generally writing in a slightly wiser and sharper manner from the same introverted homebody perspective.

Title: First Impressions of Earth
Review: Turns out what the world was waiting for really was those that saved guitars finally making a record that truly reaped the rewards of their efforts. Is this it? OH GOD YES!

Title: â€
Review: Justice does appear to be that rare breed of dance artist equally capable of stimulating the body and the mind, though neither Richard James nor the Basement Jaxx need fear this act.

Title: White Women
Review: It's not that Chromeo's run out of ideas--they've been a one-idea band all along. But now they've got more of the world singing along, so their brand of fun suddenly means a little bit more.

Title: Mirror Traffic
Review: He may mock his lack of motivation and energy, but on Mirror Traffic, Malkmus sounds more focused than he has in years.

Title: Single Mothers
Review: His gravelly croon is still sombre, but now it carries a glimmer of light in the darkness. [No. 113, p.53]

Title: No Hope, No Future
Review: A darker album, a slightly clumsier album, but an album with a strong unifying themes and a few songs worth stepping away from the bar for.

Title: Bring It Back
Review: Beneath the cheery chug and carnival-like fizz beats a sombre heart. [Oct 2006, p.117]

Title: Book of Changes
Review: Book of Changes is refreshingly exposed and intimate, as if Blakeslee has found a lingua franca for writing when it really matters.

Title: Zoomer
Review: May be the year's most surprising pure pop pleasure--precisely because it's nothing like you'd expect a pop album to be. [#224, p.61]

Title: Mangy Love
Review: There is a wonderful tension on Mangy Love between the pleasure of the music--lush, soulful, spinning out from Elliot Smith or Lambchop--and the often ugly, complex breaks and disturbances in the lyrics. [Sep 2016, p.103]

Title: Alligator
Review: Tonally and lyrically somewhere between L. Cohen, Aidan Moffett and David Berman, Berringer's cynical, world-worn love-letters and resigned croon work perfectly with the band's rock steady rhythm-section.

Title: Razorlight
Review: Up All Night is far from terrible and often a pleasant listen, but there’s nothing particularly enchanting about singer Johnny Borrell’s “vox,” and if anything seems to be lacking here, it’s perhaps a sense of musical identity. [#15]

Title: Made in China
Review: Her songs still revolve mostly around the adolescent hell of looking right and pleasing jerky guys, a shtick that would be old if Hatfield, well into her thirties, didn’t genuinely sound as if she were still living through it.

Title: Remember Us to Life
Review: On Remember Us To Life, Regina Spektor exhibits stronger affinities with Randy Newman, thanks to a turn of phrase often leaning towards the ironic, and a deceptive worldview which, like the sardonic string arrangements and ominous piano settings, gives most of these songs a slightly sour sting in the tail.

Title: Our Blood
Review: Our Blood doesn't leave me wanting more, it doesn't leave me drooling over another listen, and it sure doesn't leave me interested in more of Richard Buckner's work. But on the same measure, it doesn't leave me sick or angry.

Title: Short Movie
Review: Often she sounds like she’s having a conversation with herself. If that sounds distancing, the honesty and intelligence behind it draws us close.

Title: Heart
Review: You'd be hard-pressed to ask much more from a record.

Title: You Know Who You Are
Review: A well-drilled exercise in slick, sumptuous songwriting.

Title: The Mouse and the Mask
Review: Even though the album maintains a barely serious attitude from start to finish, it's impossible to doubt the talent and style present.

Title: Fireflies
Review: Alterna-folkie Lori McKenna's contributions save Hill from schlock overdose. [5 Aug 2005, p.65]

Title: Local Honey
Review: Svelte, mostly acoustic collection is so refreshing. [May 2020, p.94]

Title: Us
Review: A more confident, more stoutheartedly tuneful and just plain better successor to Loss. [3 Apr 2003, p.70]

Title: Revelation
Review: Where Newcombe continues to find inspiration from, who knows, but the music still keeps on coming. And the world is a better place for it.

Title: Little Broken Hearts
Review: There is a lot at play here, both sonically and lyrically, and the album rewards repeated listens. Most importantly, Little Broken Hearts is an album that just works.

Title: Stereo
Review: Mono and Stereo would be fine records from any musician-- that Westerberg himself is the source makes it all the sweeter.

Title: English Oceans
Review: Hood and Mike Cooley, the only original members left, handle all of the songwriting for the first time since the band's 1998 debut, and it makes for a unity of vision that prevents the grief from sounding gratuitous, that makes the uncertainties resonate with our own.

Title: These Walls of Mine
Review: The unshrouded nature of these compositions reveals interesting and insightful aspects of the creator and his practice.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: So if you can make it to track six - the lush “Only Love Can Set You Free” - Love Songs For Patriots becomes far more palatable from then on in.

Title: Lazers Never Die
Review: Not everything on this EP is stellar material, but the five tracks together are greater than the sum of their parts, because they come across as a murkier, more varied rewrite of Guns Don't Kill People…Lazers Do.  With any luck, this is a sign of things to come, and not simply an experimental lark.

Title: Forcefield
Review: For all its lack of idiosyncrasies, however, there’s a credibly unashamed attitude to creating perfectly fine pop songs.

Title: Monkeytown
Review: When the band sticks to this wheelhouse, they're as successful as they've ever been. When they divert from it, the results are wishy-washy.

Title: Noise
Review: Noise is probably Boris’ most accessible record to date, and the overall feeling is that it has, once again, managed to mould its inspiration while remaining quintessentially “Boris”.

Title: Paris
Review: An enjoyable pop romp.

Title: Born in the Echoes
Review: The Chems remain committed to their singular vision, still plying those swooning synths, continuing to breathe new life from the echoes. [No. 123, p.55]

Title: The Return
Review: It’s a sweet snapshot of London 2018--an encapsulation of a newly brewing jazz community, uniting numerous cultural strands that make up the city. When the scene needed him most, Kamaal Williams returned to show the way.

Title: Chronology
Review: This debut long-player has been greatly anticipated, and does not disappoint. Skating an agreeably fine line between conscious dancehall and complex nu-roots, Chronixx delivers 15 deeply personal explorations of Jamaica and the challenges it faces.

Title: High on Jackson Hill
Review: A letdown after Fables; whether haughty, homesick, or ha-ha, on the way toward frankness, the album gets bogged down in simplicity.

Title: Lost and Found
Review: Some of the playful songs are as joyously boisterous and willfully corny as anything in Smith's past, making Lost and Found an entertaining and thoughtful album for young kids and their parents to listen to and talk about.

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: Teeth Dreams isn't a failure. But it's an album that doesn't play to its creators' strengths. [Feb/Mar 2014, p.72]

Title: King's Disease
Review: Nas is more ruminative and measured, like he's found his stride again, even as he flagrantly contradicts himself and waylays men and women with relationship advice that rings hollow. Going strictly by the conviction and feeling in each line, King's Disease is the MC's best work since 2008.

Title: Untilted
Review: Autechre certainly aren't launching any new styles, and there's no innovative music to be heard here, but Untilted does represent the duo returning to the green fields of their youth after a few years sowing their wild oats.

Title: Voxtrot
Review: The majority of the record's new tracks need to either be more focused or show more dynamic range.

Title: Morph the Cat
Review: At his best he spins these tales with a mix of literary craft and jazzman's cool, animating his narratives with vivid and colorful language. [5 Mar 2006]

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: Their eighth album, Oblivion With Bells, showcases a more refined approach. [Nov 2007, p.176]

Title: The Bronx (IV)
Review: The Bronx IV is enough evidence that these guys show no signs of easing off the aggression accelerator any time soon.

Title: Spirit
Review: Though the 21-year-old's faithful, capable rendition of 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face' proves that the timelessness of the song should remain unquestioned, the album's adult-skewed material sounds even more jarring next to two fresh new tracks, the bouncy and youthful 'Forgive Me' and urban club jam 'Misses Glass,' added for American consumption.

Title: Milk Man
Review: So horribly untrendy it’s a new-black must-have, ‘Milk Man’ is the essential oddity of 2004, and a more-than-worthy successor to 2003’s magnificent ‘Apple O’’.

Title: Cardinology
Review: A thin line between revelation and revivalism, Adams and the Cardinals make an album worthy of high praises.

Title: Acid Tongue
Review: Impressively, she pulls off both sympathy and empathy. [Oct 2008, p.138]

Title: I'll Be The Tornado
Review: I'll Be The Tornado is highly focused, driven and a record that never seems content

Title: Redemption
Review: Throughout Jay fixates on a specific sort of paranoid despair, chasing bottles of Henny with painkillers. His favorite move is to not move at all, finding a good flow and digging into it, often delivering tiny clipped phrases like a boxer practicing his jab.

Title: Voices
Review: Occasionally, the band comes close to falling back into old habits, but with their new enthusiasm for sounding nothing like they used to, they've successfully created an album's worth of intelligent music for the Warped crowd.

Title: Ashes Grammar
Review: Ashes is A Sunny Day’s stripes, their first truly great album of scope.

Title: Blondes
Review: The meandering, incidental quality of their music works alternately in their favor and against them.

Title: Oh My God, Charlie Darwin
Review: They're intriguingly ambivalent, but the conundrums are so beautifully and hauntingly put, you'll want to revisit them. [Jul 2009, p.125]

Title: Have a Nice Life
Review: “I Miss Mikey” speaks not only to Murs’ own deceased homies, but acts as an inspirational call to ignore fears of mortality in the face of death and leave a lasting mark. With Have A Nice Life, an album that will not only impress longtime admirers but newcomers as well, Murs should have no problem with that task.

Title: Warpaint
Review: It feels more like a primer for live shows rather than an end in itself, a set of water colour sketches to be inked in later.

Title: Indigo Meadow
Review: The Black Angels don’t meander or mince words, and Indigo Meadow is a testament to that ideology.

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: Alternately recalling the best work of Blondie, Leonard Cohen, Depeche Mode, and dozens more, 69 Songs About Love is a sprawling masterpiece of White Album-like proportions.

Title: Little Red
Review: Katy B weaves various threads of London clubland into glittering pop flax, and this second LP is a triumphant consolidation of her position as the voice of nocturnal youth. [Mar 2014, p.78]

Title: Temple Beautiful
Review: He never strays outside his comfort zone, but the strongest moments ... have a familiar charm. [April 2012, p.102]

Artist: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
Title: Planetarium
Review: Moments of spine-tingling transcendence outweigh those of aimless noodling. [Aug 2017, p.110]

Title: Astro Coast
Review: What could have been a sterling six-track EP is still a solid album to blast until the weather matches its summertime mood. [Feb 2010, p.97]

Title: Mess
Review: All of Mess has an enjoyably menacing feel that will prove inviting to Liars fans and new listeners alike.

Title: Glory
Review: Not everything is glorious, but it might be something better: human. Finally, Spears is having as much fun as her songs sound.

Title: Crack-Up
Review: The band has always prided itself on ornateness, and in that sense, Crack-Up is its richest release to date. But more often than not, all that fussiness robs it of any impact.

Title: Ice Cream Spiritual
Review: The sound is bigger too, strengthening a band that's all guitars-drums-vocals sonics -- including Molly Siegel's yelping vocables, without which the sound's faux-tween soul and wise-ass tempo shifts would evanesce into abstraction.

Title: The Bride
Review: Khan refuses to yield crossover hits like 2009’s ‘Daniel’ (only the frenetic rhythms of ‘Sunday Love’ come close) opting instead for a slow style of storytelling that rewards the patient listener.

Title: Sheezus
Review: Songs recycle uniform beats with nods to hip-hop and electronic influences, but Allen falls short of a revitalizing comeback. Even so, her bold statements are truly worth deeper consideration.

Title: In Your Dreams
Review: In Your Dreams, Nicks' first studio album since 2001, is also streaked with the witchy-woman weirdness only she can bring.

Title: Give Up
Review: Gibbard's delicate voice matches the subtle electro arrangements far more precisely than it does the folky guitars of his real group.

Title: Pure Heroine
Review: It's not only Joel Little's minimalist production, all clicks, bass and empty space. The restraint lies also in Ella Yelich-O'Connor's treatment of orthodox pop themes.

Title: Riot On An Empty Street
Review: If you sort of liked the first record but wished it was more interesting, that it had more punch of both the sonic and emotional variety, then your wishes have come true.

Title: Egypt Station
Review: Egypt Station is easily one of the most forward-thinking records of McCartney’s later career and a surprisingly welcome return. We might wish he could be more thoughtful and elegant in his older age, and maybe even a little bit cooler, but that wouldn’t make him Paul McCartney. Thankfully, he generally keeps his groan-worthy impulses to a minimum.

Title: Manipulator
Review: It's a beautiful behemoth. [No. 112, p.56]

Title: Stars Are The Light
Review: Stars Are The Light is an aural journey, one which forces the listener to reconnect, or at least reconsider, their relationship with nature. In doing so, it encourages individuality and challenges one to break-up with the conventions of modern life.

Title: Young Prayer
Review: 'Young Prayer' is a piece of work that feels both mysterious and honest; a truly rare combination.

Title: LAX
Review: The Game goes surprisingly mellow in comparison to his first two efforts.
Thankfully, concessions aren't made at many other places on the album, and that may be why the thing works so well.

Title: Perpetual Motion People
Review: Perpetual Motion People is the restless sound of a genuine one-off in a generic world.

Title: Close Ties
Review: Crowell’s brutally honest musings on his life and loves is a case-study that makes the reflective Close Ties a poignant and emotionally affecting portrait of one of American music’s most captivating, talented and honest artists.

Title: Alpine Static
Review: The hooks fail to sink in, and Kinski is occasionally too clever for its own good. [#68, p.100]

Title: Depart From Me
Review: He abetteed by vibrant backdrops full of guitar-driven samples, which push the disc closer to rock than hip-hop and keep the energy high. [Aug 2009, p.106]

Title: Whole New Mess
Review: Whole New Mess has a singular power. The songs are spare but still feel electric, and despite their lower volume compared to All Mirrors, you couldn’t necessarily call them quiet. Their slow-strummed chords and finger-picked patterns are at times deliberately brittle and blown-out. Whole New Mess amplifies a different source of loudness.

Title: Get Color
Review: Get Color builds on the success of HEALTH in all the right ways, proving the band worthy of an intimidating amount of hype while defying the expectations that come with it.

Title: Seventh Tree
Review: Seventh Tree is the inevitable comedown, a pastoral holiday that trades glittery hedonism for quiet contemplation.

Title: La Di Da Di
Review: La Di Da Di comes across a tad too studied, never lifting out of the complex math of the group’s music.

Title: Ripe
Review: Ripe rides a similar vibe to 2005's "Awake Is the New Sleep": quick-and-dirty pop melodies polished with chiming guitars, piano fills, and Lee's exuberant, boyish vocals.

Title: More Is Than Isn't
Review: The record feels experimental and alive because of it. That unpredictability breeds some missteps but for the most part the album is peppered with pleasant, sometimes unsettling surprises.

Title: Settle
Review: It’s a shame that their debut album is so short on variety and surprises, and doesn’t capture the imagination past a couple of listens.

Title: House of Sugar
Review: As with earlier albums, it’s studded with experiments: “Project 2,” an interlude of fluting vaporwave synths, and “Sugar,” where melodramatic violin and piano are coated in Vocodered gurgles. They’re less interruptions than camouflage.

Title: A Minor Thought
Review: The result are suitably soothing. [Mar 2016, p.95]

Title: Roosevelt
Review: Roosevelt listens less like a dynamic pop album and more like a static soundtrack that only becomes more and more significant as time goes on.

Title: Distortion
Review: There is plenty to enjoy, although it never comes close to recapturing the eclectic brillance of 1999's career high, "69 Love Songs. [Feb 2008, p.99]

Title: Infinity Overhead
Review: The fluidity is back, all the parts gelling easily into a whole.

Title: Crack-Up
Review: They've upped their prog ambitions--tracks wash together, song titles abound with opaque punctuation, and the sweeping melodies often wander into moody places, away from the safety of the campfire.

Title: Amber
Review: Frequently gorgeous but over-lubed, the album forges soundscapes so lush they're almost narcotic.

Title: Relaxer
Review: That’s the half of Relaxer that I can live with, the half that strives actively to dispel alt-J’s pretentious front and swing for the top of the charts. But then, my friends, we return to the 'House of the Rising Sun'--because here, on this wikkle precious cover version with the cyclical Leonard Cohen guitar, we’re reminded of every reason to hate the three blokes.

Title: Rabbit Habits
Review: With its grunted refrain and tinkling xylophone, this strange group manage to out-weird even Waits himself. [May 2008, p.141]

Title: Make Up the Breakdown
Review: One of the more unique pop albums of the year.

Title: Dear Catastrophe Waitress
Review: The danger for B&S was that they would become trapped in a world of knee socks and introspection; the reality is that they’ve produced their best album since ‘Boy With The Arab Strap’, while proving that they can cut it in the world of well-adjusted adults.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: The result is the sun-drenched sister of an opiate-subverted Sonic Nurse, the musical equivalent of Coleridge in the afterglow of an acid trip.

Title: Distractions
Review: Any and all of the bands they draw influence from would be happy to add them to the noise club; if they keep making records as good as Distractions, they may end up ruling the club someday.

Title: 1000 Days
Review: This is a fine effort by Wand and well worth seeking out for those with a taste for garage rock not yet sated by releases this year from Mikal Cronin, Warm Soda and Thee Oh Sees.

Title: Playing the Angel
Review: [A] remarkable return to form. [Oct 2005, p.75]

Title: Kveikur
Review: No two songs sound similar and, while Jonsi’s vocals confirm that this is, really, the artist on the album sleeve, it is far from more of the same.

Title: Sing When You're Winning
Review: A collection of workmanlike whimsy... [12/2000, p.225]

Title: Sempiternal
Review: With all the ingredients for success laid bare, Sempiternal comes as the lightbulb moment--the clicking into place of every cog and spring, Bring Me The Horizon more than ready to accept the gauntlet thrown to them.

Title: Watershed
Review: A substantial addition to the band's catalog.

Title: Revel In The Drama
Review: Yet even at its most downbeat and damaged, this music gleams with a steely determination to be heard. [May 2020, p.87]

Title: Key Markets
Review: Beneath the swearing there’s a sharp sense of humour and even sharper powers of observation, Williamson’s freeform wordplay painting vivid pictures of an at times uncomfortably recognisable contemporary Britain.

Title: Natalie Prass
Review: This is music inspired by what you remember hearing as a kid from your parents’ and grandparents’ record collections, but it’s been made fresh and totally original again.

Title: The Courage of Others
Review: This could well be Midlake's masterpiece, which is saying something considering the esteem in which The Trials Of Van Occupanther is held.

Title: Eternal Turn of the Wheel
Review: There are moments here worth returning for time and again, but not much to put Eternal Turn of the Wheel in the same level of esteem as its distant predecessors.

Title: The Stepkids
Review: Everything's easy and natural, and the Stepkids sound more like purveyors of the genre than imitators. Quite an accomplishment.

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: So Divided
Review: [It] depends less on the band’s gear-smashing antics than on their sense of tunecraft, which isn’t as highly developed.

Title: The Boombox Ballads
Review: In places, The Boombox Ballads is too shambling for its own good. [Oct 2015, p.113]

Title: The Excitement Plan
Review: Todd Snider relates his hilariously heartbreaking hard-luck tales with a deadpan sing-speak delivery while superproducer Don Was gives the scrappy bar-band arrangements a glimmer of studio-pro warmth.

Title: Luminous
Review: Though songs including the shimmering So Now You Know and the Manuel Gottsching-like In And Out Of Sight maintain a stirring balance of shimmying pop appeal and experimentation, elsewhere the momentum is compromised and peaks are obscured. [Jun 2014, p.88]

Title: Broken Boy Soldiers
Review: It's a hugely enjoyable record, with songs on it as good as anything the individuals involved have produced elsewhere. It's simply that high standards achieved elsewhere aren't consistently obtained throughout.

Title: The Datsuns
Review: You've heard this album before then, but it's never sounded quite this crazed and pressed for time.

Title: Nothing's Real
Review: Her videos make clear the subjects of these songs are often women, but on record her work is open-ended--a map to a treasure that's just never there.

Title: Tarpaper Sky
Review: While it remains to be seen if any of these eleven tracks yields another legendary moment on the order of the ones Crowell has already penned, the organic Tarpaper Sky is a welcome reminder that at 63 he remains capable of releasing beautifully crafted music that can stand toe to toe with his best.

Title: Sunshine Rock
Review: Rather than singing from inside the darkness, he steps back and tries to find glimmers of hope and, dare it be said, happiness. The dozen songs offer a more forgiving perspective on time, memory and the past and how to live with and move beyond it.

Title: Victorious
Review: The second Floorplan album feels triumphant enough to bear the title Victorious. It's a stellar follow-up to Paradise.

Title: In The Wild
Review: The charm of the disconnected, breezy path that starts the album--seeming interludes punctuated by the odd story of a more solid, structured track--quickly wears thin when you realize said path meanders, the tracks mostly underdeveloped, only occasionally rolling into a bigger sound with tangible depth.

Title: Crazy Itch Radio
Review: 'Crazy Itch Radio' bumbles along with mid-paced beats and, it seems, too many disparate influences to really hold together.

Title: Psychedelic Pill
Review: Psychedelic Pill is a maximalist work from Young; he has taken the central premise of one of his many musical sides and stretched its vision as far as it will go.

Title: Rheia
Review: The sound is top-notch and very effective. But the songwriting often comes up short.

Title: truANT
Review: Alien Ant Farm's songs may be catchy, but their wishy-washy personality makes it hard to care. [Sep 2003, p.118]

Title: Bon Iver, Bon Iver
Review: A wonderful, worthy follow-up.

Title: Garden of Ashes
