Review: With Garden Of Ashes he secures his position as not just a musician’s musician, but one who looks set to grow a wider following.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: Playful yet profound, baffling but very beautiful, sticking with Panda Bear Meets The Grim Reaper until it reveals its full dizzying array of riches most certainly is [worthwhile].

Title: Dreamt for Light Years in the Belly of a Mountain
Review: Back is the blend of lo-fi and hi-fi, and back are the completely odd lyrics. [#22, p.94]

Title: Monuments to an Elegy
Review: It's hard to shake the sense that these songs ape Corgan's past but too often lack the spark of inspiration that fuelled his previous masterpieces. [Jan 2015, p.100]

Title: Palookaville
Review: Cook's dance music has seen better days. [Oct 2004, p.115]

Title: Losing
Review: Lyrically, she’s never been better. Vocally, never more dynamic. Those two alone should make for another breakout record, but unfortunately, the core of the band is left faint, robbing the music of the pulsating energy and raw sensation that initially made Bully such a head-turner. Thankfully, Bognanno’s voice and words are more than enough to carry a record.

Title: MCIII
Review: Though it manages to be both lovely and adventurous, too often MCIII sounds like Cronin falls back on the string beds instead of utilizing them with the same fervor he used to reserve for crunchy, just-this-side-of-DGAF riffs.

Title: What's It All About
Review: For those with open minds and without unfair expectations of artists, it will be another fascinating addition to a long and exceptional career.

Title: Widow City
Review: No one does puzzle-pop quite like the Fiery Furnaces, and despite the multi-genre pileups and lofty literary pretension, when they get it right it's enough to forgive them for when they get it wrong.

Title: Persuasion System
Review: It certainly sounds diminutive in scope after the triumph of Iteration, and, despite the new gear, there's not much that sounds especially new or exciting here, just the usual Com Truise stuff in a slightly reduced register.

Title: Mo Beauty
Review: Almost every tune on Mo Beauty equals or betters those on CYHSY's lauded 2005 debut.

Title: Centres
Review: Centres has the ability to both mollify and unnerve, and to think that most of it was assembled through sensitive means speaks volumes of Craig’s greater ambitions.

Title: Black Radio 2
Review: The follow-up to Robert Glasper’s Grammy-winning breakthrough builds on its predecessor by reframing the sound of contemporary urban music.

Title: Be The Void
Review: Be the Void might be the band's least accessible offering yet, but it's certainly their bravest--and given some breathing room, it might just prove their most rewarding.

Title: BE
Review: The vocals, the terrible rhymes... it's business as usual then for Liam; it's just scrubbed up a bit.

Title: Phrenology
Review: The Roots have never sounded this raw on record, this much like an actual band playing in an actual room. [Jan 2003, p.95]

Title: Surfing Strange
Review: Surfing Strange has a bit more substance and variety [than its first LP]. Neither betters the other but they complement each other nicely forming the bulk of the band’s discography.

Title: Back To Forever
Review: A disc of dark corners couched in defiantly bright pop.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: Blak and Blu throbs more like a lava lamp turned upside, a red-line splat of molten nightlife served on a huge sonic bed only achieved by major label productions.

Title: Anna Calvi
Review: Italian-blooded debutante rocks passionately. [March 2011, p. 96]

Title: The Papercut Chronicles II
Review: It works when they jettison their limp rap-rock instincts and plunge into crossover pop.

Title: Popular Problems
Review: As intimate, beautiful and witty as ever, there’s an impassioned life in Leonard that's missing from many artists a quarter of his age.

Title: Meet Glen Campbell
Review: What appear to be strange song choices on paper are risks that pay off.... Although he has his moments of sentimentality on John Lennon's 'Grow Old With Me' and the Velvet Underground's 'Jesus,' Campbell is still a formidable interpreter of song who even overcomes heavy-handed production to remind us why he was always our favorite charismatic pop-music cowboy.

Title: Value
Review: Carnell captures his negotiation with vulnerability in the process of its unfolding, and his relationship with his sonic language feels in-process as well--a generative path, to be sure, if sometimes an uneven one.

Title: Breakout
Review: Harmless fluff. [Nov 2008, p.114]

Title: The Catastrophist
Review: They're best when dabbling in the exotic, the offbeat, the slightly unsettling. Smooth surfaces are never quite what they seem in the best Tortoise songs.

Title: Seefeel
Review: Slightly more upfront and extroverted than their early recordings, this album is still instantly recognizable, and fans who go back to their last Warp LP, Succour, might be surprised at how little has changed with Seefeel over 15 years.

Title: Band of Joy
Review: "Satan, your kingdom must come down," Plant croons on the penultimate track. Take that, Jimmy Page.

Title: Dumb Flesh
Review: Dumb Flesh strikes a fabulously oxymoronic tone: euphoric dread. [Jun 2015, p.100]

Title: Remember the Night Parties
Review: Unlike the groups' prior albums, Remember the Night Parties carries less heft due to its shimmering pop mindset.

Title: Teeth Dreams
Review: The more reflective moments on the album are some of the best.

Title: Live from the Underground
Review: After listening to Live from the Underground in its entirety, you'll notice the album's cohesiveness and Southern harmony. [#253, p.88]

Title: Meet the Humans
Review: The element of smoothness cloaking the emotions could either impress the listener with its beauty or wash over them completely. The hit rate here perhaps isn’t quite high enough for the former, but the album deserves some attention for illustrating the exuberant joy of the black dog turning away from one’s door and walking on down the street.

Title: Youth and Young Manhood
Review: The band shows an incredible level of bravado on their album of fun summer hymns, but has a hard time breaking through the barrier the lackluster vocals create.

Title: Five
Review: White Lies have succeeded in creating an album with much more scope that is a testament to the enduring nature of their sound. Five denotes a chapter in the band’s career but it does by no means symbolise the end of White Lies.

Title: Black Traffic
Review: It doesn't quite hit the consistent heights of Stoosh or Post Orgasmic Chill, but Black Traffic more than justifies Skunk Anansie's re-existence.

Title: Steam Days
Review: Midway through Steam Days, Harnser does dark pizzicato things befitting a 90s warehouse rave, while elsewhere, the analogue-melting-into-digital influence of Four Tet is palpable.

Title: We Come From The Same Place
Review: It still sounds like them--just an improved, sharpened up them. And it’s wonderful for it; their best yet.

Title: Potential
Review: Whether you're aware of the conceptual backstory behind Potential or come into the project blind, Hinton makes the album just as conceptually moody as it is conceptually aural.

Title: The Highway
Review: It’s an album that defines an artist, proving that the Williams name (the daughter of Bocephus, Holly comes from the Hank lineage) remains as trailblazing and unique as ever.

Title: A Seat at the Table
Review: A Seat demands a careful listen, and rewards it richly. This is Solange's strongest album to date.

The emphasis put on the soundscapes for these songs--unprecedented for the singer/songwriter--results in her lyrics occasionally getting buried under the synth swooshes, but for the first time in a long time, the majority of Taylor's lyrics don't really demand your attention anyway.

Title: Walking Like We Do
Review: It's a heavy theme to handle, but thankfully (or perhaps to its chagrin), most of these topics go unnoticed if you submit to its simple guitar-pop pleasures.

Title: Havilah
Review: Restraint dominates elsewhere, but brillance comes when The Drones throw musical sanity to the wind. [Winter 2009, p.78]

Title: Discover a Lovelier You
Review: If the songs go down too easy, that's part of the deal -- monster hooks or guitar freakouts would only upset the balance Pernice has taken a decade to perfect.

Title: Heyoon
Review: Heyoon is an often confusing collection that depicts a mad mind, but one that at times offers enough intrigue to warrant attention.

Title: The Fall
Review: It shouldn't work, but ultimately it does, which is pretty much The Fall all over.

Title: Moh Lhean
Review: For better or for worse though, Moh Lhean mostly moves to the beat of its own, strangely laid-back drums. It just would have been nice to have a little more variation buried within those meditative vibes.

Title: Mosquito
Review: Divided between these sorts of small successes and outright failures, Mosquito is nowhere near a coherent album, which at this stage in the band's career feels like a refreshing return to form.

Title: For Emma, Forever Ago
Review: As good as it is, it’s clear that Vernon still has room to grow. A few songs could have used a little extra instrumental kick, and while his songs are great, you can tell he has more to offer. Keep an eye on this one.

Title: Derdang Derdang
Review: While Derdang Derdang has killer hooks aplenty, they're all too often obscured by stop-start rhythms and the unhinged-sounding vocals of Sam Windett. [Apr 2006, p.119]

Title: Renaissance
Review: Although there are no ballads as moving as "Hello," "Truly," or "Say You, Say Me," the album does offer a nice collection of pop tracks that, for the most part, don't suffer from the stiflingly bland over-production that's characterized other adult-contemporary albums of recent years.

Title: V
Review: They are sketches--nothing more, nothing less. But it all changes on the final, aptly-named, track Opulent Decline.

Title: AIM
Review: If this is her last record then she hasn’t gone out on her finest note, but that’s certainly not to undermine the album. Maya Arulpragasam’s body of work remains an important reminder of the exciting prospects of cultural exchange and the immigrant experience. Taken in that light, AIM is a fitting addition to her oeuvre.

Title: To Pimp a Butterfly
Review: On Lamar’s longer, denser, and even richer follow-up To Pimp A Butterfly, he stops holding the listener’s hand.

Title: Garden of Arms
Review: The rest of the album, despite a few detours into semi-indulgent, atonal glitch that shakes the fluidity of the record yet never really derails the train, keeps looking forward, hoping to find a light at the end of the tunnel, while knowing full well that it's only the first of many.

Title: To Dreamers
Review: On his fifth full-length, this '60s-pop obsessive mostly ditches the balmy homemade chorales of his earlier work for folk-rock verities, crafting his tightest, fullest-sounding record yet.

Title: Bad Witch
Review: While 2016's Not the Actual Events explores dissociative identities and 2017's Add Violence brims with paranoia about our increasingly simulated reality, Bad Witch moves past such insular anxieties and more directly acknowledges that society's chaos is the result of our collective hubris. ... Reznor conveys a bleaker and more visceral sense of desperation on the album's two instrumental tracks.

Title: Disarm the Descent
Review: This is direct, explosive and packed with big choruses. [May 2013, p.99]

Title: Welcome oblivion
Review: Welcome Oblivion is not an album that comes on forcefully, and by many measures, it's the most measured record of Reznor's career, yet it's also his most melodic, showing that this former angry young man has a design to grow old gracefully.

Title: POWER
Review: On Power they fully engage their inner Depeche Mode and LCD Soundsystem. ... Ordinarily this could point to an identity crisis, but it works. [Mar 2020, p.122]

Title: Star Wars
Review: Star Wars may have been released on the spur of the moment, but Wilco’s alchemistic gifts ensure that it’s a moment which fans will want to keep on reliving.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: Decades from now, Petty people will wonder at how a modest marvel like Hypnotic Eye aged into a late-career riff rocket.

Title: Bobbie Gentry's The Delta Sweete Revisited
Review: They carefully remodel Gentry's Southern storytelling. [Mar 2019, p.116]

Title: Rock Steady
Review: Rock Steady certainly isn't that good, and at times it's rather bad (usually when Ocasek gets a bit Cars). But it does have its moments, most of which come at the hands of [co-producer Nellee] Hooper...

Title: Milkteeth
Review: While his lyricism is filled with youthful nostalgia, his sound here is more mature than ever. Introducing an auto harp, his soundscapes are filled with a toned-down joie de vivre which makes the album stand out with its lucid simplicity.

Title: Piramida
Review: The fact that Efterklang have managed to cultivate such an effortless sounding exercise in sonic geographies is sheer testament to their skill as master artisans.

Title: I Am Easy to Find
Review: I Am Easy to Find is littered with these ambitious flourishes, all of which add up to make a much broader and more pointed statement of offbeat intent.

Title: Sing the Sorrow
Review: The songs may have opened up around him, but Havok's lyrics are as pained and sharp as they ever were.

Title: Caracal
Review: Caracal is about Disclosure maturing, moving on and showing the listener how to rave respectably. This is dance music for grown-ups.

Title: Piano
Review: In its second half, Piano begins to suffer from its stripped-back simplicity, when its sparse arrangements and slow pace start to feel plodding rather than profound.

Title: Mirrored
Review: Some listeners may find the album samey or too similar but one aspect of Mirrored that can't be disputed is that it is a unique album with little to no similar peers.

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: Ultimately, too many of these tunes are rehearsal room grooves in search of a hook.

Title: Stronger with Each Tear
Review: Although Stronger with Each Tear may not be one of her greatest works, it ensures that Blige remains as relevant as any of her more recent contemporaries.

Title: Universal Mind Control
Review: He is a mimic of fine abilities, but he has always sounded like whatever group he’s glommed onto.

Title: Specter At The Feast
Review: They have made a patchy record that’s very much intended for loyal followers who have completely bought into their long established aesthetic.

Title: Okemah and the Melody of Riot
Review: Okemah replaces Farrar's indulgence with a gently rocking back-porch feel. [28 Jul 2005, p.82]

Title: The Hunting Party
Review: Linkin Park certainly know their audience, and here delicately navigate the gulf between their own aspirations and a fanbase who will celebrate the band's loud return to rocking hard.

Title: Better Oblivion Community Center
Review: The best parts of the album, though, are the moments where it doesn't sound exactly like anything either artist has released before (songs like "My City," and closing pair "Big Black Heart" and "Dominos"), yet still shows two songwriters at the height of their talents.

Title: "Awaken, My Love!"
Review: What's missing is a sense of Glover himself as a defining character. [Feb 2017, p.112]

Title: This Is Happening
Review: This is a fantastic record, one of the year's best, but perhaps one that suggests that Murphy has said what he needed to say. [Jun 2010, p.122]

Title: The Female Boss
Review: When she sticks to the disco-pop staples of celebrating youth and dancing and fun, in tracks like "Young", "Live It Up" and "Live Your Life", once the energy dissipates, so do the songs, evaporating as if they never existed.

Title: Home
Review: The pinnacle is the tidal rhythms of 'Sickness, Bury,' but there's plenty more here to admire and absorb. [Nov 2008, p.98]

Title: The Worm's Heart
Review: Die-hard fans may appreciate the musical switcheroos on The Worm's Heart, but others may not understand the need for them.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: Pecknold enthusiastically revealed how the album was a direct result of his indulgence in MP3 piracy, as he tracked back to discover Fairport Convention, Roy Harper, Crosby, Stills & Nash, Joni Mitchell, Paul Simon, Bob Dylan and all the heroes of the Sixties folk boom.

Title: Pangs
Review: Parlay music that while irrefutably folk, gleefully shoves aside traditionalist tropes in favour of a buoyant, full-bodied combo sound, that, passingly, recalls prime Fairport Convention while proffering a beguilingly mellifluous identity of its own. [Apr 2017, p.98]

Title: Fly or Die
Review: More realized than 2002's In Search Of..., they hit all of their marks, rubbing guitar licks against '70s funk and sexy R&B that's bound to get any club flying high.

Title: Exit
Review: Tokumaru counters the tweeness of his Japanese-language croon (plus the unrelenting innocence of his twinkly, trebly melodies) with arrangements that densely interweave oddly organic twittering to suggest psychedelia without ever stooping to its cliches.

Title: Murray Street
Review: Sonic Youth find a balance--between formlessness and structure, melody and cacophony--that's eluded them for a while. [28 Jun 2002, p.142]

Title: Lost and Found
Review: A CD packed with the sort of undeniable pleasures only the most churlish thug could deny. [15 Apr 2005, p.78]

Title: Ultimate Success Today
Review: It’s music for uncertain times, something Protomartyr seem to be almost eerily skilled at producing.

Title: The DEFinition
Review: There’s a distinct lack of personality, meaning that LL Cool J’s eleventh long player is merely good, and his reputation (and bank balance) will be neither tarnished nor expanded.

Title: Suicide Songs
Review: Far from being a downer, these songs are frequently sublime. [Feb 2016, p.113]

Title: It's Me Again
Review: Too many of these fluttering tunes never quite get off the ground. [25 Mar 2005, p.72]

Title: I Will Be
Review: I Will Be is undeniably derivative--but exhilarating with it.

Title: H-p1
Review: Rock music's era of overarching influence on culture has no doubt passed into the historical twilight, but artistry and ambition in the form is alive and well on records like Hp-1.

Title: Strangers
Review: te. For the most part Strangers succeeds because of its strangeness, but when that strangeness slips, the album as a whole does too.

Title: Midwest Farmer's Daughter
Review: By the time Price sings about losing a first-born and crying out to God, bruised stoicism muting the sound of her knees hitting the floorboards, you're reminded of the incredible power that lies in tradition well-used. It's a power the rest of this record makes plain.

Title: Love Is Magic
Review: Flawed but unbowed, it is a fascinating but frustrating listen.

Title: The Big Roar
Review: Say this for The Joy Formidable's debut effort, The Big Roar: It tells no lies and seeks no modest ambitions.

Title: Invicta
Review: There are enough early anthems included to warrant picking this up, if only as a gateway to their back catalogue.

Title: Avenged Sevenfold
Review: While their willingness to experiment is admirable, despite the fact that they've gone overboard with their overdubs, the overabundance of studio polish leaves one to wonder if it's not because the songs just aren't as strong this time around.

Title: What We Lose in the Fire We Gain in the Flood
Review: Nothing sounds overworked. If anything, Burhenn and Swift present the songs in an understated manner, confident in the quality of the material and the strength of her voice.

Title: Graveyard Whistling
Review: Any doubts that the Old 97's could sustain this creative resurgence are summarily dismissed with Graveyard Whistling. [No. 141, p.60]

Title: Smoke + Mirrors
Review: Smoke + Mirrors puts across strong feelings, but it refuses to reveal how they work.

Title: Pacific Daydream
Review: As a collective work, Pacific Daydream is ultimately a step below the resurgent greatness of the White Album, but it still soundly ranks in the upper tier of Weezer’s new-millennium output. It’s peppered with some of the band’s best songs in recent memory.

Title: The Libertines
Review: Some of these songs are excellent, in an unfinished but inspired way. But many of the album's tracks evidence a band that's bursting at the seams with talent, only to stumble on unfocused, scattershot song-writing.

Title: The Con
Review: The pared-down moments of The Con seem to long for the clusterfuckedness of the album’s meatier tracks, and for the most part, rightly so.

Title: The Blue Depths
Review: The Blue Depths can be a mesmerizing album to listen to. Tapscott's voice creaks with emotion, haunting these songs with a vital humanity that keeps their cold feel from being mechanical.

Title: Live from the Kitchen
Review: Overall, the album has a good balance of solo tracks and features.

Title: Rock Island
Review: Palm do stand out from their contemporaries on Rock Island, especially since they equally embrace and rile against indie rock as a conservative movement. Their nonconformist aesthetic is imbued with an independent spirit, even if the sources they pull from prevents them from really taking off.

Title: The Hunger for More
Review: The one thing Banks lacks is Fiddy's natural charisma--he's also about eight bulletholes short in the "life-experience department."

Title: Atlas
Review: If Real Estate captured the essence of summer, and Days maintained an unmistakably autumnal aura, then Atlas, the most thematically mature of the three, could easily be classified as Real Estate's wintery opus.

Title: Parallel Play
Review: The 13-track Parallel Play is a decidedly less ambitious effort, but it’s no less brilliant in its execution.

Title: The Flying Club Cup
Review: Condon has a tendency to over-emote vocally, but even at its most melodramatic this music's rhapsodic swirl is undeniable. [Nov 2007, p.104]

Title: Give My Love To London
Review: Charged with Warren Ellis’s plaintive violin, the cracked world-weariness of Marianne Faithfull’s voice imbues the song with real life and contemporary meaning and affirms that Give My Love To London is the album with which she is able to finally reconcile her past and present.

Title: Prairie Wind
Review: In the autumn of his career, this is one of Shaky's best.

Title: My Old Familiar Friend
Review: Brendan Benson expertly assembles pop music using the manual.

Title: A Gun Called Tension
Review: Short, blunt, and skitless, A Gun Called Tension seethes with everything post-aught genre-fucking needs.

Title: Winchester Cathedral
Review: Music as taut, spare and ominous as The Bad Seeds at their most malevolent. [21 Aug 2004, p.49]

Title: Lovers
Review: If his eccentricity was tamed and the pained attempts to hop genres were avoided, Luke Steele could just produce something close to sublime. As it stands, Lovers is a fairly pleasant application of some charming reference points, but please, let's stop pretending that that's good enough.

Title: Forever and Then Some
Review: All of this impeccable accompaniment wouldn’t amount to much without terrific songs sung with emotion and drive, which is where Mae excels.

Title: Hypnotic Eye
Review: Hypnotic Eye mostly returns to their earliest days of razor-edged guitars and garage rock.... The listless You Get Me High and Burnt Out Town's clunky blues may let the side down, but it feels good to finally have the real Heartbreakers back. [Aug 2014, p.94]

Title: After Laughter
Review: The grooves they always possessed are brought to the forefront on this peppy, vibrant record, a contrast to its lyrical themes, which cover masking misery (“I’m going to draw my lipstick wider than my mouth”), spiralling depression and the anxiety of ageing, only with a knowing wink.

Title: Lambs Anger
Review: As good as some of the tracks are, it's just discouraging to think how solid the record could've been if it had been just ten tracks of more fleshed-out material.

Title: Freedom
Review: An enormous leap forward, Freedom finds Amen Dunes grappling with his abilities, with the passing of the time; a superb record, it’s one that deserves the widest possible audience.

Title: Rainbow
Review: It’s a bold, focused, universal statement about freedom--from self-hatred, from paralyzing internal conflicts, from gender expectations, from negative influences, and (especially) from other people’s shit.

Title: Lonely at the Top
Review: As methods go it can be messy, but it also throws up some interesting hybrids.

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: So no, this is not a cohesive crew album, but has there really been one since Marley Marl's In Control, Vol. 1 came out 24 years ago?

Title: Head Cage
Review: One of the year’s best and most urgent metal records, Head Cage is a fitting counterpart to another essential bit of 2018 heaviness, Thou’s Magus.

Title: Avonmore
Review: That search for perfection, his own predilection, goes on, gorgeously lit by this. [Feb 2015, p.99]

Title: Tomorrow Morning
Review: The tender optimism of tracks like "The Morning" and the gorgeous, harpsichord-led symphony "Oh So Lovely" are wonderfully uplifting, but there's still room for some snarky self-deprecation on "Baby Loves Me" too.

Title: Fall to Pieces
Review: Fall To Pieces exists in this oxymoronic hinterland of nihilism and resilience, evocative of the contradictions of grief. [Oct 2020, p.64]

Title: Bad Habits
Review: Guest spots by Young Thug and the Weeknd inject some much-needed personality into Bad Habits, but it's not enough to save the album from its own blandness.

Title: The Young Machines
Review: Terrific stuff. [Dec 2003, p.129]

Title: Everything to Everyone
Review: To be sure, Everything to Everyone certainly packs in the humorous moments that were largely lacking from the group's last album, 2000's Maroon. But it also shows principal songwriters Steven Page and Ed Robertson reflecting on weightier topics related to the band's double-edged popularity.

Title: Blue Film
Review: Beautiful in places, but falling flat on an emotional level elsewhere, there is an air of duality in Lo-Fang’s work as light and dark elements intertwine and clash with each other. For someone who has done so much travelling, it is clear that Lo-Fang is still finding his feet.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: [The album] is suitably haunted and becalmed. [Mar 2013, p.98]

Title: Hypermagic Mountain
Review: The compressed, cleaned-up ferocity of Hypermagic Mountain is a leap of refinement in every way, a sign that the band, while lushly unripe, is ripening gracefully.

Title: Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes
Review: While Desperate Youth, Blood Thirsty Babes could have become an exercise in studio-based formalistic noodling, Adebimpe and Malone’s vocals and lyrics give the songs structure and direction.

Title: Paramore
Review: It's daring and rarely less than dazzling. [6 Apr 2013, p.52]

Title: Uncaged
Review: A genre-bending, head-turning collection that vaults ZBB to the top of the roots-rock pedestal.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: While Talkie Walkie lacks some of Legend's nerve, it makes for a more immediately pleasing experience.

Title: Two Vines
Review: The credentials are there, the ability is clearly there, but for now these emperors are yet to truly shine.

Title: When I Get Home
Review: It's a reclamation of a history that often doesn't tells stories about black cowboys or black musical innovations. However, it is a recollection of what inspires Solange, and more importantly, how she wants to inspire the next generation from Houston.

Title: The Ugly Organ
Review: Kasher's jagged, jarring song cycle suggests an unholy fusion of the Cure's Robert Smith and Sebadoh's Lou Barlow.

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: Parker’s long-awaited Currents follow-up, The Slow Rush, isn’t quite as interesting as its predecessors in terms of songwriting and production, and this gap makes Parker’s lyrical weaknesses more challenging to ignore.

Title: Godfather
Review: If Godfather really is the conclusion of Wiley's recording career, he's ending it on an extremely high note.

Title: The Shadow of Heaven
Review: If there is one fault, it may be that, at times, the production and backing is a little too restrained.... [But] It really is a thing of beauty, and gets better with every listen; one of the surest signs of something that will ultimately be deemed timeless.

Title: Personal Record
Review: It’s Friedberger’s lyrics and delivery that unite these various touchstones, as fresh and distinctive as ever, incredibly poignant and powerfully aware of her self and the signifiers that surround her.

Title: Government Plates
Review: Government Plates is a challenging listen, but as one of the most transgressive records of the year.

Title: Heavy Light
Review: It's another huge step forward for the uncontainable U.S. Girls organism, one that skillfully combines the immediacy of personal memories with Remy's uncanny ability to inject her singular creative voice into every sound she touches.

Title: Maths + English
Review: It's Dizzee Rascal's pop album: catchy and danceable.

Title: TH1RT3EN
Review: Subtracting pretentious weight from a band that boasts several loose concept records in its catalog, TH1RT3EN might not don a full sense of humor, but it is 13 tracks of unadulterated hard rock in a classic package

Title: Dead Cross
Review: The result is an album that sounds as if it was a blast to make and one that’s immensely enjoyable to listen to.

Title: Preoccupations
Review: Preoccupations, by design, neither grips nor pays off with the same level of gleeful improvisational intensity [as 2015's Viet Cong].

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: Ultimately, Everything Will Be Alright in the End is not a perfect album, but then again it really didn’t need to be.

Title: Snapshot of a Beginner
Review: At times they meander a little too much, as on the ponderous Fool Thinking Ways, but this is far from the work of beginners. [Jun 2020, p.105]

Title: Glad All Over
Review: Jakob Dylan's group has picked up where it left off: with sharp roots-rock songs full of sturdy hooks, deadpan jokes and pathos that sneaks up on you.

Title: Hypersonic Missiles
Review: Fender drew plenty of early comparisons to Bruce Springsteen – on Hypersonic Missiles they’re entirely warranted, as much for the instrumentation as the lyricism and his vignettes of working-class struggle.

Title: Hip Hop Is Dead
Review: Nas can still dazzle on the mic. [Jan/Feb 2007, p.87]

Title: Ones and Sixes
Review: While some may argue that Ones and Sixes sounds too familiar, it could be said that the trio are simply playing to their strengths.

Title: Alight of Night
Review: The sound on Alight of Night is a swinging, noisy, glammy and overall dark evolution of garage rock.

Title: Haha Sound
Review: Ha Ha Sound is the sort of album that will sweetly move you towards slumber. [#23, p.82]

Title: Us and the Night
Review: Us and the Night offers some bland, platitude-driven positivity, but only once shadowed by equally vague problems. There’s a thin line between building out themes for an album and getting stuck in a rut, and this one unfortunately sounds like it falls towards the latter.

Title: The Magic Numbers

Title: The Dirty South
Review: Class warfare meets gangsta-rock.
