Review: Where [Time Out Of Mind] stared down heartbreak and mortality with somber melancholy, Love and Theft finds Dylan taking on those same themes loaded up with piss and vinegar. [Nov 2001, p.127]

Title: Ultraviolet
Review: With Ultraviolet, Kylesa has once again established themselves in the great tradition of hard-rockers who've realized it's possible to make a "dark" album without sacrificing accessibility, further proving that heavy riffs and great hooks aren't mutually exclusive.

Title: Transference
Review: Careful consideration shows that Transference really is exactly the record that Spoon intend it to be. It's just not a record that anyone really needs, one from which our feelings will all-too-easily transfer the next time that Spoon put out a record that inevitably reminds us of Spoon.

Title: Revival
Review: At 77 minutes, Revival is a heavy listen, going deep on ballads with guests like Ed Sheeran and X Ambassadors. But a certain indulgent messiness has always been part of the Eminem experience. ... When Revival's confessionals work, it's proof that, when the real Marshal Mathers stands up, he can still pull us into his evocative dramas.

Title: II Trill
Review: His second solo album (which he dedicates to Pimp C, his partner in the pioneering Houston rap duo UGK who died of a codeine overdose last December) features blunts, ho's and Caddy-shaking beats galore--but also elegantly constructed takedowns of corrupt politicians, covetous ministers and crooked police.

Title: Get Hurt
Review: A stylistically diverse collection that reaches for the stars, but can't touch the gold standard of the Jersey boys' 2010 hit American Slang.

Title: Silent Alarm
Review: What is truly magical on Silent Alarm is how it astutely grafts the accoutrements of wiry post-punk austerity to pop hooks fortified with soulful melodic intent.

Title: You're the One
Review: Paul Simon still has it.

Title: I Am
Review: This one is so packed and bold, it even exits on a turned-up club stunner ("Act Right" with Jeezy and YG), so consider it the big longevity payoff after years of rocky Yo Gotti albums.

Title: Mama, I'm Swollen
Review: For a band like Cursive to produce an album as self-pitying and mournful as Swollen is, frankly, a disappointment, especially considering the fact that the Omaha quartet tackled twenty-something melodrama with such delightful insolence on "Ugly Organ."

Title: Varshons
Review: Overall, there is sufficient sun-kissed pleasure on Varshons to extend the patience of Evan Dando-devotees a little bit longer but not enough to surpass past makeover masterstrokes.

Title: Come Home To Mama
Review: Having gotten an Édith Piaf tribute (and a baby) out of her system since, she reorients herself admirably with Come Home to Mama.

Title: Hero Brother
Review: [An] intense and atmospheric instrumental debut. [Sep 2013, p.92]

Title: Glitterbust
Review: Though it too often lingers when a punch is needed, Glitterbust carries plenty of weight.

Title: I Am King
Review: The almost unbearably intense ‘Slowburn’ and ambient ‘My World’ are just two cuts of an album littered with highlights, meaning by the end of this 33-minute pummeling, you’ll only need one word: breathtaking.

Title: Awake
Review: Even as Tycho adds more depth and variety to his sound, his music's main success is giving listeners an attractive backdrop for whatever they might be doing.

Title: So Long Forever
Review: Palace show they have matured-yet-remained faithful, and expanded-yet-honed. So Long Forever is an album from a band who know what they want, and how they want to get there.

Title: Government Plates
Review: Those instrumentals stop and start, throb and zap, sprint and lurch, empty out or swarm with noise, and they often completely switch texture in midtrack--the more disorienting the better.

Title: Sound Loaded
Review: The relentlessly likable and danceable Sound Loaded plunges listeners once again into Ricky's hothouse world, with its lush evocations of exotic climes ("St. Tropez"), Spanglish salsa-club blowouts (the irresistible "Amor") and voodoo hussies (oh, pick one -- "Jezebel"). The singing sounds a little tired, but the monstrously effective production is firmly in place, with arena-size swells swamping the ballads ("Come to Me" eventually drowns) and Latinate curlicues (like the arabesque-ing guitar that redeems "Nobody Wants to Be Lonely") peeping from the corners.

Title: In The Spirit World Now
Review: This band knows how to break new ground, yet they sound as though they’re trying to summon songs that will miraculously slot in with their old material. It’s a balancing act that’s holding them back.

Title: The Moon & Antarctica
Review: The Moon and Antarctica is darker and colder than their previous stuff, but maintains the very particular blend of peculiar lyrics and uncompromising rock that consistently weaves through all their records.

Title: Hypermagic Mountain
Review: Essentially, the Brians don't really need to innovate that much anymore and instead are just fine-tuning their craft in glorious ways.

Title: Bruiser
Review: There is plenty here to admire, leaving the feeling that this is an album to grow to love.

Title: The Hard Way
Review: Serviceable g-funk for gin-and-juice-swilling house parties. [10 Sep 2004, p.164]

Title: Slugger
Review: The energy of that debut track [“Basement Queens”] carries over into Slugger, which weaves catchy pop synthesizers around stylized guitar effects and melodic choruses.

Title: Just Like The Fambly Cat
Review: This time, the gorgeous harmonies and lo-fi ELO homages remain, but the lyrics are more personal.

Title: Wrong Creatures
Review: With BRMC, the curtains match the drapes in terms of words and music.  [No. 150, p.51]

Title: Two-Way Mirror
Review: Two-Way Mirror produces a handsome cacophony as is, but cutting away some of the gunk would have made it sweeter.

Title: Ratchet
Review: Evolution will silence all but the omnivores, and Shamir has the right taste buds. But he also has a great voice, a stunning countertenor that some have mistaken for female.

Title: How To Become Clairvoyant
Review: At times, Robertson can sound fresh and current while, other times, he can sound predictably dated.

Title: Not So Much to Be Loved as to Love
Review: Magic is liberally scattered throughout the album.

Title: Visions of a Life
Review: It has a head, a tail and a massive great beating heart. [Nov 2017, p.92]

Title: Mid-Thirties Single Scene
Review: There is a minimalist anti-folk vibe to Dermody's songs. [Nov 2016, p.37]

Title: Iron Flag
Review: The rhymes are gangsta shit at its laziest and most drearily noxious. [Mar 2002, p.111]

Title: Thrice Woven
Review: I can easily see it lacking the longevity of their other albums, but for now it’s damn good to see the Weavers doing what they do best...screaming about natural nonsense and making some excellent black metal.

Title: Valhalla Dancehall
Review: For most of Valhalla Dancehall, the diversity in sound works to British Sea Power's advantage, but it also leaves the album feeling weirdly unsatisfying.

Title: Deafman Glance
Review: Deafman Glance picks up the thread he's laid down with the stronger songs on Golden Sings That Have Been Sung. [Jun 2018, p.34]

Title: Von
Review: When layers of choir-boy vocals are added to the group's singing ("Hun Joro"), when feeble, naturalistic sounds are used in questing improvisations ("Sigur Ros"), or when acoustic instruments coalesce with a swath of electronics ("Dogun"), you'll find your jaw on the floor, too, stunned as ever.

Title: The Suburbs
Review: You barely detect it at first, but something miraculous happens on Arcade Fire's revelatory third album. The songs breathe--occasionally in long exhales, sometimes in staccato gasps.

Title: The Mirror Conspiracy
Review: Thievery Corporation sets a new standard in the downbeat discography.

Title: Wiretap Scars
Review: Under intense pressure to "prove itself," Sparta has done perfectly fine.

Title: Home Again
Review: It's Kiwanuka's staggering voice that makes you wince at its unrestrained sincerity and tenderness.

Title: Groove Denied
Review: Curiously, this bold new direction isn’t sustained; the further into the album Malkmus gets, the more normal service resumes, as if he isn’t entirely convinced of his new direction.

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: Haunting anecdotes make Carrie & Lowell consistently compelling and elevate the storytelling from murky religious contemplation to relatable human struggle.

Title: Young Enough
Review: Young Enough is a big pop influenced record that rings authentic and hits every mark both lyrically and musically--an album to dance the pain away.

Title: I Need a New War
Review: I Need a New War delivers its stories with the skill we've come to expect, and fans will likely be more than satisfied. At the same time, Finn's been telling these stories for a while, and the completion of a trilogy suggests it he might be starting to look elsewhere. If so, War makes for a nice conclusion to this run.

Title: Declaration of Dependence
Review: Declaration of Dependence offers a sense of cohesion their previous albums don’t, a complete story through melody.

Title: Overjoyed
Review: Half Japanese hasn’t returned on Overjoyed. They just found something they wanted to write songs about.

Title: Yours Truly, The Commuter
Review: This album cherry-picks a lot of the best ideas from his past work and sets a new baseline, which will simultaneously please fans of his old band and allow him to vault into the future. [Spring 2009, p.66]

Title: Cala
Review: Cala is a beautifully crafted addition to his collection. The record will appeal to those who enjoy soothing melodies and imaginative lyrics, as the Irishman continues to follow his own wonderful path.

Title: Evolution Theory
Review: It's all full-tilt anthemic intensity, whether they're tearing through drum'n'bass (Sunlight), grime (Burn, which has MCs Footsie and D Double E competing to extol the wonders of weed) or Skrillexish metalstep (Show Me a Sign).

Title: The Far Field
Review: While the album’s rear end succumbs to repetition, redemption arrives in the wistful Day Glow Fire and a bright-eyed duet with Debbie Harry on Shadows, where romantic doubts are treated as a spur to dream bigger.

Title: Ladyhawke
Review: It's all craftily entertaining, but loopy lead single 'Paris Is Burning' is the one track that escapes pastiche. [Oct 2008, p.94]

Title: Fresh Blood
Review: Fresh Blood is a much more consistent album than its predecessor. But with it, White has lost some of the sparkle that makes him so compelling.

Title: Other Truths
Review: Far from a unified artistic statement, Other Truths refuses to pin itself down, and marks itself simply and modestly as a showcase of some of the best talent in genre. A minor miracle, if you will.

Title: Dead Throne
Review: For the Devil Wears Prada's fourth album, Dead Throne, the Christian metalcore six-piece is at its most technical and most brutal.

Title: Immunity
Review: Immunity is nothing if not consistent in providing Clairo's confessional lyrics and seemingly thematically detached vocals with a cushiony-soft landing. What she loses here in charm, she makes up for in lyrical depth and an enveloping sense of comfort, if drowsy melodies tend to waft by rather than stick around.

Title: Game Theory
Review: The Roots' energy is claustrophobic and thus, jaded. It still has a prominent place on Game Theory, but when it's not subdued, it's downright bitter. [Sep 2006, p.142]

Title: Perfect Symmetry
Review: That means when Perfect Symmetry is at its best, you’ll think of a-ha, and when it’s at its worst...Go West, anyone? And yet, the more things change, the more they stay the same, and underneath it all, this is very much a Keane album.

Title: Old Growth
Review: In full flight of one of their frequent psychedelic crescendos, Dead Meadow are among rock's most eloquently deafening joys.

Title: Kamikaze
Review: A dozen svelte and self-assured songs that are ear-catching in terms of being both highly accessible while being imaginatively arranged. [3 Dec 2016, p.53]

Title: The Neon Skyline
Review: Shauf is as musically jaunty as Josh Rouse. [Mar 2020, p.92]

Title: Parcels
Review: Parcels have taken control of their destiny with a project that’s well-thought out and engaging from start-to-finish. It feels both timely and from a different era--a very rare feat.

Title: OK Cowboy
Review: This debut album took three years to make and could almost be his greatest-hits collection. It's a cracker, too; all clean, punchy metal beats and blistering, drunken synth lines in the finest italo-disco style.

Nash doesn't seem like he's willing to fully own up to his shortcomings and take a full and deep-enough personal-via-lyrical inventory. It works against him on 1977, but the music, as usual, is on point.

Title: The Flaming Lips and Heady Fwends
Review: What at first seems rather silly actually proves to be quite purposeful.

Title: Hallelujah Anyhow
Review: Hallelujah Anyhow is the group’s third. And it’s a neatly balanced work: intimate in certain moments and larger in scale at others. What makes this album work, ultimately, and what makes much of Hiss Golden Messenger’s music work on a larger scale, is the use of implicit contradictions that run through it.

Title: The Bluegrass Album
Review: In the end, Jackson's foray into bluegrass seems easy and natural, as if he'd been playing it all along.

Title: Loose Fur
Review: Tweedy, O'Rourke and Kotche push each other in exciting directions, with songs building on the contributions of each.

Title: Carry the Ghost
Review: Old fans of Gundersen’s EPs and Ledges might want something that seems less polished, as well as songs that dive even deeper into religious matters--this is not a somewhat inaccessible indie album. It is, however, melancholy beautiful pop that explores some of living’s hard questions.

Title: So Much for the City
Review: Sure, this is a very *accomplished* album by a band who can play their instruments: organs, pianos and strings sit gracefully beside each other, and there are some deft vocal harmonies, but The Thrills simply don’t have the songwriting skill or the sheer personality to make this anything more than a passable debut.

Title: Human Voice
Review: Human Voice gently nudges him back into the spotlight to speak his mind alone, and even if his voice isn't the most exciting and innovative one in today's electronic music landscape, it is unmistakably his own.

Title: In Defense of the Genre
Review: Bemis has concocted a deliciously confounding album that transcends emo more than defends it.

Title: TUTTI
Review: Situated at the border of ambient, new age, techno and industrial music, the album could just as easily fit into a meditative practice as a gritty basement rave. It is also a testament to her technical prowess as an electronic composer. But perhaps more importantly, it lives and breathes her insistence on exploring new sounds and techniques.

Title: Poetry of the Deed
Review: Poetry of the Deed still isn’t the perfect Frank Turner album, as a few songs sound a little generic due to the full-band arrangements not shouldering their part of the load. But Poetry‘s a darn good one, showing that the striving, complicated songs of the past weren’t flukes.

Title: Looping State of Mind
Review: Boundless and ecstatic, this is house music at its very best. [Dec. 2001 p. 126]

Title: This Island
Review: Theirs is an unwelcome indie lyricism that lives in a vacuum, devoid of guttural expression and left to vacant, bumper-worthy slogans.

Title: Under the Skin
Review: Of the 11 tracks, five are lovely, three are makeweights and an equal number excellent. [Dec 2006, p.133]

Title: The Great Escape Artist
Review: The Great Escape Artist does not dampen Jane's Addiction's legacy, but doesn't advance it either.

Title: Everything Now
Review: The concept of the record is solid, but the execution is lacking.

Title: Cynic's New Year
Review: On "Cynic's New Year," Portland, Ore., indie-folk duo Horse Feathers stick so firmly to their sonic guns that it becomes tightly constricting.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: The great news is that even the bad news is good news: Alabama Shakes have a hell of a lot of growing to do, but even their slightest tunes pack a punch.

Title: Acoustic Dust
Review: Acoustic Dust, really, is one for Youth completists; it’s not that Ranaldo doesn’t possess a mastery of the acoustic guitar, but rather that he’s failed to adequately display it on an album that sounds every bit as hastily recorded as it actually was.

Title: Sallows
Review: Far from immediate, Sallows demands further listens; a full surrender to the sublime. Headphones required.

Title: Natural History
Review: Nupping proved it, and Natural History amplifies the point that Dope Body are a completely unimpeachable unit from a musical standpoint: able to fit in with contemporaries while still sounding undoubtedly like themselves, carrying on the proud outsider-rock tradition of their hometown.

Title: Nothing Valley
Review: Add it up and it's an impressive display of indie rock knowledge and ability, enough to make anyone thinking they should give the band a pass (despite their unfortunate moniker) some deep second thoughts.

Title: Pursuit of Momentary Happiness
Review: Pursuit of Momentary Happiness manages to harness even more of the band’s unpredictable live energy while careering between boggle-eyed riffy bangers and booze-sodden self-reflection in truly inimitable fashion.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: The really great thing about this heavy, intense album, as punishing as it is beautiful in its resolve, is that it shakes to the core the philosophies that Björk laid out so methodically on Biophilia, but she still finds a dark difficult way back to hope and love.

Title: Biophilia
Review: The singer's greatest strength remains the glistening natural resource flowing from her throat.

Title: Fifth
Review: Much of the material here harks back less to the 1960s acoustic folksiness it's shooting for and lands disappointingly closer to the more plodding end of 1990s Britpop also-rans. [Feb/Mar 2014, p.80]

Title: Asiatisch
Review: The immaculate emptiness is, in a sense, Asiatisch’s masterstroke, helping bolster the pervading sense of dislocation of being exposed to a society that’s been fed through the photocopier one too many times.

Title: Fear Fun
Review: Fear Fun leaves his previous work in the dust.

Title: Mothertongue
Review: Connecting blue-haired symphony subscribers to indie-rock bedheads, the twentysomething New York composer is all over the place with his second disc. [Aug 2008, p.106]

Title: Family & Friends
Review: That eye for harrowing detail is Cohn's greatest strength as a writer and occasionally his biggest weakness, as one minute he's effortlessly bringing to life sons who shoot heroin with their fathers and the next stumbling into awkward rhymes about UFC fighters. [Jul 2011, p.91]

Title: Fits
Review: As 'Syncn' lilts to a close, it’s hard not to feel that White Denim would be better if they channelled a little of their chaotic diversity towards consistency, and focused upon being the very biggest, dumbest and craziest bunch of garage revivalists, rather than striking towards a uniqueness that is momentarily out of reach.

Title: Lotta Sea Lice
Review: While the album isn’t exactly synergistic in its coupling of the two singers--neither Kurt nor Courtney achieve their lyrical or musical apex here--Lotta Sea Lice nevertheless intimates an unrelenting kinship between its two auteurs.

Artist: Neil Young & Promise of the Real
Title: The Visitor
Review: Diggin’ A Hole is scratchy blues; Almost Always could have graced Harvest Moon; Stand Tall and Children Of Destiny are earworms; but if you want beauty, you’ve got it on Carnival, once the cackling stops. Neil Young is reborn, yet again.

Title: We Were Dead Before The Ship Even Sank
Review: We Were Dead... is denser than its predecessor with tunes that seem willfully harder to penetrate.

Title: You, Forever
Review: You, Forever isn’t a soft-rock record, but it is a record that reframes a certain kind of softness as strength.

Title: Camp
Review: It's wholly derivative, self-pitying emo rap that owes everything in its essence to Drake, Weezy, Cudi, and Kanye. That said, Glover is an incredibly compelling and talented rapper.

Title: ANIMA
Review: It's an excellent album born out of modern dread. He's in his element. [Aug 2019, p.106]

Title: Ditherer
Review: Broder’s voice adds an extra source of dynamism to the mix. It all adds up to a sound that revels in rock’s limitations while working to redefine them.

Title: The Fire Theft
Review: Too much of the edge is gone, too much emphasis is placed on guitar solos, and the guitars sound, at times, rather flat and listless.

Title: Salad Days
Review: The progression that Salad Days shows is encouraging, even if the album starts to peter out at the end.

Title: Radum Calls, Radum Calls
Review: O'Hagan has taken apart what he's known for and put it back together in an entirely fresh ways. [Jan 2020, p.89]

Title: Ulfilas' Alphabet
Review: In all respects, Sundara Karma have come out with a winner, mining choice bits from rock's mighty canon and fusing their own quirks and imagination to a complex but engaging set of songs.

Title: Kasabian
Review: Takes the most accessible aspects of the house-soaked, pre-Britpop scene and crafts a swaggering debut that places songwriting suss firmly above pointless posturing. [Oct 2004, p.97]

Title: Fundamental
Review: 'Fundamental' will not only be rated up there among the Pet Shop Boys finest albums -- it's also arguably the best electro pop record we've heard in years.

Title: Under Cold Blue Stars
Review: His sound, gender-neutral swooning folk dressed in quirky analog jazz keyboards, would fit nicely on a mix tape alongside The Smiths and Nick Drake.

Title: Everythangs Corrupt
Review: While it's not quite a classic like his seminal late '80s to early '90s run, Everythang's Corrupt is a return to form, especially after Cube's rudimentary 2000s releases like Laugh Now, Cry Later and I Am the West. It's heartening to hear an icon with nothing left to prove rap with the hunger of a youngster so far into his career.

Title: Oh Fortune
Review: Highlights include the waltzing "About As Helpful As You Can Be Without Being Any Help At All" and a breathless canter through the Broken Social Scene stylings of "Post-War Blues." [Jan 2012, p.93]

Title: Party Store
Review: If the band is innately familiar with the rules of this kind of territory, they sound completely out of their depth in other attempts.

Title: OutRun
Review: It’s not perfect--a couple of tracks slightly overdo the asthmatic-sounding compression--but mainly it’s a really impressively consistent and well-structured listen, and definitely worth the wait.

Title: Burst Apart
Review: Burst Apart is full of wonderful little surprises like this, that add up to two big ones: that The Antlers didn't try to follow up Hospice by repeating themselves, and nevertheless, that they have delivered a more than worthy successor.

Title: Brigid Mae Power
Review: Power sings in an emotion-laden, ever-modulating voice that summons the spirits of Tim Buckley and Tim Hardin as readily as Sibylle Baier or Sandy Denny. [Aug 2016, p.93]

Title: White People
Review: What carries the album is, I swear, the skits.

Title: Heartbeat Radio
Review: Steady but not stupendous. [Fall 2009, p.64]

Title: Pink Friday: Roman Reloaded
Review: Here both the production and Nicki's delivery border on absurdist theater, at one point devolving into Nicki literally making noises.

Title: Flat Worms
Review: An intriguing, undeniable gem. [Dec 2017, p.92]

Title: The Conversation
Review: Texas have gone back to basics, reconnecting with the solidly crafted simplicity of their earliest albums, Southside and Mother's Heaven. [Jul 2013, p.90]

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: Sure, the societal spying and corruption Reznor forecast in The Slip has played out, but Hesitation Marks is a triumphal I-told-you-so, still whispering for rebellion.

Title: Tinsel and Lights
Review: While the low-key arrangements and melancholic song choices may make Tinsel And Lights an EastEnders special of a Christmas album, if you're planning on a microwaved turkey dinner for one this year, there's probably no better soundtrack.

Title: Junk
Review: Gonzalez's more sincere side peeks through in moody, orchestral tracks like "Solitude," and the harmonica-heavy ballad, "Sunday Night 1987." Still, as its title implies, Junk leans too heavily on the quirks from the past, rife with the least flattering odds and ends of a time long gone.

Title: Youth Authority
Review: Youth Authority is a testament to the resilience of their energy, even as the band headbangs towards middle age. It's an energy that manifests itself sometimes in cringey nostalgia, other times in uninspired sentimentalism, but mostly it's anthemic and endearing.

Title: Burn Something Beautiful
Review: There are no weak tracks, proving that this collaboration with Buck & McCaughey provided the energy and creativity to help Escovedo’s 12th studio release be one of his finest, which is no small feat in his already exceptionally productive, creative and influential career.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: This good old-fashioned rock and soul quartet make good on their buzz with a debut that not only shakes, but also rattles and rolls.

Title: Let the Ocean Take Me
Review: While the majority of tracks like ‘FML’ and ‘The Weigh Down’ continue in a similar vein, with crushing slabs of aggression offset by sing-from-the-rooftops choruses, the Aussies venture into less formulaic territory with ‘Forest Fire’ and ‘Give It All’, allowing Let The Ocean Take Me to work out its own identity.

Title: Claustrophobia
Review: Scuba's music has always sounded wonderful--warm, rich, enveloping, ultra-vivid--but Claustrophobia feels like a major step up; the sonics are simply dazzling.

Title: Animal Lover
Review: Not for the unquesting. [Mar 2005, p.101]

Title: Incidental Music
Review: There’s much on this sleek and self-confident debut to suggest that the young band are wholly capable of sculpting their own unique voice amongst all the others.

Title: Kiss of Death
Review: When he's undone, it's by tinkertoy production on tracks such as the insipid Mariah Carey Vehicle "U Make Me Wanna." [5 Aug 2004, p.106]

Title: Come Around Sundown
Review: Come Around Sundown's drawling Joshua Tree sprawl, engaging enough on album opener The End and gospel-tinged first single Radioactive, soon grows shopworn.

Title: Kamaal the Abstract
Review: If we measure Q-Tip's success at "abstractionism" in terms of how his voice, message, and golden ear complement each other to bring out hip-hop's full musical potential, then Kamaal is a clear success on the artist's own terms.

Title: La Radiolina
Review: Though his global messages aren't particularly deep, his skilled, spirited execution sets him apart from other peacenik troubadours. [Oct 2007, p.101]

Title: Mary Casio: Journey to Cassiopeia
Review: Occasionally the electronic sounds can seem too familiar and overused.

Title: Girls In Peacetime Want To Dance
Review: A very weird album, but a very intriguing one too.

Title: Four
Review: Their best record since their 2005 debut.

Title: For All My Sisters
Review: The band's insistence on shouty, over-the-top moments like 'Pacific Time' or 'Mr. Wrong' still grates, but this is offset by the likes of 'City Storms', 'Summer Of Chances' and 'Different Angles', which possess some of the most urgent pop hooks and catchy anthemic choruses The Cribs have ever delivered.

Title: Umbrella Weather
Review: This music is as much fun to listen to as it is serious and vital.

Title: Southern Hummingbird
Review: Provides a refreshing change of pace from the current formulaic R&B chanteuses.

Title: Kindness Is The New Rock And Roll
Review: ‘You Don’t Walk Away From Love’ is an iconic stomp, ‘Silverlined’ is custom-made for arms-around-shoulders festival singalongs, holding court with the best of the foursome’s anthems, while ‘Magnificent’ showcases Harry’s duality perfectly: at one moment, he’s both primed to take on the world, and doubting his every step.

Title: Everything Is New
Review: The album sings from start to finish with the hard-won joy of an artist coming to terms with his own mortality and finding himself all the better for it. [Summer 2009, p.62]

Title: Freedom
Review: The writing on this third album's greatest strength. [Feb 2009, p.109]

Title: Songs for Singles
Review: With such a tight, urgent sound, Songs for Singles is an EP that'll give Torche fans enough new music to whet their appetites, but it's definitely going to leave them hungry for more.

Title: The Midsummer Station
Review: They [Adam Young's fans] deserve better. We deserve better. Come to think of it, Adam Young deserves better.

Title: Mothertongue
Review: Muhly makes more pastiche-y compositions, whose power comes from the incongruity of the comparators.

Title: Crazy Clown Time
Review: Crazy Clown Time, recorded in Lynch's personal studio with engineer Big Dean Hurley, isn't exactly fart-blank, but this visual master shouldn't quit his day job.

Title: Ma Fleur
Review: The songs are almost too precious, demanding total attention to appreciate the subtle fluctuations in texture and tone. [#25, p.102]

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: Their most accessible collection of songs to date. [#13, p.83]

Title: Shields
Review: Shields is both well-mannered and demanding, subdued but always bubbling under the surface.

Title: Home Life
Review: Home Life follows Andrew Cedermark’s displacement in this world, searching for answers as he rides a train with no set destination in sight; and along the way he was able to create a rollicking, bemused album that highlights his skills as a lyricist, allowing us to join in on the journey.

Title: Pop Etc
Review: This album marks a transition rather than an arrival.

Title: Love 2
Review: Love 2 is a triumph, effectively representing a now veteran act capable of returning to its roots yet managing still to produce novel results.

Title: Out My Window
Review: It’s not yet his "Up in Flames" or his "Pause," which is admittedly a pretty tall order.  With these 17 songs, though, it’s not a far cry to suggest that such an album might be waiting just around the bend, just a little further through that windowpane looking glass.

Title: Zoo
Review: At its best Zoo prowls menacingly and intensely, shrouded in sheets of steely guitar and fogs of squall and distortion... [But] this mood-heavy mix doesn't always work.

Title: This (is what I wanted to tell you)
Review: It feels in some ways much more of a post-Lambchop album than FLOTUS. [Apr 2019, p.24]

Title: Fuckbook
Review: As an homage to bands that paved the way, though, Fuckbook succeeds.

Title: North
Review: Arid and mannered. [Nov 2003, p.112]

Title: Hurricane
Review: Her throaty vocals and winsome lyrics recall the Jamaican patois and patience of her youth, while the title track shows off a Grace Jones delighting in a frightening form of future-forward decadence.

Title: July Flame
Review: It has such an unassuming, homespun quality that you're constantly surprised by how expansive and richly textured its songs are.

Title: Modern Times
Review: While he has never sounded quite so full of empathy, this is a grumpy old record. [Oct 2006, p.114]

Title: LUMP
Review: With each track melting into each other, LUMP feels like a self-contained trip, giving no hints as to the future of the project outside this release, but holding plenty of wonder inside.

Title: Port of Morrow
Review: An aesthetically perfect long play er that dithers in the background. [Jun 2012, p.155]

Title: Major
Review: Not be the most inspiring stuff, perhaps, but it is bloody good fun.

Title: Untilted
Review: So listener-unfriendly that it's almost amusing. [16 Apr 2005, p.51]

Title: Pura Vida Conspiracy
Review: Their sixth learns from those mistakes [on their fifth album], sounding rougher, tougher and altogether more like the raucous joy of their live shows.  [Sep 2013, p.102]

Title: Satin Panthers
Review: Easily Hud-Mo's best work yet. [Aug 2011, p.67]

Title: Shout It Out
Review: Other than the trio's weakness for trite turns of phrase, the major flaw on Shout It Out is its spit-polished production....What's encouraging about the record, though, is that Hanson's instincts are more or less on point.

Title: I Wasn't Born to Lose You
Review: I Wasn’t Born to Lose You likely won’t replace any fan’s favorite Swervedriver album, but much like the entire shoegaze revival, it’s an organic, heartfelt piece meant for those fans as much as the musicians making it.

Title: Belladonna of Sadness
Review: Her boiled up fury and velvety voice pair together to make something special, resulting in the album that Del Rey would kill to make.

Title: Wallop
Review: It’s the ‘meh’ shruggable moments of filler around them that dog the consistency of ‘Wallop’. There’s not the high-octane fuel or direction to take the record to the heights that it so constantly teases.

Title: The Diet
Review: The songs are beautifully crafted, shimmering with an alluring magic and aura, existing in their own time and space.

Title: Slowdive
Review: Slowdive delivers nearly everything their fans desire in a return: familiarity, innovation, and vast atmospheres to get lost in.

Title: Feel the Sound
Review: Those who invest the time will be rewarded with a record rife with glorious hooks, harmonies, and heart. [#39, p.69]

Title: Slow Air
Review: At its best it's a combination that offers a kind of Lynchian allure. ... Elsewhere, thought, it can all seem a little passive, a chill-out zone somewhere along Route 66. [Sep 2018, p.118]

Title: Float
Review: Most of the time, however, the band's blazing energy and instrumental swagger is able to lift your spirits despite the depressing subject matter.

Title: Blowback
Review: Tricky's most upbeat and accessible album ever, occasionally hinting at his noirish trip hop masterpiece, Maxinquaye.

Title: Sigh No More
Review: Sigh No More sees four-piece Mumford and Sons strike out for equally distinctive territory, carving out a mostly winning--if nigglingly naive--debut that deserves an audience to match its impressive convictions.

Title: The Coincidentalist
Review: The torrid, languid, gritty tones of Tuscon—as a lyrical set piece as well as an active, ire-filled ambient swell--so overwhelm Gelb’s every spiritual and physical inch, it’s as if sand and silt oozes from his pores on moments.

Title: Transgender Dysphoria Blues
Review: Free of misguided anger but with healthy amounts of trademark anxiety and angular riffs, Grace’s expression is powerful.

Title: Machineries of Joy
Review: Valhalla Dancehall found British Sea Power somewhat becalmed, but Machineries Of Joy gets them moving again, albeit in a variety of directions.

Title: commontime
Review: Commontime isn’t perfect--it’s slightly too long, and could happily have lost a couple of less distinguished tracks--but there’s still more than enough here to suggest that the reason Field Music are critically acclaimed might have less to do with the kind of band they are than the quality of what they do.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: There's still enough trail dust on the seat of their experimental pants to delight country rock eggheads. [May 2006, p.123]

Title: Tomorrow's Harvest
Review: There’s a sense of purpose and forward motion on this record where old tracks had a feeling of circling in place until the tape eroded.

Title: It Won't Be Soon Before Long
Review: The only surprising thing about It Won't Be Soon Before Long is its complete avoidance of sophomore slump.

Title: Let England Shake
Review: Perhaps it's no surprise that eighth album Let England Shake is the first for which Harvey does not appear on the sleeve.

Title: In Animal Tongue
Review: Bozulich's gloom is top quality gloom, as far as that goes, but nothing here lights up the heart like [2008's] Voyager's blistering "Truth Is Dark Like Outer Space." [Sep 2011, p.51]

Title: Strange Little Birds
Review: “Teaching Little Fingers To Play” is a bit hokey and clichéd. But on “If I Lost You,” the vibe connects massively: Serene loops and swift beats recall vintage Portishead, while Manson’s lyrical meditation on insecurity is stark, vulnerable and remarkably honest. [No. 132, p.53]

Title: Bioprodukt
Review: Its tracks are elliptical and abstract even as they stretch towards forming actual grooves. But in that respect it’s close to being the most rewarding for those who can stomach this strange, out-of-sync universe.

Title: Mermaid Avenue Vol. II
Review: Volume II is like an unnecessary b-sides compilation.... Nonetheless, the album has its high points.

Title: Feelin Kinda Free
Review: Feelin Kinda Free could be the best apocalypse soundtrack you’ll ever hear.

Title: A World Lit Only By Fire
Review: A World Lit Only By Fire finds Godflesh on pleasingly resolute form. [Dec 2014, p.57]

Title: The First Lady
Review: There's little in the way of fire or grit here.

Title: Hardcourage
Review: A record for bedroom chilling that has more than enough clout to slot into dance floor sets, it’s a refreshingly vital take on the heavily worked over source material.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: This album is rather better when it is winking at you, rather than seeking to cryogenically preserve emotion.

Title: Shine
Review: Only the fuzzy reggae of "Power of One" is lively enough to rouse a dozing listener and hint at what the record might have been with a little less midnight meditation. [May 2003, p.121]

Title: New Leaves
Review: New Leaves benfits from Kinsells'a vibrant looping and somber monotone lyricism. [Nov 2009]

Title: Songs In The Dark
Review: It’s a wonderful collection, with even Richard Thompson’s cold-comfort message in “End Of The Rainbow” imbued with a warm glow.

Title: There Is No Year
Review: Sitting right at the cross-section between optimism and pessimism, There Is No Year is an enlivening experience, and a mostly successful artistic rendering of a world on fire.

Title: SR3MM
Review: Exactly how delicately balanced their chemistry together is becomes apparent on the two solo albums that round out this three disc set. Both are decent in their own right but pale in comparison to the group disc. [Jul 2018, p.62]

Title: Hardcourage
Review: Hardcourage is a rich experience that rewards return visits. Add a near perfect flow from start to finish, and this fun bundle of irresistible future garage can be considered crafted, even when the spirit is as easy as Sunday morning.

Title: Blood Red Shoes
Review: Blood Red Shoes is an album firmly wedged in comfort, occasionally straying out into more interesting waters, but usually retreating to old tricks. For an album that tries so hard to be angry it’s just mild.

Title: Here Before
Review: This fifth album shouldn't disappoint them [their fans]. [Jun 2011, p.114]

Title: La Bella Mafia
Review: La Bella Mafia is one of the top hip-hop albums of 2003, so far.

Title: Silence Is Sexy
Review: Silence Is Sexy retains that beauty, and redoubles the degree to which it compels. The chaos has been reigned in, channeled and focused, losing none of its fervor, but perhaps gaining power in its linearity.

Title: Born Again Revisited
Review: If the audio quality is a mite cleaner this time, it seems the band have made the songs a little more prickly. [Oct 2009, p.112]

Title: Hurricane
Review: Hurricane is her first new album since 1989, and it's her best ever.

Title: Warpaint
Review: Second LP Warpaint stirs, stews, beats, and swells far more amniotic, evoking the seminal psych greeting, ladies and gentlemen we are floating in space.

Title: Mama, I'm Swollen
Review: Tim Kasher is emo's grown-up hero--a punk who pays his mortgage. So it's a little awkward to find the Omaha native stricken with Peter Pan syndrome on Cursive's sixth album, Mama, I'm Swollen.

Title: The Desaturating Seven
Review: As ever, the Californian threesome's pervasive wackiness is matched by a breathtaking sense of musicality punctuated by Claypool's manic basslines. [Nov 2017, p.112]

Title: Shadow of the Sun
Review: The swell and squall lets up just once, on the transcendental In A Cloud, but it's in  the moments of pure sonic abandon, like Wilding, that the group truly find themselves. [Apr 2015, p.95]

Title: Since I Left You
Review: Everything sounds like it's been triggered by hand and mixed on the fly, practically improvised yet brilliant in scope. [#32, p.54]

Title: Our Love to Admire
Review: The New York quartet retains its flair for dramatic images and ominous guitar lines on its major-label debut, but with producer/ mixer Rich Costey onboard, these signatures uncoil into more complex soundscapes.

Title: Long Distance Song Effects
Review: Overall, it’s fair to say that Long Distance Song Effects is pretty much what you’d expect if you were one of the few who heard Goldheart Assembly’s debut album, without some of the instant hit that record delivered, but with plenty of depth to be found once you’ve peered beneath the skin.

Title: How Big How Blue How Beautiful
Review: Welch isn't the most rhythmic singer; she's more about powerful held notes and dramatic articulation, and her rock moves have sometimes felt fussy in the past. But here, she punches like a prizefighter.

Title: Altogether
Review: Altogether is perhaps the lightest and most pop-oriented release in the band's canon, doubling down on bright guitar tones and jazzy chord voicings, and relying even more heavily on lush synth parts to augment their sound. While its feather-soft tone flirts with the smooth banality of easy listening, parts of the album are far more clever and well-structured than first impressions might suggest.

Title: Embracism
Review: If this album works, it’s because of moments like “Landslide”: those that cut through the density of an artist in flux, one susceptible to myriad influences, managerial grumblings, and producer cues, overeager to pass off his work as undeniably unique.

Title: Â¡Tre!
Review: Too often, ¡Tré! falls back on a formula--fast, box-ticking choruses fashioned from chords you can count on the fingers of one hand--that Green Day have pretty much stretched to breaking point.

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: Heretic Pride is a stunning, well-rounded piece of music that only The Mountain Goats could pull off.

Title: Good Apollo, I'm Burning Star IV, Volume Two: No World for Tomorrow
Review: Coheed have picked up more prog nuances so it fits that this, the last in the sequence, is their most ambitious yet, best embodied in the eight-minute 'The End Complete.'

Title: Yuck
Review: An overall sense of exclusivity permeates their blithe, sassy melodies, not to mention that its “adorableness” can occasionally irritate (cussing with fey charm is just so earnestly dopey). Still, Alpine’s transformation into a breezier, more cosmopolitan ensemble suits them.

Title: Human Animal
Review: The echo-saturated clang works as background music if you’re washing dishes in a haunted house or performing at-home knee surgery, but hunker down with the sound by itself and it evaporates like stale smoke.

Title: placeholder
Review: Meg Duffy’s humble, comforting vocals will help cushion the blow that will inevitably come with any relationship, and their poetic aptitude results in a record that’s just as therapeutic and affecting on the written page as it is in sung form.

Title: Adrian Thaws
Review: Expectations are, as ever, moderate for Tricky's latest album, and he doesn't disappoint. [Sep 2014, p.60]

Title: Temper Temper
Review: Though Bullet for My Valentine still have just enough post-hardcore and screamo in their sound to keep metal purists from coming completely around to their way of thinking, Temper Temper feels like a gateway album into thrash.

Title: BLACKsummers'night
Review: For those who like their pop delicate and unapologetically deep, this is one for turning up loud and wallowing.

Title: Christopher
Review: The occasional burst of incredible, disposable pop goes a long way, but sadly not long enough to make Christopher an entirely engaging experience.

Title: Vile Child
Review: Vile Child is a debut LP that is rife with a resounding honesty and an airtight dexterity.

Title: West
Review: Often harrowing, although Williams's emotional odyssey finds resolution on the title track.

Title: Fantasy
Review: If the songs on the first half of Fantasy trigger the chemicals in your brain, the captivating tracks that comprise the second half implore you to submit to them completely.

Title: The Blueprint 2: The Gift & the Curse
Review: Releasing two strong outings in the past year drained him of the juice necessary to make a compelling two-fer.

Title: Marry Me
Review: What Marry Me may lack in innovation, it makes up for in attitude and execution.

Title: Limits of Desire
Review: The only trouble is that nearly every track captures the same sense of John Hughes-worthy nostalgia, with no cut standing out above the rest.

Title: The Only Place
Review: Musically, it's business as usual as they follow up their 2010 debut with more indie pop infused with the melodrama of The Ronettes and The Shangri-Las. [Jun 2012, p.69]

Title: My Woman
Review: Here she sounds more assured, even in her darker moments, and her strong, versatile voice is as extraordinary as ever.

Title: Inclusions
Review: Inclusions is not an album for any typical audience, though those with more esoteric and adventurous tastes may embrace it.

Title: b'lieve i'm goin down
Review: Of course, songs like the playful “Lost My Head There” and the searching “Dust Bunnies” could just as easily be about the consequences of excessive drug consumption or no-less excessive levels of modern stress, yet the persistence of the self-alienation motif amid slanted nods to his career in music end up strongly insinuating that his growing status as a rock icon is weakening the already weak hold he has over himself.

Title: Goddess
Review: A bewitching, and surprisingly diverse debut, it looks like Jillian Banks more than lives up to the hype.

Title: El Pintor
Review: Ultimately El Pintor feels a like a blast of icy fresh air after a sticky, sweltering summer’s day.

Title: Transference
Review: Sure, Transference may not reach the same dizzying heights as "Kill the Moonlight" or "Gimme Fiction" did, but it's still better than half the indie-rock music that's out there today. Why? Because, in short, it's a Spoon album.

Title: Carry On
Review: Another entry in Cornell's catalogue of partial successes. [Jun 2007, p.91]

Title: My Love is Cool
Review: My Love Is Cool is no pioneering sonic masterpiece, no, but it’s definitely possessed with that ol’ black magic snap, the “electric kick” that might just inspire other manic street creatures to ignite a guitar and exorcise their own demons. This incendiary infection, pass it on.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: Beyond anything, A Moon Shaped Pool feels like the beginning of a new chapter--the first time these five have merged their own idiosyncrasies without compromising or crossing wires.

Title: Quality
Review: In the end, his big head seriously weighs down the quality of Quality.

Title: Illegals in Heaven
Review: The intelligence and emotions of the lyrics also capture the accidental complexities of the pop of yesteryear when light entertainment could find itself the place for heavy themes. [Oct 2015, p.60]

Title: It's Me Again
Review: Though few songs are second-rate, their similarities make them bleed into each other too much.

Title: Oxymoron
Review: For those unfamiliar with Q's pre-Interscope material, his official debut provides insight, and an appetizer of what his more than respectable discography can do to not only entertain fans of 2010s rap, but inspire them. [Apr/May 2014, p.81]

Title: Follow Me Home
Review: For now, Follow Me Home is a lowrider journey to California, with many ups and some downs included.

Title: Babes Never Die
Review: With barbed lyrics and messy, thrumming guitars a Honeyblood speciality, things never get overly pretty on thes 11 tales of "horror, lust and laughs," while new Honeyblood drummer Cat Myers, successor to Shona McVicar, has bedded-in nicely. [Dec 2016, p.90]

Title: Look At Us Now Dad
Review: This is a hugely promising debut. [Apr 2020, p.106]

Title: Whatever It Takes
Review: This terrific follow-up [to 2016's Hold On] captures the sparks again, and there are plenty of them. [Mar 2018, p.97]

Title: HYMNS
Review: Guitarist Russell Lissack does his best to insert some typically wiry licks where possible, but there’s none of the claustrophobia or unease that used to make Bloc Party so vital.

Title: Being
Review: Everything about the album is deliberately simple, but with some inspired production choices added to the mix.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: We’re left with many songs that could have used some voices, or ones where the voices dominate proceedings, taking the focus away from the creators.

Title: International Teachers of Pop
Review: It might not quite measure up to the very tall order of being another Dare or Different Class, but the record comes close and that is something the band should be very proud of.

Title: Cabinet of Curiosities
Review: While Gardner's music isn't exactly anything new or groundbreaking, it serves as an appropriately nostalgic reminder of a time when it would have been.

Title: Gallipoli
Review: With Condon's warm quaver and bevy of brass instruments, acoustic and electric guitars, electronic and acoustic drums, accordion, and mix of pianos, organs, and synthesizers including modular synths gathered under a production ethos that dials up already colorful arrangements to Technicolor spectacle.

Title: Special Affections
Review: O'Regan's voice is the centerpiece. Unlike seemingly every other bedroom music maker these days, there's a real power and discernable confidence to his croon.

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: It's as much fun as it needs to be--as it should be. Reflective, restless, fiercely engaged, it feels like it's in constant process of rethinking and remodeling, slicing off bits of musical flesh and slapping them back on elsewhere as it dips and bounces along the street. [Feb 2018, p.94]

Title: Whiteout Conditions
Review: Animating even the slowest songs on the album is a sense of play and possibility, the realisation that these musicians can shake off the dust and still surprise us. [May 2017, p.36]

Title: Big Station
Review: Sometimes, it's hard to remember who's influencing who. [Aug 2012, p.70]

Title: Wraith
Review: Wraith finds those heterogeneous elements [post-punk, industrial Krautrock and Angelo Badalamenti-like soundtrack atmosphere] fusing even more satisfyingly than [2015's Highly Deadly Black Tarantula]. [Mar 2019, p.97]

Title: Liars
Review: Liars is all about that Liars blueprint, and in that sense the album can get redundant.

Title: Automaton
Review: They’re still figuring it out, but somehow, even their mistakes feel fresh.

Title: Amerikaz Nightmare
Review: They've sounded stuck and overconfident before, but this old-school-styled, true hip-hop album finds the Mobb hungry again.

Title: In Stormy Nights
Review: On In Stormy Nights, Ghost does what they do best--compress decades of psychedelic and avant-garde music into a modern melange that will please fans from the folk end of the spectrum to the harshest of noiseniks. [#16, p.99]

Title: No Love Lost
Review: Budden's raw energy and experience enriche otherwise throwaway pop, even when saccharine hooks (Kirko Bangz) and amphibian croaks (Lil Wayne) threaten to cheapen it.

Title: Turn The Lights Out
Review: The Ponys continue to revel in the two-guitar rock song, naturally, but they step out stylistically. [#17, p.92]

Title: Atlas Vending
Review: There’s no point on Atlas Vending that feels wasted, no meandering or time-sucks; it’s just pure adrenaline rock expertly produced and delivered piping hot.

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: At most, half the songs on this album are capable of successfully fusing Finn’s compelling narratives with rather less than impressive instrumentation for an effect that’s worth some merit. Unfortunately, it just doesn’t ‘hold’ for the remainder.

Title: The Colour in Anything
Review: The result is a staggeringly impressive and confident third album from an artist who has reached the very peak of his powers.

Title: Lungs
Review: The best bits feel like being chased through a moonless night by a sexy moor witch.

Title: New Blood
Review: This album's a string-driven thing swinging between bravado and bleakness, and always beautiful.

Title: From All Purity
Review: From All Purity at once epitomizes Indian’s sound and represents a leap forward into new levels of intensity.

Title: Go With Me
Review: Go With Me is assuredly worth more than a few listens. The fact that this collection of sun-bathed rock tunes have arrived just in time for summer makes it all the better.

Title: None The Wiser
Review: While their true believers might not mind the record’s overall lack of variety, for anyone new to the band there’s little on None The Wiser to separate them from the indie-rock chaff.

Title: The Civil Wars
Review: The Civil Wars is a testament to the power of their undeniable musical chemistry. It’s even better than their Grammy-winning debut, Barton Hollow.

Title: Pillowfight
Review: Pillowfight is technically flawless but thoroughly unexciting.

Title: Dry Food
Review: Kempner has a knack for these odd little about-turns that elevate Dry Food above the usual plainspoken acoustic indie fare.

Title: Distant Relatives
Review: it's disappointing that collaborative projects featuring prominent artists from these fields haven't yet delivered a worthwhile album. Marley's 2005 release Welcome to Jamrock was a step forwards, but Distant Relatives represents an accomplished attempt to go further, fusing traits with few discernable flaws.

Title: Cinder
Review: This is a step forward, and the new studio approach is a constructive development.

Title: Cruise Your Illusion
Review: The highs on The Men’s album are higher than Milk Music’s, but Cruise Your Illusion is the more cohesive statement.

Title: The Bravery
Review: Endicott, who jumps skin from Julian Casablancas to Robert Smith to the guy from the Killers in just three tracks, has less charisma than a mustard plug.

Title: The Hum
Review: Hookworms have a huge, infectious energy, best evidenced on the wild organ grooves and ridiculously weighty drumming of ‘Radio Tokyo’, but some of the finest moments come when they adopt a more considered, less-immediate approach.

Title: Aufheben
Review: Newcombe is a master at turning the minimal into maximal, layering myriad swirling textures into a dizzying head-rush of a tune (see: "Seven Kinds of Wonderful"), but crafty production only takes him so far.

Title: Spokes
Review: This is a disc that springs to life under closer inspection but also serves quite capably as background music -- the kind that draws in casual listeners and gets them asking questions.

Title: No More Drama
Review: The multiproducer arrangements are expansive yet warm, and Blige's pushy rasp has never sounded better.

Title: Rooms Filled with Light
Review: It's not exactly love at first sight with Rooms Filled with Light. But like all the best love affair it endures, and reveals new sides of itself with each listen.

Title: Cause I Sez So
Review: The unlikely resurrection of the New York Dolls is solidified by this second recent album, an output that now matches in quantity and mirrors in quality their epic early-'70s sprint.

Title: The Old Believer
Review: The Atlas Moth hope to be heavy and heavenly, aggressive and accessible, to exist in worlds of light and dark simultaneously. In this instance, they wind up in the shadows of their own intentions, hidden in flat gray instead of beautiful white or harrowing black.

Title: Prior to the Fire
Review: Long on tweedly solos, rambling structures, and songs about being trapped in space and time, Prior to the Fire--love the title, dudes, despite my disappointment--is sure to satisfy hardcore stoner-metal devotees with no fear of the occasional eight-minute track length. Everybody else should seek out "Hello Master."

Title: Bloom
Review: With Bloom, they have mastered their sultry formula.

Title: The Facts of Life
Review: Haines' secret weapon lies in the hands of vocalist Sarah Nixey -- a cross between Olivia Newton-John and St. Etienne's Sarah Cracknell. Her singing style supports Haines' music with a deceptive beauty, as she wraps her voice around lyrics that belie that sweetness.

Title: Manslaughter
Review: Pure metal it ain’t. Pure fun, it sure is.

Title: Love Travels at Illegal Speeds
Review: A fine album that, while not likely to win any prizes for Gorillaz-style innovation, will resonate, both musically and lyrically, with fans young rather than old.

Title: White Stuff
Review: White Stuff is a welcome return even if it is uneven.

Title: The Future and the Past
Review: There is evolution on The Future and the Past and a real sense that Prass has done what she set out to do: make an album that, like the work of Marvin Gaye, gets people thinking and resolving to take action, all the while shaking their hips to the undeniable groove.

Title: Coles Corner
Review: If there is a difference it's in the richness of the emotions and textures.

Title: A Healthy Distrust
Review: A Healthy Distrust reinforces Sage Francis’ standing as one of the most verbally gifted rappers currently in the game, but it lacks the cohesive flow of Personal Journals and complains about a host of worldly ills without offering much in the way of a positive solution.

Title: Spell My Name
Review: The material tends toward routine, but Braxton's elegant distress cuts through everything with conviction.

Title: It's a Wonderful Life
Review: Musing, eerie and oddly lovely, It's a Wonderful Life is almost minimalist - it captures fleeting moments in a few chords and peculiarly evocative phrases.

Title: Traffic and Weather
Review: Front to back, this 14-song slice of bop-worthy Americana hits the spot like hamburgers and coffee.

Title: Don't Believe The Truth
Review: The Gallaghers sound more comfortable than ever in their skins. [Jun 2005, p.102]

Title: Be The Void
Review: Too often, Be the Void finds Dr. Dog unleashed, letting their wilder ideas get the better of them.

Title: Made in China
Review: Everything here roars. [May 2006, p.108]

Title: Reunion Tour
Review: The fourth disc from this Winnipeg, Manitoba quartet proves to be its strongest and most consistent. [Fall 2007, p.83]

Title: The Deserters
Review: This an attention-grabbing debut album from a unique and fascinating talent, who has more than demonstrated her validity and potential as a solo artist.

Title: The Lemon of Pink
Review: The Lemon Of Pink is built in much the same way that its predecessor was, and while it conjures up similar feelings at times, it also takes off in different directions entirely with the addition of actual vocals.

Title: Sleeping with Ghosts
Review: Sound-wise, 'Sleeping With Ghosts' is pretty much flawless.

Title: Exit 13
Review: While this 76-minute album flags near the end, there’s still more than enough smooth-tongued, quick-witted rhyming to justify his boasts.

Title: From the Top of Willamette Mountain
Review: From the Top of Willamette Mountain sounds more confident than the UK debut he released earlier this year.

Title: Sleeping Through the War
Review: All Them Witches have conjured fresh landmarks all their own. [18 Feb 2017, p.52]

Title: Volume 3
Review: When Volume 3 soars above its status as just a nice summer soundtrack are the moments when Deschanel lets some deeper emotions break through the carefree demeanor of the songs.

Title: Frances The Mute
Review: Within this impressive, ambitious, often stupid whole, are moments of melthing human beauty. [29 Feb 2005, p.65]

Title: Odditorium or Warlords of Mars
Review: Any ad creatives hoping for mobile phone campaign music will be disappointed. [Oct 2005, p.102]

Title: Give a Glimpse of What Yer Not
Review: Everything that 30 years ago made Dinosaur Jr a lightning bolt of enervated languor is present here. [Sep 2016, p.59]

Title: A River Ain't Too Much To Love
Review: An exquisite mix that conjures train tracks and piney woods. [3 Jun 2005, p.86]

Title: American Band
Review: Taken as a whole, American Band is the group’s most thematically coherent work since their pinnacle of Jason Isbell-assisted records in the early 2000s.

Title: In Mind
Review: The first record without co-founder and lead guitarist Matt Mondanile, who left last year to focus on his Ducktails project, it finds the band struggling to find their footing in his absence.

Title: Seeds We Sow
Review: His lyrics philosophize about love, loss and passing time. But his guitar geekery is the album's governing force, and it's usually for the better.
Not quite the step forward he needed. [Sep 2001, p.122]

Title: All We Are
Review: All We Are has potential, but it's squandered on their debut in an attempt to make a spacey, moody soundtrack.

Title: Paranormal
Review: Tremendous fun throughout. [Sep 2017, p.87]

Title: I Am Easy to Find
Review: With new voices, new avenues of exploration and new lyrical viewpoints, The National, alongside producer-director Mike Mills, once again show their ability to reinvent themselves to produce something that is more than just an album.

Title: Electric Circus
Review: To be filed alongside the Root's recent Phrenology. [Mar 2003, p.95]

Title: Love Letters
Review: Love Letters [is] not quite a glorious failure, but more of an intermittently-glorious muddle.

Title: Themes for Dying Earth
Review: Musically the album moves in a more organic way from one song into another than if it were just a collection of ten songs.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: It stands tall as the best R&B album in a long while, if not the best album in a long while.

Title: Tirtha
Review: This album is clearly not one you would want to put on in the background of your next party. In every aspect (its forms, melodies, instrumentation, etc.) it is a challenging and engaging hour of music.

Title: So There
Review: So There is both ambitious and down-to-earth, impeccably constructed, and utterly accessible.

Title: England Keep My Bones
Review: England Keep My Bones finally gets the combination right and stands right alongside Love, Ire and Song as one of Frank Turner's best works.

Title: Lookaftering
Review: Lookaftering is some kind of miracle. [Nov 2005, p.100]

Title: Multiply
Review: The heritage soul signposts multiply with almost hallucinatory rapidity. [Aug 2005, p.104]

Title: Tha Carter V
Review: Relationships with women are at the forefront of Tha Carter V, including a desperate cry for help from his mother on "I Love You Dwayne," which leads into the sorrowful "Don't Cry," featuring a chorus from the late XXXTENTACION. ... Despite the revelations, the album is not without its expected bangers.

Title: Third Mouth
Review: "Third Mouth" is arrestingly pretty, with its delicate guitars and looming, swelling synth notes, but also unfathomable.

Title: Mondo Amore

Title: Try Not To Freak Out

Title: Lay It Down
Review: Lay It Down is almost indistinguishable from green's past hits. Then again, maybe that was the point. [May 2008, p.74]

Title: Sodium
Review: Sodium is liable to leave you just as drained as its creator, but it’s the sort of exhaustion that feels valorous and victorious. After all, losing your voice is a small price to pay for saving your sanity.

Title: Semper Femina

Title: Temple Beautiful
Review: It is the details that make Prophet explode.

It captures a performer truly at the top of their game, throwing everything into a project so that not one second is wasted. It’s a record that makes you fall in love with music again, a record you feel privileged to experience and a record that imparts fundamental human truths.

Title: Redemption

Title: Last Summer

Title: Dirty Computer

Title: Wildflower
Review: It’s testament to the power of their original vision that it all still sounds so fresh.

Title: Nashville

Title: Zonoscope
Review: Clocking in at just a shade over an hour, Zonoscope is – as its cover art of Manhattan being engulfed by a waterfall suggests – a very surreal leviathan, an object that surely mesmerizes as we all wait for the oncoming Armageddon.

Title: Skelethon
Review: Skelethon is funky, freaky and heavy on the drums.

Title: Out of Nothing
Review: [Their] apathy really detracts from the heartfelt nature of the music, which, produced by the anthemic hand of Youth, is mostly of the passionate, chest-thumping variety.

Title: Damogen Furies
Review: Even on an album as wholly electronic-sounding as Damogen Furies, Jenkinson's musicality remains organic and responsive.

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Sometimes is the work of probably the best lyricist writing today, and roundly deserves to be an album for the ages. If it’s not, that’s only because she’ll have found a way to top it next time around.

Title: Forever
Review: Despite its ridiculous lyrical moments, Forever advances the trend of mashing together disparate styles in metal and hardcore.

Title: Severant

Title: Aha Shake Heartbreak
Review: Wrongly cast as a chicken-fried version The Strokes after 2003’s stellar Youth & Young Manhood, on their latest, Aha Shake Heartbreak, The Kings prove that they’re a band of significant depth and originality.

Title: Distance Inbetween
Review: Heavier, weirder and bleaker than anything they've released, Distance Inbetween is weighty but never hard work. [Apr 2016, p.84]

Title: Barbara
Review: Listening to Barbara is like watching the England football team; expectations are high at the outset and true to form, things get off to a rousing start. Title: Fortune
Review: Fortune reveals an artist more concerned with calculating than creating.

Title: Foundations of Burden
Review: As long as their attention spans can accommodate the extremely lengthy tunes, any fan of heavy music would do well to pick up Foundations of Burden. Highly recommended.

Title: Undertow
Review: Undertow makes great use of Baljo’s guitar and Olson’s saxophone; looping them into churning, oozing grooves that recall the metallic swamp of Gnod’s Infinity Machines LP. Within this sickly ambience, bursts of electronic noise erupt and sputter but never dominate. [Apr 2017, p.59]

Title: neo
Review: Feeling comfortable is not something neo, and by extension So Pitted, is concerned with. Instead, exploration of the darkness and sickness of life are the key drivers and if neo is any indication, it is pretty compelling material.

Title: No One Deserves Happiness
Review: The experience is nothing less than fully immersive by the time we’ve made it through “Shelter Is Illusory,” the closest the album gets to true pop (aside from Armstrong’s co-written “Adamah”), replete with a gorgeous quasi-operatic upward-searching chorus from Armstrong and a keening processed-strings backing.

Title: Burned Mind
Review: Every track is a pure battle, with searing bursts of abrasion chopping at lava flows of insane density.

Title: Pura Vida Conspiracy
Review: Drenched with joy in its own noisiness, the album is nonetheless easier listening than some of the group’s earlier work.

Title: Thee Physical
Review: He remains in the club for his passable sophomore effort. [Jul 2011, p.91]

Title: Partie Traumatic
Review: Youngbloods triumph with unpretentious pop.

Title: Moondagger
Review: It's exhausting but charming. [Aug 2009, p.104]

Review: Amos doesn't record as much as most artists, and it must be tempting to give fans everything she can, but in this case, it's hurt her a bit. Still there, are many tracks here worth adding to one's Amos shelf.

Title: Await Barbarians

Title: The Soul Sessions

Title: Random Access Memories

Title: 21st Century Breakdown
Review: The story is hard to follow, but after a few listens the band’s rallying cries take shape.

Title: Mirrors the Sky

Title: Slow Focus
Review: Slow Focus is the album Fuck Buttons were born to make.

Title: Visions

[#210, p.60]

Title: Local Business

Some will jump around and pump their fists to every chorus without giving the lyrics much thought; some will live and die by every word. Some will even find it all kind of funny. Nobody is necessarily wrong.

Title: Chrissybaby Forever

Title: Holding All the Roses
Review: The sub-Quo thud of Rock and Roll Again aside, this is an eminently likable upholding of 40-year-old principles.

Title: Homesick

Title: Perpetual Motion People
Review: If you're willing to get on board with Ezra Furman and the beautifully messy world that he celebrates here, Perpetual Motion People is a ride worth taking.

Title: Sistrionix

Title: Watersports

Review: The LP gets bogged down in chilled-out trap pop (see the Lil Wayne-​assisted "Lonely"). But slow jams like "Concentrate" perfectly balance the downtempo and the energetic.

Title: Timeless
Review: When Timeless succeeds, it's beautiful, boundary-breaking music.

Title: Starboy
Review: There are things worth hearing on Starboy. Starboy hedges its bets and tries to do both. You can see why, but it makes for a curiously uneven album.

Title: Swim
Review: As mesmerising as it is innovative, Swim is a record you want to dive in to. [May 2010, p.120]

Title: The Wind
Review: It's not so much what Zevon says as how he says it: with an air of ragged, nothing-to-lose spontaneity. [Sep 2003, p.133]

The second half of the record is quieter, with a more musing outlook.

Title: Empire

Title: Modern Mirror

But even that doesn't stop Modern Mirror from being something Drab Majesty haven't accomplished before, which is an album that has no use for the "skip" button. It is a very good Drab Majesty album. Title: Death Magnetic

Title: Make Another World
Review: For Idlewild fans, especially of the older school, there is more than enough here to warrant a pilgrimage to your local record shop.

Title: Confident

Title: What Comes After The Blues

Title: Mind Hive

Review: Be it maturity, empathy, professionalism, or what have you, whatever Dinosaur Jr.'s doing is working.

Title: Untethered Moon

Title: Light Up Gold

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool

Title: Process

Title: Grid of Points

Title: Graffiti on the Train

Title: Funeral
Review: Encompassing chamber pop melodies, angular art-rock, lavish orchestration and post-punk vocals, its sheer sonic size and ambition goes some way towards justifying the amount of gushing praise that's been heaped upon this album since its September release on Merge last year. The fact that the music is so paradoxically life-affirming and euphoric makes it much easier to write, what now feel like, trite hyperboles.

Title: Through the Windowpane
Review: Here lie gorgeous tunes that are lithe enough to cope with the little bursts of sonic madness that flit around like overproduced Eighties butterflies.

Title: Sermon on the Rocks
Review: With his latest, Ritter has achieved the near impossible, fully reimagining his own art while still holding close to what's always made him special.

Title: Dark Young Hearts
Review: Clearly full of ideas and enthusiasm, FrYars suffer from a cheapness of sound, the instrumentation often too basic and one-dimensional to give songs od potential the lick of sonic paint they deserve. [Nov 2009, p.94]

Title: It's Alright Between Us As It Is
Review: It’s Alright Between Us As It Is feeds the body and soul.

Title: Yuck
Review: Tracks like "Georgia" and "Holing Out" tear by with sandpaper efficiency and no little impact. Yet they have more than one idea. [Mar 2011, p.107]

Title: Cheatahs
Review: While the band leads us down roads we have assuredly traveled before, that doesn’t make the sights and the sounds any less interesting or intoxicating this time around.

Title: Love Sign
Review: The slick varnish he [producer John Agnello] slathers on doesn't do this group any favors. Still, the melodies stick to your brain like flypaper.

Title: Noah's Ark
Review: Noah's Ark is not an end-to-end stunner. But there are bright spots throughout, and the sisters display a consistent penchant for deviating from standard folk and twee pop lyrical imagery.

Title: Ellipsis
Review: This is one of Biffy Clyro's best records yet. [Aug 2016, p.106]

Title: No One Is Lost
Review: No One Is Lost is the best kind of pop music: the universal made intimate (and vice-versa), one note at a time.

Title: Fears Trending
Review: As a companion album or on its own two legs, Fears Trending was worth another trip to well.

Title: The Most Lamentable Tragedy
Review: Where TMLT fails, it’s because of Stickles’ long-windedness and the self-obsession at the heart of this work; almost certainly a by-product of his diagnosis. Mostly, though, this lament is no tragedy, but a spirited two-fingers; a celebration of the artistic payload of atypical brain chemistry.

Title: The Courage of Others
Review: These musicians came into their own and have created another standout record without repeating themselves.

Title: Only By The Night
Review: Much of Only By the Night is unmistakably the work of a band making music with arenas in mind. Sometimes it's intriguing.

Title: schlagenheim
Review: A rousing debut that constantly eschews genre conventions. As a result, the record manages the impressive juxtaposition of perpetual unfurling in unpredictable ways yet remaining tonally coherent. [Aug 2019, p.26]

Title: Welcome oblivion
Review: Reznor's undeniably present, but Maandig provides a strong focal point. [Mar-Apr 2013, p.92]

Title: CLPPNG
Review: CLPPNG is the work of hip hop auteurs delivering the shock of the new.  [Jul 2014, p.88]

Title: Making Time
Review: Making Time has some really great tracks, but maybe with a little more time spent on a few less ideas it could perhaps have been a great album.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: Despite being one of the weaker albums Wilco has released, A Ghost is Born is nonetheless the most fascinating.

Title: Time on Earth
Review: The economy of Ethan Johns' and Steve Lillywhite's production helps, as do the straightforward arrangements and, most important of all, Finn's most commercial and least quirky set of songs since 1991's "Woodface," or even the group's self-titled 1986 debut.

Title: Romantica
Review: Nothing here is as strong as any of the standouts on Luna's mid-Nineties classic, Penthouse, but each of Wareham's songs is well-rounded and pleasantly wispy.

Title: The Afterman: Descension
Review: There’s a slight dipping point of ‘Away We Go’ and ‘Iron Fist’, and this album doesn’t stand up quite as well as either of the ‘Good Apollo, I’m Burning Star’ epics, but nonetheless this is a thoroughly thrilling entry in to Coheed and Cambria’s rich canon.

Title: Greetings from California
Review: While the music might be chilled-out, an innate tension invites deeper listening.

Title: Foil Deer
Review: This album makes you work, forces you to hit repeat not to relive sweet, instantly gratifying thrills, but to let it root into your brain to understand it better.

Title: Man on the Moon: The End of Day
Review: Cudi deserves credit for such an audacious high-concept debut. It falls a bit flat, but at least it falls forward.

Title: Exclusive
Review: Brown's gotten a stronger grip on his Stevie Wonder croon, and it's hard to imagine he doesn't have an album's worth of hits here.

Title: Rewind The Film
Review: Rewind the Film seems immediately poised for lost-classic status-- for all its clumsiness and flaws, it’s the kind of album that wants you to let it sink in, or even gather dust, until you remember it’s there.

Title: A Colores
Review: Though A Colores is rather uneven, it's a compelling-- and more than competent-- effort.

Title: Immunity
Review: At just an hour in length, Immunity savours every moment, pulling on your heartstrings, lifting you off your feet and inviting you right back for more.

Title: V For Vaselines
Review: The tunes offer a smooth enough ride, but The Vaselines aren’t really stretching themselves here.

Title: Red Bedroom
Review: When Red Bedroom ditches the choppy guitar riffs... the results are as much of a buzzkill to Bedroom's jumpin' vibe as cops busting up a raging house party. [Aug 2004, p.116]

Title: Blank Project
Review: It’s as beguiling and bewitching as you’d expect.

Title: Violence
Review: It’s clear with Violence that Editors are working to build upon their new sound instead of re-inventing and re-producing, and though their efforts of combining dark indie disco pop with more morose lyrics and guitar undertones, it is a refreshing new direction.

Title: White Men Are Black Men Too
Review: The band fails to make a significant statement of their immediate necessity with this sophomore effort.

Title: Dept. of Disappearance
Review: Department of Disappearance does sound strangely complacent and monochromatic, offering no twists on the technorganic aesthetic he's been plying since Grandaddy were still a bedroom act.

Title: Strapped
Review: Long and lush isn't a bad look for the Soft Pack, so long as they're keeping the beat.

Title: Fire from the Sky
Review: Fire from the Sky fully returns the band to what made Shadows Fall so appealing in the first place--without taking a step backward.

Title: American Doll Posse
Review: Trading obscure metaphors for assertive personae, Amos sings with a remarkably forceful focus. [Jun 2007, p.92]

Title: Revival
Review: While Em’s bullheaded decision to experiment with the flow should be heartily respected, it doesn’t shroud the fact that he’s not charting any new territory, at least topically. But it’s largely the retreads of past glory where he hits stride the hardest.

Title: The Hope Six Demolition Project
Review: Harvey set out to bring listeners and the underprivileged subjects of her record together, and the exciting thing is that that final moment should surely do that.

Title: Proof of Youth
Review: The Go! Team are clearly committed to the lo-fi, DIY aesthetic, but with songs as strong as these it’s rather a shame they didn’t apply a little depth and finesse to their production.

Title: Diviner
Review: Diviner retains much of what Wild Beasts did best. [Jul 2019, p.37]

Title: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light I
Review: Angels of Darkness, Demons of Light 1 contains some of the finest work Earth has produced to date.

Title: Alphabetical
Review: Despite the '80s tag and influences worn plainly on sleeves, Phoenix always come across strangely earnest and never cheesy. [#11, p.98]

Title: Warmth
Review: Blondes' third album sees them take several steps forward, delivering a piece that's often mesmeric and always distinctively theirs.

Artist: The Knife in Collaboration with Mt. Sims and Planningtorock
Title: Tomorrow, in a Year
Review: The soundtrack version of The Knife's (in association with Planningtorock and Mr. Sims) first opera, Charles Darwin homage Tomorrow, In a Year, is such a frustrating experience.

Title: Going Places
Review: Yellow Swans' literal swan song found the two still exploring their way through often majestic drone--if the roots of the band had always been as much in uncontrolled experimentation as in serene contemplation, here the two sides found a fine fusion.

Title: Where You Want to Be
