Review: It's the album most bands wish they could make. [Aug 2004, p.101]

Title: Cocoa Sugar
Review: Cocoa Sugar isn’t a filtered version of what came before. Instead, it cements their status as riled-up oddballs determined to reinvent the wheel.

Title: Everything Is Borrowed
Review: On his fourth set, he addresses loftier themes--religion, mortality, ecology--without sounding dorky; it's like he's been woodshedding with Obama's speechwriting team.

Title: Saltwater
Review: All told, Saltwater's the most refreshing indie pop LP since Sufjan Stevens' Illinois.

Title: Sun
Review: Sun is the light at the end of one hell of a tunnel, a record brimming with an assurance and playfulness that, if a little dorky in places, is about as cathartic as pop gets.

Title: The Friends EP
Review: In the end this is a nice EP to play and a timely release considering the season and what they're releasing it right before.

Title: Cool Uncle
Review: Eclectic, soulful and refreshing, Cool Uncle is a must-hear.

Title: Soldier of Love
Review: Lovely listening.

Title: Mixed Race
Review: Mixed Race brims with well-formed songs played and sung with clear-headed emotion.

Title: Car Alarm
Review: Maybe all of Car Alarm is about conflict, but Prekop glides and sighs over every vowel, making it difficult to hear what he’s saying or to detect a hint of tension beneath the gloss.

Title: The Further Adventures of Lord Quas
Review: What's beyond doubt is the magical blend of the surreal and the fantastical that made 'The Unseen' so memorable is once again in the fullest effect on this showcase of fearlessly skewed production, dense organic vibes and hemp & helium-fuelled raps that make up this smoked-out saunter through the back streets of the cosmo-according-to-Lord Quas.

Title: Loney, Noir
Review: His high, thin voice won't grab everyone, but will generate a gentle glow for many. [May 2007, p.125]

Title: Brand New Eyes
Review: Emo kids kick up a riot on surprisingly edgy third outing.

Title: Jade Bird
Review: Across twelve polished tracks, Jade switches from piano ballad to stomping singalong and back again, full of bold choruses and raw, ricocheting vocals.

Title: Man Alive
Review: Everything Everything's debut LP, Man Alive, is proof that enthusiastic experimentation can't save your end product when the underlying elements are so incompatible and unappetizing.

Title: Club Nites
Review: Even rushing through the time between songs so as to maintain momentum, the endless energy and refusal to stay still is admirable of Dumb. Unfortunately, the pace results in some items ultimately being left undone.

Title: Yours Truly, Angry Mob
Review: 'Yours Truly...' is a rip-roaring pop record - sprightly, lean and adventurous - a bold leap skyward from 'Employment'.

Title: Planet High School
Review: So maybe Mux Mool can't literally do everything--but for the bulk of Planet High School, he's got himself an engaging something.

Title: Sun
Review: At times things seem a touch over-produced--something that's always a risk when you spend half a decade working on 11 tracks. But mostly, Marshall's thickly layered studio shenanigans make Sun shine.

Title: IV Play
Review: The-Dream barely breaks new ground artistically and the set doesn’t approach his finest effort, “Love vs. Money,” but the music is often so seductive it’s easy to ignore a misstep (“New Orleans”) and often distracting auto-tuning.

Title: Stars Are The Light
Review: There's a uplifting buoyancy to these eight tracks. [Oct 2019, p.30]

Title: Gimme Fiction
Review: Gimme Fiction may not be your favorite Spoon record right now, but give it a few years.

Title: Platform
Review: It doesn’t always work: Lonely At The Top is a minimalist, spoken-word piece set to odd clicking noises that doesn’t really bear repeated listens. For the most part, however, this is a brave, forward-thinking collection that will be required listening for any fans of electronica.

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: Landing is an apt reflection of an artist restarting after several years, but without sacrificing the eccentricity that initially made him such a compelling figure.

Title: Run Fast
Review: The album’s 13 tracks hit some serious highs and a few middling snags, but that’s to be expected from a band’s debut, even if that band features a modern day hero like Hanna.

Title: Love Songs for Patriots
Review: Funny, heartbreaking and at glorious odds with the world. [4 Sep 2004, p.73]

Title: Palindrome Hunches
Review: The quality, depth, and otherworldliness that Halstead has achieved here elevates it above being just another folk album.

Title: My Friend Fish
Review: This record is a lot of fun and show great song writing promise.

Title: Sagara
Review: Sagara shows the Norwegian to be an equally effective mood painter without his trusty beats, and in some respects, his accomplishment here is his most adept and impressive yet.

Title: Mixed Race
Review: Another smart and limber record. An astute choice of collaborators plays its part. [Oct 2010, p.116]

Title: Under the Sun
Review: Twenty-five years into his undaunted career, he has created an album that brings him proudly from behind the curtain and into the foreground for all to appreciate.

Title: A Mineral Love
Review: On the whole, the album suffers from a bout of dullness, with the majority of tracks mingling in a grey area, struggling to push through their apparent amalgamation and stand on their own.

Title: Reflection
Review: It's pleasant enough, it hardly transcendent, and feels--whisper it--ever so slightly old fashioned. [Feb 2017, p.95]

Title: Demon Days
Review: A much more consistent and coherent album, equaling Gorillaz’s high points and easily besting its shortcomings.

Title: The Republic
Review: As much as consistency has forever been The Sea and Cake’s stock in trade, doing away with it has served Prekop’s own progression well.

Title: Weather
Review: For the most part, Cottrell reliably prevents the listener from getting engulfed in the aural haze that has become Hansen’s trademark. That said, with her distinct vocal character, it seems like she could invest her singing with more spiked edges if she chose to—or if the music called for it.

Title: Welcome Joy
Review: This time around they've learnt to loosen up slightly, enlisting the help of Amber Webber from Black Mountain and adding a pleasingly West Coast sensibility to what was previously a rather monochromatic Americana mix. [Sep 2009, p.81]

Title: The Defenestration of St Martin
Review: Raving, romantic and graceful, it's what might happen if Britpop had gone to finishing school, and even includes a final guitar treat for anyone who tuned in the hope of another round of Olympian.

Title: Nothing Was the Same
Review: With the themes, moods and issues displayed here, Drizzy has shared another moment of his life, and now the only thing left to prove is if his crossover powers can last him a decade from now.

Title: Wondrous Bughouse
Review: Like the most memorable trips, this one creates some sublime eidetic imagery.

Title: Gravity the Seducer
Review: Gravity The Seducer has its fair share of tremendous moments, but unfortunately those moments begin to lose their gloss when entangled with fragments of inconveniently placed filler.

Title: Meaning of Life
Review: As cohesive and self-assured as this collection feels, Meaning doesn’t seem especially interested in scaling the heights of early smashes like “Since U Been Gone” or “Because of You.” Instead, it swings low and sweet--a refreshingly real dispatch from an artist expressing exactly what she feels in this moment, and nothing less.

Title: A Crow Looked at Me
Review: This record possesses immense power to make listeners reflect on their own relationships and mortality.

Title: One Day I'm Going to Soar
Review: Intense, painfully frank, hysterically funny,and in the end, exultant... OSIGTS isn't always an easy listen, but it does offer a fearless experience that invests pop with more theatricality than the form can usually tolerate. [Jul 2012, p.80]

Title: Pyramid of the Sun
Review: Throughout the album, Fuchs' playing is exemplary, but not in a showy or needlessly florid manner; he simply gets to work and gets the job done, content with being just one part of a greater whole.

Title: The Woods
Review: The Woods feels almost nostalgic, exalting the era when noisemakers Nirvana, Sonic Youth, NIN, Fugazi and PJ Harvey were the touchstones of artistic merit. [#9]

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: These songs are generally not the type to grab you right away, but there's enough mystery and melody there to call you back.

Title: Feminist Sweepstakes
Review: Feminist Sweepstakes does occasionally stumble.

Title: Excuse My French
Review: Rather than allowing the first three tracks to help craft a template for the rest of the LP, the other 10 tracks are watered down by concept-less, feature-heavy songs. [Jul 2013, p.87]

Title: AM
Review: Five albums in, they may not be a buzz band anymore, but they've become something much more interesting: a good band.

Title: LA Spark
Review: Winter and Benge often seem to be living out their fantasy of being Cabaret Voltaire members as the bloops, the bubbles, and the time-rips are all familiar devices, but so be it, and more please, and another listen for this one as well.

Title: Peaceful, the World Lays Me Down
Review: The vivaciousness and bright energy of the instrumentation offsets the melancholic subject matter perfectly, so that the listener is lost in the composition. [Fall 2008, p.82]

Title: Sex & Food
Review: Nielson is comfortable enough in his own songwriting to settle into airtight grooves--with the assistance of the clattering, shifty drums from his brother--and allow them to simmer for a few golden moments. His guitar playing is sensational, and his use of warping effects to achieve the right mix of tightness and sensitivity gets better with each UMO record.

Title: MIEN
Review: Mien's experiments are sometimes a little too formless, but the album's standouts prove they weren't keeping all their best ideas for their main bands.

Title: Man About Town
Review: Man About Town doesn't boast much in the way of radical steps forward. But it confirms the man is still very good at what he does.

Title: Heartache City
Review: As always, the beauty of the duo's music makes these moments all the more haunting.

Title: Electric Version
Review: The awe fades quickly as this album progresses. [Jun 2003, p.100]

Title: Let's Go Eat the Factory
Review: It shouldn't work at all, but the overall product--while a bit uneven--is something to celebrate.

Title: Dye It Blonde
Review: Dye It Blonde has unexpectedly crept into contention for being my favourite record of 2011 so far.

Title: No Color
Review: The new directions that they have managed to find on No Color are certainly interesting to explore for listeners.

Title: Eskmo
Review: His throaty, gnarled vocals--best showcased on the meandering, Dilla-esque Cloudlight--lend his music a gothic mood. [Nov 2010, p.109]

Title: Incredibad
Review: It's a hilarious comedy album that's just as hip, inventive, and inappropriate as their digital shorts.

Title: Fall to Pieces
Review: Tricky has injected so much raw emotion into Fall to Pieces that it can't help but stand out as one of his most notable, memorable and authentic releases.

Title: Stuffed & Ready
Review: Their sound has never been fuller. [Mar 2019, p.112]

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: This is Lopatin's most cogent record yet. [Dec 2015, p.91]

Title: The Magic Position
Review: Akin to Bowie's 'Hunky Dory', in its senseless but brilliant eclecticism.

Title: Valere Aude
Review: Although Romans is a collaborative effort between two dance floor heavyweights in their own right, the largely dark sound that has distinguished previous releases from Haslam emerges as this record's strongest aspect.

Title: Fake Sugar
Review: Fake Sugar is a real reinvention for Beth Ditto, but it’s not so much of a reinvention that her signature traits are unrecognisable.

Title: Feedback
Review: Feedback, for the most part, disintegrates into a cloud of unremarkable noise.

Title: Burn Burn
Review: The textures are right but Our Lady Peace remain deficient in hooks and melodies, something that didn't matter as much when their sound boiled with indignation instead of merely simmering, as it does here.

Title: Shrines
Review: The final outcome is a trebly plastic-fantastic quality, rendering Shrines closer in tone and texture to coke-rap than ethereal indie.

Title: I Had A Dream That You Were Mine
Review: It’s not that Leithauser has dramatically changed since his days in the Walkmen; rather, pairing with Rostam has brought out the best in him. It’s rare for collaborative albums between known entities to feel like equal reflections of both parties, but Rostam find a middle-ground in mutual longing for the past.

Title: Continuous Portrait
Review: There's a charming looseness to the album; while never abrasive, the samples sometimes clash with each other a bit, and it all has the feeling of a cut-and-paste collage, sounding far less refined than Eluvium or Explosions' dramatic, labored-over epics. ... The album is a poignant, playful collection of future memories.

Title: AMOK
Review: AMOK is an album you'll need to spend time unpacking, which means it's cut from the same cloth as every good Radiohead album. But with this one, maybe you'll get to dance a little along the way.

Title: Life On Earth
Review: While the similarly mystical/mewling Joanna Newsom seems adrift in fantasy, Tiny Vipers finds wonder in being rooted firmly to the terra.

Title: La ForÃªt
Review: No question, it's not for everyone; it's both fey and aggressive. But it's quite real. [11 Jul 2005]

Title: If I Should Go Before You
Review: The album's languid pace and lack of real bite often renders it a little pedestrian. [Dec 2015, p.69]

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: This time, the one flaw may simply be that the group doesn't know when to say when.

Title: Amaryllis
Review: Even with this change of tone, the album is still classic Shinedown, and though this kind of triumphant mood will probably disappoint fans looking for something to cut loose and pump their fists to.

Title: Wait For Me
Review: So it’s possible that the songs on Wait For Me will end up in the same coffeehouses and car commercials and other small, sterile environments as those on Play, but Hall’s drawing inwards as hard as he can, to the great benefit of his compositions, and Wait For Me is unabashedly majestic.

Title: Golden Sings That Have Been Sung
Review: This time round Walker has brought influences from his native Chicago scene to the forefront of his music, loosening up and expanding his sound with frankly blinding results.

Title: Some Loud Thunder
Review: The songs start running together till they’re not distinct tracks so much as guitars and bass and drums and yelpy indie vocals that happen to have been recorded at the same time.

Title: The Innocents
Review: It's a stellar record, one that captivates both the heart and the imagination with an almost imperceptible grip, clutching the listener's attention with its painstakingly beautiful construction and a sadness that is all-consuming but somehow warm and comforting.

Title: Is This It
Review: The biggest draw is the Iggy-Jagger sexual charisma of 22-year-old singer Julian Casablancas, whose self-possessed cool is astonishing. [Aug/Sep 2001, p.130]

Title: Four Lost Souls
Review: Although many songs lack the fire and passion that defined his earlier work, with the exception of the race-relation lyrical content of "What's My Name?" and the growling "Snake Behind Glass," Four Lost Souls is simply unlike anything else in Jon Langford's sprawling discography.

Title: The Trinity
Review: Sean Paul is a gifted songbird, and on The Trinity his vocal gifts and Jamaica’s continued creative vitality are a surefire formula for thrilling music.

Title: A Steady Drip, Drip, Drip
Review: Here and throughout A Steady Drip, Drip, Drip, Ron and Russel Mael riff on their history deftly, and the results are both timely and quintessentially Sparks.

Title: Love the Future
Review: Too intelligent and well-crafted to dismiss but too disjointed and self-indulgent to really embrace, Love the Future is equally frustrating and promising.

Title: Peanut Butter Blues & Melancholy Jam
Review: Peanut Butter ... might be just a little too left-field to capture the zeitgeist in the same way that Skinner did a decade previously, but it's a hypnotic and ultimately rewarding debut which, along with recent efforts from James Blake and Jamie Woon, proves that the words chill-out and challenging don't have to be mutually exclusive.

Title: The Chair In The Doorway
Review: No boundaries are being broken this around, but Living Colour still hold their own. [Jan 2010, p. 102]

Title: A Place I'll Always Go
Review: A Place I'll Always Go makes you forget about the good, the bad, and the ugly, and proves the fact that Palehound are one of the most relevant indie rock bands to date.

Title: The Good the Bad and the Funky
Review: At first listening, this feels vexingly inconsequential, but after a few loosening listens the music's slight but simple pleasures shine through.

Title: Sunny Side Up
Review: This one leaves its generational competition in the dust and is wise beyond this songwriter's years, and to be frank, leaves his own previous identity as simply a bedroom balladeer to history.

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: Viscerals
Review: On 2018's King of Cowards they proved they were a truly forward-thinking doom act, and on Viscerals they've proved it wasn't a fluke. They just need to shed a few more layers before they are ready to assume their final form.

Title: Aimlessness
Review: As you unspool slowly into Aimlessness, you can't help but wish for a more mediating human touch.

Title: Restless Ones
Review: Restless Ones establishes Heartless Bastards as a straightforward arena-rock band, one that's grown more refined with time.

Title: Ten New Messages
Review: The problem is not that The Rakes haven't sought to evolve; it's that they've done so too self-consciously and slipped out of their depth.

Title: Ibifornia
Review: The whole thing comes across as a bit of a mish- mash, a bit cobbled together. It’s an album all too reliant on the guest singers to give the songs identity.

Title: Paralytic Stalks
Review: Barnes has definitely taken a step in right direction.

Title: Within and Without
Review: The album drowns in atmospherics to the point where it could be entirely instrumental. Greene casts an enjoyably suggestive spell but it wafts right through you.

Title: Asunder, Sweet and Other Distress
Review: Asunder, Sweet And Other Distress’ is not a failure; it’s merely familiar.

Title: Slugger
Review: Slugger is low-key but, true to form, leaves a mark. [Dec 2016, p.37]

Title: Jerusalem
Review: Most of the music here finds Earle in admirable form. [Oct 2002, p.106]

Title: Exclusive
Review: Brown is riding on the coattails of artists greater than he is, but he is clearly a talented performer who can deliver high-octane club hits.

Title: Discipline & Desire
Review: A skillful balance of harshness and beauty, Discipline + Desire is a welcome reintroduction to a band that is among the best at keeping this sound not just alive, but vital.

Title: Is the Is Are
Review: At its best, Is the Is Are is a fine album with plenty of immediate pleasures to offer. However, digging deeper won’t unveil anything really tangible.

Title: Dreams and Nightmares
Review: Meek has made the move from mixtapes to the majors with a solid vision.

Artist: Sufjan Stevens, Bryce Dessner, Nico Muhly & James McAlister
Title: Planetarium
Review: In its entirety, the ambition and scope of the project is matched by the combined talent and imagination of four musical friends whose association seemed to just emerge from the ether.

Title: In Between Dreams
Review: The songs on "In Between Dreams" (Universal) are so light and self-effacing they might scatter in a tropical breeze. [13 Mar 2005]

Title: It's All True
Review: Greenspan's singing is the best it's ever been on It's All True, proving the band's mixing desk skills aren't the only thing that's matured over the past eight years.

Title: The Altogether
Review: A quirkier affair than their previous works.

Title: Take Care
Review: Drake shares [Kanye] West's love for mood and never-ending existential analysis.

Title: Off With Their Heads
Review: Off With Their Heads affirms the undying pleasures of smart, catchy pop music does well. [Oct 2008, p.137]

Title: Plastic Anniversary
Review: Plastic Anniversary is unfamiliar, strange, unsettling, and wonderful.

Title: Happenstance
Review: Evokes the singer-songwriter atmospherics of Carole King and Elton John. [24 Jun 2004, p.170]

Title: We Are Undone
Review: Two Gallants can swagger and rage like The Black Keys, but they can also find moments of ambient bliss to complement songs of helplessness and regret. [Mar 2015, p.82]

Title: All the Things That I Did and All the Things That I Didn't Do
Review: Tastefully arranged, high-spec country-folk introspection. [Aug 2018, p.96]

Title: The Take Off and Landing of Everything
Review: The Take Off and Landing of Everything is better still [than 2011's Build a Rocket Boys!], demonstrating that the band knows how to seize the spoils of success.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: Tart modern pop performed with a sly sense of homour. [Mar 2009, p.105]

Title: Get Awkward
Review: Singer and girl-Iggy Jemina Pearl's the star, bringing admirable conviction to her tales of boredom, drug-taking and, in the case of the Perky 'Food Fight,' "extra cheese in your face." [Apr 2008, p.102]

Title: Held In Splendor
Review: Held in Splendor is a good example of a record that successfully executes the tropes of psych--it sounds like it could’ve been recorded in 1967 without directly ripping off any artist in particular--without every truly transcending them.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: Like almost everything on Neon Bible... "No Cars Go" is excess with a point: We are drowning in the unspeakable and running out of air and fight. If only everything else on Neon Bible made that point with the same dynamic overkill.

Title: Wait To Pleasure
Review: Wait To Pleasure shows new facets, but that shoegaze tag isn’t likely to disappear soon.

Title: Liz Phair
Review: This is turgid, formulaic guff. [Nov 2003, p.114]

Title: Karmacode
Review: At once loud and elegant, Karmacode raises Lacuna Coil's heaviness tenfold without sacrificing a drop of the band's mystical ambience. [May 2006, p.168]

Title: Luck or Magic
Review: All in all, the sparks are overshadowed by poor choices and general lack of direction.

Title: Devotion
Review: Tirzah has made 11 raw, honest, and beautifully unusual pop songs that will remain with you whether you like it or not, bringing you back time and time again, motivated by your devotion to this record.

Title: Testimonium Songs
Review: Taken alone, these six tracks are fascinating enough from a conceptual standpoint, and listening to a band audibly restraining themselves is quite scintillating. But it's hard to shake the feeling that these pieces would likely have a significantly greater impact when connected with the entire Testimony performance.

Title: The Glass Passenger
Review: With plain-spoken songs like these, he's already made a more honest album than many of his emo peers.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: Wincing the Night Away is the sound of the Shins acknowledging where they've been and moving on to new territory, and while it probably won't change your life, it probably will make it more enjoyable.

Title: Bury Me in My Boots
Review: Alternating between bro country that's just past its sell-by date, summertime party tunes so breezy they get silly, and a heavy dose of southern rock, the Cadillac Three demonstrate versatility but they also seem scattered, as if they're scrambling for an audience.

Title: Devil
Review: Not only do tracks like Looking For A Tornado sound great, they also have a distinct air of authenticity about them. [5 Apr 2014, p.53]

Title: Ventriloquism
Review: The results are frequently transformative, and always enjoyable.

Title: Blank Face LP
Review: Blank Face stalls near its end with pedestrian raps and an awkward R&B crossover bid, but when Q locks into the streetwise grooves of "Dope Dealer" and the lush psychedelia of "That Part," he hints at the masterpiece he came tantalizingly close to making.

Title: Gang Signs & Prayer
Review: The striking thing about Signs and Prayer isn’t so much Stormzy’s way with a well-timed and dexterous diss so much as the the quality of his lyrics when he turns his attention to other topics. ... He writes affectingly about depression on the closing Lay Me Bare, a purgative howl of a track that also tackles, in pretty painful detail, his estrangement from his father.

Title: Still Life
Review: While there aren’t any revelatory moments of creative growth here, the best songs on Still Life suggest Morby still had plenty left in the NYC tank.

Title: Golden Hour
Review: Previously, her cleverness was her strong suit, but on Golden Hour, she benefits from being direct, especially since this frankness anchors an album that sounds sweetly blissful, turning this record the best kind of comfort: it soothes but is also a source of sustenance.

Title: Never, Never, Land
Review: A work of intense drama but little importance.

Title: Content
Review: Newcomers might just wonder why these old dudes are ripping off Bloc Party.

Title: Evil Friends
Review: Portugal. The Man have created something special with Evil Friends. The core songwriting and performances are top notch, and Danger Mouse’s input adds a plethora of valuable modifications and ideas.

Title: White Bird Release
Review: White Bird Release is a solid, completely contained work.

Title: Love Behind The Melody
Review: DeVaughan simultaneously sounds like every soul singer who has raised bumps on your arms and none of them at all, which is to say he's an artist no matter what banner he flies.

Title: Dalliance
Review: Dalliance is a brief half an hour expression of energy, without too much angst. It will never be considered a highly innovative venture, but the five-piece do manage to include some interesting twists on an old formula.

Title: Hunting My Dress
Review: Hunting My Dress rejoices in an off-the-cuff dreamlike sensuality, pitching and rolling in all sorts of pleasingly unexpected directions. [Dec 2009, p. 115]

Title: La Isla Bonita
Review: This is an album of difficult rhythms, squawking guitars and bohemian eccentricities that will leave fans delighted and everyone else baffled--just as their 12 others have done. Business as usual, then.

Title: Rokstarr
Review: On his second album, Rokstarr, British pop-soul artist Taio Cruz croons about the highs and lows of love over a wide variety of electronic-influenced beats.

Title: Present Tense
Review: On their past albums Wild Beasts have shown us their savage and raw sides, which have been gloriously charming and exciting, but by opening up on Present Tense and revealing their true hearts, their music has ascended to new heights.

Title: Nostradamus
Review: The songs themselves are hit or miss, with the emphasis falling on the latter, due mostly to an over-reliance on three-chord, midtempo filler, but as is the case with nearly every Priest offering, when they're on they're dead on.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: Perfect Pussy constantly find new ways to stimulate that teenage bit of your brain that wants to scream and punch things and has a lot of things to say but doesn’t know how to say them.

Title: Alight of Night
Review: Simply put, it's a decent album. There are a handful of great tracks and handful of tankers. The rest is just kind of there.

Title: Murderburgers
Review: File with the rest of your King Khan records under "readily accessible." [No. 148, p.59]

Title: Stuck on Nothing
Review: Stuck On Nothing is a boozy, lusty hug of a record--an album so loving and large-hearted that its virtues essentially cancel out its flaws.

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: The Atlanta singer delivers soulful, socially conscious meditations.

Title: Relapse
Review: Now in his 30s, he doesn't surf the beat so much as box with it, with both brutality and no small degree of grace. That a rapper of this much verbal gymnastic ability is still making Perez Hilton cracks is too bad, but the bigger problem is that Eminem's recipe of gore and gay jokes sounds like the past.

Title: Immunity
Review: By concentrating on his own endeavors, Jon Hopkins has created one of the year's most intriguing electronic recordings. [Jun-Jul 2013, p.99]

Title: I Like To Keep Myself In Pain
Review: This is a merely pleasant album, and especially after 11 long years, pleasant is a low hurdle for such an inimitable singer.

Title: Blank Face LP
Review: Blank Face LP isn’t Schoolboy Q’s first great album, but it’s the first one where he lives up to his utmost potential.

Title: Pull Up Some Dust and Sit Down
Review: In the transition from imitator to originator, the old boy has made one of his best albums ever. [Oct 2011, p.83]

Title: Tiger, My Friend
Review: Sure, greater dynamic variety and some selective risktaking would be nice, but these precocious upstarts already got the tough part pinned down: subtlety. Psapp have laid themselves a remarkably self-assured template for subsequent outings.

Title: Hard Believer
Review: It’s respectable enough but a stronger dose of Fink’s maverick tendencies would be welcome.

Title: Oxnard
Review: There are plenty of moments where Oxnard clicks, like the chugging, bum-rush rhythm “Who R U?” ... Still, there are missed opportunities.

Title: This Generation
Review: For reggae fans of a certain vintage, This Generation will rule the nation. [Apr 2013, p.94]

Title: Science Fiction
Review: A lifetime away from the Long Island quartet's emo and pop-punk origins, Science Fiction is a complex and nuanced beast of introspective indie rock and detailed production.

Title: Celestial Lineage
Review: The latest of those hymns is Celestial Lineage--and as great as the group's two previous full-lengths were, Lineage is the first to truly, fully capture the Weavers' unholy vision of sylvan majesty and pagan mystique.

Title: Lung Bread For Daddy
Review: While single ‘Angel’ uses the simplest, scrappiest riffs and Beth’s sonorous tones to make something more than the sum of its parts. Du Blonde continues to be one of UK guitar music’s best kept secrets.

Title: Open Up Your Head
Review: This band clearly has a solid vision for their sound, and with a debut this satisfying, you’ll definitely want to see where that vision takes them next – especially if that involves more experimentation.

Title: Oh No I Love You
Review: Far more stripped back than the Charlatans frontman's previous offerings, Oh No flits between affecting moments (the rather gorgeous 'Hours') and repetitive down-beaters ('A Case For Vinyl') that seem to go nowhere.

Title: Sunlit Youth
Review: ures might underplay institutional factors, Local Natives deliver these ideas knowingly. The beauty of Sunlit Youth is in its optimism rather than its pragmatism--a record that cements their status as one of our most special proponents of emotionally-charged guitar music.

Title: Celebration Castle
Review: The Ponys do what they do so brilliantly, and yet so casually, they make it seem simple.

Title: Tween
Review: This scattershot feel makes Tween something mainly for die-hard Wye Oak fans who want a peek behind the curtain, or for anyone curious about how they managed to make the daring stylistic leap from Civilian to Shriek.

Title: Ukulele Songs
Review: Like a lot of Vedder's experiments, the spirit is easier to admire than the final product. The ukulele might be a great campfire instrument, but sometimes what works best at the campfire should stay there.

Title: Writer's Block
Review: The first two songs eclipse any other songs on the album, but I'm not saying the rest of the material is weak.

Title: Hebrews
Review: Hebrews is a wholly new kind of album for the band. Is it cheesy, over the top and a little too saccharine? Yeah, but the first two of those apply in spades to the first couple Say anything records anyways, and honestly I’d rather have someone singing sweet nothings to me when they’re in their 30’s than try and continue spewing venomous bile that they haven't believed in since their early 20's.

Title: Songs of Mass Destruction
Review: With her explosively satisfying fourth solo album, Annie Lennox delivers her best recording since her Eurythmics' heyday, eclipsing even 2003's marvelous "Bare."

Title: Famous First Words
Review: As a record that Geffen plus Newell and co expect anyone to pay for, this album is a distillation of all that is wrong with British guitar music, peddled by a band so consumed by their own deluded egotism that they think of themselves as its saviours.

Title: Fear Fun
Review: A striking funereal stomp, considering its bleak subject matter, it really shouldn't be quite as sensationally sexy as it is.

Title: Aaltopiiri
Review: The sort of disc that inevitably prompts skeptics to ask, "You call that music?"

Title: A Hundred Miles Off
Review: The concentrated unity of form and content that elevated sterling sophomore effort  Bows & Arrows has been replaced by a footloose approach to songwriting and style that fails to mesh.

Title: The Secret Migration
Review: With The Secret Migration, the band completely deserts the peculiarities that distinguished them from both peers and progeny in favor of a dull collection of pastoral fantasias that frequently wander dangerously close to adult contemporary.

Title: Leaders Of The Free World
Review: A mostly brilliant, though occasionally lackluster, album.

Title: Collector
Review: Excellent from start to finish. [May 2020, p.103]

Title: Folie A Deux
Review: While Folie A Deux at times feels like the band are showing off the contents of their Rolodex, the album's standouts are so good that they will undoubtedly become standards for the band's live shows for years to come.

Title: Apex Predator - Easy Meat
Review: Untrained ears might shrivel in terror, but those who appreciate the joy of noise will recognise the sound of veteran masters on unassailable form.

Title: Partie Traumatic
Review: While Youngblood fills his sardonic twinkle with playful sexual allusions and gender ambiguity, there’s too many clunky lines and rhymes-for-rhyming’s sake for Partie Traumatic to be anything more than lyrically intriguing.

Title: Embryonic
Review: Surprise and relief are the words that best describe an initial reaction to Embryonic. [Fall 2009, p.90]

Title: Harlequin
Review: There are very few moments on Harlequin that don’t click either sonically or thematically. Izenberg has established himself as a gifted songwriter with a firm grasp on the strange side of things, and his beguiling debut plays like the nexus of Mac DeMarco and Anna Meredith.

Title: New Eyes
Review: Sometimes great, often fun, but mostly quite confused, it’s not a focused LP--though it’s certainly an expression of the oddness of 2014.

Title: Partie Traumatic
Review: Kissing goodbye to the obsolete racial and gender roles that pop, hip-hop, or indie rock still demand, Youngblood and pals throw a thrillingly subversive victory party to lift the country out of eight years of anguish.

Title: Super Critical
Review: To be honest, Super Critical is simply a cute record that shows they are back on track after a few years of less successful experiments.

Title: The Disco's of Imhotep
Review: Where previous releases under the moniker have explored the grittier, DIY side of house, here Moss leans towards the lush, psychedelic end of the spectrum, and delivers a kaleidoscopic sonic journey that commands you to keep going back.

Title: One Day All of This Wonâ€™t Matter Any More
Review: Slow Club's metamorphosis feels organic and, more importantly, embraced: this is their record, and the sound you're hearing is Slow Club overcoming their struggles.

Title: Different Creatures
Review: Part of what makes Circa Waves so compelling is that they are able to match the sound of their influences while still believably making the results sound their own. They've grown into an assured rock entity, but they've retained their fundamental sense of working-class Liverpudlian blues.

Title: Signal Morning
Review: The decaying aural ellipsis felt hanging in the aether marks the dusky road of the album’s fist half. This is dark stuff, darker than our main man Hart is known for.

Title: Colors
Review: The glossy production here sometimes neuters Beck's wilder inclinations. ...  Still, as his first upbeat album in nearly a decade, Colors proves that Beck is still one of rock's most intrepid inventors. [13 Oct 2017, p.58]

Title: Invincible
Review: It simply isn't his best work.

Title: Dirty Vegas
Review: Deeply anonymous.

Title: Paracosm
Review: You couldn't call the album a brave leap into the unknown, but nor does it feel hackneyed. Instead, it subtly shifts the boundaries of what Greene does in a way that makes you intrigued to hear what he does next.

Title: Sister Faith
Review: It’s clear Patterson put a lot of thought into Sister Faith, but a looser hand on the reins might have allowed for a more precarious, thrillingly unstable balance between post-hardcore and the world beyond.

Title: The Gathering
Review: The Gathering should be a hoot, at the very least, but this Baltimore clan's fourth release is more of a slog, shackled by monochromatic guitar churn and a slack pulse.

Title: Separation Sunday
Review: The group sounds a bit like Guided By Voices at times, only a Guided By Voices that want to kick your sorry can up and down the length of the bar.

Title: Brassbound
Review: A band slowly escaping the weight of their still-obvious influences. [Aug 2005, p.104]

Title: Automata II
Review: The transition between blasting drums and metal riffs on "Blot" from Automata I into "The Proverbial Bellow" is surprisingly smooth without feeling like there is any disconnect between records. Overall, splitting up the release made it much easier to digest a full Between the Buried and Me album, which is never an easy task.

Title: Frank Black Francis
Review: Unfortunately, disc two’s cache of amorphous, New Age-y, re-recorded Pixies standards falls flat.

Title: Invented
Review: Invented, as tuneful as it may be, still plays an odd role in Jimmy Eat World's discography, since it can't quite figure out how to transcend a genre -- one that Jimmy Eat World helped invent, no less -- that exclusively caters to younger listeners.

Title: The High Country
Review: Richmond Fontaine should be commended for bucking the singles trend and crafting an album that functions best, possibly only, as a whole, especially amid rumors of the album's impending demise.

Title: Pick Me Up Off The Floor
Review: It’s fortunate that Jones chose to hold on to these songs – they form one of the most intriguing records she’s released in years.

Title: Shadows
Review: Shadows would do the reclusive southerner [Alex Chilton] proud too, providing a dozen tracks of earnest and intelligent guitar-driven pop music. [Spring/Summer 2010, p.108]

Title: Megafaun
Review: For their third studio album...Megafaun dial back the more progressive elements of their sound in favor of a languid, Laurel Canyon-inspired foundation that treads the middle ground between Blitzen Trapper's experimental, neo-Southern rock romancing, and Will Oldham's post-Palace Music infatuation with American Beauty-era Grateful Dead.
The Icelandic quartet again create an ethereal stir with sparse, atmospheric melodies and a falsetto wail, often recalling the sonic swirl of Stateside slow-core acts like Low. [1 Nov 2002, p.70]

Title: Rehearsing My Choir
Review: There might be a compelling story in there, but when the Furnaces' songs come in to elaborate on her tales... it's all but impossible to figure out what's going on. [6 Nov 2005]

Title: Wash the Sins Not Only the Face
Review: Taken as a whole, it's an arresting step towards the light. [Feb 2013, p.90]

Title: Reality Tunnels
Review: A wide-ranging, guest-heavy collection that keeps one foot rooted in grimy, shuddering, low-end sonics while exploring multiple alternative avenues. [Aug 2020, p.34]

Title: Untitled
Review: For every moment of clarity on this album, there’s an eyebrow-archer to match.

Title: Reaching for Indigo
Review: Reaching for Indigo transcends the traditional appeal of a singer-songwriter. Whenever Haley Fohr sings, it’s as if the instrumentation around her is momentarily frozen in time; quite the compliment for an album that surrounds her with so many uncommon vibrations.

Title: Black Sheep Boy
Review: Okkervil River continue to deliver the quality of Down the River of Golden Dreams, and though sonic evolution is barely existent from that recording, perhaps it doesn't need to be; certainly Sheff's songwriting still floats above that of his peers.

Title: Paul Walker
Review: Paul Walker’s not for everyone but will at least get the 40-somethings to quit bitching about Green Day.

Title: Figure 8
Review: Smith is capable of subtle introspection, but too many of his new songs sound like the self-pitying complaints of an adolescent venting in his diary.

Title: In Waves
Review: In Waves is not Trivium's finest moment by any stretch of the imagination but it does point towards the band having found direction and its own voice for the first time in quite a while.

Title: Lianne La Havas
Review: ‘Lianne La Havas’ is a far more cohesive record than any of its predecessors, focused around a primary nucleus of intimate vocals, nimble guitar-work and driving percussion.

Title: Inform Educate Entertain
Review: Inform-Educate-Entertain is a flawed but fascinating curiosity.

Title: Maraqopa
Review: The risks that Damien Jurado and producer Richard Swift take on Maraqopa are small and subtle adjustments to those already made on Saint Bartlett, but they are small steps which reap exquisite rewards for the listener.

Title: We Are the Pipettes
Review: The Pipettes have none of Winehouse’s soul aspirations--just better songs and more sex.

Title: Diamond Eyes
Review: Usually, though, Chino Moreno's lyrics go for cathartic images (shaking coffins, fading faces) set to chopping riffage, whirlpool distortion and dark, soaring melodies that sound more like the Cure than Korn.

Title: Routines
Review: It’s a summer record if ever there was one--with even the opening track being named Sun’s Out. It’s a great introduction to the record, where a punchy snare, an uncomplicated bassline and a heat-warped guitar lick combine so easily that it takes a few of Drew Auschermann’s lyrics to be delivered before you even realize they’re there.

Title: Beyond
Review: Apparently evolution is overrated.

Title: Trouble Maker
Review: There’s no formal breakthroughs on Trouble Maker beyond the astounding economy, unless you think the harmonica on “Buddy” or Clash-goes-“Ring of Fire” chords on “Telegraph Avenue” makes this the band’s folk-punk album.

Title: Timez Are Weird These Days
Review: London is far more charming when he's given some space and sings, as he does very sweetly in the chorus of "Why Even Try," featuring Tegan & Sara's Sara Quin. Those moments are scant.

Title: Waking Lines
Review: They're better when operating at full-throttle, as on the muscular Blood and carefree Our Ego, but for music intended to elevate, the rest remains strangely earthbound. [Feb 2014, p.118]

Title: God's Favorite Customer
Review: The singer-songwriter is more sympathetic when tackling his struggles with mental health. Indeed, God's Favorite Customer hits its stride with its most emotionally naked pair of songs.

Title: Wincing The Night Away
Review: Mainly, the new disc is just more tentative than Chutes Too Narrow, with a lot of songs—like the first single, "Phantom Limb"—sounding like foggier, heavier versions of what The Shins have done before.

Title: American Supreme
Review: The raw, first-take sound of most of these songs is impressive--Suicide remain the most genuinely punk of electronic bands. [#11, p.144]

Title: Comfort of Strangers
Review: The music on Comfort of Strangers is at times so complex and distracting that it often overshadows Orton's winsome voice.

Title: Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace
Review: Throughout, the Foos are as tight as ever, even if the songs are mostly unmemorable. [Oct 2007, p.108]

Title: Innocents
Review: Majestically sad (“Almost Home,” “Saints”), soulfully sad (“A Case For Shame”), atmospherically sad (“Going Wrong”), trip hop sad (“The Last Day,” “Tell Me”), Northern soul sad (“Don’t Love Me”) are all interesting but often too subtle variations that almost make you want to force feed him Zoloft at times.

Title: On Oni Pond
Review: It's poppier than ever before, with big hooks played with funk and bossa nova fills, fat Balkan brass and imaginative lyrics full of bug-eyed images. [Oct 2013, p.71]

Title: Album
Review: Realised with friend Chet JR White in San Francisco on reel-to-reel tapes, the songs grab from Phil Spector, Beatles, Beach Boys, JAMC and Spiritualized, and are all the more enticing for it. [Jan 2010, p. 103]

Title: Neighborhood Watch
Review: Here's a group at the top of its game.

Title: Careless World: Rise of the Last King
Review: [Tyga] flings just about everything at the wall here. [9 Mar 2012, p.80]

Title: Youth Novels
Review: Youth Novels is a twinkle-toed debut that dares to suggest what others can only make tediously plain, and leaves us in the rarely-enjoyed position of actually wanting more.

Title: Carry On
Review: The arrangements can be flabby, but what you'll hear at the heart of Carry On is the voice of one of music's great troubadours.

Title: Choice of Weapon
Review: Choice Of Weapon sees The Cult back to doing what they do best, which is producing slightly dark and remarkably catchy rock 'n' roll.

Title: Sound the Alarm
Review: Sound The Alarm shows that while they're still very much an acquired taste, these guys are much more capable than many would have liked to think.

Title: The Politics of Envy
Review: However distinguished the guests, though, there's no doubt who the commanding presence is. [May 2012, p.82]

Title: Codes and Keys
Review: There's an ease and comfort about the songs that suggests they fell into place naturally, rather than suffering endless alterations; and the band seem content to let them breathe and take on a life of their own, rather than freight them with unnecessary adornment.

Title: Unknown Mortal Orchestra
Review: Combined with an expert use of space rare for such a lo-fi record, UMO manages a unique immersive and psychedelic quality without relying on the usual array of bong-ripping effects.

Title: Ape in Pink Marble
Review: Ape in Pink Marble doesn’t do anything innovative because it doesn’t really have to. So go ahead, Devendra, celebrate.

Title: Idealism
Review: 'Idealism' is dusted with the kind of metallic house glitter caking LCD's 'Sound Of Silver', and, just as promisingly, the title track could have been carved from Daft Punk before they decided they were human after all.

Title: Boys & Girls
Review: Their talent and impossible-to-fake passion merit the sudden attention.

Title: The Shepherd's Dog
Review: Intimate, literate and wonderfully executed, Iron & Wine seem to have made one of the albums of the year. Don’t let it pass you by.

Title: Odditorium or Warlords of Mars
Review: Mostly, the sound of The Dandy Warhols spreading their wings suits them. [Oct 2005, p.115]

Title: Vision Valley
Review: Vision Valley might be a little predictable, but at least the Vines sound like they're back in control of their lives and music again.

Title: The Incident
Review: It's a bit like Lance Armstrong placing second in the Tour de France--not the finish one is accustomed to, but still a remarkable achievement. [Fall 2009, p.98]
Much of 4 feels like beautifully baroque soundtrack music desperately seeking a movie about a rainy afternoon.

Title: III
Review: Never self indulgent, this is enquiring music that's frequently beautiful. [Dec 2008, p.81]

Title: Out of the Woods
Review: A tasteful disco effort. [23 Mar 2007, p.61]

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: It’s the crafting of timeless, crest-fallen melodies infused with gripping characterisations that elevates Darnielle into the upper-crust of musical virtuosity. And that’s exactly where Heretic Pride leaves him: perched atop the pile of today’s try-hardy singer/songwriters.

Title: The Orbserver In The Star House
Review: Paterson's deep respect for Perry's improvised vocals ultimately handicapping the eccentricities of each man's production prowess.

Title: The Fame Monster
Review: The lead single is a powerhouse of dance waves and infectiously produced beats, but the album doesn't always stand out as definitive, even though it's consistently fresh and innovative.

Title: Sleep of Reason
Review: Sleep of Reason then is a ponderous rolling through complexly changing scenery, no one drive-through ever seeming the same, more than a roller-coaster ride that promises the same loops each time.

Title: Is This It
Review: It's a welcome change to the current hard-rock juggernaut.

Title: Something More Than Free
Review: The achingly good Something More Than Free, captures the mix of excitement and fear that comes when the sun rises on a new day.

Title: Born This Way
Review: Beyond all else, perhaps, think of this zero as the massive bedazzled orifice out of which our heroine has spawned a new era of popular culture.

Title: A Bad Wind Blows In My Heart
Review: There's a disarming openness to the lyrics and a warmth to the arrangements that make this an album that rewards repeated listening.

Title: The Moon & Antarctica
Review: Remarkably mature and absorbing.

Title: Walking Cloud and Deep Red Sky, Flag Fluttered and the Sun Shined
Review: The disappointments of Walking Cloud are really quite perplexing, given Mono's limited but impressive history and the promise of their collaboration with Albini. Still, if it fails to live up to the heights of One Step More and their debut Under the Pipal Tree, it has its share of moments.

Title: Nursing Home
Review: It's all strung together with punk-drunk pace and some properly good melodies. This is the real deal.

Title: Compton: A Soundtrack by Dr. Dre
Review: Compton has replaced the abandoned Detox project with a surprisingly vivid soundtrack of frustration inspired by the forthcoming NWA biopic.

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: A warm, enjoyable effort, but perhaps short on the Jews' best asset: Berman himself.

Title: Innundir Skinni
Review: The album's titular track, which translates to "Within Skin," is a reference to pregnancy, but it's also a manifesto of the album's purpose as an arbiter of overwhelming feeling bound up in a neatly-tied package of folk tunes--the emotional intensity lying under the surface rather than on the sleeve.

Title: Destroyer of the Void
Review: Destroyer of the Void is a fitting reminder of what’s possible when you already have such a strong catalog of music under your belt: exceptional music that always seems to beautifully connect, no matter how varying the sounds may be.

Title: Want Two
Review: This is too classical, too romantic, and too I-yam-what-I-yam all at once.

Title: Hero Brother
Review: Her playing, while technically impressive, may not have quite Stetson's jaw-dropping virtuosity, but her pieces have a highly comparable mesmeric, minimalist intensity. [No. 101, p.58]

Title: I'm Not Well
Review: It’s an astounding record from a trio still at the most embryonic of stages. We’ll go on record and get this out there now--it has the potential to be a world-beating album.

Title: The Man Who Died in His Boat
Review: The Man Who Died in His Boat may be a smaller-scale album than either Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill or A I A, but it's no less lovely or moving because of that.

Title: Apologies to the Queen Mary
Review: One to watch. [Jan 2006, p.128]

Title: The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me
Review: The Devil and God Are Raging Inside Me builds on its predecessor's articulate wordplay, with lush tones that evidently evolved over the band's extended break.

Title: Ravedeath, 1972
Review: Each of Hecker's layers are shards, something incomplete, but with just enough shards, a fragmented, disturbed image is formed, and that is the result of Ravedeath, 1972.

Title: Un Dia
Review: Un Día takes everything the former Argentine TV star used to establish her musical style in the 12 years since she released her first album--her sometimes grainy voice, folk-leaning acoustic guitar, odd sampled sounds, and an impossible degree of looping-- and shows Molina’s music in its weirdest, most mesmerizing, ideal version of itself.

Title: Love + Fear
Review: On LOVE + FEAR, Marina shoots for stripped-bare big pop, and for the most part, she achieves it, but various clichéd lyrics occasionally stop her sincerity in its tracks.

Title: Talk That Talk
Review: True, she's still got two token I-like-it-rough tracks--"Birthday Cake" and "Cockiness (Love It)"--but they're just filler on an album that's all about dragging you out of the bedroom and onto the dance floor.

Title: Chris
Review: A breathless, breathtaking achievement, Chris is a fascinating, infectious, endlessly suggestive work, an ode to 80s pop bombast that uses those splinters to build and then de-construct countless glimpses of Héloïse Letissier. Somewhere in amongst these myriad of definitions is Christine And The Queens, a shape-shifting pop entity perpetually aiming for something greater.

Title: Do You Want the Truth or Something Beautiful?
Review: Faith takes every single ounce of her experiences and infuses them into her music. It results in one hell of a theatrical roller-coaster ride that holds attention from beginning to end.

Title: Cocoa Sugar
Review: This is a far more stripped down, stream-lined record that remains just as essential and urgent as all their output so far with little to no compromise.

Title: Let's Stay Friends
Review: They've retained some of the tighty wound post-punk angularity they've always favored and even bust a bit of old school punk, but the real advances are melodic. [Nov 2007, p.160]

Title: Coexist
Review: If letting the world in has resulted in an album this beguiling, there's nothing to fear. [Oct 2012, p.80]

Title: Mettavolution
Review: A long and winding and faithfully atmospheric cover of Pink Floyd's Echoes that closes the album is perhaps the main attraction here, but too much of what precedes it tends to waft away into the ether. [Jul 2019, p.114]

Title: Make Believe
Review: In striving for Zen-like purity, the songs often end up eerily blank. [Jul 2005, p.122]

Title: Hippies
Review: With drunken charm and incessant jangle, Hippies may be Harlem's slop-pop consummation.

Title: FORGET
Review: The album's palette feels broad, with electronics switching from twinkling and melodic to antagonistic industrial clangs. [Apr 2017, p.40]

Title: Feed The Animals
Review: A DJ is only as good as his taste, and Girl Talk is immaculate. [Sept 2008, p.78]

Title: Nextdoorland
Review: This is witty English guitar rock of the highest calibre. [Nov 2002, p.114]

Artist: ...And You Will Know Us By the Trail of Dead
Title: The Century of Self
Review: The Century of Self finds the pride of Austin, Texas, continuing to push baroque prog-rock to orchestral new heights. [Mar 2008, p.112]

Title: Blackstar
Review: Blackstar is a ricochet of textural eccentricity and pictorial-shrapnel writing.

Title: The Innocents
Review: The Innocents is earthy melodrama for catacombs that deserves to be heard above ground. Weyes Blood’s gothic, magical realm has a dozen more doors to be opened on her sophomore LP. It’s just a matter of when the record ends up in your hands.

Title: Canopy Glow
Review: Earnest and joyful throughout, they don't make records like this anymore, so be glad Anathallo didn't listen and made one anyway.

Title: California Nights
Review: California Nights peels] away the layers of haze to reveal a mature ambivalence that feels more sincere--and less forced--than anything Cosentino’s done since Crazy for You.... Production flourishes might not appeal to those who fell in love with Best Coast for its bedroom sensibilities, and there’s probably a significant subset of fans who will resent California Nights as the moment the band abandoned indie for good.

Title: On Top
Review: Throughout this collection, Rye Coalition shamlessly worships at the altar of Kiss, Grand Funk Railroad, and Spinal Tap via weathered, punk-inspired chord progressions, muddy bass lines, lead-footed drum patterns, and hammer-handed guitar riffs that will shake, rattle, and roll hockey arenas until the end of time.

Title: Endless Scroll
Review: Blistering, incisive and occasionally even surprising, Endless Scroll is anything but dull.

Title: Kicking The National Habit
Review: Grand National's main skill lies in their ability to twin their fine songs to tight electronic productions, striking the perfect midpoint between live organics and cool digital sequencing.

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: It is a complex beast of shade and mood, and it's Lopatin's best work yet.

Title: I'm Not Bossy, I'm The Boss
Review: It's a shame that the album starts so blandly. [Sep 2014, p.109]

Title: Effluxion
Review: A power-pop potpourri that falls between the Beatlesque formalism of Cotton Mather and the eruptive emotionality of Car Seat Headrest. [Mar 2019, p.34]

Title: The Cautionary Tales of Mark Oliver Everett
Review: Eels may not tread any new ground musically (aside from being generally less noisy), but never before have we seen such raw emotion on show.

Title: Broken Dreams Club
Review: This EP sounds, in many ways, like a showcase of new equipment and technology, proof that White just might be one of the best pop producers working right now. However, the songs might be too cerebral, lacking the brevity, structural simplicity, and dare I say petulance that made "Lust For Life" so easy to fall so hard for.

Title: Need You Now
Review: Lady Antebellum have potential, but they're mostly dull--by design.

Title: Motion
Review: His largely straight-ahead approach will rankle EDM devotees who are searching for boundary-busting beats, but he's taking his chances with the most unpredictable technology of all: the human voice.

Title: Survivor
Review: As contrived and calculated as a Mariah Carey record, only without the joy.

Title: The Lookout
Review: Much of The Lookout is subtly fraught.

Title: Beat The Devil's Tattoo
Review: If there were ever a reason for Black Rebel Motorcycle Club's existence, this would be it, and despite the false dawns of albums past, Beat The Devil's Tattoo can hold its head high as their most compulsive body of work to date.

Title: The Desired Effect
Review: On The Desired Effect, Flowers aims to be loose and have some fun, but he also sounds more focused than ever. Flowers has spoken of a desire to write an album full of singles, and these songs almost reach that goal.

Title: The Night Creeper
Review: If you've grown tired of the retro-metal sound of recent years, The Night Creeper is a good place to re-engage. Uncle Acid might not be sonic visionaries, but they're masters of their craft.

Title: Sukierae
Review: There are a lot of songs here, and it overwhelms in one sitting, but even in small pieces, it’s clear that Tweedy takes home the songwriting ribbon at the father-son picnic.

Title: Conspiracy of One
Review: The Offspring's hit-making machinery is as efficiently well-oiled as ever. [#3, p.106]

Title: Universal High
Review: All told: a summer soul smash. [Sep 2017, p.93]

Title: You & Me
Review: The album’s majestic brilliance reveals itself through subtle perfections that appear with repeated listens.

Title: The Diary
Review: A supremely confident collection from an artist just gearing up for greatness. [Jun 2016, p.111]

Title: Special Affections
Review: Even if Diamond Rings' rapidly evolving aesthetic has already moved beyond Special Affections' bedsit R&B, the album still stands as an exemplary model of how one can live out blinged-out fantasies on a cubic zirconia budget.

Title: California Nights
Review: Best Coast still have delivered an overall solid album with California Nights, but it remains hard to see how the simplification of their craft and the softening of their image will allow Consentino to attract new listeners without losing the older ones.

Title: Big Inner
Review: A genuine classic, in fact.

Title: Holograms
Review: It's never uninteresting on Holograms.

Title: Awfully Deep
Review: Awfully Deep, on the whole, is a bold, ambitious swing for the fences. But, like it or not, the game's done changed, and Manuva '05 sounds way too much like Manuva '01.

Title: Flesh Tone
Review: Whatever her bad luck might be down to, Kelis can take some small comfort in having made her best album since Kaleidoscope.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Daybreaker's more conventional nature puts a greater and more intriguing challenge on Orton's vocal cords to be the album's main instrument; that voice, a breathless cry that falls somewhere between Natalie Merchant and Bjork, is more than equal to the task.

Title: Down There
Review: Down there, his most accessible work outside the confines of Animal Collective, revels in that upside-down gravity. [Nov 2010, p.61]

Title: American Band
Review: An album that's both sad and angry, thoughtful and impassioned, and desperate for America to escape its chequered past. [Nov 2016, p.18]

Title: This Time Around
Review: This Time Around scores with more sophisticated harmonies and storytelling.

Title: Xenophanes
Review: Only staunch Volta cultists would claim every minute of Xenophanes is worth your precious leisure time. But damn if the best bits don't make an excellent in-car soundtrack for pretending you're on your way to something more dramatic than your day job.

Title: Mind Elevation
Review: A blissed-out menagerie of subtly morphing beats and elegant melodies within a dub framework. [Oct 2002, p.88]

Title: Noah's Ark
Review: CocoRosie sound, blissfully, like no one else. [Sep 2005, p.102]

Title: When It Was Now
Review: Though the songs can come off as occasionally sterile (“On A Day” quickly comes to mind), it’s still a pretty impressive collection of songs from a band that’s only been around for a few years.

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: Unless you are severely depressed the laggard pace of this record will make it very hard to sit through. Yet each track is delightfully insteresting in its own right. [#5, p.100]

Title: Blazing Gentlemen
Review: 16 lightly fried examples of his gift for surrealist pop/classic rock synthesis. [Jan 2014, p.104]

Title: Live a Little
Review: [It] revisits the chamber pop of their 1998 debut... equalling it in beauty and surpassing it in punch. [Nov 2006, p.123]

Title: Beneath the Skin
Review: This album has the feel of a “for us” record, one that rewards the band for making it and decides that it’s okay to create something deeply personal and a little self-indulgent.

Title: Rare
Review: There is a lot to like about Rare. But it never quite gets out from beneath the shadow of half a decade of behemothic bangers.

Title: Daybreaker
Review: Yeah, she’s sticking with the formula that got her going six years ago, but when it actually works, why bother messing with it?

Title: Black Dialogue
Review: Black Dialogue: a hip-hop classic? Maybe not, but pretty damn close.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: Fink's still a thoughtful guy with angst to spare but his new tunes inch happily toward pop.

Title: Humbug
Review: Humbug ruminates, but doesn't quite offer an extraordinary reply. [Fall 2009, p.61]

Title: Big Whiskey and the Groogrux King
Review: Steady as she goes on AOR eighth outing.

Title: Settle
Review: The only thing Settle succeeds at is repurposing generic late 90s funky house into a sound that people seem to have been brainwashed into thinking is new and exciting.

Title: Manic
Review: Manic revels in the explorative genre-pop bombast, letting the delicates twinkle, and the snarls bare their teeth; yet it's the soul that shines dominantly. It's her most complete work to date.

Title: Sam's Town
Review: The album doesn't lend Flowers the gravitas he apparently yearns for, but it does prove that few are better at irrepressible pop hooks and fist-pumping choruses.

Title: Rebel Heart
Review: Ultimately, Rebel Heart feels like a wasted opportunity.

Title: Impersonator
Review: If the easily distracted are at risk of sleeping through this, fans of emotional tours de force will have a great new addition to their 'best albums of the year' list.

Title: Visions
Review: When it works, it makes for gloriously contradictory pop--it's just a shame that the formula isn't a little more consistent.

Title: The Search
Review: There are more nuanced (and enjoyable) approaches to records focused on depression. Elzhi’s “Lead Poison” is still the one I’d recommend first but NF impresses on “The Search”. ... By stripping that away, his barrage of words – married with the booming, cinematic production (credited as NF and Tommee Profitt) – is surprisingly digestible.

Title: Hymnal
Review: Hymnal's serene beauty may make it his most sublime music yet.

Title: Black Dog Barking
Review: Keen observers will note that Black Dog Barking is a more polished affair than 2010's No Guts No Glory, but it is the ageless and tireless uniformity of the band's approach that makes this an honest and brazen delight.

Title: Love in the Future
Review: All of Legend’s strengths are present: keen melodies, smooth vocal understatement, and artful arrangements.

Title: Reverie
Review: As you'd expect, his 12th album sounds wonderful. [Nov 2011, p.86]

Title: Push the Sky Away
Review: There are some wonderful moments, the single ('We No Who U R') and the title track are starkly magnificent, but the general feel is a bit of a comedown.

Title: The Spirit of Apollo
Review: Naturally, Sam Spiegel (a.k.a. Squeak E. Clean, and Spike Jonze’s brother) and DJ Zegon’s attempt at album unity is flawed. The real question: Can The Spirit Of Apollo transcend its built-in Achilles’ heel? The short answer is yes, as there’s something to like on every song.

Title: Savage Mode II
Review: ‘Savage Mode 2’ matches ruthless entertainment to phenomenal artistry, a collaboration that works on a number of levels. Once more exposing fresh layers to 21 Savage and Metro Boomin.

Title: Hello Everything
Review: This... might just be too scatterbrained for its own good.

Title: A Mad & Faithful Telling
Review: A Mad & Faithful Telling, however, comes off as their most focused and researched work yet, incorporating traditional and pop culture aspects without getting cluttered or seeming like they’re trying too hard to find a niche.

Title: A River Ain't Too Much To Love
Review: You’re going to want to hear this one.

Title: OIL OF EVERY PEARL'S UN-INSIDES
Review: Sophie’s defining hyper-minimalism has given way to a new lushness. While enduringly “other”, tracks like Infatuation and Pretending lack focus, and this wafty iteration isn’t as original as Sophie’s other modes.

Title: The Dusk In Us
Review: On this form, there are few around who can match them.

Title: The Invisible Invasion
Review: The Coral's trade has made them less rumbling and more meandering, more coherent but less mysterious.

Title: Life for Rent
Review: Its best moments suggest that Armstrong is unfairly maligned.... At worst, it's twee and bland, aural wallpaper that only someone who didn't really like music could care about. Either way, it isn't going to change anyone's mind about Dido.

Title: The Undisputed Truth
Review: They're a tight fit: Ant likes to experiment, and Ali's nimble enough to keep up and make it work.

Title: A Black Mile to the Surface
Review: This is a painstakingly composed work of art--and an absolute masterpiece at that. [15 Jul 2017, p.50]

Title: Mature Themes
Review: A bit of editing and self-control, and this could have been one of the albums of the year.

Title: Music's Not for Everyone
Review: Music may lack the crazy ambition of his previous acts or some of the unexpected goofiness of the Gang's debut, but it's still a modest pleasure and a fine addition to Svenonius' catalog.

Title: Another Day on Earth
Review: Another Day is nowhere near as invested with ideas as Eno's name-making work, but its easy pleasures still rub and float away.

Title: Infinite Arms
Review: Infinite Arms is a confusing, schizophrenic work. Several of its earlier tracks find the band clicking like never before and exploring fresh ideas while sounding more aerodynamic than ever. But so much else seems to have been haphazardly thrown together, as if the band never even entered the same room during the recording process.

Title: Obadiah
Review: Ford's transporting voice is let down by tunes that are anything but. [Aug 2010, p.92]

Title: Animal Nature
Review: A solid offering that could have been improved by swapping some of the remixes for the originals.

Title: Starboy
Review: The Weeknd is a self-described pop star, and proves his worth on Starboy, an album with plenty to love.

Title: Callus
Review: It's the kind of record that needs to be approached in increments, but the rewards reveal themselves when given the patience and time that Callus deserves.

Title: A Deeper Understanding
Review: Lovers of the plush paranoia of 2014’s breakthrough album ‘Lost In The Dream’ will be relieved that his fourth outing doesn’t touch that dial. From the opening highway piano judder of ‘Up All Night’ it’s like losing yourself once more in some lost golden age of MOR.

Title: Electric Cables
Review: The uninitiated may find the unrelenting nerve-soothing a little too much like anaesthesia. [May 2012, p.100]

Title: This Is Not The World
Review: It's mildly disappointing that the Futureheads' first independently released music sounds more conventional than what they issued on other labels, but This Is Not the World is still a solidly enjoyable album on its own terms.

Title: Ray Guns Are Not Just The Future
Review: Ray Guns Are Not Just the Future is not an enormous departure from their self-titled debut; after all, why mess with a good thing?

Title: Engravings
Review: Engravings sees the artist employing fractured choral voices, militant drums, swirling guitars and the occasional harpsichord (notably on album standout "The Weight of Gold") to create a tapestry of sounds both experimental and organic.

Title: Crazy for You
Review: Best Coast's music wishes for that innocence – for when a pop song could sum up your whole torment in three perfect minutes, before your heart truly gets broken that first time – and successfully evokes it with Crazy for You's immediate classic-pop hits.

Title: Revolve
Review: Track after track follows the same formula, with Newman’s subdued introductory verse swallowed by a huge, anthemic refrain that never lets up, his voice drowned in a tide of orchestra and chorus, all dialled up to 11. It’s quite frustrating.

Title: The College Dropout
Review: 2004's first great hip-hop album. [9 Feb 2004]

Title: No Hope, No Future
Review: It sounds like the Good Shoes are tired and mildly sick of it all--and unfortunately, it’s catching.

Title: In Glendale
Review: Like the rest of his comedy oeuvre, Heidecker pulls no punches. In Glendale arrives as a fully formed beast, equal parts parody and confession of our universal lameness.

Title: Boxer
Review: The National were worried that they wouldn't be able to follow up Alligator, that fans would be disappointed. Boxer proves their fears ungrounded - and that Alligator was no one classic wonder.

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: For its epic length, the collection occasionally (rarely) drags, but when it does, it doesn't for long.

Title: Big Talk
Review: More than anything, Big Talk reflects the Vegas background of its middling maestro.

Title: 20 Years In A Montana Missile Silo
Review: [“Monkey Bizness” is] the most animated Ubu has been in ages, with an atmosphere of vertiginous dark energy accreting around the jagged guitar riff of “Red Eyed Blues”, while even the slower, more subdued melancholia of “The Healer” wields a strangely sinister poignancy as a desolate Thomas regretfully confesses, “I see too much”. But what visions!

Title: There is No Enemy
Review: Despite the bounty of overdubs, however, there’s little self-indulgence to There Is No Enemy; Martsch’s overloaded approach might scream ‘prog’, but he also possesses a perfectly-disciplined, ‘pop’ songwriting sensibility, with every lengthy instrumental coda married to contagious choruses and melodic barbs that lodge in the mind.

Title: Pleasureland
Review: There is an easy grace to the material. Even the shrillest cuts, such as "Syrup" that features a distorted, dirty, electric guitar line, are subdued because they were recorded with silence as an essential feature of the song. The result is evocative in the same way that one's own bodily noises like a heartbeat and breathing can seem so loud in a soundless place.

Title: Old Growth
Review: This fifth album gets progressively less fuzztoned and more overtly tuneful as it progresses. [Mar 2008, p.85]

Title: Reeling Skullways
Review: Reeling Skullways is a paean to the previous step on techno's evolutionary ladder: the analogue acid sounds of Detroit, Chicago, and Manchester. [Jul 2012, p.69]

Title: The Sciences
Review: Roughly half the tracks being available prior to this release isn’t much of an issue when they are of such high quality, and the fresh tracks are some of the best the band have ever written. The group seem rejuvenated with a long road ahead of them.

Title: Nothing Bad Will Ever Happen
Review: Nothing Bad Will Ever Happen has flashes of brilliance and moments where they're still figuring out what to do, but overall, it shows them growing into something new as gracefully as they can.

Title: Blame It On Gravity
Review: The players' tight grip on the material reveals a first-rate band in peak form. [June 2008, p.98]

Title: Grim Town
Review: Grim Town is a concept in itself: it is a fictitious location, an embodiment of feeling that has been brought to life by the sentiment and memory that revolve around it. Through it, SOAK is able to explore emotion and turn it into something tangible.

Title: New Blood
Review: Though hardly essential, New Blood nevertheless features many fine performances, and there's room for the record to prove the true depth of its merits upon further listens.

Title: Everything Ever Written
Review: Everything Ever Written is a welcome return for a band that's long been held in high regard.

Title: Woman
Review: Even if Woman sometimes sounds more like two EPs than a cohesive set of songs, it's still an enjoyable album--especially when Justice use their flair for looking back creatively.

Title: Migration Stories
Review: The result is one of his most varied but distinct albums. [May 2020, p.35]

Title: Vivian Girls
Review: I believe in the Vivian Girls. In every gorgeous harmony that coats bitterness, in every ambition subjugated to truncated song structure and muffled production, in every bouncy beat beneath a baleful drawl somehow made of equally bouncy elements.

Title: Happy in Galoshes
Review: Sticky melodies crop up here and there, but they're badly outnumbered by turgid power ballads and indulgent experiments.

Title: A Weekend in the City
Review: There's barely a song that isn't kneecapped by one of Okereke's lyrical clangers.

Title: Come Feel Me Tremble
Review: A collision of punk-fuelled cacophony, halting balladry and guttersnipe sensibility. [Dec 2003, p.112]

Title: Centralia
Review: Centralia is by far the most satisfying release to date by the Brooklyn-based minimalist post-rock duo Mountains.

Title: For Screening Purposes Only
Review: For Screening Purposes is worth checking out for those who like their music prickly but with an undercurrent of pop to it, too.

Title: Wakin on a Pretty Daze
Review: Wakin’ On A Pretty Daze strikes with a gust of pent up emotions, a trailblazing record that openly affirms a personal accountability for self without slipping into heavy-handedness.

Title: Take Control
Review: It’s still simplistic and limited but it’s meant to be. That’s the whole idea. The converted will remain.

Title: Optometry
Review: Optometry is a success in terms of both sound and vision. [#221, p.53]

Title: Persona
Review: As the album comes to a close, "Rest" and "Hidden" begin to work off of fuzzy, pulsating beats and slow, trancelike synth passages, proving that Rival Consoles certainly holds a blueprint to the dreamworld contained within Persona.

Title: Collections
Review: The production drips with gloss, but unlike Acolyte, it’s a gloss that obscures rather than glimmers.

Title: Love in the Future
Review: Legend is content to adopt a croonerific sound that doesn't challenge existing soul genre parameters in the least. That's fine, in theory, but rather yawn-worthy in execution.

Title: ye
Review: Over a brief seven tracks, the 40-year-old superstar confirms his production prowess, veering between sparse, hyper-modern styles and compositions which hark back to the soulful bent of the producer-turned-rapper’s early career; a volatile mix of the sweet and the acrid, the sentimental and the tendentious.

Title: In Between Dreams
Review: Listening to the surfer/artist’s third album is like sitting on a barstool alongside a good friend, knocking back pints and rappin’ it down about, y’know, life and whatever.

Title: Handcream for a Generation
Review: Handcream for a Generation is a festive crash of cultures, a Babel of loops and ethnic body language. Dixie R&B, Bollywood kitsch, Crooklyn hip-hop, Eurotrash electronics -- singer-songwriter and producer Tjinder Singh shakes 'em up like rats in a box, finding kicks and connections in aggressive pastiche.

Title: Tender New Signs
Review: Fortunately, adding more shape to their songs doesn't pin down their sounds too much.

Title: Fountain
Review: This is a life-affirming album which is not held back by the restrictions of linguistics and the limitations that words bring, and it may be just what you need to lift you out of yourself in these troubled times.

Title: De Vermis Mysteriis
Review: De Vermis Mysteriis gets up in your face, and it never really steps back until it's over.

Title: The Rose Has Teeth in the Mouth of a Beast
Review: Easy to admire, but hard to really love. [27 May 2006, p.31]

Title: The Rip Tide
Review: By leaving behind the experimentations and the peculiarities of their former albums, Beirut create an album that's all too easy to hold on to and all too easy to let go of.

Title: If I Should Go Before You
Review: Most of the songs exceed the four-minute mark and the lack of an obvious single makes If I Should Go Before You feel even more like a single, lovingly crafted entity.

Title: Let the Blind Lead Those Who Can See But Cannot Feel
Review: It's an uneven and at times painfully intimate record, but one that confirms the talent of a songwriter obsessed with illuminating his interior truth.

Title: It's All True
