Review: A non-household album by an oft-overlooked electronic artist/producer, Queen of Golden Dogs is an intriguing, mysteriously intelligent dark horse of a record. Fans of broader electronic/experimental pieces, prepare to be delighted in the delirious lunacy of Vessel’s apex-to-date.

Title: Hi Beams
Review: Added up, it's a departure for sure, but it's a swerve that's easy to follow.

Title: Naomi
Review: Competent. Completely forgettable.

Title: Nobody Knows
Review: A masterful song cycle of raw confessionals, ghostly R&B and gritty stompers, all channelled via intense vocals that razor and soothe. [Nov 2013, p.94]

Title: Last Summer
Review: For all her internal chaos, Friedberger's debut is a concise, considerate effort.

Title: AQUÎ›RIA
Review: Despite its depth of ideas and imagery, AQUARIA starts to feel a little thematically one-dimensional until you get to 'Only', a straight ahead piano-driven, introspective slow jam.

Title: Standards
Review: Given that Tortoise's previous recordings have spawned a procession of remixes and re-imaginings, is Standards to be judged on its own merits, or as the raw material for music yet to come? As always, the band is poised between capturing a momentary, malleable inspiration and shaping that moment into some timeless anthem, and as always, it chooses to dither and delay, settling for a sometimes pleasant, sometimes maddening, almost always stimulating exploration of atmospherics.

Title: Compton: A Soundtrack by Dr. Dre
Review: Despite its vocal flaws, if anything, there is a great amount of care in Compton.

Title: Junk
Review: Junk is deeply uncool, uncoolly deep, and utterly magnifique. [May 2016, p.115]

Title: The Pinkprint
Review: The Pinkprint is her third studio album, and like the first two it’s full of compromises and half-successes.

Title: Touch
Review: Marked by stronger grooves, darker lyrics and catchier hooks, Touch pushes July Talk's musical vision forward without sacrificing their core elements. It's an album that should cause anyone who'd previously dismissed the band reason to reconsider their stance, while exceeding existing fans' expectations.

Title: Without You
Review: Much like its musical parent, Without You effortlessly inhales and exhales strands of musical influence past, present and future.

Title: You Have Already Gone To The Other World
Review: At a hair under 60 minutes long, You Have Already Gone to the Other World is daunting by nature of its sheer length, let alone its impenetrable subject material.

Title: The Path of Totality
Review: It is samey, ugly and spectacularly stupid at the same time.

Title: Quiet Is the New Loud
Review: Though this is limp-wristed stuff, it's also undeniably beautiful, often recalling Nick Drake and Belle & Sebastian. [#154, p.82]

Title: Wild Ones
Review: Wild Ones is an unfilfilling [sic] and detached listen.

Title: Kubrick
Review: Redolent of soundtrack ace Danny Elfman, if Kubrick is a pitch for work in cinema it's a sound move. [Jan 2016, p.94]

Title: LCD Soundsystem
Review: Marries raw rock attitudes to the sonic spread and kinetic energy central to dance music.

Title: Psychic Chasms
Review: While it lacks the freshness that saw it named one of Pitchfork's best albums of last year, there's no doubting that Palomo's best efforts retain their charm a year since they were first heard.

Title: Scream Above the Sounds
Review: Stereophonics don’t have the lyrical potency of their earlier incarnation, often erring on the side of grand generalisation--as is the way when you have to appeal to enough people to fill your next arena tour. But frontman Kelly Jones has got one of the damn finest voices in rock ‘n’ roll, and that’s surely worth the price of admission in itself.

Title: Yawn
Review: The end result is an album that you sink into, which gradually envelops you: moving, painful and elating in equal measure.

Title: Beast Moans
Review: Completely uninhibited both to its credit and fault, Swan Lake doesn’t always reach the towering combined height set by it’s forerunners, but is able to stand alongside each of them individually. [#15]

Title: Big
Review: The lyrics -- which seesaw manically between exhortations to a no-goodnik to get out and purrings about being glad to have a lover by her side -- won't get nominated for any poetry awards, but Gray makes her case on the strength of her nutty soul charms.

Title: Beware of the Dogs
Review: Beware of the Dogs is a triumph on its own terms, going from high point to high point as she maps the pains, pleasures and anxieties of her personal patch of twentysomething bohemia.

Title: Electric Version
Review: The kind of album that functions as both background BBQ beat and windows-down sing-along. [Jul 2003, p.112]

Title: Food & Liquor
Review: Food & Liquor is one of the year's fresher efforts and future classics.

Title: Havilah
Review: This more relaxed style allows a somewhat more forthright exploration of the defeat/desolation that runs through much of Liddiard’s material. In fact, the structure of the album as a whole reflects this neatly.

Title: Songs of Praise
Review: Delivered with a heavy dose of grit and honesty, there’s some teeth marks there, but not the whole bite. It makes for their own, unique brand of sociopolitics-lite, done with a nudge, a wink, and just enough of the unexpected.

Title: V
Review: There are enough hooks here to show how the LA band have shifted 17m albums, but also evidence as to why most people can't remember a Maroon 5 song two seconds after it finishes.

Title: Divine Providence
Review: Though Deer Tick has moonlighted as a Nirvana tribute band, it's the group's love for the Replacements that shines on Divine Providence. [#82, p. 55]

Title: Vapor City
Review: On Vapor City, Machinedrum steers clear of dramatic style makeovers, opting to focus on sharpening his craft while leaving the listener with a collection of songs that operates on pure magnetism and unbridled confidence.

Title: Everything's Fine
Review: Although Everything’s Fine is well-crafted from front to back, there are a few hiccups.

Title: Unexpected
Review: Cutting to the chase, this album is full of Rihanna b-sides that sound like a carbon copy of everything in the charts right now and are completely personality free.

Title: Omni
Review: Minus The Bear is still boasting its trademark funkadelic rock grooves meshed with electro-pop quirk, but now with a smoother and more linear structure. [Spring/Summer 2010, p.108]

Title: Descended Like Vultures
Review: Unlike Rogue Wave's timid debut, Vultures blazes forward with the kind of assured bravado not usually seen this side of U2.

Title: Connector
Review: Connector tries to juggle too much in too short of moments, confining juxtaposing or conflicting elements to 15-20 second bursts, often between choruses.

Title: Gloss Drop
Review: The record stands as a solid collection from a trio of exceptionally talented individuals.

Title: Rated O
Review: The cuts are manic psychedelic jams--there’s even a sitar--riding electronic drones and throbbing, insistent riffs. Timbres of instruments are barbed with fuzz tone and static; the voices that infrequently appear might be shouting unintelligibly or nearly buried in the mix.

Title: New York City
Review: The album bumps from electronica to cabaret to jazz and back again; it's busy but never feels schizophrenic.

Artist: Beth Jeans Houghton & The Hooves of Destiny
Title: Yours Truly, Cellophane Nose
Review: A great start.

Title: Atrocity Exhibition
Review: Atrocity Exhibition is Danny Brown at his least diluted, almost unrelentingly grim and completely engrossing.

Title: Devotion
Review: A lack of polish--notably on the title track, which features Curl collective member Coby Sey--is part of the appeal, and if "Gladly" plays it very straight, then it's hard to carp at its loved-up optimism. [Sep 2018, p.39]

Title: Heretic Pride
Review: While he looses some duds ("New Zion," "So Desperate," and "How to Embrace a Swamp Creature" are skippable) and a set of slightly duller lyrics, the conceits of the songs—the central images of good floundering in an evil world, of contented monsters, of the naiveté of the faithful—serve to substantiate the album as a whole more than any one line, verse, or song does.

Title: White Hills
Review: All that said, it’s only about a third as bad as it sounds. It’s fairly tolerable as far as extreme self indulgence goes.

Title: Zonoscope
Review: After the ubiquitous presence of '80s-indebted music last year, a follow-up with little stylistic deviation isn't a thrilling proposition: Take Me Over steals a hook from fellow Australians Men At Work, adds ooh-ooh backing vocals and just about gets away with it.

Title: One Day All of This Wonâ€™t Matter Any More
Review: ODAOTWMA will do little to challenge the Sheffield band's twee reputation, but the record crosses genres with far greater experimentation than they're known for.

Title: End Times
Review: This may not be Elels' best record, but it's damn close to it, and a uniquely idiosyncratic deposit in an increasingly diverse discography that's getting harder and harder to ignore. [Holiday 2009, p.76]

Title: Italian Ice
Review: The whole album is stuffed with hooks and brilliant ideas. This is peak Nicole Atkins.

Title: Waiting out the Storm
Review: With his rock solid, half Crazy Horse-half Heartbreakers sounding band, the Extraterrestrials, Ivey not only expands his sound from last year’s The Dream and the Dreamer, but he brings a passionate sense of urgency too.

Title: Phantom Birds
Review: His tidiest folk-pop tunes to date. ... Irresistible. [Oct 2020, p.27]

Title: The Evens
Review: A set of faintly sad songs so minimal that they're often barely there at all. [May 2005, p.96]

Title: Secret House Against the World
Review: Buck's monotone and his lack of truly cutting statements make this a dour experience. [Sep 2005, p.100]

Title: At Best Cuckold
Review: At Best Cuckold is much like the autumnal vibe it tries to project in that, like autumn, you don't mind its existence but you kind of just want to go back to that excellent summer again.

Title: 13 Degrees of Reality
Review: It's got the breadth of a comprehensively adventurous band, able to balance a steady motorik churn midway between Kraut and deep soul while letting the pull of improvisational tangents and dub distortion shift the picture.

Title: Darling of the Afterglow
Review: While she is hardly the only artist mixing traditional musical forms with contemporary electronics, she does so with her unmistakable touch. Her latest album broadens and expands the reach of her already deft compositions.

Title: Eating Us
Review: Eating Us is their fourth full-length, and it’s a delight.

Title: Day & Age
Review: In this day and age, though, people would be better off cherry picking the best tracks for download.

Title: Maximum Balloon
Review: Maximum Balloon is by no means a perfect album, but there are some fantastic performances to be found (Karen O, Ambrosia Parsley's sultry Pink Bricks). It's a shame that Sitek never steps up to the mic, but when you've got friends like these it doesn't really matter.

Title: In Flesh Tones
Review: In Flesh Tones is sensitive, unsure and guarded, yet it's comfortable and inviting despite this.

Title: Longwave
Review: Longwave is languorous and amiable. ... The largely unchanging pace prompts yearnings for more frequent shifts from second gear, however. [May 2018, p.26]

Title: Crosseyed Heart
Review: Crosseyed Heart could have been issued at any time in the past four decades. It’s full of influences he’s spent his creative life exploring, and there’s nothing viral or meme-worthy about them. That Richards keeps discovering nuance within those original texts is a testament to his seemingly infinite muse.

Title: Carry Fire
Review: Each of Plant's albums are distinctly different from the others (a tradition that started in Led Zeppelin). On this self-produced triumph, Plant finds fresh ways to present his voice and express his venerable perspective.

Title: Do It Again
Review: Do It Again isn’t as downright amazing as it could have been, but there are far more pros than cons.

Title: As If Apart
Review: Whether autobiographical or artistic, As If Apart is a powerful, exquisitely realized journey, the sort of bummer that sounds strongest in that alien hour between when you’re supposed to fall asleep and when you should be jerking awake.

Title: Morning Phase
Review: True to his transformer's nature, the sequel is better than the original.

Title: Aaltopiiri
Review: Rich in imagery and suggestive of enviroment -- arctic, urban and mental -- Pan Sonic chisels a sound contradictory in its makeup, utterly synthetic and metallic yet somehow deeply organic. [#82, p.144]

Title: Convenanza
Review: There's a pleasing, ad hoc nature to these loose-limbed grooves. [Mar 2016, p.97]

Title: Save Rock and Roll
Review: Save Rock And Roll is the band’s most personal album yet, a tribute to being passionate and young when time makes the former difficult and the latter impossible.

Title: Return of Saturn
Review: One of the better pop albums of 2000, a multi-faceted offering that resists easy labeling while extending the band's mighty grip on the popular imagination.

Title: Hell on Heels
Review: Hell on Heels is one beautiful amble.

Title: Chain Gang of Love
Review: A miasma of retro cool. [Sep 2003, p.116]

Title: Walking With Thee
Review: Walking With Thee feels more like a transition record than a definitive statement in its own right.

Title: Electric Version
Review: It's an album's worth of smart, solid pop music that lingers in the memory.

Title: Highly Evolved
Review: The album definitely has a few remarkable moments, but it’s really just not very good.

Title: Lil Durk 2X
Review: Records like this are what will eventually outmode the contradiction of “too street for the industry,” eschewing both categories in the unique accomplishment of a profit-driven truth-telling venture. More like this.

Title: Anthems for Doomed Youth
Review: With the buzz silenced and the rag headlines but a thing of the past, it’s encouraging to see that The Libertines have lost none of what made them worth the hype in the first place.

Title: Phantom Radio
Review: It's decent and fairly enjoyable, but nothing astounds.

Title: Boys and Diamonds
Review: This follow-up to their debut shows more polish and a firmer grasp on rhythm. [Apr 2011, p.106]

Title: Before the Dawn Heals Us
Review: Before The Dawn Heals Us is a very twilight album, a very urban record. It never quite achieves the variegated subtlety of Dead Cities..., but it doesn’t reach for the same frosty rural pastures as that record either.

Title: Walking With Thee
Review: Walking with Thee is neither an album of triumph nor of disappointment.

Title: Quicksand / Cradlesnakes
Review: It's roots music that hums and rattles, hearing the dissonant sound of America singing and finding beauty in the collision of opposites. [Apr 2003, p.73]

Title: Sound of a Woman
Review: Sound of a Woman quickly reveals itself to be a crafty bait and switch. With its scratchy trip-hop beat, soulful vocals, and sparsely placed keyboards and synthesized string stabs, "Losin' My Mind" is more Blue Lines than Big Fun, while the Jessie Ware-esque electro-soul ballads "So Deep" and "Vietnam" find the singer dabbling in drum n' bass and freestyle, respectively.

Title: Earth Sound System
Review: The group's love and knowledge of folk and psychedelia is really to the fore on this collection, as they unravel both and knit them back together in bolder, even wiggier patterns. [Jun 2011, p.57]

Title: Hebrews
Review: Bemis may have grown up, but he's still a master at crafting poignant lyrics that take a sharp look at his fears of becoming irrelevant and thoughts about God. [Jul 2014, p.97]

Title: Koi No Yokan
Review: At the end of the day, I don't know exactly where I'd rank Koi No Yokan--somewhere in the top three, but really it's not important. What's important is that this is a f***ing great album.

Title: Lucky
Review: The Brooklyn-based veterns have beefed up the arrangements on LP number five, and Matthew Caws' material happily carries that weight. [Mar 2008, p.96]

Title: Dumb Flesh
Review: You can't accuse Powers of resting on his laurels--although it's at the expense of some of that first record's unique character. [Jul 2015, p.91]

Title: AMOK
Review: As a product of Yorke’s mind, AMOK represents a measurable progression over The Eraser. It’s more experimental, varied, nuanced, and likeable.

Title: Mixed Emotions
Review: Mixed Emotions is a shiny bear-hug of an album--sometimes short on fresh ideas, but never lacking in heart.

Title: Bird Songs of a Killjoy
Review: Overall, Bird Songs Of A Killjoy is the sound of someone recording exactly what they want to. Nothing here feels out of place, or sounds like a pastiche of another era. Bedouine has found herself a winning formula.

Title: Nobody Wants to Be Here and Nobody Wants to Leave
Review: The mastery on display here is that the mix comes out as sublime as it does.

Title: Coma Witch
Review: An impressive effort. [Nov 2014, p.98]

Title: NO DREAM
Review: Jeff Rosenstock is a Regular Joe, something that genuinely matters, and No Dream reminds us that sometimes the right kind of ordinary guy is something very special; may he never become jaded about the music and scene he clearly loves.

Title: Alone
Review: The songs throughout Alone may rebel with their quiet solitude and reflection, but that’s a quality worth exploring when solo albums intervene and collaborators return.

Title: This Island
Review: Those who can overlook this slightly dumbed-down approach will find This Island is not without its moments.

Title: Come Home To Mama
Review: Wainwright's vocals might be dressy but her thoughts are naked, heartbreakingly so on All Your Clothes, a graveside conversation with Kate McGarrigle.

Title: Hot Thoughts
Review: Spoon is a master of hooky songwriting, but Hot Thoughts seems so bent on undermining it that the band undersells itself. Maybe Hot Thoughts is an apt title after all--it’s got great ideas, but the execution is lacking.

Title: All a Man Should Do
Review: This album does find the fine band reaching for something different, and they hit their target with skill, assurance, and clarity.

Title: All This I Do For Glory
Review: There’s a pervading darkness over All This I Do for Glory that makes it a tricky listen at points.

Title: Free TC
Review: Free TC could use some editing, but Ty has enough charm to carry bedroom jams, Cadillac bangers, and folk-funk experiments all at once.

Title: Antarctica
Review: Though Antarctica positions itself as an assessment of worldly chaos and isolation, it’s never clear whether the stance is earnest or apathetic. Even Albini-tier fidelity can’t make this formula sound fresh.

Title: Absolute Zero
Review: The disc is only 42 minutes long, but he’s pushing the envelope in so many directions, you’ll likely get dizzy playing this through for the first time. Regardless, there’s enough of a method to his madness for those open minded enough who enter this occasionally dark, always circuitous musical tunnel to enjoy, or at least appreciate, the ride.

Title: Moth
Review: With Moths, Chairlift make a strong claim to being one of pop music's best songwriting teams, with the production and vocal chops to bring their compositions fully and vibrantly to life.

Title: Stay Positive
Review: Stay Positive is the most sophisticated and erudite THS have ever sounded, and that's a mixed blessing.

Artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
Title: Viscerals
Review: Viscerals takes their abject menace to the next level its predecessor King of Cowards threatened.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: Honeymoon will be an immediate boon to fans of heart-on-sleeve indie bands like That Dog, Waxahatchee, Charli Bliss, and the Beths. Trifilio is a very good songwriter with a lovely, somewhat folk-toned voice, and Beach Bunny are all good musicians who’ve attained an impressive amount of musical know-how in their few years together.

Title: The Creek Drank The Cradle
Review: The ambiguity in the songs adds to their haunting quality.

Title: Rainier Fog
Review: Rainier Fog has enough highs mind to comfortably recommend as a must-listen--a lot of this material is what Chains do best.

Title: At Mount Zoomer
Review: The two men’s reedy voices come across as more harried than heroic. And often the keyboard bits are linked into structures that are neat yet crowded; just when one riff grows familiar and hummable, an eager new one shows up to displace it. It’s invigorating during a song, but a little exhausting over the length of an album.

Title: Music For Men
Review: Ditto’s lyrics are still a blend of sex and politics, always delivered with enough passion to fill the dance floor and keep it sweaty.

Title: Tangerine Reef
Review: I have no doubt that Tangerine Reef will be a remarkable experience when paired with its visual stimuli, but without it, it is an album hard to recommend.

Title: Transference
Review: Transference is a good album, just not in league with what's become par.

Title: Souled Out
Review: It’s nice to see Aiko atypically solo (Common provides the only rap feature), but more variety would be welcome.

Title: Worldwide Underground
Review: Some songs are just completely uninspired.... There are definitive highlights on Underground, however, that make this collection essential. [Nov 2003, p.147]

Title: Olympus Sleeping
Review: They’re not reinventing the wheel, but pulling the Harley out of the ditch.

Title: There's a Riot Going On
Review: The pulsing, nodding, whisper-y grooves are a kind of accomplishment, too. Subdued, sure, enveloping and lucidly becalmed, you can float on them like warm salt water, no effort required at all.

Title: Selling Live Water
Review: Bottle of Humans was an amazing album, immediately hailed as a classic. Selling Live Water improves upon that album in every identifiable category.

Title: Heartthrob
Review: By the end, it feels as if Tegan And Sara need to sharpen their edge before they lose their point completely. [Mar 2013, p.110]

Title: CLPPNG
Review: This was, at least until two days ago, the most ambitious and powerful underground hip-hop album to be released this year. But leave it to Death Grips to drop a surprise record on us and steal the spotlight from their fellow Californians. We’ll have to wait before we find out which one stands the test of time, but for the moment, advantage: Clipping.

Title: Jukebox
Review: The journey is less emotionally fraught than her best work, but just as revealing.

Title: Feel That Fire
Review: Having good taste in collaborators and influences doesn't make up for how often Bentley repeats himself here though, and it isn't enough to keep Feel That Fire from being more than a tremendous disappointment.

Title: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love
Review: Ordinary Corrupt Human Love isn't going to change detractors' minds about Deafheaven. Instead, with its searing depictions of emotional and spiritual struggle in a relentlessly ambitious musical presentation, it should attract a new legion of listeners as well as deliver assurance and solace to those who found their earlier records so compelling.

For the most part, it’s the moments that pivot between shadow and light that provide the most pleasure. “L’Inconnue” emerges from its chrysalis around the 1:40 mark, Legrand singing in French as a heavenly choral loop begins to surround her voice. Both musically and lyrically, the development feels closer to the sound of falling in love than anything they’ve made, an ecstatic payoff that ranks among their finest work.

Title: Mr Beast

Title: Something For All of Us

Title: Feel the Sound
Review: For the most part, though, from robotic-but-rambunctious opener "Runaway" to the late-album one-two closing swoon of "It's You" and "Overtaken", Feel the Sound leans on Imperial Teen's puppyish charm and love for soft-rock's smooth bliss.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: Through it all they maintain a charmingly chiming and cheery vibe that's probably the closest humans can get to making elf music.

Title: iridescence
Review: As a highly experimental album, the occasional misfire is a guarantee. Ultimately, Iridescence is an exciting way to start a new trilogy and is a testament to Brockhampton’s perseverance.

Title: As I Call You Down
Review: Fistful of Mercy's sound shouldn't surprise fans of any of those acts; nor, for that matter, should the appealingly casual quality of the nine songs on "As I Call You Down," which the musicians wrote in three days.

Title: Ambulance LTD
Review: There may not be a more carefully crafted debut release this year.

Title: At What Cost
Review: At What Cost is ambitious, slickly-produced, and relies a great deal on live instrumentation. However, where Attention Deficit’s jumbled tracklist smacked of design-by-committee compromise, At What Cost is clearly guided by GoldLink’s vision from start to finish.

Title: The Age of Adz
Review: With The Age Of Adz, Stevens may simply be trying too hard.

Title: Rejoicing In The Hands
Review: Rejoicing in the Hands finds Banhart developing past his early lo-fi recordings in favor of a crisper, more succinct sound that highlights his intricate guitar picking.

Title: Lenses
Review: While this could have been a record defined by atmosphere, the near-absence of energy and long, formless instrumental sections will have listeners tuning out long before it hits any sort of stride.

Title: Puzzle
Review: Puzzle gels the Kinks/Beatles sound the group obviously adores with something less dusty. Think the Sea and Cake playing with the Stone Roses. Or a chartier Belle and Sebastian.

Title: A Rush of Blood to the Head
Review: A stronger, more distinctive album than its predecessor in nearly every respect.

Title: Computer Controlled Acoustic Instruments pt2
Review: It’s an Aphex Twin EP more than just an EP, and as those go it’s very good.

Title: Goodbye Lullaby
Review: Since her production team more or less comes through for her, it's ultimately on Lavigne's slight shoulders that Goodbye Lullaby is such a strident, ineffectual attempt at a serious pop record.

Title: Hurley
Review: If there is a compliment to be paid to Hurley, it is that the band refrains from delving into the sort of WTF territory they've explored of late.

Title: Celebration Rock
Review: Midway through, it's already tiresome to hear the anthemic shouting and seemingly non-stop drum fills. It's a celebratory listen for sure, but one that could do with a breather that shows off this duo's skills. [No.88 p.58]

Title: So There
Review: This album has its dancing shoes straddling very different musical camps and somehow manages to bind them together with skill and personality.

Title: Waiting For Something to Happen
Review: Waiting For Something To Happen, is something both sinister and sweet, dripping with shoegaze guitars and harmonies abound.

Title: The Hazards of Love
Review: It's a far-reaching and ambitious album, stronger than its predecessor and full of gallant wordplay and vivid imagery.

Title: One Day All of This Wonâ€™t Matter Any More
Review: While this album is overall a winner, it’s not revolutionary.

Title: Memorial
Review: The result of this incredible journey, Memorial, is the first landmark post-metal release since Isis’ Panopticon, Russian Circles’ greatest achievement, and unquestioningly one of 2013’s true artistic masterpieces.

Title: Sonic Highways
Review: While the band and management are careful not to peg Sonic Highways as the soundtrack to the cable television series, the Foo Fighters’ eighth studio LP certainly remains a concept album and requires that lens to be appreciated fully.

Title: Nootropics
Review: The panicked sensation of Nootropics gives way to catharsis as the surrealism intensifies to the point at which change is inevitable.

Title: A History of Every One
Review: A History Of Every One deposits its listener right up close, and seemingly the improvisations are adapted to take that into account.

Title: And After That, We Didn't Talk
Review: Even with quick, dense and precisely rhythmic flows, his rapping is like verbal dancing. Its joyous and romantic moments make the album feel more like a thematic refinement than a musical one.

Title: The Physical World
Review: Like its predecessor, The Physical World is crammed with loud, fast, short songs.

Title: Death Magic
Review: The battle between melody and noise at the heart of 'DEATH MAGIC' is a fascinating one, and the twelve songs on which it plays out are damn near bulletproof. Welcome to the most terrifying pop album of 2015.

Title: Let Us Never Speak of It Again
Review: It might take a couple of rotations, but upon spinning Let Us Never Speak of it Again, be prepared to suffer from involuntary dance fits from surfeits of jollity. Asinine lyrics be damned, I’m dancing here.

Title: Sudden Elevation
Review: In close proximity of each other, ‘Call It What You Want’, ‘Perfect’ and ‘Onwards And Upwards’ are a little too timid, each simply brushing against each other with no discernible difference. These are only minor concerns when everything else is as captivating as they are.

Title: Late for Nothing
Review: As eccentric as these tracks are, most of them wind up in a familiar place, with clean vocals ascending to growly, thundery choruses.

Title: The Appeal: Georgia's Most Wanted
Review: But for at least 10 tracks, Gucci is able to sustain a hell of a run, forming perhaps commercial rap's best dispatch this year. There have been, and probably will be, better rap albums this year. But none will be more fun.

Title: â€
Review: It stops short of SMD's effort by quite a way, but it's a fine and much welcome showing for a pair of self-professed amateurs.

Title: Fated
Review: You might only remember the songs with words, but the rest of the album puts those moments in context.

Title: Poison Season
Review: There's nothing bland about this fervid, ideasy album. [Sep 2015, p.90]

Title: rEVOLVEr
Review: By the end of these 17 tracks the head is heavy with images of the Smash robots battle-rapping against a crew from whatever planet The Clangers call home.

Title: No More Drama
Review: In the past, that voice has conveyed untold worlds of pain and anguish, but on Blige's fifth studio album, No More Drama, it's put to good use mining the foreign terrain of happiness, contentment, and other emotions seemingly antithetical to the soul singer's tragedy-filled milieu.

Title: Age Of
Review: All told, Oneohtrix Point Never’s latest album is good, but it’s also his worst ‘proper’ album since his critical breakthrough. In attempting (but not fully committing to) his most accessible release, Age Of doesn’t feel like it’ll go down well with any particular audience.

Title: Let Go
Review: Let Go is an excellent rainy-afternoon album, full of gentle and melancholic beauty, with echoes of Love and the Beach Boys.

Title: A Weekend in the City
Review: This album isn't as brash or immediate as the band's earlier work, but its gradual move from alienation to connection and hope is just as bold as Silent Alarm, and possibly even more resonant.

Title: Neck of the Woods
Review: It feels like a work in progress, skeletally over-precise and over-long.

Title: The Classic
Review: Whether or not The Classic finds that audience, it’s comforting to know that an artist like Joan As Policewoman is still out there to counterbalance the auto-tuned pop tartlets of the music business.

Title: Damita Jo
Review: Smacks of trying too hard.

Title: Band Red
Review: Kaito could be the best band in the world, but Band Red isn't the best album in the world. What it is, though, is a record that shows just how good this band can be when they get it right, even if that isn't all the time.

Title: Lost Highway
Review: This is an exciting new chapter for Bon Jovi. [23 Jun 2007]

Title: Tales of a Grass Widow
Review: Tales Of A Grass Widow won’t alter opinions; if anything it’ll cement them. But for those who enjoy CocoRosie, album number five is every bit as intriguing and fulfilling as they’d hope.

Title: With Strings Live At Town Hall
Review: Only a few moments stand out.

Title: Reflektor
Review: Reflektor is cleaner, sharper and dancier than anything the band have done before.

Title: Burials
Review: Burials is, barring a few missteps, a work of operatic melodrama set to bleak, bold, impeccable hooks. And that’s all it needs to be.

Title: Relax
Review: The production is inconsistent and largely a bit too bombastic for Das Racist's usually free-associative, untechnical rapping.

Title: Hombre Lobo: 12 Songs of Desire
Review: Everett's songwriting hasn't always kept pace with his musical and literary ambitions. But these tales of frustrated desire are vividly sketched, with the Eels delivering muddy roadhouse rockers.

Title: Dust
Review: Dust floats along meditatively, and is Halo’s warmest and most familial record to date. [Jul 2017, p.52]

Title: The House That Jack Built
Review: Certain of her likable idiosyncrasies appear to have been straightened out [since 2009's Hunting My Dress]. But while big, booming choruses bookend the album on Born To and When I'm Asleep, that's about as easy as this listen gets.   [Jul 2012, p.89]

Title: Lost Girls
Review: Like The Bride, there is a common conceptual thread running through these tracks, but unlike that record, there is less effort exerted in shaping them to fit a narrative. The songs are better for it, each unspooling like a miniature movie of its own without the same need to move the story from point A to point B.

Title: Everything Wrong Is Imaginary
Review: A beguiling mix made more loveable by its melancholic core. [Aug 2006, p.100]

Title: Total
Review: Highlights aside, Total's belligerence is as predictable as it is teeth-grinding.

Title: Two Way Monologue
Review: He ends up sounding like a confused Billy Joel.

Title: obZen
Review: They're still crisp and cold--kind of like the Terminator--but somehow unlike Ahnuld, it's possible to hear a human heart beating within the steel. [May 2008, p.138]

Title: Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea
Review: Lookout doesn’t have the feel of a major step forward for the Silver Jews: sonically, it falls pretty comfortably between "Bright Flight" and "Tanglewood" and doesn’t have the sort of big events that marked those two records.

Title: Falling Down a Mountain
Review: On Falling Down a Mountain, the most depressing thing is the sound of Tindersticks going through the motions.

Title: Sylvan Esso
Review: In one way or another, nearly the entire album feels dependable, a true achievement for a duo who are just starting to sow their musical seeds.

Title: The Concrete Confessional
Review: The whole point of Hatebreed has always been to pulverise willing participants with simplicity, power and positivity. In that regard, the furiously precise likes of Seven Enemies and Dissonance amount to jolting shots of pure musical adrenaline.

Title: Giants Of All Sizes
Review: Musically, Giants of All Sizes is richer and stranger than anything they’ve released since their commercial breakthrough. Even when it finally settles back into more comfortable lyrical terrain – My Trouble’s hymning of cosy domesticity, On Deronda Street’s paean to parenthood – the music strays beyond their usual comfort zone: ragged and underpinned by glitchy electronic beats. It suits them out there.

Title: Time To Die
Review: Time to Die bests it as far as consistency goes.

Title: Where The Action Is
Review: Overall, Where the Action Is is another reliably interesting and well-written addition to the band's latter-day renewal.

Title: The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place
Review: Most of all, though, what we find ourselves thinking of when enjoying 'The Earth Is Not A Cold Dead Place' - and, rest assured, readers, it's an enjoyable experience right the way through - is the magical spangliness that elevated the Cocteau Twins from absolutely all of their more ghettoised contemporaries way back when.

Title: PITH
Review: PITH, for all the attention it pays in getting the dressings and staging right, is best when it's replacing one genre's organs with another's, concocting an interesting if beautifully flawed, kind of Frankenstein's Monster.

Title: Horehound
Review: The first half of Horehound is just weird enough to be utterly mesmerizing, a series of ominous, fuzzed-out psycho-blues riffs that climax in the tremendous Rush-meets-Jay-Z rave-up of 'Treat Me Like Your Mother.' But creative disintegration floods the record's latter regions with less captivating bump-'n'-grindhouse grooves.

Title: Quaristice
Review: Not since "LP5" has being impressed been so obviously secondary to enjoyment.

Title: What Now
Review: At its core, What Now is a love letter to music, warts and all. About the romance, the emotional release and the sheer joy it can bring when everything feels so doom-laden.

Title: Memory of a Cut Off Head
Review: His signature restlessness tends to enhance the Oh Sees’ concussion-inducing material; for the past 10+ years, it’s sometimes seemed like the faster Thee Oh Sees produce, the harder they hit. The approach doesn’t work such wonders here.

Title: Tomorrow's Hits
Review: It makes for a focused, solid offering.

Title: Amanda Mair
Review: A wonderful debut from a truly promising singer.

Title: American Dreamer
Review: [A] rich and understated debut brimming with wisdom and heart. [Nov 2015, p.79]

Title: Garden of Delete
Review: Garden of Delete is the exceptional post-performance of the readability conjured in the wake of OPN’s work, and as a result, it critiques experimental culture’s desire to fetishize.

Title: At War with Reality
Review: This is classic ATG with freshness and vigour to spare. [25 Oct 2014, p.54]

Title: Glass Floor
Review: If there's any difference between this album and von Bohlen's lackluster recent output, it's that this collection somehow manages to be even more tepid.

Title: The Cost
Review: "The Cost"... comprises 10 tracks that range from hopeful (but triumphant!) to sorrowful (but triumphant!) to morose (but triumphant!).

Title: Weapons
Review: 'Weapons' has no shortage of big choruses, slick production and crunching riffs but is let down by tired lyrics and too many forgettable songs.

Title: Lateralus
Review: Lateralus could have been released four years ago, for all the sonic progression that's contained (or not contained) within its 79 minutes. [Jul 2001, p.57]

Title: 100 Acres of Sycamore
Review: That warmth you're feeling come its close, try to hold onto it. It's a contentment few albums leave you with.

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: In fine voice and piano, Spektor skips down the yellow-brick road, offering new diversions at every turn. Fun – but the whimsy can be exhausting.

Title: Ritual
Review: What evades White Lies is the candid charm of his Brit-gloom forebears. The sleek synth tunes are more anthemic this time out, but the lyrics are no less overwrought.

Title: Atlas
Review: It's a less daring enterprise overall. [May 2004, p.106]

Title: Hotel California
Review: Hotel California refuses to sort his over-the-top bangers into anything sensible, and without a "Rack City" to make it crossover worthy, this is a full-length to leave for the fans.

Title: Sometimes The Blues Is Just A Passing Bird
Review: Sometimes the Blues Is Just a Passing Bird is still the sound of a man who's totally comfortable in his own skin. You're also likely to find great comfort across these five tracks.

Title: Dark Comedy
Review: Eagle’s skill is in being relatable to the listener, approaching issues that could otherwise be interpreted as controversial with a soft-spoken and melodic flow that never comes off as preachy or aggressive.

Title: FLIGHT
Review: At times the songwriting just doesn't hold up to the inventive production, but there's plenty of ear candy to fill the gaps on this extremely fun LP.

Title: Teenager
Review: All in all, Teenager stands as both a distillation of the band’s strengths and an impressive step forward, and perhaps more importantly, an irony-free, immensely relatable look at the heady emotional extremes of youth.

Title: Coexist
Review: Overall, The xx have created an album that is just as interesting, attractive and sexy as it could possibly be.

Title: Everyday Robots
Review: Everyday Robots signals a sea change in Albarn's oeuvre because it is, ostensibly at least, a work that tackles its creator's origins with something close to sincerity. I say close to, because there are plenty of moments here when the familiar orientalism returns to produce slightly nauseating results.

Title: Americana
Review: It gives us songs more memorable for their grizzly narrations or the occasional doo-wop harmony than the steady performances of mostly standard-format jams.

Title: Radioactive
Review: It seems a huge effort being expended to achieve so little.

Title: Sukierae
Review: A good album is essentially buried here; at least eight songs could comfortably be axed.

Title: Strike Gently
Review: It’s Dire Straits teamed with louche New York cool--a combination that shouldn’t work, but totally does.

Title: No Cities to Love
Review: There's not enough space here to get into why Sleater-Kinney may be one of the most important bands of 2015, but one thing is clear: they've already delivered a serious contender for one of the year's best records.

Title: 22, A Million
Review: While some may sneer at the glitches and production tricks that pepper the record, thinking them mere gimmicks, those who stick around long enough will be rewarded by a string of mature, thoughtful songs emerging from their concealment, gradually revealing a little more of themselves with each play.
This is Adams at his most concise and focused. [Jan 2006, p.122]

Title: Le Noise
Review: Its eight songs containing no masterpieces and Lanois' moody noir production reining in Young's messy signature. So, Le Noise winds up as something elusive and intriguing, a minor mood piece that seems to promise more than it actually delivers.

Title: In Each and Every One
Review: Rochford's creative mix makes the album seem like an integrated, large-scale work, and the overall effect is eerily beautiful.

Title: Have Some Faith In Magic
Review: Bold, colourful and eclectic, 'Have Some Faith' displays a vivid musical palette showcasing a band growing in scope and stature.

Title: Out in the Storm
Review: This is yet another reinvention for Crutchfield, but this is the first time she’s so palpably given off the sense that she’s at peace with her own thoughts: stronger and more candid for having figured out how to best to take care of herself.

Title: Magic
Review: If Magic revisits the subject matter of previous career crests, it unfortunately recalls "The Rising" in its sound: Brendan O'Brien returns to the producer's seat, once again shuffling most of the E Street Band to the music's margins and focusing his attention squarely on the Boss.

Title: Shortly After Takeoff
Review: Shortly After Takeoff is a powerful collection made by someone who’s had to endure more than his fair share of turbulence.

Title: Ecstatics International
Review: A fluorescent, gently psychedelic record with a fat vein of Eighties pop running through it.

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: Spread over a whole CD, there is some worryingly featureless stuff. [Apr 2004, p.102]

Title: Time on Earth
Review: Finn's knack for a melodic ballad remains firmly in place as Time on Earth coasts on his dreamy voice and introspective, hook-laden pop choruses.

Title: Flock
Review: While nothing on Flock will blow the listener away with its originality, there is something about the music that draws you in and captivates. [Winter 2008, p.80]

Title: AIM
Review: If this it to be M.I.A.’s final release, it’s a fittingly confrontational, vibrant and invigorating piece of work.

Title: Jackinabox
Review: Turin Brakes’ expansive and more daring previous work held an encouraging arc that promised risks and excitement, but JackInABox, while a pleasant listen, fails to cash in on that potential, and is unfortunately a step back for the talented duo.

Title: Pala
Review: Friendly Fires are still learning how to control their talents, but boy can they move.

Title: Tara Jane O'Neil
Review: These are songs that brush up against you softly, swirl up around you like a sweet smelling breeze and leave you wistful for things you can’t quite put into words.

Title: Love Story
Review: Your enjoyment of Love Story will directly correlate with the amount that you enjoy Yelawolf’s singing, because boy howdy is there a lot of it here. If you respect Yelawolf’s progression as a musician and wish him luck on his journey to artistic self-actualization, you will be pleased.

Title: The Mosaic of Transformation
Review: Psalms like Smith’s are more than acceptable at face value as restorative, pure-of-heart acts of grace, yet your threshold for bearing this attitude of exceeding amiability may vary.

Title: Break It Up
Review: Pearl and Eatherly don't escape their past entirely on Break It Up, but they're well on their way to waving goodbye to it.

Title: Ships
Review: Smith’s abrupt changes in tempo, volume, and instrumentation are alternately inspiring and disorienting.

Title: Night Music
Review: Bathed in cloaking shadows, Night Music captures the macabre power of darkness, where ordinary shadows are stretched into ominous significance.

Title: Revolutions
Review: Revolutions is pretty breathtaking.

Title: Gone
Review: An adventurous, forward-thinking collection.

Title: Colonia
Review: Colonia is mostly careful to use its expanded palette of sounds for subtle shading rather than gratuitous effect.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: If Modern Vampires of the City makes one thing clear, it's that Vampire Weekend's just getting started here.

Title: Shrink Dust
Review: This album is much more interesting and engaging than Diaper, but just like with that album, the dancey, synth-heavy songs like Airplane's "TMNT Mask" are absent.

Title: Exotic Creatures of the Deep
Review: Exotic Creatures of the Deep is a substantial, if inconsistent treat. Even when they're treading water Sparks still cut it better than most bands half their age.

Title: Aromanticism
Review: Breathtakingly beautiful.

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: What's missing is the innovation that made Viva La Vida so dynamic.

Title: CVI
Review: Royal Thunder ultimately sound like no one but themselves.

Title: Demon City
Review: By seamlessly incorporating disparate collaborations into the fabric of this City, Crampton summons a greater collective strength than they’ve exhibited on their own--and implies that, going forward, her muse could lead her anywhere, with anyone.

Title: Radio Wars
Review: Musically, it's all mid-tempo indie-by-numbers, shimmery enough to accompany an scene of upbeat emotion in Dawson's Creek; yet sufficiently credible, as indie so often is, to provide the soundtrack to a montage of trailers in an advert for a new Film 4 season.

Title: Lianne La Havas
Review: Fans may be disappointed by La Havas' reserved lyricism here, but the femme gem "Sour Flower" and a take on Radiohead's "Weird Fishes" should be enough to compensate. [Jul 2020, p.75]

Title: American Band
Review: The songs on American Band, for the most part, are well constructed, catchy-enough tunes that don’t quite rise into the first rank of the group’s deep and impressive catalog.

Title: We Are Little Barrie
Review: Barrie's wank-free creedo makes for a bright, poppy debut. [20 May 2005, p.77]

Title: Black Radio
Review: This isn't amateur soul or faux hip-hop. But it's not a bold pop record either. It's a kind of compromise, perhaps.

Title: Kingdom of Rust
Review: On Doves’ fourth LP, Kingdom of Rust, the music is more granite than limestone, continuing 2005 album "Some Cities’" move toward cacophonous beauty.

Title: Mourn
Review: Like punk Doogie Howsers, MOURN use intellect and talent beyond their years to muscle their way in amongst the grown-ups and blow them all out of the water.

Title: Motherland
Review: These tunes don't have the big melodic hooks of "Wonder" or "Jealousy," but that doesn't lessen their beauty. [16 Nov 2001, p.172]

Title: Lights and Sounds
Review: The band shows willingness to break form. [22 Jan 2006]

Title: Alive As You Are
Review: Where 2008's 2 was frazzled and powerful, this one feels soporific, moderate, even a little slight. [Sep 2010 p.94]
Sometimes the additional flourish comes from Adele herself, who is a forceful enough singer, so confident with her agony, that she can bend words into new shapes without losing their meaning.

Title: Sule Skerry
Review: Placid moments abound. ... But "Spoot Ebb's" syncopated, Penguin Cafe rhythms indicate choppier waters, and "Flattie," introduce by poet Will Burns, hints at dark, incoming clouds. [Jun 2019, p.27]

Title: Turtleneck & Chain
Review: Parody is hard to sustain. That this follow-up provides so many laughs without flailing around in can-you-top-this? is a tribute to the comedians' musicality and their musician friends' sense of comedy.

Title: Surgery
Review: Somehow, the Warlocks have found the middle ground between the Raveonettes' Wall of Soundesque attack and the Flaming Lips' oddball fixation on love, death and outer space.

Title: Summer 08
Review: Mount remains an exceptional musical craftsman, who continues to shift and change and toy with his formula, which is proven to result in fun listens like Summer 08.

Title: Deftones
Review: Just when new metal seemed utterly played out, Deftones blows open the possibilities.

Title: The Ecology
Review: Fashawn’s sophomore release is a strong follow-up, six years in the making, that hits hard while preaching perseverance.

Title: Rise Up
Review: Unfortunately, the slick, overproduced headbanger music feels anachronistic and wouldn’t seem out of place on a Korn album. While Cypress Hill remains one of the greatest groups of all time, “Rise Up” mostly flops.

Title: Top Ten Hits of the End of the World
Review: There's a subtle psychedelic twist in these phony hits that somehow renders the best of them compulsively listenable. [Oct 2012, p.64]

Title: Stupid Things that Mean the World
Review: This is a beautiful, cohesive album that stirs so many emotions and speaks for itself. It might not be as immediate or as catchy as ADD, but does the most important thing: paving new grounds.

Title: Dragonslayer
Review: It’s another astounding album from a great band and one that we should get much, much more music from for many years to come.

Title: I can feel you creep into my private life
Review: The merger of a furrowed-brow intellect and hip-freeing rhythm has been a Tune-Yards constant since Garbus made her 2009 bedroom recording, “Bird-Brains.” I Can Feel you Creep into my Private Life is both more refined and yet more raw.

Title: Them Crooked Vultures
Review: Homme and Grohl are old hands at this kind of thing--see their excellent Zeppelin homages on the Queens' "Songs for the Deaf." But they definitely seem inspired by Jonesy's presence, and he helps them keep it light.

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: Merrie Land
Review: Rich and accomplished; beautifully played and immaculately conceptualised, Albarn’s latest trip from FitzRoy to Faeroes and back, via Dogger and Dover, is a drizzle-soaked deep-dive into a fractured land and fractured people. One of the quiet highlights of the year.

Title: Zeitgeist
Review: Thanks in part to the presence of Pantera producer Terry Date, this is the Pumpkins' hardest-rocking record ever.

Title: I Hear You
Review: It's not pretty but it's pretty effective, with tracks like "Radiant Mountain Road," "Volume Peaks" and the frantic "Babel" quickly finding a groove and then flogging it to an entertaining death. [Jun 2016, p.69]

Title: Reaching into Infinity
Review: It's hardly a reinvention, but it all adds to the OTT party DragonForce have been throwing for so long. [20 May 2017, p.53]

Title: Romance Is Boring
Review: More serious but still jittery, and not without detritus, this is the album that will decide the longevity of Los Campesinos!.

Title: Making Time
Review: For a project Woon spent four years on, Making Time is a surprisingly breezy listen. It feels a bit slight at times, especially given the lack of variance in tempo, but it’s hard to find much fault with this collection of smart, soulful work.

Title: Eighteen Hours of Static
Review: It's not noise for noise's sake--it's melodic. It's quiet at points, frantic at others. It's dark, it's messy, it's a dank and smelly basement.

Title: Lost in the Glare
Review: One of the most darkly enthralling instrumental records of the year.

Title: Frances The Mute
Review: Discipline is a crucial factor in good progressive rock, and despite Theodore's brilliant drumming, Rodriguez's flashy guitar, and Bixler's lyrical skill, there's very little of that discipline here. [Avg of two scores: 80/40]

Title: Hell Hath No Fury
Review: This time, believe the hype.

Title: Juggernaut: Alpha
Review: No matter how far they push their boundaries, the songs remain catchy. [Feb 2015, p.91]

Title: Sing in a World That's Falling Apart
Review: Some career-catchiest tunes and a lively self-production make Sing an absolute triumph in repositioning. [Mar 2020, p.91]

Title: Ferndorf
Review: It takes the music of Hauschka perhaps into more populist directions, but the experiment and joy still survive.

Title: Azel
Review: Throughout Azel, the mix of the two genres allows for an even greater sense of uplift and collectivism in a music that always carried the communal at its core. [May 2016, p.72]

Title: Oddfellows
Review: While wonderfully idiosyncratic, Oddfellows finds them at their most accessible to date. [Apr 2013, p.95]

Title: Adventure
Review: Despite the odd dreamy detour into girl-group psych-pop, this slender 10-tracker is bulked out with a little too much autopilot retro-kitsch filler. [May 2016, p.79]

Title: Year of the Black Rainbow
Review: Newcomers might well benefit from starting nearer the beginning, but this is one space saga that's worth persevering with. [Jun 2010, p.120]

Title: Chris
Review: It’s a refreshing, empowering record that embraces finding identity in a lack thereof.

Title: Portamento
Review: Everyone loves to reminisce, and we're suckers for well-crafted songs, but we also need to be challenged a little more than this boys.

Title: Impersonator
Review: At times the backdrop is so subtle that the end result is almost like an aria. Elsewhere the tunes deliver more pf a punch. [Jun 2013, p.75]

Title: Ping Pong
Review: The group has meshed all their skills acquired over the years into one vast and varied yet solid structure.

Title: War Stories
Review: The overall atmosphere is grey, too blah and insular to be colorful.

Title: Leave Your Sleep
Review: Leave Your Sleep is easily her most ambitious work, yet because of that welcoming voice, it provides familiarity enough to gather listeners inside this world of sound.

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: While it shares many similarities with the quieter side of their first record, it never quite achieves the same heart-rending beauty we know they're capable of.

Title: Waves Are Universal
Review: At times songs pass by too easily. [Sep 2004, p.104]

Title: Stories from the City, Stories from the Sea

Review: It’s a breathless record, one that threatens to last an eternity--such is the speed and dazzling depth at which James expresses himself.

Title: Seek Magic
Review: If you're the sort of person who can see music--even if you can't, perhaps--this is so colourful.

Title: High
Review: With High, they’ve recorded an almost perfect 30 minutes of indie-punk. There’s no flabbiness, no million-dollar production that adds nothing to the songs, no bloated guitar lines or pointless drum fills and nothing that even comes close to seeming in any way meaningless.

Title: Yellow House
Review: The group... get more expansive--and more pop--on their second album. [Sep 2006, p.102]

Title: Too Much Information
Review: The album feels like a grab-bag of the band’s process, but not a cohesive expression of their craft.

Title: Season High
Review: Like every Little Dragon album, Season High contains several new entries into the band’s essential catalog, but as a whole, it fails to fulfill its potential.

Title: Triple F Life
Review: While there are some highlights on the album, they don't nearly make up for the glaring flaws throughout, the lack of noteworthy lyrics or the redundancy in topics, flows, hooks and beats.

Title: All Across This Land
Review: They play one too many Springsteen cards with the dark “Cadillac Road” (at this point, Bruce pretty much owns any lyrics that revolve around mills shutting down), but the record ends on another strong track, “Across the River.” Taken as a whole, All Across This Land is one of the group’s strongest offerings in years.

Title: Nothing Violates This Nature
Review: At times, this straightforward approach, along with a smoother production sound, strips the Massachusetts quartet of the nuanced breakdowns and guitar leads that made their previous material so captivating.

Title: It's Not Me, It's You
Review: Yet something needs to be said for Allen’s ability to make cursing seem cute, and tunes about giving head sound charming.

Title: God Help The Girl
Review: God Help The Girl has real class. [Jul 2009, p.99]

Title: Where You Go I Go Too
Review: This cosmic suite evokes a steamy union between Vangelis and Santana, and is Lindstrom's strongest work by far. [Oct 2008, p.96]

Title: Glory
Review: A pop album that operates on its own terms, partly thanks to the way the white-hot notoriety of the star at its center allowed her to, after all these years, rule her own pop fiefdom.

Title: Beginners
Review: The world isn't short of observational singer-songwriters, but when the work is of this calibre it's pretty hard to resist. [Aug 2020, p.107]

Title: Tattoos
Review: All said and done, Tattoos is a pleasant album with some bright moments as well as some average ones.

Title: July Flame
Review: July Flame is a sparser effort than some of Veirs' past releases, and while there is no shortage of quality songs here, some of the most winning moments comes when the arrangements are a bit denser. [Holiday, 2009, p.77]

Title: Jay Stay Paid
Review: This might be the last material we hear from Dilla that echoes the endlessly fascinating turn his music was taking before his passing, and it couldn’t be constructed more appealingly, its jittery creativity augmented by one of Dilla’s esteemed contemporaries, himself a fan and close friend.

Title: Thr33 Ringz
Review: Thr33 Ringz shows what sets T-Pain apart. He's an inventive producer, enveloping radio-friendly hooks in Auto-Tune wackiness.

Title: The Beautiful Lie
Review: Harcourt’s sound might not suit everyone’s taste (it’s fairly dramatic), but to those who are taken with well-sung, introspective piano ballads and gloriously cascading anthems about Love and Death, The Beautiful Lie will in no way disappoint.

Title: how i'm feeling now
Review: Brimming with the prickling anxiety and stress that’s become commonplace during the pandemic, as well as the comfort Charli XCX has found in a strengthened relationship, it’s a glorious, experimental collection.

Title: Soft
Review: With his inoffensive voice and inoffensive beats (surprisingly so, considering their producers), Bodan does, if only for a brief time, achieve something exciting and intimat

Title: Humbug
Review: Humbug is another intriguing step in the evolution of Britain's most exciting guitar band.

Title: In Colour
Review: An emotive, emphatic and often joyous collection of music that plays equally for the head and the heart.

Title: Fantasies
Review: Fantasies is not only a top notch record that effectively picks up where Metric left off at "Live it Out," but with a sense of genuineness that some of the band's contemporaries have lost.

Title: Classics
Review: While sometimes Classics sees the group straying from their conceptual center, it’s never without Ratatat’s unmistakable identity and indelible gentle humor.

Title: This Island
Review: They just sound cranky here, and their beats are mostly perfunctory. [Nov 2004, p.137]

Title: The Bloom and the Blight
Review: Everything is invigorated by both the quality of songwriting and singer Adam Stephen's wrenching trouble-he's-seen vocals. [Nov 2012, p.108]

Title: Steam Days
Review: It's clear that if he wants to, he could easily command proceedings alongside his pals Walls and Four Tet. [Sep 2012, p.75]

Title: Convivial
Review: For its lack of rush-inducing highs and novel sounds, the album is immensely pleasurable, with fleet keyboard vamps and percussive effects that stab and flick ricocheting off pliant, bounding basslines.

Title: Detroit 2
Review: Big Sean makes “Detroit 2” a real and righteous place, even if he has to use a handful of holy clichés to prove it.

Title: Under the Blacklight
Review: This band brings a grubby beauty to a sound imbued with the insidious durability of the Buckingham-Nicks Fleetwood Mac. [Sep 2007, p.105]

Title: Left
Review: A monumental, spectacular achievement.

Title: Gorilla Manor
Review: At first listen that seems off-- the chops and compositional sense here are the most immediately impressive part of the album. But dig deeper and you realize Local Natives never lose sight of the pleasures of being a youthful rock band-- right down to themes of wanderlust and discovery.

Title: Welcome Home
Review: Coziness certainly has its appeal--it works as balm and a tonic--but it's hard to shake the feeling that Zac Brown Band overplays their hand somewhat by insisting they've reconnected with their roots. All those lyrics feel calculated and defensive, undercutting the grace of the music.

Title: Eyes Open
Review: Snow Patrol are poised to eclipse Coldplay as pop's greatest anthem-makers.

Title: Riot On An Empty Street
Review: Weak. [Sep 2004, p.140]

Title: The Invisible Man
Review: Eitzel does doomed introspection with more wit than the average bear, however, and more tunefully, too.

Title: Criminal
Review: In Criminal, Luis Vasquez has constructed an album dark and bleak in nature, an exploration that sees him turn his attention to creating hard hitting industrial rock in order to deal with all he's lived through. It's a record of which he can be proud.

Title: UN
Review: ((Un)) is a very impressive first record that shows tons of promise. If Black can keep the right amount of wonky in his pop, he could do something truly wonderful.

Title: The Civil Wars
Review: Whereas the debut evidenced White and Williams' exquisite knack for singing together, the set was somewhat heavy on ballads that sounded like they were made to soundtrack television dramas. The Civil Wars corrects this both in the song selection and in the way the compositions are delivered.

Title: Gunnera
Review: Gunnera is bound to appeal more to Menomena fans than to casual fans of the National, but while it's unconventional, it's even more so enthralling, loaded with worthwhile atmospheres and grooves.

Title: Fall Be Kind
Review: The new EP contains some of their strongest material to date. [Holiday 2009, p.82]

Title: Plumb
Review: Some of the straighter songs can seem a little underwhelming – for example, A Prelude to Pilgrim Street is a decidedly flat glam blowout. But such lacklustre moments are few.

Title: Turn Up the Quiet
Review: Krall has a definite vision for Turn Up the Quiet--she wants to keep things smoky and subdued, a record for the wee hours--and the end result is so elegant, it seems effortless.

Title: Libra Scale
Review: Libra Scale is a tighter, more sophisticated and compelling album that borrows not just MJ's swoony-smooth melodies, but also his taste for roleplay.

Title: Saturday Night Wrist
Review: The Deftones' fifth album turns the dial to "statesmen." [Dec 2006, p.172]

Title: Interiors
Review: The way Mesirow balances all of Interiors' concepts and sounds into songs this streamlined and appealing makes it even more akin to a marvel of modern architecture; it feels intuitive and effortless, even if it most likely wasn't to create it.

Title: Hairless Toys
Review: It's never clear where these songs are going, but the result always satisfies.

Title: Brain Candy
Review: While Brain Candy does lose creative steam towards the back end, there's still plenty here on offer for those looking for a reprieve from the oppressive reality of day-to-day life in 2020.

Title: Silencio
Review: Contrary to the urgency of the title, Silencio! is more intermission than showstopper. [No.89, p.59]

Title: British Road Movies
Review: While British Road Movies can’t quite match the shock of the new provided by The Long Blondes’ early material, it’s a strong and confident comeback, and better than we’d any right to expect from someone who hasn’t been involved in an album release for over eight years.

Title: Mountaintops
Review: This album is infectious.

Title: High Society
Review: Enon inhabit a multi-coloured Seventies soaring pop universe but with... emphasis on crunching guitar breaks, electronic textures and skewed lyrics. [Sep 2002, p.118]

Title: Contra
Review: On their second LP, the youngsters don't disappoint.

Title: Slick Dogs and Ponies
Review: Though more adventurous than 2005's "The Best Little Secrets Are Kept," the band's sophomore LP, Slick Dogs and Ponies, still rings soulless at its core.

Title: Tookah
Review: Tookah is a frustrating album because there are a couple examples of something fantastic happening in Torrini’s musical mind but it doesn’t quite deliver in the end.

Title: Aphrodite
Review: The entire album has the sonic consistency of cotton candy: It won't exactly give you a headache, but it could leave you with a stomachache.

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: At least five of these songs [out of twelve] should've remained on the cutting room floor.

Title: Lesser Evil
Review: Like a good new party drug, Lesser Evil finds a sweet spot more often than not if you let it.

Title: Vulnicura
Review: Björk’s most fully realised, accessible record in years.

Title: Giver Taker
Review: Whereas their earlier material veered towards melodic art-rock, the music on Giver Taker sounds radically gentle and confident.

Title: Saint Bartlett
Review: But for all the sonic changes and glimmers of hope, the best stuff here still sounds like boilerplate Jurado. Swift's production is at its best when it adds subtle atmospherics to the fragile melody of "Kansas City," or the dusty flourishes to the chorus of "Harborview."

Title: In This Light & On This Evening
Review: In This Light And On This Evening is a weak, ill conceived and uninspiring effort.

Title: Street Songs of Love
Review: Hints of glam and punk inform the rootsy proceedings, giving these alternately gritty and lyrical songs a satisfying glow.

Title: Combat Sports
Review: Combat Sports is their shortest album yet, with none of its 11 tracks straying over four minutes, all in bursts of compact energy. Each song has a short guitar solo, while riffs and hooks abound, in stories of combative love and sex couched in Young’s characteristically wry lyrics.

Title: Sondre Lerche
Review: The combination of intelligent and punchy songs, the sympathetic production, and Lerche's winning vocals make this a strong follow-up to Heartbeat Radio and further proof that Lerche doesn't need to mess around trying different things to keep people interested.

Title: Amygdala
Review: The root vibe is elegant techno minimalism, but that vibe is augmented with wildly eccentric detailing.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Review: Pure indie-pop to hold close to your heart.

Title: Wild Light
Review: This is an ambitious, cohesive effort from the Sheffield band, and its complex and spacious sound is both beautifully engaging and highly rewarding.

Title: Black Rainbows
Review: Nearly twenty years on from Suede's debut and he sounds pretty much unchanged.

Title: On Triple Beams
Review: On Triple Beams' marriage of the Dead Milkmen's irreverence and Wire's brilliant, repetitive simplicity makes the album one that will definitely scratch the itch for any punk fan, and will make a quick fan out of anyone not already on board with Tyvek's grinding punk goodness.

Title: Precious Art
Review: While there are unmistakable comparisons to bands like PUP and The Dirty Nil abound, Precious Art rolls on to mesh together a lot of influences while still standing on its own, carving out an identity that's as distinct as it is loud and catchy.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: Sounds miraculously unburdened by its conceptual weight.[Dec. 2011 p. 90]

Title: Slowdive
Review: This new one sounds happily like a distillation of the best of Slowdive. The effects--and the effects pedals--are still dreamy. [No. 143, p.61]

Title: Wanderer
Review: Marshall allows Wanderer to be about lots of things at once: such life-altering instances as motherhood and death as well as plentifully covered topics like love and relationships. Cat Power has stumbled at times during her lengthy and storied career, but on Wanderer, she gracefully lands on all four feet.

Title: Matangi
Review: Matangi is the best M.I.A. album since at least Kala.

Title: Garden Ruin
Review: Calexico have abandoned much of the jazzy, mariachi-infused Americana pulses that characterized their former sound.

Title: Real Gone
Review: Much of Real Gone has been stripped so bare instrumentally that its heavy accumulation of rhythmic noise -- manipulated groans and grunts (“Metropolitan Glide”) what sounds like a cracking horsewhip (“Don’t Go Into The Barn”) -- establishes a sustained, bristling mood that electrifies particular songs but bogs down the album as a whole.

Title: Dua Lipa
Review: Despite a few generic offerings (No Goodbyes is mostly just the singer breathily uttering the words “don’t go back” on loop), this is a solid pop debut that is high on summery nonchalance.

Title: Our Ill Wills
Review: At times, Shout Out Louds sounds like a bunch of former high-school band geeks trying to recreate their record collections. And on songs like the wistful, vaguely tropical 'South America,' they sound like they're in a cavernous lecture hall, describing how they spent their summer vacation.

Title: Built from Scratch
Review: With no new scratches, no innovations, and an abuse of mere battle scratches, the X-ecutioners overcompensate for their overall lack of creativity by cluttering tracks with constant restatements of reaffirmation, forcing even credible MCs to become pawns of the ornamental obsession to their own greatness.

Title: Helplessness Blues
Review: The result is almost laughably beautiful.

Title: Luck
Review: Over it all, Vek free-associates with the kind of bland monotony which serves his music--and these times--surprisingly well. [Jul 2014, p.83]

Title: Golden Era
Review: Golden Era is hit or miss, but thankfully it's more of the former than the latter.

Title: Soul is Heavy
Review: The songs themselves, delivered via polished neo-soul and roots-reggae arrangements, seldom push beyond the retro comfort zone. [Apr 2012, p.98]

Title: YU
Review: YU is a swagger drenched, masterful treatise from a woman with a new perspective, new weapons, and the confidence to use them.

Title: Altered State
Review: This is the sound of TesseracT getting even better. [25 May 2013, p.54]

Title: Wizard Bloody Wizard
Review: Conceived in antithesis to the tediously technically proficient metal that’s abundant these days, EW’s ninth album takes joy-doom to another level. Their riffs match the fuzziness of their weed-fogged minds.

Title: I Heard It Today
Review: The production throughout is more soulful and seamless than on previous efforts.

Title: I Love You, It's Cool
Review: With its bright spots marred by detachment, despondency, and meandering, I Love You, It's Cool fails to deliver on the promise of Beast Rest Forth Mouth, knocking Bear in Heaven back a tier or two in the race for indie electro-pop supremacy.

Title: Honeymoon
Review: Whereas her last album had a gently psychedelic and live-off-the-floor feel, Honeymoon plays it safer with “cinematic” arrangements occasionally pumped up (but not excessively so) with modern drum sounds.

Title: Hyacinths and Thistles
Review: Picking up where Wasp’s Nest left off, Hyacinths and Thistles finds Merritt constructing a complex sonic playground in which a host of guest vocalists have come to frolic. While the songs might initially be Merritt’s, each vocalist manages to transform each piece into something uniquely personal.

Title: All Aboard The Skylark
Review: This is no means a case of Brock and co serving up space rock comfort food to the faithful. But at the same time the final, nine-minute The Fantasy Of Faldum would be welcomed onto any Hawkwind album of the last 40 years. [Nov 2019, p.80]

Title: UNLOCKED
Review: The Denzel Curry x Kenny Beats team up is a master-class of hip hop — few artists in today's landscape have the talent and longevity to consistently deliver good music. Thankfully, Denzel Curry is one of those few.

Title: Sempiternal
Review: They've long threatened to make an album that would propel them to metal's major league. This might be it. [Jun 2013, p.95]

Title: The Haunted Man
Review: This effort is laudable, but she sounds best when pushing the envelope. A lively talent like hers shouldn't be so concealed.

Title: Let's Wrestle
Review: There’s little to get excited about here--there’s no wheel reinventing, no formula shake-up, no scrawling outside any boxes... it’s just pleasant, familiar indie-rock that verges on wishy-washy.

Title: Shaker Notes
Review: Marrying a bewildering array of influences, Shaker Notes presents a probing, unified voice on what could well be White’s finest album to date.

Title: Ohms
Review: Arguably, Ohms is at first blush nothing new for Deftones. What it is is an engrossing refinement of what they’ve become over years of risk-taking and experimentation.

Title: Anthems
Review: They deserve credit for writing and performing confidently with such specificity, but they also deserve some derision for failing to even attempt straying from the pack. Anthems is a good entry into a genre that still offers better.

Title: The Bloom and the Blight
Review: The Bloom and the Blight builds on the band's strengths and successfully maintains their idiosyncrasies, offering persuasive evidence that they are more than ready to step up a level themselves.

Title: Arc
Review: There are songs here that comprise bite-size fragments of multifarious melodies, drawing on myriad influences. But there are also tracks that sustain one tune and tempo over the duration, where previously only three or four would do.

Artist: Thao & the Get Down Stay Down
Title: We The Common
Review: It’s the witty and indirect way Thao and her band approaches the subjects in these songs that makes We The Common a minor delight.

Title: Marauder
Review: Marauder is a solid record with several decent tracks that will make it a welcome addition to the group's discography.

Title: Elytral
Review: Elytral lacks the sort of direction or structure that linger in the mind, but has a delightful exploratory freedom, as seen in the sweet, warm analogue ambience of Surprise Yourself.

Title: Passionoia
Review: The endless Anglophilia gets boring, especially when Pulp, Blur and the Auteurs have all done it better. [#61, p.86]

Title: Faded Gloryville
Review: Based on recording location alone the varied musical approach to these 10 cuts veers from straight country, to rockabilly, R&B, rootsy rock and even some pop, all connected by Ortega’s trilling, bittersweet, instantly recognizable vocals.

Title: Breakup Song
Review: No-wave krunch meets mutant disco shuffle meets snippets of global radness and, yeah, it's better than Animal Collective's new one.

Title: Simulation Theory
Review: Simulation Theory seems to fall into two territories--songs are either half-hearted nods to the best of their heavier rock-opera back catalogue, or futuristic, electronic pop-heavy tracks that borrow from bands more adept at that particular sound, and the vast majority of which are burdened with Bellamy’s political paranoia. For a new listener, it’s baffling. For a former, diehard fan, it’s disappointing.

Title: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy
Review: With My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy, Kanye West transgresses paradigms and defies the limitations of genre, thusly granting himself the highest compliment payable to an artist.

Title: Deep Fantasy
Review: hite Lung sound absolutely enormous on Deep Fantasy, and it's a testament to their stamina and technical abilities that they just do not let up on the pace.

Title: Oracular Spectacular
Review: It's a confident debut, one that features two young musicians reveling in their abilities and perhaps discovering ones they didn't know they had.

Title: Strange Dreams
Review: He's able to tap into the dark side of slackerdom without losing sight of what makes a permanent-daydream lifestyle so seductive, allowing Strange Dreams to work as both a subversive take on millennial indie's chilled-out obsessions and an album of simple pop pleasures.

Title: The Haunted Man
Review: It's safe to say that Natasha Khan has once again managed to craft an album that ticks all the boxes, while also showing a maturity and evolution from her Mercury nominated sophomore album.

Title: Happenstance
Review: Her writing can be exceptional.

Title: Movement in Still Life
Review: Looking for fresh inspiration, he relocated to Los Angeles for this third album, embarking on some musical revisions that will surprise even long-time fans.

Title: Mas Amable
Review: Cohesive and seamless, Mas Amable reaches the heart of the rhythm and the soul of the drum, aspiring to a meditative quality and tranquility that almost feels sacred.

Title: The Coincidentalist
Review: The resemblances don’t work on every song as Gelb takes some radical turns into experimental jazz and country rock that recall Charles Mingus and Neil Young more than literary Cohen, but on the whole this is the best Leonard Cohen album by someone other than Cohen himself in decades.

Title: Victory Shorts
Review: Victory Shorts is an assured, confident, and quite often brilliant album by a band that is clearly influenced by the past but never falls prey to easy nostalgia.

Title: Diotima
Review: It's strange how something so seemingly dense and difficult to fully comprehend upon first listen can be so structurally simple, each instrument clearly defined. It's one of the most fascinating aspects of this peculiar, paradoxical band, and it's something that will keep listeners riveted every time they put out new material.

Title: Learn to Live
Review: If you consider Darius Rucker's bajillion-selling voice something of an old friend, Learn to Live is worth a listen. Otherwise? Meh.

Title: Nouns
Review: Nouns showcases the appealing joy to No Age's process, the band attacking its music with relish and humor.

Title: Imaginary Man
Review: Imaginary Man presents Baxter and his material in a manner that's vividly passionate and a little swampy while avoiding cliches as he offers these sketches on life and love in the American South; it's a big step forward for Baxter, and will hopefully help him gain the audience he deserves.

Title: Young Modern
