Review: Young Modern is a highly ambitious work that happily jumps from glam rock to sweeping orchestral pastiches and almost everywhere in between.

Title: Sonik Kicks
Review: Sonik Kicks is a good record, but it doesn't have the songwriting depth and range of its two predecessors, and as admirable as it is that Weller is still playing with his formula and searching for something new to do with it, the electronics here do the songs few favors.

Title: The Hardest Way to Make an Easy Living
Review: While it can tend toward the tuneless, the upside is language that differs plenty from a Jay-Z or Eminem but stands beside them in terms of power--a flow that, once you get used to it, becomes its own form. [May 2006, p.110]

Title: Lines, Vines and Trying Times
Review: It’s a bricolage of genres, so bent on embracing a variety of musical forms that it sometimes borders on parody.

Title: 'Sno Angel Like You
Review: An immensely pleasing and happy album.

Title: A Grand Don't Come For Free
Review: 'A Grand Don't Come For Free' is proof that 'Original Pirate Material' wasn't a happy fluke.

Title: It's a Bit Complicated
Review: Here and there,  Complicated sets up some promising scenarios—worrying about a platonic friend's reaction to a mix tape, or trying to initiate sex for the sake of outdoing a girlfriend's exes—but they never pan out.

Title: North
Review: While North is a far cry from Darkstar's previous releases, it's a nice addition to the world of electronica. This album sets the duo apart from their label mates, but retains the dark atmosphere that Hyperdub artists are known for.

Title: Saint Cecilia EP
Review: The tunes on Saint Cecilia--the patron saint of music, as any Art Garfunkel fan will tell you--were largely assembled from past albums’ cutting floors. The title track crawls towards wholeness on the lovely vocal meld of Grohl and Kweller.... Meanwhile, “Iron Rooster” is a bone-tired dragger that’s probably of recent vintage but could date back to Down on the Upside.

Title: Other Worlds
Review: A lush, shimmering and fully immersive experience. [Nov 2012, p.90]

Title: Trust
Review: Amateurish, but defiantly unperturbed, this is a grave and momentous listen.

Title: 50 Words for Snow
Review: The singer does a lot of luxuriating on her 10th album; 50 Words for Snow spreads seven songs over 65 leisurely minutes, her multi-octave voice and piano mostly at the forefront.

Title: Fetch
Review: Each song on Fetch feels so meticulous and so conscientiously crafted, it's hard to listen to it without arriving at a cliched but undeniable truism: good things come to those who wait.

Title: Between Two Shores
Review: It's a decent record, even good. But am I going to be able to remember any of these songs in two months without playing them first? Experience says probably not.

Title: Object 47
Review: Even when the Wire slow way down, their densely layered riffs reward wall-shaking volumes. [Oct 2008, p.83]

Title: Starfire
Review: Jaga Jazzist's music has never been shy on the intellectual front, and for those willing to take the plunge, Starfire's innate intricacies leave as much to be discovered as the skies themselves.

Title: This Is Happening
Review: In it’s complete scope, the album contains all the master works we’re usually too scared to expect from a full-length these days.

Title: Moondagger
Review: There's nothing here that sounds di?erent to the countless other acts doing the same thing: there's nothing otherworldly about being so quotidian.

Title: The Ecstatic
Review: The Ecstatic feels like the album Mos has always wanted and intended to make. It's experimental and progressive without being too left-field and isolating.

Title: Loma
Review: Loma is also the product of atypical conditions, written and recorded as the marriage of two of its members was dissolving. The trio seem to have leaned in to that situation: Loma captures the intimacy of such heightened circumstance with layered, compelling nuance.

Title: Taking Chances
Review: The laborious 16-track record purportedly finds the queen of adult contemporary-turned-Vegas attraction taking chances by modernizing her treacly power ballad sound with lots of overdubbed guitars and of-the-moment collaborators.

Title: Achin' and Shakin'
Review: Bundy's music may not always sound like that of country legends like Parton or Loretta Lynn, but she shares with those women a clear understanding of how to create both well-crafted music and an artistic persona over the course of a set of songs.

Title: Hot Thoughts
Review: It doesn’t always work, not least in ‘Shotgun’’s iffy mix of Nashville-ready instrumentals and a chugging house beat. On the flipside, ‘Do I Have To Talk You Into It’ sticks so stubbornly to the Spoon template it could be a discarded number from any of their previous records.

Title: Caveman
Review: It's the first release for the band as an “all in” musical endeavor and it definitely feels that way.

Title: Down in the Weeds Where the World Once Was
Review: As with the best of Bright Eyes, there’s a bittersweet meeting of macabre words and folky tunefulness.

Title: Start and Complete
Review: At the end of the day, Start and Complete is hardly essential listening, but it is what it is: a dalliance.

Title: Asleep In The Back
Review: Not many of the expansive, leisurely songs on Asleep In The Back stick in the memory once they've ended, but they swoon nicely. [Mar 2002, p.127]

Title: Hollywood's Bleeding
Review: Besides a few questionable features, there’s nothing offensive or particularly bad about Hollywood’s Bleeding. It’s just Malone playing it safe and betting on the likelihood that the streaming algorithms will reward him once again.

Title: Music For Men
Review: There's nothing really to grab them: too many of the songs seem a little underweight. It may be that 'Heavy Cross' is enough to save the Gossip from indie one-hit-wonderdom, but there's no escaping the fact that Music for Men doesn't do the thing it really needs to.

Title: Sukierae
Review: If quality control on Sukierae sometimes sags amid the fecundity, all is forgotten when Jess Wolfe and Holly Laessig of Brooklyn-based new lights Lucius help gild country-folk standouts Wait For Love and Nobody Dies Anymore with calm-yet-striking backing vocals. [Oct 2014, p.94]

Title: Inner Fire
Review: Inner Fire is a showcase for the Souljazz Orchestra's depth and experience.

Title: Channel Orange
Review: While Ocean's artistic ambition is impressive, it's his haunting candour that really casts a spell. [Sep 2012, p.106]

Title: Baby I'm Bored
Review: We don't dislike anything on here, and each time we listen, we like what we hear even more.

Title: Tempest
Review: Tempest is Dylan's best musical album of this century, a vibrant maximising of strict rules and the savaged-leather state of that voice. [Oct 2012, p.84]

Title: Conceived in Sewage
Review: Guttural, brutal, and very unpleasant. [Mar 2013, p.101]

Title: Whistle Down the Wind
Review: She doesn’t shy away from political protest, but she’s careful to couch her dissent in the personal and the compassionate.

Title: The Scene Between
Review: Kaleidoscopic yet reassuringly familiar to '80s indie fans. [Apr 2015, p.98]

Title: Self Help Serenade
Review: The rich pop melodies and soft psychedelic touches of songs like "Empty Room" and "Waves" remind us of Coldplay and Grandaddy.

Title: Soft Control
Review: For an album which features a list of impressive producers, it feels though one of them should have worked on the album as a whole to give Soft Control cohesion and the platform for Welsh to jump from.

Title: I Am... Sasha Fierce
Review: While an interesting concept, neither CD contains enough strong material to match up to either of her previous releases, and at times, the constant barrage of R&B cliches and adult-contemporary production make it sound like Beyonce is rapidly transforming from hot, hip pop goddess to your standard bored diva.

Title: That Lucky Old Sun
Review: "But now I'm back." And he is, with his finest non-"Smile" album since the golden age of the Beach Boys. Lucky us.

Title: 200 Million Thousand
Review: Grimy and disheveled, clever and infectious, it's a sloppy heap of classic pop, psychedelic haze, spastic rock, and teenage disaffection mixed to lo-fi imperfection in some kid's filthy garage.

Title: The Devil, You + Me
Review: It seemed as if they'd perfected the balance of 2002's glowing "Neon Golden," but here manage to continue the evolution. [July 2008, p.108]

Title: Cruel Summer
Review: It's exactly what everyone expected this much hyped album to be like. We all guessed the Jay-Z appearance and a Wu-Tang member outshining the other acts on show. We all expected insane feats of arrogance... But don't get me wrong, it's a good album.

Title: Resistance Is Futile
Review: They sound revitalised by the radiance of these songs, liberated from the heavy burden of being the Manic Street Preachers. [May 2018, p.102]

Title: Magic
Review: Magic is a sturdy, sure-footed Bruce Springsteen album.

Title: Odeon
Review: Sticking with a winning formula can be commendable, but this is pales in comparison with past glories.

Title: Holy Ghost!
Review: Unfortunately, over 10 tracks, the band's musical limitations become ever more obvious, with songs like Hold My Breath and Jam for Jerry rummaging through the same box of retro tricks to lessening effect.

Title: Hold Time
Review: Bringing out the too-often buried pop nuances of his stylish songs and new inventions from his under-rated guitar work, it's a stylistic cloth that Ward seems very comfortable wearring. [Mar 2009, p.111]

Title: Father, Son, Holy Ghost
Review: Girls' have traded their early work's immediacy for something that requires more patience but goes much deeper if you've got the time.

Title: Language
Review: Language could afford to lose a few numbers--particularly the low-energy likes of ‘Body’ and ‘Girlfriend’--but there’s more than enough evidence here that MNEK is a potent force in his own right.

Title: Tambourine
Review: She can sound brand-new and busted-down in the same verse, and she sings like a guitar player. [Oct 2004, p.120]

Title: Extraordinary Machine
Review: In a genre hardly noted for springing surprises on its listeners, Extraordinary Machine sounds like a real achievement: however torturous the gestation, it seems worthwhile.

Title: Love and Distance
Review: The tempos drag, the lyrics are nothing special, the electronics nothing much to care about. Instead of sounding like the teenage spawn of My Bloody Valentine and Mouse on Mars, now they sound like Radiohead's very earnest cousin.

Title: Leaders Of The Free World
Review: Leaders of the Free World is a bit more rock & roll than not, with guts and heart, because Elbow have finally embraced their powerful, surrounding space this time out.

Title: Suddenly
Review: Suddenly finds Snaith in his element, writing beautifully endearing tunes and setting them to multi-layered production in a way only he can, and the results are spectacular.

Title: Slowdive
Review: This is an album comfortably on a par with the work of most of the younger artists they’ve influenced; compelling proof that the original shoegazers have stood the test of time remarkably well.

Title: Wildflower
Review: It's all too dull to make anyone care but Crow.

Title: Lonerism
Review: It may not break much new ground, certainly not for instrumentation or other reasons given, but it's one of the most solid albums all year.

Title: Chain Gang of Love
Review: Like a leather whip encased in a spun sugar cage, it is simultaneously deeply sexy yet innocent. And it’s that push-pull tension that keeps this album yanked together tighter than a PVC miniskirt.

Title: Big Black Coat
Review: Big Black Coat works best when the music is as committed to frenzied, all-consuming libidinousness as the lyrics, and on those grounds, it’s a surprisingly successful reinvention for the duo: one that feels more in line than recent efforts with the strengths (if not the tones) of their earliest material.

Title: SMiLE
Review: The end result is a great album, albeit one more lighthearted than its myth would suggest.

Title: Un Dia
Review: The organic lushness should please indie-pop fans reluctant to embrace synth music, while the emphasis on sound instead of structure holds appeal for fans of loop music who’ve grown bored of its now-familiar tropes.

Title: Metals
Review: What a beautiful record. Truly gorgeous, the kind that wins both hearts and awards--perfect for a dinner party, a drive along Pacific Coast Highway, or a good, healthy cry.

Title: Mission Bell
Review: Lee is so commanding that guests Lucinda Williams and Willie Nelson are drawn into top-of-the-range duets and still don't take over. [Feb 2011, p.96]

Title: Dirty Dancing
Review: It's that very punk rock-gone-underground-dance spirit that separates Swayzak's latest from the more rudimentary electro-art pack. [Oct 2002, p.98]

Title: Oblivion with Bells
Review: You get what sounds like Karl Hyde doing freestyle slam poetry overtop of dull beats on 'Ring Road.' 'Crocodile' starts off promising but then gives up and becomes a backdrop for a one-syllable nightclub with white sofas.

Title: Crayons
Review: Some of her tunes are more steady than sizzling, but when she taps into the likes of the soaring, synthesizer-driven 'I'm a Fire,' her smart combination of rich personality and kinetic energy invites a trip to the dance floor.

Title: American VI: Ain't No Grave
Review: There are none of the folk-alt-rock karaoke selections of previous American discs on American VI: Ain't No Grave, just 10 wholly appropriate picks that speak to the gravity of ?Johnny Cash's situation and his joy?in both life and death.

Title: Love Sign
Review: For a record that never tries to be anything more than a fun rock 'n' roll adventure, Love Sign strolls out unscathed.

Title: Tromatic Reflexxions
Review: The fact that neither side needs the other is why Tromatic Reflexxions works so obscenely well.

Title: Thing of the Past
Review: Thing of the Past show how much Cabic and his band know and love about the folk tradition, and that they’ve clearly got the chops to be an integral part of it.

Title: Everything Is Love
Review: Beyoncé impressively matches her superstar rapper husband in terms of lyrical swagger, rhythmic flow and verbal bounce. That she does it to a backdrop of samples constructed around her own extraordinary singing lends the record's mantric grooves the luxurious sheen of high-end pop.

Title: Lie Down in the Light
Review: At times the Crosby, Stills & Nash-­inspired harmony bits come off slightly overbaked, but if Oldham is angling for a summery feel-good sound that will go down well with Americana fans without alienating his sad sack indie rock fans, I’d say he knocked it out of the park.

Title: Britney Jean
Review: At a mere thirty-six minutes, it’s not a stretch to see Britney Jean as a half-baked effort, more of a commitment to be completed and shipped off than the labor of love it was touted as.

Title: Saturation III
Review: Whilst the initial surprise felt on the original ‘Saturation’ may have subsided, the erratic excitement and experimentation on that album has been executed more confidently on each subsequent chapter. The LA group are everything progressive rap music should be; forward thinking, energetic and perhaps most importantly, exciting.

Title: Ride The Black Wave
Review: By the end, listeners will feel like they've been laying out in the sun all day, warm in the glow of the Donkeys' heartfelt love for all things Cali, complete with the sound of washing waves and seagull cries.

Title: Passerby
Review: It's Randell's lovely voice, full and rounded but never overused, that gives the album its potency.

Title: Positive Songs for Negative People
Review: Rarely has such optimism sounded quite bereft of inspiration. Frankly, negative people have a right to more inventive positivism than this.

Title: Just Because
Review: There are plenty of cherishable moments to be savoured. [Jan 2015, p.96]

Title: Olympic Girls
Review: Set to music that looks toward new horizons, Olympic Girls is a gentle study into freedom’s precariousness. The quest can be exhausting and frustrating, but, here, Tiny Ruins relish its brief embrace.

Title: The Messenger
Review: As a vocalist and songwriter, Miller is in solid form here, though as with most of his solo work, this lacks a bit of the heart and soul he brings to the Old 97's. But The Messenger has a stronger individual personality that most of Miller's solo work, and he and Sam Cohen make a good team in the studio.

Title: The Naked Truth
Review: All in all, The Naked Truth is a great musical and lyrical effort, as well as a timely response to the media and the peanut gallery.

Title: Walking On A Dream
Review: His latest spin-off project sees Steele's musical wanderlust pay dividends. [Mar 2009, p.98]

Title: Unleashed
Review: Most of the time he sounds like a pipsqueak trying to play grown-up--a Lothario whose pickup lines land, time after time, with a thud.

Title: Oracular Spectacular
Review: Though the record is slightly front-loaded, there's nary a dud to be found here. [Winter 2008, p.86]

Title: Ghil
Review: Whichever end of her spectrum Lee swings toward--the harshly noisy or the hypnotically meditative--her sound always commands attention, making Ghil the biggest surprise in a career already full of them.

Title: Eliza Doolittle
Review: Eliza Doolittle is an album of potential but, for the moment, that's all it is.

Title: Here and Nowhere Else
Review: Twenty minutes of pedal-to-the-floor, tension-igniting rock ‘n’ roll can just be too much in most hands, but Here and Nowhere Else condenses these moments into more reasonable servings that are successful across the board.

Title: Dream Wife
Review: Dream Wife is brimming with grungey, glam melters and dreamy pop melodies that perfectly capture the enthusiasm and confidence of Dream Wife's live shows, without sounding too over-polished.

Title: Digital Ash in a Digital Urn
Review: Most of Digital's songs seem somewhat suffocated. [Feb 2005, p.85]

Title: Play What They Want
Review: For Play What They Want, Colpitts and Brooklyn-based ensemble TIGUE Percussion partner with some legendary guests, and the result is an expansive, writhing body of busy, ego-less playing delivered with a beating, beaming heart.

Title: My Finest Work Yet
Review: It’s a piece of masterful craftsmanship tucked snugly into the singer-songwriter tradition, filled with country-soul ballads and grungy laments driven by jangly guitars, family band harmonies, rumbling pianos and cinematic string passages that should appeal broadly to fans of the genre without alienating his own die-hards.

Title: Captain of None
Review: The whole thing carves out and inhabits a persuasively exotic world of echo that invites total immersion. [May 2015, p.97]

Title: PLECTRUMELECTRUM
Review: He and the girls trade off vocal duties, creating a bold, dynamic playfulness.

Title: I Will Set You Free
Review: By letting a few slivers of sunlight in and slightly loosening his tie, Adamson has effortlessly moved his songs into a different area while still keeping proceedings going at the slickest of clips.

Title: The Rising Tide
Review: Another remarkable, evolutionary chapter in the stormy history of one of rock's best young bands.

Title: House of Woo
Review: House of Woo suggests an artist who’s still coming into his own without being afraid to play chameleon at the DJ booth.

Title: Is Growing Faith
Review: Mostly, though, the album is burst after burst of cheerful, weird pop songs that will have you in a state of nostalgic happiness.

Title: What a Boost
Review: The combination of Rozi Plain’s curious, hopefully wistful ... songwriting and the meandering, caressing lull of the playing makes room for new, soothing life within the singer’s work.

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: Though falling short of revelatory, a few rotations of A Hero’s Death brings some good news. Outgrowing Joy Division and overblown inverted paddywhackery, it’s a largely nuanced and, most blessedly of all, believable affair.

Title: Swisher
Review: As with many dance LPs, Swisher is slightly on the long side--65 minutes is more than enough time to get your groove on. But the album never ends up sounding repetitive, the emotions behind the beats don’t allow it to.

Title: Summer Make Good
Review: Much of it is lovely, but marred somewhat by the whispery sub-Kate Bush vocals of Kristin Valtysdottir. [Apr 2004, p.117]

Title: Mylo Xyloto
Review: While the melodies on Mylo Xyloto are some of the strongest and most memorable in the band's catalogue, it's the shortcomings in their lyrics that keep Coldplay from packing the kind of emotional wallop their sound really demands.

Title: Death of a Bachelor
Review: A little more glitzy polish and loads of gloppy decadence.

Title: Alligator
Review: Like R.E.M. when they were good, [The National's] superficially simple songs have a real depth and resonance. [May 2005, p.114]

Title: Blouse
Review: Blouse is a record made for wandering inside the mind, where memory and dreams meet to form a less concrete kind of reality.

Title: Tomorrow Right Now
Review: Beans twirls and stretches his language, depicting the life of a poet-rapper, heavy on non-traditional boasts and battle rhymes. But he lacks the gulping, deep tone of former APC cohorts Priest and Sayyid, which means the beats usually usurp his rhymes.

Title: Rainbow
Review: Rainbow is a muddled hotch-potch that offers little beyond the fact it heralds her return. It's great to have Kesha back--it really is--but let's hope the quality improves in future.

Title: Lord of the Birdcage
Review: While there may not be a ton of surprises from his solo work at this point, this is still an awfully strong set from a guy who's pretty tough to beat when he's on his game.

Title: Alight of Night
Review: Every song on debut Alight Of Night seems to be falling apart, mostly because vocalist Brad Hargett’s melodies are off the map.

Title: Talon of the Hawk
Review: Under Brian Sella's smartypants lyrics and eye-catching admissions is a beating heart and a rare honesty. [1 Jun 2013, p.53]

Title: Leave It All Behind
Review: With electronic and live sounds, emotional production and excellent vocals from some of the underground scene’s best, Leave It All Behind is an open and experimental take on hip-hop and soul, highly successful, at that.

Title: The People's Key
Review: The People's Key proves Oberst has learned to balance a cutting perspective with a bleeding heart.

Title: Subjective Concepts
Review: There's not much here that departs from the blueprint Cobain establishment. Still, though, it's an undeniably exciting listen. [Aug 2015, p.80]

Title: Just Because
Review: The melodies are arranged with a cinematic sweep that elevates small moments of self-doubt and heartache into something bigger and more universal. [No. 108, p.53]

Title: Distance Inbetween
Review: It's a strong departure from the more sedate haunted seaside sounds of their last album, Butterfly House. It’s the sound of a band revitalised after a five-year-hiatus, ready to conquer the world once again.

Title: Acquiesce
Review: It's incredible how thematically cohesive a statement this record is, especially because it was recorded over a year. The music

Title: Metals
Review: Metals is a vivid evocation of a place that touches on fittingly vast themes about nature, love, and life itself.

Title: Laughter's Fifth
Review: Refreshingly, Love as Laughter doesn’t take itself too seriously: this is smart rock completely devoid of pretentiousness.

Title: Songs to Play
Review: Songs to Play is a quiet success, maybe not as quiet as it seems at first, but operating with a definite modesty and restraint. It’s a record that takes some playing before its warbly charms come clear, but it’s worth the time.

Title: Shadow of the Sun
Review: It's so soft-focus as to rarely assert itself or command attention, but fuzz-pop Free The Skull brings to mind Pink Mountaintops, boogie rocker Slow Down Low has a blissful pulse, and Thieves gets terrific mileage out of a hypnotically repetitive riff.

Title: Internal Wrangler
Review: Though not without merit, the reliance on other people's melodies (and words on the Caroline Says-pilfering Distortions) can become trying after a while.

Title: We Have Amnesia Sometimes
Review: Act as an instrumental coda to 2018's superb There's A Riot Going On. [Oct 2020, p.94]

Title: Fear
Review: Its intentions are good, but it’s stuck in trying to make itself into something that it is not: frightening or bold or looming.

Title: Ask the Dust
Review: The scope might be limited, but at least one truth shines out: he writes songs of unembellished rawness, sharp as a knife and tight as the proletariat wallet.

Title: OLD
Review: Old is a post-fame album done right.

Title: The Boy Who Knew Too Much
Review: On The Boy Who Knew Too Much, British piano-popper Mika tackles the popular songwriters' gristle of teen angst but filters it through a cracked technicolor symphony of show-tune harmonies, careening falsettos and deliciously manic productions.

Title: Cry
Review: The Nashville hottie shakes off some of her past cobwebs for slicker, bawdier rock and a collection of power ballads--most destined for a high school prom slow dance near you.

Title: Breakers
Review: Pretty, moody, and even transcendently beautiful in places, Breakers' small-scale take on dream pop is a tempestuous and emotionally unhinged listen.

Title: The Sunlandic Twins
Review: Barnes has created some utterly brilliant compositions, captured a perfect blend of melodic energy and sincerity while never sacrificing catchiness, and has used both achievements to create one of this year’s most cathartically fun albums.

Title: Peanut Butter
Review: Part of the difficulty with this is, simply, that--taken as a body of work (album) rather than a collection of individual tracks--interest can start to wane. This isn’t helped, either, by the chiefly indistinguishable lyrics: that character-and light/shade-drenched vocal might be enormously listenable, but for most of the time we aren’t able to make out what it is articulating.

Title: Trouble in Paradise
Review: Even if she doesn't match the heights of Florence, she can rest easy knowing she's made much better records.

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Paper MÃ¢chÃ© Dream Balloon
Review: It’s a lot of fun, for band and listener both (not always the easiest of tricks)--a ‘concept-less concept album’ shot through with just enough self-aware humour,

Title: Dear Heather
Review: The preponderance of slight songs marks this as a minor effort. [29 Oct 2004, p.69]

Title: They Want My Soul
Review: They just make fantastic, intricate albums that sound like they’re not even trying. Spoon are a band with nothing to prove. They Want My Soul proves everything.

Title: From the Ground Up
Review: There are songs here which recall protestant hymns, others full of Kurt Weill cabaret humour and slick, modern white blues that suggest an energised, liberal attitude to the traditions in which he's working. [May 2013, p.101]

Artist: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Title: The Good, the Bad & the Queen
Review: "The Good, the Bad and the Queen" seems to be waiting for a payoff that never materializes.

Title: Penny Sparkle
Review: They get a little too close to trip-hop for their own good on a few songs, and their widescreen drama is missed occasionally, but Penny Sparkle is still another beautiful reinvention for Blonde Redhead.

Title: Love Streams
Review: Love Streams is at once familiar and totally alien; a work of art that reminds us why we need art in the first place.

Title: Joan Shelley
Review: The 11-track set is loose, yet never directionless, with melodies that are less stately, though no less comforting than those found on the album's predecessor--Shelley's voice itself is a marvel of sonic palliation.

Title: The Year of Magical Drinking
Review: It's an album that might seem superficially bright and shiny, but the edges are sharper than they appear.

Title: The Last Rider
Review: The amiable quality of his lyrics and his enduring melodicism are in full effect on The Last Rider, which is notable in the Sexsmith canon for being the first record to employ his long-tenured touring band, a whip-smart quartet of tone-savvy sidemen who for many years have faithfully adapted the minute details of his many releases for the stage.

Title: Hush Arbors
Review: Just as David Tibet uses English folk to create his own apocalyptic mythos, so Wood takes the bare bones of Americana and makes something personal and timeless. [Oct 2008, p.58]

Title: 7 Days of Funk
Review: The two [Dam-Funk and Snoop], collaborating as 7 Days of Funk, have a loose and luxurious self-titled album (on Stones Throw) that places both men on comfortable turf.

Title: Mirrorwriting
Review: Mirrorwriting is an encouraging first offering which should neatly fill the spacious, indie R&B gap until the XX's next record comes along, but if it could have sustained the quality of its opening six tracks, it could have been much better.

Title: True North
Review: True North is another solid addition to the Bad Religion repertoire, even if it integrates itself a little too well to stand apart from the pack.

Title: Pagans in Vegas
Review: There's a patchwork of pleasantness woven throughout.... By the time the closing tracks roll around, the album has fallen apart entirely. These instrumentals are complete afterthoughts and belong nowhere.

Title: Lightning Bolt
Review: While Lightning Bolt may fall somewhat shy of that goal ["the Best Album"], it is a more than solid effort to satisfy the legions of fanboys born between ’77 and ’84, and a convincing argument for their continued existence.

Title: L'Orange, L'Orange
Review: Richly textured yet spacious and meditative, L'Orange, L'Orange is some of Kowalsky's most rewarding work yet.

Title: Under Stellar Stream
Review: If you acquiesce to its pacing and delivery it’s chantlike mix of chill and warmth can be a springboard to your own thoughts. If you’re not so inclined, I imagine that it would be like a Chinese water torture.

Title: Congratulations
Review: All in all, Congratulations pushes MGMT in the right direction. Rather than resting on their deserved laurels, Vanwyngarden and Goldwasser challenge themselves sonically, creating a follow-up that will test even the most astute audience.

Title: Krieg und Frieden (Music for Theatre)
Review: Music for Theatre frightens upon the initial listen, but ultimately stuns.

Title: Eight Gates
Review: Reminders of a great talent lost, and what might have been. [Sep 2020, p.111]

Title: Social Cues
Review: Social Cues not an overly adventurous record, but it's the sound of a band who know their niche in contemporary alternative rock and how to deliver every time.

Title: Darkness and Light
Review: Much moodier than he’s ever been, it feels as though John Legend has musically turned a corner with these 12 songs, if for no other reason than the supposed reality that in an artistic setting, feeling bad is infinitely more interesting than feeling good.

Title: All At Once
Review: You root for the good intentions and enjoy the glints of sunlight from singer/viola player Anna Bulbrook. But portentous verses thud like birds against fuselage.

Title: Love, Hate, and Then There's You
Review: Its latest album, Love Hate and Then There's You, is a stereotypical dilution of the Stooges/MC5 canon, there are a few unexpectedly tight tunes that hit as hard as, well, a sock in the eye.

Title: Return of Saturn
Review: Why, after going through a small army of producers and making us wait for half a decade, do you come back with a second rate album that seems geared towards the 13 year old girls in your audience?

Title: Worship
Review: APTBS's newest, the relentlessly brilliant Worship, seems designed to drive the listening public violently to their knees.

Title: Always Ascending
Review: This evergreen Glasgow outfit have only tweaked their sound rather than rebooting it decisively, though, making their fifth album a restatement of their core art school pop principles.

Title: What We Saw From The Cheap Seats
Review: Beyond her playing, Spektor holds together the music on Cheap Seats with her singing, which even at its most intricately melodic (as in "Oh Marcello") retains an improvisatory feel.

Title: Emily's D+Evolution
Review: Her fifth album is indeed one of the most alt-friendly jazz cycles you’ve ever heard, pivoting constantly on tight, proggy arrangements that evoke St. Vincent, tUnE-yArDs, and Incubus in their odd-angled crunch more than anything on Blue Note.

Title: Remember Me
Review: Those songs [“Gas Pedal” and “Red Nose”] are both the standouts on “Remember Me,” and also the template which Sage the Gemini tries to emulate, with varying success.... Half the songs on this album are under three minutes, and feel even shorter. Since Sage the Gemini has little to say with his words, his music does the loud talking. And as these songs speed by, they still exert strong force.

Title: I Liked It Better When You Had No Heart
Review: Walker has truly outdone himself with an album that captures all the nuances that made "Letters And Meadows" shine, and extracts them bit by bit to give every individual track its own breath.

Title: ALICIA
Review: Keys has pitched this album as genreless and, although the sonics are manifold – reggae, R&B, funk and even country – you get the sense that Keys has her eyes more on the narrative. There is genuine hope, despair, frustration and even ambivalence. In a world more in need of a key change than ever, we need this Alicia.

Title: That Don't Make Me a Bad Guy
Review: His new album is not exactly like the last or the one before that, and is pleasantly surprising in its evolution.

Title: Sugaring Season
Review: The result is a fresh, autumnal album that's unashamedly mature yet impressively free.

Title: Alive As You Are
Review: This is an album to be held close to your heart and revered as psych-pop scripture.

Title: Last Night on Earth
Review: They've made a sincere, unironic record about how great life can be if you want it to be.

Title: Everyday Life
Review: And musically, at least, that journey paid off. ... Martin can be awfully simplistic in these songs — a problem in any context but especially on an album otherwise marked by some of his most nuanced words.

Title: I Created Disco
Review: Overall I Created Disco is just a pretty confection, good for transient enjoyment at best.

Title: Brighter Than Creation's Dark
Review: Even if this type of thing isn’t your bag, it’s really pretty irresistible and is worth a shot.

Title: Gold
Review: Feels positively grand in scope. [Aug/Sep 2001, p.120]

Title: Hopeless Romantic
Review: The result is her most vulnerable and honest work to date.

Title: Goat Girl
Review: Goat Girl’s London is a murkier, and at times far more unsettling place. Creep exposes a public transport pervert, complete with a 'dirty trouser stain,' atop ominous strings and fierce percussion, while The Man with No Heart or Brain is as scornful as it sounds.

Title: Rejoicing In The Hands
Review: It sounds both brand new and old as the hills.

Title: The Helio Sequence
Review: Recalibrated as a looser, more energetic band, The Helio Sequence has created a euphoric, career-defining album.

Title: Prisoner of Conscious
Review: POC is a step above his worst material and a far cry from his glory days.

Title: Oh My God, Charlie Darwin
Review: Oh My God, Charlie Darwin is a lovely self-release in a beautiful homemade sleeve from a group who can really play.

Title: The Sun Awakens
Review: It's hugely rewarding. [Jul 2006, p.118]

Title: Carried to Dust
Review: From the way gently twanging guitar builds to toxic fuzz on 'Man Made Lake' to the whistling in 'El Gatillo' that nails the stranger-in-town vibe, the band’s best stories are in their music.

Title: Sorceress
Review: Williamson truly soars when her moving vocals combine with the vivid imagery that is painted through the lyrics.

Title: Rainwater Cassette Exchange
Review: A few tracks seem unfinished, but Deerhunter's obsession with oblivion remains as intact as always.

Title: MDNA
Review: MDNA turns out to be just another Madonna album. It's already had the biggest single-day pre-order in iTunes history: business as usual for the most remarkable business enterprise in pop.

Title: Allergic to Water
Review: In a catalog that contains over 20 studio albums, Allergic to Water is exemplary for its craft.

Title: Offend Maggie
Review: Offend Maggie isn't a huge breakthrough for Deerhoof, but it's a step toward coherence with which few fans should have a problem.

Title: The Slow Rush
Review: One of the chiefs pleasure to be had from The Slow Rush is the sheer depth of sonic treats packed into each song. [Apr 2020, p.102]

Title: Wonderful Wonderful
Review: The record charms because its ridiculousness is sincere and his sincerity is ridiculous--two qualities that make him and his art messy and quite genuine.

Title: I Am... Sasha Fierce
Review: Ironically, it's the more tame (and nameless) persona that's the most intriguing, commanding and sexual.

Title: Beyond Ugly
Review: It's a mixed bag. [May 2014, p.114]

Title: The Flower Lane
Review: It's not as challenging as previous Ducktails recordings, but a pleasant pop record nonetheless, and the band's most universally accessible yet.

Title: Tweens
Review: Battle doesn’t have Jemina Pearl’s charisma, and Tweens aren't as adept or distinct as BYOP in terms of their P.O.V.

Title: The Church of Rock and Roll
Review: The entire album is driving, clever, and bombastic.

Title: Illinois
Review: From its framing gimmick and its anti-folk folk songwriting to its he-has-to-be-kidding song titles and its show-offy instrumentation, Illinois should reduce to a simple stunt performance. That it's pop-art of the highest caliber, instead, cements Stevens as one of the most vital voices in music today.

Title: Villains
Review: Cool and calculated, it's sure to rub listeners who are anything but the wrong way.

Title: Look at the Powerful People
Review: It's still early days, but this London-based quintet have delivered a debut with all the hallmarks of a band who will continue to refine their own distinctive niche.

Title: Rated O
Review: While the latter two discs have their moments, they’re all too predictable when held up against the first disc’s ambitious blend of noise and dance.
It's a good-time record, but one intended to showcase how Mudcrutch hit harder and dig a bit deeper than they initially seemed to do.

Title: I Love You
Review: While Blank’s reference-heavy, mix-tape mentality isn’t radical in the current musical climate, it’s often fun in its familiarity.

Title: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
Review: Weezer’s big “return” is just fine.

Title: The Year of Hibernation
Review: His voice is something of an acquired taste but, this minor caveat aside, The Year Of Hibernation is a genuinely unique debut.

Title: Art Official Age
Review: Let’s call ART OFFICIAL AGE a beautiful renewal of vows.

Title: Rapprocher
Review: Harper and her cohorts have certainly created a close approximation to the heyday of Depeche Mode and Human League--but ultimately their dated sound doesn't even come close.

Title: We All Want The Same Things
Review: We All Want The Same Things finds resonant common ground in the idea that shared imperfections bring people together.

Title: Lysandre
Review: Lysandre inevitably feels a bit skimpy. It's still an unnervingly tuneful warm-up: freed from his hipster shackles, Owens is harnessing the power of the incredibly uncool--and he's all the cooler for it.

Title: 4x4=12
Review: 4x4=12 is audacious, mixing generic house grooves with eclectic fare like "Bad Selection," a kinetic jam with dog-whistle synth builds.

Title: Flavors of Entanglement
Review: Somehow, a devastating personal experience has galvanized her songwriting in a way that domestic bliss, as showcased on 2004's disappointing "So-Called Chaos," could not.

Title: No Pier Pressure
Review: No Pier Pressure is another patchy collection that includes some of his best recent work alongside his most risible.

Title: Jacuzzi Boys
Review: The album is an expertly cultivated collection of earworms that further sheds the group’s Ramones worship, instead focusing on hooky anthems that present the band’s kitsch as an accessory, rather than a focal point.

Title: Abattoir Blues / The Lyre Of Orpheus
Review: There's hardly any drop in quality over the discs' 17 tracks, and Cave maintains his ability to startle.
Dungen truely embody that dusty sleeve in some barely solvent vinyl shop, and this is just as good a find. [Fall 2008, p.75]

Title: The Moon Rang Like A Bell
Review: The Moon Rang Like A Bell is both subtly understated and completely overstated.

Title: Yeezus
Review: At first listen it sounds messy, but the more you play it, the more inspired and essential each brutal interruption becomes.

Title: Rad Times Xpress IV
Review: A psychedelic blues washout that sounds like Dave Gilmour joined MGMT ("It's Cool," "Acid Song").

Title: Operator
Review: Ultimately, their third record doesn't show MSTRKRFT to be master craftsmen.

Title: Late Registration
Review: The biggest problem with Late Registration though is Kanye's verses; he's not a great MC, but he doesn't know it.

Title: I Am Alive In Everything I Touch
Review: There's no pushing at the boundaries, but this nevertheless shows Silverstein can still turn some of the things they touch to gold. [16 May 2015, p.54]

Title: Warning
Review: Old fans who would have enjoyed such messages in the past might not like them packaged with such clean music, but they'd be missing the point. Real old school punks know that punk is about following your own path, and that's just what Green Day are doing.

Title: Arular
Review: All the elements are deftly held together by the MC/songstress' ability to make each track her own.

Title: Soft Control
Review: For an artist who has undergone so many identity experiments before her debut, Soft Control is a promising, if not groundbreaking, beginning.

Title: Swisher
Review: Swisher may not be as immediate as Blondes was, but these ambitious, accomplished tracks offer ample proof that restraint can be exciting.

Title: We Are Little Barrie
Review: So retro it's pratcially an historical document. [Mar 2005, p.100]

Title: Group Sounds
Review: Yet for all its adrenaline-rush thrills, the RFTC sound is also surprisingly complex. Like Phil Spector's '60s pop masterpieces for The Ronettes and Righteous Brothers, the sonic density of Group Sounds is actually composed of virtuoso performances and subtle nuances...

Title: Claustrophobia
Review: It's almost a back to basics approach.

Title: AIM
Review: For all its merits AIM is a muddled record, and her divisiveness is sometimes counterproductive.

Title: Thank You Happy Birthday
Review: The new album is more abrasive, rowdier, more unstable and pushier in the right ways.

Title: Dust
Review: This is a triumph of impressionism, where the digital and organic coexist in a radically beautiful whole.

Title: What About Now
Review: On the proper What About Now, the group is striving to sound big and important yet winds up sounding small.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: Despite the elongated nature of its creation, Black Messiah is a fluid, confidently cool piece.... A real showcase of his incredible talent.

Title: Rainbow Ends
Review: Despite its many-handedness, Rainbow Ends is an intensely personal vision. Indeed, it feels more like a companion piece to his great ’70s work than it does a postscript.

Title: A Moon Shaped Pool
Review: There are moments where the restraint feels almost too determined, as though the abundance of care and attention to subtle detail also places a cap on the kind of impulsive energy essential to a rock-oriented band.
Essentially, Chapman is an old-style saloon storyteller whose reflections are enhanced and coloured by his myriad guitar treatments, an old dog not afraid of new tricks.

Title: Lost & Found
Review: Sometimes it is easy to forget that Lost & Found is Smith’s first LP. The sureness and creativity that exudes from each and every song disguises what some would call a lack of experience.

Title: I Still Do
Review: I Still Do is solid, unspectacular blues. Take Clapton’s voice out and this could be one of those Jules Holland collections they promote at weekends on Radio 2.

Title: Lysandre
Review: Each song feels fully formed yet tells a unique and important chapter in this period of Owens' life.

Title: Indestructible
Review: In failing to take up the sword as they should, therefore, they wind up sounding a little lost on Indestructible, stabbing their weapons without any reasons behind each parry, setting up vague agendas they cannot follow through on. Despite this, it’s still a reliably solid, passable hard-rock soundtrack for 2008.

Title: No More Stories...
Review: What Mew have come up with here is a gently twinkling Mercury Rev-ish album of experimental percussive nonsense and occassional jazz-like noodling that somehow manage to hypnotise even while they irritate. [Oct 2009, p.114]

Title: See Mystery Lights
Review: It's a feel-good album for an era that could use a little happiness, a sweaty collection of heady, hedonistic tunes just in time for the hottest days of the year.

Title: Companion Rises
Review: Companion Rises can be the guiding light along your travel, a soundtrack-as-siren that keeps the pace as we move from point to point along the interstellar highways.

Title: Save Rock and Roll
Review: The result is the most actualized version of Fall Out Boy we've ever heard, an undeniable portrait of who Fall Out Boy is today, in 2013

Title: Realism
Review: Realism is a significant departure from the bands previous outing, Distortion, which was quite a departure from its predecessor, "i." And although the group continues to change sounds, Merritt's enthralling voice and songwriting dexterity continue to shine.

Title: i
Review: True, [Merritt] still sings in a voice that's subject to fairly strict demarcations of range and malleability, but his deft spadework in the trench of song-craft more than compensates. [May 2004, p.93]

Title: The Repulsion Box
Review: The songs on The Repulsion Box sound like they were banged out in the underlit kitchen of a crumbling Appalachian cabin. [#69, p.108]

Title: Feels Like
Review: They've reused almost every song from their EP. But that's forgivable when the band manages a knockout with almost every punch.

Title: Attack on Memory
Review: Producer Steve Albini makes sure you feel every snare slap and guitar abrasion.

Title: Engravings
Review: Engravings does find Barnes reaching new peaks, even if he’s not radically adding to his sound.

Title: Old Friends
Review: The lyrics mostly follow white-kid reminiscences, and it's best just to slot them in with all the rest of early-90s-mining that goes on on Old Friends, because they're forgettable.

Title: Qualm
Review: Sometimes producers catch a wave, sometimes they wipe out. But this theory is quickly rubbished by Hauff's own back catalogue. She's released consistent albums and EPs that said a lot with a little. Qualm achieves the same, but only in moments.

Title: Walk The River
Review: An intimate and emotive affair which manages to pursue a slightly mellower direction while still retaining their trademark oddball sensibilities.

Title: Cancer 4 Cure
Review: A set of 12 songs overflowing with bile and sonic invention.

Title: Cancer 4 Cure
Review: The production has been updated for a new, not so distant future, but retains its mechanical crunch and metallic din.

Title: The Things We Do To Find People Who Feel Like Us
Review: The album’s escapism is alarmingly potent, to the point where it verges into the downright delusional, but its lack of self-consciousness is--somewhat ironically--the thing that keeps it in check.

Title: Blackfield V
Review: The album's tempo could have been more varied, but that's a small complaint; there's plenty to enjoy here.

Title: A Ghost Is Born
Review: Wilco's ideas are unremarkable, but are worked out with intelligence and striking conception. And as it happens, the new organic emphasis tables some of Wilco's lamer stylistic obsessions.

Title: Epiphany
Review: Michele is more wry than most feel-good sisters, and never sentimental. She doesn't offer any solutions to the predicament of women caught up in sweet, rough love; like those blues queens of yore, she just takes you there. The journey is gift enough.

Title: Emerald City
Review: Both on a song-for-song basis and as singular cohesive work, Emerald City demonstrates Vanderslice's masterful control of craft at every structural level and his unrivaled ability to make the political personal.

Title: Temporary Pleasure
Review: The result of using these familiar names is that Simian Mobile Disco lose something of the edge that gave "Attack Decay Sustain Release" such a heavy clout as a sharp piece of electro.

Title: Luneworks
Review: Luneworks works best when the Rhodes, laptop and ennui work in harmony, seemingly unguided, providing moments of pure blissed-out release.

Title: Freaks of Nurture
Review: It’s unassuming and introverted, an odd mix of murk and clarity which proves to be ever more intriguing with each listen.

Title: The House
Review: You’ll discover plenty of laconic beauty wherever you drop into The House, and it glimmers with the songful club music that made its predecessor great for getting ready to go out. But a profusion of digital-pastoral vocal settings makes it unlikely to displace Pool from constant shuffle rotation.

Title: We Knew It Was Not Going To Be Like This
Review: Surf City plays with a more confident and reassured sound as the group comes into its own on We Knew It Was Not Going To Be Like This.

Title: Pain Is Love
Review: The hip-hopper's gravelly vocal style benefits greatly from the many collaborations here.

Title: In All Weather
Review: The resulting album is a thing of gossamer beauty. [Dec 2019, p.25]

Title: SVIIB
Review: The more down-the-middle SVIIB shows that these postscripts aren’t always special, but we’re grateful for the closing chapter nonetheless.

Title: Dream River
Review: Musically, Dream River sticks calmly to understated Americana, generally managing to pull off Lambchop’s neat one-inch punch trick--seemingly effortless and gentle, only to echo with far more drama and beautifully powerful resonance.

Title: Lemonade
Review: By effortlessly topping her own best work. Lemonade now sets a new standard for cross-genre collaboration.

Title: Grinderman 2
Review: While he certainly has the ability to rage in a Mel-Gibson-esque blow-me-while -I-burn-the-house-down style, Cave brings enough grace and reticence to the songs, making the proceedings even more sinister. [Oct 2010, p.113]

Title: Fun's Cool
Review: Yet despite the lyrics providing more comical punchlines than your average Adam Sandler film, the lack of variation means Funs Cool comes up just short of being a great début.

Title: The Real New Fall LP (Formerly Country on the Click)
Review: The Fall rock with scalding fury, as if it were 1981 again. [Aug 2004, p.116]

Title: Be More Kind
Review: There’s plenty more evidence here that Frank remains one of our most consistently punchy, stirring and chaff-free songwriters.

Title: Figure 8
Review: Smith makes a valiant effort to match the austere beauty of XO... Still, he falls short on the most important element of his songs, the vocal melodies.

Title: Negro Swan
Review: It's a rich and rewarding experience, one that offers a powerful glimpse into the everyday lives of those members of marginalized communities struggling for acceptance in an increasingly closed, divided, and hostile society.

Title: Swimmers
Review: The songs here are elegantly crafted, and keenly constructed, but there is absolutely nothing on the record that you haven’t heard – done better - elsewhere. Your enjoyment of the album will depend entirely on just how much soft-focus, meandering indie music you can stomach.

Title: Do to the Beast
Review: If you’re a fan of the Whigs, Do to the Beast will push all the right buttons and even add a few new ones for you to think about.

Title: Tanglewood Numbers
Review: A rhinestone-tipped treat. [22 Oct 2005, p.41]

Title: Run to Ruin
Review: Albini captures a recording full of heart, a sound quiet and full, rough and clear.

Title: We Disappear
Review: We Disappear's weak spots appear in the occasional retread "whoa-oh-whoa" pop chorus. The band is strongest in scrappy and loud moments like "Hey You."

Title: Cast of Thousands
Review: An album of moody, grungy pop with a distinctive British feel that could easily be one of this year's sleeper hits. [#23, p.97]

Title: Circuital
Review: Recorded in a Louisville church gymnasium, Circuital is just as adventurous, yet more organic and focused.

Title: Old Ideas
Review: Not to say Cohen is not an artist to be treasured, just that Old Ideas may not be entirely essential.

Title: For Years
Review: In collecting the a-sides from both of his 2012 singles and propping them up with another half-hour's worth of songs, Airhead's debut full-length only makes that stylistic restlessness more frustrating.

Title: Ta Det Lugnt
Review: Absolutely endearing. [Jul/Aug 2005, p.101]

Title: Our Bright Future
Review: The lack of any overt passion, energy and fresh ideas makes a numbing and sadly all too predictable listen. [Dec 2008, p.128]

Title: Till Death Do Us Part
Review: The combination of mournful maturity and club-ready fun they come up with on Till Death Do Us Part suits them just fine.

Title: Awoo
Review: Gibb... is the seamy, sex-fueled yang to the ascetic yin of the Magnetic Fields' Stephin Merritt. [Oct 2006, p.98]

Title: Dethalbum III
Review: Dethalbum III's tongue-in-cheek bravado delivers a more potent hour of music than many of the icons who originally inspired it.

Title: Toward the Low Sun
Review: United as a trio, their talents flare up to blinding effect. [April 2012, p. 94]

Title: My Love is Cool
Review: Even if My Love Is Cool sacrifices some of Wolf Alice's earlier fury, the album is all the stronger for it.

Title: Home Life
Review: The greatest strength of Home Life is how lived-in the tracks feel; the songs have a nostalgic, campfire quality to them.

Title: A People's History of Gauche
Review: No matter what dense subject Gauche tackle, the gang's groovy camaraderie keeps their discourse part of the action; even the Gang of Four-like march toward self-determined worth in "Running" feels whimsical, a real question pondered in every color instead of a textbook example in black and white.

Title: Collector
Review: The songs that do make up Collector are packed with interesting guitar tones, an intuition for pop magic and a message that should be shouted from the rooftops.

Title: Say Yes to Love
Review: While it's a deeply cathartic break-up record, it's both personal and political. [No. 108, p.57]

Title: You're Dead!
Review: While it may not be clear where we're headed throughout the album, Ellison maneuvers through the bedlam with such confidence that it's not just easy to get swept up in his grand vision of the Great Beyond, but to return for repeat visits.

Title: Borrell 1
Review: Ultimately Borrell 1 is a better-than-serviceable rock record complicated by myriad preconceptions, all which are further skewered by some fantastically hubristic song titles.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: Follows a smilar pattern to 2003's Monday At The Hug And Pint, fleshing out their deceptively simple songs with expanded arrangements and quicker tempos. [Dec 2005, p.148]

Title: Frances The Mute
Review: The CD has moments of undeniable beauty and power; it may prove to be one of those "difficult" records that repays with repeat listens. [4 Mar 2005, p.72]

Title: Lost Channels
Review: In a voice so fragile a strong breeze might overpower it, he offers sober ruminations on loneliness, life, love, longing, and artfully infuses each song with just the right amount of banjo, light drumming, acoustic guitar and vocal harmonies (often courtesy of the stellar Julie Fader).

Title: Smokey Rolls Down Thunder Canyon
Review: With big choruses, pristine production values, sing-alongs, and much lovelorn balladry could it be that Devendra Banhart is about to cross over?

Title: Turbines
Review: Turbines has them sounding more like a band and less like a studio project, but around their psychedelic boy-girl harmonies, circling guitar lines and insidiously weird lyrics, there are still plenty of analogue gurgles and swoops and strange, dubwise production finesse

Title: proVISIONS
Review: Though proVISIONS offers some playfully charming moments, ('Can Do,' 'Out There,' 'Increment of Love'), the dark center of this album’s middle is telling.

Title: Our Love
Review: There's a strong sense that Our Love is an important step in the evolution of Caribou. Whatever the formula is, it's working.

Title: Livin' on a High Note
Review: Livin’ on a High Note is nothing if not eclectic. While the focus is on an upbeat good time, peppered with a few life (and history) lessons, the quietest, most reflective song closes the album beautifully.

Title: Codename: Rondo
Review: Codename: Rondo showcases a softer sounding group and it's one that sounds neither confident, nor too amusing.

Title: Heavy Love
Review: Heavy Love is a fine, if ultimately inessential, summation of what Garwood does best.

Title: Zonoscope
Review: Cut Copy thrives when the ingredients are simple: melody, voice and its influences interpreted.

Title: Plumb
Review: From the ground up, Plumb is through and through the work of a band that has absolutely mastered its craft.

Title: Ten New Messages
Review: Ultimately, 'Ten New Messages' is too myopic to see beyond its own concrete cynicism.

Title: Quarantine
Review: What ultimately hits hardest is the aesthetic singularity of everything here.

Title: Future Standards
Review: A few of these songs could be standards, and most of them hold up well, but, even given the nature of the album, the occasional sonic dissipation keeps it from being a true classic, even if it’s a nice, unique addition to Gelb’s catalog.

Title: The Connection
Review: It's the sound of a band who know their craft inside out, but who aren't afraid to grow and try something new. [29 Sep 2012, p.53]

Title: The Curse of Blondie
Review: The album is engagingly eclectic, always melodic, sometimes hard and storming, but never quite so sublime [as single "Good Boys"]. [Nov 2004, p.132]

Title: kin
Review: It's a highly evolved, sometimes claustrophobic take on warm but angular Scandi-pop. [Oct 2012, p.103]

Title: Lessons in Love
Review: Between 'I'm Wit It,' 'Girls,' and a couple other standouts, Lessons and Love cannot be dismissed, but Lloyd will have to really change it up with his fourth album to evade a real holding pattern.

Title: Hifalutin
Review: Modulating between grandiosity and relative constraint helps to root the band’s sound in an eerily-wrought hinterland; a template that deters the fabled afflictions of second album syndrome, securing itself as a credible successor to their spry breakout debut.

Title: Donkey
Review: It’s not as good as its makers’ first, given the flatness of the overall production which falls well short of capturing the dynamism of the band’s live show.

Title: "Awaken, My Love!"
Review: "Awaken, My Love" is a stone-cold blast from beginning to end.

Title: Storytelling
Review: [A] tired, uninspired collection of music and songs.

Title: Prayers for the Damned
Review: [Rise] sounds like it’s been designed solely with American radio very much in mind. Things pick up quickly from there though, You Have Come To The Right Place, puts things very much back on track, wilfully over-the-top, a grand façade covering the band’s broken veneer.

Title: Lightbulbs
Review: Words are used minimally and to great effect.

Title: Central Reservation
Review: If you haven't heard the plaintive and curiously uplifting songs of longing and loss from this rising phenom, you're missing the emergence of one of the most affecting new talents of the past five years.

Title: Civilian
Review: It's impressively well-wrought music, though no longer as instantly engaging, requiring several listens before its charms truly take shape. [Apr 2011, p.122]

Title: FLOTUS
Review: A remarkable case of sonic reinvention.

Title: Lights Out
Review: While the songs on Lights Out would certainly suit a fine live atmosphere, their simplicity, repetition and generic nature create a rather weak album that fails to hold its own in today’s complicated indie rock landscape.

Title: Sleeping Operator
Review: There are less stirring points--England, for instance, never really seems to move, and album closer Please Let Me Let It Go is a little too somnambulant. [Nov 2014, p.104]

Title: Let It Come Down
Review: Let It Come Down suffers just a little from Pierce's presumably healthier outlook. [#211, p.66]

Title: Duck
Review: Duck is far from inventive, but there’s fun to be had.

Title: United States of Horror
Review: There's bountiful fun to be had pledging your inner teen's allegiance to Ho99o9's burning flag. [Jul 2017, p.93]

Title: Screaming Bloody Murder
Review: Even if there's a fair amount of affected British accents and overdriven guitars, it's a far cry from the mall-punk rebellion of Underclass Hero, the melodramatic bombast flavored with metallic flecks and solipsistic acoustic pity, all giving Screaming Bloody Murder a grander, richer palette than any other Sum 41 record.

Title: Chaos and Creation in the Backyard
Review: Sir Paul has always been an instinctive songwriter, and he sounds as surprised by these songs as his listeners may be. [12 Sep 2005]

Title: Build Me Up From Bones
Review: It’s a wild ride despite its generally non-electric trappings.

Title: Modern English Decoration
Review: A tendency to record in sequence brings its problems; a slight mid-album sag might have been remedied by tighter editing. But the end-stretch’s up-swerve in character and definition suggests renewed direction.

Title: Always Strive and Prosper
Review: The follow-up to his acclaimed 2013 debut Trap Lord sees the Harlem rapper open up with more honesty, humor and charm.

Title: At The Cut
Review: A collection of cobwebbed country and chamber-pop spiked with dark wit, it peaks with "Flirted With You All My Life", a dialogue with the reaper that Chesnutt handles with impressive dignity. [Nov 2009, p. 83]

Title: Till Death Do Us Part
Review: Only about a third enjoyable.

Title: What If
Review: On What If, Hauschka delivers an unbuttoned works that's just as revitalizing for the listener as it sounds for the artist.

Title: Street Horrrsing
Review: There are moments, however, when Hung and Power lock into something truly ecstatic, creating passages that more than account for the tremendous amount of pre-release hype that’s been softballed toward these two.

Title: Baby
Review: An impressive debut.

Title: Sex & Food
Review: On Sex & Food Unknown Mortal Orchestra are inventive, ragged, sometimes tiring, and very cool.

Title: The Money Store
Review: Death Grips appeals to the knuckle-dragging troglodyte and the smirking smart kid in us: thick-headed goonery and bookish, viscera-free nerdiness, making beautifully misanthropic music together.

Title: Disconnect From Desire
Review: This album is grounded. Slightly lost and, sadly, all too findable.

Title: ununiform
Review: It seems he's at peace with trip-hop and his legacy. However, the punky "Dark Days" with Mina Rose and a minimal take on Hole's "Doll Parts" with singer Avalon Lurks suggests he remains restless for what might be over the next smoky horizon. [Nov 2017, p.36]

Title: Be
Review: Common's naturally smooth flowing voice is a pleasure to listen to, making even the times when he is overreaching his grasp that much more tolerable in comparison to lesser peers.

Title: Paula
Review: While still frequently predictable lyrically, Thicke also occasionally takes a couple of steps away from his formula. But even cursory knowledge of their split makes this public and emotionally messy and revealing ploy for reconciliation teeter on, and sometimes fall over, the borderline into creepy territory.

Title: August
Review: There is sweetness--Shuffling Stoned's hyperfocused vignette; the title track's mystical George Harrison drone--but August feels like the product of a wandering mind deliberately slipping through the cracks. [Sep 2019, p.89]

Title: Spirit
Review: It would do well as an introduction to the group for an unfamiliar listener, but doesn’t feel necessary by any means. If anything, Spirit comes across as more mood music by design, bespoke and undemanding, and it probably already has real estate on every bedroom-themed playlist on Spotify.

Title: Dream Nails
Review: Dream Nails often surprising, forever enlightening debut album proves that the revolution will be a whole lotta fun.

Title: Hot Fuss
Review: This album’s appeal is so superficial that those who don’t cotton to guys trying to look pretty while the bombs drop should avoid this entirely.

Title: On Dark Horses
Review: Rundle explores shadowy dreams and gothic fantasies through a series of precariously balanced electrified compositions that hover around her--light as a feather one minute, heavy as lead the next. On Dark Horses rides headlong into the singer’s psyche as she pulls us into the darkest corners of her imagination and breathes out fevered secrets. [Oct 2018, p.64]

Title: This Wild Willing
Review: The Khoshravesh brothers’ Iranian sound spices things up on a few tracks, but not enough to prompt multiple listens. Hansard’s passion seems to be lacking in the way he sings on most tracks, and that ends up being a letdown. Perhaps the experience of making the album was much more magical than the music that resulted from it.

Title: Ocean Roar
Review: Ultimately, Ocean Roar works as a continuation of the feelings that were so deeply and richly explored/mined on Clear Moon.

Title: KoKoro
Review: The only way to respond to the sourpusses is to ensure the music is very, very good, something that KoKoro can more than justifiably claim.

Title: Mogic
Review: It can ramble, but their landscape is so compelling, the scenic route is no punishment. [Dec 2018, p.108]

Title: Be Your Own Pet
Review: For the most part, the band's jagged guitars and bludgeoning backbeats play by the punk rulebook. [Jul 2006, p.186]

Title: For Emma, Forever Ago
Review: The turns of phrase are usually cul-de-sacs, the flights into obscurity have bum wings, and do you really prefer, for instance, Vernon's best-in-show "Now all your love is wasted?/Then who the hell was I?" (much less "Only love is all maroon/Lapping lakes like leery loons") to this Creeley ordinaire

Title: Swoon
Review: Aubert’s dude-sings-like-a-lady tenor conjures false hope for a relationship he knows is doomed. SSPU salute misery as a kind of ideal, the opposite of love but just as beautiful.

Title: Scars
Review: Return To Form from last electro band standing.

Title: Hypnotic Nights
Review: A super-catchy mix of stadium-rock bombast and punk simplicity. [No.90, p.57]

Title: Smote Reverser
Review: Loud, hypnotic, vitriolic solos, mordant melodies with biting lyrics. It’s everything we’ve come to expect.

Title: The Beginning
Review: Simply put, this album suffers from Beyonce syndrome--it does nothing to further the group's catalogue. Last time around, the Black Eyed Peas were exploring new territory, and the results were contagious. Now, it seems as though the group, particularly will.i.am, is stuck on auto-pilot.

Title: The Obliterati
Review: Equal parts bludgeoning Art Brut and soaring pop grace. [Aug 2006, p.94]
13 is primarily a journey into familiar territory, one that yet again focuses on Black Sabbath's acumen for vintage heavy metal.

Title: American Tragic
Review: On American Tragic, Fortune rises up to squeeze every last drop of drama from her misery.

Title: James Pants
Review: Pants wraps everything effectively in a dreamy fizziness that softens some of the stranger dark edges, but he doesn't hide his increasing interest in pop song construction.

Title: In Conflict
Review: The tension between revelation and ambiguity is echoed in the music, which avoids the easy, straightforward release of pop crescendos in favor of alternating textures and rhythms.

Title: Negro Swan
Review: Perhaps Negro Swan is merely a step along the way, as Blood Orange continues to contend with monolithic, difficult ideas, but for now, this patchwork of sweltering grooves, amicable conversations, and urban ambience remains limited in its vision.

Title: Universal Beings
Review: Warrants deep exploration. [Nov 2018, p.95]

Title: John Wizards
Review: As it is now, John Wizards is an effortlessly fun, pan-global pop record that stands on its own, no qualification needed.

Title: Cigarettes After Sex
Review: The effect is a bit like pleasantly nodding off to a Mazzy Star record and, like the smoke off the titular post-coital gaspers, the intoxicating atmosphere lingers long after the tracks have played out. [Sep 2017, p.88]

Title: Noah's Ark
Review: Disconcerting and intensely beautiful. [Oct/Nov 2005, p.146]

Title: Zig Zaj
Review: Zig Zaj sounds more like a rehash than the entirely new recipe that music fans are undoubtedly looking for.

Title: Ripcord
Review: All throughout Ripcord, the electronic elements are at the forefront and foundation, but it's to Urban's credit that this never feels desperate or pandering: it's a smooth, logical progression that makes his music feel sleek and mature.

Title: Devin Dazzle & the Neon Fever
Review: It's all a welcome change from dance-scene earnestness, and worth 48 minutes of anyone's time.

Title: What We All Come to Need
Review: Divest the Smashing Pumpkins or Hum of their singers, give the bands room to jam, and this album might have ensued. Without vocals, it feels slightly empty.

Title: Ys
Review: For those willing to let go a little and drift, Ys can be an amazing journey, especially when Parks' strings and Newsom's harp lock into a seductive dance, or when her voice catches one of the fleeting snatches of melody and rides it until it escapes.

Title: Imperial Wax Solvent
Review: Throw in an evocative, anthemically chanted lyrical snapshot, some cryptic tales and a blues rock cover and almost every successful Fall trick familiar from the last two decades is also deployed. All of which amounts to a vital late period masterpice. [June 2008, p.47]

Title: Battle Born
Review: It's the band's most fully realized record, and that should keep them at the front of a dwindling pack.

Title: Glue
Review: Being so musically and thematically rich, GLUE will be a lot of things to a lot of people, and therefore act as an enduring monument to being young and looking ahead in a world that doesn’t always seem to have, or want, a future. This is an album that simultaneously makes you sad and glad to be alive. Treasure it. Use it.

Review: A riot of black humor, sex mania and mean-eyed, chaotic rock.

Title: Blood Speaks
Review: There's a gritty, lucid vein [in the album's songs] running just below the top layer of haze, the words' bite stinging all the more for their burial under all those dank guitar tones and harmonies as dark and delicate as black lace.

Title: Senior
Review: It's maybe a little older and a little wiser than Junior but it just isn't anywhere near as much fun.

Title: BE
Review: BE’] is certainly an improvement on ‘Different Gear...’, but it’s more of a tentative step in the right direction than a great leap forward.

Title: Future Crayon
Review: A welcome reminder of the Brummie art-poppers’ lighter, brighter past.

Title: MDNA
Review: Large chunks of MDNA are shockingly banal, coming across not so much as bad pop songs per se, but as drably competent tunes better suited to D-list Madonna wannabes.

Title: Loose
Review: Loose feels less like an album than a clutch of singles plus accompanying extras. [Jul 2006, p.100]

Title: Fading Frontier
Review: A remarkable album, one that only grows more awesome with each listen.

Title: Mudvayne
Review: Mudvayne has by and large returned to what it does best (or at least do frequently) on its new self-titled album.

Title: Sylvan Esso
Review: It's both club- and cafe-ready, artsy, cool, and elusive enough to woo the Williamsburg contingency, yet soulful and lightly sweetened with warm Southern honey.

Title: Write Me Back
Review: Although the flagrantly throwback Motown numbers are a bit warmed over, the album shines when Kelly blends his old-school approach with his modern club killa persona.

Title: Ego Death
Review: Ego Death is an album both suited specifically for the social media age of music listeners but simultaneously rich and permeated with the traditions of the soul and R&B music of the past.

Title: No Shouts, No Calls
Review: No Shouts, No Calls might be some of Electrelane's most accessible work, but it's far from safe; in fact, its sweet vulnerability is exactly what makes it so special.

Title: Time Will Die and Love Will Bury It
Review: The climax brings an emotional resonance to proceedings that confirms Rolo Tomassi's impressive ability to cross these genres and moods and influences but still sound undeniably them.

Title: You're Dead!
Review: Excitingly new yet classically evocative, You're Dead! is contemplative but never boring, an example of genre cross-pollination that transcends novelty and, occasionally, time and space as well.

Title: Harmonies for the Haunted
Review: Overall, the effect is post-punk Cure with swathes of Ride in heady moments and, as overblown and unlistenable as these amassed elements might sound in your head, it's actually fantastic.

Title: The Soul Sessions
Review: It’s a good voice, but it’s not a good album.

Title: Principe Del Norte
Review: Even with the album's epic length, it never feels meandering or indulgent, as Prins Thomas remains supremely focused throughout the entire journey, finding the duality between the different types of "cosmic" music.

Title: Hyacinths and Thistles
Review: As with all Stephin Merritt productions, the real stars are Stephin Merritt's wonderful songs, and the 14 love songs on Hyacinths And Thistles are as sweet and prickly as the title suggests.

Title: Thresholder
Review: Craig’s music is not concerned merely with his gadgets or the way he wants his voice to be. Thresholder is, instead, a summary of the way his voice might be heard or ignored or interpreted in a universe where activity and entropy only increase without bound.

Title: Third
Review: It's groove-deprived and difficult, and not in a particularly inventive way. [May 2008, p.78]

Title: Watching Dead Empires in Decay
Review: Although Watching Dead Empires In Decay lacks content other than song titles, it evokes spaces that need no explanation.

Title: Street Halo
Review: The six tracks divided evenly between his 20-minute 2011 return and his 30-minute 2012 stride forward, cohere almost seamlessly as the album they become when you don't have to turn any plastic over.

Title: Pieces of the People We Love
Review: The Rapture sound amazingly fresh right now.

Title: Gold Cobra
Review: The overall impression is that the Bizkit remain as annoying, entertaining and incorrigibly obnoxious as they ever were. [25 Jun 2011, p.50]

Title: Kiss Land
Review: Despite Kiss Land being The Weeknd’s major label debut release, what was once a breath of fresh air now sounds rather played out.

Title: Stripped
Review: As a pop record, Stripped is practically flawless.

Title: Preliminaires
Review: By being boring on purpose, Iggy ironically proves himself oddly more compelling than on his many past accidents. If it's not an album for the ages so much as for the aged, at least it's one you may want to hold on to a bit and give another shot when you get closer to where Iggy's at himself right now.

Title: Welcome Interstate Managers
Review: Welcome Interstate Managers is the welcome aural equivalent of a great collection of short stories, each song offering a little snippet from a life, and presenting a range of characters to fill this musical spectrum.

Title: Waiting for the Sirens' Call
Review: For the life of me I cannot fathom how people can claim this album is any sort of return to form.

Title: Hysterical
Review: CYHSY have created an album that is both jubilant and disarmingly vulnerable.

Title: Lost in the Dream
Review: An album that would sound as though it could have been made anytime in the last five decades were it not so immaculately produced, recalling Dylan and Springsteen and pretty much all of Almost Famous without ever descending into pastiche or mere homage.

Title: Traveller
Review: Everything flows naturally, and that ease is so alluring upon the first spin of Traveller that it's not until repeated visits that the depth of the album becomes apparent.

Title: Top Ten Hits of the End of the World
Review: The surreality and absurdity of dance music from the apocalypse is a joyful alternative to the surreality and absurdity of disaster movies and real life disasters.

Title: House With No Home
Review: Singer Justin Ringle often muffles his words or loses them altogether (as though a wool scarf were covering his mouth) as he trudges through cadences reminiscent of Ryan Adams or Iron & Wine's Sam Beam, delicately dotting his stanzas with multi-dimensional characters weathering the winters of their existence. Which is more enriching than it sounds.

Title: Seeds We Sow
Review: Buckingham knows his true strengths. Seeds We Sow waves goodbye, just as it began: with quiet meditation.

Title: Colour Theory
Review: Without it being a slight on Wood’s performance, it also adds to a beneficiary mix of vocal viewpoints, aimed at tightening the Orchestra’s hold over main stages and secret, more intimate tents out back.

Title: Get Lonely
Review: Darnielle's signature frantic strum is all but absent, replaced by languid tempos and quiet full-band arrangements. [Sep 2006, p.108]

Title: Blood In, Blood Out
Review: While this is an album aimed squarely at diehard metalheads, it’s also an imperious display of succinct songwriting that bulges with moments of refined catchiness...albeit of the variety that also seeks to shatter your jaw.

Title: Rock Action
Review: The subtle electronic touches give Mogwai's production a suitably enigmatic dimension. [#155, p.78]

Title: Fall to Grace
Review: Few could deny her vocal talents but you can't help but feel the character that made her stand out in a crowded pop room has been diluted somewhere along the line.

Title: O Shudder
Review: The odd lapse into trying to show how clever they are aside, O Shudder is the step up Dutch Uncles needed. [Mar 2015, p.106]

Title: Offend Maggie
Review: Offend Maggie is the sound of a group mind at work, deep in spontaneous collective play--but a kind of play taken very very seriously. As it should be. [Dec 2008, p.58]

Title: Civilized
Review: Shawn Christensen's vocals are buried in the mix, while songs fly by with no memorable structure or hooks. [Aug 2009, p.115]

Title: Reunions
