Review: With Reunions, Isbell unites the disparate aspects of his craft — soothing acoustic and fiercely electric; Hemingway's word economy dashed with Oscar Wilde-worthy asides, relatable details and otherworldly allusions. ... For listeners immersed in similar bittersweet nuances on a daily basis, there's no better musical accompaniment than Isbell's latest.

Title: Animal Joy
Review: It's aggressive, impressive, but never makes an emotional connection.

Title: Era Vulgaris
Review: QOTSA envelops many of the songs in a fog of menacing guitar squall that focuses as much on atmospherics as hooks. [16 Jun 2007]

Title: Holding All the Roses
Review: While some may disparage Blackberry Smoke’s generic stance and the fact that Holding All the Roses seems so overtly radio-ready, there’s something to be said for a band that can rock so relentlessly and still maintain its melodic appeal.

Title: Laila's Wisdom
Review: It's not only her best work, but the best amongst her peers, the sort of album that transcends the lane she was in beforehand, transcends whatever antiquated gender biases may still permeate the genre and puts her in the same category as your favourite rapper (who's now clamouring for a Rapsody feature).

Title: Fourteen Autumns & Fifteen Winters
Review: It’s a remarkable debut by a tremendous quartet. Not only does it have the raw emotion, but also the intense, glorious musicianship, absorbing hooks and grandiose arrangements to leave you utterly breathless, drained and wanting more.

Title: Purgatory
Review: Purgatory is a formidable equal to the Southern states snapshots Steve Earle took on Copperhead Road, and the largely acoustic melodies and arrangements will have some listeners checking the sleeve to make sure they’re not playing a long lost record by The Band. Yes, the likes of Price and Simpson have returned country to impressive heights, and Childers has the weaponry in his arsenal to take it even higher.

Title: Transference
Review: This is Spoon at its most Spoony.

Title: Be Brave
Review: Be Brave is not quite the barnstormer that its lead single suggests, but there is enough gumption to see The Strange Boys through any scrutiny of their credentials.

Title: Bitter Drink Bitter Moon
Review: Murder By Death reach a new plateau in the development of their ongoing pursuit of rollicking gothic indie folk, simultaneously sounding born of an era long past yet grounded in a rock 'n' roll spirit that's nothing if not contemporary.

Title: Perfect Symmetry
Review: On album three, Keane trick out their pretty piano melodies with tasty synths ('The Lovers Are Losing'), booming rap beats ('Spiralling'), and fuzzy new-wave guitars ('You Haven’t Told Me Anything').

Title: Until the Quiet Comes
Review: On this trippier, more scattered collection, it emerges in the looming calm, the open moments that peek through pneumatic melodies, beatific, druggy vocals and that throbbing, omnipresent kick.

Title: Popular Problems
Review: The great just gets greater.

Title: Audio, Video, Disco
Review: Audio, Video, Disco might just be the quintessential example of pop music in the Internet world where everything is available, and available to shuffle, but the main point is good times, great record.

Title: Forever
Review: It could be said that Forever might benefit from fewer layers of production, but its maze of sounds is part of its charm and what keeps it interesting.

Title: Hope Downs
Review: Even with the songwriting differences, Hope Downs sounds like a unified partnership between five musicians who've known each other for most of their lives.

Title: Natural History
Review: Nupping proved it, and Natural History amplifies the point that Dope Body are a completely unimpeachable unit from a musical standpoint: able to fit in with contemporaries while still sounding undoubtedly like themselves, carrying on the proud outsider-rock tradition of their hometown.

Title: Death By Sexy
Review: It's an unyielding piss-up of tattooed garage riffs, petrol-drenched blues and Marlboro-chuffing growlers. [1 Jul 2006, p.35]

Title: Make Sure They See My Face
Review: It's his overwrought vocal sensibility that really drags Make Sure They See My Face down into Starbucks country.

Title: The Something Rain
Review: There is a quiet urgency to the songs, and their cumulative effect can be a permeating of the subconscious.  [Mar 2012, p.86]

Title: Damogen Furies
Review: Some of the music is at the most extreme end of Jenkinson’s output, yet remains zanily accessible.

Title: One Breath
Review: It’s hard to say what is more ferocious on Anna Calvi’s new album: her voice, her guitar, or the interplay between the two of them. Together they launch a formidable assault on One Breath.

Title: The Weather
Review: The Weather is Pond at their most daring--and most sardonic.

Title: You Can't Go Back if There's Nothing To Go Back To
Review: It's a more poignant epitaph to their fine career than the dour and sometimes impenetrable The High Country. [Apr 2016, p.77]

Title: Get To Heaven
Review: This is spectacular. [Jul 2015, p.115]

Title: How Do You Do
Review: L.A. retro soulster Hawthorne hasn't led a major-label deal smooth out its quirk. [Oct 2011, p.119]

Title: Sensorimotor
Review: Big, warm music that doesn't shout loud, yet makes itself heard. [Apr 2017, p.97]

Title: Opposites
Review: Most of disc one consists of ponderous, blustering nonsense, with a black chandelier used as a metaphor for depression. Disc two shows more promise.

Title: Call The Comet
Review: Call the Comet is a terrific album in its own right. In context, it’s a triumph.

Title: No Love Lost
Review: With Joe’s distinct style steering every track, No Love Lost is a much more cohesive and focused work, despite similar fluctuations [to Slaughterhouse's Welcome To: Our House].

Title: Dangerous Woman
Review: While the hooks may not be as irresistible as her 2014 double whammy of “Problem” and “Break Free,” Grande compensates by having something meaningful to say with that jaw-dropping voice.

Title: The Nothing
Review: There are incredibly emotional moments throughout the record, really driving the anger and sadness of the music. Some songs lack depth and don’t land as well as others, but, overall, The Nothing remains an emotionally potent experience that longtime fans of Korn will enjoy.

Title: Songs for the General Public
Review: But for all the moments that tend towards fun-but-silly ‘70s musical theatre, there are plenty that, in isolation, ring with the kind of sepia-soaked sweetness that most genuinely don’t make anymore. The Lemon Twigs might not always take themselves seriously, but you’d be remiss to dismiss them as a joke.

Title: Boys and Girls in America
Review: Fist-pumpable rock with brains, heart and words worth coming back to. [5 Oct 2006, p.69]

Title: Repentless
Review: It's their most vital, bloodthirsty offering since 2001's God Hates Us All, with furious guitar solos from Kerry King and guest Gary Holt.hange.

Title: Prairie Wind
Review: Despite all of its strengths, neither the recording nor the songs are as memorable or as fully realized as his late-'80s/early-'90s comeback records -- Freedom, Ragged Glory, and Harvest Moon -- let alone his classic '70s work.

Title: Time
Review: Many tracks are fairly anonymous but ballad "Brighton Beach" and the anthemic "Can't Stop Me Now" serve as reminders that this is the man who brought us "Maggie May." [10 May 2013, p.67]

Title: Malibu
Review: Compared to the impressive and occasionally brilliant Venice, this album's mix of high and hard times has deeper resonance.

Title: Luminous Night
Review: Luminous Night reflects the yin-yang duality of a player whose axework has feulled Both Comets On Fire's freakout euphoria and the post-apocaltptic spok of Current 93. [Oct 2009, p.101]

Title: Lullabies to Paralyze
Review: Homme has emerged with the best songs of his career.

Title: Magnetic Man
Review: This album has failings and successes; it all adds up to a highly commendable record, there's no doubt in that.

Title: Cope
Review: The infinitely superior Cope might expand their reach further still. [May 2014, p.114]

Title: Witness
Review: The more time you spend with each song, the more it sounds like a variation on something you’ve heard done better before, a formula in search of a hook.

Title: Tooth & Nail
Review: It features some undeniably strong songs but is lacking a vitality which would make it a convincing listen. Nonetheless, it’s fascinating in its own way.

Title: Mama, I'm Swollen
Review: Kasher has zero ability to or interest in dialing down his drama and giving Cursive’s highbrow emo rock room to breathe.

Title: Sad Songs for Dirty Lovers
Review: Acoustic guitars, violin, vibes and brush stroked drums all help maintain this steady mellow tone that's about as comforting as a warm bath after three sleepless days of jetlag. [#8, p.106]

Title: Lookaftering
Review: That Vashti Bunyan had the courage to step out of seclusion and follow up her classic debut is admirable. That she was able to do so with an excellent batch of songs is a joy to behold, pure and simple.

Title: Attention Deficit
Review: In its ambitious attempts to revive conscious rap and push the envelope sonically, Attention Deficit may be one of the best rap releases of the year even while it lacks the focus of a central persona.

Title: Spend the Night
Review: If this disc has a weakness, it's in the somewhat "samey" feel of a couple of the songs, but at just under 40 minutes it's no biggie.

Title: Gung Ho
Review: A collection of hypnotic, human rock & roll that extols such seemingly antiquated virtues as moral fiber, history, and love as spirituality.

Title: A Moment Apart
Review: If you’re a little refreshed and in the midst of a heartfelt festival singalong, things might sound different. But it’s hard to get caught up in some of the grandiose gestures on offer here.

Title: A Creature I Don't Know
Review: A Creature I Don't Know takes Marling even further in her musical career than her efforts have already-and the girl's only 21.

Title: Embryonic
Review: Along with this requisite silliness come beautiful melodies (See The Leaves), exploding rock-out sections (The Ego's Last Stand) and catchy, laid-back guitar melodies (Silver Trembling Hands).

Title: The Soft Bulletin
Review: A very good slice of experimental pop.

Title: Under the Blacklight
Review: For the most part, Blacklight is far too flat to shine. [24 Aug 2007, p.130]

Title: Invitation
Review: Despite Invitation’s cinematic and often successful composition, Broderick succumbs to the passivity she’s supposedly working to renounce. The songs are ambient rather than immediate, more decorative than they are distinct.

Title: PITH
Review: PITH is a thrilling leap forward for the band that sees them hitting all the marks they hit so well on their debut and then leaping past them into new dimensions of sound and energy.

Title: Convivial
Review: while Convivial sometimes sounds urgent (as on album standouts like the soaring, gothic 'Love You All' and the bright and twitchy 'Gets Along Fine'), virtually nothing about it sounds truly fresh.

Title: One Armed Bandit
Review: Big layers of instruments dual with and complement each other via weird time signatures, and inspired, complex riffs that sound like they’re scoring a car chase from a cult Seventies film, mixed with bursts of electronic futurism--perhaps best displayed on the album’s title track--a manic, brilliant piece of instrumental songwriting that shows Jaga Jazzist to be at the top of their game.

Title: Sprinter
Review: Those who go along with her for the ride will likely connect strongly; Sprinter is not for passive listening.

Title: Ire Works
Review: Ire Works is their most controlled effort to date, even more so than 2004's mainstream-friendly (relatively speaking, of course) "Miss Machine."

Title: Clash the Truth
Review: Clash the Truth is Payseur evolving, the band shifting in a direction that’s probably unlike what they previously imagined themselves moving toward.

Title: EVOL
Review: EVOL, along with the Purple Reign mixtape, doesn’t provide that instant hit that Future’s world-class 2015 was so full of. Instead it crawls into your brain and makes itself at home; you’ll find yourself going back to it over and over without even realizing.

Title: American Slang
Review: The Gaslight Anthem's profound affection for and commitment to their forebears are just as present as they were before, but only here does the band sound as eager to bury as to praise them.

Title: Body Pill
Review: It's never a challenging listen, evoking distant, blinking skyscrapers, buzzing streetlights and echoes of the previous night's warehouse rave. [Mar 2015, p.78]

Title: Object 47
Review: Object 47 is proof that Wire’s edge remains as sharp as ever.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: The result is a fresh and invigoratingly modern take on black music and as far removed from a musical history lesson as you get. [Mar 2013, p.69]

Title: Body
Review: A keeper. ... This is still a terrific entry point into a band who repay obsession. [Oct 2018, p.87]

Title: The King of Limbs
Review: "Feral," "Codex" and "Giving Up The Ghost" finally win me over. [Apr 2011, p.62]

Title: Pick Me Up Off The Floor
Review: The music is set to do-not-disturb, but Jones has found a nuanced, emotive way to discuss loss, lies, regret, indecision and depression, along with the value of protest and defiance.

Title: Back to Land
Review: Back To Land won’t immediately blow you away, but that warm, overdriven sound makes the latest LP from this San Francisco quartet another compelling one.

Title: Ascent
Review: His extended solos during one or two-chord vamps - particularly on "Close to the Sky," "Waswasa" and "Even if You Knew," in that order of quality - are scrabbling, circular, slightly heroic, pulmonary with wah-wah and squalid with distortion. They're exciting, but they're also good for the head: they shove you into long-form listening mode.

Title: Dying to Say This to You
Review: It's like being trapped in the dressing room at Express for an hour. [Apr 2006, p.91]

Title: Carrie & Lowell
Review: It's heavy, but so very beautiful.

Title: I Don't Dance
Review: A rising Nashville star who's mastered the art of appealing to all his fans without alienating anyone. Everybody wins on songs like I Don't Dance's title track.

Title: The Understanding
Review: Too much of it passes by easily, leaving little lasting impression. [Aug 2005, p.101]

Title: Here and Nowhere Else
Review: Baldi and Co. take the best bits from Albini's tutelage, apply them to lo-fi pop-punk structures and infuse all of it with tightly wound angst.

Title: 1372 Overton Park
Review: The only problem with 1372 Overton Park is, strangely Ben Nichols' lead vocals, which in this recording, feel unusally mannered. [Fall 2009, p.75]

Title: Decimation Blues
Review: Decimation Blues examines with more boldness some of the possibilities hinted at in his previous recordings and brings them shuddering to life.

Title: Blak & Blu
Review: As is, our appetite has only been whetted and not satiated.

Title: Petrol
Review: Anenon's third album represents a confident shift in gear. [Apr 2016, p.46]

Title: American Dream
Review: The good news is that American Dream delivers, point by point, on everything you could want from an LCD Soundsystem album.

Title: Future
Review: FUTURE is a fine mix of the stylings of past Futures layered in a rich blend of sounds from a now refined sonic palette. It doesn’t communicate the same intense and complicated emotional concoction that fills his songs when he’s at his most vulnerable and compelling. But it doesn’t have to.

Title: Post-War
Review: His most striking album yet.

Title: The Magician's Private Library
Review: It's impossible to say how much ­Miranda is responsible for the shimmering, luxuriant music on this album, and how much was conjured up by her magician of a producer, TVOR mastermind Dave Sitek. What is certain is that it's the ­music that is of dramatic, hypnotic ­interest here.

Title: Half Free
Review: Chirping Half Free‘s most compelling of its many indelible hooks, she tries to convince whoever listens “You all have nothing here / You have so much to fear”. An oscillator throbs at nightmare frequency.

Title: The Grind Date
Review: There's little personality and no surprises here.

Title: Zig Zaj
Review: Abstract hiphop-heads might be turned off by the slick machismo, but others will have some good dirty fun. [Oct 2011, p.65]

Title: AM
Review: This new album's skinny-jeaned funk, Arctic Monkeys have stayed close to the spirit of their debut's title while minimizing its excess at the same time.

Title: La Radiolina
Review: The disappointment of La Radiolina is that Manu Chao’s music isn’t as arrestingly odd as it used to be. Too often his band’s ska-punk gets uncomfortably close to dull rock, and the repetition doesn’t communicate we are all singing the same song

Title: A Hero's Death
Review: It's darker and more complex than their debut, but also bigger-sounding. [Sep 2020, p.80]

Title: Remember the Night Parties
Review: Formerly a more stolidly post-punk outfit, their bread and butter on Remember the Night Parties are the kind of R.E.M.-meets-Superchunk anti-anthems of “For the Khakis and Sweatshirts” and “Return /of Burno.”

Title: Sky Full of Holes
Review: Even when Fountains of Wayne are phoning it in, they're never less than professional. Think of this as a thoughtfully-written greeting card of an album.

Title: Snapshot of a Beginner
Review: Another smartly-crafted step forward.

Title: Let's Go Sunshine
Review: At times, notably on Honey Bee, Pritchard's lyrics are sugary enough to induce toothache. However, the ever-present feel-good factor makes this an album as impossible to dislike as seeing the sun break through the clouds. [Oct 2018, p.112]

Title: The Waiting Room
Review: Imperfections define personality and The Waiting Room wears its flaws well. Don’t let them put you off. This is a rich, warm, comfort blanket of a record, marbled with veins of darkness and light.

Title: Holding Hands with Jamie
Review: Traces of Liars’ DNA persist, as do similarities to those tireless Texans Shit and Shine, but it’s hard to think of another guitar-based band conjuring fear this exhilarating and volume this rapturous.

Title: Sweet Heart Sweet Light
Review: This is probably the most uplifting album of his career... Exhilarating.

Title: Goes West
Review: Tyler sounds like he's barely breaking a sweat. It's the sound of confidence in one's abilities as an artist, one who embraces their restlessness and creativity while sounding like he's barely breaking a sweat.

Title: Luna
Review: Luna is a psychedelic delight.

Title: Radical Connector
Review: Ratchets up the accessibility quotient considerably. [Nov 2004, p.102]

Title: Dungeon Golds
Review: While plenty of folks might pick up Dungeon Golds because some well-known musicians are on board, even with a cast of unknowns Scott McCaughey would still be writing fine songs and singing them with heart and humor, and that's what makes Dungeon Golds worth your time.

Title: Replica
Review: Take off your thinking cap, and Replica reveals mostly pleasant, mellow ambient jams.

Title: Ghostory
Review: The fantastic Ghostory actually sounds more realized than their previous two full-lengths. [Mar 2012, p.98]

Title: Men's Needs, Women's Needs, Whatever
Review: This record improves on the band's earlier work and might even score them a stateside breakthrough.

Title: The Final Frontier
Review: The Final Frontier might sound alien at first, but Iron Maiden's DNA is splashed all over it.

Title: Ben Kweller
Review: While a handful of the songs sound derivative, it's hard to resist the tambourine-enhanced exuberance of standout cuts like "Penny on the Train Track" and "I Gotta Move."

Title: Wham! Bang! Pow! Let's Rock Out!
Review: Wham! Bang! Pow!, with its extravagant punctuation, is as brilliantly self-absorbed, as needlessly clever, as tightly wound and tautly played as the mid-aughts debut.

Title: Tidal Wave
Review: The guys once known for writing songs about girls who paid them no mind in adolescence aren’t here any more. Instead they’ve learned from their past, creating an album that’s both eclectic and sensitive, not just one or the other.

Title: Tio Bitar
Review: A well-considered 10-track song cycle of mostly shorter and tighter compositions that combine the catchy, guitar-oriented pop aspects of Ta Det Lugnt ... with the darker freak-folk stylings of 2002's Stadsvandringar.

Title: Ghost Blonde
Review: Despite the angst and contemplation, Ghost Blonde brings a bit of elation to a new, directionless generation of shoegazers.

Title: Beg for Mercy
Review: Mostly, it's tight but standard. [Jan 2004, p.114]

Title: Ziggy Marley
Review: On the whole it struggles to strike a light, far less catch fire. [Aug 2016, p.78]

Title: Bright Ideas
Review: Portastatic is exactly as advertised: catchy, sometimes dumb, occasionally rockin', but always at least competent pop.

Title: Jinx
Review: Jinx starts out promising, with a few well-crafted and consistently surprising gems, but the lackluster backend seems far too content to tread water.

Title: Gutter Rainbows
Review: Talib seems to be coasting just a bit on this cut-and-paste session. As in, from a pure musical standpoint, outside of a few of repeat-worthy tracks, Gutter Rainbows, is no cure for your current cabin fever.

Title: Nux Vomica
Review: Nux Vomica is a dramatic and powerful statement about uncertain futures, strong-felt regrets, and occasional, barely concealed joy.

Title: Tiger Suit
Review: Although the occasional inspired lyrical hook pokes through, all too often the need to match the amped-up production leads to generic blah in the words department.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: This is a gorgeous album, but sacrifices had to be made. They’ve undeniably lost something that made them special in the first place.

Title: BLAME IT ON BABY
Review: Blame It on Baby is pretty evenly divided between strong songs and duds.

Title: Love in the Modern Age
Review: Most of the songs are observations from an emotional distance. [Jun 2018, p.96]

Title: The Animal Years
Review: He finally has the sumptuous, sweeping arrangements to go along with his ruminative road stories and stream-of-consciousness, Dylanesque folk. [14 Apr 2006, p.86]

Title: The Golden Age of Apocalypse
Review: His mellifluous style, best exemplified on Boat Cruise and Jamboree, ebbs and flows without ever letting go of the groove. A bit like Jaco Pastorius in a space suit.

Title: Saturday Night Wrist
Review: Features the kind of envelope-pushing fans have come to expect.

Title: By The Way
Review: A near-perfect balance of gutter grime and high-art aspiration, the Rick Rubin-produced By the Way continues the Peppers' slow-motion makeover.

Title: Six Cups of Rebel
Review: The outright space exploration of Lindstrøm's previous musical outings is sometimes lost here. His dancefloor is fun, but its been grounded this year.

Title: My Love is Cool
Review: The 12-song tracklist is full of individual gems, but would have better highlighted their songwriting strengths if trimmed.

Title: Peace, Love, Death Metal
Review: A swaggering, intoxicating tight-but-loose debut. [Jun 2004, p.107]

Title: Aerial
Review: It is filled with things only Kate Bush would do.

Title: Transatlanticism
Review: There is no doubt in my mind -- and in this I seem to have a lot of company -- that Transatlanticism is Death Cab For Cutie's best album so far.

Title: Eye Contact
Review: While no commercial crossover will be gained from Eye Contact, Gang Gang Dance have released one of the most captivating albums of the year, each song different yet cohesive, challenging and ultimately highly rewarding.

Title: The Young Machines
Review: This is Bianchi’s tour de force, emotive but clever enough to avoid seeming self-centered or pathetic, and satisfying in its candid complexity.

Title: Sundowner
Review: Sundowner probably won't convert anyone who's not already a fan of Morby. It's his best album since 2016's Singing Saw, which found Morby transmuting his folk songs into a more adventurous place, but it stops short of attempting to push further into uncharted territory.

Title: Motion Graphics
Review: The album imagines pop as computer-generated architecture: vivid, plastic and physics-defying.

Title: Oxnard
Review: This meeting of joy and aggression is what defines Oxnard, and the effect is not always pleasant--it makes .Paak’s trademark grooves difficult to luxuriate in--but it is still a compelling mode, and one that rehomes his old-school tastes firmly in the present.

Title: Honest
Review: At 18 tracks, Honest doesn’t feel bloated. Future takes his time on slow, sensitive jams.... But for every tender ballad, there’s a classic Future banger in which he yelps the hook over and over, lest you forget it, on top of harsh beats.

Title: The Last Romance
Review: [Moffat] exposes a seething rage that was only occasionally revealed on the earlier albums. In the minds of some Arab Strap fans, this is a breakthrough; others, sadly, hear a betrayal.

Title: Dopamine
Review: early tracks contain all the stuff Jenkins excels at; hell, there’s even a kind of charm to cringe-worthy lines like, “Go ahead, take my heart up/ Roll it up like a joint.” Unfortunately, that charm wears off as the album drifts away from wistful pop rock and Jenkins visits some of his other, less enthralling ghosts.

Title: Emeritus
Review: No one will forget after Emeritus, an album that proves Scarface deserves accolades and titles just as much as we deserve for him not to retire.

Title: A Bad Wind Blows In My Heart
Review: A Bad Wind is a meticulously crafted album.

Title: High Country
Review: They've taken a long sidestep from Sabbath's alter.... One that sets them up to be able to go literally anywhere from here. [22 Aug 2015, p.52]

Title: Distractions
Review: Despite there being a wealth of moods and stylistic flourishes on Distractions, it nevertheless coalesces into a forceful and homogenous whole.

Title: Since We Last Spoke
Review: Terrifying, but in a good way. The bar is raised. [Jun 2004, p.105]

Title: Never Gone
Review: Never Gone [is] a solid adult contemporary album, which will please both BSB diehards and the dwindling ranks who wish that the glory days of Jon Secada never ended, but its relative strength does highlight one problem with the album: this kind of music doesn't sound quite as convincing when delivered by a group of guys as it does by one singer.

Title: Megaplex
Review: This is the second album in a row where the harder they rock, the less inspired the songs are. When they go mid-tempo and slower and add synths and other textures to their hooks, the songs sound better.

Title: Girl Who Got Away
Review: While her new dance direction leads to a fairly tame trip-hop/chill-out zone, it's a great improvement on her usual blandness.

Title: Just Enough Hip To Be Woman
Review: While the quartet's reference points (Weezer, Pavement) are hardly unusual, their sound is fresh and invigorating.

Title: Felt
Review: A brillant, beautiful album whose very nature allows it to work equally well as music for the background, where it serves as utterly unobtrusive wallpaper, or the foreground, where the little details can be noticed and treasured.

Title: Make Do With What You Got
Review: Don Was' appreciative arrangements leave room for the big man's vocal majesty. [11 Mar 2005, p.104]

Title: Ultima II Massage
Review: As an album, it’s uneven, but its stream of highlights make this a fun listen, perfect for the summer.

Title: The Marshall Mathers LP 2
Review: Even though his wit and word patterns still dazzle, they need a livelier canvas if the Eminem nostalgia experience is to be the thrilling one it should be. [Jan 2014, p.122]

Title: There is No Enemy
Review: He packs every song with parts--low, midrange and high guitars, vocal la-las and ahs--and all the layers can make the songs overstuffed and woolly, particularly the slow ones. But diligence is one way to fight complacency, and Mr. Martsch’s plaintive cantankerousness keeps breaking through.

Title: Will
Review: There are moments of a chamber ensemble compactness and clarity, but at times it all gets suspended in and blurred b clouds of ambience. [Jun 2016, p.95]

Title: Bitchin'
Review: Like so many ‘80s rockers of old, from Y&T to Lita Ford, the Donnas’ attempt at an accessible sound has come at the expense of what made them so appealing in the first place.

Title: Fall into the Sun
Review: Their best album to date, Fall Into the Sun is the sound of a band rebuilding itself one song at a time and becoming that much stronger in the process.

Title: American Goldwing
Review: Ultimately, the trip they're taking us on isn't into America, but into the past, and they show too much reverence for their forebears.

Title: Blackjazz
Review: Blackjazz was produced by Sean Beavan, who has worked with Marilyn Manson and Nine Inch Nails, and its sound skews dark but a bit cartoonish.

Title: End Times
Review: End Times is not merely Eels' best album yet, but in the highest rank of breakup albums, something with the anguished fury of Ryan Adam's "Heartbreaker," sighing with the stoic resignation of Bruce Springsteen's "Tunnel Of Love." [Feb 2010, p.83]

Title: Guilty of Everything
Review: While traces of heaviness remain--see the cacophonous climax to "B&E"--Guilty really finds itself in tender moments. [Apr 2014, p.78]

Title: Thanks for the Dance
Review: For this project Ben Cohen has taken the vocal outtakes and sketches and has crafted wonderfully rich and vibrant music around them. Is it what Leonard would have wanted? We’ll never know, but it doesn’t sound out of place in his rich canon of work, which is the important thing. Long-term fans will revel in another chance to lap up his wisdom and that captivated audiences for almost 50 years.

Title: The Expanding Flower Planet
Review: Having graduated from both Dirty Projectors and Avey Tare’s Slasher Flicks, The Expanding Flower Planet is a confident declaration of independence from a vital artist operating at the top of her creative game.

Title: Share the Joy
Review: Ultimately, this album will not convince any non-believers. But fans will find a lot to love, and perhaps even notice and enjoy the increased quality of musicianship as they bask in that all-girl garage-fuzz-pop glow and inch towards a future in hi-fi.

Title: The Diving Board
Review: The Diving Board is less engaging, widescreen lyrics paired with waddling blues and maudlin balladry. [Oct 2013, p.104]

Title: Things Change
Review: Aside from a few twangy licks, Things Change is an unabashed rock & roll record--a snapshot of a band and its reinvigorated leader.

Title: Interpol
Review: Even if Banks sticks to the "I've got two secrets but I only told you one" songwriting approach, hopefully a band shakeup will spark the soulfulness only occasionally heard in his contributions. [Oct 2010, p.118]

Title: Slave Ambient
Review: Slave Ambient as a whole may be more confused than your average reality show star at a Mensa meeting, but it's full of decent songs with a lot of heart.

Title: Battle of the Sexes
Review: The beats are solid enough, if not as universally banging as circa Luda '01. The album flows well, has some replay value and tries a few little tricks here and there.

Title: Modern Nature
Review: Modern Nature is close to classic Charlatans--no mean feat after their recent tribulation. [Feb 2015, p.74]

Title: Trouble Anyway
Review: Her solo incarnation is finer-framed, a collection of country-dusted ballads and Laurel canyon laments run through a Kurt Vile filter. [Feb 2019, p.115]

Title: Past Life Martyred Saints
Review: With her debut, the former member of art-noise cult Gowns sounds like she would quite literally rip out her heart as a sleeve adornment if it served her creative purpose. [July 2011, p. 111]

Title: Manic Expressive
Review: Merging synth orchestration and genuine strings ins't new, but [Marc] bianchi pushes the form toward and organic/technological inevitable. [#52, p.89]

Title: The Beekeeper
Review: You can delve as deeply into the lyrics and musical brain-teasers as you like, but there's plenty of surface allure for anyone who just fancies a superficial graze.

Title: Lady in Gold
Review: All things considered, Lady In Gold is a more satisfying listen than its predecessor, with a host of truly great moments.

Title: Funhouse
Review: The otherwise likeably raunchy and bratty Pink is now officially walking a fine line, leaning dangerously close to the humdrum.

Title: Heartland
Review: There are a lot of things about Heartland that feel like Pallett is presenting himself more and more fully as an artist; the scope of breadth and mood of it are all grander, more assured, making ever more of a case that the guy shouldn't be viewed as a side note (string arranger for the Arcade Fire, the Pet Shop Boys) or a minor interest.

Title: Melody's Echo Chamber
Review: Stereolab, Cocteau Twins, and Broadcast are key reference points here, though Prochet ensures that the only voice you'll recognize in the Chamber is hers.

Title: When Machines Exceed Human Intelligence
Review: From present to future at Warp factor. [Mar 2009, p.86]

Title: Immersion
Review: Immersion is less fun, harder work than In Silico. It feels like Pendulum are trying to be more than an anonymous CD you put on at a party when everyone's too boxed to DJ any more. They shouldn't.

Title: Appreciation
Review: Horse Feathers have found their way to a much richer, more confident sound, marrying Southern soul grooves and rough-hewn Americana to Paul Simon eloquence. [Jul 2018, p.28]

Title: Horses and High Heels
Review: Lou Reed guests and she's brave enough to wrestle with both Greg Dulli and Mark Lanegan's unsettling The Stations, while her four lugubrious originals show the drugs didn't turn her brain to much. [Apr 2011, p.101]

Title: Â¡Dos!
Review: While the album is agreeably jejune in a way that recalls the band's Dookie era, only a handful of its tracks are truly essential additions to the Green Day catalogue.

Title: Chrome Dreams II
Review: Chrome Dreams II, on which various Neils commingle to an extent not heard on record since perhaps 1989's "Freedom," immediately comes off as the 61-year-old artist's freshest effort in years.

Title: Need to Feel Your Love
Review: Awesome the riffs may be, one might only want to hear them in small bursts lest they risk being worn out. Still, there’s enough variation to stave off sameness, and the band is smart enough to switch it up from track-to-track.

Title: Supernature
Review: It's a curious, rather than classic, record - with the hooks to make the leap to the mainstream, but with enough residual oddness to maintain Goldfrapp's air of mystery a while longer.

Title: Live from the Underground
Review: Live From The Underground offers nothing game-changing, but is definitely enjoyable (especially on high energy jams like "Yeah Dats Me"), emulating its influences well.

Title: Smote Reverser
Review: A roaring return to a full band sound featuring twin drums, electric bass and keyboards. The secret ingredient that makes it such a blast, though, is an unabashed injection of prog pomposity. [Nov 2018, p.62]

Title: Lord Steppington
Review: The album’s content is narrow, and while there are certainly no duds here, things do get a bit predictable as the album progresses. However, the constant non-sequiturs and familiar production doesn’t take a whole lot away from the overall value of the collection.

Title: The End Is Near
Review: The New Year here occasionally let loose with a decidedly unreserved frenzy that is a joy to hear.

Title: Good Morning Revival
Review: After years and years of hating every ounce of Maryland's mall-punk icons Good Charlotte, it seems now that the actual trick to enjoying their music on any plausible level is to go into the whole thing with absolutely no expectations. Not even low expectations. Nothing.

Title: Cause I Sez So
Review: No such luck on 'Cause I Sez So, an album that, despite a few bright spots, is too flimsy and forgettable to honor the Dolls' legacy.

Title: In the Pit of the Stomach
Review: ["Boy In The Backseat" and "Human Error"] plus the resounding "Pear Tree" end the album with impressive bluster, and stirring reminders about the power of the individual: to screw up, to fight on, to howl into the night.

Title: The Stars Are Indifferent to Astronomy
Review: It's thankfully not an album of covers, and thus a wonderful return.

Title: Eleven
Review: McBride is still singing--and now occasionally even writing--songs that employ specific, substantial storytelling to speak to modern women's experiences.

Title: No End
Review: More a curiosity than a masterpiece, but a real prize for Jarrett completists.

Title: America
Review: Baltimore's Dan Deacon has piled all facets of his musical persona together here.

Title: Arular
Review: Arular's irresistible blend of crafty refugee chic and subversive digital skipping rhymes will do very nicely for the moment. [Jun 2005, p.108]

Title: Personality
Review: While the bold brush strokes of Personality may alienate some hardened purists, it may just turn out to be the defining release of Scuba's career.

Title: EARS
Review: Smith creates wide-eyed compositions with textures that cascade over one another, capturing the vast celestial wonder of synthesized sound.

Title: First Mind
Review: First Mind is captivating, full of intricacies and influences that should see it celebrated as one of the great albums of 2014.

Title: Master of Disaster
Review: While Hiatt sounds soulful as all get out (as per usual) on this set, the lingering mood is often downbeat and introspective.

Title: Hall Music
Review: The result is a seductively melancholy and unashamedly serious album that claws insistently at the heartstrings. [Nov 2011, p.91]

Title: Red Flag
Review: They return to their roots for the addictive ’90s swing of ‘Make U Love Me’ but--frustratingly--after the sultry ‘Summer Rain’ the album quickly slips off piste. ‘Who Hurt Who’ is a wet Disney ballad, while the limp dancehall and incessant pitch-shifting of ‘Ratchet Behaviour’ grates. Third time lucky it might not be, but it’s not a million miles away.

Title: Wig Out at Jagbags
Review: Sure, there’s clunky country passages (‘Houston Hades’), brassy crooning (‘J Smoov’) and Cream-y jams (‘Cinnamon and Lesbians’), but Malkmus’ wit remains more than intact in his middle-age.

Title: Singularity
Review: Structural concerns aside, Singularity still finds Hopkins exploring sonic textures as deeply as ever. It's an album that, in its best moments, finds one of electronic music's great minds operating in peak form.

Title: Hive Mind
Review: Hive Mind sounds at once strange and familiar. [Mar 2012, p.100]

Title: Lazaretto
Review: A confident, brash, inventive collection featuring songs that lock into the psyche after only a few listens, the White-produced creation is lyrically and musically challenging and filled with many fresh avenues of exploration, even as it nods to key tones and ideas from throughout the history of pre-rap American music.

Title: Thirteen Tales From Urban Bohemia
Review: One of the better albums released this year...

Title: Zoo
Review: Everything continues to feel heavy.

Title: Drastic Measures
Review: Drastic Measures’ kaleidoscope of sound will undoubtedly charm you, as Sellers himself sings “she looks like a go-getter.”

Title: Lateness of Dancers
Review: Variously heartrending and uplifting, Lateness OF Dancers is enriching stuff. [Oct 2014, p.110]

Title: Mountain Moves
Review: Whether it's the drifting of "Singalong Junk," the stripped down, jazz-cat prowling of "Mountain Moves," or the electro-tripping of "Sea Moves," Deerhoof have simply outdone themselves with Mountain Moves, an album that requires as much focus as it does imagination.

Title: Owl John
Review: The album is a mismatch of styles, moods and tempos. There is little cohesion and each song feels like a thought or idea alone on the record--like a collection of B-sides or rarities.

Title: Crush
Review: Beautifully crafted, Crush unsettles with its quiet, fervent chaos bubbling beneath its surface.

Title: BMX Bandits Forever
Review: Stewart hasn’t deviated from his love of pop music history. He understands its nooks and crannies as well as its hooks and melodies and handles them with reverent care.

Title: Enjoy the Company
Review: As with most of the band's young oeuvre, there's a sturdiness to Enjoy the Company's booming interstate anthems.

Title: Salute
Review: Ultimately, while Salute retains all of Little Mix's infectious, teen-friendly ingredients, it reveals a new recipe for fans whose palates have matured right along with the band.

Title: The Spinning Top
Review: Graham Coxon has left behind his early Jam-meets-Syd-meets-Billy Childish thrashings and his more petulant little-boy-lost vocals, and recorded an album seemingly inspired by Paul Weller's "22 Dreams." [Jun 2009, p.98]

Title: Welcome Home
Review: Somewhat lacking in real character of its ow, there is nevertheless a certain charm to this album, and it's sure to trigger a nostalgia trip in those who came of age at the turn of the current century. [Oct 2019, p.89]

Title: Foundations of Burden
Review: The album and its production make catharsis part of an evolutionary process, not an end in itself.

Title: Eyelet
Review: The formative spiral of ideas dabbled with on previous albums recedes, giving way to a pearl of accumulated wisdom - a new beginning for the three-piece that proves reflective, ambitious and openly confessional.

Title: General Dome
Review: General Dome's force is relentless, but about halfway through these 12 songs, things run together, with muddy, [mid-dy] waters polluting the mix.

Title: Nursing Home
Review: Nursing Home is notable for its lyrical successes, but doesn't have enough memorable songs to highlight them.

Title: Back to Black
Review: A wonderfully time-twisted batch of songs. [12 Mar 2007]

Title: WIT'S END
Review: No prizes for guessing who's been reading Guy Debord then, but it's these touches as well as his reverb-laden sound that makes him vaguely modern, unlike some folk artists who'd be happier pretending the 20th century never even happened.

Title: Feathers
Review: They've built upon the calm, dreamy songcraft that highlighted previous efforts, but the risky sludgefeasts have lost much of their psychedelic bluster, sounding instead like mellowed-out Mudhoney B-sides.

Title: The Party Ain't Over
Review: It's no real surprise that teaming one of today's great rockers with one of the great rockers of all time would yield such great results, but the surprise here is in how natural they sound together.

Title: Dean Wareham
Review: This is Wareham doing what he does best: making music he loves with people he holds dear. [No. 107, p.60]

Title: Ex Lives
Review: Every Time I Die are on fire again. [Mar 2012, p.102]

Title: The Lady Killer
Review: Even with his quirks dialed down, Green has a voice that can burst any melody wide open.

Title: Ultra Payloaded
Review: 'Ultra Payloaded' is largely sub-U2.

Title: How We Operate
Review: How We Operate shuffles between exuberance and wistfulness like a drunk stumbling through a crowded bar--and yet, oddly enough, it's also onoe of the more coherent albums in Gomez's career. [Jul 2006, p.192]

Title: Act Surprised
Review: This is a good record; a good Sebadoh record—and while it may not serve as the ideal access point for new fans, there's certainly something to be said for a band that is still able to create something interesting and worthwhile after both such a lengthy career and such a long time away from the recording studio.

Title: That's The Spirit
Review: Lyrically, the album is poignant and clever, though it does occasionally falter, as on the grungy nu-metal number "Happy Song."

Title: Love the Future
Review: None of the band’s stylistic flourishes are pulled off well enough to convince you they could do one style effectively, nonetheless the 10 they try out here.

Title: Pedestrian Verse
Review: An album with a self-deprecating title that belies the ambitions and talent displayed within it by this band on the verge of bigger things.

Title: The DEFinition
Review: Mostly, he's outmuscled by the production. [Oct 2004, p.122]

Title: Be
Review: Even when the music flags, Common's remarkably hungry raps push it along. [Jun 2005, p.102]

Title: In the Shape of a Storm
Review: In the Shape of a Storm is an album’s worth of that feeling. In grief many cloak themselves in distractions, or hide away entirely: Jurado treats it as an invitation to look closer, feel deeper.

Title: Possible Dust Clouds
Review: Possible Dust Clouds finds Kristin Hersh as artistically curious and inventive as ever. Committed to avoiding easy choices musically and lyrically, she remains intent on exploring the murky complexities of the mind and continuing to make the best work of her career. She is an artist that’s always evolving, and yet again the results are often dazzling and always fantastically bewildering.

Title: Pure Heroine
Review: Pure Heroine seems to hint at the truth... but the truth is, Lorde is a pop invention as much as LDR and is not nearly as honest about her intentions.

Title: Girls Can Tell
Review: Spoon deliver everything with a calm, classy Motown-pop feel, but the disc still crackles with punk intensity... [#154, p.97]

Title: The Beast In Its Tracks
Review: Happy or sad, these are fine songs. [Apr 2013, p.88]

Title: King Push - Darkest Before Dawn: The Prelude
Review: The most interesting moments of the album are when Pusha feels his way around the darkness instead of embracing it so willingly.

Title: II
Review: In other words, Moderat have stepped up to the plate and then some.

Title: Mirrorwriting
Review: Things are moving at two different speeds on Jamie Woon's casually entrancing debut album, Mirrorwriting.

Title: Live a Little
Review: The Pernice Brothers continue their string of classic pop albums with their fifth full-length, Live A Little, expanding on their already pristine pop sound.  [#15]

Title: Uniform Distortion
Review: Uniform Distortion abounds with displays of James’ fiery fretwork, but he rarely wields his other signature weapon--that angelic croon that trembles with vulnerability yet can soar high enough to rattle satellites. In the fleeting moments when it does surface, the effect is doubly stunning.

Title: SMiLE
Review: Smile's post-adolescent utopia isn't disfigured by Brian's thickened, soured 62-year-old voice. It's ennobled--the material limitations of its sunny artifice and pretentious tomfoolery acknowledged and joyfully engaged.

Title: Peace and Love
Review: Peace & Love remains something of a mood piece--it’s ruminative, not rousing, never succumbing to navel-gazing but not suited for large crowds--which does mean it doesn’t quite have the undeniable power of How to Walk Away, but when a softly melancholy mood strikes, this provides comforting consolation.

Title: Black Sun
Review: Whether consciously or not, Gold Fields have created an album whose pure, visceral pleasures are so effective they preclude much else.

Title: Not Real
Review: They pull off shifts in mood and tone with routine aplomb. [May 2015, p.83]

Title: How Does It Feel
Review: Disappointingly, How Does It Feel has a good dose of the latter [blatant variety of compositions].

Title: Wild Flag
Review: A teenage dream of a record.

Title: so sad so sexy
Review: Sadness may remain her true love, but when she flirts with other emotions, the effect can still be magical.

Title: Travelling Like the Light
Review: So where do you go when you've been a backing singer for the Pussycat Dolls? Not straight to the scrapheap but kooky la-la land, it transpires here.

Title: Hall Music
Review: This music is big enough for a hall, but soft and heartfelt enough for the quietest corner.

Title: Zammuto
Review: There's a roving chaos to the disc, not completely divorced from the springy shifts of his other band, but definitely a different animal.

Title: Recess
Review: Skrillex is good enough to kill the Brostep monster he created. He just didn't quite finish the job here.

Title: Crimes
Review: The best production values a major-label budget can buy make everything on Crimes as clear as a bell, which helps. This clarity elevates what could have easily been a sonic muddle into an album that bears repeat listenings.

Title: Ode to Joy
Review: Ode to Joy reveals that after their sabbatical, Wilco are more than willing to explore the boundaries of their music, and they do so with the confidence and sense of daring that has marked their best work from Being There onward.

Title: Everything Is New
Review: Not everything is new on Everything Is New, this young London singer's sophomore set, but enough is to make you wonder what on earth persuaded Jack Penate to ditch the ample charms of his terrific debut.

Title: color theory
Review: It’s a heavy, at times uncomfortable listen, but one that feels intensely relatable. It finds strength in the somber and the morose by paining it in bright colors and wonderful riff work. Once you’re drawn in, you won’t want to turn away, no matter how dark the journey becomes.

Title: Admiral Fell Promises
Review: Despite some lyrical cliches and careless redundancies ("Come out from the burning flame" being the most glaring example), Kozelek's songs change mood fluidly, and the contrast between the serene settings and his own tumultuous thoughts raises even the most languid instrumental passages above mere aural wallpaper, lending it the gravity of his best work while giving it a character all its own.

Title: Criminal
Review: "Young" offers brief flashes of a youthful Cure, but the fuzzy "Choke," about cocaine abuse, is underpinned by a malignant industrial beat, and the dominant mood remains that of an emaciated, homicidal Gary Numan. [Mar 2018, p.32]

Title: You're a Woman, I'm a Machine
Review: You’re a Woman, I’m a Machine is the kind of “feelings” album that fans of noise-rock or hardcore can listen to without fear of being soft. For the rest of us, it’s an indulgence of our more dramatic emotions.

Title: Black City
Review: It's the sort of album which reaches back and forward in equal measure, applying what's known about past songwriting to invigorate the present day.

Title: James Blake
Review: Full of airy vocals and synths, the album sounds as if it could lift off at any moment if not for the drum thumps tethering it down. But the beats sound weighty only in contrast.

Title: Little Hells
Review: As with previous album "Songs III," this us an enchanting record. [Apr 2009, p.109]

Title: Isla
Review: Isla boldly showcases an unconventional combination of instruments and melodic ideas, a revolutionary musical terrain that Portico Quartet will hopefully continue to explore.

Title: Smart Flesh
Review: The soul-endangering threat of our current man-machine moment is unlikely to register.

Title: The Defamation of Strickland Banks
Review: The melodramatic tunes masterfully push up against the antihero's downward narrative spiral, making Defamation the rare contemporary album that insists on being heard in full, in sequence, until the story ends.

Title: Hometowns
Review: Nils Edenloff's passionate songwriting comes across as both raucous (“The Dethbridge in Lethbridge”) and gently sweet (the harmony-rich boy-girl cupcake “Don’t Haunt This Place”), consistently marked by a joyful sonic ingenuity.

Title: An Obelisk
Review: An Obelisk is not quite as statuesque as it wants to be, though it does demonstrate the band’s ethos in a tightly-wound package, and is a solid addition to a repertoire that continues to make a Titus Andronicus release unmissable.

Title: Random Desire
Review: Random Desire doesn't necessarily sound like the Afghan Whigs in their glory days, but it does a much better job of summoning the emotional energy and musical tension that made Congregation and Gentlemen classics, and it's the best music he's made since the end of the Whigs' first era.

Title: A Brief History of Love
Review: There's nothing quite as forward looking here. [Oct 2009, p.102]

Title: A Muse In Her Feelings
Review: With their modest personas and its subtle production, it could be easy to disregard dvsn’s third record as more of the same, but repeat listens reveal a warm and unpretentious record, from an act confidently starting to evolve.

Title: Pollinator
Review: There's almost a charm in the way Blondie push so hard: it's hard to think of another legacy act so determined to play a part of the modern musical dialogue without losing their identity. If they're not always successful, there's nevertheless something ingratiating about the ambition.

Title: Hot Hot Heat
Review: This album demonstrates that the desire disappeared long ago and that they were simply prolonging their career to delay the inevitable. For Hot Hot Heat, the fire has definitely gone out.

Title: Giant Swan
Review: On Giant Swan, the duo display a fearsome mastery of techno dynamics, but it's their detachment from that world that makes their music so compelling.

Title: Throw It to the Universe
Review: A brilliant album. [Aug 2012, p.80]

Title: On Desire
Review: On Desire shows Drowners deepening and darkening the intrigue around them. [Aug 2016, p.111]

Title: Bloom
Review: Yet as easy as it should be for anyone to appreciate this thrilling and sincere record--truly, there’s no resisting the title track’s euphoric refrain--what might be most admirable about it is Sivan’s determination to make a particular group feel seen.

Title: Until Silence
Review: This is as good as the "soundtrack for an imaginary movie" gets. [Aug 2014, p.78]

Title: The Greatest
Review: Simultaneously the most-fully-realised of Chan Marshall's seven albums and yet one of missed opportunities.

Title: Keep It Like a Secret
Review: With its layers of guitars and sharp lyrics, Keep It Like A Secret is a smart, challenging installment in a career that's been as varied as it is prolific.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: Talkie Walkie is, in many ways, a return to the type of sound featured on Air's first two albums.

Title: Lantern
Review: Slightly unfocused by design, Lantern broadens HudMo’s repertoire while also reaffirming his status as the premier producer of the sound that brought him to fame.

Title: Smoke Ring for My Halo
Review: As much as one would assume that times have changed, Vile is able to supplement his strengths with newfound diversity and very simply, delivers a formidable sophomore album.

Title: C'mon, C'mon
Review: It's frustrating to imagine how much more power Crow could amp up by tattering the edges of her best songs and avoiding the crowd-pleasing delicacy that makes her sound like a Sheryl Crow cover band. Led by Bob Seger.

Title: ANTI
Review: It’s not quite the revelatory departure we might have hoped for, and has the rich but unfocused feel of something worked on perhaps too long with obsessive fervour, but it’s also subtle and interesting; an intriguing soundtrack to an era of change.

Title: Hercules And Love Affair
Review: He knows when to kick disco into action and when to just kick back and listen.

Title: Gallipoli
Review: Gallipoli is swooningly gorgeous and rich with offerings we've come to love about Condon: His weakness for exotic cities as song titles, a romance with cultures of antiquity, the combination of organ and brass fanfare, an exceptional sense for melody, and an ever-full heart. Three well-placed instrumentals punctuate and act as palate cleansers. Nowhere is this sugary, overly ornate, or maudlin: An excellent return to form.

Title: MIEN
Review: A perfect union, Mien proves the sum of its grimmest parts.

Title: Watch the Fireworks
Review: Most of the time the more streamlined approach works for the benefit of the songs, but there are a couple misteps.[ Summer 2007, p.76]

Title: Ghosts I-IV
Review: He shows here that he is much more than the swagger and smut of some of his previous releases. He has made it clear to the world that he has real vision and dexterity.

Title: Grand
Review: Matt and Kim (their real names) come on like a punked-up Mates of State--a couple so cute that you'd walk away from their frantic live shows feeling mushy, if someone hadn't just mushed you. But the love songs on their second album are for their home borough of Brooklyn as much as for each other.

Title: August By Cake
Review: The main pitfall of this record is its pacing. Bob’s best moments are lightning fast, like the 28 tracks in 41 minutes Alien Lanes. By contrast, this record is 32 tracks in 71 minutes. Its top moments are when it is moving the fastest.

Title: Desire Path
Review: OEH are a more intriguing venture when confident enough to aim for the universal. [Oct 2019, p.86]

Title: Nearer My God
Review: Pick things apart, and it’s a fine addition to the St. Louis band’s catalogue--there are several songs here that will catalyze their already electric live show.

Title: Roots & Crowns
Review: Roots & Crowns encircles the listener and flows effortlessly as each song melts into the next in bewitching bliss.

Title: Madness
Review: There are far less cringe-worthy lyrics, and a sound that seems far more natural for the band as a whole.

Title: Confessions on a Dance Floor
Review: Madonna's songwriting has always been her most underrated quality. But while Confessions absolutely hits its mark for disco functionality, its greatest strength is also its weakness. In the end, the songs blur together, relying on Price's considerable production magic to create tension or distinctiveness.

Title: Group Sounds
Review: Let's face it: Group Sounds is shit. But it's pure shit, which makes all the difference.... Everything is overdiven and mixed to within a decibel of ear-shattering heaviosity. It isn't just monstrous, it's gleefully, unapologetically monstrous. [#49, p.88]

Title: Wiretap Scars
Review: Wiretap Scars illustrates Sparta's ambition to move beyond At the Drive-In, but also the bandmembers' attempt to steer clear of mainstream emocore.

Title: Hot Shots II
Review: The group shows that their goofy sides can peacefully coexist with their harmonious, pop-song writing ones.

Title: Hardly Electronic
Review: The Essex Green direct their flawless studies in pop to disconnected friends in the 21st century; even after 12 years, they haven't slept a wink.

Title: Hungry Bird
Review: It’s a challenging album, with few of the catchy moments that have marked the band’s earlier work, but one that seems to offer a subtle new reward with each listen.

Title: The Satanic Satanist
Review: Rather than indulging the impulse to ride grooves this mellow off into the sunset, the band keeps one eye trained on the meter (most songs clock in under three minutes), while the other drifts off into the clouds, like on the ’60s-era antiwar singalong 'People Say.'

Title: Love vs Money
Review: Now, with Love vs. Money, Nash has been able to not only add a worthy addition but if this isn’t the best album the genre has seen and heard in the past year, I don’t know what is.

Title: Love and Other Planets
Review: A much grander affair [than his debut]. [Jun 2006, p.103]

Title: Majesty Shredding
Review: Infusing--as per usual--squalling, buzzsaw guitars and Mac McCaughan's high-pitched, emotionally-charged vocals with simple yet cerebral lyrics that turn commonplace existence into something sad yet (as the title suggests) splendid, Majesty Shredding--their ninth album--brings their sonic template fully into the 21st century.

Title: Strike A Match
Review: Dependent on its rich texture and brought to life by the depth of the duo’s musicianship, this is an intriguing and deeply satisfying debut.

Title: White Van Music
Review: He proves himself every bit the master his reputation promises, especially on those elbow-throwing, drm-snapping beats he does best, yet he's still unsure of himself, too willing to play cloy cat chameleon when he should be honing his own increasingly beguiling technique. [Year End 2008, p.88]

Title: Metal Moon
Review: Metal Moon could be the soundtrack to an hour from now.

Title: The Center Won't Hold
Review: What's absent about The Center Won't Hold is that it presents a powerful and necessary premise, only to find out that there's not much of a message behind it. Sleater Kinney sure have a lot to say, but overall, they don't end up saying much.

Title: Winning Days
Review: There's not much left for the Vines' frontman other than his music, which on Winning Days seems more like an afterthought--if not the work of an unbearably bad Oasis record. [Apr 2004, p.98]

Title: Hundred Waters
Review: Their debut does more than enough to stand on its own, not only ambitious in its own right, but leaving little doubt about Hundred Waters' capability of handling wherever their ambition takes them from here.

Title: American Love Song
Review: Bingham embellishes the arrangements with Exile-style female backing vocals and country-skronk raucousness. ... The reflective moments pack a wallop as well. [Mar 2019, p.24]

Title: Power in Numbers
Review: As spiritual as Talib Kweli, as musically complex as Mos Def, as joyfully syncopated as the Roots, Power in Numbers sets the standard for intelligent hip hop.

Title: Love What Survives
Review: Love What Survives, with its seductive beats and incredible production, is a strong record that finally cuts Mount Kimbie’s ties with ‘post-dubstep’. If they can avoid falling into routine, their post-post-dubstep future looks exciting.

Title: Warp and Weft
Review: This is possibly her most satisfying album to date; it is, at times, quite spellbinding.

Title: Heart Blanche
Review: The breezy Isley Brothers/Free Design hybrid "Race Against Time," the perseverance anthem "Music to My Soul," and the disco-soul/soft rock compound "Better Late Than Never" are all decked out, and are among Green's craftiest work.

Artist: The Pains of Being Pure at Heart
Title: Days of Abandon
Review: This is the third Pains record in a row that has enough memorable songs to play almost like a career-spanning Best Of collection.

Title: folklore
Review: While the album tends to lull around its middle, folklore is far less concerned with its individual tracks than the greater, twisting conversation — the sort of hours-long, sanity-affirming chats that have become vital over these last four months.

Title: Keep The Village Alive
Review: There’s an impressive yield of ace tracks from the hand of the always-reliable Kelly Jones.

Title: Spacehopper
Review: Oasis bled into mediocrity faster than you can say 'Blur were better', but just occasionally on Spacehopper in Tripwires you can see the same ambition and pop nous that made their early tracks such a thrill to the mainstream.

Title: Margerine Eclipse
Review: The band's most organic-sounding record since 1996's Emperor Tomato Ketchup. [Mar 2004, p.90]

Title: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
Review: Half of the time Barnett, sounds like she isn't even trying, shrugging out moments of brilliance with ease and nonchalance. Whether she sits and thinks or sits and does nothing, it would appear the results are still golden.

Title: Yes Lawd!
Review: NxWorries spread their undoubted talents thinly across an offering several chillies shy of the full enchilada. [Dec 2016, p.93]

Title: Harmony Avenue
Review: It's a deft endeavour in making an album that speaks to the most bombastic music of the past, and it's an enjoyable listen – just be wary of ear fatigue.

Title: Megafaun
Review: Megafaun may be their most immediately ingratiating, rewarding LP yet, as well-suited for a night strapped into headphones as it is a lazy Sunday morning, dancing around the bedroom, munching casually on a pasta breakfast.

Title: Brainwashed
Review: Beautifully fatalistic and unimposingly pedagogical, Brainwashed is quite possibly Harrison's next-to-best album and a sober reminder that his passing is a loss too large to measure.

Title: Living Proof
Review: Like Skin Deep before it, Living Proof is distinguished by these bold, clenched blasts of sonic fury, but here the production has just enough grit to make the entire enterprise feel feral, and that's a greater testament to Guy's enduring vitality than any one song could ever be.

Title: Anniemal
Review: What makes Anniemal such a strong pop effort is its refusal to drop its high standards for production, melody, and hooks.

Title: Parallel Play
Review: The album is all over the place, with traces of Queen pop excesses flowing seamlessly with crunching, almost hardcore-punk-tinged guitar rockers and some weird stuff, too. Yet each of the tracks keeps Sloan’s Big Star-sounding power-pop roots intact.

Title: Depression Cherry
Review: Anyone who doesn't fall for Depression Cherry's hypnotic splendour probably just isn't a Beach House fan, or didn't live with the album long enough. But those who do will recognize this album as the sweeping, grand gesture they've been working up to giving us for the last nine years.

Title: I'll Be The Tornado
Review: The album's strongest moments are found in the duo's ability to live in the moment and take a deep, cleansing breath. [Nov 2014, p.88]

Title: The Wolf
Review: Compared to hearing 2001's instantly gratifying I Get Wet, listening to The Wolf is like getting mindblowing sex on a first date, only to have that person get a job at the Vatican the next day. [Oct 2003, p.136]

Title: Sleep Mountain
Review: Sleep Mountain has the emotional weight of a Boxer or a Turn on the Bright Lights, but it doesn’t quite have the tunes. That said, there’s still plenty to fall in love with here.

Title: Miss Colombia
Review: Pimienta has ably realized her potential and silenced those who doubted her deservingness.

Title: Eugene McGuinness
Review: It's wittier than it is moving or insightful, but give McGuinness time.

Title: I Love You, Honeybear
Review: The lyrics are brilliant and subtle.

Title: I Am Not a Human Being II
Review: His posse cuts are finally showing some savor too, albeit not on the vestigial guns 'n' violence ones.

Title: Locked Down
Review: Most impressively of all, it comfortably lives up to the promise that Auerbach apparently made to the Doctor that he would help him craft 'the best record you've made in a long time.'

Title: Sonic Highways
Review: Despite the high concept, this isn't exactly a major overhaul for the Foos: The eight songs on Sonic Highways have the same monster guitar crunch, pummeling crescendos and hard-pleading bridges found on every album they've made this millennium.

Title: Second Love
Review: The rewards are high. [Mar 2016, p.73]

Title: Til the Casket Drops
Review: Brothers Terrence “Pusha T” and Gene “Malice” Thornton--a.k.a. Clipse--spend a surprising amount of their third official album (not counting mixtapes and collaborative showcases) sounding both upbeat and reflective.

Title: blackSUMMERS'night
Review: A few tracks (the fuzzy 'Fistful of Tears') miss the mark, but this is the necessary R&B return from one of our great--and seemingly lost--soulmen.

Title: Divisionary
Review: There's a deliciously tangy freshness to the massed voices and acoustic thrum. [Apr 2014, p.103]

Title: My Favorite Picture of You
Review: In other words, classic Guy Clark.

Title: Replica
Review: It makes for a fascinating addition to the already-extensive OPN catalogue.

Title: TLC
Review: Sure, it’s nowhere in the same league as the seminal CrazySexyCool and the innovative concept album FanMail, and the absence of Left Eye--apart from a touching brief posthumous appearance on “Interlude”--is still keenly felt. But there are still a handful of tracks here which can sit comfortably alongside their incredible mid-late 90s canon.

Title: Bent Arcana
Review: The small army of musicians continue to merrily pursue their muse, unconcerned with the human logic of time and space.

Title: Hyacinths and Thistles
Review: These music box songs never overstay their welcome.

Title: Welcome to Condale
Review: The album is quite vibrant piece of '80s-flavored pop. [Oct 2011, p.103]

Title: Empire
Review: "Empire" has an almost childlike energy and determination that makes it feel strangely charming.

Title: DS2
Review: The album is sonically pleasing. [#267, p.92]

Title: Exploding Head
Review: This is a definite progression from their earlier material and if this is an indication of where the band is ultimately headed, then Exploding Head is likely to be the first of some very exciting albums.

Title: The Woods
Review: While it's surprising to hear Sleater-Kinney act so traditional, it's more shocking how well such conventions suit them. [27 May 2005, p.135]

Title: City Beach
Review: There's charm in its corniness. [Feb 2007, p.82]

Title: Fading Trails
Review: I'd say Fading Trails is the best Magnolia's done, unless you count the nominally Songs:Ohia-made Magnolia Electric Co., which I do, and which is still the best Molina product out.

Title: Who You Are
Review: Unfortunately, the songs on Who You Are that allow Jessie J's ugly, born-that-way vocals to cut loose are in the distinct minority. In the quest to find herself, she seems to have gotten sidetracked.

Title: 69 Love Songs
Review: Each song contains its own small epiphany, but they never quite add up to the one big sweeping epiphany that you'd hope for.

Title: Wreck
Review: Chris Spencer's vocals complete the darkly uncompromising picture, oozing a disgust and despair that's as much personal as socio-political. [Jul 2012, p.85]

Title: Hiss Spun
Review: Hiss Spun is the first record from Chelsea Wolfe that commits entirely to the more catastrophic elements of her repertoire, and the results are equal parts stunning and terrifying.

Title: Push the Heart
Review: One gets the sense that this is an album recorded with white gloves, and the calculation behind the tunes is nearly tangible.

Title: Drill a Hole in That Substrate and Tell Me What You See
Review: White seems to have turned a corner, taking his songs to places they haven't gone before.

Title: Nixon
Review: The album navigates effortlessly from peak to peak.

Title: Deep Down Happy
Review: The album's length is just about right, going by in an efficient 36 minutes but feeling satisfying at the end, and while fans are bound to pick favorites, there's not a real dud in the bunch.

Title: Moth
Review: The most impressive thing about Moth is the way it manages to wrap a more compact frame around Chairlift’s spiraling colors without dulling the final product.

Title: The Loon
Review: The first must-listen record of the year.

Title: Black Sea
Review: The low tide image on the cover Black Sea suggests that this process of covering and uncovering is cyclical, and the music bears it out by adding a welcome bit of noise and depth to some stately and slowly evolving melodies.

Title: Spring Tides
Review: Amongst the other songs of Spring Tides it only serves to pull you further under the hypnotic spell of Jeniferever.

Title: Ghost Stories
Review: Rousing, downtempo pop to soothe a troubled soul.

Title: Kids in the Street
Review: J.T. Earle's latest teams him with Omaha indie-rock don Mike Mogis (Bright Eyes) for his rangiest set yet.

Title: Collagically Speaking
Review: The pace occasionally saunters, but this is an ultimately positive exercise in the group's titular "reflection and response." [Aug 2018, p.95]

Title: Human Animal
Review: The word "unnerving" doesn't account for the range of senses that get pulled down into this abyss. [#22, p.98]

Title: Dedication
Review: Zomby is a fantastically personal person whose music has never come across as less than touching. Dedication defines him as an artist to watch, and perhaps more importantly as an artist to be enjoyed.

Title: Countless Branches
Review: Countless Branches does nothing different, but seems to knock them all dead by virtue of its naked simplicity alone. Some of these tracks are scarcely crafted songs at all but simple musings, addressed to no one in particular, not even an inward self, just uttered over soft, slow piano chords. [Mar 2020, p.48]

Title: The Desaturating Seven
Review: Conceptually big but musically slight, this return of the early ’90s Primus lineup promises a lot but delivers only fragments of what we know this band is capable of.

Title: Bonfires on the Heath
Review: Bonfires is certainly a step up on its efficient, bloodless predecessor "God Save The Clientele" and stands up no matter what’s next for the band.

Title: The Campfire Headphase
Review: Ultimately, The Campfire Headphase shows continuity with the duo's previous recordings but fails to replicate the sheer beauty and awe-inspiring quality of past material, sounding at times like the work of very good Boards of Canada copyists.

Title: Broken Bells
Review: Burton builds layered, twilit soundscapes for Mercer's pensive musings; these songs are the stuff of cloudy days and sleepless nights, and that's okay.

Title: Swimming
Review: This is deeply personal material that’s as impressive if not as game-changing as anything esteemed rap figures Kendrick Lamar and Childish Gambino have produced in recent years. Miller has turned his anguish into one of the year’s most disarmingly pleasant records.

Title: Darling Arithmetic
Review: An album that delivers a gorgeous, if somewhat restrained, step forward. It’s a document of quiet, if not necessarily earth-shattering, revelations.

Title: Go Go Smear the Poison Ivy
Review: Wisely, they make no attempt  to replicate the wide-eyed wonder of their earlier work, returning to experimentation to reach a happy compromise with maturity. [Fall 2007, p.80]

Artist: King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard
Title: Infest the Rats' Nest
Review: On Infest the Rats' Nest their garage rock roots are almost imperceptible, as they commit so heartily to thrash metal and produce an album placed firmly at the top of its genre.

Title: Bare
Review: A stripped-down set of acoustic songs sung in a voice that is sometimes overly winsome but at its best is hauntingly ethereal. [Feb 2019, p.24]

Title: Humanz
Review: This is intelligent party music, but it’s also headphone listening. Production is manic and plays at an attention deficit (though really these songs are crafted with a mandala-concentration, rich in samples, styles, and sonic layering).

Title: Two Lanes of Freedom
Review: You’ll want to hit the road and play this one over and over.

Title: Modern English Decoration
Review: This is a band on a journey. Modern English Decoration nods to its predecessor, certainly, but you can hear the way in which the original duo has consolidated their appeal as a five-piece. These guys have got promise written all over them.

Title: ISAM
Review: More than any other electronic producer of the past decade, Amon Tobin's music goes places. From start to finish, ISAM is an adventure through sound and actuated potential.

Title: Weird Drift
Review: [The album] is so blatantly, almost self-consciously pleasurable it should come, like an insalubrious takeaway, with heavy duty napkins. [Apr 2014, p.65]

Title: Anoyo
Review: Because Anoyo is not just a companion work to Hecker's monumental record, but rather a fantastic conclusion to a stunning journey that started through the overwhelming presence of Konoyo, inside this world, and now finished through the beautiful, dreamlike sceneries of Anoyo.

Title: Startin' Fires
Review: A  vigorous cross-section of wallop and weepers that revels in its down-home personality.

Title: Occulting Disk
Review: The undulating, snarling “Black Transit Of Jupiter’s Third Satellite” is a bubbling 12 minute antimatter expanse, the pot of black gold at the end of this particular rainbow. The journey to get there is ravishingly bleak and massaging. [Jan 2020, p.58]

Title: Silver Ladders
Review: In Silver Ladders, Mary Lattimore brings the harp back down to earth still covered in clouds, but also threaded with veins of gloom that marble its silvery glow.

Title: Talkie Walkie
Review: Where Air's previous album failed to ignite like their classic Moon Safari, they have made some amends on Talkie Walkie. [Jan 2004, p.74]

Title: Leisure Seizure
Review: Unfortunately, Vek's voice outstays its welcome by the middle of the album. Leisure Seizure is front-loaded with its best material, such that the second half of the record becomes rather tedious.

Title: Let the Poison Out
Review: Let the Poison Out only ups the ante. Distortion is easy and lo-fi bands are a dime a dozen, but hardly any of them clean up this well.

Title: Home Again
Review: By adding little touches like a gospel call and response ("Bones") and a haunting, echoing choir ("Always Waiting"), the listening becomes a more rewarding experience.

Title: Turn The Lights Out
Review: Turn the Lights Out is the most mature and technically accomplished album the Ponys have made to date, but it doesn't lack the excitement and edge of the fine music that preceded it.

Title: Idle Labor
Review: Feeling more airbrushed than lo-fi. [Jul 2011, p.79]

Title: Scissor Sisters
Review: Scattershot.

Title: Circles Around The Sun
Review: Their new self-titled album serves as a welcome sonic elixir from the distressing realities of 2020.

Title: High Off Life
Review: Pretty much the only complaint is that, similar to all of his releases since the infamous EVOL, it delivers and lives up to the hype, but it doesn't build and surpass his previous work. It remains to be seen whether he will ever create an album that is better than everything he's done so far, but this is still an extremely solid release.

Title: Tired of Tomorrow
Review: They move a rung up on the shoegaze ladder by toning things back even more than their 2014 record and what's even more noticeable is that quite a few directions taken here, ring similar to bands Yip worked on over the past couple years. Nothing, however, still have an extra something to their music.

Title: Quiet Signs
Review: The record’s nine songs clock in at just 28 minutes total, which feels just right, the samey-ness among songs playing as a strength, conjuring a mood and maintaining it, yet never feeling predictable, in part because it’s hard to get a bead on precisely what each song is about.

Title: Meds
Review: Piles on near-emo levels of deep feelings over a plush bed of New Order synth beats and echoey atmospherics. [6 Apr 2006, p.69]

Title: Take Care, Take Care, Take Care
Review: Take Care is less ragged than Those Who Tell the Truth Shall Die, but it's otherwise a very similar album.

Title: You Know I'm Not Going Anywhere
Review: This is a fantastic record, and yet another reminder of how good this band are. Nothing seems out of place, not a single riff or beat is wasted. New styles are performed with vigour, and the band sound energised and refreshed. An essential release.

Title: Until The Colours Run
Review: Lanterns on the Lake have drawn on harsh experience to produce a beautiful record that’s anything but superficial.

Title: Complicated Game
Review: Complicated Game is brilliant album, dense and thoughtful as McMurtry swirls around inside the heads of another set of fascinating characters.

Title: FLOTUS
Review: A dozen records deep in their career, we find Lambchop at their most adventurous, and it sounds wonderful.

Title: Death Is This Communion
