Review: The deeper you go into the record, the more reassured you become that these musicians know what they’re great at.

Title: Fear Yourself
Review: Not even Linkous can prop up this house of cards for long. [#58, p.94]

Title: Black Age Blues
Review: With overwhelming heaviness tempered by blues and gospel vibes, this enthralling comeback soothes the soul even as Goatsnake crush your ears. [13 Jun 2015, p.52]

Title: Hospitality
Review: Regardless of their ability to stand out in a crowd, they write tunes sharper than a thumbtack, with words that ramble around in fascinating stream-of-consciousness webs.

Title: The Fool
Review: The beautiful skeleton of a shoe-gazing album.

Title: Oh Inhuman Spectacle
Review: It's a compelling mix, although the gaseous atmospheres and subtle melodies of Unbalancing Acts and To Swim drift too far toward shapelessness. It's a highly promising debut nonetheless. [Jul 2016, p.111]

Title: High Violet
Review: High Violet is the sound of a band taking a mandate to be a meaningful rock band seriously, and they play the part so fully that, to some, it may be off-putting. But these aren't mawkish, empty gestures; they're anxious, personal songs projected onto wide screens.

Title: Voxtrot
Review: Voxtrot’s self-titled debut album is marvelous: a collection of 11 tightly coiled songs, loud and fast and sweet.

Title: Complete Surrender
Review: Sleeker, stronger and more confident than ever, on Complete Surrender Slow Club flourish with each strum and every breath.

Title: Be The Void
Review: There's enough here to keep fans happy and even win a few more over in the process, but it's another mixed bag from a band that are easier to like than love.

Title: Brickbat
Review: Even on these quieter moments, Brickbat's invigorated feel is palpable--and contagious. It would've been easy for the members of Piroshka to rest on their laurels, but they prove they have a lot of new ideas to offer their listeners, regardless of how familiar they may be with the band's previous work.

Title: Loose
Review: Furtado is game... but Timbo brings beats, not chemistry.  Loose isn't a love child, but a bump-and-grind that never finds a groove.

Title: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
Review: T Bone Burnett's trademark production has the rhythm section thumping as if you were listening to the whole thing from a booth at your favorite pub. Which suits Earle fine.

Title: Slowdive
Review: The result is an album that can stand easily with Slowdive’s other heights and that manages the extremely tricky feat of sounding like the band that fans love and missed while at the same time marking a new step forward. The

Title: Last Man Standing
Review: On Last Man Standing, Willie Nelson continues to turn his ninth decade into a classic country song full of remembrance, regret and resilience.

Title: Marble Skies
Review: Marble Skies finds difficulty in consolidating each defining element into a smooth blend, leading to a record that’s bookended by heart-stopping tracks with a frustratingly stodgy middle passage.

Title: She Has No Strings Apollo
Review: Thrilling. [May 2003, p.106]

Title: An Imaginary Country
Review: If you've got patience it's a quiet joy; if not, it'll drive you nuts.

Title: Anika
Review: Full of lyrical and musical contradictions, such as the exhortation to 'join the revolution' in Yang Yang, it isn't exactly rabble rousing - but has a strange allure nonetheless.

Title: Tha Carter II
Review: For merely running in place, TC3 can be transfixing. But it is not enough. [20 June 2008, p.66]

Title: Paramore
Review: Paramore feels far more human and honest than anything the band have committed to tape to date, and even at its most intense, the record feels intimate (or at least like a gig happening in the back corner of your mind).

Title: Everything Not Saved Will Be Lost (Part 1)
Review: Guitars play more of a supporting role, and the tonal shifts suits the band, with Philippakis's voice given much more room to float elegantly through the record, [Apr 2019, p.29]

Title: Not To Disappear
Review: Not to Disappear is intentionally difficult to stomach. It finds a dark pit to nestle in and then digs deeper. But few acts could deliver these unceasingly grim details with such majesty.

Title: God Bless the Go-Go's
Review: Sharply written, energetically performed, and slickly produced, it actually sounds like the album Go-Go's fans have waited 17 years to hear.

Title: The Instigator
Review: Sung with the versatile confidence of a star, and impeccably assisted by ace producer Jon Brion, The Instigator's songs feel instantly familiar in the best way possible.

Title: Father Creeper
Review: Mathambo leaps about on a hotplate of styles, rarely dwelling on a groove for long. Move with him, though, because it's worth the breakneck effort.

Title: SBTRKT
Review: What these tracks are, though, are lovingly programmed, laser-dappled, preening--thanks to Sampha's buttery soul voice--and glossy reduxes of late-'90s two-step and twitchy post-house that should be filed next to James Blake and Jamie Woon.

Title: Broken Stay Open Sky
Review: A mature and complex collection.

Title: Luminous Night
Review: While normally "killer flute" and "far-out sitar" playing would feel incredibly counterfeit coming from a white guy based in California, it's his classic roots that keep it all grounded. And this album has both in spades. [Summer 2009, p.93]

Title: Have Some Faith In Magic
Review: The addition of vocals is hugely welcome, even if they are only Panda  Bear-style chants. [Apr 2012, p.77]

Title: Source
Review: Elevated throughout by Garcia's immaculate phrasing, this is music that fuses he tradition and modern with real purpose. [Sep 2020, p.110]

Title: One Second of Love
Review: Early music is fascinating to people in a way that goes deeper than anything else, and for musicians and artists, all those early things spill out in the things we make. Gonzalez does that here in a fun and remarkable way.

Title: Dreams Worth More Than Money
Review: Maybe it only all coheres in flashes, but if Meek Mill works best in bursts, then so be it.

Title: The Crucible
Review: Easily as satisfying as The Tower, The Crucible builds on its predecessor's achievement with brilliant composition, inspired performance, and consummate musicianship. It is an excellent example of how to mine rock's past in order to discover its future.

Title: All Time Present
Review: Confident and resourceful, All Time Present feels more open than its predecessor. [May 2019, p.54

Title: Down There
Review: Down There, David Portner aka Tare's debut solo joint, is a further dot on the still-empty dotted line of Animal Collective's career, built on a span of eight or so albums through which these guys have willfully, lovingly defied expectations and definitions and even maybe their own individual talents.

Title: We Mean Business
Review: Old school, but somehow not old hat. [Feb 2009, p.113]

Title: How To Die In The North
Review: An exhilarating step beyond [the 2005 and 2007] albums' late-'60s foundations. [Feb 2015, p.93]

Title: Dear Science
Review: TV On The Radio sound wise beyond their years, youthful stars whose mouthpiece contorts itself into funk shapes and whups without sounding like an out-of-depth chancer.

Title: Neon Bible
Review: If "Neon Bible" doesn't quite dazzle as "Funeral" did, that's more a measure of the latter album's benchmark brilliance, rather than the inferiority of the former.

Title: Major
Review: Major doesn't run at the consistently breakneck pace of Fang Island's debut, but the group rely less on near-ludicrous histrionics and more on exhibiting the joy of creation through complex and confident songwriting.

Title: Highway Hypnosis
Review: While brevity has consistently been a feature of Moolchan’s work, here the relatively short song lengths mean that some tracks can feel somewhat intangible, ending before they seem to be getting into their stride.

Title: Parts
Review: Altogether, Parts is stimulating, surprising, and utterly inventive. The duo demands attention from listeners, requiring mental acrobatics as they flit from one idea to another.

Title: Uneasy Laughter
Review: Uneasy Laughter is fine. It’d be much better if it was either divorced from ruminations on honesty, or if the band actually managed to define themselves without leaning on ’80s nostalgia.

Title: Game Theory
Review: Game Theory turns out to be The Roots’ finest record to date.

Title: Brotherhood of the Snake
Review: That one track ["Canna-Business"] aside, Brotherhood of the Snake is not only on par with Testament's best records during the millennium thus far, but ever.

Title: Black Messiah
Review: Black Messiah confirms that music holds the power to challenge and comfort, to take us someplace spiritual, political, and existential. It’s beautifully, devastatingly human.

Title: The Unseen In Between
Review: His strongest set of songs yet. The guitar work remains effortless and radiant, but it is no longer the dominant thing. Instead the songs, bolstered by strings and vocal harmonies, take precedence. There’s an easy, lovely coherence to this record.

Title: The Mix-Up
Review: "The Mix-Up" is thematically sound and feels like a comprehensive piece instead of a self-indulgent scheme. [30 Jun 2007]

Title: BeyoncÃ©
Review: Beyoncé's got the tour out of the way first--with this year's Mrs Carter jaunt--and released a singleless, multi-layered, head-spinning album second. Maybe she knew what she was doing after all.

Title: Similes
Review: What ultimately makes Similes so wonderful is that with every listen it seems to peel away the world around you, immersing you in its warmth, and for 43 minutes, it makes it so hard to believe that everything that might be wrong in your life actually matters at all.

Title: Cerebral Ballzy
Review: They're most fun when they're really letting loose, though, which is pretty much always.

Title: Lucifer
Review: Lucifer is definitely not for everyone, but for some it will be their album of the year.

Title: Eyes Open
Review: To sum them up in one word, "reliable" would be the most appropriate.

Title: In the Cool of the Day
Review: With his piano-playing accompanied by Daniel Joseph Dorff's drumming, the arrangements are minimal affairs, placing Moore's voice centre stage and allowing the songs to breathe. [Mar 2011, p.112]

Title: Novum
Review: A solid 11-song set. [May 2017, p.92]

Title: New Glow
Review: This 10-song effort will almost surely be a part of the soundtrack powering every block party, barbecue, summer shindig--and certainly toward the dance floor. [May 2015, p.98]

Title: Barbara Barbara, we face a shining future
Review: Near perfect and a step forward as well, Barbara Barbara, We Face a Shining Future belongs on Underworld's top shelf.

Title: Gloss Drop
Review: Clearly, these New York math-rockers have yet to learn the values of de- cluttering, with most of these dozen pieces involving furious industry to no great advantage.

Title: Wild Young Hearts
Review: The Noisettes have done a stylistic handbrake turn for the follow-up, and come up with an intoxicating blend of pop, soul and disco. [May 2009, p.116]

Title: Hesitation Marks
Review: This is the sound of a cleaner, smoother Nine Inch Nails, one that delights in complexities of rhythm more than caustic blasts of rage.

Title: Other People's Problems
Review: It's far from perfect - 'Ghost Note' sounds horribly like Skrillex in places - but there [are] enough interesting sonic detours to suggest that these agitators of sound are more than just another over-hyped gimmick band.

Title: Sour Soul
Review: The trio [Badbadnotgood] create nuanced, immersive contexts for the rapper's narratives: occasionally dialed in, at times surprising. [Mar 2015, p.71]
Ejstes' fiddle playing is certainly missed, but that's a minor complaint from an otherwise top-notch effort.

Title: Nobody Realizes This Is Nowhere
Review: After a while, Nobody--frenetic but faceless, too nonchalant for true nonconformity--starts to blur together.

Title: Beta Love
Review: Ra Ra Riot devotees will also recognize this electronic turn. The change, although typical of seemingly every 21st-century band, is respectfully executed, retaining Ra Ra Riot’s unique style, making this third album far less superfluous than most indie-rock bands’ later efforts.

Title: Heartbreak Pass
Review: There’s a lot of thought behind the offhand delivery, from the wry aphorisms of the lyrics to the structure of the album, a rambling decrescendo from rowdy to folky to nearly private.

Title: Me and Armini
Review: There is most certainly a parallel universe in which Emilana Torrini is the Next Big Thing.

Title: Li(f)e
Review: Li(f)e's major selling points are the Americana-tinged instrumentals that dutifully counterpoint Francis' rebukes. [Spring 2010, p.74]

Title: Next Thing
Review: For all its touching and personal lyrical matter, Next Thing undoubtedly boasts improved production and more developed song-structures, as well as a more fluid use of warm synths and punchy snare drums.

Title: Food & Liquor
Review: By boldly expanding the parameters of mainstream hip-hop, Fiasco's threatening to make rap a welcoming place for geeks and iconoclasts as well as pimps and thugs.

Title: Beings
Review: All in all another strong outing from the Newcastle band, it dwells in a cloudy blend of dreams and creeping nightmares, unsettling yet captivating.

Title: Transgender Dysphoria Blues
Review: Transgender Dysphoria Blues might be the most important album of the year, and its message will hopefully seep into music culture and spread till records like this don’t *have* to get made anymore.

Title: My Dinosaur Life
Review: My Dinosaur Life, with it's punchy guitars and lyrics about ennui and breaking up and video games, would fit perfectly in any blink fan's iTunes library.

Title: Chris
Review: Here, as with Grimes, percussion is used as a weapon; none of the lyrics are clichéd top 40 pap. Unlike Grimes, however, Letissier has a bold, synthetic funk payload to commend her, and her lyrics are more obviously personal.

Title: Paradise
Review: Paradise challenges its listeners to emotionally engage with their surroundings in hopes that they develop a conscious understanding that there are consequences to our daily conveniences.

Title: Stills
Review: Gauntlet Hair’s reference points are sublime, of course, but when they come up with the grudging funk of ‘Simple’, it’s something that’s all their own work.

Title: Why Love Now
Review: Why Love Now truly comes to life when the band uses their punishing sound to explore the absurdity of modern masculinity.

Title: Tourist
Review: [A] ham-fisted attempt at being exactly like everything else.

Title: A Time to Love
Review: Wonder's delivery never stumbles. His earnestness carries even the least successful of his numbers (except "Raindrops" and probably "Positivity") by being so convincing.

Title: Get Ready
Review: Negotiate Steve Osborne's rather dated stadium Techno-rock production, and there's plenty to stimulate here... [#211, p.70]

Title: American V: A Hundred Highways
Review: Unsurprisingly, American V is the most desolate of the series, bereft of the moments of playfulness that leavened its predecessors. [Aug 2006, p.92]

Title: Strangers
Review: Occasionally tracks are achingly earnest; but overall this is light in the darkness, about love and death and bravery of all kinds. [May 2014, p.94]

Title: Congotronics
Review: Stick on the nine minutes of opener Lufuala Ndonga, turn the bottom end up and stand back. What happens next is unbelievable. [May 2005, p.98]

Title: Suddenly
Review: Everywhere you turn there is something beautiful. [Apr 2020, p.114]

Title: Preparations
Review: Preparations will leave you dizzy and wondering what it all means-- which may be the point. [Nov 2007, p.124]

Title: AmeriKKKant
Review: Al Jourgensen's signature vocal bark remains unchanged, but things have slowed down musically. Fans of Ministry's lightning-fast thrash moments will be disappointed by the record's grinding pace.

Title: Grinderman 2
Review: The music veers between between a kind of funk slop with trippy organ squelches and good ol' fashioned rawk with biblical overtones, It feels a little like drowning in a bath of Jack Daniels, but not in a good way. [Sep 2010, p.53]

Title: Clockwork Angels
Review: A geekier and nerdier Rush? Yes, which is actually a very good thing.

Title: Narrow Stairs
Review: Narrow Stairs proves that with Death Cab For Cutie, it's possible to relax and let them do their own thing. Which is a remarkable thing indeed. [Spring 2008, p.75]

Title: Black Market Music
Review: Black Market Music loses its sparkle and its melodic sense whenever it grows a conscience.

Title: Transcendental Blues
Review: Earle has let the spook out of the closet, so he can bare his spiritual chest (as it were) with a Lennonesque honesty and a vocal delivery that increasingly resembles Tom Petty's sub-Dylan sneer.

Title: Goat Girl
Review: From start to finish, the album is a mix of complete swamp-rock songs, only to be broken up by confusing, short bursts of instrumentation.

Title: Cherish the Light Years
Review: Mr. Eisold's voice has the certainty of Dave Gahan and the quiver of Robert Smith, and Cold Cave's music is deeply indebted to New Order and, in weaker spots, even has a touch of A Flock of Seagulls: the synths hit hard, vibrating at a bitter frequency, and the guitars are tuned to just this side of serrated jangle.

Title: Nosebleed Weekend
Review: The 13 songs on Nosebleed Weekend communicate angst, anger, and regret by turns, but that feeling of comfort rests like a soft pillow at the very bottom of the mix, giving the trio enough confidence to explore corners of their sound they had never thought to unearth before.

Title: Pink
Review: Pink is easily the most cohesive, adventurous, and straight-ahead rocking recording of their 12-year career.

Title: The Non-Stop EP
Review: While they’re not bringing anything musically innovative to the table, they’ve re-packaged the sounds in a way that feels distinctly 21st Century. It’s extremely good fun and presented without pretence – and that feels like enough.

Title: Baby Teeth
Review: Balancing restraint with a keen ear for pop-friendly hooks inspired by Jack Antonoff, Dizzy manage to make quite the opening statement with Baby Teeth.

Title: Something
Review: Somewhere between Ladyhawke and M83, it's 1980's fetishism all the better for the apparent lack of irony.

Title: Everything in Between
Review: With the stunning Everything in Between, Randall and Spunt's emergent sonic juggernaut, No Age is continuing to build, brick by brick, a bulletproof reputation for thunderous virtuosity-all without leaning on worthless crutches like Auto-Tune, capitalized formula, compromise and other fakery that divides pretenders from those who set fire to the dustbin of musical history.

Title: Mean Everything to Nothing
Review: Though Manchester Orchestra’s dedication points to the possibility of good things in the future, Mean Everything to Nothing falls largely flat.

Title: Word of Mouf
Review: With his fashionably foul worldview, Ludacris could indeed be [Redd] Foxx's bastard son, and ''Word'' often seems like nothing so much as an extended Dolemite routine set to hip-hop beats.

Title: Unfold
Review: The Necks don't exactly break new ground with Unfold, but it's refreshing nonetheless to see that they're also not regressing--a small miracle for any band 30 years into their career.

Title: FLIGHT
Review: While the ringtone-catchy Alive and fuzzed-up Stressy are obvious standouts, it's the reckless try-anything funk of Leader that holds best claim to being Flight's spirit guide. [Jul 2020, p.106]

Title: I Learned the Hard Way
Review: I Learned the Hard Way, her fourth album with the Dap-Kings is pure joy, even when heartbreak sends her voice digging deep. This isn't just old-school; it is school.

Title: Brand New Day
Review: There’s nothing “brand new” about the Mavericks’ music; yet in this era of by-the-numbers, narrowly pigeon-holed playing, the group’s inclusive, adventurous vision is refreshingly unconventional and truly alternative.

Title: The DeAndre Way
Review: A shaky stab at Soulja manhood, the third disc from the Crank That cutie finds him hitting drinking age, torn between pup and pit bull.

Title: Duality
Review: Devilish and delicious, the album can be precious to a fault, as following all the Queen-sized arrangements and all the Adam Lambert-esque sass isn't an everyday thing for most.

Title: Melody of Certain Damaged Lemons
Review: Blonde Redhead's biggest detractors focus on the group's uncanny resemblance to Sonic Youth. But while Melody of Certain Damaged Lemons won't exactly silence such suggestions, it does seem to move conscientiously away from the influences that have marred the group's previous work.

Title: Take Control
Review: Slaves pull no punches with social and political commentary. But Take Control is also diverse and boasts sly British humor. [Nov 2016, p.90]

Title: Rockin' the Suburbs
Review: The new Ben Folds is a lot like the old one: as unpredictable as he is talented.

Title: Collapse Into Now
Review: The album clearly bounces back and forth between those moments of emotional annihilation and utter hope and optimism.  But more than that, with those tracks book-ending the effort, the record's most basic motif is clear: even as lords of rock, the men of R.E.M. still struggle daily with their own issues and the standards of the world, but welcome the battle with ever-glowing smiles.

Title: Moondagger
Review: Because the album is so continuously lush and candy-coated with a shoegaze gleam, no particular song really sticks out. Instead, hooks surface slowly from the electro-wash, rewarding repeated listens.

Title: Pay the Devil
Review: At the end of the day, it's really hard to screw up these songs with that voice--try as he might.

Title: Good Grief
Review: As put-together as Good Grief’s presentation is, and as ingratiating as its songs are, the record suffers from a distinct lack of identity.

Title: Rainbow
Review: Rainbow, her rich, masterful third LP, is far more than a kiss-off to old demons--it’s an artistic feat, as Kesha unites stylistic forays with her sharp, weathered lyricism.

Title: Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper
Review: Striking a balance between hypnotic pop and cloudy soul-searching, the album delivers all the ends of the spectrum Lennox has spent years perfecting, giving fully realized and refreshingly jubilant examples of a type of pop music so distinctive to its creator, he ends up in a class by himself.

Title: Meadow
Review: Buckner’s interest here is in a wallowing mouthful of atmosphere—dominant drums, throbbing guitar, and a fair amount of piano. This has always been the case, but the compositions are seamlessly edited and cleanly brought from instrument to recording.

Title: I Love You, Honeybear
Review: A messy, extravagant, astonishing, beguiling and honest experience: that’s love, and that’s also what I Love You, Honeybear is. Just magnificent.

Title: All My Heroes Are Cornballs
Review: Song to song, it’s genuinely exciting to see where JPEGMAFIA might go next, and you never quite know what to expect. JPEGMAFIA’s third album is his most accomplished record yet.

Title: Metropole
Review: Metropole is very close to being a masterpiece, falling just short of their own standard set by The Greatest Story Ever Told.

Title: White Trash with Money
Review: Like his last album, this one's less about attitude than song craft. [14 Apr 2006, p.85]

Title: Abandoned City
Review: The album may have been inspired by empty urban voids and desolate space but the ideas and execution found on Abandoned City conversely indicate a depth and creative vigour that is close to reaching peak form.

Title: Hurry Up and Wait
Review: While you could write off this album for not attempting to push any musical boundaries, there's an authenticity to their relatable lyricism that gives reason to their polarising popularity.

Title: hopeless fountain kingdom
Review: Hopeless Fountain Kingdom might be defiantly ambitious, but it’s surprisingly cohesive.

Title: Last
Review: Bewitching and hugely ambitious. [Apr 2011, p.110]

Title: House of Spirits
Review: House of Spirits is the saturnine successor nobody asked for, a detour though a bramble patch running parallel to a stretch of open road.

Title: Love, Hate, and Then There's You
Review: The Von Bondies' long-in-coming follow-up Love, Hate And Then There's You continues in that arena-ready modern-rock mode, but it's considerably brighter--even campier.

Title: In Rolling Waves
Review: In minor contrast to the band's previous effort, the moments of pared-down instrumentation here seem to offer a necessary respite from the intensity, providing necessary moments of calm as we anticipate the next joyous sonic wave.

Title: The Crying Light
Review: Whatever hopes you held in the aftermath of "I Am a Bird Now," they have been exponentially exceeded in poetry, music, and honesty here.

Title: Visions of Bodies Being Burned
Review: It’s been said that every era gets the monster they deserve. If this is the case then ‘Visions of Bodies Being Burned’ is everything wrong, and right, with the world distilled into 52- minutes of absurdist hip-hop. We’ve never had it so good!

Title: Gimme Fiction
Review: Some of [Daniel's] stripped-down material sounds gaunt. [May 2005, p.166]

Title: The Final Frontier
Review: Maiden have long had a knack for the lung-busting chorus, but what impresses here are the complicated arrangements.

Title: Hot Fuss
Review: Wait a minute... you mean this isn't a Duran Duran album?

Title: Free So Free
Review: He's singing better than ever--his attenuated Neil Young whine has developed into a deeper, mellower, less distracting instrument--and his arrangements of percussive punch and fuzzy guitar have rarely sounded so effortlessly rocking.

Title: The Bedlam in Goliath
Review: But even the highest highs soon crash and dissipate, wallowing once more in a proggy bog.

Title: Machineries of Joy
Review: While British Sea Power do occasionally revert back to the anthemic formula that worked so well on previous albums, on the whole, Machineries Of Joy is a more considered and composed effort.

Title: There's a Riot Going On
Review: There are flickers of the old fire on There’s a Riot Going on (which bears no similarity to Sly and the Family Stone, to the surprise of precisely no one).

Title: Lion City
Review: Global fusion at its most democratic and exhilarating. [May 2014, p.73]

Title: Last of Our Kind
Review: Ultimately, it turns out The Darkness are at their worst when doing an impression of themselves, which is exactly what Last Of Our Kind is.

Title: Ride Out
Review: There’s plenty of meat-and-potatoes rock and blues here for you to chow on and wash down with your favorite domestic beer.

Title: Modern Vampires of the City
Review: Full of heart and full of ideas, it’s big, clever and brilliantly odd.

Title: The Color Before the Sun
Review: After initial queasiness at a moment of amorousness in Eraser (‘I’m just a toy waiting for you to play me’), it quickly becomes business as usual in terms of their shamelessly enormous pop-rock music.

Title: Lines
Review: Understated, lovely. [Feb 2017, p.98]

Title: Amphetamine Ballads
Review: There are a handful of moments here when he turns himself inside-out over the course of a song, bringing him into the orbit of those artists he so obviously idolizes. Now he just needs to figure out how to emulate his starting position.

Title: Kiss Each Other Clean
Review: The equivalent of changing radio stations in his more youthful days, Kiss Each Other Clean is the result of Beam uncontrollably turning the radio knob until finding the right tune in his head.

Title: Anxiety
Review: The songs aren't strong enough to make it feel vibrant. Only the chugging Cellophane captures the giddy, filmic qualities of Ladyhawke's early songs.

Title: A Crow Looked at Me
Review: Overwhelming and beautiful. [May 2017, p.35]

Title: The Clearing
Review: This a slow-burning, intimate and accomplished disc, best enjoyed if you clear some space to let it grow.

Title: Ash
Review: This message of positivity, strength and optimism is one that is weaved throughout each track on their new album Ash.

Title: Compassion
Review: While Barnes is definitely well-versed in musical melancholy, there's also a thoughtful, sensitive part to balance all this pathos.

Title: The Beginning
Review: Although the overall plot of the album is sparse, it's hard to deny the enjoyment it can bring to you. If you know what to expect when you hear it, you can take The Beginning for what it is: a feel good album.

Title: The Magician's Private Library
Review: The ruminative, skittering TVOTR rhythmic patterns distract from Miranda's strengths even with the occasional injections of some easy-breezy horn lines or soul-jazz keys. [Winter 2010, p.100]

Title: Past Life Martyred Saints
Review: A record that is both magical and heartbreaking, Past Life Martyred Saints looks to be a beautiful start for Anderson, who has a small handful of live shows set up for the summer.

Title: FFS
Review: FFS is actually exciting to listen to, which can’t be said that often these days.

Title: The Golden Archipelago
Review: With its serene landscapes and beautiful imagery, listening to The Golden Archipelago makes waiting for the tropical temperatures of summer all the more difficult.

Title: Horrorscope
Review: The band's music and lyrics often still sound labored

Title: DNCE
Review: Now Joe’s back again with DNCE’s first full-length, and this time he’s dispensing with metaphor altogether.

Title: Sprinter
Review: These are songs that mostly get to the heart of the matter with open-hearted directness, and in balancing the coarse with the refined there’s a clearer sense of what Scott wants to find even if she struggles to understand the conditions that affect her most deeply.

Title: What Went Down
Review: There are superficial differences in aggression—slightly more electronic buzzing, harsher vocals, gristly guitars. It’s Foals’ raw record, but it’s still filet mignon tartare.... What Went Down is their most consistent, steady-handed work yet.

Title: Lay It Down
Review: Playing up his role as elder statesman, Green gets away with delivering the familiar back-in-the-day sermon because listeners expect it from an icon of the past. However, by infusing such consistent gentleness throughout the entire record, he pulls off the unthinkable in the early 21st century--a momentary respite.

Title: Wonderful, Glorious
Review: Luckily, there’s enough good on this album to hide the negatives.

Title: Surtur Rising
Review: As perfect as Twilight is, though, Surtur Rising houses it handily.

Title: Hormone Lemonade
Review: There's no straining to distance themselves from their former band [Stereolab]. [Apr 2018, p.24]

Title: Songs
Review: A profoundly, if unexpectedly, moving record. [Dec 2014, p.109]

Title: The Nature of Imitation
Review: An album of abundant imagination, if elusive meaning. [Sep 2018, p.110]

Title: Six Cups of Rebel
Review: When [the album] is all over the lingering echoes are of dizziness and disappointment.

Title: Fever Dream
Review: Alias gives us a promise that, after closing a three-year mute gap, after a decade of production and creation, there is still in him an artist to be excited about.

Title: Lifes Rich Pageant
Review: Although it shines a giant and unmistakable signal toward the direct and poppy approach the band would undertake on their next few albums, Pageant still retains the mumbles of Murmur, the jangles of Reckoning, and the rustic tones of Fables of the Reconstruction.

Title: Circular Sounds
Review: Circular Sounds takes the craft aspect to a higher level. Stoltz’s early records were scrappy, guitar-centric home recordings, and his previous LP, Below the Branches, was a piano-dominated, primary colors affair, but this one is a study in how to blend signifiers and sonorities so that they enhance each other.

Title: How to Dance
Review: This is an album to savor from a band that continues to grow and to surprise.

Title: Random Access Memories
Review: The record will remain, something that channels the past but sounds like little else right now, an album about rediscovery that's situated in the constantly-shifting present.

Title: Two Lanes of Freedom
Review: Overall, Two Lanes of Freedom is uneven but likeable, just like most Tim McGraw records.

Title: At War With The Mystics
Review: This is a band that, rightfully, just sounds tired.

Title: Oceans Apart
Review: McLennan's guitar enlivens even Forster's sketchier contributions ("Mountains Near Dellray" is a complete enigma); his own writing is harder to get behind.

Title: Landing On a Hundred
Review: Recorded live on the floor with his band, ChesnuTT's second album cuts the fat away for a lean, no-bullshit sweet soul program that hearkens back to the heyday of the O'Jays and Al Green.

Title: News From Nowhere
Review: You can sense what Darkstar wants to create--music that’s genre-less, accessible yet mysterious--but they haven’t found a way to compensate for the rougher finishes they’ve stripped from their work.

Title: Chelsea Light Moving
Review: By attempting to give us what we want, and provide reassurance that the Sonic Youth legacy is in safe hands, Moore has somehow managed to make it look weaker and less appealing than it ever was.

Title: Drift
Review: The music here is, at times, superb--it’s just hard to imagine anything (except maybe Rose On Top Of The World or Killed Someone) finding a place in your permanent playlist. And a lot of it is just average, which is probably the worst thing you could say about a band as mercurial as this.

Title: LP3
Review: LP3 hits life-affirming pinnacles upon its insistent yowls. [Nov 2014, p.98]

Title: The New Life
Review: The New Life is enjoyable, and there are times when I listen to it and quite like it. Very much. It’s just hardly groundbreaking.

Title: Aventine
Review: Certainly, some people will find Aventine a bit hard to take – at first listen, it sounds so pleasant it just washes over, and it’s only on repeated plays that its dark mysteries reveal itself.

Title: Living Thing
Review: For Living Thing, they ditch the comfortable confines of the airy, featherweight pop they perfected on Writer’s Block for more sonically adventurous territory and prove in the process that their prior success was not just a fluke.
